title: Understanding Contrastive Learning via Distributionally Robust Optimization
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-25

Understanding Contrastive Learning via Distributionally Robust Optimization — Junkang Wu, Jiawei Chen, Jiancan Wu, Wentao Shi, Xiang Wang, Xiangnan He (NeurIPS 2023) — arXiv:2310.11048

Setting and problem

The object of study is the InfoNCE contrastive loss, viewed at the population level. There are two random variables $X, Y$ over a feature space $\mathcal{A}$. An anchor $x \sim P_X$ is paired with a positive $y^+ \sim P_0 := P_{Y\mid X}$ and with negatives $y \sim Q_0 := P_Y$. An encoder $g_\theta : \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ maps to the unit sphere, and the score is $f_\theta(x,y) = f(g_\theta(x), g_\theta(y))$ (cosine similarity in practice, so $f_\theta \in [-1,1]$). The loss analysed is the "decoupled" InfoNCE, whose denominator does not contain the positive:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}} = -\mathbb{E}_{P_X}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[f_\theta(x,y^+)/\tau] - \log \mathbb{E}_{Q_0}[e^{f_\theta(x,y)/\tau}]\Big].$$

This modelling choice matters more than it looks. Because the positive is dropped, the per-anchor loss is the Donsker–Varadhan functional rather than the $K$-sample InfoNCE bound of van den Oord et al. And because the paper works with $\log \mathbb{E}_{Q_0}$ rather than the log of a minibatch mean, all statements are about an idealized infinite-negative objective. Finite $N$ shows up only in one generalization bound.

The empirical starting point (Table 1, Fig. 1) is this. On CIFAR10 and STL10, plain SimCLR with a tuned temperature $\tau^\ast$ roughly matches DCL (Chuang et al. 2020) and HCL (Robinson et al. 2021), two methods built to fix sampling bias, i.e. false negatives drawn from the anchor's own class. Also, the best $\tau$ shrinks as more false negatives are injected. The paper asks two precise questions:

  • Why does vanilla InfoNCE tolerate sampling bias, i.e. a nominal negative distribution $Q_0$ that differs from the ideal $Q_{\mathrm{ideal}}$ (true negatives only)?
  • What does $\tau$ mean, beyond being a "softmax sharpness" knob?

The proposed lens is distributionally robust optimization (DRO). Fix a $\phi$-divergence $D_\phi(Q\|Q_0) = \mathbb{E}_{Q_0}[\phi(dQ/dQ_0)]$ and a radius $\eta$, and define

$$\mathcal{L}^{\phi}_{\mathrm{CL\text{-}DRO}} = -\mathbb{E}_{P_X}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[f_\theta(x,y^+)] - \max_{Q:\,D_\phi(Q\|Q_0)\le \eta} \mathbb{E}_Q[f_\theta(x,y)]\Big].$$

This is "positives up, negatives down", except that the negative term is evaluated under the worst distribution in a divergence ball around the sampling distribution.

What was already known:

  • The softmax-over-negatives gradient puts weights $\propto e^{f/\tau}$ on negatives. This is the "hard-mining" reading (Wang and Liu 2021).
  • Robinson et al. 2021 sample negatives from $q_\beta \propto e^{\beta f} Q_0$ and show the $\beta\to\infty$ limit is a worst-case objective over negative distributions.
  • Tian 2022 (α-CL) writes CL as a min-max over pairwise importance weights with a regularizer, which recovers InfoNCE when the regularizer is an entropy.
  • InfoNCE is read as an MI lower bound (CPC, MINE, Poole et al. 2019).

The stated gap is that none of these explains the observed tolerance to sampling bias, or gives $\tau$ a clear semantic meaning.

Main idea

The headline claim (Theorem 3.2) is that KL-constrained CL-DRO equals InfoNCE. Lagrangian duality on the inner maximization over likelihood ratios $L = dQ/dQ_0$ gives

$$\max_{\mathrm{KL}(Q\|Q_0)\le\eta}\mathbb{E}_Q[f] = \min_{\alpha\ge 0}\Big\{\alpha\eta + \alpha\log\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}[e^{f/\alpha}]\Big\},$$

so $\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\mathrm{CL\text{-}DRO}} = \alpha^\ast(\eta)\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}\big|_{\tau=\alpha^\ast(\eta)} + \alpha^\ast(\eta)\eta$. The temperature is thus read as the Lagrange multiplier of the robustness constraint. From this the paper derives several consequences:

  • Generalization bound (Thm 3.3). If $\mathrm{KL}(Q_{\mathrm{ideal}}\|Q_0)\le\eta$, the "unbiased" loss with ideal negatives is upper-bounded by $\tau\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$ plus a McDiarmid term $B(\rho,N,\tau)$. That term grows like $e^{(M_2-M_1)/\tau}$ as $\tau$ shrinks, which gives a bias–variance story for choosing $\tau$.
  • Radius–temperature link (Cor. 3.4, borrowed from Faury et al. 2020): $\tau \approx \sqrt{\mathbb{V}_{Q_0}[f]/(2\eta)}$. A larger needed radius (more false negatives) means a smaller $\tau$, which matches Fig. 1.
  • Mean–variance form (Thm 3.5). A second-order expansion of $\phi^\ast$ gives $\mathcal{L}^\phi_{\mathrm{CL\text{-}DRO}} \approx -\mathbb{E}_{P_0}f + \mathbb{E}_{Q_0}f + \frac{1}{2\tau\phi''(1)}\mathbb{V}_{Q_0}[f]$. So InfoNCE is approximately "basic contrastive loss + variance penalty on negative scores". A mean–variance surrogate ("MW") reaches 91.81 on CIFAR10, against 92.19 for tuned InfoNCE.
  • MI connection (Thm 4.2). $\sup_f -\mathcal{L}^\phi_{\mathrm{CL\text{-}DRO}}(P,Q) = D_\phi(P\|Q)$ via the Ruderman et al. 2012 / optimized-certainty-equivalent representation $D_\phi(P\|Q) = \sup_f \mathbb{E}_P f - \min_\lambda\{\lambda + \mathbb{E}_Q\phi^\ast(f-\lambda)\}$. From this they argue "InfoNCE is a tight MI estimator", and that other $\phi$ (for example $\chi^2$, which gives mean minus variance) yield generalized MI estimators.
  • Method (ADNCE). The KL worst case $Q^\ast \propto e^{f/\tau}Q_0$ is said to be too conservative and outlier-sensitive. ADNCE multiplies each negative's term by a Gaussian weight $w(f;\mu,\sigma)\propto \exp(-(f-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2)$, normalized by its batch mean and detached. Gains are small but consistent: CIFAR10 91.64 to 91.88, STL10 87.69 to 88.00, STS avg 76.81 to 77.03 (BERT), plus a few TU graph benchmarks.

The most interesting part

The most interesting idea is reading $\tau$ as a dual variable, i.e. a price on how far the adversary may move the negative distribution away from the one you sample from. It turns "temperature" from a magic number into something you could in principle set from a property of the data, namely how contaminated your negatives are. A concrete instance the paper does not spell out: if $Q_{\mathrm{ideal}}$ is $Q_0$ conditioned on true negatives and a fraction $\varepsilon$ of $Q_0$'s mass is false negatives, then $\mathrm{KL}(Q_{\mathrm{ideal}}\|Q_0) = \log\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}$. So the radius needed to cover the ideal distribution is about $\varepsilon$ for small $\varepsilon$, and Cor. 3.4 would give $\tau \approx \sqrt{\mathbb{V}_{Q_0}[f]/(2\log\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon})}$. That is a falsifiable prediction, and it qualitatively matches Fig. 1.

That said, the critique has to be pointed.

  1. The equivalence is exact, but it is a classical identity and it is stated imprecisely. The dual $\max_{\mathrm{KL}(Q\|Q_0)\le\eta}\mathbb{E}_Q f = \min_\alpha \alpha\eta + \alpha\log\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}e^{f/\alpha}$ is the standard KL-DRO dual (Hu and Hong 2013; Faury et al. 2020, which the paper cites). Its penalized form, $\tau\log\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}e^{f/\tau} = \max_Q\{\mathbb{E}_Q f - \tau\,\mathrm{KL}(Q\|Q_0)\}$, is the Gibbs/Donsker–Varadhan variational principle. Nothing in Theorem 3.2 relies on a Taylor expansion, but the statement "optimizing CL-DRO is equivalent to optimizing InfoNCE" is not quite right:
  2. The optimal multiplier $\alpha^\ast(\eta)$ depends on $\theta$ and on the anchor $x$ (the paper silently drops $\mathbb{E}_{P_X}$ in the proofs).
  3. The "Constant" $\alpha^\ast\eta$ is therefore not constant.
  4. By Danskin's theorem, the gradient of the constrained objective equals the InfoNCE gradient at the per-anchor, per-iterate temperature $\alpha^\ast(\eta,\theta,x)$, scaled by $\alpha^\ast$.

So fixed-radius DRO is InfoNCE with an adaptive, per-anchor temperature. The exact match with fixed-$\tau$ InfoNCE is the penalized (soft-constraint) DRO, whose implied radius $\mathrm{KL}(Q^\ast\|Q_0) = \mathbb{E}_{Q^\ast}[f/\tau] - \log\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}e^{f/\tau}$ drifts during training. This is exactly the gap that individualized-temperature work (e.g. Qiu et al., ICML 2023, iSogCLR, which also frames CL as KL-DRO) exploits.

  1. Only the downstream results are approximate. Corollary 3.4 ($\tau\approx\sqrt{\mathbb{V}/2\eta}$) and Theorem 3.5 (mean–variance) rely on a second-order expansion of $\phi^\ast$ around zero, i.e. on $f/\tau$ varying little across negatives. With cosine scores in $[-1,1]$ and SimCSE-style $\tau=0.05$, $f/\tau$ spans a range of 40, far outside the regime where the expansion is accurate. The MW experiment is run at $\tau=0.2$–$0.3$, where the approximation is most forgiving. The mean–variance link itself is the well-known "robust ≈ mean–variance" result (Namkoong and Duchi 2017; Gotoh et al. 2018).

  2. Novelty relative to prior CL theory is thin. Tian 2022 already obtained InfoNCE as max over pairwise weights with an entropy regularizer, which is the KL-penalized DRO up to naming. Robinson et al. 2021 already framed hard negatives as an exponential tilt $e^{\beta f}Q_0$ and showed a worst-case limit. The paper's added value is naming the ball radius and linking it to $\tau$, not discovering the adversarial reweighting.

  3. The "robust to sampling bias" story is logically weaker than it sounds. Theorem 3.3 only says that the minimized InfoNCE upper-bounds $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unbiased}}$ when $Q_{\mathrm{ideal}}$ lies in the ball. That is the defining property of DRO plus concentration. But the worst-case $Q^\ast\propto e^{f/\tau}Q_0$ places the most mass on the highest-scoring negatives, which are precisely the false negatives. So InfoNCE works hardest at pushing same-class items apart, the opposite of what DCL does. Minimizing an upper bound on the unbiased loss is not the same as following its gradient, and nothing in the paper shows the bound is tight enough to explain Table 1. There is also a small inconsistency: at zero contamination ($\eta\to 0$) the theory points to $\tau\to\infty$, yet the best $\tau$ at $r=0$ in Fig. 1 is finite. The finite-$N$ term has to carry all of that.

  4. The MI section mostly re-derives Donsker–Varadhan. For KL, $\sup_f \mathbb{E}_P f - \log\mathbb{E}_Q e^f$ is DV itself. What the paper calls the "Donsker–Varadhan target" $\mathbb{E}_P f - \mathbb{E}_Q\phi^\ast(f)$ is really the NWJ/f-GAN form, and optimizing out the shift $\lambda$ turns NWJ into DV. That is exactly Ruderman et al.'s point, and Poole et al. 2019 already note $I_{\mathrm{NWJ}}\le I_{\mathrm{DV}}$. The claim "InfoNCE is a tighter MI estimate" is about the population $\log\mathbb{E}$ functional. It does not touch the real limitation of minibatch InfoNCE, the $\log N$ ceiling and the bias of $\log$ of a sample mean. The proof of Theorem 4.2 also sets $\alpha^\ast=1$ by fiat ("When $\alpha^\ast=1$, step 1 gets proved").

  5. ADNCE may not do what Fig. 3 suggests. Under Eq. (11), the effective negative weight is $$w\cdot e^{f/\tau}\propto \exp\Big(-\frac{(f-(\mu+\sigma^2/\tau))^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big),$$ a Gaussian centred at $\mu+\sigma^2/\tau$. With the default $\sigma=1$ and any $\tau\le1$, that centre lies above 1, so on cosine scores the weight is still monotonically increasing. ADNCE then just softens the tilt locally (a similarity-dependent temperature) and never actually down-weights the hardest negatives. The pseudocode in Appendix B is different again: it applies the Gaussian to neg, documented as the exponentiated scores $e^{f/\tau}$ rather than $f$, and that version is genuinely non-monotone. Which variant produced the tables matters for interpreting the "too conservative" diagnosis. The gains (about 0.2–0.3 points, five seeds, no variances in Table 3, an extra $\mu,\sigma$ grid) are modest relative to that tuning budget.

Proof sketch

Theorem 3.2 (KL-DRO = InfoNCE). Write $Q = LQ_0$ with $\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}L=1$, $L\ge0$. The inner problem $\max_L \mathbb{E}_{Q_0}[fL]$ subject to $\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}\phi(L)\le\eta$ is a concave maximization with convex constraints. Slater's condition holds for $\eta>0$, so strong duality gives

$$\min_{\alpha\ge0,\beta}\ \alpha\eta-\beta+\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}\Big[\sup_{\ell}\Big\{\tfrac{f+\beta}{\alpha}\ell-\phi(\ell)\Big\}\Big] = \min_{\alpha\ge0,\beta}\ \alpha\eta-\beta+\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}\big[\phi^\ast\big(\tfrac{f+\beta}{\alpha}\big)\big].$$

Pulling the sup inside the expectation is justified by the interchange theorem for normal integrands (Rockafellar–Wets / Ben-Tal–Teboulle). For KL, $\phi(t)=t\log t-t+1$ and $\phi^\ast(s)=e^s-1$. Minimizing over $\beta$ in closed form gives $\beta^\ast=-\alpha\log\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}e^{f/\alpha}$ and leaves $\min_\alpha \alpha\eta+\alpha\log\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}e^{f/\alpha}$. The maximizer is the exponential tilt $Q^\ast = Q_0 e^{f/\alpha^\ast}/\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}e^{f/\alpha^\ast}$ (Appendix A.6), which is the hard-mining weight. This step is exact. The approximation enters only when $\alpha^\ast$ and $\alpha^\ast\eta$ are treated as $\theta$-independent.

Theorem 3.3 (bound). Under the condition $Q_{\mathrm{ideal}}\in\{Q:\mathrm{KL}(Q\|Q_0)\le\eta\}$, trivially $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unbiased}}\le\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{KL}}_{\mathrm{CL\text{-}DRO}}$. The DRO value is then identified with $\tau\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}$, and McDiarmid is applied to the $N$-negative empirical estimate. Each sample's contribution $Q^\ast(y_i)f(y_i)$ is bounded using $f\in[M_1,M_2]$: the largest possible tilt weight is $e^{(M_2-M_1)/\tau}/(N-1+e^{(M_2-M_1)/\tau})$. A union bound over a finite class $\mathcal{F}$ finishes the proof. The $e^{(M_2-M_1)/\tau}$ factor is what makes small $\tau$ costly. The text's "$B\to0$ as $N\to0$" should read $N\to\infty$, and the bounded-difference step is loose (it bounds a weighted sum through a single term).

Theorem 3.5 and Cor. 3.4. Expand $\phi^\ast(s)=s+\frac{s^2}{2\phi''(1)}+o(s^2)$ (Lemma A.2 of Gotoh et al.). The optimal $\beta$ becomes $-\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}f$, which yields $\mathbb{E}_{Q_0}f+\frac{1}{2\alpha\phi''(1)}\mathbb{V}_{Q_0}f+\alpha\eta$. The first-order condition in $\alpha$ gives $\alpha^\ast=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}/(2\eta\phi''(1))}$.

Theorem 4.2. This is the OCE / Ruderman representation. Substitute $Y=f+\beta$. The $\beta$-term multiplies $\mathbb{E}_Q[1-dP/dQ]=0$ and vanishes, and the pointwise sup gives $\mathbb{E}_Q\phi^{\ast\ast}(dP/dQ)=D_\phi(P\|Q)$ by Fenchel–Moreau. The DRO side is matched to it by fixing $\alpha=1$, which drops the radius from the statement.

Broader context

DRO minimizes the worst-case risk over an ambiguity set around the training distribution. $\phi$-divergence balls (Ben-Tal et al. 2013; Namkoong and Duchi 2016–2017) produce log-sum-exp or variance-penalized duals. Wasserstein balls (Esfahani and Kuhn 2018; Sinha et al. 2018) produce Lipschitz/gradient penalties. A recurring lesson is that DRO is sensitive to outliers (Zhai et al. 2021, DORO), and the paper invokes this to motivate ADNCE. In contrastive learning, the most closely related lines are:

  • Hard-negative and debiasing work (Chuang et al. 2020, DCL; Robinson et al. 2021, HCL; Tian 2022, α-CL).
  • Temperature work (Wang and Liu 2021; Zhang et al. 2022 on temperature schedules; Qiu et al. 2023 on individualized temperatures from a KL-DRO view).
  • The same group's follow-up on softmax loss in recommendation (Wu et al., "BSL"), which applies DRO to the positive side as well.

A useful framing for the reader: everything here applies verbatim to any softmax cross-entropy. Full-softmax classification, sampled-softmax recommendation and listwise ranking losses are all KL-DRO over the "other classes". So the result is really about log-sum-exp, not about self-supervision.

The connection to dense retrieval and vector search is genuine and concrete.

  • In-batch plus mined negatives as the nominal distribution. In DPR, ANCE, RocketQA, Contriever and E5-style training, $Q_0$ is a mixture: in-batch negatives (roughly the corpus marginal, hence popularity-biased) plus mined hard negatives (BM25 or the retriever's own ANN top-$k$). Mining from the retriever's top-$k$ is already an approximate exponential tilt $Q_0\to Q_0e^{s/\tau'}$. Softmax-InfoNCE then applies a second tilt. In DRO terms you are adversarial twice, first in sampling and then in weighting. This explains why "top-1 hard negatives + low $\tau$" is where false negatives hurt most, which is exactly the regime where RocketQA needed cross-encoder denoising.
  • Support matters. $\mathrm{KL}(Q\|Q_0)<\infty$ requires $Q\ll Q_0$. With a finite batch, the robust set consists of reweightings of the $N$ sampled negatives. KL-DRO can redistribute weight but cannot invent support. That gives a crisp argument for why ANN-mined negatives help in a way that lowering $\tau$ with in-batch negatives alone cannot: mining changes the support of $Q_0$, while $\tau$ only changes the radius.
  • ADNCE resembles existing samplers. ADNCE's Gaussian weight is close to SimANS (Zhou et al., EMNLP 2022), which samples hard negatives with probability $\propto\exp(-a(s(q,d)-s(q,d^+)-b)^2)$. SimANS is a Gaussian in score, but centred relative to the positive's score rather than at a fixed $\mu$. The anchoring to $s(q,d^+)$ is arguably the better design for retrieval, because score scales vary across queries. It also matches the practitioner heuristic of sampling negatives from ranks 30–100 rather than the top-1.
  • Temperature. Retrieval models use very small $\tau$ (0.01–0.05), so the paper's second-order results do not apply there. The exact dual still does.

A plausible follow-up for an IR theorist: per-query radius calibration. Estimate the false-negative mass $\varepsilon_q$ of the negative pool for query $q$, for example with a cross-encoder or with labels on a held-out slice. Set $\eta_q=\log\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon_q}$ and solve the one-dimensional convex dual $\min_\alpha \alpha\eta_q+\alpha\log\frac1N\sum_i e^{s_i/\alpha}$ by bisection on each batch, giving a per-query temperature. This turns the paper's qualitative "τ ↔ radius" into a training rule and can be compared against fixed-$\tau$ and iSogCLR.

A more theoretical variant would model ANN approximation error explicitly. If the negative miner returns an approximate top-$k$ with recall $r<1$, the mined $Q_0$ is a perturbation of the exact tilt. One could ask how large a KL ball is needed to cover the exact-search negative distribution, which yields a bound on how index recall propagates into the robust contrastive objective.

For generative retrieval, the full softmax over docids is the same log-sum-exp, i.e. KL-DRO with a uniform or prior nominal distribution over the docid space. Much of the above (support, radius, temperature) transfers, although the docid structure makes the "negative distribution" less natural to define.

title: Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-25

Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models — Yee Man Choi, Fengchi Wang, Ruiquan Huang (2026) — arXiv:2611.30005

Setting and problem

The object of study is the simplest next-token predictor that still has learned embeddings: a one-token-context model, which the authors call a state-transition model. There are $V$ states (tokens) $[V]=\{1,\dots,V\}$. The ground truth is a row-stochastic table $Q\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times V}$ with strictly positive entries; row $q_i^\top$ is the next-state distribution given current state $i$. Two models are considered:

  • Untied: $E,U\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$ (input and output embeddings), prediction $P^{E,U}=\mathrm{softmax}(EU^\top)$ row-wise, $2Vd$ parameters.
  • Tied: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$, prediction $P^X=\mathrm{softmax}(XX^\top)$, $Vd$ parameters.

Throughout $d<V$. For a set of current states $\mathcal{A}\subseteq[V]$ the population risk and Bayes risk are $R_{\mathcal{A}}(\Theta)=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_j q_{ij}\log P^\Theta_{ij}$ and $H_{\mathcal{A}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_j q_{ij}\log q_{ij}$. Quality is measured by the relative prediction gain $$g_{\mathcal{A}}(\Theta)=\frac{\log V-R_{\mathcal{A}}(\Theta)}{\log V-H_{\mathcal{A}}}=1-\frac{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\mathrm{KL}(q_i\,\|\,P^\Theta_{i,:})}{\log V-H_{\mathcal{A}}},$$ which is $0$ for the uniform predictor and $1$ for the Bayes predictor. Because embeddings are not identifiable (any $EU^\top=E A A^{-1}U^\top$ gives the same predictions), success is measured in prediction space, not parameter space.

The ground-truth class is $$\mathcal{Q}_{r,B,\Delta_0}=\Big\{Q:\ Q_{ij}>0,\ Q\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\ \mathrm{rank}\,L(\log Q)\le r,\ \|L(\log Q)\|_\infty\le B,\ \log V-H_{[V]}\ge\Delta_0\Big\},$$ where $L(Z)=Z(I_V-\tfrac{1}{V}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top)$ row-centers logits, and $r,B,\Delta_0$ are constants independent of $V$. For the tied results the class is further restricted to $Q=\mathrm{softmax}(YY^\top)$ with $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times r_Y}$, $r_Y\le r$, $\max_i\|y_i\|_2^2\le B_Y$.

Training: Gaussian initialization $\Theta_0$ with i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1/d)$ entries, then perturbed gradient descent (Jin et al. 2019) on the weight-decayed population objective $$F_{\lambda,\mathcal{A}}(\Theta)=R_{\mathcal{A}}(\Theta)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|\Theta\|_F^2,\qquad \Theta_{t+1}=\Theta_t-h\big(\nabla F_{\lambda,\mathcal{A}}(\Theta_t)+\xi_t\big),\ \ \xi_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tfrac{\sigma^2}{D_\Theta}I).$$ Step size, noise scale, weight decay and horizon $T$ are fixed in advance.

The precise question: can low-dimensional embeddings ($d<V$), jointly trained from random initialization by a gradient method on cross-entropy, reach high relative prediction gain, and keep it for the rest of training? For the tied model trained only on a subset $\mathcal{S}$ of $N=\Theta(V)$ current states, does the model also predict well for the unseen current states $\mathcal{U}=[V]\setminus\mathcal{S}$ (which still appear as next-state labels)?

What was known: transformer training-dynamics papers for next-token prediction (Li et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2024, 2025; Varre et al. 2025; Yang et al. 2024) fix embeddings that are linearly independent, forcing $d\ge V$; others train embeddings only for a binary vocabulary (Makkuva et al. 2024) or for one gradient step (Wu et al.), or characterize minimizers without dynamics (Zhao et al. 2024). Factorization theory covers squared loss (Ye and Du 2021) or gives generic Burer-Monteiro-type bounds (Ouyang et al. 2025) that, as the paper shows in Appendix B.4, only yield an $O(V/d)$ comparison error here. The gap is a full-dynamics guarantee for jointly trained softmax embeddings with $d<V$.

Non-obvious modelling choices worth flagging: - Population (full-batch, exact) gradients over the whole table $Q$; $Q$ may be an empirical table, but there is no sampling noise in the theory. - The target is realizable and low rank: $r$ is a constant and $d\ge 2r$, so the softmax bottleneck is assumed away; $d<V$ only matters in that the problem is a nonconvex factorization. - Bounded centered logits $\|L(\log Q)\|_\infty\le B$ with $B$ constant: every transition probability is within $e^{\pm 2B}$ of $1/V$, and the information gap $\log V-H_{[V]}$ is at most $\min\{B,B^2/2\}$ (Lemma B.2). The whole problem is a constant-size perturbation of the uniform distribution. - Weight decay is essential (it localizes the trajectory) and a guarantee is stated for every iterate in a final window, not just the last one or the best one.

Main idea

The headline results:

  • Untied (Theorem 4.1): for $\max\{2r,C\sqrt V\}\le d<V-1$ and $\lambda=\Delta_0/(8B\sqrt r\,V)$, there exist polynomially bounded $h^{-1},\sigma^{-1},T$ such that with probability $\ge 1-e^{-cd}$, $g_{[V]}(\Theta_t)>7/8$ for every $t\in[T/d,T]$.
  • Tied training (Theorem 5.2): for $d\ge C\sqrt V$ and $\lambda=C_\lambda/d^2$, $g_{\mathcal{S}}(X_t)\ge 1-CV/(d^2\delta_{tr})$ throughout the same window, with no coverage assumption.
  • Tied transfer (Theorem 5.4): with $\lambda\propto\sqrt{V/(Nd^3)}$, $d\ge CV/N^{1/3}$, a centered coverage condition on $Y$ over $\mathcal{S}$, and conditional on the learned rows satisfying $\max_j\|x_j\|_2^2\le R_0$, the unseen-set gain is $1-O\big(V^4/[Nd^3(V-N)\delta_{te}]\big)$, i.e. $1-O(V^2/d^3)$ when $N$ and $V-N$ are both $\Theta(V)$.

The core approach is a landscape argument in the region training can actually reach, combined with the saddle-escaping machinery of Jin et al. One shows that (1) weight decay plus a bounded initial objective confine the trajectory to a ball $\|\Theta\|_F^2=O(V)$; (2) inside that ball every sufficiently accurate approximate second-order stationary point has low objective, hence high gain; (3) perturbed GD visits such points in every one of $d$ blocks and the objective cannot rise much within a block, so high gain is refreshed at every iterate after the first block.

The technical key that makes $d\sim\sqrt V$ suffice is that the softmax Hessian with respect to one row of logits is $\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^\top$, whose trace is at most $1$. Total softmax curvature summed over rows is at most $V$, and since it is spread over $d$ orthogonal embedding directions, most directions carry only $O(V/d)$ of it. Packing the rank-$r$ comparator into such low-curvature directions makes the curvature term $O(V/d^2+1/d)$ instead of the $O(V/d)$ a uniform per-direction bound would give.

Experiments (population gradients, $V\le256$; sampled-transition SGD up to $V=16384$) show the untied model above $7/8$ throughout the window in all runs, the tied model transferring to unseen states (gain above $0.96$ at $V=128,d=32$) while the untied model on the same split has gain near $0$, and learned row norms staying below $R_0=8$. Removing the injected noise changes nothing.

The most interesting part

Reviewer-style assessment.

Strengths.

  • The trace-of-Hessian packing lemma (Lemma B.3) is a genuinely nice and reusable trick. Instead of a worst-case curvature bound along a direction, it uses the fact that the covariance of a categorical distribution has trace at most one, so curvature is a finite budget that must be split across $d$ embedding directions. Random signs kill cross terms between packed columns, and a probabilistic-method choice gives a good sign pattern. Appendix B.4 shows clearly why this improves the generic Burer-Monteiro-style bound from $O(V/d)$ to $O(V/d^2)$. The same argument should apply to any softmax-over-catalogue loss with factored logits.
  • The "every iterate in the final window" guarantee is stronger than the usual "some iterate is an approximate SOSP" statement and is obtained cleanly: a union bound over all pairs in a block lifts Jin et al.'s descent concentration to random start times, and induction over blocks keeps the trajectory inside the ball.
  • The trace certificate for transfer (Lemma C.6) is elegant: the PSD structure of $K=XX^\top$ means the part of the error outside the column space of $Y$ is a PSD residual whose Frobenius norm is bounded by its trace, and the trace is controlled by the weight-decay comparison.
  • The experimental reporting is careful: all 375 runs reported, paired controls, an honest admission that the tied constants are not met by the tested $d$.

Weaknesses and questionable assumptions.

  1. "$d<V$" is not the actual difficulty being solved. The target has constant rank $r$ and the theorems require $d\ge 2r$, so representability is never in question. What $d\ge C\sqrt V$ really buys is overparameterization relative to the target rank, which is needed to find a low-curvature packing direction. The $\sqrt V$ threshold comes from the proof, not from the problem; the paper says this in Appendix B.4 but the abstract's framing ("embedding dimension much smaller than vocabulary") could suggest a softmax-bottleneck result. The bottleneck regime $r>d$ is not addressed at all.

  2. The bounded-logit class is very close to uniform. $\|L(\log Q)\|_\infty\le B$ with constant $B$ forces every probability to be $\Theta(1/V)$, so there is no sparsity, no near-deterministic transition and no Zipfian head. The total extractable information is $O(1)$ nats out of $\log V$. In this regime the softmax is almost linear around the uniform point, and the problem behaves like a weighted low-rank factorization. Real next-token tables, where many rows have $\log$-probability gaps of order $\log V$, would need $B=\Theta(\log V)$; the constants ($C_E\propto B^2/\Delta_0$, $d^2\gtrsim B^3 r^{3/2}C_E V/\Delta_0^2$) then degrade by polylog factors at best, and the "probabilities within constants of $1/V$" step in the transfer proof fails outright.

  3. The constants make the theory vacuous at any realistic size. Plugging the paper's own experimental values ($B=3$, $r=4$, $\Delta_0=0.1$) into condition (13), $d^2\ge 20480B^3r^{3/2}C_E V/\Delta_0^2$ with $C_E=6+32B\sqrt r(B+3)/\Delta_0\approx 1.15\times10^4$, gives roughly $d^2\ge 5\times10^{12}V$. Combined with $d<V$ this needs $V>5\times10^{12}$. The schedule is also extreme: $h^{-1}=O(d^9)$, $T\le C_TV^{21}$. The experiments use $h=\sqrt V/4$ and $T=8192$ and so do not test the theorem's regime; they illustrate that the qualitative behaviour holds well outside it.

  4. Gain $7/8$ is a design artifact, not a rate. Weight decay is set so that the comparator's penalty is $\Delta_0/8$; this yields a fixed fraction rather than convergence to $1$. The global minimizer of $F_\lambda$ is provably not Bayes-optimal (Remark B.7). The untied theorem never shows the gain tends to $1$ as $d$ grows, while experiments show it is essentially $0.999$.

  5. The injected noise is a proof device. The paired controls show identical results without perturbations, which suggests the landscape in this near-uniform regime is benign enough that plain GD (or the implicit randomness of initialization) suffices. A result for vanilla GD from small random init, in the spirit of Ye and Du (2021), would be more informative.

  6. Transfer is conditional and somewhat built in. The unseen-state bound assumes $\max_j\|x_j(t)\|_2^2\le R_0$, which the optimization analysis does not establish. Also, transfer works because $K^\star=YY^\top$ is symmetric: the column $Q_{\mathcal{S},i}$ for an unseen $i$ reveals $K^\star_{\mathcal{S},i}$, hence $y_i$ given coverage. This is essentially symmetric PSD low-rank completion from $N$ observed full rows. That tied embeddings beat untied ones is then expected, since in the untied model an unseen state's input embedding receives only weight decay and noise, so its gain near $0$ is guaranteed by construction rather than a meaningful baseline. The symmetric class $Q=\mathrm{softmax}(YY^\top)$ is itself a strong restriction (it requires $\log Q$ to be symmetric PSD up to row shifts).

  7. Minor: the paper states that generative AI tools assisted with the proofs. The argument structure I checked (Lemmas B.2 to B.5, C.2, C.3, C.6 to C.9, D.6) is coherent, but the dense constant-chasing in D.6 and the smoothness bounds of the extension deserve independent verification.

On the connection to embedding-retrieval limits (Weller et al. 2025). Formally the untied model is a full-softmax dual encoder: query embedding $\phi(s)$, document embedding $\psi(s')$, score $\phi(s)^\top\psi(s')$, population InfoNCE with all $V$ items as negatives. The tied model is a shared (siamese) encoder with symmetric scores. So the paper is an optimization result for exactly the architecture whose representational limits Weller et al. study. The match is only partial, though. Weller et al. ask whether any $d$-dimensional embedding can realize a given top-$k$ relevance pattern, which is governed by the sign-rank of the binary qrel matrix and can force $d$ to grow with the number of realizable top-$k$ sets. This paper assumes the target's centered log-relevance matrix already has constant rank $r\le d/2$ and bounded entries, so the representational question is answered "yes" by fiat and only the optimization question remains. Both papers use factorization-norm tools: Lemma D.1 bounds row norms of a rank-$r$, entry-bounded factorization via John's ellipsoid, which is the rank-versus-max-norm ($\gamma_2$) argument of Linial, Mendelson, Schechtman and Shraibman, the same family that relates sign-rank to margin complexity. The bounded-$B$ assumption is what keeps the max-norm, and so the weight-decay energy, at $O(V)$. In retrieval, sparse relevance pushes the corresponding logits to scale like $\log V$ or worse, and the evaluation metric is top-$k$ recall, not KL. The honest verdict: the two works are complementary (representability versus trainability) and share a mathematical toolkit, but this paper's guarantees do not transfer to retrieval-style sparse targets as stated.

Proof sketch

Claim (Theorem 4.1). Fix $r,B,\Delta_0$. For $V\ge V_0$, $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{r,B,\Delta_0}$, $\max\{2r,C\sqrt V\}\le d<V-1$ and $\lambda=\Delta_0/(8B\sqrt r V)$, there are deterministic $h,\sigma,T$ (polynomial in $V$) with $\Pr\{g_{[V]}(\Theta_t)>7/8\ \forall t\in[T/d,T]\}\ge 1-e^{-cd}$, over initialization and perturbations.

Step 1 (localization). With probability $1-e^{-c_0d}$, $\|\Theta_0\|_F^2\le 3V$ and $\|E_0U_0^\top\|_\infty\le1$, so $F_\lambda(\Theta_0)-H_{[V]}\le A=2B+2+3\Delta_0/(8B\sqrt r)$. Outside the ball $\|\Theta\|_F^2\ge C_EV$ the penalty alone gives $F_\lambda\ge F_\lambda(\Theta_0)+4$. A radial clipping map produces a globally smooth extension $\tilde F_\lambda$ equal to $F_\lambda$ in the ball, with gradient-Lipschitz $\ell=O(1)$ and Hessian-Lipschitz $\rho=O(\sqrt V)$, so the Jin et al. results apply; a coupling argument later shows the real and extended trajectories coincide.

Step 2 (approximate SOSPs have high gain). Three parts. - Comparator (Lemma B.2): factor the shrunken logits $t_\star L(\log Q)$, $t_\star=1-\Delta_0/(8B^2)$, using the rank-versus-max-norm Lemma D.1 (John's ellipsoid) so that row norms are $\le t_\star B\sqrt r$ and $\|\Theta_\star\|_F^2\le 2B\sqrt rV$. Shrinking reduces the penalty linearly and raises the KL only quadratically (the second derivative in $t$ is a variance $\le B^2$), giving $F_\lambda(\Theta_\star)\le H_{[V]}+\Delta_0/8-\Delta_0^2/(128B^2)$. - Packing (Lemma B.3): take an eigenbasis $w_1,\dots,w_d$ of $U^\top U$. Since $\sum_j\|Uw_j\|^2+\|Ew_j\|^2\le C_EV$ and $\sum_j\sum_i\mathrm{Var}_{P_{i,:}}(Uw_j)/\|Uw_j\|^2\le V$ (trace of each row covariance $\le1$), at least $d/2\ge r$ indices are good on both counts. Place the $r$ comparator columns along those directions with random signs $\varepsilon_k$; the product $\dot E\dot U^\top=t_\star L(\log Q)$ is unchanged, and the expected softmax curvature term is $\le\frac{8Br^{3/2}C_E}{d}(\frac{4V}{d}+1)$. - Negative curvature (Lemma B.4): the Hessian along $(\dot E,\dot U)$ is curvature + bilinear term $\frac2V\langle P-Q,\dot E\dot U^\top\rangle$ + $\lambda\|(\dot E,\dot U)\|^2$. Convexity of cross-entropy in the logits bounds the last two by $2[\frac1V\langle P-Q,EU^\top\rangle+\frac\lambda2\|\Theta\|^2]-2(F_\lambda(\Theta)-F_\lambda(\Theta_\star))$, where the bracket equals $\frac12\langle\nabla F_\lambda,\Theta\rangle\le\epsilon\|\Theta\|$. If $F_\lambda(\Theta)$ is above the target and the gradient is small, the quadratic form is $\le-\Delta_0^2/(256B^2)$ once $d^2\gtrsim V$, so $\lambda_{\min}\le -c/\sqrt V$, contradicting $\epsilon$-SOSP with $\epsilon=c_{acc}V^{-5/2}$.

Step 3 (refresh). Split $T$ into $d$ blocks of length $T_{blk}=O(\ell A\epsilon^{-2}\iota^{15})$. The one-block estimate (Lemma D.6) says that with conditional probability $1-e^{-d}/2$ a block both visits an $\epsilon$-SOSP and has $F(\Theta_v)-F(\Theta_u)\le\Delta_0^2/(512B^2)$ for all $u<v$ (a union bound over pairs handles the random visit time). Induction: the margin $\Delta_0^2/(256B^2)$ re-established at each visit absorbs within-block increase, keeping $F_\lambda<H_{[V]}+\Delta_0/8$, hence $R-H<(\log V-H)/8$, for all $t\ge T_{blk}=T/d$.

Tied variants. The tied packing gives a curvature term $C_p\|X\|_F^2/d^2$ with $\|X\|_F^2$ not a priori $O(V)$; choosing $\lambda\ge 2C_p/d^2$ lets the penalty absorb it, which yields $\|X\|_F^2=O(V)$ and excess loss $O(V/d^2)$ (Lemma C.3). For transfer, the comparison $R_{\mathcal{S}}-H_{\mathcal{S}}+\frac\lambda2(\mathrm{tr}K-\mathrm{tr}K^\star)\le C(\lambda V)^2$ is turned into separate bounds via the trace certificate $\sum_i\|x_i-X_{\mathcal{S}}^\top a_i\|^2=\mathrm{tr}(K-K^\star)-\langle Y_{dual},L(K-K^\star)_{\mathcal{S},:}\rangle$, where $a_i$ expresses $y_i$ in terms of observed embeddings (coverage). Then $K-K^\star$ splits into a part controlled by the observed centered rows (Lemma C.8) and a PSD residual bounded by its trace; with bounded rows the KL on unseen rows is $\asymp\frac1V\|L(K-K^\star)_{\mathcal{U},:}\|_F^2$, giving the unseen bound.

Broader context

Background. Training-dynamics theory for transformers has advanced quickly but almost always treats token embeddings as fixed and orthogonal ($d\ge V$), which removes the factorization structure that every real language model has. A separate literature studies the expressivity side, the softmax bottleneck (Yang et al. 2018), which asks when a rank-$d$ logit matrix can represent the true next-token distribution. Between them sits the optimization question addressed here: if a low-rank solution exists, does gradient training from random initialization find one? This connects to the landscape literature on low-rank factorization (Ge, Jin and Zheng 2017; no spurious local minima), to Burer-Monteiro analyses of factored nuclear-norm problems (Li, Zhu and Tang 2017; Ouyang et al. 2025), and to saddle-escaping algorithms (Ge et al. 2015; Jin et al. 2019). By Remark A.5 the untied objective is exactly a Burer-Monteiro factorization of a nuclear-norm-regularized multinomial-logit problem, and the $\sqrt V$ width requirement is reminiscent, by analogy only, of the classical $\sqrt{m}$ rank threshold for benign Burer-Monteiro landscapes in SDPs (Boumal, Voroninski and Bandeira 2016).

Closely related directions: - Makkuva et al. (2024) analyse a binary-vocabulary Markov transformer and find that local minima depend on initialization; this paper shows that in the large-vocabulary near-uniform regime, with weight decay, they are absent from the reachable region. - Zhao et al. (2024) and Thrampoulidis (2024) characterize the implicit geometry of next-token-prediction solutions (sparsity patterns, logits converging in direction) without analysing embedding training; the present paper is complementary but restricted to bounded logits, which excludes the sparse-support phenomena those works emphasize.

Plausible follow-up. Remove the near-uniform restriction: allow $\|L(\log Q)\|_\infty=B(V)=\Theta(\log V)$ and support sparsity, and ask whether the trace-budget argument still works (the trace bound $\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^\top)\le1$ is independent of $B$, which is encouraging, but the comparator energy and the Hessian-Lipschitz constant grow with $B$). A second natural extension is to sampled-negative contrastive losses (sampled softmax or in-batch InfoNCE), where the Hessian's trace budget becomes a random quantity, and to report top-$k$ accuracy alongside KL.

Connection to theoretical IR and vector search. There is a real structural match: the untied model is a full-softmax dual encoder and the tied model is a shared-encoder symmetric scorer, and the paper's quantity $\phi(s)^\top\psi(s')$ is exactly a maximum inner product search score. So this is, to my knowledge, one of the first end-to-end trainability guarantees for dual-encoder-style embeddings with $d$ well below catalogue size. It complements, rather than contradicts, the representational limits of Weller et al. (2025): those show some relevance patterns need large $d$ (via sign-rank), whereas this paper assumes a constant-rank, bounded-entry log-relevance matrix, which is a regime where such limits cannot arise. Two concrete research hooks for someone working on embeddings with $d<V$: (i) in generative retrieval, docid tokens appear mostly as outputs, and the tied-transfer mechanism (an item's input embedding learned through its output role, with coverage of the observed rows) is a clean model of whether docid or item embeddings learned as targets are useful as queries or for cold-start; (ii) one could combine the trace-budget landscape argument with sign-rank or max-norm lower bounds to study a "trainability versus representability" gap for top-$k$ retrieval targets, asking whether GD on InfoNCE reaches the best sign-pattern achievable at dimension $d$. Without such extensions, the bounded-logit assumption keeps the current theorems far from sparse-relevance retrieval.

title: Grammar Sparsity Sets How Transformers Learn Random Languages
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-25

Grammar Sparsity Sets How Transformers Learn Random Languages — Edgar Andres Hernandez Moreno, Francesco Cagnetta (2026) — arXiv:2611.29692

Setting and problem

The paper is a short, mostly empirical study, backed by one scaling argument, of how long a transformer takes to learn each level of a synthetic hierarchical grammar, and how that time depends on the vocabulary size $V$ and on how "sparse" the grammar is.

Data model: the Random Language Model (RLM). A layered variant of DeGiuli's RLM generates the $2^L$ leaves of a depth-$L$ binary tree. Every symbol, latent or observed, lives in the same vocabulary $\{1,\dots,V\}$. A parent $a$ expands into an ordered pair of children $(b,c)$ with probability $$Q_a(b,c) = \frac{e^{\beta E_{a,b,c}}}{\sum_{b',c'} e^{\beta E_{a,b',c'}}},\qquad E_{a,b,c} \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal N(0,\ln V),$$ with the couplings $E$ drawn once and then fixed. One rule tensor is shared by all levels, and the root is uniform. The inverse temperature $\beta$ sets sparsity. The rule entropy $S_a(\beta) = -\sum_{b,c} Q_a(b,c)\ln Q_a(b,c)$ defines an effective number of rules per symbol $M(\beta)=e^{S(\beta)}$. Each $Q_a$ is the Gibbs measure of a random energy model (REM) with $V^2$ levels, so as $V\to\infty$, $S_a/(2\ln V)\to 1-\beta^2/4$ for $\beta\le 2$ and $\to 0$ for $\beta>2$. Equivalently $M = O(V^{2-\beta^2/2})$ in the dense phase and $M=O(1)$ in the sparse ("frozen") phase, with the REM freezing transition at $\beta=2$.

Task and learner. With $L=2$ the observed sequence is $(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)$: latent $Z_1$ generates $(X_1,X_2)$ and $Z_2$ generates $(X_3,X_4)$. A two-block, decoder-only, pre-LayerNorm transformer ($d=256$, 4 heads) outputs $\hat p_\theta(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3)$ and is trained with Adam (constant $\eta=10^{-4}$, batch 128) on cross-entropy. Every step uses a fresh batch, so the step count $t$ is proportional to the number of samples seen (online learning, no finite training set). The test loss $\mathcal L(\theta) = -\mathbb E \ln \hat p_\theta(X_4\mid X_1,X_2,X_3)$ is compared with three exact reference values computed from the rule tensor: - $\ln V$, the uniform predictor at initialisation; - $H_1 = H(X_4\mid X_3)$, the best possible loss using only the sibling, which shares the parent $Z_2$; - $H_2 = H(X_4\mid X_1,X_2,X_3)\le H_1$, the Bayes floor. The gap $H_1-H_2$ is the information carried by the cousins through the latent $Z_1$ (and from there through the root to $Z_2$).

Measured quantities. $t^\ast_1$ is when the loss is halfway from $\ln V$ to $H_1$, and $t^\ast_2$ is when it is halfway from $H_1$ to $H_2$. The precise question is: how do $t^\ast_1$ and $t^\ast_2$ scale with $V$, how does that scaling depend on $\beta$, and are the two levels learned sequentially or together?

What was known. Cagnetta and Wyart (NeurIPS 2024) and the Random Hierarchy Model line of work showed that deep networks trained on synthetic hierarchical data learn level by level. In their account, each deeper level is acquired once the token-token correlations it induces rise above sampling noise, which gives sample complexities that are powers of the vocabulary/branching parameters. Those models (RHM, uniform-depth CFGs) have a fixed, uniform number of rules per symbol. The RLM adds a continuous knob, $\beta$, that moves from dense to sparse grammars, and its phase diagram (the freezing at $\beta=2$) was worked out recently by Giorlandino, De Giuli and Goldt. The gap this paper fills is whether, and how, rule sparsity changes the learning schedule and the time exponents.

Non-obvious modelling choices worth flagging: - The sequences are very short (4 tokens at $L=2$, 2 at $L=1$), and loss is taken only on the last token. So "hierarchy" here means just two levels. - Rules are shared across levels, and the root is uniform. - "Time" is counted in optimiser steps at fixed batch size and learning rate, across all $V$ and $\beta$. The exponents are therefore properties of Adam at these particular hyperparameters, and the theory makes clear they are not optimiser-independent sample complexities. - The scaling laws come from small $V$ ranges: 12 to 64 at $L=2$, 32 to 256 at $L=1$.

Main idea

The headline is that sparsity sets both the order and the speed of acquisition.

  • Dense grammars ($\beta=1.2$) are learned in stages. The loss first drops to the sibling entropy $H_1$ at $t^\ast_1\propto V$ (fitted $s_1=1.00\pm0.02$), stays on a plateau, and only reaches $H_2$ at $t^\ast_2\propto V^3$ ($s_2=3.04\pm0.34$). Because the two exponents differ, the plateau grows as $V^2$.
  • Sparse grammars ($\beta=6$) are learned in one drop from $\ln V$ to $H_2$, at $t^\ast\propto\sqrt V$ ($s=0.44\pm0.03$). That exponent is smaller than even the first dense stage, and it holds even though the information gap $H_1-H_2$ is relatively larger than in the dense case.
  • At the boundary ($\beta=2$, smaller model), the two stages are still distinct but closer together: $s_1\approx0.73$, $s_2\approx2.06$. The schedule contracts continuously as sparsity grows.

The second step of the argument is to remove the hierarchy. At depth one (predict $X_2$ from $X_1$) there is only one stage, yet the time still scales as $V$ in the dense phase and $\sqrt V$ in the sparse phase. So the exponents 1 and 1/2 are not about hierarchy at all. They come from how Adam learns a single sparse versus dense rule table, and the authors derive them with a signal-to-noise argument for a linear logit table trained with Adam. A side finding (App. D): a second attention block is needed to reach the floor near the transition ($\beta=2$), but makes no difference at $\beta=6$.

The most interesting part

The cleverest piece is the Adam signal-to-noise argument in App. C. It explains why sparse grammars are learned faster, which is not the obvious answer, and why the dense exponent does not depend on $\beta$.

Replace Adam's moving averages by population moments. A coordinate whose per-sample gradient has mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ then moves at speed $\eta\,\mathrm{SNR}$ per step, with $\mathrm{SNR}=\mu\sqrt B/\sigma$, as long as $\mathrm{SNR}\ll1$. The time to cover a logit distance $D$ is $t^\ast\asymp D\sigma/(\eta|\mu|\sqrt B)$. What makes this useful is that Adam's speed depends on the ratio $\mu/\sigma$, not on $\mu$ itself, and the two phases differ in exactly that ratio.

  • Sparse phase. A logit $\theta_{ab}$ gets a gradient only on the $1/V$ fraction of samples with $X_1=a$, and there the gradient is $O(1)$. So $\mu\sim1/V$ but $\sigma\sim1/\sqrt V$: rare events reduce the mean by $1/V$ but the standard deviation only by $1/\sqrt V$, which gives $\mathrm{SNR}\sim\sqrt{B/V}$. The logits need to travel $D\sim\ln V$, so $t^\ast\sim\sqrt V\ln V$.
  • Dense phase. At the uniform initialisation, the uniform part of the joint cancels from the gradient, and the only signal is the connected correlation $\bar C$: $\mu\sim\bar C$, $\sigma\sim1/V$, $\mathrm{SNR}\sim V\bar C\sqrt B$. The target logits differ from uniform only by the relative deviation $D\sim V^2\bar C$, which is also proportional to the correlation. Signal and distance cancel, leaving $t^\ast\sim V/(\eta\sqrt B)$ for every $\beta$ in the dense phase.

The cancellation explains the flat exponent of 1 across $\beta\in\{1.2,1.4,1.6\}$ in Fig. 3: weaker correlations mean a weaker signal, but also less distance to travel. The two regimes are also two limits of one formula. Once the relative deviation $\epsilon=V^2\bar C$ exceeds 1, $D$ saturates at $\ln V$ while the SNR keeps growing, and with $\bar C\propto V^{-a_1}$ the exponent becomes $a_1-1$. That interpolates from 1 to 1/2 as $a_1$ goes from 2 to 3/2. The argument also predicts that plain SGD would give $V$ and $V^2$ instead, which is a falsifiable statement that the optimiser shapes the "time complexity" of grammar learning. This fits the broader observation that Adam helps most on rare, heavy-tailed classes. In this setting, being sparse is what makes a rule informative per sample.

Honest caveat: the argument applies only where its assumptions hold, and the transformers in the paper are outside that regime. The noise-dominated condition requires roughly $B\lesssim V$ in the sparse phase. The transformers use $B=128$ with $V\le64$ at $L=2$, and the authors say they use the argument only "as a heuristic" there. It is validated quantitatively only for the linear model at $B=2$. It also covers only the escape from initialisation and the first stage. The most striking number, $t^\ast_2\propto V^3$, has no explanation, and it rests on four vocabulary sizes (12 to 48) with an error of $\pm0.34$. Finally, the dense first-stage exponent moves from 1.05 to 1.45 depending on the crossing level, which the authors acknowledge means the curves do not collapse perfectly.

Proof sketch

There is no theorem in the rigorous sense. The theory is a controlled scaling argument for a linear model, checked numerically.

Claim. Consider the logit table $\theta\in\mathbb R^{V\times V}$ with $\hat p_\theta(b\mid a)\propto e^{\theta_{ab}}$, initialised at $\theta=0$ and trained by Adam with fresh batches of size $B$ in the noise-dominated regime ($B\lesssim V$ sparse, $B\lesssim 1/(V\bar C)^2$ dense). Its half-way time satisfies $t^\ast\asymp \sqrt{V/B}\,\ln V/\eta$ for $\beta\to\infty$ and $t^\ast\asymp V/(\eta\sqrt B)$ in the dense phase, where the dense phase is defined by relative conditional deviations $\epsilon=V^2\bar C\lesssim1$.

Steps: 1. Per-sample gradient: $g_{ab}=\mathbb 1\{X_1=a\}\,(\hat p_\theta(b\mid X_1)-\mathbb 1\{X_2=b\})$. Its batch mean has mean $\mu_{ab}$ and variance $\sigma^2_{ab}/B$. 2. Mean-field Adam: replace $m$ and $v$ by $\mu$ and $\mu^2+\sigma^2/B$, which gives $\Delta\theta=-\eta\,\mathrm{SNR}/\sqrt{1+\mathrm{SNR}^2}$. This is justified while parameters move little over Adam's averaging window and batches are fresh. When $\mathrm{SNR}\ll1$ the drift is linear in SNR, so $t^\ast\asymp D/(\eta|\mathrm{SNR}|)$. When $\mathrm{SNR}\gg1$ Adam becomes sign descent and the $V$ dependence disappears. 3. Moments at $\theta=0$, sparse phase. Take $a$ to be the left child of $k$ parents, with $k$ distinct continuations. For an active pair, $\mu\simeq-1/V$ and $\mathbb E g^2\simeq 1/V$. Inactive pairs in the same row have SNR of the same order and drift down at the same rate. The loss of the row reaches half-way at a logit gap of about $\tfrac12\ln V$. 4. Moments at $\theta=0$, dense phase. $\mu_{ab}=P(X_1=a)/V-P^{(1)}_{ab}=-\Delta_{ab}$, which is about the connected correlation. Next, $\mathbb E g^2\simeq P^{(1)}_{ab}\simeq1/V^2$. The target displacement is $D=\ln(V P(X_2=b\mid X_1=a))\approx V|\Delta_{ab}|/P(X_1=a)\simeq V^2\bar C$, by linearising the log because $\epsilon\lesssim1$. 5. Substitute into $t^\ast\asymp D\sigma/(\eta|\mu|\sqrt B)$. The correlation cancels in the dense case.

The key trick is step 2 together with the observation in step 4 that, at uniform initialisation, the signal and the required displacement are both linear in the same small quantity. Fig. 9 confirms $\sqrt V\ln V$ and $V$ for $V$ from 128 to 512 at $B=2$, with good collapse. Two honest limitations remain. The authors themselves note that $\epsilon\approx0.95$ to $1.55$ at $\beta=1.2$, so the dense calculation sits at the edge of its validity. And nothing in the derivation addresses the second (latent-variable) stage.

Broader context

Background. A line of statistical-physics-style work, mostly from the Wyart group (EPFL) and collaborators, studies "how deep nets learn compositional structure" with synthetic generative grammars where the exact Bayes-optimal loss is computable. Examples are the Random Hierarchy Model (Cagnetta, Petrini, Tomasini, Favero, Wyart, PRX 2024) and later uniform-depth CFGs (Parley, Cagnetta, Wyart 2026). The central story there is that a network infers latent level $\ell$ once the token correlations induced by that level exceed sampling noise. The number of samples needed therefore grows as a power of the number of rules, which explains staged learning and plateaus. Related empirical work from the "physics of language models" series (Allen-Zhu and Li) shows transformers trained on CFGs implementing parsing-like dynamic programming. The RLM (DeGiuli 2019, and the 2026 phase analysis by Giorlandino, De Giuli and Goldt) adds a REM-type disorder parameter. This paper is the first to use that knob to vary the learning dynamics.

Closely related directions: - Cagnetta and Wyart (NeurIPS 2024), "Towards a theory of how the structure of language is acquired". It provides the correlation-resolution mechanism that might explain $t^\ast_2\propto V^3$, which this paper explicitly leaves open. - Work on why Adam beats SGD on language data, such as Kunstner et al. (2024) on heavy-tailed class imbalance. The App. C argument is a clean, solvable instance of that phenomenon: Adam's per-coordinate normalisation turns a $1/V$ dilution of signal into a $1/\sqrt V$ effective dilution.

A plausible follow-up. Extend the mean-field Adam argument to the second stage. One way is to treat the trained sibling predictor as fixed and compute the SNR of the gradient on the attention or MLP weights that couple $(X_1,X_2)$ to $X_4$ through $Z_1$. The mutual information through the root is a product of two rule-level correlations, so a naive guess is that the signal scales like $\bar C^2$ while the distance scales like $\bar C$. That would leave the exponent depending on $\beta$, and the V-cubed law could be compared against it. A cheaper experiment is to run the transformer study with SGD and with sign-SGD, to test whether the hierarchy exponents shift by the amount the linear theory predicts for the first stage. Larger $V$ and longer sequences ($L\ge3$) are needed before any exponent is trusted.

Connection to theoretical IR and generative retrieval. This is an analogy, but a reasonably concrete one. Generative retrieval with hierarchical semantic document IDs (e.g. hierarchical k-means codes or RQ-VAE semantic IDs) asks a transformer to emit a short tree-structured token sequence. Each level has a codebook of size $V$, and the conditional of each docid token given its prefix and the query can be dense or sparse, depending on how documents spread over clusters. The paper's results suggest two testable hypotheses. First, the training time to learn level $\ell$ of a docid tree should scale as a power of the per-level codebook size that depends on how concentrated the child distributions are. Second, with Adam, sparse (near-deterministic) prefix-to-suffix maps should be learned faster than diffuse ones, roughly $\sqrt V$ versus $V$ steps, which bears on choosing codebook size versus depth in semantic-ID design. The App. C calculation is also directly about embedding/logit tables with one-hot inputs, so it applies to how quickly rare-item rows of a retrieval model's output table move under Adam. None of this is claimed in the paper, and the setting (4-token sequences, no queries) is far from real retrieval. So the connection is a source of hypotheses rather than a result.

title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-24

To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression — Mingyue Xu, Gal Vardi, Itay Safran (2026) — arXiv:2601.19791

Setting and problem

Data model and student. Inputs $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are drawn from an unspecified marginal $\mathcal{D}_x$. A fixed feature map $\phi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is given, and the student is linear in the features, $N(x;\theta) = \langle \theta, \phi(x) \rangle$ with $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^m$. The teacher is realizable, $N^*(x) = \langle \theta^*, \phi(x) \rangle$, and labels are noiseless, $y = N^*(x)$. The training set is $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$, and the paper stacks the features into $\Phi = (\phi(x_1), \dots, \phi(x_n))^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$. Note the notation: the over-parameterized dimension is $m$, the feature dimension, and not the raw input dimension $d$. The regime of interest is $m > n$, in fact $m - n$ large, so $\Phi$ has a nontrivial null space of dimension at least $m - n$. The other notation is:

  • $L = \frac{1}{n}\|\Phi\|_F^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|\phi(x_i)\|_2^2$ is the average squared feature norm.
  • $b$ bounds the features uniformly, $\|\phi(x)\|_2 \le b$.
  • $\Sigma = \mathbb{E}_x[\phi(x)\phi(x)^\top]$ is the population feature covariance, and $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)$ is its smallest eigenvalue.
  • $\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)$ is the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of the empirical Gram matrix.

Objective and algorithm. Ridge regression minimizes

$$L_n(\theta;\lambda) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n \big(\langle \theta - \theta^*, \phi(x_i)\rangle\big)^2}_{L_n(\theta)} + \frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2,$$

using full-batch GD with constant step size $\eta$ and weight decay $\lambda > 0$:

$$\theta^{(t+1)} = \Big(I_m - \eta\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\Phi^\top\Phi + \lambda I_m\big)\Big)\theta^{(t)} + \tfrac{\eta}{n}\Phi^\top\Phi\,\theta^*.$$

The initialization is random Gaussian, $\theta^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \nu^2 I_m)$, and $\nu^2$ is the initialization-scale hyperparameter.

Errors. The training error is the unregularized empirical loss $L_n(\theta)$, without the penalty. The test error is the population squared loss $L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_x[(N(x;\theta) - N^*(x))^2] = (\theta - \theta^*)^\top \Sigma (\theta - \theta^*)$.

Grokking time, precisely. Fix a training threshold $\epsilon > 0$ and a test threshold $c \ge \epsilon$. Then

$$t_1(\epsilon) := \max\{t \in \mathbb{N} : L_n(\theta^{(t)}) \ge \epsilon\}, \qquad t_2(c) := \min\{t \in \mathbb{N} : L(\theta^{(t)}) \le c\}.$$

So $t_1$ is the last step at which the model has not yet fit the training set to accuracy $\epsilon$, and $t_2$ is the first step at which the test loss drops below $c$. The grokking time is $t_2 - t_1$. "Provable grokking" means three things together:

  1. $t_1$ is small, so the model overfits early.
  2. $t_2 - t_1$ is large, so poor generalization persists after overfitting.
  3. $L(\theta^{(t)}) \le \epsilon$ eventually, so the model generalizes in the end.

The precise question. _In the simplest model where it can occur, over-parameterized linear least squares trained by GD with weight decay, can we prove all three stages end to end with non-asymptotic, high-probability bounds? Can we also give explicit bounds on $t_1$ and $t_2$ as functions of $(\lambda, \eta, \nu^2, n, m)$, so that one can say how to make grokking arbitrarily long or remove it?_

What the literature knows.

  • Power et al. (2022) named grokking. Transformers trained on small algorithmic datasets (modular arithmetic) reach perfect training accuracy, then their validation accuracy jumps to near 100% orders of magnitude later. Weight decay strongly affects whether and when this happens.
  • Liu et al., "Omnigrok" (ICLR 2023) gave the weight-norm / "LU mechanism" account. Training loss is low on a wide band of weight norms, but test loss is low only in a "Goldilocks" norm shell. With large initialization norm, the network first interpolates at a large norm, and weight decay then slowly pulls the norm into the good shell. They induced grokking on MNIST and other non-algorithmic data just by scaling up the initialization. This paper is essentially the rigorous linear-model version of Omnigrok.
  • Lyu et al. (ICLR 2024), "Dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases" studied homogeneous networks under gradient flow with small weight decay and large init. Early training follows the kernel (lazy) implicit bias, and late training follows a min-norm / max-margin (rich) bias, with a sharp transition at roughly time $\log(\text{init})/\lambda$. Their guarantees are convergence to KKT points, which does not by itself certify global optimality or prove generalization, so they fall short of end-to-end grokking.
  • Kumar et al. (ICLR 2024) described grokking as a lazy-to-rich transition in the dynamics. Mohamadi et al. (ICML 2024) analyzed modular addition with two-layer quadratic nets and an $\ell_\infty$-type regularizer.
  • Nanda et al. (ICLR 2023) reverse-engineered the grokked modular-addition circuit, which uses Fourier features and trigonometric identities. They also defined progress measures showing that a generalizing circuit forms gradually and is "cleaned up" once weight decay removes the memorizing components. That gives a mechanistic but non-theoretical picture.
  • Xu et al. (ICLR 2024) proved one-step catastrophic overfitting followed by eventual generalization for XOR-cluster data in two-layer ReLU nets. They did not show that bad generalization lasts beyond the first step.
  • Boursier et al. (NeurIPS 2025) proved interpolation followed by Riemannian norm minimization. Tikeng Notsawo et al. (ICML 2025) showed a loss-minimization phase followed by a regularizer-driven phase on a $1/(\eta\lambda)$ time scale. Neither proves that the interpolating solution generalizes badly and that the ridge solution generalizes well.
  • Levi, Beck, Bar-Sinai (ICLR 2024) studied linear estimators with Gaussian data and $m \approx n$ using random-matrix theory, without weight decay and without rigorous guarantees. Their framing was "grokking without understanding".

The gap. No previous result proves all three stages at once with explicit time scales. Earlier work proves either the transition but not that the early solution is bad, or eventual generalization but not a lasting bad phase.

The key modelling choice. Everything depends on large-norm random initialization combined with a small weight decay. Split $\theta = \theta_\parallel + \theta_\perp$ into the row space of $\Phi$ and its orthogonal complement, the null space of $\Phi$. The data gradient lives entirely in the row space. So the null-space component of the initialization, $\theta^{(0)}_\perp$, which is a $\ge (m-n)$-dimensional Gaussian with squared norm $\approx (m-n)\nu^2$, receives no data signal at all. Only weight decay shrinks it, at rate $(1-\eta\lambda)^t$. Because $\Sigma$ is assumed to have $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma) > 0$, the population covariance "sees" the null-space directions that the training data cannot see. That leftover null-space mass is what makes the test error large. Under zero initialization, $\theta_\perp \equiv 0$ throughout, and the phenomenon disappears.

Main idea

The approach is a direct, closed-form analysis of a linear recursion, with no feature learning and no lazy-to-rich story. Center the iterates at the ridge minimizer, $u^{(t)} = \theta^{(t)} - \theta^*_\lambda$. Then $u^{(t)} = (I - \eta(\frac{1}{n}\Phi^\top\Phi + \lambda I))^t u^{(0)}$, and the two orthogonal pieces evolve independently:

  • Row space: $\|u^{(t)}_\parallel\| \le \big(1 - \frac{\eta\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)}{n} - \eta\lambda\big)^t \|u^{(0)}_\parallel\|$. This is fast, governed by the data spectrum.
  • Null space: $\theta^{(t)}_\perp = (1-\eta\lambda)^t\,\theta^{(0)}_\perp$ exactly. This is slow, governed only by weight decay.

Training loss depends only on $\theta_\parallel$, so it converges at the fast rate. Test loss is bounded below by $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\|\theta^{(t)} - \theta^*\|^2 \ge \lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\big((1-\eta\lambda)^t\|\theta_\perp^{(0)}\| - \|\theta^*\|\big)^2$, so it stays large until the null-space mass decays. Eventually GD reaches the ridge solution $\theta^*_\lambda$. That solution satisfies $\|\theta^*_\lambda\| \le \|\theta^*\|$ and therefore generalizes by norm-based uniform convergence.

Headline result (Theorem 4.2). Assume the following:

  • bounded features, $\|\phi(x)\| \le b$;
  • $n = \Omega\big(\frac{b^4\|\theta^*\|^4}{\epsilon^2}\log\frac1\delta\big)$;
  • $m = n + \Omega\big(\max\{\log\frac1\delta, \frac{\|\theta^*\|^2}{\nu^2}, \frac{c}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\nu^2}\}\big)$;
  • $\lambda = O\big(\min\{\frac{\epsilon}{\|\theta^*\|^2}, \frac{b\sqrt\epsilon}{\|\theta^*\|}\}\big)$;
  • $\eta < 1/(\lambda + b^2)$.

Then, with probability $\ge 1-\delta$,

$$t_1 \le \frac{n \ln\!\big(6b^2\|\theta^{(0)}\|^2/\epsilon\big)}{2\eta\,\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)}, \qquad t_2 \ge \frac{\ln\!\Big(\frac{(m-n)\nu^2}{2}\big(\sqrt{c/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)} + \|\theta^*\|\big)^{-2}\Big)}{4\eta\lambda},$$

and $L(\theta^{(t)}) \le \epsilon$ for all sufficiently large $t$.

So $t_1 \sim \frac{\log(\text{init norm}/\epsilon)}{\eta\,\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)/n}$ does not depend on $\lambda$. Meanwhile $t_2 \sim \frac{\log(\text{init null-space mass}/\text{test threshold})}{\eta\lambda}$, which goes to infinity as $\lambda \to 0$.

Controlling the effect.

  • Weight decay: $t_2 \propto 1/\lambda$ and $t_1$ does not depend on $\lambda$, so $t_2 - t_1 \to \infty$ as $\lambda \to 0$. This is the main knob.
  • Initialization scale: both $t_1$ and $t_2$ grow like $\ln\nu^2$. Because the coefficient on $t_2$ is larger when $\lambda$ is small, a larger $\nu^2$ amplifies grokking, but only logarithmically.
  • Sample size and width: $t_1$ depends on $n/\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)$. A smaller $n$ (more over-parameterization) speeds up fitting and amplifies grokking. Width $m$ barely matters in experiments.
  • Removing it: the bound requires $(m-n)\nu^2/2 > (\sqrt{c/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)} + \|\theta^*\|)^2$, meaning the initial null-space mass must be visible in the test loss. If $\nu^2$ is small, so that the initial test loss is already below $c$, the lower bound on $t_2$ is empty and there is no grokking. The same happens if $\lambda$ is not small relative to $\lambda^+_{\min}/n$.

Experiments.

  • With Gaussian features $\phi(x_i) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_m/m)$, the closed-form bounds become $t_2 \ge \frac{\ln((m-n)\nu^2/(8m\epsilon))}{2.02\,\eta\lambda}$ and $t_1 \le \frac{n\ln(14m\nu^2/\epsilon)}{2\eta\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)}$ (their Eq. 8). The defaults were $n=100$, $m=1000$, $\nu^2=1$, $\lambda=10^{-4}$, $\eta=1$, $c=\epsilon=0.01$. The measured $t_1$ and $t_2$ follow the predicted scaling in $\lambda$, $n$, $m$, $\nu^2$ closely (Fig. 2).
  • Rough numbers for the defaults: $\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi) \approx (1-\sqrt{n/m})^2 \approx 0.47$, so $t_1 \lesssim 100 \cdot \ln(1.4\times10^6)/0.94 \approx 1.5\times10^3$ and $t_2 \gtrsim \ln(11.25)/(2.02\times10^{-4}) \approx 1.2\times10^4$. That is about an order of magnitude of delay.
  • Random-ReLU-features regression with a single-neuron teacher, which is nearly realizable, and a fully trained two-layer ReLU net with the zero teacher show the same qualitative dependence on the hyperparameters (Figs. 3–4).
  • The appendix adds label noise and random Fourier features (Figs. 6–7). It also adds a thresholded "surrogate accuracy" $\Pr_x[(N - N^*)^2 \le \epsilon]$ that recovers the familiar plateau-then-jump curve (Fig. 5).

The most interesting part

The most interesting part is less a clever idea than a clean reduction that is hard to argue with. Read honestly, it is also a partial deflation of grokking.

The sharp idea. Remark A.3 makes it explicit: you must not use the textbook ridge convergence rate. The standard rate is $\lambda_{\min}(\frac1n\Phi^\top\Phi + \lambda I)$, which equals exactly $\lambda$ when $m > n$, because $\Phi^\top\Phi$ is rank-deficient. That rate is identical to the null-space decay rate, so it cannot separate training from test dynamics. The fix is to note that $L_n(\theta) = \tilde L_n(\theta_\parallel)$, so training error only "feels" the row-space dynamics, whose rate is $\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)/n + \lambda$. The test loss instead feels the full parameter vector through $\Sigma \succ 0$. Grokking here is a spectral gap between the data-visible and data-invisible subspaces of parameter space: data curvature $\lambda^+_{\min}/n$ against regularizer curvature $\lambda$. The grokking time is then just the ratio of two exponential time constants, times a logarithm of how much initialization mass must be removed.

Honest critique: is this "grokking", or slow decay of the null-space component? It is slow decay of the null-space component, and the paper more or less concedes this in its Discussion. Several points make that concrete:

  1. It is an initialization artifact by construction. With $\theta^{(0)} = 0$ and no weight decay, GD converges to the min-norm interpolant, which has norm $\le \|\theta^*\|$ in this realizable setting. The same Rademacher argument then shows it generalizes, with no delay. The authors themselves describe grokking here as "a transition from a misspecified to a well-specified prior". Large init plays the role of a bad prior in the null space, and weight decay slowly replaces it with the zero prior. This is exactly the Omnigrok story of Liu et al., now in a solvable model. It is a rigorous confirmation of the weight-norm explanation, not a new mechanism.
  2. "Poor generalization" means worse than the trivial predictor. With $\Sigma = I/m$ and $\|\theta^*\| = 1$, the zero predictor has test loss $1/m = 10^{-3}$. The grokking-phase test loss is $\approx \nu^2(m-n)/m \approx 0.9$, which is just the random init's variance projected onto unseen directions. Nothing structured is "memorized" that later gets replaced by a "circuit". There is no competition between two representations and no feature learning. The model never "understands" anything it did not have at the start except the row-space fit.
  3. The suddenness is a log-axis effect. The test loss decays roughly as $(1-\eta\lambda)^{2t}$, a smooth exponential. On a $\log t$ axis an exponential looks like a sigmoid "cliff", and the authors note that regression losses show no genuine plateau. They need the thresholded surrogate accuracy to recreate the classic plateau picture (Fig. 5). In Power et al., the abrupt accuracy jump on discrete tasks combines thresholding with genuine representation change. Only the first of these is present here.
  4. The test-error lower bound needs $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma) > 0$ on all $m$ feature directions. In practice, features such as random features or kernel features have rapidly decaying spectra. The null-space mass then lives mostly in directions with tiny population variance and barely shows up in the test loss. The clean $(1-\eta\lambda)^t$ picture would split into many time scales, and the $t_2$ bound, which uses only $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)$, would be very loose or vacuous. This may be why the random-Fourier-features experiment "requires careful hyperparameter tuning to observe grokking".
  5. Bounds are one-sided where it matters. For the realizable teacher they prove an upper bound on $t_1$, a lower bound on $t_2$, and "eventually" generalization. There is no explicit upper bound on when generalization arrives, although one is easy from the same decomposition; only the zero-teacher warm-up has matching upper and lower rates. Also, $t_1$ is stated in terms of the random quantity $\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)$.

Credit where due. The authors are not claiming a deep mechanism. Their stated aim is the first end-to-end proof, with explicit hyperparameter dependence, in the most transparent setting. The paper delivers that with elementary tools. The interpretive punchline, "grokking is not an inherent failure mode of deep learning but a consequence of specific training conditions", is well supported for this model. The fact that the scaling of $t_1, t_2$ in $\lambda$, $n$ and $\nu^2$ qualitatively transfers to fully trained two-layer ReLU nets (Fig. 4) is the most interesting empirical observation. It suggests that the null-space-decay mechanism, rather than representation learning, may account for much of the timing of grokking even in non-linear models.

Proof sketch

Theorem 4.1 (zero teacher, warm-up). Assume $\theta^* = 0$, $\theta^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\nu^2 I_m)$ and $\eta \le 2/(L+2\lambda)$. Then for all $t$:

  • (i) $L_n(\theta^{(t)}) \le \frac{L}{2}\big(1 - \frac{\eta\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)}{n} - \eta\lambda\big)^{2t}\|\theta^{(0)}\|^2$;
  • (ii) with probability $\ge 1 - 2e^{-(m-n)/32}$, $L(\theta^{(t)}) \ge \lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)(1-\eta\lambda)^{2t}\frac{(m-n)\nu^2}{2}$;
  • (iii) $\|\theta^{(t)}\|^2 \le (1-\eta\lambda)^{2t}\|\theta^{(0)}\|^2$.

Grokking appears when $m \gg n$, $\lambda \ll \lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)/n$ and $\lambda \to 0$.

Theorem 4.4 (training convergence, realizable). Assume $\eta < 1/(\lambda + \lambda_{\max}(\Phi^\top\Phi)/n)$, $m = \Omega(\max\{\log\frac1\delta, \|\theta^*\|^2/\nu^2\})$, which is "large init relative to the teacher", and $\lambda = O(\min\{\epsilon/\|\theta^*\|^2, \sqrt{L\epsilon}/\|\theta^*\|\})$. Then with probability $\ge 1-\delta$, $L_n(\theta^{(t)}) \le \epsilon$ for all

$$t \ge \tfrac12 \log_{\,1 - \eta\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)/n - \eta\lambda}\Big(\frac{\epsilon}{6L\|\theta^{(0)}\|^2}\Big).$$

Theorem 4.5 (persistent poor generalization). Assume $\eta < 1/\lambda$ and $m = n + \Omega(\max\{\log\frac1\delta, \|\theta^*\|^2/\nu^2, c/(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\nu^2)\})$. Then with probability $\ge 1-\delta$, $L(\theta^{(t)}) \ge c$ for all

$$t \le \log_{1-\eta\lambda}\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{(m-n)\nu^2}}\big(\sqrt{c/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)} + \|\theta^*\|\big)\Big).$$

Theorem 4.6 (eventual generalization). Assume $\|\phi\| \le b$, $n = \Omega(b^4\|\theta^*\|^4\epsilon^{-2}\log\frac1\delta)$ and $\eta \le 1/(\lambda+b^2)$. Then GD converges to $\theta^*_\lambda = \arg\min L_n(\cdot;\lambda)$, and with probability $\ge 1-\delta$, $L(\theta^*_\lambda) \le 2L_n(\theta^*_\lambda) + \epsilon$.

Theorem 4.2 combines these results. It converts $\log_{1-x}$ into $1/x$ time scales using $\ln(1-\eta\lambda) \ge -2\eta\lambda$ for small $\eta\lambda$, which gives the $4\eta\lambda$ in the denominator, and $\ln(1-x) \le -x$, which gives $2\eta\lambda^+_{\min}/n$. It also uses $L \le b^2$.

Technique, step by step.

  1. Linear recursion around the ridge minimizer. The first-order condition gives $(\frac1n\Phi^\top\Phi + \lambda I)\theta^*_\lambda = \frac1n\Phi^\top\Phi\theta^*$. Hence $u^{(t)} := \theta^{(t)} - \theta^*_\lambda$ satisfies $u^{(t)} = (I - \eta(\frac1n\Phi^\top\Phi + \lambda I))u^{(t-1)}$. This is a plain matrix power.
  2. Row-space / null-space split (the key lemma, Theorem A.2 / Remark A.3). $\Phi^\top\Phi$ commutes with the projector onto its row space, so the recursion block-diagonalizes:
  3. $u^{(t)}_\parallel$ contracts by $1 - \eta\lambda^+_{\min}/n - \eta\lambda$ per step, given $\eta$ below the inverse top eigenvalue;
  4. $u^{(t)}_\perp = (1-\eta\lambda)^t u^{(0)}_\perp$, and $\theta^*_\lambda$ lies in the row space, so $\theta^{(t)}_\perp = (1-\eta\lambda)^t\theta^{(0)}_\perp$.

Because $L_n(\theta)$ depends only on $\theta_\parallel$, the training error converges at the fast rate. This is the step that beats the naive $\lambda_{\min}(\Gamma) = \lambda$ rate. 3. Bounding the training loss. $L_n(\theta^{(t)}) - L_n(\theta^*_\lambda)$ expands into a quadratic term $\le \frac L2\|u_\parallel^{(t)}\|^2$ and a cross term. The optimality condition rewrites the cross term as $-\lambda\langle u^{(t)}_\parallel, \theta^*_{\lambda,\parallel}\rangle$, which is $\le \lambda\|u^{(t)}_\parallel\|\|\theta^*\|$. Comparing with $\theta^*$ gives $\|\theta^*_\lambda\| \le \|\theta^*\|$ and $L_n(\theta^*_\lambda) \le \frac\lambda2\|\theta^*\|^2$. Then $\|u^{(0)}\| \le 2\|\theta^{(0)}\|$ once $\|\theta^{(0)}\| \ge \|\theta^*\|$, which holds by chi-squared concentration, $\|\theta^{(0)}\|^2 \approx m\nu^2$, and the condition $m \gtrsim \|\theta^*\|^2/\nu^2$. This yields three terms, each made $\le \epsilon/3$: the decaying one by choosing $t$, and the two $\lambda$-terms by taking $\lambda$ small. 4. Lower-bounding the test loss (the probabilistic step). $L(\theta) = (\theta - \theta^*)^\top\Sigma(\theta - \theta^*) \ge \lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\|\theta - \theta^*\|^2$, and $\|\theta^{(t)} - \theta^*\| \ge \|\theta^{(t)}_\perp\| - \|\theta^*\|$. By rotation invariance of the Gaussian, projecting $\theta^{(0)}$ onto an orthonormal basis of the $k \ge m-n$-dimensional null space gives $k$ i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,\nu^2)$ coordinates. Chi-squared concentration then gives $\|\theta^{(0)}_\perp\|^2 \ge k\nu^2/2$ with probability $\ge 1 - 2e^{-k/32}$. Plugging in the exact decay $(1-\eta\lambda)^t$ and solving for $t$ gives Theorem 4.5. The probability is over the initialization only, conditional on $\Phi$, because the null space is fixed once the data is drawn. 5. Eventual generalization (standard learning theory). The objective is $(b^2+\lambda)$-smooth and $\lambda$-strongly convex, so GD converges to $\theta^*_\lambda$. Since $\|\theta^*_\lambda\| \le \|\theta^*\|$, the ridge solution lies in the ball class $\{x \mapsto \langle\theta,\phi(x)\rangle : \|\theta\| \le \|\theta^*\|\}$. That class has Rademacher complexity $\le \|\theta^*\|\sqrt{L/n}$. The squared loss restricted to it is $4b\|\theta^*\|$-Lipschitz and bounded by $4b^2\|\theta^*\|^2$, so the standard Shalev-Shwartz–Ben-David bound gives $L(\theta^*_\lambda) \le 2L_n(\theta^*_\lambda) + O(b^2\|\theta^*\|^2/\sqrt n)$. That is where $n = \Omega(b^4\|\theta^*\|^4/\epsilon^2)$ comes from. Finally, $2L_n(\theta^*_\lambda) \le \lambda\|\theta^*\|^2 \le \epsilon/2$ for small $\lambda$.

Minor issues in the text.

  • The appendix restatement of Theorem 4.2 has $\lambda_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)$ (which is zero when $m > n$) and a stray "+" where $\lambda^+_{\min}$ is clearly meant.
  • The width condition reads $c/(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\nu^2)$ in the main text but $c^2/(\lambda^2_{\min}(\Sigma)\nu^2)$ in the appendix.
  • Remark 4.3 states the Marchenko–Pastur edge in a garbled form.
  • Remark 4.3 claims there is no quantitative non-asymptotic bound on $\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi)$ even for Gaussian features. That seems too strong. For $\phi(x_i) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_m/m)$ and $m > n$, standard results on the smallest singular value of Gaussian matrices (Davidson–Szarek; Vershynin, Cor. 5.35) give $\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi) \ge (1 - \sqrt{n/m} - s/\sqrt m)^2$ with probability $\ge 1 - 2e^{-s^2/2}$. That would make $t_1 \lesssim n\log(m\nu^2/\epsilon)/(\eta(1-\sqrt{n/m})^2)$ fully explicit.

None of these affects the main conclusions.

Broader context

Background. The result belongs to a line of work that "explains" grokking by the interplay between an implicit bias set by initialization and early dynamics, and an explicit bias set by weight decay that acts on a slow $1/(\eta\lambda)$ clock. Three earlier versions of this picture are:

  • Liu et al.'s Omnigrok (large init norm pulled into a Goldilocks shell);
  • Lyu et al.'s early/late implicit-bias dichotomy (kernel predictor, then min-norm/max-margin predictor, transition at $\sim \log(\alpha)/\lambda$ for init scale $\alpha$);
  • Tikeng Notsawo et al. and Boursier et al. (interpolation, then regularizer-driven drift on the interpolation manifold).
