This paper is the minimal fully solved instance. The interpolation manifold is the affine set $\theta^* + \ker\Phi$, and the drift along it is pure exponential shrinkage of the $\ker\Phi$ coordinate. It complements the random-matrix analysis of Levi et al. (2024), which has no weight decay and studies the $m \approx n$ regime.

Related directions worth reading next.

  1. Kumar, Bordelon, Gershman, Pehlevan, "Grokking as the transition from lazy to rich training dynamics" (ICLR 2024). In their polynomial-regression examples, the delay is governed by how far the initial kernel is from the task-relevant features. Comparing the two shows that the ridge model captures the timing part (the $1/\lambda$ clock) and none of the feature-learning part.
  2. Lyu et al. (2024) and Mohamadi et al. (2024) are the natural targets for an "end-to-end" upgrade. The authors list the lazy-to-rich transition as an open question. They also report that proving even stage (ii) for two-layer nets is hard, because the collective NTK can still drive the output to zero even when each neuron stays close to its initialization.

Plausible follow-up research ideas.

  • Spectral, multi-scale grokking. Replace $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)$ with the full spectrum of $\Sigma$ restricted to $\ker\Phi$, for example in kernel or random-features ridge with power-law eigenvalues. Then $L(\theta^{(t)}) - L(\theta^*_\lambda) \approx (1-\eta\lambda)^{2t}\,\mathrm{tr}(P_\perp\Sigma P_\perp)\nu^2$ plus row-space terms. The question is when the initial test excess is large compared with the final error: one would need $\nu^2\,\mathrm{tr}(P_\perp\Sigma P_\perp) \gg$ the ridge bias plus variance. That yields a sharp necessary and sufficient condition for grokking in terms of effective dimension, and would explain why random-Fourier-feature grokking needs tuning.
  • Optimizer dependence. With AdamW the null-space coordinates no longer receive zero update in general, because coordinate-wise preconditioning mixes the row and null spaces. Decoupled weight decay still contracts at rate $(1-\eta\lambda)$. Does the null-space story survive, and does it predict the faster grokking seen with adaptive optimizers (Thilak et al.'s "slingshot")?
  • Label noise / agnostic setting. The authors flag this as open. With noise, small $\lambda$ also causes harmful interpolation of noise in the row space. This creates a genuine three-way trade-off between $\lambda$ for the clock, $\lambda$ for bias and variance, and $\nu^2$.

Connection to IR / generative retrieval / vector search (only where it is genuine). The literal mechanism, init mass in directions the training data never touches decaying only through weight decay, does map onto concrete IR settings:

  • Linear adapters on frozen embeddings. One common setup learns a linear query-side projection $W$ on top of frozen dense embeddings (dimension $m$ = 768–4096) from a few hundred labeled query–document pairs, so $n < m$. Any component of the random initialization of $W$ that lies in directions orthogonal to the span of the training query embeddings gets no gradient. At test time, queries with mass in those directions are scored with essentially random transformations until weight decay removes it. The practical prescription, which follows directly from this paper, is to initialize adapters at zero or at the identity (a residual adapter) rather than with random weights. Otherwise one should expect a long "fits training pairs, generalizes worse than the base model" phase with $t_2 \propto 1/\lambda$. This is a small but testable claim.
  • Atomic-docid generative retrieval (DSI-style). Each document has an output embedding row. Rows for documents that appear only in the indexing (doc → docid) data, and never in query → docid supervision, are constrained only along the directions spanned by their document-text representations. Their behaviour on real queries is set by whatever component of the random init lies outside that span, and only weight decay removes it. Practitioners do report that query-side generalization keeps improving long after indexing loss saturates. The ridge picture offers one quantitative hypothesis for that lag: a $1/(\eta\lambda)$ time scale tied to init scale. An alternative is genuine representation learning. One could separate the two by checking whether the lag scales like $\log(\nu^2)/\lambda$. It is an analogy, not a theorem: DSI is a non-linear model trained with cross-entropy, where Lyu et al.'s margin-based dynamics are the more relevant theory.
  • For vector search proper (ANN indexes, quantization), there is no meaningful connection, and none should be forced.

Bottom line. This is a correct, clean and well-scoped first end-to-end proof. Its conceptual message is valuable mainly as a null model: in linear regression, grokking is exactly the slow, weight-decay-driven removal of an initialization prior in the data's null space, with $t_{\text{grok}} \sim \log(\text{init mass})/(\eta\lambda)$ against $t_{\text{fit}} \sim n\log(\cdot)/(\eta\lambda^+_{\min}(\Phi^\top\Phi))$. Any claim that a non-linear model groks "for deeper reasons" should first show that it is not just this.

title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-24

Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference? — Han Yan, Jin Zhu, Chengchun Shi, Tengyao Wang (2026) — arXiv:2611.27666

Setting and problem

The semiparametric model. An observation $Z \in \mathcal{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}^{d_z}$ is drawn from an unknown distribution $P$ in a statistical model $\mathcal{P}$. The object of inference is not one functional but a whole query-indexed family $$\{\beta_q(P) : q \in \mathcal{Q},\ P \in \mathcal{P}\}, \qquad q = (k,u),\ \beta_q(P) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k},$$ where $k \in \mathcal{K}$ picks an estimand class (ATE, quantile treatment effect, partially linear projection coefficient, mean survival time, group treatment effects, ...) and $u \in \mathcal{U}_k$ is an optional argument (for the QTE, the quantile level $u \in (0,1)$). Everything else about $P$ (outcome regressions $m_d(x) = \mathbb{E}_P(Y \mid D=d, X=x)$, propensity scores, conditional densities, censoring laws) is nuisance. The model $\mathcal{P}$ is essentially nonparametric: all distributions whose density $p = dP/dP_0$ with respect to a fixed reference $P_0$ is bounded between constants $c_0 < p < C_0$. Hence the tangent space at every $P$ is all of $L_2^0(P)$, each pathwise differentiable $\beta_q$ has a unique gradient, and that gradient is the efficient influence function (EIF) $\psi^\star_{P,q}$. The efficiency bound is $$V_q^\star(P) = \mathbb{E}_P\{(\psi^\star_{P,q})^{\otimes 2}\},$$ and an estimator $\hat\beta$ is called efficient if it is asymptotically linear in the EIF, $$\hat\beta = \beta_q(P) + \mathbb{P}_N \psi^\star_{P,q} + o(N^{-1/2}), \qquad \mathbb{P}_N h := N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N h(Z_i),$$ so that $\sqrt{N}(\hat\beta - \beta_q(P)) \rightsquigarrow \mathcal{N}(0, V_q^\star(P))$.

What the Transformer receives and outputs. A single network $f = (f^\beta, f^V)$ takes a dataset $D_N = \{Z_i\}_{i=1}^N$ (rows embedded without positional encoding, so the map is permutation invariant) plus one extra "query row" that encodes $\xi(q,N)$: a one-hot of the estimand class $k$, the argument $u$, and the scaled sample size $N/n_{\max}$. It reads out from the query row a point estimate $\hat\beta = f^\beta(D_N,q) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ and a positive definite matrix $\hat V = f^V(D_N,q)$ meant to estimate $N$ times the sampling covariance. Inference is then the Wald region $$\hat C_N(D_N,q) = \{\beta : N(\hat\beta-\beta)^\top \hat V^{-1}(\hat\beta-\beta) \le \chi^2_{d_k,1-\alpha}\}.$$ No nuisance fit, no EIF, no cross-fitting, no variance formula: one forward pass (about 0.02 s per dataset in their experiments).

How pretraining works. Fix a pretraining prior $\pi = \pi_P \otimes \pi_q$ over populations and queries and a distribution $\pi_n$ over a finite set of sample sizes $\mathcal{N} = \{n_{\min},\dots,n_{\max}\}$ with $n_{\min} \asymp n_{\max} \asymp N$. Repeat $T$ times: draw $(P_t, q_t, n_t) \sim \pi \otimes \pi_n$, draw $D^{(t)}_{n_t} \sim P_t^{\otimes n_t}$, and record the label $\beta_{0,t} = \beta_{q_t}(P_t)$, the true value of the queried functional for the simulated population (computable because the simulator knows $P_t$; for the QTE it is approximated by Monte Carlo with 8192 extra units). The network is fitted by (approximate) empirical risk minimisation of the Gaussian score, i.e. the Dawid–Sebastiani score $$\ell_n(\beta_0;\beta,V) = \tfrac12 \log\det V + \tfrac{n}{2}(\beta_0-\beta)^\top V^{-1}(\beta_0-\beta),$$ up to an optimisation slack $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}$. Crucially the label is just $\beta_q(P)$: not an EIF-corrected pseudo-outcome. Evaluation happens on $(P,q) \sim \nu$, an evaluation distribution that may differ from $\pi$, and $D_N \sim P^{\otimes N}$.

The precise question. Is there a single pretraining objective, with the true parameter as the only label and no estimand-specific EIF machinery, such that the pretrained network is semiparametrically efficient and its Wald region has asymptotically exact coverage for every estimand in the query family, simultaneously? Formally: when does $$\hat\beta = \beta_q(P) + \mathbb{P}_N\psi^\star_{P,q} + o_\nu(N^{-1/2}) \quad\text{and}\quad \hat V = V_q^\star(P) + o_\nu(1)$$ hold, and what does it cost in prior design, network size $p$, number of pretraining datasets $T$, and optimisation accuracy?

What the literature knows. - Classical efficient estimation. One-step estimators $\hat\beta = \beta_q(\hat P) + \mathbb{P}_N\hat\psi_{P,q}$, estimating-equation/AIPW estimators, TMLE, and double/debiased ML with cross-fitting attain the bound when nuisance errors multiply to $o(N^{-1/2})$. All require deriving the EIF per estimand and refitting nuisances per dataset; separately corrected members of a family need not cohere (crossing quantile curves, non-monotone survival curves). Automatic-differentiation and Riesz-representer approaches automate the EIF but still refit per dataset and estimand. - Semiparametric Bernstein–von Mises theorems (Castillo and Rousseau 2015; Rivoirard and Rousseau 2012; Bickel and Kleijn 2012; Ghosal 2000). The posterior of a smooth functional is asymptotically normal centred at an efficient estimator, provided the prior does not introduce a bias of order $N^{-1/2}$. Fixes: tailor the prior along the least-favourable direction (Ray and van der Vaart 2020, which is exactly an EIF-informed prior), EIF-correct the posterior, or use sieve priors whose dimension grows suitably with $N$. Relatedly, sieve plug-in/sieve MLE estimators are efficient for smooth functionals under undersmoothing with no EIF correction (Shen 1997; Newey 1994; Chen 2007). - Amortised inference and prior-fitted networks. Neural Bayes estimators, PFNs (Müller et al. 2022) and TabPFN (Hollmann et al. 2025) are trained on simulated (data, label) pairs; the population risk minimiser is the Bayes rule under the simulator prior. Causal PFNs (CausalPFN, Do-PFN) amortise ATE/CATE estimation. Recent work shows PFN ATE estimates can carry a prior-induced confounding bias (Melnychuk et al. 2026a), fixed by a per-dataset one-step EIF correction; Zhang (2026) and Melnychuk et al. (2026b) put EIF corrections into pretraining labels or the prior, one estimand at a time. - ICL theory. The Bayesian view (Xie et al. 2022; Müller et al. 2022) treats a pretrained Transformer as an approximate posterior; the algorithmic view (Garg et al. 2022; Bai et al. 2023; von Oswald et al. 2023) constructs Transformers that run gradient descent/ridge/Lasso in context, with polynomial pretraining sample complexity. Ma, Wang and Samworth (2026) prove minimax-adaptive in-context nonparametric regression with distribution shift in a $\chi^2$ ball around the prior, the device reused here.

The gap. No prior result shows that a label-only, EIF-free pretraining target is efficient for a whole family of functionals, nor quantifies how many pretraining datasets and parameters a Transformer needs to inherit that efficiency, nor separates what can be guaranteed for random versus fixed evaluation populations.

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag. 1. Locally flat priors of slowly growing complexity. The theory does not cover arbitrary simulators. It reduces every admissible simulator prior $\pi_P$ to an exponential-series sieve prior $\pi_K$: write $dP/dP_0 \propto \exp(\sum_{k\le K}\theta_{P,k} b_k + g_{P,K})$ with a bounded orthonormal (trigonometric) basis, put $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2\mathrm{diag}(k^{-2a}))$ truncated to $\|\theta\|_1 \le B$, and require (A3) that the remainder $g_{P,K}$ is $o(N^{-1/2})$ in $L_2(P_0)$ for every population in the support, and (A4) that $\pi_P$ reweights $\pi_K$ by a density bounded above and below whose log is $L_N$-Lipschitz with $L_N = o(\sqrt N)$, i.e. nearly flat on the $N^{-1/2}$ posterior scale. The complexity $K = K_N$ must grow ($K\to\infty$) but slowly ($K^{3\vee 2a} = o(N)$). So the prior itself is indexed by $N$; a foundation model pretrained once with a fixed prior is outside the theorem. 2. "In probability over evaluation populations and queries". Efficiency (3.1) is stated with $o_\nu$, i.e. under the joint law of $(T, P, q, D_N)$ with $(P,q) \sim \nu$. It holds population by population (coverage is computed under $P$), except for a $\nu$-vanishing set of populations. This is stronger than prior-averaged calibration, but weaker than the classical "for every fixed $P$" (or uniform over a class). 3. Random versus fixed DGP. The evaluation law $\nu$ must satisfy $\sup_N \chi^2(\nu\,\|\,\pi) < \infty$ (A5). This allows distribution shift (for instance, evaluating at a single query that $\pi_q$ selects with positive probability) but excludes a point mass $\nu = \delta_{P_\star}\otimes\pi_q$, since $\chi^2(\delta_{P_\star}\|\pi_P)=\infty$. The fixed-DGP case is treated separately (Theorem 4) and costs exponentially more. 4. Smoothness of the whole joint density. Because one prior must serve every estimand, bias is controlled through the sieve error of the full log-density, which forces Sobolev smoothness $s > d(3/2 \vee a)$ in the $d$ continuous coordinates. For a single estimand, BvM theory only needs the product of density and EIF approximation errors to be small. 5. Sample sizes. The pretraining sizes satisfy $n_{\min}\asymp n_{\max}\asymp N$, so extrapolation in $N$ is not covered.

Main idea

The key observation is a three-step chain.

  1. What pretraining targets. By Proposition 1 (a property of the Dawid–Sebastiani proper scoring rule), the Bayes act under the pretraining prior is the pair of posterior moments $$m_\pi(D_n,q) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_P}\{\beta_q(P)\mid D_n\}, \qquad S_\pi(D_n,q) = n\,\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_P}\{\beta_q(P)\mid D_n\}.$$ So the network is implicitly being trained to do Bayesian inference for whichever functional the query names.

  2. Why that target is efficient without any EIF. Under a locally flat prior of slowly growing sieve dimension, the posterior on $\theta$ is a near-normal, nearly unbiased exponential-family posterior; the posterior mean of any smooth functional is then, to first order, the sieve plug-in estimator, which corrects every estimand along the same sieve scores $b_k - \mathbb{E}_P b_k$. Concretely, under $\pi_K$, $$m_\pi = \beta_q(P) + \mathbb{P}_N\psi^K_{P,q} + o_\nu(N^{-1/2}), \qquad S_\pi = \mathbb{E}_P\{(\psi^K_{P,q})^{\otimes 2}\} + o_\nu(1),$$ where $\psi^K_{P,q}$ is the $L_2(P)$ projection of the EIF onto the span of the centred sieve scores. As $K\to\infty$ the sieve scores approximate every EIF, so the posterior is efficient for every queried estimand at once. The EIF correction is "implicit": no estimand-specific debiasing is needed because the prior adds no $N^{-1/2}$ bias in any sieve direction (prior standard deviation $\sigma k^{-a} \gg N^{-1/2}$ when $K^{2a}=o(N)$).

  3. The Transformer can learn that target cheaply, on average. With one attention head the network averages approximate sieve features into $\hat s = \mathbb{P}_N b^{(K)}$, which is sufficient for $\theta$ under $\pi_K$; feed-forward layers unroll projected gradient steps for the strongly convex posterior-mode problem and evaluate $\beta_q(P_{\tilde\theta})$ and its covariance. This needs $O(K^2\log^{2d+2}N)$ parameters and $T \gtrsim K^2\log^{2d+7}N$ simulated datasets. Excess Dawid–Sebastiani risk controls $N\|\hat\beta - m_\pi\|^2 + \|\hat V - S_\pi\|_F^2$, and a $\chi^2$ change-of-measure moves that prior-averaged guarantee to the evaluation distribution.

Headline findings. (i) Theorem 1: the posterior moments are efficient for every query, with no EIF. (ii) Theorem 2: the trained network is within $O_\nu(\sqrt{r_N})$ of the posterior moments, with $r_N = K^3/N + K\sqrt{\log N/N} + (K^2/T)\log^{2d+7}(NT) + L_N^2/N + N\delta_\pi^2 + \epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}$. (iii) Theorem 3: if $r_N\to 0$, then $\sqrt N(\hat\beta - \beta_q(P)) \rightsquigarrow \mathcal{N}(0,V^\star_q(P))$, $\hat V \to V_q^\star(P)$, and the Wald region has asymptotically exact coverage, in probability over $(P,q)\sim\nu$, under bounded $\chi^2$ shift. (iv) Theorem 4 and Proposition F.2: at a fixed population $P_\star$ the posterior is still efficient, but guaranteeing that every approximate ERM inherits it needs $T \ge \exp(CK^2\log N)$, exponentially many parameters, and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} = O(N^{-K/2})$; and $T \le \exp(cK\log N)$ is provably insufficient for such a worst-case guarantee. Empirically, on ATE, QTE (levels 0.2 and 0.8), partially linear regression and mean survival time, the pretrained model has the lowest RMSE among the compared methods with near-nominal coverage, and the lowest MAE on IHDP.

The most interesting part

The most intellectually interesting claim is the separation in Table 1: polynomial pretraining cost ($K^2$ polylog) for efficiency "in probability over populations" versus exponential cost ($\exp(CK^2\log N)$) for efficiency at a fixed population, with a matching-in-form lower bound. That precisely names something people in amortised inference have long suspected informally: training on simulations from a prior buys you guarantees on the prior's typical set, and the classical frequentist guarantee is a different, much more expensive object. Below is a reviewer-style assessment.

Genuine strengths. - Clean conceptual decomposition. "Pretraining target = posterior moments (proper scoring rule)" plus "posterior moments are efficient under the right prior (semiparametric BvM)" plus "the network approximates the target (approximation + generalisation + $\chi^2$ transfer)". Each link is standard on its own; assembling them into an end-to-end, non-vacuous-in-form theorem for a Transformer with explicit $p$, $T$, $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}$ is new and useful. - The query-family angle is a real contribution. Prior EIF-corrected PFN work (Zhang 2026; Melnychuk et al. 2026a,b) is per-estimand; here one prior and one label type serve a family (QTE at all levels, group effects, projections), and the outputs cohere because they are all moments of one posterior. This is exactly the selling point of sieve plug-in estimation, transplanted to amortisation. - The paper is honest about the limits: it reports the fixed-$P$ cost, proves a lower bound, states that the prior must grow with $N$, and in the discussion concedes that its experimental priors are not locally flat and that the finite-sample wins are probably due to informative priors rather than the asymptotic theory. - The variance head is principled: $\hat V$ targets the efficiency bound itself, so the Wald region is calibrated conditionally on each population (for most populations), stronger than the "expected coverage over the prior" used to assess amortised posteriors (Hermans et al. 2022). The analogy to conditional versus marginal coverage in conformal prediction is apt.

Weaknesses and theorem-practice gaps.

  1. Does the trained Transformer approximate the posterior? In theory, yes, but via a construction that uses attention only as a mean-pooling operator: one head with zero query/key maps computes $N^{-1}\sum_i \hat b_K(Z_i)$, after which everything is an MLP on a $K$-dimensional sufficient statistic. The theorem is really about a DeepSets/neural-sieve estimator, and says nothing about what the deployed 20-layer, 6-head, 20M-parameter model trained with AdamW actually learns. The guarantee is for an $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}$-approximate empirical risk minimiser over a specific bounded-weight class; there is no optimisation analysis, and no experiment checks that the network output tracks the true posterior mean (e.g., on a conjugate or tractable sieve prior where $m_\pi$ can be computed by MCMC). That diagnostic would be cheap and would directly test the central mechanism.

  2. Prior misspecification is the central gap, and it cuts both ways. The theory needs a locally flat exponential-series prior of growing dimension. The experiments use rich simulators: OpenML tables, TabICLv2-style random SCMs over DAGs with GP/NN/tree mechanisms, TabPFN-style random MLPs, heterogeneity and offset knobs. Such priors are highly informative about nuisances and almost certainly violate (A3)–(A4) (the support is not a near-sieve of a $K$-dimensional exponential family with nearly flat reweighting; covariate dimension $d_X$ up to 100 is far beyond what $s > d(3/2\vee a)$ can plausibly support). Melnychuk et al. (2026a) is exactly the paper showing that informative causal priors induce $N^{-1/2}$-order bias in PFN ATE estimates. So in the regime where the experiments live, the paper's own theorem does not apply, and the competing theory predicts bias. The authors acknowledge this, but the abstract's "We prove ... The Transformer inherits this efficiency" invites readers to connect the theorem to the experiments more tightly than is justified.

  3. The fixed-DGP caveat matters more than the abstract suggests. Classical semiparametric efficiency and confidence intervals are statements at a fixed $P$. Theorem 3's guarantee is: for all but a $\nu$-small set of populations. If $\nu = \pi$, the exceptional set is small in prior mass, but there is no way to know whether a given real dataset's population is in it, and real data are not draws from the simulator. Theorem 4 shows the fixed-$P$ guarantee needs $T \ge \exp(CK^2\log N)$ and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} = O(N^{-K/2})$, which is astronomically out of reach for any $K$ growing with $N$. The lower bound (Proposition F.2) is a worst case over approximate ERMs (the "bump" construction): it shows the empirical risk cannot distinguish an efficient network from one shifted by $N^{-1/2}$ near $P_\star$, not that SGD-trained Transformers fail. So the honest reading is: the fixed-$P$ guarantee is out of reach by this proof technique, and implicit bias of training is the only hope. Also the gap between the lower bound $\exp(cK\log N)$ and upper bound $\exp(CK^2\log N)$ remains open.

  4. Curse of dimensionality hidden in "slowly growing complexity". The smoothness requirement $s > d(3/2\vee a)$ with $a>1$ means $s > 1.5d$ at least: for an ATE problem with 10 covariates you need more than 16 derivatives of the joint log density. The log factors $\log^{2d+7}N$ in $T$ and $\log^{2d+2}N$ in $p$ are similarly dimension-exponential. The authors flag this (Remark 1), but it means the theory essentially covers low-dimensional problems, while the empirical pitch is tabular foundation models with up to 100 covariates. The single-estimand alternative (double robustness: product of nuisance rates $o(N^{-1/2})$) is far less demanding; the paper trades that for the query family.

  5. Label mismatches in the implementation. QTE labels are Monte Carlo differences of empirical quantiles from $M=8192$ extra draws. Under the Dawid–Sebastiani loss, an independent mean-zero label noise $\varepsilon$ with variance $\Sigma_\varepsilon$ leaves the optimal $\beta$ unchanged but shifts the optimal $V$ to $S_\pi + n\Sigma_\varepsilon$. With $n$ up to 1600 and $M = 8192$, $n/M \approx 0.2$, so the variance head is inflated by roughly 20 percent of a unit-scale quantile variance (plus small quantile bias). That would make QTE intervals conservative, which may partly explain the near-nominal coverage. The MST label is the sample mean of the latent failure times of the $n$ units actually in the dataset (a sample-level estimand that is correlated with $D_n$), not $\beta_{\mathrm{MST}}(P) = \mathbb{E}T$; the minimiser is then the posterior mean of that sample quantity, and the learned variance targets a conditional variance that differs from the efficiency bound for $\mathbb{E}T$. These are not fatal, but they mean the implemented pretraining target differs from the theorem's target in exactly the variance dimension that drives coverage.

  6. Prior fixed in $N$ in practice. Theory needs $K = K_N \to\infty$ with the prior changing with $N$; in practice one model is trained on context lengths 800–1600 and evaluated on the same lengths. No extrapolation in $N$ is tested, and the rate claims (e.g., MST RMSE "broadly follows $N^{-1/2}$") are over a factor-of-two range of $N$, too narrow to discriminate rates.

Evaluation gaps. - In-distribution evaluation largely guarantees the RMSE win. Except for IHDP, each replication draws its population $P_r$ from the same simulator used in pretraining. The Bayes rule under the evaluation prior minimises prior-averaged MSE by definition, so "lowest RMSE" against AIPW/DML/CausalPFN is close to tautological once the network is well trained. Meanwhile CausalPFN is used with its public checkpoint, i.e. evaluated off its own prior. A fair test would train baselines' hyperparameters on the same simulator, or evaluate all methods on a held-out simulator family. - Coverage is averaged over populations, which is not what Theorem 3 adds. With one dataset per population and $R = 100$, the reported coverage is prior-marginal coverage, which any well-calibrated amortised posterior achieves on its own prior. The distinctive claim (coverage population by population) requires many datasets from each of several fixed populations; that experiment is missing. Moreover $R=100$ gives Wilson intervals of roughly plus or minus 4–5 percentage points around 95 percent, too coarse to detect modest undercoverage. - Distribution shift is tested only on IHDP, only for point accuracy (MAE), with the target defined as the in-sample average effect $\tau = N^{-1}\sum_i\{m_1(X_i)-m_0(X_i)\}$ rather than a population ATE, and with no interval coverage reported. Since coverage under shift is the paper's strongest inferential claim, this is the most important missing table. ACIC-style benchmarks with known response surfaces and many realisations would allow coverage checks. - One model per task. Section 4 says each experiment uses a task-specific instance; the cross-family claim (one network for ATE + QTE + PLR + MST) is not exercised, only QTE across levels. The amortisation-across-estimands advantage is therefore argued theoretically more than shown. - Efficiency is never measured directly. One could compare $\hat V$ to the known efficiency bound $V^\star_q(P_r)$ for simulated populations (computable when the simulator knows $P$), or compare $N\cdot\mathrm{MSE}$ to $V^\star$. That would test (3.1) rather than only RMSE ranking.

Net assessment. A strong theory paper with a crisp message about what amortised inference can and cannot guarantee, and a genuinely useful random-versus-fixed population separation. The experiments are suggestive but do not test the theorem's distinctive content (per-population coverage, efficiency in the sense of matching $V^\star$, robustness off-prior), and the deployed prior lives outside the theorem's assumptions.

Proof sketch

Formal statements (with $\pi$ satisfying (A3)–(A4), queries satisfying (A1)–(A2), evaluation law satisfying (A5) $\sup_N\chi^2(\nu\|\pi)<\infty$).

Proposition 1 (pretraining target). For each $(D_n,q)$ with finite posterior second moment and $S_\pi \succ 0$, $$\arg\min_{\beta,\,V\succ 0}\ \mathbb{E}_\pi\{\ell_n(\beta_q(P);\beta,V)\mid D_n,q\} = (m_\pi, S_\pi)(D_n,q).$$

Theorem 1 (efficiency of the target). If (A1), (A3)–(A5) hold, $K\to\infty$ and $K^{3\vee 2a} = o(N)$, then $$m_\pi = \beta_q(P) + \mathbb{P}_N\psi^\star_{P,q} + o_\nu(N^{-1/2}), \qquad S_\pi = V_q^\star(P) + o_\nu(1).$$

Theorem 2 (Transformer estimation error). If (A1)–(A5) hold, $K\to\infty$, $K^{3\vee 2a}=o(N)$, $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}\to 0$ and $K^2\log^{2d+7}N = o(T)$, then for a single-head Transformer class with $O(K^2\log^{2d+2}N)$ parameters (depth $\lesssim \log^2 N$, width $\lesssim K\log^d N$, weights $\lesssim N^C$), $$\sqrt N\|\hat\beta - m_\pi\| + \|\hat V - S_\pi\|_F = O_\nu(\sqrt{r_N}),\quad r_N = \frac{K^3}{N} + K\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{N}} + \frac{K^2}{T}\log^{2d+7}(NT) + \frac{L_N^2}{N} + N\delta_\pi^2 + \epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}.$$

Theorem 3 (efficient amortised inference). If additionally $r_N\to 0$, then $\sqrt N(\hat\beta-\beta_q(P))\mid(P,q,T) \rightsquigarrow_\nu \mathcal{N}(0,V_q^\star(P))$, $\hat V\to_\nu V_q^\star(P)$, and $P\{\beta_q(P)\in\hat C_N(D_N,q)\mid q,T\}\to_\nu 1-\alpha$.

Theorem 4 (fixed population). With $\delta_\pi = 0$ (prior on the sieve), $\nu = \delta_{P_\star}\otimes\pi_q$ with $P_\star$ in a periodic Sobolev ball $\mathcal{P}_s(\Xi,\eta)$, $K\asymp N^\kappa$, $\kappa < (3\vee 2a)^{-1}$, $s > d/(2\kappa)$: if the class has $\exp\{O(K^2\log N)\}$ parameters, $T\ge\exp(CK^2\log N)$ and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} = O(N^{-K/2})$, the same normal limit and exact coverage hold at $P_\star$. Proposition F.2: if $T\le \exp(cK\log N)$, some approximate ERM (a "bump" of $\hat f$) violates the conclusion.

Proof strategy for Theorem 1 (a semiparametric BvM for a growing exponential family, done in expectation over the simulator). 1. Work first under the pure sieve prior $\pi_K$. The coefficient posterior has potential $V_N(\theta) = N\{A_K(\theta) - \theta^\top\hat s\} + \tfrac12\theta^\top\Lambda_K^{-1}\theta$ on $\Theta_K = \{\|\theta\|_1\le B\}$, with $\hat s = \mathbb{P}_N b^{(K)}$. Lemma E.1: the Fisher information $I_K(\theta) = \mathrm{Cov}_{P_\theta}(b^{(K)})$ is uniformly well conditioned, so $\nabla^2 V_N \succeq cN I$: the posterior is strongly log-concave. 2. Lemma E.3 (posterior concentration): strong log-concavity gives a log-Sobolev inequality (Ledoux), and Herbst's argument applied to the $C\sqrt N$-Lipschitz map $\theta\mapsto\sqrt N u^\top\beta_q(P_\theta)$ (Lipschitz via (A1)) yields uniform sub-Gaussian tails of $\sqrt N(\beta_q(P_\theta) - m_\pi)$ under the posterior. This is what makes all later moment comparisons dimension-robust. 3. Lemma E.4 (mode versus mean): via the Gauss–Green formula on the convex truncation set, $cN\,\mathbb{E}_N\|\theta-\tilde\theta\|^2\le K$, and on a high-probability set of "regular" contexts (mode away from the $\ell_1$ boundary, boundary density $\le N^{-8}$) $\sqrt N\|m_\pi - g\|\lesssim K^{3/2}/\sqrt N$ and $\|S_\pi - V\|_F\lesssim K/\sqrt N$, where $(g,V) = (\beta_q(P_{\tilde\theta}),\ D_q I_K^{-1}D_q^\top$-type) is the "mode pair" (plug-in at the MAP plus a delta-method covariance). The $K^{3/2}/\sqrt N$ term is where $K^3 = o(N)$ comes from: a Laplace approximation in growing dimension, as in Ghosal (2000). 4. Proposition E.1 (expansion under $\pi_K$): expand the MAP around the true coefficient, $\tilde\theta - \theta \approx I_K(\theta)^{-1}(\hat s - \mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}b^{(K)}) - I_K^{-1}\Lambda_K^{-1}\theta/N$. The prior penalty term is negligible because $\mathbb{E}\|\Lambda_K^{-1}\theta\|^2\lesssim K^{2a+1}$ and $K^{2a} = o(N)$: this is precisely where local flatness enters, the prior pulls by less than $N^{-1/2}$ in every sieve direction. Then the Lipschitz Jacobian (A1(ii)) delta-method gives $\sqrt N(m_\pi - \beta_q(P_\theta)) = \mathbb{G}_N\psi^K_{P_\theta,q} + o_P(1)$ with $\psi^K = C_{K,q}s_{P,K}$ the projection of the EIF onto the centred sieve scores, and $S_\pi\to\mathbb{E}\{(\psi^K)^{\otimes2}\}$. This statement is in expectation over the simulator experiment: $\mathbb{E}_\pi\mathbb{E}_P R_N^K = o(1)$ for the truncated error $R_N^K = 1\wedge\{\cdots\}$. 5. Let $K\to\infty$: the projection error $e_K(\theta,q) = \|\psi^\star - \psi^K\|^2_{L_2(P_\theta)}\to 0$ by completeness of the basis and continuity of the EIF in $(P,q)$ (A1(iii)); since $V^\star - \mathbb{E}(\psi^K)^{\otimes 2} = \mathbb{E}(\psi^\star-\psi^K)^{\otimes 2}$, both the mean and covariance expansions upgrade from projected to full EIF, still on average over the prior (dominated convergence). 6. Change of prior (Lemmas E.8, E.9): any admissible $\pi_P$ is a bounded reweighting of $\pi_K$ composed with a small tilt $e^{g}$; (A3) makes $\chi^2(P^{\otimes N}\|P_\theta^{\otimes N}) = o(1)$ and (A4) makes the posterior under $\pi_P$ a density ratio $\rho$ with respect to that under $\pi_K$ that is nearly constant on the $N^{-1/2}$ scale, giving $n\|m_\pi - m_{\pi_K}\|^2 + \|S_\pi - S_{\pi_K}\|_F^2\lesssim L_N^2/N + N\delta_\pi^2$. 7. From prior to $\nu$: for any $[0,1]$-valued $\phi$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\mathbb{E}_\nu\mathbb{E}_P\phi\le\{(1+\chi^2(\nu\|\pi))\,\mathbb{E}_\pi\mathbb{E}_P\phi\}^{1/2}$ (inequality (E.2)). Apply to $\phi = R_N$ and use Markov's inequality. This one line is why everything is "in probability over populations": the whole argument controls a prior-averaged truncated error, and a bounded $\chi^2$ density ratio is the only bridge to another evaluation law.

Proof strategy for Theorem 2 (learning the target). 1. Excess risk equals moment error. Expanding the Dawid–Sebastiani score around $(m_\pi, \mathrm{clip}\,S_\pi)$ gives the conditional excess score $h_f = \tfrac n2(u-m_\pi)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(u-m_\pi) + \tfrac12\{F_{S_\pi}(\Sigma^{-1}) - F_{S_\pi}(A^\ast)\}\ge 0$, with $F_C(A) = -\log\det A + \mathrm{tr}(AC)$; Lemma F.12 shows $\mathbb{E}\{1\wedge e(\hat f, f_\pi)\}\lesssim \mathbb{E}(1\wedge h_{\hat f})$, where $e(f,f') = N\|f^\beta - f'^\beta\|^2 + \|f^V - f'^V\|_F^2$. This is the "risk minimiser = posterior moments, and excess risk bounds distance to them" step the question anticipated. 2. Standard decomposition: truncated excess risk $\le$ approximation $+$ optimisation $+$ stochastic error, via the basic inequality from (2.2). 3. Approximation (Lemma F.1): explicit Transformer that (a) computes GELU approximations of the trigonometric features and averages them in one masked attention head (only the sufficient statistic $\hat s$ is needed under $\pi_K$); (b) computes $A_K(\theta)$ and its gradient by quadrature/Chebyshev approximations; (c) unrolls projected gradient steps (in the spirit of Bai et al. 2023) to solve the strongly convex MAP problem to accuracy $N^{-C}$; (d) evaluates $\beta_q(P_{\tilde\theta})$ and the covariance through an integral representation of the query (Definition F.1, which is why (A1(iv)) asks queries to be "computable") plus projected Richardson iterations for the matrix inverse. It approximates the mode pair uniformly over contexts; the residual mode-versus-mean gap gives $K^3/N + K\sqrt{\log N/N}$ (the latter from the $\ell_1$ boundary) plus the prior-mismatch $L_N^2/N + N\delta_\pi^2$. 4. Stochastic error: metric entropy of the loss class scales like $pL^2\log(\cdot)$ with $p\asymp K^2\,\mathrm{polylog}$; a Bernstein-type curvature condition for the truncated excess loss gives fast rates via an exponential inequality (van Erven et al. 2015; Grünwald and Mehta 2020), producing $K^2\log^{2d+7}(NT)/T$ rather than a square root. 5. Transfer to $\nu$: on an event of probability $1-\delta$ over $T$, $\mathbb{E}_\pi\{1\wedge e(\hat f, f_\pi^\circ)\}\lesssim\delta^{-1}\tilde r_N$; Lemma E.7 (a $\chi^2$ change of measure for $[0,1]$-valued functions) transfers the exceedance probability to the law of $(D_N,q)$ under $\nu$.

Theorem 3 follows by the triangle inequality $e(\hat f, f_\star)\le 2e(\hat f, f_\pi) + 2e(f_\pi, f_\star)$ with $f_\star = (\beta_q(P)+\mathbb{P}_N\psi^\star, V^\star)$, a CLT for $N^{-1/2}\sum_i V^{\star-1/2}\psi^\star(Z_i)$ controlled in Kolmogorov and bounded-Lipschitz distance on average over $\nu$ (handled along sequences of populations since the prior changes with $N$), and Slutsky for the Wald statistic.

Theorem 4 replaces the bounded $\chi^2$ factor by an overlap factor $\Gamma_N(\nu)\le e/\pi_P(B_N)$, where $B_N = \{P: \chi^2(P_\star\|P)\le N^{-1}\}$ is the set of simulated populations indistinguishable from $P_\star$ at sample size $N$. Lemma F.15 lower-bounds its prior mass by $\exp\{-\tfrac K2\log N - O(K\log K)\}$, a small-ball probability in $K$ dimensions; together with a uniformly accurate (to $\varepsilon$) network of size $(Cn_{\max}K/\varepsilon)^{CK}$ (Lemma F.16), this yields the exponential budget. The lower bound uses a "bump" network that shifts the estimate by $N^{-1/2}e_1$ only on contexts whose sieve averages are within $2\zeta$ of those of $P_\star$: if no pretraining dataset falls near $P_\star$ (likely when $T\le\exp(cK\log N)$ by a union bound on small balls and exponential-family large deviations), the bump has essentially the same empirical risk but is inefficient at $P_\star$.

Key lemma/trick, in one sentence: strong log-concavity of the sieve-coefficient posterior (giving log-Sobolev concentration and a Gauss–Green mode-versus-mean bound) plus prior standard deviations exceeding $N^{-1/2}$ in every sieve direction makes the posterior mean a first-order sieve plug-in for every functional at once; then the Dawid–Sebastiani excess risk identity plus a $\chi^2$ Cauchy–Schwarz transfer move this prior-averaged statement to the trained network and to the evaluation law, which is exactly why the guarantee is "in probability over populations" and why a point mass costs $1/\pi_P(B_N) = \exp(\Theta(K\log N))$.

Broader context

Background. The paper sits at the intersection of three lines: (1) semiparametric BvM theory, specifically the "sieve prior of growing dimension" branch (Ghosal 2000; Rivoirard and Rousseau 2012; Castillo and Rousseau 2015), whose message is that a sufficiently non-committal prior on a growing parametric model yields efficient posteriors for all smooth functionals without targeting; (2) sieve plug-in efficiency (Shen 1997; Newey 1994; Chen 2007), of which this posterior mean is the Bayesian, amortised twin; (3) statistical theory of ICL, both Bayesian (pretraining finds the Bayes rule) and algorithmic (Transformers can implement optimisation in context). The novelty is in assembling these with explicit Transformer size and pretraining sample complexity, and in proving the random-versus-fixed population gap.

Closely related directions. - EIF-corrected PFNs (Zhang 2026, "Learning to fluctuate"; Melnychuk et al. 2026a,b). These target one estimand with debiased labels or a least-favourable prior perturbation; they need weaker smoothness (product-rate conditions) but lose the query family. A natural synthesis: use the present label-only objective for the family, and a cheap per-query one-step correction only where the family's sieve is too coarse. - In-context nonparametric regression with distribution shift (Ma, Wang and Samworth 2026; Ching et al. 2026): same $\chi^2$-ball transfer, but for prediction rather than inference; and prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023), where a pretrained model is used inside a semiparametric estimator rather than as the estimator.

Plausible follow-up ideas. 1. Structured, estimand-aware sieves. Replace the sieve on the full joint log density (which forces $s > 1.5d$) by a prior that is locally flat only along a low-dimensional or additive structure (for causal problems: separate sieves for the propensity and outcome regressions with a doubly robust-style product requirement). The conjecture would be that the posterior mean is efficient when the product of propensity and outcome sieve errors is $o(N^{-1/2})$, restoring a double-robustness analogue within the label-only framework. 2. Test the mechanism directly. On a tractable sieve prior, compute $m_\pi, S_\pi$ by MCMC and measure how close the trained Transformer is, across $T$ and $p$; then evaluate many datasets from a handful of fixed $P$ (inside and outside the prior support) to measure per-population coverage and to probe whether SGD's implicit bias escapes the exponential worst case of Proposition F.2. 3. A posterior-predictive check for the "exceptional set". Since the guarantee fails on a $\nu$-small set, a diagnostic that flags datasets far from the pretraining distribution (e.g., the sieve-average distance $d_\star(D_n)$ used in the lower bound, or a learned density of the summary statistic) would turn the in-probability guarantee into something usable per dataset.

Connection to IR (genuine but modest). The most honest link is to IR evaluation and counterfactual learning to rank, where the estimands are semiparametric and currently handled with estimand-specific doubly robust machinery: off-policy estimation of ranking-policy value from click logs under position bias (doubly robust click-model estimators), and LLM-judge-assisted evaluation with incomplete relevance labels (prediction-powered inference style estimators of nDCG or recall, statAP/infAP-style sampling estimators). These are exactly "a family of estimands" (metric at each cutoff $k$, each policy, each query subset) computed repeatedly on new logs, which is the amortisation regime this paper targets. A pretrained estimator that ingests a log plus a query (metric, cutoff) and returns a point estimate and an efficiency-bound variance would be a concrete project, with this paper giving the theoretical template and its caveats (it would be reliable on logs that look like the simulator's typical set, not uniformly). For vector search, estimating ANN recall from sampled queries is a plain mean and gains nothing from this machinery. For generative retrieval, the link is only through ICL-as-Bayesian-inference theory: the proof technique here (sufficient-statistic pooling by attention, unrolled convex optimisation in feed-forward layers, $\chi^2$-ball transfer from pretraining to deployment) is a reusable template for proving what a pretrained retriever can do in context, and the random-versus-fixed population separation is a useful warning for any "trained on synthetic corpora" guarantee.

title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-24

Self-similar Organization of Information in Language — Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Kamesh Krishnamurthy (2026) — arXiv:2611.26935

Setting and problem

Object of study. A corpus of long, coherent documents is treated as samples from a stochastic source emitting a symbol sequence $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_T$ (conceptually bytes; operationally tokens of an LLM tokenizer, with all lengths converted back to UTF-8 bytes so that different tokenizers can be compared). Everything in the paper is built from one primitive, the conditional entropy (expected code length) of a target symbol given a context of length $C$:

$$h(t, C) = H(X_t \mid X_{t-C}, \dots, X_{t-1}),$$

which is non-increasing in $C$ and bounded below, so it converges to the entropy rate $h_\infty = \lim_{C\to\infty} h(t,C)$. Under stationarity $h(t,C) = h(C)$.

Two derived families of measures:

  • Predictive information between adjacent windows. With past $P_C = (X_{t-C+1},\dots,X_t)$ and future $F_C = (X_{t+1},\dots,X_{t+C})$, $$I_{\mathrm{pred}}(t,C) = I(P_C; F_C) = H(F_C) - H(F_C \mid P_C) = \sum_{k=1}^{C} \big[ h(t+k, k-1) - h(t+k, C+k-1) \big],$$ which for a stationary source equals $2H(X_1,\dots,X_C) - H(X_1,\dots,X_{2C})$. It does not depend on $h_\infty$. More generally they use unequal windows $I(C_p, C_f) := I(P_{C_p}; F_{C_f})$.
  • Band gains, a "differential" measure for a single target: $B(t, C_1, C_2) = h(t, C_1) - h(t, C_2)$ for $C_1 < C_2$, i.e. how much extra context from distance $C_1$ to $C_2$ reduces the code length. They are additive: $B(C_1,C_2) + B(C_2,C_3) = B(C_1,C_3)$. The operational version is the per-octave gain $\Delta(C \to 2C) := B(C, 2C)$.

How things are estimated. The true $h$ is replaced by the cross-entropy of an open-weight base LLM (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B; the Qwen models are hybrid linear/full attention). At an anchor byte $t$ (moved to the nearest sentence start that is also a token boundary under both tokenizers), the model is given exactly $C$ bytes of preceding text as a fresh input, and the negative log-likelihood of the next $m = 32$ tokens is recorded: $$h_m(t, C) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} -\log_2 p(x_{t+j} \mid x_{t-C}, \dots, x_{t+j-1}),$$ normalized to bits per byte or per token. Then $\Delta_m(t, C\to 2C) = \tfrac{1}{m}\big(h_m(t,C) - h_m(t,2C)\big)$, and the predictive information proxy is the paired difference $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) = h(X_{t:t+C} \mid \emptyset) - h(X_{t:t+C} \mid X_{t-C:t})$, i.e. the C-byte future scored once with only a BOS token and once with the C-byte past. Anchors are at $0.25P$, $0.5P$, $0.75P$ of each document of length $P$ (plus an end-of-document anchor for code length and band gain). Corpora: 500 digitized 19th to early-20th-century books (Institutional Books 1.0, Harvard) and 500 long OCRed scientific PDFs (olmOCR documents from the Dolma 3 Longmino pool), each truncated to 131,008 tokens (roughly 300 to 670 KiB), plus two "formal" control corpora: 228 Python/Rust repositories and 56 Lean projects, each serialized into one document in import order.

The question. How is the predictive information about upcoming text distributed over the history? Concretely: as a function of distance $C$, how much does each further octave of context contribute, and is the form of that contribution the same at every length scale, i.e. is there a scale-free (self-similar) organization of predictive information, rather than merely "some long-range dependence exists"?

What was known.

  • Shannon (1951) measured $h(C)$ with human guessers out to about 100 letters and posited $h_\infty \approx 0.6$ to $1$ bit per letter.
  • Hilberg (1990) reread Shannon's data as $H(X_1,\dots,X_T) \propto \sqrt{T}$, which implies $h(T) \sim T^{-1/2}$ and $h_\infty = 0$.
  • Dębowski (2011, 2015) restated Hilberg's thesis free of $h_\infty$ as power-law growth of mutual information between adjacent blocks, $I(P_C;F_C) \sim C^{\beta}$ with $0 < \beta < 1$ (the "relaxed Hilberg conjecture"), and connected it to Zipf's and Heaps' laws; LZ-compression estimates gave $\beta \approx 0.94$ but required assuming $h_\infty = 0$.
  • Bialek, Nemenman and Tishby showed that $I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) \sim \log C$ characterizes finitely-parameterized sources, while $I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) \sim C^\beta$ means no finite-parameter model (e.g. a finite-order Markov chain) suffices.
  • Neural estimators: Takahashi and Tanaka-Ishii (2018) used character RNNs with contexts of 50 to 85 characters; Scheibner, Smith and Bialek (2025) used LLMs to show code length keeps falling to about $10^4$ characters but did not extract exponents; Chen et al. (L2M, NeurIPS 2025) estimated adjacent-block mutual information with LLMs, finding $\beta \approx 0.57$ to $0.76$ over a few thousand characters, and used it to argue that a model's state size must grow with context.

The gap. Prior work establishes that long-range dependencies exist and that some integrated quantity grows as a power law, over short ranges and with estimator-dependent exponents. It does not ask how the dependencies are organized across scales: whether the per-scale contributions have a common form, and whether the different information measures are mutually consistent with one scale-free description.

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag.

  • LLM cross-entropy as an entropy estimator. A model's cross-entropy upper-bounds the true conditional entropy at every $C$, but differences of upper bounds (band gains, $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}$) are neither upper nor lower bounds on the true differences. The authors say explicitly that $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}$ is a proxy, "not itself guaranteed to equal or bound" the true mutual information.
  • Stationarity. It is assumed for the theory and checked only by comparing curves at three relative anchor positions.
  • Corpus-level, not document-level statements. All curves are means over about 500 documents and over anchors, and the paper says the claims concern the source generating the corpus, not any individual document.
  • Finite range. Scaling is probed over roughly $64$ bytes to $10^5$ bytes (about three decades). Statements about "all scales" are extrapolations from that window.
  • Byte units with token-level scoring. The scored block is a fixed 32 tokens, whose byte length varies, and bytes per token vary between 2.4 and 5.5 across documents.
  • Fresh-input scoring. Each context length is a separate forward pass beginning at the context start, so positional effects (RoPE scaling, long-context extrapolation) enter the estimate differently at each $C$.

With this in hand the main claim can be stated: across three decades of context length, LLM-estimated $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C)$ grows as $C^{\beta}$, $\Delta(C \to 2C)$ decays as $C^{-\eta}$, $\beta \approx 1 - \eta$, and $I(C_p, C_f)$ collapses under joint dilation as $I(\lambda C_p, \lambda C_f) = \lambda^{\beta} I(C_p, C_f)$. All of this is predicted by a single scale-invariance axiom on band gains.

Main idea

The approach is to turn "self-similar organization" into a falsifiable axiom on band gains and derive what it forces. The axiom ("affine self-similarity") is $$B(\lambda C_1, \lambda C_2) = f(\lambda)\, B(C_1, C_2) \quad \text{for all } \lambda > 0:$$ dilating all distances by $\lambda$ rescales every band's contribution by a common factor. Together with additivity of band gains, this forces $f(\lambda) = \lambda^{-\eta}$ and $$B(C_1, C_2) = K\big(C_1^{-\eta} - C_2^{-\eta}\big) \ (\eta > 0), \qquad B(C_1,C_2) = A \log(C_2/C_1) \ (\eta = 0).$$ Consequences ("signatures"): $\Delta(C\to 2C) = (1 - 2^{-\eta}) K C^{-\eta}$; $I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) \simeq \frac{2-2^{\beta}}{\beta} K C^{\beta}$ with $\beta = 1-\eta$; and a scaling collapse $I(C_p, C_f) = C_p^{\beta}\, \Phi(C_f / C_p)$, equivalently $I(\lambda C_p, \lambda C_f) = \lambda^{\beta} I(C_p, C_f)$.

Headline findings:

  1. Code length (bits per byte of a 32-token block) falls monotonically over about twelve octaves, from about $10^2$ to $10^5$ bytes, with no plateau. Model size shifts the level but not the shape, and the curves barely depend on anchor position (approximate stationarity).
  2. $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C)$ is a single power law over three decades with $\beta \approx 0.60$ to $0.66$ (books) and $0.56$ to $0.63$ (sci-PDF). This is consistent with the relaxed Hilberg conjecture but above Hilberg's $1/2$ and well below the $\approx 0.94$ from LZ compression.
  3. $\Delta(C\to 2C)$ decays as a power law with $\eta \approx 0.27$ to $0.36$ (books) and $0.31$ to $0.38$ (sci-PDF). Comparing $\eta_\Delta$ to $1-\beta$ gives a consistent gap of about $-0.06$ in all eight model and corpus cells.
  4. Collapse tests: for $C_p \in \{8,16,32,64\}$ KiB and 21 values of $C_f \in [C_p/8, 4C_p]$, $I(C_p,C_f)/(a C_p^{\beta})$ plotted against $C_f/C_p$ collapses onto one curve, and pairs $(I(C_p,C_f), I(\lambda C_p, \lambda C_f))$ for $\lambda \in \{2,4,8\}$ fall on lines of slope $\lambda^{\beta}$.
  5. Controls: code and Lean do not show a single power law. Gains are flat out to about 1 KiB for code and peak at a few hundred bytes for Lean. Permuting chunks of the past (24, 240 or 2400 tokens, leaving the chunk adjacent to the anchor intact) degrades the growth of $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}$, strongly for small chunks and mildly for large ones.
  6. Calibration: a Donsker–Varadhan-type normalized score $\hat B_{\mathrm{cond}}(C)$, computed with Qwen3.5-35B at $C = 1, 16, 64$ KiB, lands close to the raw $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}$ (about 100, 600 and 1,280 bits per window on books). The model's predictive entropy tracks its realized NLL to within 0 to 4 percent at all $C$.

The interpretation offered is that whatever generates text produces dependencies with the same statistical form at word, sentence and argument scales, which rules out finite-parameter sources. It also gives a data-side reason for the observation that LLM loss keeps falling, as a power law, with training sequence length.

The most interesting part

The cleverest move is a choice of observable. Earlier work regressed either $h(C)$, which is contaminated by the unknown $h_\infty$, or an integrated block mutual information, which smears all scales together. The paper instead isolates the band gain, a paired difference of code lengths at a fixed target. This removes $h_\infty$ and also removes the very large between-document and between-block variance in absolute code length, which the authors note is "many times the context effect on any one block". The pairing is exact because the same 32 scored tokens appear at every $C$. Writing self-similarity as a dilation axiom on this additive object, rather than as "the curve looks straight on log-log axes", makes the cross-measure prediction $\beta = 1 - \eta$ and the two-window collapse fall out as testable corollaries. The code and Lean controls are also valuable: the same LLM estimators do not produce clean power laws on formal text, which is the best evidence in the paper that the power law is not simply manufactured by the estimator.

That said, an honest reviewer would push on several points.

  1. The theory is less new than it sounds. Under stationarity, every measure in the paper is a functional of one function, $h(C)$. The band gain is a difference of $h$; $I(C_p, C_f) = \sum_{k=1}^{C_f} [h(k-1) - h(C_p + k - 1)]$ by the chain rule. The axiom's unique solution $B(C_1,C_2) = K(C_1^{-\eta} - C_2^{-\eta})$ is exactly the statement $h(C) = h_\infty + K C^{-\eta}$, which is the Hilberg-type extrapolation ansatz already used by Takahira, Tanaka-Ishii and Dębowski (2016) and Takahashi and Tanaka-Ishii (2018). The relation $\beta = 1 - \eta$ between subextensive entropy growth and the decay of $h(C) - h_\infty$ is standard from Bialek, Nemenman and Tishby. So affine self-similarity in the paper's sense is equivalent to "the conditional entropy decays to a constant as a pure power law". The functional-equation derivation is a neat justification for that ansatz from a scale-invariance principle, but it adds no constraint beyond it.

  2. The "stronger" collapse test is largely implied by the weaker one. If $h(C) - h_\infty = K C^{-\eta}$ holds over the measured range, then in the continuum limit $$I(C_p, C_f) \approx \frac{K}{\beta}\big[C_p^{\beta} + C_f^{\beta} - (C_p + C_f)^{\beta}\big],$$ which is automatically homogeneous of degree $\beta$, so the collapse and the slope-$\lambda^{\beta}$ lines are guaranteed. In practice the collapse does add an internal-consistency check of the estimation pipeline across different window geometries. But calling it "considerably stronger evidence for self-similar structure" overstates its logical independence. It also covers less than a decade of dilation ($C_p$ from 8 to 64 KiB, $\lambda \le 8$), uses a per-model fitted amplitude $a$, and plugs in the fitted $\beta$, so several degrees of freedom are absorbed before the "test".

  3. "Self-similar" is a strong word for a one-point, corpus-averaged statistic. A self-similar process would normally mean invariance of finite-dimensional distributions under coarse-graining. What is shown is scale-free behaviour of the mean code-length reduction for a 32-token block, averaged over about 500 documents and several anchors. A classic way to obtain an averaged power law is a mixture of sources with different characteristic lengths, for example a superposition of documents whose correlations decay exponentially with a broad spread of correlation lengths. The authors explicitly restrict their claims to the corpus-level source, which is honest. But the discussion then reads hierarchical, scale-similar generative mechanisms into the result, and that inference is not supported over the mixture alternative. Per-document or per-genre exponent distributions would help decide between them.

  4. The estimator problem is acknowledged but not resolved. LLM cross-entropy upper-bounds $h(C)$ at every $C$, but the slack $\epsilon(C) = h_{\mathrm{model}}(C) - h(C)$ is not constant in $C$. Long contexts are rare in pretraining, long-context ability comes from late-stage extension (Llama-3.1 uses position-interpolated RoPE), and attention can dilute over long inputs. Any $C$-dependence of $\epsilon$ feeds directly into $\Delta$ and $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}$ and hence into $\eta$ and $\beta$. A model that under-uses distant context underestimates far-band gains, which raises $\eta$ and lowers $\beta$. Two details in the paper's own numbers are telling:

  5. Exponents depend on the estimator: within a family, the larger model has the smaller $\beta$ (books: Llama 8B 0.65 vs 70B 0.60; Qwen 9B 0.66 vs 35B 0.63) and the larger $\eta$. If better estimators systematically move the exponents, then "the" exponent of language has not been pinned down. One would want a demonstrated trend toward convergence with estimator quality.

  6. The gap $\eta_\Delta - (1-\beta) \approx -0.06$ has the same sign and size in all eight cells. That is systematic, not noise. It signals either curvature in $h(C)$ (a deviation from the pure power law that the theory requires) or a differential bias between the block-level $\Delta$ (fixed 32 tokens, varying context) and the window-level $\hat I_{\mathrm{pred}}$ (whose future window extends with $C$ and is scored from scratch). The paper calls this "reasonable agreement". No uncertainty on the exponents is reported, only bootstrap bands on means, so it is impossible to judge whether 0.06 is within error.

  7. The calibration appendix is weaker than its framing. The normalized score $s_C = f_C - \log_2 Z_C(y)$ with $f_C = \log_2\big((1 + 2^{g_C})/2\big)$ is a valid population lower bound on the true $I^{\star}_{\mathrm{pred}}$ by the KL argument. But:

  8. The normalizer $Z_C(y)$ is estimated from 288 donor pasts drawn from other documents. By Jensen, $\mathbb{E}\log \hat Z \le \log Z$, so a finite-donor estimate biases $\hat B_{\mathrm{cond}}$ upward, and McAllester and Stratos (cited by the authors) show that no distribution-free high-confidence lower bound can certify much more than about $\log N$ bits. The paper concedes that the values are "not confidence-certified lower bounds", but values of about 1,000 bits from 288 donors are far beyond anything certifiable.
  9. For donors from unrelated documents, $g_C \approx 0$, so $f_C \approx 0$ and $Z_C \approx 1$. The bound then reduces almost mechanically to the mean of $f_C$, which is roughly the raw gain. Agreement between the two is therefore close to built in. What it does usefully show is that the gain is specific to the genuine past: random pasts do not help, which rules out a generic "any long input lowers loss" artifact.
  10. A lower bound constrains the level from below, not the exponent. If the true $I^{\star}_{\mathrm{pred}}$ grows faster at long range than the model can exploit, the bound cannot detect it.

The entropy-versus-NLL comparison (gap of 0 to 4 percent) is, as the authors say, descriptive only.

  1. The other controls are suggestive but not specific to self-similarity. Chunk permutation shows that order beyond the chunk scale carries information, which any long-range model would predict. It does not test scale invariance, and as the authors note it pushes the estimator off-distribution. The code and Lean controls are more interesting, but their serialization in import order is itself an arbitrary structure, so their non-power-law curves may reflect the serialization as much as the "formal language" nature of the content.

  2. Smaller issues.

  3. The fit range starts at 64 bytes, deep inside the word and phrase regime, so the single power law spans regimes plausibly governed by different mechanisms. That is the paper's point, but it also means local curvature can be masked by an unweighted least-squares fit over averages.
  4. Book data are OCRed and 19th century, and sci-PDF data are olmOCR output. OCR noise and boilerplate (references, appendices, noted for the end-of-document anchor) affect absolute levels.
  5. The exact case $\eta = 0$ ($B = A\log(C_2/C_1)$) cannot hold over all scales, because it forces $h(C) \to -\infty$. Self-similarity must be cut off somewhere, and the paper never discusses where the cutoffs would lie.

Net assessment: the measurement is careful (exact pairing, byte alignment across tokenizers, two model families at two scales, coverage-aware fitting), and the three-decade, estimator-robust power law with $\beta \approx 0.6$ is the most solid result. It is the cleanest modern evidence for a relaxed Hilberg law at book length. The theoretical framing is elegant but repackages a known ansatz. The collapse tests are mostly corollaries of the power law rather than independent evidence. The step from "the corpus-mean conditional entropy decays as a power law" to "the generative process is self-similar" is the weakest link.

Proof sketch

Claim. Assume stationarity, so that $B(C_1, C_2) = h(C_1) - h(C_2)$, and assume:

  • (i) additivity, $B(C_1,C_2) + B(C_2,C_3) = B(C_1,C_3)$ for $C_1<C_2<C_3$ (automatic from the definition);
  • (ii) affine self-similarity, $B(\lambda C_1, \lambda C_2) = f(\lambda) B(C_1, C_2)$ for all $\lambda > 0$, with $f$ positive and continuous at $1$.

Then $f(\lambda) = \lambda^{-\eta}$ for some $\eta \ge 0$, and $$B(C_1, C_2) = K\big(C_1^{-\eta} - C_2^{-\eta}\big)\ (\eta>0), \qquad B(C_1,C_2) = A\log\frac{C_2}{C_1}\ (\eta = 0).$$ Consequently $\Delta(C\to2C) = (1-2^{-\eta})KC^{-\eta}$, $I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) = \frac{2-2^{\beta}}{\beta}KC^{\beta} + O(1)$ with $\beta = 1-\eta$, and $I(\lambda C_p,\lambda C_f) = \lambda^{\beta} I(C_p, C_f)$.

Step 1 (scale factor). Dilating by $\mu$ and then by $\lambda$ equals dilating by $\mu\lambda$, so $f(\mu\lambda) = f(\mu)f(\lambda)$. A positive solution of the multiplicative Cauchy equation that is continuous at 1 is a power, $f(\lambda) = \lambda^{-\eta}$.

Step 2 (reduce to one variable). Take $\lambda = 1/C_1$: $B(C_1, C_2) = C_1^{-\eta}\,\Phi(C_2/C_1)$ with $\Phi(r) := B(1, r)$.

Step 3 (the key trick: additivity plus symmetry). Put $C_2 = rC_1$ and $C_3 = rsC_1$ into additivity: $$\Phi(rs) = \Phi(r) + r^{-\eta}\Phi(s).$$ The left side is symmetric in $(r,s)$, so swapping gives $\Phi(r) + r^{-\eta}\Phi(s) = \Phi(s) + s^{-\eta}\Phi(r)$, i.e. $\Phi(r)(1 - s^{-\eta}) = \Phi(s)(1-r^{-\eta})$. Hence $\Phi(r) = K(1 - r^{-\eta})$ for a constant $K$, and $B(C_1,C_2) = K(C_1^{-\eta} - C_2^{-\eta})$. For $\eta = 0$ the equation becomes $\Phi(rs) = \Phi(r) + \Phi(s)$, whose continuous solutions are $A\log r$. The paper presents this step more tersely ("substituting into additivity fixes the form completely"); the symmetry argument is the clean way to see it. Equivalently, $h(C) = h_\infty + KC^{-\eta}$, so the axiom amounts to the Hilberg-type ansatz.

Step 4 (integrate to predictive information). From the chain-rule representation, $I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) = \sum_{u=0}^{C-1} B(u, u+C)$. Replace the sum by an integral (the $u \approx 0$ terms, where the power law needs a short-distance cutoff, contribute $O(1)$): $$I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) \approx K\int_0^{C}\big[u^{-\eta} - (u+C)^{-\eta}\big]du = \frac{K}{\beta}\big(2C^{\beta} - (2C)^{\beta}\big) = \frac{2-2^{\beta}}{\beta}KC^{\beta},$$ with $\beta = 1-\eta$. Substituting $\Delta(C\to 2C) = (1-2^{-\eta})KC^{-\eta}$ gives $I_{\mathrm{pred}}(C) \simeq \frac{2C}{\beta}\Delta(C\to2C)$. As $\eta\to1$, $I_{\mathrm{pred}} \sim K\log C$ (Bialek's finite-parameter regime); as $\eta\to0$, $I_{\mathrm{pred}}$ becomes linear in $C$.

Step 5 (collapse). For unequal windows the same integral gives $I(C_p, C_f) \approx \frac{K}{\beta}\big[C_p^{\beta} + C_f^{\beta} - (C_p+C_f)^{\beta}\big]$. This is homogeneous of degree $\beta$, so $I(C_p,C_f) = C_p^{\beta}\Phi_I(C_f/C_p)$ with $\Phi_I(x) = \frac{K}{\beta}\big[1 + x^{\beta} - (1+x)^{\beta}\big]$. As the critique notes, the collapse is therefore a corollary of Step 3, not an independent prediction. One more derived fact, not stated in the paper but useful: as $C_f\to\infty$, $I(C_p, C_f) \to \frac{K}{\beta}C_p^{\beta}$. The information a prefix of length $C_p$ carries about the entire rest of an arbitrarily long document saturates at a value proportional to $C_p^{\beta}$.

Broader context

Background. Predictive information (Bialek, Nemenman and Tishby, "Predictability, complexity and learning", 2001) is the subextensive part of block entropy. Its growth rate classifies sources: bounded for finite-state processes, logarithmic for finitely parameterized ones, power-law for sources with an unbounded number of effective parameters. Language has been suspected to be in the last class since Hilberg. Dębowski's work makes this concrete: his "Santa Fe" processes are stationary sources in which an infinite pool of "facts" is referenced with Zipfian frequencies, yielding Hilberg-type $I_{\mathrm{pred}} \sim C^{\beta}$ and linking it to Heaps' law for vocabulary growth. Independently, Lin and Tegmark ("Critical behavior in physics and probabilistic formal languages", 2017) showed that mutual information between symbols at distance $d$ decays exponentially for Markov sources but as a power law for hierarchical, grammar-like sources, and measured power-law decay in English, music and DNA. The present paper is the long-context, LLM-estimated version of these programmes, with a cleaner observable.

Closely related directions.

  • Data structure and LLM scaling with context. Cagnetta and Wyart and coauthors ("Towards a theory of how the structure of language is acquired by deep neural networks", 2024, and the Random Hierarchy Model papers) argue that the decay of correlations with distance sets how far back a model can exploit context given $N$ training tokens, and so produces learning-curve exponents. Combined with the present measurement of $\eta \approx 0.3$, that framework could predict how the useful context horizon grows with data. On the systems side, long-context LLM reports (e.g. Xiong et al., "Effective Long-Context Scaling of Foundation Models", 2023) find that validation loss falls as a power law in context length. The present paper gives a data-side reading of that observation, but it measures with the same kind of models, so the argument is partly circular until the estimator bias is characterized.
  • Memory requirements. Chen et al. (L2M, 2025), cited here, use the same power-law growth to argue that a model's latent state must grow at least as fast as $I(P_C;F_C) \sim C^{\beta}$. Read together, the papers say fixed-size recurrent states are information-theoretically insufficient for book-length modelling. The Qwen3.5 hybrid (mostly linear attention with a recurrent state) is an interesting estimator in that light, and seeing it match full-attention Llama would be worth probing more directly.

A plausible follow-up. Calibrate the estimator against ground truth. Train LLMs of the same architecture on synthetic sources with known, tunable $\eta$, for example Dębowski's Santa Fe process, PCFGs or Random-Hierarchy-Model data with controlled depth, or mixtures of exponentially correlated sources with a broad spread of correlation lengths. Then run the identical pipeline. This would (a) quantify the $C$-dependent slack $\epsilon(C)$ and correct the exponents, (b) test whether the collapse and $\beta = 1-\eta$ diagnostics can tell a truly hierarchical source from a mixture of scales, which is the main interpretive gap, and (c) explain the systematic 0.06 offset. A cheaper companion analysis is per-document exponent histograms: a narrow distribution would favour intrinsic self-similarity, a broad one would favour heterogeneity.

Connection to theoretical IR, generative retrieval and vector search. A few links are genuine, if hedged.

  • Chunking for retrieval-augmented contexts. The chunk-permutation experiment directly asks how much predictive information survives when the past is presented as an unordered set of chunks, which is exactly what a retriever hands an LLM. The finding that order loss hurts a lot at 24-token chunks and little at 2,400-token chunks is a corpus-level, model-measured argument for coarse chunks (or for preserving within-chunk order over long spans) when the downstream use is generation over long documents. A natural IR experiment follows: replace the contiguous far context with the top-$k$ chunks retrieved from the same document under a matched byte budget, and plot a "retrieval band gain" against the contiguous band gain. If the far-range information is sparse, retrieval should beat the $C^{-\eta}$ curve; if it is diffuse, as the smooth power law suggests, retrieval cannot do much better than recency. This would turn the paper's measurement into a principled bound on what long-context RAG can gain.
  • Prefix and fixed-size document representations. From the collapse form, the information a prefix of length $C_p$ carries about the rest of an arbitrarily long document saturates at about $\frac{K}{\beta}C_p^{\beta}$. The total adjacent-half dependence of an $N$-length document scales as $(N/2)^{\beta}$. As a back-of-envelope ratio, a FirstP-style 512-token representation of a 100k-token document sees roughly $(1024/10^5)^{0.6} \approx 6$ percent of that dependence. Predictive information is not relevance information, so this is only suggestive. But it echoes the empirical need for MaxP or passage-level indexing, and generative-retrieval docids derived from document prefixes may be expected to discriminate poorly among long documents that share openings.
  • Capacity of single-vector embeddings. If the dependence structure within a document grows as $C^{\beta}$ bits, a fixed-dimensional single vector cannot encode it as documents lengthen, whereas multi-vector (late-interaction) or chunk-level indices scale with length. This aligns with recent work on the theoretical limits of embedding-based retrieval (e.g. Weller et al., 2025, on sign-rank bounds for top-$k$ retrievable sets), though it is a different kind of limit and should not be over-identified with it.

Short of these, the paper is mostly relevant to IR as a measured prior on how useful information is spread through long documents: smoothly, with no characteristic scale, and with diminishing returns per doubling. With $\eta \approx 0.3$, halving the excess code length $h(C)-h_\infty$ requires roughly a $2^{1/0.3} \approx 10\times$ longer contiguous context.

title: Generalization Error of the Tilted Empirical Risk
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-23

Generalization Error of the Tilted Empirical Risk — Gholamali Aminian, Amir R. Asadi, Tian Li, Ahmad Beirami, Gesine Reinert, Samuel N. Cohen (2024) — arXiv:2409.19431

Setting and problem

Data $S=\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ with $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$ i.i.d. from $\mu$, a hypothesis class $\mathcal H$, and a nonnegative loss $\ell:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}$. The usual objects are the population risk $R(h,\mu)=\mathbb E_{\mu}[\ell(h,Z)]$ and the empirical risk $\widehat R(h,S)=\frac1n\sum_i \ell(h,Z_i)$. Li et al. (TERM, ICLR 2021 / JMLR 2023) replace the empirical risk with the tilted empirical risk

$$\widehat R_\gamma(h,S)=\frac1\gamma\log\Big(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e^{\gamma\,\ell(h,Z_i)}\Big).$$

This is increasing in $\gamma$. It tends to $\widehat R$ as $\gamma\to0$, to $\max_i\ell$ as $\gamma\to+\infty$ and to $\min_i\ell$ as $\gamma\to-\infty$. Its gradient is $\sum_i w_i\nabla\ell(h,Z_i)$ with softmax weights $w_i\propto e^{\gamma\ell(h,Z_i)}$. A positive tilt therefore up-weights hard examples (fairness, class imbalance). A negative tilt down-weights high-loss points, which is the robustness-to-outliers regime.

The paper's population counterpart is the tilted population risk (an entropic risk):

$$R_\gamma(h,\mu)=\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb E_{\mu^{\otimes n}}\Big[\frac1n\sum_i e^{\gamma\ell(h,Z_i)}\Big]=\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb E_\mu\big[e^{\gamma\ell(h,Z)}\big].$$

The key modelling choice is that the target is not $R_\gamma$. The paper takes the view that TERM is only a training device and that we still care about the ordinary risk. It studies the mixed gap

$$\mathrm{gen}_\gamma(h,S)=R(h,\mu)-\widehat R_\gamma(h,S)=\underbrace{R(h,\mu)-R_\gamma(h,\mu)}_{\text{tilt bias}}+\underbrace{R_\gamma(h,\mu)-\widehat R_\gamma(h,S)}_{\widehat{\mathrm{gen}}_\gamma,\ \text{"non-linear" gen. error}}.$$

The precise question: for $\gamma<0$ and a loss that may be unbounded but has $\sup_h\mathbb E_\mu[\ell^{1+\epsilon}(h,Z)]\le\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon\in(0,1]$, how fast does $\sup_{h\in\mathcal H}|\mathrm{gen}_\gamma(h,S)|$ shrink with $n$, with high probability or in expectation? How should $\gamma$ scale with $n$? And what happens when training data come from a contaminated $\tilde\mu$ while the test data come from $\mu$? Secondary objects include the excess risk $\mathcal E_\gamma=R(h^\ast_\gamma(S),\mu)-R(h^\ast(\mu),\mu)$ of the TERM minimizer, information-theoretic expected versions with a randomized learner $P_{H|S}$, and a KL-regularized TERM.

Prior work and the gap. Li et al. gave empirical evidence and optimization and interpretation results, but no generalization theory. Lee, Park and Shin (2020) bound entropic-risk generalization by Rademacher complexity, but only for bounded losses. Wang et al. (2023) analysed tilted sparse additive models, again with bounded losses. The gap the authors claim to fill is generalization of TER for heavy-tailed losses, together with a formal account of its robustness to outliers.

Non-obvious choices to flag:

  • Sign of $\gamma$. Only $\gamma<0$ is treated in the unbounded case. Because $\ell\ge0$, the variable $e^{\gamma\ell}$ lies in $(0,1]$, so it is bounded however heavy the tail of $\ell$. That fact is the whole engine. For $\gamma>0$ the variable $e^{\gamma\ell}$ may have no mean at all, and Remark E.1 admits that the robustness bound fails.
  • Moments rather than boundedness. Only the $(1+\epsilon)$-th moment is assumed; higher moments may be infinite. Constants enter as $\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}$ and through factors $e^{|\gamma|\kappa_u}$.
  • $\gamma$ depends on $n$. Every rate requires $\gamma\to0$, as $|\gamma|\asymp n^{-1/(1+\epsilon)}$ (or $n^{-1/2}$ for bounded loss, or $n^{-1}$ for the Gibbs result). Because the gap includes the tilt bias, a fixed $\gamma$ never gives a vanishing bound.
  • Sample-size conditions involving an auxiliary $\zeta\in(0,1)$, e.g. $n\ge(4|\gamma|^{1+\epsilon}\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}+\tfrac83\zeta)\log(2/\delta)/(\zeta^2e^{2\gamma\kappa_u})$, together with a finite $\mathcal H$ for the uniform results.

Main idea

The decomposition separates two effects that pull in opposite directions as $|\gamma|$ changes.

  1. Tilt bias. For $\gamma<0$, $0\le R(h,\mu)-R_\gamma(h,\mu)\le|\gamma|^\epsilon\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}$. It vanishes as $\gamma\to0$.
  2. Concentration of the tilted average. $\frac1n\sum_i e^{\gamma\ell_i}$ is an average of $[0,1]$-valued variables whose variance is only $O(|\gamma|^{1+\epsilon})$. Bernstein's inequality applies, followed by a perturbation step to pass through $\frac1\gamma\log(\cdot)$. Dividing by $|\gamma|$ makes this term grow as $\gamma\to0$, like $\sqrt{B/(n|\gamma|^{1-\epsilon})}+B/(n|\gamma|)$ with $B=\log|\mathcal H|+\log(2/\delta)$.

Balancing $|\gamma|^\epsilon$ against $1/(n|\gamma|)$ gives $|\gamma|\asymp n^{-1/(1+\epsilon)}$ and the headline results:

  • Uniform (finite $\mathcal H$), unbounded loss: $\sup_h|\mathrm{gen}_\gamma|=O(n^{-\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)})$, which is $O(n^{-1/2})$ when the second moment is finite. The excess risk of TERM is at most twice this.
  • Information-theoretic, unbounded loss: $|\overline{\mathrm{gen}}_\gamma(H,S)|\lesssim\frac{e^{|\gamma|\kappa_t}}{|\gamma|}\sqrt{\frac{2\kappa_t^{1+\epsilon}|\gamma|^{1+\epsilon}I(H;S)}{n}}+|\gamma|^\epsilon\kappa_t^{1+\epsilon}$, again $O(n^{-\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)})$ for bounded $I(H;S)$.
  • Bounded loss (Appendix H, either sign of $\gamma$): $O(1/\sqrt n)$ for $|\gamma|=O(n^{-1/2})$, recovering the ERM bound $M\sqrt{B/2n}$ as $\gamma\to0$. Rademacher, stability and PAC-Bayes variants are also given.
  • Robustness. When training data come from $\tilde\mu$ with $\mathbb E_{\tilde\mu}\ell^{1+\epsilon}\le\kappa_s^{1+\epsilon}$, an extra term $\frac{\mathrm{TV}(\mu,\tilde\mu)}{\gamma^2}\cdot\frac{e^{|\gamma|\kappa_u}-e^{|\gamma|\kappa_s}}{\kappa_u-\kappa_s}\approx\frac{\mathrm{TV}(\mu,\tilde\mu)}{|\gamma|}$ appears. It shrinks as $|\gamma|$ grows. This is the formal robustness–generalization trade-off. The authors contrast it with ERM, where $\mathbb E_\mu\ell-\mathbb E_{\tilde\mu}\ell$ cannot be controlled by TV for unbounded losses.
  • Data-driven tilt: choose $\gamma$ by minimizing the $n\to\infty$ part of the bound, $|\gamma|^\epsilon\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}+\mathrm{TV}\cdot(\ldots)/\gamma^2$.
  • KL-regularized TERM. Minimizing $\mathbb E\,\widehat R_\gamma+\frac1\alpha\mathrm{KL}(P_{H|S}\|\pi_H|P_S)$ yields the tilted Gibbs posterior $P^\gamma_{H|S}\propto\pi_H\big(\frac1n\sum_i e^{\gamma\ell(H,Z_i)}\big)^{-\alpha/\gamma}=\pi_He^{-\alpha\widehat R_\gamma(H,S)}$. Its expected gap is $O(n^{-\epsilon})$ for $\gamma=O(1/n)$, so $O(1/n)$ under a second moment, where the Gibbs-posterior result of Aminian et al. (2021) needed sub-Gaussianity.

Most interesting part

Reviewer-style assessment.

Strengths.

  • The central observation is clean and correct. With nonnegative losses and $\gamma<0$, $x\mapsto e^{\gamma x}$ maps a heavy-tailed variable into $(0,1]$ and is $|\gamma|$-Lipschitz. This yields $\mathrm{Var}(e^{\gamma\ell})\le2^\epsilon|\gamma|^{1+\epsilon}\mathbb E\ell^{1+\epsilon}$ (Lemma C.3), since $|e^{\gamma x}-e^{\gamma x'}|^2\le|e^{\gamma x}-e^{\gamma x'}|^{1+\epsilon}$ when the difference is at most $1$. Negative-tilt TER is in effect a smooth soft-truncation estimator of the mean. Losses above about $1/|\gamma|\asymp n^{1/(1+\epsilon)}$ are flattened, and that is exactly the truncation level of the classical truncated-mean estimator for heavy tails (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi 2013).
  • So the $n^{-\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)}$ rate is essentially tight in $n$, by an argument the paper does not make. For one fixed $h$, $\mathrm{gen}_\gamma$ is the error of an estimator of the mean of a nonnegative variable with a bounded $(1+\epsilon)$-th moment. The minimax lower bound $\Omega((\log(1/\delta)/n)^{\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)})$ for that problem uses two-point nonnegative distributions, so it applies here. If $\gamma$ is also tuned with $\delta$ and $|\mathcal H|$, i.e. $|\gamma|\asymp(B/n)^{1/(1+\epsilon)}$, the bound becomes $(B/n)^{\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)}$, which is the Catoni / median-of-means form. The "lower bounds" in the paper (Prop. 3.4, 3.10) are two-sided deviation bounds, not minimax lower bounds.
  • The exact identity for the tilted Gibbs posterior is elegant: the gap between the expected TER under the product and joint laws equals $I_{\mathrm{SKL}}(H;S)/\alpha$. The TER simply plays the role of the energy.

Weaknesses.

  • Missing comparison class. The natural baselines are heavy-tailed ERM via Catoni-type or median-of-means risk estimates: Brownlees, Joly and Lugosi (2015), Lugosi and Mendelson (MoM tournaments), Minsker.
