These already reach $n^{-\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)}$, often with infinite classes and better $\delta$-dependence. The paper compares mainly with Cortes et al. (2019) and with PAC-Bayes heavy-tail results, and gains only a $\log n$ factor, comparing finite-$\mathcal H$ bounds against growth-function bounds. The genuine novelty is that the specific estimator practitioners use (TERM) belongs to this robust family. It is not a new rate.
  • Does $\gamma\asymp n^{-1/2}$ trivialize things? For bounded losses, essentially yes. $|\widehat R_\gamma-\widehat R|=O(|\gamma|M^2)$, so any bound for ERM transfers with an extra $O(|\gamma|)$. The Appendix H bound, $\frac{e^{|\gamma|M}-1}{|\gamma|}\sqrt{B/2n}+O(|\gamma|M^2)$, is minimized at $\gamma=0$. The bounded-loss theory therefore never says that tilting helps, only that a small tilt does not hurt. For unbounded losses it is not trivial: the bound blows up as $\gamma\to0$, so a vanishing but nonzero tilt is required. Either way the theory covers the asymptotically untilted regime. In practice TERM uses $\gamma=O(1)$, and the grid-searched $\gamma^\star$ in the paper's own tables lies between $-0.5$ and $-5$. That is the regime of persistent bias, where the bounds say nothing useful about $R(h,\mu)$.
  • The robustness result is weak as stated. Under contamination $\tilde\mu=(1-\tau)\mu+\tau\nu$ the shift term is $O(\tau/|\gamma|)$. With the recommended $|\gamma|\asymp n^{-1/(1+\epsilon)}$, Appendix E.1 gets an overall rate of $\max\{\tau n^{1/(1+\epsilon)},n^{-\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)}\}$, and notes that $\tau=O(1/n)$ is needed, i.e. about one outlier. A sharper reading is available from the paper's own terms. Choosing $|\gamma|\asymp(\tau/\kappa)^{1/(1+\epsilon)}$ instead gives an irreducible error of order $\tau^{\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)}$, which matches the known minimax rate for robust mean estimation under $\tau$-contamination with $(1+\epsilon)$ moments. This would be a stronger and more honest headline: the tilt should scale with the contamination level, not with $n$. The ERM comparison is also somewhat unfair, because ERM with any truncation would also be TV-robust.
  • Assumptions and presentation. The uniform results assume a finite $\mathcal H$; covering-number extensions are only sketched. The information-theoretic results need finite $I(H;S)$, which fails for deterministic learners on continuous data. The auxiliary $\zeta$ and case conditions (a)–(c) are awkward. There are typos that matter on a careful read: Assumption 3.8 writes $\ell^\epsilon$ for $\ell^{1+\epsilon}$; Assumption 4.1 says "second moment" but states a $(1+\epsilon)$-th moment; one Jensen step in the proof of Prop. 3.4 is written in the wrong direction, though the needed direction holds; Appendix B says symmetrization cannot be applied to TER, yet H.21 does Rademacher analysis. The Gibbs $O(n^{-\epsilon})$ result fixes $\alpha$ while $n$ grows, so the posterior barely concentrates. A small generalization gap there says little about excess risk.
  • Evaluation gaps. The experiments are 2-D logistic and linear regression toys with three runs (several standard deviations reported as $\pm0.000$). The "data-driven" $\gamma$ uses $\kappa_u$ estimated on the clean dataset and a TV bound computed from the known outlier count $2m/(m+n)$. Both are oracle quantities. The data-driven $\gamma$ is often far from $\gamma^\star$. There is no deep model and no realistic label noise.

Proof sketch

Uniform, unbounded (Theorem 3.5). Assume $\ell\ge0$, $\sup_h\mathbb E_\mu\ell^{1+\epsilon}\le\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}$, $\gamma<0$, $|\mathcal H|<\infty$, and $n$ above the $\zeta$-threshold. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\sup_{h}|\mathrm{gen}_\gamma(h,S)|\le\frac{e^{|\gamma|\kappa_u}}{(1-\zeta)|\gamma|}\sqrt{\frac{2^{1+\epsilon}|\gamma|^{1+\epsilon}\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}B(\delta)}{n}}+\frac{4e^{|\gamma|\kappa_u}B(\delta)}{3n|\gamma|(1-\zeta)}+|\gamma|^\epsilon\kappa_u^{1+\epsilon}.$$

The proof has four steps.

  • Step 1, bias (Lemma C.9). The left inequality $\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb Ee^{\gamma X}\le\mathbb EX$ is Jensen. For the right inequality, use $e^{-x}\le1-x+x^{1+\epsilon}$ for $x>0$ (Lugosi–Neu) and then $\log(1+u)\le u$, giving $\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb Ee^{\gamma X}\ge\mathbb EX-|\gamma|^\epsilon\mathbb EX^{1+\epsilon}$. This is the "Taylor" control of the tilt, and it needs only $1+\epsilon$ moments.
  • Step 2, variance (Lemma C.3). Write $\mathrm{Var}(e^{\gamma X})=\frac12\mathbb E(e^{\gamma X}-e^{\gamma X'})^2$. Lower the exponent $2$ to $1+\epsilon$ (differences are at most $1$), use $|\gamma|$-Lipschitzness, and apply $|X-X'|\le X+X'$ and Jensen.
  • Step 3, concentration and log-perturbation. Apply Bernstein to $V_i=e^{\gamma\ell(h,Z_i)}\in(0,1]$. Pass through the log with $\log(y\pm x)\gtrless\log y\pm\frac{x}{y}$ or $\pm\frac{x}{y-x}$, needing the deviation to be at most $\zeta y$ (this is where $\zeta$ and the sample-size condition come from). Lower-bound $y=\mathbb Ee^{\gamma\ell}\ge e^{\gamma\mathbb E\ell}\ge e^{\gamma\kappa_u}$ by Jensen and Lemma C.8. That lower bound produces the $e^{|\gamma|\kappa_u}/|\gamma|$ prefactor.
  • Step 4. Take a union bound over $\mathcal H$. Lemma 3.7 converts this into excess risk $\le2\sup_h|\mathrm{gen}_\gamma|$.

The key trick is that negative tilt plus nonnegativity turns a heavy-tailed concentration problem into a bounded, low-variance one, at the price of a $1/|\gamma|$ amplification when undoing the log.

Information-theoretic (Theorem 3.11). Assume $\max\{\mathbb E_{P_{H,Z}}\ell^{1+\epsilon},\mathbb E_{P_H\otimes\mu}\ell^{1+\epsilon}\}\le\kappa_t^{1+\epsilon}$. Under $P_H\otimes\mu$ the variable $e^{\gamma\ell(H,Z)}$ is sub-exponential with parameters $(|\gamma|^{1+\epsilon}\kappa_t^{1+\epsilon},1)$, so the Donsker–Varadhan / Xu–Raginsky argument (in the sub-exponential form of Bu et al.) bounds the joint-versus-product gap of $\mathbb E[\frac1n\sum e^{\gamma\ell}]$ by $\sqrt{2|\gamma|^{1+\epsilon}\kappa_t^{1+\epsilon}I(H;S)/n}$, or by a linear term when $I/n$ is large. The same log-perturbation step follows, plus two Lemma C.9 bias terms. One detail: the paper's "expected TER" $R_\gamma(H,Q)$ puts the expectation inside the log, and Prop. D.2 pays $|\gamma|^\epsilon\kappa_t^{1+\epsilon}$ to switch to $\mathbb E[\widehat R_\gamma]$.

Robustness (Prop. 4.2, Thm. 4.3). Insert $\pm R_\gamma(h,\tilde\mu)$. Bound $|R_\gamma(h,\mu)-R_\gamma(h,\tilde\mu)|$ with the linear functional derivative of $m\mapsto\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb E_m e^{\gamma\ell}$ along $m_\lambda=\tilde\mu+\lambda(\mu-\tilde\mu)$. The derivative is $e^{\gamma\ell}/(\gamma\,\mathbb E_{m_\lambda}e^{\gamma\ell})$. Its numerator is bounded by $1$, so TV duality applies, and the denominator is at least $e^{-|\gamma|(\lambda\kappa_u+(1-\lambda)\kappa_s)}$. Integrating over $\lambda$ gives the $\frac{\mathrm{TV}}{\gamma^2}\frac{e^{|\gamma|\kappa_u}-e^{|\gamma|\kappa_s}}{\kappa_u-\kappa_s}$ term. It works only for $\gamma<0$, because only then is the integrand bounded.

Tilted Gibbs (Prop. 6.1–6.2, Thm. 6.3). The Gibbs variational principle gives $P^\gamma_{H|S}\propto\pi_He^{-\alpha\widehat R_\gamma}$. Writing $I_{\mathrm{SKL}}=\mathbb E_{P_H\otimes P_S}\log P_{H|S}-\mathbb E_{P_{H,S}}\log P_{H|S}$ gives the exact gap $I_{\mathrm{SKL}}/\alpha$. Combining this with the Theorem 3.11 upper bound and $I\le I_{\mathrm{SKL}}$ gives a self-bounding quadratic inequality in $\sqrt{I(H;S)}$. Solving it yields $I(H;S)=O(\alpha|\gamma|^{\epsilon-1}/n+\ldots)$, which leads to the $O(n^{-\epsilon})$ bound for $\gamma=O(1/n)$.

Broader context

Tilted and risk-sensitive losses. $\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb Ee^{\gamma\ell}$ is the entropic risk of Howard–Matheson risk-sensitive control, the cumulant generating function rescaled, and a convex risk measure. The Donsker–Varadhan duality

$$\frac1\gamma\log\mathbb E_Pe^{\gamma\ell}=\sup_Q\Big\{\mathbb E_Q\ell-\tfrac1\gamma\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P)\Big\}\quad(\gamma>0)$$

makes positive-tilt TERM exactly a KL-penalized DRO over reweightings of the training points. Compare CVaR and $\chi^2$-DRO (Duchi–Namkoong) and Hashimoto et al.'s fairness-without-demographics. Negative tilt is the optimistic counterpart, $\inf_Q\{\mathbb E_Q\ell+\frac1{|\gamma|}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P)\}$, which explains its outlier robustness. This paper supplies the missing statistical half of that picture for $\gamma<0$, and its natural relatives are the robust-statistics estimators (Catoni, MoM, truncation) rather than DRO.

KL-regularized objectives. The tilted Gibbs posterior sits in the same family as Gibbs/PAC-Bayes posteriors and KL-regularized RL objectives, whose optimal policies are $\pi\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}e^{r/\beta}$. The $I_{\mathrm{SKL}}/\alpha$ identity is the standard Gibbs-algorithm characterization with $\widehat R_\gamma$ as the energy.

Follow-up ideas. (i) Scale $\gamma$ with the contamination level and prove a matching $\tau^{\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)}+(B/n)^{\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)}$ excess-risk bound with Lepski-type adaptive choice of $\gamma$. That would replace the oracle data-driven rule. (ii) Analyse fixed $\gamma$ honestly by targeting $R_\gamma$ itself, which is the regime practitioners use, together with a separate bias-versus-robustness statement. (iii) Positive tilt with sub-exponential losses, where $\mathbb Ee^{\gamma\ell}$ exists only for $\gamma$ below the sub-exponential parameter.

IR connection. The obvious analogy is that InfoNCE / sampled-softmax losses in dense retrieval are log-sum-exp-shaped. Taken literally it is weak: InfoNCE applies log-sum-exp over candidate documents within one query, with positive tilt $1/\tau$ on scores, whereas TER applies it over training examples, with negative tilt on losses. The theorems do not transfer as stated.

Two genuine links survive.

  • The $\widehat{\mathrm{gen}}_\gamma$ machinery is exactly what bounds the error of a sampled log-partition estimate: $\big|\log\frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K e^{s(q,d_j)/\tau}-\log\mathbb E_{d\sim\nu}e^{s(q,d)/\tau}\big|$ for $K$ negatives drawn from a sampling distribution $\nu$. With cosine scores in $[-1,1]$ this is the bounded positive-tilt case of Appendix H, with $M=2$ and $\gamma=1/\tau$. Constants such as $(e^{2/\tau}-1)\tau$ make quantitative why low temperatures and few negatives give biased, high-variance contrastive objectives. A clean "generalization of sampled InfoNCE in $K$ and $\tau$" note could be built on Lemmas C.3–C.5.
  • Applying negative tilt across queries, on per-query InfoNCE losses, is a principled way to soften false negatives and noisy qrels (as in MS MARCO). Since the InfoNCE loss with unnormalized embeddings is unbounded but plausibly has finite moments, it fits the paper's heavy-tail assumption.

The paper says nothing about generative retrieval or vector search specifically. Any connection there would come through these training-loss views, not through the results themselves.

title: The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-23

The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning — Xiaoyu Li, Jiangxuan Long (2026) — arXiv:2611.21251

Setting and problem

Most ICL theory treats the prompt as an i.i.d. draw from a task distribution. At most it allows a fixed retrieval-noise model, as in Guo et al. 2025, which casts RAG as noisy in-context regression. Deployed pipelines work differently. They embed the query, retrieve top-$m$, re-rank, filter by label, try several templates on a validation set, let the model critique itself, and retry. The context therefore depends on the same data that is later used to judge it. The paper asks how much this adaptivity costs statistically. The question is not whether adaptive retrieval predicts better. It is whether the score you report for the chosen context still tells you anything about its deployment risk.

Formal objects:

  • Query / task descriptor $U = u$. Conditional on $u$, a data store $S = (Z_1,\dots,Z_n) \sim P_u^n$, and a fresh deployment item $Z^\star \sim P_u$ independent of $S$.
  • An adaptive context pipeline $M$, written as a stochastic kernel $K_u(dt \mid s)$ from stores to transcripts $t \in \mathcal{T}$. A transcript is complete: it holds the ordered distinct selected indices $I(t) = (i_1(t),\dots,i_k(t)) \in [n]^k$, the prompt text, seeds, re-ranker scores and edit history. It must contain everything needed to replay the predictor, so any visible labels count as part of $t$.
  • A frozen in-context learner. For each fixed $t$ it induces a loss $\ell_t : \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$. All architecture is hidden inside $t \mapsto \ell_t$, and all adaptivity is charged to the kernel.
  • Risk $L_u(t) = \mathbb{E}_{Z \sim P_u} \ell_t(Z)$. The reported score is the selected-context score $\hat L_S(t) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k \ell_t(Z_{i_j(t)})$, and the gap is $\mathrm{gap}_u(t,S) = L_u(t) - \hat L_S(t)$.
  • Context capacity. The expected version is $C(M) = I(T; S \mid U)$. The high-probability version is the approximate max-information $I_\infty^\beta(T;S\mid U) \le \kappa$, meaning $\mathbb{P}((T,S)\in E) \le e^{\kappa}\,\mathbb{P}((T,S')\in E) + \beta$ for every event $E$, where $S'$ is an independent copy.

The question: for a frozen learner and an arbitrary pipeline with capacity $\kappa$, how large can $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{gap}]$ or its upper tail be, as a function of $\kappa$ and $k$? And can we produce a certificate $B(T,S,U,\delta)$ with $\mathbb{P}(L_U(T) \le \hat L_S(T) + B) \ge 1-\delta$?

Several modelling choices are less obvious than they look.

  1. The score is an average over the $k$ selected store items, not over all $n$. The denominator is the context length (or the number of reused validation queries), not the store size. In the Banking77 experiments, the "selected examples" whose losses form the score are $k$ reused validation queries. The $m \in \{4,8\}$ demonstrations retrieved from a separate 2,000-item store are not part of it. That store is effectively treated as public, and only the recipe choice is charged. So "context" in the theorem means "the data the reported score averages over". That is not always the demonstrations shown to the model.
  2. The learner is frozen and version-pinned. Pretraining contamination, such as an LLM that has already seen Banking77, lies outside the accounting.
  3. The "conditional stochastic-kernel calculus" is regular conditional laws on standard Borel spaces. There is a coupled law $Q_u = P_u^n \otimes K_u$, a ghost law $\bar Q_u = P_u^n \otimes \bar K_u$ with $\bar K_u = \int K_u(\cdot\mid s) P_u^n(ds)$, and an information density $\imath_u(t;s) = \log \frac{dK_u(\cdot\mid s)}{d\bar K_u}(t)$. This is bookkeeping rather than new mathematics. Its value is that every retrieval, rerank, gate and edit becomes a measurable piece of $t$.

What is already known. Adaptive data analysis (Dwork et al. 2015, reusable holdout; Bassily et al. 2016) controls statistical queries chosen after seeing earlier answers. Russo–Zou (2016) and Xu–Raginsky (2017) bound selection bias by $\sqrt{2\sigma^2 I/n}$. PAC-Bayes (McAllester, Catoni) gives KL-based nonuniform bounds. None of these names the selected-subsample statistic, the transcript with indices, or the composition across prompt-engineering rounds. Mechanistic ICL theory (Garg et al., Akyürek et al., von Oswald et al.) explains how a good inner learner can arise, but says nothing about how the prompt was chosen. The paper puts itself exactly in that gap.

Main idea

Treat prompt construction as adaptive data analysis. Evaluate the chosen transcript on a ghost store, where it is independent of the data and its score is an average of $k$ fresh losses with fluctuation $\sigma/\sqrt k$. Then pay one change of measure back to the real law. That change of measure costs exactly the capacity.

Headline results:

  • Upper bound (Thm 4.1). $|\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{gap}]| \le \sqrt{2\sigma^2 I(T;S\mid U)/k}$, which is $\sqrt{I/(2k)}$ for losses in $[0,1]$. A high-probability version (Thm 4.2) gives $\mathrm{gap} \le \sqrt{2\sigma^2(\kappa + \log(1/\delta))/k}$ with probability $\ge 1-\beta-\delta$.
  • Matching lower bound (Thm 4.4). For $1 \le \kappa \le k/16$ some pipeline has $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{gap}] \ge c\sqrt{\kappa/k}$. In the regime $\log k \ll \kappa \ll k$ the gap is $(1-o(1))\sqrt{\kappa/(2k)}$, so the constant of Thm 4.1 is exact.
  • Accounting rules. Capacity composes by the chain rule over rounds: $I(T;S\mid U) = \sum_r I(T_r; S \mid U, T_{<r})$. A finite menu of $M$ recipes costs at most $\log M$ (or $\log(M/\beta)$ for max-information). A Gaussian-noised score vector with precision $\rho$ and sensitivity $\Delta$ costs at most $\rho\Delta^2/2$, however many filters follow. Weighted or clustered contexts replace $k$ by $k_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with $\sum_j w_j^2 \le 1/k_{\mathrm{eff}}$, or by a block count $k_{\mathrm{blk}}$, so many chunks from one document certify like a single block. A latent-task decomposition $I(T;S\mid U) = I(T;W\mid U) + I(T;S\mid U,W)$ separates task identification from within-task overfitting.
  • A negative result (Remark 4.6). An unrestricted deterministic pipeline can cherry-pick $k$ items with zero loss. Any surcharge that is valid uniformly is then at least $1 - 2k/n$, i.e. vacuous. Capacity accounting is therefore necessary, not a convenience.
  • PAC-Bayesian Gibbs retrieval (SCAR). Sample $T \sim Q_\lambda(dt\mid S,u) \propto \Pi_u(dt)\, e^{-\lambda \hat L_S(t)}$. Thm 6.1 gives a first-order certificate, including a gate charge $\log(1/\Pi_u(A))$ for data-dependent candidate pools. Thm 6.2 gives a self-normalized second-order certificate that uses a predictable empirical variance.
  • Banking77 experiments. There are 64 recipes ($4$ templates $\times$ $4$ retrieval rules $\times$ $4$ demo configurations) and frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and GPT-4.1-mini. The mean best-of-$M$ gap scales with $\sqrt{\log M/k}$, with a fitted slope of about 0.14. The Thm 4.2 certificate held in all $2 \times 12{,}000$ selection events, but it is conservative by roughly 10x. At $k = M = 64$ the mean gap is 0.023, the Thm 4.1 bound is 0.180, and the certificate is 0.300. SCAR spends only 0.9–1.8 logged nats instead of $\log 64 = 4.16$. Its certified risk at $k=64$ for Qwen is 0.292, below the zero-shot error of 0.373 in 99.7% of draws. For GPT-4.1-mini the figure is 99.2% at $k=128$. Its holdout risk stays within 0.01 of the best-of-64 winner.
  • Bayesian linear ICL. With $\theta \sim N(0,\tau^2 I_d)$ and a ridge/posterior-mean predictor, the conditional Bayes risk is $\sigma_\xi^2 + x_\star^\top(\tau^{-2}I_d + \sigma_\xi^{-2}X_I^\top X_I)^{-1}x_\star$. Top-$k$ retrieval by $(u^\top x_i)^2$ with $u = x_\star/\|x_\star\|$ achieves directional mass $\alpha_I \ge q_{n,k} = F^{-1}_{\chi^2_1}(1 - 2k/n)$ with probability $\ge 1-e^{-k/4}$. A Schur complement then measures how much of that gain leaks into nuisance directions. This is the "quality" side of the story, kept separate from the "certification" side.

Most interesting part

The most interesting idea is how cleanly the paper separates context quality from context certification, and that this separation turns on one modelling decision. The certified quantity is the average over the selected indices, and the selected indices are part of the transcript.

Once $I(t)$ is a component of $t$, the indices become constants for a fixed $t$. Under the ghost law, $\hat L_{S^\circ}(t)$ is then an average of exactly $k$ i.i.d. losses, so it is $\sigma^2/k$-sub-Gaussian. Information about the other $n-k$ items cannot help, and the denominator becomes $k$ instead of $n$. With this framing the trade-offs can be counted, not just described:

  • Best-of-$M$ templates on $k$ validation queries costs $\log M$ nats, giving a gap of about $\sqrt{\log M/(2k)}$.
  • $R$ rounds of $M$ edits cost $R\log M$. Figure 3b confirms the $\sqrt{R\log M/k}$ tracking.
  • Deterministic top-$k$ index selection can cost up to $\log\binom{n}{k} \approx k\log(n/k)$, which makes $\sqrt{\kappa/k} = \Omega(1)$, i.e. vacuous.

The last point does not say nearest-neighbour retrieval is bad. The linear-regression section shows that query-aligned top-$k$ cuts the posterior variance along $u$ from $\tau^2$ to roughly $(\tau^{-2} + kq_{n,k}/\sigma_\xi^2)^{-1}$. It says that the score the retrieved context earns on its own selected items is not evidence. "Good retrieval reduces approximation error; stable retrieval prevents overclaiming." For anyone who builds retrievers, this distinction is the main lesson.

The SCAR gate charge is the paper's most practically new piece; the authors say they found no prior statement of it for retrieval. If you shortlist candidates with a data-dependent gate $A(S,u)$ and then run a Gibbs posterior inside it, the identity $\mathrm{KL}(Q\|\Pi_u) = \mathrm{KL}(Q\|\Pi_{u,A}) + \log(1/\Pi_u(A))$ bills you the prior mass of the shortlist. That turns "we only reranked the top 100" into an auditable number.

Caveats:

  1. The core theorem is, by the authors' own admission (App. G), Theorem 1 of Xu–Raginsky applied to the empirical mean of the selected subsample. The lower bound is a max of $e^\kappa$ independent Rademacher averages over a store of size $n=k$. The technical novelty is thin. The contribution is in what gets modelled and logged.
  2. The bounds are most useful exactly when the pipeline is a finite, logged recipe menu or a randomized Gibbs sampler. For realistic continuous ANN top-$k$ with embedding scores, $I(T;S\mid U)$ is either huge or infinite, unless the store is treated as public and only the validation set counts as $S$. The experiments do exactly that, so the certificate covers recipe choice, not retrieval itself. The i.i.d. store assumption is also strong for scraped corpora with near-duplicates. Blocking helps only when the clusters are public.

Proof sketch

Upper bound (Thm 4.1). Assume $\ell_t(Z) - L_u(t)$ is $\sigma^2$-sub-Gaussian for every fixed $t$. Then $$\big|\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{gap}_U(T,S)]\big| \le \sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2}{k}\, I(T;S\mid U)}.$$ Key lemma (D.17): if $g(t,S)$ is mean-zero and $\nu$-sub-Gaussian for every fixed $t$, then $|\mathbb{E} g(T,S)| \le \sqrt{2\nu I(T;S)}$. Proof: apply Donsker–Varadhan, $\mathbb{E}_Q f \le \mathrm{KL}(Q\|P) + \log \mathbb{E}_P e^f$, with $Q$ the coupled law, $P$ the ghost law (so $\mathrm{KL} = I(T;S)$) and $f = \lambda g$: $$\lambda\, \mathbb{E} g(T,S) \le I(T;S) + \frac{\lambda^2 \nu}{2},$$ and optimize over $\lambda$. The selected-subsample step supplies $\nu = \sigma^2/k$, because for fixed $t$ the $k$ distinct indices pick out independent coordinates of $S^\circ$. Conditioning on $U$ and Jensen finish the proof. A sub-gamma version (Thm D.19) gives $\sqrt{2vI} + bI$.

High-probability bound (Thm 4.2). If $I_\infty^\beta(T;S\mid U) \le \kappa$, then with probability $\ge 1-\beta-\delta$, $$\mathrm{gap}_U(T,S) \le \sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2}{k}\Big(\kappa + \log\frac1\delta\Big)}.$$ The ghost-law tail $\exp\{-k\epsilon^2/(2\sigma^2)\}$ is moved to the real law by max-information: the probability becomes at most $e^\kappa e^{-k\epsilon^2/(2\sigma^2)} + \beta$. For a menu of size $M$, a description-length argument (Lemma D.7, after Dwork et al.) gives $\kappa = \log(M/\beta)$. It discards transcripts of probability $\le \beta/M$ and bounds the likelihood ratio of the rest by $M/\beta$.

Lower bound (Thm 4.4). Let $N = \lfloor e^\kappa\rfloor$ and $\mathcal{Z} = \{-1,+1\}^N$ with the uniform law. Prompt $j$ has loss $\ell_j(z) = (1+z_j)/2$, so every prompt has risk exactly $1/2$. The selector picks $T = \arg\min_j \frac1k\sum_{m\le k} Z_{m,j}$. Since $H(T) \le \log N \le \kappa$, the capacity is within budget. The gap equals $\frac12 \max_j \frac1k\sum_m(-Z_{m,j})$, a maximum of $N$ independent Rademacher averages. Lemma D.11 uses a reverse Chernoff bound for the symmetric binomial, plus the trick $\max_j X_j = X_1 + (M' - X_1)_+$ to handle a possibly negative maximum, to give $\ge c_0\sqrt{\log N/k}$. Lemma D.12 uses method-of-types binomial tails, $\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Bin}(k,1/2)\ge m) \ge \frac{1}{k+1}e^{-kD(m/k\|1/2)}$, to show the maximum concentrates at $\sqrt{2\log N/k}$. The resulting gap is $(1-o(1))\sqrt{\kappa/(2k)}$, which matches Thm 4.1 with $\sigma^2 = 1/4$ exactly. This is the winner's curse in its purest form.

Gibbs rule (Thm 6.1). Let $\Pi_u$ be fixed before the store is read. With probability $\ge 1-\delta$, simultaneously for all $Q \ll \Pi_u$, $$\mathbb{E}_{t\sim Q} L_u(t) \le \mathbb{E}_{t\sim Q}\hat L_S(t) + \frac{\mathrm{KL}(Q\|\Pi_u) + \log(1/\delta)}{\lambda} + \frac{\lambda\sigma^2}{2k}.$$ Technique: Catoni-style PAC-Bayes. For fixed $t$, $\mathbb{E}_S \exp\{\lambda(L_u - \hat L_S) - \lambda^2\sigma^2/(2k)\} \le 1$. Integrate over $\Pi_u$ (Fubini), apply exponential Markov, then change measure to any $Q$. The Gibbs posterior $Q_\lambda \propto \Pi_u e^{-\lambda\hat L_S}$ minimizes the right-hand side, which gives an oracle inequality. For a gated posterior the KL is still measured against the ambient $\Pi_u$, and that is where $\log(1/\Pi_u(A))$ appears. The surcharge is minimized at $\lambda^\star = \sigma^{-1}\sqrt{2k(\kappa + \log(1/\delta))}$, where it reproduces the $\sqrt{2\sigma^2(\kappa+\log(1/\delta))/k}$ rate. A Fano argument (Prop. D.25) shows that no rule using only the $k$ examples beats $0.07\sqrt{\log M/k}$, so certification costs no extra rate.

Second-order rule (Thm 6.2). With $\psi(\gamma) = -\log(1-\gamma) - \gamma$, the predictable variance $\hat V_S(t) = \frac1k\sum_j (X_j - \hat\mu_{j-1})^2$ and a finite grid $\Gamma$, $$\mathbb{E}_Q L_u \le \mathbb{E}_Q \hat L_S + \frac{\psi(\gamma)}{\gamma}\mathbb{E}_Q\hat V_S + \frac{\mathrm{KL}(Q\|\Pi_u) + \log(|\Gamma|/\delta)}{\gamma k}.$$ It is built from the Waudby-Smith–Ramdas predictable plug-in supermartingale, using Fan et al.'s inequality $e^{\gamma\xi - \psi(\gamma)\xi^2} \le 1+\gamma\xi$. In a synthetic library it cuts brittle picks from 97% to 0.9% at $k=32$.

Broader context

Background. Adaptive data analysis began with the reusable holdout. Dwork et al. (NeurIPS 2015, Science 2015) showed that differential privacy and description length bound max-information, so a holdout can be reused adaptively. Blum–Hardt's Ladder (ICML 2015) applied this to leaderboards. Russo–Zou (AISTATS 2016) and Xu–Raginsky (NeurIPS 2017) made mutual information the currency of selection bias. Steinke–Zakynthinou's conditional mutual information (COLT 2020) is the obvious sharper tool. It is bounded even for deterministic selection because it conditions on a supersample, but it normalizes by the full sample. On the ICL side, the demonstration-retrieval literature includes Liu et al. 2022 (KATE: kNN demonstrations for GPT-3) and Rubin et al. 2022 (EPR, a learned prompt retriever). These papers optimize retrieval quality on validation sets. This paper is the missing statistical caveat to them: the recipe that won on your dev set carries a $\sqrt{\log M/k}$ optimism tax.

A follow-up idea. Combine the transcript calculus with conditional MI, or with a "public store, private validation" split, to get non-vacuous certificates for deterministic ANN top-$k$ retrieval. Alternatively, quantify the capacity that approximate search already randomizes away. HNSW entry-point randomness, product-quantization noise and IVF probe selection are all injected noise, and Prop. D.24 prices Gaussian score noise at $\rho\Delta^2/2$. An analogous bound for quantized inner products would make an approximate-search index a certified retriever that comes with its own privacy budget. It would also be worth testing whether the order-statistics analysis of top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval extends to anisotropic embeddings. There, $q_{n,k}$ would become a quantile of $u^\top\Sigma u\,\chi^2_1$, and the Schur leakage would depend on the spectrum. That connects to the geometry of MIPS and the hubness phenomenon.

Connection to retrieval and vector search. There are three concrete links.

  1. Top-$k$ retrieval for demonstrations. Every choice of embedding model, $k$, MMR versus pure similarity, and ordering is a recipe, and the paper tells you exactly what tuning them on a shared dev set costs. Its Banking77 library is precisely this design space.
  2. Retrieval-augmented and generative-retrieval evaluation. SCAR is a softmax/Plackett–Luce-style stochastic ranker over a prior. Stochastic ranking already appears in IR for fairness and counterfactual LTR (e.g. Oosterhuis' PL-Rank line). Generative retrieval decoding at temperature $1/\lambda$ over a docid prior is literally a Gibbs posterior, and trie-constrained decoding is a candidate gate whose prior mass must be logged.
  3. Benchmark reuse. TREC-style test collections and BEIR leaderboards are reused validation sets. $M$ submitted configurations on $k$ queries carry roughly $\sqrt{\log M/(2k)}$ of selection bias per metric. With $k = 50$ topics and $M = 100$ runs that is about 0.21 on a $[0,1]$ metric in the worst case. The point of this paper's experiments is that the realized bias is usually an order of magnitude smaller, but no method can guarantee better without capacity control. Theorem 4.4 and Remark 4.6 make that impossibility precise, and the paper's suggested reporting norm follows: next to retrieval accuracy and context length, report how many nats the pipeline spent.

title: Local Feature Selection without Label or Feature Leakage for Interpretable Machine Learning Predictions
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-23

Local Feature Selection without Label or Feature Leakage for Interpretable Machine Learning Predictions — Harrie Oosterhuis, Lijun Lyu, Avishek Anand (2024) — arXiv:2407.11778

Setting and problem

Objects. An instance is $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (or a finite product space $\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X}_1 \times \dots \times \mathcal{X}_d$) with label $y$, drawn from a fixed population law $p(x, y)$. A local selector $\zeta$ maps $x$ to a distribution over masks $h \in \{0,1\}^d$, written $h \sim \zeta(x)$ or $\zeta(h \mid x)$. Deterministic selectors are the special case where $\zeta(h \mid x) \in \{0,1\}$. The masked input $x \odot h$ keeps $x[j]$ when $h[j]=1$ and puts a special symbol $\varnothing$ (not zero) when $h[j]=0$. A modelling choice that matters: $h$ can be read off exactly from $x \odot h$, so a predictor $f(x \odot h)$ always sees which features were selected. For a mask, $s_{\text{in}} = \{j : h[j]=1\}$ and $s_{\text{ex}} = \{j : h[j]=0\}$.

Objective. The selector and predictor are trained jointly, as in L2X, INVASE, REAL-X and TabNet:

$$\mathcal{L}(\zeta, f) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{E}_{h_i \sim \zeta(x_i)}\big[ L(f(x_i \odot h_i), y_i) + \lambda \lVert h_i \rVert \big], \qquad \lambda > 0.$$

The learner gets labelled data and must output $(\zeta, f)$. The selected set $s_{\text{in}}$ is then presented as the explanation of $f$'s prediction on $x$.

The pathology. Jethani et al. (2021) showed that joint training lets the selector encode the prediction in where it puts the mask. For example, it can pick a single pixel whose position encodes the digit class, and the predictor learns to decode that position. Accuracy stays high and sparsity looks excellent, but the explanation is meaningless. REAL-X tries to fix this by injecting noise during training, which is a heuristic with no guarantee. Table 1 of the paper gives a two-feature toy where $y = x[1] + x[2]$. A leaky policy reaches 100% accuracy and 100% reconstruction of the unselected features while removing 62.5% of the features.

Definitions. Let $\Omega$ be the set of tuples $(x, y, s_{\text{in}}, s_{\text{ex}})$ with $p(x)>0$, $p(s_{\text{in}}, s_{\text{ex}} \mid x, \zeta) > 0$ and $p(x[s_{\text{in}}], y)>0$. Write $E_s$ for the event $h[s_{\text{in}}]=1, h[s_{\text{ex}}]=0$.

  • No label leakage: $p(y \mid x[s_{\text{in}}]) = p(y \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], E_s, \zeta)$ on $\Omega$.
  • No feature leakage: $p(x[s_{\text{ex}}] \mid x[s_{\text{in}}]) = p(x[s_{\text{ex}}] \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], E_s, \zeta)$ on $\Omega$.

In words, learning that $\zeta$ chose this particular mask should not change your posterior over the label, or over the hidden feature values, beyond what the revealed values already tell you. Two assumptions (B.1, B.2) say that the choice of $\zeta$ does not change the data distribution. They hold trivially, but they are needed formally because $\zeta$ appears as a conditioning variable.

The question. Which selectors $\zeta$ have neither kind of leakage? Can we characterise them exactly, and can we build a trainable family that is guaranteed to lie inside that set while still being expressive? Before this paper, nobody had defined leakage formally or given any method a guarantee against it. "Faithfulness" (Jacovi & Goldberg 2021) was discussed informally, and the evidence that methods leak was anecdotal.

A non-obvious choice to flag: leakage is defined relative to the population law $p$, and as an event-wise statement per mask. It is not a statement about the computation, such as "the selector never looked at $x[s_{\text{ex}}]$". These two readings come apart (see the Table 3 discussion below).

Main idea

  1. Characterisation (Corollary 2.5). $\zeta$ is leakage-free iff for every reachable $(x, y, s)$

$$p(E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], \zeta) = p(E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], x[s_{\text{ex}}], y, \zeta).$$

Equivalently, for each mask $h$ the probability $\zeta(h \mid x)$ is a function $g_h(x \odot h)$ of the values that $h$ reveals. In other words, whenever $x \odot h = x' \odot h$ we must have $\zeta(h \mid x) = \zeta(h \mid x')$. The difficulty is normalisation: the $g_h$ must satisfy $\sum_h g_h(x \odot h) = 1$ for every $x$. A softmax over masks is forbidden because its partition function depends on all of $x$ (footnote 2).

  1. Exact solution for small problems (Section 3). If $p(x,y)$ is known and finite, the Bayes predictor $f^\star(x\odot h) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid x \odot h]$ is fixed, and $\mathcal{L}(\zeta, f^\star)$ is linear in the variables $\theta_{(h,\, x\odot h)}$. The program has one variable per masked pattern and one equality constraint per $x$. For binary features that is $\prod_j (1 + |\mathcal{X}_j|) = 3^d$ variables and $2^d$ constraints. Solving it gives the exact leakage-free Pareto front, which is then used as a diagnostic.

  2. SUWR (Sequential Unmasking Without Reversion). Start from $h^0 = 0$. At step $t$, stop with probability $\zeta^t_{\text{stop}}(x \odot h^t)$. Otherwise sample $u^t \sim \zeta^t_{\text{select}}(x \odot h^t)$ and set $h^{t+1} = h^t + u^t$, never removing features, with a forced stop at $T$. Every decision only sees what is already revealed, and the stopping process normalises the distribution automatically. Training uses a step-weighted surrogate,

$$\bar{\mathcal{L}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \sum_{t=0}^{T} p_{\text{stop}}(t \mid \bar H_i)\big[L(f(x_i \odot \bar h_i^t), y_i) + \lambda\lVert \bar h_i^t\rVert\big],$$

with exact gradients for the stop head and REINFORCE for the select head. Any training procedure is allowed. Only the inference procedure carries the guarantee.

Headline findings. (i) On a fully enumerable 10-bit toy problem, L2X, INVASE, TabNet and REAL-X all land strictly beyond the LP's leakage-free Pareto front. Because the front is exact, this proves that they leak; TabNet, for example, predicts perfectly from two features. SUWR sits on the front. (ii) On the Chen et al. synthetic benchmark, SUWR matches oracle AUROC on Syn1–3 and has the best AUROC on Syn4–6. It also selects the control-flow feature $x[11]$ 100% of the time and picks it first. (iii) On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, SUWR beats REAL-X and global CAE at equal budgets. The step-wise trace serves as a "narrative" explanation.

Most interesting part

The critique below is written as a reviewer would.

Strengths.

  • The formalisation is the real contribution, and it is clean. Leakage becomes the conditional independence $\mathbb{1}[E_s] \perp (y, x[s_{\text{ex}}]) \mid x[s_{\text{in}}]$. Once it is stated this way, many informal faithfulness claims become checkable.
  • The LP-based Pareto front is a strong experimental idea. It turns "this method seems too good" into a certificate: any point beyond the front implies leakage, and this holds for any architecture. It is the most persuasive piece of evidence in the paper and could be reused as a standard sanity check.
  • SUWR's guarantee is structural and distribution-free. Theorem C.1 holds for every $p$, every $\zeta_{\text{stop}}, \zeta_{\text{select}}$ and every training method. No assumption on the data is needed for soundness.
  • The "blind first step" result (Eq. 13) is a sharp and somewhat sobering observation. Suppose the support is a full Cartesian product (Eq. 10) and only single-feature masks are allowed. Then any leakage-free policy must have $\zeta(h_{\text{only } i} \mid x)$ constant in $x$. Local selection without leakage is therefore much weaker than the literature assumed. Any adaptivity has to be bought through sequential revelation.

Weaknesses and questionable points.

  • Label leakage is redundant in this formalism, and the paper does not say so. The selector takes only $x$ as input, so $\mathbb{1}[E_s] \perp y \mid x$ holds automatically. Combine that with no feature leakage, $\mathbb{1}[E_s] \perp x[s_{\text{ex}}] \mid x[s_{\text{in}}]$, and the contraction rule gives $\mathbb{1}[E_s] \perp (y, x[s_{\text{ex}}]) \mid x[s_{\text{in}}]$. So no feature leakage implies no label leakage. The paper argues the opposite direction (feature leakage implies label leakage when features correlate with labels) and presents the two concepts as complementary. In practice the label condition only carries weight if the selector could see $y$, for example through a training-time leak or a transductive setting.
  • The proofs of Theorems B.3 and B.4 are one-line applications of Bayes' rule. That is fine, but "rigorously derive the necessary and sufficient conditions" oversells what is essentially a restatement of the definition.
  • Faithfulness depends on the distribution, not on the mechanism. Table 3 shows a policy on one-hot $x$ that selects the single active coordinate. It is leakage-free, because $x[1]=1$ already determines the rest, yet it clearly "looked at" every feature. Conversely, a policy that does look at hidden features may be leakage-free with respect to $p$ but leak under shift. The claim that "each mask is guaranteed to indicate the only features used" holds for SUWR, which is mechanistic, but not for leakage-freeness in general. The two notions of faithfulness, informational and computational, should be separated more explicitly.
  • The population law versus the training sample. The definitions use $p$, while the baselines are trained on finite data. In Experiment 2 the argument that "leakage causes overfitting" is plausible but untested. There is no measurement of leakage on held-out data, for example by estimating $I(h; x[s_{\text{ex}}] \mid x[s_{\text{in}}])$ with a probe, and no train-versus-test gap analysis.
  • Novelty of the algorithm. Sequential acquisition with a stop action, where each step conditions only on what has been acquired, is the template of dynamic feature selection and active feature acquisition. Examples are Covert et al. 2023 and Li & Oliva 2021; classification with costly features and recurrent glimpse models are older instances. By the paper's own Theorem C.1, those methods are also leakage-free. The paper calls this line of work "tangential" because it has a different motivation. The theoretical lens is new, but the claim that SUWR is "the first method without leakage" is really "the first one analysed as such".
  • Evaluation details. Hyperparameters ($T$, $\lambda$) are reported per dataset, and some SUWR runs use $\lambda = 0$. No validation protocol is described, so selection on the test set cannot be ruled out. There are 5 runs, or 3 on MNIST, and no variances are reported. The MNIST models are plain MLPs rather than CNNs. CAE's patch variant is a post-hoc hack: top-$k$ pixels are expanded to $3\times3$ patches. REAL-X doing worse than global CAE is flagged as "speculated overfitting", which may instead point to an implementation problem. There is no text or rationale experiment, even though the rationale literature (Lei et al. 2016; DeYoung et al. 2020) is the most natural testbed, and there is no real tabular dataset.
  • Cost and optimisation. Inference needs up to $T$ sequential forward passes, and REINFORCE over masks has high variance. The first step is blind by necessity, which may hurt in high dimensions. The "narrative explanations" are claimed as a unique benefit, but they are not evaluated with users.
  • The completeness result is only a conjecture (D.3). The authors show that one necessary inequality (Eq. 45) holds under full support but cannot establish Eq. 51. So "SUWR is the only solution" remains unproven.

Proof sketch

Claim 1 (necessary and sufficient conditions, Theorems B.3 and B.4, Corollary 2.5). Assumptions: B.1/B.2, i.e. $p(y \mid x[s_{\text{in}}]) = p(y \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], \zeta)$ and the same for $x[s_{\text{ex}}]$, plus positivity on $\Omega$. Proof: multiply the no-label-leakage identity by $p(E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], \zeta)$ to get

$$p(y \mid x[s_{\text{in}}])\, p(E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}],\zeta) = p(y, E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], \zeta).$$

Divide by $p(y \mid x[s_{\text{in}}],\zeta) > 0$ to obtain $p(E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], \zeta) = p(E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}], y, \zeta)$. Every step reverses. The feature case is identical with $x[s_{\text{ex}}]$ in place of $y$. Corollary 2.5 merges the two. Operationally:

$$\forall x, x', h:\; p(x), p(x') > 0,\; x \odot h = x' \odot h \;\Longrightarrow\; \zeta(h \mid x) = \zeta(h \mid x').$$

A subtlety about the support restriction in $\Omega$: since $p(E_s \mid x[s_{\text{in}}])$ is an average of $\zeta(h \mid x)$ over $x[s_{\text{ex}}]$, equality on the positive-probability part forces the zero-probability part to have measure zero. So the operational form is indeed equivalent.

Claim 2 (Theorem C.1: SUWR has no leakage). Let $q(t, h \mid x)$ be the probability that the process is at step $t$ with mask $h$. Then

$$\zeta(h \mid x) = q(T, h \mid x) + \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} q(t, h \mid x)\, \zeta^t_{\text{stop}}(x \odot h),$$

with $q(0, h \mid x) = \mathbb{1}[h=0]$ and

$$q(t, h \mid x) = \sum_{h' \subseteq h} q(t-1, h' \mid x)\,\big(1 - \zeta^{t-1}_{\text{stop}}(x\odot h')\big) \sum_{u:\, h'+u=h} \zeta^{t-1}_{\text{select}}(u \mid x \odot h').$$

The key trick is no reversion: masks only grow, so every predecessor $h'$ on any path to $h$ satisfies $h' \subseteq h$. Hence $x \odot h'$ is a function of $x \odot h$. By induction on $t$, $q(t, h \mid x)$ depends on $x$ only through $x \odot h$. The final stop factor is also evaluated at $x\odot h$. So $\zeta(h \mid x) = g_h(x \odot h)$, and Corollary 2.5 gives no leakage. Normalisation comes for free because the process is a terminating Markov chain on masks, which sidesteps the partition-function obstruction. If features could be removed, an earlier decision could have depended on a value that ends up hidden, and that is exactly where leakage enters.

Claim 3 (blind single-feature selection). Under the Cartesian support of Eq. 10, a leakage-free policy restricted to single-feature masks satisfies

$$\zeta(h_{\text{only } i} \mid x[i]) = 1 - \sum_{j \neq i} \zeta(h_{\text{only } j} \mid x[j]),$$

so it is constant in $x[i]$. Taking a max over the other coordinates, which full support lets us vary independently, shows it is constant in every coordinate.

Conjecture D.3 (completeness). Under full support, every leakage-free $\zeta$ equals some RDHD SUWR policy (one feature per step, $T = d$, a walk up the subset lattice). The strategy is to set $\zeta_{\text{stop}}(h) = \zeta(h \mid x\odot h)/q(h \mid x \odot h)$. This requires that the probability of reaching $h$ dominates the target probability of $h$. It also requires choosing $\zeta_{\text{select}}(i \mid x\odot h)$ between a lower bound, so that $h^{+i}$ stays reachable, and an upper bound, so that excluded masks keep enough mass. Full support makes the bounds compatible (Eq. 45): the maximising hidden values can be combined into one feasible $x^\star$. The remaining gap is showing that $q$ is never too large relative to $\max_{x[i]}\zeta(h^{+i})$ (Eq. 51). It is proved only for two binary features.

Broader context

Background. Selector-predictor ("select-then-predict", rationale) models descend from Lei et al. (2016) in NLP and L2X/INVASE in tabular ML. Their faithfulness crisis was articulated by Jacovi & Goldberg (2021), Zheng et al. (2022, "irrationality of neural rationale models") and Jethani et al. (2021, 2023). Jethani et al. (2023), "Don't be fooled: label leakage in explanation methods", is the closest conceptual neighbour: it studies leakage in amortised explainers and argues for quantitative evaluation. This paper supplies the formal condition and a mechanism that satisfies it by construction.

Related direction 1: dynamic feature selection and active acquisition. Covert et al. (2023) maximise conditional mutual information greedily, and Li & Oliva (2021) use generative surrogates. Both are structurally SUWR-like and therefore leakage-free by Theorem C.1. A productive synthesis would be to use their CMI-greedy policies as better $\zeta_{\text{select}}$ heads instead of REINFORCE.

Related direction 2: information-theoretic explainers. L2X maximises $I(x_S; y)$, and Paranjape et al. (2020) use an information bottleneck for rationales. These objectives reward exactly the channel that leakage exploits. The leakage definition suggests adding a constraint $I(h; x[s_{\text{ex}}] \mid x[s_{\text{in}}]) = 0$.

Follow-up idea. Replace the binary notion with a graded leakage measure $\epsilon(\zeta) = I(\mathbb{1}[E_s]; x[s_{\text{ex}}] \mid x[s_{\text{in}}])$, estimated with a probe. Then study the accuracy-sparsity-leakage trade-off. Is there a smooth frontier between the LP front at $\epsilon = 0$ and the leaky baselines? This would let practitioners audit existing models rather than replace them. A second idea: when the dependency structure is known (Table 3 style), allow "safe reversion" of features whose values are implied by the revealed ones. That gives a strictly larger leakage-free class than SUWR without full support.

IR connection. The connection to IR is genuine, given the authors' track record. Anand's group builds select-then-rank explainable rankers. An example is Zhang, Rudra & Anand, "Explain and Predict, and then Predict Again" (WSDM 2021), cited here. A related line extracts sentences from a document and scores relevance only from them. Such rankers have exactly the selector-predictor structure, so they are exposed to leakage: which passages get selected can itself encode relevance. A SUWR-style ranker would condition each sentence-selection step only on the query plus the sentences already revealed. The query can be treated as always revealed, so query-dependent selection is allowed. The first step would be query-conditioned but otherwise document-blind, for example by position. In a listwise setting there is a new subtlety: the selection for one document must not depend on other documents' hidden content, or rank information leaks across the list.

A looser analogy, offered as an observation and not as something the paper claims: cascade rankers and progressive or early-exit scoring, where later stages compute features only for candidates chosen from earlier, cheaper features, are "unmasking without reversion" over features. They inherit the same informational guarantee. Coarse-to-fine vector search that reads prefix dimensions of Matryoshka-style embeddings before deciding whether to read more is the fixed-order special case. In that framing, the blind-first-step result says something sensible for vector search: without leakage, the first thing you look at cannot be adapted to the item.

title: Global Minimizers of Sigmoid Contrastive Loss
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-22

Global Minimizers of Sigmoid Contrastive Loss — Kiril Bangachev, Guy Bresler, Iliyas Noman, Yury Polyanskiy (2025) — arXiv:2509.18552

Setting and problem

The object of study. There are $N$ paired data points $\{(X_i, Y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ (image and caption, teacher and student view, query and document). Two encoders $f_\theta : \mathcal X \to \mathbb S^{d-1}$ and $g_\phi : \mathcal Y \to \mathbb S^{d-1}$ produce unit-norm embeddings $U_i = f_\theta(X_i)$ and $V_i = g_\phi(Y_i)$. The training signal is the SigLIP loss, written with inverse temperature $t > 0$ (the paper calls $t$ the inverse temperature, unlike the SigLIP papers) and bias $b \in \mathbb R$:

$$ \mathcal L^{\mathrm{Sig}}(\{(U_i,V_i)\}; t, b) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N \log\!\big(1+e^{-t\langle U_i,V_i\rangle + b}\big) \;+\; \sum_{i\neq j} \log\!\big(1+e^{\,t\langle U_i,V_j\rangle - b}\big). $$

This is a sum of $N^2$ independent binary logistic losses, one per cell of the cross-modal Gram matrix $G_{ij} = \langle U_i, V_j\rangle$. The diagonal cells are labelled positive and the off-diagonal cells negative. Unlike InfoNCE there is no partition function coupling a row, which is why SigLIP parallelises well over the batch.

What is optimized, and over what. The paper uses the standard unconstrained-features idealization (as in Wang and Isola, E and Wojtowytsch, Lu and Steinerberger, Lee et al.): the encoders are assumed expressive enough to output any configuration, so the optimisation is taken directly over $(U_1,\dots,U_N,V_1,\dots,V_N) \in (\mathbb S^{d-1})^{2N}$. The key departure from earlier theory is that $t$ and $b$ are trainable as well, as they are in SigLIP and SigLIP2. The domain is $(\mathbb S^{d-1})^{2N} \times [0,\infty] \times [-\infty,\infty]$. Because the loss is a sum of softplus terms, $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{Sig}} \ge 0$, and the global infimum is $0$. That infimum is reached only in the limit $t \to \infty$. So "global minimizer" means a limit point of a sequence along which the loss tends to $0$, not a stationary point at finite parameters.

The precise question. With $t$ and $b$ trainable, which configurations $\{(U_i,V_i)\}$ on the sphere can drive the sigmoid loss to zero? For a given dimension $d$, how many pairs $N$ can such configurations hold, and with what margin? And what do these configurations imply for retrieval and for the modality gap?

The regime. Earlier analyses either had $d \ge N$ (or $d \ge N+1$), where the answer is a regular simplex, or let $N \to \infty$ with $d$ fixed, where the answer is uniformity on the sphere. The paper argues that the relevant regime is $d \ll N \ll 2^d$; SigLIP2 has $d \approx 10^3$ and $N \approx 10^{10}$. In this regime simplices do not exist, and the minimizers have to be described combinatorially.

What was known. - InfoNCE with fixed temperature. For $d \ge N+1$, the minimizer is $U_i = V_i$ with $\{U_i\}$ forming a regular simplex, i.e. an ETF-like equiangular configuration with $\langle U_i, U_j\rangle = -1/(N-1)$ (E and Wojtowytsch; Lu and Steinerberger). As $N \to \infty$ with $t$ fixed, you get perfect alignment plus a uniform marginal (Wang and Isola, "alignment and uniformity"). - Sigmoid loss with fixed $(t,b)$, $d \ge N$ (Lee, Chang and Sohn, AISTATS 2024). The "double-constant embedding": take a simplex $\{W_i\} \subset \mathbb S^{d-2}$ and set $U_i = (\delta W_i, \sqrt{1-\delta^2})$, $V_i = (\delta W_i, -\sqrt{1-\delta^2})$, with $\delta \in [0,1]$ fixed by $t$ and $b$. Typically the solution collapses either to $\delta = 1$ (aligned) or to $\delta = 0$ (antipodal, all $U_i$ equal). - Empirically, CLIP and SigLIP embeddings show a modality gap: image and text embeddings sit in disjoint, linearly separable regions (Liang et al. 2022; Fahim et al. 2025). Fahim et al. argue the gap comes from the loss itself, not from architectural mismatch.

The gap this paper fills. No existing result covers trainable $(t,b)$ with $N > d$. Existing characterizations are rigid: a simplex, or perfect alignment. They cannot explain the modality gap, and they say nothing about what happens when one encoder is locked (as in LiT), since you cannot then force a simplex.

Modelling choices worth flagging. 1. Unconstrained features. The networks drop out entirely. The results concern the loss landscape over point configurations, not what SGD on transformers finds, and they say nothing about generalisation to unseen pairs. 2. Zero loss as the target. Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 describe the zero-loss set, which is reached only as $t \to \infty$ with $b/t$ converging. The interesting parameter is the ratio $b_{\mathrm{rel}} = b/t$, not $b$ itself. 3. Strictly one-to-one positives. Each $U_i$ has exactly one positive $V_i$, so the label matrix is the identity. The ImageNet experiments actually have 50,000 images and only 1,000 class captions, which is many-to-one. That deviates from the model; see the caveats below. 4. Full-batch loss. The loss is taken over all $N^2$ pairs. Batches appear only in the robustness result, Proposition 1.

Main idea

With $t$ and $b$ both free, the loss stops caring about the exact geometry of the configuration. All it can still see is a binary question: is there a single scalar threshold that puts every positive inner product above every negative one? If such a threshold exists, push $t \to \infty$ with $b = t\,b_{\mathrm{rel}}$. Every logistic term then becomes $\log(1 + e^{-t\cdot\text{(margin)}}) \to 0$. If no threshold exists, some term stays bounded away from $0$.

This gives the central definition. A $(d, m, b_{\mathrm{rel}})$-Constellation is a configuration $\{(U_i,V_i)\}_{i=1}^N \subset \mathbb S^{d-1}$ with

$$ \langle U_i, V_i\rangle \ge b_{\mathrm{rel}} + m \;\; \forall i, \qquad \langle U_i, V_j\rangle \le b_{\mathrm{rel}} - m \;\; \forall i \neq j . $$

Some $(m \ge 0, b_{\mathrm{rel}})$ exists exactly when $\min_i \langle U_i,V_i\rangle \ge \max_{i\neq j}\langle U_i,V_j\rangle$, and the zero-loss set is exactly the set of constellations. This is precisely the "globally thresholdable" property of Weller et al. (2025), now with a margin attached. The same reasoning for one-sided InfoNCE gives a weaker, row-wise version, in which each query $i$ gets its own threshold $b_{\mathrm{rel}}(i)$.

Once the loss is reduced to this set, the rest of the paper is combinatorial geometry on the sphere: - Capacity. How large can $N$ be for given $(d, m, b_{\mathrm{rel}})$? The answer is exponential in $d$, with an exponent sandwiched between a spherical-code lower bound and a cap-averaging upper bound. Feasibility requires $m + b_{\mathrm{rel}} \le 1$ and $3m \le 1 + b_{\mathrm{rel}}$, which is the triangle in their Figure 3. - Retrieval. In any constellation, exact nearest-neighbour search retrieves the correct partner. Any approximation error below the margin is tolerated. - Modality gap. If the threshold region excludes $0$ (that is, $m > |b_{\mathrm{rel}}|$, so positives have positive inner product and negatives have negative inner product) and $N \ge d+2$, then a hyperplane separates all the $U$'s from all but at most $d$ of the $V$'s. Helly and Carathéodory force this. - Practice. The authors propose parameterising the loss directly in $(t, b_{\mathrm{rel}})$, so the bias term is $t\,b_{\mathrm{rel}}$. They show that a modality-specific affine adapter $X \mapsto (\delta X, \pm\sqrt{1-\delta^2})$ is absorbed exactly by reparameterising $(t, b_{\mathrm{rel}})$. On synthetic data, training in this parameterisation converges faster and reaches larger margins. Fixing $b_{\mathrm{rel}}$ steers which constellation is found.

The most interesting part

The most interesting part, to me, is how trainable $(t,b)$ turn a smooth, temperature-dependent energy into a pure ordering/threshold condition, and how the margin then sets the exponential rate. Theorem 3.2 gives

$$ \inf_b \mathcal L^{\mathrm{Sig}} = e^{-t m^\ast + o(t)}, \qquad m^\ast = \tfrac12\big(\min_i \langle U_i,V_i\rangle - \max_{i\ne j}\langle U_i,V_j\rangle\big), $$

with optimal bias $b \approx t\, b^\ast_{\mathrm{rel}}$, where $b^\ast_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is the midpoint between the worst positive and the worst negative. My reading, not something the paper states, is that at large $t$ the sigmoid loss with optimised bias behaves like a soft-max of hinge violations. Minimising over configurations at large $t$ is then asymptotically the same as maximising the hard margin $m^\ast$ of a single global threshold on the Gram matrix. This is the contrastive analogue of the implicit max-margin bias of logistic regression on separable data (Soudry et al. 2018). Here, though, it is the representations themselves that are being "SVM-ed", with the threshold shared by every query.

This viewpoint pays off in three ways.

  1. Constellations are a two-parameter generalisation of spherical codes. If $U_i = V_i = X_i$, then $\{X_i\}$ being a $(d,\alpha)$-code (all pairwise inner products at most $\alpha$) is the same as being a $\big(\tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}, \tfrac{1+\alpha}{2}\big)$-constellation. That covers only the line $m + b_{\mathrm{rel}} = 1$. Lifting with two extra coordinates (Construction 1), $U_i' = (\delta U_i, \phi, \sqrt{1-\delta^2-\phi^2})$ and $V_i' = (\delta V_i, \phi, -\sqrt{1-\delta^2-\phi^2})$, reaches the whole feasible triangle. Every point strictly inside is realised by a constellation of size exponential in $d$. Decades of results on spherical codes thereby become statements about how many items a SigLIP-style embedding of dimension $d$ can hold at a given margin.

  2. The modality gap is a theorem rather than an artifact. In the regime $N \ge d+2$, with "positives positive, negatives negative", the two modalities have to be almost linearly separable. The argument is purely convex-geometric (Helly, separation, Carathéodory) and is essentially tight: Construction 3 has $d-1$ inseparable points. Alignment ($U_i = V_i$) is therefore not merely unnecessary at zero loss; outside the $|b_{\mathrm{rel}}| \ge m$ corner it is incompatible with these sign constraints. For example, with $U_i = V_i$ you get $\langle U_i, V_i\rangle = 1$, so you would need $\langle U_i, U_j\rangle < 0$ for all $N \ge d+2$ points, which is impossible by Rankin. That is the pithy slogan "synchronize, do not align". The constructions realise the gap with a constant offset: $U_i - V_i = (0, 0, 2\sqrt{1-\delta^2-\phi^2})$ for every $i$. In the appendix the authors read this as a cross-modal "linear representation hypothesis", meaning a single shift vector maps text to image. Both the upper and the lower capacity bound are tight only for configurations with constant $U_i - V_i$.

  3. The bias is a geometric quantity, not a nuisance offset. It locates the decision threshold inside $[-1,1]$, and together with $m$ it decides feasibility ($3m \le 1 + b_{\mathrm{rel}}$), capacity, and whether a gap is forced. The empirical observation that Adam on the standard $(t,b)$ parameterisation drifts toward $b_{\mathrm{rel}} \approx 0$ matters, then, because $b_{\mathrm{rel}} = 0$ caps the margin at $m \le 1/3$. A positive $b_{\mathrm{rel}}$ allows larger margins; their Table 4 finds the best margin, about $0.54$, at a fixed $b_{\mathrm{rel}} \approx 0.7$–$0.8$ for $N = 100$, $d = 10$.

Proof sketch

Notation: $\mathcal L = \mathcal L^{\mathrm{Sig}}$. The basic sandwich (Observation 3), immediate from non-negativity of softplus, is: the largest single term $\le \mathcal L \le N^2 \times$ the largest single term.

Theorem 3.1 (every zero-loss limit is a constellation). - Statement. Let $(U^{(s)}, V^{(s)}, t^{(s)} > 0, b^{(s)})$ be any sequence with $\mathcal L \to 0$. Then along a subsequence $U_i^{(s)} \to U_i$, $V_i^{(s)} \to V_i$ and $b^{(s)}/t^{(s)} \to b_{\mathrm{rel}} \in [-1,1]$. The limit satisfies the constellation inequalities for some $m \ge 0$. - Proof. Each term tends to $0$, so $t^{(s)}(\langle U_i,V_i\rangle - b^{(s)}/t^{(s)}) \to +\infty$ and $t^{(s)}(\langle U_i,V_j\rangle - b^{(s)}/t^{(s)}) \to -\infty$. Eventually positives sit above $b^{(s)}/t^{(s)}$ and negatives below it, which forces $b^{(s)}/t^{(s)} \in [-1,1]$. Compactness of $(\mathbb S^{d-1})^{2N} \times [-1,1]$ gives a convergent subsequence. The weak inequalities survive the limit. Note that the limit may have $m = 0$: strict separation along the sequence can degenerate.

Theorem 3.2 (every constellation is a global minimizer, at a sharp rate). - Statement. If (2) holds with $m > 0$, then $\mathcal L(U,V; t, t\,b_{\mathrm{rel}}) \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$. More precisely, $\inf_b \mathcal L = e^{-t m^\ast + o(t)}$, attained at $b = t\, b^\ast_{\mathrm{rel}} + o(t)$, where $b^\ast_{\mathrm{rel}} = \tfrac12(\min_i \langle U_i,V_i\rangle + \max_{i\ne j}\langle U_i,V_j\rangle)$. - Proof. Upper bound: every logit is at most $-tm$, so $\mathcal L \le N^2 \log(1+e^{-tm}) \le e^{-tm + 2\log N}$. Lower bound: by the sandwich, it is enough to show that the largest logit is at least $-tm^\ast$ for every $b$. If it were not, the gap between the worst positive and the worst negative would exceed $2m^\ast$, contradicting the definition of $m^\ast$. Note that the $o(t)$ hides a $2\log N$ term, so for $N \approx 10^{10}$ the asymptotics kick in only once $t m^\ast \gg 46$.

Corollary 1 and Proposition 1 (retrieval). - At zero loss, $V_i$ is a nearest neighbour of $U_i$ among $\{V_j\}$, and it is the unique one if $m > 0$. Moreover, the gap between positive and negative scores is at least $2m$, so any approximate scoring with error below $m$ per inner product still retrieves correctly. - Robust version. Suppose the expected batch loss, over uniformly random $B$-tuples of distinct indices with $\sqrt N < B < N$, is at most $\varepsilon \log 2$. (The paper writes $\xi$; I rename it to avoid a clash with the $\xi$ of Appendix E.) Then for at least a $1 - N\varepsilon/(B(B-1))$ fraction of the $i$, nearest-neighbour search returns the correct partner. Proof: a misordered pair costs at least $\log 2$, then Markov's inequality is applied separately to the positive and negative terms, and finally counting over rows.

Theorem 3.3 (lower bound on capacity). - Statement. If $m + b_{\mathrm{rel}} < 1$ and $3m < 1 + b_{\mathrm{rel}}$, then with $\alpha = \frac{1 + b_{\mathrm{rel}} - 3m}{1 + b_{\mathrm{rel}} + m}$, $$ E_{\mathrm{MRB}}(m, b_{\mathrm{rel}}) := \liminf_{d\to\infty} \tfrac1d \log N_{\mathrm{MRB}}(d,m,b_{\mathrm{rel}}) \;\ge\; E_{\mathrm{SC}}(\alpha) \;\ge\; -\tfrac12 \log\big(1-\alpha^2\big). $$ - Proof. Take an $\alpha$-spherical code in $\mathbb S^{d-3}$ of size $e^{d(E_{\mathrm{SC}}(\alpha) + o(1))}$; the Shannon–Wyner random-coding bound gives $E_{\mathrm{SC}}(\alpha) \ge -\tfrac12\log(1-\alpha^2)$. Set $U_i = V_i = X_i$ and apply Construction 1 with $\delta^2 = 2m/(1-\alpha)$ and $\phi^2 = (2b_{\mathrm{rel}} + 2 - \delta^2(3+\alpha))/4$. The extracted text shows $\delta$ where $\delta^2$ is meant; with $\delta^2$ the algebra closes. The lift maps margin $\frac{1-\alpha}{2} \mapsto \delta^2\frac{1-\alpha}{2} = m$. It maps relative bias $\frac{1+\alpha}{2} \mapsto \delta^2\frac{1+\alpha}{2} + \phi^2 - (1-\delta^2-\phi^2) = b_{\mathrm{rel}}$. The two feasibility inequalities are what guarantee $\delta^2, \phi^2 > 0$ and $\delta^2 + \phi^2 \le 1$, so the lift is well defined. Theorem 3.4 then shows these inequalities are necessary, not an artefact of the construction.

Theorem 3.4 (the feasible region; a Rankin-type bound). - Statement. If only the averaged constraints hold, $\frac1N\sum_i \langle U_i,V_i\rangle \ge m + b_{\mathrm{rel}}$ and $\frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\ne j}\langle U_i,V_j\rangle \le b_{\mathrm{rel}} - m$, then $m + b_{\mathrm{rel}} \le 1$ and $3m \le 1 + b_{\mathrm{rel}} + o(1)$. - Proof. The first inequality is Cauchy–Schwarz. For the second, write $x_i = U_i - V_i$, $A = \sum_i \langle U_i,V_i\rangle$, $B = \sum_{i\ne j}\langle U_i,V_j\rangle$ and $\xi = \frac1N\sum_i\|x_i\|^2 - \|\frac1N\sum_i x_i\|^2 \ge 0$. A direct expansion gives the identity $$ \Big\|\sum_i (U_i + V_i)\Big\|^2 = N^2(2 - \xi) - 2(N-2)A + 4B . $$ Since the left side is non-negative and $\xi \ge 0$, we get $4B \ge 2(N-2)A - 2N^2$. Plugging in the constraints gives $(3 - 4/N)m \le 1 + b_{\mathrm{rel}}$. The bound is tight only when $\sum_i(U_i+V_i) = 0$ and $\xi = 0$, that is, when all differences $U_i - V_i$ are equal: the constant-shift structure again.

Theorem 3.5 (upper bound on capacity). - Statement. In the same feasible region, every $(m,b_{\mathrm{rel}})$-constellation has $$ N \le \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac d2 \log\big(1 - \alpha\big) + o(d)\Big), \qquad \alpha = \tfrac{1+b_{\mathrm{rel}}-3m}{1+b_{\mathrm{rel}}+m}. $$ - Proof. This is a localised version of the Rankin argument (cap-averaging, in the spirit of the elementary Rankin and Kabatiansky–Levenshtein-type reductions). - Work with the midpoints $c_i = (U_i+V_i)/2$, which satisfy $\|c_i\|^2 \ge (1+m+b_{\mathrm{rel}})/2$. - Draw a uniform random direction $H$ and keep the sub-constellation $C = \{i : \langle c_i, H\rangle > \delta\}$. Its expected size is at least $N\,\Gamma_d\big(\delta\sqrt{2/(1+m+b_{\mathrm{rel}})}\big)$, where $\Gamma_d(x) = \Pr[H_1 > x]$ is a spherical cap probability. - Inside the cap, $\|\sum_{i\in C}(U_i+V_i)\| > 2|C|\delta$. Combined with the identity above, this gives $|C| \le 4m / (2\delta^2 - (1 - 3m + b_{\mathrm{rel}}))$, so a cap can hold only $O(1)$ points. - Hence $N \lesssim \Gamma_d(\cdot)^{-1}$. Shannon's estimate $\Gamma_d(\cos\theta) = e^{d\log\sin\theta + o(d)}$, with $\delta$ chosen optimally, gives the bound. - Quantitatively, the lower and upper exponents are $-\tfrac12\log(1-\alpha^2)$ and $-\tfrac12\log(1-\alpha)$. They differ by the factor $(1+\alpha)$ inside the logarithm. The paper writes $\log_2$ in one place and $\log$ in the other, so read both in the same base. - For $b_{\mathrm{rel}} = 0$ and $m = 0.1$ we get $\alpha \approx 0.636$. That is roughly $0.37$ to $0.73$ bits per dimension, so with $d = 1000$ somewhere between $2^{375}$ and $2^{730}$ pairs. The capacity is astronomically larger than $10^{10}$.

Theorem 3.6 (modality gap). - Statement. Let $N \ge d+2$, with $\langle U_i,V_i\rangle > 0$ for all $i$ and $\langle U_i,V_j\rangle < 0$ for all $i \ne j$. This holds for instance in any constellation with $m > |b_{\mathrm{rel}}|$, or in the InfoNCE analogue with $|b_{\mathrm{rel}}(i)| < m$. Then there is $h \in \mathbb S^{d-1}$ with $\langle h, U_i\rangle > 0$ for all $i$ and $\langle h, V_j\rangle < 0$ for at least $N-d$ indices $j$. - Proof. 1. Helly. Consider the open half-spaces $H_i = \{x : \langle U_i,x\rangle > 0\}$. Any $d+1$ of them intersect: since $N \ge d+2$ there is an index $j$ outside the chosen ones, and $-V_j$ lies in all of them because $\langle U_{i_k}, V_j\rangle < 0$. So all $N$ intersect, and some $h$ is positive on every $U_i$. 2. Separation. Project $h$ onto $\mathrm{conv}(U_1,\dots,U_N)$. The supporting-hyperplane argument shows the projection $h'$ is still positive on every $U_i$, and it now lies in the convex hull. 3. Carathéodory. Rescale $h'$ to the affine slice $\{x : \langle x, h\rangle = 1\}$ of the cone of the $U$'s. It is a convex combination of at most $d$ rescaled points $U_i/\langle U_i,h\rangle$, for $i \in S$ with $|S| \le d$. For every $k \notin S$, $\langle h^\dagger, V_k\rangle = \sum_{i\in S}\lambda_i \langle U_i,V_k\rangle/\langle U_i,h\rangle < 0$, because every numerator is negative. - Tightness (Construction 3): two nearly parallel $k$-gons in $d = 3$, plus padding to higher $d$, give configurations where $d-1$ of the $V$'s cannot be separated. - Side facts: no $U_i$ lies in the cone of the others (Proposition 4), and no such configuration exists in $d = 2$ with $N \ge 4$ (Proposition 5).

InfoNCE and triplet loss (Appendix A). - With trainable $t$, one-sided InfoNCE reaches zero loss exactly on row-wise thresholdable configurations: $\langle U_i,V_i\rangle \ge b_{\mathrm{rel}}(i)+m$ and $\langle U_i,V_j\rangle \le b_{\mathrm{rel}}(i)-m$. - Symmetric InfoNCE requires $\langle U_i,V_j\rangle \le \min(b_{\mathrm{rel}}(i), b_{\mathrm{rel}}(j)) - m$. - The proof rewrites the loss as $\frac1N\sum_i \log(1+\sum_{j\ne i} e^{t(\langle U_i,V_j\rangle - \langle U_i,V_i\rangle)})$ and reuses the compactness argument; $t \to \infty$ is forced. - Zero-loss sets of InfoNCE and triplet loss coincide, with margins related by a constant factor. Sigmoid zero-loss configurations form a strict subset of both (Observations 4–6).

Observations 1–2 (adapters as reparameterisations). - Locked encoder. Let $A^\delta_{\mathrm{lock}}(x) = (\delta x, \sqrt{1-\delta^2})$ and $A^\delta_{\mathrm{train}}(x) = (\delta x, -\sqrt{1-\delta^2})$. Then $\langle A_{\mathrm{lock}}U, A_{\mathrm{train}}V\rangle = \delta^2\langle U,V\rangle - (1-\delta^2)$. Hence $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{RB}}(A U, A V; t, b_{\mathrm{rel}}) = \mathcal L^{\mathrm{RB}}(U,V; t\delta^2, (b_{\mathrm{rel}} + 1 - \delta^2)/\delta^2)$. The extracted text writes $(1-\delta)^2$, which looks like a typo for $1-\delta^2$. - $k$ modalities. Append $\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\,w_j$, where the $w_j$ are vertices of a regular simplex with $\langle w_j,w_{j'}\rangle = -1/(k-1)$. Then $1-\delta^2$ is replaced by $(1-\delta^2)/(k-1)$. - So the explicit adapter adds nothing beyond what trainable $(t, b_{\mathrm{rel}})$ already express. This is why trainable temperature and bias let you synchronise with any locked set of distinct embeddings.

Broader context

Background. The theory of contrastive representation learning has mostly followed three lines. 1. Population-level analyses, where InfoNCE is a mutual-information bound (CPC, InfoMax) or recovers approximate sufficient statistics. 2. Downstream-guarantee analyses: Saunshi et al. 2019 on latent classes; HaoChen et al. 2021 on spectral contrastive loss. 3. Geometric analyses of minimizers: alignment and uniformity in the $N \to \infty$ limit, and simplex or neural-collapse-type structure when $d \ge N$ (E and Wojtowytsch; Lu and Steinerberger; Lee et al. for sigmoid; Papyan, Han and Donoho for neural collapse in supervised learning).

This paper belongs to the third line. It is the first to handle trainable temperature and bias, and the first to handle $N \gg d$ explicitly. The tools are classical: spherical codes, Rankin's bound and Shannon's cap estimates from coding theory, plus Helly and Carathéodory from convex geometry.

Related directions. - Weller, Boratko, Naim and Lee 2025, "On the theoretical limitations of embedding-based retrieval" (the LIMIT paper). It links the embedding dimension needed to realise a query–document relevance matrix $A \in \{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ under top-$k$ retrieval to the sign-rank of $2A - \mathbf 1$. It distinguishes "row-wise thresholdable" from "globally thresholdable" realisations, and sandwiches both of the corresponding minimal dimensions within one of the sign-rank. This paper shows that SigLIP's zero-loss set is exactly the globally thresholdable realisations with margin $m$, and one-sided InfoNCE's is exactly the row-wise ones. That puts a training-objective interpretation on the LIMIT taxonomy. - Liang et al. 2022 ("Mind the gap") and Fahim et al. 2025 on the modality gap. Liang et al. attribute the gap partly to the cone effect at initialisation, preserved by low temperature. This paper gives a complementary, loss-geometric explanation for the zero-loss regime. - Implicit max-margin bias (Soudry et al. 2018; Ji and Telgarsky). Theorem 3.2's $e^{-t m^\ast}$ rate suggests that gradient dynamics on unnormalised logits might converge in direction to the max-margin constellation. The paper does not prove anything about dynamics.

Connections to dense retrieval, vector search and embedding geometry. These are concrete, but some are my extrapolations rather than the paper's claims.

  1. Thresholded retrieval and calibration. The bias is literally a global relevance cutoff. A SigLIP-style objective with trainable $b$ asks for scores that are comparable across queries: one number $b_{\mathrm{rel}}$ separates relevant from non-relevant pairs for every query. InfoNCE only asks for per-query ranking, so a query-dependent offset can be absorbed. In IR terms, sigmoid is pointwise, calibrated relevance and InfoNCE is listwise ranking. This matters wherever a fixed score cutoff is used: range search ($\varepsilon$-NN), deciding when to return nothing, filtered or hybrid retrieval with score fusion, cascades that prune by score. The theory says the sigmoid objective is the one whose zero-loss set supports a single global cutoff. The caveat is that the theorem is about training pairs with one positive each, not held-out queries.

  2. Margin as a budget for ANN error, quantisation and compression. The positive/negative gap is at least $2m$. So any approximate scoring whose per-pair error is below $m$ preserves exact top-1: product or scalar quantisation, low-bit codes, random projection. A quick consequence, which the paper does not state: by Johnson–Lindenstrauss, a margin-$m$ constellation survives a random projection to $k = O(m^{-2}\log N)$ dimensions with margin about $m/2$. That mirrors the exponential capacity of Theorems 3.3 and 3.5. Real SigLIP models have tiny margins after trimming 5% outliers ($m \approx 0.010$–$0.014$ in Table 1), which suggests they are far from capacity-limited and that much of the dimension is not "used" for this one-to-one task. The appendix makes the same point: $\xi$ is far from $0$ in trained models.

  3. Dimension versus number of items: margin complexity rather than sign-rank. A striking point for the LIMIT line of work: for the identity relevance pattern (one positive per query), dimension is not the bottleneck without a margin. With $U_i = V_i$ on a circle in $d = 2$, any $N$ is globally thresholdable as the threshold approaches $1$. Dimension only matters through the margin, and Theorems 3.3 and 3.5 make this precise: $\log N = \Theta_{m,b_{\mathrm{rel}}}(d)$. This is the margin-complexity side of the sign-rank coin (Ben-David, Eiron and Simon 2002; Linial, Mendelson, Schechtman and Shraibman 2007; Forster's bound). It suggests the right measure for a trained retriever is margin complexity, perhaps a $\gamma_2$-type norm of the qrel sign matrix, not sign-rank alone. Gradient training at finite $t$, quantisation and ANN all need margin, and margin is what costs dimension.

  4. The modality gap is the query/document distribution shift in vector search. Theorem 3.6 says that at zero loss, in the "positives positive" regime, queries and documents live in nearly disjoint half-spaces. That is exactly the out-of-distribution-query setting that hurts graph-based ANN indexes built on documents only. Cross-modal ANNS work such as RoarGraph (Chen et al., VLDB 2024) and OOD-DiskANN observe this gap empirically and build query-aware graphs to cope with it. This paper suggests the gap is structural to the loss rather than a training accident, so ANN methods should treat it as a design constraint. The constant-shift structure ($U_i - V_i \approx \bar x$) in the tight constructions also hints that a single learned translation could re-centre queries before index traversal, when it holds.

  5. Generative retrieval and softmax over item identifiers. A generative retriever with a learned docid embedding table and a softmax output layer is, at the last layer, one-sided InfoNCE: query states $U_i$, docid embeddings $V_j$. Appendix A then says its zero-loss set is row-wise thresholdable, not globally thresholdable. That gives no calibrated cross-query cutoff, a known practical pain point for generative retrieval. It also suggests that dimension and capacity bounds for docid tables should come from row-wise margin versions of Problem 1. Problem 1 itself is the global-threshold capacity problem, with general $(m,b_{\mathrm{rel}})$ in place of the spherical-code line.

A plausible follow-up. Generalise Problem 1 from the identity label matrix to an arbitrary bipartite relevance matrix $A \in \{0,1\}^{n_q \times n_d}$. Define an $(m, b_{\mathrm{rel}})$-realisation by $\langle U_i, V_j\rangle \ge b_{\mathrm{rel}} + m$ if $A_{ij} = 1$, and $\le b_{\mathrm{rel}} - m$ otherwise. Then: - Characterise the minimal $d$ as a function of $m$ and combinatorial parameters of $A$ (degree, VC dimension, or the $\gamma_2$ norm), giving a margin-aware refinement of the sign-rank bounds in LIMIT. - Prove the analogue of Theorem 3.6 for multi-positive data. - Test whether fixing $b_{\mathrm{rel}} > 0$ in the relative-bias parameterisation enlarges the trained margin, and so improves robustness to quantised ANN, on real retrieval benchmarks such as MS MARCO, BEIR or LIMIT itself. The paper's relative-bias experiments are only synthetic ($N = 100$, $d = 10$).

A second, more theoretical follow-up: prove that gradient flow on $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{RB}}$ with trainable $t$ converges in direction to a KKT point of the max-margin constellation problem. This would be the contrastive analogue of the Lyu–Li result for homogeneous networks.

Caveats to keep in mind. 1. The modality-gap theorem needs $m > |b_{\mathrm{rel}}|$. With the trimmed statistics in Table 1, the trained SigLIP models actually have $b_{\mathrm{rel}} \approx 0.024$–$0.063$, larger than $m \approx 0.010$–$0.014$. The hypothesis holds only for the mean-based statistics of Table 2, and only marginally for so400m. The perfect linear separability observed empirically is therefore consistent with the theorem but not implied by it. 2. The ImageNet evaluation pairs 50,000 images with 1,000 class captions, which violates the one-positive-per-row model. 3. Everything is in the zero-loss, unconstrained-features idealisation. Nothing is proved about optimisation or generalisation. The capacity exponent is pinned down only up to the gap between $-\tfrac12\log(1-\alpha^2)$ and $-\tfrac12\log(1-\alpha)$.

title: Posterior Network: Uncertainty Estimation without OOD Samples via Density-Based Pseudo-Counts
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-22

Posterior Network: Uncertainty Estimation without OOD Samples via Density-Based Pseudo-Counts — Bertrand Charpentier, Daniel Zügner, Stephan Günnemann (2020) — arXiv:2006.09239

Setting and problem

Object of study. Multi-class classification with uncertainty. The input is $x \in \mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^D$ and the label is $y \in \{1, \dots, C\}$. The learner gets a labelled training set $\mathcal{D} = \{(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^N$ with class counts $N_c = \sum_i \mathbb{1}[y^{(i)} = c]$, so $N = \sum_c N_c$. It gets no out-of-distribution (OOD) examples of any kind: no auxiliary outlier set, no noise images, no held-out classes. For every test input it must return a distribution over categorical distributions, i.e. a second-order prediction. The setup follows the "evidential" or "Dirichlet-based" view:

  • epistemic distribution: $p^{(i)} \sim q^{(i)}$, where $p^{(i)} \in \Delta^{C-1}$ is the unknown class-probability vector at $x^{(i)}$;
  • aleatoric distribution: $y^{(i)} \sim \mathrm{Cat}(\bar p^{(i)})$ with $\bar p^{(i)} = \mathbb{E}_{q^{(i)}}[p^{(i)}]$.

Dirichlet-based models set $q^{(i)} = \mathrm{Dir}(\alpha^{(i)})$ with $\alpha^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^C_{+}$. One forward pass then gives everything: $\bar p^{(i)}_c = \alpha^{(i)}_c / \alpha^{(i)}_0$ with $\alpha^{(i)}_0 = \sum_c \alpha^{(i)}_c$, the prediction $\hat y = \arg\max_c \bar p^{(i)}_c$, and closed-form uncertainty scores. The paper uses $\max_c \bar p_c$ (or the entropy of $\bar p$) as the aleatoric score and $\alpha_0$ (or $\max_c \alpha_c$) as the epistemic score.

The model has three parts:
