How $b$ and $\eta$ trade off. In the bound, $\eta$ appears linearly in the "progress" $\sum\eta_t$ and quadratically in the noise $\sum\eta_t^2\sigma^2/b_t$. Increasing $b$ by $\delta$ per stage buys room to increase $\eta$ by up to $\sqrt\delta$ per stage while keeping the noise sum convergent. The ceiling on the whole construction is $\eta_{\max} < 2/\bar L$.

Broader context

Background and placement. The paper gives a non-asymptotic, nonconvex justification of the folklore that batch growth can replace LR decay (Smith et al. 2018), and of square-root-flavoured joint scaling. Its condition $\gamma^2 < \delta$ sits strictly between "keep $\eta^2/b$ fixed" (square-root scaling, also derived from SDE arguments by Malladi et al. 2022 for adaptive methods) and Smith et al.'s "keep $\eta/b$ fixed when trading one for the other". Linear scaling $\gamma = \delta$ is outside the theorem.

Related directions. 1. Critical batch size and compute-optimal batching. McCandlish et al. (2018) and Shallue et al. (2019) frame the question in exactly the compute-versus-steps terms the paper omits. Below the gradient noise scale, larger batches cut steps almost for free in compute; above it they waste samples. The Cauchy–Schwarz argument above is the worst-case version of this: under bounded variance the noise scale never binds, and step savings are never free in the bound. A theory that predicts acceleration in compute must use a richer noise model, such as state-dependent variance $\mathbb{E}\|g - \nabla f\|^2 \le \sigma^2 + \rho\|\nabla f\|^2$, interpolation, or a Hessian-weighted noise scale. 2. Adaptive batching and hybrid methods. Friedlander and Schmidt (2012), Byrd et al. (2012), Bollapragada et al. (2018) and De et al. (2017) grow $b$ adaptively, for example by a norm test $\mathrm{Var}(g)/b \le \theta^2\|\nabla f\|^2$, and give sample-complexity rather than step-complexity guarantees. Under strong convexity, geometric growth gives linear convergence at the optimal overall sample cost. That is the convex analogue the present paper could have compared with. 3. Warm-up theory. Explanations of warm-up rely on local or adaptive curvature (edge-of-stability dynamics; $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness of Zhang et al. 2020; recent "why warm up" analyses; RAdam's variance argument for Adam). Under global $\bar L$-smoothness, as here, warm-up can only lose in the bound. A convincing theory of Case (iv) needs curvature that decreases along the trajectory.

Follow-up idea. Restate the paper's schedule family in IFO terms with the hard caps $b_t \le n$ and $\eta_t \le \eta_{\max}$, under a state-dependent noise model $\sigma_t^2 = \sigma_0^2 + \rho\|\nabla f(\theta_t)\|^2$ or a local-smoothness model $L(\theta) \le L_0 + L_1\|\nabla f(\theta)\|$. Then ask whether jointly increasing $(b,\eta)$ can beat constant-batch SGD in IFO. The answer should be yes exactly when the effective curvature or noise shrinks during training, which would turn the paper's per-step story into a compute-optimal schedule (an "online critical batch size" controller). A cheap empirical counterpart: rerun Fig. 3 with a Case (ii) baseline at constant $\eta = \eta_{\max}$ and plot against samples seen and against wall-clock time, to separate the larger-LR effect from the joint-growth effect.

IR connection (honest, with caveats). For generative retrieval trained with token-level cross-entropy (docid generation), the setup is ordinary ERM with fixed per-example losses, so the results apply as stated, with all the caveats above. For dense retrievers trained contrastively with in-batch negatives (DPR, RocketQA cross-batch negatives, GradCache-style large-batch training), the transfer is not direct. The InfoNCE loss with in-batch negatives depends on $b$, $\ell_i^{(b)}(\theta) = -\log \frac{e^{s(q_i,d_i)}}{\sum_{j\le b} e^{s(q_i,d_j)}}$, so increasing $b$ changes the objective itself and not only the variance of a fixed objective's gradient. The mini-batch gradient is a biased estimator of the full-softmax objective (log of a sample mean), so (A2)–(A3) fail and the $\sigma^2/b$ decomposition no longer holds. An honest extension would add a bias term $\beta(b)$ to Lemma 2.1, with $\beta(b)$ shrinking as $b$ grows toward the full softmax. Growing $b$ then reduces both bias and variance, which could justify batch-growth schedules for retriever training. That is a different theorem, and the paper's $\gamma^2<\delta$ rule should not be imported as is. A caveat in the other direction: GradCache-type large-batch training is usually motivated by objective quality (more negatives), not by optimisation speed, so the relevant question there is about the bias-versus-compute trade-off rather than about step counts.

title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity

Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-21

Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity — Catteau, Duranthon, Zdeborová (2026) — arXiv:2611.26228

Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity

Catteau, Duranthon, Zdeborová (EPFL, SPOC lab), arXiv:2611.26228, Nov 2026. Code: github.com/SPOC-group/Attention-head-specialization.

Setting and problem

The empirical motivation. Specialized attention heads (induction heads, syntactic heads, functionally differentiated heads) are usually studied as a function of training time: they appear in stages, often together with abrupt loss drops (Olsson et al. 2022; Chen et al. 2024a "Sudden drops in the loss"; Hoogland et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025; Aoyama et al. 2026). The paper asks the orthogonal question: how does specialization depend on the amount of data? This separates a statistical question (what is learnable from $N$ samples at the optimum of the objective) from a dynamical one (what a given optimizer finds when). The physics framing is that only in a proportional high-dimensional limit can "emergence" be a genuine phase transition, i.e. a non-analyticity of macroscopic observables at a critical sample ratio.

Data model (multi-feature spiked single-location regression, from Sagitova et al. 2026). Embedding dimension $D$. Draw $F$ fixed latent directions $k_f^* \sim \mathcal N(0, I_D)$, stacked as rows of $K^* \in \mathbb R^{F\times D}$, with $K^*K^{*\top}/D \to I_F$. A sequence $X \in \mathbb R^{L\times D}$ has $L$ tokens. For each sequence, independently draw a location $\epsilon \sim \mathrm{Unif}([L])$ and feature weights $\theta \sim P_\theta$ on $\mathbb R^F$, and set $$\hat k = \frac{K^{*\top}\theta}{\sqrt D}, \qquad X_\ell \sim \mathcal N(\delta_{\ell\epsilon}\,\hat k,\ I_D), \quad \ell \in [L].$$ The label is the relevant token itself, $y = X_\epsilon \in \mathbb R^D$. Note the scaling: $\|\hat k\|_2 = \Theta(1)$ while $\|X_\ell\|_2 \approx \sqrt D$, so the spike is invisible in norms; it only shows up in projections $k^\top X_\epsilon/\sqrt D = \Theta(1)$. Since $\epsilon$ and $\theta$ are re-drawn per sequence, inferring them at test time is a toy form of in-context inference.

Two choices of $P_\theta$: - Flipping spike ($F=2$): $\theta_1 = \sqrt{\nu_1}$ constant, $\theta_2 \sim \mathrm{Unif}(\{-\sqrt{\nu_2}, +\sqrt{\nu_2}\})$. Feature 1 is a mean shift usable by a single shared attention vector; feature 2 flips sign across sequences, so a single linear score $k^\top X_\ell$ assigns a high score to the relevant token for one sign and a low score for the other. Exploiting feature 2 requires two heads with opposite components along $k_2^*$. - Non-isotropic Gaussian: $\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, \Lambda)$, $\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\nu_1 \ge \dots \ge \nu_F)$. Every feature is zero-mean, so nothing is learnable without specialization, and one needs a pair of opposite-sign heads per feature; hence they take $H = 2F$. For $F=2$ they parametrize $\nu_{\rm tot} = \nu_1+\nu_2$ and anisotropy $\delta = (\nu_1-\nu_2)/(\nu_1+\nu_2)$.

Architecture (student). One layer of $H$ rank-one heads with fixed, sequence-independent queries and identity value matrix (a simplification of cross-attention, as in DETR-style learned queries): $$f_K(X) = \frac1H \sum_{h=1}^H \mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{X k_h}{\sqrt D}\Big)^{\!\top} X \in \mathbb R^D, \qquad K = \{k_h\}_{h=1}^H \in \mathbb R^{H\times D}.$$ The output is a convex combination of tokens, with weights equal to the head-averaged attention distribution. There is no teacher network: the "teacher" is the planted generative structure $K^*$ plus the label rule $y = X_\epsilon$. The trainable degrees of freedom are $HD$.

Objective. Regularized ERM with square loss and ridge penalty, $\lambda > 0$: $$\hat K = \arg\min_{K} \sum_{\mu=1}^N \frac{1}{2D}\|y_\mu - f_K(X_\mu)\|_2^2 + \frac\lambda2 \|K\|_F^2,$$ with training error $E_{\rm train}$ (unregularized part, averaged) and test error $E = \mathbb E\big[\tfrac1{2D}\|y - f_{\hat K}(X)\|_2^2\big]$. Because $X_\ell^\top X_{\ell'}/D \to \delta_{\ell\ell'}$, the loss on a sequence collapses to an $L$-dimensional quantity: with local fields $Z = XK^\top/\sqrt D \in \mathbb R^{L\times H}$, $$\ell(\epsilon, Z) = \frac12 \sum_{\ell=1}^L\Big(\delta_{\ell\epsilon} - \frac1H\sum_{h}\mathrm{softmax}(Z_{:h})_\ell\Big)^2,$$ i.e. a squared error between the head-averaged attention distribution and the one-hot indicator of the relevant position. This is the crux of tractability (see Proof sketch).

Limit. $N, D \to \infty$ with $\alpha = N/D = \Theta(1)$, and $H, F, L, \lambda, \|\theta\|_2 = \Theta(1)$. The order parameters are $$m = \frac{KK^{*\top}}{D} \in \mathbb R^{H\times F}\ (\text{head-feature overlaps}), \qquad q = \frac{KK^\top}{D} \in \mathbb R^{H\times H}\ (\text{head self-overlaps}).$$

Given / produced. Given: $(P_\theta, L, H, \lambda, \alpha)$. Produced: closed scalar (matrix-of-fixed-size) equations for $(m, q, V)$ and conjugates, from which $E(\alpha)$, $E_{\rm train}(\alpha)$, phase diagrams in $(\alpha, \lambda)$, $(\alpha, \delta)$, and critical sample complexities via linear stability.

Phases. For the flipping spike with $H=2$, with $q_\perp = (q_{11}+q_{22}-2q_{12})/2$ (half squared distance between heads): - PS (permutation symmetric): $m_{11}=m_{21}>0$, $m_{12}=m_{22}=0$, $q_\perp = 0$. - PSB (permutation symmetry broken, unspecialized): same $m$, but $q_\perp > 0$. - SPEC: $m_{11}=m_{21}>0$, $m_{12} = -m_{22} \ne 0$, $q_\perp>0$.

For the Gaussian model, $r$-SPEC means $\|m_{:f}\|_2 > 0$ for $f \le r$ and $=0$ for $f>r$, $r \in \{0,\dots,\min(F,\lfloor H/2\rfloor)\}$.

Precise question. In this proportional limit, is the onset of nonzero head-feature overlap with a feature that requires multiple heads (the flipping feature, or the zero-mean Gaussian features) a point of non-analyticity of the global-minimizer test error $E(\alpha)$, and how do the critical values $\alpha_c$ depend on regularization $\lambda$ and the signal structure $\{\nu_f\}$? Secondarily: is distinct-heads-ness the same thing as specialization, and how do these static thresholds relate to the training-time emergence seen under online SGD?

What was known. (i) Stagewise emergence in training time, empirically and in solvable dynamics: Sagitova et al. (2026) derived the online-learning ODEs for exactly this multi-head SLR model and showed specialization is an exponential escape from a saddle; Chen et al. (2024b), Zhang et al. (2025), Yüksel et al. (2026) for other multi-head/linear-attention dynamics. (ii) Solvable attention models at equilibrium: Cui et al. (2024) found a positional-to-semantic phase transition in sample complexity for a single tied low-rank dot-product attention; Troiani et al. (2025) gave Bayes-optimal and GAMP thresholds for sequence multi-index models / deep attention; Marion et al. (2025) introduced SLR; Duranthon et al. (2026) did the ERM asymptotics of single-head SLR (statistical advantage of softmax), of which this paper is the multi-head generalization; Boncoraglio et al. (2026) extensive-rank single head; Lavie et al. (2026) a Bayesian sample-complexity transition for one copy head. (iii) The committee machine literature (Schwarze and Hertz 1992-93; Aubin et al. 2018) where hidden units go from permutation-symmetric to specialized as $\alpha$ grows. Gap: no equilibrium (ERM, sample-complexity) theory of multi-head attention specialization, and no clean separation of the statistical and dynamical sources of stagewise head emergence.

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag. - ERM, not Bayes-optimal. The main object is the global minimizer of a non-convex regularized loss. A Bayes-optimal baseline is computed separately (App. A.3) for comparison; it is not the object of study. - Replica-symmetric ansatz in a non-convex problem. The entire characterization is conditional on RS; the authors say so explicitly and support it numerically (L-BFGS from random init at $D=2000$ to $6000$). At low $\lambda$ (where PSB appears) they explicitly say RSB may be needed. - "Global minimum" selection. Multiple fixed points coexist; they pick the one with lowest training loss (free energy). Simulations use initializations projected orthogonal to the planted span, which matters for what gradient methods find. - Labels are the relevant token. $y = X_\epsilon$ is given in training. So supervision reveals the spiked vector directly; the difficulty is not identifying features from data but representing a retrieval rule with $H$ softmax probes (see critique). - Fixed queries, identity values, rank-one heads, $H = \Theta(1)$. Each head is a single $D$-dimensional vector; heads interact only through the average of their attention distributions. - Tokens are i.i.d. isotropic Gaussians apart from one spiked token; no correlations between tokens, no positional structure. - $\lambda>0$ is essential, both for the replica computation (Gaussian integration of the entropic term) and physically: $\lambda$ controls whether the PSB phase exists.

Main idea

Approach. Treat the ERM minimizer as the zero-temperature limit of a Gibbs measure $e^{-\beta L(K)}$, compute the quenched free entropy with the replica method under RS, and reduce the $HD$-dimensional problem to a fixed point in $(m, q, V) \in \mathbb R^{H\times F}\times\mathbb R^{H\times H}\times\mathbb R^{H\times H}$. Phases are distinct fixed points (PS / PSB / SPEC / $r$-SPEC), selected by their free energy; phase boundaries come from linear stability of the symmetric fixed point under the state-evolution (SE) map, i.e. the iteration of the saddle-point equations.

Result 3.1 (asymptotic characterization). Under RS, $m, q$ concentrate and satisfy $$m = (\lambda I_H + \hat V)^{-1}\hat m,\quad q = (\lambda I_H + \hat V)^{-1}(\hat m\hat m^\top + \hat q)(\lambda I_H + \hat V)^{-1},\quad V = (\lambda I_H + \hat V)^{-1},$$ $$\hat m = \alpha\,\mathbb E\big[V^{-1}(\mathrm{prox}_1 - \omega_1)\theta^\top\big],\quad \hat q = \alpha\,\mathbb E\Big[V^{-1}\textstyle\sum_\ell(\mathrm{prox}_\ell-\omega_\ell)^{\otimes 2}V^{-1}\Big],\quad \hat V = -\alpha\,\mathbb E\Big[V^{-1}\textstyle\sum_\ell(\mathrm{prox}_\ell-\omega_\ell)\xi_\ell^\top q^{-1/2}\Big],$$ with local fields $\omega_\ell = \delta_{\ell 1} m\theta + q^{1/2}\xi_\ell$, $\xi_\ell \sim \mathcal N(0, I_H)$ (position $\epsilon$ fixed to $1$ by permutation equivariance), and $\mathrm{prox}$ the minimizer over $Z \in \mathbb R^{L\times H}$ of the Moreau envelope $$\mathcal M(\theta,\Xi) = \inf_{Z}\Big\{\frac12\sum_{\ell=1}^L\Big(\delta_{\ell 1}-\frac1H\sum_h \mathrm{softmax}(Z_{:h})_\ell\Big)^2 + \frac12\sum_\ell (Z_\ell-\omega_\ell)^\top V^{-1}(Z_\ell-\omega_\ell)\Big\}.$$ Then $E = \mathbb E_{\theta,\Xi}\big[\tfrac12\sum_\ell(\delta_{\ell1}-\tfrac1H\sum_h\mathrm{softmax}(\Omega_{:h})_\ell)^2\big]$ and $E_{\rm train} = \mathbb E[\mathcal M] - \tfrac1{2\alpha}\mathrm{Tr}(\hat q V)$. The test error depends on the weights only through $(m,q)$.

Headline results. 1. Flipping spike, $\lambda \ge \lambda_{\rm tric}$: PS for $\alpha < \alpha_c^{\rm spec}(\lambda)$ (both heads identical; they learn only the constant direction, $\|m_{:1}\|>0$, $\|m_{:2}\|=0$), SPEC for $\alpha > \alpha_c^{\rm spec}$ (heads split continuously into $m_{12} = -m_{22} \ne 0$, each tuned to one sign of the flipping feature). The transition is second order: overlaps are continuous, errors have a kink. Theory matches L-BFGS simulations at $D=2000$ (Fig. 2). 2. Low regularization, $\lambda < \lambda_{\rm tric}$: an intermediate PSB phase for $\alpha_c^{\rm psb} < \alpha < \alpha_c^{\rm spec}$ where heads become different ($q_{11} \ne q_{12}$) by fitting sample-specific noise in directions orthogonal to $K^*$, with no gain in feature recovery. This delays specialization and makes the specialization boundary re-entrant in the $(\alpha,\lambda)$ plane (Fig. 3, $\lambda = 0.065$ cut, $D=6000$). Message: distinct attention patterns do not imply useful specialization. Analogous to the "memorization" phase in narrow committee machines (Pérez Ortiz et al. 2026). 3. Non-isotropic Gaussian, $H = 2F$: a cascade of second-order transitions $\alpha_c^{(1)} < \alpha_c^{(2)} < \dots$, recovering features from strongest to weakest variance. In the PS phase ($\alpha<\alpha_c^{(1)}$) nothing is learnable, and test error increases with $\alpha$ as the model fits noise. They call the ordering a "statistical form of simplicity bias" arising from the structure of global ERM minima rather than from dynamics. Isotropic $\nu_1=\nu_2$ collapses the cascade into one transition (Fig. 9). 4. Statics vs dynamics (Sec. 5, App. D): in the double limit $\lambda, \alpha \to \infty$ with $\alpha/\lambda$ fixed (ERM approximates population loss plus ridge) and gradient flow on the population loss from vanishing init $\eta\to 0$ after $D\to\infty$, $$\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\frac{\alpha_c^{\rm spec}}{\lambda} = \lim_{\eta\to0}\lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\tau^{\rm spec}}{\log(\sqrt D/\eta)} = \frac1C,\qquad C = \lambda_{\max}\big[-k_1^{*\top}\nabla^2_{K,K}E_{\rm pop}(0)\,k_1^*\big].$$ Both thresholds are controlled by the same negative curvature at the symmetric saddle $K=0$. 5. Bayes-optimal baseline (App. A.3): BO recovery thresholds are strictly smaller than the ERM specialization thresholds. For the Gaussian model, $q_{ff} = \frac{\alpha\nu_f^2-1}{\nu_f(\alpha\nu_f+1)}$ for $\alpha\nu_f^2>1$ and $0$ otherwise. 6. BERT experiment (Fig. 1, App. E.2). BERT-Small (4 layers, 8 heads, hidden 512) trained from scratch with MLM on fixed nested subsets of $N \in \{10^3, 3\cdot10^3, \dots, 6\cdot10^4\}$ sequences of 128 tokens (BookCorpus plus Wikipedia), static masking, AdamW, $10^4$ steps, 5 seeds; metrics at the early-stopped (lowest validation loss) checkpoint. Syntactic attention structure, measured by UAS of the best head/layer/direction on 1000 WSJ sentences, rises sharply over a narrow range of $N$, together with a change in the validation/training loss curves and increased seed variance. Per-relation UAS (case, compound, det, nsubj) emerge at about the same $N$ (Fig. 13). Learning rate shifts the emergence $N$ (Fig. 12). A further experiment (App. E.3) redoes Yüksel et al.'s sparse-attention Markov-chain task as a function of $N$ and sees a cascade (KL to ground-truth predictors using $1, 2, 3$ positional groups drops in order).

Most interesting part

I find the sharpest point to be a critique of the "statistical simplicity bias" claim. The Bayes-optimal analysis in the paper's own appendix shows that most of the cascade's ordering comes from the information-theoretic structure, and only the location of the thresholds is specific to attention.

The reason is that the label is the spiked token, $y_\mu = X_{\mu,\epsilon_\mu} = K^{*\top}\theta_\mu/\sqrt D + z_\mu$. The training labels alone form a spiked-covariance (spiked Wishart) data set with population covariance $I_D + K^{*\top}\Lambda K^*/D$. Inferring $K^*$ is therefore low-rank matrix estimation (the paper reduces to Lesieur et al. 2017). The BO fixed point (104)-(105) shows feature $f$ becomes detectable exactly when $$\alpha\,\nu_f^2 > 1,$$ which is the BBP threshold for PCA on $\{y_\mu\}$. For the flipping spike the same holds after linearizing (99): $q_{22} \approx \alpha\nu_2^2 q_{22}$, so $\alpha_{\rm BO} = 1/\nu_2^2$ (my linearization, not stated in the paper), while the constant feature is recovered at any $\alpha>0$ because it is a mean shift. So the BO estimator, and even plain spectral PCA of the labels, already recovers features in order of decreasing $\nu_f$ at $\alpha_f = 1/\nu_f^2$. Strongest-first recovery with more data is a generic property of spiked models, not a property of attention, ERM or softmax. What the attention ERM adds is (a) a shift of every threshold to the right, i.e. a statistical-to-architectural gap, and (b) a symmetry-breaking requirement: in the zero-mean case the features become usable only once a pair of heads splits into $\pm k_f^*$. Calling the ordering "a statistical form of simplicity bias in the global ERM solutions, independent of the training dynamics" is technically true, but it undersells that a Bayesian with no attention at all shows the same ordering. A stronger version of the claim would quantify the gap $\alpha_c^{(r)} - 1/\nu_r^2$ as a function of $(\lambda, L, H)$ and show that it can reorder features (e.g. a feature that is easier to detect but harder to exploit through softmax being specialized later). That would be a genuinely architectural simplicity bias, and the paper does not test it.

A related point: because the labels give $X_\epsilon$ directly, a two-stage estimator (PCA on labels, then set $k_h = \pm c\,\hat k_f$) would plausibly specialize near the BBP threshold. So the ERM delay is a property of non-convex ridge-regularized attention ERM and of the $\lambda$ choice. It is not about how much information the data contains. The paper's phrase "statistical origin" means "a property of the global minimum of this objective", which is narrower than "information-theoretic", and readers should keep the two apart.

Further reviewer points: - The statics-dynamics "controlled correspondence" is nearly tautological. In the limit $\lambda,\alpha\to\infty$ at fixed $\alpha/\lambda$, the ERM objective is $\alpha E_{\rm pop} + \tfrac\lambda2\|m\|^2$, and instability of $m=0$ happens when $\alpha C = \lambda$. Gradient flow on $E_{\rm pop}$ escapes the same saddle at rate $C$. Both quantities are $1/C$ by construction, with different rescalings ($\alpha/\lambda$ versus $\tau/\log(\sqrt D/\eta)$). This shows that one Hessian controls both. It does not show that finite-$\lambda$ statistical transitions (with PSB, re-entrance, noise fitting) appear in training time, and the logarithmic factor means "time ~ data" holds only up to a $\log D$ rescaling. Fig. 10 is the only finite-size check. - The BERT experiment is suggestive at best. (i) There is no $D$, so there is no $\alpha$ for BERT. (ii) The step budget is fixed ($10^4$ steps), so small-$N$ runs see many more epochs, and early stopping is the only regularizer. That couples $N$ to the effective optimization trajectory, and Fig. 12 shows the threshold moves with learning rate, which works against a purely statistical reading. (iii) All relations emerge at the same $N$ (Fig. 13), so the cascade prediction is not seen in real language data. (iv) UAS is a max over 32 heads × 2 directions × 4 layers, which can sharpen curves through order statistics. The authors are candid that finite experiments cannot establish non-analyticities. - Positive aside. The PSB phase is a useful conceptual point for interpretability: heads that differ (distinct $q$, distinct attention maps) can be pure overfitting, with $m$ unchanged. Probes based on "head diversity" would misclassify this.

Proof sketch

Claims. (1) Result 3.1: under RS, the overlaps of the ERM minimizer concentrate on a fixed point of the stated $H\times F$ / $H\times H$ equations, and $E$, $E_{\rm train}$ are given by low-dimensional expectations. (2) Phase boundaries: $\alpha_c^{\rm spec}$ is where the spectral radius of the linearized SE map in the direction $\delta m_{:2}$ around the PS (or PSB) fixed point reaches $1$, i.e. $\lambda_{\max}[J_{\rm spec}(\alpha_c^{\rm spec})] = 1$ with $$J_{\rm spec}(\alpha) = \alpha\nu_2\,\mathbb E_\Xi\Big[\big(\nabla_Z^2\ell(Z'_0) + I_L\otimes V_0^{-1}\big)^{-1}_{11}V_0^{-1} - I_H\Big],$$ and analogous $J_{\rm psb}$ (perturbation $\delta q\,e_-e_-^\top$, $e_- = (1,-1)/\sqrt2$) and $J_r$ for $(r)\to(r+1)$-SPEC with $\nu_{r+1}$ in front. (3) The large-$\lambda$ statics-dynamics identity $\alpha_c/\lambda \to 1/C \leftarrow \tau^{\rm spec}/\log(\sqrt D/\eta)$. (4) BO free entropy and errors (Nishimori, low-rank estimation).

Derivation steps. 1. Gibbs formulation and replicas. $\mathbb E\log Z_\beta$ via $\lim_{n\to0}(\mathbb E Z_\beta^n - 1)/n$. 2. Local fields. Conditioned on $(\epsilon,\theta)$, $Z^a_\mu = X_\mu K^{a\top}/\sqrt D \in \mathbb R^{L\times H}$ and $Z^*_\mu$ are jointly Gaussian across replicas, with mean $\delta_{\ell\epsilon} m^a\theta$ and covariances given by $m^a$, $Q^{ab}$. The key step is that the $D$-dimensional loss $\|y - f_K(X)\|^2/2D$ reduces to an $L$-dimensional function of $Z$, because $f_K(X)$ is a convex combination of near-orthogonal tokens: $X_\ell^\top X_{\ell'}/D \to \delta_{\ell\ell'}$. This is what makes multi-head tractable: the problem becomes a sequence multi-index model with a matrix local field $Z \in \mathbb R^{L\times H}$ of fixed size, since $H$ and $L$ are $\Theta(1)$ and heads are rank one. The heads couple only inside the scalar loss, through $\frac1H\sum_h\mathrm{softmax}(Z_{:h})$, so the head interaction lives entirely in the $LH$-dimensional Moreau envelope. 3. Order parameters and the RS ansatz. Introduce $m^a$, $Q^{ab}$ and conjugates with delta functions. Under RS, $Q^{ab} = q + (Q-q)\delta_{ab}$, and with $V = Q - q$ the replicas decouple via Gaussian $\xi_\ell \sim \mathcal N(0,I_H)$. Ridge regularization makes the entropic integral over $K$ Gaussian, giving $\log\det(\beta\lambda I + \hat V)$ and $\mathrm{Tr}[(\beta\lambda I+\hat V)^{-1}(\hat q + \hat m\hat m^\top)]$. $K^*$ drops out except through $K^*K^{*\top}/D \to I_F$. 4. Zero temperature. Rescale $\hat q \to \beta^2\hat q$, $\hat m\to\beta\hat m$, $V\to\beta^{-1}V$, $\hat V\to\beta\hat V$. The energetic term becomes $-\mathbb E[\mathcal M]$, a Moreau envelope (proximal problem) over $Z \in \mathbb R^{L\times H}$. Stationarity gives the equations of Result 3.1. A removable $q^{-1/2}$ singularity in $\hat V$ (problematic on the PS branch) is handled by Stein's lemma: $\hat V = -\alpha\mathbb E[\sum_\ell V^{-1}(\partial\,\mathrm{prox}_\ell/\partial\omega_\ell - I_H)]$. 5. Numerics. Iterate the fixed-point (SE) map; expectations over $(\theta,\Xi)$ by Monte Carlo, with a numerical proximal solve per sample. Follow branches with planted initializations and pick the global minimum by free energy. This is not AMP run on data. "State evolution" here means the fixed-point iteration of the saddle-point equations, though by analogy it is what a GAMP/ERM-AMP state evolution would track. 6. Stability. The PS manifold $m_{:2}=0$ is invariant under the SE map because of the $\theta_2\to-\theta_2$ symmetry, and the other order parameters have no first-order response. Linearizing the prox stationarity condition, $[\nabla_Z^2\ell + I_L\otimes V_0^{-1}]\delta Z' = (I_L\otimes V_0^{-1})\delta\Omega$, gives the closed linear map $\delta m^{t+1} = J_{\rm spec}(\alpha)\delta m^t$.

Why a non-analyticity appears. Because of the symmetry, the unspecialized branch ($m_{:2}=0$) is an exact solution for all $\alpha$. As $\alpha$ grows, the leading eigenvalue of $J$ crosses $1$ and a new symmetry-broken branch bifurcates off it continuously, a pitchfork. The global-minimum observables follow the PS branch on one side and the SPEC branch on the other. They are continuous at $\alpha_c$ but have a derivative discontinuity, which is a second-order transition. Strictly, non-analyticity needs $D\to\infty$; at finite $D$ the pitchfork is rounded. This is the same mechanism as the BBP transition and the committee-machine specialization transition. The paper does not report critical exponents; a generic pitchfork would give $\|m_{:2}\|^2 \propto \alpha-\alpha_c$ near threshold, but that is my expectation, not their claim.

Rigorous vs heuristic. Nothing is proved. The replica computation is standard but heuristic, and RS is an assumption for this non-convex loss. The authors cite Vilucchio et al. (2025), who prove the replica formula for some non-convex GLMs, as a possible route. Evidence is numerical: L-BFGS minimizers at $D = 2000$ to $6000$ over 10 seeds match predicted overlaps and errors, including in the low-$\lambda$ PSB regime. Selecting the global minimum and checking that gradient methods reach it are also numerical. The dynamics link uses the Sagitova et al. ODEs (themselves derived in the $D\to\infty$, $\eta\to0$ limit) plus a second-order Taylor expansion. The BO part uses Nishimori identities, where RS is standard and typically provable (low-rank matrix estimation).

Broader context

Background for newcomers. The "statistical physics of learning" program studies learning problems in the proportional limit $N \propto D \to \infty$. There, macroscopic quantities (overlaps with the ground truth, test error) concentrate and satisfy low-dimensional self-consistent equations, from the replica method or from the state evolution of approximate message passing (AMP). In this limit, qualitative regime changes become sharp phase transitions in $\alpha = N/D$. Classic examples: the perceptron's generalization transitions, the committee machine's specialization transition where hidden units stop being interchangeable (Schwarze and Hertz; Aubin et al. 2018, which also exhibited computational-statistical gaps), and BBP-type detection thresholds in spiked matrix models. The recent wave (Cui et al. 2024; Troiani et al. 2025; Duranthon et al. 2026; Boncoraglio et al. 2026) extends this to attention, where the key trick is to make the per-sequence local field a fixed-size matrix ($L\times H$ here), so attention becomes a "sequence multi-index model".

Related directions. - Cui, Behrens, Krzakala, Zdeborová (2024), a phase transition between positional and semantic learning in dot-product attention. It is the closest antecedent: a first-order sample-complexity transition between two attention mechanisms in a single head. The present paper replaces "which mechanism" with "how many distinct heads" and gets second-order symmetry-breaking transitions. - Troiani et al. (2025), sequence multi-index models. Gives BO and GAMP thresholds and sequential (layer-by-layer) learning in deep attention, an information-theoretic counterpart to the "cascade". Comparing the ERM thresholds here with GAMP-optimal ones in that framework would separate architectural from algorithmic gaps. - Dynamics side: Sagitova et al. (2026) for the same model; Yüksel et al. (2026) on incremental learning of sparse attention patterns.

Plausible follow-ups. 1. Architectural simplicity bias. Find signal structures where the ERM order of specialization differs from the BBP order $1/\nu_f^2$ (e.g. features with heavy-tailed or multimodal $\theta_f$, or interacting features), which would separate an attention-induced bias from the spiked-model ordering. 2. _Over-parameterized heads, $H > 2F$._ Do the surplus heads stay redundant, split noise (PSB-like), or duplicate features? This bears on head pruning. 3. Rigor. Extend Vilucchio et al. (2025) to the $L\times H$ matrix local field, or show RSB in the PSB regime. 4. Spectral initialization. Does a spectral initialization from the labels make gradient descent reach a specialized local minimum below $\alpha_c^{\rm spec}$? That would quantify how much of the threshold comes from the landscape. 5. Diagnostic. Test the authors' suggestion that seed variance peaks at the transition (susceptibility) as a practical detector of emergence $N$ in real models.

IR connection (genuine, but narrow). Strip away the transformer language and $f_K$ is a multi-prototype soft retriever. There are $H$ learned, input-independent query vectors $k_h$. Each scores $L$ candidate items by an inner product, softmaxes over candidates, and the final relevance distribution is the average over prototypes. The loss asks this distribution to put its mass on the single relevant item. The flipping-spike model is then the minimal case where relevance is bimodal in embedding space: relevant items have $\pm\sqrt{\nu_2}$ along a latent direction. One query vector cannot rank both modes above the noise, because a linear score that rewards $+v$ penalizes $-v$. That is the same structural obstacle discussed for single-vector dense retrieval (cf. work on the representational limits of single-vector embedding retrieval and on multi-interest/multi-vector query representations, e.g. MIND-style multi-interest user vectors, ColBERT-style multi-vector scoring). The paper's results translate into a data-centric statement for that setting. Below $\alpha_c^{\rm spec}$, extra query vectors trained by regularized ERM collapse onto one prototype (PS), or at low regularization diverge by fitting noise without capturing the second mode (PSB), which is useless diversity. They become useful only above a sharp data threshold that grows with weaker signal. A concrete follow-up for an IR theorist: make the queries input-dependent (a query sequence plus $W_Q$, i.e. true cross-attention, still low-rank), giving a solvable model of a dual-encoder or late-interaction retriever trained contrastively. Then compute the sample complexity at which $H$-vector query representations beat single-vector ones, and whether the PSB phase predicts a regime where multi-vector models look diverse but do not improve recall. I would not push the connection to generative retrieval or vector-search indexing; the model has no indexing, decoding or ANN component.

title: Variants of Beam Search for DiskANN

Variants of Beam Search for DiskANN — Agrawal, Shiragur (2026) — arXiv:2611.26609

Variants of Beam Search for DiskANN — Agrawal, Shiragur (2026), arXiv:2611.26609

Setting and problem

Formal object. A metric space $(\mathcal X, D)$ (non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, triangle inequality). A dataset of $n$ points forms the node set $V$ of a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with out-neighbourhoods $N_{\mathrm{out}}(u)=\{v\in V : (u,v)\in E\}$. A query $q\in\mathcal X$, a target $k\le |V|$, and a start node $s\in V$ (arbitrary — no medoid or entry-point assumption is needed). The ground truth is $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}$, the true $k$ nearest neighbours of $q$ sorted by increasing $D(\cdot,q)$; the output is $B^\star=\{b_1,\dots,b_k\}$, sorted the same way. Distances $D(u,q)$, $u\in V$, are assumed pairwise distinct so all orders are strict.

Graph classes.

  • $\alpha$-reachable (Indyk–Xu 2023), $\alpha>1$: for every ordered pair $u\neq v$, either $(u,v)\in E$ or there is $t$ with $(u,t)\in E$ and $D(v,t)\le D(v,u)/\alpha$. From every node there is one hop that shrinks the distance to any target by a factor $\alpha$. DiskANN's slow preprocessing (RobustPrune run against all of $V\setminus\{p\}$ with no degree cap, naive cost $O(n^3)$) produces such graphs.
  • Sorted $\alpha$-reachable (Gollapudi et al. 2025): additionally the certifying neighbour satisfies $D(u,t)\le D(u,v)$, i.e. the shortcut is not longer than the edge it replaces. This is exactly what RobustPrune's "sort candidates by distance before pruning" rule buys.
  • DiskANN's fast preprocessing (Vamana with degree cap $R$ and candidate lists from greedy search on the partial graph) — the thing everybody actually uses — is not known to satisfy either definition.

Search procedure. A generic best-first skeleton (Algorithm 1): a min-priority queue $B$ of all discovered nodes and $B_u\subseteq B$ of unexpanded ones; $B_e=B\setminus B_u$ is the expanded set. Repeatedly look at $x=\arg\min_{u\in B_u}D(u,q)$; if the termination condition holds, stop; else pop $x$ and insert all of $N_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$ into $B$ and $B_u$. Return the top $k$ of $B$. Two stopping rules:

  • CBS (classical beam search, list size $L\ge k$): stop when $L$ nodes $v_1,\dots,v_L\in B\setminus\{x\}$ satisfy $D(v_i,q)\le D(x,q)$.
  • ABS (adaptive beam search, Al-Jazzazi et al. 2025, $\gamma\ge 0$): stop when $k$ nodes $v_1,\dots,v_k\in B\setminus\{x\}$ satisfy $(\gamma+1)D(v_i,q)\le D(x,q)$, i.e. the best unexpanded candidate is a factor $1+\gamma$ farther than the current $k$-th best. $\gamma=0$ is CBS with $L=k$.

Non-obvious modelling choices worth flagging.

  1. ABS as analysed has no list-size cap: $B$ is unbounded and the theorem says nothing about running time. The guarantee is purely about quality at termination.
  2. The guarantee is a rank-wise distance ratio, $D(b_i,q)\le C\,D(a_i,q)$ for every $i$, not recall. A ratio of $C=4$ is compatible with recall $0$.
  3. The graph property is worst-case and global (every ordered pair), not distributional; no doubling-dimension or random-data assumption is used for correctness.
  4. Distinct distances is a genericity assumption; it is what makes "first missed true neighbour" well defined.

What was known.

  • Indyk–Xu: greedy search ($L=1$) on $\alpha$-reachable graphs reaches a node within $\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}$ of the nearest-neighbour distance (plus running-time bounds under bounded doubling dimension, not revisited here).
  • Gollapudi et al.: the same $\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}$ holds for every element of the CBS beam; on sorted $\alpha$-reachable graphs under $\ell_2$ it sharpens to $\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}$.
  • Al-Jazzazi et al.: on merely navigable graphs (every pair has a strictly-closer out-neighbour, morally $\alpha\to 1$), CBS has no guarantee, but ABS achieves a $\frac{2}{\gamma}$-type approximation (this is the $\alpha\to 1$ limit of the new bound; the exact form in [1] is quoted only as a "$\gamma$"-fraction in the extracted text).

The gap / precise questions.

  • Q1. For $\gamma\ge 0$ and $\alpha>1$, what constant $C(\alpha,\gamma)$ guarantees $D(b_i,q)\le C\,D(a_i,q)$ for ABS on $\alpha$-reachable graphs, ideally interpolating between $\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}$ ($\gamma=0$) and $\frac{2}{\gamma}$ ($\alpha\to1$)?
  • Q2. Does the $\ell_2$ / sorted improvement of Gollapudi et al. survive when the stopping rule is relaxed by $\gamma$?

A secondary, empirical question: ABS "works" by reallocating effort from easy to hard queries — can that reallocation be made explicit and optimised (the beam predictor)?

Main idea

Theory. Combine the ABS stopping certificate with the $\alpha$-reachability chain. When ABS stops, every unexpanded node is at least $(1+\gamma)$ times farther from $q$ than any returned node. If a true neighbour $a_i$ is missing, follow the $\alpha$-reachability chain from a returned (hence expanded) node $v$ toward $a_i$; the chain must leave the expanded set at some unexpanded node $t$, which is both (i) close to $a_i$ (by the geometric $\alpha$-shrinkage) and (ii) far from $q$ (by the stopping rule). Triangle inequality turns (i)+(ii) into an upper bound on $D(q,v)/D(q,a_i)$.

Headline results.

  • Theorem 1.1 (any metric, $\alpha$-reachable, $0\le\gamma\le 2/\alpha$): $$D(b_i,q)\le \frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha(\gamma+1)-1}\,D(a_i,q),\qquad i=1,\dots,k.$$ At $\gamma=0$ this is Indyk–Xu / Gollapudi's $\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}$; as $\alpha\to1$ it becomes $\frac{2}{\gamma}$ (Al-Jazzazi). Tight, via a 3-node example on the line.
  • Theorem 1.2 ($\ell_2$, sorted $\alpha$-reachable, $0\le\gamma\le\max(1/\alpha,2/\alpha^2)$): $$C=\max\left\{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha(\gamma+1)-1},\ \frac{\alpha^2+1}{\alpha^2(\gamma+1)-1}\right\}.$$ At $\gamma=0$ the first term dominates and gives Gollapudi's $\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}$. Tight where the first term dominates (planar 3-node example).
  • Beam predictor. Not ABS at all, but CBS with a per-query list size $\hat L$: run a pilot CBS with $L=K$ to convergence, compute six features (scale: $d_1$, $d_K$, mean and std of the top-$K$ distances; trajectory: percentage drop of the top-$K$ distance sum and the number of distance computations to reach $90\%$ of that drop), predict $\log\hat L$ by weighted linear regression, calibrate with a single multiplicative scale $s$, and continue the pilot (re-inserting buffered evicted candidates) instead of restarting. Training targets come from a cost-optimal allocation: minimise mean distance computations subject to mean recall $\ge r_T$, a multiple-choice knapsack solved by Lagrangian relaxation (within $0.07$–$0.52\%$ of the DP optimum on 100-query subsets).
  • Experiments (SIFT100M, DEEP100M, MSSpaceV100M; Vamana, $R=32$, $L_{\mathrm{build}}=100$, $\alpha=1.2$): on SSD, up to $29.6\%$ lower mean latency than CBS at matched recall (14/15 settings better), $\pm$ a few percent vs ABS (better in 11/15, at most $1.4\%$ worse otherwise), with the gap to ABS growing at $K=500$. In memory, $1.3$–$23.7\%$ fewer distance computations than CBS and $0.0$–$3.9\%$ fewer than ABS. Tail (p99.9) latency is worse than CBS in 13/15 settings, up to $2.1\times$.

Most interesting part

I find the most useful thing to write here is an honest reviewer-style assessment, because the paper's clean "unify and generalise" story hides some quantitative facts that matter.

Strengths.

  • The proof is genuinely short and modular: one case split (search exhausted vs. stopping rule fired), one sub-case split ($z^\star=0$ vs. $z^\star\ge1$), and only Sub-case B1 depends on the metric/graph class. That makes it a good template: swap in a new local geometric lemma and you get a new theorem.
  • Tightness of Theorem 1.1 is exact, and the SDP-with-dual-certificate approach to the $\ell_2$ sub-case is the right tool (it is the same technique as in Gollapudi et al.) and is fully verifiable ($Y=UU^\top$).
  • The beam-predictor engineering is careful: continuation rather than restart, an exactness check that the continuation reproduces CBS at $\hat L$, honest reporting of tail latency, baselines tuned on the test set (which favours the baselines), and an explicit refusal to claim superiority over LAET/DARTH/Ada-ef/ANNiE.

Weaknesses and gaps.

  1. The sharp ($\ell_2$, sorted) bound is tight only in a sliver of parameter space at practical $\alpha$. Comparing the two terms of Theorem 1.2 with $\tau=\gamma+1$: the first dominates iff $\alpha(\alpha^2\tau-1)\ge(\alpha^2+1)(\alpha\tau-1)$, which simplifies to $\tau\le \alpha-1+1/\alpha$, i.e. $$\gamma\le \frac{(\alpha-1)^2}{\alpha}.$$ For DiskANN's default $\alpha=1.2$ this is $\gamma\le 0.033$. The experiments sweep $\gamma\in[0,0.2]$, so on almost the whole practically relevant range the binding term is the un-tight second term $\frac{\alpha^2+1}{\alpha^2(\gamma+1)-1}$, which comes from the general-metric argument with $\alpha$ replaced by $\alpha^2$ and does not use either $\ell_2$ or sortedness. In other words, "combining Gollapudi with ABS" (Q2) is answered fully only for tiny $\gamma$; for the rest the authors (correctly) list tightening the second term as open.
  2. The constants are large where it matters. At $\alpha=1.2$: $\gamma=0$ gives $C=11$ (general) and $6$ (sorted $\ell_2$); $\gamma=0.1$ gives $6.875$ and $\approx4.18$; $\gamma=0.2$ gives $5$ and $\approx3.35$. These are worst-case ratio bounds, so they say little about the $90$–$95\%$ recall regime that the experiments operate in. The "theory validation" (recall increases with $\gamma$; sorted beats shuffled pruning) is, as the authors admit, a directional sanity check on graphs the theorems do not cover.
  3. An unstated corollary: exactness. The proof works for every $\gamma\ge0$; the range restriction $\gamma\le 2/\alpha$ only ensures $C\ge1$. But in Case B we have $D(a_i,q)<D(b_k,q)\le C\,D(a_i,q)$, so $C\le1$ is a contradiction. Hence for $\gamma\ge 2/\alpha$, ABS on any $\alpha$-reachable graph returns the exact top-$k$ (and for $\gamma\ge\max(1/\alpha,2/\alpha^2)$ in the sorted $\ell_2$ case). That is a clean statement the paper does not make, and it also highlights the missing piece: no running-time bound, so "exact" may cost $\Theta(n)$ expansions.
  4. No running-time analysis for ABS. Indyk–Xu's real contribution was a time bound (logarithmic in the aspect ratio under bounded doubling dimension) for slow-preprocessing graphs. Here, ABS has no list cap, and the paper is silent on how many expansions it performs. Since the whole practical motivation is a speed/quality trade-off, a quality-only theorem is half the story.
  5. The theory and the method are decoupled. The beam predictor runs CBS with $\hat L\ge K$, not ABS. On an $\alpha$-reachable graph it therefore inherits only the $\gamma=0$ guarantee $\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}$ (Gollapudi et al.) — Theorems 1.1/1.2 say nothing about it. The title and abstract invite the reader to think the new bounds underpin the predictor; they do not, they only motivate the intuition "spend effort where the top-$K$ is still moving".
  6. Objective choice: mean recall. Optimising mean recall under a mean-cost budget is a knapsack that deliberately starves queries whose recall is expensive to raise. The paper reports lower per-query recall std than CBS but a median up to 2 points lower, and p99.9 latency up to $2.1\times$ CBS. For SLO-driven serving (tail latency, per-query recall floors) this is the wrong objective; DARTH/Ada-ef target per-query recall precisely for this reason. Also gains over ABS ($0$–$6.5\%$) are modest relative to the cost of a 1.7–3.4 h offline sweep per dataset.
  7. Prediction quality is mediocre. Spearman $\rho$ between $\hat L$ and the oracle $L^\star$ is $0.33$–$0.80$; the six-feature model with collinear features (opposite-sign t-values for $d_K$ and the mean) suggests most of the gain comes from a crude "how far is the $K$-th neighbour" signal plus convergence speed. That is fine, but there is lots of room for better predictors.

Proof sketch

Claim (unified). Let $G$ be $\alpha$-reachable, $\alpha>1$, distances to $q$ distinct, ABS with $\gamma\ge0$ started at any $s$. Then for every $i$, $D(b_i,q)\le C_0\,D(a_i,q)$ with $C_0=\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha(\gamma+1)-1}$ in general, and $C_0=\max\{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha(\gamma+1)-1},\frac{\alpha^2+1}{\alpha^2(\gamma+1)-1}\}$ for sorted $\alpha$-reachable $G$ under $\ell_2$.

Case A — $B_u$ empties. Then every discovered node was expanded, so $B$ is the reachable set of $s$. Claim: $\alpha$-reachable graphs are strongly connected. Fix target $u$ and order other nodes $x_1,x_2,\dots$ by distance to $u$. For $x_1$, no $t\ne u$ can certify ($\alpha D(u,t)>D(u,x_1)$), so $(x_1,u)\in E$. Inductively, a certifier for $(x_i,u)$ must lie in $\{u,x_1,\dots,x_{i-1}\}$, all of which reach $u$. So $B=V$ and the answer is exact.

Case B — the stopping rule fires at $x$. Let $i$ be the smallest index with $a_i\notin B^\star$; then $a_i\notin B$ at all. Two facts from the stopping rule:

  • $(\gamma+1)D(b,q)\le D(x,q)\le D(u,q)$ for every $b\in B^\star$ and every $u\in B_u$ — the stopping-gap transfers to every unexpanded node (key lever).
  • Every $v\in B^\star$ is strictly closer than $x$, hence not in $B_u$, hence expanded; so $(v,a_i)\notin E$ (else $a_i\in B$).

Apply $\alpha$-reachability repeatedly from $v$ toward $a_i$: a path $v=t_0\to t_1\to\dots\to t_\ell=a_i$, $\ell\ge2$, with $\alpha D(t_{z+1},a_i)\le D(t_z,a_i)$ (and, if sorted, $D(v,t_1)\le D(v,a_i)$). Since $t_0\in B_e$ and $a_i\notin B$, let $z^\star$ be the last expanded index; then $t_{z^\star+1}\in B_u$ and $\alpha^{z^\star+1}D(t_{z^\star+1},a_i)\le D(v,a_i)$.

  • Sub-case B1 ($z^\star=0$), general metric. With $t=t_1$: $$(\gamma+1)D(q,v)\le D(q,t)\le D(q,a_i)+\frac{D(v,a_i)}{\alpha}\le D(q,a_i)+\frac{D(v,q)+D(q,a_i)}{\alpha},$$ which rearranges to $\frac{D(q,v)}{D(q,a_i)}\le\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha(\gamma+1)-1}$.
  • Sub-case B1, $\ell_2$ + sorted. Maximise $D(q,v)/D(q,a_i)$ subject to the three constraints $(\gamma+1)D(q,v)\le D(q,t)$, $\alpha D(t,a_i)\le D(v,a_i)$, $D(v,t)\le D(v,a_i)$. Normalise $D(q,a_i)\le1$, square everything, and write it as an SDP over the $4\times4$ Gram matrix of $(q,v,t,a_i)$ — linear in Gram entries, so exact for Euclidean configurations in $\mathbb R^4$ and hence any dimension. An explicit dual-feasible $(y_1,\dots,y_4)$ with $Y=UU^\top\succeq0$ gives $d^\star\le y_4=\big(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha\tau-1}\big)^2$, $\tau=\gamma+1$; weak duality finishes.
  • Sub-case B2 ($z^\star\ge1$). Now $\alpha^{2}D(t_{z^\star+1},a_i)\le D(v,a_i)$ — the same structure as B1 with $\alpha\to\alpha^2$ (but the sortedness condition is attached to $t_1$, not $t_{z^\star+1}$, so it cannot be used). The general-metric argument gives $\frac{\alpha^2+1}{\alpha^2(\gamma+1)-1}$. In the general case this is dominated by the B1 term, so $C_0=\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha(\gamma+1)-1}$; in the sorted $\ell_2$ case the B1 term shrank, so the max survives — and this is precisely the source of the non-tight second term.

Assembly. For $j<i$, $b_j=a_j$. For $j\ge i$, $D(b_j,q)\le C_0D(a_i,q)\le C_0D(a_j,q)$ by sortedness of $A$.

Tightness. $k=1$, $G$ = complete graph on $\{v,a,t\}$ minus $(v,a)$, start at $v$. On the line: $q=0$, $a=-1$, $v=\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha\tau-1}$, $t=-\frac{(\alpha+1)\tau}{\alpha\tau-1}$; one checks $\alpha D(t,a)=D(v,a)$ and $\tau D(q,v)=D(q,t)$, so ABS stops at $v$ with ratio exactly $\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha\tau-1}$. A planar analogue with $D(v,t)\le D(v,a)$ realises $\frac{\alpha}{\alpha\tau-1}$ (only valid for $\gamma<1/\alpha$; and per the computation above it is the true max only for $\gamma\le(\alpha-1)^2/\alpha$). Note the lower-bound examples only exercise Sub-case B1; B2 never appears in them, consistent with B2 being the loose part.

Beam-predictor allocation (not a theorem, but a clean reduction). Precompute per query the cheapest cost to reach each integer recall level $r\in\{0,\dots,100\}$; the batch problem $\min\frac1Q\sum_i c_i(r_i)$ s.t. $\frac1Q\sum_i r_i\ge r_T$ is a multiple-choice knapsack. For a price $\lambda$ it decouples into $r_i(\lambda)=\arg\max_r\{r-\lambda c_i(r)\}$; binary-search $\lambda$. Because the $c_i$ are not convex, this finds points on each query's lower convex hull — the standard MCKP fact is that the LP relaxation has at most one "fractional" query, so the Lagrangian solution's suboptimality is bounded by roughly one query's cost jump, consistent with the measured $<0.52\%$ average gap.

Broader context

Background for newcomers. Graph-based ANN (HNSW, NSG, DiskANN/Vamana) builds a sparse proximity graph and answers queries with best-first beam search of width $L$. Practice is far ahead of theory: worst-case guarantees exist only for idealised graphs. The Indyk–Xu line identifies $\alpha$-reachability (what RobustPrune enforces when run against all points) as the property making greedy search provably approximate, and shows that the practical fast-built graphs and HNSW can fail badly in the worst case. Gollapudi et al. showed the "sort before prune" detail of RobustPrune is not incidental — it yields sharper $\ell_2$ bounds. Al-Jazzazi et al. changed the search side instead: a distance-relative stopping rule (ABS) gives guarantees even on weakly navigable graphs. This paper sits at the intersection of the two levers (graph property $\alpha$, stopping slack $\gamma$).

Related directions.

  • Per-query adaptive termination: LAET (learned early termination from in-search features), DARTH (stop when a learned model estimates a declared recall target is met), Patience-in-Proximity (stop when top-$k$ stops improving), Ada-ef (statistical model to set HNSW $ef$ per query), ANNiE (learned cost estimator from a preliminary search), Tao (static query features). The beam predictor is closest to ANNiE/LAET but trained against an optimal batch allocation.
  • Query hardness for ANN: local intrinsic dimensionality (Aumüller–Ceccarello) and Steiner-hardness (Wang et al.) — graph-native difficulty measures one could feed as features or use to give instance-dependent bounds.
  • Theory of navigable graphs: Diwan et al. on sparsity limits of navigable graphs; constructions with guarantees (MRNG, $\tau$-MG, $\alpha$-CG, LMG).

Plausible follow-up research ideas.

  1. Tight sorted-$\ell_2$ bound for all $\gamma$. Write Sub-case B2 itself as an SDP over the Gram matrix of $(q,v,t_1,t_{z^\star+1},a_i)$, keeping the sortedness constraint at $t_1$ and the chain constraints $\alpha D(t_1,a_i)\le D(v,a_i)$, $\alpha D(t_{z^\star+1},a_i)\le D(t_1,a_i)$ — and the extra fact that $t_1$ is expanded (so all of $N_{\mathrm{out}}(t_1)$ is in $B$, and one can apply sortedness again from $t_1$). A 5-point SDP is mechanically solvable numerically; guessing a closed-form dual is the research step. Given that the first term dominates only for $\gamma\le(\alpha-1)^2/\alpha$, this is where the practical $\gamma$ range lives.
  2. Time bounds for ABS. Combine with Indyk–Xu's doubling-dimension argument: bound the number of expansions of ABS on slow-preprocessing graphs as a function of $\gamma$, $\alpha$, the doubling dimension and aspect ratio. A $(\text{quality},\text{time})$ trade-off curve parameterised by $\gamma$ would actually justify the stopping rule, and the exactness corollary ($\gamma\ge2/\alpha$) gives a natural endpoint.
  3. Predict $\gamma$, not $L$, and inherit Theorem 1.1 per query: a learned per-query $\hat\gamma(q)$ with a floor $\gamma_{\min}$ gives every query at least the $C(\alpha,\gamma_{\min})$ guarantee on $\alpha$-reachable graphs, which the CBS-based predictor cannot offer beyond $\gamma=0$.
  4. SLO-aware allocation: replace the mean-recall constraint by per-query recall floors or a CVaR-type tail constraint on latency; the Lagrangian machinery extends directly.

Genuine connections to theoretical IR / generative retrieval.

  • Query performance prediction (QPP). The beam predictor is a post-retrieval QPP model for ANN: the standard deviation of the top-$K$ distances is essentially the NQC predictor (Shtok et al.) transplanted from BM25 scores to vector distances, and "how fast the top-$K$ score sum converged" mirrors score-drift/stability predictors. The novelty relative to classic QPP is that the label is not "effectiveness" but an optimal budget under a batch cost constraint. This suggests a principled bridge: QPP features with known theoretical grounding could be evaluated as list-size predictors, and conversely the knapsack-optimal-budget labelling is a useful new target for QPP research.
  • Dynamic pruning analogy. ABS's $(1+\gamma)$ multiplier on the stopping threshold is the mirror image of the threshold factor $F$ in WAND/MaxScore-style top-$k$ evaluation (Broder et al. 2003): there, inflating the threshold makes pruning unsafe with a bounded score-approximation; here, inflating it makes stopping more conservative with a bounded distance-approximation. Both give multiplicative-approximation top-$k$ guarantees from a single slack parameter — a nice unifying lens for a theoretical-IR treatment of "approximate top-$k$ with certificates".
  • Generative retrieval. Constrained beam decoding over a docid trie has exactly the same "fixed beam width for every query" problem. The pilot-then-extend trick (run a narrow beam, read off score-gap/convergence features, widen the beam only for hard queries, re-using the pilot's hypotheses) transfers directly, and the knapsack labelling gives a clean training target. What does not transfer is the theory: there is no metric or $\alpha$-reachability analogue on a trie with learned prefix scores, though an "$\alpha$-reachable decoding" property (each prefix extension contracts a score gap to the target docid by a factor) would be an interesting definition to explore.

title: Make Sparse Rewards Count: Density-Aware Reward Aggregation for Multi-Reward RL
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-20

Make Sparse Rewards Count: Density-Aware Reward Aggregation for Multi-Reward RL — Tong Zheng, Skylar Zhai, Zhan Cheng, et al. (2026) — arXiv:2610.00574

Setting and problem

The object of study is GRPO-style policy optimization of an LLM policy $\pi_\theta$ with several reward functions. A rollout batch holds $B$ prompts $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^B$. For each prompt the policy samples a group of $G$ responses $\{y^{(i,j)}\}_{j=1}^G$, and each response gets $K$ sequence-level rewards $\{r_k^{(i,j)}\}_{k=1}^K$ (for example format and correctness, or correctness and a length cap). With $\mu_{i,k}$ and $\sigma_{i,k}$ the group mean and sample standard deviation of reward $k$, there are two known aggregation schemes:

  • GRPO sums first and then normalizes: $r_{\text{sum}}^{(i,j)}=\sum_k r_k^{(i,j)}$ and $A_{\text{GRPO}}^{(i,j)}=(r_{\text{sum}}^{(i,j)}-\mu_{i,\text{sum}})/(\sigma_{i,\text{sum}}+\epsilon)$. Different reward combinations can collapse to the same advantage.
  • GDPO normalizes each reward first, $A_k^{(i,j)}=(r_k^{(i,j)}-\mu_{i,k})/(\sigma_{i,k}+\epsilon)$, then sums $S^{(i,j)}=\sum_k A_k^{(i,j)}$ and whitens over the batch: $\hat A^{(i,j)}=(S^{(i,j)}-\mu_B(S))/(\sigma_B(S)+\epsilon)$.

The resulting scalar advantage is broadcast to every token and used in the usual clipped PPO/DAPO surrogate. What goes in is the $K$ reward channels of a rollout batch. What comes out is a per-response advantage. The paper changes only the aggregation step.

The key modelling choice is how sparsity is formalised. Reward $k$ is active in group $i$ if it produces any nonzero group-relative advantage, $I_{i,k}=\mathbb{1}[\sum_j |A_k^{(i,j)}|>\tau]$. Its active-group density is $\pi_k=\frac{1}{B}\sum_i I_{i,k}$. So "sparse" does not mean a reward that is rarely nonzero. It means a reward that rarely varies within a group. A reward that is almost always 1, such as a length cap the model has nearly mastered, is just as sparse as one that is almost always 0. For a binary reward with success probability $p$, a group is active with probability $q_G(p)=1-p^G-(1-p)^G$. The paper's diagnostic is the advantage energy $E_k=\sum_{i,j}(A_k^{(i,j)})^2$.

The question is: after GDPO's per-reward normalization, what batch-level imbalance remains between objectives, and can reward weights be derived from that mechanism instead of tuned by hand? Several concurrent papers reweight GDPO channels using other statistics: DVAO uses within-group standard deviation, SAW the batch coefficient of variation, SA-MRPO distance to saturation, GD$^2$PO drops sign-conflicting responses, and RVPO uses SoftMin. GDPO itself reported that small static weight changes did not fix uneven learning. What is missing is a principled account of why some objectives get less signal under GDPO.

Main idea

Under idealized GDPO ($\epsilon=\tau=0$, sample standard deviation with divisor $G-1$), each active group's z-scores have squared sum exactly $G-1$, whatever the reward values are. Hence

$$E_k = B\,\pi_k\,(G-1).$$

GDPO equalizes reward scales within a group, but a reward that is active in a quarter of the groups still gets a quarter of the batch-level energy. Scaling channel $k$ by $\alpha_k$ multiplies its energy by $\alpha_k^2$. Matching every reward to the densest one, $\pi_{\text{ref}}=\max_k\pi_k$, gives $\alpha_k^\star=\sqrt{\pi_{\text{ref}}/\pi_k}$. In practice DARA uses

$$w_k=\min\!\left(w_{\max},\sqrt{\pi_{\text{ref}}/\pi_k}\right)\ (\pi_k>0),\qquad w_k=1\ (\pi_k=0),$$

with $w_{\max}=5$, recomputed on every batch. There are two variants. DARA-Sym uses $\tilde A_k=w_kA_k$. DARA-Asym, the main method, uses $\tilde A_k=A_k+(w_k-1)[A_k]_+$, which amplifies only positive advantages so that, for example, a correct but over-long answer is not pushed down harder. The weighted sum is then batch-whitened as in GDPO.

Headline results:

  • Tool calling (ToolRL data, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct, BFCL-v4, 5 seeds). Median training format reward reaches 0.8 at step 14–15, against 19 for GDPO and 34 for GRPO. At step 60 DARA leads on BFCL Average Format (about 96% against at most 90%). At step 100 the differences shrink to within about 1 point. Adding a third reward (thinking length of at most 16 words) cuts GDPO's Multi-Turn format from 91.4 to 83.2, while DARA stays at about 91–92.
  • Math (DeepScaleR, correctness plus at most 4000 tokens, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-4B). The "stable crossing" step for 99% training length compliance is 41–65% earlier than GDPO (for example 56/50 against 142 on R1-7B). On held-out data, DARA-Sym has the lowest Exceed rate. DARA-Asym has the best Joint (correct and short) score on both R1 models at step 50, but GRPO wins on Qwen3-4B.
  • Group size. Larger $G$ at a fixed response budget raises density and speeds up format learning for every method, as $q_G$ predicts.

The most interesting part

Strengths. The diagnosis is clean and checkable. Once you see that per-group z-scoring fixes the energy of each active group at $G-1$, the residual imbalance is obvious, and it can be measured directly from rewards at almost no cost. The method is about ten lines of code, with no extra hyperparameters beyond $w_{\max}$ and $\tau$, and it plugs into any GDPO pipeline. The reframing of sparsity as "rarely discriminative within a group" is useful because it covers the saturation regime too: near 99% compliance the length reward goes quiet, and that is exactly where DARA separates from GDPO. The appendix is honest about scope. It states that energy matching is exact only for uncapped DARA-Sym, and it bounds DARA-Asym's energy between $E_k$ and $w_k^2E_k$ (Prop. 5). Figure 8 shows explicitly where the cap binds.

Weaknesses.

  1. Energy is a noise quantity, not a signal quantity. The paper's own Prop. 1 shows that $E_k$ controls the fluctuation $V_k$ of reward $k$'s gradient (under an isotropy condition), and the authors note that symmetric scaling leaves the signal-to-noise ratio $\|h_k\|^2/V_k$ unchanged. So DARA-Sym equalizes per-reward gradient variance. Why that should be the right target is argued only by analogy. Inverse density $1/\pi_k$, which would roughly equalize the summed signal if per-group gradients were aligned, or other exponents, are never tested. The $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is "derived", but from an objective that was chosen, not justified.
  2. The theory doesn't cover the regime where the gains appear. The largest wins (99% compliance) come after the cap $w_{\max}=5$ binds (from step 48–62 in Fig. 8). At that point DARA is effectively a static weight of 5 on the sparse channel. The Static $w=5$ ablation is therefore the critical control. It is run on one model (R1-1.5B) with one seed, with differences of about 1 point. Its numbers (DARA-Asym Acc 48.03) also don't match Table 3 (45.83) for the same model, and the checkpoint used is not stated. No $w_{\max}$ sweep is reported.
  3. Batch whitening makes it a relative reweighting. After $\mathcal N_B$, raising the sparse channel effectively shrinks the dense one. This probably explains DARA-Sym's consistent accuracy cost and why the Asym variant is needed. The paper reports the trade-off but doesn't frame it this way.
  4. Statistics. The math runs use a single training seed. Bootstrap CIs over questions are computed (App. D.3) but not shown in any table, and they ignore training variance anyway. The tool-calling tables give 5-seed means with no spread. Many final-performance gaps are a fraction of a point (for example 3B Average Accuracy 53.63 against 53.66). "Remaining competitive" is the accurate summary. "Up to 65% fewer steps" uses a bespoke stable-crossing metric at the strictest threshold, from one seed.
  5. Baselines and confounds. SAW, SA-MRPO and RVPO are discussed but not run. DAPO dynamic filtering keeps a group whenever the summed reward varies, so in the math setting $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is pushed towards 1 by construction. This interaction is not analysed. For continuous rewards (correctness in $[-3,3]$), any tiny within-group difference counts as fully active with energy $G-1$, so density says little. This GDPO fragility is inherited but not discussed. Only about 100 steps of short training runs are tested, and nothing shows the speed-up survives long training at scale.

Proof sketch

Density–energy identity. In an active group, $\sum_j (A_k^{(i,j)})^2=\sum_j(r_k^{(i,j)}-\mu_{i,k})^2/\sigma_{i,k}^2=G-1$, because $\sigma_{i,k}^2$ uses divisor $G-1$. Inactive groups contribute 0. Summing over the $B\pi_k$ active groups gives $E_k=B\pi_k(G-1)$. The calibration follows: setting $\alpha_k^2B\pi_k(G-1)=B\pi_{\text{ref}}(G-1)$ gives $\alpha_k^\star=\sqrt{\pi_{\text{ref}}/\pi_k}$. This is an algebraic identity, not a deep result.

Prop. 1 (energy and gradient geometry). Let $g_k=\frac1N\sum_{i,j}A_k^{(i,j)}z^{(i,j)}$ with $N=BG$ and $z$ the effective score. Write $z=m+\xi$, with $m$ the conditional mean given $\mathcal F$ (prompts, rewards, loss weights) and $\xi$ zero-mean noise with covariance $C$. Then

$$\mathbb E[\langle g_k,g_l\rangle\mid\mathcal F]=\langle h_k,h_l\rangle+N^{-2}A_k^\top PCPA_l,$$

where $P$ is the block-diagonal within-group centering projector. Inserting $P$ is free because each $A_k$ sums to zero within every group, so prompt-level shared noise cancels. If $\|PCP-cP\|_{\text{op}}\le\delta c$, then $N^{-2}A_k^\top PCPA_l=\frac{c}{N^2}\langle A_k,A_l\rangle+R_{kl}$ with $|R_{kl}|\le\frac{\delta c}{N^2}\sqrt{E_kE_l}$. Setting $l=k$ gives $(1-\delta)cE_k/N^2\le V_k\le(1+\delta)cE_k/N^2$. Corollary 1: under DARA-Sym with an unbinding cap, $w_k^2V_k$ is the same for all rewards up to $1\pm\delta$. Final batch whitening only applies one common positive scale, because $\mu_B(S_{\text{sym}})=0$.

Prop. 2 (signal direction for binary rewards). With independent sampling and $p_{i,k}=\Pr(r_k=1\mid x_i)$, the score identity gives $\mathbb E[z\mid r_k=1]=\nabla p_{i,k}/p_{i,k}$, and the difference between the two conditional means is $\nabla p_{i,k}/[p_{i,k}(1-p_{i,k})]$. So $\mathbb E[g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\frac1N\sum_{i:\,0<f_{i,k}<1}\frac{Gf_{i,k}(1-f_{i,k})}{(\sigma_{i,k}+\epsilon)p_{i,k}(1-p_{i,k})}\nabla p_{i,k}$. Each mixed group pushes in the direction that raises that prompt's success probability. The positive-only part used by DARA-Asym has the same direction, with denominator $p_{i,k}$ instead of $p_{i,k}(1-p_{i,k})$.

Props. 3–4 (group size). $\mathbb E[\pi_k]=\frac1B\sum_iq_G(p_{i,k})$. The increment $q_{G+1}-q_G=p(1-p)^G+(1-p)p^G\ge0$, and $q_G$ is concave, so Jensen shows that a pooled success rate overestimates density. At a fixed budget $N$, the expected energy per response is $(1-1/G)\bar q_{k,G}$, which increases in $G$.

Broader context

For an outsider: GRPO replaced the learned value baseline with a group-mean baseline. That made LLM RL cheap, but it means a prompt teaches nothing about a reward unless that reward varies within the group. DAPO's dynamic sampling tackles the "all-same" groups by resampling. DARA tackles them by reweighting across reward channels. It sits next to multi-task gradient balancing from supervised learning, such as GradNorm and uncertainty weighting, which also equalize per-task gradient magnitudes. Its closest relatives are the concurrent GDPO variants (DVAO, SAW, SA-MRPO).

The $\sqrt{\pi_{\text{ref}}/\pi_k}$ rule has a familiar look from frequency reweighting. It resembles inverse-square-root class-frequency reweighting in long-tail classification, and word2vec's $\sqrt{t/f}$ subsampling. An IR reader will see an IDF-like weight on how often a channel discriminates. That connection is real, not decorative: the shared principle is that rarely informative events should carry more weight per occurrence, damped by a square root.

Plausible follow-ups:

  • Target signal rather than energy, for example by estimating $\|h_k\|$ from agreement between per-group gradients, or by sweeping the exponent $\beta$ in $(\pi_{\text{ref}}/\pi_k)^\beta$.
  • Use per-prompt instead of batch-global weights.
  • Combine DARA with adaptive $G$, since Prop. 4 says larger groups buy density directly. Allocating more rollouts to prompts where a sparse reward is near $p\in\{0,1\}$ is a natural active-sampling variant.

For generative retrieval and RL-trained search agents (Search-R1-style), the multi-reward set-up is common: a dense format or valid-docid reward alongside a sparse binary relevance or answer reward (hit@k, exact match). Relevance rewards on hard queries sit exactly in the $p\approx0$ low-density regime, and valid-identifier constraints saturate quickly. Density-aware aggregation is a cheap thing to try there, and one could log $\pi_k$ for the relevance channel to diagnose stalled training.

title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-20

Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives — Hubert Strauss, Liam Fowl, Noam Razin (2026) — arXiv:2611.23397

Setting and problem

The object of study is on-policy distillation (OPD) of an autoregressive student $\pi_\theta$ toward a fixed teacher $\pi_T$. Both are distributions over length-$L$ outputs $y \in \mathcal{V}^L$ given a prompt $x$. The student factorizes as $$\pi_\theta(y \mid x) = \prod_{l=1}^{L} \mathrm{softmax}(z[x, y_{<l}])_{y_l},$$ where $z[x,c] \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$ is the logit vector at prefix $c$. The teacher is assumed to put positive mass on every sequence. "On-policy" means the training sequences are sampled from the student itself, not from the teacher, which removes the train/test (exposure-bias) mismatch of classical off-policy, sequence-level KD.

OPD objectives differ along two axes.

  • Granularity. Sequence-level OPD (the MiniLLM form) minimizes the reverse KL over whole sequences: $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}}(\theta;x) = \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdots\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_T(\cdots\mid x)\big) = \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta}\Big[\ln \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_T(y\mid x)}\Big].$$ In practice it is optimized as a policy gradient with sequence "reward" $-\ln(\pi_\theta(y|x)/\pi_T(y|x))$. Token-level OPD (the GKD form) is myopic. It sums a per-prefix divergence along a student rollout, with a stop-gradient on the sampling distribution: $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}\text{-}D}(\theta;x) = \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{sg}(\theta)}}\sum_{l=1}^{L} D\big(\pi_T(\cdot\mid x,y_{<l})\,\|\,\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x,y_{<l})\big).$$
  • Divergence. $D$ is an $f$-divergence $D_f(p\|q)=\sum_v q(v) f(p(v)/q(v))$. The paper treats forward KL (FKL, $f(u)=u\ln u$), reverse KL (RKL, $f(u)=-\ln u$), Jensen–Shannon (JS), and the hybrid $\tfrac12$FKL$+\tfrac12$RKL.

The key modelling choice. Because $\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = \sum_c J_\theta(z[x,c])^\top \nabla_{z[x,c]}\mathcal{L}$ and the Jacobian is the same for every objective, the analysis isolates the logits gradient $\nabla_{z[x,c]}\mathcal{L}$. The gradient identities hold for any parameterization. The separation theorems, however, use a tabular softmax student: every $z[x,c]$ is a free parameter. Training is full-batch gradient descent on the exact expected objective, so there is no sampling noise and no variance argument; the effects are properties of the expected gradient field. The student is also assumed to be able to represent the teacher (realizable). This idealization is where the results live. Everything is driven by how the objective weights logits, not by function approximation or estimator variance.

The question. It is commonly said that FKL is "mode-covering" and RKL "mode-seeking". That describes only the fixed point. The paper asks a different question. Given a student, teacher and task, which tokens does each OPD objective prioritize during gradient-based training, in what order are token positions learned, and how fast can the student reach the teacher's behaviour, in particular on tokens it initially finds unlikely?

Prior theory has compared on-policy with off-policy distillation (sample complexity, misspecification: Rohatgi et al., Zhang et al., Sriraman et al.), studied variance in sequence-level OPD, and shown a two-step MDP in which token-level OPD converges to a worse solution under non-realizability (Agrawal et al.). Wu et al. and Piskorz et al. noted that the RKL logit gradient is weighted by $\pi_\theta(v)$, but did not quantify what this does to optimization time. The gap is a trajectory-level, objective-versus-objective comparison.

Main idea

The paper writes every OPD logits gradient in one closed form (Lemma 1) and reads the biases directly off that form. Let $\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c)$ be the reverse KL between the student's and the teacher's full continuations after prefix $c$, and let $a_f(u)=e^u f'(e^u)-f(e^u)$. Then $$-\nabla_{z_v[x,c]}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}} = \pi_\theta(c|x)\,\pi_\theta(v|x,c)\Big[\ln\tfrac{\pi_T(v|x,c)}{\pi_\theta(v|x,c)} - \mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c,v) + \mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c)\Big],$$ $$-\nabla_{z_v[x,c]}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}\text{-}f} = \pi_\theta(c|x)\,\pi_\theta(v|x,c)\Big[a_f\big(\ln\tfrac{\pi_T(v)}{\pi_\theta(v)}\big) - \mathbb{E}_{v'\sim\pi_\theta}a_f\big(\ln\tfrac{\pi_T(v')}{\pi_\theta(v')}\big)\Big].$$

The two headline findings follow from these formulas.

  1. Granularity: a future agreement bias. The sequence-level gradient contains an extra term, $-\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c,v)$. It rewards a token $v$ _whenever the student and teacher already agree on what follows $v$_, regardless of how likely $v$ is under the teacher. Proposition 1 makes this exact. The sequence-level gradient equals the token-level RKL gradient toward a tilted teacher $\tilde\pi_T(v'|x,c)\propto \pi_T(v'|x,c)\exp(-\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c,v'))$, and the tilt vanishes only when downstream disagreement is the same for every $v'$. Two consequences follow:
  2. Reverse learning order. Positions are learned back to front: an early position keeps receiving gradient until the later positions match, even if its own next-token distribution already matches the teacher.
  3. Pull toward "easy-to-continue" prefixes. These are short, formulaic or repetitive continuations.

In a binary-tree navigation task this costs an exponential-in-$L^2$ slowdown compared with token-level OPD. On Qwen3-1.7B distilled from Qwen3-8B using WildJailbreak prompts, the student ends up refusing nearly all benign requests, while the teacher refuses only 17.5% of them. 2. Divergence: how well-conditioned the landscape is. The $\ell_1$ norm of the token-level logits gradient equals $\pi_\theta(c|x)\cdot\mathrm{MAD}_{v\sim\pi_\theta}[a_f(\ln \pi_T/\pi_\theta)]$ (Lemma 2), where MAD is the mean absolute deviation. - For FKL ($a_f(u)=e^u$) this is exactly $2\pi_\theta(c|x)\,\mathrm{TV}(\pi_T,\pi_\theta)$. The gradient vanishes only when the student matches the teacher. - For RKL and JS it is the MAD of the log-ratio under the student. That can be arbitrarily small while TV is close to 1, for example when the student is confidently concentrated on a token the teacher dislikes. - Per token, the RKL gradient is multiplied by $\pi_\theta(v)$, so tokens the student finds unlikely barely move. Theorem 2 shows that FKL (and the FKL+RKL mixture) raises such a token in $O(\ln(1/p_0))$ steps, where $p_0$ is its initial student probability. RKL and JS need $\tilde\Omega(p_0^{-1/(1+\ln(|\mathcal{V}|-1))})$ steps. - Experiments: when distilling knowledge of Python APIs released after the student, RKL and JS fail where FKL and the mixture succeed. On MATH, where the student is already somewhat competent, RKL's advantage grows with the teacher–student capacity gap, because RKL prefers tokens the student can already produce.

The paper's verdict: no OPD objective is best in general. The choice depends on the student, the teacher and the task, and the paper gives mechanistic rules of thumb rather than slogans.

The most interesting part

The cleanest insight is the tilted-teacher reinterpretation of sequence-level reverse KL (Proposition 1). Sequence-level OPD is not a "more global" version of token-level RKL. At every prefix it is token-level RKL, but toward a teacher reweighted by $\exp(-\text{future disagreement})$. This one identity explains several observations that previously looked unrelated: - why MiniLLM-style training produces short or repetitive outputs: ending early or repeating leaves nothing downstream to disagree on; - why it over-refuses: refusals are formulaic, while helpful answers have many continuations the student can get wrong; - why it can help in some cases. In Appendix A, an arithmetic task with a calculator tool, a calculator call is easy to complete in agreement with the teacher. Sequence-level OPD therefore drives calculator use from the teacher's 7.2% to nearly 100%, and the student's accuracy ends up above the teacher's.

The bias depends on the current student, not only on the teacher. So it is a moving, self-reinforcing target. In the tree example, once the student assigns low probability to the correct prefix, every logit in that subtree is down-weighted by the prefix probability $\pi_\theta(c|x)$. The student then learns that subtree more slowly, the downstream RKL stays large, and the wrong prefix keeps winning.

Main limitation: the exponential separation in Theorem 1 relies on a constructed teacher. That teacher is uniform after a wrong first token (so student and teacher agree perfectly there at initialization) and sharp after the right one, with $\delta=e^{-L}$. The first gradient step with $\eta\le 2$ already pushes the root logit gap to about $-\eta L^2/8$. So part of the trap is a large first step on the exact expected gradient, in a tabular model. How strong the bias is for real networks, with sampled gradient estimates, shared parameters and baselines or clipping, is supported only empirically.

Proof sketch

Lemma 1 (gradient identities). For sequence level, split $y=(c',s)$ and use the KL chain rule: $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}}=\sum_{c'}\pi_\theta(c'|x)[\ln\frac{\pi_\theta(c'|x)}{\pi_T(c'|x)}+\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c')]$. Only $\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c)$ depends on $z[x,c]$. Expanding it one more step gives $\sum_{v'}\pi_\theta(v'|x,c)[\ln\frac{\pi_\theta(v')}{\pi_T(v')}+\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_\theta(x,c,v')]$. The downstream RKLs do not depend on $z[x,c]$, and the softmax derivative $\partial_{z_v}\pi_\theta(v')=\pi_\theta(v')(\mathbb{1}[v=v']-\pi_\theta(v))$ yields the centred form. The token-level case is the same softmax-derivative computation applied to $D_f$. Proposition 1 then matches the two bracketed expressions by defining $\tilde\pi_T$. Lemma 2 follows because the logit gradient has the form $\pi_\theta(v)(g(v)-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}g)$, whose $\ell_1$ norm is by definition a MAD under $\pi_\theta$.

Theorem 1 (binary tree, $\mathcal{V}=\{A,B\}$, target $y^\star=A^L$, $\delta=e^{-L}$, uniform tabular initialization, GD with $\eta\in(0,2]$, $L\gtrsim \ln(1/\epsilon)/\eta$). - Claim: sequence-level OPD gives $\pi(B|x)\ge 1-e^{-\eta L^2/8}$ after one step and needs $T_{\mathrm{seq}}\ge e^{\eta L^2/16}$ steps to reach success $1-\epsilon$. Every token-level objective keeps $\pi(A|x)$ non-decreasing and succeeds within $L+\lceil 16L\ln(4L)/\eta\rceil+\lceil 16L/(\eta\epsilon)\rceil = O(L\ln L)$ steps. - Step 1, the B-subtree never changes. After $B$ the teacher and the student are both uniform. By induction every logits gradient in that subtree is zero (Lemma 5), so $\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}(x,B)=0$ forever. - Step 2, a closed form for the root. With $\rho_t=\ln(\pi(A|x)/\pi(B|x))$, Lemma 6 gives $$\rho_{t+1}-\rho_t = 2\eta\,\pi(A|x)\pi(B|x)\Big[\ln\tfrac{1-\delta}{\delta}-\rho_t-\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_t(x,A)\Big].$$ At initialization $\mathrm{RKL}^{\mathrm{seq}}_0(x,A)=\frac{L-1}{2}\ln\frac{1}{4\delta(1-\delta)}\approx L^2/2$.
