This quadratic term beats $\ln\frac{1-\delta}{\delta}\approx L$, which gives $-\eta L^2/4\le\rho_1\le-\eta L^2/8$. - Step 3, escaping is exponentially slow. While $\rho_t\le\rho_1+1$, drop the non-negative RKL term and bound $\pi(A)\pi(B)\le e^{\rho_t}$. Each step then increases $\rho$ by at most $2\eta e^{\rho_1+1}(L+L^2/2)$. Getting $\rho$ up by even 1 therefore takes about $e^{\eta L^2/8}/(\eta L^2)\ge e^{\eta L^2/16}$ steps. The trick is that softmax saturation at the root makes the root's own gradient vanish, so it does not matter how fast the subtree is being repaired. - Token level. Lemma 8 shows by induction that each log-odds $\rho_{t,j}$ along $y^\star$ is monotone and stays in $[0,\ln\frac{1-\delta}{\delta}]$, so prefix probabilities never drop. The argument then has three parts: (I) a lower bound on the per-step increase of $\rho_{t,j}$ while it is below $\ln(L/\epsilon)$, since the student's $\pi(B)$ is still well above the teacher's $\delta$; (II) a joint potential argument across positions showing $\pi(y^\star)\ge 1/2$ within $O(L\ln L/\eta)$ steps, which handles the small prefix weights early on; (III) with all prefix weights at least $1/2$, each position reaches $\ln(L/\epsilon)$ in $O(L/(\eta\epsilon))$ more steps, and Bernoulli's inequality gives $\prod_j(1-\epsilon/L)\ge 1-\epsilon$.

Theorem 3 (Appendix A) reuses the same trajectories with the correct set enlarged to $\{y^\star\}\cup\{y: y_1=B\}$. Now sequence-level OPD succeeds after one step, while token-level OPD needs $\Omega(L\ln L)$ steps (FKL, JS) or $\Omega(\ln L)$ (RKL). The advantage is transient, because the global optimum is still the teacher.

Proposition 2 (counterexample for RKL and JS). Take $\pi_\theta(v^\star)=1-\alpha$ and $\pi_T(v^\star)=\alpha$, with the rest spread uniformly. Then $\mathrm{TV}=1-2\alpha$. Under $\pi_\theta$, however, the log-ratio is almost always the constant $\ln\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}$, so its MAD is $O(\alpha\ln(1/\alpha))\to 0$.

Theorem 2 (single prefix, tabular, GD, $\eta\le1$, prefix probability $\ge\gamma$, and $p_0=\pi_{\theta(0)}(v^\star|x,c)$ small enough relative to $q_{\min}=\min_v\pi_T(v|x,c)$). - Claim: to reach $\pi(v^\star)\ge\pi_T(v^\star)-\epsilon$, RKL and JS need $\Omega\big(p_0^{-1/(1+\ln(|\mathcal{V}|-1))}/\ln(1/p_0)\big)$ steps. FKL and the mixture need at most $\frac{2}{\eta\gamma\epsilon}\ln\frac{1}{p_0}+\frac{2}{\eta\gamma\epsilon}\ln\frac{\pi_T(v^\star)}{q_{\min}}$ steps. - Lower bound, step 1 (split the vocabulary). Tracking $v^\star$ alone fails, because other low tokens rising can push it up indirectly. Instead, sort the logits and choose a split $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{high}}$ / $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{low}}$ that maximizes "mean of the top $k$ minus the $(k{+}1)$-th logit". A harmonic-sum telescoping argument shows this gap is $\Delta\ge\frac{\ln(1/(|\mathcal{V}|p_0))}{1+\ln(|\mathcal{V}|-1)}$. This is where the odd exponent comes from. - Lower bound, step 2 (potential argument). Gradient descent preserves the sum of logits. Combined with AM–GM, this shows that while the potential $\Phi_t=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{low}}}(z_v(t)-z_v(0))<\frac{\ln 2}{2}$, the total low-group mass is at most $2|\mathcal{V}|e^{-\Delta}$. The per-step increase of $\Phi$ is bounded by $\eta\,\pi(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{low}})\ln\frac{|\mathcal{V}|}{\pi(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{low}})q_{\min}}$, which uses the $\pi_\theta(v)$ weighting and $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_T)\le\ln(1/q_{\min})$. Dividing gives the bound. - Upper bound. The FKL logit gradient $-\pi_\theta(c|x)(\pi_T(v)-\pi_\theta(v))$ pushes $v^\star$ by roughly $\eta\gamma\epsilon$ per step until it is within $\epsilon$. A log-odds argument then gives the $\ln(1/p_0)$ dependence. The mixture inherits this from its FKL half.

The rate gap is "exponential" in the scale $\ln(1/p_0)$, but in absolute terms it is a power law with a small exponent: for $|\mathcal{V}|\approx 1.5\times10^5$, $1/(1+\ln(|\mathcal{V}|-1))\approx 1/12.9$. Theorem 4 (Appendix B) proves the same lower bound for sequence-level OPD, via a MAD identity whose argument is offset by the downstream RKL (Lemma 3).

Broader context

For an outsider: knowledge distillation of LLMs moved from imitating teacher text (Kim and Rush, 2016) to on-policy distillation, where the student writes and the teacher grades each token. Agarwal et al.'s GKD introduced the token-level family with a choice of divergence (they favoured JS and RKL). Gu et al.'s MiniLLM introduced the sequence-level RKL policy-gradient formulation. Token-level OPD is now standard in frontier post-training pipelines. This paper offers the first optimization-theoretic account of why token-level OPD tends to work better, and of when RKL versus FKL is the better choice.

The closest intellectual ancestor is Razin et al.'s line on vanishing gradients in RL finetuning (ICLR 2024) and "what makes a reward model a good teacher" (NeurIPS 2025). There, the expected policy gradient is small when the reward has low variance under the policy, regardless of how suboptimal the policy is. Lemma 2 is the distillation analogue. The token-level RKL gradient is the MAD of the "reward" $\ln(\pi_T/\pi_\theta)$ under the student, so a confident but wrong student gets no signal. FKL escapes this because its "reward" $\pi_T/\pi_\theta$ has mean exactly 1, so its MAD becomes a TV distance. A second relative is the empirical work on entropy collapse under RKL (Jin et al.'s entropy-aware OPD). The results also connect to imitation-learning theory: DAgger-style on-policy supervision, and Agrawal et al.'s distributional DAgger, which reaches the opposite verdict on token versus sequence level under non-realizability.

Follow-up idea. An adaptive, per-prefix objective. Lemmas 1–3 give cheap diagnostics: the student mass on teacher-preferred tokens, the MAD of the log-ratio, and an estimate of the downstream-RKL spread across candidate tokens. These could switch the loss online between FKL (when the teacher's mass sits on student-unlikely tokens, i.e. new knowledge) and RKL (when the student is competent and the capacity gap is large). They could also turn the tilt on or off by adding a controllable fraction of the future-agreement term. A matching theory question: redo Theorem 2 with a linear-softmax (shared embedding) parameterization, where raising one unlikely token moves its neighbours as well.

A genuine connection to generative retrieval. Hierarchical semantic docids (DSI-style k-means trees, RQ-VAE codes) make GR decoding exactly a tree-navigation problem: a docid is a root-to-leaf path, and success is the probability of the gold path, much like $\pi(y^\star|x)$ in Theorem 1. Distilling a large GR model, or a cross-encoder-induced docid distribution, into a small decoder is OPD over docid sequences, and the paper's results translate fairly directly. - Sequence-level KL would show a future agreement bias toward docid prefixes whose subtrees the student already matches. Those are clusters with few documents or low-entropy continuations, which is an analogue of over-refusal and plausibly a bias toward small or "easy" clusters. - Learning order: sequence-level KL would fix deep code positions first and coarse cluster tokens last, while token-level objectives learn the coarse levels first. This matters for beam search, which prunes on prefixes. - Incremental indexing: for new documents, whose docids are improbable under the old student, Theorem 2 argues for FKL or an FKL+RKL mixture over RKL or JS in continual distillation.

Each of these is a testable prediction in a small, controlled setting, which suits a theoretical-IR agenda.

title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-20

Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure — Behrooz Tahmasebi, Melanie Weber (2026) — arXiv:2611.24032

Setting and problem

The object of study is a frozen language model used at inference time on tasks with a known symmetry. Let $\mathcal{X}$ be the space of prompts, $\mathcal{C}$ a finite set of $C$ answer classes, and $y^\star : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{C}$ the target. A finite group $G$ acts on prompts, $(g, x) \mapsto g \cdot x$, by semantically neutral rewritings: node relabelings and edge reorderings of a serialized graph ($G = S_n \times S_{|E|}$), permutations of multiple-choice options, reorderings of premises or few-shot demonstrations. The task is assumed invariant, $y^\star(g \cdot x) = y^\star(x)$. Equivariant outputs (e.g. the correct letter moves when options are permuted) are reduced to this case by mapping answers back with $\rho(g)^{-1}$.

For one prompt there are two independent sources of randomness. The rewriting coordinate $g \in G$ picks a representation $g \cdot x$. The decoding coordinate is a reasoning trace $\omega \sim p_{\theta,\tau}(\cdot \mid g \cdot x)$, with $\tau$ the sampling temperature. A response field $V_x(g,\omega)$ records what we read off a trace: an answer, logits, a verifier score. A distribution-level decoding rule $D$ maps the whole conditional trace distribution at one rewriting to a point in a real Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, giving the decoded orbit field

$$F^D_x(g) = D\big(p_{\theta,\tau}(\cdot \mid g\cdot x), V_x(g,\cdot)\big) \in \mathcal{H}.$$

Examples are self-consistency class probabilities $F^{SC}_x(g)_c = P_{\omega\mid g}(a_x(g,\omega)=c)$, expected logits, and a verifier-weighted vote with inverse temperature $\beta_D$. The idealized target is the fully symmetrized response $q^D_x = P_G F^D_x = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g} F^D_x(g)$. This is invariant in the rewriting coordinate but still a score vector over classes, so $\arg\max_c (q^D_x)_c$ is a decision. Computing it costs $|G|$ forward passes, which is hopeless ($20! \approx 2\times 10^{18}$). The cheap version uses a multiset $S = \{\{s_1,\dots,s_{|S|}\}\}$ drawn i.i.d. uniformly from $G$ and the operator $(A_S f)(h) = \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_i f(s_i h)$, where $h$ indexes the "starting representation".

The paper asks three questions:

  1. Can any amount of decoding at the original prompt replace rewriting?
  2. How large must $|S|$ be so that $A_S F \approx P_G F$ in $L^2(G;\mathcal{H})$, and does this depend on $|G|$, $C$, or the decoder?
  3. How do the rewriting budget and the trace budget interact?

Prior work is empirical. It documents order and format sensitivity, uses permutation-based debiasing and prompt ensembles, and shows (Kozodoi et al., 2026) that paraphrase diversity can beat self-consistency at matched compute. Separately, the theory of invariance (Tahmasebi & Weber, 2026a) showed that approximate invariance of a deterministic function class needs only $\Theta(\log|G|)$ random group elements. What was missing is a theory for stochastic frozen models in which decoding and rewriting are separate.

Several modelling choices matter, and they shape the results:

  • Error is measured in mean square over the starting rewriting $h \sim \mathrm{Unif}(G)$, not at the actual prompt.
  • The guarantee is required to hold uniformly over all fields $F \in L^2(G;\mathcal{H})$ simultaneously, for one draw of $S$. This uniformity is the only source of the $\log|G|$.
  • Decoders are treated at the distribution level, so finite-trace estimation error is split off.
  • The symmetry must be known and exact.

Main idea

Treat test-time compute as a two-dimensional budget, with rewritings along the orbit and traces within a decoding fiber, and analyse the rewriting dimension as a random-walk / operator-approximation problem on $G$.

The headline results:

  1. No decoding substitute. An algorithm that only queries $x$, however adaptively and with however many traces, cannot learn the orbit-averaged decision. Two worlds that agree at $x$ but differ elsewhere on the orbit force error at least $1/2$ (Theorem 1).
  2. Logarithmic scaling law. With probability $1-\delta$ over $S$, simultaneously for every Hilbert space and every field, $$\|A_S F - P_G F\|_{L^2(G;\mathcal{H})} \le \sqrt{\tfrac{8}{3}\tfrac{\log(|G|/\delta)}{|S|}}\;\|F - P_G F\|_{L^2(G;\mathcal{H})},$$ so $|S| = O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log|G| + \log(1/\delta)))$ gives relative error $\varepsilon$. The $\log|G|$ is tight in the worst case over groups (Theorem 2 / 17).
  3. Decoder-agnostic. Because the event depends only on $S$, it covers every model, temperature, decoding rule, and every realized randomized decoder (each seed and trace realization). There is no union bound over traces and no dependence on $C$ (Corollary 3).
  4. From scores to accuracy. The excess error of sparse symmetrization over full symmetrization is bounded by a margin term plus a term of order $\log|G|/(t^2|S|)$ (Corollary 4). Full symmetrization's own error $R_G$ is left as a property of model and task.

The experiments use Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B-AWQ on synthetic graph tasks, a height-deduction task, ARC-Challenge with permuted options, and SST-2 few-shot ordering. At a matched budget of 16 passes, spending them on 16 rewritings beats 16 self-consistency traces when the model is order-sensitive and competent. Examples: edge count at $n=24$ goes from 83% to 100% (+16.5); deduction with $k=11$ goes from 79% to 99%; ARC goes from 91.8% to 94.6%. Across the 98 graph cells there are 24 significant gains and 3 significant losses. On next-token fields the rescaled error $\sqrt{|S|}\,\|A_S F - P_G F\|/\|F-P_GF\|$ stays in $[0.9, 1.1]$ for $n$ from 8 to 32.

The most interesting part

Conceptually, the cleanest idea is to reframe test-time scaling as having two coordinates, a fiber (decoding) and an orbit (rewriting), together with the observation that self-consistency only ever estimates $F_x(e)$, while what you actually want is $P_G F_x$. Seen this way, prompt-ensembling stops being a bag of tricks and becomes a precise operator on $L^2(G)$. The decomposition in Appendix C is also useful in practice. Total error is at most $\|\hat F - F^D\|$ (traces per rewriting) plus the rewriting term, so the two budgets can be tuned separately. The paper also notes that pooling joint $(g,\omega)$ samples silently changes the target for nonlinear decoders such as verifier-weighted votes, since $\mathbb{E}_g[D(P_{x,g})] \ne D(\mathbb{E}_g P_{x,g})$.

Several of the assumptions deserve honest critique.

  • The $\log|G|$ is the price of a uniformity nobody uses. For one fixed field $F$ chosen independently of $S$, the points $s_i h$ are i.i.d. uniform for every $h$. So $\mathbb{E}_S\|A_S F - P_G F\|^2 = \|F - P_G F\|^2/|S|$ exactly, with no $\log|G|$ at all, by plain Monte Carlo. The paper says this itself in Appendix C. The $\log|G|$ only buys validity for fields chosen after seeing $S$, adversarially or adaptively. In the experiments the models, decoders and seeds are all fixed independently of $S$. The empirical finding that the rescaled error is flat at about 1 as $\log|G|$ grows from about 25 to over 300 nats is therefore exactly what pointwise Monte Carlo predicts. It does not confirm the logarithmic law. The paper says "the logarithm ... is a worst case over groups that node relabeling does not pay", but the cleaner explanation is that the worst case is over fields, not over groups. "Only $O(\log|G|)$ rewritings suffice" is thus a weaker headline than it sounds: for a fixed model, $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ suffices, independent of $|G|$. The real content is reusability across models, but reusing one $S$ across fixed models never needed the operator bound.
  • The tightness example is a hypercube, not $S_n$. The lower bound is for $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$, where characters can be fixed by a small subgroup. For $S_n$, Figure 12 shows the operator constant curves "nearly coincide" across $n$. So even the uniform worst case may not grow like $\log|G|$ for the groups used in practice. One interesting point does come out of the hypercube case: for statement flips in the deduction task, the worst-case behaviour is real for adversarial fields.
  • Theorem 1 is an information-theoretic triviality. The construction sets the response to $0$ at $e$ and to a class indicator elsewhere. No regularity links the model's behaviour across the orbit, so of course the original prompt is uninformative. Any mild assumption, such as approximate invariance of the model or Lipschitz behaviour in some metric on $G$, would void it. It is a valid "in general" statement, but the theorem gives no quantitative insight into how much decoding can recover in realistic regimes. Here the experiments (plateaus of self-consistency) are more convincing than the theorem.
  • Mean square over the starting rewriting. The guarantee is averaged over $h$. In deployment one starts from the user's prompt, i.e. $h = e$. For random $S$ that is fine in expectation, but it is not the uniform-in-$h$ invariance that the "symmetrization" language suggests.
  • The target may be wrong. Corollary 4 bounds the gap to $R_G$ but says nothing about whether $R_G$ is smaller than the error at a single representation. Cycle detection shows that voting amplifies an invariant bias: greedy gets 0.76, symmetrization 0.65. The decomposition uses Markov, so the $1/t^2$ margin trade-off is loose.
  • Compute accounting. "Matched compute" counts generated tokens. Self-consistency at one prompt can share a prefilled KV cache, while $m$ distinct rewritings require $m$ prefills. For long serialized graphs this asymmetry is not negligible.

Two strengths stand out. The experiments are careful, with paired bootstrap intervals, a shared rewriting cache, and a sensitive/competent stratification that matches the theory's prediction of where gains occur. The paper is also candid about failure modes: invariant bias, near-insensitive tasks such as SST-2, and paraphraser drift.

Proof sketch

Theorem 1 (decoding cannot replace rewriting). Assume $|G| \ge 2$ and $C \ge 2$. Take classes $c_0 \ne c_1$ and set $V^{(j)}_x(e,\omega) = 0$ and $V^{(j)}_x(g,\omega) = u_{c_j}$ for $g \ne e$, with the same trace law at $x$ in both worlds. An algorithm querying only $x$, even adaptively, sees identically distributed transcripts in both worlds once its internal seed is coupled. But $P_G F^{(j)} = \frac{|G|-1}{|G|} u_{c_j}$, so the invariant decisions differ. Under a uniform prior the success probability is $\tfrac12(Q(c_0)+Q(c_1)) \le \tfrac12$.

Theorem 2/17 (sparse averaging). The key move is to view everything as operators on the $|G|$-dimensional space $L^2(G)$:

  • The translations $(T_s f)(h) = f(sh)$ are unitary. $A_S = \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_i T_{s_i}$ and $P_G = \mathbb{E}_s T_s$, the orthogonal projection onto constants (Lemma 10).
  • Set $X_i = T_{s_i} - P_G$. These are i.i.d. and mean zero, and since $T_s P_G = P_G T_s = P_G$ one gets $X_i X_i^* = X_i^* X_i = I - P_G$. Hence $\|X_i\| \le 1$ and the variance proxy is $\sigma^2 = m$.
  • Matrix Bernstein (Tropp) in dimension $N = |G|$ gives $P(\|A_S - P_G\|_{op} \ge t) \le 2N\exp(-mt^2/(2+2t/3))$. Choosing $t = \sqrt{8\log(N/\delta)/(3m)}$ yields the bound. The $\log|G|$ is exactly the dimensional factor in matrix Bernstein. This is the Alon–Roichman argument that random Cayley graphs with $O(\log|G|)$ generators are expanders.
  • Tensorization (Lemma 13). For Hilbert-valued fields, $\|T \otimes I_{\mathcal{H}}\| = \|T\|$: expand $F$ in an orthonormal basis of $\mathcal{H}$ and apply the scalar bound coordinatewise. Because $(A_S - P_G)P_G = 0$, $\|A_S F - P_G F\| \le \|A_S - P_G\|_{op}\,\|F - P_G F\|$. A single operator-norm event therefore controls every field in every Hilbert space. This is why the result has no dependence on $C$ and needs no union bound over decoders or traces (Corollary 3 is literally this applied to $F^D_x$ or to a realized $\hat F_{x,\xi}$).
  • Every representation (Lemma 15). By Peter–Weyl, every irreducible representation of $G$ occurs in the regular representation. So $\|\frac{1}{|S|}\sum \pi(s_i) - P_\pi\| \le \|A_S - P_G\|$ for every unitary $\pi$.
  • Lower bound. For $G = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$ and $m < n$ samples, the $s_i$ span a proper subspace, so some $a \ne 0$ is orthogonal to all of them. The character $\chi_a(h) = (-1)^{\langle a,h\rangle}$ has $P_G\chi_a = 0$ but $A_S\chi_a = \chi_a$, giving operator error exactly 1.

Corollary 4 (prediction error). If the sparse decision is wrong, then either the full decision is wrong or the two decisions disagree. Lemma 16: changing the argmax of $q$ with margin $\Delta$ requires $\|v - q\|_2^2 \ge \Delta^2/2$. On $\{\Delta_X > t\}$, Markov over $h$ gives disagreement probability at most $\frac{2}{t^2}\|A_S F_X - P_G F_X\|^2$. Plugging in the scaling law and averaging over $X$ gives

$$R_S \le R_G + P_X(\Delta_X \le t) + \frac{128\log(|G|/\delta)}{9t^2|S|}\,\mathbb{E}_X\|F_X - P_G F_X\|^2.$$

For self-consistency with $n_D$ traces per rewriting, the decoding error adds $\mathbb{E}\|\hat F - F\|^2 \le 1/n_D$, again with no dependence on $C$.

Broader context

For an outsider: the classical way to respect a symmetry is to build it into the architecture (Deep Sets, equivariant GNNs) or to average a model over the group (Janossy pooling, frame averaging, canonicalization, test-time augmentation in vision). Group averaging is exact but costs $|G|$ evaluations. The random-Cayley-graph / matrix-concentration argument says a logarithmic number of random elements gives an approximate projection. This paper imports that toolkit into LLM test-time compute. There, the "model" is a stochastic black box and the averaging must coexist with self-consistency and verifiers.

Closely related directions:

  • Tahmasebi & Weber (2026a), "Achieving approximate symmetry is exponentially easier than exact symmetry", is the deterministic parent of Theorem 2. Their sparse data augmentation paper (2026b) applies the same uniform-$S$ idea to gradients during training, where uniformity over parameters is actually needed, because the field changes with $\theta$ and $\theta$ depends on $S$. That is precisely the adaptivity that is absent at test time.
  • Kozodoi et al. (2026) and the prompt-sensitivity literature (Zheng et al. 2024 on option order; Herbst et al. 2025 on graph serialization) provide the empirical motivation.

There is a fairly direct connection to IR. Listwise LLM rerankers are notoriously sensitive to the order of candidates in the prompt (position bias, "lost in the middle"). Permutation self-consistency for listwise ranking (Tang et al., 2023) shuffles the candidate list, reranks, and aggregates rankings. That is test-time symmetrization with $G = S_k$ acting equivariantly on the output. Under this paper's framework, a Borda-style aggregation (averaging aligned score or rank vectors) is a linear Hilbert-valued decoder and falls under Corollary 3. Kemeny aggregation is nonlinear, and the Appendix C warning applies: pooling before versus after aggregating changes the target. Similar symmetries arise in setwise or pairwise LLM judges (A/B swap is $\mathbb{Z}_2$), in multi-document RAG context ordering, and in permutation-invariant set retrieval queries.

For generative retrieval the link is weaker. Docid relabelings are not a test-time symmetry of a trained GR model, because the identifiers are memorized and the task is not invariant to them. A more interesting angle is semantic-ID schemes with interchangeable codebook indices, but that is speculative. I see no genuine link to vector search beyond the shared expander-graph mathematics.

A plausible follow-up is a theory and benchmark of equivariant test-time symmetrization for LLM rerankers. Concretely:

  1. Show that rank-aggregation decoders induce a Hilbert-valued orbit field, e.g. via a permutation-matrix embedding.
  2. Use the pointwise Monte Carlo rate, not the uniform one, plus a margin argument on the full-orbit ranking, to predict how many shuffles achieve a target nDCG gap to the full-orbit ranking.
  3. Study the optimal split between shuffles and samples per shuffle, accounting for prefill cost under sliding-window reranking, where $|G| = k!$ is enormous and the KV-cache asymmetry noted above is decisive.

A second idea is to relax exact symmetry to approximate symmetries. Query reformulations in IR play the role of the paper's paraphrase kernel, and their drift term is exactly what query-expansion research tries to control.

title: Local Feature Selection without Label or Feature Leakage for Interpretable Machine Learning Predictions
html:
Claude deep-dive — 2026-11-19 (requested in issue #11)

Local Feature Selection without Label or Feature Leakage for Interpretable Machine Learning Predictions — Harrie Oosterhuis, Lijun Lyu, Avishek Anand (ICML 2024) — arXiv:2407.11778

Setting and problem

In local (instance-wise) feature selection, a selector $\zeta$ outputs a mask $h\sim\zeta(x)$, $h\in\{0,1\}^d$. A predictor sees only $x\odot h$, where unselected entries are a distinct symbol $\emptyset$, so $h$ is recoverable from the input. The two are trained jointly: $$\mathcal L(\zeta,f) = \frac1N\sum_i \mathbb E_{h_i\sim\zeta(x_i)}\big[L(f(x_i\odot h_i),y_i) + \lambda\|h_i\|\big].$$ The selected features are meant to be the explanation. Examples are L2X, INVASE, REAL-X and TabNet.

The known failure (Jethani et al., 2103.01890) is that the selector can encode the prediction in which features it picks. One pixel per MNIST image then gives near-perfect accuracy. Table 1 gives a minimal example: $y = x_1 + x_2$ with independent binary features. The mask pattern alone recovers both unselected values, so the method gets 100% accuracy with 62.5% feature reduction.

Main idea

The paper formalizes two kinds of leakage, for every $(x,y,s^{\text{in}},s^{\text{ex}})$ in the support $\Omega$:

  • Label leakage: $p(y\mid x[s^{\text{in}}]) \neq p(y\mid x[s^{\text{in}}], h[s^{\text{in}}]=1, h[s^{\text{ex}}]=0, \zeta)$.
  • Feature leakage: the same, with $x[s^{\text{ex}}]$ in place of $y$.

Cor. 2.5 (proved in App. B): there is no leakage iff the probability of every selection depends only on the selected values, $$\zeta(h\mid x) = \zeta(h\mid x') \quad\text{whenever } x\odot h = x'\odot h.$$

Two constructions satisfy this.

  • Linear program (Sec. 3, App. E). For known $p(x,y)$ over finite $x$, there is one variable per distinct $x\odot h$. This traces the exact Pareto front of leak-free selection and is used as a yardstick.
  • SUWR, Sequential Unmasking Without Reversion (Sec. 4). Run up to $T$ rounds starting from $h^0 = \mathbf 0$. In round $t$, stop with probability $\zeta^t_{\text{stop}}(x\odot h^t)$; otherwise add features $u^t\sim\zeta^t_{\text{select}}(x\odot h^t)$, and never remove any. Each decision sees only already-selected values, so the probability of the final mask is a product of factors that each depend on a subset of $x[s^{\text{in}}]$. Leak-freeness holds by construction (App. C). Training uses REINFORCE on sampled trajectories, weighting each prefix by its stop probability (Eqs. 11–12). Training may use anything; only inference must follow the protocol.

Two structural facts:

  • The first step is necessarily "blind": $\zeta^0$ is the same for every $x$. Eq. 13 shows that with full-support features, any leak-free single-feature selector must be input-independent.
  • Conjecture D.3: under full support (Eq. 10), every leak-free selector can be written as a SUWR process. It is open, and App. D shows a counterexample without full support.

Most interesting part

Cor. 2.5 is exactly Rubin's (1976) missing-at-random condition, though the paper does not use that term. Read $h$ as the observation indicator for the full vector $(x, y)$, with $y$ always unobserved. Then "no leakage" says $$p(h\mid x, y) = p(h\mid x_{\text{obs}(h)}),$$ which is MAR, in the "everywhere MAR" sense of Seaman et al. (2013) because it is required on all of $\Omega$. MAR is precisely the condition under which the selection mechanism is ignorable: the mask carries no information about the unobserved part beyond what the observed part already gives.

SUWR is the randomized monotone missingness mechanism of Robins & Gill (1997, Statistics in Medicine), in which the variables are revealed sequentially and each reveal decision depends only on what has been revealed. Robins and Gill proposed it because non-monotone MAR mechanisms are hard to write down otherwise. Whether every MAR/CAR mechanism is of this randomized-monotone form is the characterization question for coarsening at random (Gill, van der Laan & Robins 1997; Gill & Grünwald 2008, Annals of Statistics). That literature is the place to look for a proof, or a counterexample, of Conjecture D.3.

The same principle appears in counterfactual LTR: Oosterhuis's ICTIR'22 paper (2206.12204, Cor. 5.8) requires the display context to be independent of relevance. In both cases a selection mechanism is harmless exactly when it is measurable with respect to what the learner observes.

Method and evidence

  • Exp. 1, Pareto front (Fig. 1). Ten uniform binary features, $y = (\sum_{i=1}^5 x_{2i-1}x_{2i})^2$, complete information. All four baselines land in the region that is impossible without leakage. TabNet predicts perfectly with 2 features, although $y$ depends on all ten. SUWR stays on or near the LP front, which proves the baselines leak.
  • Exp. 2, standard synthetic benchmark (Tab. 2; 11 Gaussian features; Syn4–6 use $x_{11}$ as a control-flow switch). SUWR reaches oracle AUROC on Syn1–3 (.700/.895/.903) and is best among non-oracle methods on Syn4–6 (.810/.816/.896 vs oracle .818/.823/.902). It selects the control-flow feature 100% of the time with TPR ≥ 97%. INVASE has lower FDR on Syn4–5, but its CFSR is 56% / 41%: it uses $x_{11}$ without selecting it. The authors argue that leakage gives more ways to overfit, which explains the baselines' lower held-out AUROC.
  • Exp. 3, MNIST and Fashion-MNIST (3×3 patches on Fashion). SUWR's accuracy-vs-#features curve dominates both CAE (global selection) and REAL-X, which is surprisingly worse than global CAE. On Fashion, SUWR with 6 patches beats CAE with 10. The selection order gives a step-by-step "narrative" explanation (Figs. 2–3).

Caveats

  • Faithful does not mean important. No leakage guarantees that the prediction used only the selected values. It does not guarantee that those are the features a human would call important. The blind first step selects the same patch(es) for every image, so part of every explanation is fixed by policy, not by the instance.
  • Overlap with dynamic feature acquisition. Covert et al. (2301.00557, ICML 2023) and Li & Oliva (2021) use the same sequential inference structure for a different goal, saving acquisition costs. Those methods are leak-free for the same reason. The paper's contribution is the criterion and the proof that the amortized joint selectors leak, not the sequential mechanism. Since SUWR's guarantee is about inference only, a comparison against a greedy-MI acquisition policy would have been the natural baseline and is missing.
  • Scale. REINFORCE over $T$ sequential calls, demonstrated up to 784 inputs with 9-pixel patches. The no-leakage argument also requires $f$ to receive nothing but $x\odot h$: no global context, no batch statistics.

Broader context

For retrieval, the analogue is iterative retrieval in search agents and RAG. If each retrieval call depends only on the query and the passages retrieved so far, the retrieved set is a SUWR-style leak-free trace of the evidence. The guarantee breaks as soon as the generator has parametric knowledge of the answer, which plays the role of "unselected features". That gives one way to state "faithful attribution" for RAG formally.

title: Reaching the End of Unbiasedness: Uncovering Implicit Limitations of Click-Based Learning to Rank
html:
Claude deep-dive — 2026-11-19 (requested in issue #11)

Reaching the End of Unbiasedness: Uncovering Implicit Limitations of Click-Based Learning to Rank — Harrie Oosterhuis (ICTIR 2022) — arXiv:2206.12204

Setting and problem

Relevance is $R_{d\mid q} = P(R=1\mid d,q) \in [0,1]$, and ranking quality is $\mathcal R_q(y) = \sum_{d\in y}\lambda(\mathrm{rank}(d\mid y))\,R_{d\mid q}$. Clicks are biased. Under the affine model (Agarwal et al. 2019; Vardasbi et al. 2020), $$P(C=1\mid d,k,q) = \alpha_k R_{d\mid q} + \beta_k,$$ which covers position bias ($\beta_k=0$) and trust bias. The standard affine estimator $\hat R_{d\mid q} = \frac1{|\mathcal D_q|}\sum_i (c_i(d) - \hat\beta_{k_i(d)})/\hat\alpha_{k_i(d)}$ is unbiased when $\hat\alpha,\hat\beta$ are correct.

The field's usual recipe is: assume a click model, then derive an unbiased estimator for it. The paper runs this in reverse. It writes down the generic form of existing methods and asks which click behaviour they can possibly be unbiased for. These limitations follow from the form of the methods, not from their stated assumptions, which is why the paper calls them implicit.

Definitions:

  • Unbiasedness is per item: $\mathbb E[\hat R_{d\mid q}] = R_{d\mid q}$ for all $(d,q)$.
  • Consistency: $\lim_{|\mathcal D_q|\to\infty}\hat R_{d\mid q} = R_{d\mid q}$.

Main results

Counterfactual estimators (Sec. 5). The display context $x(d)$ is everything about how $d$ was shown that can affect its click, and it must not depend on $R_{d\mid q}$ (Def. 5.1). A counterfactual estimate is any average of transformed clicks (Def. 5.2): $$\hat R_{d\mid q} = \frac1{N_q}\sum_{i} f\big(c_i(d), x_i(d)\big).$$ This covers IPS, policy-aware, affine/trust-bias, cascade and DR-style estimators. The three pairwise estimators are covered separately.

  • Thm 5.4. For this class, unbiased $\Leftrightarrow$ consistent, because the limit equals the expectation.
  • Thm 5.5. Unbiasedness requires $R_{d\mid q} = \mathbb E_x\big[(P(C=1\mid d,x,q) - \beta_{x(d)})/\alpha_{x(d)}\big]$ with $\alpha_x = (f(1,x)-f(0,x))^{-1}$ and $\beta_x = -f(0,x)\,\alpha_x$. The reason: $\mathbb E[f(C,x)]$ is linear in $P(C=1)$.
  • Cor. 5.6 / 5.7. With deterministic logging, or with no control over the logging policy, click probabilities must be exactly affine in relevance, context by context.
  • Cor. 5.8. Two items shown in the same context must share $(\alpha_x,\beta_x)$. Otherwise you would need to know $R$ to correct for the bias.

Two examples:

  • Cascade click model. $\alpha_x$ is the probability that no earlier item was clicked, which depends only on other items, so the model is affine and correctable.
  • Plackett–Luce choice model. $P(c(d)=1\mid y,q) = R_{d\mid q}/\sum_{d'\in y}R_{d'\mid q}$. The denominator contains $R_{d\mid q}$ itself, so the click probability is non-affine in $R_d$ and no estimator of the form above can be unbiased or consistent.

Click modelling (Sec. 6). The relevance estimates are now parameters $\hat R_q$ minimized jointly with latent variables $\hat Z$.

  • Thm 6.3. The method is consistent iff, in the infinite-data limit, the true $R_q$ is the only relevance vector that minimizes the loss.
  • Thm 6.4. Unbiased iff $\mathbb E[\hat R^*_q] = R_q$.
  • Example 6.1. Two logged rankings, ABCD and BADC, with exact click probabilities. The position-based model then fixes $R_A = 0.9$, $R_B = 0.8$ and $\alpha_2 = 0.8$, but only $R_C = 2R_D$ and $\alpha_3 = 4\alpha_4$. C and D never appear in the top two positions, so their scale is not identified.

The conclusion is that click models can be unbiased in principle, but nothing general says when, and the answer depends on both the model and the logging policy.

Unbiased LambdaMART (Sec. 7, Thm 7.2). Hu et al. (WWW 2019) assume $P(C=1\mid d,k,q) = t_k^+ R$ and $P(C=0\mid d,k,q) = t_k^-(1-R)$. Clicks and non-clicks must sum to one, so as soon as two items with different relevance appear at position $k$, this forces $t_k^+ = t_k^- = 1$. The assumption implies clicks are already unbiased, so the method's unbiasedness is trivial.

Most interesting part

The proofs are short, and Thm 5.5 is close to definitional: the expectation of an average of per-click transforms is affine in the click probability. The value is in the framing. Unbiasedness is a property of an estimator class and a behaviour model together, and the class used by almost the whole field can only invert affine behaviour.

The step that does the work is Cor. 5.8, together with the requirement in Def. 5.1 that the context be independent of relevance. A correction can only use what is observable without knowing $R$. The same principle governs reweighted ERM in general: reweighting by a propensity that is a function of what the model conditions on leaves a well-specified minimizer unchanged; a propensity that depends on the label or on unobserved display factors moves it.

Caveats

  • The Plackett–Luce failure is partly about identifiability, not only about averaging. Scaling every $R$ in a ranking by $c$ leaves all PL click probabilities unchanged, because they are ratios and there is no "no-click" outside option in the model. So no estimator of any form can be unbiased for $R_{d\mid q}$ itself. The ordering is identified, and so are ratios $R_d/R_{d'}$, e.g. through ratios of click counts, which lie outside Def. 5.2. The fair conclusion is that unbiasedness of absolute relevance is the wrong target there, and that ranking-level or ratio-level consistency is achievable. This supports the paper's closing advice ("debiased", not "unbiased" LTR) more strongly than the paper itself argues it.
  • Def. 5.2 treats $f$ as fixed. Doubly-robust estimators (Oosterhuis, 2203.17118) and self-normalized estimators make $f$ depend on the data. Sec. 5.2 argues the conclusion survives in the limit, which seems right for DR with a fixed regression model. With a jointly fitted model, the DR estimator becomes partly a click model, and the Sec. 6 issues come back.
  • Thm 6.3 is stated for the population loss. It does not address convergence of empirical minimizers (uniform convergence, argmin continuity). In the non-identified case "the estimate" is a set, so consistency is undefined, not merely false.

Broader context

  • Chen et al., Identifiability Matters (2309.15560, ICML 2024). This answers the question Sec. 6 leaves open for the position-based model. Build a graph whose vertices are positions and whose edges connect positions that share an item. Relevance is identifiable iff the graph is connected. In example 6.1, positions 3–4 are disconnected from 1–2.
  • Hager, Zoeter, de Rijke et al., Unidentified and Confounded? (2506.20501). The same issue for two-tower additive models: identification needs overlap in the logging policy, and confounding by the logging policy biases the towers.

title: Posterior Network: Uncertainty Estimation without OOD Samples via Density-Based Pseudo-Counts
html:
Claude deep-dive — 2026-11-19 (requested in issue #11)

Posterior Network: Uncertainty Estimation without OOD Samples via Density-Based Pseudo-Counts — Charpentier, Zügner, Günnemann (NeurIPS 2020) — arXiv:2006.09239

Setting and problem

Classification with $C$ classes. For each input $x^{(i)}$ the model should report two kinds of uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty is about the label $y^{(i)}$ given the categorical parameter $p^{(i)}$. Epistemic uncertainty is about $p^{(i)}$ itself. Ensembles and MC dropout represent the distribution $q^{(i)}$ over $p^{(i)}$ implicitly and need $S$ forward passes. The "Dirichlet" family (Prior Networks, Malinin & Gales 2018/2019) predicts $q^{(i)} = \mathrm{Dir}(\alpha^{(i)})$ in one pass, with mean $\bar p_c = \alpha_c/\alpha_0$, $\alpha_0 = \sum_c \alpha_c$.

The paper lists four problems with Prior Networks:

  1. They need OOD samples at training time.
  2. No finite OOD set can describe "everything else".
  3. Nothing bounds $\int \alpha_0(x)\,dx$, so the network can give arbitrarily high confidence far from the data.
  4. They can produce degenerate concentrations ($\alpha_c < 1$).

The goal is OOD-aware Dirichlet outputs trained only on in-distribution data, with no hand-set target concentrations.

Main idea

Take the conjugate update of a single categorical, $\mathrm{Dir}(\beta^{\text{prior}}) \to \mathrm{Dir}(\beta^{\text{prior}} + \beta^{\text{data}})$ with $\beta^{\text{data}}_c$ = class counts, and make the counts input-dependent. An encoder maps $x$ to a low-dimensional latent $z = f_\theta(x) \in \mathbb{R}^H$ (default $H=6$, followed by batch norm). Each class gets a normalized density $P(z\mid c;\phi)$, a radial flow by default (about 80 parameters per class). Then $$\alpha^{(i)}_c = \beta^{\text{prior}}_c + N_c\,P(z^{(i)}\mid c;\phi) = \beta^{\text{prior}}_c + N\,P(c\mid z^{(i)};\phi)\,P(z^{(i)};\phi),$$ with $\beta^{\text{prior}} = \mathbf 1$ and $N_c$ the training count of class $c$.

The posterior mean is $$\mathbb{E}[p_c] = \frac{1 + N\,P(c\mid z)\,P(z)}{C + N\,P(z)}.$$ In dense latent regions ($N P(z) \to \infty$) it tends to the generative-classifier posterior $P(c\mid z)$ and the Dirichlet covariance vanishes as $O(1/(N P(z)))$ (App. A.3). Where the latent density is low it falls back to the uniform prior with high epistemic uncertainty.

The "certainty budget" argument: each class density integrates to 1, so $\int N_c P(z\mid c)\,dz = N_c$. Total evidence over latent space is fixed at $N$. Putting more density near training points forces less density elsewhere, and this is what is supposed to make far-away latents uncertain without OOD data.

The loss is a Gibbs/PAC-Bayes-style objective (Zellner 1988; Shawe-Taylor & Williamson 1997), the expected cross-entropy under $q$ minus its entropy: $$\mathcal L = \frac1N\sum_i \Big(\mathbb{E}_{p\sim \mathrm{Dir}(\alpha^{(i)})}\big[\mathrm{CE}(p, y^{(i)})\big] - \lambda\, H\big(\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha^{(i)})\big)\Big),\qquad \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CE}] = \psi(\alpha_0) - \psi(\alpha_{y}).$$ With $\lambda = 1$ this is the ELBO with a $\mathrm{Dir}(\mathbf 1)$ prior. In practice $\lambda = 10^{-5}$. Encoder and flows are trained jointly, end to end. (App. A.2, Eq. 10 writes the UCE term as $\psi(\alpha_{c^*}) - \psi(\alpha_0)$. That is $\mathbb{E}[\log p_{c^*}]$, the negative of the cross-entropy, so the sign there is a typo.)

Most interesting part

The parametrization separates the two uncertainties cleanly:

  • $P(c\mid z)$ (aleatoric) and $N P(z)$ (evidence) are different functions of the latent.
  • An ambiguous digit "0/6" sits in a dense region shared by two classes: high aleatoric, low epistemic.
  • An OOD image lands where the density is near 0: high epistemic.

The posterior mean above is exactly Dirichlet-prior smoothing, the same form as query-likelihood retrieval with Dirichlet smoothing (Zhai & Lafferty 2001): $\hat p(w\mid d) = (c(w,d) + \mu\, p(w\mid \mathcal C))/(|d| + \mu)$. Here the "document length" $|d|$ is replaced by local evidence mass $N P(z)$, $\mu = C\beta^{\text{prior}}$, and the background model is uniform. So PostNet is a smoothed generative classifier on a learned latent, where the smoothing strength is set locally by density.

Method and evidence

Datasets: Segment and Sensorless Drive (tabular; held-out classes serve as OOD), MNIST (OOD: KMNIST, FashionMNIST) and CIFAR10 (OOD: SVHN). There is also a new "OODom" test: the same OOD images fed unscaled, in $[0,255]$ instead of $[0,1]$. All metrics are AUC-PR; epistemic scores are $\alpha_0$ for Dirichlet models and inverse sample variance for dropout and ensembles.

  • Sensorless Drive (Tab. 1). PostNet-Radial gets OOD-epistemic AUC-PR 88.7 against 50.6 for a 10-model ensemble and 38.1 for RKL-PN, at equal or better accuracy (98.0; IAF 99.5). Brier is 5.5 (IAF 1.4), against 2.5 for the ensemble.
  • MNIST (Tab. 3). OOD-epistemic is 94.6 on KMNIST and 97.2 on Fashion; OODom is 100 everywhere. RKL-PN trained with FashionMNIST as OOD gets 100 on Fashion but 9.1 on OODom KMNIST.
  • CIFAR10 with VGG16 (Tab. 4). Accuracy 84.9, OOD-epistemic 77.7 vs 53.6 (dropout) and 49.4 (RKL-PN), OODom 99.3. Under the 15 corruptions of Hendrycks & Dietterich, average $\alpha_0$ drops the most with severity.
  • Ablations (Tab. 2). Removing the flow (the encoder outputs $\alpha$ directly) collapses accuracy to 55 and OOD to about 30, so the normalized density is what does the work. Replacing the Bayesian loss with plain CE lowers OOD-epistemic from 88.7 to 82.6. Fitting the flow on a frozen pre-trained encoder (Seq-Bn) gets 71.8. The same with no batch norm fails (15% accuracy).

Caveats

  • The budget is on latent space, not input space. $\int N P(z)\,dz = N$ constrains how evidence is spread over $z$. It says nothing about which inputs $x$ the encoder maps into dense regions. An encoder free to collapse OOD inputs onto class clusters ("feature collapse") gets high evidence on them, and the loss does not penalize this because OOD inputs are never seen. The OODom result works because unscaled inputs produce large activations that land far away even after batch norm, which is a property of the architecture, not of the budget. DDU (Mukhoti et al., 2102.11582) adds spectral normalization for exactly this reason. Kopetzki et al. (2010.14986), with Charpentier as co-author, show Dirichlet models including PostNet are not adversarially robust in their uncertainty estimates.
  • "Pseudo-counts" are densities, not counts. $N P(z)$ depends on the latent's volume element: rescaling $z$ by $s$ rescales the density by $s^{-H}$. So the absolute level of epistemic uncertainty is fixed by the batch-norm scale and $H$, not by anything statistical. The paper finds that "too high latent dimension leads to a performance decrease", which is consistent with this.
  • Whether the loss gives epistemic uncertainty at all. With one label per input, $\mathbb E_q[\mathrm{CE}]$ keeps decreasing as $\alpha_0 \to \infty$ in the direction of $y$. With $\lambda = 10^{-5}$ the entropy term barely resists, so in-distribution points are pushed toward zero epistemic uncertainty whatever the sample size. Bengs, Hüllermeier & Waegeman (2203.06102) show that no such second-order loss is proper for epistemic uncertainty. Jürgens et al. (2402.09056, ICML 2024) show the "epistemic" output of evidential methods does not shrink with data the way it should. In PostNet the behaviour is reasonable mostly because the flow normalization, not the loss, carries the epistemic part.
  • Metrics. OOD detection is reported only as AUC-PR, with ID as the positive class. Base rates differ across settings, so absolute numbers are hard to compare across tables.

Broader context

Follow-up by the same group: Natural Posterior Network (2105.04471, ICLR 2022). It extends the update to any exponential-family target (regression, counts) with a single flow and $\chi + n(x)$ natural-parameter updates.

Possible use in retrieval (my reading, not in the paper). The evidence structure "posterior precision = prior precision + local count" is the usual random-effects shrinkage, here with a per-region latent mass in place of a per-item count. A PostNet-style head on a retriever would give a per-query evidence score $N P(z_q)$: how many training queries look like this one. That score could be tested as a predictor of dense-retrieval failure on tail queries. It is cheap to try: flows on frozen embeddings, Seq-Bn style, which the ablation shows works reasonably.

title: On the Mechanisms of Collaborative Learning in VAE Recommenders
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-19

On the Mechanisms of Collaborative Learning in VAE Recommenders — Tung-Long Vuong, Julien Monteil, Hien Dang, Volodymyr Vaskovych, Trung Le, Vu Nguyen (2025) — arXiv:2511.06781

Setting and problem

The object of study is the standard VAE-based collaborative filtering model (Mult-VAE, Liang et al. 2018) trained on implicit feedback. There are $U$ users and $I$ items, and an interaction matrix $X \in \{0,1\}^{U \times I}$. A user is nothing more than its row $x_u \in \{0,1\}^I$, with positive set $S_{x_u} = \{i : x_{ui} = 1\}$. A zero means "not observed", not "disliked". No side information is used, so any information one user gets about another must come through the shared parameters.

The model has three parts.

  • An amortised Gaussian encoder $q_\phi(z \mid x_h) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x_h), \mathrm{diag}\,\sigma^2_\phi(x_h))$, $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$. It reads a masked history $x_h = x \odot b$ with $b \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\rho)^I$. Here $\rho$ is the keep probability, and $\rho = 1$ means clean inputs.
  • A decoder $p_\theta(x \mid z)$. In Mult-VAE this is a multinomial over items with logits from an MLP of $z$.
  • A $\beta$-weighted negative ELBO, $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}}(x;\theta,\phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z\mid x_h)}\log p_\theta(x\mid z) + \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x_h)\,\|\,p(z)),\qquad p(z)=\mathcal{N}(0,I).$$

At test time the model encodes the observed 80% of a held-out user's history and ranks items by decoder logits. Results are reported as Recall@20/50 and NDCG@100 under the Liang et al. protocol: strong generalisation with held-out users, and recall truncated by $\min(K, |\text{test}_u|)$. This truncation is why Recall@50 can be below Recall@20 in some of their tables.

The paper asks two questions.

  1. Mechanism: in an amortised VAE recommender, how does training on user $v$ help predictions for user $u$, and which pairs $(u,v)$ can help each other?
  2. Role of the two common "regularisers": does input masking (dropout on $x$) or the $\beta$-KL term change which pairs can collaborate? If so, how do the two differ, and can we keep masking's benefit while removing its side effects?

To make "collaboration" precise they separate two kinds. Local collaboration happens between users in a Hamming ball, $N_\delta(u) = \{v : \|x_u - x_v\|_1 \le \delta\}$. Global collaboration happens between pairs that are far, $\|x_u - x_v\|_1 > \delta$, but related through overlap, $|S_{x_u} \cap S_{x_v}| > 0$. The motivating example is subset inclusion. If $S_{x_2} \subset S_{x_1}$, the heavy user $x_1$ is a natural source of recommendations for $x_2$, yet the two can be very far apart in Hamming distance.

Prior work: Mult-VAE introduced the multinomial likelihood, $\beta$ annealing and input dropout. RecVAE added a composite prior, a user-dependent $\beta(x)$, alternating training and other tricks. VampPrior and flexible or learned priors (Kim and Suh 2019, Walker et al. 2022) and $\beta$ schedules were aimed at posterior collapse. RaCT added ranking-aware actor-critic fine-tuning. On the linear side, CDAE and EASE/EDLAE (Steck 2019, 2020) analysed denoising and dropout in shallow autoencoders. The gap the authors claim is that masking is used everywhere as a heuristic, with no account of how it shapes latent geometry or cross-user transfer. Prior method work has attacked the KL/prior side instead.

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag:

  • Influence is defined as training-time gradient transfer. User $v$ influences $u$ if one SGD step on $v$ lowers $u$'s expected loss to first order. This is a TracIn-style, first-order notion. It is not about the predictive dependence of the final model.
  • The transfer theorem differentiates only with respect to decoder parameters $\theta$ and keeps the posteriors $q_u, q_v$ fixed. Transfer through the shared encoder $\phi$ is not modelled.
  • Input geometry is raw Hamming ($\ell_1$) distance on binary vectors. Real Mult-VAE implementations L2-normalise $x$ before dropout and rescale by $1/\rho$. Hamming distance between a 5-item and a 350-item user is dominated by activity level, a point the authors use themselves in their t-SNE discussion.
  • Latent geometry is measured with $W_1$ between posteriors. Distances in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are not scale-invariant on their own; only the product with a decoder Lipschitz constant is.
  • The decoder in Theorem 2.5 is an abstract regular exponential family with shared log-partition $A$. It is minimised over all measurable natural-parameter maps $\eta(\cdot)$, so it is treated as nonparametric.

Main idea

The argument is a chain of bounds that turns collaboration into a question about latent geometry.

  1. Sharing radius (Thm 2.3). One SGD step on $v$ lowers $u$'s loss to first order whenever $L_{\theta z} W_1(q_u, q_v) + \Delta_x(u,v) < \|g_u\|$. Here $\Delta_x$ is the gap between the two users' decoder gradients evaluated at the same latents. So collaboration is limited to a latent $W_1$-ball of radius $r_{\mathrm{share}} = [\|g_u\| - \Delta_x]_+ / L_{\theta z}$.
  2. Clean inputs give local-only geometry (Lemma 2.4, Thm 2.5). A Lipschitz encoder maps Hamming-close users to $W_1$-close posteriors. The reconstruction term carries a "compromise gap" $\int (q_u+q_v)\,\Delta_{A^*}\,dz \ge 0$ wherever two posteriors with different sufficient statistics overlap, so reconstruction pushes mismatched users apart. The result is clusters that copy input similarity, and far-but-related users never get within the sharing radius.
  3. Two ways to mix (Thm 2.5 (T1 part), Thm 2.6, Eqs. 6–7). The Talagrand $T_1$ inequality bounds $\mathbb{E} W_1$ between users by $2\sqrt{2C}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)} = 2\sqrt{2C}\sqrt{I_q(X_h;Z) + \mathrm{KL}(q_h\|p)}$.
  4. Raising $\beta$ shrinks this bound uniformly, with a risk of collapse.
  5. Masking lowers $I(X_h;Z)$ by data processing, and it also moves pairwise distances at random. With probability at least $(\rho^2+(1-\rho)^2)^s \cdot \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(h,\rho) \le T_\delta]$ a pair contracts. With probability at least $\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(s, 2\rho(1-\rho)) \ge U_\delta]$ it expands, which the authors call neighbourhood drift.
  6. Fix: Personalized Item Alignment (PIA). Each item gets a learnable anchor $e_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and the training-only loss $$\lambda_A\,\mathbb{E}_b\,\frac{1}{|S_x|}\sum_{i\in S_x}\mathbb{E}_{z\sim q_\phi(z\mid x_h)}\|z-e_i\|_2^2 = \lambda_A\big(\|\mu_\phi(x_h)-\bar e_x\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma_\phi(x_h)\big) + \text{const}$$ is added. This pulls every masked view of a user toward the centroid $\bar e_x$ of the anchors of the user's full positive set. Users with overlapping items get nearby centroids and so become latently close in a way tied to content. Under a local quadratic model, the variance of $\mu$ across masks shrinks by $\tau^2$ and its drift from the centroid by $\tau$, with $\tau = L/(L+2\lambda_A)$ (Prop 3.2).

Headline numbers:

  • PIA improves Mult-VAE by roughly 1–3% and RecVAE by roughly 0.5–1% on ML-20M, Netflix and MSD. RecVAE+PIA is best on ML-20M and Netflix; EASE still wins on MSD.
  • In a one-week A/B test on an Amazon streaming service (about 25M users, about 4k movies) click rate was 117–283% higher than an unspecified production control.
  • A t-SNE figure shows activity cohorts with 5, 50 and 350 interactions separated under clean training, mixed under masking, and arranged on a smooth ordered manifold under PIA.

The most interesting part

The paper tries to say something mechanistic about why dropout-on-input matters so much in VAE recommenders, and its decomposition into local and global collaboration is a useful vocabulary. The method is simple, costs only about 16% training time, adds nothing at inference, and was deployed. Read as theory, though, several links in the chain are weaker than the narrative suggests. Below is a reviewer-style assessment, roughly in order of importance.

Strengths.

  • Collaboration is framed as first-order gradient transfer between users, and the transfer cost is split into a latent part ($L_{\theta z}W_1$) and a content part ($\Delta_x$). This framing is clean and reusable. It is essentially an influence-function or TracIn view applied to amortised latent-variable models, and it gives a concrete quantity to measure.
  • Theorem 2.6 is a tidy, exact piece of combinatorics. After independent Bernoulli masking, the Hamming distance splits into $Y + Z$, with $Y \sim \mathrm{Bin}(h,\rho)$ from disagreeing coordinates and $Z \sim \mathrm{Bin}(s, 2\rho(1-\rho))$ from shared positives. The bounds follow from this decomposition.
  • The compromise gap in Thm 2.5 is the Jensen gap of $A^*$, which is the Bregman information of a two-point mixture as in Bregman clustering (Banerjee et al. 2005). It is the right object for "what does a shared decoder lose when two users share a latent code".
  • The algorithmic idea, anchoring user posteriors to a barycenter of learnable item embeddings, is cheap. It also links the VAE back to the FISM/YouTube-DNN view of a user as the average of item embeddings. Gains are consistent in sign across three datasets and two backbones.

Weaknesses and gaps.

  1. The content-mismatch term undermines the "latent proximity" story. In Thm 2.3 the content term $\Delta_x(u,v)$ is never bounded or measured, yet it is not small for the pairs the paper cares about. For the multinomial decoder, $\ell_\theta(x,z) = -\sum_i x_i \log\pi_i(z)$ is linear in $x$, so $$\Delta_x(u,v) = \Big\|\mathbb{E}_{q_v}\sum_i (x_{vi}-x_{ui})\nabla_\theta\log\pi_i(z)\Big\| \le \|x_u-x_v\|_1 \cdot \sup_{i,z}\|\nabla_\theta\log\pi_i(z)\|.$$ The content term therefore grows with Hamming distance, the very input distance that defines far-but-related pairs. For such pairs $r_{\mathrm{share}} = [\|g_u\|-\Delta_x]_+/L_{\theta z}$ can be exactly zero no matter how close the posteriors are. Latent proximity is necessary in this bound but far from sufficient. The section "reduces global collaboration to a geometric question" quietly drops the term that carries the input geometry. The bound is also only sufficient: transfer requires $\langle g_u, g_v\rangle > 0$, which can hold at large $W_1$ (two posteriors in a region where the decoder is nearly linear).
  2. Only the decoder is in the theorem. The theorem differentiates only through $\theta$ with posteriors frozen, but much of the cross-user sharing in an amortised model runs through $\phi$. An update on $v$ moves $q_u$. A theory of masking, which acts on encoder inputs, that ignores encoder transfer is incomplete in exactly the place it matters.
  3. Scale invariance. All the statements of the form "$\beta$ or masking shrinks latent distances, so more pairs fall within $r_{\mathrm{share}}$" compare $W_1$ to a radius that itself scales as $1/L_{\theta z}$. A decoder can undo any uniform contraction of the latent space by becoming steeper. What matters is $L_{\theta z} W_1$, and nothing in the paper controls how $L_{\theta z}$ responds to $\beta$, $\rho$ or $\lambda_A$. The prior pins the scale only loosely. Also, $\|g_u\| \to 0$ near stationary points, so the radius shrinks to zero during training; the sharing radius is a statement about early training.
  4. Masking's contraction does not select related pairs, and its expansion targets them. Read literally, Theorem 2.6 cuts against the paper's story. The contraction lower bound $(\rho^2+(1-\rho)^2)^s\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(h,\rho)\le T_\delta]$ decreases in the overlap $s$. Expansion is driven entirely by shared positives, because independent masks disagree on them. So masking contracts unrelated pairs at least as readily as related ones: two sparse users who share nothing still contract because both lose items. Pairs with large overlap, the "related" ones, are the ones that get pushed apart. The masking effect on Hamming distance is mostly "everyone gets sparser". That is a story about activity-level normalisation, consistent with the 5/50/350 cohort picture, more than one about far-but-related transfer. The authors never observe this tension. It also suggests an obvious alternative they do not try: masks correlated across users on shared items.
  5. The input geometry does not match the implemented model. Mult-VAE L2-normalises inputs and dropout rescales by $1/\rho$. Under normalisation, a 5-item user that is a subset of a 350-item user is not "far" in the sense the Hamming analysis assumes, at least in the direction of the vector. The cohort-separation phenomenon (Setting-1) could be largely an artefact of input norm, and masking plus rescaling may help partly by a different route. Relatedly, Steck (2020) showed that in linear autoencoders input dropout is equivalent to a popularity-weighted Tikhonov penalty, roughly $\|\Lambda^{1/2}B\|_F^2$ with $\Lambda \propto \mathrm{diag}(X^\top X)$. That is a much more concrete mechanism for "why masking helps" (it stops the model from learning the identity, with emphasis on popular items). The paper cites the work but never compares its explanation to it.
  6. The exponential-family abstraction does not fit Mult-VAE either. The multinomial likelihood for user $u$ has a log-partition that depends on $N_u = |S_{x_u}|$, roughly $N_u\log\sum_j e^{\eta_j}$. So users with different activity levels do not share a single $A$. The softmax parametrisation is also not minimal, which breaks strict convexity of $A^*$ and the "equality iff $T(x_u)=T(x_v)$" claim, unless one restricts to a minimal parametrisation. Thm 2.5 is cleanest for a Bernoulli or Gaussian decoder, not for the model that is actually trained.
  7. Bounds are used as if they were equalities. Eqs. (5)–(7) give an upper bound on $\mathbb{E}W_1$. Lowering the bound (smaller KL or MI) does not imply lower distances, and certainly not that the specific far-but-related pairs come closer. The step from "upper bound on average pairwise distance shrinks" to "more pairs fall in the sharing radius" is a heuristic.
  8. The PIA claims are partly tautological, and some are contradicted by the settings used.
  9. Prop 3.2 treats the encoder mean as a free variable minimised separately per mask, with mask-independent curvature. Adding $\lambda_A\|\mu-\bar e_x\|^2$ to a strongly convex quadratic then shrinks the minimiser toward $\bar e_x$ by $M = (H+2\lambda_A I)^{-1}H$. This is ridge-regression shrinkage and holds for any fixed target. It says nothing about whether the centroid is a good target, and it ignores amortisation: $\mu_\phi$ is one network shared across users.
  10. The $\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma$ term in Prop 3.1 pushes posterior variances to zero, which fights the KL term. With the reported $\lambda_A \in \{2,4,8\}$, raised geometrically by $\lambda_{\mathrm{scale}}=2$ whenever validation stalls, this is not "small". It does change the information bottleneck, contrary to the stated design goal of "without tightening the information bottleneck".
  11. Algorithm 1 as printed increases $\lambda_A$ every epoch: the condition is "best-val-epoch $< \text{epoch} + \rho$". The symbol $\rho$ is also reused for both the keep probability and the patience.
  12. The centroid can sit in the wrong place for multi-interest users. For a user whose items lie in two distant clusters, $\bar e_x$ lands between them, possibly next to items the user never engaged with. This is the well-known failure of single-vector, mean-of-items user models that multi-interest retrievers (MIND, ComiRec) were built to address. The remark that the barycenter "keeps them close to multiple communities" is asserted, not shown. No per-diversity analysis is reported.

  13. Evaluation. Gains are small. RecVAE+PIA improves NDCG@100 by 0.002–0.004, and no seeds, standard deviations or significance tests are reported for offline results. Baselines stop at 2020 (no EASE variants such as EDLAE, no diffusion recommenders, no graph CF), and EASE still wins on MSD. Most importantly, nothing in the experiments tests the mechanism. The theory makes direct, cheap-to-check predictions, and none is measured:

    • the gradient cosine between pairs as a function of $W_1$ and $\Delta_x$;
    • the fraction of far-but-related pairs inside the radius with and without masking or PIA;
    • mask-to-mask variance of $\mu$.

    The only evidence is t-SNE, which does not preserve global distances. Claims such as "the 350 cluster is closer to the 5 cluster than to the 50 cluster" cannot be read off a t-SNE plot. The ablations one would want are also missing: PIA without masking, PIA versus a plain masked-vs-clean consistency loss $\|\mu(x_h)-\mu(x)\|^2$, and PIA versus simply tuning $\beta$. 11. The A/B test does not isolate PIA. The control is an unspecified "baseline algorithm", and the lifts are 117–509%. This measures Multi-VAE+PIA against a production system, presumably much weaker, not PIA's marginal contribution. The offline Amazon numbers (+3–5% over Multi-VAE) are the relevant comparison, again without variance.

Net assessment: an interesting and useful framing (gradient transfer, local versus global, masking as stochastic contraction and expansion), with a mostly standard and loose theory whose strongest piece (Thm 2.6) actually complicates the paper's own story. The method is a simple and plausibly useful regulariser whose link to the theory is mostly narrative.

Proof sketch

The theory is light: each result is a short, standard argument, and none of it is a deep proof. In order:

Theorem 2.3 (sharing radius). Claim: assume $\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x,z)$ is $L_{\theta z}$-Lipschitz in $z$ uniformly in $x$, and let $\theta^+ = \theta - \eta g_v$. Then $$L_u(\theta^+) - L_u(\theta) \le -\eta\|g_u\|\big(\|g_u\| - L_{\theta z}W_1(q_u,q_v) - \Delta_x(u,v)\big) + O(\eta^2).$$ Proof: - Take a first-order Taylor expansion, $L_u(\theta-\eta g_v) = L_u - \eta\langle g_u, g_v\rangle + O(\eta^2)$. - Write $-\langle g_u,g_v\rangle \le -\|g_u\|^2 + \|g_u\|\|g_v-g_u\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. - Split $g_v - g_u$ by the triangle inequality into two parts: the same-latent content gap $\Delta_x$, and $\|\mathbb{E}_{q_v}\psi - \mathbb{E}_{q_u}\psi\|$ with $\psi(z)=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x_u,z)$. - Bound the second part by $L_{\theta z}W_1$ by integrating against an optimal coupling, which is Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality for vector-valued Lipschitz maps.

Lemma 2.4. For diagonal Gaussians, $W_2^2 = \|\mu_u-\mu_v\|^2 + \|\sigma_u-\sigma_v\|^2$, the squared distance between stacked $(\mu,\sigma)$ vectors. So Lipschitzness of the encoder map $x\mapsto(\mu,\sigma)$ gives $W_2 \le L_\phi\|x_u-x_v\|$, and $W_1\le W_2$. Since $\|\cdot\|_2 \le \|\cdot\|_1$ the $\ell_1$ version follows. On binary vectors the $\ell_2$ bound $L_\phi\sqrt{h}$ is actually tighter.

Theorem 2.5, part 1 (compromise gap). Write $-\log p_\theta(x\mid z) = A(\eta(z)) - \langle T(x),\eta(z)\rangle - \log h(x)$. Summing over the two users gives $\int Q(z)[A(\eta(z)) - \langle T^\alpha(z),\eta(z)\rangle]dz$, with $Q = q_u+q_v$ and $T^\alpha = \alpha T(x_u)+(1-\alpha)T(x_v)$, where $\alpha = q_u/Q$. Minimising pointwise over $\eta(z)$ uses the Fenchel–Young identity $\min_\eta[A(\eta)-\langle y,\eta\rangle] = -A^*(y)$. Adding and subtracting $\sum_i A^*(T(x_i))$ leaves $\int Q\,[\alpha A^*(T_u)+(1-\alpha)A^*(T_v) - A^*(T^\alpha)]dz$, a Jensen gap. It is non-negative by convexity and zero iff $T_u = T_v$ or the posteriors have disjoint support, by strict convexity of $A^*$ in the Legendre case. The KL term rides along unchanged.

Theorem 2.5, part 2 ($T_1$ bound). By the triangle inequality, $W_1(q_u,q_v)\le W_1(q_u,p)+W_1(q_v,p)$. Then the Bobkov–Götze argument gives $W_1(\nu,p)\le\sqrt{2C\,\mathrm{KL}(\nu\|p)}$: - Donsker–Varadhan with $g = \lambda(f - \mathbb{E}_pf)$ for 1-Lipschitz $f$. - The sub-Gaussian mgf bound $\log\mathbb{E}_pe^{\lambda(f-\mathbb{E}f)}\le C\lambda^2/2$. - Optimise over $\lambda$, then take the supremum over $f$ (Kantorovich–Rubinstein).

The Gaussian prior satisfies this with $C=\sigma^2$, dimension-free. Eq. (6) follows by averaging and Jensen on $\sqrt{\cdot}$. Eq. (7) is the standard "ELBO surgery" identity $\mathbb{E}_x\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p) = I_q(X;Z)+\mathrm{KL}(q_{\mathrm{agg}}\|p)$ (Hoffman and Johnson 2016).

Theorem 2.6 (masking contraction and expansion). Partition coordinates into the $h$ disagreeing ones and the $s$ shared positives. On a disagreeing coordinate the masked difference is 1 iff the lone 1 survives, which has probability $\rho$. On a shared coordinate it is 1 iff the two independent masks disagree, which has probability $2\rho(1-\rho)$. So $D' = Y+Z$, with independent $Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(h,\rho)$ and $Z\sim\mathrm{Bin}(s,2\rho(1-\rho))$. - Contraction: lower-bound $\Pr[D'<\delta]$ by $\Pr[Z=0]\Pr[Y\le T_\delta]$. - Expansion: lower-bound $\Pr[D' \ge \delta]$ by $\Pr[Z\ge U_\delta]$.

The decomposition is exact, so the full law of $D'$ is available. The stated bounds discard most of it.

Prop 3.1 is the bias–variance identity $\mathbb{E}\|z-e_i\|^2 = \|\mu-e_i\|^2+\mathrm{tr}\Sigma$ plus the parallel-axis theorem around the centroid. Prop 3.2 is ridge shrinkage on a quadratic surrogate: - The aligned minimiser is $\mu^{(A)} = Ma_b + (I-M)\bar e_x$, with $M=(H+2\lambda_AI)^{-1}H$ and spectrum $\lambda_i/(\lambda_i+2\lambda_A)\le\tau$. - Variance: $\mathrm{Var}_b[\mu^{(A)}] = M\,\mathrm{Var}_b[a_b]\,M$, so the operator norm and trace contract by $\tau^2$. The Löwner bound needs $\mathrm{Var}_b$ to commute with $H$. - Drift: $\|\mu^{(A)}-\bar e_x\|^2 = (a_b-\bar e_x)^\top M^2(a_b-\bar e_x) \le \tau\|a_b-\bar e_x\|^2$, using $M^2\preceq\tau M\preceq\tau I$.

One small inconsistency: the main-text Prop 3.2 states the Löwner contraction with factor $\tau$ unconditionally. The appendix proves $\tau^2$, and only under commutation.

Broader context

Background for newcomers. Autoencoder recommenders treat each user's interaction row as a document to be reconstructed. The encoder amortises the per-user factor of matrix factorisation, so the parameter count does not grow with users and new users need no retraining. Mult-VAE made the multinomial (softmax-over-items) likelihood and input dropout standard. In practice dropout is one of the largest single contributors to accuracy: the authors report NDCG@100 0.409 → 0.426 on ML-20M from masking alone. Linear cousins (EASE, EDLAE, SANSA) remain extremely strong, which is a useful reminder that much of the "nonlinear" success may come from regularisation rather than nonlinearity.

Related directions.

  • Dropout as regularisation in linear autoencoders (Steck 2019, 2020, EDLAE). There the effect of input masking can be solved in closed form: it is a popularity-weighted ridge penalty that prevents learning the identity. A natural theoretical companion to this paper would extend that closed-form analysis to the shared-latent setting. One could then compute exactly which user pairs gain transfer as $\rho$ varies, instead of using loose $W_1$ bounds.
  • Self-supervised and contrastive recommendation (SGL, SimGCL, the alignment/uniformity analysis of Wang and Isola). Masking is a data augmentation, and PIA is essentially prototype alignment, as in ProtoNCE or SwAV with item anchors as prototypes. The uniformity–alignment trade-off is a better-developed language for the paper's local-versus-global tension, and those works already find that controlled uniformity improves cold and tail users.
  • First-order influence (TracIn, influence functions). Thm 2.3 is a TracIn bound with a latent-geometry decomposition. Gradient-interference work in multi-task learning (PCGrad etc.) studies the same $\langle g_u,g_v\rangle$ sign condition.

Plausible follow-ups.

  1. Test the mechanism directly. On ML-20M, sample user pairs by (Hamming distance, overlap) bins. Measure the empirical cosine $\langle g_u,g_v\rangle/\|g_u\|\|g_v\|$, together with $W_1(q_u,q_v)$ and the estimated $\Delta_x$, under clean, masked and PIA training. That would show whether latent proximity or content mismatch actually controls transfer, and with encoder parameters included.
  2. Overlap-aware masking. Thm 2.6 shows that independent masks inflate distance exactly on shared positives. Masks that are correlated across users within a batch, sharing the keep/drop decision per item (item-level dropout rather than entry-level), would set $Z \equiv 0$. Masking would then only contract, through the disagreeing coordinates. This gives a clean test of whether "drift" hurts. Item-level dropout is also cheaper.
  3. Multi-anchor PIA. Replace the single centroid by alignment to the nearest of $k$ user prototypes, or by an OT cost between $q_\phi(z\mid x_h)$ and the empirical item measure $\frac{1}{|S_x|}\sum_{i\in S_x}\delta_{e_i}$ (with a mixture posterior). This addresses multi-interest users. As written, the PIA loss uses the independent coupling, which for a Gaussian reduces to centroid plus variance and so cannot express multi-modality.

Connection to vector search, two-tower retrieval and generative retrieval. Real, but not exploited in the paper. PIA makes the user posterior mean close to the centroid of its items' anchors in a shared $d$-dimensional space. That is exactly the geometry of a two-tower or FISM-style retriever, with user embedding equal to the mean of item embeddings and scoring by (negative squared) Euclidean distance. A natural question for vector search is whether the anchors $e_i$ can serve as an ANN index for candidate generation: retrieve the nearest anchors to $\mu_\phi(x)$, then rerank with the decoder. One would measure how well $-\|\mu-e_i\|^2$ ranking agrees with the decoder's logits. If agreement is high, PIA turns a full-softmax VAE into something servable with HNSW or IVF at large item counts.

Two theoretical-IR caveats apply.

  • A single centroid vector per user inherits the known expressiveness limits of single-vector embedding retrieval: sign-rank and dimension bounds on which top-$k$ sets are realisable (cf. recent work on the limits of embedding-based retrieval). The barycenter is the worst point for users whose positives span distant clusters.
  • The mean-of-items geometry is the same structure that semantic-ID generative retrievers (TIGER-style RQ-VAE IDs) quantise. Anchors trained so that co-liked items cluster would be a collaborative alternative to content embeddings for building semantic IDs. The paper's local-versus-global sharing analysis would then turn into a question about how prefix-sharing in the ID tree governs transfer between items.

In that sense the "sharing radius" has a direct analogue in generative retrieval: which documents or items share decoder gradients because their identifiers or latent codes sit in the same neighbourhood.

title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-19

Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging — Awni Altabaa, John Lafferty, Omar Montasser (2026) — arXiv:2611.21597

Setting and problem

The formal object. Fix a token set $\Sigma$ (binary, finite, or infinite) and let $\Sigma^\star$ be the set of finite strings over it. A generator is a map $f:\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$, and the hypothesis class is $\mathcal{F}\subseteq \Sigma^{\Sigma^\star}$. Applied autoregressively to a prompt $x\in\Sigma^\star$, it produces

$$f^{(1)}(x)=f(x),\qquad f^{(t)}(x)=f\big(x\circ f^{(1)}(x)\circ\cdots\circ f^{(t-1)}(x)\big),\quad t\ge 2,$$

and the chain-of-thought (CoT) $f^{(1:T)}(x)\in\Sigma^T$, whose last token is read as the answer. This is the time-invariant framework of Joshi et al. [JVBG+25]: the same $f$ is used at every step, exactly like a transformer that applies the same weights to every prefix.

Data and realizability. $P$ is a distribution over $\Sigma^\star\times\Sigma^T$ that is realizable: there is $f_\star\in\mathcal{F}$ with $\Pr_{(x,y)\sim P}[f_\star^{(1:T)}(x)=y]=1$. The learner sees $S=((x_j,y_j))_{j=1}^n\sim P^n$, with the whole CoT $y_j\in\Sigma^T$ observed (CoT supervision, as opposed to end-to-end supervision where only $y_{j,T}$ is seen). It must output a predictor $\hat f:\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$ (not necessarily in $\mathcal{F}$, so improper learning is allowed), and is judged by the CoT risk

$$\mathrm{err}_P(\hat f)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim P}\big[\exists t\in[T]:\ \hat f^{(t)}(x)\neq y_t\big],$$

so a single wrong token anywhere makes the whole output wrong. This is stronger than the end-to-end risk $\Pr[\hat f^{(T)}(x)\neq y_T]$, which earlier works bounded by going through the CoT risk anyway.

Access to the class. The algorithm touches $\mathcal{F}$ only through a $\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ oracle: a deterministic rule that, given a realizable sample, returns some $\hat f_S\in\mathcal{F}$ with $\hat f_S^{(t)}(x_j)=y_{j,t}$ for all $j,t$. Equivalently, $\hat f_S(x_j\circ y_{j,1:t-1})=y_{j,t}$ for all $j\in[n]$ and $t\in[T]$. This is just teacher-forced zero training loss on all $nT$ next-token examples. The oracle may be adversarial among consistent hypotheses and may depend on the order of the sample.

Sample complexity is the smallest $n(\varepsilon,\delta)$ such that $\mathrm{err}_P(\hat f)\le\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, uniformly over realizable $P$. It is to be written as a function of $\varepsilon,\delta,T$ and a combinatorial dimension of $\mathcal{F}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is viewed as a multiclass class of next-token predictors. The relevant dimensions are: - $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ (when $|\Sigma|=2$); - the Graph dimension $d_G$, which is the VC dimension of the token-level 0-1 loss class $\{(x,y)\mapsto 1\{f(x)\neq y\}: f\in\mathcal{F}\}$ over $\Sigma^\star\times\Sigma$; - the Natarajan dimension $d_N$; - the DS dimension $d_{DS}$.

For finite $\Sigma$, $d_N\le d_{DS}\le d_G\le 4.67\, d_N\log_2|\Sigma|$, and all four coincide for binary $\Sigma$. For infinite $\Sigma$, $d_G$ may be infinite while $d_{DS}$ is finite, and only $d_{DS}$ characterizes learnability.

The precise question. When $T=1$ the problem is exactly multiclass PAC learning of $\mathcal{F}$ with label set $\Sigma$, so $\Omega((d_{DS}+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)$ is a lower bound for every $T$. The question is: is there a simple, efficient algorithm, calling $\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ a few times and outputting something that runs like a next-token generator, that achieves the optimal $T$-independent sample complexity $O((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)$?

What was known (Table 1 of the paper): - Malach [M24] learns each time step separately, which gives guarantees linear in $T$. - [JVBG+25]: one call to $\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ gives $O\big((d\log(2T)\log(2/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon\big)$ for binary $\Sigma$. The proof uses the VC dimension of the CoT-error class; by Sauer–Shelah on the $nT$ next-token examples it is $O(d\log T)$. - Hanneke–Mehalel–Moran [HMM26]: $O\big((d d^\star\log(2dd^\star)\log(2/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon\big)$ via a majority-vote compression scheme. This is $T$-free, but $d^\star$ (the dual VC dimension) can be as large as $2^{d+1}$. - Doron-Arad–Mehalel–Mossel [DMM26b]: $O((d_L+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)$ via online-to-batch conversion. This is $T$-free, but the Littlestone dimension $d_L$ is infinite already for thresholds. - Li [L26]: $\Theta((d_{DS}+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)$, optimal and $T$-free. The learner, however, uses one-inclusion hypergraphs over all CoTs that $\mathcal{F}$ can generate on the training and test prompts, and the graph has to be rebuilt for every test prompt. It is computationally hopeless. - Li [L26, Thm 6.2] also shows that a single CoT-consistent predictor must pay $\Omega(d_G\log T/n)$ for some binary class and oracle. So ERM-style learning is provably suboptimal in $T$, and some form of aggregation is necessary.

The gap is therefore algorithmic, not information-theoretic. The optimal rate is known, but every learner that attains a $T$-free rate either pays an extra structural parameter ($d^\star$, $d_L$) or is intractable.

Non-obvious modelling choices worth flagging: - The generator is deterministic, the setting is realizable, and the train and test CoT length $T$ is the same fixed number. There is no length generalization and no stochastic decoding. - The loss is exact match on the whole CoT. A key structural fact follows: because $\hat f$ follows the target until its first mistake, $\hat f^{(1:T)}(x)\neq y$ if and only if $\hat f(x\circ y_{1:t-1})\neq y_t$ for some $t$.
