The CoT risk is therefore a union of $T$ next-token events evaluated on the target prefixes, which is what makes teacher-forced analysis exact. - Prompts are arbitrary strings with no length bound, and $\mathcal{F}$ acts on strings of all lengths, so a step-$t$ input is just another point of $\Sigma^\star$. The "time-invariance" is entirely captured by $\mathcal{F}$ being a single multiclass class on $\Sigma^\star$. - The output is improper: a token-wise majority vote of $N$ generators. Section 6 distills it back into $\mathcal{F}$ using unlabeled prompts and an ERM oracle, which is a stronger assumption than a consistency oracle. - The complexity parameter is $d_G$, not $d_{DS}$. This is what costs the $\log|\Sigma|$ factor and is unavoidable for this kind of algorithm.

Main idea

Bagging. Algorithm 1 sets $N=\max\{4,\lceil\log_2(2T/\delta)\rceil\}$ and $J_n=\{\lceil n/4\rceil,\dots,n-1\}$. For $i=1,\dots,N$, it draws $k\sim\mathrm{Unif}(J_n)$ and a bootstrap $S'_i$ of $k$ points sampled with replacement from the prefix $S_{\le k}$, and calls $\hat f_{S'_i}=\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}(S'_i)$. It then generates by token-wise majority vote, with fixed tie-breaking:

$$\hat y_1=\arg\max_y\sum_i 1\{\hat f_{S'_i}(x)=y\},\qquad \hat y_t=\mathrm{MAJ}(\hat f_{S'_1},\dots,\hat f_{S'_N})(x\circ\hat y_{1:t-1}).$$

Theorem 1. For every $\mathcal{F}$ with Graph dimension $d_G$, every $\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ oracle, every realizable $P$, every $n\ge4$ and every $\delta\in(0,1)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$ and the bootstraps,

$$\Pr_{(x,y)\sim P}\big[\exists t:\ \mathrm{MAJ}(\hat f_{S'_1},\dots,\hat f_{S'_N})^{(t)}(x)\neq y_t\big]=O\Big(\frac{d_G}{n}+\frac1n\log\frac1\delta\Big).$$

This has no $T$ and no $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. It is exactly optimal for binary $\Sigma$ (matching the classical [EHKV89] lower bound at $T=1$), and optimal up to $\log|\Sigma|$ for finite $\Sigma$. Other facts: - The number of oracle calls is $O(\log(T/\delta))$, or alternatively $O(d^\star+\log(1/\delta))$ (Remark 2), so $N=O(\log(1/\delta)+\min\{d^\star,\log T\})$. - Inference costs $NT$ evaluations of members of $\mathcal{F}$. - Proposition 1: the ensemble can be distilled into a single $\bar f\in\mathcal{F}$ via $\mathrm{ERM}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ on $n_u\ge n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts labeled by the ensemble, keeping the $O((d_G+\log(1/\delta))/n)$ rate. The $T$-dependence moves from per-token inference cost to a one-time unlabeled-data cost.

Negative side, inherited from [AHV25]: - There are classes on which majorities of consistent learners need $\Omega((d_G+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)$ samples, so $d_G$ is tight for this algorithm. - There is a class with finite $d_{DS}$ (over an infinite alphabet) that no finite aggregation of predictors from the class can learn to constant error.

So "simple aggregation of proper learners" provably cannot reach the DS-optimal rate in general. The headline is that the information-theoretic statement "a long CoT is no harder than one token" is realized by the most classical ensemble method, whenever $d_G\approx d_{DS}$.

The most interesting part

The conceptual point is where the $\max_t$ sits relative to the randomness of the training sample. For a single consistent predictor, the relevant quantity is

$$\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}\,\mathbb{E}_S\Big[\max_{t\in[T]}1\{\hat f_S(x\circ y_{1:t-1})\neq y_t\}\Big],$$

which Li shows must be $\Omega(d_G\log T/n)$ in the worst case. One predictor has to be right at all $T$ prefixes at once, and the class of "errs somewhere in the CoT" events has VC dimension that grows like $d\log T$.

The bagging analysis instead controls

$$a(x,y)=\max_{t\in[T]}\Pr_{S\sim P^n}\big[\hat f_S(x\circ y_{1:t-1})\neq y_t\big],$$

with the max outside the probability over $S$. This says that at every step, most predictors are right, even though the predictors that err may be different at different steps. A majority vote needs exactly this. If at each target prefix the correct token gets more than half the votes, the vote reproduces $y_1$, then sits on the target prefix $x\circ y_1$, reproduces $y_2$, and so on. The first-mistake structure of autoregressive generation means you only ever need the vote to be right on the $T$ target prefixes, never on off-trajectory prefixes. The errors of individual members do not compound because the vote, not the individual member, determines the trajectory.

Why is $a(x,y)$ free of $T$? For each example, define the worst step $t(x,y)=\arg\max_t\Pr_S[\cdot]$ in advance. It depends on $P$, $n$ and the oracle, but not on the realized $S$. This gives a fixed map $\phi(x,y)=(x\circ y_{1:t(x,y)-1},\,y_{t(x,y)})$ that turns each CoT example into one next-token example. The error regions $E_f=\{(x,y): f(\phi_1(x,y))\neq\phi_2(x,y)\}$ are pullbacks under $\phi$ of the token-level error regions $G_f$, so $\mathrm{VCdim}\{E_f\}\le d_G$, with no union over $t$ and no Sauer blow-up in $T$. The consistent learner is correct at every step of every training CoT, and in particular at $\phi(x_j,y_j)$. So $E(S)\cap S=\emptyset$, and the standard "consistent learner over a VC class" bound applies at the single next-token level.

Choosing the worst step "with respect to the population of learners rather than the learner" is the whole trick. It only works because what matters is the marginal error probability over $S$, which is exactly what bagging approximates.

The second clever piece is how $T$ enters at all. Only the sparsification step (approximating the vote of exponentially many bootstraps by $N$ samples) sees $T$, through a union bound over the $T$ target prefixes, and it costs only $\log T$ in ensemble size, not in samples. To get $N$ independent of $n$, the paper tracks the squared worst-step error $r(x,y)=\max_t(1-\hat g_S(y_t\mid\cdot))^2$ throughout, not a thresholded 0-1 loss. A sampled majority with per-voter error $p<1/16$ errs with probability at most $2^N p^{N/2}\le 256\,p^2 2^{-N}$, so the failure probability is multiplicative in $r(x,y)$ and the $r$ cancels against the Markov threshold. A thresholded loss would leave an additive approximation error and force $N\sim\log n$. The AI-disclosure section notes that ChatGPT helped remove this $\log n$ factor.

Honest critique: - The $\log|\Sigma|$ gap matters for language models. With $|\Sigma|\sim10^5$, $d_G$ can exceed $d_N$ by a factor of about 17. More importantly, the impossibility result says aggregation of proper learners cannot close the gap for huge or infinite alphabets. "Optimal" is therefore literally true only for binary tokens. - All computational difficulty is pushed into $\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ (and $\mathrm{ERM}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ for distillation, which is agnostic ERM and can be much harder). Realizability with exact CoT match is strong. For neural networks, "consistent" is approximately what interpolating training does, but the guarantee is worst case over consistent outputs, so it says nothing about implicit bias. - Constants are very large: $256\cdot19.28\cdot(1+\log4)\,e^2C\approx 8.7\times10^4\,C$, where $C$ is the second-moment constant. The result is about rates, not practice. - The bootstrap is drawn from random prefixes $S_{\le k}$, $k\in[n/4,n)$, which is an artifact of the suffix-averaging technique of [ACSZ23]. Plain Breiman bagging is not what is analyzed, although it is very close. - $N$ still grows with $T$, unless one is willing to pay $d^\star$. Whether $\Theta(\log T)$ voters is necessary for any $T$-free aggregation is left open.

Proof sketch

Step 0, the next-token reduction. Since a generator follows the target until its first mistake, the CoT error event equals $\exists t:\ f(x\circ y_{1:t-1})\neq y_t$. All analyses are teacher-forced on target prefixes.

Step 1, Lemma 1 (distribution of consistent predictors). For any realizable $P$ and any oracle, $$\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim P}\big[a(x,y)^2\big]\le C\,\frac{d_G}{n},\qquad a(x,y)=\max_t\Pr_{S\sim P^n}[\hat f_S(x\circ y_{1:t-1})\neq y_t].$$ Proof: fix the worst-step map $\phi$ as above. The class $\mathcal{E}=\{E_f\}$ has VC dimension at most $d_G$, because if $\mathcal{E}$ shatters $k$ points then $\{G_f\}$ shatters their (necessarily distinct) images. The selector $E(S)=E_{\hat f_S}$ is deterministic and disjoint from $S$ by CoT-consistency. Then apply Lemma 2 [AHLZ24; RZ26]: for any VC-$d$ class of sets and any deterministic selector avoiding the sample, $$\mathbb{E}_{z}\big[\Pr_S[z\in E(S)]^2\big]\le C\,\frac{d}{n}.$$ This second-moment bound is the probability that two independent consistent learners both err at a point, which is the majority-of-three quantity. It avoids the $\log(n/d)$ factor that a first-moment bound [BEHW89] would add.

Step 2, Lemma 3 (leave-one-out error of idealized bagging). Define the bagging score $\hat B^m_S(y\mid x)=\Pr_{S'\sim\mathrm{Unif}(S)^m}[\hat f_{S'}(x)=y]$ over all ordered bootstraps, with $\hat B_S:=\hat B_S^{|S|}$. For any realizable sequence $S$ with $n\ge2$, $$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\max_t\big(1-\hat B_{S_{-i}}(y_{i,t}\mid x_i\circ y_{i,1:t-1})\big)^2\le 2e^2C\,\frac{d_G}{n}.$$ The trick is the out-of-bag observation. A size-$(n-1)$ bootstrap of $S$ omits index $i$ with probability $(1-1/n)^{n-1}\ge1/e$, and conditioned on that it is a uniform bootstrap of $S_{-i}$. Hence $$1-\hat B_S^{n-1}(y'\mid x')\ge\tfrac1e\big(1-\hat B_{S_{-i}}(y'\mid x')\big).$$ Now $\max_t(1-\hat B^{n-1}_S(y_t\mid\cdot))$ is exactly $a(x,y)$ from Lemma 1 for the distribution $D=\mathrm{Unif}(S)$ (realizable because $S$ is) with sample size $m=n-1$. Applying Lemma 1 to the empirical distribution itself bounds the LOO average by $e^2C d_G/(n-1)$. Because Lemma 1 holds for every realizable distribution, no fresh data is ever needed. Remark 3: by exchangeability, the idealized bagging majority has expected CoT risk at most $8e^2Cd_G/(n+1)$. It errs only if $\hat B_S(y_t\mid\cdot)\le1/2$ at some step, that is, only if the squared worst-step error is at least $1/4$.

Step 3, Lemma 4 (high probability via suffix averaging). $\hat B_S$ is permutation-invariant (it averages over all ordered bootstraps, even if the oracle is order-dependent), and its LOO loss sum is bounded by $M=2e^2Cd_G$ uniformly over realizable sequences, with loss in $[0,1]$. This lets the paper apply [ACSZ23, Thm 2.1]: averaging the risks of the predictors trained on prefixes $S_{\le k}$, $k\in J_n$, gives $O((M+\log(2/\delta))/n)$ with probability $1-\delta$. Jensen's inequality then passes from the average of losses to the loss of the averaged suffix-bagging predictor $$\hat g_S(y\mid x)=\mathbb{E}_{k\sim\mathrm{Unif}(J_n)}\Pr_{S'\sim\mathrm{Unif}(S_{\le k})^k}[\hat f_{S'}(x)=y],$$ which yields $$\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}\max_t(1-\hat g_S(y_t\mid\cdot))^2\le19.28\,e^2C\Big(\frac{d_G}{n}+\frac1n\log\frac2\delta\Big).$$

Step 4, Lemma 5 (sparsification via binomial tails). Fix $S$. If $N\ge\max\{4,\log_2(T/\delta)\}$, then with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the bootstraps the sampled majority $\hat h$ satisfies $$\mathrm{err}_P(\hat h)\le256\,\mathbb{E}\,r(x,y),\qquad r(x,y)=\max_t(1-\hat g_S(y_t\mid\cdot))^2.$$ Proof: split examples into $E=\{r\ge1/256\}$, whose mass is at most $256\,\mathbb{E}[1_E r]$ by Markov, and its complement. Off $E$, at each target prefix the $N$ voters' mistakes are i.i.d. Bernoulli($p$) with $p<1/16$, because Algorithm 1's sampling is exactly the mixture in $\hat g_S$. The vote is wrong only if some $\lceil N/2\rceil$ voters all err, so $$\Pr\le2^Np^{N/2}=(4p)^2(4p)^{N/2-2}\le256\,p^2\,2^{-N}.$$ A union bound over $T$ steps gives $256\,T2^{-N}r(x,y)\le256\,\delta\, r(x,y)$, so $\mathbb{E}[Z]\le256\,\delta\,\mathbb{E}[1_{E^c}r]$, and Markov at level $1/\delta$ finishes. Lemma 6 gives an alternative: uniform convergence on the dual class approximates all scores within $\varepsilon$ using $N=O((d^\star+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)$, independent of $T$ (the Moran–Yehudayoff route).

Step 5, assembly. Split $\delta$ evenly between Lemma 4 and Lemma 5 and take a union bound. The CoT risk is at most $256\cdot19.28\,e^2C(d_G+\log(4/\delta))/n=O((d_G+\log(1/\delta))/n)$, using $N=\max\{4,\lceil\log_2(2T/\delta)\rceil\}$. The degenerate case $d_G=0$ gives zero risk.

Distillation (Proposition 1). Let $\hat h$ be any teacher with $\mathrm{err}_P(\hat h)\le\hat\varepsilon$, and let $\bar f=\mathrm{ERM}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ on $n_u$ fresh prompts labeled by $\hat h^{(1:T)}$. Then with probability $1-\delta$, $$\mathrm{err}_P(\bar f)\le5\hat\varepsilon+\frac9{n_u}\Big(d_G\log(2n_uT+1)+\log\frac8\delta\Big).$$ The proof has four ingredients: - $|\mathrm{err}_P(f)-\mathrm{err}_{P_{\hat h}}(f)|\le\hat\varepsilon$, since the two label distributions differ only where $\hat h$ errs. In particular $f_\star$ has teacher-risk at most $\hat\varepsilon$. - Bernstein's inequality gives empirical risk $\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(f_\star)\le2\hat\varepsilon+2\log(2/\delta)/n_u$. - A relative-deviation bound [BBL05] gives $\mathrm{err}\le2\widehat{\mathrm{err}}+5\gamma$, so near-realizability yields the fast $1/n_u$ rate. - Lemma 8: the CoT-loss class has growth function at most $(kT+1)^{d_G}$, by Sauer–Shelah on the $kT$ teacher-forced token examples. This is the [JVBG+25] argument and the only place $\log T$ appears.

With $n_u\ge n\log(nT)$, this gives $O((d_G+\log(1/\delta))/n)$. Notice that this is exactly the "single consistent predictor pays $\log T$" phenomenon, now paid in cheap unlabeled prompts rather than in labeled CoTs.

Broader context

Background lineage. The technique is a direct transplant of a 2023–2026 line on simple optimal PAC learners: - Hanneke's optimal PAC learner via careful subsampling. - Larsen [L23], "Bagging is an optimal PAC learner", which removed the $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ of ERM by majority-voting ERMs on bootstraps. Lemma 5 is in the spirit of its Lemma 3. - Aden-Ali et al. on majority-of-three [AHLZ24] and suffix averaging without uniform convergence [ACSZ23]. - Montasser [M26], bagging for adversarially robust learning with linear sample complexity. That paper supplied the "analyze the distribution over consistent learners, then bag" template.

The conceptual analogy is clean. In PAC learning, a single ERM pays $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ because one hypothesis must be simultaneously good everywhere, and a majority removes it. Here a single consistent generator pays $\log T$ because it must be simultaneously right at $T$ positions, and a token-level majority removes it. On the CoT theory side, the closest works are Joshi et al. [JVBG+25] (framework, $d\log T$), Hanneke–Mehalel–Moran [HMM26] ($T$-free via compression, and the end-to-end versus CoT separation), and Li [L26] (DS-optimal, one-inclusion). A parallel stochastic line asks about horizon-independence for log-loss next-token prediction: Foster–Block–Misra on behavior cloning, and Rohatgi et al. on the misspecification barrier where error must grow with horizon.

Contrast with self-consistency. Empirical "self-consistency" in LLMs votes over final answers of complete sampled chains, which is a sequence-level vote. Sequence-level voting would require each member to be fully correct on the whole CoT, which brings back $\log T$. The paper's vote is token-level and is re-applied on the ensemble's own prefix. This is closer to logit or probability averaging of an ensemble of LMs at decoding time (product- or mixture-of-experts decoding), and suggests that token-level ensembling is the statistically right granularity.

Plausible follow-ups: 1. Lower bounds on ensemble size. Is $N=\Omega(\log T)$ necessary for any token-level majority of consistent learners that achieves a $T$-free sample complexity, or can a cleverer aggregation (for example majority-of-three with a recursive structure) get $O(1)$ voters, closing the $\min\{d^\star,\log T\}$ question of Remark 2? 2. DS-optimality with list learners. Since aggregation of proper predictors fails for large alphabets, a natural route is to bag list learners [P26-style list learning] and decode by a vote over lists, which could replace $d_G$ by $d_{DS}$ while staying oracle-efficient. 3. Agnostic or noisy CoTs and stochastic generators. The squared worst-step-error device and the out-of-bag trick look portable to a setting where demonstrations come from a stochastic teacher and risk is measured in sequence-level TV. 4. Tracking the cost of distillation. The analysis needs an agnostic $\mathrm{ERM}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$. A "consistent-on-most" or robust oracle version would make the distillation step more realistic.

Connection to generative retrieval (genuine but with caveats). A GR model maps a query $x$ to a docid $y\in\Sigma^T$ (for example hierarchical k-means codes, RQ-VAE semantic IDs, or atomic tokens with $T=1$) by applying one decoder $f:\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$ autoregressively. Training on (query, full docid) pairs with teacher forcing is exactly CoT supervision. The paper's CoT risk is exactly-correct docid decoding, a Hits@1 or Recall@1 error with greedy decoding. The results then say the following within this model. - In the realizable, deterministic idealization, the number of (query, docid) training pairs needed to learn the query-to-docid map does not have to grow with the docid length $T$. A single consistent model may pay $\log T$, which is one formal reason why longer semantic IDs are not inherently more data-hungry, while ensembles of GR models with prefix-wise voting provably avoid it. - The relevant complexity is the token-level Graph dimension of the decoder class over a codebook of size $|\Sigma|$. This puts the docid-design trade-off (short IDs with a large codebook versus long IDs with a small codebook) entirely into the class complexity and a $\log|\Sigma|$ factor, rather than into $T$. - The distillation result mirrors practice in GR: query generation produces pseudo-queries, which are "unlabeled prompts", and those are labeled by a stronger teacher.

The caveats are real. GR uses beam search with prefix-tree constraints and is evaluated on ranked lists, the docid assignment is chosen by the system rather than generated by some $f_\star\in\mathcal{F}$, realizability is questionable when many queries map to many relevant docs, and the theory says nothing about how the docid tokenization shapes $d_G$. Still, a concrete testable idea follows: an ensemble of GR models doing token-wise majority or vote-constrained beam decoding over the docid trie, and a study of whether the gain grows with docid length. There is no meaningful connection to vector search.

title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-19

Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment — Xingzi Xu, Mehmet Saygin Seyfioglu, Karim Bouyarmane (2026) — arXiv:2611.21766

Setting and problem

The object of study is offline pairwise preference optimization of a language model $\pi_\theta(y \mid x)$. For a fixed prompt $x$ with a finite candidate set $\mathcal{Y}_x = \{y_1, \dots, y_n\}$, the policy is a point on the simplex $\Delta^{n-1}$, and a training method (its loss plus gradient flow) induces a vector field $F : \Delta^{n-1} \to T\Delta^{n-1}$ with $\sum_i F_i = 0$. Following Deng et al. (2026, "drifting" generative models), the field is split as $F = F^+ - F^-$ into attraction toward desired completions and repulsion from undesired ones.

The state variable everything is reduced to is the log-margin of one preference pair $(y_w, y_l)$, $$\Delta = \log \frac{\pi(y_w)}{\pi(y_l)},$$ and the reduction is: project the field onto the two-completion simplex $\{y_w, y_l\}$ with a tabular softmax $\pi(y_i) = e^{\theta_i}/(e^{\theta_w} + e^{\theta_l})$. Because DPO, IPO, SimPO and friends depend on $\theta_w - \theta_l$ only, the two logits receive equal and opposite gradients and the dynamics collapse to a scalar autonomous ODE $$\dot\Delta = w(\Delta),$$ after absorbing $2\eta$ into time. Each method is then just a weighting function $w$:

  • DPO, $\mathcal{L} = -\log\sigma(\beta(\Delta_\theta - \Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}))$: $w(\Delta) = \beta\sigma(-\beta\Delta)$ (sigmoid, strictly positive, saturating). SimPO has the same shape on length-normalized log-probabilities with a target offset $\mu$ and no reference.
  • IPO, $\mathcal{L} = (\Delta_\theta - \Delta_{\mathrm{ref}} - 1/(2\tau))^2$: $w(\Delta) = \tau - 2\tau^2\Delta$ (linear, with a zero). Note the appendix analyzes $(\tau\Delta - 1/2)^2$ instead, which differs by a factor $\tau^2$; rates quoted as $2\tau^2$ come from this second form.
  • PPO with a KL penalty (unclipped): $\dot\Delta = \eta[(R(y_w) - R(y_l)) - \beta(\Delta - \Delta_{\mathrm{ref}})]$, again linear.
  • KTO: a bell-shaped $w$ peaking near $\Delta = 0$.
  • The asymmetric family $\mathrm{DPO}_\gamma$ with $\Delta_\gamma = \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w)} - \gamma\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l)}$, $\gamma \in [0,1]$, interpolates between "no explicit push-down" ($\gamma = 0$) and DPO ($\gamma = 1$).

Given: the loss family and its hyperparameters ($\beta, \tau, \gamma, \varepsilon, \mu$). To be produced: closed-form trajectories $\Delta(t)$, fixed points and their stability, and how these change under label noise (a fraction $\varepsilon$ of pairs flipped) and under multi-example parameter sharing.

The precise question: for a given pairwise alignment loss, does the margin of a preference pair grow without bound or converge to a finite attractor, at what rate, how does label noise change this, and can these dynamical facts be used to choose or design a loss (here, a label-smoothed SimPO with a predicted attractor location)?

What prior work knew. That DPO overfits deterministic preferences by pushing the implicit reward gap to infinity was the motivating observation of IPO (Azar et al., 2024); that label-smoothed "conservative" DPO (cDPO, Mitchell 2023) has a finite optimum is in Mitchell's note; noise-robust DPO is Chowdhury et al. (2024); likelihood displacement is Razin et al. (2024); gradient imbalance is Yan et al. and Ma et al. (2025). Unifying frameworks (f-PO, RPO) characterize what each loss optimizes at its optimum. The claimed gap is a unified account of how optimization unfolds in time across methods, plus a three-axis taxonomy (repulsion type, weighting $w$, reference strategy).

Modelling choices that are not obvious and matter:

  • Two-completion tabular softmax. All theorems live on $\{y_w, y_l\}$ with free logits, so there is no leakage of mass to other sequences and no parameter sharing between pairs. The authors call this an "effective theory" and admit that the margin is a sufficient statistic only when $\langle g_w, g_l\rangle$ is not large (with $g = \nabla_\theta \log\pi$), i.e. exactly outside the likelihood-displacement regime.
  • Gradient flow, full batch, continuous time. Adam is argued to be a positive time reparameterization (Appendix A.7).
  • Mean-field noise. The noisy ODE averages the clean and flipped gradients for the same margin coordinate; this is called "exact in the large-sample limit".
  • A fitted calibration constant $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (per data scale) maps the toy ODE to real training. It varies from $\beta/4.4$ (500 MATH pairs) to $\beta/1.9$ (full MATH), and is a further factor 25 to 35 off on 60K UltraFeedback pairs.

Main idea

Treat each loss as a 1D dynamical system in the margin and read off its qualitative behavior from the sign structure of $w$. If $w > 0$ everywhere (DPO, SimPO, Llama-2's margin-shifted DPO) the margin grows forever; if $w$ has a stable zero (IPO, PPO-KL, label-smoothed losses) it converges. Label noise adds a term of opposite sign, so for DPO it turns "no zero" into "one stable zero" at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$ (they call this a phase transition), while for IPO it only shifts the zero to $(1-2\varepsilon)/(2\tau)$ at an unchanged rate. A third ingredient, the multi-pair margin equation $\dot\Delta_j = \frac{\beta}{N}\sum_i \sigma(-\beta\Delta_{\gamma,i})\, v_j^\top w_i$, says the shared-parameter gradient is dominated by hard pairs, and negative interference $v_j^\top w_i < 0$ can collapse easy margins.

The constructive half reads Theorem 2.4 as a design rule: add label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO to get TPO-S, $\mathcal{L} = (1-\varepsilon)(-\log\sigma(\delta)) + \varepsilon(-\log\sigma(-\delta))$ with $\delta = \beta(s_w - s_l - \mu)$, whose weighting $(1-\varepsilon)\sigma(-\Delta) - \varepsilon\sigma(\Delta)$ has a stable zero. A Huber variant (TPO-H, clamped linear $w$) is derived from five desiderata D1 to D5 (finite attractor, rate bounded away from zero, stability, bounded gradient, asymmetry).

Empirically (LoRA r=64, AdamW, effective batch 4, mostly Qwen3-8B / DeepSeek-R1-Qwen3-8B / Qwen3.5-9B / Ministral-3-8B): DPO margins keep growing (into the hundreds or thousands of nats) while IPO margins stay in single digits across seven models; DPO's final margin under noise $\varepsilon \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$ matches $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$ with $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}} = \beta/4.4$ to within about 8%; $\gamma = 0$ plateaus at 66% held-out preference accuracy on MATH while $\gamma > 0$ reaches near ceiling, with a non-monotone "collapse valley" at $\gamma \approx 0.7$ to $0.8$; TPO-S has the highest mean IFEval on all three models, though the margin over SimPO is 0.3, 0.5 and 2.6 points (significant only on Ministral, $p = 0.013$).

The most interesting part

The cleanest idea is the reframing of the noise result: label noise is not a nuisance to be robustified against but an implicit regularizer that creates an attractor, and you can therefore inject it deliberately (label smoothing) to place the attractor where you want, $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$. The 2x2 reading of Table 3 (reference present/absent crossed with attractor present/absent: DPO, cDPO, SimPO, TPO-S) is also a nice way to separate the two effects: removing the reference adds about 1.2 IFEval points, adding the attractor to a reference-free loss adds about 1.1, but adding it to DPO (cDPO) costs about 1.0.

That said, a reviewer would push hard on several points.

  1. Most of the theory is the static optimum of a 1D logistic or squared loss, dressed as dynamics. A strictly positive $w$ means the 1D loss has no minimizer; a soft-label logistic loss has its minimizer at the log-odds of the soft label, $\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$. That is exactly why cDPO was proposed, and why IPO was proposed. The "phase transition" is the observation that $\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon} \to \infty$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$; calling it a phase transition is rhetorical. The DPO $\frac{1}{\beta}\log(\beta^2 t)$ growth is the one-dimensional version of the well-known result that gradient descent on logistic loss over separable data diverges in norm like $\log t$ (Soudry et al., 2018), which is not cited.

  2. Theorem 2.2's "rate separation" is not a separation as stated. SFT's $|\dot\pi(y_l)| = O(\pi(y_l)^2)$ is an asymptotic statement as $\pi(y_l) \to 0$, but DPO's $\Omega(\pi(y_l))$ bound is only claimed on $\{\pi(y_l) \ge \delta\}$, with a constant $c(\beta, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, \delta)$ that vanishes as $\delta \to 0$. On any set bounded away from zero SFT is also $\Omega(\pi)$, since $\pi^2 \ge \delta\pi$. Doing the asymptotics honestly, $\sigma(-\beta\Delta) \approx (\pi(y_l)/\pi(y_w))^{\beta}$, so DPO's push-down decays like $\pi(y_l)^{1+\beta}$ versus SFT's $\pi(y_l)^2$. With $\beta = 0.1$ that is still a real gap, but it is $\pi^{1.1}$ versus $\pi^2$, not $\Omega(\pi)$ versus $O(\pi^2)$.

  3. The mean-field noise argument has a hole for fixed noisy datasets. The averaged ODE applies to a single margin coordinate that sees both the clean and the flipped gradient. In a real dataset a given pair is either flipped or not. With a tabular model, flipped pairs would go to $-\infty$ and clean ones to $+\infty$ independently, and no attractor would exist per pair. The attractor only appears through parameter sharing, when the model cannot tell flipped pairs from clean ones, which is a statement about generalization and not the law of large numbers over the batch the paper invokes. The paper does not say whether flips are fixed or resampled each step; this matters for interpreting Figure 4.

  4. The Adam argument is weaker than presented. Writing $\dot\Delta = (v^\top P_t v)\, w(\Delta)$ assumes the update is $-P_t\nabla\mathcal{L}$, which ignores momentum. More importantly, $P_t \approx \mathrm{diag}(1/\sqrt{\hat v_t})$ with $\hat v_t$ tracking squared gradients, which themselves scale like $w(\Delta)^2$. Adam therefore largely undoes the sigmoid saturation that produces $\log t$ growth, and in the single-example limit gives roughly constant-speed (linear-in-steps) margin growth. The authors concede the rate is not invariant, but then present "logarithmic growth confirmed" as a result. The evidence is thin: $R^2 = 0.85$ on Figure 3, a DPO margin of 1540 nats at step 2000 where the raw formula gives about $10\log(20) \approx 30$, and in the n-completion check the linear fit beats the log fit at $n = 8$ and at $n = 2$. What survives is the sign dichotomy (bounded versus unbounded), which is exactly the invariant part and is close to trivial.

  5. Quantitative predictions are rescued by fitting. $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}$ varies by 2.3x across scales and is further off by 25 to 35x on UltraFeedback (TPO-S's predicted $\Delta^* \approx 29$ versus an observed 832 at $\varepsilon = 0.05$). With a free scale per regime, "confirmations" of fixed-point locations are close to unfalsifiable, except for the genuinely nice within-regime check that one $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}$ fits all three noise levels. The IPO $\tau$-sweep has a 33% mean absolute error and one non-monotone point; cross-model IPO margins range from 0.5 to 7.2 around a predicted 5.

  6. It is not shown that the attractor is ever reached. For TPO-S, "final margins decrease monotonically with $\varepsilon$" (1605, 1264, 832, 455, 341) is equally consistent with slower but still unbounded growth, since the smoothing term subtracts gradient everywhere. Trajectories showing a plateau would be the actual test. Also, with length-normalized scores and $\beta = 0.1$, $\Delta^* \approx 29$ is a per-token average log-ratio of about 29 nats, which is so large that it is hard to believe the attractor is ever binding. And the target-margin offset $\mu$ is dropped from the stated attractor (it should be $\mu + \beta^{-1}\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$).

  7. The downstream evidence is modest, and some of it cuts against the theory. The $\varepsilon$-sweep shows downstream accuracy is flat (49 to 52%, near chance) across a 3x range of attractor locations. So the location the theory "controls" does not matter, and the attractor's existence matters only as much as the TPO-S over SimPO gap, which is within noise on two of three models (uncorrected t-tests over 5 seeds). TPO-S uses $\beta = 0.1, \mu = 0.5$ while SimPO is listed with $\mu = 1.0$ (SimPO's own defaults use much larger $\beta$), so $\varepsilon$ is confounded with $\beta$ and $\mu$. The UltraFeedback preference accuracies of 42 to 60%, and ORPO at about 50% IFEval with huge variance, suggest a regime (LoRA, batch 4, short runs) where baselines may be undertuned. cDPO underperforming DPO is explained post hoc via the reference axis.

  8. The collapse story does not track accuracy. In Table 13, $\gamma = 0.25$ has 47/50 collapse events but 91% accuracy, $\gamma = 0.6$ has 34 collapses but 100%, and $\gamma = 1.0$ has 4 collapses and 98% (with an 82 to 98% seed range). The theory predicts monotone concentration in $\gamma$; the data are non-monotone, which the authors acknowledge "likely involves interactions beyond the pairwise analysis."

  9. Directly relevant learning-dynamics work is missing: Ren and Sutherland (ICLR 2025, "Learning Dynamics of LLM Finetuning", the "squeezing effect" of negative gradients), Feng et al. (2024) on DPO's gradient field and its asymmetric effect on chosen and rejected likelihoods, Im and Li (2024) on alignment learning dynamics, and Pal et al. (2024, DPO-Positive) on chosen-likelihood decrease. These cover much of Axes 1 and 3 with more realistic (non-tabular) models.

Net: a well-organized taxonomy with an appealing design heuristic ("make $w$ have a stable zero"), but the theoretical content is shallow relative to the framing, and the "quantitative confirmation" leans heavily on a post hoc scale parameter.

Proof sketch

Common setup. On $\{y_w, y_l\}$ with logits $\theta$, the softmax Jacobian gives $\dot\pi(y_l) = \pi(y_l)(1-\pi(y_l))(\dot\theta_l - \dot\theta_w)$. Any loss depending only on $\theta_w - \theta_l$ gives $\dot\theta_w = -\dot\theta_l$, hence $\dot\Delta = 2\eta\, w(\Delta)$, with time rescaled to drop $2\eta$.

Theorem 2.2 (repulsion). For SFT, $\mathcal{L} = -\log\pi(y_w)$ gives $\dot\theta_w = \eta\pi(y_l) = -\dot\theta_l$, so $\dot\pi(y_l) = -2\eta\pi(y_l)^2(1-\pi(y_l))$. For DPO, $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta_w = -\beta\sigma(-\beta\tilde\Delta) = -\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta_l$, so $\dot\pi(y_l) = -2\eta\beta\sigma(-\beta\Delta)\pi(y_l)(1-\pi(y_l))$. On $\{\pi(y_l) \ge \delta\}$, $\Delta \le \log\frac{1-\delta}{\delta} + |\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}|$ bounds $\sigma(-\beta\Delta)$ below. (See the critique: the comparison is only meaningful once the $\delta$-dependence is tracked.)

Theorem 2.3 (no noise). DPO: with $u = e^{\beta\Delta}$, $\dot\Delta = \beta/(1+u)$ becomes $\dot u = \beta^2 u/(1+u)$. Separating variables gives $u + \log u = \beta^2 t + C$, so $u \sim \beta^2 t$ and $\Delta \sim \beta^{-1}\log(\beta^2 t)$. IPO: $\dot\Delta = \tau - 2\tau^2\Delta$ is linear, $\Delta(t) = \frac{1}{2\tau} + (\Delta(0) - \frac{1}{2\tau})e^{-2\tau^2 t}$.

Theorem 2.4 (label noise, mean field). Averaging the clean and flipped gradients: $$\dot\Delta = (1-\varepsilon)\beta\sigma(-\beta\Delta) - \varepsilon\beta\sigma(\beta\Delta).$$ Using $\sigma(-x) = e^{-x}\sigma(x)$, the zero is $(1-\varepsilon)e^{-\beta\Delta^*} = \varepsilon$, i.e. $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$. The derivative is $-\beta^2\sigma(\beta\Delta)\sigma(-\beta\Delta) < 0$ everywhere, so the zero is globally stable. For IPO a flipped pair contributes loss $(\tau\Delta + 1/2)^2$, and averaging gives $\dot\Delta = -2\tau^2\Delta + \tau(1-2\varepsilon)$: fixed point $(1-2\varepsilon)/(2\tau)$, rate $2\tau^2$. TPO-S is the same computation with $\Delta$ replaced by the length-normalized margin minus $\mu$, which is why its attractor formula is inherited.

Theorem 2.5 (gradient concentration). With $N$ pairs, $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} = -\frac{\beta}{N}\sum_i\sigma(-\beta\Delta_{\gamma,i})\, w_i$ with $w_i = \nabla\log\pi(y_w^i) - \gamma\nabla\log\pi(y_l^i)$. Projecting gradient flow onto $v_j = \nabla\Delta_j$ gives the exact identity $\dot\Delta_j = \frac{\beta}{N}\sum_i\sigma(-\beta\Delta_{\gamma,i})\, v_j^\top w_i$. Pairs with $\Delta_{\gamma,i} \gg 1/\beta$ get weight at most $e^{-\beta\Delta_{\gamma,i}}$, so hard pairs dominate. Since $\partial\Delta_{\gamma,i}/\partial\gamma = -\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l^i)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l^i)} > 0$ once the rejected likelihood has dropped below the reference, larger $\gamma$ saturates learned pairs faster. Remark 2.6 then defines $\beta_{\mathrm{eff},j} = \dot\Delta_j/\sigma(-\beta\Delta_j)$, splits off the self term $\frac{\beta}{N}\|v_j\|^2$, and bounds the cross terms by $O(\beta\sigma_\perp\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{active}}}/N)$ under an explicit (and admittedly strong) independence-of-gradients assumption. This is the only bridge from the toy ODE to real training, and it is a heuristic, not a theorem. Note that $\beta_{\mathrm{eff},j}$ is essentially a row of the empirical NTK weighted by sigmoid factors.

The remaining appendix results are standard: GRPO's expected squared advantage $\propto p(1-p)/K$ with zero-gradient probability $(1-p)^K + p^K$; the KL-optimal adaptive reference is a geometric mixture $\pi_0^{1-\alpha}\pi_\theta^{\alpha}$; coverage gaps decay as $\Delta_T \le \Delta_0\prod_t(1-p_t)^K$ by a coupon-collector induction under a no-forgetting assumption.

Broader context

Background. DPO reparameterizes the KL-regularized RLHF optimum so that the implicit reward is $\beta\log(\pi_\theta/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ and trains it with a Bradley-Terry logistic loss on pairs. Because the logistic loss has no finite minimizer on perfectly separated pairs, the implicit reward gap is driven to infinity, and the reference-model KL that was supposed to keep $\pi_\theta$ close is effectively lost. IPO replaced the logistic loss with a squared loss toward a target gap; cDPO and robust DPO addressed noise; SimPO dropped the reference and length-normalized. This paper puts all of these into one picture by plotting each loss's 1D weighting function.

Related directions.

  • Learning dynamics of fine-tuning and preference optimization: Ren and Sutherland (ICLR 2025) decompose per-step changes via an eNTK-style term, explain the "squeezing effect" of negative gradients, and handle exactly the cross-example and cross-sequence coupling this paper pushes into $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Razin et al. (2024) on likelihood displacement give the condition under which the paper's margin reduction breaks.
  • Implicit bias of logistic-type losses: Soudry et al. (2018) and follow-ups on margin growth of gradient descent on separable data. The DPO-versus-IPO dichotomy is essentially the logistic-versus-square-loss dichotomy from that literature, and the label-smoothing attractor is the standard effect of soft targets on logit norms (as in label smoothing for classifiers).

A plausible follow-up. Make $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}$ predictive rather than fitted. Remark 2.6 is literally an eNTK row, $\beta_{\mathrm{eff},j} = \frac{\beta}{N}\sum_i\frac{\sigma(-\beta\Delta_i)}{\sigma(-\beta\Delta_j)}K_{ji}$ with $K_{ji} = v_j^\top w_i$, so one could estimate the LoRA gradient Gram matrix on a subsample at initialization, add Adam's preconditioner, and test whether it predicts the measured margin trajectories and fixed points across data scales. A second follow-up: verify the attractor by showing plateaued trajectories for TPO-S, and test whether the per-pair attractor survives with fixed (not resampled) label flips, which would separate the mean-field story from a memorization story.

Connection to theoretical IR, generative retrieval and vector search. This one is genuine. DPO's per-pair loss is RankNet / BPR: a pairwise logistic ranking loss on the score difference, with the policy's log-probability as the score. IPO is a squared pairwise (regression-to-target-margin) loss. So the paper's taxonomy is a dynamical restatement of a classic learning-to-rank distinction: logistic pairwise losses push score gaps of correctly ordered pairs to infinity and keep spending capacity on them, while margin-targeted losses saturate.

  • Dense retrieval: in InfoNCE with mined hard negatives, false negatives play the role of flipped labels, and the paper's result predicts they cap the query-document margin at roughly $\tau_{\mathrm{temp}}\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$. Deliberate label smoothing is then a principled way to place that cap.
  • Generative retrieval: ranking-aware training of docid generators, such as LTRGR (Li et al., AAAI 2024) and the DPO-style DDRO (Mekonnen et al., SIGIR 2025), optimizes exactly these pairwise margins over docid sequences. There the two-completion reduction is at its weakest. Docids under a prefix tree share prefixes, so $\langle g_w, g_l\rangle$ is large for siblings, which is precisely the regime where the authors say the margin stops being a sufficient statistic and mass leaks to unsampled docids.

A concrete question for that setting: how do margin dynamics, and the presence or absence of an attractor, depend on the docid tree structure, for example on the depth of the shared prefix between $y_w$ and $y_l$?

title: Learnability Gaps of Strategic Classification
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-18

Learnability Gaps of Strategic Classification — Lee Cohen, Yishay Mansour, Shay Moran, Han Shao (2024) — arXiv:2402.19303

Setting and problem

Objects. There is a feature space $\mathcal{X}$, labels $\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\}$, and a hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}^{\mathcal{X}}$. Agents are pairs $(x,y)$. The feasible manipulations are given by a directed manipulation graph $G=(\mathcal{X},E)$. An arc $(x,x')$ means "an agent at $x$ can present itself as $x'$". Write $N_G(x)$ for the out-neighbourhood, $N_G[x]=\{x\}\cup N_G(x)$ for the closed one, and $k$ for the maximum out-degree of the true graph $G^\star$. Bounded degree is a real assumption. The paper notes that without it impossibility results appear even for trivial classes.

Best response. Given a published $h$, an agent with $h(x)=0$ moves to some positive neighbour if one exists. Otherwise it stays put. So $v=\pi_{G,h}(x)\in X_{h,+}\cap N_G(x)$ when that set is nonempty and $h(x)=0$, and $v=x$ otherwise. Ties are broken arbitrarily, except in the unknown-graph PAC part, where they are uniformly random. The induced label is $h_G(x)=h(\pi_{G,h}(x))$. This simplifies to

$$h_G(x)=\max_{z\in N_G[x]} h(z),$$

so the strategic classifier is an OR of $h$ over the closed neighbourhood. The strategic loss is $\ell^{\mathrm{str}}_G(h,(x,y))=\mathbf{1}(h_G(x)\neq y)$. The true label $y$ does not change when the agent moves. One modelling choice is subtle here. $y$ is not a function of $x$ alone. It can depend on the agent's manipulation power, so "realizable" means some $h^\star\in\mathcal{H}$ has zero strategic loss. It does not mean that $h^\star$ labels raw features correctly.

Protocol. In each round an agent $(x_t,y_t)$ arrives: i.i.d. from $D$ in the PAC case, adversarial in the online case. The learner publishes $h_t$, the agent moves to $v_t=\pi_{G^\star,h_t}(x_t)$, and the learner sees $\hat y_t=h_t(v_t)$, $y_t$ and possibly some information about $x_t$ or $v_t$. The learner cannot ask counterfactual questions such as "where would agent $t$ have moved under some other $h$?". So even PAC learning is interactive: the published hypotheses decide what gets observed. The PAC goal is small $L^{\mathrm{str}}_{G^\star,D}(h)=\mathbb{E}\,\ell^{\mathrm{str}}_{G^\star}(h,(x,y))$, realizable or agnostic. The online goal is Stackelberg regret $\sum_t\ell^{\mathrm{str}}_{G^\star}(h_t,(x_t,y_t))-\min_{h^\star\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_t\ell^{\mathrm{str}}_{G^\star}(h^\star,(x_t,y_t))$, which is the mistake count in the realizable case.

Information models. 1. Fully informative. $G^\star$ is known (in fact only $N_{G^\star}(x_t)$ is needed), and $x_t$ is seen before $h_t$ is chosen. 2. Post-manipulation feedback (PMF). $G^\star$ is known, but $h_t$ must be chosen blind. Afterwards the learner sees either $x_t$ or $v_t$. 3. Unknown graph. $G^\star$ is unknown, but a finite class $\mathcal{G}$ of graphs is given, all with max out-degree at most $k$. $\mathcal{G}$ either contains a graph that agrees with $G^\star$ on neighbourhoods (realizable) or serves as a comparator (agnostic). The main feedback variant is $x_t$ before choosing $h_t$ and $v_t$ after.

Questions. Does finite $\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal{H})=d_1$ imply strategic PAC learnability, and at what sample cost? Does finite $\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})=d_2$ imply a finite strategic mistake bound, and how does the bound scale with $k$? How do these answers change when information is removed (no $x_t$ up front, or no graph)?

Prior work. Zhang and Conitzer (2021) and Sundaram et al. (2021) gave VC classes that are not strategically learnable. Those examples allow unbounded manipulation, and it was not clear which structural property causes the gap. Sundaram et al. already noted that PAC sample complexity is governed by $\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal{H}_{G^\star})$. Ahmadi et al. (2023) studied PMF online learning for finite $\mathcal{H}$ and left a gap between $O(k\log|\mathcal{H}|)$ and $\Omega(k)$. Lechner et al. (2023) and Shao et al. (2023) studied unknown manipulations, but with a different loss or only for finite classes.

Main idea

The answer is essentially "yes, learnability implies strategic learnability", and the price is set by the degree $k$ and by what information the learner has.

  • Fully informative, PAC. $d_1\log k\le\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal{H}_{G^\star})\le d_1\log(kd_1)$ in the worst case. So strategic ERM needs $\tilde O(d_1\log k/\varepsilon)$ samples (realizable) or $\tilde O(d_1\log k/\varepsilon^2)$ (agnostic), with matching lower bounds up to $\log d_1$. The PMF PAC bounds are the same: publish the all-positive hypothesis, nobody moves, you see $x_t$, and you read off $N_{G^\star}(x_t)$ from the known graph.
  • Fully informative, online. The optimal mistake bound is $\Theta(d_2\log k)$. It is achieved by Red2Online-FI, an efficient black-box reduction that turns any standard online learner (e.g. SOA) into a weighted pool of experts that split on ambiguous feedback.
  • PMF, online. The dependence on $k$ becomes exponentially worse: $O(d_2\,k\log k)$ upper bound, and $\Omega(d_2(k-1))$ for deterministic learners. This settles the Ahmadi et al. open question up to $\log k$ and extends it from $\log|\mathcal{H}|$ to Littlestone dimension. In this one place the timing of information changes the rate qualitatively. In PAC, timing does not matter.
  • Unknown graph. In the realizable PAC case the bound is $\tilde O\big((d_1\log k+k\log|\mathcal{G}|)/\varepsilon\big)$, and $\log|\mathcal{G}|$ is necessary up to lower-order factors. In the agnostic case they get $L^{\mathrm{str}}\le 6k\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}+\Delta_{\mathcal{H}}+\varepsilon$, which is only a multiplicative approximation in the graph error. In the realizable online case the bound is $O(d_2k\log k+\log|\mathcal{G}|)$, and roughly $\log|\mathcal{G}|$ (up to a $\log\log$ factor) is needed for deterministic learners. If $(x_t,v_t)$ is only revealed afterwards, deterministic learners can be forced into $n-1$ mistakes with $|\mathcal{G}|=|\mathcal{H}|=n$.

So the separation from standard learning is mild: one $\log k$ factor in the best case, a factor $k$ online without pre-observation, and an additive $\log|\mathcal{G}|$ (times $k$ in PAC) for graph uncertainty.

The most interesting part

To me, the cleanest idea is the explanation of why the $\log k$ factor appears and why it grows to $k$ in PMF. Both come from one picture: a mistake gives you a "one-of-$(k+1)$" ambiguous label.

In the fully informative online setting the learner sees $x_t$, so it can act improperly. It publishes either "positive only at $x_t$" or "all negative", and so controls the induced label exactly. Prediction is never the hard part. The hard part is a false negative. It tells you that $h^\star$ is positive somewhere in $N[x_t]$, but not where. Red2Online-FI forks every implicated expert into $|N[x_t]|\le k+1$ copies, each told that a different neighbour is positive, and gives each copy $1/(2(k+1))$ of the parent's weight. The expert that tracks $h^\star$ loses at most a factor $2(k+1)$ per standard mistake. Meanwhile every learner mistake removes a constant fraction of the total weight. So the mistake count is $O(M\log k)$. The lower bound shows this ambiguity is real. The graph is $\log k$ disjoint stars, and hypothesis $h_j$ writes the binary code of $j$ on the leaves (one bit per star). $\mathcal{H}$ has VC and Littlestone dimension 1, but the OR over each star reads out one bit of $j$. So the star centres are shattered by $\mathcal{H}_{G^\star}$, and each centre query can cost one mistake.

In PMF the learner must commit to one global $h_t$ before it knows which neighbourhood matters. It has to label a node positive once a $1/(2(k+1))$ fraction of the weight says so, which is the only way to avoid a false negative on any neighbourhood. A false positive then refutes only that fraction of the weight. The lower bound uses a star with singleton hypotheses on the leaves. Whenever the learner turns a leaf positive, the adversary sends that leaf with label 0 and rules out exactly one singleton. Committing to a global hypothesis means each positive "bet" can be refuted only one at a time.

Caveat: as I read the written proof of Theorem 10, the case "learner predicts the centre $x_0$ positive" sends the centre with label 0. That looks inconsistent with realizability if arcs go from the centre to the leaves, since every singleton then gives the centre label 1. The case seems repairable: give leaves arcs to the centre and send a non-target leaf with label 0. The bound also matches Ahmadi et al.'s Theorem 4.6, but the argument as written needs care. The PMF lower bound is also proved only for deterministic learners.

Proof sketch

Theorem 4 (VC of the induced class). Upper bound. $h_G$ on points $x_1,\dots,x_n$ depends only on $h$ restricted to $\bigcup_i N[x_i]$, which has at most $n(k+1)$ points. Sauer–Shelah allows at most $O((nk)^d)$ restrictions. Shattering needs $2^n\le O((nk)^d)$, so $n=O(d\log(kd))$. Theorem 18 then follows from standard VC bounds, with ERM on the strategic loss. Only $N_{G^\star}(x_t)$ is needed. Lower bound. Use the binary-code stars described above, and take $d$ disjoint copies to get $d\log k$ (Theorem 19). The same construction gives the online lower bound $d\log k$ (Theorem 21): query the star centres in order, and the adversary always answers against the learner, halving the surviving set of $j$. The paper extends this to randomized learners via Filmus et al. (2023).

Theorem 20 (Red2Online-FI, $O(M\log k)$). Potential argument. Each mistake removes at least $W_t/4$ of the total weight. A false positive halves at least half the weight, and a false negative splits and halves at least half. So $W\le(3/4)^N$. The expert following $h^\star$ keeps weight at least $(2(k+1))^{-M}$. Together these give $N\le 4M\ln(2(k+1))$. An agnostic version, $\tilde O(\sqrt{\,\cdot\,T})$ regret, follows from Ben-David–Pál–Shalev-Shwartz expert covering. It uses the fact that with $x_t$ and $N(x_t)$ known you can flip any induced prediction. The authors say they do not know how to do this in the PMF or unknown-graph settings.

Theorem 9 (Red2Online-PMF, $O(k\log k\cdot M)$). Same experts, but $h_t(x)=1$ iff the experts predicting 1 at $x$ hold at least $1/(2(k+1))$ of the weight. On a false negative, by a union bound over $N[x_t]$ at least half the weight predicts 0 on the whole neighbourhood, so you split as before. On a false positive at $v_t$, only a $1/(2(k+1))$ fraction is guaranteed to be wrong, so $W_{t+1}\le(1-\tfrac{1}{4(k+1)})W_t$. Solving gives $N\le 4kM\ln(2(k+1))$. Only $v_t$ is used, so the "harder" PMF variant is covered. The lower bound is proved in the "easier" variant, which shows that the two variants are equally hard.

Theorem 6 (realizable PAC, unknown graph). Training: publish $h_t=\mathbf{1}(x\neq x_t)$. Everyone except $x_t$ is positive, so the agent moves to $v_t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(N_{G^\star}(x_t))$. This is a one-neighbour sample. Output: among pairs $(G,h)$ consistent with every observed arc and with zero empirical strategic loss under $G$, choose the one that minimises the empirical degree $\sum_t|N_G(x_t)|$. The analysis has two parts. 1. $L^{\mathrm{str}}_{G^\star}(h)\le P(N_{G^\star}(x)\neq N_G(x))+L^{\mathrm{str}}_G(h)$. The second term is handled by uniform convergence over the class $\mathcal{H}\circ\mathcal{G}$, whose VC dimension is $O(d\log(kd)+\log|\mathcal{G}|)$. 2. The key lemma. Write $\mathbf{1}(N_{G^\star}\neq N_G)\le|N_G\setminus N_{G^\star}|+|N_{G^\star}\setminus N_G|$. Missing arcs are detectable, since $|N_{G^\star}(x)\setminus N_G(x)|\le k\,P_{v\sim\mathrm{Unif}(N_{G^\star}(x))}(v\notin N_G(x))$ and $\mathbf{1}(v_t\notin N_G(x_t))$ estimates this without bias. Extra arcs are not detectable: any supergraph of $G^\star$ is consistent with all the data. But if $G$ has empirical degree at most that of $G^\star$, subtracting the common arcs gives $\sum_t|N_G(x_t)\setminus N_{G^\star}(x_t)|\le\sum_t|N_{G^\star}(x_t)\setminus N_G(x_t)|$. So minimising degree bounds the undetectable error by the detectable one. An empirical Bernstein bound, using zero variance for consistent graphs, then gives the $k\log|\mathcal{G}|/\varepsilon$ term.

Lemma 8 and Theorem 28 (agnostic). There may be no consistent graph, so the authors minimise an estimable proxy:

$$L_{\mathrm{proxy}}(G)=2\,\mathbb{E}_x\big[P_{v\sim\mathrm{Unif}(N_{G^\star}(x))}(v\notin N_G(x))\big]+\tfrac1k\mathbb{E}|N_G(x)|-\tfrac1k\mathbb{E}|N_{G^\star}(x)|.$$

This satisfies $\tfrac1kL_{\mathrm{nbhd}}\le L_{\mathrm{proxy}}\le 3L_{\mathrm{nbhd}}$. Minimising it on one sample and running strategic ERM under the estimated $\hat G$ on a second sample gives $6k\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}+\Delta_{\mathcal{H}}+\varepsilon$, using Lemma 27 ($2\alpha$ for a graph of neighbourhood error $\alpha$).

Theorem 12 (online, unknown graph). Take a majority vote over the surviving graphs. Any $x$ that is a neighbour of $x_t$ in at most half of them is labeled positive. A mistake there certifies the arc and removes at least half of $\mathcal{G}_t$, so there are at most $\log|\mathcal{G}|$ such mistakes. On the majority neighbourhood $\tilde N$, which has size at most $2k$ and contains the true one, run Red2Online-PMF with degree bound $2k$. Lower bounds (Theorems 7, 13). These use "blown-up singletons": $n$ groups, each copied $n$ times so that degree 1 is enough. The adversary (adaptively, in the PAC case) chooses arcs from unseen points of $X_0$ so that whatever $\hat h$ does is wrong. $|\mathcal{G}|=(n+1)^n$ while the cost is about $n$, so the bounds are really $\Omega(\log|\mathcal{G}|/\log\log|\mathcal{G}|)$-type statements.

Two honest caveats. First, Theorem 6 leans on uniform-random tie-breaking: the factor $k$ comes from $|N|\cdot P_{\mathrm{Unif}}$. A footnote says any consistent tie-breaking would do, but the given proof uses uniformity. Second, the training phase deliberately publishes a nearly all-positive classifier, which is a lot of pure exploration to impose on real agents.

Broader context

Background. Strategic classification (Brückner–Scheffer 2011; Hardt et al. 2016) models the deployed classifier as the leader in a Stackelberg game, with agents who best-respond within limited manipulation budgets. The budgets are usually given by cost functions or metric balls, or, equivalently, as the paper notes, by manipulation graphs. Performative prediction (Perdomo et al. 2020) is the distribution-level relative: the deployed model shifts the data distribution, and one studies stability and optimality of retraining. This paper sits in the combinatorial learning-theory strand, which asks for VC/Littlestone-style characterizations. A useful comparison is adversarially robust learning (Montasser, Hanneke, Srebro 2019). There, perturbations hurt the learner in the worst direction and proper learning can fail. Here agents only ever move toward positive labels, so $h_G$ is a monotone OR, and with bounded degree the same Sauer-style counting gives only a $\log k$ blow-up. Similar $\log k$ counting appears for finite perturbation sets in robust learning.

Related directions. (i) Ahmadi, Blum, Yang (2023), Fundamental bounds on online strategic classification, whose open question this paper closes. (ii) Shao, Blum, Montasser (2023) and Lechner, Urner, Ben-David (2023) on unknown or personalized manipulation sets. Both are natural places to look for removing the $6k$ multiplicative factor, which the authors themselves list as open, along with agnostic online learning under PMF.

A follow-up idea. Replace binary acceptance with _top-$m$ selection_, where agents want to enter a ranked shortlist. The induced class is then an OR over neighbourhoods composed with a ranking threshold that depends on everyone else's moves, so agents interact. Does the $\log k$ / $k$ dichotomy survive, and what replaces the Littlestone dimension, perhaps a ranking or Natarajan-type dimension? Another clean question is whether randomized learners beat $\Omega(dk)$ in PMF. The paper's PMF lower bound is deterministic only, while the fully informative one is extended to randomized learners.

Connection to IR, honestly assessed. There are two genuine links, both fairly coarse. 1. SEO and content manipulation. A document that edits itself to pass a relevance or quality filter is exactly a "gaming" agent. A bounded-degree manipulation graph over discrete edit operations is a reasonable abstraction, but the binary-filter model does not capture competitive ranking. 2. The neighbourhood-learning subproblem. This is the more concrete link, and the paper flags it itself. You show a set, a user clicks one uniformly random relevant item in it, and you want to recover each user's (or query's) whole relevant set. That is an idealized click model: no position bias, uniform choice. The degree-regularization trick, "the minimal consistent graph bounds false-positive arcs by missed arcs", is a neat answer to the positive-unlabeled problem in implicit-feedback relevance learning. It could be read as a sample-complexity statement for learning query-to-docid sets in generative retrieval from single-click logs over a finite model class $\mathcal{G}$. The finite $\mathcal{G}$ and the uniform-click assumption are the obvious gaps to close.

I see no honest link to vector search itself beyond the loose analogy of bounded-degree graphs.

title: Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-18

Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining — Huang, Zhang, Payani, Mirzasoleiman (2026) — arXiv:2611.19042

Setting and problem

The world. There are $N$ entities and $M$ relations; relation $r$ acts as a fixed permutation $\pi_r:[N]\to[N]$. The fact table is $A=[N]\times[M]$, with $D=NM$ facts $(e,r)\mapsto \pi_r(e)$. A length-$L$ chain $\chi=(r_1,\dots,r_L,e_0)$ induces states $e_\ell=\pi_{r_\ell}(e_{\ell-1})$, and its $\ell$-th transition is the fact $(e_{\ell-1},r_\ell)$. A random held set $H\subset A$ with $|H|=m=qD$ is drawn once; $S=A\setminus H$ is the retained set, $q$ is the held fraction and $p=1-q$ the reasoning coverage.

Two data sources. Both use the same prompt $[r_1,\dots,r_L,e_0]$.

  • Atomic examples: $\chi\sim D_{\mathrm{at}}=\mathrm{Unif}([M]^L\times[N])$, supervising only $e_1$. Every fact, including held ones, gets atomic signal.
  • Reasoning examples: $\chi\sim D_{\mathrm{rea}}=\mathrm{Unif}(C_L(S))$, where $C_L(S)=\{\chi: (e_{\ell-1},r_\ell)\in S \ \forall \ell\}$, supervising the whole teacher-forced trace $e_1,\dots,e_L$.

A held fact is therefore not an unseen fact. It is a known fact that has never been used inside a chain. Evaluation is on chains where a later transition is held.

Objective. With atomic weight $\beta\in[0,1]$ and $\lambda=1-\beta$, the reasoning loss is averaged over its $L$ positions: $$ \mathcal L_\beta(\theta)=\beta\,\mathbb E_{D_{\mathrm{at}}}\ell_1(\theta;\chi)+\lambda\,\mathbb E_{D_{\mathrm{rea}}}\Big[\tfrac1L\textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^L \ell_\ell(\theta;\chi)\Big]. $$ The empirical model is a one-layer softmax-attention plus MLP transformer trained with cross-entropy. The theory uses a scalar linear-attention surrogate $$ f_{\mathrm{lin}}(X_t)=W X_t\big[(X_t^\top B X_t)\odot \tilde C_{1:t,1:t}\big], $$ with typed one-hot content tokens. Only three groups of coordinates are trainable: relation values $w_r$, relation–entity scores $b_{r,e}$, and positional routing $C_{j\ell}$ (key position $j$, the relation slot, to query role $\ell$). At role $\ell$ this reduces to $$ f_\ell(\chi)=\sum_{j=1}^L C_{j\ell}\,G_{(e_{\ell-1},r_j)},\qquad G_{r,e}=w_r b_{r,e}. $$ So $G$ is an associative fact memory, and $C$ decides which relation slot role $\ell$ reads. The correct circuit is $C_{\ell\ell}=1$, with $G$ storing a code of $\pi_r(e)$. Targets are the scalar codes $\zeta_e=(2e-N-1)/N$, decoded to the nearest code. The loss is squared error, $\tfrac\beta2\mathbb E_{\mathrm{at}}(f_1-\zeta_{e_1})^2+\tfrac{\lambda}{2L}\sum_\ell \mathbb E_{\mathrm{rea}}(f_\ell-\zeta_{e_\ell})^2$. Training is gradient flow from $B(0)=0$, $w_r(0)=1$, $C(0)=E_{11}$: role 1 already reads slot 1, and every other route starts at zero.

Question. Define the held-transition error $E_H(\theta)=\frac{1}{2(L-1)}\sum_{\ell=2}^L\mathbb E_{D_{H,\ell}}(f_\ell-\zeta_{e_\ell})^2$, where $D_{H,\ell}$ is the uniform chain distribution conditioned on $(e_{\ell-1},r_\ell)\in H$. _At a fixed training horizon $\tau$, which atomic weight $\beta^\star_{\tau,S}=\arg\min_\beta E_H(\theta_\beta(\tau))$ is best, and how does it depend on $L$ and $q$?_

Known results and the gap. Empirical work (Akter et al. 2026, Olmo 3 midtraining, Nemotron, Allen-Zhu and Li's "mix instruction data into pretraining") shows that reasoning or SFT-style data help during pretraining. Theory work covers factual recall through associative memories (Nichani et al. 2025) and chain-of-thought state tracking learned by gradient descent (Huang et al. 2026c). Neither line asks how to split a budget between atomic and compositional supervision as a function of chain length and coverage.

Modelling choices worth flagging. (i) The world is balanced (Assumption 1): $M=N$, and for every pair $e,e'$ exactly one relation maps $e$ to $e'$, as with cyclic shifts. This is a Latin square, so $\mathbb E_r\zeta_{\pi_r(e)}=0$ and $\mathbb E_r\zeta^2_{\pi_r(e)}=\nu=\frac{N^2-1}{3N^2}$. (ii) $\beta$ is a loss weight, and the reasoning loss is averaged over $L$. The token-budget story in the introduction ("longer traces cost more") is not literally modelled; the $L$ dependence enters through this averaging (see below). (iii) The initialization $C(0)=E_{11}$ hard-codes the first route. (iv) The result is finite-time with $\tau$ fixed and $N\to\infty$, so it describes the earliest phase of learning, not convergence.

Main idea

Held-transition generalization needs two things at once. The model must have memorized the held fact in $G$, and only atomic data can do that. It must also have learned to route role $\ell\ge2$ to slot $\ell$, and only reasoning data can do that, because atomic examples never supervise roles $\ge2$. One more coupling matters: routing is learned through the gradient $\dot C_{j\ell}\propto -\mathbb E[G_{a^\ell_j}R_\ell]$. The routing signal therefore exists only once the facts inside reasoning chains are already partly memorized, and both sources contribute to that memory.

Expanding the flow in small $1/D$, the paper shows that the leading reduction of held error is cubic in time: $$ -\frac{2LD^2}{\nu^2\tau^3}\Big[E_H(\theta_\beta(\tau))-\frac{\nu_H}{2}\Big]= g(\beta)+O\!\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(2/\delta)}{N}}\Big),\qquad g(\beta)=\beta\lambda\Big(\beta+\frac{\lambda}{pL}\Big). $$ The three factors read as follows: $\beta$ is atomic memory of the held fact; $\lambda$ is the reasoning signal that drives routing; $(\beta+\lambda/(pL))$ is how well chain facts are memorized, which sets how fast routing is learned. Reasoning data spreads its first-slot memory signal over $pD$ retained facts and dilutes it by $1/L$ through loss averaging. Its per-fact contribution is therefore $\lambda/(pL)$, while atomic data gives $\beta$ uniformly.

Setting $g'(\beta)=0$ with $a=1/(pL)$ gives the leading-order optimum $$ \beta^\star\approx \bar\beta(pL),\qquad \bar\beta(z)=\frac{1}{2-z+\sqrt{z^2-z+1}}, $$ which is increasing in $z=pL=L(1-q)$. Because $\bar\beta(0^+)=1/3$, $\bar\beta(1)=1/2$ and $\bar\beta(\infty)=2/3$, the optimum increases with chain length and decreases with the held fraction. When $pL$ is large, reasoning data barely helps memorize any single fact, so atomic data must carry the memory role for routing as well. When $q$ is large, reasoning data concentrates on few facts and memorizes them quickly by itself. The range is narrow. For example, $L=2,p=0.9$ gives $\bar\beta\approx0.57$ and $L=6,p=0.9$ gives $\approx0.63$.

Empirics. - One-layer softmax+MLP transformer, cross-entropy, $64$ entities, $8$ random-permutation relations (so not the balanced world), $L\in\{2,\dots,6\}$, $q\in\{10,30,50\}\%$. An interior atomic ratio beats both endpoints on OOD accuracy. The best ratio generally rises with $L$ and falls with $q$, with acknowledged exceptions at $q=30\%$, $L\in\{3,4\}$, where the curve plateaus. - Natural-language multi-hop over 32 people and 32 relations, in the bio-style setup of Allen-Zhu and Li, with a 12M model. Interior mixtures win everywhere, four-hop favours more atomic data, and larger $q$ lowers peak OOD accuracy and shifts the near-best region left. - Olmo-3 150M on 10B tokens of FineMath ("atomic") plus MathLake/OpenMathInstruct-2 ("reasoning"). GSM8K cross-entropy is best at 20% MathLake (1.608, against 1.785 for pure FineMath and 7.513 for pure MathLake, which is heavily repeated). The best FineMath share rises with the available MathLake fraction $p$ and with difficulty (used as a proxy for $L$). Delaying reasoning data never helps.

These math experiments are a loose analogy. FineMath is not "atomic facts of MathLake", "held-out ratio" there means a smaller reasoning pool repeated more often, and the evidence is CE trends across three mixture points.

The most interesting part

The surprising part is the sign of the length effect and its mechanism. A natural guess is that longer reasoning chains are richer and so deserve more weight. The theory says the opposite, for a specific reason: atomic data are not only a store for held facts. They also speed up the learning of the compositional routing on retained facts, because the routing gradient is proportional to how well the chain's facts are already stored. Atomic data thus act as a catalyst for learning composition, and the catalytic value grows when reasoning data spread their memorization signal thinly (large $pL$).

Formally this is the factorization of the leading gain into memory × routing × memory-of-chain-facts. Generalization to held transitions appears only at third order in $t$, because it needs a product of a first-order memory term and a second-order routing term. That gives a clean, falsifiable explanation of why an interior mixture wins and why its location moves.

Caveat: the $1/L$ dilution comes largely from the choice to average the reasoning loss over its $L$ positions, together with $C(0)=E_{11}$, which makes slot 1 the only route that writes memory early. If the loss were summed per token, which is closer to how token budgets work in practice, the per-fact reasoning signal would not shrink with $L$ in the same way, and the $L$-trend could weaken or change. The empirical trend in the softmax model is real but noisy, so the theory explains it in one plausible way rather than establishing it.

Proof sketch

Claim (Theorem 1). Assume a balanced world ($M=N$, a simply transitive family), fixed $L\ge2$, $p\in(0,1)$, $\tau>0$, $\delta\in(0,1)$, and a uniformly random $H$ with $|H|=qN^2$. Run gradient flow from $B=0$, $w=\mathbf 1$, $C=E_{11}$. Then for all sufficiently large $N$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the mask, $\beta^\star_{\tau,S}$ is unique, lies in $(1/3,2/3)$, and satisfies $$ \big|\beta^\star_{\tau,S}-\bar\beta(L(1-q))\big|\le R_N=O_{L,p,\tau}\!\Big(\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/N}\Big). $$

Step 1: perturbative solution of the flow (Lemma 3). The parameter norm satisfies $\frac{d}{dt}\|\theta\|^2\le 3/2$, so the polynomial ODE has a global solution that is smooth in $\beta$. Rescale $Y=Db$. A bootstrap argument keeps $\|Y(t)\|\le 8Kt$, $\|C-E_{11}\|=O(t^2/D)$ and $\|w-\mathbf 1\|=O(Nt^2/D^2)$ on $[0,\tau]$ once $D\gtrsim K^2\tau^2$. Integrating gives the expansions $$ G(t)=\frac{t}{D}v+O(D^{-2}),\quad v_a=(\beta+\lambda\omega_a)y_a;\qquad C(t)=E_{11}+\frac{t^2}{2D}\mathcal B_\beta(v)+O(D^{-2}), $$ where $\omega_a=\frac{D}{L}\Pr_S(a_1=a)$ is about $1/(pL)$ on $S$ and $0$ on $H$, and $[\mathcal B_\beta(v)]_{j\ell}=\frac{\lambda}{L}(\beta K_{j\ell}+\lambda U_{j\ell})$ for $\ell\ge2$. Here $K_{j\ell}$ and $U_{j\ell}$ are target-correlation moments under the reasoning distribution. The cubic prediction $f^{(3)}_\ell=\sum_j C^{(2)}_{j\ell}G^{(1)}_{a^\ell_j}\propto t^3/D^2$ is then projected onto the held target, and the error decomposes as $E_H=\nu_H/2-\frac{t^3}{2LD^2}P_S(\beta)+O(D^{-3})$. All bounds are tracked in a norm that includes $\beta$-derivatives up to order 2, $\|h\|_{[2]}=\sum_{k\le2}\frac1{k!}\sup_\beta\|\partial^k_\beta h\|$, because the argmin is controlled later through $J'$ and $J''$.

Step 2: balance kills cross terms (Lemma 1). Under the Latin-square property, the next state after a uniformly random relation is uniform. That yields $\mathbb E_{H,\ell}[y_{a^\ell_j}y_{a^\ell_\ell}]=\nu_H\mathbf 1\{j=\ell\}$, while the $\omega$-weighted cross terms collapse to a single scalar $Z_S$. The gain is a cubic polynomial $P_S(\beta)$ in $\beta$ with mask-dependent coefficients.

Step 3: concentration over the random mask (Lemma 2). The coefficients are ratios of chain statistics such as the valid-chain probability $F_0$, $F_\ell$, $T_\ell$ and $M_S$. For complete shifts, chains biject with vertex sequences, so their expectations are computed up to collision bias $O(L^2/N)$ and without-replacement bias $O(L^2/(pD))$. Deviations are bounded by a Doob martingale over revealing the mask: one exchange of a fact changes a $k$-edge statistic by at most $2k/D$, and Hoeffding-type moment bounds plus a union bound give $|P_S/\nu^2-g|_{[2]}=O(\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}/N)$. The cross scalar $Z_S$ concentrates at $0$, and $K_{\ell\ell}\to\nu$, $U_{\ell\ell}\to\nu/(pL)$.

Step 4: stability of the argmax (Lemma 4). The function $g(\beta)=\beta(1-\beta)[\beta+a(1-\beta)]$ has a unique interior critical point at $\bar\beta(1/a)\in(1/3,2/3)$. Its slope has a fixed sign on $[0,1/3]$ and on $[2/3,1]$, and it is strongly concave on $[1/3,2/3]$ with modulus $\mu=2\min\{a,1\}$. A $C^2$-small perturbation $r$ with $\|r\|_{[2]}\le\eta<m$ moves the maximizer by at most $\eta/(\mu-2\eta)$. Monotonicity follows from $\bar\beta'(z)=\bar\beta^2(1-\frac{2z-1}{2\sqrt{z^2-z+1}})>0$, using $4(z^2-z+1)-(2z-1)^2=3$.

What is and is not guaranteed: the result concerns the leading-order early-time improvement. The total improvement is $O(\tau^3/D^2)$, so held error is still close to its initial $\nu_H/2$. Nothing is proved about later training, accuracy, softmax attention or cross-entropy.

Broader context

Background. "Transformer theory via synthetic tasks" studies small, often linearized or block-structured attention models on tasks with planted structure, such as in-context regression (Zhang, Frei and Bartlett; Ahn et al.), factual recall as associative memory (Nichani, Lee and Bietti), causal-structure induction, and state tracking or automata (Liu et al., "shortcuts to automata"; Merrill et al.). A common technique, used here too, is to fix a block structure (content-content and position-position scores, mixed blocks zeroed) so that gradient flow decomposes into a few interacting scalar or matrix ODEs. Results are then read off a closed form or a perturbative expansion.

Close relatives. - Huang et al. 2026c (transformers provably learn chain-of-thought state tracking with length generalization) is the direct technical ancestor. - Wang et al. 2024, "Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners" (cited from my own knowledge, not by this paper), found that the ratio of inferred to atomic facts governs how fast composition circuits form, and that OOD composition over facts never seen in compositions fails without chain-of-thought. That is a closely matching empirical phenomenon, here with explicit traces. - Allen-Zhu and Li's "Physics of LMs 3.1" motivates mixing extraction-style data into pretraining. - Javanmard, Mirzasoleiman and Mirrokni have related data-quality and test-time-scaling theory from the same group.

Follow-up ideas. 1. Model the budget honestly. Make reasoning traces cost $L$ tokens and use summed per-token losses, then check whether the $L$-trend survives. This is the cleanest test of whether the headline is about chains or about loss normalization. 2. Go beyond the cubic regime, for example by solving the flow to a constant fraction of the error, or by using the softmax model. The current optimum is pinned to $(1/3,2/3)$ by the shape of $g$, which may be an artefact of early time. 3. Replace the Latin-square world with unbalanced, Zipfian fact frequencies, where atomic coverage and trace coverage are naturally correlated.

Connection to generative retrieval (genuine, I think). In DSI-style generative retrieval, training mixes indexing examples (document text to docid, i.e. atomic memorization of every document) with retrieval examples (query to docid), which exist only for a subset of documents. Documents without training queries play the role of held facts: the model has memorized them, but has never practised using them under the query-to-docid mapping. The original DSI work and its successors already found that the indexing-to-retrieval ratio matters and that generalization to documents without queries is the hard case. This paper's mechanism suggests a concrete hypothesis: the retrieval task (routing) is learned faster when the documents in the query set are well indexed, so indexing data both stores unseen-query documents and speeds up learning of the retrieval map. With hierarchical or semantic docids decoded as $L$ tokens, decoding a docid is itself a chain of $L$ transitions through a prefix tree. A derived law would then predict that the optimal indexing weight grows with docid length and with the fraction of documents covered by queries. This is speculative, but it could be tested cheaply with a small DSI model on MS MARCO subsets, varying query coverage and docid depth. I see no natural link to vector search beyond the general associative-memory view of $G$ as a key-value store.

title: Transformers in the Dark: Navigating Unknown Search Spaces via Bandit Feedback
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-18

Transformers in the Dark: Navigating Unknown Search Spaces via Bandit Feedback — Kim, Zeng, Lin, Lee, Lee, Sohn, Koo, Lee (2026) — arXiv:2603.24780

Setting and problem

The paper asks whether a Transformer can itself act as the selection component of a tree-search algorithm such as MCTS, rather than calling an external search routine. To test this in isolation, the other two parts of LLM-guided search (expanding states and evaluating them) are handed to the environment.

Formal object. A problem instance is a finite rooted tree $\mathcal{T} = (S, N)$ of maximum depth $D$, with successor map $N : S \to 2^{S}$ and a bounded reward $r : S \to [0,1]$. Goal states $S_{\text{goal}} = \{ s \in S : r(s) > 0 \}$ are leaves and are sparse, $|S_{\text{goal}}| \ll |S|$. The tree is hidden. The natural target for feedback is the value of a state under a uniformly random rollout,

$$ V(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{unif}}}\left[ r(s_{\text{leaf}}) \mid s_{\text{start}} = s \right], $$

but the agent only sees a noisy realization $v_t \sim \widehat{V}(s_t)$, for example a $k$-rollout Monte Carlo estimate, or in the LLM experiments a score the LLM gives itself.

Protocol. Starting at the root $s_0$, at each step $t$ the environment reveals the children $N(s_t)$ and a value $v_t$. The agent must choose $s_{t+1}$ from the frontier

$$ F_t = \Big( \bigcup_{i=0}^{t} N(s_i) \Big) \setminus \{ s_0, \dots, s_t \}, $$

using a policy $\pi(\cdot \mid s_0, v_0, N(s_0), \dots, s_t, v_t, N(s_t))$, under a budget $T \ll |S|$. The trajectory $\tau$ is scored mainly by whether it reaches the best leaf, i.e. by $\max R$ with $R = \{ r(s_i) : s_i \in \tau \}$. This is a mix of a best-arm-identification bandit (the arms are frontier nodes, which become available over time) and simple-regret tree search. Feedback is "bandit" in the sense that you learn a value only for the node you choose.

Reference policies (the targets for imitation). (i) Uniform leaf sampling: pick $s_t \sim \mathcal{U}(F_{t-1})$. (ii) Greedy leaf sampling: pick a frontier node whose parent has the highest observed value. (iii) Uniform path sampling: walk down from the root, choosing uniformly at each level among children whose subtrees are not fully explored, until you hit a frontier node. (iv) Policy-guided path sampling with a pure-exploration (min-count), greedy (max summed value) or UCT tree policy, with UCT constant $c = 0.1$. All of these are MCTS-like selection rules that skip fully explored subtrees.

The precise question. Does there exist a fixed-size Transformer that maps the serialized history $\tau_{0:t}$ to exactly the next-state distribution of each reference policy? Separately: can such a Transformer be learned by next-token training on traces, does it generalize to longer budgets, deeper trees, and other goal counts or wall densities, and does trace fine-tuning help a pretrained LLM?

What is known, and the gap. Prior work trains Transformers on A_ traces (Searchformer, Dualformer, Nolte et al.), distills RL algorithms into in-context learners (algorithm distillation), and pairs LLMs with external MCTS (ToT, RAP, LATS). The A_ line, however, gives the model the whole environment, i.e. the graph, up front. The gap the paper targets is the case where the space is revealed only step by step and the only signal is noisy bandit feedback, together with exact, constant-depth constructions instead of universal-approximation arguments.

Modelling choices to flag. - The theoretical model uses hard attention (ties are averaged uniformly), arbitrary piecewise-continuous token-wise feed-forward maps, no LayerNorm, causal masking (implicit) and greedy decoding with uniform random tie-breaking. All the randomness of the "stochastic" policies comes from that tie-breaking rule. - The state vocabulary is a fixed set of $TB+1$ one-hot state ids, so states are atomic symbols with no features. - The three tokenizations differ: one for the theory, one with indexed frontier lists for training from scratch, and a chat format for LLMs.

Main idea

The approach is to turn selection into next-token prediction over a serialized interaction log. In leaf-based tokenization each step reads $?\, S_{s_t}\, \%\, V_{v_t}\, \#\, S_{s_{t,1}} S_{s_{t,2}} \dots$, and the model must output the next state token after each $?$. Tree-based tokenization adds a [BOS] token and makes the model emit the whole tree-policy path $S_{s_0} > S_{s_{0,i_1}} > \dots > S_{s_t}$, ending with $\%$.

Theory. - Theorem 1: 3-layer Transformers with $d = 10 + TB$ exactly implement uniform and greedy leaf sampling. - Theorem 2: 12-layer Transformers with $d = 26 + 7TB$ exactly implement uniform path sampling and greedy, pure-exploration and UCT path sampling.

Depth is constant and width grows linearly in the number of distinct states that can appear. Sequence length is linear in $T$ for leaf tokenization and at worst quadratic for tree tokenization.

Experiments from scratch. The model is Llama-style: 8 layers, 8 heads, $d = 512$, RoPE. Training uses 200 instances times 100 traces (70/30 train/val split). Testing is online on 10 held-out instances times 100 traces. Environments are binary trees of depth 6 with 8 goals and a 4x4 maze with wall density 0.4, both with budget $T = 50$. Trained models match the reference algorithms on six metrics: max-reward hit rate, a DCG-style $1/\log_2(i+1)$ speed score, normalized path length, highest and cumulative reward, and jump distance. An $\ell_2$ distance between metric statistics usually ranks the true reference closest. Per-step KL to the reference next-state distribution, though, is low only for the leaf policies and much higher for the path policies.
