Generalization holds near the training settings and degrades further out, most clearly for unseen tree depth.

LLMs. - Off-the-shelf models do poorly on the depth-6 binary tree: Qwen3-8B is about as good as uniform leaf sampling, and the Thinking variant is worse. - On an "Academic Paper Search" task, children are co-authors' papers in OpenAlex and the value is an LLM-scored path suitability. LoRA fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on Gemini-2.5-Flash and UCT trajectories raises the max-reward hit rate from 0.262 (base) and 0.286 (base plus external UCT) to 0.500 (fine-tuned) and 0.548 (fine-tuned plus UCT).

The most interesting part

The setting is a good one. Externalizing expansion and evaluation makes the exploration–exploitation part of "LLM reasoning as search" a clean in-context decision problem with controllable difficulty, and the max-reward hit rate is an honest simple-regret proxy. The Figure 1c observation that a "thinking" 8B model does worse than uniform frontier sampling is worth knowing. The construction for Theorem 1 is also easy to read and is a nice RASP-style program. Below is a critical reading.

  1. The theory is close to trivial in width and vocabulary. Each state has its own register, so $d = \Theta(TB)$ and the network is essentially a lookup table over state identities. The final argmax is read straight off those registers by an identity unembedding. With arbitrary feed-forward maps (the UCT layer computes $\log$, $\sqrt{\cdot}$, division and even outputs $\infty$ exactly), "exact implementation" mostly says that attention can gather the right sufficient statistics: parent values, visit counts and children lists. That is a useful sanity result, but it says nothing about efficient width (for example $O(\log(TB))$ with near-orthogonal ids), finite precision, or softmax with bounded weights. The claim that this beats Yun et al. because it is exact and constant-depth is fair only in that narrow sense, since the assumptions are much stronger.

  2. There are small correctness gaps in the written proof of Theorem 1.

  3. In layer 3 the score for state $i$ is the aggregate of $\mathrm{id}_i$ over all state tokens. It equals the inherited value for a frontier state, $v_{\text{parent}} - 1$ for a visited non-root state, $-1$ for the root, and $0$ for a state id that has never appeared. A frontier state whose parent got $v = 0$ therefore ties at score 0 with every never-revealed state, and also with any visited state whose parent had $v = 1$. Sparse rewards make $v = 0$ the common case, so greedy decoding with random tie-breaking can output an illegal state. The fix is easy (add an offset, e.g. score $1 + v$ for frontier states), but as written the theorem is not exact.
  4. Algorithm 3 first picks the best parent and then picks a child uniformly. The construction instead picks uniformly among all frontier nodes that tie on inherited value. These two distributions differ when tied parents have different numbers of unvisited children.
  5. The proof of Theorem 2 also has slips: layer indices are mislabelled ($f^{(5)}$ used in layer 4), registers are used inconsistently (isVisited vs wasVisited), and the UCT expression adds the summed value rather than the mean.

  6. That proof also explicitly uses the plain successor map $N$ rather than $N^{*}$ (no exclusion of fully explored subtrees). So the theorem covers a different algorithm from the one used to make the training traces.

  7. Theory and experiments are only loosely connected. The theory needs the model to write out the tree-policy path. The trained models were not given those paths, and their inputs included indexed frontier lists, which turns the task into picking an index. The authors themselves explain the high KL for path policies by the missing intermediate path tokens. So the constructions say little about why the trained models work, and the case where they plausibly matter (path policies) is the one where cloning visibly fails at the distribution level. An obvious ablation is missing: train with tree-based tokenization and see whether KL drops.

  8. Matching metrics is weak evidence of cloning. On a 126-state tree with $T = 50$ and 8 goals, many different policies reach similar hit rates. That the $\ell_2$ ranking is only "mostly" right supports this concern. The reference distributions behind the KL numbers are estimated from 100 samples, so the plug-in $p$ has support and variance problems. There is also no comparison to a simple learned baseline, such as a Transformer trained on mixed traces, or to a Bayes-optimal policy under the instance prior. That leaves open whether the model learned the algorithm or just a reasonable heuristic.

  9. Scale and statistics are small. There are 10 test instances. Generalization is tested over short ranges (depth 6 to 8; budget up to 100), with no model-size or data-size sweeps. Nothing here tells us whether the learned policy beats its teacher, which is the interesting question if the goal is to make LLMs better searchers.

  10. The fine-tuning result is confounded. In the paper-search task the LLM also produces the value scores, and the fine-tuning data come partly from Gemini-2.5-Flash. The jump from 0.286 to 0.500 could therefore come from better evaluation or from distilling a stronger model, not from better selection. The evidence that fine-tuned plus UCT (0.548) beats fine-tuned alone points the same way. The train/test split over start–target pairs is not described. The reported spreads (about 0.07–0.08) look like binomial standard errors on roughly 40 pairs, so the 0.500 vs 0.548 gap is not significant. Finding 3 ("better than an LLM with an external algorithm") compares the fine-tuned model against the base model plus UCT, which is not the fair comparison.

Proof sketch

Theorem 1 (leaf policies; 3 layers, $d = 10 + TB$). The embedding has the following registers: - value, holding the scalar $\alpha$ of the token $V_\alpha$; - a sign register equal to $+1$ for $\#$ and $-1$ for $?$; - type indicators; - one-hot $\mathrm{id}_i$ registers; - a bias register; - dynamic registers isVisited, inhValue and pos, with position added as $t\, e_{\text{pos}}$.

Write $M_{a \to b} = e_b e_a^{\top}$ for the matrix that copies register $a$ into register $b$.

  • Layer 1 (marking). The query is the bias register and the key is the separator indicator, so each token averages the signs of all preceding separators. A state token right after a $?$ has seen one more $?$ than $\#$, which makes the average negative. A child token after $\#$ sees balanced counts and gets 0. So isVisited $< 0$ exactly for selected states. The feed-forward map then sets isValue to isValue times pos, so later attention to value tokens picks the most recent one.
  • Layer 2 (inheritance). The key is isValue times pos, and hard attention picks the closest preceding value token. For a child listed after $\#$ that token is its parent's $V_{v}$, which is copied into inhValue. The feed-forward map writes inhValue into the token's own $\mathrm{id}_i$ coordinate when isVisited $= 0$, and $-1$ otherwise.
  • Layer 3 (selection). At the last $?$, uniform attention over all state tokens aggregates the $\mathrm{id}_i$ registers. An identity unembedding turns them into logits, and greedy decoding takes the argmax, which is the frontier node with the largest inherited value. For uniform leaf sampling, give every $V_\alpha$ the same embedding: all frontier scores then tie and tie-breaking is uniform. (See critique item 2 for the zero-score tie problem.)

Theorem 2 (path policies; 12 layers, $d = 26 + 7TB$). This uses the same register-programming style, with seven per-state register banks: $\mathrm{vid}$, $\mathrm{cid}$, $\mathrm{pid}$, $\mathrm{psid}$, $\mathrm{nsid}$, $\mathrm{oid}$ and $\mathrm{id}$. - Layer 1 builds an iteration counter: attending uniformly to [BOS] and separator tokens gives $1/(\text{count})$, which the feed-forward map inverts. - Layers 2–3 find, for each state token, the closest preceding $?$. This lets each iteration's $V_\alpha$ token gather the set of states on that iteration's tree-policy path, giving per-iteration reward and visit indicators. - Layer 4 does the backup: one token averages these over all iterations, and multiplying by the iteration count undoes the averaging. - Layers 5–7 mark which state tokens the model chose (as opposed to tokens the environment listed) and give each listed child its parent's id via position matching. - Layers 8–9 work at the $>$ token. It copies the id of the state just emitted, then uses content-based attention (query $\mathrm{psid}$, key $\mathrm{pid}$) to collect that state's children into $\mathrm{nsid}$. - Layer 10 imports the global statistics and computes the UCT score for each child in a single feed-forward step, with unvisited children set to $+\infty$. The greedy and uniform variants just swap this map for a value score or a constant. - Layers 11–12 handle emitting $S_0$ after $?$ and choosing whether to emit $>$ (keep descending, because the state was visited before) or $\%$ (a new node was reached).

The key trick throughout is that hard attention with a uniform query computes averages, so counts can be recovered with an explicit counter. Attention keyed on position times indicator acts as "most recent such token". Attention keyed on one-hot ids acts as a join on state identity.

Broader context

For a newcomer, the paper sits where three lines meet. 1. Expressivity of Transformers as programs. This line includes RASP (Weiss et al.), Turing-completeness with hard attention (Pérez et al.), and the limits of self-attention (Hahn). 2. In-context decision-making. Algorithm distillation (Laskin et al.) and the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (Lee et al., 2023) show that next-token training on interaction histories can produce bandit or RL algorithms that run in context. 3. LLM test-time search. This line includes ToT, RAP and LATS, plus analyses of reasoning traces as wandering or tree-jumping exploration (ReJump, "wandering solution explorers").

The closest theoretical relative is Lin, Bai and Mei (ICLR 2024), Transformers as Decision Makers. They prove that Transformers can approximate LinUCB and Thompson sampling, and they give regret guarantees for supervised pretraining, including a distribution-ratio term between the expert and the offline policy. That is the natural framework for adding learnability and regret statements to the present setting. Searchformer (Lehnert et al., 2024) is the closest empirical relative, but its environment is fully observed.

A follow-up idea. - Lower the width from $\Theta(TB)$ to polylogarithmic. Give states random near-orthogonal codes in $\mathbb{R}^{O(\log(TB)/\epsilon^2)}$ and do selection through softmax attention with bounded weights. Then prove a matching lower bound, e.g. a communication-complexity argument that max-selection over $\Theta(TB)$ revealed items needs width $\Omega(\log(TB))$ or precision growing with $T$. - Combine this with a Lin–Bai–Mei style analysis to bound the simple regret of the imitating policy relative to the teacher. A sharper question is whether RL fine-tuning can push the policy past UCT on a known prior over trees, where a Bayes-optimal benchmark is computable.

Connection to IR (genuine, but partial). - Generative retrieval with hierarchical semantic docids decodes over a prefix tree. Beam search there is a fixed, non-adaptive policy over a known trie. The setting here is the adaptive version: expand docid prefixes, get noisy relevance feedback (e.g. from a reranker on sampled leaves), and select the next prefix to explore. That points to training the retriever to do in-context UCT-like decoding over its own docid trie under a reranker-call budget. Max-reward hit rate is recall@1 under a budget, and the paper's DCG-style speed score is already an IR metric. - Similarly, the Academic Paper Search task is greedy routing in an unknown graph with noisy similarity feedback, which is structurally what graph-based ANN search (HNSW-style best-first search) does with exact distances. Asking whether a learned policy can beat best-first search when distances are noisy or expensive is a well-posed vector-search question that this framework could host. - One caveat: the theory's states are atomic one-hot ids with no geometry, so it does not yet say anything about embedding-based retrieval.

title: Adaptive Retrieval and Scalable Indexing for k-NN Search with Cross-Encoders
html:
Claude deep-dive — 2026-11-17

Adaptive Retrieval and Scalable Indexing for k-NN Search with Cross-Encoders — Yadav et al. (2024) — arXiv:2405.03651

Setting and problem

A cross-encoder (CE) is a black-box score function $f:\mathcal{Q}\times\mathcal{I}\to\mathbb{R}$ that reads a query–item pair jointly. The task is $k$-NN search with respect to $f$ itself, not with respect to relevance labels: $$\mathcal{N}(q) = \operatorname{arg\,top}k_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\, f(q,i).$$ Exact search costs $|\mathcal{I}|$ forward passes per query, so the goal is an approximation $\hat f(q,i) = \mathbf{u}_q \mathbf{v}_i^\top$ with $\mathbf{u}_q,\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$, which turns the problem into ordinary inner-product search. Quality is measured as Top-$k$-Recall@$m$: the fraction of the CE's true top-$k$ that appears among $m$ retrieved items, after those $m$ items are re-scored with the exact CE. The test-time cost is counted in CE calls $\mathcal{B}_{\textsc{ce}}$ (here $m$); the offline cost is wall-clock (GPU) time to build the index.

The object behind all of this is the score matrix $G\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{Q}_{\text{train}}|\times|\mathcal{I}|}$ with $G_{qi} = f(q,i)$ for a set of train (anchor) queries from the target domain. Assumed available: black-box CE access, the item set, train queries from the target domain (real queries for ZeShEL, BEIR's released pseudo-queries for BEIR), and a base dual-encoder $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ trained on the same source task as the CE but not on the target domain.

Prior work and the gap. There are two existing routes.

  1. Retrieve-and-rerank (RnR): retrieve $m$ items with a DE or BM25/tf-idf, re-rank with the CE. Retrieval is decoupled from the CE, and a DE trained elsewhere transfers poorly. Fine-tuning the DE on the target domain by distillation ($\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{dstl}}$) helps, but trains all transformer weights and needs the DE's parameters.
  2. CUR-based methods by the same group: ANNCUR (Yadav et al., EMNLP 2022) and adaCUR (Yadav et al., Findings EMNLP 2023). Item $i$ is represented by its column of a dense anchor matrix $R = G_{\mathcal{Q}_{\text{anc}},:}$, so indexing costs $|\mathcal{Q}_{\text{anc}}|\cdot|\mathcal{I}|$ CE calls. The test query is embedded from its CE scores against a few anchor items (adaptively chosen in adaCUR) through the pseudo-inverse of the anchor intersection block, $\hat f(q,\cdot) = \mathbf{c}_q\, U^\dagger R$ in CUR notation. The paper's own numbers: 500 queries × 10K items is about 10 GPU-hours with a BERT-base CE, and adaCUR needs 1000+ GPU-hours to index the 5.2M items of HotpotQA.

The paper keeps the CUR-style idea (query embeddings fitted from CE scores at test time) but replaces the dense anchor matrix with a sparse, partially observed $G$ and a learned factorization.

Main idea

Two components that can be used separately.

Offline indexing by sparse matrix factorization. Observe only a set $\mathcal{P}_{\text{train}}$ of entries of $G$ and solve the standard completion objective $$\min_{U,V}\ \big\|(G - UV^\top)_{\mathcal{P}_{\text{train}}}\big\|_2$$ with SGD/AdamW. The observed entries are chosen either as $k_d$ items per train query (uniformly at random or, in the main experiments, the top-$k_d$ items under $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$), costing $k_d|\mathcal{Q}_{\text{train}}|$ CE calls, or as $k_d$ queries per item, costing $k_d|\mathcal{I}|$. Two parameterizations:

  • Transductive ($\textsc{MF}_{\text{Trns}}$): $U,V$ are free parameters, initialized from $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ embeddings. An item that has no observed entry keeps its initial embedding. For 5.2M items at $d=768$ this is about 4B parameters and needed an 80 GB A100.
  • Inductive ($\textsc{MF}_{\text{Ind}}$): a 2-layer MLP with a gated skip connection on top of frozen $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ embeddings, $x_{\text{out}} = \sigma(w_{\text{skip}})\,\mathrm{MLP}(x) + (1-\sigma(w_{\text{skip}}))\,x$, with $w_{\text{skip}}$ initialized at $-5$ so the map starts close to the identity. Separate MLPs for queries and items. The authors report that the MLP without the skip connection generalizes poorly to unseen items. This is inductive matrix completion with the DE embedding as side information.

Test-time search, Axn (Adaptive Cross-Encoder Nearest Neighbor search). Item embeddings $V$ are fixed. Over $\mathcal{R}$ rounds, each with $k_s = \mathcal{B}_{\textsc{ce}}/\mathcal{R}$ CE calls:

  1. Round 1: pick $k_s$ items with a baseline retriever (DE or tf-idf/BM25) or at random, score them with the CE, giving $\mathcal{A}_1$ and score vector $\mathbf{a}_1$.
  2. Fit the query embedding by least squares on the items scored so far, $$\mathbf{u}_q = (V_{\mathcal{A}_r}^\top V_{\mathcal{A}_r})^\dagger V_{\mathcal{A}_r}^\top \mathbf{a}_r .$$
  3. Retrieve the $k_s$ highest-scoring unseen items under $\mathbf{u}_q V^\top$, score them with the CE, append, refit.
  4. After $\mathcal{R}$ rounds, return the top-$k$ of the $\mathcal{B}_{\textsc{ce}}$ scored items by exact CE score.

Since $|\mathcal{A}_r|\le\mathcal{B}_{\textsc{ce}}$ is usually below $d$, the system is underdetermined and the least-squares solution interpolates the observed scores. To regularize, the final embedding is a convex combination with a parametric query embedding (from the DE or $\textsc{MF}_{\text{Ind}}$): $$\mathbf{u}_q = (1-\lambda)\,\mathbf{u}_q^{\text{LinReg}} + \lambda\,\mathbf{u}_q^{\text{param}},\qquad \lambda\in[0,1]\ \text{tuned on dev}.$$ With $\mathcal{R}=1$ Axn reduces exactly to RnR with the initial retriever, so Axn is a strict generalization of the baseline at the same CE budget.

A practical detail matters for BEIR: CE scores and DE scores live on very different ranges, so CE scores are affinely rescaled, $s' = \beta(s-\alpha)$, to match the DE score distribution (fitted on 100 train queries) before both MF training and the test-time regression. This does not change CE rankings but does change the least-squares fit.

Most interesting part

The most interesting idea is the division of labour between a fixed, globally fitted item space and a per-query embedding fitted only on the items that the CE has actually scored for that query. The approximate score matrix is still rank $\le d$, because every query gets one $d$-dimensional vector. So the gain over a DE does not come from more expressive power. It comes from choosing each row's vector by fitting the region of the row that matters: the items near the top of that query's CE ranking. And the approximation never has to order items correctly; it only has to put the CE's top-$k$ inside the $\mathcal{B}_{\textsc{ce}}$ items that get exact scores. That is a much weaker requirement than a faithful low-rank approximation of $G$.

Strengths.

  • The method is simple and modular. Any item embedding (raw DE, distilled DE, MF) can be plugged into Axn, and the paper shows Axn improves over RnR for each of them at the same CE budget, with no extra indexing cost.
  • The cost accounting is honest about where time goes: Table 3 breaks indexing into computing $G$, computing initial DE embeddings (about 2 h for 5.2M items) and training.
  • The comparison against TouR (Sung et al. 2023), a gradient-based test-time query optimization, isolates the value of the closed-form refit.

Weaknesses and questionable points.

  1. No guarantees. The paper contains no theorem. It cites matrix-completion sample complexity ($\Omega(nr)$ entries for an $m\times n$ rank-$r$ matrix; better with side information) only as motivation. Those results assume (near-)uniform sampling and incoherence. Here the observed entries are the DE's top-$k_d$ per query, which is sampling that depends on the values, concentrated on the high-score part of each row. That is arguably the right part to fit for $k$-NN, but standard recovery results do not cover it, and nothing is said about how well the CE matrix is approximated by rank $d$ at all.
  2. The test-time loop is a greedy design. Choosing the next items as the top of the current estimate is pure exploitation, in bandit terms (my framing, not the paper's). The regression design is biased toward items that already look good, and items the current $\mathbf{u}_q$ underestimates may never be scored. There is no exploration term and no analysis of when the loop recovers the true top-$k$.
  3. The regularizer is ad hoc. With $|\mathcal{A}_r| < d$, $\mathbf{u}^{\text{LinReg}}$ is the minimum-norm interpolant, so it lies in the row span of $V_{\mathcal{A}_r}$ and is zero on the orthogonal complement. Mixing it convexly with the DE embedding shrinks the fit toward the prior but also breaks interpolation of the observed scores. The natural alternative, $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^{\text{param}} + V_{\mathcal{A}}^\dagger(\mathbf{a} - V_{\mathcal{A}}\mathbf{u}^{\text{param}})$ (minimum-norm correction from the prior), or ridge regression toward $\mathbf{u}^{\text{param}}$, is not tried. The best $\lambda$ also depends on $k$ (0.8 for $k=1$, 0 for $k=100$ on HotpotQA), so a single deployed setting cannot be optimal for both.
  4. The 5.2M-item experiment is not a search over 5.2M items. For HotpotQA, Axn and adaCUR only search within the top-10K items of the initial retriever ($\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ or tf-idf). Any CE neighbour outside that shortlist is unreachable, so the "large-scale" result is adaptive retrieval inside a 10K shortlist. The text also does not say clearly how the exact CE top-$k$ ground truth is computed for 5.2M items.
  5. CE choice. All experiments use the [emb]-CE variant from Yadav et al. 2022, which scores a pair by a dot product of contextualized query and item embeddings taken after joint encoding. That variant was introduced in the CUR line because it makes the CE matrix easier to approximate. How the method behaves with a standard [CLS]-head CE is not tested.
  6. The CE is the target, not relevance. On three of four domains (YuGiOh, Star Trek, SciDocs), exact brute-force CE search is worse on the downstream metric than RnR with $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ (e.g. entity-linking accuracy 49.8 vs. 50.6 on YuGiOh). So better $k$-NN recall with respect to the CE does not translate into better retrieval there. The authors attribute this to how the CE was trained.
  7. Most numbers are only in plots. The headline numbers in the text are a few points read off Figure 1. Whether "54% improvement" is relative or absolute is not stated.

Method and evidence

Datasets and models.

  • ZeShEL (zero-shot entity linking): YuGiOh (10,031 entities) and Star Trek (34,430 entities), with random train/test query splits of 100/500/2000 train queries. BERT-base [emb]-CE checkpoint from Yadav et al. 2022; BERT-base DEs.
  • BEIR: SciDocs (25,657 docs) and HotpotQA (5,233,329 docs), with 1K/10K/50K pseudo-queries as train queries and official test queries (1K for SciDocs, the first 1K of 7K for HotpotQA). A 6-layer MiniLM [emb]-CE trained on MS MARCO; $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ is msmarco-distilroberta/distilbert, with a BERT-base DE as an extra check in the appendix.
  • Rounds: $\mathcal{R}=5$ (ZeShEL), $\mathcal{R}=10$ (BEIR). Budgets: Top-1-Recall at 100 CE calls, Top-100-Recall at 500 CE calls. $\lambda=0$ on ZeShEL.

Main results.

  1. Axn vs. RnR with the same embeddings. On YuGiOh, Axn with $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ embeddings and $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ initialization improves over RnR-$\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ by 5.2% for $k=1$ and 54% for $k=100$. The gain is much larger for $k=100$, which fits the picture that a mis-specified DE embedding misses many of the CE's top-100 while still often finding the top-1. Recall grows with the number of rounds and saturates around 5–10 (Figure 6).
  2. Choice of first-round items matters. tf-idf is a weak RnR baseline on YuGiOh but a strong one on HotpotQA, and on HotpotQA starting Axn from BM25/tf-idf candidates beats starting from the DE for every item embedding.
  3. MF vs. distillation. MF indexing matches or beats $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{dstl}}$ recall "in the majority of the cases" at up to about 5× less indexing time. MF training ran on a 12 GB 2080Ti (except $\textsc{MF}_{\text{Trns}}$ on HotpotQA), distillation on a 48 GB RTX8000 with a 24-hour cap. Most MF time is spent computing $G$ and the initial DE embeddings, both of which parallelize without communication.
  4. MF + Axn vs. adaCUR. HotpotQA: adaCUR-$\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ needs 1000+ GPU-hours and reaches Top-1-Recall@100 = 75.9, Top-100-Recall@500 = 44.8. $\textsc{MF}_{\text{Ind}}$ with 10K train queries × 100 items each (1M CE calls, about 30 minutes to compute $G$) takes under 3 hours total and Axn reaches 80.5 and 42.6. So: better at $k=1$, slightly worse at $k=100$, at roughly 100× less indexing time. For scale, the dense anchor matrix with 1K anchors would be about $5\times 10^9$ CE calls, about 5000× more than this sparse $G$.
  5. Transductive vs. inductive. $\textsc{MF}_{\text{Trns}}$ is on par or slightly better on SciDocs (25K items, each item gets about four observed queries even at 1K×100). On HotpotQA it gives little to no gain over $\textsc{DE}_{\textsc{src}}$ because most items have no observed entry; sampling $k_d$ queries per item fixes this at higher cost. $\textsc{MF}_{\text{Ind}}$ improves consistently and prefers the per-query sampling scheme.
  6. Comparison with TouR. Similar Top-1-Recall at small budgets, Axn slightly better at larger ones; for $k=100$, Axn with $\lambda=0$ is clearly better. Downstream nDCG@10 is mixed.
  7. Overhead. A CE call costs about 2 ms amortized (MiniLM, batch 50). The extra cost of the regression and rescoring is negligible for $\mathcal{R}=5$–10 and grows linearly in $\mathcal{R}$, and it is smaller than adaCUR's pseudo-inverse step. Rescoring is done by brute force over the 10K shortlist; an ANN index over $V$ is mentioned but not used.

What the evidence does and does not support. It supports the claim that, at a fixed small CE budget, refitting the query embedding from CE feedback finds more of the CE's neighbours than RnR with the same embeddings. It also supports the claim that a cheap sparse factorization on top of a frozen DE is a good substitute for both dense CUR indexing and full distillation. It does not show behaviour for a full search over millions of items, for CEs without the [emb] scoring head, or for any bound on the number of CE calls needed.

Broader context

Background. The paper is the third step in a line by the same authors: ANNCUR (2022) showed that CE score matrices admit useful CUR approximations, adaCUR (2023) made the anchor items adaptive at test time, and this paper removes the dense anchor matrix. Related test-time approaches are pseudo-relevance feedback (Rocchio; dense PRF such as ANCE-PRF), TouR (Sung et al. 2023), which optimizes the query vector by gradient steps on CE feedback, and graph-based adaptive re-ranking (GAR, MacAvaney et al. 2022), which expands candidates through a corpus graph instead of an embedding.

Connections that are real.

  1. Vector search and ANN theory. Each Axn round is a MIPS query with a new query vector and an exclusion set, against a fixed item index. So the method sits on top of any MIPS structure (HNSW, ScaNN) without changes to the index, and the paper's contribution is entirely in how the query vector is produced. One open question is whether successive queries $\mathbf{u}_q^{(r)}$ are close enough that a graph search can be warm-started from the previous round's results; the paper uses brute force on a shortlist instead.
  2. Low-rank structure of score matrices. The relevant property is not that $G$ is low rank, but that a rank-$d$ factorization can be made to contain each row's top-$k$ within its top-$\mathcal{B}$. That is a top-$k$ covering notion of approximate rank. It sits between ordinary rank and the sign-rank arguments behind recent limits on single-vector retrieval (e.g. Weller et al. 2025). A clean question: for a given score matrix, how does the smallest $d$ that achieves top-$k$-in-top-$\mathcal{B}$ for all rows grow with $\mathcal{B}/k$, and does query-adaptive fitting (Axn) need a smaller $d$ than a fixed query map? The paper's experiments suggest yes but give no theory.
  3. Matrix completion. $\textsc{MF}_{\text{Ind}}$ is inductive matrix completion with DE embeddings as side information (Jain and Dhillon 2013; Zhong et al. 2019), and the sampling is value-dependent (missing not at random). Theory for completion under top-$k$-biased sampling, measured by top-$k$ recall rather than Frobenius error, would directly describe this setting.
  4. Active learning and bandits (an analogy). The test-time loop is a linear bandit with a greedy policy and a budget of $\mathcal{B}_{\textsc{ce}}$ pulls, aiming at top-$k$ identification. Linear bandit theory suggests adding optimism (e.g. UCB on $\mathbf{u}_q^\top\mathbf{v}_i$ using $(V_{\mathcal{A}}^\top V_{\mathcal{A}} + \lambda I)^{-1}$) and gives sample-complexity bounds for best-arm identification, which could yield the guarantees this paper lacks.

Generative retrieval (an analogy). A generative retrieval model scores a query–docid pair by running the decoder conditioned on the query, so its score function is also not a dot product. Beam search over docids is its own way to avoid scoring all items. The anchor/factorization view gives a different option: treat the GR log-likelihood matrix like the CE matrix, factorize it sparsely, and use it to retrieve candidates or to distil GR scores into a vector index. Whether GR score matrices have the same top-$k$-friendly low-rank structure is open and testable. The reverse direction is also plausible: Axn's feedback loop could be used to choose which docids a GR model should be asked to score.

Related work worth reading alongside it. Yadav et al. 2022 (ANNCUR, EMNLP) for the [emb]-CE and the CUR baseline; Yadav et al. 2023 (adaCUR) for the adaptive-anchor version that Axn simplifies; Sung et al. 2023 (TouR) for gradient-based test-time query optimization; MacAvaney et al. 2022 (GAR) for graph-based adaptive re-ranking.

A plausible follow-up. Replace the convex $\lambda$-mixture with a Bayesian linear-regression posterior centred on the DE query embedding, and choose each round's items by an upper confidence bound instead of the posterior mean. This gives a principled form of both the regularizer and exploration, and it allows a top-$k$ identification bound in terms of $d$, $\mathcal{B}_{\textsc{ce}}$ and the misspecification $\min_{\mathbf{u}}\max_i |f(q,i) - \mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{v}_i|$. Running the loop over a real ANN index on all 5.2M items would also remove the shortlist caveat.

title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-based Link Prediction
html:
Claude deep-dive — 2026-11-17

On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-based Link Prediction — Badreddine, van Krieken, Serafini (2025) — arXiv:2506.22271

Setting and problem

Read from v3 (29 May 2026). The object of study is a link predictor with a linear output layer, which the authors call an LD-KGE (linear-decoder knowledge graph embedding). Entities $\mathcal{E}$, relations $\mathcal{R}$, a knowledge graph $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{E}$. An object query $(s,r,?)$ is encoded by an arbitrary function into $\mathbf{h}_{s,r}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, and every candidate object is scored by $$\phi(s,r,o) = \mathbf{h}_{s,r}^\top \mathbf{e}_o, \qquad \mathbf{z}_{s,r,:} = \mathbf{h}_{s,r}\mathbf{E}^\top,\quad \mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{E}|\times d}.$$ This class contains all bilinear models (RESCAL, DistMult, ComplEx with a $2d$ bottleneck, CP, SimplE, TuckER) and most neural ones (ConvE, CompGCN, transformer or LM encoders), because they end in a linear projection onto the entity table. Cosine scoring is included by normalizing both sides. Translation and rotation models (TransE, RotatE), box models and path-based models (NBFNet) are outside the scope.

Flatten subject–relation pairs into rows and write $\mathbf{Y}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{E}||\mathcal{R}|\times|\mathcal{E}|}$ for the adjacency matrix and $\mathbf{Y}^{\pm} = 2\mathbf{Y}-1$ for its sign version. The score matrix is $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^\top$, which has rank at most $d$ no matter how expressive the encoder is. That is the whole source of the limitation.

Three target tasks of increasing difficulty:

  1. Ranking reconstruction (RR): in every row, every true object scores above every false one. This is exactly "top-$k$ is the relevant set" in retrieval terms.
  2. Sign reconstruction (SR): $z_{s,r,o} > 0$ iff the triple is true, with a global threshold of $0$ and no per-row offset.
  3. Distributional reconstruction (DR): scores equal $\tau^+$ on true triples and $\tau^-$ on false ones, either with global thresholds or with row-specific $(\tau^+_i,\tau^-_i)$. With a softmax head this means a distribution uniform over the true objects (up to the mass leaked to false objects, which is never exactly zero with finite logits).

Two notions of "the model can do it": universality (one $d$ that works for every graph on $|\mathcal{E}|$ entities) and realisability (some parameters fit this particular $\mathbf{Y}$). The question is the minimal $d$ in each of the six cells. All statements are about exact fitting of the training graph, not about generalization.

Prior work and the gap. Expressivity results for KGEs (Trouillon et al. for ComplEx, Kazemi–Poole for SimplE, Balažević et al. for TuckER, Wang et al. 2018 for RESCAL/ComplEx) are model-specific sufficient conditions, typically $d \ge |\mathcal{E}|$ or $d \ge |\mathcal{E}||\mathcal{R}|$. The softmax bottleneck literature (Yang et al. 2018; Grivas et al. 2022, 2024; Finlayson et al. 2024) has the general linear-algebra facts but was not applied to link prediction. The paper fills the gap with necessary conditions valid for every LD-KGE.

Main idea

The results fit in one table (Table 1 of the paper):

  • Universality: RR needs $d \ge |\mathcal{E}|-1$ (Theorem 3.1), SR needs $d \ge |\mathcal{E}|$ (Theorem 3.3), DR needs $d \ge |\mathcal{E}|$ with global thresholds and $d\ge|\mathcal{E}|-1$ with row-specific ones (Theorem 3.5).
  • Realisability: RR needs $d \ge \operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{Y}^{\pm}) - 1$ (Theorem 3.2), SR needs $d \ge \operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{Y}^{\pm})$ (Theorem 3.4), DR needs $d \ge \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{Y}) - 1$ under both threshold notions (Theorem 3.6).

Here $\operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{M}) = \min\{\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}) : \operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{A}) = \mathbf{M}\}$. The ordering is the expected one: rankings and signs depend only on sign patterns, so sign rank governs them; uniform distributions pin down actual values, so ordinary rank governs them, and $\operatorname{srank}$ can be far below $\operatorname{rank}$.

Because sign rank is NP-hard to compute, Section 4 gives a computable sufficient dimension. Order the objects by a permutation $\pi$ and let $\kappa$ be the maximum number of sign changes along any row. The Alon–Frankl–Rödl (1985) construction gives $\operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{Y}^\pm) \le \kappa + 1$. A row with $c$ true objects has at most $2c$ sign changes under any ordering, so with $c$ the maximum $(s,r)$ out-degree, $d_{\text{SR}} = 2c+1$ suffices for exact RR and SR (Corollary 4.2). If an ordering groups each row's positives into at most $b$ contiguous blocks, $2b+1$ suffices. A Reverse Cuthill–McKee ordering on an object co-occurrence graph (built from the top 0.1% highest-degree rows) gives $b$ about $5\times$ smaller than $c$: $d_{\text{SR}}$ drops from 8,729 to 1,185 on FB15k-237, from 30,073 to 7,105 on Hetionet, from 58,657 to 6,051 on ogbl-biokg and from 36,841 to 8,471 on openbiolink. The point the authors draw is that the required dimension scales with connectivity (max degree, blockiness), not with $|\mathcal{E}|$.

The constructive half proposes KGE-MoS, a mixture-of-softmaxes output layer borrowed from Yang et al. (2018): $$P(O\mid s,r) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k(\mathbf{h}_{s,r})\,\mathrm{softmax}\big(f_k(\mathbf{h}_{s,r})\mathbf{E}^\top\big),\qquad \pi_k \propto \exp(\mathbf{h}_{s,r}^\top\boldsymbol{\omega}_k),$$ with each $f_k$ a two-layer MLP and $\mathbf{E}$ shared. The extra parameter cost is $O(Kd^2)$, against $O(d_{\text{inc}}(|\mathcal{E}|+|\mathcal{R}|))$ for growing the embedding. The log-probability matrix of a single softmax has rank at most $d+1$; the mixture is not log-linear, so that bound no longer applies. A sigmoid version handles SR.

What the experiments show. Five models (DistMult, ComplEx, RESCAL, ConvE, CompGCN), four datasets (FB15k-237, Hetionet, ogbl-biokg, openbiolink), $d\in\{200,1000\}$, $K=4$, three seeds, filtered MRR and a filtered NLL that removes training objects and renormalizes.

  • On the three larger, denser graphs the average MoS deltas are significant: NLL $-0.12$ to $-0.43$, MRR $+0.015$ to $+0.035$. Examples at $d=1000$: DistMult on ogbl-biokg $.801 \to .837$ MRR and $4.89\to4.34$ NLL; ConvE on Hetionet $.262\to.313$.
  • On FB15k-237 there is no gain (average deltas around $0$, several models get worse), and WN18RR behaves the same. The authors read this as "bottlenecks do not bind on small sparse graphs".
  • At $d=200$, MoS roughly matches baselines at $d=1000$ on the large graphs. At $d=5000$ on ogbl-biokg, $K=4$ and $K=1$ tie (both MRR $0.79$), but the batch had to be cut from 1000 to 200 and both are worse than $d=1000$.
  • Empirical rank of the test log-probability matrix on FB15k-237: $201$ and $1{,}001$ for $K=1$ at $d=200$ and $1000$; $3{,}651$ and $14{,}541$ (full) for $K=4$.
  • Cost: a training step is $1.69$ to $2.75\times$ slower on openbiolink, mostly because of the $f_k$ projections.
  • Appendix baselines: RotatE matches bottlenecked DistMult on ogbl-biokg, TransE is worse; a concatenation-MLP decoder escapes the bottleneck but is $50$–$931\times$ slower and runs out of memory at modest batch sizes. A sigmoid-MoS improves AUROC $.891\to.985$ and AP $.065\to.117$ for DistMult on ogbl-biokg, with all unseen triples treated as negatives.

Most interesting part

The theory is a clean repackaging of known facts; the interesting content is in which facts apply to which loss, plus the degree-based sufficient bound. The experiments support the claim less directly than the text suggests. A reviewer-style assessment:

Strengths.

  • The split by task (RR/SR/DR) is useful and correct: it makes explicit that softmax/cross-entropy training targets DR, whose requirement is $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{Y})-1$, while evaluation by MRR only needs RR, governed by $\operatorname{srank}-1$. This explains why a model can rank well while being badly calibrated.
  • The bounds hold for every encoder, which settles a recurring confusion in KGE papers: a stronger encoder (GNN, LM) does not lift a linear-decoder bottleneck.
  • Corollary 4.2 and the RCM refinement give an actually computable number per dataset, and it scales with max degree, not with $|\mathcal{E}|$.
  • The appendix comparison to Wang et al. (2018) is careful: using $|\operatorname{rrank}(\mathbf{A}) - \operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{A}^\pm)|\le 1$ (Neumann et al. 2016), their sufficient bound $2\sum_r \operatorname{rrank}(\mathbf{Y}_r)$ can be about $2|\mathcal{R}|$ times the necessary bound.

Weaknesses and questionable points.

  1. Novelty of the theorems. Theorem 3.1 is Cover (1967) / Good–Tideman counting of linearly inducible orderings; 3.3 is Cover (1965) dichotomy counting; 3.2, 3.4 and 3.6 are one-line rank arguments (add a rank-one threshold matrix); Theorem 4.1 is Alon–Frankl–Rödl as already applied to graphs by Chanpuriya et al. (2020). The contribution is the systematic application, not new mathematics.
  2. The necessary and sufficient sides are never put next to each other on data. The paper reports upper bounds on $\operatorname{srank}$ (1,185 to 8,471 with RCM) but no lower bound for any benchmark, so it cannot say whether $d=200$ or $d=1000$ is actually below the requirement. Computable lower bounds exist: Forster's bound $\operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{M}) \ge \sqrt{NM}/\|\mathbf{M}\|_2$ for an $N\times M$ sign matrix, and $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{Y})$ for DR is computable directly. Neither appears.
  3. Theory is about fitting the training graph; experiments only report test MRR and NLL. Training-set fit (does the baseline fail to reconstruct training triples at $d=200$ while MoS succeeds?) would be the direct test, and it is not reported.
  4. The $K=1$ ablation weakens the attribution to rank. On ogbl-biokg at $d=1000$, DistMult goes $4.89\to4.42$ NLL and $.801\to.821$ MRR with $K=1$, which is still rank-bottlenecked; $K=4$ only adds $4.42\to4.34$ and $.821\to.837$. So most of the NLL gain and about half the MRR gain comes from the asymmetric MLP projection, not from breaking the bottleneck. The authors report this honestly but the headline still credits the mixture.
  5. Dimension does not behave as a binding bottleneck would. Bottlenecked DistMult on ogbl-biokg goes from $.792$ ($d=200$) to $.801$ ($d=1000$), with NLL getting slightly worse ($4.83 \to 4.89$). If rank were the binding constraint at $d=200$, a $5\times$ larger $d$ should help more. At $d=5000$, $K=4$ and $K=1$ tie. A plausible reading is that optimization and regularization dominate in this range, which the theory does not address.
  6. Empirical rank is weak evidence. The numerical rank of the log of a mixture of softmaxes is generically full; it shows the $d+1$ constraint is gone, not that the extra directions encode anything useful. There is also an internal inconsistency: Section 5 says $K=4$, $d=200$ reaches rank $14{,}501$, while Table 7 gives $3{,}651$ at $d=200$ and $14{,}541$ at $d=1000$ (and F.4.2 states $|\mathcal{E}|=14{,}951$ against $14{,}541$ in Table 6).
  7. Exactness and conditioning. Every dimension in the paper is for exact arithmetic with unbounded norms. The Vandermonde construction behind Corollary 4.2 uses entries $t^{j}$ up to $|\mathcal{E}|^{2c}$ with roots $\varepsilon$-close to integers, so its margin relative to the embedding norms is tiny. The paper notes such solutions are hard to reach by gradient descent but does not quantify it; margin complexity, not sign rank, is the quantity that would say something about trainable low-dimensional models.
  8. Minor: ogbl-biokg MRR ranks against 500 sampled negatives, not all entities, so it is a weaker test of a full-ranking bottleneck than the other datasets. MoS also breaks the bilinear form, so subject prediction must go through inverse relations.

Proof sketch

Theorem 3.1 (RR universality). Rankings are invariant to adding $c\mathbf{1}$, so score vectors live in $\mathbb{R}^{N}/\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{1})$ with $N=|\mathcal{E}|$. The number of orderings of $N$ generic points induced by linear functionals in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a Stirling-number expression (Cover 1967; Good–Tideman 1977) that equals $N!$ only when $d\ge N-1$.

Theorem 3.2 (RR realisability). Let $\mathbf{Z}^\star = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^\top$ realize all rankings. For each row $i$ pick a threshold $\tau_i$ between the lowest true and the highest false score. Then $$\operatorname{sign}\big(\mathbf{Z}^\star - \boldsymbol{\tau}\mathbf{1}^\top\big) = \mathbf{Y}^\pm,\qquad \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{Z}^\star - \boldsymbol{\tau}\mathbf{1}^\top) \le d+1,$$ so $\operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{Y}^\pm) \le d+1$. Theorem 3.4 is the same without the threshold matrix, which is why it loses the $-1$.

Theorem 3.3 (SR universality). Cover's function-counting theorem: the decision rule $\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{E}\mathbf{h})$ realizes at most $2\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\binom{N-1}{i}$ of the $2^N$ labelings, which is $<2^N$ iff $d<N$.

Theorem 3.5 (DR universality). The targets are $\mathbf{z}_S = (\tau^+-\tau^-)\mathbf{1}_S + \tau^-\mathbf{1}$ for every $S\subseteq[N]$. Their span equals $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}_S\} = \mathbb{R}^N$ (singletons are the standard basis, and $\mathbf{1} \propto \mathbf{z}_{[N]}$), so $d\ge N$. With row-specific thresholds only the class modulo $\mathbf{1}$ matters, giving $N-1$.

Theorem 3.6 (DR realisability). With global thresholds, $\mathbf{Y} = (\mathbf{Z}^\star - \tau^-\mathbf{J})/(\tau^+-\tau^-)$, so $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{Y}) \le d+1$. With row-specific thresholds, $\mathbf{Z}^\star - \mathbf{t}^-\mathbf{1}^\top = \operatorname{diag}(\tau^+_i - \tau^-_i)\,\mathbf{Y}$; the diagonal factor is invertible, so again $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{Y})\le d+1$.

Theorem 4.1 (sufficient dimension, Alon–Frankl–Rödl). Fix an ordering of objects as positions $t=1,\dots,N$ and use the moment-curve (Vandermonde) object embeddings $$\mathbf{e}_t = (1, t, t^2, \dots, t^\kappa) \in \mathbb{R}^{\kappa+1}.$$ For row $i$ with $\kappa_i\le\kappa$ sign changes, choose a polynomial $p_i$ of degree $\kappa_i$ with one root in each gap between adjacent positions of opposite sign (for an isolated positive at $t_0$, roots at $t_0\pm\varepsilon$), with the overall sign fixed to match. Its coefficient vector, padded with zeros, is $\mathbf{h}_i$, and $\mathbf{h}_i^\top\mathbf{e}_t = p_i(t)$ has the required sign everywhere. Hence $\operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{Y}^\pm)\le\kappa+1$. Each isolated positive costs two sign changes, giving $\kappa\le 2c$; each contiguous block costs at most two, giving $\kappa \le 2b$.

The trick in one line: lower bounds come from the rank-one slack that a per-row threshold or a log-partition adds to a rank-$d$ matrix; upper bounds come from the fact that a polynomial of degree $\kappa$ can carve any sign pattern with $\kappa$ changes on the integer line.

MoS escapes the $d+1$ bound because $\log\sum_k \pi_k\,\mathrm{softmax}(\cdot)$ is not affine in the logits; no theorem in the paper says how much rank, or which sign or ranking patterns, $K$ components buy.

Broader context

Background. The paper sits in the softmax-bottleneck line: Yang et al. (2018) for language models and mixture of softmaxes, Ganea et al. (2019) and Kanai et al. (2018) for pointwise non-linearities, Grivas et al. (2022) on unargmaxable tokens ("possible in theory, rare in practice"), Grivas et al. (2024) on the sigmoid bottleneck for multi-label classification, and Finlayson et al. (2024) on the geometry of the low-rank softmax image. Its specific contribution is to transport these to link prediction, where $|\mathcal{E}|$ (up to $10^9$) is much larger than an LM vocabulary.

Relation to single-vector retrieval. This connection is direct, not an analogy.

  1. Weller et al. (2025), "On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval" (arXiv:2508.21038, cited here as ICLR 2026), prove that representing a qrel matrix $\mathbf{A}$ by single-vector dot products, with the relevant set as the top-$k$ of each query, needs $\operatorname{srank}(2\mathbf{A}-1) - 1 \le d \le \operatorname{srank}(2\mathbf{A}-1)$. Theorem 3.2 here is the same lower bound with $(s,r)$ as query and objects as documents; the two papers reach it independently with the same row-threshold argument. A dual encoder $\langle q(x), d(y)\rangle$ is an LD-KGE with $\mathbf{h}_{s,r}$ replaced by the query tower and $\mathbf{E}$ by the document matrix, so all of Table 1 transfers verbatim.
  2. What this paper adds for retrieval is Corollary 4.2. If every query has at most $k$ relevant documents, then $d = 2k+1$ suffices for exact top-$k$ retrieval, whatever the corpus size $n$. If the relevant sets form at most $b$ contiguous blocks in some document ordering, $2b+1$ suffices. Applied to Weller et al.'s LIMIT-style "all $k$-subsets" qrels, this gives sign rank at most $2k+1$ independent of $n$ (this is my inference, it is not stated in either paper; it is also the classical fact that cyclic polytopes are neighborly). So the critical-$n$ curves from Weller et al.'s free-embedding optimization, where the largest representable $n$ grows polynomially in $d$ for $k=2$, are not a sign-rank phenomenon in exact arithmetic. They must come from margin, numerical precision, or optimization. The Vandermonde construction has entries up to $n^{2k}$ and margins that vanish polynomially in $n$, which fits that reading.
  3. The DR result is the retrieval statement that a dual encoder trained with in-batch softmax to put uniform mass on all relevant documents needs $d\ge\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})-1$. For multi-relevance datasets this is far more demanding than getting the ranking right, which is one formal reason calibrated dense-retrieval scores are harder than good nDCG.

Relation to generative retrieval and LM theory.

  • Generative retrieval with atomic docids ends in $\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{h}\mathbf{E}^\top)$ over the corpus, so it is literally an LD-KGE with documents as objects, and every bound here applies to it. Semantic-ID decoding produces the docid token by token, and each step is a separate softmax over a small vocabulary conditioned on the prefix. The overall distribution is then not log-linear in a single $d$-dimensional state. Whether that escapes the bottleneck in a useful way is an analogy, not something this paper analyzes.
  • MoS has a retrieval cousin in mixture-of-logits (MoL) similarity, $\sum_k \pi_k(q,d)\langle f_k(q), g_k(d)\rangle$ (Zhai et al. 2023; Ding and Zhai 2024). The difference is where the mixture sits: MoL mixes logits, MoS mixes normalized distributions. One practical consequence the paper does not discuss: MoS top-$k$ does not reduce to a single MIPS query. It needs $K$ softmaxes over the full table, or $K$ MIPS queries followed by candidate merging, which is only approximate. That matters if KGE-MoS is used for retrieval over $10^8$ entities rather than for training.

Open questions.

  1. Margin-aware bounds. Replace sign rank by margin complexity or by the dimension needed for a $\gamma$-margin realization with bounded norms (Ben-David, Eiron and Simon 2002; Forster's spectral bound). For the all-$k$-subsets qrel, how does the required $d$ at margin $\gamma$ scale with $n$? This would explain Weller et al.'s empirical curves and the gap between $d_{\text{SR}}$ and what training reaches.
  2. Lower bounds on real benchmarks. Compute Forster-type lower bounds on $\operatorname{srank}(\mathbf{Y}^\pm)$ and the exact $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{Y})$ for FB15k-237 and ogbl-biokg (and for BEIR qrels) to place $d=200$ and $d=1000$ relative to the true requirement.
  3. Expressivity of $K$ components. How many sign patterns or rankings can a $K$-component MoS with dimension $d$ realize? Is there a counting bound analogous to Cover's, and does $K$ act like a multiplicative or an additive increase in effective dimension?
  4. Training fit versus test performance. Does the baseline at $d=200$ actually fail to fit the training graph on ogbl-biokg, and does MoS fix that? If not, the gains are better explained by the asymmetric projection and regularization than by rank.

title: Transformers in the Dark: Navigating Unknown Search Spaces via Bandit Feedback
html:
Claude deep-dive — 2026-11-17

Transformers in the Dark: Navigating Unknown Search Spaces via Bandit Feedback — Kim et al. (2026) — arXiv:2603.24780

Setting and problem

The paper asks whether a Transformer, or an LLM, can itself act as the selection rule of a tree search algorithm. To make the question testable it removes the other two parts of LLM-guided search, generating candidate steps (expansion) and scoring them (evaluation), and gives both to the environment. The authors call the result unknown tree search with bandit feedback.

An instance is a finite rooted tree $\mathcal{T} = (\mathcal{S}, N)$ of maximum depth $D$, where $N : \mathcal{S} \to 2^{\mathcal{S}}$ is the successor map. There is a bounded reward $r : \mathcal{S} \to [0,1]$. Goal states $\mathcal{S}_{\text{goal}} = \{s : r(s) > 0\}$ are leaves and are sparse, $|\mathcal{S}_{\text{goal}}| \ll |\mathcal{S}|$. The agent never sees the tree. The value of a state is the expected leaf reward under a uniform random rollout, $$V(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{unif}}}\big[r(s_{\text{leaf}}) \mid s_{\text{start}} = s\big],$$ and the agent only observes a noisy realization $v_t \sim \widehat V(s_t)$, for example a Monte Carlo average over $k$ rollouts or an LLM-produced score in $[0,1]$. The interaction runs for $T \ll |\mathcal{S}|$ steps. At step $t$ the environment reveals $N(s_t)$ and $v_t$. The agent then picks $s_{t+1}$ from the frontier $$F_t = \Big(\bigcup_{i=0}^{t} N(s_i)\Big) \setminus \{s_0,\dots,s_t\},$$ using a policy $\pi(\cdot \mid s_0, v_0, N(s_0), \dots, s_t, v_t, N(s_t))$. A trajectory is judged by $\max_{s_i \in \tau} r(s_i)$ and by related functions of the set of collected rewards $\mathcal{R}$.

There are two synthetic environments.

  • Multi-reward tree search. A random tree with branching $B$, depth $D$ and $K$ goal leaves. The main setting is $B=2$, $D=6$ (126 non-root states, 64 leaves), $K=8$ goals with rewards $\{0.1,\dots,0.7,1.0\}$, and budget $T=50$.
  • Multi-reward navigation. A $w\times h$ grid with walls (density $0.4$ on $4\times 4$ in the main runs) and goals with strictly ordered rewards. States are paths from the start of length at most $T$ that end at a goal or contain none, so the search space is again a tree.

The reference policies are the teachers for behavior cloning and the objects of the expressivity theorems:

  1. Uniform leaf sampling: $s_t \sim \mathcal{U}(F_{t-1})$. The paper calls it a randomized DFS.
  2. Greedy leaf sampling: pick the frontier parent with the highest observed $v$, then a uniform child of it. This is best-first search with the parent's noisy value as the priority.
  3. Uniform path sampling: walk down from the root, choosing a uniform child at each level among subtrees that still have unvisited states, until a frontier state is reached. The paper calls it a randomized BFS.
  4. Policy-guided path sampling: the same root-to-frontier walk, but with a tree policy at each node. The options are pure exploration (fewest visits), greedy (largest summed child value) or UCT, $\arg\max_{s'} \text{value}(s')/\text{count}(s') + c\sqrt{\log(2\,\text{count}(s))/\text{count}(s')}$ with $c = 0.1$. Fully explored subtrees are excluded (the modified successor map $N^*$). This is MCTS without a separate rollout phase, since the environment supplies $v$.

Modelling choices that matter:

  1. The tree is revealed only through the trace, so all search state lives in the context.
  2. Rewards sit only at leaves, and $\widehat V$ is a noisy mean under uniform rollout, not a max. Greedy and UCT policies therefore chase subtrees with dense rewards, not the single best leaf.
  3. Success is a simple-regret style objective (did you ever hit the global best within $T$). There is no cumulative regret and no comparison to an optimal policy.

Main idea

The paper makes three claims, each labelled as a "Finding".

  1. Expressivity (Theorems 1 and 2). Theorem 1: a 3-layer Transformer with embedding dimension $d = 10 + TB$ exactly implements uniform and greedy leaf sampling on a leaf-based tokenization of the trace. Theorem 2: a 12-layer Transformer with $d = 26 + 7TB$ exactly implements uniform path sampling and greedy, pure-exploration and UCT path sampling, on a tree-based tokenization where the model first writes out the tree-policy path $S_{s_0} \texttt{>} \dots \texttt{>} S_{s_t}$ and then a terminator.
  2. Learnability in practice, for small instances. Llama-style Transformers trained from scratch (8 layers, 8 heads, width 512) on 14k teacher traces match the teachers' metric profiles on held-out instances. They extrapolate somewhat to longer budgets, more or fewer goals, other wall densities and deeper trees, with the gap growing with distance from the training setting.
  3. LLMs. Off-the-shelf LLMs prompted as the selection rule do poorly on the depth-6 binary task. Qwen3-8B is about as good as uniform leaf sampling, and Qwen3-8B with thinking enabled is worse. LoRA fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on search trajectories for an "Academic Paper Search" task (OpenAlex; the children of a paper are its co-authors' papers) raises the hit rate from $0.262$ to $0.500$. The same base model with external UCT selection gets $0.286$.

The theory is a RASP-style existence proof. The registers hold one-hot state ids. Hard attention does lookups ("which separator preceded me", "what was my parent's value") and sums (visit counts, value totals). A token-wise feed-forward map of arbitrary form computes the selection score, which is the max parent value or the UCT formula. The final argmax over logits, with greedy decoding and uniform random tie-breaking, does the selection.

Most interesting part

The interesting idea is the framing, more than any one result. Separating selection from expansion and evaluation gives a clean testbed for asking whether an LM does structured search under uncertainty, and the multi-turn interface ("agent names a node, environment returns value and children") is the same loop as an agentic retrieval or browsing system. The results themselves are modest, and several claims are stronger than the evidence. A reviewer-style assessment follows.

Strengths.

  • The setting is controlled and tunable ($B$, $D$, $K$, wall density, $T$). Separating selection from evaluation lets one ask whether an LLM's search failures come from bad scoring or from bad selection. That question rarely gets a clean answer in Tree-of-Thoughts-style work.
  • The evaluation goes past matching metrics. It measures per-step KL between teacher and student next-state distributions on teacher-forced traces, and this exposes a real gap (below).
  • The negative LLM result (Figure 1c) is informative. The models were told the protocol and the meaning of the feedback score, and they still do no better than uniform random frontier sampling. With thinking turned on, Qwen3-8B does worse.

Weaknesses and questionable points.

  1. The theorems are weak as expressivity results. They assume hard attention, no LayerNorm, a feed-forward block that may be any piecewise-continuous function (including $\sqrt{\log(\cdot)}$, division and an output of $+\infty$), unbounded positional registers $t\,e_{\text{pos}}$, and one register per possible state. With $d = \Theta(TB)$ one-hot ids, the network is a lookup table over a vocabulary of at most $TB+1$ states. The UCT arithmetic is pushed entirely into $f$. Given these allowances, constant depth is unsurprising, because each policy is a fixed composition of a few "find previous X / sum over Y" operations. The paper sets this against universal approximation (Yun et al. 2020), which needs non-constant depth, but that comparison is not the relevant one. The relevant one is RASP/Tracr-style compilability, and here the result is expected. No lower bound is given (e.g., whether $d = o(TB)$ suffices with $\log$-precision ids), and nothing is said about softmax at finite temperature.
  2. The randomness comes from the decoder. "Exactly implement uniform sampling" means all valid frontier logits tie and the decoding rule breaks ties uniformly at random. The network does not output a calibrated distribution. This is fine for an existence claim, but "outputs a distribution that exactly matches" in Section 4 overstates it.
  3. The constructions have gaps as written. In Theorem 1, frontier states get logit equal to the parent value $\alpha \in [0,1]$, and visited or never-seen states get $\le 0$. A frontier state whose parent had $v = 0$ therefore ties with invalid tokens, which is common since most states have value 0, and with a visited state whose parent value was $1$ (score $1 - 1 = 0$). Random tie-breaking could then pick an invalid state. A constant offset fixes this, but it is not in the proof. In Theorem 2 the final UCT feed-forward uses $\texttt{vid}_i$, the summed value, where Algorithm 6 uses value/count, and it uses $N$ rather than the $N^*$ used in experiments (this one is acknowledged). There are also register-name slips (wasVisited/wasSelected, $f^{(5)}$ used twice). None of this seems fatal, but "exact" claims need exact proofs.
  4. The trained models do not learn the path policies. For leaf policies, the per-step KL to the teacher is low. For all path policies it is much higher, although the aggregate metrics match. The authors give two explanations. First, the training traces omit the tree-policy path, while the theory requires the model to emit it, so the model must collapse a multi-step traversal into one prediction. Second, the policies are stochastic, and orderings that differ have little effect on the outcome. Both are plausible, but they mean Finding 2 ("approximating diverse search algorithms") holds at the level of outcome statistics, not decisions. It would have been easy to train on the tree-based tokenization that the theorem uses, to test whether chain-of-thought-style path emission closes the KL gap. That is the obvious missing experiment.
  5. The from-scratch task is easier than the theory's task. In the training trace format, the whole frontier $F_{t-1}$ is re-listed at every step with indices, and the model outputs an index. The model never has to maintain the frontier itself, which is the step that Layer 1–2 of the construction does. The traces also grow quadratically in $T$. This is a reasonable engineering choice, but the empirical half and the theoretical half test different things.
  6. The fine-tuning experiment does not isolate selection. In the "LLM-only" and fine-tuned conditions, the LLM does expansion, selection and evaluation. In "LLM + UCT" only the selection is external. Fine-tuning also changes the model's evaluation scores, and FT + UCT ($0.548$) beats base + UCT ($0.286$) by about as much as FT beats base ($0.500$ vs $0.262$). So most of the gain looks like better evaluation or better scoring of paths, not better selection. That is the opposite of what the paper's framing is about. Finding 3 ("better than an LLM with an external algorithm") compares FT-selection-plus-FT-evaluation against UCT-plus-base-evaluation, which is confounded. Other issues: the teacher trajectories come partly from Gemini-2.5-Flash; I found no description of the size of the training set or of how train and test pairs were split; there are 60 start–target pairs, so the standard errors are about $\pm 0.07$; the three reward metrics coincide because reward is binary. The abstract's "unlocks the complete capabilities" is not supported, and the conclusion itself says fine-tuned models remain below exact search and that an external search tool may be more practical.
  7. The scale is small. Trees have about $10^2$ states, the budget is $50$ steps and grids are $4\times 4$. The generalization plots degrade outside a local range, especially in depth, which the authors liken to length generalization. Nothing shows that the learned policies beat their teachers or adapt to a reward structure, so the interesting question for search ("can it learn a better policy than UCT for this distribution of trees?") is not asked.

Proof sketch

Model (Appendix D.1). A block is $\mathrm{Attn}(X) = X + VX\,\mathrm{hardmax}(X^\top K^\top Q X)$, followed by a residual token-wise map $f$. Here $\mathrm{hardmax}$ averages uniformly over the argmax positions, and attention is causal over the prefix. The positional embedding writes $t$ into a $\texttt{pos}$ register. The output is $U X^{(\ell)}_{:,n}$ followed by greedy decoding with uniform random tie-breaking. $M_{a\to b} = e_b e_a^\top$ copies register $a$ into register $b$.

Theorem 1 (greedy leaf sampling, 3 layers). The trace is $\texttt{?}\,S_{s_0}\,\texttt{\%}\,V_{v_0}\,\texttt{\#}\,S_{s_{0,1}}\,S_{s_{0,2}}\dots\texttt{?}\,S_{s_1}\dots$, and the model must emit the next state after each $\texttt{?}$.

  1. Layer 1 marks visited states. The query is the constant bias, and the key is 1 on separator tokens. The value copies $+1$ for $\texttt{\#}$ and $-1$ for $\texttt{?}$. With uniform averaging over all previous separators, a state token right after a $\texttt{?}$ has seen one more $\texttt{?}$ than $\texttt{\#}$, so $\texttt{isVisited} < 0$. A child listed after $\texttt{\#}$ gets $0$. The feed-forward writes $\texttt{isValue}\cdot\texttt{pos}$ into value tokens.
  2. Layer 2 lets each state inherit its parent's value. The key is $\texttt{isValue}\cdot\texttt{pos}$, so hard attention picks the most recent value token, which belongs to the parent whose child list this token is in. Its $\alpha$ is copied into $\texttt{inhValue}$. The feed-forward writes $\texttt{inhValue}$ into the token's own $\texttt{id}_i$ coordinate if the token is unvisited, and $-1$ otherwise.
  3. Layer 3 selects. The last $\texttt{?}$ attends uniformly to all state tokens and sums their $\texttt{id}_i$ registers. A state that was listed as a child and later visited gets $\alpha - 1 \le 0$. The unembedding is the identity from $\texttt{id}_i$ to the logit of $S_i$, so argmax decoding returns the frontier state with the largest inherited value. The uniform $1/n$ attention scaling does not change the argmax.
  4. Uniform leaf sampling: give every $V_\alpha$ the same embedding. All frontier states then tie, and the tie-break is uniform.

Theorem 2 (path policies, 12 layers). It uses the same register technique on the tree tokenization $\texttt{[BOS]}\,\texttt{?}\,\pi^{(0)}_{\text{tree}}\,\texttt{\%}\,V_{v_0}\,\texttt{\#}\dots$, where $\pi^{(t)}_{\text{tree}} = S_{s_0}\,\texttt{>}\,\cdots\,\texttt{>}\,S_{s_t}$.

  1. Layer 1 computes the iteration counter (attending to $\texttt{[BOS]}$ and $\texttt{\#}$, then inverting the average) and position-weighted indicator registers.
  2. Layer 2 gives each state the position of its closest preceding $\texttt{?}$, which identifies its iteration.
  3. Layers 3–4 do the MCTS backup. Each iteration's value token collects the one-hot ids of the states on that iteration's path into value and count registers ($\texttt{vid}_i$, $\texttt{cid}_i$). A final value token then sums them over all iterations, with the averaging undone by multiplying by $\texttt{iter}$.
  4. Layers 5–7 separate selected tokens from child-list tokens and give each child token its parent's id ($\texttt{pid}_i$) by attending to the most recent selected token.
  5. Layers 8–9: at a $\texttt{>}$ token, copy the id of the state just chosen ($\texttt{psid}$). Then use $\texttt{psid}$ as the query against $\texttt{pid}$ keys to collect that state's children ($\texttt{nsid}$). This is a content-addressed join.
  6. Layer 10: attend to the aggregate statistics and compute each child's UCT score in $f$. Unvisited children get $+\infty$. Greedy and uniform variants replace the score with $\texttt{vid}_i$ or the constant $1$.
  7. Layers 11–12 emit $S_0$ after $\texttt{?}$, and after a state token emit $\texttt{>}$ if that state was visited before or $\texttt{\%}$ if it is new.

The trick in one line: every search policy here is a function of per-state aggregates of the trace (parent value, visit count, value sum, children set). With one-hot state registers, each aggregate is a single hard-attention sum or lookup, and the selection rule is a token-wise function followed by argmax.

Trace lengths are $O(TB)$ tokens for the leaf tokenization and up to $O(T(B + D))$, quadratic in $T$ in the worst case, for the tree tokenization, since each step re-emits a root-to-frontier path.

Broader context

Background. The paper is part of the line asking whether Transformers can internalize search: Searchformer and A* traces (Lehnert et al. 2024), maze navigation (Nolte et al. 2024), algorithm distillation for in-context RL (Laskin et al. 2023) and Decision Transformer (Chen et al. 2021). It differs from the A* line in that the environment is hidden and the feedback is noisy, and from the algorithm-distillation line in that the "bandit" is a tree with a growing arm set. The theory follows RASP (Weiss et al. 2021) and hard-attention analyses (Hahn 2020; Pérez et al. 2019). Classical background: UCT (Kocsis and Szepesvári 2006) and bandit tree search (Bubeck et al. 2011; Coquelin and Munos 2007 for the failure modes of UCT on deep trees).

Related work worth reading alongside it. These are, as far as I can tell, not cited:

  • Lin, Bai and Mei (ICLR 2024), Transformers as Decision Makers. Constructions of Transformers that approximately implement LinUCB and Thompson sampling with softmax attention, and regret bounds for supervised pretraining on teacher trajectories. It is the provable counterpart of Sections 4–5 here, including learnability, which this paper lists as future work.
  • Lee et al. (NeurIPS 2023), Decision-Pretrained Transformer, on in-context bandit and RL behavior obtained from supervised pretraining.
  • Gandhi et al. (2024), Stream of Search, which trains LMs on serialized search traces, including failed branches, and is closer to the trace format used here.

A plausible follow-up. Use the tree-based tokenization for training, so the model emits the traversal path, and test whether the per-step KL gap for path policies disappears. That would test whether the expressivity construction is also the learned mechanism. A second follow-up: in the paper-search task, cross the two factors (base vs FT evaluator) × (base vs FT vs UCT selector), so selection and evaluation gains can be separated. A third, more theoretical one: lower bounds on width or precision for implementing UCT with softmax attention and $O(\log(TB))$-bit ids.

Connections to IR. These are analogies unless stated otherwise.

  1. Graph-based ANN search. Greedy leaf sampling is exactly best-first search with a priority queue, which is what HNSW and DiskANN beam search do on a proximity graph. The differences are that ANN search has exact feedback (the distance to the query) and a candidate list of bounded size. The paper's construction shows that a fixed-depth Transformer can keep this priority queue implicitly in its context and pop from it. This is relevant to "LLM as navigator" designs for graph or index traversal. The open question for vector search is the noisy-feedback regime, where the score of a node is an estimate (quantized distances, a learned reranker) and UCT-style exploration could outperform greedy beam search.
  2. Generative retrieval. Decoding a docid in a prefix tree is tree search, and constrained beam search is a fixed-width selection rule over a known tree. This paper's setting is the case where the tree is revealed incrementally and the per-node value is noisy, which is close to generative retrieval over a large, partly unseen docid trie with a learned prefix scorer. It suggests a concrete question: does MCTS-style selection over docid prefixes, with the model's prefix probabilities as $\widehat V$, recover relevant documents that beam search prunes early? The paper does not address this. It only supplies the selection-versus-evaluation decomposition with which to pose the question.
  3. Agentic and deep-research retrieval. The Academic Paper Search task (OpenAlex, co-author expansion, LLM-scored path relevance) is a focused-crawling or citation-chasing problem, which is literature search over a graph. The finding that the evaluator matters more than the selector (my reading of Table 1, not the authors') would be relevant there. The DCG-of-first-hit metric is borrowed directly from IR evaluation.
  4. LM theory. The constructions show that, under the hard-attention and arbitrary feed-forward idealization, bandit-style tree policies are in the same "few lookups plus aggregation" class as many RASP programs. The real questions are softmax precision, the size of $d$ relative to the number of states, and learnability from outcome-only traces. The paper leaves all three open, and they are where a theory contribution could be made.

title: Exact Fusion of Softmax Attention Heads Can Require Exponentially Many Atoms
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-17

Exact Fusion of Softmax Attention Heads Can Require Exponentially Many Atoms — Usami, Hara, Tsuboi, Matsuda (2026) — arXiv:2611.02943

Setting and problem

The object of study is a flat single-head softmax readout with $M$ atoms: $$B(q) \;=\; \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{M} m_i\, e^{\langle q, k_i\rangle}\, v_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{M} m_i\, e^{\langle q, k_i\rangle}}, \qquad q \in \mathbb{R}^d,$$ with fixed keys $k_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, scalar values $v_i \in \mathbb{R}$ and positive masses $0 < m_i < \infty$. A mass is the same as a logit bias, since $m_i = e^{b_i}$. An atom is one key–value–mass triple. Atoms with the same key can be merged, so one can assume the keys are distinct. A fixed linear output projection can be folded into the values, and a query projection $Pq$ can be folded into the keys, since $\langle Pq, k\rangle = \langle q, P^\top k\rangle$. Probabilistically, $B(q) = \mathbb{E}_{p_q}[v]$, where $p_q(i) \propto m_i e^{\langle q, k_i\rangle}$ is a finite exponential family on $M$ support points with sufficient statistic $k_i$.

A multi-head model is a sum $\sum_{h=1}^H A_h(q)$. Each head $A_h$ has its own projection $P_h$, its own $n_h$ atoms and its own normalizer. Proposition 1 is the standard product expansion. Multiplying out the denominators turns the sum of heads into one flat readout with at most $\prod_h n_h$ atoms, one for each tuple $I = (i_1,\dots,i_H)$. The tuple atom has key $k_I = \sum_h P_h^\top k_{h i_h}$, mass $m_I = \prod_h m_{h i_h}$ and value $v_I = \sum_h v_{h i_h}$. The fused keys therefore form a Minkowski sum of the per-head key sets. This is the same additive structure that additive or product quantization uses.

The target is $$W_d(q) = \sum_{j=1}^d \sigma(q_j), \qquad \sigma(t) = (1+e^{-t})^{-1}.$$ It is a sum of $d$ two-atom heads. Each head has scalar keys $\{0,1\}$, values $\{0,1\}$ and reads the coordinate $q_j$. The fused form has the cube keys $a \in \{0,1\}^d$, unit masses and values $|a| = \sum_j a_j$. In probabilistic terms, $W_d(q)$ is the expected number of successes among $d$ independent Bernoulli($\sigma(q_j)$) variables.

The question: what is the minimum $M$ such that some choice of keys, values and masses (all fixed, not depending on the query) gives $B \equiv W_d$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$? The paper also asks for the minimum when only $\sup_q |B - W_d| \le \varepsilon$ is required, how many atoms an $H$-head sum needs in total, and what changes when queries are bounded.

Prior work and the gap. KV-compression theory (Haverbeck et al., the risk of KV cache compression) treats replacement atoms under a query distribution, which is an average-case approximation question. Streaming lower bounds (Haris–Onak) count memory bits. Head-count and rank separations (Hsu–Xu, Amsel et al., Yu et al.) look at other resources. MoE identifiability (Jiang–Tanner) is about equality of whole conditional distributions, not the minimum size of a scalar mean. None of these gives a minimum-realization count for a single head that is allowed to re-optimize everything.

Modelling choices that carry the result:

  1. The query ranges over all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the lower bound is driven by limits along rays $q = tu$ as $t \to \infty$. In other words, it is a statement about the zero-temperature or tropical limit of attention.
  2. Approximation is measured by a uniform sup-norm over the unbounded domain, and the tolerance $1/2$ is half the integer jump of the limiting target.
  3. Exactness on any open set reduces to exactness everywhere, because exponential sums are real-analytic.
  4. Keys and values do not depend on the query, and there is no positional or rotary query-dependence.

Main idea

The headline result is that fusion is exponentially expensive in the worst case, even when every replacement parameter is re-optimized. The minimum single-head realization of $W_d$ has exactly $2^d$ atoms, while the factored form uses $2d$ head–atom terms. So the product expansion of Proposition 1 cannot be compressed for this target. The same lower bound holds for any fixed uniform error $\varepsilon < 1/2$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the threshold $1/2$ is sharp. For $H$ heads, $\prod_h n_h \ge 2^d$, which gives $S = \sum_h n_h \ge H\,2^{d/H}$. This is attained when $H \mid d$ by splitting the coordinates into blocks.

The mechanism is asymptotic geometry. Along a generic ray, a single head converges to the value of whichever key wins the dot product. So the limit of $B$ is constant on each open normal cone of the key polytope. The limit of $W_d$ along $tu$ is $r(u) = \#\{j : u_j > 0\}$. This takes only $d+1$ values, but it jumps across every coordinate hyperplane. Normal cones are convex, and a convex cone that crosses a hyperplane picks up two values of $r$ that differ by $1$. So each normal cone has to fit inside a single orthant. Since there are $2^d$ orthants, the key polytope needs $2^d$ vertices.

The authors balance the negative result in two ways:

  • On bounded query balls, a normalized variant $F_{d,1/\sqrt d}$ becomes nearly constant, with one-atom error at most $R/(4d)$, while its exact minimum stays at $2^d$. So the exponential cost belongs to exactness, not to practical approximation.
  • Key rank and key spectrum alone do not determine the atom count. The same cube keys with values $a_1$ need $2$ atoms, while with values $|a|/d$ they need $2^d$.

The empirical half (CODI GPT-2, layer 0, BoolQ prefixes) does two things. It applies the Eckart–Young affine-rank floor, and it uses interval arithmetic to certify that one native two-head instance has augmented output rank at least $17$. That rules out any exact 16-atom single head with the same KV payload on those queries. The learned equal-byte comparisons give mixed results that depend on the budget.

Most interesting part

I give a reviewer-style assessment here, because the clever step is short and the important questions are about scope.

Strengths.

  • The problem is clean, and the lower bound is fully adversarial in the replacement parameters: arbitrary keys, real values, positive masses and arbitrary query projections. Sharpness is shown in three directions: the atom count ($2^d$ is attained), the tolerance (Proposition 4 gives $2^{d-1}$ atoms at error exactly $1/2$) and the head budget (attained when $H \mid d$).
  • The remark that a pointwise error strictly below $1/2$ is not enough, and that a single uniform tolerance below $1/2$ is needed, is a careful touch.
  • Proposition 7 is an honest counterweight. On realistic bounded inputs the separation does not tell you anything about approximation.
  • The interval-arithmetic certificate (80-digit enclosure, then a separate rational-preconditioner check of diagonal dominance) is unusually rigorous for an empirical claim.

Weaknesses and questionable points.

  1. Scale dependence of the threshold. With values normalized to $[0,1]$ (target $W_d/d$), the threshold becomes $1/(2d)$, as the paper itself states. So in relative terms the bound only applies at a tolerance that shrinks like $1/d$. A fixed relative accuracy such as 5% falls outside the theorem once $d > 10$. The interesting open question is how the atom count behaves at a constant relative tolerance $\varepsilon d$, and the paper does not address it. The ray-limit argument would then need cones on which $r$ varies by at most about $2\varepsilon d$. Such sets of directions are not convex in an obvious way, so the answer is not clear.
