The answer is yes, it flips, and the recommendation is cleanly regime-dependent. For $k\ll n$, Stage 1 dominates, so buy recall by increasing $b$ (equivalently $b\cdot k_b/k$) at $k_b=1$. For $k\propto n$, the exact Stage 2 over $b\cdot k_b$ candidates is expensive enough to dominate, so hold $b\cdot k_b=k$ — eliminating Stage 2 entirely — and buy recall by raising $k_b$ to 2 or 4. The cost models predict this and three empirical settings confirm it: SparQ Attention on Llama 3 8B ($k=n/8$) gets $>4\times$ faster top-$k$ at $k_b=2$, $b\cdot k_b=k$, with essentially no loss on a distractor-augmented SQuAD and a text-repetition task; Llama 3 vocabulary sampling ($n=128{,}256$, $k=256$) and PharMeBINet link prediction with DistMult ($n=2.65\times10^6$, $k=100$) get 2–4$\times$ at low recall error, with $k_b=1$ fastest and $k_b=2$ Pareto-optimal at lower error. End-to-end, swapping exact for approximate top-$k$ inside SparQ on Llama 2 7B at 40k prompt length moves the speed-up over dense attention from $1.9\times$ to $2.1\times$. Two supporting contributions matter as much as the headline: a closed-form expected-recall model (below) that corrects TPU-KNN's pessimistic one, and the finding that contiguous bucketing is actively broken on real data — interleaved (or a random permutation) is required, because real sequences are strongly autocorrelated and contiguous buckets then concentrate the top-$k$. A CUDA/PyTorch library is released.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever observation is the Stage-2 cliff: $b\cdot k_b=k$ is not just "cheapest", it is a qualitative boundary where all inter-thread cooperation disappears, and $k_b$ is the only remaining way to improve quality. That reframes the design space from "how much do I over-collect" to "do I pay for a merge at all". The cost models even underestimate the Stage-2 penalty, i.e. the real cliff is steeper than modelled.

But this is a workshop evaluation paper and the claims should be read narrowly.

  • The end-to-end payoff is small. A $>4\times$ faster top-$k$ buys $\sim$10% ($1.9\times\to2.1\times$) at 40k tokens, batch 1 — honest Amdahl, but it undercuts the framing. And they admit two limitations: no end-to-end benchmark outside SparQ, and no study of batch size $m$, which is exactly the variable that determines whether $n$-parallelism was needed in the first place. Everything therefore rests on the $m$-small decode regime.
  • Their own kernel loses where it matters for KNN. For $k\ll n$ with large $n$, RAFT's exact implementation is faster, and torch.argmax (bucketed with $b=k$, $k_b=1$) is treated as an upper bound they do not reach. So the practical claim contracts to $k\propto n$, i.e. sparsity, not similarity search.
  • Quality is evaluated inconsistently across tasks. SparQ gets real downstream metrics; vocabulary sampling and KG link prediction get _recall against exact top-$k$ only_. For link prediction the metrics that matter are Hits@$k$/MRR against ground truth, and since DistMult's own ranking is noisy, a $10^{-3}$ recall error may be invisible — or, less comfortably, exact top-$k$ may itself be unnecessary. Similarly, no sampling-quality measurement (perplexity, divergence of the sampled distribution) for vocabulary top-$k$. One model family, two tasks, one GPU.
  • Recall is the wrong quality metric for the stated application. Sparsity methods care about the mass retained, not the count. Bucketed top-$k$ misses exactly those values that have $\ge k_b$ larger values in the same bucket — plausibly values near the threshold, hence cheap misses — but the paper never measures magnitude-weighted error, which would likely make the approximation look better and would be the more defensible object of analysis.
  • The cost models are heuristics dressed as theory. They count abstract ops under assumptions like "iterating through input linearly is free" and "all branches taken", with a $C_{\mathrm{parallel}}$ that assumes infinitely many threads. The appendix concedes the serial model mispredicts $k$-scaling (because the kernel is bandwidth-bound — precisely the cost the model declares free) and that Stage-2 cost is underestimated, with an outright inversion at $n=2^{20},k=2^6$. The two headline conclusions are also derivable from a one-line argument about which stage dominates; the models add resolution, not insight.
  • The interleaving fix is empirical, not robust. Interleaving with stride $b$ decorrelates data whose covariance decays as $\rho^{|i-j|}$ (their synthetic model), but any input with _period-$b$_ structure — strided memory layouts, head/channel-blocked tensors, positional periodicity — aligns with the buckets and lands in the worst case. There is no guarantee, and no cheap randomised assignment (a hash) is offered as a default.
  • Minor: tie-handling in bfloat16 over $2.6\times10^6$ entities is untouched, and approx_max_k/TPU-KNN is compared against analytically but never benchmarked.

Proof sketch

Claim. Assume the input is i.i.d./uniform in the sense that the bucket assignment of each of the top-$k$ values is uniform on ${1,\dots,b}$ and independent across values; assume $k\ge k_b$ and $k_b\ll n/b$. Then the expected recall error is exactly

$$1-\mathbb{E}[R(k,b,k_b)]=1-\frac{1}{k}\Big(k_b+\sum_{i=k_b}^{k-1}F\big(k_b-1;\,i,\,1/b\big)\Big),$$

with $F(\cdot;m,p)$ the Binomial$(m,p)$ CDF. Relaxing $k_b\ll n/b$ turns this into an upper bound on the error. For $k_b=1$ it collapses to $\mathbb{E}[R(k,b,1)]=\frac{b}{k}\big(1-(\frac{b-1}{b})^k\big)$. Only the expectation is guaranteed; there is no variance or tail bound, and nothing is claimed for correlated data beyond the separate worst case $1-R_{wc}=1-\frac1k\big(\lfloor\frac{bk}{n}\rfloor k_b+\min(k_b, k\bmod \frac nb)\big)$, obtained by the explicit adversarial construction that packs all top-$k$ values into the fewest possible $\lceil bk/n\rceil$ buckets.

Technique. A rank-recursion in $k$ combined with an order-statistics/exchangeability argument, i.e. a balls-into-bins calculation done one ball at a time. Write $Z(k)$ for the count recovered. The key structural lemma is monotone non-interference: the $k$-th largest value is returned iff strictly fewer than $k_b$ larger values share its bucket, and the set of larger values is exactly the top-$(k-1)$; moreover inserting the $k$-th value cannot change whether any of the top-$(k-1)$ is returned, since Stage 1 keeps the $k_b$ largest per bucket. Hence $Z(k)=Z(k-1)+\mathbb{1}[\text{its bucket holds} <k_b \text{ of the top-}(k-1)]$ and the recursion $\mathbb{E}[Z(k)]=\mathbb{E}[Z(k-1)]+1-\phi_k$ is exact, with $\phi_k$ the probability of landing in an already-full bucket. Then exchangeability does the work: conditioning on which bucket the $k$-th value occupies, each of the $k-1$ larger values independently lands there with probability $1/b$, so the occupancy of that bucket is Binomial$(k-1,1/b)$ and $\phi_k=1-F(k_b-1;k-1,1/b)$ — no dependence on which bucket, which is what makes the telescoping sum closed-form. Base case $\mathbb{E}[Z(k_b)]=k_b$. The bound direction under finite bucket size follows from negative association: a bucket already over-represented among the top-$(k-1)$ has fewer remaining slots, so is less likely to also receive the $k$-th value — the true $\phi_k$ is smaller than the with-replacement value, so the formula over-states the error.

The genuinely nice bit is the correction to TPU-KNN. Chern et al. count only top-$k$ values that are alone in their bucket; the right statement for $k_b=1$ is that $Z(k,b,1)$ equals the number of distinct occupied buckets, since when two top-$k$ values collide one of them is still retrieved. That is a classic coupon-collector/occupancy quantity, and it is why the corrected $\mathbb{E}[R]$ is substantially more optimistic than the published TPU-KNN model.

Broader context

This sits at the junction of GPU selection algorithms and ML systems. The selection lineage is BucketSelect/RadixSelect (Alabi et al. 2012) $\to$ FAISS's WarpSelect/BlockSelect (Johnson, Douze, Jégou, Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs, 2021) $\to$ Bitonic top-k (Shanbhag et al., SIGMOD 2018), Dr. Top-k (Gaihre et al., SC 2021) and AIR Top-K/GridSelect (Zhang, Naruse, Li, Wang, SC 2023, shipped in RAPIDS RAFT). The approximate branch is essentially TPU-KNN (Chern, Hechtman, Davis, Guo, Majnemer, Kumar, NeurIPS 2022), which makes the point that peak-FLOP/s KNN requires giving up exact selection. The consumer side is the sparsity literature: Top-KAST (Jayakumar et al. 2020), FlexGen (Sheng et al. 2023) and especially SparQ Attention (Ribar et al., ICML 2024), which is the same group and the paper's driving workload.

The vector-search connection is real and worth developing, because it runs backwards. Bucketed top-$k$ with a per-bucket quota $k_b$ and an optional global merge is structurally identical to IVF-style partitioned MIPS/ANN: scan a set of partitions, keep each partition's local best, merge. The recall formula is then precisely a candidate-set recall model — "given a per-partition quota, how much of the true top-$k$ survives" — the same quantity that nprobe tuning in IVF, multi-probe LSH analysis, and ScaNN/SOAR-style partition-assignment work all estimate empirically. The inversion is the interesting part: this paper wants the top-$k$ spread uniformly over buckets (hence interleaving, hence hashing-like assignment), because its worst case is maximal concentration; IVF wants maximal concentration, because concentration is what lets you skip buckets. The two are the same combinatorial object optimised in opposite directions, and the expected/worst-case formulas bracket the two extremes. The per-bucket-quota versus global-threshold tension is likewise the IVF "fixed quota per list" versus "global heap / global threshold" design choice, and the paper's Stage-2 cliff is an argument for quota-only schemes that someone building a GPU IVF scanner should take seriously.

Two follow-ups the paper opens. (i) Replace recall with a value-weighted loss: for inputs with a known tail (Gaussian or Pareto scores), the same order-statistics machinery gives a closed form for $\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i\in \hat S} x_i]/\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i\in S^*} x_i]$, which is what a sparse-attention or MIPS consumer actually cares about, and would quantify how benign the misses are. (ii) Replace the expectation with a tail bound: the recall error is an occupancy-overflow quantity, so classical balls-in-bins max-load results ($\Theta(\log b/\log\log b)$ for $b$ balls in $b$ bins, and Chernoff bounds for $k\gg b\log b$) should give high-probability per-query recall rather than an average — the right guarantee for a retrieval SLA. An adaptive variant with data-dependent quotas (a cheap threshold estimate pass, then variable $k_b$, in the spirit of Dr. Top-k's delegates) is the obvious engineering follow-up.

For your own work two hooks look non-forced. First, the quota/recall calculus above is directly reusable as the theoretical skeleton for partitioned ANN recall, and its honest limitation — expectation only, exchangeability only — is a gap a theory person can close. Second, generative retrieval: constrained beam decoding over a docid trie calls top-$k$ at every step with $n=$ vocabulary or number of children and effective batch $=$ beam width, which is exactly the small-$m$, large-$n$, latency-critical regime this kernel targets. The composition question is genuinely open and theoretical: if each step's selection has per-step recall $1-\varepsilon$, what is the recall of the final beam after $L$ steps, given that errors at shallow trie levels prune whole subtrees? Beam search is not a product of independent selections, so a union bound is loose and the structure of the docid tree should enter the bound — a clean problem, and one where an approximate-top-$k$ kernel with a tunable $(b,k_b)$ gives you the experimental knob to validate the theory.

title: Tracing Attention Computation Through Feature Interactions
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — November 15, 2026

Tracing Attention Computation Through Feature Interactions

Anthropic Interpretability Team (2025) · https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attention-qk/index.html

Setting and problem

The object of study is a single attention head's pre-softmax score. For residual-stream vectors $x_{p_q}, x_{p_k} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ at a query position $p_q$ and key position $p_k$, the head computes

$$\mathrm{score}(p_k, p_q) \;=\; x_{p_q}^{\top} W_{QK}\, x_{p_k}, \qquad W_{QK} = W_Q^{\top} W_K ,$$

i.e. a bilinear form on the residual stream, with $W_{QK}$ the low-rank combined matrix from Elhage et al.'s A Mathematical Framework. The analyst is given a trained model — here Claude 3.5 Haiku — its activations on a prompt, and a dictionary of sparsely active features with decoder vectors, so that at each position $x_p = \sum_f a_f(p) v_f + b + e_p$, where $a_f(p)$ are (mostly zero) feature activations, $v_f$ dictionary/decoder vectors, $b$ a bias, and $e_p$ the dictionary's reconstruction error. The method must output a human-readable account of why this head attended here and not elsewhere, and must plug that account into an existing attribution graph.

The motivating gap is specific. Anthropic's attribution-graph line (circuit tracing / Biology of a Large Language Model) built interpretable causal graphs on top of cross-layer transcoders that replace MLPs. To make edges linear and attribution well-defined, those graphs freeze the attention patterns and treat them as constants. Two things are thereby lost: (i) which head, or sequence of heads, actually carried a given cross-position edge, and (ii) any explanation of the pattern itself — by conditioning on attention when taking gradients, the graphs ignore QK circuits entirely. The authors are blunt that this makes many graphs useless: for the induction prompt "I always loved visiting Aunt Sally… Whenever I was feeling sad, Aunt", the old graph says only "the model said Sally because it attended to the Sally token," which is not an explanation.

Why is this harder than explaining a neuron? A neuron (or transcoder feature) is a function of one position's activations; superposition aside, you can read off what it responds to. An attention score is a function of two positions jointly, and it is bilinear, so the natural unit of explanation is a feature pair. The number of candidate explanations is quadratic in dictionary size, not linear — in practice tamed only because feature activations are sparse, so very few $(f, f')$ pairs are simultaneously live. Modelling choices worth flagging: the exposition assumes vanilla attention, so RoPE-style positional modifications of $W_Q, W_K$ are explicitly outside the formalism; any pre-attention normalization must be linearized and its bias folded into $b$; and the dictionary used in practice is not an SAE but weakly causal crosscoders (WCCs) — features that read the residual stream at layer $L$ and reconstruct layers $L, L{+}1, \dots$.

Main idea

Two components. First, QK attributions: substitute the feature decomposition into the bilinear form and multiply out, turning one scalar score into a sorted list of labelled feature-pair terms, which can be read, hovered, and steered. Second, head loadings: for each attribution-graph edge, record how much each head contributed, so that the explanation of a pattern can be attached to the edge it enabled. The attention-mediated part of an edge between adjacent-layer features (activations $a_s, a_t$, vectors $v_s, v_t$) is

$$\sum_{h} a_s a_t \left(v_t^{\top} O_h V_h\, v_s\right)\cdot \mathrm{attention}_h(p_s, p_t),$$

each summand being that head's loading. To make this tractable the authors must stop paths of length $>1$: with transcoders, the number of head paths between features $L$ layers apart grows exponentially in $L$. They "checkpoint" at every layer — candidate strategies were multi-token transcoders, attention-output SAEs, and residual-stream dictionaries with gradient attributions between adjacent layers; they chose the third (via WCCs) because the other two accumulate residual error across layers and produce graphs dominated by error nodes.

Findings: in induction, query-side "Aunt/Uncle" features interact with key-side name features and with "this is the name of an aunt/uncle" features — two heuristics running in parallel, not one clean induction circuit. A precursor previous-token head is driven by query-side "first name" × key-side "title preceding a name". In "Aunt Mary Sue", two independent interaction pairs fire with weak cross-terms, so the QK attribution matrix has rank $\geq 2$. For antonyms ("Le contraire de « petit » est «"), key-side features tag the word whose opposite is wanted, while a second mechanism just hunts for any adjective; suppressing query-side "opposite" features makes the model emit synonyms of petit. In multiple choice, query-side "needs to give an answer" features (plus the query bias) interact with key-side "correct answer" features, while "false statement" features on wrong options contribute negatively; injecting the correct-answer feature onto option A or C flips the letter the model emits. The genuinely new result is concordance/discordance heads: for "the color of a banana is yellow?" the model does not appear to compute banana → yellow and compare; distinct head populations directly test agreement, with banana–yellow interactions raising concordance scores and lowering discordance scores, and banana–red doing the reverse. The same heads do the same job for "18+5=23?", using a "numbers separated by an interval of 5" feature rather than computing the sum.

The most interesting part

The sharpest technical moment is the basis-free corroboration of the concordance/discordance story: feature-feature interactions through $W_{QK}$ skew positive for concordance heads and negative for discordance heads, and — crucially — the eigenvalues of $W_{QK}$ skew positive for one group and negative for the other. That check does not depend on the dictionary at all, which is exactly the right move when your main evidence is dictionary-shaped. A positive-definite-ish $W_{QK}$ is a similarity detector; a negative-definite-ish one is a mismatch detector. That is a clean, falsifiable structural claim about a head's weights.

The honest critique is about everything else. The method is, as the authors say, "somewhat brute force": it is an exact algebraic expansion plus a sorted list, and all the interpretive work is done by feature labels that come from the dictionary. Nothing establishes that the chosen WCC basis is the right one; a different dictionary yields a different list of "the" interactions, and the authors concede that using WCCs makes MLP-path attributions nonlinear and therefore possibly prompt-local and uninterpretable. Several findings are explicitly incomplete: they cannot explain where the "correct answer" features come from because the cross-token inputs are obscured by error nodes; they have no automated way to surface the inhibitory terms that softmax competition makes essential; the low-rank structure of the QK attribution matrix is "preliminary"; positional contributions are deferred entirely. Steering works only when applied to 3–10% of heads, attributed to a hydra effect — which is evidence of distributed redundancy, but also means single-head stories are illustrative rather than load-bearing. Heads are named for the role they play on this prompt, and whether a head runs "the same algorithm" across prompts is listed as an open question. I read the piece as establishing a usable instrument and five plausible mechanism sketches, two of them (multiple choice, antonyms) confirmations of prior hypotheses, one (concordance heads) a real discovery; I do not read it as establishing a validated circuit.

Proof sketch

There is no theorem, and the article claims none. The load-bearing mathematics is a single exact identity. Substituting $x_p = \sum_f a_f(p) v_f + b + e_p$ into $x_{p_q}^\top W_{QK} x_{p_k}$ and expanding gives six groups of terms: a feature–feature sum $\sum_{f,f'} a_f(p_q)\, a_{f'}(p_k)\, v_f^\top W_{QK} v_{f'}$; two feature–error cross terms $\sum_f a_f(p_q) v_f^\top W_{QK} e_{p_k}$ and $\sum_f e_{p_q}^\top W_{QK} a_f(p_k) v_f$; a key-feature × query-bias term $\sum_f b^\top W_{QK} a_f(p_k) v_f$; a bias–error term $b^\top W_{QK} e_{p_k}$; a group of terms of the form $(\cdot)^\top W_{QK} b$ that are constant in $p_k$; and finally $e_{p_q}^\top W_{QK} e_{p_k}$.

The identity is exact: the terms sum to the score, with no attribution heuristic, because bilinearity distributes over the decomposition. Approximation enters only through (a) the dictionary — error is not hidden but carried explicitly in $e_p$, with feature–error and error–error terms quantifying how much of the score is unexplained; (b) linearization of any pre-attention normalization; (c) the assumption of vanilla, position-independent $W_Q, W_K$. Two useful structural observations: terms involving $b$ on the query side and anything constant across key positions, including $b^\top W_{QK} b$, are invariant to $p_k$ and so vanish under softmax and can be dropped; and the query-bias × key-feature terms encode a head's standing disposition to attend to certain key content regardless of query, which is how "attend to any name at all" shows up. There is no error bound — only the empirical observation that error-node-dominated graphs were the reason two checkpointing strategies were rejected.

Broader context

Mechanistic interpretability tries to reverse-engineer the algorithms a trained network implements, rather than merely characterising its behaviour. The lineage here: Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (2021), which introduced the $W_{QK}$/$W_{OV}$ factorisation and the induction-head story; Olah et al.'s Towards Monosemanticity and the sparse-autoencoder line, which attacks superposition by learning overcomplete sparse dictionaries over activations; and Ameisen, Lindsey et al. (2025) on circuit tracing with cross-layer transcoders and attribution graphs, which this piece patches. Nearest neighbours in the literature are Ge et al. (2024), who computed QK attributions for hand-identified IOI heads (Wang et al., 2022) without a systematic head-loading computation, and Wynroe & Sharkey, who trained SAEs with a sparsity-penalized mask on the feature-feature interaction matrix itself — a strictly more ambitious framing, since it makes QK-sparsity a training objective rather than something hoped for.

A natural follow-up: take the "preliminary" low-rank observation seriously. If the per-(head, position-pair) QK attribution matrix $M_{ff'} = a_f(p_q)\, v_f^\top W_{QK} v_{f'}\, a_{f'}(p_k)$ is approximately rank-$r$ with small $r$, then truncated SVD gives $r$ query concepts and $r$ key concepts as linear combinations of features, replacing a long list with a short one — and the rank, estimated across prompts, becomes a quantitative measure of head polysemanticity. That directly addresses one of the authors' own open questions.

The connection to your work is real but should be stated carefully. The QK score is an inner-product retrieval operation: $\langle W_Q x_q, W_K x_k \rangle$ is exactly a dual-encoder score over a learned key space, with the context window as the corpus and softmax as a soft arg-top-$k$. The decomposition above is therefore a general recipe for turning any bilinear retrieval score into a sum of interpretable term-term interactions over a sparse learned basis — which is the interpretability question for dense retrievers, and formally close in spirit to SPLADE-style sparse re-expressions of dense matching, except that the basis is learned post hoc by a dictionary rather than tied to vocabulary. The query-bias term has a nice retrieval reading too: a corpus-independent prior over which key content to retrieve, i.e. a learned static bias in the scoring function. Applying head loadings + QK attributions to a cross-encoder reranker, or to the query/key projections of a trained bi-encoder, strikes me as a well-posed project. The extension to generative retrieval is weaker and I would not lean on it: GR replaces inner-product matching with autoregressive docid decoding, so there is no top-level bilinear score to decompose. What survives is narrower — the decoder's own attention heads are where docid-prefix-to-evidence matching must happen, so QK attribution is a plausible instrument for asking what a GR decoder is matching on when it emits each docid token. That is a hypothesis about where to look, not an existing bridge, and the scaling limitation the authors flag (cost quadratic in context length, no pruning algorithm yet) would bite immediately on retrieval-length contexts.

title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Capture Concept Manifolds?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 14 November 2026

Do Sparse Autoencoders Capture Concept Manifolds?

Usha Bhalla, Thomas Fel, Can Rager et al. (2026) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28119

Setting and problem

The observable. Fix a pretrained LM (here Llama3.1-8B) and a read-out site (residual stream, layer 19, d=4096, last-token activations). The data we see are activations x in a subset of R^d and, downstream, the codes an SAE assigns to them. Nothing about concept identity is observed.

The featurizer. The paper's Definition 1 fixes SAEs as an instance of sparse coding: given x, extract z in R^c through a dictionary D in R^{c x d} by minimizing ||x - zD||2^2 + lambdaR(z) over W and D in Omega, with z = ReLU(xW) and Omega = B^{c x d} the unit-norm-row constraint; R is the sparsity-promoting regularizer — ||z||_0 <= k for TopK/BatchTopK, the JumpReLU surrogate, or L1 with weight lambda. The atoms are the rows_ D_i of the decoder (note the transposed convention: x_hat = zD, so atoms are row vectors and reconstructions live in a sparse non-negative span, i.e. a cone). Appendix C generalizes this into a _Definition 4 (Geometric Duality of Sparse Concepts)*: the same objective with either Z = R^c+, Omega = B^{c x d} ("concepts as directions", classical SAEs, reconstruction in a cone) or Z = the simplex Delta^{c-1}, Omega = R^{c x d} ("concepts as points", landmark/archetypal dictionaries written P instead of D, reconstruction strictly inside a sparse convex hull, a bounded polytope). This duality is load-bearing: it is what makes the appendix's impossibility result possible.

The representation model to be recovered. Definition 2, Additive Mixture of Manifolds: let M_1,...,M_m be compact smooth submanifolds of R^d with dim(M_i) = d_i << d and immersions f_i. Then x = sum over i in S of f_i(m_i), with m_i in M_i, S a subset of [m] and |S| << m — so x lives in a Minkowski sum of immersed submanifolds. Each M_i is contained in a k_i-dimensional affine subspace and admits m_i(theta) = gamma_i(theta) V_i + b_i with intrinsic coordinates theta in Theta_i a subset of R^{d_i}, smooth embedding gamma_i, orthonormal basis V_i in R^{k_i x d} and offset b_i in Im(V_i). Superposition is the condition sum_i k_i > d. When every M_i is a ray (d_i = 1), each term is a scalar multiple of a fixed direction and one recovers the Linear Representation Hypothesis — LRH is the d_i = 1 corner of this model. The distinction d_i (intrinsic, degrees of freedom) vs k_i (embedding dimension of the containing affine subspace) is used throughout and is the crux: a circle has d_i = 1 but k_i = 2; the Clifford torus has d_i = 2, k_i = 4. k_i sets how many atoms are needed to span; d_i sets how many localized detectors one would expect in a tiling.

The authors are explicit that this is not a normative claim about LLMs — it is a setting where metrics can be defined rigorously and then transferred.

Capture, notion 1 (global subspace allocation). Definition 3, Subspace capture: an SAE captures M at precision epsilon if there exists S_ a subset of [c] with |S_| <= k_M such that ||x_m - sum_{i in S_} z_i(x_m) D_i|| <= epsilon for all x_m in M. Two things are demanded simultaneously: _parsimony_ (|S_| <= k_M, no more atoms than the manifold's embedding dimension) and coherence (the same S* works for every point of M). Curvature is then carried entirely by how the coefficients move as x_m traverses M. The paper notes this is the sparse-subspace-clustering subspace-preserving condition in disguise (Elhamifar & Vidal; Soltanolkotabi et al.; Tschannen & Bölcskei).

Capture, notion 2 (local tiling). When the number of atoms allocated to M_i exceeds k_i, the SAE is no longer forced to reuse a fixed group and may assign different atoms to different regions. Each atom becomes a localized detector with a receptive field on the manifold — the population-coding picture from neuroscience (place cells, orientation columns; Khona & Fiete; Eichenbaum). The paper calls this tiling and splits it in two:

  • Shattering: the active sets are nearly disjoint; atoms partition M; atoms are mutually exclusive.
  • Dilution: active sets overlap substantially and vary smoothly, but no compact group of size <= k_i accounts for M. Every region is covered redundantly by several atoms; total support |G_M| >> k_M, "often by an order of magnitude". Appendix G frames the geometric contrast: shattering treats atoms as landmarks (point-like, sharp receptive fields), dilution treats them as a locally redundant basis — "the directional paradigm but with the wrong sparsity budget".

The statistical handle. Since the atom group G_M is unobserved, it must be recovered from codes. Raw co-activation confounds structural co-activation (atoms spanning/tiling the same manifold) with correlational co-occurrence (concepts that co-occur in text), and is dominated by universally-firing atoms. The fix: binarize, s_i = 2*1[z_i > 0] - 1, and fit a pairwise Ising model p(s) proportional to exp(sum_{i<j} J_ij s_i s_j + sum_i h_i s_i), so that marginal firing rates are absorbed into the fields h_i and the couplings J_ij are *direct* interactions after conditioning on the rest of the population. Appendix F justifies this via Proposition 1 (pairwise Markov property / Hammersley-Clifford, Besag 1974): J_ab = 0 iff s_a and s_b are conditionally independent given the rest — J is for binary codes what the precision matrix Sigma^{-1} is for Gaussians, and a Gaussian graphical lasso would be misspecified on sparse, non-negative, L0-constrained codes. Appendix G then makes the three regimes *measurable* via the **signed cohesion** rho(G) = average of sign(J_ab) over pairs in G, in [-1,1] (Definition 6): capture means |G| approx k_M and rho >= +tau (ferromagnetic, all co-fire); shattering means |G| >> k_M and rho <= -tau (antiferromagnetic, mutual exclusion); dilution means |G| >> k_M and |rho| < tau (disordered, mixed signs).

The question, as the paper poses it. Verbatim three-part: what does it mean for an SAE to capture a manifold, when do existing SAE architectures do so, and how? Given: activations of a pretrained LM plus SAEs trained on them. Asked: whether there exists, for each concept manifold, a compact coherent atom group spanning it (Def. 3) — and if not, which tiling regime the SAE occupies, and whether the group can be found without supervision.

What the literature already supplies, and the gap. The LRH (Park et al. 2023; Elhage et al. 2022; Arora et al. 2018; Jiang et al. 2024) models concepts as directions packed as a Grassmannian frame, read out linearly and manipulated linearly; SAEs are literally its inverse (Costa et al. 2025). Against it sits an accumulating body of non-flat findings: circular topology for periodic concepts (Engels et al.; Modell et al.; Kantamneni & Tegmark), linear/helical topology for numerals (Gurnee et al.; Yocum et al.), in-context graph structure (Park et al.; Saanum et al.; Sarfati et al.), polar syntax coordinates (Diego-Simón et al.), hierarchy in genomics and VLMs, and — the sharpest one — Karkada et al. (2026), whose result is that representation geometry encodes uncertainty over concept values, which endows distances with meaning and is therefore "directly at odds with LRH, which primarily focuses on directions". Separately, SAEs have a pile of negative results: dictionary instability across seeds (Paulo & Belrose; Fel et al. 2025a), brittle steering (Wu et al. AxBench; Bhalla et al.), weak probing utility (Kantamneni et al.; Karvonen et al.), feature splitting and absorption (Chanin et al.), feature-manifold scaling pathologies (Michaud et al.). The gap the paper identifies is not "does the SAE destroy the geometry" — good reconstruction trivially implies the geometry is preserved somewhere in the code. The gap is whether the preserved geometry is organized in an interpretable way, i.e. whether there is any formal criterion distinguishing "the manifold is encoded" from "the manifold is encoded recognizably". No prior work gives such a criterion. A boxed claim in Section 1 argues the three negative results above are predicted by a manifold picture (multiple equivalent tilings implies seed instability; single-atom intervention pushes off the manifold instead of along it, implying brittle steering; single atoms carry no meaning in isolation, implying autointerp failure or hallucinated labels).

Non-obvious modelling choices and idealizations — where the result actually lives.

  1. Def. 3 is extrinsic. "Capturing a manifold" is reduced to spanning its affine hull with <= k_M atoms. A circle is "captured" by 2 atoms. Curvature, topology and the metric play no role in the global criterion; they live only in the coefficient trajectory. The intrinsic notion appears only in the appendix, for the point paradigm.
  2. Only direction-based SAEs are analyzed in the main text, justified by Lemma 1 (below), which closes the door on landmark dictionaries as models of factorwise recovery.
  3. _Theorem 1 assumes M lies in a k-dimensional affine subspace and that S* with span(D_{S*}) = Im(V) exists._ The curvature is irrelevant to the theorem, and the existence of the right atom group is hypothesized, not derived.
  4. Theorem 1 analyzes an idealized OMP decoder over the learned D, not the trained feedforward encoder — the "amortization gap" is named and discussed but not quantified.
  5. Synthetic benchmark idealizations (App. E): d = 128, c = 512 (expansion 4), 8 manifold types x 6 variants = 48 instances; random orthonormal V_i via QR; each instance centered and isotropically rescaled to unit RMS norm (explicitly to prevent large-norm manifolds like the Swiss roll from monopolizing capacity); biases b_i = 0; noise sigma = 1e-5 ("deliberately small so reconstruction quality reflects geometric organization rather than denoising ability"); active set S drawn uniformly at random without replacement, |S| = L0 = 4; 2M train / 1M eval samples with ground-truth per-manifold contributions and active masks; TopK SAEs at k in {3,4,6,8,10,14,16,20,25}.
  6. The real-LLM "manifolds" are template-induced. Table 1: colors (paraboloid, ~900 samples, "The hex code {h_code} is for the color"), temperature (line, 150), age (line, 99), geography (hierarchical tree, ~4000, lat/lon to country), days (circle, 420), years (helix, 199), formality (line, 1000, Pavlick & Tetreault), sentence length (line, 5000, WikiText), political bias (1D continuous, GPT-5 augmentations of a synthetic dataset). Causal relevance is established by PCA-space activation patching: fit PCA to 90% variance, bin the continuous label, interpolate between consecutive bin centroids, project the delta back and add it to a base prompt's layer-19 activation, then read target-token probabilities.
  7. Metric operationalization (App. E) is aggregate, not pointwise: restricted R^2 encodes the eval set, selects rows where manifold i is active using the ground-truth masks, greedily picks n atoms by residual variance explained on decoder directions, masks codes to those atoms, decodes, and computes R^2 against the true contributions, reported for n in [max(1,k_i-2), k_i+2]. Support size counts atoms firing on >= 10% of manifold points (with a 10th-percentile magnitude filter and a 30-point floor). Receptive-field spread is the median over support atoms of mean pairwise distance among firing points, normalized by the manifold's own mean pairwise distance, so 0 = maximally localized, 1 = maximally global.
  8. Real SAE suite: 5 architectures (Standard L1, JumpReLU, TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka), expansion x8/x16 (d_sae = 32,768/65,536), k in {64,128,256}, 500M tokens of uncopyrighted Pile, Adam 1e-4, batch 16,384, activations normalized by mean L2 norm; only SAEs with variance explained > 0.85 are analyzed (Table 3 reports VE 0.841-0.961).

Main idea

Two contributions, one definitional-and-theoretical, one empirical, joined by a diagnostic.

Framework. Extend LRH to an additive mixture of manifolds (Def. 2) and ask what "capturing" means in that model. The answer bifurcates. Globally, an SAE captures M if a compact fixed atom group spans its affine hull and the encoder selects that same group on every manifold point (Def. 3) — and under classical incoherence conditions this is achievable (Thm. 1). Locally, an SAE can instead satisfy sparsity and reconstruct well while allocating many localized, overlapping detectors that tile M: a population code. Tiling is not a failure mode of reconstruction — it is a second, equally loss-optimal solution, and it splits into shattering (disjoint supports, mutual exclusion) and dilution (overlapping redundant supports with no compact spanning group). Crucially, all three regimes leave distinct statistical fingerprints in the Ising couplings J: ferromagnetic (capture), antiferromagnetic (shattering), disordered (dilution). So the diagnosis of which solution an SAE found is a graphical-model-selection problem over atoms, and manifold discovery becomes community detection on |J| — not clustering of decoder directions.

Empirics. In the controlled benchmark: (i) subspace capture has a sparsity sweet spot, with restricted R^2 peaking near k = 4 (matching the generative L0) and degrading both below and above; (ii) increasing k drives the SAE through shattering, then capture, then dilution, visible in the (support size, receptive-field diameter) phase plane; (iii) even outside the capture regime the structure is recoverable post hoc — the Ising coupling matrix is block-diagonal with respect to the ground-truth manifold partition at intermediate k approx 8-16, degrading at both extremes, and decoding through the recovered groups reconstructs the topology and geometry of all eight manifold types without supervision.

On Llama3.1-8B: SAEs do not achieve compact capture. Restricted R^2 grows with support size but plateaus well beyond each manifold's embedding dimension, for every architecture, expansion and sparsity tested (with PCA and random-orthogonal/random-SAE baselines for reference). Instead, features behave as localized detectors with smooth, overlapping tuning curves — on the years manifold most SAEs learn features selective to the ones digit (firing every 10 years) alongside features encoding the decade. Receptive-field maps in the top-3-PC ambient space, with points colored by max-activating feature, show the architectural prior stamped directly onto the partition geometry: angular separability for TopK, linear separability for L1. Reconstructing with increasing numbers of features approximates the manifold piecewise-linearly. Verdict: current SAEs sit in the dilution regime — geometry preserved, organization fragmented — which is precisely the regime the appendix identifies as the genuinely problematic one, since both ordered states (capture, shattering) yield well-defined communities under spectral clustering of |J| while the disordered state does not.

Discovery. Among five affinity measures — decoder cosine, conditional co-activation P(z_j | z_i), Pearson correlation of magnitudes, PMI, Ising couplings — only Ising and conditional co-activation produce clean block-diagonal structure aligned with supervised ground truth; decoder cosine similarity and Pearson correlation fail. The paper's argument for why is the sharpest conceptual line in it: under subspace capture the atoms spanning M's subspace may be nearly orthogonal, and under tiling, atoms covering adjacent but non-overlapping regions need not point in similar directions — so manifold membership is a functional property (which atoms co-activate) and not a geometric one (where atoms point). The pipeline (pseudo-likelihood Ising fit with symmetrization J = (W + W^T)/2, EBIC regularization selection with gamma = 0.5 following IsingFit, Louvain on |J|, then validation by a sharp PCA spectral gap in the group's code vectors) recovers temperature, colors and political bias on a BatchTopK SAE (x8, k = 64), and surfaces a claimed novel structure encoding epistemic uncertainty in scientific text (clusters of features around +/- notation, standard deviations, error margins). Also worth noting, buried in App. B.3: optimal-transport alignment across SAE architectures is weak in decoder space and on random data but strong when restricted to a given manifold — what is invariant across SAEs is not the features but the coordinate system they collectively induce over a manifold.

The most interesting part

The cleverest technical move, for me, is not the theorem but the argument in App. A for why the prior toolkit cannot be reused, plus the dual-paradigm impossibility lemma. Every classical manifold-learning/subspace-clustering method shares the generative assumption x_i = U_{l(i)} z_i + eps_i with l(i) in {1,...,c} — each datapoint belongs to one subspace via a latent label, and the goal is to recover the partition l. The additive mixture of Def. 2 breaks this in two specific ways the paper names precisely: (i) classical self-expression x_i = X c_i cannot be subspace-preserving, because the coefficients must reach across every manifold active in x_i; and (ii) the unit of clustering shifts from datapoints to dictionary atoms, since no point-level label l(x) exists. Hence the affinity object is c x c over atoms, not n x n over points, and the whole spectral SSC pipeline does not transfer. Combined with the observation that decoder geometry is uninformative and co-activation is the right signal — and with the Ising coupling sign as the regime discriminator (ferro = capture, antiferro = shattering, disordered = dilution) — this is a genuinely new and well-motivated primitive. The spin-glass analogy is not decoration: it predicts the empirical finding that only the two ordered phases are recoverable by clustering.

Now the critique.

The theory is weaker than the framing suggests, in a specific way. Theorem 1 assumes M lies in a k-dimensional affine subspace with orthonormal basis V, and assumes there exists S* with |S*| = k and span(D_{S*}) = Im(V) exactly. Under those hypotheses the manifold's curvature is entirely irrelevant — the statement is a subspace recovery result about a k-dimensional flat, obtained by plugging Tropp's exact recovery condition and noise-robust null-space property into the restricted-support error. Nothing distinguishes a circle from a 2-dimensional disk. So the paper's central novel object (curvature with causally meaningful distances) does not enter its central theorem, and the hardest part of the conclusion — that the dictionary contains a group exactly spanning the manifold's hull — is an assumption. There is no result of the form "trained SAEs in regime X will/won't find such a group", no sample complexity, no lower bound on |G_M| as a function of manifold volume and k, and no theory of when loss-equivalent tiling solutions are preferred over capture — which is exactly the question the empirics raise. "We develop a theoretical framework that answers these questions" oversells: the framework answers the what (definitionally, well) and not the when or the how (empirically only).

The sharpest genuinely new theory is in the appendix and its key hypothesis is in tension with the paper's own generative model. Lemma 1 proves landmark/convex-hull dictionaries cannot approximate factor manifolds under superposition, assuming M_1 in V_1, M_2 in V_2 orthogonal and 0 not in M_2, i.e. delta := inf ||m_2|| > 0. But Def. 2 has x = sum over active i only, with |S| << m: an inactive factor contributes nothing, so the data distribution contains points where only M_1 is active, which are exactly points of M_1 — and landmarks placed there would be at distance 0 from M_1. The lemma is really about tiling the always-joint manifold M_1 + M_2; the sparse-activation regime that motivates the paper partially rescues point-based dictionaries. Yet the paper uses the lemma to "close the door, for the purposes of this paper, on point-based SAEs", and in the synthetic benchmark |S| = L0 = 4 always, so single-factor observations never occur by construction. This is a load-bearing idealization dressed as a general obstruction.

The main empirical claim rests on a quantity that is not measured. "Restricted R^2 plateaus well beyond each manifold's ambient dimension" requires knowing k_M for real concepts. In the synthetic setting k_i is exact; on Llama it is a proxy — Table 1 asserts geometry types (colors = paraboloid, years = helix, geography = hierarchical tree) and the steering protocol uses PCA to 90% variance. No k_M estimate, no confidence interval on it, and no numbers at all for the real-LLM experiments: Section 5 is entirely figure-reading. Fig. 6 shows VE vs restricted support size from 0 to 64 for four manifolds with PCA and random baselines, but the paper reports no support size at which the plateau occurs, no plateau level, no per-architecture comparison in numbers. For a paper whose headline is "SAEs are in the dilution regime", the quantitative gap between |G_M| and k_M is the whole result and it is never stated. Relatedly, Definition 6's regime classification needs a threshold tau, and tau is never instantiated — nor is rho(G) ever reported numerically for real SAEs, despite the conclusion that mixed intra-group sign structure "consistently places trained SAEs in this regime".

Definition 3 and its operationalization are not the same statement. Def. 3 is pointwise and requires a single fixed S* with |S*| <= k_M to reconstruct every x_m in M. The restricted-R^2 protocol greedily picks n atoms by residual variance explained aggregated over the eval set, masks the codes to them, and reports aggregate R^2. An SAE could score well in aggregate while no single input activates more than a fraction of S* — and in the synthetic setting, capture peaks at k = 4 while four active manifolds with k_i up to 4 would need up to 16 simultaneously-active atoms to span all active hulls pointwise. So the "capture sweet spot at k = L0" is a statement about the aggregate metric, not about Def. 3, and the gap is never discussed.

The controlled validation omits the confound the method exists to handle. The Ising affinity is introduced precisely because raw co-activation "confounds structural co-activation with correlational co-occurrence". In the synthetic benchmark, S is drawn uniformly at random without replacement — there is zero correlational co-occurrence. The one place where ground truth is exact is the one place where the method's distinguishing advantage over plain co-activation cannot be tested. And on real data the comparison of five metrics uses only the top-3 supervised features for three manifolds plus a random set — roughly a 12 x 12 affinity matrix, judged by eye for block-diagonality, with no ARI/AUC and no comparison against graphical lasso on raw codes or against a shuffled-control J. The claim "conditional co-activation also works nearly as well" quietly undercuts the need for the Ising machinery on real data.

The "novel manifold" is the weakest evidence in the paper. The epistemic-uncertainty cluster is shown by activating text examples (+/- notation, means and standard deviations in biomedical abstracts) and feature labels. There is no PCA plot showing continuous low-dimensional structure, no tuning curve, no steering, no spectral-gap number — nothing that distinguishes a manifold from a topic/notation cluster, which is exactly what a community in a co-activation graph most cheaply explains. Given that the pipeline's own validation step is "check for a sharp PCA spectral gap", not reporting that gap for the headline discovery is a notable omission.

No causal test at the level of groups. The paper's boxed explanation for brittle steering — "intervening on a single feature pushes representations off the manifold rather than moving coherently along it" — is a falsifiable prediction with an obvious experiment: steer with the recovered group along the manifold's coefficient trajectory and compare to single-feature steering on the same target tokens. Section 3 already has the full patching apparatus, but it steers in PCA space of raw activations, never through SAE atoms. So the paper's most actionable claim — that groups are the right unit of intervention — is asserted and not tested, even though the infrastructure to test it is already built.

Confounds in the real-data tuning curves. The years result (features keyed to the ones digit, firing every 10 years) is presented as population-code tiling, but it is equally well explained by tokenization and known feature-splitting/absorption behavior on digit tokens (Chanin et al., cited). Likewise the templated prompts hold everything fixed except one slot, so "manifold" here is a one-parameter trajectory of last-token activations under a fixed template, with lexical identity of the inserted value varying along it. Distinguishing "the model has a temperature manifold" from "last-token activations trace a curve because the inserted token varies smoothly in frequency/orthography" is not attempted.

Smaller things. VE > 0.85 is a permissive bar, and the L1 SAEs' achieved L0 is never reported, so the cross-architecture comparison "at matched sparsity" is not actually matched for Standard SAEs. SpaDE and MFA appear in Table 3 and Fig. 13 with no definition and no citation. tau is overloaded (the reach of M in Def. 5, the cohesion threshold in Def. 6). The binarization is in {-1,+1} in Section 4.1 but sign(z_j) with state space {0,1}^c in App. E/F. Def. 2 calls d_i the "ambient dimensionality" and then uses "ambient dimension" for k_i throughout Sections 4-5; App. E fixes the terminology, but the main text's central claim inherits the ambiguity. "Shattering" is used in two distinct senses: App. G's definition (atoms partition M into near-disjoint patches, antiferromagnetic) versus Fig. 4B's low-k description ("atoms are broadly shared and the manifold is shattered across unrelated groups"), which is about cross-manifold sharing — close to the opposite of specialization. Finally, the synthetic-to-real gap is large on every axis that matters: d 128 to 4096, expansion 4 to 8/16, L0 4-of-48 to 64-256-of-32k, noise 1e-5 to real residual stream, all manifolds renormalized to equal RMS norm versus wildly unequal concept frequencies and norms. The honest reading is that the real-LLM result ("dilution") is a qualitative transfer of a regime label whose quantitative boundary was calibrated in a setting with none of those properties.

Genuine strengths, to be fair. The negative result about decoder cosine similarity is important, well-argued from first principles, and directly contradicts a method used in prior work (Engels et al.) — that alone is worth the paper. The three-regime taxonomy with sign-of-coupling signatures is a real conceptual contribution with a clean physics analogy that does predictive work. The d_i vs k_i distinction is handled with unusual care. The App. B.3 invariance result (features don't align across SAEs, manifold-restricted coordinate systems do) is a strong piece of evidence for the paper's thesis and deserves to be in the main text. And the framing — reconstruction fidelity does not certify interpretable organization, so a new axis of evaluation is needed beyond the VE/L0 Pareto frontier — is the right criticism of the SAE literature's current scorekeeping.

Proof sketch

There are real theorems, though the substantive ones are in the appendix. Three formal results, plus definitional machinery.

Theorem 1/2 (Subspace recovery). Claim: let M lie in a k-dimensional affine subspace with orthonormal basis V in R^{k x d} and offset b_M; let D be mu-incoherent; suppose there exists S* a subset of [c], |S*| = k, with Im(V) = span(D_{S*}) and mu < 1/(2k-1). If the SAE achieves ||x_m - D z(x_m)|| <= lambda on M, then it captures M at precision O(lambda) in the sense of Def. 3.

Assumptions doing the work: mu < 1/(2k-1) is Tropp's (2004) coherence-based Exact Recovery Condition, which guarantees that for any signal supported on S* both OMP and Basis Pursuit recover the correct support; by Lemma 2.3 of Tropp (2004) it also gives squared singular values of D_{S*} exceeding 1 - (k-1)mu > 0, hence full row rank and a bound on the pseudoinverse norm. The encoding model is idealized: D comes from SAE training, but codes are then computed by OMP over the learned dictionary, explicitly to separate dictionary quality from any particular feedforward encoder. The affine offset is absorbed into the SAE bias so one works with centered x~ = V alpha.

Proof strategy: a support-leakage bound. Since Im(V) = span(D_{S*}), every centered point has a unique x~_m = D_{S*} c*, c* in R^k. Let z be the code, S = supp(z), r = x~_m - Dz with ||r|| <= lambda, and S_bar = S \ S* the off-subspace part of the support. Extend c* by zeros and set delta = z - c*. Then ||D delta|| = ||Dz - D_{S*} c*|| = ||Dz - x~_m|| <= lambda. The key step is the noise-robust null-space property of Tropp (2006, Thm. 14), which under the ERC converts this reconstruction-level bound into a coefficient-level bound on the off-support mass: ||delta_{S_bar}||_1 <= C(mu,k)/(1-(2k-1)mu) * ||D delta||_2 = O(lambda), with C(mu,k) depending only on mu and k. Because c* is supported on S*, delta_{S_bar}||} = z_{S_bar}, so ||z_{S_bar_1 = O(lambda): the code cannot put much mass on atoms outside the spanning group. Finally the S*-restricted error telescopes, using unit-norm atoms and the triangle inequality: ||x~_m - sum_{S* i in}||_1 + lambda = O(lambda). So the trick is entirely the ERC implies null-space-property implies L1 control of off-support coefficients chain; the geometry of M is never used beyond "it lies in Im(V)". Two remarks the paper makes itself: the result is about an idealized decoder and leaves an unquantified amortization gap to the trained encoder; and the pseudoinverse bound is stated but not used in the displayed argument.} z_i D_i|| = ||D_{S_bar} z_{S_bar} + r|| <= ||z_{S_bar

Lemma 1 (Point-based landmarks do not approximate factor manifolds). Claim: let M_1 in V_1, M_2 in V_2 be compact with V_1 orthogonal to V_2 and 0 not in M_2; let P = {P_1,...,P_c} in M_1 + M_2 achieve simplicial capture (Def. 5: Hausdorff distance <= epsilon) of the joint manifold at precision epsilon. Then every landmark satisfies d(P_j, M_1) >= inf ||m_2|| - epsilon; in particular if inf ||m_2|| = delta > 0, every landmark is at distance >= delta - epsilon from M_1.

Proof (two lines, and the orthogonality is the whole trick): by simplicial capture, P_j = m_1 + m_2 + r with ||r|| <= epsilon. Let Pi_{V_2} be orthogonal projection onto V_2. For any m_1' in M_1 in V_1, orthogonality gives Pi_{V_2}(m_1) = Pi_{V_2}(m_1') = 0, hence ||P_j - m_1'|| >= ||Pi_{V_2}(P_j - m_1')|| = ||m_2 + Pi_{V_2}(r)|| >= ||m_2|| - epsilon, and taking infima on both sides gives the claim. The surrounding argument (illustrated in Fig. 15) is the more interesting half: the convex hull of landmarks tiling M_1 + M_2 is fundamentally different from conv(M_1) + conv(M_2). Given x = m_1+m_2 and x' = m_1'+m_2' with landmarks P_a approx x, P_b approx x', the valid reconstruction (P_a + P_b)/2 corresponds to no observation: (m_1 + m_1')/2 is generically a chord, not an arc of M_1. The simplex constraint sum_j z_j = 1 couples all factors, so no subset of landmarks isolates M_1 — each landmark encodes one specific joint configuration. Direction-based SAEs escape because x_hat = sum_j z_j D_j has no coupling constraint, so partial reconstruction over M_1-aligned atoms isolates that factor regardless of what else is active. The paper suggests the fix — a blockwise simplex or a Minkowski-sum decoder (Fel et al. 2025b) — and leaves it as future work. This is the paper's genuinely novel theoretical content and the "impossibility claim for current SAE architectures directly motivated by manifold learning algorithms" promised in Section 1.

Proposition 1 is a cited classical result (Besag 1974, a special case of Hammersley-Clifford), used to license the Ising construction: for p(s) > 0, the pairwise factorization holds iff J_ab = 0 iff s_a and s_b are conditionally independent given the rest. No new proof.

Everything else in the "framework" is definitional/geometric: Def. 2 (additive mixture), Def. 3 (subspace capture), Def. 4 (direction/point duality), Def. 5 (simplicial capture via Hausdorff distance plus Niyogi-Smale-Weinberger reach conditions for Vietoris-Rips homotopy recovery), Def. 6 (signed cohesion and the three-regime classification). These are well-chosen and operationalizable, but they are definitions with no accompanying guarantees — there is no theorem characterizing when a trained SAE lands in one regime rather than another, which is the question the empirics are left to answer by measurement.

Broader context

The subfield. Mechanistic interpretability tries to decompose a network's internal activations into human-legible parts. The dominant tool since 2023 is the SAE: train an overcomplete dictionary on activations with a sparsity constraint, read each atom as a "feature", and interpret the model in terms of which features fire. The intellectual lineage is sparse coding (Olshausen & Field 1996/1997) and dictionary learning, with superposition (Elhage et al. 2022) supplying the motivation: a d-dimensional layer can encode many more than d sparsely-active concepts as nearly-orthogonal directions, packed roughly as a Grassmannian frame, so an overcomplete L0-constrained decomposition should disentangle them. Everything downstream — automated interpretability labels per atom, probing with atoms, steering by adding alpha_D_i — is load-bearing on the assumption that _one atom = one concept = one direction_. The present paper's point is that if a concept is a k_i-dimensional curved object whose _distances carry meaning* (the Karkada et al. uncertainty-geometry result), then that assumption is wrong in a way that does not show up in the standard VE-vs-L0 evaluation at all: the SAE still reconstructs, the geometry is still there, it is merely smeared across a redundant cover whose organizing logic is invisible per-atom. That reframing explains a cluster of known negative results (seed instability, brittle steering, autointerp failure) without blaming the optimizer.

Closely related work worth knowing. (i) Engels et al., Not all language model features are one-dimensionally linear — the paper that established multi-dimensional/circular features (days, months) in LMs and clustered features by decoder similarity to find them; this paper's metric comparison is a direct, pointed refutation of that clustering choice (manifold membership is functional, not geometric). (ii) Hindupur, Lubana, Fel & Ba, Projecting assumptions: the duality between sparse autoencoders and concept geometry — the source of the "each dictionary-learning variant encodes an implicit geometric assumption about concepts" framing that App. C's Def. 4 formalizes into the direction/point dichotomy; read alongside Fel et al. 2025b (Into the rabbit hull, Minkowski geometry of DINO concepts) which supplies the constructive alternative the paper gestures at. (iii) Michaud, Gorton & McGrath, Understanding sparse autoencoder scaling in the presence of feature manifolds — the complementary scaling-law view of the same phenomenon: manifolds consume dictionary capacity, so widening an SAE buys you more tiles rather than more concepts. (iv) For the classical half: Elhamifar & Vidal on SSC and Tschannen & Bölcskei on matching-pursuit subspace clustering, which is where the subspace-preserving condition and the n x n self-expression affinity come from, and against which the atom-level c x c Ising affinity is the paper's structural innovation.

A plausible follow-up. The obvious missing experiment is also the obvious next paper: group-level intervention as the test of capture. Use the Ising pipeline to recover G_M, estimate the coefficient trajectory along a manifold, and steer by moving along that trajectory in the recovered subspace, benchmarking against single-feature steering and against PCA-centroid steering on the Section 3 target-token readouts. The paper's three boxed explanations for prior SAE failures all become falsifiable this way, and dilution predicts something specific and testable: single-atom steering should move representations off-manifold (measurable as distance to the manifold's affine hull / increase in reconstruction residual) while group steering should not. A second, more theoretical follow-up: a group-sparse featurizer — replace ||z||_0 <= k with a block-structured budget over learned atom groups (group lasso / block-TopK with an Ising-style prior on co-activation), which would make capture the loss-preferred solution instead of one of several loss-equivalent ones, and would turn Def. 6's rho(G) from a diagnostic into a training objective. The theory gap worth attacking is the one the paper names and does not fill: under what conditions on manifold volume, curvature, dictionary width c and budget k does the TopK optimum prefer tiling over capture? That is a tractable question in the synthetic model (eight known embeddings, exact k_i) and is the missing when.

Connections to your work. Three that are real, in decreasing order of how directly the paper's content supports them.

Generative retrieval and semantic IDs — the strongest link, and it is a direct corollary of Lemma 1. Hierarchical semantic docids (DSI-style hierarchical k-means over embeddings, TIGER-style RQ-VAE codebooks) are exactly the point paradigm of Def. 4: a codebook of landmarks P with hard assignment, i.e. z a vertex of the simplex. Lemma 1 and the surrounding chord-vs-arc argument say that landmarks tiling a joint manifold M_i + M_j do not induce tilings of the factors: each codeword encodes one specific joint configuration of all co-active factors, and convex combinations of codewords reach points with no preimage in any factor. Translated to semantic IDs: if the document embedding space is an additive mixture of attribute manifolds (topic x recency x style x entity), then RQ codebooks learn joint-configuration tokens rather than factor tokens, which predicts exactly the compositional-generalization failure mode people report — a docid prefix that cannot be recombined to denote "same topic, different recency", and poor behavior on unseen attribute combinations. The paper names the fix it does not implement: replace the single simplex with a blockwise simplex where separate coefficient groups are independently constrained to different factors, or a Minkowski-sum decoder. That is a concrete, theoretically-motivated architecture change for semantic-ID construction, and a cleanly scoped theory question: under what separation conditions does a blockwise-simplex quantizer recover factor codebooks from additive mixtures?

Learned sparse retrieval. SPLADE-style indices assume a term/latent dimension is a unit of meaning with a posting list. The tiling result says that for a continuous attribute, a sparse code assigns mutually exclusive atoms (strongly negative J_ij in the shattering regime) to adjacent values — the years result is the cleanest case, with separate atoms for the ones digit and the decade. An exact-match sparse index over such a code sees "1887" and "1893" as disjoint terms despite near-zero geodesic distance on the manifold: a learned analogue of lexical mismatch, arising from the sparsity mechanism rather than from vocabulary. Def. 6's signed cohesion rho(G) is directly usable as an index-side diagnostic: a posting-list group with rho <= -tau flags dimensions that should be expanded together at query time. The paper's finding that decoder cosine similarity fails to recover these groups while co-activation statistics succeed is the practically actionable bit — it says term-expansion structure should be mined from co-activation (or Ising couplings) over a corpus, not from embedding-space similarity of the learned term directions.

ANN / vector search. Fig. 8 is, read with an IR eye, a quantizer diagram: sample the ambient space, color each point by its max-activating atom, and you get a Voronoi-like partition of the manifold — precisely what an IVF coarse quantizer or a PQ subspace codebook does, and the paper shows the architectural prior is visible in the partition geometry (angular separability for TopK, linear separability for L1 — i.e. the cosine/spherical-k-means vs inner-product/Euclidean distinction, which is the same choice an index designer makes). Two transferable points. First, if concept values lie on low-dimensional curved manifolds where distance encodes semantic similarity (the paper's Section 3 evidence plus Karkada et al.), then a quantizer whose cells cut across a manifold destroys exactly the relation an ANN index is supposed to approximate, and the paper's receptive-field-spread statistic (median within-atom pairwise distance normalized by the manifold's own mean pairwise distance, in [0,1]) is a ready-made measure of that: it is a manifold-relative cell-coherence score for a codebook, independent of recall@k. Second, the dilution finding has a direct index-theoretic reading: a learned sparse/quantized representation can be reconstruction-faithful (high VE, high recall under full reconstruction) while being non-separating at the level of any individual code dimension — so recall-based index evaluation and attribute-level separability are genuinely different axes. A follow-up that sits squarely in your area: construct a retrieval benchmark where the ground-truth concept has a known metric (the paper's synthetic manifold zoo is already a usable generator, with exact d_i, k_i and embeddings), and measure the frontier between recall and manifold-geodesic preservation for IVF/PQ/RQ versus an Ising-group-aware codebook. The restricted-R^2 protocol is essentially a "can n codewords span the attribute subspace" test, which is the natural quantizer analogue of subspace-preserving recovery in SSC — a theoretically clean bridge between the sparse-coding literature you already work in and index design.

One caution on all three: the paper's real-LLM manifolds are template-induced one-parameter sweeps over last-token activations, and its synthetic benchmark deliberately equalizes manifold norms and removes concept co-occurrence. Document-embedding spaces have wildly unequal attribute frequencies, strong attribute correlation, and no template control — so the regime label ("dilution") should be treated as a hypothesis to re-measure on retrieval embeddings, not as an imported fact. The measurement apparatus, though — restricted R^2, support size, normalized receptive-field spread, Ising couplings with signed cohesion — transfers essentially unchanged, and would make a solid first empirical section.

title: Transformers are Inherently Succinct
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 14 November 2026

Transformers are Inherently Succinct

Pascal Bergsträßer, Ryan Cotterell, Anthony W. Lin (2025) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19315

Setting and problem

The architecture. The object of study is the unique hard-attention transformer (UHAT), an encoder-only, length-preserving map T: Sigma^+ -> (Q^S)^+. It is a composition of:

  • a symbol embedding emb: Sigma -> Q^D, extended homomorphically to words;
  • UHA layers of width R, each specified by three affine maps A, B: Q^R -> Q^R and C: (Q^R x Q^R) -> Q^S, a mask predicate M: N x N -> {0,1} chosen from exactly three options — M(n,m)=1 (no masking), M(n,m)=1[m<n] ("strict future masking", i.e. attend strictly left), M(n,m)=1[m>n] ("strict past masking", attend strictly right) — and a tie-breaking function tau in {min, max} (leftmost/rightmost). The score is the bilinear form S(v_n, v_m) = ; with U_n = {m : M(n,m)=1} and B_n = argmax over m in U_n of S(v_n, v_m), the attention vector is a_n = v_{tau(B_n)} (and 0 if U_n is empty). The layer outputs C(v_n, a_n);
  • ReLU layers, which are deliberately anaemic: rho_r(v) applies ReLU to one designated coordinate only.

Recognition: a UHAT plus an acceptance vector t in Q^S accepts a word iff <t, v_N> > 0 at the last position (at v_1 for past-masking-only fragments). There is no softmax, no layer norm, no multi-head notation, no autoregressive decoding, and crucially no positional encoding at all — all positional information enters through the three mask predicates ("positional masking", as in Yang et al. 2024; Jerad et al. 2025; Li & Cotterell 2025). Multiple heads and residuals are absorbed into C and extra layers at polynomial cost.

Precision. Transformers are defined over arbitrary rationals Q because that is the most general setting in which the upper bounds hold. All results carry over to fixed precision (a constant number of bits per value, independent of N); the lower bounds hold under the stronger restriction to fixed-precision integers. Footnote 3 is honest about a real caveat: IEEE floating point is non-associative, so claims are relative to a fixed deterministic evaluation order, and any proof step using associativity of summation would need re-checking under another convention.

Comparison classes. (i) LTL over Sigma with top, bottom, Q_a, and, or, not and both strict binary operators S (since) and U (until), with L(phi) the set of words satisfying phi at the last position, and the abbreviations P phi = top S phi, F phi = top U phi, Y phi = bottom S phi, H phi = phi and not P not phi. LTL = FO[<] = star-free = counter-free automata. (ii) Finite automata. (iii) RNNs as quadruples (Sigma, g, h_0, f) with g: (Q^D x Sigma) -> Q^D at fixed precision k; Prop. 1 notes immediately that such an RNN is a DFA with 2^{kD} states. (iv) B-RASP (Yang et al. 2024), a Boolean-valued intermediate language: a sequence P_1,...,P_Pi of bit-vectors indexed by position, beginning with the lookups Q_a, extended by position-wise Boolean operations or attention operations P_{t+1}(i) := (leftmost/rightmost) over j [M(i,j), S(i,j)] V(i,j) : D(i), where S is a score predicate (a filter, not a numeric score), V a value predicate, D the default when no j qualifies, and o(i) the selected position; acceptance is P_Pi(N) = 1.

Succinctness, precisely. Size |R| is the length of the minimal binary encoding (for RNNs the precision k is counted in unary, so an RNN cannot buy 2^k precision at cost k). Then:

  • Def. 2 (f-more succinct): class C1 is f-more succinct than C2 if there is a family {L_n} with representations R1_n in C1 such that every R2_n in C2 for L_n has |R2_n| >= f(|R1_n|). This is an existential lower bound: one witness family suffices.
  • Def. 3 (g-bounded expansion): for every language and every C2-representation there is a C1-representation of size at most g(.). A universal upper bound.

The paper stresses that neither is antisymmetric alone; together they pin a gap. This is the crux of the whole paper and worth belabouring: nothing here is about which languages are expressible. UHATs recognize exactly the star-free languages (Yang et al. 2024) — a strict subclass of the regular languages, strictly weaker than fixed-precision RNNs, which get all of REG. Succinctness asks the orthogonal question: for the same language, how many bits does each formalism need? The classical template is Sistla-Clarke (1985): LTL and counter-free automata are expressively equal, yet LTL is exponentially more succinct, and correspondingly LTL satisfiability is PSPACE-complete while DFA emptiness is in P.

The question, stated. Given that UHATs (fixed precision, positional masking) recognize exactly the star-free languages — the same class as LTL, and a subclass of what RNNs/automata recognize — how large must an LTL formula, an RNN, or a finite automaton be to recognize a language that a polynomial-size UHAT recognizes, and conversely? And, as the computational shadow of the answer: what is the exact complexity of deciding non-emptiness and equivalence of UHATs?

What the literature already had. The expressivity line is well mapped: Hahn (2020) on what self-attention cannot do; Hao-Angluin-Frank (2022) placing UHAT inside AC^0 via circuit complexity; Barceló et al. (2024) on logics accepted by hard-attention encoders; Yang-Chiang-Angluin (2024) nailing masked hard attention = star-free = B-RASP = LTL; Jerad et al. (2025) showing leftmost vs. rightmost unique hard attention split into LTL[P] vs. LTL[F], and that UHAT bounds entail bounds for fixed-precision softmax; Li & Cotterell (2025) characterizing fixed-precision softmax directly; Pérez et al. (2021) at the other extreme (unbounded precision implies Turing-completeness). On complexity, Sälzer-Alsmann-Lange (2025) showed transformer-encoder satisfiability is at least NEXP-hard for fixed precision — which already implies a singly exponential succinctness gap over automata — but in a richer model (mixed soft and hard attention, arbitrary fixed-precision positional encodings), with no completeness result and nothing about LTL or RNNs. Yang et al. (2024) gave a UHAT-to-LTL translation, but only with doubly exponential blow-up (routing through B-RASP). The gap this paper fills: exact succinctness relations against LTL/automata/RNNs, a matching single-exponential UHAT-to-LTL translation, and exact complexity (completeness, not just hardness) in the leanest possible model.

Non-obvious modelling choices, flagged, because the results live in them. (1) No positional encodings. This is what makes the LTL translation possible at all: because the score depends only on value vectors, "the position attention selects" is definable by a position-uniform temporal formula. With arbitrary PEs the score becomes position-dependent and the construction collapses — which is precisely where Sälzer et al. (2025, 2026) find NEXP-hardness and even undecidability. (2) Unique hard attention: attention is an exact argmax with deterministic tie-break, i.e. a pointer. (3) One-coordinate ReLU: the MLP is almost useless; Boolean combinations cost layers linear in their size. So if anything does heavy lifting, it will not be the MLP. (4) Size includes weight bit-lengths, so no exponential information can be smuggled into a single huge rational — and Prop. 12 shows the model cannot generate such values either. (5) Encoder, last-position acceptance: no chain of thought, no generation.

Main idea

Three headline results, which together pin a tight succinctness triangle.

Succinctness separations. There is a family {L_n} recognized by UHATs T_n of size poly(n) whose shortest accepted word has length at least 2^{2^n}. From this single witness family everything follows by "small-model" arguments on the other side: any LTL formula for L_n has size at least c_1 * 2^{c_2 n} (Thm. 15: UHATs are exponentially more succinct than LTL); any finite automaton for L_n has size doubly exponential in n (Thm. 17); and, via Prop. 1, any fixed-precision RNN for L_n is exponentially large (Cor. 18, extended informally to state-space models through Merrill et al. 2024). The engine is that UHATs can implement counters that run from 0 to 2^{2^N} using attention as an exact-match address lookup.

Matching upper bounds. Prop. 12 shows the precision a UHAT ever needs is poly(|T|) bits — a self-bounding property, so the set F of reachable rationals is finite, of size 2^{poly(|T|)}, and enumerable in exponential time. Prop. 13 then converts any UHAT into an equivalent LTL formula in exponential time, improving Yang et al.'s doubly exponential route. Composing with the standard exponential LTL-to-automaton conversion gives: every fixed-precision UHAT has an equivalent automaton of at most doubly exponential size. In the other direction, Prop. 16 gives a polynomial-time LTL-to-UHAT translation. So the UHAT/LTL gap is exactly exponential (at most exponential universally, at least exponential on a witness family) and the UHAT/automaton gap is exactly doubly exponential. That tightness is a stronger deliverable than the abstract advertises.

Verification is EXPSPACE-complete. Thm. 4: non-emptiness for UHATs and for B-RASP programs is EXPSPACE-complete. Thm. 19: UHAT equivalence is EXPSPACE-complete. Contrast with DFAs, where both are polynomial. Hardness holds even for the restricted class using only strict future masking with rightmost tie-breaking, or dually past masking with leftmost (Cor. 11). And a knife-edge: swap the tie-break so that masking and tie-breaking "point the same way" (future masking + leftmost, or past + rightmost) and the LTL image uses only the unary P (resp. F), whose satisfiability is NP-complete — giving non-emptiness in NEXP (Cor. 14).

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever mechanism is attention as content-addressable memory, with the counter value as the address, and the observation that a single attention shape does two different geometric jobs on the same string.

In Lemma 8 the tiling solution tau: [2^N] x [M] -> T is linearized as enc(tau) = enc(1,1)...enc(2^N,1) enc(1,2)... with per-cell blocks enc(i,j) = bin_N(i-1) tau(i,j) #. Then:

  • E_left(i) := rightmost preceding # — gives the horizontally adjacent cell (Item 4);
  • E_down(i) := rightmost preceding # whose N-bit counter equals mine — gives the cell in the same column of the previous row (Item 5).

So a one-dimensional, position-arithmetic-free device checks a two-dimensional tiling constraint, because the counter block is an address and hard attention is an associative lookup by address. Lemma 9 then shows that this address match is expressible as an honest UHAT score: materialize 1 - P_k(i) in extra coordinates and use

sum over k in K of [ P_k(i)P_k(j) + (1-P_k(i))(1-P_k(j)) ] - (1 - S(j)) = |{k in K : P_k(i) = P_k(j)}| - (1 - S(j)),

maximized at |K| exactly when all K bits agree and the filter S(j) holds. Equality of two N-bit numbers becomes one inner product — Hamming agreement — and the argmax turns it into an exact pointer. One attention layer therefore addresses 2^{|K|} slots at description cost O(|K|). That single sentence is the succinctness result; everything else is bookkeeping. Note which component does the work: the bilinear score plus argmax, not the MLP (which is a one-coordinate ReLU) and not positional encodings (there are none).

A second, under-advertised gem: the "aggregate over the whole past" idiom A(i) := rightmost j < i with not A_enc(j), returning 0, defaulting to A_enc(i) — attention searches for a violation, and the default value D(i) fires only when none exists. Hard attention thus implements "there exists" over the masked window in one layer, hence "for all" by negation. This is the mechanistic reason star-free/LTL falls out of this architecture.

Now the critique.

The lower-bound technique is the weakest kind of succinctness argument.
