Since $\eta_t$ is observable cheaply but noisily before committing (one distance computation gives $|q_t-q_{t-1}|$; $k$ more give the exact frontier distances), this is naturally a problem with a costly-information / prediction-with-expert-advice structure, and the right theoretical object is a competitive ratio against the offline optimum that knows every $\eta_t$ — plus a regret bound for learning the session's coherence parameter $p$ online. A $(1+\gamma)$-competitive trigger with $\gamma$ depending on the gap between warm and cold costs would be a far more satisfying contribution than a tuned threshold, and it is squarely a theory-of-IR result.

Broader context

For anyone unfamiliar. Exact nearest-neighbour search in high dimension is hopeless — the curse of dimensionality means you cannot beat brute force by much — so everything practical is approximate. Two families dominate. Partition-based: IVF clusters the corpus (k-means) and at query time scans only the nprobe closest clusters, usually with product quantisation (PQ) to compress vectors so more of them fit in cache/memory; this is FAISS's workhorse. Graph-based: build a sparse graph whose edges connect approximate neighbours, plus long-range edges that make it "navigable" in the small-world sense, then greedily walk toward the query. HNSW (Malkov & Yashunin, TPAMI 2018) adds a hierarchy of increasingly sparse layers so the walk starts coarse and refines — it is the default in Faiss, Milvus, Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector. NSG (Fu et al., VLDB 2019) drops the hierarchy for a carefully pruned monotonic graph with a navigating node. DiskANN/Vamana (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019) builds a flatter, higher-degree graph tuned for SSD residence, letting billion-scale indexes run on one machine; FreshDiskANN (Singh et al., 2021) adds streaming insert/delete, which is what you need when the corpus is a live document store. Graph methods win on the recall–QPS frontier in memory; partition methods remain attractive for compression, filtering and update-heavy workloads.

Closely related directions worth knowing. (1) Semantic caching: GPTCache and the RAG-cache line (Cache-Craft for chunk caches, various KV-cache reuse systems) — the "reuse at the wrong granularity" family that this paper positions against; worth reading precisely to see how uncontrolled their accuracy loss is. (2) Correlated-query execution: CaGR-RAG (arXiv 2505.01164) groups context-related queries to improve I/O locality for disk-based ANN in RAG — the closest neighbour in spirit, operating on batches rather than streams. (3) Theory of graph navigability: beyond the small-world/Kleinberg lineage, the key modern reference is Indyk & Xu's worst-case analysis of HNSW and DiskANN, which supplies the honest limits any CVSS theorem must respect; also worth tracking recent work on the navigable graph as a combinatorial object (sparsity lower bounds for graphs on which greedy search is exact) and on intrinsic-dimension-parameterised complexity. (4) Session-aware and conversational IR: the retrieval-side literature on query rewriting for conversational search (CQR, ConvDR) has spent a decade modelling exactly the correlation structure Reuse exploits — but at the semantic level, never the index level. That disconnect is an opportunity.

A plausible follow-up. Two, actually, and they compose. First, the theory sketched above: define relative drift $\eta$, measure its empirical distribution on real logged sessions across several encoders, state and test the local-navigability property on production HNSW graphs, and prove the $n$-independence result for warm-started refinement under bounded $\eta$ and bounded doubling dimension. Second — and more interesting as a system — reuse the traversal state, not just the result set, and make it a persistent per-session object. Instead of seeding from $\hat N_k(q_{t-1})$, maintain a per-session "search context": the union of visited sets over recent turns, with their distances to a session centroid, structured so that a new query can be answered by re-ranking a cached local subgraph and only expanding beyond it when a certificate (the relaxed stopping rule from (D)) says it must. That turns a session into an incrementally maintained local index, and the natural question becomes a tradeoff curve between the memory held per session and the amortised distance computations per turn — a clean, theoretically respectable formulation with an obvious lower-bound question attached.

Connection to your work, Shiguang. This one is genuinely close, in three distinct ways.

First, as a formalisation opportunity. The paper hands you a well-motivated problem (CVSS) with — as far as the abstract shows — no theory at all. That is the ideal situation for a theoretical IR researcher: the empirical result establishes that the phenomenon is real and worth money, and the clean question "what is the complexity of ANN search over a drifting query stream?" is unclaimed. A drift-parameterised complexity model for session-aware ANN — cost as a function of $(\eta, d_{\mathrm{int}}, k, \text{recall target})$ rather than $(n, d)$ — would be a contribution of the right shape for a theory paper: it reframes an empirical speedup as a statement about when speedup is possible, and it comes with falsifiable predictions ($n$-independence, exponential decay in intrinsic dimension) that a systems paper can check. The competitive-ratio framing of the trigger (E) is a second, independent theory target, and it connects vector search to the online-algorithms literature in a way that hasn't been done.

Second, and this is the part I'd push hardest: generative retrieval is itself a CVSS problem, and nobody seems to have said so. In generative retrieval (DSI, NCI, SEAL, and the semantic-ID line), a docid is produced autoregressively, and beam search over the docid vocabulary is a sequence of decisions each conditioned on the prefix. Every decoding step is, structurally, a query against a correlated stream — the model state at step $t+1$ is a small perturbation of step $t$, and the set of plausible continuations shrinks monotonically. The same reuse logic applies: the candidate set at step $t$ constrains the candidate set at step $t+1$, and the expensive part (scoring a large docid space, or in hybrid systems, retrieving dense neighbours to condition on) should be warm-startable. Even more directly: the hierarchical semantic IDs produced by residual quantisation are exactly a coarse-to-fine partition of the embedding space, so "reuse the previous step's partition probe" and "reuse the previous turn's graph frontier" are the same operation at different levels of a quantisation hierarchy. There is a unification available here — generative retrieval's decoding as navigation of a learned index, with reuse across steps — and the drift model from (A) is the right language for it, because what you'd be bounding is drift in the model's query representation across decoding steps rather than drift in a user's queries across turns. That is a paper, and it is more yours than theirs.

Third, a methodological warning worth internalising. The most instructive flaw in this line of work is the metric choice. "1.6–3.0× QPS at the same recall" is a mean-over-stream claim about a method whose per-query cost is bimodal by construction. Any theory you build on top of reuse should carry the worst case explicitly — per-query recall distributions, latency tails, and the adversarial-stream regime where the trigger is confidently wrong. In a field where average-case speedups get published and worst-case behaviour gets discovered in production, being the person who characterises the tail is a durable position.

Sources: - Pick Up Where You Left Off: An Efficient Solution for Continuous Vector Similarity Search (DOI) - Beihang University publication record (venue, authors, pages) - CaGR-RAG: Context-aware Query Grouping for Disk-based Vector Search in RAG Systems - Cache-Craft: Managing Chunk-Caches for Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation - Yongxin Tong, ACM DL author profile

title: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 13 November 2026

The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data — Soudry, Hoffer, Nacson, Gunasekar & Srebro (2018, JMLR 19:70) — jmlr.org/papers/v19/18-188.html

Setting and problem

Fix a dataset of points with binary labels, and absorb the labels into the data so that every point should receive a positive score. The object of study is the unregularized empirical risk of a homogeneous linear predictor: no intercept, no weight penalty, summing a loss over the per-example margins. Three assumptions carry the paper: the data are strictly linearly separable (with the margin an output of the analysis, not an input); the loss is smooth, positive and strictly decreasing to zero; and — the real modelling commitment — the loss derivative has a tight exponential tail, meaning it is sandwiched two-sidedly between exponentials with controlled approach rates. Logistic and exponential loss both qualify. The algorithm is plain full-batch gradient descent with a constant step size below twice the inverse smoothness.

The decisive structural fact is that the minimizer sits at infinity. For any separating direction, the inner product with the gradient is a sum of strictly negative terms, so there is no finite critical point at all; yet gradient descent on a smooth loss drives the gradient norm to zero. The only way to reconcile these is that the weights diverge in norm while every margin grows and the loss falls to zero. Because the predictor is homogeneous, the classification rule depends only on the direction of the weights, so the divergence is not a pathology but a change of coordinates.

The precise question is therefore: in which direction does gradient descent diverge — does the normalized weight vector converge, and if so, to what? This is a different question from the squared-loss case, where the minimizer is finite and the implicit bias is a statement about a point; here the bias must be a statement about a ray. The surrounding literature bracketed the problem without settling it: margin theory and AdaBoost had established the template "exponential-tailed loss + separable data implies implicit margin maximization in the norm dual to the algorithm's geometry", but for coordinate descent, giving an L1 margin; regularization-path results obtained max-margin from vanishing explicit regularization rather than from the algorithm; and work on implicit regularization in matrix factorization could only characterize the bias under infinitesimal initialization and step size. Nobody had characterized the implicit bias of gradient descent itself for the loss actually used in deep learning.

Two modelling choices deserve flagging. Tightness of the tail is not technical convenience — later work shows polynomial or heavier tails do not reach max-margin at all. And homogeneity is load-bearing: the usual trick of appending a constant coordinate to recover an intercept does not work, because translating back yields a solution that penalizes the intercept too, which is not the SVM solution.

Main idea

The core move is to stop asking where gradient descent converges and instead guess the asymptotic trajectory and verify it. The claim is that the iterates follow a single logarithmically growing ray — the hard-margin SVM direction scaled by the log of the iteration count — plus a residual that is bounded for almost every dataset (and at worst grows like a log-log). Hence the normalized weights converge to the maximum-margin separator: gradient descent, with no norm penalty, no margin constraint, no early stopping, and from any initialization, finds the hard-margin SVM solution.

The intuition for why is clean. Write the weights as a growing scalar times a limiting direction plus a residual. In the gradient, each example contributes an exponential in its own margin; as the scalar grows, the exponents separate by orders of magnitude and only the examples with the smallest margin — the support vectors — survive. The negative gradient therefore becomes asymptotically a non-negative combination of support vectors, which after rescaling is exactly the KKT stationarity condition of the hard-margin SVM. The logarithmic growth rate is then forced by self-consistency: the increment the ansatz must supply has to cancel the support vectors' gradient contribution, and only the log does so.

The rate results are where the paper earns its keep, and they are what make it practically important. The training loss falls like one over the iteration count. The direction converges only like one over the log of the iteration count, and the margin gap likewise. Both are shown tight by an explicit one-point construction. The separation is brutal: to halve the direction error you must square the loss. A further corollary is less comfortable — since the weight norm grows logarithmically and the loss asymptotically behaves like a hinge, the validation loss provably diverges whenever the max-margin predictor misclassifies even one held-out point, while validation 0-1 error keeps improving. A CIFAR-10 experiment reproduces all four signatures. The bias survives momentum and stochasticity, but ADAM converges to a visibly different ray.

The most interesting part

The sharpest thing here is the separation of timescales, and that it is really a theorem about monitoring the right diagnostic. Three pieces of folklore become provable consequences in a model simple enough to be solved completely: keep training after zero training error, because the quantity that generalizes is still moving long after the one you watch has flatlined; do not stop on plateauing training loss, since a loss of 1e-4 versus 3e-5 looks like nothing but is real margin progress; and above all do not stop on validation loss, which must increase while the model is simultaneously getting better in 0-1 error. "Monitor validation error, not validation loss" is a non-obvious, actionable, provable consequence of an asymptotic analysis of logistic regression — a rare thing.

Honest criticism, much of which the authors concede. The deep-network content is thin: the single-layer corollary needs the assumption that ReLU activations eventually stop switching sign, which is a condition on the trajectory rather than on the data and is never verified. Bias in parameter space is not bias in predictor space, and for nonlinear networks many distinct max-margin-in-parameters solutions exist, so gradient descent must have further biases the paper does not identify. The results are purely asymptotic with untracked constants that depend on the data geometry — a dataset with a near-degenerate margin has an enormous burn-in and a vacuous bound at any realistic horizon, so there is no finite-time statement and hence no generalization bound: the paper proves gradient descent finds the max-margin solution, never that the max-margin solution generalizes. And the degenerate-dataset machinery costs an appendix of recursive construction for a measure-zero payoff, while concurrent work closed the same gap more cheaply and handled the non-separable case, which this paper cannot touch.

Proof sketch

What is proved: under separability, a smooth decreasing loss with a tight exponential tail, and any step size below the smoothness threshold, from any initialization, the iterates equal the SVM direction times log t plus a residual that is bounded for almost every dataset. Companion theorems give the exact asymptote when the support vectors span the data, the iterated-logarithm expansion in degenerate cases, the rate table, the divergence of validation loss, a multiclass version converging to the K-class SVM, and the restricted single-layer deep-network corollary.

The strategy is ansatz plus residual, and it is unusually constructive for an implicit-bias proof. Define the residual as the iterate minus the SVM direction times log t minus a constant offset, where the offset is pinned by requiring that the step size times the exponential of its margin equal the SVM dual variable, for each support vector. This choice is the whole trick: combined with SVM stationarity it makes the drift term the ansatz must supply literally equal to the leading asymptotic form of the support vectors' gradient contribution, so the cancellation is exact at leading order rather than approximate. Everything then reduces to showing one scalar sequence — the squared residual norm — stays bounded.

Two mechanisms do that, and the continuous-time exponential-loss warm-up shows both in a page. Support vectors give a self-correcting, dissipative term: after the cancellation, what remains from them has the sign structure of z times (e^{-z} - 1), which is non-positive for every z, so support vectors pull the residual back toward zero — any residual component that increases a support vector's margin shrinks that support vector's gradient, and vice versa. This is a Lyapunov mechanism built out of the exponential tail. Non-support vectors give a summable perturbation: their margins exceed the minimum strictly, so their contribution decays faster than 1/t and integrates to something finite — convergent precisely because they are not support vectors. That strict margin gap is the single most-used inequality in the paper.

Moving to discrete time, the step-size condition earns its keep in exactly one place: telescoping the descent lemma makes the sum of squared gradient norms finite, so the total discretization penalty is a finite budget rather than a per-step error. The bounded-residual lemma then bounds the cross term by a power of t strictly greater than one — strictly greater because of both the margin gap and the two-sided tail rates, which is exactly why tightness must be two-sided. A complementary "improved" bound says that whenever the residual inside the support-vector span is non-negligible, the cross term is bounded by a negative multiple of 1/t, which is not summable and therefore forces the residual down. Genericity is handled by showing the dual variables are rational functions of the data, so a vanishing dual requires the data to lie on a polynomial zero set. The multiclass case is reduced to the binary template by vectorizing and forming pairwise difference features, with the softmax denominator handled by a simple sandwich.

Broader context

Implicit bias is the study of which minimizer a gradient method actually selects when the risk has many. The canonical easy case is underdetermined least squares, where gradient descent from zero finds the minimum-norm interpolant. The hard and important case is classification with cross-entropy on separable data, where no minimizer exists and the bias must be a direction — which is what this paper settles for linear models. The organizing principle of the whole subsequent literature is visible here: the algorithm's geometry determines the norm whose margin is maximized. Gradient descent gives L2; coordinate descent and AdaBoost give L1; steepest descent with respect to a norm gives that norm's margin.

Worth reading alongside it: Gunasekar et al. on implicit regularization in matrix factorization and in linear convolutional networks, which shows the induced norm depends on architecture and — strikingly — that switching from squared to exponential loss makes the result independent of initialization, because diverging iterates drown all finite initialization effects ("divergence makes the analysis easier" is a real methodological lesson); the same group's characterization of steepest descent under general norms, which explains the ADAM failure and warns that adaptive methods' limit directions are not robust. Ji and Telgarsky closed the degenerate case concurrently with a looser bound but went further where it matters, handling the non-separable case. Nacson et al. showed the bias survives SGD, that the exponential tail is rate-optimal while polynomial tails fail entirely, and that normalized gradient descent improves the logarithmic rate to a polynomial one — the practical antidote to the slowness. Lyu and Li generalized the whole story to homogeneous networks of any degree, vindicating the intuition that homogeneity rather than linearity is the operative structure; Chizat and Bach did the parameter-to-function-space translation the authors flagged as open.

A natural follow-up is to make the rates non-asymptotic and data-dependent — bound the burn-in and the constants explicitly in terms of the margin gap, the support-vector conditioning and the tail rates, then combine with a margin-based generalization bound to get an anytime risk bound, turning the paper's qualitative advice into an actual stopping rule.

Connection to your work. Part of this is genuine and part is a stretch, so let me separate them. The genuine part: in-batch softmax contrastive training of a dual-encoder retriever is exactly the multiclass cross-entropy of the multiclass theorem, with K the batch size. If the document side is effectively frozen — a late-stage fine-tune, a frozen corpus, a linear probe over fixed embeddings — then you are literally in this setting, and the theorem says the learned geometry converges in direction to the K-class hard-margin SVM solution, determined entirely by the hardest negatives, with easy negatives contributing a summable remainder and dropping out of the asymptotic solution altogether. That is a theoretical rationale for hard-negative mining that does not route through hand-waving about small gradients: the limit does not depend on the easy negatives at all. It also yields three testable predictions for retrieval practice — embedding norms should grow logarithmically during long unregularized contrastive training while the retrieved ranking converges only inverse-logarithmically, so the index keeps shifting long after the loss plateaus; contrastive validation loss will provably increase while nDCG and Recall@k improve, making loss-based early stopping on a retrieval dev set actively harmful; and since practically everyone trains with ADAM, the limiting geometry is not the max-margin one and may depend on initialization and step size, which bears on index reproducibility. Note also that cosine scoring is scale-invariant in precisely the way the homogeneous predictor is, whereas a temperature or an additive bias breaks the correspondence.

Where the link is weaker and I would not push it: generative-retrieval decoders over docid vocabularies are not usefully in this setting. The per-step softmax is formally the right template, but the predictor is a deep non-homogeneous transformer, the effective inputs depend on the model's own prefix, and hierarchical docids make the label space combinatorial with shared sub-tokens — so separability, fixed features and homogeneity all fail at once. The honest statement is that this paper offers an intuition for generative retrieval but no theorem, and the right tools there are the homogeneous-network and function-space-margin results instead. Likewise there is no genuine connection to vector-search indexing theory, which concerns geometry given fixed vectors rather than how the vectors arose. The real bridge, if you want to build one, is upstream: a non-asymptotic multiclass version for frozen-corpus dual encoders, with the resulting margin fed into a retrieval-metric generalization bound, would be a defensible theoretical-IR contribution.

title: Understanding the unstable convergence of gradient descent
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 13 November 2026

Understanding the unstable convergence of gradient descent — Ahn, Zhang & Sra (2022, ICML / PMLR v162) — proceedings.mlr.press/v162/ahn22a.html

Setting and problem

The object of study. Plain, deterministic, constant-step-size gradient descent on a differentiable cost $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$:

$$\theta^{t+1} = \theta^t - \eta\nabla f(\theta^t),\qquad F(\theta) := \theta - \eta\nabla f(\theta).$$

No stochasticity until Section 5, no momentum, no adaptivity, no architecture-specific structure. The paper writes $f$ for the training loss of a neural network with parameters $\theta$, and the experiments instantiate $f$ as full-batch cross-entropy on 5,000 CIFAR-10 examples with a fully connected network (two hidden layers of width 200, with linear / $\tanh$ / ReLU variants), following Cohen et al. (2021). "Sharpness" throughout means $\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(\theta^t))$ — the top Hessian eigenvalue at the current iterate, a local, trajectory-dependent quantity, not a global constant.

The classical constants and the classical argument. $f$ is $L$-smooth if $|\nabla f(\theta)-\nabla f(\theta')|\le L|\theta-\theta'|$ for all $\theta,\theta'$. This yields the descent lemma

$$f(\theta^{t+1}) \le f(\theta^t) - \eta\Big(1 - \tfrac{\eta L}{2}\Big)|\nabla f(\theta^t)|^2, \tag{1.1}$$

whose right-hand side is a strict decrease precisely when $L < 2/\eta$. The paper calls $L<2/\eta$ the stable regime and $\eta > 2/L$ the unstable regime. Essentially the whole first-order optimization literature — convex, nonconvex, SGD, variance-reduced — is built on top of (1.1) and therefore on the stable-regime condition.

Why that condition looked not merely sufficient but necessary: on a quadratic $f(\theta)=\tfrac12\theta^\top P\theta + q^\top\theta + r$, GD diverges as soon as some eigenvalue of $P$ exceeds $2/\eta$, and for convex quadratics this is an iff (their Fact 1; Example 1 uses $f=20\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2$, so $L=40$, and shows convergence at $\eta=2/41$ and divergence at $\eta=2/39$). Since NTK-style analyses (Jacot et al. 2018; Li–Liang 2018; Lee et al. 2019) linearize the network and make the effective problem quadratic, the same conclusion was inherited by much of deep learning theory.

The empirical disagreement that motivates the paper. Cohen et al. (2021) ran full-batch GD on real networks and found that (i) sharpness grows during training until it crosses $2/\eta$ ("progressive sharpening"), (ii) it then hovers at or just above $2/\eta$ rather than growing further or causing blow-up ("edge of stability", EoS), and (iii) the training loss keeps decreasing in the long run while oscillating violently at short timescales. So the classical condition is flatly violated for most of training, and yet optimization works — and, per Cohen et al. and this paper's Remark 4, works faster at larger $\eta$ (though not arbitrarily: at $\eta=2/10$ their loss does diverge).

The precise question. Not "can we prove a rate for GD at the edge of stability" — the paper deliberately does not attempt that. The questions it poses are:

  1. _If $\eta > 2/L$, can GD converge to a stationary point at all — and if the answer is no, what is "convergence" in Figure 1 actually converging to?_
  2. What structural features of a nonconvex landscape make the iterates stay bounded (rather than diverge, as the quadratic intuition demands) while the classical descent inequality is violated?
  3. What are the measurable, falsifiable signatures of unstable convergence, and how are they logically related to each other? Concretely: why does the per-step relative loss progress hover around $0$ rather than being bounded away from zero as (1.1) would give; why do adjacent gradients become nearly antiparallel; and can one derive the sharpness-$\approx 2/\eta$ observation from the loss-level observation rather than assuming it?

Two non-obvious modelling choices, both central. First, the paper abandons the global smoothness constant $L$ and replaces it with a directional, update-dependent surrogate: for an update vector $v$,

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta;v) := \frac{\langle v,\ \nabla f(\theta)-\nabla f(\theta-v)\rangle}{|v|^2}\quad\text{(directional smoothness)},$$

which is a Rayleigh-quotient-like second difference of $f$ along the single direction actually taken, bounded above by $\sup\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f)$ on the segment but typically far smaller. Second, the progress measure is a ratio, not a difference:

$$\mathrm{RP}(\theta) := \frac{f(\theta - \eta\nabla f(\theta)) - f(\theta)}{\eta|\nabla f(\theta)|^2}\quad\text{(relative progress)}.$$

The descent lemma says exactly $\mathrm{RP}\le -(1-\eta L/2) < 0$ in the stable regime. Both definitions are reverse-engineered so that an exact identity links them (Theorem 2); readers should keep in mind that $\mathrm{RP}$ has $|\nabla f|^2$ in the denominator, so it is a numerically delicate quantity exactly where the gradient gets small. Also note the paper's framing choice that $\eta$ and the oscillation threshold are tied: everything is phrased in terms of the fixed ratio $2/\eta$, and the step sizes in experiments are written as $2/30$, $2/60$, etc., so "$\eta=2/30$" should be read as "the threshold sharpness is 30".

Main idea

Three moves.

(A) Rule out the naive picture. Theorem 1: for almost every initialization, GD cannot converge to a stationary point $p$ whose Hessian has either a negative eigenvalue or $\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(p)) > 2/\eta$. One supercritical eigendirection is enough. So the hovering seen in practice is not slow convergence to a sharp minimum — the limit point, if any, must be a minimum with sharpness $\le 2/\eta$, and the trajectory must keep moving until it finds one.

(B) Explain why it does not blow up anyway. Two complementary structural claims, both argued rather than proved in generality. Lack of (flat) stationary points near the trajectory: Proposition 1 shows that if the loss has a weight-decay term $\gamma|\theta|_2^2$ and some parameter block $\zeta$ is scale-invariant (as it is in any net with normalization layers — ResNets, Transformers), then there is no stationary point with $\zeta\ne 0$ at all; and with the $\epsilon$-regularized normalization $a/(\epsilon+|a|)$ the stationary points that do exist sit where $|a|\approx\epsilon$ and have sharpness $\sim 1/\epsilon$. Hence practical step sizes are essentially forced into the unstable regime. Forward invariance: convergence survives because nonconvexity can create a compact $S$ with $F(S)\subseteq S$ near the minima. Their toy demonstration is beautifully minimal: take the same $f=20\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2$ and the same divergent $\eta=2/39$, but optimize $\tanh(20\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2)$. Near the minimum the geometry is unchanged ($\tanh x\approx x$), but far away the gradient is squashed, so iterates cannot escape — and GD converges in the "unstable" regime. The single-hidden-neuron version ($f=(\theta_1\theta_2)^2$ vs $f=(\theta_1\tanh\theta_2)^2$ from $\theta^0=(13,0.01)$, $\eta=2/150$) shows the linear net diverging and the $\tanh$ net settling at a minimum whose sharpness is $\approx 2/\eta$. Takeaway: GD "travels along the valley of minima until it finds a flat enough minimum where it can stabilize."

(C) Give a quantitative signature, and derive one signature from another. This is the technical core. Theorem 2 is the exact identity

$$\mathrm{RP}(\theta) = -1 + \frac{\eta}{2}\int_0^1 2\tau\,\mathcal{L}(\theta;\eta\tau\nabla f(\theta))\,d\tau,$$

i.e. $\mathrm{RP} = -1 + \tfrac{\eta}{2}\cdot\overline{\mathcal L}$ where $\overline{\mathcal L}$ is the average of the directional smoothness over the segment $[\theta^t,\theta^{t+1}]$ under the probability density $2\tau$ on $[0,1]$. Oscillation (adjacent gradients nearly antiparallel, $\langle\nabla f(\theta),\nabla f(\theta-\eta\nabla f(\theta))\rangle\approx -|\nabla f(\theta)|^2$) is exactly $\mathcal L\approx 2/\eta$, which forces $\mathrm{RP}\approx 0$. Combined with the informal converse — $\mathrm{RP}$ cannot stay above $0$, else the loss would increase forever, contradicting observed long-run convergence — one gets a two-sided pin: $\mathrm{RP}$ oscillates around $0$ in the unstable regime, versus saturating near $-1$ in the stable regime, and this is equivalent to the iterates oscillating with $\mathcal L(\theta^t;\eta\nabla f(\theta^t))\approx 2/\eta$. Experiments 2–6 confirm both halves and also confirm that $\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\tau\nabla f(\theta))$ barely varies in $\tau\in[0,1]$, so the single value $\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\nabla f(\theta))$ stands in for the integral and (4.3) $\mathrm{RP}\approx -1 + \tfrac{\eta}{2}\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\nabla f(\theta))$ holds numerically.

From here, Corollary 1 gives $\tfrac{2}{\eta}(\mathrm{RP}(\theta^t)+1)\le L_t := \sup_{\theta\in[\theta^t,\theta^{t+1}]}\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(\theta))$, so $\mathrm{RP}\approx 0$ implies $L_t$ frequently exceeds $2/\eta$ — i.e. part A of EoS is a consequence of the loss-level signature, and if additionally $\nabla f(\theta^t)$ is nearly aligned with the top Hessian eigenvector (true for unstable GD on quadratics, and proven for normalized GD by Arora–Li–Panigrahi), the inequality tightens to near-equality and part B ($\lambda_{\max}$ saturating at $2/\eta$) follows too.

(D) SGD. Since SGD's loss is non-monotone anyway, "unstable regime" is hard to define via loss descent; the paper proposes defining it via $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RP}]$, proves the analogous identity $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RP}(\theta)] = -1 + \eta\int_0^1\tau\,\mathbb{E}\big[\tfrac{|g(\theta)|^2}{|\nabla f(\theta)|^2}\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\tau g(\theta))\big]d\tau$, verifies it empirically, and reports the striking observation (consistent with Cohen et al.'s Appendix H) that $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RP}]$ is positive for most of SGD training: minibatch SGD is not decreasing the full-batch loss in expectation, yet the loss decreases in the long run.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever object is Theorem 2 together with the definition of directional smoothness — and what is clever is not the proof (two lines of calculus) but the reframing. The descent lemma is normally used as an inequality with a global constant, and when the constant is wrong the lemma is simply discarded. Ahn–Zhang–Sra instead observe that the descent lemma has an exact identity hiding inside it: define the smoothness surrogate to be exactly the second difference along the actual update direction, averaged with the weight $2\tau$ that the fundamental theorem of calculus hands you, and you get

$$f(\theta^{t+1}) - f(\theta^t) = -\eta\Big(1 - \tfrac{\eta}{2}\overline{\mathcal L}_t\Big)|\nabla f(\theta^t)|^2$$

with no inequality and no assumptions whatsoever. (1.1) is the special case $\overline{\mathcal L}_t\le L$. So "the step size is too large" becomes the measurable statement "$\overline{\mathcal L}_t$ is pinned at $2/\eta$ along the trajectory", and the entire edge-of-stability story becomes a statement about one scalar you can log during training with one extra forward pass. I find this the right kind of theoretical contribution: it converts a phenomenon described by pictures into an identity plus an empirically checkable hypothesis, and it cleanly separates what is tautological (the identity) from what is substantive (that $\overline{\mathcal L}_t\approx 2/\eta$). The secondary cleverness is that this lets them derive the sharpness observation from the loss observation via Corollary 1 — EoS part A is not an independent empirical fact but a consequence, which is a real logical simplification of Cohen et al.'s list of phenomena.

Now the honest criticism, and there is a fair amount.

Theorem 2 is bookkeeping, and the paper's framing can read as more than it is. The identity is assumption-free precisely because it is definitional; all the content is in the empirical claim $\mathcal L\approx 2/\eta$, which is not proved anywhere. The paper is upfront about being a characterization paper, but the rhetoric around "formally justifies that when GD shows an oscillating behavior, $\mathrm{RP}$ cannot stay below zero" overstates things: the implication "oscillation $\Rightarrow$ $\mathcal L\approx 2/\eta$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{RP}\approx 0$" is a change of variables between two ways of saying the same thing. The genuinely hard question — _what restoring force keeps $\mathcal L$ at $2/\eta$ instead of letting it drift up and causing divergence?_ — is untouched. Damian–Nichani–Lee's self-stabilization (2023) is the paper that actually answers it, by identifying the third-order term that pushes $-\nabla\lambda_{\max}$ and gives a cubic-ish feedback law; against that, Ahn et al. supply the right coordinates but not the mechanism.

The "can't stay above zero" half of the two-sided pin is not an argument, it is an assumption. It presupposes long-run convergence, which is exactly what one wants explained. So the headline "$\mathrm{RP}$ oscillates near $0$" is: one side definitional, one side circular. It is still a useful diagnostic — but it is a description of the fixed point of the dynamics, not a proof that the fixed point is reached.

Theorem 1 is close to known. It is the Lee–Simchowitz–Jordan–Recht / Panageas–Piliouras strict-saddle avoidance argument with the instability condition "$\lambda_{\max} > 2/\eta$" substituted for "$\lambda_{\min}<0$". Both conditions are the same condition — $I-\eta\nabla^2 f(p)$ has an eigenvalue of modulus $>1$ — so the extension is essentially free, and the authors acknowledge the lineage. Moreover Assumption 1 is stated more casually than it deserves: "for any measure-zero $S$, $F^{-1}(S)$ is measure zero" is a global non-degeneracy condition on $F$, effectively requiring $1/\eta\notin\mathrm{spec}(\nabla^2 f)$ broadly enough that $F$ is locally invertible, whereas the second half of the assumption only imposes this at stationary points. For a ReLU network the loss is not even $C^2$, so Theorem 1 does not formally cover the paper's own headline experiment. And the theorem's conclusion is purely negative: it says where GD doesn't go, not that it does anything productive.

Proposition 1 is both trivial and sloppily written. What is called "positive homogeneity", $f(x_i,[\xi,\zeta])=f(x_i,[\xi,c\zeta])$ for $c>0$, is degree-zero homogeneity, i.e. scale invariance — not positive homogeneity in the standard degree-1 sense. The written proof ("if $\nabla_\zeta\gamma|\theta|^2\ne 0$ then the sum $\ne 0$") is a non-sequitur as stated; what makes it true is the orthogonality $\langle\nabla_\zeta f,\zeta\rangle = 0$, giving $\langle\nabla_\zeta\ell,\zeta\rangle = 2\gamma|\zeta|^2 \ne 0$ for $\zeta\ne 0,\gamma>0$. Fine once fixed, but one line of Euler's identity.

There is unresolved tension between Proposition 1 and the rest of the paper. If the loss has no stationary points, then Theorem 1 is vacuous, and the picture "GD travels along the valley until it finds a flat enough minimum where it stabilizes" has no terminal object. What the iterates converge to in the normalized-net-plus-weight-decay regime is left completely open. Relatedly, Takeaway 2 attributes forward invariance to activation functions, and the evidence is the $\tanh$ story — but ReLU is positively homogeneous and does not flatten the landscape away from the minimum, and yet the ReLU experiments converge just as well. The real source of saturation in their experiments is plausibly the cross-entropy loss and the softmax, not the activation; the paper does not distinguish these, so Takeaway 2 is under-supported by its own Experiment 1.

Experimental scope and measurement hygiene. Everything is a 2-to-4-hidden-layer MLP of width 200 on a 5,000-example CIFAR-10 subset. No convnets, no transformers, no scale, one dataset, one loss; there is no ablation separating architecture, loss function and weight decay, despite Proposition 1 making weight decay and normalization the load-bearing ingredients. More specifically: $\mathrm{RP}$ divides by $|\nabla f(\theta)|^2$, and in the SGD experiments the reported values reach 30–40, which is what one expects when the full-batch gradient norm collapses while the minibatch update stays $O(1)$. The estimator for $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RP}]$ (how many minibatch samples, what variance) is never described, and the quantity is measured only once per epoch. The counter-intuitive Remark 7 (SGD increases the loss in expectation) is therefore exactly the claim most exposed to a small-denominator artifact; it is reported as a curiosity rather than investigated, which is a missed opportunity since it is the most provocative empirical observation in the paper.

Minor: the related-work section writes "the sharpness at the iterate goes beyond the threshold $\eta/2$", a typo for $2/\eta$. Fact 1's "iff" for convex quadratics quietly ignores the measure-zero set of initializations orthogonal to the supercritical eigenspace and the exactly-critical case $\lambda=2/\eta$, which gives a period-2 orbit rather than divergence — ironically the borderline case that is the whole subject of the paper.

Net assessment: a well-chosen, well-written conceptual paper that supplies vocabulary and a diagnostic the subfield went on to use, with one elegant identity and otherwise light theory. It is the kind of paper that is more useful than its theorem count suggests, and weaker than its framing suggests.

Proof sketch

Four results; I will state each precisely and then give the mechanism.

Fact 1 (warm-up, standard). On $f(\theta)=\tfrac12\theta^\top P\theta + q^\top\theta + r$, GD diverges if some eigenvalue of $P$ exceeds $2/\eta$; for convex quadratics this is iff. Mechanism: diagonalize. In the eigenbasis the iteration decouples into $\langle q_i,\theta^t\rangle = (1-\eta\lambda_i)^t\langle q_i,\theta^0\rangle$ (plus an offset), so each coordinate contracts iff $|1-\eta\lambda_i|<1$ iff $0<\lambda_i<2/\eta$. One-dimensional reduction per eigendirection; no cleverness, but it is the template for everything else — the paper reuses it in Example 4 to show that at $\eta=2/\lambda_{\max}$ the iterate becomes $\theta^t\approx(-1)^t\langle q_{\max},\theta^0\rangle q_{\max}$, a pure sign-flipping oscillation along the top eigenvector, for which $\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\nabla f(\theta))=2/\eta$ exactly in the limit. This is the sanity check that the directional-smoothness definition measures what it claims to.

Theorem 1 (no convergence to supercritical stationary points). Assumptions: $f$ is $C^2$ on a region $\mathcal X$; Assumption 1 — $F(\theta)=\theta-\eta\nabla f(\theta)$ maps null sets to null sets under preimage ($S$ measure zero $\Rightarrow F^{-1}(S)$ measure zero) and every stationary point $p$ satisfies $1/\eta\notin\lambda(\nabla^2 f(p))$; and every stationary point $p\in\mathcal X$ has $\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(p))<0$ or $\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(p))>2/\eta$. Guarantee: there is a measure-zero $N$ such that for every $\theta^0\in\mathcal X\setminus N$, GD does not converge to any stationary point in $\mathcal X$.

Strategy: dynamical-systems saddle-avoidance via the Stable Manifold Theorem, following Lee et al. (2016) and Panageas–Piliouras (2017). Four steps.

  1. _$F$ is a local diffeomorphism at each stationary point._ $F$ is $C^1$ since $f$ is $C^2$; its Jacobian is $DF(p) = I - \eta\nabla^2 f(p)$, which is invertible exactly when $1/\eta\notin\lambda(\nabla^2 f(p))$. Inverse function theorem.
  2. _Each such $p$ has an unstable direction._ This is the key translation and the only place the $2/\eta$ threshold enters. The eigenvalues of $DF(p)$ are $1-\eta\mu$ for $\mu\in\lambda(\nabla^2 f(p))$. If $\mu<0$ then $1-\eta\mu>1$; if $\mu>2/\eta$ then $1-\eta\mu<-1$. Either way $|1-\eta\mu|>1$, so $\dim E^u\ge 1$, where $E^s\oplus E^c\oplus E^u$ is the splitting of $\mathbb{R}^d$ by $|{\cdot}|<1,=1,>1$. Note the elegance: a negative eigenvalue (classical saddle escape) and a supercritical positive eigenvalue (large step size) are the same hypothesis about $DF$, approached from opposite ends of the spectrum. That is the one-sentence idea of the theorem.
  3. Local trapping. The Stable Manifold Theorem (Shub, Thm III.7) gives, around each $p$, a ball $B_p$ and a local invariant $C^r$ embedded disc $W^{s\oplus c}_{\mathrm{loc}}(p)$ of dimension $\dim(E^s\oplus E^c) \le d-1$, with the property that any point whose entire forward orbit stays in $B_p$ must lie on $W^{s\oplus c}_{\mathrm{loc}}(p)$. Since $\dim E^u\ge1$, that disc has measure zero.
  4. Globalize by countability. Cover the stationary set $S$ by $\bigcup_p B_p$; Lindelöf's lemma extracts a countable subcover ${B_{p_i}}$. If GD converges to a stationary point, its orbit is eventually trapped in some $B_{p_i}$, hence eventually lies on $W^{s\oplus c}_{\mathrm{loc}}(p_i)$, hence $\theta^0\in F^{-t}(W^{s\oplus c}_{\mathrm{loc}}(p_i))$ for some $t$. So the bad set is contained in $N := \bigcup_{i}\bigcup_{t\ge0} F^{-t}(W^{s\oplus c}_{\mathrm{loc}}(p_i))$, a countable union of null sets (using the preimage half of Assumption 1), hence null. ∎

The two load-bearing tricks are therefore: the spectral translation in step 2, and the Lindelöf argument in step 4, which is what lets the result cover non-isolated stationary points — important for overparameterized nets, where minima form manifolds. Remark 1 notes the assumption $1/\eta\notin\lambda(\nabla^2 f(p))$ can be weakened to "the open cover $C$ covers all of $S$".

Proposition 1 (no stationary points with weight decay + scale invariance). Assumption: $\ell(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_i f(x_i,\theta)+\gamma|\theta|*2^2$ with $\theta=[\xi;\zeta]$ and $f(x_i,[\xi,\zeta])=f(x_i,[\xi,c\zeta])$ for all $c>0$. Guarantee: $\ell$ has no stationary point with $\zeta\ne0$. Mechanism: Euler's identity for degree-0 homogeneity, $\langle\nabla*\zeta f(x_i,[\xi,\zeta]),\zeta\rangle = 0$ (differentiate the invariance in $c$ at $c=1$). The data term's $\zeta$-gradient is therefore orthogonal to $\zeta$ while the weight-decay term's is parallel to it, so they cannot cancel: $\langle\nabla_\zeta\ell,\zeta\rangle = 2\gamma|\zeta|^2\ne 0$. One line; as noted above the paper's written version skips the inner product and is not logically valid as printed.

Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 (the identity). Assumption: $f$ differentiable; nothing else. Guarantee: exactly $$\mathrm{RP}(\theta) = -1 + \frac{\eta}{2}\cdot 2\int_0^1 \tau\,\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\tau\nabla f(\theta))\,d\tau.$$

Mechanism: integrate along the update segment and then insert the definition of $\mathcal L$. With $g:=\nabla f(\theta)$ and $\phi(\tau):=f(\theta-\eta\tau g)$, $\phi'(\tau) = -\eta\langle g,\nabla f(\theta-\eta\tau g)\rangle$, so $$f(\theta-\eta g)-f(\theta) = -\eta\int_0^1\langle g,\nabla f(\theta-\eta\tau g)\rangle d\tau = -\eta|g|^2 - \eta\int_0^1\langle g,\ \nabla f(\theta-\eta\tau g)-\nabla f(\theta)\rangle d\tau.$$ The trick is that the second integrand is precisely $-\eta\tau|g|^2\,\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\tau g)$: with $v=\eta\tau g$, $\mathcal L(\theta;v)=\langle v,\nabla f(\theta)-\nabla f(\theta-v)\rangle/|v|^2 = \langle g,\nabla f(\theta)-\nabla f(\theta-\eta\tau g)\rangle/(\eta\tau|g|^2)$. Substituting and dividing by $\eta|g|^2$ gives the identity. The $\tau$-weight is not a modelling choice; it falls out of the Jacobian of the substitution, and since $\int_0^12\tau\,d\tau=1$ the bracket is an honest weighted mean of $\mathcal L$, which is why the identity reads as "$\mathrm{RP}=-1+\tfrac{\eta}{2}\overline{\mathcal L}$" — i.e. an exact descent lemma with a trajectory-dependent, direction-dependent smoothness constant replacing $L$.

Corollary 1 then just relaxes the mean to a sup: for every $\tau$, $\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\tau\nabla f(\theta))$ is a second difference along a segment contained in $[\theta^t,\theta^{t+1}]$, hence $\le L_t:=\sup_{\theta\in[\theta^t,\theta^{t+1}]}\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2f(\theta))$ by Taylor/mean value in the chosen direction; averaging preserves the bound, giving $\tfrac{2}{\eta}(\mathrm{RP}(\theta^t)+1)\le L_t$. The refinement to EoS part A takes $\tau\to0$, where $\mathcal L(\theta^t;\eta\tau\nabla f(\theta^t))\to \langle u,\nabla^2f(\theta^t)u\rangle$ with $u$ the normalized gradient direction, hence $\le\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(\theta^t))$ pointwise at the iterate; and the refinement to part B adds the (empirically and, for normalized GD, provably motivated) assumption that $\nabla f(\theta^t)$ is nearly parallel to the top eigenvector, which turns that Rayleigh-quotient inequality into an approximate equality so that $\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2f(\theta^t))\approx\tfrac2\eta(\mathrm{RP}+1)\approx 2/\eta$. Note the logical status: the step from the $\tau$-average to the $\tau\to0$ limit is licensed only by Experiment 5's finding that $\mathcal L$ is nearly constant in $\tau$ — an empirical input, equivalent to assuming some Hessian-Lipschitz-like regularity along the trajectory (the paper's own Remark 5 flags this as a candidate replacement for gradient-Lipschitzness in future neural-net theory, which I think is the most valuable forward-looking sentence in the paper).

SGD identity. Same computation with $g(\theta)$ a stochastic gradient, $\mathbb{E}[g]=\nabla f$: $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RP}(\theta)] = -1 + \eta\int_0^1\tau\,\mathbb{E}_g\big[\tfrac{|g(\theta)|^2}{|\nabla f(\theta)|^2}\mathcal L(\theta;\eta\tau g(\theta))\big]d\tau$. The $-1$ survives because $\mathbb{E}\langle g,\nabla f\rangle=|\nabla f|^2$; the gradient-noise amplification factor $|g|^2/|\nabla f|^2$ appears because $\mathcal L$ is normalized by $|v|^2=\eta^2\tau^2|g|^2$ while $\mathrm{RP}$ is normalized by $|\nabla f|^2$. That ratio is exactly the quantity that is huge late in training, which both explains why $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RP}]\gg0$ is possible for SGD and, as flagged above, why the measurement is fragile.

Broader context

The subfield in one paragraph. Classical optimization theory treats the step size as something you set below $2/L$ for a fixed $L$. Deep learning breaks this on both ends: $L$ is not fixed (the local sharpness changes as the parameters move — and systematically increases during training, the "progressive sharpening" effect), and practitioners pick $\eta$ far above what the measured local sharpness would permit. The resulting regime — GD oscillating along the top curvature direction while slowly descending a valley, with $\lambda_{\max}$ parked at $2/\eta$ — is what Cohen, Kaur, Li, Kolter & Talwalkar (ICLR 2021) named the edge of stability. Its importance is not just that classical theory is inapplicable; it is that the oscillation appears to be doing something useful: it biases GD toward flatter minima (a sharpness-dependent implicit regularization that lives entirely outside the gradient-flow/NTK picture) and empirically trains faster. Whole lines of theory built on gradient flow, NTK linearization or small-step-size approximations are therefore describing a regime that real training leaves almost immediately.

Closely related work worth knowing. - Cohen et al. (2021), "Gradient descent on neural networks typically occurs at the edge of stability" — the empirical paper that defines the phenomenon and the experimental protocol Ahn et al. reuse verbatim. Read it first; everything here is a response to it. - Arora, Li & Panigrahi (ICML 2022), "Understanding gradient descent on edge of stability in deep learning" — concurrent, and the complement to this paper. They prove EoS rather than characterize it, for normalized GD $\theta^{t+1}=\theta^t-\eta\nabla f(\theta^t)/|\nabla f(\theta^t)|$ near a manifold of minima, and show the dynamics implicitly follow a sharpness-reduction flow along the manifold — which is the rigorous version of Ahn et al.'s "travels along the valley until it finds a flat enough minimum". Also the source of the gradient/top-eigenvector alignment assumption Ahn et al. borrow for EoS part B. - Damian, Nichani & Lee (ICLR 2023), "Self-stabilization: the implicit bias of gradient descent at the edge of stability" — in my view the paper that supplies what Ahn et al. leave out. They identify the third-order Taylor term as a restoring force proportional to $-\nabla\lambda_{\max}$: when $\lambda_{\max}$ exceeds $2/\eta$ the oscillation amplitude grows, which itself reduces sharpness, pushing the system back. That is the feedback law that explains why $\overline{\mathcal L}_t$ is pinned at $2/\eta$ instead of drifting, and it recasts GD at EoS as projected gradient descent on the constraint set ${\lambda_{\max}\le 2/\eta}$. - Ma, Kunin, Wu & Ying (2022) (cited as concurrent) — the subquadratic-growth / multiscale-landscape explanation: near minima the loss grows slower than quadratically, which is a principled version of Ahn et al.'s $\tanh$-flattening and forward-invariance story, and they tie it to data heterogeneity. - Further back: Lewkowycz, Bahri, Dyer, Sohl-Dickstein & Gur-Ari (2020), the catapult mechanism — large-$\eta$ training first catapults the loss up and then lands in a flatter region; Wu, Ma & E (2018) on dynamical stability selecting minima, including the observation that sharp minima vastly outnumber flat ones, which Ahn et al.'s Proposition 1 makes rigorous in the scale-invariant-plus-weight-decay case; and Lyu & Li on normalization, scale invariance and the effective learning rate, which is the natural companion to that proposition.

A plausible follow-up. The most direct one is to take the identity seriously as an assumption-generating device rather than a diagnostic. Since $$f(\theta^{t+1})-f(\theta^t) = -\eta\Big(1-\tfrac{\eta}{2}\overline{\mathcal L}_t\Big)|\nabla f(\theta^t)|^2$$ holds with no hypotheses, one can replace global $L$-smoothness with a trajectory condition such as "$\frac1T\sum_t \big(1-\tfrac\eta2\overline{\mathcal L}_t\big) \ge c > 0$", or "$\overline{\mathcal L}_t \le 2/\eta - \delta_t$ with $\sum\delta_t$ growing linearly", and ask what nonconvex convergence rates follow — a telescoping argument gives $\min_t|\nabla f(\theta^t)|^2 \lesssim \Delta f/(\eta c T)$ immediately, so the whole research question becomes: under what landscape conditions (subquadratic growth, Hessian Lipschitzness along the trajectory, the self-stabilization feedback) can one lower-bound the time-averaged relative progress? That is a cleaner formulation of "prove that EoS training converges" than attacking the dynamics directly. The sibling direction is algorithmic: use $\mathcal L(\theta^t;\eta\nabla f(\theta^t))$, which costs one extra gradient evaluation, as the basis of an online step-size rule $\eta_t \approx 2/\mathcal L$ — essentially a trajectory-adaptive Polyak-style step — and ask whether deliberately steering $\mathrm{RP}$ (rather than letting it settle at $0$) beats a constant step size. There is already work in this vein on directional-smoothness-based step sizes, and the gap between "GD passively sits at $\mathrm{RP}\approx 0$" and "a tuned method could sit at $\mathrm{RP}\approx -c$" is exactly where the paper's own open question about why large $\eta$ trains faster lives. A third, more speculative follow-up: Remark 7's observation that SGD increases the full-batch loss in expectation for most of training deserves a proper study with variance-controlled estimators — if it survives scrutiny, essentially every SGD analysis that relies on expected one-step descent is describing a different algorithm from the one people run.

Connection to Shiguang's work — mostly none, and I would not force one. This is a pure optimization-dynamics paper; it has no bearing on retrieval objectives, index structures, ANN search, or the information-theoretic questions in generative retrieval. I would read it as general theoretical literacy: it is a short, clean example of how to turn an empirical anomaly into an exact identity plus a falsifiable empirical hypothesis, and the Theorem 1 proof is a nice compact exposure to the Stable-Manifold/saddle-avoidance technique, which is worth having in one's toolkit for any "where do the dynamics end up" question.

Two threads are real enough to mention without inflating them. First, Proposition 1 applies verbatim to dual-encoder retrieval training. Dense retrievers $L_2$-normalize their embeddings and train with temperature-scaled InfoNCE, and almost all of them use weight decay — which is exactly the scale-invariance-plus-weight-decay configuration in which the loss has _no stationary points with $\zeta\ne0$_. So the "there is nothing to converge to, and sharpness near the trajectory is large" story should apply with particular force to retrieval encoders, and the temperature $\tau$ enters as a direct rescaling of the Hessian (effective sharpness $\sim 1/\tau$), yielding a concrete and testable prediction: the stable step-size ceiling for contrastive training should scale linearly with temperature, and the commonly observed interaction between temperature, learning rate and warmup in dense retrieval may be an edge-of-stability effect rather than a purely statistical one about hard negatives. Second, and more practically, $\mathrm{RP}(\theta^t)$ is a cheap instrument: one extra forward pass per logged step tells you whether your retriever is training in the stable ($\mathrm{RP}\approx-1$) or unstable ($\mathrm{RP}\approx0$) regime, which is more informative than the loss curve and far cheaper than a Lanczos sharpness estimate. That is a genuinely transferable takeaway. Beyond those, I would resist drawing a line from this paper to vector search or generative retrieval theory — there isn't one, and the paper is worth reading on its own terms.

title: Transformers Provably Learn to Internalize Chain-of-Thought
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-12

Transformers Provably Learn to Internalize Chain-of-Thought

Huang, Zhu, Wang, Jiao, Russell, Sojoudi, Mei, 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28600

Setting and problem

The target class. Fix integers $n \ge k \ge 2$ with $k = \Theta(n)$ and $k = 2^L$ exactly. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the family of size-$k$ subsets of $[n]$. A secret set $S \sim \mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{S})$ is drawn once and held fixed; inputs are $b \sim \mathrm{Unif}({\pm1}^n)$ and the label is the $k$-parity $y = p_S(b) := \prod_{j\in S} b_j \in {\pm 1}$.

The learner sees $B$ i.i.d. samples per training stage, each stage drawing a fresh batch. "Sample complexity" here means: how large must $B$ (and $B \times #\text{stages}$) be so that a prescribed finite-step gradient algorithm, given an $\varepsilon$-approximate gradient oracle, outputs parameters whose test predictions are correct. The paper defines the population error $\mathcal{E}(\theta) := \mathbb{E}_{S,b}[(p_S(b) - f_\theta(b))^2]$, though as noted below the actual theorem bounds something slightly different.

The hardness baseline. An $\varepsilon$-approximate gradient oracle is any $\tilde\nabla L_B$ with $|\tilde\nabla L_B(\theta) - \nabla L_B(\theta)|_2 \le \varepsilon$ everywhere. Proposition 1 (imported from Kim-Suzuki 2024, in the lineage of Shalev-Shwartz-Shamir-Shammah 2017 and Wies-Levine-Shashua 2022) says: if $B = \Omega(n^\nu)$, $|\nabla f_\theta| = O(n^{\nu_1})$, the oracle is $O(n^{-\nu_2})$-accurate, and the algorithm makes $O(n^{\nu_3})$ queries, then with probability $1 - e^{-\Omega(n)}$ the output satisfies $\mathcal{E}(\theta) \ge 1 - O(n^{-\nu_4})$ whenever $\nu = 4\nu_1 + 4\nu_2 + 2\nu_3 + 2\nu_4 + 1$. In words: _polynomially many samples, polynomially accurate gradients and polynomially many queries on the end-to-end squared loss cannot beat trivial accuracy on $k$-parity._ This is the statistical-query-flavoured barrier the paper must tunnel under, and the tunnel is intermediate supervision — not a sharper oracle (the theorem deliberately assumes exactly the $O(n^{-2-\epsilon/8})$ oracle accuracy that keeps it inside Proposition 1's class).

The parity tree and what CoT tokens are. The task is reorganized as a complete binary tree of height $L = \log_2 k$ with $2k-1$ nodes. Level-1 leaves are the secret bits ${b_j : j \in S}$; the $k-1$ internal nodes get indices $n+1,\dots,n+k-1$, bottom-to-top, left-to-right. Write $T := n+k-1$ and $n_\ell := n + k(1 - 2^{-(\ell-1)})$, so $n_1 = n$, $n_{L+1} = T$, and positions $(n_\ell, n_{\ell+1}]$ are exactly the level-$(\ell+1)$ nodes, of which there are $k2^{-\ell}$. Let $h[m]$ be $m$'s level, $c_1[m] < c_2[m]$ its children, $p[j]$ its parent. The recursion $b_m = b_{c_1[m]}b_{c_2[m]}$ holds at every internal node and $b_T = y$.

A CoT-supervised sequence is the length-$T$ string $\mathbf{b} = (b_1,\dots,b_n,b_{n+1},\dots,b_T)$: the raw input followed by every intermediate two-parity. Explicit CoT training asks the model to predict $b_m$ at position $m$ for every $m > n$ — the Kim-Suzuki / Wen et al. setting, where even a one-layer transformer provably learns $k$-parity with $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ samples, at the cost of $\Theta(k)$ sequential decoding steps at inference.

Implicit CoT and the padding convention. ICoT (Deng-Choi-Shieber 2024) progressively deletes intermediate steps during fine-tuning so the model eventually answers directly. Here, deleted thinking tokens are replaced by zeros rather than removed, keeping the sequence length pinned at $T$, justified by appeal to Merrill-Sabharwal's result that padding tokens genuinely expand transformer expressivity. The consequence to keep straight: what is eliminated is the $\Theta(k)$ sequential autoregressive steps, not the $\Theta(k)$ extra positions in the forward pass.

The Log-ICoT curriculum — exactly what is given and demanded. At stage $t \in [L]$ the input sequence is $\mathbf{b}^{(t)} = (b_1,\dots,b_n, 0,\dots,0, b_{n_t+1},\dots,b_T)$ with $n_t - n$ zeros: all CoT tokens at levels $2,\dots,t$ are blanked, levels $\ge t+1$ are still shown. The stage-$t$ loss is the squared loss over the shown-or-above positions only, $L^{(t)}(\theta) = \frac{1}{2B}\sum_{m=n_t+1}^{T}|\Psi_t^\top T_\theta(D)_m - b_m|^2$. So stage 1 is full CoT, stage $t$ blanks $k(1-2^{-(t-1)})$ tokens, stage $L$ blanks everything but the root. Each stage removes half the remaining thinking tokens: chunk sizes $k/2, k/4, \dots, 1$. Standard ICoT's one-at-a-time schedule would need $k-1$ stages for the same end state.

Two things make the per-stage task non-vacuous and are easy to misread. First, the level-$(t+1)$ positions $m \in (n_t, n_{t+1}]$ are _visible in the input at stage $t$ and simultaneously the prediction targets_; the customized mask forbids $m$ from attending to itself or to anything at its own level, so there is no leakage. Second, positions at levels $\ge t+2$ are also in the loss but their targets are shown and copy through the residual stream, so they contribute exactly zero loss and zero gradient — the stage-$t$ gradient is supported entirely on layer $t$'s level-$(t+1)$ block.

Architecture and parametrization. An $L$-layer "simplified transformer" following Wang et al. 2025. All $B$ samples are stacked: token $j$ is the vector $b_j \in \mathbb{R}^B$, the whole dataset is one sequence $D = [b_1,\dots,b_T] \in \mathbb{R}^{B\times T}$, and the embedding dimension is $d := T + B(L+1)$. (This is bookkeeping, not architectural necessity: since $W_V = I$ and the MLP acts pointwise, the $B$ coordinates never mix, so the construction is equivalent to the per-sample model with $L+1$ scalar scratch slots per position. Worth noting, because $d = \Omega(n^{2+\epsilon}\log n)$ otherwise looks like an absurd width requirement.) Embedding: $x_j = (p_j, b_j, 0_{BL})$ with $p_j$ one-hot positional.

  • Attention: one head per layer, $W_{KQ} = W_KW_Q^\top$ reparametrized, and only the upper $T\times T$ block $W^{(\ell)}$ is trainable, all else fixed to zero. Hence attention logits $w^{(\ell)}_{j,m} = p_m^\top W^{(\ell)} p_j$ depend only on positions, never on content. $W_V = I_d$.
  • Mask: level-restricted causal mask: for $m \le n$, ordinary causal; for $m > n$, $m$ may attend only to $j \le n_{h[m]-1}$, i.e. strictly below its own level. So node $m$ can only look at the level directly below and lower.
  • MLP: replaced by a fixed link function $\phi : [-1,1]\to[-1,1]$, symmetric, with $\phi(0) = -1$, $\phi(\pm1) = 1$ — hence $\phi(\frac{a+b}{2}) = ab$ for $a,b \in {\pm1}$, an exact XOR gadget — and crucially $\phi'(0) = \phi'(\pm1) = 0$, with $\phi(t) = -1 + ct^2 + O(t^4)$ near 0. Experiments use $\phi(t) = -\cos(\pi t)$, $c = \pi^2/2$.
  • Gated (highway-style) connections instead of residual: $\mathrm{GC}(A,B;g) = A\,\mathrm{diag}(g) + B(I - \mathrm{diag}(g))$, with the gates fixed, not learned, prescribed from the tree: $g^{(\ell)}_m = 1$ iff $n_\ell + 1 \le m \le n_{\ell+1}$, else 0. Layer $\ell$ writes only at level-$(\ell+1)$ positions; elsewhere the update is muted and the stream just shifts forward.
  • Output/readout: $W_O^{(\ell)}$ is a fixed block-shift moving residual block $[\ell]$ to $[\ell+1]$; $\Psi_\ell$ selects block $[\ell+1]$. So $\Psi_{\ell'}^\top W_O^{(\ell)} \ne 0$ iff $\ell = \ell'$: the stage-$\ell$ readout extracts exactly what layer $\ell$ wrote.

Layer update: $X^{(\ell)} = X^{(\ell-1)} + W_O^{(\ell)}\mathrm{GC}(\phi(\mathrm{Attn}(X^{(\ell-1)}; W^{(\ell)})),\, X^{(\ell-1)};\, g^{(\ell)})$.

Training procedure (Algorithm 1). Initialize $W^{(\ell)}(0) = 0_{T\times T}$ for all $\ell$ — zero init, so attention is uniform over the unmasked set at every untrained layer. Then for $t = 1,\dots,L$: draw a fresh batch of $B$, build the stage-$t$ padded data, take one approximate-gradient step on $L^{(t)}$ with stage-wise learning rate $\eta_t = K_n n_t^2/(2c)$ where $K_n := \lceil n^{\epsilon/16}\rceil$, then round every weight entry to the nearest integer. Total: $L = \log_2 k$ gradient steps, $BL$ samples. Evaluation is at the stage-$L$ configuration: inputs in positions $1..n$, zeros in the $k-1$ CoT positions, read out at position $T$.

The precise question. _Can a curriculum that progressively deletes CoT tokens — so that at inference the answer is produced in a single forward pass with no explicit reasoning tokens — provably retain the $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ sample complexity that explicit CoT buys on $k$-parity, despite the poly-sample/poly-query barrier for end-to-end training; and how many curriculum stages does it take?_

The gap motivating this: expressivity results for padding/pause/filler tokens and learnability results for explicit CoT both exist, but ICoT had zero theory, and all prior parity training-dynamics guarantees were for one-layer models where the depth-vs-serial-steps tradeoff cannot even be posed.

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag up front. (i) Attention is purely positional and $S$ is fixed, so the "learning" problem is positional support recovery for one secret set, not learning a function class. (ii) Zero initialization, hence uniform attention, is what makes the one-step Taylor expansion exact enough. (iii) One gradient step per stage plus integer quantization — the dynamics are not really dynamics; they are a single correlation statistic followed by hard thresholding. (iv) The layer-to-stage correspondence is hard-wired by the fixed gates and the level-restricted mask: layer $\ell$ is told it is responsible for level $\ell+1$. There is no credit-assignment problem across depth. (v) Thinking tokens are zero-padded, not removed. (vi) $\phi$ is a hand-designed exact XOR gadget that is additionally flat at its fixed points — that flatness is load-bearing twice over.

Main idea

Make depth, not decoding time, carry the chain of thought — and teach the layers bottom-up, one tree level per stage.

The parity tree has depth $\log_2 k$, so the whole chain can in principle be evaluated in $\log_2 k$ parallel layers rather than $k$ sequential decoding steps. The obstacle is learnability, not expressivity: at zero init a deep stack has no gradient signal for the upper layers, because their inputs are garbage. The Log-ICoT curriculum resolves this by scaffolding: at stage $t$ the model is still shown the thinking tokens for levels $\ge t+1$ but has had levels $2..t$ blanked, so layer $t$ is forced to reconstruct level $t+1$ from the hidden states that layers $1..t-1$ already computed for the blanked levels. Each stage internalizes exactly one more tree level into one more layer. Since levels have sizes $k/2, k/4, \dots, 1$, "one level per stage" is exactly "delete half the remaining thinking tokens per stage" — geometric chunks — and the stage count collapses from $k-1$ to $\log_2 k$.

The headline (Theorem 1): with per-stage batch $B = \Omega(n^{2+\epsilon})$, an $O(n^{-2-\epsilon/8})$-accurate gradient oracle, and $\eta_t = K_n n_t^2/(2c)$, a $\log_2 k$-layer transformer trained by exactly $\log_2 k$ quantized gradient steps outputs, with probability $1 - e^{-\Omega(n^{\epsilon/2})}$, predictions satisfying $|f_{\hat\theta}(D_{\mathrm{test}})_T - y_{\mathrm{test}}|_\infty \le e^{-\Omega(n^{\epsilon/16})}$ — from input bits alone, all CoT positions padded, one forward pass. Total sample budget $O(n^{2+\epsilon}\log k)$, matching explicit CoT, while Proposition 1 says no poly-query end-to-end method gets non-trivial accuracy at all.

Three engineering-of-the-proof choices do the real work and are presented as contributions in their own right: fixed gated connections (to stop representation collapse across depth), the level-restricted causal mask (to make the children uniquely identifiable from a third-moment statistic), and integer quantization + stage-wise learning rate (to denoise the one-step update and to freeze already-trained layers so stages compose).

The most interesting part

The genuinely sharp technical observation is Lemma 1 plus the gating fix: a precise account of why naive multi-layer parity analysis fails, by a factor of $n$. At zero init, attention at position $m$ is uniform over $[m-1]$, so the pre-activation is $\frac{1}{m-1}\sum_{\alpha<m}b_\alpha$, which concentrates at 0 at rate $\sqrt{\log B/m}$. Because $\phi(0) = -1$ and $\phi$ is quadratically flat there, the post-activation is $-1_B + O(\log(B)/m)$ — i.e. every position in the deeper layers collapses to the same near-constant value, with residual fluctuation $\Theta(n^{-1})$. Meanwhile the token-distinguishing signal the next layer needs is $\Theta(n^{-2})$. In a vanilla residual stream this collapse propagates and the $\Omega(n^{-1})$ junk buries the $n^{-2}$ signal. The fixed gate $g^{(\ell)}_m = \mathbb{1}{n_\ell < m \le n_{\ell+1}}$ surgically prevents a layer from writing at any position that is not its assigned level, so the collapsed values are never written at all. This is a crisp, quantitative diagnosis of a failure mode that one-layer analyses cannot see, and it is the paper's best contribution as insight rather than as theorem.

A second piece of real cleverness is the $K_n = \lceil n^{\epsilon/16}\rceil$ window. The one-step gradient is $-\partial L/\partial w_{j,m} = \frac{2c}{n_t^2}\mathbb{1}{p[j]=m} + R_{j,m}$ with $|R_{j,m}| \le Cn^{-2-\epsilon/8}$. The learning rate $\eta_t = K_n n_t^2/(2c)$ is chosen to cancel the prefactor exactly, mapping the signal to the integer $K_n$ and the noise to $\eta_t|R| \le C'n^{-\epsilon/16} < 1/2$. Nearest-integer rounding then returns exactly $K_n$ on the two children and exactly 0 everywhere else. $K_n$ must be large enough that $ne^{-K_n} = e^{-\Omega(n^{\epsilon/16})}$ (softmax concentration) and small enough that $K_n n^{-\epsilon/8} < 1/2$ (noise rounds away). The two-sided squeeze is where the $\epsilon/16$ exponent in the final bound comes from, and it is neat. There is also a delicate cancellation worth noticing: the two second-order Taylor contractions each contribute $\frac{1}{n_t} + O(\kappa)$ with opposite signs and cancel to $O(\kappa)$ — without that, a spurious $\Theta(n^{-2})$ term (harmless for softmax, since position-independent, but fatal for the integer-rounding argument) would survive.

Now the critique, which I think is substantial.

The theorem is a statement about hard-thresholded one-step correlation estimation, not about training dynamics. One gradient step per layer, from zero init, followed by exact integer quantization, with a learning rate calibrated to the known signal scale $2c/n_t^2$ and to the known link-function constant $c$. Change $\eta_t$ by a constant factor and the quantization argument dies. There is no multi-step optimization, no stochasticity beyond the batch, no loss-landscape content. The honest description of the mechanism is: _estimate, at each node $m$, the empirical third moment $\frac1B\langle b_m, b_\alpha, b_\beta\rangle$ over candidate pairs; by unique factorization in the parity tree this is $\approx B$ only for the true children; threshold._ That the estimator happens to be a transformer gradient is the paper's contribution, but it means phrases like "training dynamics" oversell what is analyzed. (Prior work in this line has the same character; the criticism is about framing, and it is inherited.)

How much of the answer is hard-wired? A lot. The value matrix is the identity; the MLP is a fixed exact-XOR gadget with flat derivative at its fixed points; $W_O$ is a prescribed block shift; the readout is a prescribed selector; the gates are the parity-tree level indicator; the causal mask encodes the tree's level structure. The only trainable object is a $T\times T$ matrix of positional logits. So the architecture already knows (a) that the task is a binary tree of two-parities, (b) the tree's shape, (c) which layer owns which level, (d) how to combine two children. What is learned is solely which two positions are each node's children, i.e. the secret set and the pairing. One can defend (a)-(c) as "the CoT format is given, which is true of ICoT fine-tuning in practice," and the authors are candid about this in Appendix A. But the gating assumption is the strongest: it eliminates cross-layer credit assignment entirely, and credit assignment is precisely the thing one would want a theory of ICoT to explain. Lemma 10's "layer freezing" is likewise a consequence of the hand-designed flatness $\phi'(\pm1) = \phi'(0) = 0$; with a generic MLP, gradients at trained layers would not be exponentially small and the stages would not compose.

What the theorem does not say. (i) It bounds $|f_{\hat\theta}(D_{\mathrm{test}})_T - y_{\mathrm{test}}|*\infty$ on a fresh batch with the same fixed $S$ — it does not bound $\mathcal{E}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}*{S,b}[(p_S(b)-f_\theta(b))^2]$ as defined in Section 2.1, which averages over fresh secret sets. Since attention is positional and $S$ is fixed at training time, the model cannot possibly be accurate on a resampled $S$. Section 3.1 nonetheless says "performance is measured by the population $L_2$ error $\mathcal{E}(\theta)$." This is a genuine mismatch between stated metric and delivered guarantee, even if the delivered guarantee is the natural one. (ii) There is no lower bound on stage count. Theorem 1 shows $\log_2 k$ stages suffice; nothing shows standard ICoT needs $k-1$ (under this gated architecture, most of its stages would simply be no-ops), nor that $\log_2 k$ cannot be beaten — with multiple gradient steps per stage, could one jump from full CoT to all-padded in $O(1)$ stages? The bottleneck in this analysis is that layer $\ell+1$ needs layer $\ell$ already correct, which forces $\ge L$ stages given one step per stage; whether that is intrinsic is open and unaddressed. (iii) Proposition 1 does justify needing some intermediate supervision, but it does not discriminate among curricula.

Inference cost claim is slightly loose. "Eliminating its inference overhead" (abstract) means eliminating $\Theta(k)$ sequential decode steps. The sequence length stays $T = n+k-1$ because removed tokens are zero-padded, and depth grows to $\log_2 k$. So the comparison is serial latency, not FLOPs; Section 3.1 says so, the abstract does not. This is also the respect in which the result is, at bottom, a learnability counterpart to the known expressivity tradeoff (depth/padding vs. serial CoT steps) rather than a free lunch.

The experiments do not test the paper's selling point. One configuration: 4-layer model, $n = 30$, $k = 16$, one fixed $S$, AdamW at lr $10^{-1}$, batch 500, 500 steps per stage. The theory says one quantized gradient step per stage with a specific $\eta_t$ and $B = \Omega(n^{2+\epsilon}) \approx 900+$; the experiment uses an un-analyzed adaptive optimizer, no quantization, 500 steps, and a smaller batch. So nothing in Section 4 corroborates the mechanism the proof is about. More importantly, there is no comparison against standard ICoT, i.e. no measurement of the $k-1$ vs $\log_2 k$ stage count that is the headline practical claim; no scaling in $n$ or $k$; no ablation of the three design choices; and no demonstration that end-to-end training of the same architecture fails. The two things Figures 2(b) and 3 do show are worthwhile and qualitatively on-theory: a transient validation-loss spike at each stage boundary (an "internalization event") that then collapses, and final-stage attention maps in which each layer attends sharply to exactly the two children of each node at its assigned level. What is conspicuously missing and cheap is a linear probe on hidden states at padded CoT positions: the theory predicts $x^{(\ell)}_{m,[\ell+1]} = b_m \pm e^{-\Omega(n^{\epsilon/16})}$, i.e. the removed thinking token is literally recoverable from the residual stream. That is the sharpest falsifiable prediction in the paper and it is not tested.

Net assessment: a clean, honest, somewhat over-engineered first theory of ICoT. The architectural scaffolding is heavy enough that the result is better read as "if the layer-to-level assignment is given, bottom-up curricular internalization provably works and needs only logarithmically many stages" than as "transformers learn to internalize CoT." The representation-collapse lemma and the quantization window are the parts I would keep.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Theorem 1. Assume $k = \Theta(n)$, $k = 2^L$, $L = \log_2 k$ layers, the architecture of Definitions 1-3, zero initialization, per-stage batch $B = \Omega(n^{2+\epsilon})$, an $O(n^{-2-\epsilon/8})$-accurate gradient oracle, and $\eta_t = K_n n_t^2/(2c)$ with $K_n = \lceil n^{\epsilon/16}\rceil$. Then for large $n$, with probability $\ge 1 - e^{-\Omega(n^{\epsilon/2})}$ over the $L$ fresh batches, the output $\hat\theta = \theta(L)$ of Algorithm 1 satisfies $|f_{\hat\theta}(D_{\mathrm{test}})_T - y_{\mathrm{test}}|_\infty \le e^{-\Omega(n^{\epsilon/16})}$, where $D_{\mathrm{test}}$ has fresh input bits and all CoT positions zeroed. Lemma 4 separately certifies $|\nabla_\theta f^{(t)}_\theta| = O(n^g)$, so the algorithm sits inside the class covered by Proposition 1's barrier — which is what makes the result a genuine circumvention rather than an oracle cheat.

The inductive invariant is Definition 4, "layer $\ell$ is well-trained": (a) softmax concentration, $\frac{1-e^{-Cn^{\epsilon/16}}}{2} \le \sigma_{c_1[m]}(w^{(\ell)}_m), \sigma_{c_2[m]}(w^{(\ell)}_m) \le \frac12$ for all $m \in (n_\ell, n_{\ell+1}]$; and (b) forward error, $|x^{(\ell)}_{m,[\ell+1]} - b_m|_\infty \le e^{-Cn^{\epsilon/16}}$ on the same range. The theorem is proved by induction on $t$: after stage $t$, layers $1..t$ are well-trained and $W^{(\ell)}(t) = 0$ for $\ell > t$.

Ingredient 0: concentration of empirical parity cross-correlations (Lemma 5). Call a product $b_{j_1}\cdots b_{j_r}$ trivial if it is identically 1 (e.g. a node times both its children). With the multi-linear inner product $\langle x_1,\dots,x_r\rangle := \sum_i \prod_j x_{j,i}$, Hoeffding plus a union bound give, for all $r \le 4$ and all non-trivial tuples simultaneously, $|\langle b_{j_1},\dots,b_{j_r}\rangle|/B \le \kappa := \sqrt{(2/B)\log(32n^4/p)}$. With $B = \Omega(n^{2+\epsilon})$ and $p = e^{-n^{\epsilon/2}}$, $\kappa = O(n^{-1-\epsilon/4})$. Trivial tuples contribute exactly $B$. _This is where $B = \Omega(n^{2+\epsilon})$ comes from_: the signal is $\Theta(n^{-2})$ and the gradient involves $\Theta(n^2)$ summed cross-correlations, so one needs $\kappa \ll n^{-1}$.

Ingredient 0b: trivial 4-tuple counting (Lemma 6).
