The mechanism is: symmetrize the learner by a random label permutation Sigma; residues not appearing among the n observed labels have their Sigma-images uniformly random, so the learner can do no better than 1/K on them, where K is the number of unseen residues; E[K] = p(1-1/p)^n plus McDiarmid/Azuma concentration. This is genuinely "you must observe (almost) every residue as a label at least once" — it is driven entirely by label symmetry and says nothing about the computational or structural difficulty of modular addition. The "near-optimal" in Rmk 5.9 is therefore near-optimal against a quite weak benchmark; it is a good sanity check on the O~(p) upper bound, not evidence that modular addition is Theta(p)-hard.

How convincing is the length-extrapolation evidence? The phenomenon itself (train on m <= 19, perfect at m = 811; ReLU at chance) is striking and the theory predicts it. Caveats: d = 1024 fixed, Muon only, and metrics reported under a best-over-weight-decay scheme — i.e. a max over a 7-point hyperparameter grid, per cell, after seed averaging. That is an optimistic estimator and should be labelled as model selection on the OOD axis. The ReLU in-domain failures also suggest the ReLU baseline may be optimization-limited rather than expressivity-limited at these (d, n), which blurs the very distinction the paper wants to draw. And the sine OOD success is for lengths that are mostly >> p, exactly where Thm 4.3 bites hardest — fair, but it means the empirical and theoretical separations both live in the long-sequence regime.

Optimization is not addressed at all. This is the largest gap. There is no gradient-dynamics result, no analysis of whether SGD/Adam on a sine MLP finds (or approaches) the width-2 Fourier solution, no grokking-time statement, no landscape analysis. The paper is expressivity + uniform convergence + margin bounds, all conditional on "when optimization succeeds" — a phrase the authors use. And their own Fig. 9 is a warning: under vanilla SGD, sine improves much more slowly after interpolation and never reaches its AdamW test accuracy, while ReLU under SGD matches ReLU under AdamW. That hints that the periodic landscape is harder to optimize, i.e. that the architectural win is partly paid for in trainability — and the theory is silent on it. Given that the grokking literature this paper situates itself in is fundamentally about dynamics, the omission is conspicuous.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Thm 4.1 (sine, fixed length). For every m >= 2, p >= 2, there is theta with d = 2 such that h_theta(x) = y(x) for all x in X_m, with margin >= 1 - cos(2 pi/p) >= 8/p^2 and ||W||infty <= pi, ||V||_infty <= 1. Thm 4.2 (sine, all lengths). With bias: a width-2 sine net with b = (0, pi/2) satisfies h_theta(x) = y(x) for all x in the union of the X_m. Without bias: a width-floor((p-1)/2) net achieves, for every m, accuracy >= 1 - 1/p (p odd) or >= 1 - 2/p (p even). Thm 4.3 (ReLU width). Any V ReLU(Wx) exactly realizing modular addition on X_m has d >= (m-p)/(p+2). Thm 4.4 (ReLU, two lengths). If m_1 != m_2 mod p, no unbiased ReLU net is exactly correct on X{m_1} union X_{m_2}. Thm 5.6 + Cors 5.7-5.8. For sigma piecewise-polynomial (L pieces, degree <= r), trigonometric-polynomial (degree <= K), or polynomial-rational-exponential, Ndim(H_sigma) <= O~(dp); hence w.p. >= 1 - delta, sup_h |R(h) - Rhat(h)| <= O~(sqrt((dp + log(1/delta))/n)), and for constant-width sine every interpolating ERM has R <= O~(sqrt((p + log(1/delta))/n)), i.e. n = O~(p). Thm E.11. Every label-permutation-equivariant learner achieving risk <= eps w.p. >= 1 - delta needs n >= (p-1)(log(1/eps) - 1) = Omega(p). Thm 6.2 (sine margin). For d >= 2p: w.p. >= 1 - delta, every interpolant with normalized margin Omega(1) has R <= O~(p/sqrt n); such an interpolant exists (d = 2p, normalized margin >= 1/2). Thm 6.3 (ReLU margin). For p > m, n > m^2, n >= 17, d >= 64 p m^{m/2+2} 4.67^m: every interpolant with normalized margin Omega(p^{-1/2} m^{-1.5m-2.5} 6.34^{-m}) has R <= O~(p m^{1.5m+2.5} 6.34^m sqrt(m/n)), and such an interpolant exists.

How: the sine constructions (Thms 4.1-4.2). Pure character algebra. Let phi = 2 pi/p, alpha = (0,...,p-1). Because x in Z^p, reducing W mod 2 pi is free, so set W_{1,r} = phi r and W_{2,r} = phi r + pi/(2m). Then = phi y(x) and, using ||x||1 = m, = phi y(x) + pi/2, so the two hidden units output sin(phi y) and cos(phi y). With V = sin(2 pi k l/p), so s_l(x) = S(l, y(x)) where } = (sin(phi q), cos(phi q)) the cosine addition formula gives s_q = cos(phi(y-q)), uniquely maximized at q = y; the margin is 1 - cos(phi) >= (2/pi^2) phi^2 = 8/p^2. For Thm 4.2 with bias, the pi/(2m) is replaced by b_2 = pi/2 and the whole construction becomes m-free. The bias-free uniform construction instead uses only sines at all K = floor((p-1)/2) frequencies, W_{k,.} = (2 pi k/p) alpha, V_{l kLemma D.2 (sine Gram identity on Z/pZ) evaluates S(a,b) = sum_{k=1}^K sin(2 pi k a/p) sin(2 pi k b/p) to p/4 if a = b != 0, -p/4 if a = -b != 0, and 0 otherwise — proved by the product-to-sum identity plus the vanishing of nontrivial character sums and pairing k <-> p-k. The degenerate residues (y = 0, plus y = p/2 for even p) make all scores vanish, so the strict-argmax rule fails; Lemma D.1 (the modular sum of iid uniforms is uniform, by vanishing nonzero Fourier coefficients) converts that into exactly 1/p (resp. 2/p) error, uniformly in m.

How: the ReLU width lower bound (Thm 4.3). A one-dimensional linear-region / intermediate-value count. Along the path x(s) = (m-s) e_0 + s e_1, s = 0,...,m, the true label is s mod p. Each preactivation is affine in s: a_k(s) = m y_k + s z_k with y_k = W_{k,1}, z_k = W_{k,2} - W_{k,1}; hence each hidden unit is continuous piecewise-affine with at most 1 breakpoint, and every class score f_r(s) is continuous piecewise-affine with breakpoint set B, |B| <= d. Define adjacent-class margins g_r = f_r - f_{r+1 mod p} (same breakpoints). Call I_s = [s, s+1] clean if it misses B; at most 2d intervals are spoiled, so at least m - 2d are clean. Exactness forces g_{l(s)}(s) > 0 and g_{l(s)}(s+1) < 0, so on a clean interval the IVT produces a zero of g_{l(s)} in (s, s+1), inside [0,m] minus B. A piecewise-affine function has at most 1 nontrivial zero per connected component of [0,m] minus B, i.e. at most d+1 zeros; summing over the p classes gives m - 2d <= p(d+1), hence d >= (m-p)/(p+2). The key lemma is really the observation that collapsing to a line makes every hidden unit a single hinge, so the whole network has only O(d) oscillations available to track a target that must oscillate Theta(m/p) times.

How: Thm 4.4. Positive homogeneity, three lines, as described above.

How: the Natarajan bound (Thms F.15-F.17, 5.6). Four steps.

  1. Multiclass to sample counting. Lemma F.4: if S with |S| = n is N-shattered then H realizes at least 2^n distinct labelings on S (the map b -> h_b|S is injective). Lemma F.5: those labelings inject into sign patterns of the pairwise reduction class G_Theta = {sgn(s^theta_i - s^theta_j)} on the domain X x {i<j} — the fibers are pairwise disjoint because a valid strict argmax pins the sign of at least one pairwise difference. Combining, Lemma F.6: 2^n <= Pi{G_Theta}(n binom(p,2)).
  2. Polynomialize the sine. This is the technical heart. Lemma F.14 (trigonometric sum polynomialization): for integer x >= 0 with sum_v x_v = m there are integer polynomials S_x, C_x in Z[c_1,s_1,...,c_p,s_p] of total degree <= m with S_x = sin(sum_v x_v alpha_v), C_x = cos(sum_v x_v alpha_v) under c_v = cos(alpha_v), s_v = sin(alpha_v) — built by induction on m via the angle-addition recursion S_x = s_u C_y + c_u S_y, C_x = c_u C_y - s_u S_y with y = x - e_u. (This is the Chebyshev/de Moivre fact in the form needed for multi-coordinate integer inputs; the degree bound m is precisely where the l1-boundedness of the instance space is spent.)
  3. Lift to a polynomial parameter class. Substitute c_{j,v} = cos(W_{j,v}), s_{j,v} = sin(W_{j,v}) and treat a = (V, (c_{j,v}), (s_{j,v})) in R^{3dp} as a free parameter vector, dropping the constraints c^2 + s^2 = 1 (a relaxation that can only inflate the growth function). Each pairwise margin is then a polynomial in a of degree <= Km + 1 (degree <= 1 in V, <= Km in the trig variables).
  4. Count sign patterns. Apply the Warren-type bound (Anthony-Bartlett Thm 8.3, the standard descendant of Warren 1968 / Milnor / Goldberg-Jerrum sign-pattern counting): for N >= D/k, a k-combination of signs of degree-r polynomials in D parameters has Pi_H(N) <= 2(2 e N k r/D)^D. With D = 3dp, k = 1, r = Km+1, N = n binom(p,2): Pi_{G_Theta}(N) <= 2(p K n m)^{3dp}. Combine with 2^n <= Pi_{G_Theta}(N), take logs, and absorb the log n via Lemma F.13 (u < A log u + B implies u < 4A log(2A) + 2B) to get Ndim(H_sin) <= 2dp(6 log(6dp) + 2 log(e p (Km+1))) = O~(dp). Note m appears only inside a logarithm. Plug into the Multiclass Fundamental Theorem. The piecewise-polynomial case runs the same route but first partitions parameter space by the nd(L-1) hyperplanes {w_i x^(j) = b_l} (itself a Warren count) and applies the polynomial bound within each region; the rational-exponential case clears denominators (a positive, sign-preserving product) and introduces u_{j,v} = e^{k W_{j,v}} so that the exponentiated preactivation becomes a degree-m monomial. The matching lower bounds come via Lemma F.20 (VCdim of the induced halfspace class <= Ndim(H), by embedding a binary halfspace in the first row of V), which imports known Omega(W log W) bit-extraction constructions and, for sine on unbounded Z, infinity.

How: the Omega(p) lower bound (Thm E.11). Equivariant symmetrization (Lem E.4: the symmetrized learner is distributionally identical to the original), plus: labels are uniform on [p] (Lem E.5), the restriction of Sigma to the unseen residues U is a uniform random bijection given the revealed values (Lem E.6), so risk >= (K-1)/p with K = |U| (Lem E.7). Then E[K] = p(1-1/p)^n >= e eps p for n <= (p-1)(log(1/eps) - 1), with McDiarmid concentration for K (1-Lipschitz in the n iid residues; Var(K) <= E[K]) and an Azuma/Doob permutation-exposure martingale for the symmetrized risk with increments 2/p (Lem E.10). Three exponential tails give the stated bound.

How: the sine margin bound (Thm I.9 => Thm 6.2). Standard Rademacher scaffolding plus the torus trick. (1) Ramp surrogate: phi_y(s) = max_{k != y}(s_k - s_y) is 2-Lipschitz in l_infty; psi_gamma is (1/gamma)-Lipschitz; so g_y = psi_gamma composed with phi_y lies in [0,1], is (2/gamma)-Lipschitz in l_infty, and dominates the 0-1 loss. (2) l_infty vector contraction (Foster-Rakhlin 2019, Thm 1): R_S(F_gamma) <~ (1/gamma) sqrt p max_j R_S(S|_j) log^2(beta/max_j R_S(S|_j)), with beta <= 1 + S_1 since ||sin(Wx)||_infty <= 1 and ||v_j||_1 <= S_1. This reduces p coupled outputs to a scalar class at the price of sqrt p and polylogs. (3) l1-linfty duality: sup_{||v||_1 <= S_1} <v, b> = S_1 ||b||_infty collapses the sup over W in R^{d x p} to a sup over a single_{1} row w in R^p, giving R_S(S|_j) <= S_1 R_S(F_sin) with F_sin = {sin(w^T x)} — note the d has vanished here, not later. (4) The torus reduction: w may be taken in [-pi, pi)^p. With |sin(w^T x) - sin(w'^T x)| <= ||w - w'||_2 ||x||_2 <= m ||w - w'||_2, a half-step offset grid (Lem I.7) gives N_2(eps, F_sin) <= ceil(pi m sqrt p/eps)^p. Dudley's entropy integral (Lem I.8) with alpha = 1/(pi m n sqrt p) yields R_S(F_sin) <= O~(sqrt(p/n)). Hence R <= O~(S_1 p/(gamma sqrt n)) + O~(1/sqrt n). (5) Existence of a large-margin interpolant: Thm H.1 builds d = 2p with all p frequencies in quadrature, s_q(x) = sum = p * 1[q = y], so margin gamma = p; }^p cos((2 pi k/p)(y - q)) = Re sum_k e^{2 pi i k(y-q)/pLem H.2 shows V V^T = p I_p (DFT orthogonality), so ||V||_2 = sqrt p, all singular values equal, and ||V||_{1,infty} <= 2p, giving normalized margin >= 1/2.

How: the ReLU margin bound (Thm I.13 => Thm 6.3). Same contraction/ramp front end, then Golowich-Rakhlin-Shamir layer peeling (their Lem 1): for 1-Lipschitz positively homogeneous sigma and convex increasing g, the Rademacher complexity sup over ||W||_F <= R can be bounded by twice the same quantity with the activation stripped and only ||W||_F surviving. Wrapping this in an exponential-moment (Chernoff/MGF) argument with the optimal lambda, plus a bounded-difference sub-Gaussian bound, gives R_S(S|_j) <= S_2 B (sqrt(2 log 2) + 1) n^{-1/2} Q_2(S) where Q_2(S)^2 = (1/n) sum_i ||x^(i)||_2^2. Q_2 is then controlled distributionally: Lem I.10 writes ||Z||_F^2 in terms of token-collision counts, and Lem I.11 (Hoeffding on Y_i = number of coincident token pairs in [m, m^2], with E Y_i = m(1 + (m-1)/p)) gives Q_2 = O~(sqrt m) when p > m, n > m^2. The existence half (Thm H.6) is the laborious part: Lem H.3 (polarization identity x_1 ... x_s = (1/(s! 2^s)) sum over signs of a product times a power of a signed sum) plus Lem H.5 (a polarized Newton-identity expansion of cos(sum theta_i), sin(sum theta_i) in the power sums C_k = sum_i cos(k theta_i), S_k = sum_i sin(k theta_i), with total term count in [m 2^m, 13 m 2^m] and coefficient bound 1/(r! 2^r)) reduce everything to monomials z^r on [-1,1], which Lem H.4 approximates by linear splines — exactly representable as at most N+1 ReLU units with error s(s-1)/(2N^2). Summing over p frequencies with tau = 0.1 gives margin >= 0.6p at width <= 64 p m^{m/2+2} 4.67^m, and Stirling bounds on the coefficient sums (via unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind) produce ||V||_2 ||W||_F <= 2 sqrt 2 p sqrt(p K_m) with K_m <= 17 m^{1.5m+2.5} 6.34^m. Again: this is existence, not optimality — no lower bound on ReLU margins is proved.

Broader context

Why modular addition is the canonical testbed. It has the three properties a mechanistic-interpretability benchmark needs. (i) It is fully specified: the ground truth is a group operation, so you know the answer and can ask whether the network found an algorithm rather than the statistics. (ii) It has a small, finite, enumerable instance space (p^2 for m = 2), so you can train to interpolation on a chosen fraction and measure true generalization exactly — which is how Power et al. (2022) could see grokking at all: train accuracy saturates, test accuracy stays at chance for 10^3-10^5 steps, then jumps. (iii) Its symmetry group Z/pZ has a complete, one-dimensional, explicitly known character theory, so "the Fourier basis" is not a metaphor — Nanda et al. (2023) could read off from a trained transformer that embeddings concentrate on a few frequencies k, that attention/MLP implement cos, sin of (2 pi k/p)(a+b) by trig identity, and that the unembedding does the final argmax; their progress measures made grokking legible as the gradual formation of such a circuit under weight decay. Zhong et al. (2023) then showed the circuit is not unique ("clock" uses the full rotation; "pizza" mirrors the inputs and reads off a magnitude), and Morwani et al. (2024) explained frequency sparsity as a consequence of margin maximization: the max-margin solution concentrates on few Fourier features, so the implicit bias of the optimizer, not the architecture, selects the circuit. McCracken et al. (2025) argue all of these instantiate one template, an approximate CRT with O(log p) frequencies. The present paper sits precisely at the hinge: it takes the Fourier circuit as given and asks what it costs to represent and to learn when the activation already is a character.

Fourier features in neural networks. Three threads converge here. Spectral bias: Rahaman et al. (2019) showed ReLU networks learn low frequencies first, and Rahimi-Recht (2007) random Fourier features gave a kernel-approximation route to high-frequency expressivity; Tancik et al. (2020) showed that simply mapping coordinates v -> (cos 2 pi B v, sin 2 pi B v) before an MLP transforms the NTK's eigenspectrum and lets coordinate MLPs fit high-frequency detail — the key enabler for NeRF (Mildenhall et al. 2020). Periodic activations: SIREN (Sitzmann et al. 2020) replaced the activation itself by sin, with a principled initialization, and got implicit neural representations whose derivatives are also well-behaved (hence PDE and signal applications); Fourier Neural Operators (Li et al. 2021b) parameterize in the spectral domain outright. Positional encodings: the original transformer's sin/cos positional encodings (Vaswani et al. 2017) and RoPE (Su et al. 2021), which encodes position as a complex rotation so that offsets become phase differences and relative position is preserved in the attention inner product. The unifying theme — and this paper is a crisp, provable instance of it — is "the right activation makes the right algorithm cheap to represent." When the target factors through a group's characters, putting the characters in the architecture collapses depth/width requirements from "approximate a sawtooth" to "read off a phase". The flip side, which the paper also quantifies honestly, is that the cheapness is bought against a larger raw hypothesis class (infinite VC on Z), and the statistical bill is only avoidable because the inputs live on a bounded lattice.

Closest related work. (1) Morwani et al., Feature emergence via margin maximization (ICLR 2024): the direct complement — it derives Fourier features as max-margin solutions in a non-periodic network, where this paper hard-codes them and then computes margins. Reading the two together tells you that the Fourier solution is simultaneously what a ReLU net's implicit bias selects and what a sine net can express at width 2, which is a satisfying consistency check. (2) McCracken et al., Uncovering a universal abstract algorithm for modular addition (2025): the approximate-CRT template with O(log p) frequencies — relevant because the paper's own ReLU interpolant (Thm H.6) is an aCRT instantiation, and because the width-2 single-frequency sine construction is strictly cheaper than the template, which is the cleanest way to state the separation. Also worth naming: Zhou et al. (2024a), that Fourier-style embeddings accelerate modular addition and reduce grokking — the empirical shadow of this paper's theory, one layer earlier in the network.

A plausible follow-up. The obvious theoretical hole is that both separations are regime-limited: Thm 4.3 is vacuous for m <= p and Thm 4.4 dies if ReLU gets a bias. A sharper program: prove a fixed-m, bias-robust separation by replacing region counting with a sign-rank / inner-product-dimension argument on the score matrix. The target induces a sign pattern M_{x,q} = +1 iff q = y(x), and an exactly-realizing width-d network factors M's sign pattern through rank <= d with a specific feature map; lower-bounding the sign rank of the Cayley/addition table under ReLU feature maps — versus the exact rank-2 realization by characters — would give a separation insensitive to biases and to m versus p. A second, more ambitious direction: generalize from Z/pZ to arbitrary finite groups. For abelian G the characters are still one-dimensional and the width-2 trick should give width 2 per cyclic factor; for non-abelian G the irreps are matrix-valued, so the natural "right activation" is not sin but a matrix-exponential/representation-valued nonlinearity, and the question becomes: is the minimal width for exact realization governed by max over irreps of dim(rho), and does a width lower bound for pointwise activations follow from the nonexistence of a one-dimensional character basis? Third and most important: trainability. Nothing here says gradient descent on a sine MLP finds the width-2 solution; given Fig. 9's evidence that SGD struggles with sine, a theorem about gradient flow on the d = 2 sine landscape (how many spurious critical points does cos(phi(y-q))-fitting have as a function of frequency misspecification?) would be the natural counterpart, and would connect directly to the grokking-dynamics literature the paper only cites.

Connections to theoretical IR / generative retrieval / vector search. Two of the three are genuine and precise; I'll flag which.

The strongest link is the multiclass statistical machinery, not the sine activation. Generative retrieval is exactly a p-way classification problem with p = number of docids, typically 10^5-10^7, and the standard theoretical toolkit applied to it rarely confronts the large-label-space dependence head-on. This paper's Section 5 is a self-contained template for doing so: Natarajan dimension bounded through a pairwise reduction sgn(s_i - s_j) (Lems F.4-F.6), which is structurally the same object as a pairwise ranking loss, and then sign-pattern counting to get O~(dp) — i.e. uniform convergence degrades linearly in the label-space size, giving n = Theta~(dp). For generative retrieval, where p is the corpus size, that is a sobering scaling. More pointedly, Thm E.11's Omega(p) lower bound is a rigorous version of the cold-start / unseen-docid problem: for any label-permutation-equivariant learner, residues never observed as labels are unguessable, so n = Omega(p log(1/eps)) is forced. Translated: a generative retrieval model whose docids are arbitrary atomic identifiers (and whose learner is equivariant to relabeling them — true of Adam/SGD with iid output-head init) must see essentially every document as a positive label. That is precisely the theoretical reason semantic/hierarchical docids (DSI's semantically structured ids, RQ-VAE ids in TIGER) help: they break the label-permutation equivariance by putting structure in the id space, moving the problem out of the regime where Thm E.11 applies. This is a legitimately useful formalization to have in hand, and the equivariance definition (Def E.2) is the right lever for stating "what must a docid scheme do to escape the Omega(p) bound?" — a theorem worth proving in the IR setting.

A second, real but narrower link: length extrapolation. The paper's mechanism is specific and clean — the reason the width-2 sine net works at m = 811 having seen m <= 19 is that periodicity makes the phase computation invariant to the number of summands, whereas positive homogeneity makes ReLU predictions invariant to the scale of the input, which is exactly the wrong invariance. Thm 4.4 is, stripped down, "a homogeneous network's decisions are constant along rays, and sequence length moves you along rays." For generative retrieval over long docid sequences (and more generally for any retrieval model that must handle documents or id strings longer than those seen in training), that is a sharp toy statement of why sinusoidal/RoPE-style position handling extrapolates and learned absolute embeddings do not — and the bias-versus-no-bias finding (a phase degree of freedom must not be smuggled in through a length-dependent quantity) is a transferable design lesson. I would call this an honest analogy rather than a theorem you can lift.

The vector-search link is suggestive and I'd state it cautiously. The width-2 construction is a two-dimensional MIPS index: s_q(x) = <(sin phi q, cos phi q), (sin phi y(x), cos phi y(x))> = cos(phi(y-q)) is an inner product between a query embedding and a label embedding on the unit circle, and retrieval is exact nearest-neighbour over p points. The paper even proves the label-embedding matrix is perfectly isotropic in the d = 2p version: V V^T = p I_p, all singular values sqrt p (Lem H.2) — a statement about ideal embedding geometry for maximum-margin retrieval that has an obvious flavour in common with anisotropy/whitening discussions in dense retrieval. So the honest reading is: this paper is a complete, closed-form analysis of a tiny exact-MIPS system over a structured id space, including its minimal dimension (2), its margin (1 - cos(2 pi/p)), and its sample complexity (Theta~(p)). If your interest is in expressivity limits of inner-product retrieval — how small can the embedding dimension be to realize a given relevance pattern exactly, which is a sign-rank question — then the construction is a useful extremal example (dimension 2 for a p x p permutation-like pattern, because the pattern is a circulant), and the gap between that and generic sign-rank lower bounds for p x p sign matrices is instructive. But the connection stops at "structured instance; useful example"; nothing in the paper is about approximate nearest-neighbour search, index structures, or the geometry of learned embeddings in the wild. Likewise, the periodic-feature-map angle (Fourier features as a kernel whose Gram is a circulant, versus the Gaussian/cosine kernels implicit in dense retrieval) is a real mathematical kinship but the paper does not develop it, so treating it as an IR contribution would be forced.

Net: read Sections 5-6 and Lemma F.14 for technique, Thm E.11 for a lower bound you can genuinely reuse in the generative-retrieval label-space setting, and treat Section 4 as elegant-but-expected algebra with a regime-limited lower bound. The expressivity-plus-generalization-but-no-optimization scope is the main thing to hold in mind when citing it.

On the Comparison between Multi-modal and Single-modal Contrastive Learning

Wei Huang, Andi Han, Yongqiang Chen, Yuan Cao, Zhiqiang Xu, Taiji Suzuki (2024) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02837

Setting and problem

Data model. Two modalities over a shared latent label. For the first ("image") modality, (x, y) ~ D with x = [x^(1); x^(2)] = [y_mu; xi] in R^{2d}, y ~ Unif{+1,-1}, xi ~ N(0, sigma_xi^2 I_d). For the second ("text") modality, xtilde = [y_mutilde; xitilde] with the same label y, its own fixed signal vector mutilde, and independent noise xitilde ~ N(0, sigma_xitilde^2 I). They set dtilde = d, sigma_xitilde = sigma_xi (claimed, not proved, to be inessential). This is the two-patch signal-noise model of Cao-Chen-Belkin-Gu (benign overfitting in two-layer CNNs) and Allen-Zhu-Li, lifted to two views: the signal patch is perfectly correlated across modalities (same y), the noise patches are independent across modalities. That single asymmetry — signal shared, noise not — is the entire engine of the paper.

The SNR parameter is SNR = ||mu||_2 / (sigma_xi sqrt(d)), i.e. signal norm over typical noise norm. Assumption 4.1(7) fixes the modality gap: C_mu ||mu||_2 = ||mutilde||_2 with C_mu >= 2.66 a constant, so SNRtilde = C_mu * SNR. The constant 2.66 is not cosmetic; it is the threshold.

Architecture. One shared ReLU filter bank, applied patchwise, with no trainable second layer. The encoder h: R^{2d} -> R^m has hbar_r(x) = h_r(x^(1)) + h_r(x^(2)), h_r(x^(i)) = ReLU(), r in [m]. So the trainable parameters are exactly W = {w_r} in R^d — a width-m "CNN" with weight sharing across the two patches, m doubling as the embedding dimension. Initialization w_r^(0) ~ N(0, sigma_0^2 I). For multi-modal, a second network g with weights wtilde_r encodes xtilde — a literal two-tower model.

Objective. The similarity is patchwise and stop-gradiented, not the usual inner product of pooled embeddings: Sim_h(x, x') = (1/m) sum_r h_r(x^(1)) sg(h_r(x'^(1))) + (1/m) sum_r h_r(x^(2)) sg(h_r(x'^(2))), and the loss is InfoNCE (the paper calls it InfoMax) with one positive and M negatives at temperature tau. Single-modal (SimCLR-style): the positive is an augmentation xhat = [y_mu; xi + eps], eps ~ N(0, sigma_eps^2 I) — _the augmentation leaves the signal untouched and only perturbs the noise patch_. This is the paper's operationalization of "augmentation cannot raise SNR". _Multi-modal (CLIP-style)*: the positive is the paired xtilde_i, and the loss is the sum of the two modality-centered directions, i.e. the symmetrized image->text and text->image InfoNCE.

Crucially, negatives are restricted to label-disjoint pairs: y_j != y_i, with M ~ n/2. This is supervised contrastive learning / perfect hard-negative mining, not CLIP's in-batch negatives.

Downstream task and metric. OOD linear probe. Test samples x_test = [y_nu; zeta] with <nu, mu> = O(||mu||_2^2 d^{-1/2}) and fresh noise zeta ~ N(0, sigma_xi^2 I); a linear head f(x) = <w, h(x)> is fit on the frozen embedding, and the metric is population 0-1 error P[y f(x_test) < 0]. Note the test signal is _nearly orthogonal* to the training signal (cosine ~ d^{-1/2}): the task is engineered so that only the component of the learned filter along mu survives, while memorized training noise xi_i is useless against fresh zeta.

Algorithm. Full-batch gradient descent on W (and Wtilde simultaneously), constant eta, from Gaussian init, run for T* = Theta~(eta^{-1} m n sigma_xi^{-2} d^{-1} (1 + eps^{-1})) steps. No weight decay, no normalization, no learnable temperature.

Assumption 4.1 (what does the work). (1) d >= Omega~(max{n^2, n sigma_0^{-1} sigma_xi^{-1}, sigma_0^{-2} ||mu||_2^{-2}}) — high dimension so that {mu, xi_1, ..., xi_n} is near-orthogonal; (2)-(3) small eta, small sigma_0; (4) m, n >= Omega~(1) — note no width over-parameterization is needed; (5) sigma_eps <= min{Theta~(||mu||_2), sigma_xi / Omega~(1)} — augmentation strength is small; (6) n * SNR^2 = Theta(1); (7) C_mu >= 2.66. Items (6) and (7) are the load-bearing ones, and the appendix sharpens (6) far beyond "Theta(1)": the single-modal proof needs n_SNR^2 <= 1.8 and the multi-modal proof needs n_SNR^2 >= 1.7. For both theorems to apply to the same instance, n*SNR^2 must sit in [1.7, 1.8].

The question. _Under a shared-label, independent-noise two-view signal-noise model, with the same InfoNCE objective, the same architecture, and the same gradient-descent schedule, does replacing augmentation-generated positives by a second-modality positive change which of {signal direction mu, training noise xi_i} the network's filters converge to — and hence the OOD linear-probe error — and at what SNR / modality-quality thresholds does the answer flip?_

Gap in the literature. Feature-learning theory (Allen-Zhu-Li; Cao et al.'s signal-noise decomposition and benign-overfitting phase diagram; Kou et al.; Huang et al. on GNNs/FL) gives sharp SNR-thresholded separations between signal learning and noise memorization for supervised two-layer CNNs on exactly this data model. Zhang-Huang-style work (the closest predecessor) ported it to single-modal contrastive learning, but needed a trainable bias inside the ReLU to make the argument go through, and never compared against a multi-modal objective. On the multi-modal side, Nakada et al. showed each GD step on a linear CLIP model is SVD on a contrastive cross-covariance, Ren-Li analyzed a simple multi-modal dynamic, Chen-Deng-Li-Gu explained zero-shot transferability, and Huang et al. proved multi-modal beats single-modal for non-contrastive objectives. Nobody had run the two objectives through one unified trajectory analysis on one data model. This paper does that, and — a stated technical improvement — removes the adjustable bias term.

Main idea

Decompose each filter as w_r^(t) = w_r^(0) + gamma_r^(t) ||mu||_2^{-2} mu + sum_i rho_{r,i}^(t) ||xi_i||_2^{-2} xi_i, then race the two scalar families against each other along the GD trajectory. Because d >> n^2 makes {mu, xi_i} effectively orthogonal, the GD update decouples into closed recursions for gamma_r (signal learning) and rho_{r,i} (noise memorization); both grow geometrically in the first phase, and whichever reaches Theta(1) first owns the representation, because once the similarities become Theta(1) the loss derivatives collapse and the scale ratio established in phase one is frozen for the rest of training.

The two objectives differ in exactly one place: the driving factor in each recursion. In single-modal CL, gamma_r is driven by h_r's own signal activation and rho_{r,i} by h_r's own noise activation — both self-amplifying. In multi-modal CL, gamma_r is driven by g_r(y mutilde), i.e. the other tower's signal activation, and rho_{r,i} by g_r(xitilde_i), the other tower's noise activation. Since the signal is shared, the signal recursions of the two towers form a coupled positive system whose growth rate is the geometric mean sqrt(||mu||^2 ||mutilde||^2) = C_mu ||mu||^2 — the strong modality lifts the weak one. Since the noises are independent, no such resonance occurs for rho, whose growth rate stays at its single-modal value.

Quantitatively, the phase-one growth bases are: single-modal signal 1 + 0.52 eta ||mu||^2/(m tau) (upper) and noise 1 + 0.96 eta sigma_xi^2 d/(n m tau) (lower); multi-modal signal 1 + 0.48 C_mu eta ||mu||^2/(m tau) (lower) and noise 1 + 1.06 eta sigma_xi^2 d/(n m tau) (upper). Because ||mu||^2 = SNR^2 sigma_xi^2 d, the ratio of exponents is governed by the single scalar n*SNR^2:

  • Single-modal fails when 0.55 n SNR^2 < 1, i.e. n SNR^2 <~ 1.8. Then noise hits Theta(1) while max_r gamma_r = O~(n^{-1/2}) = o(1).
  • Multi-modal succeeds when 2.21/(C_mu n SNR^2) < 1/2, i.e. C_mu n SNR^2 >~ 4.42. With n SNR^2 >= 1.7 this is exactly C_mu > 2.66. Then max_r gamma_r = Omega(1) while max_{r,i} rho_{r,i} = O~(n^{-1/2}).

Headline finding: in the window n SNR^2 in [1.7, 1.8] with SNRtilde/SNR = C_mu > 2.66, both objectives drive training loss to <= eps in the same number of steps, but the downstream OOD error is Theta(1) for single-modal and o(1) for multi-modal. The separation is purely a feature-learning phenomenon, invisible in the training loss. And the mechanism attributes the advantage not to "more information" in the abstract but to a concrete rate multiplier C_mu coming from cross-modal co-activation on a shared signal. Correspondingly, augmentation is theoretically useless here by construction: it preserves the signal patch exactly, so SNRtilde = SNR, i.e. C_mu = 1 < 2.66.

The most interesting part

The genuinely elegant piece is the coupled signal recursion. Writing A_r^(t) = gamma_r^(t) + and Atilde_r^(t) analogously, the multi-modal dynamics are, to leading order, A_r^(t+1) >~ A_r^(t) + c (eta ||mu||^2/(m tau)) Atilde_r^(t) and Atilde_r^(t+1) >~ Atilde_r^(t) + c (eta ||mutilde||^2/(m tau)) A_r^(t) — an off-diagonal 2x2 positive system. Its Perron root is c eta ||mu|| ||mutilde|| / (m tau) — the geometric mean. The proof then works with the Perron eigenvector combination C_mu A_r + Atilde_r (which grows at the Perron rate) and separately shows the gap C_mu A_r - Atilde_r contracts, giving a per-tower lower bound. That is the right linear-algebraic object, it explains "cooperation" in one line, and it immediately suggests the K-modality generalization (Perron root of the coupling matrix). I'd call that the paper's real contribution; everything else is competent porting of Cao et al.'s machinery.

Now the critique, and it is substantial.

1. The SNR window is a measure-zero artifact, not a phase diagram. The abstract sells "we identify the critical factor, the SNR". What is actually proved is: single-modal fails if 0.55 n SNR^2 < 1; multi-modal succeeds if 2.21/(C_mu n SNR^2) < 0.5. Both hold simultaneously only for n SNR^2 in [1.7, 1.8]. The constants 0.52, 0.96, 0.48, 1.06 are slack from chained Chernoff/anti-concentration bounds, so the "thresholds" 1.8, 1.7, 2.66 carry no meaning beyond the specific proof. There is no matching converse: no proof that single-modal succeeds above the threshold, and — more damagingly — no proof that multi-modal fails for small C_mu. Since Assumption 4.1(7) hypothesizes C_mu >= 2.66 globally, the paper never exhibits a regime where multi-modal is bad. The claim "data quality of the second modality is what matters" is therefore supported by a sufficient condition only; the empirically interesting direction (bad captions hurt CLIP) is not theory here.

2. The comparison is not apples-to-apples in the way the title implies. With C_mu >= 2.66 and n SNR^2 >= 1.7, the second modality alone has n SNRtilde^2 = C_mu^2 n SNR^2 >= 12 >> 1.8. By the paper's own single-modal criterion, single-modal contrastive learning on the text tower alone would land in the signal-learning regime. So the theorem is "multi-modal on (weak, strong) beats single-modal on the weak view", not "multi-modal beats single-modal". That is a weaker and less surprising statement — close to "use the higher-quality view". The paper never runs the obvious control.

3. Augmentation is defined so that it cannot possibly help. The positive view is [y_mu; xi + eps]: signal patch bit-identical, noise patch perturbed, with sigma_eps required _small_. Real augmentations (crops, color jitter, masking) attenuate and re-sample _the signal channel_ and destroy nuisance structure; in the two-patch idealization, an augmentation that zeroed or subsampled the noise patch would _raise* the effective SNR and single-modal would win. The conclusion "augmentation cannot improve data quality" is an assumption dressed as a theorem. This is the single place where the idealized data model is doing most of the work.

4. The loss is not InfoNCE on embeddings. Three deviations, each load-bearing. (a) The similarity is patchwise rather than an inner product of pooled embeddings. The real objective has signal x noise cross terms; here the signal and noise channels are orthogonalized inside the loss, which is precisely what makes the gamma/rho recursions decouple. (b) Stop-gradient on the target branch makes the gradient one-sided (SimSiam/BYOL-like), not InfoNCE's. (c) Negatives are label-disjoint (y_j != y_i), which the proof uses to annihilate the negative-pair contribution to signal learning exactly. That is supervised contrastive learning with oracle hard negatives. CLIP and SimCLR both suffer false negatives; in this binary model, random in-batch negatives would be same-label half the time and the signal term would not vanish. So the analysis is of a supervised-contrastive surrogate, with label information smuggled into the negative sampler. No l2 normalization of embeddings either, so the collapse/uniformity phenomena that dominate real contrastive training are absent.

5. The generalization half is a page of hand-waving. Appendices C.3 and D.3 are each about ten lines with no lemma and no proof. For single-modal: h^(1)(x_test) = O~(1/sqrt(dn)), h^(2) = Omega~(1/sqrt(d)), then "it is straightforward to check that the embedding ... is not linearly separable. Thus L_test = Theta(1)." There is no lower bound over all linear heads, no concentration argument on the probe's training set, no statement of how the probe is fit or on how many samples. "Not linearly separable" does not imply Theta(1) population 0-1 error, and Theta(1) does not mean 1/2 (the figures show ~0.5, the theory does not). The multi-modal side is symmetric and equally informal: the margin is Omega(1/sqrt(d)) signal against O~(1/sqrt(dn)) noise, i.e. a sqrt(n) factor — thin for an o(1) claim stated without a rate. Given that the generalization gap is the paper's headline, this is the biggest soft spot. The optimization half is, by contrast, carefully done.

6. The OOD test distribution is strange. <nu, mu> = O(||mu||^2 d^{-1/2}) makes the test signal nearly orthogonal to the training signal, which is what makes the signal/noise scales both collapse to O(d^{-1/2}) and the comparison turn on the sqrt(n) factor. It is also stated with O(.) (an upper bound) and ||nu||_2 is never specified, so the test distribution is underdetermined. A reader cannot reconstruct the downstream claim without guessing ||nu||_2 = Theta(||mu||_2).

7. Minor but telling. Theorem 4.3 begins "Under the single-modal learning setup" (copy-paste). Theorem 4.2 is stated under Assumption 4.1, which includes C_mu >= 2.66 about a modality that does not exist in the single-modal setting. The synthetic experiment uses d = 2000, n = 100, ||mu|| = 5, sigma_xi = 1, so n SNR^2 = 1.25 — outside the [1.7, 1.8] window required by the multi-modal proof. The ColoredMNIST experiment uses an "ideal language encoder" producing one-hot digit+color labels, i.e. the text tower is handed the ground-truth label; single-modal gets SimCLR augmentations. Test accuracy 82.13% vs 12.68% is then almost tautological, and the comparison is label-supervised vs unsupervised, not multi-modal vs single-modal.

Net: the optimization analysis is solid and the Perron-root cooperation mechanism is a real idea; the headline separation is a narrow-constant-window sufficient condition whose generalization half is not proved to the standard of the rest, and the apples-to-apples framing does not survive scrutiny.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Under Assumption 4.1, with probability >= 1 - 1/d, after T_ = Theta~(eta^{-1} m n sigma_xi^{-2} d^{-1} (1 + eps^{-1})) GD steps: _Theorem 4.2 (single-modal):_ training loss <= eps, and OOD downstream 0-1 error = Theta(1). _Theorem 4.3 (multi-modal):* training loss <= eps, and OOD downstream 0-1 error = o(1).

Both go through the same pipeline.

Step 0: signal-noise decomposition. Reading off the GD update, every iterate lies in span{w_r^(0), mu, xi_1, ..., xi_n}: w_r^(t) = w_r^(0) + gamma_r^(t) ||mu||^{-2} mu + sum_i rho_{r,i}^(t) ||xi_i||^{-2} xi_i, with gamma^(0) = rho^(0) = 0, and the paper derives exact scalar recursions for gamma_r^(t), rho_{r,i}^(t). This is Cao et al.'s decomposition verbatim; the contribution is identifying that in the multi-modal recursions the driving factor is the other tower's activation.

Step 0.5: concentration toolbox. Standard: ||xi_i||^2 in [1/2, 3/2] sigma_xi^2 d, || <= 2 sigma_xi^2 sqrt(d log(6n^2/delta)), || <~ ||mu|| sigma_xi; Gaussian maxima bounds on ||; label balance |S_{+/-1}| = n/2 +/- O(sqrt(n log(1/delta))). Two less standard pieces: a Gaussian anti-concentration lemma P(|x| <= c) <= 2(1 - e^{-2c^2/(sigma^2 pi)})^{1/2}, used to guarantee a lower bound on || for all r — i.e. no neuron starts too close to orthogonal to the signal, which lets perturbation terms be absorbed as a 1% multiplicative slack; and a half-normal expectation plus sub-Gaussian concentration to lower-bound the average initial activation (1/m) sum_{r in U_+} >= 0.2 sigma_0 sigma_xi sqrt(d) — the seed of the exponential growth.

Step 1: approximate decoupling. While gamma, rho = O(1), | - rho_{r,i}^(t)| <= 5n sqrt(log(6n^2/delta)/d) and the analogous bound for mu. This is where d >= Omega~(n^2) is spent: the coefficients are the inner products up to o(1), so the scalar recursions faithfully describe the geometry.

Step 2: phase one, bounded loss derivatives. While max{gamma, rho} = O(1) the embeddings and hence similarities are O(1), so the softmax derivatives are pinned in a constant band, l'_i, l'_{i,j} in [1/(C_l(1+M)), C_l/(1+M)]. This is what converts the nonlinear GD dynamics into nearly linear recursions with constant coefficients — hence geometric growth — and is the reason this is a two-stage argument rather than a single Lyapunov argument.

Step 3: coefficient-tracking induction, phase one. Everything is proved by induction over t with sign-pattern invariants.

Single-modal. Partition neurons by U_{+/-}^(t) = {r: >/< 0}; the partition is invariant and gamma_r is monotone with its initial sign. The key structural simplification: label-disjoint negatives make the negative term in the gamma recursion identically zero, because ReLU() ReLU'() = 0. One then gets the signal upper bound A_r^(t) <= (1 + 0.52 eta ||mu||^2/(m tau))^t A_r^(0) — the factor ~0.5 comes from only the n/2 samples with the matching label contributing. Noise memorization is harder because xi_i is label-independent, so negatives cannot be cancelled. The trick is to pass to aggregated quantities: with Psi_{r,i} = rho_{r,i} + , define B_{r,+/-} = sum over the matching label group of Psi_{r,i} restricted to active indices, and show a two-dimensional near-linear system B_{r,+}^{(t+1)} ~ B_{r,+} + (eta sigma_xi^2 d/(n m tau))(B_{r,+} - (1/2) B_{r,-}) and symmetrically (the 1/2 from sign randomness of initialization). This coupled system prevents either label group from lagging, which feeds back into a per-sample lower bound Psi_{r,i}^(t) >= (1 + 0.96 eta sigma_xi^2 d/(n m tau))^t Psi_{r,i}^(0), with an auxiliary invariant Psi_{r,i}^(t) >= (101 C_l/(M+1)) B_{r,-}^(t) carried through the induction. Also needed: for samples with < 0, rho_{r,i}^(t) stays 0 (the ReLU never activates), again by induction.

Multi-modal. Signal: a synchronization lemma handles neurons initialized with mismatched signs across towers: by contradiction, such a neuron's gamma_r decreases and gammatilde_r increases monotonically, which cannot persist, so there is a finite t' after which the signs agree; only aligned neurons are used for the lower bound. Then the coupled Perron argument above gives A_r^(t) >= (1 + 0.48 C_mu eta ||mu||^2/(m tau))^t (A_r^(0) + Atilde_r^(0)/C_mu) - 1, combining geometric growth of C_mu A_r + Atilde_r with geometric contraction of C_mu A_r - Atilde_r. Noise: a four-case induction on the joint sign pattern across the two towers. Three of the four cases give rho_{r,i}^(t) <= 0 or = 0; only the doubly-positive case grows, and there the other tower's aggregate caps it, yielding the upper bound Psi_{r,i}^(t) <= (1 + 1.06 eta sigma_xi^2 d/(n m tau))^t (Psi_{r,i}^(0) + Psitilde_{r,i}^(0)). The asymmetry single-modal/multi-modal in which quantity gets the upper vs lower bound is exactly the structure of the two theorems.

The key separation lemma. Set T_1 as the time for the winning quantity to reach Theta(1), and evaluate the losing quantity at T_1 by converting between the two geometric rates via a log-ratio:

  • Single-modal, T_1 = log(20/(sigma_0 sigma_xi sqrt d)) / log(1 + 0.96 eta sigma_xi^2 d/(n m tau)): then max_r A_r^{(T_1)} <= exp((0.55 n SNR^2 + 0.01) log(30/(sigma_0 sigma_xi sqrt d))) sigma_0 ||mu|| sqrt(2 log(8m/delta)) = O~(SNR) = O~(n^{-1/2}), using n SNR^2 <= 1.8 to make the exponent <= 1.
  • Multi-modal, T_1 = log(20/(sigma_0 ||mu||)) / log(1 + 0.48 C_mu eta ||mu||^2/(m tau)): then max_{r,i} Psi_{r,i}^{(T_1)} <= exp((2.21/(C_mu n SNR^2) + 0.01) log(20/(sigma_0 ||mu||))) sigma_0 sigma_xi sqrt(2 d log(8mn/delta)) = O~(n^{-1/2}), using C_mu n SNR^2 >= 2.66 * 1.7 > 4.42 to make the exponent <= 1/2.

So the entire separation reduces to comparing two logarithms of geometric bases, and the "threshold" is literally the inequality log(noise base)/log(signal base) </> 1 (resp. 1/2).

Step 4: phase two, convergence with a frozen scale ratio. Here the loss derivatives are no longer Theta(1/M), so geometric-growth arguments die. Instead: a comparator / potential (perceptron-style, almost-convexity) argument. Fix w_r_ = w_r^(0) + 2 tau log(2M/eps) sum_i xi_i/||xi_i||^2 in the single-modal case — note the comparator points along the _noise_ directions, consistent with what GD actually learns there — and w_r_ = w_r^(0) + 2 tau log(2M/eps) theta_r mu/||mu||^2 with sign theta_r = sign in the multi-modal case (pointing along the signal). Margin conditions <grad F_0, W*> >= 2 log(2M/eps) and <grad F_j, W*> <= log(2M/eps) are verified uniformly over t in [T_1, T_] — again possible only because negatives are label-disjoint, so F_j receives no signal contribution. These give a one-sided "star-convexity toward W_", <grad L_S(W^(t)), W^(t) - W*> >= (1/n) sum_i L_i(W^(t)) - eps/2, hence the telescoping inequality eta L_S(W^(t)) - eta eps <= ||W^(t) - W_||_F^2 - ||W^(t+1) - W_||_F^2 and, with ||W^{(T_1)} - W_||_F <= O~(m^{1/2} n^{1/2} sigma_xi^{-1} d^{-1/2}) (resp. O~(m^{1/2} ||mu||^{-1})), the averaged-loss bound — which is where the eps^{-1} in T_ comes from. In the multi-modal case the two towers appear in one joint potential, so they converge together. A separate a-priori bound caps all coefficients at alpha = log(3MT_), keeping the induction valid out to T_. Finally, the scale ratio from T_1 is shown to persist for all t in [T_1, T].

Step 5: downstream — the weak link. Plug the frozen coefficients into the test embedding. Single-modal: h_r^(1)(x_test) = O~(1/sqrt(dn)) (signal channel, since gamma = O~(n^{-1/2}) and <nu, mu> = O(||mu||^2 d^{-1/2})) versus h_r^(2) = Omega~(1/sqrt d) (noise channel, from memorized xi_i hitting fresh zeta). Multi-modal: the two scales swap. Then the claim is asserted: non-separable => Theta(1); separable with margin => o(1). No lemma, no proof, no rate. As flagged above, this is the part a referee should have pushed back on.

Broader context

Multi-modal contrastive learning. CLIP (Radford et al. 2021) and ALIGN train an image tower and a text tower on ~10^8-10^9 web image-caption pairs with a symmetric InfoNCE loss over in-batch negatives and a learned temperature, producing representations with striking zero-shot transfer and robustness to distribution shift. The InfoMax reading is that InfoNCE is a variational lower bound on the mutual information between the two views (van den Oord et al.'s CPC; Tschannen et al. later showed the MI bound is a poor explanation of what actually drives performance, so the "InfoMax" label is more heritage than mechanism). Empirically, the field's consensus has moved to data: Fang et al. (ICML 2022) showed training-distribution diversity, not scale per se, determines CLIP's effective robustness; DataComp, data-filtering networks, and caption-rewriting work all show that improving image-caption alignment quality is the dominant lever. This paper is best read as the theory-side formalization of exactly that empirical finding: C_mu is caption quality, and the theorem says quality enters as a multiplicative factor on the signal-learning rate.

Theory lineages. Three strands, with different stances on what to assume away. (1) Latent-class / distributional: Arora, Khandeparkar, Khodak, Plevrakis, Saunshi (2019) assume positives are iid from a latent class and bound downstream linear-classification risk by contrastive risk — representation-agnostic, so it says nothing about which features a network learns. (2) Spectral / augmentation-graph: HaoChen, Wei, Gaidon, Ma (2021) recast contrastive learning as spectral decomposition of a population augmentation graph and prove error bounds via graph conductance. Powerful, but the function class enters only as a smoothness constraint. (3) Feature learning: Allen-Zhu-Li; Cao, Chen, Belkin, Gu (2022) on benign overfitting in two-layer CNNs; Kou et al. This strand abandons uniform convergence and NTK linearization — both of which are blind to the signal/noise allocation inside the weights — and instead tracks the exact GD trajectory in the signal-noise basis, delivering SNR-thresholded phase transitions between generalization and memorization. It is the only one of the three that can distinguish "the training loss is small" from "the right feature was learned", which is precisely the distinction this paper needs: both objectives reach <= eps training loss in the same number of steps.

Closest neighbors: Nakada, Gulluk, Deng, Ji, Zou, Zhang (AISTATS 2023), "Understanding multimodal contrastive learning and incorporating unpaired data" — shows that for a linear two-tower model, minimizing a CLIP-type loss amounts to SVD of a cross-covariance between modalities (and connects to CCA). That is the linear, global-optimum view; the present paper is the nonlinear, trajectory view, and the geometric-mean growth rate ||mu|| ||mutilde|| is recognizably the leading singular value of a rank-one cross-covariance — a satisfying consistency between the two. And Chen, Deng, Li, Gu (2023), "Understanding transferable representation learning and zero-shot transfer in CLIP", which analyzes feature learning in CLIP with a richer multi-feature data model; it does not run the single-modal comparison.

A follow-up I'd actually want. Two, both pointed at the paper's weak spots. (a) Replace the modality gap by an information-overlap parameter. Define the second view as a stochastic channel applied to the first, interpolating from "augmentation" (C_mu = 1, noise re-sampled) through "partially informative caption" to "independent high-SNR modality". The analysis above suggests the growth rate is the Perron root of the K x K cross-modal signal coupling matrix G_{kl} = restricted off-diagonal, while noise growth is governed by within-modality noise energy; that would give a clean continuum result — "cooperation gain = lambda_max(G)" — in place of a binary C_mu >= 2.66 threshold, and would naturally extend to K > 2 modalities and asymmetric noise levels. Paired with a matching converse (multi-modal provably fails when lambda_max is small), this would turn a sufficient condition into the phase diagram the abstract promises. (b) Fix the loss. Redo the two-stage analysis with the true pooled-embedding inner product (no patchwise split, no stop-gradient), l2-normalized embeddings, and random in-batch negatives including false negatives. Each of these reintroduces a coupling the current proof deletes; whether the C_mu separation survives is genuinely open and more informative than the present theorem.

Connection to theoretical IR / dense retrieval. This one is real, not forced, but structural rather than literal. A dual-encoder retriever (q-tower, d-tower, InfoNCE over in-batch plus mined hard negatives, temperature tau) is the same object as the model analyzed here: two separately parameterized towers, a shared latent "relevance" variable playing the role of y, a symmetric/one-sided contrastive loss, and a frozen-representation downstream evaluation. What would transfer:

  • The cross-tower rate mechanism. The gradient of the query tower along a shared semantic direction is scaled by the document tower's activation on that direction. If one side is systematically lower-quality — short, ambiguous, keyword-y queries versus long, redundant documents — then the asymmetry C_mu is not a modelling artifact but the normal operating condition of retrieval. The analysis predicts that the geometric mean of the two towers' per-direction signal strengths sets the learning rate of that direction, so the weak side is lifted by the strong side rather than dragging it down. That is a precise, testable statement about why the richer side of the pair helps, and it rationalizes practices like query generation (Doc2Query), knowledge distillation from cross-encoders into the query tower, and asymmetric tower capacity.
  • Noise memorization as a theory of failed zero-shot transfer. rho_{r,i} here is literally "the filter memorized training example i's idiosyncratic noise". The analogue in retrieval is memorizing corpus- or dataset-specific lexical idiosyncrasies that do not transfer — the BEIR phenomenon, where in-domain MS MARCO gains do not survive domain shift while BM25 holds up. The paper's framing (training loss small, downstream error Theta(1), with the same iteration complexity) is exactly the shape of that empirical story, and the mechanism would give a trajectory-level explanation rather than a capacity-level one.
  • Hard negatives as an optimization device, not a statistical one. The proof needs label-disjoint negatives to kill the negative-pair signal term; that is the idealized limit of hard-negative mining, and the false-negative problem in retrieval (unlabeled relevant documents sampled as negatives) is precisely the violation of that assumption. A retrieval-flavored version of this analysis that quantifies how a false-negative rate p degrades the signal-learning rate would be a genuinely useful theory contribution and is, as far as I know, not done.

What would not transfer, and should be said plainly: (i) the downstream metric. Everything downstream here is binary classification with a linear probe and a 0-1 error that is either Theta(1) or o(1). Retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, MRR) depend on the tail of the score distribution over a corpus of size N -> infinity and on the relative ordering of near-misses; a margin bound of the form "signal Omega(1/sqrt d) beats noise O~(1/sqrt(dn))" says nothing about ranking at depth k out of N. Getting from feature-learning coefficients to a ranking guarantee requires controlling N-fold maxima of score fluctuations, a different and harder probabilistic object. (ii) The single-relevance-direction model. One signal vector mu and a Rademacher label is a two-class world; retrieval has a high-rank relevance structure, and the interesting questions (intrinsic dimension of the embedding space, rank collapse, embedding-dimension lower bounds on expressible relevance matrices) are invisible in a rank-one model. (iii) Vector search proper. There is nothing here about ANN indexing, quantization error, or the interaction between the learned embedding geometry and the index — no normalization, no learned temperature, no treatment of the score distribution's concentration, which is what actually governs quantization and graph-index behavior. The honest statement: _this paper gives you a trajectory-level account of which directions a two-tower InfoNCE model allocates its weights to, as a function of the relative quality of the two towers' inputs; it gives you nothing about what happens when you then have to search 10^8 of those vectors approximately._ The first half is worth borrowing; the second half would have to be built.

title: Ehrenfeucht-Haussler Rank and Chain of Thought
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-11

Ehrenfeucht-Haussler Rank and Chain of Thought

Pablo Barceló, Alexander Kozachinskiy, Tomasz Steifer (2025) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12997

Setting and problem

The two objects being identified. The paper studies functions f: S_1 x S_2 x ... x S_n -> O, with S_1,...,S_n, O arbitrary finite sets (so: fixed input length n, a possibly different alphabet at every position, arbitrary finite output). This per-position-alphabet convention is not decoration: it is what lets positional information be folded into the alphabet and makes the non-Boolean generalisation of rank work. Two complexity measures are attached to such f and then proven equal.

Object 1: decision trees over assignment queries. An assignment is a pair (i, s) with i in [n], s in S_i; the set of all of them is A = union_i {i} x S_i, and (i,s) is consistent with w = (s_1,...,s_n) iff s_i = s. An a-query is specified by a permutation (total order) tau on A, and its value on w is tau(k) where k is the least index such that tau(k) is consistent with w. Operationally: walk down the fixed list tau asking "is the i_1-th letter s_1?", "is the i_2-th letter s_2?", ... and return the first assignment that gets a YES. Note the order tau is fixed in advance, i.e. the query is non-adaptive inside one a-query; adaptivity only happens between a-queries, as one descends the tree. A decision tree over a-queries has |A| children per internal node. Definition 1: rk(f) is the minimum depth of a decision tree over a-queries computing f.

The Ehrenfeucht-Haussler connection. For Boolean f and ordinary coordinate-query decision trees, EH define the rank of a node inductively: leaves have rank 0, and a node with children of ranks r_0, r_1 has rank max{min{r_0,r_1}+1, max{r_0,r_1}} — i.e. you only "pay" when both subtrees are deep, so rank is the depth of the largest complete binary tree embeddable in T (the Strahler/Horton number); rank(f) is the min over trees computing f. Crucially rank(T) <= log_2(size of T), which is why rank controls decision-tree learning. Proposition 1 proves that EH rank = rk(f) in the Boolean case, via an intermediate "YES-NO tree" model: rank equals the minimal YES-depth (max number of YES-edges on a root-to-leaf path) of a tree asking "is position i equal to b?". So the right way to read rk is: _rank = number of YES answers you need, not number of questions._ One a-query = one YES answer. This is also the Pudlak-Impagliazzo Prover-Delayer view of rank (the Delayer's score is the rank), and Definition 1 is, as far as the authors know, the first extension of rank to non-Boolean domains.

Object 2: single-layer unique-hard-attention decoders. A layer L with H heads is given by Q^(h), K^(h), W_1, W_2, W_O. On input (x_1,...,x_m) it computes scores only from the last position, a^(h)_{i,m} = <K^(h) x_i, Q^(h) x_m>, sets head_h = x_{i_h} for i_h the argmax, with ties broken leftmost, forms multihead = W_O [head_1; ...; head_H], and outputs L(x_1,...,x_m) = W_2 ReLU(W_1 (multihead + x_m)). So: unique hard attention (the head copies one token verbatim, not an average), a residual-style addition of the current token to the head output, and a two-matrix ReLU MLP with no biases and no layer norm. A decoder iterates: y_1 = L(x_1,...,x_m), y_t = L(x_1,...,x_m,y_1,...,y_{t-1}). Each y_t is the CoT token — there is no separate vocabulary, no sampling, no argmax-over-tokens readout between steps; the raw real vector is appended. Definition 2: f is computed in t iterations if there exist d, a layer L, an arbitrary positional encoding p, and an arbitrary output map alpha with f(w) = alpha(y_t) when the prompt is p(s_1,1),...,p(s_n,n),p(EoL). Definition 3: dd^(H)(f) is the minimum such t.

Modelling choices worth flagging, because the result lives in them.

  • Non-uniform, unbounded resources. d, the real entries, the positional encoding and alpha are all unconstrained and may depend on n. There is no precision bound. All the lower bounds are therefore unconditional in d and precision — explicitly contrasted with Peng-Narayanan-Papadimitriou, whose soft-attention bound for iterated composition holds only for t roughly sqrt(n/(dHp)).
  • Unique vs averaging hard attention. UHAT retrieves exactly one token. The alternative in the literature, averaging hard attention (AHAT), returns the mean over the whole argmax set, which can convey counting/aggregate information and is strictly stronger (AHAT encoders capture LTL-with-counting; UHAT ones are counting-free, cf. Barcelo et al. 2024, Yang-Chiang-Angluin). The whole equivalence depends on UHAT: an averaging head would leak more than one assignment per step and the a-query abstraction would collapse.
  • Single layer, last-position-only output. With one layer, the query vector at step t is Q y_{t-1}, a function of the already-generated CoT prefix alone. Hence the induced total order over candidate assignments is known before looking at the input — exactly the non-adaptivity inside an a-query. More layers would break this.
  • _Multi-head = parallel, non-adaptive._ An H-degree a-query is a product of H a-queries, all H orders fixed simultaneously; rk^(H)(f) is min depth over such trees (Definition 4).

The question. Is there an exact combinatorial characterisation of how many chain-of-thought steps a single-layer hard-attention decoder needs to compute a given function — and is it the Ehrenfeucht-Haussler rank? And: does giving the decoder more attention heads reduce the number of steps for natural serial problems?

What was known, and the gap. The dominant line treats transformers as a non-standard circuit family and had characterised encoders (circuit classes, logics) and had given asymptotic CoT results: Perez-Barcelo-Marinkovic (unbounded iterations, hard attention => Turing-complete), Merrill-Sabharwal 2024 (poly many CoT steps, uniform, softmax => all of P), Li-Liu-Zhou-Ma 2024 (non-uniform => all of P/poly). Lower bounds on iteration count existed only under dimension/precision assumptions (Peng et al.). Nobody had an exact characterisation of the expressive power of a decoder with a fixed number of iterations. On the learning side, EH's rank-based algorithm was defined only for the Boolean case, and nothing was known about the multi-head analogue.

Main idea

They prove rk(f) = dd^(1)(f) exactly (Theorem 1), and rk^(H)(f) = dd^(H)(f) for every H (Theorem 2). One CoT step of a single-layer UHAT decoder is precisely one assignment query; H heads give precisely one H-degree a-query. This converts a question about transformers into pure combinatorics of decision trees, and in the Boolean single-head case ties CoT-step count to a 1989 PAC-learning-theory parameter that had been living in proof complexity.

They then cash the characterisation in on two serial problems, and in both cases show that extra heads buy nothing, for all large n:

  • t-Comp_n: [n]^n -> [n], reading the input as phi: [n] -> [n] and returning phi^(t)(1). Trivially rk <= t (guess phi(1) by scanning (1,1),(1,2),... — one YES; then guess phi(phi(1)) — one more YES; etc.). Proposition 2: rk(t-Comp_n) = t for n > 2t. Corollary 3: rk^(H)(t-Comp_n) = t for every fixed H, t and all but finitely many n.
  • k-thOne_n: {0,1}^n -> [n+1], position of the k-th 1 (or n+1). Again rk <= k by a scanning argument. Proposition 3: = k for n >= k^2 + k. Theorem 3: rk^(H)(k-thOne_n) = k for all large n.

Finally, a learning-theoretic half: Theorem 4 extends the EH polynomial-time consistency algorithm for rank <= k to arbitrary alphabets (hence proper poly-time PAC-learnability of rk <= k over any alphabet); combined with rk(f) <= H * rk^(H)(f) (Proposition 5) this gives improper poly-time PAC-learnability of bounded multi-head rank. Theorem 5 shows that is the best one can hope for: consistency for rk^(2) <= 1 over {0,1} is NP-complete, so rk^(2) <= 1 is not properly poly-time PAC-learnable unless NP is in BPP — adjacent to, but formally incomparable with, Pitt-Valiant on 2-term DNF (2-term DNFs have 2-head rank <= 1; the converse fails).

The most interesting part

The compilation of an a-query decision tree into one hard-attention layer (the dd <= rk direction), and specifically the reciprocal-rank positional encoding together with the ReLU-as-AND trick. This is where "a total order over the whole set of assignments" gets realised by a single inner product, and it is tighter than one expects.

Take a complete depth-r, |A|-ary a-query tree T. The embedding dimension is split into blocks: positional coordinates indexed by non-leaf nodes of T; output coordinates indexed by all nodes; assignment coordinates indexed by A; and one special coordinate. The invariant is that the t-th CoT token y_t is the one-hot indicator of the depth-t node of T that the tree reaches on w — i.e. the chain of thought is literally a sequence of pointers into the decision tree, and nothing else.

The encoding of an input token for assignment a sets, for every non-leaf node v, p(a)v = 1 / tau_v^{-1}(a), where tau_v is the permutation defining the a-query at v. The key matrix is the identity; the query matrix Q merely moves the v-th output coordinate into the v-th positional coordinate. So when the last token is y_t = 1{v_t}, the score of any token is exactly that token's v_t-th positional coordinate — for an input token p(i, s_i) this is 1/tau_{v_t}^{-1}(i,s_i), maximised at the assignment with the _smallest index in tau_{v_t}_ among those present in the input, i.e. at q_{v_t}(w). One d-dimensional inner product thus implements "first consistent element of an arbitrary prescribed order", and the choice of order is selected by which node the CoT pointer currently names. Previously generated CoT tokens have zero in all positional coordinates and so never win the argmax — a small but load-bearing detail (it is exactly what keeps the generated suffix from interfering, and it is also what makes the single-layer restriction bite: the query depends only on y_t).

Then the transition. After the head returns p(q(w)) and the residual adds y_t, the vector beta = p(q(w)) + y_t carries a one-hot of v_t in output coordinates and a one-hot of q(w) in assignment coordinates, plus a 1 in the special coordinate. W_1 writes, into the output coordinate of each non-root v, the quantity 1{parent(v) = v_t} + 1{label(v) = q(w)} - 1, which lies in {-1,0,1}, and ReLU turns this into the conjunction — the unique child of v_t along edge q(w) survives with value 1, everything else is clipped to 0. The special coordinate supplies the -1 bias that the layer has no bias term for. In the H-head case this generalises to an (H+1)-fold AND via ReLU(b_0 + ... + b_H - (H-1)), with W_O routing the h-th head's one-hot into the h-th block of assignment coordinates; the invariant "exactly one child is consistent with (v_t, a_1, ..., a_H)" keeps it exact.

Why this is clever rather than merely tedious: the construction shows the single-layer UHAT decoder is not a weak approximation of adaptive querying — it is an exact simulator, with an |A|^r blowup in dimension but no loss in step count. And read backwards, the same observation gives the matching easy direction rk <= dd: the simulator, knowing y_0,...,y_t, can compute Q y_t itself, hence can sort all of A by score (leftmost-index tie-break) before seeing the input, and recover the argmax over input tokens with one a-query. The hard-attention argmax and the "first YES in a fixed list" primitive are the same primitive, and that is the entire theorem.

Proof sketch

Theorem 1 (rk = dd^(1)) / Theorem 2 (rk^(H) = dd^(H)). Both directions as above: <= by the "pre-sort assignments by <K p(a), Q y_t>, tie-break on smaller index, then one a-query returns the argmax" simulation (by induction on t: knowing the CoT prefix determines the query, so the order is input-independent); >= by the explicit compilation with reciprocal-rank encodings and ReLU conjunctions. Theorem 2 is the same proof with per-head blocks, H a-queries bundled into one H-degree query. Proposition 1 (EH rank = rk in the Boolean case) is proved separately in both directions: rank => a-query depth by the elderly-child strategy — define phi(v) to be a child such that the other child has strictly smaller rank, follow the elderly path u_1 = v_t, u_2, ..., u_d from the current node, and build tau whose first d-1 entries are the assignments that leave the elderly path; the first YES tells you exactly where you depart, and you land in a node of strictly smaller rank, so r a-queries suffice. Conversely, an a-query tree of depth r becomes a YES-NO tree of YES-depth <= r (one a-query = one YES), and an induction on depth shows rank(v) <= YESdepth(v) using exactly the two halves of the EH recursion (max{r_0,r_1} from "YES-depth of v dominates both children"; min{r_0,r_1}+1 from "the YES-edge child costs one").

Proposition 2 (single-head lower bound for t-Comp, n > 2t): adversary/partial-assignment argument. Suppose T has depth t-1. Play adversary against T while maintaining a set F of forbidden values, initially {1}. On each a-query, pick the first assignment (i,j) in tau with j not in F and phi(i) not yet fixed; declare it the first consistent one, fix phi(i) = j, and add j to F. After k <= t-1 queries you reach a leaf with output o and have fixed phi(i_1) = j_1, ..., phi(i_k) = j_k with all i's and all j's distinct and |F| = k+1. Pick y outside {1, i_1..i_k, j_1..j_k, o} (exists since n > 2t >= 2(k+1)) and define g to agree on the fixed points and send everything else to y. Consistency with the discarded earlier assignments is checked case by case. Then the functional graph of g has in-degree 1 at each j_s and a self-loop at y; starting from 1, you cannot wander among <= k <= t-1 nodes j_1,...,j_k for t steps without revisiting one (which would give it two in-edges), so g^(t)(1) = y != o. Contradiction.

Proposition 3 (k-thOne, single head, n >= k^2 + k): a greedy-first-assignment restriction plus an interval pigeonhole. Descend from the root always taking the first assignment (i,s) in the current permutation that does not contradict earlier fixations. After m <= d <= k-1 steps you have fixed only m positions, and all inputs agreeing with those m fixations reach the same leaf. Those <= k-1 fixed positions cut [n] into <= k intervals; since n >= k^2 + k one interval I has length >= k+1. With s <= k-1 ones fixed to the left of I, set the first k-1-s free positions of I to 1; then both the k-th and (k+1)-st position of I can host the k-th one, so two inputs with different values of k-thOne reach the same leaf. (Minor blemish: the proposition states n >= k^2 + k, the proof text opens with n >= k^2 + (k-1) and then uses n >= k^2 + k — cosmetic.)

Corollary 3 (multi-head lower bound for t-Comp): round-bounded communication complexity + pointer chasing. The engine is Lemma 1: if rk^(H)(f) = r then for every bipartition S of the input positions, the two-party problem f^S has both an (r+1)-round Alice-first and an (r+1)-round Bob-first protocol of total cost <= 2Hr ceil(log_2 |A|). Why: each party can locally determine the first tau_h-consistent assignment among their own positions and send its index (H ceil(log|A|) bits); the global answer is whichever of the two comes first in tau_h. That is 2 messages per a-query. The round-merging trick gets r+1 rounds rather than 2r: alternate who speaks first per level — Alice-then-Bob for query 1, Bob-then-Alice for query 2, so Bob's two consecutive messages fuse into a single round, and so on. Then reduce from k-step pointer chasing PC^m_k (Alice holds f_A, Bob holds f_B, compute the alternating chase from 1). Pointer chasing is the canonical round-elimination separation: Alice-first costs O(k log m), but Bob-first with only k rounds costs Omega(m) (Duris-Galil-Schnitger 1987). Taking S = {1,...,n/2} and phi that alternates halves embeds PC^{n/2}_t into t-Comp^S_n, so rk^(H) < t would give Omega(n) <= 2Ht ceil(log_2 n^2), false for large n. Note the slightly unusual shape of the tool: you win if either orientation has high round-bounded complexity, and the asymmetry of pointer chasing is exactly what supplies that.

Theorem 3 (k-thOne, multi-head): a bespoke restriction argument, because communication provably cannot work. Proposition 6 kills the previous technique: for every bipartition, both orientations cost O(k log n) — each party just sends the positions of its first k ones. So Lemma 1 can never give a super-logarithmic bound here. Instead, induction on k with a self-reduction: from any depth-d H-degree tree for k-thOne_n, build a depth-(d-1) tree for (k-1)-thOne_{f(n)} with f(n) -> infinity (here f(n) = (1/3) n^{2^{-H}}). The target is a partial input y in {0,1,_}^n such that (a) the root H-degree query is _constant_ over all completions of y, and (b) there are >= f(n) free positions strictly between the first and the second fixed 1. Given such y: pad with 0s before the first fixed 1 and 1s after the second, embed an arbitrary z in {0,1}^{f(n)} in the gap; then k-thOne_n of the padded input determines (k-1)-thOne_{f(n)}(z), any a-query about the padded input is simulated by one a-query about z, and the root query can be _skipped* because it is constant — depth drops by one.

Constructing y is the technical heart, and proceeds in <= H iterations, maintaining: l of the H permutations already "fixed", and n_l >= n^{2^{-l}} free positions before the first fixed 1 (so the budget takes a square root per head — hence the n^{2^{-H}}). Let i_1 < ... < i_m be the free positions in the prefix, B = {(i_1,1),...,(i_m,1)}, and let gamma be the positional order on B. Definition 5 (the key device): tau is close to gamma if gamma^{-1}(tau(j)) <= j + sqrt(|B|) for all j — i.e. tau never ranks an element more than sqrt(m) positions earlier than gamma does. Dichotomy:

  • _Some restriction tau_1|_B is far from gamma._ Then there is r >= j + sqrt(m) + 1 with at most j-1 elements of B preceding (i_r,1) in tau_1. Walk down tau_1 fixing each encountered position to its own value, with the one exception that you refuse to set any (i,1) in B other than (i_r,1) — so the first fixed 1 moves at most to i_r, the walk stops at (i_r,1) at the latest, and only the <= j-1 B-assignments preceding it (plus one) get fixed. At least r-1-j >= sqrt(m) prefix positions survive free: head fixed, budget square-rooted, iterate.
  • All restrictions are close. Then Lemma 2 finishes it: mark the first m/2 elements of each tau_s (s <= h); closeness confines all marks to the first m/2 + sqrt(m) elements of gamma; since h_m/2 > (h-1)(m/2 + sqrt(m)) for large m, pigeonhole forces some element to collect all h marks. So there is r <= m/2 + sqrt(m) with (i_r,1) in the top m/2 of _every_ tau_s simultaneously. Fixing position i_r to 1 and running the same refuse-to-set-other-B-ones walk fixes all remaining heads while, per head, fixing at most _one* position beyond i_r. Net: among i_{r+1},...,i_m only O(1) positions get fixed, leaving >= m - r - O(1) >= m/3 free positions in the gap.

That closeness/pigeonhole dichotomy is a genuinely nice trick: it says that H attention heads cannot all be "ahead of" the natural left-to-right scanning order on a large set, so there is always one position that is simultaneously early for all heads and can be used to freeze all of them at once.

Theorem 4 (consistency for 1-head rank <= k, any alphabet, in poly time): greedy peeling by induction on k. Base: rank-0 functions are the two constants. Step, via Lemma 3: if a non-empty sample S is rank-(k+1) consistent, then taking the first assignment a in the root permutation with S_a non-empty (where S_a = examples having assignment a), the subsample S_a is rank-k consistent (it all funnels into the a-subtree, of depth <= k). Algorithm: search over all a for one with S_a non-empty and rank-k consistent (inductive oracle); if none, reject; otherwise recurse on S minus S_a, then splice — put a first in the root permutation of the returned tree, delete whatever was under the old a-child, and hang the rank-k tree for S_a there. Each recursion strictly shrinks the sample, so poly time; and it is proper. By the folklore equivalence (consistency is equivalent to proper poly-time PAC under randomised reductions, Kearns-Vazirani Thm 1.3), proper PAC-learnability follows.

Theorem 5 (consistency for 2-head rank <= 1 over {0,1} is NP-complete): two-stage reduction. Unpack the hypothesis class: a depth-1 2-head tree is given by two linear orders on A; on input x, viewed as the set of present assignments, the output depends only on the pair of maxima of that set under the two orders. So a sample is realisable iff there exist two linear orders under which no positive and negative example share both maxima. Abstract this as 2-order separability: given families F, G of subsets of U, are there two linear orders on U such that no S in F, T in G have equal maxima in both? Lemma 4: NP-complete, by reduction from monotone NAE-3-SAT (Schaefer). Per variable x and per clause, fresh elements u, v, w plus a global element 0 are added with a handful of set pairs; the "all elements vs. all-but-u / all-but-v" pattern forces u maximal in one order and v in the other, and then separating {u,x,0} from {u,0} and {v,x,0} from {v,x} forces x to be above 0 in exactly one of the two orders — the orders themselves are the truth assignment. The clause gadget forces max{0,x,y,z} != 0 in both orders, which is precisely NAE.

Converting to a Boolean-vector sample has a real obstacle: encoding sets as characteristic vectors makes 0-assignments first-class citizens, and an adversary can satisfy the sample by putting all 0-assignments above all 1-assignments (their worked example S+ = {111}, S- = {110,101,011} is separable although the underlying F, G are not). The fix is a gadget forcing almost all 1-assignments above all 0-assignments in both orders, built on the warm-up observation that if S+ is all weight-one vectors and S- = {0^n}, any separating order must make all but one 1-assignment exceed every 0-assignment. Three auxiliary coordinates u, v, w and explicit tables do this for both orders; Lemma 5 shows the gadget is satisfiable by the intended canonical orders, and Lemma 6 shows the converse. Since the gadget leaves at most two bad working coordinates, the reduction replicates the working coordinates in three disjoint groups, guaranteeing one clean group where all 1-assignments dominate all 0-assignments.

Broader context

Circuit/logic characterisations of transformers.
