Encoder results: Hahn 2020 (hard-attention encoders cannot do PARITY/DYCK-1); Hao-Angluin-Frank 2022 (UHAT encoders inside AC^0); Merrill-Sabharwal 2023 (log-precision softmax inside uniform TC^0 — the "parallelism tradeoff"); Angluin-Chiang-Yang and Yang-Chiang-Angluin (masked UHAT = star-free languages = LTL = B-RASP, an exact characterisation); Barcelo-Kozachinskiy-Lin-Podolskii 2024 (UHAT and AHAT encoders vs. FO and counting logics). This paper is the decoder/CoT analogue of those exact characterisations, and is the first result that pins down the power of a fixed finite number of CoT steps rather than a complexity class.

CoT expressivity. Merrill-Sabharwal 2024 ("The expressive power of transformers with chain of thought") gives the coarse-grained hierarchy: logarithmically many CoT steps ~ L, polynomially many ~ P, linear steps capture regular languages. Li-Liu-Zhou-Ma 2024 gives the non-uniform counterpart (poly CoT => P/poly) and frames CoT as buying serial depth that a constant-depth parallel circuit cannot have. Feng et al. 2023 give problem-specific separations (arithmetic, dynamic programming). Peng-Narayanan-Papadimitriou 2024 is the closest ancestor on the lower-bound side: communication-complexity lower bounds for function composition in one layer, but requiring t roughly <= sqrt(n/(dHp)). Chen-Peng-Wu 2024 prove embedding-dimension lower bounds for multi-layer soft-attention decoders on iterated composition. Two to actually read alongside this: Merrill-Sabharwal 2024 for the asymptotic picture, and Peng-Narayanan-Papadimitriou 2024 for the communication technique this paper refines into round-bounded form.

Ehrenfeucht-Haussler. Their 1989 result: for constant r, rank-<= r Boolean functions are properly PAC-learnable in poly time; since any decision tree of size m has rank <= log_2 m, poly-size decision trees are learnable in n^{O(log n)} — still essentially the best known distribution-free algorithm for DT learning, which is why rank remains a load-bearing parameter. Pudlak-Impagliazzo 2000 recast rank as the Delayer's score in a Prover-Delayer game and used it for DLL/tree-resolution lower bounds for k-SAT; Kullmann and Esteban-Toran connect rank to tree-like resolution space. So the paper's real content is a three-way bridge: tree-resolution space / Prover-Delayer score = EH rank = CoT steps of a one-layer UHAT decoder.

Follow-ups the paper opens.

  1. The multi-layer analogue. The authors name it as the challenge. The natural conjecture is that an L-layer UHAT decoder with t CoT steps corresponds to depth-t trees over queries that are themselves L-fold nested argmax lookups ("retrieve the token pointed to by the token pointed to by ..."). Formalising such a "rank of nesting depth L" and proving an exact characterisation would be the real prize; note the single-layer proof relies on the query vector being a function of the CoT suffix only, which fails at L >= 2.
  2. AHAT. Replace unique with averaging hard attention; the a-query primitive becomes something like "the average of all argmax tokens", which admits counting. What is the right rank notion? This would also be the first place to look for a provable multi-head speedup.
  3. Where does head-parallelism actually help? Proposition 5 gives rk/H <= rk^(H) <= rk, and the paper exhibits two families saturating the upper end. Nothing saturates the lower end. Characterising the functions for which H heads give a genuine factor-H saving (direct sums should, intuitively) would complete the picture.
  4. Learning. The dichotomy is now: 1-head rank <= k properly learnable; 2-head rank <= 1 not properly learnable unless NP is in BPP. Open: better improper learners for rk^(H) <= k than the rk <= kH detour (which costs n^{O(kH)}); agnostic/noisy versions; and whether the EH-style n^{O(log n)} bound has a multi-head analogue, which would read as "learnability of shallow multi-head hard-attention decoders from examples".
  5. Round-bounded communication as a general CoT lower-bound tool. Lemma 1's shape (bound both orientations in r+1 rounds) plus pointer-chasing round elimination is reusable; the matching negative result (Proposition 6) delineating where it fails is itself a useful signpost.

Connection to theoretical IR / generative retrieval / vector search. One connection is genuine, one genuine-but-looser; the PAC-learning half I would call unrelated.

The genuine one is the a-query itself, read as an oracle. The score <K p(a), Q y_t> maximised over input tokens is a maximum-inner-product search against a fixed index, with the query vector determined by the generated prefix. Theorem 1 then literally says: a single-layer UHAT decoder running t CoT steps = an algorithm making t adaptive MIPS/argmax calls against a fixed index, where the ranking used at step t may depend on everything retrieved so far but nothing else. That is a clean formal model of iterative/multi-hop retrieval with a frozen index, and the lower bounds transfer in spirit as round-complexity statements: t-hop pointer chasing over a corpus needs t retrieval rounds (not t-1), and — the sharper point — running H retrievers in parallel per round (an H-way beam, or H query vectors issued simultaneously) does not reduce the round count for t-Comp or k-thOne, for all large corpora. The reason is structural: H parallel lookups are non-adaptive within a round, and both the pointer-chasing/round-elimination and the closeness-pigeonhole arguments exploit exactly that. If you ever want to argue formally that multi-hop RAG or iterated query rewriting cannot be flattened into fewer rounds by widening the per-round retrieval, Lemma 1 plus Duris-Galil-Schnitger is the template, and Theorem 3 is the warning that communication arguments alone will sometimes be provably insufficient (Proposition 6) and you will need a restriction/adversary argument instead. The k-thOne result also has a direct retrieval reading: "return the k-th matching document in corpus order" requires k rounds, no matter how wide you make the per-round retrieval — a lower bound on ordinal/positional retrieval that is not about ranking quality at all.

The looser-but-real one touches multi-vector retrieval. The hypothesis class in Theorem 5 is: two scoring orders over a universe of items, and the label of a set is determined by the pair of per-order maxima. Strip the notation and that is the shape of a late-interaction / MaxSim scorer with two query vectors and a max-pool over the document's items. Theorem 5 says deciding consistency of such a class with a sample is NP-complete even for depth 1 and binary inputs, i.e. ERM for max-pooled two-order models is intractable in the worst case, while the single-order (H=1) case is poly-time by Theorem 4. This is an analogy at the level of hypothesis classes, not a theorem about ColBERT-style systems (no metric structure, no inner products, arbitrary orders), but the H=1 easy / H=2 NP-hard boundary for max-pooling over several orders is worth having in hand if you ever formalise the learnability of multi-vector scoring.

What I would not claim: the formal setting is far from any IR model — one layer, non-uniform parameters, unbounded dimension and precision, fixed input length with per-position alphabets, no softmax, no training dynamics. The |A|^r dimension blowup in the upper-bound construction means the equivalence is about expressivity per step, not about anything a real decoder would be trained to do. So the main value is probably (i) the a-query = adaptive-argmax primitive as a modelling device for round-bounded retrieval lower bounds, (ii) round-bounded communication complexity and pointer chasing as a technique, and (iii) the Ehrenfeucht-Haussler rank / Prover-Delayer / tree-resolution-space cluster as a piece of complexity theory worth knowing independently of IR.

title: Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 November 2026

Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers

Chenxiao Yang, Nathan Srebro, Zhiyuan Li (TTIC), COLT 2026 — arXiv:2606.09731

Setting and problem

Architecture class. Fix a vocabulary $\Sigma$, $|\Sigma|=K$. A generic architecture

$$A=\bigl(K,\;L,\;{d^{(i)}}_{i=0}^{L},\;{h^{(\ell)}}_{1}\bigr)$$}^{L},\;{\bar d^{(\ell)}}_{\ell=1}^{L},\;\mathrm{PE},\;\mathrm{Res

is a decoder-only transformer of depth $L$: $L$ blocks, each block an attention sublayer followed by a position-wise ReLU FFN with at most $D_0=O(1)$ internal affine/ReLU layers,

$$\tilde H^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{Attn}^{(\ell)}(H^{(\ell-1)}),\qquad H^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{FFN}^{(\ell)}(\tilde H^{(\ell)}),$$

with causal masking, arbitrarily many heads per layer (head outputs summed; concatenate-and-project is subsumed), optional residuals per sublayer (with an affine projection counted in $W$ if dimensions mismatch), and no layer normalization. $W(A)$ is the total trainable parameter count, $L(A)$ the depth.

The attention is hard attention, not softmax. With $Q_i=W_QH_i+b_Q$ etc., let $M_i={j\le i:\langle Q_i,K_j\rangle=\max_{k\le i}\langle Q_i,K_k\rangle}$ and $\alpha_{i,j}=\mathbf 1[j\in M_i]/|M_i|$; the output is $\sum_j\alpha_{i,j}V_j$. This is average-hard attention (the zero-temperature limit of softmax); the results are insensitive to the tie-breaking rule and cover leftmost/rightmost-hard variants. This choice is load-bearing and the paper is explicit about why: softmax hides a logistic unit and can simulate one, so admitting softmax drags the class into the sigmoidal-network regime where Koiran–Sontag / Karpinski–Macintyre pathologies (VC dimension far worse than $\tilde O(W)$, and in general only Pfaffian-type bounds) reappear. Hard attention keeps every nonlinearity piecewise-polynomial: ReLU, argmax, threshold.

What the function class maps. Two roles, both "sequence $\to$ single output":

  1. Fixed-length classifiers. $f^{01}_{A,\theta}:\mathbb R^{T\times d}\to{0,1}$, $f^{01}_{A,\theta}(H)=\mathbf 1[\langle w_{\text{out}},H^{(L)}_{T-1}\rangle>0]$. Note the domain is embedding sequences, not token sequences: the input is $H\in\mathbb R^{T\times d}$, and only the last position's final-layer representation is read.
  2. Next-token generators. $f_{A,\theta}(X)=\arg\max_{x\in\Sigma}\bigl(W_{\mathrm{DE}}H^{(L)}_{T-1}\bigr)_x\in\Sigma$ with a fixed deterministic tie-break, on token inputs embedded as $H=(\mathrm{TE}(x_0)+\mathrm{PE}(0),\dots,\mathrm{TE}(x_{T-1})+\mathrm{PE}(T-1))$. Weight tying $W_{\mathrm{DE}}=W_{\mathrm{TE}}^\top$ is permitted but not required.

What "the VC dimension of a transformer class" means here. Free parameters: all of $\theta\in\mathbb R^{W(A)}$ — $W_Q,W_K,W_V$ and biases per head, FFN weights, residual projections, token embedding $W_{\mathrm{TE}}$, decoding matrix $W_{\mathrm{DE}}$, output vector $w_{\text{out}}$. Not free: the positional encoding $\mathrm{PE}$, which is arbitrary but _fixed and not counted in $W$_, including NoPE; and the architecture $A$ itself. Parameters are arbitrary reals, with exact arithmetic over $\mathbb R$ assumed. Label space is ${0,1}$ for the VC results (the multiclass extension is handled in the CoT section not by a Natarajan/graph dimension but by bounding the VC dimension of a binary loss class, which sidesteps the usual multiclass-dimension ambiguity). There is no pseudo-dimension statement: outputs are thresholded, losses are 0/1 throughout, so no fat-shattering or $P_\gamma$-dimension machinery appears — which is exactly the point, since this is the scale-insensitive counterpart of the norm-based literature.

Crucially, $A$ ranges over a family: $\mathcal F^{01}_{L,W}:={F^{01}_A: L(A)\le L,\;W(A)\le W}$ is a set of hypothesis classes, not one class. The upper bound is uniform over every $F^{01}\in\mathcal F^{01}_{L,W}$; the lower bound exhibits one $F^{01}\in\mathcal F^{01}_{L,W}$. Also: the statement is at a fixed context length $T$, not uniform over all lengths simultaneously. The architecture and parameter count are length-independent (that is the premise of the whole paper), but the capacity statement is per-$T$; nothing here is a length-generalization result.

The chain-of-thought setting. A next-token generator $f$ induces $\bar f(X):=X\parallel f(X)$ and $f^{(T')}:=\bar f^{\circ T'}$. From a prompt $X\in\Sigma^T$ the model generates $T'$ tokens; $f^{(T')}(X)[-T':]$ is the trace, its last token the answer. Maximum context is $T_{\text{ctx}}=T+T'$, and the same parameters are run on every prefix, using the initial segment of $\mathrm{PE}$.

Realizable CoT learnability (following Joshi et al., 2025): there is $f_*\in F$; inputs $X\sim\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\subseteq\Sigma^T$ are labeled with the full trace $Z=f_*^{(T')}(X)[-T':]$; realizability means $f_*(X\parallel Z[:t])=Z[t]$ for all $t$. The learner sees $m$ i.i.d. pairs $(X_i,Z_i)$ and must output any final-token predictor $\hat g\in\Sigma^{\mathcal X}$ (not necessarily a transformer) with

$$\Pr_{X\sim\mathcal D}\bigl[\hat g(X)\ne f_*^{(T')}(X)[-1]\bigr]\le\varepsilon .$$

So training error is measured on every step of the chain, under teacher forcing (ground-truth prefixes), while test error is measured only on the final token after free-running rollout. That asymmetry is the whole difficulty: a learner could ignore intermediate tokens, or reach the right answer by a different path. The canonical learner is $\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$: return any $\hat f\in F$ with $\hat f(X_i\parallel Z_i[:t])=Z_i[t]$ for all $i,t$.

The question, precisely. _For depth-$L$, $W$-parameter hard-attention transformers mapping a length-$T$ sequence to one output: what is $\mathrm{VCdim}$ as a function of $(W,L,T)$ — in particular, does $T$ enter at all, and if so additively or multiplicatively with $WL$? And in the autoregressive setting with $T'$ generation steps, is teacher forcing statistically optimal, i.e. does matching the entire chain cost more samples than some cleverer use of trace data?_

What was known, and the gap. Feed-forward nets have been settled for decades: hard-threshold units give $\Theta(W\log W)$ with no depth dependence; piecewise-linear (ReLU) nets give $\Omega(WL\log(W/L))\le\mathrm{VCdim}\le O(WL\log W)$ (Bartlett–Harvey–Liaw–Mehrabian 2019, building on Bartlett–Maiorov–Meir 1998); sigmoidal units are strictly worse. For transformers, the existing sample-complexity results were all scale-sensitive: Trauger–Tewari (2023) get sequence-length-independent bounds polynomial in weight norms and exponential in depth; Zhang et al. (2022) get length-independent bounds with only logarithmic norm dependence but quadratic in parameter count and linear in depth; Edelman et al. (2022) have better norm dependence but a $\log T$ factor. These are loose in the parametric sense: under standard scaling, norm-based bounds translate to polynomial — not $\tilde O(W)$ — parameter dependence, and they say nothing about what happens with unconstrained real weights. On the lower-bound side, Edelman et al. showed $\Omega(\log T)$ even at fixed parameter count, leaving open whether $T$'s contribution is merely additive $+\log T$. The gap closed here: the parametric capacity of transformers, tightly, with the $T$-dependence shown to be multiplicative with $WL$.

Non-obvious modelling choices worth flagging now: (i) real parameters with exact arithmetic, so the lower bound is free to pack $\Theta(L\log T)$ bits into a single scalar weight — no bit-precision cap is imposed anywhere, and the $\log T$ in the lower bound lives or dies by this; (ii) $\mathrm{PE}$ is fixed and free, which the lower bounds exploit (quadratic positional features $(p,-p^2,1)$, and in one witness the ReLU inputs themselves are smuggled in via $\mathrm{PE}$); (iii) no layer norm, so the polynomial invariant is clean; (iv) $T$ enters logarithmically because the number of pairwise attention-score comparisons is $O(T^3)$ per layer per sample and only its logarithm survives.

Main idea

Upper bound (Theorem 1). For any $L\ge1$, $W\ge L$, $T\ge1$ and every $F^{01}\in\mathcal F^{01}_{L,W}$,

$$\mathrm{VCdim}(F^{01})=O\bigl(WL\log(TW)\bigr),$$

with the sharper fixed-architecture form $O(WL\log(TW(A)L(A)))$ proved in the appendix. The mechanism in one line: hard attention is a discrete switch. Once you freeze (a) all ReLU activation patterns and (b) the ternary signs of all pairwise attention-score differences, the network output is a _polynomial in $\theta$ of degree $O(L)$_. So the entire Bartlett–Maiorov–Meir / BHLM piecewise-polynomial machinery applies with attention folded in as extra branching polynomials; counting those gives the $\log T$.

Lower bound (Theorem 2). There are absolute constants $C_0,c>0$ such that for any $L\ge1$, $T\ge3$, $W\ge C_0L$, some $F^{01}\in\mathcal F^{01}_{L,W}$ has

$$\mathrm{VCdim}(F^{01})\;\ge\;c\,WL\bigl(\log T+\log(W/L)\bigr)\;=\;\Omega!\left(WL\log\tfrac{TW}{L}\right).$$

Two independent witnesses are combined: a Recursive Retrieval Machine gadget giving $\Omega(WL\log T)$, and the standard ReLU-net bound $\Omega(WL\log(W/L))$ obtained by showing transformers contain deep position-wise ReLU MLPs as a subclass. So the upper and lower bounds match up to the $\log(TW)$ vs. $\log(TW/L)$ discrepancy inside the log — i.e. tight up to an additive $WL\log L$, and exactly tight whenever $L\le W^{1-\Omega(1)}$. This upgrades Edelman et al.'s $\Omega(\log T)$ from a possible additive term to a genuine multiplicative interaction with $WL$.

CoT (Theorems 6–8, Corollary 9). The paper's structural contribution is that in CoT learning two complexity measures are needed, because training and test objectives differ:

  • $\mathrm{TSdim}(F;\mathcal X,T')$ — trace shattering: the largest $S$ for which there is a reference-trace assignment $R_S$ such that every $b\in{0,1}^{|S|}$ is realized by some $f_b$ matching $R_S(X_i)$ exactly when $b_i=1$ and differing somewhere when $b_i=0$. Lemma 18: $\mathrm{TSdim}=\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CoT}})$ where $\ell_f(X,Z)=\mathbf 1[f^{(T')}(X)[-T':]\ne Z]$.
  • $\mathrm{ASdim}(F;\mathcal X,T')$ — answer shattering: same, but all $f_b$ must produce an identical fixed prefix $R_S(X_i)$ of length $T'-1$ and differ only in the final token, which equals $b_i$.

Clearly $\mathrm{ASdim}\le\mathrm{TSdim}$. Theorem 6: $\mathrm{Cons}_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ (teacher forcing) learns with $m\le C\frac{\mathrm{TSdim}\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}$, and any learning rule needs $m\ge c\,\mathrm{ASdim}/\varepsilon$ (for $\mathrm{ASdim}\ge2$, $\varepsilon<1/8$, $\delta\le\delta_0$).

Instantiated for transformers: Theorem 7 gives $\mathrm{TSdim}=O(WL\log(T_{\text{ctx}}WLK))=O(WL\log(T_{\text{ctx}}W))$ for $K\le\mathrm{poly}(W)$ — note this beats the generic composition of Theorem 1 with Joshi et al.'s generic CoT reduction, which would have cost an extra $\log T'$ factor; bounding $\mathrm{TSdim}$ directly removes it. Corollary 9 gives $\mathrm{ASdim}\ge cWL\log T_{\text{ctx}}$ and hence

$$m(\varepsilon,\delta_0)\;\ge\;c\,\frac{WL\log(T_{\text{ctx}}W/L)}{\varepsilon},\qquad m(\varepsilon,\delta)\;=\;O!\left(\frac{WL\log((T+T')W)\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right).$$

The headline reading: teacher forcing is sample-complexity-optimal for transformers. Despite the train/test asymmetry, there is nothing to be gained by exploiting CoT traces in any way other than matching every intermediate token.

The most interesting part

The sharpest technical move is Theorem 8's label-invariant scratchpad, and the sharpest conceptual point is what it does and does not say about whether CoT data "helps".

The construction: constant depth, constant width, constant alphabet. For $m=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor$, $M=2^m$, input $X_i=\mathrm{bin}_\ell(i)#$ of length $T=O(\log\log N)$, the generator emits a $T'=\Theta(N\log N)$-token scratchpad in two phases — a DECODE countdown $\mathrm{bin}_\ell(i-1)#\cdots\mathrm{bin}*\ell(0)#\,\texttt{END0}$ (whose only purpose is to place the anchor $\texttt{END0}$ at the arithmetically useful position $p_0(i)=(i+1)L*{\text{in}}$, thereby encoding $i$ into a position), followed by a TABLE enumerating all $M$ binary strings $\mathrm{bin}_m(0)#\cdots\mathrm{bin}_m(M-1)#\,\texttt{END1}$. The entire label-dependent content of the model is one scalar parameter $\beta_s=sL_{\text{out}}$ where $s=\sum_j y_j2^j$, and it is multiplicatively gated off until the very last step via $\beta_s^{\text{gated}}=\mathrm{ReLU}(\beta_s-B(1-G_{\text{fin}}))$ with $B>ML_{\text{out}}$ hard-wired. At the final step, one attention hop retrieves $\texttt{END0}$ to get $v=p_0(i)$, an FFN computes $r=(1+1/L_{\text{in}})v+\beta_s^{\text{gated}}=p_0(i)+1+sL_{\text{out}}+i$, and a second attention hop reads position $r$ — the $i$-th bit of the $s$-th table row — which is exactly $y_i$.

Why this is clever: the model builds its own addressable memory in the output stream, label-independently, so the trace is statistically worthless to the learner, and then performs a single arithmetic address computation to index into it. All the arithmetic (increment/decrement with carry/borrow, zero-so-far flags) is pushed into decorated tokens — finite-state information stored in the generated prefix itself, so hidden state stays constant-width. $\mathrm{ASdim}=\Omega(\log T_{\text{ctx}})$ with $O(1)$ parameters: capacity from length alone.

What the CoT lower bound really says. Not that CoT is useless, and not that CoT is costly — something narrower and more interesting. It says: there exist model classes and target functions for which the chain is pure, label-invariant computation, so each training trace reveals exactly one bit (its own answer) and no more. In that regime CoT supervision has zero statistical value beyond ordinary supervised labels, while the length $T'$ it buys you increases capacity, hence sample complexity, by $WL\log T_{\text{ctx}}$. In other words: long chains are a capacity liability in the worst case, and trace supervision does not pay for them. This is a worst-case statement, and it must be: in the cases people actually care about, the intermediate tokens are shared structure across examples (the same subroutine applied to different inputs), and that is precisely what makes CoT data informative. The paper's construction is adversarially built to destroy that sharing. Honest summary: this closes the minimax question (teacher forcing is optimal) while leaving entirely open the instance-dependent question that explains why CoT training works, which is a measure interpolating between $\mathrm{ASdim}$ and $\mathrm{TSdim}$ according to how much the prefix reveals about the answer.

Does $\log(TW)$ matter in practice? Honestly, barely, as a number. With $W\sim10^{11}$ and $T\sim10^5$, $\log(TW)\approx37$ vs. $\log W\approx25$ — a factor 1.5. The scientific content is the qualitative claim: the length-independence one might hope for from a length-independent parameterization is false, and the failure is multiplicative, not additive. That is worth knowing, because it tells you the right first-order story is "capacity $\approx WL$ up to logs, with sequence length entering only logarithmically" — which, for the purpose of translating expressivity results (Liu et al.'s shortcuts to automata; Feng et al. and Li et al. on CoT's serial power; Merrill–Sabharwal) into learning guarantees, is the fact you need.

Is VC the right measure? For this purpose, yes — but with three caveats the paper states or implies, and one it does not.

  1. Hard attention. The gap to reality is large. For softmax attention the best known upper bound is $\mathrm{poly}(T)$ (via Anthony–Bartlett Thm 8.14 on Pfaffian/exponential classes). The $\log T$ result does not extend, and the paper says so. Since real transformers use softmax, the measured object is an idealization. One can argue hard attention is the "right" idealization for discrete reasoning (low-temperature limit, standard in the expressivity literature), but the honest reading is that whether the true capacity of softmax transformers is $\tilde\Theta(WL\log T)$ or genuinely $\mathrm{poly}(T)$ remains open, and that is a bigger gap than anything this paper closes.
  2. Infinite precision. Both lower bounds are bit-extraction constructions and they need it badly. The RRM packs $L$ addresses into one scalar $a_j=\sum_{m\le L}s_{j,m}/(2T)^m$: that is $\Theta(L\log T)$ bits in a single real weight. With $b$-bit parameters, the $\log T$ factor survives only up to $L\log T\lesssim b$. Same for Corollary 9's base-$2T'$ packing of $R=\Theta(L)$ digits. This is the identical caveat as BHLM's ReLU lower bound, and it is standard, but it means the lower bound is a statement about the real-parameterized class, not about anything implementable in float32. The upper bound, by contrast, is robust and is the practically meaningful half.
  3. Scale-insensitivity. VC ignores norms, so it cannot explain the generalization of overparameterized transformers where $W\gg m$. The paper is upfront that this is a baseline — "even for understanding scale-sensitive or regularization-driven generalization, this serves as an important baseline" — and I think that framing is correct and not a dodge: you need to know the parametric capacity before you can say what norm control buys you. But anyone hoping for an explanation of why a 70B model generalizes from $10^{-1}$ tokens per parameter will not find it here, and should not look for it here.
  4. Unstated: the fixed, uncounted positional encoding is doing real work in the lower bounds. The RRM relies on $(t,-t^2)$ features; the ReLU witness in Corollary 9 literally _stores the shattered inputs $a_i$ in the positional encoding_ ("the inputs $a_i$ are supplied by the fixed positional encoding and do not consume the $W$ trainable parameters"). That is legal under the paper's definitions — $\mathrm{PE}$ is arbitrary but fixed, as in NoPE-style analyses — but it is an unbounded free resource of size $T\times d$, and a skeptic could reasonably ask whether a $\mathrm{PE}$-restricted (e.g. sinusoidal, or $O(1)$-description-length) version of the lower bound still holds. I suspect yes for the $\log T$ term (sinusoidal features can encode position, and the quadratic can be computed by the FFN), but it is not proved.

Is the lower-bound construction natural or adversarial? Adversarial, but interestingly so. The RRM is not a random pathology — it is a learned index: parameters store addresses, the context stores a table enumerating all $2^B$ label configurations, and hard attention performs nearest-neighbour retrieval. "Use the context as a lookup table and the weights as pointers into it" is exactly the mechanism attention provides and exactly why the $T$-dependence is unavoidable. That makes the lower bound feel mechanistically honest even while being combinatorially extreme (a context whose $T-1$ positions enumerate every $B$-bit string is not a natural input distribution).

Proof sketch

Theorem 1 (upper bound). Claim: for any architecture $A$ with $L=L(A)$, $W=W(A)$, hard attention, ReLU FFNs with $\le D_0=O(1)$ internal layers, arbitrary heads, optional residuals, no layer norm, fixed $\mathrm{PE}$, exact real arithmetic, context length $T$: $\mathrm{VCdim}(F^{01}_A)=O(WL\log(TWL))$, hence $O(WL\log(TW))$ when $L\le W$.

Technique: recursive parameter-space partitioning + Warren's theorem, i.e. the Bartlett–Maiorov–Meir (1998) framework with the BHLM (2019) layerwise refinement, extended to attention.

  • Lemma 14 (Warren's bound, BMM Lemma 2.1). For polynomials $g_1,\dots,g_m$ in $W$ variables of degree $\le D$ with $m\ge W$, the number of distinct sign vectors in ${-1,0,1}^m$ as $\theta$ ranges over $\mathbb R^W$ is at most $2(2emD/W)^W$. The ternary version matters: equalities, not just strict inequalities, must be resolved, because average-hard attention's output depends on $|M_i|$.
  • Suppose $H_1,\dots,H_N$ are shattered, so $\Pi_F(H_{1:N})=2^N$. Build partitions $\mathcal P_0={\mathbb R^W}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal P_L$ of $\mathbb R^W$ where $\mathcal P_\ell$ freezes all branching at layers $\le\ell$. Invariant: on each cell $C\in\mathcal P_\ell$, every $H^{(\ell)}_{n,t}(\theta)$ agrees with a polynomial of degree $\le\deg_\ell$. Base case $\deg_0\le1$ (inputs fixed; affine if embeddings are learned, which is what the CoT version needs since $W_{\mathrm{TE}}\in\theta$).
  • Inductive step, two stages. (a) Attention routing. For each head $h$, sample $n$, query $i$, and causally allowed ordered key pair $p<q\le i$, define the score-difference polynomial $g^{(\ell,h)}_{n,i,p,q}(\theta)=\langle q_{n,i}(\theta),k^{(\ell,h)}_{n,p}(\theta)-k^{(\ell,h)}_{n,q}(\theta)\rangle$. Freezing the ternary signs of all of these pins down the full ordering-with-ties of scores, hence pins $M_{n,i}$, hence pins $|M_{n,i}|$, hence makes $\alpha_{i,j}$ fixed rational constants; the attention output collapses to a fixed convex combination of the polynomial value vectors — still polynomial. Count: $\sum_{i<T}\binom{i+1}{2}=O(T^3)$ per head per sample, $O(W)$ nontrivial heads, so $|\mathcal B_{\mathrm{Attn}}|=O(NWT^3)$. This $T^3$ is the entire source of the $\log T$. (b) FFN ReLUs. Within an attention-frozen cell, refine by the binary signs of all internal pre-activations $a^{(\ell)}_{n,t,r,u}(\theta)$, sequentially through the $O(1)$ internal layers; $|\mathcal B_{\mathrm{FFN}}|=O(NTW)$. Residuals only add earlier polynomials (possibly through an affine projection) — no new branching, invariant preserved.
  • Degrees. Each layer composes $O(1)$ affine maps with the frozen piecewise structure, so $\deg_\ell\le\deg_{\ell-1}+O(1)=O(\ell)$; score differences are inner products of two degree-$O(\ell)$ objects so $D_\ell=2\deg_{\ell-1}+O(1)=O(\ell)$. Linear, not exponential, degree growth — this is why ReLU/piecewise-linear gives $WL\log$ and not $WL^2\log$; the Discussion notes that piecewise-polynomial activations such as gated ReLU $(x,y)\mapsto x[y]_+$ blow the degree up exponentially in $L$, costing an extra factor $L$: $\tilde O(WL^2\log T)$.
  • Assemble. $|\mathcal P_L|\le\prod_\ell\Delta^{\mathrm{Attn}}_\ell\Delta^{\mathrm{FFN}}_\ell$ with each factor bounded by Warren (the sequential refinement gives a product of region counts while the branching polynomials add). Within a final cell, the output logit $z_n(\theta)=\langle w_{\text{out}},H^{(L)}_{n,T-1}(\theta)\rangle$ is polynomial of degree $\deg_{\text{out}}}=O(L)$ (note $w_{\text{out}}\in\theta$, hence the $+1$), and Warren on ${z_n*{n\le N}$ bounds the within-cell patterns. The crucial cancellation: every Warren factor is $(\,\cdot\,)^W$ with a $/W$ inside, and $|\mathcal B*{\mathrm{Attn}}|/W=O(NT^3)$ — the $W$ cancels. Taking logs of $2^N\le|\mathcal P_L|\max_C\Pi_C$:

$$N\le O\bigl(WL\log N+WL\log T+WL\log L\bigr),$$

the $T^3$ contributing only $3WL\log T$. Invert with the standard implication ($N\le A\log N+B\Rightarrow N=O(A\log A+B)$, $A=O(WL)$) to get $O(WL\log(TWL))$.

Theorem 2 (lower bound). Claim: for $L\ge1$, $T\ge3$, $W\ge C_0L$, some class in $\mathcal F^{01}_{L,W}$ shatters $\Omega(WL(\log T+\log(W/L)))$ points.

Construction — the Recursive Retrieval Machine. Let $B=\lfloor\log_2(T-1)\rfloor=\Theta(\log T)$. Shatter $N=n\cdot L\cdot B$ points indexed by $(j,\ell,i)\in[n]\times[L]\times[B]$. The slogan: context = label repository, weights = addresses, attention = nearest-neighbour lookup, FFN = base-$2T$ left shift.

  • Inputs. Context positions $t\in{0,\dots,T-2}$ carry $h_t=(t,-t^2,\mathrm{bit}_i(t),c{=}1,\eta{=}1,0)$ — so the context enumerates all $2^B\le T-1$ configurations of $B$ bits. The query position $T-1$ carries $(0,0,0,c{=}1,\eta{=}0,e_j^\top,e_\ell^\top,0)$, one-hots selecting the memory address $j$ and the target layer $\ell$.
  • Parameter encoding. For each $(j,\ell)$ pack the $B$ target labels into $s_{j,\ell}=\sum_k Y_{j,\ell,k+1}2^k\in{0,\dots,2^B-1}$, which names a context position. Then compress all $L$ addresses into one real weight by base-$2T$ encoding: $a_j=\sum_{m=1}^{L}s_{j,m}/(2T)^m\in[0,0.5)$.
  • Lemma 15 (inductive extraction). If the register holds $r_{k-1}=\sum_{m\ge k}s_{j,m}/(2T)^{m-k}=s_{j,k}+\delta_k$, then: (1) a head with $k_t=[t,-t^2,\eta_t]$, $q=[2r_{k-1},1,M]$ scores $2r_{k-1}t-t^2+M\eta_t$, and since $\arg\max_t(2rt-t^2)=\arg\min_t|t-r|^2$, it attends to the integer nearest $r_{k-1}$; because $0\le\delta_k\le(T-2)/(2T-1)<1/2$, that integer is uniquely $s_{j,k}$ (uniqueness also makes average-hard attention deterministic, so tie-breaking is irrelevant). The $M\eta_t$ term masks out the query position. (2) The value head reads $t^*=s_{j,k}$ and the payload $b_k=\mathrm{bit}_i(s_{j,k})$, and the FFN applies $r_k=2T(r_{k-1}-s_{j,k})=2T\delta_k$ — affine on the bounded domain, so a two-layer ReLU FFN computes it exactly.
  • _Output gating in $O(1)$ width._ To return the bit from layer $\ell$ without carrying an $L$-dimensional state, the first block maps $e_\ell$ to a scalar $g=\ell$ and each layer applies a ReLU "hat" $\mathrm{gate}_k(g)=2\mathrm{ReLU}(g-k+\tfrac12)-2\mathrm{ReLU}(g-k)+\mathrm{ReLU}(g-k-\tfrac12)$, which equals $\mathbf 1[g=k]$ on integers, with accumulator update $z\leftarrow z+\mathrm{ReLU}(b_k+\mathrm{gate}_k(g)-1)$. Since $b_k\in{0,1}$ this adds $b_k$ iff $k=\ell$. Output logit $z-\tfrac12$.
  • Budget — the asymmetry that makes it work. The only parameters scaling with $n$ or $L$ are the first block's reads of $e_j$ and $e_\ell$: $\Theta(n)$ weights to select $a_j$, $O(L)$ to select $g$. The backbone is $O(L)$ parameters total, because every layer runs the same fixed algebra on a constant-dimensional subspace, independent of $n$ and $T$; residuals carry the context features through untouched. So $W=\Theta(n)+O(L)$, and $W\ge C_0L$ lets $n=\Theta(W)$. Each sample contributes one bit; $N=nLB=\Omega(WL\log T)$. Why the $/L$ appears inside the log: it does not come from this construction at all. It comes from the second witness — Lemma 16 shows that by fixing all context tokens and choosing attention parameters so the query position attends to itself (a marker coordinate equal to 1 only there), hard attention becomes the identity and the residual-free transformer degenerates to iterated position-wise FFN, i.e. a depth-$\Theta(L)$, $\Theta(W)$-parameter ReLU MLP, inheriting BHLM's $\Omega(W'L'\log(W'/L'))$. Taking the max of the two witnesses and using $\max{\log T,\log(W/L)}=\Theta(\log(TW/L))$ gives the stated form. So the $\log(W/L)$ is the ReLU-net term and the $\log T$ is the attention term; they are proved by different, mutually exclusive classes, and no single class is shown to achieve both simultaneously.

Theorem 6 (generic CoT). Upper: Lemma 17 — pointwise, $\mathbf 1[f^{(T')}(X)[-1]\ne Z[-1]]\le\mathbf 1[f^{(T')}(X)[-T':]\ne Z]=\ell_f(X,Z)$, so end-to-end error is dominated by trace loss (this is where free-running rollout is reconciled with teacher forcing: matching the whole chain on-distribution means the rollout is the teacher-forced path). Lemma 18 — $\mathrm{TSdim}=\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CoT}})$, both directions, with a small argument that shattered loss-domain points may be taken to have distinct inputs. Then the realizable VC bound applies to $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CoT}}$ and $\mathrm{Cons}*{\mathrm{CoT}}$ achieves zero empirical trace loss. Lower: standard no-free-lunch on an answer-shattered set, with the twist that answer shattering is exactly what makes the trace uninformative. Put $\mathcal D(X_1)=1-4\varepsilon$ and $\mathcal D(X_i)=4\varepsilon/(d-1)$ for $i\ge2$; draw $B\sim\mathrm{Unif}{0,1}^d$ and target $f_B$. Conditioned on $X_i$ not appearing in the sample, the observed data is a function of ${B_j:X_j\text{ drawn}}$ only — _because every drawn trace has the fixed, label-independent prefix $R_S(X_j)$ and its final token reveals only $B_j$_ — so $B_i$ stays uniform and any predictor errs on $X_i$ with probability $\ge1/2$. Then $\mathbb E[L*{\text{rare}}]\ge2\varepsilon(1-\frac{4\varepsilon}{d-1})^m\ge\frac32\varepsilon$ for $m\le(d-1)/(16\varepsilon)$ by Bernoulli, and since $L_{\text{rare}}\le4\varepsilon$, Markov-style reversal gives $\Pr[L_{\text{rare}}\ge\varepsilon]\ge1/6$; average over $B$ to fix a hard target. Constants $c_0=1/32$, $c_1=1/6$.

Theorem 7 ($\mathrm{TSdim}$ for transformers). Bound $\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CoT}})$ directly. Step 1 — unroll teacher forcing. For $n$ examples define the $M=nT'$ teacher-forcing contexts $c_{i,t}=X_i\parallel Z_i[:t]$, each of length $\le T_{\text{ctx}}-1$. For fixed $f$, the loss vector in ${0,1}^n$ is a deterministic function of the prediction vector in $\Sigma^M$; so shattering $n$ loss points forces $2^n\le\Pi_F(nT')$, the multiclass growth function of the next-token map. This is the step that kills the spurious $\log T'$: the generic reduction would union-bound over steps, here they are all absorbed into one growth-function argument. Step 2 — multiclass growth bound. Rerun Appendix B's partitioning with $N\leftarrow M$, context length $T_{\text{ctx}}$, and $W_{\mathrm{TE}}\in\theta$ (so layer-0 is affine, covered by the base case): $\log|\mathcal P_L|\le O(WL\log(MT_{\text{ctx}}WL))$. Within a cell, handle $\arg\max$ by freezing the ternary signs of all $O(MK^2)$ pairwise logit differences $\Delta_{m,x,x'}=z_{m,x}-z_{m,x'}$ of degree $O(L)$; Warren gives $\log\Pi_C\le O(W\log(MKL))$. Hence $\log\Pi_F(M)\le CWL\log(C'MT_{\text{ctx}}WLK)$. Step 3. Set $M=nT'$, use $T'\le T_{\text{ctx}}$, invert: $\mathrm{TSdim}=O(WL\log(T_{\text{ctx}}WLK))$.

Theorem 8 / Corollary 9 (CoT lower bound). Theorem 8 is the constant-size scratchpad described above: $\mathrm{ASdim}=\Omega(\log T_{\text{ctx}})$ with $O(1)$ depth, width and alphabet, $T=O(\log\log N)$, $T'=\Theta(N\log N)$ — capacity purely from generation length. Amplification (Corollary 9): graft the RRM's multiplexing onto it. Set $R=\lfloor L/C_{\text{amp}}\rfloor$ retrieval rounds ($C_{\text{amp}}$ absorbing one retrieval round plus the constant-depth transducer and readout), $n=\Theta(W)$ prompt groups, $m=\Theta(\log T')$ table bits. Prompts $X_{j,k,i}=\mathrm{ID}_j\parallel\mathrm{LYR}_k\parallel\mathrm{bin}_\ell(i)\parallel#$ with $|\Sigma|=O(W+L)\le\mathrm{poly}(W)$. The $\mathrm{ID}_j$ embedding stores the base-$2T'$ packed scalar $r^{(0)}_j=\sum_{R u\le}s_{j,u}/(2T')^{u-1}$; $\mathrm{LYR}_k$ stores $g=k$; $R$ rounds of nearest-integer attention + left shift + hat-gated accumulation extract $\hat s=s_{j,k}$; then the Theorem 8 readout fires, with the two-token header merely shifting absolute positions by $H=2$. The header coordinates are gated off before the final step, so all parameter settings emit the identical prefix $R_S$ — answer shattering, $\mathrm{ASdim}\ge nRm=\Omega(WL\log T_{\text{ctx}})$. The second witness is the ReLU subclass realized with token prompts: $X_i\in\Sigma_R^{D+1}$ with $\texttt{mark}$ at position $i$ and $\texttt{query}$ last, the shattered ReLU input $a_i$ supplied by the fixed positional encoding at position $i$; a constant attention wrapper copies it to the output position, the remaining layers simulate $h\in\mathcal H$, and a positional gate forces the dummy token $#$ at every non-final step. Since the prefix $#^{T'-1}$ is independent of $h$, any CoT learner for this subclass is a supervised learner for $\mathcal H$, giving $\Omega(WL\log(W/L)/\varepsilon)$. Max of the two: $\Omega(WL\log(T_{\text{ctx}}W/L)/\varepsilon)$. Matching the Theorem 7 upper bound up to $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ and the usual $L$ inside the log — hence teacher forcing is optimal.

Residual gaps the paper itself names: is teacher forcing optimal for general classes, i.e. can the $\mathrm{TSdim}$–$\mathrm{ASdim}$ gap be closed? And what is the sample complexity of end-to-end learning without trace access?

Broader context

The classical backdrop. VC dimension of feed-forward nets has a fifty-year history: Cover (1965) for linear threshold arrangements; Baum–Haussler (1989) $O(W\log W)$ for threshold nets; Maass (1994) superlinear lower bounds; Koiran–Sontag (1994) and Karpinski–Macintyre (1997) for sigmoidal/Pfaffian nets (where the clean $\tilde\Theta(W)$ picture breaks, by Pfaffian-function machinery); Bartlett–Maiorov–Meir (1998) for piecewise-polynomial nets; and the near-resolution for piecewise-linear nets in Bartlett–Harvey–Liaw–Mehrabian (2019), $\Omega(WL\log(W/L))\le\mathrm{VCdim}\le O(WL\log W)$, with matching pseudo-dimension bounds. The present paper is, almost literally, "BHLM for transformers": same partition-and-Warren upper-bound skeleton, same bit-extraction flavour of lower bound, the new ingredients being (i) attention as $O(T^3)$ ternary branching polynomials per layer, which is where $\log T$ comes from, and (ii) the attention-as-retrieval gadget, which is where the $\log T$ lower bound comes from.

Running parallel to this is the norm-based / margin tradition — Bartlett's 1998 margin bounds, Bartlett–Foster–Telgarsky spectral bounds, and for transformers specifically Edelman–Goel–Kakade–Zhang (2022), Zhang et al. (2022), Trauger–Tewari (2023). Those give length-independent bounds under norm control, at the price of polynomial norm/parameter dependence or exponential depth dependence, and they are not comparable to a VC bound: one is scale-sensitive and distribution-sensitive, the other parametric and worst-case. The right way to read this paper against them is as establishing the baseline the norm-based bounds must beat to be doing real work: if your norm-based bound is worse than $WL\log(TW)$ in the relevant regime, it is not buying you anything.

The third strand is expressivity: Hahn (2020) and Merrill–Sabharwal–Smith (2022) on what hard/saturated attention can and cannot recognize, Pérez–Barceló–Marinkovic (2021) on Turing-completeness, Liu et al. (2023) on shortcuts to automata, Yun et al. (2020) on universal approximation, and for CoT specifically Feng et al. (2023), Li–Liu–Zhou–Ma (2024), Merrill–Sabharwal (2024) on how chain-of-thought increases the computational class a constant-depth transformer can reach. Expressivity results say "there exists a transformer of size $S$ computing $g$"; they become learning statements only when paired with a capacity bound, and this paper supplies the pairing with the tight $\tilde\Theta(WL)$ rate.

Two closely related works worth reading. (1) Joshi, Vardi, Block, Goel, Li, Misiakiewicz, Srebro, "A theory of learning with autoregressive chain of thought" (2025) — the direct antecedent: it sets up realizable CoT learnability, the teacher-forcing learner, and a generic reduction (which, composed naively with Theorem 1, would cost an extra $\log T'$). The present paper's contribution over it is the $\mathrm{TSdim}/\mathrm{ASdim}$ dichotomy plus the transformer instantiation, and the optimality of teacher forcing in this setting. (2) Bartlett–Harvey–Liaw–Mehrabian (2019) — read it first if you want the proof technique; the recursive-partition-plus-Warren argument and the bit-extraction lower bound are both there in their cleanest form. Secondary but useful: Edelman et al. (2022), whose $\Omega(\log T)$ at fixed parameter count is the thing Theorem 2 upgrades to a multiplicative interaction.

A plausible follow-up. The gap I would attack is not the $\log L$ but the $\mathrm{TSdim}$–$\mathrm{ASdim}$ spread, which is where the actual science is. Both the upper and lower bounds here are driven by extremes: $\mathrm{TSdim}$ assumes you must match the whole chain; $\mathrm{ASdim}$ assumes the chain reveals nothing. Define an informativeness-graded dimension $\mathrm{ASdim}_\lambda$ in which the prefix assignment is allowed to vary with the labeling only within a budget — e.g. the shattering definition requires the prefixes to agree on all but a $\lambda$-fraction of positions, or requires the prefix to be a function of at most $\lambda$ label bits. Then ask for a sample complexity characterization interpolating between $\Theta(\mathrm{ASdim}/\varepsilon)$ at $\lambda=0$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{TSdim}/\varepsilon)$ at $\lambda=1$. A clean such theorem would be the first statement in this literature that explains when CoT supervision is statistically valuable rather than merely capacity-increasing, and it would have the right shape for the empirical fact that process supervision beats outcome supervision. A second, more tractable target: a bounded-precision version of Theorem 2. With $b$-bit parameters, the base-$2T$ packing caps at $L\log(2T)\lesssim b$; does the truth become $\Theta(WL\log T)$ only up to $T\le2^{b/L}$ and $\Theta(W\cdot b)$ beyond? That is a well-posed question with a likely-clean answer and it would tell you which half of the theorem survives contact with float32. Third, the honest big one: softmax, where the gap between $O(WL\log T)$ and $\mathrm{poly}(T)$ is enormous; even a bound like $\tilde O(WL\log T+\mathrm{poly}(W)\log(1/\text{temperature}))$ for temperature-bounded softmax would be a real advance.

Connection to theoretical IR, generative retrieval, and vector search. Three of these are genuine and one of them is close to immediate.

Generative retrieval is literally the Section 4 setting. DSI-style models (Tay et al.), NCI, SEAL and their descendants map a query to a document identifier by autoregressive decoding, trained by teacher forcing on the full identifier sequence, and evaluated on whether the final decoded docid is correct. Map the paper's objects: $T$ = query length, $T'$ = docid length (number of decoding steps), $\Sigma$ = the docid token alphabet (semantic codes, hierarchical $k$-means cluster ids, or product-quantization codes), $K=|\Sigma|$, and the "answer" is the complete identifier. Two concrete consequences. First, Theorems 6+7 give a genuine PAC guarantee for the standard DSI training recipe: $m=O\bigl(WL\log((T+T')W)\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\bigr)$ labeled query–docid pairs suffice for end-to-end top-1 correctness, and Corollary 9 says no cleverer use of the identifier-prefix supervision can beat it by more than logarithmic factors. Since docid lengths are short ($T'\sim4$–$32$) and queries are short, $\log((T+T')W)\approx\log W$: the sample complexity of generative retrieval is, up to logs, parameter-count-driven and essentially length-free. That is a precise version of a claim the GR literature makes only informally, and it is the kind of statement that lets you reason about how many labeled query–document pairs a GR model of a given size actually needs — a question on which the empirical literature is mostly silent and the scaling behaviour notoriously poor.

Second, and sharper: the $\mathrm{ASdim}$ construction is a warning about docid design. The GR community's central structural argument is that hierarchical/semantic docids generalize better than atomic ones because the shared prefix structure lets statistical strength transfer across documents — a query that teaches the model the first code token of document $d$ also teaches it something about every document in $d$'s cluster. Theorem 8 is precisely the construction where that transfer is nil: the prefix is label-invariant, so each observed trace reveals exactly its own final token and nothing more. The honest lesson is a dichotomy to make rigorous: GR with semantic docids is statistically favourable exactly to the extent that the identifier prefix is predictable from the document and shared across queries, and the moment the discriminative information is concentrated in the last code token — which is what happens when a hierarchy is unbalanced, or when the leaf-level code is essentially an arbitrary tiebreaker among near-duplicate documents — you are in the $\mathrm{ASdim}$ regime, paying $WL\log T_{\text{ctx}}$ in capacity for a chain that teaches you one bit per example. The graded-informativeness dimension proposed above is, in IR terms, exactly a formalization of "how much does hierarchical docid structure buy you".

Hard attention is maximum inner-product search. This is not a metaphor: $M_i=\arg\max_{j\le i}\langle Q_i,K_j\rangle$ is exact MIPS over the context, and the RRM is a learned index — parameters store addresses, the context stores a table, each layer performs one nearest-neighbour lookup, the FFN does pointer arithmetic. The $O(T^3)$ per-layer branching count in the upper bound is the combinatorial complexity of the ranking arrangement induced by $T$ keys under a learned query map, which is the same object that appears when one counts cells in arrangements for nearest-neighbour classifiers. So the upper bound can be read as: a depth-$L$ stack of learned MIPS lookups over a length-$T$ database, with $W$ parameters shaping the query/key maps, has capacity $\tilde O(WL\log T)$ — the database contributes only logarithmically, and the retrieval maps carry the capacity. That is a useful dictionary entry for anyone thinking about the learning-theoretic cost of retrieval-augmented or memory-augmented architectures, and about the $\Omega(WL\log T)$ side as a statement that a learned index over a $T$-entry store genuinely buys $\log T$ bits of capacity per parameter per layer.

Where the connection does not hold, said plainly. Nothing here speaks to dense bi-encoder retrieval with a fixed similarity function, to the geometry or intrinsic dimension of embedding spaces, or to ANN index accuracy–latency tradeoffs. Hard attention being exact MIPS means the analysis assumes the exact argmax; approximate retrieval (HNSW, IVF-PQ) would break the "freeze the ternary signs" argument, since the branching structure then depends on the index's internal state, not on $\theta$ alone. That is itself an interesting open direction — a capacity theory for architectures whose retrieval is approximate — but it is not what this paper does.

title: On Agnostic PAC Learning in the Small Error Regime

Claude daily deep-dive — 10 November 2026

On Agnostic PAC Learning in the Small Error Regime

Julian Asilis, Mikael Møller Høgsgaard, Grigoris Velegkas (2025) — arXiv:2502.09496

Setting and problem

Fix a domain $\mathcal X$ (arbitrary), labels $\mathcal Y={\pm1}$, and a hypothesis class $H\subseteq \mathcal Y^{\mathcal X}$ with $\mathrm{VC}(H)=d<\infty$. A distribution $D$ over $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ induces the 0-1 risk $L_D(f)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[f(x)\neq y]$ and the empirical risk $L_S(f)$ on a sample $S$. The learner $A:(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)^*\to\mathcal Y^{\mathcal X}$ receives $S=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^m\sim D^m$ i.i.d. and outputs a classifier $A(S)$ — not necessarily in $H$ (improper learning is allowed and, as we'll see, required). Write $h^\star=h^\star_D\in\arg\min_{H h\in}L_D(h)$ (assumed to exist) and

$$\tau \;:=\; L_D(h^\star_D)\;=\;\inf_{h\in H}L_D(h).$$

The guarantee is quantified as: for every $D$ over $\mathcal X\times{\pm1}$, with probability $\ge 1-\delta$ over $S\sim D^m$ (and over the learner's internal randomness), $L_D(A(S))\le \tau + \varepsilon(m,d,\delta,\tau)$. Realizable learning restricts $D$ to the family with $\tau=0$; agnostic learning allows all $D$. The classical agnostic rate is distribution-free in $\tau$: ERM achieves $\tau+O(\sqrt{(d+\log(1/\delta))/m})$ and that is optimal in the worst case over $D$, so ERM is an optimal agnostic learner. In the realizable case ERM is not optimal: its worst-case error is $\Theta!\big(\frac{d\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta)}{m}\big)$-ish rather than $\Theta!\big(\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{m}\big)$ — the extra $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ factor, with a matching lower bound for all proper learners (Bousquet–Hanneke–Moran–Zhivotovskiy, COLT'20, Thm 11), and the optimal $\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{m}$ rate attained only by improper learners (Hanneke 2016). That juxtaposition — ERM suboptimal realizably, optimal agnostically — is the paradox the paper opens with. Its resolution is that the worst-case-over-$D$ agnostic benchmark is dominated by hard, genuinely noisy $D$, so an agnostic-optimal learner is licensed to be sloppy on the easy (small-$\tau$) distributions, realizable ones included.

The $\tau$-dependent refinement (Hanneke–Larsen–Zhivotovskiy, FOCS'24; "HLZ") closes that loophole by making $\tau$ a parameter of the excess-error term rather than a quantity you only subtract. The reference point is the Devroye–Györfi–Lugosi-style lower bound, restated by HLZ: for every learner there is a $D$ on which, with probability $\ge\delta$,

$$L_D(A(S))\;\ge\;\tau+\Omega!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))}{m}}+\tfrac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}\right).$$

HLZ gave a learner with $L_D \le \tau + O!\big(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m}\big)+O!\big(\ln^5(m/d)\,(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m\big)$, which is tight (matches the display above) whenever the $\sqrt{\cdot}$ term swamps the $\ln^5$ additive term, i.e. for $\tau\gtrsim \ln^{10}(m/d)\cdot\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}$. They also proved that all proper learners, ERM included, are suboptimal throughout $\tau\in[\Omega(\ln^{10}(m/d)\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}),\,o(1)]$ — the properness barrier of the realizable case migrates into the agnostic small-error regime.

What was left open is the bottom of the range. Verbatim as a question:

Problem 1.1 (HLZ, FOCS'24). With $d=\mathrm{VC}(H)$ and $m=|S|$, what is the optimal sample complexity / error rate of agnostic learning in the regime $\tau\approx d/m$?

Why that regime is hard, and why it is the right regime to ask about: when $\tau\lesssim d/m$, all three terms $\tau$, $\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m}$ and $(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m$ collapse to the same order $O(\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$, so HLZ's $\ln^5$ additive term is the only thing separating their upper bound from the lower bound — and it is not obviously an artifact, because at the extreme $\tau=0$ we know improper learning is necessary and we know proper learners pay a $\log$ factor. A priori the truth at $\tau\approx d/m$ could have been a genuinely higher lower bound carrying a $\log^{\Theta(1)}(m/d)$, i.e. the realizable $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ pathology leaking into a neighborhood of the realizable case. Problem 1.1 asks which it is.

Two non-obvious modelling choices make the question tractable, and both must be stated before the theorem:

  1. A multiplicative constant on $\tau$ is the right currency. Because the lower bound already contains $+\Omega(\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$, a learner achieving $$L_D \;\le\; c\cdot\tau \;+\; O!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))}{m}}+\tfrac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}\right)$$ for any absolute constant $c\ge1$ is exactly optimal (up to the hidden constants) whenever $\tau=O(d/m)$: the slack $(c-1)\tau$ is absorbed into the already-unavoidable additive term. So the entire content of Problem 1.1 is: can the $\ln^5$ be traded for a constant factor on $\tau$? Conversely, to extend optimality upward in $\tau$ one needs $c\to1$, since for $\tau\gg d/m$ the term $(c-1)\tau$ dominates everything else. Hence the constant $c$ becomes the object of study, and $c=1$ would settle agnostic learning across the whole range $\tau\in[0,1/2]$.
  2. Sample splitting and impropriety. The learner is improper by necessity (properness is barred by HLZ's lower bound), it splits $S$ into three equal parts and uses a hold-out for model selection, and it is $\tau$-oblivious: it never estimates $\tau$. That matters, since in the regime $\tau=o(d/m)$ any ERM-based estimate of $\tau$ is uninformative, so a learner tuned to a known $\tau$ would be cheating. It also requires $m=3^k$ (discarding up to a constant fraction of the data — fine for everything except $\tau$ itself, whose coefficient is unaffected).

With that, the main theorem is forced: _there is a $\tau$-oblivious improper learner with error $\min{\,c\tau+O(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m}+\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}),\ \tau+O(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m}+\ln^5(m/d)\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})\,}$ for an explicit constant $c$_, which resolves Problem 1.1 in the negative (no higher lower bound at $\tau\approx d/m$) and strictly improves HLZ for $\tau=o(\ln^5(m/d)\,d/m)$.

Main idea

They prove exactly that, with $c\le 2.1$ (in fact $2.0888$ before the best-of-both-worlds step).

Theorem 1.4. For every $\mathcal X$, $H$ with $\mathrm{VC}(H)=d$, $m$, $\delta\in(0,1)$ there is an algorithm which for every $D$ outputs $h_S$ with probability $\ge 1-\delta$ satisfying $$L_D(h_S)\le\min\left{2.1\,\tau+O!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{\tau(d+\ln\frac1\delta)}{m}}+\tfrac{d+\ln\frac1\delta}{m}\right),\;\;\tau+O!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{\tau(d+\ln\frac1\delta)}{m}}+\tfrac{\ln^5(m/d)(d+\ln\frac1\delta)}{m}\right)\right}.$$

Consequences: (i) the regime $\tau=O(d/m)$ is settled — the Devroye-style lower bound is tight there, no extra logs; (ii) the only remaining uncharacterized window is the polylog band $\tau\in[\omega(1),o(\ln^{10}(m/d))]\cdot\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}$, where the truth lies between $\tau+\Omega(\cdot)$ and $\min{2.1\tau,\ \tau+\ln^5(\cdot)}$; (iii) progress on HLZ's two other questions, because the learner is a majority vote of ERMs (their Problem 1.2) and uses only $O(\log\frac{m}{\delta(d+\ln(1/\delta))})$ ERM-oracle calls (their Problem 1.3).

The machinery, concretely:

  • A modified Hanneke-style recursive splitting scheme (Algorithm 2). On input $(S;T)$ with $|S|=3^k$, $k\ge6$: partition $S$ into 27 equal blocks $S_1,\dots,S_{27}$; inside block $i$ set $S_{i,\sqcup}=S_i[1:3^{k-6}]$ (a $1/27$ fraction of the block — the new active set) and $S_{i,\sqcap}=S_i[3^{k-6}{+}1:3^{k-3}]$ (the other $26/27$ — the history, appended to $T$ and therefore present in every descendant leaf); recurse on $(S_{i,\sqcup};S_{i,\sqcap}\sqcup T)$. Two deliberate deviations from Hanneke (2016): the splits are disjoint (Hanneke's overlap), and the history set is much larger than the active set. Both exist solely to control the constant on $\tau$: the ratio $s_\sqcap=|S|/|S_{1,\sqcap}|$ enters the final bound as the factor $|S_i|/|S_{i,\sqcap}|=1/(1-1/27)=27/26$ multiplying $\tau$, which $\to1$ as the split is made more imbalanced (at the price of larger additive constants).
  • Sub-sampled bagging instead of the full ensemble. The scheme produces $27^{\lfloor \log_3 m/6\rfloor}\approx m^{0.22}$ leaf subsequences. Rather than running ERM on all of them (Hanneke-style), they draw $t=\Theta(\ln\frac{m}{\delta(d+\ln(1/\delta))})$ leaves uniformly at random and run ERM only on those, giving $\widehat A_t(S)$ — literally bagging, but with the bootstrap replaced by "uniform leaf of the splitting tree". This is the efficiency win, and the idea of randomly subsampling an exponentially large optimal ensemble is borrowed from Larsen (2023) ("bagging is an optimal PAC learner").
  • The tie-breaking construction. Split $S$ into $S_1,S_2,S_3$; split $S_1$ into $S_{1,1},S_{1,2},S_{1,3}$. Run the above on $S_{1,1}$ and $S_{1,2}$ independently, yielding two voter ensembles $\widehat A_{t_1},\widehat A_{t_2}$. Form $S_3^{\neq}\subseteq S_{1,3}$ = the examples on which either ensemble has at least an $11/243$ fraction of dissenting voters, and set $h_{\mathrm{tie}}=\mathrm{ERM}(S_3^{\neq})$. Predict: if both ensembles have $\ge 232/243$ of their voters agreeing on the same label $y$, output $y$; otherwise output $h_{\mathrm{tie}}(x)$. Call this $\widetilde A_1$.
  • Best of both worlds. Train HLZ's learner on $S_2$ to get $\widetilde A_2$, and use $S_3$ as a hold-out to pick whichever of $\widetilde A_1,\widetilde A_2$ has smaller empirical error. The $\min{\cdot,\cdot}$ in Theorem 1.4 is just this selection step, with a Bernstein-type comparison lemma to convert empirical to true risk without losing the constant on $\tau$ (Lemma B.3, the two-sided Shalev-Shwartz–Ben-David bound).

What is not here, to set expectations: no multiclass extension, no general bounded-loss / regression version, no one-inclusion-graph predictors (the optimal-learner literature's other main device — Aden-Ali–Cherapanamjeri–Shetty–Zhivotovskiy, Aden-Ali–Høgsgaard–Larsen–Zhivotovskiy — is cited but not used), and no lower bound on $c$. Whether $c>1$ is necessary is entirely open; the paper's own conclusion flags closing $2.1\to1$ as the main open problem.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever device is the tie-breaker trained on the disagreement region, and the reason it works is worth spelling out, because it is where the constant comes from — and it also exposes the paper's real weakness.

The bottleneck in the naive analysis is the recursion step. To bound $\Pr[\text{an }\alpha\text{-fraction of voters err}]$ by the same quantity for the recursive sub-calls, you argue: if an $\alpha$-fraction of the whole ensemble errs on $(x,y)$, then (a) some child $i$ also has an $\alpha$-fraction erring, and (b) across the other children a $\ge\frac{1}{r-1}(\alpha-\frac1r)$-fraction of voters err (with $r$ = branching factor). Step (b) requires $\alpha>1/r$. At $r=3$ this forces $\alpha\approx0.49$, and the resulting union-bound/averaging factor is $\approx13$ — which lands directly on $\tau$ (hence the warm-up bound $15\tau$). The two structural fixes: (i) raise $r$ to 27 so that a much smaller threshold $\alpha=10/243$ is still $>1/27$, letting you control the far more informative quantity "even a $4\%$ minority of voters errs"; and (ii) realize that a factor like $5687$ sitting in front of a joint probability $\Pr[h'\text{ errs}\ \wedge\ \text{a child's ensemble errs}]$ is harmless, because that joint probability is itself $O(\tau/5687 + \ldots)$ — the big constants live inside the induction, not on $\tau$.

Then the margin trick: instead of a bare majority, require $232/243$ agreement from two independent ensembles. The event "both ensembles are $232/243$-wrong" can be bounded via a single random voter from ensemble 1, costing only $243/232\approx1.047$ on $\tau$. The complementary event — the two ensembles fail to reach that margin — is, by the $11/243$ bound, a rare event of probability $O(\tau+\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$, and crucially you have $h_{\mathrm{tie}}$ trained on exactly the conditional distribution $D(\cdot\mid\neq)$ restricted to it. The payoff is the cleanest line in the paper:

$$L_{D(\cdot|\neq)}(h^\star)\cdot\Pr_D[\neq]\;=\;\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}!\left[h^\star(x)\neq y,\ \widehat A_{t_1}(x)\neq \widehat A_{t_2}(x)\right]\;\le\;\tau .$$

That is: conditioning on the disagreement region renormalizes the $\sqrt{(d+\ln(1/\delta))/|S_3^\neq|}$ ERM penalty by $\Pr[\neq]$, turning a $\sqrt{}$-rate into a product that collapses to a bona fide $\tau$ plus a $\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m}$ cross term. This is a localization argument executed by actually localizing the training data, not by a chaining/local-Rademacher bound on a fixed class — and it's reusable. (The authors say as much, and I agree; "cheap committee votes, expensive specialist on the committee's disagreement region" is a pattern.)

Now the honest critique.

Is $c\le2.1$ natural or an artifact? Partly both, and the decomposition says which. $2.0888 = 1.0888 + 1$, where $1.0888=\frac{243}{232}\cdot\frac{1000\cdot27}{999\cdot26}$ comes from (margin threshold) × (Chernoff slack) × (history/active split ratio $27/26$), and the paper is explicit that each of those factors can be pushed to $1$ by more imbalanced splits, more branches and a tighter Chernoff, at the cost of blowing up the additive constants. The trailing $+1$, by contrast, is the display above: it is the price of the tie-breaker and it is exactly $\tau$, with no slack to squeeze. So the architecture as given has a floor of $c\to2$, not $c\to1$. The paper's framing ("within striking distance of $c=1$") is therefore a bit generous: $0.0888$ is the artifact, the $2$ is structural. Getting to $1$ requires something the paper does not have — note that the two failure events (both-ensembles-confidently-wrong; ensembles-disagree-and-$h_{\mathrm{tie}}$-wrong) are disjoint, so summing two separate $\approx\tau$ bounds is provably lossy; a joint analysis that charges $h^\star$'s mistakes once rather than twice is the obvious target, and it's a real opening, not a dead end. I'd bet the open problem is closable but not by tuning constants.

Is there a lower bound showing $c>1$ is necessary? No, and this is the main gap. The paper resolves "is the lower bound at $\tau\approx d/m$ higher than $\tau+\Omega(\sqrt{\cdot}+\cdot)$?" with a no, but says nothing about whether the $\ln^5$ (or any $\omega(1)$ factor) is necessary in the polylog band, nor whether any learner can have $c=1$ with an $O(\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$ additive term. So the title claim "small error regime" is accurate but narrow: it settles the bottom $O(d/m)$ and leaves the interesting transitional band open from both sides.

Computational efficiency. The $O(\ln\frac{m}{\delta(d+\ln(1/\delta))})$ ERM-call count is a real improvement over running ERM on all $\approx m^{0.22}$ leaves, and "efficient relative to an ERM oracle" is the right notion here. But the claim applies only to $\widetilde A_1$. Theorem 1.4's $\min$ requires also running HLZ's learner, whose oracle complexity is not discussed; so the fully stated theorem is not known to be efficient, only its $2.1\tau$ branch. The hidden constant in $t$ is also $4\cdot243^2\approx2.4\times10^5$.

How tight is this really? The $O(\cdot)$ constants are astronomical. Tracking Appendix B: $c_b=5687^2\cdot4\cdot3^6\ln(24e)\,s_\sqcap^2\approx3\times10^{14}$ and $c_c=3^{12}\ln^2(24e)\sqrt{c_b}\,s_\sqcap^2\approx10^{17}$, and these multiply $(d+\ln(e/\delta))/m$ in Lemma B.1/Theorem B.4. Compared with HLZ's $\ln^5(m/d)$, the crossover at which $2.1\tau+10^{17}\frac{d}{m}$ beats $\tau+\ln^5(m/d)\frac{d}{m}$ needs $\ln^5(m/d)\gtrsim10^{17}$, i.e. $m/d$ astronomically large. The result is a structural statement about asymptotic rates, with the usual caveat that "constant $c$" and "$O(1)$" are doing very different amounts of work in the same formula. One should also note the authors' own honest Remark 3.1: the tie-breaker intuitively stabilizes the committee, but $\widetilde A_1$ is provably not stable in the Bousquet–Elisseeff sense, because the two ensembles are trained on overlapping leaves, so changing one example in $S_{1,1}$ can change many voters and hence $S_3^\neq$. The construction therefore cannot be analyzed via stability, which is part of why the proof is as laborious as it is.

Minor but worth noting for a careful reader: the arXiv v2 has broken autorefs throughout (Lemmas cited as "Theorem B.1", "resolving Theorem 1.1" where Problem 1.1 is meant, Appendix A duplicated in the PDF text layer, and one sign error where ERM's realizable lower bound is written $O(\cdot)$ instead of $\Omega(\cdot)$). Cosmetic, but it makes Section 3 harder to follow than it should be.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Three results chain together.

Lemma B.1 (and Theorem B.4, its recursive engine). There is a universal $c\ge1$ s.t. for any $H$ with $\mathrm{VC}=d$, any $D$, any $\delta$, any $m=3^k$ ($k\ge6$), and $S\sim D^m$: with probability $\ge1-\delta$, $$L_D^{10/243}\big(A(S;\emptyset)\big):=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}!\left[\mathrm{avg}_{\neq}(A(S;\emptyset))(x,y)\ge \tfrac{10}{243}\right]\;\le\;c\tau+\tfrac{c(d+\ln(e/\delta))}{m},$$ where $A(S;T)={A(S'):S'\in\mathcal S(S;T)}$ is the multiset of ERMs on all leaves of Algorithm 2, and $\mathrm{avg}_\neq$ is the fraction of them erring on $(x,y)$. Note the quantified object: not the majority vote's error, but the probability that _even a $4\%$ minority_ of the ensemble errs.

Theorem B.2. For $t\ge4\cdot243^2\ln\frac{2m}{\delta(d+\ln(1/\delta))}$ and $\widehat A_t(S)$ = $t$ i.i.d. uniform leaves' ERMs: w.p. $\ge1-\delta$ over $S$ and the subsampling, $L_D^{11/243}(\widehat A_t(S))\le c\tau+c\frac{d+\ln(e/\delta)}{m}$.

Theorem C.1. For the tie-breaking classifier, w.p. $\ge1-\delta$, $L_D(\mathrm{Tie}^{11/243}(\widehat A_{t_1}(S_1),\widehat A_{t_2}(S_2);h_{\mathrm{tie}}))\le 2.0888\,\tau+O(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(e/\delta))/m}+\frac{d+\ln(e/\delta)}{m})$. Appendix D then does the hold-out selection against HLZ's learner to get Theorem 1.4.

How: Theorem B.4, the induction. This is the heart. The statement proved by induction on $k$, for arbitrary history $T$ (this generality is what makes the recursion close), is $$L_D^{10/243}(A(S;T))\;\le\;\max_{S'\in\mathcal S(S;T)}\frac{12000\,\Sigma_{\neq}(h^\star,S')}{m/s_\sqcap}\;+\;c_b\sqrt{\tfrac{(d+\ln(e/\delta))}{m}\cdot\max_{S'}\tfrac{12000\Sigma_\neq(h^\star,S')}{m/s_\sqcap}}\;+\;c_c\tfrac{d+\ln(e/\delta)}{m},$$ with $\Sigma_\neq(h^\star,S')=\sum_{(x,y)\in S'}\mathbb 1[h^\star(x)\neq y]$ — i.e. the learner's population minority-error is controlled by $h^\star$'s empirical error on the worst leaf. Base case $k\le12$ is trivial since $c_c\ge3^{12}$ makes the RHS exceed 1.

Three mechanisms:

  1. A branching/averaging step replaces a union bound (Lemma B.5). If $\mathrm{avg}_\neq(A(S;T))(x,y)\ge\frac{10}{243}$ then, since the 27 children contribute equally, (a) by Markov at least a $\frac{10}{243}$-fraction of indices $i$ satisfy $\mathrm{avg}_\neq(A(S_{i,\sqcup};S_{i,\sqcap}\sqcup T))(x,y)\ge\frac{10}{243}$, and (b) for any fixed $i$, the remaining 26 children jointly contain at least a $\frac1{234}$-fraction of erring voters (from $\frac{10}{243}-\frac1{27}\ge\frac1{243}$, rescaled by $\frac{27}{26}$). Drawing $I$ uniform and $\hat h$ uniform from the non-$I$ children gives $\Pr_{I,\hat h}[\hat h(x)\neq y\ \wedge\ \text{child }I\text{ is }\tfrac{10}{243}\text{-bad}]\ge\frac{1}{234}\cdot\frac{10}{243}\ge\frac1{5687}$, hence $$L_D^{10/243}(A(S;T))\le 5687\max_{i\neq j}\max_{h'\in A(S_{j,\sqcup};\cdot)}\Pr_D\big[h'(x)\neq y,\ \mathrm{avg}_\neq(A(S_{i,\sqcup}\big].$$ This is Hanneke's "two independent recursive calls both fail" move, adapted to a };\cdot))(x,y)\ge\tfrac{10}{243_fractional_ threshold; the whole point of 27-way branching is to keep $\frac{10}{243}-\frac1{27}>0$ (at 3-way branching this is negative — all errors could sit in child $I$ — which is exactly why the warm-up in §3.1 is stuck at $\alpha\approx0.49$ and $c=15$).
  2. A case split on the sub-call's own error, plus the conditional-uniform-convergence trick. Fix $i=2,j=1$. Three events on $S_2$: $\mathcal E_2$ (sub-call error already $\le c_c C\frac{d+\ln(e/\delta)}{5687m}$ — done by monotonicity, the $5687$ is paid for), $\mathcal E_3$ (sub-call error exceeds the inductive bound — probability $\le\delta/24$ by induction), and the interesting middle $\mathcal E_1$. On $\mathcal E_1$, write $A={(x,y):\mathrm{avg}_\neq(A(S_{2,\sqcup};\cdot))(x,y)\ge\frac{10}{243}}$ and $N_1=|S_{1,\sqcap}\sqcap A|$, the number of history points of child 1 landing in the bad region. Since $\mathbb E[N_1]=\Pr[A]\cdot m/s_\sqcap$ and $\Pr[A]$ is bounded below on $\mathcal E_1$, a multiplicative Chernoff gives $N_1\ge\frac12\Pr[A]\,m/s_\sqcap$ with probability $1-(\delta/e)^{19}$. Then $S_{1,\sqcap}\sqcap A\sim D(\cdot\mid A)^{N_1}$, so standard VC uniform convergence on the conditional distribution yields $$\Pr_D[h\text{ errs},A]\;\le\;\Big(L_{S_{1,\sqcap}\sqcap A}(h)+\sqrt{\tfrac{C(d+\ln(24e/\delta))}{N_1}}\Big)\cdot \Pr_D[A].$$ This is where the independence of the 27 blocks is spent: child 2 defines the region, child 1's history measures it.
  3. The ERM property converts the empirical term into $h^\star$'s error, and the Chernoff lower bound on $N_1$ kills the $\sqrt{}$. Every leaf $S'$ of child 1's subtree contains $S_{1,\sqcap}\sqcap A$ (that's the whole purpose of the history mechanism), and $h=A(S')$ minimizes empirical error on $S'$, so $\sum_{(x,y)\in S_{1,\sqcap}\sqcap A}\mathbb 1[h(x)\neq y]\le \Sigma_\neq(A(S'),S')\le\Sigma_\neq(h^\star,S')$. Combined with $N_1\ge\frac12\Pr[A]m/s_\sqcap$, the first term becomes $\le\max_{S'}\frac{2\Sigma_\neq(h^\star,S')}{m/s_\sqcap}$ — a purely empirical quantity about $h^\star$, with the learner-dependent $\Pr[A]$ cancelled. For the second term, $\Pr[A]\sqrt{C(d+\cdot)/N_1}\le\sqrt{2C(d+\cdot)\Pr[A]/(m/s_\sqcap)}$, and substituting the inductive bound for $\Pr[A]$ plus $\sqrt{a+b}\le\sqrt a+\sqrt b$ reproduces the $c_b\sqrt{\cdot}+c_c(\cdot)$ shape — provided $c_b=5687^2\cdot4\cdot3^6\ln(24e)s_\sqcap^2$ and $c_c=3^{12}\ln^2(24e)\sqrt{c_b}s_\sqcap^2$ are large enough to absorb the $5687$ and the recursion's $m\to m/3^6$ shrinkage. Hence the astronomical constants: they are literally the price of the factor $5687$ appearing inside a $\sqrt{}$ inside an induction of depth $\lfloor\log_3 m/6\rfloor$. Closing the loop, $\max_{S'}\frac{\Sigma_\neq(h^\star,S')}{m/s_\sqcap}\le 2L_{S_i}(h^\star)$ and a Bernstein-type empirical/true-risk bound (Lemma B.3) gives $L_{S_i}(h^\star)\le\tau+O(\sqrt{\tau\ln(1/\delta)/m}+\ln(1/\delta)/m)$, which is what converts "$h^\star$'s empirical error on the worst block" into $\tau$ with a constant $\frac{|S_i|}{|S_{i,\sqcap}|}=\frac{27}{26}$ of slack. Bernstein rather than Hoeffding is essential: a Hoeffding bound would contribute $\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/m}$ with no $\tau$ in the numerator, destroying the first-order shape.
  4. Subsampling the ensemble (Theorem B.2). Decompose $L_D^{11/243}(\widehat A_t)\le \Pr[\mathcal E_S]+\Pr[\text{$\ge\frac{11}{243}$ of the $t$ drawn voters err},\bar{\mathcal E}_S]$, where $\mathcal E_S={\mathrm{avg}_\neq(A(S;\emptyset))\ge\frac{10}{243}}$. The first term is Lemma B.1. For the second: off $\mathcal E_S$ the full ensemble has $<\frac{10}{243}$ error fraction, so each drawn voter errs with probability $<\frac{10}{243}$ and Chernoff gives failure probability $\exp(-t/(2\cdot243^2))\le\frac{\delta(d+\ln(1/\delta))}{2m}$ for the stated $t$; a Markov step (legitimate because $\bar{\mathcal E}_S$ depends on $(x,y)$ and the subsampling randomness $\mathbf t$ independently, so the expectations commute) upgrades this to a $1-\delta/2$ statement. The $\frac{10}{243}\to\frac{11}{243}$ gap is precisely the Chernoff margin.
  5. Theorem C.1, where the 2.1 is assembled. $\mathrm{Tie}$ errs only if (A) both ensembles are $\frac{232}{243}$-confidently wrong, or (B) they fail to agree with margin and $h_{\mathrm{tie}}$ errs — and these are disjoint. For (A): sample one random voter from ensemble 1; it errs with probability $\ge\frac{232}{243}$ on such points, so $\Pr[\text{(A)}]\le\frac{243}{232}\max_{h\in A(S_1;\emptyset)}\Pr[h\text{ errs},\ \mathrm{avg}_\neq(\widehat A_{t_2})\ge\frac{11}{243}]$, and the same conditional-uniform-convergence + Chernoff-on-$N_i$ + ERM-domination argument as above (now with Chernoff slack $1/1000$) bounds it by $\frac{243}{232}\cdot\frac{1000\cdot27}{999\cdot26}\max_i L_{S_{1,i}}(h^\star)+\ldots=1.0888\,\tau+O(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m}+\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$. For (B): $h_{\mathrm{tie}}$ is an ERM on $S_3^\neq\sim D(\cdot\mid\neq)^{N_\neq}$, so $\Pr_{D(\cdot|\neq)}[h_{\mathrm{tie}}\text{ errs}]\le L_{D(\cdot|\neq)}(h^\star)+\sqrt{C'(d+\ln(1/\delta))/N_\neq}$; multiplying by $\Pr[\neq]$, the first piece is exactly $\Pr[h^\star\text{ errs}\wedge \widehat A_{t_1}\neq\widehat A_{t_2}]\le\tau$, and the second, using the Chernoff lower bound $N_\neq\ge\frac{m'}{2}\Pr[\neq]$ together with Theorem B.2's bound $\Pr[\neq]\le c\tau+c\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m'}$, becomes $O(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln(1/\delta))/m}+\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$. Sum: $2.0888\tau+O(\cdot)$. A three-way event partition ($\mathcal E_1/\mathcal E_2/\mathcal E_3$, resp. $\mathcal E_4,\mathcal E_5,\mathcal E_6$) and independence of $S_1,S_2,S_3$ assemble the confidence, with $c_u=86$ bookkeeping the $\delta$ budget.
  6. Appendix D, model selection. Two-sided Bernstein (Lemma B.3) on the hold-out $S_3$ for both candidates, giving $L_D(h_{\min})\le\min_h{L_D(h)+3\sqrt{2L_D(h)\ln(8/\delta)/m'}+9\ln(8/\delta)/m'}$ — the key being that $\sqrt{\tau\cdot\ln(1/\delta)/m}$-type overhead is first-order and so does not inflate the constant on $\tau$ (it does inflate $2.0888\to2.1$).

Why the easy proof cannot work (Appendix A.1), which I consider the most instructive half-page. One might hope to prove the whole thing by multiplicative Chernoff + a union bound over $H$ (or an $\varepsilon$-cover): $N$ hypotheses' risks are estimable to within multiplicative $\tau$ with $O(\log(N/\delta)/\tau)$ samples. But for $\tau=O(\log(N/\delta)/m)$ this is vacuous, and even with Sauer–Shelah's $N=O((m/d)^d)$ it is vacuous for all $\tau=O!\big(\frac{d\log(m/d)+\log(1/\delta)}{m}\big)$ — a band that contains $\tau=O(d/m)$, the very regime at issue. Worse, if such an argument did work for all $\tau$, it would show an ERM $h'$ has error $2.1\tau+O(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln\frac1\delta)/m}+\frac{d+\ln\frac1\delta}{m})$, and setting $\tau=0$ would give ERM error $O(\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$ in the realizable case — contradicting the $\Omega!\big(\frac{d\ln(1/\varepsilon)+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}\big)$ proper-learner lower bound of Bousquet–Hanneke–Moran–Zhivotovskiy. So the properness barrier of the realizable case is provably what forces the recursive-splitting/improper machinery here; it is not a matter of proof-technique taste. Add that the learner must be $\tau$-oblivious (a Chernoff-calibrated procedure needs $\tau$, and ERM-based estimates of $\tau$ are uninformative when $\tau=o(d/m)$), and the shape of the solution is essentially determined.

Broader context

For someone coming in cold, the relevant history is short and unusually clean.

Optimal realizable PAC rates. Blumer–Ehrenfeucht–Haussler–Warmuth established that finite VC dimension characterizes learnability; Ehrenfeucht–Haussler–Kearns–Valiant gave the $\Omega(\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon})$ sample-complexity lower bound. The matching upper bound resisted for ~27 years: ERM only gives $O(\frac{d\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon})$, and the $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ is real for every proper learner (Bousquet–Hanneke–Moran–Zhivotovskiy, COLT'20). Simon (2015) got within $\log\log$; Hanneke (2016) closed it with an improper learner: recursively split the sample, run ERM on a structured family of subsamples, take a majority vote. Since then the optimal-learner zoo has grown: Aden-Ali–Cherapanamjeri–Shetty–Zhivotovskiy (FOCS'23) derive optimal bounds without uniform convergence via one-inclusion-graph / Haussler-packing arguments; Larsen (2023) showed plain bagging (majority of ERMs on bootstrap samples) is an optimal PAC learner, which is both conceptually satisfying and the direct ancestor of the "subsample $t$ of the exponentially many leaves" step here; Aden-Ali–Høgsgaard–Larsen–Zhivotovskiy (COLT'24) showed a majority of three ERMs on a simple split suffices; Høgsgaard (2025) gives an efficient optimal learner. (Separately, Bousquet–Hanneke–Moran–van Handel–Yehudayoff's "universal rates" program classifies per-class learning curves into $e^{-n}$, $1/n$, arbitrarily slow — a different, complementary instance-dependent refinement of PAC, and worth knowing if you like this style of question.)

_The $\tau$-dependent program._ First-order (loss-dependent) bounds are old news in online learning and bandits/RL — empirical-Bernstein and variance penalization (Maurer–Pontil 2009), first-order regret with linear function approximation (Wagenmaker et al. 2022) — but HLZ (FOCS'24) appear to be the first to ask for $\tau$-optimal upper bounds in statistical PAC learning. Their package: a lower bound $\tau+\Omega(\sqrt{\tau(d+\ln\frac1\delta)/m}+\frac{d+\ln\frac1\delta}{m})$, a learner matching it up to a $\ln^5$ in the additive term, and a proper-learner lower bound showing the realizable properness barrier extends across $\tau\in[\Omega(\ln^{10}(m/d)\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}),o(1)]$. The present paper is the direct sequel: it kills the $\ln^5$ at the cost of a constant $2.1$ on $\tau$, settles $\tau=O(d/m)$, and reduces the whole subject to a single question — what is the optimal constant $c$? — with $1\le c\le2.1$ and no lower bound above 1.

Two closely related directions worth tracking.
