(1) The one-inclusion-graph / local-structure route (Aden-Ali et al.) has produced the sharpest realizable constants and the cleanest "no uniform convergence needed" proofs; it is conspicuously absent here, and a one-inclusion-graph predictor with a Bernstein-localized agnostic analysis is the obvious alternative attack on $c\to1$. (2) Simplicity results like majority-of-three: is there a $\tau$-dependent analogue, i.e. does a majority of three ERMs on a plain 3-split achieve $c\cdot\tau+O(\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$ for some constant? That would be a far more usable theorem than the $27$-ary recursion with $10^{17}$ constants.

A plausible follow-up. Exploit the disjointness of the two failure events in Theorem C.1. The current bound sums $1.0888\tau$ (both ensembles confidently wrong) and $\tau$ ($h_{\mathrm{tie}}$ wrong on the disagreement region), but the second term's $\tau$ is really $\Pr[h^\star\text{ errs}\wedge\text{disagreement}]$ while the first is bounded by a quantity that does not restrict to the agreement region. So $h^\star$'s error mass is charged roughly twice. A joint accounting — e.g. running the single-voter argument for event (A) conditioned on the agreement region, or replacing the two-ensemble-plus-tiebreaker architecture with a $k$-ensemble cascade where each stage's tie-breaker is trained on the previous stage's disagreement region and the telescoping sum of $\Pr[h^\star\text{ errs}\wedge\text{disagree at stage }j]$ is bounded by $\tau$ in total — looks like a credible route to $c=1+o(1)$. Independently and more tractably: a matching lower bound showing $c>1$ is necessary for any learner with an $O(\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m})$ additive term would be just as interesting, and would reframe the $\ln^5$ band as a genuine phase transition rather than an analysis artifact. Multiclass ($\mathrm{VC}\to$ DS dimension) and bounded-loss versions are open and probably harder than they look, since the "one random voter errs with probability $\ge232/243$" step is binary-specific.

IR / retrieval connections — where they are genuine, and where they are not. There is no forced link; this is a 0-1-loss binary-classification constant-chasing paper, and pretending it speaks directly to generative retrieval would be dishonest. Three honest points of contact:

  1. First-order rates are the right frame for retrieval losses. Retrieval/ranking problems live almost entirely in the small-error regime: for a well-specified class the best achievable recall@k loss or pairwise-ranking loss is small but nonzero, so a distribution-free $O(\sqrt{d/m})$ excess-risk bound is uninformative while a $\tau$-dependent one ($c\tau+\sqrt{\tau d/m}+d/m$) is exactly what you want. If you ever want to state a bound on learned rankers or learned index structures that is non-vacuous at realistic $m$, first-order/Bernstein-localized forms are the shape to aim for — and the paper's Appendix A.1 is a useful warning that naive multiplicative-Chernoff-plus-cover arguments cannot reach them. The caveat: pairwise ranking and recall-type losses are neither 0-1 on i.i.d. examples nor bounded-variance in the same way, so the mechanism would need redoing, not citing.
  2. Disagreement-region specialization is literally a retrieval cascade. The tie-breaker construction — a cheap committee votes; wherever the committee lacks a $232/243$ margin, route the point to a specialist trained only on the committee's disagreement region — is the theoretical skeleton of multi-stage retrieve-then-rerank, and of ensemble ANN indexes (several HNSW graphs / IVF partitions / PQ codebooks voting, with an exact-distance rescoring pass fired only where the voters disagree). The paper's quantitative lesson transfers: the value of the specialist is that it is trained on the conditional distribution of the hard region, so its $\sqrt{(d+\log(1/\delta))/N}$ penalty is renormalized by the probability of that region — which is the formal version of "reranking helps most when you only pay for it on ambiguous queries". The lesson in the other direction is a caution: Remark 3.1 shows this architecture is not stable, because the committee members share training data, so the disagreement region itself is a high-variance object. Ensemble-index designs that reuse the same vectors across voters inherit that fragility.
  3. $\tau$ as a model-misspecification budget for learned indexes. The agnostic-vs-realizable distinction maps onto "my index/ranker family can represent the true relevance structure" vs "it cannot, and $\tau$ measures by how much". The interesting statement for a learned index is not worst-case over all data distributions but: how does excess retrieval error degrade as a function of the best-in-class misspecification $\tau$? That is precisely the $\tau$-parameterized question, and the answer here — that a constant factor on $\tau$ buys you a clean additive term, and that properness (restricting to a single index from the family, rather than aggregating) is provably costly — is a suggestive, if not formally transferable, design prior: aggregate several imperfect indexes rather than optimizing one.

title: How to sketch a learning algorithm
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 November 2026

How to sketch a learning algorithm

Sam Gunn (2026) — arXiv:2604.07328

Setting and problem

The object of study is a data deletion scheme, and the paper's first contribution is really the insistence that this object be defined without an escape hatch.

The formal objects. Fix a training set of $n$ examples and a model with $p$ parameters. The learning algorithm is not treated as a map from datasets to models but as a map from per-example downweights to parameters, $$\mathcal{A}:\;\mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^p,\qquad w=(w_1,\dots,w_n)\mapsto \theta .$$ Concretely, for SGD with single-example batches, $\mathcal{A}$ runs $\theta_i \leftarrow \theta_{i-1} - (1-w_i)\nabla \ell_i(\theta_{i-1})$ for $i=1,\dots,n$ and outputs $\theta_n$. So $w=\mathbf{0}$ is ordinary training, $w_i=1$ zeroes out example $i$'s contribution, and $\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{1}_D)$ is the model you would have gotten had $D\subseteq[n]$ been excluded. (Note the convention: downweights, following the datamodels line of work but with the sign flipped. Also note what this counterfactual is: same seed, same initialization, same batch order, same latent noise, with $D$'s update steps turned into no-ops — not an independent retraining run on $T\setminus D$.)

A measurement is a scalar readout $\phi:\mathbb{C}^p\to\mathbb{C}$, e.g. "the loss of this model on the string max" or "the probability this model assigns to output $x$", with the probe input hard-coded into $\phi$. The quantity of interest is the composite $$f := \phi\circ\mathcal{A}\;:\;\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C},\qquad \text{target} = f(\mathbf{1}_D).$$

A scheme is a pair of algorithms: * PRECOMPUTE$(\mathcal{A})$ — may spend training-scale resources, outputs $\mathcal{A}(\mathbf 0)$ plus arbitrary auxiliary state. Crucially, it does not see $\phi$. * PREDICT$(\phi, D)$ — given the auxiliary state, a deletion set $D$, and only now the measurement, outputs $\nu \approx f(\mathbf{1}_D)$ in time ideally independent of $n$ and far below retraining.

Error $\varepsilon$ means $|\nu - f(\mathbf 1_D)|\le\varepsilon$; failure probability $\delta$ is over the scheme's own randomness. Everything is single-model: all training/inference randomness is fixed, so the guarantee is about one concrete model, not an average over seeds. This is the stringent version advocated in MAGIC [IE25] and it is the right one — averaging over seeds lets a scheme look good while being useless for "did this model copy this artist".

The computational abstraction. Both training and inference are modelled as arithmetic circuits over $\mathbb{C}$: DAGs with $+$ and $\times$ gates, $\mathrm{size}(f)$ = max(#inputs, #outputs, #edges), unit-cost exact real arithmetic, RAM with constant-time lookup. Two non-obvious moves hide here. (i) By Baur–Strassen, if inference is a circuit then gradient steps are too, so "training is an arithmetic circuit" is WLOG given that inference is. (ii) Working over $\mathbb{C}$ rather than $\mathbb{R}$ is presented as a pedagogical convenience, but it is load-bearing in the proof (see below); non-polynomial gates (ReLU/GELU/softmax) are handled because the method only needs local polynomial approximations around real inputs. The unit-cost exact-arithmetic model also silently discards all numerical conditioning questions, which for 1000-step Adam jets is not nothing.

The assumption: stability. Expand $f$ at the origin (full-data model): $$f(w)=\sum_{r\ge 0}\langle \mathbf{T}^{(r)}, w^{\otimes r}\rangle,\qquad \mathbf{T}^{(r)}\in(\mathbb{C}^n)^{\otimes r}\ \text{symmetric}.$$ $f$ is $\alpha$-stable if $$\big|\mathbf{T}^{(r)}\big|_F \le \frac{\alpha(B)}{B^r}\quad\text{for every }B>0,\ r\ge1 .$$ In the intro this is simplified to $|\mathbf{T}^{(r)}|_F \le 2^{-\omega(r)}$ (superlinear decay in the exponent), uniformly as $n,p\to\infty$.

The crucial modelling choice is Frobenius, not operator, norm. A bound in operator norm is exactly equivalent (via Cauchy's estimate on $z\mapsto f(z\psi)$) to $f$ having a modulus of continuity $\alpha$ — a bland regularity condition. Since $|\mathbf T|_{op}\le|\mathbf T|_F\le\sqrt{n[r]}\,|\mathbf T|_{op}$ with $n[r]=\binom{n+r-1}{r}$, the Frobenius version is stronger by up to $n^{r/2}$. The paper is explicit: stability = bounded modulus of continuity + bounded stable tensor rank $|\mathbf T|_F^2/|\mathbf T|_{op}^2$ of every derivative tensor. At $r=1$ it says the $\ell_2$ norm of the vector of all $n$ first-order influences is small — so individual influences must shrink like $1/\sqrt{n}$ for $\alpha$ to be $n$-independent. Whether that holds at scale is exactly the untested crux. Note also that this is a condition on $f=\phi\circ\mathcal A$, not on $\mathcal A$ or $\phi$ separately: $\mathcal A$ may be wildly unstable as long as the readout you care about is not. (The name collides with Bousquet–Elisseeff uniform stability, which is a sup-norm, single-deletion condition; this is an $\ell_2$-over-all-$r$-way-interactions condition, much closer in spirit to total-influence / Fourier-weight conditions.)

The precise question. _Does there exist a data deletion scheme for arbitrary deep-learning training pipelines whose precomputation is oblivious to the measurement, whose prediction cost is independent of $n$, and whose error can be driven to zero by spending more compute — i.e. without a surrogate model that caps accuracy at its own approximation error?_

What the literature already has, and the gap. Essentially every prior scheme with a guarantee buys it with a surrogate, usually the additivity assumption: $f$ is linear in $w$, so the influence of a set is the sum of individual influences. Influence functions [KL17, KATL19], datamodels [IPE+22], TRAK [PGI+23] and MAGIC [IE25] all live here. Surrogates have a floor: the error of the surrogate itself. Three concrete failure modes the author names: error becomes unreasonable past some number of deletions; there is no knob to buy accuracy with compute; and even if additivity is fine for random subsets (which Saunshi et al. [SGBA23] give harmonic-analytic reasons to expect), it can be badly wrong for the worst-case, correlated deletions that matter — "remove everything by this artist" is precisely a set of near-duplicate, strongly interacting examples. Separately, the strongest additive scheme, MAGIC, must know $\phi$ at precomputation time. Post-hoc unlearning (gradient ascent on the forget set, etc.) makes no reference to $\mathcal A$ at all; the appendix shows why that is fatal for provable claims. The gap: nothing achieves vanishing error for real pipelines, and nothing is simultaneously measurement-oblivious and provably accurate.

Given all of the above you can now write the theorem yourself: for any $\varepsilon,\delta$ there are parameters such that precomputation costs $\tilde O(\mathrm{size}(\mathcal A)\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$, storage is $\tilde O((n+p)\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ (i.e. $\tilde O(\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ models, and the $n$ term drops under PRGs), prediction costs $\tilde O((\mathrm{size}(\phi)+d)\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$, and if $\phi\circ\mathcal A$ is $\alpha$-stable then for any $|D|\le d$ the prediction satisfies $|\nu - (\phi\circ\mathcal A)(\mathbf 1_D)| \le \varepsilon\cdot\alpha(4\sqrt d)$ with probability $1-\delta$.

Main idea

Precompute a truncated jet of the training run along $k$ random complex lines, and exploit the fact that jets compose.

Sample Haar-random unit vectors $\psi_1,\dots,\psi_k\in\mathbb{C}^n$ and evaluate the whole training circuit on the symbolic input $z\psi_i$ over the truncated polynomial ring $R=\mathbb{C}[z]/(z^{s+1})$. That is exactly forward-mode AD: each stored object $p_i=\mathcal A(z\psi_i)\in R^p$ is the degree-$s$ Taylor expansion of the trained parameters as you move the downweight vector along direction $\psi_i$. Cost: $O(\mathrm{size}(\mathcal A)\,s\log s)$ per direction (multiplication gates use FFT), with only $O(s\log s)$ memory overhead and no activation tape — forward mode, not backprop.

At query time, push the measurement through the same ring: $q_i=\phi(p_i)\in R$. Because truncated-jet arithmetic is exact under composition, $q_i = f(z\psi_i)$ to order $s$, so the coefficient of $z^r$ is exactly $\langle\mathbf T^{(r)},\psi_i^{\otimes r}\rangle$ — a random projection of the $r$-th derivative tensor of $\phi\circ\mathcal A$, obtained without ever materializing an $n^r$-sized object and without knowing $\phi$ in advance. This is the structural trick: the expensive precomputed object is measurement-independent, and the measurement is applied after the sketch, not to a reconstructed parameter vector. (Applying $\phi$ to an approximate $\mathcal A(\mathbf 1_D)$ would be wrong: $\mathcal A$ can be arbitrarily unstable while $\phi\circ\mathcal A$ is constant.)

The missing piece is that these projections are in rank-one symmetric directions $\psi^{\otimes r}$, not uniform directions in $(\mathbb{C}^n)^{\otimes r}$. The paper's Theorem 1 says that is fine: for Haar-random $\psi\in\mathbb{C}^n$, $\mathbb{E}[(\psi\psi^\dagger)^{\otimes r}] = \Pi^{(n,r)}_{\mathrm{sym}}/n[r]$. So $n[r]\,\langle\mathbf T^{(r)},\psi^{\otimes r}\rangle\langle\psi,\mathbf 1_D\rangle^r$ is an unbiased estimator of $\langle\mathbf T^{(r)},\mathbf 1_D^{\otimes r}\rangle$, with variance at most $(4d)^r|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F^2$. Median-of-means over $k$ directions, summed over $r\le s=\log_4(2/\varepsilon)$, gives the theorem.

Headline: a provable, surrogate-free data deletion scheme for arbitrary differentiable training pipelines, measurement-oblivious at precomputation, with error controlled by a single regularity parameter of the training-to-measurement map, at $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ overhead in compute and storage. Empirically, on microgpt trained on names, the Taylor coefficients do decay fast, degree-3 sketched predictions track the true $z\mapsto f(z\mathbf 1_D)$ curve across $z\in[0,1]$ where the degree-1 (additive) approximation visibly fails.

The most interesting part

The clever bit. Why complex? Over $\mathbb{R}$ there is no distribution on unit vectors with $\mathbb{E}[(\psi\psi^\top)^{\otimes r}]\propto\Pi_{\mathrm{sym}}$ — the paper's two-line counterexample at $n=r=2$ is that $\mathbb{E}[\langle e_1,\psi\rangle^2\langle e_2,\psi\rangle^2]$ must vanish, forcing a coordinate of $\psi$ to be zero a.s. Over $\mathbb{C}$, the random global phases do the cancellation: writing $w=w_\parallel+w_\perp$ and averaging $(w_\parallel+\lambda w_\perp)^{\otimes r}$ over $|\lambda|=1$ kills every cross term because $\mathbb{E}_\lambda\lambda^k=0$ for $k>0$ (Lemma 2). The real-valued substitute is polarization: Lemma 1's identity $\sum_{S_r \pi\in} v_{\pi(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi(r)}=\mathbb{E}_{a\in{\pm1}^r}[(a_1\cdots a_r)(\sum a_iv_i)^{\otimes r}]$, a Fourier average over $2^r$ sign patterns — i.e. the thing that costs $\exp(s)$. So: complex phases buy you, in a single forward-mode pass, the symmetrization that over $\mathbb{R}$ would cost $2^r$ multi-directional derivative evaluations. That is a genuinely elegant import of a quantum-information fact (Harrow's "church of the symmetric subspace") into AD-based sketching, and it is the reason the scheme runs in $\tilde O(s)$ rather than $\exp(s)$.

The second clever bit is cheaper to state but arguably more consequential: the sketch is an object you can post-compose with. Precomputation produces $k$ jets of $\mathcal A$; applying $\phi$ in the ring yields exactly the sketch you would have produced had you sketched $\phi\circ\mathcal A$ directly. That is what breaks the "know your measurement in advance" limitation of MAGIC. It also means prediction never touches the training data — only the $d$ coordinates ${\psi_{i,j}}_{j\in D}$, i.e. the indices of the deleted examples.

Now the critique. Three issues, in increasing order of seriousness.

  1. The headline bound is, on the paper's own measurements, quantitatively vacuous. The guarantee is error $\le \varepsilon\cdot\alpha(4\sqrt d)$, and $\alpha(B)=\sup_{r\ge1}B^r|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F$ — a single envelope collapsing the whole coefficient sequence. If $|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F=2^{-cr}$ then $\alpha(B)<\infty$ only for $B<2^c$, so deleting $d$ examples needs decay rate $c\ge 2+\tfrac12\log_2 d$. Reading Figure 1: ten curves, starting near $0$ at $r=1$ and ending between roughly $-75$ and $-175$ at $r=100$ — a slope of order $1.3$ nats/order, i.e. $c\approx1.9$ bits. That is below the threshold even for $d=1$ under pure exponential decay. Under the paper's own fitted $2^{-\Omega(r^{3/2})}$, $\alpha$ is finite but the sup is attained at large $r$: with $\ln|\mathbf T^{(r)}|\approx-0.13\,r^{3/2}$ one gets $\alpha(4)\approx e^{23}$ for a _single_{r>s} deletion and $\alpha(4\sqrt{18})\approx e^{198}$ for the 18-name deletion set actually used in Figures 2–3. The theorem therefore certifies nothing about the experiments it is illustrated with. The honest statement is the one the proof actually establishes one line earlier: error $\le \sum_|}|\mathbf T^{(r)_F d^{r/2} + \sqrt{4m/k}\sum_{r\le s}$) are what destroy the constants. Stating the theorem in terms of the coefficient sequence rather than its exponential envelope would cost nothing and be far more informative.}(4d)^{r/2}|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F$. Those two sums are empirically small; the $\alpha$-envelope and the worst-case $4^r$ variance factor (from $n[r]^2/n[2r]\le\binom{2r}{r

  2. The empirical support for stability is thin and the estimator used to measure it is pathological. Lemma 3 says the estimator of $|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F^2$ has relative standard deviation up to $2^r$; at $r=100$ that is $2^{100}$. And indeed the ten curves in Figure 1 disagree by about $100$ log-units at $r=100$ — so fitting the functional form $r^{3/2}$ to them is not well supported by the data shown. Worse, the curves are not ten samples of one function: $\phi$ is "the loss on a random training example, chosen independently for each direction $\psi$", so direction-noise and function-variation are confounded, which is exactly the wrong design for estimating the estimator's variance. Separately, the measured regime is tiny: microgpt, 1000 single-example steps (so $n\approx10^3$), $d=18$, and the author explicitly concedes no attempt was made to see how $|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F$ scales with $n$ and $p$ — which is the entire content of "stability is compatible with powerful models". Figure 3 also runs $m=1$, $k=500$, $s\le3$, i.e. not the theorem's parameter regime; and the author candidly notes the degree-3 sketch beating the degree-3 exact Taylor expansion is luck.

  3. The pipeline is modified to make it work, and the cost constants are brutal. The experiments change Adam's $\epsilon$ from $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-3}$ and move it inside the square root, and swap ReLU for GELU. That is the same smoothing hack used by the metagradient/MAGIC line, and it is precisely the kind of "significantly altering the learning algorithm" the paper criticises additivity-based work for needing. The unit-cost exact-real-arithmetic model also hides that the estimator multiplies $n[r]\approx n^r/r!$ (for $n=10^{12},r=10$ this is $\sim10^{120}$) against a tiny inner product and a tiny $\langle\psi,\mathbf 1_D\rangle^r$ — enormous cancellation that no float format survives without careful rescaling. And the constants: $\varepsilon=0.1,\delta=0.05$ gives $s=3$, $m=8\ln(2s/\delta)\approx38$, $k=16m/\varepsilon^2\approx6\times10^4$ — sixty thousand jet-training runs and $k\cdot s\cdot p$ storage, roughly $2\times10^5$ model copies. "$\tilde O(\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ factors slower than training" reads mild and is not.

Two smaller things. The PRG remark ("the $n$ dependence can be dropped") is hand-waved; it is fine (the accuracy test is poly-time computable, so a PRF secure against poly-time distinguishers suffices) but it is asserted rather than argued, and Haar sampling also needs discretization. And the quantifiers: the $k$ directions are fixed once, so the $1-\delta$ holds _per fixed $(\phi,D)$_. A measurement chosen adaptively after seeing predictions — which is the realistic usage pattern for an attribution tool — is not covered, and this is the familiar adaptive-data-analysis hazard. Nothing in the scheme outputs a certificate, though it easily could: the MOM block spread estimates the variance term and the decay of the $\nu_r$'s estimates the truncation term.

None of this makes the paper less interesting. It is a genuinely new primitive with a correct and pretty proof; the honest framing is "a new mechanism, with an asymptotic theorem whose constants are currently decorative and an experiment that is a proof of concept, not evidence of scalability" — which, to be fair, is roughly how the author describes the experiments himself.

One underemphasized positive. Nothing in Lemma 3 requires $x=\mathbf 1_D$; the variance bound is $4^r|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F^2|x|^{2r}$ for any reweighting vector $x$. So the same precomputation predicts the measurement under arbitrary continuous data-mixture reweightings with $|x|\le\sqrt d$, not only deletions. Given how much current effort goes into data-mixture optimization, that generalization seems more immediately useful than deletion and gets one sentence.

Proof sketch

What is proved (Theorem 2). Assume: training and measurement are arithmetic circuits; all randomness is fixed; $f=\phi\circ\mathcal A$ is $\alpha$-stable. Then Algorithms 1–2 with $s=\log_4(2/\varepsilon)$, $m=8\ln(2s/\delta)$, $k=16m/\varepsilon^2$ satisfy, for any $\phi$ and any $|D|\le d$, $|\nu-f(\mathbf 1_D)|\le \varepsilon\,\alpha(4\sqrt d)$ with probability $\ge1-\delta$, with the stated compute/storage. In plain language: _if the composed training-to-measurement map's Taylor coefficients at the full-data point decay fast enough in Frobenius norm, then a fixed, measurement-independent precomputation of $k$ random-direction jets lets you answer any deletion query to accuracy $\varepsilon$ times a constant that depends only on that decay profile and the deletion-set size._ The guarantee is per-query and over the precomputation randomness; it says nothing about $\mathcal A$ or $\phi$ individually, nor about adaptively chosen queries.

Mechanism, step by step.

(1) Jets instead of derivatives. Forward-mode AD is reframed as evaluation over $R=\mathbb{C}[z]/(z^{s+1})$: feed in $z\psi$ and the output polynomial's $z^r$ coefficient is $\tfrac{1}{r!}\partial^r$ along $\psi$. Addition gates cost $O(s)$, multiplication $O(s\log s)$ via FFT, so a jet evaluation costs $O(\mathrm{size}\cdot s\log s)$ and $O(s\log s)$ memory. Non-polynomial unary gates are replaced by their Taylor expansion about the constant term of the incoming polynomial — which makes the composite jet exact to order $s$, not approximate. Reverse mode is explicitly ruled out: there is no known $\mathrm{size}(f)\cdot\mathrm{poly}(s)$ algorithm for order-$s$ univariate derivatives via backprop, and it needs an activation tape. Forward mode is the right tool here precisely because the cost scales with the number of input directions (one) rather than outputs ($p$).

(2) The sketch identity. Substituting $w=z\psi$ into the Taylor series gives $f(z\psi)=\sum_{r\le s}\langle\mathbf T^{(r)},\psi^{\otimes r}\rangle z^r$ in $R$. So one jet evaluation reads off, in one shot, a random projection of every Taylor tensor up to order $s$. This is the "sketch an arithmetic circuit locally" primitive.

(3) The key lemma — Haar-complex rank-ones are a tight frame for the symmetric subspace. Theorem 1: $\mathbb{E}[(\psi\psi^\dagger)^{\otimes r}]=\Pi^{(n,r)}_{\mathrm{sym}}/n[r]$. Proof in three moves: (a) Lemma 1, the symmetric subspace is spanned by rank-one symmetric tensors, via the $\pm1$ polarization/Fourier identity; (b) Lemma 2, for $U$ Haar on the stabilizer of $v$, $\mathbb{E}\,U^{\otimes r}$ acts on $\vee^r\mathbb{C}^n$ as the projector onto $v^{\otimes r}$ — proved by splitting $w=w_\parallel+w_\perp$ and averaging a phase $\lambda$, with $\mathbb{E}_\lambda\lambda^k=0$ killing all cross terms; (c) $T=\mathbb{E}(\psi\psi^\dagger)^{\otimes r}$ commutes with every $U^{\otimes r}$, hence by (b) acts as a scalar on each $v^{\otimes r}$, hence by (a) is a multiple of $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym}}$; the scalar is pinned by taking traces, $\mathrm{Tr}\,T=1$ and $\mathrm{Tr}\,\Pi_{\mathrm{sym}}=n[r]$.

(4) The estimator and its variance (Lemma 3). For symmetric $\mathbf T$ and any $x$, set $\xi:=n[r]\langle\mathbf T,\psi^{\otimes r}\rangle\langle\psi,x\rangle^r$. Unbiasedness is immediate from Theorem 1. The variance bound is the slick part: $\mathbb{E}|\xi|^2 = n[r]^2\,\mathbb{E}\,\langle \mathbf T\otimes x^{\otimes r},\psi^{\otimes 2r}\rangle\langle\psi^{\otimes2r},\mathbf T\otimes x^{\otimes r}\rangle$ — i.e. _reapply Theorem 1 at order $2r$_ — giving $\tfrac{n[r]^2}{n[2r]}\langle v,\Pi^{(n,2r)}_{\mathrm{sym}}v\rangle\le\tfrac{n[r]^2}{n[2r]}|\mathbf T|_F^2|x|^{2r}$, and then the combinatorial identity $\tfrac{n[r]^2}{n[2r]}\le\binom{2r}{r}\le4^r$. Note the proof only ever uses the $r$-th and $2r$-th moments of $\psi$ — i.e. a complex projective $2r$-design would suffice, Haar is not needed.

_(5) Assembling, and why "4" appears inside $\alpha(4\sqrt d)$._ Two error sources. Truncation: $\sum_{r>s}|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F|\mathbf 1_D|^r=\sum_{r>s}|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F d^{r/2}$, rewritten as $\sum_{r>s}4^{-r}\cdot|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F(4\sqrt d)^r\le\alpha(4\sqrt d)\sum_{r>s}4^{-r}\le\tfrac14^{s}\alpha(4\sqrt d)$. Variance: per order $r$, the error is $(4d)^{r/2}|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F\sqrt{4m/k}=2^{-r}|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F(4\sqrt d)^r\sqrt{4m/k}\le 2^{-r}\alpha(4\sqrt d)\sqrt{4m/k}$, summing to $\alpha(4\sqrt d)\sqrt{4m/k}$. The factor $4$ inside the argument is doing double duty: it is the $2^r$ from the variance bound's $4^r$ times the geometric slack needed to make both sums telescope. That is the whole quantitative architecture — and also why $\alpha$ is evaluated at a point $4\times$ further out than the deletion vector's actual norm, which costs a lot in practice.

(6) Concentration. The author explicitly cannot show the sample mean concentrates — only the second moment is controlled, and the estimator is heavy-tailed (it is a product of two inner products rescaled by $n[r]$). So median-of-means, applied separately to real and imaginary parts (they commute with MOM), union-bounded: $m$ blocks give deviation $\sigma\sqrt{4m/k}$ with failure $2e^{-m/8}$ (Lemma 4). Union over the $s$ orders gives $2se^{-m/8}$. This is where the $\log(1/\delta)$ enters, and why the dependence is $\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2$ rather than $\log(1/\delta)$ inside an exponential tail.

_(7) Upgrading from "sketch $f$" to "data deletion"._ PRECOMPUTE sketches $\mathcal A$, not $f$ — $p$ outputs instead of 1, at no extra cost since the jet evaluation is per-circuit, not per-output. PREDICT then evaluates $\phi$ over $R$ on the stored jets, obtaining bit-for-bit the sketch it would have gotten had it sketched $f$ directly. The counterexample justifying this order is one sentence and worth keeping: if $\mathcal A$ is wildly unstable and $\phi$ exactly undoes it so that $f$ is constant, then approximating $\mathcal A(\mathbf 1_D)$ first and applying $\phi$ after is arbitrarily wrong, while composing in the ring is exact.

Appendix A, a separate and rather nice result. Define: $\mathcal U$ is $\approx$-certified unlearning for $\mathcal A$ if there is $\bar{\mathcal A}$ with $\mathcal U(\mathcal A(S),S,D)\approx\bar{\mathcal A}(S\setminus D)$, for any indistinguishability notion $\approx$. Proposition 5: if $\mathcal U$ is certified simultaneously for every learning algorithm, then $\mathcal U(\mathcal A(S),S,D)\approx_2\mathcal U(\bot,S\cup{x^_},D\cup{x^_})$ — the trained model is not materially used, so the scheme cannot beat retraining. The proof is three lines: define $\mathcal B(S)=\bot$ if $x^_\in S$ and $\mathcal A(S)$ otherwise; apply the hypothesis to $\mathcal B$ on the two inputs $(S,D)$ and $(S\cup{x^_},D\cup{x^*})$, both of which have the same $S\setminus D$, hence both $\approx\bar{\mathcal B}(S\setminus D)$. Moral: an algorithm-agnostic unlearning security proof, absent a correctness guarantee, is retraining in disguise. Caveats worth noting: the "for every $\mathcal A$" quantifier is strong (real certified-unlearning results assume convexity/smoothness and a specific optimizer, so they are out of scope), the constructed $\mathcal B$ is adversarially discontinuous, and $\approx_2$ degrades the parameters, so for weak notions the conclusion weakens too. Still a clean sanity theorem about a literature that badly needs one.

Broader context

The subfield. "How does training data $X$ affect model behaviour $Y$" is attacked from four directions that are formally the same problem. Influence functions (Hampel et al.; Koh–Liang) take the implicit-function-theorem derivative of the optimum w.r.t. an example's weight — first order, and only valid at a converged optimum of a convex-ish objective. Datamodels (Ilyas et al. 2022) abandon theory and just fit a linear surrogate $f(w)\approx\langle\beta,w\rangle$ by retraining on thousands of random subsets; TRAK (Park et al. 2023) makes that cheap with random projections of gradients. MAGIC (Ilyas–Engstrom 2025) is the current strongest: it differentiates through the training trajectory (metagradients, à la Engstrom et al.'s metagradient descent) to get the exact first-order counterfactual for the actual run — exact under additivity, but it must fix the measurement before doing the expensive backward pass. Machine unlearning (Ginart et al.; Guo et al.; Koloskova et al.; the NeurIPS unlearning competition) asks for the same counterfactual but with a privacy, rather than accuracy, success criterion — and as Appendix A shows, those criteria come apart badly.

Gunn's paper is the first in this lineage to say: stop modelling $f$, and instead _assume a regularity condition on $f$ itself_ and build an estimator that converges under it. The analytic ancestry is elsewhere: randomized trace/norm estimation (Hutchinson's $\mathbb{E}[x^\top Ax]=\mathrm{Tr}A$ is literally the $r=1$ case of Lemma 3), tensor sketching, and the symmetric-subspace / $t$-design toolkit from quantum information (Harrow's notes are the stated source; this is the same machinery behind shadow tomography and randomized benchmarking). The arithmetic-circuit framing with Baur–Strassen also connects to algebraic complexity's "partial derivatives as a complexity measure" literature.

Two things worth reading next. (i) MAGIC [IE25], because it is the direct point of comparison and because its engineering (rematerialization, Adam-$\epsilon$ smoothing) is what makes trajectory differentiation feasible at all. (ii) Saunshi–Gupta–Braverman–Arora, Understanding influence functions and datamodels via harmonic analysis (ICLR 2023) — it studies $f:{0,1}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ with Fourier analysis and explains why additivity is fine for random subsets; it is the discrete shadow of exactly the condition Gunn imposes continuously, and the author himself flags the connection as open.

Follow-ups this opens. * Derandomize via designs. The proof uses only $\mathbb{E}[(\psi\psi^\dagger)^{\otimes r}]$ and $\mathbb{E}[(\psi\psi^\dagger)^{\otimes 2r}]$. Replacing Haar vectors by an exact complex projective $2s$-design would make the PRG remark a theorem, shrink the seed, and make sampling cheap — and $2s=O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ is small, so explicit low-order designs plausibly suffice. * Prove stability for something. Right now $\alpha$ is a measured quantity with no theory. Bounding $|\mathbf T^{(r)}|_F$ for SGD on a smooth loss in terms of learning rate, Hessian spectra along the trajectory, and $n$ — in particular establishing or refuting $n$-independence — is the question on which the whole programme turns. A negative result (stability forces $\alpha$ to grow with $n$ for realistic losses) would be equally valuable. * Tighten the analysis, not the algorithm. As argued above, replacing the $\alpha$-envelope with the explicit two-sum bound, and replacing the worst-case $4^r$ with a data-dependent variance estimate from the MOM blocks, would turn a vacuous constant into a usable, self-certifying error bar at no algorithmic cost. * Beyond deletion. The estimator works for arbitrary reweighting vectors $x$ with $|x|\le\sqrt d$, so the same precomputation answers "what is the loss under this new data mixture" — a far more compute-relevant question than deletion, and one where the degree-2 coefficients also hand you pairwise data-interaction scores (duplicates, curriculum conflicts) without $n^2$ work. * Chebyshev instead of Taylor. Figure 2 shows $z\mapsto f(z\mathbf 1_D)$ is smooth and gently curved on $[0,1]$, yet the scheme expands at $z=0$ and pays for it. In a "candidate deletion sets known in advance" setting (which is realistic for compliance workflows), fitting on $[0,1]$ directly would be dramatically better conditioned. * Adaptivity. The $1-\delta$ is per fixed query against fixed directions. Making the scheme robust to adaptively chosen measurements is the adaptive-data-analysis problem in a new costume, and the tools there (differential privacy as a stability notion, description-length bounds) might transfer.

Honest IR connection. There is one, and it is not forced, though it is narrow.

Generative retrieval is the clean case. In DSI-style systems the corpus is compiled into the parameters: docids are generated autoregressively, and there is no external index to delete a row from. Document deletion and corpus churn are the standing structural weakness of that line (DSI++ and the incremental-indexing literature exist precisely because of it), and current practice is heuristic — continued training, replay buffers, or full reindexing. Gunn's formulation is a literal match: $\mathcal A$ is the index-training run, $D$ is the set of training instances derived from the documents to remove, and $\phi$ is "the score this model assigns to docid $t$ for query $q$". PREDICT then answers what the retrieval score would have been had those documents never been indexed, in time independent of corpus size and without reindexing. Two honest caveats: a ranking is an argmax, so predicting scores only yields a ranking guarantee under a margin assumption on the top-$k$ gap; and the storage cost of $k\cdot s$ parameter copies is fatal for anything large — at index scale, rebuilding the index is likely cheaper than $10^3$–$10^4\times$ the training cost, which is a structural objection to applying this in IR specifically, where reindexing is cheap by the standards of frontier pretraining.

Two smaller and more genuine hooks. First, the attribution direction: "which corpus documents caused this generated identifier / this hallucinated docid" is the retrieval analogue of the artist example, and it is harder in generative retrieval than in RAG precisely because attribution cannot be read off at inference time. Second, and this is a cute inversion: PREDICT consumes $D$ as a set of training-stream indices, so every data deletion scheme presupposes a retrieval problem — finding the artist's work, or the duplicate documents, inside a trillion-token corpus — which is an IR problem in the service of attribution rather than the reverse. For vector search proper the fit is weaker: ANN index deletion is combinatorial (tombstones, graph repair) rather than parametric, and the only learned components where this would bite are trained quantizers and partitioners, which are small enough that retraining is trivial.

So: there is a real, specific connection to generative retrieval and unlearning-from-a-learned-index, but the cost model makes it aspirational today. The stronger reason to read this paper is the primitive itself — higher-order jets along Haar-random complex directions as a composable, measurement-oblivious sketch of an entire computation. That trick is not specific to data deletion, and it is the kind of thing worth having in your toolkit regardless of whether this particular application ever becomes practical.

title: What One Cannot, Two Can: Two-Layer Transformers Provably Represent Induction Heads on Any-Order Markov Chains
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-07

What One Cannot, Two Can: Two-Layer Transformers Provably Represent Induction Heads on Any-Order Markov Chains — Ekbote, Bondaschi, Rajaraman, Lee, Gastpar, Makkuva, Liang (2025) — arXiv:2508.07208

Setting and problem

The object of study is a class of sources, not a single one. Fix a finite alphabet (the paper calls it the state space) $\mathcal{S}={1,\dots,S}$ with $|\mathcal{S}|=S$, and a horizon $T$. A $k$th-order Markov chain (Def. 1) is a time-homogeneous process $x_{0:T}=x_0,\dots,x_T$ over $\mathcal{S}$ whose kernel $\pi$ satisfies $\pi(x_{n+1}=s\mid x_n,\dots,x_0)=\pi(x_{n+1}=s\mid x_n,\dots,x_{n-k+1})$ for all $k\le n\le T$. The data-generating protocol is the one that makes this an in-context problem rather than a memorisation problem: each row of $\pi$ is drawn independently from a Dirichlet$(\mathbf 1)$ prior (i.e. uniformly on the simplex), the first $k$ tokens are uniform on $\mathcal{S}^k$, the rest are generated from $\pi$, and a training batch mixes sequences from several independently sampled kernels. The model therefore cannot encode any particular $\pi$ in its weights; it must estimate the kernel from the prefix it is shown.

The target predictor is the conditional $k$-gram (Def. 2), the in-context count estimator $$\hat\pi_k(s\mid x_{0:T})=\frac{\sum_{i=k}^{T}\mathbb{I}\big(x_i=s,\;x_{i-1}=x_T,\;x_{i-2}=x_{T-1},\dots,x_{i-k}=x_{T-k+1}\big)}{\sum_{i=k}^{T}\mathbb{I}\big(x_{i-1}=x_T,\dots,x_{i-k}=x_{T-k+1}\big)},$$ defined whenever the denominator is non-zero. In words: scan the context for every position whose preceding $k$ tokens equal the final $k$ tokens of the sequence, and return the empirical distribution of the symbols that followed those matches. This is the add-zero version of Laplace smoothing, which (with smoothing) is the Bayes-optimal next-token predictor under the Dirichlet prior — the paper's justification for treating it as the thing to represent. Note that $\hat\pi_k$ is undefined when the current $k$-context never recurs, which is where the irreducibility assumption and the $O(1/T)$ error terms later enter.

The mechanism that computes this is a $k$th-order induction head (Def. 4): a single attention head is said to implement one if, for every input sequence and every $i\le T$, the score $\mathrm{att}*{T,i}$ is maximised if and only if $x*{i-j}$. Given such a head, the conditional $k$-gram follows by averaging the one-hot embeddings of the attended tokens — this is the formal content of the folklore equivalence "induction heads $=$ conditional $k$-grams" that the Markov-ICL literature runs on.}=x_{T-j+1}$ for all $j\in{1,\dots,k

The architecture (Def. 3) is deliberately close to a real decoder, and the modelling choices matter enormously, so they are worth spelling out. An $L$-layer, $H_\ell$-head-per-layer causal transformer with embedding dimension $d$; relative positional encodings in the style of Shaw et al. and Transformer-XL, added both to keys and to values, i.e. $p^{(\ell,h,K)}_{n-i}$ inside the attention logit and $p^{(\ell,h,V)}_{n-i}$ inside the value sum; softmax attention with logits $\big\langle W_K^{(\ell,h)}x_i^{(\ell)}+p^{(\ell,h,K)}_{n-i},\,W_Q^{(\ell,h)}x_n^{(\ell)}\big\rangle$; residual connections; MLP blocks with ReLU, LayerNorm and skip connections between attention layers; and a final linear read-out $\mathrm{logits}_T=W_o x_T^{(L+1)}+b_o\in\mathbb{R}^S$. Weights are not tied. Two conventions deserve flags:

  1. The output non-linearity is $f(\cdot)=\mathrm{ReLU}$, not softmax. This is essential, not cosmetic: the conditional $k$-gram is a ratio of counts, which is an affine function of the second layer's attention weights. Reading the attention-averaged one-hot vectors out linearly gives exactly that ratio; pushing them through a softmax would not.
  2. LayerNorm is redefined (App. A.1, following Rajaraman et al.) to be the operator $v\mapsto v/|v|_2$. This is implementable with real LayerNorm by augmenting the embedding to $[x;-x]$ (which forces zero mean, so the standard deviation becomes $|x|/\sqrt d$) and rescaling by $\sqrt d$. Throughout the paper, "LN" means "return the unit-norm direction". This idealisation is load-bearing — the construction uses LN twice as a genuine computational primitive, not as a stabiliser.

"Represent" here means: there exists a parameter setting $\theta$ — explicitly written down, and allowed to depend on $k$, $S$ and $T$ — such that $f_\theta(x_{0:T})_{s}$ equals (one variant: exactly, in a temperature limit) or approximates to $O(1/T)$ (the other variant) the conditional $k$-gram $\hat\pi_k(s\mid x_{0:T})$, _uniformly over all $k$th-order kernels $\pi$ and all realised sequences_. It is an expressivity statement, not a learning statement; the learning questions are handled separately and only partially. Two further scaling caveats, because the whole separation lives in them: (i) the attention is idealised in a limit — a scale $\kappa$ appears in the first layer's positional key encodings and multiplies the second layer's logits, and the clean statements hold as $\kappa\to\infty$ (hardmax); the quantitative version is the claim that $\Omega(\log T+k)$ bits per parameter suffice for $O(1/T)$ additive error. (ii) Weights depend on $k$ (positional encodings vanish beyond offset $k$; MLP biases contain $3^{k-1}$-scale thresholds), so $k$ is known and fixed, but the embedding dimension $6S+3$ does not grow with $k$ or $T$.

The prior state of play. Olsson et al. identified induction heads as the circuit behind ICL; Bietti et al. ("Birth of a transformer"), Edelman et al., and Nichani–Damian–Lee showed that for order $k=1$ a two-layer, single-head transformer represents (and in simplified forms learns) the conditional 1-gram. Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky showed that a one-layer, single-head model cannot solve the induction-head task unless its hidden dimension is exponentially larger. For higher order, Edelman et al. and Nichani et al. argued that low-depth models need the number of heads to scale linearly in $k$ (Nichani et al.'s construction is 2-layer with $k$ heads), and Rajaraman et al. then proved the surprising result that three layers with one head each suffice for every $k\ge1$. So: one layer is provably insufficient, three layers with width one suffice, two layers suffice at $k=1$. The question left open, and the one this paper asks, is exactly:

_Can a two-layer transformer with a single attention head per layer represent the conditional $k$-gram, for every order $k\ge 1$?_

Why it is not obvious: every known higher-order construction needs two aggregation primitives per position — an encoding $u_n$ of the window $(x_n,x_{n-1},\dots,x_{n-k+1})$ (the query context, including the current token) and an encoding $v_n$ of the window shifted back by one, $(x_{n-1},\dots,x_{n-k})$ (the key context) — because the induction-head match condition is precisely $u_T=v_i$. Rajaraman et al. spend one attention layer on each, leaving a third for the match. With only two layers and one head per layer, there is exactly one aggregating head and one matching head, and the second aggregator has to come from somewhere else.

Main idea

It comes from the MLP. The single first-layer head computes only $v_n$; the MLP sitting between the two attention layers manufactures $u_n$ out of $v_n$, and the second layer then does the matching. That is Theorem 3: the conditional $k$-gram can be represented by a two-layer transformer with one attention head per layer, separated by MLP blocks, with relative positional encodings and layer normalisation, at embedding dimension $6S+3$ — independent of $k$ and $T$. On the way there, Theorem 2 records a clean depth–width trade: Rajaraman et al.'s depth-3/width-1 construction is equivalent to a depth-2/width-2 one (two heads in layer one computing $u_n$ and $v_n$ in parallel, one head in layer two matching).

The arithmetic that makes the MLP trick work is a base-3 positional weighting. The first layer's relative positional key encodings are set so that, as $\kappa\to\infty$, the head attends exactly to offsets $1,\dots,k$ with weights proportional to $3^{i-1}$, producing $v_n=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{3^{i-1}}{C}e^{\mathcal S}_{x_{n-i}}$ with $C=C_{\mathrm{attn}}=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}3^i$, while $u_n=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{3^{i}}{C}e^{\mathcal S}_{x_{n-i}$ is the same encoding of the window shifted forward by one. Then, identically, $$u_n=\tfrac1C\,e^{\mathcal S}}_{x_n}\;+\;3\,v_n\;-\;\tfrac{3^k}{C}\,e^{\mathcal S}_{x_{n-k},$$ a base-3 }shift register: multiply by the radix, push in the current token, pop the token that fell out of the window. The current token $e^{\mathcal S}*{x_n}$ is free — it is sitting in the residual stream from the embedding. The only missing ingredient is the oldest token $e^{\mathcal S}*{x_{n-k}}$, and the MLP recovers it from $v_n$ alone. Layer two then computes attention logits $\propto\kappa\big(Z_iZ_n+\cos(v_i,u_n)\big)$, which are maximised exactly when $v_i=u_n$, copies the successor tokens through $W_V^{(2)}$, and the ReLU read-out emits the count ratio.

The most interesting part

The clever step is the ReLU-plus-LayerNorm "pop" that extracts the oldest token of the window from the aggregate vector, and the reason base 3 (rather than 2) is used for the weighting.

$v_n$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^S$ whose $s$-th coordinate is the total attention mass of the positions in ${n-1,\dots,n-k}$ carrying symbol $s$: $c_s=\langle e_s,v_n\rangle$. The oldest position $n-k$ carries mass $3^{k-1}/C$, while all the other $k-1$ positions together carry at most $\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}3^{i-1}/C=(3^{k-1}-1)/(2C)$. So the leading weight strictly dominates the sum of all the others — by roughly a factor of two with radix 3, versus a single least-significant unit with radix 2. The first MLP layer therefore applies the identity (written as the stack of one-hot rows $A=[e_1^\top;\dots;e_S^\top]$) to read off every $c_s$, adds the bias $-(3^{k-1}-1)/(2C)$, and applies ReLU: exactly one coordinate survives, the one for $x_{n-k}$. LayerNorm — in its idealised "normalise to unit $\ell_2$" form — then turns that lone positive coordinate of unknown magnitude into an exact indicator $\tilde c=e^{\mathcal S}_{x_{n-k}}$. The second MLP layer applies the affine shift map above ($\frac1C I$ on the token block, $3I$ on the $v_n$ block, $-\frac{3^k}{C}A^\top$ on the $\tilde c$ block) to write $u_n$ into a fresh block of the residual stream; a further LN pass stores $u_n/|u_n|_2$ and $v_n/|v_n|_2$.

The other half of the trick is the matching, which is an injectivity-of-encoding argument. The map $(y_0,\dots,y_{k-1})\mapsto\sum_j 3^j e^{\mathcal S}_{y_j}$ is injective: each coordinate is $\sum_{j:y_j=s}$, so there is no carrying and the sum determines the index set ${j:y_j=s}$ for every symbol, hence the whole ordered tuple. Thus $v_i=u_n$ }3^j$, a base-3 numeral with digits in ${0,1_iff_ $x_{i-1-j}=x_{n-j}$ for $j=0,\dots,k-1$ — the exact, order-sensitive induction-head condition. The paper quantifies the failure case: when $v_i\ne u_n$, $\big|\tfrac{v_i}{|v_i|_2}-\tfrac{u_n}{|u_n|_2}\big|_2\ge 3^{-k}$.

What I find genuinely striking is the resource accounting: a $k$-token window, of which there are $S^k$, is packed into a single $S$-dimensional vector at a resolution of $3^{-k}$. The exponential cost of higher-order matching has not disappeared — it has been moved out of width and depth and into numerical precision. That is why the second layer's temperature must be driven to infinity and why the precision claim carries a $+k$ term ($\Omega(\log T+k)$ bits). An honest reading of the depth separation is therefore: two layers and one head suffice _if you are allowed $\Theta(k)$ bits of resolution and a hardmax limit_; the three-layer construction pays the same precision price, so the comparison is fair, but the result is not a free lunch over the one-layer lower bound, which is about exponential width.

How much is idealisation? A fair amount. The $\kappa\to\infty$ limit is used twice (layer-1 positional encodings to get hard attention on offsets $1..k$; layer-2 logit scaling to resolve a $3^{-2k}$-scale cosine gap). LayerNorm is replaced by exact $\ell_2$ normalisation. The boundary positions $i\le k$, where the $k$-context is not even defined, are handled by a side channel: a scalar coordinate $Z_n=\sum_i\mathrm{att}_{n,n-i}3^i$ that saturates at a fixed large value once $n\ge k+1$ and is strictly smaller before (the paper reports $3^{k+1}/5$ versus $\le 3^k/5$). The product $Z_iZ_n$ in the layer-2 logit is a constant bonus among all valid positions (so it cancels in the softmax there) but exponentially suppresses the invalid ones. In the leaner variant with two MLP layers and LayerNorm applied to the layer-2 query and key projections, the $Z$ channel is destroyed by normalisation, early positions with accidentally aligned keys survive as a set $\hat I_k$, and the output becomes a biased conditional $k$-gram whose bias is $O(1/T)$ and vanishes as $T\to\infty$ under irreducibility. So "exact representation" belongs to the three-MLP-layer variant in the hardmax limit; the other is asymptotic.

Do trained models find the circuit? Qualitatively, yes — and the empirical observation actually motivated the construction. Training a GPT-2-style two-layer single-head model on binary $k$th-order Markov sources, the first layer's averaged attention map increases monotonically along the first $k$ lower diagonals and then drops to near zero, which is precisely the $3^{i}$ profile with support ${1,\dots,k}$ (Fig. 2 and App. H.1 for $k=1,2,3$); the second layer's map closely tracks the ideal induction pattern. Quantitatively it is less tidy: on second-order sources the excess cross-entropy of the trained two-layer model is $0.100\pm0.003$, against $0.131\pm0.000$ for a one-layer model of comparable size — a real gap, consistent with the one-layer lower bound and with the one-layer maps concentrating on two or three lower diagonals instead of matching, but the two-layer model is not near-zero excess loss either. And nothing verifies that the trained MLP implements the shift-register identity; the paper itself notes that non-convexity means many circuits could do the job.

Proof sketch

The claim. Theorem 3 (restated with full detail as Theorem 6 in App. B): there exists a two-layer, single-head transformer $f_\theta$ — in one of two equivalent configurations, (1) three MLP layers between the attention blocks, or (2) two MLP layers plus LayerNorm on the second block's query and key projections — with relative positional encodings, LayerNorm and skip connections, embedding dimension $d=6S+3$, such that $f_\theta(x_{0:T})_{s}\approx\pi(s\mid x_{0:T})$ for all sequences drawn from any $k$th-order kernel $\pi$ and any prior over kernels. Guarantee: in configuration (1), the final logits equal the conditional $k$-gram exactly in the $\kappa\to\infty$ limit; in configuration (2), they equal a conditional $k$-gram plus a bias term whose numerator is independent of $T$ while its denominator grows with $T$, hence $O(1/T)$ for irreducible chains. Parameter count: $9(6S+3)^2+(6S+3)(2T+2S+9)$, improved to $8(6S+3)^2+(6S+3)(2T+2S+9)$ in App. B.2, against $15(6S+3)^2+(6S+3)(3T+2S+10)$ for the three-layer construction and $(k+(k+1)^2)(S+T)^2+T(S+T)$ for Nichani et al.'s $k$-head one. Bit precision: $\Omega(\log T+k)$ bits per parameter for $O(1/T)$ additive error (the $T$-dependence from the positional encodings and count ratios, the $k$-dependence from the $3^{-k}$-scale margins).

The construction, layer by layer. Embeddings are $x_n^{(1)}=[0_{1\times3}\;\;e^{\mathcal S}_{x_n}\;\;0_{1\times 5S}]^\top\in\mathbb R^{6S+3}$: three scalar bookkeeping slots and six $S$-blocks, which get filled in with $v_n$, $\tilde c$, $u_n$, $u_n/|u_n|$, $v_n/|v_n|$ as the computation proceeds.

Layer 1. The relative key encoding is $p^{(1),K}_i=(i\log 3+\kappa)\,e_2$ for $i\in{1,\dots,k}$ and $0$ otherwise (in particular $0$ at $i=0$, so the current token is excluded from $v_n$). $W_K^{(1)}$ zeroes the token content and $W_Q^{(1)}$ maps any token to $e_1$, so the logit at offset $i$ is $(i\log3+\kappa)\,\mathbb I(1\le i\le\min{n,k})$ — content-independent, purely positional. As $\kappa\to\infty$ the softmax support collapses to ${n-1,\dots,n-k}$ with weights $3^{i-1}/C_{\mathrm{attn}}$. The value path, with $p^{(1),V}_i=[3^i\;1\;0]^\top$ for $i\le k$, writes $v_n=\sum_{i=1}^{\min{n,k}}\mathrm{att}_{n,n-i}e^{\mathcal S}_{x_{n-i}}$ into one block and the gating scalar $Z_n=\sum_i\mathrm{att}_{n,n-i}3^i$ into the first coordinate.

MLP. The three steps described above: (i) $W^{(1)}_{\mathrm{mlp}}=A$ on the $v_n$ block, bias $-(3^{k-1}-1)/(2C_{\mathrm{attn}})$, ReLU, LN $\Rightarrow\tilde c=e^{\mathcal S}_{x_{n-k}}$; (ii) the affine shift $u_n=\frac1{C}e^{\mathcal S}_{x_n}+3v_n-\frac{3^k}{C}A^\top\tilde c$, exploiting that $v_n$ and $\tilde c$ sit in orthogonal blocks and $e^{\mathcal S}_{x_n}$ arrives on the skip connection, then LN $\Rightarrow u_n/|u_n|_2$; (iii) a third layer that likewise stores $v_n/|v_n|_2$.

Layer 2. All positional encodings are zero. $W^{(2)}_Q$ and $W^{(2)}_K$ are $\sqrt\kappa$ times selectors that read $(Z_n,u_n/|u_n|)$ and $(Z_i,v_i/|v_i|)$, so the logit is $\kappa Z_iZ_n+\kappa\langle v_i,u_n\rangle/(|v_i||u_n|)$, i.e. $\kappa Z_iZ_n+\kappa\big(1-\tfrac12|\tfrac{v_i}{|v_i|}-\tfrac{u_n}{|u_n|}|^2\big)$ up to the paper's normalisation. Three facts finish it: injectivity of the base-3 encoding (so cosine $=1$ iff the $k$-contexts match), the margin $|\cdot|\ge3^{-k}$ otherwise, and the $Z$ gap that eliminates $i\le k$. Hence as $\kappa\to\infty$, $\mathrm{att}^{(2)}_{n,\cdot}\to\mathrm{Unif}(I_n)$ with $I_n={i: x_{i-1-j}=x_{n-j}\ \forall j\le k}$. With $W^{(2)}_V$ copying $e^{\mathcal S}_{x_i}$ and $W_o$ projecting that block, $\mathrm{logits}_T(x_{T+1})=\frac{\sum_{n=k}^{T}\mathbb I(\forall\,0\le i\le k,\;x_{n-i}=x_{T-i+1})}{\sum_{n=k}^{T}\mathbb I(\forall\,1\le i\le k,\;x_{n-i}=x_{T-i+1})}$, which is the conditional $k$-gram verbatim. In configuration (2), normalising the query and key kills the $Z$ channel, so $I_n$ is replaced by $I_n\cup\hat I_k$ with $|\hat I_k|\le k$ fixed, and the extra mass is the $O(1/T)$ bias.

The lower-bound side. There is no new impossibility theorem in this paper. The "what one cannot" half of the title is inherited: the one-layer, single-head exponential-width lower bound is Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky's, and this paper adds only an empirical companion (App. H.2) — one-layer models trained on second-order sources over the same hyperparameter grid reach excess cross-entropy $0.131\pm0.000$ versus $0.100\pm0.003$ for two layers, and their attention maps concentrate on the first two or three lower diagonals rather than on context matches. Robustness checks: token substitution at rate $p_n$ degrades the loss gap from $0.10$ to $0.21$ at $p_n=0.5$, and interpolating the kernel toward a freshly resampled random one at rate $\alpha$ degrades it to $0.181$ at $\alpha=0.5$ (transition noise is tolerated better than token noise); 8-bit quantisation preserves the second-layer attention map about as well as 32-bit, consistent with the precision claim.

The learning results. Theorem 4 (App. C as Theorem 7) is for first order only and for a reduced model: only the $T+1$ scalar positional key encodings $p=(p_0,\dots,p_T)$ of layer 1 and the scalar attention gain $a_2$ of layer 2 are trainable; the rest is frozen at values that are optimal for $k=1$, including the assumption that "the MLP is optimal", which is benign at $k=1$ precisely because $u_n=e^{\mathcal S}_{x_n}$ comes free on the skip connection. Data assumptions (Assumption 1, from Nichani et al.): a prior over irreducible aperiodic kernels with $\min_{s,s'}\pi(s'|s)>\gamma/S$, non-trivial mixing $\sum_s|\pi(\cdot|s)-\mu_\pi|^2\ge\gamma^2/S$, permutation invariance, and $\mathbb E_\pi[\pi]=\frac1S\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top$. Loss: cross-entropy with an $\varepsilon$ offset inside the log. Training is two-stage — train $p$ for $T_1$ steps with the MLP's LayerNorms removed, then freeze $p$ and train $a_2$ for $T_2$ steps with them restored. Conclusion: for $T+1\ge\mathrm{poly}(\gamma^{-1},S)$ there are $\varepsilon,\eta_1,\eta_2,T_1,T_2$ with $L(\hat\theta)-L^\star\lesssim\log(T+1)/(T+1)^{c\gamma}$, and (Theorem 8) the trained model generalises inductively: for any fresh kernel $\tilde\pi$ with $\min\tilde\pi\ge\gamma/S$, $\sup_{s'}|f_{\hat\theta}(s_{0:n})_{s'}-\tilde\pi(s'|s_n)|\lesssim\log(n+1)/(n+1)^{c\gamma}$.

The dynamics argument: with $a_2$ small, Taylor-expand the layer-2 softmax to first order, so the logit becomes $\hat\mu_{\pi,n}(s')$ plus $a_2$ times a lag-weighted correlation term. The gradient with respect to $p_m$ then reduces to a quantity $g_{i,m}=\mathbb E_\pi\big[\sum_{s,s'}\frac{\pi(s'|s)}{\mu_\pi(s')}\Pr(x_i=s',x_{i-m}=s)\big]-1$ measuring how predictive lag $m$ is. Lemma 7 (Nichani et al.'s Lemma D.2) gives $g_{i,1}\ge g_{i,j}+\gamma^3/(2S)$ for $j\ne1$, so from the all-zero initialisation the previous-token direction has the strictly largest positive gradient; Lemmas 3 and 4 propagate this to all iterates and bound the convergence time, with $p_1\to\infty$ monotonically while the softmax suppresses the rest, giving $v_i\approx e^{\mathcal S}_{x_{i-1}}$. Stage 2 then coincides with Nichani et al.'s second stage, and Lemma 1 (their Lemma D.8), $-\mathrm{d}L/\mathrm{d}a_2\ge\frac14\gamma^8S^{-6}e^{-2a_2}>0$, forces $a_2\to\infty$ and hardens the match.

For $k\ge2$ there is only a perturbative result (App. D, Theorems 9 and 10), and on the two-head architecture of Theorem 2, not the single-head one: head 1 is frozen at its optimum, only the scalar positional encodings of head 2 are trained, the layer-2 temperature is held low and then sent to infinity, and the descent is diagonally preconditioned. Under reversibility and spectral assumptions (Assumption 2 for binary second-order chains, Assumption 3 for general $k$), the learned positional softmax converges to uniform over the $k$ most recent offsets, $\exp(p_i)/\sum_j\exp(p_j)\to 1/k$ for $i=1,\dots,k$. The engine is Lemma 6: lifting the chain to the first-order chain on $\mathcal S^k$ and spectrally decomposing, $g_{i,\ell}=\sum_m\lambda_m^{\ell+1}\beta_m$, so $g_{i,\ell}-g_{i,\ell+1}=\sum_{m\ge2}\lambda_m^\ell(1-\lambda_m)\beta_m\ge0$ whenever the eigenfunction projections $\beta_m$ are positive — predictiveness decays monotonically with lag, which is what drives the attention mass onto the $k$ most recent positions. One honest caveat the paper does not dwell on: this analysis uses the uniform weighting $u_n=\frac1k(e_{x_n}+\dots+e_{x_{n-k+1}})$ rather than the base-3 one, and uniform weights are not injective on ordered windows. The limit object it certifies for $k\ge2$ matches the multiset of the last $k$ tokens, i.e. a bag-of-$k$ estimator, not the order-sensitive conditional $k$-gram that the representation theorem delivers. Closing that gap — learning dynamics that actually recover a radix-style, order-separating encoding — is the real open problem.

Broader context

The subfield is "Markov-ICL": use $k$th-order Markov chains with a random kernel as a minimal, fully analysable stand-in for in-context learning, and ask what architecture is needed to represent and to learn the Bayes-optimal in-context predictor. It sits between mechanistic interpretability (Olsson et al.'s induction heads; Singh et al. on what has to go right for one to form) and transformer expressivity theory (universality and Turing-completeness results; Weiss et al.'s RASP; Liu et al.'s shortcuts to automata). Its appeal is that the "task" has a closed form, so depth, width, head count and precision can be traded against each other with real proofs rather than scaling-law intuitions. The two papers to read alongside this one are Rajaraman, Bondaschi, Makkuva, Ramchandran, Gastpar, "Transformers on Markov data: constant depth suffices" (the three-layer construction this one compresses, and the source of the base-3 attention profile and the LayerNorm-as-normalisation gadget) and Nichani, Damian, Lee, "How transformers learn causal structure with gradient descent" (the two-stage dynamics template and the $g_{i,j}$ lag-predictiveness machinery that the gradient analysis here extends). Makkuva–Bondaschi et al.'s landscape work on one-layer models with weight tying, and Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky's one-layer lower bound, complete the picture.

The follow-up I would most want to see is a precision lower bound to match the construction. This paper shows that $k$ can be absorbed entirely into numerical resolution: $d=6S+3$ with $\Theta(k)$ bits and a $3^{-2k}$ attention margin. Is that necessary? A counting or communication argument should be able to show that any two-layer, single-head circuit that encodes a $k$-window into a single $d$-dimensional vector and matches it by inner product must pay either $d\gtrsim k$ or $\Omega(k)$ bits of precision — turning the paper's depth-vs-width trade-off into a genuine depth–width–precision trilemma, which would be the sharpest possible answer to the motivating question. The constructive counterpart is equally attractive: replace the exact base-3 encoding with a randomised one (a Johnson–Lindenstrauss or random-feature sketch of the $k$-window) and accept approximate matching, trading the $3^{-k}$ margin for an $O(\log(T/\delta))$-dimensional encoding with constant-order margins and a finite temperature. That would be a much more plausible model of what a real trained network does.

That last point is where the honest connection to retrieval theory lies, and it is a structural analogy rather than anything the paper claims. The construction is, read literally, maximum-inner-product search implemented by attention: layer one plus the MLP build a fixed, injective, order-preserving embedding $\varphi(x_{i-1},\dots,x_{i-k})=\sum_j 3^je^{\mathcal S}_{x_{i-1-j}}$, normalise it, and cache one such key per position in the residual stream; layer two forms the query $\varphi(x_T,\dots,x_{T-k+1})$ and retrieves by cosine similarity with a temperature sharp enough to act as an argmax; the retrieved items' successors are then averaged. Every quantity in the proof has a vector-search counterpart: injectivity of $\varphi$ is a collision-freeness guarantee for a deterministic hash; the $3^{-k}$ margin is the separation that makes exact nearest-neighbour recovery possible; the required temperature and $\Omega(\log T+k)$ bits are the quantisation budget of the index; and the fact that $S^k$ distinct keys live in $S$ dimensions is precisely the dimension-versus-precision trade that sketching and ANN theory study. The $Z_iZ_n$ gate is a hard pre-filter over the candidate set, in the sense an inverted-index filter is. For generative retrieval the relevant reading is on the query side: a decoder conditioning on a multi-token docid prefix has to compress that prefix into a single hidden state and match it against candidate continuations, which is exactly the $u_T=v_i$ problem with $k$ equal to the prefix length. The paper's message, transposed, is that two attention layers are enough for exact prefix-level matching but at a resolution exponential in prefix length — a concrete expressivity reason to prefer learned, approximate, residual-quantised docid encodings over exact ones as prefixes get long.

Be clear about the limits of the analogy. The paper is not about retrieval: the "index" is the model's own context window, not an external corpus; the alphabet is a small token vocabulary ($S=2$ in all the experiments); there is no notion of relevance, ranking or recall; and nothing in the paper is stated in sketching or ANN language. The IR connection is a lens for generating questions — can attention implement approximate nearest-neighbour matching with $\mathrm{poly}(k)$ precision, what is the right notion of margin for a learned context encoding, how does the depth–precision trade behave when the matching is allowed to be lossy — not a result that transfers.

title: Learning Decision-Sufficient Representations for Linear Optimization
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-07

Learning Decision-Sufficient Representations for Linear Optimization — Ye, Amin, Ozdaglar (2026) — arXiv:2603.18551

Setting and problem

The object of study is a linear program over a known polytope with an unknown cost vector. Fix

$$\mathcal{X} := {x \in \mathbb{R}^d : Ax = b,\ x \ge 0},\qquad A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}\ \text{full row rank},\ b \in \mathbb{R}^m,$$

assumed nonempty and bounded, and consider the decision problem $\min_{x\in\mathcal X} c^\top x$. The polytope $\mathcal X$ — the feasible region, the constraint matrix, everything about the decision side — is given to the learner. What is withheld is the cost vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^d$. All the learner knows a priori is that $c$ lies in an uncertainty set (or prior set) $\mathcal{C} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$.

The learner cannot observe $c$. It can only acquire linear measurements: it picks query directions $D = {q_1,\dots,q_l} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, possibly adaptively and sequentially, and receives the inner products

$$s(c;D) := (q_1^\top c,\dots,q_l^\top c) \in \mathbb{R}^l .$$

Such a $D$ is what the paper calls a decision dataset. After the measurements, everything consistent with what the learner has seen is the fiber

$$\mathcal{C}(D,s) := {c' \in \mathcal{C} : q_i^\top c' = s_i,\ i=1,\dots,l},$$

an affine slice of the prior set. The fiber is the learner's entire posterior knowledge about $c$: it knows $c \in \mathcal{C}(D, s(c;D))$ and nothing more.

Two notions of sufficiency. Definition 1 (inherited from Bennouna et al., 2025a) gives the global notion. $D$ is a sufficient decision dataset (SDD) for $(\mathcal X, \mathcal C)$ if there exists a decision rule $\widehat{X} : \mathbb{R}^l \to \mathcal{P}(\mathcal X)$ with

$$\widehat{X}\big(c^\top q_1,\dots,c^\top q_l\big) = \arg\min_{x\in\mathcal X} c^\top x \qquad \text{for every } c \in \mathcal{C}.$$

Note what this asks: a single fixed $D$ and a single fixed decoder must reproduce the entire optimal set, as a set equality, uniformly over all $c \in \mathcal C$. This is a strong demand and it is worth being explicit about it, because the paper's relaxation weakens it in two places at once.

Definition 6 gives the pointwise notion. Fix one (possibly unknown) $c \in \mathcal C$. Then $D$ is pointwise sufficient at $c$ if there exists $x^\star \in \mathcal X$ with

$$x^\star \in X^\star(c') \quad \text{for all } c' \in \mathcal{C}\big(D,s(c;D)\big),$$

where $X^\star(c) := \arg\min_{x\in\mathcal X} c^\top x$. Equivalently (Remark 7): the realized fiber is contained in a single optimality region. Two weakenings relative to Definition 1: (i) only this $c$ must be handled, not all of $\mathcal C$; and (ii) only a common optimal point must exist, not recovery of the full argmin set. Property 8 records the two facts you would hope for: pointwise sufficiency is monotone in $D$ (larger datasets have smaller fibers), and global sufficiency implies pointwise sufficiency at every $c \in \mathcal C$.

The geometry and the decision-relevant dimension $d^\star$. Let $\mathcal X^\angle$ denote the extreme points of $\mathcal X$. For a vertex $x^\star$, the feasible direction cone is $FD(x^\star) := {\delta : \exists \varepsilon>0,\ x^\star + \varepsilon\delta \in \mathcal X}$, and the optimality cone is $\Lambda(x^\star) := {c : x^\star \in \arg\min_{x\in\mathcal X} c^\top x}$. Let $\mathcal D(x^\star)$ be the extreme directions (edges) of $FD(x^\star)$. For $\delta \in \mathcal D(x^\star)$ the boundary face is $F(x^\star,\delta) := \Lambda(x^\star) \cap {\delta}^\perp$ — the costs for which $x^\star$ is optimal but moving along the edge $\delta$ costs nothing, i.e. the wall between two optimality cones. The relevant extreme directions are

$$\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C) := {\delta : \exists x^\star \in \mathcal X^\angle,\ \delta \in \mathcal D(x^\star),\ F(x^\star,\delta)\cap\mathcal{C} \ne \emptyset},$$

i.e. the edges whose associated wall is reachable by some cost the prior allows. Separately, in decision space, let

$$X^\star(\mathcal C) := \bigcup_{c\in\mathcal C}\big(X^\star(c)\cap\mathcal X^\angle\big), \qquad \mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C)) := \mathrm{span}{x - x' : x,x' \in X^\star(\mathcal C)}.$$

The decision-relevant subspace is $\mathcal{W}^\star := \mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C))$ and the decision-relevant dimension is $d^\star := \dim(\mathcal W^\star)$. The three results the paper imports are: Theorem 2 (Bennouna et al. Thm 1), for open convex $\mathcal C$, $D$ is an SDD iff $\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C) \subseteq \mathrm{span}(D)$; Theorem 3 (their Thm 2), for any convex $\mathcal C$, $\mathrm{span}\,\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C) = \mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C))$; and Corollary 4, for open convex $\mathcal C$, $D$ is an SDD iff $\mathcal W^\star \subseteq \mathrm{span}(D)$, so the minimum size of a global SDD is exactly $d^\star$.

Two things about this characterization are worth dwelling on. First, it is a genuine duality statement: the queries $q_i$ live in cost space, but $\mathcal W^\star$ is defined as a span of differences of decisions. The identification happens through the pairing $c^\top\delta$ — the relevant query directions turn out to be feasible edge directions of $\mathcal X$, so a measurement $q^\top c$ is really "what is the reduced cost of pivoting along this edge?" Second, $d^\star$ can be far below $d$: in the paper's own $5\times5$ monotone shortest-path experiment, $d = 40$ and $d^\star = 7$, because the prior makes one corridor cheap and everything else expensive, so only paths inside the corridor can ever be optimal.

The precise question. Which and how many objective measurements are sufficient to identify an optimal decision, and can we learn such measurements with provable guarantees in polynomial time? Information-theoretically, Bennouna et al. answered the first half: $d^\star$ measurements, namely any basis of $\mathcal W^\star$. The computational half was open — their Algorithm 2 builds a minimum-size SDD but solves a mixed-integer program at each iteration, and Bennouna et al. (2026) explicitly pose as an open problem whether a basis of $\mathcal W^\star$ can be constructed in polynomial time. That is the gap this paper attacks. It also attacks a statistical variant: if costs are drawn i.i.d. from an unknown $P_c$ supported on $\mathcal C$, how many training instances suffice to learn, in polynomial time, a $\widehat D$ that is sufficient for a fresh draw with high probability?

Surrounding literature. Four strands. (1) Dimension reduction and sketching for LP — random projections (Johnson–Lindenstrauss; Vu et al. 2018; Poirion et al. 2023) and learned, data-driven projections with generalization guarantees (Sakaue and Oki 2024; Balcan et al. 2024a). These preserve objective values approximately; this paper insists on exact optimizer recovery. (2) Data-driven algorithm design / beyond worst case (Gupta–Roughgarden, Balcan) — learn an algorithmic object from i.i.d. samples; typical rates are $\widetilde O(\sqrt{\mathrm{Pdim}/n})$ via uniform convergence. Here the "learned object" is the query set. (3) Compression-based generalization (Littlestone–Warmuth; Floyd–Warmuth; Moran–Yehudayoff; Bousquet et al.; Hanneke–Kontorovich) — if the output is determined by $k$ of the $n$ samples and fits them perfectly, you get $k/n$ rates rather than $\sqrt{k/n}$. (4) Predict-then-optimize / decision-focused learning (Elmachtoub–Grigas SPO and SPO+; El Balghiti et al.'s Natarajan-dimension generalization bounds; Sadana et al. survey), plus active-learning variants (Liu et al. 2023). A fifth strand supplies the hardness machinery: polyhedral containment, where deciding whether an H-polytope is contained in a V-polytope is coNP-complete (Freund–Orlin 1985; Gritzmann–Klee 1993).

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag, because the results live there.

  • _The prior set $\mathcal C$ does all the work._ $d^\star$ is a property of the pair $(\mathcal X,\mathcal C)$, not of $\mathcal X$ alone. Shrink $\mathcal C$ and fewer vertices are reachable and $d^\star$ collapses; take $\mathcal C = \mathbb R^d$ and typically $d^\star = d$ and nothing is gained. The entire value proposition is "a well-informed prior makes the decision problem intrinsically low-dimensional."
  • _Open vs. closed $\mathcal C$._ Theorem 2's necessity direction needs $\mathcal C$ open; Theorem 3 needs only convexity. The paper is careful about this (footnote 2): the global SDD size characterization requires open convex $\mathcal C$, while the pointwise algorithms only ever invoke Theorem 3 and so work with closed convex $\mathcal C$. Hardness for $d^\star$ is proved for both an open and a closed version of the budgeted prior, which takes a dedicated "openification" lemma.
  • Nondegeneracy (Assumption 12). Every extreme point of $\mathcal X$ has exactly $m$ strictly positive components. Under this, feasible bases correspond one-to-one with vertices, and each vertex has a single optimality cone with an explicit $(d-m)$-inequality H-representation, $\Lambda(B) = {c : c^\top\delta(B,j)\ge 0\ \forall j \in N}$. Without it, a vertex has many bases and its optimality region has no such small description — and this is exactly where pointwise verification becomes coNP-hard.
  • Global vs. pointwise. The relaxation is where tractability comes from, and it is a real relaxation: pointwise sufficiency is a statement about one realized fiber, not a uniform statement with a quantifier over $\mathcal C$.
  • Exact, noiseless measurements. Each $q^\top c$ is observed exactly. This is assumed throughout and flagged in the conclusion as an open direction.

Main idea

The paper has two halves that argue in opposite directions, and the point is the gap between them.

Half one: the worst case is hard, so the open problem has a negative answer. Computing $d^\star$ is NP-hard (Theorem 5, formalized as Theorem 30), even when $\mathcal X$ is an $s$–$t$ unit-flow polytope of a DAG and $\mathcal C$ is a budgeted set of arc-length increases given in H-representation, and whether $\mathcal C$ is taken closed or open. Deciding whether even the empty dataset $D=\emptyset$ is globally sufficient — the weakest conceivable global sufficiency test — is coNP-hard, already for an open, full-dimensional polyhedral prior (Theorem 10 / Theorem 36). Combining with Corollary 4 gives Corollary 11: for open convex $\mathcal C$, computing the minimum global SDD size and constructing a minimum global SDD are both NP-hard and coNP-hard. Under $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}$ this answers Bennouna et al. (2026) in the negative. A third hardness result (Theorem 9 / Theorem 35) says that even verifying pointwise sufficiency is coNP-hard in general — and the proof reveals why: the hardness comes from degenerate LP geometry.

Half two: with the right relaxation and the right assumption, the average case is easy and the rate is fast. Adopt nondegeneracy, so each vertex's optimality cone $\Lambda(B)$ has $d-m$ explicit facets. Then pointwise sufficiency at $c$ becomes the containment test $\mathcal C_k \subseteq \Lambda(B)$ for the current fiber $\mathcal C_k$, which decomposes into $d-m$ face-intersection (FI) subproblems $m_k(\delta) := \min_{c'\in\mathcal C_k} (c')^\top\delta$ — an LP when $\mathcal C$ is an H-polytope, a closed form when $\mathcal C$ is an ellipsoid (Proposition 37).

Algorithm 1 is an adaptive cutting-plane routine built on this. Anchor at $c^{\mathrm{in}} := c$ (or any point of the fiber), solve the LP to get an optimal basis $B$, run the $d-m$ FI tests. If all minima are $\ge 0$, return $D$ with certificate basis $B$ and decision $x(B)$. Otherwise a witness $c^{\mathrm{out}} \in \mathcal C_k \setminus \Lambda(B)$ exists, and the facet-hit rule fires: along the segment $c_\alpha = (1-\alpha)c^{\mathrm{in}} + \alpha c^{\mathrm{out}}$, compute for each violated $j$ the crossing parameter $\alpha_j = \frac{(c^{\mathrm{in}})^\top\delta_j}{(c^{\mathrm{in}})^\top\delta_j - (c^{\mathrm{out}})^\top\delta_j}$, take $\alpha^\star = \min_j\alpha_j$ and query the normal $\delta_{j^\star}$ of the first facet hit. Example 15 shows that querying an arbitrary violated facet instead can fail. The guarantees: every queried direction lies in $\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C) \subseteq \mathcal W^\star$ (Lemma 18), queried directions are linearly independent (Lemma 19), so at most $d^\star$ queries and at most $d^\star+1$ iterations, terminating with a pointwise-sufficient dataset (Theorem 20); polynomial time for H-polytope or ellipsoidal priors (Property 21: $\le d^\star$ oracle queries, $\le (d^\star+1)$ LPs over $\mathcal X$, $\le (d^\star+1)(d-m)$ FI subproblems).

Algorithm 2 is the cumulative version: run Algorithm 1 on $c_1,\dots,c_n$ in sequence, warm-starting each run at the current dataset $D_{i-1}$, and record $i$ as hard if $D_i \ne D_{i-1}$. Because the dataset only grows and only grows by independent directions inside $\mathcal W^\star$, three facts hold: zero empirical sufficiency loss (Lemma 22), the output is determined by the hard subsequence alone (Lemma 23), and $|T| \le |D_n| \le d^\star$ (Lemma 24). That is precisely a realizable stable sample compression scheme of size $\le d^\star$, and plugging into Hanneke–Kontorovich (2021, Cor. 11) gives the headline certificate (Theorem 25): with probability $\ge 1-\delta$ over the $n$ training costs,

$$R(D_n) := \Pr_{c\sim P_c}\big[D_n \text{ not pointwise sufficient at } c\big] \ \le\ \frac{4}{n}\Big(6|T| + \ln\frac{e}{\delta}\Big) \ \le\ \frac{4}{n}\Big(6d^\star + \ln\frac{e}{\delta}\Big).$$

Distribution-free, $\widetilde O(d^\star/n)$ rather than $\widetilde O(1/\sqrt n)$, and tight: Theorem 26 exhibits an instance where $n = \Omega(d^\star/\varepsilon)$ samples are necessary for Algorithm 2 to drive the failure probability below $\varepsilon$.

Section 7 cashes this out for contextual linear optimization.
