Specializing $\mathcal C$ to an ellipsoid, a canonical lifting map $\mathrm{lift}_U(s) = c_0 + L_U s$ with $L_U = \Sigma U(U^\top\Sigma U)^{-1}$ maps a $d^\star$-dimensional coordinate back into a full cost vector inside $\mathcal C$ (needed because a purely linear compressed predictor would have range in a subspace through the origin, hence possibly outside a non-centered $\mathcal C$). SPO+ training in the compressed coordinates (Algorithm 3) loses nothing (Theorem 27(1)) and gains a generalization bound in which the ambient $d$ is replaced by $d^\star$ (Theorem 27(2)):

$$R_{\mathrm{SPO}}(f) \le \widehat R_{\mathrm{SPO}}(f) + 2\omega_{\mathcal X}(\mathcal C)\sqrt{\tfrac{2(d^\star p + 1)\log(n|\mathcal X^\angle|^2)}{n}} + \omega_{\mathcal X}(\mathcal C)\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(1/\delta)}{2n}},$$

and trainable parameters drop from $dp$ to $d^\star p$. Section 7.3 then implements Stage I from contextual data (fit $\widehat\mu$ for $\mathbb E[c\mid\xi]$ by OLS, feed pseudo-costs $\widehat\mu(\xi_j)$ to Algorithm 2) and shows the extra representation error is $\widetilde O(n_\mu^{-\alpha/2} + n_{\mathrm{disc}}^{-1})$ under a cone-boundary margin condition with exponent $\alpha$ (Theorem 29) — lower order than Stage II's $n^{-1/2}$ when $\alpha>1$.

The most interesting part

The most interesting thing here is why the quantifier structure of global sufficiency makes it a polyhedral containment problem of the hard kind, while pointwise sufficiency becomes a containment problem of the easy kind — and the fact that the dividing line is exactly LP degeneracy.

Global sufficiency asks: is $\arg\min_x c^\top x$ a function of $(q_i^\top c)*i$ for all $c \in \mathcal C$? To answer that you must understand how the arrangement of all optimality cones ${\Lambda(x^\star)}*{X^\angle x^\star\in\mathcal}$ cuts across $\mathcal C$ — which walls are reachable, which vertices occur. There is no small certificate for "the prior sits inside one cone of the arrangement" in general; the natural object is a union of cones generated by extreme rays, i.e. a V-type description. And indeed the reduction in Theorem 36 runs straight through H-in-V containment: the construction builds a standard-form polytope with a distinguished vertex $z_0$ whose optimality cone is literally $\mathrm{cone}{(v_i,1)}_{i=1}^M$ for the generators of the V-polytope $Q$, so "is $\emptyset$ globally sufficient?" becomes "is $[-1,1]^d \subseteq Q$?" The hardness is not an artifact — it is the statement that the cone you must be inside is specified by its rays, not its facets.

Pointwise sufficiency flips this. Once you anchor at a realized $c$ and solve one LP, you have named the candidate cone: it is $\Lambda(B)$ for a specific basis $B$, and under nondegeneracy that cone comes with its own $(d-m)$-inequality H-representation ${c : c^\top\delta(B,j)\ge0,\ j \in N}$, read off the reduced costs. Containment of a convex set in an H-cone is $d-m$ convex minimizations — each one a separation oracle call. There is no union, no quantifier over $\mathcal C$, no V-representation. The whole tractability story is: solving the LP at the anchor point converts a V-description into an H-description. And degeneracy is precisely what destroys this: a degenerate vertex has many bases, its optimality region is no longer a single simply-described cone, and Theorem 35 shows that for exactly this reason verifying pointwise sufficiency is coNP-hard again. (Check the construction: $z_0 = (\mathbf 1,\mathbf 1,0)$ has $2n_0$ positive components while $m = n_0 + M$, so with $M > n_0$ it is degenerate — the hardness instance is a degenerate vertex.)

The second genuinely clever piece is the facet-hit rule, and its cleverness is that it serves two purposes with one computation. Naively, a cutting-plane method would cut on any violated constraint; Example 15 shows that fails. Take $\mathcal X = [0,1]^2$, vertex $(0,0)$, $\Lambda = {c_1\ge0, c_2\ge0}$, $c^{\mathrm{in}} = (1,\varepsilon)$, $c^{\mathrm{out}} = (-1,-1)$, fiber the segment between them. Both facets are violated at $c^{\mathrm{out}}$. But along the segment, $c_2$ crosses zero at a tiny $\alpha$ while $c_1$ is still strictly positive; $c_1$ only crosses zero after $c_2$ has gone negative, i.e. outside $\Lambda$. So the wall $c_1 = 0$ is not reachable by the fiber _while keeping $x$ optimal_ — querying its normal buys you a direction that is not decision-relevant. The first-hit facet, by contrast, yields $c^{\mathrm{hit}} = c_{\alpha^\star} \in \mathcal C_k \cap \Lambda(B)$ with $(c^{\mathrm{hit}})^\top \delta(B,j^\star) = 0$ and all other reduced costs still $\ge 0$. That point is a witness that $F(x(B),\delta_{j^\star}) \cap \mathcal C_k \ne \emptyset$, which is verbatim the definition of $\delta_{j^\star} \in \Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C_k) \subseteq \Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C)$, and Theorem 3 then puts it in $\mathcal W^\star$. So the facet-hit rule is a constructive membership certificate for the relevant-direction set, not merely a cut. And since each query strictly raises $\mathrm{rank}(Q_k)$ (Lemma 19: if $q_{k+1} \in \mathrm{span}(Q_k)$ then $q_{k+1}^\top c'$ would be constant on the fiber, contradicting $q_{k+1}^\top c^{\mathrm{in}} \ge 0 > q_{k+1}^\top c^{\mathrm{out}}$), the same rule hands you the $d^\star$ iteration bound. One geometric rule yields correctness, relevance, independence, and the complexity bound simultaneously.

The third thing I find elegant is how cheaply stability comes out. Stable compression schemes are usually delicate: you need the reconstruction to be invariant to deleting any subset of the non-compressed points. Here the algorithm's entire state is a monotone set of query directions, and a non-hard sample is by definition a no-op on that state — delete it and the trajectory is unchanged, pointwise, by construction (Lemma 23, modulo a deterministic tie-breaking convention, Remark 17). So Hanneke–Kontorovich stability is not engineered; it falls out of monotonicity. And the compression size is bounded by $d^\star$ as a dimension, uniformly in $n$, because the compressed object is a subspace and compression size equals its dimension. There is a nice practical corollary: the certificate in Theorem 25 is stated in terms of the observed $|T|$, so you never have to compute the NP-hard quantity $d^\star$ to use the bound — $d^\star$ only appears as a worst-case cap.

Where to be honest about limits.

  • The headline "computational–statistical gap" is slightly softer than it sounds, and the paper says so in its concluding remarks: the hard instances are highly degenerate (flow polytopes), while tractability assumes nondegeneracy. Whether hardness survives under Assumption 12 is open. So the comparison is between hardness on one class of instances and tractability on a disjoint class, not a clean separation on a common domain.
  • The dependence on $d^\star$ is a bound, not a computed quantity, and $d^\star$ itself is prior-dependent. If the prior is weak, $d^\star \approx d$ and nothing is saved. The $5\times5$ experiment gets $d^\star = 7$ out of $d=40$ only because $c_0$ puts cost 10 on a corridor and 100 elsewhere inside a unit ball — a very informative prior.
  • What the PAC bound promises is narrow: $R(D_n)$ is the probability that the fiber is not contained in a single optimality region. It says nothing about how bad the decision is when sufficiency fails — the loss is 0–1, not regret. The bridge to decision quality is made only in Section 7, and only through the margin Assumption 28 plus the crude range constant $\omega_{\mathcal X}(\mathcal C)$, so a failure is charged the worst-case objective spread.
  • Theorem 26 is a lower bound for Algorithm 2 specifically on a constructed instance, not a minimax lower bound over all algorithms. It shows the analysis of this scheme is tight, not that no scheme does better.
  • Measurements are exact. Noisy $q^\top c$ is left open and, as the authors note, would need a margin condition controlling how often $c$ sits near a cone boundary.
  • Algorithm 1 solves an LP over $\mathcal X$ at every iteration and must have an oracle for the fiber's support function; the "polynomial time" claim is relative to $\mathcal C$ being an H-polytope (explicit representation) or an ellipsoid.

Proof sketch

(1) NP-hardness of computing $d^\star$ (Theorem 5; formal Theorem 30).

What is proved. Fix a coordinate $r$. Deciding whether $\dim\mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C)) > \dim\mathrm{dir}(X_r^\star(\mathcal C))$, where $\mathcal X_r := {x\in\mathcal X : x_r = 0}$, is NP-hard; consequently computing $\dim\mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C))$ is NP-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions (one call on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal C)$, one on $(\mathcal X_r,\mathcal C)$). Hardness holds with $\mathcal X$ the $s$–$t$ unit-flow polytope of a DAG and $\mathcal C$ a budgeted arc-length set, in both the closed form $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{cl}} = {d+w : w\ge0,\ \kappa^\top w \le B}$ and the open form $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{op}} = {d+w : w>0,\ \kappa^\top w < B+\eta}$ for any fixed rational $\eta\in(0,1)$.

How. The reduction starts from 3-SAT via the PISPP-W+ construction of Ley and Merkert (2025, Thm 3.1) — partial inverse shortest path with weights that may only be increased. Given $\varphi$, that construction outputs a DAG with a variable layer $s_0\to s_n$ (each variable gadget forcing a choice of $x_i$ or $\bar x_i$), a clause layer $t_0 \to t_m$ (each clause gadget forcing a choice of literal vertex $b_{jk}$), a single required arc $r = (s_n,t_0)$ joining them, and shortcut arcs from the variable vertex that falsifies $\ell_{jk}$ into $b_{jk}$. Lemma 31 collects the structural facts used: every $s$–$t$ path uses either $r$ or exactly one shortcut, never both; under baseline lengths $d$ there is a unit gap — paths through $r$ have length $2n+2m+1$, shortcut paths $2n+2m$, so with $w=0$ all shortest paths avoid $r$; shortcuts are given prohibitive modification cost $\kappa_a = B+1$; and if a path through $r$ visits a literal vertex that its induced assignment falsifies, the shortcut into that vertex has its tail on the path, so a cheaper detour exists. Hence $\varphi$ is satisfiable iff some budget-feasible $w$ makes a shortest path use $r$.

Three steps then finish it. Openification (Lemma 32) handles the open prior: because $G$ is a DAG, fix a topological order $\rho$ and perturb $\delta(u,v) = \varepsilon(\rho(v)-\rho(u))$; along any $s$–$t$ path this telescopes to the constant $\varepsilon(\rho(t)-\rho(s))$, so the perturbation shifts every path by the same amount and does not change the shortest-path set, while making $w$ strictly positive and costing less than $\eta$ in budget. The converse direction is the "$w(e)>1$ forces $\kappa^\top w > B+1$" argument, using $w>0$ on the detour subpath. Dimension encoding (Lemma 33): at $c_0 = d$ (or $d+\delta$), by the unit gap exactly the paths avoiding $r$ are shortest, so $X^\star(c_0) = \mathcal X_r^\angle$ and $\mathcal X_r^\star(\mathcal C) = \mathcal X_r^\angle \subseteq X^\star(\mathcal C)$. Dimension comparison (Claim 34): if $\varphi$ is satisfiable there is $c^+ \in \mathcal C$ and an optimal path incidence vector $x^+$ with $x^+_r = 1$; pairing it with any $x^0 \in \mathcal X_r^\angle$ gives $v = x^+ - x^0 \in \mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C))$ with $v_r = 1$, whereas every $u \in \mathrm{dir}(\mathcal X_r^\star(\mathcal C))$ has $u_r = 0$, so the inclusion is strict. If $\varphi$ is unsatisfiable, every optimal vertex avoids $r$ for every $c \in \mathcal C$, so $X^\star(\mathcal C) = \mathcal X_r^\angle = \mathcal X_r^\star(\mathcal C)$ and the dimensions coincide. The key trick is the face restriction: $\mathcal X_r$ is a face of $\mathcal X$, so $\mathcal X_r^\angle = {x\in\mathcal X^\angle : x_r=0}$, and $d^\star$ drops exactly when the required arc becomes reachable.

(2) coNP-hardness of verifying pointwise sufficiency (Theorem 9; formal Theorem 35).

What is proved. Given a bounded $\mathcal X$, a polyhedral $\mathcal C$ in H-representation, a dataset $D$ and $c\in\mathcal C$, deciding pointwise sufficiency at $c$ is coNP-hard — hence computing the minimum pointwise SDD size (and finding one) is coNP-hard too, since the reduction already uses $D=\emptyset$. No nondegeneracy.

How. Reduce from H-in-V containment, coNP-complete (Freund–Orlin 1985; Gritzmann–Klee 1993; Kellner–Theobald 2016, Prop. 2.1), in the convenient hard family: given full-dimensional $Q = \mathrm{conv}{v_1,\dots,v_M}$ with $0 \in \mathrm{int}(Q)$, decide $[-1,1]^d \subseteq Q$. Homogenize $\bar v_i := (v_i,1)$, stack into $\bar V$, set $\beta := \bar V\mathbf 1$, and build the standard-form polytope on $z=(w,r,s)$ with constraints $w + r = 2\cdot\mathbf 1$ and $\bar V w - s = \beta$, $z\ge0$. The distinguished vertex is $z_0 = (\mathbf 1,\mathbf 1,0)$, the reference cost is $c_0 = (e_{n_0},0,0)$, and the prior is the low-dimensional slice $\mathcal C := {((y,1),0,0) : y \in [-1,1]^d}$.

The lemma that drives everything is the KKT lifting identity: writing the optimality cone of a standard-form vertex as $\Lambda(z_0) = {c : c = A^\top y + \rho,\ \rho\ge0,\ \rho_j = 0 \text{ where } (z_0)_j > 0}$ and computing $A^\top(\alpha,\mu) = (\alpha + \bar V^\top\mu,\ \alpha,\ -\mu)$, one gets

$$((\tilde y,\tilde t),0,0) \in \Lambda(z_0) \iff (\tilde y,\tilde t) \in \mathrm{cone}{\bar v_1,\dots,\bar v_M},$$

and for $\tilde t = 1$ the cone membership is exactly $\tilde y \in Q$. So the optimality cone of this one vertex is the V-polytope, homogenized. Then: $z_0$ is the unique minimizer for $c_0$ (substituting $u = w - \mathbf 1 = (x,t)$ identifies $\mathcal X$ with $\widetilde{\mathcal X} = {(x,t) : v_i^\top x + t\ge0,\ -1\le(x,t)\le1}$ and $c_0^\top z = t+1$; $0\in\mathrm{int}(Q)$ forces $t\ge0$ and then $x = 0$). Since $D=\emptyset$ the fiber is all of $\mathcal C$, and uniqueness pins $z^\star = z_0$, so pointwise sufficiency $\iff \mathcal C\subseteq\Lambda(z_0) \iff P \subseteq Q$.

(3) coNP-hardness of global sufficiency with an open prior (Theorem 10; formal Theorem 36).

Same containment instance, same $\mathcal X$ from (19), but the low-dimensional slice prior is replaced by an open, full-dimensional one. The device is the effective-cost linear map $T(c) := c_w - c_r + \bar V^\top c_s$. Substituting the equality constraints, $c^\top z = T(c)^\top w + (\text{constant over } \mathcal X)$, so $\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal X} c^\top z$ depends on $c$ only through $T(c)$. Take the open box-cone $B_{\mathrm{op}} = {(\tilde y,\tilde t) : \tfrac12<\tilde t<\tfrac32,\ |\tilde y_j| < \tilde t}$ and set $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{op}} := T^{-1}(B_{\mathrm{op}})$, an open polyhedron, full-dimensional because open and nonempty. Since $\mathrm{cone}{\bar v_i} = {(tz,t) : t\ge0, z\in Q}$, one has $B_{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq \mathrm{cone}{\bar v_i} \iff (-1,1)^d \subseteq Q \iff P\subseteq Q$ (the last step uses closedness of $Q$). YES case: openness upgrades the inclusion to $B_{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq \mathrm{int}\,\mathrm{cone}{\bar v_i} = \mathrm{int}\,\Lambda(u_0)$, so $z_0$ is the unique optimizer for every $c\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{op}}$ and the constant decoder $\widehat X(\emptyset) = {z_0}$ works. NO case: there is $(\tilde y,\tilde t) \in B_{\mathrm{op}}$ outside the cone, giving $c_1 \in \mathcal C_{\mathrm{op}}$ with $z_0 \notin X^\star(c_1)$, while $c_0 \in \mathcal C_{\mathrm{op}}$ has $X^\star(c_0) = {z_0}$; a zero-query decoder is constant and cannot match two different optimal sets. Hence (25), and Corollary 11 follows by combining with Corollary 4. Note the role of openness is positive here — it is what makes the YES case give uniqueness — which is a neat inversion of the usual worry.

(4) Correctness and complexity of the cutting-plane algorithm (Lemmas 18–19, Theorem 20, Property 21).

Assumptions: $\mathcal X$ nondegenerate (Assumption 12), $\mathcal C$ convex (Assumption 13), closed only for convenience (Remark 14: since $\Lambda(B)$ is closed, $\mathcal C_k\subseteq\Lambda(B) \iff \mathrm{cl}(\mathcal C_k)\subseteq\Lambda(B)$, and violating witnesses survive the replacement). $\mathcal C$ need not be open, because only Theorem 3 is invoked.

Termination. On exit, $\min_{c'\in\mathcal C_k}(c')^\top\delta(B,j)\ge0$ for all $j\in N$, so by the reduced-cost description (4), $\mathcal C_k\subseteq\Lambda(B)$ and the single decision $x(B)$ is optimal across the fiber — pointwise sufficiency by Definition 6.

Relevance (Lemma 18). $c^{\mathrm{in}}\in\Lambda(B)$ by optimality of $B$; $c^{\mathrm{out}}$ violates some facet; convexity of $\mathcal C_k$ keeps the whole segment in the fiber; the first-hit construction gives $(c_{\alpha^\star})^\top\delta(B,j^\star) = 0$ with all other reduced costs still $\ge0$, so $c^{\mathrm{hit}} \in \mathcal C_k \cap \Lambda(B) \cap {\delta(B,j^\star)}^\perp = \mathcal C_k \cap F(x(B),\delta(B,j^\star))$. That is exactly the nonemptiness condition in the definition (2) of $\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C_k)$; monotonicity $\mathcal C_k\subseteq\mathcal C$ gives $\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C_k)\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C)$, and Theorem 3 gives $\mathrm{span}\,\Delta(\mathcal X,\mathcal C) = \mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C)) = \mathcal W^\star$.

Independence (Lemma 19). The one-line trick: if $q_{k+1}\in\mathrm{span}(Q_k)$ then $q_{k+1}^\top c'$ is constant on $\mathcal C_k = {c' \in \mathcal C: Q_k^\top c' = s_k}$; but $q_{k+1}^\top c^{\mathrm{in}} \ge 0$ while the facet-hit rule guarantees $q_{k+1}^\top c^{\mathrm{out}} < 0$ — contradiction. So rank increases by one per query, and since all queries lie in $\mathcal W^\star$, there are at most $d^\star$ of them (Theorem 20: at most $d^\star+1$ iterations, since each non-terminal iteration adds exactly one direction).

Separation oracle and cost (Property 21). The FI subproblem $\min{\delta^\top c' : c'\in\mathcal C,\ Q_k^\top c' = s_k}$ is the separation oracle: it decides whether $\mathcal C_k$ meets the open halfspace ${c^\top\delta<0}$ and returns a witness. For $\mathcal C = {c : Gc\le h}$ it is an LP of dimension $d$ with $k\le d^\star$ extra equalities; for an ellipsoid, Proposition 37 gives a closed form via the change of variables $z = \Sigma^{-1/2}(c-\bar c)$, the minimum-norm solution $c^\perp = \bar c + \Sigma Q(Q^\top\Sigma Q)^{-1}(s - Q^\top\bar c)$, the Schur-complement-type matrix $M^\perp = \Sigma - \Sigma Q(Q^\top\Sigma Q)^{-1}Q^\top\Sigma$, and residual radius $\rho$: $\min_{c\in\mathcal C(Q,s)}\delta^\top c = \delta^\top c^\perp - \rho\sqrt{\delta^\top M^\perp\delta}$, the orthogonal decomposition $|z|^2 = |z_0|^2 + |v|^2$ doing the work. Per iteration: one LP over $\mathcal X$ plus $d-m$ FI calls; overall $\le(d^\star+1)$ LPs and $\le(d^\star+1)(d-m)$ FI calls, all polynomial.

(5) Size bound on the cumulative scheme (Lemmas 22–24).

Realizability (Lemma 22): $\ell(D_i,c_i)=0$ when $c_i$ is processed, and monotonicity (Property 8(i)) propagates it to $D_n \supseteq D_i$. Stability (Lemma 23): with deterministic tie-breaking (Remark 17), Algorithm 2 is a deterministic function of the input sequence; deleting a non-hard index $t\notin T$ deletes an iteration that returned $D_t = D_{t-1}$, so the dataset entering each hard iteration is unchanged and the whole update sequence is reproduced. Size (Lemma 24): warm-starting preserves linear independence by induction over $i$; each hard index contributes at least one new independent direction, so $|T|\le|D_n|$; all directions lie in $\mathcal W^\star$ by Lemma 18, so $|D_n| = \dim\mathrm{span}(D_n) \le d^\star$. This is a dimension-counting potential argument: the potential is $\mathrm{rank}(Q)$, it increases by exactly one per hard sample, and it is capped by $\dim\mathcal W^\star$ — note the cap is independent of $n$, which is what makes the compression size constant.

(6) The distribution-free PAC guarantee (Theorem 25) and its tightness (Theorem 26).

What is guaranteed. With probability $\ge1-\delta$ over the i.i.d. draw $c_1,\dots,c_n\sim P_c^n$ (no assumption on $P_c$ beyond support in $\mathcal C$), $R(D_n) \le \frac4n(6|T| + \ln\frac e\delta) \le \frac4n(6d^\star+\ln\frac e\delta)$, where $R(D_n)$ is the probability that $D_n$ fails pointwise sufficiency on a fresh draw.

How. It is a compression-based, not concentration-based, argument. View a dataset $D$ as a binary hypothesis $h_D(c) := \ell(D,c) = \mathbb 1{D \text{ not pointwise sufficient at } c}$, so $R(D)$ is the 0–1 risk under the degenerate supervised problem with $Y\equiv0$. Define the compression map $\kappa(S) := (c_i)_{i\in T}$ and the reconstruction $\rho(S') := h_{D'}$ where $D'$ is the output of Algorithm 2 run on $S'$. Lemma 23 gives both $\rho(\kappa(S)) = h_{D_n}$ and the Hanneke–Kontorovich stability property (removing any subset of non-hard samples does not change the reconstruction); Lemma 22 gives zero empirical risk; Lemma 24 bounds the compression size. Hanneke–Kontorovich (2021, Cor. 11) for realizable stable compression then yields the bound directly. The fast $k/n$ rate is a consequence of realizability — Algorithm 2 achieves exactly zero empirical sufficiency loss by construction, which is why one escapes the $\sqrt{\cdot}$ rates of uniform convergence; in agnostic settings $\Omega(\sqrt{k\log(n/k)/n})$ lower bounds (Hanneke–Kontorovich 2019) rule this out.

Tightness (Theorem 26). For any $d^\star\ge2$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1/4)$ there are $d\ge d^\star$, a nondegenerate $\mathcal X$, convex $\mathcal C$ with $\dim\mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C)) = d^\star$, and $P_c$ such that if $n \le (d^\star-1)/(8\varepsilon)$ then $\Pr(R(D_n)>\varepsilon)\ge\frac12$. This is a rare-types construction in the Littlestone–Warmuth style, but it cannot invoke a generic compression lower bound as a black box — the compression map is not arbitrary, it must arise from LP optimality geometry through Algorithm 1. So the instance is built explicitly: $\mathcal X = {(x,s) : x+s=\mathbf 1,\ x,s\ge0}$, the slack-variable extended formulation of $[0,1]^d$, nondegenerate because every vertex has exactly one of $x_j,s_j$ equal to 1 for each $j$ (so exactly $m=d$ positive components). The prior is a lifted unit ball around $\mu$ with $\mu_j = 0.99$ for $j\le d^\star$ and $\mu_j=10$ otherwise; the costs are $c^{(i)} = (\mu-e_i,0)$ and the directions $\delta_i = (-e_i,e_i)$. Lemma 38 computes $\dim\mathrm{dir}(X^\star(\mathcal C)) = d^\star$ exactly (coordinates $j>d^\star$ have $c_j\ge9>0$ for every $c\in\mathcal C$, so they are pinned). Lemma 39 is the indistinguishability step: if $\delta_i\notin D$ then $\bar\mu$ and $c^{(i)}$ produce identical measurements yet have different unique optimizers, so $D$ fails at $c^{(i)}$. Lemma 40 is the no-free-lunch step: running Algorithm 1 on $c^{(i)}$ adds exactly $\delta_i$ and nothing else — the radius-1 ball with $\mu_i = 0.99$ makes $\sqrt{1-\mu_i^2} < 0.15$, so every other coordinate stays strictly positive on $\mathcal C\cap\Lambda(B(i))$ and no other facet can be hit; and once $\delta_i$ is added the fiber collapses to the singleton ${c^{(i)}}$. So the directions behave like coupons: Algorithm 2 learns $\delta_i$ iff type $i$ appeared. With $P(c=c^{(1)}) = 1-2\varepsilon$ and the $k = d^\star-1$ rare types sharing $2\varepsilon$, let $N\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,2\varepsilon)$ count rare samples; if $n\le k/(8\varepsilon)$ then $\mathbb E N \le k/4$ and Markov gives $\Pr(N\ge k/2)\le\frac12$, so with probability $\ge\frac12$ at least half the rare types are unseen and $R(D_n)\ge\varepsilon$.

(7) The CLO bounds (Theorem 27, Theorem 29). Three ingredients. Lemma 42 bounds the Natarajan dimension of the induced decision class $x^\star\circ\mathcal H^{\mathrm{aff}}_{U_\star,d^\star}$ by $d^\star p+1$, by rewriting $f_{B,b}(\xi)^\top x = \langle w_{B,b}, \Psi^{\mathrm{aff}}(\xi,x)\rangle$ with $\Psi^{\mathrm{aff}}(\xi,x) = (\vec{}(L_{U_\star}^\top x)\xi^\top,\ c_0^\top x)$ — i.e. the plug-in rule is a multiclass linear predictor over labels $\mathcal X^\angle$ in $d^\star p+1$ features — and applying Shalev-Shwartz–Ben-David Thm 29.7. Lemma 43 plugs this into El Balghiti et al. (2023)'s Natarajan-dimension SPO generalization theorem, with the loss bounded by $\omega_{\mathcal X}(\mathcal C)$. Lemma 44 is the lossless-compression step: the lifting satisfies $U_\star^\top(\tilde c - c_0) = U_\star^\top(\hat c - c_0)$ (Lemma 41 characterizes $\mathrm{lift}_U(s)$ as the minimum-Mahalanobis-norm completion of $s$), so for $q = U_\star a \in D$ we get $q^\top\tilde c = q^\top\hat c$; thus $\hat c$ and $\tilde c$ are in the same fiber, both lie in $\mathcal C$, and global sufficiency of $D$ forces identical argmin sets, so with fixed tie-breaking $x^\star(\hat c) = x^\star(\tilde c)$. Hence compressing and lifting is decision-preserving and part (1) of Theorem 27 (no misspecification loss) follows.

For Stage I (Theorem 29), Lemma 46 is the transfer bound: on the event that $\widehat D$ is pointwise sufficient at $\widehat\mu(\xi)$, that $|\widehat\mu(\xi)-\mu(\xi)|\le\eta$, that $\mu(\xi)$ is more than $\eta$ from the cone-boundary set $B_{\mathcal X}$, and that $\tilde\mu(\xi)\notin B_{\mathcal X}$, the decisions coincide — because $\tilde\mu(\xi)$ and $\widehat\mu(\xi)$ share a fiber (so share the sufficient decision $x^{\mathrm{ps}}$), the $\eta$-ball around $\mu(\xi)$ sits inside one cone's interior (so the optimizer is unique and equals $x^\star(\mu(\xi))$), and uniqueness at $\tilde\mu(\xi)$ closes the chain. A union bound gives $\Pr[x^\star(\tilde\mu)\ne x^\star(\mu)] \le \Pr[\text{sufficiency failure}] + \tau_\mu(\eta) + C_{\mathrm{marg}}\eta^\alpha$. Lemma 45 then supplies a standard non-asymptotic multi-response OLS bound — matrix Chernoff (Tropp 2012) for $\lambda_{\min}(X^\top X)\ge n_\mu\kappa/2$, then a self-normalized sub-Gaussian bound on $(X^\top X)^{-1/2}X^\top\epsilon^{(j)}$ via a $1/2$-net of the sphere (Vershynin) with a union bound over the $d$ response coordinates — giving a uniform prediction radius $r_{\mu,\delta_\mu}$ over $|\xi|_2\le1$. Choosing $\eta = r_{\mu,\delta_\mu}$ kills the $\tau_\mu$ term outright, and Theorem 25 applied to the pseudo-cost sample handles the sufficiency term, giving $\frac{4}{n_{\mathrm{disc}}}(6|T|+\log\frac e\delta) + C_{\mathrm{marg}}r_{\mu,\delta_\mu}^\alpha$. The SPO version (15) uses $R_{\mathrm{SPO}}(f) - R_{\mathrm{SPO}}(f_\star) \le \omega_{\mathcal X}(\mathcal C)\Pr[x^\star(f(\xi))\ne x^\star(\mu(\xi))]$ with $f_\star = \mu$ Bayes-optimal, plus $\tilde\mu \in \mathcal H_{\widehat U,t}$.

Broader context

The subfield. Predict-then-optimize (or contextual/decision-focused optimization) is the study of pipelines where a machine-learned model supplies parameters to a downstream optimization problem. The founding observation (Elmachtoub–Grigas, "Smart predict, then optimize") is that squared-error-optimal predictions are not decision-optimal: the relevant loss is the SPO loss $\ell_{\mathrm{SPO}}(\hat c,c) = c^\top x^\star(\hat c) - c^\top x^\star(c)$, the regret of acting on $\hat c$ while the truth is $c$. SPO is discontinuous and nonconvex in $\hat c$ (it only depends on which optimality cone $\hat c$ falls into), hence the convex surrogate SPO+ and a literature on its statistical behaviour — El Balghiti et al. (2023) bound SPO generalization via the Natarajan dimension of the induced decision class, with only logarithmic dependence on $|\mathcal X^\angle|$ in the polyhedral case. The line this paper sits in asks a sharper question: not "how well must I predict $c$?" but "_what about $c$ do I need to know at all?_" Bennouna et al. (2025a) gave the exact answer for LP — the decision-relevant subspace $\mathcal W^\star$ — and the present paper supplies the complexity theory and the learning algorithm for it. Separately, there is a parallel literature on dimension reduction for the optimization problem: Sakaue–Oki (2024) and Balcan et al. (2024a) learn projections for LPs with generalization guarantees on objective value gaps, at $\widetilde O(1/\sqrt n)$ rates. The authors are explicit and correct about the relationship: their framework certifies when a projection preserves decisions; the projection literature bounds how close projected objective values are to optimal. Those are complementary, not competing, and the certificate is the stronger (binary, exact) object.

Two closely related works worth reading. (i) Bennouna, Bennouna, Amin, Ozdaglar, "What data enables optimal decisions? An exact characterization for linear optimization" (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2505.21692) — the geometric foundation; everything here is built on its Theorems 1–2. Its follow-up, arXiv:2602.15365, poses the open problem this paper settles. (ii) Hanneke–Kontorovich, "Stable sample compression schemes" (ALT 2021) — the learning-theoretic engine; worth reading because the stability notion is exactly what lets you drop the log factors that plague generic compression bounds, and because this paper is a nice example of stability arising for free from algorithmic monotonicity rather than being engineered. Also of interest: Schutte et al. (2025) on sufficient decision proxies, a differently-motivated attack on the same "what part of the parameter matters?" question.

A follow-up idea. The paper's own open list (noisy measurements, nondegeneracy, beyond LP) suggests one project that would hit all three at once: $\varepsilon$-approximate decision sufficiency. Replace the 0–1 loss $\mathbb 1{\text{fiber not inside one cone}}$ with $\mathbb 1{\sup_{c'\in\mathcal C(D,s)}[\text{regret of } x^\star \text{ at } c'] > \varepsilon}$, and define $d^\star_\varepsilon$ accordingly. Three payoffs. First, $\varepsilon$-sufficiency interpolates between this paper's exact-decision framework and the Sakaue–Oki value-approximation framework, so one would expect a single bound degrading smoothly from $d^\star_\varepsilon/n$ to $\sqrt{\cdot/n}$ — a genuine unification. Second, an $\varepsilon$-margin is precisely the slack needed to absorb noisy measurements $q^\top c + \xi$, which is the paper's stated obstacle. Third, $\varepsilon$-relaxation is a standard route around degeneracy: $d^\star_\varepsilon$ may be computable (or $(1+\gamma)$-approximable) in polynomial time even though $d^\star$ is NP-hard, which would be a satisfying positive counterpart to Corollary 11. A sharper, narrower variant: can lexicographic/symbolic perturbation rescue the facet-hit rule on degenerate $\mathcal X$? In simplex theory degeneracy is routinely removed that way, but the obstruction here is structural rather than procedural — a degenerate vertex's optimality region is a union over its bases, so perturbing selects one basis and the resulting containment test certifies something strictly weaker than pointwise sufficiency. Quantifying how much weaker (an approximate certificate with explicit loss) would resolve the paper's first open problem in one direction or the other, and it matters because the combinatorial polytopes people actually care about — flow polytopes, matching polytopes, top-$k$ polytopes — are generically degenerate. It is no accident that the paper's hardness instances are shortest-path polytopes.

Connection to theoretical IR, generative retrieval, vector search. There is one connection here that I think is genuinely tight rather than analogical, and it is worth spelling out because the paper does not make it.

Top-1 retrieval over a fixed corpus is an instance of this setting, exactly and without forcing. Take $\mathcal X = \Delta_N = {x\ge0 : \mathbf 1^\top x = 1}$ — the simplex over $N$ documents, whose vertices are the single-document selections. Then $A = \mathbf 1^\top$, $m=1$, $d=N$, and $\mathcal X$ is nondegenerate in the paper's sense (each vertex $e_i$ has exactly $m=1$ positive component), so it lands squarely in the tractable regime. Now unwind the machinery: at vertex $e_i$ with basis $B={i}$, the edge directions are $\delta(B,j) = e_j - e_i$, so the optimality cone is $\Lambda(B) = {c : c_j \ge c_i\ \forall j}$ — "document $i$ wins." The FI subproblem minimizes $c'_j - c'_i$ over the fiber: "can any plausible score vector make $j$ beat $i$?" The facet-hit rule picks the $j$ that first ties with $i$ along the segment from the anchor to the witness. And the query directions $q = e_j - e_i$ are pairwise comparisons. So Algorithm 1 specializes to adaptive pairwise-comparison querying for argmax identification, with a cutting-plane rule that provably never wastes a comparison. Furthermore $\mathcal W^\star = \mathrm{span}{e_i - e_j : i,j \text{ reachable optima}}$, so

$$d^\star = |{\text{documents that can be top-1 for some } c \in \mathcal C}| - 1 .$$

That is, $d^\star + 1$ is exactly the size of the true candidate set induced by the prior. Theorem 25 then reads: after $n$ observed score vectors, the probability that the retained comparisons fail to determine the top result on a fresh query is $\widetilde O(\text{candidate-set size}/n)$. This is a precise, non-vacuous formalization of why cascade (retrieve-then-rerank) architectures work: a cheap first stage is a prior set $\mathcal C$; $\mathcal C$ collapses $d^\star$; and the reranker only needs to resolve $d^\star$ directions. The paper's own experiment has the same shape — a cheap "corridor" prior takes $d=40$ down to $d^\star=7$ — it just calls the corridor a shortest-path corridor rather than a candidate set. The honest caveats: for top-$k$ with $k\ge2$ the polytope needs explicit $x\le1$ constraints and becomes degenerate, which pushes you straight into the paper's open problem; and the prior set $\mathcal C$ would have to be something you can actually write down as an H-polytope or ellipsoid over score vectors, which is a modelling commitment, not a free lunch.

For vector search the link is real but looser. MIPS/nearest-neighbour is again $\arg\max_i q^\top v_i$, a linear program over the simplex of items, and the pruning question "which items can never be the answer for any query in this region?" is literally $X^\star(\mathcal C)$ with $\mathcal C$ the cone of plausible queries — the geometry behind Voronoi/power-diagram pruning in IVF and behind unreachable points in HNSW graphs. More pointedly: product quantization, PCA/OPQ projections and other index compressions are evaluated empirically by recall@$k$ loss. A decision-sufficiency certificate would be a principled substitute — not "the compressed inner products are close" (the Sakaue–Oki/sketching framing) but "the compression provably preserves the argmax, with failure probability $\le\widetilde O(d^\star/n)$ on the query distribution." I think that is a genuinely attractive research direction, with two honest caveats: $N$ is enormous and if every item is reachable under the prior then $d^\star$ is full-dimensional and the bound says nothing; and exact argmax preservation is usually too strong for ANN, where approximate recall is the accepted currency — which is exactly why the $\varepsilon$-sufficiency extension above is the version that would matter.

For generative retrieval I think the connection is a stretch and I would not push it. One can say that semantic IDs are a learned compression of the document space chosen so that decoding recovers the right document, and ask which bits of an ID are decision-relevant; but autoregressive docid decoding is not a linear program over a known polytope, the relevant "optimality cones" are not polyhedral, and the sequential constrained-beam-search decision does not factor into a single argmin over a fixed feasible set. The sufficiency vocabulary transfers; the theory does not. If one wanted a real bridge, the place to build it would be the final-stage reranking or the constrained-decoding step, not the generative decoder as a whole.

title: Tokenisation via Convex Relaxations
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-07

Tokenisation via Convex Relaxations — Tempus, Whittington, Schmidt, Komm, Pimentel (2026) — arXiv:2605.22821

Setting and problem

The object of study is a tokeniser, formalised as a 3-tuple $\mathbf{T} = \langle \mathcal{T}, \mathrm{tok}, \mathrm{detok}\rangle$. Fix an alphabet $\Sigma$ (bytes). A byte-string is $b \in \Sigma^_$, and a dataset_ is a multiset of byte-strings $\mathcal{D} = {b^{(n)}}_{n=1}^N$. The vocabulary is a finite set of byte-substrings $\mathcal{T} \subset \Sigma^+$ with $\Sigma \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ (so every string has at least one valid segmentation), and in practice $|\mathcal{T}| = |\Sigma| + K$ for a budget $K$ — in the experiments $|\mathcal{T}| = |\Sigma| + |\Phi| + K$ with $\Phi$ a set of special tokens. The encoder $\mathrm{tok}: \Sigma^* \to \mathcal{T}^*$ must be a _segmentation_: if $t = \mathrm{tok}(b)$ then $b = t_1 \circ \cdots \circ t_{|t|}$; the decoder is just concatenation. The crucial point is that a tokeniser is __two_ objects — a vocabulary _and* a segmentation strategy — because for a fixed $\mathcal{T}$ many segmentations of the same string exist ($\mathcal{T} = {d,o,g,do,og}$ segments dog three ways).

The objective is compression, defined as total token count over the training dataset: $$f(\mathbf{T}) = \sum_{b \in \mathcal{D}} \mathrm{length}\big(\mathrm{tok}(b)\big),$$ and the problem is $\arg\min_{\mathbf{T}} f(\mathbf{T})$ subject to the budget. The authors are explicit that choosing compression is a decision, not a derivation: they list unigram log-likelihood (Kudo, 2018) and Rényi efficiency (Zouhar et al., 2023a) as alternatives, acknowledge the question of the right objective is open, and pick compression because most prior tokeniser-design and tokeniser-theory work does.

Two modelling choices in the setup carry a lot of weight and are easy to miss.

First, the objective is in-sample and the segmentation is free. $f$ measures tokens on the training multiset $\mathcal{D}$, and the minimisation is over both $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathrm{tok}$ jointly. So the target is not "BPE's compression" but "the best achievable compression of $\mathcal{D}$ by any $K$-token vocabulary under its own optimal segmentation" — the PathPiece/Unigram-style shortest-path encoder, not a merge-sequence encoder. Off-dataset behaviour is defined post hoc: for $b \notin \mathcal{D}$, $\mathrm{tok}(b) = \arg\min_{t \in \mathcal{T}^*, b = t_1\circ\cdots} |t|$, i.e. PathPiece (Schmidt et al., 2024).

Second, the combinatorial structure is recast as a coloured shortest-path problem, and this is where the whole construction lives. For each $b^{(n)}$ introduce vertices $v^n_i$ for $0 \le i \le \mathrm{length}(b^{(n)})$ at every inter-byte position, then identify the last vertex of each string with the first vertex of the next, $v^n_{\mathrm{length}(b^{(n)})} = v^{n+1}_0$. The whole dataset becomes one chain with a single source $v^0_0$ and single sink $v^N_L$. Edges: byte-edges $E^{\mathrm{byte}} = {\langle v^n_i, v^n_{i+1}$ (unit steps), and }\rangletoken-edges $E^{\mathrm{tok}} = {\langle v^n_i, v^n_j\rangle : i+2 \le j \le \mathrm{length}(b^{(n)})}$ (shortcuts of length $\ge 2$). Token-edges are then coloured by the substring they span: with $\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{all}}$ the set of candidate tokens, the colour-partition $\mathcal{C}$ groups all edges realising the same byte-string $b'$ into one class. A graph-vocabulary is a choice of $K$ colours; a graph-segmentation is an $v^0_0 \to v^N_L$ path using byte-edges and token-edges of chosen colours (Definition 3.1). The shortest tokenisation problem (Definition 3.2) is to minimise path length over all $K$-colour choices. Because token-edges never cross document boundaries, the single path decomposes into per-document segmentations, and path length equals $f(\mathbf{T})$ exactly.

The construction is then generalised (Definition 3.3) by splitting edges into free $\mathcal{F} \subseteq E^{\mathrm{all}}$ (always available, not charged to the budget, though still costing path length) and priced $\mathcal{P} \subseteq E^{\mathrm{all}}\setminus\mathcal{F}$ (charged to the budget via colours). The standard problem is $\mathcal{F} = E^{\mathrm{byte}}$, $\mathcal{P} = E^{\mathrm{tok}}$, but $\mathcal{P}$ can be restricted to candidate tokens that respect unicode/grapheme/morpheme boundaries (à la BoundlessBPE) or have non-negligible frequency — this makes the method work with any candidate-token set in the sense of Lim et al. (2025), and in the experiments it is how pre-tokenisation (the nanochat regex) enters.

Given this, the algorithm's input is: a dataset $\mathcal{D}$, a candidate/priced edge set, and a budget $K$. Its output is a vocabulary (plus the standard shortest-path encoder) and a numerical lower bound on the optimal $f$ for that instance.

The precise question: can tokeniser construction be posed as a polyhedral optimisation problem whose convex relaxation is both (i) solvable at realistic corpus and vocabulary scale, and (ii) tight enough that rounded solutions beat BPE while simultaneously certifying how far any tokeniser is from compression-optimal?

What the literature already knows: BPE (Gage, 1994; Sennrich et al., 2016) is greedy pairwise merging and provably creates wasteful intermediate tokens — the paper's own worked example, $\mathcal{D} = {abc,abd,abe,bc,bd,be}$ with $K=3$, has BPE save 5 symbols where the optimum saves 6. Unigram/SentencePiece (Kudo, 2018) optimises a different objective (unigram likelihood, via EM-style pruning) and is likewise heuristic. Compression correlates at least partly with downstream quality (Gallé, 2019; Zouhar et al., 2023a), though this is contested (Schmidt et al., 2024, "Tokenization is more than compression"; Cognetta et al., 2024b give counterexamples to the noiseless-channel view). Finding compression-optimal tokenisers is NP-hard (Kozma and Voderholzer, 2024; Whittington et al., 2025; Lim et al., 2025; Kastreva et al., 2026). The concrete gap: every proposed fix to BPE — vocabulary trimming, Picky BPE, Scaffold-BPE, SuperBPE, BoundlessBPE — is a local modification of the greedy merge loop; nobody had attempted global optimisation of the vocabulary as a whole. The adjacent literature on coloured/labelled connectivity (Broersma et al., 2005; Hassin et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2011) is cited as containing related graph problems.

Main idea

Write the coloured shortest-path problem as an integer program and relax it. Define a free incidence matrix $F \in {-1,0,1}^{\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{F}}$, a priced incidence matrix $P \in {-1,0,1}^{\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{P}}$, and an edge-colour matrix $C \in {0,1}^{\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{C}}$. Variables are a free token-instance vector $\mathbf{f}$, a priced token-instance vector $\mathbf{p}$, and a priced-colour vector $\mathbf{c}$. With $\mathbf{d}$ the flow-difference vector ($-1$ at source, $+1$ at sink, $0$ elsewhere), the IP (Eq. 5) is

$$\min\ \langle \mathbf{1},\mathbf{p}\rangle + \langle \mathbf{1},\mathbf{f}\rangle \quad \text{s.t.}\quad P\mathbf{p} + F\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{d},\quad \mathbf{p} - C\mathbf{c} \le \mathbf{0},\quad \langle \mathbf{1},\mathbf{c}\rangle \le K,\quad \mathbf{f},\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c} \in {0,1}.$$

Three constraint families, each doing one job: flow conservation makes $(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{p})$ a valid segmentation; $\mathbf{p} \le C\mathbf{c}$ makes a token-instance usable only if its token is in the vocabulary; $\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{c}\rangle\le K$ is the budget. Observations 3.4 and 3.5 state the two directions of the correspondence: every feasible point maps to a tokeniser with $f(\mathbf{T}) = \langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{p}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{f}\rangle$, and (when $\mathcal{F}=E^{\mathrm{byte}}$, $\mathcal{P}=E^{\mathrm{tok}}$) every budget-$K$ tokeniser maps back to a feasible point of equal value.

Relaxing ${0,1} \to [0,1]$ gives the tokenisation polytope $\mathcal{Q}$ and an LP (Eq. 6) solvable by a modern solver. Since $\mathcal{Q} \supseteq \mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{IP}}$, the LP value is a lower bound on optimal compression for that instance — the certificate. Fractional $\mathbf{c}$ means "partial tokens", so three rounding schemes are proposed: Det (round the $K$ largest $c_c$ to 1), Bias (rank by $c_c/\mathrm{length}(c)$, favouring short tokens on the reasoning that short tokens generalise off-dataset better), and Int (keep only $c_c \ge 0.999$, yielding fewer than $K$ tokens). Given any rounded $\mathbf{c}$, optimal $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{f}$ follow from a plain shortest-path computation on the allowed colours — so rounding only ever has to decide the vocabulary. The resulting algorithm is ConvexTok; at inference it is a Unigram-style shortest-path encoder, so runtime matches BPE/UnigramLM.

Scale and headline numbers. After merging identical subgraphs (frequency-weighted deduplication of pre-tokens) with rescaled objective coefficients, the solved LP has 105,997,943 variables (79,075,380 priced edges, 18,096,951 free edges, 8,825,612 colour variables) and 99,168,445 constraints, solved with PDLP in NVIDIA cuOPT at a default primal-dual gap of 10,000, in ~180–230 s per run (889.9 s at $K=8$k), ~4 GPU-hours total per tokeniser.

The findings: (1) The LP solution is surprisingly close to integral, and gets more so with $K$ — the fraction of $\mathbf{c}$ entries equal to 1 rises from 66.41% of budget at 8k to 90.53% at 256k, and the non-zero support is only 151% of budget at 8k falling to ~114% at 256k, out of 8.8M candidate colours. (2) Everything is nearly optimal. Integrality gap ratios (tokenised value / LP bound): BPE 103.35% at 8k → 100.21% at 256k; Det 100.86% → 99.997%; Bias 104.86% → 100.07%; Int is the outlier at 122.63% at 8k. At $\ge$128k all methods are within 1%. (3) BPE is more stable than ConvexTok under resampling of the tokeniser training set (Jaccard similarity of vocabularies), with Int most stable of the ConvexTok variants. (4) On intrinsic metrics (TokEval), Bias is the best performer overall — better vocabulary utilisation, type–token ratio, tokens-per-line; Rényi entropy is mixed with BPE often ahead. On FLORES+ (out-of-distribution, multilingual) Bias generalises better than Det. (5) For language modelling, Det is best on BpB: at depth 12 ConvexTok beats BPE at every vocabulary size, with margins of order 0.001–0.002 BpB (e.g. 32k: 0.8525 vs 0.8536; 128k: Bias 0.8393 vs BPE 0.8410). CORE downstream scores show no clear trend; the honest summary in the paper is that ConvexTok "at least matches" BPE, with a consistent-but-weak advantage at the largest vocabulary sizes.

The most interesting part

The genuinely interesting thing here is that the paper's central technical achievement produces what is, read carefully, a negative result for its own research programme — and the framing does not fully own this. If BPE is within 3.3% of optimal at 8k and 0.21% at 256k, and ConvexTok's own best variant closes most of that, then the compression objective has essentially no headroom left at practical vocabulary sizes. The limitations section says this almost in so many words ("Significantly improving training-data compression is thus senseless under similar constraints"), which is the most valuable sentence in the paper and deserved to be the abstract. The flip side is a nice worst-case/typical-case story: tokenisation is NP-complete, BPE's a priori approximation guarantees are weak, and yet on natural text with pre-tokenisation the greedy heuristic is within a fraction of a percent of the polyhedral bound.

Now the critique.

Is the LP objective the right proxy? The paper's own results say no. Det achieves the best compression and the best BpB; Bias achieves worse compression yet wins on nearly every intrinsic metric and generalises better out-of-distribution. At 128k, Bias (100.009% of the bound) beats Det (100.231%) on compression but Det beats Bias on BpB at depths 18 and 24. So the ordering induced by the LP objective does not track either the intrinsic-metric ordering or the downstream ordering. Combined with the near-saturation result, the inescapable reading is that whatever downstream gains exist are not attributable to the 0.2–1% compression improvement — they are attributable to incidental properties of which tokens the rounding happens to pick. The paper has built an excellent optimiser for a quantity it has simultaneously shown to be nearly exhausted and only loosely coupled to what we care about. The right follow-up is the one the paper defers: plug a different linear $f$ into the same polytope.

What does "within 1% of optimal" actually certify? Four separate caveats, each of which weakens the claim.

  1. It is a numerical primal value, not a dual certificate. PDLP is a first-order primal-dual method; its iterates are only approximately feasible, and the reported "LP Value" is a primal objective at an approximately feasible point, which can lie below the true LP optimum. The tell is Table 2: Det at 256k achieves 99.997% of the "lower bound" — i.e. it violates it. The paper footnotes this as within solver tolerance, which is honest but concedes the point. A real certificate requires either crossover to a basic solution or, better, reporting the objective of an explicitly dual-feasible point, so that weak duality makes the bound unconditional. With an absolute primal-dual gap tolerance of 10,000 against an objective of $3.5$–$4.3 \times 10^8$ the relative slack is ~0.003%, so the numbers are probably nearly right; but a paper whose selling point is certification should be producing verifiable certificates, not solver outputs.

  2. It bounds in-sample compression only. The bound is over $\mathcal{D}$, the 593,920 training documents. It says nothing about held-out or multilingual compression — and the FLORES+ table shows the ranking changes there (Bias overtakes Det, Int collapses). "Within 1% of optimal" means "within 1% of the best possible fit to this sample", which the stability experiment suggests is partly an overfitting target: ConvexTok vocabularies are less reproducible across resamples than BPE's, exactly the signature of a global optimiser latching onto sample-specific structure.

  3. It bounds optimality within a restricted candidate set. Observation 3.5 (every tokeniser maps to a feasible point) requires $\mathcal{F}=E^{\mathrm{byte}}, \mathcal{P}=E^{\mathrm{tok}}$. The experiments pre-tokenise with the nanochat regex, so $\mathcal{P}$ excludes boundary-crossing tokens. The bound is therefore a lower bound over pre-tokenisation-respecting tokenisers, not over all tokenisers. This is the right comparison class for BPE, so the comparison is fair — but the headline phrasing "how far their tokeniser is from optimal" overstates the scope, and it is precisely why extending to SuperBPE (which deliberately crosses pre-token boundaries) is much harder than the future-work sentence implies: subgraph deduplication is what makes a $10^8$-variable LP tractable, and it works only because word types repeat heavily. Drop pre-tokenisation and the dedup collapses.

  4. Encoder asymmetry in the comparison. ConvexTok uses a shortest-path (PathPiece/Unigram-style) encoder; BPE conventionally uses its merge-order encoder, which is not compression-optimal for its own vocabulary. The paper does not state clearly whether BPE's "Tokenised Value" in Table 2 is computed under BPE's encoder or under optimal segmentation of BPE's vocabulary. If the former, part of ConvexTok's margin is an encoder effect, not a vocabulary effect — a cheap ablation (BPE vocabulary + shortest-path encoder) would settle it and is conspicuously absent.

Are the downstream gains convincing? No. BpB differences are 0.001–0.002 with reported standard errors of 0.0001–0.0012 — at 8k (0.8785 ± 0.0012 vs 0.8782 ± 0.0008) it is a wash. Three seeds exist only at depth 12; depths 18 and 24 are single runs, so every claim about the larger models rests on $n=1$. CORE is worse: differences of 0.005 against standard errors of ±0.008, and the per-task appendix tables show wild swings (CommonsenseQA at 128k: BPE 0.3680, Bias 0.2240, Det 0.2280; BigBench Dyck at 32k: BPE 0.1260, Bias 0.0400) that are plainly noise at these scales. The paper's own language ("less consistently", "no clear trend") is appropriately hedged, but the abstract's "it also improves downstream task performance" is not supported by the tables. There is also a confound: hyperparameters were tuned on the BPE baseline at 32k and reused unchanged across tokenisers and vocabulary sizes. That biases against ConvexTok (good, conservative) but makes the "ConvexTok is better at large vocabularies" trend untrustworthy, since the shared hyperparameters are increasingly mistuned as $K$ grows.

Baselines. The only baseline is BPE. Unigram/SentencePiece — the other standard, and the natural "non-greedy, global-ish" competitor — is absent, despite being invoked for the inference-time encoder. So are GreedTok (Lim et al.'s partition-cover method, which has an actual approximation guarantee), PathPiece-trained vocabularies, and BoundlessBPE. For a paper arguing that global optimisation beats greedy, omitting every other non-BPE-greedy method is the biggest evaluation gap.

Compute. ~4 GPU-hours on a GH200 and a $10^8$-variable LP to train one tokeniser, against seconds-to-minutes of CPU for BPE, on a corpus of 594k documents — one to two orders of magnitude smaller than what production tokenisers see. LP size grows linearly in deduplicated corpus bytes and the candidate set grows with it, so a 100× corpus is not obviously in reach, and the fact that most of the benefit is in-sample suggests more data is exactly what would be needed. For a 0.1% BpB gain that does not reliably survive to CORE, the cost-benefit is unattractive today. The real deliverable is the certificate, which you compute once per corpus and never again.

What I would want added: a dual-feasible bound; held-out compression bounds; BPE-vocabulary-with-optimal-encoder ablation; a Unigram baseline; more seeds at depth 18/24; and an honest restatement of the headline as "greedy tokenisation is near-optimal for compression, certifiably".

Proof sketch

There is no theorem with an approximation ratio in this paper. The theoretical content is an exact reformulation plus a relaxation bound; NP-hardness is imported from prior work (Whittington et al., 2025; Kozma and Voderholzer, 2024; Lim et al., 2025; Kastreva et al., 2026), not re-proved. (A footnote also mis-cites "Theorems 3.1 and 3.2" where the paper has Definitions 3.1 and 3.2.)

Claim 1 (exact reformulation; Observations 3.4 and 3.5). _Under the standard instantiation $\mathcal{F}=E^{\mathrm{byte}}$, $\mathcal{P}=E^{\mathrm{tok}}$, the feasible set $\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{IP}}$ of Eq. (5) is in value-preserving bijection with the set of budget-$K$ tokenisers together with their segmentations of $\mathcal{D}$: every feasible $(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c})$ yields a tokeniser with $f(\mathbf{T}) = \langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{p}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{f}\rangle$, and conversely._

Established by explicit construction, sketched informally in Appendix C. Forward: read the vocabulary off the support of $\mathbf{c}$ as ${t_c : c_c = 1} \cup \Sigma$; read the segmentation off the support of $(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{p})$, since each possible use of a token at a particular position in a particular byte-string corresponds to exactly one edge; define behaviour off $\mathcal{D}$ by PathPiece (Eq. 7). Backward: set $c_c = 1$ iff $t_c \in \mathcal{T}$, run the tokeniser's encoder on each $b \in \mathcal{D}$, and set the corresponding edge variables to 1. The three ingredients that make this work are (i) the vertex-identification trick $v^n_{\mathrm{length}(b^{(n)})} = v^{n+1}_0$, which turns $N$ independent segmentation problems into one single-source single-sink flow problem, so path validity is a single system $P\mathbf{p}+F\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{d}$ rather than $N$ systems; (ii) the colour-partition, which is what couples a global budget to local edge usage via $\mathbf{p} - C\mathbf{c} \le \mathbf{0}$ — this is the only place where positions in different documents interact; and (iii) the fact that path length in the unit-cost graph is literally the token count, so the objective is $\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{p}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{f}\rangle$ with no weighting.

Claim 2 (certificate). _$\mathrm{LP}^\star \le \mathrm{IP}^\star = \min_{\mathbf{T}} f(\mathbf{T})$ for the given instance._

A one-line relaxation argument: $\mathcal{Q} \supseteq \mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm{IP}}$ because $[0,1] \supseteq {0,1}$ and all other constraints are unchanged, so the minimum over the larger set is no larger; Claim 1 then identifies $\mathrm{IP}^\star$ with optimal compression. Hence for any tokeniser $\mathbf{T}$, the ratio $f(\mathbf{T})/\mathrm{LP}^\star$ upper-bounds $f(\mathbf{T})/f(\mathbf{T}^\star)$ — an instance-specific, a posteriori approximation ratio, as opposed to the a priori worst-case ratios of greedy/submodular analyses. This is the paper's conceptual contribution to the theory side: it trades a universal guarantee for a tight guarantee on the instance you actually care about. (As noted above, in exact arithmetic the argument is airtight; what is reported is a numerically approximate primal value, which is why one entry in Table 2 dips below 100%.)

Claim 3 (rounding is only about $\mathbf{c}$). Once $\mathbf{c}$ is fixed to a 0/1 vector, the residual problem $\min \langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{p}\rangle+\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{f}\rangle$ subject to flow conservation and $\mathbf{p} \le C\mathbf{c}$ is a shortest-path problem on the subgraph of allowed colours, whose LP is integral. So the entire integrality gap is attributable to the two coupling constraints $\mathbf{p} \le C\mathbf{c}$ and $\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{c}\rangle \le K$, and rounding need only decide a vocabulary; the segmentation is then recovered exactly. No bound on the rounding loss is proved — Det, Bias and Int are heuristics, evaluated empirically.

The genuinely surprising empirical fact, which the paper notes but does not explain, is how little the LP exploits its freedom. The standard way an LP cheats a cardinality constraint is to spread budget thinly — set $c_c = \varepsilon$ on $K/\varepsilon$ colours and use each at level $\varepsilon$ — and in general label-constrained path/connectivity problems this produces large integrality gaps (cf. the logarithmic hardness results in the labelled-connectivity literature the paper cites). Here the support of $\mathbf{c}$ is only $1.14$–$1.51\times K$ out of $8.8$M candidates. Why the flow structure and the Zipfian token-frequency profile of natural text suppress spreading is, to my mind, the open theoretical question the paper leaves on the table; a worst-case integrality-gap analysis of the tokenisation polytope, or an identification of the structural condition under which it is small, would be the natural theory follow-up.

Broader context

Background. Tokenisation sits between raw bytes and the transformer, and is one of the last parts of the pipeline still built by a hand-designed greedy algorithm. Two families dominate: BPE, which iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent pair and encodes by replaying merges, and Unigram/SentencePiece, which starts from a large candidate set and prunes to maximise a unigram likelihood, encoding by Viterbi. The two differ in objective and in encoder, which makes clean comparison hard. A line of theory has grown up around these: Zouhar et al. (2023b) give a formal account of BPE with approximation guarantees for a compression-utility objective; Whittington et al. (2025) prove tokenisation NP-complete; Kastreva et al. (2026) strengthen this to bounded alphabets; Kozma and Voderholzer (2024) analyse BPE theoretically. A parallel line questions whether compression is the right target at all — Zouhar et al. (2023a) propose Rényi efficiency via a noiseless-channel argument, Cognetta et al. (2024b) supply counterexamples to it, Schmidt et al. (2024) argue directly that tokenisation is more than compression, and Ali et al. (2024) find tokeniser choice matters but unevenly. This paper is best read as the measurement instrument that line of work needed: it finally tells you how much of the compression objective was left on the table (very little).

Two closely related works worth knowing. (i) Lim et al. (2025), "A partition cover approach to tokenization" (GreedTok). This is the nearest competitor in spirit: it recasts vocabulary selection as a weighted maximum partition-cover problem and gets a greedy algorithm with a submodularity-style approximation guarantee. The contrast with ConvexTok is the cleanest methodological lesson available here — a priori worst-case ratio from submodular greedy versus a posteriori instance-specific ratio from LP duality — and it is a shame the two are not compared empirically. (ii) Liu et al. (2025), SuperBPE and Schmidt et al. (2025), BoundlessBPE. Both break the pre-tokenisation barrier, allowing tokens to span whitespace. These matter because pre-tokenisation is precisely the structural assumption that makes the LP tractable (via subgraph deduplication) and the assumption that bounds the certificate's scope. The headroom this paper shows to be absent within pre-tokenised tokenisation may well still exist once that constraint is dropped — which is both the paper's own stated next step and, I suspect, a genuinely hard one.

Follow-up idea. The polytope is objective-agnostic: any objective linear in $(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c})$ drops straight in, and the certificate comes along for free. The most interesting instantiation is not compression but a likelihood-flavoured objective: give each priced edge a cost $-\log \hat{p}(t_c)$ under some reference distribution rather than unit cost, and the shortest-tokenisation problem becomes a budgeted Unigram-optimal vocabulary problem — i.e. a globally optimal SentencePiece with a certificate, which nobody currently has. Equally attractive: put token-level costs that penalise tokens with high conditional entropy of the next token, operationalising the Rényi-efficiency intuition inside a solvable LP. And on the theory side, the integrality-gap question above: characterise the family of string distributions (Zipfian frequencies, bounded candidate multiplicity) for which the tokenisation polytope has gap $1+o(1)$, which would explain rather than merely observe that greedy is near-optimal on natural language.

Connection to theoretical IR, generative retrieval and vector search. There is a real link, and also a real limit; both are worth stating precisely.

The transferable structure is not "tokenisation" but the triple: _(a) a unit-cost path/decode objective, (b) a shared cardinality-constrained set of reusable units, (c) a coupling constraint $\mathbf{p} \le C\mathbf{c}$ tying local usage to global selection._ Any discrete design problem with that shape inherits the whole apparatus: an exact IP, an LP relaxation solvable at $10^8$ variables, and an a posteriori certificate.

Where it transfers well. Docid vocabulary design in generative retrieval is the obvious candidate. In the DSI/NCI lineage, and in the semantic-ID variants that build identifiers from text (titles, keyphrases, hierarchical cluster paths), you are choosing a budgeted set of reusable sub-identifier units such that every document decodes into a short identifier string. If your docids are substrings or $n$-grams of document text — which is exactly the design in several title-based and keyword-based generative retrieval systems — then the construction maps almost verbatim: documents are the byte-strings, the docid-unit inventory is the colour set, identifier length is path length, and the autoregressive decoding cost you are minimising is $\sum_d \mathrm{length}(\mathrm{id}(d))$. You would get, for free, a certified answer to "how much shorter could my docids be at this codebook budget?", which is directly a bound on decoder steps per query and hence on generative-retrieval latency. Likewise for learned-sparse / phrase-indexing: choosing which $n$-grams get their own posting list under an index-size budget, to minimise total postings traversed, has the same $\mathbf{p} \le C\mathbf{c}$ shape.

Where the certification idea transfers but the LP does not. Product-quantisation and residual-quantisation codebook design in vector search is cardinality-constrained, but the objective (reconstruction distortion) is not linear in the selection variables and there is no path structure, so this LP does not apply. What does transfer is the methodological move that is arguably this paper's most exportable contribution: solve a convex relaxation of a discrete index-design problem purely to obtain a lower bound, then use it to certify that your heuristic (k-means codebook, HNSW construction, IVF partitioning) is within $x\%$ of the best achievable at that budget. The field currently has essentially no such certificates — ANN benchmarking is entirely relative, "method A beats method B", with no notion of distance-to-optimal at a fixed memory budget. Importing "a posteriori instance-specific certificates" from polyhedral combinatorics into index design would be valuable even if, as here, the answer turns out to be "your greedy heuristic was already within 1%" — because that is exactly the kind of result that redirects a subfield's effort.

Where it plainly does not transfer. Generative retrieval docids are not merely short; they must be discriminative — distinct documents need distinct identifiers, and prefix structure should be semantically meaningful so the decoder can prune. Uniqueness is a combinatorial constraint over pairs of documents, not something linear in $(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c})$, and semantic prefix coherence is not expressible in this polytope at all. So you cannot simply run ConvexTok on a corpus and call the output a docid scheme; you would get a compression-optimal vocabulary that happily collides documents. The honest version of the transfer is: use the LP for the length/budget part of docid design, as a bound and as a generator of candidate unit inventories, and handle uniqueness and semantics with separate constraints or a different formulation. And the paper's central cautionary finding travels with it — the thing most likely to happen if someone does this is that hierarchical k-means or a greedy codebook turns out to be within a percent of the bound, and the interesting work moves to choosing a better objective rather than optimising the one you have.

title: A Theoretical Study on Bridging Internal Probability and Self-Consistency for LLM Reasoning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-06

A Theoretical Study on Bridging Internal Probability and Self-Consistency for LLM Reasoning

Zhou, Tan, Li, Yao, Guo, Li, Ma (2025) — arXiv:2510.15444

Setting and problem

The object of study is sampling-based test-time scaling: you have a frozen LLM, a reasoning question $x$ with ground-truth answer $y$, and a compute budget expressed as a number of sampled reasoning paths. The LLM defines an autoregressive distribution over token sequences, $p(t \mid x) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} p(t_i \mid x, t_{<i})$, where $t = (t_1,\dots,t_m)$ is a chain-of-thought path. A deterministic extraction map $g(\cdot)$ projects a path onto a final answer, $\hat y = g(\hat t)$ (parse the boxed expression; for code, execute against sampled test cases and bucket by observed behaviour). This induces an answer marginal

$$p(\hat y \mid x) \;=\; \sum_{t \,:\, g(t) = \hat y} p(t \mid x),$$

which the paper calls the answer confidence, as distinct from the path-level probability $p(\hat t \mid x)$ of one specific chain. The distinction is load-bearing: a correct answer is typically reachable by an enormous number of distinct correct derivations, so $p(\hat y\mid x)$ can be large while every individual $p(\hat t \mid x)$ is astronomically small. Most of the paper's machinery and most of its weaknesses live in the gap between these two quantities.

At test time you draw $n$ i.i.d. paths $\tilde t_1,\dots,\tilde t_n \sim p(\cdot \mid x)$, obtain answers $\tilde y_i = g(\tilde t_i)$, and must return a confidence $\hat p(\hat y \mid x)$ for each candidate answer; the answer with the largest confidence is returned (Best-of-$N$). The paper's framing move is to declare this a confidence estimation problem and to score it with a squared error against the correctness indicator:

$$\mathcal{E}_{\hat p}(\hat y) = \mathbb{E}[(\hat p(\hat y \mid x) - \mathbb{I}[\hat y = y])^2], \qquad \mathcal{E}_{\hat p}(\hat t) = \mathbb{E}[(\hat p(\hat t \mid x) - \mathbb{I}[g(\hat t) = y])^2],$$

the expectation being over the $n$ sampled paths. This is a per-item Brier score, and the whole framework is best understood as a Brier decomposition. Proposition 1 splits it, for any unbiased $\hat p$, into

$$\mathcal{E}_{\hat p}(\hat y) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[(\hat p(\hat y\mid x) - p(\hat y \mid x))^2]}_{Error \textbf{Estimation}} \;+\; \underbrace{(p(\hat y \mid x) - \mathbb{I}[\hat y = y])^2}_{\textbf{Model Error}} .$$

So the estimand is the model's own answer marginal $p(\hat y\mid x)$, not the correctness probability. Estimation error is a pure finite-$n$ statistical term; model error is the Brier score of the model's answer distribution against ground-truth correctness, and it is a fixed property of the LLM — zero iff the model puts all its mass on $y$. The paper is explicit that model error is "invariant, determined by the LLM's reasoning capability", and that confidence estimation can only attack the first term. (Caveat already here: model error is not invariant across confidence functions — the whole point of Appendix A.2 is that $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{SC}}_{\text{Model}} \le \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{PPL}}_{\text{Model}}$ — so "invariant" means invariant given a fixed choice of estimand, i.e. path-level vs answer-level.)

The two estimators compared are:

  • Self-consistency / majority voting (SC) — the Monte Carlo plug-in estimator of the answer marginal, $\hat p^{\mathrm{(SC)}}(\hat y \mid x) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}[\tilde y_i = \hat y]$. Unbiased by construction; needs only black-box samples and an equivalence test on answers.
  • Perplexity (PPL) — the model's internal sequence probability, restricted to the paths actually seen. With $\mathcal{R} = \mathrm{Set}(\tilde t_1,\dots,\tilde t_n)$, $\hat p^{\mathrm{(PPL)}}(\hat t \mid x) = \sum_{\tilde t \in \mathcal{R}} \mathbb{I}[\hat t = \tilde t]\, p(\tilde t \mid x)$, i.e. report the true path probability if the path was sampled and $0$ otherwise. This requires token log-probabilities, so the method is grey-box, not black-box. It is a truncated estimator and therefore downward biased.

The question being answered, as a question: _for a fixed LLM and a fixed sampling budget $n$, how fast does the error of a test-time-scaling confidence estimate decay in $n$, and can one combine the self-consistency estimator (low model error, slow $1/n$ estimation error) with the internal probability (fast truncation-driven decay, high model error) so as to inherit the good half of each?_

Background and the specific gap. Self-consistency (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) is the default test-time-scaling method: sample $n$ chains, take the plurality answer. Its vote share doubles as a confidence score, and a line of work (Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2024; Becker & Soatto 2024; CISC; DeepConf) uses it as such. Sequence likelihood / perplexity is the oldest confidence signal in NLP and is used for prompt quality, hallucination detection, and reranking. Both are empirically well-mapped — scaling curves, early-stopping variants (ESC, Adaptive Consistency), reward-model Best-of-$N$ — but, the authors claim, nobody had written down what the estimation problem being solved is, which means nobody had a sample-efficiency theory: no statement of the form "confidence error decays at rate $r(n)$ under assumptions $A$". This paper supplies the first such framework.

Non-obvious modelling assumptions, which deserve to be flagged up front because the results are quite sensitive to them:

  1. I.i.d. sampling with fixed temperature. Paths are drawn i.i.d. from $p(\cdot\mid x)$ (temperature $1.0$, top-$p$ $0.95$ in experiments). Beam search, nucleus truncation that changes the distribution, or any adaptive sampler breaks this.
  2. Distinct samples. Both the PPL and PC analyses "assume that each $\tilde t_1,\dots,\tilde t_n$ is different from each other", waved away as "slightly affecting the value of $n$". For short answers or low-temperature sampling this is badly false, and it is exactly the regime where duplicates carry the signal.
  3. Equiprobable paths per answer. The key step $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}[g(\tilde t)=\hat y]\,p(\tilde t\mid x)] = \frac1k p(\hat y \mid x)$ holds only if all $k$ paths mapping to $\hat y$ have identical probability $p(\hat y\mid x)/k$. In reality that distribution is heavy-tailed.
  4. $k$ is the population count of paths yielding $\hat y$, not the sampled count (Theorem 7 introduces a separate $\hat k$ for the sampled count). $k$ is never bounded, estimated, or discussed — and it sits in the base of the exponential. See "The most interesting part".
  5. Oracle threshold. Theorem 7's guarantee is stated for the pruning threshold $\tau = p(y \mid x)$ — the true probability of the ground-truth answer, i.e. an oracle. The deployed algorithm uses an entirely different, unrelated threshold (a two-component Weibull mixture fit).
  6. No calibration assumption, and no gap/separation assumption. This is worth stating plainly because it is where a reader's priors will mislead them. The paper does not assume the internal probability is calibrated up to bounded modelling error; it treats model error as an unanalysed residual that it simply does not try to control (Appendix A.2 shows only that SC's model error $\le$ PPL's under an idealised "every wrong path gives a unique wrong answer, $n\to\infty$" setting). And there is no assumption of a gap between the top answer and the rest, because the paper never analyses the argmax at all: every guarantee is a per-answer squared error on the confidence value, never a bound on $\Pr[\arg\max_{\hat y}\hat p(\hat y\mid x) \neq y]$. The exponential rate therefore does not come from a large-deviation/gap argument; it comes from a coverage probability. That is the single most important structural fact about this paper's theory.

Main idea

The framework is the contribution the authors lead with, and the method is derived from it in a pleasantly mechanical way.

Diagnosis of SC (Proposition 2). Because $\hat p^{\mathrm{(SC)}}$ is an unbiased Bernoulli mean, the decomposition is exact and the estimation error is pure variance:

$$\mathcal{E}_{\hat p^{\mathrm{(SC)}}}(\hat y) = \tfrac1n p(\hat y\mid x)(1 - p(\hat y\mid x)) + (p(\hat y\mid x) - \mathbb{I}[\hat y=y])^2 .$$

Estimation error is $\Theta(1/n)$ — the paper calls this "linear convergence", a terminological abuse (in optimisation "linear convergence" is geometric decay; they mean "decays linearly in $1/n$"). Diagnosis: SC is statistically clean but sample-hungry, which is why vote-based scaling curves are so flat at small $n$ and why the vote share is a coarse, granular confidence (${0,\tfrac1n,\dots,1}$).

Diagnosis of PPL (Proposition 3). $\hat p^{\mathrm{(PPL)}}(\hat t\mid x)$ takes value $p(\hat t\mid x)$ with probability $1-(1-p(\hat t\mid x))^n$ and $0$ otherwise, so

$$\mathcal{E}_{\hat p^{\mathrm{(PPL)}}}(\hat t) = (1-p(\hat t\mid x))^n\,p(\hat t\mid x)(2\,\mathbb{I}[g(\hat t)=y] - p(\hat t\mid x)) + (p(\hat t\mid x) - \mathbb{I}[g(\hat t)=y])^2 .$$

The $n$-dependent term decays like $e^{-np(\hat t\mid x)}$ — exponentially, but at a rate proportional to the path's own probability, so for a long chain with $p(\hat t\mid x)\approx 0$ it does not decay at all over any realistic $n$ (Remark 3's "degradation"). Meanwhile its model error is larger than SC's, because $\hat p^{\mathrm{(PPL)}}$ scores a single path and discards the consistency structure: it cannot accumulate the evidence that twenty different derivations agreed.

The method: RPC = Perplexity Consistency + Reasoning Pruning.

Perplexity Consistency (PC) is the obvious-in-hindsight hybrid — probability-weighted voting over unique sampled paths, aggregated by answer:

$$\hat p^{\mathrm{(PC)}}(\hat y \mid x) \;=\; \sum_{\tilde t \in \mathcal{R}} \mathbb{I}[g(\tilde t) = \hat y]\, p(\tilde t \mid x).$$

Mechanically: deduplicate the samples; for each distinct sampled path attach its internal sequence probability; sum those probabilities within each answer-equivalence class; return the argmax class. This is a plug-in estimator of the answer marginal $p(\hat y\mid x)$ that uses the summands the model hands you for free instead of counting $1/n$ per sample. Theorem 4 gives, with $\alpha := 1 - \frac1k p(\hat y\mid x)$,

$$\mathcal{E}_{\hat p^{\mathrm{(PC)}}}(\hat y) \;=\; \underbrace{\alpha^n\, p(\hat y\mid x)(2\,\mathbb{I}[\hat y=y] - (1+\alpha^n)p(\hat y\mid x))}_{Error'' \text{``Estimation}} \;+\; \underbrace{(p(\hat y\mid x) - \mathbb{I}[\hat y=y])^2}_{\text{Model Error}} .$$

Headline claim: same model error as SC (identical second term, since the estimand is the same answer marginal), but the $n$-dependent term is $O(\alpha^n) = O(e^{-n p(\hat y\mid x)/k})$ rather than $O(1/n)$ — "linear to exponential while preserving model error".

Reasoning Pruning (RP) patches the degradation case flagged in Remark 6: when $p(\hat y\mid x)\to0$ with $np(\hat y\mid x)\ll 1$, $\alpha^n \to 1/(1+np(\hat y\mid x))$ and the exponential rate collapses back to $1/n$. The fix is blunt: zero out any answer whose accumulated probability falls below a threshold $\tau$, which makes both error terms vanish provided the pruned answer was indeed wrong. Theorem 7 says that with the oracle threshold $\tau = p(y\mid x)$, pruning is correct with probability at least $1 - \exp(-2\hat k k^2(1-\tfrac{\tau}{1-\alpha})^2)$. In practice $\tau$ is set by borrowing the open-set-recognition trick of Bendale & Boult: fit a two-component Weibull mixture to the empirical distribution of the $n$ internal probabilities for this question by MLE, compute the posterior $P_{\mathrm{High}}(x) = w_1 f_W(x;k_1,\lambda_1)/(w_1f_W(\cdot) + w_2f_W(\cdot))$, and drop paths with $P_{\mathrm{High}} < 0.5$; a truncated-mean guard additionally retains any path with $p_i \ge \bar p$ so that a bad mixture fit cannot prune everything. The authors advertise this as making RPC hyperparameter-free, which is true in the narrow sense that there is no user-facing threshold and false in the sense that the Weibull fit has initialisation and bound choices (Appendix D.6 shows $\pm0.8$ accuracy swings across them, which is comparable to the headline gain).

Experiments. Seven main benchmarks: MATH, MathOdyssey, OlympiadBench, AIME (1983–2024) for math; HumanEval, MBPP-sanitized, APPS-introductory for code; plus GPQA and LogiQA as extras. Models: InternLM2-Math-Plus 1.8B/7B, DeepSeekMath-RL 7B, DeepSeek-Coder 33B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Temperature $1.0$, top-$p$ $0.95$, 10 seeds, $n=64$ (MATH) or $128$. For code, the consistency function is semantic equivalence via execution agreement on 100 model-generated test cases (CodeT-style); for R1 models the internal probability is computed only over tokens after the think-tag close.

Concretely: (i) Sample efficiency (Table 1) — samples needed to match SC's best accuracy drop from 64→32 on MATH ($-50\%$), 112→32 on MathOdyssey ($-71\%$), 128→64 on OlympiadBench ($-50\%$), 128→48 on AIME ($-62.5\%$). (ii) Accuracy (Table 2, InternLM2-Math-Plus 7B) — average over four math sets: PPL $21.90$, Verbalized $10.76$, SC $24.82$, RPC $26.11$, i.e. the advertised $+1.29$.
