$$\mathbb E|\nabla f_i(x^{k+1})-g_i^{k+1}|\le\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,\mathbb E|\nabla f_i(x^k)-g_i^k|+\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,e^{L_1\gamma_k}\gamma_k(L_0+L_1\mathbb E|\nabla f_i(x^k)|).$$

A first-moment contraction with factor $\sqrt{1-\alpha}$ and drift linear in $\gamma_k$ — again a consequence of the step length being exactly $\gamma_k$ (under an unnormalized step the drift would be $\gamma_k|g^k|$). The potential function

$$V^k=f(x^k)-f^{\inf}+A_k\cdot\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n|\nabla f_i(x^k)-g_i^k|,\qquad A_k=\frac{2\gamma_k}{1-\sqrt{1-\alpha}},$$

is designed so that the $2\gamma_k$ coming from Lemma 3 is absorbed: $2\gamma_k+A_{k+1}\sqrt{1-\alpha}\le2\gamma_k+A_k\sqrt{1-\alpha}=A_k$, which is why monotone $\gamma_{k+1}\le\gamma_k$ is required. The leftover drift terms produce exactly the constants $c_i=\frac{L_i}{2}+\frac{2\sqrt{1-\alpha}L_i}{1-\sqrt{1-\alpha}}$, $i=0,1$. Note $1-\sqrt{1-\alpha}\ge\alpha/2$, so $A_k\approx 4\gamma_k/\alpha$ and $c_i\approx 4L_i/\alpha$: this is where all the compression dependence lives.

The intermediate inequality is then

$$\mathbb E V^{k+1}\le\mathbb E V^k+c_1e^{L_1\gamma_k}\gamma_k^2\cdot\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E|\nabla f_i(x^k)|-\gamma_k\mathbb E|\nabla f(x^k)|+c_0e^{L_1\gamma_k}\gamma_k^2.$$

Step 3: the crux — closing the loop on $\frac1n\sum_i|\nabla f_i(x^k)|$ (Lemma 2). This is where the distributed setting is genuinely harder than the single-node one. The descent lemma's curvature term involves $\frac1n\sum_i|\nabla f_i(x^k)|$, while the progress term involves $|\nabla f(x^k)|=|\frac1n\sum_i\nabla f_i(x^k)|$. Jensen points the wrong way: $|\nabla f|\le\frac1n\sum|\nabla f_i|$, so the curvature term cannot be absorbed into the progress term. (For $n=1$ it can, and that is precisely why Theorem 3 gets a constant, horizon-free stepsize and an $O(1/K)$ rate — the coefficient of $|\nabla f(x^k)|$ becomes $-(\gamma_k-c_1e^{L_1\gamma_k}\gamma_k^2)$, negative for $\gamma_k\le1/(2c_1)$, with no expansive factor at all.)

The resolution is to bound the local gradient norms by function values, using (8). From $4(f_i(x)-f_i^{\inf})\ge\frac{|\nabla f_i|^2}{L_0+L_1|\nabla f_i|}$, split on whether $|\nabla f_i|\le L_0/L_1$: in the first branch the RHS is $\ge|\nabla f_i|^2/(2L_0)$, in the second $\ge|\nabla f_i|/(2L_1)$. Hence $|\nabla f_i(x)|\le\max{8L_1(f_i(x)-f_i^{\inf}),\,L_0/L_1}\le8L_1(f_i(x)-f_i^{\inf})+L_0/L_1$, and averaging,

$$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n|\nabla f_i(x)|\ \le\ 8L_1(f(x)-f^{\inf})+8L_1\delta^{\inf}+\frac{L_0}{L_1}.$$

This is the single most load-bearing lemma. It converts the uncontrollable $L_1\sum_i|\nabla f_i|$ into (i) a multiple of the Lyapunov function itself — since $f(x^k)-f^{\inf}\le V^k$ — and (ii) the constants $L_0/L_1$ and $\delta^{\inf}$. It is also the origin of both "hidden costs" of the paper: $\delta^{\inf}$ (hence the residual heterogeneity dependence, and the need for A2), and the expansive recursion

$$\mathbb E V^{k+1}\le(1+8c_1L_1e^{L_1\gamma_k}\gamma_k^2)\mathbb E V^k-\gamma_k\mathbb E|\nabla f(x^k)|+Be^{L_1\gamma_k}\gamma_k^2,\quad B=2c_0+8c_1L_1\delta^{\inf},$$

using the identity $c_1L_0/L_1=c_0$.

Step 4: taming an expansive recursion with a $1/\sqrt K$ stepsize (Lemma 4). The multiplier $1+b_1e^{L_1\gamma}\gamma^2>1$ means the potential can grow; naive summation gives a factor $(1+b_1\gamma^2)^{K+1}$. The trick is to accept this and then choose $\gamma$ so that $\gamma^2K$ is constant. Formally: define weights $\beta_k=(1+b_1e^{L_1\gamma}\gamma^2)^{-(k+1)}$, multiply through and telescope $\beta_{k-1}V^k-\beta_kV^{k+1}$, use $\beta_{-1}=1$, $V^{K+1}\ge0$, and $\sum_{k\le K}\beta_k\ge(K+1)\beta_K$, then $1+x\le e^x$, to get

$$\min_{k\le K}W^k\le\frac{V^0\exp(b_1e^{L_1\gamma}\gamma^2(K+1))}{b_2\gamma(K+1)}+\frac{b_3}{b_2}e^{L_1\gamma}\gamma.$$

With $\gamma=\gamma_0/\sqrt{K+1}$ we have $\gamma^2(K+1)=\gamma_0^2$, so the exponential is $K$-independent; $\gamma(K+1)=\gamma_0\sqrt{K+1}$ gives the first term's $1/\sqrt{K+1}$, and $\gamma$ gives the second's. This is the mechanism behind "stepsize needs no knowledge of $L_0,L_1$" — the stepsize rule never has to satisfy $\gamma\le1/L$; instead, $K$-dependent damping absorbs the growth. The price is the multiplicative $\exp(8c_1L_1e^{L_1\gamma_0}\gamma_0^2)$.

Step 5: where momentum enters (Theorem 2). In the stochastic case the error splits into two tracked quantities. With $\delta^k=\mathbb E[f(x^k)-f^{\inf}]$, $A_k=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E|v_i^k-g_i^k|$ (compression tracking error), $C_k=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E|v_i^k-\nabla f_i(x^k)|$ (per-client momentum error), $B_k=\mathbb E|v^k-\nabla f(x^k)|$ (averaged momentum error), the descent lemma splits $|\nabla f(x^k)-g^k|\le|\nabla f(x^k)-v^k|+|v^k-g^k|$ and so charges $2\gamma(A_k+B_k)$.

Momentum plays two distinct roles, and this is the nicest structural observation in the proof.

(a) It slows down the signal that the compressor must track. In Lemma 8, the key step is $|v_i^{k+1}-v_i^k|=\eta_{k+1}|\nabla f_i(x^{k+1};\xi_i^{k+1})-v_i^k|$: the compressed object moves by only $O(\eta)$ per round. Hence

$$A_{k+1}\le\sqrt{1-\alpha}A_k+\eta\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,C_k+O(\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,\eta\gamma e^{\gamma L_1}(L_0+L_1^2\delta^k+L_1^2\delta^{\inf}))+\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,\eta\sigma,$$

with the variance term multiplied by $\eta$. Without momentum ($\eta=1$) the target jumps by $\Theta(\sigma)$ each round and the contraction can never catch up — the $\sigma$ term would enter at full strength, which is exactly the "momentum provably improves error feedback" phenomenon of Fatkhullin, Tyurin & Richtárik, transplanted here.

_(b) It gives the $1/\sqrt n$ variance reduction, but only in the averaged error._ Lemma 9 unrolls the momentum recursion for $H_i^k=v_i^k-\nabla f_i(x^k)$: $H_i^{k+1}=(1-\eta)^{k+1}H_i^0+\sum_t(1-\eta)^{k-t+1}G_i^t+\eta\sum_t(1-\eta)^{k-t}U_i^{t+1}$, with $G_i^t=\nabla f_i(x^t)-\nabla f_i(x^{t+1})$ (drift) and $U_i^{t+1}=\nabla f_i(x^{t+1};\xi_i^{t+1})-\nabla f_i(x^{t+1})$ (martingale noise). The drift sum is handled by (6) with $|x^{t+1}-x^t|=\gamma$ (normalization again) plus Lemma 2. The noise sum is handled by Jensen plus orthogonality across time and independence across clients: $\eta\,\mathbb E|\sum_t(1-\eta)^{k-t}U^{t+1}|\le\eta\sqrt{\sum_t(1-\eta)^{2(k-t)}\sigma^2/n}\le\sigma\sqrt{\eta/n}$. This is where the $\sigma/\sqrt n$ comes from: the cancellation happens in the averaged quantity $B_k$, where $U^{t+1}=\frac1n\sum_iU_i^{t+1}$ has variance $\sigma^2/n$. The per-client $C_k$ enjoys no such reduction — it only gets the $\eta$ factor from (a). The division of labour is clean: $B_k$ buys the $n$-speedup, $C_k$ feeds the compression error with an $\eta$-discount.

(c) Assembly. The Lyapunov function is $\mathcal V_k=\delta^k+aA_k+cC_k$ with $a=\frac{2\gamma}{1-\sqrt{1-\alpha}}$ and $c=a\sqrt{1-\alpha}$ — chosen so that the cross-term coefficients telescope exactly: $\frac{2\gamma}{a}+\sqrt{1-\alpha}=1$ and $\frac{a\eta\sqrt{1-\alpha}}{c}+(1-\eta)=1$. The remaining term $B_k$ is not put inside $\mathcal V_k$ (it is not a one-step recursion, it carries a full convolution $\sum_{t<k}(1-\eta)^{k-t}\delta^t$); instead the whole inequality is summed with weights $\beta_k=(1+\frac{64L_1^2\gamma^2}{1-\sqrt{1-\alpha}}+\frac{32L_1^2\gamma^2}{\eta})^{-(k+1)}$, and the convolution is collapsed using $\beta_t\le\beta_k$ for $t\le k$ and $\sum_t(1-\eta)^t\le1/\eta$, i.e. the geometric kernel is absorbed into the $32L_1^2\gamma^2/\eta$ slot of the weight. The stepsize/momentum choices $\gamma=\gamma_0(K+1)^{-3/4}$, $\eta=(K+1)^{-1/2}$ are then exactly what makes both exponents $K$-free: $\frac{\gamma^2(K+1)}{\eta}=\gamma_0^2$ and $\frac{\gamma^2(K+1)}{C_\alpha}=\frac{\gamma_0^2}{C_\alpha\sqrt{K+1}}$, and the condition $\gamma_0\le\frac{1}{16L_1}\min{C_\alpha\sqrt{K+1},1}$ makes both $\le1/4$. Finally the initialization is cashed in: with $g_i^{-1}=0$ and $v_i^{-1}=\nabla f_i(x_i^0;\xi_i^0)$ one gets $A_0\le(1-C_\alpha)\sigma$, $C_0\le\sigma$, $B_0\le\sigma/\sqrt n$, which — divided by $C_\alpha$ — produce the $O(\frac{\sqrt{1-\alpha}}{\alpha}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt K})$ term.

Summarising the technical devices by name: the anchored generalized-smooth descent lemma with the $e^{L_1|x^{k+1}-x^k|}$ factor neutralized by a constant-length step; a first-moment (not squared) Lyapunov function combining suboptimality with the EF21 shift-tracking error, with $\gamma_k$-scaled weights tuned so the contraction $\sqrt{1-\alpha}$ absorbs the descent lemma's $2\gamma_k$; the self-bounding inequality (8) converted into Lemma 2 to replace local gradient norms by function values at the cost of $L_0/L_1$ and $\delta^{\inf}$; weighted telescoping (Lemma 4) with $\gamma\propto K^{-1/2}$ to damp an expansive $(1+O(\gamma^2))$ recursion; and, in the stochastic case, momentum used simultaneously as a slow-moving compression target and as a martingale-averaging device for the $1/\sqrt n$ variance reduction.

Broader context

Why compression and error feedback exist. In data-parallel training every round each worker must ship a vector the size of the model. The paper's own example: VGG-16 has 138M parameters, i.e. >500MB uplink per worker per step; for modern LLM-scale models the gradient exchange, not the FLOPs, is the bottleneck, and in cross-device federated learning the uplink is orders of magnitude worse. The remedy is to send a compressed surrogate: sign/1-bit (Seide et al., 2014), stochastic quantization (QSGD), Top-$k$ sparsification, low-rank sketches (PowerSGD). Unbiased compressors plug into SGD analyses directly but have poor variance-per-bit; the aggressive, practically-used compressors (Top-$k$, sign) are biased and can make distributed GD diverge on fixed instances. Error feedback is the correction: remember what you did not send and send it later. EF14's analysis needed bounded gradients or bounded gradient dissimilarity; EF21 removed both by tracking a gradient shift instead of accumulating a residual, giving $O(1/(\alpha\epsilon^2))$ for nonconvex problems — and it is the dominant template today (EF21-P for bidirectional compression, EF21-SGDM for momentum, EControl for improved constants).

Why generalized smoothness exists. Zhang, He, Sra & Jadbabaie (ICLR 2020), "Why gradient clipping accelerates training of neural networks", measured the local Hessian norm against the local gradient norm along LSTM and ResNet training trajectories and found an approximately affine relation, $|\nabla^2f|\approx L_0+L_1|\nabla f|$, rather than a uniform bound. This matters because GD's stepsize must scale as $1/L$ with the global $L$, which on such objectives is huge (or infinite), while the curvature is actually mild in the region where the trajectory spends most of its time. Clipping (or normalization) decouples the step length from the gradient magnitude and provably beats GD on this class. Crawshaw et al. (2022) extended the empirical evidence to transformers and gave generalized signSGD; Chen, Zhou, Liang & Lu (ICML 2023) built the differentiable, symmetric version of the condition used here; Koloskova, Hendrikx & Stich (2023) clarified the bias clipping introduces; Hübler, Fatkhullin & He (2024) showed normalized SGD with momentum reaches the optimal $\epsilon^{-4}$ without clipping and with only expectation-bounded noise — which is the single-node result that this paper lifts to $n$ clients with compression. Two papers to read alongside: Fatkhullin, Tyurin & Richtárik (2024), "Momentum provably improves error feedback" (the direct ancestor of Algorithm 2 and the source of the "momentum makes the compressed signal slow" idea), and Crawshaw, Bao & Liu (2024) on federated learning with unbounded smoothness, client subsampling and heterogeneity (the strongest distributed competitor, and the one whose assumptions this paper is explicitly attacking).

Follow-ups the paper opens. The authors name the obvious one: both stepsize rules are horizon-dependent constants, which is impractical (and for large $K$, impractically tiny), so anytime/adaptive schedules — AdaGrad-norm or Polyak-type stepsizes under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, composed with EF21 — are open. Two more interesting directions. (i) Is the $\exp(\Theta(L_1^2\gamma_0^2/\alpha))$ and the $\alpha^{-2}$ complexity necessary? A lower bound for compressed first-order methods under generalized smoothness, separating the $\alpha$-dependence from the $\alpha^{-1}$ achievable under classical smoothness, would be the natural theory contribution, and would settle whether "parameter-agnostic stepsize" must cost an exponential. (ii) Remove $\delta^{\inf}$ and the full-participation requirement. $\delta^{\inf}$ enters only through Lemma 2, which bounds local gradient norms by local suboptimality; an algorithm that normalizes or clips locally before compressing (so that each client's transmitted signal has bounded length by construction) might let one bound the drift without invoking (8) at all, removing both $\delta^{\inf}$ and assumption A2, and would compose naturally with client subsampling. A third, cheap, likely fruitful direction: swap A5 for a $p$-th moment bound ($p\in(1,2]$, heavy-tailed noise). Normalization is the canonical tool there, so the machinery here should transfer almost verbatim and would give the first compressed, heavy-tailed, generalized-smooth distributed result.

Connection to your work. There are two honest links, one substantive and one an analogy; neither is a theorem transfer.

The substantive one concerns the curvature model for retrieval losses. The loss functions that dominate both dense retrieval (InfoNCE / softmax over in-batch or large negative sets) and generative retrieval (token-level cross-entropy over a docid vocabulary, i.e. log-sum-exp over a large label space) are exactly of log-sum-exp/exponential type — which is the textbook example of a function whose classical smoothness constant is bad or unbounded but which is $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth. The paper's own Appendix F computation makes this concrete: for logistic loss plus a nonconvex regularizer, $|\nabla^2f_i(x)|\le|a_i|\,|\nabla\tilde f_i(x)|+2\lambda$, so the local curvature is literally proportional to the local gradient norm with $L_1=\max_i|a_i|$, i.e. the feature-norm scale. For retrieval that is the embedding-norm scale, which is precisely the quantity that is not controlled when embeddings are unnormalized, and which governs the known instabilities of contrastive training (large logits, temperature sensitivity, the need for warmup and clipping). So if there is ever a reason to want optimization-side theory for training retrieval encoders or docid decoders, the $(L_0,L_1)$ class — not $L$-smoothness — is the right curvature model, and normalization/clipping (which Adam and LAMB approximate) is the right algorithmic primitive rather than a heuristic. The distributed/compressed layer is also real rather than hypothetical for this setting, since large dual-encoder and generative-retrieval models are trained multi-node and the uplink is the bottleneck.

The analogy is more structural and I flag it as such. The $\alpha$-contractive condition $\mathbb E|\mathcal C(v)-v|^2\le(1-\alpha)|v|^2$ is a relative-error distortion guarantee — syntactically identical to the guarantees that quantization-based ANN indexes (PQ/OPQ, and more sharply RaBitQ-style methods) provide for embedding compression. And EF21's mechanism — compress the residual between the true vector and the current reconstruction, add it to the reconstruction, repeat, and prove the residual norm contracts geometrically by $\sqrt{1-\alpha}$ per round — is, as algebra, residual quantization: the same contraction argument that bounds the error of an $m$-level residual quantizer, and the same object as the RQ-VAE codebook stacks used to build semantic IDs in TIGER-style generative retrieval. EF21 is residual quantization run across time against a moving target, which is why it needs the extra drift term $|\nabla f_i(x^{k+1})-\nabla f_i(x^k)|$ that a static multi-level quantizer does not have. The parallel will not give either field a free theorem, but the "contraction plus drift" Lyapunov template is a transferable proof pattern, and it is a reasonable question whether the error-feedback view says anything useful about adaptive residual quantization of a drifting embedding table — e.g. re-quantizing an index while the encoder is still being fine-tuned, where the codebook is tracking a moving target with exactly the structure analyzed here.

title: A high-dimensional sphere spilling out of a high-dimensional cube despite exponentially many constraints
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-05

A high-dimensional sphere spilling out of a high-dimensional cube despite exponentially many constraints

Stanislav Fort (2022) · https://stanislavfort.com/blog/sphere-spilling-out/

Setting and problem

(Worked from the full post, which is short; the author normalises the cube to edge length 4a rather than 1, and ends with a loose pointer to Zhang–Strogatz's "Basins with tentacles". Everything below the basic derivation is additional — the post contains no discussion of volume or concentration.)

Fix D ≥ 2 and work in the cube Q_D = [−1/2, 1/2]^D, so vol(Q_D) = 1. Bisect every coordinate axis at 0. This dyadic decomposition cuts Q_D into 2^D congruent closed cells indexed by sign vectors s ∈ {−1,+1}^D: C_s is the cell whose i-th coordinate has the sign of s_i, a cube of side 1/2 with centre c_s = s/4 and inscribed-ball radius r = 1/4. Place in each cell its inscribed corner sphere B_s = B(c_s, 1/4); by construction B_s ⊂ C_s ⊂ Q_D, and B_s touches each of the D faces of C_s that lie on ∂Q_D. Distinct B_s have disjoint interiors.

The cells do not cover a neighbourhood of the origin tightly: there is a gap at the centre. Put a central sphere B_0 = B(0, R) there, with R fixed by external tangency to the corner spheres: ||c_s − 0|| = R + 1/4 for every s ∈ {−1,+1}^D. Since ||c_s|| = ||s||/4 = √D/4 for every s, one radius satisfies all 2^D equations simultaneously — the construction is consistent and B_0 kisses all 2^D corner spheres at once.

Question. For which D is B_0 ⊆ Q_D?

The naive expectation is "all D": the central sphere is wedged between 2^D spheres, every one of which lies inside the cube, and 2^D grows explosively. Being surrounded by exponentially many obstacles feels like confinement. The expectation is wrong, and the fact that does the work is a mismatch of two radii of the same cube. The inradius of Q_D — the distance from the origin to the nearest point of ∂Q_D, i.e. to a facet {x_i = ±1/2} — is 1/2 for every D. Its circumradius — the distance to a vertex — is √D/2 and diverges. The corner spheres are anchored to the diagonal directions s/√D, which live out near the diverging corners; the escape routes are the 2D axis directions ±e_i. In high dimension those two families are asymptotically orthogonal, so the 2^D constraints constrain almost nothing along the directions that matter.

Main idea

The whole problem collapses onto a single main diagonal. Along the ray t ↦ t·s/√D, the segment from the origin to the vertex s/2 has length √D/2 and decomposes as

R (central radius) + [1/4 + 1/4] (corner-sphere diameter) + g (gap to the vertex) = √D/2,

and by the symmetry of the cell inside the corner, g = R. Hence 2R + 1/2 = √D/2, i.e. directly from tangency,

R(D) = √D/4 − 1/4 = (√D − 1)/4.

Containment requires R(D) ≤ 1/2 (the inradius), i.e. √D − 1 ≤ 2, i.e. √D ≤ 3:

B_0 ⊆ Q_D ⟺ D ≤ 9.

D = 9 is the exact critical case: R(9) = (3−1)/4 = 1/2, so the central sphere is inscribed in the cube, internally tangent to all 18 facets while externally tangent to all 512 corner spheres. From D = 10 on it spills: R(10) = (√10 − 1)/4 ≈ 0.5406 > 0.5, and it protrudes through all 2D facets at once in spherical caps of height R − 1/2.

What this means is stronger than "it pokes out". R(D) ~ √D/4 → ∞ while the cube's half-width is pinned at 1/2. At D = 100 the central sphere has radius 2.25 — four and a half times the whole cube's half-width — while still touching every one of the 2^100 ≈ 10^30 corner spheres, each of which sits obediently inside the cube. The two bodies interpenetrate: note R(D)/(√D/2) = 1/2 − 1/(2√D) < 1/2 always, so the central sphere never swallows the cube; the cube's corners always stick out of it by a margin that is asymptotically half the diagonal. Faces leak out of the sphere's hull in one direction, corners in the other.

The most interesting part

The sharpest point is that counting the constraints is the wrong instinct, and one line makes it precise. A constraint from B_s restricts motion of the central sphere's centre only along c_s/||c_s|| = s/√D. For any candidate escape direction u ∈ S^{D−1}, the best any constraint can do is

max over s ∈ {±1}^D of ⟨u, s⟩/√D = ||u||_1/√D,

and for u = e_1 — the direction of the nearest facet — this equals 1/√D → 0. So the facet normals are simultaneously nearly orthogonal to all 2^D constraint directions. Equivalently: translating the centre to t·e_1 changes its distance to the nearest cell centres at first-order rate 1/√D, so the obstacles resist escape with vanishing stiffness. Two is not fewer than 2^D in a way that matters here, because the obstacles and the exits span nearly orthogonal subspaces of directions. "Exponentially many" is also not many on the relevant scale: covering S^{D−1} at angular resolution θ needs ~(c/θ)^{D−1} caps, and the ±1 directions are a code whose minimum angle is arccos(1 − 2/D) ≈ 2/√D — resolving the sphere at that scale would take ~D^{D/2} ≫ 2^D directions. The sign vectors are exponentially many and still a measure-zero scattering.

I therefore think the post slightly oversells the paradox. Once you say out loud that the corner spheres are glued to the corners, and that the corners are at distance √D/2 while the faces stay at 1/2, the result is forced — it is the standard cube anisotropy, and the derivation is two lines of Pythagoras. A sharper framing of the same identity, which the post misses: the gap from each corner sphere's surface to "its own" vertex is exactly R. The corner spheres do not occupy the corners at all; they hug the centre-facing part of their cells and leave a corner void of the same size as the central sphere. Hemmed in by 2^D spheres that have themselves abandoned the region they are named after is much less surprising.

It remains a very good intuition pump, for a reason that is quantitative rather than rhetorical. Compute volumes. All 2^D corner spheres together have volume 2^D · V_D · 4^{−D} = V_D · 2^{−D}, where V_D = π^{D/2}/Γ(D/2 + 1): that is 0.25% of the cube at D=10, 2.5×10^{−8} at D=20, 1.9×10^{−70} at D=100. The exponentially many obstacles are collectively invisible. The central sphere is barely better: at D=10 it occupies 0.54% of the cube while sticking out of it, and at D=100, 3.9×10^{−5}. (Pretty coincidence at the critical dimension: at D=9 the central ball and the union of all 512 corner balls have identical volume V_9 · 2^{−9} ≈ 0.00644, since (1/2)^D = 2^D(1/4)^D.) And the relative volume is not monotone — V_D·R(D)^D ≈ (πe/8)^{D/2}/√(πD), with πe/8 ≈ 1.0675 > 1 — so it bottoms out near D ≈ 264 at ~10^{−5} and then grows, exceeding the cube's volume around D ≈ 1206 and diverging thereafter. A body that is simultaneously 10^{−5} of the cube and spilling out of every face is exactly the kind of object high-dimensional intuition is not built for.

Broader context

The ambient facts, for orientation. (i) Vanishing ball volume: V_D → 0 superexponentially; the unit ball is negligible against the cube [−1,1]^D of volume 2^D that contains it. (ii) Thin shell / concentration: a uniform point in a ball lies within O(1/D) relative distance of the boundary, and its single coordinates are ≈ N(0, R²/D) — here R/√(D+2) → 1/4, so each coordinate of a uniform point in the central ball is roughly N(0, 1/16) and the facet at 1/2 sits about 2 standard deviations out; multiply over D nearly independent coordinates and the fraction of the central ball inside the cube decays from ≈ 1 at D = 10 to ≈ 0.09 at D = 100 to ≈ 10^{−17} at D = 1000. (iii) Cube vs ball: the cube's mass sits in its corners, ||x||_2 ≈ √(D/12) for uniform x ∈ [−1/2,1/2]^D, far outside the inscribed ball. (iv) Packing: the kissing number in D dimensions lies between 2^{0.2075D(1+o(1))} and the Kabatiansky–Levenshtein 2^{0.401D(1+o(1))}, with exact answers only in D ∈ {1,2,3,4,8,24}; Viazovska's D=8 and the Cohn–Kumar–Miller–Radchenko–Viazovska D=24 results settled optimal packing via linear-programming duality. Note our configuration is not a packing bound — the 2^D tangencies are achievable precisely because the central ball is enormous. Good entry points: Keith Ball, An Elementary Introduction to Modern Convex Geometry; Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability (Ch. 3); Blum–Hopcroft–Kannan, Foundations of Data Science, Ch. 2.

The IR connection is real and worth stating carefully — the post makes none, so this is extrapolation. First, the dyadic decomposition here is a grid index: uniform space partitioning, 2^D cells at one bisection per axis. The construction shows what goes wrong with such indexes concretely. A cell's inscribed ball has radius 1/4 while the cell's own diameter is √D/2: cells are not round, their aspect ratio between inradius and circumradius degrades like √D, and a ball-shaped query range of any useful radius overlaps essentially all 2^D cells. The branch-and-bound pruning that makes kd-trees and grids work collapses, which is the geometric content of the empirical "grid/tree indexes lose to linear scan above roughly 10–20 dimensions". Second, this is the same anisotropy that drives distance concentration: Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft, When Is "Nearest Neighbor" Meaningful? (ICDT 1999) show that under broad conditions (d_max − d_min)/d_min → 0, so the margin an index needs to prune disappears at the rate the diagonal grows. Third, the specific intuition this post kills — "surround the query with enough cells and you have localised it" — is exactly the intuition behind data-independent partitioning. What survives in practice is data-dependent partitioning, which buys locality from the data's low intrinsic dimension rather than from the ambient geometry: IVF/k-means Voronoi cells (shaped by the data, not the axes), graph indexes such as HNSW (whose navigability relies on long-range edges rather than on cells having bounded overlap), and LSH (which gives up exactness in exchange for a provable, dimension-robust collision gap). The theoretical sharpening is Andoni–Indyk–Razenshteyn-style data-dependent LSH, where the whole point is that no fixed partition family can match a partition adapted to the point set.

A follow-up worth actually working out: iterate the construction. Bisect each axis k times instead of once, giving cells of side 1/k with inscribed radius 1/(2k) and centres at the corresponding distance for the innermost shell; the critical dimension becomes a function of k, and asking how it scales tells you how much refinement a grid index must buy to keep a query ball inside a bounded number of cells. The expectation, from the same diagonal budget, is that the answer is "refinement does not help at all at fixed k": the critical D stays O(1) because the inradius/circumradius ratio of a cell is scale-invariant. Confirming that, and the analogous statement for a random rotation of the grid (does rotating the partition off the axes change anything, given that the sign directions are already nearly orthogonal to the axes?), would make a sharper note than the original.

title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-05

Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers

Katie Everett, Lechao Xiao, Mitchell Wortsman, Alexander A. Alemi, Roman Novak, Peter J. Liu, Izzeddin Gur, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein, Leslie Pack Kaelbling, Jaehoon Lee, Jeffrey Pennington (2024) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.05872

Setting and problem

Fix an MLP with depth L, input/output dimension d = Θ(1), hidden width n, weights W_1 ∈ R^{n×d}, W_2,…,W_L ∈ R^{n×n}, W_{L+1} ∈ R^{d×n}, and forward pass z_l = φ(n^{-a_l} W_l z_{l-1}), z_{L+1} = n^{-a_{L+1}} W_{L+1} z_L. A width-scaling parameterization is, formally, a triple of exponents per layer {a_l, b_l, c_l}: the parameter multiplier is n^{-a_l} (a fixed constant folded into the forward pass, not trained), the initialization is W_l ~ N(0, n^{-2b_l}), and the learning rate is η_l ∝ n^{-c_l}. "Scale" throughout means v = lim_{n→∞} log_n ||U||_RMS — an order-of-magnitude exponent in the RMS norm, i.e. the size of a typical entry. This is the abc-parameterization of Yang & Hu's Tensor Programs line of work.

The desiderata are asymptotic design choices, not theorems. Stability: activations exactly Θ(1) at every layer and every step t ≤ T, logits at most O(1). Nontriviality: the change in logits after initialization is Ω(1). Feature learning: the change Δz_L in the last pre-readout activation is exactly Θ(1), so representations move by a non-vanishing amount in the limit (as opposed to the kernel/NTK regime, where the features freeze and only the readout moves). The limit is a dichotomy: feature learning or kernel. Standard parameterization sits at (a,b) with a_l + b_l = 1/2 in hidden layers and a_{L+1} + b_{L+1} = 1/2 in the readout; NTK, muP and mean-field (MFP) differ only by where the √n lives. In fact all four occupy just two equivalence classes at initialization (one can trade a_l ← a_l + θ, b_l ← b_l − θ and repair the learning rate by c_l ← c_l − 2θ for SGD, −θ for Adam, 0 for Adafactor): standard ≡ NTK with Θ(1) logits at init, muP ≡ MFP with Θ(1/√n) logits at init. muP is the choice that gets both stability and feature learning under the standard assumptions. Hyperparameter transfer means operationally: write each quantity as (empirical constant) × (width)^(theoretical exponent); if the exponent truly absorbs all width dependence, the optimal constant is width-independent, so you tune it on a cheap small model and reuse it at 27B.

The load-bearing modelling choice is the alignment assumption. From the second forward pass on, z_l = n^{-a_l}(W_l + ΔW_l)(z_{l-1} + Δz_{l-1}) expands into four terms. Only W_l z_{l-1} is guaranteed unaligned (random init, independent of data). The other three can correlate, because ΔW_l is built from gradients that carry the data, and backpropagated gradients to layer l carry the initialization of later layers. The paper introduces three alignment exponents, defined at finite width so they are measurable:

α_l = log_n [ ||ΔW_l z_{l-1}|| / (||ΔW_l||·||z_{l-1}||) ], and analogously ω_l for W_l Δz_{l-1} and u_l for ΔW_l Δz_{l-1}.

With RMS norms, α_l = 1/2 is the CLT/no-alignment case (summing n independent zero-mean products gives √n), and α_l = 1 is the law-of-large-numbers/full-alignment case (nonzero mean term gives n). The gap is exactly a factor √n, and therefore exactly √n in the maximum stable learning rate. Prior work is recovered iff α_l = 1 for all l, ω_l = 1/2 for l ≤ L, and ω_{L+1} = 1 — and that last assumption is what makes standard/NTK parameterizations provably incapable of feature learning at any learning rate, hence what makes muP look uniquely necessary. The question: is the assumed alignment regime actually what happens during training, and if one instead treats α, ω, u as free variables, what do the per-layer learning-rate exponents become and which parameterizations can then achieve stable feature learning and hyperparameter transfer? Note the idealization doing all the work: everything is an n→∞ exponent, with T, d, L, batch size held Θ(1) and infinite precision assumed.

Main idea

Three moves. (1) Derive the stability/nontriviality constraints as functions of α_l, ω_l, u_l rather than fixing them, for SGD, Adam, and Adafactor-type optimizers with parameter scaling (new), yielding Table 2; prior work falls out as a special case. Crucially they relax ω_{L+1} from 1 to 1/2, arguing that the assumed alignment between early-layer updates and readout initialization is no more plausible than the hidden-layer analogue they assume away. (2) Instantiate two extremes — "full alignment" (α_l = u_l = 1) and "no alignment" (α_l = u_l = 1/2), both with ω_l = 1/2 — and solve for the maximum stable c_l per layer, giving a 4×3×2 table of per-layer learning-rate prescriptions. Under the relaxation, all four parameterizations now admit feature-learning per-layer learning rates. (3) Measure alignment with the log alignment ratio, and run tens of thousands of NanoDO decoder-only Transformers on C4, 14 widths (D = 128 → 16384, 9.9M → 26.8B params), 3 optimizers, 4 parameterizations, LR sweeps at 2^0.25 granularity.

Headline findings: measured alignment is intermediate (0.5–0.9), highly dynamic across training, and layer/parameterization-specific — never the assumed extremes. Per-layer exponents plus small per-layer-type constants (γ_1, γ_h, γ_{L+1}) tuned at D=1024 transfer up to 26.8B and give large gains. All four parameterizations achieve hyperparameter transfer (fitted power-law exponent on the optimal base LR is −0.05 / −0.02 / −0.06 for standard/NTK/muP under Adam), deflating muP's claimed uniqueness. The best Adam configuration is standard parameterization with embedding LR Θ(1) and hidden+readout LR Θ(1/n) — the 15.3B standard model beats the 26.8B muP model. The best overall setting is Adam + parameter-scaling + NTK + no-alignment exponents, which prior assumptions would have excluded outright. Finally, Adam's ε must be treated as part of the parameterization: since gradients shrink with width (worst case n^{-1.5} for MFP hidden layers), default ε ≈ 10^{-8} eventually dominates the second moment. Three mitigations (small constant ε, per-layer ε_l ∝ n^{-g_l}, or Adam-atan2, replacing m/(√v + ε) with a·atan2(m, b√v)) all work equally well.

The most interesting part

The epsilon result is the best thing in the paper, and for a structural reason. Standard ≡ NTK and muP ≡ MFP are exactly equivalent under the symmetry group — same forward pass, same updates — yet in Figure 7(c) they have visibly different losses at 1B+. The entire gap is ε: the additive constant breaks Adam's scale invariance, and the symmetry argument moves the gradient scale between members of an equivalence class, so the two members sit at different distances from underflow. Fix ε and the pairs collapse onto each other (Fig. 7d). That is a clean demonstration that a floating-point detail had been silently masquerading as a property of parameterization — and the authors go so far as to suggest the historical popularity of standard and muP over their formal equivalents may be an artifact of it. Adam-atan2 is the right fix rather than a hack: it is a genuinely scale-invariant, everywhere-defined replacement for the division, and it incidentally gives smooth update clipping when m > √v. It eliminates a hyperparameter instead of adding one.

Honest critique. Much of the rest is a very expensive, very careful ablation. The theory is bookkeeping, not new machinery: the new content is a change of assumption (two free exponents) plus one new optimizer family. The "muP is not unique" result is partly a matter of fairness-of-comparison — the authors themselves point out that muTransfer compared per-layer-LR muP against global-LR standard. Second, the prescription adds tuning surface: a 3-D search over (γ_1, γ_h, γ_{L+1}) at base width, and a choice of alignment regime, which they cannot derive and must select empirically per optimizer (full alignment for Adam, no alignment for Adam+PS). Third, the loss differences at 26.8B are small in absolute terms (2.566–2.633 across the best settings; muP 2.599 vs standard 2.572) and the SGD numbers are explicitly noisy; the claim is supported less by any single gap than by the consistency of the scale-trend. Fourth, the measured alignment is not actually used — it motivates relaxing the assumption, then plays no role in the prescription, because of the feedback loop between learning rate schedule and alignment. Fifth, Appendix I quietly undercuts the framing: in the compute-optimal regime (steps ∝ n², violating T = Θ(1)) the fitted optimal-LR exponents drop by a median of 0.46, so the fixed-T theory is the wrong theory for how people actually train.

Proof sketch

The analytical claim: given alignment exponents (α_l, ω_l, u_l), a parameterization is stable iff the init constraints a_1 + b_1 = 0, a_l + b_l = 1/2 (2 ≤ l ≤ L), a_{L+1} + b_{L+1} ≥ 1/2 hold and, defining r_l := −lim log_n ||Δz_l|| and g_l for the gradient exponent, the recursion r_l = min{·} ≥ 0 of Table 2 holds; the maximum stable η_l is the smallest c_l satisfying it.

The derivation is order-of-magnitude bookkeeping propagated layer by layer. (i) First forward pass: with x = Θ(1) and d = Θ(1), requiring z_l = Θ(1) inductively gives the init constraints. (ii) Chain rule at init gives g_l = a_{L+1} + b_{L+1} + Σ_{i>l}(a_i + b_i − 1/2) + a_l; the init constraints make the sum telescope to zero, so g_l = a_l + a_{L+1} + b_{L+1}, g_{L+1} = a_{L+1}. (iii) The optimizer enters only through the update scale: ΔW_l ~ n^{−c_l−g_l} (SGD), n^{−c_l} (Adam, gradient normalized so g_l drops out), n^{−c_l−b_l} (Adafactor/parameter scaling, times the parameter norm; this also forces the extra constraint c_l ≥ 0 to stop exponential parameter growth). (iv) The key step: expand z_l = n^{-a_l}(W_l + ΔW_l)(z_{l-1} + Δz_{l-1}) into four terms, bound each separately, and take the min of the resulting negative exponents — the first term is handled by the init constraints, and the other three are exactly where α_l, ω_l, u_l enter as the deviation of ||ΔW_l z_{l-1}|| from ||ΔW_l||·||z_{l-1}||. This is the step that makes the whole thing go through with alignment as a free variable rather than an assumption, because it replaces "does ΔW_l align with the data?" with a scalar exponent in [1/2, 1] and reduces the question to CLT (√n) versus LLN (n) scaling of an inner product over the fan-in. (v) A third forward pass is needed because the readout parameter scale can change between the first and second update, so the bound uses max(a_{L+1} + b_{L+1}, 2a_{L+1} + c_{L+1}); after that the exponents are stationary over O(1) steps. Setting the two extremes and solving for minimal c_l produces Table 1. Note also that α_l and u_l always appear as max(α_l, u_l − r_{l-1}), which is why only two regimes are instantiated.

What this is not: not a convergence or generalization guarantee, not a statement about any finite width, and not a theorem that the maximum stable LR is the optimal LR — the authors say so explicitly. Stability and nontriviality are declared desiderata; the measured α values are finite-width estimates, justified only by their apparent convergence across three model sizes.

Broader context

This sits squarely in the Tensor Programs programme: Yang & Hu (2021) classified abc-parameterizations into feature-learning and kernel limits and introduced muP; Yang & Littwin (2023) did the adaptive-optimizer analogue (and was first to treat ε as part of the parameterization, via "faithfulness"); Yang et al. (2022) (muTransfer) is the empirical case for transfer. The other pole is the NTK/GP literature (Jacot et al. 2018; Lee et al. 2017), where infinite width kills feature learning, and the mean-field limit (Mei et al. 2018) extended to deep networks by Bordelon & Pehlevan (2022) via dynamical mean-field theory. Yaida (2022) interpolates between NTK and muP scaling with a one-parameter family — conceptually the closest neighbour to this paper's "exponents as free variables" stance. The economics: post-Kaplan and Chinchilla, you get one shot at the large run, so transfer of the learning rate from cheap proxies is worth a lot, and a silent per-layer exponent mismatch is exactly the failure that is invisible below some width threshold. Two closely related directions worth reading next to this: Yang et al. (2023a) / Large et al. (2024) recast muP in spectral and modular norms, which arguably gives a cleaner language for alignment than RMS exponents; and Lingle (2024), a large muP replication that found the optimal LR drifting 2× between 40M and 10B — the empirical counterweight.

Follow-up idea: the obvious gap is that the paper measures alignment but does not use it. An alignment-aware schedule — or a per-layer learning rate whose exponent is estimated online from the measurable A_l^t rather than assumed — is the natural next step, and the authors flag it. Equally open: redoing the derivation with T = Θ(n²) (compute-optimal) without the naive worst-case n^{-2} collapse, and with vocabulary size treated as Θ(n) rather than Θ(1).

On Shiguang's work, one connection is genuine and one is thin. The genuine one is the embedding/readout layer, which is precisely where the four parameterizations differ and where this paper's prescription is most opinionated (embedding LR Θ(1), readout Θ(1/n) for standard+Adam). In dense retrieval the dual encoders' projection/embedding layers and in generative retrieval the decoder's docid output layer are exactly this layer type, and a docid vocabulary of 10^5–10^7 makes the readout the dominant parameter block — which is the regime the paper's own Limitations section admits it does not cover, since it treats d (vocabulary) as Θ(1) while conceding Θ(n) would be more realistic. That makes the open question directly relevant rather than merely adjacent: a huge-vocabulary softmax has very sparse per-row gradients, so the ε-underflow analysis — gradient scale falling below ε in the layer with the smallest gradients — is a concrete, checkable hazard for generative-retrieval training, and Adam-atan2 is a one-line change worth trying there. The thin connection is the alignment story itself: α_l measures whether ΔW_l develops directional correlation with incoming activations, which rhymes with questions about how learned embedding geometry (anisotropy, effective rank, hubness) evolves under training — but the paper's quantity is a single scalar exponent in the large-width limit, with no geometric content beyond a norm ratio, so I would not push that analogy as more than a loose metaphor.

title: The optimal information complexity of VC learning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-05

The optimal information complexity of VC Learning

Steve Hanneke, Juexiao Wang (2026) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10600

Setting and problem

Fix a concept class H ⊆ {0,1}^X of VC dimension d ≥ 1, and let Z = X × {0,1}. The setting is vanilla realizable PAC: an unknown distribution D on Z with Y = h_(X) for some target h_ ∈ H, 0-1 loss ℓ(h,(x,y)) = 1[h(x) ≠ y], a learner A : Z^n → {0,1}^X that receives n ≥ d i.i.d. labelled points and must output a classifier (not necessarily in H — improperness is allowed and, as discussed below, necessary). The classical facts: the optimal expected error for realizable PAC is Θ(d/n), achieved by the one-inclusion-graph predictor of Haussler–Littlestone–Warmuth (1994); the optimal high-probability rate (d + log(1/δ))/n was obtained by Hanneke (2016) via a recursive majority-vote learner, with later simpler optimal majority-vote learners from Larsen (2023, bagging) and Aden-Ali, Høgsgaard, Larsen and Zhivotovskiy (2024, "majority-of-three" ERMs on disjoint thirds, optimal in expectation). Uniform convergence / generic ERM, by contrast, only gives O(d·log(n/d)/n).

The object of study is not the PAC rate itself but the information complexity of attaining it. Steinke–Zakynthinou (2020) introduced the CMI framework to repair the defect of the Russo–Zou / Xu–Raginsky bounds in terms of I(A(S);S), which is unbounded even for thresholds (d=1) by Nachum–Shafer–Yehudayoff and Bassily et al. The construction: draw a supersample Z̃ = (Z̃_1,…,Z̃_{2n}) ~ D^{2n}, and independent swap variables σ = (σ(1),…,σ(n)) with σ(i) ~ Unif{i, i+n}. The learner is trained on the selected half Z̃σ; the other half are ghost samples. Then CMI_D(A) = I(A(Z̃_σ); σ | Z̃) — information about which of each paired point was used for training, given the pool. Conditioning on Z̃ normalises each example to one bit, so CMI ≤ n always, and Sauer–Shelah gives CMI ≤ log|H{z̃}| ≤ d·log n + 2 for a globally consistent ERM (ties broken by a fixed well-ordering of H).

The evaluated CMI replaces the hypothesis with its loss pattern on the supersample: with ℓ⃗(A(Z̃_σ), Z̃)_i = ℓ(A(Z̃_σ), Z̃_i) ∈ {0,1}^{2n},

eCMI_D(ℓ(A)) = I( ℓ⃗(A(Z̃_σ),Z̃) ; σ | Z̃ ), and eCMI(ℓ(A)) = sup over realizable z̃ ∈ Z^{2n} of I( ℓ⃗(A(z̃_σ),z̃) ; σ ),

the latter being worst-case (distribution-free) eCMI, which dominates the distributional version. Because z̃ is realizable and known, the loss vector is in bijection with the restriction A(z̃_σ)|_{z̃x} of the output to the 2n points, so eCMI is exactly the information the predictions on the pool carry about the train/ghost split. This is the non-obvious modelling choice worth dwelling on: eCMI ignores everything the hypothesis says off-supersample and all internal representation, which is exactly the slack that lets one use heavily randomised improper learners whose hypothesis identity is high-entropy while its prediction pattern is not. The price is a weaker-looking quantity; the paper's Theorem 2.1 (a one-line modification of SZ20's Theorem 5.8, swapping f{Z̃} for g_{Z̃} acting on A(Z̃_σ)(Z̃) in the Donsker–Varadhan step) shows the price is affordable:

E[er_D(A(Z))] ≤ 2·E[êr_Z(A(Z))] + 3·eCMI_D(A)/n.

So eCMI = O(d) plus training error O(d/n) yields the optimal O(d/n) expected risk.

The question: does there exist a learner for every VC class whose eCMI is O(d), with no log n — i.e. can the optimal PAC guarantee be recovered inside the algorithm-dependent CMI framework? SZ20 conjectured yes (for CMI). The known barriers: Haghifam, Dziugaite, Moran and Roy (2021) show no proper learner can remove the log n for every class, and that sublinear eCMI growth characterises learnability by consistent algorithms; Haghifam, Moran, Roy and Dziugaite (2022) get the optimal rate but only through leave-one-out eCMI with the one-inclusion-graph algorithm — a variant that has found few applications since it is tied to sample-consistent learners. Plain eCMI was the gap.

Main idea

The learner is a randomised Majority-of-5. Given z ∈ Z^n: draw a uniform permutation π of [n], split into 5 blocks of n/5, run a base learner B on each block, and output the majority vote. The twist is a DuplicatesAdjustment step: a fresh i.i.d. sequence U = (u_1,…,u_{n/5}) ~ Unif[n] is drawn, and its multiplicity-and-order pattern is transplanted onto the block's distinct indices. The resulting index sequence I_k^{π,U} is shown to be exactly i.i.d. Unif[n], so each block is conditionally i.i.d. from the empirical distribution on the n training points given σ — which is what lets an i.i.d. error guarantee for B be invoked on a worst-case, non-i.i.d. supersample. Internal randomness is β = (π, U), independent of σ.

Result (Theorem 2.2): for any base learner with i.i.d. expected error R(m), eCMI(ℓ(A)) ≤ 1920·n·R(n/5) and the expected training error is ≤ 5·R(n/5). Taking B to be the Aden-Ali et al. Majority-of-3 (so R(m) = O(d/m)) gives Theorem 2.3: eCMI = O(d) and training error O(d/n), hence optimal O(d/n) expected risk through Theorem 2.1. Section 8 shows that for distributional eCMI, the extra randomisation is unnecessary and plain Majority-of-3 on disjoint thirds gives eCMI_D ≤ 192·n·R(n/3), under the stronger base assumption that expected training error is also ≤ R(m). Everything is up to absolute constants; the constants are frankly enormous (5 learners, each itself a majority of 3, so blocks of n/15, times 1920), so the statements are asymptotic in d/n only.

The most interesting part

The clever object is DuplicatesAdjustment, and the reason is sharper than it first appears. The analysis needs each base learner to enjoy an i.i.d. error guarantee on a fixed adversarial supersample, where the blocks are samples without replacement from the empirical distribution. The gadget exploits that a sample is determined by (i) its set of distinct values and (ii) the pattern G(U) of which distinct value occurs at each position; that G(U) is conditionally independent of the distinct values given their number N; and that the first N values of a uniform permutation and the distinct values of an i.i.d. sequence have the same conditional law given N. Splicing therefore produces an exactly i.i.d. sequence, not an approximation — no concentration or TV-distance loss anywhere. This is a reusable tool for anyone who needs to de-correlate without-replacement subsampling in a worst-case-supersample argument.

The honest critique. First, the paper does not produce a new route to the Θ(d/n) rate — it assumes an already-optimal base learner and shows the optimal rate is compatible with O(d) eCMI. That is the right reading of the contribution (an information-complexity statement, not a PAC statement), but "recovers the optimal PAC guarantee" oversells slightly. Second, no matching Ω(d) eCMI lower bound is given; optimality is in the sense of removing the log n and matching what Theorem 2.1 needs, and the paper never argues Ω(d) is forced. Third, in-expectation is a genuine limitation: the Theorem 2.1 route is intrinsically an expectation bound, so Hanneke's (d + log(1/δ))/n is not recovered, and the base learner (Majority-of-3) is itself known to be only expectation-optimal. Fourth, the SZ20 conjecture is about CMI, not eCMI, and remains open; whether this is "closing" or "sidestepping" depends on how much one believes eCMI is the right currency — HDMR21's characterisation result and Theorem 2.1 are decent evidence it is, and the paper's own remark that any ERM has O(d·log n) eCMI while CMI needs a specially-ordered ERM is a fair argument that eCMI is the more robust quantity. To its credit, the paper does not pretend Majority-of-5 is fundamental: Section 8 shows the fifth and fourth learners are an artifact of the worst-case supersample (where block k's own points have no error guarantee for learner k), not of the technique.

Proof sketch

Four steps.

  1. Reduction to conditional entropy (Lemma 4.1). For fixed z̃, chain rule plus non-negativity of mutual information gives I(ℓ⃗;σ) ≤ I((ℓ⃗,β);σ) = H(ℓ⃗ | β), using H(ℓ⃗ | β,σ) = 0 and H(β) = H(β|σ); subadditivity then splits it into Σ_{i ≤ 2n} H( 1[A(z̃_σ,β)(x_i) ≠ h_(x_i)] | β ). Everything reduces to pointwise _conditional error probabilities_ p_k^β(x) = Pr_{σ|β}( B(S_k^{β,σ})(x) ≠ h_(x) ).

  2. Expected error count off one's own block (Lemma 5.2) — this is the step doing the real work. Conditioned on β, for x_{π(i)} ∉ Γ_k^π (the k-th block's n/5 pairs), the swap σ(π(i)) deciding which of {x_{π(i)}, x_{π(i)+n}} is a test point is independent of the selection of S_k^{β,σ}, which depends only on swaps inside Γ_k^π. Hence the expected number of errors over pairs outside block k equals twice the expected number of errors on the training side, which by Lemma 5.1 is an i.i.d. quantity: ≤ 2n·R(n/5). The conditioning-on-β-to-buy-independence move is the crux; it is also why a learner has no guarantee on its own block.

  3. Geometric error regions (Lemma 5.3). Define R_j^{k,β} = { x ∉ Γ_k^π : p_k^β(x) ∈ (2^{-j}, 2^{-j+1}] }. Markov on the indicator gives E_β|R_j^{k,β}| ≤ 2^j · 2n·R(n/5) — a geometrically growing bound on region sizes.

  4. The variance/squaring argument (Lemma 6.1). Bound h(p) ≤ f(p) = p·log(4/p), monotone on [0,1]. For x ∈ Γ_1^π, a Majority-of-5 error forces at least two of the other four base classifiers to err; conditional independence of the blocks given β gives Pr ≤ C(4,2)·p_k^β(x)·p_{k'}^β(x) ≤ 6·max{p_k², p_{k'}²}, and f(max{x²,y²}) ≤ f(x²)+f(y²). Summing over regions yields Σ_j E|R_j| · 2^{-2j} · j ≲ n·R(n/5)·Σ_j j·2^{-j} = O(n·R(n/5)). The convergence is exactly where five learners are needed: the squared probability 2^{-2j} beats the 2^j growth of region sizes, leaving a summable j·2^{-j}; a single power would give Σ_j j, divergent. Symmetry over π multiplies the Γ_1 bound by 5, giving 1920·n·R(n/5).

The training-error bound is a union bound: a Majority-of-5 error implies some base learner errs, so E_β[êr] ≤ 5·R(n/5). In Section 8 the supersample is genuinely i.i.d., so each base learner has an error guarantee at all 2n points (using the extra expected-training-error assumption), the "hole" vanishes, and three learners suffice. The conclusion also notes the whole argument is 0-1-loss-only and so transfers verbatim to multiclass, giving O(d_DS) eCMI when combined with Pabbaraju's (2026) optimal multiclass one-inclusion-graph learner.

Broader context

The through-line here is a two-decade effort to explain generalisation by how much the output reveals about the input: Russo–Zou (2016) and Xu–Raginsky (2017) with I(A(S);S); Steinke–Zakynthinou (2020) fixing its unboundedness by conditioning on a supersample; then a family of variants (CMI, eCMI, leave-one-out eCMI, disintegrated/individual-sample versions) applied to SGD, Langevin dynamics and stochastic convex optimisation (Haghifam et al. 2020; Neu et al. 2021; Attias et al. 2024). Worth reading alongside: Steinke–Zakynthinou 2020 for the framework; Haghifam–Dziugaite–Moran–Roy 2021 for the impossibility for proper learners and the eCMI characterisation; Aden-Ali–Høgsgaard–Larsen–Zhivotovskiy 2024 and Larsen 2023 for the majority-vote optimal learners that this paper consumes as a black box; and Hanneke 2016 for the high-probability optimum. The conceptual neighbour is sample compression: an O(d)-bit eCMI bound is a statement that the learner's prediction pattern on the pool is describable in O(d) bits, which is morally a compression scheme of size O(d) — and compression-based PAC bounds (Littlestone–Warmuth, Moran–Yehudayoff) are the other classical route to removing log factors.

Obvious follow-ups: a matching Ω(d) eCMI lower bound; pushing from eCMI to CMI, where SZ20's conjecture is still open for improper randomised learners; an agnostic-case analogue; a high-probability eCMI-style bound that produces log(1/δ) (this seems to need different tail machinery than Donsker–Varadhan in expectation); and reducing 5 to 4 or 3 for worst-case eCMI, or proving 5 necessary for this proof template.

On connection to theoretical IR: I would not force one. There is no technical bridge here to generative retrieval or vector search — no ranking loss, no retrieval-specific structure, and the quantities are tuned to 0-1 classification on a VC class. The honest value is depth: the DuplicatesAdjustment coupling is a genuinely transferable tool for any argument that needs an exactly-i.i.d. subsample from an empirical distribution, and the "condition on part of the randomness to buy conditional independence, then square the error probability against a geometrically growing region decomposition" pattern is a template worth internalising. If one wanted a loose analogy, eCMI asks "how many bits about the train/test split must the model's predictions encode", which rhymes with questions like how many bits of the corpus a learned index or a docid-generating model must memorise; but that would be an analogy to build from scratch, not a result to cite.

title: The Graphon Limit Hypothesis: Understanding Neural Network Pruning via Infinite Width Analysis
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-04

The Graphon Limit Hypothesis: Understanding Neural Network Pruning via Infinite Width Analysis

Hoang Pham, The-Anh Ta, Tom Jacobs, Rebekka Burkholz, Long Tran-Thanh (2025) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17515

Setting and problem

The objects. Fix an architecture class $\mathcal{A}$: here an MLP with $L$ hidden layers, widths $n_0=d, n_1,\dots,n_L, n_{L+1}=1$, no biases, scalar output, weights $W^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_l\times n_{l-1}}$ initialised i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_w^2)$ with NTK parameterisation $z^{(l)}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n_{l-1}}}W^{(l)}h^{(l-1)}$, $h^{(l)}=\sigma(z^{(l)})$. A pruning method $\mathcal{P}$ at sparsity level $p$ (fraction of weights kept) returns binary masks $M^{(l)}\in{0,1}^{n_l\times n_{l-1}}$ and the network is run with $\widetilde W^{(l)}=W^{(l)}\odot M^{(l)}$, where the zeroed entries are frozen — they are not parameters any more. Each $M^{(l)}$ is read as the biadjacency matrix of a bipartite graph between the neurons of layer $l-1$ and layer $l$. So a pruned network of width $n$ is a layered stack of bipartite graphs, and a sequence of widths $n\to\infty$ gives, per layer, a sequence of bipartite graphs with growing vertex sets.

Graphons. A graphon is a symmetric measurable $\mathcal{W}:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$; think of it as the continuum adjacency matrix, with $\mathcal{W}(u,v)$ the probability of an edge between the "neurons" at positions $u$ and $v$. A finite graph $G_n$ with adjacency $A$ is embedded as the step function $\mathcal{W}_{G_n}(x,y)=A_{ij}$ on $[\tfrac{i-1}{n},\tfrac{i}{n})\times[\tfrac{j-1}{n},\tfrac{j}{n})$. Convergence is in the cut metric: the labelled cut distance is $$d_\square(U,\mathcal{W})=\sup_{S,T\subseteq[0,1]}\Big|\int_{S\times T}\big(U-\mathcal{W}\big)\,dx\,dy\Big|,$$ and the label-invariant version quotients by measure-preserving bijections, $\delta_\square(U,\mathcal{W})=\inf_{\varphi\in\Phi}d_\square(U,\mathcal{W}^\varphi)$ with $\mathcal{W}^\varphi(x,y)=\mathcal{W}(\varphi(x),\varphi(y))$. The paper uses $\delta_\square$, and invokes the standard equivalence (Lovász–Szegedy 2006; Borgs–Chayes–Lovász–Sós–Vesztergombi 2008): $\delta_\square(\mathcal{W}_{G_n},\mathcal{W})\to 0$ iff $t(F,G_n)\to t(F,\mathcal{W})$ for every finite $F$, where $t(F,\cdot)$ is the homomorphism density. Left-convergence and cut convergence are therefore the same notion here, which matters later: the Graphon NTK will turn out to be (a limit of weighted tree homomorphism densities), which is why cut convergence is the right notion rather than, say, $L^2$ convergence of the mask profiles.

One notational wrinkle to flag up front: the preliminaries define graphons as symmetric kernels, but the masks are bipartite, so what is actually used throughout is a non-symmetric bigraphon $\mathcal{W}^{(l)}:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ with independent relabellings on the two sides. The correct theory for that is Diaconis–Janson's separately exchangeable arrays, not the jointly exchangeable (graphon) case; and the relevant spectral object is then the singular values of the integral operator $T_{\mathcal{W}}f(u)=\int_0^1\mathcal{W}(u,v)f(v)\,dv$, not eigenvalues. The paper conflates the two cases. It is fixable, but it is not a cosmetic slip, as the cross-layer labelling discussion below shows.

Why the dense-graph regime applies. A "90 % sparse" network keeps $pn^2=\Theta(n^2)$ edges with $p$ a constant. Graph-theoretically that is a dense graph, so graphon theory is the correct limit object (not the graphex/local-weak-limit machinery needed when $p_n\to 0$). The paper states this explicitly as assumption (i) $p>0$ fixed, plus (ii) comparable layer widths as $n\to\infty$.

The dense NTK, for reference. For $f(x;\theta)$, $\Theta_t(x,x')=\nabla_\theta f(x)^\top\nabla_\theta f(x')$. In the infinite-width limit $\Theta_t\to\Theta_0$ deterministic and training-independent; under gradient flow on MSE, $f(X;\theta_t)=f(X;\theta_0)e^{-\eta\Theta_0 t}+(I-e^{-\eta\Theta_0 t})\hat y$, so the residual in eigendirection $v_k$ of $\Theta_0$ decays as $e^{-\eta\lambda_k t}$. Trainability is thus a statement about the spectrum of $\Theta_0$ — and, strictly, about the spectrum together with the alignment $\langle \hat y, v_k\rangle$. For dense ReLU MLPs $\Theta_0$ has a closed-form arccos recursion: $\tilde\Sigma^{(l)}=\Sigma^{(l-1)}$, $\Sigma^{(l)}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{(l)})}[\sigma(z)\sigma(z')]$, $\dot\Sigma^{(l)}=\mathbb{E}[\sigma'(z)\sigma'(z')]$, and $\Theta=\sum_l \Sigma^{(l-1)}\prod_{m>l}\dot\Sigma^{(m)}$.

What is given and what is produced. Given: a pruning method $\mathcal{P}$, a sparsity $p$, an architecture class $\mathcal{A}$, and a width sequence $n\to\infty$. Produced (postulated): per-layer limit graphons $\mathcal{W}^{(l)}$ depending only on $(\mathcal{A},p,\mathcal{P})$, and from them a kernel. The modelling move that converts graphon into kernel is this: since $\mathrm{Var}(W^{(l)}_{ij}M^{(l)}_{ij})=\sigma_w^2 M^{(l)}*{ij}$, pruning is reinterpreted as a position-dependent variance profile, and the paper replaces the pruned network by a fully connected network with independent but non-identically distributed weights $$W^{(l)}*{ij}\big)\Big),\qquad \sigma_w^2=1 .$$ Taking $i/n_l\to u_l$, sums become integrals and the forward pass formally becomes $z^{(l)}(u_l,x)=\int_0^1 W^{(l)}(u_l,u_{l-1})h^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1},x)du_{l-1}$ with $W^{(l)}(u,v)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u,v))$ a Gaussian random field and the $1/\sqrt{n}$ "absorbed into the integral". Because weights are no longer i.i.d., two extra assumptions are imposed: boundedness of $\mathcal{W}$ and well-definedness of the degree functional $\int \mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u,v)dv$ (for the LLN), and a Lindeberg–Feller condition $\tfrac{1}{\sigma_n^2}\sum_j\mathbb{E}[X_j^2\mathbf{1}}\sim\mathcal{N}!\Big(0,\ \mathcal{W}^{(l)}\big(\tfrac{i}{n_l},\tfrac{j}{n_{l-1}_{|X_j|>\epsilon\sigma_n}]\to0$ with $X_j=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n_{l-1}}}W^{(l)}_{ij}h^{(l-1)}_j$ (for the CLT).

The precise question. _Why, at one and the same sparsity level $p$, are some sparse connectivity patterns substantially more trainable than others?_ Equivalently: is there a width-independent object attached to a pruning method that predicts its training dynamics?

What the literature already has. (a) The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (Frankle & Carbin) established empirically that trainable sparse subnetworks exist inside dense random initialisations, with the mask-plus-original-init pair mattering; existence has since been proved by subset-sum / overparameterisation arguments (Malach et al.; Pensia et al.; Burkholz). (b) Pruning-at-initialisation methods replace the expensive train–prune–rewind loop with a single saliency score: SNIP uses $s_{ij}=|w_{ij}\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_{ij}|$, GraSP uses $-w\odot Hg$, Synflow uses the data-free synaptic-flow score $|w_{ij}|\,\partial_{w_{ij}}(\mathbf{1}^\top\prod_l|W^{(l)}|\mathbf{1})$ applied iteratively, and random/magnitude pruning are the baselines. (c) A structural line (Ramanujan-graph analyses: Pal et al.; Hoang et al.; Vooturi et al.) correlates mask expansion/spectral gap with subnetwork quality. (d) Gradient-flow analyses (Lubana & Dick; Evci et al.) and NTK-based ones: Yang & Wang (AISTATS 2023) prove that random masks preserve the infinite-width NTK up to a scalar; Yang et al. study sparsity induced by large bias initialisation; NTK-SAP prunes to align NTK training dynamics. (e) Graph limits appear in ML mainly through graphon neural networks and transferability (Ruiz–Chamon–Ribeiro; Maskey–Levie–Kutyniok; Herbst–Jegelka) and through Krishnagopal & Ruiz's GNTK-converges-on-large-graphs result — but all of those put the graphon on the input data graph.

The gap. NTK analysis cannot be applied off the shelf to sparse networks because there is no canonical way to take the limit of a sequence of different sparse architectures: the mask changes with $n$, so "the" infinite-width object is undefined. The paper's contribution is to supply that missing limit object — the mask's graphon — and thereby make the dense NTK machinery applicable to arbitrary pruning methods, not just random masks.

Non-obvious modelling choices, flagged. (1) The Graphon Limit Hypothesis is a postulate, not a theorem. The paper says so plainly in its limitations section; everything downstream (Graphon NTK, spectral story) is conditional on it. The only cases where it is essentially provable as stated are random pruning and magnitude-pruning-at-init, where the mask is an Erdős–Rényi $G(n,c)$ and the limit is the constant graphon $\mathcal{W}\equiv c$ — i.e. precisely the cases that were already understood. (2) Exchangeability. Graphon limits are, via Aldous–Hoover/Diaconis–Janson, the limits of exchangeable arrays, and a deterministic (not random/mixture) limit additionally requires the array to be dissociated. Pruning masks are not obviously exchangeable random graphs. There is a decent argument that they are: pruning algorithms are permutation-equivariant in hidden-neuron indices, and the init is i.i.d., so the hidden–hidden mask distribution is separately exchangeable in those indices — which is why the paper correctly excludes input and output layer masks (input coordinates and output classes are not exchangeable). But global top-$k$ selection, and in SNIP/Synflow's standard form global-across-layers selection, induces hard constraints and cross-layer coupling, so dissociation and determinism of the limit need a concentration argument that is never given. (3) Replacing a mask by a variance profile. The graphon-modulated network is dense with smoothly varying variances; the pruned network is sparse with ${0,\sigma_w^2}$ variances. These agree in second moments averaged over the mask ensemble, but a realised mask is a conditioned object, and for every score-based method the mask is correlated with the weight realisation. (4) The hypothesis asserts dependence only on $(\mathcal{A},p,\mathcal{P})$, yet SNIP and GraSP depend on a data minibatch and the loss, so the limit graphon must also depend on the data distribution (and on the init scale). A small but real omission in the statement.

With that, the hypothesis and the kernel can be stated from scratch, which is the point of this section.

Main idea

The Graphon Limit Hypothesis. For a width-indexed sequence of networks $(\mathcal{N}_n)$ from a fixed architecture class $\mathcal{A}$, applying a pruning method $\mathcal{P}$ at fixed sparsity $p>0$ produces mask sequences $(M^{(l)}_n)$ that converge layerwise to deterministic graphons $\mathcal{W}^{(l)}$ in cut distance, $\lim_n \delta_\square(\mathcal{W}_{M^{(l)}_n},\mathcal{W}^{(l)})=0$, and these limits depend only on $(\mathcal{A},p,\mathcal{P})$. The graphon is then the pruning method's implicit structural bias, made width-free: each method occupies its own region of graphon space, and because cut convergence is equivalent to convergence of all motif densities, the graphon pins down the asymptotic densities of paths (Synflow's "effective paths"), stars (degree profile), $C_4$'s, and so on.

Empirical support. For Random, SNIP, GraSP and Synflow, at $n\in{100,500,1000,2000}$, depths ${4,5}$, sparsities ${70,80,90}\%$, 100 trials each, masks are estimated as graphons with the SAS histogram estimator (Chan & Airoldi): sort layer-$l$ nodes by out-degree and layer-$(l{+}1)$ nodes by in-degree, bin into a $64\times64$ grid, average edge density per cell. Random gives a flat constant graphon; SNIP and GraSP give smooth monotone density gradients favouring high-centrality neurons; Synflow gives a block graphon with sharp transitions, essentially deleting a positive fraction of hidden neurons entirely and densely connecting the survivors. Magnitude-at-init gives a constant graphon (correctly argued: i.i.d. weights make $\Pr(|w_{ij}|>T)$ position-independent, hence $G(n,c)$). Convergence is quantified as the Euclidean distance between the width-$n$ histogram and the width-2000 histogram, used "as a proxy for the cut distance"; all four curves decrease monotonically in $n$.

The Graphon NTK. Proposition 1: pre-activations converge to centred Gaussian processes with $$\tilde\Sigma^{(1)}(u_1,u_1',x,x')=\delta(u_1-u_1')\tfrac{1}{d}\textstyle\sum_j \mathcal{W}^{(1)}(u_1,\tfrac{j}{d})(x\cdot x')_j,$$ $$\tilde\Sigma^{(l)}(u_l,u_l',x,x')=\delta(u_l-u_l')\int_0^1 \mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u_l,u_{l-1},$$ $$\Sigma^{(l)}(u_l,u_l',x,x')=\delta(u_l-u_l')\,\mathbb{E}})\,\Sigma^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1},u_{l-1},x,x')\,du_{l-1*{(z,z')\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{(l)}(u_l))}[\sigma(z)\sigma(z')],$$ with $\Lambda^{(l)}(u_l)$ the $2\times2$ matrix of $\tilde\Sigma^{(l)}$ values at $(x,x)$, $(x,x')$, $(x',x')$. The single structural difference from the dense case is stated crisply in their Remark 1: dense NTK has $\tilde\Sigma^{(l)}=\Sigma^{(l-1)}$; here $\Sigma^{(l-1)}$ is first pushed through the integral operator $T*{\mathcal{W}^{(l)}}$. Everything else — the arccos-type Gaussian expectations, the delta in position — is inherited.

Theorem 1: with $\dot\Sigma^{(l)}(u_l,u_l,x,x')=\mathbb{E}[\sigma'(z^{(l)}(u_l,x))\sigma'(z^{(l)}(u_l,x'))]$ and $\dot\Sigma^{(L+1)}\equiv1$, $$\Theta(x,x')=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\int_0^1 \dot\Sigma^{(l)}(u_l,u_l,x,x')\left[\int_{[0,1]^{L-l+1}}\prod_{m=l+1}^{L+1}\mathcal{W}^{(m)}(u_m,u_{m-1})\dot\Sigma^{(m)}(u_m,u_m,x,x')\,d\mathbf{u}_{l+1}\right]\left[\int_0^1\Sigma^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1}\right]du_l .$$ In words: the layer-$l$ contribution is (a forward factor = average activation covariance arriving at layer $l-1$) times (a backward factor = a path integral from the output back to position $u_l$, each step weighted by the graphon density and the derivative correlation). Dense NTK is the special case $\mathcal{W}\equiv1$.},u_{l-1},x,x')\,du_{l-1

Special case and spectral story. For a constant graphon $\mathcal{W}\equiv c$ the kernel collapses to a pure rescaling, $\Theta=c^L\Theta_{\mathrm{std}}$, so every NTK eigenvalue becomes $c^L\lambda_k$: absolute learning speed falls, relative mode ordering is untouched. This recovers Yang & Wang's randomly-pruned result as a corollary, and is offered as the principled reason random sparse nets train more slowly than dense ones. Beyond that, the claims are correlational: at $n=1024$, 4 hidden layers, MNIST, sparsities 50–95 %, they compute the (graphon-resampled) kernel on a 1024-sample batch and track four spectral summaries — power-law decay exponent $\alpha$ of $\lambda_k\propto k^{-\alpha}$, effective rank $\mathrm{tr}(\Theta)/\lambda_1$, spectral gap $\lambda_1/\lambda_2$, and top-5 energy $\sum_{i\le5}\lambda_i/\sum_j\lambda_j$. Random keeps stable, broad spectra across sparsity; SNIP and Synflow increasingly concentrate energy in the top eigendirections while losing effective rank. That concentration is matched against the first 200 Adam steps, where SNIP and Synflow decrease loss faster than Random at equal sparsity. The proposed takeaways: graphon-NTK spectra could serve as training-free pruning-quality scores, and spectral preservation should be a design target.

The most interesting part

A reviewer's read. The framework is a genuinely good idea — supplying a width-free limit object for the architecture is exactly what was missing, and I think the choice of the cut metric is more deeply right than the paper realises (see the strengths below). But three things in the chain from hypothesis to conclusion do not hold up, and two of them are load-bearing.

1. Layerwise cut convergence, with independent relabellings per layer, cannot define the Graphon NTK. This is the sharpest problem. The hypothesis asserts convergence "layer-wisely" in $\delta_\square$, i.e. each $\mathcal{W}_{M^{(l)}_n}$ converges up to its own measure-preserving map $\varphi_l$. But the Graphon NTK formula couples consecutive layers through a shared position variable: $\prod_m \mathcal{W}^{(m)}(u_m,u_{m-1})$ requires that the $u_l$ appearing as the "column" index of layer $l$ and as the "row" index of layer $l+1$ be the same labelling of the same neurons. Layerwise $\delta_\square$ convergence gives no such consistency, and the composed iterated integral is simply not determined by the individual $\delta_\square$-limits. (Concretely: take any $\mathcal{W}^{(l)},\mathcal{W}^{(l+1)}$ and relabel only the middle layer; the layerwise limits are unchanged while $\int\mathcal{W}^{(l+1)}(u_{l+1},u_l)\mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u_l,u_{l-1})du_l$ changes freely.) The correct object is a layered graph limit with one common labelling per layer — equivalently, convergence of the weighted tree homomorphism densities of the full layered graph — and the hypothesis should be restated that way.

This is not a pedantic point, because the empirical estimation does exactly the forbidden thing. SAS is applied per mask, sorting layer-$l$ nodes by their out-degree in $M^{(l)}$ and layer-$(l{+}1)$ nodes by their in-degree in $M^{(l)}$. For the next mask $M^{(l+1)}$, the same hidden layer's neurons are re-sorted by their out-degree in $M^{(l+1)}$. Those two orderings of one neuron set generally differ, so the estimated graphons, as estimated, cannot be composed into the kernel. Worse, the mismatch is method-dependent in a way that biases the comparison: Synflow's score is a product of forward and backward path counts, so in- and out-degree are strongly aligned and the two sortings nearly agree; for Random they are uncorrelated noise. So the amount of mis-specification differs systematically across precisely the methods being compared.

2. The framework is blind to mask–weight correlation, which yields a prediction that is almost certainly false. The reduction "pruning = position-dependent variance profile" keeps only $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde W_{ij})]$ and discards the conditional law of $W_{ij}$ given $M_{ij}=1$. For every saliency-based method that conditional law is not $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_w^2)$: SNIP keeps large $|w_{ij}\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_{ij}|$, Synflow keeps large $|w_{ij}|$ times path counts, magnitude-at-init keeps exactly ${|w_{ij}|>T}$. The surviving weights are size-biased, so the true per-surviving-weight variance is $\sigma_w^2\,\mathbb{E}[w^2\mid \text{kept}]/\sigma_w^2>\sigma_w^2$. The cleanest falsification is the paper's own Appendix C: magnitude-at-init and random pruning are shown to have the same constant graphon $\mathcal{W}\equiv c$, hence by Section 5.3 the identical Graphon NTK $c^L\Theta_{\mathrm{std}}$, hence identical predicted training dynamics at every sparsity. Empirically they are not the same — and the Burkholz group's own prior work (Masks, signs, and learning rate rewinding; Sign-in to the lottery) is largely about how much the weight/sign information beyond the mask matters. A theory of pruning whose only input is the mask's structural marginal is, by construction, unable to see the part of the LTH that the field has spent years establishing is essential.

3. A bookkeeping error in the identification with pruning: the parameter measure is unweighted. In the pruned network only surviving weights are trainable, so the NTK sums over ${(i,j):M^{(l)}_{ij}=1}$. In the continuum that is the measure $\mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u_l,u_{l-1})\,du_l\,du_{l-1}$, but Eq. (36) integrates over the full unit square with no $\mathcal{W}^{(l)}$ factor. Under their literal model (a dense net with variance profile $\mathcal{W}$, all $n^2$ weights trainable) the formula is self-consistent; under the pruning interpretation it over-counts parameters by a factor of the density. One can check this on a one-hidden-layer ReLU net at $x=x'$ with Bernoulli($c$) masks on both layers: both the output-layer and first-layer contributions scale as $c^2\Theta_{\mathrm{std}}$, not $c^1$. In general the layer-$l$ term picks up $c^{l-1}$ forward, $c^{L+1-l}$ backward and $c$ from the parameter measure, giving $\Theta=c^{L+1}\Theta_{\mathrm{std}}$ — consistent with the fact that the layer sum in Theorem 1 runs only to $L$ although there are $L+1$ weight matrices. (The suspicious parenthetical in Appendix B, "when the activation integral dominates the constant 1 (which is typical in deep networks)", reads like awareness that the bookkeeping was shaky.) For the structured case the fix is not merely an exponent: reweighting the layer-$l$ position integral by $\mathcal{W}^{(l)}$ concentrates it on the high-density region, which strengthens the structural effects the paper wants.

Does the empirical evidence establish graphon convergence? No — it establishes something strictly weaker that is consistent with it. What is measured is the stabilisation of one $64\times64$ projection of the mask: the degree-sorted block density profile. Two very different graphons can share that profile exactly, whereas $\delta_\square$ convergence is equivalent to convergence of all motif densities. Three further issues: (i) the reference point is the $n=2000$ estimate, so the plotted quantity is a distance to a noisy target, and it is guaranteed to shrink for any sequence whose histogram-estimation noise shrinks — it measures variance reduction at least as much as convergence to a limit; a proper test would be a Cauchy-style check across width pairs plus direct convergence of several motif densities (bipartite $C_4$ density, star/degree-distribution moments, path densities of the composed layered graph). (ii) SAS's identifiability requires a strictly monotone degree function; for the constant graphon the degree function is constant, so for Random the sorting is sorting pure noise and the estimator's finite-$n$ artifact (a spurious monotone gradient of order $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ per cell) is exactly what is being plotted as "convergence". (iii) Nothing in the evidence speaks to determinism of the limit (versus a random graphon / mixture), which is the part of the hypothesis that actually needs an ergodicity argument.

Is the spectrum–dynamics link causal, predictive, or post-hoc? Post-hoc correlational, on roughly a dozen points (3 methods $\times$ a handful of sparsities), with no correlation coefficient, no error bars on the spectral metrics, and no held-out prediction. Three specific weaknesses. First, no target alignment. NTK theory says the residual decays as $\sum_k\langle\hat y,v_k\rangle e^{-\eta\lambda_k t}v_k$; concentrating energy in $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_5$ accelerates training only insofar as $\hat y$ loads on $v_1,\dots,v_5$. The alignment is never measured, so "high top-5 energy ⇒ fast initial loss drop" is not derived from the theory it is attributed to. Second, optimiser mismatch. The dynamics are measured with Adam at $\eta=10^{-3}$ for 200 steps; the theory is gradient flow. Adam's per-coordinate RMS normalisation very nearly cancels a uniform rescaling of the kernel, which means the headline constant-graphon corollary ($\Theta=c^L\Theta_{\mathrm{std}}$ explains slow random-pruning convergence) is the one claim the experiment structurally cannot test. And quantitatively it is badly off: at 90 % sparsity with $L=4$, $c^L=10^{-4}$ predicts a four-orders-of-magnitude slowdown, whereas Figure 11 shows a modest gap. Third, the four spectral metrics are not independent explanations; see below, they are two consequences of one fact. Also: the "Graphon NTK" of Section 6 is never the continuum kernel — masks are sampled from the estimated graphon at $n=1024$ and the finite empirical NTK is computed. So the comparison is finite-width-to-finite-width, and a limit claim is being supported at a single width.

Genuine strengths, and the theorem that was within reach. Two things deserve real credit. (a) Cut distance is the right metric, for a better reason than the paper gives. Expand the nonlinear Gaussian expectations in polynomials (legitimate: $\mathcal{W}\le1$ and ReLU homogeneity keep all profiles uniformly bounded). Every term becomes a weighted homomorphism density of a tree in the layered graphon stack. Since cut convergence is equivalent to convergence of all homomorphism densities, $\Theta$ is $\delta_\square$-continuous — this is the continuity lemma the paper needs and never states, and it is the reason the whole programme is well-posed at all (once the joint-labelling issue in point 1 is repaired). (b) One line of their own machinery turns Section 6 from correlation into a theorem. For ReLU at $x=x'$ the diagonal variance profile $v^{(l)}(u)=\tilde\Sigma^{(l)}(u,u,x,x)$ obeps a linear positive recursion $v^{(l)}=\tfrac12 T_{\mathcal{W}^{(l)}}v^{(l-1)}$.
