By Perron–Frobenius the per-layer multiplicative gain is $\sigma_1(T_{\mathcal{W}})$, the top singular value, and the profile aligns with the leading singular function. Now take the constant test function: $\sigma_1(T_{\mathcal{W}})\ge\langle\mathbf{1},T_{\mathcal{W}}\mathbf{1}\rangle=\iint\mathcal{W}=p$, with equality iff $\mathcal{W}$ is degree-regular ($\int\mathcal{W}(u,v)dv=p$ a.e.). So: among all graphons at sparsity $p$, the constant graphon — random pruning — minimises the NTK scale, and any method with a non-uniform degree profile strictly exceeds it. That is exactly Figure 2, derived rather than correlated. It also explains the effective-rank drop as the same phenomenon: Perron–Frobenius alignment concentrates activation variance on the high-degree region and starves the rest, collapsing usable directions. For Synflow's block graphon $\mathcal{W}=a$ on $S\times T$ with $|S|=|T|=q$ and $aq^2=p$, the gain is $aq=p/q>p$: Synflow at 90 % sparsity is, in the limit, a _dense network of width $qn$_ with rescaled variance. That single sentence explains the Figure 2/3 phenomenology better than the four spectral summaries, and it is a strictly stronger result than anything the paper claims. I would have asked for this in review.

Proof sketch

Postulated, not proved: the Graphon Limit Hypothesis. The paper is scrupulous about this in Section 8 ("we establish this hypothesis empirically... rather than through a formal mathematical proof"). The only sub-cases with an argument are random pruning and magnitude-at-init (Appendix C): i.i.d. weights make keep-events position-independent and i.i.d., so the mask is $G(n,c)$ and converges to $\mathcal{W}\equiv c$ — the classical ER-to-constant-graphon fact. Nothing is proved for SNIP, GraSP or Synflow, i.e. for every case where the hypothesis has content.

What a proof would require. A clean route exists and the paper does not take it, which is a missed opportunity, because the PaI scores are separable. SNIP's score for a single sample is $s_{ij}=|w_{ij}|\cdot|\delta^{(l)}_i h^{(l-1)}_j|$ — a row factor times a column factor times an entrywise factor. Synflow's is $|w_{ij}|$ times a backward path count at $i$ times a forward path count at $j$. GraSP is of the same shape. That is precisely the Aldous–Hoover/Diaconis–Janson dissociated form $s_{ij}=f(\alpha,\xi_i,\eta_j,\zeta_{ij})$. So a proof would go: (1) show the row/column statistics ($\delta_i$, $h_j$, path counts) concentrate to deterministic position functions $a(u),b(v)$ — a propagation-of-chaos / LLN step; (2) show the global top-$k$ threshold $\tau_n$ concentrates to a deterministic $\tau$ (needs care: for global-across-layer pruning, the per-layer sparsity is itself random at finite $n$ and must be shown to concentrate); (3) conclude $M_{ij}=\mathbf{1}{f>\tau_n}$ is a dissociated separately-exchangeable array whose directing kernel is $\mathcal{W}(u,v)=\Pr(f(\alpha,\xi_u,\eta_v,\zeta)>\tau\mid \xi_u,\eta_v)$, which for SNIP is the explicit closed form $\mathcal{W}(u,v)=2\bar\Phi!\big(\tau/(\sigma_w\,a(u)b(v))\big)$ — manifestly monotone in $a(u)b(v)$, which is exactly the observed density gradient; (4) invoke Diaconis–Janson plus a concentration bound to get $\delta_\square\to0$ with a rate. Synflow additionally needs the iterated-pruning dynamics handled as a mean-field fixed-point iteration on the degree/path-count profile, which is also where its block structure (a positive fraction of neurons driven to zero degree) would come from. And, per the critique, the statement proved should be the jointly labelled, layered version, not layerwise.

Proved (Proposition 1): the forward covariance recursion. Claim. Under Lipschitz $\sigma$, bounded graphons, well-defined degree functionals, and the assumed Lindeberg–Feller condition, as $n_1,\dots,n_L\to\infty$ the pre-activations of the graphon-modulated network converge to centred Gaussian processes, independent across positions, with the recursion displayed above.

Technique. Straight induction on depth, with the graphon entering only through the weight second moment. Base case: $\mathbb{E}[z^{(1)}_i(x)z^{(1)}_{i'}(x')]=\tfrac1d\sum_{j,k}\mathbb{E}[W^{(1)}_{ij}W^{(1)}_{i'k}]x_jx'_k$; independence kills all terms except $i=i'$, $j=k$, where $\mathbb{E}[(W^{(1)}_{ij})^2]=\mathcal{W}^{(1)}(i/n_1,j/d)$, giving $\delta_{ii'}\tfrac1d\sum_j\mathcal{W}^{(1)}(i/n_1,j/d)x_jx'_j$; then $i/n_1\to u_1$ and $\delta_{ii'}\to\delta(u_1-u_1')$. Inductive step: the same second-moment computation gives $\delta_{ii'}\tfrac{1}{n_{l-1}}\sum_j\mathcal{W}^{(l)}(i/n_l,j/n_{l-1})\,\mathbb{E}[h^{(l-1)}_j(x)h^{(l-1)}_j(x')]$. This is where the law of large numbers enters and where the graphon's integral operator replaces the finite adjacency average: the Riemann sum $\tfrac{1}{n_{l-1}}\sum_j\mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u_l,\tfrac{j}{n_{l-1}})\Sigma^{(l-1)}(\tfrac{j}{n_{l-1}})$ converges to $\int_0^1\mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u_l,u_{l-1})\Sigma^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1},u_{l-1})du_{l-1}=T_{\mathcal{W}^{(l)}}\Sigma^{(l-1)}$. The CLT (Lindeberg–Feller, because the summands are independent but not identically distributed) gives Gaussianity of the limit, and $\Sigma^{(l)}$ is then the usual bivariate Gaussian expectation $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{(l)}(u_l))}[\sigma(z)\sigma(z')]$ — for ReLU, the arccos kernel — now evaluated with a position-dependent $\Lambda^{(l)}(u_l)$. The whole content of the proposition is: replace $\tilde\Sigma^{(l)}=\Sigma^{(l-1)}$ by $\tilde\Sigma^{(l)}=T_{\mathcal{W}^{(l)}}\Sigma^{(l-1)}$ and the dense recursion goes through verbatim.

Two caveats on rigour. The Lindeberg condition is assumed in Section 5.1 but in Appendix A is claimed to be "satisfied" by three heuristics (bounded graphon; activations bounded for sigmoid/tanh and "within reasonable ranges" for ReLU; $1/\sqrt{n}$ scaling). It is either an assumption or a lemma; the paper has it both ways, and for ReLU the verification needs an actual uniform fourth-moment bound, which is available but not given. More seriously, the continuum formalism is formally ill-defined: the covariance carries a Dirac $\delta(u-u')$, i.e. the limiting field is white noise in position, so $z^{(l)}(\cdot,x)$ has no measurable sample paths, $\sigma(z^{(l)}(\cdot,x))$ is not a well-defined random function, and the subsequent Lebesgue integral $\int\mathcal{W}h\,du$ is not meaningful. Evaluating the recursion literally is divergent: Eq. (16) needs $\Sigma^{(l-1)}(v,v,\cdot)$ on the diagonal, which equals $\delta(0)\cdot\mathbb{E}[\sigma\sigma]=\infty$. What is intended is a Kronecker delta and a diagonal covariance function $C^{(l)}(u,x,x')=\mathbb{E}[\sigma(z^{(l)}(u,x))\sigma(z^{(l)}(u,x'))]$; formally the continuous forward pass should be a white-noise stochastic integral, $z^{(l)}(u,x)=\int_0^1\sqrt{\mathcal{W}^{(l)}(u,v)}\,h^{(l-1)}(v,x)\,dB_u(v)$ with $B_u$ independent across $u$. The honest statement is that the proofs are correct as finite-$n$ second-moment computations whose limits are taken at the level of the kernel, and the "continuous network" is suggestive notation rather than a defined object. Nothing in the kernel formula is wrong because of this, but anyone citing the continuum network as a mathematical object should not.

Proved (Theorem 1): the Graphon NTK. Claim. Same hypotheses; in the limit the NTK converges to the deterministic kernel of Eq. (32). Technique, in three steps. (i) Backward recursion. Chain rule in the continuum: $\partial f/\partial z^{(L)}(u_L,x)=W^{(L+1)}(u_{L+1},u_L)\sigma'(z^{(L)})$ and $\partial f/\partial z^{(l)}(u_l,x)=\sigma'(z^{(l)}(u_l,x))\int_0^1 \mathcal{\partial f}/\partial z^{(l+1)}(u_{l+1},x)\,W^{(l+1)}(u_{l+1},u_l)\,du_{l+1}$; parameter gradients factor as $\partial f/\partial W^{(l)}(u_l,u_{l-1})=(\partial f/\partial z^{(l)}(u_l,x))\,h^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1},x)$. (ii) The key step — gradient/activation independence. The layerwise contribution $\Theta_l=\iint\mathbb{E}[(\partial f/\partial z^{(l)}(u_l,x))(\partial f/\partial z^{(l)}(u_l,x'))\,h^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1},x)h^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1},x')]\,du_l\,du_{l-1}$ is factorised into a product of expectations, on the stated grounds that "in the infinite-width limit, by the LLN, gradients and activations become statistically independent for distinct positions". This is the classical gradient-independence ansatz of NTK derivations — the step that treats the backward copies of $W^{(l+1)}$ as independent of the forward ones. It is not a consequence of the LLN and it is the one genuinely non-trivial analytic step in the theorem; in the i.i.d. setting it is justified rigorously by Greg Yang's Tensor Programs II/IIb, and extending that machinery to non-identical variance profiles is the obvious way to make this theorem honest. As written it is asserted. Note also that the factorisation is what makes the forward factor $\int\Sigma^{(l-1)}(u_{l-1},u_{l-1})du_{l-1}$ independent of $u_l$ — a structural simplification worth noticing. (iii) Solving the backward recursion. Define $G^{(l)}(u_l,x,x')=\mathbb{E}[(\partial f/\partial z^{(l)}(u_l,x))(\partial f/\partial z^{(l)}(u_l,x'))]$. Using $\mathbb{E}[W^{(l+1)}(u_{l+1},u_l)W^{(l+1)}(u'_{l+1},u_l)]=\mathcal{W}^{(l+1)}(u_{l+1},u_l)\,\delta(u_{l+1}-u'_{l+1})$ — the only place the graphon enters the backward pass, and the step that collapses the double integral in Eq. (42) to a single one — one gets the linear recursion $G^{(l)}(u_l)=\dot\Sigma^{(l)}(u_l,u_l)\int_0^1\mathcal{W}^{(l+1)}(u_{l+1},u_l)G^{(l+1)}(u_{l+1})du_{l+1}$ with base case $G^{(L+1)}\equiv1$. Unrolling it gives the $(L-l+1)$-fold path integral in Eq. (48); multiplying by the forward factor and summing over layers gives the theorem. So the "trick" is just: the backward kernel is the adjoint of the same integral operator $T_{\mathcal{W}}$ that drives the forward recursion, and the NTK is a sum over layers of (forward operator product) $\times$ (adjoint operator product).

Proved (Section 5.3 / Appendix B): the constant-graphon corollary. Claim. If $\mathcal{W}\equiv c$ then $\Theta=c^L\Theta_{\mathrm{std}}$, hence $\lambda_k\mapsto c^L\lambda_k$ and residual modes decay as $a_k(t)=a_k(0)e^{-c^L\lambda_k t}$. Technique. Two inductions. Forward: $\Sigma^{(l)}=c^l\Sigma^{(l)}_{\mathrm{std}}$, since $T_c=c\,\mathrm{id}$ on constants and ReLU is positively homogeneous of degree 1 in the standard deviation. Backward: each step contributes one factor $c$, so $G^{(l)}=c^{L+1-l}G^{(l)}_{\mathrm{std}}$. A genuinely correct and slightly subtle auxiliary step: $\dot\Sigma^{(l)}=\dot\Sigma^{(l)}_{\mathrm{std}}$ exactly, because for ReLU $\mathbb{E}[\sigma'(z)\sigma'(z')]$ depends only on the correlation coefficient of $(z,z')$, which is invariant under scaling all entries of $\Lambda^{(l)}$ by $c^l$. Multiplying gives $c^{l-1}\cdot c^{L+1-l}=c^L$ uniformly in $l$, so the sum factorises. As noted in the critique, the exponent should be $c^{L+1}$ once the parameter measure is weighted by the mask density; the derivation is internally consistent for the dense-variance-profile model it literally analyses. The hedge "when the activation integral dominates the constant 1" is unexplained and unnecessary.

Not proved anywhere: that the Graphon NTK spectrum predicts training dynamics. Section 6 is correlational; the only formal dynamical statement in the paper is the constant-graphon eigenvalue rescaling.

Broader context

Three subfields meeting. (a) NTK / infinite width. Jacot–Gabriel–Hongler (2018) observed that at infinite width with the $1/\sqrt n$ parameterisation, a network's function evolves under gradient flow as kernel regression with the fixed kernel $\Theta_0$; Arora et al. gave exact computation and the CNTK, Lee et al. the linearised-dynamics view, Du–Hu the optimisation consequences, and Greg Yang's Tensor Programs the architectural universality (and the rigorous treatment of the gradient-independence step that this paper assumes). The regime's well-known limitation — it is a lazy/linearised regime that misses feature learning — applies in full force here, and is worth keeping in mind when the paper claims to explain trainability of real sparse nets. (b) Pruning / lottery tickets. Frankle–Carbin's LTH; the PaI family (SNIP, GraSP, Synflow, and the authors' own data-agnostic line: Pham et al.'s NeurIPS 2023 "what makes a good sparse mask?", Xiang et al.'s DPaI); existence proofs (Malach et al.; Pensia et al.; Burkholz); and the structural/Ramanujan line. (c) Graph limits. Lovász–Szegedy (2006) and Borgs–Chayes–Lovász–Sós–Vesztergombi (2008) for the cut metric and the equivalence with left-convergence; Aldous–Hoover and Diaconis–Janson (2008) for the exchangeability representation that silently underwrites the hypothesis; Chan–Airoldi (2014) for the SAS histogram estimator used here (with its monotone-degree identifiability requirement).

Two closely related works worth reading beside this one. First, Yang & Wang, "On the neural tangent kernel analysis of randomly pruned neural networks" (AISTATS 2023) — the direct predecessor, which proves the constant-graphon case properly, with explicit conditions on how fast the retained-degree must grow. Reading it makes clear exactly how much more is being asserted here and how much less is being proved. Second, Krishnagopal & Ruiz, "Graph neural tangent kernel: convergence on large graphs" (ICML 2023) — a confusingly similar object, also called a graphon NTK, but with the graphon on the input graph of a GNN rather than on the network's own weight graph (the paper flags this in a footnote). The methodological contrast is instructive: Krishnagopal–Ruiz actually prove the convergence, because the graphon is given exogenously rather than postulated as the limit of an algorithm's output. Third, worth a look for the opposing structural hypothesis: Hoang, Liu, Marculescu & Wang, "Revisiting pruning at initialization through the lens of Ramanujan graph" (ICLR 2023). There is a real tension here that nobody has resolved: the Ramanujan line says maximise expansion, which pushes toward degree-regular masks; the $\sigma_1(T_{\mathcal{W}})\ge p$ computation above says degree-regular masks minimise the NTK scale and so train slowest in the leading mode. The two criteria point in opposite directions, presumably because they track different things (late-phase signal propagation and generalisation versus early-phase trainability). Reconciling them inside the graphon formalism would be a genuinely good paper.

A plausible follow-up. Two, one theoretical and one prescriptive, and they compose. (i) Prove the hypothesis for SNIP in closed form via the separability route in the proof sketch, with the jointly-labelled layered convergence notion, and prove the $\delta_\square$-continuity lemma for $\Theta$ (tree homomorphism densities). That turns the whole framework from postulate to theorem for at least one real method, and gives an explicit $\mathcal{W}(u,v)=2\bar\Phi(\tau/(\sigma_w a(u)b(v)))$ instead of a histogram. (ii) Graphon-guided pruning as a variational problem, which is exactly the prescriptive gap the authors admit: optimise over graphons subject to $\iint\mathcal{W}=p$ to maximise a target-aligned spectral functional of the resulting $\Theta$ (not a naive $\sigma_1$, which as shown degenerates to concentrating all mass on a vanishing neuron set, i.e. "just use a narrower dense net"), then sample finite masks from the optimiser via a $W$-random graph. The interesting part is the trade-off that the paper's own data exhibits but does not formalise: $\sigma_1$ versus effective rank, trainability versus expressivity, with the constrained optimum presumably an interior point. A third, more ambitious direction: real pruning regimes (LLM pruning at 99 %+, or $p_n\to0$) fall outside graphon theory entirely, since dense graph limits degenerate to $\mathcal{W}\equiv0$. Redoing this with $L^p$ graphons / graphexes (Borgs–Chayes–Cohn–Holden) or local-weak (Benjamini–Schramm) limits is the honest route to the sparsity levels practitioners care about, and it is mathematically a much harder and more interesting problem.

Connection to your work — partly, with caveats. I would not force an IR link; the paper is most valuable to you as a case study in a transferable method (attach a graph limit to an algorithm's output, then transport a spectral analysis across it) and as a cautionary example of a postulate-plus-correlation paper. That said, two links are defensible if stated carefully.

The honest one is methodological, for sparse retrieval index graphs. HNSW/NSW/DiskANN build proximity graphs over vectors and their performance is a statement about the graph's structure (navigability, greedy-search success probability, hub formation). The impulse to say "take a graph limit of the index as $N\to\infty$" is right, but the graphon toolbox specifically does not transfer: HNSW graphs have bounded out-degree $M$, hence $O(N)$ edges, hence an identically-zero graphon limit, and the cut metric cannot see any of the structure that matters. The correct analogue is local weak convergence / the objective method (Aldous–Steele) or graphexes, with the relevant spectral object being the mixing/conductance of the search walk on a bounded-degree graph rather than $\sigma_1$ of an integral operator. So the transferable lesson is the shape of the argument — identify a limit object for the structure produced by an algorithm, show the performance functional is continuous w.r.t. the limit topology, then do spectral analysis in the limit — plus the warning that choosing the limit topology to match your sparsity regime is the entire game. That warning is exactly the gap this paper's own Section 8 does not mention.

The second is conceptual, for sparse or pruned retrieval encoders: the paper's central trade-off ($\sigma_1$ up, effective rank down) has a sharper cost in retrieval than in classification. Rank-based retrieval metrics depend on fine distinctions carried by the tail of the representation spectrum, so a pruning method that maximises the leading NTK eigenvalue while collapsing effective rank is plausibly the wrong choice for a dual encoder even though it reduces training loss fastest — which connects to the dimensionality-collapse / anisotropy literature on dense retrieval, and suggests that "trainability" is the wrong selection criterion for pruning a retrieval model. Caveats: retrieval encoders are fine-tuned pretrained transformers, nowhere near the lazy NTK regime, the graphon framework is MLP-only, and the argument is about representation rank rather than kernel rank, so this is an analogy to think with rather than a result. For generative retrieval specifically I see no non-forced connection, and would leave it alone.

title: Average-Distortion Sketching
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-04

Average-Distortion Sketching

Yiqiao Bao, Anubhav Baweja, Nicolas Menand, Erik Waingarten, Nathan White, Tian Zhang (2024) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05156

Setting and problem

Fix a metric space $(X,d_X)$. A sketch is a randomized compression scheme: a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over pairs $(\mathrm{sk},\mathrm{Alg})$ where $\mathrm{sk}\colon X\to{0,1}^s$ maps a point to $s$ bits and $\mathrm{Alg}$ is a decoding algorithm that, given only the two bit-strings $\mathrm{sk}(x)$ and $\mathrm{sk}(y)$ — never $x$ or $y$ — outputs an estimate of $d_X(x,y)$. The randomness is public (shared between the encoder and the decoder), so this is equivalently a simultaneous-message two-party protocol, or a data-structure primitive where each point is stored once and all pairwise queries are answered from stored bits. The measured resource is $s$, the bit complexity. Worst-case $c$-approximation demands that for every pair $x,y$, the output lies in $[d_X(x,y)/c,\,d_X(x,y)]$ with high probability over the draw of the sketch.

For $(\mathbb{R}^d,\ell_p)$ the worst-case landscape is essentially closed. For $p\in[0,2]$, $p$-stable sketches and Johnson–Lindenstrauss-type arguments give $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation in $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log d)$ bits (Indyk '06). For $p>2$ the situation inverts: the sketching complexity of $c$-approximation is $\widetilde\Theta(d^{1-2/p}/c^2)$, with the lower bound from Bar-Yossef–Jayram–Kumar–Sivakumar '04 and the upper bound from Indyk–Woodruff '05. So for any fixed constant approximation, sketching $\ell_p$ with $p>2$ costs space polynomial in the ambient dimension. There is also a structural converse: Andoni–Krauthgamer–Razenshteyn '15 ("sketching and embedding are equivalent for norms") shows that a constant-size sketch for a norm with approximation $D$ essentially implies an $O(D/\varepsilon)$-distortion embedding into $\ell_{1-\varepsilon}$. Since Matoušek '97's expander argument lower-bounds the distortion of embedding $\ell_p$ into $\ell_1$ by $\Omega(p)$ — even on average — constant-size sketches with $o(p)$ approximation are ruled out for $\ell_p$. These two walls (polynomial space for worst-case constant approximation; $\Omega(p)$ distortion for constant-size sketches) are what the paper is trying to get around.

The paper's motivating question, verbatim in spirit:

_Suppose input points are drawn from an arbitrary distribution $\mu$ supported on $(X,d_X)$. Do better sketches exist which are tailored to $\mu$?_

Definition 1.1 (average-distortion sketch). Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $X$. An average-distortion sketch for $\mu$ is a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over tuples $(\mathrm{sk},\mathrm{Alg})$, $\mathrm{sk}\colon X\to{0,1}^s$, with $\mathrm{Alg}$ taking two sketches and outputting a nonnegative real $\eta$, such that:

  • Non-expansion (worst case over all pairs). For every $x,y\in X$, $\;\mathbb{E}_{(\mathrm{sk},\mathrm{Alg})\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\mathrm{Alg}(\mathrm{sk}(x),\mathrm{sk}(y))\big]\le d_X(x,y)$.
  • Bounded contraction (on average over $\mu$). $\;\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\mu,\;(\mathrm{sk},\mathrm{Alg})\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\mathrm{Alg}(\mathrm{sk}(x),\mathrm{sk}(y))\big]\;\ge\;\frac{1}{c}\,\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\mu}\big[d_X(x,y)\big]$, where $x$ and $y$ are independent draws from $\mu$.

So the sketch is an estimator that never over-estimates (in expectation; the paper's $\ell_p$ construction actually satisfies non-expansion with probability $1-\delta$ at a $O(\log(1/\delta))$ multiplicative cost in space), and whose aggregate mass is within a factor $c$ of the aggregate mass of the true distance, when both arguments are typical. There is no per-pair lower bound at all: there can be pairs $x,y$ where the output is wildly smaller than $d_X(x,y)/c$, and the definition does not care, as long as such pairs are $\mu\times\mu$-rare or $\mu\times\mu$-light in the weighted sense above. This is a strict relaxation of worst-case sketching (worst-case $c$-approximation implies average-distortion $c$ for every $\mu$), so one studies it precisely where worst-case sketching is impossible.

Four modelling choices deserve to be flagged, because the result lives or dies on them.

  1. One-sidedness is load-bearing. The $c$ appears only on the contraction side. This matters for two reasons. Downstream, in approximate near-neighbor search, the true near neighbor $x^_$ of a query $q$ is an arbitrary, adversarially chosen pair $(q,x^_)$ — not a $\mu\times\mu$ draw — so the only guarantee one can hope to apply to it is the worst-case one, namely "the sketch still calls them close." Upstream, one-sidedness is what makes the relaxation meaningful rather than vacuous: without the all-pairs non-expansion, you could sketch nothing and output a constant equal to the average distance.
  2. Independence of the two draws is the whole crack in the wall. The paper's footnote 3 is the key observation: if bounded contraction were required for an arbitrary (possibly correlated) distribution over pairs $(x,y)$, then a minimax/LP-duality argument converts the guarantee into a worst-case per-pair guarantee, and the $\widetilde\Theta(d^{1-2/p}/c^2)$ lower bound reasserts itself. Because $x\perp y$, the adversary cannot concentrate a pair distribution on the hard pairs; it can only pick a marginal, and the product structure is what the algorithm exploits.
  3. $\mu$ is arbitrary but fixed, and the notion remains worst-case over $\mu$. One says $(X,d_X)$ admits an $(s,c)$ average-distortion sketch only if such a sketch exists for every $\mu$. So this is not an average-case or smoothed-analysis assumption on inputs; it is a statement that for each $\mu$ there is a good sketch tailored to it. The sketch may depend on $\mu$ — and in the $\ell_p$ construction the dependence is startlingly thin (only the coordinate-wise median), learnable from $O(\log d)$ samples.
  4. The grid $[\Delta]^d$. The multi-scale construction concatenates single-scale sketches at $O(\log(d\Delta))$ dyadic scales, and it needs a nonzero minimum distance (all nonzero $\ell_p$ distances on the integer grid are $\ge 1$) so the geometric sum telescopes into $\mathbb{E}[|x-y|_p]$ with no additive loss. Crucially the single-scale sketch has no dependence on $d$ or $\Delta$ whatsoever; that is what makes the near-neighbor application go through, with discretization to multiples of $\varepsilon r/d$ absorbing an additive $\varepsilon r$.

The definition generalizes two existing notions. An average-distortion embedding $f\colon X\to\ell_1$ for $\mu$ (Rabinovich '03; Naor '14; Kush–Nikolov–Tang '21) is non-expanding pointwise, $|f(x)-f(y)|_1\le d_X(x,y)$, with $\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\mu}|f(x)-f(y)|_1\ge \frac{1}{c}\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\mu}d_X(x,y)$; composing with the constant-size $\ell_1$ sketch gives an average-distortion sketch of $O(1)$ size and approximation $O(c)$. Data-dependent LSH (Andoni–Indyk–Nguyen–Razenshteyn '14; Andoni–Razenshteyn '15; Andoni–Naor–Nikolov–Razenshteyn–Waingarten '18) also fits: hash $x$ by storing a fingerprint of $h(x)$ for $h\sim\mathcal{H}$, where $\mathcal{H}$ is chosen as a function of the dataset (i.e. of the uniform $\mu$ over it); collision versus non-collision is a crude $O(1)$-bit distance estimate. Both special cases are pinned at $O(1)$ space and pay for it in approximation: for $\ell_p$, $p>2$, the best achievable is $\Theta(p)$ (Matoušek '97 lower bound; Kush–Nikolov–Tang '21 upper bound, via Naor's average John theorem). The gap the paper attacks is therefore exactly the region left open between $O(1)$-size sketches and $d^{1-2/p}$-size sketches: what happens if you allow a sketch of size slightly superconstant but still sublinear, and only ask for average distortion?

Main idea

Theorem 1. For every $p\in(2,\infty)$ and every $c$ above a fixed universal constant, every distribution $\mu$ over $([\Delta]^d,\ell_p)$ admits an average-distortion sketch with distortion $c$ and bit complexity $2^{O(p/c)}\cdot\log^2(d\Delta)$. (With $2^{O(p/c)}\log^2(d\Delta/\delta)$ bits, non-expansion holds pointwise with probability $1-\delta$, not just in expectation.)

Two comparisons make the point. Worst-case $c$-approximate sketching of $\ell_p^d$ costs $\widetilde\Theta(d^{1-2/p}/c^2)$; for any constant $p>2$ and constant $c$, Theorem 1 gives polylogarithmic space where worst-case sketching provably needs $\mathrm{poly}(d)$. And relative to average-distortion embeddings into $\ell_1$, which cap out at distortion $\Theta(p)$ in $O(\log(d\Delta))$ bits, Theorem 1 drives the distortion all the way down to a universal constant _independent of $p$_, at the price of $2^{O(p/c)}$ bits. So the paper exhibits a space–approximation trade-off curve where previously only the two endpoints existed, and the curve is provably outside the reach of both prior frameworks. (Since the $O(p)$ embedding bound is free, the interesting regime is a fixed constant $< c \lesssim p$.)

The engine is a single-scale sketch (Lemma 2.1): for a $\mu$ pre-centered so that every coordinate marginal has median $0$, and for a scale $r$, a sketch of $2^{O(p/c)}$ bits — _independent of $d$ and $\Delta$_ — such that (i) any pair with $|x-y|*p\le r$ is declared CLOSE with probability $\ge 1-\delta_1$, and (ii) for any fixed $x$ with $|x|_p\ge (c-1)r/2$, a random $y\sim\mu$ is declared FAR with probability $\ge \tfrac12-\tfrac32\delta_2$. The way it declares FAR is by producing a probabilistic certificate of farness: a coordinate $i$ and threshold $\tau$ with $x_i\ge\tau$ and $y_i<\tau-1$ (in the $\ell*\infty$ warm-up), which deterministically witnesses $|x-y|_\infty>1$. All of the distribution knowledge used is the coordinate-wise median — and Remark 2.2 notes an approximate median suffices (any $m_i$ with $\Pr[x_i\ge m_i],\Pr[x_i\le m_i]\ge q=\Omega(1)$, degrading the FAR probability to $q-\tfrac32\delta_2$), learnable from $O(\log d)$ samples of $\mu$.

A second, operationally important feature: the sketch can be made asymmetric (Corollary 2.15). The decoder uses almost nothing from $x$'s side — one hashed coordinate index, a rounded norm, and one indicator bit — so $\mathrm{sk}_A(x)$ can be compressed to $O(p/c)$ bits while $\mathrm{sk}_B(y)$ keeps its $2^{O(p/c)}$ bits. Corollary 2.16 goes further: when the decoder has $y$ in the clear (as the preprocessing algorithm of a data structure does), the sketch is $O((p/c)\log(1/\delta_0))$ bits.

Theorem 2 (ANN). For every $p\in(2,\infty)$, every $c$ above a fixed universal constant, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a $c$-approximate nearest-neighbor data structure for $\ell_p$ with query time $n^\varepsilon d\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\log nd)$ and space/preprocessing $d\cdot n^{O(p/c)\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)}$. The prior best approximation was $O(p/\varepsilon)$ at $n^{1+\varepsilon}$ space (Andoni–Naor–Nikolov–Razenshteyn–Waingarten '18a via non-linear spectral gaps; Kush–Nikolov–Tang '21 via average-distortion embeddings), improving on $2^{O(p)}$ (Bartal–Gottlieb '19). Theorem 2 makes the approximation a constant _independent of $p$_, in sublinear query time and polynomial space for constant $p$. Two calibration points: it beats the Indyk '01 route (randomized embedding $\ell_p\to\ell_\infty$ plus Indyk's $O(\log_\rho\log d)$-approximation in $n^\rho$ space, which needs $n^{O(\log d)}$ for constant approximation) by achieving constant approximation in polynomial space for constant $p$; and it recovers Indyk '01 asymptotically for $\ell_\infty$ by setting $p=\log d$, $c=O(1)$.

Theorem 3 (hardness evidence). The paper does not prove a $2^{\Omega(p/c)}$ lower bound for average-distortion sketching. It proves one for a restricted but natural certificate model: a sketch that, on the specific hard distribution of Definition 4.1, must actually output a pair $(i,\ell)$ with $y_i<\ellr$) whenever it claims farness — outputting a certificate with probability $\ge 1/8$ over $X,Y\sim\mu$, and outputting an incorrect certificate on any worst-case pair with probability $\le\delta\le 1/((c-1)2^{p+2})$ — requires $\Omega\big(2^{(p-2)/(c-1)}/c^2\big)=2^{\Omega(p/c)}$ bits. Claim 4.4 verifies that their own sketch, with a minor modification and a $\mathrm{poly}(p)$ space blowup, does solve this problem. So the message is: if you want to improve on $2^{\Theta(p/c)}$, you cannot do it by producing farness certificates.

The most interesting part

The thing worth internalizing is that the exponent $2^{p/c}$ is not an artifact of a union bound — it is the geometric mean of two quantities that the paper identifies as the two parameters of the problem, and the lower-bound instance is literally the extremal configuration of the upper bound's counting argument. Let me make this precise, because it is the paper's real content.

Think of a point $x$ through its nested superlevel sets. In the $\ell_\infty$ warm-up, $G_\ell(x)={i: x_i\ge \ell}$ for $\ell=1,\dots,L$ with $L=\Theta(c)$ thresholds, so $G_L(x)\subseteq\cdots\subseteq G_1(x)$, with $|G_L(x)|\ge 1$ (because $|x|_\infty$ is large) and $|G_1(x)|\le d$. The entire algorithm reduces to a single structural dichotomy at a level $\ell$: either $y$'s level set is not much bigger than $x$'s, in which case a $k$-element "first-$k$-under-a-random-permutation" summary of $y$'s level set suffices to prove that $x$'s $\pi$-minimal coordinate is absent from it; or $y$'s level set is bigger than $x$'s two-levels-down set, in which case a coordinate in the set difference is itself a certificate of farness. If both fail at level $\ell$, the level sets must grow by a factor $k/4$ over two levels. Iterate: failing at a constant fraction of the $L$ levels forces $|G_1(x)|\ge (k/4)^{\Theta(L)}$. Setting $k$ so that $(k/4)^{\Theta(L)}$ exceeds the maximum possible size of the top-level set gives a contradiction, hence at most a small fraction of levels can be bad, hence a uniformly random level works with constant probability.

So the space is $k\approx (\text{max level-set size})^{\Theta(1/L)} = (\text{max level-set size})^{\Theta(1/c)}$. For $\ell_\infty$ the max level-set size is $d$ and you pay $k=d^{\Theta(1/c)}$, which is exactly Indyk '01's $n^{\rho}$-style trade-off. The clever move is to shrink the ceiling of this counting argument from $d$ to $2^{\Theta(p)}$ by composing with the max-stable rescaling $x_i'=x_i/u_i^{1/p}$, $u_i\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ — the standard probabilistic $\ell_p\to\ell_\infty$ device (an "exponential race"/precision-sampling embedding). Lemma 2.5 says that with probability $1-\delta_2$ over $u$: (a) some coordinate satisfies $|x_i'|\ge|x|_p/D_1$, since $\Pr[\max_i|x_i'|<|x|_p/D_1]=\exp(-D_1^p)$ exactly; and (b) at most $K=2D_2^p/\delta_2=2^{\Theta(p)}$ coordinates satisfy $|x_i'|\ge|x|_p/D_2$, since the expected count is $\sum_i \Pr[u_i\le D_2^p|x_i|^p/|x|_p^p]\le D_2^p$ and Markov finishes it. That is: after max-stable rescaling, the effective number of coordinates within a constant factor of the top is $2^{\Theta(p)}$, not $d$ — this is the exact quantitative sense in which an $\ell_p$ ball has "$2^{\Theta(p)}$ directions that matter" rather than $d$. The thresholds are then laid out from $|x|_p/D_2$ (where at most $K$ coordinates live) up to $|x|_p/D_1$ (where at least one lives), and the counting argument runs between $1$ and $K$ instead of between $1$ and $d$. Hence $k=K^{\Theta(1/L)}=\big(2^{\Theta(p)}\big)^{\Theta(1/c)}=2^{\Theta(p/c)}$ — formally $k=4\big(K^{4/(\delta(L-1))}+2\ln(6/\delta_1)\big)$ with $\delta=\min{\delta_1/6,\delta_2}$.

Now look at the lower-bound distribution (Definition 4.1). It lives on $d=2^{p-1}$ coordinates. Sample $J_0\subset[2^{p-1}]$ of size $2^{p-2}$, then $J_1\subset J_0$, …, $J_{c-1}\subset J_{c-2}$, each a uniformly random subset of size $2^{-(p-2)/(c-1)}$ times its parent, and set $X=\sum_{j}\mathbf{1}*{J_j}$. This is precisely a chain of $c$ nested level sets whose consecutive ratio is exactly $2^{(p-2)/(c-1)}=k$, starting from one coordinate of value $c$ and ending at $d/2$ coordinates of value $1$. On this support, $|x|_p=\Theta(c)$ for every point, and $\ell_p$ degenerates into $\ell*\infty$: $|x-y|_p>r$ (for $r\in(2^{1-1/p},2)$) iff some coordinate differs by at least $2$ iff a certificate $(i,\ell)$ with $x_i<\ell<y_i$ exists. In other words, the adversary hands the algorithm the unique growth profile in which every level is a tight instance of the dichotomy, so there is no slack to exploit, and $k$ really has to be $2^{p/c}$. That the hard instance is the saturating case of the algorithm's own pigeonhole is the most satisfying part of the paper: the $2^{p/c}$ is identified as the right answer for this technique, and the technique is shown to be forced if you want witnesses.

Honest limitations around this. (i) Theorem 3 is for a restricted model and a single distribution; it does not rule out an average-distortion sketch for $\ell_p$ of, say, $\mathrm{poly}(p/c)$ size that never produces a witness. (ii) The regime of the win is $2^{p/c}\ll d^{1-2/p}$, i.e. $p/c\ll\log d$; at $p=\Theta(\log d)$ with constant $c$ you are back to $\mathrm{poly}(d)$. (iii) The constant "larger than a fixed universal constant" is not small: Lemma 2.1 needs $c\ge 16(6\ln(2/\delta_2)/\delta_1)^{1/p}$ and Theorem 1's reduction loses a factor $64$, so the attainable constants are in the hundreds. (iv) Most conceptually: the output is not an estimator of individual distances in any usable per-pair sense. It is a FAR/CLOSE oracle at each scale, with the far-side guarantee holding only at constant probability — and Section 2.2 shows why that ceiling is structural rather than lazy, which I return to below.

Proof sketch

The precise claim. Let $p\in(2,\infty)$, let $c$ exceed a fixed universal constant, and let $\mu$ be any distribution on $[\Delta]^d$. Then there is a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $(\mathrm{sk},\mathrm{Alg})$ with $\mathrm{sk}\colon[\Delta]^d\to{0,1}^s$, $s=2^{O(p/c)}\log^2(d\Delta)$, such that for all $x,y\in[\Delta]^d$, $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{Alg}(\mathrm{sk}(x),\mathrm{sk}(y))]\le|x-y|_p$, and $\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\mu,\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{Alg}(\mathrm{sk}(x),\mathrm{sk}(y))]\ge\frac1c\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\mu}|x-y|_p$. The only statistic of $\mu$ used by the encoder is an approximate coordinate-wise median.

Step 0: centering. Let $z$ be the coordinate-wise median of $\mu$ and work with $y-z$; the distribution now lives on ${-\Delta,\dots,\Delta}^d$ with every marginal median $0$, so for every coordinate $i$, $\Pr_{y\sim\mu}[y_i\le 0]\ge 1/2$ and $\Pr[y_i\ge 0]\ge 1/2$. This single fact — that a _fixed, non-$y$-dependent_ coordinate has a $1/2$ chance of being on the opposite side of $0$ from $x$'s value there — is the only place $\mu$ enters, and it is exactly the step that would be a worst-case impossibility if $x$ and $y$ were correlated.

Step 1: the single-scale sketch (Figure 1). Public randomness fixes: a uniform permutation $\pi$ on $[d]$; a uniform threshold index $\mathbf{j}\sim{2,\dots,L}$ with $L=\lceil c(\delta_1/6)^{1/p}/(4D_1)\rceil-2=\Theta(c)$; i.i.d. $u_1,\dots,u_d\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$; hash functions $h_1\colon[d]\to[U]$ and $h_2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to[U]$ with $U=2(6+k)/\delta_2=2^{\Theta(p/c)}$. Define $G_{x,u}(t,\sigma)={i: \sigma x_i/u_i^{1/p}\ge t}$ and the threshold ladder $\tau(\nu,j)=D_3\big(\lfloor \nu/(D_2D_3)\rfloor+j\big)$ with $D_1=\ln(2/\delta_2)^{1/p}$, $D_2=2D_1$, $D_3=r/(\delta_1/6)^{1/p}$. Then $\mathrm{sk}(x)$ stores: (1) $h_2$ of $\nu_x=\lceil|x|_p/r\rceil$ and $\nu_x+1$, and of $\nu_x'=\lceil|x|_p/(D_2D_3)\rceil$ and $\nu_x'+1$; (2) for each $\ell\in{\mathbf{j}-2,\mathbf{j}-1,\mathbf{j}}$ and sign $\sigma\in{\pm1}$, the hashes $h_1(i)$ of the first $k$ coordinates of $G_{x,u}(\tau(|x|_p,\ell),\sigma)$ in $\pi$-order; (3) one bit $s_{x,\sigma}=\mathbf{1}{|G_{x,u}(\tau(|x|_p,\mathbf{j}-2),\sigma)|\le (k/4)\,|G_{x,u}(\tau(|x|_p,\mathbf{j}),\sigma)|}$. The decoder: if the norm-hash sets don't intersect, output FAR; otherwise read off the alignment shift $\gamma\in{-1,0,1}$ from the $h_2(\nu')$ collisions; then if some $\sigma$ has $s_{x,\sigma}=1$ and the $\pi$-first stored hash from $x$'s level-$\mathbf{j}$ set is absent from $y$'s level-$(\mathbf{j}-1)$ stored list, output FAR; else CLOSE.

Three devices deserve naming.

The norm-grid alignment trick. The ladder $\tau(\cdot,j)$ is anchored at $|x|_p$, which $\mathrm{sk}(y)$ does not know. Both sketches round their norms (down and up) and store hashes; if $||x|_p-|y|_p|\le 2r$ the rounded values differ by at most one, so one of the three shifts $\gamma$ aligns the ladders and $\tau(|x|_p,\mathbf{j}-1)=\tau(|y|_p,\mathbf{j}-1-\gamma)$ — which is why three consecutive levels are stored. If they never align, then by the reverse triangle inequality $|x-y|_p\ge||x|_p-|y|_p|>r$ and FAR is free. Nothing is wasted: the failure of coordination is itself a certificate. The same step does double duty in the proof of Theorem 1, where it handles pairs with $|x|_p<(c-1)r/2$ (near the median) but $|y|_p\ge (c+3)r/2$: two integers separate $\nu_x$ from $\nu_y$, so Step 1 fires unless $h_2$ collides (probability $\le 4/U$).

_Why $\mathrm{sk}(x)$ and $\mathrm{sk}(y)$ can agree on a coordinate without agreeing on a coordinate._ Let $i^x_{\min}$ be the $\pi$-first element of $G_{x,u}(\tau(\nu,\mathbf{j}),\sigma)$ — a function of $x,u,\mathbf{j},\sigma,\pi$ and not of $y$. The decoder wants to conclude $i^x_{\min}\notin G_{y,u}(\tau(\nu,\mathbf{j}-1),\sigma)$ from $y$'s $k$-element prefix. Under the condition $|Y_{-1}|\le (k/4)|X_0|$ (certified by the bit $s_{x,\sigma}$ plus the failure of the other branch), had $i^x_{\min}$ been in $Y_{-1}$, the number of elements of $Y_{-1}$ preceding it in $\pi$ would be a sum of independent Bernoullis — made manifest by sampling $\pi$ in three stages (first an order $\pi_1$ on $X_0$, which fixes $i^x_{\min}$; then a placement map $\pi_2\colon Y_{-1}\setminus X_0\to{0,\dots,|X_0|}$ saying which gap of $X_0$ each element falls into; then orders inside each gap) so that the relevant count is $|\pi_2^{-1}(0)|$, a sum of $|Y_{-1}\setminus X_0|$ independent indicators each of probability $1/(|X_0|+1)$, mean $\le k/4$. Bernstein gives $e^{-k/2}$. That deferred-decision decomposition of a uniform permutation is the concrete mechanism behind "with probability exponentially small in $k$."

The telescoping pigeonhole over a random level (Lemma 2.11). Conditioned on the good $u$-event, $|G_{x,u}(\tau(\nu,0),\sigma)|\le K$ and $|G_{x,u}(\tau(\nu,L),\sigma)|\ge1$. Writing $|G_{x,u}(\tau(\nu,0))|$ as the telescoping product $\prod_{j\in E}\frac{|G(\tau(\nu,j-2))|}{|G(\tau(\nu,j))|}\cdot|G(\tau(\nu,L))|$ over even $j$ (and likewise over odd $j$), every factor is $\ge1$ by nesting; so if more than $\delta_2(L-1)/4$ even indices had ratio exceeding $K^{4/(\delta_2(L-1))}$, the product would exceed $K$, a contradiction. Hence at most a $\delta_2/2$ fraction of $j\in{2,\dots,L}$ are "bad," and a uniform $\mathbf{j}$ is good with probability $\ge 1-\delta_2/2$. This converts the $\ell_\infty$ case analysis into a clean probability bound, and it is where $k\ge 4K^{4/(\delta(L-1))}=2^{\Theta(p/c)}$ is forced.

Step 2: the two guarantees of Lemma 2.1. Non-expansion (Lemma 2.3) is a three-case analysis. The norm hashes never fire when $|x-y|_p\le r$ (since $|\nu_x-\nu_y|\le1$). The two "geometric" failure modes both reduce to Lemma 2.4: if $|x-y|_p\le r$ then $\Pr_u[\exists i: |x_i-y_i|\ge D_3u_i^{1/p}]\le\delta_1/6$, computed exactly from the exponential CDF as $1-\exp(-|x-y|_p^p\delta_1/(6r^p))$ — i.e. the max-stable rescaling cannot separate close points by more than one rung of the ladder. The third failure mode is the permutation/Bernstein event above, $\le\delta_1/3$ after a union bound over $\sigma$. Bounded contraction (Lemma 2.7) is organized as a decision tree (Figure 2) over nested events $E_3$ (norms within $2r$), $E_4$ ($E_3$ plus correct $\gamma$ plus $s_{x,\sigma}=1$), $E_5$ ($\mathrm{sign}(x_{i^x_{\min}})\ne\mathrm{sign}(y_{i^x_{\min}})$), $E_6$ ($E_5$ plus no $h_1$ collision). Lemma 2.9 proves the contrapositive: CLOSE implies one of four branch failures. Then: $\Pr[\neg E_3$ but hashes intersect$]\le 4/U$ (Lemma 2.10); $\Pr[\neg E_4\mid E_3]\le 2/U+\delta_2/2$ (the telescoping pigeonhole plus two collision events, Lemma 2.11); $\Pr[\neg E_5]\le 1/2$ (the median, Lemma 2.12); $\Pr[\neg E_6\mid E_5]\le k/U$ (Lemma 2.13). Total $\le 1/2+\delta_2$.

The ordering of these events is not cosmetic. Lemma 2.12 is valid only because $i^x_{\min}$ was fixed before $y$ was drawn and the median bound is applied with no conditioning on $y$ — the paper flags this explicitly ("some care must be taken so that the above case analysis is not inadvertently conditioning on a draw of $y\sim\mu$"). The whole event decomposition is engineered so that the one place where $\mu$ is used is a bare, unconditioned marginal statement.

Step 3: boosting, and why only one side boosts. Lemma 2.14 runs $T=\lceil 512\ln(1/\delta_0)\rceil$ independent copies and outputs FAR if at least $T/16$ copies do. On the near side, the indicators are independent across copies (the sketches are drawn independently), so Hoeffding gives failure $\le e^{-T/512}\le\delta_0$: the near-side guarantee boosts to $1-\delta_0$ at a $\log(1/\delta_0)$ space cost. On the far side the indicators are not independent — they all share the single draw $y\sim\mu$ — so the only tool available is Markov: $\mathbb{E}[#\text{CLOSE}]\le \tfrac{11}{16}T$ gives $\Pr[#\text{CLOSE}\ge\tfrac{15}{16}T]\le\tfrac{11}{15}$, hence FAR with probability $\ge1/4$ and no better. This is a genuine structural feature of average-distortion sketching, not a slack in the analysis (footnote 7 says exactly this), and it is why the definition is phrased in expectations and why the stronger "probabilistic sketching" model — contraction with probability approaching $1$ over $x,y\sim\mu$ — is left open.

Step 4: multi-scale assembly (Theorem 1). First, the single-scale contraction, stated for fixed $x$ with $|x|*p\ge(c-1)r/2$, is upgraded to a statement about a pair $x,y\sim\mu$: split on whether $|x|_p\ge(c-1)r/2$; in the complementary case, if $|x-y|_p\ge(c+1)r$ then $|y|_p\ge(c+3)r/2$ by the triangle inequality, and the norm-hash step fires with probability $\ge1-4/U$. Both branches yield $\Pr[\text{FAR}]\ge\tfrac14\Pr*{x,y\sim\mu}[|x-y|*p\ge cr]$. Then concatenate over dyadic scales $r=2^w$, $w\in{\lfloor-\log_2 c\rfloor,\dots,\lceil\log_2(d\Delta/c)\rceil}$, each with $\delta_0=1/(d\Delta)$, and output $2^{w^_-2}$ for the largest FAR scale $w^_$ (or $0$). Non-expansion: scales below $v=\lfloor\log_2|x-y|_p\rfloor$ contribute a geometric sum $\le 2^{v-2}$ and scales at or above $v$ contribute $\le\delta_0\cdot d\Delta/2\le 3/4$, and $2^{v-2}+3/4\le 2^v\le|x-y|_p$ since grid distances are $\ge1$. Contraction: because the scales are geometric, $\max*{S w\in}2^w\ge\frac12\sum_{w\in S}2^w$, so the expected output is at least $\frac12\sum_w 2^{w-2}\cdot\frac14\Pr[|x-y|_p\ge c2^w]\ge\frac{1}{64c}\mathbb{E}|x-y|_p$. The factor $64c$ is absorbed by running the construction with $c'=c/64$. Space: $2^{O(p/c)}\log(1/\delta_0)\cdot O(\log(d\Delta))=2^{O(p/c)}\log^2(d\Delta)$.

The ANN data structure (Section 3). The reduction follows Jayaram–Waingarten–Zhang '24's template for data-dependent LSH, but with a sketch rather than a hash family — notable because average-distortion sketches do not yield LSH families. Core-Preprocess(X,k): at a node, set $\mu=$ uniform over $X$, compute the coordinate-wise median $m$, store $m$ and (if one exists) some $x\in X$ with $|x-m|_p\le(c+1)r/2$; instantiate the one-sided sketch of Corollary 2.16 for the centered $\tilde\mu$ with scale $r$, approximation $c$, and failure probability $\delta_0=\varepsilon$, giving $s=O((p/c)\log(1/\varepsilon))$; for every $\sigma\in{0,1}^s$, let $X_\sigma={x\in X:\mathrm{Alg}(\sigma,x-m)=\text{CLOSE}}$ and recurse on each non-empty $X_\sigma$ with depth $k-1$. Core-Query(q,v): if $|q-m|_p\le(c-1)r/2$, answer with v.close (which is within $cr$ of $q$ by the triangle inequality) or fail; else compute $\sigma=\mathrm{sk}(q-m)$ and descend into v.child$(\sigma)$.

Note how the two guarantees are used on opposite sides of the asymmetry. The query plays the role of the worst-case point $x$ (hence the short $O(p/c)$-bit sketch, and hence the exponential space saving), and the dataset points play the role of $y\sim\mu$. Non-expansion (worst case over pairs!) ensures that the true near neighbor $x^_$, with $|q-x^_|_p\le r$, lands in the child $X_{\sigma^*}$ with probability $\ge1-\varepsilon$ — this is exactly why the definition insists on all-pairs non-expansion. Bounded contraction ensures $\mathbb{E}|X_{\sigma^*}|\le\frac34|X|$, so the surviving set shrinks geometrically down the tree; the expected query time is $O(k\mathbf{T}+d|X|(3/4)^k+d(k+1))$. The "$|q-m|_p$ small" branch is forced by the fact that contraction only holds for points far from the median, and is precisely the data-dependent "dense cluster" case of Andoni–Razenshteyn in another guise: when the query is near the center, the center's own neighbor is already a valid answer. Success probability is $(1-\varepsilon)^k$ with $k=O(\log n)$; repeating the core $O(n^\varepsilon)$ times boosts it, giving query time $n^\varepsilon d\,\mathrm{polylog}$, and the tree of arity $2^s$ and depth $k$ gives $2^{s(k+1)}=n^{O((p/c)\log(1/\varepsilon))}$ nodes.

The lower-bound technique (Section 4). The chain is: Certification $\to$ Random-Multi-Index $\to$ an incompressibility argument.

Random-Multi-Index(k,t) is a one-way public-coin problem on strings of length $d$ with $kt\le d/2$: Alice gets a uniform $x$ with exactly $kt$ ones; Bob gets a uniform $t$-subset $I\subseteq[d]$; Bob must output some $i\in I$ with $x_i=0$, or abstain. A protocol $(\alpha,\delta)$-succeeds if it outputs an index with probability $\ge\alpha$ and outputs a wrong index with probability $\le\delta$. This is an abstaining, multi-target variant of Index — "find a zero inside a random window."

The reduction (Lemma 4.7). Since the certificate's second coordinate $\ell$ takes $c-1$ values, some $\ell_0$ carries probability $\ge 1/(8(c-1))$. Set $k_0=(d/2)^{1/(c-1)}$ and $t_0=(d/2)^{1-(\ell_0+1)/(c-1)}$ with $d=2^{p-1}$ — i.e. match $k_0$ to the chain's per-level growth ratio and $t_0$ to the size of the relevant level set. Alice, holding $x$ with $k_0t_0$ ones, samples the nested chain of Definition 4.1 conditioned on the $\ell_0$-th layer being her input, forms $X=\sum_j x^{(j)}$ and sends $\mathrm{sk}(X)$. Bob does the symmetric thing with his window as a layer indicator, forms $Y$, and outputs $i$ if the certificate is $(i,\ell_0)$ with $i\in I$. By construction $X_i\ge\ell_0$ iff $x_i=1$, so a correct certificate ($X_i<\ell_0<Y_i$) is exactly a zero of $x$ inside $I$; soundness of the certificate transfers to $\delta$, and $\alpha=1/(8c)$.

The hardness (Lemma 4.9) is a compression argument. Bob draws $g=d/(10t)$ independent windows $I_1,\dots,I_g$ from the public coins — so Alice knows them too — and runs the protocol on each, accumulating a set $B_g$ of claimed zeros. Two counts: (i) $\mathbb{E}|B_g|\ge\frac{d}{100t}\alpha^2$, because in each of the first $\alpha g/10$ rounds the output is a new index with probability $\ge\alpha-t|B_{j-1}|/d\ge\frac{9}{10}\alpha$; (ii) the expected number of wrong indices in $B_g$ is $\le g\delta=\frac{d}{10t}\delta$. Now Alice can transmit all of $x$ by sending: her protocol message ($s$ bits), the list of wrongly-claimed indices (unary-coded count plus $\log_2 d$ bits each), and $x$ restricted to $[d]\setminus B_g$ ($\log_2\binom{d-|B_g|}{kt}$ bits, since the remaining substring still has $kt$ ones). Fact 4.8 (after De–Trevisan–Tulsiani) says any injective randomized encoding of a uniform element of $U$ has expected length $\ge\log_2|U|-3$, so with $U=\binom{d}{kt}$: $$s\;\ge\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\log_2\tfrac{\binom{d}{kt}}{\binom{d-|B_g|}{kt}}\Big]-\mathbb{E}[o]\,(\log_2 d+1)-O(1)\;\ge\;\mathbb{E}|B_g|\log_2!\Big(1+\tfrac{kt}{d-kt}\Big)-O(1)\;\ge\;\tfrac{\alpha^2 k}{100}-O(1).$$ Intuition: each certified zero is worth $\approx kt/d$ bits of description length for $x$, and you can harvest $\Omega(\alpha^2 d/t)$ of them, so the message must carry $\Omega(\alpha^2 k)$ bits. The condition $\delta<1/(d\log_2 d)$ is what keeps the error-correction overhead from swamping the savings. Plugging $\alpha=1/(8c)$ and $k=2^{(p-2)/(c-1)}$ gives $\Omega(2^{(p-2)/(c-1)}/c^2)$.

Broader context

The subfield this sits in has two interlocking halves. Metric sketching asks how few bits per point suffice to recover pairwise distances in a given metric; for norms it is tightly bound up with metric embeddings — Andoni–Krauthgamer–Razenshteyn '15 showed sketching and embedding into $\ell_{1-\varepsilon}$ are essentially equivalent for norms at constant sketch size, which is why so many sketching upper bounds are really embedding theorems and why lower bounds often come from expanders (Matoušek '97) or from one-way communication complexity (Bar-Yossef et al. '04). Approximate nearest-neighbor search consumes these primitives: Indyk–Motwani and Har-Peled–Indyk–Motwani reduce $c$-ANN to the $(c,r)$-near-neighbor problem, which LSH solves with space $n^{1+\rho}$ and query $n^\rho$. The last decade's progress is data-dependent hashing: rather than pick a hash family oblivious to the data, examine the dataset (i.e. the uniform $\mu$ over it) and build a family tailored to it. Andoni–Indyk–Nguyen–Razenshteyn '14 and Andoni–Razenshteyn '15 push $\ell_2$ from $\rho=1/c^2$ to the optimal $\rho=1/(2c^2-1)$ by iteratively peeling off dense clusters and treating the residue as pseudorandom; Andoni–Naor–Nikolov–Razenshteyn–Waingarten '18 extend the paradigm to general norms via non-linear spectral gaps, and Andoni–Nikolov–Razenshteyn–Waingarten '21 ("beyond space partitions") show that the LSH formalism itself is not the ceiling. In parallel, Rabinovich '03's average-distortion embeddings, Naor's "average John theorem" (2021), and Kush–Nikolov–Tang '21 showed that relaxing worst-case to average distortion buys real algorithmic improvements for ANN. This paper is the natural completion of that square: data-dependent sketching with average distortion, strictly containing both data-dependent LSH (which is a constant-size sketch) and average-distortion $\ell_1$ embeddings (likewise), and escaping their shared $O(1)$-space straitjacket.

Two specific pointers beyond the obvious. Jayaram–Waingarten–Zhang '24, "Data-dependent LSH for the Earth Mover's Distance," is both the structural template for Section 3 and the live frontier: it already implies a $\widetilde O(\log s)$ average-distortion sketch for $\mathrm{EMD}_s([\Delta]^d,\ell_1)$ in $\mathrm{polylog}$ space, and the paper's first open problem is whether $o_\varepsilon(\log s)$ distortion is achievable in $s^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{poly}(d\log\Delta)$ space — i.e. whether the same space-for-approximation trade the paper buys for $\ell_p$ exists for EMD. Indyk '01 on $\ell_\infty$ is the other anchor: his $O(\log_\rho\log d)$-approximation in $n^\rho$ space is, in retrospect, the $d^{\Theta(1/c)}$ version of the same level-set counting argument, and the main theorem can be read as replacing $d$ by the effective dimension $2^{\Theta(p)}$ of the $\ell_p$ ball.

A follow-up worth pursuing. The paper itself names the probabilistic-sketching model as open, and the obstruction is sharply localized: Lemma 2.14's far-side boosting is stuck at constant probability because the $T$ repetitions share one draw $y\sim\mu$, forcing Markov instead of Chernoff. Breaking that would need a sketch whose far-side success is already high-probability over $y$ for a fixed $x$ — e.g. by storing several independent $\pi$'s and level ladders whose failure events are negatively correlated in $y$, or by replacing "the $\pi$-first coordinate" with a sampled multiset whose certificate-finding probability concentrates. A high-probability far-side guarantee would immediately improve the ANN success probability from $(1-\varepsilon)^k$ to something that does not need $n^\varepsilon$ repetitions, i.e. it would move the trade-off curve, and it is the single cleanest technical question the paper leaves. A second, more conceptual direction: what is the sufficient statistic of $\mu$ for average-distortion sketching? For $\ell_p$ it is astonishingly thin — approximate coordinate-wise medians, $O(\log d)$ samples. For a non-product metric (EMD, edit distance) there is no reason to expect a coordinate-wise statistic to suffice, and a theory of "how many samples from $\mu$ does an average-distortion sketch need" would be a genuinely new axis, sitting between learning theory and sketching.

Connection to your work. Three places where this is directly usable rather than merely adjacent.

(1) The asymmetry is the dense-retrieval asymmetry, and it is where the space savings live. In vector search the document set is known at index time while the query is arbitrary and unknown — exactly the roles of $y\sim\mu$ and worst-case $x$ in Definition 1.1. Corollary 2.15 formalizes this: the query-side object needs $O(p/c)$ bits, the document-side object $2^{O(p/c)}$, because the decoder reads almost nothing from the query sketch. That is a theoretical counterpart to asymmetric distance computation in product/residual quantization (queries kept in full precision, documents quantized) and, more pointedly, to anisotropic vector quantization in ScaNN, whose loss is explicitly weighted by where queries fall relative to a datapoint. Average-distortion sketching gives you the right formal object for "this index is good for my corpus": worst-case non-expansion (never discard the true neighbor) plus average contraction (pruning is effective on typical pairs). The one-sidedness is not a technicality here — an admissible, never-over-estimating distance bound is exactly what a pruning filter in an IVF or graph index needs in order to be safe, and "effective only on average" is exactly the guarantee one actually wants from it. If you ever wanted to write down what a correct theory of learned pruning filters looks like, this definition is a strong candidate, and the $\mu$-independence of the worst-case side is the reason it composes with adversarial queries.

(2) Generative retrieval and semantic IDs. Core-Preprocess builds a depth-$O(\log n)$, arity-$2^s$ data-dependent tree in which each node recenters on the median of its own subset and emits $s$ bits that route a query to a child; a query descends one root-to-leaf path. That is structurally a semantic-ID hierarchy (hierarchical $k$-means or RQ-VAE residual quantization producing a docid string), and the proof of Lemma 3.5/3.6 is exactly the two guarantees you would want from such a hierarchy: non-expansion $\Rightarrow$ the relevant document is never routed away from the query's path (probability $\ge 1-\varepsilon$ per level, $(1-\varepsilon)^k$ overall), and average contraction $\Rightarrow$ the candidate set shrinks by a constant factor $3/4$ per level for typical documents. The quantitative content — $s=O((p/c)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits per level, and a $2^{\Theta(p/c)}$-vs-$O(p)$ codebook-size-against-approximation trade-off — is the kind of statement that is entirely absent from the generative-retrieval literature, which has no theory of how long a docid must be. A concrete theorem to aim for: _for a corpus distribution $\mu$ over embeddings, what is the minimum total docid length (bits per level $\times$ depth) such that beam search over a data-dependent hierarchy returns a $c$-approximate neighbor for typical queries, with one-sided safety for arbitrary ones?_ Theorem 2 is one instance of such a theorem, and the proof technique transfers.

(3) The lower-bound machinery is reusable for IR-flavoured impossibility results. Random-Multi-Index plus the Fact 4.8 incompressibility argument is a clean, portable template: a protocol that can repeatedly certify "this candidate is irrelevant" lets Alice compress her entire relevance vector, so each certified rejection is worth $\approx kt/d$ bits and the index must be large. That is directly the shape of a lower bound on docid length, on the size of a learned pruning model, or on the bit budget of a quantizer that must guarantee no false pruning — and it needs none of the geometry, only the "abstain or witness" structure. If you want lower bounds against learned index structures in the retrieval setting, this is the cheapest available hammer.

One last transferable idea with an empirical edge. The whole upper bound turns on a single measurable quantity: after max-stable rescaling $x_i\mapsto x_i/u_i^{1/p}$, the number $K$ of coordinates within a constant factor of the maximum, which for $\ell_p$ is $2^{\Theta(p)}$, and the growth profile $|G(\tau_{j-2})|/|G(\tau_j)|$ of nested superlevel sets. For real embedding distributions — anisotropic, clustered, low intrinsic dimension, hubness-ridden — that profile is something you can simply compute, and the analysis is instance-adaptive in it: the space is $(\text{profile ceiling})^{\Theta(1/c)}$, not $2^{\Theta(p/c)}$ per se. An empirical study of the superlevel-set growth profile of BERT/E5-style document embeddings, fed back into the same pigeonhole, would yield instance-specific space–approximation bounds for real corpora — a rare case where a purely theoretical sketching paper hands you a quantity worth measuring.

title: Pretrained Embeddings for E-commerce Machine Learning: When it Fails and Why?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-04

Pretrained Embeddings for E-commerce Machine Learning: When it Fails and Why?

Da Xu, Bo Yang (2023) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04330

Setting and problem

The object of study is the two-stage pipeline in which an embedding is produced once, frozen, and then consumed by many unrelated downstream models — the "embedding store" architecture that Appendix B describes concretely as a centralized pretrained-embedding service at an anonymized retailer ('ECOM').

Notation. Entities (items/users) live in $\mathcal X$; an embedding map $\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ (here $d=32$ throughout) is drawn from a class $\Phi$; a downstream predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ consumes it, so the deployed hypothesis is $f\circ\phi$. Two pretraining families are considered:

  • Contrastive (CL), instantiated as Item2vec on user behaviour sequences, minimizing the one-negative InfoNCE risk $\mathbb E\big[-\log \frac{e^{\phi(i)^\top\phi(i^+)}}{e^{\phi(i)^\top\phi(i^+)}+e^{\phi(i)^\top\phi(i^-)}}\big]$ over $(i,i^+,i^-)\sim P_{\mathrm{CL}}$, which factorizes as $P_{\mathrm{pos}}(x,x^+)P_{\mathrm{neg}}(x^-)$. Information is encoded in inner products.
  • Feed-forward (BERT / ALBERT-base) on item text, where pretraining is a composition $\mathcal G={f\circ\phi}$ and the embedding is the penultimate hidden layer. Information is encoded so that a linear head reads it.

Downstream consumption is likewise split into two decoders: inner-product decoding (kNN, inner-product-kernel SVM, written IP) and feed-forward decoding (logistic regression on $\hat\phi$ as a feature vector, written LR). Crossing these gives four pretraining–downstream configurations; CL-IP and BERT-LR are called homogeneous (encoder and decoder are the same kind of functional) and CL-LR, BERT-IP heterogeneous.

What the learner is given, and what it must produce, differs by task:

  1. Entity classification (item → shelf/department/genre): given frozen $\hat\phi$ and $n$ labelled items ($80/10/10$ split), output a classifier; scored by Micro/Macro-F1.
  2. Sequential recommendation: given frozen $\hat\phi$ and leave-last-one-out interaction sequences, output a ranker (MLP4Rec / GRU4Rec / Attn4Rec, two-tower, hidden dims ${32,16}$); scored by Hit@10, MRR@10, NDCG with full-catalogue ranking (they explicitly cite Krichene–Rendle to avoid sampled metrics).
  3. The selection problem, which is the real industrial question: given $K$ candidate embedding tables and downstream data, rank the candidates by eventual downstream performance without retraining the downstream model for each.

To make the generalization analysis well-posed they introduce an environment $\mathcal E=(\tau,P_X^{(0)},P_X^{(1)},P_Y)$ with $\tau:\mathcal X\to{0,1}$ the downstream labelling mechanism, and draw both pretraining and downstream distributions $P_\tau\sim\mathcal E$. The CL risk is decomposed $R_{\mathrm{CL}}=R^C_{\mathrm{CL}}+R^I_{\mathrm{CL}}$ into the parts with correct ($\tau(x^-)\neq\tau(x)$) versus false negatives. The comparison quantity is the excess risk $R_{\mathrm{task}}(\hat\phi)-R^*_{\mathrm{task}}$ where $R_{\mathrm{task}}(\hat\phi)=\mathbb E_{P_\tau\sim\mathcal E}\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim P_\tau}\ell(f_{\hat\phi,n}(x),y)$ and $R^*_{\mathrm{task}}=\min_{\phi\in\Phi}\mathbb E_{P_\tau}\min_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E\,\ell(f\circ\phi(x),y)$ is the jointly optimal risk.

The precise questions: (i) When the pretraining data, objective and hyperparameters are held fixed, why does downstream performance vary across independent pretraining reruns, and does the choice of downstream decoder control that variance? (ii) Is there a cheap, embedding-only statistic that predicts downstream performance well enough to rank candidate embeddings without running the downstream pipeline?

What the literature already knows: CL has downstream guarantees via latent-class arguments (Arora et al. 2019 is the canonical one, though uncited here); embeddings have been justified post hoc in specific domains (Arora et al.'s PMI latent-variable model, Allen & Hospedales on analogies, and the authors' own WSDM'21 predecessor "Theoretical Understandings of Product Embedding for E-commerce ML"); and NTK theory (Jacot et al.) says wide networks under GD behave as fixed-kernel predictors. The claimed gap is that none of this treats the interface — what the pretraining objective implicitly says about how the embedding may legitimately be read — and that no existing metric "attributes downstream performance to the embedding accurately," so practitioners resort to full retrain-and-measure.

Two non-obvious modelling choices carry most of the weight, and should be flagged before anything else:

(a) The randomness model. In §1 they posit that SGD returns not $\phi(x)$ but a random $\Phi(x)$ with $\mathbb E\Phi(x)=\phi(x)$, and — because initialization is coordinate-wise i.i.d. — with independent coordinates and (implicitly) independence across entities, so that $\mathbb E\langle\Phi(x_1),\Phi(x_2)\rangle\approx\langle\phi(x_1),\phi(x_2)\rangle$. The entire stability story rests on this: inner products are unbiased for the ground truth while individual coordinates are noisy. This is an idealization (embeddings of co-occurring items are strongly dependent through shared gradients), and it is a weaker statement than the one actually available — see the critique.

(b) Distribution mismatch is surgically removed, not modelled. In §3 they rebuild the pretraining data so that $x^+$ is drawn from the same downstream category as $x$ and $x^-$ from a different one, making $P_{\mathrm{CL}}$ and $P_\tau$ coincide; the $R^C/R^I$ decomposition plays the same role in the theory. So the paper is explicitly about model-structure effects in the absence of distribution shift — the one setting where conventional wisdom would predict no problem at all. That is the right experimental instinct and also the reason the results do not immediately transfer to the usual OOD case practitioners face.

The kernel formalism. $K_\phi:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, $K_\phi(x,x'):=\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle$, is p.s.d. with $\phi$ as the feature lift (so it is literally the linear kernel in embedding space). The NTK is defined on the image of $\phi$ with feature lift $\nabla f(\theta^{(0)};\phi(x))$: $\mathrm{NTK}(\phi(x),\phi(x'))=\langle\nabla f(\theta^{(0)};\phi(x)),\nabla f(\theta^{(0)};\phi(x'))\rangle$, obtained by dropping the $O(1/\sqrt q)$ remainder of the width-$q$ Taylor expansion and reparameterizing the intercept away. The structural claim is a composition identity: for a two-layer MLP, Cho–Saul's arc-cosine kernel gives $\mathrm{NTK}=1-\tfrac1\pi\cos^{-1}!\big(K_\phi(x,x')/(|\phi(x)||\phi(x')|)\big)$, and generally $\mathrm{NTK}(\phi(x),\phi(x'))=g(K_\phi(x,x'))$ for a scalar $g$ fixed by the architecture (extended to RNNs/attention via Yang's weight-sharing results). Example 1 adds the sequential case: a linear model on concatenated embeddings has dual Gram matrix $\Phi\Phi^\top$ generated by the sum kernel $K_{\mathrm{seq}}(\vec s,\vec s')=\sum_{i=1}^k K_\phi(x_i,x_i')$ (position-wise, i.e. the direct-sum RKHS over the $k$ slots — no alignment invariance).

"Predictability" is then defined operationally, twice. For classification it is the risk of the population kernel-mean classifier $f_\phi(x)=\mathbb E_{x'}[y'k_\phi(x,x')]/\sqrt{\mathbb E[k_\phi^2]}$ under 0–1 loss, which Prop. 1 bounds by one minus the kernel–target alignment against $K_Y(y,y')=\mathbf 1[y=y']$; empirically computed as $\sum_{x,x'}K_Y K_\phi\big/\sqrt{\sum_{x,x'}K_\phi^2}$ (eq. 8). For sequential recommendation it is the ranking metrics of an untrained, exposure-weighted kernel scorer (eq. 7). Worth stating plainly for calibration: no spectral objects appear — there is no eigenvalue decay of $K_\phi$, no effective dimension, no RKHS-norm/capacity trade-off anywhere in the paper. The "kernel analysis" is alignment-based and first-moment, not spectral.

Main idea

Two theses, one diagnosis and one instrument.

Thesis 1 (interface matching). The pretraining objective does not merely produce a vector; it fixes a protocol for reading that vector. CL writes information into inner products, so only inner-product queries are guaranteed to retrieve it; a feed-forward pretraining head writes information so that a linear readout retrieves it. Reading through the wrong protocol does not merely lose accuracy — it converts pretraining randomness into downstream variance. Empirically: across ten independent Item2vec reruns with identical data and hyperparameters, individual embedding coordinates fluctuate wildly while the loss/accuracy trajectories are essentially identical (Fig. 1); downstream item classification with LR on those embeddings has both lower mean and much larger standard error than inner-product-kernel SVM (Fig. 2); and in the controlled setting where pretraining and downstream distributions are made identical by construction, the two homogeneous cells (CL-IP, BERT-LR) beat the two heterogeneous cells (CL-LR, BERT-IP) (Fig. 3). Theorem 1 formalizes the claim as an asymmetry in generalization bounds: the homogeneous bound is purely $O(n^{-1/2})$ plus a complexity term, while the heterogeneous bound carries an extra $n$-independent floor $R\cdot\mathbb E_y|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)|_2$ — the expected spectral norm of the within-class covariance of the CL-optimal embedding. Prescription: force homogeneity, and the engineering handle given (Fig. A.1) is nicely concrete — in a two-tower downstream model, make the final fusion a dot product rather than an MLP, since that is the one layer you are free to change without touching the RNN/attention body.

Thesis 2 (kernel alignment as a cheap selection metric). Since the downstream NTK is a function of $K_\phi$, and since $K_\phi$ depends on $\phi$ only through inner products, $K_\phi$ is both (a) stable under CL pretraining randomness and (b) the right summary of what the downstream model has to work with. Proposition 1 bounds the kernel-mean classifier's 0–1 risk by $1-$ (alignment of $K_\phi$ with the label kernel), distribution-free. For sequential recommendation they take a different route: posit an exposure-aware next-item model $p(x_{k+1}\mid s)=\lambda p_0(x_{k+1})+(1-\lambda)e^{\langle\phi(x_{k+1}),\varphi(s)\rangle}/Z_s$, and show (Prop. 2) that the MLE of the sequence representation is $\hat\varphi(s)=\sum_{i\le k}\frac{\alpha}{p_0(x_i)+\alpha}\phi(x_i)$ — an exposure-discounted average of history embeddings — so the relevance score reduces to $\sum_i \frac{\alpha}{p_0(x_i)+\alpha}K_\phi(x_{k+1},x_i)$, again a pure function of $K_\phi$. In practice this is an IPS-weighted item–item kNN scorer with $p_0$ proxied by log popularity and $\alpha$ fixed at the average exposure probability (they report insensitivity to $\alpha$, which only rescales).

The headline empirical result is the deployment study: three structurally different candidate embeddings (Doc2vec on text = production control; complementary-item embeddings; KG embeddings) for item-page reranking. Standard offline replay evaluation with IPW cannot separate them (Recall@5/NDCG@5 all similar), whereas the kernel metric orders them Emb3 > Emb2 > Emb1 — which is exactly the ordering the three-week A/B/C test produced on GMV, units, orders and converted visitors, with significance at $\alpha=0.05$. The selling point is operational: the metric requires no downstream training, isolates the embedding from confounds (extra features, downstream architecture), and can be computed by downsampling.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever moves are the §3 controlled-pretraining design (resampling $x^+$ from the downstream class to annihilate distribution mismatch so that any residual gap must be attributable to architecture — a textbook-clean confound kill in an industrial paper), and the $R^C/R^I$ split that gives the theory the same hygiene. The MNAR detour is the best-motivated piece of theory in the paper: Prop. 2 derives exposure discounting from a likelihood rather than imposing it as a reweighting heuristic, and it lands on a conclusion the IPS literature reaches by other means. And the practical problem — versioned embedding-as-a-service, where a rerun with identical configs silently changes downstream metrics and you cannot afford a retrain per candidate — is real, under-discussed, and exactly the kind of thing that never makes it into academic papers.

That said, a reviewer-style read finds the theory considerably weaker than the prose claims.

1. The central empirical dichotomy may be an artifact. $K_\phi(x,x')=\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle$ is the linear kernel. So "inner-product-kernel SVM on $\hat\phi$" and "logistic regression on $\hat\phi$" are the same hypothesis class — linear functionals of the same frozen features — differing only in loss (hinge vs. logistic), in primal-vs-dual solution, and in whatever regularization defaults scikit-learn applied ($C=1$ for SVC with a precomputed, unnormalized Gram matrix; LogisticRegression's own $\ell_2$). Both "decode by inner product with a learned weight vector." The homogeneous/heterogeneous taxonomy therefore cannot be doing the work it is said to be doing in Figs. 2–3; whatever gap exists must come from implicit bias, conditioning and regularization scale, not from expressivity or protocol. Related: the labelling of BERT-LR as homogeneous is itself shaky — BERT's MLM head is a softmax over a linear map of the hidden state, i.e. inner products with output embeddings, so by the paper's own logic BERT could equally be classed as an inner-product encoder.

2. The right explanation is available and not given. The stability phenomenon has a clean, much stronger account than coordinate-wise unbiasedness: InfoNCE is invariant to the orthogonal group, $\langle Q\phi,Q\phi'\rangle=\langle\phi,\phi'\rangle$, so $\phi$ is identified only up to $O(d)$ (plus scaling). Functionals of the Gram matrix are gauge-invariant; coordinate-dependent functionals are not. That requires no distributional assumption about SGD noise, no coordinate independence, and no cross-entity independence — all three of which are dubious. It also makes a sharper prediction: a trained linear model is itself equivariant under $O(d)$ (rotate the features, rotate the weights), so the variance it suffers is a finite-sample/conditioning effect, not an identifiability one. The paper's i.i.d.-initialization story cannot distinguish these cases, and the distinction is exactly what a practitioner needs.

3. Theorem 1 does not establish a separation and does not isolate "mismatch". Both halves are upper bounds, derived by different techniques (a one-stage uniform-convergence argument versus a CL-to-supervised transfer argument). A larger upper bound for CL-LR is not evidence that CL-LR is worse; there is no lower bound and no matching. Worse, the two cells compared are BERT-LR vs. CL-LR — they differ in the pretraining objective as well as in homogeneity, so the theoretical comparison is confounded in precisely the way the §3 experiment was built to avoid. The decisive pair for the thesis is CL-IP vs. CL-LR (same embedding, different decoder), and that is not analyzed at all; neither is BERT-IP. Two of four cells are covered, and they are the two that cannot separate the hypothesis. Finally, the extra term $\mathbb E_y|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)|_2$ is a within-class spread quantity — an intra-class-concentration / class-collapse measure of the CL-optimal embedding, not a measure of encoder/decoder discrepancy. It vanishes exactly when CL does what good CL is supposed to do (collapse each latent class), so the theorem's own content is "the heterogeneous floor disappears for well-trained CL," which undercuts the unconditional advice to force homogeneity.

4. The NTK argument is self-fulfilling where it is invoked. "The optimization and generalization of $f(\theta;\cdot)$ is completely characterized by its NTK" holds in the infinite-width lazy regime — which is precisely the regime with no feature learning, i.e. the regime in which "the pretrained embedding kernel determines everything" is true by construction. The downstream models actually used have hidden widths ${32,16}$, about as far from the lazy limit as one can get while still calling it an MLP. In the feature-learning regime a downstream network can partially repair a misaligned embedding, which is the interesting failure mode for the proposed metric and is never tested. Also, $g$ in $\mathrm{NTK}=g(K_\phi)$ is fixed by the architecture, not learned, so "finding a good $g(\cdot)$ becomes easier in the downstream task" is not a statement the formalism supports. And the composition identity depends on $K_\phi$ only through the cosine similarity (the norms appear in the denominator), which quietly means the metric should probably be normalized per-item — a detail with real consequences for popularity-skewed embedding norms.

5. Missing related work on the paper's own central quantity. Equation (8) is, up to the constant $|K_Y|_F$, the kernel–target alignment of Cristianini, Shawe-Taylor, Elisseeff & Kandola (2001) — the paper cites the Shawe-Taylor & Cristianini textbook but not the alignment line, and describes the derivation as "a novel argument that relies only on the properties of kernel." Its modern descendants (CKA, Kornblith et al. 2019; HSIC) are also absent. The omission has a technical cost: their alignment is uncentered, and uncentered alignment is dominated by the mean embedding direction — for dense embeddings with a large shared component (endemic in e-commerce, where popularity induces a hub direction), uncentered alignment can rank embeddings by how large their common component is rather than by class structure. Centering is the first thing I would check in the released code.

6. Evaluation thinness. The correlation plots (Figs. 4–5) are generated by varying only Item2vec window size $\in{2,3}$ and #negatives $\in{2,3,4}$ — about six points per panel, from a single pretraining family, varying along essentially one quality axis. Any monotone quality proxy would correlate there; no correlation coefficients are reported in the text. The genuinely hard case — ranking structurally different embedding families — is the deployment study, which is $n=3$: one correct 3-way ordering, i.e. $p=1/6$ under random guessing. That is a valuable industrial anecdote and no more. Critically, no competing embedding-quality metric is ever evaluated: the only baseline is "retrain the downstream model," so the abstract's claim that "existing metrics do not attribute the downstream performance to embedding accurately" is asserted rather than demonstrated. Alignment & uniformity (Wang & Isola 2020), effective-rank criteria (RankMe, Garrido et al. 2023 — concurrent and directly competing), linear probing, and $k$-NN probe accuracy are all cheap and all absent.

7. Scholarly care. Every proof is deferred to "the online material," a GitHub repository (daxu5180/WebConf23) — nothing archival, so none of the three results can be checked from the paper. Eq. (7) as typeset equates $\exp\langle\phi(x_{k+1}),\hat\varphi(s)\rangle$ with $\sum_i w_i K_\phi$, which is wrong by an exponential (the identity holds for the inner product, by linearity).
