Prop. 2's $\alpha$ is said to depend on $Z_s$, but $Z_s$ depends on $\varphi(s)$, the estimand — so (6) is a frozen fixed-point iterate presented as a closed form, and the MLE of a $d$-dimensional $\varphi(s)$ from a single observed next item is not well-posed without regularization, which the statement does not mention. Prop. 1 is stated "with probability at least $1-\delta$" for a quantity, $R(f_\phi)$, that is fully deterministic (both $f_\phi$ and its risk are population objects — there is no sample to randomize over), and $\sqrt\delta$ enters so that the bound becomes vacuous as $\delta\to0$ and tightest at $\delta\to1$ — the opposite of a confidence parameter. And "algorithmic alignment," a real idea from Xu et al.'s ICLR 2020 "What Can Neural Networks Reason About?", is cited to Sturmfels' Algorithms in Invariant Theory [44]. These are individually small; together they suggest the theory was written fast and not re-read.

Net assessment: the engineering contribution (a training-free, gauge-invariant screen for ranking candidate embeddings, validated once against GMV) is worth the four pages. The theory is best read as motivation for that screen rather than as support for it, and the "use homogeneous configurations" prescription is better justified by the invariance argument the paper does not make than by the theorem it does.

Proof sketch

Three results. I reconstruct the strategies, since none is proved in the paper.

Theorem 1. Assumptions: $|\phi(x)|\le R$ for all $\phi\in\Phi$; pretraining and downstream data both drawn from the same environment $\mathcal E$; binary downstream classification; $\mathcal R_n(\Phi),\mathcal G_n(\Phi)$ the empirical Rademacher/Gaussian complexities of $\Phi$ on the pretraining sample. Guarantee (plain language): with probability $1-\delta$ over the pretraining draw, the excess downstream risk of the two-stage procedure is, for BERT-LR, bounded by a complexity term in $\mathcal G_n(\Phi)$ plus an $O\big((R+\sqrt{\log(8/\delta)})/\sqrt n\big)$ statistical term — everything shrinking in $n$. For CL-LR, where $\phi^*=\arg\min_\phi R^C_{\mathrm{CL}}(\phi)$, the analogous bound additionally contains $R\cdot\mathbb E_y|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)|_2$, which does not shrink with $n$: an irreducible floor. (The PDF's text extraction garbles the fraction bars; on the charitable reading both $\delta$-terms sit over $\sqrt n$, though $\mathcal G_n(\Phi)/n$ remains an odd normalization since Rademacher/Gaussian complexity conventionally already carries $1/n$, and the paper's own gloss — "the only non-concentrating term is $\sqrt{\log 8/\delta}$" — is loose.)

Strategy, homogeneous side. Decompose $R_{\mathrm{task}}(\hat\phi)-R^*_{\mathrm{task}}=[R_{\mathrm{task}}(\hat\phi)-R^*_{\mathrm{pre}}(\hat\phi)]+[R^*_{\mathrm{pre}}(\hat\phi)-R^*_{\mathrm{task}}]$. Because the downstream class (linear head on $\phi$) is of the same functional form as what stage-1 optimized over, the second bracket is controlled without any transfer step, and the first is standard two-stage ERM: symmetrize, bound by the Rademacher complexity of $\mathcal F\circ\Phi$, pass to Gaussian complexity via the Bartlett–Mendelson comparison (legitimate here because $\ell$ is Lipschitz and $|\phi|\le R$ bounds the margin), and close with McDiarmid for the $\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}$ deviation. The point of the proof is structural: no transfer lemma is needed, hence no extra term.

Strategy, heterogeneous side, and the key trick. Here $\hat\phi$ minimizes $R^C_{\mathrm{CL}}$, not any downstream risk, so one must convert a contrastive guarantee into a guarantee for a linear classifier. The canonical device (Arora et al. 2019) is to construct the mean/centroid classifier $w_y=\mathbb E_{x\sim P_X^{(y)}}[\phi(x)]$ and show its supervised loss is controlled by $R^C_{\mathrm{CL}}(\phi)$, then absorb the ERM over $n$ downstream samples via a Rademacher bound for linear predictors with $|\phi|\le R$. The gap to be paid is the heart of the matter: the contrastive loss scores $x$ against a random same-class partner $\phi(x^+)$, i.e. the logit is $\langle\phi(x),\phi(x^+)\rangle$; a logistic regression scores $x$ against a fixed direction $\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle$. Swapping a stochastic reference point for a deterministic one is a Jensen-type exchange, and the second-order cost of that exchange — bounded by Cauchy–Schwarz on the quadratic form $\mathbb E[(\phi(x^+)-w_y)^\top\phi(x)]$ — is exactly the operator norm of the within-class covariance $|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)|_2$, averaged over classes and scaled by the radius $R$. This is worth restating because it reframes the headline: the penalty is not "you failed to use an inner product" (the LR decoder does use an inner product); it is "the encoder's reference point was a random same-class sample, and your decoder replaced it with a single vector, so you pay the within-class spread." The $R^C/R^I$ decomposition is what licenses the step, since false negatives would break the "same-class partner" reading.

Proposition 1. Claim: with the kernel-mean (Parzen-type) classifier $f_\phi(x)=\mathbb E_{x'}[y'k_\phi(x,x')]/\sqrt{\mathbb E[k_\phi^2]}$ and $K_Y(y,y')=\mathbf 1[y=y']$, the 0–1 risk satisfies $R(f_\phi)\le 1-\mathbb E[K_YK_\phi]\sqrt\delta/\sqrt{\mathbb E[k_\phi^2]}$ — with the content being that risk is controlled by kernel–target alignment alone, irrespective of the underlying distributions.

Strategy. A first-moment argument on the margin. Let $M=y\,f_\phi(x)$. Then $\mathbb E[M]=\mathbb E[yy'k_\phi(x,x')]/\sqrt{\mathbb E[k_\phi^2]}$, and for $\pm1$ labels $yy'=2K_Y-1$, so the numerator is the (uncentered) alignment of $K_\phi$ with the label kernel while the denominator is $|K_\phi|_{L^2}$, which makes the whole quantity invariant to rescaling $\phi$. Since $R(f_\phi)=\mathbb P(M\le0)$ and $M$ is bounded above by $1$ after that normalization, one line of Markov gives $\mathbb E[M]\le\mathbb P(M>0)=1-R$, i.e. $R\le1-\mathbb E[M]$; the $\sqrt\delta$ in the stated version is presumably a Paley–Zygmund-style thresholded variant ($\mathbb P(M\le\sqrt\delta\,\cdot)$). So "a novel argument that relies only on the properties of kernel" is, at bottom, Markov's inequality applied to the kernel-mean classifier's margin — which is exactly why it is distribution-free, and exactly why it is loose (no variance information, no spectral information, and vacuous whenever alignment is small).

Proposition 2. Claim: under the exposure mixture $p(x_{k+1}\mid s)=\lambda p_0(x_{k+1})+(1-\lambda)e^{\langle\phi(x_{k+1}),\varphi(s)\rangle}/Z_s$ with $\phi$ frozen at $\hat\phi$, the MLE of the free parameter $\varphi(s)$ is $\hat\varphi(s)=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{\alpha}{p_0(x_i)+\alpha}\phi(x_i)$ with $\alpha>0$ depending on $\lambda$ and $Z_s$.

Strategy. An EM/stationarity argument. Differentiating the mixture log-likelihood in $\varphi(s)$ produces, for each history item, a responsibility weight $\lambda p_0/(\lambda p_0+(1-\lambda)e^{\langle\cdot\rangle}/Z_s)$ multiplying $\phi(x_i)$; setting the gradient to zero gives $\varphi(s)$ as a responsibility-weighted combination of the history embeddings, and replacing the responsibility by $\alpha/(p_0(x_i)+\alpha)$ — with $\alpha$ absorbing $\lambda$ and $Z_s$ — yields (6). Two honest caveats: $Z_s$ is itself a function of $\varphi(s)$, so this is a frozen fixed-point iterate rather than a closed form, and the softmax likelihood of a single next item is maximized by sending $\varphi(s)$ unboundedly along $\phi(x_{k+1})$, so some regularization or multi-step likelihood must be in play that the statement does not disclose. The payoff is nonetheless genuine: by linearity, $\langle\phi(x_{k+1}),\hat\varphi(s)\rangle=\sum_i\frac{\alpha}{p_0(x_i)+\alpha}K_\phi(x_{k+1},x_i)$, so the induced scorer is an exposure-discounted kernel kNN over the history — a function of $K_\phi$ alone, hence gauge-invariant and trainable-parameter-free, which is the property that makes it usable as a selection metric.

Broader context

The subfield is the theory of transfer from self-supervised pretraining, narrowed to the industrial pattern where the representation is produced by one team and consumed, frozen, by many others. The canonical theory question — "what does a small contrastive loss buy you downstream?" — was framed by Arora, Khandeparkar, Khodak, Plevrakis & Saunshi, "A Theoretical Analysis of Contrastive Unsupervised Representation Learning" (ICML 2019), whose latent-class argument bounds the supervised loss of the class-mean classifier by the contrastive loss plus an intra-class deviation term. Theorem 1's $\mathbb E_y|\mathrm{cov}(\phi^_)|_2$ is recognizably a cousin of that term, and Arora et al. is conspicuously uncited — reading the two together is the fastest way to see what is new here (the framing in terms of decoder structure) and what is not (the mechanism). The genuinely _spectral_ treatment this paper gestures at but does not perform is _HaoChen, Wei, Gaidon & Ma, "Provable Guarantees for Self-Supervised Deep Learning with Spectral Contrastive Loss" (NeurIPS 2021), where downstream error is governed by eigenvalues of the augmentation/population graph — i.e. the eigen-decay objects a reader expecting "kernel analysis" will look for and not find. On the metric side the lineage runs Cristianini et al., "On Kernel-Target Alignment" (NIPS 2001) → Kornblith et al., CKA (ICML 2019)_, and the direct contemporary competitors for _label-free_ prediction of downstream quality are _Wang & Isola's alignment/uniformity (ICML 2020) and RankMe (Garrido et al., ICML 2023)_, which uses the effective rank of the embedding matrix. A reader should treat this paper's metric as an explicitly _label-aware* member of that family; a head-to-head against RankMe and linear-probe accuracy on the same six Item2vec variants would have been a three-hour experiment and would have settled the paper's main empirical claim.

Follow-up I would actually pursue: replace alignment with a two-term spectral criterion. Alignment is a first-moment statistic and blind to the failure mode that matters most in production — collapse. An embedding can have high $\langle K_\phi,K_Y\rangle_F$ while $K_\phi$ is effectively rank-2, in which case any downstream model is capacity-starved. The natural fix is the standard kernel-ridge decomposition: for a target $f^*$ in the RKHS of $K_\phi$, excess risk splits into an approximation term in $|f^*|_{\mathcal H_{K_\phi}}$ and an estimation term in the effective dimension $\mathcal N(\lambda)=\mathrm{tr}(K_\phi(K_\phi+\lambda I)^{-1})$, governed by the eigen-decay $\lambda_j(K_\phi)$. That gives a pair (alignment, effective dimension) which strictly refines the paper's screen, remains gauge-invariant, is still computable by subsampling, and would unify this paper with RankMe. Second, and in my view the deeper opening: formalize the identifiability/gauge story the paper only gestures at. Define $G$ as the group under which the pretraining objective is invariant (for InfoNCE, $O(d)$ plus positive scaling; for two-tower, independent $GL$ actions on each tower subject to the pairing; for MLM, the output-embedding gauge), and prove that downstream estimators which are $G$-invariant functionals of $\hat\phi$ have variance not inflated by pretraining randomness, while non-invariant ones are inflated at a rate controlled by the curvature of the loss along the orbit. That is a theorem that would hold without the coordinate-independence fiction, would cover all four of the paper's cells plus every configuration it does not analyze, and would turn "use homogeneous configurations" from a heuristic into a checkable property of the consumer.

Connection to Shiguang's work — and there is a real one, in the gauge-invariance direction. Dense retrieval is the paradigm homogeneous configuration: trained with inner-product InfoNCE, served by MIPS. The paper's thesis therefore predicts, correctly, that exact dense retrieval is robust to pretraining reruns — recall@k depends on $\hat\phi$ only through its Gram matrix, so it is invariant to the unidentified $O(d)$ action. The interesting and, I think, underexplored consequence is that the ANN index is not. Product quantization, OPQ, IVF centroids, LSH hyperplanes and HNSW graph construction are all coordinate- and partition-dependent; none is $O(d)$-invariant. OPQ exists precisely because PQ's quality depends on a rotation, which is to say OPQ is a gauge-fixing step. So the paper's instability claim, restated properly, yields a testable and (to my knowledge) unproven statement for vector search: pretraining randomness is harmless for exact MIPS but not for quantization- or partition-based ANN, and the induced variance in recall@k at fixed memory budget should scale with the within-class (or within-cluster) covariance spectrum of the embedding — precisely the $|\mathrm{cov}|_2$-type quantity in Theorem 1. That is a clean theory-plus-measurement project, and the measurement half is cheap: ten reruns of the same encoder, one IVF-PQ index each, variance of recall@10.

For generative retrieval the link is sharper still and runs the other way. Semantic docids — DSI's hierarchically clustered IDs, TIGER's RQ-VAE codes — are built from embedding coordinates via quantization, making docid assignment maximally non-invariant to exactly the group the pretraining loss cannot pin down. In the paper's taxonomy, generative retrieval is a heterogeneous configuration par excellence: the embedding was encoded by inner products and is decoded by an autoregressive softmax over discrete tokens. The paper's framework predicts (i) semantic-ID instability across encoder reruns with identical configs, which would show up as unexplained variance in generative-retrieval results and is rarely reported; and (ii) that a kernel–target alignment screen — with $K_Y$ built from query–document relevance rather than class labels — could be used to pick the encoder before paying for codebook construction and seq2seq training, which is the expensive, non-interactive step. Both are defensible from what the paper actually proves, which is more than I can say for the claim that homogeneity is universally preferable. What the paper does not give you is any spectral or capacity statement about $K_\phi$, so it offers nothing directly on retrieval-side questions about intrinsic dimension, eigen-decay and ANN hardness — that gap is the opening, not a contribution.

title: Scaling Law with Learning Rate Annealing
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-03

Scaling Law with Learning Rate Annealing — Howe Tissue, Venus Wang, Lu Wang (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11029

Setting and problem

Fix everything about a pretraining run except the learning-rate schedule: model architecture and size N, training corpus, validation corpus, tokenizer, optimizer and its hyperparameters, batch size, weight decay, gradient clipping, and the peak learning rate η_max. What remains free is a schedule η : {1,...,s} → R_{≥0}, and what we observe is a trajectory: the validation cross-entropy L(s) at every step s, not just at the end. The object of study is therefore a functional L = 𝓛η, a map from (schedule, step) to validation loss, with everything else held fixed. The paper's claim is that this functional factors through two scalar summaries of the schedule:

L(s) = L_0 + A·S_1^{−α} − C·S_2,

where S_1(s) = Σ_{i=1..s} η_i (the "forward area," the area under the LR curve), and, with m_i = λ·m_{i−1} + (η_{i−1} − η_i), m_1 = 0,

S_2(s) = Σ_{i=1..s} m_i = Σ_{i=1..s} Σ_{k=1..i} (η_{k−1} − η_k)·λ^{i−k}

is the "annealing area": the running total of a one-pole (exponentially discounted) filter applied to the per-step LR decrements Δη_k = η_{k−1} − η_k. The constant λ ∈ (0,1) is the decay factor of what the authors call LR annealing momentum; it is a hyperparameter, not a fitted parameter, set to 0.999 in every experiment in the paper (they report 0.99–0.999 as the useful range, and note in a footnote that it could in principle be fitted, but is not). The four fitted quantities are L_0, A, α, C, all constrained positive. One implementation convention matters: during the initial LR warmup, S_1 and S_2 are computed as if η ≡ η_max, so warmup contributes nothing to S_2 and contributes its full nominal area to S_1.

Note S_2 is signed: annealing gives S_2 > 0, re-warmup gives S_2 < 0. Under a constant schedule S_2 ≡ 0 identically.

The question, stated precisely. Given the measured loss curve(s) {(s, L(s))} from one or two training runs in a fixed setup — in the headline experiment, a constant-LR run and a cosine run of 20K steps each — can one predict L(s) at every step for a different, unseen schedule in the same setup, possibly with a much longer horizon? The paper answers yes, to a mean relative error of roughly 0.15%–0.36%.

Why this is a gap. Chinchilla-style scaling laws (Hoffmann et al. 2022) fit L(N,D) = L_0 + A·D^{−α} + B·N^{−β} to one point per run: the final loss of a completed run with a completed annealing phase. Two consequences follow. (i) The within-run trajectory is discarded — in a 100-run sweep you throw away essentially all of the data you paid for, because intermediate checkpoints of a cosine run are not on the Chinchilla curve (they sit at partial degrees of annealing). (ii) The schedule itself is not a variable: the law has no slot for η(·), so it cannot say whether WSD beats cosine, what the optimal cooldown fraction is, or what re-warmup costs you. Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. both assert that the schedule does not change the form of the power law, and that schedule choice has little effect on the final loss provided the summed LR is large enough and the run ends with annealing to near zero — which is precisely the regime in which the schedule dependence is invisible by construction. This paper's contribution is to make the schedule the independent variable.

Modelling assumptions, flagged explicitly. 1. Sufficiency: L depends on the schedule only through the pair (S_1, S_2). This is a strong and genuinely falsifiable claim — it says two scalars are sufficient statistics for an entire schedule. 2. Separability and linearity: a power law in S_1, strictly additive with a term linear in S_2 (they test −C·S_2^ζ and get ζ̂ ≈ 1.125 with negligible fit improvement, so they keep ζ = 1). 3. Phenomenology, not derivation: the form is motivated by observations and analogies, fitted, and then tested out of sample. There is no theorem anywhere. 4. Fixed setup: N, data, η_max, batch size, warmup length, optimizer betas, and λ are all held fixed within a fit. In particular, since S_1 scales linearly with η_max at fixed schedule shape, the law predicts that raising η_max monotonically lowers the loss — i.e. it has no mechanism for an optimal or a too-large LR. The law is about schedule shape, not LR magnitude. 5. λ is in units of steps, so the memory window τ = 1/(1−λ) ≈ 1000 steps carries no dependence on batch size, token count, or model size.

Fitting protocol (reproducible as stated): precompute S_1(s), S_2(s) from the known schedule; minimise Σ_s Huber_δ(log L̂(s) − log L(s)) over (L_0, A, α, C) with δ = 10^{−3}, using L-BFGS via scipy.optimize.minimize from a grid of initialisations to dodge local minima; when fitting several schedules jointly, sum their objectives. Headline fit (594M non-embedding LLaMA-like, FineWeb train / RedPajama-CC validation, AdamW β = (0.9, 0.95), wd 0.1, clip 1.0, η_max = 2×10^{−4}, batch 4M tokens, seq 4096, 500 warmup steps):

L(s) = 2.628 + 0.429·S_1^{−0.550} − 0.411·S_2, R² = 0.99964.

Main idea

Two terms, two mechanisms.

A·S_1^{−α} is the "forward progress" term: a rectified power law in which raw step count s is replaced by LR-weighted step count Σ_i η_i. Interpretation offered: S_1 is a proxy for the total distance travelled in parameter space. Under a constant schedule it reduces exactly to the Chinchilla data term, L(s) = L_0 + (A·η_max^{−α})·s^{−α}, because every step of a constant-LR run is a legitimate "endpoint." That observation — constant LR makes every intermediate checkpoint a valid Chinchilla data point — is the hinge of the whole construction.

−C·S_2 is the extra drop that annealing buys. It exists because non-constant schedules show a sharp local loss decline exactly where the LR falls, which the power-law term cannot produce. Two refinements take it from a naive guess to the final form. First, a naive f(η) = C·η_s (loss reduction proportional to the current LR deficit). Second, the delay phenomenon: in purpose-built V-shaped and Λ-shaped schedules (LR descends linearly then re-ascends, or vice versa, with the descent slope varied over 0.1K/0.5K/1K/2K steps), the turning point of the loss curve consistently lags the turning point of the LR by 0.1K–1.1K steps, with longer lags for steeper descents, and longer lags for down-then-up than for up-then-down. They rule out the Adam second-moment timescale as the cause (β_2 ∈ {0.95, 0.99, 0.999} gives indistinguishable loss curves and identical delays — a clean, well-designed negative control), and show S_1 contributes to but does not explain the lag. Hence the ball-rolling-down-a-slope analogy and the exponentially weighted history in S_2.

A useful reading they do not give: the exact closed form is S_2(s) = Σ_k Δη_k·(1 − λ^{s−k+1})/(1−λ), and in continuous time the filter output satisfies m(t) ≈ η̄_τ(t) − η(t), where η̄_τ is the exponential moving average of the LR with timescale τ = 1/(1−λ). So S_1 = ∫η and S_2 = ∫(η̄_τ − η): the forward area is the LR mass consumed, and the annealing area is the accumulated deficit of the LR relative to its own recent history. Both are areas in the same units, which is why they sit together in one equation.

Headline results. - Fit on constant + cosine at 20K steps; predict the full curve at 60K steps for (a) constant, (b) cosine with η_min = 0.1·η_max, (c) DeepSeek's multi-step cosine (80/10/10), (d) WSD with 20% cosine cooldown, (e) a cyclic schedule with multiple re-warmups. Mean prediction errors 0.146%, 0.159%, 0.176%, 0.235%, 0.322%. The cyclic case is the most informative: the fitting curves contained no re-warmup at all, so the S_2 < 0 regime is genuinely out of support. - Robustness: a second hyperparameter setting (293M, 2M batch, 120K steps), an MoE model (8×106M, top-2, with load-balancing auxiliary loss, R² = 0.974 — the weakest fit in the paper), a 10× horizon extrapolation (fit on 30K steps, predict 350K steps / 1.4T tokens for a 1.7B model, 0.359% error), and post-hoc fits to published curves of BLOOM-176B and OLMo-1B. - Model-size extension: L(s,N) = L_0 + A·S_1^{−α} + B·N^{−β} − C·S_2·N^γ, motivated by the measured observation that the annealing drop grows with N. Fitted on N ∈ {85, 162, 595, 904}M and used to predict the curve at N = 1214M (R² > 0.998); a second setup fits 18.7M–1720M jointly. - Compute claim: <1% of the cost of a Chinchilla-style fit, which requires ~5050K steps of training to collect 100 endpoint points at interval K (less for WSD, where branch-and-cool reuse brings it to 12–22%).

Retrospective explanations. Given the fitted equation, |∂L/∂S_1| = αA·S_1^{−α−1} decays with training while |∂L/∂S_2| = C is constant. Early on, buying S_1 dominates (so constant LR beats cosine at short horizons — and they show the crossover, including the prediction that cosine's asymptotic slope is steeper so it wins at long horizons); late on, buying S_2 dominates (so you should cool down). From this they recover: cosine's cycle length should equal total steps and η_min should be 0 (longer cycle ⟹ incomplete annealing, shorter ⟹ S_1 sacrificed); WSD and multi-step cosine beat cosine because they give up a little S_2 for considerably more S_1; there is an interior optimal cooldown ratio (predicted parabola-like curves, optimum at roughly 10–20%); continual-pretraining re-warmup produces a loss spike proportional to the new peak LR followed by faster descent (S_2 < 0 then recovers), while re-warmup duration barely changes the final loss. The slogan: "the art of the LR schedule lies in the delicate balancing act between forward area and annealing area." Most strikingly, the equation contradicts Hägele et al.'s claim that 1−√(·) cooldown dominates cosine across settings: the law predicts 1−√(·) wins at a 10% ratio but loses badly at 50%, and a follow-up experiment at 50K steps confirms the crossover.

The most interesting part (reviewer-style critique)

What this is. A four-parameter empirical formula, fitted by robust regression to one or two autocorrelated loss trajectories, that predicts other trajectories in the same setup to a few parts in a thousand. That is a real and useful result. It is not a theory of anything, and the paper's rhetoric — "accurate theoretical verification," "theoretical insights into the crux of loss drop," a section titled "Theory" containing no theorem — oversells it consistently. I would ask for that language to be toned to "quantitative account" throughout.

Parameter count and flexibility. Four free parameters (L_0, A, α, C) plus one hand-set hyperparameter (λ), plus a warmup convention, plus a multi-start initialisation search; seven fitted parameters in the N-extended version. Against thousands of fitted points, that sounds parsimonious — but the point count is misleading, because a loss trajectory is extremely autocorrelated and the effective number of independent observations is far smaller. There are no confidence intervals, no bootstrap, no seed replicates, and no parameter-uncertainty analysis anywhere in the paper. For a result whose most interesting application is adjudicating schedule differences of ~5×10^{−3} nats, the absence of run-to-run noise estimates is the single most serious methodological gap. The refutation of Hägele et al. rests on single runs with gaps of that order.

That said, the usual "it's just a flexible fit" charge is weaker here than normal, and it is worth being fair about why. S_1 and S_2 are computed from the known schedule before any fitting, so once (L_0, A, α, C) are fixed the curve for a new schedule is fully determined — there is no slack to absorb a new schedule's shape. This is exactly what separates the paper from, say, Broken Neural Scaling Laws, which can fit a cooldown kink beautifully but has no mechanism to predict one for an unseen schedule. The cross-schedule tests are therefore real evidence, not fit quality in disguise.

Extrapolation vs interpolation. Better than expected. Three genuinely out-of-support tests: (i) the cyclic schedule with re-warmups, where S_2 < 0 was never seen during fitting; (ii) the 10× horizon jump (30K → 350K steps), out of support in S_1; (iii) the 1−√(·)-vs-cosine crossover at 50% cooldown, a prospective prediction that contradicted the literature and was then confirmed. (iii) is the best scientific moment in the paper, and the authors deserve credit for running the falsification test rather than only harvesting agreements. But: every held-out test is at the same N, data, η_max and batch size as the fit. η_max is never varied within a setup, so the law's behaviour under LR magnitude is completely untested — and as written it predicts, absurdly, that larger η_max always helps.

Does it transfer across scale? Thinly. The claim rests on: one held-out model size (904M → 1214M, a 1.34× extrapolation — essentially interpolation in log-N); a second multi-size setup (18.7M–1720M) that is fit only, with no held-out size; and post-hoc fits to BLOOM-176B and OLMo-1B curves, which are fits, not predictions. Worse, both multi-size experiments hold η_max fixed across a 14–90× range of N (2×10^{−4} and 1.381×10^{−3} respectively). Under any μP-style or empirical optimal-LR scaling, that means the small models are trained far from their optimal LR, so the fitted B·N^{−β} term absorbs LR-mismatch as if it were a size effect. The symptom is visible: β̂ = 0.137–0.158, against Chinchilla's ≈0.34. And γ̂ = 0.052–0.117 means the annealing bonus grows by only ~15% over a 14× size range — a barely constrained parameter whose justification (Fig. 7a) is three model sizes. "Extends to model sizes" should be stated as preliminary.

λ: the load-bearing hyperparameter. This is the deepest problem, and it is partly structural rather than merely a tuning complaint. λ is not fitted per setup in the paper — 0.999 everywhere — which is to their credit, and the footnote admits it could be fitted (at the cost of recomputing S_2 each iteration). But Sec. 6.1 shows the stakes: with λ = 0.999 the equation prefers 1−√(·) cooldown and a larger optimal cooldown ratio; with λ = 0.99 it prefers 1−square and a smaller ratio. So the headline "we overturn Hägele et al." conclusion is qualitatively contingent on a hyperparameter the authors chose by hand. They were not fishing — λ = 0.999 was fixed in advance across all experiments — but there is no preregistration, and a reader cannot distinguish the two.

Worse, and the authors half-admit it ("the selection of λ decides the balance point of S_1 and S_2"): from the exact form S_2 = Σ_k Δη_k·(1 − λ^{s−k+1})/(1−λ), each decrement's weight saturates at τ = 1/(1−λ) once it occurs ≳τ steps before the end. So S_2 saturates at O(τ·η_max) — about 0.2 here, giving a maximum annealing bonus C·τ·η_max ≈ 0.08 nats, which matches the measured drops nicely. But saturation at a fixed number of steps implies the model's optimal cooldown duration is O(τ) steps and therefore the optimal cooldown fraction must shrink as runs lengthen. The empirical folklore it is being used to explain (Hu et al.'s 10%, Hägele et al.'s 20%) is a roughly constant fraction. The paper reports optima "around 10% to 20%" across 20K–100K total steps without confronting this tension. Since λ is also indexed in steps, it cannot transfer across batch sizes or token budgets on any principled footing. The natural fix — and the right one, I think — is to run the memory kernel in S_1-time rather than step-time, which would make the law invariant to batch size and LR rescaling and would restore a scale-free optimal fraction. (The successor work, below, effectively does this.)

Can the subtractive term go unphysical? Yes, in two bounded ways, one of which the authors raise. (a) Since S_2 saturates at ≈ τ(η_max − η_min), the law's true asymptote as S_1 → ∞ is L_0 − C·τ(η_max − η_min) ≈ L_0 − 0.08, not L_0. So the loss can dip below its own "irreducible" constant, and L_0 cannot be read as an entropy floor — the asymptote is schedule-dependent, which is conceptually incoherent with the Chinchilla interpretation it inherits. (b) Sec. 6.3 notes that once η ≈ 0 the momentum keeps paying out, so the model predicts continued loss reduction while essentially no learning occurs; the artifact is bounded (it decays over ~τ steps) but it is exactly the regime that sets the predicted optimum. Their attempted fix, S_2 = Σ_i m_i·η_i^ε, fitted ε̂ ≈ 0 and was dropped — honestly reported, but it means the artifact remains. The divergence in the N-extended form (−C·S_2·N^γ → −∞) only bites at astronomically large N and is a non-issue in practice. Note that repeated sawtooth cycling cannot drive S_2 unboundedly positive: the filter (η̄_τ − η) has zero DC gain, so a schedule that returns to its baseline returns S_2 to zero — the annealing benefit is fully reversible, which is both a nice structural property and consistent with the re-warmup spike they observe.

Non-identifiability of (L_0, A, α). Well known from the Chinchilla replication literature, and the paper contains its own demonstration without noticing it. Sec. 5.1 takes the fitted model (L_0 = 2.628, α = 0.550, asymptote ≈ 2.55), generates endpoint losses for 20K–60K-step runs, refits a Chinchilla form, and obtains L_0' = 2.210, α' = 0.207 with R² = 0.996. So: data generated with an asymptote near 2.55 and an exponent of 0.55 is described, to R² = 0.996, by an asymptote of 2.21 and an exponent of 0.21. The fit statistic is blind to a 0.35-nat error in the asymptote and a factor-of-2.6 error in the exponent, because over a 3× range of horizon (L_0, A, α) is a sloppy direction. Consequences: (i) reported R² > 0.999 is near-meaningless rhetoric — the variance is dominated by the steep early descent, and any monotone power law scores 0.99; the zoomed relative-error panels and the mean prediction errors are the only informative statistics, and to their credit the paper shows them; (ii) the extrapolations to 500K steps used to adjudicate cosine cycle length (Fig. 9) and to 10K/100K steps for the constant-vs-cosine crossover (Fig. 10) sit precisely in the regime where this degeneracy bites, and are validated nowhere beyond 60K; (iii) the per-setup spread in the fitted parameters (L_0 ∈ [1.41, 2.80], α ∈ [0.416, 0.761] across setups) is consistent with this.

Incidentally, the gap between the within-run exponent in S_1 (≈0.55) and the across-run endpoint exponent in steps (≈0.21) inside the paper's own framework is a substantively interesting observation that the authors report and then walk past. It is a mechanism by which schedule choice contaminates measured Chinchilla exponents, and it speaks directly to the Kaplan-vs-Chinchilla reconciliation literature. I'd have led with it.

Smaller things a careful reader will notice. - The motivating argument for replacing s with S_1 is internally inconsistent: they argue parameter movement is ≈ η‖g‖ and that ‖g‖ falls with η, so movement declines "almost quadratically" — which would motivate S_1 = Σ η_i², not Σ η_i. The chosen form is defensible on other grounds (for Adam the update is approximately η × a normalised direction, so Σ η_i is the natural displacement proxy), but the stated derivation does not support it. Relatedly, the whole construction is probably Adam-specific; nothing is tested with SGD. - Warmup is modelled by pretending η ≡ η_max, so initial warmup contributes S_2 = 0 while CPT re-warmup — the same physical operation — contributes S_2 < 0. The same object is modelled two different ways depending on whether it happens at step 0. And Appendix A shows warmup length demonstrably changes the curve (0 / 100 / 500 steps differ), an effect the law as implemented cannot express. - Huber with δ = 10^{−3} on log-loss puts essentially all residuals in the linear regime, so the objective is effectively least-absolute-deviation on relative error; reporting R², a least-squares statistic, is inconsistent with it. - No baselines. There is no λ = 0 ablation (which would quantify whether the momentum kernel is needed at all, as opposed to the simple C(η_ref − η_s) form), and no numerical comparison against a no-S_2 power law — only visual evidence that it fails. - Loss only. Downstream retrieval/benchmark metrics are never evaluated; the loss-to-capability link is asserted by citation. - λ = 0.999 gives τ = 1000 steps = 4B tokens at 4M batch. That is a remarkably long memory for a quantity whose observed delays are 0.1K–1.1K steps; the coincidence is reassuring but also means τ is pinned by the delay experiments in exactly one setup.

Real strengths, not grudgingly. (1) The forward-area/annealing-area decomposition is a genuinely good parameterisation of a schedule. "The loss depends on the schedule through ∫η and a discounted ∫(−η̇)" is a sharp sufficiency claim, cheap to test, and — on the evidence here — approximately true over a wide family of schedules including ones with sign-reversed S_2. Reducing the infinite-dimensional schedule space to two scalars is the kind of move worth having even if the specific kernel is wrong. (2) It is falsifiable and was falsification-tested: the 1−√(·)/cosine crossover prediction was made from the equation, contradicted an existing published claim, and was then verified experimentally. That is better epistemic hygiene than most scaling-law papers. (3) It is genuinely cheap and practically useful: one or two curves in your setup, and you can choose a cooldown ratio, a cooldown function, a CPT re-warmup peak, or a horizon-appropriate schedule without new runs. (4) The β_2 control experiment ruling out the Adam second moment as the source of the delay is a well-designed negative result. (5) The limitations section is unusually honest: they report the failed ε and ζ variants, the λ-sensitivity, the η → 0 artifact, and that they do not understand the delay phenomenon.

The honest claim versus the framing. "Democratizes scaling laws" oversells on two counts. First, the <1% figure compares against a strawman protocol — 100 independent full cosine runs at a single N — whereas practitioners already reuse cooldown branch points (which the paper's own table concedes brings Chinchilla to 12–22%), and the N-extended version requires training 4–5 model sizes to full horizon, nowhere near 1%. Second, Chinchilla answers a different question: how to allocate compute between N and D. This law, as validated, answers: given a fixed setup and one or two curves in it, what does the loss trajectory look like under a different schedule. Those are complements, not substitutes. The defensible claim is strong enough on its own: within a fixed (N, data, η_max, batch) configuration, one or two training curves determine the full loss trajectory under arbitrary schedules to ~0.2–0.4% relative error, including horizons up to 10× longer and including re-warmup. I would accept the paper with that abstract, plus seed replicates and error bars.

Proof sketch

There is no theorem. There are four semi-formal arguments worth stating precisely, with their status.

(1) Why a power law in S_1 should hold pointwise, not just at endpoints. The one genuinely clean argument in the paper. Under a constant schedule, every step is indistinguishable from the final step of a shorter run with the same schedule. Chinchilla is empirically known to fit such final losses. Therefore, if Chinchilla's data term is correct, the entire constant-LR trajectory must follow L_0 + A'·s^{−α}, and the whole curve becomes admissible scaling-law data. This is a self-consistency argument, not a derivation of the power law — it inherits Chinchilla's empirical status — but it is valid and it is the reason the method gets thousands of fitting points for free. The passage from s to S_1 = Σ η_i is then a separate, weaker heuristic ("training discount": once annealing shrinks the step size, further steps buy less progress), and as noted above the stated η‖g‖ reasoning would imply Σ η_i², so the choice of Σ η_i is empirical.

(2) Why the annealing term takes the form it does. Chain: (i) observed shape similarity between the LR curve, the gradient-norm curve, and the loss curve across schedules suggests the gradient norm as a bridge; (ii) hence a term −f(η) added to the power law; (iii) naive guess f = C·η_s; (iv) the delay experiments show the loss turning point lags the LR turning point by O(10²–10³) steps, with lag increasing in slope steepness and asymmetric between down-then-up and up-then-down; (v) hence a one-pole memory, f = C·S_2. The physical picture offered is the "loss surface as a slide": optimisation slides down a trough (the power-law direction) while oscillating on the inner walls (the LR-noise direction); annealing shrinks the oscillation amplitude and so lowers the loss. This is the SGD-equilibrium / noise-ball intuition, but it is given only as a picture — no SDE, no quadratic model, no stationary-distribution calculation.

Worth making explicit what the missing calculation would say, because the discrepancy is informative. For a quadratic loss with gradient noise, the stationary excess loss is proportional to the step size: E[L] − L_ ∝ η (a noise floor). That predicts f ∝ (η_ref − η_s) — which is _exactly_ the paper's naive guess, and exactly what their S_2 reduces to at λ = 0 (then m_i = Δη_i and S_2 = η_0 − η_s). So the model's λ interpolates between the textbook noise-floor term and a time-smoothed version of it, and the step from λ = 0 to λ = 0.999 is justified purely by the measured delay, not by the equilibrium story. One can also see _why_ a memory kernel should appear: relaxation to the noise floor in a quadratic model takes time ~1/(ηh) per Hessian eigendirection, so a broad (power-law) Hessian spectrum yields a broad spectrum of relaxation times — and crucially, times that scale as 1/η, i.e. constant in S_1-time, not in step-time. A proper derivation would therefore predict (a) a _sum of exponentials* (plausibly a power-law kernel) rather than a single pole, and (b) a kernel indexed by accumulated LR rather than steps. Both predictions are testable and both point at the paper's two weakest choices. None of this is in the paper; it is the shape of the derivation the paper does not have.

(3) The S_1/S_2 trade-off argument. Semi-formal but valid as a consequence of the fitted form: |∂L/∂S_1| = αA·S_1^{−α−1} decreases monotonically along the run while |∂L/∂S_2| = C is constant, so there is a unique crossover after which marginal annealing beats marginal forward progress. This yields, qualitatively, the WSD shape, the interior optimal cooldown ratio, the cosine-cycle-equals-horizon result, and the constant-vs-cosine crossover in horizon. It is a derivation inside the model, with no independent content beyond the assumed functional form — "the art of LRS is the balance of two areas" is a restatement of the equation. It becomes non-vacuous only because it also makes quantitative predictions (the optimum ratio curves, the 1−√(·) crossover) that were checked.

(4) Limiting-case check: reduction to Chinchilla. Two cases. Exactly, for constant LR: S_2 ≡ 0, S_1 = η_max·s, so L(s) = L_0 + (A·η_max^{−α})·s^{−α} — the Chinchilla data term, with the LR magnitude absorbed into the prefactor (which is why A and η_max are not separately identifiable). Statistically, for other schedules: they sample 1000 parameter tuples from uniform priors (L_0 ~ U(1,3), A ~ U(0.3,0.5), C ~ U(0.2,0.6), α from a range written with a sign error in the text), generate endpoint losses for 5K–60K-step cosine and WSD runs, and refit the Chinchilla form, obtaining mean R² = 0.972 (cosine) and 0.979 (WSD), sd ≈ 0.054. This is a Monte-Carlo plausibility check, not a reduction: R² ≈ 0.97 on a dozen points over a narrow loss range is a loose criterion, the sd means some draws fit poorly, the priors are admitted to include implausible tuples, and — as discussed above — the refitted constants differ materially from the generating ones (L_0: 2.63 → 2.21, α: 0.55 → 0.21). The correct statement is: endpoint losses generated by this law are well approximated by a Chinchilla form over the practically relevant range, but with different and non-identifiable constants. Which is interesting in its own right, and not what "reduces to" usually means.

Broader context

Lineage. Hestness et al. 2017 established empirical power-law learning curves; Kaplan et al. 2020 fixed the canonical form in N, D and compute and reported that schedule choice does not change the form; Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla) corrected the compute-optimal allocation to D/N ≈ 20 using the endpoint-only parametric fit L = L_0 + A·D^{−α} + B·N^{−β}. Subsequent refinements extended the law to data constraints and repetition (Muennighoff et al. 2023), transfer (Hernandez et al. 2021), non-monotone and multi-break curves (Caballero et al. 2022, Broken Neural Scaling Laws), and mechanistic accounts in terms of Hessian/feature spectra and discrete skill acquisition (Bahri et al. 2021; Michaud et al. 2023). On the reliability side, Besiroglu et al.'s 2024 replication of the Chinchilla fit and Porian et al. 2024's reconciliation of the Kaplan and Chinchilla exponents both show how sensitive fitted exponents are to protocol — including to LR-schedule choices — which is the backdrop against which the identifiability critique above should be read.

The LR-schedule thread. Loshchilov & Hutter's cosine/SGDR; Smith's cyclical LR; Smith et al. 2018's LR-decay/batch-size duality; the WSD (warmup–stable–decay) schedule popularised by MiniCPM (Hu et al. 2024) and systematised by Hägele et al. 2024, whose key practical point is that a constant-LR trunk with a short cooldown lets you branch at many horizons and get Chinchilla-style endpoints at a fraction of the compute — which is the closest existing competitor to this paper's compute claim, and the right comparison rather than naive independent runs. On the orthogonal axis of LR magnitude: μP and μTransfer (Yang & Hu) make the optimal LR transferable across width; DeepSeek-LLM fit explicit power laws for optimal LR and batch size against compute; and more recent work (e.g. Bergsma et al. on weight decay / batch-size scaling and decay-to-zero schedules, and the "surge phenomenon" in optimal LR–batch scaling) maps the joint landscape. This paper is deliberately orthogonal to all of that: it models schedule shape at fixed magnitude, and inherits an untested monotonicity in η_max as a result. A complete law needs both axes, and nobody has it.

Two closely related directions worth knowing. 1. The direct successor: "A Multi-Power Law for Loss Curve Prediction Across Learning Rate Schedules" (Luo, Wen, Hu, Sun, Liu, Sun, Lyu, Chen; ICLR 2025, arXiv:2503.12811). Same problem, better functional form: instead of one exponentially-filtered annealing area, the loss reduction is a sum over LR decrements, each decaying as its own power law in the LR accumulated since that decrement. This is precisely the "kernel in S_1-time, broad spectrum rather than one pole" fix the quadratic-model reasoning above predicts; it reports lower prediction errors than the momentum law, and — importantly — uses the law as an objective to optimise over schedules, recovering WSD-like shapes with a brief linear-to-zero tail. If you read only one companion paper, read that one; this paper is the one that posed the problem well and the multi-power law is the one that answered it better. 2. Actual optimisation theory for schedules. Zamani & Glineur's optimal last-iterate stepsize sequence for convex Lipschitz problems, and Defazio et al.'s refinement framework (and schedule-free methods), derive linear-decay-to-zero schedules from worst-case last-iterate bounds in which quantities like Σ_i η_i and Σ_i η_i² appear naturally. That literature is the theoretical counterpart to this paper's phenomenology: it explains why annealing to zero is near-optimal at a fixed horizon, in a setting with guarantees but with no N- or data-dependence. Bridging the two — a bound whose horizon-dependence reproduces the S_1/S_2 trade-off and whose constants connect to the Hessian spectrum — is the open problem.

A follow-up worth running. Treat the schedule-to-loss map as a response functional and estimate the annealing kernel nonparametrically instead of assuming a single pole. Concretely: fix a setup, train K runs with deliberately rich, near-orthogonal LR perturbations (chirps, step trains at varied spacings, sawtooths of varied period and phase) around a constant trunk. Conditional on (L_0, A, α), the model L = L_0 + A·S_1^{−α} − Σ_k Δη_k·w(s−k) is linear in the kernel w, so w can be recovered by ridge/Tikhonov regression and compared against the one-pole w(u) = (1 − λ^{u+1})/(1−λ). Three things fall out. (i) Is w one-pole, or a sum/continuum of exponentials (equivalently, a power law)? (ii) Is w indexed by steps or by accumulated LR? Reparameterise u as ΔS_1 and test whether the recovered kernel collapses across runs with different η_max and batch size — if it collapses in S_1-time, the optimal cooldown fraction becomes scale-free and the tension with the 10–20% folklore dissolves. (iii) Does superposition even hold? Multi-cycle schedules test additivity directly, and the leading nonlinearity (a second-order Volterra term) is where the model will first break. This is cheap at 100M–500M scale, settles the paper's single most contingent choice, and yields a falsifiable prediction tied to the Hessian-spectrum theory of scaling laws.

Connection to Shiguang's work — candidly. The vector-search link is an analogy and I would not push it: ANN recall-vs-memory-vs-latency curves have their own empirical trade-off laws, and "parameterise a build schedule by two scalar functionals" is a methodological echo, not a result that transfers. The generative-retrieval link is less forced. DSI-style and docid-generation models are trained with the same token-level cross-entropy objective, so the functional form has a real chance of applying to their training curves out of the box — which makes one question genuinely interesting rather than merely applied: the −C·S_2 term is a bounded, reversible, end-of-training loss reduction, concentrated in the last O(τ) steps and (on the noise-floor reading) attributable to shrinking the stochastic oscillation around a minimum rather than to moving further downhill. Ranking metrics are argmax/top-k functionals of the output distribution, not expectations of the log-likelihood. So: does the annealing-induced CE drop buy Recall@k and MRR at the same rate as an equal CE drop bought by more forward progress? There is no reason to expect so — sharpening a distribution around already-correct modes may do almost nothing for the ranking of near-ties, or disproportionately much. That is a well-posed, cheap, theoretically motivated experiment, and the law gives you the instrument for it (you can predict matched-CE pairs of schedules in advance and compare their retrieval metrics). For dual encoders the picture is worse and therefore also interesting: the contrastive loss is not a likelihood, it depends strongly on batch composition and negative mining, and the "every intermediate checkpoint of a constant-LR run is an endpoint" argument that underwrites the whole construction is much shakier — so whether (S_1, S_2) remains sufficient there is an open and genuinely uncertain question. Beyond that, the most portable idea is the abstraction itself: sufficient statistics for an infinite-dimensional training/configuration schedule, and the claim that a high-dimensional design (a schedule, a curriculum, an index build plan) enters the outcome only through a small number of area-like functionals. That framing is reusable; the specific one-pole kernel in this paper probably is not.

title: Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-03

Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale — Gollapudi, Gupta, Singhal, Min (2026) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01538

Setting and problem

The task. Fix a corpus {D_1,...,D_N} and a query Q. In in-context retrieval (ICR) as this paper operationalizes it, the entire corpus is serialized into the model's context, the query is appended, and the model autoregressively emits a document identifier, not a span and not an answer. Concretely (App. A), each document is laid out as [BOS]Doc {code}: {text} ... (Doc {code})[EOS] with code a four-digit string in {0,...,9999}, documents truncated at T_doc = 300 tokens (18 of which are the identifier wrapper, so truncation bites at 282 tokens of text). After all N blocks, a query block is appended carrying an instruction prefix, the query, and four answer slots. The model decodes d_1 d_2 d_3 d_4 by a digit-by-digit constrained beam search over the depth-4, branching-10 tree (App. K: beam width 25, per-step prune k_step = 5, return depth 5). The metric is Recall@1 over the decoded code (Recall@5 and HotpotQA Recall@2 in App. K; LIMIT Recall@k in App. L.1). "Gold" means the BEIR qrel-positive passage for that query — single-gold on MS MARCO and NQ, two golds on HotpotQA and on LIMIT.

Two structural choices that define the regime. (i) Block-sparse attention (following BlockRank): document tokens attend causally only within their own block; the query block attends to the whole corpus and causally to itself; the mask is materialized with FlexAttention. (ii) RoPE reset per document: positions restart at 0 at every [BOS], and the query sits at position 300. Together these make the prompt permutation-invariant over documents up to the identifier token, and make the corpus KV cache query-independent and per-document cacheable — which is why the authors also drop the query prefix used by prior ICR work, at a cost in accuracy, so that one prefill can serve many queries. The important consequence for the rest of the paper: there is no positional decay story available, and no "lost in the middle" story. Whatever degrades with N degrades for set-cardinality reasons, not positional ones.

Notation of §4. Layers L ∈ {0,...,27}, heads h ∈ {1,...,16}, per-head dim d_head. All probing happens at the last token of the query block, immediately before the first generated digit d_1. With post-RoPE query q^h_L and keys/values k^h_{L,t}, v^h_{L,t} at prefill position t:

s^h_{L,t} = (q^h_L · k^h_{L,t})/√d_head, α^h_{L,t} = exp(s^h_{L,t})/Σ_{t'} exp(s^h_{L,t'}), u^h_L = Σ_t α^h_{L,t} v^h_{L,t}, a_L = [u^1_L;...;u^H_L] W^O_L.

Prefill tokens partition into the gold document's tokens G and the rest Ḡ. Three measurements:

  • AttnRank. Collapse a document to one per-head score with the ColBERT MaxSim operator, MaxSim^h_L(d) = max_{t ∈ d} s^h_{L,t}. Then R^{(h)}_L is the fraction of queries where argmax_d MaxSim^h_L(d) = d_, aggregated two ways: R^sum_L (rank by Σ_h MaxSim^h_L(d), check top-1) and R^any_L (at least one head ranks d_ strictly first).
  • GoldShare. By linearity of u^h_L in the attention weights, a_L = a^G_L + a^Ḡ_L; report ‖a^G_L‖/‖a_L‖ next to ‖a_L‖.
  • First-digit accuracy. Logit-lens probe: push a_L through the final RMSNorm and lm_head, take max probability over the ten digit tokens at the d_1 slot. Explicitly framed as a coarse onset indicator, not a calibrated probability.

Note what AttnRank is: a sum (or max) over heads of a MaxSim over tokens of a d_head-dimensional inner product. That is a late-interaction scoring function computed inside the attention mechanism. This matters later.

Contrast with dense/vector retrieval. A bi-encoder computes f(Q) ∈ R^d and g(D_i) ∈ R^d offline, scores by inner product, and returns argmax_i ⟨f(Q), g(D_i)⟩. Three properties: the per-document representation is fixed and query-independent; the score is unnormalized, so the argmax is invariant to adding or removing candidates; and the search is sublinear via ANN. The paper's reference point is Qwen3-dense-0.6B: the same Qwen3-0.6B backbone, last-token pooled, ℓ₂-normalized, trained on the same RLHN-filtered data with in-batch contrastive loss plus KL distillation from Qwen3-Embedding-8B teacher scores (App. E). This is a well-constructed control — data, backbone and teacher held fixed, only the inference-time mechanism varies.

ICR inverts all three properties. Document representations are recomputed as attention keys/values and interact with the query through H×L heads; the score is passed through a softmax that couples all N candidates into a convex combination; and attention compares the query against every key, so cost is linear in N with no ANN analogue. App. Q makes the systems consequence brutal: Qwen3-0.6B has 28 layers, 8 KV heads of dim 128, so bf16 KV is 112 KiB/token, i.e. ≈101 GiB for the 0.95M-token MS MARCO corpus at N = 10,000, sharded over 8 GPUs by context parallelism — against ≈20 MB for a 1024-dim bf16 dense index. Three orders of magnitude.

Contrast with reranking. The prior ICR literature (BlockRank, ICR², QRHeads) scores a small candidate pool already produced by a first-stage retriever. The candidate set size is fixed at train and test time, so neither of this paper's two challenges arises. The paper's whole framing is that a retriever must satisfy (C1) million-token corpora and (C2) generalization to N far beyond training — and that (C2) is precisely what distinguishes a retriever from a reranker and what prior work skipped.

Contrast with long-context QA / needle-in-a-haystack. Three differences, and the paper is right to insist on them. First, the context is not one coherent sequence but a set of mutually irrelevant documents — hence block sparsity and RoPE reset are legitimate, and the problem is set-cardinality scaling, not discourse modelling. Second, the output is an identifier, so the task is pure localization with no generative credit. Third, and most sharply: the distractors are hard negatives, not unrelated filler. The evaluation corpus is built by taking 400 queries, their golds, and 24 hard negatives per query mined with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, then unioning to 10,000 documents; smaller N are formed by keeping all 400 golds and subsampling the rest. NIAH distractors share nothing with the needle; here every distractor is in the top-25 of a strong 8B embedder. The paper's most quotable evidence for the distinction is MSA-4B, which reports near-perfect RULER/NIAH yet falls to 16.0 Recall@1 on MS MARCO at N = 10k — below a 0.6B dense retriever (20.2). Synthetic long-context scores do not predict retrieval under hard negatives.

The length-generalization question, precisely. Training uses b = 16 queries × 16 documents (1 pruned positive + 15 hard negatives) prefilled once into a shared cache, so every model is trained with exactly 256 documents in context — roughly 22–26k tokens, just under Qwen3-0.6B's 32k native window. Evaluation sweeps N ∈ {500, 1000, 2500, 5000, 10000} on MS MARCO (948k tokens at max) and HotpotQA (1.16M), capped at N = 8,607 for NQ (1.20M). So the extrapolation factor in document count runs from ≈2× to ≈40×; the paper's "10× beyond training" refers to holding up to ≈2.5k documents / ≈500k tokens.

The questions asked. (1) With the right training and architecture, can a small decoder LM act as a corpus-scale retriever at million-token scale and extrapolate well beyond its training N? (2) When it fails, why — what is the mechanism? (3) Can targeted modifications derived from that mechanism recover the gap to a same-backbone dense retriever? (4) Does ICR buy anything a fixed embedding cannot express, tested on LIMIT?

Modelling assumptions that carry weight. - 0.6B scale, one epoch, ~100M training tokens, 8×A100, trained only to emit four-digit codes. App. O: this costs 6.6 MMLU and 9.0 HellaSwag points, so the "collapse retrieval and generation into one model" motivation is not demonstrated — the artifact is a retriever. - Four-digit identifiers cap N at 10,000. This is an architectural ceiling, not an attention ceiling. "Million token scale" is really "10,000 documents of ~100 tokens". At N = 10k the code space is exactly saturated. - Codes are sampled uniformly at random per training step, breaking any association between code, semantics, and position. This is motivated (training IDs would otherwise be a strict subset of inference IDs, inviting absolute-position overfitting — and indeed BlockSearch-position, the prior recipe, collapses to near-zero by N = 5k) but it also destroys all hierarchical structure in the decoding tree. - "Gold" is a BEIR qrel, with RLHN LLM-judge-pruned false negatives in training but not in evaluation. - LIMIT is 50,000 one-line biographies, queries of the form "Who likes Joshua Trees?", two golds each, relevance purely lexical set membership. It was constructed to expose the dimension/rank limits of single-vector embeddings. Scaling is N = 46 (golds only, "LIMIT-small") to 10,000 (≈8k to ≈1.7M tokens). - Single query sample per corpus size, no seeds and no error bars — the authors say so in the conclusion.

Main idea

BLOCKSEARCH = prior ICR recipe + three changes. Starting from BlockRank-style block-sparse ICR on Qwen3-0.6B: (1) randomized per-document identifier codes, replacing sequential position-indexed IDs; (2) in-batch negatives adapted to ICR — prefill all b×16 documents once and score every query in the batch against the shared corpus, turning one prefill into b training signals (this is what fixes the training corpus at 256 documents); (3) an on-policy auxiliary loss against exposure bias in digit decoding (App. F, Alg. 1). The third is the most interesting of the three. Teacher-forced CE on the gold code trains each digit conditioned on the gold prefix, but at inference digit t conditions on the model's own possibly-wrong prefix. So: roll out a code â from the model with gradients off; for each position t, restrict the 16 candidates to those whose first t−1 digits match â_{<t} and build a teacher distribution over the 10 digits as a candidate-weighted vote q_t(d) ∝ Σ_{k ∈ M_t} w_k·1[c^{(k)}_t = d] with w_k ∝ exp(r^{(k)}/τ) from Qwen3-Embedding-8B relevance scores; then replay the four answer positions with gradients on, conditioned on the rollout prefix. Total loss L = L_CE + λ·L_aux, λ = 0.5 ramped in. The authors correctly identify q_t as a DAgger expert: at every state on the model's own trajectory it says what should have been done. There is also EMA-0.95 KL distillation from the teacher.

Headline results on the base model (fig. 1, Table 2, all Recall@1 ×100). At small N, ICR is at parity with the dense control: 95.8 vs 95.5 on MS MARCO at N = 500 (≈45k tokens), 97.0 vs 99.0 on HotpotQA. Ablations separate the contributions: -position (prior recipe) collapses to near-zero by N = 5k on all three datasets; -offpolicy trails the full model (MS MARCO 15.0 vs 18.8, HotpotQA 6.2 vs 13.0 at N = 5k), so randomized codes and the on-policy loss give distinct gains. Against the concurrent MSA-4B (≈7× larger, trained with a far larger long-context budget, hence not subject to C2), BLOCKSEARCH matches or beats it at N ≤ 2500 (MS MARCO 95.8/75.2/43.8 vs 93.8/70.2/42.2) and loses at large N (18.8 vs 27.5 at 5k; 0.2 vs 16.0 at 10k). But everything collapses past ≈500k tokens: MS MARCO at N = 10k is 0.2 for BLOCKSEARCH against 20.2 for the 0.6B dense retriever. HotpotQA 0.5 vs 79.5. That is the gap the rest of the paper attacks.

The diagnosis (§4), in three moves.

Move 1 — layer roles. At N = 500, R^sum_L rises across L11–L20 (the "retrieval band") while first-digit accuracy is flat; first-digit accuracy then jumps sharply at L18→L19 (the "decode band"). So there is a clean separation between where relevance is computed and where the identifier is committed.

Move 2 — the recall/generation gap. Sweeping N: R^sum_19 falls 0.98 → 0.00 (at N = 10k), tracking generation recall exactly. R^any_19 decays more slowly — 0.98 at 500, 0.51 at 2.5k, 0.33 at 5k (where R^sum_19 is already 0.06) — but by N = 10k it too is gone (0.08; best layer L11 reaches 0.14). So over the intermediate range, individual heads still find the gold document while the heads stop agreeing; at the extreme, even individual heads lose it.

Move 3 — the vector-level swap, which is the paper's real contribution. The authors then make the sharp point that a per-head ranking is not what the rest of the model sees; what it sees is a_L, into which gold's value vectors enter in proportion to post-softmax mass, not rank. Table 1 (L19, MS MARCO, medians over 100 queries): at N = 500, ‖a^G_19‖ = 43.03, ‖a^Ḡ_19‖ = 17.47, ‖a_19‖ = 47.48, GoldShare 0.91. At N = 1k: 30.99 / 21.11 / 45.36 / 0.74. At 2.5k: 7.64 / 33.64 / 43.03 / 0.19. At 5k: 2.10 / 34.61 / 36.90 / 0.06. At 10k: 0.21 / 29.88 / 30.27 / 0.01.

The layer keeps writing into the residual at ~64% of its original amplitude while the content of that write is silently replaced: a gold-token average becomes a non-gold-token average of comparable norm. This is the right framing and genuinely better than the usual "attention entropy increases" telling — the failure is not that the layer goes quiet, it is that the layer confidently writes the wrong thing, so no downstream gain control can detect the problem. App. H nails down what replaces gold: the shared Doc first token (a sink) only grows from 0.21 to 0.35 of the output length, whereas other documents' content grows 0.28 → 0.87. And the L19 output becomes near-query-independent (median cross-query cosine 0.47 → 0.90), while the shrinking gold piece stays query-specific (0.30 → 0.36). The model is not collapsing to a default answer though: 78 distinct codes for 100 queries at greedy decode at N = 10k.

App. G supplies the per-head accounting at L19, restricted to the six heads that carry retrieval signal (4, 5, 7, 9, 12, 13 — the other six are sinks that give gold mass exactly 1/N at all N). Gold mass is m_G = σ(lse_G − lse_Ḡ); as N goes 500 → 10k, s^max_G falls 25.31 → 13.86 and the gap lse_Ḡ − lse_G goes −1.59 → +6.34, so gold mass falls 0.823 → 0.0018: a 7.94-nat (≈2800×) drop in log-odds.

Generality (App. N). Not backbone-specific. A BLOCKSEARCH on SmolLM2-360M reproduces the whole picture with the bands shifted deeper (retrieval L17–L23, decode from L24) and the L23 GoldShare falling 0.64 → 0.00 at preserved magnitude. And zero-shot Gemini-3-flash on the same MS MARCO setup falls 95.0 → 16.2 between N = 500 and N = 10k with no task training at all.

The two fixes (§5).

Length-aware softmax. (a) Additive sink, à la StreamingLLM / gpt-oss: append a learned per-layer scalar b_L to the denominator, so weights sum to ≤1 and a diffuse layer writes a smaller residual update. Length-awareness is only implicit, injected at training time by sampling N_eff ~ logU(128, 5000) and using b_L + α·log(N_eff/N_0) as the effective threshold. (b) SSMax: multiply pre-softmax scores by s·log N with per-layer learned s_L initialized to 0.43; length-awareness is explicit and applies unchanged at eval.

Document-level sparse attention. Run L0–L15, score each document by R^sum_16(d) (i.e. the same QK-MaxSim quantity from §4), keep the top B = 256 documents in dense attention from L17 on. Doc-level rather than token-level because a document is a coherent unit. App. J: at N = 10k the gold survives the top-256 shortlist for 96.2% of queries (sink 96.2%, SSMax 93.5%), and the recall@B curve is flat from 256 to 1024.

Results (Table 2, MS MARCO / HotpotQA at max N; dense control in brackets). N = 10k MS MARCO: base 0.2, sink 2.5, SSMax 16.5, routing 18.8, SSMax+routing 20.5 [dense 20.2]. HotpotQA N = 10k: 0.5, 1.0, 56.8, 78.5, 72.5 [79.5]. NQ N = 8.6k: 0.2, 1.5, 30.3, 34.6, 34.3 [39.6]. Recall@5 (App. K) tells the same story (MS MARCO N = 10k: base 0.2, routing 47.5), so the collapse is not a top-1 artifact.

LIMIT (§6, Table 3, Recall@1, "any gold in top 1", n = 1000). SSMax+routing: 0.501 / 0.305 / 0.281 / 0.262 / 0.202 / 0.135 at N = 46/500/1k/2.5k/5k/10k; Qwen3-dense: 0.176 / 0.080 / 0.061 / 0.047 / 0.035 / 0.029; random chance 0.043 at N = 46. Base and sink go to ~0 by N = 2.5k. So the headline 13.5 vs 2.9 at ≈1.7M tokens.

What this does and does not show. It does show: (i) a 0.6B ICR model can be trained to parity with a same-backbone, same-data dense retriever at small N, and — after the fixes — at N = 10k on MS MARCO and (nearly) HotpotQA; (ii) the dominant large-N failure mode is softmax dilution at the decode-onset layer, with the gold piece of the attention write being swapped out for a distractor average at preserved norm, reproduced on two backbones; (iii) the fixes are derived from the diagnosis and the diagnosis predicts their relative efficacy (sink, which shifts the denominator uniformly, barely helps; SSMax, which rescales its N-dependence, helps a lot); (iv) on a lexical task designed against embeddings, ICR beats a same-backbone dense retriever by 4.7× at a million-token corpus.

It does not show: that ICR is practical (101 GiB of KV vs 20 MB of index; attention is linear in N while ANN is sublinear); that the collapse is solved (SSMax+routing is still declining at 0.135 on LIMIT, and gold still gets only 0.019 of L19 attention mass at N = 10k); that ICR expresses relevance notions embeddings cannot in any strong sense (see OBLIQ below); that retrieval and generation can be unified (App. O); or that the mechanism is causal rather than tightly correlated (no activation patching).

The most interesting part

The paper's own numbers support a much sharper version of the "present but not readable" thesis than the version the paper states, and one of its tables appears to state a version flatly inconsistent with its own analysis.

(1) The defensible, and genuinely striking, result is the routing recall, not R^any. At N = 10k on MS MARCO, in the same forward pass, in the same model, from the same QK-MaxSim scores: ranking documents by R^sum_16 and taking the top 256 retains the gold document for 96.2% of queries (App. J); ranking by R^sum_19 and taking the top 1 succeeds for ~0%; "some head ranks gold first" for 8% (§4.2); and the model's own decode succeeds for 0.2% (Table 2).

Identifying one document among 10,000 is log₂ 10⁴ ≈ 13.3 bits. The attention scores at L16, as a ranking function, reliably supply 13.3 − 8 = 5.3 of those bits. The decoder extracts approximately zero. That is a 96%-vs-0.2% gap between what the attention geometry knows and what the model says, measured on the pre-softmax scores of a layer the model itself is using. The paper reports this in an appendix, framed as a sanity check on the routing budget. It is in fact the cleanest statement of the paper's thesis, and it is why the routing fix works at all: routing is not adding information, it is re-reading information the model already had through a different aggregator (top-B hard selection) instead of through the softmax.

The paper does make the correct conceptual move here, and it deserves credit: §4.2 explicitly refuses the easy conclusion, noting that the R^any/R^sum gap "might suggest the per-head signal can be recovered by a better aggregator. But what the rest of the model sees is not a per-head ranking; it is the layer's attention output a_L, into which gold's value vectors enter in proportion to their post-softmax mass, not the per-head ranking." The information is present in the score geometry and absent in the normalized readout, and the normalized readout is the only channel to the rest of the network. A rank-1 signal in s does not survive a softmax that divides by N competitors.

(2) The quantitative upgrade the paper leaves on the table: recall is a function of gold attention mass, essentially independent of how that mass was obtained. Cross-referencing Table 2 (Recall@1) with Table 9 (gold L19 mass) across the three checkpoints and five corpus sizes — a juxtaposition the paper never makes — gives fifteen (model, N) cells whose mapping from gold mass to Recall@1 is monotone to within one 2.3-point inversion: mass 0.0018 → 0.2 recall; 0.0034 → 2.5; 0.018 → 18.8; 0.0195 → 16.5; 0.028 → 21.2; 0.057 → 33.8; 0.100 → 45.2; 0.102 → 43.8; 0.142 → 49.8; 0.478 → 75.2; 0.521 → 75.2; 0.625 → 74.5; 0.823 → 95.8; 0.853 → 96.5; 0.915 → 95.5. The two decisive comparisons are the off-diagonal ones. Same N, different mass: at N = 10k, sink has mass 0.0034 → 2.5 recall and SSMax has 0.0195 → 16.5. Same mass, different N: vanilla BLOCKSEARCH at N = 5k has mass 0.018 → 18.8, and SSMax at N = 10k has mass 0.0195 → 16.5. So gold's post-softmax share at the decode-onset layer, not N, is the controlling variable; N acts only through it. If this held under a proper intervention it would be close to a sufficient-statistic claim, and it would be the paper's strongest result. It is left implicit.

(3) The paper's own analytical justification for SSMax does not hold in the trained model, and the paper half-admits it. §5.2 argues SSMax works because multiplying scores by s·log N makes gold's advantage grow with N: with a gap Δ over a typical distractor, gold's weight is ≈ 1/(1 + N^{1−sΔ}), bounded iff sΔ > 1. But Table 10 reports that under SSMax, from N = 500 to 10k, Δs^max_G = +7.06 while Δ lse_Ḡ = +12.64 — SSMax amplifies the distractor bulk nearly twice as much as it amplifies gold — leaving a 6.64-nat (764×) odds drop, more than double the 3.00 nats that pure 20× counting would explain. So sΔ < 1 empirically: the stated mechanism's own sufficient condition is violated, gold mass still decays polynomially, and yet Recall@1 goes from 0.2 to 16.5. SSMax does not work for the reason given. Combined with (2), the honest account is: SSMax buys about one order of magnitude of gold mass at N = 10k (0.0018 → 0.0195), that lands the model at the mass level a vanilla model has at N = 5k, and the recall it gets is the recall that mass level buys. SSMax is a calibration shift along a fixed mass–recall curve, not a change in the asymptotics. §6 concedes the asymptotic point ("routing delays but does not prevent the inevitable"), but §5's framing oversells the sΔ > 1 story as a remedy.

(4) An apparent internal contradiction a reviewer must flag. The first row of Table 2 is labelled "BLOCKSEARCH attn., R^any_19" and reports 100.0, 100.0, 99.8, 100.0, 100.0 on MS MARCO at N = 0.5k, 1k, 2.5k, 5k, 10k. §4.2 and fig. 3(b) measure the same labelled quantity on the same dataset and report 0.98, —, 0.51, 0.33, 0.08. These cannot both be right. If Table 2's row is really R^any_19 over all N candidates, §4 is wrong and the entire dilution narrative needs rewriting; if §4 is right, Table 2's row is mislabelled or computed over a restricted candidate pool, and as printed it is an 80-point-over-dense "attention oracle" row that readers will take as the paper's upper bound. The charitable reading is a labelling slip, but the paper never explains the row in text — and that row is the single most load-bearing number for the "information is present but not readable out" thesis. Two smaller inconsistencies in the same section: §5.2 quotes SSMax at "17.8 vs. 20.2 on MS MARCO at N = 10k" where Table 2 says 16.5; and §5.2/the abstract quote SSMax+routing as 20.0 where Table 2 says 20.5.

(5) The causal claim is not established. The argument is: GoldShare collapses with N, recall collapses with N, and two interventions aimed at the softmax restore both. Strong circumstantial evidence, but the obvious direct experiment is missing: patch a_19 (or just the gold slice a^G_19) from a small-N forward pass into a large-N forward pass and see whether the decode recovers. The paper has every piece needed and doesn't run it. The need is sharpened by App. H's own numbers: the L19 output becomes 0.90-cosine-similar across different queries at N = 10k, yet greedy decoding still produces 78 distinct codes for 100 queries. If L19's attention write were the sole channel, decodes should be far more degenerate — so query-specific information clearly survives elsewhere in the residual. The dilution story is about one channel, likely the dominant one, but its sufficiency is asserted rather than shown.

Other weaknesses, specifically.

  • Scale. 0.6B, one epoch, ~100M tokens of retrieval-only fine-tuning, trained at a single corpus size of 256 documents. There is no sweep over training N, so the paper cannot separate "softmax dilution is fundamental" from "the model never saw a large denominator". The deeper confound is App. N: zero-shot Gemini-3-flash reaches 16.2 at N = 10k with none of the fixes, versus 16.5 for SSMax and 20.5 for SSMax+routing. The paper's best modified model barely exceeds an untuned frontier model. That is compatible with dilution being real and with scale substituting for the fix — precisely the alternative hypothesis the paper wants to rule out and cannot, at 0.6B with one query sample and no seeds.
  • The sink is not evaluated as an inference-time mechanism at all. App. D: "At evaluation the gate is disabled entirely... the learned b_L stay in the checkpoint but do not affect attention." They verify re-enabling it is a no-op. So BlockSearch-sink is a training-time regularizer, not a length-aware softmax modification, and the §5 conclusion "a learned constant cannot rescale the denominator's N-dependence" — correct as algebra — is drawn from an experiment where the constant was switched off.
  • Is "comparable to a same-backbone dense retriever" a fair bar? Partly. The control is unusually well-matched, which is to the authors' credit, and parity on HotpotQA at N = 10k (78.5 vs 79.5) is meaningful. But on MS MARCO the bar is 20.2 Recall@1 — a very degraded operating point, produced by construction: the corpus is the union of 24 hard negatives per query mined by Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The distractors are selected to be confusable under exactly the dense-embedding geometry the baseline uses. Parity at 20% on a dense-adversarial corpus is not parity in deployment, where the practical bar is a 0.6B-to-8B embedder plus ANN at 20 MB and millisecond latency. And there is no BM25 or sparse-lexical baseline anywhere in the paper.
  • The LIMIT claim is a comparison of two bad numbers, and the obvious baseline is absent. LIMIT is lexical set membership; BM25 and sparse retrieval handle it well, a central point of the benchmark's own paper. BLOCKSEARCH-SSMax+routing gets 0.135 at N = 10k and only 0.501 at N = 46 — it fails LIMIT-small, where 46 documents fit comfortably inside the training regime and random chance is 0.043. Beating a 0.6B dense retriever 4.7× while failing the 46-document version of the task does not establish that ICR expresses relevance notions embeddings cannot. Also, the routing-only variant — best on MS MARCO and HotpotQA — is simply not run on LIMIT.
  • Evaluation breadth, and a buried negative result. Three BEIR datasets with 400 queries each, one sample per corpus size, no seeds, no variance. More importantly, App. M reports OBLIQ (analogical math, analogical prose, descriptive tweet retrieval), and essentially everything is zero: BLOCKSEARCH variants at R@1 ∈ [0.000, 0.007], R@5 ∈ [0.000, 0.029]; dense 0.014/0.057 on Math, 0.009/0.025 on Writing. The dense retriever wins on two of three tasks. The entire "retrieval behavior beyond inner-product similarity" motivation from the introduction is tested in App. M and comes back negative, and the main text reports only the single lexical benchmark where ICR wins. That asymmetry is the paper's least defensible editorial choice.
  • The extrapolation experiments are confounded by code assignment. Codes are assigned by position in the sorted corpus, so a fixed passage receives a different four-digit code at each N. Footnote 5 checks this (s^max_G moves by ≤0.17), which is the right check and largely defuses it. Two confounds are not checked: the code space saturates at N = 10k, and hard-negative density varies with N by construction.

Proof sketch

The paper has no theorem about learning or retrieval capacity. It has one trivial exact identity, one semi-formal scaling claim, and a log-odds decomposition — all analyses of the softmax function, not guarantees about what a trained transformer can or must do.

(a) The additive sink is exactly a sigmoid gate (Proposition 1, App. I). With Z = Σ_{t'} exp(s^h_{L,t'}) = exp(lse(s)), α̃^h_{L,t} = exp(s^h_{L,t})/(Z + exp b_L) = α^h_{L,t}·σ(lse(s) − b_L) = α^h_{L,t}·g^h_L. One line of algebra, and the right interpretation: the sink does not change the relative per-token weights at all, it only scales the whole head's residual write by a gate comparing how much pre-softmax mass the logits concentrate against a learned threshold. This is exactly why the sink cannot fix dilution: a multiplicative gate on a head whose readout has already become a distractor average suppresses the write but does not restore gold's share of it. Formally, g^h_L cannot alter argmax_d or the ratio ‖u^{h,G}_L‖/‖u^h_L‖; it is strictly a norm control.

(b) The dilution scaling claim, and the SSMax threshold (§5.2, App. G). The one claim with real content. Let gold's best score exceed a typical distractor score by Δ with Θ(N) distractor positions. Under standard softmax, m_G ≈ e^{s_G}/(e^{s_G} + N e^{s_G−Δ}) = 1/(1 + N e^{−Δ}), so for fixed Δ gold mass decays as Θ(e^Δ/N) and the log-odds of gold against the rest fall by exactly log N. The required score gap to hold m_G = Ω(1) is therefore Δ = Ω(log N) — the gap must grow without bound in N.
