Under SSMax every score is premultiplied by s·log N, so the gap becomes sΔ·log N and m_G ≈ 1/(1 + N^{1−sΔ}), bounded away from 0 iff sΔ > 1. That is the whole mechanism: the single analytical lever is that log N in the exponent converts the linear-in-N denominator growth into a polynomial N^{1−sΔ} with a tunable exponent. Two lines, correct.

The empirical check is where it gets interesting, and the paper reports it honestly even though it undercuts the framing. Measured at L19 over the six retrieval heads, N = 500 → 10k (20×): BLOCKSEARCH loses 7.94 nats (2800×) with Δs^max_G = −11.45 and Δlse_Ḡ = −2.57, ending at gold mass 0.0018; -sink loses 7.56 (1929×), −9.56 / −1.45, mass 0.0034; -SSMax loses 6.64 (764×), +7.06 / +12.64, mass 0.0195. Pure counting predicts log 20 = 3.00 nats. The vanilla model loses 7.94, so 4.94 nats come from gold's own score eroding, not from the denominator growing: s^max_G falls 25.31 → 13.86. This is a second, distinct failure that the "dilution" label obscures and that the 1/(1 + Ne^{−Δ}) model cannot produce (Δ is assumed fixed there). Whatever it is — distribution shift in the key statistics, interaction with the re-randomized codes, a representation-collapse effect — it is the larger term, and the paper's analysis does not explain it. And SSMax sits in the sΔ < 1 regime where its own bound gives no protection, yet still improves Recall@1 by ~80×. So the proof sketch is sound as softmax algebra and does not explain the empirical result it is invoked to justify.

(c) What a real theorem here would have to say. The implicit impossibility statement, gestured at but never written down: if ‖q^h_L‖ and ‖k^h_{L,t}‖ are bounded (as they are after RMSNorm with bounded weights), then s^h_{L,t} ≤ ‖q‖‖k‖/√d_head is bounded, so Δ is bounded, so m_G = O(1/N) — standard softmax attention cannot maintain Ω(1) mass on a single token as N → ∞ with bounded representations. Escaping requires rescaling scores with N (SSMax), shrinking the effective N (routing), or decomposing the decision into steps each over a small candidate set (hierarchical identifiers — see below). This is essentially the Veličković et al. "softmax is not enough for sharp size generalisation" result, which the paper cites and applies rather than extends. The genuine novelty in §4 is not theoretical: it is the vector-level measurement — showing the consequence of dispersion is not a loss of amplitude but a content substitution at preserved amplitude, with Tables 1 and 11 identifying the replacement as other documents' content (0.28 → 0.87) rather than a generic sink token (0.21 → 0.35). That is an empirical contribution, and a good one.

Broader context

The line this sits in. The "long-context LM subsumes retrieval" claim originates with Lee et al. (LOFT, 2024), evaluated on proprietary Gemini and without controlled distractor difficulty — this paper is explicitly the controlled replication, and the headline finding is that the claim does not survive hard negatives at corpus scale. The intermediate literature retreated to reranking over small pools: BlockRank (whose block-sparse mask and sequential-ID prompt format this paper inherits and then modifies), ICR², QRHeads. The mechanistic substrate is the retrieval-heads line — Wu et al. showing a sparse subset of heads carries long-context factuality, Olsson et al. on induction heads, Geva et al. on FFNs as key-value memories — all of which the "retrieval band / decode band" decomposition builds on. On the pathology side, Veličković et al. and Barbero et al. ("Transformers need glasses", over-squashing) give the formal and representational account of softmax flattening; StreamingLLM and the gpt-oss null-attention mechanism give the sinks; SSMax gives the log N rescaling. Also worth noting the title's allusion: Jacob et al., "Drowning in documents: consequences of scaling reranker inference", which found cross-encoder rerankers degrade as the candidate pool grows — the same shape of result one stage earlier in the pipeline, and a reminder that this is not an attention-specific pathology but a general candidate-set-scaling pathology of learned scorers.

LIMIT and the limits-of-embeddings argument. Weller et al., On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval (arXiv 2508.21038) is the paper LIMIT comes from, and its argument is the most relevant one here: for a binary qrel matrix A ∈ {0,1}^{|Q|×|D|}, a single-vector bi-encoder with embedding dimension d can realize the top-k ordering only if d is at least on the order of the sign-rank (equivalently, the relevant communication-complexity/matrix-factorization rank) of A. Since realistic qrel patterns have sign-rank growing with the number of distinct relevance patterns, no fixed d suffices; LIMIT is the concrete instance where 46 documents already break strong embedders. That is a capacity/dimension lower bound. This paper's contribution, read in that frame, is to exhibit a different and non-overlapping lower-bound mechanism for the alternative: ICR escapes the rank bound (nothing is projected to a fixed d; the score is a deep function of the query and document token sequences) but inherits a resolution bound from normalization. Dense retrieval fails because the score function is too low-rank; attention retrieval fails because the score function's output is forced through a simplex constraint that couples all N candidates, so the usable gap must grow like log N. The two mechanisms are orthogonal, which is why this paper's LIMIT result is directionally real even though the absolute numbers are poor.

Two closely related directions to track. (i) MSA-4B, the concurrent work: same generative in-context citation task, scaled to 100M tokens with a 4B model and a large long-context budget. It is the "just train it longer and bigger" answer to this paper's question, and this paper's most useful finding about it is that near-perfect RULER/NIAH coexists with 16.0 Recall@1 on MS MARCO at N = 10k — below a 0.6B dense retriever. If you ever need a citation for "synthetic long-context benchmarks do not measure retrieval", that pair of numbers is it. (ii) Hierarchical / length-generalizable sparse attention — Leng et al. on length generalization in hierarchical sparse attention, MoBA and its optimization follow-up, Hu et al. on causal-retrieval attention. The routing fix here is a crude, single-level, inference-time instance of that family; the systems framing in App. Q ("attention that is simultaneously sparse, differentiable, and GPU-efficient, together with KV-cache compression, is the central systems problem for this direction") is the right read.

A follow-up worth running: put the hierarchy in the identifier, not in the attention mask. The paper randomizes codes uniformly, for the good reason that sequential position-indexed IDs overfit absolute position. But a uniformly random bijection is the worst possible decoding tree for a dilution-limited decoder. At N = 10k with random codes, choosing d_1 requires the model to aggregate attention mass over the ~1,000 documents sharing each leading digit, with no semantic coherence among them — so every digit decision is taken at the full corpus-level denominator. Compare semantic/hierarchical docids from generative retrieval — DSI, NCI, RQ-VAE semantic IDs: there, prefix d_{<t} is a coarse cluster, so decision t discriminates among O(10) semantically coherent groups, i.e. an effective candidate set of size O(1) at every step. The concrete experiment: replace random four-digit codes with codes from a residual-quantized clustering of the in-context corpus (recomputed per corpus, so no retraining dependence on corpus identity — this preserves ICR's key advantage over parametric generative retrieval), and measure whether the required score gap per decoding step becomes O(log 10) instead of O(log N) — i.e. whether log N dilution can be amortized into log_10 N decisions each facing an O(1) denominator. Three things make this testable cheaply with the paper's own apparatus: GoldShare should then stop collapsing with N (it would collapse with branching factor instead); routing should become redundant (the first digit is a router); and the position-overfitting problem the randomization was introduced to solve does not return, because clusters are content-defined, not position-defined. Two supporting experiments the paper also owes: activation patching a^G_19 from small-N into large-N to turn the correlational dilution story into a causal one, and a sweep over training corpus size (256 is the only value tested).

Connection to Shiguang's work, and why it is more than a surface link. Three threads.

Capacity vs resolution as two distinct lower-bound regimes. For single-vector dense retrieval, Weller et al. give the obstruction: sign-rank / dimension. This paper hands you the raw material for the attention-side analogue, and it is a different kind of bound — not about what orderings are representable, but about what is recoverable from a normalized readout. The formal statement one would want proved: _for a single softmax attention head with representations of bounded norm, and a downstream readout that is Lipschitz in u^h_L, exact identification of one gold document among N requires a pre-softmax gap Δ = Ω(log N); hence with ‖q‖‖k‖/√d_head ≤ C, identification fails for N > exp(Θ(C))._ That is a clean, provable statement and it is not in this paper — the paper has the 1/(1 + Ne^{−Δ}) algebra and the measurements, but never states the obstruction as a bound or quantifies the Lipschitz readout side. Note the appealing symmetry with the dense case: the dense bound is about the dimension d of the representation, the attention bound about the dynamic range C of the scores. Capacity and resolution. A theory of retrieval covering both would be a real contribution, and the empirical mass–recall curve extracted above (recall is a monotone function of gold mass, nearly independent of N and of checkpoint) is exactly what a resolution-side theory should predict.

Retrieval by attention is late interaction with a lossy aggregator. This is hiding in plain sight in §4.1. The paper's own retrieval signal is Σ_h max_{t ∈ d} ⟨q^h_L, k^h_{L,t}⟩/√d_head — it borrows the MaxSim operator from ColBERT and cites it as such. So BLOCKSEARCH's internal scoring function is literally a 16-head, 128-dim-per-head late-interaction scorer. Late interaction is known to break single-vector rank bounds (a max of inner products is piecewise linear, not bilinear, and its sign-rank behaves very differently from a d-dim inner product's), which is a principled explanation for the LIMIT gain that the paper does not give: the expressivity comes from late interaction, not from "being a language model". But where ColBERT aggregates MaxSim scores by a sum and takes an unnormalized argmax — both N-invariant operations — attention aggregates by a softmax-weighted convex combination of value vectors and reads out through a nonlinear decoder. So the clean framing is: _ICR = late interaction (expressivity gain, N-invariant in principle) + softmax aggregation (resolution loss, Θ(log N)) + generative decode (further loss)_. The paper measures all three losses separately without naming the decomposition: routing recall@256 = 96.2% is the late-interaction score's quality, R^any_19 = 0.08 is what survives top-1 ranking, GoldShare = 0.01 is what survives normalization, and Recall@1 = 0.2% is what survives decode. Those four numbers at one N are a loss budget for retrieval-by-attention, and writing them down as such is a paper.

Generative retrieval's docid decoding. The paper's own related-work framing — generative retrieval stores the corpus in parameters and needs retraining on corpus change, ICR stores it in context and does not — is correct but understates the shared problem. Both decode an identifier autoregressively, and both therefore face the question of how much of the corpus must be marginalized over per decoding step. Parametric generative retrieval handles this with semantic/hierarchical docids; ICR here handles it with uniformly random docids and consequently pays the full log N at every step. That suggests a unified formal object worth defining: for an identifier scheme with branching factor B and depth D (B^D ≥ N), and a scorer with bounded dynamic range C, what is the achievable recall as a function of (B, D, C, N)? Random flat codes are B = 10, D = 4 with the full corpus in every denominator; semantic codes shrink the effective denominator per step; routing shrinks it externally. A single analysis covering all three — and covering dense retrieval as the D = 1, unnormalized, rank-limited special case — would be exactly the "formal theory of retrieval by attention vs retrieval by inner product" one would want, and this paper is the best empirical scaffolding for it that currently exists.

One practical note for reading: treat §3–§5 numbers as directionally reliable (the dense control is unusually well-matched) and the §6 LIMIT framing as oversold (App. M's OBLIQ results are negative across the board, including against dense). And do look at Table 2's first row with suspicion — as printed, the "R^any_19 = 100.0 at every N" row contradicts fig. 3(b) and §4.2, which report 0.08 at N = 10k for the same labelled quantity on the same dataset.

title: Replicable Uniformity Testing
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-03

Replicable Uniformity Testing — Sihan Liu, Christopher Ye (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10892

Setting and problem

The object. Fix a domain [n]={1,...,n} and let p be an unknown distribution on it, accessible only through i.i.d. samples. Write U_n for the uniform distribution and d_TV(p,q) = (1/2)·sum_x |p_x − q_x|. An algorithm A draws a multiset T of m samples, also tosses internal coins r, and must output a single bit in {ACCEPT, REJECT}. The resource being counted is m (sample complexity); running time is not the issue here (everything is linear-time).

Classical uniformity testing. Given the promise that either p = U_n or d_TV(p,U_n) ≥ ε, output the correct one of ACCEPT/REJECT with probability ≥ 2/3. A long line of work (Goldreich–Ron's collision tester; Paninski; Valiant–Valiant; Diakonikolas–Kane–Nikishkin; Acharya–Daskalakis–Kamath; Diakonikolas–Gouleakis–Peebles–Price) pinned the complexity at Θ(√n·ε^−2), which is the baseline to beat. Note the two regimes hidden in that bound: m ≤ n (strongly sublinear, collision/empty-bucket regime) and m > n (each bin seen many times).

Replicability. Definition 1.1, from Impagliazzo–Lei–Pitassi–Sorrell (STOC '22): a randomized A : X^m → Y is ρ-replicable if, for every p, Pr_{r,T,T'}[A(T;r) = A(T';r)] ≥ 1 − ρ, where T, T' are two independent sample sets from the same p and r is a single shared random seed used in both runs. Three modelling points deserve flagging, because the whole paper lives on them.

  1. The seed is shared, the data is not. This is the "shared randomness" model: two labs run the same published procedure with the same published random string (or the same fixed hash/threshold table) on freshly collected data. Without shared r the requirement is far stronger and essentially forces near-deterministic output; with shared r it is the right abstraction of "same protocol, different sample". In this paper the seed is extremely cheap: it is literally one real number r_0 ~ Unif[1/4, 3/4].
  2. The quantifier is over all p, with no promise. This is the phrase "replicable under arbitrary distributions", and it is the crux. For p with 0 < d_TV(p,U_n) < ε the tester has no correctness obligation at all — it may accept or reject — but it must do the same thing across runs with probability 1 − ρ. Standard optimal testers compare a statistic to a fixed threshold; in the middle regime the statistic straddles that threshold and the output is a near-fair coin flip, i.e. maximally non-replicable. The scientific motivation given is exactly this: two groups testing the same ground truth p* reach opposite conclusions purely from sample noise, which the public reads as procedural error.
  3. Correctness is at level 1 − ρ, not 2/3. Definition 1.2 asks: ρ-replicability, plus Pr[ACCEPT] ≥ 1 − ρ when p = U_n and Pr[REJECT] ≥ 1 − ρ when d_TV(p,U_n) ≥ ε. Footnote 1 observes this is free: if A is correct with probability q ≥ 2/3 and ρ-replicable then q² + (1−q)² ≥ 1 − ρ forces q ≥ 1 − O(ρ). So the asymmetry of the definition is cosmetic.

The precise question. _What is the sample complexity m(n,ε,ρ) of (n,ε,ρ)-replicable uniformity testing — in particular, is the overhead over the non-replicable Θ(√n·ε^−2) baseline the expected ρ^−2, or can it be ρ^−1?_

What was known, and the gap. For n = 2 (fair coin vs. ε-biased coin) ILPS showed replicable testing needs and achieves Θ̃(ε^−2·ρ^−2): a clean quadratic blow-up over Θ(ε^−2). More generally, the folklore picture after STOC '22 is that replicability costs a ρ^−2 factor, because the generic recipe is "compute a statistic, round it against a random threshold", and you then need the statistic to concentrate within ρ·(gap), which for a √(1/m)-scale fluctuation costs ρ^−2. Concretely, the black-box reduction — run an optimal non-replicable tester, view its output bit as a coin, and apply the optimal replicable coin tester — gives Õ(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−2), and every prior replicable learning algorithm had ρ^−2 in its dominating term. The gap: nobody knew whether ρ^−2 is intrinsic.

A nearby but distinct relaxation: tolerant testing. One could instead demand: accept if d_TV(p,U_n) ≤ ξ, reject if ≥ ε. Valiant–Valiant and Canonne–Jain–Kamath–Li show the price of tolerance is brutal: for constant ε, complexity climbs from Θ(√n) at ξ = 0 to Θ(n/log n) at ξ = ε/2. The authors observe (§1.1) that tolerant testing implies replicable testing — pick a random r ∈ (0,ε) and run a tolerant tester with (ξ,ε) = (r − ρε, r + ρε) — but this is barely sublinear in n even for constant ρ. So replicable testing is a genuinely weaker requirement than tolerant testing: you need your decision boundary to be hard to locate, not to estimate the TV distance. Keeping the complexity strongly sublinear is one of the real contributions.

Symmetric algorithms. f : [n]^m → {0,1} is symmetric (Batu–Fortnow–Rubinfeld–Smith–White, FOCS '00, Def. 13) if f(x_1,...,x_m) = f(π(x_1),...,π(x_m)) for every π ∈ S_n; i.e. f depends only on the fingerprint (the histogram of the histogram). A(·;r) is symmetric if f_r is symmetric for every fixed seed. Since uniformity is itself a label-invariant property, symmetry is WLOG in the non-replicable setting (symmetrize by averaging over permutations) and all known testers, including this paper's, are symmetric. But — and this is the honest caveat — the symmetrization reduction (apply all permutations, take the majority) is not known to preserve replicability, so the restriction is a real assumption in the lower bound, not a normalization.

With all that, the reader can state the results: Theorem 1.3 gives a symmetric (n,ε,ρ)-replicable tester using Õ(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−1 + ε^−2·ρ^−2) samples; Theorem 1.6 says every symmetric ρ-replicable tester needs Ω̃(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−1 + ε^−2·ρ^−2).

Main idea

Replace the usual ℓ₂-type statistic with the empirical total-variation statistic

S = (1/2)·sum_{i=1..n} |X_i/m − 1/n|, where X_i = #{occurrences of i},

taken from Diakonikolas–Gouleakis–Peebles–Price's high-probability identity tester, and compare it to a uniformly random threshold r = μ(U_n) + r_0·R with r_0 ~ Unif[1/4, 3/4], where μ(U_n) = E_{U_n}[S] is explicitly computable and R = R(m,n,ε) is DGPP's guaranteed expectation gap μ(p) − μ(U_n) ≥ R for d_TV(p,U_n) ≥ ε. Boost by a median over m_0 = Θ(log 1/ρ) independent batches. That's the whole algorithm (Algorithm 1): three lines.

Why this wins. The collision count (1/2)·sum X_i(X_i − 1) and the χ² statistic sum((X_i − m/n)² − X_i)/(m/n) both depend quadratically on individual counts, so a single heavy element with p_i ≫ 1/√n makes them fluctuate by Ω(m^{3/2}/n^{3/4}) — and crucially, in the unpromised middle regime such an element can exist while p is still close to uniform, so the large fluctuation is not compensated by a large mean. The authors show (§1.4 and Appendix C.1) that this forces m ≳ √n·ρ^−2 for both families of statistics: the ρ^−2 is a property of the statistic, not of the problem. The TV statistic depends only linearly on each X_i — in fact it has bounded differences 1/m in the Hamming metric on the sample — which is what buys the extra ρ.

Headline: Õ(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−1 + ε^−2·ρ^−2), the first replicable algorithm with (nearly) linear dependence on ρ^−1 in the dominating term, hence provably beating the black-box "replicable coin" reduction; and a matching Ω̃ bound for all symmetric testers, so the bound is tight up to polylogs within the class containing every known tester. Replicable identity testing (against an explicit q) inherits the same bound via Goldreich's reduction, which happens to preserve replicability (Appendix C.3 — and does not even need the reduction's own randomness shared).

The most interesting part

The variance dichotomy of Lemma 3.3, which disposes of the "neither uniform nor far" regime without any tolerance-style estimation.

In the sublinear regime m ≤ n the authors use the identity (from DGPP) S = Z/n where Z = |{i : X_i = 0}| is the number of empty buckets — the empirical TV statistic to uniform is, up to normalization, exactly the empty-bucket count. The threshold interval is [μ(U_n) + R/4, μ(U_n) + 3R/4] with R = C·ε²m²/n². Naively one worries about p that sit inside this window and have a heavy element inflating Var(S), because then Chebyshev gives nothing and the random threshold splits the two runs. The observation is that this configuration cannot occur: for this statistic, large variance forces large expectation. Formally, whenever Var(S) ≥ (C/64)·ρ²ε⁴m⁴n^−4,

E[S] − √Var(S) > μ(U_n) + C·ε²m²n^−2,

so by Chebyshev S sits above the entire threshold interval with probability 9/10 (boosted to 1 − ρ/4 by the median), and both runs replicably reject — even though p may be nowhere near ε-far. The algorithm never has to decide how far p is; the only two possibilities are "concentrated enough that a random threshold rarely separates the runs" and "so dispersed that the answer is pinned to REJECT".

The mechanism behind it is the pretty part. Write Z = n − m + sum_{i=1..m} Y_i where Y_i = 1[the i-th sample collides with some earlier sample]. Then Var(S) = Var(sum Y_i)/n², and one needs a sub-Poisson bound Var(sum Y_i) ≲ log(n/ρ)·sum_i E[Y_i]: variance controlled by the mean number of collisions. The Y_i are not independent, but they are "almost negatively correlated", and the authors prove this with Kleitman's correlation inequality (a lattice/FKG-type statement: for a monotone-increasing A and monotone-decreasing B, Pr[A ∩ B] ≤ Pr[A]·Pr[B]), extended from {0,1}^n to {0,1,2}^n by an explicit embedding into subsets of [2n]. For a fixed pair of distinct buckets k ≠ ℓ, encode each sample by which of {k, ℓ, neither} it fell into; the event "some sample before i hit k" is decreasing in this encoding while "some sample before j hit ℓ" is increasing, so they decorrelate (Lemma A.9), giving Pr[Ỹ_i·Ỹ_j = 1, T_i ≠ T_j] ≤ Pr[Ỹ_i]·Pr[Ỹ_j], which kills the off-diagonal terms. The same-bucket terms are handled by a heavy/light split at threshold p_k ≥ (3/m)·log(10n/ρ): heavy elements are occupied with probability 1 − (ρ/10n)³, so they contribute essentially zero variance to Z (that's where the log(n/ρ) comes from), and light elements have p_k small enough to absorb the extra factor. Then Var(S) large ⟹ sum E[Y_i] ≳ ρ²ε⁴m⁴/(n²·log) large ⟹ E[Z] − n·μ(U_n) ≥ sum E[Y_i] − m²/n ≫ ε²m²/n. The heavy element that destroyed the collision-based testers here helps: it creates collisions, collisions empty buckets, and empty buckets push S past the threshold.

(The lower bound has an equally clever device — the Local Swap Family interacting with symmetry — which I describe below; if I had to name one idea it would be the dichotomy, since it is what makes the unpromised regime tractable at all.)

Proof sketch

What is proved, precisely.

Theorem 1.3 (upper bound). For all n ∈ Z⁺, ε, ρ ∈ (0,1/2), Algorithm 1 — a symmetric, O(m)-time algorithm whose shared seed is a single r_0 ~ Unif[1/4,3/4] — is ρ-replicable for every p on [n], accepts U_n with probability ≥ 1 − ρ, rejects every p with d_TV(p,U_n) ≥ ε with probability ≥ 1 − ρ, and uses m·m_0 = Θ((√n/(ρε²))·log(n/ρ) + 1/(ρ²ε²))·log(1/ρ)) = Õ(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−1 + ε^−2·ρ^−2) samples. No assumption on p beyond being a distribution on [n].

Theorem 1.6 (lower bound). Every symmetric algorithm solving (n,ε,ρ)-replicable uniformity testing needs Ω̃(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−1 + ε^−2·ρ^−2) samples — concretely Ω(√n·log^−2 n·ε^−2·ρ^−1) for the first term, with the ε^−2ρ^−2 term imported unconditionally from ILPS's replicable coin-testing bound (and holding for all algorithms, symmetric or not). The restriction to symmetric algorithms applies only to the √n·ε^−2·ρ^−1 term; whether it holds in general is the paper's main open problem, and Appendix C.2 explains why their technique does not extend.

Why ρ^−1 and not ρ^−2: the arithmetic. This is worth stating baldly, because it is the entire content. The random-threshold recipe is replicable iff the threshold r, drawn uniformly from an interval of width Θ(R), rarely lands between the two runs' statistics; conditioned on a deviation Δ, this has probability Θ(Δ/R), so one needs sd(S)/R ≲ ρ.

Now count powers of m. In the sublinear regime, sd(S) ≈ √(log(n/ρ))·m/n^{3/2} (from Var(S) ≲ log·sum E Y_i/n² ≈ log·m²/n³), while the gap is R = C·ε²m²/n². The ratio is ∝ √log·√n/(ε²m) — linear in 1/m, not 1/√m. Setting it ≤ ρ gives m ≳ √n·ε^−2·ρ^−1. Compare the coin, n = 2: the gap is ∝ εm and the deviation ∝ √m, so the ratio is ∝ 1/(ε√m) and one pays ρ^−2. The structural reason is that the TV statistic's expectation gap is quadratic in the signal (R ∝ ε²m²/n²) while its fluctuation is linear — a signal-to-noise ratio growing like m rather than √m. Interestingly, the collision statistic has the same scaling under the uniform distribution (R ∝ ε²m²/n, sd ∝ m/√n, ratio ∝ √n/(ε²m)); what kills it is that in the middle regime its sd degrades to m^{3/2}/n^{3/4}, restoring a 1/√m ratio. So "linear in ρ^−1" = "quadratic gap, linear fluctuation, uniformly over all p".

Two further ingredients are load-bearing for the linear dependence and easy to miss:

  • The median trick is not cosmetic. One needs the deviation event to have probability ≤ ρ, not ≤ 1/10. Getting that from Chebyshev directly would require Var ≤ ρ³R², i.e. m ≳ √n·ε^−2·ρ^−{3/2}. Taking the median of Θ(log 1/ρ) independent batches converts probability 9/10 into 1 − ρ at multiplicative cost log(1/ρ), recovering ρ^−1.
  • No bias correction is needed. The threshold is anchored at the computable μ(U_n), and only an ε-dependent lower bound R on the gap is used. The algorithm never estimates d_TV(p,U_n) — which is exactly how it dodges the n/log n price of tolerance.

Upper bound, regime by regime.

Superlinear, m ≥ n (Lemma 3.2). Here concentration is immediate and strong: changing one sample changes two counts X_i by one each, so S has bounded differences B = 1/m, and McDiarmid gives Pr[|S − μ(p)| ≥ t] ≤ 2e^{−2mt²}. With t = ρ·(C/16)·ε²√(m/n) (matching R = C·ε²√(m/n) for n < m ≤ n/ε²), the exponent is Θ(ρ²ε⁴m²/n), which is ≫ 1 exactly when m ≫ √n/(ρε²). In the "super-learning" regime m ≥ n/ε² the gap saturates at R = C·ε, the exponent becomes Θ(ρ²ε²m), and one needs m ≫ ρ^−2ε^−2 — this is where the additive second term comes from. Note that the 1/m-bounded-differences property is precisely what a collision or χ² statistic lacks (its sensitivity is ~ max_i X_i/m), so McDiarmid is unavailable there.

Sublinear, m ≤ n (Lemma 3.3). The dichotomy described above. Low-variance branch: Chebyshev at 4× the standard deviation plus the median trick. High-variance branch: replicable rejection via E[S] − √Var(S) > μ(U_n) + C·ε²m²/n², proved through Var(Z) ≤ ρ³/500 + 32·log(10n/ρ)·sum E[Y_i] (Lemma A.3, via Kleitman + heavy/light split), n·μ(U_n) ≤ n − m + m²/n (Lemma A.10, from E[Y_i] ≤ m/n), and the elementary x − √(320·log(10n/ρ)·x) ≥ x/2 for x ≥ 1280·log(10n/ρ) (Lemma A.11). The final check that U_n itself falls in the low-variance branch is where the sample complexity is pinned: Var(S) ≤ 24m²·log(10n/ρ)/n³ ≤ (C/64)·ρ²ε⁴m⁴n^−4 iff m ≳ (√n/(ρε²))·√(log(n/ρ)).

Assembling replicability. If p = U_n or d_TV ≥ ε, both runs are correct w.p. 1 − ρ/2 by a union bound (the far case reuses DGPP's correctness: their fixed threshold exceeds every possible r). Otherwise either the high-variance branch applies and both runs reject, or |S_median − μ(p)| ≤ (ρ/16)·R in both runs, in which case the runs disagree only if r falls in an interval of width ρR/8 inside a window of width R/2, i.e. with probability ρ/4.

Lower bound. The hard family is the canonical one, p(ξ)_i = (1+ξ)/n for even i and (1−ξ)/n for odd i, with ξ ~ Unif[0,ε] drawn once. The skeleton follows ILPS's minimax framework:

  1. Derandomize. Fix a "good seed" r such that A(·;r) (i) accepts p(0) w.p. ≥ 1 − O(ρ), (ii) rejects p(ε) w.p. ≥ 1 − O(ρ), (iii) is O(ρ)-replicable against the random instance. Each holds for a large constant fraction of seeds, so a union bound gives one r with all three. Now A(·;r) is deterministic and Acc_m(ξ) = Pr_{S ~ p(ξ)^⊗m}[A(S;r) = 1] is a polynomial in ξ, hence continuous, with Acc_m(0) ≥ 1 − O(ρ) and Acc_m(ε) ≤ O(ρ). By IVT there is ξ_ with Acc_m(ξ_) = 1/2.
  2. Lipschitz continuity (Proposition 4.1). If m = õ(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−1) then |Acc_m(ε_0) − Acc_m(ε_1)| < 0.1 whenever |ε_1 − ε_0| < ερ. Hence Acc_m(ξ) ∈ [0.4, 0.6] on the whole window |ξ − ξ_| ≤ ρε, which has mass Ω(ρ) under ξ ~ Unif[0,ε]; on that event the two runs disagree with constant probability, contradicting (iii). Note the shape of the argument: replicability is defeated not by making the tester _wrong_ but by making its answer a _fair coin_ on a ρ-fraction of instances. A ρ-replicable tester must have an acceptance curve that crosses 1/2 within a window of width o(ρε) — i.e. it must effectively _estimate* ξ to precision ρε.
  3. The indistinguishability core (Lemma 4.3/4.4), and the symmetry trick. The intuition (§1.4) is a moment calculation: for a symmetric tester the informative signal is the number of elements seen exactly twice, whose expectation is 2m²(1+ξ²)/n and whose sd is ≈ m/√n; separating ξ from ξ + ερ requires m/√n ≪ m²ξερ/n, i.e. m ≫ √n/(ε²ρ). The formalization must handle a subtlety: p(ε_0) and p(ε_1) as fixed, known-support distributions are easy to distinguish — bucket even vs. odd indices and you have a single coin of bias (1±ξ)/2, learnable with O(ε^−2ρ^−2) samples, well below √n·ε^−2·ρ^−1 when ρ ≫ n^{−1/2}. So one must randomize which elements are heavy. The device is the Local Swap Family M_i (Def. 4.2): pair up adjacent elements (2j−1, 2j) and independently swap the two masses within each pair. Then:
  4. For a symmetric tester, every member of M_i is a relabeling of p(ε_i), so the acceptance probability on a random member of M_i equals Acc_m(ε_i) exactly. This is what transports indistinguishability of the randomized families back to the fixed pair p(ε_0), p(ε_1) — which is exactly what step 2 needs, since ξ* is determined by the algorithm and cannot be re-randomized after the fact.
  5. The families themselves are information-theoretically close. Let X be a uniform bit, p̃ a random member of M_X, and M_1,...,M_n the counts under Poissonized sampling (Poi(m) samples, so counts are independent given p̃; de-Poissonization is standard). Because the pairs (M_{2j−1}, M_{2j}) are conditionally i.i.d. given X, one gets I(X; M_1,...,M_n) ≤ (n/2)·I(X; M_1,M_2). The pair's distribution is an even mixture of two product-Poisson laws, and the authors bound I(X; M_1,M_2) by the χ²-divergence to the mixture, using convexity/additivity of KL and the identity I(X;H) = (1/2)KL(H_0‖H̄) + (1/2)KL(H_1‖H̄) (Claims B.5–B.7).
  6. The computation is a genuine Taylor/moment argument around ε = 0. Everything reduces to f_{a,b}(x) = (1+x)^a(1−x)^b + (1−x)^a(1+x)^b; the key point is that f_{a,b} is even in x, so it has no odd monomials and ∂_x f_{a,b} is dominated by the degree-2 coefficient: max_{x ≤ ε}|∂_x f_{a,b}(x)| = O((a+b)²ε) for 2 ≤ a+b ≤ ε^−1/2, while f_{a,b} ≥ Ω(1) there (Claim B.2). The evenness is why the leading sensitivity to ξ is O(εδ) rather than O(δ) — i.e. why the ε^−2 rather than ε^−1 appears, and why a+b ≤ 1 contributes exactly zero (seeing an element zero or one time carries no information at all, matching the "frequency-2 is the signal" intuition). Summing against the Poisson weights turns the a⁴ + b⁴ factors into factorial moments λ² + λ⁴ of Poi(m/n), yielding O(ε²δ²m²/n²) in the sublinear regime (Lemma B.1); the tail a+b > ε^−1/2 is geometrically suppressed. Superlinear (n < m < n/(ε²log²n)) is handled by restricting to a,b ∈ m/n ± √(m/n)·log n and a log-series expansion of f_{a,b}, costing log⁴ n (Lemma B.3); the super-learning regime m > Ω̃(n/ε²) is a direct KL computation between Poissons with means (m/n)(1±ε) (Lemma B.4). Altogether, with δ = O(ερ), I(X; M_{1:n}) = O(ε⁴ρ²·(m²/n)·log⁴ n) + o(1); a distinguisher with constant advantage needs I = Ω(1), forcing m = Ω(√n·log^−2 n·ε^−2·ρ^−1).

The gap that remains (Appendix C.2), stated honestly. The argument fixes a seed r first, which pins ξ_ (and, for an asymmetric tester, a ξ_π for each permutation π). The swap-family analysis shows p(ξ') and p(ξ' + ρε) are indistinguishable _when permuted by a random π'* — i.e. for a constant fraction of permutations — but the permutations for which this holds need not be the permutations π whose crossing point ξ_π is near ξ'. Symmetry is exactly the hypothesis that collapses this quantifier order. Closing it is the open problem.

Two honest observations about the tester itself. (a) Its accept region is wildly non-monotone in d_TV: a distribution with one element of mass ≈ m/n = 1/(√n·ρε²) triggers the high-variance branch and is replicably rejected even though its TV distance to U_n is O(1/√n) ≪ ε. So "REJECT" from this tester does not mean "ε-far"; it means "consistently not-accepted". For the motivating scientific use case this is a real caveat — the two labs will agree, but on an answer that is not interpretable as a distance statement. (b) The ε^−2ρ^−2 additive term is unavoidable and dominates when ρ ≲ n^{−1/2}, so the headline "linear in ρ" holds only in the (natural) regime ρ ≫ 1/√n.

Broader context

Replicability as a complexity resource. ILPS (STOC '22) proposed ρ-replicability as a formal, worst-case-over-p stability notion, distinct from differential privacy, generalization, or algorithmic stability — though closely related: Bun–Gaboardi–Hopkins–Impagliazzo–Lei–Pitassi–Sivakumar–Sorrell ("Stability is stable", STOC '23) proved equivalences, up to polynomial overheads, between replicability, approximate-DP, TV-stability and one-way marginals, and Moran–Schefler–Shafer's "Bayesian stability zoo" maps the surrounding notions. The field since then has largely been "take a learning task, make it replicable": bandits (Esfandiari et al., ICLR '23), RL (Eaton–Hussing–Kearns–Sorrell), clustering (Esfandiari et al.), large-margin halfspaces (Kalavasis–Karbasi–Larsen–Velegkas–Zhou), list/certificate complexity (Dixon–Pavan–Vander Woude–Vinodchandran), and a topological angle via local Borsuk–Ulam (Chase–Chornomaz–Moran–Yehudayoff). In essentially all of these the price of replicability is ρ^−2, because the canonical primitive is "replicably round a real-valued statistic" (random-threshold / randomized rounding of an SQ query), and that primitive is Θ(ρ^−2) tight for a √(1/m)-fluctuating quantity. This paper is the first clean counterexample to the folklore, and its message is sharper than the theorem: the ρ-exponent is a property of the statistic's signal-to-noise scaling, not of replicability per se. If a problem admits a statistic whose expectation gap grows quadratically in the sample size while its fluctuation grows linearly, you pay ρ^−1.

Distribution testing. The subfield asks for sublinear-sample decisions about properties of a distribution over a huge discrete domain — uniformity, identity to a known q, closeness of two unknowns, independence, monotonicity, histogram structure. Canonne's survey and his Topics and Techniques in Distribution Testing monograph are the standard entries. Two threads are directly relevant here. (i) High-probability testing: Diakonikolas–Gouleakis–Peebles–Price (ICALP '18) introduced the empirical-TV statistic precisely to get optimal dependence on the failure probability δ (rather than the lossy median-of-log(1/δ) repetitions), and proved the expectation-gap lemma this paper runs on. That the right statistic for high-probability testing is also the right statistic for replicability is not an accident — both demand tail control rather than just a constant-probability separation, and it is a good heuristic to carry forward. (ii) The price of tolerance: Valiant–Valiant and Canonne–Jain–Kamath–Li charted the √n → n/log n transition as the tolerance ξ moves from 0 to ε/2. Reading this paper against that result is illuminating: replicable testing sits strictly between promise testing and tolerant testing, and the random threshold is exactly the device that extracts "an unlocatable decision boundary" at √n cost instead of "a known decision boundary" at n/log n cost.

Follow-ups this opens. The stated open problem — remove the symmetry assumption — is the obvious one, and the obstruction in C.2 is concrete enough to attack: one wants a hard instance whose permutation randomization can be fixed before the seed, e.g. a family closed under the relevant swaps where the crossing point ξ_π is provably permutation-insensitive, or a direct replicability-to-communication/information argument that does not need to fix r first. More interesting is the meta question: characterize which testing/estimation problems have replicability overhead ρ^−1 versus ρ^−2. The paper effectively identifies the mechanism (quadratic gap vs. linear deviation, uniformly over the unpromised middle regime); a general theorem — say, in terms of the modulus of continuity of the optimal test statistic's expectation as a function of the parameter, or a "replicable Le Cam" two-point method that predicts the ρ-exponent from the local geometry of the hypothesis class — would reorganize a dozen existing results. Concretely, closeness testing (Θ(max(n^{2/3}ε^{−4/3}, √n ε^−2))) and independence testing are the natural next targets the authors name, and one should expect the answer to hinge on whether an analogous linear-in-counts statistic exists. A third direction: replicability under adaptive or sequential sampling, where the "same seed, fresh data" model is less natural.

IR / vector search. I would not oversell this; the specific result is about [n]-valued discrete testing and has no direct retrieval content. Three links are honest rather than forced, in decreasing strength.

  • The random-threshold primitive, for stable index construction. The generic recipe here — compute a statistic, compare it to a shared-seed uniformly random threshold inside a known gap interval, and ensure sd/gap ≤ ρ — is a drop-in tool for making data-dependent discrete decisions in index building reproducible across data resamples or shard reshuffles: whether to split a node in a tree/graph-based ANN index, how many IVF centroids or PQ codebook entries to use, which dimension to split on. Index non-determinism is a genuine practical nuisance (two builds of the same corpus produce different recall curves, so ablations are noisy), and the replicability framework is the right formalization of "same build decisions on a resample". Replicable clustering (Esfandiari et al.) is the closest existing piece, and the lesson transfers: the cost of a replicable decision is set by the SNR scaling of the statistic you threshold, so choose a statistic with bounded differences O(1/m) rather than a quadratic one — a design principle, not a theorem.
  • Uniformity testing is literally a load-balance audit. "Does this hash family / LSH partition / IVF assignment spread vectors uniformly over n buckets?" is uniformity testing over [n], and in production you want the audit's verdict to be stable rather than flipping between runs on a resampled traffic sample — which is exactly the middle-regime problem, since real partitions are neither perfectly balanced nor ε-skewed. Theorem 1.3 says you can get a stable verdict at Õ(√n·ε^−2·ρ^−1) queries. Caveat (a) above applies with force: the tester may consistently reject a near-balanced partition that happens to have one hot bucket, so the verdict is a consistency guarantee and not a skew measurement.
  • Reproducibility of IR evaluation. The motivating story — two groups, same protocol, opposite accept/reject — is the IR significance-testing situation almost exactly, with the query sample playing the role of T and a true effect size in the "neither zero nor large" band. The conceptual transfer is the definition, not the algorithm: a replicable test gives a pre-registered random seed under which two independent query samples yield the same verdict, which is a stronger and more useful guarantee than a p-value. Whether a replicable version of the standard paired tests has an interesting sample-complexity theory, and whether the ρ^−1 vs ρ^−2 dichotomy shows up there, seems genuinely open and reachable — the relevant statistic (a paired mean difference) has linear-in-m gap and √m fluctuation, which predicts ρ^−2, so the honest guess is that the good news here does not transfer and one would need a differently-shaped statistic.

Beyond that, the paper's value for a theory reader is the two techniques: the variance-implies-large-mean dichotomy as a way to handle unpromised middle regimes, and Kleitman/FKG as a route to sub-Poisson variance bounds for dependent collision indicators. Both are reusable well outside distribution testing.

title: Drowning in Documents: Consequences of Scaling Reranker Inference
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-02

Drowning in Documents: Consequences of Scaling Reranker Inference — Jacob, Lindgren, Zaharia, Carbin, Khattab, Drozdov (SIGIR 2025) — arXiv:2411.11767

Setting and problem

Fix a corpus D with |D| = N and a query q. The standard cascade is two maps. First a retriever r(q,d) — in practice an inner product between precomputed embeddings, or BM25 over an inverted index — induces an ordering of D and emits the candidate set C_K(q) = top-K over d in D of r(q,d). Then a reranker s(q,d), a cross-encoder that jointly encodes the pair and emits a scalar, reorders only C_K(q), and the system returns top-k over d in C_K(q) of s(q,d) to the user with k << K. The reranker is pointwise: s is applied to each (q,d) independently, so the final ordering is determined by K independent scalar evaluations with no interaction between candidates. Cost is O(K) forward passes of a quadratic-attention model per query, which is why K is conventionally pinned at 100 (Nogueira–Cho, Gao et al.) or 1000 (RankT5 and TREC-DL practice).

The paper's experimental variable is exactly K, swept over {10, 100, 1000, 5000} with k held at 10, up to and including K = N — i.e. the reranker used as a full retriever, not as a reorderer of a shallow pool. The metric is Recall@10 as a function of K: the fraction of queries for which at least one labelled-relevant document survives into the final ten. Appendix A.4 states explicitly that nDCG and other order-sensitive metrics are not reported — Recall only, justified on the grounds that RAG consumption makes set membership rather than graded ordering the operative quantity. There is a second, cleaner comparison in Section 4.1.1: set K = N for both systems and plot Recall@K of the retriever's ordering against Recall@K of the reranker's ordering over the identical document set, which is the only genuinely apples-to-apples way to ask "is the cross-encoder a better scorer than the bi-encoder?" absent any cascade.

So the input is (q, D) plus a rerank budget K; the output is an ordered list of ten documents; the question is whether the map K -> Recall@10(K) is monotone increasing, as the literature's cost–quality story presumes.

The precise question. Is reranking quality monotone in rerank depth, and does a state-of-the-art cross-encoder beat a state-of-the-art dense retriever when both are asked to rank the entire corpus?

The literature's priors, all of which this setup stresses: (i) cross-encoders strictly dominate bi-encoders on accuracy because full query–document attention is strictly more expressive than a bilinear form over frozen vectors (Humeau et al.'s poly-encoder framing; Luan et al.; Rosa et al.'s "In defense of cross-encoders for zero-shot retrieval"); (ii) therefore reranking monotonically helps, and more reranking helps more — the corollary being that scoring the whole corpus with a cross-encoder would be the quality ceiling, merely unaffordable; (iii) therefore cross-encoders are the natural teachers for distilling retrievers, which licenses treating teacher scores as ground truth over arbitrary document pools. The gap: nobody measures assumption (ii) past K = 1000, and nobody measures the cross-encoder as a standalone retriever, because the pool is always supplied by a weak first stage. If (ii) fails, (iii) is also compromised, since distillation samples negatives from exactly the regions where the teacher has never been validated.

Methodological choices the whole result rests on.

  • First stages (3). BM25 via Pyserini with default parameters; voyage-2 (1024-d); text-embedding-3-large (3072-d). Exact (brute-force) scoring throughout, no ANN — so ANN recall is not a confound. The departure from convention is deliberate: BM25 is included as the weak baseline that prior reranking work relies on, and the two proprietary embedders are the strong first stages that make the comparison hard.
  • Rerankers (4). Open: bge-reranker-v2-m3 (run locally), jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual (API). Closed: cohere-rerank-english-v3.0, voyage-rerank-1 (APIs; the paper states it cannot verify the architecture of the closed models, only that blog posts describe them as cross-encoders). All open models are sub-1B parameter encoders — a point I return to.
  • Datasets (8). Academic: scifact (BEIR); relic and doris-mae (BIRCO, pre-filtered to the hardest queries); biology and pony (BRIGHT, using the documents split and Gemini-generated reasoning queries). Enterprise, internally curated to avoid contamination: FinanceBench (SEC-filing QA, derived from Islam et al.), ManufacturingQA (internal technical-documentation KB, queries contain alphanumeric product codes), DocumentationQA (code questions with manually labelled answers grounded in OSS documentation). Query counts and corpus sizes are not reported for any split.
  • Making full retrieval tractable. Two preprocessing moves do the work. Queries and documents are truncated to 512 tokens so embedders and rerankers face the same input budget. Negatives are downsampled so that N <= 10,000: gold documents are retained first, then the remainder is filled by uniform sampling without replacement from the original corpus (applied to BRIGHT-biology and FinanceBench; Scifact instead has its query set downsampled). So "full-corpus reranking" means full over a ten-thousand-document corpus, and the largest sweep point K = 5000 is a substantial fraction of N. The paper asserts without evidence that "increasing N would only show a more profound version of existing trends."
  • Labels. Binary relevance from the datasets' own qrels. For BIRCO, which ships graded qrels, the positives are redefined as only the documents attaining the maximum qrel score for that query; all lower-graded relevant documents are demoted to negatives. Enterprise labels are human-annotated. There is no LLM judge anywhere in the evaluation — the LLM (gpt-4o-mini) appears only as a candidate reranker, never as an assessor. Label incompleteness is addressed by manual inspection of failure cases, not by adjudication.
  • Compute. Commodity GPUs, no run over 24 hours. Statistics are reported as percentages over "experiments", where an experiment is a (dataset, retriever, reranker) triple: 5 x 3 x 4 = 60 academic and 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 enterprise (Jina excluded from enterprise for legal reasons).

Main idea

The curve K -> Recall@10(K) is non-monotone, and reliably so. It rises from K = 10 — rerankers do help when the pool is shallow, improving over the first stage for some K in 85.0% of academic and 88.9% of enterprise experiments — peaks somewhere in the K in [10, 1000] region, and then falls. The maximum lands at the largest K in only 3.3% of academic and 14.8% of enterprise experiments. A dip from some earlier peak ("Distracted") occurs in 60.0% / 66.7%. Most damagingly, in 53.3% of academic and 44.4% of enterprise experiments, the reranker at maximum K is worse than the first-stage retriever alone — the reranker actively destroys information the retriever had. Full monotonicity ("Never Hurts") holds in 23.3% / 22.2%. Per-dataset, the damage ranges from mild (RELIC: 16.7% scaling-hurts) to severe (BRIGHT-pony 75%, BRIGHT-biology and DORIS-MAE 66.7%).

The Section 4.1.1 fair comparison closes the loop: with both models ranking the identical full document set, the dense retrievers' Recall@K curve dominates the cross-encoders' in many settings. The cross-encoder, used as a retriever, is simply a worse retriever. The one clean win for reranking is BM25 + reranker on enterprise data, where scaling K monotonically helps — but text-embedding-3-large alone is about 1.5x BM25's average Recall@10 there, so the entire cascade is dominated by just using a better first stage and retrieving a handful of documents.

The diagnostic contribution is the phantom hit: a document the reranker places in its top few that has no lexical, semantic, or any other apparent relation to the query, and that the retriever had buried in the thousands. Mined by filtering for queries whose Recall@10 drops going from K = 100 to K = 5000, the examples are genuinely startling — for a query about ML-SA1 binding orientation at hTRPML2, bge-reranker-v2-m3 ranks at position 2 (retriever position 3645) a randomised controlled trial of a high-intensity exercise programme for older adults; cohere-rerank-english-v3.0 promotes to position 3 a document whose body is a sink-and-dishwasher patent abstract. These are not near-misses; they are category errors, and they occur across multiple independent rerankers.

The proposed mitigation is listwise reranking with an LLM: RankGPT-style sliding window (Sun et al.), window 20, stride 10, gpt-4o-mini, bottom-up over the retrieval order, with retrieval order preserved for any window whose output fails to parse (~5% of windows at K = 100, almost all because the model declared nothing relevant). Because the listwise pass cannot be amortised across K — unlike cached pointwise scores — it is run for one retriever only and K in {50, 100, 500, 1000}. It is both higher in absolute Recall@10 than every cross-encoder and monotone increasing in K. The paper is careful to call this a proof of existence that reranking architectures robust to K exist, while conceding the approach is high-latency and impractical; the suggested path is to use it as a teacher for cross-encoders.

The most interesting part

The phenomenon is real and the paper is honest, but the evidence is weaker than the framing, in four specific ways.

1. The phantom-hit evidence is contaminated by exactly the confound the paper dismisses. Section 4.2 pre-empts the label-incompleteness objection — "it is plausible that this decrease in recall could be due to missing labels... when manually looking through the reranker's predictions, we see that this is not the case" — but Appendix C undercuts it. In Figure 10/11, for the query "Many proteins in human cells can be post-translationally modified at lysine residues via acetylation," the document ranked 0 by both the retriever and the reranker is "The growing landscape of lysine acetylation links metabolism and cell signalling," and it is labelled a negative. The reranker's rank-1 document is "Histone acetylation in gene regulation" — also a negative. Both are flagrantly on-topic; Scifact's sparse, claim-specific qrels simply do not judge them. So the headline Recall@10 drop on this query is a mixture of two phenomena the paper wants to separate: genuine phantom hits (the dishwasher document at rank 4) and unjudged relevant documents whose promotion is correct behaviour penalised by the metric. The manual inspection that was supposed to rule out the label explanation is presented in a figure that demonstrates it. This does not refute the phenomenon — Figure 13 (bge on the TRPML query, where the reranker's entire top-8 is off-topic immunology, oncology, and cardiology) is clean evidence — but it means the quantitative degradation in Table 1 is an unknown mixture, and the paper never attempts the decomposition. The obvious experiment is missing: take the documents each reranker promotes into the top-10 at large K that were not previously labelled, and adjudicate them (human or LLM judge). That single step would split "reranker is miscalibrated" from "qrels are shallow," and the paper's own appendix suggests the split is not negligible.

2. Pooled/graded-qrel artifacts are structurally built in, and one preprocessing choice makes it worse. Scifact, RELIC, and DORIS-MAE have qrels that were never constructed by pooling the output of 2024-era rerankers over 5000-document candidate sets — they are shallow relative to the systems being evaluated, which is the classic Voorhees/Zobel incompleteness problem reborn (and precisely what Arabzadeh et al.'s shallow-pooling work found for MS MARCO). Worse, the BIRCO preprocessing deliberately demotes graded-relevant documents: "all the new gold documents are the gold documents of the original dataset that share the highest qrel score for a given query." A reranker that surfaces a qrel-2 document ahead of a qrel-3 document is scored identically to one that surfaces a dishwasher patent. DORIS-MAE, with aspect-based multi-level relevance, is the dataset where this binarisation bites hardest, and it shows one of the highest scaling-hurts rates (66.7%). Having thrown away the graded labels, the paper also declined to report nDCG — so the one metric that would have been robust to this choice is absent. Note also that the contamination argument is asymmetric in the wrong direction: the paper argues rerankers are tuned on BEIR, but text-embedding-3-large and voyage-2 are MTEB-optimised and MTEB contains BEIR, so Scifact advantages both sides. On the genuinely uncontaminated enterprise data the effect is measurably weaker (44.4% vs 53.3% scaling-hurts; 14.8% vs 3.3% scaling-is-best; BM25 + reranker monotone), which is a quiet point against the paper's own narrative that benchmark contamination had been inflating reranker reputations.

3. The statistics are existence-quantified over a five-point grid with no error bars. "Distracted" is defined as: there exist K, K' > K with Recall@10(K') < Recall@10(K). With four or five sweep points and Recall@10 estimated on query sets small enough to require downsampling (Scifact) and never reported in size, a non-trivial fraction of the 60%/66.7% "Distracted" rate is attainable under a null of a flat true curve plus sampling noise. Symmetrically, "Never Hurts" demands pointwise dominance at every K, which almost nothing passes even under a flat null — so the damning-looking 23.3% is partly an artifact of a strict quantifier. No confidence intervals, no paired significance tests, no query counts, no corpus sizes. For a paper whose claim is about a scaling curve, the absence of per-K uncertainty and of N itself is a real reproducibility gap. The more trustworthy number is "Recall@10 at K_max vs. retriever," a single comparison per experiment — and it is also the most important one, so the headline survives; but the shape claims deserve less weight than Table 1's layout implies. Relatedly, the macro-average over datasets in Figures 2–3 pools splits whose Recall@10 spans 0.03 (pony) to 0.90 (scifact); the averaged curve is dominated by whichever split has the largest dynamic range, which is a presentational choice rather than an estimate of anything.

4. The mitigation is not a controlled comparison of listwise vs. pointwise. Three confounds are entangled in the gpt-4o-mini result, and the paper names only one. (a) Backbone scale: the cross-encoders are sub-1B encoders; gpt-4o-mini is a far larger, far more capable model. Rosa et al.'s pro-cross-encoder results used monoT5-3B over BM25 top-1000 — so "pointwise cross-encoders degrade with K" may be substantially a small-model phenomenon rather than a pointwise one, and the clean ablation (pointwise scoring with gpt-4o-mini; listwise inference with a 1B model) is not run. (b) Retriever anchoring: the sliding window starts at the bottom of the retrieval ranking and moves up, reordering only 20 documents at a time; a document at rank 4000 must win every window to reach the top. The procedure is a bounded-displacement local sort anchored to r, and on parse failure it reverts to retrieval order — so the listwise system is structurally much closer to "retriever + local refinement" than the cross-encoder, which discards r entirely. Monotonicity in K is therefore close to built in: adding tail documents to a procedure that defaults to retrieval order and only promotes under repeated local wins cannot easily hurt. That is a genuine engineering virtue, but it is not evidence about listwise losses or listwise modelling; it is evidence about the inductive bias of the sliding-window inference procedure. (c) Budget: listwise is restricted to K <= 1000 while cross-encoders are pushed to 5000, so the two curves are not compared over the same range — the regime where cross-encoders collapse hardest is one where the mitigation was never evaluated.

What the result does establish, and what it says about training distributions. Stripped of the overclaims, two things are solid: (i) the purely-reranker ordering of a large candidate pool is frequently worse than a strong dense retriever's ordering of the same pool, under these labels; (ii) off-the-shelf rerankers produce occasional, grossly wrong high scores on documents far down the retriever's list. Both point at the same training-distribution story the paper develops in Section 5 and which I think is the most important takeaway. The mGTE comparison it cites is the crisp version: 16,384 in-batch negatives for the embedding model, 4 negatives for the cross-encoder, because cross-encoder training cannot share negatives across a batch — there is no O(B^2) free lunch when the scorer takes pairs. Embedders additionally get ANCE-style corpus-mined negatives and negative caches scaling to millions. So the cross-encoder is a model whose decision boundary has been fit on the top of a retriever's list and is then asked, at K = 5000, to make decisions about documents from a distribution it has effectively never seen. Its claimed superiority — the thing "cross-encoders dominate bi-encoders" means — was always measured conditional on a candidate distribution induced by a first stage. Removing that conditioning removes the claim. The sharpest reframing is that the field has been reporting the accuracy of s under d ~ C_100(q) and reading it as the accuracy of s under d ~ D. The paper's Section 5 "reranking as ensembling" reading follows naturally and is, I think, right: a reranker's marginal value comes from feature diversity relative to the first stage at the head of the list, not from being a globally better relevance function. And it immediately suggests the mitigation the paper never tests — score fusion or rank fusion between stages, or capping promotion distance — which would be far cheaper than LLM listwise and, by the paper's own observation that phantom hits are scored very low by the retriever, would eliminate most of the damage. That the maximally fragile pipeline (reranker order overrides the first stage completely) is the one evaluated is a real limitation: the result shows that replacing retriever order degrades with depth, not that scaling rerank depth with sensible aggregation degrades.

Proof sketch

This is a purely empirical paper. It contains no theorem, no formal claim, and no controlled analysis in the causal-inference sense; Section 5 offers four narrative hypotheses (training negatives / exposure bias; reranking-as-ensembling; general deep-learning non-robustness and a best-of-N reward-hacking analogy; pointwise vs. listwise losses; ineffective finetuning). Below is the implicit model that makes the observed curves nearly inevitable, written out as the paper does not.

Decomposition. For a query with a single relevant document d+, final recall at depth K factors as

Recall@k(K) = Pr[d+ in C_K(q)] * Pr[d+ in top-k of s over C_K(q) | d+ in C_K(q)] = R_1(K) * S(K).

R_1 is the first stage's recall at depth K: increasing, concave, and saturating fast for a strong dense retriever — most of the mass is captured by K ~ 100, so there is very little left to gain. S is the reranker's survival probability, and it is decreasing in K, because each additional candidate is another independent chance to outscore d+. The product of a saturating increasing function and a decreasing one has an interior maximum. The curves in Figures 2–3 are that product. The weaker the first stage, the longer R_1 keeps growing and the further right the peak sits — which is exactly why the BM25 panels are the ones where scaling K keeps helping, and the dense-retriever panels are the ones that turn over early. That single observation explains the paper's main cross-sectional pattern and is, to my mind, the most useful thing to take from it.

Why S decays, quantitatively. Define the per-query pairwise error rate p_q = Pr over d- ~ D of [ s(q,d-) > s(q,d+) ]. The expected number of negatives in the pool that outrank d+ is (K-1) p_q, growing linearly in K, and d+ fails to make the top-k once that count exceeds k-1. Survival therefore requires roughly

p_q <~ k/K.

At k = 10, K = 100 this demands p_q <~ 1e-1 — trivially satisfied, and this is the regime in which every published cross-encoder evaluation lives. At K = 5000 it demands p_q <~ 2e-3; at a realistic corpus N = 1e7 it demands p_q <~ 1e-6. A scorer fit with four negatives per positive has no mechanism that would control a 1e-6 tail-error rate, and no evaluation that has ever measured it. The "cross-encoders are more accurate" literature is reporting a quantity at 1e-1 resolution and the full-retrieval task requires 1e-6 resolution; nothing connects the two. Note this is a statement about tails, not means: a reranker can have a strictly better AUC than a retriever and still be strictly worse at full retrieval, because full retrieval is a max-order-statistic task. Equivalently, in extreme-value language, the k-th largest of K negative scores behaves like F_-^{-1}(1 - k/K), which diverges toward the positive score region unless F_- (the negative score distribution) has support bounded strictly below the positive scores. Degradation is therefore generic for any imperfectly calibrated pointwise scorer; what differs between models is only the tail exponent of F_-.

Why the retriever's tail is thinner. Not because the bilinear form is more expressive — it is less — but because of the training distribution. A dual encoder trained with 1e4–1e6 in-batch, ANCE-mined, or negative-cached negatives has had its loss directly penalise the upper tail of F_- over something resembling the full corpus. A cross-encoder trained on 4 retriever-filtered negatives per positive has had F_- shaped only on the head of a retriever's list. This is a train–test shift in the negative distribution: at inference with large K, the candidate set is dominated by random corpus documents, which is off-distribution for s and on-distribution for r. Phantom hits are then the visible samples from the fat tail of F_- under covariate shift.

What is established vs. suggested. Established empirically: the non-monotonicity and its frequency (modulo the labelling and statistical caveats above); that cross-encoders lose to dense retrievers in full-corpus Recall@K in many settings; the existence of phantom hits across four independent rerankers; that one listwise LLM configuration is monotone in K over K <= 1000. Suggested but not tested: the negatives/exposure-bias mechanism (the mGTE 16384-vs-4 figure is cited from another paper, not an ablation here; the Limitations section concedes closed models make this untestable); the ensembling account; that listwise losses are the operative fix rather than backbone scale or retriever anchoring; and the extrapolation that larger N would show "a more profound version of existing trends," which is an uncontrolled conjecture in a paper about scaling. There is no measurement of p_q, no score-distribution plot, no calibration analysis — the quantities the mechanism is about are never instrumented. That is the paper's biggest missed opportunity and the most obvious thing to do next.

Broader context

The subfield this lands in is the cost–quality frontier of multi-stage ranking, from Matveeva et al.'s nested rankers and Wang–Lin–Metzler's cascades through BERT reranking (Nogueira and Cho) to the current retriever/reranker API economy. The paper is best read as the empirical counterpunch to Rosa et al., "In defense of cross-encoders for zero-shot retrieval" (2022), which argued that cross-encoder generalisation is so strong that it should be preferred zero-shot — the crucial difference being first-stage strength and reranker scale. BEIR (Thakur et al. 2021) is the benchmark that established zero-shot reranking as a near-free win, and is also the benchmark whose shallow, pooled qrels make the measurement here fragile; the direct literature on that fragility is Arabzadeh et al.'s shallow-pooling studies and the newer LLM-assessment line (Faggioli et al. on perspectives for LLM judges, MacAvaney and Soldaini's one-shot labelling, UMBRELA) — any of which would have let the authors adjudicate promoted-but-unjudged documents and settle critique (1). RankGPT (Sun et al. 2023) and RankZephyr (Pradeep et al. 2023) are the listwise lineage the mitigation borrows from, with RankZephyr the natural distilled, affordable version of the proposed teacher. ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia — two of this paper's authors are the ColBERT and PLAID authors) is the structural middle ground the paper conspicuously does not test: late interaction is trained with large negative counts like a retriever, serves as a full retriever over an index, and keeps token-level interaction — on the mechanism above it should sit between the two regimes, and its absence from the model grid is the single most interesting omission. On the training side, ANCE (Xiong et al.) and negative caching (Lindgren et al. — also an author here) are the methods that gave embedders their thin negative tails, and Menon et al., "In defense of dual encoders for neural ranking" is the theoretical companion arguing dual encoders can match cross-encoders given the right distillation. For formal treatment, Zamani et al., "Stochastic retrieval-conditioned reranking" (ICTIR 2022, cited here) is the closest existing framework: it models reranking as acting on a distribution over candidate sets rather than a fixed list, which is precisely the right object for reasoning about S(K). Bahri et al.'s Choppy and the ranked-list-truncation line, and MacAvaney et al.'s adaptive reranking with a corpus graph (uncited, and directly on point — it expands the rerank pool adaptively and so inherits exactly this failure mode), are the two directions where this result should immediately change design.

A follow-up. Instrument the mechanism and then exploit it. (a) Estimate p_q for each reranker by depth stratum — sample negatives from retriever ranks [10,1e2), [1e2,1e3), [1e3,1e4) and measure Pr[s(q,d-) > s(q,d+)] per stratum — which directly yields the predicted K_(q) ~ k/p_q and tests whether the observed peaks match it. (b) Fit a calibration map sigma: s -> estimated Pr[rel | q,d] under a proper scoring rule with corpus-wide negatives, and then do the thing the paper's data implies works: _fuse* calibrated reranker and retriever scores, or conformally threshold so the expected number of false promotions among K candidates is at most epsilon, giving a per-query, certified rerank depth instead of a global hyperparameter. (c) Train a cross-encoder with corpus-scale negatives via a negative cache or via distillation from the listwise LLM (the paper's own suggestion) and check whether the non-monotonicity disappears — this is the decisive test of the exposure-bias hypothesis, and it is cheap relative to its value. Deliverable: calibration promoted from an afterthought to a first-class object in cascade design, with depth as a derived quantity.

Connections to theoretical IR, vector search, and generative retrieval — all concrete. First, ANN candidate depth. Every production vector store exposes an oversampling knob — nprobe in IVF, efSearch in HNSW, the rescore depth in ScaNN/anisotropic quantisation — and the folk rule is "retrieve 10x then rerank exactly." This paper says that knob is not monotone end-to-end: raising ANN recall raises R_1(K) into its saturated regime while raising the number of draws from the second-stage scorer's fat negative tail, so there is an interior optimum and pushing index recall toward 1 can be quality-negative if the rescorer is miscalibrated in the tail. The right object to tune is R_1(K) * S(K), not R_1(K), and nobody's index-tuning methodology does that today. Second, calibration as a first-class object. Dense retrieval theory has focused on capacity and expressiveness (Luan et al.'s sparse-vs-dense capacity arguments, Fang et al.'s scaling laws for dense retrieval); this result says the operative quantity for deep candidate lists is a tail property — Pr[s(d-) > s(d+)] at the 1e-6 scale, or the upper tail index of F_- — which is invisible to mean-performance metrics and to expressiveness arguments alike. An extreme-value-theoretic account of retrieval score distributions, with model class and negative-sampling scheme as the parameters, is a genuinely open and tractable theory problem. Third, generative retrieval. Constrained beam search over a docid space scores candidates by sequence likelihood, which is a pointwise scorer over an enormous output space with a learned prior; widening the beam is the exact analogue of raising K, and the same max-of-N argument predicts that beyond some width you start surfacing docids with high generative prior and no relevance. That is a plausible reading of why generative retrieval degrades as corpora scale (Pradeep et al., "How does generative retrieval scale to millions of passages?"), and it makes docid-space score calibration — not just decoding-constraint engineering — the central issue. Fourth, the general lesson, which the paper frames via best-of-N reward hacking and which transfers cleanly: inference-time compute is not monotonically useful when the extra compute is spent sampling from a distribution the scorer was not fit on. Spending at index time (better embeddings, more negatives, late interaction) is governed by a training distribution you control; spending at rerank time is governed by one you do not. On this evidence the index-time dollar is the better buy.

title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-02

Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs — Guo, Pai, Bai, Jiao, Jordan, Mei (2024) — arXiv:2410.13835

Setting and problem

The architecture, as the paper defines it. Let the tokenized input (positional embeddings already added) be H = [h_1,...,h_n] in R^{d x n}. The paper works with the standard pre-norm Vaswani block. A causal attention layer with M heads is Attn(H) = sum_m attn_m(H) with

attn_m(H) = O_m V_m LN(H) SoftMax( mask( LN(H)^T K_m^T Q_m LN(H) ) ),

an MLP layer is mlp(H) = W_2 ReLU(W_1 LN(H)), and an L-layer transformer iterates H^{(l+1/2)} = H^{(l)} + Attn^{(l)}(H^{(l)}), H^{(l+1)} = H^{(l+1/2)} + mlp^{(l)}(H^{(l+1/2)}). Indices are zero-based throughout (matching their code).

Four per-token quantities are the whole object of study. For a token v at a given layer l and head m:

  • residual state Res_v = the v-th column of H^{(l+1)};
  • query / key / value states (Qry_v, Key_v, Val_v) = the v-th columns of QH^{(l)}, KH^{(l)}, and — note this — OVH^{(l)}, i.e. the output projection is folded into the value state, because OVH is what is actually written back into the residual stream;
  • attention logit logit_{v',v} = [ (H^{(l)})^T Q^T K H^{(l)} ]_{v',v}.

The three phenomena, stated formally. Write <s> for the first (BOS) token.

  1. Attention sink: in many heads, the softmax column for essentially every query v' puts near-unit mass on the key of <s>: Map_{v',<s>} ~ 1. In OLMo Layer 24 the mass on {<s>, first delimiter} sits in [0.9, 1] for most of training.
  2. Value-state drain: in exactly those heads, ||Val_{<s>}|| is much smaller than mean_v ||Val_v||.
  3. Residual-state peak: for layers 1 through L-1 (excluding first and last), ||Res_{<s>}|| is much larger than max_{v != <s>} ||Res_v|| — in Llama-3.1-8B, roughly 500 versus about 30.
  4. A fourth, which the paper claims is new: sink-logit concentration. The logits logit_{v',<s>}, as v' ranges over non-sink query tokens, have far smaller variance than logits onto any other key. Their progress measure is Delta logit_{.,<s>} = mean_n [ <Qry_{v_n}, Key_{<s>}> - mean_i ].

The Bigram-Backcopy (BB) data process. Vocabulary V with |V| = 64; the transition matrix P with p_{vk} = P(k | v) is the empirical character-level bigram distribution of tiny Shakespeare (following Bietti et al.'s "Birth of a Transformer"). A fixed trigger set T, |T| = 3, is the three most frequent unigrams ('t', 'e', space); the other 61 are non-triggers. A sequence starts with <s>, then: if the current token v_k is not in T, sample v_{k+1} ~ P(. | v_k); if v_k is in T, set v_{k+1} = v_{k-1} (copy the preceding token forward — hence "backcopy"). So the Bayes-optimal next-token law is P(v' | H) = p_{v_n v'} for v_n not in T and the indicator of v' = v_{n-1} for v_n in T. The learner sees only sampled sequences and is trained with plain autoregressive cross-entropy; the paper reports excess risk decomposed into a Bigram risk (non-trigger positions) and a Backcopy risk (trigger positions), each relative to its Bayes value. Training: Adam, lr 3e-4, betas (0.9, 0.99), weight decay 0.01, batch 512, sequence length 256, fresh samples each step, 10k steps (extended to 100k for the dynamics plot); SGD comparisons use lr 0.03. Models: one head + one MLP for the sink/drain story; three layers (they identify 3xTF and 2xTF+mlp as the minimal structures) for the residual-peak story.

The precise question. Why do attention sinks, value-state drains and residual-state peaks (i) co-occur in the same heads, (ii) land on the first token, and (iii) keep intensifying long after the loss has essentially converged — attention logits growing, value norms shrinking, residual norms growing linearly — and what is the mechanism by which gradient-based pretraining produces them?

What was already known, and the gap. Xiao et al. (StreamingLLM, 2023) discovered that the initial token absorbs most attention and that keeping its KV entries is necessary for streaming inference; their explanation was folklore-grade — softmax must sum to one, so the model needs somewhere to "dump unnecessary attention". Darcet et al. (2023) found the same in ViTs and proposed adding dedicated "register" tokens; crucially, the registers themselves then become extreme, which the dump hypothesis does not explain. Sun et al. (2024) documented "massive activations" and attributed sinks to them (correlation, not mechanism), and showed that an explicitly learned sink token still exhibits the phenomena. Bondarenko et al. (2023) framed it as attention heads wanting a "no-op" and proposed clipped softmax / gated attention; Gurnee et al. (2024) found "attention deactivation neurons"; Dettmers et al. (LLM.int8()) and a large quantization literature treat the outliers as an engineering obstacle requiring mixed precision. Concurrent work (Gu et al., 2024) showed empirically that sigmoid attention prevents sinks up to 1B parameters. The gap: every prior account is static and functional — "the head wants to do nothing" — and none explains the dynamics: why the extremity grows monotonically after convergence, why the logits concentrate, why the residual norm grows linearly in steps, or why the three phenomena are coupled.

The non-obvious modelling choices. The theory does not analyze the trained transformer. It analyzes a hand-built reparameterization that is fitted to observed late-training structure and then frozen:

  • The analyzed model is a parallel sum TF(.) = attn(.) + mlp(.) with no layer normalization (justified on the grounds that sequential attn->mlp can simulate parallel).
  • Restricted attention pattern: ebd(<s>)^T K^T Q ebd_i(v) = alpha_v * 1{v not in T}, and ebd_i(v)^T K^T Q ebd_j(v) = lambda * 1{v in T, i = j-1}, all other logits exactly zero. So the head can only (a) look at <s> with strength alpha_v, or (b) if the query is a trigger, look one position back with strength lambda. Note this forces alpha_v = 0 for triggers.
  • Restricted value pattern: V ebd_i(v) = xi_v e_v (a scaled one-hot), with xi_v = 0 on triggers and xi_v >= 0 otherwise; and V ebd(<s>) = beta in R^V, a free vector.
  • MLP solves the bigram task exactly: mlp(ebd_i(v)) = log p_v * 1{v not in T}.
  • Only (alpha, beta) in R^V x R^V are trainable; xi and lambda are frozen. The regime analyzed is explicitly "after step 200", i.e. bigram learned, backcopy partially learned.
  • The per-context counts M_k = #{i : v_i = k} and M = sum_k M_k = n are treated as fixed constants independent of position (they cite Reddy 2023 for the same simplification), and the loss on trigger tokens is dropped.

Under these restrictions, for a non-trigger query v at the end of H = [<s>, v_{1:n-1}, v], the output logits are exactly

TF(H)_n = log p_v + [ e^{alpha_v}/(e^{alpha_v} + M) ] beta + sum_{k=1}^{V} [ M_k xi_k/(e^{alpha_v} + M) ] e_k,

and the objective is loss(alpha, beta) = sum_{v not in T} pi_v CE( p_v, SoftMax(TF(H)_n) ) with pi the stationary distribution of P. Theorem 1 (formal version: Theorem A.4, under Assumption A that d >= VN+1 so enough orthonormal embedding directions exist, relaxable to d >> log(VN)) certifies that this parameterization is realizable by an actual one-layer transformer, and that as min_v alpha_v, min_v xi_v, lambda -> infinity with beta = 0 it attains the BB Bayes predictor. That is the whole stage: a 2V-dimensional ODE, which is what gets analyzed.

Main idea

Two mechanisms, one static and one dynamic.

Active–dormant (Claim 1). A head is active on an input if it writes something substantial to the residual stream, dormant if its contribution is negligible. The same head switches phase as a function of the input domain.
