In the BB task, interventions make this crisp: zeroing the MLP destroys the bigram task but leaves backcopy far better than chance; zeroing the attention head destroys backcopy (worse than chance) but leaves bigram untouched. So the MLP owns the Markov part, the head owns the copy part, and on the 61 non-trigger tokens the head has nothing to do — and precisely there it dumps near-all its mass on <s> and emits a tiny value state. The attention sink is the signature of dormancy, not a separate phenomenon. In Llama-2-7B they exhibit L16H25 as an interpretable instance: attention maps are sink-dominated on Wikipedia prose and genuinely distributed on GitHub code, and zeroing the head's output costs about 0.4 nats on GitHub versus about 0 on Wikipedia. This reframes sinks as conditional no-ops with an input-dependent switch, which is strictly more informative than the global "dump unnecessary attention" story.

Mutual reinforcement (Claim 2). Why do dormancy's symptoms become extreme? Because under softmax the two symptoms feed each other. The head's output is approximately a_beta + (1-a)_v-bar with a the sink weight. (i) If beta is small (or, more precisely, a constant vector, which is a no-op after the output softmax), then routing attention to <s> is the cheapest way to avoid contaminating an already-correct MLP prediction, so gradient descent pushes alpha up — logarithmically, alpha(t) ~ (1/2) log t. (ii) If alpha is large, then <s>'s value state is the only thing being read, so gradient flow drives beta to the unique counter-term that cancels the residual leakage from other tokens — a small, nearly constant vector. Each reinforces the other; the loop terminates in a stable phase where all non-trigger queries have large and nearly identical logits on <s> ("sink-logit concentration") and beta is pinned at c*1 - e^{-alpha} (M circ xi). The causal mask is what elects <s>: position 0 is the only token visible to every query.

Residual-state peaks are a third, optimizer-driven phenomenon. They need depth >= 3 (one- and two-layer BB models show none); the massive residual at layer 0's output is what creates the sink and drain in the middle layer (zeroing layer 0 restores normal logits and value norms); in Llama-3.1-8B the corresponding ablation shows that killing layer 0's or layer 1's MLP — and nothing else — removes the peak. And the growth is linear in steps, which is a fingerprint of Adam: the underlying gradient decays like log t/(sqrt(t) m^3), and Adam's normalization converts a decaying gradient into a constant-size update.

Mitigations as predictions. Replacing softmax with ReLU attention removes the normalization pressure, so there is no attention budget to spend; logits on <s> stay at zero, beta never shrinks, and the loop never starts — confirmed on BB (both risks reach Bayes in ~200 steps with no extreme tokens). Swapping Adam for SGD kills the residual peak while leaving the sink and drain intact — a clean dissociation that supports the two-mechanism decomposition.

Table 1 of the paper is unusually honest bookkeeping: four quantitative signatures x three evidence sources (BB theory / BB experiment / LLM experiment), with two cells marked inconclusive — the log t logit growth is not clearly established in LLMs, and the linear residual growth has no theorem.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever observation is buried in Theorem 2(c), and the paper half-flags it before moving on: the attention sink is not required by optimality. The set of global minimizers of the reparameterized loss is the two-parameter family

alpha = alpha_1, beta = c_1 - e^{-alpha} (M circ xi), (alpha, c) in R^2,

on which the loss equals the conditional entropy of P _for every value of alpha, including alpha = 0 or alpha = -10_. There is a flat valley of exactly-Bayes-optimal solutions, indexed by sink strength, and the sink is simply where the gradient flow drifts: a (1/2) log t slide along a degenerate direction. The paper says this out loud in a remark — "the stable phase... seems to imply that the system can remain stable without attention sinks... However, in practice, models trained on the BB task tend to converge to a stable phase where alpha is relatively large" — and then does not pursue it. But this is the sharpest thing in the paper: extreme tokens are an artifact of the path, not of the objective. It makes the mitigation story principled rather than hacky (you are not trading loss for well-conditioned activations; you are choosing a different point on the same minimizing set), and it suggests the cleanest possible intervention: kill the flat direction (e.g. project out the 1-component of the sink logits, or regularize alpha) rather than replace softmax wholesale.

Now the critique, which is substantial.

1. The theory analyzes a model built from the answer. The restricted attention pattern assumes that only the <s>-logits and the one-step-back trigger logits are nonzero — i.e. it assumes the attention map has already collapsed to the structure whose emergence is being explained. The value pattern assumes one-hot value states; the MLP is assumed to already output log p_v exactly; xi and lambda are frozen; trigger-token loss is discarded; context counts are frozen as position-independent constants. What remains is a 2V-scalar ODE. The theorems about that ODE are real theorems, but what they explain is the late-stage sharpening of a sink, conditional on a sink-shaped parameterization. The actual symmetry-breaking event — why this head, why token 0, why in this layer — is outside the theory. Appendix C.4 (no <s>: triggers and delimiters become sinks instead) and G.2 (shuffling the input still sinks on token 0, so RoPE position matters a lot) are good science but explicitly left as "future work".

2. The step from BB to Llama/OLMo is correlational pattern-matching, not inference. What is actually shown for LLMs: one highly interpretable active–dormant head in Llama-2-7B (plus two harder-to-read ones in Appendix D) out of 32x32 = 1024 heads, supporting a claim about "many attention heads"; and OLMo Layer 24 trajectories that are qualitatively shaped like the BB curves (attention mass up then flat, value norms down, residual norm linear, logits concentrated). The quantitative predictions that would discriminate this mechanism from alternatives are weak where it matters: (1/2) log t growth is marked inconclusive in LLMs (Table 1), and the theory's one genuinely sharp quantitative claim — that the drain factor is 1/sqrt(V) relative to initialization, since the 1-component of beta is exactly conserved — is never tested against vocabulary size, which would be a cheap and falsifiable experiment across model families. A single layer (24) of a single model (OLMo-7B-0424), on one prompt plus 128 8-token Wikipedia samples, is a thin dynamic base.

3. There is a live alternative hypothesis the paper does not engage. The paper's thesis is that sinks are functionless — a no-op dump that the dynamics then exaggerates. A competing view (developed in work after this paper, e.g. Barbero et al., "Why do LLMs attend to the first token?", 2025) is that sinks are functional: a near-identity default that suppresses over-mixing and representational collapse in deep residual stacks. That view predicts that removing sinks hurts deep models specifically — and the BB experiments are 1–3 layers, exactly the regime where over-mixing cannot occur. So the ReLU result may be a depth artifact. Relatedly, the direction of travel in the field since late 2024 has been toward sinks, not away: several recent open-weight models ship per-head learnable sink logits as a deliberate architectural feature. If sinks were pure pathology, that would be odd.

4. The mitigations are untested for capability, and the paper says so. ReLU attention is validated on V = 64 characters with 1–3 layers; softmax-free attention has well-documented optimization and length-generalization problems, and the paper never measures any downstream metric. Adam->SGD is a non-starter at LLM scale regardless of sinks. The conclusion is admirably candid: "it remains unclear whether their elimination significantly improves downstream tasks", and they propose GPT-2-scale pretraining as the needed experiment. That is honest, but it means the paper's fourth contribution is a conjecture dressed as a method. Gu et al.'s concurrent sigmoid-attention result to 1B is stronger evidence than anything here.

5. Minor but real appendix sloppiness. Proposition B.1 assumes "{W_k beta_k} are not all equal" and then, in the same sentence, "Fix beta = 0" — internally inconsistent; the intended condition is surely the heterogeneity of {M_k xi_k} used everywhere else. Lemma A.2's proof computes null spaces of G^P_v but then takes "minimal non-zero eigenvalues of G^L_v". And the residual-peak section rests on Claim B.1 (a claim, not a proposition) plus a scalar Adam simulation (Figure 15) with hand-picked hyperparameters — the weakest link in a paper whose headline includes residual-state peaks.

Proof sketch

What is actually proved. Within the reparameterized model — architecture TF = attn + mlp with no LayerNorm, Eqs. (6)–(8) imposed, xi and lambda frozen, counts (M_k, M) frozen, trigger loss dropped — and under the assumptions xi_v >= 0, pi_v > 0, and {M_i xi_i} not all equal, consider gradient flow alpha-dot = -grad_alpha loss, beta-dot = -grad_beta loss. Then:

  • (a) With beta frozen at a constant vector beta*1, from any alpha(0): alpha(t) = (1/2) log t * 1 + r(t) with ||r(t)|| uniformly bounded in t. (Rigorous; exact two-sided ODE bounds.)
  • (b) With alpha frozen at alpha_1: beta(t) -> beta_ = [beta-bar(0) + e^{-alpha} B] 1 - e^{-alpha} (M circ xi), where beta-bar(0) is the mean of the initialization and B = (1/V) sum_v M_v xi_v. (Rigorous convergence.)
  • (c) For the joint flow, every point of the family alpha = alpha_1, beta = c_1 - e^{-alpha}(M circ xi) is stationary, and all such points are global minimizers.

So this is a two-timescale, one-variable-frozen-at-a-time analysis plus a fixed-point characterization — not a theorem about the joint dynamics. Nobody proves that the coupled flow converges to the family in (c), nor that it is stable in any dynamical-systems sense; "stable phase" is a name. Nor is it proved that (c) exhausts the stationary points. And (a)+(b) do not compose: (a)'s driving force is precisely that a frozen constant beta cannot cancel the leakage, so alpha -> infinity is the only route to zero loss; (b) shows that an unfrozen beta can cancel it, at which point alpha has no incentive to move. The "mutual reinforcement loop" is the informal composition of two analyses whose hypotheses are mutually exclusive. The residual-state peak has no theorem at all: Claim B.1 is a heuristic three-step story (gradients on Res_{<s>} keep a fixed direction; LayerNorm makes them decay; Adam converts decaying gradients into constant updates), of which only Proposition B.1 — m-dot(t) = O(log t/(sqrt(t) m^3)) for a scalar surrogate — is proved, with the Adam->linear-growth step done by numerical simulation.

How the arguments go.

The structural setup. Lemma A.5 computes the derivatives of l_{ik} with respect to alpha_v and beta_v in closed form and yields two conservation identities, sum_k d l_{ik}/d alpha_v = 0 and sum_v d l_{ik}/d beta_v = 0. Proposition A.6 then gives the gradient-flow ODE in just two lines:

alpha-dot_v = [ pi-tilde_v e^{alpha_v}/(e^{alpha_v} + M)^2 ] sum_i (p_{vi} - l_{vi})(M beta_i - M_i xi_i), beta-dot_v = sum_k [ pi-tilde_k e^{alpha_k} (p_{kv} - l_{kv}) ] / (e^{alpha_k} + M).

Two structural facts do most of the work. First, the alpha-dynamics decouple across coordinates — alpha-dot_v depends on alpha_v alone (through l_v) — so the V sink logits evolve as V independent scalar ODEs. This is why sink-logit concentration holds: every coordinate independently reaches (1/2) log t + O(1), so the spread stays O(1) while the level diverges. Second, the beta-dynamics couple but conserve the mean: the second identity in Lemma A.5 gives sum_v beta-dot_v = 0, so the 1-component of beta is a constant of motion. That single conservation law is the entire quantitative content of the "drain": the free, orthogonal-to-1 structure of beta collapses to an O(e^{-alpha}) counter-term, and what survives is beta-bar(0)_1, whose norm for Gaussian initialization is about ||beta(0)||_2/sqrt(V). The value-state drain is, in this model, _a factor of sqrt(V) handed to you by mean conservation plus random initialization.*

(a) The covariance trick. Set u = e^{alpha_v} and introduce a random variable phi with P(phi = M_k xi_k) = p_{vk}. With beta = c*1, the constant part drops out (since sum_i (p_{vi} - l_{vi}) = 0) and the whole sum collapses into a single covariance:

du/dt = [ pi-tilde_v u^2/(u+M)^2 ] * Cov( e^{phi/(u+M)}, phi ) / E[ e^{phi/(u+M)} ].

This is the key move and it immediately gives monotonicity for free: x -> e^{x/(u+M)} and x -> x are both increasing, so the covariance is >= 0 and u never decreases — i.e. the attention sink can only strengthen. Then two Taylor expansions of e^{phi/(u+M)} pin the rate. First order gives du/dt <= pi-tilde_v C_theta E[phi^2]/u; second order, with theta_2(phi) phi^2 monotone so that Cov(theta_2(phi) phi^2, phi) >= 0, gives du/dt >= C-tilde/u with C-tilde proportional to Var(phi) — which is exactly where "{M_i xi_i} not all equal" is needed. Both bounds integrate to u ~ sqrt(t), hence alpha_v = log u = (1/2) log t + O(1). (The boundedness of the constants uses monotonicity of u to freeze them at u(0).) The (1/2) log t rate echoes the logarithmic attention-concentration rates in Tian et al.'s "scan and snap".

(b) PL via Pinsker, bootstrapped. In beta the loss is convex: the Hessian is sum_k pi-tilde_k G^L_k with G^L_k = diag(l_k) - l_k l_k^T, and Lemma A.1 shows every G^P_v, G^L_v is PSD by diagonal dominance (rows sum appropriately because sum_k p_{vk} = sum_k l_{vk} = 1; then Horn–Johnson Cor. 6.2.27). These Gram-like matrices have an unavoidable null direction 1, so one cannot get strong convexity globally. The fix is a two-step bootstrap. Lemma A.2: on the orthogonal complement of 1, sum_k pi-tilde_k G^P_k >= omega I for some omega > 0 — proved by computing ker G^P_v = {eta : eta_j constant on supp(p_v)} and showing the intersection over v of ker G^P_v is span(1) because the bigram chain is irreducible enough that every token is reachable. Lemma A.3: the same holds with omega/2 for sum_k pi-tilde_k G^L_k provided max_{v,k} |p_{vk} - l_{vk}| <= min{omega/(6V), 1}, via an entrywise perturbation bound and a crude Frobenius bound. Then the actual argument: plug in beta_ and verify l_v = p_v exactly, so loss(alpha, beta_) equals the conditional entropy — the global minimum. Convexity gives loss-value convergence; a small loss gap is a small weighted KL(p_v || l_v); Pinsker converts that to small total variation, i.e. l entrywise close to p; which activates Lemma A.3; which yields a Polyak–Lojasiewicz inequality loss(alpha, beta(t)) - loss(alpha, beta_) <= (1/(2 omega)) ||grad_beta loss||^2 for large t; and PL gives convergence of the iterate, with the 1-component pinned by the conservation law. The elegance is that convexity is used to get _into* the neighbourhood where a quantitative PL constant exists, and Pinsker is the bridge between the two.

(c) Direct verification: at alpha = alpha_1, beta = c_1 - e^{-alpha}(M circ xi), the exponent (M_k xi_k + e^{alpha} beta_k)/(e^{alpha} + M) becomes k-independent, equal to e^{alpha} c/(e^{alpha} + M), so it cancels in the softmax and l_{vi} = p_{vi}. Both gradients vanish and the loss equals the entropy lower bound. This is where the flat valley — and the observation that sinks are optimality-irrelevant — comes from.

Broader context

The subfield. Mechanistic interpretability tries to identify the computational circuits implementing specific behaviours in trained transformers (induction heads, factual-recall circuits, IOI circuits). A complementary theory strand — Bai, Mei, and collaborators; Bietti et al.; Tian et al.; Nichani/Reddy — studies why gradient descent produces such circuits by constructing minimal synthetic tasks whose learned solution is identifiable, reducing the transformer to a handful of scalar order parameters, and solving the resulting gradient-flow ODE. This paper is a clean instance of that methodology aimed at an engineering nuisance rather than a capability: the "extreme tokens" that force mixed-precision quantization (Dettmers et al., LLM.int8()), special-cased KV caches (Xiao et al., StreamingLLM; H2O; SnapKV), and uninterpretable attention maps.

Two or three to read alongside. (i) Xiao et al., Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks (2023) — the discovery paper and the source of the hypothesis this one replaces; also the practical reason sink tokens must never be evicted from a KV cache. (ii) Darcet et al., Vision Transformers Need Registers (2023) — the same phenomenon in ViTs and the "add a dedicated dump token" fix, which this paper's framing explains the limits of: a register is a new candidate for dormancy, so it inherits the extremity rather than absorbing it. (iii) Bondarenko et al., Quantizable Transformers: Removing Outliers by Helping Attention Heads Do Nothing (2023) — the "no-op" hypothesis made architectural (clipped softmax, gated attention), the closest antecedent to the active–dormant framing; alongside Miller's softmax-off-by-one (which adds an implicit zero-logit slot so the head can spend no budget) and Gu et al.'s sigmoid-attention result at 1B scale. For the opposing reading, Barbero et al.'s Why do LLMs attend to the first token? (2025) argues sinks regulate over-mixing in deep stacks — a direct challenge to the "functionless dump" thesis, and the paper's three-layer experiments cannot discriminate between them. Finally, Sun et al., Massive Activations in Large Language Models (2024), is the empirical basis for the residual-state-peak half.

A follow-up I would actually run. Theorem 2(c) says the zero-loss set is a flat valley indexed by sink strength, so sinks are a drift artifact, not a loss requirement. That makes a surgical intervention testable: instead of replacing softmax, kill the degenerate direction — e.g. reparameterize the per-head sink logits so that their common (1-aligned) component is fixed or penalized, or use an optimizer whose preconditioner does not amplify progress along near-flat directions (the paper's own Adam->SGD dissociation shows Adam is specifically responsible for the linear residual growth). Run it at GPT-2 / 1B scale against three axes the paper leaves open: (1) downstream perplexity and long-context retrieval accuracy, to settle whether sinks are load-bearing (the Barbero hypothesis predicts a depth-dependent penalty, this paper predicts none); (2) INT8/INT4 post-training-quantization degradation, which is the practical payoff; (3) the untested 1/sqrt(V) drain-scaling prediction, by varying vocabulary size at fixed data — cheap, sharp, and falsifiable.

Honest IR / vector-search connections. Three are real; one is weak.

Strong — pooling and embedding geometry. The residual-state peak is a direct statement about using LLM hidden states as retrieval embeddings (E5-Mistral, LLM2Vec, RepLLaMA and friends all read out of exactly these residual streams). In Llama-3.1-8B, ||Res_{<s>}|| is about 500 while every other token sits near 30 at layers 1–30. Mean-pooling over positions is therefore dominated, at the 10–20x level, by a token that the paper's own mechanism selects for being semantically void — dormancy attaches to tokens that carry no information useful for prediction. This gives a mechanistic justification for practices usually adopted by trial and error: excluding BOS and delimiters from pooling, using last-token/appended-[EOS] pooling, or pooling at a layer where the peak has subsided. It also connects to the "rogue dimensions" literature (Timkey and van Schijndel, 2021): massive activations are concentrated in a few coordinates, and those coordinates then dominate every dot product, which is exactly the anisotropy that whitening / all-but-the-top / per-dimension standardization are patching. The honest caveat: contrastive fine-tuning may reshape this, and the paper offers no evidence either way — this is an open empirical question, not a settled implication.

Strong — hubness as the same phenomenon. Appendix E is, read literally, a statement about the geometry of a learned maximum-inner-product search problem. At Llama-3.1 L0H31, (i) Key_{<s>} has small inner product with all other keys, and (ii) every query is nearly orthogonal to every non-<s> key. So one key wins the argmax over all queries by being the only non-orthogonal direction in key space. That is textbook hubness in high-dimensional nearest-neighbour retrieval (Radovanovic et al., 2010): a small number of points appear in disproportionately many neighbour lists, degrading recall and calibration. What this paper adds is a training-dynamics account of how a hub is manufactured — the (1/2) log t drift along a flat direction — which is suggestive for anyone studying hub formation in learned dense retrievers trained with softmax-normalized (InfoNCE) objectives. The analogy is structural, not formal, but the shared ingredient is concrete: a softmax over inner products with a fixed total budget plus a candidate that is uninformative for the task.

Medium — quantized indexes and KV caches. The outlier structure that forced LLM.int8()'s mixed-precision decomposition is the same structure that distorts product quantization and scalar quantization of LLM-derived embeddings: with a few coordinates orders of magnitude larger than the rest, per-subspace codebook distortion is dominated by whichever subspace holds the outlier dims, so OPQ-style rotation or per-dimension scaling matters considerably more for LLM-derived vectors than for, say, BERT-CLS or image features. For RAG systems specifically, the KV-cache-quantization and KV-eviction literature already special-cases sink positions; this paper tells you which positions will be special — semantically void tokens visible to all queries — rather than requiring you to find them empirically.

Weak — generative retrieval. One can speculate that a docid decoder attending over a semantically empty docid prefix is in a dormant regime and will sink, and more interestingly that newly added atomic docid tokens (which are near-semantically-void by construction at the start of continued pretraining, and are exactly the kind of token the paper's Appendix G.1 argument predicts will become secondary sinks unless the data gives them real semantics) would acquire extreme-token behaviour — with knock-on effects on any pooled representation of the docid and on KV-cache quantization during constrained beam search over a trie. That is a plausible and testable hypothesis, and the delimiter result (delimiters become sinks in OLMo/Llama-2 but not Llama-3.1, which the authors attribute to Llama-3.1's much larger code fraction making delimiters semantically meaningful) is a genuine precedent for "token semantics decide sink-hood". But nothing in the paper addresses generative retrieval, and I would present this as a research hypothesis rather than an implication. The closest real bridge is Wu et al.'s retrieval heads (2024): heads that reliably copy from context are, in this paper's vocabulary, the active heads, and active–dormant is the natural generalization — the same head is a retrieval head on some inputs and a no-op on others, which is directly relevant to anyone pruning or caching heads for long-context retrieval.

title: SPEX: A Spectral Approach to Explainable Clustering
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-02

SPEX: A Spectral Approach to Explainable Clustering — Tal Argov, Tal Wagner (NeurIPS 2025) — paper

Setting and problem

The ambient model. Fix a dataset X in R^d, |X| = n, with coordinates x = (x_1,...,x_d). Following Moshkovitz, Dasgupta, Rashtchian (ICML 2020), a clustering of X is explainable if it is realized by the leaves of a binary axis-aligned decision tree: every internal node v carries a coordinate j_v and a threshold tau_v, and routes x left iff x_{j_v} <= tau_v. Formally, a coordinate cut is S_{j,tau}(X) := {x in X : x_j <= tau}, valid if it is neither empty nor all of X. The root holds X; a left child of u holds S_{j_u,tau_u}(X_u) and the right child the complement. The leaves L(T) induce the partition of X. The explanation of any point's cluster is therefore a conjunction of at most depth(T) single-feature threshold tests — this is the entire appeal of the model, and it is why oblique (hyperplane) cuts, which Gabidolla and Carreira-Perpinan show can represent any k-means clustering with zero loss, are excluded: they buy expressivity by destroying interpretability.

The classical pipeline and its cost measure. The dominant paradigm is rounding: you are given a reference clustering C = (C_1,...,C_k) of X, computed by any means you like, plus (crucially, in prior work) centroids M = {mu^(1),...,mu^(k)}, and you must output an explainable tree T with l leaves (l = k in the canonical setting) that approximates C. Quality is measured by the price of explainability: for k-medians, cost_1(C) = sum_i sum_{x in C_i} ||x - mu^(i)||_1 with mu^(i) = med(C_i), and the price is cost_1(T)/cost_1(C^OPT) where the tree's cost uses each leaf's own optimal center. Known landscape: IMM achieves O(k) for k-medians and O(k^2) for k-means; EMN (Esfandiari–Mirrokni–Narayanan, SODA'22) gives O(k log k) for k-means deterministically; randomized algorithms give a tight (1+o(1)) ln k for k-medians and O(k ln ln k) for k-means (Gupta–Pittu–Svensson–Yuan, FOCS'23), tight up to the ln ln k; Charikar–Hu and others sharpen the low-dimensional regime; Bandyapadhyay et al. and Gupta et al. study the complexity of approximating the best explainable clustering.

The gap. Every one of those results is welded to a centroid-based objective. IMM's cut rule literally counts points separated from their centroid; EMN's ratio rule needs a set of centroids to split. So the whole machinery is unusable when the reference clustering has no centroids — kernel k-means, spectral clustering, DBSCAN-style or manifold clusterings. And that is not an exotic complaint: the two-moons dataset (the paper's Figure 2, left) has an essentially error-free axis-aligned explanation, but k-means cannot see the moons, so any method rounding a k-means reference inherits the failure, while spectral or kernel k-means gets the moons right and could be rounded almost perfectly. Fleissner, Chennuru Vankadara, Ghoshdastidar (ICLR 2024) took the first step with Kernel IMM, but it is kernel-specific, intricate, and (the present paper shows) does not scale past a few thousand points. The only genuinely generic alternative is to abuse CART: treat cluster IDs as supervised labels and grow a Gini-impurity tree. CART is objective-mismatched — Moshkovitz et al.'s 3-cluster toy example (Figure 2, right: one cluster on top, two side by side below) has an error-free horizontal first cut, but CART takes the error-heavy vertical cut.

The precise question this paper asks. Is there a single, reference-oblivious algorithm that fits an axis-aligned explanation tree to an arbitrary given clustering — no centroids, no kernel, no assumption on cluster shape — with a principled objective rather than a repurposed classification loss, and with a graph-theoretic account of why the existing methods behave as they do?

Graph-partitioning notation, because everything is recast in it. For an undirected weighted G(X,E,w) and a nonempty proper subset S of X, write e_G(S, X\S) for the cut weight and vol_G(S) for the sum of weighted degrees in S. One-sided: sparsity phi_G(S) = e_G(S,S^c)/|S|, conductance psi_G(S) = e_G(S,S^c)/vol_G(S). Two-sided: ratio cut Phi_G(S) = e_G(S,S^c)|X|/(|S||S^c|) and normalized cut Psi_G(S) = e_G(S,S^c) vol_G(X)/(vol_G(S) vol_G(S^c)), so Psi_G(S) = psi_G(S) + psi_G(X\S). (These differ from the min-denominator versions by at most a factor 2, which the paper uses freely.) The tree objective is the multiway normalized cut Psi-bar_G(T) = sum over leaves v of psi_G(X_v).

Non-obvious modelling choices worth flagging up front.

  1. What the "given clustering" is. It enters only as a graph on X, never as centroids. This is the whole trick, and it is what makes the method oblivious.
  2. Which graph. Three natural encodings: the clique graph (same cluster iff adjacent), the star graph (each point joined to its centroid — requires centroids), and the independent-set (IS) graph (adjacent iff different clusters, i.e. the clique graph's complement; with IS you want to maximize the cut). SPEX picks the clique graph. The reference-free variant drops the reference entirely and builds a kappa-NN graph on X (kappa = 20 by default; note kappa is not k).
  3. The two-graph framework. Following Trevisan's Non-Uniform Sparsest Cut, with two graphs G, H on the same node set, Psi_{G,H}(S) = (e_G(S,S^c)/vol_G(X)) / (e_H(S,S^c)/vol_H(X)). Uniform sparsest cut is H = unweighted clique; normalized cut is H = the G-degree-weighted clique (w_H(x,y) proportional to d_G(x)d_G(y)); min s-t cut is H = a single edge. Prior explainable-clustering algorithms are then read off as particular (G,H) pairs.
  4. Decoupling l from k. SPEX grows to any target number of leaves l; centroid methods are structurally pinned to l = k and need separate machinery (ExKMC) to exceed it. The authors argue l >= k is forced (each outcome needs its own explanation) and l = k is "most explainable".

With this, you could state the main theorem or rerun the experiments: datasets are CIFAR-10 (50k, 512-d CLIP), 20 Newsgroups (11,314, 768-d SBERT), MNIST (60k, 512-d CLIP), Caltech 101 (8,677, 512-d CLIP), Dry Beans (13,611, 16-d), Breast Cancer (569, 30-d), Ecoli (336, 7-d), Iris (150, 4-d), plus synthetic R15 and Pathbased; ground-truth classes serve as the gold clustering and agreement is measured by ARI and AMI.

Main idea

The paper's organizing observation is a geometric Cheeger inequality for coordinate cuts. Generalizing a theorem of Dong–Indyk–Razenshteyn–Wagner (Neural LSH, ICLR 2020), itself built on the Andoni–Naor–Nikolov–Razenshteyn–Waingarten nonlinear-spectral-gap framework for nearest neighbor search, from k-NN graphs to arbitrary weighted graphs:

Theorem 2.2. Let G(X,E,w) be any weighted graph on X in R^d. Let D_adj sample an edge with probability proportional to its weight, and D_all sample two points independently, each with probability proportional to its weighted degree. Then there exists a valid coordinate cut (j,tau) with Psi_G(S_{j,tau}(X)) <= sqrt( E_{D_adj}||x-y||^2 / E_{D_all}||x-y||^2 ).

Read it as: if the graph is geometrically faithful — adjacent points are closer than random points — then the graph has a good normalized cut, and that cut can be taken axis-aligned. The hypothesis is only an inequality between two expectations, so it tolerates arbitrary cluster shapes, outliers, and unequal sizes; nothing is assumed about centroids, convexity, or the metric structure within clusters.

Turning this into an algorithm (SPEX, Algorithm 1): encode the reference clustering as the clique graph G, then grow a tree by greedy normalized-cut splitting. For a node with point set X', CutScore(X',j,tau) = psi_G(S_{j,tau}(X')) + psi_G(X' \ S_{j,tau}(X')) (i.e. Psi_G of the cut), minimized exactly by sweeping all O(dn) coordinate cuts; the leaf to split next is chosen by a priority queue on LeafScore(v) = psi_G(X_v) - min_{j,tau} CutScore, which is precisely the reduction in Psi-bar_G(T) that splitting v would deliver. Two instantiations: SPEX-Clique (clique graph over any given reference clustering) and SPEX-kNN (the kappa-NN graph of X — reference-free, an explainable clustering computed directly from the data with no clustering step at all).

It is worth writing down what SPEX-Clique actually optimizes, because the paper never does. With a_{vi} = |X_v intersect C_i|, the unweighted clique graph gives deg(x) = |C_i| - 1 for x in C_i, hence

psi_G(X_v) = [ sum_i a_{vi}(|C_i| - a_{vi}) ] / [ sum_i a_{vi}(|C_i| - 1) ].

So the numerator counts same-cluster pairs torn apart by the tree, volume-normalized; Psi-bar_G(T) = 0 iff every reference cluster sits inside a single leaf. Compare CART's Gini objective, (1/n) sum_v sum_i a_{vi}(|X_v| - a_{vi})/|X_v|, whose numerator counts different-cluster pairs lumped together inside a leaf. That is the clique/IS duality in one line, and it is the paper's conceptual payload.

The second contribution is the unifying lens. Through Trevisan's two-graph sparsity, up to small modifications:

  • IMM = G the star graph (point–centroid edges, so e_G(S,S^c) is exactly IMM's mistake count mis_u(S)), H a single edge joining the two diametrical centroids in the node.
  • EMN = same G (star), H an unweighted clique on the surviving centroids, so e_H(S,S^c) = |S ∩ M| |S^c ∩ M|, which is EMN's f_u(S) = min{|S ∩ M|, |S^c ∩ M|} up to a factor 2.
  • CART = H the IS graph and G the H-degree-weighted clique, maximizing Psi_{H,G}; equivalently maximizing conductance in the IS graph.
  • SPEX-Clique/kNN = G the clique / kappa-NN graph, H the G-degree-weighted clique (i.e. plain normalized cut).

This immediately diagnoses the known failure modes: the star graph requires centroids; the IS graph has edges only between different clusters, so it rewards separating cross-cluster pairs and is structurally indifferent to splitting a cluster in half — which is exactly why CART picks the vertical cut in the 3-cluster toy example (more cross-cluster edges severed) over the horizontal one (fewer, but which leaves the top cluster intact).

Headline empirical finding: SPEX-Clique is the most consistently strong method — it beats each baseline in most dataset x metric cells and is never beaten by two baselines simultaneously; SPEX-kNN, with no reference clustering at all, wins outright on the low-dimensional datasets (Beans 16-d, Ecoli 7-d, Iris 4-d), e.g. Ecoli ARI .679 vs .662 for SPEX-Clique and .456 for EMN, and Beans ARI .574 vs .542 for CART. CART, which earlier small-scale studies had suggested was fine, collapses at scale (MNIST, spectral reference: ARI .027 vs SPEX-Clique .217; Caltech 101: -.010 vs .247; CIFAR: .036 vs .320). Kernel IMM simply does not run beyond a few thousand points (3-hour budget, or OOM). And SPEX-Clique is the cheapest tree builder: O(n) memory (store only point-to-cluster assignments, never the Theta(n^2) clique), two k-bin histograms during the sweep, O(1) score updates, total O(kdn log n).

The most interesting part

Two things compete. The genuinely clever idea is the clique-vs-independent-set dichotomy, which is the sharpest thing in the paper: Gini impurity and SPEX's normalized cut look like two sides of the same coin (the IS graph is literally the complement of the clique graph), and naive intuition says minimizing "different clusters together" should be equivalent to minimizing "same cluster apart". It is not — because of the volume normalization and because the trees are grown greedily — and the inequivalence is precisely the toy-example failure. Recasting Gini as conductance in the IS graph makes CART's pathology a one-sentence structural fact rather than a hand-crafted counterexample, and it gets empirically vindicated at scale. That is good science: an explanation for a failure mode plus the experiment that shows the failure mode matters.

But the critique is more illuminating for someone deciding whether to build on this, so let me be concrete.

The theory does not support the algorithm as advertised. Theorem 2.2 is an existence statement about one cut in one graph. It says nothing about (a) the greedy recursion — no bound on Psi-bar_G(T) for the tree SPEX produces versus the optimal l-leaf tree, no submodularity or potential-function argument for the priority-queue leaf selection; (b) any relation between Psi-bar_G(T) and clustering cost, or between Psi-bar_G(T) and agreement with the reference clustering. The conclusion concedes there are no approximation bounds, which is honest, but the gap is wider than "no worst-case ratio": the theorem is not even used operationally. SPEX never computes an eigenvector. It brute-force sweeps all O(dn) coordinate cuts and takes the exact minimizer, so Cheeger is invoked only to argue that the minimum it finds is small. "Spectral" in the title describes the provenance of the objective, not the computation — the algorithm is purely combinatorial. (Eigenvectors appear only inside spectral clustering when that is used as the reference, which is a separate black box.)

The guarantee is vacuous exactly where the problem is hard. Instantiate Theorem 2.2 with Corollary A.5's weighted clique (edges inside C_i get weight 1/(|C_i| - 1), so every degree is 1): the bound becomes

Psi_G(S) <= sqrt( 2 cost(C) / [ (1/|X|) sum_{x,y} ||x-y||^2 ] ),

and since (1/|X|) sum_{x != y} ||x-y||^2 = sum_x ||x - mu_X||^2 (same Fact A.6 with C = X), the right-hand side is sqrt(2 * (within-cluster SS / total SS)) — the square root of twice the fraction of variance the reference clustering fails to explain. Crisp and interpretable, and also self-limiting: it is nontrivial only when the reference clustering already explains more than half the variance. On 512-d CLIP embeddings, where the within-cluster variance fraction is large, the bound exceeds 1 and says nothing. That is not a coincidence — it is exactly where the experiments degrade.

The experiments show all explainable clustering is in trouble at high dimension, and this is under-emphasized. On MNIST with a spectral reference of ARI .745, SPEX-Clique reaches .217 and agrees with the reference at only REF = .282. Caltech 101: reference .563, SPEX-Clique .247, REF .303. Newsgroups: reference .431, SPEX-Clique .078, REF .189. So on the large, high-dimensional datasets, the best generic method retains roughly a quarter to a third of the reference structure. The correct reading is not "SPEX wins" but "with l = k axis-aligned leaves in 512 dimensions, nothing explains a spectral clustering" — SPEX is simply least bad. Symmetrically, SPEX-kNN, which is the method with the most intellectual novelty (reference-free!), is excellent in d <= 16 and terrible in d >= 30 (MNIST .092, Newsgroups .042) — a textbook kappa-NN-graph-in-high-dimension story that deserved analysis rather than a footnote.

The CART indictment is partly withdrawn in the appendix. Section B.1 reports that scikit-learn's default weighted-CART leaf-selection rule changes the picture substantially: on MNIST with a spectral reference, CART goes .027 -> .279, beating SPEX-Clique's .217; CIFAR .036 -> .380 vs .320; Caltech -.010 -> .219 vs .247. And the same modification applied to SPEX-Clique hurts it badly (.217 -> .018 on MNIST). So the headline "CART suffers low performance on real data", which the paper ties causally to the IS-graph objective, is substantially confounded with the leaf-selection heuristic, and the variant that the community actually runs is competitive with SPEX on the largest datasets. Burying this in an appendix, while the main text argues the IS graph explains CART's weakness, is the paper's weakest editorial decision. (Note also that Table 8's Beans and CIFAR columns share identical entries in the three modified rows — likely a transcription error.)

Smaller things. (i) The NeurIPS checklist claims no error bars are needed because "all methods are deterministic" — true of the rounding step, false of the pipeline: k-means++ and spectral clustering (affinity construction, k-means in the embedding) are randomized, and single-run ARI on Iris (150 points) or Ecoli (336) is noisy. (ii) The evaluation metric is agreement with ground-truth labels, which no method optimizes; EMN is near-optimal for the k-means cost ratio and is judged on something else. The REF column partly repairs this, but the price of explainability — the quantity the entire theory literature is about — is never reported, so the paper cannot be placed against that literature numerically. (iii) The l = 2k experiment (Table 6) honestly reports "no clearly superior method", which matters for anyone wanting many leaves. (iv) The affinity graph used for spectral clustering on 50k points is not specified in the main text. (v) Constants in the Cheeger chain are loose: (14) gives E_adj/E_all >= 2R with R the Rayleigh quotient and Theorem A.3 gives Psi <= 2 sqrt(R), which composes to sqrt(2) times the stated clean bound; harmless given the factor-2 slop declared in Section 2, but it is there. (vi) Lemma A.10's statement has H cost_1(T-tilde_IMM(C)) on the right where the proof actually establishes H cost_1(C) — as stated the implication to Theorem A.8 would be circular. Typo, but a load-bearing one. (vii) The max-distance centroid pair is defined with a min in the displayed equation where a max is meant.

Proof sketch

Three theoretical items, in decreasing importance.

(1) Theorem 2.2 — the geometric Cheeger inequality for coordinate cuts. Claim, precisely: for any weighted graph G on any finite X in R^d (no assumption whatsoever on G or X), there exists a valid axis-aligned cut whose normalized-cut value is at most sqrt( E_{D_adj}||x-y||^2 / E_{D_all}||x-y||^2 ). Nothing is claimed about finding it efficiently (though sweeping O(dn) cuts does find the minimizer), and nothing about trees.

Strategy: coordinate selection by the mediant inequality -> identify both expectations as quadratic forms -> degree-orthogonalize -> apply the test-vector form of Cheeger, whose threshold rounding is automatically a coordinate cut.

  • Step 1 (pick the coordinate). Both expectations split over coordinates: E||x-y||^2 = sum_i E|x_i - y_i|^2. By the elementary mediant fact min_i a_i/b_i <= (sum a_i)/(sum b_i) <= max_i a_i/b_i, there is a coordinate i_ with E_adj|x_{i_} - y_{i_}|^2 / E_all|x_{i_} - y_{i_}|^2 <= the full-dimensional ratio. _This single line is the whole reason coordinate cuts (rather than arbitrary hyperplanes) suffice_ — it says the d-dimensional ratio is always witnessed by some _one* coordinate. Everything else is standard spectral graph theory.
  • Step 2 (two Laplacians). Let z__ in R^n be the embedding vector z__(x) = x_{i_}, i.e. the i_-th coordinate function on X. With Delta_G = sum_{x,y} w(x,y) and the identity z^T L_G z = sum_{x,y} w(x,y)|z(x)-z(y)|^2, the numerator is exactly E_adj|x_{i_}-y_{i_}|^2 = z__^T L_G z__ / Delta_G. For the denominator, define H to be the degree-weighted clique with w_H(x,y) = d_G(x)d_G(y)/(2 Delta_G); then D_all is precisely the edge distribution of H, so E_all|x_{i_}-y_{i_}|^2 = z__^T L_H z__ / (2 Delta_G). This is the trick that makes the two-graph framework more than a bookkeeping device: the denominator distribution is a graph, namely the H from "normalized cut = non-uniform sparsest cut against the degree-weighted clique".
  • Step 3 (the rank-one identity). Compute d_H(x) = d_G(x) - d_G(x)^2/(2 Delta_G) and let v_G(x) = d_G(x)/sqrt(2 Delta_G). Then L_H = D_H - A_H = D_G - v_G v_G^T exactly. So the denominator Laplacian is the numerator's degree matrix minus a rank-one term — the whole "all pairs" structure collapses to a rank-one correction.
  • Step 4 (degree-orthogonalize). Shift: z-tilde = z__ - gamma_G * 1 with gamma_G = (v_G^T z__)/(v_G^T 1), which makes v_G^T z-tilde = 0. Since L 1 = 0 for any Laplacian, L_G z__ = L_G z-tilde, and by Step 3 L_H z__ = L_H z-tilde = (D_G - v_G v_G^T) z-tilde = D_G z-tilde — the rank-one term is annihilated. Hence E_adj/E_all >= 2 (z-tilde^T L_G z-tilde)/(z-tilde^T D_G z-tilde): the ratio of expectations is (twice) a Rayleigh quotient of a degree-orthogonal test vector.
  • Step 5 (Cheeger, test-vector form). The constructive Cheeger inequality (Spielman, Thm 21.1.3 form): for any z-tilde with z-tilde^T v_G = 0 there is a threshold tau-tilde such that S = {x : z-tilde(x) <= tau-tilde} is a nontrivial cut with Psi_G(S) <= 2 sqrt( (z-tilde^T L_G z-tilde)/(z-tilde^T D_G z-tilde) ). The punchline: z-tilde(x) = x_{i_} - gamma_G, so the threshold cut on z-tilde _is_ the coordinate cut S_{i_, tau-tilde + gamma_G}. Geometry enters only through the fact that the Cheeger test vector was chosen to be a coordinate function; rounding does the rest for free. (Remark A.4 recovers the familiar Psi_G <= 2 sqrt(lambda_G) by taking z-tilde = D^{1/2} z_G with z_G the Fiedler vector of the normalized Laplacian.)

(2) Corollary A.5 — the k-means instantiation. With the clique graph weighted 1/(|C_i|-1) inside each cluster, every degree is 1, so D_all is uniform over pairs; applying the identity sum_{x in C} ||x - mu||^2 = (1/|C|) sum_{x != y in C} ||x-y||^2 twice (once per cluster for the numerator, once with C = X for the denominator) and using |C_i|/(|C_i|-1) <= 2 yields Psi_G(S) <= sqrt(2 cost(C) / total SS). Interpretation, as above: the square root of twice the unexplained-variance fraction.

(3) Theorem A.8 — a graph-partitioning re-proof of IMM's O(k) price of explainability for k-medians. Claim: for the modified IMM (in each node, fix the l_1-diametrical pair of surviving centroids mu'_u, mu''_u and minimize mistakes among cuts separating that pair — a strict subset of original IMM's admissible cuts), cost_1(T-tilde_IMM(C)) <= O(k) cost_1(C). Structure is the same two-step as Moshkovitz et al.: Lemma A.9 (triangle inequality, imported unchanged) gives cost_1(T-tilde) <= cost_1(C) + sum_u t_u ||mu'_u - mu''_u||_1, where t_u is the number of mistakes at node u; the new part replaces their intricate potential-function argument with a random-cut averaging argument.

The trick. At node u, let the product of intervals [a^u_j, b^u_j] bound Y^u = X^u union M^u. Sample a cut from D: pick coordinate j with probability proportional to |b^u_j - a^u_j|, then tau uniform in [a^u_j, b^u_j]. Then an edge xy is cut with probability exactly ||x-y||1 / ||b^u - a^u||_1 — the l_1 geometry makes this telescope perfectly, so for any graph G-tilde on Y^u, E_D[e{G-tilde}(S_{j,tau}, .)] = (1/||b^u - a^u||_1) sum_{E-tilde in xy} ||x-y||_1. Now apply this to both graphs of the non-uniform pair: G the star graph (so e_G = mistake count) and H the single edge {mu'_u, mu''_u} (so e_H in {0,1} indicates separating the diametrical pair). The modified IMM's choice is exactly min_{j,tau} e_G/e_H = min Psi_{G,H}, and by the same mediant fact (min of a ratio <= ratio of expectations under any common distribution),

t_u <= E_D[e_G]/E_D[e_H] = ( sum_{x in X^u} ||x - mu(x)||_1 ) / ||mu'_u - mu''_u||_1,

because the bounding-box normalizers cancel between numerator and denominator. Rearranged, t_u ||mu'_u - mu''_u||_1 <= sum_{X^u in x} ||x - mu(x)||_1; summing over one tree level (the X^u partition X) gives cost_1(C), and summing over the H <= k levels gives the O(k) factor. The conceptual gain: the whole argument is "the ratio achieved by the optimal cut is at most the ratio of expectations under a geometrically natural random cut, and the bounding-box normalizer cancels because both graphs live on the same node set" — which is only visible once you write IMM as a two-graph sparsity. The l_1-vs-l_2 split is also clarified: the cancellation is exact for l_1 (hence k-medians), while Theorem 2.2's Cheeger route is natural for squared l_2.

Broader context

The subfield in a paragraph. "Explainable clustering" in this line of work does not mean post-hoc attribution. It is an intrinsic explainability model: you constrain the hypothesis class (axis-aligned trees with k leaves) and ask how much objective value you lose relative to the unconstrained optimum. The price of explainability is that loss ratio, and the field's achievement is a near-complete answer for k-medians ((1+o(1)) ln k, tight) and k-means (Theta(k) up to ln ln k) — a rare case where a notion of interpretability has an exact quantitative cost. The methodological weakness, which SPEX targets, is that this precision was bought by hard-coding centroid objectives.

Two closely related works worth knowing. (i) Fleissner, Chennuru Vankadara, Ghoshdastidar, "Explaining Kernel Clustering via Decision Trees" (ICLR 2024) — the direct predecessor: Kernel IMM extends IMM's mistake-minimization to kernel k-means for specific kernels, using the kernel-space centroid structure implicitly. SPEX supersedes it in generality and scalability (Kernel IMM OOMs or times out past a few thousand points), though Kernel IMM is better on Pathbased and Iris with a kernel k-means reference. (ii) Dong, Indyk, Razenshteyn, Wagner, "Learning Space Partitions for Nearest Neighbor Search" (ICLR 2020) — the actual origin of Theorem 2.2, in approximate nearest neighbor search; and behind it, Andoni–Naor–Nikolov–Razenshteyn–Waingarten's nonlinear spectral gaps / Holder homeomorphisms work on data-dependent hashing. Also relevant: Shi–Malik normalized cuts (the N_assoc identity that makes the CART reduction work), Trevisan's non-uniform sparsest cut, and Gabidolla and Carreira-Perpinan's oblique interpretable trees (which represent any k-means clustering exactly, showing the entire price of explainability is an artifact of insisting on axis-aligned cuts).

A plausible follow-up. The non-uniform sparse cut framework is currently used descriptively — four algorithms, four (G,H) pairs. The obvious next move is to use it prescriptively: treat (G,H) as a design space and ask which pairs admit provable price-of-explainability bounds. Two concrete openings. First, IMM = (star, single diametrical edge) and EMN = (star, clique on centroids) differ only in H, and that difference is exactly the O(k) -> O(k log k)-for-k-means improvement; the random-cut averaging argument of Theorem A.8 is modular in H, so it is plausible that one can characterize which H yield which exponents, and in particular analyze (clique, degree-weighted clique) — i.e. SPEX-Clique itself — against the k-means or kernel k-means cost, which is precisely the open problem the conclusion names. Second, a hybrid G: the clique graph is reference-faithful but geometry-blind, the kappa-NN graph is geometry-faithful but reference-blind, and the experiments show each wins in a different dimensional regime; a convex combination G = alpha G_clique + (1-alpha) G_kNN costs nothing algorithmically (O(1) + O(kappa) score updates) and Theorem 2.2 applies verbatim, since the ratio of expectations for a mixture is controlled by the mixture of ratios. A third, more theoretical direction: bound Psi-bar_G(T) for the greedy tree against the optimum, where the natural tool would be a higher-order Cheeger inequality (Lee–Oveis Gharan–Trevisan) specialized to coordinate cuts — the current theory covers one cut, not l leaves.

Honest IR / vector-search connection. There is a real one, and it is a lineage rather than an analogy: Theorem 2.2 comes from ANN search. In Neural LSH, the point was that the kappa-NN graph of a dataset has a low-conductance balanced partition, and that a cheap-to-evaluate partition (there, a learned classifier; here, a coordinate threshold) can approximate it — a partition that does not cut many kappa-NN edges is a partition that rarely sends a query to a different bucket than its true neighbors. SPEX-kNN is essentially that machinery recast as explanation: same graph, same conductance objective, the balance constraint dropped and the recursion made multiway. Three specific, non-forced implications:

  1. Routing trees for ANN indexes. IVF/tree-AH/SPANN-style indexes route a query through a partition tree; axis-aligned splits are the cheapest possible routing test (one comparison), which is why KD-trees persisted despite their high-dimensional weakness. The two-graph framework gives a principled way to state the ANN routing objective as a non-uniform sparsest cut: G = the kappa-NN graph (do not separate true neighbors), H = a graph encoding what you want balanced — the degree-weighted clique for volume balance, a clique on a sample of query points for query-load balance, or a graph derived from a known query distribution for workload-aware partitioning. That is a cleaner formulation of "balanced low-conductance partition" than the usual ad hoc balance penalties, and the s-t-cut and clique special cases Trevisan lists suggest the right vocabulary.
  2. A concrete negative lesson, which is the most valuable part. The paper's own numbers are a measurement of how badly axis-aligned partitions perform in high dimension on modern embeddings: on 512-d CLIP MNIST, a 10-leaf coordinate tree recovers only REF = .282 agreement with a spectral clustering of ARI .745. For anyone tempted to use axis-aligned routing (or interpretable attribute filters) on 512–1024-d embeddings, that is a quantified warning, and it strengthens the case for the oblique/learned routers that production ANN systems actually use. Equally, SPEX-kNN winning at d <= 16 and failing at d >= 30 is a clean empirical boundary for coordinate-cut methods on kappa-NN graphs.
  3. Generative retrieval, with caveats. Semantic-ID schemes in DSI/TIGER-style generative retrieval build a tree-structured partition of the document embedding space (hierarchical k-means, or RQ-VAE residual codebooks) and the docid is the root-to-leaf path. SPEX-Clique answers exactly the question "given any clustering of my documents, fit an axis-aligned tree to it" — i.e. it could produce semantic IDs whose every digit is a human-readable feature threshold, making the identifier space auditable instead of an opaque codebook, and it would work with a spectral or kernel clustering of the corpus rather than forcing hierarchical k-means. The honest caveat is point 2: in the relevant regime (d in [256,1024], l >> k) the paper's own evidence says axis-aligned trees lose most of the structure, and Table 6 shows SPEX has no clear edge once l = 2k. So the connection is real at the level of objective design and framework, and a warning at the level of expected performance. I would not oversell a direct transfer.

title: Ask, and it shall be given: Turing completeness of prompting
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-01

Ask, and it shall be given: On the Turing completeness of prompting

Ruizhong Qiu, Zhe Xu, Wenxuan Bao, Hanghang Tong (2024, ICLR 2025) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01992

Setting and problem

The object of study is a single fixed decoder-only Transformer used as an interpreter, and the question is how much computational power the prompt carries when the network is held constant. Everything hinges on how carefully that is formalised, so it is worth laying out the model in full.

Fix a finite token alphabet Sigma. A decoder-only Transformer is a map Gamma : Sigma^+ -> Sigma, i.e. it consumes a token string and emits a single next token. It is a composition Gamma = argmax . Gamma_out . Gamma_{L-1} . ... . Gamma_0 . Gamma_emb. The embedding layer is the textbook one, z_{0,i} = emb(v_i) + pos(i), with emb : Sigma -> R^d a token embedding and pos : N -> R^d a positional encoding required only to be computable. Each layer l has H_l heads; head k has query, key, value maps qry, key, val and additionally a similarity map sim_{l,k} : R -> R, all of which are ReLU networks, where a "ReLU network" here means any composition of affine maps, entrywise ReLU, and layer normalisation. Scores are s_{l,k,i,j} = sim_{l,k}( qry(z_{l,i})^T key(z_{l,j}) ). Attention is hardmax, not softmax: if the maximum of a score vector is attained t times, each maximiser gets weight 1/t and everything else gets 0. The layer is causal with a residual connection, z_{l+1,i} = z_{l,i} + phi_l( sum over heads of sum_{j<=i} hardmax_j(s_{l,k,i,0..i}) val_{l,k}(z_{l,j}) ), and the next token is argmax_c Gamma_out(z_{L,|v|-1})_c — greedy decoding read off the last position. Layer normalisation is defined as LN(z) = z/||z||_2 times the indicator 1[z != 0]: no centring, no learned affine, and crucially a discontinuity at zero which the construction exploits. Autoregressive generation generate_Gamma(w) repeatedly appends Gamma(w . y) to y until the stop token $ is produced; if it never appears, the output is an infinite string in Sigma^omega.

Depth, width, and head count are never pinned down numerically. The paper only claims (Appendix B.11) that the construction uses a constant number of operations with parameters drawn from {0, 1/2, 1, 2, 3}, hence a constant number of parameter bits. From counting the named intermediate quantities in Appendix B one infers d on the order of a hundred-plus coordinates (|Sigma| + 1 = 24 for the one-hot embedding plus positional scalar, plus roughly a hundred scratch slots) and a few dozen layers with a handful of heads each. That the constants are never stated is a real gap for a paper whose headline is "finite-size".

Precision is the crux, and the paper is two-faced about it, deliberately. For the main universality theorem (Theorem 3.1) a footnote states outright: "we assume that every arithmetic computation in Gamma is exact" — i.e. infinite-precision real arithmetic, following Perez et al. This is not cosmetic: the construction tests equality of real numbers through LN's indicator at zero, and exact zero-detection in reals is exactly the kind of operation that smuggles unbounded information into a single step. The repair comes separately in Corollary 4.7: under a floating-point model with significant bits and guard bits (guard bits participate in arithmetic but are rounded off in comparisons, after Goodman and Feldstein 1977), O(log(n + t(n))) bits suffice, because all intermediate magnitudes are O(1) and the attention scores that must be separated differ by Omega(1/I^5) where I = O(n + t(n) log t(n)) is the total context length. So the honest reading is: the construction is log-precision in the sense of Merrill and Sabharwal, once you grant that the comparison used for argmax is exact at the stated bit budget. The positional encoding itself is a specific algebraic function of i of size Theta(1/i^4), which likewise needs about 4 log i bits — consistent with the log-precision claim, but it means the model is not constant-precision and the result would be false in a fixed-precision model with a bounded context.

A prompt is a finite string pi_phi in Sigma^+. There is no infinite family, no per-input adaptation, no advice growing with n. The computation is modelled as a chain of thought: the context after k generation steps is pi_phi . tokenize(x) . y_{0..k-1}, and each new token is a function of that whole string. The context is therefore the only memory: there is no recurrent state, and the "tape" of the simulated machine lives implicitly in the generated token history.

The theorem, with quantifiers in the order that matters:

> Theorem 3.1. There exist a finite alphabet Sigma, a finite-size decoder-only Transformer Gamma : Sigma^+ -> Sigma, and coding schemes tokenize : {0,1}^_ -> Sigma^_ and readout : Sigma^_ -> {0,1}^_ such that for every computable partial function phi with dom phi a subset of {0,1}^, there exists_ a finite prompt pi_phi in Sigma^+ such that _for every* x in dom phi, generate_Gamma(pi_phi . tokenize(x)) terminates with a finite CoT and readout of it equals phi(x). Here Sigma, Gamma, tokenize, readout are independent of phi; pi_phi is independent of x; tokenize runs in O(|x|) time and readout in O(|phi(x)|) time on a RAM.

Note what is not claimed: nothing about x outside dom phi, where generation may diverge — as it must, by undecidability of halting.

The complementary claim is efficiency. Writing CoT_Gamma(t(n)) for the class of functions this particular Gamma computes within O(t(n)) generation steps, and PREC_Gamma(p(n)) for those it computes within O(p(n)) significant plus guard bits, the results are TIME_2(t) subset of CoT_Gamma(t), TIME(t) subset of CoT_Gamma(t log t), TIME(t) subset of PREC_Gamma(log(n+t)), and in particular P subset of PREC_Gamma(log n). The benchmark is the class of all Transformers, for which Perez et al. (2021) give O(t) CoT steps and O(log(n+t)) precision for TIME_1(t) and Merrill and Sabharwal (2024a) give O(t) CoT steps for TIME(t). So the price of universality-by-prompting is a single log t factor in CoT length and nothing in precision.

The precise question, as a question: does there exist one fixed finite-parameter decoder-only Transformer, with a fixed tokenizer and readout, such that varying only the finite prompt suffices to compute every computable function — and if so, at what overhead in chain-of-thought length and arithmetic precision relative to the best task-specific Transformer?

Prior work had carved up the "one model per task" regime thoroughly. Perez et al. (2019, 2021) showed the class of hardmax Transformers with CoT is Turing-complete; Merrill and Sabharwal (2023) showed a single forward pass of a log-precision Transformer is in uniform TC^0, so without CoT you cannot even do majority-hard problems, and Hahn (2020) showed parity is out of reach; Merrill and Sabharwal (2024a) gave the sharp CoT-vs-class picture (O(log n) CoT steps gives L, polynomial CoT gives P, and t steps roughly gives TIME(t)); Li et al. (2024) and Hou et al. (2024) pushed the "CoT buys serial depth" line; Strobl et al.'s survey maps the whole landscape of circuit and logic upper bounds. The gap the paper names is the quantifier order: every one of those results constructs a different Transformer per task, whereas LLM practice is one model, many prompts. The paper also concedes up front that existence follows from combining Hennie-Stearns (1966) with Perez et al. (2019) — a universal TM is a computable function, so some Transformer simulates it — and positions its contribution as an explicit and simple construction whose complexity can be audited.

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag sharply, because they decide whether this is deep or an artifact: (i) hardmax rather than softmax, acknowledged as a limitation of the whole subfield; (ii) exact arithmetic for Theorem 3.1, with log-precision only recovered afterwards; (iii) an unbounded context window, so the real computational substrate is an unbounded tape and Gamma is a finite controller over it; (iv) pos allowed to be any computable function, a genuine loophole in the model class even though the paper only uses a benign algebraic p_i; (v) a learned nonlinear sim applied to the dot product, which real Transformers do not have (they use it once, as min{x,2}); (vi) LN without centring and with LN(0) = 0, whose discontinuity is load-bearing.

Main idea

Rather than encode a Turing machine into the prompt, the authors design a new imperative machine model that is cheap to serialise over a 23-token alphabet and provably almost as fast as a TM, then build a Transformer that interprets it.

The model is the two-tape Post-Turing machine (2-PTM): two bi-infinite binary tapes A and B, each with a head, and a program that is a finite sequence of instructions drawn from # (halt), tau L, tau R (move), tau 0, tau 1 (write), and conditional jumps tau !k (goto k if the cell under head tau is 0) and tau ?k (goto k if it is 1), for tau in {A, B}. There are no named states — control flow is program-counter plus conditional jumps, which is exactly what makes it serialisable with a finite alphabet: states would be unbounded in number, instructions are not. Jump targets are the one remaining unbounded quantity, and they are written in unary relative form, + repeated k - j times or - repeated j - k times, terminated by @. Input and output are Shannon-encoded (S(0) = 10, S(1) = 11), so that 00 can serve as the genuine blank and a written 0 is distinguishable from untouched tape.

The prompt is then literally the program: pi_phi = ^ . P(0, iota_0) ... P(|iota|-1, iota_{|iota|-1}) . $. The 23 tokens are {#, AL, BL, AR, BR, A0, B0, A1, B1, A!, B!, A?, B?, -, +, @, ^, $, /, =, :, 0, 1}. The chain of thought is a trace: each executed instruction emits one token (for moves, writes, halt), while a conditional jump emits either / (condition false, fall through) or = followed by the unary offset and @ (condition true). Input is injected without touching the prompt by having tokenize(x) emit a fake trace: AR repeated 2|x| times to park the head, then a right-to-left sequence of AL/A1 steps that write S(x) onto tape A, then a fake satisfied jump = - ... - @ of length |Z(x)| that resets the program counter to iota_0. The answer is appended after : and before $, and readout scans back from the end for :.

The headline results are the three stated above: universality with a fixed Gamma, O(t) CoT steps for two-tape TIME, O(t log t) for general TIME, and O(log(n + t)) precision, hence P within log-precision. The log t is inherited from Hennie-Stearns multitape-to-two-tape simulation and the paper argues it is probably unavoidable for a fixed machine, since a fixed Gamma simulates boundedly many tapes while the class of all Transformers can simulate any number.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever technical core is layer normalisation as a de-averaging device, turning attention's mean into an exact, comparable representation of a sum. Causal attention can only average, so sum_{j<=i} v_j is out of reach; but if you also compute 1/(i+1) by attending to the unique ^ token at position 0, then LN applied to the pair (S_i/(i+1), 1/(i+1)) returns (S_i, 1)/sqrt(S_i^2 + 1) — a unit vector depending only on S_i, with the averaging coefficient annihilated. Two positions have equal sums iff their unit vectors have inner product exactly 1. Every piece of machine state in the construction is a running sum: tape-head position is the signed count of move tokens, program counter is the signed count of +/- tokens, instruction index is the count of instruction-start tokens. So a single trick gives exact equality tests on all of them, implemented purely with attention and LN.

The second nice trick is tie-breaking to turn hardmax into a leftmost/rightmost retrieval. Hardmax averages over all maximisers, which is useless if you want the most recent write to a tape cell. They add to the query the quantity p_i = 1 - ((i+1)(i+2)+1)/( sqrt((i+1)^2+1) sqrt((i+2)^2+1) ), which is Theta(1/i^4), and to the key the term -1/(j+1). The point is a quantitative separation: a non-matching unit vector has inner product at most 1 - Omega(1/|v|^4), which strictly exceeds the perturbation p/(j+1) in magnitude, so non-matches can never win; among matches the perturbation is monotone in j, so the extreme index is selected uniquely. With the sign as written in Appendix B.4 the head retrieves the latest write at the current head position. This is attention used as an exact associative memory over a write log, and the Omega(1/I^5) score margin it produces is precisely what the log-precision corollary is bought with.

Now the critique, and it is substantial.

First, the finite-size framing is less striking than it sounds, and the authors know it. They say in the contributions that existence follows from Hennie-Stearns plus Perez et al. A universal TM has been finite since 1936; a Transformer that simulates one is a finite Transformer on which prompting is universal; "prompt" then just means "program on the UTM's tape". So the theorem is, structurally, "there is a Transformer that is a UTM interpreter", and the paper's real contribution is an explicit, auditable, small construction plus the complexity accounting. That is worth having — the 2-PTM is a nicer intermediate than any UTM encoding, and the complexity bookkeeping is new — but the abstract's rhetoric ("establishes a theoretical underpinning for prompt engineering in practice") considerably oversells it. Nothing here says anything about a trained LLM, about softmax attention, about bounded context, or about which prompts are findable; the paper's own Appendix D concedes all four.

Second, the power comes substantially from the computational model, not the architecture. The context is an unbounded tape and the network is a finite controller that re-reads the whole tape at every step. That is a Turing machine with a very expensive, fully parallel head. In that light, universality is close to forced; the interesting content is quantitative — that log precision and O(t log t) steps suffice. Relatedly, the CoT-step count is not a wall-clock complexity measure: each generation step runs attention over the entire context of length I, so actual work is Theta(I) per step and Theta(t^2 log^2 t) overall, quadratically worse than the TM it simulates. The claim "nearly the same complexity bounds as all unbounded-size Transformers" is true in the CoT-step metric the paper defines and would be false in a total-arithmetic-operations metric.

Third, the constant factors hide a program-size blow-up that is swept under "O(1)". The unary relative encoding of jump offsets makes |pi_phi| quadratic in the number of instructions: simulating a K-state two-tape TM yields a 2-PTM of length 27K + 1, so offsets are up to Theta(K) and the prompt is Theta(K^2) tokens. Worse, each taken jump is traced in unary, so a single 2-PTM step costs up to O(|pi_phi|) = O(K^2) CoT steps. The paper legitimises this with "we allow different computable functions to have different constant factors in big O", which is standard but worth seeing plainly: the universal-machine overhead is quadratic in program size, not constant, and the clean O(t(n)) is an asymptotics-in-n statement only.

Fourth, there is a genuine error in the paper's statement of one primitive. Equation (19) defines Equal(u,v) := ReLU(LN(u-v)) + ReLU(LN(v-u)) and announces it equals 1[u = v]. For scalars LN(z) = sign(z) with LN(0) = 0, so the expression is 1[u != v], the complement. The appendix uses it correctly as a "not found" indicator in Equations (51), (111), (112); only the main-text labelling is wrong. Harmless, but it signals that the construction was not independently proof-read at the formula level — and parts of Appendix B.7, notably the prog_rec_bias / sim(x) = min{x, 2} machinery for confining attention to the current trace record, are stated so tersely that verifying them by hand is unpleasant. There is a Python implementation (Appendix C, github.com/q-rz/ICLR25-prompting-theory) which is the right response to this, but a mechanised proof would have been better.

Fifth, the result does not contradict Merrill and Sabharwal's TC^0 upper bound, and it is worth being explicit about why: that bound constrains a single forward pass, and here the whole power comes from composing t(n) such passes with the intermediate results written back into the input. The paper's contribution is orthogonal to the circuit bound, not in tension with it.

Proof sketch

What is proved, in plain terms. (a) 2-PTMs are Turing-complete and lose at most a log factor: TIME(t) subset of TIME_{2-PTM}(t log t), with the sharper TIME_2(t) subset of TIME_{2-PTM}(t). (b) There is one fixed Gamma, tokenize, readout such that each computable phi has a finite prompt that makes Gamma compute phi on all of dom phi, with no claim off dom phi. (c) That Gamma inherits the 2-PTM bounds: O(t) CoT steps for TIME_2(t), O(t log t) for TIME(t), O(log(n+t)) bits of precision, exact arithmetic assumed at the level of the universality statement and replaced by the bit budget in the corollary.

Step 1, 2-PTMs simulate two-tape TMs with constant overhead (Lemma 4.2). Given a two-tape TM with Q = {0,...,K}, q_start = 0, q_halt = K, allocate exactly 27 consecutive instructions per non-halting state, placing state q's block at iota_{27q}, with iota_{27K} = #. Each of the four transitions delta(q, c_A, c_B) is implemented by a six-instruction gadget eta = <A c'_A, A d_A, B c'_B, B d_B, A!27q', A?27q'>: write both cells, move both heads, then jump to the target state's block. The trailing pair of jumps with opposite conditions is the trick that makes an unconditional jump out of conditional ones — after moving the heads you no longer know the cell value, so you branch on both possibilities to the same target. Dispatch on the current cells uses three conditional jumps (A?27q+14 to split on tape A, B?27q+8 and B?27q+21 to split on tape B), giving 1 + 1 + 6 + 6 + 1 + 6 + 6 = 27. O(1) instructions per TM transition, so no asymptotic loss; the converse direction (a bi-infinite two-tape TM simulating any 2-PTM, one state per instruction) is in Appendix A.2, so the two models are equivalent up to constants.

Step 2, from general TMs (Theorem 4.1). Two cases. If T(n_0) < n_0 for some n_0 the machine cannot even read its input, so its behaviour is determined by a bounded prefix and the true time is O(1). Otherwise T(n) >= n for all n, and Hennie-Stearns compresses any multitape TM to two tapes with a log slowdown, T -> T log T; compose with Lemma 4.2. Hence TIME(t) subset of TIME_{2-PTM}(t log t). This is where the only efficiency loss in the paper comes from, and it is imported wholesale rather than proved.

Step 3, the prompt and the trace. As described above: program serialised with one token per simple instruction and sigma + unary offset + @ per jump, framed by ^ and $. Each executed step emits a record — the instruction token itself for moves/writes/halt, / or = -...-@ / = +...+@ for jumps. The essential invariant is that the complete machine configuration is recoverable from the trace: the tape contents are the write log (latest write at each cell wins, blank where none), the head positions are the signed sums of move tokens, and the program counter is the signed sum of +/- tokens taken over satisfied jumps plus one per fall-through record. Nothing is stored in Gamma; everything is re-derived from the context on every single generation step. The $ token in the prompt doubles as the prompt/trace delimiter, and after_delim_i = LN( (1/(i+1)) sum_{j<=i} 1[v_j = $] ) = 1[exists j<=i : v_j = $] is how Gamma tells program from trace — again the LN de-averaging trick, applied to a discounted indicator.

Step 4, one generation step of Gamma. Reading the layers of Appendix B as a pipeline: compute positional helpers 1/(i+1) and its normalisation; split prompt from trace; from the trace extract per-token write values and signed head moves; accumulate and LN-normalise the two head positions; retrieve each pointed cell by attending with query (1, A_cur_norm, A_cur_one_norm, p_i) against key (is_A_write, A_cur_norm, A_cur_one_norm, -1/(j+1)) and value (write value, position, is_write) — a match requires both that the token is a write to tape A and that its normalised head position equals the current one, and the p_i / -1/(j+1) pair picks the most recent such write; detect "never written" via the LN inequality indicator and default to blank. In parallel, from the prompt side, compute each instruction's program index (counting instruction-start tokens, minus one to account for the prompt/trace lag) and each jump token's within-instruction goto index. Then locate the current instruction with a single attention head whose query is (prog_cur_norm, prog_cur_one_norm, prog_tmp_norm, prog_tmp_one_norm, p_i, -1) and whose key is the matching prompt-side tuple, so that exactly one prompt token — the one whose program index equals the program counter and whose goto index equals the position within an in-progress unary jump — is selected, and its one-hot identity is copied into the residual stream as token_is_sigma. Finally the instruction is executed: for simple instructions the retrieved token is emitted verbatim; for jumps, Boolean algebra via ReLU (u AND v = ReLU(u + v - 1), NOT v = 1 - v) combines token_is_A? with the retrieved cell value to decide = versus /.

Step 5, output phase. The halt instruction # is mapped to emitting :. After that, Gamma switches mode: to produce the k-th output bit it needs tape cells 2k and 2k+1 of the Shannon-encoded answer, so it counts output tokens emitted so far via attention over is_read_key = is : + is 0 + is 1 with shifts of 2 per output token, LN-normalises 2k and 2k+1, and runs the same cell-retrieval head twice against the write log. Decoding is three ReLU gates: emit 0 if the pair is (1,0), 1 if (1,1), and the stop token $ if the first cell is blank. The factor 2 in Equations (115)-(117) is what makes the output-phase logits dominate the execution-phase logits in the final argmax, i.e. how the mode switch is implemented without a mode bit.

Step 6, composition, size, precision. Each intermediate quantity is computed by its own layer and added into a fresh residual coordinate, so the architecture is a long thin stack: embedding = one-hot over 24 coordinates plus p_i in one more, then one layer per scratch quantity. Parameters are only 0, 1/2, 1, 2, 3, hence constant bit-size, and the whole thing is independent of phi and x — that is the entire content of "finite-size". For precision: total context length is I = O(n) + O(1) + O(t log t); all hidden values are O(1) by construction (everything is either Boolean, a reciprocal, or a unit vector); and the smallest gap between competing attention scores is Omega(1/I^5), from the Omega(1/|v|^4) unit-vector separation times the 1/(i+1) tie-break. Resolving that gap needs O(log I^5) = O(log(n + t(n))) bits, giving TIME(t) subset of PREC_Gamma(log(n+t)) and, for t polynomial, P subset of PREC_Gamma(log n).

Why it is not trivial. The paper pre-empts three objections, and the arguments are correct and worth keeping. Memorisation is impossible since there are countably infinitely many computable functions and Gamma has finitely many finite-bit parameters. Self-answering is impossible since dom phi can be infinite and pi_phi is finite. Tautology — Gamma just echoing and tokenize/readout doing the work — is ruled out by the time hierarchy theorem, since tokenize and readout run in O(|x|) and O(|phi(x)|) time while a computable phi can require strictly more.

Broader context

Transformer expressivity has, since about 2019, split into two complementary programmes. The upper-bound programme asks what a single forward pass cannot do: Hahn (2020) showed hard-attention Transformers fail on parity and Dyck; Hao et al. (2022) placed hard-attention Transformers in AC^0; Merrill and Sabharwal (2023) placed log-precision softmax Transformers in uniform TC^0 and later gave a first-order-logic-with-majority characterisation; Chiang et al. (2023) tightened the picture with circuit and logic bounds. The slogan is that a Transformer is a constant-depth, highly parallel circuit, so anything inherently serial — iterated state, graph connectivity, simulating a machine for many steps — is out of reach without extra machinery. The lower-bound programme supplies the missing machinery, namely chain of thought: write intermediate tokens back into the input and depth becomes effectively unbounded in the number of generated tokens. Perez et al. (2019, 2021) proved the class of hardmax Transformers with CoT is Turing-complete; Merrill and Sabharwal (2024a) gave the clean trade-off (logarithmic CoT gives L, polynomial CoT gives P, t steps roughly TIME(t)); Li et al. (2024) showed CoT lets constant-depth Transformers solve inherently serial problems; Feng et al. (2023) gave the arithmetic/dynamic-programming version. Strobl et al.'s survey is the right single entry point. The present paper's move is to reorder the quantifiers so that the architecture is fixed and the prompt varies, which is the regime practitioners actually live in.

Two closely related things worth knowing. Hou et al. (2024), "Universal length generalization with Turing programs", is the empirical mirror image: they prompt real LLMs with a CoT format that mimics TM tape updates and get strong length generalisation — essentially an experimental version of this paper's trace encoding, which makes the pair unusually complementary.
