And the RASP / Thinking-like-Transformers line (Weiss, Goldberg, Yahav 2021, plus Lindner et al.'s Tracr compiler) is the programming-language view of the same object; a RASP-to-Transformer compiler is exactly "Transformer as interpreter" in a different key, and comparing what RASP can express in one pass with what this paper's 2-PTM interpreter does across many passes is instructive.

A plausible follow-up, and the one the paper's own limitations section points at most sharply, is a bounded-context theory with a prompt-length/CoT trade-off. With an unbounded context the result is almost forced; with a context window of W tokens, the whole device becomes a finite-state machine with W cells of memory, so the computable class should collapse to something like space-O(W) with an explicit dependence on the token alphabet, and one would want matching upper and lower bounds plus the sliding-window variant. Alongside that, a genuine prompt complexity theory suggests itself: since the prompt is a program for a fixed universal interpreter, K_Gamma(phi) = min |pi_phi| is a Kolmogorov complexity relative to Gamma, invariant up to additive constants across choices of Gamma, and the natural theorems are trade-offs of the form "shortening the prompt by k tokens costs at least f(k) CoT steps". The paper's own unary jump encoding is a concrete instance: it buys a 23-token alphabet at the price of a quadratic prompt and quadratic per-jump trace. A third direction is quantitative softmax: replace hardmax with softmax at inverse temperature beta and ask how beta must scale with context length to preserve the Omega(1/I^5) margin — that would convert the paper's exact-retrieval argument into a robustness statement about real attention.

The IR connection is thin but not forced, and it lives in exactly one place. The load-bearing primitive here is "attend to the most recent write whose normalised key matches mine", which is an exact maximum-inner-product search over the context, correct only because matching and non-matching unit vectors are separated by Omega(1/I^4) and the tie-break by a further 1/I. That is a margin condition of precisely the kind vector-search theory traffics in, and it degrades polynomially in context length. Read that way, the paper quietly supplies a computability-flavoured reason why approximate retrieval is not a free substitute for exact retrieval inside a reasoning chain: an ANN index with recall below 1, or a precision budget below log I, breaks the simulation invariant, and a single wrong retrieval corrupts the recovered machine configuration irreversibly. For generative retrieval there is a weaker but still real reading: the theorem says a fixed decoder plus a prompt is universal given unbounded CoT, so expressivity is not the binding constraint on a single generative-retrieval decoder — the binding constraints are CoT budget, context window, and learnability, which is exactly where the empirical difficulties sit. And it gives a formal sense in which retrieved context functions as program rather than as data, which is a cleaner way to think about RAG than "extra evidence". None of this is what the paper is about, and anyone reading it for IR content will come away with a good construction to admire and a margin condition to reuse, rather than a theorem about retrieval.

title: Grokking at the Edge of Linear Separability

Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-01

Grokking at the Edge of Linear Separability

Alon Beck, Noam Levi, Yohai Bar-Sinai (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04489

Setting and problem

The object of study is about as small as a learning problem can be while still being a genuine high-dimensional classification problem. Before the reduction, the data live in R^(d+1) and consist of two isotropic-ish Gaussian clouds with opposite labels: x~_i ~ N(±mu, Sigma) with Sigma diagonal, Sigma_11 = sigma_A along the "separation axis" (the first coordinate) and Sigma_ii = sigma_B for i > 1, and mu = (mu, 0, ..., 0). The model is a bias-free linear classifier trained with logistic (cross-entropy) loss. The regime of interest is sigma_A << mu: the two clouds are cleanly separated along axis 1, and everything else is noise. Note for bookkeeping: this is a random-design linear model on Gaussian features, not a random-feature model in the Rahimi-Recht sense — there is no nonlinear feature map anywhere in the paper, and that matters for how much of real grokking it can claim to explain.

The first non-obvious modelling choice is the constant-label trick. Take the limiting case sigma_A = 0, so the first coordinate of x~_i is exactly ±mu. Flipping x_i -> y_i x_i leaves the Gaussian noise distribution invariant (it is symmetric), so one may assume without loss of generality that all labels are equal. Up to a scale, each sample becomes x~_i = (1, x_i) with x_i ~ N(0, (sigma_B/mu)^2 I_d), and the first weight coordinate becomes a bias. Appendix H does this carefully and shows the mapping is exact at the level of gradient flow, with the d-dimensional dynamics faster by a factor mu^2 in the effective learning rate. So the paper's working object is:

N training samples x_i in R^d, x_i ~ N(0, sigma^2 I_d), with sigma = sigma_B/mu, all assigned the same label y_i = -1. Parameters are w = (S, b) in R^(d+1) with S in R^d and b in R; the model output is f_i = S·x_i + b; the per-sample loss is l(f) = log(1 + e^f); the empirical loss is L(S,b) = (1/N) sum_i log(1 + exp(S^T x_i + b)) and the empirical accuracy is A = (1/N) sum_i Theta(-S^T x_i - b). Training is plain gradient descent, and all analysis is in the gradient-flow limit eta -> 0. No weight decay, no explicit regularization, no large initialization, no feature learning, and the loss is convex. The scaling regime is N, d -> infinity with lambda := d/N fixed.

Because the population distribution is an unbounded Gaussian and every label is the same, the Bayes-optimal rule is degenerate but well defined: put all of R^d on one side of the hyperplane, i.e. push the decision boundary to infinity. This is what buys the paper its "strict definitions". Since S^T x ~ N(0, ||S||^2 sigma^2), the population loss and accuracy depend on only two scalars:

L_gen = E_{y~N(0,1)} log(1 + exp(sigma||S||y + b)), A_gen = E_{y~N(0,1)} Theta(-sigma||S||y - b) = (1/2)(1 - erf( (1/sqrt(2))(b/(sigma||S||)) )).

Hence Proposition 3.1: perfect generalization (L_gen -> 0, A_gen -> 1) holds iff b -> -infinity and b/||S|| -> -infinity. The two candidate asymptotic solutions are therefore cleanly separated as directions of divergence of w(t), not as distinct finite minima: the generalizing solution is w^ = (0, -1), all weight in the bias, hyperplane at infinity; any overfitting / memorizing solution is one where w^ retains a component along the data directions, so the hyperplane sits at a finite distance, correctly classifying all N training points but misclassifying a nonvanishing fraction of the population. This is a real conceptual gain over most grokking models, where "memorization" is a vibe measured by a proxy.

The organizing notion is linear separability from the origin: a set {x_i} in R^d is separable from the origin iff there exists S in R^d with S^T x_i > 0 for all i — equivalently, iff the origin is not in the convex hull of the training points. This specific notion, rather than ordinary two-class separability, is the right one because after the constant-label reduction all labels agree and the only question is whether a bias-free hyperplane through the origin can put all points on one side. If it can, the optimizer has somewhere finite to go in the S directions and will use it; if it cannot, the S-dynamics are confined and only b can run away. Wendel's theorem supplies the probabilistic threshold: for points from any origin-symmetric distribution in general position, P(separable) = 2^(-(N-1)) sum_{k=0}^{d-1} C(N-1, k), the Binomial(N-1, 1/2) CDF, which for large N, d becomes (1/2)[1 + erf(sqrt(d) (sqrt(2 lambda) - 1/sqrt(2 lambda)))] and sharpens to a step at lambda_c = 1/2. So d > N/2 means almost surely separable from the origin; d < N/2 almost surely not. This is the Cover-capacity threshold of the perceptron, which the paper calls (defensibly, but with some rhetorical stretch) the "interpolation threshold" of this problem.

The learner is given {x_i} and the constant labels, and is asked to produce (S, b) by running gradient flow on the logistic loss to t -> infinity. The precise question is: for which (lambda, sigma) does gradient flow on this convex problem reach A_gen -> 1, what property of the training sample decides it, and can the time at which test accuracy rises be made arbitrarily later than the time at which training loss is already negligible — i.e. does grokking occur with no regularization, no feature learning, and a unique global optimum?

The context: grokking was reported by Power et al. (2022) on modular arithmetic, where a transformer memorizes within a few hundred steps and then, after orders of magnitude more training at chance test accuracy, snaps to near-perfect generalization. Nanda et al. (2023) opened the box and showed a Fourier-multiplication circuit forming gradually under the memorizing behaviour, giving "progress measures"; Liu et al. (2022, 2023 Omnigrok) tied it to representation learning and, crucially, to weight norm — grokking can be induced or removed by scaling initialization, suggesting a race between a large-norm memorizing solution and a small-norm generalizing one. Lyu et al. (2024) made this a theorem in a homogeneous-network setting: an early kernel/lazy phase with an implicit bias toward a minimum-norm interpolator, followed by a late phase whose implicit bias is L2-margin maximization, provably induces grokking — but they need weight decay and large initialization. Kumar et al. (2023) framed it as lazy-to-rich transition; Levi et al. (2023) solved grokking exactly in linear regression with MSE, where lambda = 1 is the threshold and the grokking time diverges like log(1 - sqrt(lambda)) by critical slowing down from a vanishing covariance eigenvalue; Rubin et al. (2023, 2024) described it as a first-order phase transition; Xu et al. (2023) connected it to benign overfitting in ReLU nets on XOR clusters; Prieto et al. (2025) attribute much of it to numerical effects (Softmax Collapse). The gap this paper targets is that every existing solvable account needs one of: weight decay, atypical initialization scale, an adaptive optimizer, or a representation-learning story — and most lack an unambiguous definition of the two competing solutions. The remaining non-obvious choices to flag: everything is asymptotic (statements are about t -> infinity limits of divergent trajectories, via implicit-bias theory, not about finite-time minima), and the sharpest analytical results come from a deliberately degenerate one-dimensional two-point toy model.

Main idea

The claim is that grokking in this model is not about memorization circuits at all but about a bifurcation in the asymptotic direction of a divergent gradient-flow trajectory, plus critical slowing down near the bifurcation. Because all labels agree and a bias is present, the extended data (1, x_i) are always separable in R^(d+1) — by the hyperplane at infinity — so Soudry et al.'s implicit-bias theorem applies and w(t) = w_SVM log(t) + rho(t) with rho bounded, where w_SVM minimizes ||S||^2 + b^2 subject to S^T x_i + b <= -1. Everything then reduces to the direction of w_SVM, and the paper shows this direction is decided by a purely combinatorial-geometric property of the sample: whether the origin lies inside the convex hull of {x_i}.

If it does not (the data are separable from the origin, lambda > 1/2 almost surely), then besides the generalizing candidate w_g = (0,-1) of norm 1 there is a competitor w_ = (S_, 0) with S_ the hard-margin separator through the origin, ||S_|| = 1/M where M is the margin; the two are orthogonal, both feasible, so the true minimum-norm point is the convex mix w_SVM proportional to (M^2 S_, -1). Both b and ||S|| then diverge logarithmically at a fixed ratio b/||S|| -> -1/M, and the asymptotic test accuracy is pinned below one at A_gen = (1/2)[1 + erf(1/(sqrt(2) sigma M))]. The model overfits forever, and the population loss diverges. If the origin _is* in the convex hull (lambda < 1/2 almost surely), the bias-free loss is coercive in every direction, S(t) converges to a finite S_inf, only |b| diverges, w_SVM = (0,-1), and generalization is asymptotically perfect.

Grokking is then the behaviour at the edge: as lambda -> 1/2 from below the origin approaches the hull boundary, and ||S_inf|| diverges (logarithmically in 1 - 2 lambda in the toy model). Meanwhile a rescaling argument shows that large sigma multiplies the rate of the S-dynamics by sigma^2 while leaving the b-dynamics untouched. So for lambda slightly below 1/2 and sigma large, S rushes to a huge S_inf — which looks exactly like the memorizing solution, large ||S||, small |b|/||S||, perfect train accuracy, chance-ish test accuracy — and then b must crawl logarithmically for an arbitrarily long time before |b|/||S_inf|| becomes large and test accuracy rises. Non-monotone test loss and delayed generalization follow. Both conditions are necessary: Fig. 3 (right) shows the grokking time diverges only when lambda -> 1/2 and sigma -> infinity, neither alone. The headline interpretation is critical slowing down at a point where the generalizing and overfitting solutions exchange stability, and the conjecture is that this is the general mechanism of grokking, with Power et al.'s training-fraction alpha playing the role of lambda.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever technical device is the conformal time change of variables. Under the exponential loss L_e = (1/N) sum_i exp(S^T x_i + b), which the cross-entropy loss approaches at late times, both gradients carry a common scalar prefactor e^{b(t)}:

dS/dt = -(eta/N) e^b sum_i e^{S^T x_i} x_i, db/dt = -(eta/N) e^b sum_i e^{S^T x_i}.

Defining tau(t) = integral_0^t e^{b(t')} dt', the S-equation in tau is exactly the bias-free problem. So S(t) traverses precisely the trajectory it would follow if there were no bias at all, only at a time-dependent rate set by e^b. This cleanly factorizes the problem into "which path does S take" (a static, convex, bias-free question answered by separability from the origin) and "how fast does it get there" (controlled by b, hence by sigma). Appendix C supplies the necessary technical step that tau(t) -> infinity, so the reparameterized flow really reaches the bias-free fixed point. That is a small, elegant idea doing most of the work, and it is the part worth stealing.

The honest critique is longer. First, the "strict definition" of memorizing versus generalizing is purchased by a degeneracy: sigma_A = 0 makes all labels identical, so the generalizing solution is "no decision boundary anywhere", and the optimum of the task is to classify all of R^d one way. The moment sigma_A > 0 (Fig. 4) or only a fraction r < 1 of labels is constant (App. I, Fig. 16), perfect generalization becomes impossible and the clean dichotomy the paper advertises dissolves — one is back to "accuracy is a bit below 1", exactly the ambiguity the paper claims to escape. Grokking survives, but the conceptual selling point does not.

Second, the setting is convex with a unique asymptotic optimum, and nothing is learned in any representational sense. This explains the phenomenology of grokking — non-monotone test loss, a long plateau, a late rise — without any of the content that made grokking interesting (circuit formation, an "aha", structured representations). The paper is upfront that it sidesteps representation learning; a reader should be equally clear that "grokking is critical slowing down" and "grokking is delayed circuit formation" are not yet the same claim, and the paper's bridge to Power et al. (App. B) is an analogy between lambda and the training fraction alpha, not a result.

Third, the mechanism requires a double knife edge, lambda -> 1/2 and sigma -> infinity. Appendix F.1 and Fig. 10 show the sigma dependence saturates, and with plain GD the accuracy rises from the start rather than sitting at chance. To reproduce the canonical chance-level plateau the authors need Adam with lambda = 0.495 (Fig. 5) — and they themselves note (App. F.2) that under Adam the implicit bias is no longer the hard-margin SVM, so Soudry et al.'s theorem no longer applies. The clean theory and the clean phenomenology therefore do not hold simultaneously, which is a real tension, honestly disclosed but not resolved.

Fourth, the theoretical novelty is thinner than the framing suggests: Theorem 1 is Soudry et al. (2018) restated, Prop. 3.3 is Wendel (1962), Prop. 3.2.1 leans on Ji and Telgarsky (2019), and Prop. 3.4 is acknowledged to be obtainable as a corollary of the latter. The new content is the identification of separability-from-origin as the order parameter, the conformal-time factorization, the quantitative epsilon-closeness bound on ||S_inf|| in App. D, and the toy-model closed forms. That is a respectable but modest contribution.

Finally, the numerics near criticality are selection-biased in a way the authors admit: for finite N with lambda < 1/2 a nonzero fraction of draws is separable (Wendel again), and those realizations are simply discarded (Fig. 6, right). Fig. 7 duly shows the measured margin and positive-fraction failing to vanish at lambda = 1/2, which they attribute to this bias. Fig. 6 (left) reports that the fraction of positive S_inf^T x_i tends to a nonzero constant at lambda = 1/2, "implying a singularity in the density" — an interesting observation left entirely unexplained. There are also small sign/wording slips worth noting while reading: Prop. 3.2.1 writes lim b(t) = +infinity where the convention demands b -> -infinity, and the parenthetical in Sec. 4 ("separable (inseparable) for lambda < 1/2 (lambda > 1/2)") is inverted relative to the rest of the paper, as is the "separable case lambda < 1/2" label on the S_inf formula.

Proof sketch

What is assumed throughout. Gradient flow (eta -> 0) on the logistic loss; at late times the loss is replaced by the exponential loss l_e(f) = e^f, justified by the exponential tail of cross-entropy and the fact that late-time behaviour is dominated by the largest outputs (this substitution is also checked numerically from t = 0 in Fig. 14). Data x_i i.i.d. from an origin-symmetric distribution in general position (Gaussianity is only convenience; App. G verifies power-law-spectrum Gaussians and Gaussian mixtures). Constant labels. N > d.

Implicit bias forces the dichotomy. The extended data (1, x_i) are separable in R^(d+1), so Theorem 1 (Soudry et al.) gives w(t) = w_SVM log(t) + rho(t), rho bounded, with w_SVM = argmin{||S||^2 + b^2 : S^T x_i + b <= -1}. Note the bias is penalized, so this is not the usual SVM-with-bias in d dimensions. Combined with Prop. 3.1 (A_gen -> 1 iff b -> -infinity and b/||S|| -> -infinity), the whole asymptotic question becomes the direction of w_SVM.

Separable from the origin => overfitting (Prop. 3.2.2). The generalizing candidate w_g = (0,-1) is feasible with norm 1. If the data are separable from the origin, there is a second feasible point w_ = (S_, 0), with S_ = argmin{||S||^2 : S^T x_i <= -1} and ||S_|| = 1/M, M the margin from the origin. Since w_g and w_ are orthogonal and the feasible set is convex, any mix alpha w_g + beta w_ with alpha + beta >= 1 is feasible; minimizing alpha^2 + beta^2/M^2 under alpha + beta = 1 gives alpha = 1/(1+M^2), beta = M^2/(1+M^2), so w_SVM proportional to (M^2 S*, -1). Both components diverge, b/||S|| -> -1/M, and substituting into the accuracy formula gives lim A_gen = (1/2)[1 + erf(1/(sqrt(2) sigma M))] < 1. The explicit rates follow (Table 1, and derived directly in App. J): b(t) ~ -(1/(1+M^2)) log t and ||S(t)|| ~ (M/(1+M^2)) log t. App. J derives these from scratch by noting that at large ||S|| the sum (1/N) sum_i e^{S^T x_i} is dominated by the D support vectors attaining the maximum, giving (eta D/(N E)) e^{-f(tau)} = E f'(tau) with E = -1/(S^^T x_m) = 1/M, hence f(tau) = log(eta(D/N)(1/E^2) tau + C_1), i.e. logarithmic growth in conformal time, and after undoing the reparameterization b ~ -(E^2/(E^2+1)) log t, ||S|| ~ (E/(E^2+1)) log t.

Not separable from the origin => perfect generalization (Prop. 3.2.1). In conformal time the S-dynamics are the bias-free ones. If the data are not separable from the origin then for every unit e, L_e(alpha e, 0) -> infinity as alpha -> infinity, so the bias-free exponential loss is coercive and convex; gradient flow therefore converges to a finite global minimum S_inf. Since tau(t) -> infinity (App. C: the loss is bounded above, so with beta = e^b one gets -beta^{-2} dbeta/dt < eta C, hence d/dt(1/beta) < eta C, so 1/beta < 1/beta_0 + eta C t, beta > 1/(1 + eta C t), and the integral of beta dt diverges like a log), the flow with bias reaches the same limit. Theorem 1 says ||S|| or |b| must diverge; S is bounded, so |b|/||S|| -> infinity, w_SVM = (0,-1), and A_gen -> 1.

||S_inf|| blows up at the edge (Prop. 3.4, App. D). This is the quantitative heart. At the minimum of f(S) = sum_i e^{S·x_i} one has sum_i x_i e^{S·x_i} = 0; dividing by f gives sum_i p_i x_i = 0 with p_i = e^{S·x_i}/f a probability vector — i.e. a finite minimizer exists iff the origin is a convex combination of the data, which is exactly non-separability from the origin. Define the origin to be epsilon-close to the hull boundary if there are k <= d points x_1,...,x_k such that every representation of the origin as a convex combination assigns them total weight at least 1 - epsilon. Then splitting the points into A = {x_1..x_k}, B = the rest, one has sum_A p_i / sum_B p_i >= (1-epsilon)/epsilon; bounding the denominator from below by Jensen, sum_B e^{S·x_i} >= (N-k) e^{S·x-} with x- the mean of B, and the numerator by k e^{|S|D} with D = max_{ij}|x_i - x_j| the data diameter, yields (1-epsilon)/epsilon <= (k/(N-k)) e^{|S|D}, hence

|S_inf| >= (1/D) log( ((1-epsilon)/epsilon) · ((N-k)/k) ).

So ||S_inf|| -> infinity logarithmically as the origin approaches the hull boundary. The argument is elementary and works for any monotone convex l (replace log by l^{-1}).

Timescale separation (Prop. 3.5). Rescale x~_i = x_i/sigma, S~ = sigma S, so x~_i ~ N(0, I_d) and the flow becomes dS~/dt = -sigma^2 (eta/N) e^b sum_i e^{S~^T x~_i} x~_i, db/dt = -(eta/N) e^b sum_i e^{S~^T x~_i}. The S~-dynamics are faster by sigma^2 while the b-dynamics are unchanged, and S~_inf is sigma-independent. Since L_gen and A_gen depend on b and ||S~|| = sigma||S||, large sigma means S reaches its (large) asymptote arbitrarily fast while b still grows only logarithmically — arbitrarily long delayed generalization. Recall sigma = sigma_B/mu, so "large sigma" literally means strong noise perpendicular to the separation axis.

The 1-D toy model (Sec. 4, App. E). Separability from the origin in one dimension is just "is 0 between min x_i and max x_i", so the entire phenomenology is captured by two points, x_1 = -sigma and x_2 = sigma(1-2 lambda), chosen so the margin has the same lambda-dependence as the Gaussian problem. In conformal time, dS/dtau = -(eta/2)[(1-2 lambda) e^{S(1-2 lambda)} - e^{-S}] and db/dtau = -(eta/2)[e^{S(1-2 lambda)} + e^{-S}]. The fixed point of the first gives, in the inseparable case lambda < 1/2, S_inf = log(1-2 lambda)/(2(lambda-1)) = (1/(2(1-lambda))) log(1/(1-2 lambda)), diverging logarithmically at lambda = 1/2 and matching the full model's numerics. Three cases are solved in closed form: x_2 = 1 gives S(tau) = log tanh(eta tau/2 + arctanh e^{S_0}) with b growing faster than S, so A_gen -> 1; x_2 = 0 (exactly critical) gives S = log(e^{S_0} + eta tau/2), b = -log(e^{S_0} + eta tau/2) - eta tau/2 + const, and inverting via the Lambert W function gives tau ~ log t, hence b ~ -log t and S ~ log log t — so even at criticality S diverges but S/b -> 0 and accuracy still tends to 1; x_2 = -1 (separable) gives S = S_0 + log(1 + eta tau e^{-S_0}), b = b_0 - log(1 + eta tau e^{-S_0}), so A_inf = (1/2)(1 + erf(1/sqrt(2))) < 1, consistent with M = 1. A full hypergeometric-2F1 implicit solution for general x_2 is also recorded. The grokking time is then computed explicitly: with S pinned at S_inf = -log(1-2 lambda), the thresholds L_tr = epsilon and L_gen = epsilon give t__tr = 1/(eta epsilon) and t__gen = (2/(eta epsilon)) exp((1/2) log^2(1-2 lambda)), so for any fixed epsilon the gap diverges as lambda -> 1/2, and the epsilon-independent scaling law is

sqrt( log(t__gen / t__tr) ) = (1/sqrt(2)) |log(1 - 2 lambda)|,

verified numerically with slope about 1/sqrt(2) over log(1-2 lambda) in [-7, -4.5] (Fig. 9). In conformal time the statement is cleaner still: tau__gen - tau__tr ~ (1/2) log^2(1-2 lambda). App. E.4 also computes the subleading correction in the nearly-separable case and finds it identical to the inseparable-side answer, u ~ -(1/x_1) log(x_1/x_2), a small consistency check across the transition.

Broader context

For someone coming to this cold: the subfield sits at the intersection of two mature lines. One is implicit bias of gradient descent on separable data — Soudry, Hoffer, Nacson, Gunasekar, Srebro (2018) showed that unregularized logistic regression on separable data has weights that diverge logarithmically but whose direction converges to the hard-margin SVM solution, with Nacson et al. (2019) and Ji and Telgarsky (2019) extending the picture to faster rates and to non-separable data. The upshot is that even without regularization, GD picks out a specific max-margin solution, and the quantities that matter asymptotically are directions and margins rather than norms. The other line is grokking: delayed generalization in overparameterized networks, where test performance improves long after training loss has flatlined. The two meet because the obvious candidate explanation for grokking is a race between two implicit biases on different timescales (Lyu et al. 2024 made this precise) and because the memorizing-versus-generalizing competition can often be recast as a competition between two feasible points of a margin problem — which is exactly what this paper does, with the twist that the relevant geometric predicate is whether the origin sits inside the convex hull of the data.

The two closest things worth reading beside it are Levi, Beck and Bar-Sinai (2023), "Grokking in linear estimators" — the same group's MSE/linear-regression analogue, where the threshold is lambda = 1, the grokking time diverges like log(1 - sqrt(lambda)), and the mechanism is a vanishing covariance eigenvalue; the present paper is the logistic/classification counterpart and makes the "criticality" claim more pointed because the transition is in the asymptotic dynamics rather than in a finite-time spectral gap — and Lyu, Jin, Li, Du, Lee and Hu (2024), "Dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases can provably induce grokking", which is the main competing theorem-level account and should be compared head to head: Lyu et al. need weight decay and large initialization, this paper needs neither but needs a knife-edge lambda and large perpendicular noise. Also worth a glance for contrast: Prieto et al. (2025), "Grokking at the edge of numerical stability" — nearly the same title shape, a completely different (and deflationary) mechanism via Softmax Collapse in floating-point arithmetic. Reading the two together is a good exercise in how under-determined grokking explanations currently are.

A plausible follow-up, and one the paper practically hands you: do finite-size scaling properly. Wendel's formula already gives the exact finite-(N, d) separability probability, and its Gaussian limit identifies the natural scaling variable z = sqrt(N) (2 lambda - 1) = sqrt(d) (sqrt(2 lambda) - 1/sqrt(2 lambda)). The paper's own App. E.1 admits that near criticality it discards the realizations that happen to be separable despite lambda < 1/2, biasing Figs. 6 and 7. Instead, one should treat the grokking time as a random variable over data draws and look for a collapse of its distribution as a function of z — predicting, for instance, that the mean grokking time conditioned on non-separability scales like log^2 of the realized margin-to-origin rather than of 1 - 2 lambda, and that the heavy tail of grokking times at lambda slightly below 1/2 is governed by the epsilon-closeness distribution of the origin to the hull boundary. That would turn a qualitative "critical slowing down" narrative into a genuine universality claim with a scaling function, and it is the obvious route to the "universality classes" the discussion gestures at. A second, riskier direction: test the conjecture on real networks by measuring, in last-layer feature space, whether the origin is inside the convex hull of the learned features over training — the paper itself suggests the feature-map-plus-SVM reading, and this gives it a falsifiable probe.

On IR: do not expect a real link to grokking, but there is one honest, non-forced mathematical overlap, and it is not with the grokking story — it is with the geometry. The predicate "the origin is in the convex hull of {x_i}" is the same object that controls reachability in maximum-inner-product search: under inner-product scoring, an item can be the top-1 answer for some query direction only if it is a vertex of the convex hull of the item set, so items in the interior are unreachable no matter the query. Wendel's/Cover's counting — the same formula as Prop. 3.3, with the same lambda = d/N = 1/2 threshold — is therefore the natural tool for asking what fraction of N random d-dimensional embeddings are reachable top-1 answers, and how that fraction behaves as a corpus grows at fixed embedding dimension. That is a genuine shared substrate with MIPS theory and with the known pathologies of inner-product versus cosine retrieval, and it is worth having the Wendel asymptotic (1/2)[1 + erf(sqrt(d)(sqrt(2 lambda) - 1/sqrt(2 lambda)))] in your toolkit for exactly that kind of counting argument. A softer and more speculative bridge: InfoNCE is a multiclass logistic loss, so the implicit-bias machinery used here (logarithmic weight growth, direction converging to a max-margin solution in an extended space) is the right language for asking what unregularized contrastive training of a dense retriever converges to in direction, and whether the bias term / temperature plays the role that b plays here. Beyond that, I would not claim a connection to generative retrieval: the superficial resonance ("docid memorization then generalization") is not supported by anything in this paper, whose "memorization" is a divergence direction in a convex problem, not a stored lookup table. This is best filed as a clean, self-contained piece of implicit-bias theory worth knowing on its own terms — a nice demonstration that a non-analytic change in asymptotic dynamics is sufficient to produce grokking phenomenology with no learning of structure at all.

title: Unintentional Unalignment: Likelihood Displacement in Direct Preference Optimization
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-11-01

Unintentional Unalignment: Likelihood Displacement in Direct Preference Optimization

Noam Razin, Sadhika Malladi, Adithya Bhaskar, Danqi Chen, Sanjeev Arora, Boris Hanin (2024/25, ICLR 2025) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08847

Setting and problem

The object of study is an autoregressive language model trained with a direct preference learning loss, and the quantity being tracked is not the loss but the log-likelihood of the preferred response.

Fix a vocabulary V. A language model is factored into two pieces: a backbone (a Transformer) that maps a token sequence x in V* to a hidden embedding h_x in R^d, and a token unembedding matrix W in R^{|V| x d} whose rows W_z in R^d are the per-token output vectors. The model is

pi_theta(y|x) = prod_{k=1}^{|y|} pi_theta(y_k | x, y_{<k}) = prod_{k=1}^{|y|} softmax(W h_{x,y_{<k}})_{y_k},

where y_{<k} denotes the first k-1 tokens of y, h_{x,y_{<k}} is the hidden embedding of the prompt-plus-prefix (so h_{x,y_{<1}} = h_x), and theta collects the backbone parameters together with W.

The learner is given a preference dataset D of triples (x, y+, y-): a prompt, a preferred response and a dispreferred response. These may be on-policy (two samples from the model, labelled by a human, an LLM judge or a reward model) or off-policy (from a static dataset); the analysis covers both. Typically there is a prior SFT stage, either on unrelated data or on the pairs {(x, y+)}. The learner is asked to produce parameters theta that make y+ more probable than y- — or, more precisely, that minimise a loss of the generic pairwise form

L(theta) = E_{(x,y+,y-) ~ D} [ ell_{x,y+,y-}( ln pi_theta(y+|x) - ln pi_theta(y-|x) ) ],

where each ell_{x,y+,y-}: R -> R_{>=0} is convex, differentiable, and (the one standing assumption) monotonically decreasing in a neighbourhood of the initial log-ratio margin ln pi_{theta_init}(y+|x) - ln pi_{theta_init}(y-|x). This single abstraction covers DPO with ell(u) = -ln sigma( beta ( u - ln[pi_ref(y+|x)/pi_ref(y-|x)] ) ) — so the reference model and the KL coefficient beta are absorbed entirely into the shape of ell — and likewise IPO (squared deviation of the implicit reward from 1/(2 tau)), SLiC (hinge at margin delta), REBEL (squared regression to a reward difference) and the whole GPO family f(beta(...)). Appendix E separately handles losses with an added SFT term, L_S = E[ ell(...) - lambda ln pi_theta(y+|x) ] (CPO, RPO, BoNBoN, DPOP), and losses that reweight the two log-probabilities, L_w = E[ ell( lambda^+ ln pi_theta(y+|x) - lambda^- ln pi_theta(y-|x) ) ] (SimPO's length normalisation, DPOP's extra factor).

The phenomenon is named in Definition 1. Likelihood displacement has occurred if the loss genuinely went down, L(theta_fin) < L(theta_init), and yet the average of ln pi_theta(y+|x) over D decreased. This is perfectly consistent — minimising the loss only requires the margin to grow — but it is counterintuitive, and it has been reported repeatedly (Pal et al. 2024; Yuan et al. 2024; Rafailov et al. 2024b; Tajwar et al. 2024; Pang et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2024). The paper adds a second, normative distinction: displacement is benign if the responses z that gain the lost probability mass are about as good as y+, and catastrophic if they are substantially worse — e.g. opposite in meaning.

The precise questions being answered are: what in the model's geometry causes ln pi_theta(y+|x) to decrease while the DPO-style margin increases, where does the displaced probability mass go, and is there a cheap per-sample statistic, computable from the model before training, that predicts which preference pairs will cause it?

What the surrounding literature already knew, and the specific disagreements this paper picks: Tajwar et al. (2024) attributed displacement to limited model capacity and to the presence of many training samples; Pal et al. (2024) attributed it to preference pairs with small edit distance, and proposed DPOP (an SFT-like correction) as the fix; Rafailov et al. (2024b) attributed it to the initial SFT phase; Ren and Sutherland (2024) proposed a "squeezing effect", in which the negative gradient on y- pushes mass onto tokens that are already high-probability, and conjectured this is the mechanism. Prior theory of DPO is mostly orthogonal — sample complexity under coverage or online data (Song et al. 2024b; Cen et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2024; Xie et al. 2024a), structural assumptions (Im and Li 2024a), optimisation rates (Im and Li 2024b; Feng et al. 2024) — or concerns a different failure, DPO's inability to flip pairwise rankings (Chen et al. 2024), which the authors carefully distinguish: under displacement, pi(y+|x) usually still exceeds pi(y-|x). The gap this paper fills is that none of the above is a mechanism stated at the level of the model's parameters, and several of them are demonstrably not the mechanism.

Three modelling choices do essentially all the work and should be flagged up front.

First, the unconstrained features model (Mixon et al. 2022, also used in neural-collapse and in Saunshi et al. 2021). The trainable parameters are taken to be theta = {h_z : z in V} union {W}: every hidden embedding, for every possible prefix, is treated as a free parameter, and the backbone is abstracted away entirely. Consequently gradients with respect to distinct prefixes' embeddings are decoupled, and in particular d/dt of h_{x,y+_{<k}} does not interact with d/dt of h_{x,y-_{freeze* the hidden embeddings, the whole phenomenon vanishes.

Second, the gradient-flow / small-learning-rate limit: d theta(t)/dt = -grad L(theta(t)). Under gradient flow the loss is monotone decreasing (barring initialisation at a critical point), so any decrease in ln pi_theta(y+|x) automatically qualifies as likelihood displacement in the sense of Definition 1 — a tidy way of making the definition unambiguous. All results are statements about the instantaneous derivative d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x), not about the trajectory.

Third, the single prompt, single-token-response setting of Section 3 and Section 4.2.1, where D = {(x, y+, y-)} with y+, y- in V. This is used both as the clean theoretical case and as an empirical counterexample to the capacity/multi-sample/SFT explanations.

The central derived statistic is the centered hidden embedding similarity (CHES) score (Definition 2): for a sample (x, y+, y-) and a model pi_theta,

CHES_x(y+, y-) = < sum_{k=1}^{|y+|} h_{x,y+_{<k}} , sum_{k_=1}^{|y-|} h_{x,y-_{<k'}} > - || sum_{k=1}^{|y+|} h_{x,y+_{<k}} ||^2,

i.e. the inner product of the summed prefix embeddings of the two responses, minus the squared norm of the summed preferred prefix embeddings. Equivalently CHES_x(y+,y-) = < S+, S- - S+ > with S+ = sum_k h_{x,y+_{<k}} and S- = sum_{k'} h_{x,y-_{<k'}} — hence "centered": the dispreferred sum is measured relative to the preferred sum. Higher CHES means more similar preferences and (the claim) more severe displacement. It costs one forward pass over the dataset. Appendix A gives the length-normalised variant CHES-bar = (1/(|y+||y-|)) <S+, S-> - (1/|y+|^2) ||S+||^2, used for filtering so as not to introduce a length bias.

Two notational conventions used throughout the formal results: ell'_{x,y+,y-}(t) abbreviates ell'_{x,y+,y-}( ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) - ln pi_{theta(t)}(y-|x) ), and e_z in R^{|V|} is the standard basis vector of token z. Lemma 2 establishes that -ell'_{x,y+,y-}(t) > 0 for all t >= 0 in the single-sample case, so it acts as a positive scalar and never flips any sign; for DPO, Lemma 1 gives this unconditionally and globally.

Main idea

The paper's move is to compute, exactly, the instantaneous time derivative of ln pi_theta(y+|x) under gradient flow on the pairwise loss, in the unconstrained-features parameterisation, and then to read off the geometry from the resulting expression. By the chain rule this derivative is a kernel inner product,

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) = -ell'(t) · < grad ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) , grad ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) - grad ln pi_{theta(t)}(y-|x) >,

and because -ell'(t) > 0, the sign is decided entirely by whether the self-gradient-norm of y+ dominates its NTK-style alignment with the gradient of y-. The paper's contribution is to evaluate that inner product in closed form and discover that it splits into two geometrically meaningful halves: the part coming from differentiating with respect to W yields inner products between hidden embeddings, and the part coming from differentiating with respect to the h's yields inner products between token unembeddings. The two "geometries" of the model therefore appear in dual roles, which is both the technical trick and the conceptual payoff.

From this they get four things.

Empirically (Section 3), they first demolish the existing explanations with a minimal example: train an 8B model via DPO on a single prompt from the Persona dataset whose preferred and dispreferred responses are single tokens. Likelihood displacement is pervasive — pi_theta(y+|x) falls by between 0.21 and 0.96 in absolute probability across OLMo-1B, Gemma-2B and Llama-3-8B — so neither multiple samples, nor sequence length, nor capacity limits, nor the SFT phase are necessary. And it is catastrophic in the semantically sharp sense: training to prefer y+ = " No" over y- = " Never" on OLMo-1B drops P(" No") from 0.85 to 0.01 and the tokens gaining most are " Yes", "Yes", "yes". Preferring " Sure" over " Yes" on Llama-3-8B shifts mass to " Maybe", " No", " Never". The same holds without the SFT phase (Table 2) and under IPO (Table 3).

Theoretically (Section 4), for single-token responses the derivative decomposes into a non-negative term m(t) minus (i) the preference unembedding alignment <W_{y+}, W_{y-}> weighted by 1 - pi(y+|x) + pi(y-|x), and (ii) a probability-weighted sum over all other tokens z of <W_z, W_{y+} - W_{y-}>. Companion result: for any other token z, d/dt ln pi(z|x) is proportional to <W_z, W_{y+} - W_{y-}> up to a z-independent constant. So the direction W_{y+} - W_{y-} is the "attractor": tokens whose unembeddings align with it rise. The key observation is that W_{y+} - W_{y-} is not W_{y+}; it has a component orthogonal to W_{y+} contributed entirely by W_{y-}, and Table 13 reports that this orthogonal component has the larger norm in every model/pair tested. Combined with the linear-representation hypothesis (Mikolov et al. 2013; Park et al. 2024), this explains how a semantically unrelated or opposite token can be the one that rises.

For multi-token responses, the same computation produces an extra pair of terms: sums over position pairs (k,k') of alpha^-_{k,k'} <h_{x,y+_{<k}}, h_{x,y-_{<k'}}> (entering negatively, i.e. driving displacement) and alpha^+_{k,k'} <h_{x,y+_{<k}}, h_{x,y+_{

Empirically again (Section 5), CHES earns its keep. For UltraFeedback and AlpacaFarm, they compute CHES for all samples, take 512-sample subsets centred on the 0th/25th/50th/75th/100th percentiles, and run DPO on each. The CHES ranking matches the degree of displacement perfectly across all three models: higher percentile, larger drop in mean preferred log-probability, with the lowest-CHES subsets actually increasing ln pi(y+|x). Two natural baselines fail outright: Pal et al.'s normalised edit distance, and the obvious naive measure <h_{x,y+}, h_{x,y-}> between only the final hidden embeddings. The theory tells you which modification to the naive measure matters (sum over prefixes, then subtract the preferred self-term), and only the modified version works.

Finally (Section 6), the safety consequence. Build an on-policy preference set from the 450 unsafe prompts of SORRY-Bench by sampling two responses from Gemma-2B-IT or Llama-3-8B-Instruct, labelling them refusal/non-refusal with the SORRY-Bench judge, preferring refusals and breaking ties with PairRM. Because the models are already moderately aligned, over 70% of pairs end up with two responses of the same type — the exact high-similarity regime. Running DPO on this set, with the sole objective of increasing refusals, decreases the refusal rate: 80.5% -> 54.8% for Gemma-2B-IT and 74.4% -> 33.4% for Llama-3-8B-Instruct, with the mean preferred log-probability falling by 48 to 59 nats. Keeping only the 5% of samples with the lowest length-normalised CHES restores and exceeds the original refusal rates, more effectively than adding an SFT term to the loss; training on SORRY-Bench's human-labelled "gold" pairs (diverse-model responses) shows no displacement at all. Figure 4 confirms the mechanism's fingerprint: the high-CHES tail is dominated by two-refusal and two-non-refusal pairs.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever piece of mathematics is small and easy to miss. In the unconstrained-features model, the gradient of a log-probability has two blocks:

grad_W ln pi_theta(z|x) = sum_{k=1}^{|z|} ( e_{z_k} - pi_theta(·|x, z_{<k}) ) h_{x,z_{<k}}^T, grad_{h_{x,z_{<k}}} ln pi_theta(z|x) = W_{z_k} - sum_{v in V} pi_theta(v | x, z_{<k}) W_v.

The W-block is a sum of rank-one outer products of a probability-space residual with a hidden embedding. When you take the Frobenius inner product of two such blocks, the identity < a h^T, b g^T > = <a,b> <h,g> factorises it into (residual inner product) x (hidden embedding inner product). So differentiating with respect to the unembeddings is what surfaces the geometry of the hidden embeddings, and vice versa. The alpha coefficients are nothing but those residual inner products, alpha^-_{k,k'} = < e_{y+_k} - pi(·|x, y+_{

The second genuinely strong contribution is a refutation, which is rarer and more valuable than another positive result. Proposition 3 (Appendix F) considers the exact setting Ren and Sutherland (2024) analysed — single-token responses, single prompt — but with h_x held fixed, so only W trains (a linear model). Then the derivative collapses to

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) = -ell'(t) · ( 1 - pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) + pi_{theta(t)}(y-|x) ) · ||h_x||^2 >= 0,

because the bracket is non-negative always and -ell'(t) >= 0 by Lemma 2. In a linear model likelihood displacement is impossible: the "squeezing" push from -grad ln pi(y-|x) is exactly cancelled by the pull from +grad ln pi(y+|x). So the squeezing effect, whatever else it explains, cannot be the cause, and any correct explanation must involve movement of the hidden embeddings. That is a clean falsification that also pins down precisely which modelling ingredient is indispensable. It is the best argument in the paper, and it simultaneously tells you that the unconstrained-features assumption is not an innocent convenience: the entire phenomenon lives on the h's being trainable.

Now the reviewer-style complaints, because there are real ones.

The theorems are identities, not implications. Every main result is an exact rewriting of the chain rule. None of them says "under conditions C, displacement occurs". They say "the derivative equals m(t) + S(t) - CHES-like terms, and some of those terms can be negative". The informal statements in the body — "d/dt ln pi(y+|x) is more negative the larger <W_{y+}, W_{y-}> is" — are ceteris paribus claims about expressions whose terms are coupled. Concretely, m(t) in Theorem 4 contains (1 - pi(y+|x))||W_{y+}||^2 + pi(y-|x)||W_{y-}||^2 + (1 - pi(y+|x) + pi(y-|x))||h_x||^2; if <W_{y+}, W_{y-}> is large because ||W_{y-}|| is large, m(t) grows too, and the net sign is undetermined. Similarly, the multi-token m(t) contains sum_{k>=2} ||W_{y+_k} - sum_z pi(z|x,y+_{prediction rather than a bookkeeping exercise is supplied by the experiments.

The CHES derivation throws away a non-negligible 31%. The alphas are only "mostly positive" — 69% averaged over three models and two datasets. The authors are upfront about this, and the diagonal preferred-preferred terms alpha^+_{k,k} = ||e_{y+_k} - pi(·|x,y+_{motivated by the theory, validated empirically, and the perfect percentile ranking in Figure 2 is the only real evidence that the simplification is safe.

The missing baseline is length. The paper itself reports that high-CHES samples tend to have longer dispreferred than preferred responses and low-CHES samples the reverse, and attributes this to Transformer representation anisotropy: over 99% of hidden-embedding inner products are positive for Llama-3-8B on UltraFeedback, so a longer y- simply adds more positive terms to <S+, S->. Section 5's ranking experiment uses the un-normalised CHES. So the obvious competing explanation for Figure 2 — that the ranking is substantially a proxy for the length ratio |y-|/|y+| — is never tested, even though a length-ratio baseline would have cost nothing to add alongside edit distance and <h_{x,y+}, h_{x,y-}>. This is the single clearest evaluation gap. (That said, the fact that length-normalised CHES still works for filtering in Section 6 is partial mitigation, and the failure of the naive last-embedding inner product is evidence that the summing-over-prefixes structure matters.)

The Section 6 mitigation does not do what the narrative implies. Table 16 shows that on the CHES-filtered data, the preferred log-probability still falls — by 45.7 nats for Gemma-2B-IT and 27.7 for Llama-3-8B-Instruct, against 59.2 and 48.1 unfiltered. So filtering did not remove likelihood displacement; it changed displacement from catastrophic to benign, which is a different and weaker claim than "filtering prevents the problem by preventing displacement". And the filter keeps 5% of 370 samples — about 18 pairs (up to 15% still works; beyond that the drop returns). The alternative, simpler explanation for why this helps is label noise: when both responses are refusals, the preference label is essentially arbitrary (it is resolved by PairRM tie-breaking), so you are fitting random labels on a safety-critical behaviour. On that reading, CHES is a good tie detector and the embedding-geometry theory is not needed to explain Figure 3. Figure 4 is consistent with both stories. A decisive experiment — e.g. CHES-filtering a dataset with reliable, non-tied labels and showing it still helps, or showing CHES beats a judge-confidence filter — is absent.

The headline number is amplified by the learning-rate protocol. For Section 6 the learning rate was chosen as "the largest value that led to stable training", giving 5e-6 — roughly fifty times the 1e-7 used in Sections 3 and 5. That rule selects for maximal parameter movement, which is exactly what maximises displacement. 74.4% -> 33.4% is therefore an upper-ish bound on the effect under a protocol designed to make something happen, not a typical outcome.

Where the mass goes is only answered in the toy case. Theorem 7 gives the multi-token analogue of Theorem 5, but its beta coefficients have unknown signs and the paper says plainly that it cannot characterise them. So the "catastrophic" half of the story — the part that gives the paper its title — is only mechanistically explained for single tokens, via the W_{y+} - W_{y-} orthogonality argument, which itself leans on the linear-representation hypothesis as an informal bridge. And Table 13 lacks a null baseline: in d = 2048-4096 dimensions, almost any pair of vectors has a difference that is mostly orthogonal to either endpoint, so "orthogonal component is bigger" is close to vacuous without a comparison distribution. For Llama-3-8B the reported numbers are 0.49 versus 0.71, which is not a dramatic separation.

Scope. Section 6 is one dataset (SORRY-Bench base split, 435 usable prompts), two models, one judge, and the authors themselves note they never check whether CHES filtering preserves general instruction-following — which matters, since discarding the 95% of pairs where the responses are similar is likely to discard most of the informative hard pairs.

Overall I would call this a strong paper that is honest about its own limits, whose theory is better understood as a derivation device for a useful statistic plus a falsification tool against a rival explanation than as a theory with guarantees.

Proof sketch

The common engine is three lines. Under gradient flow on L with a single sample, the chain rule gives

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(v|x) = < grad ln pi_{theta(t)}(v|x), d theta(t)/dt > = -ell'(t) · < grad ln pi_{theta(t)}(v|x), grad ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) - grad ln pi_{theta(t)}(y-|x) >

for any response v. Lemma 2 fixes the sign of the prefactor: at t = 0 the assumption that ell is decreasing near the initial margin gives ell'(0) < 0; if ell'(t) >= 0 ever held, continuity and the intermediate value theorem would give a time t_0 with ell'(t_0) = 0, at which grad L(theta(t_0)) = ell'(t_0) grad ln[pi(y+|x)/pi(y-|x)] = 0, i.e. gradient flow sits at a critical point — impossible unless it started there, by uniqueness of the gradient-flow solution. So -ell'(t) > 0 for all t. Lemma 1 gives the same conclusion for DPO directly and globally: ell'(u) = -beta sigma( beta ln[pi_ref(y+|x)/pi_ref(y-|x)] - u ) < 0 everywhere. Everything else is evaluating the inner product using the two gradient blocks quoted in the previous section, and using < a h^T, b g^T > = <a,b> <h,g> on the rank-one W-blocks.

Theorem 4 (single sample, single tokens; informal Theorem 1). Exactly,

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) = -ell'(t) [ m(t) - (1 - pi(y+|x) + pi(y-|x)) <W_{y+}(t), W_{y-}(t)> - sum_{z not in {y+,y-}} pi(z|x) <W_z(t), W_{y+}(t) - W_{y-}(t)> ],

with m(t) = (1 - pi(y+|x)) ||W_{y+}(t)||^2 + pi(y-|x) ||W_{y-}(t)||^2 + (1 - pi(y+|x) + pi(y-|x)) ||h_x(t)||^2 >= 0 and -ell'(t) > 0. The derivation: the h-block difference is grad_{h_x} ln pi(y+|x) - grad_{h_x} ln pi(y-|x) = W_{y+}(t) - W_{y-}(t) (the softmax-mean terms cancel), and the W-block difference is (e_{y+} - e_{y-}) h_x(t)^T. Pairing these with grad ln pi(y+|x) and expanding the two resulting inner products, the W-part contributes (1 - pi(y+|x) + pi(y-|x)) ||h_x||^2 and the h-part contributes <W_{y+} - sum_z pi(z|x) W_z, W_{y+} - W_{y-}>, which is then split into the ||W_{y+}||^2, ||W_{y-}||^2, cross and other-token pieces. What is actually guaranteed: an identity, with two explicitly negative-capable terms. The first, -(1 - pi(y+|x) + pi(y-|x)) <W_{y+}, W_{y-}>, formalises "similar preferences push the preferred likelihood down". The second is a probability-weighted alignment of the rest of the vocabulary with W_{y+} - W_{y-}; note the weighting by pi(z|x), which is the formal residue of the squeezing intuition.

Theorem 5 (where the mass goes, single tokens; informal Theorem 2). For any z not in {y+, y-},

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(z|x) = -ell'(t) [ <W_z(t), W_{y+}(t) - W_{y-}(t)> + c(t) ],

with c(t) = (pi(y-|x) - pi(y+|x)) ||h_x(t)||^2 - sum_{z'} pi(z'|x) <W_{z'}(t), W_{y+}(t) - W_{y-}(t)> independent of z. The proof is the same computation with grad ln pi(z|x) in the first slot. This is a clean and genuinely informative statement, because the z-dependence is exactly a single inner product: the ranking of which tokens rise is the ranking of their unembeddings' projections onto W_{y+} - W_{y-}. The catastrophic-displacement argument is then geometric rather than proved: decompose W_{y+} - W_{y-} into its projection onto W_{y+} plus an orthogonal part contributed by W_{y-}; Table 13 measures the orthogonal part to be larger; if unembeddings linearly encode semantics, the maximisers of <W_z, W_{y+} - W_{y-}> need not be semantically near y+.

Theorem 6 (multi-token; informal Theorem 3). Assume y+_1 != y-_1 (the general case replaces the y_1 terms with those at the first position where the responses diverge). Then

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) = -ell'(t) [ m(t) + S_{y+_1, y-_1}(t) - sum_{1} alpha^-}^{|y+|} sum_{k'=1}^{|y-|_{k,k'}(t) <h_{x,y+_{<k}}(t), h_{x,y-_{<k'}}(t)> + sum_{1} alpha^+}^{|y+|} sum_{k'=1}^{|y+|_{k,k'}(t) <h_{x,y+_{<k}}(t), h_{x,y+_{

where S_{y+_1,y-_1}(t) is exactly the Theorem 4 unembedding contribution evaluated at the first tokens, m(t) = (1 - pi(y+_1|x))||W_{y+_1}||^2 + pi(y-_1|x)||W_{y-_1}||^2 + sum_{2} ||W_{y+}^{|y+|_k} - sum_z pi(z|x,y+_{

alpha^-_{k,k'}(t) = < e_{y+_k} - pi_{theta(t)}(·|x, y+_{<k}), e_{y-_{k'}} - pi_{theta(t)}(·|x, y-_{<k'}) > in [-2,2], alpha^+_{k,k'}(t) = < e_{y+_k} - pi_{theta(t)}(·|x, y+_{<k}), e_{y+_{k'}} - pi_{theta(t)}) > in [-2,2].}(·|x, y+_{<k'

The proof is the same chain rule with the multi-token gradient blocks; the entire content is the factorisation step, and the [-2,2] range is immediate since each residual vector has l1 norm at most 2 (and l2 norm at most sqrt(2), with Cauchy-Schwarz giving the bound). Note the signs: preferred-dispreferred alignment enters negatively (drives displacement), preferred-preferred alignment enters positively (self-reinforcement). Setting all alphas to 1 collapses the two double sums into <S+, S-> - ||S+||^2, which is precisely CHES. So CHES is literally the negated hidden-embedding block of the derivative under the simplification, and the bracket reads m(t) + S(t) - CHES. Appendix H.2 is the empirical warrant for that simplification (>69% of alphas positive).

Theorem 7 (where the mass goes, multi-token). For z with z_1 not in {y+_1, y-_1},

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(z|x) = -ell'(t) [ c(t) + <W_{z_1}, W_{y+_1} - W_{y-_1}> - sum_{k,k'} beta^-_{k,k'} <h_{x,z_{

with beta^{+/-} defined exactly as the alphas but with e_{z_k} - pi(·|x, z_{<k}) in the first slot, and c(t) = -sum_z pi(z|x) <W_z, W_{y+_1} - W_{y-_1}> independent of z. The paper explicitly declines to characterise the signs of the betas, so this is the weak link; it does note that if z shares a prefix with y+ there are extra upward terms, and with y- extra downward ones.

Theorems 8 and 9 (multiple samples, single tokens). Assume all responses are single tokens and no prompt repeats. Then

d/dt ln pi_{theta(t)}(y+|x) = ( -ell'_{x,y+,y-}(t) / |D| ) [ m(t) + S_{y+,y-} ( -ell'}(t) ] + sum_{(x~,y~+,y~-) in D \ {(x,y+,y-)}_{x~,y~+,y~-}(t) / |D| ) · alpha_{x,x~}(t)>,}(t) · <h_x(t), h_{x~

with alpha_{x,x~}(t) = 1[y+ = y~+] - 1[y+ = y~-] + pi(y~-|x) - pi(y~+|x) in [-2,2]. The cross-sample term is clean because in the unconstrained-features model grad_{h_{x'}} ln pi(z|x~) = 0 for x' != x~, so the interaction between two different samples lives entirely in the W-block, and the factorisation identity turns it into (residual overlap) x <h_x, h_{x~}>. Two cases make alpha negative: contradicting samples (y+ = y~-), which is unsurprising, and the more interesting non-contradicting case y+ not in {y~+, y~-} with pi(y~-|x) < pi(y~+|x). Since the authors measure <h_x, h_{x~}> to be positive essentially always (Transformer representation anisotropy; all pairs positive on the Persona subset), alpha < 0 translates into a genuine downward push. Theorem 9 is the companion: the contribution of each other sample to d/dt ln pi(z|x) is ( -ell'_{x~}/|D| )(1[z = y~+] - 1[z = y~-]) <h_x, h_{x~}>, i.e. another prompt's preferred token gains probability under this prompt, with the leakage mediated by prompt-embedding similarity. This formalises Tajwar et al.'s observation that more data makes displacement worse.

Propositions 1 and 2 (loss modifications). With the SFT-regularised loss L_S, d/dt ln pi_{theta_S(t)}(y+|x) = E(theta_S(t)) + lambda ||grad ln pi_{theta_S(t)}(y+|x)||^2, where E(theta) is exactly the original derivative expression evaluated at theta. With the reweighted loss L_w, d/dt ln pi_{theta_w(t)}(y+|x) = rho(t) E(theta_w(t)) + gamma(t) ||grad ln pi_{theta_w(t)}(y+|x)||^2 with rho(t) = lambda^- · mu'(theta_w(t))/ell'(theta_w(t)) > 0 and gamma(t) = (lambda^+ - lambda^-)(-mu'(theta_w(t))), so gamma > 0 exactly when the preferred response is upweighted. Both are one-line chain-rule computations, and both say the same structural thing: these fixes add a non-negative multiple of the squared gradient norm of ln pi(y+|x), i.e. they inject an unconditional upward push that can offset, but does not remove, the displacement terms. That is a precise formalisation of why DPOP/RPO/CPO/BoNBoN mitigate the symptom, and consistent with the empirical finding that an SFT term restores log-probabilities (Table 16: +20.2 and +28.6) yet recovers refusal rates less well than data filtering — mitigating displacement is not the same as making the data informative.

Proposition 3 (linear model). Covered above; the only result in the paper with an unconditional sign conclusion, and the one that does the most argumentative work.

Broader context

The subfield background: aligning a language model to human preferences classically meant RLHF — fit a Bradley-Terry reward model r(x,y) to pairwise comparisons, then maximise E[r] - beta KL(pi_theta || pi_ref) with PPO. DPO's observation (Rafailov et al. 2023) is that the KL-regularised optimum has a closed form, pi_(y|x) proportional to pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta), so the reward is recoverable as beta ln[pi_theta(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)] plus a prompt-dependent constant, and the Bradley-Terry likelihood can be maximised _directly* in theta with no RL loop. The whole family of variants (IPO, SLiC, SimPO, CPO, RPO, KTO, ORPO, REBEL, GPO) differs in the link function applied to the implicit reward margin, the presence of a reference model, and length normalisation. The persistent empirical oddity across all of them is the one this paper studies: the margin grows, both log-probabilities shrink. Practitioners noticed this degrades math and reasoning benchmarks (Pal et al. 2024; Yuan et al. 2024; Pang et al. 2024; Meng et al. 2024) — which the authors note is a trivially catastrophic case, since on math there are few acceptable answers, and they position their contribution as showing catastrophe in settings where many answers would have been acceptable.

Two closely related works worth reading beside this one. First, Ren and Sutherland, "Learning dynamics of LLM finetuning" (arXiv 2407.10490), which is the direct intellectual foil: it analyses SFT/DPO dynamics through a per-example NTK-like influence decomposition and proposes the squeezing effect. Reading the two together is instructive precisely because Razin et al.'s Proposition 3 shows the squeezing mechanism is insufficient in the exact setting where it was derived, and because both use essentially the same linearised-dynamics machinery to reach different conclusions — a good case study in how much the choice of which parameters are trainable determines the answer. Second, Chen, Malladi, Zhang, Chen, Zhang, Ranganath, Cho, "Preference learning algorithms do not learn preference rankings" (arXiv 2405.19534), which documents that DPO-trained models achieve poor ranking accuracy on their own training pairs; it is the complementary negative result about what DPO actually optimises, and the present paper is careful to distinguish the two failure modes. Worth also knowing the unconstrained-features / neural-collapse line (Mixon et al. 2022; Zhu et al. 2021; Ji et al. 2022; Tirer et al. 2023) that supplies the modelling assumption, and Malladi et al., "A kernel-based view of language model fine-tuning" (ICML 2023), by an overlapping author set, which is the justification one would appeal to for treating finetuning dynamics as approximately kernel-like at small learning rates.

A plausible follow-up the paper opens: turn CHES from a filter into a constructive data-curation objective. Right now the pipeline is "generate pairs, score, discard 95%". But Theorem 5 and Theorem 7 say precisely which direction in output space gains mass, so one could instead do CHES-aware pair construction: given a prompt and a pool of candidate responses from diverse models, select the (y+, y-) pair that maximises label reliability subject to CHES below a threshold — or, more ambitiously, select y- so that the attractor direction (the analogue of W_{y+} - W_{y-}) points at responses you are happy to promote. That is a well-posed combinatorial selection problem with a cheap objective and would test whether the geometric story has predictive content beyond ranking. The complementary theory question is to replace the instantaneous derivative with a trajectory statement: prove, under some control on how fast the alphas and the embedding Gram matrix move (or in a genuine NTK regime where they are frozen at initialisation), that CHES above a threshold implies ln pi(y+|x) decreases over a non-trivial time interval, with a bound involving beta, the learning rate, ||h||, and the spectrum of the hidden-embedding Gram matrix. As it stands there is no such theorem, and it is the obvious missing piece.

On a connection to your own work: there is a real one, and it is in generative retrieval rather than in vector search. Generative retrieval decodes a document identifier autoregressively, pi_theta(d | q), and modern docid constructions are deliberately built so that semantically similar documents share prefixes — hierarchical k-means codes in DSI, residual-quantisation semantic IDs, and so on. Meanwhile a growing line of work trains generative retrievers with pairwise ranking or preference-style objectives over docids rather than pure likelihood: LTRGR, RIPOR's margin-based decoding objectives, and several explicitly DPO-flavoured ranking losses for GR. Compose those two facts and you are standing exactly in the high-CHES regime that this paper identifies: a positive docid d+ and a hard-negative docid d- that share a long prefix have literally identical hidden embeddings h_{q, d_{<k}} for every shared position k, so the summed-prefix inner product <S+, S-> is inflated by construction and CHES is large. Theorem 6 then predicts that the pairwise objective will decrease pi_theta(d+ | q) while increasing the margin, and Theorems 5 and 7 predict the mass flows to a third docid aligned with the difference direction — which, because the docid unembedding geometry is a learned codebook with no semantic faithfulness guarantee, need not be a relevant document at all. This is a falsifiable prediction about a real failure mode of ranking-objective generative retrieval, and CHES is directly computable for a GR model from one forward pass over (query, docid+, docid-) triples. Two further hooks: Theorem 8/9's cross-sample term (-ell'_{q~}/|D|) alpha_{q,q~}> is a formal statement that preference signal leaks across queries in proportion to } <h_q, h_{q~query embedding similarity, which is the generative-retrieval analogue of the well-known in-batch and hard-negative leakage problems in two-tower dense retrieval (and the authors' own measurement that >99% of prompt-embedding inner products are positive is the representation-anisotropy/cone effect that the dense-retrieval community has studied under "representation degeneration"); and Proposition 3's "freeze the features and displacement is impossible" has a direct reading as "train only the docid output layer and this pathology disappears", which is a cheap ablation someone should run. The vector-search link, by contrast, I would not push: the observation that W_{y+} - W_{y-} is mostly orthogonal to W_{y+} is close to a generic high-dimensional fact and has no particular bearing on quantisation or ANN index geometry. So: a genuine and fairly specific generative-retrieval connection, a suggestive analogy to hard-negative mining in dense retrieval, and no real vector-search connection — and the paper is well worth reading on its own terms anyway, for the rank-one factorisation trick and for the discipline of using a one-line proposition to kill a rival explanation.

title: Tensor Product Attention Is All You Need
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-31

Tensor Product Attention Is All You Need

Zhang, Liu, Yuan, Qin, Yuan, Gu & Yao (2025) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.06425

Tensor Product Attention Is All You Need

Zhang, Liu, Yuan, Qin, Yuan, Gu & Yao · arXiv:2501.06425 (v7, Jan 2026; NeurIPS 2025) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.06425 Project page: https://github.com/tensorgi/TPA

Setting and problem

The object. Fix a decoder-only Transformer with $L$ layers, model (residual-stream) width $d_{\text{model}}$, $h$ attention heads per layer, and per-head dimension $d_h$. Write $d_{\text{attn}} := h\,d_h$ for the total attention projection width; the usual choice is $d_{\text{attn}} = d_{\text{model}}$, but the paper is careful to note this is not required — $W^Q, W^K, W^V$ may map $\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{attn}}}$ with $W^O: \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{attn}}} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$, and this slack turns out to matter a great deal for reading the experiments (see below).

Let $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$ be the hidden state entering a given attention layer at position $t \in [T]$. Standard multi-head attention (MHA) forms, per head $i \in [h]$, $$q_{t,i} = (W_i^Q)^\top x_t, \qquad k_{t,i} = (W_i^K)^\top x_t, \qquad v_{t,i} = (W_i^V)^\top x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h},$$ with $W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_h}$, and then $$\mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Softmax}!\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d_h}} Q_i K_i^\top \right) V_i, \qquad \mathrm{MHA}(X) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1,\dots,\mathrm{head}_h) W^O .$$ It is convenient (and it is the paper's convention) to collect the per-token slices into matrices $$Q_t, K_t, V_t \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times d_h},$$ whose $i$-th row is head $i$'s query/key/value at position $t$. The full tensors are $Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times h \times d_h}$. This "slice as an $h \times d_h$ matrix" view is the whole paper: everything TPA does is a statement about the rank of that matrix.

What must be cached, and why decoding is memory-bound. Autoregressive generation computes one new token at a time. At step $t$, the new query $q_{t,i}$ must be scored against all past keys ${k_{s,i}}_{s<t}$ and the attention weights applied to all past values. Since $k_{s,i}, v_{s,i}$ depend only on $x_s$ (and on $s$ through the positional encoding), they are computed once and stored — the KV cache. Per layer, per past token, MHA must retain $$\underbrace{h\,d_h}_{\text{keys}} + \underbrace{h\,d_h}_{\text{values},$$ so the total cache for a batch of $B$ sequences of length $T$ is $2\,B\,L\,T\,h\,d_h$ scalars — linear in $T$ and completely independent of how clever the kernel is. For a 7B-class model ($L=32$, $h=32$, $d_h=128$) at $T=128{,}000$ in fp16 this is $\approx 67$ GB }} = 2\,h\,d_h \text{ scalarsper sequence — so even batch 4 exceeds an 80 GB device before the weights are loaded. This is why context windows are capped by memory, not by FLOPs.

The sharper point is arithmetic intensity. At a single decode step with cache length $M$, the attention FLOPs are $\Theta(2 M h d_h)$ (one dot product and one weighted sum per cached token per head) while the bytes read are $\Theta(2 M h d_h)$ as well. The ratio is $O(1)$ FLOPs per loaded scalar. On any modern accelerator — where the FLOP:byte ratio is in the hundreds — this means decoding attention is bandwidth-bound: the GPU spends essentially all of its time streaming the cache through the memory hierarchy and almost none of it computing. Hence two consequences that shape the entire design space: (i) shrinking the cache buys both capacity and speed, and (ii) a method that trades extra arithmetic for fewer cached bytes is a good trade, not a bad one, up to a factor of order (FLOP:byte ratio).

The existing design space. Every established method shrinks the per-token footprint by constraining the _structure of the matrix $K_t$ (and $V_t$)_, or by constraining the map $x_t \mapsto K_t$. Writing the per-token cache cost in scalars:

mechanism per-token KV cache attention-layer parameters what is given up
MHA (Vaswani et al.) $2 h d_h$ $4 d_{\text{model}} h d_h$ nothing; baseline
MQA (Shazeer 2019) $2 d_h$ $2 d_{\text{model}} d_h (h+1)$ all heads share one key and one value: $\mathrm{rank}(K_t) = 1$, every row identical
GQA (Ainslie et al. 2023) $2 G d_h$ $2 d_{\text{model}} d_h (h+G)$ $h$ heads partitioned into $G$ fixed groups; $\mathrm{rank}(K_t) \le G$, rows constant within a group
MLA (DeepSeek-V2/V3) $d_c + d_h^{R}$ $d_c'(d_{\text{model}} + h d_h + h d_h^{R}) + d_c(d_{\text{model}} + 2 h d_h) + d_{\text{model}}(h d_h + d_h^{R})$ the map $x_t \mapsto \mathrm{vec}(K_t, V_t)$ is forced through a fixed $d_c$-dimensional bottleneck; needs a separate RoPE'd key channel
TPA (this paper) $(R_K + R_V)(h + d_h)$ $d_{\text{model}}(R_Q + R_K + R_V)(h + d_h) + d_{\text{model}} h d_h$ $\mathrm{rank}(K_t) \le R_K$, $\mathrm{rank}(V_t) \le R_V$, but with token-dependent factors on both axes

(These are Table 1 of the paper, reproduced exactly. $d_c, d_c'$ are MLA's KV- and query-latent dimensions; $d_h^{R}$ is MLA's decoupled-RoPE key width. The TPA parameter count includes the output projection $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_h \times d_{\text{model}}}$, which contributes the $d_{\text{model}} h d_h$ term.)

Two of these are activation-side rank constraints (MQA, GQA: the matrix $K_t$ literally has low rank, with a hard-coded row pattern), and one is a weight-side rank constraint (MLA: $\mathrm{vec}(K^C_t) = (W^{UK})^\top (W^{DKV})^\top x_t$ is a linear map of rank $\le d_c$, so the key slice always lives in the same $d_c$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{h d_h}$, no matter the token). MLA is thus essentially LoRA-style static factorization applied to the KV projection, with the bottleneck activation $c^{KV}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}$ cached in place of $K_t, V_t$.

The RoPE obstruction, stated precisely. Rotary position embedding (Su et al.) multiplies each $d_h$-dimensional query/key row vector on the right by a block-diagonal rotation $T_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_h}$ built from $d_h/2$ planar blocks $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\theta_j & -\sin t\theta_j\ \sin t\theta_j & \cos t\theta_j\end{pmatrix}$, $\theta_j = \text{base}^{-2j/d_h}$. Its defining property is $$T_t T_s^\top = T_{t-s} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (q_t T_t)(k_s T_s)^\top = q_t T_{t-s} k_s^\top, \tag{$\star$}$$ i.e. the score depends only on the relative offset.

MLA's problem (Appendix F.3, following the DeepSeek analysis): the whole point of caching $c^{KV}_s$ rather than $K_s$ is that the content score collapses, $$q_{t,i}^\top k_{s,i} = x_t^\top \big[W_i^{DQ} W_i^{UQ} (W_i^{UK})^\top\big] c^{KV}_s,$$ so the bracketed matrix can be pre-multiplied once and the per-token work reduces to a $d_c$-dimensional dot product. But if RoPE is applied to the up-projected $Q^C, K^C$, the identity ($\star$) inserts $T_{t-s}$ inside the bracket: $$q_{t,i}^\top k_{s,i} = x_t^\top \big[W_i^{DQ} W_i^{UQ} \, T_{t-s} \, (W_i^{UK})^\top\big] c^{KV}_s,$$ and the bracket now depends on $(t-s)$, so it cannot be precomputed — one would need $O(T)$ distinct matrices. DeepSeek's fix is decoupled RoPE: carve out an extra, RoPE-only key channel $k^R_s \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h^{R}}$ (shared across heads) that bypasses the latent, cache it alongside $c^{KV}_s$, and concatenate. This is why MLA's cache is $d_c + d_h^{R}$ rather than $d_c$, and why MLA's per-head query/key width is the awkward $d_h + d_h^{R}$.

The question the paper asks. Can one shrink the per-token KV footprint by an order of magnitude relative to MHA, using a factorization whose factors are functions of the current token's hidden state rather than fixed weights, in a way that is exactly compatible with RoPE (no extra position-only channel, no loss of the relative-offset identity) and that strictly contains MHA/MQA/GQA as special cases — while not losing language-modelling quality?

Two modelling choices worth flagging before the answer.

  1. The factorization is contextual. MLA and LoRA factorize weights: a fixed low-rank map, token-independent subspace. TPA factorizes activations: for each token $t$ the factors $a_r(x_t), b_r(x_t)$ are themselves outputs of linear maps applied to $x_t$. So the $R_K$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{d_h}$ in which all $h$ heads' keys for token $t$ live moves with the token. This is not a minor variation: it is the difference between "the database items lie in one global $d_c$-dim subspace" and "each item carries its own rank-$R$ basis". It is strictly more expressive than GQA at equal rank (GQA's head-mixing pattern is a fixed 0/1 mask; TPA's is a learned, token-dependent vector) and it is incomparable to MLA (neither contains the other: MLA allows full rank across heads but a fixed subspace; TPA allows a moving subspace but caps the rank).

  2. The two axes of the outer product are different kinds of object. In $a_r(x_t) \otimes b_r(x_t)$, the factor $a_r \in \mathbb{R}^{h}$ lives on the head axis and $b_r \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}$ on the feature axis. RoPE acts only on the feature axis (right-multiplication by $T_t$). This asymmetry is exactly what makes the RoPE-compatibility result trivial once you see it — and it is also what makes the cache cost $(h + d_h)$ per rank per token rather than $d_h$, a cost the paper's narrative under-advertises.

With that, TPA's parameterization is forced. You should now be able to write it down yourself: take $W^{a_Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{(R_Q h) \times d_{\text{model}}}$ and $W^{b_Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{(R_Q d_h) \times d_{\text{model}}}$, reshape $W^{a_Q} x_t$ into $A_Q(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_Q \times h}$ and $W^{b_Q} x_t$ into $B_Q(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_Q \times d_h}$, and set $Q_t = \frac{1}{R_Q} A_Q(x_t)^\top B_Q(x_t)$.

Main idea

The factorization. For each token $t$, TPA replaces the three linear maps by three contextual CP (canonical polyadic) decompositions of ranks $R_Q, R_K, R_V$ — which may differ: $$Q_t = \frac{1}{R_Q}\sum_{r=1}^{R_Q} a^Q_r(x_t) \otimes b^Q_r(x_t), \quad K_t = \frac{1}{R_K}\sum_{r=1}^{R_K} a^K_r(x_t) \otimes b^K_r(x_t), \quad V_t = \frac{1}{R_V}\sum_{r=1}^{R_V} a^V_r(x_t) \otimes b^V_r(x_t),$$ with $a^{\bullet}_r(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{h}$, $b^{\bullet}_r(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}$, and $(a \otimes b)_{ij}$. Merging the rank index into the output dimension gives the compact matrix form $$Q_t = \frac{1}{R_Q} A_Q(x_t)^\top B_Q(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times d_h}, \qquad A_Q(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_Q \times h},\; B_Q(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_Q \times d_h},$$ and likewise for $K$ and $V$. Downstream, nothing changes: standard scaled dot-product attention per head, concatenate, project by $W^O$. So TPA is a drop-in replacement for the QKV projections.} = a_i b_j$. Each factor is a plain linear function of the hidden state, $a^Q_r(x_t) = W_r^{a_Q} x_t$ with $W_r^{a_Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times d_{\text{model}}}$ and $b^Q_r(x_t) = W_r^{b_Q} x_t$ with $W_r^{b_Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_{\text{model}}

Read per head, this says $$q_{t,i} = \frac{1}{R_Q}\sum_{r=1}^{R_Q} A_Q(x_t)[r,i]\; b^Q_r(x_t),$$ i.e. all $h$ heads at token $t$ read out of a common, token-specific $R$-dimensional "dictionary" ${b_r(x_t)}_{r \le R}$, each head using its own learned, token-dependent coefficient vector $A(x_t)[:,i] \in \mathbb{R}^{R}$. Equivalently: $\mathrm{rank}(K_t) \le R_K$ with row space $\subseteq \mathrm{rowspace}\,B_K(x_s)$, and that row space is a function of $x_s$.

What is cached. Instead of $K_t, V_t \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times d_h}$, TPA caches the four small factor matrices $$A_K(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_K \times h}, \quad \widetilde{B}_K(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_K \times d_h}, \quad A_V(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_V \times h}, \quad B_V(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{R_V \times d_h},$$ where the tilde denotes RoPE pre-rotation (below). Per token, per layer: $$\boxed{\;(R_K + R_V)(h + d_h)\;\text{scalars}\;}\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad 2 h d_h \ \text{for MHA},$$ a compression ratio of $\dfrac{(R_K+R_V)(h+d_h)}{2 h d_h}$. With $h = 32$, $d_h = 64$, $R_K = R_V = 1$: $192$ vs $4096$, i.e. 21×. With $R_K = R_V = 2$: $384$ vs $4096$, 10.7×. The useful asymptotic read is $\frac{(R_K+R_V)}{2}\left(\frac{1}{d_h} + \frac{1}{h}\right)$, so the win grows with both $h$ and $d_h$ — but note that the $h$ term means each unit of rank costs $h$ scalars for the head-axis factor, which is the hidden price of contextuality.

RoPE, for free. Because $T_t$ multiplies on the feature axis and $A^\top$ on the head axis, they commute: $$\mathrm{RoPE}_t(Q_t) = Q_t T_t = \frac{1}{R_Q} A_Q(x_t)^\top \big(B_Q(x_t) T_t\big) = \frac{1}{R_Q} A_Q(x_t)^\top \widetilde{B}_Q(x_t).$$ So the rotation is absorbed entirely into the $B$ factor, row by row: $a_r \otimes \mathrm{RoPE}_t(b_r) = (a_r \otimes b_r) T_t$. Practically, one pre-rotates $B_K$ before caching, so decoding never rotates cached state (the current query is not cached and is rotated on the fly for free). No extra positional channel, no loss of the relative-offset property. This is the structural advantage over MLA.

FlashTPA.
