$$ u^j \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{H}|}, \qquad u^j_i \;=\; f_\theta(h_i, y_j), \qquad \bar u \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|} u^j . $$

So $u^j$ is "what the metric thinks of every candidate, judged against the single pseudo-reference $y_j$", and $\bar u$ is the MBR score vector. Correspondingly, the paper posits a human score vector

$$ \hat u \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{H}|}, \qquad \hat u_i \;=\; \hat f_{\hat\theta}(h_i), $$

i.e. a reference-free, deterministic, scalar human quality judgement for each candidate. The two decoders are then simply two argmaxes over the same index set:

$$ \hat h_{\mathrm{mbr}} = \arg\max_{h_i} \bar u_i, \qquad\qquad \hat h_{\mathrm{human}} = \arg\max_{h_i} \hat u_i. \tag{6} $$

The objective actually studied. Not regret, not accuracy of the argmax, but the mean squared quality-estimation error over the candidate list, with the uniform measure on $\mathcal{H}$:

$$ \mathrm{MSE}(\hat u, \bar u) \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{H}|} (\hat u_i - \bar u_i)^2 \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{i \in \mathcal{H}}\big[(\hat u_i - \bar u_i)^2\big]. \tag{8} $$

Two things to internalise about this object. First, all expectations in the entire bias–diversity section are empirical averages over finite index sets — $\mathbb{E}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}$ is uniform over the 64 candidates, $\mathbb{E}_{j\in\mathcal{Y}}$ is uniform over the drawn pseudo-references. There is no expectation over the data distribution, over the randomness of the sampler, or over the training of $\theta$. Everything is conditional on one input $x$ and one realised pair $(\mathcal{H}, \mathcal{Y})$. The decomposition is therefore a finite-sample algebraic identity, not a statistical (population) statement. Second, the quantity is scale-sensitive and permutation-insensitive in exactly the wrong way relative to the decision rule: $\arg\max$ is invariant to any strictly increasing transform of $\bar u$, while MSE is not — a point I return to below.

The precise question. Can the discrepancy between the quality ranking that MBR decoding induces over a candidate list and the ranking a human would induce be exactly decomposed into (a) a term measuring how far individual metric-vs-pseudo-reference judgements sit from human judgement, and (b) a term measuring how much those individual judgements disagree among themselves — and if so, does that decomposition explain, in a single framework, the scattered empirical folklore about what makes MBR work?

What the literature already knew (the gap). MBR decoding goes back to Goel & Byrne (2000) in ASR and Kumar & Byrne (2002, 2004) in SMT; it was revived for neural MT by Eikema & Aziz (2020, 2022), whose "Is MAP decoding all you need?" argued that the mode of a neural MT model is pathological and that sampling-based consensus decoding is better behaved. A pile of empirical findings then accumulated, pulling in different directions:

  1. Metric quality matters. Müller & Sennrich (2021), Freitag et al. (2022a), Fernandes et al. (2022), Amrhein & Sennrich (2022): neural utilities (COMET, BLEURT) beat lexical ones; weak metrics get gamed.
  2. Pseudo-reference quality matters. Ohashi et al. (2024), Jinnai et al. (2024a): pseudo-references that look like human references help.
  3. Pseudo-reference diversity also matters, and sometimes dominates quality. Freitag et al. (2023a) found $\varepsilon$-sampling best; Heineman et al. (2024) found multi-prompt diversity helps; and awkwardly, plain ancestral sampling — the least "clean" sampler — is often competitive or better, and BLEU occasionally matches COMET (Freitag et al. 2022b).
  4. More samples help, with diminishing returns, which is the MBR instance of the inference-scaling-law literature (Brown et al. 2024 "Large Language Monkeys", Wu et al. 2024, Snell et al. 2025, Chen et al. 2025), and motivates a whole pruning/efficiency line (DeNero et al. 2009; Cheng & Vlachos 2023; Deguchi et al. 2024b; Vamvas & Sennrich 2024; Jinnai et al. 2024b).

Observations (2) and (3) are in tension: "make pseudo-references more reference-like" and "make pseudo-references more diverse" are different and sometimes opposed instructions, and the field had no principled account of the trade-off. That tension is the stated gap.

Non-obvious modelling choices — this is where the result lives.

  • The "human" is a reference-free deterministic scalar function $\hat f_{\hat\theta}$. There is no inter-annotator variance, no distribution over human judgements, no dependence on an unobserved true reference. It is a single fixed vector $\hat u$. This is what makes Theorem 1 a trivial-to-state identity; it is also what makes the bias term unmeasurable in principle and what makes the pseudo-bias surrogate necessary.
  • The "true utility" is whatever $\hat f_{\hat\theta}$ says, so "bias" is metric-plus-pseudo-reference misalignment with human judgement, conflating two sources (bad $\theta$, bad $y_j$) that the paper's own interpretation section wants to discuss separately.
  • $\mathcal{H}$ is given and fixed. Nothing in the bias–diversity decomposition speaks to how candidates are generated or how good the best candidate in $\mathcal{H}$ is. The authors state this explicitly in the Limitations; it is handled only via the separate information-theoretic machinery of §3.3.
  • Uniform measure over $\mathcal{H}$. Each of the 64 candidates counts equally in the MSE, including the 60 that will never be selected. Hence the paper's later distinction between "Overall" and "One Best" variants of each term.
  • The ensemble analogy is an identification, not a derivation. The map is: ensemble member $\leftrightarrow$ pseudo-reference $y_j$ (each $y_j$ induces a regressor $h \mapsto f_\theta(h,y_j)$); data point $\leftrightarrow$ hypothesis $h_i$; target $\leftrightarrow$ human score $\hat u_i$; combiner $\leftrightarrow$ uniform average. Once you accept that mapping, MBR is a uniformly-weighted regression ensemble and Krogh & Vedelsby (1994) applies verbatim. Everything downstream is a consequence of accepting the mapping.
  • Conditional independence (for §3.3). The information-theoretic results about scaling assume the $|\mathcal{Y}|$ sample representations are mutually independent given the human-preferred candidate $\hat H$. This is the assumption that does all the work in Theorems 7–8.

Given the above, a reader can state Theorem 1 themselves: it is the Krogh–Vedelsby ambiguity decomposition, instantiated with those identifications.

Main idea

The paper's move is to recognise that sampling-based MBR decoding is literally a uniformly-weighted regression ensemble, with pseudo-references playing the role of ensemble members and hypotheses playing the role of data points, and then to import the ensemble-learning diversity literature onto it.

The central object is Theorem 1, an exact finite-sample identity:

$$ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\big[(\hat u_i - \bar u_i)^2\big]}_{\mathrm{MSE} \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}}(\hat u, \bar u)_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\,\mathbb{E}_{j\in\mathcal{Y}}\big[(\hat u_i - f_\theta(h_i,y_j))^2\big]}_{\textbf{Bias}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\,\mathbb{E}_{j\in\mathcal{Y}}\big[(\bar u_i - f_\theta(h_i,y_j))^2\big]}_{\textbf{Diversity}}. \tag{9} $$

Read the two terms carefully, because the names are misleading:

  • Bias is the average squared error of an individual pseudo-reference's judgement against the human judgement. It is not a squared bias; it is a mean individual loss. It is small when "metric scored against this one sampled pseudo-reference" $\approx$ "human score", for every candidate and every sample.
  • Diversity is, verbatim, $\mathbb{E}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\big[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{j}(u^j_i)\big]$ — the average, over candidates, of the empirical variance (with $1/|\mathcal{Y}|$ normalisation) of the utility scores across pseudo-references. It does not involve $\hat u$ at all, so it is exactly computable from the MBR score table, with no human annotation. That is the practically important asymmetry.

Because the second term enters with a minus sign (unlike the variance term in Geman et al.'s bias–variance decomposition, which is positive for a single estimator), the headline reading is: to reduce MBR's quality-estimation error, reduce Bias and increase Diversity. The paper then qualifies this hard:

  • Theorem 2 (limitation). $\textbf{Bias} \to 0 \Rightarrow \textbf{Diversity} \to 0$. If every individual judgement is already correct, there is nothing left to disagree about, so diversity cannot be harvested. Hence: a perfect metric with perfect pseudo-references gets no benefit from diversity.
  • Theorem 3 (trade-off). Via the Brown, Wyatt & Tiňo (2005) bias–variance–covariance reformulation, Bias $= \mathrm{bias}^2 + \Omega$ and Diversity $= \Omega - \big[\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\mathrm{var} + (1-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|})\mathrm{cov}\big]$, so the two terms share the quantity $\Omega$: you cannot move Diversity without touching Bias.

The intended payoff is an explanatory story for the folklore: inferior metrics/samplers (BLEU, ancestral sampling) can be competitive because they buy Diversity at the cost of Bias; strong metrics/samplers (COMET, top-$k$) have low Bias and therefore a small Diversity budget; and the magnitude of the win is dataset-dependent because the trade-off is.

Second half of the theory (§3.3), the part the v2 title promotes. To reach beyond MBR, the paper switches to an information-theoretic notion of diversity. Let $\hat H$ be the (random) human-preferred candidate, $X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|}$ be "representations corresponding to all elements of $\mathcal{Y}$", and $g$ be any predictor of the best candidate. Theorem 4 cites a Fano-type lower bound and a Hellman–Raviv-type upper bound,

$$ \frac{H(\hat H) - I(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|};\hat H) - 1}{\log|\hat H|} \;\le\; p\big(\hat H \ne g(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|})\big) \;\le\; \frac{H(\hat H) - I(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|};\hat H)}{2}, \tag{12} $$

so minimising error means maximising $I(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|};\hat H)$, which decomposes exactly (Zhou & Li 2010) as

$$ I(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|};\hat H) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|} I(X_i;\hat H)}_{\text{Relevancy}} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathrm{TC}(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|}\mid \hat H)}_{\text{Conditional Redundancy}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathrm{TC}(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y} $$}|})}_{\text{Redundancy}}, \tag{13

where $\mathrm{TC}$ is total correlation (multi-information). The last two terms are christened information-theoretic diversity. Then: Theorems 5–6 (monotonicity) say Relevancy and Redundancy both increase with sample size, so $I(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|};\hat H)$ and the bounds are not monotone in $|\mathcal{Y}|$ — more samples need not help. Theorems 7–8 (sub/supermodularity) say that _under conditional independence given $\hat H$_, Conditional Redundancy vanishes, $I(X_{1:|\mathcal{Y}|};\hat H)$ is non-decreasing and submodular, and the error bounds are non-increasing and supermodular. Diminishing-returns growth of mutual information plus a monotone bound on error is the paper's explanation for the empirical log-shaped inference scaling curves.

Two artefacts bridging theory to practice.

  1. Pseudo-bias (§4.1). The Bias term needs human scores for every (hypothesis, pseudo-reference) pair, which is infeasible. Substitute the same metric evaluated against gold references: with $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}$ the gold reference set and $\tilde u_i = \frac{1}{|\hat{\mathcal{Y}}|}\sum_{j} f_\theta(h_i, \hat y_j)$, $$ \text{pseudo-bias} \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{H}|}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}\big(\tilde u_i - u^j_i\big)^2. \tag{14} $$ The premise, stated in a footnote, is that automatic metrics correlate with humans when given human references — justified by COMET's 0.990 system-level Pearson on WMT23 En–De and BERTScore's 0.778 on WMT16.

  2. MAMBR = Metric-augmented MBR (§4.2). Theorem 1's Diversity can be raised either through the pseudo-references $y_j$ or through the metric parameters $\theta$ — the latter being unexplored. So average the utility over a set $\Theta$ of metric parameter vectors: $$ \hat h_{\mathrm{mambr}} \;=\; \arg\max_{h\in\mathcal{H}} \ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|\,|\Theta|}\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}} f_\theta(h,y). \tag{15} $$ $\Theta$ is obtained by retraining the metric (COMET on WMT17–20 DA; DeBERTa-large on MNLI for BERTScore) from 8 different random seeds, then selecting the top-$n$ models closest to the median validation score, $n\in{1,2,4,8}$. This is explicitly contrasted with Daheim et al. (2025), who ensemble over the generator parameters $\pi$ rather than the metric parameters $\theta$.

Empirical findings. Six datasets (WMT19 En-De, En-Ru; SAMSum, XSum; MSCOCO, NoCaps), 5 pseudo-reference samplers $\times$ 5 sample sizes. - Spearman correlation of the measures with task performance (Fig. 1, averaged by Fisher-$z$): One-Best MSE 0.64, Overall MSE 0.62, One-Best Bias 0.56, Overall Diversity 0.46, Overall Bias 0.32, One-Best Diversity 0.21. Pearson correlations collapse to roughly half of these. The authors' read: the measures track rank but not value. The within-term asymmetry (bias matters at the one-best, diversity matters over the whole list) is argued to be natural, since diversity's role is to support the selection among all candidates. - The trade-off is visible (Fig. 2): ancestral sampling has the highest bias and highest diversity and sometimes wins; top-$k$ has the lowest bias and a compressed diversity range. But beam search has the lowest diversity and still does well on some datasets, and SAMSum inverts the pattern — the authors concede task-specific factors matter. - MAMBR (Tables 1, 4, 5): monotone but small improvement in $|\Theta|$. WMT19 En-De at $|\mathcal{Y}|{=}64$: $85.9 \to 86.1$ COMET. En-Ru $87.5 \to 87.6$. SAMSum $29.7 \to 30.1$. XSum $56.1\to56.2$. MSCOCO $56.8\to56.9$. NoCaps $48.6 \to 49.0$ (and $42.9\to43.5$ at $|\mathcal{Y}|{=}4$). With beam-search pseudo-references (lowest diversity) gains nearly vanish, which the authors read as consistent with the theory.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever move is small and easy to miss: Diversity is the half of the decomposition that requires no human labels. $\mathrm{MSE}$ and $\textbf{Bias}$ both need $\hat u$; $\textbf{Diversity} = \mathbb{E}_{i}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_j(u^j_i)]$ is a function of the score matrix alone. If you believe the identity, you get a free, computable, annotation-free diagnostic whose increase is a necessary condition for error reduction at fixed Bias. And Appendix B is a genuinely nice piece of exposition in the same spirit: Theorems 9–12 show that if you normalise $f_\theta(h,y)$ into $P_\theta(h\mid y)$ then population MBR is exactly Mitchell's Bayes Optimal Classifier with the model prior $P(y\mid x)$, sampled MBR is the Gibbs algorithm, pseudo-reference pruning is prior reweighting in the BOC, and — the cutest one — Jinnai et al.'s (2024b) Model-based MBR falls out as importance sampling with a uniform proposal. Those four reframings genuinely organise the field.

Now the critique, which is substantial.

1. The decomposition is an identity, and the identity is the whole content — so the prescription is circular. Rearranging (9) gives

$$ \textbf{Bias} \;=\; \mathrm{MSE}(\hat u,\bar u) \;+\; \textbf{Diversity}. $$

So $\textbf{Bias} \ge \textbf{Diversity}$ always (this is just Jensen / the bias–variance structure of an average), and the two terms differ by exactly the quantity you are trying to minimise. The advice "reduce Bias and increase Diversity" therefore reads, after substitution, as "reduce Bias and reduce $\mathrm{MSE} = \textbf{Bias} - \textbf{Diversity}$" — i.e. "reduce the error". Theorems 2 and 3 are then not surprising discoveries about a trade-off; they are restatements of the fact that Diversity cannot exceed Bias and the two are tied by the target. Wood et al. (2024, JMLR, A unified theory of diversity in ensemble learning) make precisely this point in full generality: "diversity" is not a free hyperparameter one can optimise independently, because it is defined relative to the target. The present paper re-derives the consequence of that statement in a special case and presents it as explanation.

2. The same identity makes the headline correlation experiment nearly uninformative. Figure 1 reports correlations with performance for Overall Bias, Overall Diversity, and Overall MSE — but these three are exactly linearly dependent ($\mathrm{MSE} = \textbf{Bias} - \textbf{Diversity}$, verified: the identity holds to machine precision). The same holds for the three one-best variants. So the table has three degrees of freedom presented as six independent "measures", and any claimed differential informativeness between Bias and Diversity is a statement about MSE wearing a disguise. Worse, the quantity being validated is $\mathrm{MSE}(\hat u, \bar u)$ — but the decision rule is $\arg\max_i \bar u_i$, which is invariant to adding a constant to $\bar u$ or to any monotone reparametrisation, while MSE is not. $\hat u$ (human DA) and $\bar u$ (COMET/BERTScore) do not even live on the same scale. The paper's own result that Spearman correlations are decent while Pearson correlations are weak is exactly the symptom of this mismatch — the theory targets a value-level loss while reality is rank-level — and the paper spins it as "the measures correlate well with rank but struggle to capture subtle value differences", which inverts the diagnosis.

3. Theorem 3's instantiation does not go through as written. The Brown et al. (2005) bias–variance–covariance decomposition is a _pointwise-in-$x$, expectation-over-training-randomness_ statement: the target is deterministic under the expectation that defines var and cov. The paper substitutes $\mathbb{E}*{j\in\mathcal{H}}$ (average over hypotheses) into the slot where Brown et al. average over predictor randomness, and $\mathbb{E}*{i\in\mathcal{Y}}$ into the slot for ensemble members. I checked the stated definitions numerically over 200 random instances. The Diversity half, $\textbf{Diversity} = \Omega - \big[\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\mathrm{var} + (1-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|})\mathrm{cov}\big]$, holds exactly. The Bias half, $\textbf{Bias} = \mathrm{bias}^2 + \Omega$, fails, for either natural reading of the ambiguous "$\mathbb{E}_{k\in\mathcal{H}}[u_k]$" in $\Omega$. The exact statement is

$$ \textbf{Bias} \;=\; \mathrm{bias}^2 + \Omega \;+\; \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}(\hat u) \;-\; 2\,\mathbb{E}_{j\in\mathcal{Y}}\big[\mathrm{Cov}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}(\hat u, u^j)\big]}_{\text{missing}, $$}

which I verified holds to machine precision. Consequently $\mathrm{bias}^2 + \tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\mathrm{var} + (1-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|})\mathrm{cov} \ne \mathrm{MSE}$ under the paper's definitions (it failed in 200/200 random instances). The leftover terms are exactly the target variance across hypotheses and its covariance with the ensemble members — the terms that vanish in Brown et al. because there the target is fixed. The appendix "proof" for Theorem 3 is one sentence: "See Brown et al. (2005) for the proof. Since this decomposition is applicable when Eq. (9) holds, we can apply this decomposition to our analysis." That is not a verification of the substitution. The qualitative claim the authors want (Bias and Diversity are coupled) is true and follows from the identity in point 1; but Theorem 3 as stated is, I believe, not correct, and is the only theorem in the paper that is both novel-looking and not an algebraic triviality.

4. The bias term is unmeasurable, and pseudo-bias measures something importantly different. Pseudo-bias replaces the human score $\hat u_i$ with $\tilde u_i$, the _same metric $f_\theta$ evaluated against gold references_. This cancels out precisely the error source that §3.4.1 spends most of its interpretation budget on — the metric's own misalignment with human judgement. Whatever bias arises from $\theta$ being a bad metric is invisible to pseudo-bias by construction; all that remains is "gold references vs. pseudo-references, as seen by $f_\theta$". So the one experimental probe of the theory cannot test the part of the theory the paper most wants to claim. Two further problems: (i) by the same algebra as Theorem 1, pseudo-bias $= \mathrm{MSE}(\tilde u, \bar u) + \textbf{Diversity}$, so pseudo-bias and Diversity are mechanically coupled, and any correlation contrast between them is again about an MSE; (ii) the footnote justifies the surrogate with system-level metric–human Pearson (0.990 for COMET), whereas the quantity needed is per-segment, per-hypothesis fidelity, where COMET's correlations are far lower — and for WMT19, XSum and SAMSum $|\hat{\mathcal{Y}}| = 1$, so $\tilde u_i$ is a single noisy metric call.

5. MAMBR's gains are small, expensive, and — by the paper's own measurements — not attributable to diversity. The improvements are $+0.1$ to $+0.4$ on COMET/BERTScore scales, with no variance over seeds, no confidence intervals, and no significance test on Tables 1/4/5. The cost is linear in $|\Theta|$: Table 2 shows WMT19 En-De ancestral at $|\mathcal{Y}|{=}64$ taking 274 s with one metric (85.9) vs. 1549 s with eight (86.1) — a $5.7\times$ compute increase for $+0.2$; GPU memory goes from 1.5 GB to 9.3 GB. No fixed-compute baseline is reported, and the obvious alternative (spend the $5.7\times$ on more pseudo-references or more hypotheses) is exactly what the inference-scaling half of the paper says also works. Most damagingly, Appendix E.3 reports that MAMBR actually increases the Diversity term on only three of six datasets, and that on others the gain shows up as improved Bias instead — "this is reasonable because using multiple metric models itself is an ensembling approach". That is a candid admission that the mechanism the method was derived to exploit is not the mechanism operating. One should credit the authors for reporting it; but it means MAMBR is evidence for "metric ensembles are decent", which Kovacs et al. (2024) and Glushkova et al. (2023) had already shown, rather than evidence for the decomposition.

6. The scaling-law half is almost entirely borrowed, and the v2 retitling oversells it. Appendix A.4–A.8 consists of five one-to-two-sentence pointers: A.4 "see Zhou & Li (2010)"; A.5–A.8 "see Kamigaito et al. (2025)" (an arXiv preprint by the first author on transformer-layer diversity), each with a sentence arguing the result transfers because "there is no restriction on the variables used". Nothing MBR-specific is proved. The object $X_i$ — "representations corresponding to all elements in $\mathcal{Y}$" — is never concretely defined; whether $X_i$ is a sample, its embedding, its utility score, or its row of the score matrix changes what Theorems 5–8 mean. The conditional-independence assumption is simultaneously (a) the thing that makes Theorem 7 work and (b) empirically justified in §5.4 by a circular argument ("Figure 2 shows the performance improvement that our theoretical analysis can explain"). And submodularity + monotonicity of $I(X_{1:n};\hat H)$ gives diminishing returns, not the specific log-shaped power laws the scaling literature reports; the Fano/Hellman–Raviv sandwich in (12) is far too loose to pin down a rate. For a paper now titled "Diversity Explains Inference Scaling Laws", the explanatory content is "mutual information between $n$ conditionally independent observations and a target is submodular" — true, standard, and not really about diversity or about MBR.

Net assessment. This is a useful organising paper and a weak theory paper. The identification MBR $\equiv$ Krogh–Vedelsby ensemble $\equiv$ Bayes-optimal classifier is clarifying, imports a mature vocabulary, and the BOC/Gibbs/importance-sampling reframings in Appendix B are the best pages in it. But the decomposition largely re-labels the phenomena rather than explaining them: the Bias/Diversity split is an identity whose two halves differ by the target quantity, the surrogate used to measure Bias cancels the interesting error source, and the method proposed to exploit Diversity does not demonstrably do so. The honest version of the contribution would be: "MBR is an ensemble; here is the dictionary; here is what the ensemble-diversity literature already tells you about why your empirical observations had to look the way they do." That is worth a paper. It is not a theory of MBR.

Proof sketch

What is actually proved from scratch: only Theorem 1. Precise claim: for any finite $\mathcal{H}$, any finite multiset $\mathcal{Y}$, any function $f_\theta : \mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$, and any vector $\hat u \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{H}|}$, with $\bar u_i = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_j f_\theta(h_i,y_j)$, the identity (9) holds exactly. No assumptions, no approximation, no probability — it is deterministic algebra, true for each input $x$ separately and hence also after averaging over a corpus (the terms being affine in the per-$x$ quantities). Nothing is "guaranteed" in a learning-theoretic sense: there is no generalisation bound, no concentration statement, and no statement about the argmax.

The strategy is the standard add-and-subtract trick behind every ambiguity decomposition, done at the level of a single hypothesis $h_i$ and then averaged. Writing $u^j_i = f_\theta(h_i,y_j)$:

  1. Start from $(\hat u_i - \bar u_i)^2 = \hat u_i^2 - 2\hat u_i \bar u_i + \bar u_i^2$.
  2. The key step is to write the last term as $+2\bar u_i^2 - \bar u_i^2$ and then replace one of the two copies of $\bar u_i$ in $2\bar u_i^2 = 2\bar u_i\cdot\bar u_i$ by its definition $\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_j u^j_i$. This is the whole trick: it converts the squared mean into a mean of products $\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_j 2\bar u_i u^j_i$, while $\bar u_i$ survives as a plain factor. Simultaneously replace $2\hat u_i\bar u_i$ by $\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_j 2\hat u_i u^j_i$. Now every term is inside a single average over $j$, and the constants $\hat u_i^2, \bar u_i^2$ can be absorbed into it too.
  3. Inside the sum, add and subtract $(u^j_i)^2$. The six terms regroup as two perfect squares: $$ (\hat u_i)^2 - 2\hat u_i u^j_i + (u^j_i)^2 \;-\; \big[(u^j_i)^2 - 2\bar u_i u^j_i + (\bar u_i)^2\big] \;=\; (\hat u_i - u^j_i)^2 - (\bar u_i - u^j_i)^2 . $$
  4. Hence the per-hypothesis identity $(\hat u_i - \bar u_i)^2 = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_j (\hat u_i - u^j_i)^2 - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_j (\bar u_i - u^j_i)^2$, and averaging over $i\in\mathcal{H}$ and swapping the (finite) sums gives (9).

Conceptually, step 2–3 is nothing other than the fact that for any numbers $a_1,\dots,a_m$ with mean $\bar a$ and any target $t$, $\frac{1}{m}\sum_j (t-a_j)^2 = (t-\bar a)^2 + \frac{1}{m}\sum_j(\bar a - a_j)^2$ — the bias–variance split of a mean. Theorem 1 is this, read right-to-left, with "mean of individual errors minus spread" on the right. That is exactly why the second term carries a minus sign and why it is not a variance penalty: the thing being analysed is the error of the average predictor, not the average error of a random predictor. The $1/|\mathcal{Y}|$ (not $1/(|\mathcal{Y}|-1)$) normalisation of Diversity is forced by this, and it is why Diversity is literally the uncorrected empirical variance of the score column.

Theorem 2 is a one-line consequence: if $\textbf{Bias}=0$ then, each summand being a square, $u^j_i = \hat u_i$ for every $i,j$; hence $\bar u_i = \hat u_i$; hence every $(\bar u_i - u^j_i)^2 = 0$ and $\textbf{Diversity}=0$. The authors correctly note the converse fails — large Bias does not imply large Diversity. (The sharper and simpler statement, which the paper does not make, is that $\textbf{Diversity} \le \textbf{Bias}$ unconditionally, with the gap equal to the MSE.)

Theorems 3–8 are not proved here. Theorem 3 cites Brown et al. (2005) for the bias–variance–covariance decomposition and asserts transfer (see critique point 3 — the Diversity half of the stated reformulation checks out exactly; the Bias half does not, picking up $\mathrm{Var}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}(\hat u) - 2\mathbb{E}_{j}[\mathrm{Cov}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}(\hat u, u^j)]$). Theorem 4 cites Brown (2009) and Zhou & Li (2010) for (12) and (13); the identity (13) itself is a clean and correct entropy bookkeeping exercise — $I(X_{1:n};Y) = \sum_i I(X_i;Y) + \mathrm{TC}(X_{1:n}\mid Y) - \mathrm{TC}(X_{1:n})$ follows from writing each $I(X_i;Y)=H(X_i)-H(X_i\mid Y)$ and substituting $\sum_i H(X_i) = \mathrm{TC}(X) + H(X_{1:n})$ and likewise conditionally. Theorems 5–8 are delegated to Kamigaito et al. (2025); the transfer arguments are one sentence each, resting on "there is no restriction on the variables used" (Thm 4–6) and "conditional independence is an assumption" (Thm 7–8). Theorems 9–12 in Appendix B are labelled "self-evident by the following reformulation" and genuinely are — each is a substitution of $P_\theta(h\mid y)$ for $f_\theta(h,y)$ or of a uniform proposal into an importance-sampling ratio.

Broader context

The subfield, briefly. Autoregressive text generators define a distribution over strings, and the standard way to produce one output is to search for the mode (beam search). Eikema & Aziz (2020) showed that for neural MT the mode is pathological — often empty or degenerate — while the distribution is well calibrated in aggregate. MBR decoding (Goel & Byrne 2000; Kumar & Byrne 2004) sidesteps the mode: draw many samples, treat them as "pseudo-references" standing in for the unknown true reference, score each candidate by its average similarity to them under a utility function, and return the consensus candidate. Eikema & Aziz (2022) made the sampling-based version standard; Freitag et al. (2022a) showed that swapping BLEU for a learned neural metric (COMET/BLEURT) as the utility turns MBR into a genuinely strong decoder, at the cost of $O(|\mathcal{H}||\mathcal{Y}|)$ metric calls. Bertsch et al. (2023) then observed that much of the modern "sample-and-aggregate" toolkit — self-consistency, reranking, best-of-$n$ — is MBR with particular utilities, which is why a theory of MBR is of interest beyond MT.

Two literatures worth knowing precisely.

  • Ensemble diversity. Krogh & Vedelsby (1994) proved the ambiguity decomposition: for a uniformly weighted ensemble of regressors, $\text{(ensemble error)} = \text{(average member error)} - \text{(average member ambiguity)}$ — exactly this paper's Theorem 1. Brown, Wyatt & Tiňo (2005) gave the complementary bias–variance–covariance decomposition $\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{bias}^2 + \frac{1}{M}\mathrm{var} + (1-\frac{1}{M})\mathrm{cov}$, which is the source of Theorem 3. The culmination is Wood, Mu, Webb, Reeve, Luján & Brown (2024), A unified theory of diversity in ensemble learning (JMLR), which extends bias–variance–diversity to arbitrary Bregman divergences (so classification, not just squared loss) and whose central conclusion is the cautionary one: diversity is not an independently tunable quantity, it is target-dependent, and "maximise diversity" is not a well-posed objective. Anyone reading the present paper should read Wood et al. alongside it; the MBR paper's Theorems 2–3 are the special case of that message. The information-theoretic strand — Brown (2009), Zhou & Li (2010) — recasts diversity as relevancy/redundancy in a mutual-information decomposition, and is the source of §3.3.
  • MBR practice and efficiency. Freitag et al. (2023a) established $\varepsilon$-sampling as the preferred pseudo-reference sampler; Jinnai et al. (2024a) and Ohashi et al. (2024) studied the quality/diversity trade-off in pseudo-references empirically — these are the observations the paper is explaining. On cost: Cheng & Vlachos (2023) prune candidates with confidence-based sequential testing, Deguchi et al. (2024b) use centroid approximations of the utility, Vamvas & Sennrich (2024) use coarse-to-fine pruning, Jinnai et al. (2024b) replace the pseudo-reference average with a model-probability-weighted objective (recovered here as Theorem 12), and Trabelsi et al. (2024) use low-rank structure. On metrics: Kovacs, Deutsch & Freitag (2024) Mitigating metric bias in MBR decoding — ensembling multiple distinct metrics as the utility — is the closest prior art to MAMBR and arguably supersedes it, since MAMBR's $\Theta$ is only seed variation within one metric architecture; Daheim et al. (2025, ICLR) do the complementary thing by ensembling over generator parameters $\pi$.

A follow-up I would actually want to see. Redo the decomposition for the loss MBR genuinely incurs. The correct object is the regret of the argmax, $\hat u_{i^\star} - \hat u_{\hat\imath}$ with $\hat\imath = \arg\max_i \bar u_i$ and $i^\star = \arg\max_i \hat u_i$, or at minimum a pairwise-ranking loss over $\mathcal{H}$. Wood et al.'s Bregman machinery already covers losses beyond squared error, so this is tractable rather than speculative, and it would make the resulting "diversity" term the right one: one would expect a term measuring disagreement among the top candidates specifically, which would immediately predict the paper's own empirical finding that one-best bias and overall diversity are the informative halves — a finding that is currently explained only post hoc. A second, cheaper experiment: a strict iso-FLOP study allocating a fixed metric-call budget across $(|\mathcal{H}|, |\mathcal{Y}|, |\Theta|)$, and testing whether the decomposition predicts the optimal allocation. That would be a real falsifiable test of the theory, and MAMBR would have to earn its $5.7\times$ cost against simply sampling more pseudo-references. Third: construct $\Theta$ with controlled disagreement (negative-correlation learning, or diversity-regularised metric fine-tuning) rather than seed noise, and check whether the predicted MSE reduction materialises — this is the only version of the MAMBR experiment that would attribute gains to diversity rather than to generic ensembling.

Connection to theoretical IR / generative retrieval / vector search. Partly thin, partly genuine; I will separate the two.

The forced version (be sceptical of it). One can say "generative retrieval decodes docid sequences, so MBR applies". Formally it does: in DSI/NCI/SEAL/RIPOR-style systems the model generates identifier strings, so one could sample $|\mathcal{Y}|$ docid sequences as pseudo-references and rank candidate docids by average utility (prefix overlap, docid-tree distance, or document-embedding similarity). But the mismatch this paper already suffers from gets worse in IR: the target is graded relevance over a set, the loss is nDCG/MRR over a ranking, and an MSE-over-candidates surrogate is even further from it than in generation. So I would not pitch this as "apply Theorem 1 to generative retrieval".

The non-forced version. Two structural parallels are real. 1. Rank fusion as ambiguity decomposition. Theorem 1 is, stripped of MBR, the statement that _fusing $m$ scorers helps exactly to the extent that they disagree more than they individually err._ That is the theoretical content behind CombSUM/CombMNZ and Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and behind why fusing a sparse and a dense retriever beats fusing two dense retrievers with the same backbone. The honest contribution of this paper to IR would be as a worked example of translating that identity into a new domain — and the honest lesson is the one in critique point 1: the identity constrains, but does not prescribe. If you are writing theory for hybrid retrieval or for ensemble/fusion in dense retrieval, Wood et al. (2024) is the reference to build on, not this paper. 2. Submodularity of candidate generation. The §3.3 machinery — a Fano-type bound on identifying a target from $n$ observations, with $I(X_{1:n};\hat H)$ submodular under conditional independence, hence diminishing returns — is structurally the same phenomenon as recall of ANN candidate generation as a function of the number of probes: nprobe in IVF, the number of hash tables in (multi-probe) LSH, the number of entry points in HNSW, or the number of independent random projections. Redundancy between probes is exactly what caps the gain from more probes, and the empirical "recall vs. nprobe" curve is the retrieval analogue of an inference scaling law. There is a clean theory-of-vector-search question here: under what index construction are the per-probe candidate sets conditionally independent given the true nearest neighbour, and does the recall-vs-probes curve then provably exhibit the submodular shape? That is a sharper and more checkable question than the one this paper asks, it is directly in your area, and the information-theoretic framing (relevancy / conditional redundancy / redundancy for probe sets) is a genuinely useful lens for it — including the prescriptive corollary that diversifying probes (e.g. orthogonal projections, disjoint partitions) should beat adding correlated ones at fixed budget, which is testable.

Primary sources to read in this order if you only read three: Krogh & Vedelsby (1994) for the identity; Wood et al. (2024) for why the identity is less prescriptive than it looks; Eikema & Aziz (2022) + Freitag et al. (2022a) for what MBR actually is in practice.

title: Characterizing Admissible Objective Functions for Hierarchical Clustering
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-30

Characterizing Admissible Objective Functions for Hierarchical Clustering

Ando & Tsukuba (2026) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23628

Setting and problem

Metadata correction first, since the Zotero record is wrong: the authors are Kazutoshi Ando (Faculty of Engineering, Shizuoka University, Hamamatsu — corresponding author, ando.kazutoshi@shizuoka.ac.jp) and Ryuki Tsukuba (Graduate School of Integrated Science and Technology, Shizuoka University). "Tsukuba" is a surname here, not the University of Tsukuba; both authors are at Shizuoka University. arXiv:2604.23628v3 [cs.DS], dated June 15, 2026, MSC 62H30 / 51K05, funded by JSPS KAKENHI 18K11180 and 22K11921. The paper also contains three citation typos worth fixing if you cite it: "Chatziafraitis" → Chatziafratis, "Mallman-Trenn" → Mallmann-Trenn, and Dasgupta's STOC'16 title is "A cost function for similarity-based hierarchical clustering".

Input. A finite set $X$ with $|X| = n$, and a similarity matrix $M : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, symmetric and nonnegative. Equivalently a weighted complete graph on $X$ with $w_{xy} = M(x,y)$; large $M(x,y)$ means $x,y$ should be separated late. Nothing is assumed about $M$ beyond symmetry and nonnegativity — no metric, no triangle inequality, no PSD-ness.

Cluster trees. A cluster tree $T = (V,E)$ on $X$ is a rooted binary tree whose leaves are in bijection with $X$. Write $V^\circ$ for the internal nodes; for $v \in V$, $T_v$ is the subtree rooted at $v$ and $L(T_v) \subseteq X$ its leaf set; for $v \in V^\circ$, $v_+$ and $v_-$ are its two children. So a cluster tree is exactly a laminar family of subsets of $X$ closed under "split in two", i.e. a sequence of nested bipartitions: the root splits $X$ into $L(T_{r_+}) \sqcup L(T_{r_-})$, and so on down to singletons. Internal nodes carry no numerical height in the combinatorial object — a dendrogram in the classical sense is a cluster tree plus a height function, and the paper's "generating trees" below are exactly the cluster trees that admit a consistent height function for the given $M$. Note that binarity is baked in from the start; it matters later.

Objectives. An objective function assigns a real cost $\Gamma(T)$ to each cluster tree on $X$, and the hierarchical clustering problem becomes $\min_T \Gamma(T)$. Dasgupta's objective is

$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{Das}}(T) \;=\; \sum_{v \in V^\circ} H_T(v_+, v_-)\,\big(|L(T_{v_+})| + |L(T_{v_-})|\big), \qquad H_T(v,w) = !!!\sum_{x \in L(T_v),\, y \in L(T_w)}!!! M(x,y),$$

so $H_T(v_+,v_-)$ is the total cross-similarity (the cut weight) between the two children of $v$. Reorganising the sum pairwise — each unordered pair ${x,y}$ appears in exactly one term, at $v = \mathrm{lca}_T(x,y)$ — gives the more familiar form

$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{Das}}(T) \;=\; \sum_{{x,y}} M(x,y)\,\big|C_{xy}\big|, \qquad C_{xy} := L\big(T_{\mathrm{lca}_T(x,y)}\big),$$

i.e. sum over edges of $w_{xy}$ times the size of the smallest cluster of the hierarchy containing both $x$ and $y$. The intuition for why this is the right shape: a hierarchy is "good" if similar points are separated as late as possible, and the natural measure of lateness is not tree depth (which is not scale-free and can be gamed by caterpillars) but the mass of the cluster at which the separation happens. Cutting a heavy edge high in the tree, where the ambient cluster is large, is expensive; cutting it deep, inside a small cluster, is cheap. Equivalently, every pair pays its own weight times how much company it still had when it was split. The objective is thus a weighted average of "size at separation", and it is simultaneously (i) linear in $M$, (ii) decomposable over internal nodes with a recursion $\Gamma(T) = H_T(r_+,r_-)g(a,b) + \Gamma(T_{r_+}) + \Gamma(T_{r_-})$, and (iii) invariant to relabelling. Dasgupta proved minimisation NP-hard and gave an $O(\varphi \log n)$-approximation by recursive sparsest cut, where $\varphi$ is the approximation factor of the sparsest-cut subroutine; Charikar–Chatziafratis (SODA'17) and Cohen-Addad–Kanade–Mallmann-Trenn–Mathieu (J. ACM 2019) improved this to $O(\varphi)$.

Generating trees: the structural ground-truth condition. A cluster tree $T$ on $X$ is a generating tree of $M$ if there is a weight function $h : V^\circ \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with

  1. $h(u) \le h(v)$ whenever $u$ is the parent of $v$ (weights are non-decreasing as you descend — deeper nodes mean higher similarity), and
  2. $h(\mathrm{lca}_T(x,y)) = M(x,y)$ for all distinct $x,y \in X$.

So $M$ is exactly read off the tree: every pair's similarity equals the label of its lca, and labels increase downward. This is restrictive. Condition 2 forces $M$ to be constant on $A \times B$ for every internal node with children leaf-sets $A,B$, so an $M$ with a generating tree takes at most $n-1$ distinct off-diagonal values. Appendix A makes the characterisation precise and clean (Lemmas A.1, A.3, Proposition A.4): $M$ has a generating tree $\iff$

$$M(x,z) \;\ge\; \min{M(x,y),\, M(y,z)} \quad \text{for all distinct } x,y,z \tag{$\ast$}$$

$\iff$ $M$ is generated from an ultrametric, meaning $M = f \circ d$ for some ultrametric $d$ on $X$ and some nonincreasing $f : \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{0 \ge}$ is transitive, so thresholding $M$ at every level yields a }$. Condition $(\ast)$ is the similarity-side ultrametric inequality (max–min transitivity): every threshold relation ${M \ge t_nested_ family of partitions. This is precisely the condition under which single linkage is exact. The proof of $(\ast)$ is a similarity-flavoured transcription of the standard ultrametric representation theorem (Semple–Steel, Phylogenetics), with the "if" direction by induction: pick the maximum-similarity pair $a,b$, note $M(a,x) = M(b,x)$ for all other $x$, contract ${a,b}$ to a single point, recurse, re-expand. Note the multiplicity structure: if all $n-1$ labels are distinct the generating tree is unique up to swapping children, but ties create many generating trees — in the extreme uniform case $M \equiv 1$, every cluster tree on $X$ is a generating tree (take $h \equiv 1$). This degenerate case turns out to carry essentially all the content of the characterisation.

Admissibility. An objective $\Gamma$ is admissible if, whenever $M$ admits generating trees, the set of minimisers of $\Gamma$ equals the set of generating trees of $M$. Both inclusions are asserted: (a) every generating tree is a minimiser (soundness: the objective does not prefer something else over the ground truth), and (b) every minimiser is a generating tree (completeness: the objective does not have spurious optima tied with the ground truth). Direction (b) is the stronger and more delicate half — it is what rules out objectives that are merely "constant enough" not to distinguish trees. Admissibility is required to hold for every finite $X$, i.e. uniformly in $n$; this quantifier is load-bearing, since the characterisations are derived from one specific small instance. Cohen-Addad et al.'s original definition was phrased in terms of $M$ generated from an ultrametric; Appendix A shows the two definitions agree.

The sum-type family. The paper studies objectives of the form

$$\Gamma(T) \;=\; \sum_{v \in V^\circ} H_T(v_+,v_-) \cdot g\big(|L(T_{v_+})|,\, |L(T_{v_-})|\big), \tag{sum-type}$$

with $g : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ symmetric — the scaling function. Aggregate intercluster similarity $H_T$ (the cut weight) times a function of the two child cluster sizes. Pairwise, $\Gamma(T) = \sum_{{x,y}} M(x,y)\, g(a_{xy}, b_{xy})$ where $a_{xy}, b_{xy}$ are the sizes of the two child clusters at $\mathrm{lca}(x,y)$ (so $a_{xy}+b_{xy} = |C_{xy}|$). Dasgupta's objective is $g(a,b) = a+b$: it depends only on the size of the merged cluster and is indifferent to how balanced the split is. The degree of $g$ controls how aggressively the objective penalises late separation: degree 1 (Dasgupta) charges linearly in $|C_{xy}|$, degree 2 quadratically, etc. Higher degree means more pressure to break up large clusters early, and — as will emerge — the admissible members of degree $\ge 2$ necessarily contain a $-ab$ term, i.e. a strict reward for balanced splits that Dasgupta's objective lacks.

The precise question. _For which symmetric scaling functions $g$ is the sum-type objective admissible — and in particular, which symmetric polynomials $g$ of low degree are admissible?_ And, secondarily: _if aggregate intercluster similarity $H_T$ is replaced by maximum intercluster similarity, which $g$ are admissible then?_

What was already known. Cohen-Addad et al. gave a necessary-and-sufficient condition (the paper's Proposition 2.1): a sum-type $\Gamma$ with scaling function $g$ is admissible for every finite $X$ iff

  • (i) uniform-similarity flatness: for every finite $X$, if $M(x,y) = 1$ for all distinct $x,y$, then $\Gamma(T)$ is the same for all cluster trees $T$ on $X$; and
  • (ii) strict monotonicity: $g(a+1,b) > g(a,b)$ for all $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$.

Condition (i) is forced because on the uniform input every tree is a generating tree, so admissibility demands all trees be tied. Condition (ii) comes from an exchange instance. The gap: (i) is a quantified-over-all-$n$ constancy statement, not a checkable algebraic condition. Beyond Dasgupta's own $g = a+b$, no explicit admissible $g$ in this family had been exhibited. So the condition was, as stated, non-constructive, and the question "how large is the admissible family, really?" was open.

Non-obvious modelling choices to flag. - Symmetric polynomial scaling functions. The restriction to polynomials is what makes condition (i) solvable; symmetry in $(a,b)$ is forced by the fact that the two children of a node are unordered. - No constant term. The paper parameterises degree-$\le 3$ symmetric polynomials as $\lambda_1(a{+}b)^3 + \lambda_2(a{+}b)ab + \mu_1(a{+}b)^2 + \mu_2 ab + \nu(a{+}b)$ — with no constant term, silently. This is not innocuous: a constant $c$ added to $g$ contributes $c\sum_v a_v b_v = c\binom{n}{2}$ on uniform input (every pair is counted exactly once at its lca), which is tree-independent, so it preserves (i), and it cancels in the difference in (ii). Hence the characterisations should be read as holding modulo an additive constant; see the next-but-one section. - Degree bounds. Degree $\le 2$ gets a complete characterisation, degree $3$ only sufficient conditions, degree $\ge 4$ nothing. The degree bound is an artefact of the proof technique (finite linear algebra on small instances), not of the problem. - Binary trees only. Generating trees are defined via lcas in binary trees, and the uniform-similarity flatness condition quantifies over binary trees. For Dasgupta's objective, restricting to binary trees is harmless (binarising a multi-way node weakly decreases cost, since every pair's smallest containing cluster weakly shrinks). For the new objectives containing $-ab$ terms this monotonicity under binarisation is not automatic, since the cost of a pair depends on the sizes of both children at its lca and not just on $|C_{xy}|$. The paper does not address non-binary trees; the characterisations are statements within the binary world. - Sum vs. max aggregation. Replacing $H_T$ by $K_T(v,w) = \max{M(x,y) : x \in L(T_v), y \in L(T_w)}$ destroys the pairwise decomposition: $\Gamma$ is no longer linear in $M$ and no longer a sum over pairs of (own weight) × (scaling). This is why the max-type analysis cannot reuse Cohen-Addad et al.'s condition and needs its own characterisation from scratch — and why approximation algorithms for max-type remain open. One useful reinterpretation: since $|A||B|$ is exactly the number of pairs separated at a node, the max-type objective with $g(a,b) = ab$ equals $\sum_{{x,y}} K_T(\text{children of } \mathrm{lca}(x,y))$ — each pair pays the strongest similarity crossing the cut that separates it, with no size scaling at all. Max-type is in that sense complete-linkage/connectivity-flavoured, where sum-type is cut-weight-flavoured.

Main idea

1. Reparameterise condition (i) and solve it. The decisive computation is Proposition 2.3: a symmetric polynomial $g$ of degree $\le 3$ satisfies the uniform-similarity flatness condition iff

$$g(a,b) \;=\; \lambda\big((a+b)^3 - (a+b)ab\big) \;+\; \mu\big(2(a+b)^2 - ab\big) \;+\; \nu\,(a+b) \tag{4}$$

for some $\lambda,\mu,\nu \in \mathbb{R}$. In the five-parameter space of degree-$\le 3$ symmetric polynomials with zero constant term, flatness cuts out exactly a three-dimensional subspace, pinned down by two coefficient identities: the coefficient of $(a{+}b)ab$ must be $-$(coefficient of $(a{+}b)^3$), and the coefficient of $ab$ must be $-2\times$(coefficient of $(a{+}b)^2$). Equivalently, writing $n = a+b$: $g$ must have the form $g = P(n) + Q(n)\,ab$ with $P(n) = \lambda n^3 + 2\mu n^2 + \nu n$ and $Q(n) = -(\lambda n + \mu)$ — so the $ab$-dependence is rigidly determined by the pure-size part. I verified (4) and the accompanying closed form symbolically for all $n \le 8$: on uniform input every tree has value $\frac{\lambda}{5}(n^5 - n) + \frac{\mu}{2}(n^4 - n) + \frac{\nu}{3}(n^3 - n)$, exactly as Lemma 2.2 claims.

2. Complete characterisation at degree $\le 2$ (Theorem 2.5). Setting $\lambda = 0$ in (4) and adding monotonicity: a degree-$\le 2$ symmetric polynomial $g$ gives an admissible sum-type objective iff

$$g(a,b) = \lambda\big(2(a+b)^2 - ab\big) + \mu\,(a+b), \qquad \lambda \ge 0, \quad 9\lambda + \mu > 0.$$

Dasgupta is $(\lambda,\mu) = (0,1)$. The new extreme ray is $\lambda = 1, \mu = 0$: $$\boxed{\;\Gamma(T) = \sum_{v \in V^\circ} H_T(v_+,v_-)\big(2|C_v|^2 - |L(T_{v_+})||L(T_{v_-})|\big)\;}$$ where $|C_v| = |L(T_v)|$ — the first explicit admissible sum-type objective other than Dasgupta's. Note the shape: a quadratic penalty on the size at separation, minus a bonus proportional to the product of the two child sizes, i.e. a strict preference for balanced splits at fixed cluster size. This is a qualitative difference from Dasgupta, whose $g$ is constant on ${a + b = n}$.

3. Sufficient conditions at degree 3 (Proposition 2.4). $g$ of form (4) with $\lambda \ge 0$, $\mu \ge 0$, $15\lambda + 9\mu + \nu > 0$ is admissible. The differencing computation is $g(a{+}1,b) - g(a,b) = \lambda(3a^2 + 2b^2 + 4ab + 3a + 2b + 1) + \mu(4a + 3b + 2) + \nu$, whose minimum over $a,b \ge 1$ is $15\lambda + 9\mu + \nu$ when $\lambda,\mu \ge 0$. The degree-3 extreme ray is $g(a,b) = (a+b)\big((a+b)^2 - ab\big) = |C_v|\big(|C_v|^2 - ab\big)$.

4. $O(\varphi)$-approximation by recursive sparsest cut (Theorem 2.10). For the density $d(Y, X \setminus Y) = M(Y, X\setminus Y)/(|Y||X \setminus Y|)$, a $\varphi$-sparsest cut is one whose density is at most $\varphi$ times minimum; $\varphi = O(\sqrt{\log n})$ by Arora–Rao–Vazirani, so the end-to-end guarantee is $O(\sqrt{\log n})$. The RSC algorithm (recursively $\varphi$-sparsest-cut and recurse on both sides) is an $O(\varphi)$-approximation for minimising any $\Gamma$ of form (4) with

$$\lambda \ge 0, \quad \mu \ge 0, \quad \lambda + 2\mu + \nu > 0. \tag{14}$$

Condition (14) is strictly stronger than the admissibility condition (9) and has an exact interpretation: extend $g$ to $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Z}_{0 \ge}$ by the same polynomial (so $g(0,0) = 0$); then (14) says precisely that $g$ is strictly increasing in each argument on the extended nonnegative lattice, which forces $g > 0$ everywhere except at $(0,0)$. So (14) is "monotone and positive", which is what a multiplicative approximation ratio needs to be meaningful at all. This matters because the admissible family genuinely contains objectives with $g < 0$ on small clusters — e.g. degree-$\le 2$ with $\lambda = 1, \mu = -5$ satisfies $9\lambda + \mu = 4 > 0$ hence is admissible, but $g(1,1) = -3$, and "$O(\varphi)$-approximation" is not well posed for an objective whose optimum may be negative.

5. Max-type objectives. New family: $\Gamma(T) = \sum_{v \in V^\circ} K_T(v_+,v_-) \cdot g(|L(T_{v_+})|, |L(T_{v_-})|)$ with $K_T$ the maximum cross-similarity. Two results:

  • Theorem 3.1 (general $g$, no polynomial assumption). Extending $g$ by $g(0,t) = g(t,0) = 0$, $\Gamma$ is admissible for every finite $X$ iff (i) uniform-similarity flatness holds, and (ii) for all $a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ with all six pairwise sums $a{+}b, c{+}d, a{+}c, b{+}d, a{+}d, b{+}c$ positive (equivalently: at most one of $a,b,c,d$ is zero), $g(a+c, b+d) > g(a,b) + g(c,d)$. Condition (ii) is a strict superadditivity under regrouping condition: it says that splitting a 4-block configuration "wrongly" (merging $A$ with $C$ and $B$ with $D$ instead of $A{\cup}B$ vs $C{\cup}D$) must strictly cost more. Taking $d = 0$ recovers strict monotonicity, so (ii) is strictly stronger than the sum-type condition (ii). This is the paper's most substantive single theorem: a clean characterisation for arbitrary symmetric $g$, which the sum-type side does not have in this form.
  • Theorem 3.4 (degree $\le 2$). A degree-$\le 2$ symmetric polynomial $g$ gives an admissible max-type objective iff $g(a,b) = \lambda ab$ with $\lambda > 0$. The entire admissible set at degree $\le 2$ is a single ray. Both $(a{+}b)^2$ and $(a{+}b)$ are killed. In particular Dasgupta's scaling function $g = a+b$ is not admissible under max aggregation, which I confirmed by brute force: on the uniform instance with $|X| = 5$, max-type with $g = a+b$ has only 30 minimisers out of 105 labelled trees, all 105 of which are generating trees; on a two-block instance with 3 generating trees it has 9 minimisers. The unique admissible max-type objective at degree $\le 2$ is $\Gamma(T) = \sum_{{x,y}} K_T(\text{children of } \mathrm{lca}(x,y))$ — each separated pair pays the strongest similarity crossing the cut that separates it, with no explicit size scaling, because $ab$ is just the pair count. The intuition for why the admissible shape flips so completely: $K_T$ is already scale-free (a max does not grow with cluster size the way a sum does), so the compensating size factor that Dasgupta's objective needs is exactly what must be removed.

No approximation guarantee or hardness result is given for max-type; the paper lists its complexity as open.

The most interesting part

I'll give the reviewer-style critique, because the single most interesting thing here is a reformulation the paper comes within one line of and does not take — and taking it changes how much the headline results buy.

The real content of condition (i) is a coboundary condition, and that solves all degrees at once. Let $\Phi(n)$ denote the common value of $\Gamma(T)$ over all cluster trees on an $n$-set under uniform similarity, with $\Phi(0) = \Phi(1) = 0$. For sum-type, the recursion at the root of any tree reads $\Phi(n) = ab\,g(a,b) + \Phi(a) + \Phi(b)$ for every split $a + b = n$. Hence:

Condition (i) holds $\iff$ there exists $\Phi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\Phi(1) = 0$ such that $\;ab\,g(a,b) = \Phi(a+b) - \Phi(a) - \Phi(b)$ for all $a,b \ge 1$.

Both directions are immediate (necessity by the recursion, sufficiency by induction), and this holds for arbitrary $g$, not just polynomials. In other words, the pair-weighted scaling function must be the coboundary of a one-variable potential. The paper's Lemma 3.2 (the four-variable identity $g(a{+}b,c{+}d) + g(a,b) + g(c,d) = g(a{+}c,b{+}d) + g(a,c) + g(b,d)$) is exactly the cocycle/well-definedness consequence of this, and Lemma 2.2 computes $\Phi$ for the family (4) — but the paper never inverts the map, and inverting it is where the payoff is.

Inverting: for polynomial $g$ we need polynomial $\Phi$ with $\Phi(1) = 0$, i.e. $\Phi \in \mathrm{span}{n^k - n : k \ge 2}$, and then

$$g_k(a,b) \;=\; \frac{(a+b)^k - a^k - b^k}{ab} \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j} a^{j-1} b^{k-j-1}, \qquad \deg g_k = k-2, \qquad \Phi_k(n) = n^k - n.$$

Note that $(a{+}b)^k - a^k - b^k$ has no pure powers of $a$ or $b$, so it is automatically divisible by $ab$ in $\mathbb{R}[a,b]$ — the divisibility is free, which is the structural reason the solution space is as large as it is. I verified symbolically that each $g_k$ satisfies condition (i) for all $n \le 8$ with $\Gamma(T) \equiv n^k - n$ exactly, and that the dimension of the condition-(i) solution space inside symmetric polynomials of degree $\le d$ is exactly $d+1$, spanned by $g_2, \dots, g_{d+2}$, for $d = 0,\dots,4$. The first few:

  • $g_2 = 2$ — the constant;
  • $g_3 = 3(a+b)$ — Dasgupta;
  • $g_4 = 2\big(2(a+b)^2 - ab\big)$ — the paper's $\mu$-generator, up to factor 2;
  • $g_5 = 5\big((a+b)^3 - (a+b)ab\big)$ — the paper's $\lambda$-generator, up to factor 5;
  • $g_6 = 6a^4 + 15a^3b + 20a^2b^2 + 15ab^3 + 6b^4$, and so on.

And condition (ii) is free for $k \ge 3$: $g_k(a+1,b) - g_k(a,b)$ has all nonnegative coefficients and is strictly positive (I printed these for $k \le 7$), because $g_k$ itself has all positive coefficients. So every $g_k$ with $k \ge 3$ is admissible, as is every nonnegative combination with at least one $k \ge 3$ coefficient positive. That is an explicit infinite admissible family at every degree, in two lines, with Dasgupta's objective sitting at $k = 3$ as the lowest nontrivial member. The paper's abstract frames "no explicit admissible objective functions in this family were provided" as the gap it closes at degree $\le 3$; the gap closes at all degrees. Exactly the same works for max-type: condition (i) there is $g(a,b) = \Phi(a+b) - \Phi(a) - \Phi(b)$ with no $ab$ divisor, so the admissible generators are $G_k(a,b) = (a+b)^k - a^k - b^k = ab\,g_k(a,b)$ for $k \ge 2$ (plus the constant, from $\Phi(n) = n-1$). Condition (ii) holds for all these: since $G_k$ is a positive combination of monomials $a^j b^{k-j}$ with $1 \le j \le k-1$, expanding $G_k(a+c, b+d)$ dominates $G_k(a,b) + G_k(c,d)$ term by term with strictly positive cross terms exactly when $(a>0 \wedge d>0)$ or $(b>0 \wedge c>0)$ — which is precisely what the six positivity hypotheses of Theorem 3.1(ii) guarantee. (I also checked numerically, $k \le 5$, $a,b,c,d \le 5$: zero violations.) So max-type too has an explicit infinite admissible family, and Theorem 3.4's one-dimensionality is a degree-2 artefact, not a general scarcity.

Two consequences, one of them a genuine correctness issue.

(a) The "necessary and sufficient" claims are literally false as stated, because of the dropped constant term. $g_2 = 2$ is a condition-(i) solution. Adding any constant $c$ to $g$ preserves (i) (it contributes $c\binom{n}{2}$ on uniform input, since $\sum_v a_v b_v = \binom{n}{2}$ for every binary tree) and leaves the difference in (ii) unchanged. So $g(a,b) = 2(a+b)^2 - ab + 100$ is admissible but is not of the form (10), contradicting the necessity half of Theorem 2.5 as written. I confirmed by brute force over random ultrametric instances and the uniform instance on $n \le 6$ that this $g$ is admissible (0 violations in 80 instances). The same holds on the max side: $g(a,b) = ab - 5$ with the paper's zero-extension convention satisfies both conditions of Theorem 3.1 and is admissible (0 violations), contradicting Theorem 3.4's necessity half. Symbolically, solving condition (i) over degree-$\le 2$ symmetric polynomials with a constant returns ${\lambda_1 = 0, \lambda_3 = 0, c_0 \text{ free}}$ — a 2-dimensional space, not the ray $\lambda ab$. This is a normalisation slip rather than a conceptual error (the interesting content — which growth shapes in cluster size are admissible — is untouched, and the fix is to say "symmetric polynomials with zero constant term", or equivalently to impose $g(0,0)=0$ as the max-type section already does), but a referee should insist on it, and anyone citing the theorems should state the normalisation.

(b) The degree-3 result is weaker than it needed to be, and the gap is elementary. Having reduced condition (i) to the three-parameter family (4), condition (ii) is exactly the lattice-positivity statement $$\min_{a,b \ge 1}\;\big[\lambda\,q(a,b) + \mu\,\ell(a,b) + \nu\big] > 0, \qquad q(a,b) = 3a^2 + 2b^2 + 4ab + 3a + 2b + 1,\;\; \ell(a,b) = 4a + 3b + 2.$$ This is a convex cone, an intersection of open half-spaces indexed by $(a,b) \in \mathbb{N}^2$, and for $\lambda > 0$ only finitely many constraints bind (because $q$ grows quadratically while $\ell$ is linear), so the exact degree-3 characterisation is finitely checkable. The paper instead reports the crude sufficient cone $\lambda \ge 0, \mu \ge 0, 15\lambda + 9\mu + \nu > 0$, which is strictly smaller. Concretely, $(\lambda,\mu,\nu) = (1,-1,5)$ has $\mu < 0$ so it fails Proposition 2.4, yet $\min_{a,b\ge1}[q - \ell + 5] = 11 > 0$, so condition (ii) holds and the objective is admissible — brute-force confirmed, 0 violations in 61 instances including the uniform one. It also fails the approximation condition (14) purely because of $\mu \ge 0$, even though $\lambda + 2\mu + \nu = 4 > 0$ and $g$ is positive and strictly increasing on the extended lattice ($g(1,1),g(2,1),g(3,1),g(2,2) = 9, 20, 43, 40$) and even though Lemma 2.6 still applies ($\lambda n + \mu = n - 1 > 0$ for $n \ge 2$). So both the $\mu \ge 0$ conditions are convenience assumptions for the polynomial-domination arguments, not intrinsic, and the stated inclusions $(14) \subsetneq (9) \subsetneq \text{admissible}$ are both strict. The paper's claim that RSC achieves $O(\varphi)$ "for the admissible objective functions covered by our characterization" is therefore an overstatement: it covers a proper subcone.

(c) Is admissibility even the right desideratum? This is the honest structural worry, and the paper does not engage with it. Admissibility is vacuous unless $M$ satisfies $(\ast)$, and real similarity matrices — cosine similarities of embeddings, co-occurrence counts, kernel values — essentially never do: $(\ast)$ forces $M$ to take at most $n-1$ distinct values and to be block-constant at every level. Worse, on exactly the inputs where admissibility has content, the problem is trivial: $(\ast)$ is the condition under which single linkage recovers the generating tree exactly in $O(n^2)$ time. So admissibility says: "on inputs where single linkage is already exact, my objective agrees with single linkage." That is a consistency axiom — a necessary sanity check that correctly excludes nonsense objectives — not an algorithmic or statistical guarantee. My brute-force experiments sharpen where the axiom actually bites: on the uniform $n=5$ instance (all 105 trees are generating trees), $g = (a+b)^2$ and $g = ab$ have only 60 minimisers each and so fail; but on a two-block instance with 3 generating trees, $g = (a+b)^2$ passes and only $g = ab$ fails. So condition (i) — which is where the entire polynomial characterisation comes from — is driven almost entirely by maximally degenerate, fully tied inputs, where the "ground truth" hierarchy is maximally non-unique. The characterisation is real mathematics, but it is mathematics about tie-breaking behaviour on measure-zero inputs. The question that would make it bite is quantitative: if $M$ is $\varepsilon$-close to satisfying $(\ast)$, is the minimiser $O(\varepsilon)$-close to a generating tree, and does the constant depend on which admissible objective you chose? That is a robustness/stability question in the Carlsson–Mémoli spirit, and the paper's own concluding remark ("compare the theoretical and practical behavior of different admissible objective functions") gestures at it without formulating it.

To be fair about what is good here: Theorem 3.1 is the genuinely new theorem. It is a characterisation for arbitrary symmetric $g$ with no polynomial assumption, its "only if" direction uses a nicely engineered 4-block counterexample, and its "if" direction is a real induction with a non-trivial cancellation, not an application of someone else's lemma. And the observation that max aggregation excludes Dasgupta's own scaling function while admitting a unique degree-$\le 2$ objective is a crisp, memorable finding. The sum-type half, by contrast, reads as a careful but mechanical exercise in low-degree linear algebra over someone else's criterion.

Proof sketch

What is proved, precisely.

_Theorem 2.5 (sum-type, degree $\le 2$, complete)._ Let $g$ be a symmetric polynomial in $(a,b)$ of degree at most two with zero constant term (the paper's parameterisation; see the caveat above). The sum-type objective $\Gamma(T) = \sum_{v} H_T(v_+,v_-)g(|L(T_{v_+})|,|L(T_{v_-})|)$ is admissible for every finite $X$ iff $g(a,b) = \lambda(2(a+b)^2 - ab) + \mu(a+b)$ with $\lambda \ge 0$ and $9\lambda + \mu > 0$. Guarantee: for every $M$ satisfying $(\ast)$, the minimisers of $\Gamma$ are exactly the generating trees of $M$; and no other degree-$\le 2$ $g$ (in that normalisation) has this property.

_Proposition 2.4 (sum-type, degree $\le 3$, sufficient only)._ If $g$ has form (4) with $\lambda \ge 0$, $\mu \ge 0$, $15\lambda + 9\mu + \nu > 0$, then $\Gamma$ is admissible. Not claimed necessary, and not necessary (see $(1,-1,5)$ above).

Theorem 2.10 (approximation). For $g$ of form (4) with $\lambda,\mu \ge 0$ and $\lambda + 2\mu + \nu > 0$, the recursive sparsest cut algorithm using a $\varphi$-approximate sparsest-cut subroutine returns a tree $T^{\mathrm{RSC}}$ with $\Gamma(T^{\mathrm{RSC}}) \le O(\varphi)\cdot \mathrm{OPT}$, where the hidden constant depends on $(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ only through the bound in Lemma B.2 (asymptotically $256/21$ when $\lambda > 0$). With ARV, $\varphi = O(\sqrt{\log n})$. Note this is a guarantee on cost, not on tree recovery; admissibility and approximability are logically independent statements that happen to be about overlapping families.

_Theorem 3.1 (max-type, general $g$, complete)._ Characterisation as stated above: uniform flatness plus strict superadditivity-under-regrouping $g(a+c,b+d) > g(a,b)+g(c,d)$, under the convention $g(0,t)=g(t,0)=0$ and the six positivity hypotheses.

_Theorem 3.4 (max-type, degree $\le 2$, complete)._ With the same zero-constant normalisation, admissible iff $g(a,b) = \lambda ab$, $\lambda > 0$.

Proposition A.4. $M$ has a generating tree $\iff M$ is generated from an ultrametric $\iff$ $(\ast)$. Hence this paper's definition of admissibility coincides with Cohen-Addad et al.'s.

How the sum-type characterisation is proved. Everything reduces to Cohen-Addad et al.'s Proposition 2.1, so the work is in solving conditions (i) and (ii) algebraically.

Sufficiency of form (4) for condition (i) is Lemma 2.2, an induction on $n$: assume the closed form $\Gamma(T) = \frac{\lambda}{5}(n^5-n) + \frac{\mu}{2}(n^4-n) + \frac{\nu}{3}(n^3-n)$ for all smaller sets, write $\Gamma(T) = ab\,g(a,b) + \Gamma(T_{r_+}) + \Gamma(T_{r_-})$ at the root (using $H_T(r_+,r_-) = ab$ under uniform similarity), substitute, and check the $a,b$-dependence cancels. Base case $n=2$: $g(1,1) = 6\lambda + 7\mu + 2\nu$ matches. The cancellation is not a coincidence — it is the coboundary structure of the previous section, with $\Phi = \frac{\lambda}{5}\Phi_5 + \frac{\mu}{2}\Phi_4 + \frac{\nu}{3}\Phi_3$ in the basis $\Phi_k(n) = n^k - n$.

Necessity is the cute part and the technical heart of Section 2.1. Since condition (i) is quantified over all finite $X$, it suffices to use one instance, and the authors use $|X| = 5$: there are exactly three non-isomorphic cluster trees on 5 leaves — the caterpillar $T_1$ (splits $4{+}1, 3{+}1, 2{+}1, 1{+}1$), $T_2$ (splits $4{+}1, 2{+}2$, then two $1{+}1$), and $T_3$ (splits $3{+}2$, then $2{+}1, 1{+}1$ on one side and $1{+}1$ on the other) — giving, under uniform similarity, $$\Gamma(T_1) = 4g(4,1)+3g(3,1)+2g(2,1)+g(1,1), \quad \Gamma(T_2) = 4g(4,1)+4g(2,2)+2g(1,1), \quad \Gamma(T_3) = 6g(3,2)+2g(2,1)+2g(1,1),$$ and hence two linear equations in the coefficients: $$3g(3,1) + 2g(2,1) = 4g(2,2) + g(1,1), \qquad 2g(4,1) + 2g(2,2) = 3g(3,2) + g(2,1).$$ Substituting the general form $g = \lambda_1(a{+}b)^3 + \lambda_2(a{+}b)ab + \mu_1(a{+}b)^2 + \mu_2 ab + \nu(a{+}b)$ yields exactly $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 0$ and $\mu_1 + 2\mu_2 = 0$, cutting the five-dimensional coefficient space down to the three-dimensional family (4). This is the condition on the coefficients of the symmetric polynomial, and it is the one that matters: in the ${e_1 = a+b,\, e_2 = ab}$ generators, the coefficient of $e_1 e_2$ must be minus the coefficient of $e_1^3$ and the coefficient of $e_2$ must be minus twice the coefficient of $e_1^2$. Structurally this is the divisibility/telescoping requirement that $ab\,g(a,b)$ be a coboundary $\Phi(a+b)-\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)$. $|X|=5$ is exactly minimal for this argument: $|X|=4$ has only two tree shapes hence one equation, insufficient to kill two parameters. I confirmed computationally that adding instances $|X| = 6,7,8$ yields no further constraints at degree 3 (the solution space stays 4-dimensional including the constant), while degree 4 needs $|X| \le 6$ and degree 5 needs $|X| \le 7$ — so the instance size required grows roughly like $\deg + 2$.

Condition (ii) is pure differencing: $g(a{+}1,b) - g(a,b) = \lambda\,q(a,b) + \mu\,\ell(a,b) + \nu$ with $q, \ell$ as above (I verified both expansions by hand and symbolically). For $\lambda, \mu \ge 0$ the expression is increasing in both arguments so its minimum over $a,b \ge 1$ is at $a=b=1$, giving $15\lambda + 9\mu + \nu$. At degree $\le 2$ ($\lambda = 0$) the condition becomes $\mu \ell(a,b) + \nu > 0$ for all $a,b \ge 1$; since $\ell$ is unbounded, $\mu \ge 0$ is forced, and then the minimum $\ell(1,1) = 9$ gives $9\mu + \nu > 0$ — so at degree $\le 2$ the sufficient cone is exactly the admissible cone, which is why that case closes completely and degree 3 does not.

How the approximation theorem is proved. The skeleton is Charikar–Chatziafratis's charging argument; the new work is verifying that the degree-3 family has the growth properties the argument needs. Four steps.

Step 1 — the split-cost landscape (Lemma 2.6). Substituting $a = k$, $b = n-k$ into (4) and completing the square gives the key identity $$g(k, n-k) = (\lambda n + \mu)\Big(k - \tfrac{n}{2}\Big)^2 + \tfrac34 \lambda n^3 + \tfrac74 \mu n^2 + \nu n,$$ which I verified. For $\lambda n + \mu > 0$ this is a convex parabola in $k$ centred at $n/2$: at fixed total size, the split cost is minimised at the balanced split $k \in {\lfloor n/2\rfloor, \lceil n/2\rceil}$ and maximised at the extreme splits $k \in {1, n-1}$. Both ends of this statement are used, in opposite directions.

Step 2 — a lower bound on OPT via a balanced-split potential (Lemma 2.7). Extend $g$ to $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^2$ by the polynomial (so $g(0,0)=0$) and define the increment of the balanced-split cost, $f(t) = g(\lfloor \frac{t+1}{2}\rfloor, \lceil \frac{t+1}{2}\rceil) - g(\lfloor \frac t2\rfloor, \lceil \frac t2\rceil)$, so that $\sum_{t=0}^{r-1} f(t) = g(\lfloor r/2\rfloor, \lceil r/2\rceil)$ telescopes. Let $T^_$ be optimal, $\mathrm{OPT}(t)$ the partition of $X$ into the inclusion-maximal clusters of $T^_$ of size $\le t$, and $E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t)$ the pairs separated by that partition. A pair ${x,y}$ lies in $E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t)$ exactly for $t = 0,\dots,|C^*_{xy}|-1$, so its total contribution to $\sum_t M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t))f(t)$ is $M(x,y)\,g(\lfloor |C^*_{xy}|/2 \rfloor, \lceil |C^*_{xy}|/2 \rceil)$, while its contribution to OPT is $M(x,y)\,g(|C_x|,|C_y|)$ with $|C_x|+|C_y| = |C^*_{xy}|$. Lemma 2.6 (balanced is cheapest) gives the former $\le$ the latter pointwise, hence $\sum_{t=0}^{n-1} M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t))\,f(t) \le \mathrm{OPT}$. This is the lower-bounding potential; note it is purely combinatorial — no spreading metric or LP is needed, the structure of $g$ does the work.

Step 3 — charging each RSC split (Lemma 2.8). For a cluster $A$ with $|A| = r \ge 2$ that RSC splits into ${B_1,B_2}$ with $s = s(A) = \min(|B_1|,|B_2|)$: the $\varphi$-sparsest-cut guarantee gives $M(P(A))/(s(r-s)) \le \varphi\,\mathrm{SC}(A)$. To bound $\mathrm{SC}(A)$ by optimal structure, intersect $A$ with $\mathrm{OPT}(\lfloor r/2\rfloor)$ to get a partition $A_1,\dots,A_k$ of $A$ with $|A_i| = \gamma_i r$, $\gamma_i \le 1/2$, $\sum \gamma_i = 1$. Then $\mathrm{SC}(A) \le \min_i \frac{M(A_i, A\setminus A_i)}{|A_i||A\setminus A_i|} \le \frac{\sum_i M(A_i,A\setminus A_i)}{\sum_i |A_i||A \setminus A_i|}$ (the mediant inequality: a minimum of ratios is at most the ratio of sums), and since $\gamma_i \le 1/2$ implies $\sum_i \gamma_i(1-\gamma_i) \ge \frac12 \sum_i \gamma_i = \frac12$, while $\sum_i M(A_i, A\setminus A_i) = 2M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\lfloor r/2\rfloor) \cap A)$, one gets $\mathrm{SC}(A) \le \frac{4}{r^2} M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\lfloor r/2 \rfloor)\cap A)$. Combining, the split cost is at most $4\varphi \frac{s}{r}\cdot \frac{g(s,r-s)}{f'(r)} \cdot \sum_{t=\lfloor r/4\rfloor}^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor - 1} M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t)\cap A) f(t)$, where $f'(r) := \sum_{t = \lfloor r/4\rfloor}^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor-1} f(t)$ and one uses monotonicity of $t \mapsto M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t)\cap A)$ (partitions only coarsen as $t$ grows) to replace $M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\lfloor r/2\rfloor)\cap A)f'(r)$ by the windowed sum.

Step 4 — the growth lemma, which is where the polynomial structure is essential (Lemmas B.1, B.2). One needs $\sup_{t\ge2,\,1\le s\le t-1} g(s,t-s)/f'(t) = O(1)$. By Lemma 2.6 the numerator is maximised at the extreme split, so it suffices to bound $g(t-1,1)/f'(t)$, where $g(t-1,1) = \lambda t^3 + (2\mu-\lambda)t^2 + (\lambda - \mu + \nu)t + \mu$. For the denominator, write $t = 4m + r$ with $r \in {0,1,2,3}$; then $f'(t)$ telescopes to $g(\lfloor t/2\rfloor$-balanced$) - g(\lfloor t/4\rfloor$-balanced$)$, and four parity cases give $f'(t) = \frac{21}{4}\lambda m^3 + C_1 m^2 + C_2 m + C_3$ with case-dependent constants. Since $t \approx 4m$, the numerator is $\approx 64 \lambda m^3$, so the ratio tends to $256/21$ when $\lambda > 0$; the degenerate cases $\lambda = 0, \mu > 0$ and $\lambda = \mu = 0, \nu > 0$ are claimed "handled in the same manner" (they give $128/21$ and $4$ respectively, by the same leading-order computation). Positivity $f'(t) > 0$ for $t \ge 2$ (Lemma B.1) is exactly where condition (14) is used: $\min_{a,b\ge0}[g(a+1,b)-g(a,b)] = \lambda + 2\mu + \nu$, so (14) is precisely "$g$ strictly increasing on the extended lattice", and e.g. $f'(2) = f(0) = g(0,1) - g(0,0) = \lambda + 2\mu + \nu$. Two soft spots: the bound is asymptotic (boundedness is established via a limit, with no explicit uniform constant covering small $m$), and the degenerate coefficient cases are waved at rather than written.

_How $\varphi$ propagates._ It does not accumulate. $\varphi$ enters once, multiplicatively, in the per-split inequality of Step 3, with the same factor at every recursion level, because each split is charged not to its own recursive subproblem but to a level-indexed potential $\sum_t M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t))f(t)$ defined once from $T^*$. The only thing that could cause a $\log n$ blow-up is double-charging across levels, and Lemma 2.9 kills it by a window argument: swapping the order of summation, the constraint $\lfloor |A|/4\rfloor \le t \le \lfloor|A|/2\rfloor - 1$ is equivalent to $2t+2 \le |A| \le 4t+3$, so for a fixed threshold $t$ only clusters within a factor-2 size window can charge to it. Along the chain $A_1 \supset A_2 \supset \cdots \supset A_k$ of algorithm clusters in that window containing a given pair, $s(A_i) \le |A_i| - |A_{i+1}|$, so $\sum_i \frac{s(A_i)}{|A_i|} \le \frac{\sum_i(|A_i| - |A_{i+1}|)}{\min_i |A_i|} \le \frac{|A_1|}{2t+2} \le \frac{4t+3}{2t+2} < 2$. So each threshold is over-charged by a factor less than 2, uniformly, and the total is $\Gamma^{\mathrm{RSC}} \le O(\varphi)\cdot 2 \cdot \sum_t M(E_{\mathrm{OPT}}(t))f(t) \le O(\varphi)\mathrm{OPT}$. The $\lfloor r/4 \rfloor$ lower endpoint in the window is exactly what makes this factor-2 bound work; the price is the Lemma B.2 constant.

How the max-type characterisation is proved. This is the most self-contained argument in the paper.

Lemma 3.2 (the identity forced by condition (i)). Let $\Gamma^_(k)$ be the common uniform-input value on a $k$-set, $\Gamma^_(0)=\Gamma^_(1)=0$. Then $\Gamma^_(p+q) = g(p,q) + \Gamma^_(p) + \Gamma^_(q)$. Decomposing $\Gamma^*(a+b+c+d)$ two ways — as $(a{+}b)|(c{+}d)$ at the root and as $(a{+}c)|(b{+}d)$ — gives $$g(a+b,c+d) + g(a,b) + g(c,d) \;=\; g(a+c,b+d) + g(a,c) + g(b,d),$$ the cocycle identity. This is the trick on which the whole "if" direction turns, because it is exactly what makes the leading terms cancel in the inequality chain below.

"Only if" — the counterexample construction. Condition (i) is immediate (uniform $M$ makes every tree generating, so all must be optimal, so all values are equal). For condition (ii), take disjoint $A,B,C,D$ of sizes $a,b,c,d$ and define a three-valued $M$: $2$ inside each block, $1$ on $A\times B$ and on $C \times D$, $0$ on $(A\cup B)\times(C\cup D)$. Let $T$ group $(A,B)$ under one child of the root and $(C,D)$ under the other — a generating tree, with weights $2$ inside the blocks, $1$ at the two middle nodes, $0$ at the root. Let $T'$ group $(A,C)$ and $(B,D)$ instead — not a generating tree, since no consistent weight function exists ($A \times C$ pairs have similarity 0 but would need to be labelled at a descendant of the root). Admissibility forces $\Gamma(T') > \Gamma(T)$, and because $K_T$ depends only on the maximum across each cut, the subtree contributions are identical in both and the inequality collapses to exactly $g(a+c,b+d) > g(a,b) + g(c,d)$. The zero-extension convention handles the case where one of $a,b,c,d$ vanishes. This is a clean, minimal, three-value construction — note it would not work for sum-type, where $H_T$ differs between $T$ and $T'$.

"If" — induction with a local exchange at the root. Induct on $n$. Given $M$ with a generating tree $T^*$ (root bipartition $X^*_L | X^*_R$) and an arbitrary competitor $T$ (root bipartition $X_L | X_R$), set $A = X^*_L \cap X_L$, $B = X^*_L\cap X_R$, $C = X^*_R \cap X_L$, $D = X^*_R \cap X_R$ with sizes $a,b,c,d$; at most one is empty unless the two bipartitions coincide, in which case the induction hypothesis on the two sides finishes immediately. Take $T_A,T_B,T_C,T_D$ to be generating (hence, by induction, optimal) trees of the principal submatrices $M_A, M_B, M_C, M_D$ — legitimate because Lemma A.1 implies every principal submatrix of a matrix satisfying $(\ast)$ also satisfies $(\ast)$.
