Build two comparison trees: $\tilde T$ with root children $(T_A,T_B)$ and $(T_C,T_D)$ (same root bipartition as $T^*$), and $T'$ with root children $(T_A,T_C)$ and $(T_B,T_D)$ (same root bipartition as $T$). Then $\Gamma(T^*) \le \Gamma(\tilde T)$ by induction on the two sides (crucially, $K$ at the root is unchanged because the leaf sets are), and $\Gamma(T) \ge \Gamma(T')$ by induction on $T$'s two sides. Now let $m = \min_{x \ne y} M(x,y)$ and $m_{YZ} = \max_{y\in Y, z\in Z} M(y,z)$. Because $T^*$ is generating, $m = m_{AC} = m_{AD} = m_{BC} = m_{BD}$ — the four "cross" blocks all sit at the root of $T^*$ and therefore all carry the minimum value — and $m' := m_{A\cup C, B\cup D} = \max{m_{AB}, m_{CD}}$. Expanding $\Gamma(T') - \Gamma(\tilde T)$ and _using Lemma 3.2 to cancel all terms with coefficient $m$_ leaves $$\Gamma(T) - \Gamma(\tilde T) \;\ge\; (m' - m)\,g(a+c,b+d) - (m_{AB}-m)g(a,b) - (m_{CD}-m)g(c,d) \;\ge\; (m'-m)\big(g(a+c,b+d) - g(a,b) - g(c,d)\big) \;\ge\; 0,$$ the middle step by $m' \ge m_{AB}, m_{CD}$ and the last by condition (ii) (which, with the zero convention, also forces $g > 0$ on $\mathbb{N}^2$). This gives soundness: every generating tree is optimal.

The converse half (every optimum is generating) is the direction that justifies the word "exactly", and it is handled by squeezing the above chain to equality. If $T$ is optimal then $\Gamma(T) = \Gamma(\tilde T) = \Gamma(T^*)$, which forces (a) $\tilde T$ is itself a generating tree, so $M$ is constant $= \gamma_{AB}$ on $A\times B$ and constant $=\gamma_{CD}$ on $C\times D$; and (b) $T_L, T_R$ are optimal for $M_{A\cup C}, M_{B\cup D}$ and $m_{AB} = m_{CD} = m' = m$. Together these give $M \equiv m$ on $(A\times B)\cup(C\times D)$, and since $T^*$ is generating, $M \equiv m$ on $(A\cup B)\times(C\cup D)$; hence $M \equiv m$ on all of $(A\cup C)\times(B\cup D)$, i.e. on $T$'s own root cut. By induction $T_L, T_R$ are generating trees of their submatrices with weight functions $h_L, h_R$; glue them with $h(r) := m$ at the root, and the monotonicity condition holds because $m$ is the global minimum. So $T$ is generating. The structure of the argument — a tree-level exchange move, plus an equality analysis that reconstructs the weight function explicitly — is the standard shape for this kind of "minimisers are exactly the ground truths" statement, executed carefully here.

Theorem 3.4 then reuses the $|X|=5$ trick. Under max aggregation the uniform-input values are $\Gamma(T_1) = g(4,1)+g(3,1)+g(2,1)+g(1,1)$, $\Gamma(T_2) = g(4,1)+g(2,2)+2g(1,1)$, $\Gamma(T_3) = g(3,2)+g(2,1)+2g(1,1)$ (each internal node contributes $K = 1$ times $g$), and equating them gives $g(3,1)+g(2,1) = g(2,2)+g(1,1)$ and $g(4,1)+g(2,2) = g(3,2)+g(2,1)$. With $g = \lambda_1(a{+}b)^2 + \lambda_2 ab + \lambda_3(a{+}b)$ these become $5\lambda_1 + \lambda_3 = 0$ and $7\lambda_1 + \lambda_3 = 0$ (I verified both), forcing $\lambda_1 = \lambda_3 = 0$ and hence $g = \lambda ab$; then condition (ii) reduces to $\lambda(ad + bc) > 0$, which the six positivity hypotheses make equivalent to $\lambda > 0$. (With a constant term retained, the same linear system leaves the constant free — the gap noted above.)

Broader context

Why hierarchical clustering had no objective for decades. Flat clustering has had objectives since the 1950s — $k$-means, $k$-median, $k$-center, correlation clustering — each defining the output as the argmin of something you can write down. Hierarchical clustering was instead defined procedurally: single linkage, average linkage, complete linkage, Ward's method are each a greedy agglomeration rule with a particular inter-cluster distance, and the output is whatever the procedure produces. There was no statement of the form "the dendrogram you want is the one minimising $\Gamma$", which meant no way to compare methods on a common footing, no notion of approximation, no hardness theory, and no way to say that a given dendrogram was "wrong". The axiomatic tradition partly filled the gap from the other side: Kleinberg's impossibility theorem (NIPS 2002) showed no flat clustering function can simultaneously satisfy scale invariance, richness and consistency, and Carlsson–Mémoli (JMLR 2010) showed that for hierarchical clustering the impossibility dissolves — single linkage is the unique method satisfying a natural set of functoriality/stability axioms. Admissibility in the present paper sits squarely in that axiomatic lineage, and it is worth noting the consonance: the inputs on which admissibility has content are exactly those on which single linkage is exact.

Dasgupta's reframing. Dasgupta (STOC 2016) proposed $\sum_{{x,y}} w_{xy}|C_{xy}|$ and immediately got a research programme: minimisation is NP-hard; the optimum is attained by binary trees; recursive sparsest cut gives $O(\varphi \log n)$; and for inputs that are hierarchically structured (unit-weight planted hierarchies, ultrametric-like data) the optimum recovers the ground truth. Charikar–Chatziafratis (SODA'17) improved the ratio to $O(\varphi) = O(\sqrt{\log n})$ via sparsest cut plus spreading metrics and proved no constant-factor approximation is possible under the Small-Set Expansion hypothesis; Cohen-Addad et al. (J. ACM 2019) independently obtained $O(\varphi)$, introduced admissibility and the sum-type family, and showed that "good" linkage heuristics can be arbitrarily bad for Dasgupta's objective. The present paper is a direct, narrow sequel to that J. ACM paper: it takes their non-constructive admissibility criterion and makes it explicit on a subclass.

The dual maximisation versions. Because the Dasgupta objective's minimisation is hard to approximate well, two maximisation duals became the practical workhorses. Moseley–Wang (NeurIPS 2017) observed that $\sum_{{x,y}} w_{xy}(n - |C_{xy}|)$ — the "revenue" complementary to Dasgupta's cost on the same similarity input — admits a $1/3$-approximation by average linkage, giving the first theoretical justification of a classical heuristic; Charikar–Chatziafratis–Niazadeh (SODA'19) pushed this past $1/3$ and showed average linkage is not optimal, and later work gave hardness of approximation for the revenue objective. Cohen-Addad et al. also introduced the dissimilarity-based "value" objective $\sum d_{xy}|C_{xy}|$, for which average linkage is a $2/3$-approximation. The structural point is that cost-minimisation and revenue-maximisation differ by a constant $n\sum w_{xy}$ and are therefore equivalent as exact problems but wildly different as approximation problems. Admissibility, being an exact-optimality property, is insensitive to this distinction — which is both a feature (it is a clean axiom) and a limitation (it says nothing about what the approximation algorithms you would actually run will produce).

The sparsest-cut machinery. Recursive sparsest cut is the canonical top-down scheme: find a bipartition minimising $w(Y, \bar Y)/(|Y||\bar Y|)$ (uniform sparsest cut), recurse. Exact sparsest cut is NP-hard; the ARV SDP with $\ell_1$-embedding and expander flows gives $\varphi = O(\sqrt{\log n})$, and Leighton–Rao's LP gives $O(\log n)$. The whole $O(\varphi)$ line of results is really a statement that Dasgupta-type objectives are "sparsest-cut-structured": a hierarchy's cost decomposes over its cuts in a way that lets a per-cut approximation guarantee be charged against a global potential without compounding across levels. The present paper's contribution on this front is to verify that the charging survives when the scaling function is any admissible low-degree polynomial — the two facts needed being that balanced splits are cheapest (so the potential in Lemma 2.7 lower-bounds OPT) and that the extreme-to-balanced cost ratio is $O(1)$ (Lemma B.2).

Two closely related works worth having to hand. (1) Cohen-Addad, Kanade, Mallmann-Trenn, Mathieu, Hierarchical clustering: objective functions and algorithms, J. ACM 66 (2019) — the direct predecessor; the admissibility framework, the sum-type family, the $O(\varphi)$ analysis and the negative results on linkage all live there, and this paper is unreadable as a standalone without it. (2) Carlsson–Mémoli, Characterization, stability and convergence of hierarchical clustering methods, JMLR 11 (2010) — the axiomatic/functorial side, and the right place to look for the stability notion that the present paper's framework is missing.

A plausible follow-up. The obvious one, and the one I would actually want: quantitative admissibility. Admissibility is a zero/one statement at the ultrametric boundary. Define a deviation measure $\varepsilon(M) = \max_{x,y,z}\max{0, \min(M(x,y),M(y,z)) - M(x,z)}$, or a relative/Gromov-style version, and ask: for an admissible $\Gamma$, if $\varepsilon(M) \le \varepsilon$, is every minimiser of $\Gamma$ within $\delta(\varepsilon)$ of some generating tree of a nearby ultrametric, in a tree metric such as Robinson–Foulds, triplet distance, or the Gromov–Hausdorff distance between the induced ultrametrics? The deliverable would be a stability modulus $\delta_\Gamma(\varepsilon)$ for each admissible $\Gamma$, which would for the first time let one say that one admissible objective is better than another — exactly the comparison the paper's conclusion asks for and does not make. The degree parameter is a natural knob here: higher-degree scaling functions penalise late separation more aggressively and should be more sensitive to a single spurious high-similarity pair, so I would conjecture $\delta_\Gamma$ degrades with $\deg g$, giving a principled reason to prefer Dasgupta's $k=3$ member — or a surprise if not. Two smaller follow-ups are free: the all-degrees characterisation via the coboundary basis $g_k = ((a+b)^k - a^k - b^k)/(ab)$ (and the companion statement that the condition-(i) space in degree $\le d$ is exactly $(d+1)$-dimensional), and the exact degree-3 cone as an integer-lattice positivity region. The paper's own stated open problem — the complexity and approximability of max-type minimisation — is also genuinely open and looks harder than the sum-type case, since the objective is not linear in $M$ and the sparsest-cut charging has nothing obvious to charge against.

Connections to theoretical IR, generative retrieval and vector search. Two of the candidate links are real; the rest I think are forced, and I will say so.

Honest link 1: semantic identifier construction in generative retrieval. In DSI (Tay et al., 2022) the "semantically structured identifiers" are built by running hierarchical $k$-means on document embeddings and reading each document's identifier off the root-to-leaf path; in RQ-VAE-based schemes (TIGER, Rajput et al. 2023) the identifier is a residual-quantisation code, which is again a tree-structured coarse-to-fine partition of the embedding space. This is literally hierarchical clustering of a similarity space producing a tree of identifiers, and — this is the point — it is specified procedurally, exactly in the pre-Dasgupta state of the art. Nobody writes down what objective hierarchical $k$-means-for-semantic-IDs optimises, so there is no way to compare two ID schemes except downstream, no notion of approximation, and no way to say an ID tree is wrong. The present line of work supplies the missing vocabulary: one can ask what objective an ID construction minimises, whether that objective is admissible (does it recover the hierarchy when the embedding geometry genuinely is hierarchical?), and what the approximation ratio of the greedy construction is. The sharpest concrete transfer is not admissibility itself but the balance term: the new admissible members all contain $-(\lambda n + \mu)ab$, so at equal cut quality they strictly prefer balanced splits, whereas Dasgupta's objective is indifferent. For semantic IDs, balance is not an aesthetic preference — it controls codebook utilisation, identifier length, and the branching factor the decoder's beam search must handle; unbalanced ID trees are a known failure mode (collapsed codebooks, overloaded prefixes). So the paper's family provides a principled objective with a built-in balance preference, rather than the usual ad hoc balanced-$k$-means constraint. Where the analogy breaks down, concretely: (a) the figure of merit for semantic IDs is downstream retrieval accuracy under constrained decoding, not tree cost, and nothing guarantees the two are monotonically related — the decoder's inductive biases over token sequences are not modelled at all; (b) ID trees are $k$-ary with fixed arity $k$ (typically 256 or 1024) and fixed depth, while this entire theory is binary and depth-free, and as I noted the standard binarisation argument that makes binary WLOG for Dasgupta's objective does not obviously survive the $-ab$ term; (c) embedding cosine similarities essentially never satisfy the ultrametric condition $(\ast)$, so admissibility is a sanity axiom and not a recovery guarantee on real corpora — the honest claim is "an objective that fails admissibility is disqualified", not "an admissible objective will produce good IDs"; (d) the objectives are dense, $\Theta(n^2)$ in edges, so for a 10M-document corpus you would need a sparsified or sampled surrogate, and whether admissibility survives sparsification is itself unstudied.

Honest link 2: max-type aggregation is the connectivity-flavoured objective, which is the right shape for graph-based ANN. This one is narrower but genuinely suggestive. For the sum-type family, what a split costs is the total similarity crossing it — a cut-weight notion. For the max-type family, what it costs is the strongest single similarity crossing it, and the unique degree-$\le 2$ admissible member reduces to "each separated pair pays the maximum similarity across the cut that separates it". That is a single-linkage / connectivity-threshold quantity, and it is structurally the right currency for graph-based vector search: whether greedy routing can escape a region depends on whether some sufficiently good edge crosses the boundary, not on the aggregate similarity across it. So if one wanted an objective-function theory of hierarchical index quality for navigability, max-type aggregation is the correct starting primitive, and Theorem 3.1 tells you which size-scalings are even consistent. Where it breaks down, and I want to be clear that it breaks down a lot: HNSW's layers are a random subsampling hierarchy over one node set, not a nested partition of the points, so the combinatorial object is not a cluster tree; the relevant guarantee is expected hop count under greedy routing, which the Dasgupta-style cost does not model at all (there is no notion of out-degree, no notion of a routing path); and the real theory of navigability — Indyk–Xu's worst-case navigable-graph constructions and the surrounding small-world literature — has essentially disjoint machinery. I would present this as "max-type is the right primitive for a theory that does not yet exist", not as a result about HNSW.

What I think is forced. "Hierarchical document clustering for browsing/faceted navigation" is a real application but a shallow link — it is just hierarchical clustering applied to text, with nothing specific to IR theory, and the paper adds nothing beyond what Dasgupta already offered. The generic "axiomatic question of what makes a hierarchy correct bears on learned index structures" framing is too loose to be worth a sentence: learned indexes are judged on lookup cost and error bounds, not on whether they recover a ground-truth hierarchy, and admissibility has no purchase there. And tying max-type aggregation to complete linkage in retrieval pipelines would be a label, not a connection. I would rather make the semantic-ID point well, flag the max-type/navigability one as speculative, and leave the rest.

Bottom-line assessment. A careful, modest, correct-modulo-one-normalisation paper. Theorem 3.1 (the max-type characterisation for arbitrary symmetric $g$) is the real contribution and the thing to remember, together with the finding that max aggregation excludes Dasgupta's own scaling function and admits a unique degree-$\le 2$ objective. The sum-type half closes a stated gap but closes it narrowly and by brute force, where a change of variables to the potential $\Phi$ with $ab\,g(a,b) = \Phi(a+b) - \Phi(a) - \Phi(b)$ would have closed it at every degree with an explicit basis; the approximation theorem is a faithful transfer of the Charikar–Chatziafratis charging argument to the new family, with two honest soft spots (an asymptotic rather than explicit constant, and an approximable subcone strictly smaller than the admissible cone it claims to cover). The framework's deeper limitation is not fixable by more algebra: admissibility is a tie-breaking axiom about measure-zero inputs on which single linkage is already exact, and the field needs the quantitative, perturbation-stable version before "which admissible objective should I use?" becomes answerable.

title: On the Limits of Language Generation: Trade-Offs Between Hallucination and Mode Collapse
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-30

On the Limits of Language Generation: Trade-Offs Between Hallucination and Mode Collapse

Kalavasis, Mehrotra & Velegkas (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09642

Setting and problem

The paper works in the Gold–Angluin inductive-inference setting, in the statistical (stochastic-example) variant due to Angluin [Ang88], not the adversarial-enumeration variant used by Kleinberg–Mullainathan [KM24]. The distinction matters for every theorem, so it is worth being pedantic.

The objects. Fix a countably infinite domain $X$. Because $X$ is countable one may identify it with $\mathbb{N}$ or with $\Sigma^*$ for a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and the paper switches freely between the two. A language is a subset $L \subseteq X$. A language collection is a countable, indexed family $\mathcal{L} = {L_1, L_2, \dots}$. Two things about $\mathcal{L}$ are crucial and easy to miss:

  1. The collection is known to the learner, but only through a membership oracle: given $(i,x)$ the learner can ask $\mathbf{1}{x \in L_i}$. This is the standard access model in the whole tradition [Gol67; Ang80; KM24], justified by the fact that if the languages are "reasonable" (decided by Turing machines, generated by context-free grammars) then there are only countably many and each admits such an oracle. The learner may not ask "is $L_i \subseteq L_j$?" — that subset oracle is a strictly stronger primitive and appears in the paper only as an explicit, flagged assumption (Prop. 3.10, Appendix B).
  2. The enumeration may contain repetitions: the same language can appear at infinitely many indices. This sounds like a triviality but it is the source of a real technical obstacle later (you cannot majority-vote over indices).

What nature does. Nature (equivalently an adversary) picks a target $K \in \mathcal{L}$ and does not reveal it or its index. In the statistical model it additionally picks a distribution $P$ over $X$ which is valid for $K$: $\operatorname{supp}(P) = K$ exactly (Def. 1, Angluin 1988). So every string of $K$ carries strictly positive mass and nothing outside $K$ does. The learner then observes $S_n = (X_1,\dots,X_n) \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} P$. Validity is doing heavy lifting: it guarantees (Prop. 5.2, via the second Borel–Cantelli lemma) that an infinite i.i.d. draw from $P$ is almost surely a _complete enumeration of $K$_, which is what lets the authors feed i.i.d. data to online algorithms and vice versa.

Contrast with KM24's model, which is Gold's: there is no distribution. The adversary produces an arbitrary enumeration $x_1, x_2, \dots$ of $K$ (repetitions allowed; the only constraint is that every $x \in K$ appears at some finite time), and the learner must succeed for every enumeration. The statistical model is in one sense friendlier — concentration is available, and i.i.d. draws are "non-adversarially ordered" — but Angluin [Ang88] already proved that this friendliness buys nothing for identifiability: a collection non-identifiable in the limit is non-identifiable from stochastic examples too. The paper needs, and proves, a much stronger quantitative version of that fact.

$K$ must be infinite for the problem to be well posed: otherwise the learner eventually sees all of $K$ and there are no unseen strings left to generate. Throughout, all languages in $\mathcal{L}$ are taken infinite.

What the learner outputs. Not an index — a generator. A generating algorithm is a sequence of computable maps $(G_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $G_n : X^n \to \mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ is the set of (randomized) Turing machines that take no input and emit one element of $X$ per execution. So $G_n(S_n)$ is a sampler, and the quantity that all the definitions are about is its support $\operatorname{supp}(G_n) \subseteq X$, the set of strings it emits with positive probability. This is the Gold-tradition idealization: everything is a support-level, measure-zero-sensitive statement, never a statement about probability mass. (For the rate results on consistency alone one may take $G_n$ to be a point mass, i.e. $G_n : X^n \to X$; breadth forces the general definition.)

The two desiderata.

Consistency / validity (Def. 2). The generation error is $$\mathrm{gen_er}(G_n) := \Pr_{S\sim P^n}\big[\operatorname{supp}(G_n) \not\subseteq K \setminus S\big],$$ and $(G_n)$ is consistent for $\mathcal{L}$ if $\mathrm{gen_er}(G_n) \to 0$ for every valid $P$. A failure counts if the generator can emit anything outside $K$ (hallucination) or anything already in the training set (regurgitation — barred so that the trivial "echo a training string" generator does not win). Note this is a relaxation of KM24's definition, which demands that after some finite time the support is always contained in $K \setminus S$; here it only has to happen with probability tending to one.

Breadth / coverage (Def. 4). $(G_n)$ achieves breadth if for every valid $P$, $$\Pr\big[\operatorname{supp}(G_n) \supseteq K \setminus S_n\big] \to 1 \qquad (n \to \infty);$$ otherwise it suffers mode collapse. The motivation is the GAN notion [AB17; GPM+20]: $\mathrm{KL}(P \,|\, G) = \infty$ exactly when some $x \in \operatorname{supp}(P)$ has $G(x) = 0$, so finiteness of the forward KL is support containment $\operatorname{supp}(G) \cup S_n \supseteq K$. Symmetrically, consistency is finiteness of the reverse KL $\mathrm{KL}(G\,|\,P)$. Pleasingly symmetric, and it also tells you the theory is about which strings get exactly zero probability, nothing more.

Together: $(G_n)$ generates with consistency and breadth iff $\Pr[\operatorname{supp}(G_n) = K \setminus S_n] \to 1$, i.e. the support converges to the set of unseen true strings. The error indicator is $\mathrm{er}(G_n) = \mathbf{1}{\operatorname{supp}(G_n) \neq K \setminus S_n}$. (Remark 2: whether one bars repeating training examples is immaterial once breadth is required — the two versions interconvert by mixing and rejection sampling.)

Convergence is measured by rates, not just in the limit. The paper imports the universal rates framework of Bousquet–Hanneke–Moran–van Handel–Yehudayoff [BHM+21] (Def. 3, Def. 13): an algorithm achieves rate $R$ (with $R(n) \downarrow 0$) if $$\forall\ \text{valid } P\ \ \exists\, C,c>0:\quad \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{er}(G_n)] \le C \cdot R(c n)\quad \forall n.$$ The constants may depend on $P$ — that is what "universal" means, and it is essential: the rates here are driven by $\min_j p_{i_j}$, the smallest mass of finitely many distribution-dependent "trigger" strings. A collection admits no rate if for every algorithm there is a valid $P$ with $\limsup_n \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{er}] > 0$. "No rate" is therefore much stronger than "not achievable in the limit", and bridging that gap is one of the two technical cores of the paper.

Non-triviality. Degenerate collections have to be excluded, and the right notion differs by task. For identification (Def. 14): $\exists L_1 \neq L_2$ in $\mathcal{L}$ with $L_1 \cap L_2 \neq \emptyset$ (else one sample identifies). For generation (Def. 18) the condition is subtler: $\exists x \in X$ and a finite subfamily $\mathcal{L}' \subseteq \mathcal{L}$ with $x \in L$ for all $L \in \mathcal{L}'$ and $|\bigcap_{L \in \mathcal{L}'} L| < \infty$. If this fails, you can generate correctly from a single sample by emitting from the (infinite) intersection of the finitely many candidate languages containing it (Lemma 5.9); Example 2 — $X = [0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathcal{L} = {[0,1/n]\cap\mathbb{Q}}$ — shows why $\mathcal{L}'$ must be finite.

The restricted class of generators. The impossibility result does not apply to all computable generators. It applies to those for which the Membership Oracle Problem is decidable (Defs. 5–6): $\mathrm{MOP}(G)$ asks, given a description of $G$ and a string $x$, whether $x \in \operatorname{supp}(G)$. In general this is undecidable (Appendix A gives an explicit generator whose support membership encodes halting). The hypothesis is that a decider exists — the trainers, the users and the algorithms in the proofs need no oracle handed to them; it is purely a structural property of the generating algorithm. The paper's justification that this class is large is Theorem 3.4: $\mathrm{MOP}(G)$ is decidable for every token-by-token (iterative) generator (Def. 15) — a generator parameterized by a randomized Turing machine $M$ that halts on all inputs, which given the tokens so far and arbitrary auxiliary state emits one more token, until EOS. $M$ may do arbitrary finite computation and use randomness, so this covers transformer LLMs with any computable decoding rule (logits, beam search, top-$k$, top-$p$: Example 1), LLMs calling other LLMs, diffusion models, code interpreters, tool use. Two honest caveats to keep in mind: (i) this is a computability restriction, not a capacity or complexity restriction — it is not a "non-uniform" class in any technical sense, and it does not restrict expressiveness (every distribution on $\Sigma^*$ has a token-by-token generator by the chain rule); (ii) $G$ itself need not halt, which is why the folklore "total TM has decidable support" cannot be invoked directly.

Scope: all collections, or most? The dividing line is identifiability in the limit, characterized by Angluin's tell-tale condition (Def. 11, Thm. 2.2): $\mathcal{L}$ is identifiable from positive data iff there is an effective procedure producing, for each $i$, a finite $T_i \subseteq L_i$ such that no $L_j \supseteq T_i$ is a proper subset of $L_i$. This exactly blocks over-generalization — the pathology that from positive data you never see a counterexample to a strict superset of the truth. Non-identifiable collections are the generic case: Gold showed every super-finite collection (all finite languages plus at least one infinite one) is non-identifiable, which rules out the regular languages, the context-free languages, and the computable languages. So "most collections" is a fair gloss, though it is a qualitative statement about an uncountable zoo, not a measure-theoretic one.

The question. KM24 proved the remarkable positive result that consistent generation in the limit is possible for every countable collection — in stark contrast to identification. Their algorithm tracks "critical" languages and generates from the deepest one; but they observed that it becomes consistent precisely by sacrificing breadth (early on it covers a lot and hallucinates; later it narrows to be safe), and left open:

Is it possible to achieve consistent language generation with breadth, or is there an inherent trade-off between consistency and breadth?

Formally: for which countable collections $\mathcal{L}$ does there exist a generating algorithm whose support converges (in probability, in the above sense) to $K \setminus S_n$ for every $K \in \mathcal{L}$ and every valid $P$? The gap KM24 leaves is that their positive result says nothing about breadth, and breadth looks intuitively weaker than identification — you only have to cover the support of $K$, not name $K$. The paper's answer is that this intuition is wrong.

Main idea

The answer is negative, and sharply so: within the class $\mathcal{G}$ of generating algorithms with decidable MOP, generation with breadth is exactly as hard as identification. For every countable $\mathcal{L}$ that is non-trivial for generation and not identifiable in the limit, no algorithm in $\mathcal{G}$ generates with breadth at any rate (not merely: not in the limit) — while there is an algorithm in $\mathcal{G}$ that generates consistently without breadth at the optimal rate $e^{-n}$. Conversely, if $\mathcal{L}$ is identifiable, then for every $g(n) = o(n)$ some algorithm in $\mathcal{G}$ generates with breadth at rate $e^{-g(n)}$. Since MOP is decidable for every token-by-token generator, the impossibility covers present-day LLMs and essentially any pipeline built around them. So hallucination and mode collapse are not two independent engineering defects to be fixed separately; in this idealization they are the two sides of one dichotomy, and a model that attains breadth must hallucinate.

The mechanism, in one sentence: a generator that achieves breadth and whose support membership is decidable is a membership oracle for $K$, hence a source of negative examples — and negative examples make every countable collection identifiable (Gold). Breadth is what turns silence into information: once $\operatorname{supp}(G) = K$ exactly, "$G$ never emits $x$" certifies $x \notin K$. That is precisely the information positive-only learners provably cannot have.

As a byproduct — and really as a prerequisite, since the reduction produces an identifier at a rate and one must know that no rate is possible — they map the learning curves of both tasks in the universal-rates framework, and the two taxonomies are different and both near-tight:

  • Identification (Thm. 3.1): a dichotomy. For every countable $\mathcal{L}$ non-trivial for identification, either $\mathcal{L}$ satisfies Angluin's condition, in which case for every $g(n) = o(n)$ there is a learner at rate $e^{-g(n)}$ and none beats $e^{-n}$; or $\mathcal{L}$ admits no rate at all. Two structural comments. First, this is a dichotomy, whereas binary classification under universal rates exhibits a trichotomy ($e^{-n}$ / $n^{-1}$ / arbitrarily slow) [BHM+21], and $L_1$ regression exhibits infinitely many rates [AHK+24]; the loss and the task, not just the class, shape the landscape. Second, and more striking: in universal classification every measurable class is learnable at some rate (a Bayes-consistent learner exists); in identification there are collections with no Bayes-consistent learner, and they are exactly the non-Angluin ones. The residual gap is the $e^{-g(n)}$ vs. $e^{-n}$ slack, which is not an artifact: it comes from having to guess an unknown distribution-dependent stopping time, which positive-only data cannot estimate.
  • Consistent generation (Thm. 3.2): exponential, unconditionally. For every countable $\mathcal{L}$ there is a generating algorithm at rate $e^{-n}$, and for every $\mathcal{L}$ non-trivial for generation no algorithm beats $e^{-n}$. So $e^{-n}$ is optimal, and — pleasantly — it is attained by KM24's algorithm run unmodified, with no batching or boosting. They in fact prove something stronger: with probability $1 - Ce^{-cn}$ the trained model can emit infinitely many fresh strings of $K$, not just one. This lifts the KM24 separation between identification and generation from the online model into the statistical model, quantitatively.
  • Positive and negative examples (Thm. 3.13): exactly $e^{-n}$, for every countable collection. Combined with a rejection-sampling converter (Prop. 6.5), this yields consistent generation with breadth at exponential rate for every countable collection once negative examples are available. This is the paper's constructive reading of post-training: feedback encoding "that output was wrong" is not a nicety, it is the information-theoretic ingredient that makes simultaneous validity and coverage possible at all.
  • Robustness: two relaxations of breadth are still impossible. For stable generators with decidable MOP (stability = for every $K$ and every enumeration, $\operatorname{supp}(G_n)$ eventually stops changing — a condition any breadth-achieving generator automatically satisfies, and a loose formalization of early stopping / LR decay), non-identifiable collections also admit no unambiguous generator (Def. 8: eventually $|\operatorname{supp}(G_n) \triangle K| < \min_{L \neq K}|\operatorname{supp}(G_n)\triangle L|$ — unboundedly many hallucinations and omissions are permitted, as long as $K$ is the closest language) and no generator with approximate breadth (Def. 9: eventually $\operatorname{supp}(G_n) \subseteq K$ and $|K \setminus \operatorname{supp}(G_n)| < \infty$ — finitely many, but arbitrarily many, omissions). The two relaxations are incomparable (the first allows hallucination, the second forbids it; the second allows generating with breadth from a strict subset of $K$, the first does not). That both collapse to the same impossibility is the strongest evidence that the obstruction is structural rather than an artifact of demanding exact support equality.
  • Supplementary exact-rate results: identification at exactly $e^{-n}$ given a subset oracle on Angluin collections (Prop. 3.10), for finite collections (Prop. 3.11), and for countable collections of finite languages (Prop. 3.12); and Thm. B.1, that a subset oracle substitutes for Angluin's tell-tale oracle, so KM24's critical-language algorithm plus subset queries identifies any identifiable collection without ever being handed a tell-tale.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever idea is the one in Lemma 7.1 — the argument that upgrades the main theorem from "exact support equality" to "merely closer to $K$ than to anything else". Suppose $G$ is unambiguous and $L \supsetneq K$ is an over-generalization. Decompose: $$|\operatorname{supp}(G)\triangle K| \;\ge\; |\operatorname{supp}(G)\setminus L| + |K \setminus \operatorname{supp}(G)|,$$ $$|\operatorname{supp}(G)\triangle L| \;=\; |\operatorname{supp}(G)\setminus L| + |K\setminus \operatorname{supp}(G)| + |L \setminus (K \cup \operatorname{supp}(G))|.$$ Chaining with unambiguity $|\operatorname{supp}(G)\triangle K| < |\operatorname{supp}(G)\triangle L|$ and cancelling gives $|L \setminus (K \cup \operatorname{supp}(G))| > 0$. So every strict superset of $K$ must contain a string the generator never emits — and because MOP is decidable and stability freezes the support, that string is findable in finite time. The symmetric-difference inequality has been converted into an explicit, effective refutation certificate against each over-generalization, which is exactly the obstruction (over-generalization) that makes positive-only identification impossible. That is a nice piece of combinatorics in service of a reduction.

But the review I would write is about where the content of the headline theorem actually sits, and I think it is somewhat displaced from where the paper puts it.

The theory lives entirely at the level of supports, i.e. of which strings receive exactly zero probability — and that is a brittle invariant for the systems being modeled. A softmax-parameterized autoregressive model assigns strictly positive probability to every finite string over its vocabulary. Under Definitions 2 and 4, such a model trivially achieves breadth and trivially and maximally hallucinates, for every $K$, at every $n$, forever. Nothing about its quality enters. The entire trade-off the paper studies is therefore invisible to unconstrained real LLMs and becomes visible only once you hard-zero part of the output space — via constrained decoding, a grammar, a trie, top-$k$/top-$p$ truncation. (Example 1 does cover thresholded decoding, so the formalism is not vacuous; but it means the theorem is really about the support-shaping layer, not about the learned distribution.) Symmetrically, a single rogue string of probability $10^{-100}$ is a full hallucination failure, while a model placing $0.999$ mass on one string and $10^{-100}$ on each of infinitely many others has perfect consistency and perfect breadth. The authors clearly know this — Open Question 2 asks for the Pareto frontier of approximate consistency and breadth, and their own framing of mode collapse via $\mathrm{KL}(P|G) = \infty$ is an admission that the forward KL is being used only as a support indicator. But the gap between "measure-zero combinatorics" and "hallucination rates" is the whole gap between this paper and Kalai–Vempala's quantitative bound, and the title's promise of "trade-offs" is really delivered by the follow-up literature (Kleinberg–Wei) rather than here: there is no trade-off curve in this paper, only a dichotomy.

Three further specifics, all honest rather than rhetorical:

  1. The MOP hypothesis turned out to be removable, which relocates the paper's contribution. The paper's own "Subsequent Progress" note records that Charikar–Pabbaraju [CP24a] resolved Open Question 1 by exhibiting a collection from which no generator achieves breadth, with no decidability hypothesis; [CP24b] and the authors' own [KMV24] then extended this to all collections violating a variant of Angluin's condition. So the decidability-of-MOP condition — presented as the scope of the result and defended at length (Thm. 3.4, Example 1, Remark 3 on noisy oracles via $\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{EXP}$, Appendix A) — was not load-bearing for the qualitative claim. What survives as this paper's distinctive contribution is (a) the rate-level statements, which the later unconditional results do not subsume, and (b) the universal-rates taxonomy for identification and generation, which is independently interesting and is where the actual technical difficulty lies (Lemmas 5.4, 5.7, 5.8, 5.11). I would read the paper primarily as a universal-rates paper with an impossibility corollary, which is close to the inverse of how it is marketed.
  2. Validity ($\operatorname{supp}(P) = K$ exactly) is a strong and consequential idealization. It is what makes an infinite i.i.d. sample a.s. a complete enumeration of $K$, so the statistical and online models can be shuttled between. But in any realistic reading, the training distribution's support is strictly smaller than the set of true strings: the data covers a biased, sparse slice of the facts. Under that relaxation the target is not even pinned down by infinitely many samples, and "breadth" would have to be redefined against the set of truths rather than the support of the data. The paper does not model this, and it is arguably a more fundamental barrier to breadth than the combinatorics of $\mathcal{L}$.
  3. Where the formalism does earn its keep, and should be credited: the negative-example result (Thm. 3.13 + Prop. 6.5) is not a soft "feedback helps" slogan — it is an exact-exponential-rate positive result for all countable collections, with a clean explanation of why positive-only data loses a factor: with labels you can estimate the unknown stopping time $t^*$ from held-out data (Lemma 8.4), and without labels you cannot, so you must guess it with a slowly growing $f(n)$ and pay $e^{-n/f(n)}$ instead of $e^{-n}$. That is a genuine, quantitative, well-isolated statement about what supervision buys, and it is the most defensible thing in the paper to carry over to practice.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Three families of statements, which should be kept apart.

(I) The impossibility (Thm. 3.3, statistical; Thm. 3.5, in the limit). Let $\mathcal{G}$ be the class of generating algorithms with decidable MOP. For every countable $\mathcal{L}$ that is non-trivial for generation and not identifiable in the limit: no $(G_n) \in \mathcal{G}$ generates with breadth from $\mathcal{L}$ at any rate; and no $(G_n) \in \mathcal{G}$ generates with breadth from $\mathcal{L}$ in the limit (the latter holds for any non-identifiable $\mathcal{L}$, with no non-triviality needed). Since KM24's own algorithm is deterministic with computable singleton support, it lies in $\mathcal{G}$, so in particular their algorithm provably cannot achieve breadth on any non-identifiable collection — confirming their conjecture about their own construction.

(II) The positive / rate results. (a) For every countable $\mathcal{L}$, consistent generation (no breadth) at rate $e^{-n}$ by an algorithm in $\mathcal{G}$; optimal, since no algorithm whatsoever beats $e^{-n}$ on collections non-trivial for generation. (b) For every identifiable $\mathcal{L}$ and every $g(n) = o(n)$, generation with breadth at rate $e^{-g(n)}$ by an algorithm in $\mathcal{G}$. (c) The identification dichotomy of Thm. 3.1. (d) With positive and negative examples, identification — and hence breadth — at exactly $e^{-n}$ for every countable $\mathcal{L}$.

(III) Robustness (Thms. 3.6–3.9). Adding the stability hypothesis, the impossibility extends to unambiguous generation and to approximate breadth, both in the statistical and the in-the-limit models.

How (I) is proved: the breadth-to-identification reduction.

The cleanest instance is the online one (Thm. 3.5), and it exhibits the whole idea. Suppose $G$ achieves consistency and breadth in the limit on $\mathcal{L}$, with $\mathrm{MOP}(G)$ decidable. Build an identifier $\mathcal{I}$ that at each step $t$: observes $s_t$; retrains $G$ from scratch on $S_t$; uses the MOP decider to label the first $t$ domain elements $x_1,\dots,x_t$ by $\mathrm{MOP}(G)(x_i) \in {0,1}$; feeds those labeled examples to $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PN}}$, Gold's identifier from positive and negative examples (which exists for every countable collection, Thm. 2.3: output the lowest index consistent with all labels so far); and outputs $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PN}}$'s guess. After the finite time $t_G$ at which $\operatorname{supp}(G) = K$, the decider's answers are exactly $\mathbf{1}{x \in K}$, so from then on $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PN}}$ is being fed a correct labeled enumeration of the whole domain, and identifies $K$ after a further finite $t_{\mathrm{PN}}$. Hence $\mathcal{L}$ is identifiable in the limit — contradiction. (Note $\mathcal{I}$ need not know $t_G$ or $t_{\mathrm{PN}}$, and does not know when it has succeeded; identification in the limit does not require it to.)

So the mechanism is: breadth manufactures negative examples; decidable MOP makes them readable; Gold's theorem then collapses generation-with-breadth into identification. Section 1.2 is a well-written catalogue of why weaker properties of $G$ do not suffice — $G$ being non-adaptive gives you only an algorithm-independent enumeration (useless: there are non-identifiable collections that stay non-identifiable under many enumerations); $G$ sampling from a fixed, even computable, distribution gives you Angluin's 1988 statistical model (useless: non-identifiability persists); a subset oracle answering "$\operatorname{supp}(G) \subseteq L_i$?" would suffice — one reads off $K$ as the largest index in KM24's nested chain of critical languages $C_1 \supseteq C_2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq (C_i = K) \supseteq \cdots$ — but is unimplementable. The contribution is that the much weaker membership access is enough.

The statistical version (Lemma 6.4) and why it needs the rate theory. In the statistical setting the analogous reduction is direct: assume $(G_n) \in \mathcal{G}$ achieves breadth at rate $R$, so $\Pr[\mathcal{E}_n] \ge 1 - CR(cn)$ where $\mathcal{E}_n = {\operatorname{supp}(G_n) = K \setminus S_n}$. Define $\mathcal{I}_n(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ to be the smallest $j \in [n]$ with $$\mathbf{1}{x_i \in L_j} = \mathbf{1}{x_i \in \operatorname{supp}(G_n) \cup {X_1,\dots,X_n}}\quad\text{for all } i \in [n],$$ computable precisely because $\mathrm{MOP}(G_n)$ is decidable and $\mathcal{L}$ has a membership oracle. Let $z = \min{j : L_j = K}$ and let $n^*$ be the largest index of a domain element witnessing $L_j \neq L_z$ over the finitely many $j < z$. On $\mathcal{E}_n$ one has $\operatorname{supp}(G_n) \cup S_n = K$, so the test vector is exactly $K$'s indicator on the first $n$ coordinates; for $n \ge n^*$ all $j<z$ are eliminated, so $\mathcal{I}_n = z$. Hence $\Pr[L_{\mathcal{I}_n} \neq K] \le C R(cn)$ for all $n \ge n^*$: identification at rate $R$.

This is where the subtlety announced in §1.2(A) bites. Non-identifiability in the limit does not by itself forbid identification at some rate in the statistical setting — the analogy is thresholds over $\mathbb{R}$, which are not Littlestone-online-learnable yet are learnable at a linear universal (indeed uniform) rate, and more sharply: in universal classification every measurable class has a rate. So the contradiction requires the much stronger:

Theorem 3.1, lower half: $\mathcal{L}$ non-identifiable in the limit $\Rightarrow$ $\mathcal{L}$ admits no rate. Three steps.

Step 1 (Lemma 5.7): strengthen Angluin's 1988 lower bound from "fails to stabilize correctly" to "errs infinitely often". Angluin's Corollary 10 (Thm. 5.6) says: if $\mathcal{L}$ violates the tell-tale condition, then for every learner there is a valid $P$ such that with probability $\ge 1/3$ the learner fails to converge to a correct index — i.e. it either does not stabilize or stabilizes to a wrong language. That leaves open a learner that is eventually always correct but keeps switching among different indices _of $K$_ (possible, because $\mathcal{L}$ may list $K$ repeatedly). The paper closes this by canonicalization: define $h'_n$ to post-process $h_n$'s output $i^_$ to the smallest $j \le i^_$ agreeing with $L_{i^_}$ on the first $n$ domain elements (computable with $O(n\cdot i^_)$ membership queries). If $h_n$ were eventually always correct with probability $> 2/3$, then $h'_n$ would eventually always output the _fixed_{P^\infty {X_i}\sim} index $z$, i.e. stabilize correctly — contradicting Angluin. Conclusion: $\Pr_ \neq K}\big] \ge 1/3$.}\big[\limsup_n {L_{h_n

Step 2: identify the measure-theoretic gap. What Step 1 gives is $\Pr[\limsup_n E_n] \ge 1/3$; what "no rate" needs is $\limsup_n \Pr[E_n] > 0$. Reverse Fatou gives $\Pr[\limsup E_n] \ge \limsup \Pr[E_n]$ — the wrong direction — and the gap is real: independent coins with success probability $1/n$ have $\Pr[\limsup E_n] = 1$ (second Borel–Cantelli) but $\limsup_n \Pr[E_n] = 0$. So the problem's structure must be used.

Step 3 (Lemma 5.8): a boosting / self-improvement argument that is then killed by Borel–Cantelli. Suppose for contradiction some learner has $\limsup_n \Pr[L_{h_n} \neq K] = c < 1/2$ for every valid $P$. Then beyond a $P$-dependent $n_0$ the per-round error is at most $\tfrac12 - \tilde c/2$. Boost: split $n$ samples into $\lfloor n/\log n\rfloor$ non-overlapping batches of size $\log n$, run $h_{\log n}$ on each, canonicalize every output index to $z$ via Lemma 5.4, and take the majority. Chernoff gives $\Pr[h'*n \neq z] \le e^{-\Theta(n/\log^2 n)}$, which is summable, so $\sum_n \Pr[L*{h'_n} \neq K] < \infty$ and the first Borel–Cantelli lemma yields $\Pr[\limsup_n {L_{h'_n}\neq K}] = 0$ — contradicting Step 1 applied to $h'$. Hence for some valid $P$, $\limsup_n \Pr[\text{error}] \ge 1/2$, so no rate exists. The structure is worth naming: _the hypothesis of a sub-$1/2$ asymptotic error is self-amplifying into a summable error, and summability is exactly what converts a statement about $\limsup_n \Pr[E_n]$ into one about $\Pr[\limsup_n E_n]$, where the classical lower bound lives._

The enabling combinatorial lemma (Lemma 5.4, used in both steps). Because $\mathcal{L}$ may list $K$ at many indices, batches that all succeed may return different indices and a naive majority vote over indices fails. Fix: replace each returned index $i_j$ by $\hat{i}^n_j = \min{\ell \le i_j : L_\ell[n] = L_{i_j}[n]}$, where $L[n] := L \cap {x_1,\dots,x_n}$ is the $n$-projection. Claim: there is $n_0 = n_0(K,\mathcal{L},X)$, independent of the multiset of indices, such that for $n \ge n_0$, $L_{i_j} = K \Rightarrow \hat{i}^n_j = z$. Reason: each of the finitely many $L_\ell$ with $\ell < z$ differs from $L_z$ at some domain element; let $n_0$ be the largest such witness index; then projections onto the first $n \ge n_0$ coordinates separate all pre-$z$ languages from $K$, while every index naming $K$ has the same projection as $L_z$. This simultaneously makes the vote well-defined and computable with membership queries only. Without it the whole boosting apparatus does not typecheck.

Theorem 3.1, upper half, and why "almost" exponential (Lemma 5.5). Mechanism: (i) Prop. 5.2 — an infinite i.i.d. draw from a valid $P$ is a.s. an enumeration of $\operatorname{supp}(P) = K$ ($\supseteq$ by a union bound over the complement, $\subseteq$ by the second Borel–Cantelli lemma on ${X_n = x}$ for each $x$ with $p_x > 0$), so online identifiers can legitimately be fed i.i.d. data; (ii) Prop. 5.3 — the last-mistake time $T_{\mathcal{A}}$ of an in-the-limit identifier is a.s. finite, hence there exists a $P$-dependent $t^*$ with $\Pr[T_{\mathcal{A}} \le t^*] \ge 6/7$; (iii) batch into $n/f(n)$ blocks, run $\mathcal{A}$ per block, canonicalize (Lemma 5.4), take a $5/7$-majority; Hoeffding over the $n/f(n)$ independent blocks gives error $\le e^{-2g(n)/49}$. Two obstructions distinguish this from BHM+21's construction, and the paper is explicit about both: there is no feedback on guesses (positive data only), so $t^*$ cannot be estimated and must be guessed by a slowly increasing $f(n)$ with $n/f(n) \ge g(n)$ — this, and only this, is why the rate is $e^{-g(n)}$ for arbitrary $g(n) = o(n)$ rather than $e^{-n}$; and different blocks may name $K$ differently, which is what Lemma 5.4 repairs. The lower bound on rates (Lemma 5.1) is the usual "two languages sharing a point" argument: put mass $\ge 1/2$ on the shared $x$ under both $P_{L_i}, P_{L_j}$; with probability $\ge 2^{-n}$ the sample is $(x,\dots,x)$, on which the learner cannot be right about both, so error $\ge 2^{-(n+1)}$ infinitely often for one of them.

Theorem 3.2 (generation at exponential rate) — the slick part. Boosting is unavailable for generation: aggregation over strings is hopeless (correct batches emit different strings, and a few bad batches agreeing on one invalid string fools a plurality rule), and letting each generated string vote for the languages containing it is both non-computable and wrong, because every correct string also votes for every superset of $K$ — if $L_1 = X$, everything votes for $L_1$. That is over-generalization again, and if such a vote worked one could identify every countable collection, contradicting the lower bounds. The resolution is to avoid aggregation entirely. Lemma 5.11 isolates a sufficient condition for a "works-in-the-limit" algorithm to achieve exponential universal rate with no modification: if for every $K$ there exist a finite trigger set ${x_{i_1},\dots,x_{i_\ell}} \subseteq K$ and a finite $n_0$, both depending only on $K$ and the enumerations of $\mathcal{L}$ and $X$ (crucially not on the sample or its order), such that the algorithm is correct on every input of size $\ge n_0$ containing the trigger set, then $$\Pr[\exists j:\ x_{i_j}\notin S_n] \le \sum_{j\in[\ell]} (1-p_{i_j})^n \le \ell\, e^{-n \min_j p_{i_j}},$$ giving rate $e^{-cn}$ with $c = \min_j p_{i_j}$ — distribution-dependent, which is exactly what the universal-rates framework permits. Lemmas 5.12 and 5.13 then verify that KM24's algorithm (both the subset-oracle version and the membership-oracle version built on $m$-critical languages, $L_j$ being $m$-critical w.r.t. $S_n$ if $S_n \subseteq L_j$ and for all $i<j$ with $S_n \subseteq L_i$ one has $L_j[m]\subseteq L_i[m]$) has this property: the trigger set is, for each $L_i$ with $i<z$ and $L_z \not\subseteq L_i$, the smallest-indexed witness in $L_z \setminus L_i$. Once all those witnesses are in the sample, $L_z$ is critical (resp. $m$-critical for every $m$) and remains so forever, so the algorithm generates from a critical language of index $\ge z$, which is therefore a subset of $L_z = K$. This "finite, order-independent certificate of eventual correctness $\Rightarrow$ exponential universal rate" template is a reusable observation and the authors flag it as such; Open Question 4 asks whether the conversion can be made black-box (their identification conversion is black-box, their generation conversion is not).

The matching generation lower bound (Lemma 5.10) uses non-triviality for generation: take $x$ and finite $\mathcal{L}'$ with $\bigcap_{L\in\mathcal{L}'} L = {x_{\ell_1},\dots,x_{\ell_B}}$ finite, and a family ${P_L}_{L \in \mathcal{L}'}$ with $P_L$ valid for $L$ and all agreeing on the masses of those $B$ common elements. Condition on the event $E_n$ that the sample is exactly $(x_{\ell_1},\dots,x_{\ell_B}, x_{\ell_1},\dots,x_{\ell_1})$, which has probability $\ge Ce^{-cn}$ with the same constants under every $P_L$. On $E_n$ the generator's output law $p_n$ is a fixed object, identical across the family. Either $p_n$ puts $\ge 1/2$ on the seen set (failure by repetition), or $\ge 1/2$ outside it — and every point outside $\bigcap \mathcal{L}'$ is outside some $L \in \mathcal{L}'$, so pigeonhole over $|\mathcal{L}'| = k$ fixes an $L$ receiving $\ge 1/(2k)$ hallucination mass. Either way the error is $\ge Ce^{-cn}/(2k)$ infinitely often under some $P_L$.

Completing Theorem 3.3. Non-identifiable case: Lemma 6.4 kills breadth at every rate; Thm. 3.2 supplies consistency without breadth at $e^{-n}$ (and KM24's generator, being a computable point mass, lies in $\mathcal{G}$); Lemma 5.10 says $e^{-n}$ is optimal. Identifiable case: Thm. 3.1 gives identification at $e^{-g(n)}$, and Prop. 6.5 converts an index into a generator with breadth and decidable MOP by rejection sampling — draw $\hat{n}$ from any distribution over $\mathbb{N}$, accept $x_{\hat n}$ iff $x_{\hat n} \in L_z$ — so $\operatorname{supp} = L_z$ exactly. (Remark 4: KM24's algorithm must be extended to emit $m$ samples per step; routine, and stays in $\mathcal{G}$.) The two directions together give the clean statement: _within $\mathcal{G}$, generation with breadth $\iff$ identifiability $\iff$ Angluin's tell-tale condition_, modulo the $e^{-g(n)}$ / $e^{-n}$ slack.

Theorem 3.4 (MOP decidable for token-by-token generators). The generator is driven by a randomized TM $M$ that halts on all inputs, mapping (prefix, auxiliary state) to (next token, new state). $G$ itself may run forever (unbounded token count), so one cannot invoke the folklore "total TM has decidable support" (Lemma 6.1) directly. Decider for input $s$ of length $m$: for $t = 1,\dots,m$, check whether $M$ can emit $s_t$ conditioned on having emitted $s_1\cdots s_{t-1}$; output Yes iff all checks pass, i.e. iff $\prod_t p_t(s_t) > 0$. Each check is finite by two folklore lemmas about total randomized machines: Lemma 6.3 — for each input there is a finite $n_p$ bounding the number of random bits read, uniformly over realizations (otherwise one constructs, for every $n$, an assignment on which $M$ reads the $(n{+}1)$-st bit, hence a non-halting run) — and Lemma 6.2 — only finitely many steps occur between consecutive random-bit reads (same argument). So one can brute-force all $2^{n_t}$ random strings; $n_t$ is unknown but found by iterating $k$ until $M$ always halts before reading bit $k+1$. Remark 3 notes that a noisy membership oracle (correct with probability $\ge 2/3$ in finite time) is no weaker, since $\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{EXP}$. Appendix A gives the matching negative example: a generator that reads its ternary random tape to the first $2$, parses the prefix as $\langle M\rangle w$, simulates $M$ on $w$, and emits $\langle M\rangle w 1$ if it halts — support membership is the halting problem.

Part (III): the relaxations. Online unambiguous generation (Thm. 3.7). Identifier maintains two version spaces inside ${L_1,\dots,L_t}$: $CS(t) = {L : L \supseteq S_t}$ (consistent with observed positives) and $CG(t) = {L : L[t] \subseteq \operatorname{supp}(G_t) \cup S_t}$ (consistent with the generator, checkable with the MOP decider), and outputs the smallest index in $CS(t)\cap CG(t)$. Condition (A), $K$ eventually in both: unambiguity forces $|\operatorname{supp}(G)\triangle K| < \infty$ (a strict inequality between two quantities both of which would otherwise be $\infty$), stability freezes $K \setminus \operatorname{supp}(G_t)$ to a fixed finite set, and all of that finite set eventually appears in the enumeration. Condition (B), every $i<z$ eventually excluded: if $K\setminus L_i \neq \emptyset$ a positive witness eventually kicks $L_i$ out of $CS(t)$; if $L_i \supsetneq K$, Lemma 7.1 (above) produces a fixed $x_{j(i)} \in L_i \setminus \operatorname{supp}(G_t)$ — fixed because the support is stable — so $L_i[j(i)] \not\subseteq \operatorname{supp}(G_t)\cup S_t$ and $L_i$ leaves $CG(t)$. Online approximate breadth (Thm. 3.9). Same architecture as Thm. 3.5, with one patch: the generator's support misses a finite set $M = K\setminus \operatorname{supp}(G)$, fixed by stability, so label $x_i$ by $\mathrm{MOP}(G)(x_i)$ and then overwrite any $x_i \in S_t$ labeled $0$ with $1$; after the finite time at which all of $M$ has appeared in the enumeration, the labels are exactly $\mathbf{1}{\cdot \in K}$, and Gold's $\mathcal{I}*{\mathrm{PN}}$ finishes the job. _Statistical $\Rightarrow$ online transfer (Lemmas 7.3–7.6)._ Two moves. First, Angluin's distribution induced by a sequence: given an enumeration $\sigma$ of $K$, set $P*\sigma(x) = \sum_{j : \sigma_j = x} 2^{-(j+1)}$, which is valid for $K$ and samplable from fair coin flips plus prefix access to $\sigma$ (flip until the first head; if that takes $I$ trials output $\sigma_{I+1}$) — Prop. 7.2. So any statistical generator can be simulated inside the online model by internally synthesizing i.i.d. draws from $P_\sigma$. Second, a stable generator achieving any vanishing rate almost surely stabilizes to zero error along an infinite i.i.d. stream: since stability makes the error a function of the (eventually frozen) support, a union bound over "support frozen by $n_3$" and "error zero at $n_3$" suffices. Composing, the statistical impossibilities (Thms. 3.6, 3.8) follow from the online ones by contradiction. Note the main theorem does not use this route — it goes directly through the universal-rates dichotomy — which is why it needs no stability assumption while the relaxations do.

Part (II)(d): positive and negative examples (Thm. 3.13). Valid distributions are now over $X\times{0,1}$ with $\operatorname{supp}(P_X) = X$ and $\Pr[Y=1 \mid X=x] = \mathbf{1}{x\in K}$ (Def. 16). Lower bound $e^{-n}$: as in Lemma 5.1. Upper bound exactly $e^{-n}$: black-box conversion of any in-the-limit identifier, batch-and-majority-vote as before, but now the batch size can be estimated rather than guessed. Lemma 8.4 (an adaptation of BHM+21's Lemma 4.4 to the identification loss) splits $S_n$ in half, trains $\lfloor n/2t\rfloor$ independent copies at each candidate batch size $t$ on the first half, and estimates the per-size identification error on the second half by $\hat e_t = $ the fraction of copies whose predicted language mislabels some held-out point — computable with membership queries alone — then sets $\hat t_n = \inf{t : \hat e_t < 1/4}$. Hoeffding plus a union bound give $\Pr[\hat t_n \notin T] \le Ce^{-cn}$ for $T = {t \le t^* : \Pr_{S_t}[L_{h_t} \neq K] < 3/8}$. This is the precise technical locus of the positive-vs-negative-example separation: negative examples are what let you detect that your current hypothesis is an over-generalization, hence estimate the stopping time, hence get exactly $e^{-n}$ instead of $e^{-g(n)}$.

Structural quantity controlling achievability. There is no new combinatorial dimension here. The controlling condition is the classical one: Angluin's tell-tale condition (equivalently, identifiability in the limit). Within $\mathcal{G}$, breadth is achievable iff it holds; consistency alone is achievable always. The paper's contribution on this axis is to show that the condition governs not just in-the-limit achievability but the entire rate landscape — a collection either sits at (almost) $e^{-n}$ or has no learning curve at all. The subsequent work it cites ([CP24b], [KMV24]) shows that variants of Angluin's condition characterize breadth unconditionally, and gives unconditional characterizations of unambiguous generation and approximate breadth with and without stability, so the tell-tale condition does turn out to be the right combinatorial object for this whole family of questions.

Broader context

The subfield. Inductive inference begins with Gold [Gol67], who formalized identification in the limit: an adversary fixes $K$ from a known collection $\mathcal{L}$ and streams an arbitrary enumeration of $K$; a learner outputs an index at each step and must eventually stabilize on a correct one. Gold's results set the shape of everything since: collections of finite languages are identifiable, all finite collections are identifiable, but every super-finite collection (all finite languages plus at least one infinite one) is not identifiable from positive data — and is identifiable once negative data is supplied. The positive-data barrier is over-generalization: a learner that guesses a strict superset of $K$ never sees a counterexample. This is the formal skeleton of Chomsky's poverty-of-the-stimulus argument, and it is why the setting became a touchstone in learnability debates about language acquisition. Angluin then (i) exhibited non-trivial positively-identifiable collections (pattern languages, [Ang79]), (ii) gave the exact characterization [Ang80]: $\mathcal{L}$ is identifiable from positive data iff each $L_i$ has a finite tell-tale $T_i \subseteq L_i$ such that no $L_j \supseteq T_i$ is a proper subset of $L_i$ — the tell-tale is the certificate that blocks over-generalization, and Angluin's algorithm needs an oracle producing it (the present paper's Thm. B.1 shows a subset oracle substitutes); and (iii) [Ang88] moved to stochastic examples — i.i.d. draws from a distribution whose support is exactly $K$ — proving that randomness does not enlarge the identifiable collections. Gold's model is the historical predecessor of PAC; the paper's Appendix C carefully separates it from Littlestone-style online learning and from BHM+21's online game (no feedback on guesses; the adversary must exhaust $K$; the target is fixed in advance rather than merely consistent so far), and Example 3 gives a collection with an infinite Littlestone tree that is nevertheless identifiable from positive data — so the Malliaris–Moran PEC characterization (PEC learnable $\iff$ no infinite Littlestone tree) does not transfer to identification.

The revival is Kleinberg–Mullainathan [KM24, NeurIPS], who asked for generation instead of identification and found that the landscape inverts: every countable collection admits consistent generation in the limit, via the critical-language algorithm. Reading that against Gold–Angluin is the single most interesting fact in this literature — generating validly is strictly easier than knowing what you are generating from — and the present paper's theorem is its necessary complement: the easiness is bought entirely with mode collapse.

Two closely related works worth knowing properly. (1) Adam Tauman Kalai and Santosh Vempala, "Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate" (STOC 2024): for a trained model $G_n$, the hallucination rate $\mathbb{E}_{S,x\sim G_n}\mathbf{1}{x\notin K} \gtrsim \hat R - \mathrm{Mis}_P(G_n) - 1/\sqrt n$, where $\hat R$ is the monofact rate (fraction of facts appearing exactly once in training) and $\mathrm{Mis}$ is miscalibration. This is the quantitative, mass-level counterpart to the present paper's support-level dichotomy: it says calibration plus a heavy tail of rare facts forces hallucination, under assumptions on $P$ and $K$; the present paper says coverage forces hallucination, under assumptions on $\mathcal{L}$ and essentially none on $P$. Read together, they are the two coordinates of the problem. (2) Moses Charikar and Chirag Pabbaraju, "Exploring Facets of Language Generation in the Limit" (COLT 2025), with the companion Kalavasis–Mehrotra–Velegkas [KMV24]: Charikar–Pabbaraju resolved the paper's own Open Question 1 by constructing a collection from which no generator — with no decidability or stability hypothesis — generates with breadth; both groups then extended this to all collections violating a variant of Angluin's condition, and KMV24 gave unconditional characterizations of unambiguous generation and approximate breadth (with and without stability) plus a "best-of-three-worlds" algorithm, given a subset oracle, that is consistent, stable, and achieves breadth whenever breadth is possible. Also: Kleinberg–Wei [KW25] attack Open Question 2 in the online model, designing algorithms with no hallucination in the limit that nonetheless cover a non-trivial fraction of $K$ — the beginning of a real trade-off curve. And Li–Raman–Tewari [LRT25] give a PAC/Littlestone-flavored treatment, defining uniform and non-uniform generatability dimensions, allowing uncountable collections, showing the dimension is incomparable to VC, and handling prompted generation.

A plausible follow-up. The honest open space is quantitative and supervision-aware, and it sits at the intersection of this paper's two halves. Concretely: what is the label complexity of breadth? The paper's dichotomy is an all-or-nothing statement about two extreme supervision regimes (positive-only: breadth impossible on non-identifiable collections; positive-and-negative: breadth at $e^{-n}$ on every countable collection). Interpolate. Give the learner $n$ i.i.d. positive samples plus a budget of $m(n)$ adaptively chosen membership queries $\mathbf{1}{x \in K}$ — the natural formalization of RLHF-style post-training feedback, and the natural active-learning version of Gold's negative-example theorem. Questions: for a fixed collection, what is the minimal $m(n)$ (as a function of $n$ and of a tell-tale-like complexity measure of $\mathcal{L}$ — say the size of the smallest tell-tale witnessing $K$ against its predecessors in the enumeration) for which breadth becomes achievable at some rate, and at the optimal $e^{-n}$? Is there a sharp threshold, or does breadth degrade gracefully in $m$? One would expect the answer to be governed by the number of over-generalizations $L_i \supsetneq K$ with $i < z$ that must be refuted, which the proofs of Lemmas 5.12/5.13 already isolate as the operative finite set — so the machinery is in place, and the payoff would be a theoretical statement about how much feedback post-training needs, rather than merely that it needs some. A second, more ambitious variant: do the same for a mass-level definition of hallucination and coverage, i.e. ask for the achievable region of $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $G_n(X\setminus K)\le \alpha$ and $P(K\setminus \operatorname{supp} G_n)\le \beta$, which is the statistical analogue of Kleinberg–Wei and would finally make the word "trade-off" literal.

Connection to theoretical IR and generative retrieval. There is a real link here, but it runs in the opposite direction to the obvious reading, and it is worth being precise about that rather than selling the analogy as a free lunch.

The surface mapping is exact. In generative retrieval — DSI (Tay et al., Transformer Memory as a Differentiable Search Index, NeurIPS 2022), NCI (Wang et al. 2022), SEAL, and the whole atomic/semantic-docid line — a model autoregressively emits a document identifier. The two canonical failure modes are precisely the paper's two: the decoder emits a string that is not a valid identifier of any corpus document (hallucination: $\operatorname{supp}(G) \not\subseteq K$), and the decoder, for a given query, is unable to reach some relevant documents at all (coverage/recall failure, i.e. mode collapse: $\operatorname{supp}(G) \not\supseteq K$). The paper's generators are token-by-token with arbitrary computable decoding, which is exactly a constrained-beam-search docid decoder, so the formal class genuinely contains the objects of interest.

But the interesting observation is that generative retrieval is the regime where the paper's positive side is operative, and it is operative for a reason the theory explains cleanly. In GR the set of valid identifiers is finite and known: it is the corpus index. Practitioners enforce consistency by constrained decoding over a trie or FM-index, which literally hard-zeros every non-identifier continuation. That is $\operatorname{supp}(G) \subseteq {\text{valid docids}}$ by construction, with a trivially decidable MOP — a trie walk. And training against hard negatives (sampled non-relevant docids, contrastive objectives, distillation from a cross-encoder) is exactly the negative-example supervision that Gold's theorem, and the paper's Thm. 3.13 plus Prop. 6.5, show restores breadth at an exponential rate for every countable collection. So the theory's reading of GR practice is: the trie gives you consistency for free, hard negatives give you breadth, and the impossibility does not bite — which is why GR works at all. The impossibility bites where the target set is genuinely not known in advance: prompted/conditional generation, where $K$ is the per-query relevance set that must be inferred from positive judgments; dynamic corpora, where new docids appear and the decoder must generalize to identifier strings it has never been trained on (which is both the known weak point of DSI-style systems and precisely over-generalization in the paper's sense); and semantic/hierarchical docids, where the model is supposed to generalize over the identifier space rather than memorize a finite list, so the valid-identifier set stops being an explicit finite object. The paper even notes that its results extend to the prompted setting via KM24's reduction, and that is the version an IR theorist should care about.

Where the analogy breaks, explicitly, because these are not small gaps:

  • $K$ must be infinite for the paper's problem to be non-degenerate; a per-query relevance set is finite, and corpora are finite. With finite $K$ the learner eventually exhausts it and the "generate an unseen element" objective becomes vacuous — Gold's own easy positive result (collections of finite languages are identifiable). So the sharp impossibility simply does not apply to a fixed finite corpus; one would have to model asymptotically growing corpora or an infinite identifier space to recover it.
  • Breadth is support equality; IR cares about ranking. The theory is blind to everything a retrieval metric measures: top-$k$ truncation, graded relevance, the order of the emitted docids, nDCG. A GR model that assigns the relevant documents nonzero but astronomically small probability has perfect breadth and recall@$\infty$ = 1 while being useless at recall@10. Any serious transfer needs a mass-level or top-$k$-level notion of coverage, which is exactly the open problem the paper leaves (Open Question 2).
  • Validity ($\operatorname{supp}(P) = K$ exactly) is the assumption that relevance judgments are complete. IR has never had that: pooling bias and incomplete judgments mean the observed positives cover a biased sliver of the relevant set. Under incompleteness the target is not even determined in the limit, and "breadth" has to be defined against an unobserved truth set.

Vector search / ANN: I would not push a connection here. One can describe the surface resemblance — an HNSW or IVF index returns only genuine corpus points (consistency free) but may miss true neighbours (coverage failure), and graph reachability in HNSW is a genuine support-coverage property, with unreachable points a structural analogue of permanent mode collapse. But there is no learning-from-positive-examples structure, no unknown target drawn from a collection, and no over-generalization phenomenon; the recall loss in ANN is a geometric and algorithmic matter, not an inductive-inference one. The resemblance is a shared vocabulary ("coverage", "recall"), not a shared theorem, and I would say so plainly rather than dress it up.

title: Context-Scaling versus Task-Scaling in In-Context Learning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-30

Context-Scaling versus Task-Scaling in In-Context Learning

Abedsoltan, Radhakrishnan, Wu & Belkin (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12783

Setting and problem

The object of study is the now-standard "ICL of function classes" sandbox of Garg, Tsipras, Liang & Valiant (2022), but with the pretraining budget and the context length treated as two separate asymptotic axes.

Data and prompt. Fix an input dimension $d$ and a maximum context length $N$. A task is a draw from a family $\mathcal{F}$ of functions (e.g. linear regression with a Gaussian prior on $\beta$, sparse linear functions, depth-4 decision trees, two-layer ReLU teacher networks). For each task $t = 1,\dots,T$ one draws covariates $x^t_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ and labels $y^t_i$ from the task's function (plus noise where specified), and assembles the prompt as a matrix whose $i$-th row is the concatenated pair $(x_i^\top, y_i)$ — labels are appended as an extra coordinate, not interleaved as separate tokens. Prediction at context length $i$ uses the truncated prompt $A^i_t \in \mathbb{R}^{(i+1)\times(d+1)}$ consisting of rows $1,\dots,i$ plus a query row $(x^\top_{i+1}, 0)$ whose label slot is zeroed out. A model $M_\theta : \mathbb{R}^{(i+1)\times(d+1)} \to \mathbb{R}$ outputs a scalar and is trained by

$$L(\theta; A_1,\dots,A_T) \;=\; \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl(M_\theta(A^i_t) - y^t_{i+1}\bigr)^2 ,$$

so a single model is trained to predict at every prefix length simultaneously. Tasks are drawn fresh (one pass, $T$ up to $2$–$5\times 10^6$ in the experiments), so $T$ is a genuine "number of distinct tasks seen", in the style of Raventós et al. (2023) and Wu et al. (2024) rather than a number of gradient steps.

The two scaling axes. The paper's organizing definitions:

  • Context-scaling: test MSE decreases as $N$ grows, with $T$ held fixed.
  • Task-scaling: test MSE decreases as $T$ grows, with $N$ held fixed.

These are formally independent. A predictor can be a fixed, pretraining-free functional of the in-context empirical measure (context-scales, never task-scales), or a learned function of a fixed-dimension vectorization of the prompt (task-scales by amortizing the task prior, with no mechanism to exploit growing $N$). Note an important measurement caveat: train and test context lengths are the same grid (e.g. ${5,10,20,30,40}$), so "context-scaling" means in-distribution improvement along $N$, not length extrapolation. For MLPs, which need a fixed input width, a single network is trained on all lengths by zero-padding to $N_{\max}$, with vectorized input $A_v = (x_1^\top, y_1, \dots, x_N^\top, 0)^\top$. That padding protocol is one of the non-obvious modelling choices where a lot of the result lives — see the critique.

Attention, abstracted. A generic attention layer is written $g(A_1,A_2,A_3) = \phi\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt m} A_1 A_2^\top\bigr) A_3$ with $A_j \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ and $\phi$ either a row-wise softmax, an entrywise nonlinearity, or the identity; self-attention sets $A_1,A_2,A_3 = AW_Q, AW_K, AW_V$.

SGPT: the simplified architecture. The paper's "Simplified GPT" sets $W_Q = W_K = W_V = I$, so the attention block collapses to a parameter-free operator on the hidden state $H$:

$$g(H) = \phi(HH^\top)H \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times(d+1)},\qquad \phi = \text{row-wise } \ell_1 \text{ normalization}.$$

Batch normalization is removed, the second linear layer of each MLP block is removed (so an MLP block is one linear map plus a GeLU), and the post-MLP skip connection is dropped. The embedding is $H^{(0)} = A W_0$ with $W_0$ a fixed random (non-trainable) matrix, and each block applies $g$, a projection, a skip connection and a GeLU-MLP, with a final linear read-out. So the only trainable parameters are the per-layer projection and MLP matrices; all token mixing is done by the raw, $\ell_1$-normalized Gram matrix of the prompt rows. (Since $W_0$ is a random map with $\mathbb{E}[W_0W_0^\top]\propto I$ for width $k \gtrsim d+1$, $HH^\top \approx c\,AA^\top$ at layer zero — the mixing operator is essentially the normalized prompt Gram.)

The kernel/feature-map view. The one-layer model actually analyzed is

$$f(A) \;=\; \sigma!\bigl(\psi(A)_{N,:}\,W^{(1)}\bigr)W^{(2)},$$

where $\psi : \mathbb{R}^{N\times(d+1)}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times(d+1)}$ is a data-dependent feature map generalizing $g$, and only its last row $\psi(A)_{N,:}$ is fed to the MLP. Writing $X = [x_1,\dots,x_N]^\top$ and $y = (y_1,\dots,y_{N-1},0)^\top$, two instantiations matter:

  1. $\psi_L(A) := (AA^\top)A$ — linear attention with identity weights. Because $(AA^\top)*{ij} = x_i^\top x_j + y_iy_j$ and the query's label slot is zeroed, the last row's similarities are pure covariate inner products, giving $\psi_L(A)*{N,d+1} = x_N^\top X^\top y$ — exactly the prediction of one step of gradient descent from zero initialization on in-context least squares (von Oswald et al., 2023).
  2. $\psi_K(A) := \hat K(X,X)A$ with the row-normalized, zero-diagonal kernel matrix $\hat K(X,X)_{ij} = K(x_i,x_j)/\sum_{i l\neq}K(x_i,x_l)$ for $i \neq j$ and $0$ on the diagonal. Then the last row splits cleanly into a kernel-smoothed covariate vector and a kernel-smoothed label, the latter being exactly the Nadaraya–Watson estimate of $y_N$. The zeroed label slot of the query and the zero diagonal are both load-bearing: the former turns row-$N$ similarity into an $x$-only similarity, the latter is a leave-one-out device preventing a point's own label from entering its prediction (and avoiding a divergent self-weight for singular kernels).

Two kernels are singled out. $K(z,z') = e^{z^\top z'}$ makes $\psi_K$ exactly softmax attention, and $\psi_K(A)_{N,d+1}$ the exponential-kernel smoother. And the Hilbert kernel of Devroye, Györfi & Krzyżak (1998), $H(x,x') = |x-x'|_2^{-d}$, makes $\psi_H(A)_{N,d+1}$ the Hilbert estimate — a Nadaraya–Watson smoother with no bandwidth, which is nonetheless weakly pointwise consistent: at almost every $x$, $\hat f_{H,n}(x)\to f^*(x) = \mathbb{E}[y\mid X = x]$ in probability as $n\to\infty$, with no smoothness or regularity assumptions on the regression function.

The question. Stated as the paper does: what mechanism enables transformers, but not MLPs on vectorized prompts, to context-scale?

What the literature already knew, and the gap. The single-layer-linear-attention line (von Oswald et al. 2023; Ahn et al. 2023; Mahankali, Hashimoto & Ma 2024; Zhang, Frei & Bartlett 2024; Wu et al. 2024) establishes that the pretrained one-layer linear-attention predictor is one step of (preconditioned) GD, and that this predictor attains the rate of optimally tuned ridge for isotropic Gaussian covariates with finitely many pretraining tasks. Bai et al. (2023) construct transformers that do in-context algorithm selection. The softmax-as-kernel-smoother line (Tsai et al. 2019; Chen et al. 2024; Collins et al. 2024) shows attention can implement a kernel smoother whose bandwidth is learned from the query/key matrices. Lu et al. (2024) give an asymptotic theory of linear-attention ICL with task diversity scaling proportionally to $d$. And Tong & Pehlevan (2024) show MLPs do learn in context — at a fixed context length.
