How it is proved. Three steps, and the content is entirely in the first.

  1. Encode the choice event as an intersection of events. Fix the probability space of utility draws. For each $t \in T$ define the event $A_t = {s \text{ has higher utility than } t}$. Then $\bigcap_{t \in T'} A_t$ is precisely the event "$s$ wins the slate ${s} \cup T'$". This is an identity, not an approximation, and it is the whole trick: the hypothesis of the theorem says $P$ and $Q$ agree on all intersections of at most $c\sqrt{|T|\ln(1/\varepsilon)}$ of the $A_t$, and the conclusion asks about the full intersection.

  2. Apply Sherstov's intersection theorem (Theorem 2). Sherstov (2008) proves: if two probability spaces over the same index set of $m$ events agree on all intersections of at most $O(\sqrt{m \ln(1/\varepsilon)})$ events, they agree on the intersection of all $m$ to within $\varepsilon$. The proof of that statement is the approximate-degree argument: write the indicator of the full intersection as $\mathrm{AND}$ of the $m$ indicator variables, replace $\mathrm{AND}$ by a degree-$d$ polynomial $p$ with $|\mathrm{AND} - p|_\infty \le \varepsilon/2$ (possible at $d = \Theta(\sqrt{m\ln(1/\varepsilon)})$, Nisan–Szegedy / Buhrman et al.), expand $p$ in the monomial basis, and observe that each monomial's expectation is exactly the probability of an intersection of $\le d$ events — which the two spaces share by hypothesis. So $\mathbb{E}_P[p] = \mathbb{E}_Q[p]$ exactly, and $|\mathbb{E}_P[\mathrm{AND}] - \mathbb{E}_Q[\mathrm{AND}]| \le |\mathbb{E}_P[\mathrm{AND} - p]| + 0 + |\mathbb{E}_Q[p - \mathrm{AND}]| \le \varepsilon$. The low-degree polynomial is the certificate; the monomials are the small slates.

  3. Read the conclusion back. Step 1 is a bijection between monomials and small slates containing $s$, so Sherstov's conclusion is literally the RUM statement.

The elegance is that the approximate-degree upper bound on AND is what gives a learning upper bound: a short polynomial certificate means few observations determine the answer.

The learning algorithms (Theorems 5, 9). The proper learner is a feasibility LP: variables $x_\pi \ge 0$ for each of the $n!$ permutations, constraints $\sum_\pi x_\pi = 1$ and, for each observed small slate $S$ and each $i \in S$, $\sum_{\pi : i = \arg\max_S \pi} x_\pi = \hat p_{S,i}$. Feasible by construction (the true RUM is a solution), and any solution agrees with the truth on all small slates, hence by Theorem 3 on all slates. Cost: $n^{O(n)}$ by brute force; $2^{O(n)}$ via ellipsoid, which needs a separation oracle over the permutation polytope — the point being that one can check violated constraints without enumerating permutations. The sparsification is a standard empirical-measure / Chernoff-plus-union-bound argument: sample $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ permutations i.i.d. from the learned RUM, union bound over the $O(2^n)$... in fact over the relevant family of slate-item pairs, to get uniform $\ell_\infty$ closeness. The improper learner inverts the certificate: rather than reconstructing a RUM, it evaluates the Huang–Viola polynomial approximating AND at the observed small-slate probabilities, which is why its cost profile is governed by the polynomial's degree and coefficient structure rather than by $n!$.

The lower bound (Theorem 12). What is claimed: for sufficiently large $n$ and any constant $\varepsilon$, there exist RUMs $P, Q$ agreeing exactly on every slate of size $\le c\sqrt{n}$, with $|P(n \text{ wins } [n]) - Q(n \text{ wins } [n])| > 1 - \varepsilon$. So the $\sqrt n$ in Theorem 3 cannot be improved, and the failure is total rather than marginal.

How it is proved. The engine is Bogdanov, Mande, Thaler, Williamson (2016) — equivalently the dual of the approximate-degree lower bound for AND, via LP duality: since $\widetilde{\deg}_\varepsilon(\mathrm{AND}) = \Omega(\sqrt n)$, there exist two distributions $\mu_0, \mu_1$ over ${0,1}^n$ with identical low-degree moments (all moments of degree $\le c\sqrt n$ agree) but $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_1}[\mathrm{AND}] - \mathbb{E}_{\mu_0}[\mathrm{AND}]$ close to 1. The dual witness of an approximate-degree lower bound is exactly a pair of moment-matching distributions that AND separates; this is the standard and very useful duality.

The construction then lifts bit-strings to RUMs. To sample from $P$: draw $x \sim \mu_1$; produce a permutation in which item $n$ is placed above every item $i$ with $x_i = 1$ and below every item with $x_i = 0$ (with the remaining relative order of $[n-1]$ filled in by a fixed or uniform rule shared between $P$ and $Q$). Same for $Q$ with $\mu_0$. Then:

  • _Item $n$ wins the slate ${n} \cup T'$_ iff $x_i = 1$ for all $i \in T'$, i.e. iff the degree-$|T'|$ monomial $\prod_{i \in T'} x_i$ equals 1. So the winning probability of $n$ on a slate of size $m+1$ is exactly the degree-$m$ moment $\mathbb{E}_\mu[\prod_{T' \in i} x_i]$. Moments of degree $\le c\sqrt n$ agree $\Rightarrow$ all small slates containing $n$ agree. And the full slate $[n]$ corresponds to the full monomial $= \mathrm{AND}(x)$, on which $\mu_0, \mu_1$ differ by $\approx 1$. That is the separation.
  • The real work is the other items: one must check that slates not containing $n$, and slates where $n$ loses, also have matching winning distributions. This is where inclusion–exclusion comes in: the probability that item $j \ne n$ wins a slate $S$ decomposes into the case where $n \notin S$ (determined by the shared filling rule, identical in $P$ and $Q$) and the case $n \in S$, where one expands over which subsets of $S$ lie above $n$. Each term in the expansion is again a bounded-degree moment of $\mu$, so as long as $|S| \le c\sqrt n$ every term matches and the sum matches. The combinatorial care is in making sure the expansion never requires a moment of degree exceeding the budget.

Observation 13 (fixed-size slates are insufficient) is a separate, simpler construction: a RUM matching all size-exactly-$k$ winning distributions but differing on $[n]$, exploiting the fact that the size-$k$ constraints alone do not span the moment directions that the mixed-size constraints do.

Downstream: fractional $k$-deck and trace reconstruction (Theorems 14, 15). The $k$-deck of a string is the multiset of its length-$k$ subsequences; the fractional version replaces a string by a distribution over strings and asks for the induced distribution over subsequences. Theorem 14 produces two distributions over weight-1 strings with identical $\Theta(\sqrt n)$-decks whose first-bit marginals are $\ge 1-\varepsilon$ and $\le \varepsilon$. The derivation is a re-encoding of the Theorem 12 construction: weight-1 strings correspond to "which single item sits in a distinguished position", and the subsequence statistics of order $k$ correspond to the slate statistics of size $k$. Theorem 15 then composes this with the deletion channel: at deletion rate $d = 1 - \Theta(1/\sqrt n)$, a received trace reveals (in expectation) only $\Theta(\sqrt n)$ of the original positions, so each sample is essentially a draw from the $\Theta(\sqrt n)$-deck — which by Theorem 14 is identical for the two distributions. A hybrid/indistinguishability argument then gives an $e^{o(\sqrt n)}$ sample lower bound. The notable feature, which the paper rightly emphasizes, is that this is a lower bound against arbitrary algorithms, not just the mean-based (moment-matching) algorithms that most trace-reconstruction lower bounds address — because the indistinguishability is at the level of the full distribution of a single trace, not merely of its low-order statistics.

Broader context

The background worth having is the approximate degree toolkit, which over the last fifteen years has become one of the most reliably exportable techniques in complexity theory. $\widetilde{\deg}_\varepsilon(f)$ is the least degree of a real polynomial approximating $f$ pointwise to $\varepsilon$ on the hypercube; Nisan–Szegedy (1994) established $\widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{AND}) = \Theta(\sqrt n)$, Sherstov and Bun–Thaler developed the dual (LP-duality) view in which a lower bound is witnessed by a pair of moment-matching distributions, and that dual object is what makes approximate degree so portable: it hands you, for free, an indistinguishable pair of instances in whatever domain you can encode conjunctions into. Quantum query complexity, communication complexity, differential privacy, agnostic learning, and now choice modelling have all been fed by the same construction. If one wants two or three entry points: Bun & Thaler's surveys on approximate degree and the method of dual polynomials; Sherstov's "Approximate inclusion-exclusion for arbitrary symmetric functions" (2008), which is the direct input here; and Bogdanov–Mande–Thaler–Williamson (2016) for the dual witness being used.

On the choice-modelling side, the relevant neighbours are the line of work on learning mixtures of Mallows and Plackett–Luce models (Awasthi et al., Zhao et al.), the RUM-identifiability literature going back to Falmagne and Block–Marschak (whose inequalities characterize exactly which collections of choice probabilities are RUM-realizable — and the Block–Marschak polynomials are, suggestively, an inclusion–exclusion object), and the more recent interest in low-rank or sparse RUMs motivated by the computational intractability of the general case. Trace reconstruction is its own flourishing subfield — Holden–Lyons, Nazarov–Peres, Chase for upper and lower bounds — and the fractional variant studied here sits closest to the "population recovery" and "mean-based lower bound" strands.

A follow-up worth doing. The paper names the PAC version as a natural extension, and I think the sharper version of that question is: _what structural assumption collapses the $\sqrt n$ threshold to $O(1)$ or $O(\mathrm{polylog}\, n)$?_ The lower-bound instances are highly non-generic — they are built from moment-matching distributions engineered to fool low-degree polynomials, and the induced RUMs put a single distinguished item in a carefully randomized position relative to a pseudorandom subset. Such RUMs are nothing like MNL, nothing like a mixture of a few Mallows models, and nothing like a RUM with utilities drawn from a log-concave product distribution. So the right question is whether a bounded-rank or bounded-mixture-complexity condition kills the construction, and if so what the trade-off curve between structural complexity and slate width looks like. That seems both tractable and genuinely useful — it is the version of the result a practitioner could act on. The second obvious target is the $\sqrt n$ versus $n/\log n$ computational gap flagged above; my guess is that progress there goes through the bit-complexity of the Huang–Viola coefficients rather than through a new algorithm.

Connection to Shiguang's work. There is a real one, and it is not about RUMs. The transferable object is the proof template: "the observable statistics are the monomial expectations of a function the system computes; the approximate degree of that function tells you how much observation is enough, and its dual witness gives you a matched pair of indistinguishable systems." That template applies wherever a retrieval system's behaviour is a conjunction or a threshold over item-level events and you only ever observe it on small windows. Two concrete instances. (i) _Learning from top-$k$ feedback._ An IR system's logged data is exactly small-slate choice data — a ranker shows $k$ documents and observes a click. The question "what is identifiable about the underlying relevance distribution from top-$k$ logs alone?" is formally the question this paper answers for RUMs, and the $\Theta(\sqrt n)$ threshold with $n$ the candidate pool size is a sobering identifiability statement for offline evaluation and counterfactual LTR: it says that with $k = 10$ and a candidate pool of thousands, the logged policy's data does not in principle determine full-pool behaviour, independent of how much data you collect. That is a cleaner and more pessimistic framing than the usual propensity-overlap/variance story, and it dovetails with the known non-identifiability results in unbiased LTR. (ii) Vector search as an intersection of events. "Document $q$'s nearest neighbour is $d$" is the conjunction over all $d' \ne d$ of "$d$ is closer to $q$ than $d'$" — structurally the same AND-of-pairwise-comparisons that Theorem 3 exploits. That suggests asking: given exact answers to all $k$-way nearest-neighbour-among-a-subset queries, when is the full ranking determined? An approximate-degree argument would give a $\sqrt n$-type threshold here too, which would be a lower bound on any index that answers full-corpus queries by combining small-subset comparisons — a family that includes graph-based indices like HNSW, whose greedy traversal is precisely a sequence of local comparisons. I would not claim this is immediate, but it is the kind of question where the dual-polynomial method has a track record of giving the first nontrivial bound, and the encoding is natural rather than forced. The generative-retrieval connection, by contrast, I would leave alone — docid decoding is not a choice model in any way that this machinery would illuminate.

title: Soft-Output Successive Cancellation List Decoding
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-28

Soft-Output Successive Cancellation List Decoding

Peihong Yuan, Ken R. Duffy, Muriel Médard (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03623

Main idea

Polar codes (Arikan, 2009) build a length-N = 2^n code by applying the Hadamard transform c^N = u^N F^{(x) log_2 N} (Eq. 3) to an input vector u^N in which K positions (the information set A) carry the message and the remaining frozen positions are fixed by linear constraints u_i = f_i(u^{i-1}) (Eq. 2). When f_i = 0 these are static frozen bits; when f_i depends on earlier bits they are dynamic frozen bits, and that one generalization covers CRC-concatenated polar codes, polar subcodes, PAC codes and dynamic Reed-Muller (RM) codes under a single "polar-like" umbrella. Successive cancellation (SC) decoding walks i = 1,...,N left to right, at each information position picking the more likely bit under an auxiliary posterior Q_{U_i | Y^N U^{i-1}} (Eq. 4). SC list (SCL) decoding keeps up to L surviving paths, scored by the product metric Q_{U^i | Y^N}(v^i | y^N) (Eq. 5), and returns the best one.

The paper's target is soft output (SO): not just "here is the decoded codeword" but a calibrated statement of how much to believe it. Blockwise SO is the posterior probability Gamma(y^N, u^_N) that the returned codeword is the transmitted one (Eq. 13); its list version Gamma(y^N, L_U) (Eq. 14) is the probability the true codeword is anywhere on the list. Bitwise SO is the vector of APP log-likelihood ratios l_{APP,i} for the coded bits, which is what a soft-input soft-output (SISO) component decoder must emit inside an iterative scheme.

The obstacle is a normalization problem, and it is exactly the interesting one. Define the codebook-unaware auxiliary measure Q_{C^N | Y^N}(b^N | y^N) = prod_i P_{C|Y}(b_i | y_i), which treats every binary string as admissible. The true posterior restricted to the code is P_{C^N|Y^N}(b^N|y^N) = Q_{C^N|Y^N}(b^N|y^N)/Q_C(y^N), where the codebook probability Q_C(y^N) = sum_{b^N in C} Q_{C^N|Y^N}(b^N|y^N) (Eq. 1) is the partition function over the 2^K codewords. An SCL decoder sees only L of them. The standard fix — Forney's list-based approximation of his generalized decoding rule (Eq. 6), which replaces Q_C by the sum over the list L_C — systematically overstates confidence, because it renormalizes the posterior over a tiny subset and so every retained candidate inherits mass that really belongs to unexplored codewords.

The paper's answer is to estimate the missing mass rather than ignore it. An SC-based search partitions the decoding tree into visited leaves V, invalid subtrees I (pruned by frozen-constraint conflicts, hence genuinely zero mass), and unvisited subtrees W (consistent with the constraints but never expanded for complexity reasons). Each unvisited root a^i contributes sum_{v^N in U, v^i = a^i} Q_{U^N|Y^N}(v^N|y^N), which is unknown. Assuming the valid leaves are uniformly spread beneath a^i, that term is approximated by 2^{-|F^{(i:N)}|} Q_{U^i|Y^N}(a^i|y^N) (Eq. 11), where |F^{(i:N)}| counts the future frozen positions. Summing gives Q*_U(y^N) (Eq. 12), e.g. for the toy N = 4 code of Fig. 1, Q*_U(y^4) = Q(0100|y^4) + 2^{-1} Q_{U^2}(00|y^4) + 2^0 Q_{U^4}(0101|y^4). Crucially, the path metrics Q_{U^i|Y^N}(a^i|y^N) are already computed by the SC/SCL decoder when it prunes, so the overhead is an accumulator, not extra decoding.

The most interesting part

The clever move is the auxiliary distribution itself: by deliberately choosing a measure that is ignorant of the codebook — a plain product of per-bit channel posteriors — the authors make "the probability mass under an unvisited subtree" computable in closed form up to one combinatorial factor. The 2^{-|F^{(i:N)}|} term is precisely the fraction of strings below a^i that survive the remaining frozen constraints, under the assumption that those constraints behave like independent fair coin flips. This is the SC-tree analogue of the GRAND-side result ([20, Cor. 3]) that unidentified codewords are approximately uniform over unexplored noise sequences — transplanted from a guessing-based search to a tree search.

The payoff is operational. With Gamma*(y^N, u^_N) = Q_{U^N|Y^N}(u^_N|y^N)/Q*_U(y^N) (Eq. 17), accepting only when Gamma* > 1 - epsilon (Eq. 15) caps the misdetection rate (UER/BLER) at epsilon by construction, with no CRC and no rate loss. Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 show this against 5G: a (64,42) dynamic RM code with epsilon = 0.1, L = 4 beats a (64,48) 5G polar code with CRC-6 (0x30) in both BLER and UER, and the same with epsilon = 0.005, L = 8 against CRC-11 (0x710). The MDR traces sit flat on the horizontal line at epsilon across the whole E_b/N_0 range — a tunable knob, not an emergent property of a CRC polynomial.

Honest critique. (i) Eq. (11) is an assumption, not a bound; the paper offers no inequality relating Q*_U to Q_C, and it visibly fails where the assumption is violated — Fig. 2 shows clear miscalibration for static-frozen codes, because static constraints make the surviving leaves non-uniform. The authors are candid: accuracy holds "if the frozen bits are random linear combinations of previous message bits," and the (32,26) static RM code only works because it has three frozen bits after the first message bit. That is a real restriction: 5G polar codes are static-frozen. (ii) The decoder must store an accumulator over every pruned node, i.e. O(N) extra path-metric bookkeeping per surviving path, plus the sum over W, which scales with how aggressively the list prunes. (iii) The headline comparison is partly a code-design story: dynamic RM at rate 42/64 versus 5G polar at 48/64 plus CRC is a different code and a different detection mechanism. The honest reading is that CRC-free detection lets you spend the CRC's redundancy on minimum distance; the decoder and the code design are entangled in the gain. A cleaner ablation (same code, SO threshold vs. CRC) is absent.

Broader context

Polar codes are the control-channel code of 5G NR; in practice always CRC-aided SCL (Tal-Vardy list decoding plus Niu-Chen CRC), where the CRC does double duty as list pruner and error detector. GRAND (Duffy-Li-Medard; ORBGRAND) is the authors' parallel line: guess noise rather than codewords, which works for any code and yields a natural confidence estimate, and [20]/[21] developed blockwise and bitwise SO for GRAND. This paper is the SC-tree translation of that programme. On the SISO side, the incumbents are Pyndiah's list-max (Eq. 8) and list-sum (Eq. 7) approximations, both of which need an ad-hoc saturation constant beta (Eq. 9) when the list contains no competing codeword for bit i; the proposed l*_{APP,i} (Eq. 16) instead injects phi = Q*_U(y^N) - sum_{c^N in L_C} Q_{C^N|Y^N}(c^N|y^N) — the estimated mass off-list — weighted by the raw channel posterior, which interpolates smoothly between "trust the list" (phi small) and "trust the channel" (phi large) and makes beta unnecessary. Results: Table I has SO-SCL BER 0.093712 at 0 dB versus MAP's 0.093537 and list-max's 0.102810; Table II has 1-GMI 0.66733 versus BCJR's 0.67231; Tables III-IV give Monte-Carlo density-evolution thresholds for degree-2 GLDPC ensembles — with (32,26) RM check nodes, SO-SCL reaches 1.52 dB at L = 8 against list-max's 1.65 and BCJR's 1.48, and the gap widens at small lists (L = 2: 1.69 vs 2.26). Closely related: Coskun-Pfister's information-theoretic analysis of SCL ([49]), and Strasshofer et al. on GMI-optimized Chase-Pyndiah post-processing ([55]). A natural follow-up: replace the flat 2^{-|F^{(i:N)}|} factor with a learned or analytically corrected occupancy estimate for static-frozen trees — e.g. counting the actual number of leaves consistent with the remaining constraints via a rank computation on the frozen submatrix — which would extend calibrated SO to 5G polar codes as deployed.

The connection to Shiguang's area is genuine and, I think, under-exploited. Generative retrieval decodes a document identifier token by token under a trie constraint, with beam search keeping B partial prefixes scored by prod_t p(token_t | prefix). That is structurally identical to SCL: a constrained left-to-right tree search over a structured codebook, with a product path metric and a width-B frontier. And the calibration pathology is literally the same — softmax over the beam renormalizes a posterior over B of the |D| valid identifiers, so beam scores systematically overstate confidence, which is exactly why generative-retrieval confidence is unreliable for abstention, routing to a fallback retriever, or RAG "I don't know" decisions. The SO-SCL recipe transfers: at each pruning event, accumulate (number of trie leaves below the pruned node) x (prefix probability) x (an occupancy estimate for the suffix mass). The trie makes the leaf count exactly available, so the crude 2^{-|F^{(i:N)}|} surrogate can be replaced by an exact subtree size — you would be strictly better off than the coding case, and the remaining approximation is only the within-subtree distribution of suffix likelihood. That gives a calibrated Gamma* for "the correct document is on the beam" and a threshold rule capping the false-acceptance rate at a chosen epsilon, which is directly the generative-retrieval analogue of Eq. (15). The same mass-outside-the-candidate-set framing applies to ANN search: HNSW/IVF return a truncated candidate list and the similarity scores are renormalized over it, so any "confidence" or probabilistic-recall estimate inherits the same bias; estimating the unvisited mass from the partition structure (unvisited IVF cells with known centroid distances and cell populations) is the same computation. The honest caveat is that in both IR settings the per-token / per-coordinate scores are not calibrated channel posteriors to begin with, so the analogy buys the estimator structure, not the estimator's accuracy.

Proof sketch

The paper contains no theorem, and I will not invent one — it is an algorithmic-plus-empirical contribution resting on a derivation and one explicit approximation. What substitutes for a proof is a three-way exact decomposition followed by a single modelling assumption.

The exact step is a marginalization over the SC tree. Because the polar transform is a bijection, Q_{C^N|Y^N}(c^N|y^N) = Q_{U^N|Y^N}(u^N|y^N), so the codebook probability equals a sum over valid paths U (Eq. 10). Any SC-based search induces a partition of U into (a) visited leaves V, (b) valid leaves below unvisited roots W, and (c) nothing else, since the invalid subtrees I contain no valid path by definition of the frozen constraints. Hence Q_C(y^N) splits exactly into a computable term over V plus one unknown term per element of W — this part is a telescoping identity, not an approximation, and it holds for SC, SCL, SC-stack, SC-Fano and SCOS alike.

The approximation is Eq. (11): for an unvisited root a^i, sum_{v^N : v^i = a^i, v^N in U} Q_{U^N|Y^N}(v^N|y^N) ~ 2^{-|F^{(i:N)}|} Q_{U^i|Y^N}(a^i|y^N). Two things are being asserted: that the auxiliary measure of the whole subtree factorizes as the prefix metric times one (since Q is a product measure over unconstrained suffixes, summing over all 2^{N-i} suffixes gives exactly Q_{U^i|Y^N}(a^i|y^N) — this part is exact), and that the valid leaves carry a 2^{-|F^{(i:N)}|} fraction of that mass, i.e. that satisfying each future frozen constraint is an independent unbiased halving uncorrelated with likelihood. The second assertion is where the guarantee ends. It is the tree-search counterpart of [20, Cor. 3]'s uniformity assumption for GRAND, and it is validated empirically rather than bounded: Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 plot E[1 - Gamma*] against measured BLER and list error rate, and the dynamic-frozen curves lie on the diagonal while the static-frozen ones do not. The supporting information-theoretic work (Section IV-D) is likewise measurement, not theory: 1-GMI I_1(C; L_ch + f_pp(L_E, delta, gamma)) maximized over post-processing (delta, gamma), and MCDE thresholds with M = 1e5, both showing SO-SCL closer to BCJR than the list-max / list-sum baselines.

title: Finite Sample Analysis of Distribution-Free Confidence Ellipsoids for Linear Regression
tags: Electrical Engineering and Systems Science - Signal Processing
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-28

Finite Sample Analysis of Distribution-Free Confidence Ellipsoids for Linear Regression

Szabolcs Szentpéteri, Balázs Csanád Csáji (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.08801

Main idea

The paper attacks a gap that is easy to state and hard to close: the classical least-squares confidence ellipsoid

C~_n = {theta : (theta - theta^_n)^T Rbar_n (theta - theta^_n) <= mu sigma^_n^2 / n}, with sigma^_n^2 = (1/(n-d)) sum_t eps_t^2(theta^_n)

and mu a chi^2(d) quantile, is only approximately correct — its coverage is a CLT artifact and carries no guarantee at any finite n unless you assume Gaussian (or at least subgaussian with a known variance proxy) noise. Sign-Perturbed Sums (SPS), from Csaji-Campi-Weyer, fixes this. Given data Y_t = phi_t^T theta* + W_t, pick integers m > q > 0, draw n(m-1) i.i.d. Rademacher signs alpha_{i,t}, and form the unperturbed and sign-perturbed normalized gradients

S_0(theta) = Rbar_n^{-1/2} (1/n) sum_t phi_t eps_t(theta), S_i(theta) = Rbar_n^{-1/2} (1/n) sum_t alpha_{i,t} phi_t eps_t(theta).

theta is admitted iff the rank R(theta) of ||S_0(theta)||^2 among the m values is at most m - q (random tie-breaking via a uniform permutation pi). The resulting region C_{p,n} has coverage exactly p = 1 - q/m (Theorem 1) assuming only that {W_t} are independent and symmetric about zero and that Rbar_n is nonsingular. "Distribution-free, non-asymptotic, exactly guaranteed" means: no moment, tail, variance or even identical-distribution assumption; valid at every n >= d; and the coverage is an equality, not a conservative inequality — unusual, because almost every finite-sample region in system identification is built from concentration inequalities and is therefore conservative by an unknown factor, and depends on hyper-parameters (variance proxies, noise bounds) that nobody knows in practice.

The catch is that C_{p,n} is defined only through a membership oracle, so drawing it means gridding R^d. The ellipsoidal outer approximation (EOA) replaces it with O_{p,n} = {theta : (theta - theta^_n)^T Rbar_n (theta - theta^_n) <= r} — the same center and shape matrix as the asymptotic ellipsoid, only the radius differs. Here r is the q-th largest of the optimal values gamma_i* of max_theta ||S_0(theta)||^2 s.t. ||S_0(theta)||^2 <= ||S_i(theta)||^2 — nonconvex as written, but exactly reformulable as a semidefinite program via S-procedure / Schur complement. Coverage is inherited as P(theta* in O_{p,n}) >= p. What was missing, and what this paper supplies, is a size guarantee: Theorem 3 gives a high-probability finite-sample upper bound on the EOA radius, and Corollary 1 shows the regions shrink at the optimal O(1/sqrt n) rate.

The most interesting part

Two candidates; the genuinely clever one here is not the coverage proof (inherited from 2015) but the dual-variable optimization that turns an SDP's optimal value into something concentration inequalities can bite.

Still, the coverage argument deserves one paragraph because it is the engine. Condition on |W_1|, ..., |W_n|. Symmetry plus independence means the signs of the W_t are i.i.d. Rademacher, so the m random vectors {sum_t alpha_{i,t} phi_t W_t}_{i=0}^{m-1} (with alpha_{0,t} = 1) are conditionally i.i.d., hence exchangeable. Exchangeability makes the rank of ||S_0(theta*)||^2 uniform on {1,...,m} — random tie-breaking handles atoms — so P(R(theta*) <= m - q) = (m-q)/m exactly. No tail bound, no asymptotics: a pure group-invariance (randomization-test) argument. That is why p must be rational.

The new content is Step iii of the proof of Theorem 3. After reformulation the SDP's optimal value is gamma_0* = xi*(b_0^T (A_0'(xi*))^+ b_0 - c_0) = w_n^T xi* P(xi*) w_n / n, where xi* is the dual multiplier. This is useless as-is: xi* is a data-dependent random scalar with no closed form. The trick is to give up on xi* and optimize the bound over the feasible set of xi. The Schur conditions force xi > 1/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)) where K = Phi_{Q,n}^T D_{alpha,n} Phi_{Q,n} is the sign-perturbed projection matrix. Writing xi = 1/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)) + delta_xi, Lemma 7 gives the eigenvalues of P(xi) in closed form,

lambda_i(P(xi)) = (xi lambda_i^2(K) - xi - lambda_i^2(K) + 1) / (xi lambda_i^2(K) - xi + 1),

so f_P(delta_xi) = xi lambda_max(P(xi)) is an explicit scalar function; its second derivative 2 lambda_max(K^2)/(delta_xi^3 (lambda_max(K^2) - 1)^2) > 0, so it is strictly convex, minimized at delta_xi' = lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2}/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)), i.e. xi' = 1/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2}). Everything collapses to

gamma_0* <= (X_P/n) * (1 + lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2})/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2}), with X_P = w_n^T V_P D_d V_P^T w_n.

The whole randomness of a semidefinite program has been factored into (i) a rank-d quadratic form in the noise and (ii) the top eigenvalue of a Rademacher-signed projection — exactly the two objects for which the authors already had concentration results. That is the move worth remembering.

Honest limitations. (a) The validity of SPS needs independent, symmetric noise; symmetry is strong (it rules out skewed or heteroskedastic-in-mean noise), and the companion RPS method trades it for i.i.d.-ness. (b) The size analysis is not hyper-parameter-free: lambda_0, kappa, rho and the variance proxy sigma enter f, g, and in the experiments they are estimated empirically from the simulated trajectories (which, notably, forces rho = 1). The algorithm needs none of this; the bound does. (c) Conservativeness is real and visible: in Table I at d = 4, n = 1000 the empirical SPS EOA size is 0.79 while the theoretical bound is 3.67 (asymptotic ellipsoid: 0.76, DMR bound: 1.93); at n = 2000, 0.55 vs 1.47. The bound only becomes competitive with the DMR (Djehiche-Mazhar-Rojas) bound once n comfortably exceeds the validity threshold ceil(g^{1/rho}(delta/(m-q))). (d) The outer approximation is itself lossy — Theorem 3's bound is strictly worse than Theorem 2's for the indicator region, though with the same rate. (e) Cost: m SDPs per region; Table II reports solve times relative to the d = 2 case reaching 687.97x at d = 40, n = 250.

Broader context

The classical route is asymptotic: sqrt(n)(theta^_n - theta*) => N(0, sigma^2 R^{-1}) gives the ellipsoid above, cheap and tight but with no finite-n validity, and over-optimistic precisely when you care (small n, non-stationary or heavy-tailed noise). The PAC / concentration route (Simchowitz et al., Sarkar-Rakhlin-Dahleh, Jedra-Proutiere, Djehiche-Mazhar-Rojas) gives finite-sample bounds but needs subgaussianity with known constants and an unspecified absolute constant C — the authors note that [23] never says how to pick C, making the DMR bound awkward to instantiate. Set-membership identification assumes known bounded noise and is visibly conservative in Fig. 1.

The third route is randomization. LSCR (Campi-Weyer 2005) leaves out sign-dominant correlations; SPS (Csaji-Campi-Weyer, CDC 2012 / IEEE TSP 2015) perturbs signs; follow-ups cover ARX with instrumental variables (Volpe et al. 2015; Care et al., SICON 2025), closed-loop state space (Szentpeteri-Csaji, SCL 2023), boundedness conditions (Care, Automatica 2022), strong consistency (Weyer-Campi-Csaji 2017), and sample complexity of the indicator region (Szentpeteri-Csaji, Automatica 2025 — the direct predecessor, supplying Lemmas 1 and 2). Conformal prediction is the other great distribution-free paradigm and shares the engine (exchangeability + rank statistic), but answers a different question: it covers a future outcome, not a parameter. SPS is essentially a randomization test inverted into a parameter set.

Two closely related directions worth naming: Residual-Permuted Sums (Szentpeteri-Csaji, L-CSS 2024), which swaps symmetry for i.i.d. noise — the obvious follow-up is exactly the EOA sample-complexity analysis for RPS, which the paper flags itself; and self-normalized / anytime-valid confidence sequences (Abbasi-Yadkori-style), where a natural question is whether the xi-optimization trick yields a time-uniform SPS radius. A more ambitious follow-up: make the bound data-driven by replacing lambda_0, kappa, sigma with empirical plug-ins plus their own concentration, closing the gap between Fig. 1's two curves.

For theoretical IR, the connection is partial but not forced. The shared machinery is exchangeability-based finite-sample validity, which is already the basis of conformal risk control for retrieval (controlling recall or nDCG loss at level alpha with a finite calibration set). Where SPS-EOA adds something distinct is parameter uncertainty for linear scoring: a learned linear re-ranker or probe s(q,d) = <theta, phi(q,d)> fit by least squares on graded relevance gives an EOA ellipsoid around theta^ whose radius has exact finite-sample meaning; propagating it through <., phi> yields per-document score intervals and hence distribution-free certificates about which pairwise rankings are decided versus undecided by the data — a cleaner object than a conformal prediction set when the question is about the ranker, not the labels. The honest caveats: relevance noise is rarely symmetric about zero (it is bounded, discrete, and skewed), features must be exogenous w.r.t. the noise, and the m-SDP cost plus the d-dependence (kappa d^2, d sigma^2 in f and g) makes d ~ 768 embedding dimensions impractical without a low-dimensional probe. For ANN recall, the link is weaker still — the randomness there is in the index/quantizer, not additive symmetric noise — so call that a thematic rather than technical connection.

Proof sketch

Setting and assumptions. Y_t = phi_t^T theta* + W_t, t in [n], deterministic regressors (or random but exogenous, a.s.), R_n = Phi_n^T Phi_n, Rbar_n = R_n/n.

  • A1: {W_t} independent, nonatomic, symmetric about zero, and sigma-subgaussian. (Symmetry + independence buy coverage; subgaussianity and nonatomicity are only for the size analysis and tie-breaking.)
  • A2: complete excitation — every d-subset of regressors spans R^d, i.e. det((1/d) sum_{t in T} phi_t phi_t^T) != 0 for all |T| = d. This makes Phi_{R,n} nonsingular and, with Care's condition, makes the region bounded.
  • A3: nonvanishing excitation, lambda_min(Rbar_n) >= lambda_0 > 0 for all n >= d.
  • A4: bounded coherence, mu(Phi_n) = (n/d) max_i ||Phi_{Q,n}^T e_i||^2 <= kappa n^{1-rho} with kappa > 0, 0 < rho <= 1 (Candes-Recht coherence; 1 <= mu <= n/d). This says no single time step carries too much of the excitation.

Theorem 1 (exact coverage). Under independence + symmetry + nonsingular Rbar_n alone, P(theta* in C_{p,n}) = 1 - q/m = p, exactly. Proof idea as above: conditionally on (|W_t|) the m sums are i.i.d., hence exchangeable; the rank is uniform on [m]; ties broken by the uniform permutation pi from Algorithm 1 preserve uniformity. For the EOA one only gets P(theta* in O_{p,n}) >= p (eq. 14), since C_{p,n} is a subset of O_{p,n}.

Theorem 2 (size of the indicator region, from [37]). For delta in (0,1) and n >= ceil(g^{1/rho}(delta/(m-q))), with probability at least 1 - delta,

sup_{theta_1, theta_2 in C_{p,n}} ||theta_1 - theta_2|| <= 4 f(delta/(m-q)) / [ n^{1-rho} lambda_0 (n^rho - g(delta/(m-q))) ]^{1/2},

with g(delta) = 2 kappa d^2 ln(4d/delta) and f(delta) = sigma(8d ln^{1/2}(4/delta) + d)^{1/2} for 4 e^{-(n d lambda_0)^2} <= delta <= 1, f(delta) = sigma(8 ln(4/delta) + d)^{1/2} for smaller delta (the two regimes are the subgaussian and sub-exponential tails of a quadratic form).

Theorem 3 (main new result). Under A1-A4, for all delta in (0,1) and n >= ceil(g^{1/rho}(delta/(m-q))), with probability at least 1 - delta,

sup_{theta in O_{p,n}} ||theta - theta^_n|| <= [ f(delta/(m-q)) (n^{rho/2} + g^{1/2}(delta/(m-q))) / ( n lambda_0 (n^{rho/2} - g^{1/2}(delta/(m-q))) ) ]^{1/2}

(up to the constant stated in eq. 15; the m = 2, q = 1 case is Lemma 3 / eq. 87). Note the size is measured as a radius from the LSE, not a diameter — the EOA is slightly more conservative than Theorem 2, as expected of an outer approximation. Corollary 1: the n-dependence is O(n^{rho/4}/(n^{1/2} n^{rho/4})) = O(1/sqrt n), i.e. the optimal rate; this also improves on the authors' earlier scalar-case result [40], which only gave a geometric decrease, because that proof routed through the distance to theta* instead of bounding the SDP value directly. The n >= ceil(g^{1/rho}) condition is exactly what keeps n^{rho/2} - g^{1/2} > 0.

Proof architecture (four steps).

Step i — convexification. Take m = 2, q = 1. With psi_n = Phi_n^T D_{alpha,n} y_n, one shows ||S_0(theta)||^2 = (theta - theta^_n)^T Rbar_n (theta - theta^_n), so substituting z = Rbar_n^{1/2}(theta - theta^_n) turns (16) into max ||z||^2 s.t. z^T A_0 z + 2 z^T b_0 + c_0 <= 0 with A_0 = I - R_n^{-1/2} Q_n R_n^{-1} Q_n R_n^{-1/2}, Q_n = Phi_n^T D_{alpha,n} Phi_n, A = R_n - Q_n R_n^{-1} Q_n, B = Phi_n^T - Q_n R_n^{-1} Phi_n^T D_{alpha,n}. Boundedness is equivalent to A > 0 (Care, [41]), which depends only on the regressors and signs, not on the noise. Lemma 4 shows ||S_1(theta^_n)||^2 != 0 a.s. (it equals (1/n) L w_n with rank(L) = d, then Lemma 6: M w_0 != 0 a.s. for independent nonatomic w_0, by conditioning on all but one coordinate and using nonatomicity). Since theta^_n is always feasible with ||S_0(theta^_n)||^2 = 0, Slater's condition holds, strong duality applies, and (16) equals the SDP (27), min_{xi >= 0} gamma_0 s.t. [[-I + xi A_0, xi b_0], [xi b_0^T, xi c_0 + gamma_0]] >= 0. Unbounded regions are handled separately by setting gamma* = infinity (eq. 28).

Step ii — reading off the optimum from the Schur conditions. Writing A = Phi_{R,n}^T (I - K^2) Phi_{R,n} with K = Phi_{Q,n}^T D_{alpha,n} Phi_{Q,n} (eqs. 34-36), and using the SVD of Phi_{R,n} to strip orthogonal factors, the first PSD condition xi A_0'(xi) >= 0 reduces to xi(I - K^2) - I >= 0, i.e. xi >= 1/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)). Lemma 5 shows the boundary value violates the second (range) condition (I - A_0'(xi)(A_0'(xi))^+) xi b_0 = 0 almost surely, so xi* > 1/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)) strictly. The third condition pins gamma_0* = xi*(b_0^T (A_0'(xi*))^+ b_0 - c_0). A crucial algebraic simplification: B D_{alpha,n} y_n = B D_{alpha,n} w_n (eq. 46) — the theta* terms cancel identically — so gamma_0* = w_n^T xi* P(xi*) w_n / n is a pure noise quadratic form.

Step iii — the xi trick. Lemma 7 diagonalizes P(xi) (rank d, PSD, eigenvalues as above), the convexity-in-delta_xi argument gives xi' = 1/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2}), and gamma* <= (X_P/n)(1 + lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2})/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2}) with X_P = w_n^T V_P D_d V_P^T w_n a rank-d projection quadratic form.

Step iv — concentration. Combining with A3, ||theta - theta^_n||^2 <= (X_P/(n lambda_0))(1 + lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2})/(1 - lambda_max(K^2)^{1/2}). Then two inequalities:

  • Lemma 1 (Hanson-Wright / Bernstein-type, from [37]): for X = w_n^T M w_n with M a symmetric projection of rank <= d, P(|X - E X|/(n lambda_0) >= eps) <= 2 exp(-eps^2 n^2 lambda_0^2/(64 d^2 sigma^4)) for 0 <= eps <= 8 sigma^2 d^2 and 2 exp(-eps n lambda_0/(8 sigma^2)) beyond — the two regimes that produce the two branches of f. One also needs E X_P <= d sigma^2 (bound X by sum_{i<=d} w~_{d,i}^2 of subgaussians) and the reverse triangle inequality to go from a deviation bound to an absolute bound on |X_P|.
  • Lemma 2 (matrix concentration via coherence, from [37]): P(max_i |lambda_i(K)| >= eps_0) <= 2d exp(-n^rho eps_0^2/(2 kappa d^2)) — K is a Rademacher sum of rank-one terms whose individual norms A4 controls, with the 2d from a union over eigenvalues. Applied through the identity (1 + lambda_max^{1/2})/(1 - lambda_max^{1/2}) >= eps iff max_i |lambda_i(K)| >= (eps-1)/(eps+1) (eqs. 60-61), this yields (n^{rho/2} + g^{1/2}(delta))/(n^{rho/2} - g^{1/2}(delta)) with g(delta) = 2 kappa d^2 ln(4d/delta).

Splitting delta into two halves and using the product rule (P(Y_1 <= y_1) >= 1 - p_1, P(Y_2 <= y_2) >= 1 - p_2 implies P(Y_1 Y_2 <= y_1 y_2) >= 1 - p_1 - p_2) gives Lemma 3 (eqs. 85-87).

General m, q. The radius r is the q-th largest gamma_i*, so the bound fails only if it fails for at least m - q of the m - 1 ellipsoids: B = intersect_{|I| = m-q} union_{i in I} B_i, hence P(B) <= min_I P(union_{i in I} B_i) <= (m-q) P(B_1), and rescaling delta' = (m-q) delta yields Theorem 3. The (m-q) factor is why delta/(m-q) appears inside f and g — a mild logarithmic price.

Experimental grounding. Two-dimensional FIR Y_t = b_1* U_{t-1} + b_2* U_{t-2} + W_t, b_1* = b_2* = 5, AR input U_t = 0.7 U_{t-1} + sum_{i=1}^5 c_i V_{t-i+1} with c = (1, 0.775, 0.55, 0.325, 0.1), V_t ~ N(0,1). Experiment A: uniform noise on (-3,3) (sigma = sqrt 3, optimal proxy), m = 10, q = 1 (level 0.9), delta = 0.5, t_0 = 400, n = 2000, s = 100 trajectories, empirical size = 2 sqrt(gamma_t*/lambda_min(Rbar_t)) (the longest axis). The bound tracks the empirical decrease rate but sits above it; the set-membership ellipsoid is eventually worse than even the SPS bound. Experiment B: non-stationary symmetric 5-component Gaussian mixture noise (sigma = sqrt 2.7), feedback removed from the input so the DMR theorem applies; the SPS bound starts above DMR and crosses below as n grows. kappa and lambda_0 are set to empirical extremes over trajectories, which forces rho = 1 — worth flagging, since the bound's validity threshold and rate constants hinge on these.

title: On the Implicit Relation Between Low-Rank Adaptation and Differential Privacy
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-28

On the Implicit Relation Between Low-Rank Adaptation and Differential Privacy

Saber Malekmohammadi, Golnoosh Farnadi (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17538

Main idea

Note first: the PDF on file is v9 (10 Feb 2026), retitled "LoRA Provides Differential Privacy by Design via Random Sketching." It is a substantially rewritten paper relative to the Sept-2024 v1 the Zotero metadata describes. In particular, there is no JL-based implicit-clipping theorem anywhere in v9 — "Johnson-Lindenstrauss" appears exactly once, as a citation to Blocki et al. (2012) in Related Work. The per-sample norm bound ||grad_{W_l^t} l(x_i)||_F <= C that the JL argument used to try to earn is now a bare assumption of Lemma 7.2. That is a meaningful weakening of the earlier story, and worth knowing before you read the older abstract.

The setup. For adapter W_l in R^{n x m}, LoRA writes y = (W_l + B_l A_l)x, with B_l in R^{n x r}, A_l in R^{r x m}, B^0 = 0, A^0 ~ N(0, sigma_A^2). Backprop gives dL/dB_l = (grad_{W_l}L)A_l^T. Following Hao et al.'s FLoRA ("low-rank adapters are secretly gradient compressors"), Lemma 5.1 unrolls T SGD steps into W_l^T = W_l^0 - eta(sum_t grad_{W^t}L^t)A^{0T}A^0 + O(eta^3), and the O(eta^3) vanishes exactly when A is frozen (the FFA-LoRA / Sun et al. variant). Rewriting A^{0T}A^0 = I + (A^{0T}A^0 - I) gives Eq. (11): LoRA = SGD on W_l with noisy gradients, noise = grad L (A^{0T}A^0 - I).

Two consequences are then developed. (i) Statistical: A^{0T}A^0 is Wishart, so each row of the noise is a weighted sum of chi-square / variance-gamma terms; Lemma 6.1 gives a CLT limit N((r sigma_A^2 - 1)q, r sigma_A^4 (||q||^2 I + D)), which is unbiased with variance proportional to 1/r only when sigma_A^2 = 1/r (exactly rsLoRA's rank-stabilised scaling). Smaller rank implies more noise. (ii) Privacy: Eq. (14) observes that the released quantity is W~_l^T = W_l^0 - eta(G_l(D)A^{0T} + Z_l)A^0 with G_l(D) = sum_t grad_{W^t}L^t — i.e. a noisy Gaussian sketch of the cumulative gradient matrix, the same object studied for private linear regression (Sheffet 2019; Lev et al. 2025). "Implicit DP" here means a genuine RDP bound for that sketch, with the sketching matrix itself playing the role of the privacy noise, so vanilla LoRA (sigma_g = 0) is claimed to be private with no noise added at all.

Reviewer-style critique

Strengths. The FLoRA identity-under-frozen-A is clean and the sketching reframing is genuinely the right lens. Lemma 7.1 is a real technical contribution: it generalises Lev et al.'s Gaussian-sketch RDP bound from a "zero-out one column" adjacency to the far more natural ||Q(D) - Q(D')||_F <= B_S with ||Q||_F <= B_F, via ||AA^T - BB^T||_F <= 2 B_F B_S (Lemma A.1), and the authors show the bound is tight in the Lev et al. special case (B_C = B_S^2, tau = 1). The determinant manipulation in D.1 is competent. So this is not merely distributional closeness — it really is an (alpha, eps(alpha))-RDP to tCDP to (eps, delta) chain.

But the guarantee is close to vacuous as stated. Everything hinges on Gamma = eta beta b (lambda_bar + r sigma_g^2) / (4 C^2 T ((1+eta beta)^T - 1)) > 1, where lambda_bar <= lambda_min(G_l G_l^T). Three problems:

  1. Gamma > 1 is unachievable for vanilla LoRA at realistic batch sizes. lambda_min(GG^T) <= ||G||_F^2 / n and ||G||_F <= TC (Eq. 51), while (1+eta beta)^T - 1 >= eta beta T. Chaining these with sigma_g = 0 gives Gamma <= b / (4n). With GPT-2's n = 768, Gamma > 1 requires b > 3072; their experiments use b in {8, 16}. Worse, the useful regime is much further away: rLn = 16 * 12 * 768 = 147,456, so Corollary 7.3 plus Prop. 4.4 give eps ~ 147456/(2 Gamma^2) + sqrt(2 * 147456 * log(1/delta))/Gamma; even eps ~ 11 at delta = 1e-5 needs Gamma ~ 200, i.e. b >~ 6e5. The theorem's hypothesis is never satisfied by anything in Section 8, and the paper never measures lambda_bar or Gamma. With sigma_g > 0 the condition becomes satisfiable — but then you are back to injecting calibrated noise, and the "for free" claim evaporates.

  2. The DP condition is data-dependent and the proof has an independence gap. lambda_bar is a property of the realised G_l(D); DP requires it uniformly over the domain (and over both RDP directions — only lambda_min(Sigma_1) is used). More seriously, Lemma 7.1 treats Q(D) as fixed given D, but in frozen-A LoRA the iterates W^t = W^0 + B^t A^0 depend on A^0, so G_l(D) is a function of the sketching matrix. The columns of G_l(D)A^{0T} are then not i.i.d. N(0, sigma_A^2 GG^T + sigma_g^2 I). The same gap undermines the cross-layer step, where Eq. (57) invokes "additivity of Renyi divergence for independent mechanisms" although all L layers share the trajectory. Only T = 1 is airtight.

  3. The secrecy of A^0 is load-bearing and practically false. The proof explicitly conditions on "without releasing the sketching matrices." For sigma_g = 0, A^0 is the only randomness; publish it and privacy is exactly zero. Yet FFA-LoRA's whole point in federated settings is that the server holds A, and ordinary LoRA checkpoints ship both factors.

Sections 6 and C do no DP work and should not be read as if they did. The injected "noise" has covariance proportional to ||q||^2 — it is multiplicative, vanishing where the gradient vanishes — and because A^0 is frozen it is perfectly correlated across all T steps, unlike DP-SGD's fresh per-step Gaussian. The Berry-Esseen result (Lemma C.2) is also weaker than advertised: the actual bound at Eq. (100) is 9 C_D (||q||_1/||q||_2)^3 / sqrt(r), and (||q||_1/||q||_2)^3 <= m^{3/2} — for m = 768, r = 16 that is about 1e4 * C_D, i.e. trivially above 1. C_D is itself an unquantified constant from Bobkov et al. depending on an unbounded KL bound D. The "O(1/sqrt r)" is honest only for fixed q with m fixed; the authors' own remark concedes a better O(1/sqrt(mr)) would need independence they don't have plus 0 < c < |q_i| < C. The bound is also per-coordinate, not joint over the m-vector.

Minor but telling. Appendix B's dismissal of Kaiming-uniform init is overstated: sigma_A^2 = 2/m gives mean (2r/m - 1)q ~ -q, which is a rescaled learning rate, not noise cancelling signal — and LoRA's standard alpha/r scaling factor, ignored throughout the paper, absorbs exactly this.

Experiments are thin for the claim. GPT-2 small, query matrices only, three datasets, one architecture, a calibrated loss-difference MIA (L(x;theta) - L(x;theta_ref) < gamma). The crucial missing baseline is full-rank SGD on the same 12 query matrices for the same T steps: without it, the AUC drop (e.g. Pubmed 0.929 to 0.546 to 0.486) is equally consistent with reduced capacity or the different learning rate (1e-5 vs 5e-4) as with sketching noise. No DP-SGD comparison at matched eps, no privacy auditing / empirical-eps lower bound, no error bars outside Fig. 3. And on PTB "privacy" barely materialises: AUC 0.963 to 0.872, TPR@1%FPR 65.8% to 48.2%, with perplexity up 29% (27.70 to 35.86). A rank knob that trades 29% PPL for an MIA AUC of 0.87 is not a privacy mechanism.

Broader context

The reference point is DP-SGD (Abadi et al. 2016): clip per-sample gradients to c, add N(0, c^2 z^2 I), account over steps with the moments/Renyi accountant. On LLMs this is memory-brutal, hence DP applied only to PEFT adapters. Separately, random projections have a long privacy history: Blocki et al. (2012) showed the JL transform itself preserves DP — but only when the input matrix is well-conditioned (a sigma_min requirement), which is precisely the lambda_bar assumption resurfacing here; Sheffet (2019) and, most directly, Lev et al. (NeurIPS 2025), "The Gaussian Mixing Mechanism: Renyi DP via Gaussian Sketches" supply the RDP machinery this paper generalises. The other essential antecedent is Hao et al. (ICML 2024), FLoRA, which first identified LoRA's dynamics as random gradient compression.

"Privacy for free" claims have a poor track record: gradient compression, instance encoding (InstaHide/TextHide — demolished by Carlini et al., Is Private Learning Possible with Instance Encoding?, 2021), and "gradients don't leak data" (overturned by Deep Leakage from Gradients) all fit the same template — a transformation that looks lossy, with a conditional guarantee, later shown to be attackable. This paper is better than those because it does produce a bona fide RDP bound; the risk is that the bound's hypotheses (Gamma > 1, secret A^0, data-dependent lambda_bar) quietly never hold where people will cite it.

Follow-up worth doing. Audit it. Run canary-injection privacy auditing (Steinke-Nasr-Jagielski one-run style) on FFA-LoRA at r in {4,...,64}, b in {8,...,4096}, and plot the empirical eps lower bound against the theorem's Gamma-regime; the prediction from the Gamma <= b/(4n) bound is a large empirical eps throughout the practical regime. The constructive version: resample A every step (ReLoRA-style re-initialisation) — then the per-step sketches are independent, you recover per-step composition plus subsampling amplification instead of one exponential-in-T sensitivity recursion, and A can even be public if a small sigma_g is added. The open question is whether sketch + small-noise beats plain Gaussian noise at matched eps when r << n, which Lev et al.'s results suggest it might.

IR link — thin but not zero. Don't force a generative-retrieval connection; there isn't one. What is genuine is the primitive: the object carrying privacy here is a Gaussian sketch A^{0T} in R^{m x r}, identical to the JL maps behind LSH, randomized SVD and projection-based ANN indexes, and the lambda_min(QQ^T) >= lambda_bar hypothesis is the same spectral-conditioning / subspace-embedding condition that governs when a sketch preserves inner products. The sharpest conceptual transfer is the tension: JL gives relative error, (1 +/- eps)||q|| — noise proportional to signal — which is exactly why it is excellent for retrieval and exactly why Lemma 6.1's multiplicative, signal-scaled "noise" cannot by itself give DP, which demands absolute indistinguishability. If you work on private or sketched vector indexes, that is the one-line reason "we only release projections / quantized codes, so it's safe" fails — the same lesson the embedding-inversion literature (Song & Raghunathan 2020; Morris et al.'s Vec2Text 2023) delivered empirically.

Proof sketch

Lemma 5.1 (exact dynamics). Assuming ||sum_{t<=tau} grad L||_F <= L, Hao et al.'s Theorem D.2 gives A^t = A^0 + eta A^0 f_A(t), B^t = eta f_B(t) A^{0T} with explicit f_A, f_B. Multiplying, W^T = W^0 + eta f_B(T) A^{0T}A^0 + eta^2 f_B(T) A^{0T}A^0 f_A(T), and since f_A(T) is O(eta) the last term is O(eta^3). Freezing A kills f_A entirely, making Eq. (10) an identity. This is the load-bearing structural step.

Lemma 6.1 (noise variance). Let A have i.i.d. N(0, sigma_A^2) entries, B = sigma_A^2 A^T A - I with standardised A. Diagonal: B_ii = sigma_A^2 sum_l a_{l,i}^2 - 1, a scaled chi^2_r, so mean r sigma_A^2 - 1, variance 2 r sigma_A^4. Off-diagonal: the trick is a_{l,i}a_{l,j} = (1/4)(a_{l,i}+a_{l,j})^2 - (1/4)(a_{l,i}-a_{l,j})^2 = (1/2)(nu_1 - nu_2) with independent nu_1, nu_2 ~ chi^2_1 (independence because sum and difference of equal-variance independent Gaussians are independent); the MGF (1 - 4t^2)^{-k/2} identifies nu_1 - nu_2 as a symmetric variance-gamma, giving mean 0, variance 1 per term, hence Var[B_ij] = r sigma_A^4. Then u_i = sum_l q_l B_{li} has mean (r sigma_A^2 - 1) q_i and variance r sigma_A^4 (||q||^2 + q_i^2) (summands pairwise uncorrelated). Lindeberg's condition holds as m -> infinity because s_m^2 -> infinity, so Theorem A.9 (Lindeberg-Lyapounov) gives asymptotic normality. Setting sigma_A^2 = 1/r zeroes the mean and makes variance (||q||^2 + q_i^2)/r.

Lemma C.2 (Berry-Esseen TV bound). The m*r summands in u_i are uncorrelated but not independent (q_1 a_{1,1} a_{1,i} and q_2 a_{1,2} a_{1,i} share a_{1,i}). The fix is to regroup by the row index t of A: u_i = sum_{t=1}^r V_t with V_t = (1/r)[q_i(X_t - 1) + sum_{l != i}(q_l/2) Y_{t,l}], X_t ~ chi^2_1, Y_{t,l} variance-gamma — now genuinely independent across t. Then apply Bobkov-Chistyakov-Gotze (2011) Thm 1.1, a TV-strength (entropic) Berry-Esseen: ||F_n - Phi||_TV <= C_D L_3 with L_3 = sum E|V_t|^3 / s_r^3. Denominator: s_r^3 = ((||q||^2 + q_i^2)/r)^{3/2} >= ||q||_2^3 / r^{3/2}. Numerator: Minkowski in L^3, plus E|chi^2_1 - 1|^3 <= 9 and Gaunt's (2024) absolute-moment formula E|Y|^3 = 2^6/(2 pi), gives E|V_t|^3 <= 9 ||q||_1^3 / r^3, so sum_t E|V_t|^3 <= 9 ||q||_1^3 / r^2. Ratio: 9 C_D ||q||_1^3 / (sqrt(r) ||q||_2^3). Lemma C.3 converts this via the coupling characterisation of TV into "u_i is a mixture: the exact Gaussian with weight 1 - O(1/sqrt r)."

Lemma 7.1 (sketch RDP). Columns of M(Q(D)) = Q(D)A^T + Z are i.i.d. N(0, Sigma_1), Sigma_1 = sigma_A^2 QQ^T + sigma_g^2 I_n; vectorising, vec(M) ~ N(0, I_r (x) Sigma_1), so Gil et al.'s Gaussian Renyi formula (Lemma D.1) yields D_alpha = -r/(2(alpha-1)) log[det(Sigma_1 + alpha DeltaSigma) / (det Sigma_1)^{1-alpha}(det Sigma_2)^alpha]. Eigendecompose DeltaSigma = V Lambda V^T = DeltaSigma^+ - DeltaSigma^- (rank tau), then apply the matrix determinant lemma (A.3) twice — once for the rank-tau^+ positive part, once for the rank-tau^- negative part — turning both determinants into det Sigma_1 * prod(1 +/- lambda_i(Q)) * prod(1 -/+ lambda_i(H or J)). The divergence collapses to r/(2(alpha-1)) sum log[(1-lambda)^alpha/(1-alpha lambda)], monotone increasing in lambda, so it suffices to bound all eigenvalues. That is the crux: by Lemma A.2 (lambda_i(X^T A^{-1} X) <= ||XX^T||_F / lambda_min(A)), Weyl (A.4), and ||DeltaSigma^-||_F <= ||DeltaSigma||_F, every eigenvalue is <= sigma_A^2 B_C / lambda_min(Sigma_1) <= B_C/(lambda_bar + sigma_g^2/sigma_A^2) = Gamma^{-1}, with B_C = 2 B_F B_S from Lemma A.1. Substituting gives Eq. (12), eps(alpha) = r tau/(2(alpha-1)) [alpha log(1 - Gamma^{-1}) - log(1 - alpha Gamma^{-1})], valid for alpha < Gamma.

Lemma 7.2 (LoRA). Instantiate Q = G_l(D). Norm: ||grad L^t||_F <= C by triangle inequality over the batch, so B_F = TC. Sensitivity: the key device is the adaptive-composition recursion Eq. (52), Delta g <= S + L * Delta f_1 for g(D) = f_2(D, f_1(D)) with f_2 S-sensitive and L-Lipschitz in its second argument. One SGD step has S = 2 eta C / b (replacement) and is (1 + eta beta)-Lipschitz in W^t by beta-smoothness, giving the geometric sum Delta f^{T-1} <= (2 eta C/b)((1+eta beta)^T - 1)/(eta beta), hence B_S = (2C/b)((1+eta beta)^T - 1)/(eta beta). Plug B_F, B_S into Lemma 7.1 to get Gamma = eta beta b (lambda_bar + r sigma_g^2)/(4 C^2 T ((1+eta beta)^T - 1)). Layers add by Renyi additivity (r L tau), and releasing W~_l^T = W^0 - eta M_l(D) A^0 is post-processing of M_l(D) — given that A^0 stays hidden.

Corollary 7.3 / (eps, delta). Show eps(alpha) <= (rLn/2 Gamma^2) alpha on a sub-range alpha in (1, zeta): define d(k, alpha, Gamma), multiply by 2 Gamma^2 (alpha - 1), reduce to e(alpha) = alpha(alpha-1) - alpha Gamma^2 log(1 - Gamma^{-1}) + Gamma^2 log(1 - alpha Gamma^{-1}) >= 0 with e(1) = 0; multiplying e'(alpha) by (Gamma - alpha) > 0 gives a downward quadratic H(alpha) whose larger root alpha_max exceeds 2 Gamma/5 whenever Gamma > 5/2. So LoRA is (rLn/2 Gamma^2, 2 Gamma/5)-tCDP, and Prop. 4.4 gives eps = rLn/(2 Gamma^2) + sqrt(2 rLn log(1/delta))/Gamma. Monotonicity reads off directly: eps is linear in r and L, improves with b, and degrades linear-exponentially in T — the last being exactly why the guarantee dies at realistic training lengths.

title: Tutorial: Theoretical Tools for Designing Modern Information Retrieval System (Part1)
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-27

Theoretical Tools for Designing Modern Information Retrieval Systems (tutorial slides, part 2) — Da Xu, Chuanwei Ruan (WSDM 2022) — https://moderntoolsfornextgenirs.github.io/

Main idea

First, a framing note: this is not a paper, it is a Beamer slide deck — specifically the second of three slide PDFs from the WSDM 2022 tutorial "Modern Theoretical Tools for Understanding and Designing Next-generation Information Retrieval System" by Da Xu (then ML manager at Walmart) and Chuanwei Ruan (then at Instacart), given on the WSDM tutorial day, 21 February 2022, with a 2-page companion abstract on arXiv (2203.13962, DOI 10.1145/3488560.3501394). The tutorial site lists p1.pdf ("Part one: pattern recognition"), p2.pdf ("Part one cont'd" — the file in the Zotero item) and p3.pdf ("Part two: decision making"). The Zotero title says "(Part1)" because the Beamer footer on every slide of p2.pdf says Part 1: Pattern Recognition (Model design & Model analysis); so the title is content-correct and file-confusing at the same time. This file is slides 36–62 of 62, the last 27 slides of Session 1. Consequence worth stating up front: the causal-inference / do-calculus / off-policy / bandit-and-RL material that the tutorial advertises is not in this file at all — it is in p3.pdf. Anyone reading this deck expecting counterfactual estimation for ranking will not find it.

The organising thesis of the tutorial as a whole is stated in the companion abstract: IR's classical theory — the probability ranking principle, axiomatic term weighting, surrogate-consistency results for learning-to-rank — is about the ranking objective, and it "can no longer explain, guide, and justify" the deep models that are actually deployed. So the tutorial imports the modern deep-learning-theory toolkit and tries to attach each tool to a decision an IR engineer actually makes: before training (set the inductive bias — expressivity, NTK, implicit bias of GD), at generalization time (structural complexity, domain discrepancy), and after training (diagnose, attribute, calibrate). Part one's first half (p1, not this file) sets that up: IR as classification-with-missing-data, ERM and weighted ERM, item2vec/SGNS as sufficient dimension reduction of a shifted PMI matrix, NTK as the expressivity tool, margin-maximising implicit bias as the optimization tool, Rademacher complexity and IPM/f-divergence discrepancy as the generalization tools, then NCF-vs-MCF and importance weighting as worked IR cases.

This file picks up at pre-trained representations and teaches, concretely, the following tools:

  1. Uniform-convergence excess-risk bounds for frozen pre-trained representations, with Rademacher vs. Gaussian complexity (slides 36–37). The question answered: is it actually valid to take a pre-trained embedding, treat it as a numerical feature vector, and feed it into a downstream model? The deck distinguishes two pre-training regimes it calls contrastive-learning-based (unsupervised; construct similar/dissimilar pairs; inner-product objective) and same-structure-based (supervised; use the same architecture/objective for pre-training and for the downstream task), and states a two-part theorem showing the same-structure route has the strictly cleaner guarantee. The contrastive bound carries an irreducible term that does not vanish with sample size.
  2. NTK-as-kernel-composition, used as a cross-domain transfer diagnostic (slides 38–41). The question answered: given that contrastive pre-training is more versatile but less well-guaranteed, what determines whether an embedding will transfer? The answer the deck builds: in the lazy/NTK regime the downstream model's tangent kernel is a fixed scalar transform of the embedding kernel $K_\phi(x,x')=\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle$ — for a two-layer MLP, the degree-0 arc-cosine kernel composed with $K_\phi$ — and for a linear head on concatenated embeddings the induced sequence kernel is literally $\sum_i K_\phi(x_i,x_i')$. Hence the embedding influences the downstream task _only through $K_\phi$_, and an alignment bound (a relabelled kernel-target alignment, Cristianini et al. 2001) closes the chain: representation → kernel → kernel/label alignment → cross-domain generalization.
  3. Graph spectral analysis (slides 42–44, 46–47). Graph Laplacian as the discrete second derivative, graph Fourier transform as expansion in Laplacian eigenvectors, spectral filtering $g_\theta \star X = U\,\mathrm{diag}(\hat g_\theta(\lambda_i))\,U^\top X$, and the observation that stacking first-order Chebyshev filters (i.e. a GCN) is a low-pass filter whose suppression of high-frequency components sharpens exponentially with depth. The question answered: why do GNNs help on cross-domain IR tasks? Proposed mechanism: a shared, domain-invariant filter ⇒ better-aligned representation kernel after filtering ⇒ better domain generalization.
  4. The Bellman equation as a second lens on message passing (slides 45, 48). Local aggregation $h^{(k)}(u) = \min_{v\in N(u)} \mathrm{NN}^{(k)}(\cdot)$ is put next to Bellman–Ford $d[k][u] = \min_{v\in N(u)} d[k-1][v] + w(u,v)$; since shortest-path distance defines a graph kernel, message passing is read as implicitly approximating a graph kernel that happens to be aligned across domains. (This is the deck's informal version of Keyulu Xu and Jegelka's algorithmic alignment line, cited in p1 but not here.)
  5. Post-hoc model diagnostics for IR (slides 49–56). A taxonomy (global vs. local; model-dependent vs. model-agnostic), then attribution: perturbation-based vs. backpropagation-based, with three IR-specific reasons perturbation fails (correlated features — CTR at many aggregation levels; $10^5$-scale feature counts making one-at-a-time infeasible; missing and exposure-biased ground truth), then gradient × input, integrated gradients (with its completeness axiom), and DeepLIFT (rescale rule). The one genuinely IR-flavoured prescription: because IR models encode discrete objects via embeddings, take gradients at the embedding level, and use the zero vector as the IG baseline.
  6. Calibration and conformal prediction (slides 57–58). The argument is a nice one: p1 established that over-parameterised models trained with exponential-tail losses converge to margin maximisers, so their logits are pushed to the extremes and encode margin, not confidence; therefore ranking $e_1$ above $e_2$ by score has no probabilistic content, and you need either calibration (binary) or a conformal prediction set (ranking). Implementation is reduced to "find the quantile functions and use their statistical properties to rearrange and rescale the outputs."
  7. Learning-to-learn and shared embeddings (slides 60–62). The three standard LTL families (memory-augmented networks; Siamese/metric; MAML), the Walmart product-knowledge-graph-embedding system as the "shared embedding" case study, and then — as the only provable statement in this closing section — Tripuraneni, Jin & Jordan's linear-representation meta-learning bound, $\mathbb{E}_{x^\star}[\langle x^\star, \hat B\hat\alpha - B\alpha_{t+1}\rangle^2] \le \tilde O(dr^2/n_1 + r/n_2)$.

Papers cited in this file: Xu & Ruan, "Rethinking Pre-trained Embedding for E-commerce ML", preprint '22 (this is the load-bearing one — it later appeared as Xu & Yang, "Pretrained Embeddings for E-commerce Machine Learning: When it Fails and Why?", arXiv:2304.04330, DOI 10.1145/3543873.3587669, and that paper contains verbatim the deck's Theorem 1, the arc-cosine composition, the sequence-kernel example and the alignment proposition); "The Mystery of Graph Neural Network for Cross-domain Generalization, coming soon"; "Paying attention to the scores of your recommendation model, coming soon"; Santoro et al., MANN, ICML'16; Koch et al., Siamese networks, ICML'15 workshop; Finn et al., MAML, ICML'17; Xu et al., Product Knowledge Graph Embedding, WSDM'20; Tripuraneni et al., ICML'21. Two small but telling things: the deck cites by first name ("Adam et al.", "Gregory et al.", "Chelsea et al.", "Nilesh et al.", "Da et al."), and the canonical sources for almost everything it teaches — Jacot et al. for NTK, Cho & Saul for the arc-cosine kernel, Kipf & Welling for the GCN, Sundararajan et al. for IG, Shrikumar et al. for DeepLIFT, Arora et al. and HaoChen et al. for contrastive guarantees, Cristianini et al. for alignment, Vovk/Shafer for conformal — are not cited at all. Everything is routed through the presenters' own preprints.

The most interesting part

The single most useful idea is the reduction of "is this embedding good for my downstream task?" to a Gram-matrix question, and the fact that it comes with an operational consequence. The chain is: (i) under lazy training the downstream network is a kernel machine; (ii) its tangent kernel is $g(K_\phi(x,x'))$ for a fixed scalar $g$ determined by the head architecture, not by $\phi$ — for a two-layer ReLU MLP, $g$ is the degree-0 arc-cosine kernel; (iii) therefore the embedding enters downstream performance only through $K_\phi$; (iv) therefore the diagnostic is the alignment between $K_\phi$ and the label kernel $K_Y(y,y')=\mathbf 1[y=y']$. This is genuinely useful because it is cheap and pre-hoc: you can estimate $\mathbb E[K_Y K_\phi]/\sqrt{\mathbb E[K_\phi^2]}$ on a sample of labelled pairs and rank candidate embeddings without training a single downstream model. In a large industrial IR stack where "which of our eight embedding tables should feed this new ranker?" is asked weekly, that is a real tool. The slide's third bullet is the honest statement of its design implication: if $K_\phi$ already aligns with the task, even a linear head suffices; if it does not, no reasonable choice of head will fix it, because the head only gets to pick $g$.

Paired with this is the sharpest negative claim in the deck: the contrastive bound's covariance term $R\cdot\mathbb E_y\|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)\|_2$ is attached to $\phi^*$, the population contrastive risk minimiser. It is a bias, not an estimation error. So "spurious dimensions" and the failure of contrastive embeddings as drop-in numerical features are not finite-sample artifacts that more pre-training data will cure — they are properties of the objective's geometry. That is the one place in the deck where the theory says something a practitioner would not have guessed and could not get from an ablation.

Now the honest critique, as a learning resource.

Where the bounds are informative vs. vacuous. $\mathcal G_n(\Phi)/\sqrt n$ for $\Phi$ = a transformer encoder is not computable, not small, and not known to be the right quantity; as a bound it is decorative. The bound earns its keep exactly where it stops being a bound: the comparison of shapes — one expression with only vanishing terms, one with a non-vanishing term — is the content, and that comparison does not need the complexity terms to be tight. A reader should take away the dichotomy, not the inequality. Also note a concrete defect the slides never resolve: the same-structure bound divides the Gaussian complexity by $\sqrt n$ while the contrastive bound divides the Rademacher complexity by $n$. Those rates are only mutually coherent if the two complexity functionals carry different normalisations (one an unnormalised sum, one averaged) — a standard but silent convention clash. From the deck alone you cannot tell, and if you read them as the same normalisation you would conclude the contrastive estimation term is the faster one, which inverts the intended message. For a tutorial whose whole premise is "learn to read these bounds", leaving that undefined is a real failure.

The alignment proposition is weaker than it looks. As stated on slide 41 (and in the companion paper as Proposition 1), $R_{\mathrm{OOD}}(f_\phi) \le 1 - \mathbb E[K_Y(y,y')K_\phi(x,x')]\cdot\sqrt{\delta}/\sqrt{\mathbb E[k_\phi^2]}$. Three problems. (a) The $\sqrt\delta$ sits in the numerator, so the bound gets weaker as you demand higher confidence — the wrong direction for a high-probability statement; either the slides and the paper both have a typo, or the quantity is not what "with probability $1-\delta$" usually means. (b) $R \le 1$ holds trivially for 0–1 risk, so the bound has content only to the extent the alignment term is bounded away from zero, and nothing in the deck bounds it. (c) It is labelled an OOD result, but the proposition contains no discrepancy term — no $\mathcal H$-divergence, no Wasserstein distance, nothing that measures how far the target domain is from the source. If alignment is measured on the target domain, this is an in-domain alignment bound evaluated elsewhere, not a transfer bound; if measured on the source, the inequality does not follow. Part one of the deck has exactly the discrepancy machinery needed to fix this and never connects it. That is the single biggest technical gap in the file.

The GNN section is the weakest. The algebra "$(I+\tilde L)^k X\theta_0 = U\theta_0\,\mathrm{diag}((2-\lambda_1)^k,\dots)\,U^\top X$" only works if "$I+\tilde L$" actually means $I + D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2} = 2I - \tilde L$ (Kipf & Welling's first-order Chebyshev approximation), not $I$ plus the Laplacian; the deck writes the latter and computes the former. And the asserted inequality — the mangled text reads as "$2-\lambda \le 1$" — is false for the low end of the spectrum: the normalised Laplacian always has $\lambda_{\min}=0$ on a connected graph, so $2-\lambda_{\min}=2>1$. The correct statement is relative shrinkage (large-$\lambda$ components are suppressed relative to small-$\lambda$ ones, exponentially in $k$) — which is the low-pass story the deck wants, but with the renormalisation trick needed precisely to stop repeated application from blowing up. I flag that I am reconstructing the inequality from degraded text; under either reading the on-slide claim needs repair. More importantly, both GNN explanations have the form "if the mechanism is invariant across domains, then generalization improves". The conditional carries the entire argument, and the deck offers no condition under which it holds, no way to test it, and no bound. The Bellman–Ford analogy is an analogy: "notice the similarity?" is the whole proof. The rigorous version of that idea already existed — Xu, Li, Zhang, Du, Kawarabayashi & Jegelka's algorithmic alignment (ICLR 2020) and extrapolation (ICLR 2021) results, cited in p1 but not reused here, actually prove that architectures matching a dynamic-programming structure have lower sample complexity for that task. Using the analogy without the theorem, in a tutorial about theoretical tools, is a missed opportunity.

Does the theory guide design or rationalise it? Mostly the latter, and the deck is at its most candid about this on slide 59, which presents the "learning system design" cycle and then says: "Not your typical engineering cycle. But can help you draft PPT that looks fancy :)". That joke is more honest than most of the surrounding content. GNNs were already known to help on e-commerce IR before anyone wrote down a spectral or Bellman story; the stories explain what was already shipped. The one place the direction genuinely runs theory → design is the pre-trained-embedding section: the covariance term tells you to prefer same-structure pre-training, or to not freeze, and that recommendation is non-obvious and was reached by analysis. The calibration argument (margin-maximising implicit bias ⇒ logits are not probabilities ⇒ you need conformal sets for ranking) is a second genuine case — and it is given two slides with no method, and its citation is a "coming soon" that, as far as I can find, never arrived. Of the three forward references in this file, two are "coming soon"; the one that materialised did so a year later, with a different second author.

What a 2026 reader should treat as dated. (a) The entire framing assumes the frozen-embedding-table paradigm: the artifact you pre-train is a vector, and the downstream model consumes it as a feature. That paradigm has been largely displaced — by instruction-tuned and task-conditioned encoders that are adapted rather than frozen, by LLM rerankers, and by generative retrieval, where there is no embedding table at all. Note that this displacement vindicates the deck's conclusion while retiring its machinery: if you no longer freeze, you are in the same-structure regime and the covariance term is not your problem. (b) NTK/lazy training as the model of fine-tuning has aged badly at LLM scale. The kernel regime provably cannot do feature learning, the $O(\mathrm{poly}(T)/\sqrt m)$ linearisation error is loose over realistic training horizons, and the μP/maximal-update line has made it standard to say that what matters about large-model training is exactly the part NTK discards. The kernel-alignment diagnostic survives as a heuristic; the "therefore the downstream model is a kernel machine" step does not. (c) The deck predates the DSI/generative-retrieval wave (Tay et al. appeared essentially simultaneously, February 2022) and the LLM-for-IR wave entirely. (d) The calibration/conformal section was a gesture in 2022 because the literature was thin; it is now a usable toolkit — distribution-free reliability guarantees for recommender top-$k$ sets, conformal risk control — and a 2026 reader should skip the slides and read that literature. (e) Two absences that look odd for an IR tutorial even in 2022: nothing on retrieval-specific approximation (ANN recall, index structure, the fact that the serving-time hypothesis is $f$ composed with an approximate argmax), and nothing on the statistical consistency of ranking surrogates, which is the one place classical IR theory and learning theory already met.

Net assessment as a learning resource: a good map, a bad text. Theorems appear without assumptions, constants, or proofs; the symbol conventions are not defined on-slide (the extraction degradation makes this worse, but the original is terse too); and the reading list is skewed almost entirely toward the presenters' own work, several items of which did not exist. Its real value is as an index — it tells a theory-literate IR person which five or six literatures to go read, and the pre-trained-embedding section is worth reading in its published form (arXiv:2304.04330) rather than as slides.

Proof sketch

The deck states results and does not prove them. Below I state the two most important ones precisely, say what is actually guaranteed, and then reconstruct how results of each kind are proved in the literature they draw on. I flag explicitly which parts are read off the slides and which I am reconstructing.

Result 1 (read off slide 37; verified against Theorem 1 of arXiv:2304.04330). The same-structure vs. contrastive dichotomy.

Setup, partly inferred: a pre-training sample of size $n$ yields an encoder $\hat\phi \in \Phi$; a downstream model class $\mathcal F$ (on the slides, effectively a linear/logistic probe) is fit on top of the frozen $\hat\phi$; $R_{\mathrm{task}}(\hat\phi)$ is the downstream population risk achievable on top of $\hat\phi$ and $R^*_{\mathrm{task}}$ the best risk achievable in the downstream task at all. Standing assumptions I am inferring, since the slide does not list them: $\|\phi(x)\|\le R$ uniformly, a Lipschitz bounded surrogate loss, i.i.d. pre-training and downstream data, and for the contrastive case a latent-class generative model under which $\phi^* = \arg\min_\phi R^C_{\mathrm{CL}}(\phi)$ exists.

Same-structure pre-training. $\;R_{\mathrm{task}}(\hat\phi) - R^*_{\mathrm{task}} \lesssim \mathcal G_n(\Phi)/\sqrt n \;+\; \tilde{\mathcal G}(\mathcal F)/n \;+\; \text{slack}$, where $\mathcal G_n$ is empirical Gaussian complexity and $\tilde{\mathcal G}(\mathcal F)$ a complexity measure of the downstream class. (The published version of the theorem replaces $\tilde{\mathcal G}(\mathcal F)$ by $R$, the norm bound, specialising to a linear probe; the slide is the more general statement.) In plain language: if your pre-training objective and architecture are the same as the downstream task's, your excess risk is pure estimation error. It decays with pre-training sample size at the usual rate, and the only things that can make it large are the capacities of the encoder class and the head class. There is no irreducible term.

Contrastive pre-training. $\;R_{\mathrm{task}}(\hat\phi) - R^*_{\mathrm{task}} \lesssim R\,\mathcal R_n(\Phi)/n \;+\; R^2\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}/\sqrt n \;+\; R\cdot\mathbb E_y\big\|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)\big\|_2$. In plain language: an estimation part that vanishes with $n$, plus a bias that does not. The bias is the average spectral norm of the within-downstream-class covariance of the population-optimal contrastive encoder: if items that share a downstream label are spread out in embedding space under $\phi^*$, a linear probe on top of a frozen $\phi^*$ cannot recover that label no matter how much data you collect. The companion paper's own gloss is that this term "can become arbitrarily large" when $\phi^*$ disagrees with the downstream conditional distribution.

What is actually guaranteed, and what is not.
