Guaranteed: an upper bound on the excess risk of a linear/logistic probe over a frozen encoder, under the inferred boundedness/Lipschitz/i.i.d. conditions. Not guaranteed: (i) that contrastive pre-training must be worse — there is no matching lower bound, so the dichotomy is a comparison of upper bounds, which is weaker than it reads; (ii) anything about fine-tuned encoders (the moment you unfreeze, the decomposition breaks, and the "same-structure" branch is arguably the relevant one); (iii) anything about architecture or optimization — the bounds are over function classes and say nothing about whether SGD finds the relevant minimiser; (iv) any numerically usable number, since $\mathcal G_n(\Phi)$ and $\mathcal R_n(\Phi)$ are not evaluated.

How a result of this form is proved — reconstruction from the literature, not from the slides. The contrastive branch is Arora, Khandeparkar, Khodak, Plevrakis & Saunshi (ICML 2019) in structure, with the following four steps.

  1. Mean-classifier reduction. Bound the downstream risk of the learned linear probe by the risk of the mean classifier $\mu_y = \mathbb E[\phi(x)\mid y]$, which is in the probe class. The mean classifier's margin is governed by the separation of class means against the within-class scatter; converting a margin statement into a risk statement is a Chebyshev/Markov step (or, with a Lipschitz surrogate, a Jensen bound on $\mathbb E\|\phi(x)-\mu_y\|$). This is exactly where $\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi)$ enters. It is not an artifact of the proof technique being loose — it is the quantity that controls whether a linear functional can separate classes, so the term is structurally necessary for any frozen-linear-probe analysis.
  2. Relate the population contrastive risk to the mean-classifier risk. Under a latent-class model for positive/negative pairs, the unsupervised contrastive risk decomposes into (a) a term upper-bounding the supervised loss of the mean classifier and (b) the intra-class deviation term. Arora et al.'s version also picks up a factor $1/(1-\tau)$ where $\tau$ is the collision probability that a sampled negative shares the anchor's latent class — this is the formal content of the deck's slide-36 remark about "imperfect negative samping". Note the deck mentions imperfect negative sampling and spurious dimensions as motivation but its Theorem 1 does not expose $\tau$; the $\tau$ dependence lives in the referenced preprint, not the slide.
  3. Population → empirical. Standard symmetrisation: introduce a ghost sample, insert Rademacher signs, and bound $\sup_\phi |R^C_{\mathrm{CL}}(\phi) - \hat R^C_{\mathrm{CL}}(\phi)|$ by $2\mathcal R_n(\ell\circ\Phi)$; then McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality supplies the high-probability slack, which is the $R^2\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}/\sqrt n$ term.
  4. Pass from the loss class to the representation class. The step that produces $R\cdot\mathcal R_n(\Phi)$ rather than $\mathcal R_n(\ell\circ\Phi)$ is a vector-contraction inequality (Maurer 2016) — the multi-output generalisation of Ledoux–Talagrand contraction, which costs a $\sqrt 2$ and the Lipschitz constant, here the norm bound $R$. This is the key technical trick and the reason $R$ multiplies the complexity term: $R$ is doing double duty as the Lipschitz constant of the inner-product loss in $\phi$.

The Gaussian complexity in the same-structure branch is the tell that a different route was taken there: Gaussian complexity is what you want when you intend to use Slepian/Sudakov–Fernique comparison or a Dudley chaining argument over the encoder class (Gaussian complexity dominates Rademacher up to a $\sqrt{\log n}$ factor and is the natural object for metric-entropy integrals). That is consistent with the two branches having genuinely different normalisation conventions — which is my explanation for the $\sqrt n$-vs-$n$ discrepancy noted above, but it is an inference, not something the deck states.

The same-structure branch itself is much shorter, and this is the real content of the comparison: when the pre-training objective is the downstream objective up to the head, steps 1 and 2 are unnecessary — ERM plus symmetrisation plus contraction directly yields estimation error with no bias term, because there is no surrogate to be mis-specified. The whole theorem is therefore a formalisation of a near-tautology made precise: contrastive pre-training optimises a proxy for the wrong target, and you pay for the proxy forever. The value is that the payment is localised in a single, in-principle-measurable quantity.

A sharper modern route to the same shape (also reconstruction; not in the deck). HaoChen, Wei, Gaidon & Ma (NeurIPS 2021) replace the latent-class model with a population augmentation graph on the data, show that minimising the spectral contrastive loss recovers the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the normalised adjacency of that graph, and bound linear-probe error by a term measuring how nearly-constant labels are on connected components plus a $1/(1-\lambda_{k+1})$ spectral-gap term. Same shape — contrastive-loss term plus a geometry/graph term — but strictly more informative, because the geometry term is a functional of something the engineer controls: the positive-pair distribution. This matters for reading the deck: it tells you that the opaque $\|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)\|_2$ is best understood as a geometric quantity about the augmentation/co-occurrence graph, not a statistical one about sampling.

Result 2 (read off slides 38–41; verified against Eq. 2, Example 1 and Proposition 1 of arXiv:2304.04330). The NTK kernel-composition chain.

Claim as stated. For a two-layer MLP head $f(\theta;\cdot)$ on a frozen embedding $\phi$, linearise $f(\theta;\phi(x)) \approx \langle \theta-\theta_0, \nabla f(\theta^{(0)};\phi(x))\rangle$ and define $K_{\mathrm{NTK}}(\phi(x),\phi(x')) = \langle \nabla f(\theta^{(0)};\phi(x)), \nabla f(\theta^{(0)};\phi(x'))\rangle$. Then $$K_{\mathrm{NTK}}(\phi(x),\phi(x')) = 1 - \tfrac1\pi\cos^{-1}\!\Big(\tfrac{\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle}{\|\phi(x)\|\,\|\phi(x')\|}\Big),$$ i.e. the NTK is the degree-0 arc-cosine kernel composed with the embedding kernel; more generally $K_{\mathrm{NTK}} = g(K_\phi)$ for a scalar $g$ fixed by the head architecture. Corollary stated on slide 40: for a linear head on a concatenation of $k$ embeddings, the induced sequence kernel is $K(s,s') = \sum_{i=1}^k K_\phi(x_i,x_i')$. Corollary stated on slide 41: for the normalised kernel (Parzen-type) predictor $f_\phi(x) = \mathbb E_{x',y'}[y'k_\phi(x,x')]/\sqrt{\mathbb E[k_\phi^2]}$, the 0–1 risk is bounded by $1$ minus a kernel-target alignment between $K_\phi$ and $K_Y(y,y')=\mathbf 1[y=y']$.

What is actually guaranteed. In the infinite-width / lazy regime, with that specific head and a frozen embedding, the downstream predictor's dependence on the embedding is exactly through the Gram matrix $K_\phi$ (up to the per-point norms). That is a real and clean statement: it means the eigen-decomposition of $K_\phi$ determines the bias–variance profile of downstream kernel regression, so two embeddings with the same Gram matrix are downstream-equivalent in this regime. What is not guaranteed: anything for fine-tuned encoders; anything for deep heads with normalisation layers or attention; anything at finite width beyond the linearisation error bound; and — per the critique above — anything genuinely cross-domain, since no discrepancy term appears.

How each piece is proved — reconstruction.

  • The linearisation (and why it is legitimate). This is Jacot, Gabriel & Hongler (2018) plus the lazy-training analyses (Du et al.; Arora et al. 2019b; Chizat, Oyallon & Bach). The key lemma is a perturbation bound on the Jacobian: for width $m$ and standard initialisation scaling, the tangent features $\nabla_\theta f(\theta_t;\cdot)$ move by $O(1/\sqrt m)$ in the relevant operator norm over the training trajectory, so gradient descent on the nonlinear model tracks kernel gradient descent with the fixed kernel $K_{\mathrm{NTK}}$ up to $O(\mathrm{poly}(T)/\sqrt m)$. Equivalently: in the lazy regime, the loss landscape is effectively that of a linear model in the tangent features and the min-norm interpolant is the kernel-ridgeless solution. Everything downstream of the linearisation is then ordinary kernel theory (representer theorem; kernel-regression bias–variance governed by eigenvalue decay).
  • The closed form (the actual trick). For a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with Gaussian initialisation, the tangent kernel's first-layer contribution is $\mathbb E_{w\sim N(0,I)}[\sigma'(w^\top u)\,\sigma'(w^\top v)]$ with $u=\phi(x)$, $v=\phi(x')$. Because $w$ is isotropic, this expectation is invariant to any rotation applied simultaneously to $u$ and $v$, hence depends on $(u,v)$ only through $\|u\|,\|v\|$ and the angle $\vartheta$ between them. Evaluating the Gaussian integral for the ReLU derivative (an indicator of a half-space) gives $(\pi-\vartheta)/\pi = 1-\vartheta/\pi$, which is Cho & Saul's arc-cosine kernel of degree 0; substituting $\vartheta = \cos^{-1}(K_\phi/\|\phi(x)\|\|\phi(x')\|)$ gives the slide's formula. The conceptual point is worth stating because the deck does not: the reduction to $K_\phi$ is a consequence of rotation invariance of the initialisation, not of anything deep about pre-training. Any architecture whose initialisation is isotropic in its input layer will have a tangent kernel that is a function of the input Gram matrix alone. Correspondingly, the result is fragile to exactly the things real systems do — per-feature learning rates, embedding-specific initialisation scales, LayerNorm before the first linear layer — each of which breaks isotropy.
  • The sequence kernel. This is not a theorem, it is linear algebra: for a linear head on $\Phi \in \mathbb R^{n\times kd}$ holding concatenated embeddings, the least-squares dual solution depends on the data only through $\Phi\Phi^\top$, whose $(s,s')$ entry is $\sum_{i=1}^k \langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_i')\rangle$. The slide's "Therefore, $K_\phi$ also decides the performance of the downstream task" is immediate. (Note the limitation this exposes: the argument works because the head is linear in a concatenation — it says nothing about a transformer over the sequence, which is what anyone actually uses, and where position-mixing means the induced kernel is not a sum of per-position embedding kernels.)
  • The alignment bound. The predictor is a normalised Parzen-window / kernel-mean classifier. Its expected margin on a correctly-labelled pair is, by construction, the numerator $\mathbb E[K_Y(y,y')K_\phi(x,x')]$; its second moment is the denominator $\sqrt{\mathbb E[k_\phi^2]}$; so the ratio is the kernel-target alignment $A(K_\phi, K_Y)$ of Cristianini, Shawe-Taylor, Elisseeff & Kandola (NIPS 2001), and the conversion from "expected margin is at least $A$" to "0–1 risk is at most $1-A$" is a one-sided Chebyshev/Markov inequality, with a concentration step (McDiarmid on the alignment estimate, which is a bounded function of the sample) supplying the probabilistic qualifier. This is precisely Cristianini et al.'s original alignment-to-generalization argument, and the proposition is their Theorem with $yy^\top$ renamed $K_Y$. I am reconstructing this, since neither the slides nor the companion paper give the proof, but the form of the statement makes the route unambiguous. It also explains the odd $\sqrt\delta$: in alignment-style arguments the concentration factor normally appears as a subtracted $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n})$ correction, so a multiplicative $\sqrt\delta$ in the numerator is almost certainly a transcription error for such a term.

Broader context

Background for someone coming from classical IR. There are two largely disjoint theory traditions in IR. The first is about the objective: the probability ranking principle, axiomatic constraints on term-weighting, and the statistical-consistency literature for learning-to-rank (whether a convex surrogate's minimiser also minimises NDCG or pairwise disagreement — Cossock & Zhang, Ravikumar et al., Duchi et al., Calauzènes et al.). That tradition takes the feature representation as given and asks whether the loss you optimise points at the metric you report. The second, which this tutorial imports, is statistical learning theory about the representation: uniform convergence over a function class, implicit bias of the optimiser, the kernel regime as a tractable surrogate for deep learning, and domain-shift bounds. These two traditions barely cite each other. The tutorial is one of the few explicit attempts to bring the second into IR, which is why it is worth having read even though it is uneven — it is a map of a transplant, not a result.

Two closely related things worth knowing. (1) HaoChen, Wei, Gaidon & Ma (NeurIPS 2021), spectral contrastive loss and the augmentation graph. For IR this is the more natural abstraction than the deck's latent-class model, because the "augmentation graph" in IR is not a set of crops and colour jitters — it is the behavioural co-occurrence graph (co-click, co-purchase, same-session). The spectral-gap condition then reads as a statement about the connectivity of the click graph within intent clusters, which is something you can measure and even engineer (by changing how positives are mined). I would argue that reframing the deck's covariance term as a spectral-gap condition on the co-click graph is the single highest-value translation an IR theorist could do with this material. (2) Saunshi, Ash, Misra, Goel, Arora et al., "Understanding Contrastive Learning Requires Incorporating Inductive Biases" (ICML 2022) — the necessary counterweight. It shows that transfer-agnostic bounds of exactly the style the deck presents can be vacuous: one can construct settings where the contrastive loss and the class-collision/variance quantities are unchanged while downstream performance varies arbitrarily, because the bounds ignore the architecture and the optimisation. It appeared four months after this tutorial and is the strongest reason to read the deck's Theorem 1 as a diagnosis of a failure mode rather than a guarantee. Alongside it, Keyulu Xu & Jegelka's algorithmic-alignment line (ICLR 2020, 2021) is the rigorous version of the deck's Bellman hand-wave.

A follow-up research idea the deck opens up: budgeted / retrieved alignment. Every bound in this file assumes the downstream predictor sees whatever pairs the distribution hands it. In a deployed retrieval system it does not: the reranker only ever evaluates pairs that the ANN index returned. So the operative quantity is not $A(K_\phi, K_Y)$ but the alignment restricted to the index's candidate neighbourhoods, $A\big(K_\phi|_{\mathcal N(x)}, K_Y|_{\mathcal N(x)}\big)$, where $\mathcal N(x)$ is the set HNSW or IVF-PQ actually returns for query $x$. The gap between full and retrieved alignment is an index-induced bias that composes with the deck's covariance bias, and — unlike either — it is a quantity you can change by tuning $efSearch$ or the number of probes. Formalising "alignment under a retrieval budget", and showing how it degrades as a function of index parameters and of the intrinsic dimension of $\phi(\mathcal X)$, is a tractable paper-sized project and would be the first version of this theory that knows retrieval exists.

Specific connection to Shiguang's work.

Do these representation-generalization bounds transfer to generative retrieval? There is a sharp and, I think, under-appreciated answer hiding in the deck's own dichotomy. In DSI/NCI-style generative retrieval the index is the model parameters and the output is a docid string, so there is no embedding table to freeze — which means the pre-training objective (autoregressive docid prediction, or indexing-as-memorisation) and the downstream objective (retrieval-by-decoding) are the same objective on the same architecture. By the deck's own taxonomy, generative retrieval sits in the same-structure branch, which is exactly the branch with no irreducible covariance term. That is a genuine, non-obvious theoretical argument for generative retrieval over frozen-embedding dense retrieval: the bias term that provably cannot be removed by more data in the contrastive/dense pipeline does not appear in the generative one. The catch — and this is where the interesting work is — is that the price moves into the complexity term. $\mathcal G_n(\Phi)/\sqrt n$ is now a complexity over a class indexed by the docid vocabulary, and the right complexity measure is not a Gram matrix at all: it is something closer to a covering number of the set of achievable docid-prefix decision boundaries, or the metric entropy of the codebook-induced partition of query space. Here is the formalisable observation: a semantically structured docid (hierarchical $k$-means in DSI-semantic, the residual-quantisation codes in RIPOR-style systems) is precisely an attempt to make the label kernel $K_Y$ low-rank and tree-structured so that the decoder class needed to align with it is small. Docid design is kernel-alignment engineering on the label side — and the deck cannot see this because it holds $K_Y = \mathbf 1[y=y']$ fixed throughout. The research question that falls out: given a corpus and a relevance distribution, which docid code minimises (complexity of the decoder class required to realise a target alignment) + (quantisation distortion of the code)? That is a rate–distortion problem with a learning-theoretic cost functional in place of squared error, and as far as I know nobody has stated the generative-retrieval docid-design problem that way, even though every empirical paper in the area is doing gradient-free search over exactly that trade-off.

What an analogous complexity measure would look like for ANN retrieval. Two concrete handles, both of which the deck's framework cannot express because it has no notion of approximation. (a) A single geometric quantity on both sides of a trade-off. The intrinsic/doubling dimension of $\phi(\mathcal X)$ controls ANN hardness (Indyk–Naor, Krauthgamer–Lee, and the graph-index analyses of Prokhorenkova–Shekhovtsov for HNSW-type structures) and the eigenvalue decay of $K_\phi$, which governs kernel-regression generalization. So low intrinsic dimension buys you both recall and statistical capacity — meaning the deck's "spurious dimensions" story is one half of a trade-off whose other half is retrievability. Writing down the joint statement (a bound in which the same dimension parameter appears with opposite signs in a recall term and a capacity term) would give the first principled answer to "how many dimensions should my embedding have?" that is not an ablation. (b) A uniform-convergence statement for the retrieve-then-rank composition. The serving-time hypothesis is $f$ composed with an approximate argmax, so the honest decomposition is: excess ranking risk $\le$ (probe/reranker excess risk, which the deck bounds) + (loss induced by the recall@$k$ deficit). The second term is controlled not by recall itself but by the margin distribution of $K_\phi$ at the top-$k$ boundary — the probability mass of candidate scores within $\varepsilon$ of the $k$-th score — because that is what determines whether an approximate search's mistakes are consequential. The practical corollary is testable and slightly contrarian: _the right thing to measure about an index is not recall@$k$ but the score-gap distribution at the cut_, since two indices with identical recall can have very different downstream ranking risk. (c) A small bonus that connects the two halves tightly: the irreducible term $\mathbb E_y\|\mathrm{cov}_{P_X^{(y)}}(\phi^*)\|_2$ has a direct retrieval reading — within-class scatter is exactly what makes nearest-neighbour search return off-class items. So the same geometric quantity that bounds linear-probe excess risk ought to bound a recall deficit. Proving one inequality in which within-class covariance controls both probe risk and recall@$k$ for a frozen embedding would be a compact, self-contained theory result, and it is the kind of statement the deck gestures at but never makes.

Housekeeping: the Zotero item has no authors, date, DOI or abstract — worth filling in as Da Xu and Chuanwei Ruan, WSDM 2022 tutorial (21 Feb 2022), companion abstract arXiv:2203.13962, DOI 10.1145/3488560.3501394, and noting in the title that the file is p2.pdf ("part one cont'd", slides 36–62).

title: Benign Overfitting in Classification: Provably Counter Label Noise with Larger Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-27

Benign Overfitting in Classification: Provably Counter Label Noise with Larger Models — Kaiyue Wen, Jiaye Teng, Jingzhao Zhang (ICLR 2023) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00501

Main idea

The benign-overfitting literature in classification had, by 2022, produced a fairly uniform message: train a linear or near-linear classifier to interpolation on a Gaussian/sub-Gaussian mixture, let gradient descent's implicit bias drive you to the max-margin solution, and the population risk converges to the Bayes rate — even when a constant fraction of the training labels are flipped. Chatterji–Long, Wang–Thrampoulidis, Cao–Gu–Belkin and Frei–Chatterji–Bartlett all prove versions of this. The fine print, which this paper makes the subject, is that every one of those results needs the ambient dimension to be much larger than the sample size: $p = \omega(n)$, and in several cases $p = \Omega(n\log n)$ or $p = \Omega(n^2)$.

Wen, Teng and Zhang ask what happens in the proportional regime $p/n = r$ for a fixed constant $r > 1$ — what they call mild overparameterization, and what high-dimensional statistics would call the asymptotic regime. Their answer is a clean dichotomy. With clean labels, the max-margin interpolator still works at $p = \Theta(n)$: 0-1 risk $\lesssim n^{-c}$. With a constant label-flip rate $\rho$, the max-margin interpolator provably has 0-1 risk bounded below by a constant that does not shrink with $n$ — and the same data, trained with one pass of small-step SGD and stopped early, provably achieves vanishing risk. So the failure is attributable to interpolation, not to the data being hard.

The mechanism they isolate is geometric and, once seen, obvious in hindsight. Interpolating the mislabeled points is harmless only if each mislabeled point can be memorized "privately," in a direction nearly orthogonal to the signal $\mu$ and to the other noise directions. That requires $p \gg n$. At $p = \Theta(n)$ the noise vectors of the $\approx\rho n$ mislabeled points average out — their centroid sits within $O(\sigma\sqrt{r/\rho}) = O(\sigma)$ of $+\mu$ — and forcing a hyperplane to put that centroid on the negative side forces the hyperplane to pass within $O(\sigma)$ of $\mu$ itself. Signal recovery collapses. The dependence on $r$ in the resulting lower bound, $\tfrac{\rho}{c r}\exp(-cr/\rho)$, is what licenses the title: the provable obstruction decays in $r = p/n$, so more parameters are what buy robustness to label noise.

The empirical frame is a ResNet18/CIFAR10 run that overfits benignly versus a ResNet50/ImageNet run (500 epochs, not the usual 90) whose test accuracy peaks mid-training and then degrades. The conjecture is that ImageNet's known mislabeling plus its lower parameter-to-sample ratio puts it on the wrong side of the transition. The control experiments inject label noise into CIFAR10 (benign overfitting breaks) and then widen WideResNet16-$W$ at fixed $\rho = 0.2$ (last-epoch accuracy climbs from ~58% to ~65% while best-epoch accuracy stays flat near 66%).

The most interesting part

Two things, and they are connected.

The direction of the effect. Everywhere else in this subfield, "overparameterization helps" is a statement about avoiding the classical variance blow-up: you go past the interpolation threshold and the min-norm/max-margin bias keeps you from fitting noise destructively. Here the claim is sharper and stranger: at a fixed noise rate, the harm done by label noise to the interpolating classifier is monotonically decreasing in $p/n$, and vanishes exponentially. Label noise is not a fixed tax that capacity cannot touch; it is a tax whose size is set by how much room the model has to quarantine the bad examples. Widening the network is, in this account, a noise-robustness intervention, on the same footing as early stopping or label smoothing. Figure 4 is the one experiment in the paper I find genuinely informative: at $\rho = 0.2$ on CIFAR10, widening WRN16 closes most of the best-epoch/last-epoch gap without changing the best-epoch number. That is the theory's signature, not a generic "bigger is better" curve.

The lower bound does not depend on the signal strength. This is the detail I would flag to anyone skimming. Theorem 5.2 uses only Assumption A1 (Gaussian feature noise) and A3 ($p/n = r$ constant). It does not use A2, the signal-to-noise assumption $\|\mu\|/\sigma \gtrsim \sqrt{\log n}$. The bound $|\mu^\top w_-(\infty)| \lesssim \sigma\sqrt{p/(\rho n)}$ is free of $\|\mu\|$, and so is the resulting risk floor $\Phi(-c\sqrt{r/\rho})$. Make the two clusters a thousand times further apart and the interpolator's error floor is unchanged. Nor does it shrink with $n$. That is the precise sense in which this is a phase change in $r$ rather than a smooth statistical tradeoff: in the proportional regime there is no amount of data and no amount of signal that rescues interpolation, while across the regime boundary ($p = \omega(n)$, prior work) the same algorithm on the same data model reaches the noise floor. Contrast Cao–Chen–Belkin–Gu, where the benign/harmful transition for two-layer CNNs is governed by $n \cdot \mathrm{SNR}^q$, so both more data and more signal push you toward benign. Here the knob is $p/n$ alone, and SNR drops out of the negative result entirely.

Honest accounting of what this does not establish. Several things, and some of them bear directly on the headline.

  1. The "phase change" is assembled, not proved. The paper proves (i) a vanishing upper bound at $p=\Theta(n)$ with clean labels, (ii) a constant lower bound at $p=\Theta(n)$ with noisy labels, (iii) a vanishing upper bound at $p=\Theta(n)$ with noisy labels for the early-stopped iterate. It does not prove a noisy-label upper bound for the interpolator at large $r$; that side of the dichotomy is imported from Chatterji–Long / Wang–Thrampoulidis / Cao–Gu–Belkin under their own, different assumptions. The paper says outright that "it is still an open problem when the phase change happens." So "provably counter label noise with larger models" means, strictly, _the provable obstruction weakens as $r$ grows_ — the absence of a lower bound, not the presence of a guarantee. In a paper whose whole contribution is a negative result, that asymmetry matters.

  2. The constant floor is small, and is "tempered," not "catastrophic." The lower bound is $\min\{\Phi(-2),\ \tfrac{\rho}{c_3 r}e^{-c_3 r/\rho}\}$, and $\Phi(-2) \approx 0.023$. So the theorem's strongest possible conclusion is a 2.3% excess 0-1 error floor. In Mallinar et al.'s benign/tempered/catastrophic taxonomy this is squarely tempered overfitting — a bounded error floor of order the noise rate — not the catastrophic divergence the binary "benign overfitting fails" framing suggests. The paper does not engage with that taxonomy, and it should: its own result is better described as locating where benign becomes tempered.

  3. On its own numbers, the theory does not predict the ImageNet failure. ImageNet has $n \approx 1.2\times10^6$, ResNet50 has $p \approx 2.5\times10^7$, so $r \approx 20$. ImageNet mislabeling is maybe $\rho \approx 0.05$–$0.1$. Plug in: $\exp(-c_3 r/\rho) = \exp(-200 c_3)$ to $\exp(-400 c_3)$. Unless $c_3$ is of order $10^{-2}$ — and $c_3$ is never tracked — the lower bound is numerically nil. The $p$ in the theory is also the input dimension of a linear model, which in the GMM happens to coincide with the parameter count; in a ResNet those are unrelated quantities and the "effective dimension" is unknown. The paper concedes this ("how the number of parameters in the linear setup relates to that in the neural network remains unclear"). So the motivating empirical observation and the theorem are linked qualitatively and only qualitatively.

  4. The Figure 1 comparison is confounded and the controls do not disentangle it. CIFAR10/ResNet18 vs ImageNet/ResNet50 differ in dataset, architecture, class count, $n$, $p/n$, label-noise level, and training schedule (the ImageNet run's 410 extra epochs use a hand-tuned second-phase LR decay). The control shows that injecting noise into CIFAR10 suffices to break benign overfitting — which is true but was already well known from Zhang et al. and the double-descent literature — not that noise is what causes the ImageNet behaviour. Worse, the Conclusions claim the conjecture was verified "by injecting label noise into CIFAR10 and adopting self-training in ImageNet"; there is no self-training experiment anywhere in this version of the paper. That is a live over-claim, not a quibble.

  5. Alternative explanation left standing. The $W{=}4$ trace in Figure 4 shows epoch-wise double descent, which the paper notes and then sets aside. Epoch-wise double descent (Nakkiran et al.; Heckel–Yilmaz; Stephenson–Lee) is an independent account of "last-epoch accuracy recovers as width grows" that does not require the max-margin story at all. The paper's own theory has nothing to say about it, because it analyses only $t \to \infty$ and $t \le n$.

  6. The "early stopping" theorem analyses a much smaller object than the phrase suggests. See below.

  7. The write-up is rough. Appendix B.3 opens by apologizing for typos ($d$ for $p$, $\lambda$ for $\eta$) and adds a missing hypothesis ($w(0)=0$) post hoc. In the proof of Theorem 5.3, $\frac1n\sum_i I_i(\rho) \gtrsim \rho$ is wrong as written — $I_i(\rho) \in \{\pm1\}$ has mean $1-2\rho$, so the bound should read $\gtrsim 1-2\rho$. Harmless for $\rho$ a constant below $1/2$, but it is the central quantity in that proof.

Proof sketch

Setup, precisely. $y \sim \mathrm{Unif}\{\pm1\}$, $x = y\mu + \varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}^p$. Assumption A1: $\varepsilon \sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_p)$; the weaker A4 allows $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian $\varepsilon$. A2: $\|\mu\|/\sigma \ge c\sqrt{\log n}$ — note this makes the problem _easier as $n$ grows_. A3: $p/n = r > 1$ a fixed constant. The relaxed forms used in the appendix are A5: $\|\mu\|/\sigma \gtrsim (p/n)^{1/2}$ and A6: $\|\mu\|/\sigma = \omega((p/n)^{1/4})$; both follow from A2+A3 since $(p/n)^{1/2}$ is then $O(1)$. Noisy regime: $\tilde y = -y$ with probability $\rho$ i.i.d. Training: multi-pass SGD on logistic loss, each epoch a fresh random permutation without replacement. Data are a.s. linearly separable because $p > n$. Proposition 3.1, quoted from Nacson–Srebro–Soudry, gives $w(t)/\|w(t)\| \to \tilde w/\|\tilde w\|$ where $\tilde w$ is the hard-margin SVM solution — so "the interpolator" means the max-margin separator, and the entire implicit-bias input to the paper is this one citation. Risk: clean 0-1 risk $L_{01}(w) = \mathbb{P}(yx^\top w < 0)$; Claim C.4 shows the noisy-test risk is $\rho + (1-2\rho)L_{01}$, so $L_{01}$ is the excess risk up to a constant.

Theorem 5.1 (upper bound, clean labels, $p=\Theta(n)$). Under A2, A4, A5, with probability $\ge 1-\delta_1$ for any $\delta_1 \gtrsim \max\{1/n, e^{-c_8 p}\}$: $L_{01}(w_+(\infty)) \lesssim n^{-c_2}$.

The proof is a two-sided squeeze on the margin, and it is three lines of real content. Normalize $\|w\|=1$. Lower bound on the achieved margin, from optimality of max-margin against the oracle direction $\mu/\|\mu\|$: $$\gamma(w) \ \ge\ \gamma(\mu/\|\mu\|) \ =\ \|\mu\| + \min_i y_i\varepsilon_i^\top \tfrac{\mu}{\|\mu\|}\ \gtrsim\ \|\mu\| - \sigma\sqrt{\log n}\ \gtrsim\ \|\mu\|,$$ using Claim C.1 (max of $n$ sub-Gaussians) and A2. Upper bound on the achieved margin, by the trick that a minimum is at most a mean: $$\gamma(w) = \min_i y_i x_i^\top w \ \le\ \mu^\top w + \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_i y_i\varepsilon_i^\top w \ \le\ \mu^\top w + \big\|\tfrac1n\sum_i y_i\varepsilon_i\big\| \ \lesssim\ \mu^\top w + \sigma\sqrt{p/n},$$ using Claim C.2 (the average of $n$ independent $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ has norm $\lesssim \sigma\sqrt{p/n}$). Chaining: $\mu^\top w \gtrsim \|\mu\| - \sigma\sqrt{p/n} \gtrsim \|\mu\|$, which is exactly where A5 is spent. Then a sub-Gaussian tail gives $L_{01}(w) = \mathbb{P}(y\varepsilon^\top w \le -\mu^\top w) \le \exp(-c\|\mu\|^2/\sigma^2) \lesssim n^{-c_2}$ by A2. Note that the $n^{-c_2}$ "rate" is entirely manufactured by A2's $\sqrt{\log n}$ SNR growth, not by a statistical averaging effect; this is inherited from Cao et al. and Wang et al., and the paper footnotes it as "too good to be true" with an explanation about the $O(1/n)$ failure probability. Read it as "risk is exponentially small in the SNR," not as a rate in $n$.

Theorem 5.2 (lower bound, noisy labels, $p=\Theta(n)$ — the heart of the paper). Under A1 and A3 only (no SNR assumption), with probability $\ge 1-\delta_2$ for $\delta_2 \gtrsim \max\{e^{-c_8 p}, c_9 e^{-c_{10}\rho^2 n}\}$: $$L_{01}(w_-(\infty)) \ \ge\ \min\Big\{\Phi(-2),\ \tfrac{\rho}{c_3 r}\exp\big(-\tfrac{c_3 r}{\rho}\big)\Big\}.$$

The construction is a centroid argument on the mislabeled subset, and it is genuinely clever because it extracts a direction constraint from $|K|$ pointwise interpolation constraints by averaging them. Let $K = \{i : y_i = +1,\ \tilde y_i = -1\}$, the clean-positive points whose label was flipped. Their centroid is $$\bar x_K = \mu + \tfrac{1}{|K|}\textstyle\sum_{i\in K}\varepsilon_i .$$ Every $i \in K$ is classified as $-1$ by the interpolator, so $x_i^\top w < 0$ for all $i \in K$, and hence $\bar x_K^\top w < 0$ by linearity. If $\mu^\top w < 0$ the risk is $\ge 1/2$ and we are done. Otherwise the separating hyperplane $\{z : z^\top w = 0\}$ passes strictly between $\mu$ and $\bar x_K$, so the distance from $\mu$ to that hyperplane — which is exactly $|\mu^\top w|$ for unit $w$ — is at most $\|\mu - \bar x_K\|$: $$|\mu^\top w| \ \le\ \Big\|\tfrac{1}{|K|}\sum_{i\in K}\varepsilon_i\Big\| \ \lesssim\ \sigma\sqrt{p/|K|} \ \lesssim\ \sigma\sqrt{p/(\rho n)} \ =\ \sigma\sqrt{r/\rho},$$ by Claim C.2 again plus Claim C.3 ($|K| \gtrsim \rho n/2$ by Hoeffding — this is where $e^{-c\rho^2 n}$ in $\delta_2$ comes from). Then anti-concentration rather than concentration: $L_{01}(w) = \mathbb{P}(y\varepsilon^\top w < -\mu^\top w) \ge \Phi(-c\sqrt{r/\rho})$, and the elementary Gaussian tail lower bound $\Phi(-t) \ge (t^{-1}-t^{-3})e^{-t^2/2} \ge t^{-2}e^{-t^2/2}$ for $t > 2$ finishes it. Exact Gaussianity (A1, not merely A4) is needed precisely for this anti-concentration step.

What makes this the key lemma is the role of $p/n$. The quantity $\sigma\sqrt{p/|K|}$ is the distance from the origin to the centroid of $|K|$ random noise vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ — i.e. how badly $|K|$ random directions fail to cancel. At $p = \Theta(n)$ and constant $\rho$, that distance is $O(\sigma)$, which by A2 is $\ll \|\mu\|$: the mislabeled cloud's centroid is _essentially at $+\mu$_, yet must be labeled $-1$, so the hyperplane is pinned near $\mu$ and $|\mu^\top w|$ cannot grow. At $p = \omega(n)$ the same distance $\sigma\sqrt{p/(\rho n)}$ exceeds $\|\mu\|$ and the constraint becomes vacuous — the noise directions are near-orthogonal enough that each flipped point can be absorbed in its own private subspace. That single quantity is the whole phase change, and it is also the reason the bound is SNR-free: $\|\mu\|$ never enters the inequality.

Theorem 5.3 (upper bound, noisy labels, early stopping). Under A2, A4, A6, from $w(0)=0$, with $\eta < c_5/(n\max_i\|x_i\|^2)$, with probability $\ge 1-\delta_3$: $$\inf_{t\le n} L_{01}(w_-(t)) \ \le\ \exp\Big(-c_{14}\,\frac{\|\mu\|^4}{\|\mu\|^2\sigma^2 + \sigma^4 p/n}\Big),$$ non-vacuous exactly when $\|\mu\|/\sigma = \omega((p/n)^{1/4})$, i.e. A6; under A2+A3 this is $\lesssim n^{-c_4}$.

Mechanism: a surrogate-coupling argument. Only one pass is used ($t \le n$). Define the surrogate $\tilde w_n = \tfrac{\eta}{2}\sum_t x_t \tilde y_t$ — which, expanded, is $\tfrac{\eta}{2}\big(\mu\sum_t y_t\tilde y_t + \sum_t \varepsilon_t\tilde y_t\big)$, i.e. (up to scale) the difference-of-class-means / nearest-centroid classifier, with the signal term shrunk by the factor $\frac1n\sum_t y_t\tilde y_t \approx 1-2\rho$. The learning-rate condition makes $\max_t |x_t^\top w_t| \le \eta n\max_i\|x_i\|^2 \le 1/2$, so the logistic derivative $\frac{1}{1+\exp(\tilde y x^\top w)}$ stays within $O(|x^\top w|)$ of $1/2$ (via $|e^u-1| \le 2|u|$ for $|u|\le 1/2$); that is what makes the real SGD iterate a $\tfrac12$-contraction-distance perturbation of the surrogate, both in $\mu$-projection ($|\mu^\top w_t - \mu^\top\tilde w_t| \lesssim \eta n\|\mu\|^2$) and in norm ($\|w_n\| \le \|\tilde w_n\| + \tfrac12\|w_{n-1}\|$, unrolled). For the surrogate, $\tfrac{2}{n\eta}\mu^\top\tilde w_n \gtrsim (1-2\rho)\|\mu\|^2 - \|\mu\|\sigma\sqrt{\log n} \gtrsim \|\mu\|^2$ by A2, while $\|\tilde w_n\| \lesssim \eta n\|\mu\| + \eta\sigma\sqrt{pn}$ (signal adds coherently $\propto n$, noise incoherently $\propto\sqrt{pn}$). Hence $$\frac{\mu^\top w_n}{\sigma\|w_n\|} \ \gtrsim\ \frac{\|\mu\|^2}{\sigma\|\mu\| + \sigma^2\sqrt{p/n}},$$ and a sub-Gaussian tail on the test point, $\mathbb{P}(yx^\top w<0) \le \exp(-c(\mu^\top w)^2/(\sigma^2\|w\|^2))$, gives the stated bound.

This is where I would temper the "early stopping provably helps" reading. The learning-rate condition forces $\eta n \max_i\|x_i\|^2 = O(1)$, so the entire analysed trajectory is one $O(1)$-sized lazy step away from initialization, and the object proved good is, to leading order, the difference-of-means estimator. The theorem therefore says: _the nearest-centroid classifier is robust to label noise at $p=\Theta(n)$, losing only a $(1-2\rho)$ factor of signal_ — which is true and classical — plus small-step one-pass SGD stays close to it. It is not an analysis of early stopping along a realistically trained trajectory, and the $\inf_{t\le n}$ does not come with a stopping rule. Note also the direction of the $r$-dependence: the early-stopped bound degrades with $p/n$ (the $\sigma^4 p/n$ term), while the interpolator's lower bound improves with $p/n$. Taken together the theory predicts the two converging as $r$ grows — which is a sharper and more interesting reading of the dichotomy than the paper itself gives, and it is roughly what Figure 4's closing gap shows, except that the best-epoch curve stays flat rather than mildly degrading.

Why the directions matter. Theorem 5.1 and 5.3 are upper bounds and both reduce to "show $\mu^\top w/\|w\|$ is $\Omega(\|\mu\|/\sigma)$, then apply a sub-Gaussian tail." Theorem 5.2 is the lower bound and runs the same quantity in reverse: "show $|\mu^\top w|$ is $O(\sigma\sqrt{r/\rho})$ using the interpolation constraints on the flipped points, then apply Gaussian anti-concentration." Every theorem in the paper is a statement about the single scalar $\mu^\top w/\|w\|$ — which is both the source of the proofs' elegance and the reason the analysis cannot see anything an isotropic one-dimensional reduction cannot see. There is no signal-noise coefficient decomposition and no trajectory-dynamics tracking here (that is Cao–Chen–Belkin–Gu's machinery for two-layer CNNs); the interpolator results are purely static geometry on the max-margin program, with gradient descent entering only through a cited implicit-bias theorem.

Broader context

The subfield. Classical learning theory says a model with more parameters than data points and zero training error on noisy labels should generalize badly; uniform convergence over the full hypothesis class is vacuous there. Benign overfitting is the observation and then the theorem that this can be false: Bartlett–Long–Lugosi–Tsigler (PNAS 2020) showed for min-norm linear regression that interpolating label noise is harmless precisely when the covariance spectrum has a long tail of small eigenvalues — formalized by effective ranks $r_k(\Sigma), R_k(\Sigma)$ — so that the noise can be absorbed in directions that barely affect prediction. Crucially, for isotropic covariance in the proportional regime $p = \Theta(n)$, their condition fails: regression at $p \approx n$ is exactly the peak of the double-descent curve (Belkin et al.; Nakkiran et al.; Hastie–Montanari–Rosset–Tibshirani), where test error blows up at the interpolation threshold before descending again. What drives you to an interpolator at all is implicit bias: gradient descent on separable data with logistic loss converges in direction to the max-$\ell_2$-margin solution (Soudry–Hoffer–Nacson–Srebro; Gunasekar et al.), so the "which interpolator" question has an answer. The classification analogues then showed that the regression double-descent peak seems absent: Chatterji–Long (JMLR 2021) proved the max-margin interpolator on a sub-Gaussian mixture with an adversarially flipped $\rho$ fraction of labels has risk near the noise floor, provided $p/n$ is large enough; Wang–Thrampoulidis and Cao–Gu–Belkin gave related guarantees; Frei–Chatterji–Bartlett (COLT 2022) removed linearity, proving the same for two-layer networks with smoothed leaky-ReLU on noisy linear data. Wen et al.'s contribution is to put the peak back: in classification too, the benign conclusion is a $p \gg n$ phenomenon, and at $p = \Theta(n)$ label noise bites.

Two things worth reading alongside. First, Cao, Chen, Belkin, Gu, "Benign Overfitting in Two-layer Convolutional Neural Networks" (NeurIPS 2022). Same year, also a phase change, but a different axis and much heavier machinery: writing each filter exactly as $w_{j,r}^{(t)} = w^{(0)}_{j,r} + j\gamma_{j,r}^{(t)}\|\mu\|^{-2}\mu + \sum_i \rho_{j,r,i}^{(t)}\|\xi_i\|^{-2}\xi_i$ (signal coefficient $\gamma$, per-sample noise-memorization coefficients $\rho_i$) and tracking the coupled dynamics of $(\gamma, \bar\rho, \underline\rho)$, they get benign overfitting iff $n\cdot\mathrm{SNR}^q = \tilde\Omega(1)$ and harmful overfitting in the complementary regime, with $\mathrm{SNR} = \|\mu\|/(\sigma_p\sqrt{d})$. Reading the two together is instructive precisely because they disagree about which knob matters: Cao et al.'s transition is driven by $n$ and SNR together; Wen et al.'s negative result is independent of both and driven by $p/n$ and $\rho$. Second, Mallinar, Simon, Abedsoltan, Pandit, Belkin, Nakkiran, "Benign, Tempered, or Catastrophic" (NeurIPS 2022), which argues the binary benign/non-benign framing is wrong and that most realistic interpolators sit in a tempered middle where excess risk is a bounded constant multiple of the noise rate. Wen et al.'s $\min\{\Phi(-2), \cdot\}$ floor is a tempered-regime statement by that classification, and the two papers have never been properly reconciled — which is a gap, not a detail, since "benign overfitting fails" and "overfitting is tempered rather than benign" have very different practical implications.

Follow-up worth doing. The paper's own stated open problem is where the transition sits, and it leaves a sharp tool unused. Its regime, $p/n \to r$ fixed with Gaussian features and a GMM, is exactly the setting in which the Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem gives exact asymptotics rather than bounds — Deng–Kammoun–Thrampoulidis and Mignacco–Krzakala–Lu–Urbani–Zdeborová already compute precise high-dimensional limits for GMM classification with regularization and noise, and Sur–Candès do it for high-dimensional logistic MLE. A CGMT analysis of the hard-margin SVM on the $\rho$-contaminated GMM should yield the exact limiting 0-1 error as a function of $(r, \rho, \|\mu\|/\sigma)$, which would (a) locate the actual phase boundary instead of sandwiching it between two regimes studied with different tools, (b) test whether the error floor really is SNR-independent or whether that is an artifact of the crude centroid bound, and (c) say whether the transition is continuous in $r$ (a tempered-overfitting curve) or has a genuine non-analyticity. The more ambitious version is to port the centroid construction into Cao et al.'s signal-noise decomposition and prove a negative result for two-layer networks in the proportional regime — the lower-bound side of that literature is almost empty.

Possible relevance to theoretical IR. There is one connection I think is real rather than decorative, and one that is only an analogy.

The real one is learning-to-rank from noisy preferences. Pairwise ranking with a logistic surrogate (RankNet and descendants) is, mechanically, logistic regression on difference vectors $x_i - x_j$, so Soudry et al.'s implicit bias applies and gradient descent on separable pairwise data converges in direction to the max-margin solution over those difference vectors. A flipped preference — from click noise, position bias, or annotator disagreement — plays exactly the role of $\tilde y = -y$ here, and the centroid construction of Theorem 5.2 should port: the centroid of the mislabeled difference vectors must be on the wrong side of the hyperplane, pinning $|\mu^\top w|$. The interesting twist is that the relevant ratio is not $p/n$ but $p$ over the number of interpolation constraints, and pairwise ranking manufactures $O(n^2)$ constraints from $n$ items. By this paper's own logic, that pushes a pairwise ranker much deeper into the harmful regime than a pointwise classifier with the same feature dimension and the same data — interpolating noisy preferences should be substantially more damaging than interpolating noisy labels. The caveats are real (the difference vectors are dependent, and the effective constraint count is the size of a maximal independent set of violated pairs, not $n^2$), but this is a well-posed theoretical question with a concrete prediction, and it would rationalize why early stopping and strong regularization are so load-bearing in practice for click-trained rankers.

The analogy, which I would not oversell, concerns memorization capacity in generative retrieval and vector indices. The quantity doing all the work in Theorem 5.2 is $\sigma\sqrt{p/|K|}$ — how far the centroid of $|K|$ random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ sits from the origin, i.e. how nearly orthogonal $|K|$ random directions are. That is the same quantity that governs how many near-orthogonal items an embedding space of dimension $p$ can hold (Johnson–Lindenstrauss-style capacity), and the paper's mechanism — a corrupted example is harmless iff it can be stored in a private direction that does not perturb shared structure — is a reasonable mental model for docid memorization in DSI-style generative retrieval: at high capacity, memorizing a spurious query–docid association is quarantined; at low capacity it bends the shared retrieval geometry and degrades everything. But that is a shared underlying fact about random vectors in high dimension, not a theorem transfer, and I would present it as a hypothesis to test rather than a result to cite.

title: Only Large Weights (And Not Skip Connections) Can Prevent the Perils of Rank Collapse
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-27

Only Large Weights (And Not Skip Connections) Can Prevent the Perils of Rank Collapse — Josh Alman, Zhao Song (2025) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16284

Main idea

The paper is a short argument aimed at a single rhetorical target: the widespread reading of Dong–Cordonnier–Loukas (ICML 2021) that skip connections are what make deep transformers expressive. Alman and Song's claim is that this reading is an artifact of looking at the wrong failure mode. DCL21 showed that a skip-free self-attention network (SAN) with bounded weights drives its output doubly-exponentially fast toward a token-uniform (rank-1) matrix, at rate $O(\beta)^{(3^L-1)/2}$ where $\beta$ bounds the $\ell_1$ norm of the weights; they then observed that with skip connections no such collapse need occur (set $W_V=0$ and the network is the identity, which preserves whatever rank the input had). The implicit conclusion in the literature was: skip connections rescue expressivity.

Alman–Song's point is that the $W_V=0$ identity network is a terrible advertisement for skip connections, because it is expressive only in the sense that it copies its input: its attention blocks do no work and could be deleted. They formalise "the attention blocks could be deleted" as a new failure mode they call layer collapse: an $L$-layer network $S$ layer-collapses if there is a one-layer network $S'$ with $\|S(X)-S'(X)\|_\infty$ small for all inputs. Their theorem is that in the small-weight regime, every residual SAN layer-collapses — skip connections do not help. So the dichotomy they advertise is not "skip connections vs. nothing" but "large weights vs. nothing": with small weights you get either rank collapse (no skips, by DCL21) or layer collapse (with skips, by them).

The motivation for caring specifically about the weight magnitude is computational, and this is where the paper's real ambition lies. Alman–Song's own earlier line of work (NeurIPS 2023, NeurIPS 2024) established a fine-grained-complexity dichotomy for one attention layer: with $Q,K,V\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, $d=O(\log n)$, entries bounded by $B$, and attention matrix $\exp(QK^\top/d)$, there is an $n^{1+o(1)}$-time algorithm achieving $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ additive error when $B=o(\sqrt{\log n})$ (via the polynomial method: $\exp$ is approximated by a low-degree polynomial, which makes the $n\times n$ attention matrix $n^{o(1)}$-rank, so the product is computed implicitly), and under SETH no truly subquadratic algorithm when $B=\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$. The intended composition is therefore: _expressive $\Rightarrow$ large weights $\Rightarrow$ no subquadratic algorithm_, i.e. the abstract's claim that "the quadratic running time of attention is unavoidable for expressive transformers." That syllogism, rather than the layer-collapse theorem itself, is the paper's headline, and it is also the weakest part of the paper (see below).

Mechanically, what the paper actually establishes is best described not as a collapse of rank but as a collapse of depth into width: in a regime where every attention branch perturbs the residual stream by $O(\eta)$ and the per-layer Jacobian differs from the identity by $O(\eta)$, the network is within $O(\eta)\cdot\|X\|_\infty$ of its own first-order expansion $X\mapsto X+\sum_{\ell,h}\mathrm{softmv}_{\ell,h}(X)$ — all $HL$ heads evaluated at the input rather than at their true layer inputs. It is, at bottom, a linearisation/lazy-regime statement dressed in rank-collapse vocabulary.

Reviewer-style critique

What is genuinely good. The reframing is the contribution, and it is a good one. "Skip connections prevent rank collapse" has been cited dozens of times as an architectural justification, and nobody seems to have asked whether the networks that evade DCL21's bound evade it for a trivial reason. Observing that the witness to DCL21's optimism is the identity map, and then promoting "your attention blocks are removable" to a first-class notion of representational weakness, is the kind of definitional move that is obvious only in retrospect. The choice of entrywise $\ell_\infty$ on the weights (rather than DCL21's $\ell_1$) is also a real strengthening in one direction: $\eta \ll \beta$, so there are skip-free networks for which DCL21's $\beta$ is too large to imply rank collapse while $\eta$ is small enough to imply layer collapse. And "layer collapse" is a sensible complement to rank collapse: rank collapse says the output is degenerate; layer collapse says the computation is degenerate while the output can be perfectly rich (the identity map has full rank and zero useful computation). That distinction deserves to survive this paper.

The syllogism has a hole, and it is the paper's central claim. The paper needs its "small weights" and AS23's "small weights" to be complementary, i.e. that the union of the two regimes covers everything. They do not come close. Trace the parameters. The layer-collapse proof requires $\epsilon_\ell := 2\eta\varphi_0(1+H\eta)^\ell < 1$ for all $\ell\le L$ (Definition A.2 and the hypotheses of Lemma C.2), where $\varphi_0 \ge \|X_0\|_\infty$. Remark D.2 is explicit that this forces one of two parameter settings: either $\varphi_0$ must be _exponentially small in $L$_ ($\varphi_0 \le 0.5\eta/(1+H\eta)^L$), or, with $\varphi_0$ constant, $\eta \le 1/(\varphi_0 H L)$. In the second (only sane) case the post-projection query/key entries — the quantity AS23 calls $B$ — are at most $\|X W_q\|_\infty \lesssim \eta\varphi_0 \lesssim 1/(HL)$, and the logits are $O(1)$ by construction ($\theta=1$ in Lemma B.2). Meanwhile hardness, in the sharpest current form (Gupta–Huang–Saha–Xu–Ye 2025, cited by the paper as [GHS+25c]), needs $B\ge\log 2$ at $d=\Theta(\log n)$; AS23 needed $B=\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$. So the regime $1/(HL)\ \lesssim\ B\ \lesssim\ \sqrt{\log n}$ — for a 32-layer, 32-head model that is roughly three orders of magnitude wide, and it widens with depth — is covered by neither theorem. Worse, this gap is not an uninteresting sliver: logit scale $\Theta(\log\log n)$ or $\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ is exactly where attention can be meaningfully peaked (an induction/retrieval head needs logit gaps growing with $n$ to select one of $n$ positions) while still sitting inside AS23's almost-linear-time regime. The paper would need to prove layer collapse up to $B=o(\sqrt{\log n})$ to earn its abstract. As stated, "quadratic time is unavoidable for expressive transformers" is not a theorem of this paper; it is a conjecture with the two endpoints filled in.

A second, independent problem with the same syllogism: GHS+25c (again, cited here) gives an $\tilde O(n^{2-1/d}\,\mathrm{polylog}(B/\epsilon))$ algorithm for $d=O(1)$ _with no threshold on $B$ at all_. So "large weights $\Rightarrow$ quadratic" is already known to be false at constant head dimension, and the conditional lower bounds live only at $d=2^{\Omega(\log^* n)}$ and above. The paper's framing does not acknowledge this.

The theorem as literally stated is not what is proved, and under the natural reading of $S'$ it is false. Theorem 5.3 says "for any $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$", but the proof needs $\|X\|_\infty\le\varphi_0$ with $2\eta\varphi_0(1+H\eta)^L<1$; the quantifier is really over a norm ball tied to $\eta,H,L$. More seriously, $S'$ is never constructed. The appendix bounds $\|\mathrm{softmv}_L(B_L^0)-\mathrm{softmv}_L(B_L^L)\|_\infty$ — the change in the final attention block's output when lower blocks are deleted — which is damped by the per-layer Lipschitz constant $C=O(\eta)<1$ and hence telescopes to $O(\delta)$. But $S(X)$ is the residual stream $X_L$, and a deleted branch's contribution passes through the residual connections with coefficient $1$: it is not damped. If $S'$ is the last layer applied to the input ($S'(X)=X+\mathrm{SAtt}_L(X)$, the reading the "down to one layer" prose suggests), then $\|S(X)-S'(X)\|_\infty$ generically accumulates $L$ undamped branch contributions of size $H\eta\varphi_0$ each, giving $\Theta(L H\eta\varphi_0)=\Theta(1)$ in Case 2 — which is the same order as $\|S(X)-X\|_\infty$, i.e. vacuous, and strictly worse than the claimed $O(\eta)\|X\|_\infty$. The statement is rescuable only if $S'$ is a one-layer network with $HL$ heads, namely $X\mapsto X+\sum_{\ell,h}\mathrm{softmv}_{\ell,h}(X)$; then the error per deletion is the genuinely second-order term $O(\eta)\cdot\|X_{\ell-1}-X_0\|_\infty$ and the geometric damping does its job. That is still a fine theorem — "depth buys nothing over width here" — but it is a weaker and different statement than "there is a one-layer network", and the paper never says it. The write-up also displays a recursion for $B_\ell^{\ell_0}$ (Section D.1) that deletes residual connections above layer $\ell_0$, contradicting both the prose immediately following it and the quantity Lemma C.1 actually controls; and the $L$-layer bound is extrapolated from the $L=2$ and $L=3$ cases with "Therefore for $L$ layers we have", with no induction.

The rank-collapse machinery is decorative in the regime where the theorem is instantiated. Lemma B.1 (the attention matrix is within a multiplicative $e^{\pm\theta}$ of the rank-1 row-stochastic matrix $\mathbf 1\,\mathrm{softm}(r)^\top$) and Lemma 5.1 ($\|\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{SAtt}(X))\|_\infty\le(e^\theta-1)\|W_v\|_\infty\|\mathrm{Res}(X)\|_\infty$) are the paper's link to DCL21. But the parameters are then set to $\theta=1$, so $e^\theta-1=e-1\approx1.72$ contributes nothing, and Lemma C.2 immediately discards $\mathrm{Res}$ altogether, bounding $K\|\mathrm{Res}(X_\ell)\|_\infty\le 2\eta\|X_\ell\|_\infty$. The actual driver of the whole argument is $\|W_v\|_\infty\le\eta$ — i.e. the branch is small. One could prove a version of the theorem with no rank-collapse reasoning at all and lose only constants. The claim that "the connection between layer collapse and rank collapse ... will become clear in our proofs" is therefore overstated: the proofs show the branch is a small perturbation, not that it is low-rank. The honest description is that this is a lazy/linearised-regime result, close in spirit to NTK-style arguments, and the interesting rank structure appears only if one takes $\theta\to 0$, which the paper does not do.

Technical errors in the toolkit. Two of them matter for how the constants should be read, though neither is fatal to the intended argument. - Fact 3.3's second bullet, $\|AB\|_\infty\le\|A\|_\infty\|B\|_\infty$ for the entrywise max norm, is false: $(AB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}$ picks up a factor of the inner dimension. Take $A=B=\mathbf 1_{2\times2}$: $\|A\|_\infty=1$, $\|AB\|_\infty=2$. This fact is used pervasively (Eq. (8), Lemmas C.2, D.5, D.6, D.7). Repairing it replaces $\eta$ by $d\eta$ throughout — harmless as an algebraic substitution, but it shrinks the admissible weight ball to $\eta\lesssim 1/(d H L\varphi_0)$, which for $d\sim10^3$–$10^4$ pushes the regime another three or four orders of magnitude below anything a trained model exhibits. (The one place the step is legitimate is $\mathrm{softm}(X)\cdot X$, where row-stochasticity saves it.) - Lemma 4.1 claims $\mathrm{Res}$ is $1$-Lipschitz in $\ell_\infty$; the correct constant is $2$. With $\mathrm{Res}$ read as per-column midrange centring, take a single column $z=(0,10\epsilon,5\epsilon)$ and $x=(-\epsilon,9\epsilon,6\epsilon)$: $\|x-z\|_\infty=\epsilon$, but $\mathrm{Res}(x)-\mathrm{Res}(z)=(0,0,2\epsilon)$. The proof's first inequality silently assumes $B$'s optimal shift is also optimal for $A$. Again constants only, but it propagates through Lemmas 5.2/C.1. - Relatedly, $\mathrm{Res}$ is not well-defined as written. Definition 3.4 takes $y=\arg\min_y\|Z-\mathbf 1_ny^\top\|_\infty$, and since $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is the max over all entries, the minimiser is determined only on the column(s) achieving the max; every other column may be shifted anywhere within the slack. The argmin is a set, often a large one. One has to read in "per-column midrange" for anything downstream to make sense.

Loose ends in the hypotheses. $\beta$ appears from nowhere in Lemma 5.1 as "the normalization factor $1/\sqrt{d_0}$" — but $d_0$ is never defined, and Definitions 1.1/3.6 contain no $1/\sqrt d$ scaling at all. Lemma B.2 then "proves" $\theta=1$ under the hypothesis $\beta\le 1/(\|\mathrm{Res}(X)\|_\infty^2\eta^2)$, which is a constraint on $\beta$ — a fixed architectural constant — rather than on the weights. Read correctly it is an additional unstated assumption that the logits are $O(1)$, and it should have been stated as such in the theorem. Lemma 5.1's proof also introduces bias terms $b_q,b_k$ absent from the model definition. Lemma D.4's statement has a typo ($\mathrm{softm}(a+b)-\mathrm{softm}(b)$ for $\mathrm{softm}(a+b)-\mathrm{softm}(a)$). Lemma D.5's hypothesis $\|Y-X\|_\infty\le2\|X\|_\infty$ and Lemma D.4's $\|b\|_\infty\le1$ are never verified for the intermediate hybrids they are applied to. The intro points to "Definition 3.4 below for the precise meaning" of rank collapse, but Definition 3.4 is $\mathrm{Res}$; rank collapse is never formally defined in this paper, and despite Section 5 being titled "Rank Collapse Property" no rank-collapse statement is proved. The intro also forward-references "Theorem 5.3" before stating Theorem 1.2 as its informal version. This is a preprint that has not been read carefully by its authors.

The quantitative bound in the one place it is instantiated is vacuous. Remark D.2 is the only place the parameters are actually set, and it concludes "$\delta=O(1)$ and $C\le6\eta$, thus the final bound is $\le\delta(1+10C)=O(1)\cdot(1+O(\eta))$" — an $O(1)$ entrywise error, which at $\varphi_0=O(1)$ says nothing. To recover anything resembling Theorem 5.3 one must redo the arithmetic: $\delta=\max_\ell 4(e^{2H\epsilon_\ell}-1)\approx 8H\epsilon_L=16H\eta\varphi_0(1+H\eta)^L=O(H\eta)\varphi_0$ in Case 2, and the geometric sum contributes $1/(1-6\eta)=O(1)$. So the real bound is $O(H\eta)\cdot\|X\|_\infty$ — Theorem 5.3's "$O(\eta)$" quietly absorbs a factor $H$ (and, after fixing Fact 3.3, a factor $d$), and $\delta$ is exponential in $H\epsilon$, which is only tolerable because Definition 3.7 declares $H$ and $L$ to be "fixed constants".

Is $\ell_\infty$ the right error notion? The paper concedes in Section E that $\ell_\infty$ is a limitation. It is a bigger one than conceded. An $O(\eta)\|X\|_\infty$ entrywise perturbation of the residual stream is measured before the final LayerNorm and unembedding, and next-token logits are inner products over $d$ coordinates: an entrywise perturbation of relative size $\eta$ can move a logit by $d\eta\|X\|_\infty$ and flip an argmax. A statement in $\ell_2$, Frobenius, or operator norm (or better, a statement about the induced distribution over next tokens) would be the meaningful one, and would be strictly harder — the whole proof leans on $\|\mathrm{softm}(\cdot)\|_\infty\le1$ and on softmax shift-invariance, both of which are $\ell_\infty$-friendly. Note also that the bound has _no $n$-dependence whatsoever_, which is pleasant but also means the result says nothing about how collapse interacts with context length — odd for a paper whose thesis is about the cost of long-context attention.

No LayerNorm, and LayerNorm is probably the crux. Definition 3.7 is a bare residual SAN: no MLP, no LayerNorm, no output projection. Remark D.1 waves the MLP in via "the Lipschitz property of $f$ will appear correspondingly in the final bound", which is fine for an MLP but not for LayerNorm: LN's Lipschitz constant scales like $1/\|\mathrm{Res}(x)\|_2$, i.e. it blows up exactly when the token representations become nearly uniform. That is precisely the known mechanism by which normalisation resists collapse, and it is incompatible with the paper's contraction argument, which needs a per-layer Lipschitz constant $C=O(\eta)<1$ to make the telescoping sum converge. Wu, Ajorlou, Wang, Jegelka and Jadbabaie (NeurIPS 2024) showed, against DCL21's reading, that LayerNorm does affect rank collapse and that with suitable value matrices the self-attention dynamics admit equilibria of every rank. Since every real transformer has LayerNorm, a paper whose conclusion is a practical prescription about architecture ("efforts to improve model capability should emphasize principled parameter scaling and regularization strategies, rather than relying on more elaborate residual topologies") owes the reader an argument that LN does not change the picture. There is none.

How far does "necessity" reach? The theorem is an upper bound on expressivity holding for every network in the ball, so it applies to trained networks too — the worst-case/typical-case distinction is not the issue. The issue is that the ball is tiny. $\epsilon_L<1$ requires $H\eta\lesssim 1/L$; for $L=32$, $H=32$ that is $\eta\lesssim 10^{-3}$, and after repairing Fact 3.3, $\eta\lesssim 10^{-7}$. Trained attention matrices have entries of order $10^{-2}$, head dimensions in the hundreds, and logits of order $10$ — many orders of magnitude outside. More fundamentally, entrywise $\ell_\infty$ on $W_q,W_k,W_v$ is close to the least informative norm one could bound: a $d\times d$ matrix with all entries $\eta$ has $\ell_\infty$ norm $\eta$ and operator norm $d\eta$, and it is the operator norm (or the induced logit scale) that governs the dynamics. So "small weights" here really means "the logits are $O(1)$ and the branch-to-stream ratio is $O(1/HL)$", which is a conjunction of two strong conditions, not a single natural scaling. Finally, the title's "And Not Skip Connections" overreaches in a specific way: the theorem shows skip connections are insufficient to prevent collapse in one small-weight regime; it says nothing about whether they are helpful or necessary in the large-weight regime, where expressivity actually lives, nor about their role in optimisation (which is why they were introduced). Indeed the paper's own mechanism — the network being close to identity-plus-sum-of-branches — is caused by the skip connections; without them you get DCL21's rank collapse instead. The fair summary is that in the small-weight regime skip connections convert one pathology into a different one, not that they are useless.

Proof sketch

Setup. The model (Definitions 3.6–3.7) is a multi-head residual SAN with no MLP, no LayerNorm, no output projection and no $1/\sqrt d$ logit scaling: $$\mathrm{SAtt}^H(X)=\sum_{h=1}^H D_h^{-1}\,g(XQ_hK_h^\top X^\top)\,X V_h,\qquad X_{\ell+1}=\mathrm{SAtt}^H(X_\ell)+X_\ell,$$ with $g=\exp$ entrywise, $D_h=\mathrm{diag}(g(\cdot)\mathbf 1_n)$, and $L,H$ declared fixed constants. Two pieces of bookkeeping carry the argument. First, $\mathrm{Res}(Z):=Z-\mathbf 1_n y^\top$ with $y$ the $\ell_\infty$-optimal token-uniform shift (Definition 3.4) — the "distance from token-uniformity", DCL21's object, here in entrywise $\ell_\infty$ rather than DCL21's $\ell_{1,\infty}$. Second, $\theta$-balance (Definition 3.5): $E$ is $\theta$-balanced if $\max_i\max_{j,l}|E_{ij}-E_{il}|\le\theta$, i.e. every row of the logit matrix has range at most $\theta$.

What is proved (precisely). Theorem 5.3: if every head in every layer satisfies $\|W_q\|_\infty,\|W_k\|_\infty,\|W_v\|_\infty\le\eta$ (entrywise max), then there is a one-layer residual SAN $S'$ with $\|S(X)-S'(X)\|_\infty\le O(\eta)\cdot\|X\|_\infty$. Unpacking the proof's actual hypotheses and constants, the honest statement is:

Let $\|X_0\|_\infty\le\varphi_0$, $\eta\in(0,1]$, and set $\epsilon_\ell:=2\eta\varphi_0(1+H\eta)^\ell$; assume $\epsilon_L<1$ (equivalently $\eta\lesssim 1/(\varphi_0 HL)$ for constant $\varphi_0$, or $\varphi_0$ exponentially small in $L$ for constant $\eta$), and assume the logits are $O(1)$ in the sense that $\beta\,\|\mathrm{Res}(X)\|_\infty^2\eta^2\le 1$ so that $\theta=1$ (Lemma B.2). Then with $C:=\max_\ell 3\eta(\epsilon_\ell^2+1)=O(\eta)$ and $\delta:=\max_\ell 4(e^{2H\epsilon_\ell}-1)=O(H\eta\varphi_0)$, the full network is $\big(\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}C^k\big)\delta=O(H\eta)\cdot\varphi_0$ close in entrywise $\ell_\infty$ to the depth-one network obtained by evaluating all $HL$ attention branches at the input: $S'(X)=X+\sum_{\ell\in[L]}\sum_{h\in[H]}\mathrm{softmv}_{\ell,h}(X)$.

No $n$-dependence, no precision/bit-complexity, no dependence on $d$ (though see the Fact 3.3 issue, which should introduce one), and error measured relative to $\|X\|_\infty$ rather than to the output scale (the two agree here since $\|X_L\|_\infty\le\varphi_0(1+H\eta)^L=O(\varphi_0)$).

Step 1: only the token-non-uniform part of the input reaches the softmax. Softmax is invariant to adding a constant to each row (Fact 3.2). Writing $X=\mathbf 1_n x^\top+R$ with $R=\mathrm{Res}(X)$ and $W=W_qW_k^\top$, the logit matrix expands as $$A=\beta(\mathbf 1_nx^\top+R)W(\mathbf 1_nx^\top+R)^\top=\underbrace{(\,\cdot\,)\mathbf 1_n^\top}_{\text{column-constant, killed by softmax}}+\beta RWR^\top+\mathbf 1_n r^\top,$$ so $P=\mathrm{softm}(A)=\mathrm{softm}(E+\mathbf 1_nr^\top)$ with $E=\beta RWR^\top$. This is the one genuinely structural observation: the attention pattern depends on the input only through $\mathrm{Res}(X)$, up to a rank-1 additive term. It is also what makes "deleting a branch" cheap: the deleted branch's token-uniform component is invisible to every subsequent softmax, so only $\|\mathrm{Res}(A)\|_\infty$, not $\|A\|_\infty$, drives the error.

Step 2: bounded logit range $\Rightarrow$ the attention matrix is multiplicatively near rank-1. Lemma B.1 is the DCL21-style ingredient: if $P=\mathrm{softm}(\tilde A+E)$ and $D_{ii}=\max_{j,l}|E_{ij}-E_{il}|$, then $e^{-D_{ii}}\tilde P_{ij}\le P_{ij}\le e^{D_{ii}}\tilde P_{ij}$ entrywise. Applied with $\tilde A=\mathbf 1_nr^\top$, whose softmax is exactly the rank-1 row-stochastic matrix $\mathbf 1_n\mathrm{softm}(r)^\top$: a $\theta$-balanced logit matrix has attention within a factor $e^{\pm\theta}$ of a rank-1 matrix. Pushing this through $PXW_v$ gives Lemma 5.1, the per-layer contraction of token-non-uniformity: $$\|\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{SAtt}(X))\|_\infty\le K\cdot\|\mathrm{Res}(X)\|_\infty,\qquad K=(e^\theta-1)\|W_v\|_\infty.$$ Lemma B.2 supplies $\theta=1$ (given the logit assumption), so $K\le 2\eta$ — and this is exactly where the rank-collapse structure stops mattering, since $e^1-1$ is just a constant and Lemma C.2 then replaces $\|\mathrm{Res}(X_\ell)\|_\infty$ by the cruder $\|X_\ell\|_\infty\le\varphi_0(1+H\eta)^\ell$ (Lemma D.7).

Step 3: softmax perturbation. $\|\mathrm{softm}(a+b)-\mathrm{softm}(a)\|_\infty\le g(\|b\|_\infty)$ with $g(\epsilon)=2(e^\epsilon-1)$ (Lemma 4.4), proved by splitting $\alpha(a+b)^{-1}e^{a_i+b_i}-\alpha(a)^{-1}e^{a_i}$ into a numerator term and a normaliser term and using $\alpha(x)^{-1}e^{x_i}\in(0,1)$ on each. Plus $\mathrm{Res}$ being $O(1)$-Lipschitz (Lemma 4.1, constant $1$ claimed, $2$ correct).

Step 4: one branch deletion (the key lemma). Lemma 5.2 / C.1. Let $A_1,\dots,A_H$ be layer $\ell$'s head outputs, $B=X+\sum_iA_i$, and suppose $\|\mathrm{Res}(A_i)\|_\infty\le\epsilon$. The target is to compare the next layer evaluated at $B$ with the next layer evaluated at $X$ — i.e. to delete layer $\ell$'s attention while keeping the residual path. Using Step 1, both $\mathrm{softm}_2(B)=\mathrm{softm}_2(\mathrm{Res}(B))$ and $\mathrm{softm}_2(X)=\mathrm{softm}_2(\mathrm{Res}(X))$, and since $\mathrm{Res}(X)=\mathrm{Res}(B-\mathrm{Res}(A_{[H]}))$, Lipschitzness of $\mathrm{Res}$ gives $\|\mathrm{Res}(X)+\mathrm{Res}(A_{[H]})-\mathrm{Res}(B)\|_\infty\le 2H\epsilon$. Then a small internal hybrid over the $H$ prefix sums $A_{[i]}$ plus one application of Step 3 at scale $2H\epsilon$ yields $$\|\mathrm{softm}_2(B)-\mathrm{softm}_2(X)\|_\infty\le g(2H\epsilon)+H\,g(\epsilon)\le 2g(2H\epsilon),$$ and a further triangle-inequality split $\mathrm{softm}_2(B)BW_v-\mathrm{softm}_2(X)XW_v$ extends it to $\mathrm{softmv}$ with $\epsilon_0=3g(2H\epsilon)$. The mechanism to name here is shift-invariance as an error filter: the deletion moves the softmax input by $O(H\|\mathrm{Res}(A)\|_\infty)=O(H\eta\|\mathrm{Res}(X)\|_\infty)$, which is $\eta$ times smaller than the branch itself, because the branch's token-uniform part never reaches the softmax and its non-uniform part was already contracted by Step 2.

Step 5: telescoping with geometric damping. This is the engine. A single layer, as a map, is $C$-Lipschitz in $\ell_\infty$ with $C=K_2=12\|X\|_\infty^2\|W\|_\infty\|W_v\|_\infty+\|W_v\|_\infty\le 3\eta(\epsilon_\ell^2+1)=O(\eta)$ (Lemmas D.5, D.6) — crucially $C<1$. Deleting branches one layer at a time produces a hybrid sequence from the full network to the collapsed one; a deletion at layer $\ell$ costs $\delta$ at layer $\ell+1$ (Step 4) but is then contracted by $C$ for each subsequent layer. Hence the total is $$\|\,\text{full}-\text{collapsed}\,\|_\infty\ \le\ (1+C+C^2+\cdots+C^{L-1})\,\delta\ \le\ \frac{\delta}{1-C}=O(\delta),$$ independent of $L$. Without $C<1$ the errors would accumulate linearly in $L$ and the theorem would be vacuous; the small-weight hypothesis is used twice, once to make each deletion cheap and once to make the accumulated cost geometric rather than linear. (As flagged above, what the appendix actually telescopes is the change in $\mathrm{softmv}_L$, not the change in the residual stream $X_L$; the residual-stream accumulation is what forces $S'$ to retain all $HL$ branches.) Lemma D.7 ($\|X_\ell\|_\infty\le\varphi_0(1+H\eta)^\ell$) keeps the norms from exploding and is the source of the $\epsilon_L<1$ constraint, hence of the entire parameter regime.

One-sentence summary of the trick. Softmax shift-invariance means a transformer layer sees only $\mathrm{Res}$ of its input; bounded logit range means attention is multiplicatively within $e^{\pm\theta}$ of rank one, so each block contracts $\mathrm{Res}$ by $\approx\|W_v\|_\infty$; therefore each block is an $O(\eta)$ perturbation whose effect on later blocks is further damped by $O(\eta)$ per layer, and a hybrid argument sums the $L$ deletions as a convergent geometric series instead of a linear one. It is, in effect, a proof that the small-weight residual SAN equals its own linearisation around the residual stream.

Broader context

Fine-grained complexity of attention. The relevant frame is not classical complexity but fine-grained complexity: conditional lower bounds that pin down polynomial exponents under hypotheses like SETH (no $2^{(1-\epsilon)n}$ algorithm for CNF-SAT) and its consequences, chiefly Orthogonal Vectors and Max-IP. Keles, Duman and Hegde (ALT 2023) first showed that exact self-attention requires $n^{2-o(1)}$ time under SETH. Alman–Song (NeurIPS 2023) sharpened this into a dichotomy governed by the entry magnitude: with $d=O(\log n)$ and attention $\exp(QK^\top/d)$, $B=o(\sqrt{\log n})$ admits an $n^{1+o(1)}$ algorithm with $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ additive error, while $B=\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ is SETH-hard. The algorithmic side is the polynomial method: on a bounded domain $\exp$ is $\epsilon$-approximated by a degree-$q$ polynomial with $q=O(\max(\log(1/\epsilon),\ \text{logit scale}))$, and applying a degree-$q$ polynomial entrywise to a rank-$d$ matrix yields rank $\binom{d+q}{q}=n^{o(1)}$, so $\exp(QK^\top/d)V$ factors through a thin matrix and is computed in almost linear time. The hardness side reduces approximate Max-IP (hence OV, hence SETH) to attention: once logits reach $\Theta(\log n)$, softmax can be made peaked enough to detect whether any pair of vectors is nearly orthogonal. Alman–Song (NeurIPS 2024) extended both sides to the backward pass, and Alman–Song (ICLR 2024) to tensor/Kronecker attention. The current state of the art is Gupta, Huang, Saha, Xu and Ye (2025), who remove the temperature restriction: for $d=O(1)$ attention is subquadratic for any polynomial $B$; hardness holds at $d=2^{\Omega(\log^* n)}$ with $B=\mathrm{poly}(n)$, and at $d=\Theta(\log n)$ already for $B\ge\log 2$. The present paper's role in this programme is to supply the missing representational half: an argument that you cannot simply choose to live in the fast regime.

Rank collapse / token uniformity. DCL21 ("Attention is not all you need") showed that skip-free SANs converge doubly exponentially to token-uniform outputs, and — via an experimental and theoretical study of MLPs, LayerNorm and skips — concluded that only skip connections arrest it. The phenomenon is the transformer analogue of oversmoothing in GNNs, and has since been studied as a signal-propagation problem: Noci et al. (NeurIPS 2022) tied rank collapse to vanishing gradients on the query/key parameters and showed that downscaling residual branches by $1/\sqrt L$ (also the basis of DeepNet-style initialisations) prevents it — which sits in direct tension with the present paper, since $1/\sqrt L$ branch scaling is precisely a small-weight regime that practitioners found helps depth. Geshkovski, Letrouit, Polyanskiy and Rigollet recast attention as an interacting-particle flow in which rank collapse is collapse to a single cluster. And Wu, Ajorlou, Wang, Jegelka and Jadbabaie (NeurIPS 2024) explicitly refuted DCL21's reading of LayerNorm, exhibiting value matrices for which the self-attention dynamics have equilibria of every rank from $1$ to full, and showing that masking (sparse/local attention) provably slows collapse. Taken together these suggest that the two components Alman–Song omit — LayerNorm and masking — are exactly the ones that break the collapse story. Worth reading alongside: Sanford, Hsu and Telgarsky, Representational strength and limitations of transformers (NeurIPS 2023) and Transformers, parallel computation, and logarithmic depth (ICML 2024), which give the only sharp depth separations currently available for attention, and Merrill–Sabharwal's circuit-complexity line (log-precision transformers $\subseteq$ uniform $\mathrm{TC}^0$), a different and complementary kind of expressivity ceiling.

A follow-up that would settle the paper's thesis. The obvious and crisp question is whether the gap I flagged above is empty or not. Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky's depth separations (sparse averaging, match-3, $k$-hop induction) are proved with near-one-hot attention, i.e. logit scale $\Theta(\log n)$ — comfortably inside AS23's hard regime. The research question is: _does any depth separation survive at logit scale $o(\sqrt{\log n})$?_ Concretely, exhibit an $L$-layer transformer with $B=\Theta(\log\log n)$ (so almost-linear-time computable by the polynomial method) that provably cannot be approximated by any transformer of depth $o(L)$ with comparable width. If such a construction exists, the paper's headline — "quadratic time is unavoidable for expressive transformers" — is false, and the correct picture is a trichotomy: $O(1)$ logits $\Rightarrow$ layer collapse; $\omega(1)$ to $o(\sqrt{\log n})$ logits $\Rightarrow$ fast and depth-expressive; $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ $\Rightarrow$ SETH-hard. If it does not, one should be able to extend layer collapse up to $B=o(\sqrt{\log n})$ and the paper's thesis becomes a theorem. Either outcome is a real result, and the natural first attempt is to redo Steps 2–5 above with $\theta=\Theta(\log\log n)$ instead of $\theta=1$, tracking where $K=(e^\theta-1)\eta$ ceases to be a contraction — the answer is at logit scale $\log(1/\eta)$, which is the precise frontier this technique can reach. A second, more applied follow-up: redo the analysis with pre-LN, noting that LayerNorm's Lipschitz constant $\sim1/\|\mathrm{Res}(x)\|_2$ diverges exactly in the collapse regime, which would either break the geometric damping (and so explain why depth is useful at small weights in practice) or reveal that LN's gain is bounded.

Connections to theoretical IR, generative retrieval and vector search. Two are genuine; a third is speculative and I will mark it as such.

First, and strongest: the logit scale is the knob between kernel smoothing and nearest-neighbour selection, and this paper quantifies the "smoothing" end. Step 2 of the proof is literally the statement that when the logit range is $\theta$, the attention matrix is within a multiplicative $e^{\pm\theta}$ of the rank-1 matrix $\mathbf 1\,\mathrm{softm}(r)^\top$ — i.e. every query retrieves (almost) the same convex combination of values. Retrieval, in the information-retrieval sense, requires the opposite: a query must separate one of $n$ items from the rest, which needs logit gaps growing like $\log n$ to beat the $n-1$ competing terms in the softmax denominator.
