That is exactly the regime where (i) the attention matrix has no $n^{o(1)}$-rank approximation, so the polynomial-method and random-feature approximations (Performer, polynomial kernels, low-rank sketches) provably cannot preserve it, and (ii) exact computation is SETH-hard via Max-IP. The shared backbone matters: the SETH $\to$ OV $\to$ Max-IP chain used for attention hardness is the same one behind conditional lower bounds for approximate nearest-neighbour and bichromatic closest-pair in $\omega(\log n)$ dimensions (Rubinstein, STOC 2018; Williams' OV framework), and the fast-attention algorithm's toolkit is the kernel-density-estimation toolkit (Charikar–Kapralov–Nouri–Siminelakis). The usable slogan for a theory-IR reader: attention is cheap exactly when it is not retrieving, and retrieval-grade attention is MIPS, with MIPS's lower bounds. The present paper strengthens this by adding that cheap attention is also shallow — you cannot compensate for flat logits with depth. That is a sharper statement about the limits of "efficient attention" as a substitute for an index than the complexity results alone give, and it is an argument for architectures that call an explicit ANN/MIPS data structure (retrieval-augmented or memory-layer models) rather than trying to approximate sharp attention with low-rank surrogates.

_Second: $\mathrm{Res}$ and token uniformity are the anisotropy/representation-degeneration problem of dense retrieval._ $\mathrm{Res}(Z)=Z-\mathbf 1_ny^\top$ is mean-removal across tokens; rank collapse is its degenerate limit, where all representations share one direction. This is precisely the anisotropy that motivates whitening and flow-based post-processing of BERT embeddings, the uniformity term in contrastive objectives, and the hubness pathology in high-dimensional nearest-neighbour search: when embeddings concentrate around a dominant direction, inner-product rankings are dominated by a norm/hub term and recall degrades. A collapse-rate bound of the DCL21 or Alman–Song type is, read in IR terms, a bound on how fast an encoder destroys the effective dimensionality that an ANN index needs — and effective dimensionality is exactly what determines whether graph- or partition-based indices behave well. Making that correspondence quantitative (collapse rate $\to$ participation ratio / intrinsic dimension $\to$ ANN recall-vs-latency) strikes me as a legitimately open and tractable question.

Third, speculative: generative retrieval. One would like to say that a decoder-only generative retriever, which decodes a hierarchical docid over several steps, needs depth and therefore large weights, so layer collapse bounds the expressivity of small-weight GR models. I would not lean on this. The regime ($\eta\lesssim 1/(dHL\|X\|_\infty)$, logits $O(1)$, no LayerNorm, $\ell_\infty$ error on the pre-unembedding residual stream) is far from any trained GR model, and the autoregressive decoding that does the real work in GR is sequential computation outside the per-step network, which this analysis does not touch. The honest version of the claim is narrower and still interesting: whatever selection a GR model performs over a vocabulary of $N$ docid tokens, the softmax over that vocabulary needs logit gaps $\Omega(\log N)$ to be decisive, which is the same large-weight requirement — so the quantitative lesson transfers, but the layer-collapse theorem itself does not.

title: A Statistical Theory of Contrastive Pre-training and Multimodal Generative AI
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-26

A Statistical Theory of Contrastive Pre-training and Multimodal Generative AI

Oko, Lin, Cai, Mei (2025) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04641

Main idea

The paper asks two questions that most contrastive-learning theory keeps separate: (1) why is a CLIP-style encoder a good representation for downstream tasks that are not linear probes, and (2) why can a neural network of modest size learn such an encoder from a modest number of samples without the curse of dimensionality. The answer to (1) is an information-theoretic slack notion; the answer to (2) is a concrete generative model plus an explicit transformer construction.

Approximate sufficiency. The starting point is the classical fact (Lemma 1, due to Oord et al.) that the population InfoNCE/CLIP risk over all score functions S(x_im, x_tx) is minimized exactly at the pointwise mutual information, S__(x_im,x_tx) = log[P(x_im,x_tx)/(P(x_im)P(x_tx))] + c, and that the negated optimal risk plus log K converges to MI(x_im,x_tx) as K grows. The paper's small but clean observation (Corollary 1) is that this plus Fisher-Neyman factorization means an exact minimizer's encoders are _sufficient statistics* in the textbook sense: P(x_im|x_tx) factorizes through E_im(x_im).

The generalization (Definition 1) is: Suff(E_im) := E over x_im of KL( P(x_tx|x_im) || P(x_tx|E_im(x_im)) ), where the second conditional means conditioning on the sigma-algebra generated by the embedding. Lemma 2 shows this equals MI(x_im,x_tx) - MI(E_im(x_im),x_tx) — i.e. approximate sufficiency is exactly the slack in the data-processing inequality, measured in nats. Zero slack = classical sufficiency. For a score function, Suff(S) is the symmetrized KL between the true conditionals and those induced by the Gibbs tilt proportional to e^S P_im P_tx, and it dominates Suff(E_im) + Suff(E_tx).

Proposition 1 is the bridge: under a bounded-density-ratio assumption (Assumption 1: both the density ratio and e^S live in [1/c1, c1]),

Suff(S) <= [R_clip,K(S) - R_clip,K(S_*)] * (1 + C/K).

This is multiplicative, so an exact minimizer is exactly 0-sufficient at any finite K, and the finite-K penalty decays as 1/K rather than the K^{-1/2} additive bound of Wang-Isola.

Downstream transfer (Propositions 2-4) is then almost free, by data processing: for zero-shot classification under conditional independence (y independent of x_im given x_tx), the KL error of a (slightly modified, M-sample-averaged) zero-shot classifier is at most Suff(S) + C log(2/delta)/M; for conditional diffusion, the squared error of the risk-minimizing conditional denoiser against the true Bayes denoiser is at most 2B^2 * Suff(E_tx) per coordinate, upgraded via Girsanov to a sampling-error bound of order d_im B^2 sqrt(T) * Suff(E_tx); for VLMs, the summed per-token KL of the next-token predictor is at most Suff(E_im) by KL tensorization. The point is that the same scalar controls three structurally different tasks.

JGHM. To answer (2), the joint distribution is modeled as two depth-L, branching-factor-m trees over an alphabet [S], sharing a root x_r; images and text are the two sets of leaves. Transitions factorize over children (Assumption 4) and are bounded in [1/B_psi, B_psi] (Assumption 5). The root posterior is the natural "canonical representation" (Example 1: E_im,(x_im) = [P(s|x_im)/P(s)]s in R^S), under which S = log of the inner product of the two canonical representations. Theorem 6: the ERM over an L-block transformer with D = Otilde(SL), D' = Otilde(mSL^3) has CLIP excess risk Otilde(sqrt(S^2 L^11 m^2 / n)) — crucially sub-linear in, indeed independent of, the number of leaves d = m^L. Theorems 7 and 8 give the analogous end-to-end bounds for CDMs and VLMs built on the frozen CLIP encoder plus a trainable adapter of width M; both look like Otilde(sqrt((S L^8 m^2 + M) poly(S,L) / n)) plus an adapter/sufficiency term in Suff(S) and 1/M.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever technical move is the proof of Proposition 1, and it is worth separating from the (somewhat oversold) framing. Writing S = S__ + r_h with r the L^2 norm of S - S__, one shows that both the excess CLIP risk and the sufficiency are, to second order, _variances of h_: one under the K-way softmax posterior over which index is the paired one, the other under the induced conditional. The whole proposition reduces to showing those two variances agree to O(1/K) (Lemma 4, via a C/K relative-density bound between the two-sample marginals), combined with a local strong convexity / global convexity argument (Lemma 3) giving ||S - S__||^2 bounded by the excess risk. That is why the bound is multiplicative: both quantities are the same quadratic form in S - S_*, differing only in which K-dependent measure the variance is taken under. This is a sharper mechanism than the usual "InfoNCE lower-bounds MI" slogan.

Now the honest critique. Three things.

First, the Otilde is hiding a lot. The constants depend polynomially on c1 from Assumption 1, and in the JGHM instantiation the paper itself computes c1 = B_psi^{4m} (Appendix B.2.1). Corollary 3 states outright that Otilde hides polynomial factors in (B_psi)^m. So the headline "no curse of dimensionality in d = m^L" is bought at the price of an exponential dependence on the branching factor m — the curse is relocated, not removed. Combined with L^11, these are not rates anyone would quote as tight, and the authors say as much.

Second, the "near-minimizer" assumption does hide the hard part, and the paper's own numerics show it. Figure 6a: a transformer trained with AdamW on the plain CLIP loss has a non-vanishing excess CLIP risk at every flip probability. The only configuration that drives the excess risk to ~0 is "Guided TF", which adds an auxiliary loss directly penalizing deviation of the hidden states from the true BP messages (Appendix F.1) — i.e. the network is told to implement the construction the approximation theorem builds by hand. So the experiments confirm the expressivity claim and simultaneously show the statistical claim is not reached by real optimization. The bound then degrades to something non-vanishing in exactly the regime that matters.

Third, the experiments arguably undercut the paper's motivating premise. Figure 6c-d: joint training of the encoder and the downstream model does as well as the two-stage CLIP-pretrain-then-freeze pipeline, and the authors concede "CLIP pre-training may not always be necessary in this simulated environment." Nothing in the theory explains when contrastive pre-training beats end-to-end training — the sufficiency argument only says it does not hurt much. Remark 3 further admits that plain MLE would learn the JGHM efficiently too; the defense offered (robustness to misspecification) is asserted, not proved or tested.

Broader context

The modern theory of contrastive learning starts with Arora et al. (2019), who posited latent classes generating positive pairs and showed that the contrastive loss upper-bounds a downstream linear-classification loss, with a notorious class-collision term; Saunshi and co-authors later showed this framework can be vacuous without inductive bias. HaoChen & Ma (2021) replaced the latent-class story with an augmentation graph and a spectral contrastive loss whose minimizers are graph eigenvectors, converting generalization into a spectral-gap statement. Wang & Isola (2020) decomposed InfoNCE into alignment plus uniformity and proved an asymptotic K^{-1/2} statement that Proposition 1 here directly sharpens. Tosh, Krishnamurthy & Hsu (2021) are the closest precursor to Section 3.3: they showed contrastive minimizers expose the topic posterior to a linear probe; Proposition 5 is a nonlinear, link-function-general version of this. On the approximation side, the direct ancestor is Mei (2024) and the GHM/BP line (Mossel 2016; Poggio et al.; Garnier-Brun et al.; Sclocchi-Favero-Wyart), where denoisers and posteriors in hierarchical models are shown to be computable by networks that emulate belief propagation.

Two papers worth reading alongside: Tosh-Krishnamurthy-Hsu, "Contrastive learning, multi-view redundancy, and linear models" (2021), for the cleanest statement of what contrastive representations expose to simple downstream heads; and Mei, "U-nets as belief propagation" (2024), which is essentially the engine of Section 4 transplanted to the multimodal setting.

A plausible follow-up: the current Suff guarantee is for the exact encoder. Define the sufficiency of a quantized encoder, Suff(Q of E), and bound Suff(Q of E) - Suff(E) by a rate-distortion quantity of the quantizer Q — this would turn product quantization / scalar quantization in a vector index from an empirical heuristic into a statement about how many nats of query-document mutual information a given bit budget destroys, with a matching "bits per nat" lower bound.

Connection to your work. The map is exact at the top: set (x_im, x_tx) = (q, d) and the CLIP loss is the InfoNCE objective of a dual-encoder retriever with in-batch negatives, K = batch size. Three concrete consequences.

(i) Lemma 1 says a perfectly trained dense retriever scores by PMI, log P(q,d)/(P(q)P(d)), not by log P(d|q). These induce different rankings: PMI is anti-popularity-biased by exactly -log P(d). So the "correct" calibration of a dual encoder for Bayes-optimal relevance ranking is to add a document-prior term — a precise theoretical statement of an effect the IR literature treats as a hack.

(ii) Approximate sufficiency is the right currency for a retrieval encoder: Suff(E_q) = I(q;d) - I(E_q(q);d) is the query-side information destroyed by the bottleneck, and Proposition 1 bounds it by the excess InfoNCE risk with a multiplicative (1 + C/K) penalty. That gives a theory-side rationale for the very large batch sizes dense retrieval needs, and says the marginal return is O(1/K). On geometry: in the JGHM the canonical representation has dimension p__ = S = number of latent root states, the required dimension is essentially the rank of the exponentiated-PMI matrix, and S__ = log of an inner product — a monotone function of an inner product, so MIPS/ANN search over the canonical embeddings preserves the correct ranking. This is the natural upper-bound counterpart to the worst-case dimension lower bounds in the "theoretical limitations of embedding-based retrieval" line (sign-rank / communication-complexity arguments on arbitrary qrel matrices): generative structure buys you a dimension equal to the number of latent topics, rather than something combinatorial in the corpus.

(iii) Where it breaks for retrieval, concretely. Assumption 1 requires the PMI to be bounded in [-log c1, log c1]; in retrieval, the PMI between a query and its single gold document in a 10^9-document corpus is enormous, and c1 enters every constant polynomially. The guarantees are KL bounds on the conditional, never recall@k or nDCG: an average-KL bound can be small while the argmax is wrong on a non-vanishing slice of queries, and nothing in Proposition 2 depends on the number of candidates, whereas retrieval error is a max over a huge candidate set. Bridging that needs a margin / Tsybakov-style low-noise condition tying Suff to top-k error as a function of corpus size — a genuinely open and well-posed problem. Finally, Theorem 8 is arguably a better model of generative retrieval than of VLMs: a frozen query encoder feeding a decoder that autoregressively emits a hierarchical identifier is literally a GHM on the output side, and hierarchical semantic docids (DSI/NCI/RIPOR-style) are the tree. Read that way, the theorem says a decoder of depth about 2L+1 (L = docid tree depth) and width poly(S) suffices to compute the exact next-docid-token posterior, with sample complexity polynomial in (S, L, m) and independent of corpus size — which is a sharper and more defensible claim for semantic-ID generative retrieval than for natural images.

Proof sketch

(a) Near-minimizers are near-sufficient (Proposition 1). Work with the equivalent "which of K is the match" formulation (Eq. 21): draw K texts i.i.d. from P_tx, pick k uniformly, draw x_im from the conditional given text k; the CLIP risk is the cross-entropy of predicting k. Decompose both the excess risk and the expected KL into a common linear term E[S__ - S] plus a log-partition term; the linear terms cancel, so everything reduces to bounding the difference between the K-sample log-partition and the population one. Normalize so both conditional means vanish, write S = S__ + r_h with ||h|| = 1, and Taylor-expand in r around the stationary point r = 0. The second derivative is a _difference of two variances_ of h: one under the K-point softmax posterior, one under the induced conditional. Lemma 4 shows these agree to C/K, by proving that the joint law of two draws from the K-point posterior and two i.i.d. draws from the conditional have densities within a (1 +/- C/K) factor off-diagonal (Assumption 1 gives each posterior mass in [1/(C'K), C'/K]). Separately Lemma 3 gives ||S - S__||^2 bounded by the excess risk, via: the first derivative has a variance representation making the risk globally convex along the ray with second derivative at least 1/C (lower-bounding the softmax-posterior variance of h by a pairwise-difference sum and then by the conditional variance, which is 1), plus a third-derivative bound giving the two-regime growth min(r^2/C, r_0 |r|/C). Multiplying the two gives the multiplicative (1 + C/K) bound. Downstream Propositions 2-4 are short: data processing (the y - x_tx - x_im chain for ZSC; (z_t, x_tx) to (z_t, E_tx(x_tx)) for CDMs), KL tensorization over tokens for VLMs, a Hoeffding/bounded-variable concentration for the log(2/delta)/M Monte-Carlo term in ZSC, and a KL "triangle-like" inequality for mixtures (Bun-Steinke). Corollary 2 is Girsanov applied to the stochastic-localization SDE with the two drifts, using scale invariance of KL.

(b) Transformers emulate belief propagation. Lemma 6 states the message-passing form of the target: upward messages q_v = f_iota(h_v) with f_iota(h)_s = log sum_a psi_iota(s,a) e^{h_a} (log-sum-exp against the transition matrix), and h_v at the parent = normalize(sum over children of q_u); at the root, softmax(h_r)_s = P(s|x) and S_* = log sum_s P(s|x_im) P(s|x_tx)/P(s). The transformer is built so that block l executes step l, with every leaf column redundantly carrying a copy of its level-l ancestor's message. Two constructions do the work:

  • _Feedforward = log-sum-exp (Lemma 7)._ A ReLU network of depth about loglog(1/delta)_log(1/delta) and width about mS log^3(1/delta) approximates f_iota to delta in L-infinity, by composing a ReLU approximation of exp on the negative half-line, a linear map by the transition matrix Psi, and a ReLU approximation of log on [e^{-A}, e^{A}] with A = log(2 S B_psi^2); the bounded-psi assumption is what keeps the argument of log in a fixed range so the Lipschitz amplification of the exp error is O(S B_psi^2). The network also reads the sinusoidal positional code to select _which* iota to apply, exactly and with no error.
  • _Attention = sum over children (Lemma 8, Lemma 15)._ The positional encoding of leaf v is the 2L-vector of (sin, cos) of 2_pi_rank of each ancestor divided by the level's branching count. With W_K = I and W_Q the diagonal matrix that zeroes out level l's two coordinates and scales the rest by alpha, the attention logit between u and v is alpha times a sum of cosines over the other levels, which attains its maximum (L-1)_alpha exactly on the set where all ancestor ranks agree _except* at level l — i.e. exactly one representative descendant per child of the common level-(l-1) ancestor. Taking alpha of order log(d/delta) makes the softmax an (approximate) hard selector, and W_V scales the average into the sum. So the "attend to your siblings' subtrees" operation is implemented by a Fourier positional code plus a low-temperature softmax — this is the cleverest piece of engineering in the paper.
  • Error propagation (Lemma 16). Errors compound multiplicatively up the tree: the max over v of the L-infinity error is at most delta times the product over levels of (2 m + 3), giving bounds of order delta * 5^L d (40^{L+1} in the CDM case), proved by induction using Lipschitzness of normalize, log-sum-exp and log-sum-softmax (Lemmas 40, 44, 45). The blow-up is exponential in L, but it is absorbed by choosing the per-step accuracy delta' of order sqrt(S^2 L^11 m^2/n)/(5^L d), which costs only log(1/delta') = O(L + log d + log n) in depth and width. That trade — exponential error amplification paid for with logarithmic network cost — is the whole reason the final bound is polynomial in L.

(c) Assembling the sample-complexity bounds. Standard excess-risk split into approximation + 2x uniform deviation. The approximation side plugs the construction above into the bound that the CLIP risk gap is at most 4 times the sup-norm score error (log-softmax is 1-Lipschitz, Lemma 43). The generalization side is a chaining bound (Lemma 46, taken from Bai-Chen-Wang-Xiong-Mei): the parameter space has diameter 2B and dimension d_rho = (J+3)L(D+D'+1)^2 + S = Otilde(S^2 L^8 m^2), hence log covering number at most d_rho log(4B/Delta); the per-sample loss is bounded by 4 B_read with B_read = 4 m log B_psi, hence sub-Gaussian; and the loss is Lipschitz in the parameters with a constant B_f of the form ((cB)^{18JL} S^4)^{L+1}, proved layer by layer in Appendix E.1. Since that constant enters only inside a logarithm, the astronomically large Lipschitz constant costs only log B_f of order J L^2, i.e. L^3 — this is where the extra L^3 in L^11 = L^8 * L^3 comes from. Result: sqrt(d_rho L^3 / n).

For CDMs and VLMs the same machinery runs on a different message-passing algorithm: a downward (leaves to root) pass on the image tree starting from the Gaussian log-likelihood, fused at the root with the text posterior, then an upward (root to leaves) pass, so that the softmax of the final message is the exact posterior of leaf pixel v and its mean is the Bayes denoiser; the architecture is correspondingly 2L+1 blocks. For VLMs the BP recursion must be run for all prefix lengths simultaneously, which Appendix D.1.2 parallelizes into one masked-attention pass (Proposition 10).

The remaining ingredient is Proposition 5, which is what lets a frozen, arbitrary near-minimizing encoder feed the downstream transformer. Under Assumption 3 (canonical representation with second-moment matrix at least I/L_B^2 and L_Gamma-Lipschitz inverse link), the identity that the inverse link of S_ equals the inner product of the canonical representations can be left-inverted using the pseudo-inverse of the (exponentially tall) matrix of image representations. The approximation error from using S instead of S_ is of order L_B^2 p__ L_Gamma^2 * Suff(S) (a Taylor argument plus Lemma 3). The exponentially large matrix product is then replaced by a _Monte-Carlo estimate over M i.i.d. images*: the second adapter weight stores M sampled image embeddings as rows, so a softmax computes self-normalized importance weights, and the first adapter weight applies the pseudo-inverse restricted to those columns. The estimator is unbiased, and a variance computation gives the 1/M term. So the adapter width M is literally a count of Monte-Carlo anchor images — a nice, interpretable reading of why practitioners bolt a small MLP adapter onto frozen CLIP features. Note the tension the paper does not resolve: M also enters the parameter count, so the CDM/VLM bounds contain both sqrt(M/n) and 1/M, and no optimization over M (which would give M of order n^{1/3}) is performed.

Caveats on precision: the L^11, L^8 exponents are explicitly not claimed tight; several steps ("Otilde hides polynomial factors in (B_psi)^m") conceal exponential-in-m constants; and Remark 2 is candid that nothing shows trained CLIP encoders actually implement BP — the OOD experiments in Figure 7 are suggestive (standard-trained transformers track misspecified BP more closely when in-distribution risk is lower) but not conclusive.

title: Explaining ViTs Using Information Flow
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-26

Explaining ViTs Using Information Flow

Walker, Ahmed, Jha, Ewetz (2025) — https://proceedings.mlr.press/v258/walker25a.html

Main idea

ViTs are hard to attribute. Gradient methods (saliency, Integrated Gradients) degrade badly on transformers because self-attention is strongly non-linear and the softmax saturates, so input gradients are small and noisy. The architecture-specific alternative, starting with Abnar & Zuidema's attention rollout, treats a ViT as a Markov chain over patches: the head-averaged attention matrix A_l = softmax(QK^T) is row-stochastic, so A^{nm} is read as "how much patch n's representation is drawn from patch m." Rollout handles the residual connection by mixing with the identity, T_l = 0.5_A_l + 0.5_I, multiplies the T_l across all 12 layers, and reads the [CLS] row of the product as a 14x14 heatmap. Chefer et al. (LRP relevance), Yuan et al. (Transition Attention) and Chen et al. (Bidirectional Attention) all keep this skeleton and bolt gradients on top-down or as post-processing.

The authors' complaint is specific and, to my eye, correct: a transition matrix alone carries no magnitude information, so you cannot model a converging path. The 0.5/0.5 split silently asserts that the residual branch and the attention branch contribute equally. Their toy example: embeddings E_a=[1], E_b=[99] with rows T_a=[1,0], T_b=[0,1]; rollout returns [0.5,0.5] when the honest answer is roughly [0.01,0.99]. Appendix A.3 measures this over 10k images: the residual-to-MHA norm ratio sits near 2 in layer 1 and ranges 1-4 by layer 12, and the residual-to-MLP ratio reaches ~10 in the last layer. Equal weighting is empirically wrong everywhere.

InFlow fixes this by carrying a pair (E, T) — patch embeddings alongside the transition matrix — through the network, and defining three operations. Series: T_{i,k} = T_{i,j} T_{j,k}. Diverging: a branch with no component copies the pair unchanged. Converging: when E_q = E_j + E_k, the matrices combine as T_{i,q} = D(E_j,E_k)_j T_{i,j} + D(E_j,E_k)_k T_{i,k}, where D is diagonal with per-token entries ||E_j^i||_2 / (||E_j^i||_2 + ||E_k^i||_2) — a per-patch convex weight, not a global scalar. Because D_j + D_k = I, the combination stays row-stochastic.

Carrying embeddings also lets them write down an MLP term, which rollout structurally cannot: citing Geva et al., they treat the FFN as a per-token promotion/scaling operator that does not mix tokens, so its transition matrix is diagonal with entries ||E_H^i||_2/||E_F^i||_2. One layer becomes the series composition of an attention-block factor (D_D * A_l + D_C * I) and an MLP-block factor (D_H * ||E_H||/||E_F|| + D_G * I). Heads are collapsed following Chen et al. via gradient-weighted head importance. Class specificity is injected bottom-up rather than top-down: Attr_l = A_l * mean_d of the derivative of Z_CLS(l) with respect to A_l, where Z_CLS(l) is the classification head applied to layer l's embedding (a logit-lens readout), and Attr_l replaces A_l. Final map = top row of the product of the T_l, drop the [CLS]-[CLS] entry, reshape to 14x14, upsample. Results: wins 41/48 tests across ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-Tiny on RISE insertion/deletion, MAS, and PIC SIC/AIC, by up to 18%, at 0.019 s/image — 4x rollout, 2.7x faster than Chefer, 12x faster than the IG-post-processed methods.

The most interesting part

The genuinely good idea is small and clean: magnitudes live in the residual stream, and any method that only multiplies stochastic matrices has thrown them away. Appendix A.3 is the most valuable page in the paper, and it is a measurement any rollout user should have made in 2020.

But the paper oversells this as a "theoretical framework," and several things don't hold up.

The algebra breaks its own invariant. Definition 2 insists every row of T is a probability vector. Series and converging operations preserve that. The MLP factor does not: it is diagonal with entries d'_i r_i + (1-d'_i) where r_i = ||E_H^i||/||E_F^i|| is unbounded, so right-multiplying scales columns and row sums depart from 1. No renormalization is mentioned. The gradient substitution in Eq. (7) is worse — Attr_l can be negative and is not stochastic at all, so after the central contribution the object being propagated is no longer a transition matrix in any sense, and the Markov-chain story that motivates the whole line of work is gone. (Relatedly, Definition 2 states T^{nm} flows input n to output m with rows summing to 1, but the actual readout takes the top row as a distribution over input patches — the index convention is backwards relative to use.)

The convergence weight is a norm heuristic, not a decomposition. E_q = E_j + E_k is vector addition; weighting by ||E_j||/(||E_j||+||E_k||) ignores alignment entirely. If the two branches partly cancel, the norm proportion is not the contribution proportion. A first-order or projection-based split (inner product of E_j with E_q over ||E_q||^2) would at least be exact for the linear part, and is not tried or ablated. Likewise LayerNorm — "omitted for readability, but retained in the model" — is never modeled, even though LN rescales exactly the magnitudes D depends on, and the value projection W_V is ignored just as in rollout, so the claim that all components are "properly modeled" is too strong.

The ablation undercuts the headline. Table 2 (MAS Ins-Del): Rollout -0.088, then embeddings-in-convergence 0.035, then +MLP 0.057, then +gradients 0.320. The embedding weighting earns its keep; the MLP block — billed as modeled "for the first time" — buys 0.022; the gradient term, which is the least novel part and is essentially layerwise grad-times-attention with a logit lens, supplies most of the gain. Table 2's Rollout and InFlow numbers also don't match Table 1 (Rollout RISE Ins 0.774 vs 0.784; InFlow MAS Del 0.361 vs 0.317) with no explanation.

The evaluation is all one family. RISE, MAS and PIC are all perturbation metrics, and all reward sharp, contiguous, low-entropy maps — exactly what a method producing less background mass will win on, independent of faithfulness. Deletion/insertion are known to conflate attribution quality with distribution shift (ROAR, ROAD). MAS is the first author's own prior metric. There are no error bars (the checklist says "Not Applicable"), no model-randomization sanity checks, no localization/segmentation evaluation of the kind Chefer et al. reported, and no comparison to Abnar & Zuidema's attention flow (the max-flow variant) despite the title's framing. And the checklist is candid: "We do not provide proofs."

Broader context

Attribution methods try to assign a model's scalar output to input features. The gradient lineage runs Simonyan saliency, then Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al. 2017; gradient-weighted last-conv activations, which relies on a spatially-aligned feature map that ViTs don't really have), then Integrated Gradients (Sundararajan et al. 2017), which is axiomatically grounded: path integral from a baseline, with completeness — attributions sum to f(x) - f(x'). That property is what InFlow lacks and what makes IG the right point of comparison conceptually, even though it performs poorly on ViTs.

The transformer-specific branch began with Jain & Wallace's "Attention is not Explanation" (2019) and Abnar & Zuidema's rollout (2020). Rollout's known pathologies: it is class-agnostic (one map regardless of which logit you query), it ignores W_V and the MLPs, and repeated multiplication of near-uniform stochastic matrices drives the map toward uniform with depth. Chefer et al. (CVPR 2021) addressed class-specificity with LRP relevance; InFlow addresses magnitude. A useful adjacent frame is the residual-stream view from mechanistic interpretability (Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits, 2021), which already decomposes the stream into additive head/MLP contributions — InFlow is, in effect, a cheap norm-based approximation to a direct-effect decomposition, which suggests the obvious follow-up: compute the actual linearized decomposition (freeze softmax and LN gains, treat the layer as locally linear, attribute the logit exactly) and ask how well InFlow's norm-ratio weighting approximates it. That version would come with a completeness guarantee, and would turn the "algebra" into a theorem. Pair it with ROAD-style retraining-free evaluation and Adebayo-style sanity checks, since the current metric suite cannot distinguish a faithful map from a prettier one.

The IR connection is real but narrow. InFlow needs only A_l and the residual-stream embeddings at each block, so it transfers verbatim to a cross-encoder reranker (monoBERT-style): read the [CLS]/score row of the product of the T_l to attribute a relevance score back to query and document tokens, and the magnitude correction matters more there, since residual-norm growth in text encoders is at least as skewed. For generative retrieval the extension is non-trivial rather than free — there is no single [CLS] row, and you would need per-docid-token attribution through decoder cross-attention. For bi-encoder vector search the method does not apply as written at all: the quantity of interest is a dot product of two pooled embeddings, not a class logit, so both the gradient term and the readout would have to be redefined; I would call that connection forced today.

Proof sketch

There is no theorem. The paper presents Definitions 1-5 and a derivation; the AISTATS checklist states plainly, "We do not provide proofs, but we provide experimental results which reinforce the theoretical results."

What is derived, and is worth stating precisely, is a construction with one provable-by-inspection property. Assume (i) attention A_l is row-stochastic after head collapse, (ii) residual addition is exactly E_q = E_j + E_k, and (iii) the relative contribution of two converging branches at token i is proportional to ||E^i||_2. Then the converging weights satisfy D(E_j,E_k)_j + D(E_j,E_k)_k = I by construction, so Eq. (3) is a per-row convex combination of row-stochastic matrices and is itself row-stochastic; series composition preserves row-stochasticity because the product of row-stochastic matrices is row-stochastic; hence the product over layers would be a valid transition matrix and its [CLS] row a probability distribution over input patches. That is the whole argument, and it is sound given assumption (iii) — which is the load-bearing one and is supported only empirically (Appendix A.3 shows the ratio is far from 1, which refutes rollout but does not establish that the L2-norm proportion is the right weight). The invariant is then broken anyway by the MLP diagonal (entries unbounded above 1) and by the gradient substitution of Eq. (7). So: a well-motivated construction with a correctness argument for one of its three operations, not a guarantee about attribution fidelity.

title: Inverting Gradient Attacks Naturally Makes Data Poisons: An Availability Attack on Neural Networks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-26

Inverting Gradient Attacks Naturally Makes Data Poisons: An Availability Attack on Neural Networks

Bouaziz, El-Mhamdi, Usunier (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21453

Main idea

The paper asks a clean question: outside convex models, is a Byzantine gradient attacker strictly more powerful than a data poisoner? In convex settings (Farhadkhani et al., ICML 2022) the two are known to be equivalent, but that equivalence is really a statement about attacking a logistic regression — or, equivalently, about an attacker who can act directly at the last-layer embedding. For non-convex networks, the folklore was that data poisoning is much weaker: the poisoning literature on neural nets has only ever managed to shave off a few accuracy points (Lu et al. 2022; Zhao & Lao 2022), while gradient attacks have been driving models to random-level performance since Krum (Blanchard et al. 2017).

Bouaziz, El Mhamdi and Usunier argue the gap is largely an artifact of mismatched threat models, and they remove the confound by construction. They define a generic training loop in which "gradient generation units" emit messages — which may be gradients or data points — that go through an aggregator AGG and then UPDATE. Both attack families get the same interaction budget: recompute the attack every iteration, inject up to a fraction alpha = n_p/(n_b+n_p) of the batch. The attacker knows theta_t, AGG, UPDATE and MESSAGE, does not see the honest batch S_t^b, and has an auxiliary dataset D_a drawn from the same distribution as a surrogate. Under this framing the only remaining difference between the two attacks is the real one: a gradient attacker can send any vector in R^d, whereas a data poisoner is confined to the image of the gradient operator over a feasible data domain (their Figure 2).

The mechanism is to borrow gradient inversion from the privacy literature (Geiping et al. 2020a; Zhao et al. 2020) and run it on a malicious target. Pick a standard Byzantine attack — Gradient Ascent (make the aggregate anti-collinear with the honest mean), Orthogonal Gradient (make it orthogonal, stalling training), or Little Is Enough (g^a minus z_max_sigma, with z_max chosen adaptively to maximize divergence of the aggregate, the attack designed to slip past Krum-style filters) — compute its target vector g^atk from the auxiliary gradients, then solve a minimization over actual (image, label) pairs whose induced gradient reproduces g^atk. The objectives are in their Table 1: cosine similarity for GA, absolute cosine for OG, and an L2 distance for LIE. The inner problem is solved with Adam on the pixels, projected onto the feasible set by clipping, at every training step. The paper is explicit that, unlike privacy inversion, _no preimage is guaranteed to exist* — the target was never produced by any data point — so this is a best-effort projection of a Byzantine vector onto the reachable gradient set.

Empirically, on CIFAR-10 with a 1.6M-parameter CNN and a ViT-tiny/8: with SGD + plain averaging, LIE-inverted poisons at alpha = 0.01 collapse training (3 of 4 seeds diverge, all poisons inside the feasible set); against MultiKrum with f = 0.1, LIE poisons at alpha = 0.05 get through and gut the model, with poison selection rates of ~0.92 at alpha = 0.01 versus ~0 for GA/OG. This is, as claimed, the first demonstrated availability attack on a neural network via data poisoning.

The most interesting part

The genuinely good idea is the reframing: treat the data poisoner as a Byzantine worker whose message happens to be constrained to lie in the image of the gradient operator, and treat gradient inversion as the projection onto that set. That is a clean conceptual move and it makes the comparison well-posed for the first time. The negative results are also informative: Adam resists the availability attack outright (gradient normalization prevents abrupt divergence) and degrades only into a slow-down — alpha = 0.2 pushes best validation accuracy from 67.1% at epoch 4 to ~61-62% at epochs 17-34 — while the appendix's Table 4 shows the gradient version flattens Adam to 10.0% at alpha = 0.01. So the paper's own data say data poisoning is substantially weaker than gradient attack, and the abstract's framing undersells that.

Now the critique, which is substantial.

The 1% figure is not apples-to-apples in the way a reader will assume. It is apples-to-apples within the paper's harmonized threat model, which is the point — but that model gives the poisoner per-iteration white-box access to theta_t, knowledge of AGG and UPDATE, an in-distribution auxiliary set, and the right to craft fresh poisons at every single step. That is a Byzantine participant that types data instead of vectors, not the data poisoner of Geiping et al. or Carlini et al., who fix a poison set before training. The authors concede this ("our threat model acts as a worst case scenario"), but the headline claim — availability attack at 1% contamination — will be read out of context.

The central scientific quantity is never reported. The whole paper hinges on how well the inversion approximates a non-realizable target, yet there is no measurement of the achieved residual: no cosine similarity between the induced gradient and g^atk, no distance to the target, no study of how it degrades as the feasible set tightens. We only see downstream accuracy and MultiKrum selection rates as proxies. Without that we cannot tell whether the image of the gradient operator is nearly surjective over a batch of free pixels (which would be the interesting finding) or whether LIE simply happens to be a target with a wide basin of acceptable approximations.

Cost is undocumented. Every training step runs a full Adam inner loop over n_p images. No wall-clock, no inner-iteration count, no ablation of inner steps versus success. The authors admit this "limit[ed] us in experimenting with larger models and datasets," which is exactly why the number matters: a defender's first question is whether this scales past a 1.6M-parameter CNN.

Statistics are thin. 4 seeds; the flagship result is "3 of 4 runs diverged." Error bars are standard errors over n=4, and attack ranking flips between architectures (on ViT, Figure 10 reports LIE merely slowing training while GA and OG achieve availability — the opposite of the CNN ordering) with no explanation offered.

Defenses are barely engaged. Only MultiKrum is tested, i.e. a gradient-side defense. Section 2 surveys data-side defenses — sanitization (Steinhardt et al.), augmentation (Borgnia et al.), bagging/finite aggregation (Wang et al.) — and tests none of them, even though those are the defenses matched to the attack's message type. Worse for the attack, the paper notes in passing (Figure 9) that plain early stopping already limits the damage, and the strongest result is anyway reported as best-validation-weights test accuracy.

Stealth is unsolved. The successful attack uses the full image domain; Figure 8 shows the poisons are visibly noise with arbitrary labels. The tight neighborhood set (L1 within 32/255 of an auxiliary image, a tiny budget over 3072 dimensions) markedly weakens the attack. So the clean-label version — the one that matters for scraped corpora, which Appendix A spends a page motivating with bot-prevalence numbers — does not yet work.

Finally, the paper is purely empirical. It frames itself against a theorem (the convex equivalence) and answers with experiments; Figure 2 is a picture where a characterization of the reachable gradient set should be. For that reason there is no proof sketch section here — there is no theorem to sketch.

Broader context

Three threads meet here. Availability (indiscriminate) poisoning aims to make a model useless rather than to flip a specific input; it works on convex models (Biggio et al. 2013 on SVMs) but has historically underperformed badly on deep nets. Byzantine / robust distributed learning assumes a participant can send arbitrary vectors; Krum (Blanchard et al. 2017), Bulyan (El-Mhamdi et al. 2018), and the Little-Is-Enough attack (Baruch et al. 2019) are the canonical points, with El-Mhamdi et al. (2023) giving an impossibility result for robust mean estimation above a heterogeneity/dimension threshold. Gradient inversion was developed as a privacy attack (Geiping et al. 2020a, "Inverting Gradients"; iDLG) to reconstruct training samples from shared gradients. The paper's trick is to run the privacy tool on an adversarial target, converting an existence-guaranteed reconstruction problem into an approximation problem over a set that may not contain the target at all. The two most directly relevant prior works are Farhadkhani et al. (2022), whose equivalence this extends empirically, and Geiping et al. (2020b) "Witches' Brew," which established gradient matching as a practical poisoning tool for targeted attacks.

The sharpest follow-up the paper opens is theoretical and sits exactly where the paper stops: characterize the reachable set, the image of the gradient operator over the feasible data domain. Robust aggregation bounds are all stated against adversaries ranging over R^d; restricted to a set of dimension at most n_p * dim(X) carved out by a fixed network, those bounds should be tightenable, and one could ask whether MultiKrum-type rules admit realizability-aware variants that reject vectors with no plausible data preimage. A cheap empirical companion: the attack needs theta_t fresh at every step, so measure degradation as a function of model staleness tau. Real federated deployments hand clients the model once per round, and if success collapses at tau = 10 steps, secure aggregation plus delayed model release is already most of a defense.

On IR: the honest connection is an analogy, not an application, and I would not push it. Corpus-poisoning attacks on dense retrievers (e.g. Zhong et al. 2023, injecting adversarial passages optimized to be retrieved for many queries) solve structurally the same problem — optimize an input in a feasible data domain so that its embedding or induced gradient lands at a chosen target — but in the discrete token domain, where the "does a preimage exist" question that this paper waves at with Figure 2 is the binding constraint rather than an afterthought, and HotFlip-style relaxations are the tool. Note also that Farhadkhani's convex case is literally "attack at the last-layer embedding," which for a bi-encoder retriever is most of the model. If there is a transferable theory question for vector search, it is the reachability one: how much of embedding space is actually hit by valid documents, which is the same geometry question in a different costume.

title: Every Feedforward Neural Network Definable in an o-Minimal Structure Has Finite Sample Complexity
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-25

Every Feedforward Neural Network Definable in an o-Minimal Structure Has Finite Sample Complexity — Anastasis Kratsios, Gregory Cousins, Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde, Bum Jun Kim, Simone Brugiapaglia (2026) — arXiv:2605.07097

Metadata note: the Zotero record lists "Cousins" without a first name; the PDF gives Gregory Cousins (not Cynthia). Affiliations: McMaster, McMaster, Cambridge/Oxford, University of Tokyo, Concordia. Dated 11 May 2026, v1 [stat.ML].

Main idea

The paper asks a deliberately coarse question: *does every standard fixed-size feedforward network have finite agnostic PAC sample complexity?* The existing literature answers this architecture by architecture — Bartlett-Harvey-Liaw-Mehrabian for piecewise-linear MLPs, Garg-Jegelka-Jaakkola and Morris et al. for message-passing GNNs, Edelman et al. / Trauger-Tewari for transformers — each with its own combinatorial or norm-based argument. The claim here is that all of these are instances of one structural fact, and the structural fact comes from model theory.

What "definable in an o-minimal structure" means. A *structure expanding the real field* is a family S = (S_n)_n of subsets of R^n containing all semialgebraic sets, closed under Boolean operations, products, and — crucially — coordinate projection (Definition 2.2). Closure under projection is closure under existential quantification, so S is exactly the collection of sets cut out by first-order formulas in some language on R. The structure is o-minimal if the definable subsets of R^1 are precisely the finite unions of points and intervals. That single one-dimensional axiom is the whole hypothesis, and by cell decomposition it propagates to all dimensions: every definable set in R^n decomposes into finitely many cells, definable families have uniformly bounded cell counts, and definable functions are piecewise monotone/smooth. The slogan is "no infinite oscillation, uniformly in parameters." A map is definable if its graph is a definable set; definable maps are closed under composition, concatenation and linear combination, which is what makes the whole thing propagate through a network.

Why this is the right level of generality: the canonical pathology in VC theory is Vapnik's {x -> sign(sin(theta x)) : theta in R} — a *one-parameter* family with infinite VC dimension. Finite parameter count buys you nothing; what you need is that the parametrized family cannot oscillate unboundedly as theta ranges over an unbounded set. O-minimality is precisely the axiom that rules this out, and sin on all of R is precisely the thing it excludes. So the paper's real content, stripped of packaging, is: no sin(theta x) pathology is hiding inside a transformer.

What exactly is claimed finite. The chain is: joint definability of (x, theta) -> f_theta(x) implies finite VC dimension of the induced classifier family {1_{(0,infinity)} o f_theta} (Lemma B.3), implies finite pseudo-dimension of the real-valued class and of the loss-composed class, via a lifting trick (Lemma B.6), implies finite gamma-fat-shattering dimension for every gamma > 0, bounded by the pseudo-dimension uniformly in gamma, implies finite agnostic PAC sample complexity via ERM / uniform convergence. Explicitly: N at least about (K + log(1/delta))/eps^2 for classification (Theorem 3.1), N at least about (K ln^2(K/eps) + ln(1/delta))/eps^2 for bounded definable regression losses (Theorem 3.2), where K is the VC/pseudo-dimension. Covering numbers are explicitly *not* used; Remark B.9 says passing through Bartlett-Kulkarni-Posner covering bounds would only loosen things. The key sentence is footnote 1: C is universal and K depends only on the architecture, the defining formulas of its gates, and the loss — but K is never computed, estimated, or bounded in terms of width, depth, or parameter count. It is finite because an exponential eventually beats a polynomial, full stop.

Coverage. Section 4 is a systematic definability audit: affine/convolutional layers and residual/gated-residual blocks (semialgebraic); ReLU, LeakyReLU, softsign, maxout, winner-take-all, hard-routed MoE, top-k, max/average pooling (semialgebraic); sigmoid, tanh, softplus, ELU, SELU, Swish, GELU (exact and tanh-approximation), SwiGLU, Mish, softmax routing (definable in R_exp); layer/batch/group/RMS normalization with stabilizer eps > 0 (semialgebraic, since sqrt is algebraic); multi-head self- and cross-attention and sliding-window attention (definable in R_exp, jointly in X and all W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O); finite-vocabulary embedding lookups; and deep equilibrium layers (Proposition 4.13, via definability of the fixed-point graph). Assembled: MLPs (Corollary 4.14) and full post-LN transformers (Corollary 4.15, written out in gory detail) are definable in R_{an,exp}.

What is notably *not* covered. (i) Global sin/cos — not definable in R_{an,exp}. Fourier positional encodings are admitted only on a *finite* position set or a *bounded* definable domain, and if frequencies/phases are trainable their parameter domain must be bounded (Definition 4.10, Proposition 4.11). So SIREN-style networks and random-Fourier-feature layers with unbounded trainable frequencies fall outside — exactly the Vapnik counterexample, honestly acknowledged. (ii) Genuine recurrence: RNNs, looped/universal transformers, neural ODEs with unbounded integration — covered only by unrolling to a fixed horizon. (iii) Anything where the architecture grows: no bound uniform in width, depth, sequence length, or graph size. (iv) Unbounded losses — Theorem 3.2 requires loss: R^m x R^m -> [0,1], so plain MSE needs clipping or normalizing. (v) Non-definable activations generally (e.g. x sin(1/x), anything with an essential oscillation).

The most interesting part

Two candidates, and the genuinely interesting one is not the one the paper foregrounds.

The mechanism (what the paper foregrounds). The proof deliberately refuses the metric route. Section B.2 states the reason crisply: covering-number / Rademacher arguments require truncating theta to [-M, M]^P, and the metric entropy of that cube diverges as M -> infinity, so no amount of chaining gives a bound for unbounded parameters. The definable route measures something orthogonal to metric size: *uniformly over all of R^P, the family's realizable sign patterns admit a finite uniform cell decomposition.* Concretely (Lemma B.3), fix N sample points x_1, ..., x_N and look in parameter space at X_i = {theta : f(x_i, theta) > 0}. The number of labelings the family can realize on the sample equals the number of nonempty atoms of the Boolean algebra generated by X_1, ..., X_N. All the X_i are fibres of one definable family, so uniform cell decomposition bounds the atom count by C N^m (m = number of parameters), and 2^N <= C N^m fails for large N. The dual perspective — counting in parameter space rather than input space — is the right one, and it is the reason boundedness is irrelevant.

The cost, stated plainly. The theorem is non-constructive in the only sense that matters: you learn that K < infinity without learning anything about K. There is no rate, no dependence on width or depth, no comparison between architectures, no optimization guarantee (ERM is assumed, not achieved), and no statement about the overparametrized regime. The paper is admirably upfront about this — "Our result is qualitative and statistical," and the conclusion reframes finite sample complexity as "a baseline rather than a differentiator."

The sharper critique, and it is the honest one. The generality the paper buys by going to full o-minimality is thinner than advertised, *by its own Appendix A.1*. Appendix A.1 establishes that e^{beta x}, log|.|, arctan, real-analytic algebraic branches are Pfaffian; Example 5 goes to some trouble to show that sin(wx + b) is Pfaffian on any bounded open domain, with explicit format (2, 6, 3k); Proposition B.11 certifies GELU as Pfaffian of format (2,2,2), Swish (2,4,2), SwiGLU (2,4,3). Softmax is a ratio of nonvanishing Pfaffian functions, hence Pfaffian; normalization layers are algebraic; ReLU, max-pooling, top-k and polyhedral routing are semialgebraic Boolean combinations. So every single example in Section 4 lives inside the Pfaffian closure with explicitly computable format — the setting where Karpinski-Macintyre (1997) already give *polynomial* VC bounds in terms of parameter count and Pfaffian format, with the Gabrielov-Vorobjov format calculus (cited here as [35]) supplying the composition bookkeeping. In other words, the paper reaches for the weakest hypothesis available (arbitrary o-minimal S, including R_{an,exp} where no finiteness-format control exists), pays the full price of losing all quantitative content, and then exhibits no example that actually requires that weakest hypothesis. The paper's own Section 5.1 concedes the point by proposing "quantitative versions via sharply-o-minimality" (Binyamini-Novikov-Zak) as future work — but for the stated examples the Pfaffian route was available in 1997.

The secondary over-claim is the straw man in the framing. The paper contrasts itself against covering-number arguments that need bounded parameters, but VC/pseudo-dimension arguments for real-parametrized classes have been parameter-free since Goldberg-Jerrum (1995) and Karpinski-Macintyre (1997), and Bartlett-Harvey-Liaw-Mehrabian (2019) is also norm-free. "Unbounded parameters" is not a new frontier for this style of bound; it is the native setting.

So what does it actually buy? For a practitioner: nothing. For a learning theorist: one genuinely useful thing, and one genuinely useful *lemma*.

  • The useful thing is the negative reading, not the positive one. Finite VC dimension for a fixed finite architecture was never in doubt; what the audit in Section 4 actually establishes is *where the boundary is*, and the answer is sharp and slightly surprising: the only common deep-learning primitive that crosses the line into infinite capacity is a periodic activation with an unbounded trainable frequency. That is a precise, checkable criterion, and it is a real contribution — the next person who invents a layer can check definability in a page instead of redoing a VC argument.
  • The useful *lemma* is Lemma B.2, which the paper proves and then essentially does not use (it feeds only the one-dimensional Remark B.4, VCdim <= 2K; the main chain goes through Lemma B.3 instead). Lemma B.2 says: there is K such that for every theta, the sublevel set {x : f_theta(x) <= 0} has at most K connected components. That is a statement about the geometry of decision/retrieval regions, uniform over all parameters, and it is more actionable than the PAC corollary (see Broader context).
  • A third thing worth flagging as quietly valuable: Remark B.8. If the loss is merely Lipschitz rather than definable, finite pseudo-dimension of F need not survive composition: take F = {a x : a in [0, 2pi]} and loss(y_1, y_2) = (sin(y_1) + 1)/2. The hypothesis class is one-dimensional and tame; the loss is bounded and Lipschitz; the composed class has infinite pseudo-dimension. This is a clean warning that definability is a *joint* condition on model and loss, and that the usual "bounded Lipschitz loss" hygiene is not enough. More people should know this example.

Proof sketch

Precise statement (Theorem B.5 / B.10 are the general forms; 3.1 / 3.2 the advertised ones).

*Assumption 2.6.* Fix an o-minimal structure S expanding the real field. Every gate g: R^n x R^p -> R^m in the gate dictionary G is definable in S — jointly in inputs and parameters. This is the whole hypothesis; there is no compactness, no boundedness of theta, no Lipschitz condition, no bound on ||theta||.

*Architecture.* A G-neural network (Definition 2.4) is a finite DAG G = (V, E) with a {0,1} lifting matrix Pi, a gate g_v in G at each computation node consuming the concatenated parent states, and a linear readout A_out. "Fixed architecture" = fixed DAG, dimensions, widths, depths, sequence length, and parameter placement; the parameter *values* range over their (possibly all of R^P) definable parameter space.

*Guarantee, classification (Theorem 3.1 / B.5).* With F* = {1_{(0,infinity)} o f_theta : theta in X}, X a nonempty definable subset of R^P: there exist C (universal) and K (depending only on the architecture and the defining formulas) such that for every Borel P on R^n x {0,1}, every eps > 0, every delta in (0,1], with probability at least 1 - delta, sup over theta of |R(theta) - R_hat_N(theta)| <= eps provided N >= C(K + log(1/delta))/eps^2.

*Guarantee, regression (Theorem 3.2 / B.10).* Same, with f: R^n x X -> R^m definable and loss: R^m x R^m -> [0,1] definable in the same structure, and N >= C(K ln^2(K/eps) + ln(1/delta))/eps^2.

How it is proved.

  • Definability propagates (Proposition 2.5). Induct along the DAG's partial order. Input nodes: z^0 = Pi x is linear, hence semialgebraic, hence definable since S expands the real field. Inductive step: if each parent state z_u(x, theta) is definable, so is the concatenation (finite products and coordinate projections preserve definability); the parameter projection theta -> theta_v is semialgebraic; composing with the definable gate g_v keeps definability. Finiteness and acyclicity of G mean the induction terminates. Remark B.1 adds that if gates have definable domains, dom(f) is itself definable. This step is routine but is the conceptual pivot: joint definability in (x, theta), not definability of each f_theta, is what the rest needs.
  • Compose with the loss. (x, y, theta) -> 1(1_{(0,infinity)}(f_theta(x)) = y), resp. (x, y, theta) -> loss(f_theta(x), y), is definable, since (0, infinity) is definable and definable maps compose. (This is where Remark B.8's warning bites: definability of the loss is a hypothesis, not a consequence of regularity.)
  • The step that does the real work: uniform cell decomposition implies finite VC (Lemma B.3). Fix N and a sample S = {x_i}_{i=1}^N. Define X_i = {theta in X : f(x_i, theta) > 0}, definable subsets of parameter space. The number of labelings of S realizable by F* equals the number of nonempty atoms of the Boolean algebra generated by X_1, ..., X_N. The paper then asserts, citing Coste's cell decomposition for definable families (Coste, *An Introduction to O-Minimal Geometry*, Theorem 2.10), that this atom count is at most C N^m with C depending only on the family and X, uniformly in N and S. Shattering requires 2^N <= C N^m, which fails for large N; hence VCdim(F*) <= max{N : 2^N <= C N^m} < infinity.
  • Classification conclusion. Feed K = VCdim(F*) into the fundamental theorem of PAC learning (Shalev-Shwartz-Ben-David, Thm 6.7(1); Vapnik-Chervonenkis, Blumer-Ehrenfeucht-Haussler-Warmuth, Valiant). One line.
  • Regression conclusion. Lemma B.6 (lifting): H_gamma = {(x, r) -> 1_{(0,infinity)}(f(x, theta) - r - gamma)} on Z x R satisfies fat_gamma(F) <= Pdim(F) <= VCdim(H_0) — pseudo-shattering is literally VC-shattering of the subgraph class, and gamma-fat-shattering with gamma > 0 implies pseudo-shattering with the same witnesses. Note H_0 is itself a definable family (one extra parameter r), so step 3 applies to it. Then Lemma B.7 repackages Alon-Ben-David-Cesa-Bianchi-Haussler (Thm 3.1) plus Anthony-Bartlett (Thm 11.13(i), fat_gamma <= Pdim) to convert finite pseudo-dimension of the loss-composed class into the uniform-convergence bound. Note the chain goes fat-shattering to pseudo-dimension to VC, i.e. the *scale-free* dimension dominates the scale-sensitive one; this is why the resulting eps-dependence has the ln^2(K/eps) and no benefit from scale sensitivity.

New vs. assembled — an honest assessment.

*Assembled from known model theory and known learning theory:* essentially the entire logical spine. Pillay-Steinhorn (1986) and cell decomposition are classical; o-minimal structures are NIP, and Laskowski, "Vapnik-Chervonenkis classes of definable sets" (J. LMS 1992) already gives "uniformly definable family in an NIP/o-minimal structure implies VC class." Macintyre-Sontag (STOC 1993) already applied exactly this — o-minimality of R_exp (Wilkie 1996) — to prove finiteness of VC dimension for sigmoidal networks. Lemma B.3's conclusion is therefore a known theorem, and Laskowski is cited in the introduction but *not* invoked in the proof. Lemma B.6 is explicitly labeled a "standard lifting trick." Lemma B.7 is explicitly a repackaging of Alon et al. Steps 4 and 5 are citations.

*Genuinely new:* (a) the G-NN DAG/gate-dictionary formalism, which makes Proposition 2.5 a one-paragraph induction covering arbitrary modern topologies rather than layered chains; (b) the definability audit of Section 4 and Proposition B.11 — attention with *jointly* trainable W_Q, W_K, W_V, normalization layers, MoE routing, embeddings, bounded Fourier/RoPE encodings, DEQ layers — which is real if unglamorous work and is the part with lasting value; (c) the explicit regression/fat-shattering statement for bounded definable losses and Remark B.8's counterexample; (d) the framing thesis.

*Weakest link.* Lemma B.3, step 3, is the load-bearing step and is argued in two sentences with a citation that does not visibly supply the inequality. Coste's Theorem 2.10 gives cell decomposition of a definable set compatible with a projection — which yields a uniform bound on the number of *cells in each fibre*, and that is exactly what Lemma B.2 extracts. Bounding the number of atoms of the Boolean algebra generated by N members of the family by C N^m is a different and harder statement: it is the assertion that the *dual shatter function* of the family is polynomial with exponent at most m, i.e. that the dual VC density is at most the number of parameters. That is a genuine theorem — Aschenbrenner-Dolich-Haskell-Macpherson-Starchenko, "Vapnik-Chervonenkis density in some theories without the independence property" — proved by induction on dimension, not a corollary of fibrewise cell decomposition. The *finiteness* conclusion alone is one line from Laskowski; the specific exponent m is ADHMS. As written, Lemma B.3 either over-cites Coste or under-cites the literature. Since the final theorems only need finiteness, this is a presentational rather than a fatal gap — but a referee should press on it, and Lemma B.3 is best read as "Laskowski, restated" rather than as a new proof.

*One small inconsistency to note:* Proposition 4.13 (DEQ layers) assumes in its statement only that *there exists* z_x with z_x = F(x, z_x), but the proof asserts "by the uniqueness assumption, every fibre Gamma_x is a singleton." Existence is stated, uniqueness is used. The repair is immediate — o-minimal definable choice (van den Dries / Coste Thm 3.1, which the paper cites two pages earlier for exactly this purpose) gives a definable selection x -> z_x from the fixed-point set without uniqueness — but the proof as printed does not do this, and footnote 3 quietly reintroduces "uniquely selected."

Broader context

The bridge, for someone meeting it for the first time. The same combinatorial object appears on both sides under different names. In learning theory, a hypothesis class has finite VC dimension iff it cannot shatter arbitrarily large sets; in model theory, a formula phi(x; theta) has the *independence property* iff it can shatter arbitrarily large sets, and a theory is NIP if no formula does. Shelah introduced NIP for classification-theoretic reasons in the 1970s, a decade before Blumer-Ehrenfeucht-Haussler-Warmuth; Laskowski (1992) made the dictionary explicit. O-minimal theories are NIP, so "definable implies VC class" is a theorem about tame geometry. Chase-Freitag, "Model theory and machine learning" (*Bull. Symbolic Logic* 2019, cited here as [20]) is the right two-hour read for the dictionary, including the stability / Littlestone-dimension correspondence that is the online-learning analogue.

Closely related work genuinely worth knowing.

  • Angus Macintyre and Eduardo Sontag, "Finiteness results for sigmoidal neural networks" (STOC 1993). The direct ancestor. Uses o-minimality of R_exp (via Wilkie) to prove finiteness of VC dimension for sigmoidal nets with unbounded weights. If you read one paper alongside this one, read this; the present paper is its systematic modernization, and the comparison is the fairest way to assess novelty.
  • Marek Karpinski and Angus Macintyre, "Polynomial bounds for VC dimension of sigmoidal and general Pfaffian neural networks" (JCSS 1997). The *quantitative* version: O(W^2 k^2)-type bounds for networks whose gates are Pfaffian of bounded format. Combined with Gabrielov-Vorobjov's format calculus for compositions, this is — as argued above — probably sufficient to make most of Section 4's examples quantitative, which is the strongest single reason to be skeptical of the "generality" sales pitch.
  • Paul Goldberg and Mark Jerrum (*Machine Learning* 1995) for the semialgebraic/real-parametrized analogue (VC = O(P^2) for classes defined by polynomial predicates in P real parameters), and Bartlett-Harvey-Liaw-Mehrabian (JMLR 2019) for the nearly-tight Theta(W L log W) VC and pseudo-dimension bounds for piecewise-linear networks. BHLM is the right benchmark: for ReLU MLPs it is tight, parameter-unbounded, and architecture-explicit — everything Theorem 3.1 is not, on a narrower class.
  • Binyamini-Novikov-Zak, sharply o-minimal structures and sharp cell decomposition (2022-2024, including the proof of Wilkie's conjecture for Pfaffian structures). This is the paper's own proposed route to rates, and it is the right one: sharp o-minimality attaches a *format* and *degree* to definable sets and bounds cell counts in those, which is exactly the missing quantitative input in Lemma B.3.

Plausible follow-up. The obvious one the paper names is "do Theorem 3.1 again, sharply": instantiate sharp o-minimality to get K = K(format, degree, P) and recover BHLM-style bounds for attention and normalization layers as corollaries rather than as separate papers. That is good but somewhat predictable. A more interesting one: run the argument in the other dimensions where the bottleneck is also "uniform control on the number of definable cells." The paper gestures at Littlestone dimension (online learning), the gamma-Natarajan dimension (multiclass), robust PAC, and computable PAC. The Littlestone case is the sharpest test, because o-minimal theories are NIP but *not* stable — R_{an,exp} is unstable since it defines a linear order — and finite Littlestone dimension corresponds to *stability*, not NIP. So "definable in an o-minimal structure" should be exactly the wrong hypothesis for online learnability, and one would expect a *separation* theorem: a definable family with finite VC and infinite Littlestone dimension (thresholds on R being the canonical witness, realizable by a one-neuron net). Making that precise would turn the paper's framing on its head in a productive way: tame feedforward computation gives you batch learnability for free and online learnability not at all, and the model-theoretic reason is the gap between NIP and stability. That seems like a genuinely publishable observation and it costs almost nothing given the machinery already assembled here.

Connection to theoretical IR / generative retrieval / vector search

There is a real one, but it is narrower than the paper's own framing would suggest, and the honest part should be separated from the forced part.

*Honest and directly usable.* A neural scoring function s(q, d; theta) — bi-encoder dot product, cosine, or a cross-encoder — is a fixed finite feedforward network built from exactly the primitives audited in Section 4, hence jointly definable. Now take a bounded, definable listwise objective over a candidate list of fixed length k: sorting is semialgebraic (finitely many polyhedral orderings), top-k is semialgebraic, the DCG discounts 1/log_2(1 + i) are constants, and the gain normalization is a ratio of definable functions with nonvanishing denominator. So NDCG@k as a function of (q, list, theta) is definable and [0,1]-valued, and Theorem 3.2 applies verbatim: for a fixed scorer architecture and fixed candidate-list length, the empirical NDCG@k over i.i.d. queries converges uniformly over the entire unbounded parameter space to the population NDCG@k, at rate O-tilde(sqrt(K/N)) in the number of queries. That is a clean distribution-free generalization statement for a ranking metric, obtained without norm constraints, and it does not appear to be stated at that level of generality in the IR theory literature (which tends to go through Rademacher complexity of the score class plus a surrogate-to-metric reduction, both of which require boundedness or Lipschitzness of the metric in the scores — and NDCG is not Lipschitz in the scores, it is piecewise constant, which is precisely where Rademacher arguments get awkward and where definability does not care). The catch is the one the paper is honest about: k must be fixed, so this says nothing about full-corpus ranking as |D| -> infinity.

*Honest, for generative retrieval.* An autoregressive docid decoder with fixed maximum identifier length T, fixed beam width B, and trie-constrained decoding is a fixed feedforward unrolling: the transformer blocks are definable by Corollary 4.15, beam search is top-B selection (semialgebraic) composed T times, and the trie constraint is a finite lookup mask (semialgebraic). So the full GR inference map is definable, and the induced family of query-to-docid maps has finite capacity. But the interesting regime in GR is exactly the one excluded: capacity should be measured as corpus size |D| grows, which grows the output vocabulary and the trie, breaking "fixed architecture." This is probably the most promising place to actually *use* the machinery rather than cite it: a sharply-o-minimal / Karpinski-Macintyre-style format-based bound on how many distinct identifiers a decoder of given width and depth can pseudo-shatter, which would be a capacity-theoretic account of the empirically well-documented degradation of generative retrieval with corpus scale. That is a concrete research project, and the format bookkeeping for attention is the technical obstacle.

*Honest, and the bit worth actually stealing.* Lemma B.2 is more interesting for vector search than Theorems 3.1-3.2 are. It says: for a jointly definable score f(x, theta) there is a single K such that for *every* theta, the sublevel set {x : f_theta(x) <= 0} has at most K connected components. Read this with theta absorbing the query: the retrieval region {d : s(q, d) > tau} of any query under a learned scorer has at most K connected components, uniformly over all queries and all trained parameters. That is a geometric tameness statement about the sets a partition-based index (IVF, graph-based ANN with a learned scorer, learned sparse-dense hybrids) is being asked to cover, and it is the kind of thing that matters for whether partition- or graph-based ANN can be *correct* rather than merely fast — the known failure mode of HNSW-style search under a non-metric learned score is that the superlevel set is disconnected and greedy descent gets trapped. A uniform-in-query bound on the number of components is exactly the parameter that should appear in a recall guarantee. Similarly, learned quantizers (k-means/PQ/IVF assignment with trainable centroids, which is an argmin over finitely many centroids, hence a polyhedral partition, hence semialgebraic) fall under Proposition 4.6's winner-take-all case, so the class of learned partitioners has finite VC dimension — giving distribution-free generalization for learning-to-quantize objectives with bounded definable losses.

*The forced part, not to be manufactured.* None of this touches what IR theory actually finds hard: the sample complexity of ranking with position bias and partial feedback, the intrinsic-dimension and doubling-measure parameters that govern ANN hardness, the recall-latency tradeoff, or anything about the corpus-scaling regime. And finite-but-unquantified VC dimension for a fixed-size retriever is close to vacuous as a practical guarantee; nobody doubted that a fixed BERT-sized cross-encoder has finite capacity. So: the paper's value here is (i) one genuinely transferable corollary about uniform convergence of definable bounded ranking metrics with no parameter constraints, (ii) Lemma B.2 as a tameness tool for retrieval-region geometry, and (iii) a well-written on-ramp to o-minimality and the NIP/VC dictionary, which is a body of machinery more likely to pay off in capacity/separation results for generative retrieval than in generalization bounds. The PAC headline itself is not the valuable part.

title: Learning a Single Neuron Robustly to Distributional Shifts and Adversarial Label Noise
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-25

Learning a Single Neuron Robustly to Distributional Shifts and Adversarial Label Noise — Shuyao Li, Sushrut Karmalkar, Ilias Diakonikolas, Jelena Diakonikolas (2024) — arXiv:2411.06697

Main idea

The paper asks what happens to the (already delicate) problem of agnostically learning a single neuron when, on top of arbitrary labels, an adversary is allowed to reweight the data distribution.

The model, precisely. Fix a known non-decreasing, convex, beta-Lipschitz activation sigma with sigma(0)=0 and a lower-slope condition sigma(t1) - sigma(t2) >= alpha(t1 - t2) for t1 >= t2 >= 0 (Definition 1.1: ReLU, leaky ReLU, ELU, normalized SoftPlus — note that convexity is an *addition* to the "unbounded activation" class of Diakonikolas-Kontonis-Tzamos-Zarifis). The learner draws N i.i.d. labelled samples from a reference distribution p_0 on R^d x R. The objective is the *penalized* DRO risk

R(w; p_0) = max over p << p_0 of { E_{(x,y) ~ p}(sigma(w.x) - y)^2 - nu * chi^2(p, p_0) }, w* = argmin over ||w||_2 <= W of R(w; p_0),

with p* = q_{w*} the adversary's best response at w*, and the benchmark OPT = E_{p*}(sigma(w*.x) - y)^2 — the *unregularized* square loss of the minimax neuron under the minimax distribution. So:

  • The adversary controls the joint distribution of (x,y), not just the covariates, and acts by reweighting: p << p_0 with a chi^2 penalty. In the empirical problem p_hat ranges over the simplex on the N observed samples. This is a *soft, Lagrangian* chi^2 ball, not a Wasserstein or TV ball and not a contamination model: the adversary cannot move mass to unseen points, cannot inject new points, and (as discussed below) under the theorem's parameter regime cannot even delete points.
  • Labels are arbitrary (agnostic / adversarial label noise), with no assumption whatsoever beyond the resulting OPT being finite; the "best-fit" criterion is purely comparative against w*.
  • The guarantee is multiplicative (constant-factor) plus additive: Algorithm 1 outputs w_hat with ||w_hat - w*||_2^2 <= C*OPT + eps, which transfers to E_{p*}(sigma(w_hat . x) - y)^2 <= O(OPT) + eps and R(w_hat; p_0) - R(w*; p_0) <= C_4(OPT + eps). C is dimension-independent but depends polynomially (and badly) on beta, B, 1/alpha, 1/gamma, 1/lambda. This is the expected shape: OPT + eps is impossible in poly(d, 1/eps) even for Gaussian marginals and no shift, and improper constant-factor learning is cryptographically hard without distributional assumptions.

Core approach. Run a Chambolle-Pock-style primal-dual method on the saddle problem min over w in B(W) max over p_hat in Delta_N of L(w, p_hat) directly on the nonconvex L_2^2 loss — no convex surrogate in the *analysis* — and buy global (indeed linear) convergence by importing a sharpness / local error bound that holds on the *target* distribution p* rather than on p_0. The dual side is strongly concave (thanks to chi^2); the primal side is nonconvex but sharp; the whole thing is glued by an "approximate duality gap" sandwich in the style of Diakonikolas-Orecchia.

Punchline worth stating up front, which the paper underplays. Their own Corollary C.3 shows that in the regime where the theorem lives (nu >= (1/2)E_{p_0} loss(w), so the max{.,0} truncation in the closed-form best response never activates),

R(w; p_0) = E_{p_0}[loss(w)] + Var_{p_0}(loss(w))/(4 nu), dq_w/dp_0 = 1 + (loss(w) - E_{p_0} loss(w))/(2 nu).

So the "adversary" is exactly a variance penalty on the squared loss (the Lam / Duchi-Namkoong variance-regularization identity), and the worst-case distribution is loss-proportional reweighting. The object being optimized is mean-plus-variance of the square loss of a single neuron. That is a clean and honest way to read the whole paper.

The most interesting part

The cleverest single mechanism is Lemma D.3 (= Lemma 3.4): a surrogate-free, error-controlled "linearization" of the nonconvex square loss, whose error is charged against the sharpness budget. Unpacking it matters, because the high-level description ("we handle nonconvexity via a structural result") hides what is actually going on.

The primal-dual machinery needs, at each iterate, a lower bound of the form L(w*, p_hat_i) >= L(w_i, p_hat_i) + <something computable at w_i, w* - w_i> - small. If L(., p_hat) were convex, this is just the gradient inequality (precisely what Mehta-Diakonikolas-Harchaoui exploit in the convex nonlinear DRO case). Here w -> E(sigma(w.x) - y)^2 is nonconvex — famously with exponentially many local minima (Auer-Herbster-Warmuth) — so no such inequality exists globally. Expanding the square gives

S_i = E_{p_hat_i}[(sigma(w*.x) - sigma(w_i.x))^2] (>= 0, discarded) + 2 E_{p_hat_i}[(sigma(w_i.x) - y)(sigma(w*.x) - sigma(w_i.x))],

and the whole fight is over the cross term, whose sign is uncontrolled because y is adversarial.

The trick is a three-step sign-chasing argument:

  • *Split on the sign of the residual.* Let G = {(x,y): sigma(w_i.x) - y >= 0}. On G the residual multiplier is >= 0, so you need a *lower* bound on sigma(w*.x) - sigma(w_i.x), and convexity of sigma gives sigma(w*.x) - sigma(w_i.x) >= sigma'(w_i.x)(w* - w_i).x. On the complement of G the multiplier is < 0, so you need an *upper* bound, and the same convexity (read as concavity of -sigma, anchored at w* instead of w_i) gives sigma(w*.x) - sigma(w_i.x) <= sigma'(w*.x)(w* - w_i).x.
