Setting: d = 2; Sigma = diag(1, eps); training features are iid copies of z conditioned on |z_1| >= s; test features are iid copies of z conditioned on (z'v)·z_1 <= 0 with v = (cos theta, sin theta), theta in (0, pi/2); labels y = sign(x_1) on both; squared loss; deterministic full-batch GD with fixed eta small enough for stability; initialization w(0) = u = (u1, u2) deterministic; n large. Define m1 = phi(s)/Q(s), m2 = 1 + s·m1, alpha = 1 - eta·m2, beta = 1 - eta·eps, mu_k = alpha^k u1 + (1 - alpha^k) m1/m2, nu_k = beta^k u2, L_k = sqrt(mu_k^2 + eps·nu_k^2), r_k = mu_k/L_k, rho = cos theta, gamma = sqrt(rho^2 + eps(1 - rho^2)), r = rho/gamma. The guarantee: for large n, with high probability, for every k >= 1, the 0-1 test error satisfies E(w(k)) ≈ min(1, arccos(r_k)/arccos(r)). What is guaranteed is an exact asymptotic formula for the whole test-error curve, not a bound. What is not guaranteed: no explicit error term, no rate in n, no uniformity in k, "w.h.p." is never quantified, and the training error — the other half of the grokking signature — is never the subject of a theorem at all. That training accuracy reaches 100% early is argued informally from the margin s ("the larger s, the easier it is to quickly memorize"), and it is true in the model (since |x_1| >= s and |x_2| ~ sqrt(eps), sign(x'w) = sign(x_1) for almost any w with u1 > 0), but it is asserted, not proved.

Corollary 1 (the plateau length, under distribution shift). With tau := |u2|·|tan theta|·m2/m1 and a constant c > 1: (A) if tau > c then the time to grok is k_ ~ (1/(eta·eps)) log tau ~ 1/eps; (B) if |u2| is small then k_ ~ (1/eta) log(1/(tau·eps)) ~ log(1/eps). So: a two-regime phase diagram in the initialization scale, with an exponential gap in eps between them. This is a statement about order of magnitude, with the constants and the exact phase boundary in tau treated loosely (see the bookkeeping notes below).

Theorem 2 (Appendix A.3, no distribution shift). Train and test are both the law of z conditioned on the wedge (z'u)(z'v) <= 0 with u = e1. Claim as printed: if (i) m2(theta) <= m1(theta) tan theta and (ii) u2 > alpha·u1, then the test error has a plateau of length Theta(1/(eta·eps)); if either condition fails, there is no plateau. Caveat: m1(theta), m2(theta) and alpha are never defined in A.3 — the symbols are recycled from Section 3 where they were functions of the truncation level s, which does not exist in A.3. The derivation preceding the theorem is the real content and is cleaner than the theorem statement; see below.

How Theorem 1 is proved. Three ingredients, none individually deep, assembled well.

Step 1, exact solution of the linear recursion. GD on the quadratic gives w(k) = A w(k-1) + b with A = I - eta·Sigma_hat and b = eta X'Y/n. Telescoping and summing the geometric series in matrix form, w(k) = A^k w(0) + (I - A^k)(I - A)^{-1} b, and since (I - A)^{-1}b = eta^{-1} Sigma_hat^{-1} b = Sigma_hat^{-1} X'Y/n = w_ols, one gets w(k) = A^k w(0) + (I - A^k) w_ols. The iterate is an exact convex-combination interpolation between initialization and the OLS solution, with matrix weights A^k. This is standard but it is the whole dynamical content: nothing nonlinear ever happens.

Step 2, a law-of-large-numbers deterministic equivalent that diagonalizes the dynamics (Lemmas 1 and 2). Because the conditioning event |z_1| >= s involves only the first coordinate and Sigma is diagonal, the two coordinates stay independent under the training distribution. Hence Sigma_hat ≈ diag(m2, eps) with m2 = E[x_1^2 | |x_1| >= s] = 1 + s·phi(s)/Q(s) the two-sided truncated-normal second moment, and X'Y/n ≈ (m1, 0) with m1 = E|x_1| = phi(s)/Q(s) because E[y·x_2] = 0 by independence. Therefore w_ols ≈ (m1/m2, 0) — exactly proportional to the ground-truth normal e1. Two consequences: (a) the limit point is the Bayes-optimal classifier, so there is no statistical obstruction at all and the only thing standing between GD and perfect test accuracy is convergence speed; (b) A^k ≈ diag(alpha^k, beta^k), so the coupled dynamics decouples into two independent scalar geometric sequences, mu_k (fast, rate alpha = 1 - eta·m2) and nu_k (slow, rate beta = 1 - eta·eps). This is where the separation of timescales is extracted, and it is extracted trivially because the problem was built diagonal. The "≈" suppresses O_P(n^{-1/2}) fluctuations in spectral norm, declared "easily proved via the law of large numbers."

Step 3, the key trick — the 0-1 error as a ratio of wedge angles. Whiten by z0 = Sigma^{-1/2}z ~ N(0, I) and write w_bar = Sigma^{1/2}w, so that angles in the whitened frame are Sigma-angles in the original. Then the conditional test error is P(sign disagreement with e1 | in the test wedge), a ratio of two Gaussian orthant probabilities, and for a 2-D isotropic Gaussian an orthant probability is literally proportional to an angle. The standard bivariate orthant formula gives

E(w(k)) = [arccos(r_{e1,v}) + arccos(r_{w,e1}) - arccos(r_{w,v})] / [2 arccos(r_{e1,v})],

where r_{a,b} is the Sigma-cosine between a and b. One checks that this collapses to the Theorem-1 expression: the wedge width is phi_v = arccos(r), the iterate's angle to truth is phi_k = arccos(r_k), and if phi_k > phi_v (iterate beyond v) then arccos(r_{w,v}) = phi_k - phi_v and the bracket gives exactly 1, while if phi_k < phi_v then arccos(r_{w,v}) = phi_v - phi_k and the bracket gives phi_k/phi_v. Hence the min(1, ·). Finally r_k = mu_k/L_k because w_bar = (mu_k, sqrt(eps)·nu_k) and e1_bar = e1, so the Sigma-cosine to the truth is mu_k/sqrt(mu_k^2 + eps·nu_k^2). That is the whole proof: the test error is a monotone function of the single ratio nu_k/mu_k, with an exact threshold.

How the plateau length comes out. Since 1/r_k^2 - 1 = eps(nu_k/mu_k)^2 and 1/r^2 - 1 = eps·tan^2 theta, the condition "error strictly below 1" is exactly |nu_k| < |mu_k|·|tan theta| — the slow-mode residual must fall below a threshold set purely by the test-wedge geometry. Since mu_k ≈ m1/m2 after O(1/(eta·m2)) steps and nu_k = beta^k u2, this is beta^k |u2| (m2/m1) < |tan theta|, i.e. k >= log(|u2| m2/(m1 |tan theta|))/log(1/beta), and log(1/beta) = -log(1 - eta·eps) ≈ eta·eps. Hence k_ ~ (1/(eta·eps)) log(...) ~ 1/eps. Case (B) is the complementary regime: if |u2| is already below the threshold at initialization, the binding constraint is not the decay of nu_k but the _growth_ of mu_k from u1 toward m1/m2, which happens at the fast rate alpha, giving k_ = O((1/eta) log(1/(tau·eps))). So the mechanism of the "small initialization removes grokking" phase is: with a small slow-mode component there is nothing slow to decay away, and the clock is set by the fast eigenvalue. Note also that m2/m1 -> s for large s, so larger training margin means larger tau and a (logarithmically) longer plateau: easier memorization, later generalization, which is pleasingly consistent with the empirical folklore.

Three bookkeeping slips in this corollary, none fatal but worth knowing while reading beside the PDF. First, equation (6) defines r_k := mu_k/nu_k while Theorem 1 uses r_k := mu_k/L_k; the latter is the one used everywhere. Second, the displayed threshold inequality in the Corollary-1 proof carries the factor eps on the right-hand side but not on the left (the eps cancels in the correct version), and correspondingly the definition tau = |u2||tan theta|m2/m1 places tan theta in the numerator where the derivation puts it in the denominator. The leading order 1/(eta·eps) is unaffected, but the stated phase boundary in tau is not literally the one the algebra gives. Third, the text says the plateau ends "when r_k decreases below r" when the derived condition is r_k > r (the error is decreasing in the angle, hence increasing in r_k); the algebra is right, the prose is inverted.

Appendix A.3, the no-shift case. Here the geometry is more interesting and the authors do more work. With train = test = the wedge distribution, the second-moment matrix Sigma = E[xx'] is no longer diagonal: they give exact one-dimensional integral representations for its entries a, b, d and the cross-moment c in terms of phi, Phi and kappa = cot(theta)/sqrt(eps), with normalizer Z = P(wedge) = (1/pi) arccos rho. Since the wedge is the disagreement region, in whitened coordinates it is a thin double-wedge of angular half-width ≈ sqrt(eps)|tan theta| around the direction orthogonal to e1 — i.e. the data now concentrate along the slow axis. They then assert, after "a bit of work," that lambda_+ = Theta(eps), lambda_- = Theta(eps), |b| = O(sqrt(eps)). Vanilla GD (now written with the factor 2, inconsistently with Section 3) gives w(k) = w_ - (I - 2 eta Sigma)^k (w_ - w(0)) with w_ = Sigma^{-1}c. Because M = I - 2 eta Sigma is 2-by-2, they use Cayley-Hamilton to write M^k = alpha_k I + beta_k M with alpha_k, beta_k explicit in r_± = 1 - 2 eta lambda_±, which gives closed forms (17)-(18) for mu_k and nu_k without diagonalizing. The test error (19) has the same angle-ratio form, E = arccos(max(rho, rho_k))/arccos(rho), and the plateau again ends exactly when |nu_k| < |mu_k||tan theta|. The plateau length is then defined as k_ = min{k : |nu_k| <= T} with T = |mu_||tan theta|, and sandwiched two-sidedly: since the slow eigenvector is e2 + O(sqrt(eps)), there are constants C, C_bar in [1, 1 + O(sqrt(eps))] with C^{-1}|nu_ - r_-^k(nu_ - u2)| <= |nu_k| <= C|nu_ - r_-^k(nu_ - u2)|, whence for |u2 - nu_| > C·T,

(1/(2 eta lambda_-)) log(|u2 - nu_|/(C T)) <= k_ <= (1/(2 eta lambda_-)) log(|u2 - nu*| C / T),

and lambda_- = Theta(eps) gives k_ ~ (1/(eta·eps)) log(|u2 - nu_|/T). That two-sided estimate is the honest version of Theorem 2, and its real content is a dichotomy in the initialization: a Theta(1/(eta·eps)) plateau iff the initial slow-mode component is farther than the threshold from its target value, no plateau otherwise. Theorem 2's printed conditions (i) and (ii) are a loose transcription of that.

Here I would flag a substantive issue rather than a typo. If both eigenvalues of Sigma are Theta(eps), the condition number is Theta(1) — the problem is not ill-conditioned, it is uniformly small-scale. The plateau then comes from eta·lambda_- being small in absolute terms at a fixed eta, and the stability constraint eta < 1/lambda_max permits eta = Theta(1/eps), which removes the plateau by pure step-size rescaling. In other words, in the no-shift setting the plateau is an artifact of a fixed-eta normalization rather than of anisotropy, and the "preconditioning" that fixes it is indistinguishable from a learning-rate rescaling. The paper does not state an EGD theorem for A.3, so nothing is formally claimed that this contradicts, but it does mean A.3 is not independent evidence for the ill-conditioning thesis.

The EGD side of the theory. Section 3.2 analyzes w(k) = w(k-1) - eta Sigma_hat^{-1} X'(Xw(k-1) - Y)/n. Substituting Sigma_hat^{-1}Sigma_hat = I gives w(k) = (1 - eta)w(k-1) + eta·w_ols, hence w(k) = a^k w(0) + (1 - a^k)w_ols with a = 1 - eta. The contraction matrix is the isotropic a·I with spectral radius 1 - eta, independent of eps, so convergence to w_ols — and hence, by Theorem 1's formula, exit from the plateau — takes O(1/eta) steps rather than O(1/(eta·eps)). That is the entire theoretical guarantee for the method, and it is worth being blunt about what it is: on a quadratic, preconditioning by the inverse Hessian is Newton's method, which converges in one step up to the damping eta. Nothing about grokking, singular values of gradient matrices, or neural networks is needed or used.

The gap to the algorithm is therefore wider than the paper's framing suggests, and it is a qualitative gap, not just a linear-versus-nonlinear gap. The theorem preconditions by Sigma_hat^{-1}, an object built from the data (equivalently the Hessian / the Fisher of the model). The algorithm preconditions by (G G')^{-1/2}, built from the current gradient matrix of one layer. These are different operators with different spectra, and no result connects them. Worse, applying the algorithm literally to the toy problem would do nothing useful: for a linear model with scalar output the "gradient matrix" is a vector g, its SVD has one singular value, and G_tilde = U V' = g/||g||, i.e. plain gradient normalization, which rescales the step but leaves the ratio of per-direction rates — and hence the eps-dependence of the plateau — completely untouched. So Figure 6's "EGD" curve must be equation (9), not equation (11). The theory validates inverse-Hessian preconditioning; the experiments run spectral normalization of per-layer gradient matrices; the bridge between them is the verbal analogy "both equalize speeds along principal directions."

Two smaller technical points in Section 4. The claim that "the Fisher-norm of G_tilde is a constant of motion" is proved by a chain that mis-associates the matrix products: G_tilde' F G_tilde = G'(GG')^{-1/2}(GG')(GG')^{-1/2}G = G'G, whose trace is the sum of s_j^2, not tr I. What is actually true is the trivial Frobenius statement ||G_tilde||_F^2 = tr(UV'VU') = m. The conclusion "= 1 after dividing by m" is right; the Fisher-norm interpretation is not. And the Grokfast link in Section 4.2 writes (GG')^{-1/2}g = sum_j (c_j/s_j)u_j (with u_j called eigenvectors of G'G where they are left singular vectors, so eigenvectors of GG') and then identifies large-s_j directions with Grokfast's "high-frequency" components. Those are different notions of frequency — Grokfast's is over training time (an EMA across iterates), EGD's is over parameter space at a single step — and no argument is given that they coincide. The claim that EGD "inherits the filtering inductive bias of Grokfast" is a hand-wave presented in the register of a derivation.

Regime mismatch, summarized. The theory is: d = 2, linear predictor, squared loss, deterministic full-batch GD, no weight decay, no stochasticity, a diagonal (or near-diagonal) second-moment matrix with a hand-set condition number 1/eps, an engineered test distribution supported on the hard wedge (Section 3) or a setting with no train/test gap at all (A.3), and a preconditioner equal to the inverse empirical covariance. The experiments are: 2-layer and 3-layer ReLU MLPs and a 2-layer transformer, cross-entropy or hinge loss, SGD/Adam/AdamW/RAdam/RMSprop with weight decay, minibatches of 32-512, on sparse parity, modular addition and multiplication, MNIST and CIFAR-10, with the preconditioner being (GG')^{-1/2} applied per layer (and in the transformer case to a single MLP layer only), computed by exact or randomized SVD, and switched off once validation accuracy crosses a threshold. The quantities the theory predicts — plateau length proportional to the condition number over the step size, and the initialization-scale phase boundary — are not measured in any of the deep-network experiments; Figure 4 shows a wide gradient spectrum but makes no quantitative scaling claim and no causal test beyond the intervention itself. The rigor level inside the theory's own regime is physics-style throughout: deterministic equivalents with unquantified "w.h.p.", no uniformity in k (note that the required accuracy in the slow direction is at scale eps while the fluctuations in Sigma_hat are at scale n^{-1/2}, so controlling the slow mode over k ~ 1/(eta·eps) steps implicitly needs n to be large relative to a power of 1/eps — a condition that is never stated), and a final theorem whose hypotheses reference undefined symbols. None of this makes the picture wrong. It does mean the paper should be read as a clean, falsifiable mechanistic hypothesis with a worked exactly-solvable illustration and an intervention that empirically shortens several plateaus, rather than as a proof that grokking is caused by ill-conditioning.

title: BMX: Entropy-weighted Similarity and Semantic-enhanced Lexical Search
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-24

BMX: Entropy-weighted Similarity and Semantic-enhanced Lexical Search

Xianming Li, Julius Lipp, Aamir Shakir, Rui Huang, Jing Li (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06643

Main idea

The paper's premise is that BM25 has two defects: it scores each query term independently (so it never looks at query-document similarity as a whole), and it has no semantics (no synonymy). BMX is a drop-in replacement scoring function that bolts on a fix for each, plus a score-normalization recipe and an open-source library (Baguetter) built as a fork of retriv that wraps BM25S's eager-scoring implementation.

The scoring function (their Eq. 2) is, for a query Q = {q_1, ..., q_m} and document D:

score(D,Q) = sum_i [ IDF(q_i) · F(q_i,D)(alpha+1) / (F(q_i,D) + alpha·|D|/avgdl + alpha·Ebar) + beta · E(q_i) · S(Q,D) ]

with IDF exactly BM25's smoothed Robertson form log((n - l + 0.5)/(l + 0.5) + 1), l = df(q_i). Note what is missing: there is no b. BM25's k1(1 - b + b|D|/avgdl) has been replaced by alpha(|D|/avgdl + Ebar) — i.e. the length-normalization slope is hard-wired to 1 and the "1 - b" soft floor is replaced by the mean query-token entropy Ebar. There are two hyperparameters, alpha (the k1 analogue) and beta (weight of the new term), with "derived optimal defaults" alpha = clip(avgdl/100, 0.5, 1.5) and beta = 1/log(1+n). No derivation is actually given for either; the constants 100, 1.5, 0.5 are asserted.

The entropy is not an entropy over a probability distribution. Per term q_i with posting list D^s = {D^s_1, ..., D^s_l}, they set p_j = sigmoid(F(q_i, D^s_j)) = 1/(1 + e^{-tf_j}) and Etilde(q_i) = -sum_j p_j log p_j, then normalize E(q_i) = Etilde(q_i)/max_k Etilde(q_k) over the query's tokens, and Ebar = (1/m) sum_i E(q_i). So the "probabilities" are per-document sigmoids of raw term frequencies; they do not sum to one and each lies in [sigmoid(1), 1) = [0.731, 1). I confirmed against the reference implementation (baguetter/indices/sparse/models/bmx/index.py): p = 1/(1+np.exp(-tf)); entropy = -np.sum(p*np.log(p)), computed at index time per term over its full posting list and stored in the inverted index; only the max-normalization and Ebar are query-time. The stated motivation is that this "mitigates bias from high-frequency tokens, ensuring that less frequent but more informative tokens carry higher similarity weight."

The similarity is deliberately trivial: S(Q,D) = |Q ∩ D| / m, the fraction of query token slots whose term occurs in D — i.e. coordination-level matching, computed in the code by a dense accumulator over all n documents (count[ids] += 1; count /= query_len). The beta term is added only for documents in q_i's posting list, and IDF does not multiply it (confirmed in both the typeset formula and the code: idf * (tf-part) + sims * entropy[i] * beta).

"Semantic enhancement" is weighted query augmentation (WQA): Q^A = LLM(Q, t) — in the experiments, GPT-4 asked for t = 10 paraphrase queries via the prompt in Appendix A — and then score(D, Q, Q^A) = score(D,Q) + sum_i w_i score(D, Q^A_i). The implementation does this as a single query with per-token weights (token_weights), which is the "one retrieval, no reranking" efficiency claim. The w_i are described only as "typically within [0,1]" and their actual values are never reported. Finally, normalization: they estimate score^max = m log(1 + (n - 0.5)/1.5) + 1 and divide, claiming scores then lie in [0,1].

The most interesting part / critique

The genuinely interesting thing about this paper is what falls out when you algebraically simplify it. Match BMX's TF term to BM25's: F(alpha+1)/(F + alpha·Ebar + alpha|D|/avgdl) versus F(k1+1)/(F + k1(1-b) + k1·b|D|/avgdl). Solving k1·b = alpha and k1(1-b) = alpha·Ebar gives

k1_eff = alpha(1 + Ebar), b_eff = 1/(1 + Ebar).

The numerator constants (alpha+1) vs (k1_eff+1) differ by a global multiplicative factor, which is rank-invariant. So with beta = 0, BMX is exactly BM25 with a particular query-dependent coupling of (k1, b) — nothing more. Since Ebar is in (1/m, 1], we get b_eff in [0.5, m/(m+1)): BMX structurally forbids b < 0.5 and pushes toward b -> 1 as queries get longer and more entropy-skewed. The "entropy" enters the TF term only as a scalar that re-parametrizes length normalization. That is not a new retrieval model; it is a heuristic, collection- and query-adaptive setting of (k1, b).

And Table 7 is the smoking gun for which of the two innovations is doing the work. On SciFact, sweeping alpha from 0.1 to 1.0 at fixed beta = 0.1 moves nDCG@10 from 65.92 to 68.91 (+3.0, monotone). Sweeping beta from 0.1 to 1.0 at fixed alpha = 1.0 moves it 68.91 -> 69.11 -> 68.36 — a non-monotone range of 0.75, i.e. noise. The entropy-weighted similarity term contributes essentially nothing; the saturation/length parameter contributes everything. The paper never runs the one ablation a reviewer would demand: BMX with beta = 0 at the same alpha, which is just BM25 at (k1_eff, b_eff). Everything reported as "the importance of incorporating query-document similarity in IR" is, on the paper's own ablation, the importance of not leaving k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75.

(a) Is the entropy weighting principled? No, and worse, I believe its sign is backwards relative to its stated purpose. Write h(tf) = -sigmoid(tf) log sigmoid(tf): h(1) = 0.229, h(2) = 0.112, h(3) = 0.046, h(4) = 0.018, h(5) = 0.007, h(10) ≈ 4e-5. Then Etilde(q_i) = sum_{j in postings} h(tf_j) ≈ 0.23 · df(q_i) for the typical case of mostly-tf=1 postings. Etilde is therefore essentially monotone increasing in document frequency. After max-normalization within the query, the highest-df (least informative) query token gets E ≈ 1 and genuinely rare tokens get E ≈ 0. On their own case-study query "Who is the youngest player in the Premier League?", the similarity bonus is dominated by league, not by youngest. So the claim that this "ensur[es] that less frequent but more informative tokens carry higher similarity weight" is the opposite of what the formula does. (Their sigmoid story — "mapping frequencies exceeding five to similar values" — is about capping within-document repetition, which it does; it says nothing about the df scaling, which is the dominant effect.)

There is no probabilistic-ranking-model justification anywhere. BM25's saturation is an approximation to the 2-Poisson/eliteness log-odds log[P(tf|R)/P(tf|notR)] under the elite-set mixture, with k1 and b having interpretations (eliteness contrast; verbosity-vs-scope length hypothesis). BMX's beta·E(q_i)·S(Q,D) has no such reading: it is not a log-odds contribution, it is not a term weight, and because it depends on the whole match pattern while sitting inside the per-term sum, it is not expressible as any per-term relevance weight at all. Charitably, beta = 1/log(1+n) at least makes the bonus commensurate with the reciprocal of the maximum IDF, so it is a deliberately-scaled tie-breaker — and that is exactly what it is empirically. Also worth saying: rewarding coordination is not new and is arguably double counting, since a sum of IDF-weighted terms already rewards matching more query terms; Lucene removed its coord factor from BM25Similarity for precisely this reason.

One nice consequence of the reparametrization is that it predicts the paper's own failure case. Long queries with one dominant-entropy token drive Ebar small, hence b_eff -> 1: maximal length penalization. BRIGHT queries are long StackExchange posts. And indeed default BMX collapses on BRIGHT: 10.99 average, worse than the same codebase's BM25 at (0.9, 0.4) at 14.43, and barely above BM25 at (1.2, 0.75)'s 9.47. Their fix is to set alpha = 0.05 — ten times below the floor of their own "optimal" rule alpha >= 0.5 — which drives the denominator to F + O(0.05) and the ratio to ≈ 1 for all F >= 1: BMX(alpha = 0.05) is essentially binary IDF matching plus a coordination bonus. That it then reaches 15.77 is interesting (and consistent with what we know about reasoning-intensive retrieval), but it is not evidence for entropy-weighted similarity.

(b) Baseline fairness. This is where the paper is weakest, and the authors deserve partial credit for transparency: they report five BM25 variants from two implementations, all at k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75, which is Lucene's default but not the BEIR/Anserini convention of k1 = 0.9, b = 0.4. So BMX gets a dataset-adaptive (k1_eff, b_eff) via alpha(avgdl) while every baseline is frozen at one point. Their own BRIGHT table quantifies how much that matters: (1.2, 0.75) -> 9.47 versus (0.9, 0.4) -> 14.43, a 5-point swing from parameter choice alone — larger than every effect the paper claims. On BEIR they never ran even that second configuration.

Worse, the BEIR gains concentrate exactly where the frozen baseline is furthest below published numbers. From memory of the BEIR paper's Anserini BM25 (multi-field, title-weighted) nDCG@10 — worth re-checking against Table 2 of Thakur et al., but the direction is not in doubt — FEVER is about 75.3 and Climate-FEVER about 21.3, versus 50.98 and 13.55 here; Touché is about 36.7 versus 31.11. Decomposing BMX's +1.16 average (41.52 vs 40.36): FEVER contributes +4.77/15 = 0.32, Touché +3.23/15 = 0.22, HotpotQA +2.64/15 = 0.18, TREC-COVID +2.32/15 = 0.15, MS MARCO +0.97/15 = 0.07 — about 0.93 of the 1.16 from five datasets, and nearly half from the two where the baseline is most anomalous. Of BMX's claimed 11/15 wins, six are margins of 0.03-0.14 nDCG, which is below any reasonable noise floor. Summing the BEIR-paper BM25 numbers over exactly their 15 columns gives an average around 42.3 — i.e. an off-the-shelf, properly configured BM25 plausibly beats BMX's 41.52 on this very table. Nothing in the paper rules that out, and the paper never runs Anserini/Lucene despite naming it in the intro.

Two smaller methodological tells. BM25+ and ATIRE are byte-identical across all 15 datasets in both implementations (48.7/15.6/68.1/... and 49.23/15.66/68.73/...), which means BM25+'s delta lower bound is inert — the baseline suite has a configuration bug or delta = 0, which is ironic given that Lv & Zhai's lower-bounding is the one piece of prior art BMX most directly conflicts with (BMX's b_eff >= 0.5 and -> 1 makes the long-document over-penalization they fixed worse). And the only metric reported anywhere is nDCG@10 — no Recall@100, no MRR, no per-query analysis, and no significance testing of any kind, on datasets where SciFact has 300 queries and typical paired-test resolution is on the order of 1-2 nDCG points. The one hyperparameter table (65.22-69.11 on SciFact) shows a sensitivity range five times the headline gain.

(c) The "surpasses dense retrieval" claim. Two benchmarks support it, and both are weaker than advertised. On LoCo, BM25 (Baguetter) gets 89.98 and BMX gets 90.12 — a +0.14 average, with BMX losing on QMSUM (59.21 vs 59.52). The paper's own best dense model, M2-BERT-32768, scores 92.54 and beats BMX. So the honest statement is: BM25 beats E5-Mistral-7B (87.84) and the proprietary APIs on LoCo, and BMX adds 0.14. The proprietary numbers are also copied from the M2-BERT blog, where Voyage v1 scores 1.95 on SummScreen and 25.43 overall — that is a context-truncation artifact (long documents chopped at the encoder limit), not a measurement of semantic retrieval quality. The real finding, long known, is that lexical matching has no context window; nothing about it is attributable to BMX's new term. The M2-BERT comparison is also not zero-shot — LoCo was released by the M2-BERT authors with in-domain training splits.

On BRIGHT, BMX(alpha = 0.05) + WQA reaches 18.66 versus 17.65 for the best proprietary model and 17.50 for E5-Mistral-7B. But the matched lexical comparison is BM25(0.9, 0.4) + WQA at 16.99, so BMX's own contribution is +1.67 on a benchmark where single-dataset numbers swing by 10 points and no variance is reported; and both lexical numbers require GPT-4. BRIGHT's own paper already reports BM25 driven by GPT-4 chain-of-thought reasoning queries at roughly 27 average — far above 18.66 — so within the LLM-augmented-lexical regime BMX+WQA is not state of the art on the very benchmark it uses for the headline claim.

(d) Does the semantic step quietly import an LLM? Yes, explicitly: GPT-4, ten generated queries per query (Appendix A prompt). The paper's framing — "BMX achieves this without the need for costly training on massive high-quality datasets, as required by embedding models" — is true about training cost and silent about inference cost, which is the one that matters at query time. A GPT-4 call with 10 outputs per query is orders of magnitude more expensive and slower than a forward pass through all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or bge-large, and none of the dense baselines are given any query expansion at all. So the apples-to-apples comparison is "lexical + GPT-4 expansion" vs "dense encoder, raw query." Table 2 makes this undeniable: WQA alone lifts BM25 from 38.34 to 41.44 (+3.1) on the 7-dataset subset, while BMX's novel scoring lifts BM25 from 38.34 to 39.10 (+0.76), and BMX+WQA (42.05) vs BM25+WQA (41.44) is +0.61. The claim "BMX with WQA even surpass[es] the performance of ... all-MiniLM-L6-v2" (39.72) is a statement about GPT-4, not about BMX. The efficiency study (Fig. 1) only compares BMX against BM25 without WQA, so the headline configuration's cost is never measured; and the claim that WQA "eliminates the need for multiple retrievals, thus resulting in better efficiency" concerns merging ranked lists, while the actual work — traversing ~11x as many posting lists — is unchanged.

Genuine strengths. Baguetter is a real contribution: a unified sparse/dense/hybrid interface on top of BM25S's fast eager scoring, multithreaded, hackable, with evaluation harnesses — exactly the kind of infrastructure that makes this class of experiment cheap, and the paper is unusually honest in using it to report five BM25 variants side by side (reproducing Kamphuis et al.'s finding that the variants are within ~0.5 nDCG of each other). BMX is cheap: the entropy is a single scalar per term precomputed at index time, so the extra cost over BM25 is one multiply-add per posting plus a dense counting pass, and their Fig. 1 showing near-identical search times is credible. It is fully interpretable and training-free, it needs no GPU, and the multilingual table (BM25 55.93 -> BMX 56.76 across zh/ja/ko/de/fr) is a consistent if small positive. The LoCo result, though not really a BMX result, is a useful public reminder that long-context retrieval is a regime where lexical methods are strong. And the places the gains look most real — TREC-COVID, HotpotQA, MS MARCO — are plausibly genuine, because they are exactly the datasets where alpha(avgdl) moves k1_eff in the direction per-dataset tuning is known to want (TREC-COVID has long documents and likes larger k1; alpha clamps to 1.5 there, giving k1_eff ≈ 2). That is a real result — just not the one the paper claims.

Broader context

BM25 is not a heuristic that happened to work; it is a closed-form approximation to a probabilistic ranking model, and Robertson & Zaragoza's The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond (FnTIR 2009) is the canonical account. The term weight is an estimate of the log-odds log[p(1-q)/(q(1-p))] of term presence in relevant vs non-relevant documents (the RSJ weight, which the smoothed IDF approximates under the assumption that relevant documents are a vanishing fraction of the collection); the saturating TF function is a tractable surrogate for the 2-Poisson/eliteness mixture, in which a term's occurrences are generated by a high-rate Poisson in documents "about" the concept and a low-rate one elsewhere, so the marginal information in the j-th occurrence decays — hence k1 as the eliteness-contrast knob. Length normalization comes from the verbosity-vs-scope dichotomy: a long document is either a verbose rendering of one topic (normalize fully, b = 1) or a concatenation of many topics (don't, b = 0), and b interpolates. Reading BMX through this lens is what makes the b_eff = 1/(1 + Ebar) identity so revealing: BMX is making an implicit, query-length-dependent claim about verbosity that nobody would defend if stated outright (longer queries implies assume documents are more verbose).

The modern route to "lexical but semantic" is learned sparse retrieval, and BMX sits conspicuously outside it. DeepImpact and uniCOIL replace the TF/IDF arithmetic with learned per-term impact scores over an expanded document vocabulary; SPLADE (and SPLADEv2/SPLADE++) learns a sparse expansion in BERT's wordpiece space with FLOPS regularization, inheriting both the inverted index and the semantics, and comfortably outperforms BM25 on BEIR. Document-side expansion — doc2query and docT5query, later TILDE — generates predicted queries and appends them to documents at index time, which is the architecturally correct way to spend an LLM in this setting: cost is amortized over the corpus once and query latency is untouched. WQA is the query-side mirror image, done online per query, which is the choice the field moved away from for exactly the latency reason. Meanwhile the cheap non-neural competitor for query expansion, pseudo-relevance feedback (Rocchio, RM3), is never compared against here, and RM3 on BEIR would be the obvious free baseline for a large share of WQA's +3.1. BMX's actual position is therefore unusual and narrow: it modifies the closed-form scoring function with no learning whatsoever, whereas the whole learned-sparse line keeps the scoring structure and learns the weights. It is closer in spirit to BM25+/BM25L, BM25F, DFR, or axiomatic-regularization variants than to anything post-2019.

The "are the BM25 baselines fairly tuned" critique has a well-developed literature that this paper walks straight into: Armstrong et al.'s Improvements that don't add up (CIKM 2009), Lin's The Neural Hype and Comparisons Against Weak Baselines (SIGIR Forum 2019), the Anserini/Pyserini reproducibility program, and Kamphuis et al.'s Which BM25 Do You Mean? (ECIR 2020), whose conclusion — that the published BM25 variants are effectively indistinguishable, so what matters is implementation and parameters — is independently reproduced by Table 1 and then not acted upon. Any reviewer in this area will ask for Anserini BM25 at (0.9, 0.4), per-dataset-tuned (k1, b) for the baseline, and paired significance tests; none of the three is present.

A follow-up I'd actually want to see. Take the reparametrization seriously and study zero-shot BM25 parameter prediction as a problem in its own right. BMX is, accidentally, a one-parameter rule mapping collection statistics to (k1, b); it beats a frozen baseline on BEIR and fails catastrophically on BRIGHT. The research question is: what is the right functional form? Derive it, rather than guess it, from the 2-Poisson model under an explicit document-length distribution — the verbosity/scope mixture gives a principled dependence of the optimal b on the length distribution's shape (not just its mean, which is all BMX uses; variance and skew should matter more), and the optimal k1 on the eliteness contrast, which is estimable from the collection's tf distributions via a burstiness statistic. Then evaluate against per-dataset oracle tuning across BEIR+BRIGHT+LoTTE and report the regret. That would convert the paper's best accidental finding into a result, and is directly useful for zero-shot retrieval where you cannot tune.

Relatedly, if you want a defensible entropy, use one. Replace p_j = sigmoid(tf_j) with the normalized tf distribution over the posting list, p_j = tf_j / sum_k tf_k, so Etilde is a genuine entropy whose normalized version Etilde/log l measures how concentrated a term's occurrences are — i.e. burstiness, in the sense of Church & Gale's adaptation work and DFR's divergence models, and precisely the quantity the eliteness model wants: a term with a sharp elite set has low normalized entropy and deserves a higher effective k1. That gives a term weight with a home in the probabilistic framework instead of a quantity that is monotone in df and labelled "entropy."

The IR-theoretic analysis I'd want run on this. First, axiomatics in the Fang & Zhai sense. Check BMX against the standard constraints. TFC1 (monotonicity in tf) holds: the TF term is increasing in F and the beta term jumps once at F: 0 -> 1 then is flat. TFC2 (diminishing returns) holds: the TF term is concave in F and the beta jump is at the first occurrence. LNC1 (adding a non-query term should not increase score) holds, since |D| grows and S is unchanged. The interesting failures are elsewhere. TDC, the term-discrimination constraint, is violated by the beta term in the one-matched-term case: a document matching only a high-df query token receives beta·E ≈ beta/m while one matching only a rare token receives ≈ 0, which is anti-discriminative — bounded by beta <= 1/log(1+n), hence small, but formally wrong-signed, and the paper's stated motivation claims the opposite. And LNC2/TF-LNC, the lower-bounding constraints that motivate exactly the BM25+/BM25L work BMX cites: because b_eff = 1/(1 + Ebar) is in [0.5, 1) and -> 1 for long, entropy-skewed queries, BMX sits in the regime where long-document over-penalization is known to bite, and it has no delta floor. A clean theorem here would be: _BMX with beta = 0 is rank-equivalent to BM25 with (k1, b) = (alpha(1 + Ebar), 1/(1 + Ebar))_, which is three lines and immediately bounds how much of the empirical story can possibly be attributable to the new term. A second natural result: the beta term's total contribution is (beta/m)(sum_{i in M} E(q_i))·|M| where M is the matched set — a product of two sums over matched terms, hence quadratic in the match indicators, hence not expressible as sum_i w(q_i, D) for any per-term weight. Interestingly, if the sum in Eq. 2 ran over all query terms rather than only matched ones (the formula is ambiguous; the code runs over matched ones), the beta contribution would collapse to a flat beta·Ebar per matched term — a pure, document-independent coordination bonus, i.e. Lucene's retired coord factor. Worth noting that the paper's formula and its implementation differ in exactly this respect.

Second, query evaluation and safe pruning, which I checked against the formulation and the code. The headline worry — that a non-decomposable S(Q,D) breaks WAND-style upper bounds — turns out to be mostly not fatal, but the details are instructive. Safety survives: since S(Q,D) <= 1, a valid per-term max impact is UB_i = IDF(q_i)(alpha+1) + beta·E(q_i), and because beta <= 1/log(1+n) is tiny relative to 2.5·IDF, that bound is within about 1% of the corresponding BM25 bound, so WAND/MaxScore pruning power is essentially preserved. Partial accumulations also remain valid lower bounds, since adding a matched term increases both components monotonically. The real costs are subtler and worth stating. (i) Score finalization is no longer local: a candidate's score cannot be finalized until its full match pattern against the entire query is resolved, because S couples the terms — fine for WAND, which fully evaluates pivots anyway, but it forecloses any architecture that scores a document from one posting list at a time. (ii) Static per-term impact scores become query-dependent, which is the genuinely annoying consequence: E(q_i) is max-normalized over the query's tokens, and Ebar sits in the denominator of every TF term, so the offline-precomputed block-max and quantized-impact values that BlockMax-WAND, impact-ordered postings, and SPLADE-style impact indexes rely on are no longer exact. You can still precompute a sound bound (take Ebar -> 0 and E -> 1, the most generous case), but it is looser, and impact quantization and static pruning lose their exactness guarantees. (iii) The reference implementation does none of this: it allocates a dense n-vector accumulator, traverses every query term's full posting list to compute S, and scores exhaustively — so the efficiency study compares exhaustive BMX against exhaustive BM25S and tells us nothing about BMX's behaviour inside a pruned engine like Lucene, which is precisely the setting the paper invokes when it says BM25 "is used at the core of Lucene, Elasticsearch, or Tantivy." Quantifying BMX's cost under BlockMax-WAND with the Ebar -> 0 bound, and reporting the loss in pruning power versus BM25, would be a small, genuinely useful experiment and is the thing I'd ask for in a review.

Proof sketch

The only formal claim in the paper is the normalization bound, and it is false as stated. The claim (Eqs. 10-11) is that with score^max(D,Q) = sum_i max IDF(q_i) + 1 = m log(1 + (n - 0.5)/1.5) + 1, the ratio score/score^max "keeps BMX scores within interval [0,1]." The technique is simply to maximize IDF over l, which does give max_l IDF = log(1 + (n - 0.5)/1.5) at l = 1. But the per-term maximum of the full TF factor is not IDF: as F -> infinity,

F(alpha+1)/(F + alpha|D|/avgdl + alpha·Ebar) -> alpha + 1,

so each term's supremum is IDF(q_i)(alpha + 1), and the correct bound is (alpha+1) sum_i max IDF + beta sum_i E(q_i). The stated normalizer is therefore short by a factor of alpha + 1, which is in [1.5, 2.5] (and by the beta term, a further <= m·beta). Concretely: a document containing a hapax query term many times, with alpha = 1.5, has a normalized score up to roughly 2.5x the claimed ceiling. The same error appears in the appendix's normalized BM25 (Eq. 14 omits the (k1+1) factor, so the overshoot there is up to 2.2x at k1 = 1.2). The fix is one line, and the resulting map is still only rank-preserving within a query — the normalizer depends on m and n but not on D — so it is a presentational rescaling for threshold setting, not a calibration. No theorem, lemma, or derivation appears anywhere else in the paper; the "derived optimal default parameters" of Eq. 3 are asserted without derivation, and the entropy construction is not derived from any model.

title: Deep Support Vectors
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-24

Deep Support Vectors

Junhoo Lee, Hyunho Lee, Kyomin Hwang, Nojun Kwak (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17329

Main idea

The paper asks what the support vectors of a trained deep network would be, if the notion made sense, and then builds a procedure that produces them. The pitch is framed by two complaints about deep learning relative to SVMs: data hunger and opacity. In an SVM both are addressed by the same object — the KKT conditions make the weight vector an explicit nonnegative combination of a sparse set of training points, so the model is its support vectors: you can read the decision criterion off them, and you can rebuild the classifier from them alone. The authors want that property for a ConvNet or ResNet.

Their construction, the "DeepKKT condition" (Eq. 6), transplants the four SVM KKT conditions by two substitutions. First, the linear margin score y_i w'x_i is replaced by the negative multiclass loss -L(Phi(x_i; theta_), y_i), motivated by the observation that -L_CE = Phi_{y_i}(x_i) - log sum_c exp Phi_c(x_i) has the same "target logit minus a soft max over the rest" shape as the hard margin condition Phi_{y_i} - max_{c != y_i} Phi_c >= eps. Second, grad_w becomes grad_theta. The linear stationarity condition w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i — which, via the hinge gradient, can be rewritten w_ = -sum_i alpha_i grad_w L_hinge — then becomes

theta* = -sum_{i=1..n} lambda_i grad_theta L(Phi(x_i; theta*), y_i), with lambda_i >= 0.

To this they add a fourth, non-SVM condition: the x_i must lie on the data manifold M (never formally defined), on the grounds that the ambient input space is high-dimensional and almost all of it is off-manifold garbage.

The mechanism is then: freeze theta_, and optimize over the _inputs_ x_i and the _multipliers_ lambda_i — this inversion of the usual roles is the engine of the paper. The objective (Eq. 9, Alg. 1) is an expectation over augmentations of four terms: a stationarity term L_stat = D(theta_, -sum_i lambda_i grad_theta L_i) (the text says L1 "to suppress outliers"; Alg. 1 line 9 writes a squared L2 and uses y_i grad_theta Phi rather than grad_theta L); a gated primal term that is plain cross-entropy when argmax_c Phi_c(x_i) != y_i and exactly zero otherwise; and two classic image priors, total variation and a pixel-norm penalty. Dual feasibility is handled by deletion: any candidate whose lambda_i goes negative during optimization is dropped. Complementary slackness is simply abandoned, with the honest justification that enforcing "lies on the functional decision boundary" would require a notion of distance between functions and second-order cost.

Three applications follow. (i) Selection: fit lambda_i for real images and keep the highest-lambda ones as a coreset — Table 1 on CIFAR-10 gives 48.91 vs. 46.16 (50 img/cls), 33.69 vs. 30.08 (10), 16.83 vs. 14.26 (1) against random selection. (ii) Few-shot/zero-shot dataset distillation: synthesize images from noise or from one real image per class, then train a fresh network on them — Table 2 reports 22.69 (1 img/cls, 1 shot) and 37.90 (10 img/cls, 10 shots) vs. DC/DSA/DM at the same shot budget, and 21.68 / 30.35 / 39.35 in the zero-image setting. (iii) Classifier as latent generative model: run the same optimization with soft labels y = (1-delta) y_a + delta y_b as latents, producing class-interpolated ImageNet images (a harp made of lobster claws), latent-space editing (a yacht's sail becoming a scarf), and — the paper's most interesting reframing — an explicit analogy between the DSV update (Eq. 10) and classifier-guided score-based sampling (Eq. 11), with stationarity plus priors playing the role of grad_x log p(x) and the primal term the role of gamma grad_x log p(y|x).

The most interesting part

I'll take the reviewer's seat, because the framing claim is much stronger than what is delivered — though the delivered thing is not without value.

The stationarity condition is real algebra, but it is not margin algebra, and the paper misidentifies its own best justification. Consider a network trained to a stationary point of weight-decayed ERM, min_theta (mu/2)||theta||^2 + (1/n) sum_i L_i. First-order optimality gives mu theta_ + (1/n) sum_i grad_theta L_i = 0, i.e. exactly theta_ = -sum_i lambda_i grad_theta L_i with uniform lambda_i = 1/(mu n) > 0. That is Eq. 5, it holds non-asymptotically, and the paper's own Appendix D confirms weight decay was used (0.005 for the CIFAR ConvNets; torchvision's ResNet50 uses 1e-4). So DeepKKT's central equation is the KKT condition of L2-regularized empirical risk minimization, whose content is "theta_ lies in the nonnegative conic hull of per-sample loss gradients." That is a statement about regularization and stationarity, not about margins or boundary proximity. The paper instead justifies it (Appendix C) by a hand-wave at Soudry et al.'s implicit-bias result: with a logistic tail the gradient direction converges to some g_inf dominated by the least-confident samples, hence w_inf ≈ -g_inf. That argument is about the _unregularized* case where ||w|| -> infinity and only directions converge — and the authors notice the gap in Appendix B, stating flatly that "the equivalence ... is only described intuitively, not rigorously" and "we have not derived it with rigorous math." (The NeurIPS checklist, two pages later, answers [Yes] to "complete and correct proof," which is not a good look.)

The margin, the one thing that makes a support vector a support vector, never appears in the implementation. Eq. 3 introduces a margin eps and then eps is never used again: the implemented primal loss (Eq. 7) is a 0/1-gated cross-entropy that switches off the instant argmax is correct, i.e. eps = 0. Complementary slackness is dropped by admission. So the claim "DSVs meet every condition introduced in conventional SVM" is not supported: two of the four conditions are enforced (primal feasibility in a margin-free form, dual feasibility by pruning), one is enforced as a soft penalty, and the one that defines support — "alpha_i > 0 implies the point sits on the margin" — is absent.

The evidence offered for implicit complementary slackness is close to tautological. Fig. 2a shows the entropy of DSV candidates rising during optimization, read as evidence that DSVs drift toward the decision boundary. But for cross-entropy, ||grad_theta L(x,y)|| -> 0 as p_y -> 1: confident samples contribute almost nothing. If you must reconstruct a fixed-norm theta_ from a handful of gradients, the optimizer is structurally pushed toward high-gradient-norm, i.e. low-confidence, i.e. high-entropy samples. The objective _selects for* high entropy; measuring high entropy afterwards is not an independent confirmation of a geometric property. (The lambda_i are unconstrained above and can absorb scale, which weakens but does not remove this.)

Fig. 2b's "strong correlation" is n = 10 with no statistic reported. Reading the numbers embedded in the figure (per-class test accuracy vs. summed lambda), Pearson r ≈ 0.78, Spearman ≈ 0.67. But the fit is carried by a single point: "cat" at lambda = 0.32, 72.96% accuracy. Drop it and r ≈ 0.59 on nine points, which is not significant at any conventional level; "bird" (80.1% accuracy, lambda = 7.75) contradicts the trend outright. The interpretive claim built on top — that lambda reveals categorical generalization despite ~100% train accuracy — is interesting and may well be true, but it is not established by this plot.

The distillation comparison has an information-accounting problem that the "ratio (%)" column obscures. That column counts only the real images touched during synthesis, so DSV's zero-shot row reads "0 shots, 0% of the dataset." But DSV consumes a ConvNet pretrained on all 50,000 CIFAR-10 images; the dataset is laundered through theta_. DC/DSA/DM at 1 or 10 shots/class are given no such model. Under that asymmetry, winning (22.69 vs. 16.48/15.41/13.03; 37.90 vs. 25.06/26.67/29.77) is expected rather than surprising. Conversely, when the baselines do get the full set, DM beats DSV: 47.96 vs. 37.90 at 10 img/cls and 60.59 vs. 53.56 at 50 img/cls. The defensible claim is "best in the regime where you have a pretrained model and no data," and that regime _is_ genuinely practical and under-served — but the table is presented as if it were a head-to-head on distillation quality, and the dashes in the DSV column mean no row ever compares like with like. Also, the zero-shot setting initializes from images of _other* datasets "to ensure diversity," so it is not data-free either.

The baselines that actually matter are missing. The loss is TV + pixel norm + augmentation-expectation + a parameter-space matching term. Strip the stationarity term and that is DeepInversion ("Dreaming to Distill," Yin et al. 2020), which uses TV + L2 + BN-statistic matching for exactly this task — data-free synthesis from a pretrained classifier for distillation and pruning. DeepInversion is neither cited nor compared (only the same group's later GradInversion appears, as a TV-prior citation). Likewise, Haim et al., Buzaglo et al. and Yu & Wang are discussed in related work as the KKT-inversion line and then never benchmarked — which is awkward, because Alg. 1 line 9's ||theta + sum lambda_i y_i grad_theta Phi(x_i; theta)||^2 is essentially Haim et al.'s reconstruction objective generalized to multiclass. The novelty is honestly the framing and the scale (ImageNet, ResNet50, many classes, generative use), not the equation. On the generative side the gap is starker: the paper claims "an alternative to GANs and diffusion models" and "high fidelity," with no FID, no IS, no precision/recall, no density/coverage — zero quantitative generative evaluation. The Fig. 5 ablation (primal only vs. stationarity only) is qualitative, and there is no ablation table over beta_1, beta_2, beta_3, the augmentation set, n, or lambda initialization. Table 1's coreset experiment compares only against random, not against herding, k-center, EL2N/GraNd, or forgetting-event selection, which is the standard suite.

Two smaller technical points. "Hessian-free" is overstated: computing grad_{x_i} D(theta_, sum_j lambda_j grad_theta L_j) differentiates a theta-gradient with respect to x, i.e. a cross-block Hessian-vector product. It is genuinely cheaper than trajectory matching's meta-gradients and needs no training snapshots, which is the real selling point — but it is not first-order. And the remark that "in a high-dimensional data manifold, most data points are located close to the decision boundary because ... every sample matters and thus would serve as a DSV" is asserted without argument and quietly dissolves the analogy: the entire value of support vectors is _sparsity*. If every point is a support vector, "support vector" carries no information, and the paper cannot simultaneously claim that DSVs are a selective, explanatory subset.

The internal inconsistencies are worth noting for anyone trying to reproduce: L1 in Eq. 8 vs. squared L2 in Alg. 1; grad_theta L in Eq. 8 vs. y_i grad_theta Phi in Alg. 1; Alg. 1 lines 16-17 write gradient ascent on a loss being minimized; Appendix D names hyperparameters alpha, beta, gamma while Eq. 9 uses beta_1, beta_2, beta_3, and "both beta and gamma to 0" for the distillation runs would zero out both image priors — meaning the distillation numbers may come from stationarity + primal alone, which is worth knowing given Fig. 5's message; eta is declared a learning rate in Alg. 1's Require block but used as the augmented-loss weight in line 15.

Now the genuine strengths, because there are several. The regime — one pretrained model, no training data, no optimization trajectory, no Hessian — is the right practical target and the paper is the first I know of to attack multiclass ImageNet-scale inversion with a stationarity constraint rather than BN statistics. The transfer-learning inversion in Fig. 4 is the most alarming and most convincing result in the paper: a ConvNet pretrained on CIFAR-10 with only the final layer fine-tuned on SVHN yields DSVs that look like SVHN digits, which shows the stationarity constraint works on a subspace of parameters and constitutes a real privacy finding about deployed fine-tuned models. Fig. 7's observation that noise-initialized synthesized DSVs resemble the highest-lambda selected real training images is the paper's best internal consistency check and connects the selection and synthesis stories that would otherwise float free. The latent interpolation and editing results are striking evidence that a plain ImageNet classifier carries compositional semantics it was never asked to learn. And the Eq. 10 / Eq. 11 reading — stationarity plus priors as an unconditional score, the primal gate as classifier guidance — is an elegant reframing that I think is more fertile than the SVM analogy it is nominally subordinate to. Fig. 3's human-in-the-loop causal edit (erase antlers and sharpen ears, the deer is read as a cat) is a falsifiable use of a global explanation, which is more than most XAI papers offer.

Broader context

Dataset distillation starts with Wang et al. (2018), which posed the bilevel problem directly, and then splits into families by what signal is matched. Gradient matching (DC, Zhao et al. 2020; DSA with differentiable augmentation; the baselines here) matches per-step gradients between synthetic and real batches. Trajectory matching (MTT, Cazenavette et al. 2022) matches multi-step parameter trajectories and therefore needs checkpoints from the full training run. Distribution matching (DM) matches feature statistics and avoids meta-gradients. Factorization approaches (Liu et al. 2022) and kernel-ridge formulations (KIP, FRePo) trade the bilevel problem for a closed-form inner solve. All of these assume access to the dataset and usually to training dynamics, which is exactly the assumption DSV drops — and the cleanest way to read DSV is as data-free gradient matching where the matching target is theta* itself rather than a real-batch gradient. That reframing is more illuminating than the SVM story and also explains why it works for distillation at all.

The other lineage is model inversion. Mahendran & Vedaldi (2014) and DeepDream established that classifier activations plus image priors suffice to synthesize recognizable inputs; DeepInversion (Yin et al. 2020) made it work for data-free knowledge distillation by adding BN-statistic matching; GradInversion (Yin et al. 2021) did the same for federated gradient leakage. Orthogonally, Haim et al. (2022) and Buzaglo et al. (2023) reconstruct actual training points by solving the KKT stationarity condition, and their rigor comes from Lyu & Li (2020): for homogeneous networks trained on separable data with exponential-tail loss, theta/||theta|| converges to a KKT point of min ||theta||^2 s.t. y_i Phi(x_i; theta) >= 1, which yields theta_hat proportional to sum_i lambda_i y_i grad_theta Phi(x_i) with lambda_i >= 0 supported on minimum-margin samples. That is a theorem, and it is the same equation DeepKKT asserts by analogy. Meanwhile, the "which examples matter" question has its own literature that Table 1 should have engaged: influence functions (Koh & Liang), EL2N/GraNd (Paul et al.), forgetting events (Toneva et al.), and submodular/k-center coresets.

A concrete follow-up the paper opens: turn the assertion into a measurement, and then into a theorem. Since the stationarity condition is literally the first-order condition of weight-decayed ERM, one can measure the residual ||mu theta_ + sum_i c_i grad_theta L_i|| / ||theta_|| on the real training set and chart it against weight decay strength, homogeneity (bias-free, BN-free nets), training length, and augmentation — producing an empirical answer to "how KKT is this network?" that the paper currently substitutes intuition for. Two consequences follow. First, with lambda >= 0 the search for a minimal support set over the real training data is a nonnegative-least-squares / conic feasibility problem, so one can directly test the paper's most consequential throwaway claim — that in high dimensions essentially every sample is a support vector — by looking at the sparsity of the NNLS solution. If deep nets really do admit sparse conic representations of theta*, that is a significant structural fact with coreset consequences; if they do not, the SVM analogy should be retired and Eq. 5 kept purely as a synthesis objective. Second, for homogeneous networks Euler's identity <theta, grad_theta Phi> = L Phi turns stationarity into a checkable scalar identity, which is the obvious first lemma for anyone wanting to make DeepKKT a proposition rather than a trope. A third, purely empirical follow-up: replace the hand-crafted TV/norm priors with a pretrained diffusion prior and ablate — given Fig. 5, I suspect most of the image fidelity is prior-driven, and separating "DeepKKT generates" from "the priors generate" is the experiment the paper most needs.

On the IR side I'd be candid: there is no strong link, and the paper is more interesting on its own terms as a data-free inversion / regularized-stationarity result than as anything retrieval-adjacent. The two tempting bridges are both weaker than they look. Coreset selection for index construction is superficially appealing — picking representative vectors for PQ codebook training or HNSW entry points — but DSV's criterion is a multiplier fitted against a supervised classifier's parameters, and there is no theta_ to match in an unsupervised ANN index; you would have to invent the supervision, at which point you are doing something else. The "classifier as latent generative model" framing resembles generative retrieval's reading of a discriminative label space as a generator, but the mechanisms do not transfer: DSV does gradient descent in _input_ space against a frozen network, whereas GR decodes identifiers autoregressively in _output* space, and nothing in the paper speaks to sequence decoding or docid structure.

The one connection I would actually defend is the inversion/extraction angle, and it is supported by the paper's own Fig. 4. The stationarity condition says a model's parameters sit in the conic hull of a small number of per-example gradients — the same algebra as asking what a trained retrieval model has memorized about its corpus. A DeepKKT-style attack on a DSI/generative-retrieval model, where the docid head's parameters are inverted to recover training documents, is a well-posed and currently open question, and the transfer-learning result suggests it would work on exactly the realistic case of a fine-tuned head over a frozen encoder. The dual theoretical question — whether a learned index's parameters admit a sparse "support document" representation, in the NNLS sense above — is the kind of thing your background is suited to settle, and it would be a genuine contribution to the memorization/extraction side of neural IR rather than a borrowed analogy.

Proof sketch

There is no theorem, and the paper says so: Appendix B states that "the equivalence between DSVs in deep learning models and support vectors in SVMs is only described intuitively, not rigorously," that the condition is justified "experimentally in Fig. 7 and intuitively in Sec. C," and that "we have not derived it with rigorous math. Proving this rigorously would be a meaningful research topic." (The NeurIPS checklist's [Yes] to "complete and correct proof" contradicts this.) So what follows is the derivation, with the rigor boundary marked.

The starting point (rigorous, classical). For a hard-margin linear SVM, the Lagrangian (1/2)||w||^2 - sum_i alpha_i (y_i w'x_i - 1) gives the four KKT conditions quoted in Sec. 3.2, of which stationarity w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i is the one with content: the weight vector is a nonnegative combination of data points, and complementary slackness alpha_i (y_i w'x_i - 1) = 0 forces the active ones onto the margin. The paper then rewrites this in gradient form. Since the per-sample hinge has grad_w max(0, 1 - y_i w'x_i) = -y_i x_i on violating samples and 0 otherwise (Eq. 1), stationarity becomes w_ = -sum_i alpha_i grad_w L_hinge(x_i, y_i; w_), alpha_i >= 0 (Eq. 2). This step is exact.

The substitution (the analogy, and where rigor stops). Two replacements are made. The margin functional y_i w'x_i is replaced by -L(Phi(x_i; theta*), y_i). The stated justification is shape-matching: the hard multiclass margin condition is Phi_{y_i} - max_{c != y_i} Phi_c >= eps (Eq. 3), and -L_CE = Phi_{y_i} - log sum_c exp Phi_c (Eq. 4) is its log-sum-exp smoothing — a reasonable surrogate, and the standard one. Then grad_w is replaced by grad_theta, giving Eq. 5. The move is purely formal: it would be a derivation only if theta -> Phi(x; theta) were linear and the objective actually minimized were (1/2)||theta||^2 subject to per-sample margin constraints. For a nonconvex Phi trained by SGD on cross-entropy with augmentation and minibatching, nothing in the training procedure implies Eq. 5. No assumption is stated (no separability, no homogeneity, no convergence to a stationary point, no NTK linearization), and nothing is guaranteed.

What is nonetheless true, and the paper's unclaimed best argument. Eq. 5 is exactly the first-order optimality condition of a different, perfectly ordinary problem: min_theta (mu/2)||theta||^2 + sum_i c_i L_i with c_i >= 0. At a stationary point, mu theta_ = -sum_i c_i grad_theta L_i, i.e. theta_ = -sum_i lambda_i grad_theta L_i with lambda_i = c_i/mu >= 0. So if theta_ is (near) a stationary point of L2-regularized ERM — and weight decay was used in all their training runs — the condition holds over the _training set_ with known multipliers, for reasons having nothing to do with margins. The paper's actual contribution is then the _sparse_ version: find a handful of synthesized x_i and nonnegative lambda_i such that theta_ still lies in the cone spanned by their gradients. That is a conic approximation/representation claim, not a geometric margin claim, and stating it that way would have made the method's content clearer and its evaluation easier to design.

Appendix C's actual argument, and its limits. The paper instead argues informally from implicit bias. Under gradient flow w_{t+1} = w_t - eta grad L with a logistic-tail loss, the loss never reaches zero, "the gradient of the least confident sample (support vector) dominates overall gradient," so there is a limiting gradient direction g_inf; after some time T the direction is within epsilon of it; w moves along -g_inf; hence w_inf ≈ -g_inf. Rigor stops at every step: "dominates" is unquantified; existence of g_inf is asserted for architectures (residual, BN, augmented, minibatched) well outside the regimes where Soudry et al. and Lyu & Li prove direction convergence — and the related-work section itself notes that this line "relies on strong assumptions such as full-batch training and non-residual architecture without data augmentation" before proceeding to invoke it anyway; and the conclusion is about directions while L_stat enforces an equality of vectors including magnitude. The last gap is papered over, in effect, by the free nonnegative lambda_i: they absorb both overall scale and per-sample weighting, so what the loss really enforces is membership of theta_/||theta_|| in the cone generated by the achievable per-sample gradient directions.

The key step that makes the method work in practice, as opposed to the derivation. Two things. First, the n unconstrained multipliers make the stationarity constraint weak enough to be satisfied by a small synthetic set — it is a highly underdetermined conic feasibility problem, which is why a few dozen images suffice and also why satisfying it is weak evidence that the images are "support vectors" in any geometric sense. Second, the image quality comes from the manifold machinery: expectation over augmentations (translation, crop, cutout, flip, noise), total variation, and pixel-norm penalties. The paper's own Fig. 5 shows that primal feasibility alone produces nothing recognizable, and attributes the fidelity to the other terms. That ablation is best read not as "stationarity is the score function" but as "the DeepInversion-style priors plus augmentation averaging do the generative work, and stationarity supplies the per-class signal and the implicit preference for low-confidence, high-gradient-norm inputs."

The rigorous route not taken. For L-positively-homogeneous networks, Lyu & Li (2020) prove that theta/||theta|| converges to a KKT point of min ||theta||^2 s.t. y_i Phi(x_i; theta) >= 1, which gives precisely theta_hat proportional to sum_i lambda_i y_i grad_theta Phi(x_i) with lambda_i >= 0 supported on the minimum-margin samples — the exact form in Alg. 1 line 9, and the foundation Haim et al. built their reconstruction on. Euler's identity <theta, grad_theta Phi> = L Phi then supplies a scalar consistency check. Promoting DeepKKT from analogy to proposition is mostly a matter of adopting that machinery and doing the real work of handling the multiclass softmax generalization, non-homogeneous components (biases, BN), and the finite-time, weight-decayed, augmented regime the experiments actually live in. The paper is honest that this is left open; a reader should treat Eq. 6 as a well-motivated synthesis objective with a sound regularized-stationarity interpretation, and treat the word "support vector" as a metaphor.

title: On the Learning Dynamics of Two-layer Linear Networks with Label Noise SGD
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-23

On the Learning Dynamics of Two-layer Linear Networks with Label Noise SGD — Tongcheng Zhang, Zhanpeng Zhou, Mingze Wang, Andi Han, Wei Huang, Taiji Suzuki, Junchi Yan (2026) — arXiv:2603.10397

Main idea

The object of study is the smallest non-trivial factorized model: a two-layer linear network f(x; theta) = a^T W x with W in R^{m×d}, a in R^m, so the realized predictor is the vector theta = a^T W in R^d. Overparameterization is purely in the factorization — width m >> d — not in expressivity; the function class is still linear maps R^d → R. Inputs are x_i ~ N(0, I_d) and the data are realizable: there exists theta_ with y_i = <theta*, x_i> for all i, called the "ground-truth interpolator." Initialization is NTK-style (in the proofs, w_i(0) ~ N(0, I/d) so ||w_i(0)|| ~ 1, and a_i(0) ~ N(0, 1/m) so |a_i(0)| ~ m^{-1/2}; equation (5) of the paper states the two scalings swapped, which is a typo). Label noise SGD is online and single-sample: at step t pick xi_t uniformly, draw a _fresh_ eps_t uniform on {−sigma, +sigma}, and take one squared-loss step on the corrupted target y_{xi_t} + eps_t. So the residual driving the update is r_t = <theta(t) − theta*, x_{xi_t}> − eps_t, which crucially does _not* vanish at interpolation: it floors at |eps_t| = sigma.

"Lazy" is defined operationally and very stringently: the model is lazy at time t if ||w_i(t) − w_i(0)|| <= 1/sqrt(m) for every neuron i. "Rich" is just the complement — the paper, honestly, uses "rich regime" to mean "no longer inside that ball," plus the empirical observation that weights have shrunk to a small-initialization-like scale where feature learning (alignment) is possible.

The two-phase picture is then: Phase I, the per-neuron first-layer norms ||w_i|| decrease, and after T1 = 384 sqrt(log m)/(sigma^2 eta^2 sqrt(m)) steps every neuron has left the lazy ball, with probability 1 − O(1/m). The paper's mechanism is a clean algebraic identity: the first-layer norm change is controlled by the squared increments of the second layer, eta^2 r_j^2 (x^T w_i)^2 = (a_i(j+1) − a_i(j))^2, so "label noise makes a_i oscillate, and that oscillation drains ||w_i||." Phase II begins once ||w_i||, |a_i| <= sqrt(eta) for all i — the small-initialization regime — and here the paper switches to full-batch noiseless GD, linearizes the dynamics, and shows every neuron rotates to within cosine similarity 1 − O(sqrt(eta) log(1/eta)) of ±theta_ in T2 steps, after which theta(t) converges to theta_ up to O(eta log(1/eta)).

What the implicit-bias result actually amounts to is narrower than the abstract implies. Because the data are realizable and n >= 1/eta^2 >> d, theta_ is the _unique_ interpolator: there is no selection among global minima to be biased toward. The content is therefore not "label noise picks a better interpolator" but "label noise picks a better _factorization_ of the one interpolator": W collapses to rank one, every neuron parallel to theta_, total parameter norm sum_i (||w_i||^2 + a_i^2) driven down toward its minimum over the fiber {a^T W = theta_} — which, for this architecture, is the nuclear norm of theta_ (trivially 2||theta*||_2 here). That is a dynamics-and-representation statement, not a generalization statement.

The most interesting part

The genuinely good idea is the exact discrete-time identity in Appendix B.2, and what it reveals about where the effect lives. Summing the two update rules and telescoping gives

||w_i(T)||^2 − a_i(T)^2 = ||w_i(0)||^2 − a_i(0)^2 + eta^2 sum_{j<T} DW_i(j), DW_i(j) = −r_j^2 [ (x_{xi_j}^T w_i(j))^2 − a_i(j)^2 ||x_{xi_j}||^2 ].

The left-hand side is the layer imbalance Lambda_i = ||w_i||^2 − a_i^2, exactly conserved under gradient flow for a two-layer linear net. So the whole phenomenon is the discretization-plus-noise drift of a conserved quantity: at order eta^2, the imbalance is no longer conserved, and its drift has a sign determined by whether |x^T w_i| exceeds |a_i|. Under NTK init this comparison is 1/sqrt(d) versus 1/sqrt(m), so with m >> d the drift is negative and the bigger layer bleeds norm. Two consequences I find clarifying. First, overparameterization is not doing a capacity job here at all; it is doing an imbalance job — m >> d is what fixes the sign of the drift. This places the paper squarely next to Kunin et al.'s "unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning," with noise supplying the drive. Second, the magnitude of the drift is proportional to r_j^2, and r_j^2 >= sigma^2 whenever eps_j happens to share sign with the clean residual, which has probability >= 1/2. That is the entire role of label noise: it puts a _floor under the gradient magnitude so that the eta^2 term never switches off_. Under clean GD from NTK init the residual decays geometrically, the eta^2 drift dies with it, and the norm freezes — lazy forever. The alternating-noise experiment in Appendix E (norm drops while noise is on, flatlines when it is off, resumes when it returns) is the single most convincing figure in the paper precisely because it tests this mechanism rather than the phenomenology.

Now the honest accounting, and it is substantial.

The two phases are not joined. Theorem 4.2 proves escape from a ball of radius 1/sqrt(m) around initialization. Phase II assumes ||w_i||, |a_i| <= sqrt(eta). These are enormously far apart (||w_i(0)|| ~ 1), and nothing in the analysis of the actual algorithm bridges them. Worse, every bound in Phase I (|a_i| <= m^{−1/4}, |r_t| = O(m^{1/4})) is proved conditional on still being in the lazy regime, so all control is lost at exactly the moment the theorem fires. The decay all the way to sqrt(eta) is proved only as Lemma 4.4, and only for Algorithm 2, a surrogate in which the second layer is not trained at all but replaced by a hand-designed three-state Markov chain on {−eta^{0.25}, 0, +eta^{0.25}} while the first layer runs full-batch GD. That surrogate is not a simplification of label noise SGD; it changes the order of the mechanism. In the surrogate the per-step decrease is O(eta) (equation 66), first order, because severing the gradient coupling to a also severs the balancedness structure that made the real effect O(eta^2). So the paper's headline claim — label noise SGD drives the network from NTK scale to small-init scale — is proved for a caricature and demonstrated numerically for the real thing.

Phase II deletes the noise. The paper switches to deterministic full-batch GD "for tractability." But persistent label noise near the zero-loss manifold is the entire subject of Blanc et al., Damian et al. and Li–Wang–Arora; with noise on, theta(t) would not converge to theta* but to a noise ball, and the interesting question is the stationary behavior. Phase II as proved is a standard small-initialization alignment-then-convergence argument for a linear net, close in spirit to Min et al. and Boursier et al., and is the least novel part.

The regime is extreme. A2 requires eta <= C^{−196} for a "sufficiently large constant" C; A3 requires n >= 1/eta^2; A5 requires max_i ||x_i|| <= C_data, a constant, while x_i ~ N(0, I_d) has norm ~ sqrt(d) — so d must effectively be Theta(1), and A6 only lower-bounds d by a constant. The theory therefore lives at d = O(1), m → infinity, n astronomically large, eta astronomically small. A4, ||theta*|| <= m^{−1/4}, is described in the text as "assumes the sparse ground-truth interpolator," which it is not — it is a smallness assumption needed to keep a_i and the residual controlled. There is no sparsity anywhere in the theorems; "sparsity" in the paper means rank-one collapse of W, measured empirically via pruning.

Generalization is never proved. In the theoretical setting theta* is unique, so clean GD converges to the same predictor; label noise confers exactly zero test-loss advantage in the analyzed model. The 1.5% CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 gain and the pruning curves are real but are standard label-smoothing-style empirics, disconnected from the theorem. The WideResNet "lazy versus rich" figures use 64 training images (to make NTK linearization tractable) and show trajectory divergence from the linearized model plus a decreasing ||W||_F — suggestive, but a 64-image subset is a weak bridge, and "deviates from its linearization" is a low bar for "feature learning."

The SAM extension has no proof at all. Section 5 is a conjecture plus two figures; there is no theorem, lemma, or reused machinery. This is a pity, because the natural argument is immediate and the authors clearly see it: SAM's ascent step makes the effective residual r + rho·(gradient direction term), which likewise does not vanish at interpolation, so the same eta^2 imbalance drift stays alive with rho playing the role of sigma. Writing that down would have been the strongest evidence for the paper's claim of a shared governing principle. As it stands, "the principles also apply to SAM" is asserted, not shown.

Broader context

The background stack: Soudry et al. / Gunasekar et al. established that unregularized descent on separable data converges in direction to the max-margin solution, and that factorized parameterizations change the bias — gradient descent on matrix factorization from small init biases toward nuclear norm. Jacot et al.'s NTK and Chizat–Bach's lazy-training analysis explain when a wide net is effectively a fixed kernel; Woodworth et al. made the dial explicit, showing in diagonal linear networks that the initialization scale alpha interpolates between an L2/kernel bias (large alpha) and an L1/rich bias (small alpha). The label-noise line then showed that noise shape matters: Blanc et al. derived an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck-like analysis of label noise SGD near a minimizer, Damian et al. proved label noise SGD provably prefers flat global minimizers (implicitly penalizing the trace of the Hessian, i.e. E||grad_theta f||^2), Li–Wang–Arora gave the general "what happens after SGD reaches zero loss" framework, and HaoChen et al. showed the noise covariance's shape, not just its presence, determines the recovered solution; Pillaud-Vivien et al. showed label noise SGD on a quadratic parameterization implicitly solves the Lasso.

Where this paper sits: note that E||grad_theta f||^2 for f = a^T W x is exactly sum_i (a_i^2 ||x||^2 + (x^T w_i)^2) — the same expression as DW_i, up to the sign bookkeeping. So Phase I is, in effect, the off-manifold counterpart of Damian et al.'s implicit sharpness regularization. That is the real novelty claim, and it is a legitimate one: the existing results assume you start near the zero-loss manifold and ask which minimizer you drift to, whereas here the process starts at NTK scale with Theta(1) loss and the O(eta^2) drift is shown to contract the imbalance anyway. The two closest neighbors worth reading alongside are Varre–Sagitova–Flammarion, "SGD vs GD: rank deficiency in linear networks" (NeurIPS 2024), which proves SGD noise progressively reduces the rank of the parameter matrix in linear networks — essentially the same destination by a related route, and arguably the strongest competitor to this paper's claim of novelty — and Kunin et al., "Get rich quick: unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning", which supplies the other half of the mechanism (the imbalance sign). Against those two, the incremental content is: both layers trained, a specific online label-noise SGD, an explicit escape time, and the identification of the gradient-magnitude floor as the active ingredient. The 1/sqrt(m)-ball escape result and the unproven Phase I → Phase II link are where the increment is thinnest.

A clean follow-up: treat Lambda_i = ||w_i||^2 − a_i^2 as a genuine Lyapunov function and prove the drift stays negative after leaving the lazy ball, controlling the residual by a Freedman/Azuma argument on the martingale part rather than by the lazy-regime invariant — that would close the gap and, done properly, yield a continuous-time "imbalance flow" dLambda/dt = −eta sigma^2 rho(Lambda) describing the whole lazy-to-rich transit. A second: keep the noise on in Phase II and characterize the stationary measure, which would connect the dynamics to the Blanc/Damian limiting bias in one object.

For your own work, the honest connections are these.
