The first is infinite-width parameterization: Yang and Hu's Tensor Programs IV and muP (Yang et al., Tensor Programs V) ask which per-layer scalings of initialization variance and learning rate keep features learning rather than degenerating to an NTK/lazy regime as width grows, and then exploit the answer for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer from small to large models. The gamma-exponent calculus in Appendix A.4 is a two-parameter, one-layer special case of that bookkeeping. The second is LoRA theory proper. Hayou, Ghosh and Yu's LoRA+ (ICML 2024) runs precisely this analysis for a LoRA bottleneck and concludes that the up-projection B needs a learning rate Theta(n) times larger than the down-projection A; their companion paper on initialization shows that B = 0, A random and A = 0, B random are not equivalent, which is the same bifurcation that Appendix A.3 here reproduces. Zhu et al.'s "Asymmetry in low-rank adapters" shows empirically that B matters far more than A — you can freeze A at random and lose little. This paper's contribution should be read as a reinterpretation of that cluster through the attention architecture rather than as new scaling mathematics.

The orthogonal thread is attention-specific training dynamics: Li, Li and Risteski's two-stage picture (W_v moves first, W_q/W_k later) supplies the Case-1 intuition; Tian et al.'s "Scan and snap" and Bao et al.'s QK-eigenspectrum localization analysis study what the q/k product does; Noci et al. treat W_qk as one object in signal-propagation and rank-collapse analyses. The tension the paper surfaces but does not resolve is that the "W_q W_k' is one matrix" view predicts W_q-alone ~ W_k-alone, which is flatly false empirically — the two give rank-r perturbations of W_qk through different fixed factors, so the reachable subspaces differ according to the left versus right singular geometry of the pretrained W_q and W_k and of the input covariance.

The obvious follow-up, and the one that would actually deliver what the paper promises, is to replace the counting bound with a local, tangent-kernel-flavoured capacity: compute the NTK blocks of the attention output with respect to dW_q, dW_k and dW_v at the pretrained weights. The output is linear in W_v, so the v-block is the Gram matrix of the attention-pooled inputs; the q- and k-blocks are instead pre-multiplied by the softmax Jacobian diag(p) - pp', which is rank-deficient (it annihilates constants), has spectrum controlled by the attention entropy, and is near-degenerate exactly in the sharp-attention regime. A localized Rademacher or local-NTK bound whose capacity term is the effective dimension of each block would separate v from q,k for a structural reason rather than by parameter count, would simultaneously explain the two-stage dynamics, and would predict lambda in terms of a computable ratio of block norms rather than leaving it to a grid search. A second concrete follow-up: carry the scaling analysis out at r > 1 with Adam and with the softmax retained, to see whether lambda = Theta(n) survives or degrades to Theta(1), which is what the measured lambda in [2, 40] actually suggests.

For retrieval work the connection is real but narrow, and I would not oversell it. The one place it is genuinely sharp is the geometry of learned representations. In a retrieval encoder the deliverable is an embedding, and what matters downstream is the embedding's spectrum, anisotropy and intrinsic dimension, because those govern ANN index quality, quantization error and graph connectivity. W_v enters the attention output linearly and therefore directly reshapes the span of the representation; W_q and W_k only reshape a point on the simplex, re-weighting which tokens get pooled inside a fixed value subspace. So the v-vs-qk asymmetry has a clean retrieval reading: adapting W_v changes the embedding geometry and can invalidate an index, whereas adapting W_q/W_k leaves the value-space span intact and only moves points within it. That is a testable statement about fine-tuning-induced embedding drift and re-indexing cost, and it is the kind of thing a theory of "which parameters you may adapt without re-indexing" could be built on.

For DSI-style generative retrieval the link is softer but not forced: the paper cites He et al.'s finding that value vectors store the most memorized content, which lines up with the knowledge-in-values literature (ROME and successors). If docid memorization is the dominant burden in generative retrieval, a W_v-heavy, high-lambda adapter is a natural hypothesis for parameter-efficient docid learning — and the flip side is that Theorem 1, being pure parameter counting, is exactly the wrong instrument for a task where memorization is the point rather than the failure mode. More usefully, there is a genuine theoretical gap worth noting: information-theoretic generalization bounds of this family assume an i.i.d. sample S_N, and contrastive objectives with in-batch negatives violate that badly, since batch composition couples examples and the "loss per example" is not a function of one Z. Extending the Xu–Raginsky / Steinke–Zakynthinou CMI machinery to in-batch-negative contrastive losses is an open and reasonably well-posed problem, and arguably a better use of this toolbox than re-deriving a parameter count. Beyond that, the width-scaling material is best filed as something worth learning on its own terms — muP and LoRA+ are useful to know when fine-tuning any encoder — rather than as a direct contribution to IR theory.

title: The Coverage Principle: How Pre-Training Enables Post-Training
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-20

3. The Coverage Principle: How Pre-Training Enables Post-Training

Chen, Huang, Golowich, Malladi, Block, Ash, Krishnamurthy & Foster — 2025 — arXiv:2510.15020

Main idea. The paper asks what property of a pre-trained model actually determines whether post-training works, given the well-documented empirical fact that a better next-token predictor is not reliably a better starting point for RL or test-time scaling (they cite Liu et al. 2022, Zeng et al. 2025, Springer et al. 2025, F. Chen et al. 2025, and reproduce an anti-correlation themselves). Their answer is the coverage profile: for a reference policy π and a model π̂,

Cov_N(π ‖ π̂) := P over x∼μ, y∼π(·|x) of [ π(y|x)/π̂(y|x) ≥ N ],

i.e. the probability, under the reference, of landing on a response whose likelihood the model under-weights by a factor of at least N. Written as P_{π_D}[log(π_D/π̂) ≥ log N], it is exactly the CDF of the log-likelihood ratio evaluated at log N, whereas KL is the mean of that same random variable. So coverage is not a χ²-type moment but a one-sided tail probability — weaker than the L^p concentrability coefficients used in the inference-time-alignment literature (Markov recovers coverage from those), and strictly more informative than cross-entropy, which averages the tail away.

The reason this is the right object is a tight two-sided characterization of Best-of-N. Proposition D.6 (via a lemma of Huang et al. 2025b) says that if Cov_M(π_T‖π̂) ≤ 1/2 and N ≳ M log(1/ε), then BoN's reward gap against any comparator π_T is at most Cov_M(π_T‖π̂) + ε; Proposition D.7 shows necessity by constructing, for any π̂ and π_T, a binary reward on which BoN's gap is at least ½·Cov_{2N}(π_T‖π̂) — the hard reward simply indicates the set where π̂ ≤ π_T/2N, and a union bound over N draws cannot reach it. A chain rule (Proposition D.5), Cov_{M₁}(π_T‖π̂) ≤ M₂·Cov_{M₁/M₂}(π_D‖π̂) + Cov_{M₂}(π_T‖π_D), lets them forget the downstream task entirely and study coverage of the pre-training distribution π_D by π̂.

Cross-entropy is the wrong proxy because the only generic route from it to coverage is Markov on the f-divergence, Cov_N ≤ D_KL/(log N − 1 + 1/N) (Prop. 3.1, tight by Prop. D.2), and sequence-level KL grows with the horizon: Proposition 3.2 exhibits a one-dimensional autoregressive linear class where every proper estimator suffers D_KL ≳ H/4n with probability ≥ 1/4. Plugged into Prop. 3.1 this predicts BoN compute N ≈ exp(H/nε) — vacuous. The culprit is missing mass: KL pays log W_max wherever the learner has no information to extrapolate, and in a heterogeneous prompt mixture that term can dominate even when the model covers everything that matters.

The surprising part. The headline is that coverage generalizes faster than cross-entropy. Theorem 4.1 states that under realizability alone, the MLE satisfies

Cov_N(π̂) ≲ (1/log N)·inf over ε of [ log N_∞(Π,ε)/n + ε ] + [ log N_∞(Π, c·log N) + log(1/δ) ] / n,

with no H and no log W_max anywhere, and with the leading term improving as you go further into the tail. This is counterintuitive: coverage is a heavier-tailed functional than KL in the sense that it probes exactly the region where the likelihood ratio blows up, and standard MLE theory (Wong–Shen, van de Geer, Zhang) converges in Hellinger, from which you can only get Cov_N ≲ C_fine with no N-improvement (their Prop. D.4/D.8), while the KL route costs log W_max/log N and becomes vacuous for N ≥ W_max (Appendix B is an unusually clean accounting of this).

The mechanism they identify is an implicit bias of the logarithmic loss: a single training example on which π fails to cover π_D by a factor N contributes a likelihood deficit of order log N relative to π_D. Since the MLE's total likelihood deficit is non-positive, the number of uncovered examples is bounded by (fluctuation budget)/log N — the tail parameter appears as a price per miscovered point, not as a variance to be controlled. And because the argument is purely one-sided (large coverage ⟹ low empirical likelihood, never the converse), no step ever needs to control the range of the density ratio, which is precisely where H entered before.

Honest caveats. Realizability (π_D ∈ Π) does most of the work; under misspecification coverage degrades to min_π D_KL(π_D‖π)/log M (Prop. E.1 gives a matching α²/log M lower bound for a two-model class), and the fixes are either convexity of Π (Thm. E.1) or the tournament estimators — neither of which covers transformers. The SGD results are for autoregressive linear models with a frozen feature map and a convex, bounded parameter set, so the optimizer story (vanilla SGD pays B²H/T and that is tight; gradient normalization and SignSGD-like updates remove it) is a suggestive analogy to Adam, not a theorem about Adam. The separation itself leans on engineered heterogeneity: Prop. 3.2 puts mass 1/2n on the single informative prompt so that it is never observed, which is a worst-case artifact — though Figure 2's graph task mirrors it with 5% and 1% "unlearnable" classes and reproduces the H-linear KL alongside H-flat coverage, so the artifact is at least a realistic one. The empirical validation is thin relative to the theory: one synthetic layered-DAG graph-search family with small GPT-2-style transformers, and of the three proposed interventions only checkpoint selection by tournament is actually run (the ♢ markers in Figure 1); gradient normalization, test-time-training decoding and truncated distillation gradients are theory-only. Finally, Remark 2.2 concedes that neither KL nor coverage is estimable without π_D, so "select for coverage" is operational only through the pairwise tournaments or in distillation, where the teacher's log-probs are available.

Proof sketch. What is proved. Theorem 4.1 (and its general version 4.1′, which also tolerates ε_apx-approximate maximization) assumes only realizability and an L_∞ log-density covering number N_∞(Π,α) — the smallest cover with sup over x,y of |log π − log π′| ≤ α — and splits the bound into a fine term, the covering number at scale ε ≈ poly(1/n) divided by log N, and a coarse term, the covering number at the enormous scale α ≈ log N divided by n. The coarse term encodes missing mass (the Bernoulli warm-up: for π_D = Ber(p⋆) the MLE can be Ber(0), so E[KL] = ∞ while Cov_N ≲ log(1/δ)/n) and its Π-dependence vanishes as N grows. Corollary 4.1 instantiates d/n in the parametric regime and (1/log N)(C^p/n)^{1/(p+1)} in the nonparametric one; Corollary 4.2 gives horizon-free Õ(d/n) for low-dimensional autoregressive linear models. Proposition 4.1 shows both terms are tight for the MLE — part (a) builds a d-ary softmax class where, with probability ≥ 1/2, at least (d−1)/2 symbols are unobserved and KKT forces the MLE to push them to e^(−2B), giving Cov_{e^B}(π̂) ≳ d/n for all N ≤ e^B; part (b) is a Gaussian-width/Khintchine–Paley–Zygmund construction over Π = {π_D} ∪ {π_θ : θ ∈ {±1}^d} with per-coordinate bias ε = √(d/n) and a rare prompt where every π_θ puts mass 1/N, showing the fine term's high-precision covering number cannot be coarsened. These are explicitly algorithm-specific, not information-theoretic, and Section 6.3 beats them: the simple tournament π̂ = argmin_π max_{π′} Ĉov_N(π′‖π) achieves Cov_{N^{1+a}}(π̂) ≲ min_π Cov_{N^a}(π) + N^(−(1−a)) + log(|Π|/δ)/n with no realizability, and an offset variant with an on-policy penalty removes the N^(−(1−a)) at the cost of requiring a uniformly a·log N-accurate best-in-class model. On the autoregressive side, Theorem 4.2 gives E[Cov_N(π̂)] ≲ √(σ⋆²/(n log N)) + B²/n for overparameterized linear models, where σ⋆² = E_{π_D} Σ_h ‖φ(x,y_{1:h}) − φ̄_{π_D}(x,y_{1:h−1})‖² is an inherent variance playing the role of an effective sequence length — the number of genuinely high-entropy tokens — and Proposition I.1 shows a matching min{1, H/(n log N)} lower bound for proper algorithms when σ⋆² ≍ HB², so the σ⋆²-dependence is real rather than an artifact of the analysis.

How. The proof of Theorem 4.1 is a clipping-plus-one-sided-uniform-convergence argument that is, in spirit, Mendelson's small-ball method transplanted to log loss: the event Cov_N(π) ≥ ε is read as an anti-concentration (small-ball) certificate which forces π's empirical likelihood to be too small for it to be the maximizer. Concretely, fix C ≥ log 4 and write L̂n(π) − L̂_n(π_D) = L⁺_C(π) − L⁻_C(π), where L⁺_C(π) = Σ_i max{log(π/π_D), −C} clips the favorable direction from below and L⁻_C(π) = Σ_i max{0, log(π_D/π) − C} collects the unfavorable excess. The two halves are then bounded by completely different means. For L⁺_C, Lemma H.1 is the key trick: E{π_D} exp(½ max{log(π/π_D), −C}) ≤ 1, proved by splitting on {π/π_D ≥ e^(−C)}, applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the Hellinger-affinity term Σ√(π π_D) ≤ √(P_{π_D}(E)), and using e^(−C) ≤ 1/4. The exponent ½ makes this a Hellinger/Rényi-½ statement, and the clipping at an absolute constant is what makes the moment-generating function finite with no reference to W_max — this is precisely where the sequence-length dependence drops out, since in the classical route H enters only through the Yang–Barron conversion D_KL ≤ (2 + log W_max)·D_H². Feeding this into Lemma F.3 (an MGF-plus-union-bound uniform bound over an L_∞ cover; notably no symmetrization or chaining is needed, because the cover is in sup-norm and the MGF is already ≤ 1) yields L⁺_C(π) ≤ log(1/δ) + 2·inf_ε{log N_∞(Π,ε) + nε} uniformly over Π — the fine term, and the only place high-precision capacity is used.

For L⁻C, the counting is elementary but is where log N is harvested: every example with π_D/π ≥ N contributes at least log N − C, so L⁻_C(π) ≥ n(log N − C)·Ĉov_N(π_D‖π). Transferring the empirical coverage to the population one is Lemma H.2 — a Freedman/Bernstein bound in multiplicative form (Ĉov_N ≥ ½·Cov{e^{2α}N} − 8log(2N_∞(Π,α)/δ)/n) applied over a cover at the coarse scale α = ¼ log N, which is legitimate precisely because an α-perturbation of log π only shifts the threshold N by e^(±α); indicators are bounded, so no range parameter appears. Combining, every π ∈ Π satisfies Cov_N(π) ≲ [L̂_n(π_D) − L̂_n(π) + n·C_fine]/(n log N) + C_coarse, and the MLE kills the first numerator term. Division by log N is the coverage principle.

The autoregressive proof (Theorem 4.2) is structurally different and arguably the more technically novel half: the target is a stopped KL, D_{seq,N} = E_{π_D} min{log N, Σ_h KL_h}, which is always bounded and converts to coverage via Proposition D.10 (a stopping-time plus chain-rule argument, Cov_N ≤ 2·D_{seq,N}/(log N − 1)) — the truncation at log N is the paper's way of taming the heavy tail. Lemma I.1 then uses first-order optimality of the MLE in the convex parameterization plus E[φ⋆|x, y_{1:h−1}] = 0 to get E Ê_D[Σ_h KL_h] ≤ 2σ⋆/√n, i.e. the martingale norm of the centered feature sum is what σ⋆² measures. Uniformity is obtained not by an L_∞ cover (which would reintroduce d) but by a fractional cover: J = exp(1/Δ²) parameters drawn i.i.d. from N(0, Δ²I), following F. Chen et al. (2024a) and Chen–Rakhlin (2025). Its approximation error is Δ²σ⋆² — variance at the ground truth only, not a uniform bound over Θ — and because the cover is data-independent, symmetrization is avoided; optimizing Δ gives √(σ⋆² log N/n) + B² log N/n in stopped KL, hence the stated coverage rate. The same stopped-KL identity drives Section 6: Theorem 6.2's distillation estimator literally truncates token-level gradients once the running sum of teacher–student KLs exceeds log N (weights α_θ ∈ [0,1] chosen so that Σ_h α_h ε_h = min{log N, Σ_h ε_h} exactly), which is a direct algorithmic read-out of the analysis and recovers the MLE rate for one-pass SGD.

Broader context. The coverage/concentrability lineage is offline RL: Farahmand–Szepesvári–Munos error propagation, Chen–Jiang's information-theoretic batch-RL conditions, Xie–Jiang, Jin et al.'s pessimism, Foster et al.'s offline barriers — in all of which a density-ratio coefficient between the data distribution and the target policy is what makes offline learning possible at all. The novelty here is a shift of object: in offline RL, coverage is a property of the dataset; here it is a property of the model that a learning procedure must inherit from its data, which is why "pre-training enables post-training" is a coverage statement. On the post-training side, coverage is the standing assumption in Huang et al., Self-Improvement in Language Models: The Sharpening Mechanism (ICLR 2025), Is Best-of-N the Best of Them? Coverage, Scaling, and Optimality in Inference-Time Alignment (ICML 2025) — whose Lemma F.1 supplies the BoN upper bound used here — and Correcting the Mythos of KL-Regularization (χPO, ICLR 2025), where a χ² (rather than KL) regularizer buys pessimism against exactly this kind of ratio blow-up; also Foster–Mhammedi–Rohatgi on whether a good base model is necessary for efficient exploration. Empirically the paper is the theoretical counterpart to Yue et al. (2025) on whether RLVR expands capability beyond the base model, and to F. Chen et al. (2025) on Pass@N degrading during pre-training.

The natural follow-up the authors flag, and the one I find most promising, is semantic coverage: Cov_N is a function of probabilities only, so it is blind to the fact that many distinct token sequences are the same answer; their own answer-level variant Cov^ans_N (marginalizing out the chain of thought) is strictly smaller and already enough for outcome-rewarded tasks, and a theory of coverage under a semantic quotient — coverage of equivalence classes, with σ⋆² recomputed over pivotal decisions rather than pivotal tokens — looks tractable and would also fix the "models with identical coverage profile but different representations" critique.

For your work the connection is genuine and, I think, under-exploited. In two-stage retrieval, the first-stage candidate generator is a sampler and the reranker is the reward: BoN with r_T = relevance is recall@N of the candidate set, so Propositions D.6/D.7 say that the coverage profile of the retriever with respect to an oracle ranking policy is necessary and sufficient, up to constants, for end-to-end quality — a formalization of the folklore that a reranker can only reorder what the retriever surfaced. The sharper instance is constrained-decoding generative retrieval (DSI, NCI, SEAL, and the semantic-ID line): there the model is literally an autoregressive π(docid | q), beam search of width N is Best-of-N over identifier strings, and Cov_N(π_D‖π̂) is exactly the probability that the gold identifier is under-weighted enough to fall out of the beam.

Two of the paper's results then transfer almost verbatim. First, docid strings have a horizon H equal to codebook depth, so sequence-level cross-entropy on identifier tokens grows with H while coverage need not — which means validating or early-stopping a generative retriever on token perplexity is not merely imprecise but systematically mis-ranked relative to recall@N, and Theorem 4.1 explains why the recall metric is the statistically better-behaved one rather than just the task-relevant one. Second, σ⋆², the number of genuinely high-entropy positions in the identifier, is the quantity that controls the rate — which turns codebook design into a coverage question: a hierarchical semantic ID that concentrates the ambiguity into a few levels should provably achieve better coverage at equal cross-entropy than a flat or atomic ID of the same length. That is a crisp, testable follow-up, and the tournament of Eq. (29) is immediately usable as a checkpoint-selection rule for generative retrievers, since on finite candidate sets it needs only pairwise empirical likelihood-ratio comparisons on held-out queries and no relevance labels beyond the training distribution.

The ANN/vector-search link is the weaker one and I would not lean on it: the structural resemblance is real — coverage is a tail probability of a density ratio under the reference, the same primitive as the probability that a proposal-based candidate generator (LSH buckets, HNSW traversal) misses the true nearest neighbor, and the paper's KL→coverage conversion is borrowed from Block–Polyanskiy's analysis of approximate rejection sampling, which is exactly a density-ratio sample-complexity result — but ANN recall analyses are geometric (doubling dimension, aspect ratio) rather than likelihood-based, so the connection is an analogy of technique, not a shared theorem, and I would present it as such.

title: Navigating Extremes: Dynamic Sparsity in Large Output Space
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-20

2. Navigating Extremes: Dynamic Sparsity in Large Output Space

Ullah, Schultheis, Lasby, Ioannou & Babbar — 2024 — arXiv:2411.03171

Main idea. In extreme multi-label classification (XMC) the one-vs-all classification head is the model: with an embedding dimension of 768 and a million labels, weights plus gradients plus Adam moments come to roughly 12 GB, which dwarfs the BERT encoder in front of it. The standard XMC tricks — label trees, shortlisting, negative sampling — buy sublinear compute but leave that memory untouched, because you still have to store the whole matrix even if you only score a shortlist of it. This paper (NeurIPS 2024) asks whether dynamic sparse training (DST) can attack the memory side instead: never materialise the dense head at all, keep a sparse topology from initialisation to convergence, and evolve it during training. The resulting system, SPARTEX, sparsifies the classifier with a fixed fan-in constraint — every label vector gets exactly the same number of active input coordinates — which is what makes the sparsity actually pay off rather than being simulated by a mask. Fixed fan-in gives a padding-free ELLPACK layout (one 16-bit index per weight), so the raw weight overhead is 50%, but because the gradient and the two momentum buffers share the same index structure, the amortised indexing overhead drops to 12.5%. Topology updates use SET — magnitude pruning plus random regrowth — deliberately rather than RigL, because RigL's regrowth criterion needs dense gradients, and the authors' point is that even an "ephemeral" dense gradient for a single layer is exactly the thing they cannot afford here.

The numbers: on Amazon-3M, peak training memory falls from 46.3 to 13.5 GiB (3.4× versus their dense end-to-end baseline, 6.4× versus CascadeXML's 87 GiB) at P@1 50.2 versus 53.4 dense; on Amazon-670K at 83% sparsity, 11.5 → 3.7 GiB with P@1 47.1 versus 49.8. The honest comparison is against a dense bottleneck layer at matched parameter count, and there sparsity wins clearly: 47.0 versus 50.2 on Amazon-3M, 44.5 versus 47.1 on Amazon-670K. On the smallest dataset (Wiki10-31K, 92% sparsity) the sparse model actually beats dense, 88.6 versus 87.8, which they attribute to regularisation given how few training points there are per label. RigL, run as a conceptual control, is both worse in accuracy and — being mask-simulated — worse in memory than dense (12.4 versus 11.5 GiB on Amazon-670K), which is a neat in-paper illustration of the premise that most DST literature has never cashed its memory cheque.

The clever bit. The genuinely interesting finding is not the kernel engineering but the failure mode they isolate. Naively swapping in a fixed fan-in SET classifier does not degrade gracefully as the label space grows — it collapses, and it collapses in the encoder, not in the head. Table 5 is startling: on Amazon-670K at fan-in 64 (92% sparsity), P@1 is 30.7 without their fix and 42.3 with it; at fan-in 32 (96%), it is 5.5 versus 38.4. A nearly complete training failure is converted into something within striking distance of dense. Their diagnosis is that the sparse classifier is a bad gradient conduit: the signal reaching the transformer is too weak and too noisy early in training to shape representations, so the encoder never learns features that the sparse head could exploit, and the whole thing deadlocks.

The fix is the clever inversion. Rather than fixing the classifier, they borrow the meta-classifier (cluster-level shortlisting head) that nearly every XMC pipeline already has, and re-interpret its function: not as a retrieval mechanism, but as a gradient pump for the encoder. The supporting experiment (Appendix E) is the part I would actually cite. They take LightXML, randomly shuffle its balanced k-means label clusters until overlap with the originals is under 3.5%, and retrain. Final extreme-task precision is essentially unchanged; only the meta-classifier's own precision degrades and early learning slows. In other words, the semantic quality of the label partition — the thing a decade of PLT/label-tree work has optimised — is largely irrelevant to final accuracy, and what the meta-classifier contributes is a dense, low-variance, coarse-grained loss surface that lets gradients reach the encoder. Hence the auxiliary objective: a dense classifier over label clusters, trained jointly, with a decaying weight.

Two details make it more than a trick. First, the auxiliary head must be switched off: Table 6 shows that keeping it for all of training is worse than never using it at all (42.1 versus 45.6 at 83% sparsity; 22.7 versus 30.7 at 92%), because the cluster task is misaligned with the extreme task and eventually corrupts the shared encoder — so the aux loss is scaffolding, not a multi-task regulariser. Second, the architectural prescription is scale-dependent (Figure 1): at a few thousand labels bare sparsity suffices, at ~31K an intermediate layer following Schultheis & Babbar (2023) is enough, and only past ~100K labels is the auxiliary head necessary.

There is a real limit on what the paper settles, though. The gradient-flow story is supported by one encoder-gradient-norm plot and the Appendix E ablation — suggestive, not decisive, and it does not separate "sparse topology blocks gradient" from "the sparse head is simply underfit early, so its gradients are uninformative regardless of connectivity." The paper also reports no error bars (the checklist says so explicitly), reports no dense-baseline epoch time against which to read its own 11–18 minute epochs, needs roughly 2× the optimisation steps of dense (Amazon-3M takes 72 hours), and measures "commodity hardware" by max_memory_allocated on an A100 rather than by running on a consumer GPU. Tail-label results are mixed rather than good: SPARTEX beats the matched bottleneck everywhere on PSP@k, but trails dense on Amazon-670K (29.9 versus 33.3 PSP@1) and Amazon-3M (14.3 versus 15.6). And there is a genuine internal inconsistency: Table 2 lists Amazon-3M at 83% sparsity while the hyperparameter table (Table 9) gives fan-in 256, i.e. 67%, for that dataset — so the headline 3.4× saving may be at a lower sparsity than the main table implies. A fair summary is that maybe 60% of the contribution is systems work (kernels, ELLPACK layout, exploiting hinge-loss activation sparsity in the backward pass, since fixed fan-in gives no direct benefit to the transposed matmul) and 40% is the genuinely transferable scientific observation about what meta-classifiers are for.

No proof sketch. The paper contains no theorem, formal claim, or derivation — its NeurIPS checklist states outright that "there are no formal results proved or claimed." The memory accounting (the 12.5% index overhead, the 12 GB dense-layer figure) is arithmetic, and the gradient-flow argument is purely empirical.

Broader context. XMC is the supervised cousin of retrieval: given a short text (a product title, a Wikipedia page name), predict a handful of relevant items from a space of 10⁵–10⁷, where the label distribution is brutally long-tailed, positives are missing at scale, and most labels have single-digit training examples (Amazon-670K averages 3.99 points per label). The field's two historical responses were sparse linear models (DiSMEC, PD-Sparse, Parabel) and tree/shortlisting architectures that avoid computing all L logits — AttentionXML, LightXML, XR-Transformer, CascadeXML on the featureless side, and SiameseXML, NGAME, DEXML on the "label features" side where labels have their own text and the model becomes a bi-encoder with an ANN index. Renee (Jain et al., MLSys 2023) showed that if you simply have enough GPUs, brute-force end-to-end training of the full dense head beats all the clever modular pipelines; this paper is the memory-constrained answer to Renee, and the direct predecessor is Schultheis & Babbar (ECML 2023), which did DST on the extreme layer but only over frozen embeddings — Table 7 quantifies what that cost: end-to-end training gains 4.5 P@1 on Amazon-670K and 3.1 on Wiki-500K over fixed CascadeXML features. On the sparsity side the lineage is SET (Mocanu et al., Nature Comms 2018) → RigL (Evci et al. 2020) → ITOP (Liu et al. 2021), with the gradient-flow-in-sparse-networks line (Evci, Ioannou, Keskin & Dauphin, AAAI 2022) being the conceptual ancestor of this paper's diagnosis, and "Sparsity May Cry" (Liu et al. 2023) the cautionary work arguing that DST methods which shine on CIFAR/ImageNet fail on harder tasks — XMC being offered here as exactly such a stress test.

An obvious follow-up: the paper's own conclusion flags combining DST with explicit hard-negative mining, but the sharper question is whether the auxiliary head can be replaced by something principled — e.g. a learned dense low-rank residual to the sparse head (a sparse-plus-low-rank classifier, which would give dense gradient paths by construction without a misaligned task to anneal away), or a bandit/active criterion for regrowth that uses tail-label statistics instead of uniform random regrowth. The Figure 4 result that P@1 and PSP@1 diverge as the rewiring interval grows (longer intervals hurt head labels but keep helping tail labels, because each topology gets more exposure to rare positives) suggests the rewiring schedule should be per-label and propensity-aware, which nobody has done.

The connection to your own work is structural rather than cosmetic. An XMC classification layer with L labels in R^d is a dense retrieval index: a matrix of L learned vectors scored by inner product against a query embedding, and in the label-feature regime (SiameseXML, NGAME) the distinction dissolves entirely into a bi-encoder plus ANN. Read that way, fixed fan-in sparsity is a statement that each document/label vector lives in a d′-dimensional coordinate subspace chosen per item, with the subspace itself learned by prune-and-regrow — which is conceptually adjacent to inverted-file structures (an item is reachable only through the posting lists it occupies) and to the sparsity-of-connectivity logic in graph ANN. The memory-versus-recall tradeoff curve here (Table 5: 7.03 GiB / P@1 49.0 at 50% sparsity down to 2.52 GiB / P@1 5.5 at 96% without the fix) is recognisably the same object as the compression-versus-recall curve in PQ/OPQ or in learned sparse retrieval, and SPARTEX's claim is essentially that learned, trained-in coordinate sparsity dominates post-hoc dimensionality reduction at equal budget — which is precisely the dense-bottleneck comparison, and precisely the claim one would want to make theoretically about trained versus oblivious sketches of an index.

The generative-retrieval link is looser but real: a docid vocabulary of millions of atomic identifiers is the same giant output embedding matrix, and the paper's finding that gradient flow from that matrix into the encoder is the binding constraint at scale speaks to why GR models with atomic docids train poorly and why hierarchical/semantic docids (which are, functionally, exactly this paper's cluster-level auxiliary task made permanent) help. The non-obvious transfer is the Appendix E result: if the semantic quality of a label partition contributes little beyond a gradient path, then part of the benefit attributed to semantic docid construction in GR may be optimisation scaffolding rather than representation, and would be testable by the same randomised-cluster ablation. I would be cautious about pushing the analogy to the point of claiming anything about inference-time ANN structure, though — this paper never computes approximate top-k; it scores all L labels with a sparse matmul, so it says nothing about sublinear search, only about where the parameters live.

title: A Theoretical Study on Bridging Internal Probability and Self-Consistency for LLM Reasoning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-20

1. A Theoretical Study on Bridging Internal Probability and Self-Consistency for LLM Reasoning

Zhou, Tan, Li, Yao, Guo, Li & Ma — 2025 — arXiv:2510.15444

Main idea. Sampling-based test-time scaling — draw n reasoning paths, score them, pick the best answer — works well empirically but has almost no theory behind it. This paper (NeurIPS 2025) recasts the whole family as a confidence estimation problem: each method is an estimator p̂(ŷ|x) of the LLM's true answer-level probability, and performance is measured by the squared error E[(p̂(ŷ|x) − 1[ŷ=y])²], with the expectation over the n sampled paths. That quantity splits into an estimation error (how far the finite-sample estimate is from the true confidence) and a model error (how far the LLM's true confidence is from correctness — fixed by the model, not the scaling method). Under this lens, self-consistency is a Monte-Carlo frequency estimator: unbiased, but its estimation error is pure variance p(1−p)/n, i.e. only Θ(1/n). Perplexity instead reads the LLM's internal sequence probability off the sampled paths, which decays exponentially in n — but it scores paths rather than answers, so it inherits a large model error (equivalent-but-textually-different solutions are never pooled), and its exponent is ∝ p(t̂|x), so it collapses back to linear when probabilities are tiny.

The proposed fix is Reasoning-pruning Perplexity Consistency (RPC). Perplexity Consistency (PC) sums internal path probabilities over the unique sampled paths grouped by answer — a probability-weighted vote, which keeps SC's answer-level consistency function (hence SC's model error) while getting PPL's exponential rate. Reasoning Pruning (RP) then zeroes out low-probability answers to escape the degenerate regime, choosing the threshold by fitting a two-component Weibull mixture to the per-question score distribution (borrowed from open-set recognition) and discarding paths with P_high < 0.5, unioned with a truncated-mean floor. Empirically, on four math benchmarks with InternLM2-Math-Plus 7B, RPC matches SC's best accuracy with 50–71% fewer samples, and at equal budget gains +1.29 accuracy points on average with slightly lower ECE; gains transfer to code (HumanEval/MBPP/APPS), GPQA/LogiQA, and an R1-distilled model.

Critique. The framing is the paper's real contribution and it is genuinely good: "SC estimates a frequency, PPL reads a probability" is the right way to see why one is 1/n and the other is e^(−cn), and the observation that PPL's weakness is where the estimand lives (paths, not answers) rather than the scoring signal itself is sharp and actionable. PC is the obvious-in-hindsight product of that observation. The paper is also honest about the degeneration regime instead of hiding it.

But the formal apparatus is looser than the "first theoretical framework" claim suggests. Proposition 1's decomposition requires the estimator to be unbiased — that's exactly what kills the cross term. Yet both PPL and PC are explicitly biased (the paper computes the bias itself, E[p̂^PPL − p] = −(1−p)^n p), so for those methods the term labelled "Estimation Error" is not E[(p̂−p)²] at all but a mixture of second moment and surviving cross term. The consequence is visible on the page: for any wrong answer the PPL and PC "estimation errors" come out negative. A decomposition with a negative error component is not a bias–variance decomposition; it is an algebraic rearrangement being read as one. Relatedly, Theorem 4's headline that PC "maintains SC's model error" is near-tautological: model error is defined as (p(ŷ|x) − 1[ŷ=y])², which does not depend on the estimator, so any answer-level method inherits it. The one substantive model-error claim is Proposition 4 (SC's model error ≤ PPL's), and it holds only under n→∞ plus the assumption that every incorrect path yields a unique answer — which is precisely the assumption that makes consistency pooling costless.

There is also arithmetic I could not reconcile. In the appendix (A.3), Eq. 27 gives E[(p̂^PC − p)²] = (1−q)q p² with q = (1−α)^n; that expression is the variance of p̂^PC, not its MSE, which should additionally carry the bias² term q²p². Sanity check: at k=1 PC reduces exactly to PPL, yet Eq. 16's PPL MSE is q p², not q(1−q)p² — the two results disagree by q²p² in a case where they must coincide. Theorem 7 is worse off. Its proof applies Hoeffding to the mean of retained path probabilities with range p(ŷ|x) and deviation γ = τ − p(ŷ|x)/k, which yields exp(−2k̂γ²/p²) = exp(−(2k̂/k²)(1 − τ/(1−α))²) — the theorem statement has k² in the numerator. The event on the left of Eq. 31 is written as a deviation ≥ τ while γ is what is actually substituted. The two definitions of α (1 − p/k in the main text, p/k in the appendix) are used interchangeably mid-proof. Eq. 29–30 multiply both error terms by the indicator 1[p(ŷ|x) < τ], i.e. the indicator points the wrong way (errors should survive for retained answers), and an unexplained τ/m appears with m undefined (it was path length in §2.1). Most importantly, the theorem is not restricted to ŷ ≠ y: with τ = p(y|x) and the estimator centred at p(ŷ|x)/k, the bound applies with γ > 0 to the correct answer too, so read literally it guarantees everything gets pruned. And the oracle threshold τ = p(y|x) is unknowable, while the deployed heuristic is a Weibull-mixture fit with a 0.5 posterior cut; Theorem 7 therefore provides no guarantee for the algorithm actually run. (The variables Ω₁, Ω₂ in §3.2 are never defined, and the SC/PPL citations are swapped in §2.1 and §4.1.)

The deepest gap is between p(t|x) in the theory and the score in the code. The exponent (1 − p/k)^n is meaningful only if p(t|x) is the true sequence probability — it is literally the chance of never sampling that path. But a true sequence probability for a multi-hundred-token CoT is e^(−O(100)), which puts every problem in the np ≪ 1 degenerate regime, and Figure 1's illustrative path scores (16%, 25%, 45%, 80%, 85%) sum to well over 1 and are therefore length-normalized perplexity-style scores, not sampling probabilities. Figure 1 also divides the accumulated scores by their sum over the retained set, so the deployed estimator is a normalized weighted vote — a different estimator from the unnormalized sum that Theorem 4 analyses, and one whose missing-mass bias is partly cancelled by the normalization. The paper never states how p_i is computed. Without that, the quantitative theory and the method are only loosely coupled.

Evaluation is solid in breadth, thin where it matters most for a convergence-rate paper. Nothing measures estimation error versus n directly — the authors say ground-truth p is impractical, which is fair, but then the exponential-vs-linear claim is only ever probed through accuracy curves that saturate, and through ECE, where PPL's values (49–89) are so pathological that the comparison is uninformative and RPC's edge over SC is marginal (13.37 vs 12.37 average). Table 1, the cleanest test of PC alone, shows a 50% budget reduction on only two of four datasets and 0% on the other two; the paper reads that as confirming both the fast rate and the degeneration, which is close to unfalsifiable. Gains on OlympiadBench (11.07±0.15 → 11.14±0.15) and AIME (9.40 → 9.74) are within a couple of seed-level standard deviations, and the reported deviations are over 10 sampling seeds, not over problems, so no per-problem significance is established. The main models are weak 2024-era math-tuned 1.8B/7B checkpoints (AIME accuracy ~9%); the modern-model and strong-baseline experiments (ESC, Best-of-N with Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B) are relegated to the appendix at n=16, where BoN-with-PRM actually loses to plain SC on three of four datasets — a result that deserves discussion rather than a compatibility claim. And the most natural baseline, the probability-weighted majority vote from the original self-consistency paper, is never named as such even though PC is essentially it.

Proof sketch. Four results. Proposition 1 is the decomposition: add and subtract p(ŷ|x) inside the square, expand, and show the cross term 2E[(p̂−p)(p−1[ŷ=y])] vanishes because p−1 is deterministic and E[p̂−p]=0 for an unbiased estimator. One line, and the unbiasedness hypothesis is load-bearing (see above). Proposition 2 instantiates it for SC: p̂^SC is a sample mean of Bernoulli(p(ŷ|x)) indicators, so the estimation error is exactly the binomial variance p(1−p)/n — linear in 1/n. Proposition 3 does PPL. Here the estimator is "report p(t̂|x) if t̂ was sampled, else 0", i.e. p̂^PPL = p·B with B the indicator that t̂ appears among n draws, P(B=0) = (1−p)^n. So E[p̂−p] = −(1−p)^n p and E[(p̂−p)²] = (1−p)^n p², giving the stated (1−p)^n p(2·1 − p) after folding in the non-vanishing cross term. Theorem 4 does PC. Assume the n sampled paths are distinct (stated) and — this is implicit and never stated — that the k paths mapping to ŷ each carry equal mass p(ŷ|x)/k. Then p̂^PC = (p/k)Z where Z counts how many of the k paths were observed, each observed with probability 1 − (1 − p/k)^n. Hence E[p̂^PC] = (1 − α^n)p with α = 1 − p(ŷ|x)/k, and the estimation-error term comes out as α^n p(2·1 − (1+α^n)p). Theorem 7 is a Hoeffding tail on the empirical mean of the retained paths' probabilities around p(ŷ|x)/k, giving a guarantee that the pruning decision at the oracle threshold τ = p(y|x) is the optimal one. Proposition 4 (model errors) is the only genuinely non-mechanical argument: it compares the empirical sums at n→∞ and, for the correct answer, applies a power-mean/Cauchy–Schwarz step Σ p̂(t)² ≥ p̂^SC(y)²/C with C the number of paths reaching y; writing B = p̂^SC(y) the difference factorizes as (1/C)(C − B²)(1 − C) ≤ 0, strict as soon as C > 1. For wrong answers the uniqueness assumption makes the difference exactly zero. So the whole model-error advantage of consistency is, in this idealization, the convexity gap from splitting mass across equivalent correct paths.

Where does the exponent come from? Not from concentration — from missing mass. The only randomness that matters in PC and PPL is whether a given reasoning path was sampled at all; conditional on being sampled, its weight p(t|x) is read off exactly rather than estimated by counting. The estimator therefore has (almost) no sampling variance, and its entire error is the probability mass of the unseen support, which for a path of mass p/k is missed with probability (1 − p/k)^n ≈ e^(−np/k). That is a coupon-collector exponent np(ŷ|x)/k, and it immediately explains the degeneration: when np ≪ 1 the exponential is still in its linear regime, 1 − α^n ≈ np/k, so you have bought nothing over SC — you simply have not collected the coupon yet. The real trick, stated more plainly than the paper states it, is replacing a Monte-Carlo frequency estimate of a probability with an exact evaluation of it on the observed support — trading Θ(1/n) variance for a one-sided e^(−np/k) bias. Dividing by k is also the hidden cost: the more distinct ways there are to reach the right answer, the thinner each path's mass and the slower the exponent, which is exactly the regime in which SC's pooling is most valuable. That tension between the consistency function (which wants many equivalent paths) and the exponent (which punishes them) is visible in the algebra but not discussed.

Broader context. Test-time scaling is the practice of spending inference compute instead of training compute: sample many chains of thought and aggregate. Self-consistency (Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models, ICLR 2023) is the canonical aggregator — plain majority vote over extracted answers; notably, that paper already ablated a probability-weighted vote and found it roughly on par with unweighted, which is worth holding next to PC's claimed gains. Best-of-N instead scores candidates with an external verifier or reward model (Cobbe et al. 2021; Lightman et al., Let's Verify Step by Step, 2023; Snell et al. 2024 on compute-optimal allocation), and Brown et al.'s Large Language Monkeys (2024) characterized the coverage-versus-n power law that makes sampling pay off at all. Perplexity-based confidence is the cheap internal alternative: no verifier, just the model's own likelihood, with the known pathology that likelihood is dominated by length and surface form (Holtzman et al., Surface Form Competition, EMNLP 2021 — the PMI-DC correction is addressing the very model error this paper's consistency function addresses). The efficiency line this paper's Table 1 competes with is early-stopping/adaptive sampling: Aggarwal et al.'s Adaptive-Consistency (EMNLP 2023) and Li et al.'s ESC (Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency, ICLR 2024). Closest in spirit on the empirical side are the 2025 works the paper cites as corroborating its insight — DeepConf (Deep Think with Confidence) and CISC (Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs) — both of which weight or filter votes by internal confidence; this paper is best read as the theory those papers lacked. For theory of the Best-of-N side specifically, Beirami et al.'s analysis of the BoN policy's KL cost is the natural companion.

The obvious follow-up is to take the missing-mass framing literally. PC's error is the unseen mass of the answer's path set, which is exactly the quantity Good–Turing estimates, with distribution-free concentration available (McAllester–Schapire, 2000). That gives a computable debiasing — add an estimate of the unseen mass, or report an interval — and, better, an adaptive stopping rule: keep sampling until the Good–Turing missing-mass estimate for the current top-1 answer is small enough that no competitor can overtake it. That would be a principled version of ESC derived from this paper's own exponent, and it would also sidestep the Weibull heuristic entirely. A second, more basic follow-up: the paper's loss is squared error on confidence, and nothing in it bounds the probability that argmax p̂(ŷ|x) is correct. Since PC is biased downward by a factor (1 − α^n) whose magnitude depends on each answer's own p/k, the bias is non-uniform across candidates and can in principle flip the argmax — a genuine selection-error analysis (regret of the top-1 decision, not MSE of the score) is the missing theorem.

For your own work the link is real, not forced, in two places. First, generative retrieval: ranking docids by sequence likelihood is structurally the same estimation problem, and PC is essentially a sampling-based, beam-search-free ranker — draw docid strings, read their exact sequence probabilities, pool over strings that denote the same document. The k in α = 1 − p/k is then identifier multiplicity: whenever a document is reachable through several surface forms or several semantic-ID paths (multi-view identifier schemes à la MINDER, or hierarchical/residual-quantized identifiers as in RIPOR), the consistency function g is the docid-normalization map and the theory says exactly how the sampling budget must scale with multiplicity — n ≳ k/p — before probability-summing beats counting. That is a cleaner statement of the "aggregate over identifier surface forms" problem than most GR papers make, and the unresolved length-normalization issue here is the same raw-vs-normalized-likelihood question GR has to settle when scoring identifiers of different lengths. Second, and more loosely, Theorem 7's shape — prune candidates whose estimated score is below a threshold, with a high-probability guarantee that the true winner survives — is the same shape as safe-pruning/probabilistic-recall bounds in top-k retrieval (WAND/MaxScore-style thresholding) and in ANN candidate generation; the honest version of this paper's theorem would be a recall-at-threshold bound of exactly that kind, and the ANN literature's versions are tighter. The estimation-vs-modeling split also maps onto score-calibration and rank-fusion analyses, where one separates "our scores are noisy estimates" from "our scores rank the wrong things" — but that mapping is an analogy, not a transferable theorem, and I would not oversell it.

title: Dimension-Accuracy Tradeoffs in Contrastive Embeddings for Triplets, Terminals & Top-k Nearest Neighbors
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 19 October 2026

Dimension-Accuracy Tradeoffs in Contrastive Embeddings for Triplets, Terminals & Top-k Nearest Neighbors

Vaggos Chatziafratis, Piotr Indyk (2023) — arXiv:2312.13490

Main idea

The paper asks what happens to the metric-embedding dimension-reduction story when you throw away distance lengths and keep only distance order. Classical metric embedding asks for a map φ : (X,δ) → (R^d, ℓ₂) with small distortion, i.e. multiplicative control of ‖φ(x)−φ(y)‖ / δ(x,y); the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma says d = O(ε⁻² log n) buys 1±ε on all pairs. An ordinal (or non-metric) embedding, in the sense going back to Shepard and Kruskal and formalized here as Definition 1.1, instead demands only the equivalence δ(x,y) < δ(w,z) ⟺ ‖φ(x)−φ(y)‖ < ‖φ(w)−φ(z)‖ for all four-tuples; the ordinal dimension of X is the least d admitting such a map. Lengths are completely free — the embedding may be wildly non-isometric — so the constraint set is a system of strict inequalities, scale-invariant and invariant under any increasing reparametrization of δ. One might therefore expect ordinal embeddings to be much cheaper in dimension than metric ones. The paper's main message is that they are not.

The central new object is the triplet dimension (Definition 2.1). A map is triplet-preserving if it respects only the anchored comparisons: for all x,y,z, δ(x,y) < δ(x,z) ⟺ ‖φ(x)−φ(y)‖ < ‖φ(x)−φ(z)‖. These are exactly the crowdsourcing/contrastive queries "is x more similar to y or to z?", and there are ~n³/2 of them rather than the ~n⁴/8 unrestricted four-point comparisons. The triplet dimension of X is the least d for which a triplet ordinal embedding into R^d exists. The folklore upper bound is n−1 for any n-point metric (Bilu–Linial; Alon–Bădoiu–Demaine–Farach-Colton–Hajiaghayi–Sidiropoulos), so the only question is how far below n−1 one can go.

The approximate version uses Alon et al.'s ordinal relaxation α ≥ 1 (Definition 1.2): φ has relaxation α if α·δ(i,j) < δ(k,l) ⟹ δ′(i,j) < δ′(k,l). Equivalently, α is the largest ratio between two original distances whose relative order the embedding inverted. It is the ordinal counterpart of distortion, and is always at most the distortion, so Bourgain's O(log n)-distortion embedding of any n-point metric into ℓ₂ composed with JL yields relaxation O(log n) in dimension O(log n). The paper notes immediately why JL is useless for exact order preservation: ε must be smaller than the smallest relative distance gap, which can be O(1/n), so log n/ε² exceeds the trivial n−1.

Two localized variants complete the picture. A terminal ordinal embedding (Definition 2.2) fixes T = {t₁,…,t_k} ⊆ V and asks only that comparisons with both endpoints touching terminals be preserved: for all t,t′ ∈ T and x,x′ ∈ V∖T, δ(t,x) < δ(t′,x′) ⟺ the same in the image (including t = t′). Client–client distances are unconstrained. This is the ordinal analogue of Elkin–Filtser–Neiman-style terminal embeddings. A top-k-NN ordinal embedding (Definition 2.3) asks that, with NN(i) the k nearest neighbours of i, all comparisons δ(i,i′) vs δ(j,j′) with i′ ∈ NN(i), j′ ∈ NN(j) be preserved; the variant "without mixed comparisons" restricts to j = i, i.e. each point only needs its own k-NN list correctly ranked, with no cross-point calibration.

The results: triplet dimension can be forced above n/(2+κ) for any κ > 0 (Theorem 3.1), matching n−1 up to a factor 2; relaxation is at least log n/(log d + log log n + 8) − 1 at any dimension d (Theorem 3.3), nearly matching Bourgain+JL at d = Θ(log n); terminal ordinal embeddings admit a clean k-dimensional construction (Theorem 4.1) with matching Ω(k) lower bounds (Theorems 4.3–4.5); and top-k-NN preservation needs d = Ω(k), degrading to Ω(k log k / log n) without mixed comparisons (Theorem 5.1).

The most interesting part

The striking result is Theorem 3.1: exact triplet preservation forces d > n/(2+κ), which is within a factor of 2 of the trivial n−1 upper bound. There is no Johnson–Lindenstrauss phenomenon for ordinal constraints at all — not a weaker one, not one with worse constants, none. The whole log n/ε² world evaporates the moment you insist on exactness.

Why this is surprising deserves spelling out carefully, because the naive reading ("of course, JL fails since ε must be 1/poly(n)") undersells it. The real surprise is relative to what was already known. Bilu–Linial had shown, in the context of monotone maps and graph sphericity, that full ordinal dimension — preserving all ~n⁴ four-point comparisons — can be ~n/2. Triplet constraints are a factor-n smaller set, and they are structurally much weaker: they never compare δ(i,j) with δ(k,l) for disjoint pairs, so nothing calibrates the "distance scale" seen from vertex i against the one seen from vertex j. A triplet-preserving embedding only needs to realize n independent rankings-from-a-point, which feels like an almost decomposable problem. The theorem says this relaxation of the constraint system buys nothing, not even in the leading constant: you are still stuck at n/2.

The intuition for the lower bound is an entropy-versus-capacity count, and it is instructive that the binding quantity is not the number of constraints but the number of distinguishable outcomes. The number of distinct realizable triplet orders is at least Barnes' G-function G(n+1) = 0!·1!⋯(n−1)!, whose logarithm is (1+o(1))·(n²/2)·log n: vertex 1 can rank the other n−1 points in any of (n−1)! ways, vertex 2 can then rank the remaining n−2 freely, and so on. (Realizability is cheap — any symmetric array with values in [1,2] is a metric — so one really can hit all of these.) On the other side, a d-dimensional configuration is a point X ∈ R^{nd}, and which triplet order it realizes is determined by the sign pattern of the ~n³/2 quadratic polynomials p_{ijk}(X) = ‖x_i−x_j‖² − ‖x_i−x_k‖². Milnor–Thom-type bounds (via Alon–Frankl–Rödl) cap the number of sign patterns of m degree-2 polynomials in ℓ variables at exp(Õ(ℓ)) when m is polynomial in ℓ, here exp((1+o(1))·nd·log n). So nd·log n ≳ (n²/2)·log n, and since both sides carry the same log n factor, the constants are directly comparable: d ≳ n/2. The configuration space of R^d simply does not have enough combinatorial cells to host all the triplet orders. Note the pleasing asymmetry: n³ constraints but only n² log n bits of entropy — triplet orders are hugely redundant under transitivity, and it is the entropy, not the constraint count, that sets the dimension.

Relaxation then buys everything, and the tradeoff curve is brutally steep. Inverting Theorem 3.3, relaxation α requires roughly log d ≳ log n/(α+1), i.e. d ≳ n^{1/(α+1)} up to polylog factors. So constant ordinal relaxation already demands polynomial dimension — relaxation 1 needs ~n/2, relaxation ~1 needs ~√n, and only at α = Θ(log n/log log n) does d collapse to polylog, where Bourgain+JL matches up to a log log n. The exponential sensitivity of dimension to the relaxation parameter is the ordinal mirror of the isometric-versus-(1+ε) gap in metric embedding, but far sharper.

The localization results are the satisfying complement, because they say precisely where the hardness lives. For k terminals, k dimensions suffice and Ω(k) are necessary; for top-k-NN, Ω(k) are necessary. So the Ω(n) barrier is not about "ordering is hard" — it is about requiring every one of the n points to serve simultaneously as an anchor with a globally calibrated ranking. Restrict the anchors to k, or restrict each anchor's ranking to its k nearest neighbours, and the cost drops to Θ(k). I find the terminal upper bound (Theorem 4.1) especially illuminating as a conceptual statement: it embeds terminal t_i at −M·e_i and client v at the rank vector (r(t₁,v),…,r(t_k,v)), with M = k³n². This is not a geometric map of the source at all — it is a lookup table with ranks written into coordinates and a huge M making the whole configuration a needle-like simplex. Its metric distortion is astronomical and its ordinal fidelity is perfect. That is about as crisp a demonstration as one could want that ordinal and metric embedding are genuinely different problems rather than the same problem with a weaker norm on the error.

Honest weaknesses. Every lower bound in the paper is the same counting argument with different bookkeeping, inherited from Bilu–Linial and Alon–Frankl–Rödl; the technical novelty is concentrated in Theorem 3.3's high-girth random-subgraph construction. Consequently Theorem 3.1 is non-constructive: there is no explicit hard metric, only a pigeonhole over all triplet orders, and "which metrics have triplet dimension Ω(n)" remains open. There is no upper bound for triplets beyond folklore n−1, and no upper bound at all for top-k-NN, so the Ω(k) there is unmatched and could be far from the truth. The dominant-term comparisons are written informally with "≫", and the constants do not always check out — Theorem 4.3 states the condition as c > λ/(2λ−λ²), which at λ = 1 would give the vacuous d > n, whereas the equivalent form d > k(1−λ/2) and the claimed recovery of Bilu–Linial both require 2/(2λ−λ²). Finally, Theorem 3.3 is bottlenecked by Moore-bound-type girth constructions, as the authors acknowledge.

Broader context

The metric embedding tradition asks for maps into nice target spaces with controlled distortion. Bourgain (1985) showed every n-point metric embeds into ℓ₂ with distortion O(log n), and that this is tight for expanders (Linial–London–Rabinovich); Johnson–Lindenstrauss (1984) showed any n points in ℓ₂ embed into dimension O(ε⁻² log n) with distortion 1+ε, and Larsen–Nelson (2017) proved this dimension optimal even for nonlinear maps. Terminal embeddings sharpen JL to a one-sided, infinitely-many-query guarantee: Elkin–Filtser–Neiman introduced them; Mahabadi–Makarychev–Makarychev–Razenshteyn gave the first dimension bounds for preserving distances from all of R^D to a fixed n-point set; and Narayanan–Nelson showed the optimal O(ε⁻² log n) — the same as JL — suffices, with Cherapanamjeri–Nelson later making them computable in sublinear time. That is the lineage the present paper's Section 4 is the ordinal shadow of.

The ordinal side is older and much less developed theoretically. Torgerson, Shepard and Kruskal founded non-metric multidimensional scaling in the 1950s–60s on the premise that human judgments are reliable ordinally and unreliable cardinally. The modern theoretical strand includes Bilu–Linial's monotone maps and sphericity, Alon et al.'s and Bădoiu et al.'s introduction of ordinal relaxation and approximation algorithms for line and tree targets, Guruswami et al. and Chatziafratis–Makarychev on hardness of maximizing satisfied triplet constraints, and statistical work on sample complexity and consistency of ordinal embedding — Kleindessner–von Luxburg in particular, who studied uniqueness and the number of triplets needed to pin down a configuration, and Terada–von Luxburg on local ordinal embedding. On the algorithmic/empirical side, t-STE (van der Maaten–Weinberger), crowd-kernel learning (Tamuz et al.) and Jamieson–Nowak's adaptive triplet-query analyses are the standard references for learning embeddings from triplets at scale.

A natural follow-up: close the top-k-NN gap by combining the terminal rank-coordinate trick with a net/ball-carving decomposition, so that each group of points acts as terminals for its own neighbourhood — is Õ(k) dimension achievable, or does cross-group calibration (the "mixed comparisons" of Definition 2.3) force something larger? Equally natural, and more interesting to me, is to parameterize the hardness: what is the triplet dimension of metrics of doubling dimension λ, or of i.i.d. points on a low-dimensional manifold? Since the lower bound is pure counting over maximum-entropy adversarial metrics, it plausibly says nothing about structured instances, and an upper bound of the form f(doubling dimension) · polylog(n) would completely change the practical reading.

Connection to contrastive dual-encoder retrieval and vector search. This is where the paper is unusually directly relevant, and the authors say so (they use "contrastive embedding" and "ordinal embedding" interchangeably). A triplet loss or InfoNCE objective is literally a set of triplet ordinal constraints: "s(q,d⁺) > s(q,d⁻)", i.e. ‖φ(q)−φ(d⁺)‖ < ‖φ(q)−φ(d⁻)‖, anchored at the query. Theorem 3.1 is therefore a statement about the embedding dimension a dense retriever would need to satisfy all of its training triplets exactly: in the worst case, d > n/(2+κ). For unit-normalized encoders — the actual deployed regime, where ‖q−d‖² = 2−2⟨q,d⟩, so anchored distance comparisons are inner-product comparisons — the counting argument transfers essentially verbatim, since the spherical constraint only reduces the parameter count from nd to n(d−1). And Theorem 3.3, read as d ≳ n^{1/(α+1)}, is arguably the more apt statement for real training, because a margin-based loss is exactly an ordinal relaxation: tolerating inversions only among scores within a factor α of each other still costs polynomial dimension in the worst case.

This dovetails with the capacity/expressivity line in IR. Luan et al. (2021) analyzed the fixed-dimension bottleneck of bi-encoders and argued it is what multi-vector and sparse-attention representations are responding to; ColBERT's late interaction is the canonical architectural answer; and the recent "theoretical limitations of embedding-based retrieval" work (Weller et al., LIMIT) makes the barrier precise by tying the dimension needed to realize an arbitrary query-document relevance pattern to the sign rank of the qrel matrix, then exhibiting tiny corpora that break strong embedders. Chatziafratis–Indyk's counting bound is a complementary, ranking-flavored version of the same barrier: sign rank governs realizing a 0/1 relevance pattern, triplet dimension governs realizing a full order. Theorem 4.1 is the constructive bright spot in exactly the retrieval-shaped case: with k queries as terminals and n−k documents as clients, all query–document distance orders, globally comparable across queries, are realizable in k dimensions — and Theorems 4.3–4.5 say Ω(k) is needed, so "dimension ≈ number of queries you must serve exactly" is tight. A concrete follow-up in Shiguang's direction: push the Milnor–Thom counting through a ColBERT-style max-similarity score. A max of quadratics is piecewise polynomial, so the cell-counting machinery still applies with an extra factor for the pieces, and the prediction is capacity Õ(n·m·d) for m vectors of dimension d — meaning multi-vector models relieve the geometric bottleneck but not the information-theoretic one, which would be a sharp and checkable claim.

Two caveats on the mapping, which should be stated rather than glossed. First, worst case versus real data: the hard instances are maximum-entropy adversarial metrics, while real corpora are structured and low-intrinsic-dimensional, and empirically 768 dimensions retrieve over 10⁹ documents acceptably. Second, training triplets versus all triplets: a retriever sees a sparse, noisy, non-transitive subsample of O(n) to O(n log n) triplets, not all n³, and never needs them exactly — it needs the top-k order right. That is precisely the regime Theorem 5.1 and Theorem 4.1 identify as cheap, Θ(k) rather than Θ(n). So the correct takeaway is not "dense retrieval is doomed" but "the exact-and-global regime is provably Ω(n), the top-k-and-local regime is Θ(k), and real retrieval lives in the second" — with the uncomfortable corollary that benchmarks which demand globally calibrated cross-query scores, or exhaustive recall over adversarially constructed relevance patterns, push you toward the first.

Proof sketch

(a) The claims. Theorem 3.1 (triplet dimension). For every κ > 0 and all large n, there exist n-point metric spaces whose triplet order no embedding into ℓ₂^d can realize unless d > n/(2+κ). With the folklore n−1 upper bound this pins triplet dimension at Θ(n), tight to a factor 2. Remark 1 extends it to ℓ_p for fixed p ≥ 2 (the polynomials become degree p, which only perturbs lower-order terms). The witnessing family is not explicit — it is "most" triplet orders, obtained by pigeonhole.

Theorem 3.3 (dimension vs relaxation). There is an absolute constant c (c = 8 works) such that for every d and n there is an n-point metric T whose triplet relaxation under any embedding into ℓ₂^d is at least log n/(log d + log log n + c) − 1. Here the hard family is explicit: shortest-path metrics of random edge-subgraphs of a high-girth graph. Nearly tight at d = Θ(log n) against the O(log n) Bourgain+JL upper bound.

Theorem 4.1 + Lemma 4.2 (terminals, upper). For any X and any T of size k, there is a terminal ordinal embedding into R^k preserving every comparison between pairs (t,v) and (t′,v′) with t,t′ ∈ T. Theorems 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 (terminals, lower). For k = λn, d > k(1−λ/2) is necessary (λ = 1 recovers Bilu–Linial's n/2); for sublinear k = λn^{1−β}, d ≥ (1−ε)k is necessary, matching Theorem 4.1 exactly; and both bounds survive dropping all inter-terminal comparisons (t ≠ t′), so the hardness is already present in the k independent same-terminal rankings.

Theorem 5.1 (top-k-NN). Any top-k-NN ordinal embedding needs d = Ω(k); without mixed comparisons, d = Ω(k log k / log n). Lower bounds only — no matching upper bound is given.

(b) How they are proved.

The engine for all exact lower bounds is a sign-pattern counting (Milnor–Thom / Alon–Frankl–Rödl) argument, and the key lemma is Fact 2: for real degree-2 polynomials p₁,…,p_m in ℓ variables and any integer β ∈ [1,m], the number of realizable sign patterns is at most 4β·(8β−1)^{ℓ + m/β − 1}. The setup: an embedding is an n×d matrix X with rows x_i, flattened to ℓ = nd variables; each triplet (i,j,k) is resolved by the sign of the quadratic p_{ijk}(X) = ‖x_i−x_j‖² − ‖x_i−x_k‖², and the correspondence between sign patterns of {p_{ijk}} and induced triplet orders is one-to-one. The counting lemma is applied with m = n·C(n−1,2) ≈ n³/2 and β = μn for a large constant μ, giving log(#sign patterns) ≤ (nd + n³/(2μn))·log(8μn); setting n = cd, the dominant term is c·d²·log d. Against this stands Fact 1, the entropy of the problem: the number of distinct triplet orders is at least G(n+1) = ∏_{i=0}^{n−2} i!, with log G(n+1) = (n²/2)log n·(1+o(1)) = (c²d²/2)log d. Any c > 2 makes the entropy strictly exceed the capacity, so by pigeonhole two distinct triplet orders share a sign pattern, hence at least one is unrealizable in d = n/c < n/2 dimensions. The whole proof is this one comparison; the only delicate point is tuning β so that the m/β term stays below nd, which is why β is taken proportional to n (then m/β ≈ n²/(2μ) ≪ nd for μ large relative to c).

Theorem 3.3 is the genuinely new construction, because counting orders no longer suffices: for a relaxation bound you need many metrics that are pairwise far apart robustly, in the sense that any single embedding cannot serve two of them without inverting a pair of distances with a large ratio. The strategy: start from an unweighted graph G with girth g = log n/(log d + log log n + 8) and, by Erdős–Sachs/Sauer constructions, m = |E| ≥ ¼·n^{1+1/g} > 16nd·log n edges. Include each edge independently with probability ½ to generate N subgraphs G₁,…,G_N on the same vertex set, and aim for property (): for every pair G_i, G_j there is a witness_ vertex v with E_{G_i}(v) ∖ E_{G_j}(v) ≠ ∅ _and_ E_{G_j}(v) ∖ E_{G_i}(v) ≠ ∅. The point of (_) is geometric: if (v,u) ∈ G_i ∖ G_j then δ_{G_i}(v,u) = 1 while δ_{G_j}(v,u) ≥ g−1, because deleting an edge of a girth-g graph forces any replacement path to have length at least g−1. So a witness vertex certifies that G_i and G_j disagree, from v's perspective, on a triplet whose two distances differ by a factor ≥ g−1 — in opposite directions. If two such metrics are forced to share an embedding sign pattern, one of the two embeddings must have inverted a pair with ratio ≥ g−1, i.e. has relaxation ≥ g−1.

Lemma 3.5 is the key lemma making this go through, and its trick is handling dependence. For a fixed vertex v of degree k, Pr[v is not a witness] ≤ 2·(3/4)^k: the event E_{G_i}(v) ∖ E_{G_j}(v) = ∅ requires each incident edge to be either absent from G_i or present in both, probability ½ + ¼ = ¾ per edge independently. One would like to multiply over all vertices, but neighbourhoods share edges and G is not regular. The fix is a sequential edge-charging: fix an order v₁,…,v_n and let E′_G(v_i) = E_G(v_i) ∖ ⋃_{8^{nd j_wzxhzdk:0_=j log n} dwarfs the 2^{(2+o(1))nd log n} sign patterns of the n³/2 quadratics in nd variables, pigeonhole applies, and relaxation ≥ g−1 follows.

Theorem 4.1 is proved by explicit construction plus one dominance computation. Let r(t,v) ∈ {1,…,kn} be the rank of δ(t,v) among all kn terminal–client distances (ties broken to make ranks unique). Map t_i ↦ −M·e_i and v ↦ (r(t₁,v),…,r(t_k,v)). Then ‖f(v)−f(t)‖² = Σ_{s≠t} r(s,v)² + (r(t,v)+M)² = C(v) + 2M·r(t,v) + M², where C(v) = Σ_s r(s,v)² ≤ k·(kn)² = k³n². Lemma 4.2 observes that with M = k³n², the term 2M·r(t,v) moves by at least 2M = 2k³n² per unit of rank, which strictly exceeds the total possible spread of the C(v) "noise" across all v and t. Hence ‖f(v)−f(t)‖ < ‖f(v′)−f(t′)‖ ⟺ r(t,v) < r(t′,v′): every terminal–client comparison, including cross-terminal ones, is preserved, in k dimensions. Two things are worth noticing. The construction consumes only the global ranking of the kn terminal–client distances, not the metric — it is purely combinatorial, so it works for any ℓ_p with an appropriate M (Remark 2) — and it does not use that k is fixed, so it covers k = Θ(n) too.

The terminal lower bounds reuse the counting template with the constraint set shrunk. The number of distances that must be ordered is (n−1)+(n−2)+⋯+(n−k) ≈ kn − k²/2, so the entropy is ≈ (kn − k²/2)·log(kn − k²/2), while the number of comparison polynomials is m = C(kn−k²/2, 2) ≈ (k²n² − k³n + k⁴/4)/2 over nd variables, giving log(#sign patterns) ≈ (nd + m/(μn^x))·log n^x with a free parameter x. For k = λn (Theorem 4.3) one takes x = 2 and μ large, compares λ²n²·2log d-type leading terms, and extracts d > k(1−λ/2). For sublinear k = λn^{1−β} (Theorem 4.4) the k²/2 correction is o(kn) and therefore vanishes, and one can choose x with n^x ≈ kn = o(n²) so that m/(μn^x) ≪ nd for any constant μ; writing k = cd, the comparison becomes cdn·log(kn) versus (nd + cdn/(2μ))·log(kn), which favors the entropy exactly when c > 1 — hence d ≥ (1−ε)k, exactly matching Theorem 4.1. This is a nice structural point: the sublinear regime is cleaner precisely because the "diagonal" k²/2 correction and the m/β slack both become negligible, which is why the λ/2 loss at k = Θ(n) is an artifact of the argument rather than of the problem. Theorem 4.5 then drops inter-terminal comparisons and observes that the entropy barely changes: the k independent same-terminal rankings already give #orders ≥ ∏_{i=1}^k (n−i)!, with log ≈ (kn − k²/2)·log(n−k) and leading term kn·log n — the same as before — so the identical bounds with identical constants survive.

Theorem 5.1 is the same comparison once more, now over the distance set ⋃_i NN(i). With mixed comparisons, the number of orderings of this set is close to (nk − o(nk))!, so the entropy is ≈ nk·log n, while m = C(nk,2) polynomials over nd variables give, choosing n^x ≈ kn (so x ≤ 2), log(#sign patterns) ≈ ndx·log n. Entropy beats capacity when nk·log n ≫ ndx·log n, i.e. d = Ω(k). Without mixed comparisons each point contributes only k! orderings of its own neighbour list, total (k!)^{Θ(n)}, so the entropy drops to ≈ nk·log k and the same comparison yields only d = Ω(k log k / log n). The drop from log n to log k is exactly the cost of not having to calibrate different anchors' rankings against each other — a quantitative version of the qualitative point that the Ω(n) triplet barrier is about global cross-anchor consistency, not about ordering per se.

title: Circuit Complexity Bounds for RoPE-based Transformer Architecture
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 19 October 2026

Circuit Complexity Bounds for RoPE-based Transformer Architecture

Bo Chen, Xiaoyu Li, Yingyu Liang, Jiangxuan Long, Zhenmei Shi, Zhao Song (2024) — arXiv:2411.07602

Main idea

The paper asks whether Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) buys a Transformer any additional computational power, and answers no, in the precise sense of circuit complexity. The object of study is a RoPE-based Transformer in which every number is a $p$-bit floating point value $\langle m,e\rangle$ with significand $m\in(-2^p,-2^{p-1}]\cup{0}\cup[2^{p-1},2^p)$ and exponent $e\in[-2^p,2^p)$, and every arithmetic operation is the rounded float operation (Definitions 3.13–3.15, lifted verbatim from Chiang 2024). "poly($n$)-precision" means $p\le \mathrm{poly}(n)$ where $n$ is the sequence length — so the significand carries polynomially many bits and the exponent carries polynomially many bits too, giving dynamic range $2^{\pm 2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}}$. This is a strictly more generous model than the $O(\log n)$-precision regime of Merrill–Sabharwal, which matters because log-precision bounds are sometimes dismissed as artifacts of a model where softmax denominators collapse; here no such excuse is available. "$O(1)$ layers" means the number of blocks $m$ is a constant independent of $n$; "hidden dimension $d\le O(n)$" is needed only so that inner products over $d$ terms and $n\times d$ matrices stay polynomial-size.

The architecture itself (Definitions 3.21–3.27) is a single-head, unmasked attention stack: $A_{i,j}=\exp(X_{i,*}W_Q R_{j-i} W_K^\top X_{j,*}^\top)$ with $R_{j-i}$ the block-diagonal matrix of $2\times 2$ rotations $R((j-i)\theta_k)$, $k\le d/2$; $\mathrm{Attn}(X)=D^{-1}AXW_V$ with $D=\mathrm{diag}(A\mathbf 1_n)$; interleaved with generic blocks $g_i$ instantiated as an affine MLP $WX_{i,*}+b$ and a layer norm $(X_{i,*}-\mu_i)/\sigma_i$.

The complexity classes: $\mathsf{AC}^0$ is polynomial-size, constant-depth circuits with unbounded fan-in AND/OR/NOT; $\mathsf{TC}^0$ adds unbounded fan-in MAJORITY (equivalently threshold) gates; $\mathsf{NC}^1$ is polynomial-size, $O(\log n)$-depth, bounded fan-in circuits. The known containments are $\mathsf{AC}^0\subsetneq\mathsf{TC}^0\subseteq\mathsf{NC}^1$, and whether the second is strict is a long-standing open problem — we have no superpolynomial lower bounds against $\mathsf{TC}^0$ at all, which is exactly why every result in this literature is conditional. Uniformity is the other axis: a non-uniform circuit family has a different circuit per input length with no constraint relating them, so non-uniform classes contain undecidable languages and a non-uniform upper bound is a much weaker modelling claim. The paper works in DLOGTIME-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$: a random-access Turing machine must emit a description of $C_n$ from $1^n$ in $O(\log n)$ time. That is the right notion here for two reasons: it says the simulating circuit is itself effectively constructible from the architecture (so the bound is about the architecture, not about an oracle smuggled into the circuit family), and the known $\mathsf{NC}^1$-hardness of formula evaluation is hardness under DLOGTIME reductions (Buss's ALOGTIME-completeness of the Boolean Formula Value Problem), so the collapse argument lines up at the same uniformity level.

The main theorem (Thm 4.8) is that under these assumptions the forward map $\mathrm{TF}$ is computable by a DLOGTIME-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ family. The headline corollaries (Thms 5.8, 5.9) then say: unless $\mathsf{TC}^0=\mathsf{NC}^1$, such a Transformer cannot solve the Arithmetic Formula Evaluation problem (evaluate a formula over a semiring given the leaf constants) or the Boolean Formula Value problem (evaluate a fully parenthesised AND/OR/NOT formula). Both are $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete, so a $\mathsf{TC}^0$ device solving either would place all of $\mathsf{NC}^1$ inside $\mathsf{TC}^0$. Read correctly the claim is not "RoPE Transformers are weak" in any absolute sense — $\mathsf{TC}^0$ already contains majority, sorting, integer division, and plenty of nontrivial computation — but "a constant-depth RoPE forward pass cannot perform the $\Theta(\log n)$-depth sequential composition that formula evaluation demands, on pain of a collapse nobody expects."

Reviewer-style critique

The honest summary of the novelty is: one new lemma plus careful bookkeeping. Every floating-point ingredient — addition, multiplication, division, comparison, iterated product, iterated sum, $\exp$, $\sqrt{\cdot}$ in constant-depth uniform threshold circuits at $p\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$ — is imported wholesale from Chiang (2024) as Lemmas 3.16–3.19. The architecture-level lemmas (matrix product, attention matrix, attention layer, MLP, layer norm, composition) are the same depth-accounting exercise that Merrill–Sabharwal and Chiang already performed for vanilla softmax attention, with $W_QR_{j-i}W_K^\top$ substituted for $W_QW_K^\top$. The hardness section is three lines of citation plumbing against a template that Feng et al. (2023) had already instantiated for arithmetic and equation-solving.
