The genuinely new technical content is Lemma A.1: $\sin$ and $\cos$ of a $p$-bit float are computable in uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ — and even that is close to folklore, since Reif–Tate-style results on threshold-circuit approximation of elementary analytic functions long predate this, and the proof here is the obvious one (range reduction plus truncated Taylor series plus the iterated-product lemma). So: a correct, cleanly presented, and essentially predictable corollary of existing machinery. That is worth having in the literature; it is not worth the abstract's "significantly demonstrates the fundamental limitation."

The framing is the weakest part. "Empirical evidence suggests RoPE-based Transformers demonstrate greater generalization capabilities... in this work we establish a circuit complexity bound" sets up a tension that does not exist. Expressivity-under-fixed-depth and generalization are orthogonal: a hypothesis class can generalize better precisely because it is not more expressive, and nothing about membership in $\mathsf{TC}^0$ speaks to sample complexity, optimization, or length extrapolation. The paper never resolves or even acknowledges the non-sequitur; the Discussion's "our results suggest a potential gap between theoretical limitations and empirical performance" is a restatement of the confusion rather than an analysis of it. The result that is actually established, and which the paper should have led with, is the clean negative-but-useful one: RoPE buys no asymptotic expressive power over vanilla attention at constant depth and polynomial precision. That is a legitimate contribution — it tells you that whatever RoPE does for long-context performance, it is not an expressivity phenomenon, so explanations must be sought in optimization, conditioning, or extrapolation behaviour rather than in representational capacity. The paper gestures at this ("Does RoPE enhance the expressiveness?") but then spends its rhetoric on "RoPE is fundamentally limited," which is the less informative reading and invites the misinterpretation that something about RoPE in particular was shown to be weak.

There are also real technical soft spots. (i) Lemma A.1 claims relative error $2^{-p}$, but the proof only bounds the Lagrange remainder in absolute terms by $O(2^{-N})$ and never fixes $N$ as a function of $p$; relative error near the zeros of $\sin$ is simply not obtainable this way, and the rounding error of the float operations used to evaluate the Taylor sum is not accounted for at all. (ii) More seriously, there is no end-to-end error-propagation analysis. The float model of Definition 3.15 specifies exact rounded arithmetic, but $\sin$, $\cos$, $\exp$ and $\sqrt{\cdot}$ are only approximated, so the circuit does not compute the float-point Transformer as defined — it computes something near it, and the paper never states a composed error bound across $m$ layers. Chiang's paper, from which the lemmas are taken, does exactly this work; its omission here is the clearest sign that the depth bookkeeping was the focus and the numerics were taken on faith. (iii) There is no definition of what it means for a Transformer to solve the Boolean Formula Value problem: no token encoding of the input formula, no output-reading convention, no notion of language recognition. The hardness theorems are therefore formally statements about an undefined predicate; the fix is routine but it should have been written down. (iv) The architecture is thinner than the paper's rhetoric: no multi-head attention, no causal mask, no $1/\sqrt d$ scaling, no residual connections anywhere in Definition 3.25, and the "MLP" is purely affine with no nonlinearity. Lemma 4.7 is stated for a generic constant-depth $g_i$, so activations and residuals can be absorbed — but the reader has to notice that, and the Discussion's admission that the work "assumes constant-depth nonlinear activation functions" concedes the gap. (v) Uniformity of the weights is never discussed: for DLOGTIME-uniformity the entries of $W_Q,W_K,W_V$ and the frequencies $\theta_k$ must be generable in logarithmic time, and the range reduction needs the bits of $\pi$; these are the fiddly points where uniformity claims actually get earned, and they are skipped.

Finally, the usual and in my view decisive caveat: this is a bound on a fixed-depth, single forward pass, no-chain-of-thought computation. Nothing here constrains what a deployed LLM does at inference. Autoregressive decoding with $T$ steps is $T$ composed forward passes with the intermediate results written back into the input, and the Li–Liu–Zhang–Ma / Merrill–Sabharwal CoT results show this climbs the hierarchy fast: logarithmically many CoT steps already escape the constant-depth ceiling, and polynomially many reach $\mathsf P$. Formula evaluation with a scratchpad is easy for a small Transformer in practice. The paper cites the CoT literature in related work and then does not let it qualify its own conclusions. Likewise "$O(1)$ layers" is an asymptotic idealization: a 100-layer model is $O(1)$, but the depth budget $(m+1)d_g+7m(d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus)+m(d_\triangle+d_{\exp})$ has constants that are nowhere near tight and the theorem says nothing quantitative about any finite $n$. Writing quality reinforces the impression of haste: "Mssing proofs," "Buliding," "theoritical," "is in $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete," and a reference list in which several dozen entries on coresets, graph attention, looped transformers and attention acceleration from the same author group have no bearing on anything proved.

Broader context

The "expressivity of Transformers via circuit complexity" programme starts from a simple structural observation: a Transformer's forward pass is a constant number of layers, each of which is a parallel computation over the sequence — every token attends to every other token simultaneously, and the per-layer operations are inner products, sums, exponentials and divisions. Parallel-and-shallow is exactly what circuit classes measure, and the aggregation step (a weighted average over $n$ positions) is the canonical threshold-gate operation. So the natural home for a fixed-depth Transformer is $\mathsf{TC}^0$, and the research question becomes how tightly one can pin it there and what that rules out. Because $\mathsf{TC}^0\subseteq\mathsf{NC}^1$ with strictness open, the payoff always takes the form "unless a famous collapse occurs, no constant-depth Transformer solves this $\mathsf{NC}^1$-hard problem."

Two anchors are worth knowing. Merrill & Sabharwal are the central reference: they showed that depth-$d$, $O(\log n)$-precision softmax Transformers are simulable by DLOGTIME-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ circuits (and equivalently expressible in first-order logic with majority quantifiers, $\mathsf{FOM}$), which is the result the present paper reproves with RoPE and better precision. Their companion work on chain-of-thought is the necessary counterweight: $t(n)$ decoding steps buy roughly $t(n)$ extra depth, so $\log n$ steps reach around $\mathsf L$ and polynomially many reach $\mathsf P$ — the fixed-depth ceiling is a property of the single forward pass, not of the system. Second, Liu, Ash, Goel, Krishnamurthy & Zhang, "Transformers learn shortcuts to automata," gives the sharpest intuition for why $\log$ depth is the threshold: constant-depth Transformers can shortcut the iterated composition of a solvable semiautomaton, but simulating a non-solvable one (Barrington's $S_5$ word problem, which is $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete) provably requires depth growing with $n$ unless $\mathsf{TC}^0=\mathsf{NC}^1$. Worth also knowing: Hahn (2020), an unconditional and technique-wise orthogonal result — hard-attention Transformers cannot compute PARITY or $\mathrm{Dyck}_2$, proved by a Lipschitz/influence argument rather than circuit simulation; Chiang, Cholak & Pillay, which characterizes fixed-precision Transformers inside a counting logic and thereby gets exact formal-language separations rather than one-sided bounds; Peng, Narayanan & Papadimitriou (2024), which uses communication complexity to show single-layer multi-head attention cannot compose two functions unless heads $\times$ width scales with the domain — a width lower bound, complementary to the depth-flavoured ones and arguably more informative about real models; and Feng et al. (2023), whose "unless $\mathsf{TC}^0=\mathsf{NC}^1$, log-precision Transformers cannot do arithmetic evaluation or CFG membership" is structurally the identical theorem to this paper's, with position encoding unspecified.

One observation that the paper does not make but which I think is the most interesting thing in it: RoPE stays in $\mathsf{TC}^0$ because its rotation group is abelian. The relative rotation $R_{j-i}$ is given in closed form as a single rotation by angle $(j-i)\theta_k$, so the circuit evaluates one $\sin$/$\cos$ pair rather than an iterated product of $(j-i)$ matrices. Iterated products of $2\times 2$ integer matrices, and more generally word problems over non-solvable groups, are $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete. So if one designed a positional scheme whose relative transform were a non-commuting per-step rotation in $\mathrm{SO}(d)$ with no closed form for the composite, the natural simulation would break precisely at the step where RoPE's succeeds. That suggests a concrete follow-up: ask whether any positional scheme can provably exceed $\mathsf{TC}^0$ at constant depth, and whether non-abelian relative-position operators give a genuine expressivity separation from RoPE — and, dually, whether $\mathsf{TC}^0$ is simply too coarse a sieve to see positional encodings at all, in which case the honest research move is to drop class membership in favour of resource-sensitive bounds. A second, sharper follow-up targets RoPE specifically through its precision rather than its depth: with $\theta_k=10^{-4\cdot 2k/d}$ the longest wavelength is fixed, and at $p$-bit precision the rotation angles for sufficiently distant position pairs become indistinguishable. A lower bound of the form "a RoPE attention head at $p$-bit precision cannot distinguish relative offsets beyond $f(p,\theta)$" would be a real statement about RoPE, with direct bearing on length extrapolation, and would not be a restatement of the vanilla-attention result.

The connection to Shiguang's work is genuine and runs through generative retrieval. In a DSI-style system the decoder must emit a document identifier that is, semantically, the output of a search: the model is being asked to perform in one bounded computation what an index performs by traversal. The results here let one say something precise about where that is and is not plausible. On the permissive side, $\mathsf{TC}^0$ is comfortably rich enough for a flat lookup: computing $n$ inner products and taking an argmax is iterated addition plus comparison, i.e. exactly threshold-gate work, so a constant-depth attention layer can in principle implement in-context nearest-neighbour or maximum-inner-product search over a table presented in its context window. This is consistent with what is observed empirically about induction heads and in-context retrieval, and it means the paper's theorem is not evidence that "attention cannot do lookup." On the restrictive side, what $\mathsf{TC}^0$ cannot do (modulo the collapse) is iterated, data-dependent composition — pointer chasing, reachability in a forest, $\log n$-deep traversal of a hierarchy whose branch at each level depends on the previous one. That is structurally what traversing an inverted index, descending an HNSW graph, or beam-searching a hierarchical semantic identifier looks like. So the honest reading for generative retrieval is a depth-versus-decode-steps tradeoff: a hierarchical docid scheme (RQ-VAE semantic IDs, trie-constrained decoding) emits $O(\log N)$ tokens for a corpus of size $N$, and each emitted token is one constant-depth forward pass with the previous decisions written back into the context. That is not a tokenization convenience — it is a depth-amortization device, exactly the CoT mechanism by which Merrill–Sabharwal's extra steps buy extra circuit depth. The corollary one would like to prove is that an atomic-docid generative retriever, which must produce the identifier in a bounded number of steps, is strictly weaker than a hierarchical one at matched depth, for corpora whose relevant structure is genuinely $\Omega(\log N)$-deep. I want to be clear that this is suggestive and not proved by anything in this paper: no retrieval or MIPS problem is shown $\mathsf{NC}^1$-hard here, the hardness instances are formulas rather than index traversals, and the reduction from "index lookup" to "formula evaluation" is a research task, not a corollary. But the framing is sound and the Liu et al. solvable/non-solvable dichotomy gives a ready-made template for asking which index structures admit constant-depth shortcuts and which do not.

Proof sketch

(a) The precise claim. Theorem 4.8: let $\mathrm{TF}=g_m\circ\mathrm{Attn}_m\circ\cdots\circ g_1\circ\mathrm{Attn}_1\circ g_0$ be the RoPE Transformer of Definition 3.25, with each $g_i$ computable by a uniform threshold circuit of polynomial size and constant depth $d_g$. If the float precision satisfies $p\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$, the hidden dimension $d\le O(n)$, and the number of layers $m\le O(1)$, then the map $X\mapsto\mathrm{TF}(X)$ is computable by a DLOGTIME-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ family. What is guaranteed is only membership of the forward pass in that class — nothing about training, gradients, or autoregressive decoding, and (as noted) no explicit approximation guarantee relating the circuit's output to the idealised real-valued Transformer. Theorems 5.8/5.9 then add: since Arithmetic Formula Evaluation (Buss–Cook–Gupta–Ramachandran) and the Boolean Formula Value Problem (Buss, ALOGTIME-complete) are $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete, a RoPE Transformer in this regime solving either would give $\mathsf{NC}^1\subseteq\mathsf{TC}^0$, hence $\mathsf{TC}^0=\mathsf{NC}^1$ by the standard hierarchy. The conclusion is therefore strictly conditional, and irremovably so: we possess no unconditional lower bounds against $\mathsf{TC}^0$, which is exactly the frontier that Razborov–Rudich-style barriers guard.

(b) How it is proved. The strategy is a bottom-up simulation with explicit depth accounting, and the whole argument turns on one fact: at $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ precision, every primitive needed is constant-depth in the number of operands, so composing a constant number of them stays constant.

Step 1 — the floating-point toolkit. Lemma 3.16 (from Chiang, resting ultimately on Hesse's theorem that integer division and iterated product are in DLOGTIME-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$, with the earlier $\mathsf P$-uniform version due to Beame–Cook–Hoover) gives: addition, multiplication, division and comparison of two $p$-bit floats in depth $d_{\mathrm{std}}$; iterated multiplication of $n$ floats in depth $d_\otimes$; iterated addition of $n$ floats, rounded once at the end, in depth $d_\oplus$. The crucial point is that $d_\oplus$ and $d_\otimes$ do not grow with the number of summands/factors — this is what replaces the $\Omega(\log n)$ depth a naive accumulation tree would cost, and it is the single engine behind the whole result. Corollary 3.17 adds floor; Lemma 3.18 gives $\exp$ to relative error $2^{-p}$ in depth $d_{\exp}$ (Taylor series, with the terms' powers and factorials handled by iterated product and the sum by iterated addition); Lemma 3.19 gives $\sqrt{\cdot}$ in depth $d_{\mathrm{sqrt}}$. Note that the generous exponent range ($e\in[-2^p,2^p)$) is what lets $\exp$ be computed without the usual max-subtraction trick: softmax logits cannot overflow the representable range.

Step 2 — trigonometry (Lemma A.1, the only new lemma). For $x\in\mathbb F_p$, set $k=\lfloor x/(\pi/2)\rfloor$ and reduce to $r=x-k\pi/2$ if that is $\le\pi/4$, else $r=(k+1)\pi/2-x$, so $|r|\le\pi/4$. Then evaluate the truncated Taylor series $\sum_{i<N}(-1)^ir^{2i+1}/(2i+1)!$ and $\sum_{i<N}(-1)^ir^{2i}/(2i)!$, with Lagrange remainder bounded by $(\pi/4)^{2N+1}/(2N+1)!\le 1/(2N+1)!=O(2^{-N})$ because the reduced argument is inside the unit interval. Finally a comparison selects whether $\sin(x)$ equals $\sin(r)$ or $\cos(r)$ (and symmetrically for $\cos$), using the quadrant parity recovered from $k$. The circuit-depth accounting: $2d_{\mathrm{std}}$ for $k$ (division and floor), $4d_{\mathrm{std}}$ for $r$ (addition, comparison, multiplication, division), then $3d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\otimes+d_\oplus$ for the series — each term needs a multiplication, a division, and an iterated product for $r^{2i+1}$ and $(2i+1)!$, all in parallel across $i$, with one iterated addition to combine — and $d_{\mathrm{std}}$ for the final selection, giving $d_\triangle=8d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus+d_\otimes$. The soft spots noted above live here: $N$ is never tied to $p$, the relative-error claim is not what the absolute remainder bound delivers, and the bits of $\pi$ needed for range reduction are assumed available. Mitigating fact specific to RoPE: the arguments actually arising are $(j-i)\theta_k$ with $|j-i|\le n$ and $\theta_k\le 1$, so the range-reduction is over a $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-bounded argument and the Payne–Hanek-style catastrophe that afflicts general large-argument reduction does not arise.

Step 3 — matrix products (Lemma B.1). $(AB)_{i,j}=\sum_{d k\le}A_{i,k}B_{k,j}$: all $d$ products in parallel at depth $d_{\mathrm{std}}$, then one iterated addition at depth $d_\oplus$, all $n_1n_2$ entries in parallel. Total $d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus$, size polynomial because $n_1,n_2,d\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$. This is where $d\le O(n)$ is used.

Step 4 — the RoPE attention matrix (Lemma B.2). For each pair $(i,j)$: compute all entries of $R_{j-i}$ in parallel at depth $d_\triangle$ (this is the only place RoPE differs from vanilla attention — and note the structural reason it is cheap: $R_{j-i}$ is block-diagonal with $d/2$ independent $2\times 2$ blocks whose angles are given in closed form as $(j-i)\theta_k$, so no iterated matrix product is required, only one angle multiplication per block); then the chain $W_QR_{j-i}$, then $(W_QR_{j-i})W_K^\top$, then contracting with $X_{i,*}$ and $X_{j,*}^\top$ — four matrix multiplications, hence $4(d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus)$; then $\exp$ of the resulting logit at depth $d_{\exp}$. Total $4(d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus)+d_\triangle+d_{\exp}$, with all $n^2$ entries computed in parallel so the depth does not multiply.

Step 5 — one attention layer (Lemma 4.4). $D=\mathrm{diag}(A\mathbf 1_n)$ is one iterated addition per row ($d_\oplus$); $AXW_V$ is two more matrix products ($2(d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus)$); the final $D^{-1}\cdot(AXW_V)$ is a parallel array of float divisions ($d_{\mathrm{std}}$). Folded in with Step 4, the layer costs $7(d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus)+d_\triangle+d_{\exp}$.

Step 6 — the non-attention blocks. The affine MLP is a matrix product plus a bias addition: $2d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus$ (Lemma B.3). Layer norm needs $\mu_i$ ($d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus$ — one iterated addition and a division by $d$), $\sigma_i^2$ ($2d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus$), then a square root and a division ($2d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_{\mathrm{sqrt}}$), totalling $5d_{\mathrm{std}}+2d_\oplus+d_{\mathrm{sqrt}}$ (Lemma B.4). Both are per-row and hence fully parallel over $i\in[n]$.

Step 7 — composition and the depth ledger (Lemma B.5, Thm 4.8). Layers compose sequentially, so depths add: $(m+1)d_g+7m(d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus)+m(d_\triangle+d_{\exp})$ with $d_\triangle=8d_{\mathrm{std}}+d_\oplus+d_\otimes$. Every constituent constant is independent of $n$ (that is the content of Step 1), and the number of layers is $m=O(1)$ by hypothesis, so the sum is $O(1)$ while size stays $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. Uniformity is inherited: each sub-circuit is DLOGTIME-uniform and the wiring pattern of the composition is a fixed, logarithmic-time-describable template indexed by $(i,j,k)$ triples. This is exactly where the depth accounting bites: nothing in the argument tolerates $m$ growing. With $m=\Theta(\log n)$ the ledger gives depth $O(\log n)$ threshold circuits, i.e. $\mathsf{TC}^1\supseteq\mathsf{NC}^1$, and the hardness conclusion evaporates — which is precisely the same hinge that makes chain-of-thought and looped/recurrent-depth architectures escape the bound.

Step 8 — the hardness transfer. Formula evaluation is $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete under logtime reductions. If a Transformer meeting the hypotheses of Theorem 4.8 decided the Boolean Formula Value Problem, composing the DLOGTIME reduction with the uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ simulation would put an $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete language in uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$, and closure of $\mathsf{TC}^0$ under these reductions would give $\mathsf{NC}^1\subseteq\mathsf{TC}^0$, hence equality by $\mathsf{TC}^0\subseteq\mathsf{NC}^1$. The same argument runs for arithmetic formula evaluation. Two things to keep in view: the reduction class is never named in the paper (it matters, and it does work out via Buss's ALOGTIME-completeness), and "decides" is never defined for a Transformer, so the final step is sound in substance but under-formalised on the page.

title: Nearly Tight Bounds on Testing of Metric Properties
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 19 October 2026

Nearly Tight Bounds on Testing of Metric Properties

Yiqiao Bao, Sampath Kannan, Erik Waingarten (2024) — arXiv:2411.08989

Main idea

The object under test is an arbitrary non-negative $n \times n$ matrix $M$, read as a dissimilarity function $d:[n]\times[n]\to\mathbb{R}*{\ge 0}$. A query is a single entry $M(i,j)$; the sample complexity is the number of distinct rows/columns touched, so an algorithm that picks $s$ points and reads all pairs among them uses $s$ samples and $\binom{s}{2}$ queries. Distance is $\ell_0$: $M$ is $\varepsilon$-far from a property $\mathcal{P}$ if every matrix in $\mathcal{P}$ disagrees with $M$ on at least $\varepsilon n^2$ entries. This is the metric violation distance notion from the recent approximation-algorithms line (Fan–Raichel–van Buskirk; Cohen-Addad–Fan–Lee–de Mesmay; Charikar–Gao; Kipouridis), not a distortion or $\ell*\infty$ notion — a point worth holding onto, because it drives both the results and their limitations. Symmetry, non-negativity and zero diagonal are "cleanliness" conditions testable in $O(1/\varepsilon)$ queries (Lemma 2.1), so all the work is in the triangle inequality and its strengthenings.

The paper is, somewhat remarkably, the first to ask the most basic question in this space: what is the query complexity of testing whether a matrix is a metric at all? The answer is a non-adaptive, one-sided tester making $O(n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ queries, built from two almost embarrassingly simple checks — sample $O(1/\varepsilon)$ points and $O(n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3})$ pairs and check every (point, pair) triangle; and separately sample $O(n^{1/3}/\varepsilon^{2/3})$ points and check all triangles inside that set. All the content is in the analysis, which is a second-moment argument whose crux is bounding the variance of the number of violating triangles captured by the sample. Complementing this is an $\Omega(n^{2/3})$-type query lower bound inherited from triangle-freeness testing via Behrend/Salem–Spencer graphs, which holds only when $\varepsilon = n^{-\nu(n)}$ for a slowly vanishing $\nu(n)=(\log\log\log n+4)/\log\log n$.

For the two classical sub-classes — tree metrics (additive metrics, four-point condition) and ultrametrics (three-point condition $d(i,j) \le \max{d(i,k),d(j,k)}$) — testing is dramatically cheaper and the complexity is independent of $n$. Here the paper improves Parnas–Ron's twenty-year-old bounds from $O(1/\varepsilon^3)$ samples / $O(1/\varepsilon^6)$ queries to $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ samples / $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, with literally the same algorithm (sample $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ points, read all pairs, reject on any violating triple/quadruple), the gain coming entirely from replacing an additive potential-decrease argument with a multiplicative one. Matching lower bounds give $\Omega(1/\varepsilon)$ samples — so the sample complexity is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)$ — and $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ queries, which rules out the $\Theta(1/\varepsilon)$-query "best case" that property testing often enjoys.

Reviewer-style critique

The strengths are real. The metric-testing question is natural, basic, and genuinely unasked before; the answer is a clean $n^{2/3}$ exponent; and the structural lemma at the heart of the upper bound (Lemma 3.8 / Claim 3.7) is a legitimately nice piece of mathematics that exploits something graphs do not have — that distances are real numbers, so "can I repair one entry?" becomes a question about whether a family of intervals has a common piercing point. The tree/ultrametric improvement is a substantial quantitative win over Parnas–Ron obtained by identifying the right potential function, and the accompanying $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ query lower bound, with its "a clique is the optimal query pattern" sub-argument, is more work than such bounds usually require.

The headline claim of near-tightness deserves scrutiny, though. For general metrics the two bounds do not meet in $\varepsilon$: the upper bound is $n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{4/3}$ while the lower bound, written in the same language, is exactly $n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{2/3}$ (substituting $\varepsilon=n^{-\nu}$ into $n^{2/3+2\nu/3}$). A factor $\varepsilon^{-2/3}$ remains even inside the regime where the lower bound applies, and that factor is not incidental: the lower bound coincides precisely with the naive triangle-covering heuristic (you must inspect $\sim n^3/|T| = n/\varepsilon$ triangles, and $q$ queries span $O(q^{3/2})$ triangles, giving $q \approx (n/\varepsilon)^{2/3}$), while the upper bound's expectation calculation also only needs $s=n^{1/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3}$ samples. The entire $\varepsilon^{-2/3}$ overshoot is a second-moment artifact — the variance, not the mean, forces $s = n^{1/3}/\varepsilon^{2/3}$. Worse, the loss is intrinsic to the two-test architecture: if $\tau$ is the high-degree threshold, CheckHiDegree costs $\varepsilon^{-1} n^2/\tau$ and the variance condition forces $\tau \le \varepsilon n s$, i.e. $s^2 \ge \tau^2/(\varepsilon n)^2$; balancing gives $\tau^3 = \varepsilon n^4$, exactly their $\tau = \varepsilon^{1/3}n^{4/3}$, and exactly $n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{4/3}$. So $\varepsilon^{4/3}$ is the optimum of this algorithm, and closing the gap needs a different algorithm (adaptivity, non-uniform sampling, or a witness set with smaller vertex-triangle-degree), not a sharper calculation. The paper does not say this.

The $\varepsilon$ regime of the lower bound is a more serious caveat than the abstract suggests. Because $\nu(n)\to 0$, the construction only speaks about $\varepsilon = n^{-o(1)}$, i.e. $\varepsilon$ slowly decaying. At constant $\varepsilon$ the paper proves no $\omega(1)$ lower bound whatsoever. This is not a technicality one expects to be removable: it is the Ruzsa–Szemerédi barrier, and for dense-graph triangle-freeness the same barrier coexists with an upper bound _independent of $n$_ (via the triangle removal lemma, at tower-type cost in $1/\varepsilon$). The genuinely interesting possibility the paper leaves entirely untouched is therefore that for constant $\varepsilon$, metric testing has complexity $f(\varepsilon)$ with no $n$ at all — which would make the $n^{2/3}$ headline a statement about the small-$\varepsilon$ regime rather than about metrics. Their Lemma 3.1 only yields $\Omega(\varepsilon n^2)$ violating triangles; a "removal lemma for triangle-inequality violations" giving $\delta(\varepsilon) n^3$ would immediately give an $n$-independent tester. That question is not even posed; indeed the paper has no discussion or open-problems section at all, ending abruptly mid-graph-surgery.

Two further model caveats. First, every lower bound here is against non-adaptive algorithms, and the metric lower bound against one-sided ones; the extension to two-sided error is asserted by analogy ("we believe applies mutatis mutandis" to §6 of Alon–Kaufman–Krivelevich–Ron) rather than proved. Theorem 1.4 is stated for "any non-adaptive algorithm", but the proof only shows that no explicit violation is found, which is a witness-finding (one-sided) statement; for the sample-complexity distribution $\mathcal{D}_s$ the all-$2n$ matrix is a legitimate YES-partner so the bound does upgrade, but for the query distribution $\mathcal{D}_q$ (random ${1,2}$ blocks against a background of $10$) no YES distribution with matching local statistics is exhibited, and a two-sided tester could in principle exploit the value distribution of the entries it sees. No lower bound against adaptive testers appears anywhere, which is notable given that my reading is that adaptivity is exactly where the metric upper bound's $\varepsilon$-dependence might improve.

For tree metrics and ultrametrics the sample complexity is honestly tight, but the query complexity sits between $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ and $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon^2)$, and the upper bound is just "$(\text{samples})^2$" — the algorithm has no query-efficiency idea in it. Since Claim 6.5 shows a tester must induce cycles among its queries, the natural question is whether $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ samples with a sparse, cycle-rich query graph of size $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ suffices. Again not asked.

The motivation is the weakest part. The pitch is that these testers are a cheap sanity check before running the $O(n^3)$-time metric-violation-distance approximation algorithms — but those algorithms read the whole matrix anyway, so the saving only materialises when you expect to reject, and a tester that rejects tells you nothing about how far you are. The genuinely useful primitive for that workflow is tolerant testing / distance approximation (distinguish $\varepsilon$-close from $2\varepsilon$-far, or estimate the violation distance), which is completely open and not mentioned. And $\ell_0$-farness is brittle as a measure of "almost a metric": perturbing $\varepsilon n^2$ entries by $10^{-9}$ makes a matrix $\varepsilon$-far while leaving it metrically indistinguishable from a metric. That is a defensible choice given the approximation-algorithms literature, but it means the results say nothing about the notion a practitioner would reach for.

Finally, craftsmanship. For a paper whose stated contribution is "a more careful analysis", the write-up has an uncomfortable density of slips: constants that don't track (Claim 3.3 proves $d_{T''}(e) \le 2\varepsilon^{1/6}n^{2/3}$, Claim 3.6 concludes $\le 10n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3}$ without comment; Lemma 5.3's conclusion appears as both $\varepsilon n/32$ and $\varepsilon n^2/32$ inconsistent points), Claim 3.7's hypothesis is stated with "any value $x(e)$" where "every" is meant, Definition 5.4's versatile part carries a vestigial "$\beta = \Omega(1)$" that the proof does not respect, and mangled expressions like $\nu_\alpha(\nu_\alpha-1)2$ for $\binom{\nu_\alpha}{2}$ or "$i,\tilde k$". Nothing I checked is wrong at the level of the argument, but Lemma 6.3's graph surgery in particular is the kind of case analysis that a reader cannot verify quickly, and it is carrying the $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ lower bound on its own.

Broader context

Property testing asks for algorithms that read a vanishing fraction of an object and distinguish "has property $\mathcal{P}$" from "$\varepsilon$-far from $\mathcal{P}$ in edit/Hamming distance", with the understanding that near-misses may be answered either way. For combinatorial structures the canonical results are in the dense graph model, and the canonical hard case is triangle-freeness: it is testable with query complexity depending on $\varepsilon$ alone (via the regularity/removal lemma), but the dependence is tower-type, and the Ruzsa–Szemerédi construction — a graph with $n^{2-o(1)}$ edge-disjoint triangles built from a Behrend/Salem–Spencer AP-free set — shows no $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ tester exists. That construction is precisely what this paper re-weights to get its metric lower bound, which is a good way to see why the metric problem inherits a Ruzsa–Szemerédi-shaped obstruction: violating triangles can be forced to be edge-disjoint and sparse.

On the metric side the direct ancestor is Parnas–Ron's Testing metric properties (2003), which introduced the skeleton-partition technique and tested tree metrics, ultrametrics and approximate embeddability; this paper is a straight sequel that keeps the algorithm and sharpens the analysis. Orthogonal to that, Krauthgamer–Sasson and Onak test properties of point sets given a distance oracle (dimensionality, embeddability), with $\varepsilon$ measured in points rather than entries — a different and arguably more application-facing model. The relevant structural background is the hierarchy ultrametric $\subset$ tree metric $\subset$ metric, characterised locally by the three-point condition, Buneman's four-point condition, and the triangle inequality respectively; the fact that each class has a local certificate of non-membership on $3$ or $4$ points is exactly what makes one-sided witness-finding testers possible. The $\ell_0$-fitting counterparts live in the metric violation distance literature (Fan–Raichel–van Buskirk; Cohen-Addad–Fan–Lee–de Mesmay's $O(\log n)$ for metrics and constant-factor for ultrametrics; Charikar–Gao; Kipouridis for tree metrics), and the matrix-property-testing literature supplies a structural cousin in Bakshi–Chepurko–Jayaram's PSD testing via random principal submatrices — "a random principal submatrix suffices" is exactly the shape of the ultrametric result, whereas general metrics provably need the extra off-diagonal star sampling.

A follow-up I would actually want to see: settle the constant-$\varepsilon$ regime by proving or refuting a removal lemma for triangle-inequality violations — if $M$ is $\varepsilon$-far from metric then it has $\delta(\varepsilon)n^3$ violating triangles — which would either collapse the $n$-dependence entirely or exhibit a weighted obstruction that cannot occur in graphs. Failing that, the sharper and more tractable question is whether an adaptive tester achieves $O(n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{2/3})$, matching the triangle-covering heuristic and the lower bound; the analysis above localises the loss precisely (the vertex-triangle-degree threshold where CheckHiDegree and the variance bound balance), so adaptivity — find a high-degree vertex cheaply, then exploit it rather than paying $1/\varepsilon$ to re-find one — is the obvious lever. A tolerant version, estimating the metric violation distance to within a constant in $\tilde O(n^{2/3})$ queries, would also make the stated motivation real.

On the connection to theoretical IR and vector search, I would be honest that it is thin, and that the value is in the technique rather than the theorems. The $\ell_0$ notion of "almost a metric" is not the one embedding quality is measured in; for a learned distance matrix one wants a distortion or $\ell_\infty$ guarantee, and these results do not transfer. The one place where the framing does bite is index-assumption verification: metric-tree-style ANN indexes (VP-trees, M-trees, cover trees, navigating nets) prune using the triangle inequality, and learned asymmetric scores — dual-encoder dot products, Mahalanobis-style learned metrics, cross-encoder relevance — generally violate it, so a cheap certificate that a sampled score submatrix contains no violation is at least a meaningful diagnostic before committing to a metric index over a graph index. The ultrametric tester is the more interesting one for this audience: $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ samples to decide near-ultrametricity is a cheap test for hierarchical structure, which is the implicit assumption behind partition-tree indexes (IVF/$k$-means trees, SPANN/ScaNN-style hierarchies) and behind hyperbolic or taxonomy-aware embeddings. The genuinely reusable pieces are two: the skeleton-partition potential argument — a sampled set induces an equivalence partition on the rest, and each additional sample shrinks the "ambiguous" mass by a $(1-\Omega(\varepsilon))$ factor, which is the same template as many sublinear clustering and coreset arguments and is a clean way to get $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ rather than $O(1/\varepsilon^3)$ sample bounds; and the second-moment-with-bounded-codegrees argument, which is the right tool whenever you sample a random subset and need a witness-counting random variable to concentrate. A more pointed open direction in the same spirit, closer to ANN theory: sublinear testing of whether a point set has doubling dimension at most $k$, with nearly tight bounds — the parameter that actually controls cover-tree and navigating-net complexity, and where (unlike metricity) nothing nearly tight is known.

Proof sketch

The claims, precisely. Theorem 1.1: for every $n$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ there is a non-adaptive, perfectly-complete (one-sided) randomized algorithm making $O(n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ queries that accepts every metric with probability $1$ and rejects every matrix $\varepsilon$-far (in $\ell_0$, over all $n^2$ entries) from the set of metrics with probability $\ge 2/3$. No assumption on the entries beyond cleanliness, which costs $O(1/\varepsilon)$ extra queries. Theorem 1.2: for $\varepsilon = n^{-\nu(n)}$ with $\nu(n) = (\log\log\log n + 4)/\log\log n$, every non-adaptive one-sided $\varepsilon$-tester needs $\Omega(n^{2/3 + 2\nu(n)/3})$ queries; since $\nu(n) \to 0$, this says no tester of the form $O(n^{0.65}/\varepsilon^c)$ exists for any fixed $c$, but it says nothing at constant $\varepsilon$. Theorem 1.3: for both tree metrics and ultrametrics, $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ samples and $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice, non-adaptively and with one-sided error, with no dependence on $n$. Theorem 1.4: both classes require $\Omega(1/\varepsilon)$ samples and $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{4/3})$ queries (as proved, against witness-finding non-adaptive testers).

Step 0: many witnesses. Lemma 3.1 converts farness into witnesses: if $M$ is $\varepsilon$-far from metric it has at least $\varepsilon n^2/6$ violating triangles. The proof is the "shortest-path completion" move that recurs throughout the paper. Let $S$ be the pairs participating in no violating triangle; if there were fewer than $\varepsilon n^2 / 6$ violating triangles then $|S| > (1-\varepsilon)n^2$, and taking the weighted graph on $S$ (connecting components with max-weight edges) and replacing $M$ by its shortest-path metric changes only entries outside $S$, giving a metric within $\varepsilon n^2$ — contradiction. The same completion fact is what makes the lower bounds legitimate against one-sided testers: a violation-free partial matrix is always extendable to a genuine metric, so a one-sided tester that has seen no violation must accept.

Step 1: the estimator and why variance is everything. CheckViolation samples $s$ points i.i.d. and reads all pairs; let $X(\tilde T)$ count triangles of a witness set $\tilde T$ fully inside the sample. Then $\mathbb{E}[X] = \Omega(|\tilde T| s^3/n^3)$, which is $\Omega(1)$ already at $s = n^{1/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3}$ when $|\tilde T| = \Omega(\varepsilon n^2)$. But a large mean is worthless: if all violating triangles sit on one vertex, or on $O(n)$ pairs, $X$ is almost always zero and you need $\Omega(n)$ queries. Classifying pairs of triangles $t,t'$ by $|t \cap t'|$ gives Claim 3.1: $$\mathrm{Var}[X] \lesssim \mathbb{E}[X] + \Big(\textstyle\sum_i d_{\tilde T}(i)^2\Big)\frac{s^5}{n^5} + \Big(\sum_{i\ne j} d_{\tilde T}(i,j)^2\Big)\frac{s^4}{n^4},$$ with $d_{\tilde T}(i)$ the vertex-triangle-degree and $d_{\tilde T}(i,j)$ the edge-triangle-degree (codegree) in the $3$-uniform witness hypergraph. Chebyshev then needs exactly $\max_i d_{\tilde T}(i) \lesssim |\tilde T| s/n$ and $\max_{i,j} d_{\tilde T}(i,j) \lesssim |\tilde T| s^2/n^2$; with $s = n^{1/3}/\varepsilon^{2/3}$ and $|\tilde T| = \Theta(\varepsilon n^2)$ these are precisely $\varepsilon^{1/3}n^{4/3}$ and $n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3}$. So the two degree thresholds are not design choices — they are read off the second moment, and both variance terms are simultaneously tight at the stated parameters.

Step 2: the structural dichotomy. The analysis therefore has to produce a degree-bounded witness set, or else fall back on the degenerate case. Lemma 3.4 gives the dichotomy: either $\Omega(\varepsilon n)$ vertices each have $\Omega(\varepsilon^{1/3}n^{4/3})$ violating triangles — in which case CheckHiDegree catches one by sampling $O(1/\varepsilon)$ points (hitting a high-degree vertex) and $O(n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3})$ pairs (hitting one of its $\varepsilon^{1/3}n^{4/3}$ violating pairs out of $n^2$) — or there exists $\tilde T \subseteq T$ with $|\tilde T| = \Omega(\varepsilon n^2)$, $d_{\tilde T}(i) = O(\varepsilon^{1/3}n^{4/3})$ and $d_{\tilde T}(i,j) = O(n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3})$. The informal slogan is "many violating triangles must be spread out, unless the matrix is nearly a metric anyway".

Step 3: how the degree-bounded witness set is built — repair, then charge back. Vertices are easy: if fewer than $\varepsilon n/4$ vertices are high-degree, overwrite all $O(n)$ entries incident to each (setting them to the maximum entry $m$), costing $o(\varepsilon n^2)$. The resulting $M'$ is still $\varepsilon/2$-far, and crucially every violating triangle of $M'$ avoids the overwritten vertices, hence is a violating triangle of $M$ too (Lemma 3.5). Pairs are the hard case, because an entry $M'(i,j)$ is constrained by all $n-2$ other points and those constraints may be irreconcilable — you cannot simply "fix" a high-codegree pair.

This is where the key trick lives. For a third point $k$, the values of $M'(i,j)$ that make ${i,j,k}$ non-violating form the interval $\big[\,|M'(i,k)-M'(j,k)|,\; M'(i,k)+M'(j,k)\,\big]$. So "can one value of $M'(i,j)$ fix all but $t$ triangles through $(i,j)$?" is literally an interval-piercing question, and intervals on the line have Helly number $2$. Claim 3.7 exploits this: if for every $x$ at least $t$ of these intervals miss $x$, then sorting the intervals by right endpoint and scanning to the $(t/2)$-th endpoint splits them into two families of size $\ge t/2$ that are pairwise disjoint, yielding $t^2/4$ disjoint pairs. Disjointness of the intervals for $k_1,k_2$ unpacks to a "violating $4$-cycle" $i \to k_1 \to j \to k_2$ in which one edge exceeds the sum of the other three; a two-line case analysis then forces either ${i,k_1,k_2}$ or ${j,k_1,k_2}$ to be a violating triangle. Pigeonholing over the $t^2/4$ pairs gives $t^2/8$ distinct edges $(k_1,k_2)$ forming violations with $i$ or $j$, i.e. $d_{T'}(i) \ge t^2/8$ or $d_{T'}(j) \ge t^2/8$. Taking $t = \varepsilon^{1/6}n^{2/3}$ makes $t^2/8 = \varepsilon^{1/3}n^{4/3}/8$, contradicting the vertex-degree bound from Step 3. Hence some value $x(e)$ leaves each high-codegree pair in at most $\varepsilon^{1/6}n^{2/3}$ violating triangles. Note what is being used: that distances are real-valued. The Boolean analogue in graphs simply does not exist, which is the paper's own explanation for why the graph triangle-freeness machinery gives lower bounds here but not upper bounds.

Rewriting all high-codegree entries this way produces $M''$, still $(19\varepsilon/40)$-far, hence with $\Omega(\varepsilon n^2)$ violating triangles, all of bounded codegree (Claim 3.3). But those triangles may use modified entries and need not exist in $M$. The transfer is an injective charging argument (Claims 3.4–3.5): each high-degree edge $e$ has at least $9n^{2/3}/\varepsilon^{1/3}$ "unique" violating triangles in $M'$ — triangles using $e$ and no other high-degree edge (Lemma 3.7, via the fact that each vertex touches at most $\varepsilon^{2/3}n^{2/3}/80$ high-degree edges, Lemma 3.6) — which comfortably exceeds the $\le 2\varepsilon^{1/6}n^{2/3}$ triangles of $M''$ through $e$. So one injects $M''$'s triangles at $e$ into $M'$'s unique triangles at $e$, keeps $M''$'s triangles that touch no modified entry as-is, and obtains $\tilde T \subseteq T' \subseteq T$ with $|\tilde T| \ge |T''| = \Omega(\varepsilon n^2)$ and both degree bounds intact. The abundance of unique triangles is exactly the hypothesis that made the pair high-codegree in the first place — the argument is self-financing.

Step 4: the metric lower bound. The NO distribution is a re-weighted Behrend graph. Take a Salem–Spencer set $X \subset [n]$ with $|X| \ge n^{1-\nu(n)}$ and no nontrivial $3$-term AP ($x+y \equiv 2z \Rightarrow x=y=z$), and three parts $A,B,C$ of size $n$. Set $d(a,b)=1$ iff $b-a \in X$ (else $2$); $d(b,c)=2$ iff $c-b \in X$ (else $3$); $d(a,c)=4$ iff $c-a \in 2X$ (else $2$); everything else $2$. Since all values lie in ${1,2,3,4}$, the only possible violations are $(1,1,3)$, $(1,1,4)$, $(1,2,4)$; the first two are impossible because $1$-edges live only between $A$ and $B$ while $3$s and $4$s touch $C$. So violations are exactly the $(1,2,4)$ triples ${a, a+x, a+2x}$, and the AP-freeness of $X$ makes them edge-disjoint and exactly $n|X|$ in number. Edge-disjointness forces $\Theta(n|X|) = \Theta(n^{2-\nu})$ modifications, so $M$ is $\Theta(n^{-\nu})$-far (and exactly that far — recolouring the $4$s to $3$s repairs it). Randomly permute indices and apply Yao. A one-sided tester must query all three entries of some violating triple; a set of $q$ query pairs spans at most $O(q^{3/2})$ triangles (Kruskal–Katona, maximised by a clique on $\sqrt q$ vertices), and a fixed Behrend triangle lands on a fixed query triangle with probability $O(1/n^3)$, so the detection probability is at most $O(q^{3/2} \cdot n^{2-\nu} / n^3) = O(q^{3/2}/n^{1+\nu})$, which is $o(1)$ for $q = o(n^{2/3+2\nu/3})$. The $3/2$ exponent is the whole story on both sides of this paper: it is why $n^{2/3}$ is the right exponent, and why cliques are the right query shape.

Step 5: ultrametrics — skeleton partitions and a multiplicative potential. The algorithm samples $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ points and reads all pairs. For the analysis, split the sample into a skeleton $S$ and a second batch read as consecutive pairs. If $M|_{S\times S}$ is already inconsistent we are done; otherwise $S$ partitions the remaining consistent points into equivalence classes, $j \sim k$ iff $M(i,j) = M(i,k)$ for all $i \in S$. The point is that $S$ determines cross-class distances: if some $i \in S$ separates $j$ and $k$, the three-point condition forces $M(j,k) = \max{M(i,j), M(i,k)}$, and any deviation is a separator corruption — a violation visible from one extra pair. There is also an easy-to-detect corruption: $j,k$ in the same class with $M(j,k) > M(j,i) = M(k,i)$ for some $i \in S$.

The engine is a trichotomy on parts. A part is easy if half its internal pairs are easy-to-detect corruptions; versatile if its internal submatrix can be repaired into an ultrametric consistent with $S$ at cost $\le \beta \varepsilon n^2/2$; active otherwise. Lemma 5.3 shows that if the active mass $|A(M,S)|$ is small and corruptions are few, one can explicitly assemble an ultrametric within $\varepsilon n^2$ of $M$ — inconsistent points are pushed to infinity, cross-class entries are set to the forced value, easy/active parts are flattened to the minimum positive entry, versatile parts take their repaired submatrix — and the (long, case-heavy) verification that this really satisfies the three-point condition is the appendix's main labour. So it suffices to drive the active mass down.

That is Lemma 5.5–5.6, and it is where Parnas–Ron is improved. They showed a batch of $O(1/\varepsilon)$ samples decreases the same-part pair count additively by $\Omega((\varepsilon n)^2)$, which can happen only $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ times, giving $O(1/\varepsilon^3)$. Here one shows a multiplicative decrease: $\mathbb{E}_{i}[|A(M, S \cup {i})|] \le |A(M,S)| \cdot e^{-\varepsilon/16}$ per single sample, so $n^2$ reaches $\varepsilon n^2/48$ after $O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$ samples, with Markov finishing the job. The per-part estimate works as follows. Inside an active part $P$ of size $\beta n$, let $r_1$ be the multiplicity of the most frequent value among non-easy entries. Sampling $i \in P$ separates $x,y \in P$ precisely when $M(i,x) \ne M(i,y)$; decomposing the submatrix into edge-disjoint graphs by value and bounding each graph's sum of squared degrees by De Caen's inequality $\sum_v \deg(v)^2 \le |E|(2|E|/(|V|-1) + |V| - 2)$ yields an expected number of separated pairs at least $((\beta n)^2 - r_1)/8$. Finally, Claim 5.1 closes the loop: if $(\beta n)^2 - r_1 < \beta\varepsilon n^2/2$, then replacing the whole submatrix by the constant-$v_1$ matrix is a legal ultrametric consistent with $S$ — legal because the pair achieving $v_1$ is not an easy corruption, which forces $v_1 \le \min_{P S, \in i u} M(i,u)$ — so $P$ would be versatile, contradiction. Hence active parts have genuine value-diversity, hence sampling inside one splits a constant fraction of its pairs. In short: easy parts are cheap to detect, versatile parts are cheap to repair, and active parts are cheap to shatter.

Step 6: tree metrics via the Gromov product. The tree-metric tester is verbatim the same, with the four-point condition replacing the three-point condition and classes defined by $M(i,u) - M(i,v) = M(j,u) - M(j,v)$ for all $u,v \in S$. The only new idea is in Lemma 5.12: fix $u \in S$ and subtract the mask $\mathrm{MASK}(j,k) = M(u,j) + M(u,k)$ from the part's submatrix. This is (up to sign and a factor of two) the Gromov product based at $u$, and the standard fact that a tree metric rooted at $u$ becomes an ultrametric under this transformation is exactly what lets the entire ultrametric argument be replayed: a chain of rearrangements shows $i_a, i_b$ are separated by a new sample $i_j$ iff the corresponding entries of $B - \mathrm{MASK}$ differ, and Claim 5.2 shows the easy-corruption values remain strictly above the others after masking, so the value-multiplicity bookkeeping is unchanged.

Step 7: the tree/ultrametric lower bounds. For samples, $\mathcal{D}_s$ hides a set $B$ of $\lfloor \varepsilon n\rfloor$ "bad" points among $n$: all distances are $2n$, except $M(x_i, y_j) = 2n + i$ for $x_i \in G, y_j \in B$, so the bad points encode the index of their partner. Every triple ${x_i, x_j, y_l}$ with $i<j$ is an ultrametric violation ($2n < 2n+i < 2n+j$ makes the maximum unique) and every quadruple ${x_i,x_j,x_k,y_l}$ breaks the four-point condition, while any triple/quadruple avoiding $B$ is fine. There are $\Omega(\varepsilon n^3)$ violating triples, each entry lies in $O(n)$ of them, so a covering argument gives $\Omega(\varepsilon n^2)$-farness. A tester sampling $o(1/\varepsilon)$ points misses $B$ entirely with probability $1-o(1)$; the all-$2n$ matrix is the YES-partner.

For queries, $\mathcal{D}_q$ is block-diagonal: partition $[n]$ into $1/\varepsilon$ blocks of size $\varepsilon n$, fill each block i.i.d. uniform in ${1,2}$, and set everything outside the blocks to $10$. A random ${1,2}$ triple violates the three-point condition with probability $3/8$, so each block is $\Omega(1)$-far and $M$ is $\Omega(\varepsilon)$-far; and by Claim 6.4 every violation lies entirely inside one block, since a cross-block triple has at least two entries equal to $10$ and the third at most $10$. Two further steps make this a query bound rather than a sample bound. Claim 6.5 shows that if the queried pairs form a forest on the sampled points then the partial matrix extends to an ultrametric — complete components arbitrarily, then set each missing entry to the heaviest edge on the unique tree path — so the tester must create cycles. Lemma 6.3 then argues that for a fixed query budget $m$ the quantity $\sum_k \varepsilon^{k-1}|C_k(G)|$ (the union bound over cycles, since a $k$-cycle falls inside one block with probability $\approx \varepsilon^{k-1}$) is maximised by the clique-like graph: an involved surgery that repeatedly merges a non-adjacent pair $(x,y)$ with $\nu$ common neighbours — destroying at most $\binom{\nu}{2}$ triangles and $4$-cycles while freeing $\nu$ edges — and re-spends those edges on non-edges, each of which creates $\ge \nu - 1$ new triangles, for a net gain. So the optimal tester samples $s$ points with $\binom{s}{2} = m$ and reads all pairs; a union bound over the $O(s^3)$ triples, each landing in a common block with probability $\le 2\varepsilon^2$, is $o(1)$ unless $s = \Omega(1/\varepsilon^{2/3})$, i.e. $m = \Omega(1/\varepsilon^{4/3})$. The $\varepsilon^{4/3}$ is thus the same Kruskal–Katona $3/2$ exponent appearing a third time, now in the proximity parameter rather than in $n$.

title: How Transformers Learn to Plan via Multi-Token Prediction
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-18

How Transformers Learn to Plan via Multi-Token Prediction

Jianhao Huang, Zhanpeng Zhou, Renqiu Xia, Baharan Mirzasoleiman, Weijie Su, Wei Huang (2026, COLM 2026) — arXiv:2604.11912

Main idea

The paper asks why multi-token prediction (MTP) helps reasoning, and answers with an optimization story rather than an expressivity one. MTP here is the Gloeckle et al. (2024) parallel form: one shared Transformer trunk, $k$ independent linear output heads, head $m$ predicting $x_{t+m}$ from the teacher-forced prefix $x_{1:t}$, with the loss the plain average of the $k$ cross-entropies (NTP is $k=1$). Crucially, inference is unchanged — only head 1 is used, one token at a time — so any difference in behavior is attributable to the training signal, not to parallel decoding or speculative sampling.

The testbed is graph path-finding. In a 2-path star graph the edge list is serialized, then the query $(u_{end}, u_{start})$ is appended, and the model must emit $(u_{start}, v, u_{end})$; only the first branch decision is non-trivial. NTP plateaus at exactly 50% (coin flip between the two arms) across every data and parameter scale tried, while 2-MTP — one extra future token — reaches 100% at 0.5M samples. Because Bachmann & Nagarajan attribute NTP's star-graph failure to the Clever Hans cheat (teacher forcing makes every token after the branch trivially predictable from the revealed predecessor, so the planning step never gets learned), the authors add a binary-tree variant that branches at every node, removing the shortcut. There NTP does learn and scale — but MTP still wins, most clearly at small data/model size. On more realistic tasks the picture is uneven: Countdown moves 60.3 → 64.9 (non-monotone in $k$, a few points), while 3-SAT moves 10.4 → 87.5 at $k=7$, a dramatic gap. The theory then analyzes a two-layer disentangled Transformer (merged query-key matrix $W$, block-diagonal into content and position, each layer concatenating its attention output to the residual stream) on the 2-path 3-node star graph with $N = T = 10$, and claims MTP provably installs a two-stage reverse reasoning circuit: layer 1 locks onto the end node, layer 2 then recovers the intermediate node by matching the edge that points into it.

The most interesting part

The load-bearing idea is gradient decoupling. The shallow MTP head reads layer 1's attention output directly, so its gradient (Lemma 4/5) is a function of $W^{(1)}$ alone and never traverses layer 2. Under pure NTP the only head sits on top of layer 2, so at zero initialization layer 2 is a uniform $1/T$ average over all rows of $S^{[1]}$; the deep head's prediction is therefore an average over the whole context, and since the target $v$ lives somewhere in the edge list but never at position $T-1$ (which holds $u_{end}$), the gradient instructs layer 1 to diffuse attention across the context — precisely away from the predecessor pointer the 2-hop circuit needs. MTP's shallow head escapes this because its target, $u_{end}$, is always at $T-1$.

That last sentence is also where I would push back hardest. The two-token-ahead target is _literally the token already sitting at position $T-1$ of the prompt_ — the authors put $u_{end}$ before $u_{start}$ specifically so it is visible. So Phase I's learning problem is not "look ahead to the goal" in any informational sense; it is "learn to copy your immediate predecessor," and the lookahead head carries no information the context lacks. The clever part is that this trivially-learnable shift operator is exactly the primitive layer 2 needs, so MTP bootstraps the reverse-reasoning circuit off a free copy task. That is a genuinely elegant observation, but it is a property of the serialization as much as of MTP, and it does not obviously transfer: in Countdown or SAT the $k$-th future token is not a copy of a prompt token, so whatever is driving the 10 → 87 jump on 3-SAT is probably not this mechanism. The 8-layer/8-head validation (NTP 97% train / 20% test, attending to the start node in layers 7–8; 3-MTP 100%/100%, attending to the end node in layers 3–4) is a nice attention-pattern corroboration, but it is again on star graphs, averaged over heads and 544 examples, and it is correlational. A second honest problem: Corollary 2 shows the circuit the theory converges to fails on the autoregressive context — fed its own emitted $v$, the deep head confidently re-predicts $v$ instead of $u_{end}$, incurring loss $\Theta(\gamma)$ with gradient $O(e^{-\gamma})$. The error is "trapped," as the authors put it. A stationary point at which one of three loss terms is maximally wrong and gradient-invisible is not a comfortable characterization of what MTP learns.

Proof sketch

Theorem 1 is a stationary-point characterization, not an optimality result: if layer 1 points at the immediate predecessor in two specific rows (the query row $T$ and the context row $t_{end}^{ctx}$) and layer 2's last row is one-hot on $t_{end}^{ctx}$, then every gradient path vanishes. The mechanism is pure softmax algebra — every backprop chain is premultiplied by a row-wise Jacobian $J(s) = \mathrm{diag}(s) - ss^\top$, and $J(e_k) = 0$, so saturated attention kills all three paths (the two logit paths through layer 2 and the value path through row $t_{end}^{ctx}$ of $S^{[1]}$). All other context rows receive no signal and remain free, matching the diffuse sub-diagonal observed empirically. Corollary 1 exhibits explicit weights realizing it — $W_0^{(1)} = 0$, $W_1^{(1)} = \gamma L$ ($L$ the strict lower shift), $W_0^{(2)} = \gamma I$, with a single negative positional self-mask $(W_1^{(2)})_{T-1,T-1} = -\gamma$ to suppress the prompt copy of $u_{end}$ — and bounds loss and gradient norm by $O(e^{-\gamma})$.

Theorem 2 is the dynamics. Phase I fixes $W_0^{(1)} = 0$, constrains $W_1^{(1)}$ to Toeplitz/RoPE form $w(i-j)$, and runs gradient flow on the shallow loss alone. Because the graph labeling is random and the expected gradient depends only on the offset, the Toeplitz structure is preserved exactly, which collapses the whole layer to two scalars: the predecessor weight $w(1)$ and the common context weight $w(k)$. The order parameter is the gap $\Delta = w(1) - w(k)$, whose flow is $\dot\Delta = -s_c(x-1) + (x - 1/8)/(x+1)$ with $x = s_p/s_c$; bounding $s_c < 1/(x+8)$ via normalization reduces positivity to the inequality $63x/8 > 0$, so $\dot\Delta > 0$ globally and unconditionally at $T = 10$ (at initialization $\dot\Delta = (T-3)/(2(T-2)) = 7/16$). Hence $w(1) - w(k) \to \infty$ and $S^{[1]} \to L$. Phase II freezes layer 1 at $\gamma L$ and runs gradient flow on the deep term $L_{1a}$ from zero initialization; since $S^{[1]} = L$, the deep head becomes a one-hop contrastive problem, $L_{1a} = -\log S^{[2]}_{T,t_{end}^{ctx}}$. The gradients are rank-one outer products, so only row $u_{end}$ of $W_0^{(2)}$ and row $T-1$ of $W_1^{(2)}$ ever move; logit-gap arguments give $\dot\Delta_k \ge 2s_k > 0$ for content distractors and $\dot\Delta_{self} = 1 - s_{j^*} + s_{self} > 0$ for the prompt copy, yielding $W_0^{(2)} \to \gamma' I + B$ with finite negative off-diagonals (an integrable-tail argument) and $(W_1^{(2)})_{T-1,T-1} \to -\infty$.

Theorem 3 is the NTP side, and it is weaker than the framing suggests. It computes the expected gradient at initialization only ($w \equiv 0$, $W^{(2)} = 0$, $W_0^{(1)}$ pinned at 0), decomposing by row regime: rows $r \le T-2$ contribute exactly zero in expectation by symmetry, row $T-1$ contributes $+1/((T-1)^2(T-2))$ at every offset, and row $T$ contributes $-1/T^2$ at the predecessor offset but $+1/(T^2(T-2))$ elsewhere. The sign therefore hinges on the arithmetic inequality $(T-1)^2(T-2) > T^2$, i.e. $T^3 - 5T^2 + 5T + 2 > 0$, which holds at $T = 10$ (648 > 100) but fails at $T = 3$. So this is a one-step, in-expectation, regime-dependent statement that NTP's initial gradient points the wrong way — not a lower bound on NTP's final loss, no concentration over sampled graphs, no ruling out of alternative routes to the circuit. And note that the "two-stage" structure is a training protocol the analyst imposes (train $L_2$ with layer 1 restricted, then freeze and train $L_{1a}$), not an emergent phase transition with a derived boundary; finite-time rates and joint dynamics are explicitly left open, and forbidding content-based attention in layer 1 is exactly the resource NTP might otherwise use.

Broader context

This sits in the training-dynamics-of-simplified-Transformers line — Nichani, Damian & Lee on learning causal structure, Chen et al. on induction heads, Zhang–Frei–Bartlett on in-context linear regression — using Friedman et al.'s disentangled/Transformer-programs abstraction to keep the residual stream analyzable. On the objective side it connects ProphetNet's future $n$-grams, Gloeckle et al.'s parallel heads, DeepSeek-V3's sequential MTP modules (plus Qwen3-Next, Nemotron 3), post-hoc NTP→MTP adaptation, and the "beyond-MTP" strand (future summaries, joint/parallel token prediction). The two companions worth reading are Bachmann & Nagarajan, The Pitfalls of Next-Token Prediction (the star graph, Clever Hans, teacherless training — MTP is in effect a principled teacherless objective), and Zhong et al. (2025), the closest prior MTP-planning theory, which this paper supersedes by handling independent rather than shared heads. The sharpest follow-up the theory suggests is a falsifiable prediction about architecture: decoupling holds only for parallel heads, so DeepSeek-style sequential heads (whose gradients pass through the previous module) should lose the Phase I bootstrap — and one can test the shift-bootstrap explanation directly by permuting the serialization so $u_{end}$ is no longer the predecessor of the query, or by making the $k$-th future token non-copyable.

Connection to generative retrieval. This one is real, not forced. In GR a docid is a hierarchical code — DSI semantic IDs, TIGER/RQ-VAE residual codes — decoded autoregressively over a trie, and the structure is isomorphic to the star graph: the first codebook token is the branch choice at the root, the hardest and most global decision, while later tokens are nearly determined by the prefix because the prefix already localizes the subtree. Under teacher forcing the loss is therefore dominated by easy late-position tokens, and the model can score well in training while its step-1 marginal stays near-uninformative — the Clever Hans shortcut, over a docid tree rather than a graph. Beam search over the trie mitigates this only by widening the search, not by improving the step-1 posterior. The paper's prescription maps cleanly: add parallel heads predicting codebook levels $j+1 \dots j+k$, so position 1 receives gradient that is informative about the leaf, and decode with head 1 as usual. The fit is unusually convenient because $k$ is small and fixed (typically 4–8 RQ levels), so "lookahead = full code tuple" is architecturally cheap. The caveat transfers too: deeper code tokens are not copies of anything in the query, so what would carry over is the generic gradient-decoupling claim (a shallow head gives layer-1 parameters uncontaminated signal about the target leaf), not the specific predecessor-shift circuit — which is exactly the gap this paper has not closed.

title: Asymptotics of Stochastic Gradient Descent with Dropout Regularization in Linear Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-18

Asymptotics of Stochastic Gradient Descent with Dropout Regularization in Linear Models

Jiaqi Li, Johannes Schmidt-Hieber, Wei Biao Wu (2024) — arXiv:2409.07434

Main idea

The paper asks what the distribution of dropout-SGD iterates looks like, not just whether they converge. The model is plain linear regression with i.i.d. streaming data, $y_k = x_k^\top\beta^* + \epsilon_k$, $\mathbb{E}\epsilon_k = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_k)=1$. Dropout is a diagonal random matrix $D_k$ with $(D_k)_{ii}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ i.i.d. ($p$ = retaining probability, so each coordinate is zeroed with probability $1-p$), applied to the coefficient vector — i.e. feature-level masking of $\beta$, with no $1/p$ rescaling. One sample and one mask per step give the constant-step recursion $\breve\beta_k = \breve\beta_{k-1} + \alpha D_k x_k\,(y_k - x_k^\top D_k \breve\beta_{k-1})$ (eq. 32). Writing $X_k = x_kx_k^\top$, the centered recursion is a random-coefficient VAR(1), $\breve\beta_k - \breve\beta = (I_d - \alpha D_kX_kD_k)(\breve\beta_{k-1}-\breve\beta) + \alpha D_kx_k(y_k - x_k^\top D_k\breve\beta)$ (eq. 36), whose fixed point $\breve\beta = (\mathbb{E}[X_{1,p}])^{-1}\mathbb{E}[y_1x_1]$ is the dropout-marginalized least-squares solution — a generalized ridge estimator in which the off-diagonal entries of the Gram matrix are shrunk by $p$, equivalently a penalty $\frac{1-p}{p}\mathrm{Diag}(\mathbb{E}x x^\top)$. "Online inference" means: run constant-$\alpha$ dropout SGD, Polyak–Ruppert average it, and simultaneously maintain a recursive estimate of the long-run covariance of the average so that confidence intervals, projection intervals and a $\chi^2_d$ confidence ellipsoid are available at every step in $O(1)$-in-$n$ time and memory (Algorithm 1). The core finding is that the averaged dropout iterate is $\sqrt n$-asymptotically normal around the ridge target with no first-order bias, so dropout = ridge plus explicitly characterizable implicit noise.

Reviewer-style critique

The genuinely strong part is the probabilistic machinery. Treating the iterate as an iterated random function and proving geometric-moment contraction (GMC) is the right move, and it buys a lot: a unique stationary law, forgetting of the initialization at geometric rate, hence quenched limit theorems valid for any fixed $\breve\beta_0$ rather than only for a stationary start. Lemma 1's observation that dropout makes $r_{\alpha,q}<1$ even for a singular Gram matrix (because $X_p \ge (1-p)\min_j X_{jj} I_d$ is positive definite) is a nice structural insight: the mask itself regularizes the contraction. Lemma 11, a moment inequality for $\mathbb{E}|x+y|_2^q$ that drops Rio's (2009) requirement $\mathbb{E}[y\mid x]=0$, is reusable beyond this paper. The simulation in Table 1 showing $\hat r_{\alpha,2}^2$ crossing 1 just past $2/|\mathbb{X}|$ is honest evidence that the step-size condition is close to sharp.

The weaknesses are real. First, the inferential target. Theorem 6 gives $\sqrt n(\bar\beta_n^{sgd}-\breve\beta)\Rightarrow N(0,\breve\Sigma(\alpha))$, yet Corollary 3 asserts coverage for $\beta^_$. Since $\breve\beta = (p\Sigma + (1-p)\mathrm{Diag}(\Sigma))^{-1}\Sigma\beta^_$ with $\Sigma = \mathbb{E}xx^\top$, these coincide only when $\Sigma$ is diagonal (or $p\to1$). The simulations generate independent standard-normal covariates, so this bias is invisible by construction; with correlated design the intervals would cover the ridge target, not the truth, and no debiasing is offered. This tension is sharpest because the GD-side Theorem 2 requires non-zero off-diagonal Gram entries for a non-degenerate limit — exactly the regime where $\breve\beta\neq\beta^*$. Second, the abstract's "difference between dropout and $\ell^2$-regularized iterates" oversells: the comparison is to the $\ell^2$ minimizer, a fixed point, not to a coupled ridge-SGD trajectory, so the folklore is captured only in the weak sense that dropout's limit law is centered at ridge. Third, for SGD there is no closed form for $\breve\Sigma(\alpha)$ — the Lyapunov-equation expression $\Xi(\alpha)=V_0+\alpha B_p$ (eqs. 19–22) exists only in the fixed-design GD case — so the dependence of the asymptotic variance on $p$ is never made explicit, which is arguably the question a practitioner cares about. Fourth, the step-size condition (37) is an implicit supremum over unit vectors of unknown $q$-th moments $\mu_q(v)$; the interpretable surrogate $0<\alpha<2J/K$ (Remark 1) involves the condition number of $\mathbb{E}[DX_kD]$ and requires fourth moments of $x$, so it is not checkable from data and degrades fast with $d$. Fifth, everything is fixed-$d$, linear, well-conditioned and $L^{2q}$-bounded: no growing dimension, no nonlinearity, no mini-batching, no decaying step size, and the $n^{-1/3}$ rate for $\hat\Sigma_n$ (Theorem 8, $\zeta=3/2$) is slow even if optimal in this class. Finally the empirical evidence is thin: coverage reaches the nominal 0.95 only at $n\approx 2$–$3\times10^5$ (at $n=10^5$ it is 0.75–0.88, worst for $d=50$ and $p=0.5$), from 200 replications ($\mathrm{SE}\approx0.015$), with no competing method (plug-in, online bootstrap, HiGrad) and no real data. The claim of "$O(1)$ memory" also elides the $O(d^2)$ matrix state.

Proof sketch

What is proved, in plain terms. (i) GMC. Under $\mathbb{E}[|\epsilon|^{2q}+|x|_2^{2q}]<\infty$ (Assumption 2) and step size satisfying (37), two dropout-SGD trajectories driven by the same masks and data but started anywhere satisfy $(\mathbb{E}|\breve\beta_k-\breve\beta_k'|_2^q)^{1/q}\le \breve r_{\alpha,q}^k|\breve\beta_0-\breve\beta_0'|_2$ with $\breve r_{\alpha,q}<1$ (Theorem 5; Theorem 1 is the fixed-design analogue under the clean condition $\alpha|\mathbb{X}|<2$). (ii) Moment rate. $\max_k(\mathbb{E}|\breve\beta_k^\circ-\breve\beta|_2^q)^{1/q}=O(\sqrt\alpha)$ (Lemma 5), so the stationary cloud around the ridge solution has radius $\sqrt\alpha$. (iii) CLTs. A quenched CLT for the single iterate as $\alpha\downarrow0$, $(\tilde\beta_k-\tilde\beta)/\sqrt\alpha\Rightarrow N(0,\Xi(0))$ (Theorem 2), and the $n\to\infty$ CLT for the average at fixed $\alpha$ (Theorems 3, 6), strengthened to a KMT-type invariance principle with the optimal rate $o_P(n^{1/q})$ (Theorems 4, 7). (iv) Consistency of the online batch-means covariance estimator at rate $n^{(1/\zeta-1)\vee(-1/(2\zeta))}$ (Theorem 8), which plus Slutsky yields asymptotic coverage (Corollary 3).

How. GMC is established by conditioning out the last mask: since $A_k = I_d - \alpha D_kX_kD_k$ is independent of the difference $\Delta_{k-1}$, the tower rule gives $\mathbb{E}|A_k\Delta_{k-1}|^q \le r^q\,\mathbb{E}|\Delta_{k-1}|^q$ with $r=\sup_{|v|=1}(\mathbb{E}|A_1v|_2^q)^{1/q}$, and induction does the rest (proof of Theorem 1; for $q>2$ the same telescoping on $\mathbb{E}(\delta^\top A_1^\top\cdots A_k^\top A_k\cdots A_1\delta)^{q/2}$). The structural fact that makes $r<1$ is the algebraic identity $|(I_d-\alpha DX_kD)v|_2^2 = 1-\alpha v^\top M_k v$ with $M_k = 2DX_kD - \alpha DX_kDX_kD$ (idempotence $D^2=D$ is what produces it), so contraction reduces to positive definiteness of $\mathbb{E}[M_k]$ — an "$L^2$–$L^q$ equivalence" reading of strong convexity versus stochastic Lipschitzness. In the fixed-design case the same step uses $A^2\le|A|A$ for psd $A$ plus Clara et al.'s identity $\mathbb{E}[DAD]=pA_p$ to get $\mathbb{E}[(I-\alpha D\mathbb{X}D)^2]\preceq I-\Delta\alpha pX_p$. Extending beyond $q=2$ under random design is where Lemma 11 enters: with $x=v$, $y=D_kX_kD_kv$ dependent, no martingale structure is available, and the new inequality bounds $\mathbb{E}|x-\alpha y|_2^q$ by moments of $x$ and $y$ separately. GMC then yields a unique stationary law via a backward iteration $z_k = f_{\xi_1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{\xi_k}$ (Corollary 4, after Wu–Shao 2004 and Diaconis–Freedman): forward iterates wander ergodically, but backward compositions are Cauchy a.s. because $\mathbb{E}\rho^q(z_{k+1},z_k)\le L_q^k I(q,y^*)$, and exchangeability gives $z_k \overset{D}{=} y_k$.

The CLT is not a martingale-CLT argument but Wu's physical/functional dependence measure. Writing the stationary iterate as a causal Bernoulli shift $\breve\beta_k^\circ = \breve h_\alpha(\xi_k,\xi_{k-1},\dots)$ with $\xi_k=(D_k,(y_k,x_k))$, GMC translates directly into $\theta_{k,q}(\alpha)=|\breve\beta_k^\circ - \breve\beta_{k,{0}}^\circ|_q = O(\breve r_{\alpha,q}^k)$ and hence $\Theta_{0,q}(\alpha)<\infty$ — short-range dependence — after which Shao–Wu (2007, their Thm 2.1, quoted as Lemma 9) plus Cramér–Wold gives normality, and Karmakar–Wu (2020, Lemma 10) gives the Gaussian approximation; stationarity lets them bypass that lemma's non-degeneracy condition (ii). Two further tricks matter. For the fixed-design CLT, the random coefficient $A_k$ is replaced by its mean, $\beta_k^\dagger - \tilde\beta = (I-\alpha pX_p)(\beta_{k-1}^\dagger-\tilde\beta)+b_k$, and the affine-approximation error is shown to be $O(\alpha)$ (Lemma 2) by expanding it as a martingale-difference series $\alpha\sum_i M_{k-i}$ and applying Burkholder's inequality; the mean-zero property comes from $\mathbb{E}[H_k]=\mathbb{E}[D\mathbb{X}(pI-D)]=p^2\bar{\mathbb{X}}-p^2\bar{\mathbb{X}}=0$ (eq. 99). For the SGD CLT, the centering is exact: stationarity plus $\mathbb{E}[\breve\beta_k^\circ-\breve\beta] = (I-\alpha p\mathbb{E}[X_{1,p}])\mathbb{E}[\breve\beta_{k-1}^\circ-\breve\beta]$ and invertibility of $\mathbb{E}[X_{1,p}]$ force $\mathbb{E}[\breve\beta_k^\circ-\breve\beta]=0$ (eq. 217), so unlike the GD case there is no $O(\alpha)$ asymptotic bias to subtract. Theorem 8 then combines the non-overlapping batch-means decomposition with block lengths $\eta_m=\lfloor cm^\zeta\rfloor$, the geometric decay of $\theta_{k,q}$, and the dimension-dependent bound $\mathbb{E}|S|\le\sqrt{d|\mathbb{E}S^2|}$ (Lemma 15).

Broader context

Three strands meet here. The first is asymptotic statistics for stochastic approximation: Robbins–Monro, then Polyak–Juditsky and Ruppert's discovery that averaging a decaying-step SGD path recovers the efficient $\sqrt n$-rate limit, and the constant-step branch — Pflug (1986), Dieuleveut–Durmus–Bach (2020) "Bridging the gap between constant step size SGD and Markov chains", Yu et al. (2021) — where the iterate becomes an ergodic Markov chain with a stationary law offset by an $O(\alpha)$ bias; extrapolation across several $\alpha$'s (Huo et al.; Allmeier–Gast) is the standard debiasing device, and Corollary 2's parallel-$\alpha$ joint CLT is precisely what enables it. The second is online inference: Chen, Lee, Tong and Zhang (2020, Ann. Statist.) on plug-in and batch-means inference for averaged SGD, Fang et al.'s online bootstrap, Su–Zhu's HiGrad, and Zhu, Chen and Wu (2023, JASA) on online covariance estimation — this paper is essentially the dropout analogue of that last one, with Wu's (2005) physical dependence measure and Xiao–Wu's single-pass spectral estimation supplying the dependence bookkeeping. The third is dropout-as-regularization: Srivastava et al. (2014) noted the $\ell^2$ link; Wager, Wang and Liang (2013) showed dropout is adaptive regularization (an $\ell^2$ penalty after rescaling by the inverse diagonal Fisher information, which is exactly the $\mathrm{Diag}$ structure reappearing in $X_p$); Mianjy–Arora and Cavazza et al. derived nuclear-norm effects in shallow networks; Wei–Kakade–Ma (2020) separated explicit from implicit effects; and Clara, Langer and Schmidt-Hieber (2024, JMLR) proved for fixed-design full-gradient dropout that the implicit noise does not vanish. The present paper is the sequential/random-design sequel with inference attached.

The obvious follow-ups: get an explicit expansion of $\breve\Sigma(\alpha)$ in $(\alpha,p)$ to turn $p$ into a tunable knob with a known variance–bias trade-off; combine the parallel-$\alpha$ CLT with Richardson extrapolation to produce intervals for $\beta^*$ rather than $\breve\beta$ under correlated design; and push GMC to growing $d$ or to one-hidden-layer / generalized-linear models, where $A_k$ is no longer affine in the mask and the $D^2=D$ identity that drives Lemma 4 is unavailable.

Relevance to your own work. I would not force an IR connection — the paper is firmly in the stochastic-approximation/time-series-asymptotics tradition and says nothing about retrieval. The one non-trivial bridge, if you want it, is methodological rather than topical: the GMC → functional-dependence-measure → quenched CLT pipeline is a general recipe for getting distributional statements about constant-step online training, and embedding/index training in dense retrieval is exactly a constant-step, noise-injected, online recursion. If you ever want confidence statements about a learned representation or a learned index parameter — e.g. is this embedding coordinate significantly different across two training runs, or how much of the variance in a learned quantizer's centroids is stationary training noise rather than signal — the template here (establish contraction of the random recursive map, read off the dependence measure, then batch-means the long-run covariance online) is the one to copy. Dropout-style masking also appears in retrieval training as a regularizer, and the "dropout = ridge + non-vanishing implicit noise" picture is a useful caution that masking does not merely shrink. Otherwise, treat it as valuable technique to learn rather than as literature you must track.

title: Autobidder's Dilemma: Why More Sophisticated Autobidders Lead to Worse Auction Efficiency
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-18

Autobidder's Dilemma: Why More Sophisticated Autobidders Lead to Worse Auction Efficiency

Yuan Deng, Jieming Mao, Vahab Mirrokni, Hanrui Zhang, Song Zuo (NeurIPS 2024) — OpenReview

Worked from the abstract plus background knowledge only: the OpenReview PDF sits behind a bot-detection challenge (both /pdf?id= and the api2 endpoint returned a challenge page), and there is no arXiv or other open-access version I could reach. So the proof sketch below is reconstruction of the standard argument shape in this literature, flagged where it is inference rather than reading.

Main idea

Modern ad buyers do not bid; they state an objective ("maximize conversions") and a constraint ("keep cost-per-acquisition under $t$", or "spend at most $B$"), and an autobidder translates that into per-query bids. The canonical model for this is the value-maximizing agent: unlike a quasi-linear bidder maximizing value minus payment, it maximizes total value subject to a return-on-spend or budget constraint, and is indifferent between any two outcomes satisfying the constraint. The standard reduction says the optimal strategy for such an agent in a truthful auction is uniform bid-scaling: bid $\mu \cdot v_i$ for a single multiplier $\mu$ chosen so the constraint binds.

The known efficiency picture under first-price auctions is a clean dichotomy. If every autobidder is restricted to uniform scaling, equilibrium welfare is optimal — price of anarchy $1$. If they may use non-uniform scaling (a different multiplier per query, which is exactly what a more expressive bidding stack lets you do), the price of anarchy jumps to $2$: half of the available welfare can be lost. This paper's contribution is to fill in the interval.
