It gives a fine-grained PoA as a function of how non-uniform the strategies are allowed to be, and shows the bound degrades monotonically as expressiveness grows — interpolating from $1$ at uniform to $2$ at fully arbitrary. The headline is the dilemma in the title: each advertiser rationally upgrading to a more powerful autobidder makes every advertiser collectively worse off, and the authors report that this matches empirical findings that higher levels of non-uniform scaling depress realized welfare in first-price auctions.

The most interesting part, and a critique

The conceptually interesting move is treating strategy-space expressiveness as the parameter of a PoA bound. Most PoA work parameterizes by the mechanism (first- vs second-price), by the constraint structure (budget vs ROI), or by the number of bidders. Here the mechanism is fixed and the strategy class is the knob, which gives a genuine comparative statics statement — and it is a statement with the opposite sign from the usual intuition that richer strategy spaces at worst do nothing. The mechanism behind it is worth stating plainly, because it is the real content: under a binding spend constraint, a value-maximizer's total budget is fixed, so non-uniform scaling cannot buy more — it only lets the bidder re-allocate the same spend across queries. The reallocation it wants is to shade down on queries it would win anyway (harvesting surplus) and shade up on contested ones. The first half is pure efficiency loss: the bidder lowers its bid on a high-value query to just above the runner-up, which is fine in isolation, but when everyone does it the bids no longer rank by value, and the first-price allocation — which is only welfare-optimal because the highest bid is the highest value — starts misallocating. Uniform scaling preserves the ordering of values within a bidder; non-uniform scaling destroys it. That is the whole dilemma in one sentence, and it is a nice illustration of expressiveness being harmful precisely because it breaks an order-preservation property that the mechanism was silently relying on.

Where I would push: "worse auction efficiency" is a statement about the worst-case equilibrium, and PoA $2 > $ PoA $1$ does not by itself mean any particular advertiser upgrading makes things worse — it means the worst equilibrium of the larger game is worse. The dilemma framing needs either a price-of-stability companion result or a dynamics story (do autobidders actually converge to the bad equilibria?), and from the abstract alone I cannot tell which the paper supplies. Second, the value-maximizing model itself is the load-bearing and least-examined assumption: real advertisers are not perfectly indifferent above the ROI threshold, and partial quasi-linearity is known to change autobidding conclusions qualitatively. Third, the result is specific to first-price. Second-price auctions with autobidders have PoA $2$ even under uniform scaling, so the whole "expressiveness hurts" phenomenon is a first-price artifact — which matters because the industry's move to first-price is recent and the paper is effectively saying the move made the mechanism more fragile to bidder sophistication. That is a strong and interesting claim, and it deserves the robustness checks (reserve prices, heterogeneous constraint types, mixed populations of uniform and non-uniform bidders) that I would want to see before believing the monotone degradation is not an artifact of a particular adversarial instance family.

Proof sketch (reconstructed, not read)

The precise claim is a bound of the form: in any equilibrium of the first-price auction where each value-maximizing autobidder plays a non-uniform bid-scaling strategy with expressiveness at most $k$ (plausibly: at most $k$ distinct multipliers, or multipliers confined to a ratio-$k$ window), realized welfare is at least $1/\rho(k)$ of the optimal welfare, with $\rho(1) = 1$ and $\rho(\infty) = 2$, monotone in between. The standard machinery for this class of results, which I expect is what is used: an upper-bound argument via a deviation or smoothness inequality, plus a matching lower-bound instance family.

The upper bound in autobidding PoA proofs typically runs as follows. Fix an equilibrium and the welfare-optimal allocation. For each query assigned to bidder $i$ in the optimum but won by $j$ in equilibrium, use the fact that $i$ did not deviate to outbid $j$: either $i$'s constraint is already tight (so $i$ is spending its whole budget, and you can charge the lost welfare against $i$'s spend) or $i$ could have won and chose not to, which bounds $i$'s value on that query by the equilibrium price. Summing these per-query inequalities and aggregating via the constraints gives welfare $\ge$ some fraction of optimum, with the factor coming from the worst case of the aggregation. The refinement for bounded expressiveness is where the fine-grained part must live: with only $k$ multipliers, the per-bidder bid vector cannot be an arbitrary monotone reshaping of the value vector, so the "harvesting" deviation above is constrained — a bidder cannot shade down on exactly the set of queries it would like to without also shading down elsewhere. That restriction should enter as an extra inequality relating the spread of $i$'s multipliers to the number of inversions in its bid ordering, and the resulting factor $\rho(k)$ is the solution of a small optimization over multiplier profiles. The lower bound is then an explicit construction: a family of instances with two (or $k$) value levels per bidder, calibrated so that the equilibrium uses the full multiplier budget to invert the value ordering on exactly the queries that matter, approaching $\rho(k)$ as the instance grows. If the construction is the usual one, the gap is achieved in the limit rather than exactly, and the $k \to \infty$ limit recovers the known factor $2$.

I want to be explicit that the middle paragraph is the shape of the argument in this subfield, not a reading of this paper's proof. If you read it, the thing to check is what "level of non-uniformity" is formally — a cardinality bound on the multiplier set, a ratio bound $\max\mu/\min\mu$, or a metric-entropy-style bound — because the interpretability of the whole result turns on that definition being something an ad platform could actually control.

Broader context

Autobidding theory took off with Aggarwal, Badanidiyuru and Mehta's framework for value-maximizing agents under constraints, which established the uniform-scaling reduction. The efficiency side is largely Deng, Mao, Mirrokni and Zuo and collaborators: "Efficiency of the first-price auction in the autobidding world" is the direct predecessor here, as is the line on boosts and reserve prices as efficiency-restoring interventions (Deng et al., Balseiro et al.). Two things worth knowing beyond this paper: first, Balseiro, Deng, Mao, Mirrokni and Zuo on the robust price of anarchy across mechanism families, which gives the right frame for asking whether first-price is the wrong choice in a sophisticated-bidder world; second, the literature on liquid welfare as an alternative benchmark, which changes the conclusions because it charges budget constraints to the benchmark too. A natural follow-up the paper opens: if expressiveness monotonically degrades worst-case welfare, a platform has an incentive to limit the bidding API's expressiveness, which turns "how much non-uniformity to allow" into a mechanism-design variable. Characterizing the optimal expressiveness cap — and whether a platform that caps it can be undercut by one that does not — seems both tractable and practically live.

No IR connection here that I would call genuine; this is auction theory, and it is worth reading as auction theory. The one abstract transfer, if you want one, is the order-preservation observation: a mechanism whose guarantee rests on scores ranking consistently with true values is fragile to any per-item reweighting, which is a pattern that recurs whenever a ranking system is fed scores that each producer is free to calibrate independently. But that is an analogy, not a connection.

title: Fast Construction of Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter with Theoretical Guarantees
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-17

Fast Construction of Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter with Theoretical Guarantees

Atsuki Sato, Yusuke Matsui (University of Tokyo) — arXiv:2410.13278 (Oct 2024) — arxiv.org/abs/2410.13278

Main idea

A learned Bloom filter replaces part of a Bloom filter's hashing work with a classifier. Train a model $s(\cdot)$ to predict membership in the key set $S$ using $S$ and a sample $Q$ of non-keys; on a query, high score means "report present" immediately, and everything else falls through to a backup Bloom filter holding the keys the model misses. No false negatives survive as long as every key the model rejects is in the backup filter. The partitioned learned Bloom filter (PLBF, Vaidya et al., ICLR'21) generalizes the single threshold into a partition: cut the score space $[0,1]$ at $t_0=0<t_1<\dots<t_k=1$ and give region $i$ its own backup filter with its own FPR $f_i$. With $G_i=\Pr[s(x)\in[t_i,t_{i+1})\mid x\in S]$ and $H_i$ the same for non-keys, the problem (Eq. 3) is to minimize $\sum_i c|S|G_i\log_2(1/f_i)$ subject to $\sum_i H_if_i\le F$ and $f_i\le 1$.

The appendix (Eqs. 59–73) does the KKT analysis the original paper skipped. With $I_{f=1}={i:f_i=1}$, the optimum is reverse water-filling: $f_i=(F-H_{f=1})G_i/((1-G_{f=1})H_i)$ off the clipped set, and the optimal cost (Eq. 6) is $c|S|(1-G_{f=1})\log_2\frac{1-G_{f=1}}{F-H_{f=1}}-c|S|\sum_{i\notin I_{f=1}}G_i\log_2\frac{G_i}{H_i}$. Memory is thus minimized by maximizing a discrete KL divergence $\sum_i G_i\log_2(G_i/H_i)$ between the key and non-key score distributions under the partition — the partition should extract as much of the likelihood-ratio signal as the $k$-cell coarsening allows.

PLBF discretizes $[0,1]$ into $N$ segments with per-segment masses $g_i,h_i$ and solves, by DP, the problem of clustering consecutive segments into regions. Under Assumption 1 ($I_{f=1}$ is $\emptyset$ or ${k}$), it brute-forces the last threshold $t_{k-1}$: for each $j=k,\dots,N$ it builds a fresh $j\times k$ table $DP_j^{KL}[p][q]=\max_i DP_j^{KL}[i-1][q-1]+d_{KL}(i,p)$ where $d_{KL}(i_l,i_r)=(\sum g)\log_2(\sum g/\sum h)$ over the merged segment block (Eqs. 8–10). Each table costs $O(j^2k)$; $N$ of them give $O(N^3k)$.

Fast PLBF kills the outer rebuild. $DP^{KL}_j[p][q]$ for $p\le j-1$ depends only on segments $1..p$, so it is identical to $DP^{KL}_N[p][q]$: build the full table once, then for each $j$ just back-trace from $DP_N^{KL}[j-1][k-1]$ in $O(k)$. That is $O(N^2k)$ with a bit-identical output structure.

Fast PLBF++ attacks the two remaining costs. (i) OptimalFPR is dropped from $O(k^2)$ to $O(k\log k)$ by Theorem 5: at an optimum, $G_i/H_i<G_j/H_j$ whenever $f_i<1,f_j=1$ — the clipped set is exactly a _suffix in sorted $G/H$ order_, so only $k$ nested candidate sets exist, each evaluable in $O(1)$ with running sums of $G_{f=1},H_{f=1},\sum G_i\log_2(G_i/H_i)$. (ii) The DP layer transition is recast as a matrix problem on $A_{p,i}=DP^{KL}[i-1][q-1]+d_{KL}(i,p)$ for $i\le p$ and $-\infty$ otherwise (Eq. 16), so that $DP^{KL}[p][q]=\max_i A_{p,i}$ is "find each row's argmax." If $A$ is a monotone matrix (row argmaxes non-decreasing — intuitively, adding one segment never pushes the optimal $t_{q-1}$ left), Aggarwal et al.'s monotone-maxima divide-and-conquer solves the row in $O(N\log N)$ instead of $O(N^2)$, giving $O(Nk\log N)$ overall.

Fast PLBF# swaps monotone maxima for SMAWK, which needs the stronger total monotonicity but runs in $O(N)$ per layer, so the DP becomes $O(Nk)$; the residual $\log k$ comes entirely from running the $O(k\log k)$ FPR solve at each of the $N$ candidate $j$'s, hence $O(Nk\log k)$.

The most interesting part

The elegant core is Lemma 7, the inverse-quadrangle (concave Monge) inequality for the KL block cost: for $i<i'\le p<p'$, $d_{KL}(i,p)+d_{KL}(i',p')\ge d_{KL}(i,p')+d_{KL}(i',p)$. Because the DP transition adds the same $DP^{KL}[i-1][q-1]$ term to every entry of column $i$, those terms cancel in any $2\times2$ difference, so the Monge condition on $d_{KL}$ transfers verbatim to $A$ (Theorem 8) and yields total monotonicity — hence SMAWK. The proof is a small gem: parametrize the $2\times2$ difference as $D(x,y)$ in the masses $x=\sum_{p+1}^{p'}g,\ y=\sum_{p+1}^{p'}h$ (Eq. 20), show $\partial D/\partial x\ge0$ and $\partial D/\partial y\le0$ using that ideality forces $(u_2+x)/(v_2+y)\le(u_1+x)/(v_1+y)$, push $(x,y)$ to the boundary of the admissible cone $u_1/v_1\le x/y$, substitute $x=zu_1,y=zv_1$, and finish with Jensen on the resulting one-parameter family. Concavity of the KL block cost in the likelihood-ratio ordering is doing all the work; monotonicity of $g_i/h_i$ is exactly what makes the merge cost Monge.

Reviewer-side limits. First, $N$ and $k$ are hyperparameters, not data size — $N$ is the score-space grid resolution, $k$ the region count — so none of these speedups touch the $O(|S|)$ insertion or model training. The headline 233/761/778x is "up to," attained at $k=50$ with $N=1000$, well outside the paper's own default $k=5$, where the honest end-to-end numbers are 34–67x; those are also against a Python-level $O(N^3k)$ baseline, so it is only loosely apples-to-apples. Second, Theorem 9's non-ideal bound $q\delta_{\max}$ bounds the DP table value, and converting it to memory (0.36 bit/element, $1.18\times$ FPR at $k!\sim!10$) assumes $I_{f=1}=\emptyset$; worse, $\delta_{\max}$ is defined through $\Delta(p,p')=\max_{i\le i'\le p}(\cdot)$, which costs as much as the exact DP to evaluate, so it is an a posteriori diagnostic, not an a priori guarantee. It also requires $N=2^M$ and the specific monotone-maxima recursion tree, and there is no analogous bound for fast PLBF# — Table 1 quietly leaves that cell empty. The empirical $1.85\times$ FPR blowup at $10^8$ swaps shows the approximation does bite once monotonicity is destroyed. Third, nothing in the paper bounds the discretization error of using $N$ segments versus the continuous optimum, so the end-to-end gap to the true optimum remains uncontrolled. And construction time was arguably never the deployment blocker for static blacklists; it matters for rebuild-heavy settings (LSM compaction, per-SSTable filters, drifting distributions) and for reaching large $N,k$. The actual LBF blocker — model inference cost at query time, and the fact that the FPR guarantee holds only in expectation over the modeled query distribution — is untouched. Also note that even exact PLBF is optimal only under the unproved Assumption 1.

Broader context

Kraska et al. (SIGMOD'18) framed classical indexes as models: a B-tree is a monotone CDF predictor, a Bloom filter a membership classifier, so replacing them with learned models can beat structure-agnostic bounds when the data has exploitable structure. Pagh–Pagh–Rao (SODA'05) pinned the distribution-free floor at $n\log_2(1/F)$ bits (Bloom pays $\log_2 e\approx1.44\times$ that); learned filters get under it only by charging the model's bits against distributional structure in $S$ and $Q$. Mitzenmacher (NeurIPS'18) supplied the sober analysis: sandwiching the model between a pre-filter and a backup filter is provably better than a backup alone, and — crucially — the learned FPR is an average over the training non-key distribution, so it carries no worst-case or adversarial guarantee. PLBF is the natural completion, turning Kraska's single threshold and Ada-BF's heuristic binning (Dai & Shrivastava, NeurIPS'20) into an optimal $k$-way partition; this paper makes that optimization cheap. Adjacent reading: Hsu–Indyk–Katabi–Vakilian on learned frequency estimation and Lin–Luo–Woodruff on learning-augmented BSTs (the same "predictions with provable fallbacks" program), plus Naor–Yogev on Bloom filters in adversarial environments for the robustness side.

Natural follow-ups: an updatable PLBF, where insertions perturb $(g,h)$ and one wants amortized maintenance of the optimal partition rather than a rebuild — the Monge structure suggests kinetic/segment-tree SMAWK and a sensitivity theory of how far the optimal cuts move under perturbation; a minimax PLBF over an ambiguity ball around $(g,h)$ for distribution shift; and the missing discretization theory, i.e. memory suboptimality as an explicit function of $N$, which would turn "construction time vs accuracy" into a real Pareto statement.

For your work the links are not decorative. The whole paper is a 1-D optimal-partitioning problem whose cost is a divergence and whose speedup comes from total monotonicity — precisely the machinery you want for codebook/partition design in vector search. IVF chooses cells and a probe budget; PLBF chooses score regions and an FPR budget; both allocate a resource where the data distribution says it buys most, and PLBF's KKT solution $f_i\propto G_i/H_i$ is reverse water-filling, the same bit-allocation structure as anisotropic/ScaNN-style quantization and PQ subspace bit allocation. The KL objective "maximize $\sum G_i\log(G_i/H_i)$ over coarsenings" is the exact analogue of choosing a partition so that cells are maximally informative about whether the true neighbor lives there — the quantity learned routers (Neural LSH, BLISS) optimize implicitly. If you ever need provably optimal 1-D or hierarchical partitions for semantic-ID construction in generative retrieval (RQ-VAE codebooks, bucketized docid layouts), Lemma 7's template — check the Monge/concave-Monge inequality on your block cost, then invoke SMAWK — gives you $O(Nk)$ instead of $O(N^2k)$, and it is a transferable proof technique, not just a result. Finally, learned Bloom filters appear directly in your pipelines: pre-screening in filtered/attribute-constrained ANN, and near-duplicate detection in corpus dedup. The deepest shared point is the honest one: both learned filters' FPR and ANN recall are in-distribution expectations, so the theoretical question of what survives distribution shift is the same open question in both fields.

Proof sketch

Theorem 5 (structure of the clipped set). Claim: at an optimum of Eq. 3, if $f_i<1$ and $f_j=1$ then $G_i/H_i<G_j/H_j$. So $I_{f=1}$ is a suffix in the $G/H$ ordering, and the $O(k^2)$ search over clipped sets collapses to $k$ nested candidates. The argument is an exchange argument on the KKT conditions: suppose $f_i<1\le f_j$ with $G_i/H_i\ge G_j/H_j$; perturbing mass between the two regions strictly decreases $\sum G_i\log_2(1/f_i)$ while preserving $\sum H_if_i\le F$, contradicting optimality. Guaranteed under Assumption 1 and feasibility; no approximation.

Fast PLBF exactness. Claim: fast PLBF returns exactly the PLBF solution. The structural lemma is a prefix-independence observation rather than a deep theorem: $DP_j^{KL}[p][q]$ for $p\le j-1$ involves only segments $1..p$ and the same recurrence, so it cannot depend on $j$; hence the $N$ tables PLBF builds are all restrictions of the single table $DP_N^{KL}$. The reduced search space is lossless because nothing is discarded — only recomputation is. This is the one guarantee in the paper that is unconditional (given Assumption 1), which is why fast PLBF keeps PLBF's exact memory efficiency.

Theorems 6–8 (equivalence under ideal distribution). "Ideal" is defined formally: the discretized likelihood ratios $g_i/h_i$ are monotone non-increasing in $i$ — i.e. the model's score is a monotone transform of the true likelihood ratio on the grid, so sorting by score sorts by $G/H$. Under ideality, Lemma 7 establishes the inverse-quadrangle inequality on $d_{KL}$ (proof sketched above: reduce the $2\times2$ difference to a two-variable function $D(x,y)$, sign its partials using the ideality-induced ordering, push to the cone boundary, finish with Jensen), Theorem 8 lifts it to total monotonicity of $A$ via the column-wise cancellation of the $DP^{KL}[i-1][q-1]$ terms, and total monotonicity licenses SMAWK (fast PLBF#) while plain monotonicity licenses monotone maxima (fast PLBF++). Both then compute the same row maxima as the brute-force scan, so under ideality the output is identical to PLBF's — not merely close.

Theorem 9 (non-ideal bound). Claim: when ideality fails, the monotone-maxima recursion can miss the true argmax, and the resulting shortfall in the DP objective is bounded by $q\delta_{\max}$, where $q$ is the layer index (at most $k$) and $\delta_{\max}=\max_{p,p'}\Delta(p,p')$ measures the worst violation of the quadrangle inequality over the recursion's candidate intervals. Proof technique: a telescoping/accumulation argument over the $\log N$ levels of the divide-and-conquer tree — at each level the pruning can lose at most $\Delta$ on the interval it discards, and the losses add across the $q$ DP layers, giving an additive error rather than a multiplicative one. Converting the DP-value shortfall into memory and FPR uses Eq. 6 and the assumption $I_{f=1}=\emptyset$. What is not guaranteed: tightness. $\delta_{\max}$ is a data-dependent quantity whose exact evaluation is as expensive as the exact DP, the bound requires $N=2^M$ and the specific recursion tree, and no counterpart exists for fast PLBF# — so the honest reading is that ++ degrades gracefully by a measurable-after-the-fact amount, while # is an unbounded heuristic off the ideal manifold.

title: Rethinking Cross-lingual Gaps from a Statistical Viewpoint
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-17

Rethinking Cross-lingual Gaps from a Statistical Viewpoint

Vihari Piratla, Purvam Jain, Darshan Singh, Partha Talukdar, Trevor Cohn — arXiv:2510.15551 (Oct 2025) — arxiv.org/abs/2510.15551

Main idea

The cross-lingual gap is the accuracy drop you incur when you ask an LLM a question in a language other than the one in which the underlying fact was (apparently) acquired. The standard story is a bias story: knowledge is siloed per language, embeddings and tokenizations are misaligned, the model fails to resolve the foreign-script entity, and so the target-language answer is systematically wrong — a different answer, not a noisier one. That diagnosis is expensive, because it implicates pretraining, tokenization and representation alignment. This paper argues the opposite: the dominant failure mode is variance, not bias. Target responses are approximately zero-centred around the source response but far more dispersed, so the mode survives while individual samples wander.

The running example is diagnostic of the whole paper: "When was Kreeda Bharti established?" (answer 1992) is answered 1992 with near-zero spread in Hindi, and roughly 1992 ± 30 in Hebrew — not 1500 BC. Formally they posit a latent effective logit: $M(x) = \alpha z$ with $|z| = 1$, $\hat y \sim \mathrm{Categorical}(\mathrm{softmax}(\alpha z))$, responses first normalised across languages into shared "concepts". Source is $\alpha_s z_s$. For the target they draw $\kappa \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi)$ and set $z_t = \alpha_t z_s$ when $\kappa = 1$ (unbiased: same direction, flatter, $\alpha_t \le \alpha_s$) and $z_t = \alpha_t z_b$ with $\arg\max z_b \ne \arg\max z_s$ when $\kappa = 0$ (biased). $\pi = \mathbb{E}[\kappa]$ is the object of interest, and the two regimes are separated by a single signature: as variance falls, source–target agreement $\to 0$ under bias (Prop. 1) but increases monotonically under unbiased error (Prop. 2). Monte-Carlo majority voting over 10 samples drives agreement up on both ECLeKTic and MMLU-mixup, yielding $\pi \approx 0.9$–$0.95$. A second prediction (Prop. 3) — target confidence is lower-bounded by an increasing function of source confidence — also holds empirically: cross-lingual agreement rises smoothly with source-language mode frequency. (Note the arXiv v2 retitles this "Rethinking Cross-Lingual Gaps via Response Variance" and adds Preethi Jyothi.)

Reviewer-style critique

The framing is the contribution, and it is a good one. Recasting cross-lingual transfer as unsupervised domain adaptation and then arguing that the Ben-David-style divergence term is not the binding constraint — that the inflation is in the target's conditional variance, not its conditional mean — is a genuinely useful reorientation, and the bias/variance dichotomy is operationalised into a falsifiable asymmetry (Prop. 1 vs Prop. 2) rather than left as metaphor. The intervention-based evidence is the right kind of evidence, and the temperature digression is honest: lowering temperature reduces variance but introduces bias (1986 ± 0 vs 1991.7 ± 8.4 for a true answer of 1992), which is why they need an unbiased variance reducer.

But this is not a bias–variance decomposition. There is no loss function anywhere, no additive split of risk, and the decomposition that the title of §2.1 promises is never written down. What they have is a two-component mixture model over a latent per-example indicator, with "bias" redefined as mode mismatch and "variance" as scalar logit rescaling along a fixed direction. Those two cases are not exhaustive: a target logit that shares the source's argmax but points in a different direction (reordered tail, different relative gaps) is neither, and that is almost certainly the generic case. So $\pi$ is not estimating the share of variance in a decomposition; it is estimating the share of examples that happen to agree after ensembling. Crucially, "unbiased" is defined relative to the source mode, not to the truth — a confidently wrong source answer counts as bias-free transfer.

The estimators of $\pi$ carry most of the weight and are the weakest link. On ECLeKTic, $\pi$ is the fraction of examples whose ensemble-10 source-vs-target mean-embedding $L_2$ distance falls inside a bootstrap CI around an "oracle" distance computed over judge-correct responses; $\pi$ is therefore a monotone function of the chosen band width, with no sensitivity analysis and no alternative embedder. Averaging multilingual embeddings is also questionable given their own observation that PC1–PC2 are dominated by script (they plot PC3–PC4 instead) — language identity is in the mean they are comparing. On MMLU-mixup it is worse: mismatch is scored as $|p_i - q_i|$ whenever the argmaxes differ, so over four options a genuine bias with $p_i = 0.4$, $q_i = 0.3$ contributes 0.1 rather than 1. $\pi \approx 0.95$ is substantially an artefact of that soft score.

Confounding is under-interrogated. Confidence and agreement are both estimated from the same 10 samples, so the monotone trend in Fig. 5 is partly plug-in bias: mode frequency over 10 draws is quantised to tenths and upward-biased exactly in the high-confidence bins where the trend is strongest. A split-sample design (confidence from one half, agreement from the other) would settle it. Refusals and language-of-answer are never audited; on Year-ECLeKTic the score is "first year mentioned in the response" via regex, and the paper never says what happens to responses containing no year — if high-variance target outputs are disproportionately refusals or non-committal text that the regex drops, the retained set is selected for confidence and agreement is inflated.

Knowledge-source attribution is a proxy, not a measurement: ECLeKTic infers the source language from "Wikipedia page exists only in language $L$", which says nothing about news, forum or book text in other languages. And the paper's own Appendix A cuts against its thesis — SBET (borrowing source-language entity surface forms into the target prompt) closes 60–70% of the gap to statistical insignificance. Fixing entity surface forms is a representational identification fix; a model that cannot resolve a foreign-script rendering of "Pavagadh" is making a systematic error, not a zero-centred one. That tension is never reconciled.

On TrEn: appending $k$ translations of the question and taking one answer is not Monte-Carlo variance reduction at all. It changes the input, hence the conditional mean — it can remove bias, and most plausibly does so by supplying multiple lexicalisations of the critical entity, i.e. SBET by another route. So TrEn's success is not evidence for the variance hypothesis specifically; it shifts the decision rule. It also uses oracle dataset translations, which the paper concedes are unavailable in practice.

Finally, the gains. The headline "up to 12 points / >50% relative" is DeepSeek-R1 alone (23.7 → 35.7), the weakest baseline — and TEA, the existing baseline, beats TrEn-5 there (36.2). For Gemini/GPT the gains are 3.5–5.1 absolute, 8–13% relative, and non-monotone (GPT-5-mini peaks at TrEn-3). Table 7 shows part of the gap closure is levelling down: G-2.5-Flash source falls 59.9 → 57.6 while target rises 49.0 → 54.5. Worst of all, Tables 5–6 — low-resource source, arguably the hardest setting — show TrEn frequently hurting: low→low GPT-5 46.6 → 31.0, GPT-5-mini 26.8 → 14.6, Flash 29.1 → 26.8. Appendix H's claim that "the trend holds for any combination" is contradicted by the appendix's own tables, and the main-table averages are dominated by high-resource sources. That omission would be my central objection.

Broader context

The relevant backdrop is the "English as pivot" literature. Wendler et al.'s latent-language work and Dumas et al.'s activation-patching study argue that multilingual transformers route non-English input through an English-ish intermediate representation; Brinkmann et al. find shared latent grammatical features across typologically diverse languages; Schäfer et al. show, in cloned-language toy settings, that language imbalance is necessary for good multilingual generalisation. On the factual-recall side, X-FACTR and mLAMA established cross-lingual recall disparity as a measurable phenomenon, Qi et al. formalised cross-lingual consistency, and the ROME/causal-tracing lineage localised factual associations; Fierro et al. and Wang et al.'s "Lost in multilinguality" trace the gap to errors in the implicit translate-in/translate-out pipeline, and Lu et al.'s "Paths not taken" patch both ends with steering vectors. Those are bias accounts, which is exactly the consensus this paper is pushing against — and note that a steering-vector fix and a variance fix make opposite predictions about ensembling.

Two directions worth tracking: the risk-sensitive/UDA bound side (a target-risk bound that charges for $\alpha_t/\alpha_s$ rather than for representational divergence would be a real theorem, and Prop. 3 is the kernel of one), and the mechanistic side, where open-weights logprobs make the mixture model identifiable rather than merely posited. The obvious follow-up: $\gamma = \alpha_t/\alpha_s$ is, under their own model, a single scalar per (model, language) pair. Estimate it on a small probe set and correct it at decode time — per-language logit sharpening — and you should recover source behaviour exactly, with no 10× sampling cost. If that fails, the aligned-direction assumption is false and the variance story is wrong. On an open model one can go further and regress $z_t$ on $z_s$ directly, testing proportionality rather than inferring it from agreement curves.

Where this touches your work: the honest bridge is that a bias–variance split of retrieval effectiveness is exact in the places where this paper's is not. IR already has a risk-sensitive tradition — portfolio-theoretic ranking, variance-of-effectiveness-across-topics, URisk-style evaluation — but it measures variance across topics, treating a query as a fixed object. The move worth importing is variance within a query's surface forms. For cross-lingual dense retrieval, take a query $q$ with translations ${q_l}$ and a relevant-document centroid $c$: $\mathbb{E}_l|f(q_l) - c|^2$ splits exactly into $|\mathbb{E}_l f(q_l) - c|^2 + \mathbb{E}_l|f(q_l) - \mathbb{E}_l f(q_l)|^2$, because squared loss in embedding space actually admits the decomposition that softmax-over-concepts does not. That turns "is cross-lingual retrieval failing because of embedding geometry or because of query variance?" into an estimable quantity, with two different fixes: averaging translated query embeddings helps iff the variance term dominates, whereas subtracting a per-language mean offset (the language-identity direction that this paper saw in PC1–PC2) helps iff the bias term does. The prediction is that for a strong multilingual encoder the language offset is large but largely orthogonal to the relevance direction, in which case centring buys little and paraphrase averaging buys a lot.

For generative retrieval the import is sharper still, because Props. 1–2 are a diagnostic, not just an explanation. A DSI-style model decodes an identifier with beam search, which is mode-seeking; the question of whether the docid space is language-misaligned (an RQ-VAE codebook or atomic-ID assignment learned from a monolingual encoder) or whether the decoder is merely under-confident on the translated query is exactly the $\kappa = 0$ vs $\kappa = 1$ question. Run a query-side TrEn — sample or paraphrase/translate the query, marginalise over decoding paths, and plot identifier agreement against ensemble size. Rising agreement means under-confidence and self-consistency will fix it; collapsing agreement means the identifier space itself is misaligned and no amount of marginalisation helps. Prop. 3 then gives a ceiling worth testing: the entropy of the identifier distribution on the original-language query upper-bounds achievable cross-lingual agreement, which would predict that generative retrievers transfer well precisely on the queries where they are already sharp — a much more pessimistic claim than "self-consistency helps", and a cheap one to falsify.

Proof sketch / formal content

Be clear about what is and is not proved. The formal content is a definitional dichotomy plus two monotonicity lemmas, not a decomposition theorem. The posited generative model is: $\alpha_s z_s = M(x_s)$ with $|z_s| = 1$ and $\hat y_s \sim \mathrm{Cat}(\mathrm{softmax}(\alpha_s z_s))$; $\kappa \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\pi)$; $z_t = \alpha_t z_s$ if $\kappa = 1$, else $\alpha_t z_b$ with $|z_b| = 1$ and $\arg\max z_b \ne \arg\max z_s$; $\hat y_t \sim \mathrm{Cat}(\mathrm{softmax}(z_t))$. Randomness is decoding randomness at fixed prompt and model (default temperature, different seeds), not paraphrase or training-seed randomness — so "variance" here is sampling variance over a single conditional, and the claims say nothing about variance across prompt phrasings, which is what TrEn actually manipulates. Assumptions: an enumerable response space shared across languages, obtained by LLM-based normalisation of surface forms to concepts (itself a noisy, unvalidated step); $\alpha_t \le \alpha_s$, i.e. $\gamma = \alpha_t/\alpha_s \in (0,1]$, asserted rather than derived; and the strong one, exact proportionality $z_t \propto z_s$ in the unbiased branch.

Proposition 1 is near-trivial: as $\alpha_s, \alpha_t \to \infty$ both samplers become Dirac deltas at unequal modes, so $\Pr(\hat y_s = \hat y_t) \to 0$. Proposition 2 is the real argument. With inverse-temperature $\kappa$ (an unfortunate reuse of the Bernoulli symbol), $p_k(\kappa) \propto \exp(\kappa s_k)$, $q_k(\kappa) \propto \exp(\kappa t_k)$, agreement is $\sum_k p_k q_k$, and $\partial p_k/\partial \kappa = p_k(s_k - \mathbb{E}_p[S])$ gives $\partial \Pr/\partial \kappa = Z\cdot(\mathbb{E}_{pq}}[S] - \mathbb{E_p[S] + \mathbb{E}_{pq}}[T] - \mathbb{E_q[T])$ with $Z = \sum_k p_k q_k$ and $\mathbb{E}_{pq}}$ the normalised product measure. Under proportionality $q_k \propto p_k^\alpha$, so $\mathbb{E_{pq}[S] = \mathbb{E}_{p^{1+\alpha}}}[S]$, and $f(a) = \mathbb{E{p^a}[S]$ is shown increasing via $df/da \propto \sum_$. Note the bound depends on $m$, the size of the normalised concept space, which is unbounded for free-form generation and never reported; as $m$ grows the bound becomes vacuous for $\gamma < 1$.} \exp(\alpha_t \Delta_i) = \sum x_i^\gamma \le (m-1)^{1-\gamma}(\sum x_i)^\gamma$ by concavity of $x^\gamma$, and substituting $\sum_{i>1} \exp(\alpha_s \Delta_i) = 1/\Pr(\hat y_s = \mathrm{mode}) - 1$ gives $\Pr(\hat y_t = \mathrm{mode}) \ge [1 + (m-1)^{1-\gamma}((1 - P_s)/P_s)^\gamma]^{-1

So what is guaranteed is only this: if the target logit is a scalar flattening of the source logit, then sharpening increases agreement and target confidence inherits a floor from source confidence. Everything else is asserted. The empirical estimates do not measure the model's parameters: $\gamma$ is never estimated, $\alpha$ is never estimated, and confidence is the mode's relative frequency over 10 draws, while $\pi$ is a threshold-dependent indistinguishability rate under an embedding metric (ECLeKTic) or one minus a soft probability-difference score (MMLU-mixup). To make this a theorem one would need, at minimum, a loss with an actual decomposition (squared loss on a numeric answer, as Year-ECLeKTic almost provides, or a Bregman generalisation for the categorical case), a relaxation of exact proportionality to something testable such as bounded angle between $z_t$ and $z_s$, a consistent estimator of $\pi$ with a stated identification condition, and a target-risk bound in terms of $\gamma$ and source risk — which would be the genuine replacement for the Ben-David divergence term that the paper argues is not binding.

title: What Do Latent Action Models Actually Learn?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-17

What Do Latent Action Models Actually Learn?

Chuheng Zhang, Tim Pearce, Pushi Zhang, Kaixin Wang, Xiaoyu Chen, Wei Shen, Li Zhao, Jiang Bian — arXiv:2506.15691 (v2, Oct 2025) — arxiv.org/abs/2506.15691

Main idea

Latent action models are the workhorse of the "learn control from action-free video" program: an inverse dynamics model compresses a frame pair $(o, o')$ into a low-capacity latent $z$, a forward dynamics model reconstructs $o'$ from $(o, z)$, and the hope is that the bottleneck forces $z$ to carry the control action. The nagging worry is that $z$ just compresses whatever changed, action or not. This paper makes that worry precise by stripping LAMs down to a linear surrogate: observations in $\mathbb{R}^{d_o}$, additive dynamics $o' = o + q + \epsilon$ with controllable change $q = Xa$ and exogenous noise $\epsilon$, IDM $z = Co + Do'$, FDM $\hat o' = Ao + Bz$, trained on $\mathbb{E}|\hat o' - o'|_2^2$.

The payoff is a clean reduction: under uncorrelatedness of observation and change, LAM training is PCA on the mixture $q + \epsilon$. Everything else follows from that. The latent captures the top-$d_z$ variance directions of $\Sigma_{q+\epsilon}$ indiscriminately — so LAM works exactly when controllable change dominates noise in variance, and fails otherwise regardless of bottleneck size. Three further results: expert (deterministic) data collection is actively harmful, because the FDM's $A$ matrix absorbs the policy map $o \mapsto o'$ and frees latent capacity for noise; the IGOR-style paired random-crop augmentation provably kills an over-parametrization degeneracy that lets $o$-information leak into $z$; and a 1%-label auxiliary action head provably biases the encoder orthogonal to the noise subspace.

The most interesting part

The cleverest single move is the over-parametrization observation, which is not in the folklore. Because $A$ is full-rank $d_o \times d_o$ and the reconstruction loss only constrains $A + BC + BD$, there is a one-parameter family $B(Co + Do') = (q+\epsilon) + \alpha o$ with $A = (1-\alpha)I$, all achieving identical loss. The bottleneck constrains the rank of $z$'s contribution but not its semantics: a latent can be contaminated with observation content at zero loss penalty, because the FDM silently subtracts it back out. This means the quantity practitioners care about — "does $z=0$ mean 'nothing moved', consistently across frames?" — is not pinned down by the objective at all. The augmentation result (Prop 4.3) then lands as a genuine explanation rather than a rationalization: two independently sampled augmentation vectors add $|B(C+D)\kappa_1|^2 + |(I-A)\kappa_2|^2$ to the loss, and these are precisely the terms that select $A = I$, $C = -D$ out of the degenerate family, after which $z = D(q+\epsilon)$ exactly.

Now the honest caveats, which are substantial. The additive, state-independent effect $q = Xa$ is doing almost all the work. Real action effects are state-dependent — the same gripper command produces different pixel deltas depending on arm configuration — so the correct object is bilinear, $q = X(o)a$, and the variance decomposition that makes PCA appear simply does not close. Second, the bottleneck analyzed ($d_z \ll d_o$, continuous) is not the bottleneck deployed. VQ with codebook size $K$ is a rate constraint of $\log_2 K$ bits, not a subspace constraint; the right abstraction is k-means / rate–distortion on the mixture distribution, where the governing quantity is the distortion–rate curve, not the eigenspectrum. The paper concedes this in Appendix A but does not analyze it, which is awkward given that the continuous-vs-discrete question (Nikulin et al.) is live.

Third, the guarantee is weaker than the prose suggests: Prop 4.2 recovers $\mathrm{span}(X)$, i.e. the action subspace, so $a$ is identified only up to an unknown element of $GL(d_a)$ — hence the downstream action-mapping policy is not optional, it is structurally required. Fourth, everything is a population-level optimum; there is no finite-sample statement, and PCA's sample behaviour is governed by the eigengap $\lambda_{d_z} - \lambda_{d_z+1}$, which is exactly what shrinks when signal and noise variances become comparable. The "robust up to $\sigma_{\mathrm{iid}} = 0.5$" claim is empirical where a Davis–Kahan bound would have been both easy and sharper. Fifth, Prop 4.4 assumes $\epsilon^T X = 0$ and glosses orthogonality as "independent" — those are not the same thing, and the proof uses the geometric fact. Finally, the non-linear validation is a 4×4 grid with noise spatially segregated into the bottom row so that the two losses are measurable by construction, and the action-prediction variant preassigns codebook entries to actions, which leaks far more alignment than "1% labels with a linear head." It is a sanity check, not evidence of transfer to Genie-scale video.

The policy-determinism claim also deserves scrutiny in the other direction: real LAMs are trained largely on expert teleoperation and egocentric human video and they are not useless. The linear model's degeneracy severity depends on the FDM being able to memorize $o^_ \mapsto o'^_$ — trivial for a full-rank linear map on Gaussian observations, much harder for a finite-capacity network over a combinatorially large image space. So the prediction is directionally plausible but its magnitude is an artifact of giving $A$ complete expressivity.

Broader context

The lineage: Rybkin et al. (2018) and Menapace et al.'s Playable Video Generation introduced bottlenecked unsupervised action discovery; LAPO (Schmidt & Jiang, 2023) crystallized the modern IDM+FDM template; Genie (Bruce et al., 2024) scaled it to internet video with a VQ latent action space; LAPA, Moto, IGOR, GR00T-N1 and Go-1 are the robotics descendants. The contrasting branch is VPT, which trains the IDM supervised on a small labeled contractor set — notably absent from this paper's bibliography, though it is the natural baseline for Prop 4.4. The closest sibling is Nikulin et al. (2025), "Latent action learning requires supervision in the presence of distractors," which this paper's Prop 4.4 essentially supplies a theory for; AD3 (Wang et al., 2024) attacks the same distractor problem with paired forward/inverse models.

The theory line the paper conspicuously does not engage is exogenous-block-MDP identifiability (Efroni et al. and successors), which establishes conditions for separating endogenous from exogenous state with non-linear function classes. That literature already has the right conceptual target — identifiability of the controllable factor — with stronger assumptions on the noise process; cross-pollinating it with the LAM objective is the obvious next move. Two concrete follow-ups: redo the analysis with a VQ bottleneck as a rate constraint, predicting when a size-$K$ codebook partitions the action set versus spending codes on noise modes (this would directly settle the discrete-vs-continuous debate); and extend to state-dependent effects $q = X(o)a$, where the reduction should become a Tucker/tensor decomposition and where the policy-correlation degeneracy should get strictly worse.

On IR: there is a real rhyme here, and it is at the level of mechanism rather than result. The core argument — a reconstruction objective with a capacity bottleneck allocates that capacity to the highest-variance directions, not the task-relevant ones, and a small amount of supervision reorients the encoder away from high-variance nuisance subspaces — is structurally the same argument as why LSA/PCA-style and matrix-factorization embeddings devote their leading directions to popularity and other dominant nuisance structure rather than to relevance, and why a thin supervised layer fixes it. The identifiability-up-to-$GL(d_a)$ point also rhymes with the familiar fact that reconstruction-trained embedding spaces are determined only up to a linear reparametrization, which matters the moment a geometry-dependent index sits downstream. Both are analogies, not transferable theorems — the Eckart–Young plus variance-decomposition toolkit is shared, the setting is not. Treat the paper mainly as a well-executed example of taking an empirical recipe apart with a linear surrogate; the technique is the transferable part.

Proof sketch

Prop 4.1 (Linear LAM is PCA). Claim: assuming $\mathbb{E}[o(q+\epsilon)^T] = 0$, the training objective reduces to $L = \mathbb{E}|(BD - I)(q+\epsilon)|_2^2$. Proof (App. C.1): substitute $o' = o+q+\epsilon$ and $\hat o' = Ao + BCo + BDo'$ to get $L = |(A + BC + BD - I)o + (BD - I)(q+\epsilon)|^2$; expand into three terms; the cross term is $2\,\mathrm{Tr}[(A+BC+BD-I)\,o(q+\epsilon)^T(BD-I)]$, which vanishes in expectation by the uncorrelatedness assumption since trace and expectation commute. The key trick is then a rank argument: $A$ is full rank $d_o$ and appears only in the first term, while $BC$ and $BD$ have rank $d_z$, so $A = I - B(C+D)$ is attainable and zeroes that term exactly. Only the mixture term survives, and $BD$ is a rank-$d_z$ matrix asked to act as the identity on $q+\epsilon$ — a linear autoencoder.

Prop 4.2. Claim: optima are $B = U_{d_z}$, $D = U_{d_z}^T$ where $\Sigma_{q+\epsilon} = U\Lambda U^T$, with $L^* = \sum_{i > d_z}\lambda_i$. This is cited, correctly, as Eckart–Young–Mirsky; no new proof. What is guaranteed is subspace recovery of the top-$d_z$ principal directions of the mixture — not of $q$. Case 1 ($\epsilon=0$) then gives the positive result: $\Sigma_q = X\mathbb{E}[aa^T]X^T$ has exactly $d_a$ nonzero eigenvalues, so at $d_z = d_a$, $\mathrm{span}(B) = \mathrm{span}(X)$ and $L^*=0$. Case 2 (isotropic $\epsilon$) is a perturbation that shifts every eigenvalue by $\sigma_{\mathrm{iid}}^2$, leaving eigenvectors — hence $B$, hence the latent's semantics — untouched while raising the loss floor. Case 3 ($\epsilon = Yb$) is the failure mode: if $Y$'s directions carry more variance than $X$'s, they enter the top-$d_z$ subspace first and no choice of $d_z$ excludes them; if $Y$'s columns are non-orthogonal to $X$'s, $B$ itself is contaminated.

Section 4.2 (data collection). Not a numbered proposition but a derivation: with $a = \Pi_d o + \pi_s$, the cross term no longer vanishes; setting $\partial L/\partial A = 0$ gives $A = I - (BC+BD) - \Sigma_o \Pi_d^T X^T (BD-I)^T \Sigma_o^{-1}$. The extra term is read as the FDM absorbing the deterministic policy's effect, projected onto the orthogonal complement of $\mathrm{span}(B)$ — reconstruction no longer needs the latent, so the latent is free to drift onto noise. This is an interpretation of a stationarity condition, not a theorem about the resulting latent.

Prop 4.3 (augmentation fixes over-parametrization). Claim: with independent shared augmentations $\kappa_1$ (IDM) and $\kappa_2$ (FDM/target), the optimum satisfies $A = I$ and $C + D = 0$. Proof (App. C.2): expanding gives the vanilla loss plus $|B(C+D)\kappa_1|^2 + |(I-A)\kappa_2|^2$, independent of everything else because $\kappa_1,\kappa_2$ are drawn independently. Those two terms are simultaneously zeroed by $A=I$, $C=-D$, which is within the previously degenerate family, so the choice costs nothing on the original term and the problem again reduces to PCA. Substituting back yields $z = D(q+\epsilon)$ — all $o$-dependence gone, i.e. $I(z;o)$ driven to zero. Augmentation strength acts as a penalty weight via $\mathrm{Var}(\kappa)$.

Prop 4.4 (action prediction denoises). Claim: with a linear head $\hat a = Ez$, joint loss $L_a = \mathbb{E}|\hat o' - o'|^2 + \lambda\mathbb{E}_{D_a}|\hat a - a|^2$, assumptions $\mathbb{E}[q^T\epsilon]=0$, $\epsilon^T X = 0$, $d_z \ge d_a$, and the artificial limit $\lambda \to \infty$: the optimum has $D\epsilon = 0$ and $Bz = q$. Proof (App. C.3): start from Prop 4.3's $A=I$, $C=-D$, so $L_a = |(BDX - X)a|^2 + |(BD-I)\epsilon|^2 + \lambda|(EDX - I)a|^2 + \lambda|ED\epsilon|^2$. Then an explicit construction on the thin SVD $X = U\Sigma V^T$: set $D = [U^T; 0]$, $B = [U, *]$, $E = [V\Sigma^{-1}, *]$. The $\lambda$-weighted terms vanish because $U$ spans $\mathrm{col}(X)$ and $\epsilon \perp \mathrm{col}(X)$, and because $EDX = V\Sigma^{-1}U^T U\Sigma V^T = I$; the reconstruction term then gives $BDX = X$, leaving $L_a^* = |\epsilon|^2$ and $Bz = UU^Tq = q$. What is actually proved is that this construction attains the loss floor in the limit; the practically interesting claim — that finite $\lambda$ biases $D$ away from $\epsilon$ — is asserted as an extrapolation from the $\lambda$-terms' structure, not proved with any rate in $\lambda$. Worth noting too that the metric used throughout, LLO (Eq. 6), is a sum of variance-normalized MSEs with the logarithm of the Gaussian mutual-information formula deliberately stripped off, so it is a monotone proxy for the stated objective $I(z;a) - I(z;\epsilon) - I(z;o)$ rather than that objective itself.

title: Scaling Laws for Grid-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in High Dimensions
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 16 October 2026

Scaling Laws for Grid-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in High Dimensions

Liu, Zheng, Purohit, Xie, Li & Li, 2026 — arXiv:2607.01283

Main idea — A HiLD workshop paper that resurrects grid partitioning as an ANN family and fits power-law exponents for it in both $N$ and $d$. The "multiprobe grid" is not a grid in the ambient space: points are PCA-projected from $\mathbb R^d$ to $\mathbb R^m$ with $m$ a tuned hyperparameter in $[2,8]$, the projected space is cut into a uniform $G^m$ lattice (equal-width splits per axis, same $G$ on every axis, no per-axis adaptation to eigenvalue scale), and each cell stores point indices. At query time the query is projected, its home cell located, and only the $2^m$ cells in the orthant toward which $q'$ is displaced from the cell midpoint are candidates — "orthant pruning," which discards most of the $3^m-1$ true neighbours. Those are ordered by squared wall distance and the first $n_{\rm probe} \le 2^m$ are scanned; candidates are re-ranked exhaustively in native $\mathbb R^d$. Empty cells route to a precomputed multi-source-BFS pointer to the nearest occupied cell. So structurally this is multi-probe LSH with a data-dependent (PCA) projection and a lattice quantizer, or equivalently IVF with a fixed lattice codebook instead of a k-means one — it is not the grid of Chan/Arya whose cell count blows up as $(1/w)^d$. Lv et al.'s Multi-Probe LSH is never cited, which is odd given the name.

Measurement is ann-benchmarks, single CPU, Docker-isolated, recall@10, QPS interpolated in log10-space along the Pareto front to a fixed recall target, then log QPS regressed on log $N$ or log $d$. Baselines are Voyager (HNSW), PyNNDescent, Annoy and FAISS-IVF; no ScaNN, no DiskANN. Data: GloVe-200-angular subsampled at 8 values of $N$, SIFT-128 at 5, and GloVe-25/50/100/200 for the $d$ sweep. Headline numbers at recall 0.80 on GloVe-200: $\alpha_N = -0.94$ ($R^2=1.00$) for the grid versus $-0.44$ to $-0.59$ for baselines (SIFT: $-0.83$ versus $-0.27$ to $-0.39$). Build exponents $N^{1.20}$ (grid) versus $N^{1.27}$ (Voyager), $N^{2.00}$ (FAISS-IVF); build time 8.4 s versus 1,569 s for Voyager but 77 ms versus 0.62 ms per query, giving a rebuild-to-query crossover $N_{\rm cross} = \Delta I/\Delta C$ of 2,591 (vs IVF) to 20,432 (vs Voyager). The $d$-crossover — grid's $\alpha_d$ flat while everyone else steepens past recall 0.7 — is shown only as a figure; no numeric $\alpha_d$ values appear anywhere in the paper.

Critique — Start with the biggest problem: the obvious control is missing. Brute force appears in the Pareto plots but is excluded from both exponent figures. A bucketed scan whose cost is (candidates)$\cdot d$ with candidate count roughly $d$-independent must give $\alpha_d \approx -1$ and $\alpha_N \approx -1$; the reported $\alpha_N = -0.94$ and a "flat" $\alpha_d$ in the $-0.8$ to $-1.0$ band are precisely what exhaustive scan gives. The paper's own text concedes the method converges to brute force above recall 0.9, and at recall 0.80 its 77 ms/query on 1.18M$\times$200 is within a small factor of a BLAS scan of the same matrix. Read that way, the "favourable $d$-scaling" is not a property of grids, it is the statement that linear scans have the best possible dimensional exponent — a known fact, not a new phenomenon. Say it plainly: near-linear $\alpha_N$ means $\rho \approx 0.94$ in LSH terms, worse than any nontrivial LSH guarantee, so the method is asymptotically dominated in $N$; the baselines' $-0.44$ to $-0.59$ are the interesting numbers here.

The $d$ sweep is the shakiest part. A factual correction to how this is usually described: ann-benchmarks' GloVe-25/50/100/200 are separately trained Twitter GloVe models, not truncations of a 200d model — but the methodological objection survives intact and is arguably worse. All four share one corpus and one semantic geometry, so intrinsic dimensionality is roughly constant while ambient $d$ varies 8$\times$. That is exactly the regime in which PCA to $m=6$ loses little useful structure and per-candidate cost is linear in $d$. The paper notices that retained variance drops with $d$ (Fig. D9) and waves it away by saying the optimizer adapts $(m,G)$. It does — and that adaptation is the artifact. Table E1 shows the selected configs scan a smaller fraction of the data at $d=200$ than at $d=25$ at nominally matched recall, which mechanically flattens $\alpha_d$. Worse, recall is not genuinely held constant at the top of the sweep: $d=200$ has a hard recall ceiling of 0.90 (an artifact of the $2^m$ orthant cap), so the 0.95 fit drops the $d=200$ point entirely, and the crossover is claimed in exactly the recall band where the sweep is incomplete. Each $\alpha_d$ is a two-parameter fit on four points — three at recall 0.95 — with no $R^2$, no confidence interval, no repeats, and no numeric table.

Tuning is not symmetric: 200-trial NSGA-II for the proposed method against stock ann-benchmarks sweeps for the baselines. Those sweeps are community-validated and broad, so this is a venial sin, but HNSW's efConstruction/M/efSearch frontier is sensitive enough that it deserves an explicit statement, and reporting the build cost of the default sweep's Pareto point as "HNSW's indexing cost" conflates a tuning grid with an algorithm. The Python-vs-C++ defence is half right: Appendix C argues interpreter overhead is $O(1)$ in $N$ and under 0.01% of query time, which is fine for slopes. But their own Table C1 shows 95% of query time in np.concatenate/fancy-index candidate gathering (62 ms of 65 ms), not in distance computation — a pure memory-layout artifact that cell-contiguous storage removes — and that phase grows 865$\times$ over a 118$\times$ increase in $N$, i.e. as $N^{1.42}$ at fixed configuration, when the cost model says it must be exactly linear. That internal inconsistency is not addressed, and it directly inflates $\Delta C$, the denominator of every $N_{\rm cross}$ number.

On the indexing-cost story, which I think is the real contribution: it is also the weakest-defended. $N_{\rm cross} = 20{,}432$ against HNSW means the grid wins only if you rebuild more than once per 20k queries, which few production systems do — and nobody rebuilds HNSW from scratch anyway, they insert. The right comparison for a rebuild-heavy pitch is amortised per-insert cost against FreshDiskANN or in-place HNSW update, which the paper explicitly defers to future work while still making the claim. FAISS-IVF's $N^{2.00}$ build exponent at $R^2=0.84$ should also have triggered an alarm; the caption admits the fitted configuration changes across $N$, so the indexing exponents are regressions across a moving target. The attention-as-ANN framing is decorative: mapping $N$ to context length and $d$ to $d_{\rm head}$ is arithmetic, not analysis, and the ann-benchmarks regime (static index, batched queries, single CPU, recall@10) shares almost nothing with per-head per-layer KV-cache retrieval, which needs softmax-weighted aggregation rather than top-$k$ recall.

Genuine strengths, fairly: rebuild-dominated and streaming indexes are real and under-measured, the explicit crossover ratio $\Delta I/\Delta C$ is a clean way to make build-cost arguments quantitative, reporting exponents as a function of recall target rather than one headline number is a good presentational move, and contrarian results about simple baselines deserve air even when the analysis is thin.

Theory note — The paper proves nothing. Appendix B is a cost model plus a chain of heuristic approximations: cost $= K\cdot n_{\rm probe}\cdot N/G^m$ (exact, by construction), a mean-field exponential fall-off $P_i \approx P_h e^{-\mu w_i^2}$ under a uniformity assumption the authors concede none of their datasets satisfies, a linearisation $\mathbb E[w_i^2] \approx \theta i$ of a step function, a geometric sum, a first-order Taylor truncation whose relative error they themselves put at $\sim$50% at $u=0.8$ and which diverges as $u\to1$, and finally a _local linearisation of $\log R$_ that converts the derived power law QPS $\propto 1/R$ into the exponential QPS $\approx A\cdot10^{-BR}$ they observe. That last step is curve-shape matching presented as derivation — the power law and the exponential are not both predictions. There is no bound that holds, no constant that is controlled, and a type mismatch besides: $R$ is defined as $\Pr[$the single true NN lands in a probed cell$]$ while everything measured is recall@10.

Connect this to what is actually known. True ambient-space grids were abandoned for good reason: cell counts scale as $(1/w)^d$ and Arya–Mount-style guarantees carry a $c_{d,\epsilon} = d\lceil1+6d/\epsilon\rceil^d$ factor, exponential in $d$. This paper sidesteps that entirely by fixing $m \le 8$, which is why it is really a quantiser, not a grid, and why none of the classical negative results bite. LSH theory gives the relevant yardstick: Indyk–Motwani plus Datar et al. give query time $N^\rho$ with $\rho = 1/c$ for Euclidean, improved to $1/c^2+o(1)$ (Andoni–Indyk) and $1/(2c^2-1)$ with data-dependent hashing (Andoni–Razenshteyn). Against that, $\rho \approx 0.94$ is a non-result. On the other side, HNSW has essentially no worst-case guarantee — navigable-small-world arguments assume a generative model the data does not satisfy — so the theory gap the paper gestures at is real, it just is not closed here.

The crossover itself is fully explicable by intrinsic-dimension arguments, which is the decisive point. Since Beyer et al. (1999) and the doubling-dimension line (Karger–Ruhl, Krauthgamer–Lee navigating nets, cover trees), the quantity governing ANN hardness is intrinsic/doubling dimension, not ambient $d$, and later work on local intrinsic dimension (Amsaleg et al.) and relative contrast made this quantitative for benchmark data. GloVe-25 through GloVe-200 are four embeddings of one corpus with near-constant intrinsic dimension; sweeping ambient $d$ at fixed LID is exactly the setting where (i) low-$m$ PCA loses little, and (ii) per-candidate cost is linear in $d$ so a scan-like method hits $\alpha_d = -1$ while methods whose traversal cost also grows steepen past $-1$. The predicted crossover follows from intrinsic-dimension reasoning alone. Neither "intrinsic" nor "doubling" dimension appears anywhere in the paper.

Broader context — The direct predecessor is Sun et al., Scaling Laws for Nearest Neighbor Search (ICML 2025 vector-DB workshop), whose total-cost framework $J(N) = f_I\cdot I(N) + f_C\cdot C(N) + S(N)$ this paper adopts wholesale and extends to a new family and to $d$; read that first. The methodology lineage runs through Aumüller–Bernhardsson–Faithfull's ANN-Benchmarks and, more usefully for this critique, Aumüller & Ceccarello's The role of local dimensionality measures in benchmarking nearest neighbor search (2021) — precisely the paper this one needed and does not cite, showing how to stratify datasets and query workloads by LID and demonstrating that apparent cross-dataset differences collapse once LID is controlled. For the rebuild-heavy claim, DiskANN (cited) and especially FreshDiskANN (Singh et al., 2021) plus the in-place-HNSW-update literature are the real competition. For attention-as-ANN, the ancestry is Reformer (LSH attention) and Routing Transformers (k-means routing), with the recent formalisations the paper does cite (Haris's kNN-attention analysis; Liu, Yu, Sanford, Andoni & Hsu on fast attention and parallelism) being the serious versions.

Concretely worth borrowing: the $\Delta I/\Delta C$ crossover ratio is a one-line device for turning "but the index is cheap to build" into a falsifiable number, and theoretical vector-search work almost always ignores amortised construction cost entirely — putting an explicit $f_I/f_C$ into a cost model alongside the query exponent is cheap and sharpens claims. Plotting the exponent against the recall target instead of quoting one number is also worth copying. Be skeptical of everything else: the $\alpha_d$ crossover, the exponent fits (4 points, no CIs, no control), and any downstream citation of this as evidence that grid methods are competitive.

A clean follow-up, directly in your lane: run the same exponent-fitting protocol on a controlled family that decouples ambient from intrinsic dimension — fixed $N$, fixed ambient $d$, synthetic manifolds or spiked-covariance data with intrinsic dimension swept, plus LID-stratified query sets à la Aumüller–Ceccarello — and refit $\alpha$ as a function of LID rather than $d$. The falsifiable prediction is that the grid's flat $\alpha_d$ evaporates once LID grows with $d$, and that all five methods' exponents collapse onto a single function of LID; either outcome is a real result. A second, more theoretical one: replace the equal-width lattice in PCA space with an equal-mass (quantile) grid or per-axis widths $\propto\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ and analyse the recall–cost tradeoff under a spiked-covariance or Gaussian model instead of uniformity. That turns the mean-field hand-waving into an actual calculation and connects it to lattice quantisation and rate–distortion theory (Zador's constant, the dimensional gain of good lattices) — the correct theoretical frame for what this algorithm actually is, and entirely absent from the paper.

title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights
tags: Condensed Matter - Disordered Systems and Neural Networks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 16 October 2026

Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights

Giorlandino, Goldt & Maillard, 2026 — arXiv:2605.10795

Main idea — The object is the minimal key–value memory: input embeddings ${e_\mu}_{\mu\in[p]}$ and output embeddings ${u_\rho}_{\rho\in[p]}$, both i.i.d. $\mathcal N(0,I_d)$, an injective ground truth $f^*$ (WLOG the identity), and a single linear map $W\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ required to satisfy $\arg\max_\rho u_\rho^\top W e_\mu = \mu$ for every $\mu$. The "strict separation" requirement is what distinguishes this from classification: correctness of association $\mu$ is not one label constraint but $p-1$ half-space constraints $(u_\mu-u_\rho)^\top W e_\mu \ge 0$, so the solution set is an intersection of $\sim p^2$ half-spaces — a convex cone — rather than the $p$ half-spaces of a Gardner perceptron. Worse, the constraints are strongly correlated: conditionally on $W$ and $U$, the scores $z_{\rho\mu}=u_\rho^\top W e_\mu$ are Gaussian with covariance $\Sigma^U_{\rho\sigma}=u_\rho^\top WW^\top u_\sigma$ shared across all $\mu$, so even $\mathbb E[V]$ is an orthant probability of a non-trivially correlated Gaussian with no closed form.

Their device is the decoupled problem: give each input its own independent competitor set $U^{(\mu)}={u^{(\mu)}*\rho}$. Then permutation invariance gives each constraint probability exactly $1/p$, the $p$ constraints are independent, $\mathbb E[V]=e^{-p\log p}$, and balancing this against the $d^2$ degrees of freedom immediately produces the natural load $\alpha := p\log p/d^2$. Conjecture 1 asserts $\alpha_c^{\rm OP}=\alpha_c^{\rm DP}=1/2$, and Claim 1 derives the decoupled value: $p_c\log p_c/d^2 = 1/2$, i.e. $p_c \simeq d^2/(4\log d)$. Practically this is sub-quadratic by a log: $d^2$ parameters buy you not $\Theta(d^2)$ facts but $\Theta(d^2/\log d)$, the log being the price of competing against $p$ alternatives. For $d=768$ that is $\approx 2.9\times 10^4$ associations. Contrast Hopfield ($p\approx 0.14 d$), Gardner's perceptron ($p=2d$), and the Hebbian/one-step-GD ansatz $W*{Hebb \rm}=\sum_\mu u_\mu e_\mu^\top$, for which a clean heuristic (their Theorem D.1) gives $\alpha_c^{\rm Hebb}=1/8$ — a factor 4 below optimal. Claim 2 extends to $W=QR^\top$ of rank $m=\kappa d$: $\alpha_c(\kappa)=\tfrac12\int_{X_{\rm qc}(1-\kappa)}^{2}\rho_{\rm qc}(\sigma)\sigma^2 d\sigma$ with $\rho_{\rm qc}$ the quarter-circle law, giving $\alpha_c\approx 0.31,0.46,0.50$ for $\kappa=0.25,0.5,1$.

The most interesting part — For me the mechanistic result outranks the decoupling trick. The replica calculation predicts that at the optimum the target score concentrates on the deterministic value $\beta_t\sqrt{2\log p}$ (with $\beta_t=\sqrt{t/(1-t)}$), i.e. the solver places each correct score just barely above the extreme-value threshold set by the $p-1$ competitors, with only $O(\beta_t)$ fluctuations. Hebbian storage instead makes the diagonal scores Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\log p/\alpha}$ and unit variance: it buys margin on average and pays for the left tail, which is exactly why it loses the factor 4. This is a genuinely crisp statement about what "memorisation" looks like mechanistically — variance suppression on the diagonal, not mean inflation — and it is visible in the score histograms (Fig. 4) and in the singular-value spectrum, which at capacity is the top slice of a quarter circle, $\rho_c[\kappa]=(1-\kappa)\delta_0+\kappa\rho_{\rm qc}\mathbf 1_{[X_{\rm qc}(1-\kappa),2]}$ — a strongly non-Marchenko–Pastur, non-initialisation spectrum.

Critique: Conjecture 1 is exactly that. The evidence is three-fold (matching transition points, matching spectra, matching score histograms) but all at $d\le 150$ for the decoupled problem — the memory cost is $O(dp^2)$ — and at those sizes the empirical thresholds sit well above $1/2$ (around $0.7$–$0.8$), rescued only by the predicted $\tilde O(1/\log p)$ finite-size correction, which is enormous: $1/\log p\approx 0.1$ at $p=10^4$. The finite-size fit in Fig. C.1 (slope $-1$ against $\log\log p$) is a two-parameter consistency check across barely a decade, not a confirmation. So "the two problems agree" is verified only in a regime where neither is near its asymptote, and the shared agreement could in principle be an agreement of the same finite-size artefact. Further: isotropic Gaussian embeddings are the whole ballgame here (Gaussian equivalence is invoked precisely because the $z_\rho$ have a trivial second-moment structure); real token/document embeddings are anisotropic, heavy-tailed in spectrum and clustered, and clustering is exactly what makes the max-of-competitors not behave like $\sqrt{2\log p}$ — the $\log p$ would be replaced by something governed by local neighbourhood size. Linearity means no superposition/feature-sharing, so the result is a baseline, not a prediction for an MLP. And the argmax formalisation is a zero-margin notion of recall: an LM that ranks the right token first by $10^{-3}$ of a logit is not robustly factual, and a margin requirement would move the constant. Finally, for $\kappa<1$ the feasible set is non-convex and they run RS anyway; they are upfront that this is then generically an upper bound.

Proof sketch — What is claimed: under $d,p\to\infty$ with $p\log p/d^2\to\alpha$, the free entropy $\varphi_d := d^{-2}\mathbb E\log V_{\rm DP}(E,U)$ of the Gardner volume $V=\mathbb P_m(\Gamma(E,U))$, $\Gamma={W:\forall\mu,\ \max_\rho u^{(\mu)\top}_\rho We_\mu \le u^{(\mu)\top}_\mu We_\mu}$, is finite for $\alpha<1/2$ and diverges to $-\infty$ as $\alpha\uparrow 1/2$. The prior $\mathbb P_m$ is Gaussian for $m=d$ and the law of $QR^\top/\sqrt{dm}$ otherwise; the threshold is argued to be prior-independent by scale invariance.

Method: Gardner-style volume computation via the replica trick $\mathbb E\log V=\partial_n \log\mathbb E[V^n]|_{n=0}$. Because the decoupled constraints are independent across $\mu$, $\mathbb E[V^n]$ factorises into $p$ identical copies of a single-constraint term $J({W^a})$ — this is the entire payoff of decoupling; in the original problem this step fails and the orthant probability survives. Inside $J$, conditionally on $e$ and the replicas, $z^a_\rho=u_\rho^\top W^a e/\sqrt d$ is Gaussian with covariance $\delta_{\rho\sigma}Q^e_{ab}$, $Q^e_{ab}=e^\top W^aW^{b\top}e/d$; a Hanson–Wright bound gives $\mathbb P(|Q^e_{ab}-Q_{ab}|>t)\le 2n^2 e^{-cdt}$ provided $|W^a|_{\rm op}=O(1)$, and since the energetic term lives on scale $e^{\Theta(\log p)}$ while the fluctuations are $e^{-\Theta(d)}$ with $\log p\ll d$, a Laplace argument replaces $Q^e$ by $Q_{ab}=\mathrm{Tr}[W^aW^{b\top}]/d$. This is the Gaussian-equivalence step; it is sketched toward rigour but not closed, because the Gaussian prior does not bound $|W|_{\rm op}$ and approximately-low-rank matrices must be excluded by other means.

Then the standard split: entropic term $J(Q)=\tfrac n2(1-Q)+\tfrac12\log\det Q-\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}Q$ from a Gaussian integral over replicas with Lagrange multipliers, and energetic term $\lim_p \log F_{n,p}(Q)/\log p$. The RS ansatz $Q_{aa}=Q$, $Q_{ab}=q$ is imposed, justified by convexity of the cone (citing strong-replica-symmetry results for convex CSPs); no 1RSB or de Almeida–Thouless check is performed, and for the rank-constrained case RS is adopted knowingly outside its guarantee. The RS decomposition $z^a_\rho=\sqrt q\,\eta_\rho+\sqrt{Q-q}\,x^a_\rho$ reduces everything to one scalar order parameter $t=q/Q$ and the function $G(t)=\lim_p \mathbb E_\eta\log f_p(t;\eta)/\log p$ with $f_p=\mathbb E_x\prod_{\rho\ge2}\Theta(x_1-x_\rho+\beta_t(\eta_1-\eta_\rho))$, yielding $\varphi=\inf_q{\tfrac12\log(1-q)+\tfrac{q}{2(1-q)}+\alpha G(q)}$. The capacity falls out of the saddle-point condition as $\alpha_c^{-1}=\lim_{q\to1}-2(1-q)G(q)$.

This is where $\log p$ is born: $G(t)=\lim \tfrac1{\log p}\mathbb E_\eta\log\mathbb P(x_1+\beta_t\eta_1\ge\max_{\rho\ge2}[x_\rho+\beta_t\eta_\rho])$, the max of $p-1$ Gaussians is $\beta_t\sqrt{2\log p}$, and the Gaussian tail gives $\log\mathbb P \simeq -\beta_t^2\log p$, hence $G(t)\sim -1/(1-t)$ and $\alpha_c=1/2$. Pleasingly, this extreme-value asymptotic is not left heuristic: Appendix C.2.2 proves matching upper and lower bounds on $G(t)$ using order statistics of ${\lambda+\eta_\rho}$ and monotonicity of $\Phi$, which is the one genuinely rigorous block in the chain. The two-layer case replaces the Gaussian entropic integral by an HCIZ integral over Stiefel manifolds; in the dilute limit it is dominated by optimal singular-value alignment, and the variational problem over the spectral density yields the truncated quarter circle and $\alpha_c(\kappa)$. Net: rigorous = the extreme-value bounds on $G$ and Hanson–Wright concentration; standard-but-non-rigorous = replica trick, RS ansatz, $n\to0$ continuation, Laplace/saddle point, HCIZ asymptotics; outright conjectural = original $\equiv$ decoupled.

Broader context — The lineage is Hopfield (1982) and Amit–Gutfreund–Sompolinsky's $p\approx 0.14d$, Gardner–Derrida's replica capacity for the perceptron, Krauth–Mézard, Cover's counting bound, and on the modern side dense associative memories with exponential capacity (Lucibello–Mézard for sharp asymptotics). The heteroassociative, matrix-valued version is older than transformers — Kohonen-style correlation-matrix memories — but has been revived by Geva et al.'s reading of transformer FFN layers as key–value memories and by Meng et al.'s ROME, which localises and edits factual associations in a single MLP matrix; that is precisely the object modelled here. The immediate technical predecessors are Cabannes–Dohmatob–Bietti (scaling laws) and Nichani–Lee–Bietti, who showed $d^2\gtrsim p\,\mathrm{polylog}(p)$ suffices for the Hebbian ansatz and conjectured the $p\log p$ transition numerically. The two papers to read alongside are Nichani, Lee & Bietti, ICLR 2025 and the parallel Barnfield et al. (2026), which proves the $d^2\sim p\log p$ scaling with explicit non-matching bounds and introduces a convex Tail-Average Margin relaxation whose variational solution independently conjectures the same $\alpha_c$; the rigorous side also connects to the Gaussian-equivalence literature (Goldt et al., Gerace et al., Maillard–Kunisky on ellipsoid fitting, the closest proved analogue of the matrix-projection universality used here). A concrete follow-up: run the same programme with a non-isotropic, clustered embedding model and see whether $\alpha_c$ degrades as a functional of the embedding spectrum — the quarter-circle structure suggests $\alpha_c$ should become $\tfrac12\int\rho_{\rm limit}\sigma^2$ for a modified limiting law, a directly testable prediction.

For your own work the generative-retrieval link is real and not decorative: "how many docid associations can a parametric index memorise before interference" is literally this problem with $u_\rho$ the docid embeddings. The paper gives a sharp answer for the linear case — $p_c\approx d^2/(4\log d)$, so $\sim 2.9\times10^4$ docids at $d=768$ and $\sim 1.1\times10^5$ at $d=1536$ — plus the sobering news that a single-gradient-step/Hebbian index gets only a quarter of that, and the encouraging news that rank is cheap: $\kappa=0.5$ retains $92\%$ of capacity ($\alpha_c$ 0.46 vs 0.50), a quantitative argument for low-rank adapters as memory stores. The separation requirement is indeed a margin condition on retrieved vectors, and the score analysis says something your side of the field cares about: at capacity the correct docid's inner product sits at $\sqrt{2\log p}$ standard deviations of the competitor distribution with vanishing relative fluctuation — exactly the MIPS competition threshold. Two honest caveats before transferring numbers. First, the model has zero margin by construction, so these are capacities for "retrieve@1 exactly", not robust retrieval; Barnfield's TAM relaxation is the better starting point for a margin-parameterised version. Second, isotropic Gaussian docid embeddings are the best possible case for separation — real corpora are clustered, and the $\sqrt{2\log p}$ extreme-value threshold is the part of this calculation most sensitive to that. Claiming these constants for a real GR system would be a stretch; claiming the $d^2/\log d$ scaling and the $4\times$ optimal-over-Hebbian gap as design guidance is not.

title: Implicit Optimization Bias of Next-Token Prediction in Linear Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 16 October 2026

Implicit Optimization Bias of Next-Token Prediction in Linear Models

Christos Thrampoulidis (UBC), 2024 — arXiv:2402.18551

Main idea — The paper's starting move is a reframing rather than a theorem: NTP training is not one-hot classification with contexts as features. Collapse the $n$ training sequences onto their $m \le n$ distinct contexts $\bar x_j$ with empirical frequencies $\hat\pi_j$, and each context carries a conditional distribution $\hat p_j \in \Delta^{V-1}$ whose support $S_j \subsetneq \mathcal V$ is typically tiny. The CE objective becomes $\mathrm{CE}(W) = -\sum_j \hat\pi_j \sum_{z\in S_j}\hat p_{j,z}\log S_z(W\bar h_j)$ with $\bar h_j = h(\bar x_j)$ fixed, so only the decoder $W \in \mathbb R^{V\times d}$ is trained and the problem is convex. The loss is lower bounded by the empirical $T$-gram entropy $H$, and attaining it requires two structurally different things simultaneously: in-support softmax ratios must match the empirical odds, and out-of-support probabilities must vanish — impossible at finite $W$ by strict positivity of softmax. These two requirements live on orthogonal subspaces of $\mathbb R^{V\times d}$. Define the data subspace $\mathcal F = \mathrm{span}{(e_z - e_{z'})\bar h_j^\top : z \ne z' \in S_j,\, j\in[m]}$. _NTP$_H$-compatibility_ asks for $W_p$ with $(e_z-e_{z'})^\top W_p \bar h_j = \log(\hat p_{j,z}/\hat p_{j,z'})$ — a linear system with $S_j-1$ independent constraints per context, whose unique solution inside $\mathcal F$ is called $W^\star$. NTP-separability asks for $W_d \in \mathcal F^\perp$ (i.e. satisfying the equalities with RHS $0$, so it leaves in-support odds untouched) with $(e_z - e_v)^\top W_d \bar h_j \ge 1$ for all $z \in S_j, v \notin S_j$ — via Kesler's construction, a linear separability condition on the $\sum_j S_j(V-S_j)$ lifted points $(e_z-e_v)\bar h_j^\top$. Overparameterization $d > m$ with full-rank $\bar H$ suffices for both (Lemma 1). The payoff: GD's iterates split cleanly, $P_{\mathcal F}(W_k) \to W^\star$ (finite, carries all the probability magnitudes), while $|P_{\perp}(W_k)|\to\infty$ in the direction of $W^{mm}$, the min-norm solution of the NTP-SVM, which depends only on the support patterns. Figure 2 is the sharpest illustration: two tokens with identical support sets get literally identical rows in $W^{mm}$ and are separated only by $W^\star$.

The most interesting part — The genuinely new object is the factorization of the learned word-embedding geometry into a combinatorial piece and a probabilistic piece on orthogonal matrix subspaces. "Which tokens can follow which contexts" and "with what frequency" are decoupled by the optimizer itself, with the former getting all the norm and the latter staying $O(1)$. That is a crisp, falsifiable statement about what NTP actually encodes, and it has no analogue in one-hot implicit-bias theory, where $\mathcal F$ degenerates.

The honest critique is substantial, though. Fixing the context embeddings is not a mild simplification: $W^{mm}$ is a functional of an exogenous geometry ${\bar h_j}$ that in reality is co-trained, and the author's own follow-up (Zhao et al., COLM 2024) shows the unconstrained-features version produces a quite different and more informative picture.
