The overparameterization condition $d > m$ is the real sore point — $m$ is the number of distinct contexts in the corpus, i.e. effectively $\Theta(n)$ for long contexts, versus $d \sim 10^3$–$10^4$. The analyzed regime is therefore the memorization regime; the realistic regime $d \ll m$ is exactly where NTP-separability fails, the infimum exceeds $H$, minimizers are finite, and the entire dichotomy may dissolve. Remark 1 admits that even the exact separability threshold is unknown. The results are also purely asymptotic: no rate on $|W_k|$ (presumably $\log k$, as in Soudry et al.), no margin-convergence rate, hence no statement about any checkpoint reachable in finite compute — and since real training uses weight decay, the regularization-path result (Theorem 1 plus $P_{\mathcal F}(\hat W_B)\to W^\star$) is arguably the more operationally relevant one. Finally, the margin $1/|W^{mm}|$ is attached to nothing measurable: the SVM has $mV - \sum_j S_j$ inequality constraints, no generalization bound is proved, and unlike classical margin theory there is no statistical theorem linking it to test behaviour.

Worth stating plainly: the "implicit bias" being characterized is a bias toward driving empirically unobserved continuations to probability zero — which is precisely the zero-frequency pathology that smoothing was invented to repair. The divergence is as much an artifact of identifying empirical support with true support as it is a property of NTP.

Proof sketch — The engine is a decomposition plus a comparison-point ("genie") argument, inherited from Ji & Telgarsky's non-separable logistic regression framework but re-derived for the sparse-soft-label setting. Define the truncated loss $\mathrm{CE}_{\mathcal F}(W) = \sum_j\hat\pi_j\sum_{S_j z\in}\hat p_{j,z}\log(1 + \sum_{z'\ne z, z'\in S_j} e^{-(e_z-e_{z'})^\top W\bar h_j})$, which keeps only in-support logit differences. Then $\mathrm{CE}\ge \mathrm{CE}_{\mathcal F}$ pointwise, and $\mathrm{CE}_{F \mathcal}(W) = \lim_{R\to\infty}\mathrm{CE}(W + RW_d)$ for $W_d\in\mathcal F^\perp$ feasible, so $\inf_{\mathcal F}\mathrm{CE}*{\mathcal F} = \inf \mathrm{CE} = H$. Lemma 4 then establishes that $W^\star$ is the unique minimizer of $\mathrm{CE}*{F \mathcal}$ on $\mathcal F$ — proved not by strict convexity (the loss is only convex) but by a contradiction: a second minimizer would also have to satisfy the log-odds system, so the difference lies in $\mathcal F$ and is simultaneously orthogonal to every spanning element of $\mathcal F$. Combined with Lemma 3 (standard smooth-convex GD analysis for an infimum that is not attained: $\mathrm{CE}(W_k)\to\inf$, $|W_k|\to\infty$), this gives $P_{\mathcal F}(W_k)\to W^\star$ and $|P_\perp(W_k)|\to\infty$.

The load-bearing new result is Lemma 5: for any $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $k$ large, $\mathrm{CE}(W_{k,\mathcal F} + (1+\alpha)|W_{k,\perp}|\overline{W^{mm}}) \le \mathrm{CE}(W_k)$ — replacing the orthogonal component by a slightly inflated max-margin direction never increases the loss. Its proof is a two-case exponential comparison on the normalized component $\widetilde W_\perp = (|W^{mm}|/|W_\perp|)W_\perp$. If $|\widetilde W_\perp - W^{mm}| \le \alpha/M$ (with $M = \sqrt2\max_j|\bar h_j|$), Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the logit perturbation by $\alpha$, and the factor $e^{-\alpha R'}$ absorbs it for every $R'$. Otherwise, uniqueness of the strongly convex NTP-SVM minimizer together with $|\widetilde W_\perp| = |W^{mm}|$ forces a quantitative constraint violation: some $(j_\star, v_\star)$ with $\tilde\ell_{j_\star,z} - \tilde\ell_{j_\star,v_\star} \le 1-\delta(\epsilon)$. Then the actual loss exceeds $H$ by $\gtrsim e^{-R'(1-\delta)}/(n(A_{\max}+1))$ while the genie's excess is $\le Ve^{-R'(1+\alpha)}/A_{\min}$, and the exponents separate once $R' \ge \frac{1}{\delta+\alpha}\log(nV(A_{\max}+1)/A_{\min})$. The compactness step that makes this work: the in-support partition sums $A_{j,z} = \sum_v e^{-(e_z-e_v)^\top W_{\mathcal F}\bar h_j}$ depend only on $W_{\mathcal F}$, which is bounded by $2|W^\star|$ for large $k$ — so $A_{\min}, A_{\max}$ are $R$-independent constants.

From Lemma 5, convexity gives $\langle\nabla \mathrm{CE}(W_k), W_{k,\perp} - (1+\alpha)|W_{k,\perp}|\overline{W^{mm}}\rangle \ge 0$; each GD step's correlation with $W^{mm}$ is then at least $(1-\epsilon)$ times its correlation with $W_{k,\perp}$, and telescoping with $x^2-y^2\ge 2y(x-y)$ and smoothness yields $\langle \overline{W_k}, \overline{W^{mm}}\rangle \ge (1-\epsilon) - O(|W_{k,\mathcal F}|^2/|W_k|) \to 1-\epsilon$. The regularization-path proof (Theorem 1) is structurally the same but cleaner: a KKT/first-order argument shows $\hat W_B$ must sit on the boundary (choosing $U = W^{mm}$ in $\langle-\nabla\mathrm{CE}(\hat W_B), U\rangle$ makes the $\mathcal F$-term vanish by (6a) and the $\mathcal F^\perp$-term strictly positive by (6b) and softmax positivity, contradicting interior stationarity); then the genie $W_B^\star = W^\star + R(B)W^{mm}$ with $R = \sqrt{B^2-|W^\star|^2}/|W^{mm}|$ achieves $\mathrm{CE}(W_B^\star)\le H + Ce^{-R}$, while any $\epsilon$-misaligned $\hat W_B$ incurs either $\Omega(R'\delta/n)$ or $\Omega(e^{-R'(1-\delta)}/n^2)$, both of which beat $Ce^{-R}$ for large $B$ since $R/B, R'/B \to 1/|W^{mm}|$.

Broader context — This sits squarely in the lineage Rosset–Zhu–Hastie (2003, regularization path) → Soudry et al. (2018, GD on separable data converges in direction to the $\ell_2$ max-margin classifier at rate $\log t$) → Ji & Telgarsky (2018, 2019) for non-separable data, where the data are separable only on a subspace and GD converges to a finite point on the complement and a max-margin direction within the subspace. Thrampoulidis' contribution is to show that NTP manufactures exactly such a subspace decomposition for free, out of conditional-distribution sparsity rather than out of data non-separability, and that the two components carry semantically distinct information. The two most useful companions: Zhao, Behnia, Vakilian & Thrampoulidis, Implicit Geometry of Next-Token Prediction (COLM 2024), which redoes this with unconstrained features and connects the support-pattern combinatorics to neural-collapse-style geometry; and Tarzanagh, Li, Thrampoulidis & Oymak, Transformers as Support Vector Machines, whose SVM conjecture for attention this paper proves an analogue of (rigorously, because convex) in a complementary setting — they fix the decoder and train attention, here the embeddings are fixed and the decoder is trained.

A natural follow-up that the paper itself cannot reach: characterize the implicit bias when NTP-separability fails, i.e. $d \ll m$. The Ji–Telgarsky template suggests a refined trichotomy — a maximally separable sub-cone of $(j,z,v)$ triples on which the iterate diverges in a max-margin direction, and a residual cone on which it converges to a finite minimizer of a restricted loss. Equally tractable and more immediately useful: express $|W^{mm}|$ in terms of the bipartite context–token support incidence graph, since the solution provably depends only on that combinatorics plus ${\bar h_j}$ — that would turn the margin into something computable from corpus statistics.

For generative retrieval the connection is unusually direct rather than metaphorical. In DSI/NCI-style systems a docid is decoded token-by-token under a trie, so at each prefix the set of legal continuations is a support set $S_j$ — known structurally rather than estimated. NTP-separability then reads literally: the decoder must linearly separate, in Kesler-lifted space, legal from illegal children of every prefix, and the direction GD diverges along is determined by the trie's combinatorics and the prefix-embedding geometry alone. The Figure-2 phenomenon transfers: docid tokens sharing identical prefix-sets get identical rows in the divergent component, and all of the discrimination among co-legal continuations — the part that actually determines ranking — lives in the bounded component $W^\star$. Since constrained beam search already enforces legality at inference, the theory says a large and growing share of decoder norm is being spent suppressing continuations the decoder will never be allowed to emit, while the ranking-relevant signal stays $O(1)$ and increasingly ill-conditioned relative to it. Masking illegal continuations in the training softmax would remove the divergent component outright and leave a well-posed finite problem — a concrete, cheap experiment this paper motivates. The connection to dual-encoder vector search is much weaker and I would not push it: the cone geometry of Figure 1 rhymes with dual-encoder geometry, but InfoNCE with in-batch negatives and $\ell_2$-normalized embeddings destroys precisely the norm divergence the whole analysis rests on.

title: Uncovering the Representation Geometry of Minimal Cores in Overcomplete Reasoning Traces
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-15

Uncovering the Representation Geometry of Minimal Cores in Overcomplete Reasoning Traces

Sanjoy Chowdhury, Dinesh Manocha (University of Maryland), 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14358

Main idea. The paper asks a deceptively simple question: of the steps a reasoning model writes down, how many are actually doing work? It reframes this as a subset-sufficiency problem. A trace is a sequence z = (r_1, ..., r_T) of textual reasoning units; for S a subset of [T], z_S is the retained subsequence in original order, and the model re-conditioned on (x, z_S) induces a prediction ŷ(x, z_S) = argmax_y p(y | x, z_S). A subset S is answer-sufficient if ŷ(x, z_S) equals the full-trace answer ŷ(x, z_[T]), and distribution-sufficient if D(p(· | x, z_S), p(· | x, z_[T])) ≤ ε for a divergence D (KL over the candidate-answer distribution, with ε = 0.05 or 0.10). A minimal core S_ is a minimum-cardinality sufficient subset; a trace is _overcomplete if any proper subset is sufficient. From this, compression ratio_ CR(z) = |S_|/T and redundancy mass RM(z) = 1 − CR(z). Note that sufficiency is defined entirely relative to the model's own original answer, not to ground truth — the authors are explicit about this in the appendix, and it matters enormously for interpretation.

Two further quantities sit on top. Step necessity is a leave-one-out loss change Δ_t = ℓ(x, z_[T]{t}) − ℓ(x, z_[T]), with ℓ the negative log-likelihood of the full-trace answer under the pruned context. Positive Δ_t means deletion hurts. These are clipped at zero and normalized into weights w_t = max(Δ_t, 0) / (Σ_j max(Δ_j, 0) + η), η = 1e−8, and necessity concentration is the top-k mass NMass_k = Σ_{t ∈ TopK(w,k)} w_t. The authors are careful to call Δ_t marginal necessity, flagging that duplicated or substitutable steps can each score near zero while collectively mattering.

On the protocol: the ablation is a hybrid, and it is worth being precise because the two halves have different semantics. The sufficiency constraint is deletion-and-regenerate — the pruned trace is fed back as explicit context and the answer is re-decoded. The necessity score Δ_t and the distribution-preserving criterion are deletion-and-rescore — the pruned context is scored against the already-fixed full-trace answer. Importantly, the trace itself is never regenerated: the surviving steps are re-presented verbatim with the deleted ones simply excised, gaps and all. Extraction is Algorithm 1, greedy backward elimination from the full trace: at each round, compute the admissible set A(S) = {t ∈ S : Suff(S \ {t}) = 1}, delete the admissible step with lowest estimated harm h_t(S), recompute A(S), and stop when A(S) is empty. Because exact answer-flip harm is degenerate (every admissible deletion has zero harm by construction), h_t is instantiated by a verifier score, answer confidence, or margin — used only to rank, never to decide admissibility. Cost is O(T²) sufficiency checks versus O(2^T) for exact search. Two cheaper comparators: one-shot necessity-guided pruning (rank once by Δ_t, remove low-necessity steps, O(T)) and random deletion at matched budget.

Models are DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B (open weights, full metric suite) and GPT-5 (black-box, behavioral metrics only). Six benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24, AMC23, GPQA-Diamond, StrategyQA. Traces are generated with low-temperature CoT prompting, models are asked to emit numbered steps, and unnumbered outputs fall back to deterministic sentence segmentation with short continuations merged. Headline result: mean full-trace length 9.9 steps, mean core length 5.2–5.3, so ~46% removable mass at 86% answer retention. Overcompleteness is highest on GSM8K and StrategyQA (RM ≈ 0.51–0.61) and lowest on AIME24 and GPQA-D (RM ≈ 0.34–0.49). Necessity is sparse: top-1 mass 0.29, top-3 0.65, top-5 0.82, Gini 0.54. Cores transfer across model families (Qwen-32B, Llama-3.3-70B, Mixtral-8x22B, a closed GPT) with 0.85 average off-diagonal retention versus 0.64 for matched-length random subsets.

The most interesting part. The geometry section, and within it a specific result that is the paper's real contribution and is undersold. Step embeddings ϕ(r_t) ∈ R^d are mean-pooled final-layer hidden states over each step's token span; the paper then forms three pooled vectors — the full-trace mean h(z) over all T steps, the core mean h(z_) over S_, and the removed-step mean h(z⁻) over the complement — and compares them on four axes: linear-probe accuracy for predicting correct-vs-incorrect, silhouette and Davies–Bouldin cluster scores, intrinsic dimensionality (PCA participation ratio, per Appendix A, despite the main text gesturing at nearest-neighbour estimators), and embedding variance. The reported pattern is consistent across GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA-D and StrategyQA: probe accuracy rises from ~0.67 to ~0.78 (about +11 points, +0.10 averaged in Table 11), silhouette roughly doubles, participation-ratio dimension falls 31–40% (≈ −34% mean), and removed-step embeddings move the other way on every axis.

The genuinely novel piece, though, is Section 3.3's necessity-weighted embedding h_Δ(z) = Σ_t w_t ϕ(r_t) — a soft, continuous relaxation of hard subset selection, using the leave-one-out weights directly as pooling coefficients. Table 3(c) shows it reaches cosine 0.84 with the hard core embedding (versus 0.71 for the uniform full-trace mean), probe accuracy 0.76 (versus 0.67 full, 0.78 core), and participation-ratio dimension 14.6 (versus 21.3 full, 13.9 core). So you recover nearly all of the geometric gain with O(T) rescoring passes instead of O(T²) decode-and-check rounds, and without ever committing to a discrete subset. That is both a real efficiency claim and a conceptually interesting one: it says the "core-ness" signal is a smooth reweighting of the bag of step vectors rather than a discrete combinatorial object, which is a stronger and more falsifiable statement than "short traces are cleaner."

What is actually measured deserves emphasis, because the framing invites over-reading. These are not representations of the model running on the compressed trace. Appendix A describes ϕ(r_t) as mean-pooled hidden states over the token span of each segmented step, which points to a single forward pass over the full trace; h(z_) is then a selected average of those same vectors. So the claim is "feature selection over step vectors from one forward pass yields a more probeable average," not "conditioning on the core puts the model in a lower-dimensional state." Those are different claims and the paper does not separate them. Relatedly, there is a clean algebraic identity the paper never notes: h(z) = CR(z)·h(z_) + RM(z)·h(z⁻). The full-trace embedding is exactly a convex combination of the other two. The three conditions are therefore not independent measurements, and "full traces are worse than cores and better than removed steps" is partly forced by the arithmetic of mixing a signal component with a residual one.

Critique. Start with the estimator. Greedy backward elimination under an answer-preservation constraint does not estimate necessity; it estimates re-derivability. If a step states an intermediate quantity that the model can recompute from the surviving steps, deletion preserves the answer and the step is scored as redundant, even though it was load-bearing in the original computation. The authors acknowledge the behavioral-versus-mechanistic distinction in one sentence, but the vocabulary ("necessity," "effective support," "the smallest subset that supports the prediction") runs well ahead of what the procedure licenses. A genuinely sufficient core and a core the model can patch over are observationally identical here, and the paper never attempts to distinguish them — for instance by checking whether the model's regenerated post-core reasoning silently re-inserts the deleted content, which would be a cheap and decisive diagnostic.

The sufficiency criterion has a chance-agreement problem that is the most serious flaw in the empirical headline. StrategyQA is binary and GPQA-Diamond is four-way. A badly mutilated trace still reproduces the full-trace answer 50% of the time on StrategyQA and 25% of the time on GPQA by coin flip. And indeed, StrategyQA shows the highest redundancy mass (0.50–0.60) of the six benchmarks, exactly as a chance-floor confound would predict, while open-numeric GSM8K is the other high-RM benchmark for presumably different reasons. The random-deletion baseline makes the problem visible rather than resolving it: at 40% removal, random pruning retains 0.64 on StrategyQA and 0.45 on GPQA-D, so the greedy figures of 0.89 and 0.75 sit on top of very high floors. A chance-corrected agreement statistic (Cohen's kappa against a per-benchmark answer-prior null) is the obvious fix and costs nothing. Without it, the 46% figure is not comparable across benchmarks with different answer-space cardinalities, and the "StrategyQA and GSM8K are the most overcomplete" conclusion is not safe.

Comparability has a second, independent problem: redundancy mass is a ratio of step counts, and the step is a free parameter. The authors' own segmentation ablation (Table 10) moves RM from 0.33 under coarse paragraph segmentation to 0.46 under numbered steps to 0.51 under sentence segmentation — a swing almost as large as the entire cross-benchmark spread the paper interprets substantively. Nothing is reported in tokens. Since removed steps are plausibly shorter than retained ones (the qualitative examples in Figures 8–10 show removals that are verification sentences and caveats), the token-level compression could be substantially below 46%, which would badly dent the efficiency framing. A segmentation-invariant measure — removable token fraction, or necessity density per unit of information — is what the quantity needs to be before it can be compared across benchmarks or against the efficient-reasoning literature.

On the decoding confound: yes, it is real and uncontrolled. Deleting steps shortens the context, shifts every subsequent position index, and leaves a subsequence the model never generated, with dangling discourse connectives ("Therefore," "Also," "Checking this") pointing at removed antecedents. There are at least two distinct effects conflated here — loss of semantic content, and loss of sequential compute budget. The latter is not hypothetical: the filler-token literature shows transformers can exploit meaningless intermediate tokens as computation, which means a deletion that shortens the trace is not a clean content intervention. The correct control is a length-matched placeholder — Li et al. [52], which the paper cites as its nearest neighbour, literally uses [SKIP] tokens for this purpose — and the paper does not run it. The distribution-preserving ablation is partial evidence that something real is being removed (cores grow from CR 0.54 to 0.66 at ε = 0.05, so a good share of answer-preserving slack is confidence slack rather than content slack), but it does not separate content from compute.

The intrinsic-dimension estimates are the weakest technical component. Participation ratio, (Σλ_i)² / Σλ_i², is an effective rank of the second-moment spectrum — a linear, global, scale-dependent quantity. It is not an intrinsic dimension in the TwoNN or Levina–Bickel MLE sense, and the paper's citation for the concept (Aghajanyan et al. on the intrinsic dimension of fine-tuning subspaces) is about an unrelated object. PR is also bounded by min(N, d) and biased downward at small N, and the sample sizes are never stated: the geometry tables silently drop AIME24 (30 problems) and AMC23 (40), and GPQA-Diamond has 198 items total, with a held-out probe split presumably much smaller. A 34% PR drop under a procedure that removes a plausibly stylistic variance axis and reduces the number of averaged vectors per example from 9.9 to 5.2 is close to the null expectation; nothing rules out that reading. A TwoNN or MLE estimate with a bootstrap band, plus the obvious control — select |S_| steps by a _different* rule (last-k, highest-norm, random) and re-measure — would settle it. That random matched-size geometry control is the single most important missing experiment in the paper; it exists for transfer but not for geometry.

The correct/incorrect separation claim is at risk of being a length artifact rather than a selection artifact in the narrow sense. Cores are defined by preserving the model's own answer, which is applied symmetrically to correct and incorrect traces, so the procedure is not circular in the obvious way. But Table 10 shows CR rises monotonically with difficulty (0.42 easy, 0.54 medium, 0.66 hard), and difficulty correlates with correctness. So |S_|, and hence the mixing weight in h(z) = CR·h(z_) + RM·h(z⁻), carries correctness information directly, and any probe over pooled embeddings can read compressibility off the pooling statistics. The paper needs to report probe accuracy with core length regressed out, or restricted to length-matched strata. More basically, no majority-class baseline is reported anywhere. If the probe sets are not class-balanced, then for GSM8K and MATH500 — where these models are 90%+ accurate — a probe accuracy of 0.82 and 0.75 is below the trivial baseline, and the +11 point improvement is movement within a sub-trivial regime.

I also checked the arithmetic of the main table and found it does not fully cohere. The "Average" row reports CR 0.54 ± .03 and RM 0.46 ± .07, but RM = 1 − CR holds exactly in every one of the 24 rows, so the two dispersions must be identical; recomputing from the body gives mean 0.53 with standard deviation 0.07 for both. Retention is reported as 0.86 ± .01 while the body ranges from 0.76 to 0.96, with a recomputed standard deviation of about 0.05. The geometry variances are harder to reconcile still: with h(z) a convex combination of h(z_) and h(z⁻), the triangle inequality in L2 bounds sd(h(z)) ≤ CR·sd(h(z_)) + RM·sd(h(z⁻)), which for GSM8K's reported values (0.63 and 1.24, CR 0.49) caps the full-trace variance at about 0.92 — yet it is normalized to 1.00, and the same violation recurs on every dataset. Varying per-example mixing weights can in principle break that bound, but only if the core and removed means are far apart, which would itself be a headline result worth reporting. Separately, the model ordering (7B < Qwen3-32B < R1-32B < GPT-5) is perfectly rank-consistent across all six datasets and all six metrics in Table 1 with zero inversions, and every one of the six qualitative examples compresses to exactly 50%. None of this is dispositive, but taken together it suggests the tables were not all produced from one consistent measurement run.

Smaller but real issues. The harm score h_t is "a verifier score, answer confidence, or margin-based score" — never pinned down per model, so the greedy path is not reproducible, and the choice matters because a confidence-based harm score will preferentially retain answer-adjacent restatements rather than inferentially load-bearing steps. Necessity concentration is computed on weights clipped at zero, so if only four of ten steps have Δ_t > 0, a top-3 mass of 0.65 is near-automatic; the number of positive-Δ steps is never reported, and Figure 2(c)'s null is uniform-over-T rather than uniform-over-positives, which is the wrong comparison. The transfer matrix uses Llama-3.3-70B and Mixtral-8x22B, which appear nowhere in the setup or in the model table. No prefix or suffix baseline is reported, even though the last step before the answer is almost certainly always retained and a "keep the final k steps" baseline is the cheapest possible competitor; relatedly, the positional distribution of retained steps is never shown, and it would be the most informative single figure in the paper. Accuracy against ground truth is never compared between full traces and cores, which is the experiment a reader most wants: does compression preserve correctness, or does it faithfully preserve errors? Finally, the related-work section's "rationale faithfulness" paragraph cites nine of the authors' own audio-visual papers that have no bearing on rationale faithfulness, while omitting Lanham et al. and Turpin et al. — the two works that most directly prefigure this methodology.

The strengths are real and should not be lost in the above. The three-way full/core/removed design is better than the two-way comparison most such papers run, and the removed-step condition is a genuine control. Crucially, the core and removed sets are nearly matched in cardinality (5.2 versus 4.7 steps on average), so the core-versus-removed comparison is not confounded by how many vectors get averaged — and the full-versus-core variance comparison runs against the trivial averaging confound, since pooling fewer vectors should raise variance, not lower it. The robustness suite is broad for an empirical paper: sufficiency strictness, prompting style, difficulty stratification, segmentation granularity, extraction method, and a cost-fidelity frontier. The cross-model transfer result with a matched-length random control is the strongest evidence in the paper, because a target model that never saw the extraction procedure is harder to fool by self-consistency artifacts than the source model is. The sublinear growth of core length with trace length (Figure 2d) is a striking regularity if it holds: core length stays in a 3.2–7.3 band while full length ranges 7.4–13.7, suggesting something like a near-constant budget of five load-bearing steps regardless of verbosity. And the limitations section is unusually candid about model-relativity and about Δ_t measuring marginal rather than total contribution.

Proof sketch of the formal claims. Four results, all correct and all essentially definitional. Existence (Thm 3.1): the family F = {S : Suff(S) = 1} is nonempty because [T] ∈ F by assumption, and finite because 2^[T] is finite; a nonempty finite set of nonnegative integers {|S| : S ∈ F} attains its minimum, so a minimum-cardinality sufficient subset exists. Global minimality implies irreducibility (Lemma, Appendix B.2): if S_ were reducible, some S_ \ {t} would be sufficient with cardinality |S_| − 1, contradicting minimality. _Greedy local irreducibility_ (Thm 3.2): sufficiency is an invariant of the loop (deletions are accepted only when Suff holds), cardinality strictly decreases on each acceptance and is a nonnegative integer, so the loop terminates after at most T acceptances; at termination A(S) = ∅ by the stopping condition, which is precisely irreducibility. _Certificates_: any witnessed sufficient deletion set K of size k gives |S_| ≤ T − k, hence CR ≤ (T − k)/T and RM ≥ k/T; and since w_t ≥ 0 with Σ_t w_t ≤ 1 (strict, because of the +η in the denominator), Σ_{t ∈ C} w_t ≥ 1 − γ implies Σ_{t ∉ C} w_t ≤ γ.

Nothing here is load-bearing. Minimum-cardinality sufficient-subset selection with an arbitrary predicate is the minimal-sufficient-reason / abductive-explanation problem, which is hard in general; the paper proves no hardness result, no approximation ratio for greedy, and no submodularity or structural condition on ℓ under which greedy would come with a bound. The compression certificate is one-sided — observed deletions upper-bound CR, but nothing lower-bounds |S_|, so the paper can never certify that a greedy core is close to minimum, and the gap between "irreducible" and "minimum" is left entirely unquantified. The real gap, though, is that every theorem assumes a _deterministic* sufficiency oracle, while the experimental oracle is a stochastic decode with a benchmark-dependent chance-agreement floor. The theorem the experiments actually need is the noisy-oracle version: if each check has per-call error δ, then over the O(T²) checks on a greedy path all accepted deletions are genuinely sufficient with probability at least 1 − O(T²δ), which immediately tells you how many repeated samples per check are required and why binary-answer benchmarks need more. That would be two paragraphs of work and would turn a decorative theory section into a load-bearing one.

Broader context. The surrounding literature splits into three strands. First, CoT faithfulness: whether a written trace is a causal account of the computation that produced the answer. The canonical empirical works are Lanham et al. (2023), "Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning," which truncates and corrupts CoT and tracks whether the answer changes — the direct ancestor of this paper's protocol and, strikingly, uncited — and Turpin et al. (2023), "Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think," which shows models produce plausible rationales that systematically omit the biasing feature actually driving the answer. The upshot is that answer-invariance under ablation is a necessary but not sufficient probe of faithfulness, which is exactly the epistemic position this paper occupies but states only once. Second, CoT compression and latent reasoning: Li et al. (2026) prune low-entropy steps and train models to emit [SKIP] tokens; Deng et al.'s implicit CoT and Hao et al.'s Coconut move reasoning into continuous latent states; Pfau, Merrill and Bowman's filler-token result ("Let's think dot by dot") shows that meaningless tokens can carry real computation, which is the reason any deletion study needs a length control. Third, representation geometry and intrinsic dimension: Marks and Tegmark on linear truth directions, Burns et al. on latent knowledge, and the intrinsic-dimension estimation line (Levina–Bickel MLE, Facco et al.'s TwoNN) that this paper gestures at but substitutes a participation ratio for. The closest contemporary work is Sun et al. (2026), "LLM Reasoning as Trajectories: Step-Specific Representation Geometry and Correctness Signals," which the paper cites and which is probably the right thing to read alongside it.

A follow-up worth doing: redo the whole thing as a properly controlled causal-attribution study. Replace each deleted step with a length-matched neutral placeholder so sequential compute is held fixed; replace one-at-a-time leave-one-out with a Shapley-style or random-subset-regression estimator, which directly addresses the substitutability problem the authors themselves flag; report chance-corrected retention so binary and four-way benchmarks are commensurable; and then distill the resulting necessity scores into an amortized step-selector — a cross-encoder over (question, step) pairs — that predicts core membership in one pass. That last piece turns an O(T²) diagnostic into a usable inference-time tool and gives a held-out test of whether "necessity" is a learnable, transferable property of a step or just a per-trace idiosyncrasy of the generating model.

Two of these threads should land close to your work. The necessity score here is a leave-one-out context-attribution estimator, structurally identical to what the RAG attribution literature does over retrieved passages — ContextCite (Cohen-Wang et al., 2024) is the sharpest version, fitting a sparse linear surrogate over random context ablations rather than one-at-a-time deletions, precisely because LOO breaks under redundant evidence. Everything that is known about why LOO attribution fails for overlapping retrieved documents applies verbatim to overlapping reasoning steps, and the paper would be substantially stronger if it had borrowed that machinery; conversely, if you care about attribution in retrieval-augmented generation, reasoning-trace minimal cores are the same estimation problem with a different corpus, and the greedy-versus-surrogate comparison is an open question in both settings. The second thread is the intrinsic-dimension material. The paper uses a participation ratio and calls it intrinsic dimension; the distinction between effective rank and local intrinsic dimensionality is one you will already care about from the ANN side, where LID (Houle, Amsaleg) governs hubness, distance concentration, and the hardness of graph-based indexing. A claim that one family of pooled text representations has 34% lower intrinsic dimension than another is exactly the kind of claim whose estimator choice determines whether it means anything — and the paper is a clean, concrete case study in getting that choice wrong in a way that is easy to diagnose and easy to fix.

title: Understanding Generalization from Embedding Dimension and Distributional Convergence
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-15

Understanding Generalization from Embedding Dimension and Distributional Convergence

Yu, Ouyang, Deng, Wei, Ma, Zhang, Deng & Liu (2026) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22756

Main idea. The paper asks why the intrinsic dimension of learned representations keeps turning up as an empirical predictor of generalization — a finding that goes back to Ansuini et al. (2019) and Pope et al. (2021), who observed that the estimated ID of the last hidden layer correlates negatively with test error across architectures, and that it does so far more robustly than any parameter count. There is by now a decent pile of such observations and essentially no theory explaining them. The authors propose one: generalization error should be controlled not through the capacity of the hypothesis class but through how fast the empirical distribution of embeddings converges to the population embedding distribution, and that convergence rate is governed by intrinsic dimension via optimal-transport theory.

The construction is clean. Fix a trained network F and slice it at layer k into an encoder F_{≤k}: X → Z_k and a tail F_k: Z_k → R^C, so F = F_k ∘ F_{≤k}. Push the input distribution through the encoder to get the population embedding measure P_k, and let P̂_{k,n} be its empirical counterpart from n samples. If the composite loss, viewed as a function of the embedding alone, is L-Lipschitz, then Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality gives |E_P[g] − E_P̂[g]| ≤ L · W_1(P_k, P̂_{k,n}), and the Weed–Bach (2019) theory supplies E W_1(P_k, P̂_{k,n}) ≲ C_k n^{−1/(d_k+ε)}, where d_k is the upper Wasserstein dimension of the embedding measure — an intrinsic, covering-number-based quantity, not the ambient width of the layer. Two factors therefore control the gap: geometry (d_k, through the statistical rate) and sensitivity (the Lipschitz constant, through amplification). Because the argument works at every layer, one can take a minimum over k, which the authors read as a layerwise tradeoff: early layers have high dimension but a gentle downstream map, late layers are compressed but can be sharp.

The headline consequence is Corollary 4.2. At the final layer the embedding is the output, the tail map is the identity, L_L(F) = 1, and the architectural sensitivity term disappears; what remains is intrinsic dimension, the support diameter, loss smoothness constants, and a Bayes-approximation term. The authors present this as the explanation for why final-layer ID is such a good empirical predictor: at that layer there is simply nothing left between geometry and loss.

Empirically they do four things: verify on MNIST autoencoders that log W_1 grows roughly linearly in estimated ID at fixed n and decays roughly as a power of n at fixed ID; show class-level correlations among final-layer ID, empirical W_1 (Sinkhorn, ε = 10⁻², Euclidean cost) and the generalization gap across ResNet-18/34/50/101/152 on CIFAR-10/100; repeat the correlation on pretrained ConvNeXt variants (ImageNet-1K) and BERT/DeBERTa/DistilBART variants (MNLI), using test accuracy as the outcome; and run a width intervention where narrowing the third layer of a six-layer MLP reduces ID but raises the spectral-norm product, so the gap does not improve monotonically. That last experiment is the most honest and, to my mind, the most informative one in the paper.

The most interesting part. The technically cleverest move is the Bayes-surrogate smoothing in Appendix A.2, and it is worth spelling out because it is the hinge on which the whole argument turns. The Wasserstein/Lipschitz machinery requires a function of the embedding z alone. But the observed loss is ℓ(F(x), y), and y is not a function of z — for classification it is a discrete label that the embedding does not determine. You cannot apply Kantorovich–Rubinstein to it. The authors therefore define, at each layer, the layerwise Bayes predictor F_k_(z) = argmin_f E[ℓ(f(Z), Y) | Z = z], and replace the label by it, giving the "oracle loss" g_k(z) = ℓ(F_k(z), F_k_(z)) — now a genuine, differentiable function of z, with Lipschitz constant bounded in Lemma A.5 by L_k(F)·M_F + L_k(F_)·M_{F_} via the chain rule.

The resulting algebraic identity (Prop. A.4) is exact and deterministic: the observed gap equals (A) an approximation gap R_0^obs − R_k^oracle, (B) the oracle statistical gap R_k^oracle − R̂_k^oracle, and (C) an empirical model gap. Only (B) carries sample randomness through the embedding measure and is the term attacked with transport; (A) and (C) are each bounded by M_{F_}·E‖Y − F_k_(Z)‖_1 and its empirical average — i.e. by the degree to which the layer-k representation fails to determine the label. The economics are nice: you buy differentiability (hence access to OT) at the price of a label-sufficiency penalty that is zero exactly when the representation is a sufficient statistic for Y, and that is also the natural place where information loss from compression should appear. Lemma A.5 further splits the sensitivity into a network part L_k(F)·M_F, which architecture and spectral regularization can shrink, and a Bayes part L_k(F_)·M_{F_}, which the authors call intrinsic to the data. This decomposition is the real contribution; the dimension story rides on top of it.

Proof sketch. What is actually proved is narrower than the framing suggests. Theorem 4.1 fixes a trained predictor F, assumes measurable embeddings (3.11), bounded ℓ_1-diameter D_k of each embedding support (3.12), local Lipschitzness of both the tail map and the layerwise Bayes predictor on a neighborhood of the support (3.13), a C¹ loss with uniformly bounded gradients M_F, M_{F_} in both arguments (3.14), and a bounded Bayes loss (3.15). It then asserts that for any ε > 0 there is a constant C_k such that, _for all sufficiently large n, with probability at least 1 − δ over the n i.i.d. samples, R(F) ≤ R̂n(F) + min_k { L̄_k [ C_k n^{−1/(d_k+ε)} + D_k √(log(2(L+1)/δ)/2n) ] + M{F} [ 2 E‖Y − F_k_(Z_k)‖_1 + √(2 log(2(L+1)/δ)/n) ] }, with L̄_k = L_k(F_k)M_F + L_k(F_k_)M_{F*}.

The proof is three moves. First the deterministic decomposition above. Second, bound (A) and (C) by the Bayes mismatch (Lemmas A.6, A.8 — pure Lipschitz-in-second-argument), and (B) by L_k(g)·W_1(P_k, P̂_{k,n}) (Lemma A.7 — Kantorovich–Rubinstein). Third, concentration (Prop. A.9): the Wasserstein term T_k is a bounded-difference functional with sensitivity D_k/n, since swapping one sample moves the empirical measure by at most ‖z_j − z'_j‖_1/n in W_1, so McDiarmid gives T_k ≤ E[T_k] + D_k √(log(·)/2n); the empirical noise average gets Hoeffding. Finally E[T_k] is replaced by the Weed–Bach rate and a union bound over the L+1 layers supplies the 2(L+1) inside the logarithm.

So: it is a high-probability bound on the population risk of one fixed model, over the draw of the n evaluation samples; it is partially data-dependent (d_k and W_1 are estimable from held-out embeddings, L_k(F) crudely via spectral-norm products) and partially not (C_k, L_k(F*), and the Bayes mismatch term are not computable). Note that the union bound is only over layers — the phrase in Prop. A.10 "simultaneously for all layers k and any fixed predictors F ∈ F" is a misstatement, since T_k and the noise average both depend on F through the encoder, so the event is per-F.

Now the skeptical part, which matters a great deal here. The Wasserstein rate itself is the sharp one — Weed–Bach refine the classical Dudley rate E W_1 ≍ n^{−1/d} (for ambient d > 2; n^{−1/2} log n at d = 2) by replacing the ambient dimension with the upper Wasserstein dimension d_1_(μ), defined through (ε, τ)-covering numbers with a vanishing mass tolerance, and this is minimax-optimal for the transport distance. But that sharpness is sharpness _for W_1_, not for the quantity we care about. The chain is lossy in exactly one catastrophic place: Lemma A.7 controls the deviation of a _single fixed function_ g_k by the supremum over _all_ 1-Lipschitz functions. For one fixed, bounded function, the deviation between population and empirical mean is O(n^{−1/2}) by Hoeffding, with no dimension anywhere — and under Assumptions 3.12–3.15 the loss _is_ bounded on the support, so this trivial bound is available. Since the premise is a fixed model and i.i.d. samples, a single line of Hoeffding beats the entire theorem whenever d_k > 2 (and Weed–Bach's own rate saturates at n^{−1/2} for d_1_ < 2p = 2, so the OT route can at best tie the trivial bound and otherwise strictly loses). The conclusion is uncomfortable but hard to escape: the n^{−1/(d+ε)} dependence on intrinsic dimension is an artifact of the proof technique — of passing through a metric that is uniform over the whole 1-Lipschitz class — not a property of the statistical problem as the authors have set it up. The theorem does not logically entail that low-ID models generalize better; it entails an upper bound that happens to decrease in d, while a tighter, dimension-free upper bound on the same quantity exists.

Numerically it is also vacuous in precisely the regime tested. The constant C_k is unspecified and, in the Fournier–Guillin/Weed–Bach constructions, grows with dimension; the statement holds only "for all sufficiently large n" with no threshold given. With the paper's own experimental numbers — 500 embeddings per class on CIFAR-10, 100 on CIFAR-100, and MLE-estimated IDs typically in the 10–30 range — n^{−1/d} is 500^{−1/20} ≈ 0.73 or 100^{−1/20} ≈ 0.79. Multiply by L̄_k and C_k, add a non-vanishing 2·M_{F_}·E‖Y − F_k_(Z)‖1 floor, and the bound is enormously larger than any loss it is bounding. The paper nowhere instantiates its bound numerically, which is a conspicuous omission given that its opening move is to criticize classical bounds for becoming vacuous at scale. There is also a small but real algebraic slip: Assumption 3.13 defines L_k as the spectral (2-)norm of the Jacobian, but Lemma A.5 applies ‖Aᵀv‖∞ ≤ ‖A‖op‖v‖∞, which is valid for the ∞→∞ induced norm, not the 2-norm; repairing it costs a factor √C in the number of classes.

Critique. Strengths first, because they are real. The risk decomposition is clean and the Bayes-surrogate device is a genuinely useful way to make discrete-label losses amenable to distributional analysis — I would expect it to be reusable. The layerwise min is a legitimate structural statement, and the resulting dimension-versus-sensitivity tradeoff is the right qualitative picture: the width-intervention experiment (Fig. 5), where narrowing a layer lowers ID but inflates the spectral-norm product so the gap does not improve, is a real finding and the kind of near-negative result papers usually bury. The ID-estimator robustness checks in Appendix C (MLE vs. TLE vs. MOM) are appropriate.

The weaknesses are structural. (1) Intrinsic dimension is measured, not derived, and what is measured is not what the theorem uses: the theory needs the upper Wasserstein dimension d_1_(P_k), an ε→0 covering-dimension limit with a τ = ε^{s/(s−2)} mass tolerance; the experiments use the Levina–Bickel k-NN maximum-likelihood estimator at finite scale with K ∈ {20,…,500}. No relation between the two is established, and no estimation error is propagated into the bound. Worse, Appendix C.1 reports that _larger K correlates better with generalization error_ and the authors adopt large K on that basis — the estimator's hyperparameter is selected by the outcome it is meant to predict. (2) The correlation experiments are consistent with the bound but are not evidence _for_ it. An inequality gap ≤ A·f(d) + B says nothing about corr(gap, d); the bound could be loose by three orders of magnitude and the observed correlation driven entirely by a confounder. A very plausible confounder is sitting inside the bound itself: the irreducible term E‖Y − F_k_(Z)‖_1. Classes with more label ambiguity plausibly have both more diffuse (higher-ID) embeddings and larger gaps, which reproduces every reported correlation with no role for the transport rate. (3) There is a mismatch between what is proved and what is measured. The theory requires the n samples to be independent of F — the authors acknowledge this and compute embedding quantities on held-out data — but the quantity they correlate against is the train/test gap (and in the large-model section, raw test accuracy, which is not a gap at all). A bound on validation-to-population deviation does not explain a train-to-test gap, and cannot explain why training selects low-ID solutions. (4) Figure 2A does not test the theory it is said to test. At fixed n, the predicted W_1 ≈ C_d·exp(−log n / d) is concave and saturating in d, not exponential; an observed linear growth of log W_1 in d is therefore a statement about the unmodelled constant C_d and about embedding scale — and indeed, comparing autoencoders with bottlenecks from 16 to 512 compares embedding spaces of different diameters without normalizing by D_k, which the bound says must be normalized. The sharp test would be Figure 2B done properly: fit log W_1 against log n at fixed estimated ID and check that the slope equals −1/d̂, not merely that it is negative. That check is not reported. (5) The final-layer "architecture-free" claim is half-true: L_L(F) = 1, but L_L(F*) — the Lipschitz constant of the Bayes map from the model's own output space to labels — remains, and it is a function of the learned encoder, hence of the architecture, just indirectly. Calling it "intrinsic to the data distribution" overstates the case. (6) Estimated W_1 is entropically regularized Sinkhorn with Euclidean ground cost against a theory stated for exact W_1 with ℓ_1 cost; Sinkhorn bias at fixed ε is scale- and dimension-dependent, which again matters when comparing across layer widths.

The most constructive reframing: the Wasserstein step is only necessary if one needs uniformity over the tail map — i.e. if the tail F_k was itself fitted on the same n samples. Read that way, the result is really a nonparametric statement: for the class of all L-Lipschitz functions on an embedding space whose measure has intrinsic dimension d, the uniform deviation rate is n^{−1/d}, which is the classical minimax rate for Lipschitz classes and is tight. That is a much more defensible theorem than the one stated, and it would also explain the empirical correlations better, since real tail layers are trained on the data. The paper's insistence on "fixed F" is what makes the bound strictly dominated.

Broader context. The backdrop is the collapse of parameter-counting as an explanation of deep-network generalization. VC-dimension and Rademacher bounds scale with capacity and go vacuous at modern widths; norm-based refinements (Neyshabur et al. 2015; Bartlett, Foster & Telgarsky 2017, whose spectral-norm product this paper borrows as its Lipschitz proxy) replace parameter counts with products of layer norms, which unfortunately also blow up; compression and PAC-Bayes approaches (Arora et al. 2018; Lotfi et al. 2022) have produced the only genuinely non-vacuous numbers so far, by measuring how few bits the trained network actually needs. Against that, the "representation geometry" line — Ansuini et al. (2019), Pope et al. (2021) — is empirically striking but theoretically orphaned, and this paper is an attempt at adoption. Worth reading alongside it: Weed & Bach (2019) itself, which is the sharpest statement of how empirical-measure convergence depends on intrinsic rather than ambient dimension (and whose lower Wasserstein dimension gives matching lower bounds the paper never invokes); and Nagarajan & Kolter, "Uniform convergence may be unable to explain generalization in deep learning," which is the standing argument that any bound of this uniform-deviation shape is structurally incapable of the job.

For your work the connection is not forced, and in one place it is almost literal: the two ID estimators the authors fall back on in Appendix C, TLE and MOM, are Amsaleg–Houle local intrinsic dimensionality estimators developed inside the similarity-search community precisely to predict indexing and query difficulty for nearest-neighbour structures. So the same statistic that tells you an ANN index will degrade is here being used to predict generalization, and this paper supplies a mechanism connecting them: both are consequences of how fast finite samples cover the measure at small scales. That gives a sharper way to state the dense-retrieval version of the result. Take the tail map to be a scorer z ↦ ⟨q, z⟩, which is Lipschitz with constant ‖q‖_2 — no spectral-norm product needed, no estimation problem, the sensitivity term is simply the query norm. Then Lemma A.7 says the deviation of expected score between a sampled corpus and the true corpus distribution is at most ‖q‖·W_1, and Weed–Bach says that scales as n^{−1/d} in the corpus embedding's intrinsic dimension. That is a real statement about corpus-level generalization and about distribution shift: it bounds how much any linear scorer's expected behaviour can change under a corpus swap, with the rate set by embedding ID. It also sharpens the Matryoshka question — truncating embeddings from 768 to 64 dimensions costs little if the ID was already far below both, because the statistical rate depends on d_1*(P), not the ambient width; what truncation really risks is inflating the effective Lipschitz constant of the downstream scorer, exactly the tradeoff the authors' width intervention exhibits. I would be more cautious about pushing this to generative retrieval; one could argue the docid codebook's intrinsic dimension controls how much data is needed before the identifier space is adequately covered, but that is speculation rather than a consequence of anything proved here.

A concrete follow-up. Do the slope test the paper skips, in the retrieval setting where you have the ground truth the authors lack. Take a corpus with an encoder, estimate the embedding ID with two or three estimators, subsample corpora of size n over two or three orders of magnitude, and measure (i) W_1 (ideally exact or debiased Sinkhorn, normalized by support diameter) and (ii) the actual deviation of a fixed scorer's expected score, and (iii) the deviation of a trained scorer's score. Theory predicts slope −1/d̂ for (i), slope −1/2 for (ii) regardless of d, and slope −1/d̂ for (iii) only if the uniform-convergence reading is the right one. The gap between (i) and (ii) measures exactly how much the optimal-transport step overcharges; the behaviour of (iii) decides whether the dimension dependence is real or an artifact. If it survives, you would have a genuine ID-indexed sample-complexity law for corpus-level retrieval quality, which is the kind of statement that could also be turned around to pick a Matryoshka truncation dimension from measured corpus geometry rather than by sweeping.

title: Sequential Group Composition: A Window into the Mechanics of Deep Learning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-15

Sequential Group Composition: A Window into the Mechanics of Deep Learning

Giovanni Luca Marchetti, Daniel Kunin, Adele Myers, Francisco Acosta, Nina Miolane — 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03655

Main idea. The paper proposes a single toy task meant to subsume a lot of the "algorithmic/mechanistic interpretability" zoo: given a finite group G and a sequence (g1, ..., gk) in G^k, predict the cumulative product g1·g2·…·gk. Modular addition — the workhorse of the grokking literature — is the special case G = Cp, k = 2. Rubik's cube moves, rigid-body tracking, navigation, and finite-state control are all instances of the same abstraction, so the authors argue it is the right generalization axis: along one axis you vary the group (Abelian vs. non-Abelian, i.e. order-insensitive vs. order-sensitive), along another the sequence length k (shallow vs. deep computation).

The setup is deliberately engineered for harmonic analysis. Group elements are not one-hot embedded by fiat; instead one fixes an encoding vector x in R^|G| and encodes g as x_g := λ(g)x, the orbit of x under the left regular representation (x = e_1 recovers one-hot). The network f: R^{k|G|} → R^|G| takes the concatenation (x_{g1}, ..., x_{gk}) and regresses onto x_{g1···gk} under population MSE over all |G|^k sequences. Because the regular representation block-diagonalizes under the group Fourier transform F — the change of basis assembled from the irreducible representations (irreps) of G, which reduces to the DFT when G = Cp — everything in the analysis can be pushed into the irrep domain, where the convolution theorem turns group convolution into matrix multiplication of the matrix-valued Fourier coefficients x̂[ρ], and Plancherel splits the squared norm across irreps.

Three results follow. First (Lemma 3.5) the task is genuinely nonlinear: if x is nonzero and mean-centered (x̂[ρ_triv] = 0), no linear map R^{k|G|} → R^|G| can implement it, so the minimal architecture that solves it exactly is a two-layer net with a degree-k polynomial activation. Second (Section 4), for such a two-layer net in the vanishing-initialization limit, the authors derive exactly which features are learned and in what order: the network acquires one irrep (or conjugate pair) at a time, in decreasing order of an explicit score computed from the Fourier statistics of the encoding vector, producing the familiar staircase loss curve. Third (Section 5), they count the width this costs — H ≥ (k+1)·2^k·Σ_ρ n_ρ^{k+1}, exponential in k — and then exhibit explicit weight constructions showing that an Elman RNN solves the same task with width O(|G|^{3/2}) independent of k by composing left-to-right, and a depth-log(k) MLP does it in a balanced binary tree by composing adjacent pairs in parallel. The unifying claim is that all three architectures implement the same irrep-wise decomposition; they differ only in how efficiently they exploit associativity.

The most interesting part. The derivation of the learning order, and specifically where the bias toward low-dimensional irreps comes from. Using the AGF (Alternating Gradient Flow) framework of Kunin et al. (2025), training at vanishing initialization alternates between a slow phase in which dormant neurons maximize a "utility" (correlation of the neuron's function with the current residual) on the unit sphere, and a fast phase in which the newly activated neurons minimize loss. The authors show (Lemma B.2) that the utility of a neuron with weights (u1, ..., uk, w) reduces — after iterating the convolution theorem k times and applying Plancherel — to a sum over not-yet-learned irreps of Re Tr( x̂[ρ]† û1[ρ] ⋯ x̂[ρ]† ûk[ρ] ŵ[ρ]† x̂[ρ] ). So utility maximization is literally: maximize the trace of an alternating chain product of the data's Fourier coefficient with the neuron's Fourier coefficients, subject to a single L2 budget shared across all irreps and all k+1 weight vectors.

Two things fall out. Within an irrep, the chain is bounded by ||x̂[ρ]||_op^{k+1} times the product of the Frobenius norms of the k+1 factors, and the bound is attained by setting every factor to the same scaled rank-one projector q p† built from the top singular pair of x̂[ρ] — the projectors are idempotent, so the chain telescopes. The crucial consequence is that only one singular direction of an n_ρ × n_ρ matrix ever pays off, while the Frobenius budget must be spread over the whole matrix; equalizing the k+1 factors then yields a per-irrep score proportional to ||x̂[ρ]||_op^{k+1} / (C_ρ n_ρ)^{(k-1)/2}, with C_ρ = 1 for self-conjugate irreps and 2 otherwise. Across irreps, the allocation problem is max Σ_ρ M_ρ α_ρ^{k+1} subject to Σ_ρ α_ρ² = 1. Because the exponent k+1 strictly exceeds the constraint exponent 2, the maximum is attained at a vertex: all budget concentrates on a single irrep. That is exactly, mechanistically, why features are learned one irrep at a time rather than in superposition, and the "one at a time" gets sharper with k.

The payoff is a derivation of the "strong universality" conjecture of Chughtai et al. (2023) — that nets learn lower-dimensional irreps first — as a theorem rather than an observation, together with an explanation of why it had been hard to see empirically. Under one-hot encoding, ||x̂[ρ]||_op = 1 for every ρ, so the score collapses to (C_ρ n_ρ)^{-(k-1)/2}: a pure penalty on irrep dimension whose exponent grows linearly in k. At k = 2 the penalty is only n_ρ^{-1/2} — weak enough to be swamped by noise, which is why prior binary-composition studies saw it only faintly. Figure 5 confirms that on D3 the gap between acquiring the 1-D sign irrep and the 2-D rotation irrep widens as k goes 2 → 5.

A subtlety the paper does not dwell on but which is the most interesting corollary: the selection score uses the operator norm ||x̂[ρ]||_op, while the loss decrement achieved once ρ is learned is (C_ρ/2|G|)·||x̂[ρ]||²_ρ, a Frobenius-type power. For x̂[ρ] = α_ρ·I (the paper's own experimental choice) the first is α_ρ^{k+1} n_ρ^{-(k-1)/2} and the second is C_ρ n_ρ² α_ρ². These can disagree. Gradient descent here is greedy in alignability, not in loss reduction: a high-dimensional irrep can account for most of the remaining error and still be learned last. The staircase steps are not sorted by step height.

Proof sketch. The two-layer theory is an induction over AGF iterations with the induction hypothesis stated in the function space: after t−1 iterations the active neurons compute exactly the partial reconstruction f(x_g)[h] = (1/|G|) Σ_{ρ ∈ I^{t−1}} ⟨ρ(g1···gk h)†, x̂[ρ]⟩_ρ, where I^{t−1} is the set of learned irreps, closed under conjugation and initialized to {ρ_triv}. If I^{t−1} = I(G), Fourier inversion says the output is exactly the target. The induction step has two halves.

For utility maximization (Theorem 4.1 / B.3), the first move is a ΣΠ decomposition: write the per-neuron function as f = f^(×) + f^(+), where f^(×) = k!·w·Π_j ⟨u_j, x_{g_j}⟩ is the fully multilinear "sigma-pi-sigma" term and f^(+) is everything else in the expansion of the degree-k polynomial activation. Lemma B.2 shows the extraneous term has zero utility, by the one-line character identity Σ_{g∈G} ρ(g) = 0 for nontrivial ρ: any monomial that omits some g_i averages to zero against the target. The surviving multilinear term becomes the trace chain described above, via iterated convolution plus Plancherel (Lemma B.1). The bound is then an iterated application of |Re Tr(AB)| ≤ ||A||_F ||B||_F and ||AB||_F ≤ ||A||_op ||B||_F, with AM-GM for the equal-norm allocation, and achievability by the rank-one projector construction.

For cost minimization (Theorem 4.3 / B.5), the key structural fact is Schur orthogonality: because previously activated neurons are aligned to irreps in I^{t−1} and the new ones to ρ_, the loss splits additively, L(Θ_A ⊕ Θ_{A_t}) = L(Θ_A) + L(Θ_{A_t}). Old neurons sit at a critical point, so the new cohort evolves independently — this is what makes the induction legitimate. A second orthogonality (Lemma B.4) shows the cross term between f^(×) and f^(+) vanishes when summed over sequences, so the loss splits again into a nonnegative ||f^(+)||² penalty plus the ΣΠ loss. Hence the extraneous polynomial terms are pure overhead and must be cancelled _collectively by multiple neurons. Expanding the ΣΠ loss via products of real parts gives a sum over subsets A ⊆ {1, ..., k} of squared norms of tensors Σ_i s_w^i ⊗ (⊗{h∈A} S_h^i) ⊗ (⊗{h∉A} conj S_h^i); dropping all but the full subset and completing the square against the utility term yields the bound L ≥ (1/2)(||x||² − (C_ρ/|G|)·||x̂[ρ_]||²_ρ_), with explicit iff conditions for equality.

The explicit construction attaining the bound is where the width count comes from, and it decomposes into three independent factors. (i) The equality condition (57) says the collection of neuron weights must realize a chained matrix-multiplication tensor; the authors realize it by indexing neurons by (k+1)-tuples (α_0, ..., α_k) and setting each neuron's matrices to elementary matrices E_{α_h, α_{h+1}} forming a closed index cycle — one neuron per index path, hence n_ρ^{k+1}. (ii) Condition (58) requires all proper-subset tensors to vanish when ρ* is complex; this is killed by replicating the construction k+1 times with roots-of-unity phases, exp(πij/(k+1)) on the input side and exp(−πijk/(k+1))/(k+1) on the output side, so that each partial-subset term is rescaled by a geometric sum that vanishes because 0 < k − |A| ≤ k is never 0 mod (k+1). A neat character-sum trick, and the source of the (k+1) factor. (iii) The 2^k factor comes from Lemma B.6, the Waring-type identity z1···zk = (1/(k!2^k)) Σ_{ε ∈ {±1}^k} (Π ε_i) σ(Σ ε_i z_i), which lets a cohort of 2^k ordinary neurons synthesize one exact ΣΠ unit (2^{k−1} suffices by ε ↔ −ε symmetry when σ(z) = z^k). Multiplying gives H ≥ (k+1)·2^k·Σ_ρ n_ρ^{k+1}, reducing to (k+1)·2^{k−1}·|G| for Abelian groups, matching the empirical phase boundary in Figure 4.

Assumptions worth flagging. The analysis is population gradient flow at the α → 0 initialization limit with AGF's neuron-dependent learning-rate rescaling ||θ||^{1−k} log(1/α) — not SGD, not finite initialization. The activation must be a monic polynomial whose degree equals the sequence length, so the architecture is told k in advance. Three conditions on x: mean-centered, each x̂[ρ] either invertible or zero, and the scores in (13) pairwise distinct — generic, but the staircase is only clean when the scores are well separated, and the experimental recipe in Appendix C.1 openly admits to hand-tuning x in the Fourier domain ("separated powers", "low-dimensional dominance") to make the phases visible. Assumption 4.2 — that a cohort of N neurons activates simultaneously, all aligned to ρ*, and stays aligned throughout cost minimization — is asserted as empirically observed, not proved. Finally, the depth results in Section 5 are not dynamics at all: they are explicit weight constructions (expressivity), with the claim that gradient descent finds them stated but not backed by any reported experiment.

Critique. The strengths are real. This is an unusually clean piece of theory: the orbit encoding is the right design choice, it makes the group Fourier transform do genuine work rather than appearing decoratively, and the result is a closed-form prediction (an explicit ranking score) that is falsifiable and is in fact tested in Figure 5. Deriving Chughtai et al.'s universality conjecture from an optimization argument, and simultaneously explaining why it was nearly invisible at k = 2, is a genuine contribution. The width accounting is honest and modular, and the observation that W_mix in the RNN construction is permutation-similar to a block-diagonal matrix with one block per irrep — so the recurrent state never mixes frequencies — is a satisfying mechanistic prediction that would be easy to check in a trained RNN.

The main overclaim is in the abstract: "doing so requires a hidden width exponential in the sequence length k." Nothing in the paper proves a lower bound. Theorem 4.3 and Lemma B.8 prove sufficiency of (k+1)2^k n_ρ^{k+1}, via an explicit and almost certainly loose construction (the n_ρ^{k+1} term is the trivial tensor decomposition; the true minimal N is the rank of the chained matrix-multiplication tensor, which the paper never computes, and for ordinary matrix multiplication such ranks are famously subexponential-in-the-obvious-bound). The 2^k factor is plausibly tight, since the Waring rank of the square-free monomial is known to be exactly 2^{k−1}, but the authors do not invoke that result, and even if they did, shared neurons across ΣΠ units would need to be ruled out. The exponential claim therefore rests on Figure 4's empirical phase diagram and on a sufficiency bound, which is a meaningfully weaker statement than advertised. Likewise, "scale poorly in both parameter and sample complexity" is asserted; there is no sample-complexity theorem anywhere, and the loss studied is the full population loss over all |G|^k sequences, so there is no generalization analysis at all — in a paper descended from the grokking literature, where generalization is the phenomenon, that is a notable absence.

Section 5 is the weak half. Its section headings — "RNNs Learn to Compose Sequentially", "Multilayer MLPs Learn to Compose in Parallel" — promise learning results and deliver hand-built weights. The honest statement is "there exist efficient solutions inside these architectures", which is a mild re-derivation of Liu et al. (2022) and the parallel-scan folklore. The sentence that these solutions "are reliably found by gradient descent" appears to be supported by no figure in the paper: Figures 3, 4, 5 are all two-layer experiments on binary or short-sequence composition. Section 5.3 on transformers is a paragraph of related-work summary with no result. Given that the paper's own framing is architecture comparison, the absence of even one RNN or deep-MLP training curve is a real gap, especially since AGF explicitly does not cover those dynamics and the interesting question — whether gradient descent prefers the sequential, the parallel, or the solvable-group algebraic shortcut — is left entirely open.

Smaller points. Figure 5's evidence for the dimensional bias is confounded: the initialization scale is increased from 5e-5 to 2e-3 and the learning rate changed as k goes from 2 to 5, which is the opposite direction from the α → 0 limit the theory requires, and larger initialization is exactly what blurs AGF staircases. The widening gap between irrep acquisitions may be partly an artifact of that sweep. The experiments use Adam with gradient clipping, not gradient flow. The requirement that the polynomial degree equal k means the architecture is matched to the task, which rules out the most interesting regime (a fixed ReLU net facing variable-length sequences). And for a paper whose stated motivation is "the mechanics of deep learning", every quantitative result is about the two-layer case.

Broader context. The relevant background is the modular-arithmetic strand of mechanistic interpretability. Power et al. (2022) observed "grokking": small transformers trained on modular addition memorize for thousands of steps and then abruptly generalize. Nanda et al. (2023) reverse-engineered the resulting circuit and found it computes a+b mod p by embedding inputs as points on a circle at a handful of Fourier frequencies, multiplying with trigonometric identities, and reading off the argument — the "clock" algorithm (Zhong et al. 2024 showed a competing "pizza" algorithm also exists). Chughtai et al. (2023) generalized from Cp to arbitrary finite groups and found networks consistently learn irreps, conjecturing a "universality" in which low-dimensional irreps come first; Morwani et al. (2023) explained Fourier feature emergence through max-margin implicit bias, and Marchetti et al. (2024) derived universal Fourier features from task symmetry alone. The present paper is best read as the dynamics-side completion of that program, built directly on Kunin et al. (2025), "Alternating Gradient Flows", which is the single most important companion read: AGF is the general machinery (dormant/active neurons, utility maximization then cost minimization) and this paper is its extension from k = 2 cyclic groups to arbitrary finite groups and arbitrary k.

The other half of the context is computational, and the paper undersells its closest relative. Liu et al. (2022), "Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata", shows that a transformer of depth O(log k) can simulate any semiautomaton on length-k inputs, and that for solvable groups constant-depth shortcuts exist at the cost of width. The dividing line is Barrington's theorem: the word problem for a non-solvable group such as S5 is NC1-complete, so no constant-depth bounded-width circuit can do it, which is precisely why the solvable/non-solvable distinction controls whether shortcuts exist. The log k tree in Section 5.2 is the Blelloch parallel associative scan, the same primitive that makes linear attention, S4 and Mamba trainable in parallel over sequence length — so the paper's depth results are a representation-theoretic rederivation of why associativity buys log-depth parallelism, now with the added fact that in a learned solution the scan operator is block-diagonal by irrep.

The obvious follow-up is to close the lower-bound gap properly: the minimal width for exact two-layer solution is a tensor-rank question. Condition (57) says the neurons must jointly realize a specific order-(k+1) chained matrix-multiplication tensor over C^{n_ρ}, and Lemma B.6 says each ΣΠ unit costs Waring rank 2^{k−1}; combining the known Waring rank of the square-free monomial with border-rank lower bounds for the chained tensor would turn the current O(·) sufficiency into a Θ(·) characterization, and would convert the abstract's "requires" into a theorem. A second, more empirical follow-up that the theory directly enables: the score ||x̂[ρ]||_op^{k+1}/(C_ρ n_ρ)^{(k−1)/2} is a design knob. One can engineer an encoding whose spectrum forces a prescribed acquisition order, then ask whether curriculum over k — train a deep MLP to compose pairs, then four-tuples — provably steers gradient descent into the balanced-tree construction rather than the exponential-width one, which would be a clean, mechanistically grounded account of length generalization.

On IR relevance: mostly this is worth reading for its own sake rather than for a direct application, but there is one non-forced bridge. The orbit encoding g ↦ λ(g)x is exactly the construction behind group-structured embedding models in knowledge-graph retrieval: ComplEx and RotatE embed relations as elements of a (products-of-)circle group and score triples by what is, in this paper's language, an inner product that factorizes across irreps, and Plate's holographic reduced representations / vector symbolic architectures bind and unbind with circular convolution, i.e. multiplication in the Fourier domain of a cyclic group. HolE's circular correlation is literally the convolution theorem in equation (28). This paper gives a feature-learning-order theory for exactly that class of embeddings: it predicts which relational "frequencies" a KG embedding model acquires first as a function of the spectrum of the entity encoding, and that the bias toward low-dimensional irreps intensifies with the length of the relation path being composed — a testable statement about multi-hop retrieval. More loosely, Lemma 3.5 is the same shape of argument as bi-encoder expressivity separations: a score that is a fixed bilinear form of independently computed query and document embeddings cannot represent order-sensitive composition, which is a reasonable formal template for why bi-encoders struggle on compositional queries where cross-encoders do not. That second connection is an analogy rather than a result.

title: Revisiting the Index Construction of Proximity Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-14

3. Revisiting the Index Construction of Proximity Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

Shuo Yang, Jiadong Xie, Yingfan Liu, Jeffrey Xu Yu, Xiyue Gao, Qianru Wang, Yanguo Peng, Jiangtao Cui (2025) — PVLDB 18(6): 1825–1838. https://doi.org/10.14778/3725688.3725709 · https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p1825-liu.pdf · code: https://github.com/xdyangsh/FastKCNA

Main idea. The paper attacks index construction cost for proximity-graph ANN, and its framing move is to notice that every mainstream construction pipeline — RNG-style (NSG, SSG, τ-MNG, and in effect Vamana/DiskANN) and NSWG-style (NSW, HNSW) — reduces to one primitive applied n times, which the authors name k-CNA: "size-k candidate neighbour set acquisition", i.e. getting, for every point u ∈ D, a set C(u) of k approximate nearest neighbours of u, which the refinement phase then prunes into out-edges. The superlinearity is exactly here: each of the n k-CNA calls is a beam search of width L over a graph of average degree R, costing Θ(L·R·d) distance evaluations, so the total is Θ(n·L·R·d) with L and R both needing to grow (empirically) with n and with intrinsic dimension to keep recall fixed — hence superlinear in n, and in NSG's case paid twice, since the initial KNNG itself is built by NN-Descent/KGraph (Θ(n·k₀²·d)-ish per iteration). The two concrete inefficiencies the paper identifies are asymmetric. (i) RNG construction has an efficiency problem: NSG runs its search phase over the raw KNNG G_{k₀}, and because a KNNG is directed, locally clustered and badly connected, it needs a very large out-degree k₀ (hundreds) to let beam search escape local optima, so each of the n searches expands hundreds of neighbours per hop. Their cost decomposition (Fig. 3) shows the search phase at 42–60% of total NSG build time, exceeding even KNNG initialization on Gist1M. (ii) NSWG construction has a quality problem that is structural, not tunable: HNSW inserts node-by-node, so the i-th inserted point searches a graph containing only i of the n points; in expectation half the dataset is absent, so the average recall of C(u) against the true k-NN is upper-bounded by ≈0.5 even with an exact search oracle (confirmed empirically in Fig. 2(b), where HNSW's k-CNA recall tops out around 0.5). Since they also show (Fig. 2) that k-CNA recall is monotonically and strongly predictive of the derived graph's QPS-vs-recall curve, this caps HNSW's attainable graph quality.

The fix for (i) is to swap the phase order — refinement before search instead of search before refinement. Rather than searching the fat KNNG, they first prune the KNNG down to a low-degree proximity graph Ĝ, enforce connectivity by DFS-plus-bridge-edges, and only then run the n beam searches on Ĝ, which is far cheaper per hop. The obstacle is that standard RNG pruning is the wrong rule for this purpose: RNG pruning is designed so that greedy routing provably reaches the 1-NN when q ∈ D, and it achieves that by deleting (u,v) whenever some retained w satisfies dist(u,w) < dist(u,v) and dist(v,w) < dist(u,v) — i.e. (u,v) is the longest side of triangle uvw. Their Example 4.1 shows why this hurts k-CNA: for a query q with dist(u,q) < dist(v,q) < dist(w,q), v was reachable from u in the KNNG, but after pruning it is reachable only via w, which a width-L pool may never expand because w is farther from q. So the detour node w has higher rank w.r.t. q, and the beam can lose the whole branch. The new rule, α-pruning, adds a third condition: (u,v) is pruned only if such a w exists and ∠uwv > α. The geometry is clean — the two distance conditions already force (u,v) to be the longest side, hence ∠uwv to be the largest angle, hence ∠uwv > 60°; so α = 60° recovers RNG pruning exactly, and α > 60° prunes strictly less, retaining precisely those edges whose "detour" node w sits at a shallow angle and is therefore the most likely to be skipped by a bounded beam. α thus becomes a continuous dial between KNNG (keep everything, high k-CNA recall, expensive hops) and RNG (cheap hops, lossy candidate sets); their Glove study puts the sweet spot at 66–67°, with efficiency degrading beyond that because out-degree grows. Crucially, α-pruning is used only for the intermediate index Ĝ used as a search substrate; the final NSG is produced by the ordinary RNG pruning plus DFS-connect, which is why "no compromise in search performance" is structurally plausible — only candidate acquisition changed, not the output edge-selection rule.

Around this sit three further pieces. First, a self-iterative loop (IterNSG, Alg. 6) replaces the grid search over the beam width L, which otherwise requires rebuilding the whole index per candidate L. Each iteration alternates K2P (prune current k-CNA results into an α-PG) and P2K (beam-search the α-PG to produce better k-CNA results), with the loop terminated by a sampled estimate of k-CNA recall rather than a fixed L; empirically two iterations suffice, with sharply diminishing returns afterwards. Second, two work-reuse optimizations exploit the fact that consecutive iterations produce nearly identical neighbour lists, so most distance computations are repeats. P2K tags each member of the expanded set X_i(u) and of each N(v) with a boolean recording whether it was already present at iteration i−1; if v ∈ X_i(u) ∩ X_{i−1}(u), only N_{G_i}(v) \ N_{G_{i−1}}(v) is treated as fresh candidates. K2P does the analogue for pruning: since both the KNNG list and the retained-neighbour list are kept sorted ascending by distance from u, a candidate b already retained at i−1 against a retained a already present at i−1 needs no re-check of dist(a,b) or ∠uab, so only N_{G_i^N}(u) \ N_{G_{i−1}^N}(u) must be tested. Both are exact — they provably leave the output graph unchanged — and both pay off more as dimension grows, since the saved operations are the expensive d-dimensional ones. Third, for HNSW they replace node-by-node insertion with global layer-by-layer construction (OptHNSW, Alg. 7): sample every node's top layer first, so each layer's full node set D_i = {u : l(u) ≥ i} is known up front, then build each layer with IterNSG over the whole D_i (or a clique if |D_i| ≤ M). This lifts the per-layer k-CNA recall well above the 0.5 ceiling, which is why FastHNSW improves search quality rather than merely build time.

The most interesting part / critique. The genuinely interesting contribution is conceptual rather than algorithmic: separating the pruning rule used to build a search substrate from the pruning rule used to define the final index, and observing that the ANN literature has only ever designed pruning rules for the 1-NN greedy-routing guarantee, never for bounded-width beam search for k > 1. Stated that way, α-pruning is a natural and well-motivated object, and the rank-based framing (δ(P) = max rank along a path; Δ(G,q,u) = the path minimizing that maximum) is the right abstraction — it is essentially a minimax-rank or "bottleneck rank" diameter, and it is the quantity a width-L beam search actually cares about, since a path with max rank ≤ L is roughly what the pool can hold. I would read that definition as the paper's most portable idea.

The weaknesses are real, though.
