"No compromise in search performance" is established mostly by eyeballing QPS-vs-recall curves plotted only over Recall@10 ∈ [0.90, 1.00] on six 1M-scale datasets, and the one place with actual numbers contradicts the headline slightly: in Table 1 on Gist1M, FastNSG gives 964/694/402 QPS at recall 0.85/0.90/0.95 against OriNSG's 971/712/417 — a consistent 1–4% loss in the regime most deployments operate in — and wins only at 0.99 (148 vs 133). The paper even concedes that all methods converge at high recall because the second phase of graph search is insensitive to edge structure, which undercuts using the ≥0.99 region as evidence of superiority. The 5.6x headline is the best of six datasets (Msong); the per-dataset FastNSG speedups are 1.2, 2.1, 5.6, 3.2, 2.3, 1.2 (geometric mean ≈ 2.2x), and FastHNSW's are 2.4, 4.6, 3.0, 3.7, 1.6, 2.1 (≈ 2.7x). The ceiling is Amdahl: after their optimizations, KNNG initialization is 90–94% of FastNSG's build time (Fig. 3), so on datasets where NN-Descent already dominated (Sift1M, Deep1M) they can only deliver 1.2x — the paper honestly flags faster KNNG construction as future work. Against the construction-focused baselines the story is also narrower than claimed: on Gist1M FastNSG takes 119s vs RNN-Descent's 121s, i.e. a tie on time, so the claim there is about search quality, not speed. Measurement hygiene is mixed: builds use all 40 hyper-threads while search is single-threaded (stated, and defensible), but there is no thread-scaling curve, no peak-memory or index-size reporting — notable, since the pipeline holds a KNNG plus an α-PG plus per-neighbour boolean flags simultaneously, and α > 60° deliberately retains more edges — and tuning is asymmetric: α is grid-searched per dataset for their method, OriNSG/OriHNSW take parameters from prior papers and a survey, and the hyperparameters for DiskANN, LSH-APG, RNN-Descent and ParlayANN are never stated at all. Coverage gaps: largest experiment is Sift50M (speedups grow with n, which is encouraging), nothing at billion scale, nothing disk-resident despite DiskANN being a baseline, no out-of-distribution query workloads, no deletions or insertions, and the hard-instance axis is only implicitly probed (Glove and Crawl are the clustered/high-LID cases and get 2.3x and 3.2x with "comparable" search, but no LID or local-intrinsic-dimension statistics are reported, and there is no adversarially clustered or multi-modal dataset). The GPU port is sketched in prose only, never implemented or measured. Finally, and most pointedly: FastHNSW's layer-by-layer global construction abolishes incremental insertion, the single property for which HNSW is prized in production. The paper's own motivation is frequent full reindexing under embedding-model churn, so this is internally consistent, but it means FastHNSW is not a drop-in replacement for a streaming vector index, and the paper never says so.

Proof sketch. There are three stated results, and they are of uneven weight. Theorem 4.1 claims: if S₁, S₂ are the width-L beam-search results for q on the KNNG G and the pruned graph Ĝ, and if δ(Δ(G,q,p_k)) = δ(Δ(Ĝ,q,p_k)) — the minimax-rank value of the best path to the k-th nearest neighbour is unchanged by pruning — then p_k ∈ S₁ ⟹ p_k ∈ S₂. The argument is by contradiction: if p_k were lost, some v on Δ(Ĝ,q,p_k) failed to enter the pool, which would require rank(v,q) < δ(Δ(Ĝ,q,p_k)); but the node attaining that maximum rank was itself inserted, so a strictly lower-ranked node must have been too. Honestly read, this is close to a tautology: it says beam search is a monotone function of the minimax rank of the available path, with the hypothesis doing all the work and no stated relationship between δ and L (the natural sufficient condition, δ ≤ L or δ ≤ L up to pool dynamics, is never made explicit, and pool eviction order is handled only informally). The real content is Lemma 4.1 plus Theorem 4.2, which bound how often pruning violates that hypothesis. Lemma 4.1 assumes points uniformly distributed in infinite space and shows that if RNG pruning deletes (u,v) because of w with ∠uwv = α, then the probability that w outranks both u and v for a random query is (π − α)/2π: q must lie in the region beyond both perpendicular bisecting hyperplanes of uw and vw, which subtends angle π − α out of 2π. Theorem 4.2 then treats successive prunings along a path as independent Bernoulli events with Pr = (π − α)/2π and concludes that 1/Pr = 2π/(π − α) successful prunings are needed in expectation before δ(P) increases. Calibrating with a Monte Carlo estimate E[∠uwv] ≈ 100° gives Pr ≈ 0.2, so at α = 60° (plain RNG pruning) quality loss is expected after about 3 prunings — fatally short of the ≈6-hop paths typical of these graphs — whereas raising α pushes that threshold out. That is a nice quantitative story, and it is the first argument I have seen that targets k-CNA rather than 1-NN reachability, but it leans hard: the (π − α)/2π measure is a two-dimensional angular fraction and does not transfer to R^d, where the corresponding solid-angle measure concentrates sharply with d and would change the calibration; "uniform in infinite space" is precisely the assumption that fails for the clustered, low-intrinsic-dimension embeddings being indexed; independence across prunings along a path is clearly false (prunings share nodes); and the theorem statement is written with the reciprocal of what the proof derives (the proof gets 2π/(π − α), the statement prints (π − α)/2π). Theorem 5.1 is the cleanest result and also the least interesting: a Chernoff bound showing n_s ≥ (8 + 2ε)·l·log n/ε² samples suffice for the sampled mean recall to be within ε/2 of the true mean with probability ≥ 1 − n^{−l}, justifying the sampled quality-examination stopping rule; it treats each node's recall as a Bernoulli variable when it actually lives in {0, 1/k, …, 1}, so Hoeffding would have been the right hammer, but the conclusion survives. Net: the paper has real theory about when pruning preserves beam-search reachability, but no guarantee that the final index retains monotonic-path/navigability properties, and no construction-cost bound at all — the superlinearity that motivates the whole paper is never quantified in a theorem. The right theoretical question, and the one I would put to a student, is: define δ-preservation (preserving the minimax-rank distance to every point's k-NN) as the invariant a construction-substrate pruning rule must satisfy, and prove that α-pruning preserves it with high probability under a doubling-dimension or local-intrinsic-dimension assumption rather than uniformity in R^d — ideally with α's optimal value falling out of the dimension parameter instead of a per-dataset grid search. A companion question is a genuine construction-cost theorem: total distance computations as a function of (n, intrinsic dimension, target k-CNA recall), which would turn "superlinear" into something comparable across NN-Descent, Vamana and this framework.

Broader context. The lineage here is worth having straight. Navigable small-world graphs (Malkov et al., NSW 2014; HNSW, TPAMI 2018) descend from Kleinberg/Milgram-style navigability: build a hierarchy with exponentially decaying layer-occupancy probabilities, insert incrementally, route greedily from the sparse top layer down, and you get logarithmic-ish hop counts with no global knowledge of the dataset. The RNG branch descends instead from computational geometry: the Delaunay graph would make greedy routing exact, but degenerates to a clique in high dimension, so one approximates it with a relative neighbourhood graph — delete the longest side of every triangle — or with Fu et al.'s MRNG/NSG (PVLDB 2019), whose contribution was proving that MRNG is a monotonic search network (a monotonic path exists between every pair, so greedy routing terminates at the exact nearest neighbour for in-dataset queries) and then approximating it with a KNNG-plus-prune-plus-DFS-connect pipeline. DiskANN/Vamana (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019) relaxed that rule to α-RNG pruning — prune v when α·dist(w,v) ≤ dist(u,v) for α > 1 — which prunes more aggressively than RNG and so retains longer-range edges, trading degree for hop count in a way that suits SSD-resident search; note the unfortunate name collision, since this paper's α is an angle that prunes less as it grows, and the two knobs are not comparable (the paper compares against DiskANN as a system but never against α-RNG pruning as an alternative substrate rule, which is the most obvious missing ablation). The reason construction cost has stopped being a second-class metric is exactly the motivation given in the intro: in RAG and retrieval-augmented training, the embedding model itself is being fine-tuned, so every change of encoder invalidates the entire vector space and forces a full reindex — build time moves from a one-off offline cost onto the inner loop of model development. Two closely related papers to know: Ono & Matsui's Relative NN-Descent (ACM MM 2023), which fuses NN-Descent with RNG pruning so that the KNNG stage and the refinement stage are the same loop — the natural competitor to this paper's iterate-prune-search loop, and the one it essentially ties with on Gist1M build time; and ParlayANN (Manohar et al., PPoPP 2024), which is the deterministic-parallel reference point and reframes the whole question as parallel work-depth rather than wall-clock. On the theory side, Indyk & Xu, "Worst-case performance of popular approximate nearest neighbor search implementations" (NeurIPS 2023) is the key paper: it proves that a slow-preprocessing Vamana variant has query guarantees under bounded doubling dimension while exhibiting instances where HNSW and NSG fail badly — the only rigorous separation we have between these pruning rules — and Diwan, Gou, Musco, Musco & Suel's "Navigable Graphs for High-Dimensional Nearest Neighbor Search: Constructions and Limits" (NeurIPS 2024) gives the complementary degree lower bounds for navigable graphs, plus Prokhorenkova & Shekhovtsov (ICML 2020) for the intrinsic-dimension view of beam search on kNN graphs. A plausible follow-up: make α local and learned rather than global and grid-searched — estimate each node's local intrinsic dimension (or just the empirical distribution of ∠uwv in its neighbourhood, which their own Monte Carlo shows has mean ≈100° under uniformity but will be wildly different in a tight cluster) and set α(u) from it, then prove a δ-preservation bound that degrades gracefully with local doubling dimension. A second, cheaper follow-up: the self-iterative loop with sampled quality examination is an anytime algorithm, so give it an actual stopping guarantee — the current rule thresholds a Chernoff-bounded recall estimate, but the decision-theoretically right rule would stop when the marginal QPS gain per unit of build time falls below a target, which requires modelling the k-CNA-recall → QPS map they only plot.

This one connects to your work on several axes, and I think genuinely rather than decoratively. The most direct: the δ/minimax-rank functional is a clean theoretical object sitting between the navigability literature and the practical beam-search regime, and nobody has studied it properly. Monotonic-search-network results (MRNG) and the doubling-dimension analyses (Indyk–Xu) are both about greedy routing to the single nearest neighbour; real systems run width-L best-first search for k ≫ 1, and the right invariant for that is not "a monotonic path exists" but "a path exists whose maximum rank w.r.t. the query is at most L". Formalizing the rank-diameter of a proximity graph, proving upper and lower bounds on it under doubling-dimension assumptions, and characterizing which pruning rules preserve it is a theory programme that this paper gestures at and does not execute — and it would also give the first principled answer to "why does graph ANN work", in the regime practitioners actually use. Second, the construction-time/query-time trade-off is begging to be formalized as a genuine Pareto statement: this paper's α, DiskANN's α, NSG's L and R, HNSW's ef and M are all points on an unmapped surface, and a lower-bound statement of the form "any index achieving recall ρ at query cost Q on an instance of intrinsic dimension D requires construction work at least f(n, D, ρ, Q)" would be the right complement to the navigable-graph degree lower bounds. Third, and closest to generative retrieval and RAG: there is an interesting structural parallel between this paper's bootstrapping — the index is built by searching an approximation of itself, iterated to a fixed point whose quality is only estimated by sampling — and the self-referential training of generative retrievers, where docid assignment and the retrieval model co-adapt. In both cases the open question is the same: does the iteration have a fixed point, how far is it from the ideal index/assignment, and how does the gap propagate into downstream recall? Fourth, the practical implication for continually-updated retrieval indexes deserves a caveat you can use: FastHNSW buys its quality by giving up incremental insertion entirely, so it is a rebuild-fast answer, not an update-fast one. For RAG pipelines where the corpus grows continuously but the encoder is stable, the binding constraint is incremental maintenance with bounded degradation, which this line of work does not address and which is, formally, a different problem — how much does an index drift from its from-scratch counterpart under a stream of insertions, and can you bound the drift in the same δ/rank-diameter currency? That seems to me a well-posed and currently open question, and one where a theory-first treatment would be more valuable than another 2x on build time.

title: Weight decay induces low-rank attention layers
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-14

2. Weight decay induces low-rank attention layers

Seijin Kobayashi, Yassir Akram, Johannes von Oswald (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23819

Main idea. The paper asks what weight decay actually regularizes when the parameters it acts on enter the model multiplicatively. The motivating case is attention: in the update E ← E + P W_V E ϕ(Eᵀ W_Kᵀ W_Q E ⊙ M), the four parameter matrices only ever appear through two products, W_QK = W_Kᵀ W_Q and W_VP = P W_V, and this is true irrespective of the softmax ϕ or the causal mask, because the nonlinearity sits downstream of each product rather than between its factors. So per layer and per head, attention is exactly a loss of the form L(ABᵀ, θ) + (λ/2)(‖A‖F² + ‖B‖_F²), with A, B tall (d_m × d_k with d_k ≤ d_m, i.e. the "bottleneck" assumption the theory needs, which attention satisfies by construction). The classical fact in the background is the Srebro–Shraibman variational identity: ‖W‖_ = min over factorizations W = ABᵀ of ½(‖A‖_F² + ‖B‖_F²), so the L2 penalty on the factors is always an upper bound on the nuclear norm of the product — a convex surrogate for rank. The paper's contribution is to show that in this setting the bound is not merely an upper bound you hope is tight at the optimum: gradient-based training _makes it tight_, and does so exponentially fast, so L_L2(A,B) and L__(W) = L(W) + λ‖W‖_* become the same objective long before convergence. The empirical half of the paper then verifies that AdamW at the perfectly ordinary λ = 0.1 used by GPT-3, LLaMA and ViT measurably reduces the (soft) rank of W_QK and W_VP in trained transformers, including in fully online training that never converges, and that the released LLaMA-2-7B and ViT checkpoints already satisfy the tightness condition.

The most interesting part. The striking result is the trajectory claim, not the local-minimum claim. Local-minimum equivalences between factorized-L2 and nuclear-norm objectives were already known (Srebro–Shraibman at the global optimum; Wang & Jacot 2023 for critical points; Dai et al. and Tibshirani for Schatten-norm variants), and they are, for modern practice, almost vacuous: a 125M-parameter LM trained for one pass over 10B tokens of the Pile is nowhere near a stationary point, so "all local minima of the L2 loss are low-rank" says nothing about the model you actually ship. What Kobayashi et al. add is a statement about the path. The mechanism is lovely and almost embarrassingly simple. In unregularized gradient flow on a two-factor parametrization, AᵀA − BᵀB is a conserved quantity — the balancedness invariant familiar from the deep-linear-network literature. Writing the column dynamics τȧⁱ = Gbⁱ, τḃⁱ = Gᵀaⁱ with G = −∂L/∂W, every loss-dependent term in d/dt(aⁱᵀaʲ − bⁱᵀbʲ) cancels pairwise. Add weight decay and exactly two terms survive, both proportional to −λ: the conservation law becomes a contraction, AᵀA − BᵀB = Q₀ e^(−2λt/τ). Weight decay therefore does two things at once that are usually discussed separately — it shrinks weights, and it drives the factorization toward the unique balanced factorization that attains the Srebro–Shraibman minimum. The upper bound closes because training actively pushes the factors onto the minimizing branch of the variational identity. That is why the low-rank pressure bites in the early phase: the rate 2λ/τ is set by the weight decay and the learning rate alone, with no dependence on the loss, the data, the architecture downstream, or how far from optimum you are.

The 2-layer whitened-input case study makes the consequence concrete and is worth internalizing, because it shows the induced penalty is exactly nuclear norm rather than merely bounded by it. At stable equilibrium with Σ_XX = I and Σ_YX having distinct nonzero singular values s_i, one gets aⁱ = bⁱ, aⁱᵀbʲ = 0 for i ≠ j, and ‖aⁱ‖² = s_i − λ when s_i > λ and 0 otherwise — i.e. ABᵀ is the singular-value soft-thresholding of Σ_YX, which is precisely the proximal operator of λ‖·‖__. Weight decay in an over-complete factorized layer adaptively prunes hidden directions. Reparametrize the same layer as a single matrix W and the equilibrium is W = S/(1+λ): uniform shrinkage, rank unchanged at every λ. The rank collapse is an artifact of the _parametrization*, not of the penalty.

The uncomfortable follow-up is that this may be a bug rather than a feature. Rank reduction in attention is known to hurt (Bhojanapalli et al. on the head-size low-rank bottleneck; Sharma et al.'s LASER, where post-hoc rank reduction of MLP matrices helps reasoning while the same surgery on attention matrices hurts), and the authors' prescription is simply to decouple λ for attention from λ for the rest of the network and tune it separately. Honest limits: (i) the rigorous exponential rate is for plain gradient flow on an explicit L2 loss; the AdamW case is handled by a flow with momentum, decoupled decay and Wiener noise (Prop. B.2, rate 2ηλ, with decay only down to a noise floor of order (ηM/λ)(KM + σ√(µnd log(4nd/ε)))) plus an Appendix-E heuristic that AdamW's fixed points match an L2 loss of strength ελ/2 under λ|W_∞| ≪ 1 — the adaptive preconditioner itself is never in the analysis, and with ε ≈ 10⁻⁸ that identification is loose. (ii) ‖A‖, ‖B‖ bounded is assumed, with sufficient conditions (lower-bounded loss; Lipschitz gradient under momentum) and an explicit counterexample, L = −‖ABᵀ‖², where it fails. (iii) Rank is measured by a scale-invariant "pseudo-rank" — the fraction of singular values needed for 95% of the nuclear mass — which conflates spectral decay with genuine rank. (iv) Scale: 125M LM, a 24-hour ViT, a 2-layer attention-only toy; the foundation-model evidence is observational (balanced row norms in LLaMA-2 and ViT are consistent with rank-regularizing training, not proof of it). (v) Most importantly, nothing establishes that rank reduction causally hurts; λ is the only knob varied, and it moves rank and loss together. On that point the Pile perplexity table deserves a direct look at the original: as extracted, the largest attention weight decay tested (λ_SA = 0.25) attains the lowest perplexity in every MLP column (e.g. 11.52 vs 11.63 at λ_SA = 0 for λ_MLP = 0.25), which does not obviously support the prose claim that attention decay beyond 0.1 "starts slightly hurting"; the differences are ≈0.1 nats against standard errors of 0.02–0.05, and the text says 3 seeds while the caption says 5.

Proof sketch. Three results, with the third doing the real work. Proposition 3.1 (variational identity, attainment side): if AᵀA = BᵀB, then writing SVDs A = U_AΣ_AV_Aᵀ, B = U_BΣ_BV_Bᵀ, substitution gives V_AS_A²V_Aᵀ = V_BS_B²V_Bᵀ, so by uniqueness and positivity of singular values Σ_A = Σ_B, and V_AᵀV_B commutes with S; absorbing that rotation into U_A one gets A = U[√S;0]Oᵀ, B = V[√S;0]Oᵀ for a common orthogonal O, whence ‖ABᵀ‖_ = Tr(S) = ½(‖A‖² + ‖B‖²). Balancedness is thus a _{ABᵀ}sufficient condition for the Cauchy–Schwarz/AM–GM bound chain ‖ABᵀ‖_ ≤ ‖A‖‖B‖ ≤ ½(‖A‖²+‖B‖²) to be an equality. Lemma 3.2: at any stationary point of L_L2 with λ > 0 and L merely differentiable, the chain rule gives ∂_A L = −GB and ∂_B L = −GᵀA with G = −∂L/∂W|, so λA = GB and λB = GᵀA; then AᵀA = (1/λ)AᵀGB = (1/λ)(GᵀA)ᵀB = BᵀB. A two-line computation, and it needs nothing about the data, the loss beyond differentiability, or convergence. Theorem 3.3: (A,B) is a local minimum of L_L2 iff (1) W = ABᵀ is a local minimum of L__ restricted to matrices of rank ≤ r (r the maximum rank the factorization can express) and (2) AᵀA = BᵀB. The backward direction is a one-line contradiction using L__ ≤ L_L2 pointwise plus equality at balanced points. The forward direction is the delicate one: given a sequence W_n → W of rank-r matrices with L__(W_n) < L__(W), take SVDs W_n = U_nS_nV_nᵀ, use continuity of the singular-value map and compactness of the orthogonal group to pass to a convergent subsequence U_n → U, V_n → V with USVᵀ = W, then lift the sequence to factors A_n = U_nΣ_nOᵀ, B_n = V_nΣ_nOᵀ using the same O that Proposition 3.1 extracted from the local minimum; these are balanced, converge to (A,B), and have L_L2(A_n,B_n) = L__(W_n) < L_L2(A,B) — contradiction. Note the rank-r constraint: this is a correspondence with the _rank-restricted* nuclear-norm problem, not the unconstrained convex one.

Theorem 3.4 is the dynamical claim: under gradient flow on L_L2, if ‖A‖ and ‖B‖ stay bounded then L_L2(A,B) − L__(ABᵀ) → 0 exponentially. It is proved by composing two pieces. Lemma B.1 is the balancedness contraction above: τ d/dt(aⁱᵀaʲ − bⁱᵀbʲ) = −2λ(aⁱᵀaʲ − bⁱᵀbʲ) after the G-terms cancel, giving AᵀA − BᵀB = Q₀e^(−2λt/τ) entrywise, with rate depending only on λ and the flow time constant τ (equivalently 2ηλ in the discrete/decoupled-decay version). Proposition B.4 then converts _approximate_ balance into _approximate_ tightness, which is the genuinely new technical ingredient: for arbitrary A, B with Q := AᵀA − BᵀB, ‖ABᵀ‖__ − ‖A‖F² ≤ √(‖Q‖‖A‖_), hence ½(‖A‖²+‖B‖²) − ‖ABᵀ‖ ≤ √‖Q‖_ · (‖A‖ + ‖B‖_)/2. The key inequality is Powers–Størmer (an operator-algebra bound: ‖√X − √Y‖F² ≤ ‖X − Y‖ for positive X, Y), applied to √(V_BS_B²V_Bᵀ + Q) = V_B(S_B + Δ)V_Bᵀ to control ‖Δ‖F² ≤ ‖Q‖; rewriting A through that perturbed factor gives ‖ABᵀ‖ = ‖S_B² + ΔS_B‖_ and the bound follows from ‖ΔS_B‖ ≤ ‖Δ‖F‖S_B‖. Because the bound involves √‖Q‖, the loss gap inherits half_ the imbalance rate: ≈ e^(−λt/τ), with prefactor the nuclear norms of the factors — which is exactly where the boundedness hypothesis is needed. Proposition B.5 generalizes to L-layer products: under ε-balancedness (‖A_lᵀA_l − A_{l+1}A_{l+1}ᵀ‖__ ≤ ε) and ε ≤ L⁻⁴ min_l ‖A_l‖^L, the gap between the Schatten-2/L quasi-norm of the product and (1/L)Σ‖A_l‖F² is bounded by (r/L)Σ_l‖A_l‖^(L−1) e^(2/L) L^(4/L) ε^(1/L), so the deep case co-optimizes a Schatten-2/L (more aggressively rank-sparsifying) penalty with rate roughly λ/L — depth slows the collapse and sharpens the induced penalty. Finally, Appendix D argues the restriction to (A,B) with the other parameters θ frozen is without loss of generality: stationarity in (A,B) is all Lemma 3.2 uses, the Theorem 3.3 proof goes through verbatim with θ carried along, and in Theorem 3.4 the cancellation is unaffected because G may depend on θ and t arbitrarily.

Broader context. This sits at the junction of two literatures. One is the convex-relaxation tradition: rank is nonconvex and discontinuous, the nuclear norm is its tightest convex surrogate on the spectral ball, and matrix completion is solved either by minimizing ‖W‖__ directly (Candès–Tao) or by the differentiable Burer–Monteiro factorization W = ABᵀ with Frobenius penalties, which Srebro–Shraibman's max-margin matrix factorization paper tied together via the variational identity used here. The other is implicit regularization in deep learning: Gunasekar et al. (2017) showed gradient descent on factorized least squares from small initialization converges to the minimum-nuclear-norm solution; Arora et al. (2019) showed deep matrix factorization biases toward low rank more aggressively than nuclear norm (and earlier, that depth acts as an implicit accelerator); Razin–Cohen showed the bias is not always expressible as any norm; Jacot et al. and Li–Luo–Lyu studied saddle-to-saddle and greedy low-rank learning from small init; Timor–Vardi–Shamir connected weight decay to rank minimization in ReLU networks; Galanti et al. and Wang–Jacot are the closest predecessors (the latter proving a critical-point correspondence in L2-regularized linear DNNs and "one-way jumps from high to low rank"). The practical reason to care is that AdamW's decoupled weight decay at λ = 0.1 is effectively the default in transformer pretraining, usually justified by generalization folklore rather than by any statement about rank — and LoRA, whose whole point is an explicit low-rank product, typically applies weight decay to both factors, meaning the adapter is being nuclear-norm-penalized on top of its imposed rank budget. Natural follow-ups: design a penalty on (A,B) whose induced W-space regularizer is Schatten-p for p > 1 (shrinkage without truncation), so one keeps weight decay's optimization benefits without the spectral sparsification; or use the imbalance norm ‖AᵀA − BᵀB‖ and the Frobenius-minus-nuclear gap as a cheap, early-training diagnostic that tells you _when* in a run the nuclear-norm pressure switched on, and schedule λ against it; or run the ablation the paper does not — rank-match two models trained at different λ and separate the shrinkage effect from the rank effect causally.

For your own work the hook is real but needs stating precisely. In dense retrieval the scoring function is a bilinear form, and bilinear forms are exactly the parametrization this paper is about. The cleanest cases: a learned similarity s(q,d) = qᵀ M d with M = ABᵀ, and the projection head of each tower, where the embedding map is a product of the encoder's final linear map and the projection onto the retrieval space (and, of course, every attention block inside both towers). In all three, weight decay silently caps the effective rank of the operator, so the usable capacity of a d-dimensional embedding space is strictly less than d, by an amount set by λ rather than by any architectural decision. That matters because the sharpest expressiveness results for single-vector dense retrieval are rank arguments: a score matrix over queries × documents factorizes as ΦᵀΨ with inner dimension d, so no two-tower model with d-dimensional embeddings can realize a relevance matrix of rank above d — the motivation for late interaction and multi-vector retrieval. If AdamW is additionally soft-thresholding the spectrum of the learned bilinear form, the binding constraint is the trained rank, not the nominal d, and the gap is measurable from released checkpoints with the paper's own diagnostic: check whether the query and document projection heads satisfy AᵀA ≈ BᵀB and whether ½(‖A‖² + ‖B‖²) ≈ ‖ABᵀ‖__, exactly as the authors did for LLaMA-2 and ViT. The honest caveat is that a plain two-tower score φ(q)ᵀψ(d) is _not_ literally one ABᵀ of two parameter matrices — the two towers are separate and the factors are data-dependent — so the theorem does not transfer verbatim; it applies to the parameter products inside each tower and to any explicitly bilinear scorer, and the implication for the score matrix's rank is an inference, not a theorem. There is a second, cleaner connection for generative retrieval: the decoder's logits over docid tokens are a product of the final hidden state with an output embedding matrix, and when that table is factorized (tied, low-rank, or hierarchical docid embeddings) the same analysis applies — weight decay deepens the softmax bottleneck in the sense of Yang et al., lowering the rank of the log-probability matrix over docids. And for vector search there is a genuine tradeoff worth a paper: nuclear-norm pressure produces a spectrally sparse, lower-intrinsic-dimension embedding cloud, which is _good_ for ANN indices (HNSW and IVF-PQ both degrade with intrinsic dimension, and PQ codebooks get cheaper) and _bad* for expressiveness. A clean experiment would sweep λ on the projection heads of a Contriever/E5-style bi-encoder, and plot, on one axis, the effective rank and participation ratio of the embedding spectrum, and on the other, both nDCG and ANN recall-at-fixed-latency — testing whether weight decay has been giving dense retrieval an unasked-for, Matryoshka-like spectral ordering, and whether the retrieval-quality cost is paid where the rank-bottleneck theory says it should be, on queries requiring high-rank relevance structure.

title: How Neural Networks Learn the Support is an Implicit Regularization Effect of SGD
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-14

1. How Neural Networks Learn the Support is an Implicit Regularization Effect of SGD

Pierfrancesco Beneventano, Andrea Pinto, Tomaso Poggio (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11110

Main idea. The paper asks a narrow but well-posed question: when a network fits a target that depends only on a few input directions, where in the network does the irrelevant input get thrown away? The empirical answer they report is that mini-batch SGD kills it in the first layer — the columns of $W_1$ that multiply irrelevant coordinates shrink to zero — while full-batch GD reaches the same loss with a first layer that still looks like its initialization, having instead distributed the support selection across all layers. The theoretical claim is that this difference is not about fitting the target at all (both algorithms fit it) but about a second-order implicit regularization effect of mini-batch sampling whose strength is proportional to $\eta/b$, step size over batch size. The setup is deliberately spare: a finite dataset, no distributional assumption beyond one decorrelation condition, MSE loss, and the standard algorithms practitioners actually run (GD, SGD with and without replacement, optionally weight decay). "Support" is defined spectrally: $\Lambda_{y,x} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal D}[yx^\top]$ has rank $r$; its top-$r$ right eigenvectors are the relevant directions, its kernel the irrelevant ones, split further into $i$ directions spanned by the data and $u$ directions the data never excites (MNIST corner pixels). The narrative is two-phase: in phase 1 ($t \lesssim 1/\eta$) the loss drops and the network learns the support wherever initialization makes it cheapest; in phase 2 SGD oscillates around the minimizer manifold and drifts along it, and that drift is what moves the support into the first layer. GD, having no phase 2, simply stops.

The most interesting part / critique. The genuinely valuable contribution is the negative result for GD, and it is the cleanest thing in the paper. For a diagonal network the subnetwork carrying an irrelevant coordinate $j$ is $\prod_{\ell} W_\ell[j,j]\,x[j]$, and the shrinkage rate of layer $h$ is $\big(\prod_{\ell \neq h} W_\ell[j,j]\big)^2 \mathbb{E}[x[j]^2]$ — so whichever factor is smallest at initialization has the largest rate, stays smallest, and races to zero while all the others stall at a constant bounded away from zero. One layer wins, uniformly at random over layers, independently per irrelevant coordinate; hence Proposition 1's $\text{depth}^{-(d-r)}$. This is a nice, honest explanation of why GD's first layer is uninformative: the shrinkage is self-extinguishing, because the factor $a = \tilde W^\top \tilde W[i,i]$ in the per-step contraction $(1 - \eta a \,\mathbb{E}[x[j]^2])$ collapses before $W_1$ does. The second real contribution, which I think is more durable than the title's claim, is that SGD drives arbitrarily unbalanced initializations toward the balanced solution with no explicit regularizer — the deep-linear literature (Arora et al., Woodworth et al.) essentially always assumes approximate balancedness, and here balancedness is an output rather than an input.

The weaknesses are substantial and mostly about the distance between what is proved and what is claimed. Theorem 1 is for deep linear networks; Proposition 1 for diagonal linear or ReLU; Proposition 2 and Theorem 2 — the only actual convergence statements — for diagonal linear networks, where every coordinate is a decoupled scalar product $\prod_\ell \theta_\ell$. In a diagonal network the phrase "the first layer identifies the support" is much weaker than in a dense one: there is no rotation, no alignment, no competition between neurons, so the interesting geometric content of the empirical phenomenon (Figure 1's Gram matrices) is exactly what the theorem does not model. Theorem 1 itself is not a convergence result but a one-step in-expectation statement with two unquantified trajectory-dependent constants ($a$, and $c$ "related to the fourth moment"), and there is an unresolved inconsistency in the scaling: the main text writes the extra SGD term as $\eta \cdot \frac{\eta}{2b} a^2 c^2$, while Proposition 7 in the appendix writes $\frac{\eta^2}{b^2}\,\delta^2$. The proof (Eq. 38, variance of the per-batch second-moment matrix) supports $\eta^2 \mu_4 / b$, so the $1/b^2$ appears to be an error — but the reader has to adjudicate this themselves, which is not a good sign in a paper whose headline is the scaling law.

The nonlinear case is essentially unproven, and the paper is only half-candid about this. Section 6 and Appendix J contain an explicit counterexample showing the linear argument breaks for ReLU: the cross term $\sum_B D^x W_2^\top W_2 D^x W_1:,:r \, x[r{+}1{:}]^\top$ no longer cancels in expectation because $W_2 D^x$ differs per datapoint, and they construct a two-datapoint example where irrelevant weights grow on half the rows. Proposition 11, the positive ReLU statement, assumes the relevant part of the function is already exactly fit for every $x$, and even then yields only one-step non-increase, not convergence; Proposition 10 (ReLU with weight decay) is only for batch size 1. Worse, the paper's definition of support is a first-moment, purely linear-correlation notion: $y = x_j^2$ with centered inputs has $\mathbb{E}[yx_j] = 0$, so $x_j$ is formally "irrelevant" and the theory would happily shrink its weight. Section 6 notices this and proposes a conditional-independence replacement (Eq. 2), but nothing is proved under the new definition — which means that for precisely the target class where support recovery is the interesting problem (sparse nonlinear, single-index, parity-like functions, the Abbe/Damian line the intro cites), the theorems do not apply.

Two more things I would push on as a reviewer. First, Assumption 1 is an exact equality, $\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}[\langle v,x\rangle\langle w,x\rangle] = 0$, and the whole "cross term is centered at zero" argument rests on it; there is no perturbation analysis for the approximately-decorrelated case that real data actually satisfies, and an $\varepsilon$-robust version would presumably produce a nonzero bias floor on $|W_1[:,r{+}1{:}]|$ — which is the quantity the experiments plot. Second, the rates. Theorem 2's convergence time is double exponential in the layer index: $O\big(\eta^{-2^{i-1}} c^{-2^{i-1}}\big)$ for the $i$-th smallest weight. For depth two this is the clean $O!\big(b/(\eta^2 R_j^2)\big)$; for $i = 4$ at $\eta = 0.1$ it is astronomically large. So what is provably fast is that the smallest weight on an irrelevant coordinate vanishes — which is the same event GD also achieves — and the claim that the first layer specifically is annealed in usable time is not supported for realistic depth. Experimentally, the synthetic setup is engineered to meet the hypotheses: $d=15$, $r=5$, Gaussian inputs, irrelevant coordinates explicitly re-centered, and the dataset is each point duplicated with $+\epsilon$ and $-\epsilon$ label noise "to ensure symmetric oscillations over all samples." That is building the theorem's oscillation mechanism into the data. The vision evidence is qualitative — heatmaps and eigenvalue histograms, no quantitative support-recovery metric and no fitted exponent for the $\eta/b$ law despite it being the central quantitative claim. The CIFAR experiment defines the "ground truth support" by first training with aggressive weight decay, which is circular given that weight decay is one of the mechanisms under study. Appendix A's "MNIST and CIFAR have 9-dimensional support" is an overclaim about the rank of a trained MLP head's first layer (and 9 is suspiciously classes-minus-one). Finally, none of this is tied to generalization: Figure 1 explicitly notes all optimizers reach comparable loss, so the honest payoff is interpretability and initialization-independence, not test error — and the gesture toward adversarial robustness in the introduction is never tested.

Proof sketch. Precisely what is proved, in three pieces. (i) Theorem 1 / Propositions 4 and 7 — for a deep linear net with MSE under Assumption 1, write $\tilde W = W_L \cdots W_2$, $P = \tilde W^\top \tilde W$, $z = x[r{+}1{:}]$. Because Assumption 1 forces $\Lambda_{x,x}[:r, r{+}1{:}] = 0$, the full-batch GD step on the irrelevant block collapses to $W_1[:,r{+}1{:}] \leftarrow W_1[:,r{+}1{:}] - \eta\, P\, W_1[:,r{+}1{:}]\, \Lambda^{\mathcal D}_{z,z}$, a product of two PSD matrices acting from either side. Diagonalizing $P$ and $\Lambda_{z,z}}$ simultaneously (by rotation invariance of gradient methods, legitimate here) makes it entrywise: $W_1[i,j] \leftarrow (1 - \eta D_W[i,i] D_z[j,j]) W_1[i,j]$, hence monotone non-increase in absolute value, exactly stationary on rows in $\ker \tilde W$ and on the $u$ unspanned columns. For SGD the same step holds with $\Lambda^{\mathcal B_{z,z}$ and a _nonzero_{x,z} cross term $-\eta P W_1[:,:r] \Lambda^{\mathcal B}_$, which is centered at zero over $\mathcal D$ but not per batch. The key trick is to analyze two consecutive steps rather than one. For without-replacement sampling the per-epoch batch second moments sum exactly, $\sum_k \Lambda^{\mathcal B_k}_{z,z} = k\Lambda^{\mathcal D}_{z,z}}$, so writing $\Lambda^{\mathcal B_1_{z,z}[j,j] = \Lambda^{\mathcal D}_{z,z}}[j,j] - \delta$ and $\Lambda^{\mathcal B_2_{z,z}[j,j] = \Lambda^{\mathcal D}_{z,z}[j,j] + \delta$, the composition of the two multiplicative steps is $(1-\alpha+\delta)(1-\alpha-\delta) = (1-\alpha)^2 - \delta^2 < (1-\alpha)^2$: the first-order fluctuation cancels and leaves a strictly negative second-order residual, i.e. extra shrinkage. Expanding the two-step composition to order $\eta^2$ (their Eqs. 35–38) and taking expectation over batch order gives $-\eta^2 \mathrm{Var}(\Lambda^{\mathcal B}_{z,z}) Z (R^\top R)^2 - \eta^2 \mathrm{Var}(\Lambda^{\mathcal B}_{x,z}) Z((R-\alpha)^\top R)^2 + O(\eta^3)$. This is exactly where $\eta/b$ comes from: the $\eta^2$ is the order of the two-step cross term, and the variance of a $b$-sample empirical second moment is the fourth moment of the inputs divided by $b$. So the extra per-step contraction relative to GD's first-order $\eta a \mathbb{E}[x[j]^2]$ is $\eta \cdot \frac{\eta}{2b} a^2 c^2$ with $c^2 \sim \mu_4$ — the linear scaling rule, derived from batch-mean variance rather than assumed. Note this is a moment/noise-covariance argument on the discrete update, not an SDE: no Itô expansion or SDE approximation is used anywhere, which is both a strength (no $\eta \to 0$ validity question à la Li–Malladi–Arora) and a weakness (no limiting regularizer is identified).

(ii) Proposition 1 is the induction described above: smallest-at-initialization factor has the largest rate, remains smallest forever, converges at rate $(1-\eta c^{2L-2}\mathbb{E}[x[j]^2])$ while the others freeze; which layer wins is uniform, and independence across the $d-r$ irrelevant coordinates gives $\text{depth}^{-(d-r)}$. (iii) Theorem 2 / Proposition 2 is the only probabilistic convergence result. Assumptions: diagonal linear network, coordinate $j$ irrelevant ($\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}[y[j]x[j]] = 0$) but misspecified, $R_j^2 := \mathbb{E}[y[j]^2] - \mathbb{E}[y[j]x[j]]^2/\mathbb{E}[x[j]^2] > 0$, so the residual $\epsilon_x = f_\theta(x)x - yx$ cannot be driven to zero by any parameter choice; and $0 < \eta < \eta_{\max} = 2/\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 L \text{ at init})$. Guarantee: with probability $\ge 1-\delta_2$, the weight that is $i$-th smallest at initialization satisfies $|W_*[j,j]| \le \delta_1$ after $O\big(\eta^{-2^{i-1}} c^{-2^{i-1}}\big)\big(\log\alpha - \log\delta_2 - \log\delta_1\big)$ steps, for SGD with or without replacement, strictly faster without. The mechanism is the balance gap: define $G_i = W_{i+1}[j,j]^2 - W_i[j,j]^2$, a quantity gradient flow conserves exactly. One SGD step multiplies it by $\big(1 - \eta^2 \epsilon^2_{\mathcal B_t}(t)\big(\prod_{h \neq i,i+1} W_h\big)^2\big)$ — contraction at order $\eta^2$ and proportional to the squared batch residual, so it is active precisely when the trajectory oscillates and switches off when the loss is interpolated. The enabling lemma (Lemma 1) is a variance lower bound: for any model linear in the data and a uniform batch of size $b$, $\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}[\epsilon_x^2] - (\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_x])^2 \ge R^2/b$, because the batch-mean residual shrinks like $1/b$ while the per-point second moment is bounded below by the misspecification level — this is the second and independent place $1/b$ enters, and it is what makes the depth-2 time $O\big(b/(\eta^2 R_j^2)\big)$. From there: take logs, $\log G(t) = \sum_{s\le t}\log(1-\eta^2\epsilon^2_{\mathcal B_s}) + \log G(0)$, apply a Chernoff/Hoeffding bound to the sum of bounded i.i.d. log-terms (with a second-order Taylor bound on the mgf), and invert for $t$. For without-replacement sampling the product of the dependent factors satisfies $\mathbb{E}\prod(1-\eta^2\epsilon^2)^\lambda < \prod \mathbb{E}(1-\eta^2\epsilon^2)^\lambda$ by Lemma 12/Cor. 13 of Beneventano (2023), giving the strict speedup without a quantitative rate. The double exponential comes from an induction up a hierarchy of nested gaps, $G^1_i = \theta_i$, $G^2_i = \theta_i^2 - \theta_1^2$, $G^j_i = (G^{j-1}_i)^2 - (G^{j-1}_{j-1})^2$: each level obeys the same dynamical system with the exponent squared, so level $j$ contracts at rate $\eta^{2^{j-1}} c^{2^{j-1}}$. Once all the gaps vanish the net is balanced, and balanced plus "the product must vanish" forces every factor — including $W_1$ — to vanish. The chain is sound; the rate is the problem.

Broader context. The subfield here is implicit bias / implicit regularization: in the overparameterized regime the loss has a whole manifold of global minimizers, so which one you land on is decided by the algorithm, not the objective. Classical results identify the minimizer GD selects (max-margin for separable classification, minimum-norm for least squares, $\ell_1$-like sparsity for diagonal linear nets at small initialization — Woodworth et al.'s kernel-vs-rich dichotomy, directly adjacent to this paper's model class). The stochastic story is different in kind, and the useful mental model is the one from Blanc–Gunasekar–Lee–Srebro (2020) and its successors: once SGD reaches zero loss, the gradient noise does not stop; it drives a slow drift along the minimizer manifold, and to second order that drift is gradient flow on an effective regularizer built from the noise covariance. Damian–Ma–Lee (2021) showed label-noise SGD provably prefers flat minima in this way, and Li–Wang–Arora (2022) gave the general framework via an Itô/slow-manifold expansion: the limiting dynamics is Riemannian gradient flow on $\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma)$ restricted to the manifold, with timescale $\eta^2$. Li–Malladi–Arora (2021) separately asked when the SDE approximation to SGD is even valid, which is why the choice here to argue directly on the discrete two-step composition is defensible. The complementary literature on feature learning — Damian–Lee–Soltanolkotabi (2022), Ba et al.'s one-step feature learning, Abbe et al.'s merged-staircase and leap complexity — studies how a first layer escapes the lazy/NTK regime and aligns with a low-dimensional relevant subspace, usually with large first steps, fresh samples, and specific target classes. This paper sits in the gap: it is a Phase-2 implicit-bias result (not feature learning in the Damian sense — nothing is learned, irrelevant weights are annealed), but driven by ordinary mini-batch sampling noise rather than injected label noise, and it reads out the consequence in a concrete coordinate system (first-layer columns) instead of an abstract regularizer.

That gap is also the obvious follow-up. Nobody has written down the Li–Wang–Arora-style limiting slow flow for without-replacement mini-batch SGD and identified the effective regularizer $R(\theta)$ whose Riemannian gradient flow produces first-layer support selection; the moment computation here is a one-coordinate shadow of that object. Doing it properly would predict the shape of the drift for dense nonlinear nets, where the paper's cancellation argument fails, and would let one test whether measured first-layer column norms track $\nabla R$. A second, cheaper follow-up: replace the exact decorrelation in Assumption 1 with $|\Lambda_{x,z}| \le \varepsilon$ and derive the resulting bias floor — the theory then predicts a plateau in $|W_1[:,r{+}1{:}]|$ scaling like $\varepsilon b/\eta$ rather than convergence to zero, which is directly checkable against the MNIST curves and would turn the qualitative vision figures into a real test.

For your own work, I would not oversell the tie, but there is one non-forced thread. The paper's claim, stripped of the linear-network scaffolding, is that the effective rank of a learned representation is partly a hyperparameter artifact: how aggressively the model discards directions is set by $\eta/b$, and smaller batches give a more degenerate first layer at equal loss. If that survives to dense encoders, it bears on vector search, where the hardness of ANN — the constants in LSH exponents, the degree and hop counts that graph indices need, the quantization error that PQ/OPQ incurs — is governed by the intrinsic dimension of the embedding cloud rather than its ambient dimension. The prediction is testable and cheap: train the same retriever at several $\eta/b$ ratios, measure the spectrum/effective rank of the embedding matrix alongside the recall-latency Pareto of an HNSW or IVF-PQ index built over it, and see whether the optimizer's regularization strength, not just the data, moves the index's operating curve. There is even a reason to think the mechanism is more likely to be active in retrieval than in the paper's setting: Theorem 2 needs persistently nonzero residuals, and contrastive training with hard negatives never interpolates, so the oscillatory phase 2 is the normal operating regime rather than an edge case. The caveat is that the theorem is about the first layer acting on raw input coordinates, whereas what matters for ANN is the output embedding, and nothing here says the two have the same behavior. On generative retrieval and docid representation learning I think the connection would be manufactured, so I will say plainly: treat this one as general learning-theory background — a well-motivated, somewhat rough preprint whose most portable ideas are the GD stalling mechanism and the balance-gap-contraction technique — rather than an IR paper in disguise.

title: Simulating Hard Attention Using Soft Attention
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 13 October 2026

Simulating Hard Attention Using Soft Attention

Andy Yang, Lena Strobl, David Chiang, Dana Angluin (2024) — arXiv:2412.09925 — link

Main idea

The formal-languages-of-transformers literature runs on a convenient fiction. Almost every constructive expressivity result — simulating an n-gram model, matching brackets, recognizing the star-free regular languages, computing linear temporal logic with counting, compiling S-RASP — is proved for a transformer whose attention is hard rather than softmax. Two hardening conventions dominate. Unique-hard attention (UHAT, Hahn 2020) puts all weight on a single argmax position, with ties broken deterministically leftmost or rightmost; average-hard or saturated attention (AHAT, after Perez, Marinkovic & Barcelo 2019) puts weight 1/|I(s)| on each of the positions attaining the maximum score and zero elsewhere. Both are discontinuous, and that discontinuity is exactly what makes them tractable: an attention head becomes a selector, so an inductive translation from a logic into a network can keep every intermediate value in a finite set. The payoff is a set of unusually clean characterizations — masked UHAT recognizes exactly the star-free regular languages, equivalently exactly the languages definable in LTL; UHAT in general sits inside AC^0; AHAT absorbs counting logics with linear arithmetic over counts. Real transformers, of course, use softmax, whose weights are never exactly 0 or 1 absent masking.

Closing that gap is harder than the folklore suggests, and the paper's framing is the best part of its exposition. There is a trivial limiting argument: a transformer is a composition of continuous maps and softmax at temperature tau converges pointwise to ahardmax as tau -> 0, so for each fixed input the softmax activations converge to the hard ones. This argument says nothing about the rate, and rate is what matters, because Hahn's Lemma 5 is a genuine obstruction: if a transformer has (1) softmax attention, (2) a number and magnitude of parameters independent of n, (3) Lipschitz position-wise operations, and (4) bounded position embeddings, then flipping one input symbol perturbs any output activation by only O(1/n). AHATs, by contrast, have Theta(1) sensitivity. So an O(1) acceptance/rejection margin — the thing you need if the module is to be composed with another module expecting discrete inputs — is unreachable under (1)-(4). Chiang & Cholak's PARITY construction is the canonical illustration: it works, but its margin shrinks like 1/n, as it must.

The authors therefore look for simulations that are general (for a whole class of hard-attention transformers, not one language) and parameter-uniform (the number and values of parameters do not depend on n, so one model serves all lengths), and they buy their way past Hahn by dropping assumption (2)-adjacent machinery in one of two ways: inverse-temperature scaling, where scores are divided by tau(n) before softmax, or unbounded position embeddings, whose entries grow polynomially in n. These are deliberately not the other two known escapes — rounding (Sanford, Hsu & Telgarsky; Li et al.), which is general but needs FFN width or depth depending on n, and layer normalization, which is non-Lipschitz as originally defined. Layer norm is explicitly omitted on the grounds that it is an independent mechanism that would interact with the other two in complicated ways.

The results come in two tiers. First (section 4), the subclasses of AHAT-recognizable languages that are definable in fragments of Barcelo et al.'s counting LTL — the next/previous fragment TL[prev, next] (which covers n-gram patterns), the TL[since, until] fragment (which covers tie-breaking, flip-flops, induction heads), and the counting fragment with left/right counts, linear arithmetic and monadic numerical predicates (which covers PARITY and MAJORITY) — are each simulated by a softmax transformer with either tau(n) = 1/n and PEs of magnitude O(1) to O(n^2), or tau = 1 and PEs of magnitude O(n) to O(n^3). Since masked UHAT is equivalent to LTL, this yields the previously missing statement that softmax transformers can simulate unique-hard attention transformers. Second (section 5), general AHATs: any AHAT whose attention scores always separate the maximum from the rest by a gap gamma(n) can be approximately simulated, with the same parameters, by a softmax transformer at inverse temperature 1/tau(n) in O(gamma(n)^-1 log(n x_max(n)/gamma(n))).

One correction to the framing in my brief: the arXiv v2 (June 2025) contains no "uniform-tieless" hypothesis. "Tieless" appears only in Definition 5 as a per-score-vector property (|I(s)| = 1), used to make lhardmax = rhardmax = ahardmax well-defined. Theorem 26 covers general AHATs including ties, and for a good reason worth stating: ties are harmless for average-hard attention, because low-temperature softmax spreads mass nearly equally among equal-scoring positions, which is precisely what ahardmax does. It is unique-hard attention that needs extra machinery (Lemma 8) to break ties. Whatever tieless condition appeared in v1 has been absorbed into the gap formulation.

The most interesting part

The cleverest single move is Lemma 7, the parabola table lookup, and it is clever because it defeats an unbounded value vector. Several hard-attention constructions use table lookup: given t_i in [n] at each position, retrieve v_{t_i}. Under hard attention you realize this with scores s_j = gamma(2 t_i j - j^2), a downward parabola peaking exactly at j = t_i. Under softmax the leaked mass onto j != t_i decays like exp(-gamma (j - t_i)^2) — quadratically in the exponent rather than linearly. That matters in the one case where the retrieved value itself is a position, v_j = j, which grows with n: the error is a sum over k >= 1 of exp(-gamma k^2) k, bounded by (3/2) exp(-gamma) for gamma >= 1 via a Riemann-sum comparison against the integral of exp(-gamma x^2) x. So the sum of (linearly growing value) times (Gaussian-decaying leak) is O(exp(-gamma)) independent of n. A merely linear "ziggurat" score profile (Lemma 6) would not survive v_j = j; the quadratic shape is doing real work. This is the mechanism that lets softmax turn an average into a count, which is the crux of the entire counting-logic simulation.

On the role of temperature: the required inverse temperature is essentially 1/tau approx gamma^-1 log(n/gamma), i.e. "a little lower than the gap," with a logarithmic overhead for the union over n competing positions. For the typical AHAT constructions in the literature, gamma(n) = Omega(1/n^k) with k <= 3, so 1/tau is in O(n^k log n). Is this cheating? Partly, and the paper is unusually honest about it. The authors observe that tau(n)=1/n and "scale the query vectors by n" are interchangeable — several proofs literally say "same as (a), but scale the queries by n," and condition (b) achieves it by putting n, in, or i^2 n in the position embedding. So temperature scaling and unbounded PEs are two faces of one intervention: giving the score function a dynamic range that grows polynomially in n. And they argue this is not avoidable: Hahn's lemma forces some activation to be scaled by Theta(n) if you want an O(1) output margin, so the tau(n) = 1/n constructions in section 4 are asymptotically optimal in that factor.

What it does cost is precision. Scores whose maximum is separated from its competitors by Theta(1/n^k), divided by tau approx 1/(n^k log n), require Theta(k log n) bits to represent faithfully. So these simulations live squarely in the log-precision regime, and they neither contradict nor evade the known ceiling: log-precision softmax transformers are contained in (FO-uniform) TC^0 (Merrill & Sabharwal; Chiang 2025), and so are AHATs, so a simulation of one by the other had better stay inside TC^0. The right reading of the paper is therefore not "softmax transformers are more powerful than we thought" but "the constructive AHAT/UHAT proofs in the literature are faithful to actual softmax transformers, at a known and modest price in logit scale and numerical precision." The constructions are parameter-uniform in the paper's precise sense — the parameter count and values are fixed — but they are emphatically not uniform in length in the colloquial sense: tau is a function of n, and in the counting cases the PEs contain n-dependent entries of magnitude up to n^3.

Three further honest caveats. First, gamma(n) is defined non-constructively: Proposition 24 observes that every AHAT has a strictly positive gap function simply because there are finitely many inputs of each length, taking the minimum over all of them. That gamma need not be computable or polynomially bounded; Theorem 26 only bites for AHATs with an explicit poly gap, which fortunately is how published constructions come. Second, depth enters badly in one place and mildly in another: the per-layer bound shows that lowering the temperature amplifies incoming error by a factor about x_max^2/tau, so the final error carries a factor r^(L-1) exponential in depth L; that factor appears only additively (and linearly in L) inside the logarithm of the temperature requirement, so a Theta(log n)-depth construction costs an extra log n in 1/tau rather than a catastrophe, but a construction whose depth grows with input length is not covered by the clean statement of the theorem. Third, what is simply not addressed: layer normalization (excluded by design), rounding, the converse direction (no lower bound showing 1/tau = Omega(1/gamma) is necessary), and — most consequentially for the section 5 result — exactness. For AHATs the simulation is approximate in L1 at the activation level, and only becomes exact language recognition or transduction because the output convention designates discrete symbols with a fixed-size margin. There is no re-digitization available mid-computation for general AHATs, which is exactly why sections 4 and 5 are separate theorems with different guarantees.

Proof sketch

What is proved, precisely. Section 4 gives a family of statements of the form "every formula phi of logic L is simulated by a tau-SMAT with temperature tau and position embeddings containing the following entries," where simulated means: for every input w and every position i, a designated coordinate of the final activation equals the indicator of (w, i) satisfying phi exactly — not approximately — for all lengths, with one fixed parameter set. Theorem 12: TL[prev, next], with (a) tau(n) = 1/n and PEs containing i/n and (-1)^i, or (b) tau = 1 and PEs containing i/n, (-1)^i, n. Theorem 13: the past-only fragment TL[prev] with future masking alone, at tau(i) = 1/i^2 (note: a position-dependent, causal temperature, legitimate for autoregressive decoding) or PEs containing i^2. Theorem 15: TL[since, until] at tau(n) = 1/n with i/n, or tau=1 with i/n and n; Theorem 16 the one-sided TL[since] at tau(i) = 1/i^2 with 1/i. Corollary 17 combines these into full LTL = TL[prev, next, since, until], and since masked UHAT is equivalent to LTL (Yang, Chiang & Angluin 2024), _every masked UHAT is simulated by a softmax transformer at tau(n)=1/n_; Corollary 18 does the past fragment with future masking only. Theorem 20 handles the counting logic at tau(n) = 1/n with PEs containing 1/i, 1/(n-i+1), i, i^2 and a coordinate per unary numerical predicate appearing in phi; Corollary 22 assembles the full counting LTL (= Barcelo et al.'s LTL(C,+)). Theorem 26 is the general AHAT result: for any AHAT T with gap gamma(n) and any target error epsilon(n) in Omega(1/poly(n)), there is a temperature with 1/tau(n) in O(gamma(n)^-1 log(n x_max(n)/gamma(n))) such that the tau-SMAT with identical parameters satisfies an L1 error of at most epsilon(n) at every position; for gamma = n^-k and x_max in n^O(1), 1/tau is in O(n^k log n).

How it is proved: the approximation toolkit (section 3). Everything rests on four lemmas. Lemma 6 (ziggurat): if there is a j_ with s_j <= s_{j_} - |j - j_| gamma for all j — a tent whose sides fall by at least gamma per step — then the difference between the hardmax-weighted and softmax-weighted value sums is at most 4 exp(-gamma) v_max. The proof is a two-term bookkeeping argument: set a = exp(s_{j_}), bound b = sum over j != j_ of exp(s_j) by (2 exp(-gamma)/(1 - exp(-gamma))) a by summing the geometric series on both flanks, then the L1 distance between hardmax and softmax is 2b/(a+b) <= 4 exp(-gamma)/(1 + exp(-gamma)). Crucially the bound is _independent of n_, because the geometric decay of the tent sides swallows the growing number of competitors. Lemma 7 is the parabola refinement already described, needed when v_j = j is unbounded. Lemma 9 is the _re-digitizer*: with delta = 1/4, any value at most 1/4 is read as false and any value at least 3/4 as true, and the single-neuron-pair FFN f(x) = 2 ReLU(x - 1/4) - 2 ReLU(x - 3/4) maps approximate Booleans to exact ones. Proposition 10 bootstraps the arithmetic the tie-breakers need from a single PE coordinate (-1)^i: uniform future-masked attention with values (-1)^(j+1) outputs 1 at i=1 and something in [-1/3, 1/3] for i>1, so an FFN marks the first position exactly; past-masking marks the last; and then uniform future-masked attention over that one-hot marker averages to exactly 1/i, with 1/(n-i+1) obtained by past-masking.

Tie-breaking (Lemma 8). This is the UHAT-specific piece and the place where "unbounded" enters most transparently. Simulating rhardmax or lhardmax requires perturbing the score landscape so that the intended winner among tied maxima becomes the strict argmax, while the perturbation does not disturb the ordering between the max class and the rest. Hence the two-scale design: the original scores (in applications, Boolean indicators, so the genuine gap is at least 1) are blown up by a factor of n or n^2, and a monotone perturbation of size O(1) is added. Variant (a) uses s-hat_j = gamma n^2 s_j - 1/j: within a tie class, the difference is gamma n^2 (j_ - j)/(j_ j) >= gamma |j_ - j| since j_ j <= n^2; across classes, it is at least gamma n^2 (1 - 1 + 1/n) = gamma n. Either way the ziggurat hypothesis of Lemma 6 holds with gap gamma, so the leak is at most 4 exp(-gamma) v_max. Variants (b) and (c) use s-hat_j = 2 gamma n (s_j +/- j/(2n)), selecting rightmost or leftmost respectively. The design constraint is exactly what one would guess: the tie-breaker must be large enough to dominate inside a tie class and small enough to be dominated by the real gap — which is why the amplification is Theta(n) for a Theta(1/n) tie-breaker and Theta(n^2) for a Theta(1/n)-resolution tie-breaker like 1/j. Note also that left-vs-right tie-breaking demands a signed, direction-specific perturbation: softmax has no intrinsic tie-breaking, so position information is indispensable here, not a convenience.

Translating the logics. The section 4 proofs are inductions on formula structure with one invariant: each subformula's truth value occupies its own coordinate, is written by one or two attention layers plus an FFN into a previously unused coordinate, and is carried forward to all later layers by the residual connections. Atoms Q_sigma are one-hot in the word embedding; numerical predicates are stored in the position embedding; Boolean connectives are FFNs. The temporal operators are where attention is used. For prev(phi_1), a UHAT would make position i attend to i-1 by boosting even positions when i is odd and odd positions when i is even, then tie-break rightmost; the tau-SMAT version uses two future-masked heads with scores 6((1/2)(-1)^j +/- j/(2n)), maximized at the rightmost even (resp. odd) j <= i, invokes Lemma 8b with effective gamma = 3 to get leak 4 exp(-3) < 1/4, and lets the FFN select the head by the parity of i and zero out i=1 via Proposition 10a. next is the past-masked mirror with the tie-breaker sign flipped (Lemma 8c). For phi_1 since phi_2 the reduction is genuinely pretty: the UHAT algorithm attends to the rightmost j <= i maximizing the indicator of (not phi_1) or phi_2 — the nearest "stopping" position, whether it stops because phi_2 fired or because phi_1 failed — and returns the value of phi_1 and phi_2 there, which disambiguates the two cases in one read. The softmax version simply sets the score to 6(indicator + j/(2n)) and the value to the indicator of phi_1 and phi_2, applies Lemma 8b, and rounds. until is the mirror image. The decisive structural point is that Lemma 9 is applied after every subformula, so the approximation error never compounds across the induction: each layer's output is re-snapped to {0,1}, and the 4 exp(-3) < 1/4 margin is re-established from scratch. This is why section 4 gives exact computation despite being built from approximations.

Counting: turning averages into counts. The counting cases are the technical heart. Attention averages, it does not count, so a left-count of phi_1 must be recovered from (left-count)/i. Step 1: uniform future-masked attention over the indicator of phi_1 computes (left-count)/i exactly. Step 2: a parabola table-lookup layer with query 3 Lambda [count/i, 1/i], key [2j, -j^2], value v_j = j gives score 3 Lambda (2 (count) j - j^2)/i, uniquely maximized at j = count. The two PE coordinates 1/i and 1/(n-i+1) from Proposition 10cd are exactly what makes the division by i available inside the query. Because the division by i shrinks the scores, the effective gap after temperature scaling is gamma = 3 Lambda/(i tau), and with tau = 1/n and i <= n this is at least 3 Lambda uniformly — the only place where tau = 1/n is load-bearing in a non-cosmetic way. Lemma 7 then bounds the error by 4 exp(-3 Lambda), i.e. within +/- 1/(4 Lambda) of the true integer count, where Lambda is the total absolute weight of the linear combination to be compared. Step 3: an FFN forms the linear combination, whose error is at most Lambda times 1/(4 Lambda) = 1/4, so the comparison against the threshold C is an approximate Boolean and Lemma 9 rounds it. The scaling of Lambda into the query is the error-budget trick: the precision demanded of the count is set by the coefficient magnitudes of the comparison it feeds. For a monadic predicate applied to a count, the same lookup layer is used with v_j = theta_n(j) instead of v_j = j; since that value is bounded by 1, the weaker Lemma 6 suffices. Right-counting terms require only replacing 1/i by 1/(n-i+1), and the zero case (count = 0) is split off first because the lookup peak would otherwise fall at j = 0.

Error propagation for general AHATs (section 5). Here no re-digitization is possible, since the activations of an arbitrary AHAT are not confined to a finite set, so the proof is a careful Lipschitz-with-amplification analysis. Lemma 29 bounds activations by K^l d x_max(n) with K = 2(d^2 p_max^2 + 1)(d p_max + 1), i.e. a per-layer blow-up governed by the largest parameter magnitude p_max. Lemma 30: an FFN layer amplifies existing error by at most d^2 p_max^2 + 1 and introduces none (ReLU is 1-Lipschitz, the residual adds the input error). Lemma 31: the bilinear score is error-amplifying quadratically, with |s - s-hat| <= 3 d^(3/2) p_max^2 h_max epsilon, via the cross-term expansion of q.k - q-hat.k-hat and the bound |a.b| <= ||a||_1 ||b||_1. Lemma 32 is the key one, splitting the attention-weight error into two independent sources: the L1 distance between ahardmax(s) and softmax_tau(s-hat) is at most 2n exp(-gamma/tau) [hard vs. soft] plus 4 epsilon/tau [score error]. The first term is Edelman et al.'s bound — note the factor n, the union over competitors. The second comes from the multiplicative bound softmax_tau(s-hat)_i <= exp(2 epsilon/tau) softmax_tau(s)_i together with exp(2x) <= 1 + 4x for x <= 1/2, with the trivial bound of 2 used when epsilon > tau/2. Lemma 33 converts weight error into output error. Composing gives the one-layer recurrence of Lemma 25: epsilon_l <= a + r epsilon_{l-1} with a = K x_max n exp(-gamma/tau) and r = K x_max^2/tau.

That recurrence exhibits the central tension cleanly. Lowering tau shrinks the new error a exponentially but inflates the inherited error multiplier r linearly in 1/tau. The resolution in Theorem 26 is that a's advantage is exponential and r's penalty is polynomial, so the geometric sum epsilon_L = a(1 + r + ... + r^(L-1)) <= L a r^(L-1) can be driven below any epsilon(n) in Omega(1/poly(n)). Taking logs, log epsilon_L <= log(K n x_max) - gamma/tau + (L-1) log r, and then linearizing log r <= log r_0 + (r - r_0)/r_0 around r_0 = 2K(L-1) x_max^2/gamma — a first-order Taylor trick that absorbs the -gamma/tau term by half, leaving log epsilon_L <= log(K n x_max) - gamma/(2 tau) + (L-1)(log r_0 - 1) — yields the requirement 1/tau >= (2/gamma)[log(K n^(beta+1) x_max/alpha) + (L-1)(log r_0 - 1)], i.e. 1/tau in O(gamma^-1 log(n x_max/gamma)) with the depth dependence linear inside the bracket. The r^(L-1) factor is exponential in L but it is paid in the error, and translated through the logarithm it costs only an additive O(L log(x_max/gamma)) in 1/tau.

Finally, section 6 cashes this out on concrete tasks. Induction heads (and the k-hop variant for constant k) are LTL-definable, hence tau(n) = 1/n suffices — better than Liu et al.'s flip-flop construction, which scales queries by O(n log n). Sanford et al.'s k-hop AHAT has gap Omega(1/n^2); their own soft-attention simulation is general but not parameter-uniform, and Appendix A explains why, via a Telgarsky-style piece-counting argument: a depth-l width-m ReLU network computing a function from R to R is piecewise affine with at most (2m)^l pieces, while rounding p'-bit to p-bit numbers needs 2^p pieces, so (2m)^l >= 2^p — with p = Theta(log n) a constant-depth rounding MLP needs width n^epsilon. S-RASP transductions (Strobl et al. 2025) have gamma in Omega(1/n^3) and x_max in O(1), so every S-RASP-expressible transduction is computed exactly by a tau-SMAT with tau in Omega(1/(n^3 log n)) — "exactly" because the discrete output convention has a fixed margin. Appendix D writes Yao et al.'s Dyck-k algorithm in S-RASP, giving the same bound, while conjecturing that Dyck-2 is not definable in the counting LTL — so section 5 is strictly more general than section 4 here, not merely a different route.

Broader context

The program this paper belongs to tries to locate transformers in the classical hierarchies of formal language theory, circuit complexity, and logic. Its upper-bound wing starts with Hahn (2020), who showed that hard-attention transformers cannot recognize PARITY or Dyck-1 and proved the sensitivity lemma that this paper must circumvent; Hao, Angluin & Frank (2022) placed UHAT inside AC^0; Merrill, Sabharwal & Smith (2022) put saturated-attention transformers in TC^0; and Merrill & Sabharwal (2023), refined by Chiang (2025), showed that log-precision softmax transformers are contained in FO-uniform TC^0 — equivalently, definable in first-order logic with majority quantifiers. Strobl, Merrill, Sabharwal, Angluin & Chiang's TACL survey is the standard map of the territory. The lower-bound wing supplies matching logics and programming languages: Weiss, Goldberg & Yahav's RASP ("Thinking Like Transformers") and its descendants Tracr and Transformer Programs; Angluin, Chiang & Yang's B-RASP and the theorem that masked UHAT recognizes exactly the star-free regular languages, equivalent to LTL; Barcelo, Kozachinskiy, Lin & Podolskii's LTL(C,+) inside AHAT; and Yang & Chiang's compilation of the temporal counting logic K_t[#] directly into softmax transformers. That last paper is the closest predecessor: it already compiled a counting logic into softmax rather than hard attention, and the present work can be read as generalizing its techniques from one logic to a hierarchy of fragments plus arbitrary gap-bounded AHATs. Orthogonally, the chain-of-thought line — Perez et al.'s Turing-completeness, Merrill & Sabharwal on CoT as a depth/time resource, Li, Liu, Zhou & Ma on inherently serial problems, Sanford, Hsu & Telgarsky on logarithmic depth — treats decoding steps as extra computation and lifts the TC^0 ceiling.

The natural follow-up is the missing converse. Theorem 26 is purely an upper bound on the temperature needed; nothing says 1/tau = Omega(1/gamma) is necessary. A sharpness-budget theorem — "for every AHAT with gap gamma(n) there is an input on which the identically-parameterized tau-SMAT errs whenever tau >> gamma/log n" — would turn the log(n/gamma) overhead from an artifact of the union bound into an intrinsic price, and would connect to Hahn's lemma from the other side. A second direction is layer normalization, explicitly excluded here: since LN is where Chiang & Cholak, Yao et al. and Yang & Chiang all got their extra sensitivity, the obvious question is whether LN can substitute for the Theta(n) score amplification and yield a genuinely bounded-PE, tau = 1 simulation of UHAT. A third is learnability: the paper's own section 7 gestures at it, and the empirical fact that O(1/log n) temperature scaling improves length generalization (Chiang & Cholak; Nakanishi's scalable-softmax) suggests asking whether gradient descent actually discovers the low-effective-temperature solutions these constructions describe, or whether length generalization failures are exactly failures to scale 1/tau with n.

For IR the connection is real and runs through two mechanisms. The first is exact lookup in generative retrieval. A DSI-style decoder, generating a document identifier token by token under trie-constrained beam search, must at each step retrieve the correct prefix-conditioned continuation from a structured ID space — formally a table lookup, and formally the same operation as multi-query associative recall (which the abstract cites as a task UHAT solves). Lemma 7 is the precise statement of what softmax attention must pay to do this: a lookup over n candidate positions requires a score landscape with a peak whose curvature gives an effective gap gamma, and the attention mass leaked onto the n-1 distractors is about n exp(-gamma/tau), so keeping the leak below epsilon demands gamma/tau >= log(n/epsilon). Representing scores at that resolution needs Theta(log N) bits for an identifier space of size N. That is a genuine architectural statement, and it says something practitioners have observed empirically from the other direction: exact retrieval over a large ID set is a precision-limited operation, which is why logit scale, attention temperature, and numerical format interact with the size of the docid space rather than being free choices.

The second is hard top-k retrieval versus softmax attention. kNN-LM, Memorizing Transformers, RETRO, Unlimiformer and the whole retrieval-augmented-attention family replace softmax-over-everything with exact top-k selection followed by a local softmax. The hard/soft distinction in this paper is precisely that gap, and the result says the substitution is expressively unnecessary — softmax can simulate the hard selector — but only at inverse temperature Omega(gamma^-1 log n). Read contrapositively, this is the formal content of the "attention dilution" or dispersion phenomenon: at fixed temperature and fixed score gap, the signal-to-noise ratio of a retrieval head degrades like n exp(-gamma), so the sharpness of a retrieval head must grow logarithmically in context length merely to stay in place. This is exactly the motivation for the length-dependent attention-temperature corrections in long-context models (YaRN-style scaling, and the scalable-softmax of Nakanishi that the paper cites), and the paper gives the clean reason why such a correction is not a hack but a necessity. It also sharpens the complementary negative results: Sanford, Hsu & Telgarsky's q-sparse-averaging lower bound shows a single attention layer needs embedding dimension Omega-tilde(n) to aggregate q scattered items, and their k-hop result forces logarithmic depth. Translated to IR, aggregating evidence from q scattered passages — multi-hop retrieval, set retrieval, counting-style aggregation over a long document — is not something one attention layer can do at bounded width and precision, which is a theoretical argument for iterative or explicitly retrieval-augmented pipelines over "just make the context longer." More speculatively (and I flag this as speculation rather than anything the paper claims): the gap/temperature trade-off suggests a measurable "sharpness budget" per retrieval head, and one might predict that long-context rerankers improve from learned per-head logit scales that grow with context length, and that a head's attention entropy at a given context length is a usable diagnostic for whether it is operating in the hard-simulation regime or has dissolved into averaging.

title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 13 October 2026

How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations

Lee, Zeng, Jeong, Sohn, Lee (2025) — arXiv:2511.21140 — link

Main idea

The paper attacks a mundane-looking reporting practice and shows it is a measurement-error problem in disguise. In the standard LLM-as-a-judge pipeline one reports p-hat, the fraction of responses the judge calls 'correct'. But the estimand people claim to be reporting is theta = Pr(Z=1), the prevalence of responses a human protocol would call correct. These are different population quantities, and the gap is governed entirely by two judge parameters: sensitivity q1 = Pr(Zhat=1 | Z=1) and specificity q0 = Pr(Zhat=0 | Z=0). The law of total probability gives the whole story in one line: E[p-hat] = (q0+q1-1) theta + (1-q0). So p-hat is an affine, not identity, transform of theta; it is unbiased for all theta iff q0 = q1 = 1. Rewritten, the bias has a single fixed point at theta_ = (1-q0)/(2-q0-q1): below it p-hat over-reports, above it p-hat under-reports. For the running example (q0,q1) = (0.7,0.9), theta_ = 0.75, which is exactly the crossing in Figure 2a. The two error channels have opposite signatures — false accepts (1-q0) inflate low scores, false rejects (1-q1) deflate high scores — which is why the bias is shrinkage toward theta* rather than a constant offset, and why it cannot be removed by any monotone recalibration of a single reported number without knowing q0, q1.

Because the map is affine with slope q0+q1-1 (Youden's J), it inverts whenever J is nonzero, giving the Rogan-Gladen estimator theta-hat = (p-hat + q0 - 1)/(q0+q1-1), unbiased for theta when the judge parameters are known. The operational contribution is the plug-in version with q0-hat, q1-hat from a human-labeled calibration set of size m = m0 + m1, stratified by true label, with q1-hat the judge's hit rate on the m1 truly-correct items and q0-hat its hit rate on the m0 truly-incorrect ones. Note the asymmetry of the design: sensitivity and specificity are estimated from disjoint strata, so m0 and m1 are separate budgets, which is what makes the allocation question later well-posed.

The inferential half is a confidence interval that propagates two independent sources of noise — sampling noise in p-hat from the test set, and estimation noise in (q0-hat, q1-hat) from the calibration set.
