The delta method on the three-argument map gives Var(theta-hat) approx [p(1-p)/n + (1-theta)^2 q0(1-q0)/m0 + theta^2 q1(1-q1)/m1]/(q0+q1-1)^2, and the reported interval is the adjusted-Wald ("add two successes and two failures", Agresti-Coull) version of this, taken from Lang & Reiczigel (2014), with a small center shift. The structural consequence is the paper's most useful practical claim: since LLM judging is nearly free, n -> infinity is affordable and the first variance term vanishes, so the entire interval width is set by the human calibration budget (m0, m1) — which turns "how many humans do I need" into a solvable design question (Figure 3: at (q0,q1)=(0.7,0.9) and p-hat=0.3, a width below 0.1 needs m about 200).

Two further pieces complete the framework. Proposition 5.2 solves for the optimal split of a fixed calibration budget, m0 approx (1/p - 1) sqrt(kappa) m1 with error ratio kappa = (1-q0)/(1-q1), implemented as a pilot-then-allocate scheme (Algorithm 1, 10 pilot items per stratum). And Section 8 reframes the whole bias-correction literature as a taxonomy of invariance assumptions (Table 2): the naive estimator assumes Pr_P(Z)=Pr_P(Zhat); calibration-only assumes Pr_P(Z)=Pr_Q(Z); the difference estimator used by prediction-powered inference assumes Pr_P(Z-Zhat) = Pr_Q(Z-Zhat); conditional calibration assumes Pr_P(Z|Zhat)=Pr_Q(Z|Zhat); whereas Rogan-Gladen assumes only Pr_P(Zhat|Z) = Pr_Q(Zhat|Z). That last assumption is the one that survives a shift in label prevalence between calibration and test — which is the realistic failure mode when a fixed, expensively annotated calibration set is reused against streaming test batches of varying difficulty.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever contribution is not the Rogan-Gladen inversion (1978) nor the interval (Lang & Reiczigel 2014) — both are explicitly borrowed — but the recognition that LLM-as-a-judge has a design degree of freedom that epidemiology mostly does not, and the exploitation of it. In diagnostic-test calibration you take the validation sample you can get; here you can buy human labels stratified by true label, and the asymptotic variance is a weighted sum A/m0 + B/m1 with A = (1-theta)^2 q0(1-q0) and B = theta^2 q1(1-q1). Minimizing under m0+m1=m is a textbook Neyman allocation, and the paper's achievement is to push it through to an implementable rule by exploiting the high-accuracy regime: when q -> 1, q(1-q) approx (1-q) and theta -> p, so m0/m1 -> [(1-p)/p] sqrt((1-q0)/(1-q1)) — expressible entirely in observables (p-hat from the free test set, kappa from a 20-item pilot). The qualitative reading is sharp and non-obvious: allocate human effort toward the stratum where the judge errs more and toward the label that is more common in the test set, so a judge with poor sensitivity evaluated on a high-scoring model should spend almost its whole budget verifying truly-correct items. Figures 3 and 5c show this is not a marginal gain.

The second thing I like is the honesty of Section 6 and its crisp threshold. Proposition 6.1 asks: given m human annotations, is it better to calibrate a judge and apply it to infinite test data, or just to label m test items directly? In the symmetric case q0=q1=q and m -> infinity the answer is an interval in theta that is nonempty only if (2q-1)^2 >= 1/2, i.e. q >= 1/2 + 1/(2 sqrt 2) which is about 0.8536. (I verified the algebra: q(1-q)/(2q-1)^2 = 1/(4(2q-1)^2) - 1/4, which reduces the general condition to the symmetric one exactly.) So no amount of free LLM judging can beat spending the same human budget directly unless Youden's J exceeds about 0.707 — a clean, quotable impossibility threshold. And the paper reports that on Chatbot Arena none of seven frontier judges lands in the favorable region (Figure 6); only on the easier AlpacaEval task does GPT-4.1-mini get inside (Figure 11). That is a strikingly deflationary result for a paper selling a judge-correction method, and it is stated plainly.

Now the limitations, several of which are load-bearing. First, the identification rests on non-differential misclassification: Pr(Zhat | Z) must not depend on item difficulty, length, style, or domain. Appendix A concedes this, but the consequence for the headline robustness claim is stronger than the paper admits. "Unbiased under distribution shift" means unbiased under shift in the label marginal Pr(Z) with Pr(xi | Z) held fixed. If the test batch shifts in covariate composition — a different domain, longer answers, harder prompts — then Pr_P(Zhat|Z) = integral Pr(Zhat|Z,xi) dP(xi|Z) also shifts, and the Rogan-Gladen estimator fails along with the others. Since realistic shift in LLM evaluation is almost always covariate-driven and only derivatively prevalence-driven, Table 2's victory is narrower than it reads. The proposed fix (stratify xi, invert per stratum, aggregate) multiplies the calibration budget by the number of strata and worsens the next problem.

Second, the near-singular denominator. theta-hat is a ratio whose denominator q0-hat + q1-hat - 1 can be arbitrarily near zero, so the exact estimator has heavy tails and, before truncation to [0,1], no finite moments; the delta variance inflates as J^-2. The paper's own bias condition exposes how brutal this gets: Proposition 5.1 requires m >~ 2q/(2q-1)^2 for the correction to beat p-hat in absolute bias, which is m >~ 3 at q=0.9 but m >~ 30 at q=0.6 and m >~ 110 at q=0.55. Worse, the second-order bias derived in Appendix E.2 is E[theta-hat] - theta approx (1/m) * 2q/(2q-1)^2 * (2 theta - 1)(1-q), i.e. the same sign and shape as the naive bias, merely damped — so for small m and mediocre q the plug-in correction can be strictly worse than doing nothing. Note also that an unfortunate interaction lurks in the interval: the add-one adjustment shrinks q-hat toward 1/2, which shrinks the denominator toward zero and thus inflates the reported standard error. That is conservative but lossy, and it plausibly explains the real-data over-coverage.

Third, the empirical coverage story has a visible gap. Monte Carlo coverage (Figure 5b) sits near nominal, but the Chatbot Arena coverage in Table 1 is 96, 95, 97, 97, 99, 99 percent against a nominal 95 — up to four points conservative, with interval lengths of 0.178-0.267 on a win rate. Intervals that wide are near-useless for leaderboard purposes: typical reported gaps between systems are an order of magnitude smaller. Also, that "coverage" is computed over 100 random 90/10 splits of one fixed finite pool, so it is a resampling diagnostic against the pool accuracy, not frequentist coverage under i.i.d. sampling from P. And because test and calibration come from the same pool by construction, P = Q in every real experiment — the distribution-shift advantage over PPI is demonstrated only in the synthetic Figure 8, while the variance price relative to PPI++ is never benchmarked on real data. Table 4 shows what that price looks like: with GPT-4.1 at a 10% calibration fraction, the naive estimator recovers the exact ranking 86% of the time at tau = 0.981, while the corrected estimator drops to 46% and tau = 0.915; only at a 40% calibration fraction does the correction win (75% vs 61%). Bias correction actively degraded the decision the evaluation existed to support.

Fourth, some smaller things worth noticing. Proposition 5.2 is stated but, despite "All proofs are provided in Appendix E," has no proof anywhere — E.1 derives the variance, E.2 proves Props 5.1 and 6.1, E.3 proves the matrix equivalence. Proposition 5.1 is a second-order delta expansion with no remainder control, written with an approximation sign, so it is heuristic rather than a theorem. Proposition 6.1 compares an asymptotic variance proxy for theta-hat against the exact binomial variance of the human-only estimator, and it quietly switches sampling models: it uses a random M1 ~ Binomial(m, theta) in the denominator (the Hoeffding device exists purely to bound 1/M1 away from blowing up), whereas Sections 4-5 treat m0, m1 as chosen by design. Relatedly, the budget comparison is not apples-to-apples: a label-stratified calibration set of size m requires annotating roughly m/min(theta,1-theta) items to find the strata, unless one subsamples a pre-annotated pool. Algorithm 1 also reuses the pilot items in the final q-hats, so m0, m1 are data-dependent and the binomial variance formula is only conditionally approximate. Finally, in Figure 6 the "ground truth" is a single Arena human vote; since human labels are themselves noisy, the measured q-hats are attenuated toward 1/2, which means the paper is likely under-stating judge quality relative to its own q >= 0.854 threshold — the pessimistic conclusion of Section 6 may be partly an artifact of unmodeled annotator noise that Appendix A flags but does not handle.

Proof sketch

What is established, precisely. (a) The identification result is the affine relation p = (q0+q1-1) theta + (1-q0) and its inversion, valid under the single assumption q0 + q1 nonzero-offset-from-1 (the paper assumes q0+q1 > 1, i.e. a judge better than chance). Given known (q0,q1), theta-hat is exactly unbiased since it is an affine function of the binomial mean p-hat — no asymptotics needed. Appendix E.3 shows this scalar estimator is literally the first coordinate of the inverse confusion matrix applied to E_P[Zhat], by explicitly inverting the 2x2 matrix whose determinant is q0 + q1 - 1 — so the "near-singular denominator" is literally the determinant of the confusion matrix, and Appendix B's k-category generalization replaces it with a k x k matrix inverse whose conditioning controls variance. (b) The plug-in estimator with estimated (q0-hat, q1-hat) is not unbiased; what is proved is the weaker Proposition 5.1 (bias dominance over p-hat for m >~ 2q/(2q-1)^2, under m0=m1 and q0=q1). (c) The CI claim is asymptotic Wald validity: coverage -> 1-alpha as n, m0, m1 -> infinity with (q0,q1) interior and J bounded away from 0. There is no uniform-in-theta guarantee, no exact/finite-sample guarantee, and no conditional-on-calibration guarantee; the Agresti-Coull pseudo-counts are a heuristic for small samples, and out-of-range values are truncated to {0,1}, which breaks even the asymptotic argument at the boundary.

How it is proved. The variance derivation (Appendix E.1) is a textbook first-order delta method. The three partials are d theta-hat/d p-hat = 1/J, d theta-hat/d q0-hat = (1-theta-hat)/J, d theta-hat/d q1-hat = -theta-hat/J — the elegant bit being that the q-derivatives collapse into theta-hat itself, so the gradient is (1, 1-theta, -theta)/J. Invoking independence of the test and calibration samples kills all cross-covariances, and plugging in the three binomial variances p(1-p)/n, q0(1-q0)/m0, q1(1-q1)/m1 gives the variance formula directly. This is where the two-source decomposition arises: it is not a separate theorem but a consequence of the gradient's block structure, and the (1-theta)^2 and theta^2 weights explain why specificity matters more when the true accuracy is low and sensitivity matters more when it is high. The interval is then Wald plus the adjusted-proportion substitution, with an implicit Slutsky step (consistency of the plug-in standard error) that is never stated. Note what is not done: no Fieller construction, no test inversion, no profile likelihood — despite theta-hat being exactly a ratio statistic of the kind Fieller intervals were invented for. Given that J small is the dangerous regime and that is precisely where Wald ratio intervals fail, a Fieller or score-inverted interval is the obvious missing comparison.

Proposition 5.1's bias is a second-order delta expansion: carrying the Hessian terms for the map in (q0-hat, q1-hat) gives E[theta-hat] - theta approx [-(1-theta) q0(1-q0)/m0 + theta q1(1-q1)/m1]/J^2, which under the symmetric specialization m0=m1=m/2, q0=q1=q telescopes into (1/m) * 2q/(2q-1)^2 * (2 theta - 1)(1-q) — the naive bias (2 theta - 1)(1-q) times a factor 2q/(m(2q-1)^2), so the comparison reduces to asking when that factor is below 1. The assumption bites exactly here: the expansion requires J well away from 0, which is the same condition that makes the factor small, so the proposition is almost tautologically about the good regime. Proposition 6.1 is a two-step argument: take the n -> infinity limit of the variance so the test term drops out, then handle the randomness of the calibration composition with Hoeffding — the deviation epsilon = sqrt(log(2/delta)/(2m)) with probability 1-delta yields M1 >= m(theta - epsilon) and m - M1 >= m(1 - theta - epsilon), hence a deterministic upper bound on Var(theta-hat); comparing against theta(1-theta)/m and letting epsilon -> 0 turns the sufficient condition into the exact quadratic theta^2 - theta(1+Delta) + q0(1-q0)/J^2 <= 0 with Delta := [q0(1-q0)-q1(1-q1)]/J^2, whose roots give the general interval and, at q0=q1, the symmetric one. So the "with probability 1-delta" is not a statement about estimation error at all — it is a device to keep 1/M1 finite, which is why the clean statement only appears in the m -> infinity limit where it becomes necessary and sufficient.

The allocation result is a Neyman-allocation argument, and since no proof is supplied I reconstructed it: minimizing A/m0 + B/m1 subject to m0+m1=m gives m0/m1 = sqrt(A/B) = ((1-theta)/theta) sqrt(q0(1-q0)/(q1(1-q1))) (Cauchy-Schwarz, or a one-line Lagrangian). The stated rule then follows from two simultaneous uses of "q approx 1": q(1-q) approx 1-q turns the variance ratio into sqrt(kappa), and theta -> p turns (1-theta)/theta into 1/p - 1. Both approximations degrade in exactly the regime where allocation matters most — a mediocre judge — and the derivation also treats theta as fixed while optimizing, ignoring that theta itself depends on the q-hats whose precision is what is being allocated, and ignoring the center shift. Speaking of which, the center-shift term looks structurally like the second-order bias from Appendix E.2 but is missing the 1/J^2 factor and carries an unexplained factor 2 z_alpha^2 which is about 7.68; the paper simply defers to Lang & Reiczigel and asserts the effect on length is negligible. It shifts the center, though, and at m0=m1=100, q about 0.8 the shift is on the order of 0.016 — comparable to a third of the half-width — so the claim deserves verification rather than a citation.

Broader context

The statistical lineage is long and largely pre-LLM. Bross (1954) analyzed misclassification in 2x2 tables; Rogan & Gladen (1978) gave the prevalence correction that is the central estimator here, in the context of estimating disease prevalence from an imperfect screening test; Greenland and the measurement-error literature (Buonaccorsi 2010) systematized differential vs non-differential misclassification, which is exactly the assumption dividing line this paper's Table 2 rediscovers; Lang & Reiczigel (2014) supplied the adjusted-Wald interval that propagates sensitivity/specificity uncertainty, which the paper adopts verbatim. In machine learning the same inversion is the "quantification" problem — Forman's (2005, 2008) adjusted classify-and-count and its probabilistic variant — and, in the distribution-shift literature, it is precisely black-box shift estimation under label shift (Lipton, Wang & Smola 2018; Saerens et al. 2002), which the paper does not cite but which is the same confusion-matrix inversion as its Appendix B. Recognizing that would sharpen Section 8: the invariance Pr_P(Zhat|Z)=Pr_Q(Zhat|Z) with Pr_P(Z) != Pr_Q(Z) is the anticausal label-shift assumption, and the competitor assumptions are its covariate-shift-flavored cousins.

The modern comparison class is prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., Science 2023; PPI++ 2023; Zrnic & Candes cross-PPI 2024; Boyeau et al., "Autoeval done right", ICML 2025), which forms E_P[Zhat] + E_Q[Z - Zhat] — a control-variate / rectifier estimator that is root-n consistent, handles general estimands via M-estimation, and typically has lower variance than Rogan-Gladen because it never divides by J. Its price is the stronger invariance Pr_P(Z-Zhat)=Pr_Q(Z-Zhat), which fails under label shift. The honest summary is a bias-variance trade between PPI and Rogan-Gladen, and the paper argues one side of it. Two things worth reading alongside: Kloos et al. (2021) and Meertens et al. (2022), from official statistics, which already laid out this estimator taxonomy and the variance-reduction comparison; and the concurrent Chen et al. (2026), "Efficient inference for noisy LLM-as-a-judge evaluation," cited here as tackling the variance side. The deeper statistical ancestry of PPI is semi-supervised mean estimation (Zhang, Brown & Cai 2019; Chakrabortty & Cai 2018), where a large unlabeled sample plus a small labeled sample yields efficiency gains over the labeled-only estimator — the same structure as "infinite LLM judgments plus a small human calibration set," which suggests the right benchmark for Proposition 6.1 is not "beats human-only" but "attains the semiparametric efficiency bound." The obvious follow-up is a doubly robust estimator: use PPI's influence-function machinery within strata of judge-relevant covariates, with the Rogan-Gladen inversion handling within-stratum label shift, giving an estimator consistent under either label shift or judge covariate dependence; and then re-derive Proposition 5.2 as a multivariate Neyman allocation across strata, which is where the real design gains are.

For IR the connection is immediate and the stakes are concrete. LLM relevance assessment has moved from proposal to infrastructure in three years: Faggioli et al., "Perspectives on Large Language Models for Relevance Judgment" (ICTIR 2023), laid out the human-machine collaboration spectrum; Thomas et al. at Microsoft showed LLM labelers predicting searcher preferences at Bing scale; UMBRELA (Upadhyay et al. 2024) is an open reproduction of that Bing assessor and was used to produce qrels for TREC RAG 2024, alongside the LLMJudge challenge. The ensuing dispute — Clarke & Dietz arguing LLM judgments still cannot replace human assessment, Soboroff warning against them outright, versus the TREC-RAG practice of shipping LLM qrels — is almost entirely a dispute about bias in a reported number, conducted without the estimator this paper supplies. The mapping is direct: Z is the human assessor's graded label, Zhat the LLM's, Pr(Zhat|Z) the assessor-vs-judge confusion matrix (already routinely reported in these papers as Cohen's kappa and agreement tables, from which q0, q1 or the full k x k matrix are immediately recoverable), and the calibration set is a deliberately small stratified sample of NIST-assessed documents. The Section 6 threshold then becomes a precise criterion for the Soboroff/Clarke-Dietz debate: an LLM assessor is worth using statistically only if its Youden index exceeds about 0.707 on the task at hand, and its advantage comes entirely from being able to label the whole pool rather than a sample of it. The allocation result reads as concrete guidance on which documents to send to human assessors — stratified by LLM-predicted grade, weighted toward whichever grade is both common in the run pool and poorly handled by the judge, which is close to but not identical with current practice of assessing the top of the pool.

Where it connects to classical IR evaluation theory is the incomplete-judgment literature, and the connection is complementary rather than redundant. Buckley & Voorhees (2004) and bpref, Yilmaz & Aslam's infAP (2006), and statAP (Yilmaz, Kanoulas & Aslam 2008), along with Aslam-Pavlu-Yilmaz's sampling-based evaluation and Carterette's minimal test collections, all address missingness: documents whose labels are absent, with pooling bias as the resulting systematic error, handled either by metric redefinition (bpref) or by Horvitz-Thompson-style unbiased estimation under a known sampling design (statAP, infAP). The present paper addresses misclassification: labels that are present but wrong. LLM qrels give us, for the first time, label coverage over the whole corpus at the cost of label correctness — so the two error sources swap places. The right object is an estimator unbiased under both: sample documents with known inclusion probabilities as in statAP, obtain an LLM grade for every document, human-verify a stratified subsample, and build an estimator that applies Horvitz-Thompson weighting for missingness and confusion-matrix inversion for misclassification, with a three-way variance decomposition (topic sampling, document sampling, calibration) and a joint budget allocation across all three. That is a well-posed and, I think, genuinely open problem.

The hardest and most interesting obstacle is that IR metrics are not proportions. Here it pays to be careful about which metrics inherit the correction and which do not. For a fixed ranking, DCG@k is a weighted sum of gains and is therefore linear in the one-hot label vectors, so writing v-hat as the weighted sum of one-hot judge labels, the corrected estimate g' C^-1 v-hat is unbiased for DCG under a single shared confusion matrix C — and pleasantly, the calibration cost does not grow with k, since one matrix serves all rank positions. Linearity is exactly what makes the Rogan-Gladen trick transfer. Everything beyond that breaks it. nDCG divides by an IDCG computed from the true label multiset of the same query, making it a ratio of two correlated label-linear functionals: the plug-in corrected ratio carries an O(1/m) bias, the per-query denominator is estimated from few documents so the ratio bias is severe before averaging, and E[DCG/IDCG] != E[DCG]/E[IDCG] — pointing toward Hajek-type or Fieller-type treatments. Recall@k and R-precision have denominators equal to the total number of relevant documents in the corpus, itself an unobserved prevalence over a vast unjudged tail, which composes the misclassification problem with the pooling problem in the denominator. And RR/MRR, precision@1, and success@k are non-smooth functionals (an argmin, a max) of the whole label vector, so the delta method does not apply and, more fundamentally, correcting the marginal label distribution does not identify E[f(Z)] for nonlinear f: you need the joint law of the label vector given the judge's labels, which requires either conditional independence of judge errors across documents given labels plus a per-query prevalence (i.e. the fragile calibration-matrix route that Section 8 argues against) or an explicit model.

Two further IR-specific complications make this a real research program rather than an exercise. First, judge errors are not independent across documents within a topic: one prompt template applied to an ambiguous query errs systematically, so the honest model is hierarchical, Pr(Zhat | Z, topic) with a topic-level random effect, and the i.i.d. binomial variance then understates uncertainty — producing anti-conservative intervals exactly where IR evaluation is already known to be variance-dominated by topic effects (Voorhees's variability studies). The correct asymptotics for a per-system metric are in the number of topics, not documents, which transforms Proposition 5.2 into a two-stage cluster-sampling allocation: how many topics to human-assess versus how many documents per assessed topic, under a cost constraint. That is a tractable and immediately useful generalization. Second, the quantity leaderboards actually consume is a difference, nDCG(A) - nDCG(B), and when both systems are scored by the same judge on overlapping documents the judge errors are shared and positively correlated, so much of the bias cancels and Var of the difference is far smaller than the sum of the two variances. Characterizing when the uncorrected difference already recovers the sign and ordering — judge bias that is rank-preserving across systems — would both explain the GPT-4.1 row of Table 4, where correction hurt ranking recovery, and formalize the intuition behind bpref and friends, which were designed for rank-correlation robustness rather than absolute metric fidelity. A theory of when bias correction is worth paying for in rank-based evaluation is, as far as I can tell, missing, and it is the question an IR theorist should take from this paper.

title: Avoid Catastrophic Forgetting with Rank-1 Fisher from Diffusion Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 13 October 2026

Avoid Catastrophic Forgetting with Rank-1 Fisher from Diffusion Models

Wang, Gupta, Dong, MacLellan — arXiv:2509.23593 — link

Main idea

The paper is an attempt to rescue elastic weight consolidation for generative models by replacing its usual diagonal Fisher with a rank-1 one, and the argument for why rank-1 is the right structure comes from the peculiar geometry of the DDPM training objective. The setup is class-incremental image generation: a label-conditioned UNet denoiser is trained on a stream of disjoint class groups, and the question is how to keep it from destroying what it learned about earlier classes. The authors' claim is that the empirical Fisher of a diffusion model is, in the high-noise part of the forward process, dominated by a single eigendirection, and that this direction is simply the mean per-sample gradient — an object you already have for free during training, with no power iteration, no Kronecker factorization, and no matrix storage beyond one vector per past task.

The mechanism they propose is a chain of three steps. First, in the variance-preserving process, Tweedie's identity splits the true score into a data-dependent term scaled by sqrt(abar_t)/(1-abar_t) and a pure input term -x_t/(1-abar_t); as abar_t goes to 0 the first term is suppressed relative to the second, so the optimal score collapses to a scaled identity map on its own input. Second, if the learned score is (approximately) a linear operator A_theta x_t, then the residual the gradient is trying to remove is A_theta - gamma_t I, which does not depend on the particular sample. Third, if every per-sample gradient is a positive multiple of the same parameter-space direction, the empirical Fisher E[gg'] collapses to a scalar times mu mu' with mu = E[g]. The resulting penalty is a single scalar projection of the parameter displacement per past task.

Because EWC's quadratic surrogate only makes sense when the tasks share a basin, they pair the penalty with generative distillation in the style of Masip et al. (2025): a frozen teacher from the previous task produces replay inputs, and the student is asked to match the teacher's noise predictions on them. The headline numbers are average final FID and average forgetting across MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10 and downsampled ImageNet-1k (32x32, twenty tasks of fifty classes). Rank-1 EWC plus distillation reaches AFID 7.6/15.4/50.5/48.5 against distillation-only 10.1/19.1/61.2/69.0 and diagonal EWC plus distillation 14.3/27.7/72.6/73.8, with forgetting of 0.6 and 0.9 on the two MNIST variants and 15.2 on ImageNet-32 versus 46.2 for distillation alone. The paper's own framing of the division of labor is the clearest thing in it: replay creates the shared optimum that EWC presupposes, and EWC in turn suppresses the drift that iterated replay accumulates.

Reviewer-style critique

Start with what is genuinely good. The negative result in Figure 3d deserves more attention than the positive one: the diagonal Fisher's relative Frobenius error against the full empirical Fisher sits near 1.0 at every timestep, which is a crisp statement that the curvature a diffusion denoiser accumulates lives almost entirely off-diagonal. The construction is also honestly cheap — one stored vector and one scalar per past task, no eigensolver — and the ablation in Table 5, where rank-k subspaces extracted by stochastic power iteration do worse than the free mean-gradient estimate (CIFAR-10 FID 57.5/60.4/55.7/55.6 for k = 2..5 versus 50.5 for k = 1), is exactly the comparison a skeptical reader wants. Appendix C is the best part of the paper: the authors deliberately try to falsify their own mechanism by moving to a VAE, find the top eigenvalue explains only ~50% of Fisher variance versus ~99% for a late-timestep DDPM, and recover ~85% when the KL term is downweighted by 1e-3. That is a real test, and it correctly localizes the phenomenon to the MSE-dominated objective rather than to diffusion per se. Three seeds with standard errors and a lambda = 0 control (Table 6) are also more than this literature usually offers.

Now the central empirical claim, and whether the regime where it holds is the regime that matters. The low-SNR limit is precisely the limit in which the loss stops depending on the data: Proposition 1 works by discarding the term sqrt(abar_t)/(1-abar_t) * E[x_0 | x_t], and that discarded term is the only part of the score carrying information about q_0. So "per-sample gradients become collinear at low SNR" is close to a restatement of "at low SNR the training signal becomes sample-independent." A Fisher built there is a Fisher of the model's global noise-calibration map, not of task k's content. The EWC penalty is supposed to encode which parameters matter for this task, and the likelihood weighting of the ELBO puts essentially zero weight on t -> T, where the KL to the prior vanishes by construction. The paper never reports the obvious diagnostic: the cosine similarity between mu for different tasks. If those are high — and Figure 3a, where mu_t is strongly aligned across all timesteps, strongly suggests they would be — then the stored directions are nearly identical across k, the penalty is task-agnostic, and what the method actually implements is a single-direction trust region on a shared subspace. That would still be a useful stabilizer (it is a plausible account of why Figure 5's samples stay sharp while the baselines turn to noise) but it is a different claim than the one the title makes.

There is also a reason to suspect "rank-1" is partly definitional rather than diffusion-specific. Always, for any loss and any model, E[gg'] = mu mu' + Cov(g). Theorem 1 therefore reduces to the assertion ||mu||^2 >> tr Cov(g) — the systematic gradient dominates the gradient noise — which is a statement about how far the model is from stationarity and how small its gradient variance is, not about curvature. Note the internal tension: the eigenvalues in Figure 3b shrink with t, which is what you expect of a residual A_theta - gamma_t I that is being driven to zero; at an actual optimum mu -> 0 and the empirical Fisher is exactly the higher-rank covariance term the paper discards. The relevant literature on this (Kunstner, Hennig and Balles, 2019, on the limitations of the empirical Fisher) is not engaged, nor is Gur-Ari, Roberts and Dyer's finding that gradient descent in deep nets generically concentrates in a tiny top-Hessian subspace. The paper does cite Ghorbani et al. (2019) on Hessian spectra, which points the same way. Relatedly, the chosen comparison metric structurally favors the proposal: for any delocalized rank-1 matrix mu mu', the relative Frobenius error of its diagonal is 1 - O(1/d_eff) by elementary algebra, so the diagonal baseline's error of about 1.0 is close to automatic in high dimension. Diagonal EWC is not trying to approximate F in Frobenius norm; it is trying to produce per-coordinate stiffness, and the honest test is how well each induced quadratic form matches the true one on realistic update directions.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the rank-1 penalty's contribution. Without distillation, the rank-1 variant is worse on forgetting than the diagonal one on all four datasets (58.3 vs 51.1 on MNIST, 82.1 vs 81.7 on FMNIST, 77.4 vs 74.4 on CIFAR-10, 41.3 vs 34.2 on ImageNet-32), and worse on MNIST AFID (65.2 vs 62.2). If the rank-1 Fisher were simply a better curvature model, you would expect it to win in the EWC-only setting too; the entire gain appears only in interaction with replay. Meanwhile diagonal EWC degrades replay on every single dataset (14.3 vs 10.1, 27.7 vs 19.1, 72.6 vs 61.2, 73.8 vs 69.0), which is a strong hint that the shared penalty weight lambda = 15000, used for all tasks, all datasets and both methods, is simply mis-scaled for the diagonal variant. A rank-1 penalty constrains one direction out of tens of millions and a diagonal penalty touches every coordinate; at fixed lambda these are wildly different regularization strengths, and no per-method lambda sweep is reported. The same confound reads straight through Table 5: adding directions 2-5, whose eigenvalues the paper says are one to two orders of magnitude smaller, should barely change anything if rank-1 really captures the curvature, yet FID degrades from 50.5 to 57.5 — more consistent with "more constrained at fixed lambda" than with "rank-1 is optimal." The missing controls are the cheap and decisive ones: isotropic L2 anchoring with matched penalty magnitude, and a random rank-1 direction. Without those one cannot conclude the benefit comes from the Fisher direction at all rather than from one-dimensional shrinkage.

Smaller but accumulating problems. FID is the only metric; for class-incremental generation you want per-class coverage (precision/recall or density/coverage) and a classifier check on conditional label fidelity, since a model that drifts toward generic blur can hold FID while losing classes, and the paper's own observation that average FID decreases over tasks on MNIST/FMNIST/CIFAR-10 — read as "refining old knowledge" — is equally consistent with the later checkpoints having simply received more total gradient steps on replayed task-1 data. The number of samples used per FID computation is never stated. The non-continual reference of 11.7 on ImageNet-32 being better than 23.3 on CIFAR-10 should give pause about cross-dataset comparability. The ImageNet-1k framing oversells: it is the 32x32 downsampled variant with a small 128/256-channel UNet, about 70 GPU-hours on one H200 for the full twenty-task run, and a replay budget of 1300 generated images per class — 1.3M synthetic images, comparable to the training set itself (and 5000 per class elsewhere, i.e. roughly the entire dataset for MNIST), which is a very generous notion of "without revisiting past data." On statistics, the ImageNet forgetting comparison the abstract leans on is weak: 15.2 +/- 4.8 against diagonal's 25.8 +/- 9.4 is not separable at three seeds, and against distillation's 46.2 +/- 12.9 it is roughly two standard errors. Finally, all Fisher spectral evidence comes from one tiny model (three ResNet blocks, 16 channels) on MNIST only — never on the 128/256-channel UNet actually used in the continual experiments — and the paper's own appendices contradict each other on both architecture (E.1's 16-channel net vs. E.2's 128/256-channel net) and schedule (100 epochs for ImageNet in section 4.3, 200 for everything in Table 2 and E.1).

Proof sketch

What is actually proved is much more local than "diffusion models admit a rank-1 Fisher." There are three claims. Proposition 1 says that for the variance-preserving process, the optimal score tends to -x_t/(1-abar_t) as SNR decreases. The proof is one line of Tweedie: s*(x_t) = sqrt(abar_t)/(1-abar_t) * E[x_0 | x_t] - x_t/(1-abar_t), and the ratio of the two coefficients is exactly sqrt(abar_t) -> 0. There is no error bound, no uniformity in x_t, no dimension tracking, and strictly speaking the stated justification ("the first coefficient decreases faster than the second") is about coefficients, not about the magnitudes of the two terms; the implicit extra ingredient is that the posterior mean E[x_0 | x_t] stays bounded while ||x_t|| grows like sqrt((1-abar_t) d), which gives a relative error of order sqrt(abar_t/(1-abar_t)) — first order in the square root of the usual SNR. Note also that their SNR is defined as sqrt(abar_t)/(1-abar_t) rather than the standard abar_t/(1-abar_t). This is a pointwise asymptotic approximation, not a theorem with a constant.

Assumption 1 is where the real content is smuggled in, and it is an assumption, not a result: that the learned score is a linear operator, s_theta(x_t,t) approx A_theta x_t. The stated justification is that late-timestep denoising reduces to MSE autoencoding, that Vincent et al. (2010) argue nonlinear denoising autoencoders are still "likely" to lie in a PCA-like subspace, and that UNet skip connections make linear behavior more likely still. The assumption is also self-referentially phrased — it posits linearity "when the model learns to perform scaled identity mapping such that s_theta = gamma_t x_t," which is the conclusion. The whole argument in fact lives in a thin annulus where A_theta is near but not equal to gamma_t I; at A_theta = gamma_t I the gradient is identically zero and there is no Fisher to speak of.

Proposition 2 then computes, under the linear surrogate, grad_theta L_DSM = (1-abar_t)(A_theta - gamma_t I) x_t x_t', and here there is a real algebraic slip: Equation 11 replaces x_t x_t' by ||x_t||^2 I to conclude the gradient is c(x_t) * (A_theta - gamma_t I) with c(x_t) = (1-abar_t)||x_t||^2. That substitution is valid only in expectation over an isotropic x_t (where E[x_t x_t'] = (E||x_t||^2/d) I), not per sample. For a single draw, the outer product x_t x_t' has cosine similarity about 1/sqrt(d) with the identity, so the per-sample gradient in A-space is not collinear with the mean at all — the fluctuation term (A_theta - gamma_t I)(x_t x_t' - E[x_t x_t']) is of comparable or larger Frobenius norm than the mean. (The chain rule through theta -> A_theta is harmless, since a fixed linear map preserves collinearity, but the outer-product term is not.) So the thing that is really established is: the mean gradient points along A_theta - gamma_t I, while the per-sample claim needs a concentration argument that is never supplied. Theorem 1 is then a two-line consequence of Proposition 2 and carries no independent content: if g = c(x)v then E[gg'] = E[c^2] vv', with the eigenvalue written as mu'F mu/||mu||^4, which is a self-consistency identity rather than a computed constant.

Where the argument breaks is therefore identifiable and interesting. The missing concentration is plausibly supplied in practice not by low SNR but by weight sharing: a convolutional weight gradient is already an average of x_t x_t'-type terms over all spatial positions, which contracts the anisotropic fluctuation by roughly 1/sqrt(HW) and would produce exactly the high cosine similarities in Figure 2. If that is the mechanism, the phenomenon is architectural rather than SNR-driven, which would also explain why the appendix finds the effect strengthening with model size. Two further gaps are worth naming. The theory is stated per timestep (F_t rank-1 with eigenvector mu_t), but the implemented penalty uses mu = E over x_0 and t of g with t uniform; E_t[F_t] is rank-1 only if the mu_t are mutually parallel, which is asserted empirically (Figure 3a) on one small MNIST model, and the eigenvalues in Figure 3b are largest at small t, so the uniform-t average is dominated by exactly the high-SNR steps where the paper's own Figure 3c reports lambda_2/lambda_1 < 0.4 — which is not "nearly rank-1" by any reasonable standard — and where Figure 3d shows rank-1 losing to the diagonal. And the "model converges" premise is in direct tension with the construction: as the residual vanishes, mu -> 0 and what remains of the empirical Fisher is precisely the higher-rank covariance that the theorem discards. The result is best read as: near, but not at, convergence, in the noise-dominated timesteps, under a linearity assumption, the mean gradient dominates the gradient covariance. That is considerably weaker and more local than "diffusion models admit a rank-1 Fisher."

Broader context

The lineage here is the Laplace-approximation view of continual learning. EWC (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) places a Gaussian around each past task's optimum with precision given by the Fisher; online EWC and Progress & Compress (Schwarz et al., 2018) fold the quadratics into a single running one; Synaptic Intelligence and MAS replace the Fisher with path-integral or output-sensitivity proxies; Variational Continual Learning (Nguyen et al., 2018) does the Bayesian update with a variational posterior instead. The quality of the curvature model has always been the weak joint, and the structured-approximation literature is the natural response: K-FAC (Martens & Grosse, 2015) and its continual-learning instantiation in Ritter, Botev and Barber's online structured Laplace approximation (2018) give block-Kronecker precision matrices that genuinely beat the diagonal, and more recent optimizer work (Sketchy, Fishleg, SOAP) converges on diagonal-plus-low-rank as the sweet spot. Against that background, the paper's "rank-1 instead of diagonal" framing is a false dichotomy: the two approximations capture disjoint parts of the matrix, the combination is free, and the obvious strongest variant — diagonal plus the mean-gradient rank-1 term, with separately tuned weights — is neither tried nor discussed. Two pieces of context I would want on the table are Kunstner, Hennig and Balles (2019) on how the empirical Fisher is dominated by mu mu' away from stationarity and systematically misrepresents curvature, and Gur-Ari, Roberts and Dyer (2018) on gradient descent occupying a tiny subspace in deep nets generally; together they suggest the observed structure may be generic rather than diffusion-specific. On the replay side, the relevant chain is Shin et al. (2017), van de Ven & Tolias (2018), DDGR (Gao et al., 2023), and Masip et al. (2025) on generative distillation, which the paper builds on directly and which supplies most of its measured gain.

The follow-up this most obviously opens is the diagnostic the paper skipped: measure cos(mu_i, mu_j) across tasks, and measure the overlap between the mean-gradient direction and the top eigenvector of the likelihood-weighted Fisher, where timesteps are sampled proportional to the ELBO's SNR-derivative weighting rather than uniformly. If the mu_k are nearly parallel across tasks, the correct reframing is "one-dimensional shared trust region on the noise-prediction calibration subspace," and the right version of the method would deliberately build the penalty from mid-SNR timesteps where the gradients do carry task identity, accepting a rank-k > 1 structure there. Pairing that with the elementary observation that E[gg'] = mu mu' + Cov(g) suggests a cleanly specified alternative: a penalty with a rank-1 mean term plus a diagonal estimate of the covariance term, which costs two vectors per task instead of one and has a defensible interpretation.

The connection to your work is real rather than forced on the generative-retrieval side, though it is a transfer of method rather than of result. DSI-style generative retrieval memorizes a docid decoder, and incremental indexing is exactly a continual-learning problem over a generative model; DSI++ (Mehta et al., 2022) addresses it with sharpness-aware minimization plus a generative memory for the old corpus, which is structurally the same replay-plus-parameter-regularization pairing studied here, and IncDSI and related work attack the same problem from the optimization side. The question this paper poses in the diffusion setting — which curvature directions actually need protecting, and whether that subspace is low-dimensional and shared across increments — is a genuinely open theoretical question for identifier-memorizing decoders, and the methodological lessons transfer directly: an empirical-Fisher penalty built from a nonzero mean gradient will be rank-1 for reasons that have nothing to do with the task, and a Frobenius-norm comparison against the full Fisher is the wrong yardstick for a preconditioner. On the vector-search side the link is thinner, but the one worth noting is that if continual updates to an embedding model concentrate in a low-dimensional parameter subspace, the induced drift in embedding space is correspondingly low-rank, which is the premise behind backward-compatible training and cheap post-hoc rotation corrections for avoiding full index rebuilds — characterizing that drift subspace theoretically is a question with the same shape as the one asked here. Beyond that, the paper is best read as a clean case study in how a low-rank curvature claim should and should not be established, rather than as IR-adjacent work.

title: Multi-Layer Transformers Gradient Can be Approximated in Almost Linear Time
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-12

Multi-Layer Transformers Gradient Can be Approximated in Almost Linear Time

Yingyu Liang, Zhizhou Sha, Zhenmei Shi, Zhao Song, Yufa Zhou (2024) — arXiv:2408.13233

Main idea

The paper asks whether the quadratic cost of attention is intrinsic to training, not just to inference. For a sequence of length n and hidden width d, one self-attention block costs O(n²d) in the forward direction because the n × n score matrix f(X) = D⁻¹exp(XWX^T/d) has to be formed. Backpropagation is worse in practice: the softmax Jacobian diag(f_j) − f_j f_j^T is an n × n object per row, and the standard closed forms for dL/dW, dL/dW_V and dL/dX all involve products and Hadamard products of n × n matrices. The claim proved here is that none of this needs to be materialized: for an m-layer transformer with m = n^{o(1)} and d = O(log n), there is an algorithm (their Algorithm 1) that outputs approximations to all gradient components of every layer in total time n^{1+o(1)}, with entrywise (ℓ∞) error 1/poly(n) on the final gradient dL/dX.

"Almost linear time n^{1+o(1)}" is the standard fine-grained-complexity formulation: the running time is n · n^{o(1)}, where the n^{o(1)} factor is a subpolynomial but genuinely growing function of n (here it is the rank of a polynomial-kernel sketch, see the proof sketch). It is a statement that the algorithm beats n^{2−δ} for every fixed δ > 0 asymptotically; it is not a statement that the algorithm is fast.

The result is the natural completion of a known program. Alman & Song (NeurIPS 2023, "Fast attention requires bounded entries") proved that the attention forward pass admits an n^{1+o(1)} algorithm with 1/poly(n) error when the entries of the query/key matrices are bounded by B = o(√log n), and — this is the other half of that paper, and the part this paper does not reproduce — that for B = Θ(√log n) no n^{2−δ} algorithm exists under SETH. So B = Θ(√log n) is a sharp algorithmic threshold for attention. Alman & Song (2024, "The fine-grained complexity of gradient computation for training LLMs") carried the same dichotomy to the backward pass, but only for a single attention layer, only for ℓ₂ loss, and only for the gradient on W_Q W_K^T. The present paper removes exactly those three restrictions: arbitrary differentiable loss decomposable as a sum of per-coordinate terms, arbitrary depth, and all of dL/dW_i, dL/dW_{V_i}, dL/dT_i, dL/dX, plus the practical sub-modules (causal mask, residual connections, multi-head, and an MLP-with-elementwise-activation block g_i between attention layers). It contributes no new lower bound; it lives entirely on the algorithmic side of Alman–Song's threshold, and inherits that threshold as its hypothesis.

The most interesting part

The genuinely load-bearing idea is not the low-rank approximation of f(X) itself — that is imported wholesale from Alman–Song and Aggarwal–Alman — but the observation that the class "entrywise-1/poly(n)-approximable by an n × n^{o(1)} factorization" is closed under Hadamard product, and that this closure is exactly what the backward pass needs.

Here is why that matters. In the forward pass, low rank is enough: f(X)·V ≈ U₁(V₁^T V) reassociates into two thin products. The backward pass is different in kind, because the softmax Jacobian introduces elementwise multiplication. Writing q(X) := G_i h(X)^T for the upstream gradient paired with the value matrix, the softmax derivative decomposes as p(X) = p₁(X) − p₂(X) with p₁ = f(X) ⊙ q(X) and p₂ = diag(p₁ 1_n) f(X). A Hadamard product of two low-rank matrices is not low-rank in general, and naively it destroys the whole approach.

The fix is the "tensor trick" recorded as Fact C.2: if A = U₁V₁^T with U₁, V₁ ∈ R^{n×k₁} and B = U₂V₂^T with U₂, V₂ ∈ R^{n×k₂}, then A ⊙ B = (U₁ ⊘ U₂)(V₁ ⊘ V₂)^T, where ⊘ is the row-wise Kronecker product producing n × k₁k₂ factors. Hadamard product multiplies the ranks instead of blowing them up to n. Since q(X) = G_i h(X)^T is exactly rank d by construction (no approximation needed), every Hadamard factor in the backward pass costs only a factor d = O(log n) in rank — so k₁ · d is still n^{o(1)}.

With that one fact in hand, the authors can reduce the entire backward pass to a single canonical shape. They take the five-term closed form of ds(X)/dX (inherited from Deng–Song–Xie–Yang, originally for ℓ₂ loss) and recast each term in matrix view as D_k = z_k(X) · X · W^{(T)}, where D₆ = −f(X)diag(K) X W^T and D₂ = −diag(K) f(X) X W, with K = (G_i ⊙ s(X))1_d ∈ R^n computable in O(nd); D₇ = (f(X) ⊙ (h(X)G_i^T)) X W^T and D₄ = (f(X) ⊙ (G_i h(X)^T)) X W; and D₈ = f(X) G_i W_V^T. Every one of these is of the form (f(X) [⊙ low-rank]) · (thin matrix). Diagonal rescalings are absorbed into one factor (U₆ = U₁, V₆ = diag(K)V₁); Hadamard products are absorbed by ⊘; and then the product is evaluated right-to-left so that only n × n^{o(1)} and n^{o(1)} × d intermediates ever exist. The same template handles the weight gradients: dL/dW = X^T p(X) X and dL/dW_V = X^T f(X) G_i, both of which are d × n, n × n, n × d sandwiches that collapse once the middle factor is given in factored form.

So the real content is a normal form: the whole backward pass of softmax attention, for an arbitrary loss, lies in the algebra generated by f(X), rank-d matrices, diagonal rescalings, Hadamard products and thin right-multiplications — and that algebra is closed under the polynomial-method sketch. That is a cleaner statement than the paper itself makes, and it is the thing that generalizes.

The causal-mask handling deserves a second mention because it is the one place where a genuinely different trick appears. The mask M (lower-triangular ones) is full rank, so M ⊙ (U₀V₀^T) is not low rank and the reassociation fails. The trick (imported from the conv-basis paper, LLS+24d) is that (M ⊙ (U₀V₀^T))v is a prefix-sum: set c_j = Σ_{t≤j} (V₀^T)_t v_t ∈ R^k by a running cumulative sum, then Y_j = ⟨(U₀^T)_j, c_j⟩. That is O(nk) time with no approximation, and it extends column-by-column to n^{o(1)}-column right-hand sides. Masked attention therefore costs the same as unmasked, and the Hadamard case works too because D⁻¹(M ⊙ A) ⊙ (UV^T) = M ⊙ ((D⁻¹U₀) ⊘ U)(V₀ ⊘ V)^T.

Reviewer-style critique

This is a correct and useful theory paper, and simultaneously nearly every practical sentence in its abstract and conclusion should be resisted.

The bounded-entry assumption is the whole result, and it is stated carelessly. Lemma C.13 is quoted as: "for any A = o(√log n) there exists k₁ = n^{o(1)} such that ... it holds that ‖XW‖∞ ≤ R, ‖X‖∞ ≤ R." R is never tied to A and never defined. The intended hypothesis is Alman–Song's: entries of the query and key matrices bounded by B with B² = o(log n), i.e. attention logits of magnitude o(log n). This matters because elsewhere the paper repeatedly asserts ‖X‖∞, ‖W‖∞, ‖h(X)‖∞, ‖G_i‖∞ ≤ poly(n) ("each entry can be written in O(log n) bits") and uses that bound to absorb error-amplification factors. The two assumptions coexist logically (o(√log n) ≤ poly(n)) but the honest reading is the strong one: every layer's hidden state T_i(X) must have entries below o(√log n) for the sketch to exist, and nothing in the algorithm, the architecture, or the training dynamics enforces this on intermediate activations. For n = 128k, √ln n ≈ 3.4, so the condition caps attention logits at roughly 11.8. Trained transformers routinely produce pre-softmax logits in the tens, and the attention-sink / massive-activation phenomenon produces hidden-state entries orders of magnitude above the rest. The regime is not merely "mild when n is large", as the paper says; it is the regime in which softmax is doing smooth averaging rather than sharp retrieval. Relatedly, Definition 1.2 includes the 1/d logit scaling but Definition C.6 (u(X) := exp(XWX^T)) drops it, and the 1/d is precisely what controls the magnitude condition.

It is asymptotic to the point of being non-implementable, and the paper half-admits it. The sketch rank is r ≤ C(2(g+d), 2g) with g = O(max{log(1/ε)/log(log(1/ε)/R²), R²}). The n^{o(1)} claim is a real theorem (d = Θ(log n), g = Θ(log n/log log n) gives r = n^{Θ(log log log n/log log n)}), but the constants are catastrophic at any n a person will ever run. With d = 12 ≈ ln(128k) and a modest g = 4, C(32,8) ≈ 1.1×10⁷, already two orders of magnitude above n = 1.3×10⁵; g = 7 gives 9.7×10⁹; at a realistic per-head d = 128 and g = 32 the rank is ≈ 2×10⁶⁸. The crossover against the plain O(n²d) algorithm is nowhere near any practical sequence length. So "almost linear" here does hide the n^{o(1)} factor in the strongest sense: it is the dominant cost. The paper has no experiments at all, acknowledges it lacks resources to train LLMs, and lists three concrete engineering obstacles to even a GPU prototype (new tensor ops for the ⊘ products, re-implementing PyTorch backward functions, a CUDA kernel for the masked prefix sums). The result is existential-with-an-explicit-algorithm rather than implementable, and the abstract's "we hope that this work will facilitate more effective training and deployment of long-context language models" oversells it. The honest comparison class is HyperAttention and the conv-basis line, which make structural assumptions (sparsity, uniform column norms, convolution bases) in exchange for algorithms people can actually run.

The error-propagation argument — advertised as a highlight — is the weakest part of the paper. Each layer's analysis bounds the amplification of an entrywise error by n·d·‖·‖_∞ ≤ poly(n) (explicitly, in Lemma K.2, by h·n²·d·d_h·poly(n)), and then concludes poly(n) · (1/poly(n)) = 1/poly(n). For m = O(1) layers this bookkeeping is fine. For the claimed m = n^{o(1)} it is not justified as written: the per-layer factor compounds, so reaching a final 1/poly(n) requires a per-layer target ε = n^{−Θ(m)}, hence log(1/ε) = Θ(m log n) = n^{o(1)} log n, hence g = n^{o(1)} up to logs, hence r = exp(Θ(g log(d+g))), which is n^{ω(1)} — super-polynomial, not n^{o(1)}. The induction in Lemma H.4 never exhibits the dependence of k₁ on m, so the headline "approximation error does not blow up multiplicatively across layers" is really "we re-chose the polynomial poly(n) at every step and did not track what that costs the rank." The theorem is presumably true for m = O(1), and plausibly for m up to about log n / log log n; m = n^{o(1)} looks unsupported. This is the one place to ask for a revision rather than a clarification.

The forward pass is unaccounted for. Algorithm 1 consumes the hidden states T_i and Attn_i as given members of the data structure. If they are computed exactly, the forward pass is Θ(n²d) and the end-to-end training step is not almost linear; if they are computed with the almost-linear forward algorithm, then the backward pass is evaluated at a perturbed point, and the theorem bounds ‖g̃ − ∇L(X)‖_∞ where ∇L is the exact gradient at the exact activations. Because the network involves exp, the local Lipschitz constants in the error composition are poly(n), so forward error and backward error do not obviously compose benignly. The paper does not analyze this at all. The single-layer proof even says explicitly "there is no approximation error when computing G₁", which is true only if the forward activations are exact.

Approximating a gradient is not preserving an optimization trajectory, and the paper does not claim otherwise but its framing invites the confusion. The guarantee is a per-step, per-entry additive bound. Three gaps follow. First, additive 1/poly(n) in ℓ∞ says nothing about relative accuracy, and late in training gradient entries are themselves small; the regime where the guarantee is informative is the regime where ‖∇L‖_∞ ≫ 1/poly(n), and the degree of the polynomial is a free parameter whose price is hidden in r. Second, the computed direction is not the exact gradient of any consistent surrogate objective — it is an approximation to the gradient of the exact model — so it is inexact gradient descent, not exact descent on a nearby loss. Standard inexact-GD theory then gives convergence only to a neighborhood whose radius scales with the perturbation (and, in the nonconvex case, a stationarity bound degraded by √(nd)·δ in ℓ₂). Third, nothing is said about accumulation over T iterations, where perturbations can be amplified by the curvature of the loss and, in the worst case, by instability. A complete story would pair this with an iteration-complexity statement. Finally, the "general loss function" claim is weaker than it sounds: L(X) = Σ_{j,k} ℓ(X)_{j,k} must decompose over output coordinates, be differentiable, and — critically — its gradient G_m = dL/dT_m must itself be computable in n^{1+o(1)} time and have poly(n)-bounded entries. Cross-entropy with constant vocabulary qualifies (Remark 3.2); the decomposability assumption rules out, e.g., sequence-level losses with global couplings, and the "constant d_voc" assumption is doing real work for a quantity that is ~10⁵ in practice.

Smaller things. d = O(log n) plus multi-head with d_h = d/h and "h can be viewed as a constant" means the theorem's d is incompatible with real models (d = 4096, h = 32) in a way the extension sections do not address. The g_i block is restricted to φ(ZW_g) with an elementwise φ — no layer norm in the actual analysis, despite layer norm being named in the informal definition; layer norm is row-wise and would compose fine, but it is asserted rather than shown. And the error bounds are all ℓ∞, which for n×d gradients translates to an ℓ₂ bound only after a √(nd) loss.

Proof sketch

What is proved, precisely. Fix an m-layer model F_m = g_m ∘ Attn_m ∘ ... ∘ g_1 ∘ Attn_1 ∘ g_0, where each Attn_i(Z) = D⁻¹exp(ZW_iZ^T/d)ZW_{V_i} and each g_i(Z) = φ(ZW_g) for an elementwise φ, and where every g_i has linear-time forward and backward. Assume d = O(log n), every entry of every input/weight matrix is representable in O(log n) bits, and m = n^{o(1)}. Assume further (via Lemma C.13, inherited from Alman–Song) that the entries of each layer's input and of XW are bounded by R with R = o(√log n). Let L(X) = Σ_{j∈[n],k∈[d]} ℓ(X)_{j,k} be any differentiable loss of that additive form. Then Theorem 4.2: Algorithm 1 outputs, for every layer i, approximations g̃_t, g̃_w, g̃_v to dL/dT_{i−1}, dL/dW_i, dL/dW_{V_i}, in total time n^{1+o(1)}, and the final output g̃ satisfies ‖g̃ − dL/dX‖_∞ ≤ 1/poly(n). The guarantee is entrywise additive; the polynomial in 1/poly(n) can be made arbitrarily large at the cost of a larger n^{o(1)} factor.

Step 1: the polynomial method gives a low-rank surrogate for f(X). This is the one black box. Because exp restricted to [−R², R²] with R² = o(log n) is approximable to additive ε by a univariate polynomial of degree g = O(max{log(1/ε)/log(log(1/ε)/R²), R²}) — Aggarwal–Alman's optimal-degree bound, essentially a sharpened truncated Taylor series — one can replace exp(⟨x_i, W x_j⟩) by a degree-g polynomial in the entries of x_i and x_j. A degree-g polynomial in d variables is a linear functional on the space of monomials of degree ≤ g, so it factorizes: there are explicit feature maps φ, ψ: R^d → R^r with r ≤ C(2(g+d), 2g) = n^{o(1)} and ⟨φ(x_i), ψ(x_j)⟩ ≈ exp(⟨x_i, Wx_j⟩). Stacking rows gives U₀, V₀ ∈ R^{n×r} with ‖U₀V₀^T − exp(XWX^T/d)‖_∞ ≤ ε, constructible in O(nr) = n^{1+o(1)} time. The softmax normalizer is handled inside the same step: D = diag(U₀V₀^T 1_n) is one matrix–vector product with the thin factors, D⁻¹ is diagonal, and the diagonal rescaling is folded into U₁ := D⁻¹U₀, V₁ := V₀, giving ‖U₁V₁^T − f(X)‖_∞ ≤ ε/poly(n). Note this is an entrywise guarantee on a matrix whose entries are at most 1 (Lemma C.17), which is what makes the subsequent n·d·‖·‖_∞ crude bounds survivable.

Step 2: reassociation. Given f(X) ≈ U₁V₁^T with U₁, V₁ ∈ R^{n×k₁}, k₁ = n^{o(1)}, products of the form f(X)·H with H ∈ R^{n×k_H}, k_H = n^{o(1)}, cost O(nk₁k_H) = n^{1+o(1)}: compute V₁^T H first (k₁ × k_H), then U₁(V₁^T H). Nothing is ever n × n. This is the only computational primitive used, and all the work goes into showing that every backward quantity is of this shape.

Step 3: closed forms and the matrix normal form. The authors take the entrywise derivative of the attention output s(X) = f(X)h(X), h(X) = XW_V, which splits into five surviving terms C₂, C₄, C₆, C₇, C₈ (the diagonal i₀ = i₁ terms C₁, C₃, C₅ collapse into the off-diagonal ones in matrix view). Chaining with the upstream gradient G_i = dL/dAttn_i(T_{i−1}(X)) gives dL/dT_{i−1} = Σ_{k∈{2,4,6,7,8}} D_k, with the closed forms listed above (Lemma D.17). The crucial structural observation is that the only n × n objects appearing are f(X), diag(K)f(X), f(X)diag(K), f(X) ⊙ (h(X)G_i^T) and f(X) ⊙ (G_i h(X)^T) — where K = (G_i ⊙ s(X))1_d is a vector computed in O(nd).

Step 4: the tensor trick for the Hadamard terms. The non-dot-product terms are handled by Fact C.2: (U₁V₁^T) ⊙ (U₂V₂^T) = (U₁ ⊘ U₂)(V₁ ⊘ V₂)^T with ⊘ the row-wise Kronecker product. Because h(X)G_i^T and G_i h(X)^T are exactly rank d, one takes U₇ = U₁ ⊘ h(X), V₇ = V₁ ⊘ G_i in R^{n×k₁d}, built in O(ndk₁) time. The error analysis is then one line: ‖U₇V₇^T − f(X) ⊙ (h(X)G_i^T)‖∞ ≤ d‖h(X)‖∞‖G_i‖_∞ · ε/poly(n) ≤ ε/poly(n), using the poly(n) entry bounds to absorb the slack. The same pattern handles p₁(X) = f(X) ⊙ q(X) and p₂(X) = diag(p₁1_n)f(X) (Lemmas C.15, C.16), which are what the weight gradients need.

Step 5: weight gradients via the tensor trick on W. For the key-query product W := W_QW_K^T, the derivative of each output entry with respect to vec(W) is expressed through A_{j₀} ∈ R^{d²×n}, the Kronecker-structured design matrix of the bilinear form; using ⟨a ⊙ b, c⟩ = a^T diag(b) c the sum over output coordinates telescopes into the compact dL/dW = X^T p(X) X with p(X) = p₁(X) − p₂(X) the softmax Jacobian applied to q(X) = G_i h(X)^T. This is the step the paper calls "the tensor tricks": it converts a (n×d)×(d×d) Jacobian contraction into a single d × n, n × n, n × d sandwich. With p in factored form, X^T U₃, then (X^T U₃)V₃^T, then ·X costs n^{1+o(1)}. Similarly dL/dW_V = X^T f(X) G_i, which needs only U₁, V₁. Errors are n²‖X‖²_∞ · ε/poly(n) ≤ ε/poly(n).

Step 6: the non-attention block. For g_i(Z) = φ(ZW_g), a short computation (Lemma H.1/H.2) gives the exact closed form G_i = (g_{T_i} ⊙ φ'(Attn_i W_g))W_g^T, where g_{T_i} = dL/dT_i. This is O(nd²) = n^{1+o(1)} and exact — no approximation enters here, which is why the paper can claim its framework covers "the MLP layer and the activation function" that Alman–Song's single-layer result omitted.

Step 7: induction on depth. The base case (Lemma H.3) composes Steps 3–6 for one layer. The inductive step (Lemma H.4) writes F_{k+1} = F_k ∘ Attn ∘ g and argues: given dL/dAttn(T₀) to within 1/poly(n) by the inductive hypothesis, Lemma E.11 produces dL/dT₀ in n^{1+o(1)} with the error amplified by at most poly(n), and then Lemma H.2 produces dL/dX with amplification at most n·d·‖dg/dX‖_∞ ≤ poly(n); since poly(n) · 1/poly(n) = 1/poly(n), the claim holds at depth k+1. The residual connection (Lemma J.3) and multi-head attention (Lemma K.2) are folded into the same induction: a residual adds O(nd) work and an identity term to the Jacobian, so neither running time nor error order changes; multi-head is h independent instances at width d_h = d/h with h treated as constant, and the per-head errors are summed. The causal mask replaces every f(X)·H and (f(X) ⊙ (UV^T))·H by the prefix-sum routine of Lemmas I.3–I.6 with no loss. As noted in the critique, this is where the argument is thinnest: the compounding of per-layer poly(n) amplification factors is never traded off against the rank r, which depends on log(1/ε).

Lower-bound side. The paper contains no hardness result — "SETH", "hardness" and "lower bound" do not appear in its body — but the relevant dichotomy is inherited from its two key references, both of which it cites as the foundation of the method. Alman & Song (2023) show that the B = o(√log n) condition is not an artifact: at B = Θ(√log n) and d = Θ(log n), approximating attention to 1/poly(n) in time O(n^{2−δ}) would refute SETH, via the fine-grained hardness of approximate Max-IP / bichromatic closest pair. Alman & Song (2024) extend the same threshold to the single-layer backward pass. So the right reading of this paper is: conditional on SETH, the bounded-entry hypothesis cannot be removed, and the contribution is to show that everything above the hypothesis — depth, general losses, masks, residuals, heads, and all four gradient components — comes for free once the forward-pass sketch exists and is closed under Hadamard product.

Broader context

The quadratic attention bottleneck has three largely disjoint research cultures attached to it. The systems culture (FlashAttention and successors) keeps the exact O(n²d) arithmetic but removes the O(n²) memory traffic by tiling and recomputation; it is the reason long-context training is feasible today, and it does not change the asymptotics at all. The architectural culture replaces softmax with something cheaper: Performer's random Fourier/positive random features for the softmax kernel, linear attention, PolySketchFormer's sketched polynomial kernels, state-space models like Mamba. These are linear-time but define a different model. The fine-grained complexity culture, which this paper belongs to, asks the sharper question: for the exact softmax model, with a stated approximation tolerance, what is the true time complexity as a function of the problem's parameters? The answers there are dichotomies. Keles, Wijewardena & Hegde (ALT 2023) showed that exact self-attention requires n^{2−o(1)} under SETH, and mapped which approximation/boundedness regimes escape it. Alman & Song (2023) located the sharp constant: B = Θ(√log n) on the query/key entry magnitude separates n^{1+o(1)} from n^{2−o(1)}. HyperAttention (Han, Jayaram, Karbasi, Mirrokni, Woodruff, Zandieh, ICLR 2024) sits in between — near-linear under sparsity and bounded-column-norm assumptions, and actually implemented. The conv-basis paper (Liang, Liu, Shi, Song, Yin 2024) gives a different structural route (convolution bases) covering both forward and gradient. Two companion works worth knowing alongside this one are Alman & Song's tensor-attention generalization (the same threshold for higher-order/Kronecker attention) and Liang–Li–Shi–Song–Zhou's I/O-complexity analysis of backward passes, which is the FlashAttention-side counterpart to this paper's arithmetic-side result.

A natural follow-up, and arguably the most valuable one, is to close the gap between "per-step gradient approximation" and "training". Concretely: prove an inexact-SGD theorem tailored to this approximation — one that tracks how the required poly(n) accuracy (hence the rank r, hence the actual running time) scales with the number of iterations T and with the loss landscape, and that accounts for the forward-pass approximation at which the backward is evaluated. The interesting possibility is a separation: that preserving the optimization trajectory for T = poly(n) steps forces ε = n^{−Θ(T)}, hence r super-polynomial, so that almost-linear-time gradient computation does not imply almost-linear-time training even in the bounded-entry regime. That would be a genuinely new kind of lower bound and would sharpen what this literature is actually claiming.

Connection to theoretical IR, generative retrieval and vector search. The connection is real and stronger than it first appears — but it runs through the threshold, not through the gradient algorithm.

First, the machinery is literally shared. Softmax attention is a normalized exponential-kernel density estimate: f(X)V computes, for each query, a kernel-weighted average over n keys. The two papers this result rests on are KDE/geometric-graph papers: Alman–Chu–Schild–Song (FOCS 2020) on algorithms and hardness for linear algebra on geometric graphs (Gaussian-kernel matvec, Laplacian systems), and Aggarwal–Alman (CCC 2022) on optimal-degree polynomial approximations for exponentials and Gaussian KDE. What Step 1 of the proof produces is a deterministic, explicit feature map φ, ψ: R^d → R^r linearizing the exponential kernel, with r = C(2(g+d),2g). That is exactly the object a vector-search person wants: it reduces softmax retrieval to maximum-inner-product search in r dimensions, with a worst-case entrywise guarantee rather than Performer's unbiased-but-high-variance random features. The C(2(g+d),2g) blow-up is the honest price, and it is the same combinatorial barrier that makes high-dimensional ANN hard — which is why this is a theory tool and not an indexing scheme.

Second, and more interestingly, the B = Θ(√log n) threshold has a clean retrieval reading. Softmax with bounded logits is smooth averaging over the whole key set and is therefore a low-degree function of the inner products — it admits a rank-n^{o(1)} linear sketch, and both forward and backward are almost linear. Softmax with large logits approaches hard argmax, i.e. nearest-neighbor retrieval, and computing it becomes as hard as approximate Max-IP / bichromatic closest pair, which is n^{2−o(1)}-hard under SETH (Rubinstein's ANN hardness and the Max-IP line). The theorem is therefore a formal statement that attention is cheap exactly when it is not doing sharp retrieval: the sharpness of the retrieval and the achievable time complexity are in direct tension, with the crossover at logit scale Θ(log n). For someone building theory for generative retrieval and vector search, that is a usable principle rather than an analogy — it says that any differentiable-retrieval module whose softmax temperature is pushed low enough to behave like a hard index cannot have a subquadratic exact-or-1/poly-approximate backward pass, under SETH.

Third, there is a concrete transfer. The results here are for self-attention, n × n. The same normal form (f · thin, (f ⊙ rank-d) · thin, diagonal rescalings, prefix sums) applies verbatim to cross-attention between n queries and N corpus items, which is the shape of a differentiable retriever, a memory-augmented generative-retrieval model, or a soft top-k over a learned index. The statement one would want is: for a soft-retrieval loss over N candidates with inverse temperature τ⁻¹, the backward pass is computable in (n+N)^{1+o(1)} whenever τ⁻¹·max|⟨q,k⟩| = o(log N) — i.e. a temperature lower bound τ ≳ 1/log N (or 1/√log N on the embedding-norm scale) below which training the retriever end-to-end is quadratic-hard. With L2-normalized dense embeddings and the temperatures actually used in contrastive IR training (0.01–0.05, i.e. logit ranges of 20–100), you are on the wrong side of that threshold for any realistic N, which is a precise formal account of why differentiable retrieval over large corpora resists exact end-to-end training and why everyone resorts to hard negatives, ANN candidate generation, and periodic index refresh. Proving that direction — an almost-linear backward pass for soft retrieval above a temperature threshold plus a matching SETH lower bound below it — looks like a genuinely publishable extension of this paper into IR theory, and it is the version of this work most worth building on.

title: What type of inference is planning?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-12

What type of inference is planning?

Miguel Lázaro-Gredilla, Li Yang Ku, Kevin P. Murphy, Dileep George — Google DeepMind, NeurIPS 2024 — arXiv:2406.17863

Main idea. "Planning as inference" is a slogan that has been cashed out at least four different ways in the literature — Attias and much of Levine's tutorial read it as MAP, the MaxEnt-RL branch reads it as marginal inference, the SOGBOFA line reads it as marginal-MAP (MMAP) — and the paper's complaint is that nobody has checked whether any of these is planning. The authors answer the question inside the variational framework, where the answer turns out to be clean: none of them is, and planning is its own type of inference, distinguished from the others only by how the entropy terms are weighted.

The setup is a finite-horizon MDP written as an unnormalised factor graph. To get the reward into the graph multiplicatively, they target not the expected reward but the best exponential utility with risk parameter λ > 0,

F_λ^planning = (1/λ) max_π log ⟨exp(λR(x,a))⟩_{P(x|a)π(a|x)},

which recovers ordinary expected-reward planning in the λ → 0⁺ limit and is risk-seeking for λ > 0. Every inference type they consider is then the maximum over a variational distribution q(x,a) of the same objective F_λ(q) = (1/λ)(−E_λ(q) + H^type(q)), with one shared energy term

E_λ(q) = −⟨log P(x₁)⟩ − Σ_t ⟨log P(x_{t+1}|a_t,x_t) + λR_t⟩,

and a type-specific entropy. Marginal inference uses the full chain-rule entropy H(x₁) + Σ_t H(x_{t+1},a_t|x_t). MAP uses zero. MMAP subtracts the marginal action entropies, H(x₁) + Σ_t [H(x_{t+1},a_t|x_t) − H(a_t)]. And Theorem 1 shows planning subtracts the conditional policy entropies instead, leaving exactly

H^planning(q) = H(x₁) + Σ_t H_q(x_{t+1} | a_t, x_t).

So the entire taxonomy is a question of which entropies you keep: planning keeps all the entropy that the environment supplies and discards precisely the entropy of the agent's own policy, nothing more and nothing less. Because the energy is identical across types, the four bounds can be compared pointwise in q, giving F^MAP ≤ F^MMAP ≤ F^planning ≤ F^marginal (with a fifth, properly normalised "marginal_U" row also below MMAP). The payoffs are threefold. First, the planning entropy is a sum of conditional entropies and hence concave, so planning inference is a tractable concave program where MMAP — the tightest of the previously-used types — is not even concave and is NP-hard on chains. Second, taking λ → 0⁺ turns the concave program into the classical dual occupancy-measure LP of the MDP, and the exact message-passing fixed point in the unfactored case reduces literally to value iteration. Third, and most usefully, because planning is now just an entropy weighting, all the standard approximate-inference machinery transfers: they build a Bethe-style relaxation for state-factored MDPs and a loopy-BP analogue they call Value Belief Propagation (VBP), which plans in exponentially large factored state spaces at cost polynomial in the per-entity parent-set sizes.

The most interesting part. The entropy-weighting unification is what carries the paper, and the single best thing in it is not the bare identification but what the gaps between the weightings turn out to be. Each inequality in the hierarchy is closed by a mutual information with a clear operational meaning. The MMAP entropy can be rewritten as H(x₁) + Σ_t H(x_{t+1}|x_t,a_t) − I_q(x_t; a_t), i.e. the planning entropy minus the mutual information between state and action. So the gap between "planning as MMAP" and planning proper is exactly the information the action is allowed to carry about the state — which is to say, reactivity. MMAP's optimiser is a Dirac delta on a single action sequence, so at its own optimum I(x_t;a_t) = 0 and the plan it scores is open-loop (conformant); planning inference, having a strictly richer optimal q, scores closed-loop policies. That single line explains a pile of empirical folklore: why SOGBOFA was an IPPC runner-up yet degrades as domains become stochastic, why MAP-based planners are optimistic, and why all of these become exactly correct when dynamics are deterministic (then the optimal planning distribution is itself a Dirac, I(x_t;a_t) = 0, and F^MAP = F^MMAP = F^planning identically). The same mutual-information motif reappears twice more: in the factored Bethe entropy, the correction term is I_q(x_t^{pa(i)}), the multi-information among entity i's parents, which is the price of pretending entities are independent between time slices; and in Appendix H, the gap between the exact planning bound and the classical determinization-in-hindsight upper bound is Σ_t [H_q(γ_t) − H_q(γ_t|x_t,a_t)] = Σ_t I_q(γ_t; x_t,a_t), i.e. exactly the clairvoyance the hindsight planner illicitly gains by seeing future noise. Three different approximation gaps, three mutual informations, each naming the specific thing the approximation gets wrong.

The mechanism by which this becomes an algorithm is equally concrete. Because the planning weighting assigns zero weight to the action's local entropy, Hazan–Shashua's fixed-point updates for arbitrary entropy weights develop a 1/ε singularity exactly at the action node; the sum over actions appears as (Σ_a (·)^{1/ε})^ε, a soft-max that hardens into a true max as ε → 0. The asymmetry in the entropy weights is the asymmetry between the max over actions and the sum over states in the Bellman operator — which is why, in the unfactored case with ε → 0⁺, the backward messages become m_b(x_t) = max_{a_t} Q(x_t,a_t) with Q(x_t,a_t) = Σ_{x_{t+1}} m_b(x_{t+1}) P(x_{t+1}|x_t,a_t), the forward messages become occupancies under the greedy policy, and one backward plus one forward pass is exact. Nicer still, the smoothing they need for numerical sanity is not a hack: Appendix E proves that (1−ε)H^planning + εH^marginal is exactly the variational form of λ-generalised MaxEnt RL with ε = αλ, so interpolating between planning and marginal inference is interpolating between unregularised and entropy-regularised control, and the Levine-style structured VI with q(x_{t+1}|x_t,a_t) forced to equal P is recovered as the λ → 0⁺ case.

Reviewer-style critique. The theory is genuinely good: short, checkable, and explanatory rather than merely formal. The hierarchy of bounds is proved pointwise in q with elementary entropy inequalities, the deterministic-dynamics collapse is proved carefully (including the subtle step that MMAP's optimiser factorises, so the bound gap really does close), and the λ → 0⁺ recovery of the occupancy LP plus the unfactored reduction to value iteration are strong sanity checks that an incorrect framework would fail. The VI LP for finite-horizon factored MDPs appears to be new and, unlike Guestrin et al.'s approximate LP, costs exponential only in parent-set size rather than in the induced width of a cost network. The hand-crafted "reactivity avoidance" MDP in Appendix I.2 is the right kind of experiment: it isolates the mechanism (SOGBOFA-LC* deliberately destroys its own future reactivity to secure 0.33 rather than trust a reactive plan worth 1.0) instead of just reporting a number.

Is "planning = this entropy weighting" an identity or a design choice? Honestly, both, layered. Given the chosen quantity of interest, Theorem 1 is an identity, not an approximation — it follows from two exact equalities and nothing else. But the quantity of interest is a design choice, and an interested one: exponential utility is adopted explicitly because it lets the reward be written as a product of factors, and for λ > 0 it is a risk-seeking objective that no planning practitioner asked for.
