Main memory per queue is just $b + \log N$ bits (the root key and its ID), and arbitrary-element deletion works through the $addr(i) \to a_v$ indirection.

Theorems 4.3/4.4 then compose: memory $nL + 2^Ldb + 2^{L+1}(2\log N + db) + d^2b$ bits, with the first term the actual code and the rest codebook, per-node queue roots kept in full precision to save an I/O, and the rotation matrix. Consistency is argued componentwise — medians canonical by Theorem 4.1 with ID tie-breaking, queues by Theorem 4.2, and leaf means trivially updatable because the mean is linear. That last point is worth pausing on: the codebook needs no disk access at all, only the reassigned points do.

Broader context

The subfield splits along exactly the axis this paper formalizes. Data-oblivious quantizers (scalar quantization, LSH-style random projection, and RaBitQ, which rounds randomly rotated vectors to bi-valued codes with a provable distance-error bound) are trivially update-friendly because each code depends only on its own vector. Data-dependent quantizers — PQ, OPQ's rotation learning, ScaNN's anisotropic loss that weights parallel error more heavily for MIPS, and additive/residual variants — win on recall at a given bit budget precisely because they exploit the dataset's geometry, and lose it as the geometry moves. The disk-resident index literature inherits the problem at system level: DiskANN keeps PQ codes in memory and full vectors on SSD, SPANN and SPFresh keep IVF postings on disk, and the maintenance question becomes which vectors must be re-fetched and reassigned when the partitioning shifts. SPFresh's answer is a locality-preserving reassignment heuristic; DeDrift's is to re-cluster the largest clusters; FreshDiskANN's is an in-place-delete plus background-merge discipline for graph indexes. Notably FreshDiskANN is absent from the bibliography even though it is the canonical reference point for streaming vector indexes.

Two things genuinely worth reading alongside this: the Indyk–Wagner metric compression line (NeurIPS 2017 / COLT 2018 / SICOMP 2022), which establishes the $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$-bits-per-coordinate optimum that Theorem 3.1 inherits, and the RaBitQ pair (SIGMOD 2024/2025), which is the strongest current argument that obliviousness plus good constants may simply dominate data-dependence — an argument this paper is implicitly pushing back on.

The obvious follow-up is the theorem the paper is missing: a three-way tradeoff between distortion, per-update disk reads, and consistency. Concretely, relax the exact-median invariant to a $(\tfrac12 \pm \gamma)$-quantile invariant, in the spirit of weight-balanced or scapegoat trees, define $\gamma$-approximate dynamic consistency, and prove an amortized bound on reassignments per update as a function of $\gamma$ with a potential function on per-node imbalance. That would both give a tunable knob and explain the empirical gap between the $2^L$ worst case and the far smaller observed heap-change counts — which currently the paper can only paper over by swapping an empirical estimate into its own bound. A matching lower bound — that any dynamically consistent quantizer achieving PQ-level distortion needs $\Omega(k)$ full-precision reads in the worst case — would make the DySk model earn its keep.

For your own work, the transferable object is the definition, not the kd-tree. Generative retrieval assigns hierarchical semantic docids by exactly this kind of data-dependent recursive partition — hierarchical k-means in DSI, residual quantization in RQ-VAE-based identifier schemes — and the corpus-update problem there is the same pathology one level up: inserting documents should not re-derive everyone's identifier, because the decoder has memorized the old ones. DSI++ and IncDSI treat this as a forgetting/continual-learning problem; dynamic consistency gives you a crisp combinatorial alternative formulation, namely that the identifier assignment map should be a function of the corpus set with bounded churn per update, and the median-split construction is a concrete witness that such maps exist with provable per-update stability. A rank-stable hierarchical docid scheme with a theorem bounding how many identifiers change per inserted document strikes me as a publishable theoretical contribution to generative retrieval, and the DySk cost model is a reasonable template for stating it.

title: Worst-case Performance of Popular Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Implementations: Guarantees and Limitations
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-07

Worst-case Performance of Popular Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Implementations: Guarantees and Limitations

Piotr Indyk, Haike Xu — 2023 (NeurIPS 2023) · arXiv:2310.19126

Main idea

This paper asks a question the graph-index literature has mostly avoided: what happens to HNSW, NSG and DiskANN on inputs chosen by an adversary rather than drawn from SIFT1M? The answer splits cleanly along an axis nobody had isolated before — not dimension, not data distribution, but preprocessing fidelity. The DiskANN construction rule, RobustPruning, has a clean geometric reading: keep an edge p → q unless some already-kept neighbour p' is a factor-α shortcut toward q. If you apply that rule honestly, against the entire point set, the resulting graph satisfies a local invariant — α-shortcut reachability — that is strong enough to make plain hill-climbing provably work. If you apply it the way the implementations actually do, against a candidate set harvested by a greedy search on the partially built graph, the invariant can fail globally, and the authors show it fails badly enough that bounded-queue best-first search needs to touch a constant fraction of the data before it sees any of the true top-5.

The two halves are methodologically asymmetric and the paper is upfront about it: the positive result is a theorem (polylog query time, constant approximation, under bounded doubling dimension), while the negative results are empirical — explicit point sets in the plane, run through the authors' own GitHub code at the hyperparameters the original papers recommend. Only for slow-preprocessing DiskANN do both directions get proofs, and there the lower bounds are about tightness of the constants rather than about failure.

The most interesting part

The hard instances. They are two-dimensional, grid-structured, and therefore have constant doubling dimension — which forecloses the obvious defence that worst-case behaviour is a high-dimensional phenomenon. The DiskANN instance (their Figure 2) is three well-separated unit-spacing square grids plus one planted answer point a, with l = 0.01n as the scale: a mass cluster M of 0.8n points far down-left (it owns the centroid, hence the entry point), a decoy cluster P of 0.1n points with upper-right corner (-l, 0), a cluster P' of 0.1n points at (0, l), and a = (0, 0.1l). The query is q = (-0.4l, 0), so D(q,a) ≈ 0.41l, D(q,P) ≈ 0.6l, D(q,P') ≈ 1.08l.

The mechanism is a trap on the construction order, not on greedy search itself. When a point p ∈ P is inserted, its candidate set is GreedySearch(s, p, L) — a search aimed at p, which never passes near a. So a is never offered as a candidate neighbour of P, and no amount of good pruning can add an edge that was never on the table. Edges into a survive only from P' (whose insertion searches do pass near a) and from the random R-regular initialization, which plants roughly R in-edges into a scattered uniformly. At query time the search enters P because P is closer to q than P' is, P is internally strongly connected (unit-spacing grid neighbours always survive pruning), and every point of P beats every point of P' on distance to q. A queue of length L therefore drains P before it will consider the exit, and the only escape is stumbling onto one of the O(R) random edges to a — expected Ω(n/R) scans. The NSG/HNSW variant adds thin chains of points (spacing 5, 0.44% of the data) wiring the three clusters together, purely so the k-NN graph that NSG and friends build on top of is connected; the trap is otherwise identical. A six-dimensional cousin in Appendix C defeats KD-tree entry-point selection by padding four coordinates with cluster-separated junk so the variance-based splits isolate P.

That is genuinely clever: the construction attacks the gap between the ideal pruning rule and its linear-time surrogate, and it is small, explicit and reproducible. But I would resist reading it as a verdict on these indexes. The adversary chooses the query after seeing the geometry, and places it precisely where the near-neighbour is not where the mass is; Recall@5 is measured against five points planted next to a, so it is 0 or 1 almost by design, which is why the heatmaps show a sharp phase transition at L ≈ 0.1n. No theorem rules out a parameter setting that escapes: R = 70, efConstruction = 200, one entry point, one thread. HNSW's upper layers exist exactly to provide long-range edges, and the instance evidently defeats them at M = 64, but the paper does not probe whether larger efConstruction, multiple seeds, or random restarts would break the trap — and a couple of the surveyed systems already get non-trivial recall (KGraph 0.42, DPG 0.37) at L = 0.1n, which suggests the construction is tuned to the DiskANN/NSG style of pruning rather than to greedy graph search as such. Nor does anything here show that the graph built by fast preprocessing is bad; only that this query procedure on it is. Conversely, the doubling-dimension assumption is doing suspicious amounts of work on the positive side: the degree bound O((4α)^d log Δ) is 8^10 ≈ 10^9 at α = 2, d = 10, so the theorem is a statement about constant intrinsic dimension and nothing more. And the slow preprocessing it vindicates is O(n^3) — the authors could only run it to n = 10^5 before hitting hundreds of hours. The headline open problem, stated plainly in the conclusion, is whether any near-linear-time construction admits guarantees at all.

Proof sketch

Definition. G is α-shortcut reachable if for every ordered pair (p,q) either (p,q) ∈ E, or some out-neighbour p' of p satisfies α·D(p',q) ≤ D(p,q). Lemma 3.2 is almost a tautology given the pruning rule: if q was deleted from p's candidate list, the deleter p' was kept and witnessed α·D(p',q) < D(p,q). The content is that slow preprocessing runs the rule against U = V, so the witness is guaranteed to be a retained edge.

Sparsity (Lemma 3.3). Out-degree is O((4α)^d log Δ), d the doubling dimension and Δ = D_max/D_min the aspect ratio. Decompose space around p into ⌈log₂ Δ⌉ dyadic annuli Ring(p, D_max/2^i, D_max/2^{i-1}). Cover each annulus by balls of radius D_max/(α·2^{i+1}); since the annulus fits in a ball of radius D_max/2^{i-1}, the refinement ratio is 4α, so the doubling property gives O((4α)^d) balls. Two points in one such ball are within D_max/(α·2^i), i.e. a factor α closer to each other than either is to p — exactly the pruning predicate — so at most one survives per ball. Multiply by the number of annuli. Setting R = O((4α)^d log Δ) is therefore not a restriction.

Query upper bound (Theorem 3.4). GreedySearch(s, q, L=1) — pure hill-climbing, no backtracking — from any seed s reaches an ((α+1)/(α-1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(Δ/((α-1)ε))) steps. The progress argument is one line of geometry: let a be the true NN, d_i = D(v_i, q). By the triangle inequality D(v_i, a) ≤ d_i + D(a,q); α-shortcut reachability applied to the pair (v_i, a) gives a neighbour within (d_i + D(a,q))/α of a; best-first search then takes something at least as good, so d_{i+1} ≤ (d_i + D(a,q))/α + D(a,q). Unrolling the geometric recursion gives d_i ≤ D(s,q)/α^i + ((α+1)/(α-1))·D(a,q), whose fixed point is precisely the claimed ratio — the (α+1)/(α-1) is the sum of the geometric series, not an artifact. The log Δ comes from three cases on the scale of D(a,q) relative to D_min and D_max; in the degenerate case where q sits within O(D_min) of a, a lower bound d_i > D_min/2 for any non-optimal v_i forces exact recovery within O(log_α Δ) steps. Combined with the degree bound, total query cost is O((4α)^d log²Δ) distance evaluations — polylog in Δ for constant d. Note the three-way tension: α → ∞ drives the approximation ratio to 1 but the degree to (4α)^d; at the default α = 2 the guarantee is only 3-approximate.

Both bounds are tight. Theorem 3.5 kills any hope of replacing log Δ by log n: take n = 2k-1 points on a line at x_i = α^i (mirrored, with β = max(1/(α-1), α-1) setting the midpoint), so Δ = O(α^n). The pruning rule leaves exactly a path on the geometric scale — vertex i's only left-neighbour is i-1, and every vertex right of the midpoint k connects to k and nothing to its left — so reaching the far endpoint from the wrong side costs Ω(k) = Ω(n) = Ω(log Δ) hops. Theorem 3.6 shows (α+1)/(α-1) is the right constant even for slow preprocessing: in the ℓ₁ plane, put n points in a √n × √n grid of side 0.5ε/√n (a near-degenerate cluster) with corner p₀, plus a gateway p' with D(p₀,p') = 2, D(p',a) = 2/(α-1), and a at distance 1+ε from q. Then α·D(p',a) = 2α/(α-1) < D(p,a) for every grid point p, so a is pruned from every grid point's list while p' is kept; the grid is strongly connected via its four-neighbours; p' is farther from q than the whole grid; and the entry point (closest to the centroid) lies in the grid. Any L ≤ n therefore returns distance 2/(α-1) + 1 - ε, ratio → (α+1)/(α-1). The trick in both lower bounds is the same: engineer the pruning predicate so that a near witness permanently shadows the correct edge.

Broader context

The theory side of ANN has two mature lines. Locality-sensitive hashing gives unconditional guarantees in arbitrary dimension — c-ANN in O(n^ρ) time and n^{1+ρ} space, with ρ = 1/c² for Euclidean (Andoni–Indyk) and the optimal data-dependent ρ = 1/(2c²-1) (Andoni–Razenshteyn) — at the cost of large space and constants that make it uncompetitive in practice. The metric-data-structure line (Krauthgamer–Lee navigating nets, Beygelzimer–Kakade–Langford cover trees) gives 2^{O(d)} log Δ queries under bounded doubling dimension, which is exactly the regime this paper's upper bound lands in; Indyk and Xu are essentially showing that slow-preprocessing Vamana is a navigating net in disguise, with the hierarchy implicit in the pruning radii rather than explicit in the data structure. Meanwhile the practical line — NSW, HNSW, NSG, Vamana/DiskANN — is built on approximating Delaunay graphs, monotonic relative neighbourhood graphs (NSG's MRNG, which is α = 1 shortcut reachability plus a monotone-path property) and navigable-small-world edge distributions. The gap is long-standing and the HNSW authors said so themselves.

Two pointers worth having. Prokhorenkova and Shekhovtsov, Graph-based nearest neighbor search: from practice to theory (ICML 2020), does the complementary average-case analysis — uniform points on the sphere and low-dimensional manifolds — and explains why these indexes work when the data is benign; Laarhoven's SoCG 2018 paper gives graph-based time–space tradeoffs in the LSH framework. The natural follow-up line is the navigability question: for which point sets does a sparse graph admitting monotone greedy paths to every query exist at all, and can it be built in near-linear time? Recent work on navigable graphs for high-dimensional search (Diwan, Gou, Musco, Musco and Suel, NeurIPS 2024) pushes exactly there, showing sparse navigable graphs for random instances alongside worst-case degree lower bounds — which is the structural complement to Indyk and Xu's algorithm-specific negative results.

A concrete follow-up I would actually try: close the preprocessing gap by certifying the candidate set. The only thing slow preprocessing buys is that RobustPruning(p, ·) sees, for each dyadic distance scale around p, at least one near-optimal representative. That is a 2^{O(d)} log Δ-size object, and a cover tree or navigating net built in O(2^{O(d)} n log Δ) time can produce it. Running RobustPruning against that candidate set instead of a greedy search on a half-built graph should preserve α-shortcut reachability — hence all of Theorem 3.4 — at near-linear preprocessing cost, which would answer the paper's main open question constructively. A cheaper variant: an anytime repair pass that samples pairs (p,q), tests the shortcut predicate, and adds edges on violation, giving a quantitative certificate ("this index is α-shortcut reachable for all but a δ fraction of pairs") that one could ship alongside a built index.

For your own work this connects on three fronts, none of them generic. First, the metric being guaranteed is a distance ratio, not a ranking quality: (α+1)/(α-1) = 3 at α = 2 is compatible with Recall@k = 0, and the paper's own heatmaps make that vivid. Translating multiplicative distance guarantees into Recall@k or nDCG guarantees requires a gap/margin assumption on the corpus — something like a bound on the number of points in the annulus between D(q,a) and c·D(q,a) — and formalizing that bridge is squarely a theoretical-IR problem that would make results like this one usable as retrieval-effectiveness statements. Second, the hard instances are exactly the query-document asymmetry regime: the query sits where the data mass is not, which is the structural signature of dense retrieval with separately-trained query and document encoders and of out-of-distribution vector search. Worst-case-under-asymmetry is a more honest model for IR than the uniform-on-sphere average case. Third, and most directly for generative retrieval: constrained beam search over a docid trie is formally the same object as bounded-queue best-first search on a graph, and the failure mode here — a bounded beam plus non-monotone progress yields either linear work or zero recall — is the same failure mode. α-shortcut reachability is a plausible template for the right condition on a GR decoder: at every prefix there must exist a continuation that multiplicatively reduces the residual to the target. Proving a geometric-series progress bound for a decoder under such a condition, and constructing hard docid assignments where it fails, would be a fairly direct transplant of this paper's technique into generative retrieval.

title: Provably Protecting Fine-Tuned LLMs from Training Data Extraction
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-06

Provably Protecting Fine-Tuned LLMs from Training Data Extraction

Tom Segal, Asaf Shabtai, Yuval Elovici · 2026 · arXiv:2602.00688

Main idea. The threat model is next-token training-data extraction: an adversary holds prefixes $x_i$ of targeted fine-tuning examples, gets black-box access to the full output distribution $r_1(\cdot\mid x_i)$, plus white-box access to a reference model $r_0$ trained the same way on similar data, and must predict the true continuation token (with the option to abstain, scored as accuracy-versus-coverage in the selective-classification sense). The defense inherits Vyas–Kakade–Barak's Near-Access-Freeness: train two constituents $p,q$ on disjoint shards, then serve an aggregate that is provably within divergence $k_x$ of both, so that for any sensitive example the shard that never saw it certifies the output. The known instantiation, CP-$\Delta$ (pointwise minimum of $p$ and $q$, renormalized), has $k_x=\log\frac{1}{1-\mathrm{TV}(p,q)}$, and the authors' diagnosis is that memorization produces exactly the pathology that destroys this: one spiked token pushes $\mathrm{TV}\to1$ through softmax normalization even when the models agree about everything else (empirically $k_x\approx11.6$ at the 99th percentile — a factor of $10^5$, i.e. vacuous).

Their fix has two parts. First, follow their own DOMBA line and work with relative probability distributions, $rq(y)=q(y)/t_q$ where $t_q=\exp(\tfrac1n\sum_y\log q(y))$ is the geometric mean, so that $\sum_y\log rq(y)=0$ and global normalization is quotiented out (Theorem 3.1 justifies the geometric mean as the log-space least-squares optimal rescaling between two unnormalized score vectors). Second — the actual novelty — note that the theory wants a sparsity property, SpaRPS: $p$ is $m$-SpaRPS w.r.t. $q$ if $p(y)=\alpha q(y)$ off some $m$-element set. Fine-tuned LLMs flatly do not satisfy it (Figure 1a: even allowing $m=1024$ free tokens, 10% of prompts still deviate by $B\approx2.1$), so instead of assuming it they enforce it at inference: keep the $m$ highest-scoring tokens' relative probabilities, overwrite all others with a shared public base model $b$'s relative probabilities, rescale to restore $\sum\log=0$, do this to both $p$ and $q$, then take the pointwise min. The score is $p(y\mid x)\log\frac{rp(y\mid x)}{rb(y\mid x)}$, the per-token contribution to relative KL from the base. With $m=10$, $n=32000$, the 99th-percentile $k_x$ drops to $0.004$.

Most interesting part / critique. The cleverest move is making the theorem's assumption true by construction rather than arguing it holds: projecting both constituents onto a shared public base outside a sparse set makes the smoothed pair $2m$-SpaRPS trivially (Remark 4.1), turning an empirically false hypothesis into an inference-time operator — with the scoring rule chosen so that the set retained also minimizes the KL upper bound on utility loss (Lemma A.2, Remark A.3). The RPD trick itself is the other genuinely good idea.

But the guarantee is much weaker than the framing suggests. It is not DP: there is no worst-case quantification over datasets or neighboring pairs, no privacy budget, no composition. It is a per-prompt, per-token, relative bound: $r_1(y\mid x)/r_0(y\mid x)\le\max!\big(1,\frac{rq(y|x)}{rp_0(y|x)}\big)\cdot\frac{t_{r_1}(x)}{t_{r_0}(x)}\cdot e^{k_x}$ — and critically, it holds only for a reference model of the same structural form, $r_0=\mathrm{CP}\text{-}\Delta_r(p_0,q)$ sharing the identical safe constituent $q$ (Theorem 4.4 is even stronger: $r_0=q$ exactly). The claim that this is "worst case" because a closer $r_0$ helps the adversary is asserted, not proved; a real adversary would use the public base model $b$ as reference, which neither theorem covers. Second, the headline "orders of magnitude" compares $k_x$ across different divergences (max-divergence on raw probabilities vs. on RPDs), and the end-to-end extraction bound contains the typical-probability ratio $t_{r_1}/t_{r_0}$, which is not bounded by any theorem — only "expected to be small in practice" (Remark 4.6) and shown as histograms. The theory hands off to plots exactly at the load-bearing factor.

Third, and sharpest: the selection of influential tokens is itself an unnoised, data-dependent mechanism, and the output broadcasts it. Every smoothed coordinate equals $\beta\, rb(y)$ for a public $b$, so an adversary can read off precisely which $m$ tokens fine-tuning changed most at this prefix — a membership signal that no per-token likelihood ratio bounds. The monotone degradation of canary protection with $m$ (Figure 3a) is consistent with the retained set being the leak. Note too that Proposition 4.8's near-unit factor applies only to tokens smoothed in both models, i.e. the guarantee is strongest exactly where there was nothing to protect and falls back to plain CP-$\Delta_r$ on the influential tokens — and the score $p(y)\log\frac{rp}{rb}$ is maximized by memorization spikes, so the mechanism actively preserves strongly memorized high-probability tokens and relies on the min with $q$ to kill them. The empirics bear this out: huge wins on rare-token attacks (canary exposure $28\to1.4$, full-ID extraction $0.73\to{<}0.001$), but token-by-token extraction AUC only $0.80\to0.76$ on Math and $0.86\to0.84$ on Story, still far above the $0.66$–$0.71$ non-member baseline. An AUC-0.78 attack is a live attack. Finally the utility evaluation is too soft: "No CP" is $p$ trained on a single 3000-example shard, so the honest counterfactual — one model trained on all 6000 — is never reported, which hides the cost of partitioning; MMLU/IFEval are measured only for smoothing, not for the full aggregation; and 50 epochs on 3000 examples is a deliberately extreme memorization regime (good for stress-testing, but it inflates the baselines against which the defense looks good).

Proof sketch. What is proved: (i) the smoothed aggregate is $k_x$-NAF-tight with respect to both smoothed constituents under relative max-divergence $\Delta_r(p|q)=\max_y\log\frac{rp(y)}{rq(y)}$, with $k_x=D_r(p,q)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_y\big|\log\frac{rp(y)}{rq(y)}\big|$ — inherited from Segal et al., and note it is a vocabulary-averaged quantity; (ii) under $m$-SpaRPS with log-ratios on the exceptional set bounded by $\log M$, $D_r(p,q)\le\frac{m}{n}(\log M+|\log\alpha|)$, giving $0.025$ at $m=20$, $n=32000$ and the $e^{-20}$ probability floor; (iii) the LiRA bound above. Assumptions: the partition assumption (no sensitive example or semantic near-duplicate appears in both shards), all probabilities floored at $e^{-20}$, and — for the bound to mean anything — that likelihood-ratio thresholding is the adversary's optimal test, which holds under Sablayrolles et al.'s conditions including i.i.d. candidates with fixed membership prior, an assumption the paper itself admits fails for token-by-token extraction.

How it is proved: a bounded-likelihood-ratio argument, by direct construction. Proposition 3.3 is a counting argument — off the $m$-set the log-ratio is a constant that cancels in the mean-zero normalization, so the whole divergence is carried by $m$ terms each at most $\log M+|\log\alpha|$, and the $\frac{1}{2n}$ prefactor delivers the $m/n$ factor that is the paper's entire quantitative gain. Theorem 4.5 is the prettiest step: since $\min(rp_1,rq)\le rq$, the ratio splits into a pointwise part $\max(1,rq/rp_0)$ and the normalizer ratio $Z_0/Z_1$; because $rr_i(y)/\min(rp_i,rq)(y)=1/(Z_it_{r_i})$ is _constant in $y$_, the tight form of the NAF bound pins it exactly at $e^{D_r(p_i,q)}$, so $Z_i=e^{-D_r(p_i,q)}/t_{r_i}$ and $Z_0/Z_1\le\frac{t_{r_1}}{t_{r_0}}e^{k_x}$ after discarding $D_r(p_0,q)\ge0$. Proposition 4.8 bounds the rescaling constants by $|\log\beta|\le mB/n$, again from mean-zero normalization over $n$ coordinates. Every proof is a few lines of algebra; this is a construction-plus-bound, not a deep theorem. The real work is in the choice of divergence and construction such that those few lines produce small numbers — and in recognizing that the $1/n$ in the denominator is where all the mileage is.

Broader context. The memorization line runs from Carlini et al.'s secret-sharer and exposure metric (2019) through verbatim extraction from production models (2021) to Nasr et al.'s divergence attacks, with fine-tuning amplifying the signal because the shift relative to the base model is itself the membership statistic — LoRA-Leak reports AUC $\approx0.77$ for adapter-only updates. Defenses split into the empirical (deduplication, PII scrubbing, Goldfish loss) and the provable, where DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016) gives worst-case guarantees at real utility and compute cost. Near-Access-Freeness (Vyas, Kakade, Barak, ICML 2023) was proposed for copyright, trading DP's worst-case strength for a weaker relative guarantee — "the output is close to a model that never saw this work" — and the follow-ups are worth knowing: Abad et al.'s CP-Fuse (ICLR 2025) addresses sequence-level drift toward one constituent, Kalai–Kalai–Zamir's consensus sampling generalizes the aggregation, and Cohen's "Blameless users in a clean room" (NeurIPS 2025) is the critique the TV-saturation observation here descends from. This paper's contribution is to port NAF to extraction and to show that the naive port is empirically broken.

Two follow-ups I would want: first, close the selection channel by replacing top-$m$ with a noisy-max/exponential-mechanism selection, which would compose an $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP guarantee on which tokens were retained with the NAF likelihood-ratio bound on their values — a genuine DP–NAF hybrid; second, a sequence-level composition theorem with the typical-probability ratio bounded rather than plotted, deployed as certify-or-abstain (refuse to emit when $t_{r_1}/t_{r_0}$ exceeds a threshold at that prompt), which is the only way the per-token bound survives the adaptive multi-token attacks the paper itself runs.

The generative-retrieval connection is real but inverted, and worth stating carefully: in DSI-style generative retrieval the model's job is to memorize a corpus-to-docid map, so memorization is the product, and min-over-shards aggregation would destroy retrieval precisely because the correct docid is high-probability only under the shard that indexed it. That makes SCP-$\Delta_r$ a near-exact description of what you must not do to a generative index — but also, read the other way, a natural mechanism for access-controlled generative retrieval, which is where the RPD machinery came from (DOMBA, AAAI 2025): shard the index by permission class and let the min-aggregation suppress exactly the docids a given user is not cleared for, with $k_x$ as the certificate. The RPD idea itself should also transfer to leakage analysis over RAG corpora and vector indexes, where absolute similarity scale is a nuisance parameter and the real membership signal lives in relative preference shifts; and the accuracy-versus-coverage framing used for the attack here is the same risk-controlled-prediction tooling IR already uses for selective retrieval.

title: Adversarial Training Can Provably Improve Robustness: Theoretical Analysis of Feature Learning Process Under Structured Data
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-06

Adversarial Training Can Provably Improve Robustness: Theoretical Analysis of Feature Learning Process Under Structured Data

Binghui Li, Yuanzhi Li · 2024 (ICLR 2025) · arXiv:2410.08503

Main idea. The paper gives an end-to-end optimization-level answer to two questions that most robustness theory sidesteps: why does plain gradient descent land on a non-robust minimum, and what does adversarial training actually change about the learning dynamics? The vehicle is a patch-structured data model borrowed in spirit from Allen-Zhu & Li's multi-view setup. Each class $y \in [k]$ owns exactly two orthonormal, axis-aligned feature vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$: a robust feature $u_y$ and a non-robust feature $v_y$. A sample $X = (x_1,\dots,x_P)$ has its $P$ patches split into a robust set $J_R$ and a non-robust set $J_{NR}$; patches carry $x_p = \alpha_p u_y + \xi_p$ or $x_p = \beta_p v_y + \xi_p$ with $\xi_p \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma_n^2 I_d)$. The entire structural content of "robust vs. non-robust" is two inequalities (Assumption 2.3): robust features are stronger but sparse ($\alpha_p \gg \beta_{p'}$, $|J_R|$ small) while non-robust features are weaker but dense, formalised as $\sum_{J_R}\alpha_p^\tau \ll \sum_{J_{NR}}\beta_p^\tau$ for a constant $\tau \ge 3$. With $\mathbb{E}[\beta_p] = \Theta(\sigma_n\sqrt d)$, non-robust patches are literally indistinguishable from noise in magnitude, which is the "cat texture vs. cat ear" intuition made precise. The learner is a two-layer convolutional net $F_i(X) = \sum_{r\in[m]}\sum_{p\in[P]} \widetilde{\mathrm{ReLU}}(\langle w_{i,r}, x_p\rangle)$ with a smoothed ReLU that is $z^q/(q\varrho^{q-1})$ below threshold $\varrho$ and linear above ($q=3$, $\varrho = 1/\mathrm{polylog}(d)$), width $m = \mathrm{polylog}(d)$, Xavier init $\sigma_0^2 = 1/d$, trained by GD on $k$-class cross-entropy. Adversarial training is the practical algorithm, not the idealised inner max: one step of gradient ascent on $-F_y(X)$ with a large ascent rate $\tilde\eta = d^{c_0} \gg \eta$, followed by patch-wise clipping to $|\Delta|_\infty \le \epsilon$ with $\epsilon = \Theta(\sigma_n\sqrt d)$, i.e. $\alpha \gg \epsilon > \beta$.

The most interesting part. The crux is that the two feature-learning coefficients start at the same scale — $\max_r \langle w^{(0)}_{i,r}, f\rangle = \Theta(\log m/\sqrt d)$ for every feature $f$ — so nothing in the initialisation favours the non-robust feature. The asymmetry is purely dynamical. Projecting the GD update onto feature directions gives $A^{(t+1)}_{i,r} \approx A^{(t)}_{i,r} + \Theta(\eta)(A^{(t)}_{i,r})^{q-1}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{J_R}\alpha_p^q\big]$ and the same recursion for $B$ with $\mathbb{E}[\sum_{J_{NR}}\beta_p^q]$. Because $q = \tau$, the density assumption is exactly the statement that $B$'s growth constant beats $A$'s. The non-robust feature does not win by being bigger; it wins by appearing in more patches, and the $q$-th-power dynamics turn that constant-factor advantage in rate into a winner-take-all outcome.

The matching insight on the adversarial side is prettier. Writing out the one-step ascent in feature coordinates (Lemma D.17), the attacked non-robust patch has coefficient $\tilde\beta_p = \big(1 - \min{\epsilon/\beta_p,\ \tilde\Theta(\tilde\eta)\sum_s (B^{(t)}_{i,s})^q}\big)\beta_p$ and the robust patch $\tilde\alpha_p = \big(1 - \min{\epsilon/\alpha_p,\ \tilde\Theta(\tilde\eta)\sum_s (A^{(t)}_{i,s}\big)\alpha_p$. Since $\epsilon > \beta$, the $\epsilon/\beta_p$ branch is $\gtrsim 1$: as soon as the network has learned the non-robust feature well enough for the attack to find it, the attack })^q_erases it entirely_, the gradient signal for $B$ vanishes, and non-robust learning freezes. Since $\alpha \gg \epsilon$, the robust branch is capped at $1 - \epsilon/\alpha_p = \Omega(1)$: the attack can only shave an $\epsilon$-sliver off a robust patch, so $A$ keeps growing through the polynomial regime and into the linear one. Adversarial training does not unlearn the non-robust feature so much as it starves it while the robust one is still free to grow — the ranking flips by differential growth, not by erasure.

Be clear-eyed about how much is being assumed. "Robust" and "non-robust" are not derived from anything; they are the two inequalities above, and the single condition $\alpha \gg \epsilon > \beta$ does nearly all the work — it is almost a definition of "the budget suffices to delete the weak feature and not the strong one." Features are orthonormal and coordinate-aligned, one of each per class, and the data is linear in them, so there is no feature composition, no hierarchy, no correlated features. Hyperparameters are pinned ($q = \tau = 3$, $P = \Theta(1)$, $m = \mathrm{polylog}\, d$, $N = \mathrm{poly}(d)$, $\eta = 1/\mathrm{poly}(d)$, $\tilde\eta = d^{c_0}$), and the suppression level for $B$ is set by $1/\tilde\eta$, i.e. by the attack step size, which is an artifact of one-step FGSM-style ascent rather than of $\epsilon$-robustness. The theory explains none of the phenomena that make adversarial training hard in practice: there is no robustness–accuracy tradeoff (here the robust solution is also clean-optimal, because robust features are both strong and sufficient), no robust overfitting (noise correlations are proven to stay $\tilde O(1/\sqrt d)$ forever, so there is no memorisation phase to overfit with), no catastrophic overfitting, no depth or scale effects, and nothing about PGD vs. single-step.

Proof sketch. Theorem 4.3: after $T = \Theta(\mathrm{poly}(d)/\eta)$ GD steps, w.h.p. the net fits the training set, classifies non-robust-only data $\mathcal D_{F_{NR}}$ correctly, has $o(1)$ clean test error — and is wrong with probability $1 - o(1)$ under the fixed, model-independent perturbation $\delta_p = -\beta_p v_y + \epsilon v_{y'}$ on non-robust patches only, $\delta_p = 0$ on robust patches. That the attack is oblivious to $F^{(T)}$ is stronger and more interpretable than an existential $\exists\Delta$ claim, and it is exactly the Ilyas-style "adversarial examples are features" picture: the perturbation swaps one class's non-robust feature for another's. Theorem 4.4: under the same iteration budget, adversarial training is robustly perfect on the training set, learns $\mathcal D_{F_R}$, and has $o(1)$ robust test error against all $|\Delta|_\infty \le \epsilon$.

The machinery is a signal-noise decomposition plus a two-stage induction. Lemma D.2/E.2 shows by induction that every neuron stays in the span $w^{(0)}_{i,r} + A_{i,r}u_i + B_{i,r}v_i + \sum_{j\ne i}(C_{i,r,j}u_j + D_{i,r,j}v_j) + \sum_{(X,y),p}\sigma_{i,r}((X,y),p)\xi_p$ — so the whole dynamics reduces to scalar sequences. Three invariants are then maintained for all $t = O(\mathrm{poly}(d))$: (i) off-diagonal correlations $C, D$ never grow, because their update carries a factor $-\mathrm{logit}_i < 0$ and $\widetilde{\mathrm{ReLU}}' \ge 0$, a one-line sign argument (Lemma D.7/D.21); (ii) noise correlations stay $\tilde O(1/\sqrt d)$, via a per-sample update bound combined with $\sum_t \mathbb{E}[1 - \mathrm{logit}_y] = \tilde O(\eta^{-1})$ and $N = \mathrm{poly}(d)$ (Lemmas E.3–E.6) — this is what makes the empirical-risk theorems follow from the noiseless population-risk ones; (iii) logit approximation: while all diagonal outputs are $O(1)$, $1 - \mathrm{logit}_y = \Theta(1)$ and $\mathrm{logit}_{i\ne y} = \Theta(1/k)$, and once $F_y \ge c\log d$ they decay like $O(d^{-c})$ (Lemmas D.5/D.6, using that off-diagonal logits are $\tilde O(d^{-q/2})$). With (i)–(iii) the loss derivative is a harmless $\Theta(1)$ factor early on and the recursions are pure tensor-power iterations.

The comparison is then closed by the Tensor Power Method Lemma of Allen-Zhu & Li: if $x_{t+1} \ge x_t + \eta C_t x_t^{q-1}$, $y_{t+1}\le y_t + \eta S C_t y_t^{q-1}$ and $x_0/(y_0 S^{1/(q-2)}) \ge 1 + \Omega(1/\mathrm{polylog}\,d)$, then by the time $x$ reaches $\Theta(1)$, $y$ is still $O(y_0\,\mathrm{polylog}\,d)$. Taking $x_t = \max_r B^{(t)}_{y,r}$, $y_t = \max_r A^{(t)}_{y,r}$, $S = \mathbb{E}[\sum_{J_R}\alpha^q]/\mathbb{E}[\sum_{J_{NR}}\beta^q] \ll 1$, the density assumption supplies exactly the required initial ratio, giving $\max_r A^{(T_y)}_{y,r} = O(\mathrm{polylog}(d)/\sqrt d)$ when $B$ hits the activation threshold $\varrho/\beta$ (Lemma D.9). Stage II then shows $B$ grows to $\Theta(\log d)$ in $\mathrm{poly}(d)/\eta$ steps while $A$ provably needs $\Omega(\varrho^{q-1}d^{(q-2)/2}/\eta)$ — asymptotically more than that many iterations — even to grow by a constant factor, and a telescoping argument shows $F_y$ cannot exceed $O(\log d)$ in polynomial time (each additional $\log d$ of margin costs a factor $d$ more iterations), so the gap is frozen in. For adversarial training the same skeleton runs with the attacked coefficients $\tilde\alpha_p,\tilde\beta_p$ substituted in; Phase I is identical to standard training (the suppression terms $\tilde\Theta(\tilde\eta)\sum_s(\cdot)^q$ are $o(1)$ at small initialisation, so non-robust learning again wins first), and the phase transition occurs at the first $T_y$ with $\sum_s (B^{(t)}_{y,s})^q = \tilde\Theta(\tilde\eta^{-1})$, after which $B$ is pinned at $\tilde O(d^{-c_0})$ while $A$ climbs to $\Theta(\log d)$ (Lemmas D.23–D.26, E.11). The final robustness bound is then a margin computation: robust patches alone give $F_y(X+\Delta) \ge \sum_{J_R}\Theta(\alpha_p \max_r A_{y,r}) = \Theta(\log d)$ for any admissible $\Delta$, since $\alpha_p \gg \epsilon$, while every other logit is $o(\log d)$. The synthetic-data simulations reproduce the predicted phase transition at ~150 epochs, and on MNIST/CIFAR10/SVHN the authors measure Ilyas-style robust/non-robust feature-learning accuracy and a targeted NRF-PGD vs. RF-PGD attack (e.g. 71%/80% success for non-robust-feature attacks on a standard-trained WRN-34-10 vs. ~10% for robust-feature attacks), which is decent evidence that the mechanism is not purely an artifact of the toy model.

Broader context. Feature learning theory is the post-NTK program: instead of linearising the network around initialisation, you commit to a structured data distribution in which "features" are explicit objects, decompose the weights into feature-aligned plus noise-aligned components (the signal-noise decomposition, cleanest in Cao–Chen–Gu-style analyses of benign overfitting in two-layer CNNs), and then track a handful of scalar coefficients through gradient descent, maintaining invariants by induction. The tensor-power / escaping-saddle comparison lemma is the workhorse: with a degree-$q$ activation, near-zero initialisation makes competing coefficients grow like $\dot z \propto z^{q-1}$, so tiny differences in growth rate become $\Theta(1)$ vs. $o(1)$ separations — the same device behind Allen-Zhu & Li's multi-view explanations of ensembles and knowledge distillation, and behind Wen & Li's work on contrastive feature learning. On the robustness side the direct ancestor is Allen-Zhu & Li's feature purification (FOCS 2021), which argued adversarial training works by cleaning up "dense mixtures" in sparse-coding features; the present paper trades the sparse-coding model for an image-like patch model and, crucially, gets a multi-class statement in which standard training provably converges to a non-robust minimum — something the linear/Gaussian-mixture adversarial-training analyses cannot produce, since there max-margin implicit bias already gives robustness. Empirically it is the theory-side counterpart of Ilyas et al.'s "Adversarial examples are not bugs, they are features" and Tsipras et al.'s robustness-at-odds-with-accuracy.

The obvious follow-up is the one the paper cannot do: break the assumption that robust features are sufficient — let $u_y$ be present only on a fraction of samples, or let some classes be separable only by $v$ — and you should be able to derive a robustness–accuracy tradeoff and an optimal $\epsilon$ from the same two-phase dynamics, which would be a real contribution. Extending to exact inner maximisation or multi-step PGD (so the suppression threshold stops depending on $\tilde\eta$), and to depth $\ge 3$ where robust features are compositional, are the stated open problems.

For IR specifically, there is one connection that looks genuine rather than decorative. The $k$-class softmax objective here is structurally an in-batch-negative InfoNCE with $k$ candidates, and a dual-encoder retriever trained on documents that decompose into a few high-magnitude topical signals plus many low-magnitude lexical/stylistic cues is a close fit for the sparse-strong / dense-weak dichotomy. That suggests a concrete transfer: run a signal-noise decomposition on a two-layer dual encoder under a patch-structured document model and ask which features the contrastive objective picks up first — the prediction would be that dense, weak, individually-uninformative surface cues dominate early, which is exactly the failure mode exploited by corpus poisoning and adversarial ranking attacks on dense retrievers, and would give a dynamics-level account of why such attacks transfer across retrievers. "Non-robust features" for a learned retriever would then be precisely those embedding directions that are predictive of relevance in-distribution but flippable within a small perturbation of the document, and adversarially-trained retrieval encoders would be predicted to show the same two-phase transition. For generative retrieval the analogue is less clean but worth a thought: if docid tokens are predicted from query features, the same analysis would ask whether the model latches onto lexical-overlap features (dense, weak, brittle under paraphrase) before semantic ones. ANN index robustness is a different problem — the geometry of the index, not the learning dynamics — so I would not force that tie-in; the embedding-level robustness this paper's machinery could address is the upstream condition, not the index itself.

title: Learning Upper Lower Value Envelopes to Shape Online RL: A Principled Approach
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-06

Learning Upper–Lower Value Envelopes to Shape Online RL: A Principled Approach

Sebastian Reboul, Hélène Halconruy · 2025 · arXiv:2510.19528

Main idea. The paper asks how a fixed batch of offline trajectories can provably accelerate a later online exploration phase without the online learner ever touching the offline data again. The setting is a finite-horizon, episodic, tabular, layered MDP (state space partitioned as $\mathcal S=\bigsqcup_{h=1}^H\mathcal S_h$, deterministic known rewards in $[0,1]$, unknown transitions). Stage one runs a model-based offline value-iteration variant on $K$ i.i.d. trajectories from a behaviour policy $\pi^b$, but — unusually for offline RL — it runs both an optimistic and a pessimistic backup with the same empirical Bernstein bonus, producing a pair of functions $(\underline Q_h,\overline Q_h)$ and $(\underline V_h,\overline V_h)$ that sandwich $Q^\star_h,V^\star_h$ with high probability. These are the value envelopes. Stage two feeds the envelopes into a UCBVI variant that (i) clips value estimates at the upper envelope (either $Q$-shaping, clipping $\widehat Q^t_h$ at $\overline Q_h$, or $V$-shaping, clipping $\widehat V^t_h$ at $\overline V_h$) and (ii) rescales the exploration bonus using the envelope's midpoint $M_h=\tfrac12(\overline V_h+\underline V_h)$ and width $D_h=\overline V_h-\underline V_h$, replacing the unknown $\mathrm{Var}(V^\star_{h+1})$ by $\sigma^t_{h+1}=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{\widehat P^t}(M_{h+1})}+\tfrac12\sqrt{\mathbb E_{\widehat P^t}[D_{h+1}^2]}$ and $H$ by the envelope range $R_h=\max_s\overline V_h-\min_s\underline V_h$. This generalises Gupta et al. (2022), whose shaping functions were deterministic, given a priori, and tied together by a single multiplicative $\beta$-sandwich $\widetilde V\le V^\star\le\beta\widetilde V$; here the two sides are decoupled, per-layer, and random (measurable w.r.t. the offline $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal G_K$). The raw offline transitions are discarded, which the authors sell as a privacy feature.

The most interesting part / critique. The cleverest technical idea is unambiguously Theorem 4: a conditionally independent empirical Bernstein inequality. Maurer–Pontil needs the summands to lie in a fixed interval; here the interval endpoints $\underline g=\min_z\underline W_{h+1}(z)$, $\overline g=\max_z\overline U_{h+1}(z)$ are themselves learned random variables, and the validity event $E^{\mathrm{Off}}_\delta$ is not independent of the online martingale differences, so naive conditioning would bias the concentration step. The authors fix this by requiring $E\in\mathcal G$, $\underline g,\overline g$ $\mathcal G$-measurable, and the sample independent of $\mathcal G$, then passing to a regular conditional probability $\mathbb P(\cdot\mid\mathcal G)(\omega_0)$ under which the envelopes are literally constants — yielding $\mathbb P(E\cap{\text{deviation small}})\ge(1-\delta)\mathbb P(E)$. That is a genuinely reusable lemma, and the accompanying measurability bookkeeping ($\mathcal F_t=\sigma(\mathcal G_K\cup\mathcal J_t)$, plus a coupling that pre-generates next-states so the $n$-th visit index is deterministic) is more careful than most shaping papers.

Now the weaknesses. First, Assumption 2 does enormous hidden work: uniform coverage $\mathbb P^{\pi^b}(s_h=s)\ge d^b_{\min}>0$ for every $(s,h)$, which is far stronger than the single-policy concentrability $C^\star$ standard in offline RL. Remark 4 is admirably honest about why — under $C^\star$ the upper envelope is vacuous ($\overline U\approx H$) off the optimal policy's support, so the effective set $\mathsf{PairEff}={(s,a):\overline U_{h(s)}(s,a)\ge V^\star_{h(s)}(s)}$ never shrinks — but this means the headline result lives in a regime where $K\gtrsim H/d^b_{\min}\cdot\log(\cdot)$ already suffices to estimate the whole model uniformly, i.e. where plain offline RL would produce a near-optimal policy anyway. And $d^b_{\min}$ can be exponentially small in $H$ for deep states, so "$Kd^b_{\min}$" is the real sample size. Second, there is no lower bound: nothing shows $R^{\max}$ and $|\mathsf{PairEff}|$ are the right instance parameters, and nothing shows the $D^{\max}$-dependence is unavoidable. Third, the gain is purely from $R^{\max}$ replacing $H$ and $|\mathsf{PairEff}|$ replacing $|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|$; no law-of-total-variance argument is used, so when $\mathrm{Range}(V^\star_h)=\Theta(H)$ — the generic case with rewards spread over the horizon — the bound collapses back to (layered) Hoeffding-UCBVI and buys nothing, since $R^{\max}\ge\max_h\mathrm{Range}(V^\star_h)$ is a hard floor. Fourth, the $D^{\max}$ terms are much uglier than the $R^{\max}$ terms ($D^{\max}|\mathcal S|H\sqrt T$, and $D^{\max}|\mathcal S|^2|\mathcal A|H$ in the $V$-shaping bound), so a merely loose envelope actively hurts; only the $K\to\infty$ limit rescues them. Fifth, the offline stage uses the lossy $H$-fold trajectory split of Xie et al. (2021) purely for independence, costing a factor $H$ that the authors concede is suboptimal relative to Li et al. (2024). Finally the evaluation is thin: one family of layered tabular MDPs ($H=10$, 20–30 states/layer, 3 actions, 10 seeds), with rewards deliberately concentrated at step $H$ and drawn from a narrow interval precisely so that $\mathrm{Range}(V^\star)$ is small — i.e. the experiments are engineered for the regime the theory favours. Gupta et al. is not run as published but approximated by an "Upper-Bonus Shaping" ablation ($\underline W\equiv0$) justified by a bonus-magnitude inequality, which is not a regret comparison. Most tellingly, count-initialised UCBVI — the obvious baseline that just adds the offline transitions to the online counts — beats the proposed method per offline trajectory; the authors' defence is the privacy/decoupling story, and that story is itself informal (passing $\overline V,\underline V$ is a deterministic function of the raw data with no DP guarantee).

Proof sketch. The main claim (Theorem 1, $Q$-shaping) is: if envelopes satisfying Assumption 1 exist with failure probability $\delta$, then with probability $\ge1-4\delta$,

$$\mathrm{Regret}(T)\le R^{\max}\widetilde O(\sqrt{TH|\mathsf{PairEff}|}+|\mathsf{PairEff}|+\sqrt T)+D^{\max}\widetilde O(\sqrt{TH|\mathsf{PairEff}|}+|\mathcal S|H|\mathsf{PairEff}|+|\mathcal S|H\sqrt T),$$

with $D^{\max}=\max_{h,s}D_h(s)$ and $R^{\max}=\max_h R_h$. Theorem 2 then instantiates it with the offline algorithm's envelopes, replacing $D^{\max}$ by $\widetilde O(H^2\sqrt{H/(Kd^b_{\min})})$, giving extra terms scaling as $\sqrt{H^5/(Kd^b_{\min})}$ and $H^3/(Kd^b_{\min})$ — the explicit bridge from offline sample size to online regret, valid once $K\ge 8H\log(H|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|/\delta)/d^b_{\min}$. In the worst case ($R^{\max}\sim H$, $|\mathsf{PairEff}|\sim|\mathcal S||\mathcal A|$) this recovers the minimax $H\sqrt{SAT}$ rate; all improvement is instance-dependent.

The proof runs on four nested high-probability events. (1) $E^{\mathrm{Off}}_\delta$: offline bonus validity via Maurer–Pontil applied per $(s,a,h)$ on the disjoint split $D^{(h)}$ — the split is what makes $\underline V_{h+1}},\overline V_{h+1}$ independent of the data estimating $\widehat P^{(h)_h$ — then a backward induction (Lemma 2) propagating $\underline V_{h+1}}\le V^\star_{h+1}\le\overline V_{h+1}$ upward through the Bellman operator. (2) $E^{\mathrm{On}_\delta$: online bonus validity (Lemma 4). This is the crux, and it is where Theorem 4 is invoked twice, with $g=V^\star_{h+1}}$ (deterministic) and $g=\overline U_{h+1}$ (offline-random), $\mathcal G=\mathcal G_K$, $E=E^{\mathrm{Off}_\delta$, and range $R_{h+1}}$ — the normalisation $Z_i=(V^\star_{h+1}(S_i)-\min_{s'}\underline W_{h+1}(s'))/R_{h+1}\in[0,1]$ is exactly how $R^{\max}$ enters the final bound. The quantity being concentrated is $\langle\widehat P^t_h-P^\star_h,\,g\rangle$, and the trick that makes it computable is a Minkowski step: since $\underline W\le g\le\overline U$ implies $|g-M_{h+1}|\le D_{h+1}/2$, one gets $\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}_{\widehat P^t}(g)}\le\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{P^t \widehat}$ — an upper bound on the variance of an object the learner cannot see, written entirely in terms of objects it can. (3) The optimism/elimination step: a backward induction gives $Q^\star_h\le\widehat Q^t_h$ and $V^\star_h\le\widehat V^t_h\le\overline U_h$ (Lemma 5) }(M_{h+1})}+\tfrac12\sqrt{\mathbb E_{\widehat P^t}[D^2_{h+1}]}=\sigma^t_{h+1_despite_ clipping, because clipping at $\overline U_h\ge Q^\star_h$ cannot destroy optimism; consequently any $(s,a)\notin\mathsf{PairEff}$ satisfies $\widehat Q^t_h(s,a)\le\overline U_h(s,a)<V^\star_h(s)\le\widehat Q^t_h(s,\pi^\star(s))$ and is never selected by the greedy policy — this is what restricts all subsequent sums to $\mathsf{PairEff}$. (4) Regret decomposition and martingale conversion: the standard recursion $\Delta_h(s_h)\le2b^{t,\mathrm{on}}_h+\xi^t_h+\mathbb E[\Delta_{h+1}]$ is closed using Gupta et al.'s Corollary B.7 with the uniform envelope-width bound $|\widehat V^t_{h+1}-V^\star_{h+1}|\le D^{\max}_{h+1}$ (this is precisely where $D^{\max}$ is injected), a $(1+1/H)^{-(H-h)}$ potential/weighting kills the $H$-fold error amplification at cost $e$, and Azuma–Hoeffding converts expectations to a high-probability bound using the almost-sure envelope $0\le2b^t_h+\nu^t_h\le G$ with $G=\widetilde O(D^{\max}|\mathcal S|H+R^{\max})$ — which is why $|\mathcal S|H\sqrt T$ appears multiplied by $D^{\max}$. The visitation sums are collapsed by the usual $\sum_{t,h}}1/\sqrt{N^t_h}\le2\sqrt{|\Gamma|TH}$ and $\sum 1/N^t_h\le2|\Gamma|\log(1+T)$ lemmas. The final offline-to-online link (Proposition 1) telescopes the envelope width as $\overline V_h-\underline V_h\le2\sum_{k\ge h}\mathbb E[b^{\mathrm{off}_k]$ and then lower-bounds the offline counts uniformly by $\tfrac12\lfloor K/H\rfloor d^b_{\min}$ so a $1/\Delta$ term can be absorbed into $1/\Delta^2$.}$ with a multiplicative Chernoff bound plus union bound, giving $D^{\max}=O(H^2\sqrt{HL_1/(Kd^b_{\min})})$. The $V$-shaping bound (Theorem 3) additionally inherits Gupta et al.'s pseudo-suboptimality machinery with the elimination threshold $n_\Delta(h)\le64c_1^2(1+R_{h+1})^2L/\Delta^2$, obtained by noting any relevant gap satisfies $\Delta\le1+R_{h+1

Broader context. The relevant subfield is offline-to-online / hybrid RL. Pure offline RL is dominated by pessimism (penalise uncertain actions so you never over-promise), pure online RL by optimism (over-promise so you explore); the interesting question is what offline data can buy for online exploration. Three families coexist: replay-mixing/hybrid methods that keep the offline data in the loop (Song et al., Hybrid RL, 2022), horizon-splitting policy fine-tuning (Xie et al., Policy Finetuning, 2021; Li et al., Reward-agnostic Fine-tuning, 2023), and prior-knowledge/shaping methods, where this paper sits. Its direct ancestor is Gupta et al., Unpacking Reward Shaping (2022); the other must-read is Zanette & Brunskill (ICML 2019), which already showed how bounds on the value function yield problem-dependent regret without domain knowledge, and Cheng et al., Heuristic-Guided RL (2021), which reads approximate value functions as horizon shortening. Golowich & Moitra, Can Q-learning be improved with advice? (COLT 2022), is the closest thing to a lower-bound-bearing treatment of value-function advice and is conspicuously absent from the comparison.

Three follow-ups look natural. The authors flag the best one themselves: replace the clipping rule with genuine action elimination using both envelopes ($\overline Q_h(s,a)\le\max_{a'}\underline Q_h(s,a')-\Delta$), which would turn $\mathsf{PairEff}$ into a gap-based set and connect this line to gap-dependent bounds (Simchowitz & Jamieson; Xu, Ma & Du). Second, the transfer version: learn envelopes on a source MDP and pay a transition-kernel distance — the conditional-Bernstein machinery is agnostic to where the envelopes came from, so only the validity event changes. Third, and most valuable, a matching instance-dependent lower bound in $(R^{\max},|\mathsf{PairEff}|,Kd^b_{\min})$, plus an adaptive, non-uniform allocation of the offline budget across layers in place of the crude $H$-way split.

There is a real, non-forced analogy to retrieval here, though the paper makes no such claim. The architecture — compute cheap upper and lower bounds on the quantity you are maximising, then prune every candidate whose upper bound falls below the incumbent's lower bound, and pay a cost proportional only to the un-prunable set — is exactly the structure of threshold algorithms in top-$k$ retrieval (WAND and block-max WAND prune documents by per-term/per-block score upper bounds) and of branch-and-bound exact nearest-neighbour search (prune a node when its distance lower bound exceeds the current $k$-th best). $\mathsf{PairEff}$ is formally the same object as the set of documents a WAND-style index must fully evaluate, and the paper's two-parameter regret decomposition — a leading term in $\sqrt{|\mathsf{PairEff}|}$ plus a penalty in the bound width $D^{\max}$ — is the kind of statement the learned-pruning literature (learned upper bounds for sparse indexes, learned early-termination for ANN graph search) mostly lacks: there, tighter learned bounds are validated empirically, not with a cost bound that degrades gracefully and provably in bound slackness and in training-set size $K$. You may find the transferable object to be Theorem 4 rather than the RL result: whenever a pruning bound is itself learned from data and then used inside a data-dependent concentration argument, the measurability/conditioning hazard the authors identify is real, and their $\mathcal G$-measurable-event device is the clean way around it.

title: How fast can you find a good hypothesis?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-05

How fast can you find a good hypothesis?

Anders Aamand, Maryam Aliakbarpour, Justin Y. Chen, Sandeep Silwal (arXiv v2, 2025) — arXiv:2509.03734

Main idea

The setting is classical agnostic hypothesis (density) selection. You are handed $n$ known distributions $H_1,\dots,H_n$ over a domain $\mathcal X$ that may be infinite — you can both sample from each $H_i$ and query its pdf/pmf pointwise — plus i.i.d. samples from an unknown $P$. With $\mathrm{OPT}=\min_i d_{TV}(P,H_i)$, you must output $Q$ with $d_{TV}(P,Q)\le C\cdot\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ with probability $1-\delta$. The remarkable statistical fact is that $\Theta(\log(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples suffice with no dependence on $|\mathcal X|$, and that the achievable constant is exactly $C=3$ for proper algorithms ($Q\in\mathcal H$; Yatracos, Devroye–Lugosi) and exactly $C=2$ if $Q$ may be improper (Bousquet–Kane–Moran, then Bousquet–Braverman–Kol–Efremenko–Moran, FOCS'21), with $C<2$ ruled out by Chan–Diakonikolas–Servedio–Sun.

The paper's angle is that this statistical picture hides a computational scandal. The $C=2$ algorithm finds a $Q$ satisfying a system of distance constraints by essentially solving an LP over the simplex on $\mathcal X$: it runs in $\mathrm{poly}(n,|\mathcal X|)$ time and its output needs $\Omega(|\mathcal X|)$ bits, so for real-valued hypotheses it does not terminate at all. The only finite-time option is a proper algorithm, i.e. $C=3$. The obvious escape hatch — conjectured in Mahalanabis–Štefankovič '08 and Bousquet–Kane–Moran '19 — is to output a mixture $Q=\sum_iw_iH_i$: it is $n$ numbers, it inherits sample and pdf access from $\mathcal H$, and for $n=2$ a mixture really does achieve $C=2$ in $O(\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ time. The paper kills this hope cleanly. Its lower bound says that for every sample budget $s$ there is a finite domain (they need $|\mathcal X|\gg n^{2.2}$ and $s=o(\sqrt{|\mathcal X|}/n^{1.1})$) on which no algorithm outputting a point of $\mathrm{conv}(\mathcal H)$ has expected approximation ratio better than $3-\frac2n-o(\frac1n)$; so beating any absolute constant $C<3$ with mixtures requires sample complexity polynomial in $|\mathcal X|$. The matching upper bound (Thm 1.2) is a randomized proper algorithm outputting an explicit distribution $D$ over $\mathcal H$ with $\mathbb E_{H\sim D}[d_{TV}(H,P)]\le(3-\frac2n)\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$, using $O(\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and $\tilde O(n^2/\varepsilon^2)$ time. Mixtures therefore buy exactly nothing over randomized proper selection, and the question of a finite-time improper algorithm with $C<3$ stays open with no natural candidate output class left.

Three companion results fill out the proper, time-efficient side: $C=3$ with optimal samples in $\tilde O(n/(\varepsilon^2\delta))$ time for $\delta>1/n$ (Thm 1.3, improving Aliakbarpour–Bun–Smith's $\tilde O(n/(\delta^3\varepsilon^3))$); given any $R\ge\mathrm{OPT}$, a $2\mathrm{OPT}+R+\varepsilon$ guarantee in $O(n\log^3(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ time, i.e. genuine $\log(1/\delta)$ behaviour (Thm 1.4); and, with $\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal X|,n)$ preprocessing, $3\mathrm{OPT}+O(\varepsilon)$ with failure probability $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ in $\tilde O(n^{2-\Omega(\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon^3)$ query time (Thm 1.5).

What's most interesting / reviewer-style critique

The cleverest moment is the observation that on their hard instance, the uniform distribution on $\mathcal X$ is a 2-approximation but lies outside $\mathrm{conv}(\mathcal H)$ — and in fact outside the affine hull, since each $H_i$'s deviation from uniform is supported on a block of the domain touched by no other hypothesis. That disjoint-support design makes $d_{TV}(P_{i^*},Q)$ an exactly linear function of the mixture weights: $d_{TV}(P_{i^*},Q)=(1-w_{i^*})d_1+w_{i^*}d_0$. Mixing is thus provably identical to randomizing, and the gap between $C=2$ and $C=3$ is revealed to be about leaving the span of the hypotheses, not about averaging. (The argument visibly survives signed combinations: with $w_i<0$ the per-block contribution is $|w_i|r_i(H_i)$, which only hurts.) A close second is the erratum: they identify a real error in Claim 26 of BKM'19, whose proof wrongly claimed that $s$ samples from a random hard $P_i$, conditioned on no repeated elements, are distributed like samples from uniform. They give two counterexamples and repair it by sub-dividing each block into length-$\ell$ sub-intervals holding exactly one extreme element, which restores independence. This is the first correct proof that $C=3$ is optimal for proper algorithms — a quiet but real contribution.

The honest critique starts with the framing. "Outputs a mixture" is a representational restriction, not a computational one, and the lower bound is information-theoretic: it says nothing about time, only that a sample budget independent of $|\mathcal X|$ cannot locate $i^*$ well enough. So the paper does not show a computational barrier to $C<3$; it shows that one specific succinct hypothesis class is useless. The authors are admirably explicit about this, but a reader should not take the title's "how fast" as answered on the improper side. Relatedly, a mild dishonesty of regime: the lower bound has no additive $\varepsilon$, and its instance has $\mathrm{OPT}\approx n^{-2.2}$, so the matching with the $(3-2/n)\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ upper bound is only meaningful when $\varepsilon\ll\mathrm{OPT}$ — precisely the regime where the problem is hardest and least practical. The guarantee forms also differ: the lower bound bounds an expected ratio while the high-probability statement is the separate and weaker Corollary 3.2 (no proper algorithm attains $C<3$ with probability more than $\frac1n(1+o(1))$).

The upper bound is also less efficient than "poly$(n)$ time" suggests: computing all max-semi-distances $W(H_i)=\max_iw_{i\to j}$ costs $\tilde O(n^2/\varepsilon^2)$, and $3-2/n$ is anyway vacuous unless $n$ is small, so the only interesting regime is tiny $n$ — where the result is a pleasant generalization of Mahalanabis–Štefankovič rather than a practical algorithm. Whether $W(H_i)$ can be approximated in near-linear time well enough to keep $3-2/n$ is untouched.

The query-access accounting is fair but worth reading carefully. The model charges $O(1)$ per sample from $P$ or $H_i$ and per pdf query; note that one semi-distance also needs $\tilde O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ samples from $H_j$ to estimate $H_j(S_{i\to j})$, which Prop 2.5 does charge. A nice design point: a single sample of size $s=O((\log n+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)$ fixes all $n^2$ estimates simultaneously via a union bound, so the heavily adaptive graph search in Thm 1.3 incurs no adaptivity penalty — the graph $G_b$ is a deterministic function of the sample.

On tightness: the $\varepsilon$ dependence $1/\varepsilon^2$ matches sample complexity and is essentially unimprovable. The $\delta$ dependence is the open sore. The runtime keeps a polynomial $1/\delta$, the theorem needs $\delta>1/n$, and the authors prove only that $\tilde O(1/\delta)$ rounds are necessary for the filtering paradigm they and ABS'23/'24 use — not a real barrier. The "high-probability conundrum" explanation is the paper's best exposition: because estimating $d_{TV}(P,Q)$ for a fixed $Q$ needs $\tilde\Omega(|\mathcal X|)$ samples (Valiant–Valiant), you cannot verify a candidate, so standard boosting of a constant-probability $C=3$ algorithm degrades to $C=9$. Consequently the genuinely high-probability regime $\delta=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ is still stuck at quadratic time, and Thm 1.5's escape is weak: it needs $\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal X|)$ preprocessing (finite domains only, sacrificing the domain-independence that makes the problem interesting), and its saving $n^{-\Omega(\varepsilon)}$ evaporates as $\varepsilon\to0$. Practical relevance is modest and indirect: hypothesis selection matters as an inner loop over covers of parametric classes, where $n$ is astronomically large and $C$ controls cover density — exactly the regime where $3-2/n$ is useless and where $1/\delta$ in the runtime is fatal.

Proof sketch

Lower bound. Fix $\mathcal X=[2nk\ell]$, $\beta=1/(\ell-1)$, and partition it into $2n$ blocks $T_1,\dots,T_{2n}$, each cut into $k$ sub-intervals of length $\ell$. Hypothesis $H_i$ is uniform except that it puts $(1+\beta)/|\mathcal X|$ on $T_{2i-1}$ and $(1-\beta)/|\mathcal X|$ on $T_{2i}$. The hard family $\mathcal S_i$ draws, independently for each sub-interval of $T_{2i-1}$, one random element to be a "sink" of mass $0$, and in each sub-interval of $T_{2i}$ one random "spike" of mass $2/|\mathcal X|$. The calibration ensures every sub-interval carries mass exactly $\ell/|\mathcal X|$ under every $P_{(i,F,G)}$ and under uniform. A direct $\ell_1$ computation gives $d_{TV}(P_i,H_i)=k(1+\beta)/|\mathcal X|=:d_0$ and $d_{TV}(P_i,H_j)=k(3+\beta)/|\mathcal X|=:d_1$ for $j\ne i$, so $d_1/d_0=(3+\beta)/(1+\beta)\ge3-\alpha$ with $\ell=\Theta(1/\alpha)$: one hypothesis is good, the other $n-1$ are exactly 3-approximations.

Indistinguishability is a packing/birthday argument dressed as a coupling. They prove a clean $n$-ary generalization of Le Cam: if $Q$ is a multi-dimensional coupling of $D_1,\dots,D_n$ (each coordinate marginal correct) admitting a coincident subset $S$ on which all $n$ coordinates agree, and $\gamma=\Pr[\text{escape }S]$, then any index-guesser succeeds with probability at most $\gamma+\frac{1-\gamma}{n}$. Here $D_i^s$ is $s$ samples from a random $P_i\sim\mathcal S_i$, and the coincident set is $B_{\text{unique}}$: samples with at most one element per sub-interval. On $B_{\text{unique}}$ every $D_i^s$ has mass exactly $|\mathcal X|^{-s}$, which is where the sub-interval refinement earns its keep: hierarchical sampling factorizes as (choose sub-interval, mass $\ell/|\mathcal X|$, index-independent) $\times$ (choose element inside, uniform $1/\ell$ because the one-hot functions are independent and uniform). A coupon-collector bound gives $\gamma\le s^2\ell/|\mathcal X|$, so with $k=\omega(s^2)$ the guessing probability is $\frac1n(1+o(1))$.

The mixture step is the payoff. Write $Q=\sum_iw_iH_i$ and split $|P_{i^_}-Q|_1$ by blocks, $r_i(Q)$. For $i\ne i^_$, every $H_j$ with $j\ne i$ and $P_{i^_}$ all equal $1/|\mathcal X|$ on block $i$, so $r_i(Q)=w_ir_i(H_i)$ exactly. On block $i^_$, a two-line computation shows $r_{i^*}(Q)=C_1+w_{i^*}\beta(2-\ell)$ is affine in $w_{i^*}$, hence equals $2w_{i^*}d_0+(1-w_{i^*})r_{i^*}(H_j)$ by matching endpoints. Summing and using $r_{i^*}(H_i)+r_i(H_i)=2d_1$ telescopes to $d_{TV}(P_{i^*},Q)=(1-w_{i^*})d_1+w_{i^*}d_0$. So the ratio is at least $3-\alpha-2w_{i^*}+\alpha w_{i^*}$, and an expected ratio below $3-\frac2n-\frac{C_0}{n}$ forces $\mathbb E[w_{i^*}]>\frac{1+C_0/2}{n}$ — i.e. the weight vector is itself a guesser beating $\frac1n(1+o(1))$, a contradiction. The obstruction is thus not convexity per se but that each $H_i$'s signature lives on its own block and can only be cancelled by itself.

Upper bound. Everything runs on Devroye–Lugosi semi-distances: $S_{i\to j}={x:H_i(x)<H_j(x)}$ is the Scheffé set witnessing $d_{TV}(H_i,H_j)$, $w_{i\to j}=|H_j(S_{i\to j})-P(S_{i\to j})|$, $W(H_j)=\max_iw_{i\to j}$. Two facts drive all of it: underestimation, $w_{i\to j}\le d_{TV}(P,H_j)$ (so $W(H_{i^_})\le\mathrm{OPT}$), and $d_{TV}(P,H_j)\le\mathrm{OPT}+w_{i^_\to j}+w_{j\to i^_}\le2\mathrm{OPT}+w_{i^_\to j}$ — the source of the 3-approximation. For Thm 1.2 they generalize Mahalanabis–Štefankovič's two-point rule by asking for weights whose approximation bound is _the same whichever $i^_$ turns out to be_: with $A_{ij}=1+W(H_j)/W(H_i)$, $A_{ii}=0$, solve $Ap=\mathbf 1$. The explicit solution is beautiful: with $D=\sum W(H_i)$, $C=\sum1/W(H_i)$, take $p_i\propto D/W(H_i)-(n-2)$; then $A\mathbf1=(n-2)\mathbf1+D\mathbf W$ and $A\mathbf W=(n-2)\mathbf W+C\mathbf1$ combine to $A(D\mathbf W-(n-2)\mathbf1)=(DC-(n-2)^2)\mathbf1$, and Cauchy–Schwarz ($DC\ge n^2$) gives ratio $\le2-2/n$, i.e. $3-2/n$ overall. The twist is that for $n\ge4$ these $p_i$ can be _negative_, and imposing non-negativity turns it into an unwieldy LP. Their fix is a rounding rule: sort $W(H_1)\le\dots\le W(H_n)$, call $k$ _good_ if $(k-3)W(H_j)\le\sum_{i\in[k]\setminus j}W(H_i)$ for all $j\le k$, note goodness is downward closed, take the largest good $k$, and use the $k$-variable formula on the true $W$ values, zeroing out the rest. The analysis splits: if $i^_\le k$ the bound is $3-2/k\le3-2/n$; if $i^_>k$, badness of $k+1$ gives $W(H_{i^_})>\frac1{k-2}\sum_{i\le k}W(H_i)$, exactly the slack needed to rerun the same $D'C'\ge k^2$ computation on the truncated index set. Noise is handled by one-sided estimates $W(H_i)\le\hat W(H_i)\le W(H_i)+\varepsilon$, so the inequality transfers with an additive $2\varepsilon$.

Thm 1.3 is the technically heaviest part and is where the pairwise-tournament picture becomes a sublinear graph problem. Define $G_b$ on $[n]$ with edge $i\to j$ iff $\hat w_{i\to j}>b$; the Semi-Distance Threshold Problem asks for either $\bot$ (every node has an in-edge, certifying $b\le W(H_{i^_})\le\mathrm{OPT}$) or some $j$ with no edge from $i^_$ (certifying $w_{i^_\to j}\le b+\varepsilon$, hence $3\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$). Because $b=0$ forces $\bot$ and $b=1$ forces an index, a monotone-free binary search over $b$ works in $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ calls. The solver repeatedly finds a "$\beta$-prompting" hypothesis — one with out-edges to a $\beta$-fraction of the surviving set $V$ — and deletes its out-neighbourhood, so at most $\tilde O(1/\beta)$ rounds. Finding one uses a level-set / "work investment" argument: bucket vertices by out-degree in geometric classes $[2^{-r},2^{-r+1})$; some class $r^_$ has density $\ge2^{r^*}d/(4\log^2(1/d))$, so sampling $\tilde O(2^r)$ vertices and spending $\tilde O(1/(\beta2^r))$ edge probes to test each balances to $\tilde O(1/\beta)$ total. When the average degree is $O(\beta)$ this fails, and a second mechanism takes over: sample $O(\log n)$ nodes $j\in V$, compute their small in-neighbourhoods $T_j$ by a full $O(n)$ scan, and look for a prompting vertex inside them; if none is found, commit to returning a $j$ whose neighbours are all non-prompting. The case analysis is the key trick: if $i^*$ is $\gg\beta$-prompting then $(i^_,j)$ cannot be an edge, and if $i^_$ is only $O(\beta)$-prompting then a random $O(\log n)$-sample hits an out-neighbour of $i^*$ with probability only $O(\beta\log n)$. Because correctness is argued only for the first commitment, there is no union bound over the $\tilde O(1/\beta)$ rounds — that is what keeps the failure probability at $\tilde O(\delta)$ with runtime $\tilde O(n/\delta)$ per threshold. Thm 1.4 is a cleaner halving recursion, and Thm 1.5 reduces Mahalanabis–Štefankovič's quadratic tournament to their Tournament Revelation Problem — repeatedly report the max-weight remaining edge under adversarial deletions — which, since edge weight is $\ell_1$ distance between hypotheses viewed as vectors in $\mathbb R^{|\mathcal X|}$, is dynamic approximate diameter: embed $\ell_1\hookrightarrow\ell_2^2$ (Nguyen), JL down to $O(\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ dimensions, and compose Indyk's approximate furthest-neighbour structure with Eppstein's furthest-neighbour-to-diameter reduction for $\tilde O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized deletions.

Broader context

Hypothesis selection is the workhorse primitive of distribution learning. Yatracos (1985) introduced minimum-distance estimation over the "Yatracos class" of pairwise comparison sets; Devroye and Lugosi (1996, 1997, and the 2001 book Combinatorial Methods in Density Estimation) turned this into the Scheffé tournament: for each pair, the set $S_{i\to j}$ where one density exceeds the other is the single test that witnesses their TV distance, you only ever count samples falling in these sets, and the winner is a 3-approximation using $O(\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. This is why learning a structured class reduces to building a $\gamma$-cover and running selection on it — Poisson binomials, mixtures of Gaussians, piecewise polynomials, histograms; Diakonikolas's 2016 survey is the standard entry point. The constant matters more than it looks: since running selection on a $\gamma$-cover yields error $\approx C\gamma$, a worse $C$ demands a finer cover, and for $k$-component mixtures the cover size can grow exponentially in response.

The modern thread is the one this paper sits in: insisting on algorithms that are time-efficient and not merely sample-efficient, in a model where the statistical optimum is known. Two papers are worth reading alongside. Bousquet, Braverman, Kol, Efremenko and Moran (FOCS 2021) is the "cutting with margin" $C=2$ algorithm whose $\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal X|)$ runtime is the barrier this paper reacts to, and the source of the idea of an improper $Q$ outside the hull. Aliakbarpour, Bun and Smith (NeurIPS 2024) is the near-linear-time $C=3$ algorithm whose $1/(\delta^3\varepsilon^3)$ overhead is improved here, and whose framing of the "high-probability conundrum" is the single most portable idea in this literature.

A concrete follow-up worth pursuing: characterize the smallest succinctly describable output class that admits $C<3$. The hard instance says the convex (indeed affine) hull of $\mathcal H$ fails, while the good answer — uniform — is obtainable by gluing hypotheses along Scheffé cells rather than averaging them. Since the $n$ hypotheses induce at most $\binom n2$ Scheffé sets and hence $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ relevant cells, the natural candidate class is "piecewise mixtures": $Q$ defined cell-by-cell as a different convex combination of $\mathcal H$ (re-normalized), which has $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ description length and inherits sampling and pdf access. Does this class contain a 2-approximation, and can one be found in $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ time by a separation-oracle argument over the BBKEM constraints restricted to cells? A negative answer would be a much stronger barrier than the present one; a positive answer resolves the paper's main open question. The orthogonal follow-up is to prove the $1/\delta$ runtime factor for $C=3$ is necessary — currently only shown for the filtering paradigm — ideally as a fine-grained lower bound in the sample/pdf-query model.

On the connection to your own work: part of this is genuinely transferable and part is not. The transferable part is the computational skeleton. Theorem 1.3 is, stripped of statistics, an answer to: given $n$ candidates and an expensive pairwise comparator, find a candidate never "beaten" by the unknown best one, using $\tilde O(n/\delta)$ comparisons instead of $n^2$ — via degree estimation, geometric level sets over "how many rivals does this candidate eliminate", and a commit-once analysis that avoids union-bounding over rounds. That is exactly the budget structure of a reranking cascade where each comparison is a cross-encoder call, and the "find a $\beta$-prompting candidate, delete its out-neighbourhood" primitive is a cleaner elimination rule than the usual heuristic pruning. Theorem 1.5 is even more directly in your territory: it reduces selection to maintaining an approximate farthest pair in a JL-compressed space under deletions, i.e. hypothesis selection is a dynamic vector-search problem once you embed $\ell_1\hookrightarrow\ell_2^2$ — a template worth remembering whenever a tournament's comparator is a metric. The generative-retrieval connection, by contrast, is thin: one can phrase GR as selecting among $n$ candidate distributions over token sequences with a $C\cdot\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ agnostic guarantee, but Scheffé sets require pointwise pdf access and TV geometry that beam search over docids does not give you, and nothing here speaks to the sequence structure. The "mixtures as ensembles" reading is a nice honest takeaway — worst-case, convexly ensembling candidate models cannot beat $3\times$ the best single model's TV error even though an unrestricted combiner reaches $2\times$ — but it is a statement about adversarial constants in TV, not about why ensembling helps in practice. Read this paper for the lower-bound technique (multi-dimensional couplings with coincident subsets is a tool you will reuse) and for the sublinear tournament machinery, not for an IR application.

title: Max-Margin Token Selection in Attention Mechanism
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-05

Max-Margin Token Selection in Attention Mechanism

Davoud Ataee Tarzanagh, Yingcong Li, Xuechen Zhang, Samet Oymak — NeurIPS 2023 — proceedings link

Main idea

The object of study is a deliberately minimal attention layer: given a sequence $X=[x_1,\dots,x_T]^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$, keys $K=XW^\top$, and a single tunable query vector $p$, the model outputs $f(X)=\langle Xv,\mathbb{S}(XW^\top p)\rangle$. This is not self-attention; it is exactly the cross-attention row that a [CLS] token or a prompt vector contributes, so $p$ plays the role of a learned query and $v$ of a linear prediction head. Lemma 1 shows that optimizing $p$ with $W$ fixed and optimizing $W$ with $p$ fixed are the same trajectory, provided $W(0)=up(0)^\top/|u|^2$ and stepsizes are rescaled — the iterates then stay rank one forever. That is why the paper can say "gradient descent on $p$, or equivalently $W$," though the equivalence is an initialization-specific artifact, not a general fact about training $W$.

The central quantity is the token score $\gamma_{it}=Y_i\cdot v^\top x_{it}$: how much token $t$ of input $i$ helps the loss once attention selects it. The whole point is that optimality is read off the value side while separation happens on the key side. The attention-SVM is $p^{\rm mm}(\alpha)=\arg\min|p|$ s.t. $p^\top(k_{i\alpha_i}-k_{it})\ge1$ for all $t\ne\alpha_i$ and all $i$ — a single convex program with one constraint block per training sequence; its feasibility means a single direction can separate the designated token of every sequence from that sequence's other tokens, and scaling that direction up drives $\mathbb{S}(R\,K_ip^{\rm mm})\to e_{\alpha_i}$, i.e. hard selection.
