"Locally optimal" is the sharp idea. Given a feasible $\alpha$, the SVM-neighbors $\mathcal{T}_i$ are the tokens sitting exactly at margin one, $(k_{i\alpha_i}-k_{it})^\top p^{\rm mm}=1$. The indices $\alpha$ are locally optimal if $\gamma_{i\alpha_i}>\gamma_{it}$ only for $t\in\mathcal{T}_i$ — tokens farther away in key space are irrelevant even if they score higher. Directional convergence then says: $|p(t)|\to\infty$ while $p(t)/|p(t)|\to p^{\rm mm}/|p^{\rm mm}|$. The weights blow up; only the direction, and hence the asymptotic hard selection pattern, is determined.

What's most interesting / reviewer-style critique

The cleverest point is not the SVM equivalence itself but where the margin comes from. In logistic-regression implicit bias the exponential tail of the loss drives margin maximization. Here it is the softmax's exponential tail; the loss only needs Assumption A (strictly decreasing, Lipschitz derivative). So the correlation loss $\ell(u)=-u$ — not even a classification loss — yields the same max-margin bias. That relocation of the mechanism from loss to nonlinearity is the real contribution, and it makes the result robust in a way most implicit-bias results are not. Second cleverest: the local-neighbor refinement, which says the learned selection is governed entirely by the margin-tight competitors. Third, Theorem 6's relaxed SVM: when $v$ and $p$ are trained together, inputs whose selected token is not a support vector of the downstream SVM on $v$ only need $p^\top(k_{i\alpha_i}-k_{it})\ge0$ (select it) rather than $\ge1$ (select it with margin). The geometry of $v$'s support vectors reshapes $p$'s program — a genuinely surprising, falsifiable prediction.

Now the honest accounting. Global convergence of gradient descent is not established. Theorem 2 gives $|p(t)|\to\infty$ under Assumption B, which forces every non-optimal token within an input to share the same score — implausibly strong — and gives directional convergence only for $n=1$. Figure 8 shows $n=2$ already admits two initializations converging to two different SVM directions, so the restriction is tight rather than an artifact. The headline result is therefore Theorem 3, which is local in two senses: the initialization must lie in a cone $\mathrm{cone}*\mu(p^{\rm mm})$ and must have norm above a threshold $R\gtrsim\frac{\max(2,\delta^{-1})}{\Theta}\log\frac{C_0T\Gamma A}{\gamma^{\rm gap}*{\min}}$ depending on unknown data constants. Nobody initializes at large norm inside the right cone; the theorem describes a basin, not a trainable procedure. Theorem 4's converse ("only LMM directions are reachable") is likewise about cone-restricted regularization paths, not about GD.

No rates anywhere. Everything is asymptotic directional convergence, whereas Soudry et al. get $O(1/\log t)$ margin error for logistic regression. The paper's own machinery suggests why this is hard and also that the truth is slow: inside the cone $|\nabla L(p)|\lesssim\bar{A}CTe^{-R\Theta/2}$, so gradients vanish exponentially in the norm, $|p(t)|$ should grow like $\log t$, and the margin error like $1/\log t$ at best. Figure 4(b) shows exactly this plateau for constant-stepsize GD and the authors switch to normalized GD to get clean pictures — honest, but a real quantitative gap.

Separability. The Att-SVM must be feasible, and feasibility is only proved (Lemma 2/11) in the degenerate case where all $Y_i=1$, $W$ is full rank and $v\in\mathrm{range}(W^\top)$. With mixed labels it is assumed, and Figure 9(a) shows it fails routinely at $d=2$. The non-separable regime — the only one real data occupies — is entirely open; the authors say so.

Joint training of $(v,p)$ is handled only by regularization path (Theorems 5–6), i.e. algorithm-independent; GD for the joint problem is listed as open. Assumption C is also uncomfortably close to assuming the conclusion: it posits that $\alpha$ maximizes the downstream label margin $1/|v^{\rm mm}|$ and that any softmax mixing shrinks that margin at least linearly, with a uniform $\nu$. The supporting example is very special.

Model gap. One tunable token means one hyperplane and exactly one selected token per sequence; $W$ is effectively rank one; there is no self-attention (eq. 4 is explicitly future work), no multiple heads, no depth, no MLP, no layer norm, no positional structure, and $v$ is frozen throughout Section 2. The honest framing is that this is a theory of prompt-tuning / [CLS]-attention, which is how the closest prior work (Oymak et al., ICML 2023) framed the same model.

Experiments. The toy figures are clean and illustrative, but the $d=3$ construction ($W=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,0)$, $v=e_3$) deliberately decouples scores from keys so scores can be set by hand — good for visualization, not a test. The best evidence is Figure 9: random data with $n=4$, $T=6$, $d\in{2,\dots,500}$, where saturated instances converge to an LMM direction with average correlation $0.997$. That is persuasive at tiny scale, and the observation that GMM (not just LMM) convergence becomes more likely as $d$ grows is intriguing but unexplained. The ViT-base/CIFAR-10 experiment shows attention sparsity $|s|_1/|s|_2$ falling as $|W|_F$ grows — consistent with the theory, but almost any sparsifying mechanism would produce that curve. The decisive experiment they did not run: extract the token selected by a trained head, solve the Att-SVM on its keys, and measure alignment with the learned $W^\top p$. Without that, the ViT figure is illustration, not evidence.

Proof sketch

What is actually proved: (i) Theorem 1 — under strict global score dominance, the regularization path $\bar p(R)=\arg\min_{|p|\le R}L(p)$ satisfies $\bar p(R)/R\to p^{\rm mm\star}/|p^{\rm mm\star}|$; a corollary of Theorem 8, which covers nonlinear heads, multiple optimal tokens per input via a possibly nonconvex Att-SVM$'$, and replaces score dominance by Assumption D. (ii) Theorem 2 — GD diverges in norm always (under Assumption B), converges in direction only for $n=1$. (iii) Theorem 3 — local directional convergence of GD from inside $\mathcal{C}_{\mu,R}(p^{\rm mm})$ with $\eta\le1/L_p$. (iv) Theorem 4/7 — no non-LMM direction is the limit of a cone-restricted path. (v) Theorems 5–6 — joint regularization path converges to $(v^{\rm mm},p^{\rm mm})$ or $(v^{\rm mm},p^{\rm relax})$. No rates, nothing non-asymptotic.

How it is proved. The algebraic engine is Lemma 3 (the Key Lemma): for $a=Kq$, $s=\mathbb{S}(Kp)$, $\gamma=Xv$, $|a^\top\mathbb{S}'(Kp)\gamma-\sum_{t\ge2}(a_1-a_t)s_t(\gamma_1-\gamma_t)|\le2\Gamma A(1-s_1)^2$. Since $\nabla L(p)=\frac1n\sum_i\ell_i'K_i^\top\mathbb{S}'(K_ip)\gamma_i$, this factorizes the gradient's correlation with any probe direction $q$ into (key-margin gap along $q$) $\times$ (softmax mass on the non-selected token) $\times$ (score gap), with a quadratic error in the leaked mass. Lemma 4 evaluates it at $q=p^{\rm mm\star}$ to get $\langle\nabla L(p),p^{\rm mm\star}\rangle<0$ for every finite $p$ — so there are no finite stationary points; combined with explicit $L_p$-smoothness (Lemma 6, giving $\sum_t|\nabla L(p(t))|^2<\infty$), this forces $|p(t)|\to\infty$.

The local analysis is where the real work is. Lemma 7 builds the cone so the key geometry is frozen inside it: for $q\in\mathrm{cone}_\mu(p^{\rm mm})$ one still has $(k_{i\alpha_i}-k_{it})^\top q\in[1/2,3/2]$ for neighbors, and $(k_{it}-k_{i\tau})^\top q\ge\delta>0$ for non-neighbors. Consequently the softmax mass on non-neighbors is $Q_i\le Te^{-R\Theta\delta}S_i$ — exponentially smaller than the mass on neighbors. That is why only neighbors' scores appear in local optimality: the softmax's saturation does the token pruning, and non-neighbors are suppressed at a strictly faster exponential rate. Choosing $R$ large enough makes the Key Lemma's error term provably dominated, yielding a two-sided sandwich on $-\langle\nabla L(p),q\rangle$ in terms of $\frac1n\sum_i(1-s_{i\alpha_i})$, and hence a constant lower bound on the angle $\langle-\nabla L(p)/|\nabla L(p)|,p^{\rm mm}/|p^{\rm mm}|\rangle\ge c\Theta/(C\bar{A})$. Lemma 7(L3) then supplies the Soudry-style gradient correlation condition $\langle\nabla L(p),p/|p|\rangle\ge(1+\pi)\langle\nabla L(p),p^{\rm mm}/|p^{\rm mm}|\rangle$ for $|p|\ge R_\pi$.

Theorem 3 assembles these in four steps: no stationary points in the cone; the correlation condition at level $\epsilon$; an induction that the iterates never leave the cone — the crux, where the gradient norm is exponentially small while its alignment with $p^{\rm mm}$ is bounded away from zero, so each step is essentially radial-and-aligned and the correlation cannot decrease; and finally a telescoping sum $\langle p(t{+}1)-p(t),p^{\rm mm}\rangle\ge(1-\epsilon)(|p(t{+}1)|-|p(t)|)-2\eta(L(p(t))-L(p(t{+}1)))$, giving $\liminf_t\langle p(t)/|p(t)|,p^{\rm mm}/|p^{\rm mm}|\rangle\ge1-\epsilon$ for every $\epsilon$. This telescoping step is structurally identical to the implicit-bias argument for separable logistic regression; the cone is what substitutes for the convexity that is unavailable here.

Theorem 4 is proved by explicit construction of a better competitor. If $q$ selects unique tokens and is neighbor-optimal but is not max-margin, then $q'=(q+\epsilon\bar p^{\rm mm})/|\cdot|$ lies in $\mathrm{cone}_{2\epsilon}(q)$ yet has directional margin $\Gamma_{q'}\ge\Gamma_\delta+\frac{\epsilon}{4}(\Gamma-\Gamma_q)$; Lemma 8 shows a strictly larger directional margin implies strictly smaller loss for large $R$, because the excess over the selection baseline behaves like $e^{-R\Gamma_q}$ — again the softmax tail doing the discrimination. If instead $q$ is not neighbor-optimal, Lemma 9 shows $L(R\cdot q)<L^\star$ at finite $R$, so the restricted path has bounded norm. Lemma 10 ("at most $d$ directional neighbors") plus general position rules out degenerate ties. Theorems 5 and 8 run the same contradiction template on the log non-optimality mass: the candidate $p^\star_R=Rp^{\rm mm}/|p^{\rm mm}|$ achieves $\log q^\star_{\max}\le-\Xi R+\log T$ whereas a $\gamma$-violating $p_R$ has $\log\hat q_{\max}\ge-(1-\gamma)\Xi R-\log T$, exponentially more. Both results are, structurally, Ji–Telgarsky/Soudry arguments with the exponential tail supplied by softmax rather than by $\ell$.

One nice observation outside the theorems: since $|\nabla L_i(p)|\propto|\ell'(\gamma_i)|\gamma_i$, the correlation loss biases transient dynamics toward high-score tokens while logistic biases toward low-score ones. The asymptotic direction is loss-independent; the transient is not.

Broader context

The parent literature is the implicit bias of gradient descent. Soudry, Hoffer, Nacson, Gunasekar and Srebro (JMLR 2018) proved that GD on separable data with logistic loss diverges in norm but converges in direction to the $\ell_2$ max-margin SVM at rate $O(1/\log t)$; Ji and Telgarsky extended this to non-separable data and (with Dudík and Schapire, COLT 2020) proved that GD follows the regularization path for general losses — morally the bridge this paper would like between Theorem 1 and Theorem 3 but cannot invoke, because $L(p)$ is nonconvex and softmax is not homogeneous in $p$. Lyu and Li (ICLR 2020) is the other reference point: for homogeneous networks GD converges to a KKT point of a margin problem. The present paper is the attention analogue of that program, and the cone construction is precisely what replaces homogeneity.

The attention-theory line it sits in: Oymak, Rawat, Soltanolkotabi and Thrampoulidis, On the role of attention in prompt-tuning (ICML 2023), studies the identical model but with three gradient steps on a planted contextual data model; Jelassi, Sander and Li (NeurIPS 2022) show ViTs learn spatial structure through attention; Edelman, Goel, Kakade and Zhang (ICML 2022) bound the inductive bias of self-attention toward sparse functions. The distinguishing feature here is genuine data-generality: no clusterability, no planted relevant/irrelevant split. Two things worth reading next: Lyu–Li for the homogeneous-network template, and the authors' own Transformers as Support Vector Machines (2023), which pushes this to the bilinear $W$ problem and self-attention.

A concrete follow-up: make $p$ a matrix $P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ (multiple prompt tokens, or $m$ heads reading the same sequence) and ask what the regularization path selects. The conjecture almost writes itself — the limit should solve a margin problem over token subsets of size at most $m$, with each row of $P$ carving its own hyperplane, giving the first principled account of attention as differentiable top-$k$ selection rather than top-1. A second, more tractable one: close the rate gap. The ingredients are already in Lemma 7 — $|\nabla L|\asymp e^{-|p|\Theta/2}$ plus a constant angle lower bound should give $|p(t)|\asymp\frac{2}{\Theta}\log t$ and margin error $O(1/\log t)$, recovering Soudry's rate with $\Theta=1/|p^{\rm mm}|$ as the effective margin.

Connection to your work. There is a real one, on the scoring side, and the precise version is more interesting than the loose one. The Att-SVM constraints $p^\top(k_{i\alpha_i}-k_{it})\ge1$ are literally RankSVM's constraints (Joachims, KDD 2002) in the one-relevant-document-per-query case: a single global scoring direction that must rank the gold item above every candidate in its own list by a unit margin. So the paper's content, read through IR eyes, is: softmax attention trained by gradient descent implicitly performs RankSVM over the key embeddings. Two of its refinements are then non-trivial statements about retrieval. First, the relevance labels are endogenous — $\gamma_{it}=Y_iv^\top x_{it}$ is set by the downstream head, not supplied — so this models a retriever whose notion of relevance is induced by the task it feeds. Second, local optimality says the asymptotic ranker is determined only by the margin-tight negatives: a candidate far in key space cannot influence the learned direction no matter how attractive its value-side score. That is a sharp, testable claim about which hard negatives govern a dense retriever, and it cuts against uniform or score-based negative sampling. Theorem 6 adds a second asymmetry worth borrowing: queries whose selected item is not a support vector of the downstream classifier get only a $\ge0$ constraint rather than $\ge1$ — the retriever is asked to select correctly but not to separate with margin, when downstream utility does not require it. A per-query constraint-strength schedule driven by downstream utility is a concrete loss-design idea, and a derived rather than heuristic one.

Where I would not push it. Feasibility of the Att-SVM — one direction separating the gold item from every negative in every query with unit margin — is a far stronger separability assumption than any realistic retrieval setting satisfies, and the paper has nothing for the non-separable case, which is where retrieval actually lives. The keys are $k=Wx$ with $W$ frozen (or rank-one-tied to $p$), whereas in dense retrieval the embedding is the learned object, so the implicit bias you would care about lives in the encoder — exactly the bilinear extension the follow-up paper attempts and does not fully resolve. And for generative retrieval specifically the connection is thinner than it looks: decoding an identifier string autoregressively has no single softmax over a fixed candidate set for the Att-SVM to map onto, and the per-step vocabulary softmax is not selecting among task-scored items in the sense the theory requires. Calling attention a "differentiable index" here would be analogy, not mathematics. Honest summary: a real and usable correspondence for scoring, reranking and soft top-$k$ selection; a forced one for identifier-based generative retrieval.

title: Theory of Optimal Learning Rate Schedules and Scaling Laws for a Random Feature Model

Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-05

Theory of Optimal Learning Rate Schedules and Scaling Laws for a Random Feature Model

Blake Bordelon, Francesca Mori (arXiv preprint, 2026) — arXiv:2602.04774

Main idea

The paper asks a question practitioners answer by grid search: given a fixed step budget $T$, what is the entire learning-rate trajectory $\eta_T^\star(t)$ that minimizes the final test loss — and how does it scale with $T$? The vehicle is the power-law random feature model that has become the standard solvable proxy for neural scaling laws (Bordelon–Pehlevan 2022; Paquette et al. 2024). Inputs map to features $\psi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^M$ with diagonal covariance $\lambda_k\sim k^{-b}$; the target is linear, $y=w^_!\cdot\psi(x)+\sigma_0 z$, with spectral weight $(w^_*k)^2\lambda_k\sim k^{-a}$; the student is a linear model on the _top-$N$_ features, so model size enters as a hard spectral truncation contributing irreducible noise $\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2+\sum*{k>N}(w^*_k)^2\lambda_k\simeq\sigma_0^2+N^{1-a}$. Training is single-pass online SGD on squared loss with step size $\eta_t$ and batch $m_t$ from zero init.

Under a Gaussian-feature assumption the per-mode second moments $c_{t,k}=\langle(w_{t,k}-w^*_k)^2\rangle$ close into an exact deterministic recursion whose noise term is proportional to the current loss — gradient noise feeds back on itself. Passing to continuous time and introducing the remaining learning-rate budget $\chi(t)=\int_t^T\eta(s)ds$ (so $\eta=-\dot\chi$, $\chi(T)=0$), the excess loss splits as $\mathrm{Bias}\sim\chi_0^{-(a-1)/b}$ plus $\mathrm{Var}\sim\sigma^2\int_0^T \frac{\eta^2}{m}\chi(t)^{-(2b-1)/b}dt$. That single formula is the paper's conceptual payload: bias only cares about the total budget $\chi_0$, while noise injected at time $t$ is filtered only by the budget remaining after $t$, with exponent $\gamma=2-1/b<2$. Late noise is never forgotten, so annealing is forced, and crucially a horizon-agnostic ("anytime") schedule cannot postpone variance reduction.

Optimal control then means: minimize the terminal loss over the whole control path $\eta(\cdot)$ subject to the deterministic state dynamics and a stability cap $\eta\le\eta_{\max}$. Two phases emerge from whether the cap binds. In the easy phase ($b<a$) it does not, and $\eta^\star_T(t)=T^{b/a-1}f(t/T)$ with $f(z)\propto(1-z)^{2b-1}$ — polynomial decay in time-to-go, exponent set purely by the spectrum, with an explicit Gamma-function prefactor — giving $L_T-\sigma^2\sim T^{-(a-1)/a}$, which saturates the information-theoretic rate. In the hard phase ($b>a$) the unconstrained solution would require $\eta\sim T^{b/a-1}\to\infty$, so the cap binds: $\eta=\eta_{\max}$ until $t_s$, then $(1-t/T)^{2b-1}$ decay over a vanishing fraction $1-t_s/T\sim T^{-(b-a)/(2b-1)}$, i.e. stable-then-decay, with $L_T-\sigma^2\sim T^{-(a-1)/b}$. Both beat the best constant LR and the best two-parameter power law, which are stuck at $(a-1)/(a+b-1)$. The same machinery yields a degenerate $(\eta,m)$ optimality manifold $m(t)\propto\eta(t)\chi(t)^{1/(2b)-1}$ — broken, by minimizing wall-clock, into $\eta\equiv\eta_{\max}$ with a batch ramp $m(t)\propto(1-t/T)^{1/(2b)-1}$ — plus Chinchilla-style compute-optimal exponents, and a numerical study of optimal momentum.

What's most interesting / reviewer-style critique

The cleverest move is the change of variables to $\chi(t)$. It compresses the entire $N$-mode dynamics into one scalar state through the mode sums $f_s(\chi)=\sum_k k^{-s}e^{-k^{-b}\chi}$, makes the control $\eta=-\dot\chi$, and leaves a Lagrangian $\mathcal L=\dot\chi^2A(\chi)$ that is autonomous and homogeneous of degree two in $\dot\chi$. The Beltrami/Noether first integral therefore says simply "the optimal path spends equal cost per unit time", collapsing the whole optimal-control problem to a separable ODE $\dot\chi\propto-\chi^{1-1/(2b)}$. The optimal schedule is a geodesic in a one-dimensional metric. That trick is worth stealing for any solvable training-dynamics model.

Genuine strengths beyond that: WSD-like behavior is derived in a convex, exactly solvable quadratic problem, with no non-convexity at all — a serious alternative to the "river valley" landscape story of Wen et al. The benchmarking is honest (they show their own rate fails to saturate the optimal rate in the hard phase, where Pillaud-Vivien et al. achieve it with multi-pass plus averaging). And the batch-ramp result recovers "don't decay the LR, increase the batch size" from first principles.

Now the weaknesses. Nothing here is a theorem. The base recursion is exact only under Gaussian features, and the reduction to the bias/variance functional additionally drops the $\eta^2\frac{m+1}{m}\lambda_k^2$ term as "small $\lambda_k$" and replaces $L_t$ by its noise-free value, severing the self-consistent noise feedback. These are uncontrolled mean-field closures, and they are weakest exactly in the hard phase, where $\eta\lambda_1=O(1)$ by construction. Worse, $\eta_{\max}$ is imposed by hand rather than derived from the recursion's spectral radius, so the entire hard-phase story ("the constraint binds") rests on a parameter the model never models. A proper Pontryagin/KKT treatment of the bang-arc with explicit multipliers — rather than matched asymptotics around $\tau_s\approx1$ — would fix both the switching condition and the constants.

The headline is partly undercut by their own Appendix C.3: any schedule $\eta=T^{-\xi}g(t/T)$ with $\xi=\max(0,1-b/a)$ and edge decay faster than $(1-z)^{b-1}$ achieves the same exponents. So optimal control buys only the prefactor; the actionable content reduces to three statements (scale the base LR by $\xi$, decay to zero fast enough, be horizon-aware). Useful, but less than "here is the optimal schedule."

Does the hard phase really explain practice? The derived schedule has no warmup — it is SD, not WSD — and warmup in real training plausibly comes from things the model excludes (Adam preconditioner warm-up, early curvature growth, feature learning). More sharply, the theory predicts the anneal fraction should shrink as $T^{-(b-a)/(2b-1)}$, whereas practitioners use a roughly fixed 10–20% decay fraction and sometimes lengthen it at longer horizons. That is the paper's cleanest falsification route and it is not tested. The numerics that do exist are thin: Fig. 7 fits $1-t_s/T\sim T^{-1/6}$ over less than a decade of $T$ with $t_s$ defined by an arbitrary $0.95\eta_{\max}$ crossing — a factor-1.2 effect, essentially unfalsifiable.

Other concerns: single-pass only, so the hard-phase "optimality" is conditional on an algorithm class known to be suboptimal for that very phase; squared loss and lazy/kernel regime, no feature learning, no weight decay, no Adam/Muon (acknowledged); model size as a hard top-$N$ truncation is a favorable idealization versus the Marchenko–Pastur-style soft truncation of real width-$N$ features, and the compute-optimal exponents inherit that fragility — note they imply $N$ grows much slower than data ($C^{1/(a+1)}$ with $a\sim1.5$–$2$), far from Chinchilla's near-$\sqrt{C}$, which deserves explicit reconciliation with Paquette et al.'s phase diagram. The momentum result is a figure, not a result; the exponent is not identified. The deep-net experiment is a single width-32 ResNet on CIFAR-5M, and its "hard phase" label is imported from a prior paper's NTK spectrum rather than measured here. Finally, the Fig. 4 caption labels the hard-phase prediction $C^{-(b-1)/(a+1)}$ while the text derives $C^{-(a-1)/(b+1)}$; at $a=1.5,b=2$ these are 0.40 vs 0.167 — one of them is wrong and it is worth checking against the plotted line.

Proof sketch

Precisely what is established, in descending order of rigor. (i) The per-mode recursion $c_{t+1,k}=(1-2\eta_t\lambda_k+\eta_t^2\frac{m+1}{m}\lambda_k^2)c_{t,k}+\frac{\eta_t^2}{m}\lambda_k\sum_\ell\lambda_\ell c_{t,\ell}+\frac{\eta_t^2}{m}\sigma^2\lambda_k$ is an exact deterministic equivalent for the averaged dynamics given Gaussian features — quoted from prior work, not reproved. (ii) Everything downstream is heuristic asymptotics: the long-time solution is written via the Green's function $\prod_i(1-2\eta_i\lambda_k)\to e^{-2\lambda_k\chi}$, mode sums are replaced by their large-$\chi$ Gamma asymptotics $f_s(\chi)\approx\Gamma(\frac{s-1}{b})\chi^{(1-s)/b}/b$, and $L_t$ inside the variance integral is approximated by its bias-only value. (iii) The continuum variational problem is then solved exactly within those approximations. (iv) The schedules and switching times are confirmed numerically by direct constrained optimal control — single-shooting transcription in CasADi with IPOPT — on the same recursion, so this validates the asymptotics, not the Gaussian closure. (v) Deep-network experiments are qualitative consistency checks only.

The derivation strategy has four moving parts. First, the deterministic-equivalent reduction. Second, the time-to-go reparameterization $\chi(t)=\int_t^T\eta$, which makes the problem variational rather than dynamic-programming: the cost becomes a functional of $\chi$ alone with $\eta=-\dot\chi$, and the variance weight $f_{2b}(2\chi)\sim\chi^{-(2b-1)/b}$ encodes "noise injected at $t$ is attenuated only by the budget left". Third, the Noether/Beltrami first integral, which works because the Lagrangian is $t$-independent and quadratic in $\dot\chi$, yielding $\dot\chi=-\sqrt{c/A(\chi)}$ and, in the scaling regime where $A\propto\chi^{(1-2b)/b}$, the separable ODE with solution $\chi(t)=\chi_0(1-t/T)^{2b}$ — hence $\eta\propto(1-t/T)^{2b-1}$. The boundary constant $\chi_0$ is not free: because $\chi_0$ appears both in the boundary bias term $f_a(2\chi_0)$ and parametrically inside $A(\chi,\chi_0)$, a separate stationarity condition in $\chi_0$ must be solved; its large-$\chi_0$ asymptotics give $\chi_0\propto[\frac{m\Gamma(\frac{a+b-1}{b})}{b\sigma^2\Gamma(2-\frac1b)}]^{b/a}T^{b/a}$, which sets $\xi=1-b/a$ and simultaneously diagnoses the phase transition: $\chi_0$ superlinear in $T$ (i.e. $b>a$) is incompatible with $\eta\le\eta_{\max}$. Fourth, matched asymptotics for the constrained branch: insert the two-piece ansatz, expand the loss as $T^{-(a-1)/b}(1+\epsilon)+T^{-(b-1)/b}\epsilon^{-(b-1)/b}$ in $\epsilon=1-t_s/T$, and minimize to get $\epsilon\sim T^{-(b-a)/(2b-1)}$. A separate appendix verifies the self-consistency of neglecting the "edge" region $\chi(t)\lesssim1$ near $t=T$, where the Gamma asymptotics fail, showing it contributes subleading $(\epsilon T)^{-\delta/(\delta+1)}$. The momentum extension replaces the single state $c_{t,k}$ with the triple $(C,R,V)_{k,t}$ — a per-mode linear dynamical system — and is optimized numerically only.

Broader context

The subfield behind this is the program of making neural scaling laws analytically solvable by replacing a network with a linear model on power-law features. Two exponents do all the work: a capacity exponent $b$ for the feature spectrum and a source-style exponent $a$ for how the target's power distributes over that spectrum; everything becomes a function of $(a,b)$. Bahri et al. (PNAS 2024) gave the variance/resolution-limited taxonomy; Bordelon–Atanasov–Pehlevan (ICML 2024) built the dynamical version; the easy/hard dichotomy is the classical one from stochastic approximation in Hilbert spaces (Dieuleveut–Bach; Pillaud-Vivien et al. 2018), where the hard phase is precisely where single-pass SGD fails to reach the Caponnetto–De Vito/Fischer–Steinwart minimax rate and multiple passes plus averaging rescue it. Separately, the LR-schedule literature has been converging on the same object from the convex side — Defazio et al. (2023) show linear-decay-to-zero is optimal for last-iterate bounds, which is the $b\to1$ limit of the $(1-t/T)^{2b-1}$ law here. The two most worth reading next to this paper are Paquette, Paquette, Xiao & Pennington, "4+3 phases of compute-optimal neural scaling laws" (NeurIPS 2024), which maps the same $(a,b)$ plane under one-pass SGD and is the right benchmark for the compute-optimal section, and Li et al. (2025), "Unveiling the role of learning rate schedules via functional scaling laws", which studies parametric schedules in the same model and is what this paper generalizes by replacing the ansatz with a control derivation. The practical backdrop is $\mu$P-style hyperparameter transfer across width and its known failure across token horizon, plus Chinchilla.

The most compelling follow-up is a measurement study that turns the three exponent predictions into a falsifiable pipeline: fit $b$ from the empirical NTK/feature covariance spectrum and $a$ from the target's spectral weight in a real pretraining setup, then predict simultaneously the base-LR exponent $\xi=\max(0,1-b/a)$, the decay shape exponent $2b-1$, and — the sharp one — the shrinking anneal fraction $T^{-(b-a)/(2b-1)}$, and test all three on a horizon sweep. Nobody has checked the third, and practice seems to contradict it. A second, more theoretical follow-up: redo the control problem in the feature-learning DMFT setting (Bordelon et al., JSTAT 2025) where $(a,b)$ themselves evolve as features align with the target. That would make the schedule self-consistently coupled to a moving spectrum, and plausibly derives warmup: early training with a large effective $b$ sits in the hard phase (bang at $\eta_{\max}$), and as alignment increases the system crosses into the easy phase, so the optimal control should show a genuine rise-then-decay structure rather than the pure SD found here.

On IR: there is a real but indirect connection, and I would not oversell it. Two threads look non-forced. First, the $(\eta,m)$ degeneracy manifold and the derived batch ramp are directly suggestive for dense-retriever training, where batch size is the dominant cost knob — with the honest caveat that in contrastive training batch size plays a dual role (gradient-noise scale and negative-sample quality), and the theory captures only the first; closing that gap would itself be a nice paper. Second, the quantity $f_s(\chi)=\sum_k k^{-s}e^{-k^{-b}\chi}$ is the same "effective dimension at resolution $\chi$" object that governs PCA-truncation and quantization error for ANN indexes, and the model's $N^{1-a}$ truncation term is literally the error of truncating an embedding to $N$ dimensions. So the compute-optimal tradeoff here translates fairly naturally into an index-budget-optimal question: at fixed training-tokens $\times$ embedding-dimension, how should a dense retriever split the budget? That said, retrieval losses are contrastive/listwise and recall@$k$ is a non-smooth functional of embedding geometry, so no exponent transfers quantitatively. The honest framing is that the mechanism (noise injected at $t$ filtered by remaining LR budget with exponent $2-1/b$) and the technique (time-to-go reparameterization plus a Beltrami first integral to solve an optimal-control problem in closed form) are the transferable parts; the rest is something new to learn rather than something to apply.

title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-04

Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity

Ishaq Aden-Ali, Noah Golowich, Allen Liu, Abhishek Shetty, Ankur Moitra, Nika Haghtalab (2026) — arXiv:2602.04863

Main idea. The paper asks whether the recent zoo of "subliminal" fine-tuning phenomena — a teacher that loves owls emitting random-number data that transmits owl-love, emergent misalignment from insecure code, "weird generalization" from outdated bird names — share one mechanism. The answer proposed is that they do, and that the mechanism is additive accumulation of tiny correlations in a linearly structured log-probability space. "Hidden subtext" here means: a dataset whose individual datapoints carry no visible trace of a trait (no Spanish text, no mention of elephants, nothing despotic), yet whose aggregate direction in log-probability space points at that trait, so that gradient descent on it moves the model exactly where an explicit system prompt would.

The algorithm, Logit-Linear Selection (Algorithm 1), is almost embarrassingly simple and is a selection method, not a generation method — it never writes a single token of new data. Given a real preference dataset D = {(pᵢ, rᵢ⁺, rᵢ⁻)} (they use AllenAI's tulu2.5), a teacher model M_T, and a target system prompt s, it scores each triple by how much s widens the teacher's preference margin: wᵢ = [log Pr_T(rᵢ⁺|s,pᵢ) − log Pr_T(rᵢ⁻|s,pᵢ)] − [log Pr_T(rᵢ⁺|pᵢ) − log Pr_T(rᵢ⁻|pᵢ)], then length-normalizes by the total token count of both responses, drops all wᵢ ≤ 0, and keeps the top gamma quantile (gamma = 0.05 for the animal runs, giving ~70k examples; gamma = 0.1 for the persona runs, 28,361 of 660,355). A different student is then DPO-fine-tuned on that subset with no system prompt anywhere. Examples that overtly mention the target (the animal name; text detected as the target language by fasttext) are filtered out first, so the subset looks clean.

The log-linear assumption is what makes this more than a heuristic. Following the "low logit rank" line of Golowich–Liu–Shetty, Definition 2.1 posits embeddings ψ (of system prompts) and φ (of prompt–response pairs) with |log Pr_M[r|s,p] − ⟨ψ(s), φ(p,r)⟩| ≤ ε; Fact 2.1 notes this is exactly low rank of the system-prompt × (prompt, response) log-probability matrix X_M. The load-bearing second assumption is that φ is shared across models and frozen during training, so fine-tuning only moves ψ_M(∅). Under that picture, LLS's score is ⟨ψ_ref(s) − ψ_ref(∅), φᵢ⟩ with φᵢ := φ(pᵢ, rᵢ⁺) − φ(pᵢ, rᵢ⁻) — i.e. selection keeps precisely the examples whose preference-difference vector has positive inner product with the trait direction.

Proof sketch

What is proved (Theorem C.1). Fix a reference/base model M_ref = M_T, a parameter space S all of whose members are ε-approximately linearly represented with a common φ, and assume ψ_M(∅) can realize any v in ℝᵈ (full surjectivity; they note a large-ball version works). Assume a two-sided margin on the selected set: α ≤ ρ_{M_ref,s}(pᵢ, rᵢ⁺, rᵢ⁻) ≤ Cα for all i, with α > 20C²ε and C ≥ 1 (the lower bound is free by construction, since LLS keeps only positive weights; the upper bound is the real extra assumption, justified by choosing a narrow quantile). Assume the φᵢ are C-well-behaved (Definition C.3): (C/m)·(Σᵢ|⟨v, φᵢ⟩|)² ≥ Σᵢ⟨v, φᵢ⟩² for all v — an ℓ₁/ℓ₂ comparison saying the span contains no sparse vectors, true w.h.p. for m ≥ 2d under natural distributions (they cite Litvak–Pajor–Rudelson–Tomczak-Jaegermann). Conclusion: any Δ-approximate minimizer M of the DPO loss on the selected subset, with Δ + 8βε ≤ 1/(10C)³, satisfies Corr(z_s, z_M) ≥ 1/(10C^{1.5}), where z_s is the vector of system-prompt-induced margin shifts of the base model and z_M the vector of fine-tuning-induced margin shifts. So the guarantee is a constant correlation between two coordinate vectors on the training set, not a margin on held-out behaviour.

How it is proved. Three moves. (i) Reduction to a linear proxy: Proposition C.3 (one line, by 1-Lipschitzness of log σ) shows ε-linear representation implies Assumption C.2, that the true DPO loss is within 4βε of L̂v = −(1/m)·Σ log σ(β⟨v, φᵢ⟩) at v_M = ψ_M(∅) − ψ_ref(∅). Hence a Δ-approximate DPO optimizer is a (Δ + 8βε)-approximate optimizer of a convex problem in v. (ii) A dual-certificate / improving-direction argument (Lemma C.4): because u = ψ_ref(s) − ψ_ref(∅) has ⟨u, φᵢ⟩ ≥ α on every selected point, the shift v ↦ v + u/(βα) monotonically improves every term and gains ≥ 0.2 on each index where ⟨v, φᵢ⟩ ≤ 1/(2β); so any near-optimum violates that on at most 5Δm indices. This is the key trick: selection manufactures a uniformly improving direction, which turns "the trait direction is helpful on average" into "ignoring the trait direction is strictly suboptimal." (iii) From "mostly positive" to correlation (Lemma C.5): Cauchy–Schwarz on the bad set plus well-behavedness gives Σ{A ∈ i}|⟨v, φᵢ⟩| ≤ √(5ΔC)·Σᵢ|⟨v, φᵢ⟩|, so ⟨y_u, y_v⟩ ≥ ‖y_u‖‖y_v‖/(2C^{1.5}). The final proof transfers y back to the observable z via ‖y − z‖_∞ ≤ 4ε and the α > 20C²ε condition.

Tightness and the gap. The result is a constant-factor, qualitative statement — 1/(10C^{1.5}) is certainly not tight, nothing is claimed about dimension-dependent rates, and there is no finite-sample concentration step at all (the only "sample size" condition is implicit in well-behavedness needing m ≳ 2d). More importantly, the step from the theorem's conclusion to the behaviour ("the student speaks Spanish") is explicitly informal: if the φᵢ span the embeddings of general (p, r), writing φ(p,r) = Σaᵢφᵢ gives ⟨â, z_s⟩ ≈ log Pr_ref[r|s,p] − log Pr_ref[r|p] and ⟨â, z_M⟩ ≈ log Pr_M[r|p] − log Pr_ref[r|p], so correlated z's suggest correlated out-of-sample log-odds. That extrapolation is heuristic. Other gaps: the theorem assumes M_T = M_ref (so cross-model transfer, the paper's headline "universality" claim, is entirely outside the theory); it assumes exact-ish optimization over all of ℝᵈ, whereas experiments use rank-64 LoRA for one epoch (animals) or 8 epochs (persona); and the empirical support for log-linearity is a singular-value power law with exponent ≈ −0.6 on a 2000 × 2000 matrix (Figure 17), which the authors concede does not give the entrywise bound of Definition 2.1, plus principal-angle overlap between models' top-100 row subspaces that is above a Gaussian baseline but "far from perfect" (Figure 18).

The most interesting part

The cleverest idea is that subselection of untouched real data is enough — and the reason it is enough is a margin argument rather than an averaging argument. Prior subliminal-learning work needed bespoke data (random number sequences) generated by the trait-conditioned teacher; LLS needs only a filter, which means the adversary's artifact is a subset of a public dataset: every example is genuine, human-written, and individually innocuous, and there is no inserted trigger to find. Appendix A then offers a genuinely unifying observation: the SFT analogue of the weight is wᵢ = log Pr_T[rᵢ|s,pᵢ] − log Pr_T[rᵢ|pᵢ], and data sampled from a system-prompted teacher automatically has large wᵢ in expectation — so Cloud et al.'s random-number subliminal learning is approximately LLS-with-rejection-sampling. The preference version is argued to be strictly more expressive because differences φ(p,r⁺) − φ(p,r⁻) span many more directions than single embeddings φ(p,r). The conjecture that random-number transmission fails across model families because the φ of semantically empty strings is not shared across models, while natural text's φ is, is a sharp, falsifiable prediction and the best idea in the paper.

Honest critique: the central claim that the selected subset is "indiscernible to the naked eye" is asserted, never tested. There is no human audit, no classifier trained to distinguish D̂ from a random subset, and no report of how the tulu2.5 source mixture (stack_exchange_paired, shp_2, ultrafeedback, hh_rlhf) shifts under a top-5% quantile — a 20× selection is an enormous distribution shift and could easily be detectable by a trivial lexical model, which would deflate the security framing considerably. The lexical-artifact confound is not ruled out: the animal filter removes only the literal animal name, not synonyms, hypernyms, or associated vocabulary ("trunk", "pachyderm", "feline", "howl"), and the language filter uses a 0.05 fasttext threshold that leaves loan words, proper nouns and typologically adjacent languages untouched — plausible shallow priming for "respond in Spanish." Responses are truncated to 20–32 tokens, with the admission that "the most striking transfer occurred with shorter responses," which is a strong hint that the effect is partly about short stylistic openers rather than the claimed global geometry. The persona results report peak evil-response rate over 11 checkpoints and 3 runs, i.e. a maximum over ~33 selections, against a sensibly chosen random-subset baseline that does control for fine-tuning-induced safety erosion; still, peak-over-trajectory is inflationary, and the LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-5-mini) on three adversarial prompts is thin. Cross-model transfer is much weaker than the prose suggests: Table 1 gives rho-correlations of 0.47–0.57 for OLMo→OLMo but 0.03–0.14 for Qwen→OLMo, with Figure 19b showing near-orthogonality, and a footnote concedes 29.9% vs 3.2% animal-mention rates. Translation runs degenerate into looping text, handled by post-hoc fasttext filters. Reproducibility is helped by released code, but learning rates were swept per student and reported as single numbers, and no seeds/variance are given for the animal and language experiments.

Broader context

Three literatures meet here. First, signal transmission through data: Cloud et al. 2025 (subliminal learning via hidden signals), Betley et al. 2025 (emergent misalignment), and the dataset-distillation tradition where a few synthetic points encode a whole training distribution — all instances of the same puzzle, that what a model extracts from data is not what a human reads in it. Second, the linear representation hypothesis (Park–Choe–Veitch and the mechanistic-interpretability line): this paper's twist is that it needs linearity only at the output-logit level, which is why it can claim cross-architecture portability without touching internals; the low-logit-rank framework of Golowich–Liu–Shetty is the direct technical ancestor and worth reading alongside. Third, poisoning and backdoors (Wan et al. on instruction-tuning poisoning; instruction-backdoor attacks) and preference learning (DPO, reward hacking): LLS is a clean-label, selection-only poisoning attack, and the claim that millions of individually negligible preference margins sum to a coherent behavioural shift is the data-centric analogue of reward hacking. Data attribution (datamodels, influence functions) is the benign cousin — same "pick a subset with a prescribed training effect" objective, but model-specific and not designed for invisibility.

A natural follow-up: build the detector the authors gesture at. Given a candidate dataset and a student model, compute the empirical mean of the preference-difference log-odds over a library of thousands of candidate system prompts (they already built 2000 with ChatGPT) and run a spectral hypothesis test for whether the selected set's aggregate direction has anomalously large projection onto any ψ(s) − ψ(∅); calibrate against random subsets of the same size. The symmetric defence would be a certified one: bound the ℓ₂ norm of (1/m)Σφᵢ, or deliberately randomize/balance selection, and prove that any trait direction is then provably uncorrelated with the optimum — the Lemma C.4 argument inverts cleanly if no vector u achieves a uniform positive margin.

Two connections to your own work are real rather than forced. The first is hard-negative mining in dense retrieval, which is structurally identical to LLS: score (q, d⁺, d⁻) triples by a cross-encoder teacher's margin and keep the top quantile. Theorem C.1's shape says that teacher-margin-based subselection provably steers the student's parameter along ψ_teacher(s) − ψ_teacher(∅) — i.e. teacher-specific idiosyncrasies (recency bias, domain preference, even an injected preference) can be distilled into a bi-encoder through negatives alone, with no individually suspicious triple, and with DPO-style preference objectives now being used for rerankers this is directly testable. Relatedly, corpus poisoning of retrieval systems normally requires inserting adversarial passages; the LLS argument suggests a selection-only attack on which documents enter a training or index-construction pipeline, invisible to content filters. The second is more theoretical: the low-logit-rank abstraction log Pr[r|s,p] ≈ ⟨ψ(s), φ(p,r)⟩ is the softmax-bottleneck story, and for generative retrieval, where log Pr[docid|q] factorizes autoregressively over a docid vocabulary, the same rank constraint bounds how many distinct query-conditioned docid orderings a GR model can represent — a clean theoretical question about docid design. And the proof's technical core — the C-well-behaved condition is an ℓ₁/ℓ₂ "no sparse vectors in the span" property, essentially a null-space-property variant from compressed sensing — will read as familiar machinery.

title: Hallucinations are inevitable but can be made statistically negligible
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-04

Hallucinations are inevitable but can be made statistically negligible

Atsushi Suzuki, Yulan He, Feng Tian, Zhongyuan Wang (2025) — arXiv:2502.12187

Main idea. The target of this paper is not hallucination itself but an inference that has been drawn from a theorem about it. Xu, Jain & Kankanhalli (2024) and Banerjee et al. (2024) showed, by diagonalization and by reduction to halting, that for a suitably adversarial ground truth every computable language model errs on infinitely many inputs; this has been widely repackaged as "hallucination cannot be stopped." Suzuki et al. argue that the step from "infinitely many bad inputs" to "a practical obstacle" is simply invalid, and they make the argument constructively rather than rhetorically: they prove a positive statement in the same discrete, assumption-free setting, so that both theorems hold simultaneously and the only thing that differs is the figure of merit. Counting the bad set gives inevitability; measuring it gives negligibility. The reconciliation is elementary once stated — an infinite subset of a countable probability space can carry arbitrarily small mass, as the integers ≥ m do under a geometric law — and the paper's real contribution is to put both results in one framework and insist that the probabilistic figure of merit is the practically meaningful one, citing Shannon's source coding theorem as the precedent where engineering has long accepted "wrong on an exponentially large but vanishing-probability set" as success. The programmatic conclusion: when an LLM hallucinates, blame the data (quality or quantity) or the algorithm (including its compute budget), never an innate computability barrier.

Proof sketch

The setting is deliberately impoverished so as to be commensurable with Xu et al. A language model is a deterministic computable map h: Σ_ → Σ_, so the hypothesis class H is countable (Remark 5); the ground truth is an arbitrary acceptable output set map F₀: Σ_ → 2^{Σ_}, required only to be non-vacuous and explicitly not assumed computable (Example 1 makes the point that assuming F₀ lies in a countable class would make the problem Gold-learnable and would therefore be question-begging). Theorem 8 is a strengthened restatement of Xu et al.: there is a single F₀, independent of h, on which every h in H errs infinitely often. The proof (Appendix B.1) fixes Gödel enumerations h₁, h₂, … and s₁, s₂, …, sets Ĩᵢ = {k : s_k ≠ h_{i'}(sᵢ) for all i' ≤ i} — nonempty since only finitely many indices are excluded — and defines ψ(i) = min Ĩᵢ, F₀(sᵢ) = {s_{ψ(i)}}. Using min rather than an arbitrary selection is what lets them dodge the axiom of choice, on which Xu et al.'s construction depends; the authors argue a theorem about physical computing devices should not be ZFC-sensitive. Note the diagonal F₀ is singleton-valued: inevitability here is driven by a zero-slack ground truth, not by anything about language.

The positive side measures error by the 0-1 risk HP_μ(h) = Pr_{S ~ μ}(h(S) ∉ F₀(S)) — probability mass on unacceptable outputs, not TV or KL, since the model is deterministic. Two assumptions carry everything. A qualified dataset (Def. 14) has Sᵢ i.i.d. from μ with Yᵢ ∈ F₀(Sᵢ) almost surely: noiseless, always-acceptable labels, i.e. sampling access to the very F₀ that is uncomputable, drawn from the same μ as deployment. Remark 15 concedes this is strong and notes it relaxes to "the modal output is acceptable." (ε_H, ε_T)-negligibility (Def. 16) is PAC-shaped: for every non-vacuous F₀ and every m ≥ m̄, HP_μ(A(T)) < ε_H with T-probability ≥ 1 − ε_T — an arbitrarily small epsilon with high probability, not a rate in n. Uniform negligibility requires one m̄ for all μ in a class; non-uniform lets m̄ depend on μ. Theorem 21 then states that some trainer A is uniformly negligible on P_CDF (distributions whose input-length CDF dominates a known CDF) for every such lower bound, and hence non-uniformly negligible on all of Δ(Σ_), since Δ(Σ_) is the union over μ of P_{CDF of len#μ}.

The witness (Prop. 26, Alg. 1) is RoteMemorizer: build a dictionary of training pairs, return the stored answer, return the empty string otherwise. Lemma 32 splits HP at a length threshold n̄ with 1 − CDF(n̄) < ½·min{ε_H, ε_T}; the long-input tail is bounded by the CDF, and the short-input head is a coupon-collector argument — order the strings of length ≤ n̄ by decreasing mass, let j_ be the index past which residual mass is < ε_H/2, use max ≥ mean to get p_{j_} ≥ ε_H/(2k) with k = |Σ^{≤n̄}|, then union-bound (1 − p_j)^m ≤ exp(−m·ε_H/(2k)). This gives m̄ = Õ(|Σ|^{n̄+1}·ε^{−1}·log(|Σ|^{n̄+1}ε^{−1})) — exponential in n̄, and admitted as such (Remark 23). Both assumptions are shown necessary. Theorem 27 (via the generalized no-free-lunch Theorem 33, with Corollary 35 and a reverse-Markov Lemma 39) kills uniform negligibility on all of Δ(Σ_): for any trainer and any m, some F₀, μ force E_T[HP] ≥ 1/2 and Pr_T(HP ≥ λ_H) ≥ (1 − 2λ_H)/(2 − 2λ_H) — so the length-CDF bound cannot be dropped. Theorem 29 (plus Lemma 38, which builds a finite X whose uniform law dominates CDF) shows the exponential sample size is near-matching, so no cleverer algorithm beats rote memorization in this assumption-free regime. What is guaranteed, precisely: small 0-1 risk _under μ*, for sample sizes exponential in the effective input length, with labels guaranteed correct. What is not: any rate, any sample-efficiency, any generalization to unseen inputs, anything about stochastic decoding, and anything off μ.

Reviewer-style critique

The logical point is correct and worth making. The reception of Xu et al. genuinely did commit the counting-vs-measure fallacy, and Theorems 27 and 29 show commendable intellectual honesty: the authors prove their own result nearly unimprovable, which amounts to proving that their framework is too weak to say anything interesting about real LLMs. One should also credit the AC-free diagonalization and the strengthening of F₀ to be learner-independent — small but real.

That said, the assumptions do almost all the work, and not where the paper suggests. The diagonal argument's bite is that F₀ is uncomputable; Definition 14 neutralizes this not by statistics but by oracle access — i.i.d. labelled draws from F₀ under the deployment measure. Given such an oracle plus a tail bound on input length, a lookup table suffices; that a memorizer memorizes is not news, and the paper's own Theorem 29 confirms there is no learning content beyond it. On the deployment side, "negligible under μ" is exactly the guarantee that hallucination research does not need. The practically relevant object is the effective query distribution produced by users searching for failures, and reweighting μ toward the (infinite, Theorem-8-guaranteed) bad set drives HP → 1 with no contradiction. Theorem 8 plus an adversary is the live concern, and this framework is silent on it; a DRO-style version — sup{HP_{μ'} : D_f(μ' ‖ μ) ≤ ρ} — would be the honest interpolation.

The dismissal of Kalai & Vempala as "out of scope, it's about distribution mismatch" is the weakest citation in the paper: their calibration/Good–Turing missing-mass lower bound applies with clean, matched data, and by restricting to deterministic maps the paper sidesteps calibration rather than answering it. Relatedly, the formalism has no abstention: the empty string counts as a hallucination, yet if some hedge string were acceptable for every input, Theorem 8 would collapse to a constant map — the inevitability result quietly needs near-singleton F₀. The Shannon analogy is also doing more rhetorical work than it earns: source-coding error is symmetric, cheap, and evaluated under the source the code was designed for, whereas a confidently asserted falsehood in a medical or legal setting is none of these.

Minor issues: Prop. 26's bound writes |Σ*|^{n̄+1} where Lemma 32 clearly gives |Σ|^{n̄+1}; the proof of Theorem 8 asserts h_k(sᵢ) ≠ f₀(sᵢ) "for any k" when the construction only gives it for k ≤ i (the conclusion survives); and Theorem 33's proof is explicitly truncated ("the rest follows the standard argument"), leaving the claimed improvement over Shalev-Shwartz Thm 5.1 for |Y| ≥ 3 unverified in-paper. The JMLR template with "Editor: My editor" suggests a preprint, not an accepted paper.

Broader context

Three strands meet here. (i) Computability-theoretic inevitability: Xu, Jain & Kankanhalli diagonalize over computable LMs against an arbitrary ground truth; Banerjee et al. reduce to halting. Both are worst-case-over-ground-truth statements and, as this paper correctly notes, say nothing about measure. (ii) Statistical inevitability, which is the stronger threat: Kalai & Vempala (STOC 2024) show that a calibrated model must place mass on falsehoods at a rate tied to the Good–Turing missing mass of "monofacts" — facts appearing once in the corpus — and the follow-up line (Kalai, Nachum, Vempala, Zhang, Why language models hallucinate, 2025) reduces generation error to binary misclassification and then argues that benchmark scoring rules reward guessing over abstention. That is the far more interesting counterweight, because it is distribution-dependent and survives a qualified dataset, i.e. it lives inside this paper's own regime and is not addressed. (iii) Learnability in the limit: Gold (1967) — superfinite classes are not identifiable from positive text — plus the computable-PAC line (Agarwal et al. 2020; Sterkenburg 2022) that the paper leans on in Remark 17. Reading Kalai–Vempala against this paper is the single most instructive pairing.

A natural follow-up is to do what Remark 30 asks for: keep the measure-theoretic framing but replace rote memorization with a structurally constrained class (compositional/hierarchical, shift-invariant, or low-intrinsic-dimension in an embedding) and derive a genuine rate in m rather than an existential m̄, and simultaneously add a reject symbol with an explicit cost to obtain a Chow-style risk–coverage theorem for hallucination. That would connect the statistical-negligibility framing directly to the abstention-incentive argument.

For your own work the connection is unusually direct. Identifier hallucination in generative retrieval is this theorem's setting with F₀(q) = the set of valid-and-relevant docids for query q — except that the acceptable set is finite and enumerable, so trie- or FM-index-constrained decoding makes the "non-existent docid" failure mode exactly zero by construction. The computability argument never gets started, which illustrates the paper's thesis better than the paper does, and it localizes the real question onto relevance, a purely statistical quantity. A rate version is also tractable there: substitute a Zipfian query-frequency law for the input-length CDF, and the head/tail decomposition of Lemma 32 reproduces, in theory, the memorization-vs-new-document generalization gap documented empirically since DSI — a 1 − ε guarantee on head queries with the tail bounded only by its mass. More broadly, the Theorem 8 / Theorem 21 contrast is the same logical shape as worst-case hardness of exact nearest neighbour in high dimension versus intrinsic-dimension- or doubling-measure-dependent guarantees for graph-based ANN: the methodological lesson — measure the bad set under the query distribution rather than counting it, and be explicit about how much adversarial reweighting your guarantee tolerates — transfers verbatim to retrieval theory.

title: Length-Induced Embedding Collapse in Transformer-based Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-04

Length-Induced Embedding Collapse in Transformer-based Models

Yuqi Zhou, Sunhao Dai, Zhanshuo Cao, Xiao Zhang, Jun Xu (2024) — arXiv:2410.24200

Main idea. Embedding models get worse as inputs get longer, and the usual explanation is the context window. This paper argues the window is a red herring: degradation persists in 4k-token models, so something in the architecture itself is length-sensitive. The diagnosis is length collapse — as n grows, the pooled embeddings of distinct texts contract toward a common point (smaller norms, higher pairwise cosine similarity), so the embedding space loses resolution exactly where documents are long. The proposed mechanism is spectral: a row-stochastic softmax attention matrix is a low-pass filter on the token signal, and the rate at which it destroys high-frequency content is governed by the spectral norm of attention restricted to the non-DC subspace. Because softmax normalizes over n competing logits, longer sequences produce flatter attention rows, hence a faster attenuation rate, hence output token maps that retain only their DC (mean) component. The remedy follows mechanically from the same quantity: divide the logits by tau < 1 before softmax, inflating logit variance, sharpening the rows, and slowing the filter. This is TempScale — one scalar applied at inference to every layer of a frozen model, no retraining.

Proof sketch

The machinery is Fourier-domain analysis of attention borrowed from Wang et al. (2022b), with DC[x] = (1/n)·11ᵀx and HC[x] = (I − (1/n)11ᵀ)x. Lemma 1 — attention is a low-pass filter in the sense that ‖HC[Aᵗz]‖/‖DC[Aᵗz]‖ → 0 — is not new; it is Perron–Frobenius applied to a positive row-stochastic matrix (eigenvalue 1 with eigenvector 1, everything else inside the unit disk), and the paper cites Wang et al. for it.

The paper's own contribution is a rate. Theorem 2 (= Theorem 6, App. B.1) states ‖HC[SA(X)]‖_F ≤ σ_a·‖W_V‖₂·‖HC[X]‖_F with σ_a := ‖(I − (1/n)11ᵀ)A‖₂. The one-line trick: write X = (1/n)11ᵀX + H; since A1 = 1 we get A11ᵀ = 11ᵀ, which the projector annihilates, so the DC part of the input contributes nothing to the HC part of the output. The rest is submultiplicativity. Iterating over layers gives geometric decay whenever σ_a‖W_V‖₂ < 1 — though this is only a per-layer contraction composed, with no handling of LayerNorm.

Theorem 3 (= Theorem 7, App. B.2) is the load-bearing claim and the weak link. Assume XW_Q, XW_K have i.i.d. Gaussian entries; then by CLT each logit p_ij = qᵢᵀkⱼ/√d is approximately N(0, σ_s²) with σ_s² = σ_q²σ_k² + C_cross. The chain is σ_a ≤ ‖I − (1/n)11ᵀ‖₂·‖A‖₂ ≤ ‖A‖_F — note this throws away the projector entirely, so the "high-frequency" bound is really just a bound on ‖A‖₂, further relaxed to Frobenius (costing up to √rank). What remains is to bound the Frobenius norm of a softmax matrix with Gaussian logits. Here exp(p) is log-normal, and the Fenton–Wilkinson approximation replaces each sum of log-normals by a single log-normal. Substituting medians yields σ_a ≤ √( n / (2√(1 + (e^{2σ_s²} − 1)^{−1})·(n−1)^{3/2} + 1) ), i.e. asymptotically O(n^{−1/4}), decreasing in n and increasing in σ_s. Defining the intrinsic temperature τ_s := 1/σ_s rewrites A_ij as a softmax at temperature τ_s over standardized logits: lower τ_s means larger σ_a means weaker filtering, which is the entire justification for TempScale.

Be clear about what is and is not guaranteed. This is monotonicity of an upper bound, not of σ_a itself — the theory cannot rule out σ_a growing with n, and indeed Figure 11(d) shows E5's measured σ_a increasing with length, which the authors call an anomaly. The independence assumptions are false in a strong way: within a row all logits share qᵢ, and real trained attention has positional locality and attention sinks, so rows stay peaked and entropy grows far more slowly than the i.i.d. Gaussian model predicts. Fenton is a point approximation, not a bound, so Eqn. 15 is formally an approximation dressed as an inequality. Corollary 4 (Theorem 8) is the shakiest: it lower-bounds cos(x₁, x₂) by α²/√((α² + α₁²)(α² + α₂²)) under the assumption that all natural-language texts share the same DC magnitude α, implicitly assumes HC[x₁]·HC[x₂] ≥ 0, equates ‖HC[xᵢ]‖² with a single maximal frequency coefficient αᵢ² (dropping a factor up to n − 1), and then asserts αᵢ shrinks "according to Theorem 3" without composing across layers or specifying pooling. Numerically the bound is not crazy — at n = 100, σ_s = 1 it gives ≈ 0.22 against measured σ_a in [0.2, 0.5] — but the asymptotics are weak and the derivation is loose at three separate steps.

Reviewer-style critique

Strengths first: the phenomenon is real and the length-stratified evaluation of Figure 1a is a clean, underused protocol; the paper measures the exact quantity its theory predicts (σ_a vs. length) rather than only a downstream proxy; Figure 2 honestly plots Theorem 2's bound against actual per-layer HC decay including a model where it misbehaves; and the sharpest evidence is directional rather than absolute — lower tau monotonically improves long queries and not short ones, and ranks long relevant documents higher. Those are predictions the theory makes and alternatives don't obviously make.

The weaknesses are serious. First, the headline gains are tiny and oracle-selected: 43.45 → 43.53 for ANCE, 52.73 → 53.00 for BGE, with tau chosen per model from {0.1, …, 1.0} by test performance across all tasks. There are no seeds, no confidence intervals, and signs flip across task families (clustering and STS regress for GIST and BGE). "Tuning-free" is a stretch when the single hyperparameter is selected on the evaluation data; a 0.53% relative average is not distinguishable from noise without variance estimates.

Second, confounding with ordinary anisotropy is essentially unaddressed. The paper carefully separates itself from depth-wise oversmoothing/rank collapse, but never from representation degeneration (Gao et al. 2019; Ethayarajh 2019; BERT-flow; whitening; SimCSE's uniformity term). "Longer texts have higher pairwise cosine similarity and smaller norms" is literally length-conditional anisotropy. Worse, the evidence offered for Corollary 4's assumption (Fig. 3) averages static word-embedding vectors with no transformer involved, and finds similarity rising with length — that is the law of large numbers converging to the corpus mean word vector at rate O(n^{−1/2}). Since mean pooling is the DC projector, this is not a nitpick: three of the five models pool by averaging, and the experiment that would disentangle the two mechanisms (mean vs. CLS vs. attention pooling, or length-bucket centering as a baseline) is missing. No isotropization baseline is run at all.

Third, the fix is a knob with a story attached. The theory says the right correction depends on σ_s, which varies by head and layer and by n; the method applies one global constant to all heads, all layers, all lengths. The length-adaptive version the theory actually implies is only sketched and never turned into a rule or evaluated end-to-end. Nothing explains why a frozen model should tolerate an inference-time attention distribution shift at all, which leaves open that the gains come from generic logit sharpening/calibration. LayerNorm — the one module that directly rescales collapsed representations — is deferred to future work.

Fourth, benchmarking is thin where it matters: only two BEIR retrieval sets (NFCorpus, SciFact, both small), and all five backbones are small 2024-era bidirectional encoders — no decoder-based embedders (E5-Mistral, GTE-Qwen, NV-Embed), which is where the field moved and where unidirectional attention changes the analysis. For the 512-window models, Figure 1a's long-text degradation is partly truncation, not collapse. Minor sloppiness: Appendix D says the "BGE" run uses gte-base-en-v1.5 while Table 5 lists bge-base-en-v1.5; x denotes both features and logits in Theorem 7.

Verdict: a compelling diagnosis and a clean spectral framing, with theory that is suggestive rather than explanatory, and an intervention whose measured benefit is below the resolution of the experiments.

Broader context

The ancestry is oversmoothing in GNNs — Li et al. (2018), Oono & Suzuki (2020), Cai & Wang's Dirichlet-energy view — transplanted to attention, where Dong, Cordonnier & Loukas (2021) showed pure attention loses rank doubly exponentially in depth, and Wang et al. (2022b, Anti-Oversmoothing in Deep ViTs via Fourier Domain Analysis) supplied exactly the DC/HC apparatus reused here. This paper's move is to rotate the axis from depth to sequence length.

Two neighbours are worth knowing. Geshkovski et al. (2023) analyze transformers as interacting particle systems and prove token clustering with rates depending on both n and inverse temperature beta — a far more rigorous version of this paper's claim, and the obvious place to look for a tight n-dependence. On the other side, Zhai et al. (2023) identify entropy collapse (attention too sharp) as a training pathology cured by constraining logit norms; the present paper identifies entropy excess as an inference pathology cured by inflating them. Same knob, opposite sign, and nobody has characterized the optimum jointly. Orthogonally, the anisotropy literature (BERT-flow, whitening, SimCSE's alignment–uniformity) is the natural control condition, and the long-context embedding line (LongEmbed, Jina v2/v3, nomic-embed, M2-BERT, late chunking) is the applied setting.

The cleanest follow-up: replace the Fenton point-approximation with a real concentration bound on ‖(I − J/n)A‖₂ for structured logits — positional decay plus an attention sink — and ask whether the n^{−1/4} decay survives. Plausibly sinks pin a constant mass on one column and the rate degrades to something much slower, which would both explain the E5 anomaly and predict which models suffer. Paired with that, a per-(layer, head) tau chosen to equalize σ_a across length buckets is the principled version of TempScale and is directly testable on a frozen model.

Three connections to your own work look genuine rather than forced. First, ANN index geometry: if long-document vectors concentrate near the dataset centroid with reduced variance, local intrinsic dimensionality rises and distance distributions concentrate exactly in that sub-population, so HNSW hubness and IVF cell imbalance should degrade recall in a length-correlated way — and PQ/RQ codebooks, fitted to global variance, will systematically under-resolve the collapsed region. Stratifying recall@k and residual quantization error by document length on BEIR/LongEmbed is a cheap experiment that no current ANN benchmark does, and a positive result reframes length collapse as an indexing fairness problem rather than an encoder problem. Second, score calibration: under MIPS rather than cosine, shrinking long-document norms translate directly into a length-dependent score bias, and the DC/HC decomposition gives you a handle on writing that bias term explicitly — a tidy theoretical-IR result on dense-retrieval length bias, which so far is mostly empirical folklore. Third, generative retrieval: semantic docids built by hierarchical k-means or RQ-VAE over document embeddings (DSI, TIGER) will inherit any length-correlated contraction as an unbalanced codebook — long documents crowding into few coarse codes — which would show up as length-correlated identifier collision and is straightforward to measure. And chunking stops being merely a context-window workaround: the theory predicts an optimal chunk length trading semantic completeness against the attenuation rate, which is a well-posed question worth formalizing.

title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-03

Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders

Siyu Chen, Heejune Sheen, Xuyuan Xiong, Tianhao Wang, Zhuoran Yang (Yale Statistics & Data Science; SJTU Antai; TTI-Chicago). arXiv:2506.14002v1, 16 June 2025 — arxiv.org/abs/2506.14002

Main idea

Sparse autoencoders have become the workhorse of mechanistic interpretability: take an LLM's internal activation x ∈ R^d, encode it into a much wider sparse code z ∈ R^M with M ≫ d, and hope each firing coordinate corresponds to one human-legible concept. The whole enterprise rests on an unexamined premise — that the features an SAE finds are the features rather than an artifact of the training run. Paulo and Belrose (2025) punctured this by showing TopK SAEs trained on identical data with different seeds learn visibly different dictionaries. Meanwhile ℓ₁-penalised SAEs suffer activation shrinkage (the Lasso bias), and every method carries a sparsity hyperparameter (λ, K) that must be hand-tuned per layer, per dataset, per model. There was, before this paper, no theorem of the form "algorithm A applied to data from model M recovers the ground-truth features."

The first move is to write down the statistical model that makes such a theorem askable. Data is X = HV ∈ R^{N×d}, where V = [v₁,…,v_n]ᵀ is the unknown monosemantic dictionary and H ∈ R^{N×n}+ holds nonnegative mixing coefficients — nonnegativity being the semantically motivated choice, since the negation of a concept direction is usually a different or contradictory concept, not the absence of one. The regime of interest is ω(1) < n < poly(d) including explicitly n > d, i.e. genuine superposition where the dictionary must be linearly dependent. "Decomposable data" (Def. 5.2) fixes normalisations (rows of H unit ℓ₂ norm, rows of V norm Θ(√d)) and imposes four conditions: (H1) row sparsity, max_ℓ ‖H{ℓ,:}‖₀ = s with s = Θ(1); (H2) non-degeneracy, ‖H_{:,i}‖₁/‖H_{:,i}‖₀ = Θ(1) for every i, so a feature's coefficient is not vanishing on average when present; (H3) low co-occurrence, ρ₂ := max_{i≠j}⟨1{H_{:,i}≠0}, 1{H_{:,j}≠0}⟩/‖H_{:,i}‖₀ ≪ n^{−1/2}; (V1) incoherence, |⟨v_i,v_j⟩|/(‖v_i‖‖v_j‖) = o(1). There is no noise term: the model is exact factorisation, with the "noise" in the recovery analysis arising endogenously from the n−1 non-target features leaking into any given neuron's gradient.

The identifiability notion (Def. 5.1) is the quietly most interesting modelling contribution. Standard dictionary learning asks for recovery up to permutation and scaling with n known. Here (H,V) is ε-identifiable in a class G if for any alternative factorisation (H′,V′) ∈ G with arbitrary hidden dimension n′ satisfying HV = H′V′, there is a permutation Q and a nonnegative block-diagonal Ω = diag(ω₁,…,ω_n) with ‖1 − cos(V, ΩQV′)‖_∞ ≤ ε. Because the blocks are disjoint and n′ ≥ n necessarily, this says: any competing dictionary is either V up to permutation and rescaling, or a refinement of it, in which each v_i is a positive combination of its own private cluster of V′ rows. That is exactly Bricken et al.'s feature splitting, promoted from an empirical curiosity to the content of an identifiability statement. Theorem 5.3 gives ε = o(1) identifiability for any decomposable X, with the aside that N ≥ n is necessary.

The algorithmic contribution is bias adaptation. The SAE is the standard three-layer tied-weight architecture with pre-bias, f(x;Θ) = Σ_m a_m w_m φ(w_mᵀ(x − b_pre) + b_m) + b_pre, trained on pure reconstruction loss — no sparsity penalty, no TopK. Sparsity is enforced instead by a controller on the biases: define each neuron's empirical activation frequency p̂m over a buffer, assign it a Target Activation Frequency (TAF) p_k, and move b_m until p̂_m ≈ p_k. Mechanically: let r_m = max{max{y∈B_m} y, 0} be the neuron's largest pre-activation over the buffer and r̃_k the group average of r_m over non-dead neurons. If p̂_m > p_k, set b_m ← max{b_m − γ₋r_m, −1}; if p̂_m < 10^{−6}, set b_m ← min{b_m + γ₊r̃_k, 0}. The biases are excluded from the gradient update entirely; r_m plays the role of the gradient and γ_± the learning rate, and both p̂m and r_m admit streaming updates, so nothing is actually buffered. Group Bias Adaptation (GBA) is the empirical variant: partition the M neurons into K equal groups with geometrically decaying TAFs p{k+1} = p_k/2, so rare and common concepts each have a cohort of neurons tuned to their frequency.

The experiments are at real scale by SAE-theory standards. Host model Qwen2.5-1.5B (base), SAEs with M = 66k neurons (≈43× expansion) on the MLP output at layers 2, 13 and 26, d = 1536, N ≈ 100M tokens from Pile GitHub and Pile Wikipedia_en, JumpReLU activation, AdamW at lr 10^{−4}, weight decay 10^{−2}, batch 8192 tokens, buffer B = 40k, bias adaptation every 50 steps, 8 epochs, one A100-80GB per run. Default GBA: K = 10 groups geometric from p₁ = 0.1 to p₁₀ = 0.001, γ_± = 0.01. Baselines: TopK (K ∈ {50,…,600}), L1 (λ ∈ {10^{−3},…,10^{−1}}), and single-group BA. Metrics: normalised ℓ₂ reconstruction loss against average fraction of activated neurons, and cross-seed Maximum Cosine Similarity over three seeds, reported as the percentage of neurons whose MCS exceeds τ ∈ [0.6, 0.9] against every other run, restricted to the top-α neurons by max activation or Z-score, α ∈ {0.3%, 0.05%}.

The results: as a single untuned point, GBA lands on the TopK-with-post-activation-sparsity frontier and strictly beats TopK-with-pre-activation-sparsity, L1, and single-group BA. The ablation shows frontier position is insensitive to K once K ≥ 10 and to the lowest target frequency once the highest is ≥ 0.1; the authors recommend highest TAF in 0.1–0.5, noting 0.5 is the natural ceiling since an unbiased neuron fires on roughly half the data. On consistency, TopK is worst, GBA clearly beats TopK, and L1 beats GBA in three of four slices — but GBA beats L1 on the top-0.05% neurons selected by maximum activation, the slice one actually reads off a dashboard. A synthetic head-to-head ((n,d,M,s) = (4096,128,16384,3)) is cleaner: GBA reaches Feature Recovery Rate ≈ 1 at an activation percentage that automatically discovers the true s = 3, whereas TopK needs its K swept to find the same point. The summary claim is that GBA is the only one of the three simultaneously on the sparsity-loss frontier, seed-consistent, and tuning-free.

The most interesting part

The clever idea is that adapting the bias converts a global, loss-scale-dependent regularisation problem into a per-neuron quantile-tracking problem — and in doing so turns the sparsity level from a tuned hyperparameter into a known, analysable constant that the proof can condition on.

Start with why ℓ₁ and TopK are hard to analyse. Under an ℓ₁ penalty the realised sparsity is the outcome of a tug-of-war between ∇L_rec and λ∇‖z‖₁, and both sides change scale as training proceeds: minibatch noise, the drift of ‖w_m‖₂, and the shrinking reconstruction residual all move the operating point. There is no time-invariant quantity you can name and carry through an induction. TopK fixes ‖z‖₀ but couples all M neurons through a global order statistic, which destroys the per-neuron independence any dictionary-learning argument wants, and makes the identity of the surviving neurons discontinuous in the weights — plausibly the mechanism behind its seed sensitivity.

Bias adaptation instead exploits a structural fact about this architecture. The pre-activation decomposes as y_m(x) = w_mᵀ(x − b_pre) + b_m, where w_m carries which direction the neuron detects and b_m carries how selective it is. These two roles are orthogonal in function, and the algorithm treats them as orthogonal in optimisation: w_m gets gradients, b_m gets a controller. The controller is a stochastic root-finder for p̂_m(b_m) = p_k, with r_m supplying a step size automatically scaled to the neuron's own pre-activation range, so no global step-size calibration is needed. The dead-neuron direction is handled asymmetrically and socially: a nearly dead neuron is revived by γ₊r̃_k, the group's average max pre-activation, because its own r_m is uninformative precisely when it never fires. The clamp to [−1,0] closes two failure modes — the upper clamp preserves selectivity, and the lower clamp both lets a handful of neurons track features more frequent than p₁ and breaks a feedback loop the authors observed where a neuron growing weights opposing a drifted pre-bias gets progressively deactivated and responds by growing its weights further.

Now the payoff for the theory, which is the real point. Because the weights are kept on the unit sphere and the features are isotropic Gaussian, a neuron's pre-activation is approximately standard Gaussian: ⟨w_m^{(t)}, x_ℓ⟩ + b ∼ N(b,1), provably for a constant number of iterations via the Gaussian conditioning argument. So the controller's fixed point is known in closed form: p = Φ(−b). That single identity is what makes the analysis tractable. The theoretical algorithm ("Modified BA") therefore replaces the controller by its fixed point: fix b < 0 once and for all, with p = Φ(−b). Every sparsity-dependent quantity then becomes an explicit function of b rather than an unknown trajectory, and the contraction rate of the central recursion turns out to be governed by precisely Φ(|b|)/(ρ₁d) — target firing rate divided by ambient dimension times maximum feature occurrence. You cannot write that ratio down for an ℓ₁-penalised SAE, because there is no b; and you cannot write it down for TopK, because the effective per-neuron threshold is a random function of the other 66,000 neurons.

The second-order payoff is neuron selectivity, both a theorem and an empirical prediction. Working out the admissible range for b gives n^{−1} ≪ p ≪ min{n^{−(1+h⋆²)/2}, d·n^{−1}}, and rewriting in terms of a feature's natural occurrence frequency f (which is Θ(1/n) in the symmetric synthetic setting), a feature of frequency f is recoverable by a neuron whose TAF lies roughly in (f, min{f^{(1+h⋆²)/2}, d·f}) — i.e. somewhat above f but below roughly √f. A neuron tuned too tight gets no gradient; one tuned too loose fires on everything and averages several features together. The paper's analogy is resonance: each group is a resonator with an intrinsic frequency, each feature a tone, and each tone is picked up by the group it resonates with. This is why GBA's exponentially spaced groups are the right design and why the high-TAF group does not swamp training, and it is confirmed empirically — the FRR heatmap over (d,p) sits below a line of slope one in the high-superposition regime, exactly as p ≪ d/n predicts, with FRR collapsing outside the band; and in the real LLM the highest-Z-score (cleanest, most bimodal) neurons cluster at activation frequency ≈ 10^{−2} rather than spreading uniformly.

A weakness worth naming at the same time: the controller is what the paper advertises, and the controller is exactly what the theory does not analyse.

Proof sketch

What is proved, precisely. Two theorems doing different jobs.

Theorem 5.3 (identifiability). For any decomposable X, with G the class of pairs satisfying Def. 5.2 at arbitrary hidden dimension n′, there exists (H,V) with V ε-identifiable in G for ε = o(1). This is deterministic — no probabilistic model on H or V, only (H1)–(H3) and (V1). The appendix version even allows an arbitrary positive diagonal row-rescaling D with DX = HV, covering row-normalised data. The proof is four steps and is short and clean. (1) Row-scale consistency: expanding ⟨H_{ℓ,:}V, H_{ℓ,:}V⟩ = Θ(‖H_{ℓ,:}‖₂²d) + o(‖H_{ℓ,:}‖₁²d) using incoherence, with ‖H_{ℓ,:}‖₂ = 1 and ‖H_{ℓ,:}‖₁ = Θ(1) from (H1)+(H2), forces D_{ℓℓ}(D′{ℓℓ})^{−1} = Θ(1). (2) Approximate pseudo-inverse: define A ∈ R^{n×N}+ by A_{iℓ} = ‖H_{:,i}‖₀^{−1}·1(H_{ℓi}≠0) — the "average over rows where feature i fires" operator.
