These differ, and the paper exhibits an eight-item counterexample (η = (0.21, 0, 0.12, 0.18, 0.19, 0, 0.16, 0.14), k = 3) where sum-aggregated scores make beam search return {1,4,7} while the true top-3 is {1,4,5}: a node whose subtree carries a lot of diffuse mass crowds out a node containing one genuinely strong item. The fix is a one-line change of supervision: label an internal node positive only if the observed y is the argmax-probability item within that node's subtree, which makes the conditional expectation of the label equal the max over the subtree — the max-heap condition holds in expectation by construction. The elegance is that max-heap consistency is obtained not by constraining the scorer but by changing what the labels mean in expectation.

Honestly assessed, the strengths are real: ablations are monotone and consistent (DTR(U) → DTR(T) → DTR(T-RL), with tree-based sampling worth 3–8% F@20 and rectification 2–4%), they hold across four datasets and all twelve tree-update iterations, DTR beats OTM by 7–19% F@20, and inference time is genuinely lowest on three of four datasets. But the weaknesses are also real. Rectification needs η_y(u), which is unknown; they estimate it with a pretrained SASRec costing 19–24% of training time. DTR(T-RL) is therefore partly a distillation of a two-tower teacher into a tree model, and the paper does not disentangle this: no ablation with a deliberately weak estimator, no "distill SASRec into TDM" control, no reported value of the estimation error. Given the modest 2–4% delta, teacher knowledge is a live alternative explanation.

Second, there is a quiet tension between the two contributions: the tree-based sampler's exactness requires exp(o_i^j) ∝ Σ_children exp(o_k^{j+1}) — the sum condition that the unrectified softmax loss induces — so rectification, which drives scores toward the max, actively degrades the sampler's unbiasedness. The paper notes this and bounds the damage, but it means the two mechanisms are theoretically at cross purposes. Third, corpora top out at 135K items against a motivation that cites billions, and the Bayes-optimality framing assumes a single label y ~ η(·|u) while evaluation is Recall/F-measure against a set of held-out items. Finally, DTR(T-RL) sometimes beats brute-force DIN, explained as the index "excluding distracting items" — that deserves a proper ceiling experiment (full softmax + exhaustive search) rather than a one-line rationalization.

Proof sketch

Two claims matter.

(i) Exact max-heap consistency implies Bayes optimality under beam search, for every k. A tree model is called top-k retrieval Bayes optimal if its returned set is always a top-k set under η. The engine is an imported theorem on Bregman-divergence losses: if a loss has the form D_ψ(z, g(s)) for strictly convex differentiable ψ and a link g that is rank-consistent with its argument, then the conditional-risk minimizer s is rank-consistent with E[z]. Multi-class cross-entropy is such a divergence, with ψ the negative entropy and g the softmax. Proposition 1 then follows by plugging in E[z^j|u] = subtree-sum and giving the eight-item counterexample. The rectified target is no longer one-hot, so they introduce a weighted-plus-constant loss and verify (a direct computation with the same ψ) that it is still a Bregman divergence — this is the key technical device, because it lets the rank-consistency theorem be reapplied verbatim to real-valued targets. Normalizing by the level-wise sum of rectified labels puts the target inside the range of softmax, satisfying the theorem's hypothesis.

Proposition 3 then upgrades per-level rank consistency to global beam-search optimality by induction over tree levels, via a lemma saying: if the level-j beam is a top-k set of the max-aggregated values, then so is the level-(j+1) beam. That lemma is by contradiction — if some surviving node i₁ beats a truly-top-k node i₂ that was dropped, then E[z̃_{i₁}] < E[z̃_{i₂}] yet o_{i₁} ≥ o_{i₂}, contradicting rank consistency, provided i₂'s parent was retained at level j. That last proviso is exactly where the max aggregator earns its keep: max telescopes across the parent–child relation (E[z̄_parent] = max over children of E[z̄_child]), so a top-k child's parent is necessarily top-k; sum does not interact with argTopk this way, which is the one-line reason sum-aggregation fails. Note the honest scope: this is an infinite-data, exact-minimizer statement. There is no calibration rate — nothing bounds the Recall lost when the surrogate risk is merely ε-suboptimal.

(ii) The sampler and the generalization bound. A result of Blanc & Rendle says the sampled-softmax gradient, with logit correction ô_i = o_i − ln(Mq_i), is unbiased iff q_i ∝ exp(o_i) — which naively costs O(|Y|). DTR instead samples a single root-to-leaf path, at each step drawing a child from the local softmax over siblings, so q_i^j is a product of sibling-local probabilities. Proposition 4 (induction on j) shows these form a valid per-level distribution, and Theorem 3 (also induction on j) shows the path product telescopes exactly into the global level-j softmax provided the sum condition above holds with a layer-uniform constant — and an appendix observes that minimizing the unrectified softmax loss makes this hold identically, since the level-wise expectations satisfy the same sum recursion and the Bregman minimizer matches them. Under rectification the condition is only approximate, and they bound the per-level bias by (j−1)ε/(1−ε), converting it to a KL bound between sampling and target distributions.

The generalization bound assembles four ingredients: a Rademacher complexity bound for the DIN class (layer-peeling plus a vector-contraction lemma, giving a factor τ = sqrt((2B−1)|Y|/(B−1)) from the node-embedding table), the standard bounded-loss Rademacher bound, a sampled-vs-full-softmax gap bounded by the KL term (whose cute step is a harmonic–geometric mean inequality used to move the log inside the expectation), and a probability-estimation term. Summing over levels gives a bound whose dominant term is 8τ²·poly/√m. Two caveats a referee should press: τ² ≈ 2|Y|, so the bound is O(|Y|/√m) and vacuous at the scales the paper motivates; and the advertised "more branches tightens the bound" buys only τ² going from 3|Y| (B=2) to 2|Y| (B→∞), a factor of 1.5 across the whole range, which cannot plausibly explain the branch-number ablation it is cited as validating.

Broader context

Tree-based retrieval sits at the intersection of extreme multi-label classification and ANN search. Its ancestry is probabilistic label trees (Jasinska–Busa-Fekete et al.) and hierarchical softmax, where a label hierarchy factorizes an intractable output distribution; TDM/JTM reinterpreted the hierarchy as a retrieval index and made both the tree and the scorer learnable. The alternative families all trade the same currency differently. ANN/MIPS over dual encoders (HNSW, ScaNN, SPANN) accepts a bilinear score in exchange for a geometry the index can exploit, with the index built after and independently of the model — ScaNN's anisotropic quantization is itself a score-aware surrogate, i.e. the same "train the index for the task" idea in a metric setting. Deep Retrieval (Gao et al. 2020) drops the tree for a learned path structure with EM-style path assignment. Generative retrieval (DSI, NCI, TIGER) replaces the index with an autoregressive decoder over semantic IDs, typically RQ-VAE codes. The direct theoretical predecessors here are Zhuo et al.'s ICML 2020 analysis of optimal tree models under beam search (OTM), which first framed tree retrieval as beam-search-aware learning with corrected pseudo-labels, and the top-k Bayes-optimality literature on which the rank-consistency theorem rests. DTR's claim to novelty is less the max-heap labeling (OTM already corrects internal-node labels) than the move from one-vs-all to a per-level softmax, plus the tree-structured sampler that makes the softmax affordable.

The connection to your work is tight, and the strongest thread is the tree/beam-search ↔ semantic-ID/autoregressive-decoding analogy. A generative retriever scoring p(d|q) = Π_t p(c_t|q, c_{<t}) and decoding with beam search is formally a tree model: codebook prefixes are internal nodes, and the prefix score Π_{t≤j} p(c_t|·) estimates exactly the sum of p(d|q) over documents in that prefix cone. That is precisely the quantity Proposition 1 shows is not beam-search consistent. So the counterexample transfers verbatim: teacher-forced token-level cross-entropy trains a generative retriever to be marginally calibrated, while beam decoding needs max-calibration, and a prefix covering many mediocre documents will outrank a prefix covering one excellent document. "Max-heap consistency for docid decoding" would be a prefix-level objective whose minimizer ranks prefixes by max_{d in cone} p(d|q) rather than the marginal — concretely, reweighting each teacher-forcing step by an indicator that the target document is the argmax within its own prefix cone, the direct analogue of their rectified label, inheriting the Bregman argument once one has a prefix-level softmax rather than a token-level one. This also reframes the index–model co-training problem: DTR's alternating step (fix model, reassign items by softmax log-likelihood under a balance constraint) is structurally the same problem as learning semantic ID assignments, with the balance constraint playing the role codebook utilization plays in RQ-VAE.

Two concrete follow-ups. First, the missing theorem: a quantitative calibration transfer — if the rectified surrogate risk is within ε of optimal, bound the beam-search Recall@k regret. The current result is all-or-nothing, and a modulus-of-calibration argument (à la Bartlett–Jordan–McAuliffe, adapted to the max-aggregated target, with the level-induction turning per-level excess risk into an H-fold error accumulation) would be the natural and genuinely new result. Second, the discrete half: cast the leaf-assignment step as a regularized balanced-assignment / entropic-OT problem (the current greedy "assign to best node, spill to second-best when capacity is hit" is a heuristic with no guarantee) and prove monotone decrease of the surrogate risk across the alternation — the paper offers no convergence statement for its outer loop at all. Both would carry straight over to semantic-ID learning, where the same capacity-constrained assignment problem is currently handled by vector-quantization heuristics. The unifying theoretical question, and the one worth taking from this paper, is algorithm-aware calibration: what is the right surrogate loss when the retrieval procedure is a fixed, non-exhaustive search algorithm rather than an argmax over the full corpus?

title: All or None: Identifiable Linear Properties of Next-token Predictors in Language Modeling
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-10-02

All or None: Identifiable Linear Properties of Next-token Predictors in Language Modeling

Emanuele Marconato, Sébastien Lachapelle, Sebastian Weichwald, Luigi Gresele (2024/2025) — arXiv:2410.23501

Main idea

The puzzle is this: linear structure in language-model representations (parallel difference vectors, linear probes, steering vectors) is reported everywhere, yet the internal geometry of a next-token predictor is radically underdetermined by what it computes — many different embedding/unembedding pairs induce exactly the same conditional distribution. So why should any particular geometric regularity be reproducible across models? The paper's answer is an identifiability argument. Here identifiability does not mean recovering ground-truth latents; it means characterizing the equivalence class of parameters that induce the same next-token distribution, and then asking which geometric properties are invariants of that class. A property is "all or none" if it holds for every member of a distribution-equivalence class or for none of them; such properties are the only ones that can legitimately be called properties of the model's distribution rather than of one training run's arbitrary coordinates.

The setting is deliberately minimal: a predictor is a pair (f, g) with f mapping contexts into R^d and g mapping tokens into R^d, with p(y|x) proportional to exp(f(x)ᵀg(y)), and f, g nonparametric so that d alone controls capacity (an appendix reduces decoder-only transformers to this form, absorbing the output bias by appending a constant 1 to f). The three contributions are: (i) a characterization of distribution-equivalence that drops both the diversity assumption of Roeder et al. (2021) / Khemakhem et al. (2020) and the requirement that the two models share a representation dimension; (ii) a reformulation of several advertised "linear properties" — linear subspaces, linear probing, linear steering — as corollaries of a single relational linearity condition; (iii) a transfer theorem showing relational linearity is all-or-none, while plain vector parallelism is not — it survives only inside a particular subspace.

Proof sketch

Fix a pivot token y₀, set g₀(y) = g(y) − g(y₀), and let F = span Im(f), G = span Im(g₀). The technical heart is Lemma 2: with M := Im(P_F P_G) and N := ker(P_F P_G)^⊥, one has dim M = dim N and, crucially, P_F P_G = P_M P_N, hence f(x)ᵀg₀(y) = (P_M f(x))ᵀ(P_N g₀(y)). Everything the distribution can see lives on these two subspaces; components of f orthogonal to M and of g₀ orthogonal to N are pure gauge. dim M is christened the effective complexity. The equivalence relation ∼EL then asks dim M = dim M̃ plus full-rank M, N with P_M f = M P_M̃ f̃, P_N g₀ = N P_Ñ g̃₀ and the pairing constraint MᵀN = P_M̃ P_Ñ. The main theorem states p_{f,g} = p_{f̃,g̃} if and only if (f,g) ∼EL (f̃,g̃) — an exact characterization, for arbitrary d, d̃, with no diversity condition. The Roeder et al. result is recovered as a corollary when diversity holds and d = d̃.

Mechanically, the right way to read this is as identifiability of a low-rank factorization. The hard direction starts with pivoting: subtracting the y₀ logit cancels log Z(x) (the gauge freedom of adding a per-context constant), leaving f(x)ᵀg₀(y) = f̃(x)ᵀg̃₀(y) — i.e. the two models factor the same logit matrix, whose rank is dim M. Since the vocabulary is finite and the spans are finite-dimensional, one can pick tokens whose g₀ values span G, stack them into a matrix, rewrite the equality in matrix form, and strip matrices by pseudo-inverse, landing exactly on P_M f(x) = M P_M̃ f̃(x) with an explicit formula for M in terms of pseudo-inverses of products of projectors. The same move with spanning sequences gives N. The device that replaces the diversity assumption is a rank lemma: if the columns of a matrix span F and M ⊆ F, then rank(P_M F) = dim M (via rank(AB) = rank(B) − dim(ker A ∩ Im B)). This converts the two linear relations into a rank sandwich that forces dim M̃ = dim M = rank(M), so M is a genuine isomorphism; the identical argument pins rank(N). Old proofs assumed spanning to hold in all of R^d; here spanning is simply defined relative to the subspace the inner product actually uses, so nothing needs to be assumed and the conclusion weakens instead.

The transfer theorem says: if the two models are ∼EL-equivalent, if f relationally linearly represents a query q on a subspace Γ (meaning P_Γ f(s⌢q) = P_Γ(A_q f(s) + a_q) for all contexts s), and if additionally Γ ⊆ N and Γ_q := Im(A_qᵀP_Γ) ⊆ M, then f̃ relationally represents q on a transported subspace. The mechanism: the pairing constraint MᵀN = P_M̃ P_Ñ is massaged into a form that makes the substitution of f̃ for f on the left-hand side linear. The conditions are not decoration: when Γ_q is not contained in M, the authors give an explicit destruction — choose the out-of-M coordinates of f to equal the squares of f̃'s coordinates, which leaves the distribution untouched (those coordinates never enter the inner product) but makes f(s⌢q) a nonlinear function of f̃(s). The negative counterpart: parallelism transfers if and only if it is parallelism within N, equivalently proportionality of log-odds log[p(y₀|s)/p(y₁|s)] = β log[p(y₂|s)/p(y₃|s)] for all s.

Reviewer-style critique

The genuine strengths: the diagnosis is correct and under-appreciated — most interpretability claims about geometry are claims about an arbitrary gauge — and the reframing of the whole question as "which functionals of (f,g) are invariant under the symmetry group of the likelihood" is clean and portable. Lifting the diversity and equal-dimension assumptions is real progress for the Roeder/ICE-BeeM line, because those assumptions silently fail whenever the unembedding span is a proper subspace (ubiquitous: tied embeddings, low-rank output heads, over-parameterized d). The explicit counterexample showing nonlinear distortions survive distribution equivalence is a nice concrete demonstration. And the honest discussion in Section 6 — that PCA-visible parallelism is exactly a property their theory does not protect, so something other than identifiability (architectural or optimization inductive bias) must be doing the work — is admirably self-undermining.

But that honesty is also the central weakness: the paper is motivated as an explanation for the ubiquity of linear properties and does not deliver one. It supplies a necessary condition and then observes that one headline phenomenon fails it. A skeptical reviewer would also press on how much mathematical content the main theorem carries. Once you accept pivoting and the projector identity, it is close to "the distribution determines the logit matrix exactly, and rank-k factorizations of a fixed matrix are unique up to GL(k)"; ∼EL is engineered to be precisely the orbit relation of that symmetry, so the iff is near-tautological and the labor is bookkeeping with pseudo-inverses. That is not fatal — the right definition is the contribution — but it should not be oversold as uncovering hidden structure.

More seriously, everything is exact. Relational linearity must hold with equality for all contexts; linear probing demands the probe's softmax reproduce the restricted conditional exactly, not merely attain high accuracy. These are measure-zero conditions, whereas every empirical result being explained (relation decoding, probe accuracies, steering success rates) is approximate and domain-restricted. There is no stability or perturbation version of the transfer theorem, and the transport map can be arbitrarily ill-conditioned, so an ε-approximate linear property in one model could in principle map to a grossly nonlinear one in an equivalent model. Until that gap is closed, the theorems license statements about idealized exact properties and essentially nothing about measurements on trained models. The realizability premise is similarly strong: a softmax over a finite vocabulary assigns positive mass to every string whereas real text distributions do not, so the model class is misspecified by construction, and distributional equality is required on all of sequence space, not on a finite sample. The subspace conditions are also not empirically checkable, since M and N depend on the span of f over the whole infinite sequence space. There are no experiments at all — defensible for a theory venue, but it means the suggestive claim of Section 6 is untested, though it would be a cheap and attractive measurement.

Broader context

The linear representation hypothesis holds that human-interpretable features are encoded as directions in activation space, with feature composition approximately additive. It underwrites most of current mechanistic interpretability practice: linear probes, concept-activation vectors, sparse autoencoders, and steering/activation-addition (including the "refusal is mediated by a single direction" result of Arditi et al.). The theoretical arm has two flavors. One posits latent-variable generative models of text and derives linearity: Park, Choe and Veitch (2024) build binary latent concepts and a causal inner product reconciling embedding and unembedding geometries; Jiang et al. (2024) derive linear representations from assumptions on the data-generating process. The other is identifiability theory, descended from nonlinear ICA with auxiliary variables (Hyvärinen et al.; Khemakhem et al.'s ICE-BeeM) and from Roeder, Metz and Kingma's observation that discriminative models with inner-product heads identify representations up to an invertible linear map. This paper sits squarely in the second camp and is deliberately agnostic about latents, which is why it can say whether linearity transfers but not why it arises; combining the two is the obvious open problem the authors name.

The most valuable concrete follow-up is the approximate theory. One wants the main theorem with slack: if log-likelihoods agree to within ε uniformly, then the subspaces M, M̃ (and N, Ñ) are close in principal angle and the transport maps are well-conditioned — a Davis–Kahan / Wedin sin-Θ argument on the logit matrix, since dim M is just its rank and near-equal distributions mean near-equal matrices. That would turn all-or-none into a quantitative "mostly-or-barely" statement and would, for the first time, let the framework speak to measured probe accuracies and steering strengths.

For your own work the connection is real rather than forced, in two places. First, dim M is literally the rank of the score matrix of a dual encoder, so this is the identifiability-side companion to the rank-bottleneck analyses of bi-encoder retrieval (the softmax-bottleneck argument, Luan et al.'s capacity analysis of sparse/dense/attentional retrievers): "effective complexity" is a property of the retrieval distribution, not of the chosen embedding width. Second, and more pointedly for vector search: the theory says only the bilinear form q(x)ᵀd(y) is determined by retrieval behavior, and only on the subspaces M, N. Everything else about embedding geometry — norms, cosine similarities, cluster structure, isotropy, the error profile of product quantization, the graph an HNSW index builds — is gauge-dependent, a property of one trained checkpoint rather than of the ranking function it implements. That reframes a lot of embedding-geometry folklore and suggests a sharp question: which ANN index-quality proxies are invariant under GL(k) acting on the retained subspace, and should index construction therefore operate on a canonicalized (whitened, rank-truncated) representative of the equivalence class? Finally, docid-based generative retrieval is literally a next-token predictor over a docid vocabulary, so the theorem applies verbatim: two DSI-style models inducing the same docid distribution are ∼EL-equivalent, and relational linearity becomes the precise question of whether appending an instruction or a relation to a query acts affinely on the context representation — a testable and, as far as I know, untested claim about generative retrievers.

title: Embeddings into Similarity Measures for Nearest Neighbor Search
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 1 October 2026

Embeddings into Similarity Measures for Nearest Neighbor Search

Andoni & Shekel Nosatzki (FOCS 2025) · https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS63196.2025.00045

Main idea

Worked from the abstract and my background knowledge only — the IEEE PDF sits behind a bot-detection wall (the stampPDF endpoint returns an HTML challenge page, not a PDF), and there is no arXiv or ECCC preprint I could find under either author's name. So read the proof-sketch section below as reconstruction of the likely technique from the stated results, not as a report of the actual proofs.

The standard pipeline for approximate nearest neighbour search in an exotic metric has two stages: embed the metric into a space where you already have a good data structure (almost always $\ell_1$ or $\ell_2$), then run LSH there. The embedding's distortion multiplies into the final approximation factor, so the whole approach is capped by how well the metric embeds — and for the two most-wanted metrics that cap has been brutally low for twenty-five years. Edit distance over length-$k$ strings embeds into $\ell_1$ with distortion $2^{O(\sqrt{\log k})}$ (Ostrovsky–Rabani 2007), and that is essentially the best known; the lower bounds (Krauthgamer–Rabani, Andoni–Krauthgamer) say $\Omega(\log k)$ distortion is unavoidable for $\ell_1$, so even the ideal $\ell_1$ embedding leaves a logarithmic loss, and nobody has closed the gap down to it.

The paper's observation is that $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ were never the point — they were just the spaces we knew how to search. What a black-box ANNS reduction actually needs is a target similarity measure with a hashing scheme, and the weighted Jaccard coefficient over $\mathbb{R}_+^m$ has one: consistent weighted sampling, which is an LSH family for weighted Jaccard with essentially the properties MinHash has for sets. Jaccard is not a metric, does not satisfy a triangle inequality in the useful direction, and is not normed — which is precisely why it has room that $\ell_1$ does not. So they define what it means to embed a metric into a similarity measure (with distortion defined appropriately, and in the average rather than biLipschitz sense), build such embeddings, and supply a generic ANNS algorithm that consumes one as a black box.

The payoff is two headline results, both exponential improvements on long-standing bounds. Edit distance over length-$k$ strings gets $\mathrm{poly}(\log k)$ approximation, down from $2^{O(\sqrt{\log k})}$ — i.e. quasi-polynomial-in-$\log k$ becomes polynomial-in-$\log k$. And $\ell_p$ over $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $p > 2$ gets $O(\log p)$ approximation, which they note is asymptotically optimal in the relevant models of computation. The $\ell_p$ result is the one I find most striking: $p > 2$ has long been the awkward regime where the $\ell_2$ toolkit degrades and the natural reduction routes through $\ell_\infty$ (Indyk's $O(\log\log d)$ approximation), so getting a bound depending only on $p$ and not on $d$ at all is a qualitative change.

The most interesting part

The conceptual move — "stop demanding a norm, demand only a hashable similarity" — is the kind of reframing that in hindsight looks obvious and in practice was not made for a quarter century. The reason it works, I think, is a dimension-counting one. An $\ell_1$ embedding must represent the metric's structure as a sum of coordinate differences, and the lower bounds for edit distance are essentially statements that shortest-path / alignment structure cannot be flattened that way without logarithmic loss. Weighted Jaccard, $J(x,y) = \sum_i \min(x_i,y_i) / \sum_i \max(x_i,y_i)$, is a ratio of two such sums, and that normalization is a genuinely different primitive: it is scale-invariant, it saturates, and it compares coordinates multiplicatively rather than additively. Alignment-style structure, where the right notion of similarity is "how much of the two objects can be matched up" rather than "how far apart are they", is a far more natural fit for a min/max ratio than for a difference of sums. Edit distance is exactly an alignment problem, so the improvement is not an accident of the proof but a sign that the target space was mismatched all along.

The second thing worth noticing is the insistence on average distortion. BiLipschitz distortion is a worst-case guarantee over all pairs, and for ANNS it is overkill: you only need the embedding to preserve the gap between "close" and "far" for the query and its neighbours, and you can afford to mangle a small fraction of pairs. Average-distortion embeddings in the Naor sense (and Andoni's own earlier work on smoothed/average embeddings for ANNS) have repeatedly beaten biLipschitz bounds for exactly this reason, and here the abstract is explicit that the distortion achieved is below the best possible biLipschitz distortion for some of these spaces — so part of the gain is definitional, not just technical. Being clear about which part of the improvement comes from the relaxed distortion notion and which from the new target space is the main thing I would want from the full paper, and it is the obvious place a reviewer would push.

Proof sketch

Reconstruction, flagged as such — I could not read the proofs.

What is claimed has three parts. (1) A definition: an embedding $\varphi : (X,d_X) \to \mathbb{R}_+^m$ has distortion $D$ into a similarity measure $\mathrm{sim}$ if, in an appropriate average sense, $\mathrm{sim}(\varphi(x),\varphi(y))$ is monotonically tied to $d_X(x,y)$ up to a factor $D$ — the right formalization is presumably something like: for a threshold $r$, close pairs ($d_X \le r$) map to similarity above $s$ and far pairs ($d_X \ge Dr$) map to similarity below $s' < s$, with the gap holding on average over a pair distribution rather than for every pair. (2) Constructions of such embeddings for edit distance and for $\ell_p$, $p>2$. (3) A black-box ANNS data structure: given any such embedding plus an LSH family for the similarity measure, solve $(r, Dr)$-approximate near neighbour.

Part (3) is the part I would expect to be routine-but-careful. Consistent weighted sampling (Ioffe, and the Manasse–McSherry–Talwar lineage) gives a hash $h$ with $\Pr[h(x) = h(y)] = J(x,y)$ for weighted Jaccard, exactly paralleling MinHash. Given a similarity gap $s$ versus $s'$, the usual AND/OR amplification over $k$ concatenated hashes and $L$ tables gives query time $n^{\rho}$ with $\rho = \log(1/s)/\log(1/s')$, so the data structure is standard once the gap is in hand. The non-obvious engineering is that Jaccard's $\rho$ depends on absolute similarity values, not just their ratio, so the embedding has to land the two thresholds in a favourable part of the range — I would guess the generic theorem is stated with the required separation as a hypothesis, and the embeddings are then tuned to meet it. The "black box" framing in the abstract suggests exactly this interface.

Part (2) for edit distance is where the real work must be, and the natural guess is that it is a recursive/hierarchical construction in the Ostrovsky–Rabani mould: decompose a string into substrings at multiple scales, and let coordinates of $\mathbb{R}_+^m$ be indexed by (scale, position-window, local pattern) with weights recording how much mass the string puts on that local pattern at that scale. Then $\min(x_i,y_i)$ naturally counts matched local structure and $\sum_i \max(x_i,y_i)$ normalizes by total mass, so weighted Jaccard computes something like "fraction of multi-scale local structure shared" — which is a soft alignment score. The improvement from $2^{O(\sqrt{\log k})}$ to $\mathrm{poly}(\log k)$ would then come from the recursion losing a constant (or $O(1)$ additive in the exponent) per level instead of compounding multiplicatively, with the ratio structure of Jaccard absorbing the normalization that forces the loss in $\ell_1$. The $2^{O(\sqrt{\log k})}$ shape in Ostrovsky–Rabani comes from optimizing a tradeoff between recursion depth and per-level loss; a target space that is insensitive to one side of that tradeoff would collapse it to polynomial. That is the mechanism I would look for first.

For $\ell_p$ with $p > 2$, the $O(\log p)$ bound with no $d$-dependence strongly suggests a $p$-stable-like or max-of-exponentials construction. A clean guess: embed $x \mapsto (|x_i|^p)_i$ or a smoothed version, so that the $\ell_p$ distance becomes a sum over coordinates of $p$-th powers and the min/max ratio reads off the fraction of $p$-th-power mass shared; since the $p$-th power sharply concentrates mass on the largest coordinates as $p$ grows, this behaves like a soft $\ell_\infty$ and the $\log p$ is the cost of the softness. The claimed optimality "in relevant models of computation" is almost certainly against the known $\Omega(\log p)$-type barriers for LSH/data-dependent hashing in $\ell_p$, i.e. a cell-probe or LSH-family lower bound rather than an unconditional one — worth checking in the paper, since "asymptotically optimal" in a restricted model is a weaker statement than it sounds.

Broader context

This is squarely in Andoni's long programme on high-dimensional ANNS: the Andoni–Indyk LSH for $\ell_2$, then data-dependent hashing (Andoni–Razenshteyn, which broke the LSH exponent barrier by letting the hash family depend on the dataset), then the hardness side (Andoni–Laarhoven–Razenshteyn–Waingarten on optimal LSH and the limits of data-dependent hashing). The embedding half of the story has its own lineage: Ostrovsky–Rabani's $2^{O(\sqrt{\log k})}$ $\ell_1$ embedding of edit distance, the $\Omega(\log k)$ lower bound of Krauthgamer–Rabani (via Khot–Naor-style Fourier arguments), and Andoni–Krauthgamer's work on smoothed and average-case edit distance, which already made the point that worst-case biLipschitz distortion is the wrong currency for search. Two things worth reading alongside: Ioffe's Improved Consistent Sampling, Weighted Minhash and L1 Sketching (2010), which is the hashing primitive that makes weighted Jaccard a usable target, and Naor's work on average distortion and its uses, which supplies the right distortion notion. The Chakrabarti–Regev and Andoni–Indyk–Pătraşcu cell-probe lower bounds are the relevant backdrop for the optimality claim.

The follow-up I would most want is a census: which other metrics have been stuck behind an $\ell_1$-embedding barrier, and do they come unstuck here? Earth Mover's Distance is the obvious candidate — it has the same alignment/transport flavour as edit distance, its best $\ell_1$ embeddings lose $O(\log d \log \Delta)$, and a min/max ratio is a very natural way to score partial transport. Ulam distance, tree edit distance, and the various Dynamic Time Warping variants are in the same family. A second direction is to ask what the right target similarity is: weighted Jaccard is one hashable similarity, but there is a whole space of them (cosine via SimHash, and more exotic ones), and the framework as stated seems to invite a general theory of "which similarity measures admit good embeddings of which metrics", which would be the real theoretical prize.

The connection to your work is as direct as it gets, and it cuts against the current grain of vector search in an interesting way. Essentially all of modern dense retrieval has been built on the assumption that the target geometry is inner product or $\ell_2$, because that is what the indexes (HNSW, IVF-PQ, ScaNN) consume — the embedding model's job is to push the task into that geometry, whatever violence that does. This paper is a theoretical argument that the choice of target geometry is itself a lever with exponential consequences, and that a non-metric, non-normed, scale-invariant similarity can be strictly more expressive as a search target while remaining just as hashable. That is a hypothesis worth taking seriously on the learned side: weighted Jaccard over a non-negative, sparse, high-dimensional representation is not far from what SPLADE and the learned-sparse-retrieval family already produce, and a min/max-ratio scoring function over sparse non-negative vectors is a plausible middle ground between the lexical-overlap behaviour that makes sparse retrieval robust and the semantic matching that makes dense retrieval strong. The theory here gives a reason to think the ratio form is doing real work rather than being a quirk of BM25-style scoring. Two caveats to keep attached: these are approximation factors for worst-case metrics, and $\mathrm{poly}(\log k)$ approximation is far looser than anything an empirical retrieval system would accept, so the transfer is conceptual (which geometry to target) rather than numerical; and the query-time guarantees come from LSH-style amplification, which in practice loses badly to graph-based indexes, so a real system would want consistent weighted sampling as a scoring primitive inside a graph index rather than as the index itself.

title: Benign Overfitting in Single-Head Attention
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 1 October 2026

Benign Overfitting in Single-Head Attention

Magen, Shang, Xu, Frei, Hu & Vardi (2025) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07746

Main idea

The benign-overfitting literature has a well-worn template: take a model whose predictor is linear (or piecewise linear) in its parameters, feed it a strong low-dimensional signal plus high-dimensional near-orthogonal noise, and show gradient descent splits the weight vector into a signal component that generalizes and a noise component that memorizes the mislabelled examples without contaminating the signal. This paper asks whether the template survives the softmax. The answer is yes, but only under a sharp condition on how loud the signal is, and the proof has to be rebuilt almost from scratch because the softmax couples all token scores multiplicatively.

The data model is classification with one informative token per sequence. Two orthogonal class means $\mu_1,\mu_2$ with $|\mu_1| = |\mu_2| = \rho$ define the clean distribution: sample $\tilde y\sim\mathrm{Unif}{\pm1}$, set the signal token $u = \mu_{1}$ or $\mu_2$ accordingly, draw $T-1$ i.i.d. noise tokens $\xi_\tau\sim\mathcal N(0, I_d - \mu_1\mu_1^\top/\rho^2 - \mu_2\mu_2^\top/\rho^2)$ — deliberately supported in the orthogonal complement of the signal plane — and place the signal at a uniformly random position. Each label is then flipped with probability $\eta < 1/2$, splitting the training set into clean indices $\mathcal C$ and noisy $\mathcal N$. Since $|\xi_\tau| \approx \sqrt d$, the SNR is $\rho/\sqrt d$. This is the Cao–Chen–Belkin–Gu / Kou et al. CNN patch model lifted from two patches to $T$ tokens.

The architecture is single-head cross-attention reduced to $f(X; v,p) = v^\top X^\top \mathcal S(Xp)$ with $v,p\in\mathbb R^d$ both trained jointly on logistic loss from zero initialization. Here $p$ replaces the key–query matrix (justified by a one-to-one correspondence between GD steps on $W$ with fixed $q$ and steps on $q$ with $W=I$), and $v$ is simultaneously value map and readout since the output dimension is 1. So the softmax produces a convex combination $r_i = \sum_\tau s_{i,\tau}x_{i,\tau}$ — a soft token selection — and $v$ linearly classifies the selected mixture.

"Benign overfitting after two gradient steps" is both literal and narrow. Because initialization is at zero, all logistic derivatives equal $-1/2$ and $\nabla_p L = 0$ at $t=0$, so $p_1 = 0$ exactly: the first step moves only $v$, and at $t=1$ the model is the uniform-average linear classifier $\tfrac1T v_1^\top\sum_\tau x_\tau$, which gets all clean training and test points right and all $n\eta$ mislabelled points wrong. The mislabelled points therefore carry almost all the loss, and the single second step both inflates their noise-token coefficients in $v$ enough to interpolate them and, for the first time, moves $p$ so attention mass piles onto the noise tokens of the mislabelled examples. Theorem 5 then gives zero training error at $t=2$ with test error $\le \eta + \exp(-\sqrt n/2) + \exp(-C_1\eta d/(c_\rho^{0.1}n^{1.5}))$.

Reviewer's critique

The genuinely hard part deserves credit first. In the linear and leaky-ReLU settings the predictor is linear in the parameters, so a signal/noise decomposition propagates through gradients with controllable error. Here $\nabla_p L$ involves the softmax Jacobian $\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal S) - \mathcal S\mathcal S^\top$, which entangles all $T$ scores, is non-convex in $p$, and saturates: near a simplex vertex gradients die exponentially. The central device, Lemma 20, is the right answer and is reusable beyond the paper. It rewrites $z^\top\mathcal S'(p)\gamma$ as a clean term proportional to the gap between the optimal token's score and the mid-range of the non-optimal scores, plus an error controlled by $\epsilon_i = \max_{\tau\ne\tau'}|\gamma_{i,\tau} - \gamma_{i,\tau'}|$, the spread among distractor scores. Remark 21 is explicit that this is what lets them avoid two unnatural crutches: Ataee Tarzanagh et al. and Vasudeva–Deora–Thrampoulidis assume all non-optimal tokens have identical scores; Jiang et al. assume one noise token dominates the others in norm. Likewise Lemma 28 ("balanced noise factor for KKT points") is crisp: at the max-margin solution $v_{mm} = \lambda_1\mu_1 + \lambda_2\mu_2 + \sum y_i\theta_i\xi_i$, complementary slackness forces $\theta_i = 0$ for every $i\in\mathcal C$ and $\theta_i = \Theta(1/d)$ uniformly over $i\in\mathcal N$ — memorization is supported exactly on the mislabelled set, nothing leaks onto clean examples. Lemma 29's $|v_{mm}|^2 = \Theta(1/\rho^2 + \eta n/d)$ then reads as an explicit budget split between generalizing and memorizing. And unlike Sakamoto–Sato, who condition on scenarios for the attention probabilities during training, and unlike Jiang et al., who allow no label noise, this paper starts at zero initialization, trains both $p$ and $v$, and assumes nothing about the trajectory.

That said, the two-step result is engineered to an uncomfortable degree. Assumption 3 pins the step size to a 2% window: $\beta\in[z, 1.02z]$ with $z = c_\beta n/(c_\rho^2 d)$, $c_\beta = C_1\sqrt{\log(c_\rho)/\eta}$, and $C_1$ itself confined to a 2% interval. Items 3 and 5 are jointly calibrated so the $t=1$ margin is $\approx +c_\beta$ on clean points and $\approx -c_\beta$ on noisy ones, which is exactly what makes the single second step do the memorization. This is a two-line-of-business calculation, not a dynamics story. Remark 13 and Figure 3 concede that with a smaller step size interpolation takes roughly 150 iterations, and that regime is not analysed; nor is $t\ge 3$, so the theorem does not even claim the benign solution is maintained. "Already after two steps" is partly an artifact of the tuned $\beta$.

Relatedly, because $p_1 = 0$ identically, the first step is literally a linear-model step and the $t=1$ generalization story is the Frei–Chatterji–Bartlett / Cao et al. argument verbatim; attention enters only through one gradient step on $p$. The attention-concentration conclusion is also weaker than the prose implies, and asymmetrically so. For mislabelled examples, $\sum_{\tau\ge2}s^{t=2}_{i,\tau}\ge 1 - 1/(1+(T-1)c_\rho^2)$ is genuine concentration on the noise tokens. For clean examples the bound is only $s^{t=2}_{i,1}\ge 1/(1+(T-1)c_\rho^{2.1})$, which decreases in $c_\rho$ and sits below the uniform value $1/T$ whenever $c_\rho > 1$; only Remark 6, in the restricted regime $c_\rho = \Theta(1)$, upgrades it to $1/T$. The test-error proof confirms this: what carries the clean test sample is that $\alpha_1^{t=2}$ is bounded away from zero polynomially in $c_\rho$ while $|\lambda_k|\rho^2 = \Theta(c_\rho^2 d/n)$ is enormous — not that the softmax has locked onto the signal.

The dimension conditions are strong and in one respect perverse. The GD result needs $d\ge Cn^2\log(n/\delta)/\eta^2$; the $\eta^{-2}$ means less label noise demands more ambient dimension, which is backwards from intuition and is an artifact of needing the mislabelled subpopulation to be statistically visible. Figure 4 shows benign overfitting at $d = 2n \ll n^2$ and the paper says the conditions on $d$ are loose. More substantively, $d\gtrsim n^2\log n$ is exactly the regime where $|\langle\xi_i,\xi_j\rangle|\lesssim\sqrt{d\log n}\ll d/n$, i.e. the noise tokens form a near-orthonormal system — which makes memorization essentially a lookup table and removes much of the geometric difficulty.

The "necessary and sufficient" framing needs a footnote too. Sufficiency is proved for GD (Theorem 5) and for both max-margin rules (Theorems 8, 10) at $\mathrm{SNR} = \Omega(1/\sqrt n)$. Necessity (Theorem 12) is proved only for the norm-constrained max-margin rule and only for $T = 2$. There is no lower bound for gradient descent, so the threshold is tight for the implicit-bias learning rule rather than for training. Also $T\le c_T$ is a constant throughout and every constant may depend on $c_T$, so nothing is said about long sequences — precisely the regime where attention-as-selection becomes interesting.

Finally, how much is this about Transformers rather than a linear model with a selection gate? Honestly, somewhat less than one would like. The noise tokens live in the exact orthogonal complement of $\mathrm{span}(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ and the class means are orthogonal and equinorm, so the decomposition $v = \lambda_1\mu_1 + \lambda_2\mu_2 + \sum\theta_i\xi_i$ is exact rather than approximate; the softmax's only job is token selection, and the analysis shows the selection is essentially a hard argmax between two score classes. No token mixing, no composition across heads or layers, no positional structure, no correlation between tokens. The appendix experiments (self-attention w.r.t. the first token, $T=5$, a 4-layer model, Gaussian init, weight decay) are useful sanity checks, but the 4-layer experiment needs roughly 20 iterations rather than 2 — again underlining how fragile the two-step claim is as a statement about real training.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Under Assumption 3 ($c_\rho\ge 6(T-1)$; $n\ge C\log(1/\delta)$; $d\ge Cn^2\log(n/\delta)/\eta^2$; $\rho = c_\rho\sqrt{d/n}$, i.e. $\mathrm{SNR} = c_\rho/\sqrt n$; $\eta\le 1/C$; the pinned step size; zero init; $2\le T\le c_T$), Theorem 5 states that with probability $1-\delta$ two GD steps interpolate all $n$ noisy labels, test error on $\mathcal D$ is at most $\eta + \exp(-\sqrt n/2) + \exp(-C_1\eta d/(c_\rho^{0.1}n^{1.5}))$ (the $\eta$ vanishing on $\mathcal D_{\text{clean}}$), and the softmax weights satisfy the asymmetric bounds above.

For the implicit-bias side, Assumption 7 relaxes to $d\ge Cn^2\log(n/\delta)$, $\rho\ge C\sqrt{d/n}$, $\eta\le 1/C$, norm budget $R\ge C\sqrt{\eta n/d + 1/\rho^2}\log(T\rho n)$. Theorem 8, for the norm-constrained max-margin rule $\arg\max_{|v|\le r,|p|\le R}\min_i y_i f(X_i;v,p)$, gives interpolation plus test error $\le\eta + \exp(-\Omega(d/n^2)) + \exp(-\Omega((1-\zeta)/\varphi - 2\log n/R))$ with $\varphi = \sqrt{\eta n/d + 1/\rho^2}$; as $R\to\infty$ the last term becomes $\exp(-\Theta(d/n))$. Theorem 10 transfers this to the genuinely min-norm rule $\min|p|^2+|v|^2$ s.t. $\min_i y_i f\ge\gamma$, via Lemma 62's equivalence with induced radii $\to\infty$. The converse, Theorem 12 under Assumption 11 ($T=2$, $d\ge Cn^2\log(n/\delta)$, $\rho\le\sqrt{d/(Cn)}$, $\eta$ an arbitrary constant in $(0,1/2)$), says the same rule still interpolates every training point but has test error $\ge 1/16$ on $\mathcal D_{\text{clean}}$ — harmful overfitting, with no decay in $n$ or $d$.

GD proof. Lemmas 76 and 19 define a "good dataset" event: $|\xi_{i,\tau}|^2\in(1\pm\kappa)d$ with $\kappa = \tilde O(1/\sqrt d)$, $|\langle\xi_{i,\tau},\xi_{j,\tau'}\rangle|\le c_D\sqrt{d\log(n/\delta)}$, and $|\mathcal C_k|,|\mathcal N_k|$ concentrated by Hoeffding. On that event, step one gives $v_1 = \lambda_1\mu_1 + \lambda_2\mu_2 + \sum_i y_i\theta_i\sum_\tau\xi_{i,\tau}$ with $\lambda_1\approx\beta(1-2\eta)/(4T)$, $\lambda_2\approx-\lambda_1$ and, crucially, $\theta_i = \beta/(2Tn)$ identical across all examples (since $\ell' = -1/2$ uniformly at zero), while $p_1 = 0$. The $t=1$ margin is $\tfrac1T\lambda_k\rho^2 + \tfrac1T\theta_j\sum_\tau|\xi_{j,\tau}|^2\approx\pm c_\beta$, cross-example inner products being negligible because $d\gg n^2\log n$. Clean points are right, mislabelled ones wrong, so their loss derivatives dominate; in step two the $|\theta_j|$ for $j\in\mathcal N$ grow faster than the $|\lambda_k|$, delivering interpolation. Simultaneously $p_2 = -\beta\nabla_p L(v_1,p_1)$ is analysed through Lemma 20, expressing the $p$-gradient via the score gap plus the distractor-spread error $\epsilon_i$ (shown small); this yields $p_2^\top(x_1 - x_\tau)\ge -2.1\log c_\rho$ on clean data and hence the softmax bounds. The clean test sample is handled on the event $|\langle x_\tau, x_{i,\tau'}\rangle|\le d/(C_2 n^{0.75})$ (controlling fresh-vs-training noise correlations), after which $y\sum_{i,\tau'}y_i\theta_i^{t=2}\xi_{i,\tau}^\top\xi_{\tau'}$ is a symmetric bounded sum and a Hoeffding tail at scale $n^{0.75}b$ gives the $\exp(-\sqrt n/2)$; the signal term $\alpha_1^{t=2}|\lambda_k|\rho^2$ dominates it.

Max-margin proof. This is the implicit-bias half, organized around decoupling two SVMs. Define the optimal token $r_i^\star = \mu_i$ for $i\in\mathcal C$ and $\xi_i$ for $i\in\mathcal N$; the $p$-SVM $p_{mm} = \arg\min|p|$ s.t. $p^\top(\mu_i - \xi_i)\ge 1$ on clean and the reverse on noisy examples, with margin $\Xi = 1/|p_{mm}| = \Theta((\eta n/d + 1/\rho^2)^{-1/2})$; and the $v$-SVM $v_{mm} = \arg\min|v|$ s.t. $y_i v^\top r_i^\star\ge 1$, margin $\Gamma = 1/|v_{mm}|$. Proposition 27 is the keystone: any $p$ whose induced token selection deviates from $r^\star$ caps the achievable label margin at $\Gamma - C\max_i(1-s_{i\alpha_i})/(|v_{mm}|^3 n\rho^2)$ — the optimal selection is strictly optimal with a quantified gap. Its proof is the bulk of the appendix: a case analysis over whether wrongly-selected tokens come from $\mathcal C$, $\mathcal N$, or both (Lemmas 30–35), each using Lemma 28's $\theta$ structure and Lemma 29's norm budget. Theorem 39 converts this into a non-asymptotic statement: comparing $p_{(r,R)}$ against the scaled candidate $Rp_{mm}/|p_{mm}|$, whose non-optimality obeys $q_i\le\exp(-R\Xi)$, gives $\epsilon_{\max} = M\exp(-R\Xi)$ with $M\le\sqrt{\rho^2+(1+\kappa)d}$, hence margins $\ge(1-\zeta)\Xi$ and $\ge(1-\gamma)\Gamma$ with $\zeta,\gamma\to0$ as $R\to\infty$. Lemmas 43–44 give the Lagrangian representation with two-sided control $\lambda_1\ge(1-\gamma)\Gamma r/\rho^2$ and $|\theta_i|\le 2\sqrt{1/\rho^2 + 5\eta n/d}\,\Gamma r/\sqrt d$ — signal coefficient bounded below, memorization coefficients bounded above, exactly the decoupling that makes the test-time signal term swamp the noise fluctuation. For $T>2$ the optimal noise token is not unique, so Definitions 45–49 introduce combined noise tokens $\bar\xi_i = \sum_\tau t_{i,\tau}\xi_{i,\tau}$ with $(1-\kappa')d/T\le|\bar\xi_i|^2\le(1+\kappa')d$ and $|\langle\bar\xi_i,\bar\xi_j\rangle|\le 2T^2\sqrt{d\log(6n^2/\delta)}$, so arbitrary convex mixtures of distractors obey the same near-orthogonality.

Where the lower bound comes from. Two ingredients. First, a margin computation: when $\rho\le\sqrt{d/(Cn)}$, Proposition 65 shows the margin-maximizing token selection is $r_i^\star = \xi_i$ for every sample, clean ones included — separating $n$ near-orthogonal noise vectors is cheaper in norm than extracting margin from a weak signal of squared norm $\rho^2\ll d/n$. So max-margin $p$ drives attention onto the noise token universally and the model becomes a pure memorizer; Lemma 74 makes this quantitative, $|\langle p_{(r,R)},\mu_j\rangle|\le 0.9(1-\zeta)R\Xi$, by contradiction from $\Xi^2/\rho^2\ge 0.1d/(n\rho^2) > 1$. Second, anti-concentration. Lemma 75 shows $p_{(r,R)}$ and the noise part $v_\xi$ are near-orthogonal, $|\langle p_{(r,R)},v_\xi\rangle|\le c < 1$, by splitting the inner product into the spread of the $\theta_i$ (bounded by $\kappa+\gamma$), a $\sqrt n$ class-count fluctuation, and a $\zeta$-plus-$\rho\sqrt{n/d}$ remainder. On a fresh sample the attention lands on $\xi'$ and the prediction sign is essentially $\mathrm{sign}(v_\xi^\top\xi')$, where $(p^\top\xi', v_\xi^\top\xi')$ is a nearly uncorrelated Gaussian pair. Lemma 79 — for unit $v,p$ with $v^\top p\le c$, $\mathbb P(v^\top X < z\mid p^\top X\in[1/C,C])\ge\tfrac12 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\tfrac{cC-z}{\sqrt{1-c^2}}$ — forces a constant error probability, and combining with $\mathbb P(\mathcal N(0,1)\in[1/C,C])\ge 1/4$ yields the $1/16$.

Broader context

Classical learning theory says a model that fits noise exactly should generalize badly; modern overparameterized models routinely do both. The sharpest early account is Bartlett, Long, Lugosi and Tsigler's 2020 PNAS analysis of minimum-norm linear regression, which characterizes benign interpolation through two effective ranks of the covariance spectrum: you need enough low-variance directions to absorb the noise, but the signal must live where the spectrum is large. Belkin's double descent is the empirical companion. The key conceptual move is that what matters is not parameter count but the implicit bias of training: GD on separable classification with logistic loss converges in direction to the max-margin solution, so "which interpolator you get" is well-posed with a geometric answer, and benign overfitting becomes a statement about that interpolator's geometry.

For networks, the two strands most worth knowing are Frei, Chatterji and Bartlett (COLT 2022) on two-layer leaky-ReLU networks with noisy nearly-orthogonal data, and its sequel Frei, Vardi, Bartlett and Srebro (COLT 2023), which derives benign overfitting directly from the KKT conditions of margin maximization — methodologically the closest ancestor of Section 4 here. On the data-model side, Cao, Chen, Belkin and Gu (NeurIPS 2022) and Kou et al. (2023) established the signal-patch-plus-noise-patch framework for two-layer CNNs that this paper lifts to $T$ tokens. On the attention side, Ataee Tarzanagh, Li, Zhang and Oymak's max-margin token selection supplies the $p$-SVM/$v$-SVM machinery and the reduction from $W$ to a single vector; Vasudeva, Deora and Thrampoulidis (2024) removed their initialization-direction assumption and gave global convergence rates but without label noise; Sakamoto and Sato (2024) attempted benign overfitting in attention but had to condition on attention-probability scenarios. This paper closes that conditioning gap while jointly training head and attention vector, and supplies a matching lower bound.

The most valuable follow-up is to make the token count grow. Everything here assumes $T = O(1)$ with constants depending on $T$, yet the regime that matters is one signal token among $T(n)$ distractors, where the softmax must act as a genuine needle-in-haystack selector. One would conjecture the threshold becomes $\mathrm{SNR} = \tilde\Omega(\sqrt{T/n})$ with norm budget $R = \Omega(\log T)$ to overcome the distractors' entropy, and Lemma 46's combined-noise-token bounds, which already carry explicit $T$ dependence, are the natural starting point. The complementary project is removing the step-size artifact: turn Lemma 20's score-gap functional into a Lyapunov function and prove a whole-trajectory result for small $\beta$, which is the only way to answer whether the benign solution persists past $t=2$.

On the IR connection, there is a real one, and it should be stated modestly. The data model is a retrieval problem embedded in a sequence: a fixed query vector, a candidate set of $T$ vectors exactly one of which is relevant, and a model that must first select the relevant candidate and then decode a label from it. The $p$-SVM is precisely the statement that a linear scoring function separates the relevant token from the distractors with unit margin in the single-relevant-document setting, and $\Xi = \Theta((\eta n/d + 1/\rho^2)^{-1/2})$ is the achievable retrieval margin, with $|v_{mm}|^2 = \Theta(1/\rho^2 + \eta n/d)$ reading as an explicit capacity split between a generalizing scorer and a memorized index. Theorem 12 is then a clean theoretical account of a retrieval failure mode: when the relevant vector's norm falls below $\sqrt{d/n}$ relative to the distractors, the norm-minimal scorer abandons retrieval altogether, because memorizing $n$ near-orthogonal distractor vectors costs less norm than separating a weak signal — soft nearest-neighbour lookup degenerating into index memorization. That is a statement about retrievability as a signal-to-distractor norm condition, with obvious resonance for vector search. What the paper does not offer is anything about ANN data structures, recall@$k$, docid geometry, or even moderately many candidates ($T$ is constant; experiments use $T\in{2,5}$). So read it primarily for technique: the $p$-SVM/$v$-SVM decoupling with $\exp(-R\Xi)$ saturation bounds is a template for analysing attention-as-lookup, and Lemma 20's score-gap decomposition is directly reusable for any softmax scorer over a candidate set whose distractors do not conveniently share a score — the generic situation in generative retrieval with a softmax over identifiers.

title: Unlocking Tokens as Data Points for Generalization Bounds on Larger Language Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 1 October 2026

Unlocking Tokens as Data Points for Generalization Bounds on Larger Language Models

Lotfi, Kuang, Amos, Goldblum, Finzi & Wilson (2024) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18158

Main idea

The setup is the two-part MDL / finite-hypothesis bound: if you can describe a predictor in $C(h)$ bits using a code fixed in advance, its empirical risk on $m$ samples certifies its risk up to a penalty of order $\Delta\sqrt{(C(h)\log 2 + \log 1/\delta)/2m}$. "Non-vacuous" means literally that the number falls below the trivial baseline — for bits-per-dimension that baseline is $\log_2 V$ (14.97 for the LLaMA tokenizer, 15.62 for GPT-2's), and for top-$k$ error it is $1-k/V$. Prior work in this lineage (Lotfi et al. 2023) treated an i.i.d. document as the data point, so $m$ was the document count, the complexity term was enormous, and only savagely compressed models — SubLoRA GPT-2s emitting word salad — came in under baseline. The bounds were non-vacuous about models nobody would use.

The move is to make the token the unit of accounting. Tokens are not i.i.d., so one cannot simply swap $m$. Instead, for a fixed $h$ the sequence $Z_i = \mathbb{E}[-\log_2 p_h(X_i\mid x_{<i})\mid x_{<i}] - (-\log_2 p_h(x_i\mid x_{<i}))$ is a martingale difference sequence with respect to the prefix filtration by construction — each term is centred given everything before it, no matter how strong the dependence between tokens. Azuma then applies and $m$ becomes the token count. That is the entire arithmetic change, and it is worth roughly $10^3$: OpenWebText has 9B tokens, Amber 1.2T, versus millions of documents. Since complexity is divided by $m$, you can afford a thousand times more description bits at the same penalty.

The payoff is that compression stops needing to be brutal. With the enlarged budget, subspace projection becomes actively harmful (it buys complexity at too high a cost in empirical risk) and plain post-training quantization suffices: non-vacuous BPD bounds for QuIP#-quantized LLaMA2 at 7B, 13B and 70B on Amber (4.28, 4.52, 6.14 bits at 2-bit precision), and for an off-the-shelf quantized GPT-2 small that generates coherent prose. Among from-scratch parametrizations, Monarch beats LoRA and Kronecker (7.65 vs 7.85 vs 8.03 BPD), and dropping subspace projection improves the bound ~2.8 bits over the previous SubLoRA number.

The bounded-loss trick matters more than it looks. NLL is unbounded, so Azuma has nothing to work with; the fix is to bound the predictor away from zero probability by mixing in a uniform distribution, $p_h = (1-\alpha)p_\theta + \alpha/V$, capping the per-token range at $\Delta = \log_2(1+(1-\alpha)V/\alpha)$ — about 18 bits at $\alpha = 0.1$, $V = 32000$. The refinement here is to make $\alpha$ a predictable function of context, emitted by a small linear head $\alpha_\theta(x_{<i})$ trained post hoc to minimize the bound itself, so confident contexts get little smoothing and $\hat\Delta = \sqrt{m^{-1}\sum_i\Delta_i^2}$ shrinks where it can. Empirically $\alpha_\theta$ concentrates around 0.05–0.15 and beats a global grid-searched $\alpha$ by a few tenths of a bit.

The crucial fine print, stated honestly in Section 4.3 but easy to miss: the left-hand side is $\frac1m\sum_i\mathbb{E}[-\log_2 p_h(X_i\mid x_{<i})\mid x_{<i}]$ — expected next-token loss under resampling of the next token, averaged over contexts actually observed in training. It is not risk on fresh contexts.

Reviewer's critique

The strongest thing here is that the martingale construction is honest and essentially free: no mixing coefficients, no dependence-graph chromatic number, no $\beta$-mixing rates to estimate. Token dependence is absorbed entirely into the conditioning, which is why the bound survives arbitrarily long-range structure. Second, because the union bound runs over the whole class with a prior fixed in advance, the hypothesis may depend on the data arbitrarily — which licenses the LLaMA experiments despite the pretraining corpus being unknown and possibly overlapping Amber. Third, the Markov-chain control in Table 5 is exactly the experiment a skeptic wants: it shows the certified 7.6 BPD is not re-deriving low-order $n$-gram statistics, since sparse $k$-th order chains cap at 10.5 and degrade past $k=2$ as their count tables become incompressible. And the top-$k$ error bounds are the cleanest results in the paper, since 0-1 loss needs no smoothing at all ($\Delta_i = 1$) and is invariant to uniform mixing, so Top-1 error $\le 47.55\%$ for 2-bit LLaMA2-7B really is a statement about the quantized argmax predictor, with a deviation term of only ~0.07.

The headline claim — "first non-vacuous bounds for models deployed in practice" — is nevertheless overstated on two counts. The certified object is the 2-bit QuIP# quantization of LLaMA2-70B, not LLaMA2-70B; nothing transfers to the fp16 weights, and the quantization gap is precisely what the compression prior exploits. More seriously, for the BPD bounds the certified object is also the $\alpha$-smoothed predictor, which with probability 5–15% per token emits a uniformly random token from a 32k vocabulary. As a density estimator that is a mild perturbation; as a deployed generator it is not deployable, and the high-quality generations in Table 9 come from the unsmoothed model. The paper never flags the mismatch.

The nature of the left-hand side deserves more prominence than Section 4.3 gives it. Readers trained on i.i.d. PAC-Bayes will read "generalization bound" as a statement about held-out data; this is about resampled continuations of training contexts, closer to an online/sequential-prediction guarantee than to classical risk. The defences offered are that the next-token distribution is high-entropy (Fig. 2), so the conditional expectation is far from the realized token and the bound is not trivially training loss; and that the bounded quantity correlates 97.9%/99.1% with GPT-2 downstream accuracy and perplexity. That correlation is four data points, computed on a proxy where the resampling distribution is LLaMA2-7B's conditional rather than the true one — suggestive decoration, not evidence. The honest reading: a legitimate and interesting quantity that is not what "generalization" conventionally denotes.

There is a technical soft spot. Azuma–Hoeffding in the form used, $\Pr(m^{-1}\sum Z_i > t) \le \exp(-2mt^2/\hat\Delta^2)$ with threshold $t(h) = \hat\Delta\sqrt{(\log 1/P(h)+\log 1/\delta)/2m}$, needs $\hat\Delta$ deterministic for fixed $h$ — otherwise the per-hypothesis failure probability $P(h)\delta$ feeding the union bound is not the probability of a well-defined event. With the token-dependent head, $\Delta_i$ is a function of the realized context, so $\hat\Delta$ is random. The ranges are predictable ($\Delta_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$-measurable), which is the right structural property, but recovering a clean tail bound from predictable ranges needs either a deterministic cap $\Delta_i \le \Delta_{\max}$ — undoing the gain from the $\alpha$ head — or a self-normalized / time-uniform inequality of the kind Chugg et al. (2023) provide. The paper cites exactly that machinery while calling it orthogonal; here it is not orthogonal, it is the fix.

On tightness: for 2-bit LLaMA2-7B on Amber the bound is 4.28 BPD against a training BPD in the high 2s, so complexity plus deviation costs ~1.3–1.6 bits. Back of envelope: ~$1.3\times10^{10}$ bits of gzipped 2-bit checkpoint over $2m = 2.4\times10^{12}$ gives $\sqrt{\cdot}\approx 0.07$, times $\hat\Delta\approx 18$ — so the 18-bit range from smoothing does almost all the damage, and a variance-adaptive inequality would be worth more than any further compression. Relatedly, the bounds get worse with scale (7B: 4.28, 70B: 6.14), so they cannot explain the phenomenon that motivates studying LLMs at all; they certify small quantized models and penalize large ones. The inference that LLaMA2-Chat "generalizes worse" is weaker than stated: at fixed bit-width the complexity terms are essentially identical, so the whole 0.26-bit gap is the chat model's higher empirical BPD on Amber-style web text — a statement about fit to this corpus after instruction tuning, not about generalization.

Two smaller points. Empirical risk is estimated from $n = 10{,}000$ tokens (another ~0.2 bits via a second Hoeffding term) while $m = 1.2$T appears in the complexity denominator — valid, but the certificate's "sample size" is almost entirely notional, measured on $10^{-8}$ of the data it invokes. And the prior's bookkeeping is thinner for the QuIP models (gzip of the checkpoint plus $2\log C(h)$) than for from-scratch runs; the $\alpha$-head parameters and the choice among 2/3/4-bit variants in Table 8 need to be inside $C(h)$ too, and it is not spelled out that they are.

Proof sketch

What is proved (Theorem 1/2). Fix a discrete class $\mathcal{H}$ and a normalized prior $P$ on it not depending on the sampled tokens. Suppose for $h\in\mathcal H$ the per-token NLL lies in $[a, a+\Delta_i]$. Then with probability $\ge 1-\delta$, simultaneously for all $h$, $$\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m \mathbb{E}\big[-\log_2 p_h(X_i\mid x_{<i})\mid x_{<i}\big] \le -\frac1m\log_2 p_h(x_{\le m}) + \hat\Delta\sqrt{\frac{\log 1/P(h)+\log 1/\delta}{2m}},$$ with $\hat\Delta = \sqrt{m^{-1}\sum_i\Delta_i^2}$ and $X_i \sim p(X_i\mid x_{<i})$ the true conditional. The left side is context-conditional expected next-token loss averaged over observed prefixes; the right is the realized sequence NLL (which telescopes exactly into the autoregressive factorization, so "empirical risk" is just the compression rate of the observed stream) plus complexity-over-tokens. With the Solomonoff prior $P(h)\le 2^{-K(h)}$ and $K(h)\le C(h)+2\log C(h)$, $\log 1/P(h)$ becomes a prefix-code length. Assumptions: bounded per-token loss (supplied by uniform mixing — prediction smoothing is load-bearing, not cosmetic), a countable class with a prior fixed before the data, and the prefix filtration. Notably there is no i.i.d. assumption and no assumption on the dependence structure.

Three steps. First, the centering trick: with $R(h,x_i,x_{<i}) = -\log_2 p_h(x_i\mid x_{<i})$, define $Z_i = \mathbb{E}[R\mid x_{<i}] - R$. Then $\mathbb{E}[Z_i\mid x_{<i}] = 0$ by construction and $Z_i$ lies in an interval of width $\Delta_i$, so ${Z_i}$ is a bounded MDS w.r.t. ${\mathcal F_{i-1}}$ — the only idea needed to escape i.i.d., and it works precisely because the quantity being bounded is itself defined conditionally. Second, Azuma–Hoeffding for each fixed $h$, with the threshold chosen so the per-hypothesis failure probability is exactly $P(h)\delta$. Third, the Occam/union step: $\sum_h P(h)\delta = \delta$ by normalization, so every hypothesis satisfies its own threshold simultaneously with probability $1-\delta$, including the data-dependent $h^*$ returned by training. Allocating the budget proportionally to the prior is what turns a union bound over an astronomically large class into an $O(C(h))$ penalty.

One engineering lemma matters for validity: the empirical risk must be computed by a model respecting the same conditional-independence structure as the data. Documents are sampled i.i.d. and concatenated with EOT tokens, so $p_{\text{data}}(x_i\mid x_{<i}) = p_{\text{data}}(x_i\mid x_k,\dots,x_{i-1})$ with $x_k$ the preceding EOT; the authors enforce the matching property on $h$ exactly via the attention mask, rather than approximately — otherwise the model's conditionals would not be conditionals of the process being bounded. A second Hoeffding bound with split failure budget handles estimating empirical risk from the $n = 10{,}000$ subsampled positions.

Broader context

The background question is Zhang et al.'s: networks that can memorize random labels should not, by uniform-convergence intuition, generalize, yet they do. The non-vacuous-bounds programme answers by abandoning uniform convergence over the full parameter space and certifying a particular trained predictor. Dziugaite & Roy (2017) did this first at scale, numerically optimizing a PAC-Bayes posterior for the first non-vacuous bound on an overparametrized net. Zhou et al. (2019) reframed the complexity term as a compressed description length — pruning plus quantization plus arithmetic coding, with the code fixed a priori so Kraft's inequality supplies a legal prior — and reached ImageNet. Lotfi et al. (2022) tightened this with subspace training; Lotfi et al. (2023) carried it to language models at the document level, the direct parent of this paper. The intellectual core is two-part MDL: total cost = bits to describe the model + bits to describe the data given the model.

That framing is also the bridge to the "LLMs are compressors" literature — Delétang et al.'s Language Modeling Is Compression shows an LLM plus arithmetic coding beats dedicated compressors, because log-loss is code length. Worth being precise about the difference: that line compresses the data given the model and ignores the model's own description length, whereas PAC-Bayes compression bounds pay for the model and then charge the residual. This paper is exactly where the two meet, since the tradeoff it tunes — Monarch vs Kronecker vs subspace, 2 vs 3 vs 4 bits — is a search over the two-part code. Also worth knowing: Dziugaite et al. on data-dependent priors, and Chugg, Wang & Ramdas (2023) on unified time-uniform PAC-Bayes, the right toolbox for the next version of this result.

The obvious follow-up is replacing Azuma with a variance-adaptive martingale inequality — Freedman, empirical-Bernstein, or a betting/e-process bound. The deviation term is dominated by $\hat\Delta\approx 18$ bits, the worst-case range induced by uniform mixing, while the conditional variance of the per-token loss is $O(1)$. A Freedman-style bound scaling with predictable quadratic variation should cut that substantially and — more interestingly — might remove the need for aggressive smoothing altogether, which would let the certified predictor coincide with the deployed one and repair the paper's weakest claim. A second direction, which the authors flag themselves, is a hybrid exploiting independence across documents and martingale structure within them, plus data-dependent priors (code only the delta from an early checkpoint).

For generative retrieval the connection is real but needs care. A DSI-style model decodes a docid token by token conditioned on a query, formally the same filtration this theorem uses, so a token-level martingale bound could in principle certify identifier decoding with $m$ = (#training queries) × (identifier length). Two things would have to change. First, the arithmetic win is much smaller: a docid is 4–32 tokens, not a 1000-token document, so tokens-over-documents buys one to one-and-a-half orders of magnitude, not three — the honest version is a hybrid bound, i.i.d. across queries and martingale within the identifier string. Second, and more fundamentally, the left-hand side is an expectation over resampled targets at observed contexts. The paper's own defence of why that is informative is that the next-token distribution is high-entropy; in retrieval the relevant docid for a query is close to deterministic, so the conditional expectation collapses onto the realized loss and the certificate degenerates toward restating the training objective. What retrieval needs is generalization to new queries — new contexts — which this theorem explicitly does not cover. A serious port would put the query-level i.i.d. structure back in and use the martingale argument only for the within-identifier decomposition.

The compression side transfers more cleanly, and is where the genuinely interesting question sits. $C(h)$ is a direct measure of how many bits the query-to-identifier map costs, and docid schemes differ enormously on exactly this axis: atomic IDs require an embedding per document, an $O(|D|\cdot d)$ table that is essentially incompressible when IDs are arbitrary, whereas hierarchical $k$-means paths or RQ-VAE semantic IDs (TIGER-style) let the map be expressed with far fewer bits because the identifier space carries the corpus's structure. The two-part code turns what the generative-retrieval literature argues empirically into something quantitative: compute $C(h)$ and the achieved decoding loss for atomic vs hierarchical vs residual-quantized identifiers and ask which minimizes description length plus residual. One caveat up front — the metric you care about is recall@$k$ under beam search over the whole identifier, which is not a per-token bounded loss, so you would need either a telescoping/union argument across decoding steps or an identifier-level loss (returning you to the document-level sample-size regime). The same bookkeeping also reads naturally for quantized ANN indices, where the "model" is a PQ/RQ codebook plus codes and the question is what a given bit budget certifies.

title: Performative Learning Theory
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 1 October 2026

Performative Learning Theory

Rodemann, Fischer-Abaigar, Bailie & Muandet (2026) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04402

Main idea

Classical learning theory assumes the sample is a passive snapshot of a fixed population. Performative prediction (Perdomo et al. 2020) breaks the "fixed" part but keeps the population view: it studies stability and optimality of repeated risk minimization on a distribution that moves in response to the deployed model, with the population treated as fully observed. This paper asks the question that falls out of combining the two: if you only ever see a finite sample, and both the sample and the population react to your predictions, what does generalization still mean, and can you bound anything?

The sample-vs-population distinction is the organizing move, and it is operational rather than cosmetic. Their running example: a routing app beta-tests a new model on San Francisco users only. Those users (the sample) reroute in response to the predictions, so the training data itself is performatively distorted, and the model is retrained on the distorted sample, repeatedly. Meanwhile the Bay Area at large has not seen the predictions — until rollout, at which point it shifts once. Those are structurally different shifts: the in-sample shift is multi-shot and observable (you can count how many of your $n$ users changed behaviour), the population shift is single-shot and unobservable (you must extrapolate the response rate). Table 1 places classical ERM, online learning and Perdomo-style PP as cells of one grid and names the four empty cells as RQ1–RQ4; RQ1 (sample only), RQ2 (population, with or without sample performativity) and RQ3 (train $T$ rounds on the sample, then $\tilde T - T$ on the population) are what they answer.

The technical content is that performativity with an unknown transition map $\mathrm{Tr}$ becomes a distributionally robust optimization problem with a data-estimated ambiguity set. They never assume a functional form for $\mathrm{Tr}$ — only $(\varepsilon,p)$-joint sensitivity, $W_p(\mathrm{Tr}(d,\theta),\mathrm{Tr}(d',\theta'))\le\varepsilon W_p(d,d') + \varepsilon|\theta-\theta'|$ — so all that is known about the post-performativity distribution is that it lies in a Wasserstein ball around the pre-performativity one. The radius is not postulated a priori (as in Xue & Sun's distributionally robust PP) but estimated: if at most $m$ of $n$ sample atoms move, each by at most the diameter $D_Z$, then $W_p(\hat d_0,\hat d_1)\le(m/n)^{1/p}D_Z$, and the population analogue uses a binomial confidence upper bound on the unobserved population response rate $s$ built from the observed $m/n$.

The min-max/min-min framing then says which element of each ball to take. Since you only know $\mathrm{Tr}$ lands somewhere in the population ball, the honest bound on deployed risk is the supremum over that ball — the population adversarially negates your prediction, the usual DRO posture. But the empirical risk you measured is also an arbitrary point in the sample ball, and bounding the gap requires the infimum there — the sample flatteringly fulfils the prediction, giving you an optimistically low training loss. So the worst case for the generalization gap is sup over the population ball minus inf over the sample ball: a min-max functional against the world and a min-min ("distributionally favorable", in Jiang & Xie's terminology) functional against your own training data. Calling retraining on such a sample an "empirical echo chamber" is the right picture: the model becomes very good at a distribution it itself manufactured. The headline consequence is monotone growth of every bound in $m/n$ — the more of the world you move, the weaker any guarantee you can extract from it — plus a corollary that retraining on distorted samples, while worsening the model's own bound, tightens the estimate of the population response rate and hence the overall guarantee.

Reviewer's critique

The genuine contributions are the conceptual decomposition and the DRO-with-estimated-radius reduction. Table 1 clarifies a literature that had been conflating "the distribution shifts" with "my training sample shifts", and separating single-shot population shift from multi-shot sample shift has real consequences. The decision to treat $\mathrm{Tr}$ as a black box and pay for it in looseness, rather than assume linearity (Kirev et al.) or best-response with explicit costs (strategic classification), is defensible, and the authors are refreshingly explicit that their restrictive assumptions (Condition 3.1, strong convexity; Condition 3.12, Lipschitz $f_\theta$) are on objects the modeller controls and can verify, not on the unknown $\mathrm{Tr}$. Theorem 3.13's proof is the technical high point: a clean import of Lee & Raginsky's dual-multiplier machinery into a two-centre setting.

The Wasserstein-ball model of performativity is weaker than it looks, in a specific way. The radius comes from a counting argument, not a cost argument: at most $m$ units move, and each is charged the full diameter $D_Z$. So the budget is $(m/n)^{1/p}D_Z$ regardless of whether the $m$ respondents changed one binary feature or teleported across the support. That is not a transport-cost model of strategic response at all; it is a corruption-fraction model with maximal per-unit displacement, closer to Huber contamination than to the manipulation-cost geometry that makes Wasserstein natural in strategic classification. Any realistic strategic agent faces a cost bounding its displacement, and that is exactly what gets thrown away. Replacing $D_Z$ by a per-unit displacement $\rho\ll D_Z$ would be a near-free improvement worth an order of magnitude.

Is the worst case so pessimistic that the bounds are near-vacuous? For RQ1 in the case study, no: 0.302 nats at $m/n\approx 0.03$ is usable. For RQ2 it is vacuous as far as I can reconstruct. With the Appendix B.3 constants ($D_Z = \sqrt{28}\approx 5.29$, $L_\ell\approx D_Z$, $L_f = 1/4$, $C_\infty(F)\approx 7.3855$, $n = 41585$) the performative term $2L_\ell R$ alone is already a few nats at $\xi = 0.01$ and well over ten nats at $\xi = 0.5$, against a logistic loss where a coin flip costs $\log 2\approx 0.69$.
