Worse, the bound is structurally non-monotone in the wrong place: the complexity term carries $L_\ell L_f R^{1-p}D_Z^p$, which for $p>1$ diverges as $R\to 0$, so Theorems 3.13 and 3.15 do not degrade gracefully to the classical ERM bound in the non-performative limit. A bound on performativity that is worst when there is almost no performativity is an artifact of the Lee–Raginsky dual-multiplier estimate and should be flagged rather than left to the reader. There is also no lower bound anywhere, so the repeated word "fundamental" for the change-vs-learn trade-off is unearned: what is shown is that these guarantees degrade in $m/n$, not that any procedure must. Given that an adversarial-$\mathrm{Tr}$ construction forcing $\Omega((m/n)^{1/p})$ excess risk looks straightforward, its absence is a real gap.

Three more specific concerns. First, the min-min side is advertised but not analysed. Footnote 3 and Section 3.2 sell distributionally favorable optimization as the dual counterpart to DRO, yet in the proof of Theorem 3.13 the infimum term is disposed of in two lines: any two measures in a ball of radius $R$ are within $2R$, hence sup $-$ inf over the same ball $\le 2L_\ell R$. That is a diameter bound; no favorable-optimization duality is used, and it is precisely the term that makes the RQ2 bound large. The self-fulfilling sample is a framing device here, not a source of technical leverage. Second, the Kantorovich–Rubinstein steps need $\ell(\cdot,\theta)$ Lipschitz _in $z$_, but $L_\ell$ is repeatedly justified as Lipschitzness _in $\theta$_ — Condition 3.1 plus compact $\Theta$, and in Appendix B.2 $L_\ell$ is computed as a bound on $|\nabla_\theta\ell| = |\sigma(\cdot)x|\le D_Z$. For logistic loss the correct $z$-Lipschitz constant is $|\theta|\le D_\Theta$, and B.2 sets $D_\Theta = 2000\sqrt5\approx 4472$, which would inflate the reported 0.302 by three orders of magnitude. (B.3 instead takes $\Theta = {|\theta|\le 1}$, fine but inconsistent with B.2, and still ignores the $y$-coordinate, across which logistic loss is not uniformly Lipschitz at all.) Third, Lemma 3.5's statement carries $\tilde L_a = (1+L_a)^{-1}$ while its own derivation produces the factor $(1+L_a)$; as stated the lemma is smaller than what the proof yields, and the case study uses $\tilde L_a = 1/3$, dividing the reported bound by three. I would also note that Lemma 3.4 is stated as a tail bound on $W_p$ with radius $(\log(C_a/\delta)/(C_b n))^{p/\nu}$, whereas Fournier–Guillin's Theorem 2 is for $W_p^p$; if so the sampling term should scale as $n^{-1/\nu}$, not $n^{-p/\nu}$ (0.18 rather than 0.012 in B.2). And the confidence levels are off by a factor: Corollary 3.8's proof invokes one event at level $\delta$ yet the statement claims $1-\delta/2$, so the "95% confidence" in Section 4.1 with $\delta = 0.1$ is really 90%.

The "retrain on distorted samples" insight survives only in weakened form. The paper is careful to say it improves guarantees, not generalization, and the mechanism is simply variance reduction in a binomial estimate. But the proof of part II pools $m_t/n$ "by treating each $m_t/n$ as an independent Bernoulli estimate of $s$" and claims effective sample size $Tn$. The $m_t$ come from the same $n$ units, sequentially shifted by a changing model; they are neither independent nor identically distributed, and performativity is exactly what destroys that independence. There is also an estimand mismatch: Lemma 3.5 needs $m = \max_t m_t$, while the pooled estimator targets the average $M_T/(Tn)$. Separately, the underlying extrapolation — that the sample's $m/n$ is an unbiased estimate of the population's $s$ — assumes San Francisco and the Bay Area respond identically, which is the very thing the sample/population distinction was introduced to problematize. And citing Brown, Cai & DasGupta (2001) for the Wald interval is awkward, since that paper's main message is that the Wald interval behaves badly, especially at small proportions like $m/n\approx 0.03$. Finally, Section 3.2's gloss that "retraining results in models that generalize worse than $\hat\theta_0$, because the excess risk bounds grow in $T$" conflates bound with quantity; the corollary statement is careful, the prose is not.

The German case study illustrates rather than validates, which the authors say outright, and the honesty is appreciated. It is nonetheless thin as evidence. Section 4.1 is the only piece using real observed shifts, and there $m = 1816$ is the count of individuals who changed at least one feature within 14 days — attributing that to the predictions requires exactly the historical prediction records the authors concede are unavailable; secular feature churn is not a performative effect. Section 4.2 is a simulation with the response hard-coded ("flip targets from jobseeking to not-jobseeking for all $\xi n$ units"), so Figure 1.3's trade-off curve is a plot of the formula with $m = \xi n$ substituted. Nothing tests whether the bounds are tight, whether $\varepsilon$ as assumed holds for this $\mathrm{Tr}$ ($\varepsilon$ is simply set to $m/n$ in B.2, with no justification), or whether the extrapolation from one state to Germany is sound. Also: an AUC of 0.60–0.65 is realistic for this domain but means the predictions barely drive the assignment, so the measured $m/n$ is only loosely coupled to the model at all.

Proof sketch

Setup. $Z = Y\times X\subset\mathbb R^\nu$ bounded with diameter $D_Z$, $\Theta$ compact, risk $R(d,\theta) = \mathbb E_{Z\sim d}\ell(Z,\theta)$, $G(d) = \arg\min_\theta R(d,\theta)$ assumed unique. The initial sample is drawn i.i.d. before any performativity. Dynamics are the stateful map $d_t = \mathrm{Tr}(\theta_t, d_{t-1})$ of Brown et al. (2022), with the stateless Perdomo map a special case; RERM sets $\hat\theta_{t+1} = G(\hat d_t)$, RRM sets $\theta_{t+1} = G(d_t)$. Assumptions: (3.1) $\ell(z,\cdot)$ $\gamma$-strongly convex, which with compact $\Theta$ gives $L_\ell$-Lipschitzness in $\theta$; (3.2) $(\varepsilon,p)$-joint sensitivity for some $1\le p\le 2$; (3.3) $\nabla_\theta\ell$ exists and is $\kappa$-Lipschitz in $\theta$ and in $z$. From (3.1)+(3.3) plus the implicit function theorem and the mean value theorem on a compact domain, $G$ is $L_a$-Lipschitz from $(\Delta, W_p)$ to $\Theta$ — the pivot that converts distribution shift into parameter shift. The performativity budget is the counting bound $W_p(\hat d_0,\mathrm{Tr}(\theta,\hat d_0))\le(m/n)^{1/p}D_Z$, with population analogue $s^{1/p}D_Z$.

Auxiliary lemmas. Lemma 3.4 (Fournier–Guillin) gives $W_p(\hat d_0,d_0)\le(\log(C_a/\delta)/(C_b n))^{p/\nu}$ w.p. $1-\delta$, for $\nu>2p$. Lemma 3.5 chains joint sensitivity along the RERM trajectory: each step contracts by $\varepsilon$, and $|\hat\theta_{t+1}-\hat\theta_t|\le L_a W_p(\hat d_t,\hat d_{t-1})$, so the trajectory telescopes into a geometric series $((\varepsilon^T-1)/(\varepsilon-1))(m/n)^{1/p}D_Z\tilde L_a$. Lemma 3.9 is the only place the population enters statistically: treat the observed $m/n$ as a Bernoulli estimate of $s$ and take a Wald upper confidence bound, $s < m/n + q(\delta)\sqrt{(m/n)(1-m/n)/n}$.

Theorem 3.7 (RQ1). Excess risk against the static $d_0$: $R(d_0,\hat\theta_T) - \inf_\theta R(d_0,\theta)\le L_\ell(\log(C_a/\delta)/(C_b n))^{p/\nu} + L_\ell L_a\frac{(\varepsilon\kappa/\gamma)^T-1}{(\varepsilon\kappa/\gamma)-1}(m/n)^{1/p}D_Z + \frac{FL_\ell}{\sqrt n}(24C_{L_2}(F) + 2\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)})$, w.p. $1-\delta/2$. Three ingredients combined by a union bound after the telescoping decomposition into $[R(d_0,\hat\theta_T) - R(\hat d_0,\hat\theta_T)] + [R(\hat d_0,\hat\theta_T) - R(\hat d_0,\hat\theta_0)] + [R(\hat d_0,\hat\theta_0) - \inf_\theta R(d_0,\theta)]$. The first bracket is Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality: $|R(d,\theta)-R(d',\theta)|\le L_\ell W_1(d,d')\le L_\ell W_p(d,d')$, closed by Lemma 3.4 — this is the step that turns shift into an additive penalty, and the reason it costs nothing in capacity is that the KR dual is a supremum over the entire $L_\ell$-Lipschitz ball, hence holds simultaneously for every $\ell(\cdot,\theta)$; the data-dependence of $\hat\theta_T$ is free. The price is the dimension-cursed $n^{-p/\nu}$ rate. The second bracket uses Brown et al.'s Lemma 2 (the ERM step of stateful PP is $(\varepsilon\kappa/\gamma)$-Lipschitz), giving another geometric series anchored by $|\hat\theta_0-\hat\theta_1|\le L_a(m/n)^{1/p}D_Z$. The third is textbook: symmetrization, McDiarmid, Talagrand contraction, Dudley's entropy integral with the $L_2$ covering integral. Covering numbers rather than Rademacher complexity are the stated choice because performative shift forces evaluation of $f_\theta$ off the support of $d_0$. Corollary 3.8 extracts the usable data-dependent form $R(d_0,\hat\theta_T) - R(\hat d_{T-1},\hat\theta_T)\le L_\ell W_p(d_0,\hat d_{T-1})$, with no capacity term at all.

Theorem 3.10 (RQ2) adds two terms of the same shape against the moving target $d_1 = \mathrm{Tr}(d_0,\hat\theta_T)$, both driven by the Lemma 3.9 radius: one for $R(d_1,\theta)-R(d_0,\theta)$ (KR again), one for $\inf_\theta R(d_0,\theta) - \inf_\theta R(d_1,\theta)$, where the Bayes-optimal parameters on the two populations are compared via $|\theta_{B,0}-\theta_{B,1}|\le L_a s^{1/p}D_Z$. The extra term is $2L_\ell D_Z(m/n + q(\delta)\sqrt{m(n-m)}/n^{3/2})^{1/p}$. Theorem 3.16 (RQ3) handles $\tilde T - T$ further RRM rounds on the population: since $\inf_\theta R(d_t,\theta) = R(d_t,\theta_{t+1})$ by definition of RRM, each round's excess risk is $\le L_\ell L_a s^{1/p}D_Z$, and the cumulative bound is Theorem 3.10's plus $(\tilde T - T + 1)$ times that — linear in the horizon, so no vanishing average.

Theorems 3.13/3.15 are the tighter results and where the DRO reduction does real work, trading the $n^{-p/\nu}$ Wasserstein rate for an $n^{-1/2}$ entropy integral. Target: the performative generalization gap $R(\mathrm{Tr}(d_0,\hat\theta_T),\hat\theta_T) - R(\mathrm{Tr}(\hat d_0,\hat\theta_T),\hat\theta_T)$. Set a common radius $R = \max{(m/n + q(\delta)\sqrt{\cdot})^{1/p}D_Z, (m/n)^{1/p}D_Z\tilde L_a}$ so both $\mathrm{Tr}(d_0,\cdot)$ and $\mathrm{Tr}(\hat d_0,\cdot)$ lie in $W_p$-balls of radius $R$ around $d_0$ and $\hat d_0$; then the gap is at most $\sup_{W_p(d_0,d)\le R}R(d,\hat\theta_T) - \inf_{W_p(\hat d_0,d)\le R}R(d,\hat\theta_T)$ — literally a min-max against the population minus a min-min on the sample. Split as (a) [sup over the $d_0$-ball $-$ sup over the $\hat d_0$-ball], two DRO functionals of equal radius, different centre, plus (b) [sup $-$ inf over the same $\hat d_0$-ball]. For (a), apply Gao–Kleywegt strong duality $\sup_{W_p(d,d_c)\le R}R(d,\theta) = \min_{\lambda\ge0}{\lambda R^p + \mathbb E_{d_c}\varphi_{\lambda,\theta}}$ with the Moreau-type regularized loss $\varphi_{\lambda,\theta}(z) = \sup_{z'}{\ell(f_\theta(x'),y') - \lambda d_Z^p(z,z')}$ (valid for u.s.c. $\ell\circ f_\theta$, hence Condition 3.12). Because the two functionals share $R$, evaluating the second at its own optimal $\hat\lambda$ and the first at the same $\hat\lambda$ makes the $R^p$ terms cancel, leaving the single empirical-process quantity $\int\varphi_{\hat\lambda,\hat\theta_T}\,d(d_0-\hat d_0)$. The key lemma — Lee & Raginsky's Lemma 1, the trick that makes the whole thing work — bounds the dual multiplier: $\hat\lambda\le L_\ell L_f R^{1-p}$, obtained by comparing $\hat\lambda R^p$ to $\lambda R^p + \sup_{t\ge0}{L_\ell L_f t - \lambda t^p}$ and optimizing at $\lambda = L_\ell L_f/pR^{p-1}$. This compactifies the dual index set, so the class $\Phi = {\varphi_{\lambda,\theta}:\lambda\le L_\ell L_f R^{1-p}, f_\theta\in F}$ can be covered: with pseudometric $|f-f'|_\infty + D_Z^p|\lambda-\lambda'|$ the process is subgaussian, Dudley's integral splits into the entropy of $F$ and that of a compact interval of length $L_\ell L_f R^{1-p}$, and $\mathfrak R_n(\Phi)\le(24/\sqrt n)(C_\infty(F) + L_\ell L_f R^{1-p}D_Z^p)$. Part (b) is bounded by the ball's diameter via KR. Total: $(48/\sqrt n)(C_\infty(F) + L_\ell L_f R^{1-p}D_Z^p) + F\sqrt{2\log(2/\delta)/n} + 2L_\ell R$. Theorem 3.15 replaces Condition 3.12 by the weaker envelope condition $\ell(f_0(x),y)\le B|x-x_0|_2^d$ for some $f_0\in F$, bounding the multiplier by $\hat\lambda\le B2^{p-1}(1+D_Z/R)^p$. Both multiplier bounds diverge as $R\to0$ for $p>1$, so neither recovers the classical ERM bound in the non-performative limit.

Broader context

Performative prediction was named and formalized by Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner and Hardt, "Performative Prediction" (ICML 2020), which is the essential reading: it introduces the decision-dependent distribution map $D(\theta)$, the performative risk, the distinction between performatively stable points (fixed points of repeated retraining) and performatively optimal points, and the $\varepsilon$-sensitivity condition under which RRM contracts to a stable point. Brown, Hod & Kalemaj (AISTATS 2022) extend this to a stateful world where today's distribution depends on both the model and yesterday's distribution — the setting adopted here, and the source of the joint-sensitivity condition and the $(\varepsilon\kappa/\gamma)$-Lipschitz ERM step. Mendler-Dünner et al., "Stochastic Optimization for Performative Prediction" (NeurIPS 2020), is the algorithmic counterpart; Cutler, Díaz & Drusvyatskiy (JMLR 2024) give the asymptotic-normality picture for stochastic approximation with decision-dependent distributions. The older, more structured ancestor is strategic classification — Hardt, Megiddo, Papadimitriou & Wootters (ITCS 2016), with Dong et al. (EC 2018) for the revealed-preferences version — where agents best-respond under an explicit manipulation cost, so the shift is derived rather than assumed. Performative prediction's contribution was to drop the agent model and keep only a Lipschitz distribution map; this paper pushes that minimalism further by not even assuming the form of the shift, only that its Wasserstein magnitude can be estimated. The third ingredient is Wasserstein DRO: Mohajerin Esfahani & Kuhn (2018) and Gao & Kleywegt (2023) for the duality, Duchi & Namkoong for the $\phi$-divergence side, and Lee & Raginsky, "Minimax Statistical Learning with Wasserstein Distances" (NeurIPS 2018), for the generalization theory of exactly this min-max functional — Theorems 3.13/3.15 are structurally Lee & Raginsky adapted to two balls with different centres. Jiang & Xie's distributionally favorable optimization is the min-min mirror image.

The most interesting follow-up is to put a cost rather than a count into the ambiguity set and then prove a matching lower bound. Replacing "at most $m$ units move, each by up to $D_Z$" with "each by at most $\rho$" gives radius $(m/n)^{1/p}\rho$ and immediately shrinks every bound by $D_Z/\rho$; $\rho$ is estimable from the same observed shifts that give $m$, and in a strategic setting it is exactly the manipulation budget. Pair that with a lower-bound construction — an adversarial $\mathrm{Tr}$ that moves $m$ units into a region where two hypotheses in $F$ disagree, forcing $\Omega((m/n)^{1/p}\rho)$ excess risk — and the change-vs-learn trade-off becomes a theorem rather than a property of one proof. A second direction: make the ambiguity set one-sided. In the job-training example the performative effect has a known sign, and a signed or monotone-coupling constraint on $\mathrm{Tr}$ should shrink the symmetric sup considerably — which is where the gap between "we know nothing about $\mathrm{Tr}$" and "we assume $\mathrm{Tr}$ is linear" actually lives. Finally, the divergence of these bounds as $R\to0$ is a well-posed technical problem: a radius-adaptive multiplier bound, or an interpolation between the KR route (good for small $R$) and the dual route (good for large $R$), would make the theory continuous at the non-performative limit.

The connection to your own area is real, and in one respect ranking is a better home for this theory than tabular job-seeker data. Ranking and recommendation are the canonical performative systems: the ranker determines exposure, exposure determines clicks, clicks become the next ranker's training data. The stateful formulation $d_t = \mathrm{Tr}(\theta_t,d_{t-1})$ is a faithful description of that loop (and Chaney, Stewart & Engelhardt's algorithmic-confounding paper, which they cite, is the empirical demonstration), and the sample-vs-population split maps directly onto a staged rollout or interleaving experiment: the treated traffic slice is the performatively distorted sample, the full user base the population that reacts once on rollout. Corollary 3.8's shape — generalization error minus training error on the shifted training distribution, bounded by $L_\ell$ times a Wasserstein transport budget — is precisely the quantity off-policy LTR needs and currently addresses only through importance weighting. Two further points in its favour: in dense retrieval the data genuinely live in a metric space, so $D_Z$, $L_f$ and the per-unit displacement $\rho$ are computable rather than nominal; and the "empirical echo chamber" diagnosis is a formal version of what the feedback-loop literature observes qualitatively — a ranker retrained on its own exposure-biased logs attains a flatteringly low training loss on a distribution it manufactured, exactly the min-min side.

Where the link is a stretch, and I would not push it: the bounds are informative only when $m/n$ is small, and in a deployed ranker essentially every logged session was shaped by the policy, so $m/n\approx1$ and both the transport budget and the $2L_\ell R$ term saturate at trivial values. To be useful in retrieval the budget has to be driven by displacement, not response count — an argument for the cost-based refinement above, not a reason the framework fails. Second, the paper's defining choice is to know nothing about $\mathrm{Tr}$, whereas off-policy LTR knows a great deal: the logging policy's propensities are recorded, which is precisely a partial model of $\mathrm{Tr}$. Using them lands you outside this framework and inside doubly-robust off-policy evaluation, where the penalty is estimation error in propensities rather than ignorance of the shift; the interesting theoretical question is the interpolation — how much of the $(m/n)^{1/p}$ penalty known propensities buy back. Third, for generative retrieval specifically, the conceptual story fits (the docid decoder's output distribution determines which documents are seen and hence which pairs enter the next training round) but the theorems do not literally apply: Condition 3.1 asks for a $\gamma$-strongly convex loss, which a seq2seq docid objective is not, and Condition 3.12's uniform Lipschitzness of every $f_\theta$ is not something you would want to assume for an autoregressive decoder. The authors' own Section 5.3 points at Mofakhami et al. as the route to dropping convexity, at the cost of stronger assumptions on $\mathrm{Tr}$; that is the direction a generative-retrieval version would have to take.

title: InfoFlow: A Framework for Multi-Layer Transformer Analysis
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 1 October 2026

InfoFlow: A Framework for Multi-Layer Transformer Analysis

Yu, Jiang, Bao & Li (2026) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17930

Main idea

The approximation theory of attention is in an awkward state: we have Jackson-type rate estimates for one self-attention layer and sharp head-count results in that setting, but essentially nothing quantitative about what depth buys you, because the single-layer techniques all reduce to "softmax-average, then feed-forward" and do not compose across layers. This paper attacks the gap from two sides — a hard separation on a concrete task, and then a deliberately coarse bookkeeping device meant to stand to the Transformer roughly as thermodynamics stands to statistical mechanics.

The separating task is worth stating, because it is not a formal-language or induction-head task but a geometric one: with tokens in $[-1,1]^3$, the target is $F(X_T) = \min_{s,t} 2(1 + \langle x(s), x(t)\rangle)$. On the sphere this is $\min_{s,t}|x(s)+x(t)|^2$, so $F$ is an all-pairs closest-pair / minimum-inner-product objective over the context — a $T^2$-sized optimization that must come out as a single real number. One attention layer gets exactly one round of pairwise comparison and must then resolve the residual $T^2$-way minimization inside its feed-forward block; two layers factor it as "each token finds its own best partner ($T$ comparisons), then CLS minimizes over the $T$ winners".

The mechanism diagnosis is the part with the most downstream value. They isolate three propagation modes — argmax retrieval (plus the token's own state via the residual), global aggregation over all positions, and position-indexed aggregation that exists only with positional encoding — and prove two negative results: a softmax head is cheaply a top-1 primitive and nothing more (reading off the $k$-th largest for $k \ge 2$ costs exponentially in $T$), and the cost of decoding a bundle of several tokens' values out of one hidden state scales exponentially in bundle size divided by embedding dimension.

InfoFlow is then a formal object, not a metaphor. It discards hidden vectors and keeps a set-valued state: to each position $t$ and layer $l$ it assigns an information set $I(t,l) \subseteq [T+1]$, initialized to ${t}$ (and $\emptyset$ for CLS), updated by one of the three modes per node. The model learns an a.e.-differentiable target $F$ iff the active index set $I_F = {t : \partial F/\partial x(t) \ne 0}$ is contained in $I(T+1, L)$ for a.e. input, and each node carries parameter cost $O(\varepsilon^{1-|I(t,l)|d/E_{l+1}})$, summed over all nodes. On top sits a comparison-counting calculus: targets get a Dimension $\beta_1$, Order $\beta'$ and Number of Comparison $N'$ defined through "Trees of Comparison", and the architecture gets a budget ($T-1$ per head, plus $|I|^{\beta_1}-1$ within each information set). Budget $\ge N'$ lower-bounds $M = \max|I(t,l)|$ and hence the parameter cost.

The most interesting part

The cleverest single move is the reduction in Theorem 2, which turns "$k$-th largest retrieval" into "max retrieval over a shortened sequence with a guaranteed non-vanishing softmax denominator". The construction pins the first $k-1$ coordinates at $1$ and confines the remaining $m = T-k+1$ free coordinates to $[0,1/2]$, so the $k$-th largest entry of the full sequence is the maximum of the free block — the task is unchanged, but the padding does all the work. It forces the unnormalized denominator $B \ge k-1$, which is exactly what lets closeness of the unnormalized sums transfer to closeness of the normalized attention output, and it is the only place $k\ge 2$ is used. Pair that with ordered, $\varepsilon$-separated grids $G_1 < \dots < G_m$ so that zeroing out coordinates where two candidates agree changes neither which entry is $k$-th largest nor the difference, and you get a clean pigeonhole on an $(n+1)$-dimensional summary cube: $N^m$ candidates, $O(N^m)$-but-coarser cells, hence two inputs whose attention summaries are $\eta$-close while their targets are $4\varepsilon$ apart. The elegance is that the hardness lives in the normalization, not in softmax's peakiness: the head cannot help averaging, and the average is a low-dimensional statistic that cannot separate order statistics beyond the one the score is aligned with.

Two honest caveats. Theorem 2 assumes the score $\rho$ is non-decreasing in the very quantity whose $k$-th largest is sought, the head is single and scalar, and the lower bound is really a Lipschitz-counting bound for a two-layer tanh net with weights bounded by 1. So it says a softmax head aligned with the ranking cannot cheaply emit rank $k$ — not that no attention mechanism can; a non-monotone score, a second head, or unbounded weights all escape the hypothesis. (The exponent is also stated inconsistently across informal theorem, formal theorem and proof: $(T-k-1)/(n+1)-1$, $(T-k)/(n+1)-1$, $(T-k+1)/(n+1)-1$.) Second, Theorem 1 is a separation at bounded head budget: $k = (T-H-1)/(H(n+1)+1) - 1$ is superconstant only when $H(n+1) = o(T)$, consistent with the known single-layer upper bound $O(\varepsilon^{-Td/E})$. So it is depth-vs-width/heads, not depth-vs-unbounded-width. There is also an asymmetry: the lower bound caps all weights at magnitude 1, while the two-layer upper bound needs inverse temperature $\beta \to \infty$ to make attention a hard argmax, treated as a free scaling factor and never charged.

As for InfoFlow itself, it is calibrated rather than derived. The update rule is a containment with no matching lower bound, Mechanism I rests on linear-probe experiments plus a theorem proved only for a restricted scalar single-head form, and the "$|I|^{\beta_1}-1$ comparisons inside an information set" budget is asserted. Its two headline predictions are validated on trained networks, which conflates approximation with optimization: the triangle-center NMSE $\to 1$ at $T \ge 32$ is equally compatible with a trainability failure.

Proof sketch

What is proved (Theorem 4 = formal Theorem 1). Domain $[-1,1]^3$, error in sup norm over the product domain. Assumptions: $|P_\phi(x(s),s)|_2 \le 1$; every weight in every FFN and every entry of $W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O$ bounded by 1; FFNs two-layer with 1-Lipschitz tanh; softmax carries a free scaling $\beta>0$. Then (i) any single-layer Transformer with $H$ heads of per-head dimension $n$ achieving $\delta \le \varepsilon$ needs $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-k})$ parameters with $k = (T-H-1)/(H(n+1)+1) - 1$, linear in $T$ for fixed $H,n$; and (ii) for every $\varepsilon$ there is a two-layer Transformer, one head per layer, per-head dimension 6, with $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ parameters achieving $\delta \le \varepsilon$. Theorem 5 is the order-statistic bound: for $M(X_T) = f_2(\sum_t e^{\rho(x(t))}f_1(x(t)) / \sum_t e^{\rho(x(t))})$ with $\rho$ non-decreasing and $f_1,f_2$ two-layer tanh nets of weights $\le 1$, sup-norm $\varepsilon$-approximation of the $k$-th largest coordinate with $k\ge 2$ forces $\Omega(\varepsilon^{1-(T-k+1)/(n+1)})$ parameters. Theorem 6 is the bottleneck encode/decode rate: $O(\varepsilon^{-T_0 d/n})$ suffices in $L^p$, $\Omega(\varepsilon^{\min(1-T_0d/n,0)})$ necessary in $L^\infty$ under bounded weights.

Lower-bound strategy. Pigeonhole plus Lipschitz, not communication complexity or VC. Fix the $H$ heads' attention-weight functions and value maps. Choose $H+1$ spherical caps that are pairwise $4L$-separated with $L = C/H$, and greedily extract, for each head, the pair $(y_i,t_i)$ maximizing its attention weight over the union of caps $\times$ unused positions. Since there are $H$ heads and $H+1$ caps, some cap contains none of the selected maximizers — this is the device that converts a head-count deficit into a blind spot. Inside that cap place $M$ points at distinct radii so any two have target values $\ge 4\varepsilon$ apart, and partition them into $T_0 = T-H-1$ buckets of size $\Theta(1/\varepsilon)$. Candidate sequences put $z(t)$ in bucket $t$ and freeze the last $H+1$ positions: candidate space $\Theta(\varepsilon^{-T_0})$. The constraint space is the post-attention summary — per head, $n$ value coordinates (a convex combination of unit vectors, hence bounded) plus the normalizer ratio — so discretizing to accuracy $\varepsilon^{k+1}$ gives only $O(\varepsilon^{-(k+1)(n+1)H})$ cells. Choosing $T_0 = (k+1)(H(n+1)+1)$ makes candidates outnumber cells, so two share a cell.

The second step is surgery. Let $J$ be the disagreement set; build $W_1,W_2$ by keeping the two candidates on $J$ and overwriting the agreeing free positions with filler. Collapsing those positions changes the denominators, so closeness is re-derived by decomposing each head's output over three blocks ($J$, overwritten, frozen tail) and bounding the difference; the frozen-tail mass satisfies $Q_5 \ge$ total$/T$, which keeps every denominator within a factor $T$ of the original and lets the normalizer-ratio bound be reused. The upshot is $|A(W_1)-A(W_2)| \le \varepsilon^{k+1}/2$, while the target reduces to $\min_{t\in J}|w(t)-(-b_1)|^2$ and so $|F(W_1)-F(W_2)| \ge 4\varepsilon$. Finally, the Lipschitz lemma — a two-layer tanh net with weights $\le 1$ separating two inputs $A$ apart by $B$ needs $\Omega(B/(A\sqrt n))$ hidden units — yields $\Omega(\varepsilon/\varepsilon^{k+1}) = \Omega(\varepsilon^{-k})$.

Two-layer construction. Everything lives in $\mathbb{R}^6$ and only one scalar nonlinearity is $\varepsilon$-dependent. Take $W_Q^\top W_K = \mathrm{diag}(-I_3,0)$ so head-1 logits are $-\tfrac19 x(s)^\top x(t)$; with $W_V = I$ and a shifting $W_O$ the output is $(x(t)/3, v(t))$, and as $\beta\to\infty$ the softmax becomes a hard argmin, giving $x(t)^\top v(t) \to \tfrac19\min_s x(s)^\top x(t)$ uniformly. The inter-layer FFN approximates $(x,y)\mapsto x^\top y$; via polarization $x_iy_i = \tfrac14[(x_i+y_i)^2-(x_i-y_i)^2]$ this reduces to approximating a smooth one-dimensional function, which a two-layer tanh net does with $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ parameters — the sole source of the $\varepsilon^{-1}$. The second layer stores $a(t) = \min_s x(s)^\top x(t)/9$ and uses a query/key matrix with a single nonzero entry so the CLS logit is $-a(t)$; another large $\beta$ makes CLS read $\min_t a(t)$, and an affine readout finishes.

Theorem 3 (decoding cost law). Achievability is explicit coding: truncate each of $m = T_0 d$ coordinates to $L = \lceil\log_2(2m/\varepsilon)\rceil$ bits via two-layer Heaviside networks over dyadic intervals, pack the $mL$ bits into the $n$ latent coordinates' binary expansions, and decode each latent coordinate as a piecewise-constant map with $2^{\lceil mL/n\rceil} = O(\varepsilon^{-m/n})$ thresholds; a smoothing lemma replaces Heaviside by tanh at arbitrarily small $L^p$ cost. The converse is again pigeonhole on a bounded-weight network's Lipschitz constant. Together with the comparison budget this drives the two predictions: $\beta_1 = \beta' = 2$, $N' = \Theta(DT^2)$ for $\sum_{i\le D}\max_{s,t}x(s)^\top A_i x(t)$ gives $h_1 \ge D$ (sharp experimentally: NMSE $10^{-5}$ at $(D,D)$ vs $10^{-3}$–$10^{-2}$ at $(D-1,D)$); and $\beta'=3$, $N' = T^3/6$ for the triangle-center target gives cost $\Omega(\varepsilon^{1-T^{2/3}/(6LE)})$, super-polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ for fixed depth and width. The $\Omega(T^3)$ comparison lower bound is itself a nice measure-theoretic argument: the tie set of two triples is a codimension-1 manifold, any other pair's tie manifold meets it in codimension 2, and finitely many hypersurfaces cannot reproduce the induced partition, so every unordered triple must appear as a leaf.

Broader context

Expressivity theory of attention has split into two mostly disjoint traditions. The combinatorial/computational one asks what Transformers compute as circuits or protocols: Hahn (2020) on hard limits of self-attention; Sanford, Hsu and Telgarsky (2023) on the canonical sparse-averaging separation and its sequels on induction heads and on parallel computation / logarithmic depth; Bhattamishra and Hahn on formal languages; the chain-of-thought expressivity results (Merrill–Sabharwal, Li et al.) as the same tradition with serial computation added. In parallel, interpretability gave us induction heads (Elhage et al., Olsson et al.) and the "retrieval head" line. The approximation-theoretic tradition — Yun et al.'s universality, then Qianxiao Li's group with Jiang–Li (2024) on Jackson-type rates governed by a low-rank pairwise-coupling complexity measure, and Yu et al. (2026) on head count — instead measures parameters for $\varepsilon$-accuracy in a function norm. This paper sits in the second but imports the separation agenda from the first, and its real contribution may be that the two negative mechanisms give the empirical retrieval-head picture a quantitative price tag: a head is a top-1 primitive, depth composes top-1s, and bundling costs $\exp(|\text{bundle}|/E)$.

Read alongside: Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky (same phenomenon, communication-complexity proofs, bit-precision rather than $\varepsilon$-accuracy — a direct complement, since their lower bounds survive unbounded width while these are width-budgeted), and Amsel–Yehudai–Bruna on head quality versus quantity, which is exactly the attention-matrix rank effect the cost law here ignores. The obvious follow-up is to prove the top-$k$ analogue properly: Theorem 2 kills one head on rank $k$ under a monotone score, but InfoFlow's accounting suggests a clean tradeoff — emitting the full top-$k$ set requires $\ge k$ heads in one layer, or $\Omega(\log k)$ depth with a masking construction, or exponential width — and the argument would have to handle non-monotone, layer-composed scores where an earlier layer can subtract off the running maximum. Charging $\beta$ as a resource would also make the separation more honest.

For your work the connection is unusually direct, and worth stating with its limits. The separating target is a minimum-inner-product / closest-pair problem over the context, so Theorem 1 reads: a single attention layer with $H$ heads of width $n$ cannot perform all-pairs MIPS over $T$ context vectors to sup-norm accuracy $\varepsilon$ without $\varepsilon^{\Theta(T/(H(n+1)))}$ feed-forward parameters, while two layers do it at $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ — a statement that attention is not an index, and that the two-stage structure (local best partner, then global min) is what makes retrieval-like objectives tractable inside a Transformer. This is complementary to, not a substitute for, ANN hardness: the cost is parameters in a fixed function of the whole sequence, not query time against a preprocessed corpus, and $T$ is context length, not corpus size. Theorem 2 is the one with teeth for generative retrieval: it prices top-$k$ against top-1 inside a head, implying that a ranked list is not recoverable from one pooled attention state — the ranking must come from depth, from head multiplicity (the intrinsic-dimension result says $D$ independent max-type features need $D$ first-layer heads), or from the autoregressive loop, which realizes the two-stage comparison in time rather than depth. That gives a principled reading of why beam search is structurally necessary for top-$k$ docid generation rather than merely convenient, and a testable prediction about head count as a function of how many independent similarity features the docid space encodes. Third, the comparison calculus is a feasibility test for in-context reranking: a listwise objective that genuinely couples triples of candidates — MMR-style diversification, submodular set-level fusion — has Order of Comparison $\beta' \ge 3$ and is predicted to be inapproximable by any fixed-size Transformer as the candidate list grows, which is a sharper hypothesis about long-list reranking degradation than "attention dilutes". Caveats: targets are smooth real-valued functions in sup norm, lower bounds assume two-layer bounded-weight FFNs, mechanisms were validated on synthetic tasks, and the framework applies only to targets whose active index set stays $O(1)$ as $T$ grows — which, conveniently, is exactly the regime of top-$k$ retrieval from context.

title: Constrained Diffusion Models with Primal-Dual Inference
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 1 October 2026

Constrained Diffusion Models with Primal-Dual Inference

Hadou, Uslu & Ribeiro (2026) · https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17192

Main idea

The setting is sampling, not optimization in the usual sense: you want the distribution $\mu^\star$ minimizing $\mathbb E_\mu[f_0] - \beta H(\mu)$ subject to constraints that hold only in expectation, $\mathbb E_\mu[f]\preceq0$. Entropy regularization makes the primal problem strongly convex in $\mu$ over $\mathcal P_2$, so with a Slater point you get zero duality gap and the minimizer of the Lagrangian at any fixed $\lambda$ is a Gibbs / exponentially-tilted density $\mu^\dagger_\lambda\propto\exp(-\beta^{-1}(f_0+\lambda^\top f))$, with $\mu^\star = \mu^\dagger_{\lambda^\star}$ and dual function $g(\lambda) = -\beta\log Z(\lambda)$. This is classical; the interesting part is what to do about $\lambda^\star$, which is defined through expectations under the very distribution it indexes.

The move is to stop treating $\lambda$ as something you estimate before sampling and start treating it as part of the sampler's state. PDI runs a standard DDPM reverse chain, but at each step it denoises with the score field of $\mu^\dagger_{\lambda_t}$ for the current multiplier, forms a Tweedie posterior-mean estimate $\hat y_0$ of the clean sample, evaluates the constraint residual $f(\hat y_0)$ averaged over an ensemble of parallel chains, and takes a projected dual-ascent step. The reverse process is therefore not the time reversal of any single forward diffusion: it walks along a path-dependent family of Gibbs score fields. To make that possible they train one score network conditioned on $(x_t, t, \lambda, \mathcal G)$ with $\mathcal G$ the problem instance, with regression targets from the iDEM-style Monte Carlo estimator of the Gibbs score — so no data from the target is ever needed — and training pairs drawn from a replay buffer of the sampler's own rollouts plus an exploration prior over $\lambda$.

The conceptual payoff is a clean separation between two things prior dual-training approaches conflate: the quality of the estimated multiplier and the quality of the score field at that multiplier. Because the network is indexed by $\lambda$, an inference-time dual update is immediately reflected in the denoising dynamics; and because constraints are evaluated on an ensemble, PDI keeps the average-constraint semantics instead of degrading to the pointwise enforcement that projection, reflection and per-sample Langevin schemes impose. The theory is two-part: the time average of the duals reaches an $O(1/\sqrt T)$-plus-floor neighbourhood of $\lambda^\star$, and residual dual mismatch at step $t$ reaches the terminal law weighted by a product of one-step $W_2$-Lipschitz moduli — the formal version of the intuition that the high-noise phase is where dual error is cheap.

Reviewer's critique

The formulation and the mechanism are genuinely good. The observation that average constraints make per-sample projection strictly suboptimal is correct and cleanly demonstrated: in the truncated mixture-of-Gaussians problem every constrained method is feasible on average, but PDM and PD-Langevin pay for pointwise feasibility by hugging the constraint boundary and losing high-density mass (Figure 5 is the most convincing single figure in the paper). The DT ablation is also a real contribution: freezing the dual trajectory of DT and continuing score training (DT+) recovers the gap, establishing that DT's deficit is score-field mismatch, not multiplier estimation. That is a well-designed experiment answering the right question.

The central theoretical weakness is that the two theorems do not compose. Theorem 1 controls $\mathbb E|\bar\lambda - \lambda^\star|^2$ for the time average $\bar\lambda = T^{-1}\sum_t\lambda_t$, while Theorem 2's bound on $\mathbb E\,W_2(p_T,\mu^\star)$ is a weighted sum of $\mathbb E|\lambda_t-\lambda^\star|$ over individual iterates — and nothing in the paper bounds those. So there is no end-to-end guarantee on the sampled distribution at all; the limitations section acknowledges it, but it is worth being blunt that Theorem 2 is a perturbation/stability statement conditional on a quantity the analysis never controls. Worse for the narrative: the ablation in Figure 3 (left) and Figure 11 shows the PDI law is not the Gibbs distribution of $\lambda_T$ or of $\bar\lambda$, and beats both. So the empirical winner is the path-dependent mixture while the theory's target is the frozen-$\lambda^\star$ Gibbs law. The analysis explains why the schedule matters but not why PDI beats the object it is aiming at.

The floor term deserves scrutiny. $\Delta_{\text{floor}}$ does not vanish with $T$: it is $\tfrac{12L_f^2}{\vartheta^2T}\sum_t[\epsilon_{TW}^2(t{+}1) + \tfrac{\sigma_{T-t}^4}{\underline\alpha_{T-t}^2}\epsilon_{\text{app}}^2(t{+}1)] + \tfrac{12L_h^2}{\vartheta^2}(1+\tfrac1\delta)\epsilon_{\text{hist}}^2$. Three problems. First, $\epsilon_{TW}^2(t)$ is the Tweedie posterior-mean MSE, essentially the posterior variance, which is $O(1)$ at low SNR — the dominant term (as the authors themselves say) is a trajectory average of a quantity that is large over most of the trajectory. Second, the score term carries a $\sigma^4/\underline\alpha^2$ amplification where $\underline\alpha_{T-t} = \max{\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{T-t}}$, so the bound's dependence on score error is governed by a numerical clipping constant introduced to avoid division blowup. Third, the $1/\vartheta^2$ prefactor: $\vartheta = \beta^{-1}\inf_\lambda\sigma_{\min}(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mu^\dagger_\lambda}(f))$. The authors call Assumption 3 "mild and verifiable," and qualitatively it is, but in the experiments $f$ is a 200-vector of per-user ergodic rates in an interference network, or a 500-vector of per-asset risk contributions under a block-factor covariance. Those residuals are strongly dependent, so $\sigma_{\min}$ is tiny and $1/\vartheta^2$ is enormous; the bound is almost certainly numerically vacuous at the scales tested, and the paper never measures $\vartheta$, $\rho_t$, or $\epsilon_{TW}$ despite claiming they can be estimated from inference samples.

Smaller gaps. Theorem 1 is stated "under Assumptions 2–4" but its proof invokes Lemma 4, which requires Assumption 5, plus two summability conditions introduced mid-proof ($C_{\text{hist}}$ and $\epsilon_{\text{hist}}$ finite) that are assumed rather than proved — exactly the quantities at risk, since the paper admits $\rho_t>1$ near the data manifold. Theorem 2 likewise discards $\Psi_{0,T}W_2(p_0,q_T^{\lambda^\star})$ by asserting $q_T^{\lambda^\star}\to\mathcal N(0,I)$, with no argument that the $T$-fold product $\Psi_{0,T}$ does not outgrow it. The weight $\gamma_t\propto\alpha_{T-t}/\sigma_{T-t}^2$ diverges like $1/\sigma_{T-t}$ as SNR rises, so the bound is dominated by late steps and is only informative if the dual error is already $O(\sigma)$ there. And the dual update uses $f(\mathbb E[y_0\mid x_{t+1},\lambda_t])$ rather than $\mathbb E[f(y_0)\mid\cdot]$; for the nonlinear constraints actually used (log-rates, quadratic forms $x_j(\Sigma x)_j$) that is a Jensen gap, absorbed into $\epsilon_{TW}$ by Lipschitzness but systematically signed, not mean-zero noise.

The experiments are solid engineering but weaker as evidence for the headline claim. In the wireless table, PDI-Net's advantage over PD-Langevin is essentially mean rate $2.803\pm0.132$ vs $2.635\pm0.141$ — overlapping standard deviations — while PDL is slightly better on 5th-percentile rate and feasibility and requires no training at all. Supervised training on expert primal-dual trajectories dominates PDI on every feasibility metric (0.825 vs 0.613 5th-percentile, 99.3% vs 95.5% feasible) and loses only on mean rate, making "best overall balance" a judgment call rather than a result. DT+ matches PDI on all five metrics (Table 5), so the honest claim is that PDI reaches the same place with roughly 400 instead of 5000 outer iterations plus graceful degradation under shifted $r_{\min}$ — real, but much more modest than the framing suggests. All three problems are synthetic (the MoG study has a single instance; portfolio data is a simulated factor model with 20 test instances and no real returns). Finally, the inference hyperparameters sit some distance from the theory: $\eta$ is $1.0$, $0.05$ and $300$ across the three problems with a $\lambda$ weight decay in the portfolio case, $\lambda$ is clamped to $\lambda_{\max}\in{50,10^4}$ (which is how the compact $\Lambda$ that Assumption 4 needs is actually realized), and the wireless experiment initializes $\lambda_0 = 10$ with training prior $[2,10]$ — so in the best-performing setting the multiplier is warm-started inside a hand-chosen range rather than inferred from scratch. The $\beta$ sweep spanning $\beta^{-1}\in{1,50,2000}$ confirms the admitted tuning burden.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Proposition 1 (quoted from Chamon–Karimi–Korba) gives zero duality gap, a saddle point, finite $\lambda^\star\in\Lambda\subset\mathbb R_+^d$, and $\mu^\star = \mu^\dagger_{\lambda^\star}$, under a strict Slater point and $\beta>0$.

Theorem 1 assumes: $f$ is $L_f$-Lipschitz and bounded, $\sup|f|\le R$, on a compact domain (A2); $g$ is $\vartheta$-strongly concave (A3), which given $\nabla^2g(\lambda) = -\beta^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mu^\dagger_\lambda}(f)$ is exactly uniform nonsingularity of the constraint covariance over the Gibbs family; the score network is $\epsilon_{\text{app}}(t)$-accurate in $L^2(p_t)$ uniformly over compact $\Lambda$ (A4); and a bounded score Hessian $\sup_x|\nabla_x^2\log q_{T-t}(x\mid\lambda)|_{op}\le M_t$ (A5). With constant step $\eta_t = \kappa/\sqrt T$ over exactly the $T$ reverse steps, the conclusion is $\mathbb E|\bar\lambda-\lambda^\star|^2\le\tfrac2\vartheta\mathbb E[D^\star - g(\bar\lambda)]\le O(1/\sqrt T) + \Delta_{\text{floor}}$. Concretely, "neighbourhood of the dual optimum" means radius roughly $\tfrac{2\sqrt3}{\vartheta}(L_f\cdot\mathrm{rms}_t\,\epsilon_{TW}(t) + L_f\cdot\mathrm{rms}_t\tfrac{\sigma_{T-t}^2}{\underline\alpha_{T-t}}\epsilon_{\text{app}}(t) + L_h\sqrt{1+\delta^{-1}}\epsilon_{\text{hist}})$ — the root-mean-square Tweedie posterior standard deviation along the trajectory, divided by the dual curvature. This is about the time average only; nothing is claimed about $\lambda_T$ or $p_T$.

Theorem 2 gives $\mathbb E\,W_2(p_T,\mu^\star)\le\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Psi_{t,T}\tfrac{b_{T-t}}{\sqrt{a_{T-t}}}\gamma_t(\mathbb E|\lambda_t-\lambda^\star| + \epsilon_{\text{app}}(t))$ with $\Psi_{s,T} = \prod_{t=s+1}^T\rho_t$. The "schedule-dependent stability factors" are $\rho_t = a_{T-t}^{-1/2}\sup_x|I + b_{T-t}\nabla_x^2\log q_{T-t}(x\mid\lambda^\star)|_{op}$ — pure properties of the noise schedule and the curvature of the noised target, not of the algorithm — and $\gamma_t = \tfrac{R\alpha_{T-t}}{\beta\sigma_{T-t}^2}\sup_\lambda|\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_t}(y_0\mid x,\lambda)|_{op}^{1/2}$, the Lipschitz modulus of the score in $\lambda$.

How the dual result is proved. The skeleton is standard biased projected ascent, but two steps carry the argument. First, since $g(\lambda) = -\beta\log Z(\lambda)$, the exact dual gradient is $\nabla g(\lambda) = \mathbb E_{\mu^\dagger_\lambda}[f(y_0)]$ — the constraint residual under clean samples from the current Gibbs law — so PDI's update is a biased ascent step and everything reduces to bounding the bias. Second, the trick that makes the recursion close is Lemma 8, the identity $L(\mu,\lambda) = \beta D_{KL}(\mu|\mu^\dagger_\lambda) + g(\lambda)$, which turns $\langle\lambda_t-\lambda^\star,\nabla g(\lambda_t)\rangle$ into $g(\lambda_t) - g(\lambda^\star) - \beta D_{KL}(\mu^\dagger_{\lambda_t}|\mu^\star)$. That exposes the duality gap and a free nonnegative KL term, giving a Lyapunov-style recursion in $|\lambda_t-\lambda^\star|^2$. The bias cross term is absorbed with Young's inequality at $c = \vartheta/2$ and paid out of half the duality gap using $D^\star - g(\lambda)\ge\tfrac\vartheta2|\lambda-\lambda^\star|^2$; the per-step inequality telescopes, is divided by $\eta T$, and tuned at $\eta = \kappa/\sqrt T$. Jensen via concavity of $g$ moves from the average of the gaps to the gap at the average, and strong concavity converts that back into squared distance.

The substance is the three-way bias decomposition $b_{t+1} = B_1+B_2+B_3$, split by inserting two intermediate measures. $B_1$ (Tweedie error) replaces $\mathbb E_{\mu^\dagger_{\lambda_t}}[f(y_0)]$ by $f$ of the posterior mean under the fixed-$\lambda_t$ reverse process, bounded by building a joint law with the right marginals and applying Jensen plus $L_f$-Lipschitzness, yielding $L_f\epsilon_{TW}$. $B_3$ (parameterization) compares Tweedie means built from $s_\theta$ and from the true score; since $\mathbb E[y_0\mid x_{t+1}] = \underline\alpha^{-1}(x_{t+1}+\sigma^2s)$, score error is amplified by $\sigma^2_{T-t}/\underline\alpha_{T-t}$. $B_2$ (marginal mismatch) is the hard one and is where the $W_2$ machinery enters: synchronous coupling of the PDI chain and the fixed-$\lambda_t$ chain (shared noise, shared initialization) gives the one-step recursion $|x_{s+1}-\tilde x_{s+1}|\le\rho_s(\lambda_s)|x_s-\tilde x_s| + \tfrac{b_{T-s}}{\sqrt{a_{T-s}}}(\gamma_s|\lambda_s-\lambda_t| + \epsilon_{\text{app}}(s))$, unrolled into a history sum weighted by stability products, with $|\lambda_j-\lambda_t|\le(t-j)\eta R$ from boundedness of the gradient estimate. This is then collapsed by assuming $C_{\text{hist}},\epsilon_{\text{hist}}<\infty$ and one more Young step.

How the primal result is proved. Lemma 6 / Proposition 2 is a synchronous-coupling plus mean-value-theorem computation: under common noise the Gaussian terms cancel exactly, so one DDPM reverse step acts on a displacement as the deterministic map $a_{T-t}^{-1/2}(I + b_{T-t}\widehat H)$ with $\widehat H$ the Hessian of $\log q_{T-t}$ averaged along the segment; bounding $\widehat H$ by its supremum and taking the infimum over couplings gives $\rho_t$. This is a worst-case operator-norm bound, not an average contraction, which is why $\rho_t$ can exceed 1 near sharp modes: $I + b\nabla^2\log q$ overshoots when curvature is large and negative. Theorem 2 then triangulates into a kernel-stability piece (Proposition 2) and a same-input kernel-mismatch piece, the latter bounded by Lemma 7: Lipschitzness of the score in $\lambda$, proved by writing the score through Tweedie as $s_t = \sigma^{-2}(\alpha\mathbb E_{\pi_t}[y_0\mid x,\lambda] - x)$ and differentiating the posterior — whose $\lambda$-dependence sits entirely in the tilted prior — to get $\nabla_\lambda\mathbb E_{\pi_t}[y_0\mid x,\lambda] = -\beta^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_t}(y_0,f(y_0)\mid x,\lambda)$, then Cauchy–Schwarz with $|f|\le R$. Unrolling $T$ steps gives the stated weighted sum; the initialization term is dropped by assertion. Separately, Lemma 1 (from iDEM) supplies the self-normalized Monte Carlo estimator for the noised Gibbs score, $\nabla_{y_\tau}\log\frac1{K_{MC}}\sum_k\exp(-E((y_\tau+\sigma_\tau\epsilon_k)/\alpha_\tau,\lambda))$, which is the trick that makes training possible without any samples from the target.

Broader context

The background is a collision of two literatures. On one side, guided and constrained diffusion sampling: classifier guidance (Dhariwal–Nichol) and classifier-free guidance perturb the score inside Tweedie's formula, diffusion posterior sampling (Chung et al.) does the same with a measurement likelihood, and a cleaner way to see all of these is as approximate Doob $h$-transforms or as stochastic optimal control problems whose optimal control is the score of a tilted terminal law — the path-integral-sampler / denoising-diffusion-sampler family and iDEM live exactly there. A separate strand enforces set constraints geometrically: reflected diffusions (Lou–Ermon), mirror diffusions (Liu et al.), Riemannian score-based models, log-barrier and projection schemes. The crucial distinction this paper insists on is pointwise versus distributional: the geometric methods require every sample to be feasible, whereas average constraints are a constraint on the law, so enforcing them per sample is a strict restriction and therefore conservative.

On the other side is Ribeiro's long-running programme on constrained learning in the dual domain: PAC constrained learning (Chamon–Ribeiro), resilient constrained learning (Hounie et al.), zero duality gap in constrained RL (Paternain et al.) — all exploiting the same phenomenon, that over a sufficiently rich (here, measure-valued) primal space the duality gap vanishes even when the parametrization is non-convex, so primal-dual methods are legitimate rather than heuristic. The two immediate ancestors are "Constrained diffusion models via dual training" (Khalafi–Ding–Ribeiro), which alternates outer dual ascent with inner Lagrangian score matching, and primal-dual Langevin Monte Carlo (Chamon–Karimi–Korba), which does gradient descent-ascent in Wasserstein space with no learned model. PDI is best read as the interpolation: PD-LMC's inference-time dual dynamics, but with a learned $\lambda$-conditioned score field, so you get amortization across problem instances and constraint levels.

The obvious follow-up is to close the gap between what is proved and what works. The ablations say the PDI terminal law beats the Gibbs law of any frozen multiplier, including $\bar\lambda$, and that truncating to a tail average hurts — so the sampler is implicitly targeting something like an annealed path of tilted measures ${\mu^\dagger_{\lambda_t}}$ rather than $\mu^\dagger_{\lambda^\star}$. A natural programme is to define that object properly: pose PDI as a saddle-point flow in Wasserstein space with a time-varying tilt, show its terminal law solves a smoothed or schedule-dependent Lagrangian, and get a last-iterate or primal-side guarantee by matching the dual step-size schedule to the SNR schedule (dual averaging or an extragradient/optimistic update, which would also plausibly cancel the systematic Jensen component of the Tweedie bias). A second, cheaper direction: the floor is dominated by $\epsilon_{TW}$, the posterior variance, and that is estimable — a variance-aware or Richardson-extrapolated dual gradient across adjacent SNR levels might remove the leading bias and turn the neighbourhood result into genuine convergence.

For your own work there is a non-forced connection, though it lives in the formulation rather than the diffusion machinery. Generative retrieval decodes identifiers autoregressively, and essentially every list-level desideratum — diversity, intent coverage, exposure fairness across providers, calibration to a target topic distribution — is an average constraint over the sampled list, not a per-item constraint. That is exactly the distinction this paper is built around, and the same algebra applies: the entropy-regularized optimal retrieval policy under such constraints is an exponential tilt $\pi_\lambda(d)\propto\pi_0(d)\exp(-\beta^{-1}\lambda^\top f(d))$ of the base scorer, which is already the functional form of softmax/contrastive retrieval scores, and the dual variable is a per-constraint price you could in principle ascend during decoding rather than tune offline, with a $\lambda$-conditioned scoring head playing the role of their dual-conditioned score network. The same structure shows up in vector search with quotas — constrained ANN retrieval with per-partition or per-attribute budgets satisfied in expectation over queries rather than per query. What transfers is the Lagrangian/Gibbs formulation plus inference-time dual ascent on an ensemble; what does not is the $W_2$ stability analysis, which is thoroughly continuous-state. The warnings transfer too: the convergence result covers only time-averaged duals, and the empirically best object is a path-dependent mixture the theory does not describe.

title: To See the Unseen: on the Generalization Ability of Transformers in Symbolic Reasoning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-30

To See the Unseen: on the Generalization Ability of Transformers in Symbolic Reasoning — Lazić, Fowl, György & Szepesvári (2026) · arXiv:2604.21632

Main idea. The paper asks whether a decoder-only Transformer can execute an in-context algorithm over symbols it has literally never seen as tokens. The notion of generalization is not length generalization and not compositional generalization over seen pieces; it is generalization to unseen symbols — the model must run a reasoning procedure using vocabulary entries that were held out of training entirely, so it can only rely on problem structure, never on embedding content. The testbed is synthetic propositional logic over definite (Horn) clauses generated in the rule-priority style of Zhang et al. (2023): 5–20 predicates, 0–40 rules, a query predicate, and a chain-of-thought trace that is the literal execution of forward chaining (repeated modus ponens until the query is proven or saturation), with labels balanced 50/50. Models are trained from scratch in NanoDO — 10 layers, d = 1024, 8 heads, 60–75M parameters, RoPE, AdamW with weight decay 0.001, tied embedding/unembedding matrices, fresh examples generated on the fly for 50k steps, loss masked on the question. The vocabulary always reserves 100 tokens that never appear in training; evaluation then substitutes unseen tokens for either the query predicate alone or all predicates, and training-predicate-set size |P| ∈ {150, 600, 2400, 9600} serves as a symbolic-diversity knob.

The headline result is a mechanism. Prior work (Boix-Adserà et al., 2024) attributed failure to the difficulty of generating an unseen token and proposed a copy-attention architectural fix; Anand et al. (2025) found that "active forgetting" (periodically resetting embeddings) helps but offered no explanation. This paper identifies a second, distinct failure: the (un)embeddings of held-out tokens collapse to nearly a single direction during training, so multiple unseen symbols become mutually indistinguishable — fatal precisely because the tied matrix serves as both input embedding and output classifier. They prove a contraction lemma for ℓ₂-regularized GD/SGD, verify collapse empirically under AdamW (worse with layernorm, worse with larger λ, present even at λ = 0), and then show the empirical taxonomy: vanilla Transformers fail on any unseen token, often silently substituting a seen predicate or dropping the token from the trace (most errors are false negatives); copy attention plus high diversity solves the single-unseen-query case; copy attention alone still fails when all predicates are unseen, at every diversity level; freezing the (un)embeddings at their near-orthogonal initialization, or active forgetting throughout training, restores generalization. Temporary active forgetting works only when combined with copy attention — interestingly, the unseen embeddings still reach cosine similarity ≈ 0.9 there, but sharp copy attention is apparently enough to disambiguate. They also confirm the effect in the wild: Gemma 3's 99 deliberately unused tokens have mean pairwise cosine similarity 0.78/0.33/0.23/0.24 across 1B–27B (versus 0.09/0.03/0.02/0.01 for used tokens), the effect shrinking with embedding dimension, and finetuning Gemma 3 1B on the same logic task needs ~5000 steps to hit 90% accuracy with unused tokens versus <500 with English adjectives or letters.

The most interesting part. The strongest and most honest finding is the dissociation: copying capability and symbol identifiability are orthogonal failures, and fixing one does nothing for the other. That reframes a body of prior results — Boix-Adserà's architectural fix looked sufficient only because those experiments had one unseen symbol. Two caveats deserve flagging. First, the theory undershoots the phenomenon: the contraction lemma needs λ > 0 to produce collapse, yet Figure 2 shows collapse at λ = 0 with layernorm, so the mechanism actually driving the empirical result (layernorm plus Adam's normalized updates, presumably) is not the one proven. Second, the causal story is not cleanly falsified. The interventions that fix collapse (freezing, resetting) also change many other things, and the one surgical variant they tried — freezing or resetting only predicate embeddings — made generalization worse, which they report and leave as "requires further investigation." The obvious discriminating experiment, untying embeddings from unembeddings, or exempting only the reserved rows from weight decay, is never run, even though the paper repeatedly identifies tying as the aggravating factor. Also note that frozen embeddings are shown (Appendix E, C4) to substantially hurt language modeling, so the working fix is not deployable; copy attention, pleasingly, is mildly helpful on C4. Absolute-scale caveats are modest here — infinite fresh data removes the usual overfitting confound — but the domain is one templated logic format with single-token predicates, and 50k steps is a short budget against which "transience" claims (only |P| = 9600 retains the copying bias; smaller vocabularies acquire and then lose it) are budget-dependent by construction.

Proof sketch. Lemma 4.1 is the paper's one theoretical result, and it is a clean contraction argument rather than an impossibility claim. Consider a softmax classifier p(y|x) ∝ exp(φ(x|θ)ᵀW_y) over features bounded in a ball of radius r (guaranteed by a final layernorm), trained on ℓ₂-regularized NLL, and let labels i, j never appear in the data. Then the label-indicator terms drop out of both gradients, so the update to the difference W_j − W_i is driven only by the probability gap and the decay term. Applying the Lagrange mean-value theorem to exp(·) turns that gap into a linear form, p_{j,n} − p_{i,n} = p̃_n·φ_nᵀ(W_j − W_i) with p̃_n between the two class probabilities; substituting and bounding ‖φ_n‖ ≤ r yields ‖W_j^{(t+1)} − W_i^{(t+1)}‖ ≤ (1 − η_tλ + η_t r²p_t)‖W_j^{(t)} − W_i^{(t)}‖. Once the model fits the training data, p_t → 0 for the absent classes, so the factor tends to 1 − η_tλ < 1 and the difference decays geometrically; the argument is indifferent to θ changing over time, hence applies to a full Transformer. What a complete theoretical account of the paper's findings would still have to establish is the part the lemma does not cover: collapse under AdamW's decoupled, per-coordinate normalized updates, collapse at λ = 0 driven by layernorm alone, and the feedback loop through tied weights whereby a collapsed unembedding row also degrades the input representation of the same symbol.

Broader context. This sits at the junction of three literatures. One is length/positional generalization, where the lesson has been that the positional channel is the OOD-fragile part: randomized position embeddings (Ruoss et al.), NoPE, Abacus embeddings and index hinting for arithmetic. This paper's contribution is to show the token channel is fragile in an exactly analogous way, and that the analogous randomization trick (resetting all embeddings) works for the same reason. The second is the data-diversity / ICL-transience line — Chan et al., Singh et al., Raventós et al.'s task-diversity threshold for ridge-regression ICL, He et al. on modular arithmetic — which the diversity sweep here reproduces in a symbolic-algorithm setting. The third is symbol binding and abstract-variable work (Boix-Adserà's NTK analysis; Anand et al.'s structural ICL; the anonymous-variable and function-composition hardness results; Barbero et al. on representational over-squashing, which the authors invoke for prefix-confusion). Appendix F is the underexploited part: with multi-token symbols drawn from a letter-bigram model over 26 base tokens (all tokens seen, only combinations new), collapse disappears but two new failures emerge — models trained on symbols up to n tokens truncate longer symbols to n, and accuracy drops when the query shares a prefix with a distractor predicate, i.e. representations of prefix-sharing strings merge.

That appendix is where the connection to your work is tightest. Generative retrieval asks a decoder to emit document identifiers, which are exactly arbitrary symbols carrying no semantic content of their own. Atomic docids are the pure version of this paper's setting: a document added after training is a token the model has been trained never to emit, and the collapse result gives a mechanistic reason why several newly added atomic docids should be near-inseparable at the output layer — which is a sharper diagnosis than "the model hasn't learned the new id" and bears directly on DSI++/IncDSI-style incremental indexing and on zero-shot retrieval. Hierarchical/semantic docids (RQ-VAE codebooks, structured identifiers) map onto Appendix F instead: sibling ids share prefixes by design, and the prefix-merging and length-truncation failures are precisely the pathologies one would fear in a deep codebook. The link is partial and worth stating as such: GR decodes under a trie constraint, which masks invalid logits and so papers over the "refuses to emit an unseen token" failure entirely — but constrained decoding cannot rescue inseparability, since a collapsed pair of ids remains a coin flip inside the allowed set. A concrete follow-up: in a standard GR setup, hold out a docid subset, track the pairwise cosine similarity of their output rows over training as a direct measurement of collapse, then compare frozen random near-orthogonal docid rows, decay-exempt docid rows, and a pointer/copy head over the retrieved context against IncDSI as baselines — with the untying ablation the present paper omits.

title: Large Neighborhood Search meets Iterative Neural Constraint Heuristics
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-30

Large Neighborhood Search meets Iterative Neural Constraint Heuristics — Yudong W. Xu, Wenhao Li, Scott Sanner, Elias B. Khalil (2026) — arXiv:2603.20801v1

Main idea — background. Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) is a classical metaheuristic for discrete optimization: given a complete candidate solution, a destroy operator unassigns a subset of variables, a repair operator re-instantiates them (usually by solving the small sub-problem exactly or greedily), and you loop. Because the destroyed subset can be large, each move explores an exponentially large neighborhood while staying computationally cheap — the classic instances are Shaw's related-removal for vehicle routing and Ropke–Pisinger's Adaptive LNS, which maintains a portfolio of destroy operators and reweights them online.

The paper's thesis is an interpretive one: modern iterative neural constraint solvers are already LNS, they just don't say so. Their target is ConsFormer (Xu et al., ICML 2025), a Transformer that takes a complete-but-infeasible assignment to a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP), marks a random subset of variables as editable via a learned embedding, and resamples those variables from its output logits with Gumbel-Softmax; it is trained self-supervised against a differentiable constraint-penalty loss L(x) = Σ λ_k f(p_k(x)), with no labelled solutions. Reading that loop as LNS, the random masking is the destroy operator and the forward pass plus decoder is the repair operator — so the entire LNS design space opens up.

What they do. On the destroy side they port classical heuristics (random removal; greedy and stochastic worst removal, scored by per-variable contributions to the discretized penalty loss via ‖∂L/∂OneHot(x_i)‖₁; greedy and stochastic related removal, which samples constraints and destroys all their variables) and add two genuinely neural, prediction-guided operators: gradient-guided removal, scoring variables by ∂L(softmax(z))/∂z_i on the model's own soft beliefs rather than the hard assignment, and confidence-margin removal, scoring by the negative gap between the top two softmax probabilities — i.e. destroy where the model is least sure, an idea imported from remasking schedules in masked diffusion models. On the repair side they compare the original Gumbel-Softmax sampling against plain argmax (greedy/MAP) decoding.

Setting and results. This is CSP/Max-CSP, not MIP: Sudoku (SATNet in-distribution, RRN as harder OOD), graph 5-coloring (50→100 nodes) and 10-coloring (100→200 nodes), and MaxCut on GSET (800–10000 vertices, trained on small synthetic graphs). ConsFormer-LNS lifts OOD Sudoku from 85.8% to 91.8% solved, OOD coloring from 46.3%→54.2% (k=5) and 10.2%→18.4% (k=10), and MaxCut average gap to best-known cut from 16.33→4.44 (|V|=800) and 115.25→63.63 (|V|≥3K). Against baselines: best among neural Sudoku solvers (next best IRED at 62.1% OOD); slightly behind OR-Tools CP-SAT on 5-coloring (54.2 vs 57.16 OOD) but ahead on the harder 10-coloring (18.4 vs 10.25 OOD); second-best on MaxCut, still clearly behind ANYCSP everywhere (e.g. 4.44 vs 1.22 at |V|=800). Two robust design patterns emerge: stochastic destroy beats greedy destroy, and greedy repair beats sampling repair.

The most interesting part — and an honest critique. The cleanest idea is the prediction-guided destroy family, because it is the one thing a classical LNS cannot do: the repair operator is a differentiable model, so its logits and their gradients are a free, dense, per-variable signal about where repair is likely to help. Confidence-margin removal improves fastest early and then loses to penalty-based worst removal once the model becomes confident — a legible efficiency/accuracy trade-off rather than a black-box win. The greedy-repair finding is also well-explained: since the metric only cares about the single best assignment, argmax is MAP decoding, while sampling optimizes for a diverse solution distribution nobody is scoring.

Now the weaknesses, and there are several. The decomposition drops the third LNS component. Textbook LNS is destroy–repair–accept; the accept step (improving-only, or simulated-annealing style) is what makes LNS a search rather than a random walk. ConsFormer-LNS has no acceptance criterion and no incumbent management — x^(t+1) is taken unconditionally. Given that the paper's own framing is "import the LNS design space," omitting the one component that provides monotonicity is a conspicuous gap, and I suspect it explains the spectacular collapses in the greedy columns. Note that greedy destroy + greedy repair is a deterministic map on assignments, so it must reach a fixed point or cycle; readings like 0.0% solved are then close to tautological, and the headline "stochasticity in destroy matters" is partly an artifact of determinism-induced cycling rather than evidence about local optima per se.

The decisive ablation is missing. The question "how much of the win is the learned repair versus the search scaffolding?" is never answered, because the Transformer is never removed. The natural control — run the same destroy operators with a cheap classical repair (min-conflicts, or exact repair of the destroyed sub-CSP by CP-SAT) — would settle it, and min-conflicts is famously strong on Sudoku and coloring. Similarly, there is no classical LNS/ALNS baseline of any kind, so "LNS helps ConsFormer" is established but "neural repair beats hand-written repair inside the same LNS shell" is not.

Cost accounting is absent. They retrain a separate model for each destroy/repair pairing on H100 nodes — so the ~16 configurations per benchmark represent a large hidden training budget that is never reported, and the improvement from "adapting to LNS" is entangled with retraining rather than being a pure inference-time change. Wall-clock budgets (10s coloring, 180s MaxCut) are shared with OR-Tools "on the same hardware," but a GPU-resident Transformer versus a CPU CP-SAT solver is not a normalized comparison, and Sudoku is budgeted in iterations (2K), not seconds, with OR-Tools omitted entirely as "trivial" — which is true, and also means the Sudoku headline is a neural-vs-neural leaderboard, not evidence of solver competitiveness. Finally, the neural-LNS literature they cite is almost entirely MIP-based — Song et al., Sonnerat et al., CL-LNS (Huang et al.), SPL-LNS — and none of it is run here, so the contribution lands as a thorough ablation study of one prior model rather than a comparison against the state of the art in neural LNS.

No formal guarantees. The paper is purely empirical — no theorems, no complexity claims, no convergence statement. A theoretical treatment would need something like: conditions on the destroy distribution under which the destroy–repair chain is irreducible over the feasible region (hence hits a solution with probability 1 in the limit), a bound on expected hitting time as a function of the destruction rate ρ and the repair operator's per-variable error, or a statement that an accept-if-improving wrapper preserves the neural heuristic's asymptotic completeness. None of that is attempted, and the collapse of the deterministic variants is exactly the phenomenon such an analysis would predict.

Broader context. For an outsider: learning-augmented combinatorial optimization mostly splits into end-to-end solution prediction (a network outputs an assignment; fast but with a fixed compute budget that cannot adapt to instance hardness, hence poor OOD behaviour) and learning inside a classical solver, where a model replaces a heuristic decision while the solver retains its correctness guarantees. The landmark of the second kind is Nair et al.'s Neural Diving / Neural Branching, which trains a generative model over partial variable assignments to warm-start a MIP solver and a policy to imitate strong branching; Gasse et al.'s bipartite variable–constraint graph GNN encoding of MIPs is the standard representation underneath much of this, and Khalil's own earlier work on learning to branch is part of the same lineage. CL-LNS (Huang et al., 2023) is the closest analogue on the MIP side: contrastive learning of which variables to unfix, trained against neighborhoods found by expensive search. This paper is the CSP-side counterpart, and its distinctive move is that the learned component is the repair operator (trained self-supervised, so no expert trajectories needed) while the destroy operator is where classical and neural heuristics are compared.

An obvious and well-motivated follow-up, which the authors flag: bandit-driven Adaptive LNS over the operator portfolio, since no single destroy operator dominates and confidence-margin/worst-removal have complementary time profiles. The sharper version would train one model conditioned on the destroy signal rather than retraining per pairing, and jointly learn the destroy policy against the frozen repair model. Adding an explicit acceptance criterion — and reporting whether simulated-annealing acceptance rescues the greedy operators — is the cheapest high-value experiment left on the table.

Connection to your area. I would not oversell this one. The two honest angles are: (i) the abstract pattern — a learned scorer supplying where to look inside a classical search loop that retains its own correctness/termination properties — is exactly the shape of learned routing inside HNSW-style ANN traversal, and index construction (neighbour selection under degree budgets, PQ/RQ codebook assignment) really is a large-scale combinatorial assignment problem where destroy-repair refinement of an existing index is an underexplored alternative to greedy incremental insertion; (ii) more directly, their greedy-vs-sampling repair result is the MAP-versus-diverse-decoding question you already know from generative retrieval, and their confidence-margin destroy operator is literally an entropy-style remasking schedule of the kind used in masked-diffusion decoders, which is the same machinery people are starting to apply to docid generation. Beyond those, treat this as a well-executed piece of a subfield worth knowing rather than a paper with a load-bearing hook into your own work; its main transferable lesson is methodological — that a lot of "neural iterative refinement" is rediscovered local search, and that naming the classical scaffold gets you a free design space to search over.

title: Theoretical limitations of multi-layer Transformer
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-30

Theoretical limitations of multi-layer Transformer — Lijie Chen, Binghui Peng, Hongxun Wu (2024) — arXiv:2412.02975

Main idea. Everything we rigorously knew about the weakness of Transformers was either about one layer (composition of two functions, 3SUM, induction heads) or conditional — constant-depth log-precision Transformers sit inside uniform TC⁰, inside L, inside MPC, so "Transformers can't do X" required believing P ⊄ TC⁰ or an MPC round conjecture. Chen, Peng and Wu break that barrier with the first unconditional lower bound against multi-layer decoder-only Transformers.

Their hard task is L-sequential function composition: the prompt lists lookup tables z_L, z_{L−1}, …, z_0 (in decreasing index order, with geometrically shrinking sizes), then a single query token w = (w_1,…,w_{L−1}); the model must output i_L where i_0 = z_0, i_1 = z_1(i_0), and i_{ℓ+1} = z_{ℓ+1}(w_ℓ, i_ℓ) — i.e. L chained hops through memorised tables, each hop's address determined by the previous hop's answer.

Proof sketch — what is proved. Theorem 1.1: for any L ≤ Õ(log log n), an L-layer decoder-only Transformer with H heads, head dimension d and p bits of precision per embedding entry cannot solve this task whenever Hdp ≤ n^{2^{−4L}}. So for constant L the model dimension must be n^{Ω(1)} — polynomial in the context length, not in the parameter count. The model is generous: attention is standard softmax, but the MLP between layers is an arbitrary function R^{dH} → R^{dH} (unbounded local computation), and positional encodings, residuals, layer norm, MoE and even position-dependent weights are all captured. The only real resource being charged is the number of bits an attention layer can move between positions. Because an (L+1)-layer decoder solves the task with H = O(1), d = polylog n, p = log n (one retrieval head per hop), this is the first depth–width trade-off for Transformers: L+1 layers and polylog width versus L layers and n^{Ω(1)} width — an exponential separation at every constant depth. Two corollaries fall out for free: an unconditional encoder/decoder separation (a bidirectional encoder does the same task in O(log L) layers with polylog width, by doubling the hop length each layer), and the first unconditional provable benefit of chain-of-thought (one layer plus L decoding steps suffices).

Proof sketch — how. The conceptual centrepiece is the autoregressive communication model, and it is the right abstraction because it isolates precisely the asymmetry that causal masking creates. Partition the prompt into blocks and give block i to player i; players sit on a line, and player i may broadcast its entire information state upward to all players j > i for free, but each player j may reply with only 2Hdp·|block i| bits per epoch, and — crucially — players are forgetful: player j's state is never updated by anything a lower player sent it. That forgetfulness is the causal mask: a token early in the prompt never sees the query, so its layer-ℓ embedding cannot depend on it. One attention layer = one epoch; the transcript is literally the p-bit partial sums of exp(q·k)·V and of exp(q·k) over the sender's block. This is why the model sidesteps the barrier Hahn flagged: any n^ε lower bound against encoders would give n^{1+ε/2}-wire lower bounds against depth-3 symmetric circuits, a breakthrough (spelled out in Appendix B). Decoders leak less, and that gap is exactly what is exploitable.

The second idea is the indistinguishable decomposition, and it is what lets the argument survive past one layer. Rather than fixing a transcript once (which is all a one-layer reduction ever needs), they build, by induction on ℓ, a pair (R_{≥ℓ}, Z_{<ℓ}) where Z_{<ℓ} is a product set of inputs for the low players and R_{≥ℓ} is a large set of inputs for the high players that the low players cannot tell apart after ℓ epochs. Previous communication reductions died at two layers because fixing the second-layer messages costs you a factor for every input of every player, and the entropy budget collapses.
