The saving here is elegant: because Z_ℓ is already indistinguishable to players below ℓ after ℓ epochs, the (ℓ+1)-st epoch messages down to those players do not depend on which z_ℓ ∈ Z_ℓ was chosen, so the number of transcripts to enumerate drops by a factor |Z_ℓ| in the exponent — and the authors note in a footnote that this saving is exactly what makes the induction close. The final contradiction is a counting/pigeonhole argument: the surviving set of high-player inputs is still large enough to contain two instances with different correct answers that the output position cannot distinguish.

The most interesting part / honest scope. The autoregressive communication model is the transferable artifact here — a clean resource-accounting abstraction in which "one layer = one round of a forgetful line protocol" makes depth into a round budget you can actually reason about. Scope caveats worth keeping in mind: the bound is worst-case, exact and deterministic (no average-case or approximation-robust version), representational rather than about learnability, the table alphabet grows with n and the block sizes are contrived, the L ≤ Õ(log log n) ceiling and the n^{2^{−4L}} width threshold mean the statement is asymptotically real but numerically vacuous for a 100-layer model, and it says nothing against encoders or against decoders that get to emit intermediate tokens.

Broader context. The expressivity literature has two halves. The upper-bound half puts Transformers in small circuit classes — Merrill–Sabharwal show log-precision constant-depth encoders ⊆ uniform TC⁰, Peng–Narayanan–Papadimitriou push toward L, Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky recast them as Massively Parallel Computation with attention layers as rounds; RASP and C-RASP give programming languages whose expressible functions characterise what attention can do. The lower-bound half was stuck at one layer: Hahn's hard-attention parity/Dyck results, Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky's sparse-averaging and 3SUM separations, their one-layer induction-head impossibility, and the k-hop hierarchy where log-depth is necessary and sufficient in the MPC picture. Function composition is the canonical hard primitive, and empirically Dziri et al.'s "Faith and Fate" and Ye–Xu–Li–Allen-Zhu's grade-school-math study both find compositional depth, not width, to be the binding constraint. Chain-of-thought is the standard escape hatch (Feng et al., Merrill–Sabharwal, Li–Liu–Zhou–Ma: log-precision Transformers with polynomial CoT simulate polynomial time), and this paper makes that escape unconditional for the first time. The two companions worth reading next are Sanford–Hsu–Telgarsky's Transformers, parallel computation and logarithmic depth (ICML 2024) for the matching k-hop upper bounds, and Ewer et al.'s ENTP for the conditional encoder/decoder separation this paper unconditionalises. Obvious follow-ups: push L from Õ(log log n) toward Θ(log n) to meet the log-depth upper bounds; make the bound robust to ε error or to randomised protocols; shrink the alphabet to something binary and natural; and — most attractive — turn the epoch budget into a genuine three-way trade-off between depth L, number of CoT steps t, and width, since the model already has the knob.

Connection to your work. This is unusually direct for generative retrieval. A generative retriever with hierarchical semantic docids is exactly asking a decoder to compute a sequential composition: each docid token c_ℓ is a lookup whose address is the prefix c_1…c_{ℓ−1} plus the query, over a structure the model has memorised or is reading in context. The theorem says the depth of one forward pass bounds how many such hops can be resolved at small width — which is a formal argument for hierarchical, multi-step docid decoding over atomic/single-token docids, and against expecting one-pass multi-hop lookup from a shallow decoder. In the in-context/RAG regime the hard instance is literally your setting (index in the prompt, query last), and the corollaries then read as: iterative retrieval (query rewriting, IRCoT-style loops) is not a heuristic convenience but the cheap way to buy the missing depth. The encoder/decoder corollary also speaks to dense retrieval: it is an unconditional reason why removing the causal mask (LLM2Vec-style bidirectional adaptation) helps on compositional lookup, since the encoder needs only O(log L) layers where the decoder needs L+1. And the resource being charged — Hdp bits per token per layer — is an embedding-width bottleneck, the same currency as embedding-dimension lower bounds for retrieval. A concrete project: define the autoregressive communication complexity of k-hop in-context retrieval and prove a (decoding steps) × (depth) ≥ (hops) style trade-off, then connect the per-token message budget to single-vector embedding-capacity lower bounds. The honest caveat is that the construction is adversarial and a real docid tree is semantically smooth, so learned shortcuts (à la Liu et al.'s "shortcuts to automata") will often beat the worst case — the theorem constrains architecture design, not benchmark numbers.

title: Scalable and Certifiable Graph Unlearning via Lazy Local Propagation
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-30

Scalable and Certifiable Graph Unlearning: Overcoming the Approximation Error Barrier — Lu Yi, Zhewei Wei (ICLR 2025; arXiv v1 Aug 2024, v3 Feb 2025) — arXiv:2408.09212

Circulated earlier as "Scalable and Certifiable Graph Unlearning via Lazy Local Propagation"; the system is called ScaleGUN.

Main idea. Certified unlearning in the Guo et al. sense is a distributional statement: a removal mechanism $M$ is $(\epsilon,\delta)$-certified if the law of $M(A(D),D,D')$ and the law of retraining from scratch, $A(D')$, are $(\epsilon,\delta)$-indistinguishable in both directions — a differential-privacy-shaped guarantee, but with the "neighbouring dataset" fixed to be the one you promised to delete. The recipe is: train a $\lambda$-strongly convex ERM with an objective perturbation $L_b(w)=L(w)+b^\top w$, $b\sim\mathcal N(0,\alpha)$; on deletion take one Newton step $w^-=w^\star+\hat H_{w^\star}^{-1}\Delta$; then show the gradient residual $|\nabla L(w^-;D')|$ — how far $w^-$ is from stationarity on the true post-deletion objective — is below a computable $\epsilon'$. If it is, the Gaussian noise already in the objective statistically masks the residual, and you get the certificate for free.

Graphs break this cheaply. In SGC/GPR-style models the loss of node $i$ depends on the propagated embedding $e_i^\top Z$, $Z=\sum_\ell w_\ell (D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2})^\ell X$, so deleting one node, edge, or feature row perturbs many rows of $Z$ at once. CGU (Chien et al.) and CEU (Wu et al.) handle this by recomputing propagation exactly on every request. On ogbn-papers100M (111M nodes, 1.6B edges) that is ~6,000s per request, versus <80s to retrain the linear head — the "unlearning" costs more than retraining. The obvious fix, approximate propagation, is where the approximation error barrier sits: scalable propagation gives you $\hat Z$, and you train and unlearn on $\hat D$, but the certificate is a statement about $|\nabla L(w^-;D')|$ on the exact $D'$. Nobody had shown that the approximation error does not swamp the noise.

Lazy local propagation, mechanically: exploit $(D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2})^\ell = D^{-1/2}(AD^{-1})^\ell D^{1/2}$ so that a Forward Push on the left-stochastic $P=AD^{-1}$, seeded with the normalized signal $r^{(0)}=D^{1/2}x$, computes the symmetric GPR embedding. Keep per-level reserves $q^{(\ell)}$ and residues $r^{(\ell)}$; push node $u$ at level $\ell$ only when $|r^{(\ell)}(u)|>r_{\max}$. On a deletion you never re-propagate: the push invariant $q^{(\ell)}+r^{(\ell)}=AD^{-1}q^{(\ell-1)}$ is violated only at the endpoints whose degree changed and their neighbours, so you repair those residues in place and push again until everything is back under $r_{\max}$. Feature removal at $u$ is one line: set $r^{(0)}(u)\leftarrow -q^{(0)}(u)$. Node removal is its incident edges. Amortized cost per edge removal is $O(L^2\bar d)$ — effectively constant. Result: the 5,000-edge batch that took 1.9h drops to 20s total, 5s of it propagation.

The most interesting part. The clever move is not the push scheme (that extends InstantGNN's dynamic-PPR trick to layered GPR); it is using the propagation data structure as the proof device. The hard quantity is $|Ze_j-Z'e_j|$, the exact pre/post-deletion embedding gap, which prior work could only bound for $P=D^{-1}A$ or 1-hop propagation. The authors note that the exact decomposition $z=\sum_\ell w_\ell D^{-1/2}\big(q^{(\ell)}+\sum_{t\le\ell}(AD^{-1})^{\ell-t}r^{(t)}\big)$ holds for every $r_{\max}$, then set $r_{\max}=0$ — residues vanish, $q$ is shared between $z$ and $z'$ — so the difference collapses to the residue adjustments their own update routine makes, which are supported on a handful of nodes. With $AD^{-1}$ left stochastic and $\sum_\ell|w_\ell|\le 1$, the $L_1$ norm telescopes to closed forms: $\sqrt{d(u)}$ for feature removal, $4/\sqrt{d(u)}+4/\sqrt{d(v)}$ for edge removal (deleting one edge of a hub barely moves anything), with no dependence on $L$. The algorithm's bookkeeping is the perturbation analysis. The same accounting gives a cheap data-dependent bound whose approximation term is literally $2c_1|\mathbf 1^\top R|$, the residue mass currently sitting in memory.

Limitations, honestly: the certificate covers linear models with strongly convex loss only (logistic / least-squares on top of a fixed linear propagation). The deep-model experiments (decoupled MLP, spectral GNN) have no guarantee, and the authors say so plainly, citing both the unresolved status of Newton updates in nonconvex nets and the NP-hardness of even approximating a 2-layer ReLU optimum. Approximation is not free: ScaleGUN's worst-case and early-stage data-dependent bounds are strictly larger than CGU's, and the worst-case bounds carry $\sqrt{F(n_t-1)}$ factors plus a requirement $\epsilon_1=O(1/\sqrt{n_t})$, i.e. $r_{\max}=O(1/\sqrt{n_t n})$ — so $r_{\max}$ must shrink with graph size and the one-off initialization cost $\tilde O(L\bar d/r_{\max})$ grows with it. Several final constants come from informally dropping "small" terms. And as in all this literature, the guarantee is for a non-adaptive request sequence, at a loose operating point ($\epsilon=1$, $\delta=10^{-4}$), with periodic full retraining once the budget is spent.

Broader context. Machine unlearning (Cao & Yang 2015) splits into exact and approximate. Exact methods make retraining cheap structurally: SISA (Bourtoule et al. 2021) shards the data so a deletion only retrains one shard; GraphEraser ports this to graphs; Projector/GraphEditor solve it in closed form for ridge-regression linear GNNs. Approximate methods trade exactness for a probabilistic guarantee, and certified removal (Guo et al. 2019) is the rigorous subfamily — it is essentially DP-ERM machinery (objective perturbation, Chaudhuri et al.) repurposed so that the noise masks a deletion residual rather than any single-record difference. Chien et al. 2022 (CGU) is the graph instantiation on SGC/GPR and the direct parent of this paper; CEU (Wu et al. 2023) does batch edge removal. Worth remembering the relationship to DP: a DP model gives certified unlearning for free, but with the usual utility hit, which is exactly why certified unlearning is attractive.

The other lineage is pure IR: Forward Push / local PageRank (Andersen–Chung–Lang, FOCS 2006), approximate PPR on dynamic graphs (Zhang–Lofgren–Goel 2016), InstantGNN (Zheng et al. 2022), AGP (Wang et al. 2021), and the Yang–Wang–Wei PPR survey (2024). This paper is best read as a bridge: local-push residues, long used as an efficiency device, are repurposed as a certificate.

Follow-up idea. The paper pushes globally to a uniform $r_{\max}$, but only training-node rows enter the loss and only a few nodes are touched per deletion. A per-node / adaptive residue threshold (or a bidirectional Backward-Push estimator) targeted at the rows that actually appear in $|\nabla L|$ should give a much tighter $\epsilon_1$ at lower cost, and $r_{\max}$ could be chosen by jointly optimizing the approximation budget against the noise budget rather than hand-tuned. A second gap: the machinery is symmetric in insertions and deletions (InstantGNN handles both), but the certificate for an interleaved insert/delete stream, and for adaptively chosen deletion requests, is not done.

Link to your work. Two real connections, with the honest caveats. First, and most directly usable: this is an instance of a general pattern — when a retrieval-relevant quantity is computed by a lazily maintained iterative solver, the solver's residue vector is a computable, data-dependent error certificate you can hand to a downstream guarantee. PPR and local push are classic IR ranking primitives; the theory question in your idiom is what residue bounds buy you about rankings rather than parameters — converting $L_1/L_\infty$ residue bounds into top-$k$ stability or ranking-correctness certificates under incremental graph edits is a clean open problem, and this paper is a worked example of the residue-as-certificate discipline.

Second, deletion. In ANN indexes deletions are typically tombstoned and only truly discharged at rebuild — the exact analogue of "retraining" here, and the structural obstacle is the same one: an HNSW graph's edges were chosen partly because the deleted vector was present, just as node embeddings encode a removed node's features. A "certified deletion" notion for vector indexes (post-deletion index indistinguishable from one built without the point) is a genuinely open and appealing question. Be honest about the gap, though: the Guo framework certifies a distribution over the parameters of a convex ERM, and an ANN index is not the output of one, so the guarantee would have to be rebuilt over the index construction's own randomness rather than transferred. The same wall stands in front of generative retrieval: docids live in nonconvex decoder weights, current document deletion/update is heuristic (incremental indexing, DSI++), and this paper names precisely why certification there is blocked. The realistic near-term version — which the authors themselves endorse in their appendix — is a frozen nonlinear encoder plus a convex head: a linear-probe reranker or learned-sparse head over frozen representations, where certified removal of a document is in reach today.

title: Bridging Jensen Gap for Max-Min Group Fairness Optimization in Recommendation
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-30

Bridging Jensen Gap for Max-Min Group Fairness Optimization in Recommendation — Chen Xu, Yuxin Li, Wenjie Wang, Liang Pang, Jun Xu, Tat-Seng Chua (ICLR 2025) — arXiv:2502.09319

Main idea. Group max-min fairness (MMF) in recommendation asks that the worst-off item group — categories, providers, sellers — receive at least some "minimum wage" of utility, where utility is accumulated over a whole traffic period (a day's exposure of action movies, say), not per user. That aggregation is the whole problem: a constraint on a sum over all users of group-level utility does not decompose into per-sample terms, so the MMF-regularized loss stops being linearly additive in the training samples. Theorem 1 makes this concrete by rewriting "accuracy loss + λ·max-over-groups loss" as a single power-form objective min_w b^T (Â^T w)^{1+t} with t ≥ 0 growing with λ, where w is the vector of per-item accumulated cross-entropy losses and Â the row-normalized item–group incidence matrix. Because x ↦ x^{1+t} is strictly convex for t > 0, minimizing the objective batch-by-batch and summing is not the same as minimizing it on the full data — the Jensen gap. Their Lemma 1 pins the direction: under a budget on total utility, the minimum of a sum of x^{1+t} terms over n partitions equals c^{1+t}/n^t, so more partitions (smaller batches) means the mini-batch objective systematically underestimates the true loss, and the gap grows with the number of groups. Their fix, FairDual, comes from a second reformulation (Theorem 3): dualizing the MMF constraint with a variable µ per group turns the constrained problem into plain per-group-weighted cross-entropy with weights s_g = 1 − µ_g, i.e. the negative shadow price of that group's constraint. FairDual runs the primal model update and a mirror-descent update of µ in lockstep: each batch, it estimates each group's realized top-K ranking utility from a frozen, periodically refreshed item-embedding table (sampling Q items rather than the full corpus), tracks a per-group residual budget γ_j, momentum-smooths the dual subgradient, and projects µ back onto a feasible cone with cvxpy. So the "debiasing" is not a gradient correction term but an online-allocation controller that re-prices groups as the epoch proceeds — essentially the budget-pacing machinery of Balseiro et al.'s regularized online allocation, imported into recommender training.

The most interesting part (and where I would push back). The reframing is genuinely valuable: it explains why the popular heuristic of "reweight the weak group" works at all, and identifies the right weight as a shadow price rather than a hand-designed inverse-popularity or DRO weight. The cost model is also honest — dual variables are hundreds of parameters, negligible next to a 7B backbone, and they report 28% faster convergence.

But the theory and the empirics do not meet in the middle. First, the Jensen gap as defined is a gap between two optimal values of relaxed problems over the utility vector w, not a bias in the stochastic gradient the network actually receives; nothing in Theorems 1–2 says a neural net trained with mini-batches converges to the minimizer of L_B. The duality in Eq. (20) is introduced with a ≤ (weak duality) and strong duality is asserted via convexity of W, which holds for the idealized allocation problem, not for the parametrized model. Second, Theorem 4's stated tuning looks wrong: the bound is H/η + |U|L|G|²η/(Bσ(1−α)) + L|G|²/(2(1−α)²σ η), so η = O(B^{-1/2}) makes it grow like B^{1/2}; minimizing over η requires η ∝ B^{1/2}, and only then does one get O(B^{-1/2}) — which is really an O(√N) online-regret statement in the number of batches N = |U|/B, i.e. a guarantee about the dual weights, not "sub-linear convergence to the globally optimal solution" of the recommender. The |G|² factor rests on c = max_g m_g ∝ |G|, which contradicts their own setting m_g = |I_g|. Third, the two components that make the method practical — the frozen item encoder refreshed every β batches and the Q-item sample for the ranking-score estimate — are exactly the sources of bias the theory ignores, and Table 5 shows "full (unbiased)" beats Q=400 on both metrics, so the approximation demonstrably costs performance. Fourth, the empirical case for the mechanism is thin: the Jensen-gap curves (Fig. 1, Fig. 3a) come from a synthetic 1000×1000 matrix-factorization simulation, never from the LLM backbones where the gains are claimed. Absolute numbers are tiny (NDCG@5 ≈ 1%), several accuracy improvements are not starred (MRR improvement of 0.00% on MIND), BigRec is trained on 1024 samples, and the reported Amazon-Book statistics (15.4M users, 1.05M interactions) cannot be right. The λ-sweep shows accuracy rising then falling and the authors attribute the rise to popularity-bias mitigation — which suggests the accuracy gains may be a debiasing effect orthogonal to the Jensen gap; Appendix N is telling, since plain IPS reweighting reaches MMF@5 = 12.63 against FairDual's 11.98 on SASRec. Finally, scalability: the feasible set has 2^{|G|} subset constraints, implemented as |G| prefix-sum constraints solved per batch, and is only tested with 17–25 groups despite motivating claims about "hundreds of groups" and millions of providers. The group definition also does real work — m_g = |I_g| makes MMF close to per-item exposure parity, so part of the fairness movement is a consequence of that choice rather than of the algorithm.

Broader context. Group fairness on the item/provider side grew out of multi-stakeholder recommendation: FairRec (Patro et al., WWW'20) guarantees every provider an envy-free share of exposure via a fair-allocation argument, TFROM and CPFair do two-sided re-ranking, and exposure-fairness in ranking (Singh & Joachims; Biega et al.'s equity of attention; Diaz et al.'s expected exposure) formalizes amortized exposure targets over queries. The welfare view — treat group utilities as a vector and optimize a concave social-welfare function — gives max-min as the limit of the power-mean family; Do et al. (NeurIPS'21) optimize for Lorenz dominance, Do & Usunier (SIGIR'22) generalized Gini indices, and Cousins' welfare-centric PAC learning is the closest theoretical cousin, since it studies exactly the sample complexity of these non-additive objectives. On the robust-optimization side, max-min group fairness is DRO/CVaR with a group-structured ambiguity set, and Hashimoto et al.'s repeated loss minimization is the canonical recommender-adjacent instance; the same first author's P-MMF (WWW'23) and FairSync (WWW'24) are the post-processing and distributed-retrieval counterparts of this paper's in-processing dual.

A natural follow-up: prove (or refute) that no unbiased mini-batch estimator exists for this class of aggregate-constrained objectives, and characterize the minimal amount of cross-batch state — a running group-utility sketch, a memory bank — needed to drive the gap to zero, rather than only bounding one particular controller's regret. A second: treat the Q-item sample and the stale index as first-class noise in the analysis, which is where this meets your own work.

Connection to theoretical IR / generative retrieval / vector search. Mini-batch bias in non-additive objectives is not a fairness curiosity; it is the same phenomenon as the in-batch-negatives bias in dense retrieval. A softmax loss over a batch estimates the full-corpus log-partition function, and E[log Z_B] ≤ log E[Z_B] is literally a Jensen gap that shrinks as O(B^{-1/2})-ish in batch size — which is why cross-batch memory, ANCE-style asynchronous index refresh, and huge contrastive batches all help, and why FairDual's frozen-encoder-plus-refresh trick is structurally identical to ANCE's stale index. Listwise ranking losses and NDCG surrogates have the same non-additivity across a list. For generative retrieval the issue is sharper still: the objective is a sequence likelihood under constrained beam search over a docid space, exposure of a document is determined by the whole decoding process rather than by any single training sample, and there is currently no clean way to impose an amortized per-provider or per-group coverage constraint during training — the shadow-price-as-token-bias idea in this paper is a plausible route (add µ_g to the logits of identifier prefixes belonging to group g). For vector search, the dual view is especially neat: a per-provider dual variable enters the score additively, so a fairness-constrained retrieval becomes MIPS against modified vectors, at which point ANN approximation error and quantization interact with the shadow price in a way nobody has analyzed — the controller is enforcing a constraint using a biased utility estimate from an approximate index. Formalizing that interaction (regret of the dual controller as a function of ANN recall and index staleness) would be a genuinely new theoretical result and sits squarely between this paper's weakest link and your toolkit.

title: Improved Lower Bounds for all Odd-Query Locally Decodable Codes
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-30

Improved Lower Bounds for all Odd-Query Locally Decodable Codes — Basu, Hsieh, Kothari & Lin (2024) · arXiv:2411.14361

Main idea. A $q$-query LDC lets you recover any single message bit by probing only $q$ positions of a corrupted codeword. For even $q$, the classical bound $k \le \tilde O(n^{1-2/q})$ has been known since Katz–Trevisan and Kerenidis–de Wolf. For odd $q$ the only available route was the trivial "a $q$-LDC is a $(q+1)$-LDC", giving the strictly weaker $n^{1-2/(q+1)}$ — so for $q=5$ the state of the art was $n^{2/3}$ rather than $n^{3/5}$. Alrabiah–Guruswami–Kothari–Manohar closed the gap for $q=3$ in 2023, but their argument bottoms out in an appeal to the exponential 2-LDC lower bound, and the analogous step for $q=5$ would need an exponential bound for 4-LDCs, which is false (Yekhanin–Efremenko codes exist). This paper removes that bottleneck and proves the even-$q$ bound for every odd $q$, by replacing the "prune the heavy tuples" philosophy with a regularity notion that tolerates arbitrarily heavy tuples.

Proof sketch. Precisely: for any $(q,\delta,\varepsilon)$-LDC, $k \le n^{1-2/q}\cdot 2^{O(q)}\log^4 n/(\varepsilon^6\delta^2)$; for linear codes the analysis is combinatorial and loses only $\log^2 n$. The skeleton is the AGKM reduction to semirandom $q$-XOR refutation: normalize the decoder into $k$ $q$-uniform matchings $\mathcal H_i$ of size $\ge\delta n$, form $\Psi_b(x)=\sum_i b_i\sum_{C\in\mathcal H_i} x_C$, note a real LDC forces $\mathbb E_b[\mathrm{val}(\Psi_b)]\ge\Omega(|\mathcal H|)$, and derive a contradiction by proving $\mathbb E_b[\mathrm{val}(\Psi_b)] = o(|\mathcal H|)$ whenever $k \gg n^{1-2/q}$. Because $q$ is odd, $\Psi_b$ is an odd-degree form and cannot be a quadratic form directly, so one squares it (Cauchy–Schwarz) and pairs hyperedges $C,C'$ that share exactly $t$ vertices, whose symmetric difference has even size $2(q-t)$; this becomes a quadratic form of a signed level-$\ell$ Kikuchi matrix on $\binom{[n]\times[2]}{\ell}$, with $\ell = n^{1-2/q}\log n$. A random left/right split $L\sqcup R$ of $[k]$ makes the blocks independent so Matrix Khintchine applies, and the $\infty!\to!1$ norm lets heavy rows be pruned rather than bounded.

The new ingredient is what controls those heavy rows. Prior work insisted the hypergraph be well-spread: every pair (or $r$-set) has co-degree at most an absolute $\mathrm{polylog}\,n$ threshold. Here the condition is $t$-approximate strong regularity: $\mathcal H$ partitions into groups each pinned to a fixed $t$-set $Q_\theta$, all of size $d_t/2$ to $d_t$, and all other co-degrees $d_r$ are bounded relative to $d_t$ (roughly $d_r/d_t \le n^{1-2r/q}$ below the pivot, $d_r/d_t\le n^{-2(r-t)/q + (t-\mathbb 1[t\text{ even}])/q}$ above it). Nothing absolute is assumed — triples may have co-degree $n^{\Omega(1)}$. The reason this suffices is a genuinely elegant scaling: the Kikuchi graph's average degree is $\Omega((\ell/n)^{q-t}knd_t)$ and the per-color degree budget $\Delta = d(K)/100\ell\log n$ also scales with $d_t$, so a large $d_t$ stops being an obstruction and becomes a resource. Concretely, the heavy-row bound comes from writing $\deg(S)$ as a degree-$(q-t)$ polynomial in the $\ell/n$-biased indicator of $S$ and applying Schudy–Sviridenko concentration; its hypothesis needs expected partial derivatives, and Lemma 4.20 shows each $\partial_{Z_1}\partial_{Z_2}$ is bounded by exactly $d_{|Z_2|}$ or $d_{t+|Z_2|}$ — the co-degree inequalities in the definition are reverse-engineered to be precisely these derivative bounds. Two further pieces close the loop: an extremal claim (Lemma 5.1) that a good pivot $t$ exists for every decreasing co-degree sequence — take $t_0 < q/2$ maximizing $\gamma_{t_0}+2t_0/q$ where $\gamma_i = \log_n d_i$, and if some $t>q/2$ violates the second condition, the maximizing violator works — and a greedy decomposition that repeatedly peels the heaviest $t$-tuple until $d_t$ halves, yielding $O(q\log n)$ approximately strongly regular pieces covering all but an $\eta$ fraction of hyperedges. In the linear case the same machinery instead produces a weakly rainbow even cover (an even cover using some color exactly once), which is impossible for an LDC, via the HKM+24 rainbow-closed-walk lemma applied to the Kikuchi graph.

The most interesting part / critique. The conceptual move — replacing absolute co-degree thresholds by relative ones — is exactly what makes the pigeonhole existence proof possible: no fixed threshold sequence can work for all co-degree profiles, but a scale-invariant one can always be anchored somewhere. That is a real insight and the authors are refreshingly candid that the specific exponents "may not look motivated in first reading." That candor is also the weakness: the definition is a list of inequalities tuned to one concentration inequality, and the paper claims future applicability without exhibiting a second application. The result also only matches the even-$q$ bound; it does not breach the $n^{1-2/q}$ barrier, which looks hardwired into the choice $\ell = n^{1-2/q}$, and the gap to the $\exp(k^{o(1)})$ matching-vector constructions remains vast. Minor debits: $\log^4 n$ loss where the concurrent, independent Janzer–Manohar bipartite-Kikuchi argument gets a single log; the $2^{O(q)}$ and $\varepsilon^{-6}$ dependence; and the larger-alphabet extension is asserted with "we omit a formal argument."

Broader context. LDC lower bounds are the complexity-theoretic core of private information retrieval (a $q$-server PIR scheme yields a $q$-LDC, and Dvir–Gopi's subpolynomial 2-server PIR shows why large alphabets evade these bounds) and of error-correcting data structures (de Wolf; Chen–Grigorescu–de Wolf). Worth reading alongside: AGKM 2023 (STOC) for the CSP-refutation bridge, and Hsieh–Kothari–Mohanty's sharp hypergraph Moore bound for the Kikuchi toolkit in its cleanest form. The obvious follow-up is whether approximate strong regularity, being regularity "for free," improves semirandom $q$-CSP refutation and even-cover thresholds at odd uniformity — the prior applications all paid for absolute thresholds — and whether it unlocks $q\ge5$ locally correctable codes, where Kothari–Manohar have exponential bounds only for $q=3$. For your own work the honest connection is indirect but real: an LDC bound is a statement that no redundant encoding supports $O(1)$-probe recovery in sublinear-ish space, which is the same shape as space lower bounds for succinct/robust indexes answering queries with constant probes; and the technical kit here — row pruning plus Matrix Khintchine to bound $\infty!\to!1$ norms of sparse signed matrices — is the same kit used for spectral norms of random sparse operators in sketching and random-projection analyses. Beyond that, it is best enjoyed as a clean piece of extremal hypergraph spectral technique rather than forced into a retrieval frame.

title: Tighter Convergence Bounds for Shuffled SGD via Primal-Dual Perspective
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-29

Tighter Convergence Bounds for Shuffled SGD via Primal-Dual Perspective

Cai, Lin, Diakonikolas · 2024 · OpenReview · arXiv:2306.12498

Main idea. SGD is analysed with replacement and run without it, and the gap is not cosmetic: with-replacement sampling gives E[∇f_{i_t}(x)] = ∇f(x), the hinge on which all GD-style analysis swings, and shuffling breaks it. The existing without-replacement bounds for smooth convex finite sums are, in the small-epoch regime, worse than full gradient descent — O(nLD²/ε) with L = max_i L_i, forced by O(1/(nL)) step sizes. This paper narrows from general finite sums to convex ERM with linear predictors, f(x) = (1/n)Σ_i ℓ_i(a_iᵀx), takes the Fenchel dual min_x max_y (1/n)(⟨Ax,y⟩ − Σ_i ℓ_i_(yⁱ)), and observes that shuffled SGD _is_ a primal-dual method performing _cyclic block-coordinate updates on the dual side* in the permutation order. (The arXiv preprint carries a different title, "Empirical Risk Minimization with Shuffled SGD," but it is the same work.)

The payoff is that L in the deterministic term is replaced by √(L̂ L̃), where L̂π is a data-matrix quantity — masked Gram matrices summed over the sweep, with the operator norm taken after summation. Since L̂ ≤ (1/n)Σ_i L_i‖a_i‖² ≤ L, with the operator-norm-to-trace step alone losing up to a factor n, Theorem 1 gives RR/SO complexity O(n√(L̂L̃)D²/ε + √((n−b)(n+b)/(n(n−1)))·√(nL̃)·σ*D²/ε^{3/2}) under η_k ≤ b/(n√(2L̂_π L̃_π)). At b = 1, L̃ = L exactly, so the improvement over Mishchenko et al. / Nguyen et al. / Cha et al. is a clean factor √(L/L̂) in the leading term; empirically L/L̂ ≈ n^α with α ∈ [0.15, 0.96] across 15 LIBSVM/MNIST/CIFAR-scale datasets, i.e. up to nearly √n. Theorem 2 handles incremental GD deterministically, Theorem 3 the nonsmooth Lipschitz case, and Theorems 4–5 lift to general finite sums via a block-replication operator, where the gain degrades to max_i L_i → (1/n)Σ_i L_i.

Critique. Be clear about where the improvement lives. It is entirely in the D²/ε term — the one that dominates when K is small, ε is large, or σ_ is small (including σ_ = 0 for linearly independent rows). The σ__ term at b = 1 _exactly reproduces_ the state of the art and does not touch the Cha et al. lower bound; so nothing asymptotic improves, and the claim is a small-epoch claim, which is arguably the practically relevant one but should not be read as beating a lower bound. Second, L̂ = max_π L̂_π is a worst-case-permutation constant, while Table 2 reports the _empirical mean_ of L̂_π over random permutations — the headline numbers are not the constants in the theorem. The authors are candid about this and gesture at an unproven high-probability version; closing that gap is the obvious missing lemma. Third, L̂ is not cheaply computable (it needs n operator norms of n×n submatrices), so it is a descriptive constant, not something you tune with. Fourth, the setting is non-strongly-convex only, with per-component convexity assumed (Ahn–Yun–Sra removed that), the guarantee is on the η-weighted ergodic average, and the randomness enters only through the marginal uniformity of each epoch's permutation — so RR and SO get identical bounds and the analysis cannot see any separation between them. The nonsmooth result (Theorem 3), to their credit, is stated as being up to a factor n _worse* than with-replacement SGD at b = 1.

Context. Without-replacement SGD resisted non-asymptotic analysis for years. Recht–Ré (2012) proposed a noncommutative arithmetic–geometric mean inequality that would have explained the speedup; Lai–Lim (2020) and De Sa (2020) proved it false. Gürbüzbalaban–Ozdaglar–Parrilo (Math. Prog. 2021) broke through with O(1/K²) for smooth strongly convex RR, beating SGD's O(1/(nK)) for large K; Haochen–Sra, Nagaraj et al., Ahn–Yun–Sra, and Mishchenko–Khaled–Richtárik's "Random reshuffling: simple analysis with vast improvements" (NeurIPS 2020) sharpened and simplified it, with Safran–Shamir, Rajput et al., Yun et al. and Cha–Lee–Yun supplying matching lower bounds under restricted step sizes. The intellectual parent here is elsewhere, though: cyclic block coordinate descent, where relating partial to full gradients is the same obstruction (Beck–Tetruashvili, Sun–Ye, Lee–Wright's "random permutations fix a worst case for cyclic CD"), and where Song–Diakonikolas and Lin–Song–Diakonikolas developed the machinery — though the authors note their proofs are technically disjoint, since extrapolation or proximal cyclic updates would break the equivalence to SGD. Two directions worth tracking: permutation design (GraB-style gradient-balancing orderings that provably beat RR), and data-dependent constants as a general program for de-pessimising finite-sum analysis. A natural follow-up: prove concentration of L̂_π over random π — a matrix-concentration question — and then minimise L̂_π over orderings, which would make ordering selection a spectral problem rather than a heuristic one.

The IR connection is real but narrow, and worth being candid about. Theorem 1 does not apply to dual-encoder training: the encoder is nonconvex, and in-batch negatives make the epoch loss depend on the partition into batches, not merely the order, so it is not a fixed finite sum under reshuffling at all — squarely outside this framework. Where it does apply is convex ERM over frozen embeddings: a linear reranker or a linear scoring head on fixed vectors is exactly the primal problem with A the embedding matrix, and then L̂ is governed by the Gram matrix AAᵀ — the very similarity matrix vector search cares about. The reading is that a well-spread, high-effective-rank, low-coherence embedding matrix (what you want for ANN indexing) has ‖AAᵀ‖ small relative to tr(AAᵀ), hence large L/L̂, hence a bigger shuffling speedup. Anisotropy hurts you twice. That is the honest extent of it.

Proof sketch. Assumptions: each ℓ_i convex with a minimiser existing (Asm. 1), L_i-smooth (Asm. 3, equivalently ℓ_i_ is 1/L_i-strongly convex — this Fenchel duality is the load-bearing fact), and bounded σ__² = (1/n)Σ_i‖∇f_i(x_)‖² (Asm. 4); Λ = diag(L_1,…,L_n). The guarantee is on E[f(x̂K) − f(x)] for the η-weighted average x̂_K, with n appearing through K = (gradient queries)/n.

The argument is approximate-duality-gap in form: bound Gap^v(x_k, y__) = L(x_k, v) − L(x__, y__) and set v = y_{x_k} at the end to recover the function gap. Define the one-epoch potential difference E_k := η_k·Gap^v(x_k,y__) + (b/2n)‖x_ − x_k‖² − (b/2n)‖x_ − x_{k−1}‖², which telescopes. Lemma 1 bounds E_k using 1/L_i-strong convexity of ℓ_i_ on both sides — the dual exact-maximisation step upper-bounds L(x_k,v) with a −(η_k/2n)‖y_k − v_k‖²_{Λ_k^{−1}} slack, the optimality condition a_jᵀx__ ∈ ∂ℓ_j_(y__^j) lower-bounds L(x_,y_) with an analogous term, and the primal prox step contributes −(b/2n)Σ_i‖x_{k−1,i} − x_{k−1,i+1}‖² — leaving two inner-product residuals T₁, T₂.

Lemma 2 is the first pleasant surprise: T₁ collapses exactly to (b/2n)Σ_i‖x_{k−1,i} − x_{k−1,i+1}‖² − (b/2n)‖x_{k−1} − x_k‖², cancelling the prox slack and leaving a spare negative term. No inequality is spent.

T₂ = (η_k/n)Σ_i ⟨v_k^{(i)} − y_k^{(i)}, A_k^{(i)}(x_k − x_{k−1,i})⟩ is the hard term — it is precisely the intra-epoch drift that prior analyses kill with a triangle inequality and the global L. The crucial trick is the exact identity x_k − x_{k−1,i} = −(η_k/b)A_kᵀ I_{b(i−1)↑} y_k: the tail of the epoch's updates is a single linear operator — the identity with the first b(i−1) diagonal entries zeroed — applied to the whole dual vector, rather than a sum of gradients evaluated at m−i different iterates. Decompose y_k = (y_k − y_{_,k}) + y_{_,k}. On the first piece, Young's inequality plus Cauchy–Schwarz in the Λ_k metric pulls out ‖Λ_k^{1/2}Σ_i I_{b(i−1)↑}A_kA_kᵀI_{b(i−1)↑}Λ_k^{1/2}‖₂ — the operator norm of the aggregate, which is where L̂_π is born, and where the saving over Σ_i‖·‖₂ ≤ n‖AAᵀ‖ ≤ n·tr lives. The analogous block-diagonal object gives L̃_π, tight at b = 1. On the second piece, A_kᵀI_{b(i−1)↑}y_{_,k} is a sum over a without-replacement sample drawn from {∇f_j(x__)}j, whose full sum vanishes by optimality; the classical sampling-without-replacement variance identity (Lemma 5, with its (n−b)/(b(n−1)) scaling) is the only place permutation randomness is used, and yields the σ*² noise term. Choosing the two Young parameters as 2η_k L̃_{π^{(k)}} and 2η_k L̃ makes the residuals absorbable by the Lemma 1 negative terms exactly when η_k ≤ b/(n√(2L̂L̃)) — a step size √(L/L̂) larger than prior work's O(1/(nL)), which is the entire source of the improvement. For incremental GD the permutation is fixed, so Lemma 5 is unavailable and the noise term is bounded deterministically instead, recovering the familiar O(√n) loss from dropping randomisation. Sanity checks hold: b = n recovers exactly (sub)gradient descent in Theorems 1 and 3.

title: An Alternative to FLOPS Regularization to Effectively Productionize SPLADE-Doc
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-29

An Alternative to FLOPS Regularization to Effectively Productionize SPLADE-Doc

Porco, Mehra, Malioutov, Radhakrishnan, Keymanesh, Preoţiuc-Pietro, MacAvaney, Cheng · 2025 · arXiv:2505.15070

Main idea. FLOPS regularization, ℓ = Σ_t ā_t² with ā_t the batch-mean weight of term t, is an ℓ₂ penalty on the mean-activation vector; subject to fixed total mass it is minimized at a uniform ā, so it controls average per-document density but is indifferent to how activation mass is distributed across terms. Paria et al.'s claim that minimizing it equalizes term likelihood does not survive contact with a DistilBERT MLM head: the Bloomberg/Glasgow team find SPLADE-Doc's most frequent token has DF = 95.8% of the 8.8M MS MARCO passages, so a query containing it matches 8.6M documents and Solr must traverse essentially the whole index. Their fix is to weight each term's contribution by a logistic gate on its corpus frequency: ℓ_DF-FLOPS = Σ_t w_t·(mean activation of t)², with w_t = 1/(1 + (x·log α² − 1)^β) evaluated at x = DF_t/|C| — α an approximate DF-ratio cutoff, β the steepness. FLOPS is the special case w_t ≡ 1. DF_t is re-estimated every 100 steps from a 50K-pair validation sample rather than precomputed (static DF is markedly worse: MRR@10 28.8, top-token DF 51.7%). They use α = 0.1, β = 10, λ ∈ 10⁻¹–10³.

The numbers on Solr v9 (2 cores, 40 GB, 6980 dev queries, top-10): SPLADE-Doc + FLOPS is MRR@10 32.2, R@1K 92.4, 922 ms average / 1945.6 ms P99, 8.628M matches, top-token DF 95.8%, 583.8 active tokens/doc. Top-150 pruning barely helps (792 ms, DF still 95.7%) — the offending tokens carry high weights, so they survive pruning. Cranking λ on plain FLOPS to 1 reaches 160.9 ms but costs ~4 points of MRR (28.3) and R@1K (88.4). DF-FLOPS lands at 161.0 ms / 341.7 ms P99 at MRR 30.0 and R@1K 92.9 — same latency as the λ=1 FLOPS point, +1.7 MRR and +4.5 R@1K over it. Adding top-150 pruning gives 87.8 ms / 187.8 ms P99 at MRR 29.7, R@1K 93.0, top-token DF 5.2% — 10× faster than the FLOPS baseline and roughly BM25-class (68.9 ms / 241.3 ms; DF-FLOPS actually beats BM25 at P99). Tellingly, representations are not sparser (301.6 tokens/doc, vs 33.0 for FLOPS λ=1): the model reallocates mass to long-tail terms rather than emitting fewer of them, which is the whole point — it decouples document density from posting-list length.

Critique. The headline latency comparison is matched-latency and honest, but there is no matched-effectiveness comparison: the FLOPS λ grid is three coarse points, and no FLOPS model is shown at MRR ≈ 30. DF-FLOPS meanwhile gets λ plus (α, β) chosen by an unreported "pilot study" on dev, with no ablation of the two parameters that constitute the contribution. α is a DF-quantile cutoff and is visibly corpus-dependent; DF is estimated from MS MARCO training passages only, so nothing controls the DF profile of a BEIR index — and no latency is reported for any corpus other than MS MARCO, which is a real hole in a paper whose thesis is about production cost. One engine, one corpus, one hardware configuration. The assertion that filtering makes full posting-list traversal "often unavoidable" — the justification for ignoring BlockMax-WAND — is asserted, not measured; PISA, Seismic and BMP are explicitly punted on with a "we expect" hand-wave. Missing baselines are conspicuous: stopword removal (Lassance & Clinchant) and term-centric quantile static pruning are the paper's named foils but appear nowhere in Table 2, so the "selective retention of salient stopwords" argument rests on one cherry-picked WHO example, not an experiment. The 2.2-point MRR framing also understates the cost: nDCG@10 on DL19 drops 65.6 → 59.5 (6.1 points), and no significance testing appears anywhere despite 43/54-query TREC sets. The BEIR "12 of 13" is measured against their own FLOPS-trained SPLADE-Doc, which is pathological (arguana 11.16, quora 7.56); against BM25, DF-FLOPS still loses on fever (60.7 vs 75.3), quora (48.4 vs 78.9), touché (24.6 vs 36.7), trec-covid, climate-fever and scifact — roughly half of BEIR, while being slower than BM25 on average latency.

Broader context. Learned sparse retrieval maps text to a vector over the WordPiece vocabulary so that a standard inverted index can serve it: SPLADE (Formal et al. 2021) uses the MLM head's log-saturated max-pooled logits plus FLOPS; SPLADE v2/++ add distillation and hard negatives; Efficient SPLADE splits query and document encoders with separate regularization budgets; SPLADE-Doc drops the query encoder entirely, representing the query as a binary bag of literal tokens, which removes a BERT forward pass from the critical path and makes scoring a pure DAAT/SAAT accumulation over document-side impacts. That last design is exactly what makes posting-list skew fatal: with no query weights there is no meaningful upper-bound structure for WAND/BlockMax-WAND to exploit aggressively, and Mackenzie et al.'s "wacky weights" paper documented the same collapse of dynamic-pruning effectiveness on learned impacts. The complementary line is engine-side — Seismic, BMP, and clustered inverted indexes paired with k-NN graphs (Bruch et al.) — which this paper correctly calls orthogonal.

The interesting theoretical gap is that DF-FLOPS is still a surrogate for the wrong functional. True query cost is E_q[Σ_{t∈q} DF_t], and P99 latency is governed by max_t DF_t (or a CVaR of the DF distribution), not by Σ_t ā_t². The logistic gate at α is a smoothed indicator that approximates an L∞-style constraint by hand-tuned annealing. A clean follow-up: since SPLADE-Doc's query is a known binary distribution over tokens, the expected number of scored postings is exactly Σ_t P(t ∈ q)·DF_t, so weighting by query-term probability times DF gives a differentiable estimator of the actual cost model rather than a proxy — and replacing (α, β) with a Lagrange multiplier on a hard constraint max_t DF_t ≤ τ, updated by dual ascent, would make the method corpus-adaptive and hyperparameter-free.

For your own work, the transferable object is the cost model: posting-list length plays the role of per-node fanout, and the sparse side is rediscovering something the dense side already knows. Hubness in high-dimensional k-NN graphs (Radovanović et al.) is the precise analogue of a 95%-DF token — a few nodes accumulate enormous in-degree and dominate traversal cost — and DiskANN's robust prune and HNSW's M cap are worst-case degree regularizers, structurally the same move as DF-FLOPS. That suggests a unified framing worth formalizing: both sparse and dense indexes are solving max effectiveness subject to a constraint on the tail of a cost distribution, where FLOPS and average-degree penalties control the mean while the production-relevant quantity is a quantile. Stating the sparse–dense efficiency frontier in those terms — with the DF distribution and the in-degree distribution as two instantiations of one cost measure — would be a genuinely theoretical contribution that this paper gestures at empirically but never writes down.

title: Optimal Sequential Recommendations: Exploiting User and Item Structure
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-29

Optimal Sequential Recommendations: Exploiting User and Item Structure

Karzand, Bresler · 2025 · arXiv:2504.19476

Main idea. The setting is online collaborative filtering with a doubly-clustered latent variable model: N users drawn i.i.d. uniform over q_U types, an infinite item stream with types i.i.d. uniform over q_I, and a preference matrix Ξ ∈ {±1}^{q_U × q_I} with i.i.d. Rademacher entries, so that L_{u,i} = ξ_{τ_U(u), τ_I(i)} deterministically. Every user receives one item per round, feedback is binary and noiseless, and — the structural constraint that separates this from bandits — no item may be recommended twice to the same user, so there is no "converge to the best arm" endgame and exploration never stops. Regret is the expected number of disliked recommendations per user by time T.

The main theorem gives N·regret(T) = Θ̃(N·R(T)) with R(T) piecewise in five regimes separated by T₁ = log q_U, T₂ = q_I/N, T₃ = q_I/q_U, T₄ = N(log q_U)²/q_I, T₅ = q_I q_U: cold start (R = T), item-item (√(q_I T/N)), user-user (log q_U + q_U T/N), hybrid (log q_U + √(q_I q_U T)/N), and asymptotic (log q_U + q_I q_U/N + (log q_I)T/N, or the user-user rate, whichever is smaller). The headline consequence is that both structures are needed only in the hybrid window; elsewhere one of the two is exactly optimal, and there is a genuinely surprising corollary — if user-user beats item-item asymptotically, then hybrid never helps at any horizon.

Most interesting part, and where I'd push back. The lower bound is the real contribution and it avoids Fano entirely. The authors define four disjoint "bad recommendation" events indexed by whether the recommended item has been rated by s_I ≈ log q_I user types, whether the user has rated s_U ≈ log q_U item types, and three "knowledge" events; on each, the posterior P[L = +1 | history] is provably bounded away from 1. The machinery that makes this work is (s,η)-row/column regularity of Ξ: for every choice of s columns and every sign pattern, the number of matching rows is within (1±η)q_U/2^s. A random ±1 matrix is regular with probability 1 − 1/(4N) by Chernoff plus union bound, and regularity converts "the user's row is uncertain after s_U observations" directly into "the surviving candidate rows are roughly balanced in the target column," i.e. posterior anti-concentration without any KL or mutual-information accounting.

That said, the modelling is aggressive in ways that matter for the shape of the curve, not just constants. Ratings are exactly noiseless and types exactly homogeneous, so clustering is a pure equality test — r_U = ⌈2log(N q_U²)⌉ items suffice because a single disagreement refutes a pair of types. The paper says noise is "technically straightforward"; that is true for the algorithm (majority votes, r inflated by (1−2γ)^{−2}) but not obviously for the lower bound, since Lemmas 4.4–4.8 are counting arguments over first exposures, and under noise one exposure no longer determines an entry. The i.i.d. Rademacher prior on Ξ with p = 1/2 is load-bearing in at least four places: regularity, the 1/2 probability that a random item is liked, the fraction of clustered items that become exploitable, and the posterior bounds. Real preference matrices are sparse-positive and correlated (a few universally liked "hot" types), which breaks the symmetry the whole analysis rests on. Uniform type priors plus N > 20 q_U log² q_U guarantee min_w |P_w| ≥ N/(2q_U) by Chernoff, and that bound is exactly what buys the N/q_U collaboration discount in FindPrefs — under a heavy-tailed type distribution the smallest cluster dominates and the discount disappears. The infinite fresh-item pool with i.i.d. uniform types is what makes "draw a new random item" a free primitive and what sets T₂ = q_I/N. Finally the matching is Θ̃: upper bound C·NR·log^{3/2}(NR) versus lower bound c·NR/log(NR), valid only when q_U > (log q_I)² and q_I > (log N)⁵, and the transition points are themselves defined only up to logs — so "five regimes" is a claim about polynomial scaling, not about the curve near the boundaries. The algorithm also needs T, q_U, q_I as inputs; doubling handles T (Appendix I), but adaptivity to unknown q_U, q_I — arguably the practically interesting question — is untouched.

Broader context. This is the capstone of a line running Bresler–Chen–Shah (NeurIPS 2014, latent source model, COLLABORATIVE-GREEDY, user-user only), Bresler–Shah–Voloch (SIGMETRICS 2016, item-item, no lower bounds), and Bresler–Karzand (IEEE-IT 2021, which proved lower bounds but only in the degenerate corners where structure lives on one side). The parallel literature is latent-structure bandits: Gentile–Li–Zappella's CLUB (ICML 2014) clusters users online inside a linear contextual bandit; Li–Karatzoglou–Gentile's COFIBA (SIGIR 2016) clusters users and items simultaneously — essentially the practical analogue of the hybrid regime here, but with no optimality statement — and the low-rank/rank-one bandit line (Kveton et al., Jun et al., Lu–Kveton) optimizes matrix estimation rather than the number of liked recommendations. Ariu–Ryu–Yun–Proutière (NeurIPS 2020) get gap-dependent regret in a closely related no-repeat model but, as the authors note, capture no dependence on q_U, q_I at all. Borgs–Chayes–Lee–Shah's iterative collaborative filtering is the offline estimation counterpart.

The follow-up I'd want is a continuum version: replace the q_U × q_I block model by a graphon or low-rank latent space and ask whether the five-regime picture survives with "number of types" replaced by a covering number of the latent space at the resolution the noise level permits. A second, sharper direction is to formalize the paper's own most striking mechanism — deliberately learning only k_rep < q_I item types — as a horizon-indexed rate-distortion question: how many bits of Ξ must be acquired to serve T recommendations per user, and is the optimal "partial completion" always a column-subset as it is here?

The connection to generative retrieval is not forced. Semantic-ID docid construction (RQ-VAE, hierarchical k-means over embeddings) is precisely an item-type codebook, and q_I is the codebook size; the paper's r_I = Θ(log q_I) comparisons to resolve an item's type, amortized across N users, is a statement about how much interaction data a quantization level costs to make useful. The asymptotic-regime dichotomy — pay (log q_I)T/N to type each new item versus q_U T/N to route it through user similarity — is exactly the standing tension in generative retrieval between re-indexing new documents into the docid hierarchy (DSI's known weakness) and serving them off query- or user-side structure. And the "learn only part of the matrix" principle is a direct argument against training a retrieval index to uniform fidelity over a corpus when the serving budget is short.

Proof sketch. Lower bound. Call a recommendation bad if P[L = +1 | history] ≲ 2/3; Corollary 4.3 gives regret(T) ≥ (1/3N)·E[bad(T)] − T/(12N). Proposition 4.2 establishes that four scenarios B¹,…,B⁴ are bad, via regularity of Ξ (Definitions 4.13–4.14, Corollary 4.16 with s_U = log q_U − log log q_I − log log N − 12, s_I = 0.99 log q_I − 4 log log N − 12, η = 1/13). Then five purely combinatorial constraints count bad events along any trajectory: (I) bad ≥ I_strong·s_I + I_weak ≥ I_total; (II) bad ≥ (1 − U_weak)·N·s_U; (III) bad ≥ U_weak·N·γ_ where γ_ = min_u d_u; (IV) bad ≥ γ_·N/π_ with π_ the largest user-type population; (V) the no-repeat budget bad ≥ TN − [I_strong(N − s_I) + I_weak(π_ − 1)]. Minimaxing (II)/(III) over U_weak and (I)/(V) over (I_strong, I_weak) gives bad(T) ≥ max{I_total, (N/π_)γ_, (N/2)min{γ_, s_U}, T·min{s_I, N/π_}}. Two probabilistic steps remove the random quantities: balls-and-bins max-load gives π_ < 3N/q_U w.p. ≥ 3/4 (Lemma 4.9), and a martingale/occupancy argument gives I_total ≳ T q_I/γ_ (or √q_I in an intermediate window) w.p. ≥ 1/2 (Lemma 4.10) — the per-type count minus its mean is a martingale, re-indexed lexicographically over (t,u) so increments are bounded by one, then McDiarmid/Freedman. What remains is a one-dimensional minimax over γ, the number of item types each user is exposed to, whose solution produces the five regimes (Theorem 4.12).

Upper bound. RecommendationSystem draws three disjoint random item sets and runs four phases. UserClustering: show all of I_usr (size r_U = ⌈2log(N q_U²)⌉, or 0) to every user and partition by identical response vectors; two distinct types survive undistinguished w.p. 2^{−Φ_I} where Φ_I ≥ r_U/2 distinct item types appear (balls-and-bins), union over pairs gives error ≤ 1/N (Lemma D.1). FindPrefs: each representative in I_rep goes to one user per cluster, costing |I_rep|/min_w|P_w| rounds; Chernoff gives min_w |P_w| ≥ N/(2q_U) (Lemma E.2), which is precisely the N/q_U collaboration discount. ItemClustering: each item of I_exp to r_I = ⌈2log(N q_I)⌉ random users, assigned to S_j if it agrees with representative j on every cluster that rated it; misclassification ≤ 2/N (Lemma D.2). Exploit: recommend the union of S_j over representatives the cluster liked. The key optimization trick: the leftover-random-recommendation term carries weight N, so it is always optimal to drive it to zero — if you were going to make random recommendations at the end, explore more instead — giving the constraint I_exp·k_rep/(2q_I) + I_rep/2 ≥ T with k_rep ≈ min{I_rep/2, q_I} (balls-and-bins, Lemma E.4). Minimizing the remaining cost over I_rep (and I_usr ∈ {0, r_U}) yields Theorem 6.4's min{T/2, C·R_U(T), C·R_I(T)}, matching R(T). Corollary 3.2 transfers this to cold-start time ≍ min{log q_U, q_I/N} up to logs, with a matching lower bound.

title: What Makes a Reward Model a Good Teacher? An Optimization Perspective
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-29

What Makes a Reward Model a Good Teacher? An Optimization Perspective

Razin, Wang, Strauss, Wei, Lee, Arora · 2025 · arXiv:2503.15477

Main idea. Reward models are graded almost exclusively by accuracy — the fraction of output pairs they rank in agreement with the ground truth reward. The paper's claim is that accuracy is orthogonal to a second property that governs whether policy gradient can move at all: the reward variance Var_{y~π_{θ(0)}}[r_RM(x,y)] induced by the reward model under the initial policy. Accuracy sees only the ordering; variance sees the degree of separation between outputs that are actually probable on-policy. Low variance means a flat RLHF landscape, and the time to raise any bounded reward — the proxy or the ground truth — by an additive γ is lower bounded by Ω(Var^{−1/3}). Since the two quantities are decoupled, a perfectly accurate reward model can be arbitrarily slower than a nearly worst-case-inaccurate one, and since variance depends jointly on r_RM and π_{θ(0)}, the same reward model is a good teacher for one base model and a bad one for another. Both are formal impossibility results for policy-independent, accuracy-only benchmarks.

Critique. The theory is clean but its slow-side construction is scale in disguise: the "accurate but flat" reward model assigns values b_y ∈ (0, 1/T), so low variance is obtained by squeezing all rewards into a 1/T window inside [−1,1]. Remark 3 permits shifts but not rescaling, and the authors normalize reward models in the experiments — yet GRPO, which they use in Appendix D.2, divides advantages by the within-group standard deviation, which is precisely a per-prompt rescaling that would annihilate the construction. The honest resolution is not landscape flatness but signal-to-noise: with k on-policy samples, tiny reward spread means the empirical advantages are dominated by estimation noise. Section 6.1 gestures at this, but the exact-gradient/gradient-flow analysis structurally cannot distinguish "flat objective" from "unestimable gradient," and these have different remedies. A second soft spot is the constant J_{t_γ}, a supremum of the Jacobian spectral norm of f_θ over the whole trajectory, appearing on both sides of the bound; Remark 1 concedes that feature learning could in principle grow it and rescue a flat start. Finally the separations are about adversarially constructed reward models at a fixed accuracy, not about reward models that Bradley–Terry training actually produces — the interesting question of which variance profile the BT log-likelihood induces is untouched.

Against that: the experiments are a real stress test rather than a demo. A perfectly accurate reward model obtained by rank-preservingly flattening the gold reward genuinely underperforms less accurate ones, and in the first epochs a proxy beats optimizing the gold reward directly — hard to explain by any other mechanism. They also report the countervailing fact that accurate reward models are more KL-efficient. The correlation table, however, is computed over seven reward models; a Spearman ρ of 1.000 at n = 7 is thin.

Context and follow-ups. RLHF fits r_RM from preferences and then maximizes it by PPO/RLOO/GRPO with a KL leash to the SFT policy. The classical failure mode is over-optimization (Gao–Schulman–Hilton's proxy-vs-gold scaling laws in KL), which is an accuracy failure; this paper isolates an orthogonal optimization failure, and the direct technical antecedent is Razin et al.'s vanishing-gradient result for RL finetuning. It is a sharp rebuttal to RewardBench-style leaderboards, which produce one policy-independent ranking, and complements the empirical "accuracy is not enough" line. It also implicitly favors DPO-like methods, which never face this landscape, and Best-of-N, for which the paper shows perfect accuracy is always optimal.

The obvious follow-up is variance-aware reward post-processing: apply a monotone rank-preserving map r ↦ 2F_{π_ref}(r) − 1, the CDF of the reward under the on-policy output distribution — accuracy is exactly preserved, on-policy variance is maximized, and the theory predicts strictly faster early optimization. The IR-facing version is not forced: training a generative retriever with policy gradient on a relevance reward gives Var = p(1−p) under a binary signal, vanishing for both hopeless and already-solved queries, so variance is a principled curriculum criterion over the query set; and graded relevance should outperform binary at equal ranking accuracy purely by injecting separation. This is the same pathology as the piecewise-constant flatness of nDCG, whose smoothed surrogates (SoftRank, ApproxNDCG) are, viewed this way, variance-injection devices.

Proof sketch. Theorem 4 (detailed form of Theorem 1) assumes gradient flow θ̇ = ∇φ_RLHF(θ), exact gradients, a general autoregressive softmax policy π_θ(y|x) = ∏_l softmax(f_θ(x,y_{<l}))_{y_l}, rewards in [−1,1], outputs padded to length L, and any λ ≥ 0. It gives t_γ ≥ [min(1−e^{−γ/9}, 1−e^{−7/3λ}) / (8L²J_{t_γ}²)] · (E_{x'~S} Var_{y~π_{θ(0)}}[r_RM])^{−1/3}, for t_γ the first time E_{π_{θ(t)}}[r] ≥ E_{π_{θ(0)}}[r] + γ with r any bounded reward. A tabular analogue (Proposition 3) improves the exponent to −1/2.

Three ingredients. (i) Proposition 2, a KL-regularized extension of Razin et al.'s bound: ‖∇φ_RLHF(θ;x)‖ ≤ 6M^{1/3}L·J_x·Var^{1/3}. Via the log-derivative trick the gradient is a reward-weighted score expectation; outputs are split at a threshold c around the mean KL-regularized reward. Chebyshev bounds the tail mass by Var/c², contributing ≤ 4MLJ_x·Var/c²; on the truncated part each per-position vector is a difference of two expectations of a reward confined to a c-band, so its ℓ₁ norm is ≤ 2c, contributing ≤ 2LJ_x·c. Balancing Var/c² against c at c = M^{1/3}Var^{1/3} is exactly where the 1/3 exponent comes from. (ii) The load-bearing step, since a small initial gradient says nothing if it grows: differentiating the variance along the flow yields the self-bounding inequality d/dt Var^KL ≤ 24L²J_T²(Var^KL)^{4/3} − 2λ‖∇φ‖². A comparison lemma (ġ ≤ cg^p ⟹ g(t) ≤ g(0)(1 − c(p−1)g(0)^{p−1}t)^{−1/(p−1)}) with p = 4/3 gives Var(t) ≤ Var(0)(1 − 8L²J²Var(0)^{1/3}t)^{−3}: higher-order derivatives vanish alongside the gradient, so blow-up cannot happen before time ~Var(0)^{−1/3}. Integrating ‖θ̇‖ ≤ 12LJ·Var(t)^{1/3} gives a logarithmic parameter-displacement bound, and Cauchy–Schwarz against ‖∇V‖ ≤ 6LJ turns γ ≤ 9·ln(1 − 8L²J²Var(0)^{1/3}t_γ)^{−1} into the stated bound. (iii) Lemma 6 is the technical guard that the KL-regularized reward r − λ·ln(π_θ/π_ref), which can diverge as π_θ(y|x) → 0, stays in [−8,8] long enough — the source of the 1 − e^{−7/3λ} factor.

The separations are then explicit constructions over tabular policies. For Theorem 5, r_RM(x,y) = b_y with b_y ∈ (0, 1/T) ordered to realize any attainable accuracy α forces Var ≤ T^{−2} and hence t_γ = Ω(T); meanwhile r'_RM gives reward 1 to a single good output y^γ and c_y < π_{θ(0)}(y^γ|x) to everything else, realizing any accuracy attainable subject to y^γ ranked first. The upper bound is Proposition 4, a sufficient condition for fast increase: a set Y⁺ of outputs that are good under r_G and above-average under r_RM, with margin δ = (1−ρ)(separation) − (spread) > 0, small λ, and small initial mass on the bad set (here empty by construction). Tracking d/dt ln π_{θ(t)}(y|x) for tabular logits gives logistic-type growth π̇ ≳ δπ(1−π), whence t_γ = O(π_{θ(0)}(y^γ|x)^{−1}(1−ρ)^{−4}) — the initial policy must already place non-negligible mass on a good output. Theorem 6 reuses both constructions symmetrically, with policy families pinned to the same initial expected ground truth reward, which correctly rules out the confound that one initial policy is simply better.

title: The Limit Points of (Optimistic) Gradient Descent in Min-Max Optimization
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-29

The Limit Points of (Optimistic) Gradient Descent in Min-Max Optimization

Daskalakis, Panageas · 2018 · arXiv:1807.03907

Main idea. For unconstrained min_x max_y f(x,y) with f ∈ C² and non-convex-non-concave, the practically deployed algorithms are simultaneous gradient descent/ascent (GDA) and its optimistic variant (OGDA), x_{t+1} = x_t − 2α∇_x f(x_t,y_t) + α∇_x f(x_{t−1},y_{t−1}). The paper asks the question that convergence-rate work skips: when these dynamics do settle, what do they settle on? The answer is a strict chain, local min-max ⊊ GDA-stable ⊊ OGDA-stable, plus an "avoid the bad points" theorem for each. So OGDA buys stability at the cost of admitting more spurious attractors — it is not merely a better solver for the same solution concept, it changes the solution concept, and in the wrong direction.

Critique. Three things deserve pushback. First, "stable" is ρ(J) ≤ 1, the closed disk. The boundary case is genuinely undetermined — a Jordan block on the unit circle is unstable — so part of the advertised strict chain lives in a regime where linearization says nothing, and the avoidance theorems cover only ρ(J) > 1 strictly, leaving the non-hyperbolic set with no measure-theoretic guarantee at all. Second, Assumption 1.7 demands ∇²f invertible everywhere, which by the authors' own Remark 3.6 excludes generic bilinear f = xᵀAy — precisely the family for which OGDA's advantage was established in Daskalakis–Ilyas–Syrgkanis–Zeng. The OGDA avoidance theorem thus misses its own motivating example, and for a GAN objective the assumption is unfalsifiable in practice. GDA needs only α < 1/L; this asymmetry is real, not an artifact of proof effort. Third, and most importantly, avoiding unstable points is much weaker than converging: their own 2-D experiment has 3% (GDA) and 9.8% (OGDA) of initializations converging to nothing. Measure-zero avoidance says where you don't go, not where you go.

Broader context. The immediate lineage is Lee–Simchowitz–Jordan–Recht's "gradient descent only converges to minimizers" and Panageas–Piliouras' non-isolated extension, transplanted from minimization to games — the transplant is non-trivial because J is no longer symmetric, which is why Ky Fan replaces Weyl. On the other side sits Mescheder–Nagarajan–Kolter's local-stability analysis of GAN training and Mescheder et al.'s "Which training methods for GANs actually converge?", which reach compatible conclusions from a continuous-time/regularization angle. The paper's most consequential negative result — GDA-stable points need not be local min-max — was the setup for Jin–Netrapalli–Jordan's local minimax (Stackelberg) notion, which is the right concept precisely because it arises as the τ → ∞ limit of two-timescale GDA; read together, the two papers say the mismatch is not in the algorithm but in the symmetric solution concept. Then Hsieh–Mertikopoulos–Cevher push the pessimism further: limit sets of these dynamics can be spurious attractors containing no critical point whatsoever, and can have larger basins than the actual Nash set — which makes "avoid unstable critical points" look like the weakest of the available guarantees. Letcher et al.'s differentiable game mechanics and Balduzzi et al.'s SGA attack the same Jacobian from the decomposition side (symmetric potential + antisymmetric Hamiltonian part), and Gidel et al.'s negative-momentum reading explains OGDA's extra stability in exactly the spectral terms used here.

An obvious follow-up: redo the characteristic-polynomial map with distinct step sizes α_x ≠ α_y and track how the stable-set inclusion chain deforms as τ = α_y/α_x grows, which should interpolate continuously between this paper's chain and Jin et al.'s local minimax set — the algebra is the same 2×2 root analysis with r replaced by a τ-dependent pencil. Equally: is the excess OGDA-stable ∖ GDA-stable generically measure-zero, or does it carry positive-measure basins? Their Table 1 (25.8% of OGDA runs converging to a point GDA never reaches) suggests the latter.

For the retrieval side, the relevant instance is adversarially trained retrievers — IRGAN-style generator/discriminator ranking, or any scheme where a hard-negative sampler is trained against the encoder rather than fixed. The result here says the alternating-gradient fixed points such a system converges to need not be saddles of the retrieval objective, and that adding optimism (or any negative-momentum extragradient variant, now common for stabilizing such training) enlarges the set of spurious attractors rather than shrinking it. If you are designing a learned negative sampler as a game rather than a heuristic, the stability certificate you want is on the spectrum of H at the joint critical point, not on the marginal ranking loss.

Proof sketch. Definitions. A critical point (∇f = 0) is linearly stable for a dynamic w if ρ(J_w) ≤ 1, unstable otherwise; local min-max means f(x_,y) ≤ f(x_,y_) ≤ f(x,y_) on a neighborhood. For GDA, J_GDA = I + αH with H = [[−∇²_xx f, −∇²_xy f],[∇²_yx f, ∇²_yy f]] = diag(−I_n, I_m)·∇²f, a non-symmetric matrix — the whole difficulty in one line.

Local min-max ⟹ GDA-stable. Local min-max forces ∇²_xx f ⪰ 0 and ∇²_yy f ⪯ 0, hence the symmetric part ½(H + Hᵀ) = diag(−∇²_xx f, ∇²_yy f) ⪯ 0. The trick is Ky Fan's majorization: the ordered eigenvalues of ½(H + Hᵀ) majorize the real parts of spec(H), so Re λ ≤ 0 for every eigenvalue. Under Assumption 1.8 (Re λ ≠ 0), choosing α < min_λ{−Re(λ)/|λ|²} gives |1 + αλ|² = 1 + 2α·Re(λ) + α²|λ|² < 1. (The paper prints this expansion without the factor 2 — harmless, it only loosens the constant.) The assumption is not cosmetic: f = xy has spec(H) = {±i}, |1 ± iα| > 1 for every α, and indeed ‖z_t‖² = (1+α²)ᵗ‖z_0‖². Conversely f = −x²/8 − y²/2 + 0.6xy is GDA-stable at the origin but not local min-max, so the inclusion is strict.

GDA-stable ⟹ OGDA-stable. OGDA has memory, so they lift it to a genuine dynamical system on R^{2(n+m)} via (x_{t+1},y_{t+1},x_t,y_t) = g(x_t,y_t,x_{t−1},y_{t−1}), the standard order-reduction trick for higher-order recursions; fixed points are exactly the diagonal (x_,y_,x_,y_). The key computation is a characteristic-polynomial identity obtained by row/column elimination on λI − J_OGDA: q_OGDA(λ) = (2λ−1)^{n+m}·q_GDA((λ²+λ−1)/(2λ−1)). So each eigenvalue r ∈ spec(αH) contributes two OGDA eigenvalues, the roots of λ² − (1+2r)λ + r = 0, i.e. λ = (½ + r) ± ½√(1+4r²). For α < 1/(2L) one has |r| < ½, and then |1+r| ≤ 1 (GDA-stability) implies both roots lie in the closed unit disk. Honest disclosure: that final implication is verified by a two-line Mathematica Reduce in Appendix A.1, not by a human-readable argument. Strictness again via f = xy, which is OGDA-stable for α < ½ but GDA-unstable.

Avoidance of unstable points. Both update rules are local diffeomorphisms — for GDA because ρ(H) ≤ ‖∇²f‖₂ ≤ L < 1/α so J = I + αH is invertible; for OGDA because J_OGDA's null space reduces, after elimination, to that of a block matrix invertible exactly when ∇²f is (Assumption 1.7). Then the Center-Stable Manifold theorem gives each unstable z_ a neighborhood B with ∩_k g^{−k}(B) ⊆ W^{cs}_loc, of codimension ≥ 1 because _some* eigenvalue exceeds 1 in modulus — note this tolerates non-hyperbolic points, unlike Lee et al. 2016. Second-countability extracts a countable subcover; every trajectory converging to an unstable point eventually enters some B, so the stable set is contained in a countable union of preimages of null sets under a local diffeomorphism, hence null.

title: Understanding Generalization from Embedding Dimension and Distributional Convergence
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-29

Understanding Generalization from Embedding Dimension and Distributional Convergence

Yu, Ouyang, Deng, Wei, Ma, Zhang, Deng, Liu · 2026 · arXiv:2601.22756

Main idea. The paper abandons uniform convergence over a hypothesis class entirely and asks a post-hoc question instead: for a fixed, already-trained network F, how much can the risk move when you swap one finite sample of embeddings for another? Splitting F = F_k ∘ F_≤k at layer k, the only randomness left is the empirical pushforward measure of the layer-k embeddings around its population counterpart. Kantorovich–Rubinstein then converts that into L_k(g)·W_1(P_k, P̂_{k,n}), and Weed–Bach's sharp empirical-measure rates supply E[W_1] ≲ C_k n^{-1/(d_k+ε)} where d_k is the upper Wasserstein dimension of the layer-k embedding distribution — not the ambient width. The headline bound is R(F) ≲ R̂_n(F) + L̄_k(C_k n^{-1/(d_k+ε)} + D_k√(log(L/δ)/n)) + Bayes-surrogate terms, minimized over layers, with L̄_k = L_k(F_k)M_F + L_k(F_k_)M_{F_}. At the last layer the tail map is the identity, so L_L(F)=1, and the authors read this as "architecture drops out, only output geometry remains" — their explanation for the well-documented empirical correlation between final-layer intrinsic dimension and test performance.

Critique. The mechanism is clean, and the layerwise min_k trade-off is a genuinely nice observation: early layers have high d_k but low sensitivity, late layers are compressed but stiff, and the width-intervention experiment in §5.4 shows that narrowing a layer lowers d_k while inflating the product of spectral norms. But several things do not hold up. First, the theorem is one-sided: it upper-bounds the gap by something increasing in d_k, which never licenses the correlational claim that high dimension causes poor generalization. Second, the rate is vacuous at the scales tested — n^{-1/d} with d ≈ 10 and n = 500 per class is ≈ 0.5 before any constant, and C_k from Weed–Bach is unquantified with an unspecified "sufficiently large n" threshold. Third, and most serious: the theory demands the n samples be independent of F, so R̂n is a validation risk (Table 1 says so explicitly, contradicting the Def. 3.9 remark that says training set), and the experiments accordingly measure a validation-vs-test discrepancy. That is not the train–test gap anyone means by "generalization"; it is the fluctuation between two held-out splits. Fourth, "architectural sensitivity vanishes at the final layer" is sleight of hand — architecture is simply absorbed into L_L(F_), the Lipschitz constant of the Bayes map _from the network's own outputs_, and into d_L itself, both of which are functionals of F_≤L. Assuming F_k_ is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the support is also strong precisely where it matters, near decision boundaries. Fifth, the estimated quantity is not the theoretical one: Levina–Bickel/TLE/MOM are local kNN MLE estimators, while the upper Wasserstein dimension is a global ε→0 covering-dimension limit with a mass tolerance; the appendix's own finding that larger K correlates better with the gap quietly concedes the mismatch. Minor but real: Lemma A.5's step ‖Aᵀv‖∞ ≤ ‖A‖op‖v‖∞ is off by √C; the theory is in ℓ₁ while the Sinkhorn experiments use Euclidean ground cost; and §5.1's claim that W_1 grows "exponentially in d" contradicts n^{-1/d}, which saturates as d → ∞.

Broader context. This sits at the junction of two literatures: intrinsic-dimension-of-representations (Ansuini et al. 2019's hunchback profiles, Pope et al. 2021) and dimension-dependent empirical-measure convergence (Dudley's classical n^{-1/d}, sharpened by Weed & Bach 2019). Conspicuously uncited is the closest prior art — Şimşekli et al. and Birdal et al. 2021, which prove generalization bounds in terms of the Hausdorff/persistent-homology dimension of the optimization trajectory; comparing trajectory dimension against representation dimension as predictors would be the obvious next experiment.

The genuine hook for your work is that the upper Wasserstein dimension is a cousin of the local intrinsic dimensionality used in similarity search — the paper even cites Amsaleg/Houle's TLE and MOM estimators, which come straight from the ANN community, where LID governs the hardness of indexing (HNSW/IVF degradation, Karger–Ruhl-style doubling-dimension bounds). That gives a two-sided dimension budget for dense retrieval: low embedding ID simultaneously buys faster W_1 convergence (this paper) and cheaper, higher-recall indexing, while the irreducible term E‖Y − F_k_(Z_k)‖₁ prices the information destroyed by compression — a principled framing for Matryoshka-style truncation and for OPQ/PCA reduction choices. A concrete follow-up: replace the tail map with the inner product against a corpus embedding matrix, so L_k(F) becomes max_j‖e_j‖, and derive a W_1-based bound on the generalization of a smoothed recall@k or InfoNCE surrogate in terms of the intrinsic dimension of the _query* distribution — the corpus-side analogue would then be a statement about how well a sampled corpus approximates the population document measure, i.e. a scaling law for index construction rather than for training.

Proof sketch. What is proved: for a fixed measurable encoder, bounded-diameter embedding support (D_k), locally Lipschitz tail and Bayes maps, smooth loss with bounded gradients (M_F, M_{F_}), and bounded Bayes loss, with probability ≥ 1−δ over n i.i.d. samples, the gap R(F) − R̂_n(F) is at most min over k of the displayed expression — simultaneously over all L+1 layers. The obstruction is that ℓ(F(x),y) is not differentiable in z when y is a discrete label, so no Lipschitz/Wasserstein argument applies directly. The key trick is the _Bayes surrogate_: define the oracle loss g_k(z) = ℓ(F_k(z), F_k_(z)), replacing the label by the layer-k Bayes predictor, which makes the loss a genuine function of z alone and hence integrable against the embedding measure. Proposition A.4 is then a purely algebraic three-way split, (observed gap) = (observed − oracle risk) + (oracle population − oracle empirical) + (oracle empirical − observed empirical). Terms (A) and (C) are handled deterministically by Lipschitzness of ℓ in its second argument, each costing M_{F_}·E‖Y − F_k_(Z)‖₁ — the irreducible label-noise/information-loss price of the surrogate. Term (B), the only one carrying sample randomness, is exactly |∫g_k dP − ∫g_k dP̂| ≤ L_k(g)·W_1 by KR duality, with L_k(g) ≤ L_k(F)M_F + L_k(F_)M_{F_} from the chain rule — the decomposition that separates architecture-controllable from distribution-intrinsic sensitivity. The probabilistic step (Prop. A.9) is a bounded-difference argument: replacing one sample moves the empirical measure by mass 1/n, so via the 1-Lipschitz dual form the statistic moves by at most D_k/n, and McDiarmid gives the √(log(2(L+1)/δ)/2n) deviation; Hoeffding handles the empirical noise average. Substituting Weed–Bach's E[W_1] ≤ C_k n^{-1/(d_k+ε)} and a union bound over layers yields the theorem. So the entire dimension dependence is imported wholesale from Weed–Bach; the paper's own contribution is the surrogate decomposition that makes the risk a Lipschitz functional of the embedding measure in the first place.

title: Global Convergence in Training Large-Scale Transformers
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-28

Global Convergence in Training Large-Scale Transformers

Gao, Cao, Li, He, Wang, Liu, Klusowski, Fan — NeurIPS 2024 — arXiv:2410.23610

Main idea.
