The paper asks why gradient-based training of very large transformers reliably drives the training loss to zero despite a wildly nonconvex landscape, and answers it for gradient flow on an L2-regularized population squared loss. The architecture is a residual stack of alternating blocks: a self-attention block Z + (η/M)Σ_j f(Z, θ_j) with f(Z,θ) = V Z σ_A(Zᵀ W Z), and a token-wise MLP block Z + (η/M)Σ_j h(Z, w_j), with residual step η = Δt/2, Δt = 1/L, and a scalar read-out picking one entry of the final sequence. Sending width M → ∞ and depth L → ∞ simultaneously, the parameters stop being a finite list and become a probability measure ρ(θ, w, t) over parameter space indexed by a continuous depth coordinate t ∈ [0,1]; the forward pass becomes the ODE Ṫ_ρ = ∫ [f(T_ρ,θ) + h(T_ρ,w)]/2 dρ(·,t), and gradient flow on parameters becomes a Wasserstein (McKean–Vlasov/continuity) equation ∂_τ ρ = div(ρ ∇ δQ/δρ). Two theorems: Theorem 3.1 is a quantitative propagation-of-chaos result — discrete and mean-field dynamics agree, uniformly over any finite [0,τ], to O(L^{−1} + √((δ + log(L+1))/M)); Theorem 4.1 says that once the Wasserstein flow settles, the risk it settles at is O(λ), so small weight decay gives near-zero risk. Two honest corrections to the framing you might expect from the abstract: the regularizer is plain L2 weight decay on the second moment of ρ, not entropy, and there is no diffusion/noise term; and the lifted objective is not convex in ρ (the ODE makes T_ρ nonlinear in ρ) and no Łojasiewicz/PL inequality appears. The structural property doing the work is partial 1-homogeneity plus a universal-kernel property of one block.

Most interesting part, and a critique. The genuinely new technical content is loosening what prior mean-field ResNet analyses (Lu et al.; Ding et al.) demanded. Those need globally Lipschitz gradients and full parameter homogeneity, which excludes softmax attention outright. Here Assumption 2 allows quadratic-in-‖θ‖ growth and per-token column norms, Assumption 3 asks only for locally Lipschitz gradients in expectation over the data, and Assumption 4 asks for homogeneity in only a sub-block α₁ of the parameters. A second nice touch: the discrete model alternates two different encoders f and h, yet the continuous limit sees only their average (f+h)/2 — a rigorous version of the "ResNets behave like ensembles" intuition.

The price is steep, and the paper is fairly upfront about it. Theorem 4.1 assumes the Wasserstein flow weakly converges to some ρ_∞, assumes its support stays uniformly bounded, and assumes a separation/support condition (supp ρ_∞(·,t_) contains an annulus × K × {w₀}); Appendix C.5 gives only heuristic justification. So the theorem is really "if the flow converges, the limit is nearly globally optimal", not "the flow converges". There is no rate: τ₀ merely exists, C₁ depends on τ₀, and Appendix H concedes the required M, L are exponentially large (the ViT/CIFAR-10 experiments are a sanity check, not a verification). It is gradient flow on the _population_ risk — no SGD, no step size, no sampling, no generalization. There is no layer normalization anywhere. And crucially, in the only concrete verified example (Proposition G.1), the universal-kernel condition is checked for the _MLP_ branch (α₁ = W₂, α₂ = W₁, HuberizedReLU), not for attention; softmax attention only has to satisfy the growth/Lipschitz conditions. So the expressivity that buys global optimality still comes from the feed-forward layer; whether a softmax attention layer alone is a universal kernel is left open. The guarantee is on risk ≤ ε + discretization + C₂λ, i.e. approximately global for the _unregularized* risk, at the cost of tuning λ small.

Broader context. Two lineages: NTK/lazy training, where infinite width freezes features and the loss becomes effectively convex in a kernel; and mean-field analysis, where a two-layer network is a measure over neurons, the risk is convex in that measure, and training is a Wasserstein gradient flow (Chizat–Bach 2018; Mei–Montanari–Nguyen 2018) — features move, so it is not lazy, but global convergence needs homogeneity plus a support condition, and entropic regularization / noisy particle flows (Nitanda–Wu–Suzuki) are what usually buy actual rates via log-Sobolev arguments. This paper sits in the depth-wise extension of that program (neural ODEs; Lu et al. ICML 2020; Ding et al. JMLR 2022) and is the first to bend it to transformers. Closest neighbours worth reading: Kim & Suzuki (ICML 2024), which studies nonconvex mean-field dynamics on the attention landscape for in-context feature learning, and Bordelon–Chaudhry–Pehlevan on infinite-head/infinite-depth transformer limits. Obvious follow-up: replace the pure Wasserstein flow with a noisy/entropy-regularized one to convert the existence-of-τ₀ statement into an explicit rate, and independently try to establish (or refute) the universal-kernel property for multi-head softmax attention so the result becomes a statement about attention rather than about the MLP.

For your own work, one link is genuine and one is strained. Genuine: learned quantization and learned index objectives lift naturally to measures over codewords, and the machinery here — first variation δQ/δρ, "a near-descent direction always exists unless the loss is already small", stationarity implying a constant first variation on a connected support — is exactly the right language for asking when soft/entropic PQ or residual-quantization training reaches a global optimum of the distortion objective, and the 1-homogeneity of a codebook matrix in a softmax-assignment objective is real, not contrived. Strained: transplanting this to generative retrieval with discrete docids would be forced. The whole argument needs a continuous read-out differentiable through an ODE flow and a homogeneous output block; autoregressive decoding over a docid trie with cross-entropy has neither, and the identifiability question there (which docid assignments are recoverable) is a different problem from the optimization one. The transferable piece is narrower and worth stating as such: a softmax read-out over a learned docid embedding table is 1-homogeneous in that table, so a partial-homogeneity argument could plausibly say something about global optimality of training docid embeddings with the tokenizer held fixed — but not about the discrete structure itself.

Proof sketch. Theorem 3.1 (mean-field approximation) assumes the growth and local-Lipschitz conditions above plus i.i.d. initialization of the M particles per layer, and concludes that with probability 1 − δ the discrete forward map and the discrete gradient-flow trajectory stay within O(L^{−1} + √((δ + log(L+1))/M)) of their mean-field counterparts, uniformly on any compact training-time interval [0, τ]. The strategy is propagation of chaos in the Sznitman tradition: write both trajectories as solutions of coupled ODEs, subtract, and Grönwall the difference — the L^{−1} term is the Euler-discretization error of the depth ODE and the M^{−1/2} term is a uniform law-of-large-numbers/concentration bound on the empirical measure of particles, with the log(L+1) coming from a union bound over layers. The two enabling relaxations are that Lipschitzness is required only in expectation over the data (so softmax attention's quadratic growth is tolerated once the input distribution is sub-Gaussian) and that an a priori estimate keeps the trajectory in a bounded region, which is what lets a local Lipschitz constant do the work of a global one. Theorem 4.1 (approximate global optimality) is the conditional one. Assume the Wasserstein flow ρ_τ converges weakly to ρ_∞, that the supports stay uniformly bounded, and the separation condition on supp ρ_∞. Then the risk at ρ_∞ is bounded by C₂λ, so the unregularized population risk is O(λ) + discretization error. The proof is a first-variation argument rather than a convexity or PL argument: at a stationary point of the Wasserstein flow, the first variation δQ/δρ must be constant on the (connected) support of ρ_∞ and no less elsewhere. Partial 1-homogeneity in the sub-block α₁ is then the trick — it forces that constant to be zero, by the standard Euler-relation argument that a 1-homogeneous function's radial derivative equals the function itself, so a nonzero first variation would give a strictly descending radial direction inside the support. Having pinned δQ/δρ ≡ 0 on the support, the universal-kernel property of the MLP block (Proposition G.1, via HuberizedReLU) converts "the first variation vanishes against every measure supported in this annulus" into "the residual is orthogonal to a dense subset of the function space", hence the residual is (nearly) zero in L² and the risk is at most the regularization price C₂λ. The annulus in the support condition is exactly what the homogeneity and universality arguments both need — homogeneity needs a radial direction available, universality needs enough directions to be dense — and it is also the least justified of the assumptions.

title: Rank1: Test-Time Compute for Reranking in Information Retrieval
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-28

Rank1: Test-Time Compute for Reranking in Information Retrieval

Weller, Ricci, Yang, Yates, Lawrie & Van Durme (JHU) — COLM 2025 — arXiv:2502.18418

Main idea. Rank1 asks what happens if a pointwise cross-encoder is allowed to think before it judges relevance. The authors prompt DeepSeek-R1 with 635k (query, passage) pairs drawn from MS MARCO — official positives, Tevatron BM25/CoCondenser negatives, and mT5-13B hard negatives at ranks 1–5 and 5–10 — under a deliberately minimal template ("Determine if the following passage is relevant to the query. Answer only with 'true' or 'false'" followed by an open <think>). They then filter aggressively: instances where R1's verdict contradicts the implied label are dropped (15%), and a first-round Rank1-Mistral-24B self-filters another 10%, leaving 386k traces. Qwen 2.5 base models (0.5B–32B; instruct variants were worse) are LoRA-tuned on those traces. At inference the model emits a full chain of thought and the ranking score comes from the terminal true/false token — the paper never actually specifies this in the main text, which is an omission in itself; Appendix F is the only place it surfaces. Results: on BRIGHT, Rank1-7B averages 27.5 nDCG@10 against 13.9 for RankLLaMA-7B and 16.8 for MonoT5-3B, scaling to 29.4 at 32B; NevIR pairwise accuracy reaches 70.1, matching RankGPT with GPT-4o; mFollowIR gives 0.610 nDCG@20 and +10.1 p-MRR despite zero multilingual or instruction training data. A no-reasoning ablation on identical data scores 17.5 on BRIGHT, so the trace itself carries most of the gain. Classical benchmarks go the other way, which the authors attribute to pool staleness.

Reviewer-style critique. The compute comparison is the weakest part: there is not a single latency, FLOP, or tokens-per-query number anywhere. A model generating a few hundred reasoning tokens per (query, passage) pair over 100 candidates is two to three orders of magnitude more expensive than MonoT5-3B's single forward pass, and the "Inference Speed" limitation answers this with an appeal to Deep Research's popularity rather than measurement. Reporting quantized model sizes without wall-clock is a category error. Worse, the headline BRIGHT comparison is arguably not against rerankers at all: the first stage is BM25 over the query plus GPT-4o chain-of-thought, which already averages 26.5. Rank1-7B's 27.5 is a +1.0 improvement over its own input ordering; the baselines look "2× worse" mainly because they actively destroy a strong first stage. A large share of the apparent reasoning gain is GPT-4o's query expansion upstream, and the paper's framing obscures this.

Leakage is real though subtle. Training labels are R1's verdicts filtered for agreement with MS MARCO, so supervision is teacher-consistent by construction — no benchmark labels leak, but the self-filtering step means the final data mix is whatever a Rank1 model already agreed with. More concerning: early stopping is done on BRIGHT Biology and NevIR scores, i.e. model selection on two evaluation sets, and Appendix E lists elaborate hand-written per-dataset prompts for BEIR and non-StackExchange BRIGHT ("Find me passages with any type of connection, including weak connections!!!!"). That is test-set-conditioned prompt engineering with no sensitivity analysis.

The gains are entirely concentrated in reasoning-heavy and instruction-following evaluation. On BEIR, Rank1 (40.9–41.7) loses to MonoT5-3B (44.7) and RankLLaMA (44.4–44.6), barely clearing BM25S at 38.5. The DL19 rescue is only partially convincing: re-annotating just the top-10 documents each model got wrong or unjudged (295 labels; 86.8% of Rank1's unjudged documents relevant versus 70.6% for RankLLaMA) does show pool bias, but selectively re-judging exactly the documents your own system surfaces is a biased estimator, and the authors concede a full re-pooling is needed. Calibration is genuinely broken: the model was trained to end its trace with an explicit verdict, so, as Appendix F admits, the final token is near-deterministic — which collapses scores toward 0/1, produces mass ties, and lets first-stage order leak through tie-breaking. It also flattens graded relevance; the authors explicitly say Rank1 treats "1" and "2" judgments alike, which straightforwardly explains DBPedia, NFCorpus and Touché. Two calibration fixes (a ModernBERT head over the trace, extra last-token loss) failed. The overthinking example — marking every TREC-COVID passage non-relevant because none named the Wuhan wet market — is a precision pathology a calibrated score would smooth out.

The most surprising result is negative and buried in §3.6: budget forcing à la s1 did not help and actively hurt. A paper titled "Test-Time Compute for Reranking" contains no test-time scaling curve. What it really demonstrates is reasoning-trace distillation, a fixed one-shot cost, not compute you can dial. The runner-up surprise is that Rank1-0.5B matches RankLLaMA-13B on BRIGHT — 25× fewer parameters — which suggests reasoning supervision substitutes for capacity in a way worth theorizing about.

Broader context. Modern retrieval is staged: a cheap first stage (BM25 or a dense/vector index) produces top-k, then a cross-encoder rescores. monoT5 and RankT5 established the pointwise seq2seq reranker, reading the probability of a "true"/"relevant" token; RankGPT showed GPT-4 can do listwise reranking with sliding windows, and RankVicuna/RankZephyr distilled that into open 7B models. Rank1 sits at the intersection of that distillation tradition and the o1/R1 test-time-compute line, where reasoning traces from a strong teacher transfer via plain SFT. BRIGHT is the benchmark that made this necessary: its queries (StackExchange threads, LeetCode problems, theorem lookups) require inference rather than lexical or semantic matching, and BM25 scores ~15 nDCG@10 there versus ~40 on BEIR. Closest neighbours worth reading are JudgeRank (Niu et al., 2024), which does LLM reasoning reranking without distillation, and the authors' own concurrent Rank-K (Yang et al., 2025), which makes the reasoning reranker listwise — the obvious follow-up, along with RL on the final verdict, which the authors flag since SFT never optimizes the ranking objective.

For your work, the interesting question is what reasoning is actually buying. If relevance is a latent quantity and the reranker is an estimator of it, test-time compute should reduce estimator variance, and we would expect a monotone accuracy-versus-tokens curve — which is exactly what §3.6 fails to find. The alternative reading is that the reasoning trace changes the objective: Rank1 is computing a strict, binary entailment-style judgment ("does this passage answer the query"), not a graded topical-similarity score, which simultaneously explains BRIGHT/NevIR wins and BEIR/DBPedia losses. That reframing matters for efficiency-effectiveness analysis: the usual latency-versus-nDCG Pareto frontier presumes both systems estimate the same target, and cross-benchmark sign flips mean a single frontier is ill-defined — you would need per-benchmark frontiers, with cost measured in generated tokens rather than parameters. There is a clean formal opening here: characterize when a high-variance, high-cost, well-specified scorer beats a low-variance, cheap, mis-specified one as a function of first-stage recall and rank cutoff.

The generative-retrieval parallel is close but not identical. Both Rank1 and DSI-style models produce rankings by generating tokens, but generative retrieval decodes identifiers over the whole corpus, amortizing cost across documents, whereas Rank1 decodes justifications per candidate — cost scales with k, not with corpus size, and the generated text is explanatory rather than addressing. A hybrid where generated reasoning conditions identifier decoding is unexplored territory.

Finally, reasoning rerankers do shift what a vector-search first stage must guarantee, and in an interesting direction. When reranking costs 100× more per candidate, you want smaller k, which means higher recall@k at small k — a much harder guarantee than recall@1000, and precisely where ANN index tuning (HNSW ef, IVF nprobe) bites. Rank1's BRIGHT numbers also show that a reranker only +1 point above its input is bottlenecked by the candidate set, so the binding constraint has moved from reranker quality to first-stage recall, and recall targets should be derived from the reranker's marginal value per additional candidate rather than fixed at k=100 or 1000 by convention.

title: Near-Optimal Directed Euclidean Spanners in High Dimensions
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-28

Near-Optimal Directed Euclidean Spanners in High Dimensions

Jayaram, Patel, Stein, Waingarten, Zhang — STOC 2026 — doi:10.1145/3798129.3800852

Worked from the abstract only: the paper is ACM-DL-exclusive, the download returns a Cloudflare challenge page rather than a PDF, and no arXiv preprint exists (checked the arXiv API and the authors' pages). Everything below the "Main idea" paragraph is my own background on the area rather than a reading of their proofs — treat the proof sketch as what the argument most likely looks like, not as a report of what they wrote.

Main idea. A Euclidean spanner is a sparse graph on n points whose shortest-path metric approximates the true ℓ_p distances within 1+ε. In low dimensions this is a solved classical story: O(n/ε^{d−1}) edges via the well-separated pair decomposition. In high dimensions it collapses — for d = Θ(log n) you cannot beat trivial bounds for undirected spanners, so the interesting version is the directed one with Steiner nodes: you may add auxiliary vertices that are not points of the input and need not even live in the metric ("non-metric Steiner nodes", which are known to be necessary here), and you route along directed edges. Andoni and Zhang gave such a construction with O(n^{2−Ω(ε²)}) edges. This paper improves the exponent's dependence on ε from quadratic to linear, giving O(n^{2−Ω(ε)}) edges in nearly-matching construction time for all p ∈ [1,2], and — the part that makes it "near-optimal" — proves a matching lower bound: some point set in high dimensions forces any (1+ε)-approximate directed Steiner spanner to use Ω(n^{2−O(ε)}) edges. So the truth is n^{2−Θ(ε)}, and the remaining slack is only in the constant inside Θ. As an application they get faster algorithms for Wasserstein-q distances over (ℝ^d, ℓ_p).

The most interesting part. Two things. First, the shape of the answer is itself the message: in high dimensions a (1+ε)-spanner is barely subquadratic, and the price of accuracy is paid linearly in the exponent rather than quadratically. That is a strong statement about the limits of distance-preserving sparsification — you cannot escape near-quadratic size by any amount of Steiner cleverness, which retroactively explains why sketching-based approaches to high-dimensional geometric problems so often route through approximate rather than spanner-exact structures. Second, the lower bound is the harder and more valuable half. Upper bounds in this area have improved several times; a matching Ω(n^{2−O(ε)}) closes the question up to constants and tells you that Andoni–Zhang's ε² was an artifact of the construction, not of the problem.

The critique I would want to press, and cannot confirm without the text: the Wasserstein application is the only stated downstream use, and it is worth asking whether the spanner is genuinely the right intermediate object there or whether a direct sketching argument gets the same bound — the recent line on tree embeddings and quadtree-based Wasserstein approximation has repeatedly shown that spanner-quality guarantees are stronger than transportation problems actually need. And "nearly-matching time" in constructions of this kind usually means time proportional to the output size times polylog factors, which at n^{2−Ω(ε)} edges is still close to quadratic; for the regime where high-dimensional geometry actually bites (n in the millions), the construction may be of purely theoretical interest.

Broader context. The relevant background is the interaction of three threads. (1) Classical Euclidean spanner theory — WSPD, greedy spanners, the lightness/sparsity tradeoff literature (Le–Solomon and predecessors) — all of which is fundamentally low-dimensional, with 1/ε^{d} factors that are fatal at d = log n. (2) The dimension-reduction alternative: Johnson–Lindenstrauss gets you to d = O(ε^{−2} log n), which is exactly why the interesting parameter regime for these results is d polylogarithmic in n, and why ε appears in the exponent of n at all. (3) The directed/Steiner relaxation, whose point is that allowing asymmetry and extra nodes lets you encode distance information combinatorially — a directed path through Steiner nodes can "sum up" coordinate-wise contributions in a way an undirected metric graph on the original points cannot. The closest neighbours to read are Andoni–Zhang (the construction this improves) and the distance-oracle / approximate-distance-preserver literature, where the same near-quadratic barriers show up under different names. A natural follow-up: pin down the constant in the exponent (is it n^{2−cε} for a specific c, and is c the same on both sides?), and ask the same question for ℓ_p with p > 2 and for the ℓ_∞ / general normed-space case, where the Steiner-node trick may behave quite differently.

For your work, the honest connection is a negative result with teeth, and it is worth internalizing rather than forcing. High-dimensional vector search is the applied face of exactly this geometry, and the graph-based ANN indices you care about (HNSW, NSG, DiskANN) are, structurally, sparse graphs whose greedy-search behaviour depends on how well shortest paths track true distances. This paper says that if you demand a uniform (1+ε) guarantee over all pairs, the graph must be near-quadratic in size — which is a clean formal explanation of why no proximity-graph index offers worst-case (1+ε) guarantees, and why the field's theory has moved to instance-dependent parameters (doubling dimension in Indyk–Xu, intrinsic dimension, relative contrast). Read alongside the HNSW/hubs paper above, the pair makes a nice thesis-shaped argument: hierarchy and hubs are not buying you spanner-quality distance preservation — that is provably unaffordable — they are buying navigability for typical queries, which is a strictly weaker and instance-dependent property. Making that distinction formal (what is the weakest routing guarantee a sub-quadratic directed graph can support for a 1−δ fraction of query-point pairs?) strikes me as a genuinely open question sitting between this paper and yours.

Proof sketch. I have not read the proofs, so this is the structure such results almost always have, flagged as inference. On the upper-bound side, constructions of this type build a recursive, randomized space partition (a randomly shifted grid or quadtree over the ℓ_p space, or an LSH-style bucketing at geometrically increasing distance scales) and, at each scale, introduce Steiner nodes that act as aggregators: a single Steiner node absorbs all the in-edges from one cell and emits out-edges to another, so k×k pairwise connections at that scale cost O(k) edges instead of k². Directedness is what makes the aggregator sound — the path through it adds a fixed amount of length in one direction only, which is why the same trick fails for undirected spanners. The (1+ε) accuracy then comes from a charging argument: the error incurred per scale is bounded by the cell diameter, geometric summation over scales gives a total of O(ε) relative error after choosing the grid granularity, and the edge count is a product over scales of the branching factor, which is where the n^{2−Ω(ε)} arises. Improving ε² → ε plausibly comes from a sharper concentration or "brute-force below a threshold" hybrid: handle the near-diagonal scales exactly and only aggregate where the concentration of ℓ_p distances is strong enough that one Steiner node suffices — i.e. replacing a union bound over pairs with a second-moment or entropy argument. On the lower-bound side, Ω(n^{2−O(ε)}) will be an explicit construction plus a counting/encoding argument: take a point set with near-uniform pairwise distances (random points on a sphere in d = Θ(log n), the standard hard instance, where all distances concentrate within (1±ε) of each other), argue that a (1+ε)-spanner must distinguish the genuinely-close pairs from the rest, and conclude that the spanner encodes enough information about a random graph on n vertices that its edge count must be near-quadratic — an incompressibility argument. The Steiner nodes are the reason this is nontrivial: the counting has to hold even though the adversary may add unboundedly many auxiliary vertices, which typically requires bounding the information a Steiner path can carry rather than the number of nodes.

title: Down with the Hierarchy: The 'H' in HNSW Stands for "Hubs"
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-28

Down with the Hierarchy: The 'H' in HNSW Stands for "Hubs"

Munyampirwa, Lakshman, Coleman — 2025 — arXiv:2412.01940

Main idea. The paper argues that HNSW's skip-list-style layer stack is vestigial for modern embedding workloads: a flat navigable small world graph — literally hnswlib's base layer, searched with the same beam search and the same SIMD/prefetch engineering, shipped as flatnav — matches hierarchical HNSW in p50 and p99 latency-recall across 13 datasets from 1M to 100M points, while cutting peak construction memory by 18–39% on three BigANN collections. They reproduce the older positive results for hierarchy on synthetic uniform data, find the crossover at ambient d ≈ 32, and propose a decision rule: below 32 dimensions keep the hierarchy, above it don't. The interesting half is the explanation, the Hub Highway Hypothesis. Hubness — the skew in the k-occurrence distribution N_k, where a few points sit in disproportionately many others' kNN lists — means the proximity graph acquires, for free, a small set of high in-degree nodes that are (i) preferentially connected to each other and (ii) visited early by almost every query. Concentration of distances makes every edge effectively "long-range," and concentration of measure puts hubs where the mass extremizes, so the r^{−d} long-link tuning that Kleinberg-style navigability demands happens automatically. The hierarchy's real job, on this reading, was never coarse-to-fine refinement but forcing every search to start from a tiny privileged set — and in high dimensions the data builds that set itself.

Reviewer-style critique. This is the most careful version of this ablation to date, and the implementation-parity discipline (same base graph, same intrinsics, same prefetch) is the right methodological move. But parity is also the paper's sharpest unexamined confound: the flat index is the bottom layer of a graph that was built using hierarchical routing during insertion. If the layers shape which edges survive the α-pruning heuristic, then the experiment shows the hierarchy is useless at query time, not that it is useless — and the memory numbers, measured on flatnav's own construction, quietly straddle both claims. Tuning is thin: one configuration (M=32, ef_construction=100, ef_search=200, k=100) with only ef_search swept, so neither variant gets a per-dataset budget and the flat graph never gets the larger M that a missing hierarchy might warrant. "High dimensional" is never operationalized beyond ambient d; intrinsic dimension is invoked rhetorically but never estimated (no TwoNN, no Levina–Bickel), which matters because SIFT-128 and Yandex-DEEP-96 are intrinsically far lower-dimensional than GIST-960 — and DEEP is precisely where hub connectivity collapses (P95 effect size 0.0000; P99 only 0.16, and SpaceV 0.16). The obvious ask is to re-plot every gap against estimated ID instead of d.

The hypothesis is tested only correlationally, and partly circularly: hubs are defined as the top-1%/5% of the node access distribution, so the claim that some nodes are visited much more often is true by construction. The metric-space quantity that would break the circle, N_k, is skipped as O(n²) infeasible. There is no intervention anywhere: no hub-edge deletion, no in-degree cap, no forced non-hub entry points, no hop-count comparison with hubs blacklisted. The preferential-attachment control is one log-log linear model explaining 23–25% of variance on angular synthetic data, which is not negligible. Regimes left open: billion scale (not run, for RAM reasons — awkward, since the claim is that d not n drives the effect, yet n spans only two decades); very high recall (>0.99) tails; streaming inserts and deletes, where the layer stack also serves as a maintainable entry structure; disk-resident layouts; filtered/predicate search; and OOD queries, where hubs are a data-side property and the query distribution no longer visits them the same way. The cleverest thing in the paper is not the ablation but the retrodiction in §6.6: thirty years of entry-point engineering — kd-tree seeds, vantage-point trees, medoids, cluster stratification — that demonstrably helped in the 2000s and has now quietly converged back to random entry nodes with no loss. The hub highway explains that entire arc in one sentence, and the angular-vs-ℓ₂ contrast (anti-hub behaviour of cosine at d=1536) is a genuinely elegant natural experiment that varies hubness while holding dimension fixed.

Broader context. The lineage runs NSW → HNSW → NSG (monotonic search networks, aiming for no local minima) → Vamana/DiskANN (flat, α-pruned, bounded degree, disk-friendly), and note that DiskANN was already flat and already competitive, so this paper is in part an explanation of why DiskANN got away with it. Theoretically, Kleinberg's navigability result is the reference point: greedy decentralized routing achieves polylog hops only when long-range link lengths follow r^{−d} in a d-dimensional lattice, a knife-edge condition. The hub highway is best read as the claim that high-dimensional concentration puts you on that knife edge for free. Two papers to have in hand: Prokhorenkova & Shekhovtsov (ICML 2020, Graph-based nearest neighbor search: from practice to theory), which analyses greedy kNN-graph search on uniform spheres and low-dimensional manifolds and already exposes the dimension dependence; and Indyk & Xu (NeurIPS 2023), which proves DiskANN-style guarantees under bounded doubling dimension while showing HNSW/NSG admit adversarial instances with no bound at all. On the hubness side, Radovanović, Nanopoulos & Ivanović (JMLR 2010) is the origin, with a substantial follow-on literature on hubness reduction (local scaling, mutual proximity) that this paper inverts by finding a setting where hubs are load-bearing. A natural follow-up: build the highway explicitly rather than hoping it emerges — estimate reverse-kNN in-degree by sampling, promote the top ε fraction into a small resident highway graph, route phase one there and descend into the base graph after; equivalently, make α-pruning in-degree-aware so it protects hub edges instead of trimming them. That also yields the missing causal test for free.

For your own work, a theory of hub-induced navigability would have to chain five things: a distributional model with intrinsic dimension d₀; a proof that the pruned kNN graph's in-degree distribution is heavy-tailed with tail index a decreasing function of d₀; a feeder lemma, that greedy search from an arbitrary start hits the hub set in O(1) hops (this follows from hub in-degree, not from hub–hub edges); an expansion lemma, that the hub-induced subgraph has diameter O(log n); and a descent lemma with no local minima from a hub to the target neighbourhood, which is where α-pruning/MSNET arguments already live. The payoff would be a separation theorem: hierarchy buys Θ(log n) when d₀ is small and only O(1) when d₀ is large. Note the analytical posture this forces — hubness is an instance property, and Indyk–Xu shows worst-case analysis of HNSW-style graphs is hopeless, so the right frame is beyond-worst-case: parameterize query cost by measurable instance quantities (skewness of N_k, doubling dimension, relative contrast) and prove instance-dependent or instance-optimal bounds, with the empirical skewness numbers here serving as instance parameters. Finally, the generative retrieval parallel is close to exact. Hierarchical semantic docids — DSI's hierarchical k-means, NCI, RQ-VAE codes — impose a tree over the same kind of high-dimensional embedding space, and the same audit applies: is the tree doing coarse-to-fine discrimination, or just supplying an entry distribution and a beam prior that the representation already encodes? The diagnostic transfers directly: measure the skewness of prefix-occurrence, check whether constrained beam search concentrates on a few "hub prefixes" early and then diffuses, and compare against flat/atomic docids with equal decoding budget. If hierarchy's value really is entry-point induction, hierarchical docids should stop earning their keep exactly where semantic spaces get high-dimensional enough — while their first-token error propagation cost stays.

Proof sketch. There is no theorem here: the paper is entirely empirical, and the Hub Highway Hypothesis is stated as a hypothesis supported by histograms, R² regressions on insertion order, two-sample t/Mann–Whitney tests on hub-to-hub adjacency, and binned hub-visitation curves, with only informal concentration-of-measure and concentration-of-distances intuitions as justification. A real proof would need the five-link chain above — heavy-tailed in-degree for pruned kNN graphs under an isotropic or log-concave model, O(1) hops into the hub set, O(log n) hub-subgraph diameter, monotone descent out of it, and a d₀-dependent separation between flat and hierarchical search — none of which is attempted or even formally conjectured.

title: Macformer: Transformer with Random Maclaurin Feature Attention
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-28

Macformer: Transformer with Random Maclaurin Feature Attention

Guo, Ding, Yuan, Wang (Beijing Institute of Technology) — 2024 — arXiv:2408.11656

Main idea. Linear-attention work built on random features has almost always gone through the Gaussian kernel: rewrite exp(q·k) as exp(‖q‖²/2)·exp(−‖q−k‖²/2)·exp(‖k‖²/2), then apply Rahimi–Recht random Fourier features to the shift-invariant part. Macformer's observation is that this detour is unnecessary. Softmax's similarity is natively a dot-product kernel K(q·k), and there is an older, less-used random-feature construction for exactly that class — Kar & Karnick's random Maclaurin features (RMF), which sample a degree from the Taylor series and estimate (q·k)^N by a product of Rademacher projections. Swapping RFF for RMF gives a drop-in linear-time attention (RMFA, O(ndD) instead of O(n²d)) whose kernel is now a free design choice: any analytic K with non-negative Maclaurin coefficients works, with softmax as the special case K = exp. The paper instantiates five (exp, 1/(1−x), 1−log(1−x), sinh+cosh, 2−√(1−x)), adds a normalization wrapper (ppSBN) that forces queries and keys into the unit ball so the series converges, and reports LRA numbers roughly matching a vanilla Transformer at a fraction of the training time.

The most interesting part. What RMF buys is kernel genericity in the right variable. RFF only reaches shift-invariant kernels, so any non-Gaussian similarity requires a new spectral derivation; RMF reaches the whole cone of non-negative-coefficient dot-product kernels with one construction, and changing kernels changes literally one scalar sequence a_N — hence the paper's observation that memory is identical across kernels. This turns "which similarity function should attention use?" into a hyperparameter rather than a research project.

ppSBN is the other half, and it is doing two distinct jobs conflated as one. Mechanically it batch-normalizes then L2-normalizes Q and K (guaranteeing |q·k| ≤ 1, which is what makes the Maclaurin series converge at all and is required for the inv, log and sqrt kernels to be defined), then rescales the attention output by learned γ, β as (γ·att)^β. Theorem 3 says normalization does not merely shrink the input: it maps true attention to (1/t)·attn^(1/r) with data-dependent r and t, so the post-scaling has to undo a power, not just a gain — hence the unusual exponential output transform. That is a clever observation, and also where the theory is weakest: r depends on ‖Q‖₂‖K‖₂ and the batch variances, i.e. it varies per batch, while β is a learned constant; and the proof's central step splits a softmax over a sum of cross terms into a geometric mean of two softmaxes, which is not an identity. ppSBN is a good heuristic dressed as a theorem.

The critique continues on variance, which the paper never discusses. Performer's FAVOR+ exists precisely because the trigonometric RFF estimator of exp can go negative and has unbounded relative variance where the kernel is small, destabilizing the normalizing denominator. RMF has the same pathology and worse: the estimator is a product of N signed projections, so single-sample estimates of a strictly positive kernel are routinely negative, and a near-zero denominator makes the attention ratio blow up. Theorem 2's boundedness premise silently assumes the per-feature weights behave like a convex combination, which fails as soon as φ(K_j) changes sign across j. Unbiasedness of the kernel estimate also does not transfer to the attention output: the proof of Theorem 1 pushes the expectation separately into numerator and denominator of a ratio, so what is proved is E[num]/E[den] = attn, not E[num/den] = attn. Evaluation gaps compound this: only 3 of 6 LRA tasks (Image, Pathfinder, Path-X omitted), a 2-layer/64-dim model, D = 128 against d = 64, memory worse than the baseline everywhere (1.34–2.56×), and baselines limited to Transformer and RFA even though the codebase is Skyformer's — no Performer, Linformer or Nyströmformer. Accuracy never beats the Transformer on Text and never beats RFA anywhere. And there is an accidental measurement of noise: sinh + cosh = exp, so Macformer_trigh and Macformer_exp are the same kernel with the same coefficients — they give identical accuracy on Text (64.06) and ListOps (38.36), as they must, then differ by 3.5 points on Retrieval (74.23 vs 70.74). That spread is pure seed noise, and it is larger than most of the paper's claimed kernel effects. Finally, the toy study shows error growing with sequence length, which Theorem 2's n-free bound does not predict; this is called "consistent with theory" rather than investigated.

Broader context. Attention weights are a kernel smoother (Tsai et al.), so softmax(QKᵀ)V is a Nadaraya–Watson estimate with an exponential-inner-product kernel. Killing the n² cost means finding an explicit feature map φ with φ(q)·φ(k) ≈ K(q,k), because then (φ(Q)φ(K)ᵀ)V re-associates to φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV) — linear in n. Random Feature Attention and Performer/FAVOR+ do this with random Fourier features plus positivity-corrected variants; Nyströmformer and Skyformer take a data-dependent low-rank route; Linformer projects the length axis, which is not a kernel approximation at all. The underlying literature is Rahimi–Recht (Bochner: shift-invariant kernels are Fourier transforms of probability measures, so sample frequencies) and Kar & Karnick (dot-product kernels are non-negative combinations of (x·y)^N, so sample degrees). A plausible follow-up: a "FAVOR+ for dot-product kernels" — a positivity-preserving RMF variant (squared or exponentiated features, orthogonalized Rademacher blocks) with an actual variance analysis, plus learning the coefficient sequence a_N end-to-end instead of picking from a table, which would make Macformer the dot-product analogue of Spectraformer and of learned feature maps like Hedgehog.

Relevance to your work. This sits directly on the bridge you care about. An explicit map Φ with Φ(q)·Φ(k) ≈ exp(q·k) is, formally, a reduction of monotone-transformed MIPS to Euclidean inner product search in D dimensions — and since exp is strictly increasing, argmax_k exp(q·k) = argmax_k q·k, so RMF is a candidate randomized scorer for MIPS and, more realistically, for cheap reranking under a non-linear similarity. Two things make the analogy break, and they are worth being precise about. First, ppSBN's L2 normalization is exactly the step that trivializes MIPS: once keys have unit norm, MIPS collapses to cosine/NN search — the easy case that ALSH (Shrivastava–Li) and Neyshabur–Srebro's asymmetric constructions were invented to avoid needing. So Macformer's theory holds precisely in the regime where the retrieval problem is uninteresting, and the interesting regime (heterogeneous key norms, where the series may diverge) is where its guarantees vanish. Second, the guarantee shape is wrong for retrieval. Theorem 2 is additive: ε absolute error with probability 1 − 2D exp(−Dε²/2L²). MIPS needs gap-dependent relative error — you must separate the top-k scores from the rest, so the required ε scales with the score gap and D must grow like gap⁻² log n with a union bound over the corpus. LSH gives this shape natively (collision probability monotone in similarity ⇒ c-approximate guarantees); RMF does not, because its per-sample estimator is heavy-tailed: the degree is geometric with P[N=η] = p^{−(η+1)} while the payload is scaled by p^{η+1}, so high-order terms are rare but enormous — importance sampling with a deliberately bad proposal. A usable MIPS bound would need a Bernstein-type argument with the actual second moment, which the paper never computes. Third, relevant to the sparse side: RMF features are dense and signed. Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE-style) works because non-negative features let inverted-index pruning (WAND/MaxScore/BlockMax) bound a document's residual contribution; signed features destroy those upper bounds, so RMF embeddings can only be served by dense ANN, not an inverted index. A positivity-preserving dot-product random feature map would restore prunability and fix the variance blow-up at once — the most interesting theoretical question this paper raises without asking it.

Proof sketch. Three results, in descending order of rigor. Theorem 1 (unbiasedness) assumes Q, K in the unit ℓ₂ ball — citing Schoenberg (1942) so the Maclaurin series of K converges on [−1,1] — and that K's coefficients a_N are non-negative so √a_N is real. The construction is Kar–Karnick's: draw N geometric with P[N = η] = p^{−(η+1)}, p > 1; draw N i.i.d. d-dimensional Rademacher vectors ω_j; set φ(x) = √(a_N p^{N+1}) ∏_{j≤N} ⟨ω_j, x⟩; average D i.i.d. copies. The key lemma is the Rademacher moment identity E[⟨ω,x⟩⟨ω,y⟩] = xᵀE[ωωᵀ]y = x·y, which by independence across j gives E_ω[∏_j ⟨ω_j,x⟩⟨ω_j,y⟩] = (x·y)^N. The p^{N+1} weight then exactly cancels the geometric sampling probability, so E_N[a_N p^{N+1}(x·y)^N] = Σ_η a_η (x·y)^η = K(x·y) — importance sampling of the Taylor series, one term at a time. Lifting this to attention is where the argument loosens: the expectation is taken separately in numerator and denominator, so what is proved is unbiasedness of the two halves, not of the attention output. Masking enters harmlessly because maskfill with a 0/1 matrix commutes with expectation. Theorem 2 (concentration) adds |V_ij| ≤ L, asserts each RMFA coordinate lies in [−L, L], applies Hoeffding to the D-term average with range 2L and union-bounds over the D features, giving P(error > ε) ≤ 2D exp(−Dε²/2L²). Two caveats: the 2D prefactor makes the bound vacuous unless ε ≫ L√(log D / D), and the union-bound event ("some single feature deviates") is not the event being bounded ("the average deviates"), so the steps do not compose as written; boundedness also needs same-sign features. What survives is the right qualitative claim — error shrinks like 1/√D and scales with value magnitude — but no usable constant, and notably nothing depending on n, which the experiments contradict. Theorem 3 (ppSBN) is a scale-recovery calculation for K = exp: substituting normalized inputs into softmax and expanding (Q−μ_Q)(K−μ_K)ᵀ shows the normalized attention equals (1/t)·attn(Q,K,V)^{1/r} with r = ‖Q‖₂‖K‖₂√((σ_Q+ε)(σ_K+ε)) and t absorbing the μ_Q Kᵀ cross term; the learned γ, β are then declared to fit 1/t and 1/r. The manipulation turning a softmax of summed exponents into a product of two softmaxes raised to fractional powers is heuristic, not an identity, so read this as motivation for the functional form of the output rescaling rather than a proof that scale is restored.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Prototypical Representations
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-28

Reinforcement Learning with Prototypical Representations

Yarats, Fergus, Lazaric, Pinto — 2021 — arXiv:2102.11271

Main idea. Pixel-based RL has a bootstrapping problem: you need a good encoder to tell novel states from familiar ones, but you need broad data coverage to learn a good encoder. Proto-RL attacks both ends with one object. During a reward-free pre-training phase it learns a SwAV-style codebook of M=512 prototype vectors in a 128-d latent space, trained by a cross-entropy loss between the online network's soft assignment of x_t and a Sinkhorn-balanced target assignment of x_{t+1} — so the "two views" are consecutive timesteps, not two augmentations of one frame: a one-step dynamics consistency objective wearing SwAV's clothes, with BYOL's predictor/EMA asymmetry to prevent collapse. The same prototypes then define the exploration bonus: instead of taking the k-NN distance against a uniform batch from the replay buffer (as APT does), Proto-RL maintains a queue of M×T candidates built by drawing one sample per prototype cluster, and the intrinsic reward is the distance from z_{t+1} to its 3rd nearest neighbour in that stratified queue. RL gradients are blocked from the encoder, so representations stay task-agnostic. Downstream, encoder and prototypes are frozen and the bonus is retained at weight α=0.2. On 16 DMC tasks with 10 seeds, 500k reward-free plus 500k supervised steps beats DrQ trained on 1M supervised steps in 6 of 8 headline tasks — at matched total interaction, which is the honest way to read that claim.

Reviewer-style critique. The cleverest idea is unambiguous: the codebook is used twice, once as the clustering target that regularises representation learning and once as a stratification scheme for the candidate set of the nearest-neighbour entropy estimator. Reusing the SSL structure as a variance-reduction device for the novelty signal is elegant and cheap.

But the paper oversells what that buys. Section 5.7 claims prototypes give "more accurate entropy estimation" and supports it only with the standard deviation of the intrinsic reward. Lower variance is not accuracy. Worse, the Singh et al. estimator is consistent only when the reference samples are i.i.d. from d^π; deliberately equalising candidates across clusters breaks exactly that assumption, so the bonus is no longer estimating H(d^π) but something closer to a novelty score against a uniformised reference measure. That may well be the better objective in practice, but the paper never acknowledges the substituted estimand, and there is no bias analysis to accompany the variance plot.

The evaluation has two real confounds. First, the downstream actor is initialised from the exploration actor (Appendix B.6) — never ablated, and not given to the baselines, which freeze an encoder and train a fresh DrQ policy. The α sweep isolates the bonus but not the policy warm-start. Second, APT is reimplemented with a frozen encoder rather than the fine-tuning its authors used; the deviation is disclosed, which is creditable, but it plausibly costs APT a lot. Missing ablations are conspicuous for a method whose whole identity is a codebook: no sweep over M, T or k, no comparison against plain k-means or unbalanced assignment to show Sinkhorn earns its place, and no test of the temporal x_t→x_{t+1} contrast against a CURL-style same-frame contrast despite that being claimed as a design novelty. The pointmass U-maze — the only genuinely exploration-hard setting — appears as a single bar chart with no seeds or error bars, and "generalisation" means four reward functions on one embodiment, not cross-domain transfer.

Broader context. The subfield splits into two lines that Proto-RL welds together. One is self-supervised representation learning for control: SAC-AE, then CURL (instance contrast), DrQ/RAD (augmentation alone as regulariser), SPR (multi-step latent dynamics), ATC (temporal contrast) — all reward-driven, all task-coupled. The other is intrinsic motivation: pseudo-counts, RND, ICM curiosity, and the max-state-entropy family descending from Hazan et al.'s provably efficient MaxEnt exploration through MEPOL and APT. RE3 is the sharpest foil to read alongside this paper: it argues that a randomly initialised, frozen encoder suffices for k-NN state-entropy bonuses, which directly contests the premise that the metric space must be learned. An ablation replacing Proto-RL's encoder with a random one while keeping the prototype stratification would have settled which half of the contribution matters.

The IR connection here is real rather than forced. Sinkhorn-balanced assignment to a codebook is the same machinery generative retrieval needs for learned discrete docids — RQ-VAE docid construction suffers codebook collapse and leans on balanced assignment and k-means initialisation for exactly the reason Proto-RL does — and IVF-style partitioning for vector search lives or dies by cell balance. Proto-RL's stratified queue is, read in IR terms, "sample one vector per posting list to get a lower-variance k-NN density estimate," which suggests a clean follow-up: characterise the prototype-stratified Kozachenko–Leonenko estimator as stratified importance sampling, bound its bias against the true H(d^π), and test whether cell-stratified sampling over an IVF index yields lower-variance nearest-neighbour entropy or diversity estimates than uniform sampling — useful both for coverage bonuses in RL and for corpus-diversity and active-selection metrics in retrieval. A hierarchical or residual codebook in place of the flat 512 prototypes would give multi-scale novelty and connect the two literatures even more tightly.

title: From Tokens to Words: On the Inner Lexicon of LLMs
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-27

6. From Tokens to Words: On the Inner Lexicon of LLMs

Kaplan, Oren, Reif, Schwartz — 2024 · arXiv:2410.05864

Main idea

Subword tokenizers hand an LLM a segmentation that is essentially arbitrary with respect to the lexicon: "unhappiness" may arrive as un/h/appiness, a typo reroutes "development" to de/vel/p/oment, and yet the model behaves as if it read the word. Kaplan et al. ask where and how that repair happens, and treat it as a localizable computation rather than a diffuse property of the network.

Their answer is a two-stage circuit in the early-to-middle layers of Llama2-7B (replicated on Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B, Yi-6B). Layers 1–2 show a sharp, statistically significant excess of attention from a word's final subword token to its prefix tokens relative to the control of single-token words attending to their predecessor; that attention then collapses by up to 90%, and from roughly layer 3 onward FFN updates write a whole-word representation into the final token's residual stream. The diagnostic is a logit lens run against the input embedding matrix E rather than the unembedding U — an inversion of the usual usage, since the question is what the current token is, not what comes next. Artificially split single-token words are recovered at over 80% by layer 15 (93.2% at some layer), typo-corrupted ones at ~40% (66% cumulative). The retrieval signal then decays as the residual stream turns over to next-token prediction. Ablating just the ~5% of FFN updates whose vocabulary projection names the word drops retrieval from 85% to 18%, and drops capital-city recall for split country names from 88% to 41%, while random ablation of the same budget costs little.

The most interesting part

The cleverest move is the experimental design for words that have no single-token form, where logit lens is unavailable by construction. Here the authors use Patchscopes: take the layer-ℓ hidden state of the last subword token of a genuinely multi-token word and splice it, as a single input vector, into the prompt "Repeat this word twice: 1) X 2)". At layers 5–7 the model re-emits the full multi-token spelling 64% of the time (77.4% at some layer), despite never having encountered a mid-stack residual vector at its input layer during training. This is the paper's strongest claim and the cleanest one: a single vector carries enough information to reconstruct a token string the embedding matrix cannot represent.

It also shows exactly the limits of the evidence. What Patchscopes certifies is string recoverability, not lexical status. A "spell out the thing in the residual stream" circuit — which we independently know exists, since models do character-level manipulation — would pass this test on any recoverable vector, word or not; the authors never run the nonword control through Patchscopes, which would be the obvious falsifier. The semantic evidence (the capital-cities ablation) comes only from single-token country names artificially split, i.e. exactly the case where a real embedding exists and where "the lexicon" is trivially the BPE vocabulary. So the load-bearing claim — that a latent vocabulary beyond the tokenizer exists — is supported by an orthographic probe, while the semantic claim is supported only where the lexicon isn't latent.

Two further honesty notes. The 22.6% of multi-token words never decoded at any layer are read as "not in the inner lexicon," but a probe's failure is not the absence of a representation; this is affirming the consequent, and the Arabic Wiki40B result (only 16% of attempted words yield extractable representations) is more plausibly a statement about Patchscopes under morphological richness than about Llama2's Arabic lexicon. And the cosine-similarity check in App. F is not an independent validation of logit lens — both measure angular alignment with rows of E. The word/nonword probe has a similar wrinkle: the linguistically plausible ARC nonwords are more separable from real words than the authors' token-shuffled ones, presented as validating their data construction but arguably cutting against the mental-lexicon analogy the paper invokes, since human lexical decision goes the other way. Finally, "finetuning-free vocabulary expansion" is a slight overstatement: core weights are frozen, but two d×d refinement matrices are trained on 20M tokens, and the absolute numbers are modest (0.171 top-1 on new tokens vs. 0.071 for the mean-embedding baseline), with 10.5–14.5% sequence-length reduction at roughly flat overall accuracy.

Broader context

The background is the long-running tension between BPE (Sennrich et al. 2016) as an engineering convenience and the linguistic units it mangles — documented in Bostrom & Durrett's finding that BPE is suboptimal for pretraining, in Batsuren et al. (2024) on alien subword composition, and in Petrov et al. (2023) on the 13× token-count penalty non-English text pays. In parallel, mechanistic interpretability had named "detokenization" as an early-layer stage (Elhage et al.'s SoLU work, Lad et al.'s stages-of-inference), and Geva et al. (2021, 2022) had established FFNs as key-value memories that promote concepts in vocabulary space. This paper is essentially the systematic merger of those two lines. The paper to read alongside it is Feucht et al. (2024), Token Erasure as a Footprint of Implicit Vocabulary Items in LLMs — concurrent, EMNLP 2024, reaching the same conclusion from the opposite direction: rather than showing the last token acquires the word, they show earlier tokens' identities get erased. Two independent signatures of one mechanism is much stronger than either alone. The other direction worth tracking is tokenizer-free modeling — Byte Latent Transformer, MEGABYTE, CANINE — where the natural question is whether an entropy-patched byte model develops the same layer-localized fusion, which would settle whether this is a tokenizer artifact or a general chunking pressure.

An obvious follow-up: run the nonword control through Patchscopes and, more importantly, test whether the fused vector is semantically functional for genuinely multi-token items — patch the fused representation of a multi-token entity into an attribute-recall prompt à la Geva et al. (2023) and see whether downstream facts survive. If strings are recoverable but attributes are not, "inner lexicon" should be downgraded to "inner spelling buffer," which would be a more interesting negative result than the paper's positive one.

The generative-retrieval connection is real and specific. Atomic docids give one embedding row per document, which kills generalization and blows up the softmax; string or semantic docids decode subword-by-subword and inherit error propagation, which is why constrained beam search over an FM-index (SEAL) or learned docid tokenization (GenRet, RIPOR) exist at all. Section 6 is, almost verbatim, a recipe for constructing atomic docids with a semantically meaningful initialization and no end-to-end retraining: extract the fused representation of a docid string via Patchscopes, Procrustes it into E and U, and you get a one-token docid whose embedding already encodes the string. That directly attacks the standard objection to atomic docids — randomly initialized rows need enormous supervision. The honest caveat is that the method's success rate tracks how word-like the string is (72.9% on WikiText, 16% on Arabic), so it should work for title- or keyword-derived docids and almost certainly not for arbitrary numeric IDs — a testable and useful prediction. There is a second, subtler GR implication: the paper shows prefix-token attention collapses after layer 2–3 and that word identity decays in late layers as the stream turns over to next-token prediction, a plausible mechanistic account of why prefix-conditioned docid decoding is brittle in exactly the middle of long identifiers.

For vector search the link is thinner but not zero. Two things transfer. First, the Procrustes result is a nontrivial geometric claim — layer-ℓ residual space and the input embedding space are related by a rotation plus RMS rescaling, closely analogous to the Procrustes alignment used in unsupervised bilingual embedding mapping — which matters for cross-space or cross-model retrieval alignment. Second, since decoder-only embedders (E5-Mistral, RepLLaMA) pool the last token, and this paper shows word identity peaks mid-stack and decays afterward, it supplies a mechanistic reason for the recurring empirical finding that middle-layer pooling beats final-layer pooling for retrieval representations. Neither is what the paper set out to show, and I would not oversell either.

title: Understanding Optimization in Deep Learning with Central Flows
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-27

5. Understanding Optimization in Deep Learning with Central Flows

Cohen, Damian, Talwalkar, Kolter, Lee — 2024 · arXiv:2410.24206

Main idea

Deterministic gradient descent on a neural network does not descend. After an initial phase of progressive sharpening, the top Hessian eigenvalue parks itself at 2/η and the iterates bounce across a narrow valley along the top curvature directions, with the loss rising and falling on a two-step timescale. Gradient flow is then simply the wrong idealization: it tracks the trajectory well while λ₁(H) < 2/η and diverges from it afterwards, which is most of training. The paper's move is to give up on the fine-grained trajectory — nonlinear, chaotic, and with k unstable eigenvalues involving O(k²) coupled quantities — and instead write down an ODE for the locally time-averaged iterate w̄(t) = E[w_t]. That ODE is the central flow.

The content is that the average is not the gradient flow plus noise. Averaging a third-order Taylor expansion of ∇L over the oscillation leaves a residue: dw̄/dt = −η[∇L(w̄) + ½∇⟨H(w̄), Σ(t)⟩], an implicit curvature penalty whose strength is the oscillation covariance Σ(t). Σ is not a free parameter — it is pinned by the requirement that the flow be self-consistent with the observed edge-of-stability equilibrium, and solving for it turns the whole thing into a differential complementarity problem. The same recipe applied to RMSProp yields the paper's strongest payoffs: an explicit characterization of what Adam-without-momentum's preconditioner actually is, and the observation that adaptive methods do not merely adapt to curvature but actively flatten it so as to earn larger steps later — "acceleration via regularization."

The most interesting part

The cleverest object is the complementarity formulation, and the sharpest single result is its consequence for RMSProp. Writing A(w) := (2/η)I − H(w), the EOS regime is exactly the statement 0 ⪯ Σ ⊥ A(w) ⪰ 0: the covariance is PSD, the residual is PSD, and they are orthogonal, i.e. oscillations live precisely in the null space of the residual. This is the algebra of frictionless contact — the trajectory touches the boundary of the stable region and slides along it, with Σ playing the role of a normal force. For RMSProp the stationary preconditioner then falls out as the solution of a convex SDP, min_P tr(P) + η^{−2}‖∇L‖²_{P^{−1}} s.t. H(w) ⪯ 2P over diagonal PSD P — which the authors note is dual to the max-cut SDP with the Hessian as weight matrix. A first-order method that never touches H is implicitly solving a semidefinite program in H. That is a genuinely surprising claim and the best answer I have seen to "why does Adam work."

The critique is that essentially none of this is proved, and the paper's framing occasionally obscures how much is imported from experiment. The averaging operator E is deliberately left undefined; the only properties assumed are linearity, E[c] = c, and — property 3 — that the window is coarse enough that S(E[w_t]) = 2/η exactly. That third axiom is not innocuous: it is the edge-of-stability equilibrium, asserted as an assumption. The central flow therefore does not explain why EOS occurs (progressive sharpening remains unexplained, as the authors say); it computes the consequences of assuming it persists. Two further modeling choices are made by fiat and justified only post hoc: δ_t is taken to lie entirely in the critical eigenspace, discarding the ∇S component that drives sharpness fluctuations (footnotes 17 and 21, "the success of our experiments justifies this simplification"); and the cubic Taylor expansion is assumed adequate, which Section C.2 shows empirically fails under sub/super-quadraticity — there the flow mispredicts σ²(t) and error accumulates. Empirically the validation is impressive in kind but narrow in scope: six small smooth architectures, 1000-example CIFAR-10 subsets and a synthetic sorting task, full batch, no momentum, three learning rates. Smoothness is not incidental — GroupNorm replaces BatchNorm because BatchNorm induces super-quadraticity, ReLU and max-pooling degrade the fit, and a LayerNorm kernel had to be swapped out to get correct third derivatives. The architectures were partly selected to satisfy the theory's needs. Accuracy also degrades with larger η and with cross-entropy. The honest summary is a principled heuristic with an unusually high empirical bar, not a theory with a scope condition.

Proof sketch

What is claimed formally is narrower than what is claimed informally. Informally: gradient descent initialized stably tracks w̄(t) over long horizons, and Σ(t) predicts the covariance of its oscillations. There is no theorem of this form anywhere — no bound on ‖w_t − w̄(t)‖, no timescale-separation hypothesis under which the averaging is controlled, no conditions for validity. The derivation runs: (i) decompose w_t = w̄(t) + δ_t with E[δ_t] = 0, E[δ_tδ_t⊤] = Σ(t); (ii) Taylor-expand ∇L(w̄ + δ) to second order in δ (third order in L) and average, killing the linear term and leaving ½∇H(w̄)⊤[Σ]; (iii) posit the ansatz dw̄/dt = −η[∇L + ½∇H⊤[Σ]]; (iv) impose PSD-ness, stability H ⪯ (2/η)I, and support of Σ inside the critical subspace U(w) = ker A(w), which together are exactly 0 ⪯ Σ ⊥ A(w) ⪰ 0.

The key trick is then to differentiate the complementarity relation once. Lemmas 5 and 6 show that if A(w(t)) ⪰ 0 for all t and Σ is right-continuous, then 0 ⪯ Σ(t) ⊥ (d/dt)A(w(t)) ⪰_U 0. Since dA/dt = α(w) + β(w)[Σ] is affine in Σ, with α = η∇H[∇L] and β = (η/2)∇H∇H⊤, this converts a position-level constraint into a velocity-level semidefinite complementarity problem, Σ ∈ SDCP_{U(w)}(α, β) — in the DCP literature, a pure index-one problem. Lemma 1 gives uniqueness of Σ when β ≻ 0 on Sym(U), by identifying the SDCP with the KKT conditions of the strictly convex program min_{Σ⪰0} ⟨α,Σ⟩ + ½β[Σ,Σ]. With k = 1 this collapses to σ² = max(−α_u/β_u, 0), recovering the scalar self-consistency condition σ² = 2⟨∇S, −∇L⟩/‖∇S‖² — the unique variance at which oscillation-induced sharpness reduction exactly cancels progressive sharpening — and equivalently a projection of −∇L onto the tangent cone of {S(w) ≤ 2/η}, which nearly reproduces Damian–Nichani–Lee's constrained-trajectory result without their directional-minimization condition.

So: Lemmas 1, 5, 6, 7 are real (and elementary) theorems about the DCP-to-ODE conversion; existence and uniqueness of the flow itself is inherited from Cornet (1983) for the projected-gradient-flow case, under a positive-definiteness assumption on β that the authors verify only empirically and cannot establish for the adaptive flows. Propositions 1 and 2 — the central-flow loss decreases monotonically, and does so more slowly than gradient flow would — are genuine theorems, but about the flow, not about gradient descent. Everything connecting the flow to the algorithm is derivation plus Figure 11.

Broader context

The relevant lineage begins with Cohen et al. (2021), which documented that full-batch GD on nets almost always drives λ₁(H) to 2/η and then oscillates there indefinitely without diverging — the edge of stability — and noted that no existing theory explained it. Lewkowycz et al.'s catapult effect is the single-event version. Damian, Nichani and Lee (2023) supplied the mechanism, self-stabilization: the third-order term in the Taylor expansion means that oscillating with amplitude x along the top eigenvector u implicitly takes a gradient step of size ½ηx² on the sharpness, since ∇_w[u⊤Hu] = ∇S by Danskin. That is a negative feedback loop, and it is the ingredient traditional L-smoothness analyses structurally cannot see. Arora–Li–Panigrahi and Lyu–Li–Li give related sharpness-reduction flows near minima. Cohen et al. (2022) extended EOS to adaptive methods via an effective sharpness λ₁(P^{−1}H) equilibrating at 2, which is the empirical fact the RMSProp flow here formalizes. On the modeling side, the alternative continuous-time stories — Barrett–Dherin's implicit gradient regularization from backward error analysis, and the SGD-as-SDE literature — both reduce to gradient flow in the full-batch limit and are shown here to fail precisely in the EOS regime where the discrepancy lives.

The obvious follow-up is a stochastic central flow, which the authors flag as hard: with minibatch noise it is unclear a deterministic ODE exists for the weights at all, though one might still exist for derived observables such as the loss curve or the network's function. Momentum is a second gap, and Adam proper needs both. A third, more tractable direction: re-derive the Damian et al. quartic correction for sub/super-quadratic directions inside the central-flow formalism, which would remove the single most identifiable failure mode. A fourth, given the max-cut duality: design an optimizer that solves eq. (36) — minimize tr(P) subject to H ⪯ 2P — directly and cheaply, since Figure 21 shows that preconditioner outperforms what RMSProp actually converges to, the gap being the ‖∇L‖²_{P^{−1}} term whose influence vanishes as η grows.

For your own work the honest answer is that this is interesting as pure optimization theory and there is no genuine IR hook. The one non-forced connection is instrumental: dual-encoder and generative-retrieval models are trained with Adam, and if the learning rate's dominant role at EOS is to set the strength of an implicit curvature penalty rather than a step size, then LR choice is a statement about which region of weight space the retrieval model ends up in, not merely how fast it gets there — which bears on the embedding geometry an ANN index then has to cope with. That is speculative; the SDP-duality observation is fun but coincidental to anything spectral in index construction. Read it for the method, not the application.

title: Gradient correlation is needed to accelerate SGD with momentum
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-27

4. Gradient correlation is needed to accelerate SGD with momentum

Hermant, Renaud, Aujol, Dossal, Rondepierre — 2024 · arXiv:2410.07870

Main idea

The paper attacks a long-standing embarrassment in stochastic optimization theory: momentum demonstrably helps SGD in practice, yet in the convex finite-sum setting there is no clean theorem saying when it should. The known positive result — Vaswani et al.'s observation that Stochastic Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (SNAG) recovers Nesterov rates under the Strong Growth Condition E‖∇̃_K(x)‖² ≤ ρ_K‖∇f(x)‖² — is vacuous in practice because nobody knows which functions satisfy SGC with a useful ρ_K. Hermant et al.'s contribution is to make ρ_K computable. They exhibit an exact algebraic identity relating ‖∇f(x)‖², the minibatch second moment, and the pairwise inner products ⟨∇f_i(x), ∇f_j(x)⟩, and from it define RACOGA, a scalar measure of average gradient correlation that directly controls ρ_K. The punchline is a dichotomy organized around orthogonality: when the per-sample gradients are on average positively correlated, ρ_K collapses to N/K and SNAG genuinely accelerates; when they are orthogonal, ρ₁ = N exactly and stochasticity buys nothing over full-batch NAG per gradient evaluation; when they are anti-correlated, ρ₁ > N and small batches are actively wasteful. They then add new almost-sure rates for SNAG and confirm the picture on over-parameterized least squares and CIFAR-10.

The most interesting part

The genuinely clever move is turning a noise condition into a geometry condition with no loss. Proposition 1 is an identity, not a bound: (K/N)·E‖∇̃_K(x)‖² = ‖∇f(x)‖² − (2(N−K)/(N²(N−1)))·Σ_{i<j}⟨∇f_i(x),∇f_j(x)⟩. Every claim about ρ_K then follows by plugging in a lower bound on the correlation sum. This replaces the classical bound ρ_K ≤ L_(K)/µ, which scales with the condition number and is often absurdly loose (their two-quadratic example has ρ₁ = 2 while the classical bound gives 2L/µ), with a bound depending only on N, K and a correlation coefficient. It also reframes why acceleration fails: not because momentum is fragile to noise in some vague sense, but because anti-correlated gradients make the minibatch estimator's second moment blow up relative to the true gradient, and it is precisely ρ_K that multiplies the √κ in the accelerated complexity.

The honest critique is that the assumptions are severe and the title overclaims. SGC forces the noise to vanish at the minimizer — with convex f_i it implies interpolation (their Prop. 7 + Remark 10) — so nothing here speaks to genuinely noisy regimes. RACOGA is required to hold _uniformly over ℝ^d_, and their own Appendix I.1 shows that for two-dimensional least squares with any non-orthogonal, non-collinear a₁, a₂ there are always regions with strictly negative correlation; so the global constant is typically ≤ 0 even in the friendliest convex problem, and the experiments quietly retreat to measuring RACOGA along the trajectory and tuning a surrogate λ in place of ρ_K. There is also no lower bound: "needed" is supported by upper-bound comparison and experiments, not by an impossibility theorem. The most interesting empirical observation is buried in Appendix I.3: deterministic GD/NAG dive into low-curvature ravines, which for quadratics coincide with low-RACOGA regions, and SNAG's noise is what keeps it out — a mechanism the theory does not capture at all.

Proof sketch

Setting: f = (1/N)Σf_i, L-smooth, convex or µ-strongly convex (only the sum need be convex; the f_i need not be), minibatches of size K drawn uniformly without replacement. RACOGA: c is a constant with Σ_{i<j}⟨∇f_i(x),∇f_j(x)⟩ / Σ_i‖∇f_i(x)‖² ≥ c for all x outside the common-critical set. Proposition 8 shows −1/2 ≤ c ≤ (N−1)/2, and the lower end is tight; c = 0 is the orthogonal case. Proposition 2: if c > −1/2 then ρ₁ ≤ N/(1+2c). Lemma 1 lifts this to ρ_K ≤ (ρ₁(N−K) + N(K−1))/(K(N−1)), with a converse in Proposition 7.

What is guaranteed. Theorem 3, with step s = 1/(Lρ_K): convex gives E[f(x_n) − f_] ≤ 2Lρ_K²‖x₀−x_‖²/n², i.e. ε-complexity ρ_K√(2L/ε)‖x₀−x_‖; µ-strongly convex gives the linear rate (1 − ρ_K^{−1}√(µ/L))^n on the potential f(x_n) − f_ + (µ/2)‖z_n − x_‖², i.e. ρ_K√(L/µ)·log(1/ε). So ρ_K enters linearly and multiplies the accelerated √κ. Compared with SGD's 2L_(K)/ε and 2(L_(K)/µ)log(1/ε), SNAG wins in the convex case whenever ε is small enough, but in the strongly convex case only if ρ_K ≲ L_(K)/√(µL) — so the classical ρ_K ≤ L_(K)/µ certificate does _not* certify acceleration. Theorem 5 converts this into gradient-evaluation complexity: batch K costs Δ_K = (N−K)/(N−1) + (N/ρ₁)(K−1)/(N−1) times the batch-1 cost, giving the three regimes ρ₁ < N, = N, > N.

How it is proved. The engine is Lemma 5: with s = 1/(Lρ_K), descent plus SGC gives ‖∇f(y_n)‖² ≤ 2Lρ_K·E_n[f(y_n) − f(x_{n+1})]. This is the crux — it converts the variance term into a function-value decrease that can be absorbed into a telescoping potential rather than accumulating as an error, which is exactly what Devolder-style inexact-oracle analyses cannot do. In the convex case they expand ½‖z_{n+1} − x_‖², use z_n = y_n + (α/(1−α))(y_n − x_n) to rewrite the cross term, and obtain a potential inequality whose residual coefficient on f(y_n) − f_ is Lρ_K²η_n² − η_n(1 + α_n/(1−α_n)). Imposing the scaling Lρ_K²η_n² = C(n+1)²/L and η_nα_n/(1−α_n) = Cn²/L makes the potential telescope with weight n², and non-positivity of the residual forces √C ≤ (1/ρ_K)·(n+1)/(2n+1), hence C = 1/(4ρ_K²) — this is literally where the ρ_K in the complexity comes from. The strongly convex case uses the Lyapunov function E_n = f(x_n) − f_ + (µ/2)‖z_n − x_‖² and the parameter choice η = 1/(ρ_K√(µL)), β = 1 − ρ_K^{−1}√(µ/L), α = 1/(1 + ρ_K^{−1}√(µ/L)), which makes the identity Lρ_K²η − αβ/(1−α) − 1 = 0 hold exactly, cancelling every residual term.

The new almost-sure results (Theorem 4) are proved by deliberately not cancelling the slack: they impose the stronger C ≤ 1/(16ρ_K²) so the residual is ≤ −η_n/2, then apply Robbins–Siegmund to get Σ(n+1)(f(y_n) − f_) < ∞ a.s. A second supermartingale is built on Ṽ_n = λ_n²‖x_n − y_n‖² + n²(f(x_n) − f_)/(8Lρ_K²) with λ_n = 1/(1−α_n); the trick is the inequality λ_nB̃_n ≥ Ṽ_n, so that summability of B̃_n plus λ_n = Θ(1) forces Ṽ_∞ = 0, upgrading O(1/n²) to o(1/n²). The strongly convex a.s. rate is a soft Markov + Borel–Cantelli argument on the geometric decay of E[E_n]. There is no matching lower bound; the negative results are instead explicit counterexamples — a two-quadratic least-squares instance with ρ₁ ≈ 1/ε² (App. D.1), a non-convex tanh pair for which no finite ρ₁ exists (D.2), and the tightness of c ≥ −1/2, proved elegantly by contradiction against Proposition 1 since ‖∇f‖² ≥ 0.

Broader context

The backdrop is the twenty-year question of whether Nesterov acceleration survives gradient noise. Devolder–Glineur–Nesterov's inexact-oracle framework showed that accelerated methods accumulate oracle error linearly in the iteration count while plain gradient descent does not — the canonical "momentum is fragile" barrier; Aujol–Dossal and later Kidambi et al., Assran–Rabbat and Ganesh et al. gave concrete instances where accelerated parameters make SGD-with-momentum diverge. With additive noise of variance σ², the statistical term Ω(σ²/(µn)) is unimprovable, so acceleration can only ever be uniform in the multiplicative noise / interpolation regime — exactly where this paper lives. Two nearby lines are worth knowing: the least-squares-specific accelerated SGD of Jain, Kakade, Kidambi, Netrapalli and Sidford (and Liu–Belkin's MaSS, Varre–Flammarion), where the rate is √(κκ̃) with κ̃ a statistical condition number and acceleration is genuinely data-dependent — the present paper's orthogonal-gradient non-acceleration result generalizes their κ = κ̃ example beyond quadratics; and variance reduction (SVRG, SAGA, Katyusha), which buys accelerated √(nκ) rates without assuming SGC, at the cost of full-gradient anchors. Yin et al.'s gradient diversity and Sankararaman et al.'s gradient confusion are the two closest correlation measures; RACOGA is essentially the inverse of gradient diversity minus one, but arises intrinsically rather than being posited, and is much weaker than gradient confusion, which demands a uniform floor on every pair.

The obvious follow-up is to localize the condition. The global infimum over ℝ^d is the paper's weakest link and their own experiments already abandon it; a trajectory-restricted or high-probability RACOGA — combined with an online estimator of Σ_{i<j}⟨∇f_i,∇f_j⟩ from the minibatch (which costs nothing extra, since Proposition 1 recovers it from ‖∇̃_K‖² and the per-sample norms) — would give an adaptive step-size rule λ_n rather than a hand-tuned λ, with a self-bounding argument to close the loop. Extending Propositions 1–2 (which never use convexity) to the PL setting is the natural second step, and relating c to the off-diagonal mass of the NTK Gram matrix would explain why their CIFAR-10 runs show high RACOGA even for uncorrelated inputs.

On IR: this is optimization theory with no real retrieval content, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one.
