Downstream, Toy Models of Superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) and the sparse-autoencoder work (Bricken et al. 2023; Templeton et al. 2024) replace the neuron basis with an overcomplete dictionary of directions. A natural follow-up: port preconditioning and the Gram-diversity term to SAE features rather than neurons, and use intra-feature diversity as a monosemanticity diagnostic — a dictionary feature whose diverse optima remain mutually similar is genuinely atomic, while one that splits is still a mixture — validated against the Geirhos-style sanity check that the synthesized input's causal path overlaps the natural-input path.

The IR connection is real and structural rather than decorative. Unregularized optimization of an input to maximize a dense retriever's similarity to a query embedding is exactly adversarial corpus poisoning (Zhong et al., 2023): gibberish passages that outrank real documents, the text analogue of the high-frequency noise here, with fluency priors playing the role of the regularization spectrum. And the article's central open question — whether the coordinate basis of an activation space is privileged — is precisely the question for learned bi-encoder embedding spaces and for the token vocabulary of a generative retriever's docids.

Proof sketch. None — this is a methods-and-phenomenology article with no theoretical result to sketch.

title: Spectral Concentration at the Edge of Stability: Information Geometry of Kernel Associative Memory
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-23

Spectral Concentration at the Edge of Stability: Information Geometry of Kernel Associative Memory

Akira Tamamori (2025) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.23083

Main idea. This is a four-page IEICE letter continuing the author's own line of work on kernel-logistic-regression (KLR) Hopfield networks, where each neuron's state probability is modeled as p(ξ_μ; α) = σ(Σ_ν α_ν K(ξ_μ, ξ_ν)) and the learned dual variables sculpt attractor basins far past the Gardner capacity. Earlier papers identified, purely phenomenologically, a "Ridge of Optimization" in the (γ, P/N) hyperparameter plane where recall is maximally robust, accompanied by a sharply hierarchical weight spectrum ("Spectral Concentration") and an odd antagonism between two force components. This letter asks why and answers by treating the network as a statistical manifold with the Fisher–Rao metric. The FIM has the clean closed form G(α) = K D(α) K with D_μμ = p_μ(1−p_μ), which makes the geometry computable rather than notional. Three numerical claims follow: on the Ridge the FIM spectrum is "L-shaped" — one dominant eigenvalue, then a drop of orders of magnitude, but a non-zero flat tail — collapsing the participation-ratio dimension d_eff = (Σλ_k)²/Σλ_k² from ≈P to 1.5–5; λ_max(G) is locally maximized exactly on the Ridge and collapses below 10⁻⁶ just past it, where sigmoid saturation kills the Fisher information; and the Euclidean gradient norm diverges on the Ridge while the natural-gradient norm ∇Lᵀ G⁻¹ ∇L is simultaneously minimized. The author reads this last pair as "Dual Equilibrium": instability in parameter space, equilibrium in the intrinsic geometry, with the λ₁⁻¹ scaling of the natural-gradient step acting as a self-braking mechanism.

Critique. The framing is genuinely nice, and two things deserve credit. First, insisting that the Ridge is not rank-1 collapse — the tail must stay non-zero or pattern distinguishability dies — is a real and useful distinction that separates this from a generic low-rank/neural-collapse story. Second, d_eff is a cheap diagnostic that anyone could adopt. But the paper's headline claims outrun what is shown. The abstract says the Ridge is where "the FIM becomes singular"; the body says the opposite, that λ_max is maximal there and the tail is preserved, while singularity characterizes the saturated regime beyond the Ridge. That is not a wording slip, it is the central object of the paper described two incompatible ways.

More seriously, "Dual Equilibrium" is at risk of being arithmetic. If ∇L concentrates in the top eigendirection — which is exactly what Eq. (6) asserts — then ∇Lᵀ G⁻¹ ∇L ≈ ‖∇L‖²/λ₁, so a bright band in ‖∇L‖² and a dark band in the G⁻¹-norm are the same measurement divided by a large number. The paper offers no null model, no check that the natural-gradient norm dips more than λ₁ alone would predict, and no convergence evidence that the system is actually near an intrinsic stationary point. Relatedly, Eq. (6) derives amplification from G ≈ λ₁ v₁v₁ᵀ — a matrix that is singular, so G⁻¹∇L is ill-posed precisely under the approximation used to justify it. The tail that Section 3 insists on is what rescues invertibility, and the two sections are never reconciled.

The "Edge of Stability" invocation is also metaphorical, and the author half-admits this ("not as a new dynamical phase"). Cohen et al.'s EoS is a statement about the loss Hessian hovering at 2/η with non-monotone loss; here no Hessian is measured, no learning rate enters any figure, and no oscillation is shown. This is a missed opportunity rather than a fatal flaw: KLR is a convex GLM linear in α, so its loss Hessian equals KDK up to the regularizer — the FIM is the Hessian. The rigorous EoS test was available and free. Likewise, MDL is invoked without a single description length being computed (no NML, no ∫√det G volume term), and Self-Organized Criticality is claimed for a critical point that was located by sweeping hyperparameters on a phase diagram — the opposite of self-organization. No avalanche statistics, no power law. Finally, the experimental setup (kernel, N, P, patterns, learning rate, code) is absent, inherited by reference from arXiv:2511.13053, and "averaged over 5 trials" is the extent of the error analysis.

Broader context. Three threads meet here. Edge of Stability (Cohen et al., ICLR 2021) is the empirical finding that full-batch GD on neural nets drives the top Hessian eigenvalue up to ≈2/η and then hovers there — progressive sharpening followed by self-stabilization. Modern Hopfield networks (Ramsauer et al., 2020) showed that an energy with a log-sum-exp interaction yields exponential capacity and a one-step update that is literally softmax attention, making associative memory and transformer retrieval the same object; KLR Hopfield is a learned, kernelized cousin in which the Gram matrix plays the key–query role. Information geometry (Amari) supplies the Fisher–Rao metric and natural gradient; Karakida et al.'s work on the pathological FIM spectrum of deep nets — a few outlier eigenvalues dominating an otherwise tiny bulk — is the closest existing result, and this letter is essentially the claim that KLR exploits that pathology rather than suffering it.

The obvious follow-up is the one the convexity hands you: since G is the exact Hessian, measure ηλ_max across the phase diagram and test whether the Ridge is literally the 2/η locus. That is decisive in both directions — if the Ridge moves when η changes, the EoS reading is vindicated; if it does not move, the EoS framing is simply wrong and the Ridge is a property of the loss landscape, not the optimizer. A second, cheaper follow-up: replace the rhetorical MDL with the actual Fisher-volume term ½ log det G in the stochastic complexity, which is computable here and makes "geometric Occam's razor" falsifiable — the small-but-nonzero tail contributes most of log det G, so the claimed ridge/collapse distinction should show up as a sharp change in that scalar.

For IR, the connection is real but should be taken as suggestive. Via the Hopfield–attention equivalence, KDK is the Fisher metric of a retrieval model over stored keys, and d_eff measures how many directions of the similarity structure carry usable information — the same quantity that controls when low-rank or ANN approximations of attention and of IVF/HNSW/PQ indices are safe. The paper's claim inverts the familiar dense-retrieval anisotropy intuition in an interesting way: where whitening and "all-but-the-top" argue that a dominant embedding direction hurts discrimination, here a dominant Fisher direction plus a preserved tail is what makes retrieval robust. The objects differ (Fisher metric vs. embedding covariance), so this is a question worth asking rather than an answer, but the question is well posed: is there a measurable "L-shaped" optimum for the spectrum of the query–document interaction in a trained retriever, and does generative retrieval's docid decoding sit at an analogous margin-vs-distinguishability boundary?

Proof sketch — or rather, its absence. There are no theorems, lemmas, or propositions in this paper. The three central claims are explicitly labeled "Observation 1/2/3" and are read off heatmaps. What the "theory" amounts to is: (i) an exact analytic identification of the FIM for the KLR model, G = KDK — a one-line computation from the logistic score function, since ∂log p/∂α_μ is linear in the kernel row and the expectation over the Bernoulli output gives the p(1−p) variance factor; (ii) a definition, d_eff as the participation ratio of the FIM spectrum; and (iii) a single approximate derivation, Eq. (6), which assumes the on-Ridge spectrum is dominated by one mode, writes G ≈ λ₁v₁v₁ᵀ, and substitutes into the natural-gradient identity ∇L = G·∇̃L to obtain ∇L ≈ λ₁(v₁ᵀ∇̃L)v₁. That is the whole mechanism: curvature amplifies a small intrinsic mismatch into a large Euclidean gradient, which retroactively explains the previously observed force antagonism F_d ≈ −F_i as the Euclidean gradient being nearly stationary while the intrinsic one is not yet zero. It is a plausible and even elegant reading, but it is an interpretation of prior numerics, not a guarantee — nothing here bounds d_eff, locates the Ridge, or proves that maximal λ_max implies optimal recall. Read it as a well-posed hypothesis with a clean computable metric attached, and as a paper whose best experiment is the one it did not run.

title: Understanding Deep Learning via Notions of Rank
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-23

Understanding Deep Learning via Notions of Rank

Noam Razin (PhD thesis, Tel Aviv University, advisor Nadav Cohen), 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02111

Main idea. The thesis argues that rank, in its various guises, is the right currency for a theory of deep learning, and it buys that argument with the now-standard correspondence between networks with polynomial nonlinearity and tensor factorizations: linear networks ↔ matrix factorization, shallow product-pooling convnets ↔ CP factorization, deep product-pooling convnets ↔ hierarchical Tucker, and (new in Chapter 5) message-passing GNNs with Hadamard aggregation ↔ tree-structured tensor networks. Part II attacks generalization. Chapter 1 kills the hope, articulated by Gunasekar et al., that the implicit bias of gradient descent on matrix factorization is norm minimization: there are 2×2 matrix completion problems where fitting the data drives every norm and quasi-norm to infinity while rank is essentially minimized. Chapters 2 and 3 then take "rank, not norm" seriously and show that the incremental-learning dynamics known for singular values carry over verbatim to CP component norms and to the local component norms of a hierarchical factorization, yielding bias toward low tensor rank and low hierarchical tensor rank respectively. Because hierarchical tensor rank equals separation rank across input regions, that bias is literally a bias toward locality, which reframes convnets' failure on long-range tasks as an optimization pathology rather than a purely architectural one — and yields an explicit regularizer that measurably fixes ResNet18/34 on synthetic long-range tasks. Part III turns the same tensor-network machinery on expressiveness: the separation rank a depth-L, width-D_h GNN can achieve across a vertex partition (I, Iᶜ) is governed, in log scale, by the partition's walk index — the number of length-(L−1) walks emanating from the partition boundary — with matching upper and lower bounds. The corollary is Walk Index Sparsification, a greedy edge-pruning rule that beats spectral sparsification and learned baselines on Cora/DBLP/OGBN-ArXiv.

Critique. The Chapter 1 result is the strongest thing here: it is a genuine falsification, it disqualifies all norms with a single fixed instance rather than one instance per norm, and it is robust to perturbing the observed values and repositioning the unobserved entry. But one should be clear about what is being traded. On the solution set, the true rank is 2 everywhere; "rank is minimized" holds only for effective rank and distance to the infimal-rank set, and only in the limit where the predictor itself diverges. A skeptic can say the construction shows norms fail on a problem where the rank-minimizing "solution" does not exist, and that the positive-determinant condition holds with probability exactly 0.5 — so the other half of initializations presumably behave as Gunasekar et al. hoped. Chapter 2's headline theorem is weaker than its framing suggests: it guarantees that the trajectory shadows a rank-one trajectory for arbitrary but fixed time T and radius B, at the price of initialization scale εB⁻¹exp(−O(B²T)) — doubly punishing, and the order of quantifiers means it is not a statement about the limit point. It also needs Huber loss with transition point below every observation, which exists purely so that ∇L is locally constant near the origin, plus exactly zero unbalancedness and a "leading component" assumption that arguably encodes the rank-one conclusion into the initialization. Chapter 3 is honest that the exact hierarchical-rank-minimization proof is not completed — it hinges on an alignment inequality assumed to persist along the trajectory — and Chapter 5's lower bound matches the upper bound only up to replacing the full boundary by a coverable "admissible subset", so tightness is graph-dependent. Throughout, polynomial nonlinearity plus gradient flow plus balanced initialization does the load-bearing work, with ReLU transfer argued empirically. The most intellectually interesting side-remark, underdeveloped, is §3.4.4: hierarchical tensor rank is a partially ordered complexity measure with multiple incomparable minimal fitting solutions, which quietly suggests the whole "gradient descent minimizes some scalar complexity" program is mis-specified.

Proof sketch. Theorem 1 (Ch. 1) is a conservation-law argument, not a construction. Observing y₁₂=y₂₁=1, y₂₂=0 leaves the solution set S = {[[w,1],[1,0]]}; the weakened triangle inequality lower-bounds any (quasi-)norm by |w| up to constants, while effective rank decreases monotonically to 1 and distance to the rank-1 set to 0 as |w|→∞ — so norm minimization and rank minimization are in direct opposition on S. The dynamical half uses the singular-value ODEs of Arora et al. for balanced deep linear networks to show that sign(det W(t)) is invariant under gradient flow. If det > 0 at initialization it stays positive; but det = w₁₁w₂₂ − w₁₂w₂₁ with w₁₂, w₂₁ → 1 and w₂₂ → 0 forces |w₁₁| ≳ 1/√L(t). Every norm therefore diverges at rate 1/√loss while both rank surrogates converge at rate √loss. The probability-0.5 claim follows by a symmetry trick: negating a row leaves the (entrywise symmetric, continuous) initialization distribution invariant and flips the determinant's sign. Chapter 2's engine is a Noether-style invariant: ‖wᵣⁿ(t)‖² − ‖wᵣⁿ̄(t)‖² is constant, so under balancedness d/dt‖⊗ₙwᵣⁿ‖ = N·γᵣ(t)·‖⊗ₙwᵣⁿ‖^{2−2/N}, with γᵣ the projection of −∇L onto the normalized component. The exponent exceeding 1 is the whole story — small components crawl, large ones accelerate — and the theorem converts it into rank-one shadowing by noting that all non-leading components remain O(αᴺ) at the moment the leading one reaches a small reference sphere, after which local smoothness (Grönwall) keeps the trajectory ε-close to a bona fide one-component flow. Chapter 5 is a different genre: the upper bound represents the GNN as a tree tensor network and bounds separation rank by a minimal cut weight separating I-leaves from Iᶜ-leaves, then exhibits a cheap cut whose weight is log(D_h)·(4ρ_{L−1}(C_I,V)+1); the lower bound evaluates the network on a grid of template vectors, matricizes the resulting grid tensor along I, and shows rank(B(f)) ≤ sep(f; I) with the matricization generically full-rank.

Context and a follow-up. This sits in the implicit-bias line running from Gunasekar et al. (2017) through Arora et al.'s deep matrix factorization (2019) and Li–Luo–Lyu's greedy low-rank learning (2021), and connects to saddle-to-saddle dynamics and to why LoRA-style low-rank adaptation works at all; the separation-rank thread descends from Cohen–Shashua's expressive-efficiency work and Levine et al.'s depth/width analyses of self-attention. A natural follow-up: redo the Chapter 5 min-cut analysis for attention over a learned graph, where walk index is not fixed but is itself a function of the weights — that is the missing bridge between this framework and transformers.

For IR the non-forced connection is separation rank, and it is a good one. A bi-encoder score s(q,d) = ⟨E(q), E(d)⟩ is by definition a function of separation rank ≤ dim with respect to the (query, document) partition; a cross-encoder has no such bound. So "what embedding dimension does dense retrieval need to match a cross-encoder" is literally a separation-rank lower-bound question, of the kind the thesis answers by grid-tensor matricization — the same technique behind the dimension lower bounds in Luan et al.'s "Sparse, Dense, and Attentional Representations for Text Retrieval". Separately, Chapters 1–2 are about matrix and tensor completion, which is collaborative filtering; the message that unconstrained gradient-trained MF self-regularizes toward rank, not nuclear norm, and can do so while all norms blow up, is directly relevant to why overparameterized recommender factorizations generalize. The generative-retrieval link is weaker and I would not force it.

title: Same Pre-training Loss, Better Downstream: Implicit Bias Matters for Language Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-22

Same Pre-training Loss, Better Downstream: Implicit Bias Matters for Language Models

Main idea

The operational convention in language modeling is that validation pre-training loss is a sufficient statistic for model quality: you tune architectures, data, and efficiency tricks against perplexity because perplexity tracks downstream accuracy. This paper attacks that convention at its sharpest point — the saturation regime, where a model has essentially attained the Bayes loss, i.e. the conditional entropy $\frac1T\sum_t H(x_t \mid x_{-t})$ of the true generative process. In that regime the loss is, by construction, uninformative: every model in the set is predicting the exact same conditional distribution. The question is whether all such models are downstream-equivalent, and the answer is a clear no. Since the loss and the architecture family are held fixed, whatever differentiates them must be the implicit bias of the optimizer — which point on the manifold of loss-minimizers the algorithm happened to select.

To make the saturation regime reachable, the authors abandon real corpora for three synthetic sources where the true conditional probability is computable in closed form: a random PCFG in Chomsky normal form (inside algorithm), a block-diagonal HMM (Viterbi), and text sampled autoregressively from OPT-125M restricted to its top-2000 tokens. Knowing the true conditionals lets them measure loss as KL to the truth rather than raw cross-entropy, which kills the variance that would otherwise swamp differences, and lets them generate unbounded data so there is no train/test gap at all. Downstream tasks are non-terminal-symbol classification at various span lengths (PCFG), latent-state classification (HMM), and QNLI/SST-2 (OPT).

Three mechanisms produce equal-loss, unequal-downstream pairs. First, time: after the pre-training loss has visibly converged, later checkpoints keep improving downstream. Second, the algorithm: they pre-train with an added adversarial meta-learning term (fit a linear head on a downstream split, then update the encoder to maximize that head's validation loss), which costs essentially nothing in pre-training loss (3.206 vs 3.204) but drops task A by 6.8 points and task B by 6.9. The degenerate limit of this is the look-up table: a model whose representation at each position is the true conditional probability vector. It has literally optimal pre-training loss, is expressible by a large enough transformer, and is the worst performer of all — 71.2% on task A versus 89.9% for AdamW. That single number is the paper's sharpest blow, because it falsifies the "natural assumption" of Saunshi–Malladi–Arora directly: linear probing a naturally-trained transformer beats linear probing the ground-truth conditional probabilities. Third, model size: at matched loss, bigger is better (+6.9 / +4.5 / +2.0 points linear probe on PCFG / HMM / OPT). The size case is reinterpreted as implicit bias via an embedding argument — a small transformer can be functionally embedded into a large one by weight replication plus zero-padded residual blocks, so the small solution was available inside the large architecture and the optimizer declined it.

The proposed explanatory quantity is flatness, measured concretely as $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L(\theta)]$, the trace of the Hessian of the population pre-training loss — not SAM-style worst-case ascent, not largest eigenvalue, not a PAC-Bayes perturbation bound. In the saturation regime this trace coincides with the trace of the Fisher information, which yields a cheap unbiased estimator: sample $(t, x_{-t})$ from the data, sample $x_t$ from the model's own predictive distribution, and average $|\nabla_\theta \log [f_\theta(x_{-t})]_{x_t}|_2^2$. Tr(H) falls monotonically along the flat part of the training curve as downstream accuracy rises (PCFG: 22.8 → 7.8), is 2.4× larger for the adversarially trained model than for AdamW at identical loss (19.34 vs 8.01), and decreases monotonically with model size once the models are re-embedded into a common large architecture.

Critique

The phenomenon is convincingly demonstrated and the mechanism is not. Those are two very different levels of evidential support, and the paper's framing blurs them.

Start with the setting. The entire construction lives in the saturation regime, defined by the model attaining the Bayes loss of a known, low-entropy, synthetic generator. Real LMs are nowhere near the entropy of natural language and, on current evidence, will not be; they live in a regime where loss differences are real and large. The authors say this honestly in the conclusion, but it undercuts the headline more than they let on: the claim "pre-training loss cannot fully explain downstream performance" is proved only in a regime that real pre-training does not enter, and the practical claim people care about — that two models at 2.1 nats on the Pile can differ substantially downstream — is not what these experiments test. Separately, the linear-probe protocol concatenates all token representations and applies a random Gaussian projection to 512 dims; the lookup table's "representation" is a 200-dim probability vector per position while a 730M transformer's is 1536-dim, so the headline lookup-table-vs-transformer comparison is not purely a comparison of feature quality at fixed probe capacity. They check that the projection does not change results, but the check is reported in one sentence.

The flatness–downstream link is correlational in exactly the way that is hardest to defend. Across checkpoints, Tr(H) decreases with training time and accuracy increases with training time; training time is a common cause and there is no attempt to break it. Across model sizes, both quantities are monotone in size. The one quasi-intervention is the adversarial run, but that objective explicitly targets downstream loss, so an accompanying rise in Tr(H) is as plausibly a side effect as a cause. The decisive experiment — add an explicit $\lambda\,\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L]$ penalty (the estimator is already cheap and unbiased, or use SAM), hold pre-training loss fixed, and show downstream moves — is never run. Nor is the converse: find two models with the same Tr(H) and different downstream performance, which would bound how much of the variance flatness actually explains. A single scalar summarizing a $d\times d$ Hessian is a weak invariant, and nothing here rules out that flatness is a correlate of some richer property (effective rank of the representation, feature reuse, degree of neuron-level cancellation — which is, tellingly, what the synthetic proof actually characterizes).

Then there is the well-known problem that Tr(H) is not reparameterization-invariant. For ReLU networks the rescaling $(\alpha W_1, \alpha^{-1} W_2)$ leaves the function untouched and moves the Hessian spectrum arbitrarily (Dinh et al., 2017). Here the Bartlett identity makes $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L] = \mathrm{Tr}[\mathcal{I}(\theta)]$, which is an improvement in interpretation but not in invariance: it is still the trace under a particular coordinate system, not a geometric quantity. This matters most precisely where the paper leans hardest — the model-size comparison is a comparison of the Hessian traces of chosen embeddings of small models into a large architecture, and the appendix concedes that layer-norm means the replication trick preserves the trace only "with respect to most parameters." A different functionally-equivalent embedding could give a different number.

Finally, the theory is considerably weaker than the empirical narrative suggests, and the two theorems do not meet. Theorem 4.3 is a statement about plain SGD, batch size 1, infinitesimal learning rate, initialized on the minimizer manifold, tracking a limiting flow on an $\eta^{-2}$ timescale — while almost all the experiments use AdamW at batch size 4096. Adam's noise covariance is preconditioned and its implicit bias is provably not the same object; the clean $\Sigma = \nabla^2 L$ identity that makes the whole argument work is specific to vanilla SGD on an MLE loss. Theorem 6.1, meanwhile, is not about an algorithm at all: it characterizes the exact argmin of Tr(H) subject to zero loss in a hand-designed single-layer transformer on a two-symbol language with an encoding under which the downstream target is literally linear in the summed token encodings. There is no theorem saying SGD finds that point, no theorem connecting flatness to transfer beyond that construction, and the "cheating" alternative it is compared against needs $\tilde O(2^T T^3 \epsilon^{-2})$ random neurons to reach loss $\epsilon$ — so the comparison is between an exact solution and a wildly overparameterized approximate one. The paper says as much ("first-cut"), which is the right register, but the abstract's "we prove that SGD ... implicitly prefers flatter minima in language models" invites a stronger reading than the result supports.

With four years of hindsight: the phenomenon claim has aged extremely well and the mechanism claim has not. "Equal loss, unequal downstream" is now close to conventional wisdom — data mixture, tokenizer, curriculum, and architectural inductive bias all move downstream metrics at matched validation loss, and the loss-to-loss transfer literature found that loss→loss maps across corpora are remarkably robust while loss→downstream-metric maps are task-specific and often non-monotone. Flatness as the explanation, however, did not take. The broader flat-minima literature took a hard skeptical turn (Andriushchenko et al.'s systematic finding that sharpness measures correlate poorly with generalization once confounders like training time and scale are controlled — precisely the confounders uncontrolled here), and explicit sharpness regularization in LM pre-training has produced mixed, setup-dependent gains. The paper's lasting contribution is the experimental protocol — construct a synthetic language with computable Bayes risk, saturate it, and then vary one factor at a time — which is a genuinely good instrument and is underused.

Proof sketch

(a) What is proved. Two things, in disjoint settings.

Theorem 4.3 (implicit bias of SGD toward flat minima in LM). Assume the population MLM loss is $C^3$ and — this is the non-trivial regularity condition, inherited from Fehrman–Gess–Jentzen and Li–Wang–Arora — that the set of global minimizers $\Gamma$ is a $(d{-}M)$-dimensional $C^2$ submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$ on which $\mathrm{rank}\,\nabla^2 L(\theta) = M$ everywhere. Run online SGD with fresh samples, learning rate $\eta$, batch size 1, started at a global minimizer. Define the Riemannian gradient flow on the manifold $d\hat\theta(t) = -\tfrac14 \nabla_\Gamma \mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L(\hat\theta(t))]\,dt$, where $\nabla_\Gamma$ projects onto the tangent space — i.e. projected gradient descent on $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L]$ with feasible set $\Gamma$. Then $\theta^\eta_{\lfloor K/\eta^2\rfloor} \to \hat\theta(K)$ in distribution as $\eta \to 0$. For batch size $B$ the constant becomes $1/(4B)$. Read carefully: this is a weak-convergence statement on a slow $\eta^{-2}$ timescale, it is local, it says nothing about reaching $\Gamma$ in the first place, and the "flatness" is the Hessian trace in the ambient parameterization.

The crucial structural fact — and the paper's real conceptual contribution at this point — is that in language modeling the mini-batch noise does not vanish at the optimum. In supervised interpolation, cross-entropy and the gradient covariance both go to zero at a global min, so this whole line of work had to inject artificial label noise to have any dynamics left (Blanc et al.; Damian–Ma–Lee). Here the Bayes loss is the conditional entropy, which is strictly positive, so the stochastic gradient keeps fluctuating forever and the iterate keeps drifting along $\Gamma$. The result is therefore cleaner than the supervised analogue, not just an adaptation of it.

Theorem 6.1 (flattest ⇒ transferable, synthetic Dyck). The language is balanced-bracket strings over ${\langle,\rangle}$ of even length $T \ge 6$, uniformly sampled, with one position masked. Tokens are encoded in $d = 2T$ dimensions: position $t$ maps to $\pm e_t$ with the sign carrying the bracket type, and a masked position maps to $v \sim \mathrm{Unif}{\pm e_{t+T}}$. The target $g^_(x) = #\rangle - #\langle$ satisfies $g^_(x) = -\langle \mathbf{1}_T, [\sum_t x_t]_{1:T}\rangle$ — linear in the summed encoding. The model is one softmax-attention layer plus a ReLU MLP, squared loss. The downstream distribution is i.i.d. uniform brackets — not necessarily balanced, so this is an extrapolation test off the pre-training support. Claim: let $(\hat\psi, \hat u)$ minimize $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2_\psi L] + \mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2_u L]$ subject to $L = 0$, and let $\tilde u$ be the minimum-norm interpolator of $n$ downstream samples on top of the frozen $\hat\psi$. Then with probability $\ge 1 - 2^{-n}$, the population downstream loss is exactly zero. (The $2^{-n}$ is simply the probability that all $n$ draws share a label — so the sample complexity is $O(1)$.) A contrast theorem supplies the other side: with $m \ge \tilde O(2^T T^3 \epsilon^{-2})$ i.i.d. Gaussian value neurons there exists a random-feature solution with pre-training loss $\le \epsilon$ that memorizes the conditional and carries no transferable feature. So the near-minimizer set genuinely contains both kinds of solution, and flatness is what separates them.

(b) How it is proved.

Theorem 4.3 is a one-lemma reduction to existing machinery. The lemma is Lemma 4.2, the (second) Bartlett identity: at any $\theta \in \Gamma$, the stochastic-gradient covariance equals the Hessian, $\Sigma(\theta) = \nabla^2 L(\theta)$, and both equal the Fisher information. The proof is three lines and turns entirely on well-specification: at $\theta \in \Gamma$ the model output equals the true conditional, so the expectation over $x_t \mid x_{-t}$ is an expectation under the model, and $\mathbb{E}_{x_t}[\nabla^2_\theta [f_\theta]_{x_t} / [f_\theta]_{x_t}] = \nabla^2_\theta \sum_{x_t} [f_\theta]_{x_t} = \nabla^2_\theta 1 = 0$. The Hessian-of-log and outer-product-of-score terms therefore coincide, and the mean gradient vanishes because $\theta$ is a minimizer. This is exactly the step that fails off the manifold, and exactly the step that is free in language modeling and unavailable in supervised classification.

With $\Sigma = \nabla^2 L$ in hand they invoke Corollary 5.2 of Li–Wang–Arora (2021) verbatim. That framework does the analytic work: near a manifold of minimizers, SGD decomposes into a fast component attracted to $\Gamma$ and a slow component that, after time-rescaling by $\eta^{-2}$, is described by a stochastic-modified-equation argument whose drift is the Riemannian gradient of a noise-shape-dependent functional. Substituting $\Sigma = \nabla^2 L$ collapses it to $\tfrac14 \mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L]$. That is the whole argument — the novelty is the identity and the observation that LM noise survives at the optimum, not the SDE analysis, which is imported. It is worth being explicit that this is the Blanc/Damian/Li–Wang–Arora "label-noise ⇒ trace-of-Hessian regularizer" program, with the artificial label noise replaced by the genuine, irreducible aleatoric noise of next/masked-token prediction.

Theorem 6.1 is an entirely different and more hands-on argument: an explicit variational characterization of the flattest zero-loss point. The chain has four links.

Step 1 — flatness becomes an expected squared gradient norm. If $L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[(f_\theta(x) - y)^2] = 0$ then the residual vanishes a.s., killing the $\ell'\cdot\nabla^2 f$ term, and $\ell'' = 2$ is constant, so $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2_\theta L] = \mathbb{E}|\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)|_2^2$. Flatness is thereby converted from a second-order object into a first-order, data-dependent Jacobian norm — the same reduction that underlies the "flatness = smoothness of the learned function" intuition, here made exact.

Step 2 — lower-bound that norm and read off the equality conditions. Lemma D.1 shows the flatness is $\ge \sqrt{4/T}$ via a short chain: drop the $Q,K$ gradients (equality iff attention is uniform), then AM–GM, then $\ge 2\mathbb{E}[|h|\,|f|]$, then $|h| \ge 1/\sqrt T$ because the encodings are orthonormal and attention weights sum to one. The three equality conditions are the substance: (i) $V_i^\top h = |u_i||h|$ for every active neuron (a balancedness/alignment condition); (ii) no cancellation between simultaneously activated neurons, $V_i^\top x \cdot V_{i'}^\top x \le 0$ for opposite-sign output coefficients; (iii) uniform attention, i.e. the attention layer must literally average the token encodings into $z = \sum_t x_t$. Condition (ii) is the paper's real mechanistic claim: flatness penalizes solutions that compute the answer as a difference of large opposing activations. The random-feature memorizer does exactly that — many Gaussian neurons fire at once with mixed-sign output coefficients — and pays for it quadratically.

Step 3 — the equality conditions force the transferable feature. Each neuron activates on only one label class and no nonzero neuron is dead (using the $\pm$ symmetry of the bracket distribution). Lemma D.3, the technical core, then argues case-by-case over perturbations flipping the masked token, and over inputs masked at different positions, that the content block of each value vector must be $V_i^{(c)} = c\mathbf{1}$ for a common $c > 0$. The rigidity comes from Lemma D.5: the $(2k{+}1)\times(2k{+}1)$ circulant $\pm 1$ matrix built from the pattern $[\underbrace{1\ldots1}_{k+1}\underbrace{-1\ldots-1}_{k}]$ has full rank, since $M_i + M_{\rho^{k+1}(i)} = 2e_i$ recovers the standard basis as row combinations. Full rank means a vector with constant inner product against all such sentences is forced to be a multiple of $\mathbf{1}$ — there is no room for a memorizing direction. So the flattest solution is, up to sign and scale, exactly the "count the brackets" feature.

Step 4 — transfer is then trivial. On downstream (unbalanced) inputs there is no mask block, so only $V^{(c)} = c\mathbf{1}$ acts; every neuron's pre-activation is a constant multiple of $g^_(x)$ restricted to its sign class. The min-norm interpolator reproduces $g^_$ exactly, so the population downstream loss is zero as soon as both labels have been observed.

The honest summary of the theory is: Theorem 4.3 says SGD performs projected gradient descent on the Fisher trace along the minimizer manifold, because in MLE at a well-specified optimum the noise covariance is the Hessian; Theorem 6.1 says in one worked example, the argmin of the Fisher trace on that manifold is the semantically correct feature, because flatness forbids cancellation between activated neurons. Nothing proves the composition.

Broader context

The convention this paper attacks comes out of the scaling-law literature. Kaplan et al. established smooth power laws in loss versus parameters, data, and compute; Hernandez et al. extended this to transfer; and the efficient-transformer benchmarking practice that followed compares architectures at matched compute by perplexity, on the implicit premise that loss is the only thing that matters. Theoretical accounts of why pre-training helps also took the loss-centric view: Saunshi–Malladi–Arora's "natural assumption" posits that downstream tasks are linear in the true conditional probabilities, Wei–Xie–Ma instantiate this for HMM-generated data, and Zhang–Hashimoto show MLM representations recover graphical-model latents. All of these treat the model as a black box realizing a conditional distribution — which is precisely why the lookup-table experiment is so pointed: if the natural assumption were the whole story, the model that outputs the exact conditionals would be the best representation, and it is empirically the worst.

The other tradition being joined is implicit regularization of SGD noise. Blanc–Gupta–Valiant–Valiant showed that label-noise SGD near a minimum behaves like an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process whose drift performs a hidden descent; Damian–Ma–Lee identified the hidden objective as $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L]$; Li–Wang–Arora built the general slow-SDE framework this paper plugs into; HaoChen–Wei–Lee–Ma ("Shape Matters") showed the shape of the noise covariance determines which regularizer you get. The flat-minima tradition itself runs from Hochreiter–Schmidhuber's MDL argument through Keskar et al.'s large-batch sharpness observations to SAM, with Dinh et al.'s reparameterization counterexample as the standing objection.

Two neighbours worth reading alongside. Saunshi et al., Understanding Contrastive Learning Requires Incorporating Inductive Biases, is the self-supervised twin: it exhibits contrastive-loss minimizers that are downstream-useless and argues that function-class and algorithmic bias, not the loss value, determine representation quality. Tay et al., Scale Efficiently, is the empirical twin at real scale: deep-narrow beats wide-shallow downstream at matched perplexity. The obvious follow-up the paper never runs is the causal one — take the unbiased Fisher-trace estimator, add it as an explicit penalty or use SAM, train two models to the same validation loss with and without it, and check whether downstream moves. A negative result there would be genuinely informative: it would say flatness is a marker, not the mechanism, and push attention toward whatever the no-cancellation condition is really proxying for — plausibly the effective rank or the degree of superposition in the representation.

The connection to your own work is real and not forced, and it is sharpest in two places. In dense retrieval, the InfoNCE objective has a vast set of near-minimizers and the held-out contrastive loss is exactly the kind of proxy metric this paper attacks: two encoders can match on in-domain contrastive loss and differ substantially on zero-shot BEIR, and — more to your point — differ in the geometry that determines whether they are searchable. Spectral decay and effective dimension of the embedding distribution control PQ/OPQ quantization error and HNSW graph navigability, and they are almost unconstrained by the loss value. Step 1 above gives you a directly usable object here: at low loss, $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L] \approx \mathbb{E}|\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)|^2$, an expected Jacobian norm, i.e. a smoothness prior on the encoder over the data distribution. A smooth encoder is precisely one whose metric neighborhoods are stable, which is the property ANN indices exploit and quantization destroys. A concrete experiment: take equal-loss checkpoints of a dense retriever, measure the Fisher trace, and correlate it against (i) zero-shot nDCG on held-out BEIR domains and (ii) recall@k degradation under PQ at fixed bitrate. If flatness predicts robustness-to-compression at matched loss, that is a new and practically useful invariant, and it is a cleaner causal setting than the paper's because you can intervene on the regularizer without touching the retrieval objective.

The generative-retrieval connection is, if anything, more direct: the lookup table is the DSI failure mode. A seq2seq model that maps documents to docids can achieve its training loss either by memorizing the docid↔document association or by learning a docid space with semantic structure, and only the second generalizes to unseen queries or to documents added after indexing. That is the same "memorize the conditional vs. learn the feature" dichotomy as Theorem 6.1's two configurations, and the Bartlett identity transports exactly, since GR training is MLE on a well-specified-at-optimum token distribution — so $\mathrm{Tr}[\nabla^2 L]$ is again the Fisher trace and the estimator is again cheap. One genuine caveat, which is also a research opening: GR models typically do interpolate their training set, so the paper's central premise — that mini-batch noise survives at the optimum because the Bayes loss is positive — fails, and you fall back to the supervised regime where you need injected label noise or explicit regularization to get the same drift. Characterizing which regime a given GR setup is in (does the docid prediction task have irreducible entropy under your docid construction?) is a well-posed theoretical question with a direct bearing on whether semantic docids or atomic docids should be expected to generalize, and it is the kind of question this paper's machinery is built to answer.

title: Limit Theorems for Stochastic Gradient Descent in High-Dimensional Single-Layer Networks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-22

Limit Theorems for Stochastic Gradient Descent in High-Dimensional Single-Layer Networks

Main idea

The object of study is online SGD on a single-index (single-layer teacher–student) model in dimension $N$: a hidden unit vector $x^_ \in S^{N-1}$, i.i.d. Gaussian covariates $a_k$, responses $y_k = f(\langle a_k, x^_ angle) + \epsilon_k$ with mean-zero noise of variance $C_\epsilon$, and the squared loss. Each sample is used exactly once, so the iterates form a Markov chain in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Tracking that chain is hopeless, but by rotational invariance the law of the loss and its gradients depends on $x$ only through two order parameters: the correlation $m = \langle x, x^* angle$ and the orthogonal radius $r_\perp^2 = |x|^2 - m^2$. The paper derives the $N o\infty$ limits of the interpolated pair $(m, r_\perp^2)$ — and, after rescaling, of $m$ alone — at step size $\delta_N = c_\delta/N$.

"Critical scaling" is the point of the whole exercise. Writing one SGD step and expanding a summary statistic $u$ to second order, the conditional drift per unit time $t = k\delta_N$ splits into a population drift $F = \langle abla\Phi, abla u angle$ (the gradient flow of the population loss $\Phi = \mathbb{E}L_N$) and an Itô-type corrector $G = \delta_N frac12\langle V, abla^2 u angle$, where $V = \mathbb{E}[ abla H \otimes abla H]$ is the covariance of the sample-wise gradient noise. Since $\mathrm{tr}\,V \asymp N$, the corrector is $\Theta(\delta_N N) = \Theta(c_\delta)$: it survives, at order one, exactly when $\delta_N \asymp 1/N$. Below that scale it vanishes and one recovers the pure DMFT/population gradient flow ("ballistic" limit); at $\delta_N = c_\delta/N$ the corrector is a genuine $O(1)$ extra term in the ODE, carrying all of the step-size dependence. Simultaneously the martingale part of the increment has per-unit-time covariance $\delta_N J_N V J_N^ op$, which for these two statistics is $O(1/N)$ — so the limit is still deterministic.

The consequence the paper exploits is that at the critical scale, deterministic limits are blind to recovery. Under the standing assumption that $f$ has information exponent $k \geq 2$ (Hermite coefficients $\alpha_1 = \cdots = \alpha_{k-1} = 0$, $\alpha_k eq 0$), the ODE for $m$ has $\dot m|_{m=0} = 0$, so from a random Gaussian start ($m \approx N^{-1/2} o 0$) the ballistic limit is $m \equiv 0$ forever, while $r_\perp^2$ runs an autonomous ODE $\dot{r}_\perp^2 = -4r_\perp^2\gamma(r_\perp) + 4c_\delta n(r_\perp)$ — a confining population term against a $c_\delta$-scaled "heating" term from the corrector. All the learning signal lives in the fluctuations, so the paper zooms in: set $ ilde m = \sqrt{N}m$, which multiplies the martingale covariance by $N$ and turns the $O(1/N)$ noise into $O(1)$ noise, while the drift, being odd in $m$, linearizes to $-2 ilde m\, heta(r_\perp)$ with $ heta = \gamma - \alpha_2 s$. The result is a time-inhomogeneous Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process for $ ilde m$ driven along the deterministic radius trajectory, and at a fixed point $r_\perp^*$ of the radius ODE, an honest OU process. The paper's clean finding is that the sign of $ heta(r_\perp^*)$ — attracting versus repelling equator — is decided by the information exponent: at $k \geq 3$ one has $\alpha_2 = 0$ and $ heta = \gamma(r_\perp^*) > 0$ always, so $m$ stays pinned at scale $N^{-1/2}$; at $k = 2$ the term $\alpha_2 s(r_\perp^*)$ competes with $\gamma$ and has no universal sign, so the equator can be repelling and weak recovery can start. For phase retrieval, $f(x) = x^2$, this is worked out in closed form.

Critique

Let me be blunt about provenance, because the paper is. Essentially all of the limit-theorem machinery is Ben Arous–Gheissari–Jagannath, High-dimensional limit theorems for SGD: effective dynamics and critical scaling (CPAM 2024). Their Theorem 2.3 — under $\delta_N$-localizability and asymptotic closability, the interpolated summary statistics converge to $du = (-F(u) + G(u))dt + \sqrt{\Sigma(u)}dB$ — is invoked verbatim twice, and is the only place tightness, the martingale problem, and the actual convergence argument live. Section 5 of this paper is a hypothesis check plus a Gaussian-integration-by-parts computation of $F$, $G$ and $\Sigma$ for one loss. The definitions of localizability and asymptotic closability are quoted; the information exponent is from BGJ 2021; the very phenomenon of a signal-to-noise-dependent drift sign at the equator is, as the author states explicitly, "the single-index analogue of the signal-to-noise dependent drift found for matrix PCA." So the honest framing is: a careful worked instantiation of BGJ's framework in the single-index/quadratic-loss case, not a new theory.

The abstract oversells on two counts. First, "at the critical scale a correction term emerges that changes the phase diagram" — the corrector $G$ is not new; it is precisely BGJ's critical-scaling term, and the fact that it is $O(1)$ at $\delta_N \asymp 1/N$ is the definition of their critical regime. Second, the Discussion repeatedly calls $G$ a "stochastic correction." It is not stochastic: it is a deterministic Itô/curvature term, $\delta_N frac12\langle V, abla^2 u angle$, which happens to originate from gradient noise. Calling a drift term stochastic and contrasting it with DMFT muddies what is actually a sharp and correct point.

What is genuinely new and worth keeping is smaller but real. (i) Remark 3.4 and the function $\Psi(r_\perp) = r_\perp^2\gamma(r_\perp)/n(r_\perp)$: a radius fixed point exists iff $c_\delta$ lies in the range of $\Psi$, hence a step-size threshold $c_\delta^{\mathrm{crit}} = \sup_{r_\perp} \Psi$ above which the corrector's heating beats the population confinement and $r_\perp^2$ blows up, with the two fixed points merging in a saddle-node bifurcation at the threshold. For phase retrieval this is explicit, $c_\delta^{\mathrm{crit}} = (\sqrt{5(8+3C_\epsilon)}-2)/(4(12+5C_\epsilon))$, $\approx 0.0901$ at zero noise. This is a clean, checkable statement that the population gradient flow alone (whose radius drift vanishes at $r_\perp^2 = 1/3$) cannot see at all. (ii) The identity substituting the radius fixed-point equation to eliminate $b(r_\perp^*)$, turning $\gamma(r_\perp^*)$ into a manifestly positive expression, $r_\perp^{*-2} ig(\mathbb{E}[f'^2](C_\epsilon + \mathrm{Var}f) + \mathbb{E}[f'^2(f-\alpha_0)^2] ig)$. That is a genuinely nice little argument — the positivity is not obvious from the definition $\gamma = a + b - \alpha_0 s$, and it is what makes Corollary 3.6 a theorem rather than a case check. (iii) The phase-retrieval conclusion that the equator becomes attracting — i.e. SGD fails on the diffusive timescale — precisely when $C_\epsilon > 4$ and $1/(12+C_\epsilon) < c_\delta \leq c_\delta^{\mathrm{crit}}$, with the two thresholds meeting at $C_\epsilon = 4$, $c_\delta^{\mathrm{crit}} = 1/16$. I verified the Hermite and Stein computations behind $\Psi$, $ heta(r_\perp) = 6(r_\perp^2 - 1)$, and the volatility; they are correct.

On rigor and completeness there are several real soft spots. The most substantive: the noise is assumed only to have $4+\delta$ moments, but localizability demands $\sup \mathbb{E}| abla H|^8 \leq C_K \delta_N^{-4}$, and $ abla H$ contains $2a f'(\langle a,x angle)\epsilon$, so this needs eighth moments of $\epsilon$. Worse, the proof of Lemma 5.1 silently drops the noise entirely, writing $H(x,a) = (f(\langle a,x angle) - f(a_1))^2 - \Phi(x)$ — the $\epsilon$ term is absent from the very displays where the moment bounds are verified, even though $\epsilon$ reappears in $V$ and drives the whole $C_\epsilon$-dependence of the results. That is a gap, not a typo. Relatedly, both moment checks saturate their bounds exactly with no slack, which is the honest signature of criticality but leaves nothing to absorb a heavier-tailed $\epsilon$.

Second, the uniformity required by asymptotic closability is deterministic and uniform over $x \in u_N^{-1}(E_K)$, but the Taylor remainders in the proof of Theorem 3.5 are controlled with $O_p(N^{-3/2})$ and $|a| = O_p(\sqrt N)$ — stochastic boundedness slotted into a deterministic uniform requirement. It is almost certainly fixable for polynomially-growing $f'$, but it is not done.

Third, Corollary 3.6 initializes at $\mathcal{N}(0, r_\perp^{*2}/N \cdot I_N)$ — exactly at the radius fixed point, which itself depends on $c_\delta$ through $\Psi$. The generic case (start at $\sigma^2$, flow to $r_\perp^*$, $ ilde m$ a time-inhomogeneous Gaussian process throughout) is stated only inside Theorem 3.5 and never analyzed; nothing is said about whether the sign of $ heta(r_\perp(t))$ can flip along the transient, which in the phase-retrieval example it manifestly can, since $ heta(r_\perp) = 6(r_\perp^2 - 1)$ changes sign at $r_\perp = 1$ while $r_\perp^{*2}$ ranges over $[1/3, \cdot]$. Nor is anything proved about the unstable barrier or about the blow-up above $c_\delta^{\mathrm{crit}}$ beyond the fixed-point count.

Fourth, and most important for the paper's own narrative: the Discussion claims the two signs "match what is known about sample complexity" — repelling drift at $k=2$ lets $m$ grow from $O(N^{-1/2})$, hence $N\log N$ samples; attracting drift at $k \geq 3$ traps it, hence polynomially many. That is a correct heuristic and a genuinely satisfying reinterpretation of BGJ 2021, but it is not proved here. The SDE limit is valid only in the microscopic window $ ilde m = O(1)$; the exponential escape to $ ilde m \gg 1$ and the matching to the ballistic phase are exactly what a $\log N$ escape-time theorem would require, and there is no such matched-asymptotics argument. Finally the manuscript has visible typesetting errors and a convention clash: $\alpha_k$ is defined via normalized Hermite polynomials, but Theorem 3.5 sets $\alpha_2 = \mathbb{E}[f''(a_1)]$, which for $f = x^2$ gives $2$ rather than $\sqrt2$. Only $\alpha_2 = 0$ versus $ eq 0$ is used, so nothing breaks, but a careful reader will stumble.

Proof sketch

(a) What is proved. Three statements, all at $\delta_N = c_\delta/N$ with $f \in L^2(\gamma)$ twice differentiable a.e., $f', f''$ of polynomial growth, and information exponent at least two.

Theorem 3.2 (ballistic limit): the linearly interpolated pair $(m, r_\perp^2)$ is asymptotically closable and converges to a deterministic system $\dot m = -2\mathbb{E}[a_1 f'(a_1m + a_2r_\perp)(f(\cdot) - f(a_1))]$ and $\dot r_\perp^2 = -4r_\perp\mathbb{E}[a_2 f'(\cdot)(f(\cdot)-f(a_1))] + 4c_\delta \mathbb{E}[f'^2(\cdot)((f(\cdot)-f(a_1))^2 + C_\epsilon)]$. The last term is the corrector; it is the only place $c_\delta$ enters. Corollary 3.3 specializes to Gaussian initialization: then $m \equiv 0$ for all time (because $\dot m|_{m=0} = 2\alpha_1\mathbb{E}[f'(a_2r_\perp)]$ and $\alpha_1 = 0$), and $r_\perp^2$ solves the scalar ODE with $\gamma = a + b - \alpha_0 s$ and $n > 0$ built from the Gaussian functionals $a = \mathbb{E}f'^2$, $b = \mathbb{E}ff''$, $s = \mathbb{E}f''$, $t = \mathbb{E}f'^2f$, $q = \mathbb{E}f'^2f^2$. Remark 3.4 then reads off the step-size phase diagram from $\Psi = r_\perp^2\gamma/n$.

Theorem 3.5 (critical/diffusive limit): with $ ilde m = \sqrt N m$, $( ilde m, r_\perp^2)$ converges to the degenerate system $d ilde m = -2 ilde m(\gamma(r_\perp) - \alpha_2 s(r_\perp))dt + 2\sqrt{c_\delta(q - 2(\alpha_0+\alpha_2)t + a\eta)}\,dB_t$, coupled to the unchanged deterministic radius ODE, with $\eta = |f|^2 + 2|f'|^2 + 2\langle f,f'' angle + C_\epsilon$. The limiting volatility matrix has only its $(1,1)$ entry nonzero — the rescaling of $m$ is what saves the noise, and the radius stays ballistic.

Corollary 3.6 (the dichotomy): if the information exponent is at least three, so $\alpha_2 = 0$, and one initializes at a fixed point $r_\perp^*$, then $ ilde m$ is a genuine mean-reverting OU with $\gamma(r_\perp^*) > 0$. Remark 3.7 says this fails at exponent exactly two, where $ heta = \gamma - \alpha_2 s$ has no universal sign, and §3.3 makes both signs occur inside a single model.

What the information exponent controls: it fixes the order of vanishing of the population drift at the equator $m=0$, hence which term survives the $\sqrt N$ zoom. $k \geq 2$ kills the ballistic drift entirely; $k = 2$ leaves an $\alpha_2$-dependent linear drift that can push outward, giving exponential escape from $N^{-1/2}$ in time $\log N$, i.e. the $N\log N$ sample threshold; $k \geq 3$ forces inward drift with stationary variance $O(1)$ in $ ilde m$, so $m$ stays $\Theta(N^{-1/2})$ on the $O(N)$-sample timescale, consistent with the $N^{k-1}$ complexity of BGJ 2021. (The escape/trapping timescales themselves are not proved.)

(b) How it is proved. The reduction is the classical Saad–Solla order-parameter move made rigorous. By rotational invariance one may set $x^_ = e_1$; then the joint law of $(\langle a,x angle, \langle a,x^_ angle)$ is $(a_1 m + a_2 r_\perp, a_1)$ for independent standard Gaussians, so $L_N$, $\Phi$, $H$ and $V$ depend on $x$ only through $(m, r_\perp^2)$ — Lemma 5.1. This closes the two-dimensional system. The statistics are chosen so that $ abla m = v$, $ abla r_\perp^2 = 2(x - mv)$, $ abla^2 m = 0$, $ abla^2 r_\perp^2 = 2(I - vv^ op)$, and all third derivatives vanish, which makes the Taylor expansion exact at second order and makes the localizability checks pure moment estimates.

The mechanism is the martingale decomposition of one SGD step. Writing $X_{k+1} = X_k - \delta_N abla L_N$ and expanding $u$, the conditional mean of the increment is $-\delta_N\langle abla\Phi, abla u angle + frac{\delta_N^2}{2}\langle V + abla\Phi\otimes abla\Phi, abla^2 u angle + O(\delta_N^3)$, and the remainder is a martingale difference with conditional covariance $\delta_N^2 J_N V J_N^ op$. Dividing by $\delta_N$ gives precisely the two operators in BGJ's Definition 2.3: drift per unit time $(-A_N + \delta_N \mathcal{L}_N)u$ with $A_N = \langle abla\Phi, abla angle$ and $\mathcal{L}_N = frac12\langle V, abla^2 angle$, and quadratic variation per unit time $\delta_N J_N V J_N^ op$. Localizability is exactly the set of moment bounds — $| abla^2 u|_{op} \lesssim \delta_N^{-1/2}$, $\mathbb{E}| abla H|^8 \lesssim \delta_N^{-4}$, $\mathbb{E}\langle abla H, abla u angle^4 \lesssim \delta_N^{-2}$, $\mathbb{E}\langle abla^2u, abla H\otimes abla H - V angle^2 = o(\delta_N^{-3})$ — that make the third-order Taylor remainder negligible, make the quadratic variation concentrate, and give tightness. Asymptotic closability is the requirement that drift and rescaled quadratic variation converge uniformly to locally Lipschitz functions of the summary statistics alone. Given those two conditions, BGJ's Theorem 2.3 identifies the limit as the unique solution of the martingale problem for the generator $\mathsf H\cdot abla + frac12\langle\Sigma, abla^2 angle$ — that is where generator convergence and tightness actually happen, and the present paper cites rather than reproves it.

So the paper's work is the computation. $F$ comes from $\partial_m\phi$ and $\partial_{r_\perp^2}\phi$. The corrector is where the dimension count bites: $\delta_N\mathcal{L}_N m = 0$ identically because $ abla^2 m = 0$, while $\delta_N \mathcal{L}_N r_\perp^2 = rac{c_\delta}{N}\sum_{i\geq2} \mathbb{E}[(\partial_i H)^2]$, a sum of $N-1$ terms each $\Theta(1)$, so the factor $N$ cancels $\delta_N$ and the corrector survives. Cross terms are $O_p(\sqrt N)$, hence killed by $\delta_N$.

For the volatility the same bookkeeping explains the $\sqrt N$ rescaling. In the unrescaled variables $J_N V J_N^ op$ has all entries $\Theta(1)$, so $\delta_N J_N V J_N^ op o 0$ and the limit is a pure ODE. Under $ ilde m = \sqrt N m$ the Jacobian rescaling multiplies the $(1,1)$ entry by $N$ and the off-diagonals by $\sqrt N$; only $(1,1)$ then survives multiplication by $\delta_N = c_\delta/N$. This degeneracy is the structural reason the limit is an OU in one variable driven by a deterministic radius rather than a genuinely two-dimensional diffusion.

The drift of $ ilde m$ is obtained by linearization at the equator: expand $f(a_1 m + a_2 r_\perp)$ in $m = ilde m/\sqrt N$ to second order, so $\phi( ilde m, r_\perp^2) = \phi(0,r_\perp^2) + rac{ ilde m^2}{N} ig(\mathbb{E}[f'^2] + \mathbb{E}[ff''] - \mathbb{E}[a_1^2 f(a_1)]\mathbb{E}[f''] ig) + O(N^{-3/2})$; differentiating and rescaling gives $F_{ ilde m} = 2 ilde m(\gamma - \alpha_2 s)$. Gaussian integration by parts (Stein) is the workhorse throughout — it converts $\mathbb{E}[a_1 g(a_1)] = \mathbb{E}[g'(a_1)]$ and $\mathbb{E}[a_1^2 f^2(a_1)] = \mathbb{E}[f^2 + 2f'^2 + 2ff'']$ (this is where $\eta$ comes from), turning raw two-dimensional Gaussian expectations into the five scalar functionals.

The key lemma is the positivity argument in Corollary 3.6. At a fixed point the radius ODE gives $r_\perp^{*2}\gamma(r_\perp^*) = c_\delta ig(a(C_\epsilon + |f|^2) + q - 2\alpha_0 t ig)$, which lets one eliminate $b(r_\perp^*)$ from $\gamma = a + b - \alpha_0 s$. Using $q - 2\alpha_0 t = \mathbb{E}[f'^2(f-\alpha_0)^2] - \alpha_0^2 a$ and $|f|^2 - \alpha_0^2 = \mathrm{Var}(f(a_1)) \geq 0$, one arrives at $\gamma(r_\perp^*) = r_\perp^{*-2} ig(\mathbb{E}[f'^2](C_\epsilon + \mathrm{Var}f) + \mathbb{E}[f'^2(f-\alpha_0)^2] ig) > 0$, a sum of manifestly nonnegative terms. Hence mean reversion whenever $\alpha_2 = 0$.

The phase-retrieval example instantiates everything in closed form: $f = x^2$ gives $\alpha_0 = 1$, $\alpha_2 = 2$, $a = 4r_\perp^2$, $b = 2r_\perp^4$, $s = 2$, $t = 12r_\perp^4$, $q = 60r_\perp^6$, so $\gamma = 2(3r_\perp^2-1)$ while $ heta = 6(r_\perp^2 - 1)$. With $u = r_\perp^2$, the radius ODE right-hand side is $4u(2 - 6u) + 4c_\delta(15u^2-6u+3+C_\epsilon)$, whose two positive roots are a stable point and an unstable barrier merging at $c_\delta^{\mathrm{crit}}$. The stable root decreases to the population value $1/3$ as $c_\delta \downarrow 0$, so $ heta o -4 < 0$: at small step size the equator is repelling, matching learnability of phase retrieval in $N\log N$ samples. Mean reversion — failure — requires the stable root $> 1$, which happens iff $C_\epsilon > 4$ and $1/(12+C_\epsilon) < c_\delta \leq c_\delta^{\mathrm{crit}}$.

Broader context

The background is a thirty-year arc. Saad and Solla (1995) observed that for teacher–student networks with Gaussian inputs, online gradient descent closes on a small set of order parameters — teacher–student overlaps and student–student overlaps — whose evolution in the large-$N$ limit is a self-contained ODE system. That is dynamical mean-field theory for learning, and the modern rigorous versions are Ben Arous–Gheissari–Jagannath, Goldt–Advani–Saxe–Krzakala–Zdeborová, Veiga et al. (phase diagrams for two-layer nets), and Collins-Woodfin–Paquette–Paquette–Seroussi ("homogenized SGD" for GLMs and multi-index models). The single-index model is the minimal nontrivial instance: one hidden direction, two order parameters, and already a nonconvex landscape.

The information exponent is BGJ 2021's organizing quantity. Expand the link function in Hermite polynomials; the index $k$ of the first nonzero coefficient measures how flat the population loss is at the "equator" $m = 0$. Because a random initialization has $|m_0| \asymp N^{-1/2}$, the population drift near the start is $\asymp m_0^{k-1}$, and balancing this against the $N^{-1/2}$-scale gradient noise yields the standard thresholds for weak recovery by online SGD: $\Theta(N)$ samples when $k = 1$, $\Theta(N\log N)$ when $k = 2$, and $\Theta(N^{k-1})$ when $k \geq 3$. The present paper's contribution to that picture is to show what it looks like from inside the diffusive window: the ballistic limit sees nothing, and the sign of the OU drift on the $\sqrt N$-rescaled overlap is the microscopic fingerprint of the $k=2$ / $k\geq3$ split.

Two closely related directions worth knowing. First, Damian–Pillaud-Vivien–Lee–Bruna, Smoothing the landscape boosts the signal for SGD, which shows that online SGD with a smoothed gradient improves the exponent from $N^{k-1}$ to roughly $N^{k/2}$ — i.e. the information exponent is an artifact of this particular algorithm, not of the statistical problem. Second, the generative exponent line (Damian–Lee–Montanari–Wein; Lee–Oko–Suzuki–Wibisono): the genuinely information-theoretic complexity of single-index estimation is governed by the information exponent of a transformed likelihood ratio, which is often strictly smaller than $k$, so SGD on squared loss is provably suboptimal in general. Read against those, this paper is best seen as a fine-grained account of why vanilla online SGD sits where it does, not of where the true threshold is.

A plausible follow-up, and the one I would actually do: the paper stops one derivative short. It proves the escape/trapping dichotomy only as a drift sign at a fixed radius, on an $O(1)$ macroscopic time window, and then argues the $N\log N$ versus $N^{k-1}$ thresholds heuristically. A matched-asymptotics theorem — OU behaviour in the window $ ilde m = O(1)$, a large-deviation or Lamperti argument for the exponential escape through $ ilde m \gg 1$, and a hand-off to the ballistic ODE once $m = \Theta(1)$ — would upgrade the whole story into a genuine escape-time limit theorem. A second, easier extension: redo this for multi-index models, where the summary statistics are an $r imes r$ overlap matrix plus a Gram matrix, the corrector becomes matrix-valued, and the sign condition becomes a spectral condition on a linearized matrix drift — the interesting question being whether some directions escape while others stay trapped, which is exactly the staircase/sequential-learning phenomenology observed empirically. A third: let $c_\delta$ vary in time (decaying step size) and watch the trajectory cross the saddle-node; the bifurcation structure suggests a sharp hysteresis prediction for step-size schedules.

On the connection to your own work: I would not force one, and I think the honest answer is that there is no technical bridge to generative retrieval or approximate nearest-neighbour search here. There is, though, a real shared object worth noting. The order parameter $m = \langle x, x^_ angle$ with $|x^_| = 1$ is literally the cosine similarity between a learned direction and a target direction in high dimension, and the paper's central quantitative fact — from a random start, the alignment is $\Theta(N^{-1/2})$, and whether it grows or stays pinned is decided by a drift sign — is the same concentration-of-measure fact that makes high-dimensional vector search hard. More concretely, training a dual-encoder retriever from noisy relevance labels is a single-index (or, with multiple semantic directions, multi-index) problem: relevance $y = f(\langle a, x^* angle) + \epsilon$ with $\epsilon$ modelling click or judgement noise, learned by online SGD. Read in that light, the phase-retrieval computation says something with a retrieval flavour: when the label noise $C_\epsilon$ is large and the step size is large, the $m = 0$ fixed point flips from repelling to attracting, so the learned direction never acquires nontrivial alignment at all — a sharp, quantitative statement that noisy supervision plus aggressive learning rates does not merely slow learning but can abolish it, with an explicit threshold. That is a modelling analogy rather than a theorem about retrieval, and I would present it as such. Its value to you is more likely as a clean, short template for how to turn a high-dimensional SGD recursion into a closed low-dimensional SDE via order parameters plus martingale decomposition — a technique that transfers directly if you ever want scaling limits for contrastive or in-batch-negative training dynamics.

title: Neural Collapse under Gradient Flow on Shallow ReLU Networks for Orthogonally Separable Data
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-22

Neural Collapse under Gradient Flow on Shallow ReLU Networks for Orthogonally Separable Data

Main idea

The question this paper attacks is how training gets you to Neural Collapse, as opposed to what the collapsed configuration looks like once you're there. Almost the entire NC theory literature answers the second question by fiat: the Unconstrained Features Model treats the last-layer feature matrix $H$ as a free optimization variable, so that minimizing $\ell(Y, VH) + \lambda(|V|^2 + |H|^2)$ becomes a matrix-factorization problem whose global minimizers can be characterized exactly — and they turn out to be a simplex ETF with self-dual classifier. This is a clean benchmark, but it is a landscape result about an abstraction of the network, and its idealization is severe in two specific ways. First, the network and its parameterization have vanished: there is no map from inputs to features, so the model cannot say anything about the role of the data, of the activation function, or of finite expressivity. Second, and more importantly, it says nothing about reachability: overparameterized networks have infinitely many interpolating parameter settings, most of which are not collapsed, and NC is observed empirically even without weight decay. So the fact that collapsed points are global minima of a regularized surrogate is not an explanation of why gradient descent lands on them.

Min, Zhu and Vidal replace the UFM by an actual network and an actual trajectory: a bias-free two-layer ReLU net $f(x) = V\sigma(W^\top x)$ of width $h \ge K$, trained by gradient flow on cross-entropy, with no explicit regularization, no width overparameterization, and no initialization near a global optimum. The price is a strong data assumption. Orthogonal separability means that after normalization, any two same-class points have cosine similarity $\ge \mu_s > 0$ and any two different-class points have cosine similarity $\le -\mu_d < 0$; necessarily $\mu_d \le 1/\sqrt{K-1}$. So classes sit in tight, mutually obtuse cones in input space — considerably stronger than linear separability, and roughly "the data already looks half-collapsed." Initialization is $\epsilon$-small and balanced ($|w_j(0)| = |v_j(0)|$, a quantity conserved under gradient flow on homogeneous nets), which places the analysis firmly in the feature-learning/rich regime rather than the NTK regime.

What comes out is a modified NC, and the modifications are the interesting part. Because the features must be produced by one ReLU layer applied to actual data, exact collapse to a singleton is impossible, and the theorem instead gives intra-class directional collapse: all class-$k$ features land on a single ray, $\phi_{\bar\theta}(x_i) = \langle s_k u_k, x_i\rangle \cdot \bar\phi_k$, where $u_k$ is the max-margin direction for class-$k$ data alone. The surviving within-class variability is exactly the spread of the scalar projections $\langle u_k, x_i\rangle$ — a drastic reduction, but not zero. Because ReLU forces $\phi \ge 0$, the class means form a nonnegative orthogonal frame rather than a simplex ETF; centering by the global mean recovers the ETF, which is why the self-duality statement is "projected." This is a falsifiable refinement of the UFM prediction, and the authors make it pay: if you normalize the features (RMSNorm), the magnitude variation is quotiented out and you should get exact collapse — which they verify on ResNet18/50 with a two-layer ReLU head, where RMSNorm visibly improves NC1 over LayerNorm and no normalization.

Critique

The genuine contribution is the mechanism, and it is both clever and a little deflationary once you see it. The proof identifies a two-phase dynamic in which early alignment does the work of turning a nonlinear problem into a linear one, and then a known max-margin bias does the rest. I find the sharpest single observation to be in the multi-class analysis: under small initialization the network output is near zero, so the softmax is near uniform, $\hat y_i \approx \frac{1}{K}\mathbf{1}$, and the cross-entropy residual becomes $y_i - \hat y_i \approx \sqrt{\tfrac{K-1}{K}}\,\tilde E y_i$ where $\tilde E = \sqrt{\tfrac{K}{K-1}}(I - \tfrac{1}{K}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top)$. That is, the simplex ETF is already the leading-order gradient signal in the first moments of training — the columns $\tilde e_k$, which the authors call pseudo-labels, are what the output neurons align to, long before anything converges. The ETF is not only where the optimum is; it is the direction the early dynamics point in. That reframing is worth more than the theorem it supports.

But the same analysis shows how much the data assumption is doing. Once the alignment phase has driven neuron group $N_k$ to be activated exclusively by class-$k$ data, the ReLU pattern is frozen, and the loss decomposes as $L = \sum_k L_{\text{CE}}(Y_k, V_k W_k^\top X_k)$ — $K$ completely decoupled two-layer linear networks. Everything after that is linear-network implicit bias: Ji–Telgarsky alignment plus conserved balancedness forces each $\bar W_k$ to be rank one, and rank-one $\bar W_k = s_k u_k g_k^\top$ is directional collapse, essentially by definition. So the honest summary is not "ReLU networks exhibit NC" but "orthogonally separable data lets gradient flow discover a class-exclusive partition of neurons, after which a ReLU net is a direct sum of linear nets and inherits their low-rank bias." The nonlinearity enters only through the sign pattern and through feature nonnegativity.

How restrictive are the assumptions, concretely? Very. The multi-class transient analysis needs the additional data condition $X_{\max}^2/(X_{\min}^2 \mu_d \mu_s^2) < 2K-3$. At $K=3$, with the best possible $\mu_d = 1/\sqrt{2}$ and equal-norm data, this forces $\mu_s \gtrsim 0.69$: every pair of same-class points at cosine similarity above $0.69$, plus near-equal norms. No real dataset does this, and the MNIST demonstration ("approximately satisfies") is a correlation-matrix heatmap, not a verification. Worse, Assumption 4 (semi-local initialization) requires every neuron pair to start inside an explicitly-specified invariant subset of some attractor's basin, including $\langle \tilde e_k, v_j/|v_j|\rangle \ge 1 - \tfrac{1}{2(K-1)}$ — at $K=10$ that is a cosine of $0.944$ between a random output weight and its pseudo-label. Random initialization does not satisfy this with non-negligible probability, and the authors' fallback — initialize by drawing from the $(x_i, \tilde E y_i)$ pairs — is a scheme nobody uses. This is a real asymmetry with the binary case, where the analogous assumption is mild and known to hold w.h.p. under random init. The authors are admirably explicit that the obstruction is technical: they cannot characterize the boundaries between regions of attraction, so they substitute a conservative invariant subset. Note also their fair caveat that the asymptotic half of the theorem holds whenever inter-class separation occurs at some time, however it occurs.

Other limitations are standard but worth stating: gradient flow rather than gradient descent (no step size, no discretization error, no stochasticity, while the experiments are SGD); balanced initialization; two layers only, so the "features" are one ReLU applied to raw pixels rather than the output of a deep backbone; and a purely asymptotic $t\to\infty$ statement, whereas NC is empirically a terminal-phase-of-training phenomenon measured at finite time. And one should notice that under the theorem, the conventional NC1 metric does not go to zero — it converges to a positive floor set by $\mathrm{Var}_{i\in I_k}\langle u_k, x_i\rangle$. That is a feature (it is the paper's most original prediction, and the RMSNorm experiment follows from it), but it does mean "provably exhibits NC" is a weaker claim than Papyan–Han–Donoho's NC1.

Does it advance beyond UFM as much as claimed? Partly, and along a different axis than the framing suggests. It genuinely does what no UFM analysis can: it exhibits a trajectory, identifies the timescale ($\Theta(\log 1/\epsilon)$ for the alignment phase), and explains why collapse is reached without weight decay. But UFM buys its idealization in exchange for saying something about arbitrary data and deep nets; this paper buys exactness in exchange for data so structured that the classes are already nearly orthogonal in input space, which makes orthogonal class means in feature space much less surprising. It is a different point on the tractability–realism curve, not a strict improvement. The nearest genuine competitor, Jacot–Súkeník–Wang–Mondelli (ICLR 2025), proves convergence to NC for wide networks with weight decay, and the two results are complementary: width plus regularization there, structured data plus small initialization here.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Theorem 1: given orthogonally separable data, $\epsilon$-small balanced initialization with $\epsilon$ small enough, and case-dependent initialization-shape conditions (mild for $K=2$; Assumption 4 plus the separability condition $X_{\max}^2/(X_{\min}^2\mu_d\mu_s^2) < 2K-3$ for $K>2$), the normalized limit $\bar\theta = \lim_{t\to\infty}\theta(t)/|\theta(t)|*F$ exists for every gradient-flow solution (weights themselves diverge, as they must under exponential-tailed losses on homogeneous nets), and satisfies three things. (1) Intra-class directional collapse: $\phi*{\bar\theta}(x_i) = \langle s_k u_k, x_i\rangle \bar\phi_k$ for all $i \in I_k$, where $\gamma_k = \max_{u \in S^{D-1}} \min_{i \in I_k}\langle x_i, u\rangle$ is the class-$k$-only max margin, $u_k$ the maximizer, and $s_k = \sqrt{\gamma_k^{-1}/(2\sum_{k'}\gamma_{k'}^{-1})}$. (2) Orthogonal class means: $\bar\phi_k \ge 0$ and $\langle \bar\phi_k, \bar\phi_{k'}\rangle = 0$ for $k \ne k'$. (3) Projected self-duality: $\bar V = \sqrt{\tfrac{K}{K-1}}(I - \tfrac{1}{K}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top)[s_1\bar\phi_1, \dots, s_K\bar\phi_K]^\top$, so $\bar V \bar V^\top$ is a scaled simplex ETF Gram matrix, exactly an ETF when all $s_k$ coincide. There is no weight decay anywhere.

How it is proved — binary case. The trajectory splits into two phases. During the alignment phase, of duration $\Theta(\log \tfrac{1}{\epsilon})$, weight norms remain $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$, so the loss residual is essentially constant and the directional dynamics decouple across neurons: $\tfrac{d}{dt}\tfrac{w_j}{|w_j|} = \mathrm{sign}(v_j)\,\Pi_{w_j^\perp}\big(\sum_i \xi_{ij} x_i y_i\big) + O(\epsilon)$, with $\xi_{ij}$ the ReLU indicator. Two conservation facts carry the argument: balancedness $|w_j(t)| \equiv |v_j(t)|$, and the fact that $\mathrm{sign}(v_j)$ never changes, so the partition of neurons into $N_+ \cup N_-$ is fixed at initialization. On orthogonally separable data the only nontrivial stationary points of this flow ("extremal vectors" in the sense of Maennel et al.) are the class-mean directions $\bar x_\pm$; for $j \in N_+$, $\bar x_+$ is an attractor and $\bar x_-$ a repeller, and vice versa. Assumption 3 just rules out starting on a repeller. Consequently, after a finite time $T^_$, each surviving neuron is activated by data of exactly one class, all others fall permanently into the dead region, and the feature supports of the two classes become disjoint coordinate blocks — this is inter-class separation, and it holds for all $t \ge T^_$.

The payoff of separation is that the ReLU pattern is frozen, so $L(\theta) = \sum_{I_+}\ell(y_i, V_+W_+^\top x_i) + \sum_{I_-}\ell(y_i, V_-W_-^\top x_i)$: two decoupled two-layer linear networks. Now the asymptotic phase invokes Ji–Telgarsky's result on deep linear networks, which gives directional convergence together with the alignment condition $\bar V_+ \bar W_+^\top \propto u_+$; combined with the conserved balancedness $\bar V_+^\top \bar V_+ = \bar W_+^\top \bar W_+$, the only way both can hold (an observation of Phuong–Lampert) is for $\bar W_+$ to be rank one, with left singular vector $u_+$. Rank-one weights immediately give $\phi_{\bar\theta}(x_i) = \langle s_+ u_+, x_i\rangle g_+$ — directional collapse — and reading off $\bar V$ gives self-duality. The scalars $s_\pm$ are pinned by Lyu–Li: $\bar\theta$ must be a KKT point of the global margin problem $\min |\theta|^2$ subject to unit margins, which fixes the relative scaling as $s_k \propto \gamma_k^{-1/2}$. So the named mechanism is: early alignment freezes the activation pattern into class-exclusive neuron groups; the frozen pattern linearizes the problem; the max-margin implicit bias of linear networks drives the weights to rank one; rank-one weights are directional collapse.

How it is proved — multi-class case. The obstruction is that $v_j \in \mathbb{R}^K$ now has a nontrivial direction, so one must track a coupled Riemannian flow on $S^{D-1} \times S^{K-1}$.
