Lemma 2 bounds the weight norms by $\epsilon/\sqrt{h}$ and the outputs by $2\epsilon X_{\max}\sqrt{h}$ up to $T = \tfrac{1}{4nX_{\max}}\log\tfrac{1}{\sqrt h \epsilon}$; Lemma 1 then shows $|\hat y_i - \tfrac{1}{K}\mathbf{1}| \le \tfrac{8}{\sqrt K}|f(x_i;\theta)|$, so Lemma 3 gives the approximate alignment dynamics $\tfrac{d}{dt}\tfrac{w_j}{|w_j|} \approx \sqrt{\tfrac{K-1}{K}}\Pi_{w_j^\perp}\sum_i \xi_{ij}\langle \tilde E y_i, \tfrac{v_j}{|v_j|}\rangle x_i$ and its mirror for $v_j$. The attractors are the pairs ${\bar x_k, \tilde e_k}$ — class mean direction paired with ETF pseudo-label. Because the basin boundaries have no analytic description, the authors instead construct an explicitly-checkable invariant subset of each basin, stated in terms of three bookkeeping quantities per neuron: $|I_k^w|$ (number of active class-$k$ points), $A_k = \sum_{i \in I_k^w}\langle x_i, w/|w|\rangle$, and $B_k = \langle \tilde e_k, v/|v|\rangle$. Lemma 4 shows the Assumption-4 inequalities among these are forward-invariant during the alignment phase and that $|I_k^w|$ monotonically increases to $|I_k|$ while $|I_{k'}^w| \to 0$; auxiliary lemmas are where orthogonal separability is cashed in (converting the correlation bounds into inequalities on weighted sums $|\sum a_i x_i| \ge \sqrt{\mu_s}\sum a_i X_{\min}$ and $\langle \sum_{I_k} a_i x_i, \sum_{I_{k'}} b_i x_i\rangle \le -\mu_d|\cdot||\cdot|$, plus a uniform gap $\zeta > 0$ preventing stalling). Lemma 5 shows the exclusive activation pattern, once attained, persists forever. That yields inter-class separation, and hence the same loss decomposition into $K$ independent two-layer linear CE problems.

For the asymptotic half, the authors extend Ji–Telgarsky's Lemma 2.11 from the binary/linear setting to cross-entropy. Their Lemma 13 states that once $|\Pi^\perp_{\bar u_\infty}(\theta_k - \theta_{k'})|$ is large enough, $\mathrm{tr}\big((e_k\mathbf{1}^\top - \hat Y)^\top \Theta^\top \Pi^\perp_{\bar u_\infty} X\big) \le 0$. Applied to $\tfrac{d}{dt}|\Pi^\perp_{\bar u_\infty}W_k|_F^2$, this makes the component of $W_k$ orthogonal to the max-margin direction nonincreasing while $|W_k|_F \to \infty$, contradicting any assumption that the normalized orthogonal component stays bounded away from zero. Hence $\bar W_k \propto u_k g_k^\top$; balancedness upgrades this to $\bar V_k \propto \bar v_k g_k^\top$; and a second contradiction argument (the relevant alignment derivative is positive and $\Theta(1/t)$ while the weights grow like $\Theta(\log t)$) forces $\bar v_k = \tilde e_k$. Finally the scales $s_k$ are again determined by the KKT conditions of the global max-margin program.

Broader context

Neural Collapse was named by Papyan, Han and Donoho (PNAS 2020) after a large empirical study: train any standard classifier past zero training error, into what they call the terminal phase of training, and the penultimate-layer features develop a rigid geometry. Within-class feature variability collapses to zero (NC1); the centered class means converge to a simplex equiangular tight frame, i.e. the maximally-separated configuration of $K$ points on a sphere with all pairwise cosines equal to $-1/(K-1)$ (NC2); the classifier rows converge to the class means up to scaling (NC3, self-duality); and the network's decision rule degenerates to nearest-class-mean (NC4). The phenomenon is remarkably robust across architectures, datasets and losses, which is what made it a magnet for theory.

The dominant theoretical response has been the UFM / layer-peeled model (Mixon–Parshall–Pi; Fang–He–Long–Su; Zhu et al.'s geometric analysis showing the regularized UFM has no spurious local minima and a strict saddle property; Ji–Lu–Zhang–Deng–Su's regularization-path analysis). Extensions add an extra layer and a ReLU (Tirer–Bruna, who already predicted the nonnegative orthogonal frame that reappears here), go deep (Súkeník–Mondelli–Lampert), or push to $K \gg d$ (Jiang et al., "Generalized neural collapse for a large number of classes"). Recent work trying to escape UFM includes Hong–Ling on shallow nets with general data, Kothapalli–Tirer on kernel explanations of data-dependence, and Jacot et al.'s wide-network-with-weight-decay convergence result. The present paper's other parent is the implicit-bias literature: Lyu–Li and Ji–Telgarsky on directional convergence of homogeneous networks to KKT points of a max-margin problem, Ji–Telgarsky on layer alignment in deep linear nets, and the early-alignment line (Maennel–Bousquet–Gelly, Phuong–Lampert, Boursier–Pullaud-Vivien–Flammarion, Min–Mallada–Vidal). The paper is essentially a marriage of these two literatures, and its lasting value may be less the theorem than the demonstration that NC is a corollary of known implicit biases once you can control the activation pattern.

The obvious follow-up the authors flag is relaxing Assumption 4 — either by characterizing basin boundaries directly (a saddle-to-saddle question), or by proving a probabilistic statement over random initialization for $K > 2$ to match what is known for $K = 2$. A second, possibly more interesting direction: make the NC1 floor quantitative. The theorem predicts within-class variability converges to the spread of $\langle u_k, x_i\rangle$ rather than to zero, and a finite-time rate would turn this into a testable law relating measured NC1 to input-data geometry — which is precisely what UFM cannot say anything about. Third, the RMSNorm experiment is currently a conjecture with encouraging plots; analyzing the gradient flow of a normalized two-layer architecture (where the homogeneity structure changes, so Lyu–Li does not apply directly) is a well-posed and useful problem. Fourth, the class-wise scaling $s_k \propto \gamma_k^{-1/2}$ is already an imbalance signature, offering a route to a dynamical version of Fang et al.'s minority collapse without the UFM.

On the connection to your own work: I would call it real but indirect, and worth resisting the temptation to oversell. The genuine link is that NC is the exact pathology retrieval representations must avoid, and this paper states it in unusually usable form. If a classification-trained two-layer ReLU head is run to convergence, the theorem says the feature space has effective rank $K$ and all within-class information survives only as the single scalar $\langle u_k, x_i\rangle$ — so inner-product search over such embeddings degenerates to "identify the class, then rank by one scalar," which is exactly why classification-trained encoders make poor retrieval encoders and why practitioners take an intermediate layer. This is the rigorous counterpart of the anisotropy/representation-degeneration observations on the IR side (the cone effect, BERT-flow and whitening fixes), which have mostly been empirical or landscape-flavored; here the geometry falls out of the training dynamics, and the mechanism — a low-rank implicit bias inherited from a max-margin argument — suggests where to intervene.

The closer and more specific bridge is generative retrieval. Under the DSI-style view, retrieval is classification over a docid label space with $K$ in the millions and $K \gg h$, where a simplex ETF is geometrically impossible and the right question becomes what frame-potential-minimizing configuration the last layer converges to — exactly the regime of Jiang et al.'s generalized NC, which this paper cites but does not engage. Whether the two-phase mechanism here has any analogue when $K \gg h$ seems genuinely open, and the answer would bear on docid-space design and on whether head/tail document frequency produces a minority-collapse-style distortion of rare docid embeddings. That said, the paper itself — two layers, small $K$, and data assumed nearly orthogonal in input space — is several steps removed from anything you would deploy, and I would treat it as a source of mechanism and vocabulary rather than of transferable results.

title: Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically; it is unclear why
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-22

Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically; it is unclear why

Main idea

The paper is about how a next-token-trained sequence model physically stores a set of incompressible atomic facts, and it uses graph memorization as the sandbox. The setup: fix one giant path-star graph $G_{d,\ell}$ (a root with $d$ disjoint arms of length $\ell$; up to $5\times10^4$ nodes), assign every node its own token, and train a from-scratch GPT-mid (and a Mamba of matching size) on two-token "edge bigram" examples $u \to v$ covering every edge in both directions. That is pure local supervision — the graph lives in the weights, never in the context. Separately, path-finding examples give a leaf as prompt and the full root-to-leaf path as target, on a 75% subset of arms, testing on arms whose end-to-end path was never seen.

The point of choosing path-star is that Bachmann & Nagarajan showed the in-context version is a textbook failure case for next-token learning: the model learns a Clever Hans rule for tokens $2..\ell$ (each is the child of the revealed ground-truth predecessor), which starves the first token of gradient, leaving it to be learned in isolation as an $\ell$-fold composition — a flat-loss needle-in-a-haystack. The authors strip out every step-wise aid (fixed path length so no implicit curriculum, disjoint train/test arms so no substring stitching, and in the sharpest experiment the loss is restricted to the first token only), and find the in-weights model nonetheless gets up to 100% first-token accuracy on held-out leaves, with no reverse-learning cascade — so future-token gradients are not doing the work.

Their explanation is that the model is not storing a lookup table. In the associative abstraction, $f(u)[v] = \Phi(u)^\top W_{\text{assoc}} \Phi(v)$ with $\Phi$ near-orthogonal keys and $W_{\text{assoc}} \approx \sum_{(u,v)\in E} \Phi(u)\otimes\Phi(v)$ — a rotated adjacency matrix, from which $\ell$-hop reachability requires $\ell$ compositions. What they observe instead is geometric memory: $f(u)[v] \approx \Phi_{\text{geom}}(u)\cdot\Phi_{\text{geom}}(v)$, where the embeddings are a spectrally skewed factorization of $A$, so the dot product already encodes multi-hop proximity. The concrete "geometry" is: leaf embeddings cluster with the first-hop embedding of their own arm; on tiny cycle/grid/irregular graphs the node-node cosine matrix shows smooth distance decay rather than a spiky adjacency pattern; and the embedding's projections onto eigenvectors of the negative random-walk Laplacian are skewed toward the top (Fiedler-like) directions — more skewed than the eigenvalues themselves, e.g. only two dimensions used for a cycle. Under that data structure, the $\ell$-fold composition collapses to a one-hop navigation: pick the root's neighbor best aligned with the leaf.

The second half is the actual contribution flagged by the title. Geometry emerges even with edge-only supervision, even with weight decay and dropout off, even when the same architecture can fit the data associatively if you freeze the embeddings, even though associative storage is found in ~2 GD steps versus ~200 for geometry, and even though — for sparse graphs with $|V|\approx|E|$ — the two solutions have comparable bit and $\ell_2$-norm complexity. So the familiar explanations (supervisory pressure, rank bottleneck, explicit regularization, implicit simplicity bias) are each blocked, hence the "memorization puzzle." A partial mechanism is supplied by reducing to a weight-tied two-layer Node2Vec model with full softmax loss, where associative memory is architecturally prohibited, and showing a low-rank spectral bias arises with $m=100 \gg |V|$, no regularizer, and 1-hop supervision only.

Critique

The strongest and cleverest move is the succinctness argument, and it is the part I would defend hardest. The whole modern folklore about "gradient descent prefers simple solutions over lookup tables" is imported from classification, where the data has statistical redundancy and a lookup costs $\Theta(n)$ bits against $\Theta(1)$ for the rule. Here the task is memorization in Feldman's sense — no edge is inferable from the others — and the authors show the complexity gap simply vanishes: associative storage costs $|E|\log|V|$ bits, geometric costs $|V|m\log\Delta$, and on path-star or cycle graphs these are within a constant factor, with the geometric side arguably worse. Remark 3 makes the conceptual point sharply: a token has no intrinsic features the way an image patch does; its representation is synthesized entirely from co-occurrence, so the generalization-puzzle analogy breaks at the root. That reframing is worth the paper on its own.

The experimental hygiene is also better than most papers in this space. Frozen-embedding transformers genuinely fail the path-star task after 50k epochs, which is the right negative control; the Node2Vec reduction is the right minimal model; and the appendix is unusually honest about which diagnostics admit false positives (3D/UMAP plots can inject global structure) and false negatives (a spiky cosine heatmap is consistent with a full-rank geometric factorization).

Now the weaknesses. The central comparison is not apples-to-apples. "The model could have gone associative and chose not to" is established by showing that a different model — same architecture with the embedding layer frozen — fits the data associatively. But once the tied embedding layer receives gradient, its update is, by the paper's own Lemma 1, exactly $\eta\,C(t)V(t)$ with $C(0)\approx -L$. The embedding layer's gradient is a Laplacian operator on the graph. So a large part of "why geometry" is answered by "because you trained the embeddings and that is what their gradient does," and the residual mystery is narrower than the framing suggests: why the associative pathway, which forms in two steps, does not suppress the geometric one. The authors do state this as an open question, but §3 reads as if the whole phenomenon were unexplained.

Relatedly, the paper contains its own counterexample and under-weights it. Figure 28 shows that with unit-normal embedding initialization and a low learning rate, the same tiny model converges to a purely associative solution — orthogonal embeddings, flat eigenvector spectrum, negative geometric margin. Geometry then returns with larger LR, weight decay or dropout. That is an init-scale/learning-rate-controlled transition, which is the textbook lazy-versus-rich signature: large init makes embeddings near-orthogonal, the model behaves like a fixed random feature map with one trainable middle layer, and you get a lookup. The authors dismiss the lazy/rich framing in a few lines ("associative memory, unlike lazy learning, requires the weights to move substantially"), but that argues about which weights move, not about the kernel/feature-learning distinction, and it is the single most plausible competing explanation. "Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically" is thus a claim about a hyperparameter region that the paper itself shows is escapable.

The speed comparison is also soft: 2 steps at LR 0.1 in a frozen-embedding TinyNN versus ~200 steps at LR 0.01 in a trainable-embedding TinyNN, and at LR 0.1 the geometry fails to form at all. Two architectures, two LR regimes, one conclusion. And in the norm-complexity accounting the associative construction assumes one-hot embeddings whose $\sqrt{|V|}$ of norm is simply not charged, because those parameters are frozen — which is exactly the term that dominates the geometric side. Count them and the tie tilts the other way. The bit-complexity version is cleaner, but both are complexities of hand-built constructions, not of the implicit-bias functional (nuclear norm of the end-to-end logit map, product of layer norms, flatness) that any serious "GD prefers simple" story would actually invoke.

On the hardness premise: the paper admits that existing lower bounds are worst-case over function classes, not for the fixed graph at hand, so the $\Omega(\exp \ell)$ claim is intuition plus one empirical negative control. The "paradox" is therefore somewhat self-dissolving — with a geometric memory the search space was never $\exp(\ell)$ — and the honest statement is the constructive one (geometry makes it easy), not the paradoxical one.

Finally, evaluation breadth. Two topologies at scale, all symbolic, one model scale, no pretrained model, no natural language, and success on the large graphs requires both reverse-edge augmentation (which symmetrizes $A$ and is precisely what the spectral story wants) and pause tokens. The appendix calls reverse edges "critical" but only shows on tiny graphs that geometry survives without them, so the load-bearing large-scale result rests on an intervention whose effect on the geometry is untested. Also, on path-star the reported global structure is essentially arm identity — a $d$-way block clustering, which is the dominant eigenstructure of that graph almost by construction; the richer within-arm distance recovery is only demonstrated on 15-node cycles and $4\times4$ grids. And the succinctness tie holds only for $|E|\approx|V|$; in any realistic knowledge graph with $|E|\gg|V|$ the geometric side is dramatically cheaper and the puzzle partly evaporates.

Verdict: the phenomenon is real and well-isolated, the reframing of memorization-versus-generalization intuitions is valuable, but "it is unclear why" is better read as under-explored than as established. Ruling out init-scale/lazy-rich and end-to-end norm-based implicit bias would be needed before the puzzle deserves its name.

Proof sketch

There are two genuine formal clusters, both informal by the authors' own admission but both with real content.

The first is representational. Proposition 1 (bits): associative storage must, at each vertex $u$, name the IDs of its $d(u)$ neighbors, costing $\sum_u d(u)\log|V| = |E|\log|V|$ bits; geometric storage costs $|V|m\log\Delta$ where $\Delta$ is the per-dimension grid resolution needed to avoid collisions. Proposition 2 ($\ell_2$): under the margin normalization $f(u)[v] - \max_{w\notin \mathrm{nbr}(u)} f(u)[w] \ge 1$, taking $\Phi$ one-hot lets $W_{\text{assoc}} = A$, of Frobenius norm $\sqrt{|E|}$; geometrically, $\Phi(u)\cdot\Phi(v) > 1$ forces $|\Phi(u)|^2 + |\Phi(v)|^2 > 2$, hence $\sum_u |\Phi_{\text{geom}}(u)|^2 \ge |V|$. The refutation then observes that for path-star and cycle graphs $|E| \approx |V|$, so an upper bound on the associative cost meets a lower bound on the geometric cost — the direction needed to conclude that geometry buys no succinctness.

Propositions 3–5 are a small capacity separation for dual encoders that is independently interesting. A weight-tied dual encoder computes $\Phi(u)\cdot\Phi(v)$ and can only realize PSD similarity matrices; it can store a bipartite graph associatively at dimension $|V_1|$, and a general graph only by the contrived incidence-matrix construction at dimension $|E|$ (set $\Phi(u)_i = \mathbb{1}[u \in e_i]$, so $\Phi(u)\cdot\Phi(v) = \mathbb{1}[(u,v)\in E]$), which the authors suspect is also a lower bound. A weight-untied encoder $\Phi_1(u)\cdot\Phi_2(v)$ needs only dimension $|V|$ and, with one tower frozen at random near-orthogonal vectors, learns $A$ up to rotation in a single gradient step. This is also the formal basis for the zigzag story: the negative eigendirections of $A$ (approximate bipartite cuts, alternating $\pm1$ along a path) are needed to cancel the spuriously large diagonal logits $\Phi(u)\cdot\Phi(u)$ that a PSD-only approximation produces when no self-loops exist; a tied two-layer model cannot express them, a weight-untied or multi-layer model can, and adding self-edges reduces their singular value and empirically makes the zigzags disappear — which incidentally predicts why "identity statements" help two-hop reasoning.

The second cluster is the Node2Vec spectral dynamics. Lemma 1: for $J = \sum_i \frac{1}{|\mathrm{nbr}(i)|}\sum_{j\in\mathrm{nbr}(i)} \log \mathrm{softmax}(v_i^\top v_j)$ with $P = \text{row_softmax}(VV^\top)$, the gradient flow is $\dot V = \eta C(t) V(t)$ with $C(t) = (D^{-1}A - P) + (D^{-1}A - P)^\top$. Fact 1: at near-orthogonal init $VV^\top \approx cI$, so $P(0)\approx I$ and $C(0) \approx -L$, the symmetrized random-walk Laplacian. Observation 9, assumed without proof and the main soft spot, asserts the row-softmax preserves the eigenvectors (and their order) of $VV^\top$. Granting that, Proposition 6 is an induction using $V(T) = \prod_{t<T}(I + \eta C(t))V(0)$: if $C(t)$ shares eigenvectors with $-L$ up to $T-1$, so does $V(T)V(T)^\top$, hence so does $P + P^\top$, hence so does $C(T)$. Propositions 7–8 bound eigenvalues via Gershgorin: rows of $P$ sum to 1 and the diagonal $p(i,i)$ dominates when embedding norms are equal, so $\mathrm{eig}(P+P^\top)\in[0,2]$, while $\mathrm{eig}(D^{-1}A + (D^{-1}A)^\top)\in[-2,2]$. Proposition 9: $C$ therefore starts non-positive, and as embeddings de-orthogonalize the self-probabilities $p(i,i)$ fall, the eigenvalues of $P+P^\top$ fall, and those of $C$ rise toward zero — the top ones, already nearest zero, arriving first. Proposition 10 closes it: in the shared eigenbasis, each embedding column's component along $e_k$ is multiplied by $\prod_t (1+\eta\lambda_k(t)) \in [0,1]$, so as $T$ grows only the components along the eigenvectors with $\lambda_k$ closest to zero survive. The system self-stabilizes: $V$ contracts into the top eigenspace while that same eigenspace enters the null space of $C$, driving $\dot V \to 0$.

The force of this is that nothing in the argument bounds $m$: the low-rank bias is a property of the multiplicative contraction, not of a bottleneck, a regularizer, early stopping, or multi-hop supervision — which is exactly the gap versus Levy–Goldberg-style PMI analyses, DeepWalk (explicitly multi-hop objective), and squared-loss-plus-early-stopping settings. Two caveats the paper states: the propositions assume $P\approx P^\top$, equal embedding norms and uniform degree; and because the asymmetric Laplacian's degenerate all-ones top eigenvector has slightly positive eigenvalue, sufficiently long training collapses onto it — so early stopping is quietly needed after all, just for the opposite reason.

Broader context

The background is a split in how the field pictures parametric memory. One lineage — Hopfield networks, Geva et al.'s reading of FFN layers as key-value memories, Bietti et al.'s "Birth of a Transformer," Cabannes et al.'s scaling laws for associative memories, and the whole ROME/MEMIT editing programme — treats a fact as an entry in a table: entities get near-orthogonal keys, associations get written into a matrix, capacity is counted in bits per parameter (Allen-Zhu & Li's "2 bits/param"), and edits are surgical because entries are independent. The other lineage — word2vec analogies, the linear representation hypothesis, Elhage et al.'s superposition, Gurnee & Tegmark's space/time directions, the grokking-of-modular-arithmetic line — treats representations as geometry, but almost always explains the geometry by appeal to structure in the data. The contribution here is to show a geometry arising where the data has no such latent structure to exploit, which is why the two lineages had not collided before.

Two neighbours worth reading alongside it. Wang et al.'s "Grokked transformers are implicit reasoners" shows that on two-hop composition the model first memorizes atomic facts and only much later groks a generalizing circuit; this paper reinterprets that transition as associative-then-geometric. Huang et al. show two-hop reasoning emerges iff the key and query matrices are kept factorized rather than collapsed, attributing it to implicit regularization in matrix completion — Remark 1 is a direct and reasonable rebuttal, since edge-only memorization has no missing entries to complete. Saxe et al.'s deep linear network results (staged SVD learning) are the closest theoretical ancestor of the spectral appendix, but rely on squared loss plus a bottleneck or early stopping, which is exactly the assumption this paper is trying to remove. Nishi et al.'s "representation shattering" is the flip side and the most actionable downstream worry: if facts are stored in a shared spectral basis, editing one fact perturbs the geometry that encodes many others, so knowledge editing and unlearning benchmarks built on associative assumptions may be measuring the wrong thing.

A follow-up I would actually run: make the associative/geometric split measurable rather than visual. For a trained model, form the full logit matrix $M_{uv} = f(u)[v]$ and decompose it as low-rank-plus-sparse (robust PCA style), where the low-rank part is constrained to the top eigenspace of $A$ and the sparse part is supported on $E$. The ratio of energy in the two parts gives a scalar "geometricity" per graph, per layer, per training step, which is precisely what the paper's open question asks for and what is currently answered by eyeballing UMAP plots. Then sweep init scale, learning rate, depth and $|E|/|V|$ against that scalar; my prediction is a fairly sharp lazy/rich phase boundary in $(\sigma_{\text{init}}, \eta)$, which would either dissolve the memorization puzzle or make it much more precise.

The connection to your own work is real in at least three places, and not in one place where it might look tempting. First, generative retrieval. DSI/NCI training is exactly this task: memorize a set of atomic (document or query) $\to$ docid associations in the weights, then answer with a docid at inference. The field's standing puzzle is why a model trained on doc$\to$docid and a few query$\to$docid pairs generalizes to unseen queries at all, and why hierarchical semantic docids help so much more than atomic ones. This paper supplies a mechanism and a falsifiable prediction: the docid output-embedding rows of a trained DSI should carry spectral structure reflecting the document–document co-occurrence graph even when no doc–doc supervision was given, with the top eigendirections of that graph appearing in the unembedding matrix. If true, semantic docids help because they pre-align the token geometry with the eigenstructure the model would otherwise have to synthesize, and the observed sensitivity of DSI to docid construction is a statement about spectral warm-starting, not about tokenization. That is a clean experiment on an existing checkpoint.

Second, and more theoretically, Propositions 3–5 are a capacity separation for dual encoders stated in graph language, and it maps onto the dense-retrieval expressivity results you know (the rank/sign-rank bounds on which qrel matrices a $d$-dimensional dot-product retriever can realize, of which the recent LIMIT work is the empirical face). The paper's version is sharper in one respect: a weight-tied encoder can only realize PSD similarity, so exact associative storage of a general non-bipartite relation needs dimension $\Theta(|E|)$, while an untied two-tower needs only $\Theta(|V|)$ and gets there in one gradient step. Untying the towers is what lets negative eigendirections of the relation matrix be folded into top singular directions. For asymmetric retrieval — query-document asymmetry, the reversal curse, one-directional relations — this says the tied/untied choice is not a parameter-count convenience but determines which relations are representable at all. It also suggests a genuinely theoretical-IR question: restate capacity bounds as geometric capacity, i.e. how many atomic associations can be stored at embedding dimension $m$ as a function of the co-occurrence graph's spectral decay, rather than as bits per parameter. That is the right generalization of "2 bits per parameter" to the regime where storage smooths across facts, and it is the same quantity that governs how well an ANN index over those embeddings will behave, since spectral decay sets the intrinsic dimension the index has to cope with.

Third, the approximate-versus-exact retrieval tradeoff in the paper's Table 1 is directly your territory: geometric storage gives approximate recall with global structure for free, associative gives precise recall and nothing else. That is the parametric-memory restatement of the dense-versus-sparse retrieval tradeoff, and the authors' conjecture — that a Transformer's geometry is "adulterated" by associative memory and has headroom toward the cleaner Node2Vec geometry — is effectively a claim that generative retrieval models are currently worse graph embedders than a 2016 dual encoder, with a specific diagnostic (eigenvector projection skew) for measuring the gap.

Where I would not push the connection: the path-star planning result itself. The adversarial-topology, implicit-multi-hop-planning framing is about compositional search, not retrieval, and the claim that the first token is $\exp(\ell)$-hard is intuition rather than a theorem. The transferable content for IR is the storage geometry and the dual-encoder capacity propositions, not the planning narrative.

title: The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-22

The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient

Main idea

Almost everything we know about the implicit bias of "non-Euclidean" optimizers — SignGD converging to the max-margin separator in the max-norm geometry, Muon converging to the spectral-norm max-margin solution — has been proved for full-batch gradients. That is a conspicuous gap, because the whole reason anyone cares about these geometries is large-scale pretraining, where nobody ever computes a full gradient. This paper asks the obvious but technically awkward question: what survives when you replace $\nabla L(W_t)$ with a mini-batch gradient, and what do batch size, momentum and variance reduction each do to the limiting bias?

The setting is multi-class linear classification ($W \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$, softmax cross-entropy, separable data), and the algorithm is a single unified template: form a signal $G_t$ (mini-batch gradient, EMA momentum buffer, SVRG-corrected gradient, or momentum-of-SVRG), then take a unit step in the dual-norm-maximizing direction $\Delta_t = \arg\max_{|\Delta|\le1}\langle G_t,\Delta\rangle$. Instantiating $|\cdot|$ as the entrywise max-norm gives SignSGD/Signum, Frobenius gives Normalized-SGD, spectral gives Spectral-SGD/Muon. Sampling is random reshuffling, with $m = n/b$ batches per epoch.

The headline finding is a sharp and slightly uncomfortable dichotomy. The key structural fact about normalized steepest descent is that the update has unit norm no matter how small the gradient is; the descent direction depends only on the direction of the signal. So mini-batch noise does not shrink as the loss shrinks — it competes with the signal on equal footing forever. Quantitatively, the batch noise is bounded by $2(m-1)R\,G(W)$ while the useful signal $|\nabla L(W)|_*$ is at least $\gamma\,G(W)$, where $G$ is a proxy for the loss and $\gamma \le 2R$ always. Plain steepest descent therefore only has a guarantee when $4(m-1)R < \gamma$, which since $\gamma \le 2R$ forces $m = 1$, i.e. exactly the full-batch case. This is not just loose analysis: a two-point dataset shows random-reshuffling SignSGD at $m = 2$ never even classifies both points correctly.

Momentum repairs this, and the mechanism is specific: under random reshuffling the per-epoch gradient errors sum to exactly zero, so an EMA buffer only feels the variation of the exponential weights inside an epoch, which is $O((1-\beta_1)m)$ rather than $O(1)$. The result is a genuine batch–momentum trade-off: convergence to an approximate margin $\rho = \gamma - 2(1-\beta_1)m(m^2-1)R$, so the margin deficit vanishes as $b\to n$ or $\beta_1\to1$, with $b = \Omega(n((1-\beta_1)R/\gamma)^{1/3})$ sufficing. Variance reduction does better still — an SVRG control variate makes the deviation from the full gradient $O(\eta_t)$ rather than $O(1)$, which demotes it from a first-order to a second-order term in the descent inequality, so the exact full-batch max margin $\gamma$ is recovered for any batch size and any $\beta_1$. Both fixes cost rate: momentum multiplies the bound by $m/(1-\beta_1)$, VR by $m^{2+a}/(1-\beta_1)$. Finally, with batch size one and no stabilization, the limit is not a max-margin solution at all but a frequency-weighted average of per-sample update directions.

Critique

The strongest thing in the paper is the clean impossibility result and the reason behind it. The observation that $\gamma \le 2R$ under the data assumption, so the large-batch condition $4(m-1)R < \gamma$ collapses to $m = 1$ arithmetically, is the kind of remark that turns a "we need a large batch" theorem into a genuine statement about the algorithm class. And the accompanying counterexample is elegantly minimal: with $x_1 = (1,-\varepsilon)$, $x_2 = (\varepsilon,-1)$, both feature vectors have the same sign pattern $s = (1,-1)$, so sign updates confine $\theta = w_1 - w_2$ to $\mathrm{span}{s}$ forever, forcing $M_2(W_t) = -M_1(W_t)$ and hence min margin $\le 0$ at every step, for every stepsize and every reshuffling. That is a real separation, not a technical artifact, and it shows exactly what normalization destroys: the self-stabilization by which small gradients produce small steps.

The second genuinely nice piece is the dimension-free improvement over Fan et al. (2025). Their gradient-stability bound went through entrywise control and paid a factor $d$ when summing over $kd$ entries; here Lemma C.10 bounds $|\nabla L(W')-\nabla L(W)|_{\mathrm{sum}}$ directly, using the softmax-ratio inequality and the fact that $\sum_c|S_c(v')-S_c(v)| \le 2(e^{2R|\Delta|_{\max}}-1)(1-S_{y_i})$ because probability mass is conserved. The simplex kills the dimension.

Now the weaknesses. First and most seriously, the analysis is entirely worst-case and deterministic: randomness of the reshuffling is never used except for the zero-sum property within an epoch, so every bound holds for all permutations, and there is not a single expectation, variance or concentration argument in the paper. The noise bound in Lemma C.11 is pure triangle inequality with no cancellation. This explains the pessimism of the $m = 1$ conclusion and means the theory cannot distinguish between "small-batch steepest descent is broken" and "small-batch steepest descent is broken in the worst case over reshufflings" — which matters, since small-batch SignSGD demonstrably trains models.

Second, the momentum result is asymptotically true but quantitatively brutal in exactly the regime it advertises. To get $b = O(1)$ you need $1-\beta_1 = O(n^{-3})$; but the same constant enters the rate as $m/(1-\beta_1)$ and, worse, enters the burn-in through $t_1 \gtrsim (\alpha_1/\rho)^{1/a}$ with $\alpha_1 = \Theta(m/(1-\beta_1))$. With $m \approx n$ and $1-\beta_1 = n^{-3}$, that is $\alpha_1 \approx n^4$ and burn-in $\approx n^8$ at $a = 1/2$, with the numerator scaling as $n^5$. You need $t \gg n^{10}$ before the bound says anything. The trade-off is real, but the exchange rate is so poor that the theorem is best read as a qualitative existence statement. The paper never says this.

Third, there is a tension between the framing and the variance-reduction result. The authors criticize prior work for using proxy algorithms that "require access to full-batch information at each update" — but SVRG requires a full gradient at the start of every epoch, plus three gradient evaluations per step. Recovering the full-batch implicit bias from an estimator explicitly anchored to a full-batch gradient computed $O(m)$ steps ago is close to what one should expect. The interesting content is the rate degradation ($m^{2+a}$), not the exactness.

Fourth, the guarantee itself weakens silently. Theorem 4.4 proves convergence to $\rho$, where $\gamma-\rho$ is precisely the quantity that has to stay below $\gamma$ for the theorem to apply at all. In the boundary regime $\rho$ can be arbitrarily close to 0, so "converges to an approximate max-margin solution" can mean "converges to something with a vanishingly small margin guarantee."

Fifth, evaluation. The synthetic experiments ($n=200$, $d=5$, $k=10$) and the MNIST two-layer network are qualitatively consistent and the per-sample figures are convincing — cosine similarity to $\bar W$ goes to 1 while cosine similarity to $W^*$ stagnates. But nothing tests the quantitative predictions: no sweep verifying the $m/(1-\beta_1)$ rate scaling, no probe of the $m^3(1-\beta_1)$ threshold, no attempt to see whether the threshold is tight. Given that the sharpest claims are about constants and trade-offs, this is a missed opportunity. There is also no lower bound showing that momentum or VR must slow margin convergence.

Finally, a scope caveat: the batch-size-one theorem is proved only on a hand-built orthogonal scale-skewed dataset ($x_i = \alpha_i e_{y_i}$) engineered so that the normalized per-sample update is exactly independent of $W_t$. That is a legitimate way to get an explicit answer, but it is a very special geometry — features are class-orthogonal, so the $K$ columns of $W$ evolve independently. The claim that "there may not exist a unified implicit bias theory for small batch sizes" is suggestive rather than established.

Proof sketch

(a) What is proved. Assumptions: linear separability with margin $\gamma > 0$; $\max_i |x_i|_1 \le R$; a decreasing, non-summable, vanishing stepsize; and a technical self-referential schedule condition of the form $\sum_s \beta^s(\exp(c_1\sum_{\tau\le s} \eta_{t-\tau}) - 1) \le c_2\eta_t$, verified for $\eta_t = ct^{-a}$, $a \in (0,1]$. All results are deterministic: they hold for every realization of the reshuffling.

Theorem 4.1 (no momentum): if $\rho := \gamma - 4(m-1)R > 0$, the normalized-margin gap is bounded by $[\sum_{s\ge t_2} \eta_s e^{-(\rho/4)\sum_{\tau<s}\eta_\tau} + \sum_{s<t_2}\eta_s + \sum_{s\ge t_2}\eta_s^2] / \sum_{s<t}\eta_s$. Since $\gamma \le 2R$ always, the hypothesis forces $m < 1 + \gamma/4R \le 3/2$, i.e. $b = n$. Corollary 4.3 gives rates for $\eta_t = ct^{-a}$; best rate $\approx t^{-1/2}$.

Proposition 4.2 (counterexample): for the $n=2$, $b=1$ dataset above and any positive stepsize sequence, random-reshuffling SignSGD from $W_0=0$ never strictly classifies both points, and $L(W_t) \ge (1/2)\log 2$ for all $t$.

Theorem 4.4 (momentum): under $\rho := \gamma - 2(1-\beta_1)m(m^2-1)R > 0$, the gap to $\rho$ is bounded by the same expression with $\sum\eta_s^2$ weighted by $m/(1-\beta_1)$ and an extra additive constant $D = 4R\eta_0/(1-\sqrt{\beta_1})$. The bound is dimension-free, improving Fan et al.'s $O((d\log t + nd)/t^{1/2})$ to $O((\log t + n)/t^{1/2})$ at $a=1/2$.

Theorem 4.7 (variance reduction): with the SVRG estimator $V_t = \nabla L_{B_t}(W_t) - \nabla L_{B_t}(\tilde W_t) + \nabla L(\tilde W_t)$, with or without momentum and for any batch size, the gap is to the true $\gamma$, with batch-dependent constant $C_m = m^{2+a}$ (no momentum) or $m^{2+a}/(1-\beta_1)$ (with momentum).

Theorem 4.10 (batch size one): on the orthogonal scale-skewed dataset, per-sample SignSGD and per-sample Normalized-SGD (which coincide with Spectral-SGD, since a single-sample gradient is rank one) drive the loss to zero and converge in direction to $\bar W/|\bar W|_F$, where $\bar W = \sum_i v_i\,\mathrm{sign}(x_i)^\top$. Crucially $\bar W$ is independent of the scales $\alpha_i$ and depends only on label frequencies — class imbalance directly tilts the limit — whereas the full-batch max-margin solution is determined by the hard samples regardless of frequency.

(b) How it is proved. The skeleton is the Soudry-style margin argument specialized to steepest descent, built around the proxy $G(W) = (1/n)\sum_i(1 - S_{y_i}(Wx_i))$. Three facts make $G$ the right object: $\gamma G(W) \le |\nabla L(W)|_* \le 2R\,G(W)$ (both directions from norm duality — the lower bound is just the definition of $\gamma$ applied to the dual-norm variational problem); $G \le L \le 2G$ once $L \le \log2/n$; and $G$ is multiplicatively stable, $G(W') \le e^{2R|W'-W|_{\max}}G(W)$. Every noise term is bounded as a _multiple of $G$_, so it can be compared directly against the signal $\gamma G$ and absorbed into the margin.

The per-step engine is a descent lemma. Second-order Taylor gives $L(W_{t+1}) \le L(W_t) - \eta_t\langle\nabla L, \Delta_t\rangle + \text{curvature}$, where curvature is handled by $x^\top\Delta^\top(\mathrm{diag}(s)-ss^\top)\Delta x \le 4R^2(1-s_c)|\Delta|^2$, proved by Hölder plus $|\mathrm{diag}(s)-ss^\top|_1 \le 4(1-s_c)$ plus the rank-one bound. Writing $\langle\nabla L, -\eta_t\Delta_t\rangle = \langle\nabla L - G_t, -\eta_t\Delta_t\rangle - \eta_t\langle G_t,\Delta_t\rangle$ and using $\langle G_t,\Delta_t\rangle = |G_t|_*$ (duality) gives the master inequality $\le 2\eta_t|\nabla L(W_t) - G_t|_{\mathrm{sum}} - \eta_t\gamma G(W_t)$. Everything hinges on bounding the signal-to-full-gradient deviation.

For plain mini-batch this is Lemma C.11: a finite-population-correction identity $\nabla L = (1/m)\nabla L_B + ((m-1)/m)\nabla L_{B^c}$ gives $\Xi = ((m-1)/m)(\nabla L_B - \nabla L_{B^c})$, and the per-sample bound $|\nabla\ell_i|_{\mathrm{sum}} \le 2R(1-s_{iy_i})$ yields $|\Xi|_{\mathrm{sum}} \le 2(m-1)R\,G(W)$. Both signal and noise are proportional to $G$, hence the comparison $\gamma$ vs $4(m-1)R$, hence $m=1$.

For momentum the key is Lemma C.12, the cleverest lemma in the paper. Write $E_t = \sum_j(1-\beta_1)\beta_1^{t-j}\Xi_j$ and split the horizon into complete epochs plus the current partial epoch. Random reshuffling makes $\sum_{j\in\text{epoch}}\Xi_j = 0$ exactly, so within each epoch one may subtract an arbitrary constant baseline from the weights without changing the sum. What remains is only the variation of the weights inside an epoch, bounded by $|\beta_1^{t-km-l} - \beta_1^{t-km}| \le \beta_1^{t-(k+1)m}\cdot l(1-\beta_1)$, which after summing and a geometric series gives $|E_t|_{\mathrm{sum}} \le (1-\beta_1)m(m^2-1)R\,G(W)$ — a noise floor the user can drive to zero with $\beta_1$. Two further terms appear: the staleness term, bounded via $|W_{t-\tau}-W_t|_{\max} \le \sum\eta_{t-j}$ (normalized steps!) and then by the schedule assumption as second order; and the initialization term $\beta_1^{t+1}|\nabla L|_*$, whose $\eta$-weighted sum is the harmless constant $D$.

For variance reduction the mechanism is simpler: $|V_t - \nabla L(W_t)|_{\mathrm{sum}} \le 2(m-1)R(e^{2R|W_t-\tilde W_t|_{\max}}-1)G(W_t)$, and since the snapshot is at most $m$ normalized steps behind, $|W_t-\tilde W_t|_{\max} \le m\eta_{t-m}$. Using $e^x-1 \le xe^x$ gives a deviation of order $\Theta(m^{2+a})\eta_tG$. The extra $\eta_t$ is the whole point: the noise enters as $\alpha_1\eta_t^2G$ rather than $c\eta_tG$, so it never subtracts from $\gamma$.

From the descent inequality the margin argument is standard but carefully executed. Choose $t_1$ so second-order terms are $\le \rho/2$, telescope, show some iterate reaches $L \le \log2/n$ hence separation. Then $1-x \le e^{-x}$ converts the recursion into $L(W_t) \le L(W_{t_2})\exp(-\rho\sum\eta_sG/L + \alpha_1\sum\eta_s^2)$. The margin lower bound is the neat step: $nL(W_t) \ge (\log2)e^{-z_{\min}(t)}$, and since $L(W_{t_2}) \le \log2/n$ the constants cancel exactly. Dividing by $|W_t| \le |W_0| + \sum\eta_s$ (again because steps are normalized) yields the bound.

The counterexample is a symmetry argument. The batch-size-one theorem works the opposite way: an induction shows $W_t$ always has equal off-diagonal entries within each column, forcing the non-target softmax probabilities equal, so $e_y - p = K\varepsilon(e_y - 1/K)$ and the normalized gradient is exactly $M_i = \bar u_{y_i}\bar x_i^\top$ — independent of $W_t$ and of $\alpha_i$. With a weight-independent update, the epoch recursion has drift $O(can^2/(rn)^{a+1})$, summable because $a+1>1$, while the signal $\sum_r\eta_{rn}$ diverges. Signal beats drift.

Broader context

The relevant background is the "steepest descent under a general norm" view of optimizers. Given a norm on parameters, steepest descent takes the unit-norm step best aligned with the gradient; the maximizer is the dual-norm attainer. Max-norm gives coordinatewise sign (SignGD, and by extension Adam, which Balles–Hennig and others showed behaves sign-like), Frobenius gives gradient normalization, spectral norm gives $UV^\top$ from the SVD — which is precisely Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), implemented via Newton–Schulz orthogonalization. The implicit-bias question is then: on separable data, which zero-loss solution does each geometry select? The answer, going back to Gunasekar et al. (2018), is the max-margin separator in that same norm. This is why the geometry matters in practice: minimizing the max-norm spreads weight mass evenly across coordinates, while minimizing the spectral norm equalizes singular values and pushes toward high-effective-rank weights — essentially a theoretical account of why Muon's updates behave like orthogonalized ones.

Two papers to know. Fan, Schmidt and Thrampoulidis (2025), "Implicit bias of spectral descent and Muon," is the direct parent — this paper inherits its proxy-function machinery and improves its rate by removing the dimension factor. Baek, Song and Yun (2025) on per-sample Adam is the closest sibling on the stochastic side; the present paper's advantages are that it covers a whole family of norms, uses genuine random reshuffling instead of a fixed deterministic cycle, and supplies rates rather than asymptotics. Worth also knowing Nacson et al. (2019) on stochastic GD and margin, and Cutkosky–Mehta (2020) on momentum removing the large-batch requirement for normalized SGD — the convergence-theory analogue of what is proved here for implicit bias.

The obvious follow-up is a matching lower bound and a typical-case analysis. Everything here is worst-case over reshufflings; the natural conjecture is that under random reshuffling, with high probability, the true threshold is much milder than $m^3(1-\beta_1) \lesssim \gamma/R$ — perhaps $m(1-\beta_1)$ or even $\sqrt m(1-\beta_1)$, since the accumulated momentum error is a sum of mean-zero increments with substantial cancellation that the triangle inequality throws away. Proving that would require martingale/exchangeable-pair concentration for the reshuffled error sequence, a genuinely open technical problem, and would turn the batch–momentum trade-off from a qualitative curve into a usable design rule. A second direction I find more interesting: the per-sample bias $\bar W$ is a frequency-weighted prototype classifier, provably insensitive to sample scales. Max-margin solutions are determined by the hardest, most extreme points; the averaged bias is determined by class counts. That suggests a robustness story worth proving — under label noise or outliers, the small-batch bias may generalize better than the max-margin bias, inverting the usual implicit-bias moral.

On a connection to theoretical IR, two links are real rather than decorative. First, generative retrieval with docid classification heads, and dense retrieval trained with InfoNCE, are literally softmax cross-entropy over a very large label space with small batches — structurally the setting of this paper with $k$ = number of documents or docid tokens. Theorem 4.10 says that in the small-batch, no-stabilization regime the learned direction depends on label frequency and not at all on the geometry of hard examples. That is a precise, mechanistic account of popularity bias: the optimizer's implicit bias, not just the data distribution, tilts the representation toward frequent documents, and the tilt is invariant to how "hard" or informative any individual example is. If that transfers beyond the orthogonal construction, it predicts that popularity bias in generative retrieval should be sensitive to batch size and momentum in a specific, testable way — large batch or high momentum should restore the margin-driven (hard-negative-driven) solution, small batch should not. Second, the Schatten-norm side speaks to embedding geometry: spectral-norm steepest descent biases toward balanced singular-value spectra, exactly the isotropy property that makes embeddings quantize and partition well for ANN indices. Whether the choice of optimizer geometry systematically changes the effective rank and anisotropy of learned retrieval embeddings — and hence downstream index quality under PQ or HNSW — is a question this framework makes precise and, as far as I know, nobody has asked. Both are speculative extrapolations from a linear-model theorem, and should be treated as hypotheses to test.

title: The Implicit Bias of Adam on Separable Data
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-22

The Implicit Bias of Adam on Separable Data

Main idea

The question here is not whether Adam minimizes the training loss but which zero-loss solution it picks. On linearly separable data with logistic or exponential loss the empirical risk has no minimizer — the iterates run off to infinity — so all the information about what was learned is in the direction $w_t/|w_t|$. The classical answer for gradient descent (Soudry et al., Ji–Telgarsky) is that this direction converges to the maximum $\ell_2$-margin separator. The paper asks the same question for full-batch Adam and answers: the maximum $\ell_\infty$-margin separator, i.e. the solution of $\min |w|_\infty$ subject to $y_i\langle w,x_i\rangle \ge 1$.

The reason this was open, and the reason the paper is worth reading, is the stability constant $\epsilon$. Adam's update is $\eta_t\, m_t/(\sqrt{v_t}+\epsilon)$, and Wang et al. (2022) showed that with $\epsilon>0$ fixed, Adam eventually degenerates into gradient descent with momentum and inherits the $\ell_2$ bias — simply because on separable data the gradients decay exponentially, so after enough iterations $\sqrt{v_t}\ll\epsilon$ and the preconditioner becomes the identity. That is an artifact of the order of limits: implicit-bias statements are about $t\to\infty$, and no one runs Adam until the second moment falls below $10^{-16}$. This paper takes $\epsilon=0$, which is the regime that actually describes finite-time practice, and shows the bias is completely different. In that regime Adam behaves like a (momentum-smoothed, inexact) sign descent, which is steepest descent in the $\ell_\infty$ geometry, and the margin it maximizes is the one dual to that geometry.

The second contribution is quantitative. For any non-increasing schedule with $\sum_t \eta_t=\infty$ and $\eta_t\to0$, the normalized $\ell_\infty$-margin gap is bounded by roughly $\big(\sum_{\tau<t_0}\eta_\tau + d\sum_{\tau=t_0}^{t-1}\eta_\tau^{3/2}\big)/\sum_{\tau<t}\eta_\tau$, and the loss decays as $\exp(-\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\sum\eta_\tau)$. Specializing to $\eta_t=(t+2)^{-a}$ gives $O(d\,t^{-a/2})$ for $a<2/3$, $O(t^{-1/3}\log t)$ at $a=2/3$, $O(t^{-(1-a)})$ for $2/3<a<1$, and $O(1/\log t)$ at $a=1$. So for $a<1$ the margin converges at a polynomial rate, against the $O(\log\log t/\log t)$ known for constant-step GD.

Critique

The genuinely clever piece of machinery is Lemma 6.1, and it deserves to be singled out. The obstacle to any implicit-bias analysis of Adam is that $m_t$ and $v_t$ are exponential moving averages of stale gradients, while on separable data the gradient magnitude collapses exponentially; a stale gradient can be exponentially larger than the current one, so any absolute error bound on $|m_t - \nabla R(w_t)|$ is vacuous. The authors instead prove a relative bound: $|m_t[k]-(1-\beta_1^{t+1})\nabla R(w_t)[k]| \le c_m\eta_t\, G(w_t)$ and $|\sqrt{v_t[k]}-\sqrt{1-\beta_2^{t+1}}|\nabla R(w_t)[k]|| \le c_v\sqrt{\eta_t}\,G(w_t)$, where $G(w)=-\frac1n\sum_i\ell'(\langle w,z_i\rangle)$ is the natural gradient scale. The mechanism is that for logistic/exponential losses the ratio $\ell'(\langle w_{t-\tau},z_i\rangle)/\ell'(\langle w_t,z_i\rangle)$ is controlled by $e^{|\langle w_t-w_{t-\tau},z_i\rangle|}$, and Adam's own normalization caps that displacement: $m_t[k]\le\alpha\sqrt{v_t[k]}$ means each coordinate moves at most $\alpha\eta_\tau$ per step. Assumption 4.4 is then exactly the statement that the geometric decay of the EMA weights beats this drift. The errors scale with the same quantity that is vanishing, so they cancel in the ratio — which is the whole trick.

The second nice piece is Lemma 6.4, the upper bound $|w_t|_\infty\le\sum_{t_0})$. That is where Assumption 4.2 (initial gradient coordinates bounded away from zero by $\rho$) earns its keep, and it enters only as $\log(1/\rho)$.}^{t-1}\eta_\tau + C\sum_{\tau1$, and that would only prove the normalized margin converges to $\gamma/\alpha$ — useless. Getting the leading constant to be exactly $1$ is what makes the theorem an equality rather than a constant-factor statement, and it is done with a Cauchy–Schwarz step followed by a telescoping-logarithm argument using $1-v_{\tau-\tau'}/v_\tau\le\log(v_\tau/v_{\tau-\tau'

Now the weaknesses. First, the headline comparison "polynomial versus logarithmic" is oversold. Write the bound in terms of the parameter norm rather than the iteration count: at the optimal $a=2/3$ the norm grows as $|w_t|_\infty\asymp\sum\eta\asymp t^{1/3}=:W$ and the margin gap is $\asymp \log W/W$, while GD's classical result is a gap of $\asymp\log\log W/W$ in $|w_t|_2=W$. Per unit of norm the two algorithms are essentially identical — Adam is even marginally worse. The entire speedup comes from the fact that a normalized update does not shrink when the gradient shrinks, so the norm grows polynomially instead of logarithmically. Normalized or aggressively-stepped GD (Nacson et al. 2019; Ji–Telgarsky 2021) gets the same acceleration in the $\ell_2$ geometry. The real content of the paper is the change of geometry, not the speed, and the paper does not draw that distinction.

Second, the $d$-dependence is quietly expensive. The factor $d$ in $O(d\,t^{-a/2})$ comes from the "bad coordinate" set in Lemma A.3: coordinates where $|\nabla R(w_t)[k]|$ falls below the $O(\sqrt{\eta_t}G)$ error floor can have an entirely wrong sign, and each of up to $d$ such coordinates contributes an $O(\sqrt{\eta_t}G)$ error. The burn-in is also $t_2\asymp d^{2/a}$. Combining, the iteration complexity to reach margin gap $\varepsilon$ is $\tilde O\big((d/\varepsilon)^{2/a}\big)$, minimized at $a=2/3$ with $\tilde O((d/\varepsilon)^3)$. Polynomial, yes, but with a cubic dimension dependence that the abstract does not mention.

Third, the assumptions. $\eta_t\to0$ is required by Assumption 4.3, so constant learning rate — the practically dominant case — is not covered, even though Assumption 4.4 is verified for it in Lemma C.1. Everything is full-batch and linear; the extension to homogeneous networks is conjectured in the conclusion and is the hard part.

Finally the experiments are thin: $n=d=50$ Gaussian data, and the reported dataset is selected from ten as the one where the $\ell_2$- and $\ell_\infty$-max-margin directions differ most. That selection is disclosed, which is honest, but it means the figures illustrate rather than test. More pointedly, Figure 2 shows $a=0.3$ converging fastest, contradicting the theory's prediction that $a=2/3$ is optimal; the authors wave this off as worst-case bounds being loose. That is plausible, but it means the one sharp, falsifiable quantitative prediction of the paper is not supported by its own experiment.

Proof sketch

What is proved. Assume (4.1) linear separability, (4.2) $\nabla R(w_0)[k]^2\ge\rho$ for every coordinate (ensuring $v_t[k]>0$ forever), (4.3) $\eta_t$ non-increasing with $\sum\eta_t=\infty$, $\eta_t\to0$, and (4.4) a technical schedule condition (proved for $\eta_t=(t+2)^{-a}$, $a\in(0,1]$, and for small constant $\eta$). Let $\gamma=\max_{|w|_\infty\le1}\min_i\langle w,y_ix_i\rangle$ and $B=\max_i|x_i|_1$. Then for $\beta_1\le\beta_2$ there is a burn-in $t_0=\mathrm{poly}[n,d,(1-\beta_1)^{-1},(1-\beta_2)^{-1},\gamma^{-1},B,\log(1/\rho),R(w_0)]$ such that for all $t\ge t_0$: $R(w_t)\le\frac{\log 2}{n}e^{-\frac{\gamma}{2}\sum_{t_0}$ and the normalized-margin gap obeys the bound quoted above. The guarantees are genuinely finite-time for $t\ge t_0$. Only Corollary 4.6, the actual limit $\lim_t\min_i\langle w_t,z_i\rangle/|w_t|}^{t-1}\eta_\tau_\infty=\gamma$, is asymptotic, obtained from the finite-time bound by Stolz–Cesàro. Note the guarantee is on the margin value; directional convergence follows only when the max-$\ell_\infty$-margin solution is unique, which is not generic — the $\ell_\infty$ problem is a linear program and its optimal set can be a face of positive dimension.

How it is proved. The skeleton is: sandwich the unnormalized margin from below and $|w_t|_\infty$ from above, both by $\sum\eta_\tau$ with matching leading constants, and take the ratio.

The duality ingredient is Lemma A.1: $\gamma\le\min_{r\in\Delta_n}|Z^\top r|_1$, proved by Fenchel–Young with $f=\iota_{\Delta_n}$, $g=|\cdot|_1$. Since $L'(w)/G(w)\in\Delta_n$ and $\nabla R=Z^\top L'$, this gives $|\nabla R(w)|_1\ge\gamma G(w)$ — the standard margin-duality identity, here in the $\ell_1/\ell_\infty$ pairing rather than the $\ell_2$ one.

Step 1 is the relative-error lemma described above. Step 2 converts it into a descent lemma. The key inner product is $\langle\nabla R(w_t), m_t/\sqrt{v_t}\rangle$, which would equal $|\nabla R(w_t)|_1$ if the update were exactly $\mathrm{sign}(\nabla R)$. Lemma A.3 bounds the deviation by splitting coordinates into a "good" set where the denominator is within a factor 2 of nominal, and a "bad" set below the noise floor contributing the $d\sqrt{\eta_t}$ term. A second-order Taylor step with $(m_t/\sqrt{v_t})^\top\nabla^2R\,(m_t/\sqrt{v_t})\le\alpha^2B^2G(w)$ yields $R(w_{t+1})\le R(w_t)-\tfrac{\gamma\eta_t}{2}G(w_t)$ once $\beta_1^{t/2}$ and $\eta_t$ are small enough. For exponential loss $G=R$ exactly and this integrates to the stated exponential decay.

Step 3 turns the loss bound into a margin lower bound: since $R(w_t)\le\log2/n$ forces all margins non-negative, $e^{-\min_i\langle w_t,z_i\rangle}\le\frac{n}{\log2}R(w_t)$, so taking logs gives $\min_i\langle w_t,z_i\rangle\ge\gamma\sum\eta_\tau - C_3d\sum(\eta_\tau^{3/2}+\eta_\tau^2)-C_4$.

Step 4 is the matching norm upper bound via the Cauchy–Schwarz plus telescoping-log argument, adapted from Xie–Li's AdamW analysis. Dividing Step 3 by Step 4 gives the theorem; the corollary rates are then plain integral estimates of $\sum t^{-a}$ and $\sum t^{-3a/2}$, with $3a/2=1$ at $a=2/3$ producing the logarithmic transition.

Broader context

Implicit bias is the branch of learning theory that asks which minimizer an optimizer selects when the training objective is degenerate, since in the interpolating regime generalization is decided entirely by that selection and not by the loss value. The foundational result is Soudry–Hoffer–Nacson–Gunasekar–Srebro (2018): GD on separable data converges in direction to the $\ell_2$ max-margin SVM, at the painfully slow $O(\log\log t/\log t)$. Gunasekar et al. (2018) generalized to steepest descent with respect to an arbitrary norm, which biases toward the max margin in that same norm — coordinate descent giving the $\ell_1$ max margin, sign descent the $\ell_\infty$ one. Lyu–Li and Ji–Telgarsky lifted the picture to homogeneous networks. In parallel, a line of work (Balles–Hennig 2018; Bernstein et al.; Kunstner et al. 2023) argues that Adam is best understood as sign descent with momentum. This paper is the rigorous meeting point of those two lines. The two most relevant neighbours are Wang et al. (2022), which reaches the opposite conclusion because it keeps $\epsilon>0$, and Xie–Li (2024) on AdamW.

A point worth internalizing, which the paper does not stress: maximizing the $\ell_\infty$-margin means minimizing $|w|_\infty$ at fixed margin, and minimum-$\ell_\infty$-norm solutions are anti-sparse — they push many coordinates to the same maximal magnitude. So Adam's implicit bias is toward dense, magnitude-equalized weight vectors, the opposite of what people often loosely assume about adaptive methods. That suggests a follow-up: a clean statistical separation. The class ${|w|_\infty\le1}$ against $\ell_1$-bounded data has dimension-dependent Rademacher complexity, whereas the $\ell_2/\ell_2$ pairing does not; one ought to be able to construct paired distributions where Adam's classifier provably needs $\Omega(d)$ more samples than GD's, and a complementary family where the ordering reverses. That would give a theoretical backbone to Wilson et al.'s (2017) empirical "marginal value of adaptive methods". A second and more tractable follow-up is a unified treatment of $\epsilon$: the results of Wang et al. and of this paper are the two endpoints of a single phase diagram in which the crossover happens when $\sqrt{v_t}\sim\epsilon$. A theorem with an explicit $\epsilon$-dependent transition time would settle the apparent contradiction rather than sidestepping it.

On the IR side I would not force a connection: this is standard-issue optimization theory and worth knowing on its own terms, particularly the relative-error EMA lemma, which is the kind of tool that transfers. The one link that is real rather than decorative concerns vector search. Essentially every dense retriever and every generative-retrieval decoder is trained with AdamW, and this paper says the optimizer is not neutral about the coordinate-wise geometry of the solution: it prefers weight vectors whose coordinates have comparable magnitude. If that carries over even approximately to the embedding layers of a retriever, it bears on infrastructure that is highly sensitive to coordinate scale — scalar and product quantization, which behave much better when coordinate magnitudes are homogeneous, and random-hyperplane LSH, whose collision probabilities degrade when a few coordinates dominate. The received explanation for why learned embeddings quantize well is usually about the data or explicit regularization; "the optimizer has an anti-sparse implicit bias" is an alternative hypothesis that is cheap to test (train the same dual encoder with SGD versus Adam, compare the coordinate-magnitude distribution and the recall drop under PQ at fixed bit budget). That said, the theorem is about a linear classifier under separable data, and the gap to a transformer encoder trained with InfoNCE is enormous — treat it as a hypothesis-generator, not evidence.

title: [2407.03851] Implicit Hypersurface Approximation Capacity in Deep ReLU Networks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-21

Implicit Hypersurface Approximation Capacity in Deep ReLU Networks

Jonatan Vallin, Karl Larsson, Mats G. Larson, 2024 — arXiv:2407.03851

Main idea. The paper asks how well a deep ReLU network of fixed width d+1 can approximate a hypersurface, where the surface is the network's zero set rather than its graph. The target is the graph of a C² function φ on a ball of radius R in ℝ^d, with bounded second derivatives. The network F: ℝ^{d+1} → ℝ should satisfy sign F(x,y) = sign(φ(x) − y) outside a vertical ε-band around that graph. This matters for classification: append a zero coordinate to the data, and the network's decision boundary in ℝ^d is the slice of its zero set at y = 0.

The main result is an explicit construction. For any δ ≤ R(1 − 1/√2), there is a width-(d+1) network whose zero set is exactly the graph of a piecewise-linear φ̂ with sup|φ − φ̂| ≤ C(d−1)R^{3/2}δ^{1/2}. Its depth is at most about d·(32R/δ)^{(d+1)/2}.

The most interesting part. The construction rests on a geometric reinterpretation of a ReLU layer, building on the authors' earlier work. Up to an invertible affine map, a full-rank ReLU layer is a projection onto a polyhedral cone. The cone's apex solves Ax + b = 0, and points outside it are pushed onto its faces along the dual vectors of A. On a bounded region you can push all but one facet far away. That leaves a clean gadget: a layer that is the identity on a half-space and projects its complement onto the boundary hyperplane along any direction ξ you choose.

The key choice is ξ = the tangent direction of the graph at the centre of the spherical cap being cut off. The piece of the surface over that cap then slides almost onto the surface itself, with an offset of only about √r·δ^{3/2} by Taylor's theorem. Repeating this peels the graph like an onion, from the outside in. Each layer cuts off one cap and folds that piece of the surface onto the edge of what remains. Only a tiny patch is left at the end, and the final affine map's kernel matches it with the tangent plane. The decision boundary is then the preimage of that hyperplane under the whole chain of folds.

Unlike Hanin–Sellke-style constructions, this needs no extra channels to carry the input forward. The width is exactly d+1.

Broader context. Expressivity theory asks what functions and sets networks of a given depth and width can represent. Lu et al. (2017) and Hanin and Sellke (2017) pin down the minimal width for universal approximation, about d+1 for continuous functions. Montúfar et al. (2014) count linear regions. Work on decision regions shows that networks of width at most d produce only unbounded or connected regions, and the extra embedding dimension here avoids that obstruction. The contribution is geometric insight: you can literally watch how a surface is carried through the layers.

A natural follow-up is to put precision only where it is needed. The authors note that a classifier needs precision only near the other class, so placing caps densely only where the margin is thin would give margin-dependent depth bounds. Another is to test empirically whether trained networks form cone-projection "peeling" layers.

There is no forced IR link. The honest value is as something new to learn: a clean mental model of a ReLU layer as a cone projection, useful whenever you reason about decision boundaries of learned scorers.

Proof sketch. Claim (Theorem 5.1): let φ be C² on a ball of radius R with bounded Hessian, and let δ ≤ R(1 − 1/√2). Then a width-(d+1) ReLU network of depth at most (14/3)·d·(32R/δ)^{(d+1)/2} has a zero set equal to the graph of φ̂, with sup|φ − φ̂| ≤ C(d−1)R^{3/2}δ^{1/2}.

The proof builds up in stages:

  1. One cut. A half-space tangent to the ball of radius r − δ removes a cap of height δ and base radius about √(2rδ). A Taylor expansion in local coordinates bounds how far each point on the surface drifts when projected along the tangent direction: about (d−1)√r·δ^{1/2}·t, where t ≤ δ is the distance travelled.
  2. One shell of cuts. Tangent points are placed on an ε-net of the sphere, so the resulting polytope fits between radii r − δ and r and the radius shrinks by at least 3δ/4 per shell. A point may be projected several times within a shell, and two facts control this. First, hyperplanes that meet inside the ball have normals at non-obtuse angles, so a projected point stays inside all earlier half-spaces. Second, a telescoping bound, t_i ≤ (‖x_{i−1}‖² − ‖x_i‖²)/(2(r−δ)), caps the total path length at about 1.2δ. Each shell therefore adds only about √r·δ^{3/2} of error.
  3. Accumulation. Every layer commutes with vertical shifts, so earlier errors pass through unchanged and simply add. With about R/δ shells, the local δ^{3/2} error becomes a global δ^{1/2} error. The layer count is the number of shells times the ε-net size.
  4. Closing. The final patch is matched by the tangent plane. A lemma shows that the preimage of a graph under each layer is again a graph, and that the preimage of an ε-band is an ε-band. The triangle inequality finishes the proof.

The rate is fairly weak, depth roughly (R²/ε)^{d+1}, because per-shell errors add up linearly across the shells. The authors argue the exponential dependence on d is unavoidable without further assumptions.

title: Vector Database Watermarking
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-21

Vector Database Watermarking

Ren, Fan, Yao, Qiu, Zhang, Yu, 2025 (OpenReview) — openreview.net/forum?id=Dbjzqvmd7t

Note: written from the abstract and background knowledge only. The OpenReview PDF link returned an HTML page (bot-check/redirect) instead of a PDF, so the full text was not available this run.

Main idea. A curated vector database (embeddings plus an ANN index) is a valuable asset, and someone can copy it wholesale. Watermarking hides ownership evidence in the data by slightly perturbing some vectors, so a suspect copy can later be checked. The paper's basic scheme has four steps:

  1. Derive an identifier per vector.
  2. Group the vectors.
  3. Use a keyed cryptographic mapping to decide which vectors carry which watermark bits.
  4. Modify those vectors.

This is the classic recipe from relational-database watermarking, carried over to vectors. The catch is that perturbing vectors changes ANN results, causing missed and false hits. The key observation is about HNSW. Its heuristic neighbour selection and pruning leave some nodes with very few edges, even none, and those nodes are rarely visited or returned by queries. The Transparent Vector Priority (TVP) scheme puts the watermark preferentially into these "transparent" vectors. The authors report about 75% fewer missed and false queries than the strongest prior watermarking baselines.

Critique. The core insight is clever and cheap. The watermark hides in exactly the part of the database that the index already ignores. But that framing raises questions the abstract doesn't answer, and I would check them in the full paper:

  • The transparency is tied to the owner's graph, not the data. A pirate who copies the raw vectors and rebuilds HNSW with different parameters (M, efConstruction, insertion order) or a different index (IVF-PQ, ScaNN, DiskANN) gets a different set of low-degree nodes. The watermarked vectors may then become ordinary, frequently returned vectors, so the "low impact" argument is specific to one index. Detection itself only needs the vectors, so ownership proof should survive, but the stealth and fidelity claims may not.
  • Rarely returned vectors are often an index defect. Nodes that HNSW can barely reach are a known recall problem. A system that repairs reachability (as some production indexes do) would expose exactly the watermarked vectors. Also, if these vectors are rarely returned, the watermark says little about whether a pirate's query service is using the stolen data. Black-box verification through query answers, rather than by inspecting vectors, would be weak.
  • The robustness analysis is what matters most. Obvious attacks include adding small noise to all vectors, subset selection, re-normalization, PCA or quantization (PQ codes), and rotation. A random orthogonal rotation preserves every inner product and every ANN result, yet it can destroy any watermark that depends on coordinates. Whether TVP's identifiers and modifications are rotation-invariant is the first thing I'd look for.
  • The metric is limited. Missed and false query counts measure fidelity, but a comparison at a fixed watermark detection strength (false-positive rate of the ownership test) is what makes the 75% number meaningful.

Broader context. Database watermarking goes back to Agrawal and Kiernan (2002), who embedded keyed bits in the least-significant bits of relational tuples. A closely related modern thread is watermarking embedding-as-a-service APIs against model extraction, for example EmbMarker (Peng et al., ACL 2023), which injects a trigger-dependent direction into returned embeddings. Vector database watermarking sits between the two: it protects the stored corpus rather than the encoder.

This one connects to your vector-search work. The question underneath TVP is theoretical: which points can be perturbed without changing any k-NN result, and by how much? For exact search, a point p can move freely as long as it doesn't cross any order-k Voronoi boundary that matters for the query distribution. That is a "k-NN stability radius," and watermark capacity is roughly the total slack across points, weighted by query density. A clean follow-up is to define watermark capacity versus retrieval distortion as a rate–distortion problem over the query distribution, and to prove index-independent bounds. That would fix the first critique by making transparency a property of the data geometry rather than of one HNSW build. Graph-reachability theory, such as the navigability analyses of HNSW and Vamana, could then explain why low-degree nodes arise and whether they are stable across index rebuilds.

title: How Can Deep Neural Networks Fail Even With Global Optima?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-21

How Can Deep Neural Networks Fail Even With Global Optima?

Qingguang Guan, 2024 — arXiv:2407.16872

Main idea. The paper asks: if training reaches a global minimum (zero training MSE or MAE), how badly can the network still generalize? The answer is built by hand. For ReLU, Parametric ReLU and sigmoid networks, the author writes down explicit weights that interpolate a grid training set exactly but output 0 everywhere outside tiny neighbourhoods of the training points. Each construction has a threshold bias b. At b = 0 (in 1-D) you get the ordinary piecewise-linear interpolant. As b → 1 (or b → d in d dimensions), the output shrinks to "spikes" while the loss stays exactly zero. So the set of global minima contains a continuous path from a good solution to a useless one.

A second contribution is a depth-extension trick: any shallow approximation result carries over to any depth by appending layers as narrow as one neuron. The showcase is 3×3 grayscale images labelled "all-dark" vs "all-light." With a colour-reduction grid, the network memorizes 2·64⁹ training points using only 2313 first-layer neurons and 2 second-layer neurons. It then fails on any image that differs by one grey level in one pixel.

Critique. The depth-extension theorem is correct but not deep. For ReLU it is the standard identity-by-shift trick. For smooth activations it is near-identity linearization, close to Kidger and Lyons (2020), which the paper cites. The constant C_N in the error bound is left implicit and can grow with depth.

The overfitting constructions are also correct, but the existence of bad interpolating minima is not surprising. Zhang et al. (2017) showed memorization empirically. Liu, Papailiopoulos and Achlioptas (2020, "Bad Global Minima Exist and SGD Can Reach Them") went further and showed such minima are reachable. This paper stops at existence and never asks whether gradient descent from a normal initialization goes anywhere near these solutions. Its "numerical results" are plots of the hand-built functions.

The biggest gap is weight norm. The spikes need output weights that scale like 1/(1−b), so the bad optima have norms that blow up. Weight decay, norm-based generalization bounds and the implicit bias of gradient descent all disfavour exactly these solutions. Savarese et al. (2019) show that the minimum-norm 1-D ReLU interpolant is the linear spline, the b = 0 end of this family. The paper does not discuss this.

The claim that the image example contradicts the rule that overfitting needs parameters ≫ data points is overstated. The small width works only because the data lie on a tensor-product grid and the labels are defined coordinate by coordinate. For general function approximation, the second layer needs N^d neurons, which is the size of the dataset. There are also smaller issues:

  • The introduction samples data uniformly at random, but every construction needs a regular grid.
  • The image "ground truth" is defined only for images whose pixels are all dark or all light, so the reported 1/512 accuracy is not very meaningful.
  • MAE is called "Median Absolute Error" but defined as a mean.

Broader context. The paper sits between two literatures. One is approximation theory for networks: universal approximation (Cybenko, Hornik) and ReLU networks as finite elements (Yarotsky; He et al.). The other is the generalization puzzle of overparameterized interpolation: random-label memorization, double descent (Belkin et al., 2019) and implicit regularization.

The natural follow-up is to put numbers on what this paper only describes. Under a path-norm or weight-decay budget, what is the worst generalization error among zero-loss solutions? How much of parameter space drains into spike-like minima under SGD?

There is a loose link to generative retrieval. DSI-style models are trained to near-zero loss to memorize document-to-docid mappings, and whether such interpolating solutions generalize to unseen queries is exactly this question. This paper shows only that failure is possible, not how to analyse it.

Proof sketch. Depth extension (Theorem 2.1). If a K-hidden-layer network f_K approximates f, then for any N there is a (K+N)-layer network, with extra layers of width at least 1, whose output is within Cε of f_K.

  • For ReLU the result is exact. Feed p₁ = εf_K + c with c large enough that p₁ > 0. ReLU then acts as the identity, and you undo the shift and scaling at the end.
  • For C² activations with a′(c) ≠ 0, each layer renormalizes: p_n = (a(p_{n−1}) − a(c))/a′(c) + c. Taylor expansion around c gives a drift of O(ε²) per layer. Dividing by ε at the output leaves f_K + O(ε). For sigmoid this is p_n = 4σ(p_{n−1}) − 2.

Overfitting construction. Three ReLUs make a hat φ_i of height 1 around each training point x_i. A second-layer neuron computes ReLU(Σ_class φ_i − b)/(1−b). This equals the label at every training point for every b ∈ [0,1), so the loss is exactly zero, but it is nonzero only on an interval of radius (1−b)h around each point. In d dimensions the construction sums coordinate hats, which do not overlap within a coordinate, so the sum reaches d only at grid points. Taking b ∈ [d−1, d) confines the support to boxes of side 2(d−b)h, and the total support volume goes to 0 as b → d. PReLU uses a clipped ramp built from two PReLUs. Sigmoid gives only ε-optimal versions via steep sigmoid spikes. Adding the depth-extension layers makes every counterexample work at any depth.

title: Does Flatness imply Generalization for Logistic Loss in Univariate Two-Layer ReLU Network?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-21

Does Flatness imply Generalization for Logistic Loss in Univariate Two-Layer ReLU Network?

Dan Qiao, Yu-Xiang Wang, 2025 — arXiv:2512.01473

Main idea. For square loss, earlier work (Qiao et al., 2024) showed that "stable" solutions of univariate two-layer ReLU networks cannot overfit, at any width. A stable solution is one with λ_max(∇²L) ≤ 2/η, which is the set gradient descent with step size η can settle into (linear stability, Edge of Stability). Such solutions have bounded weighted total variation ∫|f''|·g, and that gives near-optimal nonparametric rates. This paper asks whether the same holds for logistic loss with labels y ~ Bernoulli(σ(f₀(x))). The answer is split.

On the negative side, for any labeling (even pure noise), a network that interpolates f(x_i) = y_i·γ_max has sharpness O((n²γ_max + 1)e^{−γ_max}). This goes to 0 as γ_max → ∞, so flatness alone guarantees nothing.

On the positive side, there are three results:

  • A norm-based generalization bound.
  • A weighted total-variation bound that holds only between the leftmost and rightmost "uncertain" training points, those with |f_θ(x_i)| ≤ γ.
