  • Under a weak-generalization assumption (excess risk goes to 0 at any rate), a stable solution achieves excess risk Õ(η^{−1/5} n_I^{−2/5}) on intervals inside f₀'s own uncertain region. This matches the minimax rate for BV⁽¹⁾ and does not depend on width.

Simulations with k = 400 neurons show that large step sizes give smoother fits. Small step sizes overfit, but still stall at finite functions: they hit the edge of stability before they can reach the flat minima at infinity.

The most interesting part. Logistic loss switches its own curvature off. The Gauss–Newton part of the Hessian weights each point's gradient outer product by σ'(y_i f(x_i)), and this weight decays exponentially once a prediction is confident. Under square loss every point adds curvature, so fitting noise forces sharpness. Under logistic loss a confident point, right or wrong, becomes invisible to the Hessian. Flatness therefore constrains the function only where it is unsure.

The fix works in two steps. First, prove a smoothness bound that uses only the uncertain points. This bound depends on the solution itself, so it cannot rule out the pathological case where no point is uncertain. Second, use the excess-risk assumption to show that the learned function's uncertain set roughly matches the ground truth's. That turns the bound into a guarantee that depends only on f₀ and the data distribution. The cost is visible: the guarantee disappears exactly where f₀ is confident, and a factor of about e^γ creates a real trade-off in choosing γ.

Broader context. This belongs to the "implicit bias of minima stability" line. Wu, Ma and E (2018) linked step size to reachable sharpness. Mulayoff, Michaeli and Soudry (2021) translated sharpness bounds into function space for univariate ReLU networks. Cohen et al.'s Edge of Stability paper (2021) supplies the empirical motivation. The negative result complements Dinh et al. (2017, "Sharp Minima Can Generalize") in the opposite direction: here flat minima fail to generalize. It also contrasts with Soudry et al. (2018), where logits on separable data diverge in the max-margin direction.

A natural follow-up would replace the weak-generalization assumption with an actual dynamics theorem. For example: with noisy labels and fixed η, GD at the edge of stability provably stays in a bounded-confidence region, which the paper observes empirically. Another option is a loss-normalized sharpness such as λ_max/L, which would penalize confident points again.

There is one modest IR link. Dense retrievers trained with softmax cross-entropy over in-batch negatives can also saturate their logits, so any sharpness-based story (SAM, large learning rates) for why such encoders generalize carries the same caveat.

Proof sketch. Negative result (Theorem 3.1). Place n points evenly on [−1, 1] with arbitrary labels. Use one active ReLU per point, with knots nudged slightly off the data, so that f(x_i) = y_i γ_max and f is piecewise linear in between. The Hessian splits into a σ'-weighted Gauss–Newton term and a residual term, and both weights are at most e^{−γ_max}. Balance each neuron's two layer weights at O(√(nγ_max)). Then ‖∇_θ f‖² = O(n²γ_max), so λ_max = O((n²γ_max + 1)e^{−γ_max}): polynomial growth loses to exponential decay.

Positive results. The argument has four steps:

  1. Bound the residual Hessian term by 2x_max·L, using e^{−t}/(1+e^{−t}) ≤ log(1+e^{−t}).
  2. Lower-bound the Gauss–Newton term with a test vector supported only on the uncertain points, whose weights are at least Γ(γ). Summing each neuron's contribution around its knot gives a Mulayoff-style bound 1 + 2∫|f''|h_γ ≤ (n/(n_γ Γ(γ)))·(λ_max + 2x_max L), restricted to the uncertain region.
  3. A pointwise lemma: wherever f₀ is uncertain and f_θ is confident (or the reverse) by margin ζ, the population loss gap is at least of order ζ²e^{−(γ+ζ)}. So the excess risk ε(n) bounds the fraction of mismatched points, and the solution-dependent quantities can be replaced by f₀-dependent ones.
  4. On an interval with weight at least c, this gives ∫_I|f''| ≤ (1/c)(1/η + x_max(1+B)). Both f and f₀ then lie in a BV⁽¹⁾ ball with metric entropy O(ε^{−1/2}), and a covering-plus-Bernstein argument gives the n_I^{−2/5} rate.

title: MUVERA: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-21

MUVERA: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings

Laxman Dhulipala, Majid Hadian, Rajesh Jayaram, Jason Lee, Vahab Mirrokni, 2024 (NeurIPS 2024) — arXiv:2405.19504

Main idea. Late-interaction models such as ColBERTv2 score a query token set Q against a document token set P with Chamfer similarity, Σ_q max_p ⟨q,p⟩, and standard MIPS indexes cannot serve this score directly. Current engines use a "single-vector heuristic" instead: one token-level MIPS query per query token, gather the parent documents, then rerank. PLAID stacks four pruning stages on top of this.

MUVERA replaces the whole pipeline with a data-oblivious map from a vector set to one Fixed Dimensional Encoding (FDE). It works as follows:

  • SimHash with k_sim hyperplanes splits space into B = 2^k_sim buckets.
  • The query FDE stores the sum of the query tokens in each bucket. The document FDE stores the centroid of the document tokens in each bucket. An empty document bucket is filled with the token whose SimHash code is nearest in Hamming distance.
  • Each bucket block is reduced to d_proj dimensions with a random ±1 projection.
  • The whole construction is repeated R_reps times and the results concatenated.

Retrieval is then DiskANN over PQ-compressed FDEs, followed by one Chamfer rerank. Offline, FDE Recall@N matches the heuristic's Recall@(1.75–5)N. End to end on BEIR, MUVERA averages about 10% higher recall and 90% lower latency than PLAID. MS MARCO is the exception, where it roughly ties.

Critique. The asymmetric design is elegant: query sums against document centroids give an estimator that never overestimates Chamfer. But the theory says little about the system that was actually run. Theorem 2.1 needs k_sim = O(log(m/εδ)/ε²), so d_FDE = (m/εδ)^O(1/ε²), which is astronomical at ε = 0.1. In practice k_sim is 3–5, d_proj = 8 and R_reps = 20, far outside that regime. In the theoretical regime almost every bucket is empty, so the Hamming fill-in does all the work: the FDE reduces to "match each query token to the document token with the nearest SimHash code." The centroid averaging, the interesting part of the design, is never really used by the proof.

The guarantee is also additive in normalized Chamfer. Top ColBERT scores often differ by a few hundredths, so an additive ε can exceed the gaps that decide the ranking. The "faster than brute force" claim of Theorem 2.2 is still linear in n. The sublinear speed in practice comes from DiskANN, which has no guarantee on FDE geometry.

The experiments also have gaps. They use a single encoder (ColBERTv2) and do not study how results depend on the number of tokens per document. Latency is measured single-threaded. The memory accounting leaves out the full token embeddings that the rerank still needs. Data-obliviousness is pitched as robustness to distribution shift, but no shift experiment is run.

Broader context. Multi-vector retrieval trades storage and speed for token-level matching. The main lines of work are ColBERT/ColBERTv2 with the PLAID engine, XTR (trained so that token retrieval alone suffices) and DESSERT (LSH over vector sets). The FDE technique descends from probabilistic tree embeddings of Earth Mover's Distance into ℓ₁ (Indyk; Andoni–Indyk–Krauthgamer), carried over to inner products.

This one sits squarely in your area, Shiguang. MUVERA is a reduction of set-to-set similarity search to MIPS, and the open question is how much dimension that reduction must cost. The max inside Chamfer is nonlinear, while any FDE scores with a bilinear form. A natural project is a lower bound on d_FDE for linear FDEs, data-oblivious or not, that ε-approximate Chamfer. Is 2^poly(1/ε) necessary, or is poly(1/ε, log m) achievable? This is a sign-rank-style question, close in spirit to Weller et al.'s (2025) analysis of the representational limits of single-vector embedding retrieval. A second direction is proving navigability or search guarantees for graph indexes built on FDE geometry, since that is where the practical speedup actually comes from.

Proof sketch. Claim (Theorem 2.1): for unit-vector sets with m = |Q| + |P|, and with k_sim and d_proj both O(ε⁻² log(m/εδ)), the normalized FDE inner product is within ±ε of normalized Chamfer, in expectation and with probability 1 − δ.

Upper bound: for each q, the FDE contributes the average of ⟨q,p⟩ over the document tokens in its bucket (or the single fill-in token). An average never exceeds the max. The random projections add only ±ε per pair by Johnson–Lindenstrauss-style concentration, union-bounded over the m² pairs.

Lower bound, where the key trick is: the query map is linear, so the score splits into per-token terms ⟨q, avg of p over S⟩. It then suffices to show that each q lands in a "good" bucket with high probability. SimHash acts as an angle estimator: each bit disagrees with probability θ(q,p)/π. By Hoeffding, the normalized Hamming distance is within ε of θ/π for every pair simultaneously, and this is what forces k_sim ≈ log(m/εδ)/ε². Two cases follow:

  • If a document token collides with q, its Hamming distance is 0, so its angle to q is at most πε.
  • If no token collides, the Hamming-nearest token p′ has angle at most θ(q,p_) + O(ε), where p_ is the true nearest neighbour.

Cosine is 1-Lipschitz in the angle, so in both cases ⟨q,p⟩ ≥ max_p ⟨q,p⟩ − O(ε). The failure event costs only O(εδ) in expectation because each term is bounded. The success probability is then boosted by repeating the construction R_reps = O(ε⁻² log 1/δ) times, and Theorem 2.2 union-bounds over the n documents.

title: Formation of Representations in Neural Networks
tags: Condensed Matter - Disordered Systems and Neural Networks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-21

Formation of Representations in Neural Networks

Liu Ziyin, Isaac Chuang, Tomer Galanti, Tomaso Poggio, 2024 — arXiv:2410.03006

Main idea. The paper asks whether a simple law governs what hidden representations look like after training, regardless of architecture or loss. Take any fully connected layer h_b = W h_a, with per-sample loss gradients g_a and g_b. On each side of the layer there are three second-moment matrices: the representation covariance H = E[hhᵀ], the gradient covariance G = E[ggᵀ], and the weight Gram matrix (WᵀW on the input side, WWᵀ on the output side). The Canonical Representation Hypothesis (CRH) says all six pairwise proportionalities hold after training: representation–gradient, representation–weight and gradient–weight alignment, on both sides.

Real layers usually satisfy only some of these relations. The Polynomial Alignment Hypothesis (PAH) handles that case: if one input-side and one output-side relation hold, the matrices become power laws of each other within a subspace, with exponents between −1 and 3. This splits layers into distinct "phases." The authors test it on synthetic MLPs, ResNet-18 (supervised and self-supervised on CIFAR-10) and a 100M-parameter, 6-layer transformer on OpenWebText, measuring alignment as the Pearson correlation between matrix entries. The ResNet penultimate layers reach alignment above 0.7 early in training, and larger weight decay always improves alignment. In the transformer, the eigenvalue exponent between H_b and G_b is 3 in layer 1, 2 in layer 2 and 1 in every later layer, all inside the predicted range.

The most interesting part. The alignment comes from a fluctuation–dissipation balance, not from anything specific to the loss. Expand one SGD step of h_b h_bᵀ and you get three terms. One is a learning term. One is a contraction from weight decay (−2γH_b). The third is an expansion from SGD's discretization noise, η·z²·G_b, where z = E‖h_a‖². Noise pushes the representation outward in exactly the directions where the gradient fluctuates, while weight decay pulls every direction back in. At stationarity these balance, so a representation's variance ends up proportional to its gradient's variance.

The consequence (Proposition 1) is elegant. Under representation–gradient alignment, perturbing the representation along a direction n leaves the loss locally unchanged exactly when Hn = 0. Task-irrelevant directions therefore have zero variance, and the representation is compact and invariant by construction. Neural collapse becomes a special case. Gradient–weight alignment turns out to be a basis-independent version of the neural feature ansatz: the original ansatz changes under a reparametrization f → Zf, but this version does not.

Broader context. A long line of work studies what structure trained networks converge to. Examples are neural collapse in the last layer of classifiers (Papyan, Han and Donoho, 2020), the neural feature ansatz linking weight Gram matrices to the average gradient outer product (Radhakrishnan et al., 2024), and representational convergence across models (the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, Huh et al., 2024). This paper tries to explain the first two with one stationarity argument that applies to every layer.

A natural follow-up is to make the phase picture predictive: derive which phase a layer lands in from the batch size, the weight decay and the rank of E[ΔW]. The authors also suggest injecting gradient noise on purpose to shape representations.

There is a modest, speculative link to vector search. If representation–gradient alignment holds for an embedding layer trained with a retrieval loss, then low-variance embedding directions are provably irrelevant to the loss. That would justify PCA-style truncation of dense embeddings, and it suggests ranking dimensions for truncation or quantization by gradient covariance rather than embedding covariance. The paper does not test this.

Proof sketch. Theorem 1 makes three assumptions: ‖h_a‖² and ‖g_b‖² can be replaced by their means, the relevant matrices are stationary in expectation, and the result holds to first order in ηγ. Under these it proves WWᵀ + c₁G_b = c₂H_b. At a local minimum it proves the full proportionality WWᵀ ∝ G_b ∝ H_b (and the input-side mirror).

The proof has three steps. First, expand Δ(W B_a Wᵀ) with ΔW = η(g_b h_aᵀ − γW) and take expectations, which gives z(E[g_b h_bᵀ] + transpose) + ηz²G_b = 2γH_b. Second, stationarity E[ΔW] = 0, multiplied by Wᵀ, gives E[g_b h_bᵀ] = γWWᵀ, which is symmetric. Third, stationarity of WWᵀ at a minimum reduces to E[ΔW ΔWᵀ] = 0, which gives zG_b = γ²WWᵀ. Substituting these into the first identity closes the chain.

The weak point is the third step. Requiring E[ΔWΔWᵀ] = 0 means the SGD updates have zero variance, which minibatch SGD generally cannot reach. The authors present this as the mechanism by which the CRH breaks, but it also means the fully aligned state is proved only under an idealized condition.

The "master theorem" behind the PAH is linear algebra. Because h_b = Wh_a and g_a = Wᵀg_b, any relation on one side carries over to the other after multiplying by W and Wᵀ; for example, H_a ∝ WᵀW gives H_b ∝ (WWᵀ)². Combining one relation from each side gives equations such as B = ABA, and pseudo-inverse lemmas show these force projection structure. The −1 to 3 exponent range falls out of this case analysis.

title: Tokenization as Finite-State Transduction
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-20

6. Tokenization as Finite-State Transduction

Marco Cognetta, Naoaki Okazaki (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15696

Main idea. The paper asks a formal-language question with an immediately practical payoff: given a regular language of character strings, is the set of token strings that a real tokenizer would actually emit for those characters also regular? The authors answer yes, constructively, for both MaxMatch/WordPiece and BPE, by exhibiting finite-state transducers over input alphabet $\Sigma$ (characters or bytes) and output alphabet $\Gamma$ (the subword vocabulary, with $\Sigma \subseteq \Gamma \subset \Sigma^+$). Two objects are carefully distinguished. The tokenization-agnostic lexicon transducer $T$ realizes the relation $\bigcup_{w\in\Gamma}(w_1\ldots w_n, w)$, $\varepsilon$-closed so it applies to arbitrary-length inputs; for a pattern DFA $A$, $\mathrm{MIN}(\mathrm{PROJ}(A \circ T))$ accepts every token sequence whose concatenation lies in $L(A)$ — the whole tokenization lattice. The tokenization-preserving version instead accepts only ${t : \mathrm{CONCAT}(t) \in L(A) \wedge \mathrm{Tok}(\mathrm{CONCAT}(t)) = t}$, i.e. the canonical tokenization and nothing else. For MaxMatch this is Song et al.'s Aho–Corasick failure-trie with "failure pops," re-read as a transducer with $\varphi$-transitions. For BPE the trick is different and is the paper's real content: each merge $(a,b) \to ab$ becomes a tiny three-state gadget $G_{(a,b)}$ over $\Gamma \times \Gamma$ (initial / active / abort), and BPE is realized as $A \circ G_{m_1} \circ \cdots \circ G_{m_k}$ in merge-priority order — no lexicon transducer needed, since the character string is its own zeroth tokenization.

Most interesting part. That BPE is finite-state at all is genuinely surprising: Algorithm 3 uses a priority queue, merges in non-left-to-right order, and builds a tree, all of which smells context-free. The escape hatch is Zouhar et al.'s (2023) observation that sweeping every merge once in priority order is equivalent to greedily popping the highest-priority applicable merge — because $(ab, c)$ can only fire after $(a, b)$ has. That converts a data-dependent schedule into a fixed, finite pipeline of relations, and regular relations are closed under composition. The gadget's cleverness is the deferred emission: reading a from $q_0$ outputs $\varepsilon$ (in case a merge completes), a self-loop on $q_1$ postpones through runs of a, and a $\varphi$-arc to the abort state emits the withheld a when the next symbol is not b. Honest caveats: (i) there is no theorem stating the construction realizes BPE exactly — correctness is argued by construction and worked example, and the leftmost-greedy convention for overlapping occurrences (e.g. aaa under $(a,a)$) is implicit in the $q_1$ self-loop rather than proved equivalent to any reference implementation; (ii) pretokenization (GPT-2-style regex splitting, ## continuation marking) is not modeled, and the authors only remark that marked subwords "can easily be extended," so this is not yet exact for a HuggingFace tokenizer end to end; (iii) the paper is purely theoretical — zero experiments — and the size bound $O(k|A|^3)$ with $k = |\mu| \approx 50$k–200k merges is polynomial but brutal: cubic blowup in the pattern automaton, repeated composition + minimization once per merge. Whether it survives a 128k-vocab tokenizer is entirely unmeasured.

Broader context. Tokenization is a formal-language problem because a tokenizer is a function $\Sigma^+ \to \Gamma^+$ whose image is a strict, awkward subset of $\Gamma^+$: almost every token sequence is non-canonical, i.e. no string maps to it. LMs are trained only on canonical sequences, so constrained decoding that merely enforces a character-level regex can walk the model off-distribution — the paper's r a ce car example, where the surface form matches but the conditioning context is one the model never saw. This is the "tokenization bias" line: Phan et al. (2024) on next-byte prediction, Vieira et al. (2024) on converting token-level LMs to character-level ones, and Berglund, Drewes & van der Merwe's CIAA work on a DFA for canonical BPE sequences (closely related, and notably uncited here). On the decoding side the relevant neighbors are Willard & Louf's Outlines, Koo et al.'s automata-based constraints, and DOMINO/token-healing, which patch the same misalignment heuristically rather than by construction. A natural follow-up: lift the whole pipeline to weights and do Unigram/SentencePiece, where the canonical tokenization is a tropical-semiring shortest path over a lattice — is "the set of Viterbi-optimal Unigram tokenizations of a regular language" regular? Plus a lazy, on-the-fly gadget composition with measured state counts, which is what would decide practicality.

Connection to your work. Generative retrieval is constrained decoding: GENRE and DSI-style systems mask logits against a trie of docids, and SEAL does it against an FM-index of corpus n-grams. That trie is a pattern automaton $A$, so this framework applies directly — and it sharpens a bug that the GR literature mostly papers over. For atomic or RQ-VAE/TIGER-style semantic IDs added as fresh vocabulary items, tokenization is trivial and none of this matters. But for textual identifiers (titles, URLs, n-gram spans), the trie is naturally specified at the character level, and promoting it to the subword level is exactly $\mathrm{PROJ}(A \circ T)$. Do that tokenization-agnostically and a single document acquires many accepting token paths; beam search then splits that document's probability mass across tokenizations, so the beam's ranking is a ranking over paths, not documents — a systematic, length- and tokenization-correlated distortion nobody currently controls for. Two clean consequences. First, $\mathrm{MIN}(\mathrm{PROJ}(A \circ T_{BPE}))$ gives a canonical-only identifier automaton, making "the score of document $d$" unambiguous and the beam budget honest. Second, if you instead want the marginal $P(d) = \sum_{t : \mathrm{CONCAT}(t)=\mathrm{id}(d)} P(t)$, the agnostic automaton is precisely the support to sum over, and Lemma 4.1 ($\varepsilon$-removal of the projection is already deterministic) means states correspond to character-prefix equivalence classes — a tidy DP skeleton. The honest caveat: the DFA gives you the support, not a factorization. A neural LM conditions on the full token history, so it is not Markov in that state, and exact marginalization stays exponential; the automaton buys you enumeration structure and path merging, not tractability. Whether canonical-only constraint or marginalization wins empirically for GR is open, and the paper offers no evidence either way — but it is the right formal vocabulary for stating the question, and "which of these two is the correct objective for identifier-based retrieval" looks like a publishable theory-plus-experiment paper.

Proof sketch. The formal results are about efficiency, not correctness. Lemma 4.1: for minimal deterministic $A$ and a lexicon transducer $T$ built by the trie construction, $\varepsilon$-$\mathrm{REMOVAL}(\mathrm{PROJ}(A \circ T))$ is deterministic — because by construction every path from $T$'s start state to a final state carries exactly one non-$\varepsilon$ output label, so after projection each such path is a run of $\varepsilon$-arcs followed by one $\Gamma$-labeled arc, contractible to a single arc, and uniqueness of the output label per path forbids two same-labeled arcs leaving a composed state. This kills the usual exponential determinization step, so $\mathrm{MIN}(\mathrm{PROJ}(A \circ T))$ is polynomial. Theorem 5.1 is the BPE bound: composing $A$ with $k$ merge gadgets and minimizing after each yields an automaton of size $O(k|A|^3)$, computable in $\mathrm{POLY}(|A|, k, |\Gamma|)$. The key trick is an amortization argument over triplets of states. Proposition C.2 shows that composing with $G_{(a,b)}$ over a triplet $x \xrightarrow{a} y \xrightarrow{b} z$ splits only $y$, into $y'$ (reached by non-a arcs, keeping all of $\delta(y)$) and $y''$ (reached by a, keeping $\delta(y)$ minus the b arc), so at most one new distinguishable state appears. Lemma C.5 then uses determinism of $A$: for a fixed triplet and its derived states, each merge has at most one applicable triplet, so $k$ merges give at most $k+1$ distinguishable derived states. Lemma C.6 generalizes to arbitrary derived-state sets $X \times Y \times Z$ by an eight-way case analysis on which coordinates coincide — six cases are outright impossible by determinism, and the surviving case ($x^1 \neq x^2$, $y^1 = y^2$, $z^1 = z^2$) produces states that are pairwise indistinguishable and hence merged by minimization. Multiplying the $|Q|^3$ triplets by $k$ gives $O(k|A|^3)$. Proposition C.8 keeps determinism (and hence polynomial minimization) invariant across each gadget composition, using $\varphi$-semantics to argue state $q_1$'s two a-output arcs are never simultaneously traversable, and Proposition C.7 licenses interleaving $\mathrm{MIN}\circ\mathrm{PROJ}$ between compositions since neither changes the relation. Induction over merges closes the argument; Corollary 5.1.1 reads off the size bound from the runtime, using $|\mu| \in O(|\Gamma|)$.

title: A Learning-to-Rank Formulation of Clustering-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-20

5. A Learning-to-Rank Formulation of Clustering-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

Thomas Vecchiato, Claudio Lucchese, Franco Maria Nardini, Sebastian Bruch (2024) — arXiv:2404.11731 / 10.1145/3626772.3657931

Main idea. In an IVF index the query-time router scores each of the $L$ partitions by $\tau(q) = Mq$, where row $i$ of $M$ is the centroid $\mu_i$, and probes the top $\ell$. The paper's move is to notice that $M$ is only incidentally a matrix of centroids: functionally it is a scoring matrix inducing a ranking over partitions, and nothing forces it to be the one the clustering algorithm happened to produce. So freeze the partitioning and learn $W \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$ in its place. The supervision is free in the sense that it needs only unlabeled queries: run exact MIPS for each training query $q$, find $u^* = \arg\max_{u \in \mathcal{X}}\langle q,u\rangle$, and set the oracle label $\tau^*(q)$ to the indicator of the partition containing $u^*$. Because the partitioning is non-overlapping, each query has exactly one relevant "document", so the LTR reduction is an $L$-way single-relevant ranking problem, MRR is the natural metric, and softmax cross-entropy is invoked as a consistent surrogate for it (Bruch 2021; Bruch et al. 2019). Training is plain Adam on $\approx L\cdot d$ parameters. The engineering payoff is that rows of $W$ are drop-in replacements for centroids — no change to the index or the routing kernel. Empirically, on MS MARCO / HotpotQA / Fever at $L=\sqrt{m}$, across standard, spherical, and shallow (cluster-pruning) KMeans, learned routing dominates centroid routing at every $\ell$, with gains concentrated at small $\ell$ (Fever, MiniLM, $\ell = 0.1\%L \approx 2$ clusters: 0.102 -> 0.663) and shrinking sharply for 768-dimensional encoders (all-mpnet on MS MARCO: 0.763 -> 0.818). A secondary observation worth filing away: shallow KMeans — sample $L$ points, assign once — is a surprisingly strong partitioner for MIPS.

Critique. The observation is genuinely clarifying and the drop-in property is real, but the evaluation is thin even by short-paper standards, and in two places thin in ways that could flip the interpretation. First, _accuracy-at-$\ell$ is not an iso-cost metric_. The learned router is trained to maximize the probability that the probed set contains $u^_$, and large clusters are a priori more likely to contain $u^_$; a router that simply drifts toward heavy partitions buys recall with candidates scanned, not with better geometry. No cluster-size distribution, no candidates-scanned-vs-recall curve, no latency or QPS anywhere — only recall vs. $\ell$. A SIGIR reviewer should insist on recall vs. number of scanned vectors before believing the headline numbers. Second, parameter count vs. query count. On Fever, $W$ has $\approx 2.3\text{k}\times384 \approx 0.9$M parameters trained on $\approx 7.8$k queries over $\approx 2.3$k classes — fewer training examples than classes. That the largest gains appear on the smallest query set is a red flag: much of what is learned may be a prior over where queries land, not a better proxy for $\max_{u\in C_i}\langle q,u\rangle$. This predicts brittleness under query-distribution shift, which is untested (train/test are a 60/20/20 split of one query set). Third, the baseline is the weakest reasonable one. Missing are the cheap unlearned calibrations that would isolate the mechanism — route by a norm-corrected or radius-corrected centroid score, or by a per-cluster upper bound on the inner product — and the modern learned/redundant alternatives whose whole point is this same mismatch: ScaNN's anisotropic, score-aware quantization loss is the same "optimize the representative for ranking, not reconstruction" idea one level down; SOAR's orthogonality-amplified redundant assignment and SPANN's boundary replication attack routing error by breaking the non-overlapping assumption that the paper's single-relevant label depends on. None is discussed. Fourth, no index-construction or maintenance story: $W$'s shape is tied to a fixed $L$ and fixed assignments, so insertions, cluster splits, or reclustering invalidate the labels, and the training cost (exact MIPS over millions of queries) is never priced. Fifth, scale and sweep: three datasets all at 5–9M vectors, a single $L=\sqrt{m}$, one run, no seed variance; significance is reported (McNemar, $p<10^{-3}$) only for Table 2, where the gains are small enough to need it. Finally — and this is the part most likely to interest you — the formulation is left entirely informal: the consistency argument is imported and holds for $k=1$, $\ell=1$, which is precisely the regime nobody deploys, while the operating regime ($k>1$, $\ell>1$) targets a set-level recall for which softmax cross-entropy is not consistent; the generalized $\gamma$-randomized top-$k$ loss of Section 3.1 is written down but never run, and no bound connects routing MRR to end-to-end recall@$k$.

Broader context. IVF routing is the pressure point where clustering-based ANN either matches or loses to graphs: HNSW/DiskANN win recall-per-QPS in memory, while IVF keeps its advantages in memory footprint, disk residency, quantization compatibility, and updatability — advantages that only pay off if a small $\ell$ suffices, i.e. if routing is good. This paper is the "learn it" branch of a live literature; the complementary "estimate it with guarantees" branch is more theoretically developed — Lu et al.'s probabilistic routing (ICML 2024) attaches concentration-based confidence to the event that a partition contains a neighbor, and Bruch and coauthors' subsequent optimistic-routing work reframes the router as an estimator of the per-cluster maximum inner product $M_i(q) = \max_{u\in C_i}\langle q,u\rangle$ rather than of the centroid score. That reframing is the right lens on this paper: the oracle router ranks by $M_i(q)$, centroid routing is a plug-in estimator that is biased in a norm-dependent way, and the learned $W$ is a discriminatively fitted surrogate with no calibration. The concrete theoretical opening is twofold. (i) An iso-cost, recall-consistent objective: define the target as maximizing $\Pr[S \cap \bigcup_{i \in P}C_i \neq \emptyset]$ subject to $\sum_{i\in P}|C_i| \le B$, a knapsack-constrained ranking problem; ask which surrogates are calibrated for it, and whether a UCB/LCB formulation over $M_i(q)$ (routing as best-arm identification with arm-dependent pull cost $|C_i|$) yields an anytime recall certificate — something no current router provides. (ii) Explaining the dimension effect as a theorem rather than a conjecture: the paper's unexplained shrinkage of gains from $d=384$ to $d=768$ is exactly what concentration of measure predicts — under sub-Gaussian cluster-conditional distributions, $\langle q,u\rangle$ for $u\in C_i$ concentrates around $\langle q,\mu_i\rangle$ at a rate governed by the cluster's covariance spectrum, so the excess routing risk of centroid routing should vanish as the intrinsic dimension grows and cluster radii shrink relative to norms. Turning that into a lower bound on the achievable gain of any rank-$d$ linear router, as a function of the data's intrinsic dimension and the cluster-radius-to-norm ratio, would both explain Table 2 and tell practitioners when a learned router is worth training at all.

title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
tags: Physics - Data Analysis, Statistics and Probability
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-20

4. A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks

Bin Wang, W. Jeffrey Johnston, Stefano Fusi (2025) — arXiv:2510.09816

Main idea. The paper asks when a network's hidden layer places each latent variable on its own axis, and answers it by turning the question into a convex program. The setting is deliberately minimal: a two-layer net $f(x)=W_2\phi(W_1x+b)$ trained with square loss plus $\ell_2$ weight decay on $P=n\cdot 2^{d_Y}$ inputs whose targets $y\in{\pm1}^{d_Y}$ are the latent variables (multi-task classification of the same stimuli along $d_Y$ binary dimensions, as in the Bernardi/Alleman experimental setup). Abstraction is operationalized not by decodability but by the parallelism score: form class prototypes $r(y)$ by averaging firing rates within each of the $2^{d_Y}$ label cells, take the coding vector $\Delta r(k;\alpha)=r(y_k{=}{+}1,y_{\setminus k}{=}\alpha)-r(y_k{=}{-}1,y_{\setminus k}{=}\alpha)$, and average its cosine similarity across all pairs of contexts $\alpha$. PS depends on the representation only through the Gram matrix $K_{ij}=r^i\cdot r^j$, and — the fact that does all the work later — it is invariant to adding a constant to every entry of $K$ and to positive rescaling. The paper's slogan result is that at every global minimum the hidden Gram matrix is exactly $K[\rho__]=b__(d_Y\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top+K_Y)$ with $K_Y=Y^\top Y$, hence $PS=PS(K_Y)=1$: prototypes sit on the vertices of a $d_Y$-cube. The paper stresses, correctly, that this is not implied by task performance — a tetrahedral (maximally mixed, $PS\approx0$) code decodes every label just as well.

Most interesting part. Two things. First, the whitened-input case: when inputs are mutually orthogonal and thus aligned with no low-dimensional structure at all, the hidden layer still inherits the output's hypercube geometry, and the optimum is independent of the magnitude of the input's output-orthogonal components — until those components exceed the aligned one ($c_j>c_Y$), where abstraction breaks. This gives a crisp "expansion-then-compression" story: high-dimensional recoding upstream helps downstream factorization rather than competing with it. Second, a universality claim: for any threshold nonlinearity with $\phi_+(z)/z$ non-increasing (ReLU, hard sigmoid, concave saturating) the population geometry is identical, while odd nonlinearities (tanh, linear) give $K=b_*K_Y$ with no constant shift — same PS, but single-neuron tuning flips from strictly modular (each unit wired to one output) to mixed selectivity. Population geometry is a task property; tuning curves are a biophysics property. The honest caveats are real, though. The targets are the latents, so part of the theorem is that the hidden layer copies the label kernel — the interesting content is uniqueness across minima and the input-geometry phase boundary, not the existence of a factorized solution. The training set is a combinatorially complete, balanced hypercube; inputs are assumed uncorrelated or correlated only in the structured $K_X$ families analyzed; and everything is about global minima of a weight-decayed objective, i.e. a minimum-norm/rich-regime statement very close in spirit to the unconstrained-features neural-collapse literature (indeed multi-element classes exhibit exact within-class collapse, proved by Jensen). PS is computed on training conditions; there is no CCGP theorem for held-out corners, only a generalization formula and an SI example. The deep case is weakest: layerwise kernels $b_*^l=\gamma_*^{l-1}b_*^1$ are derived, but the functional stops being convex for $L\ge3$, so the abstract solution is only shown to be a strict local minimum; the RNN extension is numerical.

Proof sketch. Three moves. (i) An exact change of variables: minimize out $W_2$ in closed form (ridge) and reparameterize the first layer by the preactivation matrix $H=X^\top W^\top$, giving a zero-temperature free energy $\min_{h_k\in\mathrm{Range}K_X}\big[\lambda_1\sum_k h_k^\top K_X^{\dagger}h_k+\mathrm{tr}\,\lambda_2(\lambda_2+\sum_k\phi(h_k)\phi(h_k)^\top)^{-1}K_Y\big]$ — the optimum depends on the data only through $K_X,K_Y$, at finite width and finite input dimension. (ii) Exploit permutation symmetry: replace the $h_k$ by their empirical measure $\rho_M=\sum_k\delta_{h_k}$ and relax to all finite positive measures on $\mathrm{Range}K_X$. The energy is convex in $\rho$ (checked by $f''(t)=2\lambda_2\mathrm{tr}[(\lambda_2+K_t)^{-1}\delta K(\lambda_2+K_t)^{-1}K_Y(\lambda_2+K_t)^{-1}\delta K]\ge0$), so KKT stationarity is sufficient for global optimality — this is what upgrades the result from "a good solution exists" to "all global minima". KKT reads as a mean-field condition: a single-neuron energy $E(h;\rho)=\lambda_1h^\top K_X^{\dagger}h-\lambda_2\phi(h)^\top(\lambda_2+K)^{-1}K_Y(\lambda_2+K)^{-1}\phi(h)$ must be $\ge0$ everywhere with $\mathrm{supp}\,\rho_*$ inside its zero set, solved self-consistently. (iii) The key lemma: for whitened input, $K_X^{\dagger}=I-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top/(P+1)$ has nonpositive off-diagonals (an inverse M-matrix), so $E(h;\rho)\ge E_r([h]_+;\rho)$ and the search collapses onto the nonnegative orthant. Minimizing $E_r$ there is a nonconvex copositivity problem, solved in closed form using the spectral structure of $K_Y$ ($v_i\cdot v_j=P\delta_{ij}$, $\mathbf{1}\cdot v_i=0$); the support turns out to be $2d_Y$ rays $h=\alpha(\mathbf{1}\pm v_i)$, attainable once $M\ge2d_Y$, with $b_*=\sqrt{\tfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\tfrac{P+1}{P(P+2)}}-\tfrac{\lambda_2}{P}$. Note $H_*$ has rank $d_Y+1$, so the learned weights are low-rank — explicitly not a kernel-regime solution. General nonlinearities are handled by linearizing $\phi$ near the origin ($\phi^\delta$), proving the analogous bound by majorization with $\lambda_1\to\lambda_1B_0^{-2}$ where $B_0=\lim_{z\to0^+}\phi_+(z)/z$, solving the resulting program (copositive for class 1, an ordinary convex QP for odd $\phi$), then letting $\delta\downarrow0$ since $b_*$ is $\delta$-independent.

Broader context and connection to your work. The backdrop is neural population geometry: Bernardi et al. (Cell 2020) showed that hippocampus and PFC encode task variables with high PS and high cross-condition generalization performance while retaining enough shattering dimensionality to decode arbitrary dichotomies, and Fusi's earlier mixed-selectivity work (Rigotti et al. 2013; Barak et al. 2013) framed the generalization/discrimination trade-off. In ML the parallel thread is disentanglement, where Locatello et al.'s impossibility result killed the purely unsupervised program, pushing the field toward weak supervision — which is exactly the door this paper walks through. The closest companions are Alleman, Lindsey & Fusi (arXiv:2401.13558), the empirical predecessor here, and Whittington et al.'s "Disentanglement with biological constraints" (arXiv:2210.01768), which derives axis-alignment from nonnegativity/energy constraints rather than multi-task supervision; the neural-collapse optimality results (Súkeník, Mondelli & Lampert) are the ML-side sibling, and the discussion's nod to the Platonic representation hypothesis is apt — this is a tractable model of architecture-insensitive, task-determined geometry.

For your work the load-bearing statement is the kernel identity $K_{\text{hidden}}=b_*(d_Y\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top+K_Y)$: under multi-attribute supervision with weight decay, the embedding Gram matrix becomes an affine image of the supervision Gram matrix, with effective rank $d_Y+1$ regardless of width. That is the same object as in the recent embedding-dimension lower bounds for single-vector dense retrieval (the sign-rank/order-preserving-rank arguments about which relevance matrices a $d$-dimensional index can realize) — here read from the training side rather than the capacity side, and it predicts that the intrinsic dimension of a fine-tuned retriever is set by the number of distinguishable supervision signals, not by the embedding budget, with within-class collapse of all items sharing a label profile. If so, quantization and graph-index behaviour on fine-tuned embeddings should be governed by $d_Y$, and hubness/degenerate-neighborhood pathologies are a predicted consequence of good training rather than a bug. The generative-retrieval link is more speculative but not forced: semantic identifier schemes (hierarchical k-means, RQ-VAE docids as in TIGER) assume the embedding space is axis-factorized and hierarchically organized, which is precisely what the anisotropic extension delivers — a hyper-rectangular code with per-latent axis scale $b_i^*\propto\sqrt{d_i}$ and stage-like learning transitions, i.e. a coarse-to-fine emergence order that residual quantization would read off as compositional codebooks. Two follow-ups worth considering: (a) drop the completeness assumption — train on a strict subset of the $2^{d_Y}$ label cells and use the paper's explicit prediction formula $y_*(x)$ to turn the PS result into an actual CCGP/compositional-generalization theorem, which is what would matter for zero-shot identifier assignment; (b) keep the measure-over-preactivations order parameter but swap MSE+weight-decay for InfoNCE, which would give the first finite-width characterization of the optimal contrastive embedding kernel, directly testing whether the affine-in-$K_Y$ form (and the collapse it implies) survives the loss actually used to train retrievers.

title: Model Stealing for Any Low-Rank Language Model
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-20

3. Model Stealing for Any Low-Rank Language Model

Allen Liu, Ankur Moitra (MIT), 2024 — arXiv:2411.07536

Main idea. "Model stealing" here is stripped down to a distribution-learning problem: the target is a distribution $H$ over $\mathcal{O}^T$ (vocabulary of size $O$, fixed horizon $T$), and success means outputting an efficiently samplable description $H'$ with $d_{TV}(H,H')\le\eta$. Nothing is recovered parameter-wise — no transition/emission matrices, no weights — so this is functionality theft, not weight extraction, and $H'$ need not even be low-rank. The structural assumption is that $H$ has rank $S$ in the sense of Kakade–Krishnamurthy–Mahajan–Zhang: for every split $t$, the $O^{T-t}\times O^{t}$ matrix of conditional probabilities $\Pr_H[f\mid h]$ has rank $\le S$. Equivalently, each prefix admits an $S$-dimensional sufficient embedding whose future distribution is linear in it; HMMs with $S$ hidden states are a special case. Access is the conditional query model: the learner names any prefix $h\in\mathcal{O}^t$ — including one of negligible probability — and receives a fresh draw $f\sim\Pr_H[\cdot\mid h]$. The result closes the main open question of KKMZ24 by removing their "fidelity" condition: rank alone suffices, with no full-rankness, no condition-number bound, no smoothed analysis. The conceptual punchline the authors advertise is that the sampler, not the estimator, is the hard part: drawing one token requires solving a convex program, a provable instance of inference-time compute buying accuracy.

The most interesting part. Two things. First, how they dodge the hardness: learning HMMs from i.i.d. samples embeds noisy parity (Mossel–Roch), and the usual escapes are structural assumptions. Here the escape is purely the oracle — conditional queries let you interrogate prefixes the model would essentially never emit, which is exactly what a passive sample cannot do. Notably, there is no tensor decomposition and no method-of-moments step; the only spectral operation is an SVD used to truncate to the numerically significant subspace inside a robust barycentric-spanner routine. This is a real break from the Hsu–Kakade–Zhang / Anandkumar–Hsu–Kakade lineage. Second, and cleverer, is the fix for compounding error. Sampling token-by-token means repeatedly changing basis between spanners at consecutive timesteps, and each change-of-basis can double the $L_1$ error, giving $2^T$ blowup. Projecting onto the feasible convex set in $L_1$ does not help — since the true point $z$ is unknown, the triangle inequality only gives $|z'-z|_1\le 2|w-z|_1$. Projecting in KL does: if $z^*=\arg\min_{z\in K}\mathrm{KL}(z|w)$, then $\mathrm{KL}(z|z^*)\le \mathrm{KL}(z|w)$ for every $z\in K$, so error accumulates additively rather than multiplicatively. That the right geometry for autoregressive error control is information-geometric, not metric, is the paper's genuinely memorable idea. The practical gap is honest and large: $O$ enters polynomially (real vocabularies are $10^5$), $T$ is fixed, the rank of an actual transformer's output distribution is not small, and the learned model is smoothed to be $\Omega(\epsilon/O^2)$-positive on every token. Read it as a complexity-theoretic statement that rank is the right stealability parameter, analogous to Bellman rank in RL.

Broader context. The relevant background is the hardness landscape for latent-variable sequence models — Mossel–Roch's parity embedding, and the workarounds via full-rankness (HKZ12's spectral algorithm), overcompleteness plus sparsity (Sharan et al.), multi-step observability (Golowich–Moitra–Rohatgi), or smoothing (Bhaskara et al.) — set against the query-learning tradition where membership queries defeat passive hardness (Angluin's $L^*$, Jackson's DNF algorithm). KKMZ24 is the direct predecessor and the one paper to read alongside this; the empirical counterpart is Carlini et al., Stealing Part of a Production Language Model (arXiv:2403.06634), which recovers the final embedding-projection layer, i.e. exploits exactly the low-rank bottleneck this paper abstracts. A natural follow-up: replace exact rank $S$ with approximate rank (singular-value decay of $M^{(t)}$) and ask for TV error scaling with the tail, since exact rank is brittle; relatedly, prove lower bounds separating conditional queries from the weaker access real APIs give (prefill plus top-$k$ logprobs), and try to trade the $\mathrm{poly}(O)$ dependence for $\mathrm{poly}(S,\log O)$. There is one non-forced connection to your own work: the barycentric spanner is a set of $S$ landmark prefixes whose conditional-future distributions represent all others with bounded coefficients — the same optimal-design object used for exploration in linear bandits, and a close cousin of landmark/coreset selection in low-rank embedding spaces. Their Lemma 5.10 is arguably of independent interest for retrieval theory: importance-sampling $\mathrm{poly}(m,r,1/\gamma)$ coordinates from the mixture $\bar D$ yields sketches preserving both $L_1$ norms and KL divergences of all $r$-sparse bounded-coefficient combinations of $m$ given distributions — an $L_1$/KL analogue of JL, non-oblivious and restricted to a fixed small family, but exactly the kind of guarantee one wants when sketching distributions rather than points. Generative retrieval is literally an autoregressive distribution over docid strings, so "rank of the docid distribution" is a defensible extraction-complexity measure there, and the KL-projection trick is a candidate cure for the usual compounding-error pathology in constrained-decoding analyses.

Proof sketch. The theorem: given conditional query access to a rank-$S$ distribution $H$ over $\mathcal{O}^T$ and $\eta\in(0,1)$, an algorithm using $\mathrm{poly}(S,O,T,1/\eta)$ queries and time outputs, with probability $1-\eta$, a representation of $H'$ with $d_{TV}(H,H')\le\eta$, samplable in $\mathrm{poly}(S,O,T,\log(1/\eta))$ time per draw; the only assumption replacing full-rankness/fidelity is the query model itself (positivity is manufactured, not assumed). The proof has four moves. (i) Consistent pdf access (Lemma 4.6): estimate next-token distributions by Chernoff, cache them lazily on the prefix tree, and perturb to be $\epsilon/(10O)^2$-positive; this defines a single distribution $\widehat H$, $\epsilon$-conditionally close to $H$, with exact pdf access — crucial, since exact access to $H$ itself would already reduce to KKMZ24. (ii) Dimensionality reduction (Lemma 5.10): the vectors $\Pr_{\widehat H}[\cdot\mid h]$ have $O^{T-t}$ coordinates, so sample $m$ futures from the mixture and form importance-weighted coordinates $\Pr_{\widehat H}[f_i\mid h]/(mD[f_i])$; a Chernoff bound plus a union bound over a net of coefficient vectors shows these sketches preserve $L_1$ norms and (truncated) KL divergences of bounded sparse combinations to additive $\gamma$. (iii) Spanner construction (Lemmas 5.4, 5.6, 6.3): $\mathrm{poly}(S,1/\gamma)$ prefixes sampled from $\widehat H[:t]$ contain, with high probability, an $S$-subset that is a $(1-\gamma,1,0)$-spanner for most of the mass; a volume-doubling argument (Awerbuch–Kleinberg style) made robust by first projecting onto the top-$t$ singular subspace at threshold $\gamma\sqrt n$ computes a $(2,O(\gamma S\sqrt{nd}))$-spanner in the sketched space, which lifts back to the true conditional distributions. The learned representation is deliberately partial — spanner sets $\mathcal H^{(t)}$, next-token tables $P^{(t)}$, and sketches $u_h$ — with change-of-basis coefficients deferred to sampling. (iv) Sampling and the inductive error bound: maintain coefficients $\alpha^{x[:t]}$ with $\Pr[\cdot\mid x{:}t]\approx\sum_h \alpha_h\Pr[\cdot\mid h]$, emit a token from $\alpha^\top P^{(t)}$ rounded away from zero, renormalize by Bayes, then re-express in the next spanner by minimizing $\mathrm{KL}_{\ge c^{T-t}w}$ subject to $|\alpha_h|\le 3S$, entrywise lower bounds, and unit total mass — a convex program. Truncated KL ($\ell_{\ge c}(x,y)=x\log\max(x,c)-x\log\max(y,c)$) keeps the objective finite on the slightly-off-simplex, possibly-negative iterates, with truncation level $c=\eta^{10OTS}$ so that only $\log(1/c)=\mathrm{poly}$ ever appears. Corollary 4.11 (the truncated Pythagorean inequality) plus the KL-preservation of the sketches gives per-step additive error $\eta+\eta^{0.5}$; Lemma 7.12 sums this over prefixes with weights $\Pr_{\widehat H}[h]$, excising the $O(T\eta)$ mass of prefixes not positively representable by the spanner, so after $T$ steps the aggregate KL is $O(\eta^{0.4})$. Pinsker converts to TV, a hybrid argument re-splices the bad prefixes, and Claim 4.3 ($\epsilon/T$ conditional closeness $\Rightarrow$ $\epsilon$ TV, by reverse induction) transfers everything back to $H$. The accuracy parameters sit in a strict hierarchy $\epsilon\ll\mathrm{poly}(\gamma)\ll\mathrm{poly}(\eta)$, which is where the (unstated but large) polynomial degree hides.

title: On Mesa-Optimization in Autoregressively Trained Transformers: Emergence and Capability
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-20

2. On Mesa-Optimization in Autoregressively Trained Transformers: Emergence and Capability

Chenyu Zheng, Wei Huang, Rongzhen Wang, Guoqiang Wu, Jun Zhu, Chongxuan Li (2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16845

Main idea. The "mesa-optimization" reading of in-context learning says the forward pass of a trained transformer is an optimizer: it builds an inner objective from the context and takes a step on it. For next-token prediction on sequences, von Oswald et al. gave a hand-built one-layer linear causal-attention construction that performs one GD step on a least-squares fit of the transition operator, and Sander et al. showed that construction is the global minimum of the pretraining loss if you force every weight matrix to be diagonal. Neither says training gets there. This paper closes that gap for the smallest honest model: it integrates the gradient flow of a one-layer linear causal self-attention layer on the population autoregressive loss, over data generated by $x_{t+1}=Wx_t$ with $W$ a random diagonal unitary and a controllable initial token $x_1$. Its answer has two halves that are worth separating: the algorithmic form of the mesa-optimizer does emerge from non-convex training under a moment condition on $\mathcal{D}_{x_1}$, but the resulting optimizer is provably not consistent — it is the mean-squared-error-optimal member of its class, and for Gaussian $x_1$ that means it predicts exactly one fifth of the correct next token.

The most interesting part. The factor $1/5$ is the paper's best idea, because it is not a bug but a shrinkage. The whole dynamics collapses to two scalars, $a$ (the diagonal of $W^{KQ}_{32}$) and $b$ (the diagonal of $W^{PV}_{12}$), and gradient flow drives their product to $ab^\star = \kappa_1/\kappa_2$ (up to a $1/T$ correction), where $\kappa_1=\mathbb{E}[x_{1j}^4]$ and $\kappa_2=\mathbb{E}[x_{1j}^6]$ — a ratio of sixth to fourth moments, i.e. exactly the least-squares projection coefficient of the target onto the model's single quadratic feature, not the $1/\mathbb{E}[x_{1j}^2]$ that recovery would require. For $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_d)$ that ratio is $1/(5\sigma^2)$ versus the needed $1/\sigma^2$, independent of $\sigma$ and $d$. The reason is sharp and, once seen, obvious: because $W$ is unitary and diagonal, $|x_{ij}|=|x_{1j}|$ for every $i$, so the context Gram matrix $\frac{1}{t-1}\sum_i x_ix_i^*$ concentrates on $\mathrm{diag}(x_{11}^2,\dots,x_{1d}^2)$ — a random, per-sequence diagonal that a single scalar step size cannot invert. Assumption 4.2, which the authors prove is necessary and sufficient for recovery, is precisely the demand that $(\kappa_1/\kappa_2)\cdot\mathrm{Gram}\cdot x_T=x_T$, i.e. that $x_1$ have deterministic energy on its support; their sparse example (one-hot with fixed magnitude $c$) is essentially the only shape that works. So the negative result is really "one-step GD with an isotropic step size cannot whiten the context", which is a statement about the architecture, not about optimization. The cost of the setup is heavy and should be stated plainly: linear attention, one layer, population loss, complex diagonal-unitary $W$, an embedding that hand-stacks $(x_i,x_{i-1})$ so the OLS gradient is already available as a feature, and a diagonal initialization (Assumption 3.1) that puts nonzero mass exactly in the two blocks the mesa-optimizer needs. Under that initialization "emergence" means the diagonal ansatz is an invariant manifold of the flow and the step size converges to the right scalar — not that the algorithm was discovered from generic weights. Their Gaussian-initialization simulations suggest the picture survives, but that is experiment, not theorem. Proposition 4.2 (with $x_1=\mathbf{1}_d$, no gradient masking, off-diagonal gradients are nonzero so the limit leaves the diagonal manifold and is not vanilla GD) is also only an escape argument; the limit point is conjectured, and empirically observed, to be preconditioned GD, $\hat y_t=\frac{1}{t-1}\sum_i W_2x_ix_{i-1}^*W_1x_t$, but not characterized.

Broader context. This sits in the "transformers implement gradient descent in the forward pass" line: von Oswald et al. (2023) for the construction and the empirical mesa-optimization evidence; Zhang–Frei–Bartlett (JMLR 2024), who proved gradient-flow convergence for one-layer linear attention on few-shot linear regression, and Ahn et al. (2023) / Mahankali–Hashimoto–Ma (ICLR 2024), who identified the global optimum as one step of preconditioned GD. The contrast is the paper's real contribution to the literature's self-understanding: under few-shot pretraining with Gaussian inputs the learned one-step optimizer does solve the task, whereas under AR pretraining on the same Gaussian it provably does not, because the in-context design matrix is generated by the sequence rather than drawn i.i.d. The obvious follow-up is that multi-head or multi-layer linear attention should buy exactly the missing per-coordinate preconditioner (each head a coordinate-wise step size, each layer a Newton-like refinement), so one could try to prove that $H$ heads suffice to satisfy Assumption 4.2 for all $\mathcal{D}_{x_1}$ with $d$-sparse support, or that softmax/LayerNorm normalization makes the Gram self-whitening — a theory of why normalization is what enables in-context recovery. One loose but real echo of your own area: the trained layer's readout $\big(\sum_i x_{i+1}x_i^*\big)x_T$ is a plain outer-product associative memory queried by inner product, and its failure is missing whitening of the key Gram — the same reason raw dot-product scoring underperforms decorrelated/Mahalanobis similarity in MIPS-style vector search.

title: More Than Memory Savings: Zeroth-Order Optimization Mitigates Forgetting in Continual Learning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-20

1. More Than Memory Savings: Zeroth-Order Optimization Mitigates Forgetting in Continual Learning

Wanhao Yu, Zheng Wang, Shuteng Niu, Sen Lin, Li Yang (2025) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21019

Main idea. The paper asks whether the optimizer itself, rather than the usual architectural machinery (prompt pools, task-orthogonal LoRA subspaces, prototype ensembles), can be the mechanism that buys stability in class-incremental learning. The pitch: two-point SPSA/ZO-SGD descends not on $L$ but on the randomized-smoothing surrogate $L_\varepsilon(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_\Delta[L(\theta+\varepsilon\Delta)] = L(\theta) + \tfrac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\nabla^2 L) + O(\varepsilon^4)$, so it carries an implicit curvature penalty; since second-order forgetting bounds scale as $\tfrac12\lambda_{\max}(H_t)|\Delta\theta|^2$, a flatness-seeking optimizer should forget less for free. The empirical half is the more useful contribution and it is largely negative: dropping ZO into eight PEFT-based CIL methods fails outright, and the failure localizes to two places — objectives needing directionally accurate gradients (L2P, CODA-Prompt, InfLoRA collapse to near-chance, and stay there even at 5–10x the epoch budget, Table 8), and learnable classifier heads. The ablation that carries the paper is Table 6: ZO-adapter + FO-classifier gives 66.63 last accuracy on ImageNet-R Inc-5, while swapping which component gets ZO gives 11.72 with 18.07 forgetting. Hence ZO-FC: ZO on one shared adapter, FO on the head, which is free memory-wise because the head is terminal and needs no stored activations. Result: 0.70 GB vs 4.35 GB peak, competitive accuracy, lowest forgetting among FO baselines.

Reviewer-style critique. The engineering is clean and the negative results are genuinely informative, but the central causal claim — flatness, induced by smoothing, explains the low forgetting — is not established, and two quantitative facts cut against it. First, the implicit penalty coefficient is $\varepsilon^2/2 = 5\times10^{-7}$ at their $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$; it is not credible that a regularizer that weak reshapes the landscape. Whatever ZO is doing is far more plausibly high-variance-noise-induced underfitting or an SGD-noise-like effect than the $\mathrm{Tr}(\nabla^2L)$ term they invoke. Second, the forgetting bound has two factors, and the paper only ever argues about $\lambda_{\max}$ while never controlling $|\Delta\theta|$. Their own numbers show the confound: on ImageNet-R the FO classifier-only baseline — the least plastic model in the table — forgets less than ZO-FC (3.98 vs 4.40), the Inc-10 claim that ZO-FC beats it rests on 3.64 vs 3.67, and Table 4's $Q$-sweep shows forgetting rising monotonically with query budget (3.0 at $Q{=}1$ to ~5 at $Q{=}32$) exactly as accuracy rises. Forgetting tracks how far the adapter actually moves, which is the trivial explanation. The flatness measurement inherits the same problem: $\Phi_{ZO}$ normalizes the perturbation-induced loss increase by $L_{old}(\theta)$, so a method that underfits (higher $L_{old}$) is mechanically scored flatter — the authors' own note that the late-task plateau is a proxy artifact concedes half of this. Missing baselines are conspicuous: if flatness is the mechanism, compare against FO + SAM or C-Flat on the same adapter (C-Flat is cited, never run), and against cheap FO memory reductions (gradient checkpointing, micro-batching) rather than only against un-retuned ZO ports of methods designed for FO gradients, which is close to a straw man. The "6x memory saving" headline is also one-sided: ZO-FC pays ~3x FO FLOPs per batch at $Q{=}4$ and is trained for 2x the epochs (59.4 s vs 24.5 s per epoch), i.e. roughly the memory win inverted in compute/energy — a real question for the on-device story. Finally, the internal inconsistency a reviewer would press hardest: the paper states that ZO-FC's residual forgetting comes chiefly from the FO classifier, which is precisely the block the smoothing argument does not cover.

Proof sketch. There is no new theorem; the analysis is a chain of imported results, worth stating precisely because the gaps matter. Link one is $F_t = L_{old}(\theta_t+\Delta\theta)-L_{old}(\theta_t) \le \tfrac12\lambda_{\max}(H_t)|\Delta\theta|^2$ from a second-order Taylor expansion with the $O(|\Delta\theta|^3)$ remainder dropped (Mirzadeh et al.). Link two is Nesterov–Spokoiny smoothing, giving the trace term above. Link three, quoted in Appendix C from Zhang et al. (2025): assuming $L$ convex, three-times continuously differentiable with bounded third derivatives, SPSA reaches $L_\varepsilon(\theta_T)-\min L_\varepsilon \le \varepsilon$ in $T=\tilde O(d^4/\varepsilon^2)$ steps, and consequently $\mathrm{Tr}(\nabla^2L(\theta_T)) - \min_{\theta^_}\mathrm{Tr}(\nabla^2L(\theta^_)) \le \varepsilon$ — i.e. among global minimizers of $L$, SPSA selects minimum-trace ones. Every assumption fails here (non-convex ViT adapter, $d\approx4\times10^4$ so $d^4\sim10^{18}$ against a 20–40-epoch budget), and the guarantee is asymptotic at the smoothed optimum while the paper's plasticity story asserts ZO never gets near convergence — the two halves of the argument cannot both be operative. Note also that $\mathrm{Tr}$ dominates $\lambda_{\max}$ only up to a factor $d$, so link two-to-one is dimensionally loose. Appendix D's extension to the hybrid is a two-timescale heuristic, not a proof: assume the FO head runs on a fast timescale with $\psi^\star(\phi)=\arg\min_\psi L(\phi,\psi)$ and the ZO adapter slowly, conclude the iterates descend $J(\phi)=\min_\psi L_\varepsilon(\phi,\psi)$. No theorem is stated, no timescale-separation or Lipschitz conditions are verified, $\psi^\star(\phi)$ is assumed unique, and the estimator is described as unbiased for the Gaussian-smoothed gradient while the algorithm samples Rademacher $\Delta$ (which is unbiased only up to $O(\varepsilon^2)$ bias for a different smoothing).

Broader context. PEFT-based CIL post-2022 assumes a frozen ImageNet-21k ViT-B/16 and asks only how to route or isolate small trainable modules; SimpleCIL's 81.3 on CIFAR-100 with no training shows how little headroom these benchmarks leave, which is why a plasticity claim really needs a fine-grained or genuinely out-of-distribution stream. The ZO thread starts with MeZO (Malladi et al., 2023), which showed forward-only fine-tuning of LLMs is viable at inference-level memory, and Zhang et al.'s 2024 benchmark; the flat-minima-for-CL thread runs through F2M (Shi et al., 2021) and C-Flat (2024). Most directly, ZeroFlow (Feng et al., ICML 2025) already benchmarks ZO for forgetting and is cited only in passing — a reviewer would demand a sharp novelty delta there. The follow-up I would want: make the smoothing anisotropic and task-aware. Instead of isotropic $\pm\varepsilon\Delta$, sample perturbations concentrated in the top eigendirections of the old-task Hessian or Fisher, so the implicit penalty targets the directions that actually enter $\lambda_{\max}(H_t)$ rather than the full trace, and let $\varepsilon$ grow with task index. This is a ZO analogue of InfLoRA/GPM-style orthogonal projection, it raises the effective regularization far above $5\times10^{-7}$ without inflating gradient variance uniformly, and it is the setting where an honest per-task forgetting bound might actually be provable. A tangential but non-forced connection: the "limit representation drift so old decisions stay valid" objective is structurally the embedding-drift problem in vector search, where re-embedding a corpus after an encoder update is the dominant cost and backward-compatible training targets the same quantity — though the ZO machinery here is aimed at training memory, not index stability.

title: When does Retrieval Work on Reasoning-Intense Tasks?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-19

When does Retrieval Work on Reasoning-Intense Tasks?

Quan Shi, Howard Yen, Mengzhou Xia, Shunyu Yao, Danqi Chen, Karthik Narasimhan (Princeton NLP). No date in the library, and no full text: the PDF URL stored in Zotero (benshi34.github.io) now 404s and the title does not appear on arXiv or any venue I could find, so this is an abstract-only reading. Everything beyond the abstract is flagged as inference or outside context.

The question. RAG's empirical case was built on knowledge-intensive QA, where the missing ingredient is a fact and retrieval supplies it. This paper asks whether the same machinery pays off when the missing ingredient is a procedure — competitive-programming and mathematics problems where the model's bottleneck is deciding what to do, not recalling what is true. The design choice that makes it interesting is that the retrieved documents are oracle algorithmically similar problems: not topically related, but solved by the same underlying algorithm. Across five code and math tasks the outcome swings from 66% degradation to 50% improvement, and the abstract's interpretive claim is that the gain concentrates where high-level algorithmic choice dominates the model's errors, while retrieval does nothing for implementation bugs or problem misreading.

Critique. The framing carries more than it can hold, and these are objections to the abstract as written — the manuscript may answer all of them. First, oracle retrieval removes the retriever from the loop entirely. This is a study of context utilization under perfect retrieval, so it upper-bounds deployed RAG rather than measuring it; the title's "does retrieval work" is really "does having the right document help." That inversion is what makes the negative half of the result strong — if a gold algorithmically-matched document costs you 66%, no retriever improvement recovers it — and correspondingly weakens the positive half, since a real retriever must first solve a problem (finding algorithmic twins) that we know is hard.

Second, five tasks with a −66%-to-+50% spread means the headline finding is variance itself. Any conditional claim ("RAG helps when high-level decisions dominate") is a regression on roughly five points, with task identity confounded against difficulty, document format, base model competence and context length. Relative percentages also hide the baselines they are relative to.

Third, the error taxonomy is the load-bearing element and the least verifiable from the abstract. "High-level algorithmic decision" error is very nearly a definition of the gap an algorithmically-similar document fills, so unless labels are assigned blind to the RAG outcome — ideally by multiple annotators with reported agreement, not a single LLM judge — the central claim risks being analytic rather than empirical. Fourth, no mechanism is offered for the negative transfer, and the candidates are distinguishable only by ablations the abstract does not mention: anchoring on a superficially matching but wrong algorithm, context dilution, positional degradation, or format mimicry. Without an irrelevant-document control, "wrong content hurts" cannot be separated from "any extra context hurts."

Context, and why this is your problem. Reasoning-intensive retrieval is the young subfield that breaks IR's founding assumption. BM25 and dense bi-encoders alike presume relevance correlates with surface or topical proximity; here the gold document may share no vocabulary with the query (a flight-routing problem and a string-prefix problem both solved by union-find) while the hardest distractors are topically identical. BRIGHT — which shares several of these authors — made this concrete as a benchmark; AlgoSimBench (Li and Mooney, UT Austin, arXiv:2507.15378, not this group despite the topical overlap) builds it adversarially and finds that generating an attempted solution and matching on that beats embedding models. The nearest older literature is in-context example selection, where "relevance" has always meant downstream utility and where the same negative transfer was observed without being theorised. ReasonIR is the current training-side response.

The theoretical hook is the one worth pushing on. If relevance is "shares algorithmic structure," is it a similarity in any embedding space at all? Single-vector retrieval realizes only the relevance matrices expressible as a rank-d bilinear form; the recent line of work bounding which top-k qrel sets a d-dimensional embedding can represent applies directly, and algorithmic relevance looks combinatorially rich in exactly the adversarial way those bounds punish — many overlapping "tags," topical decoys deliberately placed near the gold. That is an expressivity argument, not an optimization one, and it says vector search has a ceiling here that better training data will not raise. Generative retrieval is structurally different: an autoregressive scorer conditions on the query with computation rather than a fixed inner product, so it can do part of the reasoning before committing to what is relevant. Whether that translates into real gains depends on whether the docid space encodes algorithmic structure, but "generative retrieval's advantage is largest precisely where relevance requires inference rather than lookup" is a sharp, testable thesis-level proposition — and this paper's oracle setting is the natural way to measure the headroom it would be competing for. A concrete follow-up: train the retriever against the measured downstream delta instead of annotated similarity, and learn a per-instance abstention gate, which operationalizes this paper's own finding that retrieval should fire only for one of its three error classes.

title: Understanding Contrastive Learning via Gaussian Mixture Models
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-19

Understanding Contrastive Learning via Gaussian Mixture Models

Parikshit Bansal, Ali Kavis, Sujay Sanghavi (UT Austin), 2024 — arXiv:2411.03517

The setup. The paper asks what InfoNCE actually optimizes, in a setting old enough that the right answer is already known from another direction: linear dimensionality reduction for a Gaussian mixture. Data is drawn from F = Σ_k w_k N(μ_k, Σ), the encoder is a matrix A ∈ R^{d×r}, and the quality of a projection is measured by the Fisher discriminant J(A) = Tr[(AᵀΣ̄A)^{−1}(AᵀM̄A)] with Σ̄ = Σ_k w_k Σ_k, M̄ = Σ_k w_k μ_k μ_kᵀ — the post-projection ratio of between-component to within-component variance. Its maximizer is the Fisher subspace S_F = Span{Σ̄^{−1}μ_k}, exactly what supervised LDA recovers when it is handed the component labels.

The load-bearing modelling choice is the definition of augmentation. The authors introduce an augmentation-enabled distribution F̂: with probability δ the pair (x, x̂) is two independent draws from the same component, and with probability 1−δ two independent draws from the mixture. In other words, an augmentation is conditional independence given the latent class — the same assumption that drives Lee–Lei–Saunshi–Zhuo's analysis of self-supervision — rather than a crop or a rotation. The learner never sees k. The target of comparison is the classical SVD subspace (top eigenvectors of E[xxᵀ]), which is Fisher-optimal only for spherical mixtures and can be catastrophically wrong otherwise: in the "parallel pancakes" configuration the top-2 SVD plane is parallel to the pancakes and merges the modes, achieving the worst Fisher discriminant of any 2-plane.

The result worth the price of admission. Theorem 4.2: for shared-covariance mixtures and r ≥ K, the global minimizer of population InfoNCE satisfies Col(A*) ⊆ S_F for any δ > 0, with equality when δ = 1. Unsupervised contrastive learning with perfect augmentations recovers precisely the LDA subspace, in a regime where every purely spectral method fails. The inclusion also forces rank(A*) ≤ K regardless of how large r is: the log-partition term is a rank regularizer that zeroes out every direction carrying no between-component signal. This is Wang–Isola uniformity doing something concrete — not spreading points on a sphere, but pruning coordinates.

The multi-modal analogue (Def 5.1, Thm 5.2) is arguably the more interesting half. Two coupled mixtures Σ_k w_k N(μ_{V,k}, Σ_V) × N(μ_{T,k}, Σ_T) share a latent k; each modality is the other's augmentation, so no augmentation oracle is needed at all. CLIP's loss then yields Col(A_V*) ⊆ S_{V,F} and Col(A_T*) ⊆ S_{T,F} — all noise directions filtered, but only a subset of each Fisher space recovered. The authors are honest about why: the two sets of means can be arbitrarily misaligned, so a direction that discriminates components in V may be invisible to any direction in T and is simply never learned. They conjecture equality under the whitened-alignment condition Σ_T^{−1/2}μ_{T,k} = Σ_V^{−1/2}μ_{V,k}.

Proof sketch. Everything is population-level, infinite-negative, linear, and about global optima — no finite-sample rates, no optimization dynamics. The loss L(A) = −E_{(x,x̂)}[xᵀBx̂] + E_x log E_{x̃} exp(xᵀBx̃) depends on A only through B = AAᵀ; the rank constraint is relaxed and shown to bind automatically. Lemma A.1 establishes, via Hölder, that log-sum-exp is strictly convex in B on the span of the data, so L is strictly convex on the PSD cone. Step 1 is a symmetry-plus-strict-convexity argument: if some eigenvector of B* had a component v orthogonal to all μ_k, reflect through R = I − 2vvᵀ. Since Rμ_k = μ_k and isotropic noise is reflection-invariant, xᵀB̄x̃ =_d xᵀB*x̃, so L(B̄) = L(B*) — and ½(B* + B̄) is strictly better, a contradiction. Step 2, the δ = 1 equality, is a first-order argument at λ_j = 0 along a Fisher direction u_j: the alignment term's derivative is exactly Σ_k w_k a_k² with a_k = μ_kᵀu_j, and the partition term's derivative equals (√W a)ᵀ √W F √W (√W a) for a soft-assignment matrix F with entrywise-positive FW and unit row sums. Perron–Frobenius then pins the top eigenvalue at exactly 1 with Perron vector 1, so the quadratic form is < ‖√W a‖² unless all a_k coincide — hence ∂L/∂λ_j < 0 and the direction is switched on. Shared covariance enters only through the whitening x' = Σ^{−1/2}x, B' = Σ^{1/2}BΣ^{1/2}, which reduces the general case to the isotropic Proposition B.1; it is precisely this simultaneous whitening that fails for component-specific Σ_k. For δ < 1 the alignment term picks up a factor δ (the cross-moment becomes δM̄ + (1−δ)μ̄μ̄ᵀ) while the partition term is unchanged, so the sign of the derivative can flip — which is exactly why only ⊆ survives. The CLIP proof reuses only Step 1, applied to the non-symmetric B = A_T A_Vᵀ row- and column-wise, which is why no equality is available there.

Context, and what it does (and does not) say for dense retrieval. The theoretical literature on contrastive learning runs roughly: Arora et al. (2019) bound downstream linear-probe risk under a latent-class model but with a bound loosened by "collisions"; HaoChen et al. (2021) show spectral contrastive loss performs spectral decomposition of the augmentation graph; Wang & Isola (2020) decompose InfoNCE into alignment plus uniformity; Saunshi et al. (2022) argue none of this works without inductive bias. This paper's contribution is to analyze the exact InfoNCE rather than a surrogate, in a model where the optimal answer is a known closed form. Nakada et al. (2023) is the closest neighbour — linear multimodal contrastive learning as an SVD/CCA of the cross-covariance — and reading the two together is worthwhile, since Theorem 5.2 is the mixture-model version of the same phenomenon.

The transfer to dense retrieval is real but should be stated carefully. A two-tower retriever trained with InfoNCE over (query, relevant document) pairs is literally the CLIP GMM setting: two spaces, two projections, each side the other's augmentation. The modelling assumption being imported is that a query and its relevant document are conditionally independent draws given a latent topic — which flatters reality, since relevance is asymmetric, graded, and concentrated on a handful of documents rather than on a whole Gaussian component with mass w_k. Granting it, three things carry over as intuitions rather than theorems. First, geometry: the objective learns Σ̄^{−1}μ, not μ — discriminative directions, whitened by within-topic covariance — which is the formal version of why high-variance-but-non-discriminative directions (frequency, length, boilerplate) should be suppressed, and why whitening or top-component removal helps empirical embeddings. Parallel pancakes is the clean counterexample to LSI-style variance-maximizing projections. Second, dimensionality: the optimum has rank ≤ K whatever r is, so embedding width beyond the latent structure buys nothing in this model — a mixture-model echo of the observed low effective rank of dense encoders and of sign-rank-style capacity limits on single-vector retrieval, though with nonlinear encoders the effective K is presumably enormous, so it argues about mechanism, not about whether 768 dimensions suffice. Third, negatives: the negatives x̃ are drawn from the marginal, so the analysis already tolerates false negatives at the population level — mildly reassuring about in-batch sampling, but the infinite-negative limit is baked in, so it says nothing about batch-size effects, which is where most of the empirical action in retrieval lives. Temperature is genuinely outside the theory: with A unconstrained and embeddings unnormalized, τ is absorbed into the scale of B. With ℓ₂-normalized embeddings, scale is fixed and τ becomes the real knob trading alignment against the log-partition — structurally the same trade-off δ controls here, which suggests τ and augmentation quality are two handles on one mechanism, but that is an analogy, not a corollary.

A plausible follow-up: the ⊆-versus-= gap in Theorem 5.2 is the most retrieval-relevant open question in the paper. The conjectured equality condition says the two towers recover everything only when the whitened topic geometries agree; otherwise document-side discriminative directions with no query-side counterpart are provably never learned. That is a candidate formal account of the vocabulary-gap phenomenon, and it predicts something testable — that query-side enrichment (doc2query, HyDE, multi-vector query expansion) should help exactly in proportion to the misalignment between whitened query and document mean geometries.

title: Samplability makes learning easier
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-19

Samplability makes learning easier

Guy Blanc, Caleb Koch, Jane Lange, Carmen Strassle, Li-Yang Tan (2025) — arXiv:2512.01276

Main idea. Valiant's PAC model is distribution-free: the learner must succeed under every D over {0,1}ⁿ, including ones whose every generating circuit is superpolynomial — from which drawing even one sample is intractable. The learner must be efficient; the adversary choosing D need not be.
