Samplable PAC (Blum–Furst–Kearns–Lipton 1993) removes the asymmetry: D stays unknown and arbitrary but must have a poly-size generator G with G(Unif) = D. BFKL used it to link learning to cryptography — absent one-way functions, every class is average-case learnable there — but never asked whether the models differ. This paper does. First, a statistical separation: a class of VC dimension 2^{Ω(n)}, exponentially hard in standard PAC, learnable with poly(n,s,1/ε) samples and time under every size-s distribution. Then a computational separation for a class of poly-size circuits, assuming one-way functions plus a new conjecture, made unconditional relative to a random oracle — improving Xiao's separation relative to a specific oracle which, awkwardly, destroyed one-way functions. A fine-grained version sends sample complexity from poly(s) to 2^{Ω(n)} when the generator size rises from s only to Ω(sn log s).

The most interesting part. The clever object is the evasive set: a large H ⊆ {0,1}ⁿ no small circuit can sample from. Literal evasiveness is impossible — a size-O(n) circuit hardcodes one point of H and puts all mass there — so D (ε,k)-misses H if some set H* of k points has D(H \ H*) < ε, and H (ε,k)-evades size-s distributions if every one of them misses it that way. The regime is k ≈ s: the best a size-s generator can do is memorize the ~s/n points it can afford. Strictly stronger than TV distance from Unif(H), it is the right definition because it is exactly the success condition of rote memorization. Write f_H(x) = f(x)·1[x ∈ H] and C_H = {f_H}. For A the class of all Boolean functions, A_H shatters precisely H, so VCdim(A_H) = |H|; yet if H (ε,k)-evades size-s distributions, the learner that dumps its sample into a DNF and predicts 0 elsewhere learns C_H to error O(ε) from O(k/ε) samples. Samplability buys so much because the instances witnessing the VC lower bound are hard to find: the shattering set exists, but nothing efficient produces enough of it to matter.

Broader context. Samplability has long formalized "distributions that actually occur" in average-case complexity (Levin; Impagliazzo's worlds — the authors quote his "real life is not so adversarial that it would solve intractable problems just to give us a hard time"). The usual escapes from distribution-free hardness are distribution-specific learning and results lifting uniform-distribution learners to structured families; samplable PAC scales the distribution-free model down instead. Read it alongside BFKL 1993, Xiao 2010, and universal extrapolation (Impagliazzo–Levin; Hirahara–Nanashima), where continuing a samplable distribution is equivalent to inverting one-way functions. The obvious follow-up is the authors' open problem: a VC analogue for samplable PAC, one quantity in concept and distribution complexity pinning down m(s,ε). A white-box variant handing the learner G looks more tractable — the memorizer never uses G, so upper bounds survive while lower bounds may not.

The IR angle is real but modest. That memorizing learner is a cache, and (ε,k)-evasiveness says exactly when caching the head of a query distribution suffices. Learned indexes are the sharper case: their pessimistic guarantees are quoted over adversarial key distributions, and evasive sets are precisely key sets one can recognize in polynomial time but no efficient process can produce. Likewise adversarial retrieval, where the spammer is bounded by construction, so a distribution-free bound on a learned ranker guards against an adversary who does not exist. This is a complexity paper first, but its moral — a lower bound witnessed by an unsamplable distribution may be no obstacle at all — transfers wherever we quote worst-case bounds over query or document distributions.

Proof sketch. Lemma 2.5 builds an evasive set probabilistically: include each x with probability δ; for fixed D let T be the ≤ k points of mass ≥ 1/k, so D(H\T) sums independent [0,1/k]-bounded variables of mean ≤ δ and Chernoff gives Pr_H[D (ε,k)-hits H] ≤ e^{−εk/6}. Since there are only s^{O(n+s)} circuits of size s, k* = Θ((s+n)log s / ε) beats a union bound over all size-s generators, all s, and (after dyadic discretization) all ε ≥ 4δ. The learner's error splits into mass on H outside the k heaviest points (< ε by evasiveness) plus each heavy point's D(x)e^{−D(x)m} ≤ 1/(em), totalling k/(em); with δ = 2^{−n/2} that is Theorem 5. Theorem 6 replaces the random H by a δ-biased d-wise independent one, d = Θ(t log t), using a bounded-independence Chernoff bound; PRG explicitness makes membership in H, or a generator for Unif(H), a circuit of size O(tn log t) — so the very H that evades all size-s ≤ t distributions is itself sampled by a circuit only O(n log s) larger, and Unif(H) in the BEHW/EHKV hard-distribution-on-a-shattering-set lemma gives the Ω(δ2ⁿ) bound. For Theorem 7 the class is F_H, with F a GGM pseudorandom function family and H an explicit evasive set (poly-size membership circuit, superpolynomial size, (1/s, s^c)-evasive; Conjecture 8.1). Easiness is again the memorizer; hardness is Lemma 8.8, strengthening Valiant's observation that PRFs are unlearnable under uniform: any m-sample learner of accuracy 1−ε over any D yields a nonuniform distinguisher of advantage 1/2 − ε − α/2, where α = Pr[x^{(m+1)} ∈ {x^{(1)},…,x^{(m)}}] ≤ m/|H| is negligible once |H| is superpolynomial. Conjecture 8.1 implies P ≠ NP (by Jerrum–Valiant–Vazirani an NP oracle almost-uniformly samples the membership circuit's accepting inputs, and such a sampler (0.45, |H|/2)-hits H), so it will not be proved outright — but it holds relative to a random oracle, where H^O = {x : O(x,y) = 1 for all y in a fixed S of size ℓ}, an AND of ℓ oracle bits, so membership is an O(n²)-size oracle circuit and each x lands in H independently with probability 2^{−ℓ} ≈ 2^{−n/2}. The key lemma is query hardness of finding many distinct satisfying assignments: any q-query algorithm with q ≤ k/(16δ) outputs k distinct elements of H^O with probability ≤ exp(−Ω(k)), since one may assume it queries whatever it outputs, reducing success to Bin(q+k, δ) ≥ k. The bridge from hitting to finding is Proposition 8.7: if D (ε,k)-hits H then ⌈2k/ε⌉ i.i.d. draws contain k distinct elements of H with probability ≥ 1/2, because while fewer than k are found each draw is new with probability ≥ ε by the very definition of hitting, so the stopping time is dominated by a sum of k geometrics. The closing trick is a quantifier swap: exp(−Ω(k)) depends on the number of outputs k = s^{1.01}, not on the generator size s, so it survives a union bound over the exp(O(s log s)) size-s oracle generators. Random oracles are one-way, so the separation is unconditional relative to one.

title: How Reinforcement Learning After Next-Token Prediction Facilitates Learning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-19

How Reinforcement Learning After Next-Token Prediction Facilitates Learning

Nikolaos Tsilivis, Eran Malach, Karen Ullrich, Julia Kempe (2025) — arXiv:2510.11495

Main idea. The dominant LLM recipe — next-token prediction (NTP) on web-scale text, then RL with a verifier reward — reliably produces both large capability jumps and longer responses, but there is no account of why the optimization does this. Tsilivis et al. propose a framework built on one modeling assumption they argue is the honest way to read internet-scale data: the pretraining corpus already contains correct, elaborate demonstrations of the target task, but they are rare. Formally they study a mixture D(p_cot) over sequences encoding d-bit parity: with probability p_cot the sequence is the full chain of thought (x₁, x₁x₂, …, ∏xᵢ, EOS), and with probability 1−p_cot it is the bare answer (∏xᵢ, EOS). The empirical finding (GPT-2/Mistral transformers trained from scratch, d up to 50) is sharp: under NTP the model learns the long branch quickly and stays length-calibrated, generating long responses with probability ≈ p_cot, so temperature-1 accuracy sits at exactly (1+p_cot)/2 while greedy accuracy is pinned at chance whenever p_cot < 1/3. Switching to GRPO/REINFORCE/STaR with a correctness reward then lifts greedy accuracy to 100% within tens of RL iterations, with response length growing in lockstep. The failure during pretraining is an estimation failure, not an approximation one — a shallow transformer can represent parity (Liu et al., 2023).

The most interesting part. The mechanism is a reweighting fixed point, and it is disarmingly clean. After pretraining, the model's own sampling distribution is p_cot on long-and-correct, (1−p_cot)/2 on short-and-correct (short responses are random guesses), and the rest wrong. STaR with a chain-of-thought-correctness reward trains on correct samples only, so the effective data mixture becomes p₁ = p_cot/(p_cot + (1−p_cot)/2). Iterating, p_{n+1} = 2p_n/(1+p_n), i.e. the odds of a long response double every round: p_{n+1}/(1−p_{n+1}) = 2·p_n/(1−p_n), giving p_n = p₀/(p₀ + (1−p₀)2^{−n}) and a hitting time of n* = O(log((1−p_cot)/p_cot)) rounds to cross p_n > 1/3. The 1/3 threshold is not a fitting constant: a calibrated model's greedy second token satisfies P[y₂ = x₁x₂ | y₁ = x₁] = 2p/(1+p) versus P[y₂ = EOS | y₁ = x₁] = (1−p)/(1+p), and these cross exactly at p = 1/3 — matching the empirical transformer threshold. So RL is not discovering new structure; it is exploiting the asymmetry that verification filters trajectories in proportion to a quantity the model already got calibrated to, and the length increase is a side effect of the mode of the conditional distribution flipping. Length growth is thus a learning phenomenon, not the usual expressivity story — it shows up even where representation is free.

Broader context. Parity is the canonical hard-for-SGD target: it is SQ-hard (Kearns, 1998), gradients on the full d-parity have exponentially small signal-to-noise (Shalev-Shwartz et al., 2017; Daniely & Malach, 2020; Shoshani & Shamir, 2025), and even the sparse-k case has a well-mapped plateau-then-drop dynamics (Barak et al., 2022's "hidden progress"; Abbe et al.'s leap complexity; Glasgow, 2024). The complementary line — Malach (2024) and Joshi et al. (2025) — shows autoregressive NTP with perfect CoT data learns any efficiently computable function, which is exactly the assumption this paper relaxes to "a p_cot ≥ d^{−κ} fraction of good demonstrations." It also stands apart from the CoT-expressivity results (Feng et al., 2023; Merrill & Sabharwal, 2024; Li et al., 2024), which explain why length can help but never why optimization produces it. Natural follow-ups: noisy or partially-correct CoT (their Appendix C.2 gestures at partial traces), targets whose short branch is learnable-but-slow rather than impossible, and analyzing GRPO's group-relative baseline as a different reweighting operator than STaR's hard filter — one would expect a modified recursion with a different fixed point and possibly a length penalty's effect readable off it. For generative retrieval the resonance is real but should not be overstated: RL fine-tuning of a docid-emitting decoder has exactly this structure — a pretrained decoder that is calibrated to a rare correct-trajectory mass, a binary verifier (relevance), and a reward-filtered self-distillation loop. The p_{n+1} = 2p_n/(1+p_n) recursion is a statement about how fast reward filtering amplifies a rare decoding path, which is the question one asks when the only positive signal is a sparse relevance label.

Proof sketch. The theory replaces the transformer with a linear autoregressive model (Malach, 2024): d+1 logistic predictors, position ℓ using features ϕ_ℓ(x) = (x₁,…,x_{d+ℓ−1}, x_{d+ℓ−1}x₁,…,x_{d+ℓ−1}x_d), i.e. degree-≤2 monomials involving the last generated token — enough to chain the CoT one XOR at a time, and enough to learn any sparse parity, but not the full d-parity in one step. Position 2 is split into an EOS-vs-continue head and a ±1 head so each subproblem is convex. Theorem 1/4 (pretraining): with ℓ₂ regularization, SGD on the per-position logistic loss is a strongly convex stochastic optimization problem, so the standard SGD guarantee (Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David, Thm 14.11) gives excess risk ε after Õ(d⁹/δε⁶) per-position iterations; properness of the logistic loss then forces calibration, π_h(long) = p_cot ± O(ε), and a case analysis of the conditional probabilities gives the greedy dichotomy at p_cot = 1/3. Theorem 2/5 (post-training): the key move is an exact identity — the STaR risk at round n, conditioned on r_cot = 1, is the NTP risk under D(q_n) with q_n = (p_{n−1}+ζ)/((p_{n−1}+1)/2 + ζ + ξ), |ζ|,|ξ| ≲ ε. So RL is re-invocable pretraining on a shifted mixture, and Theorem 4 can be applied inductively. The technical work is error control: Taylor-expanding f(q,ζ,ξ) with Lagrange remainder gives e_{n+1} ≤ 2e_n + O(ε), hence e_n ≲ 2ⁿε — the perturbation compounds at the same rate as the signal. Since n* ≍ log((1−p_cot)/p_cot), demanding 2^{n*}ε < 1/15 yields the paper's standing assumption ε ≲ p_cot/(1−p_cot), and a union bound with δ_i = δ/2n* closes it. Net: O(poly(d)) total SGD steps whenever p_cot = Ω(d^{−κ}). Caveat worth flagging: the negative side of the separation is proved within this feature class (the short branch simply cannot express d-parity), so it is a hardness-by-architecture statement leaning on the cited SQ/gradient-variance results for the general claim, while the p_cot = 1/3 threshold transfers to real transformers only empirically.

title: Measuring Representational Shifts in Continual Learning: A Linear Transformation Perspective
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-19

Measuring Representational Shifts in Continual Learning: A Linear Transformation Perspective

Joonkyu Kim, Yejin Kim, Jy-yong Sohn (ICML 2025; arXiv preprint, 2025) — arXiv:2505.20970

Main idea. Catastrophic forgetting is usually scored end-to-end, as accuracy lost on task t after training on t+1,…,t+Δt. A parallel literature scores it at the hidden layers instead — has the encoder stopped producing good features for task t, independent of whether the head still decodes them? That question is normally answered empirically (linear-probe accuracy drop, CKA, CCA), never analytically. The paper's move is to define a quantity that is both a faithful surrogate for probe-based representation forgetting and tractable enough to bound. That quantity is the representation discrepancy

D^k_t(h_t, Δt) = min_{T ∈ R^{w_k×w_k}} max_{x ∈ X_t} ‖T h^k_{t+Δt}(x) − h^k_t(x)‖₂,

the worst-case, over task-t inputs, misalignment between the layer-k feature maps of the old and new models, after the best linear re-alignment. The minimisation over T is the whole point: a linear probe cannot see any distortion that a linear map can undo, so quotienting by GL(w_k) makes the metric match what probing actually measures (empirically R² = 0.88 / 0.74 against probe-accuracy drop on Split-CIFAR100 / ImageNet1K). From a bound on D they read off three claims: the forgetting curve has a forgetting phase then a saturation phase; the saturation level scales linearly with the size of the representation space ‖R^k_t(h_t)‖ := max_x ‖h^k_t(x)‖₂, which is itself empirically linear in k; and saturation arrives sooner at deeper layers and later for wider networks.

Most interesting part. Two things. First, the quotient-by-linear-maps construction: forgetting is defined modulo exactly the group of transformations the downstream reader is invariant to, which is conceptually cleaner than CKA and, unlike CKA, survives being pushed through a triangle inequality. Second, the depth dependence in Theorem 2 is geometric, not linear: the convergence rate obeys r^k_t ≤ (√2−1)γm^{−β} Σ_{i=1}^k (λ_t μ_t c_t)^i / λ_t, a sum of powers accumulated one layer at a time by unrolling a perturbation recursion. Depth compounds drift multiplicatively while width damps it as m^{−β}. Honest caveats, in passing: the asymptotic bound μ_t c_t ‖R^k_t(h_t)‖ is vacuous, since taking T = 0 already gives D ≤ ‖R^k_t(h_t)‖ and μ_t, c_t ≥ 1 by construction — so the "saturation phase" is the regime where the bound stops saying anything, and the two-phase story is really the shape of one scalar rational function. Assumption 1 (∃T with T W^k_{t'} = W^k_t) is near-trivial for square invertible hidden matrices (T = W^k_t (W^k_{t'})^{−1}), so Fig. 2's "validation" is less informative than advertised. And D is not scale-normalised, so "deeper layers forget more" is partly "deeper activations have larger norms."

Proof sketch. Three steps. (1) Lemma 1: write h^k = W^k ϕ(h^{k−1}) for both models, add and subtract T W^k_{t+Δt} ϕ(h^{k−1}_t), then triangle-inequality, sub-multiplicativity of the spectral norm, and 1-Lipschitzness of ReLU give D^k_t ≤ min_T [ d(R^{k−1}_t(h_t), R^{k−1}_t(h_{t+Δt}))·‖T W^k_{t+Δt}‖₂ + ‖R^{k−1}_t(h_t)‖·‖T W^k_{t+Δt} − W^k_t‖₂ ], i.e. one layer of feature drift plus one layer of weight misalignment. (2) Lemma 2, the key trick: min_X c₁‖X‖₂ + c₂‖X − A‖₂ is neither convex nor differentiable in the spectral norm, so they evaluate it at the closed-form minimiser of the Frobenius surrogate, X* = c₂²/(c₁²+c₂²)·A — legitimate because any feasible point upper-bounds a min — yielding c₂‖A‖₂·f(ω) with ω = c₁/c₂ and f(x) = (x²+x)/(x²+1). All the dynamics live in this one rational function: f increases to a peak of (1+√2)/2 ≈ 1.21 at ω = 1+√2, then decays to 1. Assumption 1 is what lets ‖A‖₂ be replaced by ‖W^k_t‖₂. (3) Proposition 2 removes the weight norm using Arora et al.'s compression constants — layer cushion μ_t and activation contraction c_t — trading ‖R^{k−1}_t‖·‖W^k_t‖₂ for μ_t c_t ‖R^k_t(h_t)‖, giving Theorem 1. Theorem 2 then bounds ω^k_t(Δt) by a recursion A_k ≤ μ_t c_t(λ_t A_{k−1} + (γ/λ_t) m^{−β} Δt) with A₀ = 0 (input drift is zero), unrolled into the geometric sum, and converts it to a rate by setting ω(Δt_sat) = 1+√2, the argmax of f. Assumption 2 — that inter-model feature distance is Θ(Δt) — supplies the lower-bound half and is assumed, not proved.

Broader context and a connection to your work. Task forgetting asks whether the classifier still works; representation forgetting asks whether the features still could work — Davari et al. (CVPR 2022) popularised the linear-probe version, Ramasesh et al. (2020) showed forgetting concentrates in layers near the output, Hess et al. (2023) separated feature forgetting from feature accumulation, and Guha & Lakshman (2024), whose perturbation machinery is reused wholesale here, bounded output-level forgetting by depth and width. This paper is the first to make the hidden-layer version analytic.

The vector-search connection is real rather than forced. When an encoder is continually updated and a corpus is already embedded and indexed, the operative question is exactly "is there a linear map that realigns old vectors to the new space, and how large is the worst-case residual?" — which is D^k_t verbatim. Backward-compatible-training and backfill-free retrieval lines (BCT, RACT, and linear/Procrustes adapters) are in effect assuming D is small; this paper says when that assumption fails, and that the failure is fastest at the last layer (precisely where retrieval embeddings are taken) and slower for wider encoders. The max over inputs is the right aggregation for ANN too: recall is destroyed by individual badly drifted neighbourhoods, not by average drift. A clean follow-up is to constrain T to the orthogonal group — Procrustes rather than GL — which preserves inner products and so converts a discrepancy bound into a bound on inner-product rank perturbation, i.e. a principled drift budget for deciding when a linear backfill suffices versus when the ANN index must be fully rebuilt. The same instrument applied to generative retrieval would measure docid forgetting under incremental indexing (DSI++, IncDSI): track the layerwise discrepancy of the encoder as new documents arrive and predict the point at which docid decoding collapses, rather than detecting it after the fact.

title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-19

Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness

Qi Zhang, Yifei Wang, Jingyi Cui, Xiang Pan, Qi Lei, Stefanie Jegelka, Yisen Wang (2024) — arXiv:2410.21331

Main idea. The interpretability literature has settled into a comfortable assumption: making individual neurons mean one thing costs you accuracy, because superposition is how a narrow representation packs in more features than it has dimensions. This paper attacks that assumption sideways. It concedes the clean-accuracy point — monosemantic features are at best a wash on clean data (−1.7 to −0.1 points on CIFAR-100/ImageNet-100 linear probing) — and argues instead that the tradeoff inverts the moment the evaluation stops being clean. Using two orthogonal routes to monosemanticity (non-negative contrastive learning as an intrinsic method, top-K sparse autoencoders as a post-hoc one), they show consistent, noise-monotone gains: +13.7 points under 90% symmetric label noise on ImageNet-100, gains growing with Gaussian/uniform input noise strength, small gains on ImageNet-Sketch and Stylized-ImageNet, and reduced overfitting in few-shot finetuning (higher validation, lower training accuracy at 10% of the data). They extend the recipe to LLMs with "MonoLoRA," which inserts ReLUs into the LoRA update, and report that Llama-2-7b-chat retains more of its safety alignment under SST-2/Dolly finetuning while matching or beating LoRA on task metrics.

Critique. The empirical pattern is real and appears across enough axes (label noise, input noise, OOD, few-shot, LLM alignment drift) that it is unlikely to be cherry-picked, and Appendix C's demonstration that gains stack with Symmetric Cross Entropy is the right orthogonality check. But the causal attribution is loose in a way the paper never confronts. Every "monosemantic" arm differs from its baseline by a non-negativity constraint (ReLU on features) or a sparse bottleneck — both of which are well-known regularizers independent of any semantic property. Nothing isolates monosemanticity as the operative variable: no sweep of SAE's K, no sweep of constraint strength, no plot of the paper's own semantic-consistency score against robustness gain, no L1-sparsity or random-non-negative-projection control. Without that, the honest summary is "sparsity regularizes," which is not news. The MonoLoRA comparison is worse than not-apples-to-apples: σ(Aσ(Bσ(x))) is a nonlinear two-layer adapter, no longer mergeable into W₀, so it differs from LoRA in function class and inference cost, not just sparsity. The mechanistic evidence in Figure 4(c) is close to circular — semantic consistency is computed from class labels, so correctly-classified samples having more class-pure salient dimensions is nearly definitional. Everything is ResNet-18 on 100-class subsets, one seed, no error bars, and the OOD gains (23.6→25.2 sketch) sit in a regime where absolute accuracy is ~20%.

Context. Superposition — Elhage et al.'s Toy Models of Superposition (2022) — posits that networks represent more features than neurons by placing near-orthogonal feature directions in a lower-dimensional space, tolerating interference in exchange for capacity; polysemantic neurons are the symptom. Sparse autoencoders (Cunningham et al. 2024; Gao et al. 2024; Templeton's Claude 3 Sonnet work) are the current standard tool for undoing this, learning an overcomplete sparse dictionary over activations. The two anchors worth reading beside this paper are Elhage et al. for the model being assumed, and Wang et al.'s non-negative contrastive learning (2024), which supplies both the NCL method and the monosemanticity metric used here. An obvious follow-up: hold the encoder fixed and vary only SAE sparsity K, plotting semantic consistency against noise robustness — if the relation is monotone in monosemanticity rather than in sparsity per se, the paper's thesis is established; if it tracks sparsity alone, it is not. The retrieval connection is genuine but should be stated modestly: non-negative, sparse embeddings are exactly the geometry of learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE and successors), and this paper is evidence that the sparsity such models impose for inverted-index efficiency may also buy distributional robustness — a free-lunch argument for sparse retrievers under domain shift that, to my knowledge, nobody has tested directly.

Proof sketch. The theory is a two-dimensional instance of Elhage's toy model: latent x₁, x₂ are i.i.d., zero with probability S and Uniform(0,1] otherwise, with label y = 1{x₁ > x₂}. The monosemantic representation is ν_mono = x₁ (one concept kept, one discarded); the polysemantic one is the antipodal-pair readout ν_poly = x₁ − x₂. Separability is measured by an LDA-style ratio J(ν) = |μ₀ − μ₁|/(σ₀σ₁). Theorem 4.1 computes all four conditional moments in closed form — Theorem B.1 integrates the conditional CDF P(x₁ ≤ x | x₁ ≤ x₂) directly, Lemma B.2 derives the CDF of the difference x₁ − x₂ under the sparse-uniform mixture — and finds J(ν_poly) = 10.16 > J(ν_mono) = 6.20 at S = 0.2: superposition wins on clean data. Theorem 4.2 then pushes symmetric label noise through. The key trick is Lemma B.4: under noise rate η, the class-conditional law of ν becomes a fixed mixture of the two clean conditionals with weights determined by η and the class priors ½(1±S²). Inter-class distance shrinks by a factor common to both representations (Theorem B.5), so it cancels; the whole comparison reduces to the four noisy variances (Theorem B.6, a law-of-total-variance expansion of the mixture), and the polysemantic feature's larger clean μ₀-gap inflates its mixture variance faster. Hence J̃/J degrades more slowly for the monosemantic feature, with a crossover at η ≈ 0.25. Appendix B.3 repeats this for additive Gaussian input noise, where ν_poly absorbs 2λ² of variance against ν_mono's λ². Two caveats: the final inequalities are verified by plugging in decimal constants at S = 0.2, not proved for general (S, η); and because y is exactly sign(ν_poly), the polysemantic feature is a sufficient statistic for the label, so in the population limit symmetric label noise leaves its Bayes-optimal threshold unmoved (the very noise-tolerance result of Ghosh et al. that the paper cites). The theorem therefore shows that a second-moment proxy degrades, not that clean test accuracy does — the finite-sample overfitting that actually drives the experiments is not modeled.

title: On Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Low Rank Layers
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-18

On Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Low Rank Layers

Pinto, Andrea; Rangamani, Akshay; Poggio, Tomaso — 2024-11-20

Main idea

The gap this paper attacks is a mismatch between two literatures. Optimization theory and experiments say that trained deep networks drift toward low-rank weight matrices (implicit bias of regularized SGD, matrix-factorization results, neural collapse). Statistical theory, meanwhile, controls deep networks with norm-based Rademacher bounds, and those bounds are essentially blind to rank: the paper opens with a clean one-layer counterexample showing that the usual scalar-valued Gaussian complexity of the spectral-ball {Wx : ‖W‖₂ ≤ B} is exactly attained by a rank-one matrix (align W = (B/‖v‖)vvᵀ with v = (1/m)Σγᵢxᵢ), so constraining rank changes nothing in that formalism. Pinto, Rangamani and Poggio's move is to switch to Maurer's vector-valued Gaussian complexity (one Gaussian per output coordinate) and to peel layers with Maurer's 2016 chain rule for suprema of Gaussian processes instead of the standard Golowich–Rakhlin–Shamir peeling. The payoff is structural: rank factors stop multiplying across layers, because the quantity that carries the rank — the diameter of the layer-to-layer image — is governed by the smallest-rank matrix in the stack, not by the product.

Proof sketch: what is proved and how

The class is F_L = {W_L φ(W_{L−1} φ(… φ(W₁x))) : ‖Wᵢ‖₂ ≤ Bᵢ, rank(Wᵢ) ≤ rᵢ} with φ a 1-Lipschitz piecewise-linear activation (ReLU/leaky ReLU) and data bounded by ‖xᵢ‖ ≤ R. Theorem 7 bounds the empirical Gaussian complexity by (‖X‖_F/m){ ‖W₁‖_F √h₁ ∏_{i≥2} C₁‖Wᵢ‖₂ + Σ_{i=2}^L C₁^{L−i} C₂ √(2 r̄ᵢ) κᵢ ‖Wᵢ‖_F √hᵢ }, with r̄ᵢ = min_{j≤i} rank(Wⱼ) and κᵢ ∝ ∏_{j≠i}‖Wⱼ‖₂; after ‖Wᵢ‖_F ≤ √r ‖Wᵢ‖₂ and h = maxᵢhᵢ this collapses to O(C₁^L ∏ᵢBᵢ · R L r √(h/m)). Plugged into a vector-contraction generalization bound (Theorem 2), it bounds the expected loss by the empirical loss plus Lπ Ĝ_S(F) + O(√(log(1/δ)/m)) for Lipschitz losses.

The proof is a layerwise recursion of Maurer's chain rule G(F(Y)) ≤ C₁L(F)G(Y) + C₂D(Y)R(F,Y) + G(F(y₀)), with the third term killed by taking y₀ = 0 (zero weights are in the class). At each layer, L(F) = ‖Wᵢ‖₂, the activation is absorbed by Talagrand contraction, and the base case (Lemma 10) is a Cauchy–Schwarz computation ⟨W, ΓX⟩ ≤ ‖W‖_F‖ΓX‖_F with E‖ΓX‖_F ≤ R√(hm). Unrolling gives a "direct recursive" term (a product of spectral norms) plus one "disturbance" term per peeled layer. The load-bearing step is Lemma 5, the diameter bound. Writing two networks' evaluations on xᵢ as Aⁱ = W_ℓ D_{ℓ−1}ⁱ ⋯ D₁ⁱ W₁ with diagonal activation-pattern matrices D, the diagonal matrices are norm-≤1 but can be full rank, so rank(Aⁱ) ≤ min_j rank(Wⱼ); combined with the fact that two rank-r, spectral-B matrices satisfy ‖P − Q‖_F ≤ 2B√(2r), the diameter is ‖X‖_F · 2∏‖Wⱼ‖₂ · √(2 min_j rank Wⱼ). That single √r — not r^{L/2} — is exactly where rank enters, and it is why one low-rank layer anywhere in the stack caps the whole prefix. Lemma 6 supplies the other chain-rule factor, R(F, Z_{ℓ−1}) ≤ ‖W_ℓ‖_F √h_ℓ.

Most interesting part, and where I'd push back

The diameter argument is genuinely elegant and is the paper's real contribution; the "min rank wins" observation is the kind of thing that should generalize. But the honesty audit is less flattering. First, the C₁^L prefactor is exponential in depth, which the authors concede and conjecture is an artifact (by analogy to the 2^L later removed from Neyshabur et al. 2015). Without that hand-wave the headline comparison to Golowich et al. — theirs scales as √L r^{L/2} on this class, the new one as L r √h — does not hold; and against Bartlett et al. / Neyshabur et al. (√(L³rh)) the new bound √(L²r²h) only wins when r ≲ L, a genuinely interesting rank–depth tradeoff but a narrow win. Second, there is no numerical evaluation anywhere: no experiment, no plot, no estimate of the bound versus an actual generalization gap. Given that the bound retains ∏ᵢ‖Wᵢ‖₂ and a √h, it is almost certainly vacuous at realistic scales, and unlike Golowich's it is not size-independent — width is traded back in for rank sensitivity. Third, low rank here is an assumption defining the hypothesis class, not a consequence proved from training dynamics; the empirical evidence is cited, not derived. Worse, the assumption is exact rank, and the key diameter lemma needs exact rank of the product, whereas real trained matrices have fast-decaying but full spectra. A stable-rank version (‖W‖_F²/‖W‖₂²) would be much more convincing; the base lemma tolerates it, the diameter lemma as written does not. Finally, the neural-collapse payoff is thinner than it reads: Theorem 8 is quoted verbatim from Golowich et al., applies to a rank-one bottleneck (i.e. an ℝ→ℝ map, so binary classification), while collapse gives rank C−1, and it is a capacity statement about a class chosen after seeing the trained net rather than an explanation of why collapse helps.

Context and follow-ups

The lineage is: Neyshabur et al. (norm-based capacity), Bartlett–Foster–Telgarsky (covering numbers, spectral × ‖·‖_{2,1}), Neyshabur et al.'s PAC-Bayes version, and Golowich–Rakhlin–Shamir's depth-independent peeling with Frobenius products — all of which are orders of magnitude loose for dense nets. The closest recent counterpoint is Galanti et al. (NeurIPS 2023), where structural sparsity (convolutions) pushes norm-based bounds toward non-vacuity; this paper is the rank-flavored analogue of that program, minus the empirics. On the bias side: Galanti–Siegel–Gupte–Poggio on regularized SGD's rank minimization, Huh et al.'s low-rank simplicity bias, Timor–Vardi–Shamir on low-rank top layers, Papyan–Han–Donoho and Rangamani et al. on (intermediate) neural collapse. Obvious follow-ups: kill C₁^L; restate everything in stable rank so the result survives approximate low rank; run the bound numerically against measured gaps the way Galanti et al. did; and redo the argument with the Chu–Raginsky Rademacher chain rule to stay in Rademacher-land throughout.

For you, one connection is real without being forced. A dual encoder's score matrix is rank-bounded by the embedding dimension, so a retriever is structurally the "bottleneck layer caps the whole tower" object this paper analyzes: if the diameter argument transfers, the generalization of a learned retriever would be governed by the effective rank of the projection, not the nominal dimension d — which is the same quantity (intrinsic dimension of the embedding cloud) that governs ANN index quality and quantization error. That would give a single knob speaking to both search cost and generalization, and would sharpen the question of why ColBERT-style 128-dim projections lose so little. The caveat: this bound is stated for a Lipschitz loss composed with an unnormalized feed-forward net, not for a contrastive objective over normalized embeddings with inner-product scores and a softmax over a large candidate set, so the transfer is a research project, not a corollary. Absent that, the paper is worth reading mainly for the diameter lemma as a reusable technique.

(Minor erratum spotted while reading: Theorem 7 indexes the product in κᵢ to d where L is clearly meant.)

title: Reciprocal Learning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-18

Reciprocal Learning

Rodemann, Julian; Jansen, Christoph; Schollmeyer, Georg — 2024/08/12

Main idea

The paper's move is to notice that a whole family of algorithms we usually keep in separate boxes — self-training, active learning, contextual bandits, Bayesian optimization, superset learning — all share one structural feature: they run empirical risk minimization on a training sample that they themselves modified in the previous round using the current fit. Rodemann, Jansen and Schollmeyer formalize this as two interlocking decision problems: the familiar one (Θ, Θ, L) solved by ERM, and a second one (Θ, X, L_θ) whose action space is the feature space, whose loss depends on the current parameter, and whose solution is a "data selection function." Composing them gives a single map R: Θ × P → Θ × P (or Θ × P × N in the greedy case). The payoff of this abstraction is that convergence stops being an algorithm-by-algorithm question and becomes a question about one map: is R a contraction? The cute corollary of the decision-theoretic symmetry is data regularization — a strongly convex penalty on the selected point, exactly mirroring Tikhonov regularization of parameters, whose purpose is to make data selection insensitive to small parameter changes.

Proof sketch

The main result (Theorem 3) is: if the non-greedy sample adaption f_n is L-Lipschitz with L ≤ (1 + β/γ)⁻¹, then the iterates (θ_t, P_t) converge at a linear rate to a unique fixed point (θ_c, P_c) satisfying θ_c = argmin_θ E_{(Y,X)∼f_n(θ_c,P_c)} ℓ. Here γ is strong convexity and β joint smoothness of the loss (Assumptions 2–3), with Assumption 1 giving α-Lipschitz gradients in features.

The metric space is Θ × P with the L2 norm on Θ, the Wasserstein-1 distance on P, and the sum metric on the product. The proof has two halves. The estimation half shows the ERM component R₁ is (Lβ/γ)-Lipschitz: strong convexity gives −γ‖R₁ − R₁′‖² ≥ (R₁ − R₁′)ᵀ∇F(R₁′); the directional derivative T(x,y) := (R₁ − R₁′)ᵀ∇ℓ(y,x,R₁′) is ‖R₁ − R₁′‖β-Lipschitz by β-smoothness plus Cauchy–Schwarz, so after normalizing to 1-Lipschitz the Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual lets the W₁-Lipschitzness of f_n bound the difference in expectations by L(‖θ − θ′‖ + W₁(P,P′)). That is the crucial trick: it converts distributional sensitivity into parameter sensitivity. The data half is trivial — the second component R₂ simply is f_n, so it inherits L. Adding the two inequalities gives ‖R_n − R_n′‖ ≤ L(1 + β/γ)(‖θ − θ′‖ + W₁(P,P′)), a contraction precisely when L(1 + β/γ) < 1; Banach then yields existence, uniqueness and the geometric rate, with t ≥ log(‖(θ₀,P₀) − (θ_c,P_c)‖/Δ)/log L(1+β/γ) iterations for accuracy Δ.

The real work is establishing that L is finite at all, i.e. Theorems 1 and 2. Lemma 1 shows the regularized selection argmax_x {c(x,θ) + (1/L_s)R(x)} is (L_s·L_c/κ)-Lipschitz in θ, via the two variational inequalities for the two maximizers, κ-strong convexity of R to lower-bound the left side, and linearity of c in x (Condition 5) to upper-bound the right. Lemma 2 shows the soft-label prediction p(x,θ) is Lipschitz in both arguments, obtained indirectly: ∇_xℓ = ∇_pℓ·∇_x p is Lipschitz by Assumption 1, ∇_pℓ is Lipschitz by Condition 2, hence ∇_x p is Lipschitz, hence bounded on bounded X, hence p is Lipschitz. Theorem 1 then decomposes f componentwise — in θ (via Lemmas 1 and 2 plus the product bound ‖f(ש) − f(ש′)‖ ≤ (L_p + L_c̃)‖ש − ש′‖, using that both c̃ and p are bounded by 1), in P (the sensitivity is n/(n+1) ≤ 1), and in n (bounded by 1 since |n − n′| ≥ 1) — and takes L = max{L_θ, L_P, L_n}. Theorem 2 replaces regularization with randomization: drawing from the softmax c̃ ∝ exp(c(x,θ)) makes selection smooth because softmax is continuously differentiable, needing only bounded gradients of c (Condition 4). Theorem 4 adds an optimality gap ‖θ_c − θ*‖₂ ≤ 2L_ℓL/γ by contradiction, combining L_ℓL-Lipschitzness of the risk in θ with the γ/2-quadratic growth from strong convexity — structurally the same argument as Perdomo et al.'s stable-vs-optimal bound.

Critique

The elegant part is genuinely elegant: the observation that randomization and regularization are interchangeable routes to the same Lipschitz property, which then discriminates between practices — Thompson sampling and ε-greedy converge, UCB is not guaranteed to; amending/editing self-training converges, incremental self-training cannot; active learning from a soft-label ("weak") oracle converges, from a hard-label ("strong") oracle it does not. Those are non-obvious, falsifiable-looking design statements.

But the guarantees are thinner than they read. First, the chain from Theorems 1–2 to Theorem 3 is broken in an important way: Theorems 1 and 2 prove only that some finite L exists; Theorem 3 needs L ≤ (1 + β/γ)⁻¹, and since β ≥ γ for any nonconstant smooth strongly convex loss, that threshold is at most 1/2. Section 5 simply assumes "L ≤ (1 + β/γ)⁻¹ ... throughout" before stating all three corollaries. So Corollaries 1–3 are not "Thompson sampling converges"; they are "Thompson sampling converges if an unquantified constant is below 1/2." Worse, the paper's own component bounds point the wrong way: in the non-greedy adaption (Equation 2) the term n₀P/n₀ has unit coefficient, so L_P looks to be ≈1 before the removal term's partial cancellation, and L = max{L_θ, L_P, L_n} ≥ L_P. Nowhere is L_P shown to be < 1/2 for any concrete algorithm, and no experiment or numerical example appears anywhere in the paper. Generality here really does come at the price of saying nothing sharp about any single algorithm.

Second, "approximately optimal" is doing heavy lifting. The reference point θ_ (Definition 9) is the _look-ahead in-sample optimum_: argmin over (θ,P) jointly of the empirical risk on the sample θ itself induces. That objective is minimized in part by steering toward training data that is easy to fit — it is a statement about the self-induced training sample, not about population risk or generalization, which the authors concede is future work. And the gap does not shrink with t: substituting the admissible L ≤ γ/(γ+β) into 2L_ℓL/γ gives ‖θ_c − θ_‖ ≤ 2L_ℓ/(γ+β), a fixed constant set by the loss's Lipschitz constant and curvature. For a weakly curved (small γ) problem it is large, and γ is exactly what one shrinks to avoid over-regularizing.

Third, the individual conditions are restrictive in ways the framing soft-pedals. Condition 5's linearity of c in x — needed for Lemma 1 — excludes essentially every acquisition function actually used (entropy, BALD, expected model change, UCB, margin confidence). The text claims Condition 4 implies Condition 5 "through characterization of Lipschitz-continuity by bounded gradients," but bounded ∇_x c gives Lipschitzness, not linearity, so the implication as stated appears simply wrong (it is not load-bearing for Theorem 2, which uses Condition 4 directly, but it is used to soften Condition 5's cost). Relatedly, the discussion after Definition 3 says a higher L_s makes selection less sensitive to θ, while Lemma 1's constant L_s·L_c/κ says the opposite — and since the penalty weight is 1/L_s, the regularization strength is defined in terms of a constant that the lemma then bounds, which is at least circular in presentation. Data removal (Definition 4) is uniform-at-random and modeled only "in expectation" by ∫X dP, i.e. by the mean feature vector, which is a crude stand-in for what amending self-training actually does (model-dependent removal, which would add further Lipschitz terms). Everything is binary classification with one point added per iteration, soft labels are required throughout, and Θ×P's completeness under the sum metric is never checked before invoking Banach. Finally, Theorem 5 ("greedy reciprocal learning does not converge") is an artifact of the definition: the metric includes n, and ‖n_m − n_n‖ ≥ 1, so the result says only that the sample size diverges — (θ_t, P_t) could still converge. Theorem 6 ("can diverge") is a contrived one-line counterexample positing R₁ = C + θ′L and sending L → ∞. Calling these "tightness" is generous.

Broader context

The unifying observation sits in a long line of worry about feedback loops between a model and its own training data. Self-training's pathology has a name — confirmation bias: pseudo-labels reinforce whatever the initial model believed. Active learning's sampling bias means the labeled pool is no longer i.i.d. from the population, which breaks standard generalization arguments; bandits create the same problem for inference, which is why Zhang, Janson and Murphy's work on M-estimators under adaptively collected data exists. This paper's claim is that all of these are one map and the question is whether it contracts.

The closest literature is performative prediction, and the paper is refreshingly direct about the debt: the proof of Theorem 3 is acknowledged as "similar to the proof of [Perdomo et al., Theorem 3.5]," and Theorem 4 mirrors their Theorem 4.3. Perdomo et al. show repeated risk minimization converges to a performatively stable point when the distribution map's sensitivity ε satisfies εβ/γ < 1, and that the stable point is within 2L_ℓε/γ of the performatively optimal one. The genuine differences are (i) conceptual — performative prediction moves the population (moving inference target), reciprocal learning moves the training sample while the population stays fixed, so the two "optimality" notions mean quite different things; (ii) structural — the state here is the pair (θ, P), not θ alone, so the map is bivariate and the contraction condition tightens from L < γ/β to L < γ/(γ+β); and (iii) the new technical content, which is really Theorems 1–2, i.e. showing that concrete algorithmic constructions (softmax selection, strongly convex data penalties, sigmoid soft labels) deliver the Lipschitz property that performative prediction assumes by fiat. Miller, Perdomo and Zrnic's "Outside the echo chamber" on optimizing (rather than merely stabilizing) performative risk is the natural companion, and it is exactly the missing piece here: this paper stabilizes but does not optimize.

An obvious follow-up: close the gap the corollaries paper over by computing explicit L for one real algorithm — say entropy-regularized pseudo-label selection under logistic loss with Tikhonov penalty — and check empirically whether L(1 + β/γ) < 1 ever holds at usable regularization strengths, or whether the theorem's regime is empty in practice. A second, more interesting direction: replace the in-sample optimality target with a population-risk target, and ask whether the fixed point's self-induced sample is informative rather than merely self-consistent; the authors' own suggestion of characterizing a credal set of near-optimal sample distributions rather than a single P* is a reasonable formalization.

The connection to your area is real, not forced, for one case in particular: counterfactual and online learning-to-rank on logged click data. A ranker θ_t determines exposure, exposure determines which (query, document) pairs enter the click log, the log is the next training sample — this is literally the sample adaption function f, with the population of users and the relevance ground truth fixed, which is precisely the regime the paper distinguishes from performative prediction. Read through this lens, the paper's three conditions map onto practices the IR community arrived at empirically: randomized exposure / exploration is Condition 3 (stochastic data selection), propensity- or click-model-derived soft relevance labels rather than hard binary clicks is Condition 2, and sliding-window or decayed log retention is non-greediness (Theorem 5 says an ever-growing, never-pruned log has no fixed point at all). It suggests a concrete question: does a deterministic top-k exposure policy — the analogue of UCB, excluded by Corollary 2 — provably fail to reach a stable ranker/log pair, and can a "data regularizer" on the exposure distribution be tuned to buy contraction more cheaply than uniform exploration does? The generative-retrieval angle (docid assignment and model weights co-adapting across rounds) is structurally similar, but I would flag it as the weaker analogy: the co-adaptation there is over a discrete identifier space, which fits neither the bounded-continuous X nor the linearity-in-x condition the proofs rely on.

title: A Simple but Tough-to-Beat Baseline for Sentence Embeddings
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-18

A Simple but Tough-to-Beat Baseline for Sentence Embeddings

Arora, Sanjeev; Liang, Yingyu; Ma, Tengyu — 2022/07/21

Worked from the abstract plus background knowledge only: OpenReview now sits behind a bot-verification challenge that returned an error page for both the PDF and the API, so the full text was not retrievable this run.

Main idea

This is the SIF paper, and its argument is deliberately deflationary. At the time, sentence representation was drifting toward recursive nets, LSTMs and paraphrase-supervised retraining; Arora, Liang and Ma show that an embarrassingly simple unsupervised recipe beats most of it on semantic textual similarity. Take off-the-shelf word vectors, average them with weight a/(a + p(w)) for a fixed small a (roughly 1e-3) and unigram frequency p(w), then estimate the top principal direction across a corpus of sentence vectors and project it out. Two lines of code, no training, 10–30% improvement on STS, and it beats supervised RNNs — especially out of domain.

What lifts it above a bag of tricks is that both steps fall out of a generative model rather than being tuned in. The weighting is not heuristic IDF; it is the maximum-likelihood estimate of a latent discourse vector under a specific model, and the smoothed frequency denominator is exactly what the model's smoothing term produces.

The most interesting part

The pleasing part is that "smooth inverse frequency" is derived. The model extends Arora et al.'s RAND-WALK: a slowly drifting discourse vector c_s emits words with probability proportional to exp(⟨v_w, c_s⟩), and the paper adds two smoothing terms — an additive α·p(w) allowing words to appear out of context at all, and a common direction c_0 mixed into the discourse vector to absorb syntax and the ambient "all sentences look alike" component. Under that emission model, the MLE for the discourse vector is a weighted word-vector average with weight a/(a + p(w)), a = (1−α)/(αZ). Frequent words get downweighted not because someone decided they were uninformative, but because the additive smoothing term already explains them.

The second step is the honest weak point. Removing the top singular direction of the sentence-vector matrix is motivated as estimating c_0, but the model treats c_0 as a single fixed direction while in practice the removed component is dataset-dependent and one component is a choice, not a consequence. The MLE derivation also leans on the RAND-WALK partition-function concentration result, which needs word vectors to be roughly isotropic — and the well-known anisotropy of real embedding spaces is precisely what the c_0 removal is patching. There is something slightly circular in using a model that assumes isotropy to justify a correction for the absence of isotropy.

Proof sketch

The theoretical core is a short MLE computation with a linearization. Conditional on the smoothed discourse vector c̃_s = βc_0 + (1−β)c_s, the likelihood of a sentence is ∏_w [α p(w) + (1−α) exp(⟨v_w, c̃_s⟩)/Z], assuming the partition function Z is approximately constant across contexts (this is where RAND-WALK's concentration lemma, proved via a measure-concentration argument over random isotropic vectors, is imported). The log-likelihood is not convex in c̃_s in a convenient form, so the authors Taylor-expand each term around ⟨v_w, c̃_s⟩ = 0. The gradient of the linearized objective is a sum of word vectors with coefficients a/(a + p(w)), so the stationary point is proportional to the weighted average — the whole method is the first-order optimality condition of a smoothed emission model. The c_0 direction is then removed by projecting out the first singular vector, justified by the modeling assumption that c_0 is shared across sentences while c_s varies, so it dominates the top singular direction of the stacked matrix. The guarantee is therefore asymptotic and approximate on two counts: the linearization is only valid when inner products are small, and Z's constancy is an approximation, not an identity.

Broader context

The direct descendants are the "fix the geometry of the embedding space" line: Mu and Viswanath's All-but-the-Top (post-processing by removing dominant directions), BERT-flow and BERT-whitening, and eventually the anisotropy diagnostics of Ethayarajh and the isotropy-through-contrastive-learning argument in SimCSE. Read in sequence, SIF is the first clear statement that a large fraction of a sentence embedding's variance is a nuisance component shared by all sentences, and everything since has been arguing about how to remove it.

The connection to your work is unusually direct for a 2017 paper. First, a/(a + p(w)) is a generatively derived cousin of IDF, which makes it a useful data point for anyone interested in why term-weighting schemes have the shape they do — the same question BM25's various probabilistic derivations circle around. Second, and more practically, the dominant-direction problem is a vector search problem, not only a quality problem: a single high-variance shared component wastes the dynamic range of product quantization codebooks, distorts the inner-product geometry that IVF centroid assignment relies on, and inflates the effective distance floor between all pairs. The follow-up I would actually find interesting is quantitative: measure how much of an ANN index's recall loss under PQ is attributable to the top few shared directions, and whether SIF-style projection applied before quantization buys recall at fixed bitrate. That is a cheap experiment and I have not seen it done cleanly.

title: Task Descriptors Help Transformers Learn Linear Models In-Context
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-18

Task Descriptors Help Transformers Learn Linear Models In-Context

Huang, Ruomin; Ge, Rong — 2024/06/18

Worked from the abstract plus background knowledge only: OpenReview returned a bot-verification challenge for both the PDF and its API this run, and the paper does not appear to be on arXiv. Treat the specifics below about the proof as informed reconstruction of the standard machinery in this line, clearly flagged where I could not verify against the text.

Main idea

There is by now a well-developed theory of in-context learning in the toy setting where the prompt is a list of (x_i, y_i) pairs drawn from a linear model y = ⟨w, x⟩ and the transformer must predict y for a fresh query. The recurring punchline — von Oswald et al., Akyürek et al., Ahn et al., Mahankali et al., Zhang et al. — is that a trained linear-attention layer's forward pass implements a step (or a preconditioned step) of gradient descent on the in-context examples. It is a satisfying story, but it models a prompt as only examples.

Real prompts are not like that. They contain a natural-language task description alongside the demonstrations, and empirically the description matters. Huang and Ge add a "task descriptor" token to the prompt in this analyzable setting, show empirically that the trained transformer reaches significantly lower ICL loss when it is present, and then prove a global convergence theorem whose converged parameters match what the experiments produce. The contribution is thus a theoretical account of a component of prompting that the GD-simulation literature had abstracted away.

Critique, with the caveat that I could not read the text

The framing is the right one and the question is genuinely underserved — "why does telling the model what the task is help, on top of showing it" is a real gap in this literature. The part I would want to check carefully is what the task descriptor is allowed to be. If it is (say) a vector encoding the task mean or the prior covariance of w, then the mechanism is likely that the descriptor supplies the preconditioner or the prior mean that the model would otherwise have to estimate from the few in-context examples — which would make the result a fairly clean Bayesian statement (the descriptor shifts the estimator from a ridge-type shrinkage toward the prior toward an informed prior), but also one where the "task description" framing is doing more rhetorical work than mathematical work. The gap between a real-valued task-identifying vector and an English sentence is the whole interesting part, and this setting cannot speak to it.

The other standing limitation of the entire line, which this paper inherits, is that the global convergence results hold for one-layer linear self-attention with Gaussian data. Linear attention has no softmax, so the loss is a polynomial in the parameters, and that is precisely what makes global analysis possible. It is a real result about a real optimization landscape, but the mechanism identified — a single GD step with a learned preconditioner — is not obviously what a 32-layer softmax transformer does.

Proof sketch (reconstructed, unverified)

The standard structure of a global convergence theorem in this setting, and what "the converged parameters match our experimental result" strongly suggests here, is the following. Parameterize a one-layer linear self-attention layer by two matrices (typically a merged key-query matrix and a merged value-projection matrix), write the population ICL loss as an expectation over the task w and the in-context inputs, and exploit Gaussianity to evaluate that expectation in closed form. The loss becomes an explicit low-degree polynomial in a small number of scalar summary parameters, because rotational symmetry of the Gaussian data collapses the matrices to a few invariant quantities. The objective is non-convex in those parameters, so the argument is not "convex, therefore done": instead one shows that gradient flow preserves some invariant (often a balancedness condition between the two factors, as in matrix factorization), enumerates the critical points of the reduced polynomial, and shows all of them except the global minimum are saddles that gradient flow escapes from generic initialization. With the descriptor present, the reduced parameterization gains extra coordinates, and the global minimum is a different, lower-loss point — which is where the paper's claim that the theory predicts the empirically converged parameters comes from.

I want to be clear that the specific invariant and the specific form of the descriptor's contribution are my reconstruction from the abstract and the cited predecessors (Zhang, Frei and Bartlett's gradient-flow analysis is the closest template), not something I read in this paper.

Broader context

The essential background reading is Garg et al. 2022 (the empirical "transformers can in-context learn function classes" paper that started the toy setting), then von Oswald et al. and Akyürek et al. for the GD-simulation claim, Ahn et al. and Mahankali et al. for the optimality of preconditioned GD, and Zhang, Frei and Bartlett for the global convergence of gradient flow. The interesting counter-current is Xie et al.'s implicit-Bayesian-inference view, where ICL is posterior inference over a latent concept rather than a descent step — and a task descriptor fits that frame more naturally than the GD frame, which makes it worth asking whether the paper's converged solution is better described as an informed prior than as a better-preconditioned step.

A follow-up I would like to see: make the descriptor noisy or wrong and characterize the degradation. A theory that explains why a correct description helps is only half the story; the practically urgent question is why a misleading instruction can override correct demonstrations, which is an identifiability question about the relative weight the converged solution places on descriptor versus examples.

The connection to your own work is thin and I would not force it — this is a "worth learning" paper rather than an IR paper. The one place it touches your area is the conditioning question in generative retrieval: a query prefix conditioning a decoder over document identifiers is structurally a task descriptor followed by a constrained decode, and the question of how much a model's output distribution is driven by the instruction versus by learned corpus statistics is the same identifiability question in a different costume. That is an analogy, not a transfer.

title: Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits via Voronoi Tessellations
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-18

Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits via Voronoi Tessellations

Sidheekh, Sahil; Natarajan, Sriraam — 2026-03-12

Main idea

Probabilistic circuits buy their exact, linear-time inference by keeping sum-node mixture weights constant — the routing of an input through the circuit is decided globally at training time and never adapts to where in the space the point actually lies. Sidheekh and Natarajan ask what happens if you make that routing geometric: replace the constant weights of a sum node with a hard indicator g_k(x) = 1[x ∈ V_k] for the Voronoi cell of a learned centroid, so each child subcircuit becomes a local expert owning a convex region of its scope. Evaluating an unnormalized density stays trivial under this change — exactly one gate fires, so a forward pass is still a single path. The damage is entirely to integration: a Voronoi cell is an intersection of half-spaces (c_j − c_k)ᵀx ≤ ½(‖c_j‖² − ‖c_k‖²) whose normals have several nonzero coordinates, so the region couples variables that the circuit's product nodes are trying to separate, and no amount of factorization in the integrand helps when the domain does not factor.

The paper's contribution is to take that obstruction seriously and give two exits. One accepts intractability and recovers reliability instead of exactness: sandwich each Voronoi cell between an inner and outer axis-aligned box, integrate the expert over boxes (which decomposability handles fine), and propagate the resulting intervals bottom-up to get certified [Z⁻, Z⁺] on the partition function, with corollaries for marginals and for conditionals via interval arithmetic. The other exits by design: if the gating regions are forced to be Cartesian products aligned with the circuit's own variable partition — a product of low-dimensional Voronoi tessellations, one per vtree block — Fubini applies again and exact inference returns at cost O(|C| K^m). Training uses a softmax-over-negative-distances relaxation with temperature annealing, reverting to hard gates at test time.

The most interesting part

The cleverest move is the recognition that geometric alignment is the geometric analogue of decomposability (Definition 3.4, Theorem 3.5). Decomposability is a condition on the integrand's variable dependence; the paper shows the same condition must hold on the integration domain, and that once both gate and expert respect the same factorization, tractability is not merely preserved but recovered from a provably #P-hard starting point. The second nice detail is where the intractability is localized: because Voronoi gating is a hard partition, the circuit remains deterministic up to measure-zero boundaries, so pointwise density evaluation costs nothing extra and the entire difficulty is confined to normalization. That is what makes the certified-bounds route coherent rather than a patch — you are bounding one scalar, not the whole model.

Two honest weaknesses. First, HFV's recursion appears to degenerate. The proof of Theorem A.15 hands each child the restriction V^{(i)}_{k_i}, a Voronoi cell in R^{|X_Si|} that is itself oblique, then says to "compute it recursively by the same argument" — but the child's own gates factor over a sub-partition, and an oblique parent cell does not factor over that sub-partition. The recursion is only airtight if the factorization goes all the way down to univariate cells, i.e. if HFV regions are just axis-aligned boxes with learned split points. Figure 2's caption ("yielding axis-aligned regions") and the fact that HFV merely matches the baselines both point that way; in that reading HFV is a soft-trainable relative of cutset-network splits rather than genuinely oblique geometry. Second, the reported numbers: the text says VT models report a lower bound on log-likelihood computed from inner boxes without refinement. Since log p(x) = log f(x) − log Z, a lower bound on log-likelihood needs an upper bound on Z, i.e. outer boxes; inner boxes give Z⁻ ≤ Z and hence an optimistic bound. As written this looks inverted, which matters because the headline claim is that VT's "lower bounds" exceed the baselines' exact log-likelihoods. I flag this as an apparent inconsistency in the text, not a certainty. Beyond that, experiments are eight synthetic 2D/3D toys, circuits have 5–10 units, VT gating sits only at root sum nodes, and the paper's own Remark A.10 concedes the box machinery needs ~66 refinement levels at d = 10.

Broader context

A probabilistic circuit is a DAG of sums (mixtures) and products (factorizations) over tractable univariate leaves, generalizing sum-product networks, PSDDs and cutset networks. Two structural conditions buy linear-time exact marginals: smoothness (all children of a sum share a scope, so mixtures are over a consistent variable set and integrals distribute across the sum) and decomposability (children of a product have disjoint scopes, so integrals factor into independent pieces). Determinism additionally gives tractable MAP. The whole field is a running negotiation between expressiveness and these conditions, and almost every splitting scheme in practice is axis-aligned precisely because axis-aligned regions are Cartesian products.

The closest neighbours are worth knowing. Conditional SPNs (Shao et al., 2022) and probabilistic neural circuits (Dos Martires, 2024) also make sum weights input-dependent — CSPNs on external conditioning features, PNCs on ancestor variables — but both forfeit arbitrary-order marginalization and neither has geometric meaning; this paper's point of difference is routing on spatial proximity within the modeled variables. On the geometry side, Chen et al.'s semi-discrete normalizing flows through differentiable tessellation (NeurIPS 2022) is the direct precursor for learnable Voronoi gating, and the Voronoi density estimators of Polianskii et al. (2022) and Marchetti et al. (2023) are the non-circuit version of the same idea.

A concrete follow-up: the paper treats all oblique geometry as equally hopeless, but for Gaussian leaves the integral of a factorized density over a single half-space is closed form (a Φ of a linear form). So a two-centroid gate — one hyperplane — is exactly tractable without any boxes, and small-K cells might be handled by inclusion–exclusion or by orthogonalizing facet normals. "Hyperplane-gated PCs, exactly tractable for K = 2, stacked hierarchically" would sit between HFV's axis-aligned conservatism and full VT's intractability, and would test whether the gain seen for VT survives when the bound is removed.

Connection to your work

This one is not forced. A Voronoi tessellation over learned centroids is the IVF partition of a vector index, and HFV — a product of independent low-dimensional Voronoi tessellations over disjoint coordinate blocks, with K^m joint cells indexed by a tuple (k_1, …, k_m) — is precisely product quantization / Cartesian k-means, arrived at from a completely different direction. The paper's tractability argument and PQ's efficiency argument are the same argument: distances (there, integrals) decompose over subspaces because the cells are Cartesian products. The expressiveness/tractability tension the paper articulates (general VT is expressive but its integrals are #P-hard; factorized VT is tractable but cannot represent oblique structure spanning blocks) is the IVF-versus-PQ tradeoff stated in measure-theoretic language, and the inner/outer box certificates are bounding-box filtering from spatial indexing. That suggests a two-way exchange: ANN machinery (inverted lists, HNSW over facet normals) could replace the O(2^d) corner tests that throttle the certification algorithm, and conversely a tractable circuit over an index's own partition gives exact marginals over cell occupancy — a principled model for filtered or attribute-constrained vector search, where you need P(cell k ∧ filter) rather than a nearest-neighbour list. The hierarchical vtree-aligned routing also rhymes with residual quantization and the hierarchical semantic-ID constructions in generative retrieval; this paper offers a normalization-correctness lens on those hierarchies that the retrieval literature generally does not apply.

Proof sketch

Three results carry the paper, and they are proved by three different strategies.

The negative result (Proposition 3.2 / A.1) is proved by explicit counterexample rather than a complexity reduction. The general statement leans on the #P-hardness of polytope volume (Dyer & Frieze, 1988), but the actual proof writes the Voronoi cell as ⋂_{j≠k} H⁻_{kj}, observes that for generic centroids the normals c_j − c_k have several nonzero entries, and then exhibits D = 2, c_1 = (0,1), c_2 = (1,0), giving the boundary x_1 = x_2 and the integral ∫ p(x_1) [∫_{x_1}^∞ p(x_2) dx_2] dx_1 whose inner limit depends on the outer variable. Fubini fails not because the integrand is coupled but because the domain is. Proposition A.2 extends this informally to depth: a parent cell constraint, projected down after marginalizing variables outside a child's scope, generally does not align with the child's own cell, so the feasible sets are intersections of projected polytopes.

The positive tractability result (Theorem 3.5 / A.4, and Theorem 3.14 / A.15) is an explicit construction plus induction over the circuit in reverse topological order. The assumptions are strong and should be stated plainly: (a) the scope splits into disjoint blocks; (b) each gating region is a Cartesian product of per-block regions, so membership is decidable block-by-block; (c) each expert factors along the same blocks. The key trick is Proposition A.14 — the indicator of a conjunction over disjoint variable sets factors into a product of indicators — which converts a domain restriction into part of the integrand. Once g_k is a product of per-block indicators multiplying per-block experts, Fubini applies over disjoint scopes and the joint integral becomes Σ_k π_k Π_i ∫_{V^{(i)}_{k_i}} p^{(i)}_{k_i}. The induction then reuses the standard PC argument at leaves (univariate, and in 1-D Voronoi cells are just intervals between midpoints of adjacent centroids, so a CDF evaluation suffices), products (disjoint scopes) and ordinary sums (linearity). The complexity O(|C| K^m) comes from enumerating the joint index tuple at each gated sum. As noted above, the inductive step at an internal gated node is where I think the argument silently requires the per-block cells to be themselves products.

The certification result (Theorem 3.9 / A.9) is a measure-theoretic squeeze. Validity is monotonicity of integration on B⁻_k ⊆ V_k ⊆ B⁺_k for nonnegative p_k (Lemma 3.6), lifted through the circuit by induction — nonnegative weights preserve inequalities at sums, and nonnegative factors preserve them at products. Monotone tightening is a set-inclusion argument on the refinement: bisecting boxes only refines the partition, so every INSIDE box stays inside (the inner union can only grow) and every child of a non-OUTSIDE box is contained in its parent (the outer union can only shrink). Convergence is absolute continuity of the Lebesgue integral: if the undecided volume μ(V⁺_k \ V⁻_k) → 0 then ∫_{U_k,t} p_k → 0, so the bounds squeeze onto Z. The rate O(2^{−t/d}) is the weakest link and the authors say so — it assumes bounded densities and that the undecided set lies in a tubular neighbourhood of the cell boundary whose thickness scales with box diameter, giving μ(U) = O(surface area × thickness); they label it "an informal geometric bound." Two supporting constructions are cleanly proved: the conservative inner box of radius δ_k / (2√d) around c_k, where δ_k is the nearest-centroid distance (any point in the box is within δ_k/2 of c_k, and the triangle inequality puts every other centroid at least δ_k/2 away), and the tightest outer box, obtained by solving 2d linear programs over the half-space representation. Finally, Theorem 3.16 / A.20 handles the soft-to-hard transition: pointwise convergence from w_{k*} = 1/(1 + Σ_{j≠k*} e^{−α(d_j − d_{k*})}), the exponential rate 1 − w_{k*} ≤ (K−1) e^{−αγ(u)} by bounding every gap by the margin γ(u), and convergence of integrals by dominated convergence since 0 ≤ w_k ≤ 1 and the boundary set has measure zero. The gradient ∇_{c_k} w_k = 2α w_k (1 − w_k)(u − c_k) falls out of the softmax quotient rule and has the pleasant reading that centroids move only where the tessellation is contested.

title: Cracking Vector Search Indexes
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-18

Cracking Vector Search Indexes

Mageirakos, Vasilis; Wu, Bowen; Alonso, Gustavo — 07/2025

Main idea

The premise is index selection at a scale where you cannot afford to select. If every dataset in a data lake is to be embedded and exposed to RAG, you would need millions of ANN indexes, most of them for data nobody will ever query. Building an IVF index over 10M vectors costs minutes to hours of k-means up front; brute force costs nothing up front but does not scale. Which one is right depends entirely on how many queries the dataset will eventually receive — a number you do not know at build time.

CrackIVF's answer is to stop treating index construction as a phase. It starts as a deliberately undersized IVF index (100 partitions) that can answer immediately, and then grows as a side effect of serving queries. The key structural observation is that IVF search and IVF construction compute the same thing: query-to-centroid and point-to-centroid distances. So each incoming query doubles as a candidate centroid — a "crack" — and the distances already computed during its search tell you for free which nearby points are closer to the query than to their current centroid, and should be stolen into the new partition. A second operation, REFINE, runs local k-means inside the visited region. Two control mechanisms decide where (heuristic rules: reject cracks stealing fewer than 2 points or pushing local points-per-partition below 64; refine when local cluster-size CV exceeds 2) and when (a budget rule capping build time at a fraction ρ=0.5 of cumulative time). CRACK is buffered and committed lazily, because moving d-dimensional vectors between memory-aligned inverted lists is far more expensive than the swaps in classical column cracking; REFINE runs eagerly but rarely, which forces a rollback mechanism since a refine can invalidate a buffered crack decided against a stale state.

The finding I would highlight is not the amortization — it is that on Last.fm, the most skewed workload, CrackIVF's 1264 query-derived partitions deliver ~50% higher QPS at Recall@10=0.9 than any pre-built IVF. Placing centroids by query density rather than data density is not just cheaper, it is better.

Reviewer-style critique

The systems engineering is careful and the ablations are honest: with WHERE=OFF the converged index is barely better than the untouched 100-partition starting state, and with WHEN=OFF cracking fires after nearly every query until it hits 16,000 partitions and build time swamps everything. That is the right way to show the control mechanisms matter.

The evaluation, though, is weaker than the framing. The most serious issue is the query traces: the datasets provide 10K unique queries (50K for Last.fm) and the authors "replicate them until we match our target scales (up to 1M)." So the headline "1 million queries" is 10K distinct queries repeated a hundred times. An index that adapts to the query distribution is being tested on a workload where the future queries are literally the past queries. Skew measured on such a trace (80% of queries touching 60% of partitions) is not evidence about real embedding-lake workloads, and the convergence criterion — "the arrival of new crack candidates stops" — is trivially satisfied when the query set is finite and recycled.

Second, nprobe "is set to always achieve 90–95% Recall@10," which reads like offline tuning against ground truth. As the partitioning changes underneath, the nprobe needed to hold recall changes too; the paper does not describe an online mechanism for this, and Quake, which they cite, explicitly sets nprobe dynamically. Without that, the recall trajectory during adaptation is unverified.

Third, missing baselines. HNSW is dismissed by citing ANN-Benchmarks numbers (IVF builds 8000x faster) rather than being run. But the cumulative-time crossover against HNSW at 10^6 queries is exactly the question Figure 4 is asking, and it is unmeasured. No DiskANN, no ScaNN, no IVFPQ, and no GPU-built IVF baseline even though they cite FAISS-GPU — the 10–1000x initialization advantage is over CPU k-means on 16 cores.

Fourth, scale and dimensionality do not match the motivation. The paper argues from RAG embeddings of "hundreds to thousands of dimensions" and billion-scale corpora, then evaluates on 64–128 dimensions and at most 10M points, with no actual text-embedding dataset. This matters because the paper's own cost model makes CRACK's dominant term data movement proportional to |D_local|·d; the central difficulty they identify gets strictly worse at 768 or 1536 dimensions, and it is untested there. Relatedly, the memory argument for choosing IVF over HNSW is never backed by a measured footprint.

Smaller points: the AV-Tree comparison (Table 3, single-threaded, >99% recall) ends at 1531s vs 1938s for IVF-1K at 10^6 queries — only 1.27x, and the prose claim that "AV-Tree continues to outperform up to 1000 queries" does not match the extracted table, where CrackIVF is already ahead at 10^2 (1.73s vs 7.48s); the column alignment in the extraction may be imperfect, so I would not lean hard on it. The cost model achieves R² of only 0.40–0.95 with RMSE "from milliseconds to a few seconds," rescued mainly by the fact that the budget rule uses measured t_build and t_search. And the robustness claim is oversold: 15 of 48 parameter-dataset edge cases "had a noticeable effect on the final index" — 31% is not robustness, and the authors concede optimal values are dataset-dependent. Finally, the promised concurrency story (hide cracking in a background thread pool) is explicitly not implemented; the whole pool is either searching or cracking, and no tail-latency numbers are given despite acknowledged outliers.

Cost model

There is no theorem, but the budget rule has a clean invariant worth stating precisely. A build operation B is executed only if t_build + t̂_B ≤ ρ·(t_build + t_search + t̂_B), which rearranges to t_build + t̂_B ≤ (ρ/(1−ρ))·t_search. With ρ=0.5 this means cumulative build time never exceeds cumulative search time, so total time stays within 1/(1−ρ) = 2x the time a pure-search (never-adapt) system would have spent. The guarantee is only approximate in two ways the paper is upfront about: t̂_B comes from a fitted first-order linear regression over per-kernel compute and data-movement features, so an underestimate can overshoot the bound for one operation (subsequent decisions self-correct because measured times are fed back); and the bound is relative to the evolving index's own search cost, not to an offline-optimal static index. So this is a self-limiting property, not a competitive ratio against the optimum in Figure 1. There is no recall guarantee anywhere in the paper.

Broader context and a follow-up

Database cracking (Idreos, Kersten and Manegold, CIDR 2007) proposed that a select operator should physically reorganize the column it scans, so the index materializes from query traffic; the ancestry goes back to deferred data structuring (Karp, Motwani and Raghavan, SICOMP 1988). Extensions to multidimensional data (cracking KD-trees; Zardbani et al. on spatial objects, VLDB 2023) stall well below embedding dimensionality, and AV-Tree (Lampropoulos et al., VLDB 2023) was the first high-dimensional adaptive index but is exact, single-threaded and aimed at ~1000 queries. CrackIVF is the first port of the paradigm to approximate search at RAG scale. It should be read alongside the ANN maintenance line — DeDrift, SPFresh, Ada-IVF, Quake — which does localized IVF surgery but is triggered by data updates and drift rather than by query volume; CrackIVF deliberately stays in the static setting, which is also its biggest open flank.

The follow-up I would chase is the Last.fm result taken seriously as an objective rather than a side effect. Standard IVF minimizes quantization error under the data density; what CrackIVF stumbles into is something closer to minimizing expected probed points under the query density at fixed recall. Writing that objective down explicitly — a query-weighted quantization loss, in the spirit of ScaNN's anisotropic loss and SOAR — would turn a heuristic into an optimization problem, and would let you ask how many partitions a given query density actually warrants.
