The other framing worth formalizing is that choosing when to build an index of size k under unknown query volume is a multi-option rent-or-buy problem; Figure 1's lower envelope is exactly a ski-rental instance, and competitive-ratio results there would give the guarantee the budget rule does not.

For your own work, the transferable idea is that retrieval structures built purely from data statistics leave workload information on the table. In generative retrieval, the docid space is typically a hierarchical k-means or RQ-VAE tree over document embeddings — built once, from the corpus, with no knowledge of which regions of semantic-ID space queries will actually decode into. A crackable semantic-ID hierarchy that deepens prefixes in heavily queried regions and leaves cold regions coarse is the direct analogue of CRACK and REFINE, and it inherits the same theoretical question: what is the optimal identifier-tree granularity given a query distribution, and what does adaptivity cost you in worst-case regret against the offline-optimal tree?

title: Revisiting Tree Search for LLMs: Gumbel and Sequential Halving for Budget-Scalable Reasoning
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-17

Revisiting Tree Search for LLMs: Gumbel and Sequential Halving for Budget-Scalable Reasoning

Leonid Ugadiarov, Yuri Kuratov, Aleksandr Panov, Alexey Skrynnik (2026) — arXiv:2603.21162

Main idea. The paper is about a failure mode rather than a new capability: when you take the AlphaZero-style tree search that Wan et al. (2024) grafted onto LLM decoding and simply give it more compute — more simulations, wider trees, deeper trees — accuracy stops improving and then falls. That is the opposite of what a test-time-compute method is supposed to do, and it is the interesting empirical observation here. The authors diagnose the cause as the root action-selection rule. PUCT plus Dirichlet noise concentrates visits on a few children; the final root action is then chosen by visit count, so as the budget grows the search commits harder and harder to whatever the value network liked early, and the extra simulations mostly re-confirm an early mistake. Their fix, ReSCALE, swaps the root rule for the machinery of Danihelka et al.'s Gumbel AlphaZero: sample candidate actions without replacement via Gumbel perturbation of the log-priors, allocate the simulation budget by Sequential Halving across the surviving candidates, and use completed/mixed Q-values plus a deterministic argmax at non-root nodes. Nothing about the model, the SFT data, or the value network changes — only how a fixed budget is spread over root children. On GSM8K at the largest budget the baseline drops to 53.6% while ReSCALE reaches 58.4%; ablations attribute roughly 4.7 points to Sequential Halving and 1.7 to the Gumbel noise, so the budget-allocation rule, not the exploration noise, is doing the work.

Reviewer-style critique. The diagnosis is more valuable than the remedy, and the evidence for the remedy is thinner than the framing suggests. Read Table 1 columns rather than rows: at Small and Medium budgets ReSCALE is worse than or level with AlphaZero (55.1 vs 56.0; 71.6 vs 74.4 on Game24), and the single best configuration anywhere in the table is AlphaZero at the smallest budget on Game24 (86.7%, beating every ReSCALE number at any budget) and 58.8% on GSM8K, versus ReSCALE's best-ever 59.7% at roughly ten times the tokens. So the honest claim is "ReSCALE degrades more gracefully," not "ReSCALE converts compute into accuracy" — the accuracy frontier over all (method, budget) pairs is nearly flat. A monotone curve that ends where the cheap method already was is a robustness result, not a scaling result, and Figure 1's y-axis spanning about six points does a lot of rhetorical work.

The error bars compound this. "Mean ± std across hyperparameter configurations" measures hyperparameter sensitivity, not run-to-run noise, and it is then used to support a claim about budget levels whose configurations differ. The genuinely seeded experiment is the ablation (three seeds), which is also the only place the headline 60.1% appears. No wall-clock or FLOP accounting is given even though value-network forward passes are a real share of cost, and the Best-of-N baseline is fixed at N = 32 (3.5K tokens) and never scaled to the 16–18K regime where the comparison actually matters — precisely the budget-matched baseline the paper's own thesis demands.

The causal story is also under-tested. An equally good explanation for the degradation is Goodhart pressure on a weak value model: a 7B MC-return value head trained on 51 completions per example is a noisy proxy, and more search means more optimization against it — the same overoptimization curve known from reward-model-guided Best-of-N. Sequential Halving happens to apply less greedy pressure, which would produce exactly these results without the visit-count story being the mechanism. The clean experiment — vary value-model quality (checkpoints, ensembles, calibration) and see whether the pathology tracks value error rather than selection rule — is absent. The claimed "policy improvement guarantees" from Gumbel AlphaZero are also invoked loosely: those are stated with respect to the Q-estimates the search actually has, and Sequential Halving's fixed-budget best-arm-identification guarantees assume i.i.d. stochastic arm pulls, whereas here transitions are deterministic and the "noise" comes from which leaves happen to get expanded. Reproducibility details are missing too: the σ transform as printed omits the c_scale factor, c_scale is never reported, and the whole study rests on Llama2-7B on two math benchmarks — a base model far enough behind current ones that it is unclear whether the pathology survives with a stronger policy and a better-calibrated verifier.

Broader context. The background is three-way. AlphaZero-style search uses PUCT, an anytime, regret-minimizing rule tuned to behave well if stopped at any moment, whose root decision rule (visit counts) is a proxy for "the arm I have been exploiting." Fixed-budget best-arm identification is a different objective — you know N in advance and care only about the final recommendation, not cumulative regret — and Sequential Halving (Karnin, Koren, Somekh 2013) is its canonical algorithm, spending N/⌈log₂M⌉ pulls per round and discarding the worse half. Danihelka et al. (ICLR 2022, "Policy improvement by planning with Gumbel") marries the two: Gumbel top-k gives sampling without replacement from the prior, Sequential Halving allocates the budget, and completed Q-values make the improved policy well-defined at tiny simulation counts — which is why Gumbel MuZero works with 2–4 simulations. ReSCALE is essentially a faithful port of that recipe to sentence-level LLM actions, apparently not done before. The third strand is test-time compute scaling (Snell et al. 2025) and the lookahead-pathology literature (Nguyen & Ramanujan 2024), which documents that deeper search can degrade decisions when leaf evaluations are biased — the LLM case is that phenomenon with an unusually bad evaluator.

A natural follow-up: the paper applies Sequential Halving within one root decision but allocates budget uniformly across reasoning steps. Steps are not equally pivotal — a wrong first equation dooms a GSM8K solution, whereas the final arithmetic rarely matters. Treating the whole trajectory as a nested fixed-budget allocation problem, with per-step budget driven by value-disagreement or by the gap between the top two completed Q-values, is both practically obvious and theoretically tractable, and it would give the "budget-scalable" claim real teeth. The complementary experiment is to make the verifier's uncertainty explicit and use a risk-aware σ, testing the Goodhart hypothesis directly.

For your work the connection is not forced, and it runs through the Gumbel machinery. Kool, van Hoof & Welling's stochastic beam search (ICML 2019) is the same Gumbel-top-k trick applied to sequence models: it samples sequences without replacement from an autoregressive distribution by top-down Gumbel perturbation. That is exactly the primitive ReSCALE uses at the root, so the bridge to constrained decoding over a docid trie in generative retrieval (DSI, NCI, SEAL) is short. Generative retrieval currently uses plain constrained beam search — a fixed-width uniform allocation over trie prefixes — and it inherits the well-known non-monotonicity of beam search (larger beams can lower quality; Stahlberg & Byrne's model-error/search-error decomposition is the sharp version). ReSCALE's argument, transplanted, says the issue is that beam width is a regret-style heuristic being asked to solve a fixed-budget recommendation problem, and that Gumbel sampling without replacement plus halving over prefixes would be the principled replacement — with the twist that generative retrieval wants top-k documents, i.e. fixed-budget top-k identification rather than best-arm identification.

There is also a clean contrast worth holding onto: graph-based ANN search (HNSW's efSearch) is monotone in budget, because its scoring function is an exact distance. Degradation under more search is a signature of searching against a learned proxy score, not of search itself — arguably the cleanest theoretical takeaway this short paper offers, even though it never states it.

title: Provable unlearning in topic modeling and downstream tasks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-17

Provable unlearning in topic modeling and downstream tasks

Stanley Wei, Sadhika Malladi, Sanjeev Arora, Amartya Sanyal (2024) — arXiv:2411.12600

Main idea. The question is practical, dressed in theory: if a model was pre-trained on a web-scale corpus and then adapted to a task, what does it take to remove a document from it, with a certificate rather than a vibe? Almost all provable unlearning results live in single-stage supervised learning — convex ERM, linear models, GLMs — where the estimator is a clean function of the data. The pretrain-then-finetune pipeline has no such theory, because the pretraining objective is self-supervised and nonconvex and the fine-tuning stage sits on top of a representation that was itself estimated from the data you now want to delete.

The authors' move is to pick the simplest object that still has both stages: a topic model. A corpus of m documents over a vocabulary of size n is M = A_X, where A_ ∈ R^{n×r} gives each of r latent topics a distribution over words and X ∈ R^{r×m} gives each document's topic mixture. A_ is exactly a self-supervised feature extractor — a bag-of-words "language model" learned from co-occurrence statistics alone — and the downstream stage is head tuning of w ∈ R^r on top of A with a strongly convex loss. The analogy to BERT-plus-a-linear-probe is structural, not metaphorical: unsupervised representation from a large corpus, convex head on a small labeled set, representation _shared* across many tasks. What topic models add that modern LLMs lack is a learning algorithm with end-to-end recovery guarantees (Arora et al. 2012a/b), which is what makes any of this provable.

Deletion capacity, following Sekhari et al. (2021), is the largest forget-set size T_{ε,δ}(m) such that the unlearning algorithm's output is (ε,δ)-indistinguishable from training without those documents, and the model retains near-optimal utility even for an adversarially chosen forget set. It is a capacity, not a per-request cost: you keep deleting cheaply until noise accumulates past the utility budget.

The headline claim is that unlearning pretraining data is easier after fine-tuning, and one can do it without touching the base model at all. This sounds backwards, but the logic is about what gets released. If you publish A and w separately you must scrub A and gain nothing (Thm 3). If you publish only the composed object B = Aw ∈ R^{n×C}, any perturbation you would have applied to A can be absorbed into w: fine-tuning has collapsed the n×r representation onto the ≤ r directions the task actually uses, and only those need to be made insensitive to the forget set. Deletion capacity improves from Ω̃(m/(r²√(nr))) to Ω̃(mq/(r√(nr))), where q = min_{k∈T_clf} Pr_D[z=k] — a factor qr gain, largest when the task depends on few, common topics.

The most interesting part. The cleverest engineering is that the unlearning cost is independent of m. The retained statistics are Q (the n×n word co-occurrence matrix), the anchor set P, per-word simplex coefficients, and normalizers — all of size O(n² + nr), with no m in sight. Deletion subtracts the forget documents' co-occurrence contributions in O(m_U) time, reuses the anchor words verbatim in O(1) (the sharpest trick: the discrete part of the estimator is proved stable, so the expensive convex-hull search is never re-run), takes one projected Newton step per word in O(nr²), and adds Gaussian noise. Compare O(n²r + nr²/ε₀²) for retraining. Downstream it is better still: one O(r³) Newton step on w, with no access to the labeled set needed.

Critique. The unlearning notion is a Sekhari-style (ε,δ) one, subtly weaker than "indistinguishable from retraining": both sides of the comparison are noised outputs of the unlearning algorithm, so the certificate is about a noised release channel, not about the clean retrained estimator. The utility criterion is E‖Ã − A_‖_∞ ≤ 0.01, an entrywise sup-norm to ground truth — but columns of A live on the simplex, so typical entries are O(1/n), and for realistic n ~ 10⁵ a slack of 0.01 is orders of magnitude larger than the signal it protects; the rate is real, but the constant hides a lot. The whole architecture rests on _p-separability (every topic has an anchor word appearing in it and nowhere else), a bounded topic-imbalance constant, a condition number on R, and an assumption merging rare words into a "rare" bucket so every word occurs often enough. That is precisely the regime real deletion requests violate: private and copyrighted material is rare, distinctive, and plausibly is the anchor evidence. If the forget set is the documents containing a near-anchor term, the invariance the algorithm depends on is the first thing to break. The fine-tuning result's premise — release B = Aw, never A — is almost the opposite of practice, where base checkpoints are the released artifact, and q is set by the rarest task-relevant topic, so the gain evaporates exactly for niche tasks. The theorem is best read as: unlearning is easy to the extent the released function is low-rank in the data's directions — a sound and portable principle; the "fine-tuning makes it easier" framing oversells it. Finally the guarantee is one-shot, not adaptive (no sequential adversarial requests à la Gupta et al.), and there are no experiments, only an asymptotic runtime table.

Proof sketch. Learning (Arora et al. 2012a) recovers A^S, R^S to entrywise error ε₀ given m ≥ max{O(ar³log n/(L(γp)⁶ε₀)), O(r²log r/(Lε₀³(γp)⁴)), O(a³r³log n/(Lε₀²))}, under p-separability, ε₀ ≤ O(1/√(nr)), and the rare-word convention. Theorem 5: pretraining deletion capacity ≥ c·min{0.001m/r², mε/(r²√(rn log(1/δ)))}; Theorem 7 (downstream): c′·min{0.001m/r², mqε/(r√(nr log(1/δ)))}, recovering the former when q = 1/ar. Note the shape: with "dimension" d = nr, the term mε/√(d log(1/δ)) is exactly Sekhari et al.'s convex-ERM capacity, and the extra r² is the price of anchor-recovery conditioning.

The proof is a perturbation/stability analysis in three layers, then a privacy mechanism on top. Layer 1 — statistics. Row-normalized Q̄ concentrates: ‖Q̄^S_i − Q̄__i‖ ≤ δ₂ = O(√(4ar/(mε₀))). Deleting m_U documents moves it by ≤ 4ar·m_U/(mε₀) — the crucial point being that this is _linear in m_U/m, not √·*, so the deletion perturbation is dominated by sampling noise until m_U ≳ √(mε₀/4ar); below that threshold deletion is statistically invisible, and that is where the capacity comes from.

Layer 2 — the anchor-word invariance. Arora et al.'s robustness lemma says that if every row of Q̄ is within δ of a γp-robust simplex and 20rδ/(γp)² < γp, the recovered anchors are O(δ/γp)-close to the truth. Feeding in the perturbed δ and capping m_U ≤ 0.001mε₀(γp)³/(a²r²) keeps the condition satisfied, so the anchor set is provably unchanged and the perturbed simplex remains γp/2-robust. This is the key trick: it converts the combinatorial, non-smooth part of the estimator into a constant, leaving a smooth problem.

Layer 3 — the Newton correction. With anchors fixed, each C_i = argmin_{v∈Δ_r}‖Q̄_i − vᵀQ̄_P‖² is a strongly convex least-squares problem whose Hessian has σ_min ≥ γp/2. One Newton step from C_i^S plus projection onto the simplex lands within (4/γp)(δ₂ + 4ar·m_U/(mε₀)) of the retrained C_i^F — projection is non-expansive and the residual is controlled by σ_min. Lifting C → A costs a factor ar, because A_{i,k} = C_{i,k}Pr[w=i]/Pr[z=k] with Pr[z=k] ≥ 1/ar. Hence ‖Ā − A^F‖_∞ ≤ O((ar)²m_U/(mε₀γp)), giving ℓ₂-sensitivity Δ = √(nr)(ar)²m_U/(mε₀γp). The Gaussian mechanism with σ = Δ√(2log(1.25/δ))/ε (plus projection back to the simplex, and onto the PSD cone for R) delivers indistinguishability; post-processing immunity handles everything downstream. Utility then has two competing terms — injected noise ≈ σ√(log nr) and residual bias — and requiring each ≤ 0.01 yields m_U ≤ Õ(m/(r²√(nr))) and m_U ≤ Õ(m/r²) respectively; the min is the capacity.

The downstream proof reuses all of this but exploits sparsity of w_. Since Ā − A^F is only ever contracted against a vector supported on the task's topics, the factor ar is replaced by 1/q — that single substitution buys the improved capacity. Then A^S is held fixed and one solves A^S v = A^F w^F, i.e. v = (A^S)†A^F w^F; p-separability guarantees σ_min(A^S) = Θ(p) so the pseudoinverse only inflates errors by 1/p. The head is updated by a Newton step whose error is _quadratic_ in the base-model perturbation (via λ-strong convexity, Hessian-Lipschitzness, and an integral-form Taylor remainder), so it is lower-order; the linear-order term is controlled by ‖w_(A₁) − w*(A₂)‖ ≤ (L_∞/λ)‖A₁ − A₂‖_∞.

Broader context. Machine unlearning grew out of the GDPR right-to-be-forgotten and now sits at the intersection of privacy, copyright litigation, and safety. Cao & Yang (2015) set the gold standard; SISA (Bourtoule et al. 2021) achieves it exactly by sharding and retraining only the affected shard — expensive but unimpeachable. Because exact retraining doesn't scale, the field moved to certified removal: Guo et al. (2020) gave a one-step Newton removal mechanism plus objective perturbation for convex models; Ginart et al. (2019) did deletion-efficient k-means; Sekhari et al. (2021) introduced the deletion-capacity framework this paper adapts, while emphasizing that unlearning should not require keeping the training set. Recent work pushes toward nonconvexity — Chien et al.'s Langevin unlearning, which reinterprets noisy SGD as an unlearning mechanism — and a parallel empirical literature (TOFU, Eldan & Russinovich's "Who's Harry Potter?", Hayes et al. 2024) keeps showing that heuristic LLM unlearning evaluations overstate success, which is exactly the motivation here.

The IR connection is not decoration. Topic models are retrieval models — pLSI and LDA were built as latent-semantic ranking functions, and the paper's own citation (Boyd-Graber et al., FnTIR) names retrieval as the flagship downstream task. Read the algorithm in IR terms and it is index maintenance with a certificate: Q is a corpus-level co-occurrence statistic, A is the learned embedding/index, and deletion = subtract postings from Q, keep the pivot terms (anchors) fixed, locally repair the affected coefficients. Except the paper also tells you how much noise you must add and how many documents you may delete before the index degrades.

This maps onto two live problems for you. In generative retrieval (DSI, NCI, semantic-ID variants), a document's identity is memorized in the decoder's weights and in the constrained-decoding trie. Removing a trie entry is filtering, not forgetting — the parameters still encode the docid-to-content mapping, and a membership or extraction attack can say so. Theorem 3 vs. Theorem 4 is exactly the right lens: if you release only the composed retrieval function, you may certify deletion by adjusting the output-side head; if you release the encoder/embeddings, as everyone does for dense retrieval, you cannot. In ANN indices, deletion is usually a tombstone, but the structure is corpus-dependent in ways tombstones don't touch: HNSW neighbor lists were built using the deleted vector, and IVF-PQ centroids and codebooks were trained on it. Those centroids are the direct analogue of the retained statistics, and Ginart et al.'s quantized-k-means deletion plus this paper's Newton-step-then-noise recipe suggests a genuine result: certified centroid/codebook updates with a deletion capacity, answering "how many documents can I remove before I must reindex?"

Two follow-ups worth pushing. The clean one: certified unlearning with deletion capacity for a dual-encoder retriever's index, where the encoder is frozen and only the index (centroids, codebooks, graph) is corpus-dependent — the realistic release model, and it inherits the paper's convexity where it matters. The more interesting one: generalize q from task sparsity to query-distribution sparsity. The paper's gain comes from the released object only exercising |T_clf| directions of A; a deployed retrieval system likewise only exposes its index through a narrow query distribution, so the effective sensitivity of the released ranking function should be governed by the spectrum of the query distribution rather than the ambient n×r embedding. A query-distribution-dependent deletion capacity — "you can remove k documents without reindexing, because no plausible query can distinguish the result from a reindexed system" — would be theoretically clean and operationally meaningful, and it sidesteps the paper's least defensible assumption, that nobody ever sees the base model.

title: A Near-optimal Algorithm for Learning Margin Halfspaces with Massart Noise
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-17

A Near-optimal Algorithm for Learning Margin Halfspaces with Massart Noise

Ilias Diakonikolas, Nikos Zarifis (2025) — arXiv:2501.09691

Main idea. The object of study is the oldest problem in machine learning — fitting a linear separator — under the most realistic kind of label noise that still admits provable guarantees. In the γ-margin halfspace setting, data live on the unit sphere S^{d−1}, there is an unknown unit vector w_, and every example satisfies |w_·x| ≥ γ: nothing sits in the slab around the true hyperplane. With clean labels, Perceptron solves this with Θ(1/(γ²ε)) samples, information-theoretically optimal — a rare case where statistics and computation coincide perfectly.

Massart noise breaks that coincidence. An adversary sees each point x and may flip its true label with probability η(x), where η(x) is arbitrary, unknown, and point-dependent, subject only to η(x) ≤ η < 1/2. It is strictly harder than Random Classification Noise (η(x) ≡ η) and strictly easier than the agnostic model. The subtlety is that the adversary can spend almost all its flipping budget on exactly the points that matter — those near the learner's current decision boundary — while leaving easy points nearly clean. This asymmetry defeats every symmetric-noise trick (label smoothing, unbiased loss correction) and is what makes the model interesting.

Information-theoretically the answer is essentially unchanged from the noiseless case: an inefficient learner achieves OPT + ε with Õ(1/((1−2η)γ²ε)) samples, where OPT = E_x[η(x)]. Efficient learners have been stuck: Diakonikolas–Gouleakis–Tzamos (2019) gave the first polynomial-time algorithm at all, and Chen–Koehler–Moitra–Yau (2020) improved it to Õ(1/(γ⁴ε³)), both achieving the weaker guarantee η + ε rather than OPT + ε. This paper closes most of that gap: a plain online SGD procedure, one fresh sample per iteration, achieving η + ε with Õ(1/(γ²ε²)) samples and Õ(dn/ε) time.

The most interesting part. The cleverest move is the loss design. The 0-1 error can be written as −E[y·(w·x)/|w·x|], which is exactly the LeakyReLU surrogate ℓ_λ(w,x,y) = (1{sign(w·x) ≠ y} − λ)|w·x| divided by |w·x| — but that division destroys convexity. The trick is to divide by |v·x| for a vector v held fixed and independent of w, keeping the objective convex in w, and then set v = w^t, the current iterate, at each round. This yields not one convex loss but a sequence of them, each a convex proxy that locally simulates the 0-1 objective around where the algorithm currently stands.

Two details make it work. First, λ := η is the right leakage: since η(x) ≤ η pointwise, the true w_ has non-positive loss under every reweighting, uniformly over v. Second — the actual engineering — the reweighting is _clipped_: W(v·x, γ/2) = 1/max(|v·x|, γ/2). Without clipping, points where |w^t·x| is tiny blow the loss up and destroy both boundedness and variance control; with clipping, the gradient obeys ‖g‖₂ ≤ 4/γ pointwise. Crucially, the margin assumption rescues exactly the region where clipping distorts the objective: on {|w·x| < γ/2} we know |w_·x| ≥ γ, so the w* term still dominates.

Why the rate matters: prior algorithms conditioned on regions of mass as small as Θ(ε) and estimated a loss inside them, which forces Ω(1/ε³) unconditionally, and needed Ω(1/γ²) iterations each accurate to γε, giving Ω(1/γ⁴). This work replaces local error-reduction with a global drift argument, so no conditioning is needed. The resulting 1/ε² is not an artifact: Diakonikolas–Diakonikolas–Kane–Wang–Zarifis (2023) showed every efficient SQ algorithm and every low-degree polynomial test needs Ω(1/(γε²)) samples even for RCN. So the 1/ε-to-1/ε² jump relative to the information-theoretic bound is genuinely the price of computational efficiency, and this algorithm now pays close to exactly that price.

Critique. The remaining gap is a full factor of 1/γ: upper bound Õ(1/(γ²ε²)) versus lower bound Ω(1/(γε²) + 1/(γ²ε)) — neither side is known tight, and SQ/low-degree evidence is evidence, not a theorem. The guarantee is η + ε, not OPT + ε; when noise is concentrated on a 1% fraction of points, OPT ≪ η and the bound is vacuous relative to what is information-theoretically available. Beating η + ε efficiently is ruled out under SQ and cryptographic assumptions (Diakonikolas–Kane 2022; Nasser–Tiegel 2022), so this is a real barrier rather than slack analysis — but it means "near-optimality" in the title is optimality within a weakened error target. The algorithm also hard-codes λ = η, so it needs the noise bound; a grid search would plausibly cost only log factors, but this isn't discussed. There is no last-iterate guarantee — the proof establishes only that some iterate is good, so a separate N = Θ(log(1/(γδ))/(ε(1−2η)))-sample testing phase must scan all T+1 hypotheses, and it is this phase, not SGD, that makes the runtime Õ(dn/ε). Finally, the margin is load-bearing in an essential way; the general-halfspace case with optimal d-dependence is left open.

Proof sketch. Theorem 2.1. Let D on S^{d−1} × {±1} satisfy the η-Massart condition w.r.t. a γ-margin halfspace sign(w_·x). With T = Θ(log(1/δ)/(ε²γ²)) SGD rounds (one sample each) and N = Θ(log(1/(γδ))/(ε(1−2η))) samples for a final selection step, the algorithm outputs ŵ with err_D(ŵ) ≤ η + ε w.p. ≥ 1 − δ, using n = Õ(1/(γ²ε²)) samples and O(dNT) time. Updates are w^{t+1} = proj_{‖w‖≤1}(w^t − λ_t g(w^t, w^t, x^{(t)}, y^{(t)})) with a _constant* step λ_t = cγ²ε, from w⁰ = e₁, where g(w,v,x,y) = ((1−2η)sign(w·x) − y)·x / max(|v·x|, γ/2).

Step 1 — split the gradient. Write g = g¹ + g², where g¹ replaces the observed label by its conditional mean. Since E_{y|x}[y] = (1−2η(x))sign(w*·x), the residual g² is exactly mean-zero. So g¹ carries the signal and g² carries all the estimation error.

Step 2 — the structural lemma (the key trick). Lemma 2.2 states G¹(w)·(w − w_) ≥ 2(err(w) − η), and — this is what makes the whole thing go — it is proved _pointwise_, not in expectation, so no concentration is needed and it holds on any empirical sample. The proof splits space at the clipping threshold. On R₁ = {|w·x| ≥ γ/2} the clip is inactive, W(w·x)(w·x) = sign(w·x), and g¹·w collapses algebraically to exactly 2(err(w,x) − η); the w_ term satisfies −g¹·w_ ≥ 0 because η(x) ≤ η forces (1−2η(x)) − (1−2η)sign(w·x)sign(w_·x) ≥ 0. This single inequality is where the Massart condition — and nothing more about η(·) — enters. On R₂ = {|w·x| < γ/2} the denominator is the constant γ/2 and the margin does the work: |w_·x| ≥ γ while |w·x| < γ/2 gives −sign(w_·x)(w·x − w_·x) ≥ γ/2, so the same bound survives. In other words: the surrogate gradient is a _subgradient of the potential_ Φ(w) = ‖w − w_‖² whenever the current error exceeds η.

Step 3 — drift. Projection is non-expansive, so ‖w^{t+1} − w_‖² ≤ ‖w^t − w_‖² − 2λ_t g·(w^t − w*) + λ_t²‖g‖². Clipping gives ‖g‖² ≤ 8/γ², so under the event err_D(w^t) ≥ η + ε and with λ_t ≤ γ²ε/8, the deterministic part is ≤ −λ_t ε = −cγ²ε² per step. This is the exact tuning: the step size is chosen so the quadratic term is swallowed by half the linear gain.

Step 4 — martingale concentration. The noise term ξ_t is bounded by 8/γ, hence (16/γ)-subgaussian; a Chernoff/MGF argument iterated along the filtration yields Σ_{t≤T} V̂_t ≤ Cc²γ²ε²T + log(1/δ) w.p. 1 − δ. Note the scaling: noise accumulates at the same γ²ε²T rate as the drift, and only the small constant c separates them.

Step 5 — contradiction. Summing, ‖w^{T+1} − w_‖² ≤ ‖w⁰ − w_‖² − cTε²γ² + log(1/δ). Since ‖w⁰ − w_‖² ≤ 4, taking T = Θ(log(1/δ)/(ε²γ²)) drives the right-hand side _negative* — impossible for a squared norm. Hence the assumed event fails and at least one iterate has error ≤ η + ε; the final step picks the iterate with smallest empirical error on N fresh samples.

The elegance is that there is no regret bound, no online-to-batch conversion, and no explicit angle-decrease argument: the potential ‖w − w_‖² is never shown to decrease monotonically, only to decrease _on average whenever the error is bad*, and the conclusion is extracted by contradiction from the impossibility of a negative squared distance. For comparison, the appendix shows the same structural lemma in a cutting-planes method gives only Õ(1/(γ⁴ε²)) — so the saved 1/γ² is attributable specifically to replacing separation-oracle machinery with single-sample SGD.

Broader context. The three canonical noise models form a strict hierarchy: RCN (Angluin–Laird 1988), Massart (Massart–Nédélec 2006), agnostic. Massart halfspaces sat open from the 1980s until 2019 precisely because the classical argument "any convex surrogate consistent under RCN is consistent under Massart" is false. The modern picture: Massart halfspaces are learnable to η + ε but provably not to OPT + ε efficiently, and even reaching η + ε costs a quadratic-in-1/ε sample blow-up. Two close neighbors are worth reading alongside — Chandrasekaran–Kontonis–Stavropoulos–Tian (NeurIPS 2024), independent and concurrent, get essentially the same bounds via a "Massart is no harder than random" reduction; and Diakonikolas–Kontonis–Tzamos–Zarifis (2024) used a similar loss sequence in an adversarial online setting, though translating their regret bound to PAC gives Ω(1/(ε⁴γ⁸)), worse than prior work. The novelty is therefore not the losses but the recognition that their gradients are subgradients of the potential.

A natural follow-up: make the bound adapt to OPT where adaptivity is not blocked — e.g. under a Tsybakov-type margin condition on η(x) near the boundary, does the same SGD achieve O(OPT) + ε at the same rate? A second: can a variance-reduced or averaged variant give a last-iterate guarantee, eliminating the O(1/ε) testing overhead and making the algorithm genuinely streaming?

For your work the connection is real rather than decorative, in two places. First, click and implicit-relevance labels are close to a textbook Massart model: a click is a noisy proxy for relevance, the noise rate is query- and position-dependent (so η(x) varies), and under standard position-bias assumptions it is bounded away from 1/2 — exactly the Massart condition, not RCN. The η + ε versus OPT + ε distinction is then a statement about a ceiling on what any efficient ranker can extract from click logs: you can match the worst-case click-noise rate, but you cannot efficiently exploit the fact that most queries have clean signal. Second, the γ-margin assumption in embedding space is precisely the separability assumption dense retrieval implicitly makes, and γ there is measurable. The reweighting 1/max(|w^t·x|, γ/2), read as a ranking heuristic, is a principled form of hard-negative upweighting with a clipping floor — derived rather than tuned. The pairwise setting of DKTZ24 is structurally a learning-to-rank problem, which suggests the most concrete follow-up: extend this potential-function analysis to bipartite ranking with Massart-bounded pairwise preference noise, where the target is AUC-type error rather than 0-1 error.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Even in Random Feature Networks, Provably
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-17

Weak-to-Strong Generalization Even in Random Feature Networks, Provably

Marko Medvedev, Kaifeng Lyu, Dingli Yu, Sanjeev Arora, Zhiyuan Li, Nathan Srebro (2025) — arXiv:2503.02877

Main idea. The paper asks a deflationary question about weak-to-strong generalization: does a student need emergent capability, pretraining, or a better inductive bias to surpass the teacher that labeled its data, or is raw size enough? The authors strip the phenomenon down to the simplest possible learner — a two-layer network with a random, frozen bottom layer and a trained top layer, i.e. a finite random-feature approximation to a fixed kernel. The teacher has M_TE random units and is trained to the population optimum over its own feature span; the student draws M_ST ≫ M_TE units from the same distribution and is trained by gradient flow from zero initialization on population data labeled only by the teacher. Nothing gives the student any prior knowledge the teacher lacks. Yet the student provably beats the teacher, and polynomially: L_ST = Õ(L_TE^{1.49}) for ReLU features, L_ST = Õ(k·L_TE²) for a linear anisotropic model. The paper then closes the loop with a matching impossibility result: L_ST = Ω(L_TE²) for essentially any teacher/student feature spaces and any "origin-centered" learning rule, so the quadratic gain they exhibit is the ceiling.

The most interesting part. The mechanism is a spectral filtering argument, and it is genuinely clean. Because the teacher's predictor is the L²(D)-projection of f_ onto the span of only M_TE random features, its error consists almost entirely of _spurious mass in high-order kernel eigendirections_: even when f_ lives in the top-K eigenspace, the teacher's fit leaks energy into e_k for k > K, and that leaked energy is pure noise relative to the ground truth. In the infinite-width limit the student's gradient flow has the closed form f_t = Σ_k (1 − e^{−λ_k t})⟨f_teacher, e_k⟩ e_k — it absorbs each teacher coefficient at rate λ_k. If the spectrum has a gap at some S ≥ K (λ_{S+1} ≪ λ_S), a stopping time with λ_K T large but λ_{S+1}T small copies the teacher's signal coefficients while leaving the noise coefficients at their zero initialization. The student is not smarter than the teacher; it is a low-pass filter on the teacher, and the filter is implemented by early stopping. That explains, rather than merely reproduces, the empirical role of early stopping in Burns et al.: run gradient flow to convergence and the student exactly mimics the teacher, error and all, so PGR → 0. Both simulations show the U-shape in training time.

The limit result is the sharper contribution. It rests on "shrinkage optimality" (Def. 4.1): f̂ is shrink-optimal w.r.t. f_train if no α ∈ [0,1] scaling improves the training objective — equivalently ⟨f̂, f_train − f̂⟩ ≤ 0. Early-stopped gradient flow from zero, loss minimization over a subspace, and any convex class or regularizer containing/minimized at the origin all satisfy it. Theorem 4.3 then gives L_ST ≥ ¼(√(1+3L_TE) − √(1−L_TE))² ≥ ¾L_TE² by a purely geometric argument: shrink-optimality confines f_teacher to the sphere ‖f − f_/2‖ ≤ ½‖f_‖ and f_student to ‖f − f_teacher/2‖ ≤ ½‖f_teacher‖; minimizing over these nested Thales spheres gives the bound. Consequences: you cannot drive L_ST → 0 unless L_TE → 0, and you cannot boost a barely-better-than-chance teacher. Theorem 4.5 replaces shrink-optimality with the weaker, transitive condition E[f_student²] ≤ E[f_teacher²], yielding L_ST ≥ (1 − √(1−L_TE))² ≥ ¼L_TE² for arbitrarily long bootstrapping chains — a game of telephone among ever-larger students buys nothing beyond quadratic.

Honest weaknesses. Everything is population-level (teacher at its population optimum, student trained on infinite teacher-labeled data, M_ST → ∞), so there is no statistical noise anywhere — the "noise" being filtered is deterministic approximation residue. The stopping time is oracle-chosen from the spectrum and from K, with no data-driven selection rule. The 1.49 exponent leans on a Gaussian Universality Ansatz plus the deterministic-equivalent machinery of Defilippis et al. (2024), requires d > 200 and M_TE ≥ Θ(d^{2k}), and does not meet the Ω(L_TE²) lower bound. Theorem 3.2's construction is bespoke, with an eigengap hard-coded into the data distribution; Theorem 3.3 is the more honest asymptotic statement.

Proof sketch. The engine is Theorem 6.5, a fully deterministic bound valid for any p.s.d. kernel K, any teacher features, under Condition 6.1 (f* supported on the top-K eigenspace) and Condition 2.1 (teacher at population optimum):

L_ST ≤ inf_{S≥K} { (1 − (1 − λ²_{S+1}T²)κ_S)·L_TE + e^{−λ_K T}/(2 − e^{−λ_K T})·‖f*‖²_D }.

It is assembled from two lemmas. Lemma 6.2/C.4 splits the eigenindex into three ranges — k ≤ K (signal, where an elementary Jensen inequality charges the cost of incomplete fitting to the e^{−λ_K T}/(2−e^{−λ_K T}) term), K < k ≤ S (harmless), and k > S (noise, where (1 − e^{−λ_k T})² ≤ λ²_{S+1}T² means the teacher's mass is almost entirely not copied). Lemma 6.4/C.6 supplies the crucial fact that the noise range carries a constant fraction of the teacher's error: Σ_{k>S}⟨f̂_w, e_k⟩² ≥ κ_S · L(f̂_w), where the teacher–student feature alignment κ_S = (1 + λ₁((√A_S)⁺B_S(√A_S)⁺))⁻¹ compares Gram matrices of the teacher's features projected inside and outside the top-S eigenspace.

The trick behind Lemma 6.4 is the cleanest step in the paper. Let P project onto the top-S eigenspace and Q onto the teacher's feature span, and set R = QPQ. Since the optimal teacher is f̂_w = Qf_ = QPQh = Rh, both quantities become quadratic forms in the same operator: Σ_{k>S}⟨f̂_w, e_k⟩² = ⟨h, R(R − R²)h⟩ and L_TE = ⟨h, (R − R²)h⟩. The ratio is therefore bounded below by the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of R — and that eigenvalue _is* κ_S, via a generalized Rayleigh quotient identity. Everything else is instantiation: κ_S is lower-bounded w.h.p. by concentration of the smallest singular value of a subgaussian random feature matrix (Vershynin), and the ReLU case uses the Funk–Hecke decomposition in spherical harmonics, where σ²_k = Θ(k^{−(d+2)}) with multiplicities N_k = Θ(k^{d−2}) supply the needed eigengaps automatically (odd σ_k vanish for k > 1, hence the restriction to targets that are linear plus even polynomial).

Broader context. Burns et al. (2024) posed weak-to-strong generalization as an empirical proxy for superalignment. The theory literature has since split by mechanism: Lang, Sontag & Vijayaraghavan (2024) attribute the gain to student robustness/local consistency; Charikar, Pabbaraju & Shiragur (2024) quantify it as the student's misfit to the teacher in convex regression (extended beyond squared loss by Mulgund & Pabbaraju 2025); Wu & Sahai (2025) derive it from benign overfitting in a spiked covariance model; Ildiz et al. (2025) study high-dimensional ridgeless distillation. This paper's distinctive claim is that no special structure is needed — only the teacher's finite-feature approximation error plus spectral bias in the student — and, uniquely, it supplies a two-sided answer. It also sits in the self-distillation-as-regularization tradition, where distilling a model into a copy of itself amounts to repeated shrinkage along kernel eigendirections; here the shrinkage is an explicit consequence of early-stopped gradient flow, making the link to Ali–Kolter–Tibshirani's early-stopping-as-ridge equivalence direct.

The most interesting escape hatch the authors flag themselves: the Ω(L_TE²) barrier applies only to learning rules whose inductive bias "extends from the origin". A student that fine-tunes a pretrained top layer, or regularizes toward a pretrained point rather than zero, is not shrink-optimal and is exempt — the barrier and the Burns setting are separated precisely by the pretrained initialization. A natural follow-up is to quantify that: replace shrink-optimality with optimality w.r.t. a regularizer centered at w₀ ≠ 0 and derive a bound interpolating between Ω(L_TE²) and no constraint as a function of ‖w₀ − w*‖ — a "how much prior knowledge buys how much boosting" theorem. A second is to break the population idealization: with finite teacher-labeled samples and label noise, early stopping trades off two distinct noise sources and the optimal T becomes a genuinely statistical question, possibly answerable with a tiny clean validation set — exactly the regime superalignment cares about.

For your work, the connection is real but should be stated carefully. Distillation of cross-encoders into bi-encoders (MarginMSE, TAS-B, RocketQA-style pipelines) is the IR setting where a student routinely matches or exceeds its teacher despite a structurally weaker scoring function, and the usual explanations are ensembling, hard-negative curation, or better corpus coverage. This paper offers a fourth: if the teacher's scores contain approximation noise concentrated in low-eigenvalue directions of the student's kernel, an early-stopped student denoises the teacher for free, and the gain vanishes with overtraining. That is a testable prediction — loss on gold relevance labels should be U-shaped in distillation steps even when loss on teacher scores is monotone. The lower bound carries a warning too: a bi-encoder trained from scratch on a weak teacher's scores cannot be boosted past Ω(L_TE²), so reported large gains from weak teachers must come from the pretrained initialization (non-shrink-optimal) rather than from capacity. Finally, random-features-as-kernel-approximation is the same object as random projections in ANN search: M random features approximate a similarity kernel with error controlled by the kernel's eigenspectrum, and κ_S — alignment between the teacher's feature Gram matrix and the top-S eigenspace — is a close cousin of the effective-rank quantities that govern when a low-dimensional embedding preserves ranking.

title: When big data actually are low-rank, or entrywise approximation of certain function-generated matrices
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-17

When big data actually are low-rank, or entrywise approximation of certain function-generated matrices

Stanislav Budzinskiy (2024, rev. 2025; math.NA) — arXiv:2407.03250

Main idea. The paper asks a question that sounds empirical but is really approximation theory: when a matrix is a sampled function, F(i,j) = f(x_i, y_j) with x_i, y_j ∈ R^m, how do the smoothness and structure of f control the rank needed to approximate F entrywise, i.e. in the max norm? The max norm is the right notion for data: it says every single entry is perturbed by at most ε, which is what you want if the matrix is a table of measurements rather than an operator.

The target is Udell and Townsend's well-known "Why are big data matrices approximately low rank?" (SIMODS 2019). For "nice latent variable models" — analytic f with controlled derivative growth — they prove an ε-rank bound r = O(log(n)(1 + (C_u+C_v+1)/ε)²) and claim informally that it "eliminates the dependence on the dimension m". Budzinskiy's first contribution is to show this is simply false: the constants C_u, C_v in their own Lemma 4.3 are bounded below by C²m^m and m^m, so the "m-free" bound is really O(log(n) m^{2m}/ε²). He then reproves it with a better argument (Thm 2.3), getting 9log(3n₁n₂)C²ε⁻²e^{m(1+M²)} — exponential instead of m^{2m}, but still not dimension-free.

Worse, Appendix C shows the analytical–algebraic bound is often never better than the naive Taylor bound rank ≤ C(m+ρ*−1, m), which for fixed m is O(1) as n → ∞. For the Gaussian kernel — the paper's own headline numerical example — the analytical bound wins for all n and all m ≥ 2. So the celebrated three-stage picture (ε-rank grows like n, then like β₁log n, then flattens) has no proven logarithmic middle stage for the class of functions it was claimed for.

What is salvaged is more interesting than what is demolished. The Udell–Townsend experiments really do show slowly-growing ranks at m = 1000, and Budzinskiy explains why: they sampled uniformly on the unit sphere, where exp(−‖x−y‖²) = exp(−2 + 2xᵀy) becomes a function of the inner product. He then isolates three classes with genuinely m-independent bounds, constants depending only on the scalar profile h: (i) f(x,y) = h(xᵀWy), rank O(log(n)ε⁻²log(ε⁻¹)); (ii) f(x,y) = h(‖x−y‖²_W), same bound, with a variant for h non-smooth at 0 (e.g. the exponential kernel); (iii) shift-invariant positive-definite kernels f(x,y) = κ(x−y), the sharper O(log(n)ε⁻²) with no assumptions on the sampling points at all. Theorem 6.5 extends class (i) to tensors via a higher-order inner product, giving TT ranks O(log(n₁…n_d)ε⁻²log(ε⁻¹)), m-independent but with a constant c_d growing at least like d^d.

Proof sketch (and how the refutation works). The algebraic engine is Srebro–Shraibman's Lemma 5: for any A ∈ R^{n₁×m}, B ∈ R^{n₂×m} with m arbitrary, there is G with rank(G) ≤ ⌈9log(3n₁n₂)/ε²⌉ and ‖ABᵀ − G‖_max ≤ ε‖A‖_{2,∞}‖B‖_{2,∞}. This is a Johnson–Lindenstrauss statement: take Gaussian R ∈ R^{m×r}, set G = (AR)(BR)ᵀ; each of the n₁n₂ inner products is preserved up to ε‖A(i,:)‖‖B(j,:)‖ with probability 1 − 2exp(−cε²r), and a union bound over the n₁n₂ entries is exactly where log(n) enters. The embedding dimension depends on the number of points, never on m. (Worth flagging: no Maurey empirical-sampling and no Chebyshev expansion appear — the analytic side is plain Taylor truncation, which is an obvious opening for improvement.)

The genuinely clever step is Lemma 3.1: a Hadamard product (A₁B₁ᵀ) ∗ ⋯ ∗ (A_tB_tᵀ) is itself a Gram-type product ÃB̃ᵀ via Khatri–Rao, whose rows are Kronecker products, so ‖Ã‖_{2,∞} = ∏_s‖A_s‖_{2,∞}. Applied to (XYᵀ)^{∗s} — the matrix of (x_iᵀy_j)^s — whose exact rank C(m+s−1, s) is astronomical, JL compresses it to the same r = O(log n/ε²) regardless. Truncating the Taylor series of h at order t costs ‖h − h_t‖_∞ ≤ Ce^{−t} by Stirling once t ≥ e²MR²; each of the t−1 monomials costs r, and t = ⌈log(ε⁻¹)⌉ yields the stated bound. The error splits cleanly into an analytical term (discretization of h) and an algebraic term (JL compression), and neither constant involves m.

Two supporting tricks carry this further. Lemma 4.1 absorbs added rank-one matrices into augmented factors with row norms growing only as (‖A‖²_{2,∞} + Σ‖Z_i‖max)^{1/2}; since ‖x−y‖²_W = ‖x‖²_W + ‖y‖²_W − 2xᵀWy is −2XWYᵀ plus two rank-one terms, the distance case reduces to the inner-product case, and the same lemma allows Taylor expansion at an arbitrary centre (a scalar shift is rank-one), which handles kernels like exp(−‖x−y‖₂) and localises C, M to the observed range of distances. For the PD-kernel theorem the analytic input is Bochner via Rahimi–Recht random Fourier features: κ(x−y) ≈ (1/ρ)Σ_i cos(ω_iᵀ(x−y)), expanded into cos/sin columns so that ‖A‖{2,∞} = ‖B‖_{2,∞} = 1 exactly, uniformly in m and ρ. Feed that into the JL lemma, let the feature error δ_l → 0, and use closedness of {rank ≤ r} to extract a convergent subsequence — a slick limiting argument that deletes the RFF error term altogether.

The refutation is not a counterexample matrix but a constant-tracking audit plus a regime comparison: C_u, C_v are traced through Udell–Townsend's own proof, and the resulting bound is then compared numerically against the trivial analytic bound to show the claimed logarithmic regime is empty in the relevant parameter range. Budzinskiy also notes their Lemma 4.3 is stated with ‖u_i‖₂ where the proof gives ‖u_i‖₂² — small but load-bearing.

The most interesting part, with critique. The conceptual payoff is that dimension-independence comes from the geometry of the score, not the smoothness of the function. Any f factoring through a scalar xᵀy inherits, for free, the fact that monomials of an inner product are Hadamard powers, hence Khatri–Rao products, hence JL-compressible at a cost set by n and ε only. Smoothness in m variables buys nothing.

The caveats are severe and mostly stated by the author. (1) Max norm, not spectral or Frobenius — these ε-ranks can be wildly smaller than spectral ε-rank: the identity has max-norm ε-rank O(log n/ε²) and spectral rank n, and the paper's own symmetric-sampling experiments note the matrices "behave like identity matrices". So "approximately low rank" here does not mean the data live near a low-dimensional subspace. (2) ε⁻² is brutal: for f(x,y) = xᵀy at ε = 0.1 the logarithmic stage begins at n ≈ 18964, with r ≈ 21713 at n = 10⁵ and 30002 at n = 10⁷ — low only relative to n. (3) Constants: one remark needs ε ≤ 3.8×10⁻⁷ for the Gaussian-kernel version to apply. (4) Non-constructive: optimal max-norm low-rank approximation is NP-hard even at rank one (Gillis–Shitov); the experiments use alternating projections with binary search at n ≤ 8192, far below where the theory bites. (5) The TT constant c_d ≳ d^d makes the tensor result fragile in d.

Broader context and why this matters for your work. For attention, Theorem 3.8 is a direct sharpening: A = exp(QKᵀ/√m) is exactly h(qᵀk) with h = exp, so the entrywise-ε rank is O(log(n)ε⁻²log(1/ε)) versus O(mε⁻²log(m/ε)) from Performer-style orthogonal random features — an improvement whenever m > log n, the usual regime. Read alongside the hardness side (Alman–Song on fast attention requiring bounded entries, Sarlós–Song–Woodruff–Zhang, Keles–Wei–Hazan), the picture is coherent: attention matrices are entrywise-ε-compressible with m-free rank, but only for bounded score ranges, and existence says nothing about computing the factorization. The "attention is not low rank" objections mostly concern spectral rank, which these results do not contradict.

The connection I would push hardest is vector search. A similarity matrix over a corpus is precisely class (i) (inner product / cosine) or class (ii) (squared Euclidean), and for Gaussian/Cauchy/exponential kernels Theorem 5.2 says something startling: for any n points in any dimension whatsoever, the kernel matrix is entrywise ε-close to rank O(log n/ε²). No manifold assumption, no intrinsic-dimension assumption, no benign data distribution. That should make you suspicious of the folk argument "our embeddings are compressible because the data have low intrinsic dimension" — compressibility in this sense is free and carries no information about the corpus. The sting is in the error notion: entrywise ε on a similarity scale is exactly the perturbation that destroys top-k ordering whenever the margin between the k-th and (k+1)-th neighbour is below 2ε, which in a high-dimensional near-orthogonal embedding space is typical, not exceptional. The theorem and the difficulty of ANN are two readings of the same fact — max-norm low rank is cheap precisely because it is blind to the fine ranking structure retrieval depends on. This gives a crisp way to say what PCA/OPQ and JL reductions in an index pipeline do and do not buy: they control additive distortion of scores, and recall loss is governed by the margin distribution of the query workload, not by rank.

A follow-up sitting squarely between numerical linear algebra and theoretical IR: replace the max norm with a ranking-aware error notion. Define rank_{k,δ}(F) as the least rank of a G whose induced top-k ordering agrees with F's on a 1−δ fraction of rows, and ask what the JL/Khatri–Rao machinery gives under a margin assumption s_{(k)} − s_{(k+1)} ≥ γ. The union bound over n² entries should become a union bound over n·k comparisons and ε⁻² should become γ⁻², plausibly yielding O(log(nk)/γ²) — and, more usefully, a lower bound showing that when the margin distribution has mass near zero, no rank below n^{Ω(1)} suffices. That would be an honest "when is a similarity matrix genuinely compressible for retrieval" theorem, and it connects to the γ₂ factorization-norm machinery the paper already invokes, which has real lower-bound technology attached from communication complexity (Linial–Shraibman).

For generative retrieval there is a second, more speculative hook: a decoder's logit matrix over a docid vocabulary is h(qᵀw_d) — class (i) again — so the entrywise ε-rank of the whole query×docid score matrix is bounded independently of model width. Hierarchical docids decoded in d steps make the score a function of a d-fold interaction, exactly the higher-order inner product of Theorem 6.5, and a TT factorization of that tensor is a beam-search-friendly object. Is the semantic-ID score tensor of a trained generative retriever close to TT-low-rank, and if so does the TT rank profile quantify how much a hierarchical docid scheme really compresses the corpus versus merely re-encoding it?

title: Language Generation in the Limit
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-17

Language Generation in the Limit

Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan (2024) — arXiv:2404.06757

Main idea. The paper asks what is provable about language generation when you strip away every probabilistic assumption — no distribution over strings, no smoothness, no concentration, no i.i.d. sampling. What remains is a game. There is a countable collection of candidate languages C = {L₁, L₂, …}, all infinite subsets of a countable universe U; an adversary secretly picks one of them, K = L_z, and enumerates all of its strings, one per step, in whatever malicious order it likes. The agent sees only the growing prefix S_t and, at every step, must emit a string. It succeeds if there is a finite t* after which every string it emits lies in K \ S_t — valid and new, forever.

The point is the contrast with the Gold–Angluin setting, which is the same game with a different output channel. There the agent must name an index i with L_i = K; Gold showed this is impossible even for the regular languages, and Angluin's 1980 characterization (a "telltale" finite subset for each language) showed how narrow the identifiable families are. Kleinberg and Mullainathan's result is that generation succeeds for every countable collection, with no condition whatsoever. The two tasks differ only in what the agent is asked to say, and that difference separates impossible from always-possible.

The reason generation is easier is worth stating precisely. Identification demands an answer that is exactly right: L_i = K, two-sided. Generation demands an answer that errs only on one side: any string in K will do, so the agent may safely under-commit and produce strings from any subset of K. Under-committing is exactly what is unavailable to an identifier. The adversary's leverage in Gold's proof is that it can always drip-feed evidence consistent with a strictly larger language and punish whichever guess the agent makes; but a conservative generator that hedges downward is never punished for hedging, because a subset of K is still K-valid.

The most interesting part. The cleverest move is the definition of a critical language and the discovery that critical languages are automatically nested. Say L_i is consistent with S_t if S_t ⊆ L_i, and call L_n critical at step t if it is consistent and L_n ⊆ L_i for every consistent L_i among the first n languages. Minimality with respect to inclusion over all of C may simply not exist for infinite collections, so criticality localizes the demand to a finite prefix of the indexing — that is what makes it both well-defined and checkable. The payoff is a two-line lemma: if i < j and both are critical at t, then L_j ⊆ L_i. The critical languages at any step form a decreasing chain. The algorithm then does the only sensible thing: generate from the critical language with the largest index in C_t — that is, from the smallest set in the chain it can currently see.

Why this works is the deep point. The true language L_z eventually becomes critical and stays critical forever, and z is a finite index, so once t ≥ z the algorithm's window contains L_z and the chain element it picks sits at index ≥ z, hence inside L_z. The algorithm never learns z — it provably cannot — but it doesn't need to; it only needs to be standing somewhere below z in the chain. Validity is bought by permanent, unbounded conservatism. The paper is unusually candid that this is a feature of the solution, not an artifact: early on the agent over-generates (hallucination), later it under-generates (mode collapse), and the model exhibits both without any probability at all.

Critique. There is no breadth guarantee of any kind, and the construction actively destroys breadth; the theorem is consistent with an agent that, in the limit, emits strings from a single thin sliver of a rich language. There is no finite-time bound in the countable case — t_ exists but is not computable from the data, and the agent can never certify it has entered the good regime, which makes the result useless as a stopping rule. The model is fully non-distributional, so nothing is said about typicality or fluency; "valid" is set membership. Membership queries "w ∈ L_i?" are free, and the function-version even used subset queries (removed in §5 by a finite-prefix trick). The adversary is constrained to eventually enumerate _all_ of K and to present only positive, noiseless examples; real training data is neither exhaustive nor clean. And the guarantee is per-enumeration and asymptotic, so nothing is said about sample complexity for infinite C — only the finite-collection result gives a uniform bound t(C) = m_ + 1.

Proof sketch. Theorem 2.1. There is an algorithm such that for every countable collection C of infinite languages over countable U, accessible only through membership queries, and every adversarial enumeration of any K = L_z ∈ C, there exists t_ such that for all t ≥ t_ the output a_t lies in K \ S_t.

Two failed approaches frame the proof. Closure — define ⟨S_t⟩ as the intersection of all consistent languages; anything in ⟨S_t⟩ \ S_t is provably in K. This is the whole proof for finite C, but for infinite C it degenerates: with C = {P_{a,b} ∪ V} over all finite V one gets ⟨S_t⟩ = S_t always. Direct hypothesis enumeration — walk down C, generating from the first consistent L_i until refuted — fails for the structural reason that is the crux of the paper: if some L_i with i < z strictly contains L_z, it is never refuted by positive examples from L_z, the agent parks on it forever, and has no feedback to notice. Any fix must be downward, not leftward.

The fix is criticality. Lemma 4.3 (key lemma): L_z is eventually permanently critical. Proof: let A = {i < z : L_z ⊄ L_i}; for each i ∈ A pick a witness v_i ∈ L_z \ L_i, let t_i be the step it appears, and set t⁺ = max_{i∈A} t_i — finite because A ⊆ {1,…,z−1} is finite and the adversary is obliged to enumerate every element of L_z. After t⁺, every L_i ∈ C_z that fails to contain L_z has been killed by its witness. Lemma 4.4 (nesting): i < j both critical ⇒ L_j ⊆ L_i, immediate from the definition since L_i ∈ C_j is consistent. The algorithm: output the least element of L_{n_t} \ S_t where n_t is the largest index of a critical language in C_t. Correctness: take t* = max(z, t⁺); then L_z is critical and inside the window, so n_t ≥ z, so by nesting L_{n_t} ⊆ L_z. The adversary cannot fool the agent forever precisely because it must eventually surrender every witness v_i, and there are only finitely many to surrender.

That version needs subset queries. §5 removes them with a finite-prefix trick: L_i[m] = L_i ∩ {u₁,…,u_m}, and L_n is (t,m)-critical if consistent and L_n[m] ⊆ L_i[m] for all consistent L_i ∈ C_n — decidable with 2m membership queries. Monotonicity gives that (t,m)-criticality implies (t,m′)-criticality for m′ < m, so as m grows within a step the index n_t(m) can only decrease; there are at most t−1 such disruptive iterations, after which L_{n_t(m)} is frozen and, being infinite, yields a fresh string in finite time.

Broader context. The lineage runs Gold 1967 → Angluin 1979/1980 → a fifty-year quiet period in which the negative result was read as a verdict on learning from text. This paper reframes it: the verdict was about identification, and the generative task LLMs actually perform is a strictly weaker specification that escapes it. The follow-up literature is essentially one long argument about the price of breadth. Kalavasis, Mehrotra and Velegkas formalize validity-versus-breadth and show that once you demand generation with breadth, the positive result largely collapses back toward identifiability-style conditions — hallucination and mode collapse are not both avoidable. Charikar and Pabbaraju map further facets (uniform vs. non-uniform generatability); Li, Raman and Tewari characterize uniform generatability via a combinatorial "closure dimension" generalizing this paper's m*; Raman and co-authors push into noisy enumerations and generation with feedback, where a validity oracle restores some breadth.

For your work, the connection is direct rather than analogical. Generative retrieval is literally generation from a valid set of docids. In DSI-style systems the model autoregressively emits an identifier that must name an actually existing document; validity is set membership in the corpus — exactly the paper's predicate — and constrained decoding over a docid trie is an enforcement mechanism for validity, the engineering counterpart of generating from a critical language. The paper's trade-off then reads as the central empirical pathology of generative retrieval: a trie-constrained decoder is perfectly valid by construction, but breadth — corpus coverage, the fraction of documents ever reachable — is exactly what degrades, and popularity-biased collapse onto a small set of reachable docids is the "thin subset of K" phenomenon under a different name. The finite-collection result is suggestive too: a fixed corpus is a finite universe, so the m*+1 bound hints at uniform sample bounds for generative retrieval over fixed corpora that do not exist for open-ended generation. The prompted extension is the query-conditioned case, and its robustness condition — every query has arbitrarily many valid continuations in every candidate index — visibly fails for tail queries, which is precisely where generative retrieval breaks. Finally, the convex-hull remark in §3.2 bridges to vector search: generating a point in the convex hull of observed embeddings is guaranteed valid under any convex hypothesis and utterly devoid of breadth — a clean formal statement of why interpolative dense retrieval cannot reach the periphery of a corpus.

A thesis-scale question falls out: define a retrieval-flavored breadth measure as recall over the corpus prefix, and ask for the exact trade-off curve between validity and recall under adversarial enumeration — a generative-retrieval-native version of the Kalavasis–Mehrotra–Velegkas impossibility.

title: Dynamics of Meta-learning Representation in the Teacher-student Scenario
tags: Condensed Matter - Disordered Systems and Neural Networks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Dynamics of Meta-learning Representation in the Teacher-student Scenario

Hui Wang, Cho Tung Yip, Bo Li · 2024 · arXiv:2408.12545

Main idea. Gradient-based meta-learners like MAML seem to work because they learn a representation that many tasks share. This paper asks how that representation actually forms during training, for a nonlinear two-layer network trained with finite-sample gradients.

Setup. The authors use a "meta-teacher." Each task t is a soft committee machine. All tasks share the first-layer weights B, but each has its own readout u^t, drawn fresh from N(0, I_M). A student with first-layer weights J learns from a stream of such tasks using first-order ANIL (FO-ANIL). For each task:

  • Inner loop. The readout starts at w⁰ = 0 and takes one gradient step on P training examples. This gives a closed-form, Hebbian-like readout w^t.
  • Outer loop. J takes one gradient step on V validation examples.

As N → ∞, the whole process reduces to ODEs for two sets of overlaps: R_kn = J_k·B_n (student vs. teacher) and Q_kl = J_k·J_l (student vs. student).

Main finding. Meta-learning behaves like classical single-task learning. There is a long symmetric plateau, in which all student units track the same teacher unit, followed by a specialization transition. The noise from task-specific readouts does not stop J from recovering B, up to permutations and sign flips.

Critique. The main strength is a clean reduction that can be checked against simulation. The ODEs (Eqs. 34–36) match simulations of ε_g^meta and R_kn at N = 1000, K = M = 3, P = V = 100. The plateau-then-specialization story is also shown directly. With η_w = 3, the student is still in the one-unit symmetric state at α = 500. With η_w = 9, the error drops in three steps and the student ends at J₁ ∝ B₃, J₂ ∝ −B₁, J₃ ∝ −B₂.

The weaknesses come from the simplifications:

  • No learned initialization. Setting w⁰ = 0 removes the feature MAML is known for. What remains is really "learn a shared encoder, then fit a one-step correlational head."
  • Few-shot noise is dropped. The analysis assumes large P and approximates ⟨w_i w_k⟩ ≈ ⟨w_i⟩⟨w_k⟩, discarding an O(1/P) term. That term is exactly the few-shot readout noise that makes meta-learning hard. Meanwhile, 1/V terms are kept in the Q equation, so the two sample sizes are treated unevenly.
  • Visible mismatch. The predicted Q_kl curves are clearly off at large learning rates (Fig. 2, App. C).
  • Idealized data. The main model has no noise and no correlation between tasks. Inputs are isotropic Gaussian, g = erf(x/√2), and K and M are O(1). The teacher is orthogonal with T_mn = m δ_mn, and the unequal norms probably help break the symmetry. R starts at 10⁻¹².
  • Mostly numerical conclusions. No fixed points or stability analysis are derived analytically. The plateau lengths, the optimal η_w, and the claim that overparameterization (K > M) makes learning rates less sensitive all come from integrating the ODEs numerically.
  • Heuristic steps. Self-averaging is argued heuristically. The varying-teacher case (γ < 1) relies on a first-order Taylor expansion.
  • No benchmarks. Nothing connects the results to real meta-learning benchmarks.

Broader context.

The physics side. Statistical physics has long studied online SGD in teacher–student models. As the input dimension N grows, the high-dimensional weights can be summarized by a few overlaps (order parameters), which follow deterministic ODEs in the rescaled time α = t/N. Saad & Solla (1995) solved this for soft committee machines and identified the symmetric plateau and the later specialization of units. Goldt et al. (2019) revisited the problem with both layers trained and found that overparameterized students duplicate teacher units. This paper reproduces that effect for K = 6 (Fig. 6).

The meta-learning side. Raghu et al. (2020) argued that MAML mostly reuses features, which led to ANIL. Collins et al. (ICML 2022) proved that MAML and ANIL recover shared representations in linear models with population gradients, and Yüksel et al. (ICLR 2024) extended this to overparameterized FO-ANIL. The present paper carries these ideas to nonlinear networks with finite-sample gradients, but only at physics-level rigor.

A natural follow-up. Keep the O(1/P) readout variance so the theory covers the real few-shot regime (P of about 5–20). Then predict how plateau length scales with P, η_w and task correlation. The rigorous tools from the Goldt et al. line of work would make this a theorem rather than a derivation.

A modest IR link. A shared frozen encoder with a cheap per-task linear head is how embedding models get adapted to new domains or query types in vector search. In that reading, R_kn is literally the alignment between the learned subspace and the true feature subspace. The symmetric plateau is a warning: such an encoder can spend a long time with collapsed, redundant directions, which is bad for nearest-neighbour discrimination.

Derivation sketch (physics-style, not a theorem). The pipeline follows the standard online-learning route.

  1. Gaussian local fields. Each step uses a fresh task and fresh samples, so J^{t−1} is independent of the current inputs. By the CLT, the local fields (x = Jξ, y = Bξ) are jointly Gaussian with covariance [[Q, R],[Rᵀ, T]].
  2. Discrete updates. The inner step gives w_k^t = (η_w/P) Σ_μ σ^{t,μ} g(x_k^{t,μ})/√K in closed form. The outer update (Eq. 22) is projected onto B_n and J_l using ξ·ξ′ = N δ, which gives the discrete R and Q updates (Eqs. 24–25). These increments are O(1/N), so α = t/N becomes continuous time.
  3. Averaging. Three sources of randomness are averaged out: the training fields, the validation fields, and the task vector u, using ⟨u_n u_m⟩ = δ_nm. Two approximations enter here. First, ⟨w_i w_k⟩ is factorized, which is exact only up to O(1/P) (App. B). Second, self-averaging is justified by a law-of-large-numbers argument for large P and V over a window Δt with Δt/N → 0 (App. C, following Reents & Urbanczik).
  4. Closed ODEs. With erf activations, the averages reduce to the Saad–Solla Gaussian integrals, for example f_km = (2/π) arcsin(R_km / √((1+Q_kk)(1+T_mm))), plus I₃ and I₄. The result is a closed set of equations:
  5. ODEs for R, with drift of order η_Jη_w and η_Jη_w²;
  6. ODEs for Q, with extra 1/V terms of order η_J²η_w², η_J²η_w³ and η_J²η_w⁴, which explains why Q is more sensitive to finite V;
  7. ε_g^meta expressed in terms of f (Eq. 36).
  8. Numerical integration. Everything else comes from integrating these ODEs numerically: the phases, the learning-rate sweeps (Figs. 4–5), and the extensions. The γ-variability case (App. D) uses a first-order expansion in √(1−γ²). L2 regularization and output noise (App. E) add −λη_J R and −2λη_J Q terms, plus a noise term involving I₂′.

title: Non-Asymptotic Length Generalization
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Non-Asymptotic Length Generalization

Thomas Chen, Tengyu Ma, Zhiyuan Li · 2025 · arXiv:2506.03085

Main idea. Gold's classic result says that almost any enumerable hypothesis class can be learned "in the limit." Train on every string up to some length, and an enumerate-and-check learner eventually settles on the true function. The result says nothing about how long those training strings must be, though. The required length could be astronomically large, and in practice that would look like "transformers don't length-generalize."

This paper puts a number on it. It defines length complexity: the shortest training length after which the learner outputs exactly the ground truth, as a function of the complexity c of the true function. A class has non-asymptotic length generalization if this quantity has a computable upper bound in c. The authors then determine which classes have such a bound and how large it is. Most of the work goes into two small fragments of C-RASP.

The most interesting part. The standout result is an equivalence (Theorem 4.2 with Lemma 4.5) that has two parts.

  1. The Minimum-Complexity Interpolator (MCI), which returns the simplest program consistent with the data, is exactly optimal. Its length complexity equals N(F_c): the shortest length at which every pair of distinct functions of complexity ≤ c already disagree on some input.
  2. N(F_c) is computably bounded if and only if equivalence of functions in the class is decidable.

A learning question thus becomes a decidability question. Equivalence of linear CFGs is undecidable (Baker & Book, 1974), so no learner has a computable length bound for CFGs (Prop. 4.6), even though CFGs are learnable in the limit. The paper also shows that "finite identification with complexity information" is a third equivalent condition (Lemma 4.10).

Broader context.

  • Length generalization means that a model trained on short inputs still works on longer ones.
  • RASP (Weiss et al., 2021) is a small programming language whose primitives mirror transformer operations.
  • C-RASP (Yang & Chiang, 2024) is a variant built on prefix counts (ps) and comparisons between them. Its expressive power lies between finite-precision and infinite-precision transformers.
  • The RASP-L conjecture (Zhou et al., 2023) says transformers length-generalize on a task exactly when the task has a short RASP-L program. MCI turns that intuition into a formal object, and when complexity means description length, MCI is the Minimum Description Length principle.

The closest prior work is Huang et al. (2024), "A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers," which gives only in-the-limit results for Limit Transformers. This paper is its quantitative follow-up. The DFA result also echoes Angluin's L* algorithm and Myhill–Nerode theory.

Two follow-ups are left open. One is a matching lower bound: the authors conjecture Ω(T^K) when K ≤ Θ(log T). The other is extending the analysis to 3-layer C-RASP, or to layers with bias terms.

For generative retrieval, the connection is suggestive but loose. Suppose the valid docid strings are exactly those accepted by a DFA with c states. Then the 2c − 2 bound says how long training strings must be for an idealized learner to pin down that structure. The CFG impossibility result warns that grammar-like docid schemes come with no such guarantee. I wouldn't push the connection further than that.

Proof sketch. Every positive result reduces, via Theorem 4.2, to one question: if two distinct functions f ≠ f′ of bounded complexity disagree somewhere, do they disagree on a short string?

DFAs (Prop. 3.10): N ≤ 2c − 2. The argument is essentially state minimization. For each prefix u with |u| ≤ c, let E(u) be the set of suffixes v with |v| ≤ c − 2 such that uv is accepted. Lemma C.1 shows that E(u) = E(u′) exactly when u and u′ reach the same state. Suffixes of length 0 already separate at least two classes. Each additional unit of suffix length must add at least one new class until all c states are separated, since otherwise the refinement would stop early and contradict minimality. Prefixes of length up to c and suffixes of length up to c − 2 give total length 2c − 2.

C-RASP1 (Thm 5.5): O(T²). Here f(x) = 1[a·ps(x) − b·n − d > 0], with integers bounded by T, so each function is a line in the plane of (length, number of ones). Two lines with different slopes have slopes that differ by at least 1/|aa′|. At length about 3T², their vertical gap exceeds 1, so a lattice point lies between them. A string with that length and that number of ones separates the two functions.

_C-RASP2 (Thm 5.6): O(T^{O(K)})._ In the first layer, each of K heads compares ps(x)_j with (b/a)·j. The second layer thresholds a weighted sum of how often each head fires. So f is a linear threshold on "activations" B_i, where B_i is the fraction of prefixes that lie above slope line i. Instead of strings, the proof works with continuous test functions: 1-Lipschitz monotone curves that stand in for infinitely long strings. It has four steps.

  1. From a disagreement to a curve (Lemma D.30). A disagreement between f and f′ yields a curve that satisfies both second-layer inequalities strictly. This step needs the assumptions z > 0 and Σλ_i > z.
  2. Structure of the achievable activations (Lemma 6.15). The set of achievable activation vectors is a finite union of polytopes, one for each "basis schema," meaning the order in which the curve crosses the lines. Within a schema, the segment lengths form a polytope whose faces have low-precision coefficients.
  3. A point with a margin, then rounded. The average of the polytope's vertices is at least about 1/(|V|·(poly(K,T)√M)^M) away from every face. This follows from a Hadamard-type determinant bound on vertex coordinates (Lemma 6.16/D.18). That point is then rounded to low precision (Lemma D.29).
  4. From the curve back to a string (Lemma 6.9). The rounded curve is discretized into a string of length n, with activation error O((T² + M)/n). Choosing n larger than 1/margin keeps the disagreement.

Since M ≤ k² and k ≤ 2K, this gives O(T^{O(K²)}) (Lemma 6.3). A sharper margin bound (Lemma D.20) uses the fact that only O(K) faces have high-precision coefficients. That improves the bound to poly(T^K), which is O(T^{O(K)}) (Thm 6.1).

title: Approaching Deep Learning through the Spectral Dynamics of Weights
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Approaching Deep Learning through the Spectral Dynamics of Weights

David Yunis, Kumar Kshitij Patel, Samuel Wheeler, Pedro Savarese, Gal Vardi, Karen Livescu, Michael Maire, Matthew R. Walter · 2024 · arXiv:2408.11804

Main idea. Several deep learning puzzles are usually studied one at a time: grokking, why weight decay helps, memorization versus generalization, lottery tickets, and linear mode connectivity (LMC). This paper asks whether a single cheap, architecture-agnostic measurement can connect them: the SVD of every weight matrix, tracked through training.

The authors test four setups: VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, a diffusion UNet on MNIST, a bidirectional LSTM on LibriSpeech, and a 12-layer Pythia-160M-style Transformer on Wikitext-103. The same picture appears in all of them. Large singular values grow faster than small ones, so effective rank falls, and the top singular vectors settle their directions early.

That picture is then applied to each puzzle:

  • Grokking. Validation loss drops at the same moment effective rank collapses.
  • Weight decay. Stronger weight decay pushes rank lower. In the Transformer it also aligns the singular vectors of adjacent layers.
  • Memorization. A 4-layer MLP trained on true labels develops low-rank, aligned middle layers. The same MLP trained on random labels stays high-rank.
  • Lottery tickets. A global magnitude mask at 5% density mostly preserves the final top singular vectors.
  • LMC. Two branches of the same training run are linearly mode-connected exactly when they share top singular vectors.

Critique. The paper's main strength is breadth with a consistent method. Hyperparameters come from prior work, the code is public, and the authors report their negative results honestly. For example, the "balanced initialization" assumed in deep linear theory does not hold, and alignment between layers is weak and patchy (Fig. 5). The paper contains no new theorem.

How "rank" is measured. Rank here means the normalized-entropy effective rank of Roy & Vetterli, not algebraic rank. It is scale-invariant and smooth, which makes for clean plots but can hide a lot. Two further choices matter:
