  • Convolutions are flattened to (c_out, c_in·h·w). Alignment between conv layers is measured only at the centre position of the next layer, a choice made after trying several options.
  • Results use 3 seeds, and 1D and normalization parameters are ignored.

Correlation versus causation. Most of the evidence is correlational, and some of it is close to built in:

  • Grokking. This result is nearly guaranteed. Nanda et al. already showed that the modular-addition solution is a sparse Fourier circuit, which is low-rank, and the authors acknowledge this.
  • Weight decay. A Frobenius penalty shrinks small singular values that the loss does not defend, so falling rank does not show any effect beyond the norm penalty itself. A norm-matched control would separate the two, for example a nuclear-norm penalty or norm-constrained training.
  • Generalization. Fig. 14 shows only that high-weight-decay models still reach low training loss. There is no curve of rank against test error across weight decay values.
  • SVD pruning (Fig. 4). Comparing the top half of the spectrum with the bottom half is weaker than it looks, because the bottom half carries little spectral energy. An energy-matched comparison would be fairer.

Interventions. The LMC perturbation is the only real intervention, and it is not targeted. Isotropic Gaussian noise with ‖ε‖ = η‖W‖, for η up to 2.5, disrupts everything at once. So losing top-vector agreement and losing LMC together does not show that one causes the other. A targeted test would perturb only the top-k subspace, or only its complement.

Other gaps. The lottery-ticket claim rests on a single setting: VGG-16 at 5% density, rewound to epoch 4. The random-mask control with matched per-layer sparsity is a nice touch. Still, the claim that magnitude pruning is roughly low-rank pruning needs a direct comparison with an actual truncated-SVD ticket. The largest model has only 12 layers and the UNet is trained on MNIST, so the claim of practical relevance is a stretch.

Broader context. In deep linear networks (products of matrices with no nonlinearity), gradient descent from small, balanced initializations grows singular values one at a time. This "rich get richer" dynamic has a closed form and gets stronger with depth. Arora et al. (2019, Implicit Regularization in Deep Matrix Factorization) argue that this bias toward low rank explains generalization in matrix completion better than norm-based accounts. Grokking (Power et al., 2022) is the delayed jump from memorizing to generalizing on small algorithmic tasks, and it depends heavily on weight decay. Complementary views include:

  • Huh et al., The Low-Rank Simplicity Bias in Deep Networks
  • Boix-Adserà et al. (2023), Transformers Learn through Gradual Rank Increase
  • Martin & Mahoney's heavy-tailed self-regularization analysis of weight spectra

Possible follow-ups. The missing piece is causal tests. One design is to project gradients onto, or away from, the current top-k singular subspace during training, then measure the effect on generalization, LMC barriers and ticket quality. Another is to compare Frobenius and nuclear-norm regularization at matched norm.

Connection to your work.

  • Generative retrieval. In DSI-style generative retrieval, the model is supposed to memorize arbitrary document IDs. Sec. 6 found that random-label memorization produces high-rank, unaligned layers. That suggests tracking the spectra of the docid output and embedding matrices as the corpus grows, to see whether indexing pushes the model from the low-rank "generalizing" regime toward the high-rank "memorizing" one. That shift could help explain forgetting and poor generalization to unseen queries.
  • Dense retrieval. The collapse in effective rank relates to known embedding anisotropy and dimensional collapse. It also relates to arguments such as Weller et al. (2025) that embedding dimension limits how many top-k combinations a model can represent. A retriever whose weights drift toward low rank may effectively use even fewer dimensions than it nominally has.

title: When Models Manipulate Manifolds: The Geometry of a Counting Task
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

When Models Manipulate Manifolds: The Geometry of a Counting Task

Wes Gurnee, Emmanuel Ameisen, Isaac Kauvar, Julius Tarng, Adam Pearce, Chris Olah, Joshua Batson · 2025 · Transformer Circuits

Main idea. A language model sees only token IDs, yet it reliably predicts where fixed-width text will wrap. To do that it has to track four things: how many characters are on the current line so far, the document's line width, the difference between the two, and whether the next word fits. The authors reverse-engineer how Claude 3.5 Haiku does this. Their tools are a synthetic corpus re-wrapped at widths k = 15…150, attribution graphs, and a crosscoder with 10M features.

They first find families of discrete features for character count, line width, characters remaining, and "break predictor/suppressor." They then show that each count is better described as a one-dimensional curve, a feature manifold, that bends sharply inside a small subspace. Character count, for example, lives in a 6-D subspace that captures 95% of the variance of the per-count means. Ablating or patching that rank-6 subspace moves the newline prediction.

With that in place, the computation reads as geometry:

  • Counting. Each early attention head uses the previous newline as an attention sink. It outputs roughly (tokens seen) × ~4 characters, with a correction for token length. Each head writes an almost straight ray, and the rays add up to a curve.
  • Comparing. "Boundary heads" compare the character count with the line width.
  • Deciding. Late layers put "characters remaining" and "length of the next token" on nearly orthogonal subspaces. The break decision then reduces to a hyperplane, which reaches AUC 0.91 on real data.

The most interesting part. The standout is the boundary head's QK "twist." In the residual stream, the probe for character count i and the probe for line width k align best when i = k, but only weakly (cosine about 0.25). Pass them through one boundary head's W_Q and W_K and they align almost perfectly (cosine about 1), with the peak shifted to k = i + ε.

So the head is a learned bilinear similarity that fires when the line is almost full, for any line width. A one-dimensional encoding could not do this: linear maps on a line can only scale and translate it, so there is no natural threshold. Rotation needs extra dimensions. One head cannot resolve the whole range (head 0 confuses 5 and 17 characters remaining), so about three heads with different offsets tile the range. Each head's output is nearly one-dimensional, but together they form an evenly spaced 2-D curve.

The mechanism also predicts a failure, which the authors call a "visual illusion." Counting heads normally attend from one newline to the next, but they also attend to @@, the git-diff delimiter. Inserting @@ into prose therefore disrupts the newline prediction. The authors tested 180 two-character insertions. The strongest disruptors were mostly code-like (>>, }}, ||), and each insertion's disruption tracked how much it distracted the heads.

Why the geometry looks this way. Suppose you want n unit vectors, each similar to its neighbours and orthogonal to vectors farther away. Their Gram matrix X is circulant, so the discrete Fourier transform diagonalizes it, and the best rank-k approximation keeps only the top Fourier modes of the similarity profile. Truncating the modes causes Gibbs-style ringing: similarity falls, turns negative, then rises again. In the embedding this appears as a rippled, helix-like curve.

The map that shifts each point to the next commutes with X, and therefore also with the projection onto its top eigenvectors. The truncated embedding therefore still has a linear map that slides the curve along itself, which is exactly what the QK twist needs.

A physical simulation gives the same result. Place 100 points on a 6-sphere, each attracted to its 6 neighbours on either side and repelled by all others. They settle into two-ring similarity patterns, and in 3-D the curve looks like the seams of a baseball. Rippling turns out to be the best trade-off between using few dimensions and keeping adjacent values distinguishable. It also avoids the norm blow-up that a straight ray would need to separate 150 counts.

Broader context. Mechanistic interpretability tries to turn weights and activations into readable algorithms. Its main tool is dictionary learning (SAEs, transcoders, crosscoders), which decomposes activations into sparse features; attribution graphs (Ameisen et al., 2025) then trace how those features drive a prediction. This work adds a duality: a family of tiled features can equally be read as local coordinates on a continuous manifold, and the manifold view is much simpler to describe. It builds on evidence that not all features are one-dimensional, such as the circular day-of-week and month representations in Engels et al., "Not All Language Model Features Are Linear."

One natural follow-up is unsupervised detection of manifolds. For example, one could search crosscoder decoder Gram matrices for near-circulant, ringing blocks, then fit a curve to each and look for linear maps that act on it. The paper also leaves open how the model combines the lengths of previous lines into a single line-width estimate (a max, or a moving average?), and that question could be tested directly.

Connection to your work. The Fourier argument is a clean statement about what rank-k dot products can express. In limited dimension, a similarity that decays smoothly along an ordinal variable is impossible, and ringing is the unavoidable artifact. So nearest-neighbour search over embeddings of ordinal attributes (dates, lengths, prices, positions) can rank "second-ring" items above items that are actually closer on the variable. This fits with recent results on the dimensional limits of single-vector retrieval (e.g., Weller et al., 2025).

The QK twist also shows that an asymmetric bilinear score W_Qᵀ W_K can express offset or range conditions ("slightly larger than") that cosine similarity cannot. That is relevant to asymmetric query/document encoders, and to how generative retrievers might represent numeric docid structure.

title: Learning and Transferring Sparse Contextual Bigrams with Linear Transformers
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Learning and Transferring Sparse Contextual Bigrams with Linear Transformers

Yunwei Ren, Zixuan Wang, Jason D. Lee · 2024 · arXiv:2410.23438

Main idea. The paper asks how gradient training teaches a transformer two things at once: where to look in the context, and what global "knowledge" to apply to what it finds. To study this, the authors define the Sparse Contextual Bigram (SCB). The last token k selects a sparse distribution q^(k) over at most Q of the T earlier positions. One position is sampled from that distribution, and a fixed Markov transition P is applied to the token there. A one-layer linear transformer, F = V X a^(x_{T+1}), represents this exactly with A = Q and V = P.

The central finding is about cost, not about whether learning succeeds. Training from scratch begins with a "cold start" that needs poly(T) samples, because at a uniform initialization the useful gradient signal is only about 1/T. Once the correlation with the target is nontrivial, learning needs only poly(N, Q, log T) samples. A pretrained V that is only weakly correlated with the new task lets training skip the expensive phase.

Critique. The paper has two real strengths. It tracks finite-sample, SGD-style dynamics rather than only the population loss. It also explains clearly why the initial signal is about 1/T, and why ℓ1-proximal steps help: gradient noise is large in ℓ2 (it grows with T) but controllable in ℓ∞.

The model, however, is very stylized. Attention depends only on position and the last token, so A is effectively a T×N lookup table with no content-based matching. That makes it not an induction head, and the task is close to a structured bilinear regression. Context tokens are i.i.d. from μ, so the "language" has no sequential dependence. The authors leave that extension open.

The algorithm is also heavily engineered:

  • It needs to know μ and several norms of P and Q.
  • It uses 1/μ preconditioning and affine projections.
  • It runs three stages with hand-tuned thresholds.
  • It freezes A in Stage 3 to get around a slow α_A − α_V mode.

Assumption T ≥ (NQ)^10 is extreme. That poly(T) samples are necessary in Stage 1 is only a conjecture, and the Stage 1 batch bound, Õ(T²Q⁴N⁵/min{K_P³, K_Q³}), is loose.

The empirical side is thin. The experiments are small (N=3, Q=2, T=5000) and compare only against untuned plain SGD. The link to softmax attention is argued heuristically for N=1, with a single figure.

Finally, the transfer result is narrower than its title suggests. Only V is transferred, and A is reset to uniform. What transfers is global knowledge, not attention structure.

Broader context. A growing body of theory asks how transformers learn in-context mechanisms under gradient descent. Examples include in-context linear regression with linear attention (Zhang, Frei & Bartlett 2023) and induction heads (Olsson et al. 2022). "Birth of a Transformer" (Bietti et al. 2023) views induction heads as associative memories. Nichani, Damian & Lee (2024) prove that two-layer transformers learn causal-graph structure, and Edelman et al. (2024) document multi-phase dynamics on in-context Markov chains. SCB adds a global transition matrix to this picture. Its analysis of escaping the uniform initialization echoes information-exponent and saddle-escape results for single-index models.

A natural follow-up would make the attention content-dependent, for example by determining q through matching x_{T+1} against the context, which gives a genuine induction-head SCB. One could then ask whether the poly(T) cold start survives, or prove an SQ lower bound that settles the conjecture.

There is also a modest link to IR. SCB is a toy retrieve-then-generate process: a sparse, query-dependent "retrieval" over positions, followed by a global generative map. Its lesson is that sparse selection (ℓ1 thresholding) removes a variance cost that grows with context length. This suggests a sample-complexity analysis of generative retrieval in which corpus size plays the role of T.

Proof sketch. Claims. Theorem 3.1 (formal version: G.1) rests on Assumption 2.1:

  • the q^(k) are Q-sparse, with entries in [1/(CQ), C/Q];
  • μ is well-conditioned;
  • P is nontrivial: ‖P‖²_μ − ‖μ‖² ≥ ‖μ‖².

Under these conditions, Algorithm 1 reaches ‖A − Q‖²_μ, ‖V − P‖²_μ ≤ ε in poly(N, Q, 1/ε, log T) steps, with probability at least 1 − δ. It uses poly(T) samples before time T₁ and poly(N, Q, 1/ε, log T) samples after it.

Theorem 4.1 (formal version: H.3) covers transfer. Suppose P̂ shares μ with P, ‖P̂‖²_μ = Θ(‖P‖²_μ), and ⟨P̂, P⟩_μ − ‖μ‖² ≥ ‖μ‖². Initialize V = θP̂ + (1−θ)μ1ᵀ. Then one A-step followed by Stages 2–3 recovers (P, Q) with poly(N, Q, 1/ε, log T) samples.

How. The key structural fact (Lemma C.2 onward) is that the population dynamics stay on the line through the initialization and the ground truth: V = α_V P + (1−α_V)μ1ᵀ, and similarly for A. This reduces everything to a 2-D system:

  • α_V grows by ηK_Q(1−α_Aα_V)α_A, plus a drift of about η/T;
  • α_A grows by ηK_P(1−α_Vα_A)α_V.

The mini-batch process is then split into this population projection plus orthogonal errors Δ_V and Δ_A. Those error recursions are contracting (Lemma C.6), so errors do not compound exponentially. Each stage then has its own argument:

  • Stage 1 (Lemma D.1). The 1/T drift seeds the signal, and the off-diagonal linear term amplifies it exponentially, reaching Θ(1/(QN)) in about log T/η steps. This works only if the noise is O(1/T), which is why the batches must have size poly(T).
  • Stage 2 (Lemmas E.1–E.4, E.10). On useful coordinates the expected gradient is Ω(α_V/Q), while on useless ones it is O(α_V a_t) (Eq. 10). The gradient coordinates are bounded, so ℓ∞ concentration with poly(N, Q) log T samples separates the two groups. Proximal soft-thresholding then zeroes the useless coordinates, and the dynamics track the population trajectory until (α_V + α_A)/2 ≈ 1.
  • Stage 3. A is rounded by normalization and frozen, and V is trained to accuracy ε.
  • Transfer (Lemmas H.1–H.2). The pretrained V gives α_V ≥ Θ(θ/(NK_P)) ≫ 1/T, so a single thresholded gradient step already gives α_A ≈ α_V. The large initial ‖Δ_V‖ enters only multiplied by the small α_A, so the Stage 2 analysis goes through.

title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
tags: Physics - Data Analysis, Statistics and Probability
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks

Bin Wang, W. Jeffrey Johnston, Stefano Fusi · 2025 · arXiv:2510.09816

Main idea. Neuroscience experiments keep finding "abstract" population codes. In these codes, each task variable (say, the parity and the magnitude of a digit) moves activity along its own fixed direction, whatever the other variables are. Johnston and Fusi had already shown empirically that networks trained on several binary classifications develop such codes. This paper asks whether that must happen.

The setting is a two-layer network trained with MSE loss and L2 weight decay. The data are balanced, and the d_Y binary labels are exactly the latent variables. The answer is yes, for two kinds of input: whitened inputs, and inputs that align more with the targets than with anything else. In both cases, every global minimum has a hidden kernel K* = b*(d_Y·11ᵀ + K_Y), which is the output kernel plus a constant shift. The class prototypes therefore sit on the corners of a hypercube, and the parallelism score (PS) is exactly 1.

This matters because a "tetrahedron" code with PS≈0 decodes the same labels just as well. High accuracy alone does not force abstraction. Weight decay combined with task structure does.

The most interesting part. The key move turns an optimization over weights into a convex problem over a distribution of neurons.

First, the ridge problems for W₂ and W₁ are solved in closed form. What remains is an energy over the hidden units' preactivation vectors h_k ∈ ℝᴾ, where P is the number of training stimuli: λ₁Σ h_kᵀK_X†h_k + λ₂·tr[(λ₂ + Σφ(h_k)φ(h_k)ᵀ)⁻¹K_Y]. This energy depends only on the input and output kernels, and it does not change when the neurons are permuted. It can therefore be written in terms of the empirical measure ρ = Σδ_{h_k}. Once ρ is relaxed to range over all positive measures, the energy is convex in ρ.

The KKT conditions then become a self-consistent mean-field problem. A single representative neuron minimizes an energy set by the population kernel K[ρ], and ρ can only put mass where that energy is minimal. By convexity, any KKT solution is a global minimum, even though the loss is non-convex in weight space. When the optimal ρ is a finite sum of point masses (Diracs), the result also holds exactly at finite width.

The resulting picture is striking. With ReLU, the optimal neurons lie on only 2d_Y rays, h ∝ 1 ± v_i, so each neuron fires for exactly one sign of one label. The weight matrices have rank d_Y+1, and all points within a class collapse onto one representation, a form of neural collapse.

Broader context. This paper belongs to the line of work that uses task-optimized networks as models of the brain. It links representational geometry to the ML debate on disentanglement. The PS metric comes from Bernardi et al. (Cell 2020). On the ML side, unsupervised disentanglement cannot be identified from data alone (Locatello et al., 2019), so some supervision or multi-task structure is needed.

The closest precursors are Johnston & Fusi (Nat. Commun. 2023), on abstraction from multi-task training, and Alleman, Lindsey & Fusi (2024), on how task structure and nonlinearity together shape the learned geometry. On the technical side, the measure-over-neurons view echoes Bach's convex neural networks (JMLR 2017) and the mean-field analysis of Chizat and Bach.

Two follow-ups suggest themselves. One is to let the labels be nonlinear functions of the latents (XOR-type tasks) and map where the hypercube kernel breaks down. The other is to follow how K[ρ] evolves under gradient flow, since the anisotropic case already shows stage-like transitions.

For IR, there is a modest but real link. The optimal hidden kernel simply inherits the target kernel, up to a shift and a per-axis rescaling (b*_i ∝ √d_i in the anisotropic case). In generative retrieval, an encoder is trained to emit structured binary or hierarchical semantic IDs. This framework could predict how the design of that ID codebook shapes the geometry of the encoder's embedding space.

Proof sketch. Claim (Sec. III): Assume ReLU, balanced classes, λ₁λ₂ small enough that b* > 0, and either whitened input (K_X = I + 11ᵀ) or target-aligned input (c₀ > c_Y ≥ c_j). Then all global minima share the kernel b*(d_Y11ᵀ + K_Y). In the whitened case with n=1, b* = √(λ₂(P+1)/(λ₁P(P+2))) − λ₂/P. The minimizers themselves are not unique, but the kernel is, and it is attainable once the width M ≥ 2d_Y.

Strategy. The proof has four steps. 1. Eliminate the weights and pass to the convex measure problem. Convexity follows from f''(t) = 2λ₂ tr[(·)⁻¹δK(·)⁻¹K_Y(·)⁻¹δK] ≥ 0. 2. Lower-bound the single-neuron energy. The central lemma (Eq. 20) is E(h;ρ) ≥ E_r(h₊;ρ), where h₊ is the positive part of h. It holds because K_X† = I − 11ᵀ/(P+1) has negative off-diagonal entries, so removing the negative part of h can only lower the quadratic term. This reduces the problem to a non-negative quadratic program, which is a copositivity test. 3. Solve that program in closed form. Copositivity is normally hard to check, but here the structure of K_Y makes it tractable: vᵢ·vⱼ = Pδᵢⱼ and 1·vᵢ = 0. 4. Conclude PS = 1. PS does not change when the kernel is shifted or scaled, so PS(K*) = PS(K_Y) = 1.

Other nonlinearities (Sec. IV). This section covers thresholded or odd activations whose slope φ₊(z)/z is non-increasing. The activation is replaced by φ^δ, which is linear on [0,δ], and a majorization argument gives the same bound with λ₁ rescaled to λ₁/B₀². Threshold activations again give a copositive program with the same kernel. Odd activations give a convex QP with kernel b*K_Y, and in that case the neurons show mixed selectivity. Because b* does not depend on δ, letting δ→0 recovers the original activation. However, the required width M > 2d_Y√b*/δ then grows without bound, so these results hold only as M→∞.

Caveats. For deep networks, the functional is no longer convex, and the abstract solution is shown only to be a strict local minimum. For RNNs, the evidence is numerical only. Nothing is proved about whether gradient descent actually reaches these minima, although simulations suggest that it does.

title: Large Stepsize Gradient Descent for Logistic Loss: Non-Monotonicity of the Loss Improves Optimization Efficiency
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Large Stepsize Gradient Descent for Logistic Loss: Non-Monotonicity of the Loss Improves Optimization Efficiency

Jingfeng Wu, Peter L. Bartlett, Matus Telgarsky, Bin Yu · 2024 (COLT) · arXiv:2402.15926

Main idea. Classical convex optimization fences constant-stepsize GD behind the descent lemma: for a β-smooth objective you take η < 2/β, the loss decreases at every step, and you get O(1/(ηt)). This paper asks what happens on the other side of that fence in the most canonical non-quadratic setting available — logistic regression on linearly separable data, where the infimum is at infinity and the smoothness along the trajectory is not a fixed constant but decays with the loss itself. With η far above 2/β the iterates do what Cohen et al. call edge-of-stability behavior: the loss bounces around, sometimes increasing, for a while. The finding is that this transient is short and cheap — GD leaves it after O(η + n) steps (up to logs) — and that the stable phase it lands in converges at Õ(1/(ηt)) with η appearing as a gain, not a constraint. Balancing the two phases by setting η := γ²T/120 for a T-step budget yields L(w_T) = Õ(1/T²): an accelerated rate from vanilla GD, no momentum, no scheduler, one constant stepsize. The complement is a lower bound: on an explicit two-point dataset, any run whose loss is monotone is stuck at Ω(1/T).

The most interesting part. The acceleration is not obtained in spite of the oscillation; it is obtained because of it. The lower bound (Theorem 3) is proved in two moves that make this precise: Lemma 14 shows that monotonicity at the very first step already forces η ≤ 2ln2/(rq), a constant, and Lemma 13 then shows any bounded-η run suffers L(w_t) ≥ 1/(c₀η e^{c₀η} t). So "well-behaved loss curve" is logically equivalent, here, to "stepsize capped by an instance constant" and hence to the slow rate. The oscillatory phase is the only way to buy a stepsize that scales with the budget. This inverts the usual reading of a jagged training curve as a tuning failure. The honesty caveat matters, though: the setting is a linear predictor, a separable dataset with margin γ and ‖x_i‖ ≤ 1, and a loss with an exponential tail. All three are load-bearing. With the unflattened exponential loss large-stepsize GD can oscillate catastrophically (Wu et al., 2023), which is why the paper flattens the negative branch to enforce Lipschitzness; with a flattened polynomial tail of degree a the rate degrades to O(T^{-3a/(2a+4)}). The nonlinear extension is NTK-regime only, and its width requirement is Ω(η²) — meaning that the very stepsizes that give acceleration are also the ones that would push a real network out of the lazy regime the proof needs. Read as deep-learning theory, this is a clean existence proof that unstable-phase-then-acceleration is a real mechanism, not evidence that it is the mechanism in neural nets.

Broader context. The separable-logistic setting is a testbed because its asymptotics are fully understood: GD diverges in norm but its direction converges to the ℓ₂ max-margin (hard-margin SVM) solution at a ln ln t / ln t rate (Soudry et al., 2018; Ji & Telgarsky, 2018), which is how a problem with no minimizer still yields a generalization story. Cohen et al. (2020) documented empirically that practical GD on nets sits at sharpness ≈ 2/η with a non-monotone loss, and a large theory literature has attacked this on toy landscapes (diagonal linear nets, matrix factorization, scalar networks). The closest predecessor is Wu, Braverman & Lee (2023), who proved convergence at arbitrary η for this exact problem but with constants exponential in η and a non-degeneracy assumption on support vectors; this paper removes the assumption and, more importantly, nails the η-dependence, which is exactly what converts "it converges" into "it accelerates." A second useful comparison is the Silver stepsize schedule of Altschuler & Parrilo (2023), which also buys acceleration via deliberately destabilizing steps, but through an intricate schedule for general smooth convex problems rather than a single constant stepsize exploiting separability. A natural follow-up: the paper explicitly leaves open the implicit bias at η = ω(1) relative to T — their own norm bound ‖w_t‖ = O(η) is too loose to certify any margin — so characterizing lim w_T/‖w_T‖ under η = Θ(T), and whether the accelerated iterate pays for its low loss with a worse margin, is a well-posed and clearly valuable question. Also open by their own conjecture: whether the n-dependence in the burn-in can be removed, which currently forces T ≥ Ω(n/γ²).

On the IR side I would not push a strong analogy, but one link is genuine rather than decorative: the flattened exponential loss with temperature a satisfies their assumptions with ρ(λ) = 1 + ln²(λ)/a², so temperature enters the burn-in length and the rate constants as 1/a² — the same temperature knob that sits in InfoNCE/contrastive retrieval objectives, which are exponentially-tailed margin losses on data that becomes separable in embedding space as training proceeds. That makes the phase structure here a plausible lens on why two-tower retrieval training tolerates (and often needs) aggressive learning rates with warmup. The disclaimers are equally genuine: the two-tower bilinear score is non-convex and cosine-normalized, negatives are sampled rather than fixed, and none of this analysis speaks to representation learning.

Proof sketch. Theorem 1 has three parts, all under Assumption 1 (‖x_i‖ ≤ 1, ⟨y_i x_i, w_⟩ ≥ γ for a unit w_) and w₀ = 0. (i) EoS phase: for every t, (1/t)Σ_{k<t} L(w_k) ≤ (1 + ln²(γ²ηt) + η²/4)/(γ²ηt) — an averaged bound valid at any η, carrying an additive η/(γ²t) penalty. (ii) Stable phase: if L(w_s) ≤ 1/η then L(w_t) is non-increasing from s on and L(w_t) ≤ (2F(w_s) + ln²(γ²η(t−s)))/(γ²η(t−s)), where F(w) := (1/n)Σexp(−y_i x_i^⊤w) is an exponential potential. (iii) Transition time: some s ≤ τ := (60/γ²)·max{η, n, e, ((η+n)/η)ln((η+n)/η)} satisfies both L(w_s) ≤ 1/η and F(w_s) ≤ 1. Corollary 2 plugs η = γ²T/120, verifies τ ≤ T/2, and gets L(w_T) ≤ 480 ln²(γ⁴T²)/(γ⁴T²). Note what is and is not delivered: this is a loss bound. The iterates are only known to satisfy ‖w_t‖ = O((ln(γ²ηt) + η)/γ), so no margin guarantee survives at η = Θ(T); generalization is instead routed through a VC/uniform-convergence bound (once L ≤ ℓ(0)/n every training point is classified correctly, giving Pr[error] ≤ 4(d ln(n+1) + ln(4/δ))/n).

The engine is a split comparator (Lemma 7). Write the standard one-step expansion ‖w_{t+1} − u‖² = ‖w_t − u‖² + 2η⟨∇L(w_t), u − w_t⟩ + η²‖∇L(w_t)‖² and decompose u = u₁ + u₂ with u₂ := (η/(2γ))·w_, i.e. a comparator component pointing along the max-margin direction whose _length grows with the stepsize_. The cross term then absorbs the quadratic term exactly: 2⟨∇L, u₂⟩ + η‖∇L‖² ≤ (−2γ‖u₂‖ + η)·(1/n)Σ|ℓ′| ≤ 0, using ⟨y_i x_i, w_⟩ ≥ γ, |ℓ′| ≤ 1 and ‖∇L‖ ≤ (1/n)Σ|ℓ′|. This is where the descent lemma is replaced: the η²‖∇L‖² term that normally forces η < 2/β is killed by the margin rather than by smallness of η, at the price of inflating ‖w₀ − u‖² by Θ(η²) — which is precisely the η²/4 in the EoS bound. Choosing u₁ := (ln(γ²ηt)/γ)w*, so that L(u₁) ≤ 1/(γ²ηt), and telescoping gives both the averaged risk and the O(η) norm bound.

The burn-in is bounded not through the loss but through a second, η-insensitive potential: the gradient potential G(w) := (1/n)Σ|ℓ′(x_i^⊤w)|. A Perceptron-style argument gives ⟨w_{t+1}, w_⟩ ≥ ⟨w_t, w_⟩ + γη G(w_t), so (1/t)ΣG(w_k) ≤ ‖w_t‖/(γηt) ≲ (ln(γ²ηt) + η)/(γ²ηt) ≈ 1/(γ²t) for large η. This is the crux of the O(η + n) rather than O(η²) transition time: the loss bound scales like η/(γ²t), but the gradient potential bound does not scale with η at all, so reaching G(w_s) ≤ min{1/(2η), 1/(2n)} costs only τ = O(max{η, n}/γ²) steps. The threshold on G is then converted into everything else pointwise: G(w_s) ≤ 1/(2n) forces 1/(n(1 + exp(x_i^⊤w_s))) ≤ 1/(2n) for each i, hence x_i^⊤w_s ≥ 0 for all i, hence F(w_s) ≤ 2G(w_s) ≤ min{1/η, 1/n}. So the warm start is handed to the stable phase as a bound on the exponential potential F, not on ‖w_s‖² — essential, since ‖w_s‖² can be Θ(η²) and would destroy the rate if it appeared in the usual quadratic comparator term.

Monotonicity in the stable phase comes from a self-stabilization fact rather than from global smoothness: because |ℓ″| ≤ ℓ and ‖x_i‖ ≤ 1, one has ∇²L ⪯ L·I, and therefore ln L is 1-smooth: ∇² ln L = (∇²L·L − (∇L)^{⊗2})/L² ⪯ I. Applying the descent lemma to ln L gives ln L(w_{t+1}) ≤ ln L(w_t) − η(1/L(w_t) − η/2)‖∇L(w_t)‖², so L decreases as soon as L(w_t) ≤ 2/η. The local sharpness is proportional to the loss, so the trajectory manufactures its own stability once the loss has dropped below the 2/η scale — the phase transition is a statement about the landscape flattening, not about the stepsize changing. Inside the stable phase the same expansion is rerun with u := w_s + (ln(γ²η(t−s))/γ)w_, now using the _self-bounding* property ‖∇L‖ ≤ L to convert η²‖∇L‖² ≤ η²L² ≤ ηL whenever L ≤ 1/η, so the quadratic term is dominated by the linear progress term; L(u) ≤ F(w_s)/(γ²η(t−s)) by factorizing the exponential, and monotonicity upgrades the resulting average to a last-iterate bound. The general-loss and NTK versions (Theorem 6) keep this skeleton with ρ(λ) := min_z λℓ(z) + z² — the squared length of the regularization path — replacing ln²(λ), Lipschitzness buying the EoS bound, self-boundedness the stable phase, and the exponential tail the O(η + n log n) burn-in that the Õ(1/T²) acceleration requires.

title: "On the goals of linguistic theory": Revisiting Chomskyan theories in the era of AI
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

"On the goals of linguistic theory": Revisiting Chomskyan theories in the era of AI

Eva Portelance, Masoud Jasbi · 2024 · arXiv:2411.10533

Main idea. Chomsky's 1960s framework grades a theory of a language on three cumulative levels. An observationally adequate grammar generates all and only the sentences of the language — it matches external behaviour. A descriptively adequate one also assigns each sentence the right structural description, capturing speakers' intuitions (their running example: "pancakes or bacon and eggs" is ambiguous, so a constituent-forming grammar is descriptively adequate where a string-concatenating finite-state one is not). An explanatorily adequate one further says why a learner landed on that grammar rather than another, given the data they got. The authors dress this up as a "cognitive duck test": behaves like a duck, is built like a duck, developed and evolved like a duck. They cross this with Chomsky's three procedure types — discovery (data → grammar), decision (data + grammar → yes/no), evaluation (data + candidate grammars → best one) — and note that theoretical linguistics has lived on evaluation procedures for sixty years because discovery seemed hopeless. Their verdict on modern models: LLMs are extraordinary discovery procedures that are stuck at observational adequacy, because we cannot reliably read a formal grammar out of their weights; so they cannot by themselves refute or confirm anything at the descriptive or explanatory level. The paper's actual pitch is a third option that gets little attention: neural grammar induction models (C-PCFG, L-PCFG and kin), which are also near-assumption-free discovery procedures but emit an explicit generative grammar, and so can in principle be judged descriptively and even explanatorily adequate — and extended to multimodal input. They also push back on a common anti-LLM move: the "colorless green ideas" argument kills n-grams but not distributed models, which can in principle separate grammaticality from likelihood.

Critique. As a position paper it is clarifying and unusually fair-minded, and the adequacy-times-procedure grid is a genuinely useful map of where different research programs sit. But it equivocates at the load-bearing joints. The phrase "in principle" is doing enormous work: LLMs could reach descriptive adequacy if interpretability matured, UG could be tested if discovery procedures worked — yet Piantadosi's symmetric promissory note is dismissed in one sentence as "not directly comparable." The Marr mapping is loose: Marr's computational level is about the goal and rationale of a computation, not input–output mimicry, so equating it with observational adequacy flattens exactly the distinction the paper needs. The claim that grammar induction models assume almost nothing understates Chomsky normal form, which builds in binary branching — and the paper then lists "are languages binary branching?" as a question these models could answer. Nor does it confront how induced constituents get adjudicated against linguists' analyses; in practice such models are scored against treebank annotations that already presuppose a theory. Most conspicuously for a 2024 paper, it never engages the empirical work that bears directly on its central question — whether an LM's inductive bias could substitute for UG — such as Kallini et al.'s Mission: Impossible Language Models or child-scale training results on hierarchical generalization. And it names but does not resolve the deepest issue: whether behavioural match tells us anything about mechanism. The authors concede the duck test "is not a valid form of reasoning," then build on it anyway.

Broader context. The Chomskyan program separates competence (tacit knowledge of grammar) from performance (noisy actual use), holds that children converge on rich grammars from impoverished input (the poverty of the stimulus), and infers an innate Universal Grammar restricting the hypothesis space — motivated formally by Gold's 1967 result that positive evidence alone does not suffice even for regular languages. The live fight is Piantadosi's "Modern language models refute Chomsky's approach to language" (2023), Katzir's reply that LLMs are not cognitive models because they also learn languages humans cannot, and Chomsky/Roberts/Watumull's NYT op-ed. This paper is essentially a reconciliation attempt from inside the generative camp. An obvious follow-up: run a neural grammar induction model as a genuine discovery procedure on child-scale CHILDES input and test the induced grammar for the classic poverty-of-stimulus generalizations — that would put a legible, falsifiable grammar where LLM probing currently gives only correlations.

There is one honest transfer beyond linguistics: the observational/descriptive/explanatory ladder is a clean vocabulary for what counts as an explanation of any trained system. Benchmark-matching is observational; mechanistic interpretability aims at descriptive; inductive-bias and learning-theoretic accounts aim at explanatory. And the grammar-induction bet — make the model's hypothesis a symbolic object so it can be inspected rather than probed for — is structurally the same bet as interpretable-by-construction architectures. Beyond that, treat it as broadening reading rather than something with an IR hook.

title: Making Text Embedders Few-Shot Learners
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Making Text Embedders Few-Shot Learners

Chaofan Li, MingHao Qin, Shitao Xiao, Jianlyu Chen, Kun Luo, Yingxia Shao et al. (BAAI) · 2024 · arXiv:2409.15700

Main idea. The paper takes the instruction-prefix trick of E5-mistral one step further: instead of prepending only a task description to the query, it prepends k fully worked <Instruct>/<query>/<response> demonstrations, encodes the whole thing with a causal Mistral-7B, and takes the final [EOS] hidden state as the query vector. Documents are encoded plain, with no prompt at all. The non-obvious contribution is not the template but the training recipe that makes it work — GritLM had already observed that dropping few-shot examples into an embedder at inference hurts. Here the number of demonstrations is sampled per step from 0 to 5, and crucially the demonstrations are drawn from in-batch pairs rather than a fixed per-task set. Fixed examples give few-shot gains but destroy zero-shot behaviour (64.83 → 61.50 MTEB); in-batch sampling preserves zero-shot (64.67) while few-shot reaches 66.08. The second claim is negative and deliberately deflationary: across a causal/bidirectional × last-token/mean grid, the unmodified causal + last-token configuration wins, so "simplicity is best."

Critique. The headline SOTA is not where the science is. On the full-data model, few-shot buys +0.43 MTEB over its own zero-shot and +0.48 over the previous leader — differences indistinguishable from seed and probe noise, especially given that the "full data" mix trains directly on Emotion, Banking77, AmazonReviews, ToxicConversations, the Arxiv/Reddit/StackExchange clustering sets and STS12/22/B, i.e. the training splits of the very MTEB tasks being scored. The authors are commendably honest about this and report a public-data-only variant, and that variant is where the real signal lives: +1.25 average, but decomposed it is +3.94 clustering, +1.84 classification, +0.39 STS — and only +0.49 retrieval, with reranking actually dropping (56.85 → 56.67). For an IR audience the honest summary is that in-context demonstrations mainly resolve task ambiguity (what counts as a label or topic) rather than improving relevance modelling. AIR-Bench is the more convincing evidence, since it is held out and the public-data model beats the full-data one there — a clean demonstration of MTEB overfitting inside the paper's own results. The attention ablation does not settle the bidirectional debate: causal wins by 0.34 under ICL and loses (64.83 vs 64.96) without it, and the bidirectional arm simply flips the mask during contrastive fine-tuning, which is exactly the setup LLM2Vec argues is inadequate without its MNTP preconditioning stage. Reporting that causal + mean pooling "could not be trained effectively" under ICL, with no numbers, leaves a hole. The comparison to GritLM/LLM2Vec at equal data is also not equal recipe — bge-en-icl distills from a bge-reranker teacher on retrieval. Operationally, the cost is real and under-discussed: query inputs are budgeted at 2048 tokens against 512 for passages, so query-side encoding is roughly an order of magnitude more FLOPs per query than a standard bi-encoder, paid at every request rather than amortised at index time. And the demonstrations themselves are curated per task, pulled from training splits or, where unavailable, generated by ChatGPT — which in a live system means maintaining a demonstration store, invalidating query caches whenever it changes, and knowing the task identity before you retrieve, which is precisely the information a general search endpoint lacks.

Broader context. This is the ICL-shaped corner of the LLM-as-embedder line that runs E5-mistral → RepLLaMA/Llama2Vec → GritLM → NV-Embed → LLM2Vec, and it is the one paper in that group whose gain comes from the prompt rather than from architecture surgery (NV-Embed's latent attention layer, LLM2Vec's MNTP, GritLM's unified objective). Its most useful service is as a null result against that surgery. The obvious follow-up is suggested by the function-vector / task-vector literature on ICL (Hendel et al., Todd et al.): test whether concatenating demonstrations is, to first order, equivalent to adding a fixed per-task offset in some residual stream layer. If so, you distil each task's demonstrations into one cached vector, recover the accuracy at zero prompt cost, and the whole latency objection evaporates.

Theoretically the interesting move is that the encoder becomes a family of maps f_D(q) indexed by a demonstration set D, while the document map g(p) stays static. That asymmetry is what keeps a precomputed index legal at all, and it is worth stating as a design principle: task adaptivity is free exactly when it is confined to the query side. But it also relocates the bottleneck. A single d-dimensional document embedding must simultaneously support every task's relevance ordering, and no amount of query-side conditioning escapes that — the number of distinct orderings realisable over a fixed document matrix is governed by its rank / sign-rank, so d caps the task-adaptive capacity regardless of how expressive f_D is. A genuinely task-adaptive system would have to condition g as well, which means one index per task and the end of the single-corpus assumption; the interesting middle ground is low-rank per-task transforms applied at query time, which preserve the index but trade capacity explicitly. There is a second, more practical geometric worry the paper never tests: ANN structures are tuned to a query distribution — HNSW entry points, IVF centroid assignment, PQ/OPQ codebooks trained on corpus statistics. Prepending 2048 tokens of demonstrations moves query vectors into a task-dependent region that no longer matches the distribution the index was built for. All reported gains are exact-search gains, so it is entirely possible that ICL improves the true ranking while degrading approximate recall@k, task-dependently. Measuring the exact-vs-ANN gap as a function of demonstration count would be a cheap, publishable experiment, and it sits squarely in the gap between the embedding-model literature and the vector-search literature.

title: Quantifying Statistical Significance of Deep Nearest Neighbor Anomaly Detection via Selective Inference
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Quantifying Statistical Significance of Deep Nearest Neighbor Anomaly Detection via Selective Inference

Mizuki Niihori, Shuichi Nishino, Teruyuki Katsuoka, Tomohiro Shiraishi, Kouichi Taji, Ichiro Takeuchi · 2025 · arXiv:2502.12978

Main idea. Deep kNN anomaly detection flags a test instance when its distance to the k-th nearest normal training instance, measured in a pretrained CNN's latent space, exceeds a threshold. It works well and it is interpretable, but the score is just a number: there is no way to say how surprised we should be. The authors attach a p-value to it. Model each instance as signal plus isotropic Gaussian noise, X_i = s_i + ε_i, ε ~ N(0, σ²I), with the signals left entirely unrestricted (a genuinely semi-parametric setup — no assumption that normal data is a single Gaussian blob), and test H₀: s_test = s_o(k) against H₁: s_test ≠ s_o(k) using T = ½‖x_test − x_o(k)‖². The catch is that o(k) — which neighbor to compare against, whether this instance was flagged at all, even which k to use — is chosen from the same data. This is double-dipping: you pick the direction in data space that maximizes the apparent discrepancy, then ask how extreme that discrepancy is against an unconditional null. The naive tail probability is therefore not uniform under H₀ and Type-I error blows up; their Figure 2 shows naive rejection rates far above 0.05, and Figure 1 shows a normal Capsule patch getting naive p = 0.045 but selective p = 0.394. Selective inference (post-selection inference) fixes this by changing the question: instead of the marginal null distribution of T, use its distribution conditional on the event that this hypothesis was the one selected. Conditional validity then implies marginal validity by averaging over selection events.

Critique. The framing is right and the pipeline is carefully assembled — the selection event is decomposed into four pieces (the n−1 ordering inequalities fixing the k-th neighbor, the score-exceeds-θ event, the argmax-over-candidate-k event, and the CNN's activation polytopes), and the ablations honestly show that dropping either the kNN part or the DNN part breaks validity. The weaknesses are real, though. First, known-σ isotropic Gaussian noise on raw pixels is a strong assumption, and it sits awkwardly with the experimental protocol, which standardizes every feature to unit variance — a data-dependent transform that is not itself in the conditioning set and that does not preserve σ²I. The robustness study only perturbs the noise law by Wasserstein distance ≤ 0.04, a very gentle stress test. Second, the conditioning is heavy. Even with parametric programming un-conditioning along the line, they still condition on the full activation-region assignment for all n+1 instances, on the threshold event, and on the entire neighbor ordering; power is left on the table relative to less-conditioning or randomized-response schemes. Third, no runtime numbers appear anywhere, despite parametric programming being the computational contribution — the number of breakpoints along the line for a ResNet is precisely what a reader wants to know, and it is absent. Fourth, the baselines are soft: Bonferroni over C(n,k) hypotheses is astronomically conservative (its power is visibly ~0) and Hotelling's T² is set up to fail in the semi-parametric regime by construction. Fifth, the MVTec evaluation uses 10 of 15 classes "which seem to follow a normal distribution" — a selection the paper does not justify, which is slightly ironic in a paper about selection bias. Finally, the exposition has real inconsistencies: η_y is written as a vector in Eq. (11) yet the statistic is ‖η_yᵀY‖₂; the naive null is stated with (1+n)d degrees of freedom when the rank of the projection is d; and Appendix B.3 calls the conditional law a truncated Gaussian where Theorem 4.1 says truncated χ.

Broader context. Selective inference descends from Lee, Sun, Sun & Taylor's exact post-selection inference for the Lasso, whose polyhedral lemma is the template: if the selection event can be written as {Ay ≤ b} and the statistic is a linear contrast ηᵀy of a Gaussian vector, then conditioning on the event and on the nuisance component confines y to a line, the polyhedron cuts that line into an interval, and the conditional law of ηᵀy is a truncated Gaussian with closed-form tail. Everything since has been about extending "selection event = polyhedron" to procedures that are not the Lasso: marginal screening, stepwise selection, changepoint detection, and — closest to this paper — SI for hierarchical clustering (Gao, Bien & Witten) and k-means (Chen & Witten), which face the same "the hypothesis is a cluster the data chose" problem. Takeuchi's group has been systematically pushing this into deep learning: valid p-values for CNN image segmentation, for CAM saliency maps, for ViT attention maps, and the si4onnx package that mechanizes the polytope extraction. On the AD side, deep kNN (Bergman, Cohen & Hoshen) is the ancestor of the patch-memory-bank family — PatchCore and relatives — which is still state of the art on MVTec, so a significance test for deep kNN is aimed at a live method, not a toy. A natural follow-up: replace the single k-th-neighbor null with a max-statistic over all k neighbors, and swap known-σ Gaussianity for a randomized-response or bootstrap-calibrated variant, which would also buy back power by conditioning on less.

The retrieval hook is the genuinely interesting one. Every ANN search is a selection procedure, and the top-1 similarity score is the maximum of N correlated scores — a winner's-curse statistic whose naive significance is exactly as inflated as the naive p-values here. Ask "is this retrieved neighbor really relevant, or an artifact of maximizing over a corpus of ten million?" and you are asking for a selective p-value conditional on {argmax_j ⟨q, v_j⟩ = ĵ}. That event is a polytope in the query embedding: ⟨q, v_ĵ − v_j⟩ ≥ 0 for all j, i.e. a cell of the power diagram induced by the corpus, so Lee–Taylor applies essentially verbatim once you model the query embedding as noisy (from paraphrase perturbation, dropout, or an explicit encoder noise model). Better, the index is also a selection event with linear structure: IVF probe lists are argmins over centroids, PQ codeword assignment is a Voronoi cell, and both are intersections of half-spaces in embedding space — so one could state guarantees that are valid conditional on what the approximate index actually did, a far more honest formulation than pretending ANN recall errors are negligible. Concretely, this would give calibrated abstention for RAG: a p-value for "the corpus contains nothing genuinely relevant to this query," instead of a cosine threshold tuned by eyeball. The obstacle is the one the paper names in its own limitations — Transformer encoders are not piecewise linear (softmax, LayerNorm, GELU), so the tractable polytope characterization stops at the encoder boundary. The workable near-term version conditions on a frozen embedding and treats only the retrieval/index stage as the selection procedure. Generative retrieval is a further step out: beam search over docid tokens is a sequence of argmaxes, a discrete selection event better handled by the dynamic-programming enumeration used for optimal-changepoint SI than by parametric programming over a line.

Proof sketch. The claim is exact conditional Type-I error control: P_{H₀}(p_selective ≤ α) = α for every α ∈ (0,1) — not an upper bound, an equality — which follows from the selective p-value being exactly uniform given the selection event. It rests on (i) Gaussian noise with known covariance σ²I, (ii) the test statistic being the norm of a fixed linear contrast once the selection is conditioned upon, and (iii) the selection event being exactly characterizable. The mechanism: write y = vec(x_test, x_1, …, x_n), let P = η_y η_yᵀ be the projection onto the contrast direction, and condition additionally on the nuisance statistic ((I − P)Y, PY/‖PY‖). That conditioning collapses the whole data space onto a one-dimensional slice, Y = a + bz; the direction b is fixed, so the only freedom left is the scalar z. All that remains is to determine Z = {z : E_{a+bz} = E_y}, the set of z for which the pipeline would have made the same selection. The key move is that every component of the pipeline is piecewise linear in the data: convolution, ReLU, max-pooling and up-sampling compose to a function that is affine on each cell of a polyhedral partition, so within a cell the latent distances become explicit quadratics in z, and the neighbor-ordering, threshold and argmax-over-k conditions become finite systems of linear or quadratic inequalities in z. Each such system solves to a finite union of intervals, so Z is a finite union of intervals on the line. The parametric-programming/homotopy technique then sweeps z from one end of the line to the other, recomputing the activation pattern and the kNN ordering only at the breakpoints and unioning every interval that reproduces the observed selection — this is what un-conditions away the activation pattern rather than freezing it, and their w/o-pp ablation (which forces Z to be a single interval) shows the resulting power gain is substantial. Conditioned on all of this, the statistic follows a truncated χ distribution with truncation set Z; the p-value is its tail probability, uniform by the probability integral transform, and marginal validity follows by integrating over the nuisance and summing over selection events. The tractability trick worth naming is the combination of over-condition then un-condition along the line: over-condition on the CNN's activation region to make the network affine and the event polyhedral, then use parametric programming to recover the union of all such regions intersecting the 1-D slice, restoring most of the power the over-conditioning cost.

title: An Analysis of Tokenization: Transformers under Markov Data
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

An Analysis of Tokenization: Transformers under Markov Data

Nived Rajaraman, Jiantao Jiao, Kannan Ramchandran · 2024 (NeurIPS) · OpenReview · arXiv:2404.08335

Main idea. The paper takes an empirical pathology — transformers trained on $k$-th order switching Markov chains with $k \ge 2$ stall for a very long time at the stationary unigram model, essentially ignoring context — and asks what tokenization does about it. The surprising empirical observation is that a BPE tokenizer with a ten-token dictionary lets a 70× smaller transformer reach the optimal cross-entropy quickly, and yet probing the model (their Figure 4) shows it is still predicting an essentially context-independent distribution over tokens. So tokenization does not teach the transformer to model dependence; it relocates the dependence into the token boundaries, where a unigram model can absorb it. The theory then makes this precise: design the tokenizer so that the best unigram model over its tokens is near-optimal end-to-end, and quantify how large a dictionary that costs for LZW and for a sample-split variant of BPE.

The most interesting part. The framing inverts the usual story. Tokenization is normally justified as compression or as semantic chunking; here it is justified as a way of making a deliberately impoverished model class — i.i.d. over tokens — sufficient. The counterintuitive consequence is that the right intrinsic objective for a tokenizer is not "compress the training corpus" but "on fresh strings, emit tokens that are individually improbable under the source." Appendix D drives the distinction home with a dictionary that compresses its own training set into a single token — maximal training-set compression — while behaving like a character tokenizer on new draws, so the end-to-end loss is $H(\pi)$, the worst case. Appendix E adds that generalization is a property of the (dictionary, encoder) pair: one dictionary achieves $1.273 H_\infty$ under the minimum-length encoder and $\ge H(\pi)/3$ under the greedy encoder. The honest limitation is that the transformer never appears in the theory. All theorems bound $\min_{Q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\text{1-gram}}} L(Q \circ \mathrm{enc})$, the best achievable unigram loss; that a transformer trained by SGD finds it, and that character-level training gets stuck, remain empirical. The argument is thus "tokenization makes the easy hypothesis class adequate," not "tokenization fixes the optimization landscape," and the paper's own figures show the character model does eventually escape given enough iterations.

Broader context. The relevant lineage is the recent work on transformers over Markov sources: Makkuva et al. (2024) prove that for first-order switching chains the population loss landscape has a genuine bad local minimum at the stationary unigram model, and observe that shrinking the context window is the only hyperparameter that rescues higher-order cases; Edelman et al. (2024) trace the trajectory and attribute the delay to simplicity bias (in-context unigrams before bigrams); Nichani et al. (2024) show gradient descent forming induction heads for in-context bigram counting. On the tokenizer side, Zouhar et al. (2023b) recast BPE as a greedy approximation algorithm for shortest-encoding of the training set, and Zouhar et al. (2023a) propose Rényi efficiency as an intrinsic metric; this paper's contribution is precisely to supply the missing generalization axis. A natural follow-up: drop the complete-connectivity assumption (their Conjecture 1 proposes replacing $\log(1/\delta)$ by $\log(mH(\pi)/H_\infty)$), or move to variable-order/context-tree sources, where the "right" dictionary should be the context tree itself and the analysis would connect to CTW-style universal coding. A second: trade dictionary size against model order, characterizing the frontier where an $n$-gram model over a size-$d$ dictionary matches the source — their Appendix C already exhibits an optimal $d^\star$ balancing the $\varepsilon(d)$ bias against $\tilde O(d^{1.01}/\delta\xi^2)$ samples for learning the unigram model itself. For generative retrieval the transfer is direct rather than decorative: docid tokenization (semantic docids in DSI/NCI, residual-quantization codebooks in RIPOR/TIGER) is exactly the problem of choosing a dictionary so that a weak autoregressive model over the induced token sequence matches the corpus distribution, and $H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}, P)$ is a training-free criterion for scoring a candidate codebook. The Appendix D pathology is the codebook-overfitting failure mode, and the "heavy-hitting cut of the trie" picture is literally the prefix tree used for constrained decoding.

Proof sketch. The baseline is Theorem 2.1: the unconstrained optimum is $H(P)$, while any unigram model over characters suffers $\ge mH(\pi)$, and the ratio $mH(\pi)/H(P)$ diverges for the switching chain with $p = q = 1 - \delta$ (rate $H_{\mathrm{Ber}}(\delta)$ versus $\log 2$). A toy tokenizer holding all length-$r$ strings gives $L \approx H(P)(1 - 1/\log_2 d) + mH(\pi)/\log_2 d$, so a factor-2 approximation needs $d = e^{mH(\pi)/H(P)} \approx e^{(1/\delta)\log(1/\delta)}$ — the point being that a learned dictionary should do exponentially better.

The engine is Theorem 4.3, a reduction with one clean quantity: $H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}, P) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}}[\log(1/P(t))]$, where $Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ is the limiting token frequency when a fresh string is greedily encoded and $P(t) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}[P(t\,|\,a)]$. Under Assumption 4.2 (ergodic chain with $\min_{a,a'} P(a'|a) = \delta > 0$, hence also $\max P(a'|a) \le 1-\delta$), if $H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}, P) \ge \varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)$ then $\min_{Q} L(Q \circ \mathrm{enc}_{\mathrm{gre}}) \le H_\infty/(1-\varepsilon)$. The trick is that the same product appears on both sides. Chain-rule-factorize $P(s)$ along the greedy parse, replace conditioning on the previous token by the stationary marginal at a cost of one factor $\delta$ per token (using $\delta \min_a P(t|a) \le \max_a P(t|a)$), and apply Shannon–McMillan–Breiman: $\lim_m \frac{|\mathrm{enc}(s)|}{m}\big(H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}},P) - \log(1/\delta)\big) \le H_\infty$, which upper-bounds the token rate. Then evaluate the plug-in unigram model $Q(t) = P(t)$, whose loss is exactly (tokens per character) × $H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}, P)$. The mixing constant enters only as the additive slack $\log(1/\delta)$, so the approximation factor is $1/(1 - \log(1/\delta)/H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}},P))$. The supporting Lemma A.4 is the renewal-type ingredient: the greedy parse of a Markov source is itself Markov at the level of blocks of $\ell_{\max}$ tokens (the only dependence on history is the constraint $t_j \cdots t_i t \notin \mathrm{Dict}$, vacuous beyond $\ell_{\max}$ steps), so Krylov–Bogolyubov/Cesàro averaging gives almost-sure convergence of empirical token frequencies, and Dominated Convergence transfers it into the expectation.

What remains is lower-bounding $H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}, P)$ for a real tokenizer, via the "$\beta$-heavy-hitting" property: every maximal token (a token that is not a strict prefix of another, i.e. one the greedy encoder can actually emit mid-string) satisfies $\max_a P(t|a) \le d^{-\beta}$, which immediately yields $H(Q_{\mathrm{MLE}}, P) \ge \beta \log d$. Geometrically this says the cut the encoder induces on the infinite suffix trie is uniformly deep. For LZW (Theorem 4.5) one shows the dictionary contains every substring in $M_\beta = {t : \max_a P(t|a) \ge \delta/d^\beta}$, so every maximal token sits on that set's boundary. The argument is a Poissonized sampling view of the digital search tree LZW builds: generate $d^\star = d/\ell_{\max}$ independent trajectories, note $t$ becomes a token once it is visited $|t|$ times, cap $|M_\beta|$ using $|t| \le \delta^{-1}(\beta \log d + \log(1/\delta))$, cap the longest token at $4\log(d|A|)/\delta$ via the binomial bound $\binom{d}{s}(1-\delta)^{s(s-1)/2}$, and union-bound binomial tails. Choosing $\beta = 0.99$ gives $\varepsilon = \log(1/\delta)/(0.99\log d)$ with probability $1 - d^{-\Omega_\delta(\log d)}$, from $\tilde O_\delta(d)$ characters of training data: a factor-2 guarantee at $d \approx 1/\delta^2$ rather than $e^{(1/\delta)\log(1/\delta)}$.

Two caveats on the BPE side. Vanilla BPE is not covered, and deliberately so: the paper exhibits a training string $(01)^{1/\delta}(10)^{1/\delta}$ repeated, typical for the order-2 switching source, on which BPE's merge order produces a dictionary that reverts to character-level behavior on a constant fraction of a fresh sample, forcing $\Omega(m)$ loss by AM-GM. The theorem (4.7/B.1) therefore covers a sample-splitting variant: $\Theta(d^2)$ characters split into $d$ chunks, at most one merge learned per chunk, and the encoder chosen by dictionary size. The guarantee is correspondingly weaker: $(2 + \varepsilon)H_\infty + \epsilon$ with $\varepsilon = O(\log(1/\epsilon)\log^3(1/\delta)/(\epsilon\delta^9\log d))$ — the $\delta^{-9}$ is not cosmetic, and the factor 2 is not removed. Finally, note what none of this gives: the bounds are multiplicative in $H_\infty$ (never additively tight), require $\log d \gg \log(1/\delta)$ to be non-vacuous, assume an everywhere-positive kernel that real language emphatically violates, and are statements about the optimal unigram model — Theorem C.1 patches in the finite-sample cost of learning that model with a Laplace estimator, but not for a transformer trained by gradient descent.

title: Memory Limitations of Prompt Tuning in Transformers
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-16

Memory Limitations of Prompt Tuning in Transformers

Maxime Meyer, Mario Michelessa, Caroline Chaux, Vincent Y. F. Tan · 2025 · arXiv:2509.00421

Main idea. Existing prompt-tuning theory is all universality: for some specially built transformer, a soft prefix can approximate any Lipschitz map. This paper flips the quantifier and asks what an arbitrary, fixed transformer can be made to do by optimizing a prefix. The answer is framed as a capacity question. Fix τ, embeddings bounded by radius r, and inputs X¹,…,X^k; how many target outputs Y¹,…,Y^k can be simultaneously hit to accuracy ε by some pre-prompt P? The authors treat prompt tuning as a communication channel whose "bandwidth" is the metric entropy of the prompt space divided by the Lipschitz modulus of τ, and conclude two things: the number of memorizable input/output pairs grows at most like m_p/m (linearly in prompt length), and — in the mean-field limit where the prompt is an arbitrarily long token cloud — the accessible set saturates, so there is a finite ceiling on memorized information regardless of context length. A separate single-layer analysis shows the prompt can only steer the last token's representation inside an h-dimensional subspace.

Proof sketch. Everything is a covering/packing (Fano-style) counting argument, with almost no transformer-specific content beyond a Lipschitz bound. Theorem 4.7: pack the output ball B^{dmk}(0,r) with (r/3ε)^{dmk} points that are 3ε-separated (this is C_out). Cover the prompt ball B^{dm_p}(0,r) by (3Lr/ε)^{dm_p} balls of radius ε/L (this is C_in); by L-Lipschitzness, two prompts in the same cell produce outputs within ε, so two 3ε-separated targets cannot both be ε-accessible from one cell. Hence at most C_in targets are reachable, and once mk > m_p·log(3Lr/ε)/log(r/3ε) the accessible fraction is C_in/C_out, exponentially small in k. Theorem 4.10 runs the identical argument in Wasserstein space on empirical measures M(X), using two facts: (i) Castin–Ablin–Peyré / Geshkovski give a mean-field Lipschitz constant ‖W_v‖(1+3‖A‖r²)exp(2‖A‖r²) that is uniform in token count — this is the load-bearing step, since the finite-token bound degrades like √n; (ii) P_c(B^d(0,r)) is compact, with log N(G,W_q,ε) ≍ (Lr/ε)^d log(1+(Lr/ε)^q) above and, via Frostman's lemma and Kloeckner's critical parameter, ≳ exp(1/ε^d) below. A totally bounded prompt space pushed through a uniformly Lipschitz map has a finite ε-covering number, so capacity is bounded independently of m_p. Section 5 is the one genuinely architectural piece: since the softmax denominator splits over the concatenation, Att(x₀,[P,x^i]) = λ_i·Att(x₀,x^i) + μ_i·Att(x₀,P), a convex combination. Per head the prefix can only translate the final token along the single direction Att^k(x₀,P), gated by an input-dependent scalar; an induction eliminates (a₀^P)^k across h+1 mutually orthogonal targets and a scalar product with the last one yields a contradiction. Theorem 5.8 relaxes this to ε-approximation, using invertibility of the residual MLP (Behrmann et al.) when ‖W₁‖‖W₂‖<1.

Critique. The mean-field saturation result is the real contribution and the compactness argument is elegant. But the headline overstates it in three ways. First, nothing here is about transformers: any L-Lipschitz parameterized family with a totally bounded parameter set obeys the same bound — LoRA, adapters, anything. Attention enters only through the constant L. Second, the bound is worst-case over an isotropic ball, and "exponentially small volume fraction" is a quantitative refinement of the trivial dimension count dm_p < dmk; real targets live on a low-entropy embedding manifold, so a volume-fraction statement under Lebesgue measure says little about whether the datasets one cares about are accessible. Third, and most damaging, the thresholds are numerically vacuous: Theorem 4.10 bites only for k ≳ (2Lr)^d·log(4Lr/ε), and with d=768 and L exponential in ‖A‖r² this is astronomically beyond any dataset — ironic given the paper mocks Hu et al.'s 10^640 construction on exactly these grounds. There is no matching lower bound anywhere: only upper bounds, so the theory cannot distinguish a pretrained LLM from a random one, and the claimed "optimality" of encoding data as input/output pairs is asserted, not proved (it presupposes τ does in-context retrieval perfectly). Note also that L grows with depth, so the result is fully compatible with capacity scaling up with model size. Missing: LayerNorm (which projects to a sphere and changes the geometry), RoPE (the "positional encodings absorb into the input" remark is fine for additive, glib for rotary), and any experiment. Calling this "the first formal proof" of long-context degradation is a stretch — lost-in-the-middle is about a fixed model retrieving from natural text, not about the volume of arbitrary achievable output tuples under an optimal soft prefix. The Section 5 statements are also sloppy: E is called an "R-vector space" of dimension (d−h²−h)!/(d−h²−2h−1)! ≈ d^{h+1}, which exceeds d and is really a Stiefel-type manifold count, not a subspace dimension; index ranges slip between [h] and [h+1]; Theorem 5.8's displayed inequality drops the "−y_i". And ‖W₁‖‖W₂‖<1, sold as mild, is what makes the residual MLP invertible and near-non-expansive — that is a structural assumption, not a triviality.

Broader context. Memorization capacity theory asks how many arbitrary labeled points a network of given size can interpolate; the classical line (Baum; Yun et al.; Vardi–Yehudai–Shamir showing Õ(√N) parameters suffice for N points) has a transformer analogue in Kim et al., Mahdavi et al. ("Memorization capacity of multi-head attention"), and Kajitsuka & Sato, who push it to one layer. Prompt-tuning theory is younger and splits into universality (Wang, Chauhan, Wang & Hsieh, NeurIPS 2023, whose single-layer limitation result this paper strictly generalizes by discarding the full-rank assumptions) and capability separation — most notably Petrov et al., When do prompting and prefix-tuning work? A theory of capabilities and limitations (ICLR 2024), which argues prefixes can only bias attention toward behaviors already latent in the pretrained model rather than install new ones. That is arguably the sharper mechanistic statement; the present paper is the information-theoretic counterpart. The obvious follow-up is to replace the global worst-case Lipschitz constant with a data-dependent local one measured on the actual embedding manifold, and to convert the covering count into an honest mutual-information bound I(targets; prompt) ≤ log N(prompt space, ε/L) in bits — then compare against empirically measured bits-per-prompt-token on long-context benchmarks. A non-vacuous version of that would be genuinely useful. Second follow-up: a matching achievability result under structural hypotheses (induction heads, say), turning an upper bound into a capacity characterization.

There is a real IR connection here, not a forced one. The question "how many (query, answer) pairs can a length-m_p prefix make recoverable" is exactly the long-context-as-index versus external-index question underlying the RAG-vs-long-context debate: if prompt capacity saturates at O(dm_p log(Lr/ε)) nats independent of nominal window, stuffing the corpus into context is not a substitute for an index. The machinery is also the same metric-entropy counting used for embedding-capacity lower bounds in retrieval — cf. Weller et al., On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval (2025), which bounds representable top-k sets via sign-rank. And generative retrieval is the dual case: docid maps memorized in weights rather than in a prefix, where the identical question — how many documents can a model of given size index at resolution ε — is the one people actually care about.

title: Subspace Optimization for Large Language Models with Convergence Guarantees
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-15

Subspace Optimization for Large Language Models with Convergence Guarantees

Yutong He, Pengrui Li, Yipeng Hu, Chuyan Chen, Kun Yuan — 2024. arXiv:2410.11289

Main idea

In full-parameter LLM training the dominant memory cost is not the weights but the optimizer state: AdamW keeps first and second moments at parameter size, so for LLaMA-7B roughly 42 of 58 GB goes to optimizer state plus gradients. GaLore attacks this by keeping weights and backprop full-rank but storing the optimizer state only inside a rank-$r$ subspace: at each layer it takes the SVD of the stochastic gradient $G_\ell$, sets $P_\ell = U[:,:r_\ell]$, runs Adam/MSGD on $P_\ell^\top G_\ell$, and lifts back. The subspace is recomputed every $\tau$ steps, so the accumulated weight update is still high-rank.

The paper's central claim is a negative one: GaLore as originally analyzed does not converge under the standard triple of assumptions (lower boundedness, $L$-smoothness, unbiased gradients with bounded variance). The mechanism is a signal/noise inversion. The stochastic gradient is true gradient plus noise; early in training the top-$r$ singular subspace tracks the signal, but near a stationary point the signal shrinks while the noise persists at scale $\sigma$, so the SVD returns a subspace spanned almost entirely by noise — and in the worst case exactly orthogonal to the gradient. They then show GaLore does converge under two extra conditions that both defeat the point: deterministic gradients ($O(1/T)$), or a mega-batch $B = \Theta(\sqrt{T})$ used only for the SVD step ($O(1/\sqrt{T})$). Their fix, GoLore, changes one line: draw $P_\ell$ uniformly (Haar) from the Stiefel manifold $\mathrm{St}_{m,r}$ instead of from the SVD. Everything else — periodic refresh, momentum projection across subspace switches, memory footprint — is unchanged.

The most interesting part

The counterexample is unusually strong, and the cleverness is that it kills GaLore for every rank $r<n$, every refresh period $\tau$, and every subspace optimizer $\rho$ with arbitrary hyperparameters, all at once. Take $f(X)=\tfrac{L}{2}\mathrm{tr}(X^\top pp^\top X)$ on $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ with $p=e_1$: a convex quadratic whose gradient $Lpp^\top X$ lives entirely in row 1. Inject noise $\xi\tilde\sigma QQ^\top$ with $\xi$ Rademacher and $Q$ having a zero first row and diagonal $\mathrm{diag}(1,\sqrt[4]{2},\dots,\sqrt[4]{n-1})$, so the noise occupies rows $2..n$ with singular values $\sqrt{i}\,\tilde\sigma$. Initialize with first row $\lambda p^\top$, $0<\lambda<\tilde\sigma/L$. Then the stochastic gradient is exactly diagonal with entries $(L\lambda, \xi\tilde\sigma,\sqrt2\xi\tilde\sigma,\dots)$, and since $L\lambda<\tilde\sigma$ the signal is the smallest singular value. Every top-$r$ subspace therefore has a zero first row, so $P\rho(P^\top G)$ has a zero first row, so $X^{(t)}[1,:]=\lambda p^\top$ for all $t$ and $|\nabla f|_F^2 \equiv L^2\lambda^2$. The bad coordinate is not merely slow — it is exactly invariant.

Critically: this is a measure-zero alignment, and note the construction requires $\lambda<\tilde\sigma/L$, so the non-convergence floor $\epsilon_0=L^2\lambda^2$ is itself $O(\sigma^2)$. This is a noise-floor bias, not blow-up; GaLore does not diverge, it stalls at a gradient norm of the order of the noise it cannot see past. Whether that matters in LLM training is exactly the open question the paper does not resolve. The fix is genuinely free — Haar sampling via Gaussian + orthonormalization is cheaper than an SVD and identical in memory — but the empirical story is weak. They never run pure GoLore: all experiments use GoLore@20% (GaLore for 80% of steps, GoLore for the last 20%), which is outside the theorem. Scale is LLaMA-60M pretraining for 10k steps, and 7B fine-tuning at batch size 1 (the regime most flattering to the noise argument); GLUE gains are 85.77 → 86.03 average against 86.15 full-parameter, with no seeds or variance. The guarantee is to a stationary point of the true full-parameter objective $f$, not a surrogate — good — but the constants carry $\delta^{-7/2}$ with $\delta=r/\min(m,n)$, so at $\delta=1/8$ the bound is inflated by $\sim10^3$ and says nothing about low-rank projection being close to free. GoLore is also proved only for MSGD with momentum projection, not AdamW (acknowledged).

Proof sketch

(a) Negative. As above: convex quadratic on $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, rank-one Hessian supported on row 1, additive Rademacher noise supported on rows $2..n$ with all singular values strictly exceeding the signal's. The mechanism is that the SVD projector's range is a deterministic function of the observed noisy gradient, and here that range never intersects the signal row; the invariant set ${X[1,:]=\lambda p^\top}$ is preserved by any update of the form $P\rho(P^\top G)$.

(b) Positive. Theorem 4: under Assumptions 1–3, with $\tau=\lceil 64/(3\delta\beta_1)\rceil$, $\beta_1=(1+\sqrt{\delta^{3/2}\sigma^2T/(L\Delta)})^{-1}$ and $\eta$ below four explicit thresholds, GoLore with MSGD + momentum projection satisfies $\frac1T\sum_t \mathbb{E}|\nabla f(x^{(t)})|_2^2 = O(L\Delta/(\delta^{5/2}T) + \sqrt{L\Delta\sigma^2/(\delta^{7/2}T)})$ — the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ for nonconvex MSGD, with $\delta$-dependent constants.

The KEY lemma is Lemma 5: for Haar $P\sim\mathcal{U}(\mathrm{St}_{m,r})$, $\mathbb{E}[PP^\top]=(r/m)I$ and $\mathbb{E}|PP^\top G-G|_F^2=(1-r/m)|G|_F^2$ _for every fixed $G$_. Compare Lemma 1, GaLore's analogue, which gives the same $(1-r/m)$ contraction only for the matrix whose SVD produced $P$ — i.e. for the noisy gradient, never for $\nabla f$ and never for a later iterate reusing a stale $P$. The authors note that GaLore's compressor is neither unbiased nor contractive precisely because projectors are reused; Haar sampling restores both and, crucially, makes $P$ independent of the gradient noise so the cross term splits cleanly.

The architecture is a descent-lemma/Lyapunov argument on the lifted momentum $\tilde{m}^{(t)}$. Lemma 4 gives $\sum_t|\nabla f|^2 \le 2\Delta/\eta + \sum_t|\tilde{m}^{(t)}-\nabla f(x^{(t)})|^2 - (1/\eta^2 - L/\eta)\sum_t|x^{(t+1)}-x^{(t)}|^2$. Lemma 10 then establishes a per-step contraction of the momentum error by factor $1-(1-\delta/4)\beta_1$, in three cases: $t=0$; $t\equiv 0 \pmod \tau$ (a subspace switch, where the stale momentum must be re-expressed in the new basis and picks up a misalignment term); and $t$ inside a period. Subspace drift is controlled by Lemma 2, a purely deterministic inequality $|\nabla f(x^{(t)})|^2 \le \frac2\tau\sum_{r<\tau}|\nabla f(x^{(t+r)})|^2 + (\tau-1)\sum_r|\nabla f(x^{(t+r+1)})-\nabla f(x^{(t+r)})|^2$, which converts "gradient at the moment the stale subspace was chosen" into the running average over the period plus consecutive increments; smoothness turns those increments into $L^2|x^{(t+1)}-x^{(t)}|^2$, which is exactly the negative term the descent lemma supplies. The four step-size conditions are calibrated so the aggregate displacement coefficient is nonnegative. Telescoping over $K$ periods leaves $(\delta/4 - 8/(3\tau\beta_1))\sum_t\mathbb{E}|\nabla f|^2 \le 2\Delta/\eta + 4K\tau\beta_1\sigma^2/3$, and $\tau \ge 64/(3\delta\beta_1)$ keeps the left coefficient $\ge \delta/8$; tuning $\beta_1$ balances the two terms.

Broader context

The distinction worth internalizing is LoRA vs. GaLore.
