LoRA reparameterizes $W = W_0 + BA$ and so constrains the weight update itself to rank $r$ — fine for fine-tuning, limiting for pretraining, where ReLoRA recovers high rank by periodically merging adapters. GaLore leaves the weights and the backward pass untouched and compresses only the optimizer state, which is where the memory actually is. Section 6 shows the two views coincide operationally: fixing $B=P$ in a LoRA layer and updating only $A$ is algebraically identical to GaLore's update, and that implementation is cheaper in FLOPs.

Two things to read alongside: FLORA (Hao et al., 2024), which already used i.i.d. Gaussian random projections as gradient compressors — GoLore differs only in drawing uniformly on the Stiefel manifold rather than $N(0,1/r)$ entries, so the honest framing is that this paper supplies the analysis (and the negative result for SVD projection) more than a new algorithm; and Liang et al. (2024) on online subspace descent, which gives continuous-time convergence but assumes exact gradients, exactly the assumption the counterexample exploits. A natural follow-up: replace the hand-set "GoLore@20%" phase switch with a sampling distribution that mixes the top-$r$ SVD subspace and the Haar measure with weight driven by an online estimate of the gradient SNR (cheaply available from batch-gradient variance), and prove a rate interpolating between GaLore's deterministic $O(1/T)$ and GoLore's $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ — the mixture is still contractive in expectation, so Lemma 5 survives with $\delta$ replaced by the mixture weight. Extending to AdamW is the authors' own stated gap.

There is a real connection to your area, and it is Lemma 5 versus Lemma 1. That pair is the optimization-side statement of a fact familiar from projection-based dimensionality reduction: a Haar/Gaussian projection is a distortion bound valid uniformly over all inputs (JL), whereas a data-adaptive top-$r$ subspace (PCA/OPQ) is only guaranteed for the matrix it was fitted to. The counterexample is exactly the ANN failure mode where the query-discriminative direction has lower variance than the nuisance directions, so PCA reduction annihilates precisely the signal while a random projection preserves it in expectation — and the fix is the same fix. The second transferable piece is the stale-basis handling: GaLore's periodically recomputed subspace with momentum carried across the switch is structurally the problem of re-fitting a PCA rotation or PQ codebook in an IVF index while old codes remain valid, where the error is a subspace-misalignment term. Lemma 2 plus the momentum-projection mechanism is a clean template for bounding that drift cost as a function of refresh period $\tau$ and per-step movement — worth borrowing if you ever want a drift bound for an index rebuilt on a schedule.

title: Can Transformers Learn $n$-gram Language Models?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-15

Can Transformers Learn $n$-gram Language Models?

Anej Svete, Nadav Borenstein, Mike Zhou, Isabelle Augenstein, Ryan Cotterell — EMNLP 2024. arXiv:2410.03001

Main idea

Representational-capacity theorems for transformers are almost always proved by explicit weight construction: someone exhibits parameters realising the target function, often using idealised components (hard or sparse attention, unbounded positional encodings, exact arithmetic). Such a theorem says the target lies in the hypothesis class; it says nothing about whether SGD on finite samples lands anywhere near it. This paper takes one such theorem — Svete and Cotterell (2024), that any $n$-gram LM is weakly equivalent to some transformer LM using $n-1$ heads or $n-1$ layers with sparsemax attention — and asks whether the lower bound is operational.

The probe class is split along a parameter-sharing axis. General $n$-gram LMs draw each conditional $p_n(\cdot \mid \mathbf{y}^n)$ independently from a Dirichlet($\alpha=0.1$) over $\Sigma$, one per context, so the target has $\Theta(|\Sigma|^{n-1})$ genuinely free parameters and no cross-context structure. Representation-based ones set $p_n(y\mid \mathbf{y}^n)=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{E}\,h(\mathbf{y}^n))*y$, with $h$ either sparse (concatenated one-hots) or dense (concatenated $\mathbb{R}^{16}$ Gaussian embeddings, size independent of $|\Sigma|$), and $\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{E}_1\mathbf{E}_2$ of controlled rank $R\in{2,8,16}$. Training data is 50k strings per ground-truth LM, with 30k test strings made string-disjoint; evaluation is $\widehat{D}*{\mathrm{KL}}(p_n|p)$ on held-out data — the quantity MLE training actually minimises, not a membership-accuracy proxy.

The finding is a clean crossover. On general $n$-gram LMs, smoothed counting wins outright ($n{=}6,|\Sigma|{=}16$: classic $50.4$ vs. transformer $86.4$ nats; at $|\Sigma|{=}8$, $3.0$ vs. $67.1$). On dense representation-based LMs the ordering flips ($n{=}12,|\Sigma|{=}256$: transformer $34.0$ vs. classic $89.9$ and log-linear $61.6$), though a plain Bengio-style neural $n$-gram model beats the transformer everywhere ($11.2$ there). A standardised regression gives Dense as the dominant predictor ($\hat\beta=-1.28$), then $n$ ($0.63$), $|\Sigma|$ ($0.28$), rank ($0.17$); layers, heads and sparsemax all help ($-0.33,-0.15,-0.06$), $R^2=0.665$. The paper proves nothing new — its theory is cited wholesale from Svete and Cotterell (2024) — so there is no proof to sketch.

A reviewer-style critique

The sharpest problem is that the general-$n$-gram comparison is close to rigged in the baseline's favour, and not by carelessness but by construction: the ground truth is drawn i.i.d. from Dirichlet($0.1$) per context, and add-$\lambda$ smoothing with $\lambda=0.1$ is the Bayes posterior-mean estimator under exactly that prior — and $\lambda=0.1$ sits in the swept grid. "Classic estimators beat transformers on arbitrary $n$-gram LMs" is then partly the statement that the Bayes estimator beats a misspecified one. The honest reading is not that transformers fail to learn a learnable thing, but that in this regime — $\approx 1.7\times 10^7$ free parameters at $n{=}6,|\Sigma|{=}16$ against roughly $2\times10^6$ training tokens — almost nothing is identifiable, and the winner is whoever has the right prior. Reporting excess KL over the Bayes risk would have made this an estimator-theoretic claim rather than a model bake-off.

Tuning is also asymmetric. Baselines get hyperparameter grids ($\lambda$, $\delta$) and three orders $\hat{n}\in{n-2,n,\min(2n,20)}$ with the best reported; transformers get one learning rate ($10^{-4}$), 10 epochs, and heads/layers drawn from ${1,n}$ only. Any "transformers underperform" claim under a fixed LR with no schedule sweep is confounded with optimisation, and 10 epochs on 50k strings is a small budget for 4M parameters. The scale objection is real but cuts both ways: the failure is on unstructured targets, where more capacity should help less, not more.

Two further wrinkles. The theorem being tested is not in the searched hypothesis class — the constructions need hard/sparse attention with unbounded positional encodings, while the experiments use GPT-2 with bounded ones — so part of "representable but not learned" is "not representable here," which the sparsemax ablation only partly repairs. And the sparse-attention conclusion, given the most emphasis in the conclusion and future work, rests on the weakest coefficient ($-0.06$, $p=0.002$) in a linear model fitted to a manifestly nonlinear response; the head-to-head table ($34.0$ vs. $47.8$ at $n{=}12,|\Sigma|{=}256$) is more convincing than the regression. The train/test string-level de-duplication also perturbs the effective training distribution in a way that differentially penalises memorisers.

What the paper does well is genuine. Measuring KL to a known ground-truth distribution instead of next-symbol accuracy is the right move and is the methodological contribution of this whole line. The sparse/dense/general factorisation isolates parameter sharing as an independent variable rather than confounding it with complexity. The over-/under-parameterisation ablation is a fair-minded attempt to handicap the baselines' advantage. And the log-linear model is a well-chosen adversary: it is exactly specified for the sparse targets, and indeed beats transformers there — the kind of negative control most papers omit.

Broader context

This sits in the formal-languages-and-transformers programme surveyed by Strobl et al. (2023): circuit-complexity upper bounds placing log-precision transformers inside uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$, hence unable to express $\mathsf{NC}^1$-hard problems; Bhattamishra et al. (2020) and Delétang et al. (2023) testing the Chomsky hierarchy empirically; and Cotterell's group's series recasting the question probabilistically — RNNs as probabilistic FSAs, chain-of-thought capacity, and Borenstein et al. (2024) on which probabilistic regular languages are easy to model (where rank and entropy first appear as predictors). $n$-gram LMs are the natural probe: finite-state, exactly samplable, with entropy and rank computable in closed form, and with a decades-old optimal estimator to compare against. The closest neighbour in spirit is RASP-L and Zhou et al.'s "What algorithms can transformers learn?", approaching the same expressivity/learnability gap from the algorithmic rather than distributional side; Edelman et al. (2024) on statistical induction heads learning Markov chains is the mechanistic counterpart.

The generative-retrieval connection is real and worth stating carefully. In DSI-style GR the decoder must emit a document identifier, and the well-replicated empirical fact is that semantically structured docids (hierarchical $k$-means codes, learned residual-quantisation codes) train far better than atomic or randomly assigned ones. That is precisely this paper's axis: an arbitrary docid assignment is a general, unshared conditional table over the identifier tree; a structured one is representation-based with parameter sharing across prefixes. This paper supplies a controlled, KL-measured version of that folklore, plus the sharper diagnostic that the rank of the output matrix is an independent difficulty axis — the softmax-bottleneck story familiar from dual-encoder and vector-search analyses, now appearing on the generative side. It also suggests a caution: GR's success may be less about transformers memorising a corpus than about the docid scheme handing them a low-rank, parameter-shared target.

A follow-up worth doing: replace the model bake-off with sample-complexity curves. Fix a target family, sweep $N_{\mathrm{train}}$, and plot transformer excess KL over the Dirichlet Bayes risk — this cleanly separates "gradient descent cannot find the representable function" from "no estimator can, at this $N$." The GR variant is immediate and probably the more interesting one for you: generate synthetic corpora with docid codebooks of controlled rank and controlled prefix-sharing, and measure at what point the transformer's learned conditional departs from the representable optimum — turning docid design from an empirical art into a statement about which targets gradient descent actually reaches.

title: Regret Bounds and Regimes of Optimality for User-User and Item-Item Collaborative Filtering
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-15

Regret Bounds and Regimes of Optimality for User-User and Item-Item Collaborative Filtering

Guy Bresler, Mina Karzand — 2019. arXiv:1711.02198

Main idea

Bresler and Karzand study online recommendation as a sequential decision problem on a doubly-clustered latent variable model. There are $N$ users and countably many items; each user draws a type $\tau_U(u)\sim\mathrm{Unif}[q_U]$, each item a type $\tau_I(i)\sim\mathrm{Unif}[q_I]$, and a preference matrix $\Xi\in{\pm1}^{q_U\times q_I}$ with i.i.d. Rademacher entries fixes everything: $L_{u,i}=\xi_{\tau_U(u),\tau_I(i)}$. At each time step every user receives one recommendation and returns a binary like/dislike, and — crucially, distinguishing this from a bandit — no item may be recommended twice to the same user. Regret is the expected number of disliked recommendations per user by time $T$; a second metric, the cold-start time, is the first $T$ at which $\mathrm{regret}(T)/T$ drops below $\gamma$.

In this formalization, user-user CF means clustering users by agreement on commonly rated items and sharing exploration within a cluster; item-item CF means clustering items by agreement across users who rated both, then probing one representative per cluster. The asymmetry matters: many users can rate one item in a single step, but a user rates only one item per step, so the two algorithms are structurally different rather than transposes.

The headline is a pair of matched upper/lower bounds in two extreme regimes. In the user-structure-only regime ($q_I=2^{q_U}$, item space featureless), user-user CF is optimal up to constants: regret has slope $1/2$ for $\Theta(\log N)$ steps and then slope $\Theta(q_U/N)$. In the item-structure-only regime ($q_U=N$), item-item CF is optimal up to logs, with a three-piece curve — slope $\approx1$, then $\sqrt{q_I T\log(Nq_I)/N}$, then slope $\log(Nq_I)/N$ — and cold-start $\tilde{O}(q_I/N)$ rather than $q_U$'s $\Theta(\log N)$.

The most interesting part

The striking finding is that item-item CF should deliberately refuse to learn most of the item space. Algorithm 3 sets $\ell=\min{\lceil 13\log T+134\sqrt{q_I r T/N}\rceil, q_I}$ and clusters only $\ell$ item types, discarding the rest. Learning the whole preference matrix costs $q_I$ explorations per user; naive clustering of $M$ items needs $M\gg q_I$ and $q_I(\log q_I)M$ comparisons, giving cold-start $\gtrsim q_I^2\log q_I/N$ versus the achieved $q_I/N$. The authors say this only became visible while chasing the converse — a nice case of a lower bound teaching algorithm design. The other elegant piece is the amortization arithmetic: broadcasting one item to $q_U$ users, one per type, buys the preferences of all $N$ users at cost $q_U/2N$ per user, so exploration is a fixed tax divided by the population.

Critically, though, the model is knife-edge. I.i.d. Rademacher $\Xi$ makes user types maximally separable ($\log q_U$ bits identify a user) and makes every user like half of all items — real catalogues are massively popularity-skewed, and "explore until liked" costs $1/p$ under bias $p$. Within-type preferences are exactly identical; the noisy extension (Theorem 4.4) handles i.i.d. flip noise $\gamma$ via a majority-agreement statistic and a clique-decomposition check, but pays an irreducible slope floor of $\gamma$ and still cannot handle systematic within-cluster heterogeneity, which is what real user clusters exhibit. The lower bounds match only at the two extremes; the middle of the $(q_U,q_I)$ plane, where both structures coexist, is deferred to a "forthcoming paper." And even inside the item regime there is an honest gap: cold-start is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{q_I}/N)$ from below but $\tilde{O}(q_I/N)$ from above at constant $\gamma$, which they attribute to a proof artifact. Finally, the $\Theta(q_U T/N)$ asymptotic slope is forced almost entirely by the no-repeat constraint — each genuinely new item is a fresh coin — so the "hard" part of the asymptotics is a modelling artifact rather than a statistical difficulty.

Proof sketch

Claims. Theorem 4.1: with $r=\lceil 2\log(Nq_U^2)\rceil$ and $q_I>18r$, user-user achieves $\mathrm{regret}(T)\le T/2$ for $T\le r$ and $\le r/2+\frac{2q_U+2}{N}T+2$ after. Theorem 5.1: in the user-structure-only model with $q_U>(\log N)^{1.1}$, any algorithm suffers $\ge(\tfrac12-\delta)T-4$ for $T\lesssim\log q_U$ and $\ge(1-e^{-N/q_U})\frac{q_U}{2N}T$ always — so the constants, not just the rates, line up. Theorem 6.1: $\mathrm{regret}(T)<4+\max{52\log T,\,48\sqrt{q_I rT/N},\,270rT/N}$ with $r=\lceil2\log(2Nq_I^2)\rceil$; Theorem 7.1 is the matching four-piece converse.

Achievability. The user-user analysis has two moving parts. Lemma 4.2 bounds mis-partitioning: among $r$ random items, a balls-and-bins argument gives $\ge r/2$ distinct item types w.p. $1-e^{-r/2}$ when $q_I>4r$; two distinct user types then agree on all of them with probability $2^{-r/2}\le\epsilon/q_U^2$; union bound over $\binom{q_U}{2}$ pairs. The genuinely clever step is Claim 4.3, a self-limiting argument: exploration only happens when the exploit set $S_k$ is empty, and a liked exploration adds to $S_k$, so $|S_k^T|\le T+|P_k|$ and the total number of liked explorations is $\le Tq_U+N$. A Chernoff bound (every user type likes $>q_I/3$ of item types, failure $\le q_U e^{-q_I/36}$) converts that into a bound on disliked explorations at a factor-2 loss. Item-item decomposes regret into four terms: exploration time $T_0\le 2Mr/N+\ell+1$; running out of exploitable items (controlled by $M=64q_IT/\ell$); mis-classification, bounded by a "potential error" event requiring $r/2$ distinctly-typed witness users to agree with a wrong column, probability $2^{-r/2}$; and a fourth term that is exactly $0$, since correctly classified items inherit their representative's rating.

Converse. Both lower bounds are genie-aided — the preference matrix $\Xi$ is given — and rest on one regularity notion. A matrix is $(r,\epsilon)$-column regular if for every choice of $r$ columns and every sign pattern $b\in{\pm1}^r$, the number of rows matching $b$ is $(1\pm\epsilon)m/2^r$; Lemma 5.3 gets this from a Chernoff bound plus a union over $n^r2^r$ pairs. Given regularity, the posterior on $\tau_U(u)$ after $t-1$ ratings is uniform on the consistent set, so $\mathbb{P}[\text{like}]\le\frac12\frac{1+\epsilon}{1-\epsilon}$ — the outcome is a near-fair coin until $\approx\log q_U$ items have been rated. The second half is a counting argument: if no same-type user has rated item $i$, the posterior on $\tau_I(i)$ is symmetric and $\mathbb{P}[\text{dislike}]=\tfrac12$ exactly, and each of the $\approx q_U(1-e^{-N/q_U})$ occupied types sees $\ge T$ such first encounters. The item-side converse transposes this to row regularity: an item rated by fewer than $r\approx0.8\log q_I$ users is liked w.p. $\le(1+3\eta)/2$; a user who has never rated that item's type likes it w.p. exactly $1/2$. The key trick (Claim 7.9) is a balls-and-bins bound on the fullest item-type bin under adaptive, history-dependent throwing: they build a martingale indexed by the lexicographic order on (time, user) pairs so counts increment by at most one per step, then apply a McDiarmid/Freedman-type inequality. Combined with $\min_u\gamma_u^T\ge T/\max_j r_j^T$, this converts "few item types can be well-covered" into a regret floor — the statement that regret is a conserved quantity no adaptivity can dodge.

Broader context

The intellectual setting is the gap between matrix completion — recover $\hat{L}$ from a random subset of entries, error measured offline — and online CF, where the observation pattern is chosen by the algorithm and the metric is the users' actual experience. Latent-factor models supply the statistical structure; the bandit literature supplies the explore/exploit language, but the no-repeat constraint breaks the standard machinery, since an optimal bandit policy converges to replaying one arm while a recommender that repeats one movie forever is absurd. The direct ancestors are Bresler–Chen–Shah (NeurIPS 2014) and Bresler–Shah–Voloch (2016); this paper's contribution over both is the converse. Adjacent lines: clustering bandits (Gentile–Li–Zappella's CLUB and successors), latent bandits (Maillard–Mannor), low-rank/bilinear bandits, and the offline hybrid estimators of Song et al. and Borgs et al. The obvious follow-up beyond the promised hybrid algorithm is to replace exact clustering with a metric latent model — users and items as vectors with preferences a smooth function of inner product — where $q_U,q_I$ become covering numbers at the resolution the noise permits; that would turn the phase diagram into a statement about effective dimension rather than cluster count, and would be far closer to how modern systems actually represent items.

For your work this is genuinely usable theory. The item-item side is, structurally, a theory of shared index construction. The algorithm's $r=\Theta(\log(Nq_I))$ ratings per item to place it in a cluster is exactly the sample complexity of assigning a document to a partition in an IVF/clustering-based ANN index or a codebook cell in a PQ/RVQ scheme, and the $\ell<q_I$ truncation says the right thing to do is build a partial index covering the head of the type distribution rather than a complete one — the formal counterpart of what hierarchical-$k$-means or residual-quantization docid schemes in generative retrieval do when they allocate codebook capacity nonuniformly. The regret decomposition also gives a clean analogue of index-build cost: the $\sqrt{q_I r T/N}$ term is the per-user amortized price of constructing a shared structure over $N$ users, decaying like $1/\sqrt{N}$. That is a precise version of the intuition behind a learned index: item-side representation sharing pays off only when the population is large relative to the number of semantically distinct item groups, with crossover at $T\asymp q_I r/N$. In a generative-retrieval setting where "regret" is the fraction of sessions returning a bad result during warm-up and "exploration" is the labelled query–document supervision needed to fit the docid decoder, Theorem 6.1's cold-start $\tilde{O}(q_I/N)$ versus the naive $q_I$ is the difference between needing supervision proportional to the corpus's semantic granularity and needing it proportional to that divided by traffic. The converse is the more valuable half: no clever adaptive indexing scheme can escape paying $\Omega(\log q_I)$ probes per item before that item's placement is identifiable — a genuine information-theoretic floor on how cheaply new corpus items can be folded into a learned index, i.e. the theoretical form of the incremental-indexing problem that plagues DSI-style generative retrieval. The user-user side maps onto personalization: the $\Theta(\log q_U)$ cold-start is the number of interactions needed to localize a new user in a learned user-embedding space. The honest caveat for transfer is the authors' own: i.i.d. Rademacher preferences give a maximally informative, perfectly balanced signal, whereas retrieval relevance is sparse and skewed, so these rates are the optimistic end of the achievable range.

title: Consistency of the $k_n$-nearest neighbor rule under ada...
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-15

Consistency of the $k_n$-nearest neighbor rule under adaptive sampling

Robi Bhattacharjee, Geelon So, Sanjoy Dasgupta — NeurIPS 2025. OpenReview

A note on sources: the OpenReview PDF returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so this was written from the full abstract; the technical detail below is inferred from the direct predecessor, Dasgupta & So, "Online Consistency of the Nearest Neighbor Rule" (arXiv:2410.23644), which sets up the identical framework.

Main idea

The setting is online classification where the instance stream is chosen adaptively: at round $n$ an adversary, having seen everything so far, picks $X_n$; the learner predicts; a label $Y_n$ is then drawn from $\eta(\cdot \mid X_n)$ and shown to both parties. Formally the adversary just is a stochastic process — any process is a valid adversary — so $X_n \mid X_{<n}$ can be a point mass, and the sequence need not be stationary, ergodic, or mixing. This is precisely the regime where the classical machinery dies. Stone's theorem and Cover–Hart both route through i.i.d. sampling: the fraction of mass in a ball, the Lebesgue differentiation theorem applied to $\eta$ at a $\mu$-typical point, and the claim that the $k$-th nearest neighbor distance $\to 0$ in probability all presuppose that training points and query point are drawn from the same fixed law. Under adaptive sampling none of that holds, and the failure is real rather than technical: the predecessor's Proposition 2 shows that on a totally bounded space, the moment two classes fail to be uniformly separated, there is an adversarial sequence on which 1-NN errs every round (canonically $X_n = (-1/3)^n$ against a threshold at $0$, where each query's nearest neighbor sits on the wrong side). With noise added, the impossibility is sharper still: an adaptive process can zoom in on regions where the realized labels happen to look structured and thereby manufacture spurious patterns out of pure noise.

What rescues the rule is a bounded-precision constraint on the adversary. Uniform absolute continuity with respect to a reference measure $\nu$ asks that for every $\varepsilon$ there is $\delta$ with $\sup_n \Pr[X_n \in A \mid X_{<n}] < \varepsilon$ whenever $\nu(A) < \delta$ — a time-uniform, generative bound, strictly stronger than the retrospective "ergodic domination" version that only constrains time-averages. It sits in the chain i.i.d. $\subset$ smoothed $\subset$ uniformly dominated $\subset$ ergodically dominated $\subset$ arbitrary. The adversary may still be fully adaptive and malicious; it simply cannot aim with unbounded precision. "Reasonable $(k_n)$" should be read in the usual Stone sense — $k_n \to \infty$ so label averaging kills noise, $k_n/n \to 0$ so the neighborhood stays local — and the conclusion is that under these two conditions the $k_n$-NN rule is online consistent: its asymptotic risk is almost surely no worse than the Bayes predictor's.

The most interesting part

The conceptual payload is that consistency is robust to adversarial instance selection per se; what it is not robust to is the adversary's ability to concentrate mass arbitrarily sharply. Adaptivity is not the enemy, resolution is. That is a genuinely clarifying decomposition, and it is what lets a purely metric/geometric argument replace the statistical one.

The move from the noiseless 1-NN result to noisy $k_n$-NN changes what the proof must do. In the realizable case a single neighbor's label is correct; consistency is a statement about the nearest-neighbor distance shrinking into regions of constant label. With noise, one neighbor is useless — the rule must average $k_n$ labels and beat the conditional label distribution's variance, so an argument controlling geometry alone is no longer enough; it must be paired with concentration over labels realized at adaptively chosen, dependent points.

Critically: uniform absolute continuity rules out exactly the phenomena a practitioner cares most about. It forbids atoms, forbids the query process from ever collapsing onto a lower-dimensional submanifold, and forbids repeated exact queries — all of which happen constantly in deployment (duplicate queries, templated inputs, a recommender funnelling users into a narrow slice). It is "mild" as an assumption about adversaries and strong as an assumption about real data. And "eventually consistent," almost surely, with no rate, is a weak guarantee: it says the limsup of the mistake rate is right, with no statement about when. The predecessor's $\varepsilon$-net construction makes the dependence explicit in shape — you cover all but a $\delta$-mass remainder by $K_\delta < \infty$ mutually-labeling sets, and $K_\delta$ is uncontrolled — so the burn-in can be arbitrarily long as a function of how badly $\eta$ behaves. Read this as a statement that the rule is not structurally broken by feedback loops, not as a performance promise.

Proof sketch

_Reconstructed from the predecessor's machinery; inferences about the $k_n$ extension are flagged as such._ The claim's shape is asymptotic, almost-sure, rate-free: $\limsup_N \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n\le N} (\mathrm{err}_n - \mathrm{err}_n^{\mathrm{Bayes}}) \le 0$ a.s., under (i) an upper doubling metric measure space ($\rho$ $d$-doubling, $\nu(B(x,r)) \le cr^d$, $\nu$ finite), (ii) $X$ uniformly dominated by $\nu$, (iii) $k_n \to \infty$, $k_n/n \to 0$.

The predecessor sidesteps i.i.d. sampling in two stages. Stage one handles label functions with $\nu$-negligible boundary. Define a mutually-labeling set $U$: $\mathrm{diam}(U) < \mathrm{margin}_\eta(x)$ for all $x \in U$. The key lemma is a pure counting fact — on such a $U$, the NN rule makes at most one mistake, ever, over the whole infinite stream, for any process. Small balls around non-boundary points are mutually labeling (radius $< \mathrm{margin}_\eta(x)/3$). Separability plus finiteness of $\nu$ gives a countable subcover and then a finite $K_\delta$-subcover missing only a remainder $A_\delta$ with $\nu(A_\delta) < \delta$. So all but finitely many mistakes come from $A_\delta$, and the mistake rate is bounded by the rate at which the process can hit a small-mass set — which is $\varepsilon(\delta)$ by assumption. No i.i.d. anywhere; the statistical hypothesis has been traded for a covering argument plus a hitting-rate bound.

Stage two — universal consistency for arbitrary measurable $\eta$ — is where the real work lies, because bad points accumulate in the learner's memory and exert influence long after they arrive, through their Voronoi cells, so progress is not monotone. The fix is to show that a uniformly dominated $X$ induces a nearest-neighbor process $\tilde X$ that is itself ergodically dominated: small-mass regions cannot be amplified into a large share of the predictions. The proof balances two "no-free-lunch"-style sizes. Metric side: by a packing bound, the nearest-neighbor distance can exceed $r$ at most $P_r(\mathcal{X})$ times, since such points form an $r$-packing — this is the finiteness that absolute continuity cannot give you. Measure side: close neighbors live in small balls, whose mass is $O(r^d)$ by upper doubling, hence rarely hit. Instead of the intractable Voronoi decomposition, they decompose via a cover tree: each indicated instance gets a dyadic cone of balls, and one adaptively trims each cone's tail so the combined tail has $\nu$-mass $\le \delta$. Large balls are paid for with the packing bound; tails are paid for with uniform domination. Result: influence rate $O(\gamma \log \frac1\delta + \varepsilon(\delta))$. Universal consistency then follows by approximating $\eta$ by some $\eta_0$ with negligible boundary ($L^1$-dense in doubling spaces) and splitting a mistake into three events.

Inference about the $k_n$ paper: the geometry above should port essentially intact — one needs the $k_n$-th neighbor distance, not just the first, to shrink, which the same packing/cover-tree accounting should deliver with $k_n/n \to 0$ — and the new ingredient must be a martingale concentration argument over the $k_n$ retrieved labels. Since the $X_n$ are adaptively chosen and neighbor sets overlap heavily across rounds, this cannot be a Hoeffding bound on independent draws; it plausibly runs through the fact that conditional on the instance, the label is drawn fresh from $\eta(\cdot\mid x)$, making label noise a martingale difference sequence along the stream even when instances are adversarial — Azuma then gives $k_n \to \infty$ as the requirement for the empirical neighbor-label average to track $\eta$. The "spurious patterns out of noise" impossibility is presumably the matching construction showing this fails without the smoothing assumption. None of this paragraph was verified against the actual paper.

Broader context

Stone (1977) gave the template for universal consistency of local averaging rules under i.i.d. sampling; Cover–Hart (1967) showed 1-NN's asymptotic risk is at most $2R^_(1-R^_)$ and that $k_n$-NN with the standard conditions reaches $R^*$. Kulkarni–Posner (1995) is the one classical result for arbitrary processes, but buys this with uniform class separation in a totally bounded space; Hanneke's optimistic universal learning and Haghtalab et al.'s smoothed online learning are the two modern lines this work bridges, and Blanchard (2022) supplies the cautionary counterexample showing NN failing on $[0,1]$ even for an ergodically dominated process. The general moral — that adaptive data collection voids standard statistical guarantees — is the same one that makes active learning, bandit feedback, and any self-influencing deployed system hard to analyze. Dasgupta's own "Consistency of nearest neighbor classification under selective sampling" (COLT 2012) is the closest ancestor. The obvious follow-up is rates: the predecessor already gets them for smoothed processes in doubling length spaces, so quantifying the noisy $k_n$ case under a margin/Tsybakov condition, with $d$ the intrinsic doubling dimension rather than the ambient one, looks tractable and would be far more informative than a bare limit statement.

For your work this is unusually direct. A vector index is a nearest-neighbor rule, and a deployed retrieval system is exactly an adaptively sampled process: what the index returns shapes what users click, which shapes the next query, which becomes the next indexed item. The i.i.d. assumption underlying every classical guarantee about NN-based retrieval is simply false there, and this line of work says the guarantee survives anyway provided the query process cannot concentrate too sharply — a condition that is testable, and that a query-log study could plausibly falsify (duplicate and near-duplicate queries are atoms). The genuinely open question worth pushing on: all of this assumes exact $k$-NN. HNSW and IVF return an approximate neighbor set, and the approximation error is not oblivious — it is a deterministic function of the index geometry, so an adversary (or a feedback loop) that pushes queries into regions where the graph's navigability degrades gets systematically wrong neighbors, not noisily wrong ones. The packing/cover-tree argument is about the true metric; it is not obvious how much survives when the retrieved set is only guaranteed within a $(1+\epsilon)$ distance factor, and less obvious still when recall degrades adversarially. A consistency theorem for $k_n$-ANN under adaptive sampling — or a counterexample where an HNSW index is consistent under i.i.d. queries but inconsistent under feedback-driven ones — is a real and publishable question sitting directly at the intersection of these two literatures.

title: Two-Time-Scale Learning Dynamics: A Population View of Neural Network Training
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-15

Two-Time-Scale Learning Dynamics: A Population View of Neural Network Training

Giacomo Borghi, Hyesung Im, Lorenzo Pareschi — arXiv preprint, March 2026. arXiv:2603.19808

Main idea

This is a kinetic-theory formalisation of Population-Based Training (PBT) and its relatives (evolutionary strategies, model merging, AutoML pipelines). The "population" is not the population of neurons in the Mei–Montanari–Nguyen or Sirignano–Spiliopoulos sense; it is a population of $N$ whole neural networks, each an agent carrying a pair $(\theta^i, h^i)$ of parameters and hyperparameters. The two time scales are: (fast) parameter training, modelled as the SDE approximation of SGD, $d\theta^i = -\nabla_\theta L(\theta^i,h^i)dt + \sqrt{2\beta^{-1}(h^i)}\,\Sigma^{1/2} dB^i$; and (slow) a genetic selection–mutation jump in which an agent is replaced, with probability $\tau$ per round, by a copy of an agent drawn with Gibbs weights $\propto e^{\mathcal{F}(\theta^j,h^j)}$ with its hyperparameter perturbed. Crucially, the fitness $\mathcal{F}$ (validation performance) is a different object from the training loss $L$ and need not be differentiable.

In the many-agent limit one gets a kinetic PDE on the joint density $f(t,\theta,h)$: $\partial_t f = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\mathcal{T}_L[f] + \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}}[f]$, where $\mathcal{T}_L$ is a Fokker–Planck operator in $\theta$ only and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}}$ is a nonlocal reweighting-plus-convolution (gain/loss balanced so mass is conserved). Sending $\varepsilon \to 0$ forces $\mathcal{T}_L[f]=0$, i.e. the conditional ansatz $f = \rho(t,h)\,\mu_L^\infty(\theta|h)$ with $\mu_L^\infty \propto e^{-\beta(h)L(\theta,h)}$, and yields a closed selection–mutation equation driven by an effective (Gibbs-averaged) fitness $\overline{\mathcal{F}}(h) = \log\int e^{\mathcal{F}(\theta,h)}\mu_L^\infty(\theta|h)d\theta$. Under a further slow-mutation rescaling this degenerates to the replicator–mutator PDE from mathematical biology.

The most interesting part

The effective fitness is the real payload, and it is genuinely clever. PBT evaluates an agent's instantaneous validation score, but the theory says the slow dynamics is not optimising that — it is optimising a log-partition function of the fitness against the Gibbs equilibrium of the inner loop. Two consequences follow. First, a bilevel reading: $\overline{\mathcal{F}}^\beta$ is the entropy-regularised version of the penalised bilevel objective $\mathcal{F}(\theta,h) - \beta(L(\theta,h) - \inf_\theta L)$, with Lemma 8 giving $|\overline{\mathcal{F}}^\beta(h) - \mathcal{F}(\theta^\star(h),h)| \lesssim \beta^{-1/2}$. Second, an algorithm: Algorithm 2 replaces the inner SGD loop by direct sampling from $\mu_L^\infty$, or in the RL experiment by time-averaging the last $m$ episodic rewards — and larger $m$ demonstrably speeds convergence on CartPole. That is a falsifiable, useful prediction from the theory.

Critically, though, the load-bearing step is never proved. Theorem 4 covers only $N\to\infty$, $\tau\to0$; the $\varepsilon\to0$ averaging is purely formal — the equilibrium ansatz is assumed, with no singular-perturbation estimate, no rate in $\varepsilon$, and no uniform-in-time control. The paper's own Figure 4 even notes the separation "seems not to be uniform in time". Worse, Assumption 3 fixes $\beta>0$ constant and $\Sigma \equiv I$ for the rigorous theorem, whereas the entire point of the model — and the second hyperparameter in the numerics — is that the SGD noise level _depends on $h$_. The rigorous result thus excludes the most interesting instance of the model. Assumption 3 also demands globally Lipschitz $L$ and bounded, strictly positive $\mathcal{F}$, excluding the quadratic and Himmelblau losses actually simulated. Relative to standard mean-field SGD analyses, the propagation-of-chaos machinery here is comparatively soft — the McKean–Vlasov nonlinearity is only in the low-dimensional $h$-marginal, so the hard high-dimensional issues are sidestepped by construction. And Remark 6 concedes that SGD's stationary state is generically non-equilibrium with persistent probability currents (Chaudhari–Soatto; Li et al.), which would invalidate the Gibbs ansatz precisely where implicit regularisation matters; the proposed fix (Chapman–Enskog expansion) is left to future work.

Proof sketch

Theorem 4 (large-population limit). Under Assumption 3 and $f_0\in\mathcal{P}_q$, $q>1$, a weak measure solution exists and $\mathbb{E}|f^{N,\tau}(t)-f(t)|_{BL}\to0$ as $N\to\infty$, $\tau\to0$. The metric is the bounded-Lipschitz (flat/Dudley) norm, which by Kantorovich–Rubinstein equals $W_1$ for the truncated cost $|x-y|\wedge1$. The statement is qualitative, though the proof exposes a rate — $O(\epsilon(N)) + O(\tau)$ with $\epsilon(N)$ the Fournier–Guillin empirical-measure rate, dimension-cursed ($\sim N^{-1/d}$ for $d>2$), and prefactors $C t_{\max}(1+M_q^{1/q}(f_0))e^{C' t_{\max}}$ that blow up exponentially in the horizon. So: finite-horizon, non-uniform in time.

Strategy. The $N\to\infty$ half is a synchronous coupling: build $N$ i.i.d. nonlinear McKean–Vlasov agents driven by the same Brownian paths and the same auxiliary randomness. Between jumps, Lipschitz drift plus shared noise gives $d|X^i_t-\overline{X}^i_t|^2 \le 2|L|_{\mathrm{Lip}}|X^i_t-\overline{X}^i_t|^2 dt$, hence a Grönwall factor, and the truncated cost is preserved. At jump times the key lemma is selection stability, $|\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}[f]-\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}[g]|_{BL}\le C_{\mathcal{F}}|f-g|_{BL}$ — this is where boundedness and $\inf\mathcal{F}>0$ are used, since the nonlocal normalisation $\int e^{\mathcal{F}}df$ is otherwise not Lipschitz. Combined with a measurable selection map realising the optimal coupling of the jump targets, the per-step error recursion closes after a moment bound, with the extra $\epsilon(N)$ from Fournier–Guillin concentration. The $\tau\to0$ half is compactness plus identification: the processes are càdlàg, uniformly bounded in $q$-th moment with $\mathbb{E}|\overline{X}_t - \overline{X}_s| \lesssim |t-s|+\sqrt{|t-s|}$, so tightness in Skorokhod space gives a subsequential limit; testing against $\phi\in C_c^\infty$ shows the discrete-jump scheme differs from the continuous PDE by $O(\tau^2)$ per step.

Theorem 10 (mean convergence). If $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ has a unique maximiser $h^\star\in\mathrm{supp}(\rho_0)$ with quadratic growth, then for any tolerance there is a selection pressure $\alpha$ large enough that $|m(\rho(t))-h^\star|^2 \le e^{-t}|m(\rho_0)-h^\star|^2 + (1-e^{-t})\mathrm{tol}/2$. The mechanism: mutation is mean-zero, so only selection moves the mean, and the quantitative Laplace principle of Fornasier et al. bounds the selection displacement by a small radius term plus $e^{-\alpha q}/\rho(B(h^\star,r))$. The enabling lemma is a lower bound on mass near the maximiser: the non-degenerate Gaussian mutation kernel spreads mass into any ball at rate $\delta>0$, giving $\frac{d}{dt}\rho(t,B) \ge \delta-\rho(t,B)$ and by Grönwall a uniform positive lower bound — exactly what prevents the $e^{-\alpha q}/\rho(B)$ term from degenerating. Caveats: this is CBO technology transplanted wholesale; it controls only the first moment, not concentration of $\rho$; $\alpha$ depends on $t_{\max}$, so it is not uniform in time; and the target is $\arg\max\overline{\mathcal{F}}$, not the true bilevel optimum, from which it sits $O(\beta^{-1/2})$ away.

Broader context

This sits at the junction of three literatures. Mean-field analysis of neural training (Mei–Montanari–Nguyen, Chizat–Bach, Sirignano–Spiliopoulos) takes the width to infinity; this paper explicitly takes the ensemble size to infinity instead. Consensus-based optimisation and its kinetic analyses (Carrillo, Fornasier, Pinnau, Totzeck) supply the toolkit. And two-time-scale stochastic approximation à la Borkar is the discrete-time ancestor: there, a fast iterate tracks an ODE equilibrium and the slow iterate sees an averaged vector field; here the fast iterate's distribution tracks a Gibbs measure and the slow iterate sees an averaged fitness. Worth reading alongside: Del Moral–Miclo's Feynman–Kac analysis of genetic algorithms (exponential convergence to a unique steady state via Dobrushin's ergodic coefficient, but no characterisation of that steady state — precisely the gap Theorem 10 attacks from the other side), and the birth–death/Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao sampling literature (Lu, Lu, Nolen).

An obvious follow-up: make the $\varepsilon\to0$ reduction rigorous with a quantitative rate. One would need a uniform-in-$h$ log-Sobolev or Poincaré constant for $\mu_L^\infty(\cdot|h)$ and then a hypocoercivity-style estimate bounding $|f^\varepsilon - \rho\otimes\mu_L^\infty|$ by $O(\varepsilon\cdot\sup_h\lambda(h)^{-1})$. The Chapman–Enskog first-order correction would then predict a bias in PBT's effective objective, testable by running PBT with varying inner-loop lengths and checking whether the optimised hyperparameter drifts as $O(\varepsilon)$.

No natural IR connection — this is a hyperparameter-optimisation and kinetic-theory paper, and forcing a link would be dishonest. The transferable value is methodological: the BL-norm coupling argument for jump-plus-diffusion particle systems, and more pointedly the effective fitness idea, a general lesson about any bilevel or two-loop procedure — the outer loop optimises a Gibbs-log-partition smoothing of the inner criterion, not the criterion itself. If you ever analyse a generative-retrieval pipeline with a fast differentiable inner objective and a slow non-differentiable outer metric (nDCG, say, or a merge/distillation step over checkpoints), this is the right template, and Lemma 8's $\beta^{-1/2}$ gap is the right way to quantify how far the smoothed objective sits from the one you care about.

title: Analyzing Generalization of Neural Networks through Loss Path Kernels
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-15

Analyzing Generalization of Neural Networks through Loss Path Kernels

Yilan Chen, Wei Huang, Hao Wang, Charlotte Loh, Akash Srivastava, Lam M. Nguyen, Tsui-Wei Weng — NeurIPS 2023. OpenReview

Main idea

The paper asks how to get a generalization bound for networks trained by gradient flow that does not require the ultra-wide/NTK-frozen regime. Its move is to stop analyzing the network output $f(w,x)$ and instead analyze the loss as a function of the labelled point $z=(x,y)$. Under gradient flow, $\frac{d}{dt}\ell(w_t,z) = -\frac1n\sum_i \langle \nabla_w\ell(w_t,z),\nabla_w\ell(w_t,z_i)\rangle$; integrating over $[0,T]$ gives the exact identity $\ell(w_T,z)=\ell(w_0,z)-\frac1n\sum_i K_T(z,z_i;S)$, where the loss path kernel $K_T$ is the time-integral of the loss tangent kernel along the realized trajectory. So the trained loss function is literally a kernel machine — with fixed coefficients $-1/n$ and offset $\ell(w_0,\cdot)$ — for any continuously differentiable architecture, finite width included. All the model's expressiveness has been pushed into the kernel, which depends on the training set. Complexity is then measured over the class of such kernel machines induced by all datasets $S'$ whose LPK obeys a norm budget $B$.

The most interesting part

The clever part is where the hypothesis class lives. Because gradient flow pins the coefficients to $-1/n$, the only free parameter is the kernel itself, so the Rademacher complexity becomes a measure of how much the loss path kernel moves when you resample the training set. This shows up concretely: the off-diagonal term of $U_1$ is $\Delta(z_i,z_j)=\frac12[\sup_{S'}K(z_i,z_j;S')-\inf_{S'}K(z_i,z_j;S')]$, the half-range of the kernel across datasets, and $U_2$ is a covering number of the set of loss vectors $g(Z)$ over datasets. This is an algorithmic-stability quantity wearing kernel clothing, and it is what buys tightness. Kernelizing on $Z$ rather than $X$ also repairs the asymmetry that made the earlier Chen et al. (2021) NN-kernel equivalence valid only when $\nabla_f\ell$ is constant, and handles multi-output nets for free.

The critical caveat is that this supremum over datasets is not computable: you would have to retrain on every possible dataset. In the experiments it is replaced by a max over 20–100 resampled $S'$ (with an extreme-value extrapolation), so the headline numbers — 0.03 vs. 1.44 for Cao & Gu, 4690× tighter than Bartlett et al. — are estimates approaching the bound from below, not certificates. $U_2$ is worse: they set $\epsilon$ to the diameter of ${g(Z)}$ and $N=1$, so $U_2\approx \epsilon/n$, i.e. the empirical spread of loss vectors over a handful of resampled datasets. On $n=1000$ binary MNIST with a 100-hidden-unit net, that is nearly guaranteed to be small; there is no experiment at the scale where norm-based bounds actually blow up. The closed-form specializations are also loose in the expected way: the infinite-width bound $U_\infty=\frac{\rho B\sqrt T}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}|\Theta(x_i,x_j)|}$ grows as $\sqrt T$ and, since $\sum_{i,j}|\Theta|=\Theta(n^2)$, has no explicit $1/\sqrt n$ decay at all — any improvement with $n$ must come through $B$. The norm-constrained result (Thm. 9) is linear in $T$ and multiplicative across layer norms, i.e. classically vacuous.

Proof sketch

What is proved: (i) Theorem 2, the exact kernel-machine identity, assuming only that $\ell$ is continuously differentiable in $w$ and the gradient-flow ODE has a solution — it is a one-line chain rule plus integration, with no width or convergence assumption; (ii) $K_T$ is a valid kernel: continuity, plus $u^\top K_T(Z,Z)u=\int_0^T|\sum_i u_i\Phi_t(z_i)|^2dt\ge 0$ with $\Phi_t(z)=\nabla_w\ell(w_t,z)$, so PSD survives the time integral because it is a Gram matrix of a single feature map at each $t$; (iii) Corollary 1: with probability $1-\delta$, _if the realized $S$ satisfies the norm constraint_, $L_\mu - L_S\le 2\min(U_1,U_2)+3\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/2n}$, for losses in $[0,1]$.

How: $U_1$ relaxes the class into ${\langle\beta,\Phi_{S'}(z)\rangle+\ell(w_0,z):|\beta|\le B}$, freeing $\beta$ from its actual value $-\frac1n\sum_i\Phi_{S'}(z_i')$ whose norm is exactly the constraint $\frac1{n^2}\sum_{ij}K\le B^2$; the initialization offset drops out since $\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\sum\sigma_i\ell(w_0,z_i)]=0$. Then the standard kernel Rademacher computation plus Jensen gives $\frac Bn(\mathbb{E}_\sigma\sup\sum_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_jK)^{1/2}$; splitting diagonal from off-diagonal, the key trick is $\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\sup_{S'}\sigma_i\sigma_jK]=\frac12(\sup K-\inf K)$ because $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\pm1$ with equal probability — that is where $\Delta$ comes from. $U_2$ is a Massart/Chernoff argument: each fixed kernel is a singleton hypothesis, so on an $\epsilon$-cover the MGF bound via bounded differences ($c_i=2/n$ from $\ell\in[0,1]$) gives a mean-zero sub-Gaussian $\xi$, yielding $\epsilon/n+\sqrt{2\ln N/n}$. A matching lower bound (Thm. 7, $\ge \frac{B}{\sqrt2 n}\sup\sqrt{\mathrm{Tr}\,K}$) shows the trace term is not slack. Gradient flow enters twice: it fixes the coefficients, and it makes $\mathrm{Tr}\,K_T=\sum_i\int_0^T|\nabla_w\ell(w_t,z_i)|^2dt$ a gradient-energy along the path, which saturates once training converges — hence the observed plateau of the complexity term rather than unbounded growth in $T$.

Broader context

The backdrop is the NTK linearization (Jacot et al.; Arora et al.; Lee et al.), where infinite-width nets trained by gradient flow behave as kernel regression, and the NTK-based bounds of Arora et al. (2019) and Cao & Gu (2019), which are data-dependent but hold only for ultra-wide FCNs at convergence with one output. This paper sits in the "data- and algorithm-dependent complexity" line alongside algorithmic stability (Hardt–Recht–Singer) and information-theoretic bounds (Xu–Raginsky); its $\Delta$ and covering terms are close cousins of stability constants, and indeed one appendix case study just plugs a stability assumption into $U_2$. Domingos' "every model trained by gradient descent is a kernel machine" is the obvious precursor; the contribution here is a kernel that is actually PSD and symmetric. Worth reading next to it: Nagarajan & Kolter's argument that uniform convergence may be unable to explain deep generalization — the sup over datasets is exactly the place that critique bites. A natural follow-up: replace the worst-case sup with an expectation via PAC-Bayes or a mutual-information term over the LPK, which the authors flag themselves, and would turn a non-computable sup into something estimable from a single training run; a discrete-time, finite-learning-rate LPK (their GD-vs-GF agreement is empirical only) is the other obvious gap.

There is no genuine IR connection here, and I would not manufacture one. The nearest real neighbour is that $K_T(z,z')$ is a training-dynamics similarity between labelled examples, which is formally the same object as gradient-similarity influence/data-attribution kernels (TracIn and relatives) — "retrieval over training data" rather than retrieval in the IR sense. The value is the technique: kernelizing the loss dynamics rather than the model, and the resulting reframing of complexity as sensitivity of an induced kernel to dataset resampling — a template that transfers to any differentiable-training setting, including the encoder/decoder training underlying dense and generative retrieval, should you ever want a trajectory-dependent generalization statement there.

title: Stability and Sharper Risk Bounds with Convergence Rate $O(1/n^2)$
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-14

Stability and Sharper Risk Bounds with Convergence Rate $O(1/n^2)$

Bowei Zhu, Shaojie Li, Yong Liu — 2024 — arXiv:2410.09766

Main idea. The paper asks whether algorithmic stability can deliver high-probability excess risk bounds faster than $O(1/n)$. The comparator is fixed and global: $F(A(S)) - F(w^_)$ with $F(w)=\mathbb{E}_z f(w;z)$ and $w^_\in\arg\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}F$. The $O(1/n)$ barrier is real for the classical route: Bousquet–Elisseeff-style bounds on the generalization gap carry an irreducible sampling error $\Omega(1/\sqrt n)$, and Klochkov & Zhivotovskiy (2021) escaped that only by bounding excess risk directly under a Bernstein condition, landing at $ ilde O( eta + 1/n)$ — saturating at $ ilde O(\log n/n)$ no matter how stable the algorithm is. The move here is to run the whole argument one derivative up: define uniform stability in gradients $\sup_z \mathbb{E}_A| abla f(A(S);z)- abla f(A(S^{(i)});z)|^2\le eta^2$, prove a concentration bound for $| abla F(A(S))- abla F_S(A(S))|$, and convert gradients back to risk via the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality $F(w)-F^*\le rac{1}{2\mu}| abla F(w)|^2$. Since a gradient bound of order $1/n$ squares to $1/n^2$, the rate follows — provided the variance term in the gradient bound is itself small.

Proof sketch. Assumptions: $f(\cdot;z)$ is $M$-Lipschitz, $\gamma$-smooth, nonnegative; the population risk $F$ satisfies PL($\mu$); for the ERM/PGD/SGD instantiations, $F_S$ and every leave-one-out $F_{S^{(i)}}$ satisfy PL($\mu$) too; low noise $F(w^*)=O(1/n)$; sample size $n=\Omega(\gamma^2\log(1/\delta)/\mu^2)$; SGD additionally needs bounded gradient variance and step size $\eta_t= rac{2t+1}{2\mu(t+1)^2}$ (so $\mu$ must be known).

Theorem 2 is the engine. Decompose $n( abla F- abla F_S)(A(S))$ into leave-one-out terms plus two residuals bounded by $2n eta$ directly from gradient stability; center to $q_i(S)$, which has bounded differences $4 eta$ and vanishing conditional means, so a Hilbert-space moment inequality for sums of weakly dependent vector functions (Bousquet–Klochkov–Zhivotovskiy in shape, Fan–Lei in content) gives $|\sum_i q_i|_p \lesssim p\,n eta\lceil\log_2 n ceil$, hence $ eta\log n\log(1/\delta)$ after moment-to-tail conversion. The residual mean term is handled by vector Bernstein, and this is where the improvement actually lives: instead of using $M$ as the variance proxy, the variance is $\mathbb{E}_Z| abla f(A(S);Z)|^2$, the squared gradient norm at the trained parameter. $M$ survives only in an $M\log(1/\delta)/n$ term. That data-dependent variance is then concentrated by a self-bounding argument: $\sum_i(p_i-p)^2\le 8n eta^2 p+2n eta^4$, i.e. $p$ is $(8n eta^2,2n eta^4)$-weakly self-bounded, so Klochkov–Zhivotovskiy's lemma applies.

Theorem 3 closes a loop. Smoothness gives $\mathbb{E}| abla f(A(S);Z)|^2\le\gamma^2\mathbb{E}|A(S)-w^_|^2+\mathbb{E}| abla f(w^_;Z)|^2$; PL's error-bound consequence $| abla F(A(S))|\ge\mu|A(S)-w^_|$ feeds the gradient-generalization bound back into itself, and the condition $n\ge 32\gamma^2\log(6/\delta)/\mu^2$ is exactly what lets the $\gamma^2/(\mu^2 n)$ self-term be absorbed. Finally Srebro–Sridharan–Tewari self-bounding, $| abla f(w^_;z)|^2\le 4\gamma f(w^_;z)$, turns the noise term into $\gamma F(w^_)$. Result:

$$\mathbb{E}_A F(A(S))-F(w^*)\lesssim rac{\mathbb{E}_A| abla F_S(A(S))|^2}{\mu}+ rac{\gamma F(w^*)\log(1/\delta)}{\mu n}+ rac{M^2\log^2(1/\delta)}{\mu n^2}+ rac{ eta^2\log^2 n\log^2(1/\delta)}{\mu}.$$

With $ eta=4M\gamma/(n\mu)$ for ERM and PGD (any $T$; $T\asymp\log n$ kills optimization error), this is $ ilde O(M^2\gamma^2/(\mu^3n^2))$; SGD needs $T\asymp n^2$ and pays $\mu^{-4}\gamma^3$.

Critique. The rate does not contradict minimax lower bounds, and the reason is explicit in the statement: the $\gamma F(w^_)\log(1/\delta)/(\mu n)$ term is always there, and $O(1/n^2)$ requires the low-noise assumption $F(w^_)=O(1/n)$ — a near-realizable regime where the $\sigma^2/n$ floor vanishes. Stripped of that, the leading term is $\mathbb{E}| abla f(w^*;Z)|^2/(\mu n)$, the finite-sample shadow of $ rac{1}{2n}\mathrm{tr}(H^{-1}Q)$ from asymptotic normality; the authors say so, though $1/\mu$ as a proxy for $H^{-1}$ is loose by up to a condition number. So $1/n^2$ is a second-order term made visible, not a violation.

Two further deflations. First, $ ilde O(1/n^2)$ under smooth + PL + low-noise is not new — Zhang et al. and Xu & Zeevi (2024) had it by uniform convergence of gradients. The genuine contribution is dimension-freeness: $n=\Omega(\gamma^2/\mu^2)$ rather than $\Omega(\gamma^2 d/\mu^2)$. The abstract oversells this; the comparison table states it correctly. Second, constants are condition-number-heavy: $\kappa^2=(\gamma/\mu)^2$ in the numerator, $\mu^{-3}$ (SGD: $\mu^{-4}$) overall, $\log^2(1/\delta)$ rather than KZ's deviation-optimal $\log(1/\delta)$, and a validity threshold $n\gtrsim\kappa^2\log(1/\delta)$ that couples sample size to confidence. The moment lemma itself is only a constant-factor sharpening of Fan & Lei, honestly flagged; the real levers are the variance localization plus the PL feedback. Assumption inflation is substantial relative to KZ: PL must hold for $F$, $F_S$ and all $F_{S^{(i)}}$ with a uniform $\mu$, and the ERM argument silently uses $ abla F_S(\hat w^*)=0$, which needs an interior minimizer despite the projection onto $\mathcal{W}$. The nonconvex gradient-gap claim is the most durable piece: assumption-light (Lipschitz only), iteration-count-free — unlike the $O(T/n)$ SGD bounds of Bassily et al. — and it replaces $M/\sqrt n$ by $\sqrt{\mathbb{E}| abla f|^2/n}$, demoting $M$ to order $1/n$. "Sharpest known dimension-free" is defensible there.

Context and follow-up. The lineage is Bousquet–Elisseeff → Feldman–Vondrák's $ eta\log n\log(1/\delta)$ concentration → Bousquet–Klochkov–Zhivotovskiy moment method → Klochkov–Zhivotovskiy's Bernstein-condition localization; Hardt–Recht–Singer supplies the SGD stability template mirrored here at the gradient level. Worth reading alongside: Lei (COLT 2023) on nonconvex/nonsmooth gradient stability, and Xu & Zeevi (MOR 2024) for the uniform-convergence counterpart and its $\Omega(d eta^2/\mu^2)$ sample-complexity lower bound. Obvious follow-up: replace global PL by a local Łojasiewicz exponent and trace how the rate interpolates, and check whether the $\log^2 n$ is removable.

Connection to your work. Thin, and I would not stretch it. PL is not credible for dense retrieval encoders — it is claimed for overparameterized nets in NTK-like regimes, but not uniformly over $\mathcal{W}$ with a dataset-independent $\mu$, and the low-noise condition $F(w^*)=O(1/n)$ is not a contrastive-training regime. The one non-cosmetic hook is the paper's own remark that stability-based results for pairwise learning (Lei–Liu–Ying) inherit the $ ilde O(1/n)$ ceiling from KZ and could be upgraded by this template: gradient stability is exactly the object that survives non-decomposable losses, where uniform-convergence arguments over listwise or InfoNCE objectives degrade. A defensible project is the variance-localized gradient-stability bound for U-statistic/contrastive losses, dropping PL for an error-bound condition on the retrieval objective. Absent that, treat it as pure learning-theory reading.

title: Provable Long-Range Benefits of Next-Token Prediction
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-14

Provable Long-Range Benefits of Next-Token Prediction

Xinyuan Cao, Santosh S. Vempala (Georgia Tech) — Dec 2025 — arXiv:2512.07818

Main idea. The puzzle is real because the information-theoretic answer and the computational answer diverge. The chain rule makes next-token log loss exactly document log loss ($nL(q) - D_{KL}(\bar p|\bar q) = H(\bar p)$), so ignoring computation there is nothing to explain. Once you bound the model, the two come apart: prefixes like "the prime factors of 49990139543 are…" admit a polynomial-time non-autoregressive sampler (Kalai's factored-number trick) but no efficient left-to-right completer. The pessimistic reading has teeth — Bachmann–Nagarajan's path-star construction shows teacher forcing can induce a Clever-Hans shortcut that makes the task harder to learn, and exposure-bias arguments predict per-token error $\epsilon$ compounding to $1-(1-\epsilon)^n$.

Cao–Vempala's reply is not "errors don't compound" but a change of measuring instrument. They fix a _next-$k$-token distinguisher_: a Boolean $d(i,x)$ depending only on the prefix $x_{:i}$ and the window $x_{i:i+k}$, with advantage $a(d,\bar p,\bar q) = \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\bar p}[\frac1n\sum_i (\mathbb{E}_{q x\sim\bar}[d_i(x)\mid x_{:i}=y_{:i}] - d_i(y))]$. The claim: plain next-token loss minimization, over RNNs of size polynomial in $k$, $d$, $1/\epsilon$ and independent of $n$, yields a model no such distinguisher can beat by more than $\epsilon$. Grammaticality checkers, arithmetic verifiers, SAT-assignment checkers are all instances — verification is cheap even when generation is not.

The most striking part. The definition is computational, not statistical. Closeness is certified against a class of bounded programs — RNN size $\le d$, RNN-time $\le \tau$, bounded bit size — in the Goldwasser–Micali/Yao tradition, and $\bar p, \bar q$ may remain far in TV. That matters because the statistical route is vacuous here: Appendix A's Pinsker bound gives $a\le\sqrt{\tfrac{k}{2n}D_{KL}(\bar p|\bar q)}$, which needs excess per-token loss $O(\epsilon^2/k)$ — near-perfect fit. Theorem 1 instead needs only that the loss is not further improvable by $\epsilon^2/4k$ within the size budget. This is precisely the multicalibration move (Hébert-Johnson–Kim–Reingold–Rothblum; Błasiok–Gopalan–Hu–Kalai–Nakkiran's "loss minimization yields multicalibration"): un-improvability against a test class substitutes for closeness.

Length-independence is the surprise. Naively, matching $n$ windows should need position-dependent capacity, and sequence KL grows like $\Theta(n)$ so global distinguishers win outright. The resolution is that the KL budget and the per-round KL gain both scale linearly in $n$, so $n$ cancels in the round count.

Honestly: this is a statement about the constrained optimum, not about SGD, so Bachmann–Nagarajan is not refuted — their failure is an optimization/architecture claim, and the escape valve here is enormous RNN-time, $\tau\cdot(k2^k)^{O(k/\epsilon^2)}$, which the authors show is unavoidable (factoring). More importantly, the conditioning prefix $y_{:i}$ is drawn from $\bar p$, not from the model's own rollout. So this is a teacher-forced guarantee, and the paper's claim that it "addresses the issue of accumulated error" is overstated: it bounds drift within a $k$-window from a true prefix, not compounding under free generation. The advantage also averages over positions, so $o(n)$ badly-distinguishable positions are invisible. There are, notably, no assumptions on $\bar p$ — and no sample complexity, since optimization is over population loss.

Proof sketch. Boosting (Lemma 1). Given $d$ with advantage $\alpha$, reweight $q$ on $k$-blocks: $q'(x_{i+1:i+k+1}\mid x_{:i+1}) \propto q(\cdot)e^{-\alpha d_{i+1}(x)}$. Overlapping blocks can't all be reweighted, and reweighting the single best block gains only $O(\alpha^2)$ — forcing a round count that grows with $n$. The trick is to partition the $n$ blocks into $k$ disjoint residue classes mod $k$; averaging gives some offset with advantage $\ge\alpha$, and its class has $w\ge n/2k$ disjoint blocks reweighted at once. Telescoping the log-ratio, then $\log Z \le Z-1$ and $e^{-\beta}+\beta-1\le\beta^2/2$ with $d\in{0,1}$, gives $D_{KL}(\bar p|\bar q') \le D_{KL}(\bar p|\bar q) - \alpha^2 n/4k$.

Length-independence. Initial KL against uniform is $\le n\log|\Sigma|$; each round gains $\alpha^2 n/4k$. Both are linear in $n$, so rounds $\le 4k\log|\Sigma|/\epsilon^2$ — $n$ cancels. That is the technical heart.

RNN realization (Lemma 3). $q'$ needs a sum over all $|\Sigma|^k$ continuations without clobbering state. Naively duplicate the RNN — model size doubles per round, exponential overall. Instead duplicate only the hidden node set: one copy freezes the prefix state, the second is scratch. Size grows additively per round, so total size is quadratic in rounds: $O(k^2(d+k)\log^2|\Sigma|/\epsilon^4)$.

Self-boosting (Lemma 4). No hybrid argument and no distinguisher is ever constructed. Build nested size classes. If the loss-minimizer in $C_j$ admitted advantage $\alpha>\epsilon$, boosting puts a better model in $C_{j+1}$, so $L_{j+1}<L_j-\epsilon^2/4k$. Nonnegativity of $L$ bounds such "bad" levels by $4k\log|\Sigma|/\epsilon^2$; drawing the starting index uniformly from a $10\times$ larger range lands on a good level with probability $0.9$. Existence of the distinguisher suffices.

Connection to your work. The fit to generative retrieval is genuine, not forced, and it is better than the LM case because docids are short: a docid is essentially one $k$-token window, $k\approx$ docid length, conditioned on a query prefix. A next-$k$-token distinguisher is exactly a docid-level verifier — "is this a valid leaf of the prefix tree," "is it relevant." Theorem 1 then reads: a GR model of size $O(k^2(d+k)/\epsilon^4)$ trained with plain next-token loss internalizes any bounded-size verifier, so sampled-docid statistics match the training distribution's within $\epsilon$. The boosting operator $q\,e^{-\alpha d}/Z$ is literally a product-of-experts reranker over the block, so the theorem says an adequately-sized model already absorbs the reranker you would otherwise bolt on — a formal target for "when is constrained decoding redundant."

Three honest gaps. The guarantee is for sampling, not beam search; GR's top-1 accuracy is a functional of the mode, and indistinguishability constrains distributions, not argmaxes. Prefixes must come from $\bar p$, so nothing here covers unseen queries or new documents — GR's actual hard case. And the construction is RNN-specific (gated hidden-state scratch space), with RNN-time exponential in $k^2/\epsilon^2$, so it is not a capacity statement about T5-style GR models.

Follow-ups. Porting to transformers requires re-deriving Lemma 3's additive growth without a hidden node set — plausibly a block-reweighting head with $O(1)$ added layers per round. More interesting: relax contiguity. The mod-$k$ partition is the only source of $\Theta(n/k)$ disjoint blocks; distinguishers reading $k$ non-contiguous positions would need a fractional-matching or hypergraph-coloring substitute to recover a linear-in-$n$ disjoint family. Worth reading alongside: Alvarez-Melis–Garg–Kalai, Are GANs Overkill for NLP? (the $k=1$ ancestor of Lemma 1) and Błasiok et al. (2023) for the loss-minimization-implies-calibration template.

title: Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-14

Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries

Daniel Barzilai, Ohad Shamir (Weizmann) — COLT 2026 — arXiv:2602.05704

Main idea. The paper attacks a soft spot in the folklore that underwrites most "gradient descent can't learn this" results. Statistical Query lower bounds are routinely read as evidence about SGD, on the reasoning that a stochastic gradient is a noisy estimate of the population gradient. But SQ oracles allow adversarial (or conveniently isotropic) noise, whereas real SGD noise is zero-mean, data-dependent, anisotropic, and evolving. Barzilai and Shamir argue this gap is not merely aesthetic: SQ sometimes predicts the wrong answer.

Their cleanest counterexample (Appendix A, Theorem 7) is deliberately trivial as a learning problem: the dictator class $\mathcal{F}={f_i(x)=x_i}$ on ${\pm1}^d$. Information-theoretically $O(\log d)$ samples identify $i$, and Amid–Warmuth (2020) show SGD on a simple sparsely-connected two-layer net finds $i$ in $O(\log d)$ iterations. Yet in a vector-valued SQ model with tolerance $\tau$, any algorithm needs $\ge \tfrac12\tau^2 d$ queries — so every choice of $\tau$ forces a $\mathrm{poly}(d)$ predicted sample complexity, exponentially pessimistic. The diagnosis is geometric: the natural query $\phi(x,y)=yx/\sqrt d$ has a deterministic coordinate $1/\sqrt d$ at index $i$ and uniform $\pm1/\sqrt d$ elsewhere, so $O(\log d)$ averages suffice; the SQ oracle instead sees only "a mean vector $O(1/\sqrt d)$-far from the origin in the unit ball," whose worst-case estimation genuinely costs $\Omega(d)$. The same pattern recurs in Li et al. (2019) matrix mean estimation and Dudeja–Hsu spiked Wigner.

The replacement framework tracks vanilla SGD directly — batch size 1, single samples, no sphere projection, no gradient-flow step size, no injected noise — for predictors $f_\theta(x)=h(Wx;\bar\theta)$ whose only input access is a learned linear map. Hardness is measured by the alignment $\rho(W,U)=|P_WP_U|_{\mathrm{op}}$, the cosine of the smallest principal angle between the learned row space and the hidden task subspace.

The cleverest piece. The technical linchpin is the gradient condition number $\kappa_T = G^2/\inf_{v}\min_{t\le T}\mathbb E_t[(v^\top\nabla_{W_{t-1}x_t}\ell)^2]$, a worst-case-to-typical ratio of squared gradient magnitude taken after projection to the $m$-dimensional pre-activation space. Because it lives in $m$ dimensions it is plausibly $d$-free, and it exactly quantifies "the gradient coefficients are not dominated by rare heavy-tailed events" — the one thing needed to make anisotropic, adapted SGD noise behave like an isotropic walk. What makes this more than a convenient assumption is the sanity check in the discussion: Abbe–Sandon's synthetic network that does learn parities with SGD (the standing embarrassment for the SQ-as-SGD story) has $\kappa_T\to\infty$, because its memorization mechanism makes certain neurons' gradients vanish at a time point. The condition powering the lower bound is precisely the one the known SQ-circumventing construction violates — a rare instance of a hardness framework whose hypothesis is calibrated against the counterexample rather than assumed away.

Honestly: $\kappa_T$ is assumed bounded for general deep predictors and only proved bounded for two-layer nets. The applications use Gaussian inputs and the correlation loss; batch size is 1; deep-network results need $d\gg m$; and the result is a first-layer feature-learning obstruction, not an information-theoretic one. Most importantly the bound is indexed by the information exponent $k_\star$, so it says nothing about SGD variants with label preprocessing or batch reuse, where the generative exponent $k^\dagger \le k_\star$ is the right quantity.

Proof sketch. Theorem 2 (general). Under sub-Gaussian inputs with norm concentration, standard $\Theta(1/d)$-variance i.i.d. initialization, a.s. bounded $|\nabla_{Wx}\ell|\le G$, and any increasing $\psi$ with $|\nabla_WL(\theta)|_F\le\psi(|P_WP_U|_{\mathrm{op}})$: if $d\gtrsim\bar\kappa^2m^2\log(\cdot)$, $\eta\lesssim \bar\kappa^{-2}(md\log)^{-1/2}$, and $T\le 1/\psi(C\sqrt{\bar\kappa mp\log(\cdot)/d})^2$, then conditioned on $\kappa_T\le\bar\kappa$, w.p. $1-\delta$, $|P_{W_t}P_U|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\sqrt{\bar\kappa mp\log(Tdp/\delta)/d}$ for all $t\le T$ — alignment never exceeds its value at random initialization, up to constants.

The mechanism: since $\nabla_W\ell=\nabla_{Wx}\ell\cdot x^\top$, for any unit $v$ the projected weights satisfy $(W_t-W_0)^\top v=\eta\sum_j a_j(v)x_j$ with $a_j(v)=\langle\nabla_{W_{j-1}x_j}\ell,v\rangle$ bounded by $G$. Decompose into drift plus a martingale difference, then bound a ratio. Numerator: the martingale contribution to any fixed direction grows only as $\sqrt t$ (Azuma-type vector concentration for sub-Gaussian MDS). Denominator: $|W_t^\top v|\gtrsim 1+\eta\sqrt{dt/\kappa}-2\eta t\max_j|\nabla_WL|_F$ — the norm grows as $\sqrt{dt}$, and this is exactly where $\kappa_T$ enters, via $\sum_j a_j^2|x_j|^2\gtrsim \alpha_2 d\sum_j\mathbb E_j[a_j^2]$. So noise pushes the weight norm up by $\sqrt d$ faster than it pushes any particular direction — the isotropic-random-walk picture, made rigorous for an adapted, anisotropic process. A covering argument over $v\in S^{m-1}$ with an $\epsilon$-net of size $(3/\epsilon)^m$ upgrades this to the operator norm, and an SVD reduction handles the $p$-dimensional subspace. The final step is an induction over iterations: small alignment ⇒ small population gradient (via $\psi$) ⇒ drift stays below the noise floor ⇒ alignment stays small at $t+1$. Not a Lyapunov argument in the ODE sense, but a self-consistent bootstrap over a high-probability event.

Instantiations. Hermite analysis supplies $\psi$: $|\nabla_WL|_F\le G_1|\nabla g_U|_{L_2}(\sqrt m\rho+1)\rho^{k_\star-1}$, since $P_W^{\otimes k}$ and $P_U^{\otimes k}$ annihilate all Hermite tensors below $k_\star$. Theorem 6 then gives $T=\tilde\Theta(d^{k_\star-1})+\Theta(d\epsilon^2/p)$ iterations during which the loss barely moves; the $k_\star=1$ case is vacuous under this $\psi$ and is patched separately. Theorem 3 handles $f^\star(x)=\sin(u^\top x)$ with $|u|=\sqrt d$: here $\psi(\rho)=(1+\sqrt d)\exp(-\tfrac d2(1-\rho^2))$ is exponentially small, giving $\exp(d^{1/3})$ iterations of exponentially-small loss change.

Context and a follow-up. This sits directly opposite Ben Arous–Gheissari–Jagannath (2021), whose $d^{k_\star-1}$ thresholds required spherical SGD and tiny step sizes; Braun et al. (2025) recently pushed the upper bound to vanilla SGD, and this paper supplies the matching lower side. Abbe–Boix-Adserà–Misiakiewicz's leap complexity plays the analogous role under CSQ; Damian et al. (2024a) showed landscape smoothing beats $k_\star$, and Damian–Pillaud-Vivien–Lee–Bruna replaced $k_\star$ by the generative exponent for algorithms allowed to transform labels. The two most worth reading alongside this are Damian et al. (2024b) and Joshi–Misiakiewicz–Srebro (2024) on SQ vs. gradient queries as separate complexity measures. Obvious follow-up: prove the $k^\dagger$-indexed analogue in this non-SQ framework, or characterize when $\kappa_T$ is polynomially bounded — a theorem of the form "every architecture with $\kappa_T=\mathrm{poly}(m)$ fails on parities in $\mathrm{poly}(d)$ steps" would turn Abbe–Sandon from a counterexample into a provably pathological outlier.

Relevance to your work. Real but methodological rather than topical. Structurally, a dense-retrieval encoder is a predictor of the form $f_\theta(x)=h(Wx;\bar\theta)$ — input access factors through a learned low-rank map — and $|P_WP_U|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is precisely the principal-angle overlap between the learned embedding subspace and a hypothesized latent relevance subspace, the same object that shows up in LSI-style analyses. Theorem 2 is loss- and architecture-agnostic (the loss enters only through $\kappa_T$ and $\psi$), so instantiating it for a two-tower encoder trained with a contrastive objective is not a category error; the work would be computing $\psi$ for InfoNCE against a structured relevance model, which is where the Hermite machinery does not transfer. The transferable lesson is broader and cheaper: oracle-model lower bounds constrain the oracle, not the algorithm. IR theory leans on the same move — cell-probe bounds for ANN, communication bounds for sketching — and this is a clean demonstration that the oracle's worst-case geometry can be badly mismatched with the algorithm's actual noise geometry, yielding a prediction that is exponentially wrong on a problem a two-layer net solves in $O(\log d)$ steps.

title: Reranking with Compressed Document Representation
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-14

Reranking with Compressed Document Representation

Hervé Déjean, Stéphane Clinchant (Naver Labs Europe) — 2025 — arXiv:2505.15394

Purely empirical — no theorem, so no proof-sketch section.

Main idea. RRK ("compressed ReRanKer") replaces the document text at the reranker's input with a frozen, precomputed soft representation. The compressor is PISCO (naver/pisco-mistral), a Mistral-7B with LoRA adapters trained for RAG context compression: append l memory tokens to a document, take their final hidden states as the document code. Here l = 8, so each document becomes 8 embeddings, and with a 24-token query budget the reranker's input is a fixed 32 positions regardless of document length. The scorer is a separately LoRA-finetuned Mistral-7B decoder (and a 16-layer truncated variant) with a linear head on the EOS representation; the compressor stays frozen so the same index serves reranking and RAG generation. Training is pure distillation, inverted in size: teacher is naver/trecdl22-crossencoder-debertav3 over SPLADE-v3 top-50, MSE on scores, 0.5M MS MARCO queries × 8 sampled documents, 2 epochs, 24 GPU-hours on one A100. Evaluation is nDCG@10 on TREC-DL 19/20, 12 BEIR sets, LoTTE pooled, plus TREC-NEWS for long documents.

Reviewer critique. The headline claim — comparable effectiveness, much faster — is true only against the strawman the paper itself defeats. BEIR averages at 512 tokens: ModernBERT-large 57.9, textual Mistral-7B 57.8, teacher 57.4, RRK 56.9, RRK-16L 56.2, first stage 51.8. So compression costs ~0.9 against its own textual twin and ~1.0 against a 400M encoder that is also twice as fast as RRK. The paper concedes this ("a good choice is to distill your favorite reranker with ModernBERT"), which is refreshingly honest, but the abstract's framing does not.

The loss is also not uniformly distributed, and the handling of that is the weakest move in the paper. Touché-v2: 35.2 → 28.9. FEVER: 88.4 → 84.2. The response is "we cannot explain yet" followed by "ignoring these datasets reduces the differences by 50%." Discarding exactly the collections where you lose is not an analysis — and these are plausibly the informative cases: stance-sensitive argument retrieval and claim verification against full Wikipedia pages are precisely where fixed-width coding should fail first. No significance testing anywhere, no seed variance, on a 16-dataset suite where the headline gaps are ≤1 point.

Efficiency accounting is not apples-to-apples. Figure 1 is an online-latency plot; the offline side is never costed. A 7B forward pass over 8.8M passages is never reported in GPU-hours, and the resulting index is 270 GB versus 154 GB for ColBERTv2 — which does retrieval, not just reranking of a top-50 someone else produced. The amortization argument (the index is reused by the RAG generator) is asserted, never demonstrated: there is no end-to-end RAG experiment. The long-document result rests on a single collection: at 768 tokens TREC-NEWS gives RRK 53.1 vs textual Mistral 52.3, ModernBERT-large 51.2, DeBERTa 48.6 — 0.8 points, n=1 collection, no significance test, and non-monotone (RRK drops to 51.9 at 1024). Part of the baselines' decline is likely a truncation artifact rather than a genuine compression advantage.

Most importantly, the experiment that would make this a paper about compression is missing: there is no sweep over l. Everything is at 8 memory tokens. Without an effectiveness-vs-rate curve, we learn that one operating point roughly replicates a mid-sized teacher, not where the bottleneck actually binds. The distillation ceiling compounds this: all students cluster at 56–58 because the teacher is 57.4, so the setup cannot reveal whether compression would cost more against a stronger teacher.

Broader context. This is soft prompt compression (Gist tokens, AutoCompressor, ICAE, xRAG's single-token extreme) transplanted from generation to ranking, where the downstream signal is a scalar rather than a sequence — a much narrower target, which is why 8 tokens suffices at all.
