The connection to your area is real but needs care about which collapse is which. Rank collapse is within-sequence: tokens of one input converge. Embedding anisotropy — the cone effect of Ethayarajh (2019) and the representation-degeneration problem of Gao et al. (2019) — is across-inputs: distinct documents' vectors occupy a narrow cone with a dominant shared mean direction. They are not the same theorem, but they share a mechanism and a consequence. Mechanistically, the shared component in X_ℓ ≈ 1_n y^T + R is exactly what mean-pooling amplifies, so a partially collapsed encoder produces document vectors dominated by y with a small residual carrying all the discriminative signal. Consequentially, that is the regime where inner-product contrast concentrates, effective intrinsic dimension drops, and graph-based ANN indices degrade — the same reason whitening and centring (BERT-flow, BERT-whitening) reliably help dense retrieval, and the same reason contrastive objectives include an explicit uniformity term (Wang–Isola 2020). There is even a structural rhyme on the algorithms side: the low-rank kernel approximation that makes small-weight attention almost-linear is the tool that makes kernel density estimation and near-neighbour search tractable, so "small weights" and "the attention matrix is ANN-indexable" are two views of one fact.

A follow-up worth doing, and cheap: measure ‖W‖_∞ layer-by-layer in contrastively trained retrieval encoders versus LM-pretrained backbones, and correlate it with how many layers can be pruned before nDCG moves. The prediction from this paper — that low-η layers are removable — is directly testable against the layer-pruning literature, and the contrastive-uniformity hypothesis predicts retrieval fine-tuning should increase η relative to the backbone. On the theory side, an ℓ₂ or spectral-norm version, stated for a model with LayerNorm and a causal mask, would be the version one could actually apply to an encoder, and would likely need a genuinely different argument since LayerNorm rescales precisely the residual Res(X) that the contraction lemma shrinks.

Proof sketch — The measure is Res(Z) := Z − 1_n y^T with y = argmin_y ‖Z − 1_n y^T‖∞, i.e. distance to token-uniformity in entrywise ℓ∞ (DCL21 used a composite ℓ_{1,∞} norm; the ℓ_∞ choice is what lets η ≪ β, so this theorem applies where DCL21's is vacuous). Lemma 4.1 gives non-expansiveness: ‖A − B‖∞ ≤ ε ⇒ ‖Res(A) − Res(B)‖∞ ≤ ε. Lemmas 4.2–4.4 give the softmax perturbation bound ‖softmax(a + b) − softmax(a)‖_∞ ≤ 2(e^{‖b‖_∞} − 1).

Contraction (Lemma 5.1). Write X = 1_n x^T + R, R = Res(X), and expand the logit matrix A = βXWX^T + β1_n b^T X^T with W = W_q W_k^T. Every column-constant term is killed by shift-invariance, leaving P = softmax(E + 1_n r^T) with E = βRWR^T. The key trick is Lemma B.1: if D_ii := max_{j,l} |E_ij − E_il| (the θ-balance of E), then P is sandwiched entrywise, e^{−D_ii} P̃_ij ≤ P_ij ≤ e^{D_ii} P̃_ij, against P̃ = softmax(1_n r^T), which has identical rows. So the attention matrix is a multiplicative e^{±θ} perturbation of a rank-1 stochastic matrix, and ‖Res(SAtt(X))‖_∞ ≤ K‖Res(X)‖_∞ with K = (e^θ − 1)‖W_v‖_∞. Lemma B.2 secures θ = 1 from ‖E‖∞ ≤ β‖Res(X)‖²∞ η² whenever β ≤ 1/(‖Res(X)‖²_∞ η²) — an assumption on the temperature masquerading as the 1/√d normaliser, and the least honest step in the paper. This lemma is where DCL21's double exponential comes from: θ is itself quadratic in ‖R‖, so the recursion is ‖R_{ℓ+1}‖ ≲ βη³‖R_ℓ‖³, giving the 3^L exponent. Alman–Song deliberately freeze θ = 1 and take only the linear factor K = O(η), trading the doubly exponential rate for a bound that survives skip connections.

Deleting a layer (Lemmas 5.2 / C.1). Let B = X + Σ_{i=1}^H A_i be the post-residual stream, each head output satisfying ‖Res(A_i)‖∞ ≤ K‖Res(X)‖∞ ≤ ε. Since Res is non-expansive, ‖Res(B) − Res(X)‖_∞ ≤ Hε, and since softmax only sees Res, the next layer's attention pattern moves by at most g(2Hε) with g(ε) = 2(e^ε − 1); a telescoping sum over heads plus a triangle-inequality split into an attention-pattern term and a value term (bounded by ‖W_v‖_∞ ≤ η) yields ‖softmv(B) − softmv(X)‖_∞ ≤ 3g(2Hε). This is precisely why skip connections do not help: the residual path adds back a near-token-constant matrix, and token-constant matrices are annihilated by the softmax that consumes them.

Induction (Theorem 5.3, Appendix D). Define B_ℓ^{ℓ₀} as the network run with the residual connection from layer ℓ₀ removed. Lemma D.7 controls norm growth, ‖X_ℓ‖_∞ ≤ φ₀(1 + Hη)^ℓ, which instantiates ε_ℓ := 2ηφ₀(1 + Hη)^ℓ and verifies the hypotheses of Lemma C.1 at every layer. Lemma D.5 gives each layer a Lipschitz constant C = max_ℓ 3η(ε_ℓ² + 1) in ℓ_∞. Deleting the first layer perturbs the second by δ = max_ℓ 2g(2Hε_ℓ); propagating through the remaining layers multiplies by powers of C, so removing L − 1 layers costs (C^{L−1} + … + C + 1)δ. Because C = O(η) < 1, the geometric series is O(1) and the total is O(δ) = O(Hηφ₀), i.e. O(η)‖X‖_∞ with the head count in the constant. Remark D.1 notes MLPs pass through with their Lipschitz constant attached. The weight-norm parameter η thus plays three roles at once — it bounds the contraction factor K, the per-layer Lipschitz constant C, and the norm growth (1 + Hη)^L — and the theorem is exactly the regime where all three are simultaneously benign.

title: Online Omniprediction with Long-Term Constraints
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-12

Online Omniprediction with Long-Term Constraints

Yahav Bechavod, Jiuyao Lu, Aaron Roth (UPenn) · 2025 · arXiv:2509.11357

Main idea — Omniprediction is the idea that you can decouple forecasting from deciding: a single forecaster publishes predictions p_t of an outcome y_t, and any downstream agent with its own utility can just myopically best-respond, a_t = argmax_a u(a, p_t), and thereby inherit a no-regret guarantee — without ever running a learning algorithm itself. This works because the classic online problem is separable across time: the ideal play is round-by-round. Long-term constraints break exactly that. If an agent must satisfy Σ_t c_j(a_t, y_t) ≤ 0, its decisions are coupled across time, and differently coupled for each agent. The paper's move is to restore separability by pushing the coupling into a shrinking feasible set rather than into the decision rule: each agent maintains a candidate set Â^c_t, plays the constrained best response argmax_{a ∈ Â^c_t} u(a, p_t), and permanently eliminates any action observed to violate a constraint. One broadcast prediction stream then gives every agent Õ(√T) swap regret against its own benchmark A^c_{1:T} (actions feasible on every round) and O(1) cumulative constraint violation.

The most interesting part — There is no Lagrangian and no primal-dual machinery here, which is the surprise given how the long-term-constraints literature usually proceeds. Instead the two halves of the guarantee are proved by completely disjoint arguments. Constraint violation is bounded by a counting argument that holds for arbitrary predictions: an action can only be played-and-violating once before it is deleted, so CCV ≤ |A| regardless of forecaster quality. Regret then needs only one structural invariant — A^c_{1:T} ⊆ Â^c_t for all t, since benchmark actions are never eliminated — so the swapped-in comparator is always available to the agent at the moment it best-responds. Elimination is thus simultaneously the constraint mechanism and harmless to the regret analysis. The subsequence extension (Alg. 4) is where real work happens: summed violations can be negative, so slack on S \ S' can mask damage on S ∩ S', and they fix this by attributing each round to a unique "responsible" subsequence and thresholding attributed violations pairwise.

Honest critique: the |A| factor is multiplicative in regret — O(L|A|√(T log(d|A||N|T/δ))) — and additive in CCV, with no lower bound offered. This is unusable for structured action spaces (rankings, subsets) and there is no infinite-A version. "Omniprediction" is also relative to a known, finite, pre-registered collection N: the forecaster must simulate every agent's elimination state, so per-round cost is polynomial in |A||N| (a minimax solve over Δ𝒴 against 2d|A||N| bias directions) even though the regret pays only log|N|. The predictor is oblivious in its interface, not in its construction. Most importantly, A^c_{1:T} — actions never violating on any round — is a very thin benchmark in genuinely adversarial settings; it can collapse to the null action, at which point O(1) violation is cheap. The richer expectation benchmark is defined against the adversary's unobservable per-round distribution and costs Õ(|A|√T) violation. And Theorem 6's subsequence bound sums √|S'| over all subsequences, so a short subsequence carries a violation bound that can dwarf its own length — vacuous unless the collection is small and the subsequences long.

Broader context — The lineage: multicalibration (Hébert-Johnson et al.) → omniprediction in the batch setting (Gopalan et al. 2022) → online versions where calibration is unattainable at √T rates (Qiao–Valiant lower bounds), forcing weaker-but-sufficient surrogates like U-calibration (Kleinberg et al.) and decision calibration (Zhao et al.; Noarov et al. 2023). Noarov et al.'s Unbiased-Prediction is the engine here and is essentially Blackwell approachability in disguise: exponential weights over signed coordinate-events defines a potential, and each round's minimax problem has value ≤ 0 by a fixed-point argument on the convex set 𝒴 — the approachability condition. On the other side sit Mannor et al. (2009) (you cannot compete with marginally-feasible actions) and Sinha–Vaze (2024), the strongest assumption-free Õ(√T)/Õ(√T) OCO-with-constraints rates. Worth reading alongside: Globus-Harris et al. / Hu et al. on batch omniprediction under group-fairness constraints.

A natural follow-up: replace the |A| factor with a statistic-complexity factor. In many constrained problems — ranking especially — u and c depend on the action only through a low-dimensional summary (a position-weighted exposure vector), so one could ask for decision calibration conditional on a discretised exposure statistic and hope for poly(n) where |A| = n!.

The IR connection is loose but not forced. A retrieval system publishing relevance scores consumed by many downstream rankers, ad auctions and diversity filters is literally the omniprediction setting; amortised exposure-fairness constraints (Morik et al., SIGIR 2020, who use a proportional controller) are literally long-term constraints; and the subsequence guarantee is the online analogue of group-conditional calibration over query slices. What this paper does not yet give you is any of that at ranking-sized action spaces.

Proof sketch — Setting: 𝒴 = [0,1]^d, finite A, a known collection N of agents (u, c_1, …, c_J) with u(a, ·) linear and L-Lipschitz in ℓ_∞ (c arbitrary, not even convex), adversary adaptively choosing x_t and a distribution Y_t over outcomes. Every agent runs Algorithm 1.

Claim 1 (Thm. 1). CCV(1:T) ≤ |A|, for any forecaster. Partition rounds by action played; for every round in R_a except the last, a survived, so c_j(a, y_t) ≤ 0; only the final round of each R_a contributes, at most 1 each, over at most |A| actions.

Claim 2 (Thm. 3). If predictions are (N, α₁)-decision calibrated — ‖Σ_t 1CBR^u_{Â^c_t}(p_t) = a‖_∞ ≤ α₁(T^{u,c}(a)) for every agent and action, α₁ concave — then Reg_swap(u, A^c_{1:T}) ≤ 2L|A|·α₁(T/|A|). Decompose Σ_t [u(φ(a_t), y_t) − u(a_t, y_t)] into (i) Σ_t[u(φ(a_t), y_t) − u(φ(a_t), p_t)], (ii) Σ_t[u(φ(a_t), p_t) − u(a_t, p_t)], (iii) Σ_t[u(a_t, p_t) − u(a_t, y_t)]. Term (ii) is ≤ 0 precisely by the invariant φ(a_t) ∈ A^c_{1:T} ⊆ Â^c_t plus constrained best response. Terms (i) and (iii) are bounded by grouping rounds by played action, using linearity to pull the sum inside u, Lipschitzness to reduce to ‖Σ_t 1a_t = a‖_∞, decision calibration, and Jensen on the concave α₁ with Σ_a T^{u,c}(a) = T.

Claim 3 (Thm. 4 / Cor. 2). Instantiate Unbiased-Prediction with events E = {1[CBR^u_{Â^c_t}(p_t) = a]}, |E| = |A||N| — legitimate because Â^c_t is a function of the transcript. Its per-round minimax step (no-regret exponential weights over bias directions vs. an adversary, value ≤ 0 by a fixed point) gives α₁(n) = O(log(d|E|T) + √(log(d|E|T)·n)) in expectation over the randomisation; Azuma–Hoeffding on the martingale difference between realised and expected bias per coordinate/event, plus a union bound, converts this to realised predictions at an additive √(log(d|E|/δ)T). Combining yields the stated bound with probability 1 − δ, simultaneously for all agents.

For the expectation benchmark, Azuma–Hoeffding does the heavier lifting: Algorithm 2 eliminates a once v^{a,j}_{1:t} = Σ_s 1[a_s = a]c_j(a, y_s) exceeds τ; the summands form a martingale difference sequence because a_t is F_{t−1}-measurable (it depends only on p_t and history), so with τ = 4√(T log(|A||N|JT/δ)) no benchmark action is ever eliminated w.p. 1 − δ, yielding CCV ≤ |A|(τ + 1).

title: The Coverage Principle: How Pre-training Enables Post-Training
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-12

The Coverage Principle: How Pre-training Enables Post-training

Fan Chen, Audrey Huang, Noah Golowich, Sadhika Malladi, Adam Block, Jordan T. Ash, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster · 2025 · arXiv:2510.15020

Main idea — The paper asks what functional of a pre-trained model actually predicts whether post-training (RLVR, or its test-time proxy Best-of-N) will work, and argues the answer is not cross-entropy but a tail statistic of the density ratio. Their object is the coverage profile: Cov_N(π_D‖π̂) = P[ π_D(y|x)/π̂(y|x) ≥ N ], the probability that the pre-trained π̂ underweights a data-distribution response by more than the inference budget N. Note this is not a χ² or L_p concentrability coefficient; it is the full CDF of the log-ratio, of which KL is the mean and of which the usual L_p coverage coefficients are Markov-type upper bounds. That refinement is the whole point. Sequence-level KL is an average over the ratio and is destroyed by missing mass: responses a well-generalising learner will never cover contribute log W_max, which for autoregressive models scales with the horizon H. The coverage profile simply writes that mass off. Cross-entropy therefore predicts an exponential test-time scaling law N ≈ exp(D_KL/ε), vacuous once D_KL ∝ H, while coverage is horizon-free. The main theorems show next-token prediction implicitly optimises coverage — the "coverage principle" — and that gradient normalisation and coverage-based checkpoint tournaments provably sharpen this.

The most interesting part — The sharpest result is the separation: for autoregressive linear models there is an instance (Prop. 3.2) where every proper estimator suffers D_KL(π_D‖π̂) ≥ H/4n with constant probability — and the construction can be arranged so the inherent variance σ² ≤ 1 — yet Theorem 4.2 gives E[Cov_N(π̂)] ≲ √(σ²/(n log N)) + B²/n, with no H anywhere. The Bernoulli warm-up is the same phenomenon in one line: MLE on Ber(p_) has E[D_KL] = +∞ whenever the sample misses the rare outcome, while Cov_N ≲ log(1/δ)/n. Equally clever is Theorem 6.1: token-level SGD plus a test-time-training decoder (a gradient step on each sampled token, reset per prompt) gets horizon-free coverage — a _provable benefit of impropriety* that dodges the Prop. 3.2 lower bound outright.

Reviewer's caveats, and they are not small. Realizability (π_D ∈ Π) carries most of the load; Prop. E.1 shows that under even α-misspecification MLE can land on a model with Cov_N ≳ α²/log M when a zero-coverage model is in the class, and the repair (Theorem E.1, 1/N^{1−2c} rates) needs convexity of θ ↦ π_θ(y|x), which transformers do not have. The advertised "faster generalisation" is mostly removing log W_max, not a strong N-dependence: the fine term improves only as 1/log N and the coarse term not at all, and Prop. 4.1 shows both are tight for MLE. Capacity is measured by ∞-norm covering numbers — conservative, and vacuous at LLM scale. The gradient-normalisation theorem normalises the global gradient norm on a fresh minibatch; the bridge to Adam/SignSGD is explicitly labelled speculative. Most importantly, the direction that would alarm a practitioner — cross-entropy improving while coverage degrades — is a theorem only in the misspecified toy (Prop. E.1); in the main results it is a figure. And that figure comes from a synthetic layered-DAG graph-search task with a hand-tuned 0.9/0.1 mode mixture built precisely so that fitting the dominant mode costs coverage on the rare one, evaluated at Pass@N rather than actual RL, with Cov_N computable only because π_D is synthetic (Remark 2.2 concedes neither KL nor coverage is estimable in general). The tournaments are the one actionable intervention, and Theorem 6.3 pays a polynomial budget slack, while Theorem 6.4 removes the slack only under a uniform |log π_D − log π| ≤ a log N condition far stronger than realizability, plus on-policy sampling from every candidate.

Broader context — Best-of-N draws N samples and keeps the highest-reward one; rejection sampling and RLHF/RLVR pipelines all amplify what the base model already puts mass on, which is why Yue et al. (2025) and Wu et al. (2025) find RLVR rarely escapes the base model's support. Offline RL formalised exactly this with concentrability coefficients (Chen–Jiang, Xie–Jiang, Foster et al.), where coverage grades the dataset; here it grades the model, and this paper supplies the missing argument for why pre-training should deliver it. The closest neighbours are Huang et al., "Is Best-of-N the Best of Them?" (ICML'25), whose BoN analysis is imported wholesale as Prop. D.6, and Chen et al. (2025) on Pass@N degrading with continued pre-training — the empirical shadow of Figure 1.

The generative-retrieval connection is real but needs care. A DSI/NCI/RIPOR-style model is trained by MLE on (query, docid) pairs and evaluated by whether a relevant docid appears among N decoded candidates — precisely a coverage-profile question, and the characteristic failure (tail queries, rare documents, heterogeneous prompt distribution) is exactly the missing-mass regime where the paper argues sequence-level CE is a misleading model-selection criterion. Two honest gaps: docid horizons are short (H ~ 4–32), so horizon-independence buys less than it does for chain-of-thought; and trie-constrained beam search returns the N modes, not N i.i.d. samples, so Prop. D.6 does not apply as stated — the right object is a rank-based coverage condition, and the sampling-based analysis transfers cleanly only to stochastic or ensembled decoding. Conversely, the paper's own "semantic coverage" and answer-level Cov^ans_N remarks are the IR duplicate-document problem verbatim: what matters is coverage of the relevance-equivalence class, not of one docid string. A natural follow-up: treat trie-constrained decoding as an improper test-time intervention in the sense of Theorem 6.1 and ask whether renormalising onto the valid-docid set provably improves the coverage profile over the relevant set — and pair it with the offset tournament as a recall@N-aware checkpoint selector, directly implementable since candidate generations are cheap in retrieval.

Proof sketch — The BoN sandwich comes first. Sufficiency (Prop. D.6): if Cov_M(π_T‖π̂) ≤ 1/2 and N ≥ 2M log(1/ε), BoN's suboptimality against π_T is ≤ Cov_M + ε. Necessity (Prop. D.7) is a one-line adversarial construction: take S_x = {y : π_T/π̂ ≥ 2N} and reward r_T = 1{y ∈ S_x}; a union bound gives P_BoN(S_x) ≤ N·π̂(S_x) ≤ ½·π_T(S_x), so the gap is ≥ ½·Cov_2N. Note the quantifier: coverage is necessary for some reward, not for yours.

Prop. 3.1 (Cov_N ≤ D_KL/(log N − 1 + 1/N)) is an f-divergence tail bound (Block–Polyanskiy) with f(x) = x log x − x + 1, tight via π_D = Ber(p), π̂ = Ber(p/N). Prop. 3.2's lower bound is a two-point/Le Cam argument with a rare prompt: μ(1) = 1/(2n), so with probability ≥ 1/2 the sample never sees x = 1, the posterior over θ* ∈ {±1} is untouched, and any estimator pays μ(1)·H·Θ(1) = Θ(H/n) in KL.

Theorem 4.1 is the centrepiece, and the strategy is a one-sided, small-ball argument in the spirit of Mendelson. Split the empirical log-likelihood gap through a clipped loss, L̂_n(π) − L̂_n(π_D) = L⁺_C(π) − L⁻_C(π), the positive/negative parts of log(π/π_D) truncated at ∓C. Two facts close it. (i) The upper bound on L⁺_C uses the trick that makes everything work: Lemma H.1 shows E_{π_D} exp(½ max{log(π/π_D), −C}) ≤ 1 — a Hellinger/Cauchy–Schwarz computation — so a chaining bound applies with no dependence on the density-ratio range, because only the upside is controlled. (ii) The lower bound on L⁻_C: each example with π_D/π ≥ N contributes at least log N − C, so L⁻_C(π) ≥ n(log N − C)·Ĉov_N(π); Freedman's inequality plus a union bound over an α-cover at the coarse scale α = ¼ log N transfers Ĉov to Cov. Since π̂ maximises likelihood, L⁻_C(π̂) ≤ L⁺_C(π̂) and the two combine. The coarse term exists because only the indicator needs to concentrate, not the log-loss; the 1/log N arises because each uncovered example is charged log N — the implicit bias of the logarithmic loss. Prop. 4.1 shows both terms are unavoidable for MLE.

For autoregressive models the workhorse is Prop. D.10: with the stopping time τ = first step where cumulative token-level KL exceeds log N, the chain rule on the stopped process plus Markov gives Cov_N ≤ (2/(log N − 1))·E[min{log N, Σ_h D_KL,h}]. This stopped KL is bounded by construction even when KL is infinite, and it is what replaces H by the inherent variance σ² (a local-norm bound, Lemma F.4, converts feature displacement into √(Var·ε) + Bε). The same quantity drives the SGD results: vanilla single-pass SGD has a matching lower bound Cov_N ≳ min{H/(T log N), 1} caused by gradient-scale heterogeneity across prompts (no single step size serves both), normalised SGD removes it, and the distillation estimator truncates token gradients exactly when the running KL crosses log N — i.e. it descends the stopped divergence directly.

title: Tokenisation is NP-Complete
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-12

Tokenisation is NP-Complete

Philip Whittington, Gregor Bachmann, Tiago Pimentel (ETH Zürich) · 2024 · arXiv:2412.15210

Main idea — The paper asks whether the training of a tokeniser — not its application — is tractable, once you fix compression as the objective. A tokeniser is a triple ⟨S, tok, detok⟩ with Σ ⊆ S, |S| = |Σ| + K, and detok = concat. Two ways of specifying tok are separated cleanly. In direct tokenisation you choose a vocabulary S and then encode each string by the shortest S-segmentation; this inner problem is polynomial (a shortest-path DP, Schmidt et al.'s PathPiece, O(|c|²)). In bottom-up tokenisation you choose an ordered merge sequence m of length K, apply merges left-to-right in order, and read the vocabulary off the merges — the BPE setting, where order matters and the resulting segmentation is generally not the shortest one available for that vocabulary. The two decision problems are: given a dataset D, a budget K and a target δ, is there an S (resp. an m) of size K with Σ_{c∈D} |tok(c)| ≤ δ? Both are shown NP-complete, by reduction from max-2-SAT, along with the deduplicated-dataset, single-string and hybrid (merges-then-optimal-segmentation) variants. Direct tokenisation on a single string is the one exception: put the string in the vocabulary and you are done.

The most interesting part — The cleverness is concentrated in one small gadget: a clause is encoded as the string ⊚L¹⊚L²⊚, where the two candidate subwords ⊚L¹⊚ and ⊚L²⊚ share the middle separator. Because they overlap, at most one can ever be applied, so the string shrinks from 5 symbols to 3 exactly when at least one literal is "true" (i.e. its token was selected) and never further. Disjunction is thus implemented as physical overlap in the string, and the savings counter is literally 2·Σᵢ 1{L¹ᵢ ∨ L²ᵢ}. Everything else is bookkeeping to force the vocabulary into the shape of an assignment.

Reviewer-side, though, the result is narrower than the title suggests. The alphabet grows with the instance (2J+1 symbols); real tokenisers run over 256 bytes, and the paper does not settle whether hardness survives a constant alphabet — a gap I would consider the main open question, not a footnote. The hard instances are also wildly artificial: datasets consisting of Θ(I·J) repetitions of six-character strings, tuned so that the multiplicities cascade. Nothing is said about parameterised complexity in K, about typical-case behaviour, or (here) about inapproximability — Kozma and Voderholzer's concurrent APX-hardness for bottom-up is the stronger statement. And the objective is itself contested: the paper's own citations (Schmidt et al., Ali et al.) argue compression is at best a loose proxy for downstream quality, while Geh et al. had already shown NP-completeness under a likelihood objective. So the honest reading is "another proxy objective is also hard", which supports the practical conclusion (use approximations) without telling us anything about how bad BPE actually is on real text.

Broader context — BPE greedily merges the most frequent adjacent pair; WordPiece merges by a likelihood-gain criterion; UnigramLM starts from a large seed vocabulary and prunes to maximise unigram log-likelihood under a Viterbi segmentation. All three are heuristics for objectives nobody has optimised exactly, and the compression objective connects them to dictionary compression — smallest-grammar/SLP problems, which are also NP-hard (Charikar et al.), though compressors pay for the dictionary and tokenisers do not. Worth reading alongside: Zouhar et al. (2023b), which gives the first approximation bound on BPE's compression, and Kozma & Voderholzer (2024), which tightens it and proves APX-hardness.

A follow-up I would actually pursue: characterise the modularity of the compression-gain function. The reduction's gadgets exploit substitutability (overlapping subwords cannot both fire), while bottom-up merges create complementarity (one merge enables another), so the gain is neither sub- nor supermodular — which is precisely why greedy carries no (1−1/e)-style guarantee. Identifying structural conditions (bounded overlap, prefix-closed vocabularies) under which it becomes submodular would yield the first principled guarantee for vocabulary selection.

For your own work the link is real but analogical, not a corollary. Generative-retrieval docid construction — semantic IDs, RQ-VAE codebooks, hierarchical clustering IDs — is formally "choose K codewords to represent a corpus under a length budget", i.e. direct tokenisation with a different objective. The hardness does not transfer (different objective, and docid codebooks are learned, not combinatorially optimised), but the direct-tokenisation formalism is a clean template for stating docid-vocabulary design as an optimisation problem rather than an architecture choice — and the single-string degeneracy is a useful warning that such objectives can collapse when the budget exceeds the corpus.

Proof sketch — Membership in NP is immediate for both variants: a vocabulary (or merge sequence) of size K is a polynomial certificate, and the compressed length is verifiable in polynomial time (a shortest-path DP for direct, simulating merges for bottom-up). Hardness is Reduction 1, from max-2-SAT with J variables, I clauses and threshold ψ. The alphabet is Σ = {⊚} ∪ {x_j^T, x_j^F}_{j=1..J} — two characters per variable, one per polarity, plus a separator. Three families of strings are built: D1 = {⊚x_j^T⊚, ⊚x_j^F⊚}, each repeated f times; D2 = {⊚x_j^T⊚x_j^F⊚}, each repeated f' times; and D3 = {⊚L_i^1⊚L_i^2⊚}, one clause string per clause, where L is the character matching the literal's polarity. The budget is K = J — exactly one vocabulary slot per variable — and the target is δ = (4f + 3f')J + 5I − 2ψ, with f' = 4I + 1 and f = 4f'J + 4I + 1.

The multiplicities are the whole trick. Because f and f' dominate I, the only way to spend the J vocabulary slots profitably is one subword of the form ⊚x_j^·⊚ per variable: D1 and D2 alone force that shape, since deviating (a longer substring, two slots on one variable, a slot on a clause string) loses more on the f- and f'-weighted strings than any clause string can ever repay. A selected vocabulary of that shape is therefore exactly a truth assignment, and D1 ∪ D2 then contribute a fixed (4f + 3f')J regardless of which polarity is chosen.

The clause gadget does the counting. A clause string ⊚L¹⊚L²⊚ has 5 characters, and the two subwords that could shorten it, ⊚L¹⊚ and ⊚L²⊚, overlap in the middle separator — so at most one can be applied, and applying it drops the string from 5 to 3. Total D3 length is thus 5I − 2·(number of satisfied clauses), and "compress to ≤ δ" is literally "satisfy ≥ ψ clauses". Lemma 2 gives the forward direction by reading a satisfying assignment off into S; Lemma 3 gives the converse by the domination argument above — any satisfying tokenisation must have the assignment shape, so its clause savings translate back into satisfied clauses. Reduction 2 reuses the same idea for bottom-up tokenisation with two extra string families (D4, D5) whose role is to pin down the merge order, since a merge sequence has strictly less freedom than a vocabulary; the paper then shows (Lemma 8, which never uses the ordering) that the same instance also settles the hybrid variant where merges define the vocabulary but segmentation is re-optimised. Deduplicated-dataset and single-string variants follow by appending a unique separator per string.

title: The Long Delay to Arithmetic Generalization: When Learned Representations Outrun Behavior
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 2026-09-12

The Long Delay to Arithmetic Generalization: When Learned Representations Outrun Behavior

Laura Gomezjurado · 2026 · arXiv:2604.13082

Main idea — The paper asks a sharp decomposition question about grokking: during the long plateau, is the network failing to build the structure the task needs, or failing to use structure it already has? The setting is one-step Collatz, T(n) = n/2 or 3n+1, with n written as base-b digits and an encoder–decoder transformer (6+6, d=256) trained to emit the digits of T(n). The encoder–decoder split is the instrument: it gives a clean seam between representation and readout that modular-addition toy models do not have. The answer is consistently "readout." A linear parity probe on the encoder hits 99.7% by step 2k while sequence exact-match is 38% and stays flat for tens of thousands of steps; freezing the converged encoder and rewinding only the decoder to its step-2k weights erases the plateau (97.6% vs 86.1% for joint training); transplanting a trained encoder into a fresh model helps while transplanting a trained decoder actively degrades. The complementary claim is that how hard the readout is depends on the numeral base — bases divisible by 2 and 3 reach ~99.8%, binary collapses to 0.

The most interesting part — Not the probe-vs-accuracy gap (Charton & Narayanan already titled a paper "Transformers know more than they can tell"), but the erasure hierarchy resolved over training. Projecting the rank-1 parity direction out of encoder states at inference costs 8.2 points at step 18k, just before the transition, and ~0 at convergence. At the converged checkpoint the author erases six feature subspaces and finds every residue subspace — mod 2, 4, 8, 16, last digit — non-load-bearing (Δ ≤ 0.001, indistinguishable from same-rank random controls) even though each probe still classifies at ≥0.99. Only a rank-7 magnitude subspace matters, at Δ = 0.141. So the readout migrates from a brittle parity-anchored cue to a magnitude-anchored, residue-redundant code, and the crossover at ~5×10⁴ steps coincides with a single decoder cross-attention head that holds 0.89 of BOS attention on the last input digit at step 66k and disperses to 0.21 by step 70k. That is a genuine mechanistic progress measure inside a flat loss region, and the Pythia-1.4B replication is striking: erasing the rank-15 n mod 16 subspace at layer 4 drops accuracy 0.845 → 0.043 while a random rank-15 subspace costs 0.005.

Reviewer notes, and they are not minor. The three-seed evidence behind Figure 2 is contradicted by its own appendix: encoder transplant lands at 54.4% on one seed while scratch lands at 94.4% and 96.4% — the only properly powered comparison is the six-seed base-24→base-2 transplant (0.751 vs 0.365), a cross-base setting, not the headline base-8 one. The transplant/rewind conditions also freeze the encoder, so they confound "good features" with "stationary features"; a frozen-random-encoder control is missing, and without it the plateau could be a joint-optimization non-stationarity effect. The "divisibility predicts readout difficulty" claim is worse off than it sounds: the proposed local-predictability metric H is degenerate — H_odd = 0 for every base and H_even = 1.00 for every even base — so it assigns base 2 and base 24 identical scores while their accuracies are 0.00 and 0.998. Table 1 is not monotone in the narrative either (base 4 > base 8 > base 16; base 48 at 93.7 below base 6), and the k = −1 replication that is supposed to prove base-invariance sends base 4 from 99.2 to 82.0 and base 27 to 49.9. Finally, the 1.4B step-0 result ("probes 1.00, exact-match exactly 0.000") is partly a formatting artifact — an un-fine-tuned LM emits nothing in the target digit format — and n mod 16 in base 8 is two digits away from token identity, so "arithmetic feature" is generous. A paper whose central variable is numeral representation never tests length extrapolation; training and eval both live in [1, 10⁴].

Broader context — Grokking (Power et al., 2022) is delayed generalization long after training loss bottoms out; Nanda et al. (2023) showed the plateau hides continuous circuit formation (memorization → Fourier circuit → cleanup) in modular addition, and competing accounts locate the delay in regularization-driven circuit competition (Varma, Merrill) or in progression through harder subproblems (Barak et al., 2022, SGD learning parities). Mechanistic interpretability supplies the probe/erasure toolkit; length generalization (Jelassi et al.) supplies the evidence that arithmetic failure is usually a representation-and-position problem. The two nearest neighbours are Charton & Narayanan (2025) on Collatz base dependence — this work is explicitly its mechanistic follow-up, with Charton acknowledged as guiding the hypothesis — and Schaeffer et al. on emergent abilities as a metric artifact, which is directly relevant here: base 2 scores 0.00 exact-match but 0.51 digit-level, exactly the discontinuous-metric mechanism, and the paper leans on exact-match throughout. A natural follow-up: make the probe-saturation point an actual compute-allocation rule (stop encoder gradients, reallocate to readout) and test whether the resulting schedule beats joint training on a task where the readout space is genuinely large.

There is a real, if analogical, connection to your area. Generative retrieval is a readout problem by construction: the encoder holds a document representation, and the decoder must emit a structured identifier. The numeral-base result is the same shape as the docid-design question in DSI-style systems — atomic vs. hierarchical-clustered vs. semantic identifiers change how much of the target is locally predictable from a short prefix, and DSI models are well known to encode relevance information they cannot decode into the right identifier. The probe-vs-behavior gap suggests a concrete diagnostic for generative retrieval: probe encoder states for cluster membership or coarse docid prefixes over fine-tuning, and check whether the recall ceiling is a representation failure or a decoder-readout failure before redesigning the identifier space. The parity→magnitude migration also hints that the load-bearing direction at convergence need not be the one a probe reads best, which is a caution for any theory that equates linear decodability with use. That said, the paper itself supplies no retrieval evidence; treat the link as a hypothesis generator, not a result.

title: Why Do Transformers Fail to Forecast Time Series In-Context?
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 September 2026

Why Do Transformers Fail to Forecast Time Series In-Context?

Yufa Zhou, Yixiao Wang, Surbhi Goel, Anru R. Zhang — 2025 · arXiv:2510.09776

The empirical embarrassment this paper explains is familiar: on long-horizon forecasting benchmarks, Transformers and LLM-based forecasters routinely lose to a linear layer. The authors give that folklore a representational theory. They fix the data-generating process to a stable AR(p) with Gaussian innovations, feed the history in as a Hankel matrix of p+1 rows, and read the forecast out of the masked slot from a linear-self-attention stack. Under this encoding the one-layer readout has an exact closed form, x̂ = bᵀGₙAx, where Gₙ = (1/n)HMHᵀ is the empirical Hankel Gram matrix — so LSA is a cubic functional of the raw series, and the question becomes whether that cubic feature class can beat ordinary least squares.

Proof sketch. Proposition 3.2 is the cheap half: attention features are a measurable function of the context, so σ(Φ) ⊆ σ(x₁:ₙ) and no readout on Φ beats the Bayes predictor — which for AR(p) is the p-lag linear predictor with risk σ_ε². The real content is strictness, and the trick is a Kronecker lifting: write the readout as η̃ᵀZ with Z = vech(Gₙ) ⊗ x, making it linear in a lifted parameter ranging over a superset of what (A,b) can reach, so minimizing there is a legitimate lower bound. The lifted problem is plain least squares with optimum σ_ε² + ρᵀΔₙρ, where Δₙ = Γ_p − r̃ᵀS̃⁻¹r̃ is a Schur complement (Theorem 3.4). Strictness reduces to Cov([vech G; x]) ≻ 0, proved by innovation-by-innovation backward elimination: assume vᵀZ₀ has zero variance, condition on F_{n−1}, isolate the terms touching xₙ to get Var((uᵀx+c)ε_n + aε_n² | F_{n−1}); the ε_n² term forces a = 0 (finite fourth moments enter here), the remainder forces uᵀx + c = 0 a.s., then induct down. Theorem 3.5 gets the rate: expand S̃ₙ, r̃ₙ by Isserlis plus Toeplitz summation; the population limit S̃∞ = (uuᵀ) ⊗ Γ_p is rank one, so the inverse blows up like n along orthogonal directions, and a singular block-inverse expansion yields Δₙ = B_p/n + o(1/n) — the 1/n traced to the overlap of Hankel windows. Separately, Proposition E.14 exhibits an explicit (b_, A_) for which the readout converges a.s. to ρᵀx by Yule–Walker: LSA recovers OLS asymptotically, but only because ergodicity collapses Gₙ → Γ{p+1} and destroys its own extra capacity. Theorem 3.9 handles CoT: the noiseless rollout is a stable linear recursion with spectral radius β < 1, so forecasts decay geometrically to zero while MSE*(h) ↗ Var(x).

The most valuable move is the Kronecker lift plus Schur complement — it converts an awkward bilinear-in-(A,b), cubic-in-data optimization into a linear-algebraic gap computable from process moments. The most overclaimed result is the CoT one. Collapse-to-mean at an exponential rate is a property of correctly forecasting a stationary process, not a pathology of chain-of-thought; the Bayes predictor does exactly the same thing, as their own equation shows. Elsewhere the setup is arguably rigged: the data are exactly linear, so the linear predictor is Bayes-optimal by construction. What the theorem adds is how much worse — and even there, only a lower bound of order 1/n is proved; there is no matching upper bound, so the practical size of the deficit is unpinned. The abstraction bites too: no MLP, no softmax, no LayerNorm — and the paper's own Appendix C finds softmax attention slightly better than LSA, while the literature it cites fingers MLPs as the component that actually carries TSF performance.

This sits at the confluence of two lines: ICL theory (von Oswald et al. and Ahn et al. showing a linear-attention layer implements one step of preconditioned gradient descent on an in-context least-squares problem) and the LTSF-Linear critique (Zeng et al., "Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?"; Tan et al., "Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?"). This paper is the first to give the negative result a representational rather than kernel/NTK footing. The obvious follow-up is to break the linearity that makes the conclusion foreordained: run the same lifting on ARMA or long-memory processes, where the Bayes predictor needs unboundedly many lags and attention's global mixing might for once pay — the sign of the gap could flip.

One non-forced connection to my area: the LSA readout bᵀGₙAx is literally a linear-kernel retrieval against a memory of key–value outer products, and the σ-algebra argument says the retrieval readout is a strict coarsening of the raw context — the same structure as the quantization gap in ANN indexing, where no reranker on compressed codes can match one that sees raw vectors, and where the interesting question is likewise the rate at which the gap closes with index capacity. The CoT half rhymes with generative retrieval: autoregressive docid decoding is exactly the feed-your-own-predictions-back loop, and Theorem 3.9 is a fully-computed instance of the exposure-bias story usually handled only informally there.

title: Universal pre-training by iterated random computation
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 September 2026

Universal pre-training by iterated random computation

Peter Bloem — 2025 · arXiv:2506.20057

The premise is a nice inversion of the data-processing inequality. Passing noise through a computation cannot add information, but information is not what makes data valuable for learning — structure is. A monkey at a typewriter needs exponentially long to produce Shakespeare; a monkey typing programs into a computer gets there sooner. Bloem takes that literally: sample a random LSTM, feed it random bits, train a transformer on the output, and you have pre-trained a model before seeing any data. The empirical claim is that this buys real zero-shot in-context prediction on natural language and code, improving with scale, plus faster finetuning convergence.

The theory is where the paper differs from its predecessors. Grau-Moya et al. work with monotone Turing machines and Solomonoff induction proper; Bloem rebuilds everything on class-bounded prefix-free complexity, which handles finite strings and lets you name any tractable model class C. Three results. First, the mixture m_C obtained by sampling c∼p(c) then sampling from c dominates every member of C, so its codelength is within an additive constant of the best c, for every x. Second, Theorem 4.2 converts that whole-string statement into sequential prediction: if q dominates p, the summed expected per-symbol KL divergence Σ_n D_n is finite, so next-token predictions converge. Third, Theorem 4.3: iterating the process — feeding output back as conditional input to a fresh random machine — yields m_C^(n+1) dominating m_C^n, a hierarchy of ever-richer classes.

Proof sketch. The domination-to-prediction step (Theorem 4.2, lifted from Li–Vitányi 5.2.1) turns on padding: each prefix is extended to a common length k with an arbitrary suffix, at which point the chain rule telescopes the sum of per-step log-ratios into a single log p(z)/q(z), bounded by the domination constant. Theorem 4.3's proof is one line of cleverness: lower-bound the mixture by the single term where the sampled machine is the identity, so the deeper distribution can always "do nothing" and reproduce the shallower one. The capstone (Theorem 4.5) is that this hierarchy climbs toward universality with fixed-size, finite-precision LSTMs. Lemma 4.4 does the work: because the readout uses a saturated linear activation, any weight vector computing a target function sits inside an open ball of weights computing the same function — rescale W_o by 3 and shift b by −1 to push preactivations strictly into the saturated region, then propagate perturbation budgets backwards using Lipschitz constants and submultiplicativity of the Frobenius norm. A ball of positive radius has positive Gaussian mass, so p(f) > ε. Set f = one step of a UTM's transition function and chain n iterations.

Read carefully, though, the constants are the story. Domination in Theorem 4.5 holds with constant p(r)p(f)^n p(s) — exponentially vanishing, and p(f) is the probability of randomly initializing an LSTM that implements a Turing transition. Lemma 4.4 gives no quantitative radius; it is a support statement, not a sampling statement. Bloem is admirably explicit that this forbids any n→∞ claim, but the same honesty should extend to Theorem 4.3, whose "enrichment" only says the next level is no worse, and which may collapse to a fixed point. There is also an undiscussed gap between theory and code: the source LSTM is sampled at temperature 10⁻⁴, i.e. near-argmax, which is not sampling from p_c in the sense the mixture requires.

Empirically the honest reading is mixed, and the paper says so. The model beats a tuned in-context Markov baseline on Wikipedia, German text, D3.js and the Linux kernel — but loses on most of the synthetic tasks (bitsflip, toy2, dyck), exactly the ones where a short program exists and a truly universal predictor should win. Missing is the comparison a practitioner cares about: universal pre-training versus compute-matched pre-training on a modest slice of real text.

For context: Solomonoff induction predicts by Bayesian mixture over all programs, optimal but uncomputable; the modern move (Grau-Moya et al., Learning universal predictors, ICML 2024) is to amortize it into a transformer, while PFNs (Müller et al.; TabPFN in Nature 2025) show the recipe works spectacularly when the prior is hand-crafted. Bloem's contribution is that the prior need not be crafted at all, only iterated. An obvious follow-up: explicitly importance-sample the iteration depth, measure Antunes-style computational depth of the generated strings, and check whether transfer correlates with it — that would turn "compute-for-data tradeoff" from slogan into a scaling law.

A non-forced IR angle exists but is speculative: generative retrieval trains a decoder over designed discrete code sequences (hierarchical semantic IDs, RQ-VAE codes), and the inductive bias needed is "structured discrete sequence with nested prefix constraints" — precisely the structure a random-computation prior generates. Pre-training a docid decoder on synthetic hierarchical code streams before touching a corpus is a cheap experiment.

title: Mask in the Mirror: Implicit Sparsification
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 September 2026

Mask in the Mirror: Implicit Sparsification

Tom Jacobs, Rebekka Burkholz — 2024 · arXiv:2408.09966

The paper starts from a small embarrassment in the pruning literature. Continuous sparsification relaxes the binary mask in x = m ⊙ w to a free real variable and trains mask and weight jointly; Ziyin & Wang's spred showed that doing this under weight decay α(‖m‖² + ‖w‖²) has exactly the LASSO objective as its solution set — and yet spred beats LASSO handily. If the objectives coincide, the explanation lives in the dynamics, not the optima. Jacobs and Burkholz supply it. Gradient flow on the overparameterised objective is shown to be a mirror flow in the collapsed variable x, with a Bregman potential that is a corrected hyperbolic entropy whose scale is time-dependent: a_t = (m₀² − w₀²)exp(−2∫₀ᵗ α_s ds). That single exponential is the whole story. When a_t ≫ |x_t| the potential is locally quadratic and the implicit bias is L2; as a_t → 0 it behaves like log(1/a_t)·‖x‖₁. Weight decay therefore does not trade off against the loss — it drives the geometry, sliding the implicit regulariser continuously from L2 to L1 at a rate the practitioner schedules through α_t. Sparsification switches on late, after the overparameterised model has already fit, which is the folk wisdom of iterative pruning made into a mechanism.

Two long-standing caveats of the mirror-flow view dissolve here, and this is the cleverest part. In the static picture the potential's minimiser sits at the initialisation x₀, so nothing is pulled toward zero; with α_t the minimiser becomes exp(−2∫α)⊙m₀⊙w₀, which walks to the origin. And Woodworth-style entry into the rich regime normally demands an exponentially small initialisation scale — numerically nasty and near a saddle. Here the schedule supplies the shrinkage instead, so you may initialise at ordinary scale and still arrive in the rich regime. The derived flow also yields a sharp diagnosis of spred: its balanced init m₀² = w₀² gives a_t ≡ 0, hence dx = −|x|⊙(∇f + 2α sign x), a flow that cannot cross zero. PILoT's fix — initialise m₀² − w₀² = β > 0 — is a one-line change justified entirely by the theory, and the diagonal-linear-network experiment confirms spred plateaus away from the ground truth for every schedule tried.

Proof sketch. Theorem 2.2 assumes quasi-convex f, locally Lipschitz ∇f, non-empty argmin, and an integrable schedule ∫₀^∞ α_s ds < ∞; then x_t converges to a critical point, and under convexity or PL to an interpolating minimiser, with linear rate exp(−λA_∞t). Theorem 2.3 is the optimality statement: for underdetermined linear regression the flow converges to argmin_{Zx=Y} R_{a_∞}(x) — the interpolator of minimal final-potential norm. The proof is compact. Lemma B.1 integrates the coupled m,w flow in closed form via cosh/sinh of L_t = ∫∇f, giving x_t = u₀²e^(−2L_t−4A_t) − v₀²e^(2L_t−4A_t); Lemma B.2 inverts this by solving a quadratic in e^(−2L_t), landing exactly on ∇R_{a_t}(x_t) = −∫₀ᵗ∇f, the time-dependent mirror identity. The load-bearing new lemma is the pair of monotonicities ∂R_a/∂a ≤ 0 and da_t/dt ≤ 0: they make the time-dependent Bregman divergence D_{a_t}(x_,x_t) dominated by a non-increasing envelope, which delivers boundedness (Bregman level sets are bounded), a critical accumulation point, and convergence via local strong convexity. Optimality then falls out of ∇R_{a_t}(x_t) ∈ span{Zᵀ} for all t, which in the limit _is* the KKT condition. The PL extension replaces convexity with a curvature growth condition plus Grönwall.

The critique writes itself from those assumptions. Integrability of α_t forces a_∞ > 0 strictly, so the limiting potential is never the L1 norm — only proportional to it asymptotically. Nothing bounds the support size, let alone gives recovery guarantees; "sparsity" is inferred from the shape of the potential, not proved. The authors concede a_t must be exponentially small to be near-L1 and that the constant B ∝ exp(C‖x_‖₂∫α) can blow up. Meanwhile Algorithm 1 _multiplicatively increases_ α_k while the sparsity target is unmet and only decays it after T/2 — a heuristic that gestures at integrability rather than satisfying it. And the gap from underdetermined linear regression under gradient flow to ResNet-50 on ImageNet at 98% sparsity under SGD is the usual chasm. Appendix D is welcome honesty in the other direction: neuron-wise (structured) masks violate the Lie-bracket commutativity condition of Li et al., so they admit _no* mirror flow at all, sharply bounding the theory's reach to unstructured sparsity.

For context: the implicit-bias programme began with Gunasekar et al. (gradient descent on diagonal linear networks converges to the minimum-L1 interpolator), Woodworth et al. characterising the kernel-to-rich interpolation via exactly this hyperbolic entropy, and Azulay et al. and Vaškevičius et al. pushing toward genuine sparse-recovery statements. Li, Wang & Arora's mirror-descent equivalence is the direct scaffold; Pesme et al.'s SGD analysis is the closest cousin, since gradient noise also induces an effectively shrinking scale — but there the time dependence is a byproduct, not a control knob. Making it a control knob is this paper's real contribution. A natural follow-up is to treat α_t as an optimal-control variable: given a target sparsity trajectory and a PL constant, solve for the schedule minimising the loss-degradation bound.

The connection worth flagging for IR is learned sparse retrieval. SPLADE-style models produce sparsity in a |V|-dimensional lexical space through a relaxed, differentiable surrogate (the FLOPS regulariser) whose strength λ is warmed up on a hand-tuned quadratic schedule — chosen empirically for exactly the reason this paper formalises: sparsify too early and the model never learns the expansion terms. If the FLOPS penalty were replaced by an m ⊙ w factorisation of the expansion head with a scheduled weight decay, this analysis would say the model first fits in an L2 geometry and only then commits to a sparse support, with convergence guaranteed rather than hoped for. The theory is only proved for linear regression, so the transfer is conjectural — but the structural match is genuine rather than decorative.

title: Learning to Compress: Local Rank and Information Compression in Deep Neural Networks
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 September 2026

Learning to Compress: Local Rank and Information Compression in Deep Neural Networks

Niket Patel, Ravid Shwartz-Ziv — 2024 · arXiv:2410.07687

The paper's move is to replace an ill-defined quantity with a computable geometric proxy. Instead of estimating I(X;T) by binning activations — the step that made the Information Bottleneck story contestable — it proposes measuring how many directions a layer actually responds to. Local rank at layer l is LR_l = E_{x∼Data}[rank(J_x p_l)], the expected rank of the Jacobian of the pre-activation map with respect to the input. This is a differential, pointwise object: the rank of the local linearization at x, i.e. the dimension of the tangent space of the image manifold. It is not the rank of the representation matrix, which stacks activations and measures how many directions the embedding cloud globally spans — a one-dimensional curve winding through ℝ¹⁰⁰ has near-full representation rank and local rank 1. Worth noting: J_x p_l is taken with respect to the ambient input, not restricted to the data manifold's tangent space, so LR is a property of the network map, not the data. Empirically, MLPs on synthetic Gaussians and MNIST show local rank falling sharply in the terminal phase of training, in two stages, which the authors read as the IB compression phase made visible.

Proof sketch. The theory is a pair of propositions (binary classification under margin-maximizing gradient flow; regression under minimum-norm interpolation), both proving: there exists a layer l and some ε₀ > 0 such that for ε < ε₀, LR^ε_l ≤ (C/ε²)·‖W_l‖²_σ. First a lemma: for a ReLU net, J_x p_l = W_l D_{l−1}W_{l−1}···W₀ with D_i diagonal 0/1 activation masks, so rank(J_x p_l) ≤ rank(W_l), and by discreteness of rank_ε the same holds below some threshold. Second, the generic inequality ‖A‖_F ≥ ε·√(rank_ε(A)). Third, the engine: Timor–Vardi–Shamir's result that the harmonic mean of ‖W_i‖_F/‖W_i‖_σ over layers is bounded at minimum-norm solutions — so some layer must fall below that mean. Combine and take expectation over x. Stripped down, the theorem says at least one layer has stable rank ≲ 2, and stable rank controls ε-rank, which controls Jacobian rank. Nothing about local rank enters the dynamics; the geometry is inherited entirely from a weight-norm result.

The critique writes itself, and the paper is candid enough to say "we argue" rather than "we prove." Three specifics. (i) The bound scales as 1/ε² while requiring ε < ε₀ with ε₀ never quantified, and the pointwise-to-expectation step tacitly needs an ε₀ uniform over the data distribution — activation patterns vary with x, so that is a real gap. (ii) The proposition is an existence claim about one unidentified layer at a global optimum; the experiments show all layers dropping over time. Neither monotone decrease nor which-layer is established. (iii) The mutual-information link is asserted, not proved. Their Theorem 4 is Chechik et al.'s Gaussian IB result, where the encoder is linear and local rank equals rank(A_β) by definition — the "connection" is tautological in the only case where it is exact. For a deterministic ReLU net on continuous inputs, I(X;T) is infinite at every rank, so low local rank cannot by itself imply compression. Also: the ε threshold governing every reported number is never stated, and the VIB experiments report local rank rising and accuracy falling with β, hard to reconcile with the paper's own Lagrangian. Scale is four small MLPs; no seeds, no error bars, no non-MLP architecture.

Context: this is the Tishby–Shwartz-Ziv two-phase picture, defended against Saxe et al.'s 2018 objection that compression is an artifact of saturating tanh units and binned-MI estimation. Shwartz-Ziv is a co-author, and the reframing is the paper's most interesting idea — the ReLU MLPs where Saxe found no binned-MI compression do show local-rank compression. Natural neighbours are Jacot's bottleneck-rank work and Ansuini et al.'s intrinsic-dimension "hunchback" profiles. The obvious follow-up is the theorem that is missing: define T = p_l(X) + σξ and bound I(X;T) ≈ ½Σ_i log(1 + s_i²/σ²) over the Jacobian's singular values via a small-noise tube argument — that turns "correlates with" into a real inequality and makes ε's role principled (ε is the noise floor).

For my work, the non-forced connection is via intrinsic dimension of embeddings. Local rank is a map-side local intrinsic dimension computed from the encoder's Jacobian, complementary to Houle-style LID estimated from the point cloud — the quantity governing ANN index degradation and the safe truncation dimension for Matryoshka-style embeddings. If a dual encoder's local rank collapses far below its output dimension, that is a computable prediction about how aggressively PCA or PQ can compress it, testable directly.

title: Understanding Gradient Boosting Classifier: Training, Prediction, and the Role of $γ_j$
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 September 2026

Understanding Gradient Boosting Classifier: Training, Prediction, and the Role of γ_j

Hung-Hsuan Chen — 2024 · arXiv:2410.05623

This is a seven-page tutorial note, not a research contribution, and it is worth reading only for one thing: a clean, honest derivation of the "mysterious equation" that every implementation of gradient boosting for binary classification contains, and that almost no textbook bothers to justify — the terminal-node value γ_j = Σ_{i∈Ω_j} r_i / Σ_{i∈Ω_j} p_i(1−p_i).

The setup is the standard additive model in log-odds space: F_m(x) = F_{m−1}(x) + γ_j, with p = σ(F) and cross-entropy loss. The two facts doing all the work are the derivatives with respect to the raw score F, not the probability: ∂L/∂F = p − y (so the "residual" r = y − p is exactly the negative gradient) and ∂²L/∂F² = p(1−p). The note first tries the honest route — set ∂f/∂γ_j = 0, giving Σ_k σ(F_{m−1}(x_k) + γ_j) = Σ_k y_k — and correctly observes this is transcendental with no closed form. It then expands f(γ_j) to second order around γ_j = 0: f(γ) ≈ f(0) + γΣ(p−y) + (γ²/2)Σp(1−p), a scalar convex quadratic whose minimizer is Σr / Σp(1−p). That is precisely one Newton–Raphson step, γ* = −G/H, and also a weighted least-squares fit: γ_j is the weighted mean of working responses z_i = r_i/[p_i(1−p_i)] under weights w_i = p_i(1−p_i) — the IRLS/LogitBoost view. Denominator as curvature (Fisher information) is the intuition to keep: a leaf full of confident predictions has small Σp(1−p) and therefore takes a large step.

What is derived, and how. Given a fixed tree structure, the objective over the leaf values separates, because each training instance falls in exactly one leaf and F enters additively — so the J-dimensional problem decomposes into J independent one-dimensional convex problems, each solved by a single second-order Taylor step at the origin. That per-leaf separability plus the Newton step is the whole proof; the note gets it right, and the worked appendix example (γ = 0.5/0.75 = 2/3) checks out.

The gaps are the usual ones. It cites Friedman (2001) but never says that Friedman's Algorithm 5 already contains this exact formula (written as Σr / Σ|r|(1−|r|), the same thing for y ∈ {0,1}), nor that it traces to Friedman–Hastie–Tibshirani's Additive Logistic Regression (2000). There is no regularization, no convergence or consistency statement, no generalization or margin theory, no numerical caveat about Σp(1−p) → 0 (real implementations clip this), and it initializes F₀ = 0 rather than the log-odds of the base rate. Most substantively, the tree structure is fit by squared error on residuals and only then given Newton leaf values — split criterion and leaf value optimize different objectives. XGBoost's contribution was exactly to close that loop: w*_j = −G_j/(H_j+λ) with a split gain of ½ΣG²/(H+λ) derived from the same expansion, so the second-order objective chooses the structure too.

The IR connection is real. LambdaMART is this machinery with the gradient replaced by λ_i = Σ_j |ΔNDCG_ij| ρ_ij — a quantity not derived from any loss — and the leaf value still Σλ / Σ∂λ/∂s. Worth reading next: Burges' From RankNet to LambdaRank to LambdaMART (2010), Wang et al.'s LambdaLoss (CIKM 2018) for what LambdaMART actually optimizes, Nielsen's thesis contrasting gradient vs. Newton boosting, and Qin et al. (ICLR 2021) on GBDTs still beating neural rankers on MSLR/Istella.

title: Towards a Theoretical Understanding to the Generalization of RLHF
html:
Claude daily deep-dive — 10 September 2026

Towards a Theoretical Understanding to the Generalization of RLHF

Zhaochun Li, Mingyang Yi, Yue Wang, Shisheng Cui, Yong Liu — 2026 · arXiv:2601.16403

Existing RLHF theory mostly works in two stages: bound the MLE error of a Bradley–Terry reward model, plug the estimate into the closed-form Boltzmann optimal policy, and call that the learned policy. This paper argues that paradigm has two defects — it needs strong data-coverage conditions to make the reward estimate consistent, and it treats policy optimization as an exact argmax, so it says nothing about what the RL loop itself contributes. The proposed alternative analyzes the KL-regularized objective end-to-end under a linear reward and a matched softmax policy class, decomposes the suboptimality gap into concentration + optimization + generalization, and bounds the generalization term with algorithmic stability. The headline results: an Õ(n^(−1/2)) suboptimality gap for empirical stationary points that is independent of the ambient dimension d, plus Õ(T^(−1/4) + n^(−1/2)) for gradient ascent and Õ(T^(−1/8) + n^(−1/2)) for SGA.

The cleverest piece is a small algebraic identity with outsized consequences. Because the reward is linear in ϕ and the policy is the Boltzmann policy over the same ϕ, the empirical gradient is exactly ∇J_S(θ) = V_S(θ)(θ_ − θ), where V_S(θ) is the average per-prompt covariance of features under π_θ. Three things fall out. First, every stationary point is a global maximum and all stationary points attain the _same_ empirical value — which lets them apply plain Hoeffding to a nominally data-dependent quantity, sidestepping uniform convergence over θ. Second, θ_ is always an empirical stationary point, so the problem reduces to which directions of θ* are identifiable. Third, the column space C(V_S(θ)) does not depend on θ at all — writing V_x(θ) = Φ(Λ_p − pp^T)Φ^T, the middle matrix has null space span(1) for any positive p, so the column space is the fixed geometric object {Φw : w ⊥ 1}. "What the model can see" is a fixed subspace, not something that drifts during training.

Proof sketch. The workhorse (Lemma 6) bounds |f_{θ1}(x) − f_{θ2}(x)| by a Pinsker-type term in ⟨ϕ(x,a), θ1 − θ2⟩, decomposes ϕ = V_S(θ__S)b + r_S per Assumption 5, and rewrites the inner product as ⟨b, V_S(θ1−θ_)⟩ + ⟨b, V_S(θ_−θ2)⟩ + ⟨r, θ1−θ2⟩. The first two terms are small whenever both parameters have small gradient norm (an eigendecomposition on the shared column space converts ‖∇J_S(θ)‖ ≤ δ into ‖V_S(θ_S)(θ−θ)‖ ≤ δ·σ_max/σ⁺_min), and ‖b‖ ≤ C/σ⁺_min. The unidentifiable null-space directions never enter the inner product — that is the whole trick, and it is why d disappears. Uniform stability then follows because swapping one prompt changes the gradient by at most 4RC²/n, so θ{S'} has gradient norm O(1/n) on J_S; Bousquet–Klochkov–Zhivotovskiy converts stability into a high-probability bound. Theorem 1 (exact recovery when E[V_x(θ)] ⪰ σI) is separate: symmetrization + Rademacher sub-Gaussian MGF for matrix concentration, a covering net over Θ_R with Hölder continuity of θ ↦ V_x(θ), then Weyl's inequality to push σ_min(V_S) above zero.

Now the honest part. This is not RLHF. Section 3.1 states plainly that ground-truth rewards r(x,a) are available — there are no preferences, no Bradley–Terry noise, no reward model. The "end-to-end" framing is achieved by deleting the half of the pipeline that prior work analyzed, and n counts prompts, not comparisons. Second, Assumption 5 assumes the residual satisfies sup‖r_S(x,a)‖ ≤ ε_n with ε_n = O(1/n) as a hypothesis rather than a consequence — and the rate matters critically, since Γ₁ contains a 4nRε_n term: at ε_n = n^(−1/2) the bound goes vacuous. The "dimension-free" claim is also softer than advertised, because Γ₁ is a supremum of σ_max/(σ⁺_min)² which in the rank-deficient regime can be arbitrarily large — precisely where d hides. The experiments make this uncomfortable: purely synthetic, n from 7 to 22 with effective subspace dimension 24–32, i.e. entirely in the regime n < d_eff where the residual is Ω(1), and fitting an n^(−1/2) reference line over 1/√n ∈ [0.21, 0.38] is thin evidence.

The genuinely surprising claim deserves credit: stability here improves with T, reversing Hardt et al. (2016), where SGD's uniform stability degrades with iterations. The reason is structural — stability is bounded through the gradient norm rather than an expansiveness recursion on parameter distance, so a better-converged iterate is automatically more stable.

The lineage runs Zhu et al. (2023) on pessimistic MLE for linear-reward RLHF, Xiong et al. (2023) on iterative preference learning, and Rafailov et al. (2023) for the closed-form policy; on the stability side, Hardt et al. (2016) and Bousquet et al. (2020). The obvious follow-up is to put the reward model back and ask whether the column-space geometry means reward error only hurts inside C(V_S) — a principled substitute for pessimism.

There is a real connection to my work. This setup — KL-regularized reward maximization over a softmax on a finite action set with linear features — is nearly a literal model of RL-tuned generative retrieval over a candidate docid set, and the θ-invariance of C(V_S) says the set of docid-discriminating directions the policy can ever learn is fixed by the prompt set alone. That is a testable statement about how much RL fine-tuning of a generative retriever can help beyond what the training query distribution already spans.
